text:
Scarlett was playing in the yard with Baani. They rolled a red ball down the hill. The ball stopped by the fence.

Scarlett ran to get it. Then she saw something small on the grass. It was a little stick with a button. It looked like a lighter.

Baani came over. "What is that?" she asked.

"I think it's a lighter," said Scarlett. She did not pick it up. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," she said.

"Let's go tell a grown-up," said Baani.

They ran to Scarlett's dad. He was watering the flowers. Scarlett held his hand and showed him the fence. Dad picked up the lighter and put it in his pocket. "Good job, girls," he said.

The sun went down. The ball went back in the toy box. Scarlett got tired and went to her bed. Dad tucked her in. "Night night, Scarlett," he said. She smiled and closed her eyes.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She smelled something sweet. "Strawberries!" she said. Her nose had smelled them first.

Her dad put a red strawberry on her plate. Aubrey touched it with her finger. It felt bumpy with tiny seeds. One, two, three, four, five seeds. Then she looked at it with her eyes. Red like her boots.

Aubrey took a bite. "Yum!" she said. Her tongue tasted the sweet. She licked her lips.

Then Aubrey had an idea. She pinched her nose closed. She took another bite. Her mouth went quiet. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much.

"Mommy, my strawberry got shy!" she said. Her mom smiled. "Open your nose and try again."

Aubrey let go of her nose. She sniffed the sweet smell. She took a bite. The sweet came back, big and strong. "There it is!" she said. She clapped her hands.

"What a lucky strawberry," said her mom. She passed Aubrey one more. Aubrey held it up. "Hello, sweet friend," she said, and took a big bite.

Miles sat at the little table in the library. Ms. Farah-Ali put the tablet in front of him. "Can you turn it on?" she asked. Miles looked for the button. He pressed it. The screen lit up. One press made the light come on. He pressed the button again. The screen went dark. One press made it go off.

Miles laughed. "Press, on. Press, off," he said. He pressed the button one more time. Then he tapped the drawing app. A rainbow of colors filled the screen. He drew a big yellow bus. He drew a heavy elephant standing by the bus. "What if the tablet gets tired?" Miles asked. "It needs the charger," said Ms. Farah-Ali. Miles picked up the charger. It was not too heavy. He carried it to her. A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall. Ms. Farah-Ali plugged it in.

"Now put the tablet away," she said. Miles pressed the button. Off went the screen. He set the tablet on the shelf, all tidy. "I did it," said Miles. "You did it," said Ms. Farah-Ali.

Thomas sat on the bathroom floor. Dad was running his bath. The water came out of the tap. Steam went up, up, up. Dad touched the water with his hand. "Too hot," said Dad. He turned the tap the other way. Now the water felt warm, not hot.

On the shelf sat Thomas's red bike helmet. It was drying there after the rain. Thomas saw his blue bike by the fence. He wanted to ride it now. He jumped up. He ran to the door. "Wait," said Dad. "You must wear a helmet when you ride a bike." Thomas ran back. He took the helmet off the shelf. The strap felt rough on his chin. Dad helped him click it.

Thomas stayed close to Dad. Summer rode by on her little bike. She had a helmet too. It was pink with stars. "Look at me!" she called. Thomas pedaled and pedaled. He did not forget his cookie in his pocket. He munched it under the tree. "Good riding," said Dad, and he clapped his hands.

Amelia went to the library with her mother. She wanted a book about dogs. A big dog book sat on a low shelf. Amelia took it and opened it. But she opened it at the last page. "That is the end," said Ms. Qureshi. "Books start at the front." Amelia turned back to the first page. There was a dog with a red ball. "Start here," she said to herself.

Then Ms. Qureshi gave out name cards. Amelia's card said Amelia. A-m-e-l-i-a. Then Amelia saw her name again. It was on her library card in her mother's bag. A-m-e-l-i-a. She put the cards side by side. The letters were the same. Same letters, same order. "Look!" said Amelia. "It is still me!"

Kiana came over with her card. Her card said Kiana. "Your name is not my name," said Amelia. Kiana laughed. "No, silly. That one is mine."

They sat down. Amelia held her dog book. She started at the front. Page by page, the dog found his red ball. At the end, the dog went to sleep. Amelia waved to the sleeping dog. "Good night," she said. "See you next time."

Sara went to the library with her dad. She wanted the big red book about bears. But a boy named Florian had it first.

Sara stamped her foot. She made a sad, angry face. Florian looked at her. He held the book tighter. Sara's dad looked worried. He did not know what was wrong.

Then Sara took a breath. "I feel sad," she told her dad. "I want the bear book." Her dad nodded. "Let's ask Florian to take turns," he said. Florian smiled. "You can have it next," he said.

Sara waited. Soon the book was in her hands. She hugged it and laughed. Ms. Navarro, the librarian, clapped softly. "A wild bear story for Sara today," she said. Sara sat down and opened the book.

Charlie stood in the kitchen. The toast was on her plate. Her dad had made it hot, and now it was cool enough to touch.

"You can try the butter," her dad said. He gave her a small knife with a dull edge. He stayed right beside her. Charlie held the knife. She poked the toast with the tip. The toast got a hole in it. Butter went on in one big lump. "Why did that happen?" she asked. Her dad said, "Try the flat side. Watch what it does."

Charlie turned the knife over. She laid the flat side on the butter. Then she pushed it across the bread. The butter spread out thin. The whole toast turned yellow. "Look!" said Charlie. "One push, then two, then three." She counted her pushes. Three pushes made it smooth.

Next came the milk. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. The milk went up the side, one inch, then two. Not one drop spilled. There was a flower on her cup, and now the flower looked like it was swimming. "Can I make more toast tomorrow?" she asked. Her dad smiled and said, "Yes, butter girl."

Livia went to the art gallery with her class. Mr. Goldberg showed them red, yellow and blue. "Blue," said Livia, pointing. April pointed at the red. Ilyan pointed at the yellow.

Then they sat at a little paint table. Livia wanted to paint the sky. She dipped her brush in blue. She made a big stripe. But the sky looked almost black. "Too dark," said Livia. Her sky was dark like night, and she wanted day.

Mr. Goldberg brought a pot of white paint. Livia stirred some white into her blue. She mixed and mixed. The paint made a sloshy noise. The blue got lighter and lighter. Now it looked like a real morning sky.

Livia looked at her dark brush. The drips made a yucky brown spot on her paper. She laughed and chased the spot with more light blue paint.

April leaned over. "Your sky is so pretty," she said.

Livia held up her painting so everyone could see.

Maria wanted to see the pot. Her dad was cooking corn in the backyard. Maria stood next to her dad. She held his hand.

The pot went bubble, bubble. White steam went up, up, up. Maria leaned in close to see.

Her dad pulled her back. "Stay back, Maria. Steam is hot. Steam can burn you." Maria took one big step. Then another big step. She held her dad's hand again.

From far away, Maria watched the bubbles. She could still see them. She could still hear them pop, pop, pop.

"Can I help?" asked Maria.

"You can put on your new hat," said Dad. "The sun is hot today too."

Maria put on her new hat. She sat on the grass. Sarah came over to play. Maria wiped her hands on her shorts.

"Look at the pot," said Maria. "But not too close. Steam is hot. Stay back."

Sarah sat down next to Maria. They watched the bubbles together. The steam went up, up, up, far over their heads.

Dad carried the corn to the table. "All done," he said. "Who wants a piece?"

Maria raised her hand. "Me! Me!"

Declan ran to the block corner. The big red blocks were all gone. Oaklynn was using them. "Can I have the red blocks?" Declan asked. "Later," said Mr. Hosseini. "Oaklynn is building now."

Declan sat down. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mr. Hosseini. Declan waited. He heard the blocks go click, click. He felt the soft rug under his hands.

He found some blue sticks. He stuck them together. His tower looked different from Oaklynn's. It was tall and blue. "Is it later yet?" he asked again. "Now it is later," said Mr. Hosseini.

Oaklynn gave him the red blocks. They clicked together. "Red blocks come after blue towers," said Declan. He laughed and built some more.

Alice went to the store with her brother. Her tummy felt hungry. "Can we get apples?" she asked. Her brother said, "We need to find aisle five."

Alice looked at her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Aisle five is this many!" Then she saw a big sign. It had a 5 on it. Alice held up her fingers next to the sign. The 5 matched her five fingers. She smiled big.

"Here!" she said. They walked down the aisle. They counted apples into a bag. "One, two, three, four, five, six." At the checkout, the cashier said, "Seven, eight, nine, ten. Ten apples!" Alice helped carry the bag. At home, she gave her brother a big red apple. "Crunch," he said.

Lydia sat high in the big stadium. Daddy held her hand. Arabella sat beside her. Down below, the blue team ran and ran. The red team ran too.

"Blue runs the most," said Lydia. "Blue wins!"

The game ended. A loud horn went, beep, beep.

"Look at the numbers," said Arabella. She pointed up high. Red had two. Blue had one.

"Red has more points," said Arabella. "Red wins the game."

Lydia looked and looked. The people cheered for red. Red got a big shiny cup.

"One, two," said Lydia, counting the points. "More points wins!"

Then Lydia did a happy skip. Her tummy felt bouncy like a ball.

"Next time I will watch the points," said Lydia. "Not just the running."

Arabella clapped for her. The last cheer rang out, and Lydia waved her little red flag.

Nora ran to the door. "Outside!" she said. Mom opened the door a little bit. The cold air came in. Brr! Nora's arms got little bumps. "Cold!" she said.

"Your coat keeps your body warm," said Mom. Nora got her red coat. She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. One, two! She pulled the zipper down low. Then she pulled it up. Up, up, up! Zip! "I did it!" said Nora.

Outside, the wind was loud. But Nora was warm in her coat. "I am a sheep!" she said. "Sheep stay warm too." Mom laughed. Nora pretended to hop like a sheep. Hop, hop, hop.

Then Nora saw Matteo at the fence. He was shivering. He had no coat. "Wait!" said Nora. She ran inside. She got his blue coat from the hook. Matteo put it on. Zip! Now he was warm too. "Warm sheep!" said Matteo. They hopped together. Hop, hop, hop, all the way to the mailbox.

Cooper was playing in the playroom. He had the red truck out. He had the blocks out too. Louie came over to play.

They pushed the truck on the floor. They stacked the blocks up high. The blocks went crash. They laughed and stacked them again.

Then Louie's dad called. Louie had to go home. Louie ran to the door. The toys stayed on the floor.

Cooper looked at the mess. He began to walk away too. But then he stopped. He thought about the truck. He thought about the blocks. He had played with them.

Cooper went back. He put the blocks in the basket. He put the truck on the shelf. The floor was clear.

There was one wet block from a spill. Cooper wiped it with a towel. It did not slip out of his hands.

Soon Louie knocked on the door again. "I came back to help," Louie said. But the room was already clean.

Louie looked around. "You did it," he said.

Cooper smiled. "We played," he said, "so I put them away."

Louie picked up one small car from under the chair. "This one is mine," he said. He put it in the basket too.

Then they sat by the window. They watched a bus go down the street. The playroom was tidy and quiet.

Emilia went to the store with her dad. She wanted to pick a present for her grandma. Near the bread, there was a little play spot. Saanjh from her class was there. He was building a tall block tower.

Emilia ran over fast. Her elbow bumped the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. All of them. Saanjh's mouth went wobbly. "My tower," he said.

Emilia felt hot in her face. She took a big, deep breath. "Sorry, Saanjh," she said. "I bumped your tower." Then she got down on her knees. She put one block on the bottom. Then another. Saanjh put the top block on. The tower stood tall again.

Saanjh smiled at her. Emilia smiled back. She held her dad's hand. "Present time," she said, and off they went to the card aisle.

Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt jumpy. "Will it hurt a lot?" she asked her dad. "Just a tiny pinch," he said. But Emilia's hands felt weak, and she wanted to hide.

A nurse came in with a small tray. Emilia looked at the line of cotton balls on it. "What do I do?" she whispered. "Smell a flower with me," her dad said. He took a slow, deep breath in. Emilia smelled the pretend flower, slow and deep. Then she let the air out. She counted one, two, three. Her tummy felt calmer.

"Ready?" the nurse asked. Emilia took one more slow, deep breath. Then the shot was done, quick as a blink. "I did it!" Emilia shouted. She got a shiny bandage with stars. "Next time I will smell the flower first," she said, and she held up her arm to show Dylan the stars.

Chloe sat at the kitchen table. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. "I can do it," said Chloe. She held the little knife. She spread the butter. The butter slipped and made a slide. Chloe laughed. She tried again, slow and soft. Now the butter covered the toast.

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup with both hands. She poured. One drop hopped out. She poured slower. The milk went into the cup, not the table. "I did it!" said Chloe. She drank some milk. It was cold and sweet.

Then Chloe ran to play. The milk sat on the table. Daddy looked at it. He looked at the wall clock. Chloe looked too. The milk was not in the fridge! She carried it with both hands. She put it back on the cold shelf. "Good job," said Daddy. Chloe smiled like a stormy cloud turning sunny. "Toast time again tomorrow?"

Today was Marlee's birthday. The party was at Grandma's house. Madeline sat on a little chair next to her friend.

"Look, the cake!" said Marlee. It was a pink cake. It smelled sweet, like sugar.

Madeline leaned in close. She counted the candles. "One, two, three, four," she said. Then she stopped. Marlee was turning five today. But there were only four candles.

"Marlee, one candle is gone," said Madeline.

Grandma looked. "You are right, Madeline. We need one more." She took a candle from the box. She pushed it in, right at the top. Now there were five.

Grandpa held the matches. He lit each candle. The little flames wobbled. "Make a wish, Marlee," he said.

Marlee took a big breath. She blew and blew. All five candles went out. A thin smoke curled up.

"Yay!" said Madeline. She clapped her hands.

Everyone got a slice of cake. Madeline's slice was cool on top, with cold ice cream beside it. Marlee gave her a big hug.

"Thank you for counting," Marlee said.

Madeline smiled and took another bite.

Chloe stood in the kitchen. Her dad was baking. He said, "You can help from here."

Chloe looked at the bowl. "I see the oats," she said. "My eyes see them."

"Good," said Dad. "Now touch this."

Chloe put her fingertips on the oats. "They feel bumpy. My skin feels them. My fingertips feel them too."

Dad held out sugar. Chloe touched it. "This feels soft. Not bumpy at all."

She touched a wooden spoon. "This feels hard and smooth."

"Stop," said Dad with a smile. "One more thing. But do not touch the pan. It is hot. I will hold it."

He poured the mix into the pan. Then he put it in the oven.

Later the oat bars came out. Chloe sniffed. "My nose smells them. Mmm."

Dad handed her a small piece. Chloe took a bite. "Crunchy!" she said. "My ears hear the crunch. My tongue tastes the sweet."

"My tummy likes the five senses," said Chloe.

Dad laughed. "My tummy likes them too." He put the last bar back in the tin. "One for tomorrow," he said.

Chloe grinned and licked her fingertips.

Hayden ran to the library playroom. His elephant toy was gone! He looked under the table. He looked in the doll bed. "My elephant is lost," he said.

Dua was filling the big toy box. She held up a block. "Block!" she said, and dropped it in. She held up a ball. "Ball!" she said, and dropped it in. She held up a doll with loose yarn hair. "Doll!" she said, and dropped it in. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," said Dua.

Hayden gasped. The toy box held toys. Maybe his elephant was in there! He dug past a red ball. He dug past a small doll. Then he felt something soft and grey. Out came his elephant, wearing a tiny paper party hat. "You came to a party!" said Hayden. He hugged his elephant tight. Dua clapped and closed the toy box lid.

Andrew was at the pool by the lake. He was learning to swim. Teo was there too. Andrew held the edge and kicked his feet. "Good kicking," said Ms. Takahashi. Andrew was a little shy in the water. But he kicked and kicked. Then it was time to get out. Andrew pulled on the side. It was too high. He slipped back. Splash! "Try the ladder," said Teo. Andrew went to the ladder. He held the rails. Step, step, step. He popped out of the water! "That was easy," said Andrew. He sat on the grass and looked at the lake. "Now I know the way out," he said. "Let me try the ladder too," said Teo.

Henry wants story time at the library. But story time is not now. The clock on the wall says later.

"Is it now?" Henry asks his dad.

"Not yet," Dad says. "Story time comes after morning. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast."

Henry and Dad sit at a little table. Henry eats his oatmeal. He licks the spoon. "Good morning," he says to Leanna, who waves from her chair. Morning is wake up time and breakfast time. Henry knows that now.

"Now can we go?" Henry asks.

"Yes, now," says Ms. Romano, the library lady. "Story time starts."

Henry sits on the soft rug. Leanna sits next to him. Eleanor sits in front. Ms. Romano reads about a bear who bakes a cake. It is the same book she read yesterday. Yesterday means it already happened.

"Will you read it again tomorrow?" Henry asks.

"Yes," says Ms. Romano. "Tomorrow means it is coming, not here yet."

She turns the last page. She claps her hands. Henry claps too, right on the soft rug.

Henry ran to the park with his teddy. He saw a big red slide. He heard Andre and Rome talk about the swings. "I want to swing high!" said Rome.

Henry smelled the flowers. "Smelly, but nice," he said. He touched the bark on a tree. It was bumpy. He ate a banana snack. It tasted sweet.

Then teddy fell down. Teddy rolled under the slide. It was dark under there. Henry could not see teddy. He tried and tried. No teddy.

"My shirt has the ocean on it," said Andre, "but my ocean picture is dark too." Ms. Bekele came over. She flipped the switch on the park lamp. The light came on.

Henry looked under the slide. There was teddy! He grabbed teddy and hugged him tight. "Big hug," said Henry.

Blake walked on the nature trail with her friend Hayden. Ms. Moose said, "Today we name our five senses." Blake wanted to say all five.

First Blake smelled a flower with her nose. Then she touched a smooth rock with her hands. She saw a red bird with her eyes. She tasted the cold water Ms. Moose poured from a bottle. That was four senses.

A big truck rumbled by. It was loud. Blake put her hands over her ears. The sound got quieter. "My ears hear!" she said. "Ears are for hearing." Hayden clapped. "You did all five!" said Ms. Moose.

A soft rain began to fall. Blake listened with her ears. "That is a neat sound," she said. Hayden covered his ears too, and the rain got quieter for him. Then they took his hands away, and they could hear it again.

William went to a big festival with his family. There were flags and drums and food smells. William saw a long table with bread and soup. He wanted to sit with his friend Maximus.

Maximus held hands with his family. They all bowed their heads. "We say grace first," Maximus said. "It is a short prayer of thanks." William wanted to say it too. He did not know the words yet. He tried. "Thank you for the food," he said. "And thank you for Maximus." Maximus smiled big. His mom squeezed William's hand.

At the playground after lunch, William fell down in the grass. Maximus helped him up. Then a lady handed out apple slices. A grown-up cut them with a sharp knife, far from the kids. William held out his hands again. "Can I say grace?" he asked. "Yes," said Maximus. "You go first."

Michael ran up the steps to Grandpa's house. Today was a big family party. He wanted to see his cousins. He had not seen them for a long time.

The door opened. Hugs and voices everywhere! But where were the cousins? Michael looked in the kitchen. He looked by the table. No cousins. His face went sad.

"Big holidays bring families together," said Grandma. "So they will come." Michael waited by the window. Then a car pulled up. The cousins jumped out, waving big!

The cousins ran to Michael. They all played with Grandpa's pet dog in the yard. They ate sweet cake at the big table. Soon Michael was sleepy in Grandma's lap.

"Best party ever," he whispered, closing his eyes.

The community hall was warm and noisy. Big pots steamed on the stove, and a grown-up stirred the soup with a long spoon. Joshua sat at the long table with Faye and Nico. A dog outside went "Woof, woof," and Nico laughed. "That dog can bark louder than my grandpa," he said.

Ms. MacLeod stood by her little desk. "Now we say our blessing," she said. Joshua did not know one. He hid his hands under the table. Then he thought about the soup. Somebody had grown the carrots. Somebody had picked them. He stood up tall. "Thank you for the carrots," he said. "Thank you for the soup. Thank you for the sun that made them grow."

Faye clapped. Nico clapped. Ms. MacLeod smiled a big smile. The windows looked cloudy and gray, but inside the hall it felt sunny. Joshua picked up his spoon. Faye leaned over and whispered, "Your blessing made my tummy extra hungry." Joshua giggled. "Then eat fast," he said, "before my blessing makes the soup disappear."

Anna went to the playground with her mama. A big kid was there, wearing a lion shirt. Anna hid behind her mama's legs. The lion shirt looked big and loud to Anna.

Then a boy waved at Anna. It was Oakley from her class. "Hello, Oakley," Anna said, peeking out. Oakley smiled a big smile. His smile got even bigger after she said hello. "Hello, Anna," he said. "Want to play lion?" Anna looked at his shirt. "Yes," she said. "Can I be a lion too?"

They crawled on the grass and roared. The dark slide was their lion cave. Anna's shoe felt funny. A little rock was inside it. "Mama, can you help me, please?" Anna asked. Her mama took the rock out. "Thank you," said Anna. The shoe fit just right again.

Anna bumped into a girl by the swings. "Sorry," said Anna. "It's okay," said the girl. It was Maira. Maira had never met Anna before. Anna hid her face for one second. Then she peeked out and said, "Hello, Maira." Maira grinned. "Hello, lion Anna," she said. "Roar!" said Anna. "Roar!" said Maira. And three lions ran to the cave together.

Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was falling outside the window. The snow made a thick white pile on the ledge. "Counting song time!" said Mr. Demetriou. He clapped his hands.

Axel loved the counting song. He jumped up and down. His friends Wylder and Wilson sat in a circle. Mr. Demetriou began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Axel sang too. "One, two, three, four, five!" Then he stopped. What came next? He bit his lip. "One, two, three, four, five, seven?" he sang.

Wylder shook his head. Wilson covered his mouth. Axel felt his face go hot. He asked, "Did I miss a number?" Mr. Demetriou nodded. He held up six fingers, then seven. "Six comes next," he sang.

Axel took a big breath. He tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Every word came out in the right spot. Wilson clapped. Wylder stomped his feet.

"Again!" said Axel. All the kids sang it together. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Axel looked out at the snow. He counted ten fat flakes falling down.

Lincoln put on his blue coat. He went to the corner store with his dad. Ms. Esposito worked at the store. She had two plates of cookies.

"Can you count them?" she asked.

Linlin counted the first plate. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the second plate. "One, two, three." He pointed at the first plate. "This one has more!"

Ms. Esposito smiled. "You may have one cookie." Lincoln ate it slowly. It was sweet and a little crunchy. Then his dad ate one. Then Ms. Esposito ate one.

"One left," said Lincoln. He ate it. He looked down at the plate. There was nothing on it. Not even one crumb.

"Zero," said Ms. Esposito.

"Zero?" Lincoln felt shy, then curious. He looked closely. "Zero cookies. The plate is empty."

Outside, kids were starting to build a snowman. "Dad, can we watch?" asked Lincoln. He counted the snowballs out loud. "One, two, three!"

Ms. Esposito waved from the door. "Come back soon, Lincoln."

Lincoln waved back. "Next time I will count to ten!"

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. She hung her coat in the kitchen. Violet looked at her own coat. It hung right next to Grandma's. When Violet moved her coat, Grandma's coat moved too. "Funny," said Violet. "They are touching."

Violet watched Mom give Grandma a big hug. "Mom, why do you hug her so much?" asked Violet. Mom smiled. "She is my mom," said Mom. Violet's eyes went wide. Grandma was Mom's mom! "So Grandma is a grandma because she has a kid who is my mom?" asked Violet. "Yes," said Grandma, laughing.

Grandma pulled a stool to the table. She got out paper and paints. Violet painted a sheep. Grandma painted a sheep too. Grandma's sheep was pink. Violet laughed and laughed. Then Mom set three cups of milk on the table. One for Mom, one for Grandma, one for Violet. "Milk for my mom and my girl," said Mom. Violet snuggled between them and took a big sip.

Brielle stood at the library door. In her hand was a new card. It was her very first library card.

She wanted a book about frogs. But the frog book was on a high shelf. Her toe could not reach it. Her fingers could not reach it either.

Ms. Suryanto came over. "Storytime is starting," she said. "A librarian reads books aloud to the children. Come and sit."

Brielle felt shy. She hid behind the big chair. Then she heard a laugh. Leonard was laughing. Arthur was laughing too.

Brielle peeked out. The librarian held up a funny book. It had a frog on the cover. She read it out loud in a silly voice. All the children giggled.

Brielle put one foot out. Then she put the other foot out. She sat down next to Leonard.

After the story, the librarian gave her the frog book. "You can take it home," she said.

Brielle held the book with her long arms. She hugged it all the way home. "My card worked," she said.

Blake went to the library with Dad. She saw a big rug and small chairs. There was a new book about a lake on the shelf. Blake wanted that book very much. A line had formed at the checkout desk. Kyson was in the line too. Blake got in line behind him. "What is a line for?" Blake asked Dad. Dad said, "It shows whose turn is next." Blake waited. She watched her shoes. She hummed a little song. Then Kyson ran up to the front and pushed in. The librarian shook her head. Kyson walked back to his spot. He stood still and waited. Soon it was his turn, and he got his books. Then it was Blake's turn. She put her new lake book on the desk. "I waited like Kyson," she said. "And the waiting worked." She held the book tight all the way home. That night Dad read it twice, and Blake said, "I win, I got the best book."

Oliver was at summer camp. He was painting a big lion. The lion had a yellow mane. His friend Elliott painted a red car.

"Look at my lion," said Oliver. "He is big and yellow."

Elliott held up his painting. "My car goes fast," he said.

Ms. Demir rang a little bell. "Time to go play," she said. Oliver put his brush in the paint cup. Then he ran outside to play.

The next day, Oliver wanted to paint more. He picked up his brush. The brush felt hard. The bristles did not bend at all.

"Why is my brush so stiff?" Oliver asked.

"Touch it," said Ms. Demir. Oliver touched it. The paint on it was dry and crusty. Elliott had rinsed his brush in water. His brush was soft and clean.

"I want a soft brush too," said Oliver. He rinsed his brush in the water cup. The water turned yellow like his lion. He watched the paint swirl away.

Then he looked in the cup. At the bottom was a tiny stone shaped just like a lion's face. "A little lion!" said Oliver. He put it in his pocket.

Aiden ran to the park with his toy chicken. The sun did shine on the swings. Aiden felt so excited.

Then Aiden saw Alia. She sat under the big tree. Tears ran down her face. She was crying.

"Why are you crying?" Aiden asked.

"My balloon flew away," Alia said. "It went far, far up. Now I feel sad."

Aiden looked at her tears. He looked at his toy chicken. He held it out. "You can hold my chicken," he said.

Alia wiped her eyes. She took the soft chicken. She hugged it close. Her tears stopped. Then she smiled a little.

"I feel better now," Alia said.

Ms. Lau came over with a new balloon. It was red and round. Alia let go of the chicken and clapped her hands.

"Thank you, Aiden!" she said. Aiden felt happy inside. They took turns pushing the red balloon high into the sunny sky.

Iris sat in her big girl bed. She pulled her blanket up to her chin.

"Papa," she said, "is today the library day?"

Papa sat on the edge of the bed. "Yes," he said. "Today is the day that is happening right now. And right now it is bedtime."

Iris frowned. She still wanted her library books. The ones with the bear who wore one red shoe. She had picked them yesterday. Yesterday was all done.

"But the library is closed now," said Papa. "It is dark outside."

Iris looked out the window. The sky was black. One little star tickled the glass, twink, twink.

"I want the bear book now," said Iris.

"The library opens later," said Papa. "Later comes after sleeping. Tomorrow you will go with Elia."

Iiris wiggled her toes under the blanket. They felt warm and cozy. "Is tomorrow soon?" she asked.

"Soon," said Papa. "First you sleep. Then it is morning. Then it is tomorrow."

Iiris closed her eyes. She thought about the bear. The bear would be there tomorrow, waiting on the shelf.

Her fingers were a little sticky from the honey bread at dinner. Papa wiped them with a soft cloth, one by one.

"Now I sleep," said Iris. "Later, the bear."

"Later, the bear," said Papa. He kissed her head.

Iris snuggled down. The house was quiet. The star kept twinkling outside the window.

"Papa," she whispered one more time. "Today is all done?"

"Today is all done," said Papa.

Iris smiled with her eyes still shut. "Tomorrow, library," she said.

"Tomorrow, library," Papa said softly, and he turned off the light.

Bennett climbed into the car. He held his little drum. "Fast, fast, fast!" he called, as the car zoomed down the big road. The sun was hot through the window. The air from the vent was cold on his face.

In the back seat, his baby sister slept. Bennett banged the drum. BANG, BANG, BANG! It was so loud. The baby woke up. She cried and cried. Dad said, "Shh, the loud drum woke her up. Try quiet."

Bennett tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. It was so quiet. The baby stopped crying. Her eyes closed. She went back to sleep. Bennett tapped and tapped, soft as a whisper. Quiet, quiet, quiet. The baby stayed asleep.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Bennett. Dad smiled. "Loud woke her. Quiet lets her sleep."

Soon the car went slow. They were home at last. Dad made yummy snacks. Bennett put his drum on his plate. The baby was still asleep. Bennett tiptoed. Tap, tap, tap.

Grandpa had a violin. It sat in a big black case. One sleepy morning, Beatrice opened the case. "Can I play it?" she asked. Grandpa smiled and said yes.

He gave her a stick with hairs on it. "This is the bow," he said. Beatrice held it the wrong way. She poked the violin with the handle. The violin made a small squeak. Beatrice jumped. "Why did it squeak?" she asked. "Try turning the bow," said Grandpa.

Beatrice turned the bow around. She pulled the hairs across the strings. One string, two strings, three strings, four strings. A long, warm sound came out. It did not squeak at all.

Then a bird began to sing outside the window. Beatrice pulled the bow again. She made another sound. The bird sang back. "It is singing with me!" said Beatrice. Grandpa laughed. Beatrice pulled the bow across the strings one more time. The little bird flew up into the morning sky, still singing.

Andrew went to the park with his mom. They walked past the swings first. The slide was long and silver. Andrew slid down, down, down. The metal felt cold under his hands. "Nice sliding," said his friend Axton.

Then they went to the little farm stand by the gate. A snowy white pig lived there. Andrew patted the pig with one finger. The pig made a happy oink. But then Andrew looked around. He could not see his mom. Too many people. His tummy felt tight.

Andrew remembered something. He saw a lady at the stand with a big red vest. She had a cash box. She worked there. Andrew walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The lady held his hand. "Let's look together," she said. They stepped past the pig, past the swings. There was Mom, right by the slide. Mom hugged him tight. "You found a helper," Mom said. "I did," said Andrew, and he waved to the lady in red.

Henri was awake early. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny, like little wings flapping inside. "My tummy is fluttery," he told Mama. Mama smiled a soft smile. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," she said. "Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay."

Henri ate his toast. It was cut into a triangle. He chased the last crumb around his plate with his finger. Then he put on his new shoes. His tummy still fluttered a little.

At the door, Henri held Mama's hand. He took one big step outside. The fluttery feeling got smaller. "I am going to school," he said. Mama kissed the top of his head. "Have a happy first day, Henri."

Henri waved and walked down the path.

Matteo loved to play outside at daycare. Behind the fence there was a small grassy hill. Kamryn counted to ten. Laurier ran to hide. Matteo wanted to hide too. He wanted to win. So he stood on the hill and covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the slide. He could not see the fence. He could not see Kamryn.

"I can't see you," he said, "so you can't see me!"

He heard Kamryn laugh. He heard feet running on the grass. Then Kamryn tapped his shoulder. "I see you, Matteo!"

Matteo peeked through his fingers. The sun made the grass glow. He saw his shoes. He saw the whole yard.

"Your eyes were covered," said Kamryn. "My eyes were not."

Matteo uncovered his face. "So you saw me the whole time?"

"The whole time," said Kamryn.

Ms. Ross called them in for crackers. Matteo smelled the cheese. He touched the warm cup. He tasted a cracker. "Yum," he said.

"Next game," said Matteo, "I will hide behind something. Then no eyes can see me!"

Kamryn giggled. "Try the short bush by the door."

Matteo smiled. "I will."

Josephine went to the park with her dad. The sun was hot on her face. The water fountain made the water cold. She put her hand under it and giggled. "How does it get so cold?" she wondered.

They sat at a picnic table to eat. Josephine stayed close to her dad, just like always. Stay close, stay close, that was their park rule. Then she saw something shiny on the next table. Little red and yellow balls sat in a small cup. They looked just like candy. "Ooh," said Josephine. "Maybe someone left candy."

Her friend Lilia ran over to play. "Can I have the candy too?" Lilia asked. Josephine looked at the little balls. They were round and bright. But was it really candy? She did not touch them. She held Lilia's hand and said, "Let's ask first."

Josephine ran to her dad. "Papa, come look," she said. Her dad looked at the cup. "Those are pills," he said. "They are medicine. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy." A kind lady came back to the table. "Thank you for not touching," she said. "I dropped my cup." She picked it up and put it away.

Later, a man made popcorn over a small fire. Josephine stood far back and watched. "Can I beg for some popcorn?" she asked. Her dad laughed and bought a bag. Josephine and Lilia shared it, drop by drop, piece by piece. The popcorn was warm. The water was cold. "Try it," said Josephine. Lilia dipped one piece in her cold cup and popped it in her mouth. "Warm and cold together!" she said.

Sara planted seeds at the farm. She put tomatoes in one row. She put carrots in another row. Then she ran to see the bunnies. Her friend Indie came to help. "Where are the tomatoes?" Indie asked. Sara looked at the dirt. She could not remember. All the rows looked the same.

Then Sara saw a stick with a picture. Mr. Suzuki had made it. It showed a carrot. It stood in the carrot row. "The stick tells us what grows here," said Mr. Suzuki. Sara clapped her hands. A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot.

So Sara made more labels. She drew a pretty red tomato. She pushed the stick down. It sank into the soft dirt. Indie drew a big orange carrot. She even drew a dog with a bone, just for fun. Day by day, tiny green leaves popped up. "Look, look!" said Sara. The leaves grew right under their pictures.

Harrison stood on his little balcony. He had three pots. One pot had lettuce. One pot had carrots. One pot had a tomato plant. Every morning he counted them. "One, two, three," he said.

One day the sun was very hot. Harrison looked at his lettuce. The leaves were drooping. They hung down like sleepy hands. He pointed at the pot. "Mom, the lettuce looks sad," he said. Mom came and looked too. "Plants droop when they are thirsty," she said. She handed him the small blue watering can. Harrison gave the lettuce a big drink. Water ran down onto the smooth leaves.

The next morning, Harrison ran outside. He counted his pots again. "One, two, three." The lettuce stood up tall. The leaves were wide and perky. "You grew back!" said Harrison. Mom smiled. Harrison watered every pot, one by one. Then he sat in his little chair beside the tomato plant. "Drink up," he said.

Claare was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big kitchen. Claire wanted to make soup, like Grandma did. But the real stove was too hot. Grandma said, "Only I touch the stove. You can play right here."

So Claire made her own kitchen on the porch. She found a pot and a spoon. She found three pinecones and some leaves. She dropped them in the pot. "Pinecone soup!" she said. She stirred and stirred. A bird began to sing its song over her head. Claire felt happy.

She lifted the spoon to her mouth. Grandma sat down next to her. "That soup is pretend food," said Grandma. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth." Claire smiled. She opened her mouth wide and made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! All gone!" The last pinecone bobbed in the pot. Grandma clapped her hands.

Lily sat at Grandma's big table. There was a pencil and paper. Lily wanted to write her name. She held the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard on the paper. The L came out fat and wobbly. "It looks like a squiggle," Lily said.

Grandma sat down next to her. "Watch me," said Grandma. She put her thumb and first finger on the pencil. Then she let it rest on her middle finger. "This is called the pinch," Grandma said. "Can you try?"

Lily pinched the pencil with her thumb and first finger. She rested it on her middle finger. She drew a letter L. It was thin and straight! Then she made an I. Then a Y. "Lily!" she read out loud. Grandma clapped her hands.

Lily looked out at the quiet street. The paper had been empty. Now her name was on it. "Can I write it again?" Lily asked. Grandma slid the pencil back across the table.

Wesley ran into the forest with Reina. He wanted to play shop. Reina said, "I will be the shopkeeper first." She set leaves and pinecones on a flat rock. "Come buy from my shop," she called.

Wesley was the shopper. He carried three acorns in his pocket. He gave one acorn to Reina. She put it in her little bag. Then Wesley had to wait. The shopper waits while the shopkeeper picks the pinecone. Reina chose a big green one. "Here you go," she said. Wesley held it like a treasure.

"Now you be the shopkeeper," said Reina. Wesley stood by the rock. Reina gave him an acorn. She looked and looked. Wesley waited and waited. At last she pointed at a red leaf.

"This one, please," said Reina.

Joshua was in bed. The room was dark. Then he heard a noise. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window.

Joshua felt scared. He pulled the blanket up. The noise came again. Tap, tap. His tummy felt tight.

Joshua got out of bed. He went to Mommy's room. "I heard a noise," he said. "I feel scared."

Mommy took his hand. Her hand was warm and soft. "Come on," she said. "We can look together."

They walked down the hall. Mommy turned on the light. The room felt less dark. Then they heard the noise again. Tap, tap.

Mommy opened the curtain. A tree branch was tapping the glass. The wind was moving it. "That is a cool branch," said Joshua. He was not scared now.

They saw Grandpa's dog outside in his bed. The dog heard them and began to bark. "Woof!" he said.

Mommy tucked Joshua back into bed. The blanket smelled like clean laundry. "If you feel scared again, you can tell me," she said. "I will help you."

Joshua closed his eyes. Tap, tap, went the branch. He smiled and went to sleep.

Natalie sat on the playroom floor. Mr. Pritchard held up a big cloth bag. "This is the feely-bag game," he said. "Put your hand in. Feel the toy. Then guess what it is."

Natalie reached in first. Her fingers found something round. It was smooth and bouncy. "A ball!" she said. She pulled it out. It was a red ball. She had not known that part.

Ezra put his hand in next. His nose scrunched up as he felt around. "A block," he said. He pulled out a yellow block. Then Soraya felt a soft car. When she pulled it out, it was blue.

Natalie wanted to try again. "Can I feel one more?" she asked. Mr. Pritchard nodded. This time she felt something small and round. A marble! "Is it green?" she asked. She peeked in the bag. No, she could not see it yet.

She squeezed the marble. Smooth. Round. Little. But what color? She could not tell. She took her hand out. The marble was green after all!

"Look at that," said Soraya. "My turn, my turn!"

Ezra was hungry for a turn too. He reached in and filled his hands with something soft. He pulled out a green frog. "Ribbit," he said, and everyone laughed.

"How many colors are in that bag?" Natalie wondered. Mr. Pritchard smiled. "Why don't you look and see?"

Natalie tipped the bag over. The toys fell out in a pile. Red, yellow, blue and green, all mixed together on the floor. "So many!" she said. She picked up the red ball one more time and held it to her eye.

Isaac was going to the store with Mom. He jumped into the family car. But his bunny was gone! "Where is Bunny?" he cried. Bunny always came along for rides.

Isaac looked on his lap. No bunny. He looked on the floor. No bunny. He spun around in his seat to check the back. Now he felt dizzy, and still no bunny. "Bunny must be under the seat," he said. He bent down low. But it was dark under there. He could not see anything at all.

Then Mom opened the glove box. She took out a flashlight and turned it on. "Here you go," she said. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots." Isaac held the bright light under the seat. The dark spot lit up. And there was Bunny! One ear was sticking up. Isaac grabbed him fast.

"Bunny, you found the light too!" Isaac laughed. He buckled Bunny in tight. The car started, and they went on their way to the store.

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. The bookshop was warm and friendly. There were books everywhere. Brooklyn saw a big poster on the wall. It had letters on it.

"Dad, what is that?" she asked.

"Those are the letters," said Dad. "The alphabet starts with A and ends with Z."

Brooklyn looked at the letter A. "A," she said. "A says ah, like apple!"

"You found the first letter," said Dad.

Brooklyn walked along the poster. She found B. Then C. Then D. She tapped each letter with her finger. She said the sound each letter made. B says buh. C says cuh. D says duh.

Then she got to the letter P. "P," she said. "Is that the end?"

"Keep going," said Dad.

Brooklyn kept walking. Q, R, S, T. She said each sound. Then U, V, W. Then X and Y.

"What comes next?" she wondered out loud.

She took one more step. There it was. The letter Z!

"Z!" she shouted. "Z says zzz, like a bee!"

Ms. Dang, the shopkeeper, smiled. "Would you like a book about Z?" she asked.

"Yes, please," said Brooklyn.

Ms. Dang found a book with a zebra on it. Brooklyn opened the book on the floor. She pointed at the zebra.

"Zebra starts with Z," she said. "Z is the last letter."

She turned to Dad. "Can we spell my name with letters?"

"We can spell it at dinner," said Dad. "First, let's pay for the book."

Brooklyn hugged the book tight. "A to Z," she whispered to the zebra. "The whole way."

Victor sat down for snack time at school. Ms. Nguyen held a big jug of apple juice. She could pour the juice into little cups.

Luciano pushed his cup forward. "Give me juice!" he said. Ms. Nguyen stood still. She did not pour. Luciano waited. Then he said, "Juice, please." Ms. Nguyen smiled. She poured the juice. One cup, full to the top.

Rafaelle held out his cup. "Juice, please." Ms. Nguyen poured. Two cups, full to the top. Victor felt a small worry in his tummy. What if no juice came for him? He took a big breath. "Juice, please," he said. Ms. Nguyen poured. Three cups, full to the top. The juice was cold and sweet. "Thank you," said Victor. "You are welcome," said Ms. Nguyen.

After snack, Victor yawned. He was sleepy. He picked a soft mat and a picture book. The book had a red fire truck on it. "Can you read to us, please?" he asked. Ms. Nguyen sat right down beside him. She opened the book and said, "Fire trucks go woo, woo, woo."

Gabriella sat on the small red mat. Mr. Banerjee played a song on his piano. He wanted her to clap along.

Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap, clap, clap! Her claps got faster and faster. Soon they were all mixed up.

"Try this," said Mr. Banerjee. He stood up tall. "March with me." He marched around the room. Step, step, step, step. His footsteps were even. They kept going. Gabriella marched behind him. Step, step, step, step.

"Now clap like your feet," he said. Gabriella marched and clapped. Clap, clap, clap, clap. The claps were even now. They kept going, just like footsteps when you march.

"Now sing," said Mr. Banerjee. Gabriella sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She clapped while she sang. She did not stop. She did not go too fast.

Mr. Banerjee smiled. "Let's do it one more time," he said. He played, and Gabriella marched, clapped and sang all the way to the end.

Margot sat at the little table. The tablet in front of her was dark. She wanted to draw a picture of winter, with snow and a red hat.

She tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped it again. Still nothing. "Why won't it work?" she asked. Mr. Boateng knelt down beside her. "Press this little button," he said, pointing to the side. Margot pressed the button. The screen lit up. It was bright and full of colors.

She touched the drawing app. It opened with a soft pop. She drew snow, lots of white snow, and a red hat too. Then she showed Dakota. "Snow!" said Dakota, and she clapped.

When the bell rang, Margot pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, all by herself. "I did it," she whispered, and ran to line up at the door.

Hazel went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a chicken. She could not find one on the low shelf. She pulled a book out. The whole row tipped over. Thump, thump, thump! Blocks fell too. Emir was building with those blocks. Now they were all over the floor.

Emir's lip wobbled. Hazel felt bad inside. "Sorry," she said. "Sorry I knocked your tower down." Emir looked at her. Then he smiled a little. "Okay. Help me fix it?" Hazel stacked the blocks again. Emir put the tall top on. The tower stood up, fresh and tall.

Then Hazel asked Mr. Aziz for help. "Please, can you help me find a chicken book?" "Thank you," she said when he handed her one. The book had a soft yellow chick on the cover. Emir sat next to her. They read about a chicken on a swing together.

Logan held his dad's hand at the library door. Inside, the room smelled like paper and warm air. Logan saw Anais at the desk. She held a small blue card. "It's mine," Anais said. "I can take books home."

Logan wanted a card too. He ran to the desk and reached up high. The librarian smiled. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," she said. Logan looked back at his dad. Dad sat down on a soft chair. Logan climbed nothing. He stood beside Dad and helped hold the pen. It felt loose in his fist, so he gripped it tighter. Dad wrote his name, and then Logan drew a wobbly line under it.

The librarian handed Logan his own card. It was smooth and cool. He picked a book about a big red truck. At the door, his knee bumped the desk, but he didn't drop anything. "Thank you," Logan told the librarian. He held the card all the way home.

Dylan looked out the window. He could see the park. The swings were over there. He wanted to go on the big swing.

"Can we go to the park?" Dylan asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Put on your shoes."

Dylan put on his red shoes. He ran to the door. Then he stopped. The park was across the street. A car went by. It was fast.

Dylan waited by the door. He did not step off the curb. He held out his hand.

Dad took Dylan's hand. "Ready?" said Dad.

"Ready," said Dylan.

They looked left. They looked right. They walked across the street together. Dylan held on tight.

At the park, Leah was there. "Dylan!" she said. "Come on the swing!"

Dylan ran to the swing. Leah pushed him. Dylan pushed Leah. The swings went up and down.

Leah had a snack in her bag. She shared her apple slices. "Crunchy," said Dylan. He took a big bite. Leah laughed.

The sun began to go down. Dad called, "Time to go home."

Dylan took Dad's hand again. They crossed the street together. At home, Dylan had a warm bath. Then he got into bed.

"Best day," said Dylan. He closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Sienna stood at the playground gate. It was her first day of school. Her new backpack sat on her back. It was very heavy. "Oof," said Sienna. She could not walk fast.

Fiona ran over. "Your bag is so big!" she said. Sienna sat down on the grass. She opened her backpack. Out came a teddy bear. Out came three toy cars. Out came a big rubber duck. The bag was not heavy now. It felt thin and light on her back.

Sienna put the toys in her cubby inside. Then she came back out. The air was warm. She mixed sand and water in the sand pit with Zaynab. They made a big round cake. Mr. Balogun clapped his hands. Sienna ran to the slide. Her light backpack bounced up and down. "Look at me!" she called. "I can run now!"

Emily was at Grandma's house. She wanted a cookie. Grandma had many jars on the shelf. But which jar had the cookies?

Emily stood on her toes. She stretched her neck up high. She could see the jars. Each jar had little marks on it. "Grandma, what are the marks?" she asked. Grandma said, "Those marks are words." Emily looked closer. The words were on labels.

She pointed to the first jar. It said "Sugar." She pointed to the next jar. It said "Flour." Then she found one more jar. It said "Cookies!" Emily clapped her hands. "Grandma, this one says cookies!"

Grandma laughed and took the jar down. "You found them," she said. "The words told you." Emily ate a warm cookie at the table. Grandma said, "Just one more, or your tummy might hurt." Emily nodded and took one more careful bite.

Later, Emily walked past the big door. There was a sign on the door. It had words too! "Grandma, what does the sign say?" she asked. Grandma read it out loud. It said "Welcome." Words were on the jars. Words were on the door. Words were all around, telling her things.

Emily held Grandma's hand. "I like words," she said. Grandma smiled and opened the door to the garden. "Then let's go find some more," said Grandma.

Zoey stood in the garage with her dad. A little guitar sat on a wood box. Zoey wanted to play a song for her friend Natalia.

Zoey picked the strings. The notes sounded funny. "That is not a song," Zoey said. She frowned.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Guitars need tuning," he said. "I will turn the pegs." He turned a little peg at the top. Zoey plucked the string again. Now the note sounded right. He turned another peg. That note sounded right too.

Zoey plucked all the strings. "Now it sounds like music!" she said. She ran to the door and called, "Natalia, come hear my song!" Natalia ran in, and Zoey began to play.

Adam sat at the little table. He wanted to make a number poster. Mr. Ma put out fresh paper and crayons.

Adam drew one big leaf. Then two leaves. Then three.

Edmund came to help. "Four, five, six," he counted.

Cataleya added more leaves. "Seven, eight, nine," she said.

Adam wrote the numbers too. One number for each. Then he wanted ten.

"Ten is written with two digits," said Cataleya. She wrote a 1 and then a 0.

Adam tried. He wrote a 1. Then a 0 next to it. "Is that ten?" he asked.

Mr. Ma smiled and nodded. "Yes. That says ten."

Adam gave his poster a little bite of tape to hang it up. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" he shouted.

Georgia sat on Grandpa's big striped chair. The game was on TV. Navy came over with her dad. Harper came too, with a bowl of popcorn.

The red team ran fast. "Go, go, go!" said Georgia. She clapped her hands. The blue team ran fast too. Everyone watched. Grandpa said, "Now we wait."

The score said two and two. Georgia frowned. She wanted the red team to win. She asked Grandpa, "Who won?"

Grandpa looked at the screen. "Nobody won," he said. "Both teams have the same score. That is called a tie."

"A tie," said Georgia. She said it again. "A tie."

Navy stood up. "Then nobody is sad," she said. Harper passed the popcorn around. Georgia took a little handful and ate it slowly.

They watched the players shake hands. Grandpa turned off the TV. The night was dark outside the window. Georgia waited for her mom by the door.

Mom came in with cold cheeks. "Who won?" Mom asked.

Georgia smiled big. "Nobody! It was a tie."

Stella stood by the blocks at school. Emaan and Ashlyn were playing house in the corner. Emaan rocked a teddy bear. Ashlyn stirred a pretend pot. Stella wanted to play too. But she did not know how to start. She walked closer. She looked at the little table they had made. Nobody asked her to join.

Then Stella had an idea. She took a deep breath. "Let's pretend I'm the baby's doctor," she said. Emaan jumped up. "Yes! The baby has a scratch on her paw!" Ashlyn clapped her hands. "Quick, doctor, come to our table!"

Stella ran over. She tapped the teddy's paw with a toy spoon. "All better!" she said. Ashlyn said, "Now let's pretend you're the pizza man." Stella laughed. "Here is your pizza, hot from the oven!" She handed over a flat block. Ms. Ahmadi smiled from her chair.

Stella felt lucky. She knew a secret now. "Let's pretend" made a game begin. "Let's pretend we're pirates next!" she said. "Aye aye!" said Emaan, waving a paper tube like a sword.

Rehmat sat on the back step. She wanted her juice to stay yummy on the sunny day. She saw her mom carry a tray. On it was a shiny bowl full of ice cubes. Rehmat heard them clink, clink. She took one little cube with her fingers. "Ooh, it feels cold," she said. She dropped it into her cup fast. Then she touched her cold, wet cup. She smelled her juice. It smelled like sweet apples. She took a sip. "Mmm, it tastes cold too," she said. Madeline came over. She held out her hand. "Can I try one?" Rehmat gave her a cube. Madeline felt it and laughed. "Cold!" Then she popped it in her own cup. Rehmat smiled and gave her a straw. "Now our drinks are cold like a mountain," said Madeline, and they called out, "Cheers!"

Peyton sat at the big table in math club. Mr. Sadeghi put down two piles of blocks. "Which pile has more?" he asked. Nolan pointed fast. "That one!" But Peyton was not sure.

She tried to count the blocks. "One, two, three, um." A block rolled away. "Oh no, I lost my count!" Nolan laughed. "Blocks are tricky walkers." Peyton giggled too. Then she looked at her hands. She put up one finger for the first block. Then one more finger. Then one more. "Six!" she said. Her six fingers stood up tall.

She counted the other pile the same way. "Four!" Peyton held up her hands. Six fingers was more than four fingers. "This pile has more!" she said. Mr. Sadeghi clapped. Timothee clapped too. "Can we count cookies next?" he asked. Mr. Sadeghi smiled. "Only if you each pick one sweet treat to take home." Peyton grinned and held up one finger for her cookie.

Colton went to the grocery store with his dad. He held his little red car. It was his favorite toy. "Stay in my pocket, little car," said Colton.

Colton looked at the apples. He looked at the milk. Then he reached for a big red apple. His little car fell down. It fell on the floor. Then it rolled. It rolled far, far away. "Oh no!" said Colton. "My car is lost!"

Colton looked by the apples. No car. He looked by the milk. No car. Mr. Whitaker, from next door, was shopping too. He had a thick warm coat on. "Can I help you look?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Colton. "My car rolled away." Mr. Whitaker bent down low. He peeked under the big cold fruit box. "Small toys can roll under things," he said. "Let's look under here." There it was! The little red car sat under the box.

Colton got down on his knees. He reached out his hand. He pulled the car back out. "Found you!" said Colton. He gave the car a big hug. Then he put it in his thick coat pocket. "Safe now," said Colton. Mr. Whitaker smiled. "That pocket is a good garage," he said. Colton laughed all the way to the checkout line.

Leo held Mommy's hand at the park. He saw the big slide first. "Slide!" he said. "Yes, we can go on the slide," said Mommy. "Stay close to me on the way."

Esteban was there too. He ran to the slide. He climbed the ladder. Then he lay down on top. His head went first, down toward the ground. "Wait," said Mommy. "Feet first on the slide." Esteban sat up. He turned around. His feet went down first, and he slid to the soft sand. "Again!" said Esteban.

Leo watched. The slide was hot where the sun shone on it. Mommy touched the top. "Too hot for bare hands," she said. She showed Leo how to hold the cool, rough side rail. Leo climbed up slowly. He sat down. He pointed his feet down the slide, feet first, just like Esteban. Whoosh! He landed on his bottom in the sand. His tummy felt tickly and happy.

Esteban waited at the bottom. "You did it!" he said. Leo laughed and kicked the sand with his toes. Then he ran back to Mommy, and she picked him up. "My big boy, feet first," she said.

Amira was in the cooking classroom. Today the class would make muffins for their families. Amira wanted to make nice muffins for her mom.

Ms. Vogel put out flour, sugar, and butter. Amira picked up the big sugar bag. She tipped it over the bowl. Sugar poured and poured. "Oh no," said Amira. "Too much sugar!" Ms. Vogel came to help. "We can start again," she said kindly. "Watch this."

Ms. Vogel held up a little cup with a handle. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Amira filled the cup with sugar. She tapped it out into the bowl. It was just the right amount. Cadence measured the flour next to her. Meredith measured a little spoon of salt. Each cup and spoon held just what they needed.

The muffins went into the big oven. Ms. Vogel, the grown-up, put them in and took them out. Amira waited at the table with her hands in her lap. Soon the muffins sat on a rack, warm and round. Amira counted them. "One for Mom, one for Dad, one for me," she said. "I know just how many we made." She carried the box home, hugging it all the way.

Jules sat at the dinner table. His tooth felt wiggly. It went back and forth when he touched it. "Will it fall out?" he asked. Dad smiled. "Yes, but not tonight."

Jules was scared. He pushed his carrots around. Then he saw Dad's face change. Dad looked worried too.

"Dad, are you scared?" Jules asked.

"Yes, a little," said Dad. "I have a big day at work tomorrow. I feel nervous."

Jules stared. "You have feelings too?"

Dad laughed. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Jules thought about that. Everybody has feelings. Even grown-ups. Even big dads with big jobs. He slid his carrots near Dad's plate. "You can have my carrots," he said. "They make me feel happy."

Dad took one and crunched it. Jules giggled. His tooth went wiggly again. Maybe tomorrow.

Brielle sat on the rug in the nursery room. Her baby sister was coming today. Mama walked in with a little blanket. "This is the baby," said Mama. The baby was so small and so cute.

Brielle wanted the baby to see her. She waved. The baby did not look. She clapped her hands. The baby did not look. "Try again," said Mr. Rajapakse. "Babies like slow things." Brielle waited. She counted one, two, three. Then she put her finger in the baby's little hand. The baby held on tight! The baby held Brielle's finger and would not let go.

Noor came to look. Isla came to look. "She likes me," said Brielle. The baby still held on. Mr. Rajapakse smiled. The sun came in the window and made a warm spot on the blanket. The baby yawned a big baby yawn. Then she let go, little by little, and fell fast asleep.

Bennett ran into the backyard. The sun made the light dance on the grass. There was a big tub of water on the porch. Bennett wanted to jump right in.

"Stop there," said his dad. "We do this first." Dad put his hand in the water. He pulled it out fast. "Hot," he said. "The sun made it hot." He added cold water from the hose. He put his hand in again. "Now it is warm, not hot. Warm water is good. Hot water can hurt you." Bennett put in one toe. The water felt nice and warm. Then he climbed in and splashed with both feet.

Kylian came to the gate. "Can I get in too?" he asked. Bennett said, "Wait! My dad has to check first." Dad felt the water. "Still warm," he said. "You can get in." Kylian took off his tall boots and jumped in. The water went splash, right onto Dad's shoes. All three of them laughed.

Sadie stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her new lunchbox with both hands.

Zakaria stood beside her. He had a lunchbox too. His looked just like hers. Both boxes were red with a little boat on the front.

At lunch time, the boxes got mixed up. Sadie picked one up. She opened the lid. Inside was a sandwich she did not like. "This is not mine," she said.

Mr. Cardinal came to help. "Open both lids," he said. Sadie looked inside one lid. There was a name. It said Zakaria. She looked in the other lid. It said Sadie.

"Here is your lunch," she said. She gave Zakaria his box. He smiled and gave her hers.

After school, Sadie found her mom. "Can we write my name on my coat?" she asked. "And on my hat?"

"Yes," her mom said. "We can do it tonight."

Sadie hugged her red lunchbox. "My name helped it come back to me," she whispered.

Levi wanted to paint a pumpkin. It had to be orange. But the paint cups had no orange. There was red, yellow, and blue. Levi counted them. "One, two, three," he said. "Red, yellow, blue. No orange." Caleb was painting a fire truck red. Vincent was painting a thin yellow duck. A picture of a big egg hung on the wall, painted orange. Levi sighed. His pumpkin sat white and plain.

Ms. Lin gave him a big brush. "Try mixing," she said. Levi dipped into the red paint. He dipped into the yellow paint too. He stirred them on his tray. The red swirled. The yellow swirled. Then something new came. "Orange!" shouted Levi. His pumpkin turned orange, just like that.

Levi painted a fast swipe. Then another. "One, two, three, four stripes," he said. His pumpkin glowed like a little sun. Caleb and Vincent came to look. "Mix red and yellow," said Levi, holding up his brush. "Watch this." He stirred again, and more orange appeared on the tray.

Noah stood at the train station with Dad. They held a big sign. It said "Grandma" in wiggly letters.

"Is that the wrong sign?" Noah asked. "It looks crooked."

"It is crooked," said Dad. "But Grandma will know it is for us."

A big train rolled in. It went slow, then it stopped. People stepped out one by one. Then Noah saw her. Grandma waved her hand high.

Grandma hugged Noah. Then she hugged Dad. "My bags are heavy," she said. "The little wheels sank into a soft spot on the platform."

Noah helped pull one bag. The wheels popped out. "You are strong," said Grandma.

At home, Grandma unpacked a photo. "Look," she said. "This is Dad when he was little."

Noah stared. Dad as a little boy? "Dad was small? Like me?"

"He was," said Grandma. "He got his first bike. It was red. He fell off seven times. Then he rode all the way down the street."

"Tell me more," said Noah. "Tell it at the sink. I can rinse the bowl while you talk."

Grandma laughed and started the story.

The sky was cloudy, but Everett ran to the playground anyway. In his bag he had all the chalk. Every piece. Red, blue, green and yellow.

"Let's draw a dragon!" said Dominik. He reached for the chalk. But the bag was on Everett's arm. Dominik had no chalk at all. He stood by the big tree with empty hands.

Everett drew one dragon. Then he drew two dragons. He looked up. Dominik was still by the tree. He was poking the dirt with a stick. His face looked sad and far away.

Everett ran over. "You can use my chalk," he said. "Sharing means letting you use it too." He gave Dominik the red piece and the yellow piece. "Let's cook dragon soup!" said Dominik. "Yes! Make it big! Make it big!" said Everett.

They drew a giant pot under the tree. They drew fire under the pot. They threw in pretend berries and pretend leaves. Two dragons came to eat the soup, they said, and slurped it all up. Then Everett gave Dominik a blue piece too. "More soup! More soup!" they shouted together. The dragons danced across the pavement.

Sebastian sat at the big table in the library. Mr. Ho put out paint and paper. "We will make butterflies," said Mr. Ho.

Sebastian painted one half of his paper. He used red paint. He made one big wing. He made one small spot. Skylar sat next to him. Colson sat across from him.

Then Sebastian folded his paper in half. He pressed it with his smooth, flat hand. The paint was still wet. He counted to five. One, two, three, four, five.

Sebastian opened the paper. "Look!" he said. The paint had printed on the other half. Now there were two big wings. Now there were two small spots. Both sides matched.

"That is a real butterfly," said Skylar. "Both wings are the same." Colson held his paper up. His wings matched too.

Sebastian looked at his red butterfly. He folded it one more time. Then he opened it again. The two wings still matched, like a mirror. "I want to hang it in our kitchen," he said.

Mr. Ho smiled and brought the tape.

James was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to play outside in the snow. "Put on your coat," said Grandpa. James tried to put it on. His arm went in the wrong hole. He pulled and wiggled. At last the coat was on.

Now the zipper. James held the bottom. He pushed it up, up, up. It went zzzzzip all the way. "I did it!" said James.

Outside, he made a snowball with Rupert. But then James lost a mitten in the snow. He looked and looked. His hand felt cold and thirsty for warmth. Rupert found the mitten. Then James saw his coat pocket. He tucked both mittens inside. The pocket held them just fine. When he took them out again, they were still there. "Thank you, pocket," said James. Grandpa smiled and called them in for a warm sandwich.

Matthew went to the farmers' market with his dad. There were big baskets of carrots and potatoes. "Let's make soup for dinner," said Dad. Matthew picked out three carrots. The carrots had dirt on them. "Dirt from the farm," said the farmer. "It means they are fresh."

At home, Matthew wanted to help. Dad said, "Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables before cooking." Matthew stood at the sink. He held a carrot under the water. He rubbed it with his fingers. The dirt came off. The water turned brown in the sink. Then the carrot was clean and shiny.

"I did it!" said Matthew. He rinsed the next carrot. Dirt off, water brown, carrot clean. He rinsed the potatoes too. "Dirt off, water brown, carrot clean," he said again. He liked saying it.

The vegetables went into a big pot. Dad put the pot on the stove. Matthew stayed back, because the stove was hot. Dad stirred the soup. "Smell it," said Dad. Matthew smelled carrots and potatoes.

At dinner, Mom filled Matthew's bowl. Matthew took a big bite. "I rinsed these," he said. "They were dirty. Now they are soup!" Mom smiled. "Best soup ever," she said. "Yum," said Matthew, and he took another bite.

Nova ran to the park with her dad. Yesterday the slide was wet, and they went home early. Today the sky was blue, and the slide was dry. Nova slid down, down, down.

Robert was there too. "When is snack time?" Nova asked. "Later," said Dad. He pointed to his phone. A clock showed what time it was. "Now the little hand points here," Dad said. "When it points to the next number, it will be snack time." Nova looked and looked. The hands moved very slowly. She slid down the slide again. She gave the slide a funny kiss, just to be silly. Then she ran back to the clock. The little hand had moved!

"It moved! Snack time now?" she asked. Dad peeked and laughed. "Almost, Nova." Nova sat on the bench and swung her legs. She waited. The little hand moved again. "Now!" said Dad. He opened the bag. Out came apples and juice. "We can come back tomorrow," said Dad. Nova smiled and took a big bite.

Margot sat at the dinner table with her peas. Under her chair, in a bag, were five toy monkeys. "Can I show you a song after dinner?" she asked.

Dad said, "First peas, then monkeys."

Margot ate fast. Then she lined the monkeys up on the table. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. She made one monkey fall off. It rolled into her cup. "One fell off and bumped his head," she sang. "Now four monkeys!"

"You take one away each time," said Dad.

"Yes! Watch. Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." One monkey fell into the peas. "Now three!" She counted them out loud. "One, two, three."

"Are you a little owl watching so hard?" said Dad.

"No, I am just Margot." She sang again. "Three little monkeys jumping on the bed." One fell behind the salt. "Two left! Then one! Then zero monkeys!"

"No monkeys at all," said Dad. "Is that scary?"

"No, it is just funny." Margot picked them up. "Can we do it again?"

She began to sing, "One little monkey jumping on the bed."

Wyatt wanted warm milk before his nap. His dad carried a little camp stove out to the backyard. He set it on the table by the fence. Wyatt stood close to his dad, like always. The grass was still wet from the rain. His shoes made little dark spots on the stones.

The stove made a soft blue flame. The milk went into a small pot. Wyatt could not see anything hot in the pot. He wanted to touch it. He pulled his hand back. "Dad, is it still hot?" he asked. "The stove can be hot even when it does not look hot," his dad said. "Only I touch it." His dad stirred the milk with a long spoon.

The milk got warm. It made little bubbles. The flame went out. The stove still did not look hot. But Wyatt kept his hands in his pockets. His dad poured the milk into Wyatt's green cup. It was warm, not too hot. Wyatt took a little taste. It was sweet. The wet grass sparkled in the sun. Wyatt sat on the step by his dad. "Warm milk is good," said Wyatt. His dad smiled and poured one for himself too.

Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. Snow! White snow everywhere. "A snow day!" she shouted.

Chome pulled on her boots. She put on her mittens. She ran into the backyard. The snow was cold and soft. She made a big snowball. She patted it and patted it. Then she made a snowman with a stick arm. Diana came over and they laughed and fell in the snow. The snow tasted cold on Chloe's nose.

"I want to go out again after lunch," Chloe said. But her mittens were soaked. Water dripped from them. Her boots were wet too. She could not wear wet mittens. Wet mittens are left out to dry after playing in the snow. So Chloe hung her mittens on the chair. She set her boots by the door.

After lunch, Chloe touched her mittens. They were warm and dry! She put them on. She pulled on her dry boots. "My turn again!" she said. She ran back out into the white, white snow.

Elias sat on the big bed at the doctor's office. His dad held his hand. "Today you get a small shot," Dad said. Elias looked around the room. He saw a red box on the wall. "What is that for?" he asked.

The nurse smiled. "That is the special hard box," she said. "Used needles go in there." Elias wondered, why a hard box? He would find out soon.

The nurse cleaned his arm with a cool wipe. Then she gave him the shot. It pinched for one second. "All done," she said. Elias watched her drop the used needle into the red box. It went in, and the lid snapped shut. Nobody got poked. "The needle went in the box," Elias said. "So nobody gets poked. Not me, not you!"

Afterward, Dad took Elias to the ice cream shop. Elias got a small cone with pink strawberry ice cream. He licked it and smiled. "My arm was brave," he said. "And the box keeps the needle safe." Dad gave him a big thumbs up, and Elias took one more happy lick.

Avery sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Where are we going now?" she asked. Mom said, "To the park. Today we play at the park." Avery clapped her hands. She wanted to see the ducks.

At the park, Avery found her friend Gwendolyn. Gwendolyn was throwing thin little sticks into the pond. "I came to this park tomorrow," said Gwendolyn. Then she stopped. She put one ear toward Avery. "No, wait. Yesterday. I came yesterday." Avery blinked. Yesterday was the day already done. Tomorrow was the day not here yet.

"I want to do that too," said Avery. She picked up a thin stick. She threw it in the water. A duck swam fast to the stick. Splash! "Look! My stick made the duck come!" said Avery. Gwendolyn threw her stick too. Another duck came. Two ducks, two sticks.

"Now it is time to go home," said Mom. Avery waved to the ducks. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. Tomorrow we will come back." In the car, Avery looked out the window. "Bye, park," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Raphael was at Grandpa's house. Today was painting day! Grandpa set out big paper and bright paint.

"I will paint a sun," Raphael said. "A big yellow sun!"

He dipped his brush. He painted a round yellow sun. It looked so good. Raphael wanted to touch it. He poked the sun with one finger.

"Oh no!" The yellow smeared. The sun had a smudge now. His finger was yellow too.

Grandpa looked over. "The paint is still wet," Grandpa said. "Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries."

Raphael made a sad face. But then he had an idea. "I will wait!" he said. "I will wait and wait."

He painted a green grass next. He did not touch it. He counted slowly. One, two, three, four, five.

Then Grandpa said, "It is dry now. Try it."

Raphael touched the sun. It felt smooth. Nothing smeared! The sun stayed round and bright.

"It works!" Raphael shouted. "I waited and it dried!"

He gave Grandpa a big hug. "Thank you, Grandpa," he said. "Waiting made the paint stay on."

Grandpa laughed. "Let's paint one more," he said.

Raphael picked up his brush. He painted a blue, squishy-looking whale. And this time, his hands stayed in his lap the whole time. He watched the paint dry, all by itself, in the sunny window.

Anthony put on his red shirt. It was the color of his team. The big game was on tonight.

At the restaurant, the big screen glowed. Nevaeh was there too. She wore a red shirt like his. Anton wore a blue shirt. Blue was the other team.

Anthony looked around. Many people wore red shirts. Many people wore blue shirts. "I cheer for red," said Nevaeh. "I cheer for blue," said Anton.

The game began. The big screen showed the players. Red team ran fast. Anthony clapped his hands. The people in red shirts stood up. They made a big noise.

Then blue team scored a goal. The people in blue shirts cheered loud. Anton jumped up and down. Anthony saw something smart. Shirt colors showed who cheered for who.

Anthony pointed at Nevaeh's shirt. "You cheer with me," he said. Nevaeh nodded. They held up their red cups.

The score got close. Everyone watched the big screen. Anthony's dad held him up high. "Kick the ball," Anthony shouted. "Kick it far."

The red team ran one more time. The player kicked. The ball went in. The red shirts all cheered at once. Anthony sent his napkin flying up in the air. It came down like a little flag. Nevaeh laughed and clapped.

"Red team wins," said Ms. Das from the next table. She wore red too. Anthony smiled big. He looked down at his shirt. "We match," he said.

Anthony looked out the window. The sky was dark and gray. Snow was falling on everything.

"No school today," said his dad. "It is a snow day."

Anthony jumped up and down. He put on his boots. He put on his puffy coat. He put on his red hat. One, two, three, and out he went.

He made a snowman, one, two, three snowballs tall. He found the biggest snowball of all. It was as big as a melon. Anthony loved it. He wanted to keep it forever.

"I will keep you in my room," he told the snowball. He carried it inside. He set it in a bowl on his table. He gave it a pat. Then he went to play with his blocks.

After lunch, Anthony ran to his room. He stopped. The bowl was full of water. His big snowball was gone.

"Dad! My snowball ran away!" he cried.

His dad came to look. "Hmm," he said. "The bowl is full of water."

Anthony thought hard. Snow outside, cold. Snow inside, warm. He scooped a fresh scoop of snow from the doorway. He put it in a cup. He watched and watched. Drip, drip, drip. The snow got smaller. The water got higher.

"The snow turns into water in here!" said Anthony. "My snowball did not run away. It melted!"

He ran outside and made a new snowman. This one, one, two, three, four snowballs tall.
