Lily did not want to put it back. Her lip went down, down, down.

Ms. Buchanan came over. She held out a small card. It was blue with Lily's own name on it. "This is a library card," she said. "A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

Lily's eyes went big. "Even the dragon book?"

"Even the dragon book."

Ms. Buchanan zapped the card on her desk. Beep! Then she zapped the book. Beep! "Now it can go home with you."

Lily held the book tight. The cover felt rough under her fingers. "Come on, dragon," she said. "You can hang out at my house."

Isha giggled. "The dragon sleeps at your house tonight!"

"He snores," said Lily. "You will hear it tomorrow."

At the door, Lily waved the blue card high. "See you soon, library!" she called.

Blake was at daycare. There was a big red box on the rug. Small cars went in the box. Blake pushed them to the bottom.

Then Maude came by. Maude took the cars out. One by one, the cars came out. Blake put them back in, fast. Maude pulled them out, slow.

"Stop," said Blake. "My cars!"

Maude laughed. She put a car in. Then she took it out.

Mr. Do sat down with them. "In and out are opposites," he said. "Want to play a game?"

Blake nodded. "In!" said Mr. Do. Blake dropped a car in. "Out!" said Maude. She took one out. They went back and forth, fast and slow.

Then the teacher called, "Snack time!" The milk was cold. The soup was hot. A grown-up helped pour.

After snack, Blake wanted to talk. "Maude, can you put them in with me?"

"Yes," said Maude. "But then I get to take them out."

"Okay," said Blake. "In first, then out."

They played together until the bottom of the box was full. Then it was empty. Then full again.

"Best game," said Maude. Blake held up a little blue car. "In you go," she said.

Maya ran into the garage with her recorder. Travis was already there, waiting by the big blue bag of toys. "Listen to this!" said Maya. She blew into her recorder. It made a loud squeak. Travis covered his ears.

"That was a bad sound," said Travis. Maya looked at her recorder. She saw the little holes on top. She tried again. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. She pressed that finger down hard. She blew. Now the recorder sang a real note.

"It works!" Maya shouted. She lifted her finger off the hole. She blew again. A different note came out. She put it back. The first note came back. Travis laughed. "Let me try!" he said. He pressed all the holes down hard. His recorder sang too. The two friends played their notes together, loud and happy.

It was a sunny morning at the pool. William was on the swim team this season. His teacher was Mr. Njoroge. William's friends Viola and Kasen swam too.

After swim practice, Mr. Njoroge put a small net on the grass. "Let's play soccer," he said. He put a round ball on the ground. "In soccer, we try to get the ball into the net to score a goal."

William wanted to score a goal. He ran to the ball. He tapped it with his foot. The ball wobbled a tiny bit. It did not go in the net. Kasen ran after it and kicked. The ball went past the net. "So close!" said Viola.

William looked at the ball. He looked at the net. He saw that the ball rolled where his foot pushed it. If he kicked it straight, it would roll straight. William took a big breath. He ran up and kicked the ball with his toe. The ball rolled and rolled, right into the net.

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Viola jumped up and down. Kasen clapped for William. William laughed. The ball was still in the net, so William ran to get it for Kasen's turn.

"Your kick, Kasen," said William.

It was Ellie's birthday at school. Ms. Halvorsen helped the class hang paper owls on the wall. "One owl, two owls, three owls," they counted. Leane gave Ellie a hug. Then Leane asked, "How old are you now?"

Ellie held up her fingers. Leane counted them. "One, two, three. You are three!"

Ellie shook her head. "No, wait!" She looked at her hand. One finger was hiding down. She pushed it up. "Now look!"

Leane counted again. "One, two, three, four. You are four!"

"Yes!" said Ellie. "Four!" Savanna held up four fingers too. "I am four also!" The three friends laughed and jumped.

Then the teacher lit the candles on the cake. Ellie took a big breath. She blew and blew. The candles went out. The smoke curled up, up, up.

"Make a wish, Ellie," said Ms. Halvorsen.

Ellie squeezed her eyes shut. Then she held up four fingers at the smoke.

Ethan wanted the red paint. It sat on the far table. But the whole class stood in his way. Darian and Amar were blocking the door like two big dragons.

Ethan tried to squeeze past. He bumped Amar's arm. Amar's tower fell down. Amar began to cry. "Sorry," said Ethan. He felt small as a mouse.

Ms. Demir knelt down. She had a gentle voice. "Say excuse me," she said. "It helps you get past."

Ethan took a breath. "Excuse me, please," he said.

The dragons became boys again. Amar stepped left. Darian stepped right. A little path opened up, wide as a doorway.

Ethan walked through. He got the red paint. He painted a big fire truck with a shiny ladder.

"Excuse me," said Amar, holding out a block. "Want to build again?"

Lucy went to the park with her dad. Sama was coming to play. Lucy could not wait.

Lucy felt so excited. She jumped up and down. She bounced near the bench. She shouted, "Sama! Sama!" But Sama was not there yet.

Her legs got tired from bouncing. Her dad said, "Sit with me. Let's color." He gave Lucy a red crayon. Lucy sat still and colored a big red flower. She looked with her eye at every petal. Waiting felt calm now.

A dog came by with a ball in its mouth. Lucy laughed. The dog dropped the ball and it rolled to her feet. Lucy picked it up gently.

Then Lucy saw Sama at the gate. Sama waved. Lucy stood up slowly. She walked over and held out the ball.

"Look what came to say hello," said Lucy. Sama patted the soft dog, and the dog wagged its tail.

Everly sat in a big red seat. Ms. Smith sat next to her. A man on the stage held a long shiny horn. "Now we clap," Everly whispered. She lifted her hands. Ms. Smith smiled and shook her head. "Not yet," she said softly. "Wait for the end."

The music began. It was slow and quiet. Everly wanted to clap so much. But she kept her hands in her lap. She watched the man blow into his horn. The music went up and down like a bird. It went on and on.

Then a fast song began. Everly felt the beat. One, two, one, two. She tapped her toes. Then she clapped her hands with the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Ms. Smith clapped too. It was like a game, and it made the song feel bouncy.

After the fast song, Ms. Smith sang a little rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Everly knew that one. She sang the next part all by herself. "How I wonder what you are." Her voice was small but strong.

At last the horn man put his horn down. He bowed. Ms. Smith clapped loud. Everly clapped too, right at the end. The man on the stage smiled at her. "One more song," he said, "and then pretzels." Everly licked her lips. She loved salty pretzels. She clapped again, and kept on clapping until her hands were warm.

Colton ran to the play table at daycare. Mr. Rossi had a big box there. "A guessing game!" said Colton. Ayman and Orion ran over too.

"First, close your eyes," said Mr. Rossi. Colton squeezed his eyes shut tight. He could not see anything at all. Mr. Rossi put something in his hands. Colton touched it with his fingertips. It felt bumpy. "A pinecone!" said Colton. "Yes!" said Mr. Rossi. Everyone cheered.

Next came something soft. "A feather!" said Colton. Then something smooth. "A stone!" said Colton. He had guessed them all. "Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy," said Ayman. "Even with eyes closed!"

Then Mr. Rossi opened the snack box. Colton heard the loud crunch of crackers with his ears. He smelled bananas with his nose. He tasted a sweet banana with his tongue. A baby in the next room made a happy sound too.

"Cracker crumbs!" said Orion. The table was messy now. "That's okay," said Mr. Rossi. "Crumbs make hungry tummies happy." Colton laughed and ate one more crunchy bite.

Jordan dug a small hole in the school garden. He dropped in a seed and patted the dirt. The hole was not too deep, just right. Mr. Karimi came over with a green watering can.

"Seeds need water to start growing," said Mr. Karimi. Jordan poured water on the dirt. The soil turned dark and wet. Jordan sat in a circle with his friends to rest.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He saw only dirt. No sprout. "It did not grow," he said. He watered the seed again. He watered it every day. Althea helped him share the big watering can. Still, only dirt.

Then one morning, Jordan saw something green. A tiny sprout stood in the dirt. "It came up!" he called. Luciano clapped. Jordan smiled and watered it again.

Margot sat on the big soft couch. Her dad was next to her. Isabella and Eyad came over too. The big game was on TV. Everyone was eating popcorn.

"Go, go, go!" shouted Eyad. A player ran fast down the field. Then another player ran too. Margot frowned. She could not tell who was who. "Dad, which team has the ball?" she asked.

Her dad pointed at the screen. "Look at the shirts," he said. "One team wears red shirts. One team wears blue shirts." Margot looked hard. The red shirt had the ball. "The red team has it!" she clapped. Then a blue shirt kicked the ball far. "Now the blue team!" she said. She was not lazy about looking now. She checked every shirt. "Red team, red team, red team," she said, over and over.

Isabella sat on Margot's left. "Your turn to see who has it," Margot said. Isabella looked at the shirts. "Blue team!" The crowd on TV roared. Margot's dad hugged her tight. "You can tell the teams apart now," he said. Margot smiled and ate one more piece of popcorn.

Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. The pumpkin was big and round.

Michael looked for orange paint. There was no orange paint. He found red paint. He found yellow paint. Michael felt sad.

Then Michael had an idea. He put red paint in a cup. He put yellow paint in too. He mixed it with his brush. The paint turned orange! Michael smiled big. He painted the pumpkin all orange. Some paint felt slimy on his fingers. He giggled.

Grandma came to see. "What a lovely orange pumpkin," she said. "My favorite color," said Michael. He held it up to the window. The pumpkin glowed like the sun.

Ethan wanted his bedtime story. He ran to get his big book about a puppy. He was in such a hurry that he opened the book from the wrong side. "The puppy found his home already," said Dad. "That is a funny ending first!" The pages went backwards. The puppy got lost, then he played, then he woke up. It was all mixed up.

"The puppy is sad, then happy, then sad again," said Ethan. He looked at the book. Then he flipped it over. The picture of the puppy was on the front. Dad smiled. "Let us try this way," he said.

Dad started at the front cover. He turned page after page. The puppy woke up. He ran in the yard. He heard a dog bark at the fence. He got lost in the long grass. At the end of the book, the puppy found his home. "That is better!" said Ethan. He hugged the book.

"Can we read it again tomorrow?" Ethan asked. Dad tucked him in. He put the book on the shelf with the front cover facing out. "Right there," said Dad. "Ready for tomorrow." Ethan closed his eyes and whispered, "Start at the front."

"Look, William!" said his mom. "We are driving to the library!" William bounced in his car seat. He wanted a book about animals. He hoped the library had a big one, with tigers in it. On the way, he played a game. "Cow!" he shouted. "That is an animal." "Truck!" he said. "That is not an animal." His mom laughed.

At the library, William ran to the first shelf. He saw books about trucks. He saw books about food. Apples and bread were on the covers. No animals. He reached up high, but the books were all wrong. "Where are the tigers?" he asked. He felt like his book was missing.

Ms. Pritchard, the librarian, came over. "Follow me," she said. "The library puts its books on shelves in groups, so people can find them." She pointed to one shelf. Every book there had an animal on the cover. Tigers! Bears! Elephants! All together on one shelf.

William grabbed a tiger book. He hugged it tight. In the car, he turned the pages fast. "Roar!" he said. His mom smiled at the red light. "That one goes back on the animal shelf next week," she said. William held it all the way home.

Blake went to the garden center with her dad. She picked out small tomato plants. "We will plant them at home," said Dad. Blake held a plant in her little hands.

At home, Blake dug a hole in the dirt. Then she saw a weed. She pulled it up. "Whoa!" said Blake. Long stringy roots hung down from the weed. Her friend Rocco came to play. "Look at the strings!" he said. "Those are roots," said Dad. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

So Blake put her tomato plant in the hole. She made sure the roots went down into the dirt. She patted the soil on top. Every day she gave it water. After some days, small green tomatoes grew. "A big number of tomatoes!" said Blake. Rocco laughed. "Can we taste one?" he asked. Dad smiled and picked one red tomato for them.

Nathan sat at the big table. His hat sat on his head, wide and blue. It was writing club time. Mr. Mansour gave him a pencil and paper. "Write your name, Nathan," he said.

Nathan held the pencil tight. He made the N. Then the A. But his lines were fat and fuzzy. "Why are my letters so big and soft?" he asked. Joelle looked over. "My pencil did that too," she said.

"Your pencil tip is dull," said Mr. Mansour. "A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull. Come, I can help." He turned the pencil in the sharpener. Bits of wood sank into the little tray.

Nathan tried again. The tip made a small, sharp line. He wrote N-A-T-H-A-N. The letters stood neat and small. Under his name, he drew Joelle wearing a wide hat too.

Gabriel was at Grandma's house. He wanted to draw a snowman. He got his red crayon, his yellow crayon and his green crayon. He also had white paper. He drew a big snowman with three balls. But the snowman did not show up. The white paper was white, and the snowman was white too. Gabriel frowned at the empty page.

Then he looked out the window. Fresh snow had fallen on the grass. It was white, just like his paper. "I know what to do," Gabriel said. He found a piece of blue paper. He drew the snowman again. Now the white snowman showed up on the blue sky.

He drew a red scarf and a green hat. Grandma made hot soup, and Gabriel chewed his bread while he drew. Grandma held up the picture. "Snow in a blue sky," she said. "Perfect."

Eliana went to the art gallery with her class. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya showed them a big table. On the table were three pots of paint. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. "These are the first colours," said Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya. "They are called primary colours."

Eliana picked up a brush. She painted a red circle. Then she wanted to touch it. The paint came off on her finger. Her fingerprint sat in the middle of the circle. The paint was still wet, and it smudged. "Oh," said Eliana. She looked at her red finger. On the wall hung a picture of a thirsty monkey holding a cup. The monkey looked like he wanted orange juice. "I will paint him some," said Eliana.

She put red paint on her brush. Then she put yellow paint on the same brush. She stirred them on her paper. The paint turned orange! She painted a big orange cup for the monkey. Elyas painted a blue cat. Huda painted a yellow sun. "Don't touch it yet," Eliana told them. "Wet paint can smudge."

They sat and waited. They watched the paint dry. Then Eliana touched her paper very gently. The orange cup stayed just the same. Later, Eliana went home. Her dad was going to cook dinner. She held up her painting. "Look," she said. "I made orange for the thirsty monkey."

Matteo sat in his warm bed. He had a big want. He wanted to go to the library.

"Is the library day tomorrow?" he asked.

Mom shook her head. "The library day is today," she said. "And today is the day that is happening right now."

Matteo looked out the window. Snow fell on the trees. The snow was falling now. It fell on his window now. Today was happening right now!

"So the library is now?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Get dressed now, and the library comes next."

Matteo jumped up. He washed his face. He put on his boots. Now he was ready.

Outside, snow landed on his hat. His mittens kept his hands warm. He and Mom walked and walked.

Soon they saw the big library door. Matteo ran to it. "We came now, and now we are here!" he said.

He picked three books about trucks. He hugged them tight.

At bedtime, Mom tucked him in again. "That was today," she said softly.

"Today we went to the library," said Matteo. "Right now I read."

He opened his truck book. Tomorrow he would read it again. But now, right now, he turned the first page.

Carter wanted to build a big tower at daycare. He found a heavy box under the shelf. He pulled it. He pulled again. The box did not move.

"Oof," said Carter. "So heavy."

Daphnee found a light feather pillow on the cot. She picked it up with one hand. "This one is light," she said. "Heavy and light are opposites."

Carter put the pillow on top of the box. He pushed the box again, slowly. Daphnee pushed too. It moved a little. They pushed and pushed, slow and steady.

Mr. Sutherland came to help. He slid the box to the rug. Carter wiped his dirty hands on his pants. Then he stacked the light pillows up, up, up.

"Fast pillows," said Carter. "Slow box."

Daphnee laughed and clapped her hands.

Hailey was playing on the rug. Her baby brother was asleep in his cot. Hailey jumped up and waved her arms. "Look at me!" she shouted.

The baby stirred. He made a little frown. He began to cry. Hailey felt sad. She wanted her brother to sleep.

Her dad came in. He put his finger to his lips. "Shh," he said softly. "Baby is sleeping. We use a quiet voice now."

Hailey took a big breath. Then she made her voice very small. "I can whisper," she whispered. Dad smiled. The baby stopped crying. He closed his eyes again. His tummy went up and down, slow and slow.

Hailey whispered to her teddy bear. She whispered to the window. Outside, a car rolled by on the street. It made no big sound inside.

Soon the baby woke up. He blinked and smiled at Hailey. Now she could be loud! She clapped and sang, "Good morning, baby!" Dad clapped too.

At nap time, the baby went back to sleep. Hailey looked at her dad. She put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she whispered. Dad picked her up for a soft, warm hug.

Madelyn woke up in her little bed. The sun was up too. It was morning now. She could smell toast.

She ran to the kitchen. Dad was at the table. Mom was pouring milk. There were eggs on plates.

"Good morning, Madelyn," said Dad.

"Good morning," said Madelyn. She climbed into her chair.

Morning was the part of the day when they woke up and ate breakfast. Yesterday it was morning too. Tomorrow it would be morning again.

Madelyn had a want. She wanted to paint. "Can we paint now?" she asked.

"After breakfast," said Mom. "First we eat. Later we paint."

Madelyn ate her eggs. She ate her toast. She was not fast, but she kept going. Then she went to get the paints.

But the paint box was stuck. The lid would not open. Madelyn pulled and pulled.

Dad came to help. He turned the box. The lid popped open. Something small fell out. It was a letter from Grandma, hidden under the box.

"Look," said Madelyn. "A letter!"

Mom read it out loud. Grandma was coming tomorrow.

"Tomorrow!" said Madelyn. "I will paint her a cat."

Dad got the water cups. Mom got the brushes. Madelyn made a big orange cat with green eyes.

"Tomorrow, Grandma will see it," said Madelyn. She set the painting by the door, right where Grandma would look first.

Hannah and her dad were going on a big trip. First they had a long drive in the car. Then they would ride a train! Hannah held her yellow bag on her lap.

The drive went on and on. Hannah watched the trees go by. Then her tummy felt funny. "I need the bathroom," she said. "Soon," said Dad. "We can stop at a rest stop. People use the bathroom there and stretch." Hannah wiggled her toes. She counted rain drops on the window. One, two, three.

At last the car turned in. There was the rest stop! Hannah ran with Dad to the bathroom. Then she stretched her arms way up high. "Look at me!" she said. "I am as tall as a giraffe." A lady next to them laughed.

Back in the car, Hannah felt much better. Soon they reached the train station. The train was big and silver. Hannah climbed the steps with Dad. They found their seats. The train made a happy sound. "Toot, toot!" said Hannah. Then the train said it too.

Harper went to the pharmacy with her dad. She saw a boy named Emrick there too. Ms. MacLeod, the neighbour, was at the counter. Harper had to use the toilet. "Dad, do I wash my hands after?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Wash with soap for twenty seconds."

Harper pumped the soap. She rubbed and rubbed. One, two, three. She counted to twenty. Then she looked at her hands. They were slippery. "Why are they still slippery?" she asked. "The soap is still on," said Dad. So Harper held her hands under the water. The water washed the soap off. Now her hands were not slippery at all.

Emrick pointed at the sink. "My hands were slippery too," he said. "I rinsed quick, quick, quick!" Harper laughed. She made a soap bubble on her finger. She rinsed it away. "Slippery, then gone," she said. "Slippery, then gone." Ms. MacLeod waved goodbye from the counter, and Harper waved her clean, dry hand back.

Ethan sat at the school table. Mr. Zhou put out two plates. One plate had apples. One plate had grapes. "Which plate has more?" asked Mr. Zhou. Ethan wanted to say the right word.

Ethan counted the apples. He touched one apple. "One, two, three, four, five." But then he touched the big apple again. "Six." He looked at the plate. "That is not six," he said slowly. Blake leaned in and watched. "Count again," said Blake. "Take your time."

Ethan put the apples in a line. He pointed at each apple once. "One, two, three, four, five." He did not touch the big apple two times. He counted the grapes too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Ethan smiled big. "The grapes have more!" he said. "The naughty big apple tried to trick me. Now I count each one just once."

Sophie dug a little hole at the community garden. Ms. Kim handed her pea seeds. "Drop them in," said Ms. Kim. Sophie dropped them and patted the dirt. Every day she came back with her watering can. Green shoots popped up. Then tall vines grew. Sophie watered and watered, but she saw no peas anywhere. "Where are my peas?" she asked. "I don't see them!"

Paris came over to look. He picked a long green pod. "Is this a bean?" he asked. Sophie was worried. Was it the wrong plant? Ms. Kim smiled. "Open it and see," she said. Sophie pressed the pod with her thumb. It popped open. Inside lay a neat row of little round peas, like green beads.

"Peas!" Sophie shouted. "They grow inside the pod!" She picked pod after pod and filled her basket. She gave one to Paris and one to Marion, who was watering the carrots. A pig puppet sat on the fence post, and Sophie made it sniff the pods. It was getting late, so Ms. Kim said, "Time to go home." Sophie held her basket tight. "We can eat these at dinner," she said.

Elias went to the big kitchen with his dad. Today they would make soup for the family. Elias wanted to help make the whole meal. His dad said, "You can be my helper."

Elias got the carrots from the bag. He put them in a big pot. His dad washed them first. Then the soup would be ready for dinner.

Next came the onion. Dad picked up the knife and cut the onion into small pieces. Then Dad rubbed his eyes. Water ran down his face. Elias whispered, "Dad, are you sad?" He felt worried, like a small mouse.

Dad shook his head. "The onion makes my eyes water," he said. "I am not sad at all." Dad cut some more. His eyes watered again. Elias watched. Every time Dad cut the onion, more water came. When Dad put the knife down, the water stopped.

"Aha," said Elias. "The onion did it." He brought Dad a soft cloth for his eyes. Then he stirred the pot with a big wooden spoon, standing far from the hot stove. Dad smiled at him. "Our soup smells good," said Dad. Elias sniffed the pot. "Dinner is ready," he said.

Ellie put on her red team shirt. She ran onto the grass at the park. Her friend Ada was on the team too. Mr. Chatterjee blew his whistle. "Time to play," he said.

Ellie kicked the ball. It went into the net. Everyone cheered. Then a boy on the other team grabbed the ball with his hands. Ellie stomped her foot. "No fair," she said. "You used your hands!"

A woman in a white shirt ran over. She wore a bright yellow card in her pocket. Mr. Chatterjee knelt down by Ellie. "She is the referee," he said. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules." The referee pointed at the boy. "Hands are not for the ball," she said. The other team had to give the ball back.

Ellie took the kick. The ball rolled to Ada. Ada kicked it in. "We can win," Ellie said. The referee gave a big thumbs up. Ellie waved back. At the end, Mr. Chatterjee handed out juice. Ada and Ellie sat on the bench by the park door and clinked their cups. "Good game," said Ada. "Good game," said Ellie.

Eleanor jumped up and down. It was Diwali night! Mama put small clay lamps on the table. "They are called diyas," said Mama. "Diyas," said Eleanor. "One, two, three, four, five!"

The diyas were cold. Eleanor could touch them. She set them in a row on the sill. "More! More!" she said. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven! "Are they messy?" Eleanor asked. "A little oil spilled," said Mama. "That is okay."

The diyas were dark. The night was dark too. Then Papa came with a long match. He was the one to light them. He touched the flame to each wick. Pop! One little light. Pop! Two little lights. Soon all seven diyas glowed! "The dark ran away!" said Eleanor. She clapped her hands. Papa laughed and gave her a warm hug.

Logan ran into the baby store. "The baby needs things!" he said. Mom said, "We need a cozy blanket." Logan followed her down the big aisle. He saw tiny shoes. He saw tiny socks. He saw a little bed with soft sides.

Then Logan saw something wonderful. His friend Sehaj was there too! Sehaj held a demo baby doll. "My mom has a real baby at home," Sehaj said. Logan patted the doll's head. Pat, pat, pat! He patted hard. Sehaj's eyes got big. "Too hard!" Sehaj said. "The baby is little. A new baby must be touched very gently."

Logan tried again. He stroked the doll's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The doll's hand wiggled, just a little. "It moved!" Logan said. Sehaj smiled. "Gentle hands make the baby happy," he said.

Mom held up two cozy blankets. "Pick one, Logan." Logan picked the blue one with stars. At home, the real baby lay in the crib. Logan reached out slowly. He stroked the baby's hand, soft, soft, soft. The baby's tiny fingers curled around Logan's finger and held on. Logan laughed. "She likes gentle hands!" he said. "Hello, baby. I am Logan."

Mila sat at the big table in the art classroom. She was drawing a yellow apple. Her friend Zaynab sat next to her. Zaynab was drawing a yellow apple too. Both apples had a green leaf and a happy little worm.

"Time to clean up," said Ms. Lawson. "Put your drawings on the shelf." The two papers went on the shelf, one on top of the other. Then Mila saw the papers side by side. She looked and looked. Both apples were the same. "Which one is mine?" she asked. Zaynab shook her head. "I don't know. They look the same."

Mila had an idea. "I will write my name on my apple," she said. She took her pencil. She wrote M-I-L-A. Zaynab wrote her own name too. Now everyone could see who made each drawing.

Ms. Lawson picked up the papers. "Look, this one says Mila," she said with a smile. "This one says Zaynab." She would send the drawings home with the right girls. Mila hugged her paper. "My apple found me," she said. Zaynab laughed and clapped her hands.

Brooks ran to the playground. He saw Bowen under the big tree. Bowen had a toy pot and a toy spoon. "We are playing house," said Bowen. "You can pick a role," said Ms. Leung, who sat near the sand. "Like the parent, or the baby."

"I want to be the parent," said Brooks. "I want to be the parent too," said Bowen. They both held the pot. The pot went clunk on the ground.

Brooks put his hand on his chin. He had to think. "We can both be it," he said. "First me, then you." "Okay," said Bowen. "Half and half."

Brooks was the parent first. He stirred the pot. He fed the baby doll. He patted the doll's bed with soft leaves. One pat, two pats, three pats. The doll went to sleep.

Then they switched. Bowen was the parent now. He stirred the pot. He rocked the doll. Brooks was the baby. He made a small baby voice. "Ba ba," said Brooks. Bowen laughed.

Leandro came to the tree. "Can I play too?" he asked. "Yes," said Brooks. "You can pick a role. There is a cat too." Leandro said, "Meow."

Lena sat in the big waiting room chair. She was wide awake, even though it was early. She held her little card with her name on it. "Lena," the nurse called. Lena pushed the door open with her hand.

The dentist smiled. "Let me brush your teeth," she said. Lena opened her mouth wide. The brush went round and round. It tickled. Soon Lena's mouth was full of minty foam. It felt bubbly and cool. Lena was about to swallow it. Then she saw the dentist hold up a little cup and point to the sink. Lena leaned over and spat the foam out. It went down into the sink. The foam was gone.

"Now your teeth are clean," the dentist said. Lena looked in the mirror. Her teeth were shiny and white. She smiled at herself. "Can I come back?" she asked.

Sara sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a bowl of soup in front of her. "Let's play the sense game," said Mom. "Five senses. Can you name them?"

Sara thought hard. "Eyes see," she said. "Ears hear." She touched the warm bowl. "Hands feel." She slurped her soup. "My tongue tastes it!"

"One more," said Mom. Sara tapped her chin. She waited. She thought some more.

Then Mom set down a plate of cookies. The sweet smell floated up. Sara sniffed with her nose. "The cookies smell good!" she said. "My nose smells them!"

Mom smiled and clapped. Sara counted on her fingers. "See, hear, feel, taste, smell. Five!"

Then Sara hugged her toy snake and held it up high. "My snake knows too," she said. "He smells cookies with his nose." She shook the snake at the plate. "But he can't have one yet. We wait for dinner first."

The lights went out. Matthew looked up. The TV was dark too. "Oh no," said Matthew. "No TV."

Dad lit a big flashlight. The whole room glowed. Matthew tried the TV button again. Still dark. "The power is off," said Dad. "It will come back later."

Matthew sat on the rug. What could he do now? He saw his new puzzle box. He opened it. The pieces did not need power at all! Dad put the flashlight on the floor so it shone on the pieces. Matthew clicked in piece after piece.

Then Mom brought a board game from the shelf. They played it right there on the rug. Matthew moved his little red bus piece around the board. He laughed when he won.

The lights blinked back on. Matthew kept playing the game by flashlight. "Let's stay here," he said. "This is fun." Dad smiled and turned the flashlight off.

"Your turn, Matthew," said Mom. "Roll the dice."

Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. Daddy made the toast, because the toaster is hot. Then he put the toast on her plate.

Aubrey took the butter from the fridge. She pressed it on her toast. The butter was hard. It made a big hole in the bread.

"Oh no," said Aubrey. "My toast has a hole."

Daddy put a new stick of butter on the table. "This one sat out all morning," he said. Aubrey touched it with one finger. It was soft. She spread it on her toast. It went on smooth and easy. No holes at all.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one hand. She poured slowly. The milk went into the cup, not onto the table. "I did it!" she said.

The dog barked at her feet. He smelled her toast. "Stinky dog," Aubrey said with a giggle. She tore a corner off her toast. She held it down low. "Here you go."

Isla ran to the playground. The sun was hot. Her towel sat in her bag, but the slide was too hot to touch. "Ow," she said, and pulled her hand back. She stood in the shade instead. The shade felt cold and nice.

Her friend Alek came up. "Let's play a word game," he said. "I say a word. You shout the word that means the opposite. Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be, like big and small."

Isla grinned. "Big!" Alek shouted. "Small!" she yelled back. They laughed. Then Isla said, "Big dog!" Alek said, "Small bug!" They tried more. Alek said, "Hot sun." Isla pointed at the shady spot and said, "Cold shade!"

A big kid zoomed by, fast on his bike. Isla walked behind him, slow, slow, slow, like a sleepy turtle. Alek laughed so hard he fell over on the grass.

Isla was wide awake now. She grabbed her towel and ran to the swings. "Opposite of slow?" Alek called. Isla pumped her legs. "Fast!" she shouted, and the swing flew high.

One morning at daycare, Zoey wanted the bunny book. She saw it on the shelf yesterday. But the shelf had so many books. Big books, red books, dinosaur books.

"Mr. Krause, I want the bunny one," said Zoey. "The one with the sweet little bunny."

Mr. Krause smiled. "Every book has a name," he said. "The name is right on the front. It is called the title."

Zoey picked up a book. She looked at the front. "Bear!" she read. That was not it. She patted the book and put it back. She picked up another one. "Trains," said Anika over her shoulder. Not it either.

Zoey counted the books as she looked. "One, two, three." On the fourth book she saw it. The front said Bunny. "Bunny! This one!" said Zoey.

She held it up high. "Your name is Bunny," she told the book. Then she sat down and turned the pages, one by one, front to back. "Read it to me, Anika!"

Edouard sat on his bed in his bedroom. His mom had a surprise for him. It was his very first library card. It was blue and had his name on it. "Now you can borrow a book," Mom said.

At the library, Edouard saw a big book about dinosaurs. He loved dinosaurs. He shouted, "A dinosaur book!" Then he looked around. People were sitting and reading. Mr. Dlamini from next door was reading too. He put a finger to his lips. Mom whispered, "We use quiet voices here so others can read." Edouard whispered too. "Sorry, Mr. Dlamini." Mr. Dlamini smiled and gave him a thumbs up.

Edouard borrowed the dinosaur book with his new card. At home, he lay on his bed and drew a picture of a dinosaur in a garden. "Best card ever," he whispered, just like at the library.

Eliana sat in the family car. Her tummy felt hungry. "Are we going to the park?" she asked. "No," said Mom. "We are going to the dentist. He will look at your teeth." Eliana wondered, how can anyone see inside a mouth? A mouth is so small.

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and down. Eliana climbed in all by herself. The dentist said, "Hello, Eliana! Let's take a look." He pointed up. A bright light hung over the chair. He clicked it on, and the light shone right at her face. Eliana squinched her eyes. So bright!

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Put these on," he said. Eliana put them on. Now the light did not hurt her eyes. She opened her mouth wide. The bright light above the chair helped the dentist see inside. "I can see all your teeth," he said. "Nice and clean!" Eliana tasted something bubbly on her teeth, like bubbles from the sink.

Then it was done. The dentist gave her a sticker. It had a shiny star on it. Back in the car, Eliana held up her sticker. She looked at her teeth in the little mirror. "I see my teeth too!" she said. Mom laughed and drove home.

Eliana stood at the gate. It was her first day of school. She looked for a friend, but everyone was running fast.

Then Nathanael ran by with a toy dog on a string. "Come play!" he said. Eliana ran after him. She wanted to race to the big slide. She started to climb the fence, just a little, to get there first.

A boy stopped her. "No climbing the fence," he said. "Ms. Rosen says so. It is one of our class rules." Eliana stepped down. "Class rules?" she asked. "Yes," said Abygael, joining them. "The whole class follows them. Everyone. Even Nathanael." Nathanael made a silly face. "Even me!"

So Eliana used the gate instead. It opened with a squeak. She raced to the slide and got there second. "Next time I will win," she said. The wind blew the clouds into a stormy grey pile. "Rain soon," said Nathanael. "Let's slide fast before it comes!" Down they went, one, two, three, wheee.

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. His dad was driving to the dentist. It was Brooks's first time going. A big plane flew over the car. Brooks watched it zoom away. He felt a little worried.

"I will sit still," said Brooks. "But what do I do with my mouth?"

His dad smiled. "You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth," he said.

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a big chair. The dentist said, "Say hello, Brooks." Brooks closed his mouth to talk. The dentist could not see any teeth then. Brooks tried again. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion's roar. Now the dentist could see every tooth.

"Very nice teeth!" said the dentist. Brooks got a sticker of a plane. He jumped down from the chair. "I want to come back!" he said.

Lillian wanted to make a happy picture for her mom. She got her crayons first. She drew a big face on the paper. Then she ran to the mirror in the hall. "Look at me," she said. She smiled a big smile. The mirror girl smiled too. Her happy feeling showed right on her face!

Lillian made a sad face next. Her mouth went down. The mirror girl looked sad too. Then she made a mad face, and a scared face, and a giggly face. Each one showed up in the glass.

Lillian had an idea. She drew a big smile on her picture. She turned on the light so her mom could see it best. When Mom came in from the shop, Lillian held it up high. "I am happy!" she said. Mom smiled a big smile back.

Ms. Sultani gave out paper shapes. "Find a rectangle," she said. Samuel held up a circle. "That is a pancake," said Winston, and he laughed. Samuel laughed too.

Samuel looked around the room. He saw a square block. Four sides, but not long enough. He saw a triangle flag. Too pointy. Then he heard the door creak. The door! Samuel ran to it and put his finger on a corner. He counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." He counted the sides. "One, two, three, four."

"A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door," said Ms. Sultani. Samuel held his paper up to the door. It matched! Josiah clapped his hands. "Samuel found the biggest rectangle in school," he said. Samuel smiled a big, quiet smile and hung his coat on the door hook, right on corner number four.

Parker sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint green grass. But the green pot was empty. "Oh no," said Parker.

Miraya sat next to him. She had a pot of blue paint. Parker had a pot of yellow paint. "Watch this," said Miraya. She put blue paint in her cup. Then she put yellow paint in too. She stirred with her brush. The paint turned green!

Parker looked with big eyes. He put yellow paint in his cup. Then he added blue paint. He stirred and stirred. His paint turned green too. "I did it!" said Parker.

He painted tall grass all over his paper. Ms. Tan came to look. "What nice green grass," she said. Parker painted a yellow sun in the blue sky. Then he hung his old painting on the wall to dry. "Blue and yellow make green," he told Oceane at the slide. "Come and see!"

Parker had a big red dragon. It was pretend, but it felt very real. He wanted to tell Ms. Hamdan all about it.

Nayla was talking. "My bear can fly to the park," she said. Parker jumped in. "My dragon is big!" Nayla stopped talking. Her face went sad. Ms. Hamdan held up her hand like a stop sign. "Wait, Parker. When someone is talking, we listen until they finish."

Parker closed his mouth. He watched Nayla. She talked about her bear and the tall trees and the dark cave where the bear slept. Then she said, "All done." Parker waited for his turn. "Now you, Parker," said Ms. Hamdan.

Parker told about his dragon. It had wings like a red cape. Nayla listened with her ears and her eyes. She did not jump in. When Parker finished, she clapped. Then Jonathan got a turn too.

"Next we all watch the dragon fly," said Parker. He zoomed the dragon over the blocks. "Roar!" said Jonathan. The dragon flew and flew, and everyone waited for the very last roar.

text:
Mila wanted to play in the playroom. She looked for her toy boat. She found it under the chair. Then she saw a puddle on the floor.

"Is the puddle big or small?" asked her friend Mckinley.

"It is small," said Mila. She pushed her boat fast. Then she pushed it slow. The boat went through the puddle. Splash! The water jumped up. It landed on Mila's socks. Her socks were wet now.

Mckinley brought a towel. "Wet and dry are opposites," he said. Mila touched her wet socks. They were not dry like before. She sat down and pulled them off. Ms. Cheung gave her warm, dry socks from the basket. Mila put them on.

"Dry socks feel nice," said Mila. She patted the towel on the floor. The puddle got smaller and smaller. Then the floor was dry too. Mila put her boat back on the shelf. Her new socks were warm and dry, and she smiled at her tail-wagging toy dog. "Let's sail again early tomorrow," she said.

Isla wanted to blast off in a rocket. At school, she found a big cardboard box. She climbed inside. Pearl climbed in too.

"We need numbers," said Pearl. Mr. Romano smiled. "Start with ten," he said. "Then go down."

Isla tried. "Ten, nine, eight." Pearl helped. "Seven, six, five!" Isla got mixed up. She said six two times. "That's okay," said Pearl. "Try again."

So Isla took a big breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" She and Pearl jumped up, way out of the box. "That was far," said Isla.

Mr. Romano clapped. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown," he said. "You did a countdown!"

Shay ran over. "Can I blast off too?" Isla grinned. She pretended to press a big red button. Then she began. "Ten, nine, eight..."

Then a loud moo came from behind the box. It was only Shay, holding a toy cow. "The cow rides in the rocket too," he said.

"Seven, six, five, four, three, two, one," they all shouted. "Blast off!"

Levi's class had a big basket. It sat by the cubbies at school. Levi put his muddy socks on the floor. He wanted to play, not clean.

His friend Ahaan picked up a sock. "Watch this," Ahaan said. He tossed the sock. It went into the basket. Swish! Levi laughed loud. "My turn!" said Levi.

Levi lifted his other sock. He threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. Sasha giggled. "Try again," she said. Levi tried again. This time it went in. Swish! "Basket!" he shouted.

Ms. Wijaya clapped her hands. "Good work," she said. "Now those dirty socks can get washed." Levi felt proud. He gave the basket a gentle pat, like a hug.

The next day, Levi wore his clean socks. They smelled like flowers. He wiggled his toes inside his shoes. "My socks got washed!" he told Sasha. She wiggled her toes too. At play time, Levi aimed one more sock. Swish! Right into the basket.

Beau sat on the little stage. Ms. Papadopoulos put a drum in front of him. "Tap it," she said. Beau tapped it. The drum made a small sound. Harrison sat next to him with a drum too.

Harrison hit his drum very hard. It made a big, loud sound. It was so loud that the babies in the back woke up. One baby began to cry. The teacher held the baby and rocked her. "Softly now," said Ms. Papadopoulos.

Beau thought about the drum. He hit his drum hard. It was loud. He tapped it soft. It was quiet. It was like a puzzle, and now he knew the answer. He tapped soft, and the baby closed her eyes.

"Your drum is quiet," said Harrison. "That is true," said Beau. He tapped again, soft as a whisper, and the baby slept on.

Jack went to the park with his bucket of blocks. His friend Frederic was there. His friend Akram was there too. Jack tipped out all the blocks. He made a big round tower all by himself.

Frederic had no blocks. Akram had no blocks. They stood and watched. Frederic's mouth turned down at the corners. Akram sat on the sand. Jack looked at his tall tower. Then he looked at his friends.

Jack chose some red blocks. He gave them to Frederic. He chose some blue blocks. He gave them to Akram. Then everyone had blocks. Frederic smiled. Akram jumped up. Now there were three towers in the sand.

Frederic wanted the tall ladder too. Jack let him go first. Then Akram had a turn. Then Jack had a turn. Mr. Nkosi, the park helper, walked by. "That looks fair," he said. Jack grinned and pushed his truck down the slide.

Declan sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "We will ride bikes at the park," said Dad. Declan looked out the window. A man was washing a car with hot water. Steam went up, up, up. "That water is hot," said Dad. "We stay back from hot things." Declan nodded and stayed in his seat.

At the park, Joel was on his bike. Joel wore a helmet on his head. Declan ran to his little bike. He put his foot on the pedal. Then he stopped. He looked at Joel again. Joel had a helmet. Declan did not. "Wait for me!" he said. He ran back to Dad. Dad helped him buckle his helmet. It sat snug on his head.

Declan pedaled his bike. He went fast on the fresh green grass. Then his wheel hit a stick. His bike began to slip. He fell down on his knee. But the helmet kept his head safe. Joel rode over. "You okay?" he asked. Declan stood up. He rubbed his knee. Then he got back on his bike. "Watch me go!" he said, and off he pedaled.

Raphael stood by the little pool next to the lake. The water looked cool and shiny. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But he did not want to put his face in the water.

The teacher smiled. "Watch me," she said. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out. Bubbles popped up. "Bubbles!" said Raphael.

Felicia ran over. "Your turn," she said. Raphael bent down. He blew out through his mouth. Big bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! He laughed. "Did you see my bubbles?" he asked. "I did!" said Felicia. "They were so big!"

He tried again. He blew harder. More bubbles came. Then he put his lips in the water and blew. The bubbles tickled his chin. "It feels funny!" he said.

"Now try a little kick," said the teacher. Raphael held her hand. He kicked his legs. He blew more bubbles. He moved through the cool water. "I am swimming!" he shouted. Felicia clapped. Raphael blew one more big bubble and giggled.

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The bell on the door went ring. Inside, Ms. Wanjiru had a big table. On it sat two baskets of apples. Clara wanted to pick the basket with more.

Ms. Wanjiru said, "Count them, Clara." Clara pointed at each apple in the red basket. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the green basket. "One, two, three, four." Carmen and Sybil watched.

"The red basket has more," said Clara. She smiled. Then Carmen said, "Can I have an apple, please?" Ms. Wanjiru said yes. Carmen took one apple from the red basket.

Clara counted the red basket again. "One, two, three, four." She looked and looked. Clara said, "The baskets are the same now."

Sybil clapped her hands. "Clara, you did it," she said. Clara held up four fingers on one hand, then four on the other. After snack, they all went out to the car. Clara saw a tall sun by the window. She said, "Dad, my basket had one less when Carmen took one."

Arlo ran into the backyard. Ms. Almeida had a bag of balls. "Time for practice," she said. Arlo made a face. He wanted to play the game now. Not practice.

A ball rolled to his feet. He tried to stop it. It bounced right past him. "Oops," said Arlo.

Charleigh ran up. "Watch me," she said. She had come to practice all week. She put her foot out. The ball stopped. Just like that!

How did she do that? Arlo wondered. He put his foot out too. The ball rolled by again. He tried again. And again. Then, thump! The ball stopped at his foot. "I did it!" said Arlo.

On Saturday, Arlo played the big game. A ball flew at him. He put his foot out. Thump! It stopped. Leonidas clapped. "Nice stop!"

After the game, Arlo ate a juicy orange. "More practice next week?" he asked Ms. Almeida. "Yes! More practice," she said. Arlo smiled big.

Levi found a big cardboard box. He sat inside it. "Beep beep!" he said. "This box is my car."

His friend Elio came over. Elio looked in the box. "No, it is a boat," said Elio. "Row, row!"

"It is a car," said Levi.

"It is a boat," said Elio.

They both frowned. Levi wanted the box to be a car. Elio wanted it to be a boat. Then Levi had an idea. "You go first," he said. "Then me."

Elio sat in the box. He rowed his arms. "Boat, boat!" he said. Levi put a block on the floor. "Here is your dock," he said.

Then it was Levi's turn. He held an imaginary wheel. "Beep beep! My car!" Elio clapped.

After that, Levi turned the box upside down. "Now it is a house," he said. "Knock knock!" Elio knocked. Levi opened the door.

They ate pretend crunchy crackers in the box house. "I remember this was a car," said Levi. "And a boat," said Elio.

"Now it is a house," said Levi. Elio smiled. "Knock knock!"

Isaac sat at the dinner table. He wore one red sock. His other foot was bare. Dad put the soup on the table. "One spoon, two spoons," said Dad. Isaac wiggled his bare toes. He wanted his other sock.

"I only have one sock," said Isaac. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks," said Dad. "We need to find the other one." Isaac slid down from his chair. He looked under the table. He heard a little noise. It was his own sock, stuck on his chair leg!

"One sock," said Isaac. He put it on his foot. "Two socks." Now he had a pair. Dad laughed and clapped. "You did it," said Dad.

They washed their hands. It was still early, so Dad said, "Want to count after dinner? One, two, three." "Four, five, six," said Isaac. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" they said together. Isaac ate his warm soup. His two socks were cozy under the table. "Ten toes in there," said Dad. Isaac laughed and wiggled them all.

Noah ran in the backyard. The grass was soft and green. Today his team came to play.

All the kids wore yellow shirts. Noah wore yellow too. Shea wore yellow. Bridget wore yellow. Even Mr. Ramos wore a yellow hat.

Mr. Ramos rolled the ball to Noah. Noah looked up fast. He saw a yellow shirt near the fence. He kicked the ball to it.

But it was not Shea. It was a boy from the other team! The other team wore blue shirts. The boy ran away with the ball.

Noah stopped and looked around. He saw lots of blue shirts. Then he saw yellow. Shea was waving by the big tree. Bridget stood beside the little horse toy in the corner.

"Here, Noah!" Shea called.

Mr. Ramos rolled the ball again. This time Noah looked for yellow. He kicked it right to Shea. Shea kicked it to Bridget. Bridget kicked it into the net between the hats.

"Goal!" everyone shouted.

The sun began to set. It was getting late. "Good game," said Mr. Ramos. "You guessed right that time, Noah."

Noah looked down at his yellow shirt. He smiled and patted it. "Yellow," he said.

Margot sat on her bed. She held her red crayon. She wanted to write a note to Mama. The note would say, "I love you, Mama." Margot knew some letters. She wrote them all together. ILoveYouMama. One big string of letters. It looked like noodle soup.

She ran to find Mama in the kitchen. "Read my note!" said Margot. Mama looked and looked. Her eyes went squinty. "Hmm," said Mama. "It says... Ilubba?" Margot sank down onto her socks. "No! It says I love you, Mama!" Her note was all squished. Squished letters were stinky.

Then Mama had an idea. She tapped the paper. "Look here," she said. "In English, there is a space between one word and the next." Margot looked. Mama pointed. "Like this. Space, space, space." Margot ran back to her bedroom. She counted her words. One, love. Two, you. Three, Mama. She wrote them again. She left a little gap after each word. I love you Mama.

"Read it now!" said Margot. Mama read it out loud. "I. Love. You. Mama." Margot jumped up and down. "Spaces! One, two, three spaces!" She gave Mama a big hug and a big kiss on the cheek. "Next I will write to Yanis," said Margot. "With lots and lots of spaces."

Leon sat on the big red couch. It was Mr. Siddiqui's house, and the game was on TV. Everyone was shouting and clapping. Prisha and Viraaj sat on the floor with popcorn. Leon took a bite of his popcorn.

"Who is winning?" Leon asked.

"The blue team," said Prisha.

"No, the red team," said Viraaj.

They both laughed. Leon could not remember the score at all. He looked and looked at the TV. Then he saw it, up high. Big shiny numbers, one set for each team.

"Look!" said Leon. "The blue team has more!"

"That is the scoreboard," said Mr. Siddiqui. "It shows how many points each team has."

Leon clapped. Now he could see who was winning all by himself. The red team got a basket. The numbers jumped. Now they were even!

"Tied!" shouted Leon.

Viraaj gave Leon a high five. Outside, a frozen puddle sat in the shade. Leon pointed at it through the window. "When the game is done, can we look?"

"After the game," said Mr. Siddiqui.

Leon watched the numbers. The blue team went up by one. Leon jumped up and cheered. The popcorn bowl tipped over. Prisha giggled.

"Look at the scoreboard, everyone!" Leon said. "Blue wins!"

Today was Sophia's birthday party at the bowling alley! The shoes were shiny and red. The balls rolled down the long floor. Boom, boom, boom went the pins. Her friends Alita and Kyro waved. "Happy birthday!" they shouted.

Sophia picked a small blue ball. She pushed it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. All the pins fell down! Everyone clapped. "Strike!" said Kyro. Sophia jumped up and down. Then Alita said, "I am four. How old are you?" Sophia said, "I am three!"

Alita shook her head. "But it is your birthday today," she said. "On your birthday, you turn one year older." Sophia thought and thought. Then she smiled a big, real smile. "I am four now!" she said. "I was three yesterday, but not today!"

They ate cake with a spoon. It was sweet and soft. The candles glowed. A grown-up blew them out. "Do not forget the wish," said Sophia. "I wish to bowl again!" She rolled the ball one more time. Boom went the pins.

Daniel was in the school cooking classroom. He was making bread for his family. Mr. Bekele gave him a big bowl. Daniel mixed flour and water. The dough got very sticky. It stuck to his fingers like glue.

"Oh no," said Daniel. "My dough is ruined!" Ahmad laughed next to him. "Mine is sticky too," said Ahmad. Daniel held up his hands. The dough hung from his fingers in long strings.

Mr. Bekele came over. "Watch this," he said. He pushed the dough with his hands. Then he folded it over. He pushed and folded again. Daniel tried it. He pushed and folded too. The dough felt less sticky. "Knead it like this," said Mr. Bekele. Daniel pushed and folded some more. Soon the dough was soft and smooth. "It's a nice round ball," said Daniel. Ahmad patted his own dough. "Mine is a turtle," he said. Daniel giggled. He put his dough in a safe spot to rest. "My family will eat this," he said. Then he went to clean his sticky hands.

Luca ran to the backyard. He had a big plan. He wanted a dark tent! Dad helped him hang blankets over the chairs. Soon the tent was dark, very dark, inside. Luca grabbed his two toy cars. He wanted the red one. He looked and looked. He could not tell which car was which. One car felt fast in his hand. But was it red or blue? He could not see. "Hmm," said Luca. He crawled out into the sun. He held up his hand. "Blue!" he shouted. The other car was red. His friend Rishi came over. "Look, Rishi!" said Luca. "In the dark tent, I could not tell!" Rishi crawled in with a green ball and a yellow ball. He came out laughing. "I picked the wrong one!" In the bright sun, the yellow ball shone like a little sun. They took turns hiding toys and guessing. Then Mom called, "Time to clean up!" Luca put the blankets away and shook them out. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "And tonight you can pick your own socks before bed." Luca picked red socks while the light was still on. He put them by his bed, both the same, both red. "Perfect," he said, and jumped up high.

text:
Wesley stood in the band room. He had a violin in his hands. He turned it upside down. He strummed the strings. The sound went boing, boing.

"That sounds funny," said Brooklynn. She held her drum. Rafaelle laughed and hit his triangle. Ding!

Ms. Holloway came over. "A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument," she said. She turned the violin right side up. She put it under Wesley's chin. She placed the bow in his hand.

Wesley pulled the bow. Now the sound went ooo, ooo, soft and sweet. Brooklynn stopped drumming. Rafaelle's mouth fell open.

"Again," said Wesley. He pulled the bow again. Ooo, ooo.

"My mom will like this," he said. He did a little swing of his hips. Then he played one more note, slow and smooth.

John sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. The sun needed a big round circle. John drew one circle. It came out wobbly. He drew another one. Wobbly again. He hid his paper under his arm.

Kasen sat next to John. Kasen was drawing a sun too. Kasen's circle was big and round. John leaned close. Kasen was tracing around the bottom of a cup. She lifted the cup off the paper. There it was, a perfect circle. "Can I try?" John asked. Kasen smiled and pushed the cup to him.

John traced around the bottom of the cup. He lifted it up. A perfect circle sat on his paper. He added curly yellow rays with his finger on the crayon. Then he drew a square house and a triangle roof. "My sun is round and fine," John said. Kasen giggled and drew one more circle too.

Camille wanted to see the bubbles. Mom put a pot on the stove. Camille took one step, then two steps, then three steps close.

"Stay back, sweet pea," said Mom. "The steam is hot. It can burn you."

Camille stopped. She saw white steam float up from the pot. It went up and up, like a little cloud. Camille took one step back, then two steps back, then three steps back. From there she could still see the pot.

"I can see the bubbles!" said Camille.

"One bubble, two bubbles, three bubbles," said Mom. They counted together. The water jumped and popped.

"You are my brave helper," said Mom. "Can you fill my cup at the sink? The sink water is cold."

Camille filled the cup. She held it with both hands. She felt the cool side of the cup.

Later, Camille sat at the table. She drew a picture of the pot. She drew the steam going up and up. Mom hung it on the fridge.

"That is my favorite picture," Mom said.

Camille smiled. "Bubbles tomorrow too?"

Madison was playing in the backyard. Her toy snake had escaped again! It was green, like the grass. It was hiding.

"Let's make snake houses," said Khadijah.

They gathered baskets. Madison put all the red toys in one basket. Khadijah put all the blue toys in another basket. Abbas put all the yellow toys in a third basket.

"We are sorting by color," said Khadijah. "All the same colors go together."

Then Abbas shut the gate tight. The snake house was safe!

But wait. Something blue was in the yellow basket. It was the green snake! No, it was a blue sock. Abbas laughed and moved it to the blue basket.

The green snake slithered into the green grass. Madison gasped. Then she saw its tail wiggle.

"I see you, snake!" she said.

Jack had big news. He had a new puppy! The puppy was small and white. Jack named him Snowy.

At home, Snowy sniffed every corner. He begged for Jack's shoe. Jack laughed and gave him a ball instead.

But then Snowy went quiet. He did not eat. He did not play. "Is Snowy sick?" Jack asked. "I think so," said Dad. "We will take him to the doctor."

Jack felt worried. Would Snowy sit in a big chair? Would he get a sticker? "Do dogs go to my doctor?" Jack asked. "No," said Dad. "Snowy goes to a vet."

"A vet?" said Jack. "What is that?"

"A vet is a doctor for animals," said Dad.

The vet's room was full of pets! A cat sat in a box. A white bird dropped one feather on the floor. Snowy barked hello.

The vet looked at Snowy. She gave him some medicine. Soon Snowy wagged his tail. At home he gobbled his food. Jack clapped. "Good boy, Snowy!"

Benjamin was at daycare. He dropped his teddy bear on the floor. The bear went bump on the tiles.

Benjamin felt scared. "Is my bear hurt?" he asked.

Ms. Baptiste picked up the bear. She gave it a big hug. "The bear cannot really feel," she said. "But you can pretend it does."

Benjamin hugged the bear too. He patted its head. He made a little bed from a scarf.

Jasmine came over with her doll. "My doll is hungry," she said.

"Pretend it can eat," said Benjamin. He held a toy cup to the doll's mouth. Jasmine made slurp sounds. Then they built a pretend mountain of soft blocks. The doll climbed to the top.

"More soup, please," Jasmine said in a tiny doll voice. Benjamin laughed and poured again.

Elijah sat on the cold bench. He held his dad's hand. The ice rink had a big screen above the skate counter. On the screen, a big soccer game was on. Iyla sat next to him. Armin sat on the other side. Mr. Ndlovu gave them each a cup of fresh, cold juice.

The players ran and ran. They kicked the ball fast. Then a man in a striped shirt blew a whistle. Toot! All the players stopped running. They stood still on the green grass. Elijah blinked his eyes. He looked at Iyla. "Why did they stop?" he asked.

Mr. Ndlovu pointed at the screen. "The referee blew the whistle," he said. Elijah watched and waited. The whistle blew again. Toot! The players ran again. Elijah leaned forward. The whistle blew once more, and the players stopped again. "The whistle makes them stop," Elijah said. Iyla clapped her hands.

Later, Elijah's mom came over. She gave him a kiss on his cheek. "Did you like the game?" she asked. Elijah pointed at the referee. "He blows the whistle," Elijah said. "Then everybody stops."

Violet went with her mom to a big house of prayer. It was a special night. Little lamps sat in rows on the floor. They looked like tiny stars.

Violet saw Mr. Ahmadi hold a long match. He touched it to a wick. The wick made a small flame. Then the flame made light all around. Violet wanted to make a flame too.

"Can I light one?" she asked.

Mr. Ahmadi knelt down. "Grown-ups light the flames," he said. "They are not safe for little hands. But you can pick the lamp you like best. Then I will light it for you."

Violet walked along the row. She saw a red lamp and a gold lamp. She pointed to the gold one. Mr. Ahmadi lit it. The flame stood up tall.

"It's not scary," Violet said. "It's small and warm."

She planted her gold lamp right at the end of the row. Then she waved to her friend Maira. "Come see my lamp," she said. "It shines!"

Violet ran to school after breakfast. She was not late today. Outside, her friend Raphaelle waved. "Let's play hide-and-seek," Raphaelle said. Leane jumped up and down. "Yes, let's play!"

"I will count," said Violet. "You go hide." Raphaelle and Leane ran to hide. Violet covered her eyes. She counted very fast. "One two three four five six seven eight nine ten!" she shouted.

Raphaelle stood by the wall. She was not hiding at all. "Violet, that was too fast," she said. "We need time to hide." Leane nodded. "Please count slowly," she said. Violet felt her cheeks get warm. "Okay," she said. "I will count slowly this time."

They played again. Violet covered her eyes. This time she counted slowly. "One... two... three..." Raphaelle ran behind the big tree. "Four... five... six..." Leane ducked under the slide. "Seven... eight... nine... ten!" Violet turned around. Now the yard was quiet. She looked by the tree. She looked under the slide. "Found you!" Violet called. "Found you both!" Raphaelle and Leane laughed and laughed. "Slow counting is the best," said Leane. "Let's play again after snack."

Clara lay on her little mat at school. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes for rest time. The room went very quiet. Then it went very dark.

Clara woke up and opened her eyes. She could not see the sun. She could not see the blocks or the easel. She saw only black. "It is morning," she said. "Time to play!" She stood up fast and bumped her toe. "Ow," she said, and sat down slow.

Mr. Moretti came over with a small lamp. He helped her look out the big window. "The sky is dark," he said. "It is night, not day." Paige was awake too, holding her bird with one paper wing. "Night and day are opposites," said Paige. "Night is dark. Day is bright." Clara held her bear and watched the wild wind move the tree.

Mr. Moretti brought warm milk. First it was too hot, so Clara waited. Then it was just right, not hot, not cold. She took small sips. One sip, two sips, three. Outside, a car went by fast. Then all was slow and still again. The lamp made a little circle of light on the floor.

Clara looked out at the dark sky one more time. "Night," she whispered to her bear. Then she lay back down. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes and waited for day.

text:
The sun was warm at summer camp. William had a red truck. It was his very special toy. He loved its bumpy wheels and its shiny paint.

Julian and Melina came to the sandbox. Julian grabbed for the truck. William held it tight. His tummy felt tight too. Then he had an idea. He ran to the shelf. He put the red truck up high, on the top. Now it was put away before his friends played. He did not have to share it at all.

William came back with a big yellow bowl. "Let's make a sand cake," he said. Melina patted the sand. Julian poured it in. The bowl made a round, soft cake. It smelled like warm sand.

"Your turn, William," said Julian. William took the bowl. He filled it up and patted it down. The cake came out perfect. Melina clapped her hands.

After camp, William got his truck back from the high shelf. He hugged the bumpy wheels. His red truck waited for him all day. "Tomorrow you can hide again," William whispered. He smiled all the way to the car.

Rehmat went to the bank with her dad. She wore her red coat. The wind blew at the big doors. Her coat flapped open like a bird.

"My apple will get cold!" said Rehmat. She had an apple in her pocket. The wind puffed her coat open again. She held it shut with both hands. But the wind was faster than her hands.

Then Rehmat looked down. She saw the zipper. It had two sides. The two sides were apart. A little tab hung at the bottom. She pulled the tab up, up, up. The two sides joined together. The coat closed all by itself. The wind could not get in anymore.

A kind cashier smiled at her. "Nice zip!" she said. Rehmat beamed. The wind tried again at the doors. It puffed and puffed. But the coat stayed shut.

"Sorry, wind," said Rehmat. "No apples for you." She patted her warm pocket. The apple was safe and snug. Rehmat marched into the bank, zipping her tab up one more time, just for fun.

text:
Miles sat in the family car. His hair was wet from a quick bath. Today he would get his first haircut at a salon. "I want to look like Dad," he said.

At the salon, the hairdresser put a blanket around Miles. Snip, snip went the scissors. A little curl fell down. The hairdresser was careful, and Miles sat very still.

Then Dad picked up the little curl. He put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Miles. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut," said Dad. "We keep it to remember this day."

Back in the car, Miles held the envelope. He saw one small curl. Now it sat in paper, saved. "I want to see it at home," said Miles. Dad smiled and buckled him in.

Joshua was in the school cooking room. Today he would bake bread for his family. Ms. Ong put the bowl on the table. Joshua got to stir! One, two, three, he stirred the dough. It looked like soft brown mud. "Not muddy mud," said Joshua. "Just pretend mud!" Luis laughed. Lilly laughed too.

Next they needed butter on the bread. Joshua took butter from the little fridge. He pushed it with his knife-safe spoon. It was hard. Too hard! The butter would not spread at all. "Rip it, naughty butter!" said Joshua.

Ms. Ong set the butter on the counter. "We will let it sit," she said. The class washed the bowls. One bowl, two bowls, three bowls.

Then Joshua touched the butter. It was soft now! He spread it round and round. One slice for Mom, one for Dad, one for baby sister. Lilly clapped her hands. "Soft butter wins!" she said. Joshua held up the warm, buttery bread. "Taste it, everyone!"

Charlie was at Milena's birthday party. There was a big bumpy ball with yellow spots. Charlie wanted to play with it right away.

Milena had the ball first. Mr. Li set a timer. "When the timer beeps, your turn is over," he said. Charlie waited and waited. Her leg bounced up and down. Then the timer beeped!

Charlie ran to the ball fast. She almost grabbed it from Milena's hands. But Mr. Li held up his hand gently. Charlie stopped. Milena smiled and held out the ball. "Your turn," she said. Charlie took it with two soft hands. She did not scratch the ball with her nails. She held it like a baby kitten.

Then Charlie rolled the ball on the grass. It went bumpy, bumpy, bumpy. The timer beeped again. Charlie ran to Thea, who was next. She handed the ball gently to Thea. Thea hugged it and laughed.

Then Thea did something funny. She rolled the ball right back to Charlie. "One more turn for you!" she said. Mr. Li laughed too. Charlie held the bumpy ball and grinned at Milena. "Best party ever," said Charlie.

Parker made a painting at school. It was a gift for his dad. The paint was wet. It had to dry.

"When can I take it home?" Parker asked.

"Not now. Later," said Mr. Joseph. "Look up there. That is a clock. A clock shows what time it is."

The little hand pointed to the ten. Parker waited. He played blocks with Blake. He looked up again. Now the little hand pointed past the ten.

"Is it later now?" Parker asked.

"Yes. Touch your painting," said Mr. Joseph.

Parker touched it. The paint was dry. It was not wet at all. The clock had moved, and the paint had dried.

"My gift is ready," said Parker. He held it up high.

"Take it home today," said Mr. Joseph. "Yesterday it was just paper. Tomorrow it will be on a wall."

Milo went to the park with Maxim. Ms. Lawson put a big hoop on the grass. She gave Milo a beanbag. "Throw it in," she said.

Milo threw the beanbag. It hit the rim. Then it went flop. It just lay there on the grass. Maxim threw his ball. The ball bounced high. It bounced again and again.

Milo picked up the beanbag. It went flop. It did not bounce at all. The ball bounced. The beanbag flopped. That was the different part!

Milo tried again. He held the beanbag up high. He let it drop onto his shoe. Flop. It sat on his toe like a sleepy cat. Maxim laughed, and Milo laughed too.

Then Maxim rolled a big ball to Milo. Milo held out both hands. The ball came fast. He squeezed it with both arms. He got it!

"Nice catch," said Maxim.

Milo stood the hoop up tall. He threw the beanbag up and up. Flop. It went right in. He jumped around in a circle until he felt dizzy.

"My turn," said Maxim, holding out both hands.

Anna was at the school playground. She had her little red bunny with her. Now bunny was gone.

"Where is bunny?" said Anna. She looked by the slide. No bunny. She looked by the park bench. No bunny. Her search was short. Anna sat down. She wanted to cry.

Then Anna saw her big sister at the gate. Dad was there too. Anna ran to them. "Bunny is lost," she said. "Will you help me look?"

"Yes," said Dad. "Now more people are searching."

Anna looked by the swings. Her sister looked by the sand. Dad looked by the fence. Anna peeked under the little bridge. She saw something soft.

"Bunny!" said Anna. She gave bunny a big hug.

Elisha and Ayzal clapped from the sandbox. "Yay, Anna!" they said.

Anna held bunny close. "Found you," she whispered.

Eli ran to the book corner at daycare. He wanted a story about a big red truck. He found a truck book on the shelf. "Ms. Costa, read this one," he said.

Ms. Costa sat down on the little chair. Eli sat next to Liam and Aminata. She opened the book from the front. "This is the top of the page," she said. She pointed at the little marks under the picture. Then she read them out loud. The words told about the truck going up a hill.

Eeli turned a page. There was a picture with no marks under it. Only a big blue sky. "Read the sky," said Eli. Ms. Costa smiled. "There are no words here," she said. "There is nothing written there to read." She turned to the next page. "Here are more words." She read them, and the truck went fast down the hill.

"Now me," said Eli. He took the book. He opened it from the front. He found a page with words and pointed. "Read it fast, Ms. Costa!" She read it, and everyone laughed. Then Eli pointed at a picture page. He looked at it all by himself. "This one I just look," he said.

Lillian went to the cultural center with her dad. There were red lanterns on the wall. Edmund and Asees were there too. "Come look!" said Edmund.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were very noisy. Lillian put her hands on her ears. "Too loud," she said. A big lion came out. It was gold and red. The lion jumped and shook its head.

Asees clapped her hands. "Watch the lion," she said. Lillian looked. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion jumped again. The lion moved to the beat of the loud drums! Lillian let go of her ears. She clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. The lion danced faster, and Lillian clapped faster. "The lion hears the drums!" she said. Mr. Russo smiled and gave her a little red paper lantern. Lillian held it up high and clapped one more time.

Henry jumped into the family car. "Are we going on a big trip?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We are going to see Grandma!"

The sky looked stormy and gray. Henry held his shoe up so it would not get wet. "Big trip means big planes!" he said. The car drove and drove.

At the airport, Henry saw the planes. They were huge! He wanted to run to them. But the place was full of people. So many legs, so many bags!

Dad held out his hand. "Stay close to me," he said. "In busy places, children hold hands."

Henry took Dad's big hand. From up close, he could still see the planes. He pointed at a red one. "I can see it from here!" he said.

Henry squeezed Dad's hand tight. Then they walked to the plane together, ready for Grandma.

Ibrahim looked out the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling on the grass. "Snowy day!" said Ibrahim.

He put on his boots. He put on his big red coat. He ran outside to play. His dad sat on the step and watched. Ibrahim made a snowball. It was cold in his hands. His hands hurt. "Ow," said Ibrahim. "My hands are cold."

His dad held up red mittens. "Look what I found." Ibrahim remembered his mittens were on the table. His dad had brought them out. Ibrahim put the mittens on. He made a new snowball. His hands felt warm now. "Good mittens," said Ibrahim. Then something moved in the snow. It was his toy robot, lost last week. "Robot!" said Ibrahim. He held it in his mittens and smiled.

Myles stood by the back door in his rain boots. He wanted to play in the backyard sandbox. "Look," he said. "The sky is all gray." Big clouds were up there. The clouds hid the sun. His friend Jeremy came over. Jeremy wore a sunny-day hat with a big brim. "My hat is for the sun," Jeremy said. "Where did the sun go?" Myles watched the sky. Would the clouds move? A wind came. The wind blew hard. The wind pushed the clouds away. Then the sun popped out! "Sun!" Myles shouted. The warm sun shone on the sandbox. The boys ran out. They found a turtle sitting by the fence. "Hello, little turtle," said Myles. The turtle walked slow, slow, slow. Jeremy laughed. "You naughty turtle, you took my spot in the sand." The sun stayed out. The boys made a big sand hill. Myles patted it flat. Then he looked up again. More clouds were coming. "Hurry," he said. "Let's finish before the clouds hide the sun again."

Kinsley ran to the park with her red ball. The grass was slippery from the rain. She wobbled, then sat down with a plop.

Her friend Phoebe came over. Kinsley rolled the ball to her. Phoebe caught it and ran away with it. Then Phoebe stopped. She turned around and said, "Thank you!"

Kinsley blinked. So that is what you say. Someone gives you a thing, and you say thank you.

Then Austin came by. He had a square cookie his dad had helped him cook that morning. He broke it and gave half to Kinsley.

Kinsley held the cookie. She remembered. She smiled big and said, "Thank you, Austin."

Austin grinned. Phoebe rolled the ball back. They all sat on the warm bench and ate the cookie together.

Evelyn sat on the red rug in her living room. Her mama played a song on the phone. Evelyn patted her knees. The song had a steady beat. She tried to clap along. Her claps went too fast. Then they went too slow.

"Try again," said her mama. She clapped one, two, one, two. Evelyn watched her mama's hands. Evelyn clapped one, two, one, two. Now her claps fit the song! Evelyn smiled big.

"Now let's sing our cat song," said mama. Evelyn sang, "The cat sat on his..." She stopped. She forgot the last word. She looked at her block tower. Hmm. What rhymes with cat? Cat... hat! "The cat sat on his hat!" she sang. Mama laughed and clapped. "Yes! Cat and hat end the same."

Evelyn stood up. She clapped and sang the whole song. One, two, one, two. "Cat and hat, cat and hat!" Her mama clapped with her. Evelyn took a bow.

Paisley got in the car with her dad. "Today we get a pet," Dad said. They drove to a place with lots of barking.

Inside, cats sat in little rooms. Dogs sat in bigger rooms. They all looked at Paisley. "Why are they here?" she asked. A kind lady said, "They wait here for a family to adopt them and take them home." Paisley walked past a big dog. Then a small one. Then a fluffy cat.

The cat put her paw out. She touched Paisley's hand. "This one!" said Paisley. Dad filled out a paper. The cat could go home with them.

At home, Paisley put a soft blanket in a basket. She put water in a bowl. She gave the cat some food. The cat ate it all up. "Yummy, right?" said Paisley. The cat licked her paw, then curled up. Paisley could see the moon in the window. The cat saw it too. She purred and purred. "Good night, Coco," Paisley whispered.

Olivia was at school. It was cold outside. Ms. Asante held up a small coat. "Time to learn zippers," she said.

Olivia pushed her arms in. The coat felt different from her sweater. The zipper tab hung down low. Olivia pulled the tab up. The zipper stuck halfway. She tried again. It stuck again. Olivia waited. She took a breath. Then she pulled the tab down, down to the bottom. The coat opened wide, all by itself!
