"Look!" said Olivia. "The tab goes down and the coat opens." Blake came over to watch. Olivia zipped it up slowly. Then she pulled the tab down again. The coat opened again. The clock on the wall ticked while she tried.

At last Olivia zipped her coat all the way up. "Ready for outside!" she said. Elsa clapped, and they ran to the door.

Aurora put on her lucky red dress. Grandma's house was full of cousins today.

"Time to eat!" called Aunt May. Everyone sat down at the big table.

Aurora saw Grandpa stand up. Then everyone held hands. Grandpa did not say the blessing. He sang it! Aurora's eyes went wide. "Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it," her cousin whispered. "Our family sings it too."

"I want to sing it," said Aurora. "Can I try?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. You can lead it next."

Aurora stood up tall. She took a big breath. But her tummy felt jumpy. She opened her mouth and sang the wrong tune. It came out like a wobbly bird. Some cousins giggled. Aurora sat right down.

"You can try again," said Grandpa. "Take your time. No hurry."

Aurora stood up again. She thought of the tune in her head. Then she sang it, slow and clear. Her voice rang out over the table. Everyone joined in with her. Grandma squeezed her hand. When the song ended, Aunt May brought out the warm bread.

"That was beautiful," said Aunt May. "Now we eat!"

Aurora grinned and reached for her plate.

Sophie sat in the family car. Her new baby brother sat in his little seat. He was very small. He slept and slept.

Mom sat in the front. Sophie looked at Mom. Then she looked at the baby. Then she looked at Mom again.

"Mom," said Sophie, "the baby sleeps a lot. He drinks a lot. He gets held a lot."

"Yes," said Mom.

Sophie took a deep breath. "I miss you, Mom. I miss having you all to myself."

Mom turned around. "It is okay to feel left out," said Mom. "Big sisters can feel that way."

Sophie nodded. Her tummy felt a little better.

Mom said, "Count with me. One hug now. Two hugs at home. Three after your cookie."

Sophie counted. "One, two, three."

Mom smiled. "And the baby can have zero cookies. He is too little."

Sophie laughed. The baby opened one eye. Then he went back to sleep.

"Home now," said Mom.

Sophie waved out the window. "One, two, three hugs," she said.

Georgia put on her big sun hat. It was a little loose, so she tugged it down. Today Ms. Chaudhry was taking the class to the farm.

"Close your eyes," said Ms. Chaudhry. "Use your hands."

Georgia held a feather in her fingers. It felt soft. Then she held a pinecone. It felt rough. She put the feather in the soft basket. She put the pinecone in the rough basket.

"My skin tells me!" said Georgia.

"Yes," said Kacey. "Skin can feel soft or rough."

Georgia found a blanket next. She touched it with her hand. "Soft," she said, and put it in the soft basket. Alexy clapped.

Then the class walked to see the sheep. Georgia listened to the baa with her ears. She smelled the hay with her nose. She saw the big red barn with her eyes. "Ears, nose, eyes, hands," said Georgia.

Ms. Chaudhry smiled. "And your mouth?"

Georgia tasted her apple snack at the picnic table. "Sweet!" she said. She patted the sheep through the fence. The wool felt soft, like her blanket.

"My skin knows," said Georgia. "It says soft!"

Jaxson was playing in the yard. He dug in the dirt with his spoon. One scoop, two scoops, three scoops. His hands turned brown and dirty.

Then he smelled soup. It was warm lunch inside the house. Jaxson ran to the table. He held out his dirty hands.

"Wash first," his mom said. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Jaxson went to the sink. His mom turned on the water. It was not too hot. The water ran over his hands. Bubbles grew, one bubble, two bubbles, lots of bubbles. The dirt went down, down, down the drain.

His hands were clean now. He climbed onto his chair. The soup was warm in his bowl. He took a bite. Then another bite.

Something was under his bowl. It was a small drawing. It showed a girl at a sink, washing two hands. "For you," said his big sister. She smiled.

Jaxson laughed and clapped his clean hands. "More soup, please," he said.

Milan ran into his classroom. The sun was bright in the window. "Story now, Mr. Mwangi?" he asked.

Mr. Mwangi smiled. "Not now, Milan. First we have snack. The story comes later."

Milan sat down at the little table. Ellis gave him a cracker. Emmeline gave him a slice of banana. Milan looked at the book on the shelf. He wanted it now. But it was not story time yet.

"Is the story now?" Milan asked.

"Not now," said Ellis. "Now we eat."

Milan ate his cracker. He drank his milk. He waited and waited.

Then Mr. Mwangi clapped his hands. "Snack is done. The story is now."

"Now means at this very moment," said Emmeline.

Milan ran to the rug. He sat down fast. "Now I am ready!" he said.

Mr. Mwangi opened the book. It was about a big pot. A dad helped cook soup in the pot. He stirred it with a long spoon.

Milan loved the soup story. He asked for it again.

"Not now," said Mr. Mwangi with a smile. "Now we go outside. The soup story can come tomorrow."

"Tomorrow," said Milan. He said the word slowly. "Tomorrow the soup story comes again."

"Tomorrow," said Ellis. He said it slowly too.

The children lined up at the door. Milan held Emmeline's hand. He looked back at the book on the shelf.

"See you tomorrow," Milan whispered to the book.

Then he walked outside with his friends.

Billie stood in the bakery kitchen with her mom. The oven door was open. It was hot inside. "Can I touch it?" Billie asked. "No, it needs a grown-up," her mom said. "You stay back here."

The kitchen lights were bright. A big door swung open and shut. Billie peeked through it. There were shelves and shelves of bread. She walked a little way. Then a little more. She turned around. She could not see her mom.

Billie looked and looked. Her tummy felt small. Then she saw the checkout counter. A worker stood there with a red apron. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. "Can you help me?" "Yes, I can," the worker said. She held Billie's hand and called out. Mom came running from the kitchen door. She hugged Billie tight. "You told the store worker," Mom said. "That was just right." Billie smiled and held on all the way to the car.

Natalie stood in her backyard with her basketball. Her team had a game on Saturday. At her last game, she kept missing the hoop. The ball would not go through. She felt worried.

"Will I ever get the ball in?" Natalie asked.

"Try again," said Mr. Diallo, her neighbor. He stood by the fence and watched.

Natalie threw the ball. It hit the rim and bounced off. She threw it again. It went under the hoop. She threw it once more. Up it went, then down, then right through the hoop! The ball dropped to the grass.

Natalie jumped up and down. A soft feather drifted past her in the air. She picked up the ball, took a bite of her crunchy apple snack, and threw the ball again.

It went through the hoop again!

"I can do it," said Natalie. Mr. Diallo clapped his hands.

Madison stood at the big running track. Ms. Munro put a hoop on the ground. "Throw the beanbag in," she said. Madison looked at her friend Jay. She threw the beanbag. It landed in the grass. Not in the hoop.

"Why did it miss?" Madison asked. "Try looking at the hoop," said Jay. Madison looked at the hoop. She kept her eyes on it. She threw the beanbag. It went in! "Yes!" said Jay. Lili clapped.

Next Lili rolled a big ball. Madison held out both hands. She looked straight at the ball. The ball came right to her. She caught it with both hands. "Again!" said Madison. Lili rolled it again. Madison caught it again. "You did it," said Ms. Munro. Madison jumped up and down. "I did it!"

Asher was at summer camp. It was time for lunch. Mr. Sow said, "Time to wash hands, team." Asher ran to the little sink. He turned on the water. He got his hands wet. Then he turned off the water. He looked at his hands. There were no bubbles at all. Hezekiah was beside him. "Look," said Hezekiah. He rubbed the soap in his wet hands. White bubbles grew and grew. They covered his fingers like cozy mittens.

Asher picked up the soap. He rubbed it on his wet hands. Bubbles! Big bubbles, small bubbles. "Bubbles!" said Asher. He sang the hand song with the class while he rubbed. "Wash, wash, wash," they sang. He rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean and shiny.

At lunch, Asher looked at his plate. His hands were clean. After the toilet, he skipped right back to the sink. Water, soap, rub. "Bubbles again!" said Asher. Maggie peeked over. "You did it," she said. Asher held up his bubbly hands. "Soap and water, that's all," he said.

Hailey was hungry. She wanted a sandwich. Mom said, "I can make one." Hailey watched Mom cut the bread. Mom made two triangles.

"Can I count the corners?" Hailey asked. "Yes," said Mom. Hailey touched each point. "One, two, three. Three corners!" She counted the sides too. "One, two, three. Three sides!"

Hailey pulled her chair to the table. She took a big bite. "Still three corners," she said. Mom laughed.

After lunch, Hailey found shapes all over the house. The clock was a circle. The window was a big square. Her pet cat slept on a rectangle rug.

Hailey drew a picture. She made a red triangle, just like her sandwich. She counted the corners again. "One, two, three," she said. "I did it!" Mom gave her a big hug.

Sofia was at the beach with her dad. Right by the sand was a big pool. "Can I swim there?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Today we start swim class!"

Sofia carried her little blue bag. Her friend Benedict was there too. A boy from her class waved from the water. Sofia ran straight to the pool steps. She wanted to jump in fast!

A coach stood by the door. She held up her hand. "Stop, Sofia. First we take a shower. Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." Sofia looked at the little shower. Water sprayed down, tick, tick, tick. "Can I go in now?" she asked. "After your shower, yes," said the coach.

Sofia stood under the warm spray. Then she got in the pool! The water went splash. Benedict splashed too. A furry dog barked on the beach. Sofia kicked her legs and giggled. "Look, Dad, I'm swimming!" she called.

Alexander stood at the bus stop with his mom. He had his blue coat in his hands. "Can I put it on all by myself?" he asked. His mom smiled and said, "Try it, Alexander."

He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat was on! Now the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He tugged again. Click, it closed. "I did it!" he said.

Little drops began to fall. Drizzle on his nose. Drizzle on his hands. Where could he hide? Then he felt the soft part on the back of his coat. He pulled it up over his head. "That's the hood," said a girl next to him. The rain stayed off his hair. The drops went tap, tap on the hood instead. Alexander looked at a turtle crossing the wet sidewalk. The turtle had a shell over its back too. "So a hood is like my shell?" he asked. "Yes," his mom laughed. The bus came, and Alexander climbed the steps, warm and dry.

Aaron brought his red car to school. He loved that little car. At play time, the sky was cloudy. Aaron ran all around the playground. Then he looked in his pocket. His car was gone!

"Help me look," Aaron said to Esmae. "Where did you go first?" she asked. "First I went down the slide. Then I rode the swing. Then I played by the fence." Mr. Perera smiled. "Go back to each place you went, in order. That is called retracing your steps." Aaron ran to the slide. He looked all around. No car. He rode the swing again. He looked under the seat. No car. He walked to the fence, near the little forest of trees. There, in the grass, sat his red car!

"Found it!" Aaron shouted. Esmae clapped. "You went back to every place," she said. Aaron held his car up high. "My car wants one more ride," he said. He zoomed it down the slide.

Leon went to the hair salon with his dad. It was his very first haircut. Leon sat in the big chair, on a booster seat. The hairdresser picked up her scissors.

There was a fish tank on the wall. It had bright fish, orange and blue. Leon liked the fish. He turned his head to look. Snip! A piece of hair went crooked. He turned again. Snip! Another crooked piece. His hair looked messy and funny, like a small rainbow that had slipped sideways.

"Sit very still," said the hairdresser. "Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly. Like a statue." Leon puffed up his cheeks. He made statue arms. He did not turn. One fish, two fish, three fish swam by, and Leon did not look. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little snowflakes.

The hairdresser held up a mirror. "Look at your neat hair," she said. Leon saw a boy with tidy hair smiling back. "Fish are nice," said Leon, "but I am a statue." Dad gave him a big hug, and Leon felt happy, not tired at all.

Bennett stood in the pool changing room. He pulled his swim bag open. Out came his little blue goggles. "Swim day!" he said.

Water was all over the floor. Bennett saw his shoes go drip, drip. Then Lydia ran past him to the door. Her feet went slip, slide. Ms. Bear caught her arm. "The floor is wet, so we walk," said Ms. Bear. Lydia slowed down. No more sliding.

Bennett looked down at the shiny floor. Would his feet slide too? He tried one fast step. His foot slipped a tiny bit. So he took small steps, one at a time. His feet stayed under him. "Walking works," he said to Lydia. She nodded and walked too.

They walked all the way to the pool. Bennett felt a splash on his toes. The water was warm. "I kept my feet dry until now," he said, not sad at all. Ms. Bear smiled. "Ready, Bennett?" He held his bag tight and said, "Ready!" Then he stepped down to the water.

Edouard wanted to find the dog page in the book corner. The book was big and red. He sat on the soft rug and opened the cover. The pages felt smooth and cool. "Where is the dog?" he asked. "I will look and look," he said.

He put his finger at the right side of the page. He slid it left to left, back to the front of the line. His friend Amiyah came to sit with him. "One page, two pages, three pages," they counted together. But no dog.

Ms. Liu knelt down beside them. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side of the page. Edouard put his finger there. He slid it from left to right, word by word. "One word, two words, three words," he said. Then he turned to the next page. Then the next.

There it was. A big brown dog with a tight red collar. "A pet dog!" said Edouard. He patted the picture with his hand. The dog looked soft. Amiyah laughed and clapped. Edouard turned one more page, from the front of the book to the back. "Good dog," he said. "Good book."

Eleanor ran to the park with her curly hair bouncing. Her tummy made a little rumble. She was hungry. Emelia and Londyn were there by the swings. Eleanor wanted a snack soon.

She sniffed with her nose. Something smelled warm and good. "I smell toast," she said. "Or maybe pancakes!" Londny listened with her ears. She heard a sizzle sound. Emelia looked with her eyes. She did not see any food yet. "The smell came first," said Emelia. They followed their noses down the path.

Near the big tree, a grown-up was cooking at a safe little grill. Mr. Bélanger stood beside it and watched the food. "You smelled it before you saw it," he said with a smile. He gave each child one warm pancake. Eleanor touched it. It was warm. She took a bite and tasted the sweet syrup. "My nose knew first!" she said, and she held Emelia's hand.

Hayden wanted to wash his hands. He stood on his step stool by the sink. His toy lion sat on the edge, watching him. "You wait there," Hayden told the lion.

Dad turned the tap. "Hot water is for me," said Dad. "Cold water is for you." The cold water ran over Hayden's hands. It felt cool and nice.

Then Hayden saw something small and red by the soap. It looked like a little candy. He wanted to pick it up. But he stopped. He kept his hands in the water. "Dad, there is a candy," he said.

Dad looked. "That is not candy. That is medicine. Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Dad picked it up and put it away high in the cabinet. Hayden washed and washed, slow and careful. He dried his hands all by himself.

Dad clapped. Hayden hugged his lion. "You are special," he whispered.

Mya stood in the storytime room. She held her very first library card. It had red stripes on it. Mya counted the stripes. "One, two, three, four," she said.

"I want a book about paint," said Mya. "I want to see all the colors." She looked on a small shelf. No paint books there. She looked on a big shelf. Still no paint books. She looked under the rug. No paint books there, either.

Then Mya saw Ms. Farah. Ms. Farah worked at the library. "Ms. Farah helps people find books," said Mya's mom. So Mya walked over, slowly and carefully.

"Can you help me find a paint book?" asked Mya.

"I can," said Ms. Farah. "I am the librarian. That is my job." She took Mya's hand. They walked past one shelf. They walked past two shelves. They stopped at a shelf with a green sign.

"Here are the art books," said Ms. Farah. Mya looked and looked. Then she found it. A paint book with a striped cat on the cover!

But there was a surprise inside. The book had a hole in the page. Through the hole, Mya could peek at the next page. "Red paint," she said. She turned the page. "Blue paint!"

The children in storytime clapped for Mya's new card. Mya held her book tight. "See you soon," she said to Ms. Farah.

Axel sat down at the dinner table. He saw his plate and clapped. "Five carrots!" he shouted. He pointed at each one. "One, two, three, four, five."

Dad put a card by his cup. It was the card from school. It had a big 5 on it. Axel tapped the card. "What is this?" he asked.

"That means five too," said Dad. "The number 5 and the word five are the same number."

Axel gasped. He held up his hand. He counted his fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." He wiggled them fast. "Five fingers! Five carrots! Five on the card!" He laughed so hard his tooth felt funny. One tooth was missing on the bottom, and the air whistled when he laughed.

"I want ten carrots!" said Axel. Dad gave him one more. Axel counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." He looked at the card. "I need a six card now!"

Dad said, "Don't forget your chicken, Axel."

Axel ate a big bite. Then he counted his peas. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" He spread his arms wide. "My plate is a counting song!"

At the end, one carrot was left. Axel held it up like a rocket. "One carrot for me!" He crunched it loud.

"Tomorrow can we count to ten?" he asked.

"Tomorrow," said Dad, and he held up a big 10 card.

Arlo woke up and put on his blue socks. "Time for school," he said. He looked out the window. The backyard was all white. Snow sat on the grass. Snow sat on the swing.

Dad came in. "No school today," said Dad. "It is a snow day." Arlo tilted his head. "What is a snow day?" he asked. "A snow day is a day when school is closed because of snow," said Dad. Arlo laughed. Snow had closed his school!

Arlo put on his boots. He pulled the laces tight. Dad helped him tie them in a bow. Then Arlo ran outside. The snow went crunch, crunch under his feet. He patted a big ball of snow with his mittens. He patted and patted. The ball got big and round. Then he rolled it across the yard. Where the snow had been, Arlo could see green grass. The ball had picked up the snow! The snow made the ball grow.

Arlo made two more balls, one big and one small. He stacked them up. Then he found two sticks and a carrot. He pushed them in. "It's a snow man!" Arlo shouted. The neighbor's pet dog barked at the fence. Arlo waved. "Hello! Want to see my snow man?" he called. The dog wagged its tail, and Arlo patted one more handful of snow right on top.

Olivia was at home. Tatum came to play. They both saw the red scooter. They both ran to it.

"Who goes first?" asked Olivia. "Can we both go?" asked Tatum.

Her dad looked at the cloudy sky. "You could take turns," he said. Olivia asked, "What is taking turns?" Her dad said, "One person goes, then the next person goes." So Olivia went first. She rode past the wall. One, two, three, four, five pedals. Then she stopped. "Your turn, Tatum!"

Tatum rode past the wall too. One, two, three, four, five pedals. Then he stopped. "Your turn, Olivia!"

They took turns and took turns. The bell on the scooter fell off. Dad helped them fix it. He held the little screw. Olivia gave him the bell. Tatum waited for his turn to ring it.

Ding! Ding! Each of them got a go, one after another. Then Dad called, "Snack time!" Olivia looked at Tatum. "You can have the first cookie," she said. Tatum smiled. Ding, ding, ding went the bell.

The car pulled up to the house. Grandma was here for a whole week! Anna hid behind Dad's legs. Grandma held out her arms. "Do you want a hug?" she asked. Anna was not ready for a hug yet. She felt shy.

Then Anna had an idea. She lifted her hand and waved. "Hello, Grandma!" she said. Grandma waved back. "Hello, Anna!" she said. Grandma did not look sad at all. A wave was a hello too! Anna counted the ways. "One, a hug. Two, a wave. Three, a hello."

In the kitchen, Grandma poured milk into a cup. Anna helped set out spoons. Anna rip, rip, ripped a paper napkin for each place. One, two, three, four. It was a little messy, but Grandma laughed. Then Anna ran to Grandma and gave her a big, big hug. "A hug!" said Grandma. "Yes!" said Anna.

Today was a big day at Luke's house. Grandma was cooking a special meal. "This food is just for today," Grandma said. It was for the holiday.

Luke wanted to help. Grandma gave him dough. He patted it flat. Then he learned to fold it over. Fold, pat, fold. The dough looked like a little nest.

"Can I taste one now?" Luke asked. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we wait for everyone." Luke's tummy grumbled. He watched the empty plate on the table.

Dad put the pan in the oven. Luke watched from his chair. The kitchen began to smell warm and sweet.

Then the door opened. Auntie and Uncle came in. Everyone sat down. The plate was full now. Luke took a big bite. It was warm and good.

Luke clapped his hands. "We made this just for today!" he said. Grandma smiled and gave him one more.

Grayson and his family were going camping. The car was full of bags. Grayson held his teddy bear tight. "We will see trees and a lake!" he yelled.

Dad drove and drove. Then the car stopped. "This is not our road," Dad said. Mom opened a big paper map. Grayson looked too. The map had little roads and little lakes on it.

Grayson put his finger on the map. He found the lake. "The lake is here!" he said. Mom smiled. "Can you find the road to the lake?" Grayson looked and looked. His finger went up one road. It went down another road. Then his spotted finger found the right one. "This way!" he said.

Dad drove that way. Soon the trees got tall. The lake got big and blue. The tent went up. Grayson jumped. "We found it! One lake, one tent, one happy bear!" he said. He waved the map in the air.

The community hall was big and warm. Snow fell past the windows. Eliana wore her thick red coat. She took it off and ran to the slide. Macey and Mya were already there.

Balloons sat on every table. A big cake sat in the middle. Three candles stood on top. "Why is everyone making a fuss today?" Eliana asked.

Grandma took a small photo from her bag. "Look," she said. "This is you on the day you were born." Eliana looked at the tiny baby. "That is me?" she asked. "A birthday celebrates the day a person was born," said Grandma. "So my birthday is my born day," said Eliana. Grandma smiled and nodded.

Dad lit the candles with a match. Eliana watched from her chair. Everyone sang. Eliana blew out the candles in one big breath. The room went dark, then bright again. Macey clapped. Mya clapped. Eliana clapped too. Then she ran back to the slide, singing happy birthday to herself.

Hailey was at the grocery store with her dad. It was cold outside. Hailey wanted to wear her red coat. "Can I put it on all by myself?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said her dad.

Hailey sat down on the bench. She pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then she pushed her other arm in too. But it went into the same sleeve! Both arms were stuck in one sleeve. "Look, I am a one-arm snake!" she said. Her dad laughed. A lady with carrots laughed too.

"Where does my other arm go?" Hailey asked. She wiggled her arm and looked. The other sleeve was empty. So she pulled her arm out. She put one arm in this sleeve. She put her other arm in that sleeve. One arm in each sleeve. The coat sat just right on her!

Now the zipper. Hailey pulled it up, up, up. Click, it closed at the top. "I did it!" she said. Her dad gave her a big smile. Outside, snow was starting to fall. Hailey stuck out her tongue to drink a snowflake. It was cold and tiny. "Snow is true," she said, and they walked to the car.

Brielle woke up early. She wanted to wear her red hat today. It was her favorite hat. She put it on her head. She looked in the mirror and smiled.

The sky outside was sunny. "Sunny day!" said Brielle. But the trees were moving. The leaves went swish, swish, swish. "It is windy too," said her dad.

Brielle went outside to play. The wind blew her hair. The wind blew the leaves. Then the wind blew very hard. Her red hat flew right off her head! "Oh no!" said Brielle. "Come back, hat!"

The hat went over the grass. It went fast. Brielle ran after it. She ran and ran. The hat stopped by a big bush. Brielle bent down and picked it up. Her nose was cold, but the hat was warm and soft in her hands.

Brielle held the hat on her head with both hands. "The wind took it," she said. "I will hold it tight." Her dad came out with a warm coat. He zipped it up for her. "Good holding," he said. "Now let's meet the wind together." Brielle laughed and held her hat all the way to the door.

Isaiah went to the store with his dad. The store was full of apples. Isaiah wanted a red apple very much.

He saw the basket. He grabbed for an apple with both hands. A lady was already reaching there. She pulled her hand back. Isaiah's dad knelt down beside him. "Try again," Dad said softly.

Isaiah looked at the lady. "Can I have an apple, please?" he asked. The lady smiled a big smile. "Yes! You waited your turn too," she said. She picked three apples and put them in her bag. Then she moved aside so Isaiah could reach.

Isaiah took one apple. He held it with both hands. "Thank you," he said. At the checkout line, a girl named Aida stood ahead of him. She was holding a banana. Isaiah waited behind her. He did not push. He kept his apple safe against his chest.

Aida turned around. "Do you want to see something?" she asked. She showed him a tiny apple sticker on her hand. Isaiah laughed. "I want one too," he said. Then he remembered. "May I have one, please?" Aida gave him a sticker from her pocket.

They walked out to the street together. Isaiah put the sticker on his shirt. He bit his apple and smiled. "Please," he said to himself, and Dad laughed all the way home.

Henri sat on the train with his dad. The train went clickety-clack. Henri looked out the window. "Are we going to the beach soon?" he asked. "Yes, very soon," said Dad. Dad gave Henri a carton of milk. It was cold and sweet.

The train stopped. Henri and Dad got off. They walked to the beach. Henri could hear the big water. He could smell the salty air. He ran ahead on the warm sand.

The water came up and made a wave. Henri wanted to splash in it. He ran to the edge. Dad called out, "Wait for me! At the beach, a child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching." Henri stopped. His legs felt a bit weak from running. He waited.

Dad came and held his hand. "Now can we splash?" asked Henri. "Now we can splash," said Dad. The wave came in. Splash! The water tickled Henri's toes. He laughed and laughed. The sun was warm on his back. Dad held his hand the whole time.

Elliot wanted to have a tea party. He wanted it very much. He got out his little cups. He got out his teddy bear and his duck. His dad had washed all the cups. The cups were clean and dry.

But there was a problem. Elliot had no tea. He looked in the cups. Empty. He looked in the teapot. Empty, too. No tea anywhere. Elliot made a sad face.

Then his mom came in. "Would you like some pretend tea?" she asked. "Pretend tea can go in empty cups," she said. Elliot tipped the empty teapot over a cup. Tilt, tilt, tilt. Nothing came out. But he pretended it did!

"One cup for teddy," said Elliot. "One cup for duck." He handed them out. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" he said. He blew on the empty cup. He blew for teddy, too. Then he pretended to sip. He smacked his lips. "Mmm, so juicy!"

Just then Marvin knocked on the door. "Come in!" said Elliot. "We are having tea!" Marvin sat down fast. Elliot poured him a pretend cup. Marvin pretended to drink it all up.

"More tea?" asked Elliot. He tipped the teapot again. "Yes, please!" said Marvin. Elliot filled every empty cup. The tea party went on and on. "Best tea ever," said the duck's voice, and Elliot laughed and laughed.

Charlotte held her mama's hand. They walked into the barbershop. Charlotte saw big chairs and little mirrors. A man with scissors sat in one chair.

"Time for your first haircut," said Mama. Charlotte did not move. "Will the scissors hurt?" she asked. "Scissors are sharp and fast."

The barber smiled. He picked up a long piece of hair. It had fallen on the floor. He snipped it with the scissors. Snip! The hair fell into two bits. "See?" he said. "Hair does not feel it."

Charlotte looked at the little bits of hair. Then she looked at her own arm. The scissors did not cut arms, only hair. And hair does not feel it. "So cutting hair does not hurt?" she asked. Mama nodded. "That is right."

Charlotte climbed up into the big chair. It rolled back a little. She held on tight. Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Charlotte waited for an ow. No ow came. She felt nothing at all.

"Look at me!" said Charlotte. Ms. Nair from next door waved from her chair. Mina and Kayce rolled in on Mina's bike. They stopped by the window. "Your hair looks short," said Kayce. "It does not hurt even one bit," said Charlotte. "Not one bit at all."

The barber held up the mirror. Charlotte saw her new short hair. She jumped down and spun around. "Snip snip," she said, and everyone laughed.

The wind blew hard at the park. Riley held her hair with both hands. Sand flew up from the sandbox. "Ow," said her friend Salem. "Something went in my eye!" He blinked and blinked. A bit of dirt fell out on his cheek.

Riley blinked too. She blinked fast, like a butterfly. Nothing went into her eyes. "How come?" she wondered. She looked at Salem's face. He had little hairs above his eyes. She had them too. She could feel them when she touched her eyelids, soft as a feather.

Riley sniffed the air with her nose. She smelled popcorn. She heard the popcorn cart, boom, boom, going over the bumps. "I hear it with my ears!" she said. Ms. Reddy, her neighbour, was buying a bag. She gave Riley one warm piece. Riley tasted the salt on her tongue. Yum.

Then a big gust of wind came. Sand flew everywhere. Riley shut her eyes tight. She felt her little hairs stand out like a fence. When she opened her eyes, they felt fine. No dirt inside. "The sand stopped at my lashes," she said. Salem leaned close and looked. "My hairs stopped it too," he said. "Our eyes stayed clean!" Ms. Reddy smiled and held out the popcorn bag for one more piece.

Alice sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Are we going to Ryland's house now?" she asked. Her dad shook his head. "Not today," he said. "We went to Ryland's house yesterday. Today we are going to the store."

Alice looked out the window. A red truck went by. A dog sat by a tree. "I want to play with Ryland now," Alice said. Her mouth turned down, just a little. Her dad said, "You will sleep tonight. Then it will be tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today. Tomorrow you can play with Ryland."

Alice held her heavy water cup. She took a slow sip. The store came into view. "First the store now," she said. "Then sleep. Then Ryland." Her dad smiled at her in the mirror.

At the store, Alice helped put apples in the bag. Later, in the car again, the sky turned pink and orange. Alice yawned. "Sleep comes next," she said. "Then tomorrow comes." She hugged her soft rabbit tight. "Night, night, rabbit," she whispered. "Tomorrow we see Ryland."

Ellie sat at the dinner table. Her dad put a bowl of soup in front of her. Steam went up, up, up.

"Tomorrow is Saturday," said Dad. "We can go to the lake and sail my boat."

Ellie tapped her spoon. "I want the boat now."

"Now we eat dinner," said Dad. "The boat comes later, tomorrow morning."

Ellie looked out the window. The sky was dark. She could not see any birds. Yesterday morning, the sky had been light, and she had eaten eggs for breakfast. Now it was night, and she had soup.

"What is morning?" Ellie asked.

"Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast," said Dad.

Ellie sipped her soup. It was warm and good. She started to feel sleepy before the bowl was empty. Later, Dad carried her to bed. He tucked her in. "Sleep now," he said. "Morning comes after."

Ellie closed her eyes. She dreamed about the little boat on blue water.

Then her eyes opened. Light came in the window. She could smell pancakes. She ran to the kitchen in her sock feet. Mom and Dad were at the table.

"Good morning!" said Ellie.

"Good morning," said Mom. "Time for breakfast."

Ellie climbed into her chair. Morning was here. The boat was coming soon.

Everly wanted her blue blocks. "Can I play with my blocks?" she asked. Dad shook his head. "You can play with them later. Now it is bedtime." Everly got into bed. She held her teddy. She looked at the blocks on the shelf. "Is it later yet?" she asked. Dad smiled. "Not yet. Later means some time after now." Everly waited. She heard the tap drip water in the bathroom. She heard Dad hum a song. She asked again. "Is it later yet?" "Not yet," said Dad. Everly closed her eyes. She tasted a little lemon on her tongue from dinner. It was sour. She made a funny face. Then she yawned a big yawn. Dad kissed her head. Her eyes got heavy. Soon she was fast asleep. In the morning, the sun came in the window. Everly sat up. "Is it later now?" she asked. Dad laughed. "Yes! Now it is later!" Everly clapped her hands. She ran to the shelf and took down her blue blocks. She stacked them tall, one, two, three. Then the door opened. Aariz came to play. "Blocks!" he said. Everly grinned and gave him the red block. "We can build a big tower," she said.

Anthony woke up early. "Is it today?" he asked. "Is it the library day?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is the day happening right now."

"Right now?" said Anthony. He wiggled his toes. Yes, right now! He ate his breakfast. Then they walked and walked. At the library, Stephanie and Veda were already there.

"Today! Today!" said Veda. "We all came today."

Ms. Brennan read a book about cake. Anthony's tummy rumbled. He was hungry.

"Yesterday we played outside," said Stephanie. "That is not now."

"Tomorrow we can come back," said Ms. Brennan. "That is not now either."

Anthony clapped. Yesterday was gone. Tomorrow was not here. Today was here, right now, at the library.

"Now it is song time!" said Ms. Brennan.

Anthony stood up. "Now is my favorite," he said.

Dylan went to the park with his dad. The weather was warm and sunny. The grass smelled fresh and green. Dylan felt excited to play.

His friend Marshall was there. Marshall pushed a red truck along the path. The truck went fast. Then Marshall tripped on a stone. He fell down on the soft grass. His face looked sad. A little tear ran down his cheek.

Dylan ran over. He bent down close. "Are you okay?" he asked. Marshall looked up at him. His sad face began to change. He rubbed his knee and smiled a small smile. "Yes," Marshall said. "My knee hurt. But now I feel better." Dylan helped him stand up. Marshall gave the truck a big push. It rolled all the way to the bench.

Then they sat on the bench together. Dylan's dad had a bag full of crackers. He shared them with both boys. The wind blew softly. The birds sang in the tree above them.

Marshall held up the red truck. "You can have a turn now," he said.

Charlie stood at the basketball court with a red beanbag. Mr. Bautista hung a hoop on the fence. "One beanbag, two beanbags, three," said Charlie. She wanted to throw them all.

Rhea stood next in line. Charlie threw one beanbag. It went in. Then she grabbed the next one fast. Rhea's face went sad. She had no beanbag at all.

Mr. Bautista knelt down. "Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn," he said. Charlie looked at Rhea. She held out the beanbag. "Your turn," said Charlie. Rhea threw it. It went in, too.

Then Mr. Bautista brought a big ball. Charlie patted it with both hands. She tried to catch it, but it rolled away like a magnet pulling to the ground. Rhea threw it gently. Charlie held out her arms. The ball landed in her hands. "I caught it!" she said. They took turns, one throw and then one throw, for a long, long time. "Again," said Rhea. "Again," said Charlie.

Michael got to school in his red shoes. He ran to the dress-up corner fast. Haisley was already there. She was putting on a big hat.

Mr. Thompson had a surprise. "We will play outside," he said. "But first, dress up like workers." Michael picked a hard hat and a vest. He was shy at first, but Haisley smiled at him.

Michael wanted to wear the big boots too. He sat on the little bench. He pushed his feet into the boots. But they hurt! They felt bumpy inside. He pulled one boot off. A sock was stuck in the toe. Michael laughed. "Socks go on your feet before your shoes," he said to himself. So he put on the socks first. Then the boots went on easy.

Corlin came over with his boots too. He put a boot on his bare foot. He made a funny face. "It hurts," he said. Michael held up two blue socks. "Try these first," he said. Corbin put the socks on. Then his boots slid right on. "Thank you," said Corbin.

The class lined up to go out. Mr. Thompson sniffed the air. "I smell fresh bread from the kitchen," he said. "We can see it on the computer later, how bread is made." Michael stomped his boots on the floor. Haisley stomped too. Then they marched out the door, all together.

Lincoln ran to the school garden. He had tiny carrot seeds in his hand. Ms. Abdi had a puzzle for him. "Plant these seeds here," she said. Lincoln pushed the little seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil down. Then he watered them with a small blue can.

Every day Lincoln ran to look. One morning he saw green leaves. "A sprout!" he shouted. His friend Messiah came to see. Messiah pointed at a tall leafy plant nearby. "Look, a big weed," he said. Messiah grabbed it to pull it out.

"Wait!" said Lincoln. "That might hurt our carrots." He looked closely. "Why does it matter?" asked Messiah. Lincoln thought hard. "A weed is just a plant in the wrong spot," he said. "It grows where you don't want it." Ms. Abdi smiled and nodded. They pulled the real weed out together. Then they washed their hands. The water felt cool and a little salty from Lincoln's sweat.

Soon fat orange carrots pushed up. Lincoln pulled one up. It was big news! "Messiah, come look!" he called. "Our snack grew right out of the dirt!"

Emmett woke up from his nap. He was hungry. He ran to the kitchen. His dad was there, and so was the big blender.

Emmett looked at it with his eyes. He touched the cold counter with his hands. He sniffed with his nose. "I smell strawberries," he said.

"I smell them too," said Dad. "Smoothie time."

Then Dad turned the blender on. Whirrrr! It was so loud. Emmett's ears hurt. He put his hands right over his ears. The loud sound got quiet, just like that.

Emmett tried it. Ears open. Whirrr! Ears covered. Quiet. "Dad! My hands make it quiet!" he said.

"That is a good trick," said Dad. "One, two, three, four, five. Count your fingers over your ears." Emmett counted. One, two, three, four, five.

The blender stopped. Emmett took a taste of the smoothie with his tongue. "Yum," he said. "Can we sweep the crumbs too?"

"Sweep later," said Dad. "First, drink your wild pink drink."

Sofia sat in the family car. Her tummy felt jumpy. "First dentist day," said Dad. He reached over and buckled her seat. The car went bump, bump, bump over three little bumps. One, two, three. Sofia counted them. Then she saw her ear in the window. The glass made a small Sofia too.

At the dentist, Sofia sat in a big chair. "Open wide," said the dentist. Sofia opened. "How can you see behind my teeth?" she asked. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. "This little mirror shows me the backs of your teeth," she said. Sofia saw her teeth in it. Small and shiny, like the window Sofia in the car.

After, Dad gave her a sticker. In the car, she counted the bumps again. One, two, three. "I was brave," said Sofia. Dad smiled and drove home.

Leah was at the little pool by the beach. Her friend Kasper was there too. Their teacher was Mr. Dang. Leah wanted to learn to float on her back. But every time she tried, she sank down. "Who can hold me up?" she asked. "I can," said Mr. Dang. He put his hands under her back. His hands held her like a soft chair.

Leah lay back on his hands. She did not sink. The water held her ears and her hair. Kasper clapped from the steps. "Look at me!" said Leah. She floated and floated. Then Mr. Dang took one hand away. Leah still floated. Then he took his other hand away. Leah floated all by herself.

After the lesson, Leah and Kasper ran to the sea to bathe in the shallow waves. The sand was warm on their toes. They ate a little cake on a towel. The cake had crunchy sugar on top. Kasper pointed at the water. "Can you float there too?" he asked. Leah smiled big. "Yes," she said. "I can float anywhere now." She lay back in the shallow water. The sky was blue above her.

Austin sat in the waiting room with his mother. He used his eyes to see fish swimming in a tank. He used his ears to hear the water go bloop, bloop. He smelled something clean and sharp in the air. The paper on the seat felt crinkly under his hands.

Then the nurse gave Austin a sticker and a red strawberry candy. "Yum," said Austin. He put it in his mouth. It tasted so sweet and fruity. His friend Amara sat beside him. She had the same candy, but she held her nose closed with her fingers. "Mine tastes plain," said Amara. Her candy tasted like nothing much at all.

Austin wanted to try. He pinched his nose. He sucked the candy. It tasted plain, plain, plain! He let go of his nose. The sweet taste came back, big and strong. He gave Amara a squishy pat on her hand. "Save your nose for good candy," he said. Amara laughed and laughed.

Grandpa had a big basket of clothes pegs. Riley wanted to help hang the blanket. "Ten pegs will hold it," said Grandpa. Riley took the pegs one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," she said. The blanket went up on the line.

Then a gust of wind came. The blanket flapped like a big bird. Two pegs popped off and landed in the grass. Riley ran to get them. She counted them back onto the line. But she went too fast. "One, two, four," she said. Grandpa laughed. "Did you skip a number?" Riley tipped her head. She started again, slow and quiet. "One, two, three, four." There it was! Three had been hiding.

She put all ten pegs back on. The blanket stayed still. The wind tried again. It flapped once, then it gave up. Grandpa patted the blanket dry corner. "Good work, counting girl," he said. Riley grinned and counted the pegs one more time, just because. "Ten," she said. "All snug."

The lights went out. Jules stood in the dark kitchen. "Mama, I can't see!" he called. Mama came with her hands out. She patted the wall. She found Jules's shoulder. "The power is out," she said. "The house has no lights now."

"I want a light," said Jules. "Where is one?" Mama thought. "We have a flashlight," she said. "But where? I can't find it in the dark." Jules thought hard. Then he remembered. "The kitchen drawer!" he said. "Down low, by the sink." He held Mama's hand. They walked slow, step by step. Mama reached into the drawer. Something rolled. "I have it," she said.

Myles pressed the button on the flashlight. It made a bright, round shape of light on the floor. Jules clapped. "It works! The lights are out but it shines!" he said. "Is that true, Mama? No power, and it still shines?" "Yes," said Mama. "The batteries make it shine."

Jules planted his feet and held the light. He made the shape dance on the wall. Then something small moved by the window. Jules jumped. The light showed a fluffy tail. It was just his cat, Felix, sitting in the dark. "Felix, you surprised me!" said Jules, laughing softly. Felix blinked in the bright beam.

Mama spread a blanket on the floor. They sat together with the flashlight glowing between them. Jules pointed it at a book. They looked at the pictures while the house stayed dark. "This is nice," said Jules. Then he turned the light onto Felix's nose. Felix gave a tiny yawn, and the round shape landed right on his whiskers.

Aiden wants the bunny book. He cannot find it on the shelf. Mr. Vogel lifts a big pile of books. The bunny book is at the bottom. "Here it is," says Mr. Vogel. He hands it to Aiden.

Aiden opens the book. He starts at the back. The pages feel wrong. The bunny is not there yet. Meghan sits down next to him. "You turned it the wrong way," she says. Aiden turns to the front. The bunny is on the first page.

Aiden points at the letters. "What do these say?" he asks. "Read them to me," says Meghan. "The bunny hopped to the garden," Aiden reads. Later, Eloise reads the same page. "The bunny hopped to the garden," she says. Aiden laughs. The words are the same! Not one letter is different. Aiden hugs the book. "Good idea, book," he says.

Hunter had a big red drum. He loved to bang it loud. BOOM! BOOM! The dog ran to hide. A bird outside flew off the fence.

Dad came out of the kitchen. "Naptime for the baby," he said. "Your drum is too loud."

Hunter looked at his drum. He tapped it very soft. Tap. Tap. That was quiet. The dog came back. The baby kept sleeping.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Hunter.

He tried it again. BOOM! The dog hid. Tap. The dog came back. Hunter laughed and laughed. It was like a game.

Then he tapped quiet, quiet, quiet. Slow taps. Soft taps. The sun began to shine in the window. The stormy clouds had gone away. Dad gave him a thumbs up.

"Shh," said Hunter to the dog. He tapped one more soft tap. Tap.

Nataly was in the nursery room. She sat on the soft rug. Her baby brother was here too, in his little seat.

The baby made a loud cry. "Waa! Waa!" Natalie covered her ears. "Why is he so loud?" she asked. Her teacher, Mr. Müller, came over. "The baby cannot talk yet," he said. "He cries to show he needs something."

Natalie looked at the baby. His face was red. His fists were small and tight. Maybe he was hungry! Mom gave the baby some milk. The baby drank and drank. Then the crying stopped. The room was quiet and warm.

Natalie smiled big. She had seen it happen. The cry meant "help me." The milk made the cry go away. "He talked to me with his cry!" she said. Later she drew a picture. She used her glue to stick a flat yellow sun on the paper. She drew a long road for the baby to walk on one day. "When you can talk, we will walk that road together," she told him. The baby blew a bubble and waved his tiny hand.

Madelyn sat on the playroom rug. She had a box of blocks and a snack. Her friend Ezra had crackers. Ezra held up a cracker. "Is this a square?" he asked. "I am not sure," said Madelyn. She found a piece of string. She laid it along one side of the cracker. Then she laid it on the next side. That side fit the string too. She checked side three. It fit. She checked side four. It fit as well. "Four sides," said Madelyn. "All the same." Ezra smiled. He stacked the cracker on a square block. It sat just right. Madelyn built a tower with square blocks and round balls. Ezra made a little sheep from two triangles. A rectangle block fell over because the tower was weak. They built it again, slow and steady. "Four sides, all the same," said Ezra, holding up his cracker. Madelyn clapped and took the last square block.

Everett sat at the dinner table. He sniffed with his nose. "Mmm, soup!" he said. He touched his cup. It felt rough on the side. He tapped it. Tink, tink! He heard the sound with his ears.

Then Everett looked down. His teddy was gone! "Where is Ted?" he cried. He ran to his room. The room was dark. He could not see Ted anywhere. He froze like a statue.

"I can't see in the dark!" said Everett. His dad came in. Dad turned on the lamp. Click! The room filled with light. There was Ted, under the bed. Everett grabbed him and hugged him tight. He kissed Ted's soft ear. "Found you!" he said.

Back at the table, Everett took a big bite of soup. "Yum! I taste carrots," he said. Dad laughed. "You used your tongue, too! What a busy summer day for your eyes, ears, nose, hands and mouth."

"Taste it, Ted," said Everett. He held the teddy up to the bowl. "Ted says it tastes like carrots," he whispered. Dad smiled and gave him one more spoonful.

At snack time, Lennon wanted the apple sauce. The jar was on the table. She grabbed the lid and pulled. The lid did not move. She pulled harder. It still did not move.

"Want me to try?" asked Kiara. Kiara pulled and pulled. The lid stayed stuck. Then Amal tried. His face went red. "It is too hard," he said. Lennon frowned. She wanted the apple sauce so much.

Then Lennon spotted Mr. Novák across the room. She walked over to him. She took a big breath. "Can you help me, please?" she asked. Mr. Novák smiled. "Of course," he said. He came to the table and turned the lid. Pop! It came off easy.

"Thank you," said Lennon. She gave Kiara and Amal each some apple sauce. "How did it open?" wondered Kiara. Lennon shrugged and took a bite.

Cooper played in the playroom. He had a big toy fridge. It had a little door. Cooper pulled the door. Now it was open. He pushed the door. Now it was shut. Open. Shut. Open. Shut. It was fun.

Charli came in with a toy ice cream. "Put it in the fridge," she said. Cooper opened the door. Charli put the ice cream in. Then Cooper ran to get his blocks. He ran fast. He came back slow. He looked at the fridge. The door was still open. He could smell the pretend strawberry inside.

Mr. Villanueva knocked on the playroom door. It was open, so he could see them. He pushed it shut. Then he opened it again. "Open and closed are opposites," he said. Cooper looked at his toe, then at the big fridge. He pushed the little door shut. "Ice cream stays cold now," said Charli. Cooper clapped his hands. Opposites were fun. He opened the door one more time, just to see.

Jasmine sat at the big table. She had paper and crayons. Today she would draw the sky.

She picked the gray crayon first. Gray, gray, gray. She made one gray line. Then she stopped. She looked out the window.

The sun was shining. The day was clear and bright. "The sky is blue," said Jasmine. She put the gray crayon down. She picked the blue crayon instead. Blue, blue, blue. She filled the whole top of her paper.

Then she drew a red ball. She drew a yellow sun. She drew green grass at the bottom. "A party in the sky," she said. "A red ball party!"

Her tummy felt hungry. Mommy came in with apple slices. "Is it snack time?" asked Jasmine. "It is," said Mommy. Jasmine waited. She looked at her picture while Mommy set out the plate.

After her snack, Jasmine marched back to the table. She looked out the window again. Still blue. Still sunny. She smiled and drew one more blue cloud. "Blue like the sky," she said.

Gabriella stood at the big table. The community kitchen smelled like warm bread. Today she would make muffins for her family.

"Can I stir?" she asked.

"Yes," said her mother. "Stir slow."

Gabriella stirred the batter. It was thick and sweet. Marcel stirred his bowl too. His batter went plop, plop. They laughed.

Her mother slid the pan into the oven. She set a little round timer. "The timer will tell us when to look," she said.

Then everyone played a game. Gabriella rolled the dice. She moved her little duck. The duck had to cross a river on the board. The duck tried to hide behind a tree. It was an old game, and the corners were soft.

Suddenly, beep, beep, beep!

Gabriella jumped up. "The muffins!" she said.

Her mother opened the oven with big gloves. The muffins were gold and puffy.

"Did the timer know?" asked Gabriella.

"It rang, so we looked," said her mother.

Gabriella carried the plate to the table, one careful step at a time.

Isla stood in the bathroom. She wanted to hide from Kenzie. Kenzie was coming to find her.

Isla covered her eyes with her hands. Now she could not see the tub. She could not see the mirror. She could not see the sink.

"I can't see you, Kenzie!" she called. Her ears heard Kenzie giggle. Her nose smelled the soap. Her hands touched the soft towel. Her tummy felt jumpy.

"I see you, Isla!" said Kenzie. "You are by the sink."

Isla peeked through her fingers. Kenzie waved at her. Kenzie could still see her!

"Oh!" said Isla. She took her hands down. Her eyes could see again. She saw Kenzie smiling.

"You find me," said Isla. "My turn to count!"

Kenzie hid behind the shower curtain. Isla closed her eyes tight. She could not see anything at all. She tasted a little snack still on her lips.

"One, two, three," said Isla. Then she opened her eyes. "I see your toes!"

Kenzie laughed. "You found me!" she said. "Now let's wash our hands. Then we can buy a snack at the shop with Ms. Torres."

The two friends washed up. The bathroom was all tidy again. Ms. Torres helped them dry their hands on the big soft towel.

"Ready," said Ms. Torres. She held out her hands.

Lena stood on her stool in the kitchen. Today was Dad's birthday. She was going to make a cake!

Dad helped her crack two eggs. Lena poured in the milk. Then she mixed and mixed. The batter was runny and wobbly, like a puddle in the bowl.

Lena looked at it and frowned. "This is not a cake," she said. "It's just goo! Will it ever be a birthday cake?"

Dad smiled. "Watch what the oven does," he said. He slid the pan in himself, because ovens are hot and only grown-ups touch them.

Lena waited by the table. She drew a fox on a card for Dad. She could smell something warm and sweet filling the kitchen.

Then the timer rang. Dad pulled the pan out. Lena leaned close to see.

It was a cake! A real cake, big and round and springy. Dad cut it with a knife, one slice, then another.

"You can slice it!" Lena yelled. "The runny goo turned into cake!"

She took a big bite. It was warm and yummy. "Happy birthday, Dad," said Lena. "Next time I will mix it even bigger."

Anna sat at the table. Dinner was ready. There was rice, and there was corn. Anna was hungry. She picked up her spoon.

"Wait," said Grandma. She put her hand on Anna's spoon. "First we say thank you. Many families say a blessing before they eat. Then we start."

Anna put her spoon down. Everyone held hands. Grandma said, "Thank you for this food." Anna said it too. Then she got to eat.

The next day, Anna's friend Vivian came over. Mom set out sandwiches. Vivian picked one up right away. Anna pointed at the sandwiches. "Wait," said Anna. "First we say thank you. Then we eat."

Vivian put the sandwich down. Anna held out her hand. Vivian held it. "Thank you for this food," they said together.

"Young Anna taught me something," said Mom with a smile.

"I know," said Anna. "Now eat your sandwich, Vivian."

Connor sat at the dinner table. His potatoes made a big splash in his milk. "Oh no," said Connor. The milk ran far and wide.

His mom wiped it up. Then she put three plates on the table. One plate had a cow, a pig and a monkey on it. "These are animals," she said. The next plate had a ball, a truck and a teddy bear. "These are toys." The last plate had a banana, bread and cheese. "These are foods."

"Now put your potatoes in a group," said his mom. Connor laughed. "Potatoes are foods!" He made a pile of bread, cheese and potatoes. "Where do I put my fork?" he asked. His mom smiled. "Make a new pile for forks. But keep the fork away from your nose. Forks are sharp!" Connor giggled and put the fork down beside his plate.

Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. It was big and warm. The chef, Mr. Charles, put warm toast on the counter. The butter was soft. Colton took a small knife. The knife was dull and safe. He spread the butter. The butter went on, bit by bit. The toast turned yellow and shiny.

"Can I pour the milk too?" Colton asked. "Yes, hold the cup with one hand," said Mr. Charles. Colton picked up the little jug. He poured. The milk rose in the cup. Then a drop ran over the edge. A small white puddle sat on the counter. Colton's face went still. "Did I break it?" he asked. "No," said Mr. Charles. "Milk can be wiped up."

Colton took a cloth from the shelf. He wiped the puddle. The counter was dry again. He looked at the cloth. The milk was in the cloth now. He hung it on the hook next to the snowy white aprons.

Then Colton poured more milk, slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. "Look, Mr. Charles," he said. "My milk is all in the cup." A turtle sat in a picture on the wall, and it seemed to smile. Someone knocked at the kitchen door. It was Jack, holding a tray. Colton held up his cup of milk like a prize.

Zoe went on a big trip. Her family drove to a national park. The car had a round wheel. Daddy turned the wheel all the way.

At the park, Zoe saw tall trees. She saw a deer by the rocks. Mom held up her phone. "Say cheese!" said Mom. Zoe smiled big. Click! The deer went into the photo too.

Then Zoe found a stick. It looked bumpy and ugly. She held it up. Click! Mom took a photo of that too. Zoe laughed and laughed.

The trip ended. The car took them home. Zoe felt sad. She missed the deer. She missed the tall trees.

Then Mom opened the photo album. There was the deer! There was Zoe with her ugly stick! There was Mom and Daddy smiling.

"Look," said Zoe. "The trip is still here!"

"Photos help us remember," said Mom. She gave Zoe a hug. Zoe looked at the pictures again and again, until bedtime.

Jordan sat in a big booth at the restaurant. A giant screen glowed on the wall. A game was on! His dad said, "Watch this. Our team has the ball." Jordan held his red cup tight. Elio and Wilder sat across from him. They were excited too.

Then the other team scored. Jordan jumped up and clapped. He cheered, "Hooray! Hooray!" But the whole room went quiet. Nobody else clapped. Elio laughed. Wilder laughed too. Jordan's cheeks turned red. "Oops," he said. "That was the wrong team!"

Jordan waited. He watched the screen. Soon his team ran fast. They scored! Everyone clapped and cheered. Jordan clapped the loudest of all. "Now that's my team!" he said. Wilder gave him a high five. On the screen, the fans waved their scarves like a river of color. Jordan waved his napkin too.

Luka sat at the paint table at summer camp. He had a pot of yellow. He had a pot of blue. His friend Ares sat next to him. Ms. Mercado said, "Try mixing two paints."
Luka was shy at first. He looked at his brush. He put a little yellow on the paper. Then he put a little blue on it. He stirred with his brush. The wet spot turned green. "Green!" said Luka. Ares laughed and clapped.
Then Luka stirred his brush in the whole yellow pot. All the yellow went into the blue pot. He dipped his brush in and pulled it out. The yellow did not come back. He poked the paint with his brush. The blue and yellow stayed one green pot. He could not pull them apart again.
"Uh oh," said Luka. He looked at the green pot. Then he got a new little cup. He put some blue in it. He kept it apart. Ares gave him a little yellow from Ares's own pot. Luka kept that apart too. He mixed just a tiny bit on the paper. Green again. Luka smiled and painted a big green frog. "Ribbit," said Luka.

Henri sat at the long table in the community hall. His friend Karam sat next to him. Big bowls of soup sat in the middle. Henri picked up his spoon. He was hungry and ready to eat.

But Karam did not pick up his spoon. Karam put his hands out. Henri saw everyone else putting their hands out too. The people on each side of him held hands. A hand reached toward Henri. It was Karam's hand. But Henri's spoon was in the way.

Henri looked at his spoon. Then he looked at the hands. He set his spoon down on the table. He took Karam's hand. He took Ms. Somsak's hand on the other side. The whole circle closed all the way around. Ms. Somsak smiled. Everyone closed their eyes. Karam's papa said the blessing in a soft voice. It was like one warm word over the soup. Outside, the thick clouds sat on the hill. Inside, the hall felt cozy.

The blessing ended. Everyone said, "Amen." Then hands let go. Henri picked his spoon back up. "Now we eat," said Karam. Henri took a big sip of soup. It was warm and good.

Liam sits in the computer lab with his class. Today he gets a tablet. He wants to draw a big sun on it. Mr. Wu hands him the tablet. Liam holds it with one hand. He walks to his chair. The tablet tips and slips. Liam grabs it fast. It wobbles in his hands.

"Try two hands," says Mr. Wu. Liam puts one hand on each side. He holds on tight. The tablet sits still in his hands now. It does not tip. It does not slip. Liam smiles and carries it to his chair.

Now he has to turn it on. He looks for the round button. He presses it with his finger. The screen lights up. His face glows in the light. The lab is quiet. He hears small taps all around him.

Liam finds the drawing app. It is a little rainbow square. He taps it. A white page opens. He picks yellow. He draws a big round sun. Then he draws tight little rays all around it. Skye leans over. "Nice sun," she says.

Time to put the tablet away. Liam presses the button again. The screen goes dark. He stands up slowly. He holds the tablet with two hands, one on each side. He walks to the shelf. He sets it down soft as a feather. He looks back at his empty hands. "I did it all by myself," he says.

Theodore went to the store with his dad. The store had big bright lights. One corner was dark. Theodore held his dad's hand in the middle of the aisle.

Theodore wanted a red apple. "Not now," said Dad. "We can buy one later." Later felt far away.

Then Theodore saw his friend Elyas. Elyas was kicking a little ball near the carts. "I went to the park tomorrow!" said Elyas. Then Elyas stopped. "No. Not tomorrow. I went yesterday. It already happened. Yesterday is the day before today."

Theodore thought about that. Yesterday was gone. Today was now, here in the store. Tomorrow was still coming.

Dad put a red apple in the bag. "You can eat it later, at home," said Dad.

Later came fast. At home, Theodore took a big bite. The apple was sweet and cold. "Today is a good day," he said.

Gabriel wanted to go to the park. He held his red ball by the door. Then the sky turned dark. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"No park today," said his mom. "We need to stay inside."

Gabriel felt sad. His lip went down. His eyes felt watery. He sat on the floor and hugged his ball.

Then his mom brought a big blanket. "We can build a fort," she said. Gabriel jumped up. He felt excited now!

They put chairs together. They spread the blanket on top. Gabriel crawled inside. It was cozy and dark. His mom gave him a little flashlight.

"Wow," said Gabriel. "My fort!"

He shined the light on the red ball. The ball glowed inside the fort. Gabriel laughed and laughed.

Just then the phone rang. It was Iqra from school. "Come to my house tomorrow," she said. "We can play at the park together."

"Okay!" said Gabriel. He was happy.

The rain still tapped outside. But inside the fort, Gabriel smiled. He gave his mom a big hug through the blanket door.

The rain tapped, and Gabriel laughed.

Iris stood on her step stool in the bathroom. She wanted to wash her hands all by herself. The tap was shiny and silver. Iris reached for the red side. Her dad caught her hand right away. "Let me test it first," he said. He turned the tap. The water got hot and steamy. Then he turned it back. Now the water was cool and just right. Iris put her hands under the cool water. She rubbed the soap and made white bubbles. "I can learn to do this," she said. Her dad smiled and gave her a small towel.

After her bath, Iris saw the red side made hot water. The blue side made cold water. She pointed at them. "Red is hot," she said. Her dad nodded. "And blue is cold," he said. Iris dried her hands on the soft towel.

Then Iris looked out the little window. She could see the park across the road. There were swings there. She wanted to swing very much. Iris ran to the front door. Her dad put on his shoes. Iris stopped at the curb and waited. She held out her hand. Her dad took it in his big warm hand. Together they stepped into the road. A car went by, and Iris held on tight. They walked straight across, side by side.

At the park, Iris ran to the swings. "You waited for my hand," said her dad. "That was good." Iris kicked her legs and went up high. Kingsley waved from the slide. Iris waved back with a big smile. "Again!" she called to her dad. He pushed the swing, and her feet touched the sky.

Luka sat in a small chair at the doctor's office. He wanted a sticker, but first he had to wait. "What can I do while I wait?" he asked his mom. "You can look around," she said.

So Luka used his eyes to see. One, two, three fish. They were orange. They did swim in a tank. He used his ears to hear. Beep, beep, beep. One, two, three beeps. He touched the chair with his hands. It felt smooth. He smelled something like soap. He sniffed with his nose.

Then Ms. Oyelaran came out with a tray. "Would you like a lemon slice?" she asked. "Yes!" said Luka. He thought lemon would taste sweet like orange juice. He put it on his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" said Ms. Oyelaran. "Very sour," said Luka.

Ms. Oyelaran laughed kindly. "Your tongue did its job," she said. Luka drank some water. Then he got his sticker, a shiny root vegetable with a smiley face. "What will we see next time?" he asked his mom. "Maybe more fish," she said. Luka waved to the fish. "Bye, one, two, three," he said.

Elizabeth sat at the little blue table. It was snack time at daycare. Mr. Moretti held a big bowl. "Peas?" he asked Gaia. "Yuck!" Gaia shouted. Her spoon went clatter on the table. Mr. Moretti's face went sad and quiet.

Then Elizabeth saw something. Mr. Moretti said, "You can say no, thank you." Gaia took a breath. "No, thank you," she said, straight and clear like a small bell. Mr. Moretti smiled big. "Crackers instead?" he asked. "Yes, please!" said Gaia. One smile. One cracker. No clatter at all.

Mr. Moretti came to Elizabeth. "Peas?" he asked. Elizabeth did not like peas. She remembered the bell. "No, thank you," she said. "But apples, please?" Mr. Moretti grinned. He cut an apple into a butterfly shape with a safe knife, far from her hands. He gave her one wing, then two wings. Elizabeth looked out the window. She could see a real butterfly, orange and small, sitting on the flower pot. "No, thank you," Elizabeth whispered to the peas. Then she munched her apple wings, one, two, and smiled at Gaia.

Henry went to the park with his mom. "When can we go home?" he asked. "Later," Mom said. Henry did not like later. Later felt very long.

Then Henry saw a big round clock on the park wall. "What is that?" he asked. "A clock," Mom said. "A clock shows what time it is." The little hand pointed to the four. Henry watched it move, very slowly. Tick, tick. The hand moved a tiny bit.

Henry ran to Mario. "Come see the clock!" he said. They watched the hands together. Henry waited and waited. Then the bell rang. "Time to go!" Mom called.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" Henry asked. "Yes," Mom said. Henry hugged his sweater. The clock had told him when. Tomorrow they would watch it again.

Zoey wanted to build a toy car at daycare. She found four square pieces of cardboard. She taped them on for wheels. She gave the car a big pull across the rug. The car would not roll. It just stopped with a bump.

"Why won't you go?" Zoey asked the car. She looked and looked at the square wheels. August rolled a toy fish truck past her. Its wheels were round like circles. Round wheels rolled. Square wheels did not.

Zoey tapped Ms. Liu on the arm. "Can you help me cut circle wheels? The scissors are sharp." Ms. Liu smiled. "You were brave to ask for help," she said. She cut four circles out of the cardboard. Zoey taped them on all by herself.

Zoey gave the car a big pull. It rolled and rolled, all the way to the block shelf. Eunice clapped her hands. "Fast car!" she said. Zoey chased it down and pulled it back again.

Claire ran to the window at daycare. The sky was cloudy today. "Ms. Lin, is it story time now?" she asked. Ms. Lin smiled. "Soon, Claire. Soon means in a little while." Claire sat down on the rug. She waited. She waited some more. "Is it story time now?" she asked again. "Soon," said Ms. Lin. "Soon means in a little while." Nathanael sat down next to her. "I want the story now too," he said. "Let's play a quiet game while we wait," said Claire. They played pat-a-cake. Pat, pat, clap. Pat, pat, clap. "Is it soon yet?" asked Claire. "Almost," said Ms. Lin. Claire and Nathanael played one more game. Pat, pat, clap. Then Ms. Lin picked up a big red book. "Now it is story time," she said. Claire clapped her hands. Soon had come! "Tomorrow we will read it again," said Ms. Lin. Claire whispered to Nathanael, "That is not soon. That is tomorrow!" Nathanael laughed. Claire leaned in close to see the first page.

Julia looked out the window. The sky was dark. "Rain is coming," said Mama. Julia put on her red sneakers. They had a triangle pattern on the side.

The rain came down. Plop, plop, plop. Julia counted the puddles outside. One puddle, two puddles, three puddles.

Julia wanted to jump in the puddles. She held Mama's hand and went out. She jumped in the first puddle. Splash! She jumped in the second puddle. Splash! Then Julia felt it. Her socks were wet. Her toes went squish, squish. "My socks are soggy," she said.

Mama held up rain boots. "Try these," she said. Julia took off the wet sneakers. She put on the yellow rain boots. She jumped in the third puddle. Splash! She looked at her toes. Dry! Rain boots keep feet dry. Julia jumped again. One puddle, two puddles, three puddles. Dry toes every time.

The wind blew. The rain stopped. The sun came out. "Sunny now," said Julia. A rainbow made a big triangle shape in the sky.

Inside, Mama made warm soup. Julia took a taste. "Tasty," she said. Her boots sat by the door, still wet, waiting for the next rainy day.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Olivier loved that. On Monday, they went to the park. Olivier saw a sign by the gate. It said "Bake Sale on Saturday." "Grandma, can we bake something?" he asked.

Grandma smiled. "I will show you my special bread," she said. "My mother made it too. Now you can learn."

On Tuesday, they stood in the kitchen. Olivier poured a little flour in the bowl. Then he poured water. He stirred. Something new appeared. It was not flour. It was not water. It was soft, sticky dough! "The water made the flour turn into dough," Olivier said. He pressed it with his hands. It squished between his fingers.

Grandma put the dough in a warm spot. "Now we wait," she said. Olivier peeked at it again and again. The dough grew bigger and bigger!

Grandma shaped the loaves. She put them in the hot oven herself. Olivier watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

On Saturday, they took the bread to the park. Felicia and Ganeev ran over. "Grandma showed me how to cook this!" Olivier said. He broke off a piece for everyone. Felicia took a big bite. "Can you teach me too?" she asked.

"Come to my kitchen," said Olivier. "I will show you."

Jordan ran to the block corner at daycare. Yesterday the blocks were all put away. Today they sat in a big pile, waiting.

"I went to the park tomorrow," said Payton. Payton stacked one block, then another. Jordan tilted his head. "Tomorrow? But that is later."

Payton thought hard. "No, wait. It already happened. I went yesterday." Jordan clapped. "Yesterday is the day before today!" said Payton. Jordan wondered: did yesterday have the park in it? Did today have the park in it too?

"Not today," said Ms. Martínez. "Today we stay here. But tomorrow we play outside." Jordan looked at the blocks. He wanted a tall tower. He stacked a red block. Then a blue one. Then a yellow one. The tower grew and grew. Jordan held his breath. Would it stay up?

Destiny ran over with a winter hat on her head. "Look! Good hat for outside," she said. Now it was time for a snack. "The tower can wait," said Ms. Martínez. "We will build more later." Jordan patted the tower. "Stay there," he said. "I will come back soon."

Later, Jordan came back. The tower was still there. He put one more block on top. "Today is a good day," he said.

Felix sat on the small red rug. He had a book about a bear in a boat. He opened it at the back. The pages felt funny that way. They went the wrong way.

"Look at this bear," said Felix. "Who drew him?" He turned the book around. He peeked behind the cover. Lea sat down next to him.

"I need the crackers," said Althea. She was passing out salty crackers for snack. She gave one to Felix. Felix munched and looked at his book.

Mr. O'Brien came over. "Start at the front," he said. "This side first." Felix turned to the very first page. There were words there. Felix pointed at them. "What do those say?"

"That part tells who made the book," said Mr. O'Brien. He read, "Pictures by Anna Lee." He pointed again. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator."

"The illustrator!" said Felix. He said it slow. "Anna Lee drew my bear."

"Turn the page," said Lea. Felix turned it. The bear sailed on. Page by page, they went front to back, all the way to the end.

"Tomorrow," said Felix, "we read it again."

Owen sat in the waiting room. He felt grumpy. The wait was long, and he was hungry. Mom gave him a piece of bread. Owen took a big bite. His tongue tasted the soft bread. It was good.

Next to him, his friend Olivier was there too. They built a tower with blocks. Owen touched each block with his hands. One block was smooth. One block was bumpy. Then Olivier bumped the tower. Crash! It fell down. "Oops," said Olivier. They laughed and built it again.

Then a nurse called, "Owen!" In the room, Owen took off his shoes and socks. His bare toes touched the cold floor. "Ooh," said Owen. "My feet can feel too!" Ms. Tanaka, the doctor, smiled. "Yes, they can," she said. She looked in his ears with a light. Owen heard a little beep. His nose smelled the sticker she gave him. It smelled like strawberries.

After the visit, Mom took Owen home. Owen ran to the backyard. He took off his shoes and socks again. He stepped on the soft green grass. The grass tickled his bare toes. Owen giggled and wiggled them. "It tickles!" he said.

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. Her bunny was gone. "Where is Bunny?" she asked. Grandma said, "Let's look together."

Aubrey looked under the bed. She looked in her cup drawer. No bunny. Then Grandpa called, "Come here, Aubrey!" He held a big box. "This is the lost and found," he said. "People put things they find in here. Then the owners can get them back."

Aubrey peeked in the box. She saw a hat, a mitten, and a spoon. Then she saw two soft ears. "Bunny!" she said. She hugged him tight.

Grandma smiled. "Grandpa found Bunny on the sofa this morning. He put him in the box for you." Aubrey kissed Grandpa's cheek. She held Bunny up to the window. "Bunny, you can share my breakfast," she said. Bunny's ears bobbed up and down as they walked to the kitchen.

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had paints and a big sheet of paper. He wanted to paint a flower for his mom. His favorite shirt was blue with a rocket on it.

He began to paint. He dipped his brush in red. Drip, drip, went the brush. A red spot fell on his sleeve. Mohamed looked down. His rocket shirt was not clean anymore. He felt like crying a little.

His dad came in with an old shirt. "Put this on," Dad said. "An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes." Mohamed pulled it over his head. It was big and soft and smelled like the garden.

He painted again. Drip, drip, went the brush. This time the paint fell on the old shirt. His rocket shirt stayed clean underneath. Mohamed smiled and painted a big red flower. Then he painted a small yellow sun, and a tiny ladybug. "Look, Dad," he said. "The paint can't get me now."

Felix stood in the band room. A big drum sat in front of him. He wanted to play it for the class.

Mr. Fortin held up a page. "See these dots and lines?" he said. "These marks are called notes. Notes show which sounds to play."

Felix looked at the dots. He tapped the drum. He looked at the dots again. He tapped once more. A bird sat by the window. It seemed to listen.

Elowyn and Kali came to listen too. Felix watched the notes. He tapped a high dot. The drum went boom. He tapped a low dot. The drum went boom again, but softer.

"You did it!" said Elowyn. Felix felt upset that the boom was not right. So he tried again. He waited. He looked at the notes. He tapped slowly.

Mr. Fortin smiled. The bird flew up. "Play it one more time," said Kali.

Felix raised his drumstick and tapped the big drum.

Ruby went to the garden center with her dad. She picked out little plants. Tomatoes, carrots, and beans. "We can plant these at home," said her dad.

Ruby planted them in a big box. She watered them every day. Then little green shoots came up. But Ruby forgot which shoot was which. "Where did I put the tomatoes?" she asked.

At school, she told her friend Christophe. "I don't know what is growing," Ruby said. Christophe smiled. "My grandma puts a label in the soil," he said. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot."

So Ruby drew pictures. She drew a red tomato. She drew a long carrot. She drew green beans. Her mom helped her cut the cards. Ruby taped each picture to a stick. She stuck one stick by each row. "Now I know what lives in each spot," said Ruby.

Soon a big leaf popped up by the tomato stick. Ruby patted the soft dirt. Bees buzzed by, noisy and busy. "Grow big, tomato," said Ruby. "I will come back tomorrow."

Stella marched into daycare. She wanted to find her cubby fast. But the tags were all mixed up on the wall. "Which one is mine?" she asked.

She looked at one tag. It said Alex. That was not her name. She looked at another tag. It said Liliane. That was not her name either. Then she saw a tag that said Stella. S, then T, then E, twice, then L, then A. "That is me!" she said. Her coat went in that cubby.
