Later, Ms. Joseph held up a card. "Whose birthday is it?" she asked. The card had writing on the front. Stella looked hard. The same letters came first. S, then T, then E, twice, then L, then A. Then more letters after. "The front says Stella!" she said. Ms. Joseph smiled. "Yes, it does."

Stella picked up a pencil. She wrote her name on paper. S, then T, then E, twice, then L, then A. She held it next to the card. Both names looked the same. Same letters. Same order. The noisy playroom went on around her, but Stella kept looking.

"Can I write it ten more times?" she asked.

Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was a white rabbit. "His name is Snowy," said his dad.

At home, Oliver fed Snowy a carrot. He cleaned the cage with his dad. Snowy had soft fur. Oliver patted him a lot.

Then Oliver ran to the kitchen. He wanted his crackers. His mom stopped him at the door. "Wash your hands first," she said. "You touched Snowy and his cage." Oliver looked at his hands. He could not see anything on them.

Oliver washed his hands with soap. The water felt nice and warm. Then he ate his crackers.

The next day, Elijah came over. Elijah patted Snowy too. Then Elijah ran to the snack plate. Oliver called, "Wait! Wash your hands first." Elijah washed his hands. Then they shared the crackers and laughed.

"Snowy is a good rabbit," said Oliver. He gave Snowy one more gentle pat.

Jacob stood in the kitchen. Papa was setting the big pot on the table. It smelled like warm soup and bread.

"Time for the blessing," said Papa. "Close your eyes, Jacob."

Jacob squeezed his eyes shut. But he wanted to peek. He peeked just a little. He saw Grandpa! Grandpa's eyes were closed too. Grandpa's head was bowed down low.

Jacob closed his eyes again. He held Papa's hand. He held Grandma's hand. Papa, Grandma, Grandpa, Jacob. Four hands, all joined together.

"Amen," said Grandpa.

"Amen!" said Jacob. That was his big word. His word felt loud and strong.

Outside, snow was falling past the window. Jacob watched the white flakes skip and spin.

"Soup time!" said Papa.

Jacob ate his bread. He slurped his soup. Then he asked, "Do it again?"

Grandpa laughed. "At supper, Jacob."

Jacob clapped his hands. "Supper! Amen again!"

Victoria went to swim class with her dad. The pool was right by the beach. She could hear the wind and see the big blue sea.

Victoria's big friend Rihaan swam in the deep end. Victoria wanted to go there too. She walked to the deep end. Her coach, Mr. Guo, held her hand. "We start here," he said. "This is the shallow end."

Victoria put her feet down. The water was low. She could touch the bottom. She looked at Rihaan. He could not touch the bottom way over there.

Victoria practiced. She kicked and kicked. The water felt slimy on her legs. Her goggles would not stay on, so she fixed them. She kicked some more.

"You are ready," said Mr. Guo. He held her tight. They went a little deeper. Victoria could not touch the bottom now. She kicked and she swam.

Rihaan clapped. "You swam past the shallow end!" he said. Victoria smiled and kicked some more.

Florence loved shape day at school. Ms. Taylor put a big clock on the table. "Look, a circle!" said Fraser. Kimberly held up a tiny button. "This is too small to be a circle," she said. Florence looked at the button. Then she looked at the big clock. She put the button right next to the clock. "It is small, but it is still round," said Florence. "A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles!" Kimberly smiled big. "My button is a circle too!"

Ms. Taylor clapped her hands. "Let's hunt for more shapes!" Florence ran to the block corner. She found a square block. Fraser found a triangle roof piece. Kimberly found a long rectangle for a door. "Let's build a house for a nest," said Florence. "A bird can pay us a visit!" The three friends stacked the blocks up high. Ms. Taylor made sure the tower was safe and steady. Florence put the button on top, like a round little sun. "Our house has a circle too!" she said. Kimberly laughed and clapped again.

Sienna was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut!" Sienna patted her curls. "My hair is big like a mountain," she said. Grandma laughed. "Off we go."

At the salon, there was a big chair. Sienna climbed up. But she was small. The hairdresser bent down low. She bent lower and lower. "I cannot reach your hair," she said. Sienna thought hard. Then the hairdresser brought a booster seat. "Small children sit on a booster seat," she said, "so I can reach." The booster seat went on the big chair. Sienna sat on it. Now she was up, up, up!

"Now I can reach your hair," said the hairdresser. Snip, snip, snip. The curls fell like soft little pieces. "Snip, snip, snip!" said Sienna. Grandma held up the mirror. "Look at you!" Sienna grinned. "Grandma, do you need a booster seat too?" Grandma laughed and laughed. "Not yet," she said. Sienna hugged her tight. "Maybe tomorrow!"

Carter sat at the kitchen table. He had a little toy slide. He wanted his toy pig to go down. First, he put the pig on top. He pushed it. The pig did not move. What was wrong?

Carter turned the pig around. Now its feet went first. He let go. The pig slid down, fast! It landed on the table with a plop. "Again!" said Carter. Feet first worked every time.

Then Carter wanted to try. Was there a big slide somewhere? "Can we go to the park?" he asked. Mom said, "Yes, after I stir the pot."

Mom stirred the hot soup. Carter stayed back. The stove was hot, and Mom was the one who touched it. Carter watched the steam move up, up, up.

At the park, Carter climbed the slide steps. He started to lie down, head at the top. His friend Azriel was waiting below. Carter turned himself around. He sat up. Feet first! Down he went, zoom, all the way. "My turn!" said Azriel.

Grayson ran to the playground with his dad. Samrath and Eesa were already there. "Come on the slide!" said Samrath. Grayson held the rail. He went up slow, one step at a time. His dad said, "Stay where I can see you." Grayson slid down. Whee! He slid down again.

The sun was warm on the slide. The metal felt hot. Grayson touched it with one finger. His dad checked the slide with his hand. "Let's find a shady spot," he said. They kept to the shade. Grayson saw the sun make the slide hot. That was real.

After the playground, Grayson had mud on his shoes. "Bath time," said his dad. Grayson wanted to jump right in. But he remembered the hot slide. He stopped and waited. His dad put his hand in the water. "Warm," he said. "Not hot. You can get in now." Grayson touched the water. It felt warm and soft. He got in slow. The bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

Then they would eat pizza together. Grayson washed his toes. He washed his tummy. "All clean," said his dad. Grayson hugged his warm towel and said, "Pizza now, please."

Lillian's soft gray bunny was gone. "Where did you go, Bunny?" she said. She looked under her bed. One sock. She looked in her toy box. Two blocks. She looked behind the big chair. Three crayons. No bunny.

Then Lillian saw something shiny under the couch. She reached in. It was a little red toy car. The car belonged to Austyn. He had played with it at her house yesterday. "That is Austyn's car," Lillian said. "I will give it back to him."

The doorbell rang. It was Austyn. Lillian ran to him. "I found your car," she said. She put the red car in his hands. Austyn smiled big. "You found it! Thank you!" Then Austyn pointed at the laundry basket. "Look," he said. Something soft peeked out from under a cold, wet shirt. It was Bunny! Bunny had gone for a sleep in the basket.

Lillian hugged Bunny tight. "Found you," she whispered. Austyn rolled his car on the floor. Zoom, zoom.

Hudson was three today. He was having a party at the bowling alley. Mom held his hand at the big door. Hudson saw Blakely and Eyad waiting inside.

Then Eyad looked sad. "I thought we would get lost," Eyad said. "I did not know where to go." Hudson had an idea. He pulled the party invitation from his pocket. He showed Eyad the paper. "See, it says the party is here," Hudson said. "It says the bowling alley. And it says today, at my party time." Blakely peeked at it too. "The invitation tells us when and where," Blakely said. Eyad smiled big now.

Ms. Girma, the bowling coach, helped them pick small balls. Hudson rolled his ball. The pins all fell down. Everyone clapped. Mom brought out a cake with three candles. Hudson blew them out with one big breath. Then he took another safe bite of cake.

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. The grass was still wet. His red shirt felt bright in the sun. His friend Jolene ran beside him. She kicked the ball to him. Cooper kicked it back. The coach blew the whistle.

The other team scored a goal. Then they scored one more. The whistle blew again. The game was over. Cooper's team had lost. He sat down on the grass. He did not want to talk. His face felt hot. Jolene sat next to him. "We lost," he said.

Mr. Kaya clapped his hands. "Line up, everyone," he said. "We say good game to the other team." Cooper stood in the line. Each player walked past. Each player said, "Good game." A boy from the other team said, "Good game, Cooper." Cooper said it back. Then a small surprise. The boy smiled and held out his hand for a high five. Cooper laughed and clapped it. Jolene took a drink of water. "Good game," she said again. "Good game," said Cooper. The sky was turning pretty and pink.

Ruby went to the doctor with her dad. Her throat hurt, and she wanted to feel better fast.

First the doctor looked in her ears. "Your ears do the hearing," said the doctor. Ruby heard a little beep. It was so funny! Then Ruby saw a big poster on the wall. Her eyes did the seeing. She saw a dog on it. Then the doctor said, "Open wide." Ruby stuck out her tongue. "Good tongue!" he said. "It does the tasting." Ruby smelled something sweet. Her nose did that! The room smelled like bubble gum.

Then the doctor gave Ruby a cup of water with an ice cube in it. Ruby touched the ice cube with her finger. It felt so cold! She dropped it fast, right into her cup. Plop!

"Can I do it again?" Ruby asked.

The doctor laughed. "Here is one more ice cube." Ruby touched it with one finger. Cold again! She dropped it in the cup too.

At the end, the doctor put a sticker on Ruby's neck. "You were so brave," he said. Ruby looked in the mirror. She saw a shiny star sticker.

"My eyes see it!" said Ruby. "My finger felt the cold ice!" Her dad smiled. Then they went home, and Ruby fell asleep in the car.

Rosalie ran into the art room. Big paper waited on the table. Mr. Castillo held up a jar of paint. "This is red," he said. "Say it with me!" "Red!" shouted Rosalie. Shea pointed at another jar. "Blue!" said Shea. "Yellow!" said Rosalie. Mr. Castillo smiled. "Those are the primary colours."

Rosalie dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She touched the paper. "Look!" she cried. The circle turned purple. "Purple! I made purple!" Shea ran over to see. "Make more!" said Shea. Rosalie painted purple all over the paper.

At home time, Rosalie set her brush down in the paint cup. She wanted to hurry and show her father. "Wait," said Mr. Castillo. He showed her the sink. "Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished." Rosalie rinsed her brush in the cool water. She laid it on the rack to dry.

The next day, Rosalie ran back to the art room. Her brush was soft and clean. It was true! She picked it up fast. "My turn for yellow and red," she said. She painted a yellow sun. She added red on top. "Orange!" she yelled. "Orange like a pumpkin!" Shea clapped. Mr. Castillo gave her a fresh sheet of paper. Rosalie dipped her clean, soft brush and wrote her name at the top in orange paint.

Hazel was hunting for her red ball in the backyard. The ball was her best toy. Instead, she found a little blue feather. It was soft and straight and shiny.

"Feathers come from birds," said her mom. "Birds are animals that have feathers."

A bird must have lost it! Hazel put the feather in her pocket. Then she listened. She heard a chirping sound by the fence. A fat blue bird sat there. It looked like her feather!

Hazel held the feather up high. The bird tilted its head. Then it flew down, snatched a crumb from her snack plate, and zoomed away.

"My crumb!" laughed Hazel. "I guess I fed the animals today." She waved the feather like a tiny flag. "Bye, bird! Come eat again tomorrow!"

Joseph ran out to the playground. The sun was very bright. He scrunched up his eyes. "Too sunny!" he said.

His friend Ahaan ran over. Ahaan wore a big sun hat. "Here, try mine," Ahaan said. Joseph put it on. He opened his eyes wide. He could see the swings now. He could see Mr. Lin by the fence.

"Your turn," Joseph said. He gave the hat back. Ahaan smiled. "I have one more," said Mr. Lin. He reached into his bag. He pulled out a little sun hat. It had a red star on it.

Joseph put it on. The sun did not hurt his eyes. The hat made shade for his face. He ran fast to the slide. Ahaan ran with him. "Sunny days need hats!" said Joseph. The two boys slid down together, again and again.

Nora was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. Grandma had set out crunchy crackers and apple slices. Nora ran to the table. "First we wash," said Grandma. "Wash with soap for twenty seconds."

Nora was hungry. She put her hands under the water and rinsed them fast. "Done!" she said. Grandma shook her head. "That was too quick. It was not twenty seconds."

Nora frowned. Twenty seconds felt so long. "How will I know?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "I will help you count." Nora put soap on her hands. Grandma said, "Let's march in place while we scrub." So Nora scrubbed and marched, and Grandma counted slowly, "One, two, three, all the way to twenty."

The bubbles grew big and white. Nora scrubbed her fingers and the backs of her hands. "Nineteen, twenty!" said Grandma. Nora rinsed the bubbles off. Her hands were clean and shiny.

"Good washing," said Grandma. Nora sat down and took a crunchy cracker. "Yum," she said. "Washing takes a long time." Grandma laughed. "It does. And now your apple is safe to eat." Nora took a big bite. She held up her clean hands to show Grandma. "Twenty seconds," said Nora. "I counted every one."

text:
Jasper sat very still on the back step. His dad said, "Sit and listen. What do you hear?"

Jasper wanted to know all five senses. He knew two already. "I see with my eyes," he said. "I smell with my nose." Dad smiled.

A sound came. Tweet, tweet! Jasper put his hands on his ears. "A bird!" he said. "I hear it!" Dad nodded. "We hear with our ears," he said. Jasper clapped. Three senses now.

Then a bee buzzed by the swing. Jasper heard the buzz too. He wiggled, but he stayed still and kept listening. A car went vroom. The wind went whoosh. Jasper giggled. His ears were busy!

Dad handed him a bright red apple. Jasper touched it. Smooth and cool. "I touch with my hands!" he said. Dad laughed. "Yes! That is four." Jasper took a big bite. Mmm! He licked his lips. "And I taste with my mouth!"

Then something soft bumped his leg. It was his cat! Jasper heard no footstep at all. "Cats are quiet," he whispered. He touched the cat's soft fur. Jasper counted on his fingers. "Five senses!" he said.

Dad gave him a hug. Jasper hugged the cat, very gently.

text:
Penelope was in the backyard with her red apple. She took a big bite. Juice ran down her chin. Xander came to play. He brought his toy cars.

"Let's make a road," said Penelope. She got the chalk. Mom helped her sweep the patio clean first. Then Penelope drew a long line. Xander drove his cars on it. One car was blue. One car was yellow.

"I need a light," said Penelope. She drew a tall box with three circles. The top circle was red. The bottom circle was green. Xander stopped his car at the red circle. "Red means stop," said Penelope. Then she pointed at the green circle. Xander zoomed his car fast. "Green means go!" he said.

Then they walked to the shop with Mom. They stopped at the big light on the pole. The light turned red. All the cars stopped. Penelope held Mom's hand tight. The light turned green. The cars went. "Just like our game," said Penelope. She skipped the rest of the way, holding her clean, sticky apple hand in Mom's.

Jaxon sat in the car with his dad. They were going to the salon. It was his first haircut ever.

At the salon, Jaxon sat in a big chair. A hairdresser named Ms. Mwangi put a cape on him. She picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. One bit, two bits, three bits. They landed on his neck.

Jaxon wiggled in the chair. "My neck feels itchy," he said. He wanted to scratch it. But the cape was in the way. Ms. Mwangi saw him wiggle. "I know what will help," she said. She took a soft brush. She brushed the little bits of hair off his neck. One sweep, two sweeps. The itchy feeling went away.

"Now I can sit still," said Jaxon. He smiled a happy smile. Ms. Mwangi cut and cut. When she was done, his hair was short and neat. The lights made his hair shine.

Back in the car, Jaxon looked at himself in the mirror. His dad gave him a high five. On the seat was an egg sandwich for a snack. "Next time," said Jaxon, "the hairdresser can brush the itchy bits off right away."

His dad laughed and started the car. "Home we go," he said.

Victor was building a house in the playroom. He wanted a door for it. He found a square block. It was red with four sides. He put it in the door spot. But the house leaned, and the block slipped. Now one corner pointed up.

Nora sat next to him. She looked at the block. "That is a new shape," she said. "It is not a square now."

Victor frowned. He needed the square for his door. He turned the block with his hands. He turned it back, corner down. It looked the same as before. Four sides. Four corners.

"It is still a square," Victor said.

"You found it out," said Nora. She gave his cheek a quick kiss, like his mom did. Then she laughed and clapped.

Victor put the square back in the door spot. It fit. He pushed the house gently. The door stayed on. The house did not fall down.

Ms. Fortin came over. "What a fine house," she said. "Can I see the door?"

Victor opened it wide. "Watch this," he said. He turned the square so a corner pointed up. Then he turned it back. Square. Square.

Ms. Fortin smiled. "May I knock?"

"Knock three times," said Victor.

Ms. Fortin knocked. Victor opened the door again. Nora made her toy bird fly over the roof and land on top.

"The bird lives here too," said Victor. "In the round window." He pointed to a circle block. He had a triangle for the roof, and a rectangle for a bed.

"Then let it sleep," said Nora. She tucked the bird in with a small cloth.

Victor closed the square door, corner down, just the way he liked it.

Livia woke up excited. "Today is shot day!" she said. She ran to find her socks. Mom said, "First we wait in the waiting room."

At the doctor's office, the waiting room was full. Families sat in rows of chairs. Livia sat next to a boy with a teddy bear. She wanted her turn now. "When is it my turn?" she asked.

Mom pointed at the door. "We sit here until the nurse calls your name."

Livia watched the door. A nurse opened it. "Ava!" she called. Ava's family stood up and went in. So that was the trick! The nurse calls a name, and that family goes.

Livia hugged her teddy bear tight. The door opened again. "Livia!" the nurse called.

"My turn!" Livia shouted. She jumped up so fast her hat fell off.

The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then the nurse gave her a shiny star sticker.

"I waited, and then it was my turn," Livia told Mom.

Mom laughed. "One more stop on the way home. Guess what's in the bag?"

Livia peeked. A computer? No. It was a new book!

"Read it next," Livia said, and held Mom's hand all the way out the door.

Elizabeth did not want to sleep. "I want to play," she said. Her mom gave her a bath. The water was warm and safe. Mom washed one arm, two arms, one foot, two feet. Then Elizabeth put on her pajamas. She pulled the zip up, up, up. She brushed her teeth, one tooth at a time. Mom read one book, two books, three books. Then Mom turned off the light. Elizabeth closed one eye. Then she closed the other eye. And she slept all night.

The next morning, Elizabeth woke up. Her friend Kehlani came to play. "Let me see you hop," said Kehlani. Elizabeth hopped one hop, two hops, three hops. She ran fast. She stacked big blocks. She laughed and laughed. "You have so much play," said Kehlani.

That night, Elizabeth yawned a big yawn. "Can sleep give me more play?" she asked Mom. Mom smiled. Elizabeth took her bath. She zipped her pajamas. She closed both eyes. She slept all night again. In the morning she hopped and hopped. "More hops for me!" she said.

Grandma had a big soft bag. "Put your hand in," she said. "Do not peek. Tell me what you find."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. "A red ball!"

Grandma smiled. "Take it out and look."

Milo pulled out the ball. It was blue! He laughed. "I felt it was a ball. But my fingers did not know the color."

Wade and Miraal were there too. They wanted a turn. Wade put his hand in. "A spoon! A yellow spoon!" He looked. The spoon was red. "My fingers cannot see," he said.

Miraal had a turn next. She felt something small and smooth. "A car! A blue car!" She peeked in the bag. "No, it is green!"

"Close your eyes," said Milo. "Now look at the ball. What color is it?" Miraal opened her eyes. "Blue. I see blue with my eyes."

Grandma yawned. She looked tired. "Time for my nap," she said. The children hurried to be quiet.

Milo held the bag shut. "No peeking," he whispered. "You have to look. Looking is how you see."

Miraal put her hand back in. "I feel it! It is a yellow duck." She pulled it out fast.

It was yellow! She jumped up and down. "I guessed it! My eyes and my hands both helped me!"

Iris needs to use the toilet at school. She goes into the little bathroom. She closes the door.

Vienna is washing her hands at the sink. Iris hears the water. "Why is the water on?" Iris asks. "I used the toilet, so now I wash my hands," says Vienna. The soap is white. Vienna rubs it on her hands. The bubbles look like little clouds.

Iris uses the toilet too. Then she runs to play with the blocks. "Wait, Iris!" says Vienna. "The toilet is still full!" Iris runs back. She forgot to flush. She presses the big button. Whoosh, the water swirls away. Then Iris washes her hands. She rubs the soap. She counts, "One, two, three." The water is warm and nice. Then Iris gets a crunchy cracker for snack time. She holds it with her clean hands. Crunch, crunch, crunch. Vienna smiles and sits down next to her.

Leo stood on the balcony. He had a big orange pot. In the pot was a little lettuce plant. Leo patted the soil with his hands. "Grow, grow," he said.

The sun came. The sun was hot. Leo played inside with his friend Alexie. They built a tower of blocks. It fell down. They laughed and built it again.

The next morning, Leo ran to the pot. The lettuce was drooping. Its leaves hung down like sad little arms. "Oh no," said Leo. He filled his watering can. He gave the plant a drink. Water dripped down into the soil.

Leo waited. He watched. Slowly the leaves lifted up. They stood tall and green. "It wanted a drink, like me!" said Leo. Alexie clapped. Ms. Bennett, from the next balcony, gave a thumbs up. Leo held the watering can high. "More water tomorrow, my friend!"

Raphael was at school. He had made a real clay star. It was red and shiny.

Then Brooklyn bumped the table. The star fell down. It broke into two pieces.

Raphael felt angry. His face got hot. He sat down and did not talk.

Mr. Clarke-Williams came over. He said, "Raphael, your face looks angry. Is that right?"

"Yes," said Raphael. "I feel angry. My star broke."

Mr. Clarke-Williams picked up the pieces. "Can you tell me what would help?" he asked.

"Fix it," said Raphael.

"Good idea," said Mr. Clarke-Williams. He got the glue. He put it on the edges. He pressed the pieces together. They fit!

Raphael watched the star dry. He felt happy now.

Brooklyn said, "I feel sad I broke your star."

"It is okay," said Raphael. "It is fixed now."

Raphael held his star up to the light. "Look, it still shines," he said.

Alexis ran to Grandpa's house. His new baby sister was here. He wanted to hold her right away. He had been waiting all day.

He ran inside from the yard. His hands were dirty. There was mud on them. His mom said, "Stop right there, big brother." She said, "Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby."

Alexis looked at his hands. They were very muddy. "Even this much mud?" he asked. "Even a little mud," said his mom. She did not sound mean. She sounded like a teacher, kind and calm.

So Alexis went to the sink. He scrubbed and scrubbed. He made soap bubbles. He blew one off his hand. Grandpa laughed and gave him a towel.

Then the clean hands worked their magic. His mom put the baby in his arms. The baby grabbed his finger. She held on tight. "She likes me," Alexis whispered. Grandpa took a picture. The baby still held the finger.

text:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. He liked it there. He liked the big chair. He liked the soft rug.

"Let's play a game," said Grandma. "Name your five senses. Tell me the body part you use." Aaron tried. "Ears," he said. "Ears hear." "Good!" said Grandma. "Now eyes." "Eyes see," said Aaron. "Eyes see. Ears hear. Eyes see."

Then Aaron smelled something sweet. He could not see anything. But he knew that smell. "Cookies!" he said. "Grandma, your nose game is fun, but I smell cookies." He followed the smell. His nose led him down the hall. His nose led him to the kitchen. There stood Grandma, taking a hot pan from the oven with her big mitts. Aaron stayed back, safe by the door.

"My nose knew first!" said Aaron. "I smelled cookies before I saw them." Grandma laughed. "Yes, your nose can smell some things before you can see them." Aaron clapped. "Nose smells. Eyes see. Ears hear." He pointed. "Tongue tastes. Hands touch." Grandma gave him a cookie when it cooled. Aaron took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "Five senses, one cookie."

Jasper wants to make a number poster for home. He gets paper and crayons. Mr. Popal helps him set up the table. Jasper writes one, two, three, four, five. Each number fits in its own small box. Then he counts on. Six, seven, eight, nine. Still one number in each box. Now Jasper needs ten. He looks at the last box. He writes a 1 in it. Then he stops. Ten needs more room. He shows Mr. Popal. "Ten is written with a 1 and then a 0," says Mr. Popal. Jasper looks hard. Ten takes two digits. The other numbers take only one. His box is too small for both.

Jasper thinks. Then he runs to get tape. He tapes a new strip of paper on the end. Now there is a big box. He writes the 1, then the 0. Ten fits at last. Jad and Davina come to see. They count all the numbers together. One, two, three, all the way to ten. Davina points at the end. "That one is the longest," she says. Jasper smiles and holds his poster up high. "It can hang by my door at home," he says.

Zoe went to the health clinic with her mom. Mr. Cheung, the friendly nurse, said, "First we check how much you weigh." Zoe stepped on the scale. She wiggled her toes. She waved her arms. The numbers jumped up and down. "Why does it keep moving?" Zoe asked. "Try standing still and see," said Mr. Cheung. Zoe planted her feet. She held her arms at her sides. She stood as still as a statue in a garden. The numbers stopped jumping. One number stayed put. "The scale shows how much you weigh," said Mr. Cheung. Zoe smiled. "That number is me!"

Next it was time for her shot. Zoe felt scared. Mr. Cheung opened a small drawer. He took out a tiny bandage with stars on it. "Can I sit very still too?" Zoe asked. "Yes," said her mom. "Still like a statue." Zoe held her arm steady. She looked at her mom, not at the needle. It was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done. Mr. Cheung put the star bandage on her arm. "You stood still twice today," he said. Zoe held up her arm and said, "Look, Mom! Stars!"

Olivier was at Grandma's house. He could not find his little blue car. "Where did you go, car?" he called.

He looked under the big chair. No car. He looked by the door. No car. Then he saw something round under the sofa. He pulled it out. It was his ball, not his car. What was that next to the ball? A little blue corner! "I found you!" said Olivier. His car had rolled under the sofa with the ball. The ball was big, so it stopped first. The car rolled far, far back.

Grandma came in with a basket. "Here is a home for your car," she said. Olivier put the car in the basket. He set the basket by his bed. The next morning, Olivier looked in the basket. There was his car, right where he put it. "Naughty sofa, you can't hide my car now," he said, and he rolled it down the hall to the park picture on the wall.

Jaxson ran into the kitchen. "Cookies for breakfast!" he said.

His dad shook his head. "Cookies are not breakfast," he said. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day. We eat it when we wake up."

Jaxson frowned. He woke up. He wanted cookies. "Cookies, cookies, cookies," he said.

"Let's pick the first meal together," said Dad. He held up an egg. Jaxson shook his head. Dad held up a banana. Jaxson giggled and wiggled it like a phone. "Hello, banana!" he said.

Dad cooked the egg on the stove. Jaxson watched from his chair. Then Dad peeled the banana and cut it. Slice, slice, slice.

Jaxson took a bite. "Mmm," he said. "Banana is yummy." He took another bite of egg.

"See?" said Dad. "The first meal can be yummy too."

Jaxson smiled. "But can I have a cookie later?"

"After lunch," said Dad.

"Okay," said Jaxson. He hugged the banana peel. "Bye bye, banana!"

Joshua went to the park with his red ball. His soft bunny came too. Joshua put bunny on the bench. Then he ran to play.

Bethany threw the ball. It was hard to catch. Joshua laughed and threw it back. Legend ran to get it. They played a long time.

Then Joshua looked for bunny. Bunny was gone. Joshua felt sad. He looked under the bench. No bunny.

Mr. Francis walked over. He held a bunny in his arms. "This tag says Joshua," he said. "So I knew it was yours." Joshua hugged bunny tight.

The tag had letters on it. His dad had written his name there. Now Joshua knew. A name on the tag helps bunny come home.

"Let's share the ball now," Joshua said. Bethany smiled and threw it high.

Zoe sat in the big waiting room chair. Her sneakers swung back and forth. The room smelled like soap. A fish tank bubbled softly in the corner. Today Zoe had to get a shot.

Hanna from her class sat there too. "I am not even sick," said Hanna. "Why do we need a shot?"

The doctor came in and smiled. "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said.

Zoe thought about that. So the shot was like a special shield. It kept her body safe before any sickness came.

"Me first," said Zoe. She held Hanna's hand. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done!

Afterward, Zoe got a shiny band aid and a sticker of a star. She and Hanna skipped down the hall together, holding their stickers up high.

"I am protected," said Zoe.

Lena wanted to read the bear book at daycare. She sat on the little rug. She opened the book and looked at it.

The bear looked funny. His feet were up. His head was down. Lena laughed. "Silly bear!" she said.

Frederic came to sit with her. He looked at the book too. "The words look funny too," he said. "They are upside down."

Lena turned the book around. Now the bear stood on his feet. The words stood up too. "Better," said Lena. She turned one page, then the next page. She went from the front to the back.

Mr. Rajapakse sat down beside her. "Read to me," he said. Lena tapped each word with one finger. "Bear eats honey," she said. Then she turned the page. "Bear kicks the ball!" At snack time, Lena used her spoon to eat yogurt. Then she picked up the book again. "This way up," she said, and she opened the front cover.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything was dark. Kai wanted his teddy bear in the kitchen.

"I will run and get him!" said Kai.

Kai ran in the dark. Bump! His leg hit a chair. "Ow," said Kai.

Dad came with a big flashlight. "In the dark, we walk slowly," said Dad. "And you hold my hand so nobody trips."

Kai held Dad's hand. They took one slow step. Then another slow step. The kitchen door was right there.

Dad shined the light on a chair. They stepped around it together. No bump this time!

"There is Bear!" said Kai. He hugged him tight.

The lights came back on. "Yay!" said Kai. "We can have a pretend party now!"

Kai found his party hat. It was red and pretty. He put it on Bear.

"More steps, Dad?" asked Kai. Dad laughed and clapped his hands.

Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. Mr. Santoso held up a big card. "This is the recipe," he said. "One, mix the flour. Two, add the milk. Three, add the egg. Four, cook the pancakes."

Max looked at the card. He could not read yet. So he mixed the flour. He added the milk. Then he thought, "The egg is too cold!" Max skipped the egg. He skipped step three.

Mr. Santoso poured the batter onto the pan. The pancakes stayed flat, flat, flat. "Oh no," said Max. His tummy felt sad. "My pancakes are flat like the rain on the sidewalk!"

Kieran looked at the card. "Step three is the egg," he said. Max got the egg. He cracked it in the bowl. Kieran laughed. "You have batter on your nose!"

They mixed again. One, the flour. Two, the milk. Three, the egg. Max said each step out loud. "One, two, three!"

This time the pancakes puffed up big and fat. Kelly clapped her hands. "They look like little clouds!" Max carried the plate to his family. Dad took a big bite. "Yum," said Dad. Max grinned. "I read the recipe, Dad!"

It was Evan's first day of school. Mr. Rao rang a little bell. "Time to walk inside," he said. All the children stood in a line, one behind the other. Evan did not know about the line. He ran ahead, fast, all by himself. The door was heavy. His foot got stuck on the step, and he almost fell.

Mr. Rao came to help. He held Evan's hand. "See the line," said Felix. Felix pointed at the children walking one behind the other. Evan looked. The line moved like a long train. Evan stepped in behind Sidney. He put one hand on Sidney's shoulder, soft and light.

The line walked and walked. It went up the steps, easy as pie. Nobody got stuck. Nobody had to stop. Evan smiled at Felix. "We walk together," said Evan. Then the whole line went inside, one, two, three, through the big door.

Eliana was at home with her friend Ruby. They played with blocks in the living room. The blocks made a big, tall tower. It smelled like lemon soap nearby, because Mama had just cleaned the table.

Then the tower fell down with a crash. Blocks rolled under the chair. Ruby stood up and walked to the sofa. Eliana wished Ruby would come back. "The blocks are everywhere," Eliana said. Ruby looked at the floor. Then she came back. Ruby picked up the red blocks. Eliana picked up the blue ones. The blocks felt hard and cool in her hands.

They put all the blocks in the box. It was their mess, so they cleaned it. Then Mama gave them each a crayon and a pencil. "You tidied up your toys," Mama said with a smile. Eliana drew a picture of the tall tower. Ruby drew herself next to it. "We build it again tomorrow," said Ruby.

Edouard ran to the playroom. Atreus was there with five toy monkeys. "Let's sing!" said Atreus. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

They sang together. Then one monkey fell off. Atreus put it under the bed. "Now we sing four!" he said. Edouard counted the monkeys on the bed. "One, two, three, four," he said. Four monkeys were left.

They sang again. One monkey fell off again. Atreus put it under the bed too. "Four, then three!" said Edouard. The number got one smaller each time! He jumped up and down. "Sing more! Sing more!"

They sang and sang. Three, then two, then one. At last the bed held one monkey all alone. Edouard put the last monkey under the bed. "Zero monkeys!" he said. Atreus laughed. Meadow came over with a small broom. She swept pretend dirt off the bed. "Time for new monkeys!" she said. Edouard turned the bed around. He put all five monkeys back on top. "One, two, three, four, five!" he sang.

Ibrahim woke up in his big bed. The sun was in the window. His dad said, "Morning time! Let's eat, then brush your teeth." Ibrahim ate his egg. Then he brushed his teeth. "One, two, scrub, scrub, scrub," he said. His teeth felt clean and good.

It was a cold day. His dad made a fire in the fireplace. Ibrahim watched from far away. The fire crackled. The room got warm. "Good and warm," said Ibrahim. He played cars on the rug. Then he had a bath. The bubbles went pop, pop. His mom helped him wash. Then he put on his soft pajamas.

Dad read him a story. Ibrahim got in bed. Dad turned off the light. Then Ibrahim popped back up. "My teeth!" he said. He had not brushed them. He ran to the sink. He brushed and brushed. "One, two, scrub, scrub, scrub." Then he hopped into bed and closed his eyes. "Good night, Dad," he said.

Rowan wanted to make cookies. His mom said yes. First they washed their hands. Then Rowan helped pour the sugar. A little bit did spill on the floor. Mom wiped it up. "We can try again," she said.

Mom rolled the dough flat. She gave Rowan some cutters. One was a square. One was a triangle. One was a rectangle. The last one was round. "Which one is this?" Mom asked. "A circle," said Rowan.

Rowan pressed the square cutter down. Out came a square cookie. It had corners. He counted them with his finger. Then he pressed the circle cutter. Out came a round cookie. Rowan looked for a corner on it. He turned the cookie all around. No corners at all. He turned it again. Still no corners at all!

Rowan set the circle cookie on the table. It began to spin. Then it rolled right off the edge! "Catch it!" Rowan laughed. Mom caught it in her hand. "Round things like to roll," she said. Rowan put the circle cookie safely on the tray. "No corners at all," he said, and gave it one more little spin.

Joshua sat in the music classroom. Ms. MacLeod had a big piano. Joshua wanted to play a growly bear sound. He pushed a key near the middle. It made a light, tinkly sound. That was not a bear. That was more like a little bird.

Joshua tried again. He pushed a key on the left side. Boom! The sound was low and deep. "That is my bear!" said Joshua. Ms. MacLeod smiled and nodded. Joshua ran his fingers along the left side. Low sounds came out, one after another. Then he tried a key on the right side. Pling! That one was high. A tiny mouse sound!

Joshua played low bear steps on the left. Then he played high mouse hops on the right. Amaya and Noura clapped. "Play it again," said Amaya. Joshua played his bear and his mouse all the way to the end. Then Ms. MacLeod said, "Time to stop and line up."

"I will play my bear tomorrow," said Joshua.

Nathan stood at the edge of the lake. The water was cool and clear. Small waves went tap, tap, tap on his toes. He wanted to jump in. He wanted to splash and kick.

His friend Vincent came running. "Let's jump now," said Vincent. Nathan looked around. No grown-up was there. Not Ms. Kaya. Not a parent. Nobody was watching the water. So Nathan sat down on the grass. "We wait," he said. A cow stood far away by the trees. It looked at them with big soft eyes.

Soon Ms. Kaya walked up. "I am here and I can see you," she said. "Now we can bathe in the water and practice swimming." Nathan held her hand. He stepped in slowly. He kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. "You are swimming," said Ms. Kaya. Nathan was happy. Vincent clapped his hands by the shore.
