text:
Zachary sat on the big rug in the living room. The tablet sat on the low table. He wanted to draw a red fire truck.

First he pressed the round button. The screen lit up. "I did it," he said. Then he tapped the little paintbrush. The drawing app opened. He picked red and drew fast circles for the wheels.

Morgan came over to watch. "Can I see the fire truck?" Morgan asked. "Yes," said Zachary. "Look at the big wheels." Then the screen went black. All the red was gone.

"Why did it go dark?" Morgan asked. Zachary thought. "Maybe it used up all its power," he said. "A tablet runs out of power after being used." His dad came in with the charger. "It needs charging," Dad said. He plugged it in, and Zachary watched from the rug.

They drank apple juice while they waited. Soon the screen lit up again. The fire truck was still there, red wheels and all. Zachary drew the ladder, nice and slow. Then he pressed the button and the screen went dark the right way. He did not forget to put the tablet back on the table. Morgan waved goodbye at the door. "Same time tomorrow?" Morgan asked. "Yes," said Zachary. "I will draw a school bus next."

Arthur was on the city bus with his dad. Snow fell past the window. Arthur looked in his bag. His little bunny was not there. "Where did bunny go?" he asked.

"I ran all over the house this morning," Arthur said. "I looked in every room so fast." Mr. Rossi, the driver, heard him. "Try one room at a time," said Mr. Rossi. "That helps you not miss any places." Arthur and his dad rode the bus home.

First they looked in the kitchen. No bunny. Then they looked in Arthur's room. No bunny under the bed. Then the living room. There was bunny, on the neat shelf, next to a book! Some dirt from Arthur's shoes sat under him. Arthur hugged bunny tight. "One room at a time," said Arthur. "We found you!"

Sofia put on her coat at the bank. The big doors opened. Cold air came in. "Time to go, Sofia," said her dad.

Sofah grabbed the zipper tab. She pulled it up. The zipper did not move. She pulled again. Still nothing. Her dad was waiting at the door. Snow began to fall outside the glass. Little white flakes floated past the window. Sofia wanted to zip up fast.

She looked down at her coat. The two sides were apart. One side had a little box at the bottom. The other side had a small end. "I wonder what that box is for," Sofia said. She pushed the small end into the little box. It clicked in. Then she pulled the tab. Up went the zipper, all the way to her chin!

"I did it, Dad!" she called. Her dad smiled and held the door. Sofia stepped out into the snow. The wind was cold, but her tummy felt warm and strong, not one bit weak. She zipped her coat again, just to hear the zip, zip, zip.

Amira sat at the big table at math club. Ms. Tran put out two buckets of blocks. "Which bucket has more?" she asked. Amira peeked in. One bucket had four blocks. One bucket had five blocks. Amira wanted to know. She hoped she could figure it out.

"Let me count," said Amira. She touched each block in the first bucket. "One, two, three, four." Then she counted the other bucket. "One, two, three, four, five." Lambert leaned in close. "That one has more," he said, pointing. "It has five!"

Then Cameron gave Amira one block from his pile. Amira dropped it into her bucket. Now she counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." She clapped her hands. "Four and one more makes five!"

Ms. Tran smiled. "You are ready for the next game," she said. She put a big pile of blocks in the middle of the table. Amira reached for the first one.

Iris went to her dad's office. She wanted to draw a monkey. Dad gave her the tablet. "The small pictures are called icons," he said. Iris looked at the screen. She saw many little icons. She tapped one. It was not the drawing app. It was a map. She tapped the top corner. The map went away. Then she saw a paintbrush icon. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. Iris drew a big brown monkey with a long tail. She gave it a banana too. "Nice monkey," said Lexie, who sat at the next desk. Iris drew a small rip on the monkey's banana leaf. Then she pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in the drawer, all by herself. "All done," she said.

Emmett went to the grocery store with his dad. "We need eggs," said his dad. Emmett put the egg carton in the cart. The eggs sat still in their little beds. At home, Emmett wanted to make dinner for his family. "Eggs for everyone!" he said.

His dad let him help at the counter. The stove stayed off for now. Emmett held an egg. He tapped it on the edge of the bowl. The shell cracked. He pulled it open, and the egg slid out into the bowl. A tiny bit of shell fell in too. Emmett took a spoon. He fished the piece out, slow and careful. It took two tries. Then he got it.

His dad cooked the eggs in the pan. Emmett waited and watched. The eggs turned from wet to firm. Soon the family sat down to eat. "Tasty!" said Emmett's dad. Emmett smiled and took a big bite.

Weston sat at the dinner table. His mac and cheese was warm and yummy. Outside, rain pattered like a little storm. Then came a knock at the door.

Weston hid under the table. His blanket tickled his nose. Dad opened the door. It was Mr. Aydın from next door. He had a big bowl of strawberries. "Hello, Mr. Aydın," said Dad.

Weston peeked out. One eye, then two. Mr. Aydın waved at him. Weston crawled out and stood by his chair. "Hello," said Weston, very small. Mr. Aydın smiled a big smile. "Hello, Weston! Would you like a strawberry?"

"Yes, please," said Weston. He held the red strawberry. It looked like a tiny magic hat. He ate it in one bite. "Thank you," said Weston. Then he bumped his cup and water spilled. "Sorry," said Weston. Dad helped him wipe it up.

Mr. Aydın sat down with them. "Hello, everybody," he said. Weston laughed. Hello was a happy word. It made people smile. Weston waved his spoon like a wand. "Hello, mac and cheese," he said.

Rowan ran to the playground. The sun felt warm on his shirt. He heard a whoosh, whoosh, whoosh above the trees.

Raven was there. She held a big red kite. The string pulled in her hands. The kite jumped in the wind.

Rowan wanted the kite very much. He reached out and grabbed at the string. The kite wobbled. It dipped down low.

"Wait," said Raven. Her voice was small and a little scared. "Please don't pull."

"Sorry," said Rowan. He let go. He put his hands behind his back.

Then he heard his dad call from the bench. "Rowan, try asking. Say, may I have a turn?"

Rowan took a soft breath. "Raven, may I have a turn?"

Raven smiled big. "Yes! May I is a nice way to ask." She put the string in his hands.

The kite went up, up, up. Rowan felt the wind pull. One hand, two hands, hold tight. "Thank you, Raven!" he called.

"Thank you for asking," said Raven. She held his elbow so he would not tip.

The red kite sailed over the swings. It sailed over the slide. Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, it sang.

Then it was Raven's turn again. "May I?" she asked.

"Yes!" said Rowan. And the string flew back to her like a friendly bird.

Miles stood in the pool changing room. He put his towel in the big basket. Then he put on his swim pants. "Where do we get in?" Miles asked. "Watch the water," said the coach.

At the pool, Miles saw his friend Mikhail. Mikhail went down the steps. Splash! The steps helped him get in. Miles went down the steps too. The water was warm. "This is fun!" said Miles.

After swimming, Miles tried to climb out over the edge. His arms were too small. His tummy got stuck. "Try the ladder," said Mikhail. Miles put his feet on the ladder. Step, step, step. He was out! "The ladder helps me get out," said Miles. "Sorry, edge. You are too tall for me." Mikhail laughed. On the wall, a picture of an owl looked down at them. "Swim again next week?" said Mikhail. "Yes!" said Miles.

Jules stood in the kitchen. He was hungry. He wanted warm toast. Mom put bread in the toaster. Jules watched with his eyes. The bread popped up high. "Pop!" said Jules.

Then he heard a knock at the door. He used his ears. It was his friend Rhea. "Toast!" said Rhea. "I smell it with my nose." Jules sniffed too. The toast smelled warm and good. Mom gave them each a piece. Jules touched it with his fingers. The top was bumpy. He took a bite. It tasted sweet with jam.

"Rhea, how many openings does your nose have?" asked Jules. "I don't know," said Rhea. Mom said, "Those openings are called nostrils." Jules ran to the little mirror. He looked and looked. He counted one, two. "Two nostrils!" he said. "Me too!" said Rhea. Then they sniffed their toast at the same time. "I can smell with both," said Jules. They giggled and ate the last bite.

Mohamed sat in his car seat. The car went zoom down the road. "We are going home," said Dad. "Then I will cook soup on the stove." Mohamed loved soup. "Is the stove hot now?" he asked. Dad said, "You can help me see." The car stopped. The parking spot was empty, so Dad pulled right in. They walked in together, Mohamed staying close to Dad's hand. In the kitchen, Dad turned the stove on. Mohamed looked at the stove. It looked just the same as before. "Is it hot?" Mohamed asked. "Let's find out," said Dad. Dad held a spoon of butter above it. Sizzle, sizzle! The butter melted fast. "Wow," said Mohamed. "It was hot even when it looked cold." Dad stirred the soup, and Mohamed watched from his chair. "Can I talk to the soup?" he asked. Dad laughed. "Sure," he said. "Tell it to yum."

Florence stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. Benson was there too. A hoop lay on the grass. "Watch me," said Florence. She threw the beanbag. It landed outside the hoop. Benson threw his beanbag. His landed in the hoop.

"I want it in," said Florence. She picked up the beanbag. She stood closer. She threw again. This time the beanbag went in. Florence clapped her hands. "Good try," said Benson. "You got it in!"

Then Mr. Van Dijk came out with a big blue ball. "Catch," he said. He rolled it to Benson. Benson caught it with both hands. Then he rolled it to Florence. Florence held out one hand, like a big kid. The ball bumped her hand and fell on the grass. "Oh no," said Florence.

Mr. Van Dijk rolled the ball again. This time Florence held out both hands. The ball went right into them. She caught it! "I did it," said Florence. She laughed and hugged the big ball. Just then, the wind began to blow. Benson's hat flew off his head and landed inside the hoop. Everyone laughed. "Now the hat is in the hoop too," said Benson.

David climbed the big school bus. It was his very first day of school. He held the tall rail and walked to a seat. His friend Amayra sat by the window. "Sit with me!" she said. David sat down fast. The bus rumbled and off they went.

At school, everyone lined up. Ms. Navarro smiled at the door. "Welcome, class," she said. David hung his bag on his hook. Then he painted a red cat with Amayra. He built a tall tower with Cassie. School was fun!

Then David needed to use the bathroom. He looked around. Where was it? He did not see it anywhere. His tummy felt tight. He asked himself, "What do I do?" He thought and thought. Amayra was painting. Cassie was building. He could not ask them.

Then David walked to Ms. Navarro. "I need help," he said. "Where is the bathroom?" She took his hand. "Come with me," she said. "If you need help at school, you can ask the teacher." The bathroom was right down the hall. David washed his hands all by himself.

Later, Cassie lost her crayon. "What do I do?" she said. David ran to Ms. Navarro. "Please help Cassie!" he said. Ms. Navarro found the crayon under the table. The bell rang, and David waved to Amayra. "See you tomorrow!" he said.

Everett sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted the tiger sticker on the desk. But first, the doctor had to check him.

"Can you see my light?" asked the doctor. Everett looked with his eyes. "Yes! It is bright." Then he heard a tick tock with his ears. It was a clock on the wall. He touched a wet cotton ball with his fingers. It felt soft and cold. He smelled soap. It came from his hands.

"Now your tongue," said the doctor. She held out a lemon slice. Everett thought it would taste sweet like orange juice. He put it on his tongue. He scrunched up his whole face! "Sour!" he said. The doctor laughed. "Sour, sour, sour," said Everett, and he giggled too.

The doctor said, "All done, big man." She put the tiger sticker right on Everett's shirt. Everett climbed down from the big chair. He waved to the doctor at the door. "Bye, bye!" he said. Then he rubbed his new sticker with one finger. It was smooth, and it was all his.

Evelyn sat at the big art table. She was painting a picture. It had a round sun and a little lion. The lion stood on green grass.

But Evelyn had no green paint. She looked in her cup. Only blue paint. She looked in the other cup. Only yellow paint. "I need green," she said.

Inaya sat next to her. Inaya pointed at the cups. "Put some blue in the yellow," said Inaya. Evelyn dipped her brush. She put blue paint into the yellow cup. She stirred it round and round with her brush.

The paint turned green! Evelyn gasped. Blue and yellow made green. She painted the grass fast. The grass was bright and soft. The lion stood on it now.

Mr. Doyle came to look. "What nice green grass," he said. Evelyn held up her brush. "I made it myself," she said. "Blue and yellow made green." Shanaya clapped her hands. Evelyn painted one more big patch of green.

Madelyn sat at the table. She wanted juice. "Give me juice!" she said. Dad did not get the juice. He just looked at her.

Madelyn tried again. "Give me juice, please." Dad smiled. He got the cup. He poured the juice. Madelyn drank it all up.

The next morning, Madelyn wanted her red shoe. It was under the chair. She could not reach it. "Help, please," she said to Dad. Dad got the shoe. "Thank you," said Madelyn.

Later, Madelyn ran fast in the hall. She bumped into the cat. The cat woke up. It was not asleep anymore. "Sorry, cat," said Madelyn. She patted the cat softly. The cat purred.

At nap time, Madelyn wanted her bear. It was on the bed. "Bear, please come here," she said. Dad laughed. He got the bear for her. Madelyn hugged the bear tight. Then she closed her eyes. Outside, a dog began to bark. Madelyn did not hear it. She was fast asleep.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her father set down the plates. The plates made a bumpy stack. Zoey's tummy felt excited. Tonight was pasta night.

Then Zoey looked at her big sister. Tears ran down her sister's face. "Why are you crying?" Zoey asked. "I feel sad today," her sister said. Zoey remembered her friend Bonnie. Bonnie felt sad at school once. Bonnie cried too.

Zoey slid down from her chair. She ran to her room. She grabbed her soft bunny. The bunny had long ears to chase and squeeze. She ran back on her bumpy socks. "Here," said Zoey. "Bunny can sit with you." Her sister smiled a little. She held the bunny close. Her tears stopped. "Thank you, Zoey," she said. "Now I feel a bit happy." Zoey grinned. The bunny got a big share of pasta sniffles that night.

Snow was falling outside the window. Kinsley had made paint footprints on paper with her blue paint. She made a snowman with five round paint toes at the bottom. Now she wanted to show it to her dad.

Her paper slipped behind the couch. Kinsley got down on her knees. She reached way in. Her hand touched the wall. There was a little white box there. It had small dark holes. She thought she could poke a finger in to feel it.

Her mom came fast and held her hand. "No, sweet one," Mom said softly. "We never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet." Mom reached in herself. She pulled out the paper. She slid the couch a little, so the box was hidden again. "That box is for plugs. Only grown-ups touch it," said Mom.

Kinsley held her snowman painting up. Dad clapped his hands. "A paint snowman on a snow day," he said. "Is that true, did you make this all by yourself?" Kinsley nodded big. She hung it on the fridge with a magnet, way up high where her little brother could not reach.

Zayn got some mail. It was a card with his own name on it. "It is a library card," said his dad. "It lets you borrow a book." Zayn put on one shoe. Then the other shoe. "Oops, wrong feet!" said Dad. They laughed and swapped them. Then they walked to the library.

Zayn found a book about a juicy red strawberry. He held out his card. Beep! The librarian smiled. "The book is yours to take home," she said. At home, Dad read it three times. Then Zayn read it all by himself. Soon the book was done. "We need a new one," said Zayn.

Back they went. Zayn gave the strawberry book back. Then he held out his card again. Beep! Now he had a book about a big blue whale. "My card works again!" said Zayn. "And again and again," said Dad. At home, Zayn hugged the card tight. "Goodnight, card," he said.

Charlie woke up and peeked out the window. Snow was everywhere. "A snow day!" said his dad. Charlie put on his boots and his coat. He went outside to the snowy street.

Charlie wanted to make a snowman. He patted the snow into a ball. The ball fell apart. He tried again. The ball fell apart again. The snow was dry and soft. It would not stick. Alex came by with a sled. "My snowman keeps falling down," said Charlie. "Try again later," said Alex. Charlie waited. He watched the snow on his mittens. It began to melt a little. The snow got a little wet.

Charlie patted the wet snow into a ball. It stuck! He rolled it and rolled it. It grew big. He patted another ball for the middle. It stuck too. Charlie gave the snowman a stick arm and a hat. He rubbed his cold ear and smiled. "Hello, snowman," said Charlie.

Carter sat on the soft rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Lili sat next to him. Eleonore sat by the couch. Dad made popcorn in the kitchen, and the smell filled the room.

"Where is the ball?" asked Carter. He looked hard at the screen. The players had sticks, but no ball. Then he saw it. It was small and flat. It slid on the ice. "It is not a ball," said Carter. "That is a puck," said Lili. A player hit the puck with his stick. The puck zoomed far across the ice. Then it went into the net. Everyone jumped up. "They scored!" said Carter.

Mr. Thompson, the neighbour, smiled from his chair. The clock on the wall said it was almost bedtime. Carter hugged his dad good night. "This game is different from soccer," Carter said. "I like the puck."

Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table with her toast. Her nose began to run. Drip, drip. Victoria sniffed it back. One sniff. Two sniffs. Three.

Then her nose ran again. Drip, drip. Victoria sniffed and sniffed. It did not help. The drips came back.

Mama looked over. "Your nose is runny," she said. "Ask for a tissue."

"A tissue, please," said Victoria.

Mama gave her one soft tissue. Victoria wiped her nose. One wipe. Two wipes. All dry. No more drips.

Victoria looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. She hoped she could play under the big tree soon.

Her nose ran again. Victoria held up the tissue herself. "Tissue, please," she said.

"Good asking," said Mama, and she smiled.

Naomi sat on her bed at bedtime. She held her beautiful book about a dragon. But she had a problem. "Who made up this story?" she asked her dad.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Look at the front cover," he said. Naomi looked. There was a name in little letters. "That name is the author," said Dad. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book."

Naomi touched the name with one finger. "Someone wrote these words," she said. "Then the words turned into a dragon!" She opened the book at the front. First page, second page, third page. The dragon came out on the fourth page. It was green with purple toes.

"One page, two pages, three pages, four," she said. Dad laughed and kissed her head. She read to the very last page. Then Naomi held the book tight. "Good night, dragon," she whispered. "Good night, author."

Alexander went to the baby store with his dad. A new baby sister was coming soon. Alexander wanted to pick a toy for her. He found a big red ball. "She can spin it," he said. "She can roll it too!"

Then he saw some tiny cups. They were slippery and shiny. He put one in the cart. His dad smiled and put the red ball in too.

At home, the baby came. Alexander held the ball up. "Wake up!" he said. But the baby was sleeping again. She had slept all morning. She slept after her milk. She slept in her cup time too. "When does she play?" Alexander asked.

Then one morning, the baby opened her eyes. Alexander spun the red ball. Slowly, slowly, the baby watched it turn. Her mouth made a little smile.

"Again," said Alexander. He gave the ball a soft push. "Spin, ball, spin."

Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and shiny. His dad held his hand. Logan wanted to swim like the big kids. But the water looked deep. He felt a little scared.

His dad said, "Hold the edge, Logan." Logan put his small hands on the cool wall. Then his dad said, "Kick your legs." Logan kicked and kicked. His legs made big splashes. The splashes were white and cold on his chin. He kicked so hard, water flew up and hit Mr. Esposito, the pool teacher. "Splash!" said Mr. Esposito, laughing and wiping his face. Logan laughed too. He was not scared anymore. He held on tight and kept kicking.

Then his dad picked him up. "You did it," his dad said. Logan looked at his cute yellow float toy bobbing in the water. "Kick more tomorrow?" he asked. His dad hugged him with a warm, soft towel. "Yes," he said. "Kick more tomorrow."

Milo ran to the library door. He saw a big sign with words on it. He pointed at the sign. "What do the words say?" he asked. Ms. Russo read them out loud. "They say, Story time at ten." Milo looked at the clock. It was almost ten.

Inside, Milo found Josh. Josh was holding a book upside down. The pictures looked wrong. The tree in the picture hung from the top of the page. Milo turned the book around. Now the tree stood up tall. "The front of the book goes first," said Josh. They opened the front cover together.

Milo picked a book about a busy bee. On the first page, the bee began to chase a red flower. Milo put his finger under the words. Ms. Russo read one word at a time. Slowly, slowly, page by page. Milo waited for each new page.

At the end, Milo ran to the shelf. He found a box marked with words. "This box says big books," he said. He read it all by himself. Josh clapped his hands.

The lights went out. Jules stood in the dark backyard. "I can't see anything," he said. Dad held his hand. Dad lit a little lamp, but it was far away by the door. Jules wanted his toy fish from the sandbox. He could not see it at all. "Wait a little," said Dad. So Jules waited. He counted softly, "One, two, three." The snow began to fall, tiny and white. Jules looked and looked. Slowly, slowly, he saw the big tree. Then he saw the swing. Then he saw the sandbox! "My eyes are working now," said Jules. He found the fish. It was not a real fish. It was orange and plastic and funny. "Hello, fish," said Jules. The snow tickled his nose, and he laughed.

Cooper put on his warm red hat. Today was the big hockey game! Mom held his hand at the ice rink. Cooper's friends Charles-Edouard and Elowen were already there, waving.

"Look, look!" said Cooper. A man in a striped shirt skated onto the ice. "Why does he have stripes?" asked Elowen. "He is the referee," said Mr. Santos-Reyes, who sat beside them. Cooper watched the referee skate round and round. He watched every player.

Then one player pushed another player. He fell down! The referee blew his whistle. It was loud. The pushing player had to sit out. "He did not follow the rules," said Charles-Edouard.

A player shot the puck. It went in! The crowd went wild. Cooper cheered and cheered. The referee watched the whole game and kept it fair.

After the game, Cooper got a hot chocolate from the stand. He held the warm cup with both hands. "When I grow up," said Cooper, "I want stripes too." Then he took a big slurp.

Layla was in her bed. It was dark outside. She held her teddy bear tight.

Then she heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. Layla felt scared. Her tummy felt small and tight. She hid under her blanket. The sound came again. Tap, tap, tap.

Layla had an idea. She could call for help. "Daddy!" she called. Daddy came fast. He sat on the bed. "I heard a noise," Layla said. "I am scared."

Daddy took her hand. They listened together. Tap, tap, tap. They walked to the window. Daddy opened the curtain a little. A tree branch was tapping on the glass. The wind made it move.

Layla looked at the branch. It looked different in the dark. In the day, it was just a small tree. "The tree says good night," she said. Daddy smiled. He built a snug nest of pillows for her bear.

Layla was not scared now. She felt happy and warm. She listened to the tap, tap, tap. Soon she closed her eyes and slept.

Grandma came to stay at Jaxon's house. She stayed for a whole week. They played in the backyard every day. They dug in the dirt. A long snake lay in the sun. "Is the snake afraid of us?" Jaxon asked. "No," said Grandma. "It slides away because we are big."

Then the week was done. Grandma packed her bag. She waved and drove away. Jaxon felt sad. He sat on the back step.

"What can we do now?" he asked his dad. "We can call her," said Dad. "On the phone?" asked Jaxon. "Yes. We can hear her voice." Jaxon called Grandma. He heard her say hello. The next day they made a video call. Jaxon saw her face on the screen. Then Jaxon drew a snake in the sun. Dad put the picture in an envelope. It was a letter for Grandma. Jaxon ran to the mailbox with it.

Edouard sat in the music room. Mr. Liu said, "Today we clap and sing." Edouard wanted to sing the whole song. But he forgot the words. His brother could sing it at home. Why not Edouard?

Nayla clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. The drum beat went slow and steady. Edouard clapped too. When he clapped, the beat got easier to feel. Clap, clap, clap. He tried the song again. The words still ran away.

"Is there a short song?" Edouard asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Liu. "A nursery rhyme. It is short, and it rhymes."

So they sang a nursery rhyme. It was not long at all. Edouard clapped the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Then the words came out too! He sang it all by himself. Avery laughed and clapped with him.

"Again!" said Edouard. "Again, again!"

They sang it one more time, all together, and Edouard did not miss one word.

Milan went to the store with his mom. There was a little shelf of books by the door. Milan saw a blue book with a truck on it. He wanted that book very much.

He picked it up. He opened the front cover. Then he turned more pages, one by one. He held it the right way, front to back, like his books at home. On the big page at the front, he saw words. "What does that say?" he asked his mom.

"That is the title," she said. "Blue Truck. The title is the book's name."

The store man could not find another copy for Alisa's birthday. "Do you know the title?" he asked Milan.

"It is called Blue Truck," said Milan.

The man went to fetch one from the back room. He came back with the book. Milan held it tight all the way home. "Alisa will like her Blue Truck," he said.

The sun was big and hot. Madison stood on the basketball court. Her team was playing a game today. Braxton ran by her. "It is so hot," he said. "I think my face is red." Madison felt warm too. Her hands were dry. Her throat felt dry too.

The coach blew the whistle. "Break time," he called. The players ran to the bench. Braxton picked up his water bottle. He drank and drank. Phillip drank his water too. Madison looked in her bag. She looked again. "Where is my bottle?" she asked. "Did I leave it at home?" She had left it on the kitchen table.

Mr. Bekele, the coach, saw her empty hands. He went to his big cooler. He filled a paper cup with cool water. He brought it over. "Here you go, Madison," he said. "Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days." Madison held the cup. The water was cold. She drank it all. It felt good in her dry throat.

The whistle blew again. Madison ran back on the court. She bounced the ball. She felt fast now. The water had made her feel new. She shot the ball. It went in! "Nice shot," said Braxton. Madison smiled big. At the next break, she was the first one in line for water.

Beatrice sat at Grandma's big soft chair. On the table was Grandma's tablet. "Can I make a picture?" Beatrice asked.

Grandma held the tablet up. "You tap the screen with your finger to choose things," she said. Beatrice pressed her whole hand on the screen. She pressed and pressed. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark.

"Try one finger," said Grandma. "A little tap." Beatrice tapped with one finger. Tap! The screen lit up. There was the drawing app, like a little red ball on the screen. She tapped the ball. The app opened. Beatrice drew a cat, then a sun, then a big blue sweep of sky.

"Grandma, look! My finger did it!" she said. When she was done, she tapped the small X and put the tablet on the table. "All done," said Beatrice.

It was Ava's first day at school. Her mom held her hand. "Will I find a friend?" Ava asked. "Yes, you will," her mom said.

In the classroom, Ms. Nowak smiled. "Time for the playground," she said. Ava saw a big slide. She ran to it fast. She went down, down, down. Then she ran to the top again.

A boy named Louis-Philippe stood there. "We take turns on the slide," he said. Ava looked. A line of kids stood waiting. Ava got in the back. She waited. She watched. Then it was her turn again. Whee! She got to go two whole times.

Later, the class ate bread for a snack. Ava sat with Louis-Philippe and a girl named Agamveer. Agamveer had pink shoes, just like Ava's.

"What a surprise," Ava said. "We match!"

Ms. Nowak laughed. Ava had learned a lot today. She had two new friends. At pick-up time, her mom waved at the door. Ava ran to her with a big smile. "Mom, I slid down the slide!"

Adam was at the playground. He saw a big red truck. Hunter was holding it. Adam wanted the truck.

Adam grabbed the truck. He pulled it out of Hunter's hands. Hunter's face got sad. Hunter started to cry. His face turned red and he stomped his foot. Adam looked at Hunter. Adam did not want Hunter to cry.

Adam gave the truck back. "Truck?" he asked. Hunter wiped his eyes. "Yes," said Hunter. "My turn first." Adam sat down on the step to wait. It was hard to wait. He watched the truck go zoom, zoom on the ground. Ms. Bear smiled at Adam. "Good waiting, Adam," she said.

Then Hunter ran over. "Your turn now," said Hunter. Adam held the truck. He made it go fast. "Thank you," said Adam. Hunter sat down to wait too. The two boys took turns and turns. Then Adam held out the truck. "Your turn, Hunter," he said.

Gabriel was at home with his friend Noam. They were building a big block tower. It was very tall. Gabriel ran to get his bear. He ran too fast. He bumped right into the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. Noam's mouth turned down. His eyes looked wet.

"Sorry, Noam," said Gabriel. "Sorry, sorry." Noam sniffled. Then Gabriel picked up a block. He put it on the carpet. Noam picked up a block too. Would they build it again? Yes! One block, two blocks, three blocks. The tower grew tall again. It stood tight and straight, like at school.

Noam gave the bear a little tickle. "He can watch," said Noam. Gabriel smiled. He held the bear very still this time. "No bumping," said Gabriel. The tower stayed up. "Yay!" said Noam, and he clapped his hands.

Charles found his crayon box in the car. He had left it there after lunch. He opened the box and peeked inside.

"Uh oh," said Charles. The crayons were soft. One orange crayon was bendy. It bent like a worm in his hand. Was it broken? He touched it again. It squished a little.

Charles showed the box to his dad. Dad held up an orange crayon. "It got hot in the car today," Dad said. Charles looked out at the sunny car. So the sun made his crayons go soft!

Charles had an idea. He put a soft crayon on his paper. He pressed it down. It made a big fat line! It drew like paint. He pressed a red one too. Soon his paper had fat, bright stripes.

Charles held up his picture. "Look! The sun helped me draw!"

Mohamed's teddy bear was sick. His friend Yasin had come over to play.

"The teddy has a tummy ache," said Yasin.

"What can we do?" asked Mohamed.

"Pretend to feed him," said Yasin. "My mom does that for my baby sister."

Mohamed found a small cup. He held it to the teddy's mouth. "Here is your medicine," he said. "Drink it all up."

The teddy still looked sick. So Mohamed got a blanket. He tucked the teddy into bed. "Now sleep," he said. "Sleep, teddy, sleep."

The sun made a warm shadow on the bed. The boys sat very still. They waited.

Soon Yasin whispered, "Look. He is sleeping. He is not sick anymore."

Mohamed smiled. He patted the teddy's head.

"Hot soup next time," said Mohamed. "Mom will make it, and I will feed him with my spoon."

"Good idea," said Yasin. "You are a good teddy daddy."

Josephine stood by the window at school. She saw a nest in the tree. It was round and brown. A bird sat in it. Outside, Ms. Hosseini was pouring seeds into a long tube. The seeds made a little sound, plip, plip, plip. The bird flew down to eat. "Ms. Hosseini, why is the bird here?" Josephine asked. "She likes the seeds we pour," said Ms. Hosseini. The bird ate, then flew back to her nest.

At circle time, Ms. Hosseini sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four," they sang. Josephine sang too. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Everyone clapped. Then Sidney looked grumpy. He had no spot on the rug. "Come sit by me," said Josephine. Sidney smiled and sat down.

Then Mitchell asked, "Josephine, how old are you?" Josephine held up her fingers. She counted them. One, two, three, four. "I am four," she said. Mitchell held up his fingers too. He counted them. "I am five," he said. Ms. Hosseini laughed and poured them each a cup of juice. Josephine took a big sip. "Four is a good age," she said. "I like being four."

Arnaud ran to the rug at school. He sat down next to Jonathan. "Story now!" he said. Mr. Pelletier shook his head. "The story is not now," he said. "It is after snack."

Arnaud made a loud sigh. He wanted the story now. "Now means at this very moment," said Mr. Pelletier. Arnaud looked at his hands. This moment felt very long.

Mr. Pelletier gave out cups. Arnaud helped fill the cups with juice. He watched the juice go up and up. Jonathan drank fast. Declan drank slowly. Then all the cups were empty.

"Is it now?" Arnaud asked. Mr. Pelletier smiled. "Yes. It is now." Arnaud clapped. He sat very still on the rug. Mr. Pelletier opened a big book. It was a book about a robot who could not stop beeping. Arnaud leaned in close. "I waited," he whispered to Jonathan, "and the story came."

Penelope went to the store with her dad. She wanted a toy animal for home. The toy shelf was low, so she could see it all.

"Look, a dog," said Penelope. "A dog is an animal." Reyna was there too. She held a cow. "A cow is an animal too," said Reyna. They laughed at the cow's big silly nose.

Then Penelope found a little toy fish. She put it down fast. "No, no. A fish has no legs. A fish is not an animal," she said.

Reyna shook her head. "A fish is an animal," she said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals."

Penelope looked at the fish. She looked at the dog. She looked at the cow. "Fish and dogs and cows? All animals?" she asked.

"Yes," said Reyna. "All animals."

Penelope hugged the fish toy. "Then I will take you home," she said. "You can swim in my bath."

At home, her dad helped her write a name on the fish's box. The name was Bubbles.

"Hello, Bubbles," said Penelope. "You are my animal."

The fish smiled its fish smile, and Penelope carried it to the bath.

Evan sat in the backyard with his friend Yousif. They had a big box of paint. Evan wanted to paint the sky.

"Blue," said Evan. He looked for blue paint. He found a dark, dark blue pot.

"That is not blue," said Yousif. "That is too dark."

"It is blue," said Evan. "I think it is."

Yousif's little sister was sleepy in the sun. Yousif gave her his hat. He was a polite friend.

Evan painted a stripe. It was very dark. He found a light blue pot. He painted a stripe next to it.

"Both are blue," said Evan. "This one is dark blue. This one is light blue."

Yousif found more blues. He lined up the pots. Light blue. Then not so light. Then very dark blue. "All blue," said Yousif.

They painted a big sky. It started light at the bottom. It got dark at the top. They painted green grass under it too. Yousif's sister clapped her hands.

"Look, a yellow sun," said Evan. "That one is just yellow."

Elias went to the mall with his dad. Elias was getting his first haircut. Nina and her mom were there too. Nina sat in the big chair first.

The hairdresser put a cape around Nina's shoulders. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell down. But the hairs did not get on Nina's clothes. They slid off the cape, onto the floor. Nina laughed and flapped her arms like a superhero.

Then it was Elias's turn. He climbed up into the big chair. The hairdresser put a cape around his shoulders too. "Now the hairs will not get on your shirt," she said. Snip, snip. Hairs fell down and slid right off. Elias giggled and flapped his arms too.

"Look at me!" he said. "I am a superhero!"

Afterward, dad said, "You look so big. We can cook lunch and eat a juicy apple at home." Elias held his dad's hand. They walked past the toy cars to the car. Elias smiled at his short hair in the shiny window.

Norah came home with a little cat. The cat was gray and soft. Norah hugged her teddy bear tight. She was scared the cat would not like her.

Then Norah wondered something. Where would the cat go potty? She looked at the cat. The cat looked at her. Norah felt worried.

Her dad brought out a small box. It was full of sand. He poured more sand in. "This is a litter box," he said. The cat sniffed it. Then the cat climbed in. The cat dug a little hole. Then the cat went potty right in the box!

Norah clapped her hands. "Good cat!" she said. The cat jumped out. It rubbed its soft head on Norah's leg. Norah giggled.

"What a smart cat," said Dad. He scooped the box clean. Norah held her teddy bear and watched. The cat curled up on the rug. It fell asleep. Norah whispered, "Good night, cat."

Xavier sat at the little table. In front of him was a tablet. He wanted to draw on it.

"Watch this," said Clare. She tapped the button. The screen lit up. Xavier tapped the button too. The screen lit up for him! He smiled big.

Mr. Tang helped him find the drawing app. Xavier tapped the green picture on the screen. A white page came up. Now he wanted to draw a sun. A big red sun.

He touched the screen with his finger. The line was blue. "Oh no," said Xavier. "My sun is blue." Clare pointed at the row of little round dots. "Tap the red one," she said. Xavier tapped the red dot. He drew a line. It was red! He drew a big red sun with sticky-looking yellow rays.

Then the bell rang. Time to go. Xavier pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the shelf, all by himself.

"Good job, Xavier," said Mr. Tang.

Xavier waved at his red sun still in his head. "Bye, sun," he whispered.

Kinsley sat at the little table in the playroom. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. It would have a big flower on it. But Grandma loved pink flowers, and Kinsley had no pink paint.

She had red paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint. She had green paint. And she had one jar of white paint. Her friend Rachel came over to look. "No pink," said Rachel. "Try red," said Rachel. Kinsley painted a red flower on the paper. It was red, not pink. She made a sad sound with her mouth.

Then she looked at the white jar. She dipped her brush in the white paint. She stirred it into the red paint. Round and round the brush went. The red paint began to change. It got lighter and lighter. It turned pink!

"Pink!" said Kinsley. She clapped her hands. Rachel jumped up high. Kinsley painted a big pink flower. Then she washed her brush in the water cup. She painted green leaves and a yellow sun. The card looked so pretty.

"Grandma will love it," said Rachel. Kinsley held the card up to the window. "A pink flower for you, Grandma," she said.

Arya went to the library with her dad. There was a craft table. Ms. Reyes put out paper squares. Each paper had four sides the same.

Arya held her square up. "Look, Kaiya! My square has four sides." Kaiya held hers up too. Then Arya folded her square. She matched the top edge to the bottom edge. She pressed it flat with her hand.

She stared at the paper. It was not a square now. "Ms. Reyes, it changed!" Ms. Reyes smiled. "That shape is called a rectangle," she said. Arya traced the long side with her finger. Then she traced the short side. It was long on top and short on the side.

Kaiya tried it too. She folded her square edge to edge. "Mine is a rectangle too!" Kaiya spun her rectangle on the table like a little card. Arya laughed and spun hers too.

Nearby, Riley had a triangle hat and a circle wheel for his toy truck. He could not reach the glue. Arya picked up the glue and gave it to him. "Thank you, Arya," said Riley.

Arya folded her rectangle again, edge to edge. It got smaller and smaller, like a sharp little point of spring grass. "Dad, look!" she said. "Squares can hide inside!"

Ruby is at Grandma's house. Grandma has made warm rice and peas. Ruby picks up her spoon fast. She wants the first bite right now.

Grandma holds up one hand. "Wait, Ruby," she says. Ruby stops her spoon in the air. Grandma puts her hands together. "We say Bismillah first," she says. "It means in the name of God. Many Muslims say it before we eat." Grandma says "Bismillah" in a soft voice. Then she takes her bite.

Ruby pats her fuzzy sleeves. She forgot yesterday. She forgot the day before, too. But today she remembers. She puts her hands together. "Bismillah," Ruby says. Grandma claps. "My smart girl!" Ruby takes a big bite of rice. "Yum," she says. "The rice tastes happy today." Grandma laughs and gives her more peas.

Zoey sat in the waiting room. She was going to get her first haircut. She wanted short hair like her friend Ruhaan. But she was scared of the scissors.

First, a lady sat in the big chair. Zoey watched. The hairdresser picked up a comb. He combed the lady's hair. One, two, three. Then he made one little snip. Zoey counted on her fingers.

A boy sat in the chair next. The hairdresser combed his hair again. One, two, three. Then a snip. Zoey saw it. The comb made the hair sit flat and neat. Only neat hair got cut. No comb, no snip.

"It's my turn," said Zoey. She climbed into the big chair. The hairdresser combed her hair. One, two, three. Snip. It did not hurt at all. Zoey counted every time. Comb, comb, comb, snip.

Soon Zoey had short hair like Ruhaan. She looked in the mirror. "Can we get dinner now?" she asked her mom. Her mom laughed and kissed her neat new hair.

Oliver went to the cultural center with his mom. Tonight was a party for Hanukkah. The room smelled like warm pancakes. His friends Otis and Kash were there too.

A grown-up stood by a big golden menorah. "Watch," said Otis. "My dad lights the candles." The dad used a long match. He lit one candle. Then he used that candle to light two more. The flames wiggled and glowed.

Oliver counted the candles. "Three are lit," he said. "How many more will there be?" Ms. Popal smiled. "We light candles on a menorah for eight nights," she said. "Tonight is night three." Otis held up his fingers. "One, two, three," he counted. "Tomorrow there will be four!"

Oliver watched the flames dance. The light made pretty shadows on the wall. Kash brought Oliver a warm pancake on a plate. "Try this," said Kash. "It has a secret inside. Applesauce!" Oliver took a bite. It was sweet and soft.

At home, Oliver held up his fingers. "One, two, three," he said to his mom. "Tomorrow we count to four." He smiled big. Then he blew a kiss to the moon.

Weston ran to the tall slide at the park. He looked up. The slide was very tall. His tummy felt funny. He felt scared.

Dad sat on the bench close by. Weston said, "I feel scared." Dad said, "I felt scared of the tall slide too, when I was little." Weston opened his eyes wide. "Even you, Dad?" Dad nodded. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Weston thought about that. He held the rail. He climbed one step. Then two. Then he was at the top! He zoomed down fast. He laughed and laughed. Now he felt happy.

Then Weston heard a cry. His friend Daphne was sad. Her ball had rolled into the bushes. Weston held out his hand. "Come on, we can find it together." They looked and looked. Then Weston saw something red behind a leaf. It was the ball, and a small ladybug sat right on top! Daphne smiled a big smile. Weston smiled too. Dad waved from the bench. "Slide again with me, Dad?" said Weston. Dad laughed and stood up.

Juliette sat at the art table. She had a big orange square of paper. Josh sat next to her. He was making a paper sailboat.

"I need two triangles for my sail," said Josh. "But I only have a square."

Juliette looked at her square. She turned it around. It was still a square. She looked at Josh's boat. The sail was not there yet.

Ms. Pritchard came over. "Let me help with the scissors," she said. "Watch. I cut from this corner to the corner on the other side." She cut slowly. Snip, snip. The square came apart.

"Two triangles!" said Josh. Juliette looked. One square had made two triangles. They were the same.

Juliette waited for her turn. Then Ms. Pritchard handed her the scissors. "You can try on the brown paper," she said.

Juliette picked up the brown square. She held the scissors. Ms. Pritchard stayed close. Juliette cut from one corner to the corner on the other side. Snip, snip, snip.

The brown square made two triangles too. Juliette clapped. Josh taped one triangle to his boat. He gave Juliette the other one.

"My sail is up," said Josh. Juliette held her triangle up high. It had a pointy tip, like a little root growing up to the sky.

"Your boat can taste the wind now," said Josh. He pushed the boat across the table. Zoom.

Juliette put her triangle on the table. Then she got another square. She wanted to see it one more time.

Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. Her dad made the toast, because the toaster was hot. He set two warm slices on her plate.

Aubrey picked up the butter knife. She spread the butter slowly. "I can do it," she said. The butter made shiny lines on the toast. First one slice, then the other. "Look, Dad! I did it all by myself."

Next came the milk. Aubrey held her cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wobbled. Milk splashed onto the table. "Oh no," said Aubrey. She set the cup down on the table. Then she poured again. The cup did not wobble at all. The milk went right in. Not one drop spilled. She took a big sip and smiled. "Dad, the cup stays still this way!"

Oliver sat at the kitchen table with a big jar of buttons. His mom poured some out. "Let's make two rows," she said.

Oliver made his row long and spread out. His mom pushed her buttons close together in a little bunch. Oliver looked at both rows. "My row has more!" he said. "My row is so long!"

"Let's count," said his mom. Oliver touched each button. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted her row. "One, two, three, four, five." He sat very still. Both rows had five!

Oliver pushed his buttons together. Then he spread them out again. He counted once more. Still five! He laughed out loud. "It is the same!" He jumped up and ran to the window. "Mom! Come see! I can count anything now!" Outside, a soft bee buzzed by the flower, and Oliver waved at it. "Five flowers, bee! I counted them!"

Evan sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. He looked in the cup. Red. Blue. Yellow. Green. No orange at all.

Evan frowned. He showed his paper to his friend Luc. "I need orange," Evan said. "I can't find any." Luc picked up the red pot. "Try red," said Luc. Then he picked up the yellow pot. "And yellow. Stir them together." Evan dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in yellow too. He stirred them in his tray. The paint turned orange!

"Neat!" said Evan. He painted a big round pumpkin. It looked just like a real one. Mr. Ferreira came to look. "What a fine pumpkin," he said. "Did you paint a green egg next to it?" Evan laughed. "No, that's a frog!" he said, and he painted two more pumpkins.

Felix went to the community kitchen with his dad. They had come to buy bread, and then to help make snacks. Mr. Kovalenko held the soft white bread. "Can I help?" asked Felix. "Yes," said Mr. Kovalenko. He put the bread in the toaster. Felix waited and counted, "One, two, three." Out came the bread. Felix touched the plate. The bread was brown and crunchy now. "It got hot in there," said Felix. "It is toast now," said Mr. Kovalenko. Toast, toast, brown and crunchy.

Iyla came to the table with butter. Felix spread the butter. One, two, three, slow little strokes. The butter melted on the warm toast. Then Felix poured milk into his cup. He poured slowly, and not one drop spilled. Iyla poured too, and clapped. Mr. Kovalenko said, "Well done." Felix bit his toast. Crunch. He smiled. "I can pour the next one," said Felix.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Elizabeth ran to the guest bedroom. The bed was empty and flat. "Grandpa needs a bed ready," said Mom. "A guest who sleeps here needs a spot all his own."

Elizabeth got to work. One pillow. It was too flat. She found a big soft one. Two pillows now. She counted them out loud. "One, two." Next she chose a blanket. Not the scratchy one. She picked her favorite blue blanket. It was soft and warm. She pulled it tight over the bed.

Grandpa arrived with his bag. He peeked into the guest room. He patted the pillows. He touched the blue blanket. "This is my cozy nest," he said. "I love it here." Elizabeth smiled. She had made it just right. Grandpa lay down and hugged the soft pillow.

Zachary sat in the computer lab with his class. Mr. Torres said, "Today you will learn the tablet." Zachary felt a little worried. The tablet looked big and shiny.

First, Zachary pressed the round button. The screen lit up! He made that happen. He smiled at his friend Aicha. Then he tapped the little paintbrush. A drawing app opened. Zachary drew a blue pond with a green frog. Aicha drew a duck on the pond.

Sacha set his juice cup right beside his tablet. Mr. Torres said, "Tablets stay away from water and drinks." Sacha picked up his cup. He set it on another table. Zachary was careful, too. He kept his hands dry. When the bell rang, Zachary pressed the button and put the tablet on the shelf. "I can do it," he told Aicha. Aicha clapped.

Paisley wanted a bedtime story. Her dad gave her a little red book. "You can read to me tonight," he said.

Paisley sat on her bed. She opened the book. The pictures looked all mixed up. A duck was in a tub. Then the duck was in the sky. "That's funny," said Paisley. The words looked wrong too.

Dad picked up his own book. Paisley watched him. He started at the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. His story went in order, all the way to the back.

Paisley looked at her book. She turned it over. The front cover had a happy duck on it. She opened the front cover. There was the duck waking up! She turned the pages one by one. The duck found a tub. The duck had a bath. At the back cover, the duck slept.

"I read it," said Paisley. Dad smiled and turned off the light.

Violet hung up her coat at daycare. It was cold outside today. Yesterday it had been cold too. Her tummy made a little growl.

Mr. Nolan was pouring milk into small cups. Violet stood by the table. She wanted her milk now.

"Is it snack time now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mr. Nolan. "Snack is soon. Soon means in a little while."

Violet sat down. She looked out the window. A bird hopped on the fence. Then it flew away.

Alejandro sat down next to her. Aura sat down too. They waited together.

Violet wiggled her feet. She counted them. One, two. Still no milk.

Then Mr. Nolan brought the cups over. "Snack time now," he said.

Violet drank her milk. It was cold and good. "It came in a little while," she said.

"Tomorrow we will have snack again," said Mr. Nolan. "And after today comes tomorrow."

Aura held up her cracker. "Now I eat this. Later I will paint."

Violet smiled. She took a big bite of her cracker. Outside, the bird came back to the fence.

Isabella wanted to sing the whole rhyme. It was about a cat with a shiny tail. She wanted to sing it all by herself.

At the music studio, Ms. Baptiste clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Isabella clapped too. But the rhyme was tricky. One cat, two cats, three cats with shiny tails. The words were hard to remember.

Mason sang it very fast. He got all tangled up. "Three cats one tail two shiny," he sang. Leonel laughed and fell over sideways.

"Let's try it slow," said Ms. Baptiste. She clapped very slowly. Clap. Clap. Clap. Isabella sang one word for each clap. One cat. Two cats. Three cats with shiny tails. The slow words came out just right.

Then Isabella tried it fast. She got tangled too, like Mason. So she went back to slow, and it was easy.

"Now the fast one!" she said, and clapped her hands.

Samuel looked out the window. The morning was quiet and sunny. He wanted to build a sand castle in the backyard. He ran out in his t-shirt.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Samuel got wet. His arms felt cold and damp. He ran back inside. "Why am I all wet?" he asked. His mom held up a red coat. "This is your raincoat," she said. "Put it on."

Samuel put on the raincoat. He went out again. The rain fell on the red coat. It dripped down the sides. But Samuel stayed dry underneath. He patted his arms. Dry! His friend Harvey came by in his blue raincoat. Harvey stayed dry too.

"Rain on top, dry under here," said Samuel. The wind blew a little. The rain went drip, drip, drip. Samuel and Harvey made a wet sand castle together. "Rainy days are good for this," said Harvey. Samuel smiled and patted the mud flat.

Jasmine ran to the park door. The sun was shiny and bright. She wanted to swing right now.

"Wait," said her mom. "Sunscreen first." Mom put white cream on Jasmine's arms and neck. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," Mom said. Then Jasmine could go.

At the park, Melody was on the swing. Melody's nose was red and sore. "Did you wear sunscreen?" Jasmine asked. "No, I ran out too fast," said Melody. The wind blew cool air, but the sun still burned Melody's skin. Ms. Hosseini gave Melody a hat. Melody put cream on her nose, too.

The next day was rainy. "Will we need sunscreen today?" Jasmine asked. "No," said Mom. "Rainy days have no hot sun." They took boots and an umbrella instead. Jasmine jumped in a puddle. "Sunny days need sunscreen," she said. "Rainy days need boots!"

Mohamed ran to bed with his turtle book. He held it out to his dad.

"Read the turtle book, please!"

Dad sat down. He opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. He read the words at the top of each page. The words told about a turtle who liked to grow flowers.

Mohamed looked at the page. He saw little black marks. "What are those?" he asked.

"Those are the words," said Dad. "I read them out loud."

Mohamed touched the marks with his finger. Dad read that line again. The same words came out!

Then they came to a page with only a picture. It showed the turtle spinning around. He looked dizzy in the picture.

"Read this page!" said Mohamed.

"There are no words here," said Dad. "Just a picture. So I will make up my own words."

Dad told a silly story about the dizzy turtle. Mohamed giggled.

"Turn the page," said Mohamed. Dad turned it. There were more words. Dad read them. Then Mohamed turned the page himself, front to back, all the way to the end.

"One more book," Mohamed whispered.

Dad smiled. "Tomorrow, you can point to the words."

Wyatt stood at the bus stop with his dad. The sun was out. "Sunny," said Wyatt. His hat kept his head warm. The wind blew. It blew his hat right off! "Silly wind," Wyatt laughed. His dad picked up the hat.

Then dark clouds came. Rain fell. Wyatt zipped up his raincoat. Drop, drop, drop went the rain. Diego came with his boots. "Rain, rain!" said Diego. Wyatt stomped in a puddle. Splash!

Then Wyatt heard a big sound. Rumble, rumble. "What is that?" he asked. "That is thunder," said his dad. "When you hear thunder, go indoors." Wyatt looked up. Rumble, rumble again. "Indoors now," said Wyatt. Everyone ran to the door. His dad held it open. "Good running, Wyatt," said Diego. They watched the rain from the window. "Warm and dry," said Wyatt. Rumble, rumble went the thunder outside.

Ava sat at the art table. She had a small wooden block. She wanted to make it pretty. "I will put a sticker on it," she said.

Ava put one red sticker on the top. Then she turned the block over. There was another flat side! She put a blue sticker there. "How many sides are there?" she wondered.

Maria came to help. "Let's count them," said Maria. They turned the block again and again. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six stickers, one on each side. Every sticker was a square! "The block has six sides," said Ava. "They are all squares!"

Mr. Novák smiled. "Ava, look at your block. You made a cube." Ava held it up. Each square sticker was a face. Six flat faces, six square stickers.

Then Ava pressed the block onto her paper. She took some paint and stamped it. A square appeared! She stamped again and again. Squares on the paper. She stamped one corner down. Now it looked like a triangle!

Tia ran over. "Ava made shapes with her block!" she said. Ava laughed and stamped one more square. "My block can paint!"

It was a cold, windy day. Snow had begun to fall outside. Mia and her mom went to the baby store. A new baby sister was coming soon!

Mia had a big idea. "I will pick a blanket," she said. She picked a soft yellow one. Then she saw a little bed for dolls. She put her doll in it. The doll's head rolled to one side. Then it rolled the other way.

"Uh oh," said Mia. The doll's head would not stay up.

A lady walked by with a real baby. She carried the baby in her arms. She put one hand under the baby's head. She kept it there the whole time.

Mia looked at her doll. She picked the doll up. She put her hand under the doll's head. The head stayed still now.

"Look, Mom!" said Mia. "I hold her head too!"

Mom smiled big. "That is just right," she said.

Mia carried her doll all through the store. She held the yellow blanket in her other hand. At the door, the snow swirled outside.

"Baby sister is so lucky," said Mia. "I will carry her like this every day."

Norah wants to make pancakes for her family. "I can help," she says. Her dad gets out a big bowl. He gets out eggs and milk. Then he gets out the flour bag.

"Pour the flour in," says Dad. Norah tips the bag fast. Poof! The flour makes a little cloud. It goes on her nose. It goes on Dad's nose too. "You have a dusty nose," says Dad. He laughs. Norah laughs. The flour is a dry powder, and it puffed up like snow.

"Now I pour slow," says Norah. She tips the bag little by little. No cloud this time. No dusty nose. Dad stirs the shiny batter round and round. He cooks the pancakes on the hot stove. Norah waits at her spot. Soon the pancakes come to the table. "These are for us," says Norah. "And I made them with my name on the helper list," she says, pointing to her drawing on the fridge.

Lucy ran into the playroom. She saw the new slide! It was big. Rohan was already there. "My turn!" said Lucy. Rohan went up the little ladder. Up, up, up he went. Then he sat at the top. Whee! Down he came, fast. "So fast!" laughed Lucy.

Lucy wanted a turn. She put her cup of juice on the floor. She climbed up. Up, up, up. The top felt very high. Her eyes went wide. "Look at me!" she called. Rohan waved at his friend. Then Lucy slid down. Down, down, down, slow at first, then fast. Her feet touched the soft mat. "Again!" she said.

Ms. Lau came in with warm cookies. "Careful, don't spill your juice," she said. Lucy drank it all. "Up and down are opposites," said Rohan. Lucy laughed. She went up again, and she came down again. "Big slide, big fun!" said Lucy.

Iris sat at the dinner table. Mom put grapes in a bowl. "You can have three grapes," said Mom.

Iris looked at the grapes. She found one big grape. She put it on her plate. She found a second big grape. Then she found a third one. "One, two, three," said Iris. She counted them with her finger.

But Iris wanted more. She pointed at a tiny grape. "Can I have this one too?" she asked. "It is so small."

Mom shook her head. "Three grapes means three grapes," said Mom. "Three is always three."

Iris looked at her plate. She had one, two, three grapes. The tiny grape would be four. Four was more than three.

The clock on the wall gave a little ring. Dinner was nearly done. Iris ate her three grapes, one by one.

Then she pushed the bowl toward Mom. "You can have three too," said Iris.

Mom smiled. She counted out one, two, three grapes. "Thank you, Iris," she said. "I will share some with Dad, near the sink."

Iris drank her milk. Her cup made a small clink on the table. "Three is three," she said, and ate her bread.

Hudson stood in the school gym. He held a red beanbag. He wanted to throw it into the big blue hoop.

He threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew way past the hoop. It landed near Sophia. "Oops," said Hudson.

Ms. Halvorsen came over. "Try this," she said. She held her arm down low. Then she swung it forward and up. The beanbag sailed into the hoop.

"Can I try that?" Hudson asked. "Yes, you can," said Ms. Halvorsen.

Hudson held his arm down low. He swung it forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop. "I did it!" he shouted. The beanbag made a soft sound on the floor.

Then it was time to catch the big yellow ball. Hasrat threw it to Hudson. Hudson held out both hands. The ball bounced off and rolled under the mat. What a messy pile of mats!

"Keep both hands close together," said Sophia. Hasrat threw the ball again. Hudson cupped both hands and squeezed them tight. The ball landed right in them.

"Nice catch," said Hasrat. Hudson laughed and threw the ball back.

Asher ran to the big slide at the playground. He was so excited. Romi was already in line. "My turn is next," said Romi. Asher wanted a turn too.

A boy pushed past and went up the stairs first. Asher felt angry. His face got hot. He stomped his foot. He wanted to shout.

Then Asher saw Mr. Kaur sit down on the bench. "Come here," said Mr. Kaur. "Try this. Breathe in slow. Now breathe out slow." Asher breathed in. He breathed out. He made a big circle with his arms, out and in. "Again," said Mr. Kaur. Asher did it three more times. Slow in. Slow out. His body began to calm down. His face did not feel so hot.

"I feel better," said Asher. "Can I try the slide now?" "Yes," said Mr. Kaur. Asher climbed the stairs. He did not feel dizzy. He slid down fast. Romi clapped. "My turn!" said Romi. Asher smiled and waited in line behind her.

text:
Ayla sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She did not want to be there. She was mad about the cold room.

The doctor smiled. "Look here," she said. Ayla used her eyes to see a tiny light. Then she heard a beep in her ears. She touched the smooth table with her hands. She smelled something like soap. The doctor gave her a sweet sticker. Ayla tasted nothing yet, but the doctor said, "Your tongue will taste lunch later."

Now the doctor pointed down. "Socks off, please." Ayla took off her shoes and socks. She put one bare foot on the floor. It was cold!

At home, Ayla ran outside. She took off her shoes again. Her bare toes touched the grass. It was soft! It tickled! "My feet can feel it," said Ayla. "The grass feels soft under my toes." She laughed and stomped. The tall green blades moved like they could float away.

Gemma came over. "Try it," said Ayla. Gemma took off her shoes too. Both girls wiggled their toes in the soft, green grass.

text:
Maya ran to the park with her bear, Bo. She wanted to play house, but Aashvi and Makai were already there. They had pots and a flat, round leaf for a plate.

"Bo is hungry," said Maya.

"I will be the cook," said Aashvi. "This leaf is a pancake!"

Aashvi held out the leaf. Maya smelled it. It smelled like grass, not pancakes. She made a sad face.

"It is not real food," said Makai.

"Pretending means acting as if something is real when it is not," said Aashvi.

Maya smiled big. "Okay! Bo loves pancakes!" She held the leaf to Bo's little mouth. Bo "ate" the whole pancake. Maya made a loud nom nom sound.

Then Makai jumped up. "Oh no! The floor is a river!" he shouted. Maya laughed and jumped too. They hopped from mat to mat. Maya held Bo up high so he stayed dry.

The pretend pancake made Bo full. The pretend river made Maya giggle. It was the best day at the park.

"More pancakes, please!" said Maya. "Bo is still so hungry!"

Isaiah sat at the little table in the school library. He wanted to write his name on his new book card. Ms. Robinson sat close by with a big alphabet book.

Isaiah wrote the letters one by one. "i, s, a, i, a, h," he said. He looked at his card. It felt small and wrong. His tummy felt funny.

His friend Viviane held up her card. Her name began with a big V. "Mine has a big letter at the start," she said. "A name starts with a capital letter," said Ms. Robinson.

Isaiah rubbed out the small i. He drew a big black I. Then he made the I shine with a yellow crayon. "Now it says Isaiah!" he said.

He turned his card into a ball of joy and then smoothed it flat again. Vivane laughed. Ms. Robinson put a gold star on it.

"Can I write Viviane next?" Isaiah asked, and he picked up his crayon.

text:
Carter went to the store with his dad. He wanted to find squishy peaches for lunch. "Stay where I can see you," said Dad. Carter nodded and skipped down the aisle. He held the cart with one hand.

Then Carter saw the peaches. They were far away, at the end of the aisle. He let go of the cart. He ran to the peaches. When he looked back, he could not see Dad. He could not see the cart either. Carter stopped. His tummy felt funny.

He walked back the way he came. Soon he saw Dad's blue coat. Soon he saw the cart. "There you are," said Dad. "I like it where you can see me," said Carter. He held the cart again. They found the peaches together. Carter picked four squishy ones. Dad let him put them in the bag. "Good picking," said Dad. Carter smiled and held on all the way to the checkout computer.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. The new baby was coming today. Bennett's baby sister would sleep in the little bed by the window. Bennett counted the things on the table. "One blanket. Two socks. Three hats." Then he counted the diapers. "One, two, three, four, five!" There were so many. Why did the baby need so many?

Bennett was sad. He wanted to give his sister a gift. He took a pencil and drew a picture of her. Then he cut the paper with safe scissors. Grandma helped him hold the paper. The picture had ten little diapers drawn on it.

Then the car came. Dad carried in a small bundle. It was Bennett's sister, Mia. "Mia cannot use the toilet yet," said Dad. "That is why she wears diapers. She needs a new one many times a day." Bennett looked at his tall stack. Now he knew why there were so many.

Mia wore a diaper and a little hat. Bennett set his picture by her bed. "That is you," he said softly. He counted again. "One blanket. Two socks. Three hats. And lots of diapers for you." Grandma smiled and tucked the blanket in.

Emmett sat at the dinner table. His friend Kacey sat next to him. There was a bowl of peas to share. "Let's count them," said Emmett. "One, two..." Then he stopped. What came after two? He felt mad at himself. He wanted to count so much!

Kacey began to sing, soft and small. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." The words rhymed! Emmett listened. Shoe rhymed with two. Door rhymed with four. "Sing it again," he said. Kacey sang all the way to "nine, ten, a big fat hen." Emmett laughed at the hen.

Then he tried it by himself. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." He did not get stuck! "Five, six, pick up sticks." He pushed one pea with his spoon. "Look, Kacey. One pea. The song taught me!"

The peas made a little green rainbow on his plate. Emmett counted them all, from one to ten.

Nova sat at the art table at summer camp. She was drawing a big cat. The cat had one, two, three kittens.

Next to her, Clyde was drawing a toy robot. "My robot is old and rusty," he said. "It creaks when it walks. Creak, creak, creak."

Nova wanted her cat to look dark and bold. She pressed her pencil down very, very hard. The line got thick and dark.

Then she pressed even harder. Snap! The pencil point broke off.

"Oh no," said Nova. "My point broke."

"Mine broke yesterday," said Clyde. "Mr. Chowdhury gave me a new one."

Mr. Chowdhury came over. He smiled and put a sharpened pencil on the table. Nova took it.

This time she pressed soft and slow. One, two, three soft whiskers. The line was still nice and dark. The point stayed on.

"Your cat looks sleepy," said Clyde.

"She is," said Nova. "Watch me draw her dreams."

Josephine sat at the little table in art class. She wanted to draw snow. She drew big white circles on white paper. She looked and looked. The white snow did not show up at all.

Sulaiman sat next to her. He was drawing a green tree. "My snow is hiding," Josephine said. She felt like crying a little. Sulaiman was not mean. He slid his blue paper across the table. "You can share mine," he said.

Josephine drew white circles on the blue paper. Now the white snow showed up, big and bright. "Snow is white," she said. "So I need blue!" She drew white snow on the sky and white snow on the ground. Then she drew a yellow sun, just a small one. Ms. Fortin came to look. "What lovely snow," she said. Josephine gave Sulaiman a hug. Then she drew one more white snowball, round as a ball.

text:
Hayden sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint grass. He looked for the green pot. The green pot was empty.

Dani sat next to him. She looked grumpy. "My grass needs green too," she said. Ms. Joshi came over. "We can mix some," she said. She put blue paint in a cup. She put yellow paint in the same cup.

Hayden stirred it with his brush. Round and round, blue and yellow. The paint turned green! "Green!" said Hayden. He painted tall grass. One blade, two blades, three blades.

"Can I try?" asked Dani. Hayden helped her add blue and yellow. She stirred and made green too. She smiled big now. Their grass looked bright and soft. Tegh held up the class pet, a small turtle. "He likes grass," said Tegh. The sun began to shine through the window. "Green grass for everyone," said Dani.

Felix was starting his first day of school. He put on his new backpack. It was very heavy. He had packed his teddy bear, three cars, and a big picture book. On the playground, Felix could not run. The heavy bag pulled him back. Emmanuel ran by him. Lev ran by him too. Felix sat down on the wooden bench.

"Your bag is too full," said Emmanuel. Felix opened his backpack. It was a bag he carried on his back, and it was full of toys. He took out the teddy bear. He took out the cars. He kept only his snack. Now the bag felt light.

Mr. Flores came over. "Do you want me to keep your toys safe in the classroom?" he asked. Felix gave him the toys. Then Felix ran across the playground. He ran fast, and the backpack bounced, small and light, on his back. "Wait for me!" he called to Emmanuel and Lev.

Grayson woke up and saw white outside. No school today! It was a snow day. He clapped his hands. Then he saw something odd in the yard. There were little holes in the snow. They went in a line, one by one, up to the big tree.

"Mom, look!" said Grayson. "The snow has marks!"

Mom looked out. "Those are footprints," she said. "Feet leave footprints in fresh snow." Grayson bent down low. He put his own boot in the snow. He lifted it up. A mark was there! His boot made a print too.

"Maybe the prints came from Mr. Luo," said Mom. "He was looking for his cat." Grayson followed the prints with his eyes. They went past the tree. They went to Mr. Luo's door. Grayson walked in his own boots, step by step, on the bumpy, crunchy path. At the door, Mr. Luo smiled. He held his cat in his arms.

"Thank you for coming to check," said Mr. Luo. "I found her under your tree." Grayson grinned and looked back at his own line of footprints in the snow.

Mateo ran to Grandpa's house. A new baby sister was coming today. He wanted to hold her so much.

Mateo tried to grab the baby from the basket. His grandpa said, "Not standing up. Wait." Mateo pouted. His bottom lip went out far.

Grandpa sat on the big couch. "A big brother can hold a baby while sitting down, with a grown-up helping," he said. "Come sit by me."

Mateo climbed up next to Grandpa. Grandpa put a pillow on Mateo's lap. Then he set the baby down, soft and slow. Mateo held still. The baby had tiny fingers. They tickled Mateo's hand a little.

The baby made a small sound. Then she grabbed Mateo's thumb. Her hand was small like a little glass. Mateo laughed. "She caught me!" he said.

Grandpa smiled. "You are a good big brother," he said.

Mateo sat very still and looked at her face. Then he said, "Hello, baby. I am Mateo."

text:
Paisley put on her little apron to wear. Ms. Bianchi took hot toast out of the toaster with a big glove. She set the toast on a cool plate.

"Now you can help," said Ms. Bianchi. Paisley picked up the knife of butter. She spread it slow, slow, across the toast. Then she stopped. The butter looked shiny. Then it was gone! "My butter is lost!" said Paisley. She looked at the plate. She looked at the floor.

Ms. Bianchi smiled. "Look at your toast," she said. Paisley looked. The toast was wet and glossy. She touched one corner with her finger. It felt soft and slippery. The butter had not run away. It had melted into the warm toast. Paisley put on more butter. She watched it melt again, just like before. "It melts!" said Paisley.

Next, Ms. Bianchi held the milk jug. Paisley held her cup with two hands. She poured slow, slow. One small drip ran down the side. She wiped it with a cloth. All the milk was in the cup.

Outside the window, a bird sat in a tree. Paisley took a sip of milk. "More toast, please," she said.

Lennon went to the store with her dad. She saw balloons by the door. She whispered, "I want a red one."
"Today we buy bread," said her dad. "Later we can look at balloons."
Later came. Lennon held the red balloon.
At the checkout she saw Tony and his mom. "Can I come to your house now?" Lennon asked.
"Not today," said Tony. "Come tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today."
"But I want to go now," said Lennon. Her voice was weak like a little mouse.
"First we sleep," said Tony. "Then it is tomorrow. Then you come over."
Lennon squeezed her balloon. "Sleep, then tomorrow," she said.
At home she ate bread. She looked at her bed.
"I will sleep now," she said. "Then it is tomorrow."
She climbed in and closed her eyes.

Charlotte went to the library with her dad. There was a big rug with pictures on it. Mr. Hughes sat on a small chair.

"Help me sort, Charlotte," said Mr. Hughes. He put down three hoops. "We need animals here, toys here, and foods here."

Charlotte found a little cat. It went in the animal hoop. Then she found a ball with a wheel inside that spun around. That was a toy. Quinton came over and put a carrot in the toy hoop.

"Is a carrot a toy?" Charlotte wondered. She rolled it on the rug. It did not bounce or spin. "That is silly," she said.

She looked at the food hoop. There was an apple there. There was bread there too. She picked up the apple and sniffed it. Then she sniffed the carrot.

"Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Mr. Hughes.

Charlotte moved the carrot to the food hoop. "You did it!" yelled Quinton.

Charlotte clapped her hands. Then she went to find more things to sort.

Ethan ran up the big steps of the bookmobile. Inside, the shelves were very tall. Tall shelves, big books, all packed tight. Ethan stood on his tiptoes. He could not see any books for him. "Too high," he said. His dad held his hand. Ms. Clarke smiled from her desk.

"Follow me," said Ms. Clarke. She walked to the corner. There was a short shelf there. It was full of little books with bright covers. "This is the children's area," she said. "The books here are just for young kids." Ethan laughed. The shelf was just his size! He pulled out a book about a squishy red ball. He hugged it tight.

"Now you get your card," said Ms. Clarke. She printed a little card with Ethan's name on it. Ethan held it up high. "My card!" he said. Novalie, standing nearby, clapped her hands. "Now the book is yours for a while," she teased. "But not for lunch!" Ethan giggled. He put the card in his pocket and patted it twice. "Home, book," he said.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled at her new swimsuit. A little tag scratched her back. "Ouch," she said. Her mom got small scissors and cut the tag off. The scratching stopped. Leah smiled. "That feels better," she said.

Then Leah looked around. The benches were made of wood. The room was quiet. Leah could hear water splashing far away. She walked to the pool with her mom. Niall from her class was there too. Leah looked up. A tall chair sat by the water. A person sat in the tall chair. "Why does she sit up so high?" Leah asked.

The lady climbed down. "I am the lifeguard," she said. "My job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it." Leah got in the shallow pool. She kicked and kicked. Then she slipped. She went under. In one moment, the lifeguard was there. She lifted Leah up. "Got you," she said. Leah blinked. The lifeguard had seen her from up high. Leah looked at the tall chair. It was like a bird spot. From up there, the lifeguard could see everyone.

Niall splashed by. Leah held the wall. "Watch me," she said. "She watches everybody," said Niall. Leah laughed and kicked some more.

Violet stood at the little pool by the lake. Ms. Mori was her swim teacher. Violet wanted to swim, but she did not want her face near the water.

"Let's try blowing bubbles," said Ms. Mori. "Put your mouth in the water and blow."

Violet held her mom's hand. She bent down. She put her mouth near the water. Then she blew.

Bloop! Big bubbles came up. The bubbles popped at the top.

Violet laughed. "Again!" she said. She blew more bubbles through her mouth. Pop, pop, pop.

Jean and Audrey blew bubbles too. The water tickled Violet's chin. She took a small bite of air and blew again.

The new pool felt warm in the sun. Violet looked at the lake and smiled.

"I did it, Mom!" said Violet. "Bloop!"

Harrison went to the library with his friend Sehaj. Ms. Tan had put out big mats. On the mats were piles of things. One pile had animals. One pile had toys. One pile had foods. "Put each thing where it goes," said Ms. Tan.
