Harrison picked up a black stuffed dog. He put it in the animal pile. Then he stopped. He looked at the dog. He listened. There was no sound. "Is it an animal?" he asked himself. He touched its nose. The nose was soft and still. "No," he said. "It does not eat. It does not run. It is not alive." He picked up the dog again. He carried it back. He put it in the toy pile. "A toy dog is a toy," he said.

Sehaj tried the same game. He put a toy cat in the animal pile. He thought again. He moved it to the toys. Then they sorted the foods. An apple went in the food pile. A banana went there too. Harrison clapped his hands. "We did it!" he said. Ms. Tan gave each boy a sticker. Harrison held his sticker up high. "A dog that is alive goes with animals," he said. "My dog stays here."

Amelia stood by the toy box at school. Mr. Wu had a new rule today. Every toy must go in the box. The room had to look tidy before snack time.

Amelia put a small mouse puppet in. Then she put in a big red ball. She turned around to get more toys. When she looked back, the mouse and the ball were out on the floor!

"Who did that?" she asked.

Maelle pointed at the baby in the stroller. The baby's hand reached for the box again. The baby pulled out a fast little car.

"Baby takes toys out," said Maelle. "In and out are opposites."

Amelia watched the baby's hand. She put one toy in. The baby took one toy out. It was like a slow game. In. Out. In. Out.

"I know what to do," said Amelia.

She put the toys in the big box. Then she pushed the box far from the stroller. The baby could not reach it now. The baby clapped and laughed instead.

The floor was tidy. Mr. Wu smiled. "Nice work, Amelia," he said.

"Would the baby grow big like us?" Amelia asked Maelle.

"Yes," said Maelle. "Then she can play in and out too."

Amelia picked up the mouse puppet and made it dance for the baby.

Nicholas wanted his bedtime story. But Mom was still in the bath. "Can Dad read it?" Nicholas asked. Dad said, "Yes, bring me the book."

Nicholas ran to his bedroom. He found the book on the floor. It had a bear on the front. He picked it up. But which way did it go? He turned it upside down. The bear looked wrong that way. He turned it back. Now the bear stood on his feet.

Nicholas brought the book to Dad. Dad opened the front. He read, "Bear put on his red hat." Nicholas looked at the page. The little marks under the picture said it. "Read it again," said Nicholas. Dad read it again. "Bear put on his red hat." The very same words came out!

The next night Mom read the book. She read, "Bear put on his red hat." Nicholas sat up. Mom said the same words Dad said! "Say it again," he said. Mom said it again. The words were the same every time.

"Now me," said Nicholas. He held the book the right way. He started at the front. "Bear put on his red hat," he said. He turned the page. "What happens next?"

Daniel went to the park with his dad. Daniel wanted to splash in the big puddle by the bench. He held his dad's hand all the way there. "Stay close," said his dad. So Daniel stayed close.

Near the puddle, Daniel saw something shiny in the grass. It was a little lighter. Daniel did not pick it up. He kept his hands in his pockets. He called, "Dad! Come see!"

His dad came over and looked. He picked up the lighter and put it in his pocket. "Good job telling me," he said. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." Daniel nodded. Then he put one toe in the puddle. Then the other toe. Then he jumped in and splashed and splashed.

The sun began to go down. It was getting late. Daniel held his dad's hand again. "Big splash tomorrow?" asked his dad. Daniel smiled and said, "Big splash tomorrow."

Lincoln was at Grandma's house. The new baby was there too. The baby was his little sister.

Lincoln gave her a soft pat. "Squishy," he said. The baby grabbed his finger. Grandma smiled.

Lincoln smelled bread. Grandma was baking. "Bread for us," said Grandma. "Milk for the baby."

The baby woke up in the night. Lincoln heard her cry. He got out of bed. Mom was already there. Mom fed the baby. Lincoln counted: one feed.

In the morning, the baby cried again. Mom fed her again. Two feeds. In the afternoon, three feeds. "Does she eat at night too?" Lincoln asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Grown-ups feed a new baby many times, day and night."

At night, the baby woke again. Lincoln listened. He heard Mom go in. The house was quiet and dark. Then the baby made a small milk sound.

"Night feed," Lincoln whispered. He counted it: four. He went back to sleep. In the morning, the baby was awake in her basket. Lincoln leaned close. "Hello, little sister. Milk time again soon."

Sofia was going on a trip. Her family would sleep at a campsite. She packed her teddy bear in a loose bag. "Time to get in the car," said Dad.

Sofia climbed into her seat. She was so excited. She held her teddy in her hand. The car did not start. Hmm. Why not? "Click your buckle, Sofia," said Dad. Sofia pushed the buckle in. Click! Now the car could go.

They drove past cows and trees. At the campsite, Sofia saw a fire. Ms. Chanthavong, the neighbour, was cooking corn. Sofia stayed back and watched. The fire popped. "I see it," said Sofia. "The fire makes the corn hot!" Later, Sofia sat by the tent with teddy. "Pretend we are driving again," she said. She clicked her seat belt buckle. Click! "We are safe, teddy."

Iris went to the pharmacy with her dad. The pharmacy sold soap, bandages and toothpaste. Iris picked a small pink soap. "For my hands!" she said.

At the sink, Iris could not reach the tap. Too high! Her dad got a step stool. He stood right beside her. Iris climbed up. Now her hands were under the water. She rubbed the soap on. Bubbles grew big and white. Her dad said, "We count to twenty." They counted together, slow and loud.

Then Iris rinsed the bubbles off. Her hands were shiny and clean. She held them up to the sun by the window. "Look, Dad! Smart hands!" she said. Her dad laughed and clapped. Iris washed her hands again after the toilet, all by herself, with the stool and Dad close by.

Jake had a runny nose. He was at home in his bedroom. He did not feel well yet. He blew his nose into a tissue. Then he put the tissue on his pillow.

"Where should that go?" his dad asked. Jake wondered. Maybe on the bed? Maybe on the floor?

Dad pointed at the bin by the door. "Try the bin," he said. Jake dropped the tissue in. It fell right down. Plop!

Jake blew his nose again. He got a new tissue. He held it up high. He dropped it in. Plop! He laughed.

Soon there were three tissues in the bin. "I can fix my messy bed," Jake said. He put his stuffed bear back on the pillow too. His shoe was under the bed. He put it by the door.

Was Jake still a little shy about missing school? Maybe. But he waved at the bin and said, "Plop, plop, plop."

Henry sat in his car seat. The car went up a big hill. Then it went down the hill. Going up was slow. Going down was fast. Henry held his cup. It was empty. Not one drop was in it. "I want water," he said. Dad stopped at a little shop. The wind outside was windy. It pushed the door hard. Dad paid for a big bottle of cold water. He also bought tea in a cup. The tea was hot. Dad held the hot cup himself. Henry sat far from it.

Dad gave Henry a small cup. It was empty too. Dad poured the water. The water went in fast. It went up and up. Henry watched it come to the top. "Stop! Stop!" he said. Dad stopped. Not one drop spilled. "Now my cup is full," said Henry. He took a slow sip. The water was cold. The tea was hot. Henry put his cup down. The cup was full. He drank more and more. Soon the cup was empty again.

The car went back on the road. A big truck went by. The truck was fast. Their car went slow behind it. Henry looked out at the windy trees. "Dad," he said, "my cup was empty. Now it is full." Dad smiled and poured a little more. Henry held his full cup with two hands. "Slow, slow," he said. "Not one drop."

Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. A woman, his grandma, put down a pencil and some paper. "Now you can write your name," she said.

Gabriel held the pencil in his fist. He pressed hard. The G came out big and wobbly. He made a rip in the paper too. "Oh no," said Gabriel. "My G is all wrong!"

Grandma smiled. She pointed to the pink end of the pencil. "Try that end," she said. Gabriel rubbed the pink end on the wobbly G. He looked close. The wobbly line was gone! The paper was clean again.

"Again!" said Gabriel. He held the pencil with his fingers, just like Grandma showed him. He wrote a slow, round G. It looked good.

"I did it!" said Gabriel. He jumped up and hugged Grandma tight. Then he sat back down fast. He wanted to write the whole name, all the way to the last letter. "Watch me, Grandma!" he said.

Bennett stood in the music room. Mr. Reyes played a song on the piano. Bennett wanted to clap and sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by himself. But his claps went everywhere. They were too fast. Then they were too slow. Vera clapped next to him. Her claps fit the song.

"Listen first," said Vera. "The song has a beat. Clap at the same time as the beat of the music."

Bennett hid his hands behind his back. He listened. Clap, clap, clap. He nodded his head with it. Then he tried. His claps landed right on the beat. Now his claps and the piano sounded like one thing.

"Now sing," said Mr. Reyes with a big smile.

Bennett sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He clapped and sang together. Myriam poured him a cup of milk at snack time after. "You can sing the yellow star song again," she said.

Bennett clapped one more time, right on the beat.

Jacob was washing his hands in the bathroom. The water felt warm on his skin. He saw white soap bubbles in the mirror. He heard the tap go drip, drip. Then he smelled something good in the air. He sniffed with his nose. "Something is cooking," he said. He sniffed again. "I think it is soup!" Jacob ran to the kitchen. His dad was stirring a big pot. "You guessed right," Dad said. "Dinner is soup. You smelled it before you saw it." Jacob laughed. "My nose knew first!" Dad gave him a spoon to hold. Jacob touched the cool spoon. Later he tasted the warm soup. "Yum," said Jacob. "I will never miss soup night again. My nose smells it first." Dad smiled and ruffled Jacob's hair.

Nova put on her clean blue dress. It was Eid morning. The street outside was full of music and balloons. "We will greet everyone today," said Mama.

At the door, Nash came with his family. "Say Eid Mubarak," Nash said. Nova tried it. "Eid Mubarak!" Nash smiled big. He gave her a sweet that smelled like honey and cardamom.

Aunties and uncles kept coming to the door. Each time, Nova said, "Eid Mubarak." Each time, she got a smile back. Grandma laughed and gave Nova two coins. Grandpa hugged her twice. Nova laughed too. Her words made the smiles happen. At the festival, the lanterns glowed above the crowd. Nova held Mama's hand. Then she saw Ms. Taylor from her class. Nova took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak!" she said. Ms. Taylor knelt down and clapped. "Eid Mubarak to you too, Nova."

Ivy went to the library with her dad. Mr. Pham had a new tablet there. "Would you like to try it?" he asked. Ivy nodded. She wanted to draw a cat.

Mr. Pham showed her the power button. Ivy pressed it. The screen lit up. "Wow," said Ivy. The dark screen was bright now. Mr. Pham tapped the drawing app. It opened with a funny pop.

Ivy drew a cat with a big hat. Lawson came to look. "Your cat is silly," he said, and laughed. Ivy laughed too. Now she was done. She remembered what to do. She pressed the power button. The screen went dark. "All done," said Ivy. She put the tablet on the shelf. "Good job," said Mr. Pham. "Can I draw next?" asked Lawson. Ivy smiled and pressed the button for him.

Oliver sat at the dinner table. He had one brown sock on his foot. The other foot was bare. "Where is my other sock?" he asked. Mom said, "Check under your chair." Oliver looked down. He saw nothing there.

"A pair means two," said Mom. "You need one more sock." Oliver slid off his chair. He walked to the rug. He counted the socks he found. "One, two, three," he said. None of them was brown. He kept looking. He waited by the toy box. Then he saw something peeking out.

Oliver reached in and pulled. It was the brown sock! "One sock, two socks," he said. "A pair!" The feeling was happy and warm. He fetched the sock back to the table. He pulled it on his bare foot. "Two feet, two socks," said Oliver. Mom smiled. "Ten warm toes," she said. Oliver wiggled them, one by one.

Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought bread, butter, milk and apple juice. "Can we have toast at home?" Ezra asked. "Yes," said Dad. "And I will teach you something new."

At home, Dad made the toast. The toast was warm and flat. Dad gave Ezra a small knife with butter. Ezra spread the butter. The butter went on slow. Then it went on smooth. "I did it!" said Ezra.

Now Ezra wanted milk in his cup. He took the big milk carton. It was too heavy. The milk almost spilled. "Too heavy," said Ezra. Dad poured some milk into a little jug. Ezra held the little jug. It was light. He tipped it, and the milk went in the cup. Not one drop spilled. "Small jug, easy pour," said Ezra. He took a big drink and smiled.

Evan had a big box of toys in the backyard. He wanted his favorite blue car. But the box was full of everything mixed up.

Kelsey came over to play. "Let's sort them," she said. She picked up the blocks. "One red, two red, three red," she said. She put all the red blocks in a pile. Then she made a pile of blue blocks. Then a pile of green blocks. The blocks were sorted by color.

Evan tried it too. But then he looked again. Some blocks were big and some were small. He made a new pile. "One big, two big, three big," he said. He put all the big blocks together. Then he put all the small blocks together. The same blocks, sorted a new way!

"Now I see everything," Evan said. He pushed the toy animals into one pile. "One cow, one duck, one sheep." He pushed the toy cars into another pile. There was the blue car, under a teddy bear!

Evan held up his favorite car. "It was hiding from me!" he said. Kelsey laughed and clapped. "Good sorting, Evan," she said. The blue car went vroom, vroom, all around the backyard.

Amelia ran into the art room. Her new shirt was pink with little stars. Today was paint day. She sat next to Hana at the big table.

Mr. Nolan held up three paint pots. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. Amelia said them back. Then she wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint anywhere. She looked and looked. No green!

"Your shirt is new," said Hana. "Put on an apron first. An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Amelia pulled a big yellow apron over her stars. It was long and floppy. Hana laughed. "You look like a duck!"

Amelia dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She mixed them on her paper. Round and round went the brush. The paint turned green! A real frog green. She painted a fat frog with big eyes. Hana painted a blue frog. "Silly frog," said Amelia. "Frogs are green!"

At the end, Amelia looked down. Her stars were still clean. Only her apron had green dots on it. "The apron did the work," she said, and she hung it up next to her favorite brush.

Mason sat on the school bus. He held his little bag on his lap. His tummy felt funny, like little butterflies inside. Today was his very first day of school.

A boy sat down next to him. "Hi, I am Azaad," he said. "This is my first day too." Azaad rubbed his tummy. "My tummy feels funny," Azaad said. Mason nodded. "Mine too," he said. "It flutters like a bird." The bus stopped in front of the school.

Mr. Singh stood at the big door. He smiled at the children. "My tummy is fluttery too," said Mr. Singh. "First days can feel like that." Mason looked up. Grown-ups felt it too? Then it must be okay. Mason took Azaad's hand. They walked in together.

The classroom had tall glass windows. Sun came through and made warm spots on the floor. Mason sat beside Azaad at a little table. They built a tall tower of blocks. Azaad pushed the lock on the toy cabinet, and the door clicked shut.

At play time, a girl named Eunice joined them. She spun the big wheel on the toy. The wheel turned, and the bell rang. Mason laughed. His tummy did not flutter anymore. "Happy tummy now," he said. Azaad laughed too, and they spun the wheel again.

Sarah walked into the big community hall. She saw a Christmas tree in the corner. It was tall and green. Her friend Katrina waved from across the room.

Sarah held a box of ornaments. She wanted to hang every ornament on one branch. She hung a red ball. Then a soft white star. Then a little wooden boat. All on the same branch! The branch began to bend. The branch began to droop. Would the branch touch the floor?

Katrina came over. "Why are they all there?" she asked. Sarah looked at the branch. It looked sad and heavy. Sarah took the boat off. The branch lifted a little. She took the star off. It lifted some more.

"I will spread them out," said Sarah. She hung the boat on a low branch. She hung the star on a high branch. She hung the red ball in the middle. Now every branch had one ornament. The tree looked full and pretty. How many branches could she count? One, two, three, four, so many!

Then Sarah found one more ornament at the bottom of the box. It was a soft little bell. It had been hiding all along. Sarah hung it on the very top branch. The bell made a tiny ring. Sarah smiled and rang it again.

Leah went to the library with her dad. There was a little playroom there. On the shelf sat blocks, dolls and balls.

Evren was there too. He tipped over the toy box. "Oh no," said Leah. "The toys fell out."

"Let's fill it up," said Evren. Leah picked up a block. "A block," she said. "A block is a toy." She put it in the box.

Evren picked up a doll. "A doll," he said. "A doll is a toy." In it went. Then a ball. "A ball is a toy too," said Leah. She patted the box.

But the box would not close. Why was it so full? Leah looked inside. Something was hiding under the balls. It was a soft grey sock. The sock made the box too full!

Leah pulled the sock out. "That is not a toy," she said. She put it on her nose like a puppet. "Hello!" said the sock. Evren laughed and laughed. The box closed with a click.

"Silly sock," said Leah. "You are too ugly to be a toy. But you can stay and play."

The wind blew hard outside Sienna's window. It howled and howled. Then all the lights went out. The whole apartment went dark.

Sienna grabbed her mom's leg. "It's dark," she said. Mom held her hand. "The big wind knocked out the power," Mom said. "The lights will come back." Mom lit a little candle on the table. Sienna watched from the couch. She did not touch it.

They sat on the floor with blankets. Sienna had a plastic cup of water. Rain tapped on the window. It sounded tap, tap, tap. Soon the rain stopped. The wind got quiet too. Then the lights came back on. The lamp glowed bright. Sienna clapped her hands. "The wind stopped and the lights came back," she said. Mom smiled and blew out the candle.

Weston was at a big festival with his class. There were flags and drums and food everywhere. A cloud shaped like a bunny sat in the sky. Weston's tummy made a loud growl.

Ms. Kowalski led them to a long table. There was warm bread, and it smelled so good. Weston grabbed a big piece right away. Then he looked up. Everyone was holding hands. Nobody was eating yet. "We wait," said Aarav. "We say the blessing first." Weston put the bread down. It was hard to wait, so he counted to ten.

An old man said the blessing. His voice was low and kind. Then everyone said "Amen!" together. Weston said it too. Now everyone picked up their food at the same time. Weston took a big bite of bread. "Mmm," he said. "Is it salty?" asked Estelle, giggling. Weston nodded with his cheeks full like a squirrel.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. Mr. Haile gave him a fat pencil and paper. "Time to write your name," said Mr. Haile.

Ryan held the pencil in his fist. It felt funny. Mr. Haile sat next to him. "Rest it here," he said, "on your fingers." Ryan tried it. The pencil sat nicely now.

Ryan began to write. He started at the right side of the paper. He made an R, then a Y. Then the paper ended. His name did not fit! Ryan made a sour face. "No room!" he said.

Mr. Haile pointed to the left side of the paper. "Start here," he said. "We go from left to right." Ryan looked at the left side. Then he looked at the right. He thought about the paper ending.

Ryan put his pencil down at the left. He wrote R, Y, A, N. The letters went across. His whole name fit! Ryan smiled big. He lifted the paper up high. "I did it!" he said. Mr. Haile clapped. "Read it to me," he said. Ryan pointed at each letter. "R, Y, A, N!"

Josephine wanted to build a big nest in the corner at daycare. She found a heavy box full of blocks. She pulled it. She pushed it. It would not move one bit. Her face got red. She sat down to rest and wait.

Henri came over. He pulled the box too. "It is too heavy," he said. Mr. Mwangi knelt down beside them. He pushed the box slowly, slowly, with one hand. It slid across the rug. "Heavy and light are opposites," he said with a smile.

Then Josephine saw a soft feather pillow on the chair. She picked it up. It went up so easy! She held it high. She carried it fast to the corner. Henri brought another light pillow. They stacked them up, one by one, slow and careful. Josephine put the last pillow on top. She kissed it gently and climbed into her cozy nest. "Soft nest," she said.

Jasper had a problem. His toy box was all mixed up. His friend Ahmad was coming to play.

Jasper looked inside the box. Toy cars were everywhere. A red car. A blue car. A yellow car. Then he saw something yellow and long. It was a banana!

"That does not belong with the cars," said Jasper. "It is the odd one out."

He put the banana in the fruit bowl. Now all the fruits sat together. Apples, oranges, and the banana. That was better.

Jasper sorted the rest. Soft animals on the shelf. Balls in the basket. Cars back in the box.

The doorbell rang. It was Ahmad! He brought gentle teddy bears to share.

"Let's play cars," said Ahmad.

Jasper opened the box. Only cars were inside. He gave Ahmad a blue car and a red one. They zoomed the cars across the floor, and the banana sat safe in the bowl.

Sienna sat at the craft table at summer camp. She wanted to make a paper sun. She had yellow paper and a red crayon. But she needed to cut out the circle. She looked at the big scissors in Ms. Fitzgerald's bag.

"Can I use those big scissors?" asked Sienna.

"Those are for grown-ups," said Ms. Fitzgerald. "I watch while kids cut with safety scissors. These are yours." She handed Sienna small scissors with round tips.

Flavie sat down next to her. "I have safety scissors too," said Flavie. "Watch me." Flavie snipped a strip of paper. Snip, snip, snip.

Sienna cut her circle. It was hard. The paper ripped a little. "Oh no," said Sienna. "My sun has a tear."

"That's okay," said Flavie. "A tear looks like a smile."

Sienna held up her sun. The tear did look like a smile. The sun was smiling! She laughed. Then her hands felt dirty from the glue. She wiped them on a paper towel.

"Look, Ms. Fitzgerald!" said Sienna. "My sun is smiling at you."

Ms. Fitzgerald taped it up high on the wall. The sun smiled down on the whole craft table.

Colton wanted Dad to read his bear book. But Dad was giving the baby a bath. "I will write him a note," Colton said. He found paper and a crayon. He wrote all his letters in one long line. ILIKETHEBEARBOOKPLS.

Colton put the note on the bed. Then he sat and waited. His tummy felt jumpy, but he waited some more. Dad came in with wet sleeves. He looked at the paper. He turned his head. He squinted. "Hmm," said Dad. "I see letters. But they are all squished together."

Colton looked at his note. The letters ran on and on, like one long word. Then he remembered his book. In the book, the words had little gaps. There was a space between one word and the next. Colton took his crayon again. He copied his letters one more time. This time he made a little gap after each word. I LIKE THE BEAR BOOK PLS.

Dad read the note out loud. He smiled. "A note for me! Now I can read it." Colton clapped. He got the bear book off the shelf. He opened the front cover, where the story starts. Dad read page one, then page two, all the way to the back.

Colton held the smooth cover. He looked at his note on the bed. Words he made. Words Dad could read. His eyes began to close. The last page turned, soft as a boat that could float on water. "Again tomorrow," Colton whispered. "You read my note, and I will write you a new one."

Sofia sat in the family car. She held her favorite toy bunny. "Are we going to see Doctor Lee?" she asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Time to hurry!"

At the office, Sofia sat in a big chair. A friendly woman looked in her mouth. She looked at Sofia's teeth. She counted them, one by one. She did not look at Sofia's ears. She did not look at Sofia's toes.

"Doctor, my tooth feels funny," Sofia said.

The woman smiled. "I am a dentist," she said. "A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth."

"Then look at my bunny!" said Sofia. She held up bunny's white smile.

The dentist laughed. "Bunny's teeth look clean and shiny," she said.

Sofia beamed. She hugged bunny all the way to the car. "Bunny did great," she told Dad. "Can bunny come next time too?"

Eloise was playing in her bedroom. Her teddy bear sat on the little table by the bed. Her friend Eline came to play.

Eline stood in the door. Her mouth turned down at the corners. Her eyebrows made a little frown.

Eloise looked at Eline's face. She saw the frown. She froze. "Eline, your face looks sad," she said.

Eline nodded. "I lost my hair clip," she said. "It was my favorite one."

Eloise wanted to help. She looked under the bed. She looked in the toy box. No clip there. Then she looked at the teddy bear. Something shiny was on the table, right next to him.

"There it is!" said Eloise. She held up the hair clip.

Eline smiled big. Her eyes went bright. Eloise saw the smile on Eline's face. Now Eline looked happy.

The two girls clipped the hair in place. They hugged the teddy bear. Then they played together until Mom called, "Snack time!"

Luca stood at the bus stop with his mom. The sky was gray. "It will rain," said Mom. She gave Luca his yellow boots. "Rain boots," she said. "Ready?"

Luca nodded. The rain began. It went tap, tap, tap. Luca's mom held a big umbrella over them.

Then the wind blew. The umbrella wiggled. "Windy," said Luca. He held his mom's hand tight. The rain came down faster. Plop, plop, plop.

Soon the rain stopped. The sun came out. "Sunny now," said Mom. Luca looked down. The ground was shiny and wet. A big puddle sat by the bench. "Look, Mom! Rain makes puddles on the ground!"

Luca jumped in the puddle. Splash! His boots kept his feet dry. He jumped again. Splash, splash! His friend Hunter came by with his dad. Hunter had red boots too. Hunter jumped in the puddle. The water went up and down.

"Cold," said Hunter, laughing. Luca chewed on his snack cracker while he watched the water shine. The bus came at last. Mom wiped Luca's boots with a cloth. "All dry," she said. Luca held her hand and climbed the steps. "Big puddle tomorrow?" he asked. "Maybe," said Mom, and she smiled.

Myles sat on his bed. He had a fresh new book. He opened the front cover first. That is where books begin.

He turned page by page. A big red dog ran across one page. A tiny cat slept on the next page. "I love the dog," said Myles. "Who drew the dog?"

He ran to his dad. "Who made the pictures?" he asked.

His dad opened the front of the book. He pointed to a name there. "This is the illustrator," he said. "The illustrator is a person who draws the pictures for a book."

Myles looked hard. There was the name. There was the name of the person who drew the dog.

He went back to his bed. He opened the front cover again. Front to back, page by page. He found the name each time.

Then came a surprise. The dog on the last page had a puppy. Myles laughed out loud.

"Now I chew my toast and read," he said. It was a good day.

He hugged the book. "Thank you, illustrator," he whispered.

Ellie went to a big family dinner. Grandma carried warm bread to the table. Ellie wanted to help. She wanted to say the bread blessing all by herself.

"Can I say it?" Ellie asked.

Grandpa smiled. "It is called the Hamotzi," he said. "Many Jewish families say it over the bread first."

Ellie practiced. "Ha-mo-tzi," she said slowly. "Ha-mo-tzi." Grandpa said it with her. Grandpa said it again. "Ha-mo-tzi," they said together. Ellie's little cousin listened from her chair.

Everyone sat down. Grandpa held up the bread. He looked at Ellie. "It is your turn," he said.

Ellie took a big breath. Her tummy felt jumpy. "Ha-mo-tzi," she said, loud and clear. Her voice did not shake at all.

The family said "Amen" together. Grandma cut the bread. Everyone ate. The bread was warm and soft. Ellie's cousin clapped her small hands.

"Ellie said the blessing!" said Grandpa.

"Yes I did," said Ellie. "I did it."

Anna climbed the school bus. It was her first day of school. She held her red lunchbox tight. Rosa was already sitting there. Rosa had a red lunchbox too.

"My plane is in my bag," said Rosa. "I painted it yellow." Anna giggled. "My plane is yellow too!" The two lunchboxes sat side by side on the seat. They looked exactly the same.

At school, Mr. Farah-Ali smiled. "Time for snacks," he said. Anna picked up a lunchbox. She opened it. Inside was a sandwich she did not like. "Hey," said Anna. "This is not mine." Rosa opened the other one. "This is not mine either!" said Rosa.

Then Anna saw writing on the lid. "That says Rosa," said Mr. Farah-Ali. Anna looked at her own box. Her daddy had written Anna on the lid that morning. "Look! This one says Anna," she said. "That is mine." They swapped the boxes. Anna munched her snack.

"Your name is like a little map," teased Rosa. Anna laughed. "My name walked my lunchbox right back to me." On the bus home, she held the box close and waved to a big grey plane in the sky. "Lunchbox one, plane zero," said Anna.

Lea sat at the big table in the art classroom. She was making a paper crown. Ms. Do gave her shiny stars and a long red strip.

"Glue, glue, glue," said Lea. One, two, three stars. She put glue on each one. Then she pressed the ends of the crown together.

Lea picked up her crown right away. Oh no. The stars slid down. The ends slid apart. Lea felt like she might cry. "My crown fell apart," she said.

Ms. Do sat down close by her side. "The glue is still wet," she said. "Wet glue needs time to dry. Then the pieces hold together."

Lea put the crown flat on the table. She counted with Ms. Do. One, two, three, four, five. She waited a little more.

Duncan came over to look. "Pretty stars," he said. Lea touched the glue very softly. It was dry now. She lifted the crown up high.

The stars stayed on. The ends stayed shut. Lea put the crown on her head. It felt like a real king's crown.

"Look, Duncan," said Lea. "One star, two stars, three stars. All stuck on tight." Duncan clapped his hands. Lea smiled a big, full smile, like a baby who just learned to wave hello. Ms. Do said, "Waiting was the magic."

After class, the teacher would cook noodles for snack time. Lea held her crown all the way to the snack table.

Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to bake blueberry muffins for the whole family. Grandma said, "Let's do it together." Parker poured the flour. He cracked the eggs in a big blue bowl. He stirred and stirred. Grandma let him ride his toy horse around the kitchen while the muffins baked.

Soon Parker smelled something sweet. He wanted to see the muffins. He ran to the oven and reached for the door. Grandma said, "Stop! The oven is hot. A grown-up is in charge of the hot stove and oven." Parker stepped back. He watched Grandma put on big mitts. She opened the door all by herself.

The muffins were tall and golden. Parker saw that Grandma opened the oven and the hot air came out. He was glad he had waited. The muffins went into a basket that looked like a bird's nest. Parker carried the basket to the table. "Muffins for everyone!" he said. Grandma smiled and gave him the biggest one.

Weston was in the backyard. He had a big red pot. His friend Saif came over with a bag of pinecones. "Let's make soup," said Weston. They put the pinecones in the pot. Weston added green leaves and little stones. He stirred the soup with a wooden spoon. Round and round he stirred.

"I want a taste," said Saif. He picked up a pinecone. He opened his mouth wide. "Stop," said Weston. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth." Saif put the pinecone down. "Show me," he said.

Weston held the spoon up. He made a big slurping sound. "Mmm, yummy soup!" he said. Saif laughed and slurped too. Nothing went in their mouths. Weston's dad watched from the porch and smiled. "More soup, please!" said Saif. Weston stirred the pot again.

Naomi sat on the playroom rug. She was hungry for a game. "Let's hunt for shapes," said Ms. Ito. "Mathys, you find a circle. Emir, you find a triangle." Mathys held up a round ball. "Circle!" he said. Emir found a yellow block with three sides. "Triangle!" he said.

"I want a rectangle," said Naomi. She looked and looked. She found a square block. She counted its sides. One, two, three, four. But the sides were all the same. That was not her rectangle. She got thirsty from all the looking. She took a drink from her little water bottle.

Then Naomi saw the playroom door. She walked over. She put her finger on the door. She counted the sides. One, two, three, four. She counted the corners. One, two, three, four. Each corner was square, just like her block. The door was a rectangle!

"I found one!" said Naomi. "The door has four sides. It has four square corners." Ms. Ito smiled. "You win the shape hunt," she said. Naomi looked at her fork on the snack table. It had pointy parts, but it was long and flat, like a little door. "That is a rectangle too!" she said, and she clapped her hands.

Nova sat at the long wooden table in the community hall. Big pots of soup sat at the end. A grown-up stirred them carefully. Nova held her spoon. She was very hungry.

But first came the blessing. Ms. Owusu stood up. She bowed her head. Jaxx and Gunnar bowed their heads too. Nova did not know when to eat. She watched and waited. Ms. Owusu said, "We thank you for this food." Nova kept waiting. Then Ms. Owusu said, "Amen." Jaxx and Gunnar picked up their spoons. So that was the end of the blessing. Nova picked up her spoon too.

The soup was warm and good. Gunnar gave Nova a present, a small napkin ring. Then Ms. Owusu stood again. She said, "We thank you for our friends." Nova whispered along. Then everyone said, "Amen." Nova smiled and took a big sip.

Rehmat sat in the playroom with her blocks. John came in with a big red ball. "Let's play the opposite game," said John. "I say a word. You shout the opposite."

John said, "Big!" Rehmat pointed at the big red ball. Then she held up her small block. "Small!" she shouted. John laughed and clapped.

Then John said, "Fast!" Rehmat threw her arms up. "Slow!" she said, and she walked like a slow turtle. John walked slow too, then fell down and got grumpy. His lip wobbled. Mr. Sow was close by. He helped John up and gave him a soft hug. "All better?" he asked. John nodded.

"Hot," said John next. Rehmat looked at her cup of cold water on the table. The grown-up had warmed John's milk, so his cup was hot. Her cup was cold. "Cold!" she shouted. Mr. Sow smiled. "Two words, as different as can be," he said. "That means they are opposites."

Rehmat hugged her cold cup. John hugged his warm one. "One more," said Rehmat. John whispered, "Night." Rehmat closed her eyes. "Day!" She opened them wide and laughed. John laughed too. The blocks sat in a heap, big ones under small ones, and the two friends played on and on.

It was a big day. Audrey and Mom went to the pharmacy. Audrey was going to get a shot. She held Mom's hand tight. The nurse said, "Come sit up on the big table." Audrey climbed up. The table was high and cold. Her legs wiggled. "It's too big," she said. Her tummy felt deep and jumpy.

Then Mom sat down on a chair. Mom patted her lap. "Sit here," Mom said. "You can sit on my lap for your shot." Audrey slid down. She sat on Mom's warm lap. Mom's arms went around her, snug like a hug. The nurse cleaned Audrey's arm. It felt wet.

"Ready?" said the nurse. Audrey took a deep breath. Poke! It was done! "All done," said the nurse. She poured a little bandage from the box and stuck it on. Audrey looked at her arm. She jumped down and smiled. "That was fast!" said Audrey. Mom said, "You pick a sticker." Audrey ran to the sticker drawer.

Audrey sat in the school library with her friend Halima. They had bumpy letter cards on the table. Audrey wanted to write the letter K on her paper. But every time she tried, the K came out wrong. The little lines went the wrong way. She rubbed her arm and sighed.

"I can't do it," Audrey said.

Mr. Marino came over with a soft smile. He put a bumpy K card by her hand. "Try this," he said. Audrey traced the letter's shape with her finger. She went up the tall line, then down the little lines. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it again and again.

Then she picked up her pencil. She wrote a K. It looked right this time! Halima clapped. "Do a B next," she said. Audrey traced the bumpy B with her finger. Then she wrote it on her paper, big and clear.

"Letters are not stuck being hard," Audrey said. "My finger can teach my hand."

Rowan went to the cultural center with his mom. There were red lanterns and paper flowers. Ms. Brown was there with a big table of food. Rowan saw his friends Jujhar and Azalea.

Jujhar held a small red envelope. "It has money inside," Jujhar said. Rowan wanted one too. He looked around. He did not see any envelopes for him.

Then Azalea's grandma came over. She gave Azalea a red envelope. Azalea took it with both hands. "Thank you," Azalea said first, before she opened it. She did not peek inside yet.

Azalea's grandma smiled. Then she took out one more envelope. She held it out to Rowan. Rowan felt shy. His mom stood close behind him. Rowan took the envelope with both hands. "Thank you," he said, just like Azalea.

"Open it now," said Azalea's grandma. Rowan opened the flap. Inside was a shiny gold coin. His eyes went wide. Jujhar laughed and clapped.

The lanterns glowed in the light. Rowan held his coin up so it sparkled. "Look, Mom!" he said. "It shines like the lanterns!"

Sadie ran to the playground with her dad. The sun was hot on her nose. She held her dad's hand at the big road. Then they were at the playground.

Sargun was there with his bike. "Want a turn?" he asked. Sadie jumped on the seat. She started to pedal. But Sargun held the wheel. "Wait," he said. "You need a helmet." Sadie got off the bike. She ran back to the bench. Her dad had her helmet in the bag. He helped her put it on. The strap made a short click.

Sadie pedaled around the path. She turned left by the swings. She turned right by the slide. Her helmet sat snug on her head. Then something surprising happened. A ball rolled right at the bike. Sadie's wheel went bump. The bike tipped over. Sadie fell onto the soft ground. Her head went clonk on the inside of the helmet. It did not hurt at all.

Sargun ran over. "Are you okay?" he asked. Sadie stood up. She patted her helmet with her hand. "Good thing I wore it," she said. Then she got back on the bike. Her dad waved from the bench. Sadie pedaled off again, one slow circle, then two.

Bennett ran in from the backyard. His hands were dusty from the sand. Grandma was mixing pancake batter in a big yellow bowl.

"I want to stir!" said Bennett.

"Cooks wash their hands first," said Grandma. She pointed to the sink.

Bennett went to the sink. He turned the water on. He rubbed the soap between his fingers. Bubbles grew soft and white. The water rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean and shiny now.

"Ready to cook," he said.

Grandma gave him the wooden spoon. He stirred round and round. The batter went swish, swish. It smelled like warm vanilla. A little splash landed on his nose. He laughed.

Grandma poured the batter into the pan. The pan was hot, so Grandma held it. Bennett watched from his stool. The batter made tiny bubbles. Then each bubble popped. That meant a pancake was ready to flip.

"I saw it," said Bennett. "The bubbles popped. Then you flipped it!"

Grandma flipped the pancake high. It spun in the air like a soft cloud. Then it landed flat in the pan. Bennett clapped his hands.

At the table, the pancakes were golden and warm. Bennett took a big bite. His grandpa gave him a thumbs up.

"Best cook in the family," said Grandpa.

Bennett grinned. His tummy felt happy and full. Outside, a bird sang at the window. "More bubbles tomorrow," said Bennett.

Alexander wanted to see the pot boil. His mom put the pot on the stove. "I want to see the bubbles," said Alexander. He took a step toward the stove. Then he stopped. White steam came up from the pot. The steam went up and up. His mom put her hand near it and pulled back fast. "Steam is hot," she said. "It can burn. Stay back." Alexander stayed back. He watched from the sunny window, far from the stove. Soon the water went bubble, bubble, bubble. He could see it all. He clapped his hands. "I see the bubbles!" he said.

Just then his pencil rolled off the table. It rolled toward the stove. Alexander did not run for it. "Mom, can you get my pencil?" he asked. His mom picked it up and put it back on the table. "Thank you," said Alexander. He sat down and drew a big pot with steam. Then he drew himself, watching from far away. "Look, Mom," he said. "I am staying back." His mom smiled and gave him a sunny orange slice. Alexander took a big bite. "Next time I will watch the tea kettle too," he said.

Grandpa had big letter cards on the wall. "A!" said Evan, pointing up high. "A is for apple!"

Then Grandma read Evan a book. Evan saw a small letter on the page. It looked round and small, not tall like the big A. "That is a different letter!" said Evan.

Grandma smiled. "That small one is the same A," she said. "Big A and small a, the same letter!"

Evan leaned close. He looked at the wall. He looked at the page. Same letter! Big A on the wall. Small a in the book.

"Let's find more!" said Evan. He turned the page fast. There was a small b. He ran to the wall and found the big B. Same! He found small c and big C. Same again!

A soft feather fell from Grandma's pillow. Evan laughed and picked it up. He held it to the wall, light as a small letter.

"Now I know all of them," said Evan. "Big and small, the same! Big and small, the same!"

Julia stood in the band room. A big piano sat by the window. Ms. Sánchez smiled. "You can try it today," she said.

Julia pressed one white key. It made a low sound. She pressed a white key up high. It made a high sound. Then she looked at the black keys. She touched one. It made a sound too, a different one. She pressed only black keys, one after another. Plink, plink, plink. It sounded like a little song.

Kyson ran over. "That sounds nice," he said. "I want a turn." He was upset because his turn was far away. Julia slid down the bench. "You can sit with me," she said. Kyson sat next to her. He played the white keys. She played the black keys. Their sounds went up and down together.

Maisy clapped her hands. "Play it again!" she said. Julia and Kyson played the black keys and the white keys, slow, then fast. Ms. Sánchez gave them each a hug. "Same time tomorrow?" she asked. Julia pressed the last key down soft. "Yes," she said.

Aubrey walked into the school computer lab with her class. Her teacher, Mr. Wardak, held up a small tablet. "We will learn to use these today," he said.

First, Aubrey pressed the round button. The screen lit up. "One, two, three, tap," she said. Then she tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared. She picked blue. Then she picked yellow. The colors mixed into green on the screen. "Look, look!" said Aubrey. Luis came to see. Daxton came too. "Green," they said together. Aubrey felt happy.

Luis made a big red circle. When the bell rang, he put his tablet on a chair and ran to line up. Mr. Wardak walked toward the chair. He was about to sit down. "Wait!" said Aubrey. She ran over fast. She picked up the tablet with both hands. "Tablet on the chair," she said. She carried it to the shelf.

Mr. Wardak nodded. Aubrey put her own tablet back too. "One, two, three, place," she said. The shelf had a soft mat. The tablets sat in a neat row. Aubrey waved at them. "Bye bye, tablets," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Grayson and Zayd played house in the kitchen corner. Grayson was the dad. He stirred a pretend pot of soup. Plop, plop, plop went the wooden spoon.

"One boot is missing!" said Grayson. The baby doll had one red boot on and one bare foot. "Where did it go?"

Zayd looked under the little table. "Here it is!" He pushed the boot onto the doll's foot.

"Is the baby alone now?" asked Grayson.

"No, she is with us," said Zayd.

Then the teacher rang a small bell. Time to go home. The soup pot was still out. The cups were everywhere.

"When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away," said Zayd, picking up a cup.

Grayson put the pot on the shelf. Zayd stacked the cups. Together they tucked the baby into her little bed, wearing both red boots.

"Night night, baby," said Grayson. He patted her soft head and waved.

Ibrahim went to Zuri's house. Zuri's dad had a tablet on the table. It was big and shiny.

Ibrahim wanted to draw on it. But first he asked Zuri's dad. "Can I use the tablet, please?" "Yes, you may," said Zuri's dad. "Children ask a grown-up first. Good job, Ibrahim."

Zuri showed him the round button. Ibrahim pressed it. The screen lit up like magic. "Whoa!" said Ibrahim. He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. He drew a green circle. Then he drew a purple cat with six legs. "Silly cat!" said Zuri. She laughed.

The cat meowed from under the sofa. A real cat! That was a surprise. "Sorry, cat," said Ibrahim. "I drew you too many legs."

Then the screen went dark. "Time to put it away," said Zuri. Ibrahim pressed the button again. He set the tablet down, face up, nice and flat. The real cat jumped on the table and sniffed it. "No drawing for you," said Zuri. "You don't have a finger that works."

Josephine ran into the library with her dad. Story time was today! "Where do we go?" she asked. Her dad looked at a big sign. It said Room 5.

Josephine held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Five fingers!" Then she looked at the door with the 5 on it. "That says five too! Five and 5 are the same!"

Her dad laughed. "Yes, that is five. Good looking, Josephine."

Down the hall they went. They passed doors with more numbers. "Six, seven, eight, nine," said Josephine, pointing at each one. The next door said ten. "Ten! Room ten!"

Inside Room 5, Mr. Pierre sat on a straight little chair. "Welcome, Josephine!" he said. "Today we will sing about counting to ten. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Josephine sat down next to her friends Krishiv and Jordan. Mr. Pierre held up a book. It had a red cross on the cover. "This book is about medicine," he said. "A doctor gives medicine to help people feel better. Listen to our song!"

They all sang together. "One, two, three, four, five!" Josephine held up five fingers. Then she looked at the door. The numeral 5 was still there, waiting.

She waved at it with all five fingers and sang louder.

Brielle got to school early. Mr. Taylor had put out pencils and paper. "Today we write our names," he said.

Brielle picked up a pencil. She waved it as she walked to her seat. Sacha held up his hands. "The point!" he said. Brielle looked at the point. It was close to his arm. She turned the pencil around. Now the point faced down at the floor. "Better," said Sacha.

Brielle sat down and gripped the pencil. She made a big B. Then an R. Then an I. "Look, Mr. Taylor!" she said. He smiled. "Two more letters," he said. Brielle wrote the E twice. She counted her letters. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!"

"That is not a joke," she said. "That is my name!"

Halle clapped. "Write mine next," she said.

Jayden was at home with Mom. Mom had a present to buy. "We will go to the big store," Mom said. Jayden put on his thin blue coat. He held Mom's hand all the way.

At the store, Jayden saw yummy apples. He let go to look at them. Then he looked up. Mom was not there. Jayden felt his tummy go tight. He did not run. He saw a lady at the checkout. She had a vest and a big smile.

"I can't find my grown-up," Jayden told her. "My mom is lost." The lady said, "Let's find her together." She spoke into her phone. Soon Mom came fast. Mom hugged Jayden close. "Stay by me now," Mom said softly. Jayden held Mom's hand and did not let go.

At home, Mom made warm cocoa. Jayden watched from his chair. Mom held the hot cup until it was cool. Then Jayden took a little sip. The marshmallow on top began to melt. It turned into a sweet white cloud. "Slow sips," Mom said. Jayden smiled and held her hand again.

Mila sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair stuck out over her ears. Today she had to get a shot. She thought a shot would be huge. She imagined a giant needle, as tall as the door.

Mila wanted to hurry out of the room. But her mom held her hand. Kyler from her class was there too. He was waiting for his turn. "I got my shot already," Kyler said. "It was one quick poke in my arm."

The nurse came in. She had a thin needle. It was small, like a tiny straw. Mila looked at her arm. She held her mom's hand tight.

The nurse counted. "One, two, three." Mila felt a quick poke in her arm. Then it was done. Mila blinked. "That was it?" she asked. The nurse put a round bandage on her arm. It had a little star on it.

Kyler walked over to see. "See? Quick poke," he said. Mila looked at her star bandage. She waved her arm in the air. "All done," said Mila.

James wanted to blast off in his rocket. It was a big box in the playroom. Lorenzo climbed in too. "We need numbers first," said Lorenzo. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." James listened. Then Lorenzo said, "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" They jumped up high. James laughed and patted the box. "Do it again," he said. James tried by himself. "One, two, three," he said. The rocket did not go. "Why not?" he asked. Lorenzo smiled. "It goes down, not up. Ten to one. That is called a countdown." James tried again. He counted ten down to one. "Blast off!" He jumped so high. Esmeralda clapped from her puzzle on the rug. "Quick, James, one more time," she said. James counted down again. Up he went, like a real rocket.

Charlotte went to Ophelia's house. Ophelia had a tablet. Charlotte wanted to draw on it too.

"Press the round button," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte pressed it. The screen lit up. The tablet made a little sound. "I hear it!" said Charlotte. She tapped the drawing app. A green hill grew under her finger. She drew a big sun over the hill. Then she drew a cat on the hill.

The screen went dark. "Oh no," said Charlotte. "The battery is low," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte found the charger on the shelf. She carried it over, carefully, with both hands. "Here," she said. Ophelia's mom took the charger and plugged it into the wall. Charlotte watched. Then she pressed the button again. The screen lit up once more. Her cat was still there, sitting on the last hill she had drawn.

"Time to put it away," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. She laid the tablet down flat on the table. "I did it all by myself," she said. Ophelia clapped.

Aurora stood by the gate at school pickup. Her dad was not there yet. The line of cars got long. Aurora held Mr. Sharma's hand and waited.

"I am hungry," said Cody. "I want my snack."

"I want my bath," said Kallie. "I always get a bath before bed."

Aurora's tummy felt tight. Then she saw her dad's blue car. It stopped at the gate. "Daddy!" she called. Her worry melted away.

At home, Dad cut an apple for her snack. Aurora ate it all up. Then Dad said, "Time to wash your hands."

Aurora put her hands under the water. She rubbed the soap. Bubbles grew on her hands! She rubbed more. The bubbles got thick and white.

"Look, Daddy! Soap and water make bubbles!"

She spread the bubbles on her chin. "I have a beard!" she said.

Dad laughed. He helped her rinse. Then they dried her hands on the soft towel.

"Snack, bath, pajamas, bed," said Dad. Aurora yawned. "Bubbles first," she said.

Isabelle went to the farm with her class. Isra and Ivory came too. Ms. Wardak had a surprise.

"Today we learn our five senses," said Ms. Wardak. "Eyes see. Ears hear. Noses smell. Hands feel. Tongues taste."

Isabelle wanted to try them all. She saw a shiny red apple. Her eyes saw it. She heard a cow. "Moo!" Her ears heard it. She smelled hay. Her nose smelled it. She felt a soft bunny. Her hands felt it.

Then Ms. Wardak held up two cups. "One is sweet. One is sour. Guess with your tongue."

Isabelle tasted the yellow lemon. Her face went squinty. "Sour!" she said. Then she tasted the strawberry. "Sweet!" said Isabelle. "My tongue can tell!"

Isra tasted the lemon too. Her eyes went big. "Whooo!" said Isra.

Then the cow came close. It licked Isabelle's hand. The tongue was big and warm.

"That cow felt me too!" said Isabelle. "Hello, cow. Your tongue is so big!"

Sarah was at Grandma's house. Ten little cars sat on the rug. "Count them," said Grandma. Sarah counted from the red car. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Then her friend Charlee came to play. Charlee counted too. She started from the blue car, at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Sarah frowned. "I got ten too!" Charlee laughed. "Ten for me too!" They counted again. Sarah started in the middle this time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Still ten! "Try it," said Sarah. Charlee started from the green car. Ten again. Grandma poured juice into two cups. "Which cup has more?" she asked. Sarah pointed. "That one." The cat walked by with dirty paws. Sarah hugged the cups. "Ten cars, and more juice for me!"

Sarah ran into the library. Today was play day! Mr. Yilmaz had big bins on the rug.

"Look, Sarah," said Mr. Yilmaz. "We sort things into groups."

One bin held toy cars. One bin held plastic animals. One bin held play food. Sarah grabbed a banana. It was yellow and smooth. She dropped it in the food bin. "Food goes here!" she said.

Then Sarah found a soft sock. It felt rough on the heel. She put it with the toy cars. She looked at it. She looked again. Then she laughed a big laugh.

"No, no, silly sock!" she said. She picked it up and moved it to the clothes bin. A shirt was in there. A hat was in there too.

Iyla held up a shirt. "Shirt goes here," she said. She dropped it in with the sock and the hat. Athena clapped her hands.

Mr. Yilmaz smiled. Sarah found a picture book about a red hat. She sat down and opened it wide.

"The hat is clothes too!" said Sarah. She turned the page.

Jaxon sat on the big couch. Mary sat next to him. Adley sat on the floor. On TV, a big soccer game was on. The room smelled like popcorn. Dad brought a warm bowl, and everyone cheered.

The blue team ran and ran. They ran so fast. "The blue team runs the most," said Jaxon. "They will win!" Mary clapped for the blue team too. The blue team kicked and kicked. But the ball went wide. No goal.

Then the red team got the ball. They kicked it into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted. Jaxon jumped up. The red team had one point. The blue team had zero points.

The game ended. The red team jumped up and down. They got a big gold cup. Jaxon looked hard at the screen. "But the blue team ran more!" he said. Mary pointed at the numbers. "The red team has more points," she said. "They won."

Jaxon leaned close to the TV. The score said red team one, blue team zero. "More points wins," said Jaxon. He marched around the room like a winner. "Next time I will watch the numbers, not the feet."

Adley held up her toy turtle. "Even the turtle knows now," she said, and everyone laughed.

Adam could not sleep. He heard a soft tap on his window. "What is that noise?" he asked. His dad smiled. "Just rain, little one. The storm is far away." Adam wanted his book about a stinky skunk. He had forgotten where he put it. It was under his pillow.

Adam opened the book himself. He put his finger at the right side of the page. "Dad, why do the words look mixed up?" he asked. His dad sat close on the bed. He took Adam's finger gently. He moved it to the left side first. Then he slid it along, slow and smooth, all the way to the right. The words lined up like little ducks in a row. "There," said Dad. "Now read with me."

Adam tried again. Left to right, left to right. His finger found the word "skunk." He laughed. "That says skunk! I read it!" Dad turned one page, then the next. Adam saw they always went front to back. The skunk found his mom at the end. Adam yawned big.

He hugged the book to his chest. The rain tap-tapped softly. "Read it again tomorrow?" Adam asked. Dad kissed his head. "Every night, if you want." Adam's eyes closed. The book sat warm beside him.

Nicholas was at Grandpa's house. He found a big cardboard box under the bed. He put his teddy bear inside it. "Now teddy has a bed," he said.

Colin came over to play. Colin stood at the door. He looked at Nicholas and the box. "What are you doing?" Colin asked. Nicholas wanted Colin to play too. But Colin just stood there. Then Nicholas had an idea. "Let's pretend this is our house," he said. Colin smiled. Colin ran over fast. "I will be the dad," said Colin. "I will cook soup." He stirred a toy pot.

Louana came in next. She looked confused. "What is this game?" she asked. "How do we play?" Nicholas said, "Just say let's pretend." Louana said, "Let's pretend I am the grumpy baby!" She made a funny face. Everyone laughed.

Grandpa heard them from the kitchen. He peeked in the door. "Can I count the soup?" he asked. "One, two, three bowls!" said Nicholas. Grandpa sat down in a small chair. He pretended to slurp the soup. "Best soup in town," said Grandpa. Teddy watched from his box bed. Nicholas tucked him in with a soft blue sock.

Clara ran to school with her red scarf. Today was scarf day! Genevieve had a scarf too. It was blue.

"Look at my scarf," said Genevieve. She spread it out wide.

Clara spread her scarf out too. Genevieve's scarf went on and on. It touched the floor. Clara's scarf was small. It did not touch the floor.

"Your scarf is long," said Clara. "My scarf is short. Long and short are opposites."

Genevieve clapped her hands. "Let's go show Ms. Qureshi!"

Ms. Qureshi was drawing a big ocean on paper. It had a big wave and a small fish. The girls held up their scarves side by side.

"A long scarf and a short scarf," said Ms. Qureshi. "What fun!"

Then Clara had an idea. "Can we use the scarves in your ocean picture?"

"Yes!" said Ms. Qureshi. The long scarf became the big wave. The short scarf became the small fish. Clara laughed and pointed.

Armaan came over to look. "The wave is so big!" he said.

At nap time, Clara was sleepy. She laid her short red scarf on her mat like a little blanket. "Good night, scarf," she whispered.

"I will wear you again tomorrow."

Alexis sat at the dinner table. His little red car sat next to his plate. Olive came for dinner tonight. She saw the car. Her eyes got big.

"Can I hold it?" Olive asked. Alexis held the car tight. His hands wanted to keep it. Olive reached out her hand. Alexis almost grabbed her wrist. Instead, he sat still. He took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His shoulders came down, soft like his pillow. The hard wait began to feel small.

"Your turn now," Alexis said. He put the car in Olive's hand. She rolled it across the table. It went past his cup and bumped his ear. Both of them laughed. Mom brought over two warm plates. She had helped wash the big pot in the sink. It was heavy, and it made a loud clang. Alexis ate his pasta. Olive rolled the car back to him.

"Now it's mine again," Alexis said. He made it zoom.

Joshua went to Toby's house. Toby had set up a little shop on the porch. It had a table and a big red door made of cardboard.

"I am the shopkeeper," said Toby. "You be the shopper."

Joshua picked up a toy carrot. He put it in his basket. Then he picked up a toy banana too.

"Wait," said Toby. "You have to pick first. Then I count."

Joshua stopped. He looked at the banana. He put it back. He walked around the table. Then he chose the carrot again.

"Good," said Toby. He tapped the carrot. "That is two coins."

Joshua gave him two blocks. Toby put the blocks in a cup. The blocks made a click sound. Joshua giggled.

"Now can I be the shopkeeper?" asked Joshua.

Toby scratched his head. "Okay. I will be the shopper."

Joshua stood behind the table. He waited. He waited some more. Toby walked around and around, looking at everything.

"Pick one," said Joshua.

Toby held up a tiny toy cake. "This one, please."

Joshua tapped it. "Three coins."

Toby paid him three blocks. Then Juniper came to the door. She had her teddy bear. "Can my teddy shop too?" she asked.

Joshua nodded. "Teddy can pick. I will wait."

His legs were tired from standing. He sat down on the step. Teddy chose a toy strawberry, very slowly. Joshua waited, just like a good shopkeeper.

Toby clapped. "You are good at this, Joshua."

Olivia went to the garden center with her dad. She held a little paper packet. It had seeds inside. The seeds were small and brown. "Can we plant these?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "We can plant carrots."

At home, they filled a pot with soft dirt. Olivia poked little holes with her finger. She dropped the seeds in. Then she covered them up with dirt. "Now they need water," said her dad. Olivia held the watering can. The water made the dirt dark and wet.

The next morning, Olivia ran outside. The weather was sunny. She looked at the pot. There was only dirt. No green anywhere. Her tummy felt worried. "Maybe my seeds are broken," she said. Her dad shook his head. "Sprouts do not come up right away," he said. "Keep watering them."

So Olivia watered the pot every day. The dirt drank the water. Then one morning, Olivia saw something tiny. A little green sprout stood in the dirt. It looked like a small smile. "It came up!" Olivia shouted. Her shout was loud. A bird flew off the fence.

Her friend Ryan came to see. He bent down close. "How did it grow?" he asked. Olivia picked up the watering can. "I gave it water," she said. She tipped the can over the pot. The water fell like soft rain.

Jake wanted to play house in the playroom. Romane was there too. She had a gray blanket and a small robot toy.

"I want to be the parent," said Romane. "I want to be the parent too," said Jake. They both frowned. The baby doll sat on the floor with nobody to hold it.

Then Jake had an idea. "I can be the parent first," he said. "Then we can switch." Romane smiled. "You can be the baby next," she said. "Babies get to nap."

Jake tucked the doll in the gray blanket. He rocked the robot toy too. He gave them pretend bottles of milk. Romane pretended to cook a pretend soup. She stirred it with a big spoon.

"Now we switch," said Romane. Jake lay down on the soft rug. He made a tiny baby yawn. Romane patted his back and sang a soft song. The doll slept next to him in the blanket.

After that, they switched again and again. "Taking turns is fun," said Jake. He held the robot up high. "Look, the baby robot is all grown up!" Romane laughed and clapped her hands.

Maverick went to Grandpa's house. Kylie was there too. Grandpa gave them a big cardboard box. "You can make it anything," he said.

Kylie put a toy pig in the box. "This is our house," she said. "The pig is our baby." Maverick rocked the pig in his arms. The pig felt soft and warm.

Then Maverick said, "A dragon is at the door!" Kylie frowned. "The dragon is scary," she said. Maverick said, "No, he is nice." Kylie thought. She looked at the pig. "Okay," she said. "The dragon can be friendly. He can help the baby pig."

The dragon knocked softly. He was polite. He swung his tail like a happy dog. The pig clapped her little hooves.

"Come in, dragon," said Maverick. "Time for snacks."

Ivy went to the cemetery with her dad. They walked on the dry, crackly grass. They came to a stone with flowers by it. "This is Grandpa Joe's spot," Dad said. Ivy put down one yellow flower. Then two small stones. Then three kisses on her hand for the wind.

Dad opened the picnic basket. "We eat here today," he said. "Grandpa Joe loved picnics." Ivy saw bread, apples, and cheese. Her tummy made a little growl. She wanted to eat right away. But Dad held her hands in his.

"First we say our blessing," said Dad. "A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food." Dad said thank you for the bread. Ivy looked at the apple in her hand. It was red and round and cool. Someone had grown that apple on a tree. She had never thought about that before.

"Now me," said Ivy. She held up the apple. "Thank you for this apple. Thank you to the tree. Thank you to the sun for helping it grow." Dad gave her a big smile. A wind moved the grass, soft and warm. It felt like a pat on her back.

"One bread, two apples, three kisses," said Ivy. She took a bite. The apple was sweet and juicy. "Grandpa Joe would like this apple," she said. Dad nodded. He put a piece of bread by the yellow flower. Ivy put her small stone next to it, and the wind went shhh through the trees.

Olivier was at the garden with Mr. Cruz. He had tiny carrot seeds in his hand. He wanted to grow big carrots to eat.

"Pat the soil," said Mr. Cruz. Olivier patted the soft dirt. He dropped the seeds in. Then he watered them with a small pink can.

One day, Olivier saw a green weed next to his carrots. "May I pull it?" he asked. Mr. Cruz nodded. Olivier pulled, and out it came. Long stringy roots hung down from the bottom! "Wow," said Olivier. "What are those?"

"The roots," said Mr. Cruz. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Olivier looked at his carrots. Did they have roots down there too? He wondered how deep they went. He gave the soil a gentle pat. "Grow down, little roots," he said. "Then I can have a carrot snack, and a cookie too."

Austin ran to the playground with his dad. He saw a big slide and a small slide. He went down the big slide fast. Then he went down the small slide slow. His friend Gus was there, too. Gus jumped in a puddle. Splash! Splash! Austin jumped too. His socks got all wet.

"Ooh, my feet feel squishy," said Austin. His dad sat on the bench near the rocking horse. "Come here, Austin," said Dad. "Wet and dry are opposites. We need dry socks." Dad took off the wet socks. He put warm, dry socks on Austin's feet. Austin touched his toes. Dry! Nice and dry.

"I like dry socks," said Austin. Gus got new socks too. Then Austin and Gus went down the slide one more time. Austin did not jump in the puddle alone this time. He held Dad's hand and stepped over it. "Big step!" said Austin. Then he gave Dad a big hug.

Max sat at the kitchen table. He found a pencil there. His brother had left it by the coloring book. Max wanted to write his name, like big kids do. He held the pencil in his fist. He pushed it hard on the paper. The M came out wiggly. The A looked like a little worm. Max frowned. "Why won't you stay?" he asked the letters.

His dad sat down next to him. Dad drew M, A and X on a new paper. But these letters were made of dots. Lots of small dots, close together. Max leaned in. What were the dots for? Could he do something with them?

Dad showed him how to pinch the pencil with three fingers, like a bird picks up a seed. Max put his pencil tip on the first dot. He slid it to the next dot. Then the next one. The dots turned into a line! He kept going, dot by dot. A real M appeared on the paper. Max gasped. He traced the dotted A. Then the dotted X. "Dad, look! The dots made my name!"

Max made a new dotted name all by himself. He traced it slowly. The letters came out clear this time. Dad taped the paper to the fridge. Then Max washed his hands and helped dry the cups. "Tomorrow," he said, "I will write MAX with no dots at all."

Eva went to the playground with her dad. The sun was hot on the slide. The shade under the tree was cool. "One, two, three steps," said Eva as she climbed.

Eva saw something red by the bench. She went close, but not too close. It was a little bottle. Inside were round dots. They looked like candy. One, two, three, four dots.

Eva did not touch the bottle. She ran to her dad. "I find something," she said. "It looks like candy, but maybe not."

Her dad picked up the bottle with two fingers. "These are medicine," he said. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy."

He put the bottle in his pocket. Then he held Eva's hand. They walked past the open gate, toward the little forest of trees by the fence.

"One, two, three swings," said Eva. She swung up high, all the way to the sky.

Ivy ran to the swings on a hot summer day. Kinsley was there with her little brother, Mathys. He wanted to count the swings. "One, two, four," said Mathys. Kinsley shook her head. "You skipped three," she said. Mathys looked sad. His foot kicked the wood chips.

Ivy wanted to help. "Let me try," she said. "Watch my mouth." She said the words slowly. "One, two, three." Mathys said them back. "One, two, three!" His sad face went away.

Then Mathys counted five hopscotch squares. He got to four and stopped. "What comes next?" he asked. Ivy held up her hand. She said, "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Mathys counted the squares with her, careful not to spill his juice cup. "Ten!" he shouted. Kinsley clapped. Then all three kids ran to the slide, counting the steps as they climbed. "Ten steps!" said Mathys.

Today was the puppet day at daycare. A puppet box was coming with Ms. Wiśniewski. Liam was so excited. He jumped up and down. He bounced on his toes. He wanted to shout, "Puppets! Puppets!"

Alicia bounced too. "I can't wait!" she said. But bouncing made Liam bump the block shelf. The blocks fell down with a noisy crash. Liam felt sad about the blocks.

Ms. Wiśniewski came over. She did not look angry. "Let's find a calm way to wait," she said. She put Liam's hand on his chest. "Pat, pat," she said softly. "Breathe slow."

Liam patted his chest. He breathed slow. His jumps got small. Then his jumps stopped. Waiting felt easier now.

Soon the door opened. The puppet box was here! Liam clapped his hands. He sat on the rug, nice and still.

"Look," said Alicia. "Liam waited so well."

Ms. Wiśniewski smiled. "Here is a puppet for you, Liam."

A red fox popped up over the box. "Hello, Liam!" said the fox in a little voice.

Liam laughed. "Hello, fox!"

Emile sat at the big art table. Today they would paint suns. A sun needs a circle. Emile picked up his brush. He drew a circle. It came out wobbly. It looked like a potato. He drew another one. That one wobbled too. "Oh no," said Emile. Celeste looked over. Her sun was wobbly too. Gurnaaz made a face at his page. All their circles went bumpy and squishy.

Then Emile saw a cup on the table. The cup was round at the bottom. He had an idea. He held the cup down on his paper. He traced his crayon all around the bottom. He lifted the cup away. "Look!" said Emile. The line went round and round and closed up. It was a circle. A real circle. "Let me try!" said Celeste. She traced a cup too. Gurnaaz traced a glue stick. His came out round as well.

Ms. Shapiro came to look. "What bright suns," she said. Emile painted his circle yellow. He added orange rays. Each ray was a little triangle. He painted a green square for a house. He added a red rectangle for the door. "My sun is so round!" said Emile. Celeste clapped her hands. Gurnaaz held up his paper for all to see. Emile grinned and traced one more cup circle, just for fun.

Florence sat on the grass in her pink hat. She wanted to learn her five senses. "I will name them all," she said. "One, two, three, four, five!"

First she touched a leaf. "Hands are for touch," she said. Then she heard a bee buzz. "Ears are for hearing!" She sniffed a flower. "Nose is for smell. That is fun."

Then Florence looked up at the sky. "I want to see the sun up close," she said. She began to peek. The grown-up ran over fast. "Stop! Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes." Florence shut her eyes tight.

"So eyes are for seeing," said Florence. "But not the sun!" The grown-up laughed. "Good guess. Look at the roses instead." Florence looked at the pink roses. "Eyes see safe things," she said. Then she ate a snack the grown-up gave her. "Mouth is for taste! Five senses, all done!"

Nova woke up early. She was going to Aanya's house. Aanya had a big box in her room. Nova crawled inside it. "Beep beep!" said Nova. "This is my bus!"

"No," said Aanya. "It is my boat." Aanya held a paper flag. "Boats need flags."

"It is a bus," said Nova. "Buses go beep."

"It is a boat," said Aanya. "Boats go splash."

They both wanted the box. They both stood very still. Then Nova had an idea. "You go first," she said. "Then me."

Aanya smiled. She sat in the box. She waved her flag. "Splash, splash!" she said. Nova pretended to be a fish. She swam around the boat. Then it was Nova's turn.

Nova sat in the box. "Beep beep!" she said. Aanya made a door with her hands. "Tickets, please," she said. Nova gave her a pretend ticket. They laughed and laughed.

Then Aanya's dad came in. "Time for a snack," he said. He looked at the box. "What is that?"

The girls looked at each other. "A boat," said Aanya. "A bus," said Nova. "And next," said Aanya, "it can be a house!"

They ate their crackers fast. Then they ran back to the box. Aanya spread a little blanket on top. "Welcome to our house," she said. Nova knocked on the cardboard wall. "May we come in?"

"Yes!" said Aanya. "Come in, come in."

Peyton was at Grandma's house. She sat at the big table in the sunny room. Grandma gave her red paint and a brush. Peyton painted a big red apple on her paper. "So red!" said Grandma.

Peyton got sleepy. She left her brush in the paint cup. Grandma said, "Time for bed, little one." The brush stayed in the cup all night.

The next morning, Peyton ran back to the room. She picked up her brush. It felt hard. It would not bend at all. "Oh no," said Peyton. "My brush is stiff."

Grandma got a fresh cup of water. She showed Peyton how to swish the brush around. The water turned pink. Then the brush felt soft again. Peyton painted a fresh green leaf next to her apple. When she was done, she swished the brush herself. "All clean," she said. Grandma smiled and clapped.

It was Everett's birthday at Grandma's house. Grandpa put four candles on the cake. He lit them with a match. Everett watched from his chair.

Everett's friend Maddison came. So did Maisy and Mr. Novák. "Time to sing!" said Grandma.

Everett hid behind his hands. He did not like loud singing.

The singing began. "Happy birthday to Everett," they all sang. "Happy birthday to Everett!"

Everett peeked through his fingers. They were singing his name! He peeked a little more. His smile grew big.

They sang his name two more times. Each time, he smiled more.

Then Grandma helped him blow out the candles. "You do it," she said. "I will help."

Everett took a big breath. He blew and blew. The candles went out, one by one.

"Happy birthday, Everett," said Mr. Novák.

"Thank you," said Everett. He clapped his hands.

Eliana was at Grandma's house. She wanted to find her own book to read. Grandma had a big shelf of books. Eliana pulled one out.

"This one," she said. She opened it. Grandma showed her the front. "We start here," said Grandma. Eliana turned the pages one by one. At the end, the pages stopped. "All done," said Eliana.

Then Eliana saw some mail on the table. There was a card with shiny purple letters. Eliana pointed. "What does that say?" Grandma smiled. "It says Eliana. It is your name."

Eliana looked at the card. Then she ran to her coat. There was her name inside it, too. She looked at both. The letters were the same. Same letters, same order, both times. "It's me!" said Eliana. "My name is the same!"

Grandma laughed. "Yes, it is you, both times."

Eliana held the card to her chest. Then a little ladybug crawled across the card. It sat right on the letter E. "Even the ladybug knows me," said Eliana. She watched it walk down to the last letter, like it was reading her name.

Connor ran to the sandbox. He had the big red truck all to himself. He filled it with sand. He poured the sand out. Then he filled it again.

Carmelo came to the sandbox too. Carmelo had no truck. He just stood there. He dug with one hand.

Connor looked at his truck. He looked at Carmelo. "Do you want a turn?" Connor asked. "Is that sharing?" Carmelo asked. "Yes," said Connor. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too." He pushed the truck across the sand.

Carmelo filled the truck. It was hard to pour with one hand. He tried again. He tried once more. Then all the sand came out in a big pile. "Good pouring," said Connor. Carmelo smiled.

Dania came over next. "My turn too?" she asked. "Yes," said Connor. "We can all use the truck." The three friends sat in a row. Fill, pour, pass. Fill, pour, pass. The sand pile grew and grew.

The sun began to go down. The kids waved goodbye. "Come back tomorrow," said Connor. "I will bring the truck again. It is a present for the whole sandbox."

Jaxson sat down at the dinner table. There was broccoli on his plate. He jumped in his seat. "Broccoli!" he said. "I am so happy!"

Markus sat next to him. Markus looked at his broccoli. His face turned grumpy. "I do not like it," he said. He pushed it far away.

Jaxson stopped chewing. He looked at Markus. Then he looked at his own plate. Same broccoli. How could that be? "You feel sad about broccoli?" he asked. "But I feel excited!"

Maria sat across from them. She held her doll on her lap. "I like broccoli a little," she said. "So we all feel different!"

Jaxson picked up a green tree piece. He made it dance on the table. "Dance, broccoli, dance!" Markus laughed. Then Markus picked one up too. He made his broccoli dance beside Jaxson's.

Maybe Markus would not eat it. Maybe he would try one bite. But they both laughed at the same little green trees. Mr. Mensah walked by with the bread. "Two dancing trees," he said. "How funny!"

Jaxson ate his broccoli up, every bit. "My tree is all gone!" he said. Markus waved his broccoli tree. "Mine is still dancing," he said.

Asher sat at the big table in the library. Ms. Buchanan put out paper and rainbow paints. "We will make butterflies," she said. Asher wanted to make the best butterfly of all.
