He painted one half of his paper. He painted a red wing and a yellow wing. Then his elbow knocked the paper. The paper folded in half on top of the wet paint. "Oh no," said Asher. His butterfly was squished!

Nikola leaned over. "Open it," she said. Asher opened the paper slowly. The wet paint had printed onto the other half. Now there were two red wings and two yellow wings. The wings matched! They were the same on both sides.

"It looks like a rainbow butterfly," said Nikola. Asher laughed. He folded it again and pressed it flat. When he opened it, the colors were brighter. Lewis came to look. "How did you do that?" he asked. Asher held up his butterfly. "Paint one half, then fold it while it's wet," he said. Lewis ran to get more paper. Asher painted another wing. He was not hungry for a snack yet. He had butterflies to make.

Matteo woke up early. The sky outside was still dark. Today was his first day of school. Matteo hid one foot under the blanket. He did not want to go. He did not know the children there.

Mama sat on the bed. "Let us play school," she said. She put Teddy in a little chair. Bunny and Duck sat on the floor. "Teddy is the teacher," said Mama. "A teacher is the grown-up who looks after the children in a class." Matteo watched. Teddy hugged Bunny. Teddy found Duck's lost shoe. Teddy helped everyone.

Matteo squeezed Teddy's paw. The paw patted Bunny on the head. Matteo laughed. He tried it again. Pat, pat. Then he held Teddy tight all the way to school. At the door, a big man smiled. "I am Mr. Fitzgerald," he said. "I am the teacher." Matteo took a slow breath. He lifted his hand and waved.

"Hello, Mr. Fitzgerald," said Matteo.

Zayn stood on the ferry with his dad. The boat went slow across the water. Zayn held his little blue bag. Inside the bag was a snack, a seed he had found, and his red shoes.

"Look, Dad," said Zayn. "The waves make the boat go up and down." The big boat pushed the water. The water made little white waves by the side. Zayn laughed and held the rail with both hands.

On the beach, Zayn took off his shoes. He ran in the sand. Then it was time to go home. The trip was done. Zayn was very tired.

At home, Dad said, "Now we unpack." Zayn put his cars away. He put his shirt in the basket. Then he picked up his red shoes. Something made a funny sound. Shake, shake. Sand came out! Sand from the beach was hiding in his shoes.

"It's stinky sand," Zayn said, and he giggled. Dad helped him sweep it up. Zayn put his shoes by the door, all clean, ready for tomorrow.

"Next time, I'll shake my shoes at the beach," said Zayn.

Elijah wanted to play hide-and-seek at school. Lilly said, "I will count, and you hide." Elijah ran to the toy shelf. He hid behind a big toy horse.

Lilly counted, "One, two, three, four, five." She counted very, very fast. She got to ten in a blink. Elijah peeked out. His legs were still showing. Ember popped up from behind a tiny chair. She was not hidden at all.

"Lilly, you counted too fast," said Ember. "We need time to hide." Lilly nodded. "Okay," she said. "I will count slowly this time."

They all started again. Lilly put her hands over her eyes. She counted, "One... two... three..." Each number came slow, like a soft song. "Four... five... six..." Elijah squeezed behind the horse. He froze like a statue. "Seven... eight... nine... ten!"

Lilly opened her eyes. "Ready or not, here I come!" She tiptoed past the shelf. Elijah held his breath. Ms. Martínez smiled from her desk. Lilly looked behind the tiny chair. She looked under the table. Then she looked behind the horse.

"Found you, Elijah!" said Lilly. Elijah laughed and jumped up. "You counted slow," he said. "Now let me hide one more time!"

Isaac sat in the waiting room with his father. Today Isaac would get a shot. He did not want a shot. "It might pinch," said his father. "I will hold your hand."

A doctor came in. A long tube hung around her neck. Isaac pointed at it. "What is that?"

"This is called a stethoscope," said the doctor. "I use it to listen to your heart beating." She put the small end on Isaac's chest. She put the other ends in her ears. "Listen," she said, and she let Isaac's father hold the ear tips. His father smiled big. "Thump, thump," he said. "That is your heart, Isaac. It is beating right now."

Isaac felt the tube on his chest. His heart was beating inside him. Then it was shot time. Isaac squeezed his father's hand. The doctor said, "All done."

Isaac looked at his arm. Just a tiny bandage. "My heart still beats," said Isaac. "Thump, thump," said his father, and hugged him tight.

Evelyn carried her blue teddy to the park. She named him Button. She set him on a rock while she played.

Then Evelyn wanted to swing. She ran to the swings with her friend Oskar. They swung high. They counted out loud, "One, two, three!"

Later Evelyn went back to the rock. Button was not there! She looked and looked. The wind had blown him. Or maybe he fell. She wanted to run far away to search alone.

But Evelyn stopped. She found her dad on the bench. "My teddy is lost," she said. "Will you help me look?"

"Yes," said Dad. "We will search together."

They held hands. They looked by the swings. No Button. They looked by the slide. No Button. They counted the places, "One, two, three." Then they looked behind the big tree. There sat Button on the grass!

Evelyn hugged him tight. "Found you, Button," she said. She put him in her pocket, safe and snug, all the way home.

Willow wanted to be a firefighter. But her fire truck toy was missing. She looked under the table. She looked by her knee. No truck anywhere.

Then Ms. Chukwu opened the dress-up box. "Look at this big red hat," she said. Willow put it on. She stood up tall. Now she felt like a real firefighter! Ismael came to play too. He put on a blue coat. "I can be the helper," he said.

The baby doll began to cry. It was pretend crying. Cecilia patted the baby so it would stay asleep. Willow ran over in her big hat. "The firefighter is here!" she said. She gave the baby a pretend bottle. The baby went right to sleep. Willow forgot all about her truck. The hat was even better. "Tomorrow I want the hat again," she said.

Emma was at the campsite with her dad. She wanted to make pancakes for the family. Dad said she could help.

Emma held the big sugar bag. She poured some into the bowl. Then she poured more. Then more! "Too much sugar," said Dad. "It will taste too sweet."

Dad gave her a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," he said. "Fill it up, then pour." Emma filled it with sugar. It was just the right amount. Dad used a measuring spoon for the salt. Just the right amount too.

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot grill. Emma watched from her chair. A little frog hopped by the table. Emma laughed.

The pancakes were golden and warm. Emma took a big bite. "Yum!" she said. "We made these!" Dad smiled and gave her one more.

Sebastian stood in the backyard. He had a red beanbag and a big blue ball. A hoop lay on the grass like a circle. He wanted the beanbag to land inside the circle.

He threw the beanbag. It fell outside the hoop. He frowned. His friend Journey came over. "Try again," she said. Sebastian threw it again. It missed again. He sat down on the grass.

But the ball rolled to his feet. He stood up. He tossed the ball up and caught it with both hands. It was too big for one hand. He tossed and caught, tossed and caught. Then he tried the beanbag again. He threw it. It went in! The beanbag sat right in the middle of the circle.

Journey clapped. "You did it!" she said. Sebastian was busy with happy jumping. He threw the beanbag again and again. It went in the hoop more and more. He picked up the big blue ball and hugged it tight. "Again!" said Sebastian.

Charles sat at the dinner table. He had a tiny pea on his fork. He wanted the apple pie on the counter.

"Can I have pie now?" asked Charles.

"Not now," said Dad. "You can have pie later."

"Is it later yet?" asked Charles.

Dad smiled. "Not yet. Later means some time after now. Not right away."

Charles ate his pea. He wiggled his toe under the table. He looked at the clock. The big hand moved a little bit.

"Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Eat your carrots first."

Charles ate one carrot. Then he ate another carrot. He picked up his cup and took a drink. The clock hand moved some more.

"Now is it later?" he asked.

Dad looked at the empty plate. "Yes," said Dad. "Now it is later."

Dad cut the pie and put a tiny piece on Charles' plate. Charles took a big bite.

"Later took a long time," said Charles. "But the pie is sweet."

"Time for one more bite," said Dad, "and then it will be bath time."

Charles giggled and ate his pie.

Olivier was at the doctor's office with his mom. They were not late. Ms. Suryanto smiled at the door.

First she checked Olivier's eyes. He looked at a chart. He saw big letters and small letters. Then she checked his ears. She put a little tool near his ear. The tool made a loud beep. Olivier did not like the beep. He put his hands over his ears. The beep got quieter. He lifted his hands. The beep got loud again. He put his hands back. Quiet again. Olivier laughed. Ms. Suryanto laughed too. "You have good hands," she said.

Next she put a cold tool on his chest. Olivier felt the cold. He smelled soap on her hands. Then she gave him a sweet pop to taste. "It is sweet," said Olivier.

In the waiting room, Olivier watched a plane fly past the window. Then he drew a picture. He drew his hands over his ears, and the quiet beep. "That is me," he said. His mom said, "That is you."

Sophie ran to the park field. Her team was there in red shirts. Today was the big game.

Sophie wanted to kick the ball right away. "Can we start now?" she asked. Ms. Korhonen shook her head. "Not yet," she said. "Teams warm up by running or stretching before a game." So Sophie ran in a little circle. Her friend Orson touched his toes. Shaurya stretched her arms up high.

Sophie felt her legs get warm. They felt fast, too. "Why do we run first?" Sophie asked. "So our legs are ready to play," said Ms. Korhonen.

The gray clouds moved away. The sun came out. Grandpa sat on the bench and waved. The game began. Sophie ran and kicked the ball. She did not fall down. Her warm legs carried her far.

Orson tripped on the grass. He began to cry. Sophie helped him up. "Run with me next time," she said. "Warm legs feel good." Orson wiped his eyes and smiled.

Then the whistle blew. Sophie looked at Grandpa. He clapped and clapped.

Zoe sat at the paint table with Ivaan. Mr. Castillo put out three pots. Red, yellow, and blue. "Make a new colour," he said.

Zoe wanted to make orange. She dipped her brush in red. Then she put the brush in the yellow pot. She stirred and stirred. But the yellow turned brown and muddy. Not orange at all.

Zoe looked at her brush. The red was still on it. She remembered the water cup. She dipped the brush in the water. She swished it until it was clean. Then she dipped it in the yellow pot. She stirred. This time the pot turned bright orange, like a fox.

"Look!" said Ivaan. "You made fox colour!"

"It's magic paint," said Zoe. She painted a big orange circle. Then she painted a small green leaf with blue and yellow, after she rinsed her brush again. Alessia clapped her hands.

Zoe held up her wet brush. "Next, I will make purple."

Elizabeth ran to the park with her mama. She saw the round merry-go-round spinning. Amir and Adem were on it already. "Can I play too?" Elizabeth asked. "Yes," said Amir. "We all take turns pushing."

Elizabeth pushed first. Round and round went the merry-go-round. Then Amir pushed. Then Adem pushed. It was fair.

Then Adem jumped on. "I push every time now," he said. "New rule." Elizabeth stopped. Amir stopped too. The merry-go-round slowed down and stopped. "We can't play like that," said Amir. Adem looked at the still merry-go-round. No one was laughing.

Adem got off. "Okay," he said. "We all take turns again." Elizabeth pushed. Amir pushed. Adem pushed. The merry-go-round spun fast and everyone laughed. Ms. Francis, the neighbour, waved from her bench.

After the game, mama had a snack. She shared a little round cake with Elizabeth. Elizabeth gave half to Amir and half to Adem. "Yum," said Amir. Elizabeth smiled. The merry-go-round went round behind them, and the children sat in the sun.

David woke up and looked out the window. Snow was everywhere. "No school today," said Dad. "It is a snow day." David put on his boots and his red hat. "Can we go to the sledding hill?" he asked. "Soon," said Dad. "First we must wait."

David watched the street from the window. The road was all white. No cars could go. Then a big yellow truck came. It had a big blade in front. It pushed the snow off the road. It pushed and pushed. The black road came back. "Look, Dad!" said David. "The truck pushed the snow away!"

"The road is clear now," said Dad. He held David's careful little hand. They walked to the sledding hill. David's friend Ally was there. She had a blue sled. David went down the hill. The cold wind touched his face. "Again!" he said. They slid down and down until the sky turned pink. "One more time," said Ally, "and then we go home for warm cocoa."

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist's office. She was waiting for her turn. Soon she would get a sticker from Ms. De Vries.

First Grace had to wash her hands. She ran to the little sink. She got her hands wet. She rubbed the soap fast, fast, fast. Then she rinsed it all off right away.

"Hmm," said Ms. De Vries. "Was that long enough? Germs can hide on hands, you know."

Grace looked at her wet hands. Had the soap really stayed on long enough? She wondered. How long is long enough?

Ms. De Vries sang a little song. "Sing while you scrub," she said. "That is the handwashing song." Grace tried again. She rubbed the soap and sang the song. It was a long song! Her hands got all fuzzy with white bubbles. When the song ended, the soap had been on for twenty whole seconds.

"Can I sing it at home too?" Grace asked.

"You can sing it anywhere," said Ms. De Vries, and she held out a shiny sticker shaped like an ice cream.

Anna came home from the windy park. Her eyes felt funny. "Something is in my eye," she said. Her mom looked. "Just a tiny bit of dust," Mom said. She helped Anna blink it out. Anna blinked and blinked. Then the dust was gone.

Anna stood by the sink. She looked in the mirror with her eyes. She saw her eyelashes. She touched them with her finger. "Do my eyelashes help?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes." Anna blinked again. She watched her lashes go down and up. They were like little brushes!

Anna sniffed lunch with her nose. Soup! She could smell it. She heard the spoon tap the bowl with her ears. She tasted the warm soup with her tongue. "Yum," she said. After lunch she found her toy robot under the sofa. She had thought she would lose it forever, and that had made her sad. But now she smiled. She held the robot tight. Then she blinked at it, slow, like a wink.

Henry stood at the classroom door. His new shoes were shiny. His backpack felt heavy on his back. Ms. Krause smiled at him. "Welcome, Henry," she said. "Come on in."

Inside, kids were playing everywhere. Henry did not know any of them. He held his truck tight. He wanted a friend, but how do you get one? He sat down all alone at the little table.

Then he saw a boy standing by the blocks. The boy looked lonely too. Henry walked over. He took a big breath. "My name is Henry," he said. "What is your name?" The boy grinned. "I am Angad. Want to build a tall tower?"

They built the tower together. It went up and up. "Can I touch the top?" asked Angad. "Only with one finger," said Henry. "It might fall!" Angad tapped it very gently. The tower wobbled but stood tall. "Safe!" said Angad, and they both laughed.

Then Violet came over with a toy stethoscope. "I am the doctor," she said. "Your bear looks sick." Angad held out his bear. Violet checked the bear very carefully. "He needs a hug," she said. So all three of them hugged the bear at once. The bear fell right onto the blocks. Down came the tower with a big crash. "Again!" shouted Henry. Angad piled up the first block.

Gianna was at Palmer's birthday party. A big box of blocks sat on the rug. Gurtaj grabbed the box first. Gianna wanted it too. She reached out her hand.

Then she stopped. She asked, "Can we play together?" Gurtaj said, "Yes! Let's build one big tower." So they did. Gianna put on a red block. Gurtaj put on a blue one. "My turn, your turn," said Gianna. "My turn, your turn," said Gurtaj.

The tower grew tall. It got a little thin at the top. Then it wobbled and fell down. They both laughed. "Again?" asked Gianna. "Again!" said Gurtaj.

Later, the mom brought out the cake. It had thin pink candles. She lit them all by herself. Everyone sang for Palmer. Then Gianna helped him dig into the party bag for candy. She found two pieces. She gave one to Gurtaj. "My turn, your turn," she said.

Myles sat at the little table in art class. The sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Mr. Eze put out paper shapes in a big box.

"We will make boats," said Mr. Eze. Myles wanted to make a boat. He picked a blue rectangle. That would be the boat's body. He picked a circle for the sun. But then he stopped. He needed a sail. He did not know which shape to pick.

Aicha held up a shape. It had pointy corners. "Is this a triangle?" she asked. Mr. Eze nodded. "Yes, that is a triangle." Myles took a triangle too. He put it on top of his rectangle. It looked like a sail. He counted the sides. One, two, three. He touched the corners. One, two, three. "Three sides and three corners," said Myles.

Then it was snack time. Mr. Eze cut the sandwiches. Each piece had pointy corners. Myles counted them before his bite. One, two, three. "Mine is a triangle too!" he said. Ophelie counted hers. "One, two, three. Mine also!"

After snack, Myles glued his boat. The triangle sail stood up tall. The circle sun shone on it. He gave one hop. "My boat can sail!" said Myles. Mr. Eze hung it on the sunny wall.

The bookmobile came to Matthew's street. It was a big blue truck full of books. Mr. Cho stood by the door. "Hello, Matthew," he said. "Today you get your very own library card."

Matthew held the card tight. It had his name on it. He felt a big smile grow on his face. He picked out a book about a red fire truck.

Nearby, his friend Elyana held her book. She looked sad. "I have to give my book back," she said. She pointed to a small hole in the side of the truck. "It goes in there."

"That is the return slot," said Mr. Cho. "You drop books in it when you bring them back."

Elyana hugged her book. "But then it is gone!"

"You can get it again," said Mr. Cho. "Or a new one."

Elyana held her book up. She waved it goodbye. Then she dropped it into the slot. Something went thunk inside the truck. A little door opened, and Mr. Cho waved back with his hand. "Safe and sound," he sang out.

Matthew laughed. "The slot ate it," he said.

"One week, and you bring yours back too," said Mr. Cho.

At home, Matthew read the fire truck book three times. He kept the card in his pocket. It was not loose. It was tucked in safe.

The next morning, Matthew put the book by the door. "I will drop you in the slot soon," he told it. Then he patted his pocket, where the card waited.

Hannah stood in the school gym. A hoop lay on the floor. Ms. Littlechild gave her a small beanbag. "Throw it in the hoop," she said. Hannah threw it. The beanbag flew past the hoop. "Missed it," said Hannah. Ronin clapped for her. "Try again." Hannah bent her knees and threw soft. The beanbag went in the hoop. "My turn next time?" asked Ronin. "Yes," said Hannah.

Then Zyon rolled a big ball to Hannah. Her hands were in her pockets. The ball hit her legs and rolled away. "Oh no," said Hannah. Zyon rolled it again. This time Hannah held her arms out. Her hands were open. The ball came right into them. "I caught it!" said Hannah. It felt smooth and warm. "Roll it fast now," she said. Zyon laughed and rolled the ball.

William wanted the fast red car. Knox had it first. Knox made it zoom across the playroom rug.

William ran to grab it. He pushed past Atlas. "Hey," said Atlas. "You were behind me." Mr. Sow put out his hand. "William, waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn."

William walked back. He stood behind Atlas. He watched Knox drive the car. The car went under the little table. Knox got down and pulled it out.

Then Knox held out the car. "Your turn," said Knox. William took it. He made it zoom fast, all the way to the toy barn. He shut the barn door so the car could hide inside.

"Next is me," said Atlas. Atlas stood still and waited. William drove the car one more time. Then he gave it to Atlas. "Good waiting," said William.

Charlotte was at home. She wanted to paint a bee. Mama set out the paints and paper. "My turn first," said Charlotte. Mama gave her the brush. Charlotte painted a big yellow bee.

Then Grandma came to visit. She brought Charlotte a new red cup. Charlotte grabbed it fast. She ran to fill it with water. Grandma sat down and looked sad.

Charlotte remembered. Grandma gave her the cup. She had not said the magic word. Charlotte ran back to Grandma. "Thank you for my cup!" she said. Grandma smiled big. "You are welcome," said Grandma. Charlotte gave Grandma a turn with the paints. Grandma painted a little flower. Charlotte clapped her hands. The bee on the paper looked asleep in the flower.

Elena looked out the window and gasped. Snow! School was closed today. It was a snow day!

She put on her boots and her red coat. Then she ran out to the sidewalk. The snow was deep and soft. But under the snow, the sidewalk was icy.

Elena ran fast. Her feet slid out. Plop! She sat down in the snow. "Ow," she said. She felt a little grumpy.

Her friend Leona was there. Leona walked past her. Leona took tiny steps. She walked slow, slow, slow. "Why are you walking like that?" Elena asked. "The ice is slippery," said Leona. "So I go slow."

Elena stood up. She let her arms hang out wide. She took small, slow steps. Careful, careful, careful. Her boots did not slide at all!

"I did it!" she shouted. "Slow feet work on ice!" Leona laughed. "Come on, slow feet," she said. "Let's find the big hill."

Elena grinned and followed her, step by step by careful step.

Lily woke up in the dark. She saw a small light on the wall. "It's morning!" she said. She got up fast and ran to the window.

Outside, the sky was dark. The moon was up. The street was quiet. No children were outside. Lily stood still. "It is not morning," she said. "It is still night."

She walked back to bed. On the way, she found her letter blocks on the floor. One, two, three, four, five. She put them in a row. The blocks made her feel calm.

At school, Lily told her friend Taya. "I woke up in the dark. I thought it was morning. But it was night!" Ms. Fortin smiled. "Night and day are opposites," said Ms. Fortin. Taya nodded. "At night the sky is dark. In the day the sky is light."

At play time, Taya ran fast around the big table. Lily walked slow around the small table. Then they sat by the window. The sun was up now. The sky was big and blue. "Day time," said Lily. She waved at the sun with both hands.

William sat in his car seat. He was going to the library. "I want a book about animals," he said. Dad smiled. "Let's go find one."

William looked out the window. He saw a red car. He saw a blue car. He saw a big bus. The wheels went round and round. The trees went by so fast.

"Red car, blue car, big bus," said William. He said it again. "Red car, blue car, big bus." Then his sock felt itchy. Dad stopped the car. He fixed the sock. "All better," said Dad.

At the library, William looked and looked. So many books! He saw a shelf. The books there were all about animals. A cat book sat by a dog book. A bird book sat by a fish book.

"Look, Dad! Animal books live together," said William. He pulled out the cat book. It was too heavy. It started to fall. Dad caught it. "Nice catch," said William.

They took the book to the table. William turned the pages. He named each animal. "Cat. Dog. Bird. Fish." Then Dad said, "Time to check it out." William held the book all the way to the car.

Elijah sat in the big waiting room. The chairs were dark and squishy. He was getting his very first haircut. His tummy felt funny.

"Will my hair fall off forever?" he asked his dad.

"No," said Dad. "Hair grows back after it is cut."

Then Mr. Khan waved him over. Mr. Khan had scissors. Only Mr. Khan touched the scissors. Snip, snip, snip. A little curl fell down. It looked like a tiny bird on the floor.

"Robin will laugh at me," said Elijah. "My hair is all gone!"

"It is not gone," said Mr. Khan. "Look in the mirror."

Elijah looked. He still had hair! It was just short now. He patted his head with both hands.

When they walked out, Dad said, "Robin will see your hair grow and grow." Elijah smiled. Maybe he would have a lion mane one day.

Sarah sat at the big table. She had paper and bright paint. Mom helped her open the paint jars. The red paint smelled like berries. Sarah painted a big yellow sun. She painted green grass, too.

"I want to put a dot on the sun," said Sarah. She pushed her finger on the sun. Oops. The yellow paint was wet. Her finger made a smudge. The sun looked yucky now. Sarah's lip wobbled. "My sun is messy."

Mom came close and patted her back. "The paint was still wet," said Mom. "Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries. We can fix it."

Sarah watched her painting. She waited and waited. She glued cotton balls on the grass while she waited. They felt soft and bumpy. At last the paint felt dry and smooth. Sarah touched the sun with one finger. Nothing moved. The sun stayed yellow.

"Now I can paint more," said Sarah. She added a little dot with her brush. The dot sat on the sun just right. Sarah held up her paper. "Look, Mom! The sun has a nose!"

Mom smiled. "Let's hang it where we can see it," said Mom. "Right by the garden window."

Emily sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. "Look," said Dad. "A red light." The car stopped. Emily saw a bird hop by the window. It had soft feathers. Then the light turned green. The car went again. At the next stop, Emily saw a little feather on the ground. "Dad, a feather! Can we take it?" Dad picked it up. It was small and gray.

"Who lost it?" Emily asked. She thought hard. Then she smiled big. "A bird! Birds have feathers." Dad laughed. "Yes, that is right." Emily held the feather up. It tickled her nose. "Birds are animals with feathers," she said, "and I am an animal with a tickly nose!"

At home, Emily knocked on her friend Elaine's door. Knock, knock! Elaine opened it. "Look, a bird feather," said Emily. Elaine peered close. "Wow." They put it in a safe box next to a toy car and a toy bear. Then they ate apple slices together. Outside, a spider climbed its web. A bird landed on the fence. "That bird lost a feather," said Emily. The bird sang. Elaine giggled and sang too.

Zoey wanted to make a special picture. Mom got out the crayons. First Zoey drew one sun. Then she drew two birds. She counted them out loud. "One, two."

Then Noor came to play. Noor asked, "How old are you?"

Zoey held up her fingers. She lifted one, two, three fingers. She looked at them. Then she said the number word.

"I am three."

Noor held up her fingers too. "I am four," said Noor. She lifted four fingers, one by one.

Zoey counted them. "One, two, three, four."

Then they sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." They sang it again. Zoey loved singing it.

Later they sat at the table to eat. Zoey held up three fingers one more time.

"Three," she said. "I am three."

Abigail woke up and looked out the window. The world was white. "Snow!" she cried. No school today. It was a snow day at home.

She ran to put on her boots. She pulled on her warm coat. She found her hat. "Where are my mittens?" she asked. She could not find them. She ran outside anyway.

The snow was cold and soft. Abigail made a snowball. She made another one. Then her fingers hurt. They were red and cold. She ran back inside fast. There were her mittens, under her wide hat on the chair! She pulled them on. Her hands got warm again.

Back outside, she clapped her mittens together. "Snow day!" Freya was there too, with Ms. Karimi from next door. Freya had no mittens. Abigail held up her own mitten hands. "Mittens keep you warm," she said. Freya nodded and ran home to get hers. Then they built a big snow frog together, all white, with stone eyes.

Maria sat at the piano in Ms. Bondarenko's studio. Her stuffed lion sat on the bench beside her. He was her audience. Maria played her song. It went "ding, ding, dong."

"Good," said Ms. Bondarenko. "Now we build a little show. Fiona and Alan will come to listen."

Fiona and Alan sat on the floor. The sun made the room hot, so Ms. Bondarenko opened the window. Maria played her song. She played it again. The notes went "ding, ding, dong."

Fiona clapped her hands. Alan clapped his hands. Maria stood very still. She did not know what to do. Then she remembered. She bent down low. She bowed.

"Bravo!" said Fiona.

"You bow when we clap," said Alan, clapping more.

Maria picked up her lion. She made him bow too.

Jasper was on the school playground. He had lost his special red car. He looked in the sandbox. No car. He looked by the slide. No car. "Where are you, car?" he said.

Rose came to help. "One, two, three places we looked," she said. Then the teacher, Mr. Sun, pointed to the playhouse. "Small toys can roll or slide under things," he said. Jasper got down on his knees. He peeked under the little bed in the playhouse. There it was! The red car had rolled under the bed.

Jasper reached in and grabbed it. He held it up high. "I found you!" he said. Rose clapped her hands. A leaf fell from the tree and landed on Jasper's head. He laughed. He put the leaf on the car like a little blanket. "Night night, car," said Jasper. Rose giggled too.

Kayden ran to the big sports field. The weather was warm and sunny. His friend Brody was already there. "The game starts soon!" said Brody. Kayden clapped his hands. He could smell popcorn from a cart. He could hear whistles and loud horns.

Kayden sat with his dad on the grass. Rhys sat close by with his mom. The players ran and kicked the ball. The crowd cheered, "Go, go, go!" Kayden jumped up and down. "Did you see that kick?" he asked Rhys.

At the end, everyone counted the score. One team had two goals. The other team had two goals too. "Who won?" Kayden asked. Ms. Côté, his neighbor, smiled. "Nobody won," she said. "When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie."

"A tie!" said Kayden. He held up two fingers on each hand. "Two and two. Same, same!" Brody laughed and held up two fingers too. The players on both teams shook hands. Kayden and Brody shook hands next. "Tie!" they shouted. "Best game ever!"

Sarah wanted to wash her hands. She stood on her little stool at the sink. Dad turned the tap for her. "Hot water comes out of this side," Dad said. "It can hurt you. I will turn it." Dad made the water warm and safe. Sarah got soap and rubbed her hands. She saw the bubbles grow and grow. Then she rinsed them and the bubbles went away.

After her bath, Sarah saw her rubber duck. She wanted to take it to the park. But the park was across the road. Sarah stood by the door and waited. Dad came with his coat on. "Ready?" he said. Sarah held up her hand. Dad took it in his big hand.

They walked out together. At the road, Sarah stopped. "Do we hold hands now?" she asked. "Yes, we hold hands when we cross the street," Dad said. They looked left, then right. Then they crossed, step by step, hand in hand. On the other side, Sarah saw the swings. She squeezed her duck and smiled. "We made it!" she said, and ran toward the sandbox.

Luke ran into the storytime room. Today he would get his first library card! He picked a big book about seeds. A round seed grew into a tall, tall tree.

Chelsea put her book back on the shelf. "Oops," she said. "I forgot which spot."

Mr. Morales held up a book. "Look at the spine," he said. "The label shows where the book belongs on the shelf." Chelsea read her label. She slid her book into the right place. It fit just right.

Then Luke dropped his book. It slid under the shelf. He pulled it out. The label was gone! "My label fell off," Luke said. Mr. Morales taped it back on.

"Now my book can go home with me," Luke said. He held his new card and his book. Chelsea clapped. "Show us your seed book next time!" she said.

Milan was at the park with his friend Naya. He saw big clouds in the sky. He heard a dog bark. He smelled something sweet. "Snack time!" said Naya's dad. He held out red strawberries. Milan loved strawberries. He wanted the sweet taste. He bit one. Mmm, so sweet! Then Naya laughed. "Look at me!" she said. She held her nose closed with her fingers. She ate her strawberry. Her eyes went wide. "It tastes plain!" she said. "Plain like water!" Milan did not know food could do that. He held his nose closed too. He took a big bite. Wow. The strawberry tasted like nothing much. He let go of his nose. The sweet taste came back! "We are lucky we can smell," said Naya. Milan touched his nose. Then he touched his ears. "Ears hear, nose helps taste," he said. "What else can we try?" Naya handed him one more strawberry. He ate it with his nose wide open.

Snow fell past the gray window. Ryan and Tate wore their warm sweaters inside. It was counting day at daycare. Mr. Sokolov put out ten crayons. Ryan counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." Tate went on. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then Mr. Sokolov asked them to write the numbers. Ryan wrote 1. Then 2. He wrote all the way to 9. Each number used one shape. But ten was a problem. Ryan drew a tall stick. "That looks like one," said Tate. Ryan tried a round loop. "That looks like zero," said Tate.

Ryan scratched his head. Then Mr. Sokolov came over. He drew on Ryan's paper. First a 1. Then a 0. "Ten," said Mr. Sokolov. "A 1 and then a 0." Ryan looked at his paper. Two little numbers, side by side. He wrote it again by himself. 1 and then 0.

"Ten!" Ryan shouted. He held up his paper. Tate clapped. Mr. Sokolov smiled and pinned it on the gray wall. Ryan grinned at his ten crayons. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," he said.

Everly walked into the big library with her dad. She held his hand. Today she would get her very own library card.

At the desk, the librarian typed on her computer. Then she handed Everly a small blue card. "All yours," she said.

Everly hugged the card. Then she heard a voice from the next room. A librarian sat in a low chair, holding a book up high. Children sat on the floor all around her.

"What is she doing?" Everly asked.

"She reads books out loud," Dad said. "It is called storytime."

Everly tiptoed to the door. The librarian opened a book about a frog. She read it in a big, funny voice. The children laughed.

Everly picked out a bear book. The librarian beeped it. "Bring it back soon," she said.

Everly blew a kiss to the storytime room. "Next time I will sit down too," she said. She waved her new card all the way home.

Grace stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her red bag tight. Through the big window she saw the street and the yellow school bus. The bus was not moving yet. Austin was on the bus. He stood up in his seat. He wanted to wave out the window. The driver said, "Sit down, please. Children stay sitting in their seats." Austin sat down fast. Then he waved from his seat instead.

Grace laughed. "Silly Austin!" she said. Then the bell rang. Grace froze. She did not know where to go. A teacher opened the last door at the end of the hallway. "This way, Grace," she said. Grace looked back at the bus one more time. Austin was still sitting. He waved and waved. Grace waved back. "Bye, Austin!" she called. Then she skipped down the hallway to her class.

Rehmat woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow!" she said. School was closed today. It was a snow day at home.

Rehmat stood in the kitchen. She was hungry. Her dad made warm toast. Then they heard a sound outside. It was the mail carrier. She was walking on the snowy path. Her feet slipped. Slip, slip, slip.

"Uh oh," said Rehmat. Dad got the big shovel. Rehmat got her small red shovel. They pushed the snow away. One scoop. Two scoops. Three scoops. Rehmat pushed and pushed. Then the path was clear. The mail carrier walked on it. She did not slip at all. She waved and said, "Thank you!"

Inside, Rehmat looked out the window. The sun came out. The snow on the steps began to melt, drip by drip. Rehmat ate her toast and smiled. "Snow day," she said, "one, two, three scoops of fun." Dad laughed and gave her one more piece of toast.

Peyton ran to the park with her dad. The sun was big and hot. "I want a cold drink!" she said.

Her dad had a cup and a small ice cube. He put the ice cube on Peyton's hand. "Ooh! Cold, cold, cold!" she cried. She dropped the ice cube into her cup fast. It went plunk. She heard the plunk with her ears. She saw the ice cube sit in the juice with her eyes.

Artemis ran over. "Can I try?" she asked. Her dad gave her one too. Artemis held it, then dropped it in her cup. "So cold!" she said, laughing.

Peyton took a sip. The juice was cold in her mouth. She smelled the orange juice with her nose. "Yum!" she said. Then she touched the wet grass with her toes. "Cold grass too!"

"More ice, more ice!" Peyton and Artemis cheered. Her dad dropped in two more cubes. Plunk, plunk.

Maeva went to the store with her dad. She wanted a book about fish. "I want the fish to swim," she said. There were shelves and shelves. One, two, three shelves of books!

Maeva found a blue book. She held it up. Oh no! The fish looked funny. The fish was upside down. The little words were upside down too. Had the store clock turned everything around? Maeva looked at the clock. No, the clock was fine.

Then Maeva turned the book around. Now the fish was right side up. The fish could swim in the deep blue sea. The words sat straight on the page.

"Read it at bedtime," said her dad.

"Can the fish swim deep down?" asked Maeva.

"Open it and see," he said, smiling.

Gabriel wanted to make a toy car. He found a small box. He found some cardboard, too. He cut four square wheels. He taped them on. "Vroom!" said Gabriel. He pushed the car on the floor. The car would not roll. It just went bump, bump, bump. "Oh no," said Gabriel.

His dad came to help. Dad held the scissors. "We need round wheels," said Dad. Dad cut four circles from the cardboard. Gabriel tapped each circle with his little arm, as if to say hello. Dad taped the circles on the car. Gabriel pushed the car again. This time it rolled! It rolled so fast. Gabriel had to catch it at the wall.

"Loud wheels!" laughed Gabriel. The circles went round and round. The car zoomed past his sock. It zoomed past the door. "My car can roll now," said Gabriel. He pushed it one more time. "Catch me, Daddy!"

Noah sat on the mat at team practice. Mr. Sánchez put one big red ball in the middle. Noah wanted it first.

Noah ran and grabbed the ball. He held it tight. Lucie stood there with no ball at all. Her face looked sad.

"Noah," said Mr. Sánchez. "Sharing means letting someone else play with it too." He knelt down next to Noah. "You can have a turn. Then Lucie can have a turn."

Noah looked at the ball. He looked at Lucie. Then he rolled the ball across the mat. Lucie caught it. She laughed and kicked it back.

They took turns. One kick for Noah. One kick for Lucie. Noah counted the kicks out loud. One, two, three.

After practice, the team sat at a little table. Noah picked crayons to write his name. Lucie had none. Noah pushed the crayon box to the middle of the table. Lucie took a blue one. She drew a big ocean with waves.

Noah was not mad. He drew a boat on the ocean too. Lucie drew a fish beside it.

"I like sharing," said Noah.

Mr. Sánchez smiled and gave them each a sticker.

Maeve was on the big city bus. She held her mama's hand. Then she looked down. Her bunny was gone!

"Where is Bunny?" Maeve asked. Her tummy felt small and scared.

Mama knelt down beside her. "Let's look," Mama said. "Where do you last remember holding Bunny?"

Maeve thought hard. "I had Bunny at the bus stop," she said. "I gave him a snack crumb."

They could not go back yet. The bus was still moving. Maeve looked under the seat. She found a red crayon. She held the crayon straight up in the air. "Not Bunny," she said.

The bus stopped. Mama and Maeve stepped off. They walked back to the bus stop bench.

There sat Bunny! His ears were flat on the wood.

Maeve caught him up in a hug. "Bunny! I remembered where I held you!"

She waved the red crayon at him too. Bunny got a ride home in her pocket.

Leah sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump down the road. She was going to the park with her dad. On the way, they played a game. "One red car," said Leah. "Two red cars," said her dad. "Three red cars!" said Leah. She laughed at the deep, silly voice her dad made.

At the park, Leah saw her friend Adelie. Adelie had a big sandcastle. Leah ran fast. Her foot hit the tower. The tower fell down. Adelie's face went sad. Leah said, "Sorry." Then she helped Adelie build it again. Pat, pat, pat went their hands. The tower stood up tall.

"Want to swing now?" asked Adelie. "Yes, please," said Leah. Adelie pushed her high. "Thank you!" Leah called from the sky. On the ride home, Leah looked out the window. "One red car," she said softly. Then she fell fast asleep.

Ayla ran into the school cafeteria. It was her first day of school! Her tummy made a little growl. She was hungry now.

"Is it lunch time?" she asked Ms. Sok.

Ms. Sok smiled. "Not yet. First we play. Then we eat."

Ayla did not know that. She thought you could eat any time you want!

She found her friends Ryan and Mikayla. They counted the tables together. One table, two tables, three tables, four tables! Then a bell rang. Ding, ding!

"Snack time!" said Ryan.

Everyone sat down. Ayla opened her lunch box. One apple, one cracker, one cookie. She took a big bite of the apple.

A boy at the next table took off his shoe. "My sock is smelly," he said. Everyone laughed.

"After snack we go outside," said Mikayla.

Ayla smiled. "I know just what to do," she said. "I wait for snack time, and then I eat!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. On Saturday, Grandpa said, "Let's take the train to the market." Bennett held Grandpa's hand at the station. They stood on the platform to wait.

Bennett heard a loud sound. "The train is coming! I want to see!" He tried to lean out far. Grandpa pulled him back gently. "Stand back from the edge," said Grandpa. "Wait until the train stops." Bennett stepped back behind the yellow line. He waited. The train whooshed in. Then it stopped. The doors opened with a ding. "Now we can go," said Grandpa.

At the market, they bought fresh bread and a small toy turtle. Bennett put the turtle in his pocket. On the way home, they waited on the platform again. Bennett stood back from the edge all by himself. The train stopped, and the doors opened. Bennett smiled up at Grandpa. "I waited, Grandpa." Grandpa gave him a big thumbs up.

Billie stood at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day, so Billie wore her hat.

"Where is the bus?" asked Billie.

"It is coming soon," said her mother.

Then the wind came. Billie felt it push her hair. She looked up. The trees began to sway. The leaves blew off the branches. They flew all around the yard next to the bus stop.

Billie ran after a big red leaf. The wind blew it left. Then it blew it right. Billie jumped and clapped her hands. "I got it!" she said. She held the thick stem tight.

More leaves blew by. Miller came to the bus stop too. "It is windy today!" he said. He wore his jacket zipped up high.

"Now the sky looks gray," said Billie's mother. "Rain may come. Get your rain boots on." Billie sat down and pulled them on.

The bus came at last. Billie jumped on with her leaf. She held it up. "Look what the wind gave me!" she said.

Madison went to the library with her dad. She saw Ms. Chen near the rug. Ms. Chen had a big basket of toy monkeys. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" sang Ms. Chen. Madison sat down fast.

"One fell off and bumped his head," sang Ms. Chen. She took one monkey out of the basket. "How many are left now?" she asked. Madison counted them. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Four monkeys!" Then they sang again. One more monkey fell off. "One, two, three," said Madison. She was thinking hard. Every time a monkey fell, there was one less.

Preston came to sit down too. "Can I sing?" he asked. "Yes," said Madison. They sang the next part. A monkey fell off. "How many now?" asked Preston. "One, two," said Madison. "Two monkeys left." They sang again and again. Then there was one monkey. Then there were none.

After the song, Madison found a book about a slippery slide at the park. She took it to her dad. "Can we read this one?" she asked. He smiled and said, "Yes, let's read it here." Madison sat close and turned the first page. "The slide looks slippery," she said. "I wonder how fast he goes." Her dad laughed and began to read.

Zayn stood on the baseball diamond. He held his bat with both hands. He wanted to hit the ball far.

The coach looked at the clock. "One more turn," he said. Zayn took a deep breath. The ball came. He swung. He missed.

"Can I try again?" Zayn asked. "Yes!" said Luke. "You can do it, Zayn!" said Maha. The whole team clapped and shouted from the bench. They did not say one cross word.

Zayn smiled. The ball came again. He swung again. Ping! The ball flew over the grass. "Run, Zayn, run!" his teammates called. His shoes went slap, slap, slap on the dirt.

Zayn stood on the base, breathing fast. "We cheered and you hit it," said Maha. "Next time I will cheer for you too," said Zayn. Then he looked at Luke. "Your turn!"

Rowan was in the backyard with his dad. He had a big basket of picture cards. The basket tipped over. All the cards fell out on the grass. "Oh no," said Rowan. "It's a big mess." His dad sat down next to him. "Let's look at them," his dad said.

Rowan picked up a card. It had a cow on it. Then he found a card with a duck. He put them together. "Animals," he said. He found a card with a ball. Then a card with a drum. He put those in a new pile. "Toys," he said. Then he found a card with an apple. A banana card came next. A carrot card, too. "Foods," he said.

Alix came through the gate. She held a card with bread on it. Rowan smiled. "Put it with the foods," he said. Alix put the bread card in the pile. Then they stacked all the piles into one big stack, animals on top. "Tea time," called his dad, and they ran inside to eat warm toast.

Mya stood at the school gate. It was her first day. The gate looked huge to her. "Do I go in?" she asked. "Yes, you go in," said her mom.

Inside, Ms. Chukwu read the class rules. "Rule one, we hang our coats. Rule two, we sit for story time. Rule three, we wait for our turn." Mya listened hard. Ayansh sat next to her. Krew sat next to Ayansh.

Then it was play time. Mya saw the toy horse. She ran fast to grab it. But Krew was already holding it. Mya grabbed too. "Mine!" she said. "No, mine!" said Krew.

Then Ayansh said, "We wait for our turn." Mya stopped. She let go. "Okay," she said. "I can wait." She sat on the floor and counted. "One, two, three." Krew made the horse jump. "Neigh!" he said. "Neigh!" said Mya, and they both laughed.

Then Krew held out the horse. "Your turn now," he said. Mya hugged the horse and made it gallop all around. "Best first day ever," she said. "Neigh!" said Krew.

Emily wanted a bedtime story. She ran to her shelf. She grabbed her book and held it upside down.

Mom sat on the bed. "Let's look at the cover first," she said. "The front has the title." Emily turned the book around. The picture of a bear looked right side up now.

"The words say 'Sleepy Bear,'" said Mom. Emily pointed at the curly letters. "That word says sleepy?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Words tell us things."

They turned the pages one by one. Front to back. Emily held the page corner and waited. She turned it slowly. Then a word on the page said BOO!

A big owl popped out! Emily laughed. "The word said boo!" she said.

Mom closed the book. "Time for sleep," she said. Emily hugged it. "Read the words again tomorrow," she whispered.

The lamp clicked off. The room felt quiet. Emily yawned and closed her eyes.

Beatrice woke up and saw snow. "No school today!" said her dad. "Snow day!" Beatrice cheered. She put on her boots and her red hat. Then she and Dad walked to the big sledding hill.

Marianne and Sebastian were there. Sebastian went zooming down on his sled. Beatrice slid down too. Then she lay down in the soft snow. She swept her arms up and down. She swept her legs out and in. "You look like a wiggly worm!" laughed Marianne.

Beatrice stood up. "Oh no!" Her boot made a big smudge. Her shape was all messy now. "Try again," said Marianne. Beatrice lay down in a different spot. She swept her arms and her legs. Then she rolled to the side and stood up carefully. There it was. A snow angel with wings! "It looks like it will fly away," said Sebastian. Beatrice smiled and waved to her angel. "Fly, angel, fly!" she called.

It was Mackenzie's birthday at the bowling alley. She got new red bowling shoes. "Your turn, Mackenzie," said her dad. Mackenzie rolled the ball. It knocked down three pins. Jenny and Sami clapped. "Happy birthday, Mackenzie!"

After the cake, Dad gave Mackenzie a big yellow balloon. Jenny held a blue one. Sami held a green one. "Let them go and they will fly to the ceiling!" said Mackenzie. She opened her hand. The balloon did not fly up. It went down, down, down. It landed on the floor. It just sat there.

Jenny let go of her blue balloon. It did not fly up either. It drifted down to the floor too. Sami laughed. "Mine fell too!" he said. Mackenzie picked up her balloon. She tossed it up high. It came right back down. Again and again, it came back down.

Then Sami found a shiny silver balloon by the shoe counter. It was on a string. It floated all the way up to the ceiling. It hung there like a star. Mackenzie looked at her yellow balloon. She looked at the silver one. "Yours stays down," said Jenny. "That one goes up."

The silver balloon came floating down on its string. Ms. Crowchild, the lane helper, held it out. "This one can sit by your cake," she said. Mackenzie smiled. She ate one more salty pretzel. Then she took her turn. Strike! All the pins fell down. "Happy birthday to me!" said Mackenzie.

Owen ran into daycare with big news. Today was his birthday. He was four now!

Ms. Hernández was talking to Clark. Clark had a wobbly tooth. Ms. Hernández leaned close and looked at it. "Let me see," she said.

"Ms. Hernández! Ms. Hernández!" Owen pulled her sleeve. She kept talking to Clark. She did not turn around. Owen frowned. His news felt too big to hold in.

He looked out the window. It was windy outside. The leaves spun in circles. Owen took a deep breath, just like the wind filling up and letting go. He stood still. He waited. Clark finished his words. Then Ms. Hernández said, "All done, Clark." Then there was a quiet space.

"Ms. Hernández," Owen said, "can I tell you something?" She turned right away. "Of course, Owen."

"It is my birthday! I am four!" Ms. Hernández clapped her hands. "Happy birthday!" she said. August ran over. "Happy birthday, Owen," August whispered, and gave him a hug.

At snack time, Owen waited for August to finish talking too. Then he said, "Please may I have the crackers?" August passed them over. "Thank you," said Owen.

Waiting was slow. But waiting made the listening come. Owen took a big bite of cracker and smiled.

Isaiah went to the store with his dad. "Let's find juice," said Dad. Isaiah loves juice. He held Dad's hand.

They passed the toy shelf. Then they passed the food. Apples, bread and cheese. Isaiah put the juice in the cart. "Good helper," said Dad.

Then Isaiah saw a big picture. It had dogs and cows. And a fish. Vincent was there too. "Look at the animals!" said Vincent.

"A fish is not an animal," said Isaiah. "It has no legs."

Mr. Ionescu worked at the store. He smiled. "A fish is an animal too," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals."

Isaiah's eyes got big. A fish with no legs, still an animal! He looked at the picture a long time.

The fish jumped out of the picture? No, better. A little dog by the door barked. Woof! The fish in the tank near the door swam fast. Both animals.

"I want to tell Madeline," said Isaiah. "She has a fish!" Dad laughed. They got the juice and went home fast.

Everly sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted to know what the doctor would do. "Open your eyes wide," said the doctor. Everly opened her eyes. She saw a poster on the wall. It had a big ear on it. She saw a shiny tool, too.

"Close your eyes," said the doctor. "Can you see the poster now?" Everly closed her eyes. It was dark. "No," she said. She could not see the poster. She could not see the doctor. She could not see her mama. But she could hear a beep from the hall. Her ears did the hearing. She could smell something like soap. Her nose did the smelling.

Then the doctor said, "Open your mouth." Everly stuck out her tongue. "Good," said the doctor. "Your tongue does the tasting." The doctor put a cold circle on Everly's back. Brrr! Everly felt it with her skin. Her skin did the touching.

Then Wrenley came in with her mama. Wrenley hid her face behind her hands. "You can't see me!" she said. But Everly could still see Wrenley's shoes. Everly could still see her red coat. "I see you," said Everly. Wrenly peeked out. Her hands were over her own eyes, not Everly's. Wrenley laughed. She pulled her hands away. "Peekaboo!" she said. Everly laughed too. She waved her hand. Wrenley waved back.

Evelyn woke up in her bed. The sun was up too. She ran to the kitchen. Her mom was at the table. "Good morning," said Evelyn. They ate eggs and toast. Morning is the time when we wake up and eat breakfast. Now it was morning.

"Now we go to the park," said Mom. At the park, Evelyn saw Mitchell and Adelie. They looked at the pond. "Where are the ducks?" asked Evelyn. "Not here now," said Mitchell. The pond was wide and empty.

Adelie had a present in her bag. It was bread for the ducks. But there were no ducks. "They come in the morning," said Adelie. "We came late. Later is not morning." Evelyn looked at the bread. She waited. They sat on the bench. They waited some more. The ducks did not come.

"Yesterday we saw them," said Mitchell. Evelyn had an idea. "Tomorrow we wake up," she said. "We eat breakfast. Then we run here fast!" Adelie smiled. She put the bread in her bag for tomorrow. "Meet you in the morning," said Evelyn. She waved to the pond, wide and shiny in the sun.

Jules ran to the community garden. He held a little bag of seeds. "Today we plant peas!" said Mr. Brown. Jules dug a small hole. He dropped the seeds in. Then he patted the dirt down. A frog hopped near the fence. Jules laughed and clapped.

Every day Jules came back. He looked for his peas. First he saw tiny leaves. Then he saw curly green vines. The vines grew tall and tall. But where were the peas? Jules could not see any. He looked and looked. He frowned. "Where are they?" he asked. Addison came over. She pointed at a long green pod on the vine.

Jules picked the pod. It felt bumpy. He squeezed it. Pop! The pod opened up. Inside sat a row of little green peas. Jules gasped. "The peas are hiding in here!" he said. Addison picked one too. They found lots of pods on the vines. Jules filled his basket. A red ladybug landed on his hand. "More pods, more peas!" Jules shouted, and ran to the next vine.

Zayn was a little boy on a big trip. He had a small blue bag. He slid the bag across the hotel room floor. "My turn to zoom!" he said. His dad laughed. "Zip, zip, slide," said Zayn. "Zip, zip, slide."

Then it was time to fly home on an airplane. Zayn sat near the window. He wanted to stand up. He wanted to see the clouds up close. He pulled at his seat belt. "I want to look out!" he said.

A kind lady next to him shook her head. "Not now. On an airplane, we all stay buckled in our seats," she said. "We buckle up for takeoff." So Zayn sat and stayed buckled. The plane went fast. Then it went up, up, up! Zayn's tummy felt funny and light. The whole plane tipped, and his feet lifted just a little off the seat. "Whoa!" said Zayn. Now he knew why. He kept his belt on tight.

The clouds slid by the window. "I can see them sitting down," said Zayn. His dad smiled. "Good boy. Buckled up like everyone." Zayn looked out the window all the way up, and the plane flew on.

Abigail was staying at Grandma's house. It was time to sleep. Grandma said, "Pick your socks in the dark room, so we don't wake Grandpa." Abigail tiptoed in. The room was very dark. She felt for socks with her hands. Two socks felt soft and warm. She pulled them on and went to sleep on the big cozy bed.

In the morning, light came in the window. Abigail looked down at her feet. One sock was red! One sock was green! "Grandma, look!" she said. "They looked the same in the dark." Grandma laughed a friendly laugh. "The dark room hid the colors," she said.

Abigail wondered about the dark room. What else was hiding in there? She peeked in again. In the light, she saw a blue blanket and a yellow hat. "In the dark I could not tell," she said. "Light helps me see!" She ran back to show Grandma her two funny socks, one foot at a time.

Ms. Chan put big letters on the rug. "Today we put them in a line," she said. Leah picked up the letter M. Lukas picked up the letter B. Lyle picked up the letter Z.

The line began to grow. A came first. Then B. Then C. But Leah did not know where M should go. She tried to slip M in after C. "No, no!" laughed Lukas. "That spot is full."

Then Leah had an idea. She began to sing the alphabet song. She sang it in her head, quietly. A, B, C, D, E, F, G. She kept singing. H, I, J, K, L. Then she stopped. "M comes now!" she said. She put M down after L. It fit just right.

Lyle held the letter Z. "I know where this one goes," he said. He ran to the end of the long line. "Last!" he said. Leah giggled. Ms. Chan clapped her hands. "Our letter door is open," she said. "Come on, let's sing it all the way through!" Together they sang the whole line, from A to Z.

Harper ran to the farm gate. Ms. Anderson waved her over. "Today we learn our five senses!" she said. Harper clapped her hands.

First they went to the sheep. The sheep said, "Baa!" "You hear with your ears," said Ms. Anderson. Harper touched a soft lamb. "I feel with my hands!" she said. Nola peeked at the beautiful red barn. "I see with my eyes," said Nola.

Then Layne ran up with warm cookies. The baker gave them out. Harper pinched her nose shut. She sniffed and sniffed. Nothing! No cookie smell at all. She let go of her nose. Sniff! Now she could smell them. "Your nose smells!" she said. She took a big bite. "And my tongue tastes chocolate!" Layne laughed and pinched his nose too. "I can't smell mine either!" he said.

Layla was at Grandma's house. It was a sunny morning. Grandma had a basket of five small things on the table. "Can you guess them with your senses?" asked Grandma.

Layla held up one hand. "I have five fingers," she said. "And I have five senses. Eyes to see. Ears to hear. Nose to smell." She stopped. She looked at her last finger. What was the fifth one? She touched a soft little peach. "Hands touch!" she said. "Touching is a sense!" Grandma laughed. "Don't forget your tongue," she said. "Tongues taste." Layla licked a bit of honey from her spoon. "Sweet! That is tasting. Now I have all five."

Then Grandma hid a bell in her apron pocket. She rang it very softly. Layla could not see it. But she heard it. Her ears found the sound! "I hear it with my ears," said Layla, and she pointed right at the pocket. Grandma clapped. "My favorite guesser," she said. Layla counted again: "See, hear, smell, taste, touch. Five!"

Oliver was at Grandpa's house. The big game was on TV today. Oliver wanted to wear his team shirt. He could not find it anywhere.

He looked in his little bag. He looked under the bed. "Not late yet," said Grandpa. "We can keep looking." Oliver walked to the laundry room. There it was, his red shirt! He pulled it on all by himself.

Soon the doorbell rang. Gurfateh came in. He wore a red shirt too. Ocean came next. She wore red too. Ms. Leung was their neighbour. She held up her red scarf. "Look, we all cheer for the same team," she said. Oliver smiled big. The room was full of red. Then the game began, and everybody cheered as one loud crowd. "Go, go, go!" they all shouted together.

Natalie sat on the floor at daycare. Blocks were everywhere. It was messy. Ms. Moose said, "Clean-up time!" Natalie looked at the big pile. "Where do I start?" she asked.

Bria made a red pile. Jayla made a blue pile. Natalie made a yellow pile. All the red blocks went together. All the blue blocks went together. All the yellow blocks went together. "I am sorting by color," said Natalie.

Then she saw something funny. One yellow block was in the blue pile. "How did it get there?" she asked. It was hiding! Natalie picked it up. She put it in the yellow pile. Now the piles were right. The floor was clean. Sun began to shine through the window. Jayla smiled and said, "All done!" Natalie clapped her hands.

Elena was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a small pool in the yard. Elena wanted to swim, but her duck float was up high on a shelf.

"Please, can you get my duck?" Elena asked. Grandma reached up and took it down. "Thank you," said Elena. She hugged the soft yellow duck.

Outside, a boy was splashing near the pool. It was Avery from down the street. Elena bumped into his arm by the gate. "Sorry," she said. Avery smiled at her.

They played in the water. The air smelled like warm flowers. Elena kicked her feet. Splash, splash! Avery handed her a red ball. "Gracias," said Avery.

Elena stopped kicking. "What did you say?" she asked.

"Gracias," said Avery. "It means thank you. It is a Spanish word." His grandma spoke Spanish, too.

Elena thought that was nice. She climbed out of the pool. She gave Avery her yellow duck. "Gracias," said Elena. Avery laughed and clapped.

Soon the sky turned pink. It was getting late. Grandma wrapped Elena in a big warm towel. "Time to come in," she said. Elena held her duck tight.

"Gracias, Grandma," said Elena. Grandma kissed the top of her wet head.

It was Victor's birthday! There was a big box on the table. The box was covered in blue paper. "What is inside?" Victor asked. "I can't see it!" He shook the box. He squeezed the box. He held it up to his ear. The paper hid everything.

Jameson came to the party. Hiba came too. Mr. Fitzgerald from next door came with a smile. "Guess what is inside," said Hiba. "Is it a drum?" asked Jameson. Victor did not know. The paper was in the way.

Dad helped Victor open the box. Dad tore the paper off. Slowly, slowly, the box showed what it was. It was a big red truck! Victor jumped up and down. "The paper was hiding my truck!" he said. "Now I can see it!" He pushed the truck across the floor. Beep, beep! Happy birthday, Victor!

Arthur had a runny nose. His cough was small but loud. Mama put him on the big couch with his red blanket.

"I want to run in the garden," said Arthur.

"Not today," said Mama. "You have a cold. Resting here helps your body get better. Sit with your sock feet and your book."

Arthur wiggled one sock foot. He sniffed. The lemon water on the table smelled sour. He took a little sip. Sour! His face went wrinkly. He let out a tiny laugh at himself.

Mama read his book about bears. Arthur looked at the pictures. He heard rain tap the window. Tap, tap, tap. The blanket was warm and soft like a cat.

Arthur slept a long time on the couch. When he woke up, his nose felt better. His cough was almost gone.

"I rested and my body got better!" said Arthur. He jumped one small jump.

Mama felt his head. "Tomorrow you can run outside," she said. "Today, one more book?"

"Yes," said Arthur. He pulled the blanket up to his chin. "The bear book again, please."

Maya stood at the school door. Her hands held her mama's hand tight. "Big school," said Maya. "Too big." The hallway was long and loud.

Mr. Whitehead smiled at her. "Hello, Maya," he said. "It is time to walk to our room." The children stood one behind another. Maya did not see why. She let go of her mama and ran ahead, fast, to catch the end of the hall. But the line went past her like a long snake. Then the line was gone, and the hall felt empty.

"Here, Maya," called Charli. "Stand in front of me!" Maya ran back and took her spot. Gus stood in front of Charli. Maya looked at the line going on and on. Then she walked with them, step by step.

Mama waved at the door. Maya caught her smile and waved back.

Emilia played in the kitchen while supper cooked. She smelled the soup. It was hot soup, and her mom stirred it. Then Mom said, "Bath time soon." Emilia wanted to jump right in. She ran to the tub and put one foot near the water. "Wait," said Mom. "I check the bath water first." Mom put her hand in the water. Emilia watched.

"Too hot," said Mom. She turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Mom put her hand in again. "Now it is just right." Emilia touched the water with her toes. It felt warm and nice. She got in and splashed. She washed her arms and her belly.

After the bath, Emilia got dressed in soft pajamas. She heard the phone ring in the kitchen. Mom swept the floor by the table. Soon Emilia yawned. She lay in her bed and closed her eyes. Her teddy sat beside her pillow. Mom kissed her head. "Warm water, warm bed," Mom whispered. Emilia fell fast asleep.

Raphael was playing house at daycare. His baby doll sat in a little chair. The doll had one sock on. The other sock was lost.

Then Raphael dropped the doll. It fell on the floor. Raphael picked it up fast. He looked at the doll's face. Was the baby sad? Raphael felt worried.

Walker came over. "The doll cannot really feel," Walker said. "But we can pretend it does." Raphael thought about that. Then he hugged the doll. He patted its back, just like a dad would. "There, there," he said softly.

The doll did not cry. The doll did not smile. It just sat still. But Raphael made a pretend smile with its mouth. Walker laughed. Then Walker found the lost sock under the rug. It was a thick, warm sock. Raphael pulled it onto the doll's foot.

"Would the baby like a bottle?" Walker asked. Raphael held the pretend bottle to the doll. "Drink up," he said. Ms. Kerr walked by and smiled. "What a good daddy," she said. Raphael hugged the doll again. "I will thank you later," he told it, "for being my baby."

Arnaud did not want to sleep. His favorite stuffed cow sat on the pillow. Arnaud held it tight. His tummy felt funny. Tomorrow was the class party, and he was excited.

"Too much thinking," he said to the cow. He got out of bed. He padded to the big mirror by the door. He looked at his face.

Arnaud smiled a big smile. The mirror smiled back. "That is my happy face," he said. Then he made his mouth turn down. The mirror looked sad. "That is my sad face," he said.

He made a scowl. His eyebrows went down. The mirror looked angry. Then he made big wide eyes. The mirror looked scared. Arnaud giggled. His face could change, and the mirror showed it. He made the happy face again. The mirror smiled at him.

Dad came in. "What are you doing, little one?" Arnaud said, "Watch!" He made his sad face. Then he made his happy face. Dad laughed and made a happy face too. Arnaud yawned. He got back into bed. He hugged the cow. His eyes closed slowly.

"Good night, cow," he whispered. "See you at the party."

Mateo sat on the soft red rug at the library. Mr. Okonkwo held up a big card. It had the letter A on it. "A says ah," said Mateo. "Very good," said Mr. Okonkwo.

They went through the letters one by one. Mateo patted the card each time he got one right. The letters felt thick and stiff, like a book cover. A girl named Ellis sat next to him. She clapped for him.

Soon Mateo reached the letter P. P says puh. "Now I know them all," he said. Mr. Okonkwo smiled and shook his head. "Sing the song with me," he said. They sang. Q, R, S, all the way to the end.

Then Mateo heard it. The last letter of the song. Z. "Z!" he shouted. "The alphabet ends at Z!" Ellis laughed and patted his back. Mateo held up the Z card. It felt cool and smooth. "Z says zuh," he said. "Now I know them all. A to Z."

Isaac ran to the backyard with a big bag. Inside were carrots and potatoes. They came from the farmers' market. Isaac wanted to make dinner for his family!

But the carrots were dirty. Little brown bits clung to them. "Yuck," said Isaac. "Can we eat dirt?"

"No," said his dad. "Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables first. Scrub them in the sink." Dad turned on the water. It was cool, not hot.

Isaac held a carrot under the water. He rubbed it with his fingers. The dirt popped off into the sink. The water turned brown. Then the carrot turned bright orange and clean!

"Look!" said Isaac. "The dirt went away!"

He scrubbed the potatoes too. They came clean as well. Isaac stacked them in a pot. Dad carried the pot to the stove, where it would be safe.

Soon the carrots were soft and sweet. Isaac's name was on a card by the plate. It said, "Dinner by Isaac."

Greyson came over to share. "This is so good!" he said.

Isaac grinned and held up a red tomato. "Next time, soup!"

Violet stood by the big blue pool. Her team was in the water. The water smelled like soap and splashed everywhere.

"Where do I stand?" Violet asked. She looked at the lanes. She looked at the ropes. She did not know.

Kane was at the wall. Macie was by the steps. Violet wondered where she belonged.

The coach blew the whistle. "Come here, Violet," she said. "I will show you." The coach teaches the team and helps the players learn the game. She held Violet's hand at the shallow end. "Stand on this line," the coach said. "Wait here for your turn."

Violet stood on the line. The water was cool on her toes. She waited and waited.

"Go!" said the coach.

Violet kicked and splashed to Kane. Kane clapped. "You know where to stand now!" he said.

It was Violet's little surprise. She knew just where to go. Macie waved from the steps. "Violet, come stand with us!"

Thomas was at a big family party. The house was full of cousins and aunts. It was a celebration with special food and songs.

Music started to play. Everyone began to dance. Thomas sat on a chair and watched. He wished he could dance too. But his feet felt shy.

His grandmother held out her hand. "Come dance with me," she said. Thomas took her hand. They stepped and spun. The music went fast, and his feet went fast. The music went slow, and his feet went slow too.

Later, his cousin Nikola laughed. "You danced the whole song!" she said. Thomas looked out the window. The street was dark. It was getting late.

"I want one more dance," said Thomas. Grandmother laughed and clapped her hands. "Play the music again!"

Wesley came to school early. He saw his friend Harnaaz at the wood table. He touched the wood. It felt bumpy.

"I smell cookies," said Harnaaz. Wesley sniffed with his nose. He smelled them too. Then Bonnie shouted, "Cookies!" Everyone laughed.

Ms. Morningstar gave out warm cookies. Wesley tasted his cookie. It was sweet. He heard a crunch. That was his own mouth.

Wesley looked at Harnaaz. He saw two little holes in her nose. "What are those?" he asked.

"Those are your nostrils," said Ms. Morningstar. "Your nose has two openings. They are called nostrils."

Wesley ran to the little mirror. He counted his nostrils. One, two. He sniffed again. The cookie smell came in both holes.

"My nose smells with two doors!" he said.

"Cookie for me too," said Harnaaz, and she took a big bite.

Ivy sat in a little chair at the doctor's office. She held her teddy on her lap. "Eyes open, please," said Mr. Nielsen. He shined a small light. Ivy saw the light go blink, blink. "Now I will tap here," he said. Ivy heard the tap, tap with her ears. She smelled something sweet from a sticker sheet on the desk.

Then the big light went off. The room got dark. "Where is teddy?" Ivy asked. She could not see him anywhere. "It is hard to see in the dark," said Mr. Nielsen. He turned on the lamp. Click. Now Ivy saw teddy on the chair. She picked him up and gave him a hug. "Good team," said Mr. Nielsen. The grumpy old light had made her wait. But waiting was fine. Ivy got a sweet sticker. She licked it with her tongue, just a tiny taste. Then she and teddy touched noses.

It was play time at school. Mr. Tesfaye put two hoops on the floor. Theodore wanted to throw his red beanbag into a hoop. He threw it. The beanbag hit the edge and fell out. Boaz clapped for him anyway. Theodore tried again. This time the beanbag went in. "I did it!" said Theodore. The hoop did not spin. It stayed still, and the beanbag landed inside.

Then Ella rolled a big ball to Theodore. He held out his hands. The ball hit his hands and bounced out. It rolled past his shoes. Ella rolled it again. The ball bounced out again. Theodore felt like crying a little. Mr. Tesfaye came close and sat by his side.

"Hug it to your chest," said Mr. Tesfaye. Ella rolled the big ball once more. Theodore caught it and hugged it to his chest. The ball did not bounce out. It stayed right there, warm and round. "My turn," said Ella. Theodore rolled the ball back to her.

Axel sat at the big table. He wanted to paint a picture of the sky. He picked up a gray crayon first. He drew one gray line. Then he looked out the window.

The sun was shining bright. The day was clear. The sky did not look gray. The sky looked blue, all over.

Axel put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He drew blue at the top of his page. "Blue," he said. He drew a big blue sky.

Then he painted a yellow sun in the corner. He painted red flowers down low. He painted green grass under the flowers. Each color was different. "Look, Mama," said Axel. His mama looked at the paint. "What a sunny blue sky," she said.

Axel held his picture up to the window. The blue on his page sat next to the blue in the sky. They looked the same. Axel smiled. "Sky match," he said.

Sienna sat in the family car. Her brown bear was not in her bag. "Oh no," she said. "Bear is lost!"

Dad buckled her seat. "Do not worry," he said. "We will find him. Let us go back to each place you went, in order. It is called retracing your steps."

First, they drove back to school. Sienna had played there with Deacon and Meher. She looked under the little table. No bear.

Next, they drove to the park. Sienna had gone there after school. Dad parked the car. Sienna held his hand.

They walked back along the path. First she stopped at the swings. She looked under her favorite swing. No bear.

Then she stopped at the slide. She peeked behind it. The sun was going down. A lamp by the slide clicked on. The light made a warm, bright circle. And there, in the circle, sat bear!

"Bear!" said Sienna. She hugged him tight. "Thank you, lamp," she said.

Dad laughed softly. They walked back to the car. Sienna held bear all the way home.

"You found him," said Dad.

"I went back to every place," said Sienna. "In order!"

Stella woke up and looked out the window. Snow! No school today. It was a snow day.

Dad made her a sled from a big red tray. "Let's make a hill," he said. They piled snow in the backyard. The hill was small, but Stella loved it.

She wanted to go down head first, like a penguin. "Watch me, Dad!" she called. Dad shook his head. "Sit up, Stella. Face the way you are going. I will stand right here and watch you."

Stella sat up on the tray. She held on with both hands. She faced forward. Dad stood by the hill and watched. Whoosh! Down she went. She did not fall off.

The wind touched her cold cheeks. The stormy sky looked gray and big. "Again!" said Stella. She climbed back up the little hill.

"This time I will be a cow," she said. "Cows do not sled." Dad laughed. "No, they just watch us." Stella went down again, sitting up, facing forward, all the way to the flat white grass.

Charles sat at the little table. It was writing time at school. Ms. Tanaka gave everyone a pencil and a paper.

"I will write my name!" said Charles.

He picked up his pencil. He made a big C. But the paper slid away. His line went crooked. He tried again. The paper slipped again. His letter went off the side.

Myla sat next to him. She put one hand on her paper. Her paper stayed still. Her letters came out neat.

Charles looked. Then he put his hand on his paper too. He held it down. He drew his C. It stayed on the line! He made an H. Then an A. Then R. Then another L. Then an E. Then an S.

"Look!" said Charles. "It says Charles!"

Ms. Tanaka came over. She clapped her hands. "Wonderful!" she said.

Myla peeked at his paper. "Your C is so round," she said.

Charles stood up. His shoe tapped a happy tap on the floor. He held up his paper high.

"I can write it again!" he said. He sat down in his cozy chair. He put one hand on the paper. The paper did not slip one bit. He started a big, round C.

Anna sat in the band room with her little drum. Ms. Cho gave out a new song. "Tap it like this," said Ms. Cho. Anna tried. She hit the wrong spot. The song stopped halfway. Mivaan and Maika played theirs all the way.

Anna frowned. "This song is too hard," she said. "I don't know how to do it." Ms. Cho smiled. "Take the drum home. Try a little bit each day." Anna was afraid the song would stay hard forever.

On Monday Anna tapped the drum after her cookie. She got two notes right. On Tuesday she tapped again. She got four notes right. On Friday her hands seemed to know the song by themselves. She played it all the way! At school, Anna played it for Mivaan and Maika. They clapped and clapped. "Again!" said Maika. Anna lifted her drumsticks high.

It was Jayden's birthday at the park. Siena and Aiden came to play. The wind blew the balloons side to side.

Mom set a big cake on the table. "Look at your candles," she said. Jayden counted them. "One, two, three, four." He counted again. "One, two, three, four."

He stopped and thought. "How old am I today?" he asked. "Five," said Mom. "One candle for each year."

Jayden looked at the cake. "Then I need one more!" Mom smiled. She put in a fifth candle. "One, two, three, four, five," they said together.

Dad lit the candles, far from Jayden's hands. Then came a small surprise. The wind puffed one out. Jayden laughed.

"Make a wish," said Siena. He did, and blew out the same candles, one by one.

Ryan ran into Ms. Dela Cruz's music studio. A big guitar sat on a stand. "Can I play it?" he asked. Ms. Dela Cruz smiled and said yes.
