Ryan tapped the guitar like a drum. Pat, pat, pat. The strings stayed quiet. No music came out. "Why is it so quiet?" he asked. Ms. Dela Cruz said, "Watch me." She swept her fingers across the strings. Pluck, strum! A happy sound filled the room.

Ryan's tummy did a little jump. He tried it too. He plucked one string. Ping! He strummed them all. Waaaah! "It works!" he shouted. His friend Clovis clapped from the corner. Ryan strummed again, faster this time. Ms. Dela Cruz clapped too, and Ryan sat up tall and proud. "One more song!" he said.

Livia could not find her bunny. She looked under the table. She looked in the toy box. No bunny. "Where can he be?" she asked. Ms. Fernando said, "Let's look together."

Livia looked behind the chair. She spotted Alison painting at the easel. "Bunny is not here," Livia said. Then she saw her own coat hanging on the hook. She asked herself, "Can things hide in pockets?" She put her hand in the pocket. Something soft was inside. It was bunny! Bunny had been tucked in her coat all along.

Alison clapped her hands. "Bunny was in your pocket!" she said. "Now let's speak to bunny at the tea table," said Ms. Fernando. Livia hugged bunny tight. At the tea table, Alison poured pretend tea. Livia set out a pretend cake. "We used pretend money to buy this cake," said Alison. Livia laughed and held bunny on her lap, safe and warm.

Wesley stood in the pet store. He held a small box with holes. Inside was his new bunny, Pip.

At home, Wesley put Pip in his cage. "Now we play!" said Wesley. He reached for the cage door. But Pip was eating a carrot. His little mouth went munch, munch. Ms. Popal, the neighbour, was visiting. "Look," she said softly. "When a pet is sleeping or eating, it is best to leave it alone." Wesley sat on his hands and waited. He watched the carrot get smaller and smaller. Soon the bowl was empty. Then something surprising happened. Pip hopped out on his own and made a circle right around Wesley's shoe.

"Now we play," said Wesley. Pip sniffed his tall sock. "Best friend ever," said Wesley. He found a soft brush and sat very still on the floor. Pip climbed onto his lap. "Goodnight, Pip," Wesley whispered.

Grandma's car pulled into the driveway. Amira ran to the door. Grandma climbed out with a big bag. "This is my suitcase," Grandma said. "I packed it full of clothes and things."

Amira helped pull the suitcase across the grass. It bumped over the stones. One, two, three bumps. It was heavy! What could be inside?

"Can I see?" Amira asked. Grandma smiled and opened it up. Amira peeked in. She saw sweaters. She saw socks. She saw a warm red scarf. One, two, three sweaters. Four, five, six socks. And there, on top, was a small sheep. It was soft and woolly. "That sheep keeps me company at night," Grandma said.

Amira touched the sheep. It felt warm from sitting in the sun. Grandma would stay for a whole week. "Do you have enough clothes for seven days?" Amira asked. Grandma laughed. "I packed one shirt for each day."

They counted the shirts together. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Then Amira showed Grandma her own room. "My toys don't live in a suitcase," she said. "They live in my toy box." Grandma zipped the suitcase shut. "Tomorrow I will wear the blue shirt," she said. "Which one will you wear, Amira?"

Jaxon ran to the sandbox at the park. He saw Malcolm there. Malcolm had a big blue truck. "Vroom, vroom," said Malcolm. He pushed the truck through the sand.

Jaxon wanted that truck. It looked so strong. He grabbed it fast. Malcolm began to cry. "My truck!" he said. Jaxon held the truck very tight. Why was Malcolm sad? Was it because Jaxon took it?

Jaxon gave the truck back. Then he tried again, a different way. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. Malcolm wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You can have a turn." Malcolm handed the truck over. Jaxon pushed it through the sand. "Vroom, vroom," said Jaxon.

What a big change! He took it, and Malcolm cried. He asked, and Malcolm smiled. Jaxon said the magic words again and again. "Can I have a turn? Can I have a turn?"

Later, Mallory came with a little green turtle toy. Jaxon looked at it. He did not grab. He said, "Can I have a turn, please?"

Mallory smiled big. "Yes! And then we splash in the puddle together." She held out the turtle. Jaxon took it gently, with both hands.

Austin went to the store with his dad. He held the list like a treasure map. The list said one word: carrot.

In the veggie aisle, a big cart blocked the way. Austin squeezed. He wiggled. He could not get past. He saw the carrots far away, glowing like orange rockets waiting for him.

"Say excuse me," Dad whispered. "Excuse me," said Austin. The lady smiled and moved her cart. The way was open! Austin ran to the carrots and picked the biggest one.

At the freezer, Austin saw frozen peas sparkle like tiny stars. He wanted to touch them, but the door was too high. "Can you help me, please?" he asked Dad. Dad reached the peas down. Austin put them in the cart.

At the checkout, Austin bumped a box of crackers. "Sorry," he said. The cashier smiled. Austin handed her the carrot like a golden wand. "Thank you," she said. "You too," said Austin. He held the carrot all the way home.

Athena put her hand in her pocket. Her little bunny was not there. "Oh no," said Athena. "Bunny is lost."

She looked under the art table. No bunny. She looked in the toy box. No bunny. Athena sat down on the winter rug. She wanted to cry.

Ms. Sutherland sat by her. "It is hard to look all alone," she said. Athena stood up. "Elora! Sunny! Will you help me look?" Elora nodded. Sunny nodded too. Now three friends were looking, not just one.

Elora looked by the book shelf. Sunny looked near the blocks. Athena looked by the snack table. Then Sunny called out, "Come here! Come quick!" There was bunny, tucked behind the crunchy cracker bin. Someone had used bunny to hold a paper the class had cut into snowflakes.

Athena hugged bunny tight. "Thank you," she said. "More eyes found him!" Sunny smiled and clapped. Elora gave bunny a little pat on the head.

"Let's put bunny somewhere safe," said Athena. She zipped him into her coat pocket, right up close to her heart.

Natalie ran to the park with her bat in her hand. Today was her first team game. Her friends Santino and Avery were there too. The coach blew a whistle. "Batters up," he called.

Natalie was first to hit the ball. She ran to home plate fast. An ant crawled by her shoe. She lifted the bat and got ready to swing.

"Hold on, Natalie," said the coach. "You forgot something." He held up a helmet. "You wear this on your head when you bat," he said. "The helmet protects your head." Natalie put it on. It felt big and warm.

She swung and missed. She swung and missed again. Santino called out, "You can do it, Natalie!" Avery clapped her hands. Natalie took a big breath. She was not shy now. She watched the ball come.

Swing! The ball went far. Natalie ran to first base. The helmet sat on her head the whole time. "Nice hit," said Mr. Saleh from the fence. He was their neighbor. He waved his hat in the air.

Avery was up next. She ran to the plate without her helmet. "Wait," said Natalie. She picked up the helmet. "You have to wear this." Avery smiled and put it on. Then she hit the ball too.

Olivia sat at the wooden table. She had red paint, blue paint and yellow paint. She wanted to paint a big blue sky.

She dipped her brush in the blue. She painted the top of her paper. "Oh no," said Olivia. "My sky is too dark. Real sky is not this dark."

She had a question. Could paint get lighter? She looked at her pots. There was one more pot. It was white.

Olivia stirred her brush in the white pot. Then she stirred it into her blue. Round and round she mixed. The blue began to change. It got lighter and lighter!

"Look, look!" she called. Her friend Lilian ran over. Lilian was painting a red fire truck. "Try it on your red," said Olivia.

Lilian added white to her red. Her red got lighter too. It looked pink like a flower. "Ooh," said Lilian. "My fire truck is a happy truck now."

Olivia painted her light blue sky. She added a big yellow sun. Then she held her paper up high.

"Mom! Come see my sky!" she shouted. "The white paint made it light, just like morning!"

Brielle stood in the gym at school. Ms. Dhillon put a hoop on the floor. "Throw the beanbag in," she said.

Brielle held the beanbag in her little hands. She looked at the hoop. She let go. The beanbag went in! Brielle jumped up and down. Oceanne clapped for her.

Then Ms. Dhillon brought out a big ball. "Now catch it," she said. She rolled it to Brielle. Brielle shut her eyes tight. The ball bumped her tummy and rolled away. "Oh no," said Brielle. She was not angry. She just wanted to try again.

Ms. Dhillon rolled the big ball again. This time Brielle kept her eyes open. She watched the ball all the way to her hands. She caught it with both hands! "I did it!" said Brielle.

Leonard was next. He shut his eyes and missed too. The ball rolled under a shelf. A tall woman came to get it out for him. "Keep your eyes open," said Brielle. "Watch the ball all the way to your hands."

Leonard watched the ball all the way to his hands. He caught it with both hands. "My turn again!" said Brielle, and she held out her arms.

Beatrice went to the mall with her dad. She was getting her very first haircut. She sat in a big chair. The hairdresser put a cape on her. It was soft and blue.

"I want to see my hair," said Beatrice. The hairdresser cut a little. Then she cut a little more. Beatrice saw the front in the mirror. But she could not see the back. She turned her head. Still no back. She stuck out her chin. Still no back. "I can't see the back," said Beatrice. "Not a bad try," said the hairdresser. "But I have a key trick for you." She picked up a small mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice's head. Now Beatrice saw the back of her hair in the big mirror too. "There it is!" said Beatrice. She smiled at her short, neat hair. "Can I look again?" she asked. The hairdresser held the mirror up one more time.

Edouard ran to the bookmobile. He saw his friend August at the steps. August held a book about trains. "I have a card," August said. He showed a little blue card. Edouard wanted one too.

He ran to the desk. "Can I have a card?" he asked. The driver shook her head. "You need a grown-up to help you sign up," she said. Edouard's dad was parking the car. Edouard ran to him. "Please come!" he begged. Dad followed him to the desk.

Dad wrote on a form. The driver made a new card. It had Edouard's name on it. Edouard picked a book about the moon. She scanned the card, and the book was his to take home. That night, Dad fell asleep, but Edouard read on by the hall light. "Moon," he whispered, turning the page.

Today was the big day. Madeline's family was having a party for the lights festival. The sky outside was stormy and grey. But inside, the house smelled sweet and warm.

Madeline had a problem. What should she wear? She held up her old play shirt. It had a paint spot on it. She held up her blue dress with gold flowers. Her mom came in and said, "You pick, Madeline." Madeline looked and looked. Then she put on the blue dress. It felt soft and shiny. She looked in the mirror and smiled.

Grandma came to the door. Grandma wore a red sari with tiny bells. Dad wore his white kurta. Everyone at the party had special clothes on. Madeline saw that. Her friends Richard and Skyler arrived too. Skyler wore a bright green kurta. Skyler said, "Your dress is so pretty." Madeline twirled around and around. She had one loose tooth, and it wiggled when she grinned.

The candles were lit by Dad, up high and safe. The little flames made the gold flowers on Madeline's dress sparkle. She laughed and clapped her hands. "More lights," she said.

Sophia sat at the dinner table. Papa put a bowl of soup in front of her. The lamp above the table made a warm circle of light. Sophia tapped her spoon. Tap, tap, tap.

Haider was eating with them today. "We went to the park tomorrow," said Haider. Then he stopped. He shook his head. "No. Not tomorrow. Yesterday. We went yesterday." Sophia looked at him. "What is yesterday?" she asked. "Yesterday is the day before today," said Haider. He took a big spoonful of soup.

Sophia counted on her fingers. "Today is soup day. Yesterday was park day." She held up one finger, then another. "One day, then one day. Yesterday, then today." Papa smiled and nodded.

"Now I want bread," said Sophia. "Later we can have berries," said Papa. "Not now. Later." "And tomorrow?" asked Sophia. "Tomorrow we can go to the park," said Haider. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Sophia clapped her hands.

She ate her soup. She ate her bread. Her chin got messy. Papa wiped it with a soft cloth. Then he brought a small bowl of berries. "Later is now," said Papa. Sophia picked up one berry, two berries, three. "Today is berry day," she said. She put a berry on Haider's plate too.

Jacob ran to the big slide at the playground. His friend Alycia was already there. She had a drum, a birthday gift from her grandma.

"Want to hear it?" said Alycia. She banged it. BOOM! The sound was loud. It was so loud that the little babies by the swings woke up. They cried and cried.

Jacob covered his ears. "Can you make it quiet?" he asked.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Alycia. She tapped the drum very softly. Tap, tap, tap. That was quiet. The babies stopped crying. One baby went back to sleep.

"Drums can be fast too," said Jacob. He patted the drum fast, fast, fast. Then Alycia patted it slow, slow, slow. They laughed.

"Race you to the slide," said Jacob. He ran fast. Alycia ran slow on purpose, like a turtle.

"I am a slow turtle!" she said. "Smelly like one too!" Jacob giggled all the way down.

"Tap, tap," went the drum, soft and quiet, all the way home.

Elijah went to the store with his dad. He wanted a book about a big red truck. He skipped down the book aisle. There were so many books. He could not find the truck book. Elijah opened a book. The pages went the wrong way. His dad turned it around. "Start at the front," his dad said. Elijah began at the front cover. Then he saw words on the cover. "Who made this story?" Elijah asked. His dad pointed to the name. "That is the author. The author wrote the words of the book." Elijah ran his finger over the name. Then he found the truck book. On the cover, he saw a name. "This author made my truck story!" he said. A girl named Beatrix was looking for a bunny book. Elijah showed her the cover. "Look for the author's name," he said. She smiled and held her cute bunny book tight.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. The trees went by the window. She held her little book on her lap.

"Is today library day?" she asked.

Mom looked in the mirror. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now. We are going now."

Kinsley looked out. "Yesterday we went to Nina's house," she said. "Yesterday is all done."

"That's right," said Mom. "And tomorrow is the day after this one. Tomorrow you will see River."

The car stopped at a red light. Kinsley watched a big dog climb out of a truck. The dog jumped down, and the light turned green. The car moved again.

"Later we can read books," said Mom. "Later means after the library."

"Can we eat apples later?" asked Kinsley.

"Yes," said Mom. "Red, juicy apples."

The library door came into view. Kinsley kicked her feet. "Today is now!" she said.

Mom smiled and parked the car. "Hold my hand," she said. Kinsley took it, and they walked in together.

Henry had a cold. His nose was red and his throat felt scratchy. So Henry stayed at Grandma's house all day. It was cloudy outside. Henry looked out the big window. He wanted to play in the garden, but not today.

Henry built a tower with soft blocks. Then his nose tickled. "Ah... ah... achoo!" Henry sneezed right into his hand. His hand felt wet and yucky. Grandma brought a tissue. She wiped his hand clean.

"Watch me," said Grandma. She lifted her arm and put her nose into her elbow. "Ah... ah... achoo!" Grandma sneezed into her elbow. "You try it," she said. Henry lifted his arm. He put his nose into his elbow. His nose tickled again. "Ah... achoo!" This time the sneeze went into his elbow. His hand stayed clean and dry.

Henry smiled big. He sneezed two more times that day. Each time, up went his arm. Each time, his elbow caught the sneeze. At bedtime, Grandma read him a story on the couch. Henry snuggled close under a warm blanket. "Night night, elbow," said Henry. Grandma kissed his head.

Mya sat on the playroom rug. She had a bowl of grapes. Auston sat next to her with his own bowl.

Mya counted her grapes out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." She pushed each grape as she said the word. Five grapes sat in a row.

Auston looked at his bowl. His grapes were very big. "My grapes are big," he said. "Maybe three big grapes are really five grapes."

Mya shook her head. "No. Three means three." She picked up his grapes. "Watch. One, two, three." Three big grapes sat in a row. "Three is three. Big or small, it is three."

Auston counted them himself. "One, two, three," he said. He laughed. "Three grapes are three grapes!"

Klara came over. "Can I have some grapes too?" she asked.

Mya looked at her bowl. She had five. She gave one to Klara. "Now I have four," she said. "One, two, three, four."

They played a counting game next. Mya hid grapes under a cup. "How many now?" she asked.

Auston lifted the cup. "One, two, three!" he said. "Three grapes!"

Klara hid grapes next. Auston guessed, "Four!" Klara lifted the cup. "No, it was two!"

They played until the grapes were gone. Then they counted blocks instead, all the way to ten.

"One, two, three, four, five," said Mya.

"Six, seven, eight," said Klara.

"Nine, ten!" said Auston. He stacked the last block on top.

"Lucky us," said Mya. "Ten blocks." The tower wobbled. Auston held it steady with one finger.

Matthew wanted to play tea party at daycare. But the teapot was empty. No real tea at all. Matthew frowned at it.

Noelie came over. She held her teddy bear. "Pour the tea," she said. Matthew tipped the empty teapot over a little cup. Nothing came out. But Noelie clapped. "Good tea!" she said.

Matthew picked up the cup. He gave it to teddy. "Careful," said Noelie. "It's pretend hot. Blow on it first." Matthew blew into the empty cup. Teddy drank and drank. "More, please," said Noelie, in a small bear voice.

Then Samy came with a tall dinosaur. "Dino is thirsty too," he said. Matthew poured pretend tea again. Samy put a pretend coin on the table. "Dino pays," he said. Mr. Carvalho smiled from across the room.

Matthew remembered the empty teapot. Empty was fine. Pretend tea was still tea. He filled every cup on the table. Noelie blew on hers. "All gone," she said. Matthew tipped the teapot one more time. "Last cup for teddy," he said.

Rosalie ran up the short front steps. Grandma opened the door wide. "Happy Diwali!" she called. Inside, the house was full. There were aunts and uncles and babies everywhere. "Why is everyone here?" Rosalie asked. "It is our special holiday," said Grandma. "We all come together to celebrate." Then Rosalie heard a laugh. It was her cousin! She had not seen him in a long, long time. They hugged and spun in a circle, like a wheel going round and round. Grandma placed little clay lamps on the windowsill. She lit each one herself. Rosalie watched the flames flicker. "So many lights," she said. "Does one lamp make the whole house glow?" Her cousin took her hand. "Come see the lamps outside too!"

Zoe rode in the car with Dad. They drove down the long road to the hospital. The sky was cloudy, but Zoe did not mind. Mom was at the hospital with the new baby.

Zoe saw Mom in a soft bed. The baby was tiny. He had small hands and a small nose. "This is your baby brother," Mom said. Zoe looked and looked. Everyone looked at the baby. Nobody looked at Zoe.

Then the baby cried. Mom needed a clean diaper. Dad could not find it. "Zoe, can you help?" Mom asked. "Big sisters can fetch things. Please bring the diaper from the bag." Zoe ran to the bag. She found the diaper. She carried it to Mom, so proud.

"Now can you fetch a small blanket?" Mom asked. Zoe got the blanket too. Mom put it on the baby. The baby stopped crying. He hid his face in the blanket and went to sleep.

Mom smiled at Zoe. "You helped him feel cozy." Zoe patted the blanket, soft and slow. "I am the diaper girl," Zoe said. Mom laughed and hugged her tight.

Mason was at Grandpa's house. He found a big pencil on the table. "Can I write?" he asked. Grandpa said, "Yes. Let us write your name."

Mason held the pencil in his fist. The M came out wiggly. The A fell over. The S looked like a sleepy cat curled on the page. "My letters are all mixed up," said Mason. "Will they get better?"

"Try again," said Grandpa. So Mason wrote his name one time. Then two times. Then three times. One, two, three, Mason! The pencil began to feel friendly in his hand. The M stood up tall. The S woke up and stretched.

The next day Mason wrote his name again. And the day after that. One, two, three, Mason! Soon the letters came out neat and small. "Look, Grandpa!" said Mason. "It says Mason!" Grandpa laughed and put the page on the fridge. The cat jumped up to look too. "That is my name," said Mason. "I wrote it all by myself."

Jules had a cold. His nose was red. His throat felt scratchy. He sat at the kitchen table in his pajamas. His blanket was around him.

Jules wanted to hide his throat. It felt bad. But then he thought of Grandma's house. At Grandma's house, his throat had hurt too. He had told Grandma. Grandma had helped him. So Jules took a big breath and said, "Mom, my throat hurts."

Mom put her hand on his head. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Let's fix that."

Mom got out a pot. She filled it with warm water. The stove was hot, so Jules stayed back. He watched from his chair. Mom added noodles to the pot. They were small noodles shaped like hearts. Jules smiled. "A heart!" he said.

Mom stirred the soup. Steam went up, up, up. Jules closed his eyes and smelled it. The smell was warm and good.

Mom set the bowl down. "Blow first," she said. Jules blew on his spoon. Then he took a little sip. The warm soup went down his throat. His throat felt softer now. Not scratchy.

Jules took another sip. Then he saw something at the bottom. He dug his spoon in. It was the biggest heart noodle of all. It had been hiding under the small ones.

Jules held it up. "Mom! Look!" he said. "The biggest one for me."

Jack waited at the airport. He held a sign that said Grandpa. The plane came in. The doors opened. People walked out, one, two, three. Then Jack saw Grandpa! Grandpa hugged him. "I will stay a whole week," said Grandpa.

At home, Grandpa brought out a card game. "We can play together," said Grandpa. "We take turns." Jack grabbed all the cards. "I want to go first every time!" he said. Grandpa shook his head, kind and slow. "No, Jack. First me, then you." Grandpa put down one card. Then Jack put down one card. Then Grandpa. Then Jack. Turn and turn and turn.

Jack saw that when he waited, the game worked. The cards went flip, flip, flip, back and forth. Grandpa smiled. "Your turn, Jack," he said. Jack clapped and played his card. Then a little ant walked across the table. "Look! The ant wants a turn too," said Jack.

Mr. Holloway held up a big red bag. "Time for the feely-bag game," he said. Scarlett ran over with her friends Bree and Arvin.

"You put your hand in," said Mr. Holloway. "Do not peek. Feel it and guess."

Arvin went first. He pushed his hand into the bag. "It is round," he said. "It is a ball!" He pulled it out. The ball was blue. "I was right about the ball," he said. "But I thought it was red."

Scarlett went next. Her fingers touched something soft. She patted it. It was small and furry. "A little toy cat," she said. She pulled it out. The cat was yellow. "I felt the cat," she said. "But my fingers did not tell me the color."

"Can fingers ever tell a color?" asked Bree.

"No," said Scarlett. "You need to look with your eyes."

Bree put her hand in the bag. "I feel something flat," she said. "Maybe paper?" She pulled out a green paper sign. It said SUN in big letters.

Then Scarlett felt one more thing. It was cold and smooth. She pulled it out. It was a tiny red apple, Mr. Holloway's favorite snack. "A surprise for the class," he said, and everyone laughed.

Wyatt ran to the playground. He wanted to build a big tower in the sandbox. His friend Bradley was already there.

"Come up," called Bradley from the top of the slide ladder.

Wyatt looked up. Bradley was high. Wyatt was low on the ground. Wyatt climbed up, up, up. Now he was high too.

"Up and down are opposites," said Bradley.

Bradley sat on the slide. He slid down, down, down. Now Bradley was low again. Wyatt was still high. Wyatt laughed and slid down too.

Then Wyatt went to the sandbox. Addilyn was there. Her cup was small. Wyatt's cup was big. They poured sand together. The tower grew fast. Then the wind blew. The tower fell down slow, so slow, and got weak at the bottom.

Mr. Aziz came over. "Hold this side," he said. Addilyn held one side. Wyatt held the other side. The tower stood up tall again.

"We did it," said Wyatt.

Addilyn smiled and poured one more cup of sand on the top.

Matteo ran to the pool. He wanted to swim so fast. He got to the water and jumped up and down. Ms. Robinson called out, "Stop right there!" Matteo stopped. His feet were wet from the shower room floor. Ms. Robinson smiled. "First we take a shower," she said. "Then we get in the pool."

Matteo looked at the showers. Raphaelle was under one. Xavier was under another one. The water came down on them. Matteo stood under a shower too. The water was warm. It tickled his hair. His towel got thick with water and he laughed.

Then Matteo saw something. When the water fell on him, soap and dirt went down and away. The water carried it all off. Now he was clean. "My turn now?" he asked. "Yes," said Ms. Robinson. "Shower first, pool after. Shower first, pool after."

Matteo walked to the pool. He sat on the step. He kicked his legs. Raphaelle splashed him. "Hey!" Matteo shouted, and splashed back. Then he let go of the side. The water held him up. He was swimming. Xavier clapped. "Matteo swam all by himself!" Matteo looked at the shower room. "Shower first," he said. "Pool after!"

Charlie ran into the backyard with a box. "My first pet!" he shouted. Inside was a little bunny named Floppy. Dad helped set up a safe pen with straw and water. Charlie wanted to pat Floppy right away. But Floppy hopped to the corner. Then Floppy hid behind the big flowerpot. Charlie could not see her at all.

Charlie felt sad. He called his friend Lylah on the phone. "My bunny is hiding!" he said. Lylah said, "Sit still and wait. New pets hide at first. They need to get used to their new home." So Charlie sat down on the grass. He filled a small bowl with carrots. He waited. He waited some more. It was very quiet.

Then two ears popped up over the flowerpot. Floppy looked at Charlie. Floppy hopped closer. Then Floppy nibbled a carrot from the bowl! Charlie laughed and clapped his hands. "She likes it here," he whispered. Floppy hopped one more time, right up to his shoe.

Hunter had a slide in his backyard. He wanted to slide down fast. His friend Zayden came over to play. Zayden brought his blocks, and they made a messy tower by the fence.

Hunter climbed up the slide ladder. He held on with both hands. He started to lie down with his head at the top. "Feet first," said Zayden. Hunter turned around. He put his little feet at the edge. Then he let go and slid down, feet first, whee!

They could smell the warm grass in the sun. Zayden went next. He went feet first too. They slid and slid until the sky turned orange. "One more time," said Hunter, running to the ladder.

Evan ran to the block corner. He wanted the big red stick to dig in the sand table. Brett had it now.

"MY TURN!" Evan shouted. Loud.

Ms. Rosen put her finger to her lips. Catherine was asleep on the little cot. Her eyes stayed shut.

Evan looked at Catherine. Would a big voice wake her? He tried something new. He made his voice very small.

"May I have a turn?" Evan whispered.

Brett looked up. He did not cover his ears this time. He nodded. "You can have it when I am done," he whispered back.

Evan waited. He watched Brett dig the sand. Slow. Careful. Evan waited some more. Waiting was hard, but Catherine kept sleeping.

At last Brett held out the red stick. "Here," he whispered. "Your turn."

Evan dug in the sand. He made a tall hill. He did it all with a tiny voice.

Catherine sat up on the cot. She rubbed her eyes. She had slept the whole time.

"Blocks?" she whispered.

"Blocks," said Evan.

Alice wanted to make soup for dinner. "I can help!" she said. Dad said, "Yes, you can."

First, Alice put carrots in the pot. Then she added little square pieces of potato. Dad cut a big onion with his knife.

Dad's eyes began to water. Big tears ran down his face. "Dad is sad!" said Alice. "The soup made him cry!"

"No, no," said Dad, laughing. "The onion makes my eyes sting and water. Grown-ups cry like this when they cut onions."

Alice looked closely. Dad was still smiling. He was not sad at all. It was just the onion. How silly!

Alice got a small towel for Dad. She patted his cheek, very gently. "There, there," she said, just like Mom. "The onion will stop soon."

Then came the surprise. Mom walked in and sniffed the air. "Mmm!" she said. "Is that soup? Can I bathe in it?"

Alice laughed and laughed. "No, Mom! You eat soup! Silly Mommy!"

Dad wiped his last tear. The soup bubbled on the stove. Alice stirred it with a big spoon, standing far back where it was safe.

At dinner, everyone ate the soup. "Best soup ever," said Mom. Alice beamed. Then she pointed at Dad. "Watch out," she said. "He might cry again!"

Dad made a funny face. "Only if I find more onions!"

Nathan was going on a trip. He and his brother rode the ferry across the big water. The boat went bump, bump, bump. The wind smelled like salt. Big black birds flew over the deck. Nathan counted them. One bird, two birds, three.

They were going to the snow. But Nathan had packed his swimsuit. "For swimming," he said. His dad smiled. He unpacked the little bag. Out came one swimsuit. Out came two sandals. Out came nothing warm.

"You pack for the place you go," Dad said. "Snow needs a warm coat." He found Nathan's red mittens instead. Nathan pulled them on. His hands went warm and cozy. He put the mittens on his brother too, one for each little hand.

That night, Nathan had a dream. He dreamed he wore his swimsuit in the snow. A penguin slid by on its belly. "Nice suit," said the penguin. Nathan laughed and laughed. Then he woke up, held his mittens tight, and ran to the window to look for snow.

Nathan was at the park with his dad. They were going to get a baby guinea pig today. Nathan wanted to carry it everywhere.

Dad held a small box. Inside was a fluffy guinea pig. "His name is Pip," said Dad.

At home, Nathan stood up and tried to hold Pip. He held Pip tight. Pip wiggled. Nathan almost dropped him!

Dad sat down on the floor. "Sit here," he said. "Hold him with two hands."

Nathan sat down on the floor. He held Pip with two hands. Pip sat in his hands. Pip did not fall.

Then Nathan saw something. When he sat down, Pip could not fall far. So Pip stopped wiggling. Pip made a soft squeak.

"I did it," said Nathan. "I held him gently."

He cleaned Pip's little bowl with Dad. Then Nathan sat on the floor again. He held Pip with two hands. "Hello, Pip," said Nathan. Pip nuzzled his thumb.

Elijah sat in a small room at the vet. A puppy slept in a box beside him. "Today we take him home," said Dad.

The vet clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. "A leash clipped to a collar keeps a dog close to the person walking it," she said. Elijah held his dad's hand. The leash went from the collar to Dad's hand. "So the puppy stays near you?" asked Elijah. "Yes," said Dad.

Outside, a bird hopped on the grass. The puppy wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash was clipped to his collar. Dad held the leash. The puppy stayed close. The bird flew away. The puppy sat down. His tummy growled. "Was he grumpy?" Elijah wondered. At home, Dad filled a bowl. The puppy ate it all up. Then he curled up on Elijah's sock.

Felix went to the library with his friend Mishka. Ms. Shin had a big game ready. "Put the animal cards in the animal pile," she said. "Put the toy cards in the toy pile." Felix loved this game. He picked up a card with a black cat on it. He put it in the animal pile. Mishka held up a card with a rabbit. "Where does this go?" she asked. "Animals!" said Felix. They clapped their hands.

Then Felix found a card with a toy dog on it. It was brown and soft. He put it in the animal pile. Mishka shook her head. "Look," she said. "The real dog runs. The toy dog does not run." Felix looked at both cards. The real dog wagged its tail. The toy dog sat still. "The toy dog is not alive," said Ms. Shin. Felix thought hard. He picked up the toy dog card. He moved it to the toy pile.

"Now show me your favorite food," said Mishka. Felix held up a card with an apple. "Foods go in the food pile," said Ms. Shin. Felix found a banana card and a bread card too. His tummy made a little rumble. Ms. Shin laughed softly. "We will get a snack soon," she said. Felix patted the toy dog card one more time. "You are a toy," he told it. "You stay with the ball and the blocks."

Chloe held her mom's hand. She wanted a big red apple from the store. The store was across the street.

They stopped at the corner. The light was red. "Red means stop," said Chloe. All the cars stood still. Then the light turned green. "Green means go!" The cars moved, and Chloe and her mom walked. Chloe saw that one little light made all the cars stop and go. It was like magic, but real.

Inside the store, Chloe helped. She put yellow bananas in the cart. The cart felt heavy. She found green grapes and a blue box of crackers. Then she saw a pink pig bank on a shelf. She wanted to swing it, but it might fall. Her mom said, "Just look, sweet pea." Chloe held it softly instead. At last, she picked the biggest red apple. "For you too," she said, and gave her mom a bite.

Rose sat at the big table. Grandpa had a new book. Rose wanted him to read it now.

Grandpa picked up the book. He held it far away. He squinted his eyes. "The words look cloudy to me," he said.

Rose watched Grandpa find his glasses. He put them on his nose. Then he smiled. "Now I can see the words," he said. The glasses helped his eyes see clearly.

Rose looked at the pictures with her eyes. She heard Grandpa's voice read the story. She smelled the warm cookies in the kitchen, because her mom was baking them.

Then Grandpa stopped reading. "Where is the cat?" he asked. Rose reached out her hand. She touched something soft. "Here she is!" she said.

Later, Mom gave Rose a small cookie. Rose tasted the sweet cookie. "Yum," she said.

Rose took her crayons. She wanted to color a cat. She drew big round circles for the cat's eyes. "These are cat glasses," she said.

Grandpa put his glasses on the cat picture. He laughed a kind laugh. "What a smart cat," he said. "Now open the book again," said Rose. "I want to hear the rest."

Violet went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about boats. Big boats, little boats, boats with sails. She could not find one anywhere.

Maci was there too. Maci held a book upside down. "The pictures look funny," Maci said. Violet peeked at the pages. The words were all mixed up. The pictures started at the end.

"Flip it over," said Mr. Jung, the library man. He smiled a kind smile. Maci turned the book around. Now the boat picture was on the front. It looked right side up.

Violet found a boat book on the shelf. She opened it from the back by mistake. The pages felt wrong in her hands. The story seemed to jump and mix. So she flipped it over to the front cover. She turned page one, then page two. The little boat sailed across each page.

Violet sat on the soft rug next to her dad. She pointed at the words under the boat. "What does that say?" she asked. Her dad read it out loud. The marks on the page were saying something! Violet turned the pages, one by one, until the back cover came. "The end," her dad read. Violet patted the empty back cover. "Again," she said. "Read it again."

Owen sat in the waiting room with his dad. There were fish in a tank. Owen watched a little fish step over a rock with its fins. "Fish can't step," said Owen. "No, they swim," said Dad.

Then the nurse called, "Owen." Owen got a shot in his arm. It was fast. He got a sticker and a nice hug from Dad.

In the car, Owen touched his arm. "Ow," he said. "My arm feels sore." Dad said, "That is okay. The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while." "Will it stop?" asked Owen. "Yes, soon," said Dad.

Owen waited. He looked out the window. He counted two cars. Then he squeezed his arm softly. It did not hurt any more. "All better!" said Owen. He put his sticker on his shirt, right over the spot.

Wyatt dug a little hole in the backyard. Mom handed him a seed. "This one will be a carrot," she said. Wyatt dropped it in and patted the dirt. He watered it with a big spoon dipped in a bucket.

Every day Wyatt looked. Would a carrot come up? Where was it? Then one morning he saw tiny green leaves. He saw another little plant too, near the fence. Wyatt pulled at it. Was it a weed? He tugged harder.

"Wait," said Mom. She knelt down beside him. "Look at this one. It is a weed. It grows where we do not want it." She pointed to the leaves by the fence. "It can stay there. But look at your carrot. These little leaves grow in a straight row, right where you planted your seed. That one is a baby carrot."

Wyatt let go of the leaves. His carrot stayed in the ground. The weed went into the bucket. Wyatt looked at the long row. Would another leaf come tomorrow? "Hello, baby carrot," he whispered, and gave it one more spoon of water.

Ava packed her small red bag. Grandma was taking her to the beach. It was a long drive in the car. Ava watched trees go by. Then she watched more trees. Her tummy felt funny. "I need the bathroom," she said. "The beach is still far away," said Grandma. Ava felt worried.

But then the car slowed down. It pulled into a big rest stop. "Here we can use the bathroom," Grandma said. "And we can stretch our legs." Ava held Grandma's hand. They walked in. Ava used the little bathroom. She washed her hands. Then they stretched outside. Ava reached her arms up high.

Back in the car, Ava felt better. Soon the water came into view. At the beach, Ava let a short stick float on a little wave. It bobbed up and down. "Look, Grandma, it floats!" said Ava. Grandma smiled and sat close by her on the warm sand.

Snow fell on the park. Athena wore her warm coat and red mittens. "Snowy day, snowy day," she sang.

Bryan ran by in his big boots. Naomie wore a hat with a pom-pom. The wind blew hard. "Windy!" said Athena. Her hat almost flew off, so she held it tight.

Athena found snow on the bench. "I will keep this snowball," she said. She put it in her glass. Then she went to play on the slide.

Later, her dad came with cocoa. Athena looked in her glass. The snowball was gone. There was only water. "Where did my snowball go?" she asked.

Her dad sat close. "Look," he said softly. Athena touched the water. It was not cold like snow.

On sunny days, she thought, snow could not stay. She tipped the water onto the brown dirt by a tree. "Grow, little tree," she said. "Drink my snow."

Ivy went to the library with her dad. She got her very first library card. It had her name on it. She picked a big book about a worm. The worm was long and wiggly on the cover.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Ivy.

"Not forever," said the librarian. "This book has a due date. That is the day it must come back. Then other kids can read it too."

Ivy hugged the book all week. She read it at breakfast. She read it in her dry, sunny spot by the window. Once she squeezed the pages too hard and the corner bent a little. It did not hurt the worm, but she said sorry to it anyway.

Then the due date came. Ivy put the worm book in her bag. She carried it back to the library. She slid it into the return slot. It went down with a soft whoosh.

"Can I take another one?" she asked.

The librarian smiled and nodded. Ivy ran to the shelf. She came back hugging a new book.

Leo ran to the play corner at school. He wanted the big red kitchen. But Diego and Faye were already there.

"Can I cook too?" Leo asked.

"You need a baby," said Faye. "We are playing house. I am the mom. Diego is the dad."

Faye held out a doll. Leo took the doll. The doll was not real. It was made of soft cloth.

"Pretend the baby is crying," said Diego. "Pretend means we act like it is real."

Leo patted the doll's back. He made a soft shush sound. One pat, two pats, three pats. The doll did not really cry. But Leo acted as if it did.

"The baby needs food!" said Leo.

He turned the red knob on the toy stove. Ms. Kaminski walked over. "That stove is pretend," she said with a smile. "It cannot get hot. But you can stir the pot."

Leo stirred the empty pot. One stir, two stirs, three stirs. He held the doll close. "Here, baby," he said. "Warm soup."

Then Faye shouted, "Oh no! The floor is a river!"

Leo looked down. The floor was not a river. It was just the floor. But everyone acted as if it was real. Leo grabbed a cushion and hopped on it. One hop, two hops, three hops.

"My turn to be the dad," said Diego.

"Okay," said Leo. "And I will be the kind big sister!"

Leo hugged the doll tight and jumped again. "Look out, river!"

Raphael stood in the pool changing room. His swim suit was tight and blue. Water dripped on the floor. The floor was wet. It made a drip, drip sound.

"I want to swim now," said Raphael. He started to run. Rex ran too. Ms. Sánchez held up her hand. "Walk, please," she said. "Wet floors are slippery. We walk here." Raphael stopped. His feet were bare. He looked down. The floor was shiny and wet. He tried one slow step. His foot slid a tiny bit. He held the wall. It was cold under his hand.

"Why do we walk?" Raphael asked. Rex smiled. "So we do not fall," said Rex. Raphael walked all the way to the pool door. His towel was warm and soft on his arm. Then he saw his rubber duck sitting by the pool. "You came too!" he said. Ms. Sánchez laughed. "Ready for the water?" she asked. "Ready," said Raphael. He stepped in, holding her hand.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had ten green peas on her plate. She wanted to count them all.

"One, two," she said. Then she stopped. She could not think of the next number. Her face got upset. She pushed her fork down.

Her big brother leaned over. "Sing it," he said. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Aubrey sang the little rhyme with him. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." The words rhymed, and they helped her remember.

"Three!" said Aubrey. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All ten peas were counted.

"Ten peas!" said Dad. "Ten big bites."

Aubrey peeked under her cup. No peas were hiding there. She ate one pea at a time.

"Nine left," she said. "Eight. Seven."

Dad poured the milk. It ran into her cup like a tiny river. Aubrey giggled and counted, "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Sara ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. It had a little orange pot and three plastic cups. Emmeline was already there. "Let's play house," Emmeline said. "You be the mom. I be the baby."

Sara held a doll. "Time to eat," she said. She stirred the orange pot. Clack, clack, clack. One cup, two cups, three cups. The baby doll got a cup too.

Then Ms. Byrne rang the bell. "Playtime is over," she said. "Time to go home." Sara started to run. But then she looked back. The cups were on the floor. The pot was tipped over. The baby doll lay under the bench.

"Emmeline, wait," Sara called. "The kitchen is a mess." The two girls picked up the cups. One, two, three. They put the pot on the shelf. Sara tucked the doll into the little bed. "Night night, baby," she said.

"Now the kitchen looks tidy," said Emmeline. They ran to the gate together, hand in hand.

Sofia sat at the kitchen table. She had a big piece of paper. She had a bag of crayons. She wanted to write her name.

Her dad was making soup on the stove. He watched from far away. Sofia picked the red crayon.

She wrote s-o-f-i-a. All the letters were small. She looked at her name. It did not look right.

Her friend Rosalyn had made a card yesterday. Rosalyn's name was on it. It started with a big R. Sofia remembered the big R.

She looked at her s. It was small. She tried again on a new line. She made a big S. Then small o, small f, small i, small a.

Sofia. Now it looked right. "Dad, look!" she said.

Her dad came over. He read it out loud. "Sofia. What a big beautiful S."

Sofia smiled. She wrote it again. Big S first. Then the small letters. She wrote it one more time, slow and careful.

"Dad, can we put it on the fridge?" she asked.

"Yes, we can," he said. He found a magnet. The paper went up. Sofia stood back and looked at her name.

"Big S," she said, pointing. "Big S for me."

Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. "I will make soup!" she said. Rosa grabbed a big pot. Emiliano put in a pinecone, a leaf and two round stones. "Yum, pinecone soup!" said Rosa.

Amelia stirred the soup with a long spoon. Then she lifted the spoon to her mouth. She opened her lips wide. Mr. Sharma came over fast. "Stop, Amelia," he said. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat." He took the spoon out of her hand.

Amelia looked at the spoon. Then she smiled a big smile. She held the spoon near her mouth. She made a loud slurping sound. "Slurp, slurp!" she said. Nothing went in her mouth. Rosa peeked into the pot. "More soup for me!" she said. She slurped too, with an empty spoon.

Emiliano patted his tummy. "I ate five bowls!" he said. Amelia poured more soup with her arm held high. "Soup for everyone!" she called. The pot went around and around the table, slurp by slurp by slurp.

Emilia wanted the sleepy bear book. She had seen it before. Now the shelf was big and full.

She pulled one book off the shelf. She opened the front cover. Page by page, she looked. No bear. She put it back.

Rafael came to help. "Ask Ms. Hu," he said.

Emilia went to Ms. Hu. "I want the bear book," she said. "The bear is sleepy."

"The title is the book's name," said Ms. Hu. "Let's look for the title on the front."

They walked back to the shelf. Emilia looked at the fronts of the books. One, two, three fronts. There it was. The title said "Sleepy Bear."

Emilia held it tight. She sat down on the soft floor. She opened the front. The bear yawned on page one.

Rafael sat next to her. "Read it to me too," he said.

Emilia turned the pages. The bear slept at the end.

"I found it by its name," said Emilia.

Lucy sat at the big table. She had a box of crayons. She wanted to draw the sky. She found a blue crayon and drew. "Too dark!" she said. Her sky looked like night. She wanted a daytime sky.

Capri came over to play. "That sky is not blue," said Capri. "It is too dark!" Lucy held up the crayon. "It says blue," said Lucy. "See? Blue." Capri made a funny face. "A dark blue? Is that still blue?"

They dumped out all the crayons. "Let's find every blue," said Lucy. They lined them up on the table. "One light blue, two blue, three dark blue," they counted. "Look!" said Lucy. "Light blue, blue, dark blue. All blue!" Then she drew a new sky with the light one. "Now it's day!" said Capri. Lucy laughed and held up the dark one. "And this can be night," she said.

Logan had a small violin. It was his dad's old one. Logan wanted to play a song for his cat.

He held the stick part in his fist. He poked it at the strings. The violin made a squeak. The cat ran under the chair.

"Oh no," said Logan. "That was a hard sound."

Mr. Okonkwo lived next door. He came over with a smile. "This is called a bow," he said. He put it gently in Logan's hand. "Pull it across the strings. Like this." He pulled the bow, slow and smooth.

The violin sang. What a pretty sound!

"My turn," said Logan. He pulled the bow across the strings. It sang again, soft and low. The cat peeked out from under the chair. It sat down close to listen.

Logan pulled the bow one more time. "Song for you, cat," he said. The cat purred and tapped the violin with one soft paw.

Liam looked out the big window. The sun was not out today. Rain dripped down the glass. Drop, drop, drop.

"Is it sunny today?" Liam asked.
"No, it is rainy," said his dad.

Liam wanted to walk to school with Joshua. But the rain was falling. His dad held up a big red umbrella. "Come under here," he said.

Liam stood close to his dad. The umbrella went up over their heads. The rain fell on the red top. It did not fall on Liam's head. His hair stayed dry. His dad's hair stayed dry too.

The wind blew a little. The umbrella wiggled. Liam held the handle straight and tight. The rain still slid off the sides.

On the way home, the rain stopped. Dad shook the umbrella. Water flew off the top. Liam laughed.

Inside, Dad gave Liam a cup of juice. Liam looked at the window again. "Will it be snowy tomorrow?" he asked.
"Maybe," said Dad. "Then you will need your warm hat."

Liam drank his juice. He put his boots by the door, all ready.

Clara was at school. It was cold outside. Snow was on the playground. Ms. Carvalho called out, "Time to wear scarves!" Clara got her scarf. It was red and soft. Youssef got his scarf. It was blue and warm.

Clara put on her scarf. It went down to her shoes. Youssef put on his scarf. It stopped at his chin. "Mine is so long," said Clara. "Mine is short," said Youssef. He shivered. His neck was cold in the wind. Clara wanted to help her friend.

Then Clara had an idea. The long scarf could wrap around two necks. She held one end. Youssef held the other end. They stood close together. "Long and short are opposites," said Youssef with a laugh. Clara laughed too. The scarf was long enough for both.

The naughty wind blew again. But now both necks were warm. They walked out to the snow, side by side, slow and careful. At the door, Ms. Carvalho had to sweep the snow away. "That wind is playing a joke on us," she said. Clara and Youssef giggled. The long red scarf swung between them as they stepped outside.

Wyatt wanted to be a rocket ship. He put a small box on his head. The box was his nose cone. His friend Veronica came over to play.

"We need blast off," said Wyatt. "But I don't know how."

"My big brother does it," said Veronica. "He counts backward from ten. It's called a countdown. Then he jumps!"

Wyatt tried. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." He wiggled his toes. "Six, five, four." A bug crawled by his shoe. "Three, two, one. Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up high.

The box fell off his head. It made a big bong sound on the floor. Wyatt laughed. Veronica laughed too.

"Again!" said Wyatt.

Veronica put the box back on his head. "Ten, nine, eight," she started.

Wyatt jumped again, even higher.

Isabella ran to Mr. Thompson. "Tell a story now," she said.

Mr. Thompson smiled. "Not now. Now is this very moment. The story is after snack."

Isabella put her hands on her hips. She wanted the story now. She looked around. The snack table had cups and crackers on it. "Is snack now?" she asked.

"Snack is now," said Mr. Thompson.

Isabella sat with her friends. Adelia shared her crackers. Jean drank his milk. Isabella ate slowly. Then the cups were empty.

"Is it after snack now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Thompson. "Now means at this very moment. And this moment is story time."

Isabella clapped her hands. She sat tall on the rug. Yesterday she had missed the story. Today she did not miss it.

"Tomorrow I will eat fast," she said.

"Today you waited well," said Mr. Thompson. He opened the big book.

"Once there was a bird who lived high in a tree," he began. Isabella leaned in close.

Mia was thirsty after her walk to shop with Dad. She wanted cold milk. She opened the big fridge door. It was open. Cold air came out onto her nose. "Ooh, cold," said Mia.

Dad was stirring hot soup on the stove. He turned fast. "The fridge is open," he said. "It should be shut. Open and closed are opposites." Mia looked at the door. Open meant she could see the milk. Closed meant she could not.

Could she make it closed all by herself? Mia pushed the door. Click. Now it was closed. She opened it again, quick and slow, then slow and fast. Open, closed. Open, closed. Dad laughed. "One, two, three pushes," he said. Mia took out the small milk cup. She shut the door and drank. "Cold milk," she said. "My door is closed."

Aurora went to the dental clinic with her dad. It was her first time. She held her little green toothbrush in her hand. "Why do I bring it?" she asked. "The dentist likes to see it," Dad said.

In the waiting room, Aurora saw her friend Molly. Molly had a toothbrush too. It was blue with a wheel on the handle that spun around. Molly spun the wheel. Round and round it went. "Can I try?" Aurora asked. She reached for the blue one.

Then she looked at her own green toothbrush. "Where is mine?" she asked. It was right there in her other hand! Aurora laughed. "Silly me. This one is mine." The dentist came out and said, "Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes." Molly giggled. "Good thing you found yours, Aurora." Aurora showed her green toothbrush to the dentist. The dentist smiled and let her sit in the big chair. It went up, up, up!

Jake stood in the backyard with his friend Carly. "We have five senses," Carly said. "Can you say them all?"

Jake tried. "Ears hear," he said. He heard a bee buzz. "Nose smells," he said. He smelled the flowers. "Tongue tastes," he said. He tasted a nice apple slice. "Hands touch," he said. He touched the warm grass.

But then Jake stopped. "I forgot one," he said. He covered his eyes with his hands. It was all dark. No bee. No flowers. No sun.

Carly laughed. "Open them!" she said.

Jake opened his eyes. The sun was bright. The bee flew by. The flowers were red and yellow.

"My eyes see!" Jake said. "We see with our eyes!"

"You got all five," Carly said. She gave him a big hug.

Jake wiped the apple juice off his chin. Then he covered his eyes again and peeked through his fingers. "Peekaboo, sun!"

Jake put on his red boots. He was so excited for the park. Then Ms. Choi looked out the window. Big raindrops fell. Tap, tap, tap on the glass.

"No park today," said Ms. Choi. Jake's face went sad. His friend Kaison was sad too. Jake sat on the rug. He held his soft bear tight.

Then Ms. Choi brought out a big clean blanket. "We can make a fort," she said. Jake stood up. Kaison smiled. They put the blanket over two chairs. Inside, it was cozy and dim. Jake heard the rain still tap, tap, tapping. But now he giggled.

"I am happy now," said Jake. Kaison said, "Me too!" Ms. Choi shined a little light inside. Jake hugged his bear.

"Wow," said Jake. "The rain was sad. Now it is fun!"

Sara ran to the park with her bunny. Then she set him on the bench. She raced to the slide. Whee! She climbed up. She slid down. One, two, three slides!

A dog barked by the swings. Sara laughed. Then she went back for bunny.

No bunny on the bench! Sara looked under the bench. She looked in the thin grass. She looked in a lost cup. No bunny anywhere.

Her friend Ally ran over. "Come with me," Ally said. "I know a place!" They ran to a little box by the park gate. It had a sign that said "Lost and Found."

"Is that where things go?" Sara asked.

Ally nodded. "People put found things in there," she said. "So owners can get them back."

Sara peeked in. A hat. A ball. Then she saw two soft ears! "Bunny!" she shouted. She hugged him tight.

Then she saw the hat. "Ally, that is your hat! It was lost too!" Ally grabbed it with a big grin.

One bunny, one hat, two happy girls. They spun in a circle all the way to the swings.

Blake's old teddy bear, Brown, sat on her bed. He looked sad. His paw hung down and his eyes looked droopy.

"Oh no," said Blake. "Brown is sick today."

She laid him on a pillow. She got a small cup. She tipped it to his mouth. "Drink your pretend medicine," she said. "It will help you feel better."

Brown did not drink. So Blake drank a tiny sip for him. "There," she said. "All gone."

Next she found a soft blanket. She wrapped Brown up, all snug. She tucked him into bed. She patted his back and sang a little song.

Then Blake pretended to be the doctor. She put a bandage on Brown's paw. "Your job is to rest now," she told him.

Brown's eyes still looked droopy. So Blake tucked the blanket higher. She gave him a kiss on his nose.

In the morning, Blake ran to the bed. Brown's paw was up! His eyes looked bright.

"You are all better!" said Blake. She hugged him tight.

Then she heard a tiny sound. It was a little squeak. Blake gasped. She looked under the blanket.

There, next to Brown, was her toy bunny. The bunny had been hiding there all night!

"You helped Brown get well too," Blake whispered. She tucked the blanket around both of them. "Now you can both rest together."

Owen ran to the playground early. The sun was warm on his face. He wanted the big swing. But Mannat was on it. Mannat sat with her head down. She did not swing at all. Owen felt angry inside. He wanted to shout. Instead, he took a breath. He asked, "Why do you sit so still?" Mannat said nothing. She looked at her shoes. Owen waited. He heard the swing creak. He smelled the wood chips. He waited some more.

Then Mannat said, "I feel sad. My dog ran away." Ms. Tehrani was nearby. She heard the words. She sat on the swing next to Mannat. She helped her look for the dog by the fence. And there he was, wagging by the slide! Mannat clapped her hands. "I feel happy now!" she said.

Owen got his turn on the swing. The wind pushed his hair back. He felt excited, way up high. Then Aviraj came to ask for a turn. Aviraj frowned and stomped his foot. Owen remembered the quiet waiting. He asked, "Do you feel sad?" Aviraj said, "Yes. I want a swing." Owen said, "You can have my turn." They took turns, up and down, until the sky turned orange. "Best playground day," said Owen.

Maeva held a small clay lamp. The street festival was loud and bright. "These are called diyas," her dad said. "Set them in a row on the step."

Maeva put down one diya. Then another. She made a slow, straight line. Maximus came to help too. He slipped his diyas next to hers. Soon the row was long.

But the diyas were dark. "When will they glow?" Maeva asked. "When the grown-ups light them," Dad said. He took a match and touched it to each little wick. One flame, then two, then all of them. The whole step grew warm and golden.

Rayne ran over with a spoon of sweet food. "Share with me," she said. Maeva sat with her friends. The little flames danced. Dad smiled and lit one more.

Alexander sat in the music classroom. A small guitar sat on his lap. He pulled the strings one by one. The notes sounded funny. They wobbled like a pig walking in mud.

Kingsley sat next to him. "Your guitar sounds silly," Kingsley said. Anna covered her ears and laughed. Alexander frowned. He wanted his guitar to sound pretty.

Mr. Jean-Louis came over. He listened to the strings. "The guitar needs tuning," he said. He turned the little pegs at the top. He turned one peg, then plucked the string. The note came out clear. He turned another peg, and the next note came out clear too. Alexander watched closely.

"Now you try," said Mr. Jean-Louis. Alexander turned one small peg. He plucked the string. The note wobbled. He turned the peg back a tiny bit. He plucked again. This time the note rang out clear and sweet. Anna clapped her hands. Kingsley tapped his knees to the beat. Alexander's itchy sweater sleeve slid down as he played, but he did not stop. He played a song, one clear note after another. "Again!" said Anna. So Alexander played again.

Sienna sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She was there to get a shot. Her tummy felt a little stormy. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said the nurse. "Then we get ice cream," said Mama.

The nurse opened a small drawer. She took out a tiny needle. Sienna wanted to see it up close. "Can I hold it?" she asked. She reached out her hand. "Only I touch the needle," said the nurse kindly. "The needle is just for me to hold. But you can hold my sticker sheet." She put the shiny sheet in Sienna's hands.

Sienna waited and held the stickers. The nurse held the needle all by herself. Then it was done, quick as that. "You picked a flower sticker," said the nurse. At the ice cream shop, Sienna licked her pink cone. "The nurse held the needle," she told Mama. "I held the stickers." Mama smiled and gave her a big hug.

Ellie went to the library with her dad. There was a playroom there. Mr. García smiled at the door.

Ellie saw a big toy box. It was empty. Blocks were all over the floor. A ball was under the chair. A doll sat on the mat. Esteban was there too.

"I will help," said Ellie. She picked up a block. She put it in. "One block," she said. Esteban picked up the ball. "One ball," he said. The ball went in. It rolled a little. Then it stopped. Julie picked up the doll. "One doll," she said.

"Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," said Mr. García. Ellie clapped. She picked up another block. "One more block," she said. It went in. Soon the floor was clean. The toy box was full.

Then Ellie found a pillow in the corner. She hugged it soft. Her eyes felt sleepy. "Shh," whispered Mr. García. He closed the toy box lid. Ellie yawned. "Story time first," said Mr. García. He sat down. Ellie sat close with the pillow. Julie sat on one side of her. Esteban sat on the other side.

"One sleepy girl," said her dad with a smile. Ellie leaned on the pillow. Mr. García opened the book. "Once upon a time," he read.

Matthew went to the store with his dad. The store was big and warm. Matthew held his dad's hand.

"Can we get new socks?" asked Matthew.

"Yes," said Dad. "You need a new pair."

"What is a pair?" asked Matthew.

"A pair means two, like a pair of socks," said Dad.

Matthew saw the sock shelf. He took one red sock. "One sock!" he said.

But Dad shook his head. "One sock can't go on two feet," he said.

Matthew looked and looked. He found another red sock hiding behind a blue one. "Two socks!" he said. He put the two socks together. They matched. Now he had a pair.

The store man helped count the socks at the till. "One, two," he said. Matthew counted too.

Then Matthew counted other things. "One cart, two carts!" he said. "One lamp, two lamps!"

A girl named Akram was there with her mom. Matthew saw her take one glove.

"That's just one," said Akram's mom. "You need two gloves to make a pair."

Akram found the other glove under a hat. "Two gloves!" she said. She clapped her hands.

Matthew smiled. "A pair means two," he said. "My socks are two!"

At home, Matthew put on his new socks. His feet felt warm. He looked down at his toes.

"One foot, two feet," he counted. "A pair of socks for me!"

Elijah sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name.

He made a letter. "That is K," he said. But the K looked funny. The little lines went the wrong way. Mom smiled at him.

Mom put a card on the table. It was the letter K. It felt bumpy under his fingers. "You can trace it," Mom said. "Use your finger as a tool." Elijah traced the bumpy K with his finger. He went down the tall line first. Then the little lines went out, up to the top.

Elijah traced it again and again. The bumpy card tickled his finger. He laughed a soft little laugh. Then he picked up his pencil. He wrote a K on the paper. This time the little lines went the right way!

"Look, Mom! A good K!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. His fingers were a little sticky from breakfast, so he wiped them on a napkin. Then he wrote K again. And again. Each K came out just right.

Elijah pointed at the paper. "That spells me," he said. "E for Elijah. K for more Elijah." Mom laughed and kissed his head. Elijah traced the bumpy K one more time, just because he liked it.

Lea rode the city bus with her dad. The bus went bump, bump, bump. "Next stop, the library," said the driver. Lea held her dad's hand.

At the library, Mr. Marino smiled. "Time for your first card, Lea." Lea got a little card with her name on it. She felt so big. She picked a book about a snowy day and a cat.

Then Mr. Marino gave Lea a crayon. He had paper too. Lea opened the library book. She wanted to draw on the cat's face. But then she saw a page with a small tear. "Someone was not careful," said Mr. Marino. "Many kids share this book. We take care not to tear or write in it." Lea looked at the tear. She closed the book. She drew a cat on her own paper instead. The cat on her paper had a big smile.

On the bus home, Lea hugged the book. "I will keep it nice," she said. "For the next kid?" asked her dad. Lea nodded. She drew a little cat on her paper all the way home.

Leon was helping Mom put things away. They had just come back from the store. On the floor sat three big bags.

Leon found a carrot. He held it up like a sword. "A toy sword!" he said. He ran to the toy box. He dropped the carrot in with the blocks.

Then he found a red apple. "A ball!" he said. He rolled it across the floor. It bumped the teddy bear.

Mom laughed. "Leon, come look at the shelf." She held up fresh bread. "This is food. The apple is food. The carrot is food. Foods go in the fridge."

Leon opened the toy box. He pulled out the carrot sword. He picked up the apple ball. He put them both in Mom's hands.

"Wait!" said Leon. He ran away fast. He came back hugging his toy dinosaur. He held it next to the bread.

"Dino is not food," said Mom. "Dino stays with you."

Leon put the dinosaur on his head like a hat. "Follow me, foods!" he said. He marched to the fridge. The apple, the bread and the carrot went inside, one by one.

The dinosaur peeked through the fridge door. "Roooaar," it said, in Leon's very best roar. Mom gave Leon one little piece of bread to munch.

Elena sat on her bedroom floor. The sun made a warm spot on the rug. Alfred came over to play. He brought his toy ducks.

Elena had made a blue scarf on the rug. It was the pond for the ducks. "The ducks can swim here," she said. Alfred laughed. He was happy.

Alfred reached for a duck. He slipped on the scarf. His elbow hit the floor. The ducks went everywhere. Alfred's face went red. His eyes got big and wet. He looked sad and a little scared.

Elena did not laugh. She did not grab the ducks. She walked over to Alfred. She looked at his face. Then she asked, "Are you okay?"

Alfred blinked. He rubbed his elbow. "It hurt," he said. "But now it is better." His mouth made a little smile.

Elena smiled too. She felt warm inside. "Good," she said. She picked up the ducks one by one. Alfred helped her. He lined them up by the pond.

"I will send this duck to you," said Alfred. He slid a duck across the rug. It went right to Elena's toes. She clapped. "Again!" she said. She was so excited.

Outside the window the trees moved. It was windy. The leaves went swish, swish. The ducks did not mind. They sat safe by their pond.

Alfred pushed a big block to make a duck house. It wobbled. It fell down with a bump. Alfred made an angry face. Then Elena asked, "Are you okay?" Alfred took a breath. "Yes," he said. "Blocks fall. We can build again."

So they built it again, side by side, slow and careful. The block house stood up tall. "Duck home," said Alfred. Elena put the last duck inside.

It was Charlie's first day of school. She ran to the playground with her new backpack. Her friend Stetson was digging by the fence. "Look, a worm!" he said. The worm wiggled in the dirt. Charlie laughed. "That worm is silly," she said.

Then Charlie needed to go to the bathroom. She looked around the playground. She did not see a bathroom. She did not know where to go. She waited by the slide. She looked and looked again. Then she saw Ms. Weiss, her teacher. Charlie walked over slowly. "I need help," she said. "I can't find the bathroom."

Ms. Weiss smiled and held out her hand. "I will show you," she said. They walked together through the big door. The bathroom was right there. "Thank you," said Charlie. Then she hurried back outside. Stetson was still watching the worm. "Come see!" he called. Charlie sat down next to him in the sun.

Layla woke up in her bed. Her hair was very messy. It looked like a bird had slept in it. "Oh no," said Layla. She patted her hair with her hand. It felt bumpy and knotty. Her tangles were everywhere.

She wanted to look nice today. Khadija and Hoorain were coming to play. Layla got out of bed. She found her soft brush on the shelf. She looked in the little mirror. Her hair stuck up on one side. It flopped down on the other. She giggled at her silly self.

Then her mom came in. "Time for breakfast first," she said. Layla ate her egg and toast. After that, her mom helped her wash her face. Layla picked her blue dress. She pulled it on all by herself. Now she only had one job left. Her hair.

Layla sat down with the brush. She started at the bottom, very slowly. "Ouch, ouch," she said, laughing. She brushed a little bit at a time. The brush went through. The bumps went away. One by one, the tangles came out. Soon her hair was smooth and shiny.

Ding dong! The doorbell rang. Layla ran to the mirror one more time. Her heart went pitter patter with joy. Her hair was all neat now. She opened the door. Khadija and Hoorain stood there. "Your hair looks so pretty!" said Hoorain. "Can I bring my brush next time?" asked Khadija. "Only if I get to brush yours too," said Layla.

Athena went to the park with her friend Shane. They saw ducks by the pond. The ducks floated on the water. Athena dropped a leaf in. The leaf floated too.

Then Shane called her to the big tree. Under the tree was a box of toy cars. There was something else in the box. "Look," said Shane. "A banana!" Athena laughed. "A banana does not go with cars," she said. Shane said, "It is the odd one out." Athena looked at the banana. It was yellow and round at the end. The cars were small and red. The banana did not belong.

Athena wanted to find the banana's owner. She asked Mr. Fortin, who sat on the bench. He was eating his lunch. "Is that your banana?" she asked. Mr. Fortin smiled big. "Yes! I lost it," he said. Athena gave it back to him. He said, "Thank you, kind girl." Then he shared his apple slices with Athena and Shane. They sat under the tree and ate together.

Elizabeth got a new coat for school. The coat had no zipper. It had big red buttons down the front. Elizabeth wanted to zip it up, like her old coat. She pulled at the top. Nothing happened. "It has buttons," said her friend Zion. "Buttons go through buttonholes to close a coat." Zion pointed to the little holes.

Elizabeth looked at a button. She pushed it. It would not go. She tried again, slow this time. She wiggled the button through the hole. Pop! It went in. The coat closed a little bit. Elizabeth laughed. "One more," she said. She pushed the next button through its hole. Pop!

Mr. Sánchez came over. "Do one more, Elizabeth," he said. Elizabeth took her time. She found the hole. She pushed the button through. Pop! The coat was all closed and warm. Elizabeth ran to the blocks. "My coat is on fast!" she said, and Zion clapped.

Splash day was here at daycare. Penelope put on her swimsuit all by herself. Mr. Paquette filled the little pool. "Not too deep," he said with a smile.

Penelope jumped in. Splash! Water went everywhere. Elodie jumped too. Arlo poured water from a cup. Drip, drip, drip ran down Penelope's arms.

Then Arlo climbed out. He ran away, still wet. "Brrr!" he said. He wiggled like a puppy. Elodie giggled. Arlo ran right back. He grabbed the big soft towel. He rubbed his arms and his legs. Now he was dry!

Penelope climbed out too. "Towel, please!" she said. Mr. Paquette handed her one, and he was kind about her drippy puddles. She dried her hair. It was fluffy like a cloud.

Then it was time for a snack. Penelope ate her crackers and colored a picture of a big yellow towel. "That is my towel!" said Arlo. "It dried me all up."

Grandma had big news at her house. "The baby is here," she said. Henri ran to the soft blanket. A tiny baby brother lay there. He was very small. Henri wanted the baby to like him.

Henri waved. The baby did not wave back. Henri made a funny face. The baby just slept. Then Henri put one finger near the baby's little hand. The baby woke up. The baby's fingers closed tight. He held on and held on! Henri laughed. "He likes me," Henri said. "He will not let go!"

Grandma smiled. Julius came over to see the baby. Julius put his finger in the baby's hand too. The baby held Julius tight as well! Then Grandma showed them a wiggly worm in the garden. The baby did not see it. The baby was frozen still, holding Henri's finger the whole time. "My finger is stuck," Henri said. "And I like it."

Leah was three today. Her party was in the backyard. Balloons sat near the fence. Danny and Mallory came to play. They hopped on the grass with bare feet.

Then Mom brought out the cake. It had three candles. Leah wanted to light them herself. She reached for the matches. Dad took them up right away. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," Dad said. "You get to make a wish."

Dad lit the candles one by one. The little flames wiggled. Leah blew out each candle with one big breath. Danny and Mallory clapped. Mom cut the cake and gave everyone a slice. Leah took a bite and smiled at her friends.
"Best cake ever," said Leah.

Madelyn loved her party dress. It was pink with sparkles. She wore it all day. She twirled in it. She ate an apple in it. "I wish I could wear it forever," she said.

At bath time, her dad helped her wash. Then it was time for bed. "I want to sleep in my party dress," said Madelyn. Dad held up soft pajamas. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said. Madelyn touched the sparkly dress. It was scratchy. She touched the pajamas. They were soft like a bunny.

She looked and looked. The dress was pretty but not cozy. Madelyn put on the pajamas. They felt warm and snug. She climbed into bed and hugged her bear. Her eyelids went blink, blink, blink. Then they closed. The pajamas were soft, soft, soft. Madelyn slept and slept.

Ava sat in her seat for the long car ride. Her bag of things sat beside her. She had a soft toy bunny, a toy car, and an apple for a snack. Outside the window, she saw cows in a field. "Look, cows!" she said.

Then Ava dug in her bag for her hat. The sun was in her eyes. She found something soft instead. It was a sock! "A sock is not a toy," said Dad from the front seat. "Silly sock." Ava laughed. She put the sock with the shirts and the hat in her bag. Shirts, socks and hats were all clothes. They went in one pile. Toys went in another pile.

Soon Ava got sleepy. She hugged her bunny. "We need to stop for milk and bread," said Dad. "And I have money for it." At the store, the cashier was kind. She gave Ava a little sticker. It was a picture of a cat. Ava smiled and stuck it on her hat. Then she closed her eyes and went to sleep.

Beatrice went to the store with her dad. She wanted a big yellow ball. But the store had so many shelves. Her ball was hiding somewhere.

Beatrice looked at a big box of balls. She put her hand in. She pulled out a red ball. Not yellow. She put the red ball in the box. She pulled out a blue ball. Not yellow. She put the blue ball in.

Then a baby by the box grabbed a ball. The baby took it out. Beatrice put it back in. The baby took it out again. "You take out, and I put in!" said Beatrice. "In and out are opposites!" The baby laughed. It was a silly game. Then Beatrice reached far in and pulled out the big yellow ball. "I found my answer!" she said. Her dad said, "Good noticing." Beatrice hugged her ball all the way home.

Harrison stood at the bus stop with his mama. He wanted to see the sun come out. "Where did the sun go?" he asked. "Look up," said mama. "The clouds are hiding it today." Big white clouds sat in the sky. They covered the sun like a blanket.

Harrison waited. The wind blew. It was windy! His hat flapped on his head. He held it with both hands. His toe was cold in his shoe. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Mama opened an umbrella over them. It kept the rain off.

"Will the sun come back?" Harrison asked. "Maybe," said mama. "Clouds can move. Let's watch together." They watched the sky. One cloud moved slowly. Then another cloud moved too. A little piece of blue showed. Then the sun peeked out. It made a yellow spot on the road. Harrison pointed at it. "There it is!" he said. He felt warm on his cheek.

The bus came. Harrison and mama got on. Harrison looked out the window. The sun followed the bus down the street. "Hello, sun," said Harrison.

Felix sat at the paint table. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. It would have a pink flower on it. But Felix looked and looked. There was no pink paint.

"Where is the pink?" he asked.

Ms. Rodríguez held up a jar. "We have red, blue, yellow and green," she said.

Felix felt a little scared. Grandma loved pink flowers. He hoped so much he could make one. He dipped his brush in the red paint. He made a red flower on the paper. It was bright like a fire truck. But it was not pink.

Erica sat next to him. She was painting with white. White like snow. A drop of white fell onto Felix's red flower.

"Oh no," said Felix.

Then he looked closely. The red spot with white on it was lighter. It was pink! Felix stared at it. He got more white paint on his brush. He stirred the white into the red. Round and round he stirred. Stir, stir, stir. The red turned pink. Soft pink. Flower pink.

"It's pink! It's pink!" said Felix.

He painted a big pink flower. Then a blue one. Then a green one. Then a yellow sun.

Zeria clapped. Zelda clapped too. "A pink flower for Grandma," said Zelda.

Felix smiled. He stirred some white into the blue next. The blue got lighter too, like the sky in the morning.

"Look, Grandma," Felix whispered to his card. "Pink, just for you."

Paisley stood at the pretend shop in her classroom. There were toy apples, toy bread, and one stinky sock. The sock was pretend stinky, made of soft yellow cloth.

"I want to be the shopkeeper," said Paisley.

Jayla put a toy bunny on the road rug. "The bunny needs to shop," said Jayla. "She wants bread."

Paisley picked up the bread right away. She put it in Jayla's bag.

"Wait," said Jayla. "The shopper picks. You are the shopkeeper. I am the shopper."

Paisley put the bread back. She stood behind the little desk. She waited.

Jayla looked and looked. The bunny sniffed the apples. The bunny sniffed the bread. The bunny hopped to the stinky sock!

"No, no, bunny," laughed Jayla. "Too stinky!"

Jayla pointed at the bread. "We will take this one, please."

Paisley rang the little bell. Ding! "Thank you," she said. "Come back soon."

The bunny waved goodbye with one soft ear.
