Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted more rice. She reached across the plates. "Say please," said Dad. "Please may I have rice?" said Wren. Dad passed her the bowl. "Thank you," said Wren. Dad smiled big. He gave her a spoon too.

Wren's baby brother dropped his hat on the floor. It fell off his high chair. "Sorry, little one," said Mum. She picked it up. She put it back on his head. He laughed and clapped.

Then Wren tried to pour the milk. The jug was too big. Milk dripped onto the table. "Sorry," said Wren. "Can you help me?" Mum held the jug with her. The milk went into the cup. It worked. "Thank you, Mum," said Wren. Mum gave her a warm hug. The baby waved his spoon. "More, more," he seemed to say. "Thank you," Wren told him, just to be kind.

Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. Big white flakes were falling. "It is snowy today," said Ms. Nielsen. Grayson jumped up and down. He loved snow.

"Snowball time!" said Billy. They put on their boots. Grayson put on his red mittens. Billy had no mittens. "I forgot mine," Billy said. His voice sounded shy.

Outside, the wind blew. "It is windy too!" said Kaitlyn. She held her hat tight. Grayson scooped up snow. He patted it into a ball. It was cold, but his hands stayed warm inside his mittens.

Billy made a snowball too. Then he stopped. "My hands are cold," he said. He held his hands under his arms. Grayson looked at his own warm, red mittens. Then he looked at Billy's cold hands. "Take one of mine," Grayson said. He pulled off a mitten and gave it to Billy.

Billy put it on. He smiled big. "Now my hand is warm!" He patted a new snowball with his mitten hand. Kaitlyn glued a snow sign onto the classroom door when they went back in. It said hello, snow. Grayson clapped his mittens together. "Snowy days are the best days," he said.

Sofia sat at the kitchen table. Mama was making soup. Sofia wanted to play the guessing game.

Mama gave her a soft bag. "Put your hand in," said Mama. "Tell me what you feel." Sofia put her hand in. She touched something round and bumpy. "A ball!" she said. She was right.

Mama held up a cold spoon. "Which body part told you it was cold?" Sofia looked at her hand. "My skin!" she said. "We feel things with our skin," said Mama. Sofia touched the table, her cup, and her sleeve. Each one felt different. Her fingertips told her so.

Then they named the other senses. "My eyes see the soup," said Sofia. "My ears hear it bubble. My nose smells it. My tongue will taste it." Mama laughed. "You learned all five senses, and it is fast soup today!" Sofia turned her cup around and around. She touched it one more time. "Smooth," she said. Mama kissed her head. Then they looked out the window at the moon. "Five senses, all done," said Sofia. "Now soup!"

Anthony rode the bus with Dad. He reached into his bag. His little red car was not there. "Where did it go?" Anthony wondered. He looked under the seat. He saw gum and a penny. No car. He looked in his coat pocket. He found a crayon. No car. Dad helped him look. Then Anthony peeked in the corner of the bag. There was the red car, hiding under his hat. "Found it!" said Anthony. At home, Anthony made a nest for the car. He put a small basket by his bed. Every night, the car went in the basket. One morning, Anthony woke up. "Is my car in the nest?" he wondered. He looked in the basket. The car was there, every time. "It is true," said Anthony. "The car is always easy to find." He drove it down the blanket, all the way to Dad's big toe. "Beep beep!"

Florence held her mother's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the first time. Florence sat near the window. She watched the cars go by.

The dentist was kind. "Open wide," she said. Florence opened her mouth. The dentist looked at all her teeth. "Your front teeth are for biting food," she said. "Your back teeth are for chewing it." Then Florence got a shiny sticker.

On the bus home, Adriel sat beside Florence. He had apple slices in a bag. He gave one to Florence. She bit it with her front teeth. The apple came off in a piece. Then she chomped it with her back teeth. Chomp, chomp, chomp.

"I did it!" said Florence. "Front bites, back chews." Adriel laughed and took a bite too. He chomped with his back teeth. The bus went bump, bump. Florence tasted the sweet apple. At home, she told her fish about the sticker on her shirt. "The dentist said my teeth are good," she said.

Leah ran to the playground with Giovanni and Thea. "Let's play hide-and-seek," said Giovanni. "You seek first, Leah."

Leah turned to face the slide. She counted. "One, two, three!" Then she peeked right away. But Giovanni and Thea were still running to find spots. "Leah, you counted too fast," said Thea. "Count slowly so we can hide."

Leah tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She counted slowly. Nobody was in sight now.

Leah looked behind the swings. Not there. She looked at the line of tires. There was Giovanni's shoe! "Found you," she called. Giovanni laughed and came out.

Then Leah heard a giggle by the sandbox. She found Thea too. "Good counting, Leah," said Thea. "You waited so long we hid so well."

Leah smiled a happy smile. "Now you seek, Giovanni. Count to ten slow!"

Amira was at school. She saw her friend Saoirse by the red block box. Saoirse had tears on her face. She was crying. Her shoulders shook, and she sniffed.

"Saoirse is sad," Amira said to herself. "When people feel sad, they sometimes cry."

Amira wanted to help. She ran to the toy shelf. She got her favorite bunny. The bunny had soft ears. She ran back fast. "Here," said Amira. "You can hold my bunny."

Saoirse hugged the bunny close. She wiped her eyes. Then she smiled a little. "Thank you," said Saoirse. Her tears stopped.

"Let's build a nest for the bunny," said Amira. Saoirse nodded. They made a nest with soft red blocks. The bunny sat in it. Romeo came over too. He added one more block.

Mr. Fernando looked over. He gave them a big smile.

Saoirse laughed now. "The bunny likes the nest," she said.

Amira clapped her hands. She felt happy inside. Her bunny had helped her friend.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna loved Grandma, but she felt shy too. Grandma seemed big and new. At the market, Sienna held Grandma's hand. The stalls smelled like bread and apples. A big clock hung above the fruit stand. "The clock says it is apple time," said Grandma. Sienna giggled.

Then Sienna saw something. Grandma picked up a red apple. "Your dad loved these," said Grandma. "When he was a little boy, he ate one every day." Sienna stopped walking. "Dad was little?" she asked. "Like me?" Grandma laughed. "Yes, just like you. He fell off his first bike and cried, then he got right back on."

Sienna's eyes went wide. Dad on a little bike! Dad crying! She could see it, like she could paint a picture in her head. At the next stall, she asked, "Tell me more about little Dad." So Grandma told her about Dad's muddy shoes, and Dad's lost sock, and Dad jumping far over a puddle.

All week, they walked to the market together. Sienna asked for a story each day. "Did Mommy like bananas?" she asked. "Yes, she hid one under her bed," said Grandma. Sienna laughed so loud that the baker smiled. On the last night, Sienna hugged Grandma tight. "Tomorrow," she whispered, "tell me about Dad's first hat."

Lillian ran to the playroom. Yousuf was building with blocks. "Look, a snake!" he said. His blocks made a long, curvy line.

Lillian wanted to add a house. She found a square block. "The house needs a roof!" she said. She put a triangle block on top. Then she found a rectangle block for the door.

Yousuf turned a square block on its corner. "Look, a new shape!" he said. He put it next to Lillian's house.

Lillian frowned. "That is not the same." She took the block. She turned it back flat. "It is a square again!" she said. Then she turned it back on its corner. Still a square! She laughed. "A square turned so a corner points up is still a square."

Ms. Taylor came in with paper. "Let's color!" she said. Lillian drew a circle sun and her silly square house.

"Time for the snake to visit," said Yousuf. The snake slid up to the house, right through the rectangle door. "Welcome!" said Lillian.

Lena wanted to go to the store with Mom. But Mom said, "Not now. Later." Lena frowned. When was later? She asked again. "Is it later now?" Mom shook her head.

Then Mom pointed up. There was a clock on the bedroom wall. "The clock shows what time it is," Mom said. "See the little hand? When it points to the three, we can go." Lena sat on her bed and watched. The hand moved very slowly. Tick, tick. She heard the loud ticking sound.

Yesterday they had gone to the store and it was fun. Today she had to wait. "Will tomorrow be too late?" she asked. Mom laughed. "No, today will be just right." The little hand crept up to the three. Lena jumped up. "Now! It is now!" She thanked the clock with a little pat on its side and ran to get her shoes.

Arthur was at Grandpa's house. He had big seeds in his hand. "Let's plant a garden!" said Grandpa. Arthur dug little holes. He put seeds in every hole. He patted the soil down.

The next day, Arthur ran outside. Tiny green leaves were peeking up! But Arthur stopped. "Grandpa! Which ones are the tomatoes?" He could not remember. All the little plants looked the same.

Grandpa smiled. He held up a stick with a picture on it. "This is a label," he said. Grandpa pushed it into the soil. The picture showed a big red tomato. Arthur jumped up and down. Now he knew!

Arthur drew more pictures. He drew a yellow carrot. He drew a green bean. He pushed a label next to every row of little plants.

Soon the garden grew tall. Arthur looked at the labels. He ran to the tomato row first. "Hello, tomatoes!" he said. Then he touched the middle leaf on the bean plant. "You grew so big!" A ladybug landed on his hand. Arthur froze. Then he giggled and watched it fly away. "Grandpa, come see!"

Kayden was in the kitchen. Lunch was coming soon. "First we wash our hands," said his mom. Kayden ran to the sink. He turned on the water. He got soap on his hands. His mom said, "One, two, three, four." Kayden rubbed the soap. "Five, six, seven, eight." More bubbles grew. "Nine, ten, all the way to twenty." Kayden rinsed the soap away.

Then Kayden shook his hands. Water went drip, drip, drip. A drop fell on the floor. Another drop fell on his shirt. His hands were still wet. Where was the towel? He looked and looked. There it was, hanging by the sink. Kayden picked up the towel and dried his hands. "One hand, two hands, all dry," he said.

The towel made his hands dry and warm. Then Kayden sat down for lunch. His hands were clean and dry. He picked up his sandwich. It did not get wet at all. "Nice washing, Kayden," said his mom. Kayden smiled and took a big bite.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Juliette waved her arms and jumped up and down. "Grandpa is here! Grandpa is here!"

On Saturday, Dad took Juliette and Grandpa to the local market. Juliette wore her red hat. They bought apples and bread and a big orange.

At home, Grandpa had a bath. Juliette waited outside the door. Then the door opened a little bit. Grandpa peeked out.

"Sorry, Grandpa," called Juliette. "I forgot to show you!"

Grandpa did not know where the towels were. Juliette held his hand. She walked him to the cupboard in the hall. She opened the little door.

"Towels are in here," she said. Grandpa took a soft blue towel. "Thank you, Juliette. You are a good host."

The next day, Grandpa needed the bathroom. Juliette ran ahead. "This way, Grandpa!" She showed him the little room with the sink. Grandpa laughed and clapped.

"Let me show you one more thing," said Juliette. She pointed up. "That is where the stars live, out the window."

Grandpa gave her a big hug. Then Juliette put on her red hat again.

Penelope sat on the low bench by the door. Yesterday she had missed story time. She had been slow to walk to the rug. Today she came fast.

"Story time starts soon," said Mr. Kang. Soon. What did that mean? Penelope tapped her shoe. She looked at the clock on the top shelf. The big hand did not move one bit.

"Soon means in a little while," said Deborah, sitting down beside her. Penelope counted to ten. Then she counted again.

Mr. Kang picked up the book. He held it up high. "It is story time now," he said.

Penelope grinned. A little while was not long at all. Tomorrow she would count again, just to see.

"Now open the book," said Deborah.

Charlie sat in her reading nook with a big letter card. It was the letter S. "I can't remember this one," she said. Her dad sat down next to her on the soft cushion.

"Make the sound with me," said Dad. "Ssss." Charlie tried it. "Ssss," she said. Then she looked around the nook. Her sun picture hung on the wall. "Sun," she said. "Ssss, sun!" Dad nodded. Charlie pulled off one stinky sock and laughed. "Ssss, sock!" She tipped over her toy bucket, and sand poured out onto the mat. "Ssss, sand!"

Charlie hugged her feather pillow. "Sun, sock and sand," she said. "They all go ssss." Dad smiled and pointed at the card. "Yes, Charlie. That is the letter S." Charlie traced the curvy shape with her finger. "Hello, S," she whispered.

Livia could not find her bunny. She looked under her bed. "Bunny, where are you?" she said. The bunny was not there.

Livia looked in her toy box. She peeked behind the big chair. She looked far across the room. No bunny. Then she saw something red under the sofa. She reached in and pulled it out. It was a small toy car. It was not her car. It was Anders' car. He had lost it when he came to play.

Livia held the car in her hand. She liked its shiny color. She wanted to keep it. But it was not hers. It belonged to Anders. When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them.

Livia put the car in her pocket. She went to find her mom. "Can we take the car to Anders?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "That is kind."

They walked to Anders' house. Anders opened the door. Livia held out the car. "I found this at my home," she said. "It is yours." Anders smiled big. "My car! Thank you!"

Then Anders said, "Wait here." He ran inside. He came back with something soft. It was Livia's bunny! "You left it here," he said. "Now I give it back to you."

Livia hugged her bunny tight. "Bunny!" she said. Anders hugged his car. They sat on the step together and played.

Emilia sat at the big table. Her tummy was hungry. Dad put warm toast on her plate. He put a little cup of milk by the toast too.

"I want to do it myself," said Emilia. Dad gave her a small, safe knife. He stayed right beside her. Emilia poked the toast with the tip of the knife. The butter made a hole. The toast broke into bits. "Oh no," said Emilia.

"Try the flat side," said Dad. "Push it across the bread." Emilia turned the knife over. She spread the butter with the flat side. She pushed it across the bread. The butter went smooth and even. The toast looked golden and shiny now.

Next came the milk. Emilia held the little jug with two hands. She poured slowly. A drop ran down the side of the cup. She waited. Then she poured again, even slower. No spill this time. The milk sat flat and white in the cup.

Emilia took a big bite of toast. It tasted good. An ant walked across the table, far from her plate. "Hello, little ant," said Emilia. "You cannot have my toast. I made it all by myself." Dad smiled and sat down to talk while she ate. Emilia raised her cup. "Cheers, Dad," she said.

Gabriel went to the park with his dad. Ms. Dlamini was there with a big hoop and some beanbags. Gabriel wanted to toss a beanbag into the hoop.

He threw the beanbag very hard. It flew over the hoop and landed in the grass. Felicia laughed and called it a silly throw. Gabriel picked up the beanbag and tried again.

This time he tossed it slow and easy. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. Plop. It sat in the middle of the hoop. Gabriel clapped his hands.

Then Felicia brought a big ball. She threw it very hard at Gabriel. It bumped his arm and rolled away. "Too fast," Gabriel said. Felicia picked up the ball. She tossed it slow and soft. Gabriel held out both hands. The big ball landed right in them. He held on tight.

They played catch by the pond. A fish jumped in the water. The sun went down behind the trees. "One more toss," said Gabriel. He sent the ball up soft and slow. Felicia caught it with both hands. "Got it," she said.

Leon was at Grandma's house. Snowy fields sat outside the window. Leon wanted to make bread for the whole family.

Grandma helped him mix flour and water. The dough felt sticky. It stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Leon. "Is it ruined?"

Grandma smiled. "Watch me show you what cooks do," she said. She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

Leon tried it too. He pushed. He folded. The sticky dough came off his fingers. It turned smooth and soft.

"Why does it feel different now?" Leon asked.

"Because you pushed and folded it, just like a cook," said Grandma.

The dough made a quiet noise when Leon pressed it. Grandma put the bread in the oven. Leon watched from far away.

Soon the bread was warm and ready. The whole family ate it together. "Leon made this!" said Grandma.

Leon took a big, happy bite.

Elizabeth had a big box of blocks. She wanted to sort them all. First she made a red pile. Then she made a blue pile. Then she made a yellow pile. "Look, Mom," she said. "All the red ones are together!"

Then her friend Enzo came over. He lived on the same street. Enzo looked at the blocks. He made a new pile of big blocks. Then he made a pile of small blocks. "I sort by size," he said.

Elizabeth blinked. The same blocks! But a new way! She tried too. She put all the big red blocks in one pile. Then all the small blue blocks. The blocks fit both ways.

Mom gave them apple slices and crackers. "Snack time," she said. Elizabeth kissed Mom on the cheek. She gave Enzo a gentle pat on his back.

"Same blocks," said Elizabeth. "Two ways to sort!"

"Let's do it again," said Enzo. He tipped the box over, and the blocks went everywhere.

James ran into writing club with his pet turtle in a little box. "Today I write my name!" he said. Mr. Dela Cruz smiled. "Get a pencil, James." James held the pencil in his fist. The letters came out wiggly and big. "My J looks sad," said James.

Mr. Dela Cruz showed him how to hold the pencil with three fingers. James tried it. His hand felt strange, but he drew a line. It popped right onto the paper, straight and neat. "Look! A J!" James drew an M too. All straight lines, like little sticks. Then he drew an A. It had lines and a little curve. Then he drew an O. The O was all curve, like a round balloon.

Piper leaned over. "My name has a curvy P," she said. "My S is curvy too," said Jasmine. James looked at his whole name. He pointed at each letter. "J, A, M, E, S," he said. He made the straight ones like sticks and the curvy ones like slides. He wrote his name again, full and clear, all the way across the page. "I did it!" said James. He held his paper up high for Mr. Dela Cruz to see.

Jasmine ran to her bed with her book. "Dad, read this one!"

Dad sat down. He opened the front cover. He turned the first page. Then the next. He read the words out loud, top to bottom.

Jasmine looked at a page full of pictures. It had a rainbow and a little dog. "Read that page too!"

Dad turned the page around so she could see. "There are no words here," he said. "Just pictures. I can't read it."

"Why not?" asked Jasmine.

"Reading is for the words," said Dad. "There is nothing written on this page."

Jasmine pointed to the lines of little marks on the next page. "Those?"

"Yes. Those are the words."

Jasmine held the book herself. She started at the front. She turned each page. On the word pages, Dad read aloud. On the picture pages, she made up her own story about the dog.

"That is not what the words say," laughed Dad. "But it is a good story."

"Is it a true story?" asked Jasmine.

"No," said Dad. "But I like it anyway."

Jasmine patted the book. "Tomorrow I will draw the dog a cat friend."

Dad kissed her head. "Good plan," he said. He turned off the light.

Aurora sat on the clean, soft rug. The big game was on TV. Daddy, Melody, and Callie sat with her. The players ran fast on the shiny floor.

One player threw the ball up. It went through the hoop. The crowd cheered loud. "They score by putting the ball in the hoop," said Daddy. Aurora clapped her hands. "I want to try that," she said.

Melody found a big bouncy ball in the bag of toys. Daddy held a laundry basket up high. "Throw it in," he said. Aurora threw the ball. It bounced off the rim. She tried again. The ball went through the basket. "I scored!" she shouted. Callie jumped up and down. Then Callie took the ball for her turn.

Aaron stood in the pool changing room. He pulled on his swim shorts all by himself. Then he sat on the big bench to wait.

"Where is Mr. Ong?" Aaron asked his dad. "He will meet us by the pool," Dad said. Aaron felt worried about the water. "It looks so big," he said. "Will I float today?"

At the pool, Mr. Ong smiled. "Lie back in the water," he said. "I will hold you while you learn." Aaron lay back. Mr. Ong's hands were under his back. Aaron did not sink. He floated like a little boat!

"Can you let go now?" Aaron asked. "Yes, just a little," said Mr. Ong. His hands stayed close. Aaron looked up at the huge ceiling and the bright lights.

Back in the changing room, Aaron saw a poster of a painted house by a lake. "Dad, I floated!" he said. "I saw a bird fly past the window!"

Charlie sat at his little table. It was writing time at school. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He grabbed the pencil in his fist. He pushed it onto the paper. The letters came out wobbly. "Oh no," said Charlie. "My C looks yucky."

Mr. Reddy sat down next to him. "Watch me," he said. Mr. Reddy pinched the pencil with his thumb and his first finger. Then he let it rest on his middle finger. "Now you try," he said.

Charlie pinched the pencil with his thumb and his first finger. He rested it on his middle finger. One, two, three, ready! He drew a big round C.

"Look, look!" said Charlie. His friend Ayansh leaned over. "That C is so good!"

Charlie wrote the next letters. H, A, R, L, I, E. Six letters, one by one. Each letter sat on the road line Mr. Reddy had drawn on the paper.

"I did it!" said Charlie. He lifted his paper up high. "That says Charlie!"

School was done. David waited by the gate with Ms. Eze. His green hat was in his hand. He had worn it all day, and now it was dirty.

"Papa is here," said Ms. Eze. David ran to Papa. Papa smiled. "Time for home," said Papa. At home, David took off his dirty shirt. He dropped it on the floor. He ran to find his socks.

Papa came in. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket," said Papa. "Then we can wash them." David looked at the basket. He picked up his shirt. He tossed it in. It went in the basket. David clapped.

Then David rolled his socks into a ball. He aimed at the basket. He threw. The socks went in too. "Score!" said David. Papa laughed. David ran back for his hat. He threw it in too. Now all his dirty clothes were in the basket. "Basketball star," said Papa. David bounced on his toes and said, "Again tomorrow!"

Aurora sat at the dinner table. Daddy put three things in the middle. "Close your eyes," he said. Aurora closed her eyes tight.

First she touched a pinecone. Her fingertips said bumpy. Then she touched a feather. Her fingertips said soft. Then she touched a stone. Her fingertips said smooth. "A pinecone!" she guessed. "Yes!" said Daddy. Aurora opened her eyes and laughed.

But one thing felt rough. What could it be? She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled like paint. She listened. It made no sound. She licked just a tiny bit. It did not taste good. The grumpy face she made told Daddy she was wrong.

"It is my old paintbrush," said Daddy. "Your fingers knew it was rough." Aurora touched it again. Rough, soft, smooth, bumpy. Her fingertips could tell her everything. She put her hands in her lap and smiled. "Again!" she said.

Jasmine was in the playroom with Ayaan. They had a small tea set. The little teapot was empty. It had nothing inside.

"I want real water," said Jasmine. Mr. Dang brought a big pitcher. "Pour slow," he said. "The cups are small."

Jasmine poured fast. The water ran over the top. It went all over the table. "Oops," she said. Mr. Dang wiped it up. "Try again," he said kindly.

Jasmine looked at the cup. It was empty. She poured slow this time. The water went up, up, up. She stopped just in time. Now the cup was full to the top.

"Full!" said Jasmine. She held it up. Ayaan clapped. Mr. Dang gave them two sour candies on a string. Jasmine licked hers and smiled.

"Tea time," said Jasmine. "Slow tea time."

Quinn went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish and birds and one small black kitten. "This one," said Quinn. Her dad smiled. They took the kitten home in a little box with holes.

At home, Quinn gave the kitten a soft blanket. The kitten drank and drank. Then Quinn saw the water bowl. It was empty. The kitten looked sad and licked the bowl.

"We need fresh water," said Quinn. "Every day, right Dad?" "Yes," said Dad. "Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day." Dad held the bowl under the tap. Quinn could not reach the sink, so she watched from her step. Dad filled it up with cool, clean water.

Quinn set the bowl on the floor. The kitten ran to it. Slurp, slurp, slurp. "You were thirsty," said Quinn. The kitten drank it all. Then it curled up on Quinn's lap and went to sleep. "Good night, kitten," Quinn whispered.

Camille ran onto the ice rink floor in her socks. Beanbags and hoops were set out. Ms. Walker smiled. "Today we throw beanbags!"

Camille picked up a red beanbag. She stood far from the hoop. She threw it. It missed. She threw again. It missed again.

"Will I ever get it in?" Camille asked Jayda.

"You can try!" said Jayda.

Camille took three little steps. Now she stood closer to the hoop. She threw the red beanbag. It sank right in!

"I did it!" Camille shouted. "Standing closer makes it easier!"

Next it was time for the big ball. Jade rolled it to Camille. Camille held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy. She grabbed it with two hands and hugged it tight.

"I caught it!" she yelled. The ball was soft like a blanket.

Ms. Walker clapped. "Great work, Camille!"

Camille threw the beanbag one more time. "Watch me, watch me!" she said. "I can get it in again!"

Connor wanted to build a big tower in the playroom. He found a heavy box of blocks. He pulled and pulled. The box would not budge. "Why is this so hard?" he wondered. His friend Nick came in. Nick picked up a light feather pillow. He carried it across the room with one hand. "Look, easy!" said Nick. "Heavy and light are opposites," said Nick. Connor tipped the heavy box over. Blocks spilled out. Now the box was empty. Connor picked it up. It felt light now! He smiled big. He stacked the blocks fast, then slow and careful. "My tower is so tall!" said Connor. The empty box sat on top, small and neat. Nick clapped. "Can I add my pillow?" he asked. "Yes," said Connor. "Put it on soft and slow."

Ella sat on her bed. She wanted to write a note for Grandpa. "What should it say?" she asked. Mom said, "It can say, I love you." Ella picked up her crayon. She wrote all her letters in a long line. They ran together like one big word. Grandpa would come tomorrow. Ella looked at her paper. It looked cloudy and mixed up, like paint stirred in a cup. She brushed the crumbs off her night table. Then she got her favourite book. Mom opened it at the front. "Books start here," said Mom. They turned the pages one by one. Ella looked and looked. "Mom, why is there a little space here?" she asked. Mom said, "There is a space between one word and the next." Ella looked again. Yes! Every word had its own space. She went back to her note. She wrote it again. She put a space after I. She put a space after love. Now the words stood apart. Each word sat alone, neat on the page. The next day, Grandpa came. He held the paper. He read it out loud. "I love you," he said. He gave Ella a big hug.

Louis stood at the little table. Ms. Cohen put bread by his hands. The toast was warm and soft. Louis held a small knife with butter on it. He spread the butter, slow and slow. "Look, it goes far across the bread," said Krishiv next to him.

Then it was milk time. Louis took the small jug. He poured into his cup. A drop ran down the side, but not much. "Good pouring, Louis," said Ms. Cohen. Louis set the milk jug down on the table.

Graham chased his rolling cup across the table. "Oops!" said Graham. Then Louis remembered. He picked up the jug. He carried it to the fridge. He put the milk inside so it would stay cold. Ms. Cohen smiled. Louis sat down and drank his milk. "I did it," he said, and his heart felt big.

Hayden went to the library. It was a cloudy day. He wanted a book about a cat. He could not find one. "Please help me," Hayden said to Mr. Eze. "Thank you," he said when Mr. Eze showed him the cat books.

Emma sat at the little table. Mr. Eze offered her a cracker. "Yuck!" Emma shouted. The book in her hand fell. It covered her crackers on the floor. "Sorry," Emma said. She picked the book up.

Mr. Eze offered the cracker again. Emma thought a bit. Then she said, "No, thank you." Mr. Eze smiled and gave her a sticker instead.

Hayden counted his cat books. One cat, two cats, three cats. Then he opened the first book. A tiny paper cat fell out. "Look!" said Hayden. "A surprise cat." Emma clapped her hands and leaned in close to see.

The car ride to the library was a little bumpy. Felix sat in his big seat and looked out the window. "I see a cow!" he said. "One, two, three cows." His dad smiled. Soon Felix said, "I see a dog. And a bird. And another dog." He wanted to find a book about animals, all about cows and dogs and birds.

The car stopped. They were at the library. Felix held his dad's hand and went inside. It was quiet and warm. It smelled like paper. Ms. Oliveira was there. "I want an animal book," said Felix. She walked with him to a shelf. "Here are the animal books," she said. "They sit together in a group."

Felix looked and looked. Then he saw it. A book with a cow on the front, a big brown cow. "This one!" he said. He hugged it tight. Next to it was a shelf of toy books, and then a shelf of food books. "Books about food live together too," said Ms. Oliveira. Felix laughed. It was a surprise, like a big family of books.

In the car, the ride home felt bumpy again. Felix held his cow book on his lap. "Cow, dog, bird," he said, one finger up for each. His dad said, "We can read it at bedtime." Felix patted the cover gently and whispered, "Book goes home with us."

Luka ran to the park with a small bag. His friend Zendaya was there. She had a game. "Name your five senses," she said. "You win a sticker if you get them all."

Luka tried. "Eyes see," he said. Zendaya clapped. "Ears hear," he said. "Nose smells," he said. "Hands touch," he said. Then he stopped. "I forgot one," he said. His face went sad.

Quentin came over with snacks. He had lemon slices and tiny strawberries. "Try one," said Quentin. Luka picked a strawberry. He put it in his mouth. He began to chew. It was sweet. Then he licked the lemon slice. His mouth went sour and his eyes went tight. "Wow!" said Luka. "My tongue can taste!"

"That is your fifth sense," said Zendaya. She gave him a rainbow sticker. Luka put it on his shirt. He looked at a butterfly on a flower. "I see it with my eyes," he said. "And I smell the flowers with my nose."

Mr. Villanueva smiled from his bench. "Nice work, Luka," he said. Luka held up the lemon slice. "Want to taste it?"

Isaiah sat in his car seat. Hasan sat next to him. "Let's play a game," said Hasan. "I say a word. You say the opposite. Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be."

"Big!" said Hasan. "Small!" said Isaiah. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on a small street. "Fast and slow!" they shouted.

Dad's coffee sat in the cup holder. It was hot. Isaiah touched his cold water bottle instead. "Hot," he said. "Cold!" said Hasan.

The car stopped at the store. Dad bought ice. The ice was cold too. Isaiah held the bag with Dad. It rattled in his hands.

They played the game all the way home. "You know so many opposites," said Hasan. "You win!"

Isaiah smiled big. "One more?"

Arlo sat at the big table. He had paper and markers. He was drawing a garden. He drew one red flower. He drew two blue flowers. He drew three green leaves.

The red marker slipped. It made a line on his hand. Arlo looked at his hand. "Oh no," he said. The red line would not rub off. "Will it stay on my skin?" he asked. He guess what a grown-up might say.

His dad came to help. "These are washable markers," said Dad. "Let's try soap and water." They went to the sink. Dad turned on the water. Arlo rubbed his hands with soap. The soap felt slippery. He rubbed and rubbed. The red line began to fade. Then it was gone!

Arlo held up his clean hand. He looked at it. Then he looked at the marker. "Marker on skin, soap and water, all gone," he said. He smiled at his hand. Then he went back to his garden.

Alice went to the playground with her friend Dax. Dax loved the big swing. It was his dream swing, he said. Alice wanted to push him ten times. She wanted to count all the way to ten.

"One, two, four," said Dax, counting the pushes.

"Where did three go?" Alice asked. "Three comes after two. Then four."

"I forgot three!" said Dax. He laughed. They tried again.

"One, two, three, four, five," said Alice.

"Six, seven, eight," said Dax.

Together they said, "Nine, ten!"

Ten pushes made the swing go high. Dax felt like a bird. Then they slid down the slide. On the ground there was a little slug on a leaf. It was slimy. Alice did not touch it. She just looked. A leaf fell down. It went bump on the slide, then bump on the ground.

"Do leaves always fall down?" Alice asked.

"Yes," said Dax. "Down to the ground, every time."

They watched one more leaf fall. Then they counted it. "One," they said together.

Avery sat at the little table. It was art time at school. Outside the window, snow was falling. The snow piled up on the grass. The snow looked white and soft.

"I want to paint the snow," said Avery. She got white paper. She painted a big white snow hill. But the white paint did not show. The white paint looked like nothing at all. Ms. Smith came over. "Try blue paper," said Ms. Smith. Avery was careful as she got a blue sheet. She painted a white hill on the blue paper. Now the white snow showed up. "I see it!" said Avery. Waylon leaned over. "The snow looks so soft," he said.

Avery mixed yellow and red. She painted a red mitten. She painted a green tree. "Almost done," she said. She reached for her cup of water. The cup began to tip. "Careful," said Enoch. Avery caught it. Not one drop did spill. Then she painted one last thing. A small yellow sun, way up in the sky. "Snow day," said Avery. "All done."

Grandpa was coming on a plane. Myles wanted to see him first. So Dad took Myles to the airport. "Families wait here," said Dad. They stood by the arrivals doors. Many people walked out. Not Grandpa. Not Grandpa. "That lady is not Grandpa!" said Myles. Dad laughed. "No, she is not."

Myles kept looking. A tall man came out. Not Grandpa. A boy with a hat came out. Not Grandpa. Myles began to frown. "Where is Grandpa?" he asked. "The plane is big," said Dad. "It takes a long time to empty."

Then the doors opened again. A man waved his hand. He had a big smile and a red bag. "Grandpa!" Myles shouted. He ran and hugged him tight.

Grandpa stayed a whole week. Each day they went to the park. They fed the ducks. They looked for spring flowers. Grandpa pushed Myles on the swing, high, high, high.

At night, the park gate was closed. "No more park today," said Grandpa. "But we can come back tomorrow." "And the next day?" asked Myles. "And the next day," said Grandpa. Myles grinned and held Grandpa's hand all the way home.

Lucy put on her red hat. "It keeps my head warm," she said. Then she and Oscar ran to the park. The sun was hiding. Big clouds were up above. The wind began to whoosh.

The wind blew hard. Whoosh, whoosh. The wind blew Lucy's hat right off her head! "My hat!" cried Lucy. The hat rolled over the grass. Lucy chased it. The wind blew it again. It landed in the dirt by the bench.

Lucy was scared her hat was gone. But Ms. Bighorn, the kind teacher, ran with her. Ms. Bighorn picked up the hat. "Hold it tight," she said. Lucy held it with both hands. Then rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip.

"Rainy days need hats too," said Ms. Bighorn. Lucy smiled. She kept her hat on all the way home.

Nora was at Marius's house. She saw a tablet on the table. "Can I draw?" she asked. Marius nodded. "Press the round button," he said. Nora pressed it. The screen lit up. How did that happen? She had made the light come on with one little press.

Marius tapped a colorful square. A drawing app opened. Nora touched the screen with her finger. She slid it across, and a line followed! A long, messy, squiggly line. She wiggled her finger more. The line wiggled too. "It looks like a snake!" she said. She added two dots for eyes. Where would the snake go next? She drew a big loop around it.

Then Nora yawned. The picture was done. "Time to put it away," said Marius's mom. Nora pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She set the tablet down, flat and safe. Then she picked up her book and read about real snakes. "Mine had more wiggles," she said.

The bookmobile came to Paisley's street. It was a big truck full of books. Paisley held her dad's hand and walked up the steps.

"I want that one," she said. She pointed to a book about a red fox. The cover felt rough when she touched it. Ms. Çelik smiled at her.

"You can take it home," said Ms. Çelik. "This is your library card. A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

Paisley looked at the little card. It had her name on it. Her name, right there! "My very own card?" she asked.

"Your very own," said Ms. Çelik. She scanned the card. Then she scanned the fox book. Beep, beep!

Paisley hugged the book tight. "I get to take it home to read," she said. "I get to take it home to read!"

Her friend Mae was there too. Mae picked out a book about the moon. "Can you take yours home too?" Paisley asked her.

"Yep," said Mae. "My card works the same way."

On the walk home, Paisley skipped the whole way. She read the fox book at lunch. She read it again at bedtime.

"Again," said Paisley, turning to page one.

Ibrahim sat in his car seat. Dad was driving. They were going to Mr. Owusu's house. It was still early in the morning. The sun was just coming up. Out the window, Ibrahim saw a river. The water moved slow and shiny. He waved at the river as they passed.

At Mr. Owusu's house, there was a big jar of cookies. Ibrahim wanted one very much. He pulled the lid. It did not open. He pulled again. It was too hard. His face felt hot and his eyes felt watery.

Then he remembered something. He looked up at Mr. Owusu. "Can you help me, please?" he said. Mr. Owusu smiled. "Of course," he said. He turned the lid, and it popped open. One small turn did it.

Dad passed Ibrahim a cookie. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. He took a big bite. Mr. Owusu laughed and passed him a napkin. "Sorry, it's a bit crumby," Ibrahim said. "That's okay," said Mr. Owusu. "Cookies are meant to be crumby."

Sarah went to the store with her dad. She wanted to buy ten apples for a snack. She put apples in the bag. Her dad helped her count. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten apples!

Then Sarah saw a sign. It had the number ten on it. But ten looked funny. It had a 1 and then a 0. Sarah asked, "Why does ten need two numbers?" Her dad said, "Ten is written with two digits, a 1 and then a 0." Sarah touched the sign. The 1 came first. The 0 came after.

Sarah saw a cute cookie shaped like a triangle. "Can you guess what it costs?" her dad asked. "Ten!" said Sarah. And there it was again, a 1 and then a 0. Sarah smiled and carried the bag of apples all the way home.

Charlie was in the sandbox. She dug a big hole with her blue shovel. Mud got all over her hands. Then Dad called, "Snack time!"

Charlie ran to the table. There were warm muffins. Mom had helped bake them after school. Charlie reached for the biggest one.

Mom shook her head. "Wash your hands first," she said. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Charlie looked at her muddy hands. "Will the mud go on the muffin?" she asked.

"Yes, if you touch it," said Mom.

Charlie went to the sink. Dad turned on the water. It was warm and bubbly. Charlie rubbed her hands. The mud went down, down, down the drain. Her hands were clean and pink.

She ran back to the table. She picked up the big muffin. No mud went on it. Not one bit.

"I washed, so the muffin stayed clean," said Charlie. "I am so smart!"

Mom laughed. "Eat your muffin, smart girl."

Charlie took a big, big bite. "Yum," she said. "Clean hands taste good with muffins."

James sat at the paint table with his friend Paxton. Paxton wanted to paint green grass. But the green paint pot was empty. "Oh no," said Paxton. "No green." Ms. Santos-Re Reyes came over. She smiled and let them try something. "Take your time," she said. "Paint can surprise you."

James looked at the pots. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. He put a big blue dot on his paper. Then he put a yellow dot on top. He mixed them with his brush. He stirred slow. He stirred some more. The paint turned green! "Look, Paxton!" said James. "Blue and yellow make green!"

Paxton scooped some blue. Then he scooped some yellow. He mixed and mixed. His paint turned green too. Paxton painted tall grass. James painted a green frog. Aira came to look. "Can I try?" she asked. James gave her his brush. Outside, the snow was frozen on the window. Inside, the grass grew on every paper.

Athena stood in the kitchen in her curly socks. She wanted to help make breakfast. But her socks were wet. She had splashed in a big puddle outside.

"Wet socks feel squishy," said Athena. Her mom knelt down. "Let's find dry socks," said Mom. Mom pulled off the wet socks. Wet and dry are opposites, Mom said. Then Mom brought small socks from the basket. They were dry and warm.

Athena put them on. Her toes felt happy. She stomped fast, then slow. Stomp, stomp, stomp! Now she could help.

Mom poured cold milk into a cup. Mom used the big pan on the hot stove. Athena stayed back and watched from her chair. The pan went sizzle, sizzle. Athena clapped.

"My socks are dry," said Athena. She twirled around the kitchen like a small dancing star. Then she carried the spoons to the table, one by one.

Milo loved the red blocks at school. Gabrielle was playing with them now. Milo asked Ms. Bear, "Can I have the blocks?"

"Not right now," said Ms. Bear. "You can have them later."

"Is it later yet?" asked Milo.

"Not yet," said Ms. Bear. "Later means some time after now."

Milo sat at the little table. He looked at the clock. He paid attention to the big hand. It moved a tiny bit. The blocks were still with Gabrielle.

He drew a loose circle on his paper. It looked like a ball. He drew another one. He drew a whole page of circles.

"Is it later yet?" he asked again.

"Not yet," said Ms. Bear.

Milo stacked some soft cubes. He made a tower. He made it tall.

Then Gabrielle walked over. "You can have the blocks now," she said. "I made a long train already."

Milo looked up. The big hand had moved far. "Now it is later!" he said.

He took the blocks. He built a big red house.

"Tomorrow," said Ms. Bear, "you can have them again."

"Tomorrow is after today," said Milo, and he put one more block on top.

Addison went to the library with her dad. There was a story time about shapes. Mr. Gupta held up a red square. "A square has four sides," he said. Then he held up a blue triangle. "Look, three sides and pointy tips!"

After the story, it was craft time. Everyone got paper shapes and glue. Addison wanted to make a sun. She found a yellow circle.

Drew sat next to her. He was cutting a green square. "I start at a corner," he said. Snip, snip. Matias cut his purple triangle. "Corners are easy to cut," he said.

Addison looked at her yellow circle. She wanted to cut it in half. She looked for a corner to start. She turned the paper round and round. She looked again. There was no corner anywhere!

"It has no corners!" she said. "A circle is just round, round, round." Drew peeked over. "Your shape is sneaky," he said. Addison laughed.

Mr. Gupta came to help. He gave her child-safe scissors and held the paper. Addison made one snip on the round edge. Then she turned the paper a little. Snip. Turn. Snip. Soon she had two half circles.

"The mean scissors did not scratch my paper," she said. "They made two happy faces!" Drew giggled. Matias put a rectangle under his triangle. "My house has a roof," he said.

Addison glued her two half circles on a big paper. Then she added the whole circle in the middle. "My sun has smiling friends," she said. Mr. Gupta put it up on the shelf by the window.

James went to the bank with his dad. It was cold outside. James had to put on his coat.

He pushed one arm in. One sleeve was full. Where was the other sleeve? It hid behind his back. James could not touch it. He wiggled and turned. The sleeve still hid.

A lady at the bank saw him. She smiled. "Want to see a trick?" she asked. "Lay your coat on the floor. Put your arms in the sleeves. Then flip it over your head."

James put his coat on the floor. He pushed both arms in. He flipped it over his head. The coat was on! Both sleeves were on! James looked down. How did that happen? He patted his chest. The zipper hung open.

James pulled the zipper up, slow, slow, up. It stopped at the top. His dad clapped. James touched the good warm coat.

Outside, snow fell on the bank steps. James said, "I did it all by myself."

Lillian had a cold. Her nose was red. Her throat felt scratchy. She sat on the couch with her blanket.

"I don't want water," Lillian said. "I am not thirsty."

Her grandma smiled. She brought a cup with a pink straw. A little paper plane was taped to the straw. It looked like it could fly.

Lillian took one little sip. Then she took another. The water was cool and fresh. Sip by sip, the plane went up and down.

Soon Lillian sat up a bit taller. She looked at her blocks across the room. She wanted to build a tower.

"Water helps when you are sick," Grandma said softly. "Take your cup."

Lillian carried her cup to the blocks. She sipped while she stacked. She made a tall, tall tower.

Grandma sat beside her. "Can I add one block?"

"Yes," said Lillian. She took one more sip, and the tower reached all the way up to her chin.

Beatrice stood by the blocks at school. She wanted to play with Jayke and Penny. But they were busy feeding a teddy bear with a tiny spoon.

Beatrice did not know how to start. She looked at her shoes. She looked at the toy shelf. Then she had an idea.

"Let's pretend I am the bear's doctor," she said. Jayke looked up right away. "Okay, doctor!" he said. Penny handed her a toy phone. "The bear is sick," said Penny. "He needs one hug, two pats, and three songs."

Beatrice got to work. She bent down low. She listened to the bear's tummy with a block. "Hmm," she said. She gave one hug, two pats, and three little songs. The bear smiled. Then the bear jumped up and danced.

"Now let's pretend the bear is a pirate," said Jayke. "Let's pretend I am the pirate's parrot," said Penny. Beatrice laughed. She flapped her arms like wings.

The teacher, Mr. Han, walked by. "A pirate, a parrot, and a doctor," he said. "What a happy crew." Beatrice held the bear up high. "Sail the ship!" she called.

Abigail sat at the little red table. Ms. Lau put a tablet in front of her. The screen was dark and still. Abigail tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. Still nothing. Her friend Julia leaned over. "Mine did that too," Julia said.

Ms. Lau came to help. She pointed to a small round button on the side. "Press this," she said. Abigail pressed it. The screen lit up. She smiled big. Now she could draw. She tapped the paint app and drew a bird. She made it fly across the sky with her finger. She drew an apple, round and red, with one little root like a tiny tree.

Then it was time for snacks. Abigail pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, just like Ms. Lau showed. "You did it all by yourself," said Julia. Abigail sat down and took a big bite of her apple.

Max saw the red truck on the rug. He wanted it so much. Porter was holding it and driving it slow. Max ran over and grabbed the truck. Porter said, "Hey!" Max held it tight. Ms. Abdi came and sat down. "Max, you can ask for a turn," she said. Max gave the truck back to Porter. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. Porter said, "Yes, after two more drives." Max sat on the pillow and waited. It was hard. His sweater felt itchy. He did not grab. Then Porter put the truck in Max's hands. "Thank you, Porter," Max said. Porter smiled a big smile. Then Porter handed Max the blue car too. "You can hold both," said Porter. Max drove the trucks fast down the rug. "Thank you again!" he called.

Gianna stood at the airport with Mom. She held a big paper sign. It said "Grandma" in red letters. "The plane will land soon," said Mom.

A lady with a blue bag walked out. "Grandma!" cried Gianna. She ran and hugged her. Then Gianna had a question. "Grandma, are you my mom's mom?" Grandma laughed. "Yes, I am your mom's mom. A grandma is a mom of your mom or your dad."

Gianna thought about that. Grandma was a mom too! Grandma was Mom's Mom. "Say it again," said Gianna. "My mom's mom," she said. "My mom's mom," said Gianna. "My mom's mom!"

At home, Gianna got a snack for Grandma. Grandma shared a cookie. Grandma had a small fish toy in her bag. It was for Gianna! It wiggled its tail.

The week went by fast. They played, and painted, and read books. Then it was airport day again. Gianna gave Grandma the red sign to keep. "So you remember me," she said.

Grandma waved from the long line. "My Gianna," she called. "My mom's mom!" Gianna waved back, high and wide.

Mason was at Grandma's house. His spotted toy monkey was lost. "Where did Monkey go?" Mason asked. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. He looked behind the big chair. No monkey.

Grandma helped him look. They checked one basket, two baskets, three baskets. No monkey anywhere. Then Grandpa came in. He held Monkey up high. "Monkey fell behind the couch," he said. "But I did not know whose monkey it was." Then Grandpa smiled. "Then I saw the tag."

Mason looked at the tag. It said Mason in big letters. "That is my name!" he said. "Grandma wrote it there." Grandpa nodded. "The tag told me." Mason hugged Monkey tight. "Now everyone will know you are mine," he said. He kissed Monkey's soft ear. "Hello again, my spotted friend."

Rosalie was going on a big trip. First came the airport. It was very busy. So many people! So many feet.

Then Rosalie saw the planes. Big planes! One was taking off. "Look, look!" she called. She wanted to run to the window. But the crowd was thick like soup. Where was her grown-up?

Rosalie looked down. She saw Mommy's hand. She held it tight. In busy places, children hold hands. She did not let go. Mommy smiled and squeezed back.

Later they got to the beach. The sand was warm. Rosalie found a tiny shell. "Where did you come from, little shell?" she asked. The wind blew. The waves went swish, swish. Rosalie held Mommy's hand again, just because it felt nice.

"Look, Mommy, the sea goes on and on!"

Riley sat on the blue rug. She held a book about apples. On the wall, there was a big letter A. It was made of red paper.

Riley pointed at the page. "That is a little circle with a tail," she said. "That is not the A." Sloan came to look. "The wall A is big," said Sloan. "This one is small."

Riley put her finger on the small a. Then she looked up at the big A. She looked down again. "Little a," she said. "Big A." Ms. Kobayashi knelt down beside her. "Same letter," said Ms. Kobayashi. "A can be big or small."

Riley turned the page. She found a small m. She ran to the wall and found the big M. "Same letter!" she said. Payton clapped. Then Riley found a small t and a big T. "Same letter," she said again.

At dinner that night, Riley held up her milk cup. She drew a big R in the air with her finger. Then she drew a small r. "Same letter," said Riley. "That is me." She took a sip and smiled.

Kai was at Grandma's house. Grandma was playing the piano. She played a song. Kai wanted to sing it. But the words ran away from him. He only hummed.

"Let's clap," said Grandma. She clapped. Clap, clap, clap. The beat was steady, like feet walking. Kai clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. His hands went with the music.

Then Grandma sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Kai knew that song! He tried. "Twinkle, twinkle..." He lost the words again.

Kai sat and thought. He hummed a song from school. It was the ABC song. A, B, C, D... He hummed and hummed. Then he stopped. It sounded the same! The ABC song sounded just like "Twinkle, Twinkle"!

Grandma smiled. "Try it, Kai," she said. Kai sang the ABC tune. He put new words on it. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" It worked! He clapped while he sang. Clap, clap, clap.

Their naughty cat jumped on the piano. It wanted to sing too. Kai laughed and hugged his gift of a song. He sang it one more time, all by himself. "How I wonder what you are."

Jaxon was at Grandma's house. He wanted to play outside in the leaves. Grandma said, "First we get dressed." Jaxon was shy about the big red boots by the door.

He sat on the small step. He pushed his feet into the boots. Then he tried to push his socks on top. The socks would not stay. They slid right off. Jaxon laughed and laughed.

Grandma smiled. "Want to try again, sweet boy?" Jaxon pulled the boots off. He wiggled his blue socks onto his toes. They felt soft and warm. Then he pushed his boots on over them. This time they stayed!

There was a line of orange leaves by the gate. Jaxon jumped along the line, one jump for each leaf. He heard a knock at the fence. His friend Ayansh was there, waving. "Come play with me!" Ayansh called. Jaxon ran to the gate, boots stomp-stomping on the path. The leaves crunched under his feet. Ayansh handed him a big red leaf. Jaxon held it up to the sun. It glowed like fire. "Wow," said Jaxon. "Grandma has the best yard." Ayansh laughed, and they jumped in the leaves together.

Eva climbed the school bus. She held the rail with both hands. She sat by the window. Her friend Tom sat next to her. "First day of school," said Tom. Eva looked out. She saw a red car. She saw a big dog. She saw a pink flower by the road. One, two, three things, counted Eva.

At school, the bus stopped. Mr. Tesfaye helped everyone off. Eva ran to the slide. It was tall and yellow. She went down fast. Whee! She wanted to go again right away. She ran to the front. But the other children stood in a line. Tom was in the line. Rylee was in the line. "We take turns on the slide," said Rylee. So Eva walked to the back. She waited. She counted the children. One, two, three, four. Then it was her turn again.

Eva went down the slide a second time. At the bottom, a leaf landed on her nose. It was a small yellow leaf. Eva laughed. She held it up. "Look, Tom!" said Eva. Tom laughed too. Then he showed her the line. Eva ran to the back again, and she held the leaf in her hand all the way down.

Florence went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a mouse who moved to a new house. The pictures were big and bright. Florence loved them.

"Who drew this mouse?" she asked. She wanted to know. Mr. Bear, the library man, came to help. "Look here," he said. He pointed to the front of the book. "This name is the illustrator. An illustrator draws or paints the pictures for a book." Florence touched the name with her finger. "The illustrator made my mouse," she said.

She opened the book at the front page. "We start here," said Mr. Bear. "Then we go page by page." Florence turned each page herself. At the end, the mouse had a new friend. "Again!" said Florence. Her dad laughed and turned the book back to the front.

Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her tummy felt fluttery, like little wings inside. She held her mama's hand very tight.

"Mama, my tummy feels funny," said Elizabeth.

Mama knelt down. "Mine felt that way too, on my first day of school. Feeling nervous is okay." She kissed Elizabeth's head and waved goodbye.

Elizabeth walked in slowly. She saw blocks, paints, and a big red carpet. A girl with two braids was hiding behind the easel. Her face looked worried.

"Hi, I'm Elizabeth," she said. "My tummy felt fluttery at the door."

The girl peeked out. "Mine feels fluttery right now," she whispered. "I'm Isabel."

Elizabeth took Isabel's hand. "Come on. We can feel fluttery together."

They walked to the block corner. Isabel's hand stopped squeezing so hard. Together they built a tall, tall tower.

Ms. Guo came over with a smile. "What a big tower!"

"It wobbles," said Isabel. Elizabeth pulled one block out, and the whole tower leaned. She pushed it back in, and the tower stood straight again.

"Isabel, look!" said Elizabeth. "The block holds it up."

Isabel laughed and put the next block on top. "Let's make it taller than us."

Emile wanted to read a book to Rosa. He found a thick book on the shelf. The cover had a red flag on it. He sat down and opened the front cover first.

Emile put his finger on the page. He started at the right side of the page. Rosa shook her head. "That sounds funny," she said. Ms. Das knelt down beside them. She moved Emile's finger to the left side. "Start here," she said. Emile slid his finger across the words. Left to right. Then he went to the next page. "Why do I start here?" he asked. "The words go this way," Ms. Das said. Emile tried again. His finger went left to right. "The flag is big!" he read. Rosa clapped.

Emile turned page after page. He always started on the left. At the end, he closed the back cover. "Now you read one to me," he said. Rosa ran to the shelf to find a book.

Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. His friend Zayd sat next to him. There were paper cups of paint on the table.

Hudson looked for orange paint. "There is no orange," he said. His pumpkin paper had red paint and yellow paint. Hudson dipped his brush in the red. He painted the pumpkin red. Then he dipped the brush in the yellow cup. He painted yellow on top of the red. The pumpkin turned orange!

"Look, Zayd!" said Hudson. "Red and yellow make orange!" Zayd clapped his hands. Ms. Chatterjee came to see. "What a big orange pumpkin," she said. Hudson painted a small bear next to the pumpkin. The bear was brown. Then he painted a green grass hill, and a sun in the sky. After all that painting, Hudson gave a big yawn. "I think my paper wants to sleep," he said. Zayd laughed, and Ms. Chatterjee hung the pumpkin up on the wall.

Sadie sat at the dinner table. She had a big want. "Can I go to Aayra's house now?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Dad. "Aayra is busy today." Sadie put down her spoon. "Is tomorrow far away?" she wondered. "Tomorrow is the day after today," said Dad. Sadie looked at her peas. She counted them. One pea, two peas, three peas. Tomorrow was not on her plate. "What do we do first?" she asked. "First we eat dinner," said Dad. "Then we sleep. Then it is tomorrow." Sadie ate her peas. She drank her milk. She talked about the color of her cup. It was red and it made her happy. After dinner, Dad tucked her in. "Now I sleep," she said. "Later I wake up. Then it is tomorrow." She closed her eyes. In the morning, the sun was in her window. Sadie ran to the door in her pajamas. "Dad! I slept! Is it tomorrow now?" Dad laughed. "It is tomorrow," he said. "Go get dressed." Sadie got dressed fast. At Aayra's door, she knocked two times. The door opened. Aayra smiled. "You came!" said Aayra. "I waited," said Sadie. "I had dinner, then I slept, and now it is today!"

Ava sat at the dinner table. Her dad put warm soup in her bowl. Ava took a bite. Yum. Then she asked, "Can I stay up late tonight?" Her dad said, "You can try, but it is almost bedtime." Ava begged, "Please, just a little more?" She got to stay up and up. The sky outside turned stormy. Thunder went boom. Ava watched a cow in the rain from the window. Her eyes felt heavy. She fell asleep on the big chair.

The next morning, Ava woke up slow. Yousuf came to play. "Let's run!" he said. Ava tried to run. Her legs felt slow. Her arms felt slow. "Why am I so tired?" she wondered. At dinner, she ate her food and said, "I want to go to sleep now." She slept all night. The next morning, her legs felt fast again. She ran and ran with Yousuf. "Night sleep makes me ready!" she laughed, and off they went.

Lennon went to the cultural center with her mom. There were little lamps everywhere. They glowed like small warm suns. The room smelled like flowers and sweet rice.

Lennon wanted to light one. She reached for a match in a box on the table. "Not that one," her mom said. "Matches are for grown-ups." Lennon felt her face go hot. It seemed wrong to just watch.

Then Ms. Fernando knelt down beside her. "Would you like to pick a lamp for me to light?" she asked. Lennon pointed to a blue lamp. Ms. Fernando lit the wick. It sent up a small flame. The lamp glowed bright.

Lennon picked a red one next. Tatum picked a yellow one. Ms. Fernando lit each one. Soon all the lamps were shining. The whole room glowed.

"Thank you for helping," said Ms. Fernando. Lennon smiled and held her mom's hand. She waved at her little blue lamp, shining far across the room.

Blake ran to Azariah's house. Azariah's big sister had a song on. The song had a steady beat. Boom, boom, boom, boom.

"Let's clap!" said Azariah. Blake tried to clap. She clapped too fast. She clapped too slow. She would lose the beat every time. "It's not easy," said Blake.

Then Azariah's big sister held up her hand. "Listen," she said. "I will count. One, two, three, four." On four, they clapped. Boom, boom, boom, boom. It worked!

"Now we sing," said Azariah. Blake started right away. Too soon! The song had not started yet. "Wait for the count," said Azariah. "One, two, three, four." Then they sang together.

Twinkle, twinkle, little star. Blake knew every word!

The song ended. A small voice came from the door. Azariah's cat was meowing to the beat!

"One, two, three, four," said Blake. The cat meowed on four.

"Again! Again!" said Blake. And they all clapped.

Isla went to the pharmacy with her dad. She held his hand at the door. On a shelf she saw a little fox toy. It was soft and red. Dad bought soap, and Isla got the fox too.

At home it was lunch time. Isla held up her hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said. They looked clean in the light.

Dad turned on the tap. The water was warm. Isla rubbed the soap all over. It smelled like flowers. She sang her fox song while she washed. Singing the whole song took a long time.

Then Isla ate her sandwich. Her hands felt slippery, then soft, then clean.

After lunch, Isla ran to the sink all by herself. "Fox needs washing too," she said. Dad laughed and turned on the tap.

Beau sat in his car seat. The car went zoom, zoom. "I want to show Anika my book," said Beau. "It is a book about animals." Mom said, "We will see Anika soon. First we wait at the red light."

The light was long. It was windy outside. A little feather floated by the window. It went up. It went down. It tapped on the glass. Beau opened the window a tiny bit. He caught the feather in his hand. "Mom! Look!" he said. "A feather!"

"Where did it come from?" asked Mom. Beau looked up. A bird sat on a wire above the car. "The bird!" said Beau. "Birds have feathers. This one is his." He held the feather in his book. At the next stop, Anika got in. "Look, Anika!" said Beau. "A bird gave me this!"

Hailey sat in the cafe with her mom. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her own name.

She pressed the pencil down hard. She made a big H. Then the tip snapped off. The pencil could not make marks now.

"Uh oh," said Hailey.

Her mom got a new pencil from her bag. "Try again," she said. She gave Hailey's hand a little kiss.

Hailey held the pencil softly this time. She made light, small lines. H. A. I. The letters came out neat, not ugly and smudgy like before.

"I did it!" said Hailey.

A waitress came by with warm muffins. She looked at the paper. "Is that your name?" she asked.

"Yes! I wrote it all by myself," said Hailey.

She wrote L, E, and Y too. Then she wrote the whole name again. Press soft, write letters. Press soft, write letters. Her name sat on the paper, pretty as a little painting.

Hailey held the paper up for everyone to see.

Raphael went to the dentist with his mom. The waiting room had a friendly fish tank. His friend Erica was there too.

Raphael needed to use the toilet. He ran out fast when he was done. He wanted to skip back to the fish tank. Erica called to him. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet." Raphael stopped. He turned around.

He went back to the little sink. He pushed the soap pump. He rubbed his hands. Bubbles grew in the middle of his palms. He rubbed and rubbed until his hands were slick and white. Then he rinsed the bubbles away. The water carried them down the drain.

His hands smelled like soap now. Erica gave him a big smile. The nurse opened the door and said, "Raphael, you're next." Raphael sat in the big chair. The friendly dentist, Mr. Girma, looked at his teeth. "Nice clean hands," said Mr. Girma. Raphael held them up high and grinned.

Asher ran to the little pool at the park. He wanted to jump right in. "Wait," his dad said. Dad put his hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot. Now you can get in." Asher stepped in. The water felt nice and warm on his toes. A rubber duck floated by. "Quack," said Asher. That was a surprise! He splashed and the duck bobbed up and down.

Then Asher saw the slide. The sun sat on the slide all morning. Asher put his hand near it. It felt hot. He pulled his hand back. Dad moved the duck and Asher to the shady pool. Splashing made the water fly up. Asher's face got wet. He was happy.

"Time for juice," said Dad. Asher helped bring the cup to the bench. The bench sat in the shade, so it was not hot. Asher sat down and drank. Warm pool, cool juice, quacking duck. "Again," said Asher, and he pointed at the water.

Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find the letter M. It was the first letter of her name. But the big letter rug had all the letters mixed up. Brooklyn could not find M anywhere.

Adriano was there too. He sat on the letter B. "I found my letter," he said. Brooklyn looked and looked. She sat down on a letter, but it was a W. "Oh no," she said. "That is not my letter. This feels bad."

Then Mr. Dela Cruz came over. He was the library man. He sat down on the rug with them. He began to sing, very soft. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." Brooklyn knew that song. She sang along too. The song went on and on, all the way from A to Z. When the song got to L, Brooklyn looked at the rug. L was next to a letter. And after L came M. There it was.

Brooklyn jumped up and put her feet on the M. "This is mine," she said. "M is for Brooklyn." The sun did shine in the window. It made the M on the rug bright. Then Mr. Dela Cruz said, "What letter comes after M?" Brooklyn took a deep breath and sang, "N, O, P."

Lily sat in the school computer lab. Mr. Popescu held up a tablet. "Who wants to learn this?" he asked. Lily raised her hand high.

First, she pressed the little button. One press. The screen lit up. Lily smiled. The button made the light come on.

Next came the drawing app. Mr. Popescu showed her the small blue square. One tap. Two taps. There it was. Lily moved her finger on the screen. A straight green line followed her finger. She pressed the stick on the side, and the line turned red. She drew a sun, a cat, and a big round tree.

Then it was time to put the tablet away. Lily picked it up with one hand. She walked to the shelf. The tablet slipped. It tipped and wobbled in her hand. She caught it just in time.

Yasin was watching. "Two hands," he said. Lily looked at her hands. She put one hand on each side. She held the tablet with two hands, and it sat still, like a bird on a nest.

Lily carried it to the shelf. One step, two steps, three steps. She set it down on the shelf, soft and slow. The tablet did not tip. It did not fall.

Mr. Popescu clapped. "All done," he said. Lily looked back at the shelf. The tablet sat safe and straight, and Lily waved good night to it.

Lydia stood at the baseball diamond. Mr. Pereira put a purple hoop on the grass. "Throw the beanbag in," he said.

Lydia threw her ball first. The ball hit the ground. It bounced up and up. "My ball can jump!" said Lydia.

Then she threw the beanbag. It hit the ground. It went flop. It did not jump at all. It just sat there, soft and still. Lydia poked it with her toe. Flop, flop.

Zaviyar ran to her. "Try again," he said. Lydia tried again. The beanbag went flop. Emil clapped. "It always goes flop!" said Lydia.

Then Lydia had an idea. A bouncing ball would hop right out of the hoop. But a beanbag would stay inside. She held the beanbag tight. She aimed. She threw it.

Flop. The beanbag landed in the hoop. It stayed put.

"Bring me the big ball," said Lydia. Zaviyar brought it. Lydia held out both hands. The ball came down. She caught it.

"I got it, Mr. Pereira!"

Mateo sat at the little table in art class. In front of him was a snack cracker. He held it up and looked at it.

"Is this a square?" he asked. "I'm not sure."

Ilyana leaned over. "It has four sides," she said. "I counted them."

"But a square has four sides that are all the same length," said Aspyn. She said it fast, like a song she knew.

Mateo frowned. How could he check? Then he saw the basket of purple string. Ms. Sun used it for necklaces. He pulled out one long purple string.

He put the string on the top side of the cracker. He pinched the string where the side ended. Then he moved the string to the bottom side. Same pinch! He moved it to the left side and the right side. Same pinch every time.

"It fits all four sides," Mateo said. "The sides are all the same length!"

"So it's a square!" said Ilyana. She clapped.

Mateo laid the cracker on his paper. He traced around it with his crayon. Then he traced it again and again. The squares made a big purple train on his paper.

Ms. Sun came by. "What a long train," she said. "Can I add one car?"

"Yes," said Mateo. He poured some glue next to his train, and Ms. Sun pressed on a triangle for the roof. "A baby house," Mateo said, "for a baby train."

Jayden was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa put a small pumpkin on a plate. "Can I paint it?" Jayden asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "We can paint it after lunch."

Jayden looked at the paint cups. He named them one by one. "Red, blue, yellow, green." There was no orange. That felt bad. "I want an orange pumpkin," said Jayden. "But there is no orange paint."

Yaseen came over to play. He looked at the cups too. "Stir red and yellow," said Yaseen. Jayden dipped his brush in red. He dipped it in yellow. He stirred them together in a big cup. The paint turned orange! Jayden painted the pumpkin with slow, careful strokes. The orange covered the whole pumpkin. "Red and yellow make orange," said Jayden. Yaseen laughed. Grandpa set the pumpkin on the plate by the window, next to his red tomatoes and green basil.

Henri sat in the waiting room. He held his doll tight. Today he would get his first haircut. He did not want his hair to go away. His hair was his. Asher came in with his mom. "I had a haircut here," Asher said. "It did not hurt one bit." Henri still held his doll.

Then the barber called Henri's name. Henri walked slowly. The barber's scissors went snip, snip. Little curls fell down. Some fell on the floor. Henri watched one curl land on the cape. His mom picked it up. She put the curl in a small envelope. "Why?" Henri asked. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it," his mom said. "Now we can look at it any time we want."

Henri peeked in the mirror. His hair looked short and neat. He made a silly face. The mirror made a silly face back. He laughed and almost spilled the envelope. His mom caught it just in time. "All safe," she said. Henri hugged his doll and waved the envelope at Asher. "Look," said Henri. "This is my hair, and I get to keep it."

Amira lost her favorite sock. She wanted to find it before lunch. "Let's look in your room," said Dad.

Amira counted as they searched. "One bed, two pillows, three books." She looked under the bed. Her arm could not reach. Dad helped her pull out a box. Something went scratch on the floor. It was just the box sliding.

Then Amira saw a paper on her door. It had a big 5 on it. She held up her hand. "One, two, three, four, five," she said, touching each finger. "Look, Dad! My fingers say five. The door says 5 too."

"Yes," said Dad. "The 5 means five." Amira smiled. It was like a new word in her world.

She counted five toys, then put them in the box. Six, seven, eight toys went in too. Then she looked in the box one more time. There was her sock, tucked at the bottom! "Nine and ten!" she shouted, waving both hands. Dad laughed and held up the sock. "Lunch time," he said. "Sock found, just in time."

Raphael had to go to the doctor. He took his old toy truck along. "Big day!" said his dad.

First the doctor looked in Raphael's ears. Raphael could hear the truck beep. Beep, beep! Then the doctor said, "Look here." Raphael used his eyes to see a red chart. He could smell something clean and sharp in the room. The doctor let him touch a soft cotton ball with his fingers.

Then the doctor held up a yellow lemon slice. "Taste this," she said. Raphael thought it would be sweet, like orange juice. He took a little lick. Wow! His whole face scrunched up. Sour! Sour, sour, sour!

The doctor laughed. "Your tongue knows," she said. Raphael laughed too. He hugged his truck. His tongue tasted the sour lemon, and his face went funny all by itself.

Henry sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. He looked for orange paint. He could not find any.

"I need orange," said Henry. "My pumpkin has to be orange."

Samar held up a jar. "We have red," she said. "We have yellow. One, two, that's all."

Henry dipped his brush in the red paint. He made a red stripe on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He put yellow on top of the red. He stirred it round and round with his brush.

The paint turned orange!

Henry looked and looked. "Samar, come see!" he said.

Samar ran over. "Orange!" she said. "Red and yellow make orange."

Henry painted his pumpkin. He painted one big pumpkin. He painted two small pumpkins. Ms. Brennan came to look.

"What a fine orange pumpkin," said Ms. Brennan. "Would you like to paint a white cat too?"

Henry nodded. He painted a white cat on a soft pillow. The cat looked sleepy. Henry added a little feather to tickle its nose.

"My cat will wake up," said Henry with a giggle.

Samar mixed red and yellow too. Now she had orange as well. They painted pumpkins side by side all morning.

Owen ran to the park with Selina. They went to the big slide. Owen felt so excited. "Watch me go fast!" he said. He slid down and laughed.

Then Owen heard a loud bark. A big dog was near the fence. It barked and barked. Owen felt scared. His tummy felt tight. He wanted to run, but he stood very still.

Selina saw Ms. Vu on the bench. "Let's tell her," Selina said. Owen walked over slowly. "Ms. Vu, that dog is loud," he said. "I feel scared." Ms. Vu held his hand. She knew the dog's name was Buddy. She called, "Buddy, come!" The dog ran to her and sat down. "Good boy, Buddy," she said.

Buddy licked Owen's hand. His fur was warm. His breath was a little smelly, and Owen giggled. "He does not bite," said Ms. Vu. "He just wanted to say hi." Owen patted Buddy's soft ear. The dog wagged his tail. Owen saw that telling a grown-up had made the scared feeling go away. "Buddy, can we play more?" he asked. Buddy bounced up and barked once.

Mohamed went to the farmers' market with his dad. He held the big cloth bag. The bag was loose on his arm. It kept sliding down. "Silly bag," Mohamed said with a giggle.

Mohamed bought a round loaf of bread. He bought fresh butter in a little jar. Landon and Frederic were there too. They waved and laughed. A fly buzzed near the apples. It landed on Frederic's hat. "A fly likes your hat," Mohamed teased. Frederic laughed and shooed it away.

At home, Mohamed wanted to make bread and butter for his family. He took the butter from the fridge. He poked it. It was hard, like a little hammer. He tried to spread it on the bread. The hard butter tore the bread. "Oh no," said Mohamed.

His dad said, "Let's leave it out on the counter." They set the butter on the counter. They waited. They washed apples. They set out plates. Then Mohamed poked the butter again. Now it was soft. His knife went smooth and easy. The bread stayed whole. Mohamed spread butter on every slice.

"Time to eat," said Mohamed. His family sat down together. Mohamed took a big happy bite. "Soft butter is the best," he said. "Better than the hammer butter." Everyone laughed, and the bread was gone fast.

Nova loved art class. Today the paint jars were in a big mess. Red, blue and yellow jars were all mixed up on the shelf. "We need sorting," said Ms. Chowdhury. "Sorting means putting all the same colors together in one group." Nova clapped her hands. "I can do it!" She made a red pile. Then a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. The jars clinked as she set them down. Jaxton found a green jar. "Where does green go?" he asked. Nova looked at her piles. She made a new pile, just for green. Then Etienne held up a jar. "This one goes in the red pile," he said. But Nova looked close. The jar was yellow! "It was hiding in the wrong pile," she said, and moved it. The shelf looked so pretty now. "Nice work," said Ms. Chowdhury. Nova smiled. She had a dream to paint a high mountain and a cow. She dipped her brush in blue.

Brooks had a cold last night. His nose ran and his head felt hot. So Mom took him to the pharmacy. Mr. Castillo worked there. He smiled at Brooks.

Mom talked to Mr. Castillo. He gave her a small bottle. It was medicine for Brooks. Brooks wanted to hold it. Mom said, "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine." She put the bottle in her bag.

At home, Brooks waited on the sofa. He watched Mom set the bottle on the counter. She opened it. She filled a little cup. She read the lines on the cup so it was just right. Then she held it out. "Here you go," she said.
