Brooks drank it all down. It tasted like grapes. He gave Mom the little cup back. Only Mom had poured it. Brooks had waited. Now his blanket felt soft and his cup of water sat close by. Mom sat down next to him and opened a book. "Show me the cat," she said. Brooks pointed at the page.

Julia stood in the kitchen next to her mom. Baby Sam was fast asleep in his little seat. Julia wanted to play her drum. She loved her drum so much.

She banged the drum. BANG! BANG! It was very loud. Baby Sam woke up. His face went red. He began to cry.

Mom said, "Loud and quiet are opposites." She held Julia's hand. "Try a little tap."

Julia looked at her drum. She tapped it very softly. Tap. Tap. It was quiet now. Baby Sam stopped crying. He blinked his big eyes. Then he made a small smile.

Julia tapped again, slow and quiet. Sam's eyes began to close. Soon he was asleep again.

Mom gave Julia a warm hug. The gray cat came in and sat on the floor. Julia tapped her drum one more time, very quiet, very soft.

"Good night, Sam," she whispered.

Eleanor turned four today. There was a big cake on the table. Her friends Duncan and Waris came to play. There were presents everywhere.

Eleanor opened a present from Duncan. It was a red truck with a big wheel. "I love it!" she said. Then she ran to the next box. She tore the paper off. It was a stuffed bear from Waris. Eleanor hugged the bear. Her mom bent down and smiled at her. Eleanor looked at the red truck. Then she looked at Duncan.

Eleanor ran back to Duncan. "Thank you for the truck," she said. Duncan smiled a big smile. "You are welcome," he said. Eleanor ran to Waris too. "Thank you for the bear," she said. Then she pushed the truck across the floor. The big wheel spun fast. The bear rode on top. "Beep beep!" said Eleanor, and everyone laughed.

Amelia woke up and saw snow. "Snow day!" said Mom. Amelia put on her boots and mittens. She ran out to the backyard. She made a big snowball. She patted it and patted it. Her mittens got all wet.

Amelia wanted to make a snow train. She came inside for more snow. "My mittens are soaked," she said. Mom shook her head. "Wet mittens need to dry first." They hung the mittens on the chair near the warm vent. They set the wet boots by the door to dry too.

Amelia waited by the window. She watched her mittens drip, drip, drip. Her friend Moksh waved from his yard. He was sad. "My mittens are wet too," he called. "Come dry them here," said Mom. Moksh came over with the neighbor. He hung his wet mittens next to Amelia's. The two mittens sat side by side.

Soon the mittens were warm and dry. Amelia clapped her hands. Moksh put his on. Amelia put hers on too. They ran back out to the snow. "Choo choo!" said Amelia. She rolled a long line of snowballs. Moksh rolled the last one. "The snow train is so pretty," said Moksh.

Felix was at Grandpa's house. He wanted the big cat book from the shelf. It was too high.

"Can you help me?" Felix asked.

Grandpa reached it down. Felix opened the book. He held it upside down. The pictures looked funny.

Grandpa turned it around. "The front goes first," he said. "We read this way."

Grandpa read a page. "The cat sat on the noisy box."

Later, Grandma read the same page. "The cat sat on the noisy box."

Felix looked up. "Grandma, you said the same words!"

"That's right," said Grandma. "The words are printed here."

Felix touched the letters with his pencil. "Do they spell cat?"

"Yes, they do."

Felix grinned. The words would say the cat again tomorrow. And every day after that.

Kinsley went to Remington's house. A big box sat on the floor. It was full of dress-up clothes.

Remington put on a red hat. "Now I am a firefighter," he said. He ran to a pretend fire. He sprayed it with a toy hose.

Kinsley looked in the box. She found a white coat. She put it on. "Now I am a doctor," she said. She found a teddy bear with a hurt paw. She wrapped it with a soft cloth. "You need rest," she told the bear.

Then Kinsley put a big apron over her coat. "Now I can be a cook too," she said. She pretended to clean the top of the toy stove. She stirred a pot of pretend soup. Remington sat down at her little table. "I am hungry," he said. Kinsley gave him a bowl.

Remington took off his hat. He became just Remington again. He laughed. "Your turn with the hat," he said.

Kinsley put the big red hat on her head. Then she ran to the pretend fire. "Here comes the firefighter!" she called.

Matteo ran to the park with his bucket. He wanted to find treasures for his sand castle. He saw the red slide. He heard the swings squeak. He smelled the flowers near the gate. "Treasure time!" he said.

Pia and Norah were by the grass. They took off their shoes. "Come feel the grass," said Pia. Matteo sat down. He was careful with his shoes. Then he pulled off his socks.

He put one bare foot on the grass. "It tickles!" he said. He wiggled his toes. "My feet can feel it too!" The grass was soft and cool under his toes. He laughed and stamped his feet.

"Let's take the buckets to the grass," said Norah. They sat down together. Pia gave Matteo a juicy orange slice. He tasted the sweet juice on his tongue. He touched the bumpy peel with his fingers. "The grass tickles my feet again!" said Matteo. Pia giggled and wiggled her toes next to his.

Luke went to the mall with his dad. They were going to the salon. Luke was getting his very first haircut. "Will it tickle?" Luke asked. "A little," said Dad.

Luke sat in a big chair on a low booster seat. The hairdresser put a cape on him. Then Luke saw a fish tank. Bright fish swam inside. Luke turned his head to look. Snip, snip went the scissors. A piece of hair fell onto the cape. Was it crooked? Yes, it was crooked.

"Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly," said the hairdresser. Luke tried again. He looked straight ahead. He sat like a statue. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little pins. It felt tickly on his neck.

At the end, Luke looked in the mirror. His hair was nice and neat. The hairdresser gave him a sticker shaped like a magnet to bring home. "Why a magnet?" Luke asked. "Because it sticks to your fridge," she said, "just like you stuck to that chair."

Kai stood in the garage with his dad. The radio played a song. Kai wanted to sing "The Itsy Bitsy Spider" all by himself. But he did not know the hand actions yet.

His dad showed him. "The spider climbs up," Dad said. His fingers wiggled up, up, up his arm. Then the rain came down. Then the sun came out. Kai tried it. He wiggled his fingers down, down, down. "Silly spider!" said Dad with a laugh. "Spiders climb up, not down." Kai giggled. His spider was going the wrong way!

Kai tried again. Up went the spider. Down came the rain. He clapped along to the steady beat. Clap, clap, clap. The cold garage air made his nose feel frozen, so Dad gave him a big hug. Then Kai sang the whole song. He did not stop, not once.

Andres ran in from the driveway. "Do it again!" he said. Kai smiled and wiggled his fingers high in the air. "The itsy bitsy spider climbs up the spout," he sang, "one more time!"

Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a green frog. He knew just where the green paint sat. "Green is next to the red," he said.

Then the room went dark. The lights went out. Mr. Clarke said, "Stay calm, everyone. A storm is outside." Rain tapped on the window. A dog outside began to bark.

Miles reached for the green paint. It was too dark to see. He dipped his brush anyway. He made a big frog shape on the paper.

Then the lights came back on. Miles looked at his frog. His frog was red! Not green, but red. He laughed and laughed. "I could not see the colors in the dark," he said.

Sylvie laughed too. "Try again," she said.

Miles found the green. He painted a new frog, all green. "There you are, green," he said.

Charles sat at book club with Cade and Abygael. Ms. Goldberg held up big letter cards. She held up A. "A," said Charles. She held up P. "P," said Charles. "P is the last letter," he said. "The alphabet is done!"

Cade laughed. "No way," he said. Ms. Goldberg kept going. She held up more cards. Q. R. S. Charles counted them. "Four more letters," he said. T. U. V. W. X. Y.

Then Ms. Goldberg held up the last card. "What is this one?" she asked. Charles looked hard. "Z," he said. "Z! The alphabet ends at Z!"

"I thought it ended at P," said Charles. "It ends at Z," said Abygael. Ms. Goldberg smiled.

"Now sing the song," she said. Charles sang it all the way. He sang A, and he sang Z. His itchy sweater made him wiggle, but he kept singing. After the song, his hands were dry from clapping.

"Does the alphabet end at P now?" asked Cade, teasing.

"No, it ends at Z," said Charles. "A first, Z last, forever!" He turned over the Z card and made a sleepy animal snore. "Zzz," he said, and everyone giggled.

Xavier ran through the grocery store. His soft blue bunny was lost somewhere.

"Where is Bunny?" he said. He ran to the fruit. He ran to the bread. He ran past the milk. No Bunny anywhere. He ran so fast his shoes went tap, tap, tap.

Mr. Wanjiru worked at the store. He knelt down by Xavier. "Slow down, little friend," he said with a smile. "Try one room at a time. Then you will not miss any places."

Xavier took a big breath. He walked slowly into the fruit room. He looked up. He looked down. He looked behind the apples. No Bunny. He walked into the bread room. He looked up. He looked down. He looked behind the big bread shelf.

There was Bunny! Bunny sat on a soft bag of flour, like a little bed.

"Found you!" said Xavier. He hugged Bunny tight. "You were sleeping in the flour!"

Mr. Wanjiru laughed. "Bunny wanted a nap before lunch," he said.

Xavier held Bunny's paw. "Let's go home," he whispered to Bunny. "Tap, tap, tap, we go."

Leah woke up in the dark. "Is it morning?" she whispered to her doll. Her dad laughed. "No, it is still night," he said. "Night and day are opposites." Leah hugged her doll. Dark outside, then light later. What a big idea!

"But we can still go to the store soon," said Dad. Leah got dressed fast. At the store, everything felt exciting. The freezer was so cold. Inside was frozen ice cream! Dad reached in with a big glove. Leah touched the cold glass from far away. "Brrr!" Then they walked past the bakery. It was hot there. Fresh bread, hot and big!

At checkout, the belt moved slow. Then the cashier made it go fast. Slow, then fast! Leah held her little carton. It was small, but the ice cream inside was cold. At home, Dad scooped a big bowl. Outside, the sky turned light. Night was gone. Day was here. "Opposites again!" said Leah, and she took a big, cold bite.

Mateo was going to the store with his dad. He had his toy truck in his hand. "We will look at cars that are for sale," said Dad. Mateo loved the red truck best.

But when they got in the car, the truck was gone. "Oh no!" said Mateo. "My truck! I lost my truck!" He looked down at the floor. It was dark under the seat. He could not see a thing.

"Here," said Dad. He handed Mateo a flashlight. Dad turned it on for him. The light made a bright circle. Mateo pointed it under the seat. Now he could see! There was his truck, sitting in the dark spot. "My truck!" Mateo shouted. "The light shows me!"

At the store, Dad talked to the man who sells cars. Mateo sat alone in the big seat for just a minute, holding his truck tight. A lady with long hair walked by and smiled at him.

On the ride home, Mateo shined the flashlight under the seat again. Just to check. The dark spot was empty now. All clean. "No more lost toys," said Mateo. He hugged his truck and grinned. "Light on, dark goes away!"

Levi ran to school with his new backpack. Today Ms. Yoon had a shape hunt! She held up a card. "Find things that are circles," she said. Levi was so excited. He ran to the big clock on the wall. "I found a circle!" he shouted. It was big and round.

Then he looked down. A button had fallen on the floor. It was round too, but so tiny. Georgia came over. "That button is too small," she said. "It can't be a circle like the big clock." Levi put the button on his hand. He held it up next to the clock. Round like the clock. Round like the button. Both were round! "The big circle stays a circle, and my tiny one is still a circle," he said. Georgia clapped. "Big circles and tiny circles are both circles!"

Jasmin ran up with a picture of an animal. "Look, my lion has circle eyes!" she said. Levi found more circles all day. The dot on the letter i. The wheel on a toy car. The plate at snack time. He put the button in his pocket. It could stay there, safe and round. "Circle," he whispered, and grinned.

Thomas put on his red coat. It was cold outside. Mom said they would walk to the grocery store. Thomas tried to zip his coat. He pulled the zipper up. It went up a little. Then it stopped. He pulled again. It still stopped. "I can't do it," said Thomas. Mom said, "Try again, Thomas." Thomas lined up the bottom of the zipper. He pushed it in. Click! It stayed. Then he pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up. It stopped again, right under his chin. "Almost," said Mom.

At the store, they saw Ms. Lewandowski. She was his neighbour. "What a neat coat," she said. "Did you zip it all by yourself?" "Some of it," said Thomas. He looked down at the zipper. He pulled it up a tiny bit more. It moved! He pulled again. Zip! It went all the way to the top. "I did it!" said Thomas. Ms. Lewandowski clapped. Thomas smiled and zipped it down, then up again. "Look, Mom! Zip, zip!"

Max was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big book about the ocean. Max wanted to learn his five senses. "Eyes see," said Grandpa. Max pointed to his eyes. He looked at the ocean pictures.

Then a big truck went by. Rumble, rumble! Max put his hands over his ears. The truck noise got quieter. He took his hands off. The noise got loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again! "My hands make it quiet," said Max.

"Will I miss the cookie bell?" Max asked. Grandpa smiled. "No, the bell is soft. Listen." Ding! Max heard it with open ears. "Ears hear!" said Max. He felt brave now. Grandpa rang the bell again, and Max laughed and ran for cookies.

Harper sat in a big blue chair. It was her first day at the dentist. She held her gray toy mouse tight. "One mouse, two hands, three big breaths," she counted. The dentist waved hello.

Harper looked at the dentist's hands. They were blue. "Your hands are blue!" she said. The dentist wiggled his fingers. "These are gloves," he said. "I wear gloves when I put fingers or tools in your mouth." Harper peeked at the gloves up close. They went over each finger, one, two, three, four, five.

Then the dentist pulled one glove off. His hand was not blue underneath. It was just a hand. Harper's eyes got wide. "The blue comes off!" she said. The dentist laughed softly. He put on a new glove. Snap. It was clean and blue again. "One glove, two glove," said Harper.

The dentist let her look in a little mirror. Harper opened her mouth wide. "Say ahh," said the dentist. "Ahh," said Harper. Her toy mouse watched too. Then it was all done. Harper got a shiny sticker. She held it up next to her mouse. "Look, mouse, we did it," she whispered.

Arya went to the library with her dad. She saw a big box of toys. Inside were five little monkeys. "Look, monkeys!" she said. Her friend Nova was there too. "Let's sing the monkey song," said Nova.

They put the five monkeys on the top of a little bed. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," they sang. Then one monkey fell off! Nova took that monkey away. Now they sang four. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." One fell off again. Arya laughed. "The number gets one smaller!" she said. They kept singing. Four, then three, then two, then one.

At last all the monkeys were off the bed. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!" they sang. Arya lined the monkeys up on the rug. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." Mr. Pritchard, the library man, clapped. "Sing it again!" he said. So Arya put all five monkeys back on the bed.

Ella put her teddy bear in a box bed. "Time to sleep," she said. She patted his soft head. Then Douglas ran over. He made a big dragon voice. "ROAR!" he said. Ella jumped. She hugged her teddy tight. "The dragon is scary," she said. "It will wake my teddy."

Douglas stopped roaring. "My dragon is friendly," he said. "But your face looks scary," said Ella. Ms. Farah-Ali knelt down beside them. "You can decide together," she said softly. Ella thought. She asked, "Can the dragon be friendly and quiet?" Douglas smiled. "Yes! The dragon says shhh."

The dragon curled up like a big green cat. It did not scratch the floor. It just snored a tiny snore. Ella covered her teddy with a small blanket. "Sorry I was scared," she whispered to Douglas. "It's okay," he said. The teddy slept. The dragon slept. Ella yawned and patted them both. "Goodnight, dragon," she said.

Nora looked out the window. The sky was gray. Rain tapped on the glass. "Rainy day!" said Nora. She put on her orange raincoat. She ran to the door in her sneakers.

Outside, a big puddle sat by the steps. Nora stepped in it. Splash! Water went in her sneakers. Her socks got soggy. Soggy socks felt cold. Nora stomped back inside. "Yucky wet socks," she said.

Dad brought her red rain boots. "Try these," he said. Nora slid them on. She marched outside again. She stepped in the puddle. Splash! This time her feet stayed dry. "Dry feet! Dry feet!" she cheered.

Then the wind blew. It was windy now. The wind pushed Nora's hood back. She held it on with one hand. A leaf flew past her like a little orange kite. "Look, Dad! The wind paints the sky!" she said, pointing at the clouds moving fast.

Nora found a toy turtle by the door. She set it on the step. "Turtle, you need boots too," she said. She stomped in the puddle one more time. Splash! Still dry. Nora laughed all the way back inside.

Avery went to the store with her dad. Zoravar and Sadie were there too. They saw a big bin of apples. Avery wanted to pick the first apple.

But Sadie was already talking. She was telling Mr. Ferreira about her new shoes. Avery opened her mouth. Then she closed it. She looked at her dad.

"Do I have to wait?" Avery asked.

"Yes," Dad said. "When someone is talking, we listen and wait until they finish."

So Avery waited. She kept her hands still. She watched Sadie's face. Soon Sadie was all done talking. Then it was Avery's turn. "I want a red apple," said Avery. "The shiny one, please."

Mr. Ferreira smiled. "Good waiting, Avery," he said. "Now you can pick."

Avery reached into the bin. There were sharp stickers on some apples. She picked one without a sticker. She put it in the basket, not in her pocket. Then Zoravar picked an apple. Then Sadie picked one too. Everyone got a turn.

At the checkout, Dad used his phone to pay. Avery held the basket with both hands. The apples did a little dance when she walked. Bump, bump, bump.

"That was fair," said Zoravar. "Everyone got an apple."

Avery bit into hers on the way home. It was sweet and crunchy. "My turn came fast," she said.

Anthony sat in the car. Mom was driving. "We will meet the hair lady today," said Mom. Anthony held his ears. "Will the scissors hurt me?" he asked.

At the salon, a lady with pretty red hair waved. She was Ms. Cruz. Anthony sat in a big chair. Ms. Cruz picked up her scissors. They went snip, snip. Anthony closed his eyes tight.

Nothing hurt. Not one bit. He opened his eyes. Snip, snip, snip. It felt like nothing at all. "Hair does not hurt when you cut it," said Ms. Cruz. Anthony watched a curl fall down. It landed on his shirt like a little soft worm. He laughed.

In the car, Mom smiled at him. Anthony looked in the mirror. "Look at my new hair!" he said. Mom said, "Snip, snip."

Ivy walked home with her dad. She held the red leash in her hand. At the end of the leash was a small puppy. The puppy had soft white fur and a new collar.

"Poor puppy has no tag," said Ivy. "His collar is empty." Her dad had a shiny tag in his pocket. It was small and round. On the tag was their phone number. Dad let Ivy hold it. She clipped it on the puppy's collar. It went jingle, jingle, jingle.

Just then, the neighbor's cat ran by. The puppy pulled hard. The leash slipped out of Ivy's hand. The puppy ran down the street. "Come back!" called Ivy.

Mr. Eze was watering his flowers. He saw the puppy. He read the tag. Then he called the number on it. Dad's phone rang in his pocket. "Our puppy is at Mr. Eze's house," said Dad. They walked to the big blue door. The puppy wagged his tail.

Ivy hugged him tight. "Your tag helped you come home," she said. The puppy licked her hand.

Ava sat at the big table. Writing club was starting. Ms. Whitehead gave her a yellow pencil.

"Can you write your name?" asked Ms. Whitehead.

Ava held the pencil in her fist. She pressed hard on the paper. The first letter was A. But the lines came out fat and fuzzy.

"My A looks like a sleepy bee," said Ava.

Beckett laughed next to her. "My B is fuzzy too!"

The pencil tip had gone dull and flat. Ava looked at it. "My pencil got tired," she said.

Ms. Whitehead smiled. "Bring it here. I can sharpen it."

Ava watched from her seat. Ms. Whitehead turned the pencil in the sharpener. Shavings curled down like little flowers. Then the tip was pointy again.

Ava took the pencil back. She held it the new way, with her fingers, not her fist. Now her A had thin, neat lines.

"Look, Beckett!" said Ava. "My A woke up!"

Beckett ran to Ms. Whitehead with his pencil. "Sharpen mine too!"

Then Ava wrote the V. It was two lines, sharp as a kite. She wrote the last A. It looked just like the first one.

"Ava," she read out loud.

She held up the paper. "My whole name! And a pointy pencil did it."

Ms. Whitehead clapped. Ava tapped the paper and grinned at her fuzzy, sleepy-bee A from before. "That one can stay sleepy," she said.

Riley sat in the waiting room. The sky outside was cloudy. She held a small box with holes in the top. Inside was her new puppy, Dot.

Riley wanted to give Dot a treat. She had a chocolate coin in her pocket. She held it out to the box.

Ms. Huang, the vet, came over. She shook her head. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick," she said. "Dogs are never given chocolate."

Riley put the coin back in her pocket. Ms. Huang handed her a bone-shaped dog treat. Riley held it near the box. Dot sniffed it. Then Dot took it and crunched.

On the table, a nurse was helping a green snake. Dot watched the snake. Riley helped sort the treats into a jar. She kept one out for later.

"Good puppy," Riley said. Dot wagged her tail.

Ali sat in the backyard with his toy truck. Today his new baby sister was coming home. Ali could not wait to pat her. Dad came out with a small blanket. The baby was inside it, fast asleep. "Can I pat her?" Ali asked. Dad sat down on the grass beside him. "You can," said Dad. "But be very gentle." Ali reached out his hand. He patted the baby on her head. He patted too hard. The baby woke up and began to cry. Ali felt his face go hot. He thought he might lose his turn to hold her. "It's okay," said Dad. "Try again. A new baby must be touched very gently. Stroke her hand softly, like this." Dad showed him how. Ali held out one finger. He stroked the baby's small hand, very softly. The baby stopped crying. Her little fingers curled around Ali's finger and held on tight. "She likes me," Ali whispered. "She likes you," said Dad. The last light of the sun warmed the yard. Ali sat very still, so the baby could keep holding on.

Elena went to the park with her new water bottle. It had her name on it in red letters. The gate was closed. She pushed it. It did not move. "Let me help," said Etienne. They pushed together. The gate swung open! "Open and closed are opposites," said Ms. Wong. "Like a door that is open or shut."

Elena ran fast down the path. Then she walked slow. Big dogs ran by. A small bug sat on a leaf. The sun felt hot on her face. The water fountain made her hands cold.

Elena wanted a drink. But her bottle top was closed. She turned it and turned it. She waited. She tried again. Pop! The top was open. She drank and drank. "You did it," said Etienne. Elena drew a big smile in the dirt with her toe.

Eli sat on his bed. He had lots of books. He wanted the dog book. But which one was it?

He looked at a birthday card on his shelf. The card was from Naya. On the front it said Eli. The letters were E, L, I. Mom opened the card. She read the first page, then the next. "She reads it front to back," Eli thought.

Then Eli saw a paper tag on his toy box. It said Eli too. E, L, I. The same letters. The same order. He held the card next to the tag. "It looks the same!" he said. His name always looked like that.

Eli picked up a book. He opened the front cover. The dog on the cover looked ready to jump over a big red ball. Inside, a little note said Eli. The same letters again. E, L, I. This book was his! He put his toy pot back on the shelf to make room.

Eli held the book on his lap. He turned the first page, then the next. He went front to back, just like Mom did with the card. Mom sat down beside him. "That one," said Eli. "It says me."

Matteo sat in his car seat. The car rolled down the road. His friend Cade sat beside him. They were going to a birthday party!

Matteo wanted to know how old the birthday girl would be. "I will ask her!" he said. He could not wait.

A song came on. It counted one, two, three, four, five. Then six, seven, eight, nine, ten! Matteo sang along. He held up his fingers too.

Cade sang too. "I am four," Cade said. He held up four fingers. Matteo held up four fingers too. "I am four too!" he said.

The car stopped. They were at the party! The birthday girl stood by the door. Matteo ran to her. "How old are you?" he asked.

She held up five fingers. "I am five!" she said.

Five! That was one more than four. Matteo clapped his hands. "Happy birthday!" he shouted. Cade shouted it too.

"Happy birthday!"

Jasmine ran to the playground with her teddy bear. Alanna was already at the little playhouse. "Let's play house," said Alanna. Jasmine smiled big.

"I will be the mommy," said Alanna. "No, I want to be the mommy," said Jasmine. They both stood still. The teddy bear sat on the step with no mommy at all.

Then Alanna had an idea. "You can pick a role, and I can pick a role. Maybe one of us can be the baby." Jasmine clapped her hands. "I will be the baby first!" She sat down small and pretended to cry. Alanna patted the teddy bear and mixed pretend soup in a little pot with a stick. "Here, baby, time to eat," she said.

Then they switched. Jasmine became the mommy. She wrapped the teddy in a friendly yellow scarf. "Sleep tight, little baby," she said. Alanna yawned like a baby and closed her eyes. Jasmine rocked the teddy side to side, singing a soft song to her little playhouse family.

Jake went to the library with his dad. There was a big green dragon rug by the shelves. There was also one toy dragon with shiny wings. Jake wanted that dragon. But Keenan ran up and grabbed it first. Jake grabbed the tail. Keenan grabbed the wings. The dragon almost ripped. Ms. Martínez walked over. "One dragon, two boys," she said. She held up her hand like a stop sign. Both boys had to freeze.

"Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another," said Keenan. Jake nodded. Keenan went first. He made the dragon fly over the book shelves. He made it buzz like a bee. Then he gave the dragon to Jake. Jake made it swoop and roar. It flew over a messy pile of books. The pile did not fall. Then Jake gave the dragon back to Keenan. Keenan handed it back again. They went on and on, one after another.

At story time, everyone sat in a circle. Everyone got a turn to hold the dragon. Jake smiled at Keenan. "Your turn now," said Jake.

Wyatt ran to the door of the grocery store. He wanted to see the big truck outside. He did not put on his coat. "Wait," said his dad. But Wyatt pushed the door open fast. The cold air hit him. Brrr! Wyatt shivered and hugged his arms. His fingers felt like little ice cubes.

He ran back inside. There sat his coat on the cart. Wyatt pushed his arms in the sleeves. He lined up the zipper. Pull, pull, pull. It went up, up, up! "I did it myself!" Wyatt said. His dad smiled big.

Then something amazing happened. The coat made him warm. The shivering stopped. Wyatt bounced on his toes. "Cold outside, warm in my coat!" He walked out to the truck like a feather, light and cozy. The truck honked hello. Wyatt waved his warm hand.

Rosalie jumped into the big pool. The water was cool and light sparkled on top. She loved swim team. Every day she practiced with Nirvair and Etienne. Mr. Otieno was their coach.

Today Rosalie wanted to swim all the way to the wall. She kicked her legs. She splashed and splashed. But she stayed in one spot. "Why am I not moving?" she asked. Mr. Otieno smiled. "Try kicking your feet flat, like a frog," he said. So Rosalie kicked her feet flat, not pointy. Suddenly she zoomed through the water like a little fish! The kick made her go forward.

After swimming, the friends played soccer on the flat grass. Nirvair kicked the ball hard. It rolled and rolled into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted, and they all clapped. Rosalie wondered, could she kick the ball into the net too? She ran up to the ball and kicked it with her wet toes. It went straight in!

"Goal! Goal! Rosalie got a goal!" Etienne shouted.

Rosalie clapped her hands and did a happy jump.

Aubrey wanted to find the pretend kitchen. She looked all around daycare. She could not remember which corner it was in.

Benedict stood by a shelf. He held a big box. "This box has words on it," he said. "I want to know what they say." Aubrey peeked at the box. There were marks in rows. "Maybe they are the picture blocks," she said. Benedict shook his head. "No, they are words."

Mr. Silva came over. He turned the box so Aubrey could see. "These words say play kitchen," he read. Aubrey's eyes got big. "It is in the box?" she asked. "The words tell us," said Mr. Silva. He opened the box. The pots and cups were inside. The words had told them!

Aubrey helped put the pots on the shelf. Then she found a book on the rug. She opened the front cover first. She turned the pages one by one, front to back. On a page she saw the word stop. "Benedict, look!" she said. "That word says stop." Benedict leaned in close. Aubrey pointed at the word and smiled. "Words tell us things," she said, and she turned the page.

Isaiah sat on the big rug in the living room. Dad sat beside him. Brendan and Eden sat on the floor too. The big game was on TV.

The players ran and kicked. One player kicked the ball. It began to spin through the air. "Watch!" said Isaiah. "The ball will go over the net!"

Then the ball went into the net. The crowd cheered loud. Everyone in the room jumped up.

"Goal!" Dad shouted, arms open wide.

Isaiah's mouth fell open. He showed a missing tooth and grinned. "It went in the net! That's how they score!"

"Goal again!" said Eden, pointing.

The referee blew the whistle. Isaiah clapped and clapped.

"They kick it in," Isaiah said. "I want to try that at the park tomorrow."

"Then that's our plan," said Dad, and he held up his hand for a high five.

Declan needed to wash his hands. There was paint on them, blue paint from art time. He went into the bathroom with his dad.

The sink was big and white. The faucet had two knobs. One knob had a red dot. One knob had a blue dot. Which one was cold? Declan wondered about that. His dad turned the blue knob. Cool water came out. It felt nice on his painty fingers. Bubbles grew, one, two, three. The bubbles squeaked between his hands.

Then Declan saw something small on the wall. It was a little face with two holes. It sat low, near the floor. What lived in there? His fingers wanted to poke it, just a tiny poke. But he kept his hands in the water instead. "Dad, there is a hole face on the wall," he said.

His dad looked. "That is an outlet," he said. "We never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet. Not toys, not sticks, nothing. I will put a cover on it." The cover went click, and the little face was gone.

Where did it go? Declan crouched down and looked. He touched only the smooth cover with one clean fingertip. Then he ran back to class to build a tall tower with Sacha, his hands all clean and shiny.

Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. Her class was having a picnic. Ekam and Luca were there too. A man had a little stove on a table. He was making warm soup for everyone.

Elizabeth wanted to see the soup. She walked to the table. She looked at the stove. It did not look hot at all. Nothing was red. Nothing was smoking. She wondered, is it still hot? Her hand came up close.

"Stop there," her dad said, gentle and quick. He took her hand. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," he said. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot."

Elizabeth watched from far back. The man put his hand near the stove. "Still hot," he said. He poured the soup with a big mitt on. The soup steamed and steamed.

Ekam got his cup. Luca got his cup. Then it was Elizabeth's turn. The cup felt warm in her two hands. She blew on it, one big blow. "Not too hot now," she said. She sat on the bench and took a little sip. "Warm soup is the best," said Luca.

Billie went to the playground after school. Her dad sat on a bench near the swings. "Stay where I can see you," he said.

Billie ran to the slide. Then she ran to the swings. Then she saw something far away. It was a big red ball by the fence. The fence was at the far end of the playground. Billie started to walk to it.

She walked and walked. She looked back at the bench. She could not see her dad. The trees were in the way. Billie stopped. She turned around and walked back. When she got close, she could see her dad again. He waved at her.

"Can you get my red ball by the fence?" she asked. Her dad held her hand. They walked to the fence together. The sun had made the ball hot, so her dad picked it up and let it cool in the shade.

Back at the bench, Billie sorted leaves into little piles. One pile was big. One pile was small. A lazy bee buzzed by and rested on a warm stone.

"I can see you the whole time," said Billie. Her dad smiled and clapped his hands. "Roll it to me," she said.

It was Miles's birthday at the park. There was a big table with juice and cake. Miles wore a paper hat that tickled his ears. His friend Ainsley came running over. "Happy birthday!" she said.

A boy named Robert was there too. Robert was new. He did not know Miles yet. "How old are you?" Robert asked.

Miles looked at his hands. He held up some fingers. Robert counted them. "One, two, three," said Robert. "You are three!"

Miles felt worried. He was not three. He shook his head. Then he looked again at his hand. One finger was hiding under his thumb! Miles let that finger pop up. Now there were four fingers standing tall.

Robert counted again. "One, two, three, four," he said. "You are four!"

"Yes!" said Miles. He wiggled the four fingers. Ainsley held up four fingers too. Robert held up five. Then everyone laughed and held up fingers together.

Dad brought the cake to the table. Dad lit the little candles with a match. Miles watched from his seat. Everyone sang the birthday song. Miles took a big breath. He blew and blew. The candles went out, one by one. Smoke curled up like a thin gray ribbon.

Miles ate cake from a glass plate. The frosting was sweet and cold on his tongue. Robert sat next to him and shared his juice. "Hold up four again," said Robert. Miles grinned and held up four fingers high in the air.

Charlotte went to the store with her dad. She held his hand in the parking lot. Inside, the store was bright and full.

They walked down the crayon aisle. Charlotte saw red crayons. She saw yellow crayons. She saw green ones too. "Can I try them?" she asked. Her dad said yes. He picked a small box for her.

In the cart there was a pizza box. "That pizza is hot," her dad said. "We wait for it to cool." Charlotte sat in the cart. She wanted to draw while they waited. She picked a gray crayon for her sky.

Then she looked out the big window. The sun was shining. The sky over the parking lot was not gray. On this clear, sunny day, the sky looked blue. Charlotte put the gray crayon down. She picked the blue one instead.

Her friend Jordyn came by with her mom. "Your sky is blue," Jordyn said. Charlotte smiled and held up her paper. "It's a sunny day," she said. She drew a big yellow sun in the blue sky. Her dad gave the crayons a safe home in her pocket.

Lea packed her little red bag. "We are going to the beach!" she said. The car ride was long, long, long. Lea counted three cows, then she fell asleep.

At the beach, the sand was warm and soft. Lea found a shell. "Look, Mom, a pink shell!" The waves went splash, splash. Lea's hat flew off. It did not fall down. It floated on the water! Dad waded in and got it. "Silly hat," said Lea.

Dad held up his phone. "Smile, Lea!" Click. Click. He took a photo of the shell. He took a photo of the floating hat. He took a photo of Lea's sandy toes. "Why so many photos?" asked Lea. "You will see," said Dad.

Then it was time to go home. Home looked different from the beach. No sand. No waves. Lea felt sad. "I miss the beach," she said. Mom opened the photo album. "Look here," said Mom. There was the pink shell! There was the silly hat! There were the sandy toes! Lea laughed and laughed. "Now we can see the beach every day," she said. She hugged the book tight.

Nolan ran to the community garden with his watering can. Mr. Tse had given him three little lettuce plants. "Let's plant them!" said Nolan. He dug in the smooth brown dirt. Minha helped pat the soil down. Everest poured water from the pond in his big can.

The sun came out. It was a hot day. The next morning, Nolan ran to see his plants. But the lettuce was drooping. The leaves hung down low. "Are you sad?" Nolan asked the lettuce. Mr. Tse smiled and handed him the watering can. Nolan gave the plants a big drink.

The sun was warm on his back. The water sparkled on the leaves. The next day, Nolan ran to look again. The lettuce stood up tall! "It likes water!" said Nolan. Minha clapped her hands. "Look how big they are!" said Everest. Nolan filled his can again. "More water for you," he said. "Drink up, little plants!"

It was snack time at school. Ruby stood by the little table. Ten chairs sat around it. Ten cups sat in a big pile.

Mr. Demetriou gave Ruby a job. "Put one cup by each chair," he said. Ruby picked up a cup. She set it by a chair. One cup, one chair. She picked up another cup. One cup, one chair. Saoirse came to watch. "Do you have enough cups?" Saoirse asked. Ruby did not know yet. She kept going. One cup, one chair. Mckenzie counted the chairs with her finger.

At last the pile was empty. Every chair had a cup. Every cup had a chair. Not one cup was left over. Not one chair was empty. "We have enough," Ruby said. "One for each chair."

Then Mr. Demetriou held up two baskets of shiny apples. "Which basket has more?" he asked. Ruby took an apple from the small basket. She set it by a cup. She took an apple from the big basket. She set it by another cup. She matched them one by one. The big basket still had apples left. "This one has more," Ruby said, and she lifted it high. "Apples for everyone!" said Saoirse.

Madelyn went to the library in the morning. Mr. Tran sat on the big red rug. Kids were singing a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," they sang. Then they sang, "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Madelyn clapped along.

Mr. Tran had a jar of stickers. "You may pick three stickers," he said. Madelyn looked and looked. She found a big sun sticker. She found a big star sticker. Then she found a tiny cat sticker. She held them up. "Are these three?" she asked. "The cat one is so small." Harris leaned over to see. "Maybe big ones count more," he said. Madelyn worried. What if three was not three?

Mr. Tran smiled. "Count them out loud," he said. Madelyn touched each sticker. "One. Two. Three." Three stickers, big, big and small. Three still meant three. The cat did not hide or vanish. It sat right there in her hand. Harris counted his own stickers too. "One, two, three," he said. His three had a dinosaur and two dots. Still three. Madelyn was not alone on the rug. The kids sang the song again. Madelyn stuck the tiny cat on her shirt. "Three," she said.

Eloise sat high in the big stadium. Her dream was to see a real game. Her friend Oliver sat beside her. Ms. Chaudhry sat on her other side.

The players ran out onto the green grass. Eloise frowned. "I can't tell who is who," she said. "Everyone is running fast. I see so many players. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!"

Ms. Chaudhry pointed. "Look at the shirts," she said. "This team wears red. That team wears blue."

Eloise looked hard. Yes! The red team had the ball. A red player kicked it. The blue team ran after him.

"Red team, red team," Eloise said. "Blue team, blue team." She named every player on the field.

A red player kicked the ball into the net. The crowd jumped up. Eloise clapped and clapped.

Oliver wiped his seat with a napkin to clean off some spilled juice. Then he clapped too.

"My favorite team is the red team," Eloise said. "They won because I kept watching them!"

Ms. Chaudhry laughed. "They won because they kicked the ball well," she said. "But you watched very well too."

Eloise looked down at the field one more time. The red players waved. "Goodbye, red team," she whispered.

Lucy looked out the window. No school today! Snow was everywhere. "Snow day!" said Mom.

Lucy put on her red boots. She and Mom walked to the big sledding hill. Lucy's friend Ila was there. They went down the hill on the sled. Zoom! The snow felt soft and cold. Lucy laughed and laughed.

Then Lucy made a snowball. It was round and white. She wanted to keep it. She put it in her mitten and brought it inside. She set it in a bowl on the table. "Now I will have snow in the house," she said.

After lunch, Lucy came back to look. The bowl had water in it. No snowball! Lucy touched the bowl. A wet leaf had stuck to her mitten, and now it floated in the water. "My snow turned into water," said Lucy. "The house is warm."

She ran back outside. "Ila!" she called. "I made a puddle inside!" Ila laughed. "That's funny!" she said. Lucy scooped up new snow. Down the hill she went, fast and happy, one more time before the sun went down.

Jacob sat in the waiting room. His tummy felt weak and funny. "I will be brave," he said.

"Jacob," called Ms. Demetriou, the doctor. She looked at his eyes. "You see with these." She rang a little bell. "You hear with your ears." She held out a sticker. "Touch it with your hands." Then she said, "Open wide." Jacob stuck out his tongue. "Now sniff," she said. Jacob sniffed with his nose. "All done. You may go home."

At home, Jacob played blocks in his room. Then he smelled something warm. He sniffed and sniffed. "Soup!" he said. "I smell it before I see it."

His dad laughed. "Come and look."

Jacob ran to the kitchen. There was the pot of soup. He had guessed right.

"I remember soup night," said Jacob. He touched his nose. "Good nose."

Theo went to music class at the community center. He wore his favorite blue shirt. Mr. Khan gave each child a recorder. Natalie got one too. Theo held his recorder up.

Theo blew into it. It made a loud squeak. Natalie put her hands over her ears. Theo tried again. Squeak, squeak. He looked at his fingers. One finger was not on a hole. He pressed the finger down flat. Then he blew. A clear note came out.

Mr. Khan smiled. "Nice note, Theo," he said. Theo lifted one finger a little. He blew again. A different note came out. Theo laughed. Natalie scooted close to hear. Theo lifted another finger. The note changed again.

Then Theo covered all the holes. He blew a long, low note. Natalie clapped. Theo played his duck song, up and down. Mr. Khan tapped his knee in time. Theo blew the last note and held it.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a little bag of crackers. Emilio sat next to her. Tina sat on the other side.

"Crackers, please?" said Emilio.

Sadie gave him one. "Thank you," said Emilio.

Sadie did not know what to say. She sat very still. She thought and thought.

The car went bump, bump, bump. Tina held a small puzzle. One piece fell on the floor. "Can you help me, please?" Tina asked.

Sadie reached down. She got the puzzle piece. She gave it to Tina.

"Thank you," said Tina.

Sadie still did not know what to say. Then Daddy spoke from the front seat. "You're welcome," he said to Tina.

Sadie heard it. She tried it in her mouth, quiet and slow. "You're welcome."

Emilio gave Sadie one cracker back. "Thank you," said Sadie.

Emilio smiled. He waited. He did not know either.

"You're welcome," said Sadie, nice and clear.

Emilio laughed. Tina clapped. "That sounds cool!" said Tina.

Daddy kept driving. "Good helping in there," he said.

Sadie looked out the window. She read the big stop sign to herself. Then she shared one more cracker.

"Thank you," said Emilio.

"You're welcome," said Sadie.

Maverick sat at the big art table. He was painting a cat. The cat had a long tail. One, two, three whiskers on each side. Sehaj sat next to him. She was painting a cat too. Her cat had a long tail as well.

Mr. Das called out, "Bring your paintings to the drying rack." Maverick put his cat on the rack. Sehaj put her cat on the rack. The two paintings looked almost the same.

Mr. Das held up a painting. "Whose cat is this?" he asked. Maverick looked hard. "Is it mine?" he asked. He did not know. Sehaj did not know either. Both cats were orange. Both tails were long. Nobody could tell.

Then Sehaj pointed at her paper. "Look. I wrote my name," she said. There it was. S-E-H-A-J. Mr. Das found the other paper. It had Maverick's name at the bottom. Maverick smiled big. "That one is mine!" he said.

Mr. Das gave him a crayon. "You can write your name too," he said. Maverick wrote M-A-V on his cat. "Now everyone knows," said Sehaj. "You are kind to show me," said Maverick. "Thank you." He painted one more whisker. Then he hung his cat up high.

Claare stood at the front door with her boots on. She wanted to play at the park. "Is it rainy today?" she asked. Her dad looked outside. "No, it is sunny," he said. "But it is windy, too. Hold on to your hat."

Claire could not find her hat. She looked in the box by the door. She found mittens for snowy days. She found a raincoat for rainy days. No sun hat. The wind blew the door hard. The tree leaves went round and round.

Then Claire saw her sun hat on the hook. She put it on and pulled the string snug. At the park, her friend Rome was playing. He made his face small and squinty. "The sun is too bright," he said. Claire had an extra hat in her bag. "Wear this sun hat," she said. Rome put it on. His eyes went big and open. "Better!" he said.

They sailed a paper boat on the puddle by the bench. The wind pushed the boat fast. Claire laughed and held her hat tight. "Race you to the swings!" said Rome.

Athena went to Ms. Virtanen's music studio. It was a stormy day. Rain tapped on the window. Athena was learning to play the drums.

Nivaan came in too. He had a little drum. Athena and Nivaan sat side by side. A big picture of a band hung on the wall.

They began to play. Athena tapped fast, fast, fast. Nivaan tapped fast too. Soon their drumming was a jumble. It did not sound like music at all. Athena stopped. "Why does it sound so mixed up?" she asked. Ms. Virtanen smiled. "Let's try a steady beat," she said. She clapped one slow clap, then another, then another. Tap, tap, tap.

Athena watched Ms. Virtanen's hands. The claps were all the same size. Athena copied them on her drum. Tap, tap, tap. Nivaan copied too. Tap, tap, tap. Their drums matched! It sounded like one big drum. Athena laughed out loud. That was the surprise. Same speed meant same sound.

They played a long song together. Ms. Virtanen danced in a circle. "Thank you, Athena!" said Nivaan at the end. Athena patted her drum. Outside, the rain kept its own tap, tap, tap on the window.

Leah sat in the living room. She held the tablet in her two hands. "How do I make it turn on?" she asked. Her dad sat beside her. "Press the round button," he said. Leah pressed it. The screen lit up. "It worked!" she said.

Next she wanted to draw. Her dad helped her tap the little paintbrush. A big white page appeared. Leah wanted to draw a red sun. She looked at the colours at the top. She tapped the blue. Her finger made a blue line. "That is not red," she said. She tapped the red spot. Now her finger made a red line. She drew a big round sun. "I did it!" she said.

Then Leah drew green grass. She drew a yellow bird. Her picture was full. "Time to put the tablet away," said her dad. "Where does it go?" Leah asked. "On the shelf, next to your bed things," he said. Leah pressed the button and the screen went dark. She carried it slowly with both hands. She set it on the shelf, safe and snug. "Goodnight, tablet," she whispered.

Florence sat in the car with her mom. They were going to the hospital. A new baby was coming. Florence held her stuffed mouse tight. "I miss it being just us," she said. Mom held her hand. "It is okay to feel left out," Mom said. "Big sisters can feel that way." Florence squeezed the mouse.

At the hospital, the baby was small and soft. He yawned a tiny yawn. He smelled like soap. Florence drew a picture of him. She pressed too hard, and the crayon snapped. "That was wrong," she said. Mom smiled. "You can try again."

Florence drew a new picture. It was the baby with her mouse. She gave it to Mom. Mom kissed her head. The baby opened his eyes. Florence waved at him. "Hello, baby," she whispered. "This is my mouse."

Michael ran to the kitchen. Cookies sat on a plate. They smelled sweet and warm. His tummy said, "Eat now!"

His hands stopped in the air. He looked at his fingers. They had sandbox dirt on them. Dirt was under each finger. Smooth cookie, dirty hand. That was not good.

Michael marched to the sink. He pushed the soap pump. Bubbles grew big and white. They felt slippery on his hands. He rubbed and counted. "One, two, three." He counted to twenty. The water rinsed the bubbles away. His hands came out clean.

He ran back to the plate. He picked up a cookie. It was still warm. He took a big bite. The cookie tasted sweet. Michael looked at his clean hands and smiled. Then he held the plate out to his dad. "Your turn to wash," he said.

David stood in the school cooking classroom. He was making muffins for his family. Ms. Pritchard helped him mix the batter. Marianne and Raiden scooped flour beside him.

"Watch this," said Ms. Pritchard. She turned a small dial. It went tick, tick, tick. "The timer will beep when the muffins need checking," she said. David put the pan in the oven. Only Ms. Pritchard touched the hot oven. She slid the pan in with a big mitt.

The class played a game while they waited. They acted like foxes, hopping and leaping. David jumped too. Then he heard it. Beep, beep, beep! The timer rang out loud. "The muffins!" said David. Ms. Pritchard pulled the pan out. Sweet smells filled the room. David read the card that said "Blueberry." "Muffins for my family," he said. "And one for me."

Emile sat at the snack table at daycare. He had a square napkin. All four sides were the same. He pointed at the sides. "Square," he said. Emile wished for a rectangle for his paper house. A rectangle was long on two sides.

He tried pulling the napkin. It stayed a square. He tried pushing it. It stayed a square. His friend Saif watched. "Try folding it," Saif said.

Emile folded the square napkin in half, edge to edge. He patted it flat. He looked. The napkin was not a square anymore. It was a rectangle.

"It changed!" said Emile.

"Let me see," said Zoelie. She held it up to the window. The glass was cold near her fingers.

Emile folded another square napkin in half, edge to edge. Again, a rectangle appeared. He folded and folded more napkins.

Ms. Visser came over. "You made many rectangles," she said.

Emile carried the rectangles to the art table. His shoe squeaked on the floor. He lined them up like doors on his paper house. One rectangle made a roof.

Saif tapped the roof. "Nice house," he said.

Emile smiled and put the last rectangle on top.

Maeve sat on a high bench by the sports field. Her tummy felt fluttery. Today was the big game. Palmer and Azriel sat beside her. Ms. Pereira waved from the other side of the field.

The players ran and ran. They chased one ball. Maeve clapped her hands. Then she heard a loud sound. Tweet, tweet! A referee blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. They stood very still.

Maeve pulled Palmer's sleeve. "Why did they stop?" she asked. Palmer pointed at the referee. "The whistle means stop," Palmer said. Maeve watched the referee's mouth. The whistle went into it. Tweet! Everyone stopped again. The whistle came out. The players ran again.

Then the whistle fell into the grass. The referee looked down. He could not find it. The players kept running. Nobody stopped. Maeve skipped to the edge of the field. She pointed at the shiny whistle. The referee picked it up. He smiled at Maeve. Tweet! All the players stopped. The game was over. Azriel gave Maeve a big hug.

Layla ran to the toy corner at school. A big red truck sat on the mat. Adrian wanted it too. He grabbed one side. Layla grabbed the other side. "My truck!" said Layla. "No, my truck!" said Adrian.

The truck did not move. Layla pulled hard. Adrian pulled hard. Then Layla remembered something. At Noa's party, two kids pulled on a doll. They asked a grown-up for help. The grown-up helped them take turns.

Layla let go of the truck. "Let's ask Ms. Tesfaye," she said. Adrian held the truck. They walked to the teacher fast. "We both need the truck," said Layla. Ms. Tesfaye smiled. "Adrian can go first," she said. "Layla, you go next."

Layla sat on the mat. She waited. Adrian pushed the truck. It rolled far. He laughed. Then he gave the truck to Layla. "Your turn," he said. Layla held it tight. It was her present to herself, waiting like this. She pushed the truck. It rolled under the table. Adrian got it out for her. "Again?" he asked. "Again," said Layla.

Everly was at Grandma's house. A new baby was there too. The baby was her new little brother. His name was Ben. He was small and warm, like a fresh bun.

Everly had a cracker in her hand. She wanted to share it. She held it out to Ben. "Eat," she said. Grandma shook her head. "Babies don't eat crackers," said Grandma. "A newborn baby drinks milk or formula. Not regular food."

Everly looked at Ben. He was not chewing. He was drinking from a bottle. His mouth made little sounds. Suck, suck, suck. His eyes closed slowly.

Everly wanted to help. She fetched a soft blanket from the table. It was cool and smooth. Grandma smiled. "That will keep him cozy," she said. Everly patted the blanket down, very gently. Ben drank his milk. Everly watched him. "More milk for you," she whispered. "Crackers for me." She sat close by his chair and took a big bite.

Nova loves daycare. She loves the blocks and the paint. But today the class will sing for the parents. Nova feels afraid. Her tummy feels small and tight.

"I can't sing," Nova tells Mr. Ortiz. "My voice will shake." Mr. Ortiz sits down beside her. He stays very close. "You know what?" he says. "I feel nervous too. My tooth even chatters when I sing in front of people." Nova looks up. "Grown-ups get nervous?" she asks. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups," says Mr. Ortiz. He smiles. "My hands get sweaty. Then I take a big breath."

Nova takes a big breath too. Her friend Gianluca takes one. Her friend Kolton takes one. Then they all sing together. Nova's voice does not shake at all. The parents clap and clap. Nova feels so happy. "Again!" she says. "Let's sing it again!"

Isabelle went to the cultural center with Mama. It was a rainy day, so the party was inside. There were red lanterns on the wall. Felix was there too.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were very loud. Isabelle covered her ears. "Why is it so loud?" she asked. Mama knelt down. "The drums make the beat," she said. "Watch."

A big lion came in. Its mouth opened and closed. It jumped and shook. Isabelle peeked at the drums. The drummer hit the drum. The lion jumped. The drum went boom. The lion bowed.

The lion moved to the beat of the loud drums! Isabelle clapped along. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. Felix clapped too. The lion danced right up to them. It blinked its big eyes. Isabelle laughed and waved.

Aaron was at Grandpa's house. He wanted his favorite book. It was on the big shelf.

"Grandpa, read to me," said Aaron. Grandpa sat down in his soft chair. He held the book. He turned to the front. "We start here," he said. "The front comes first."

Aaron looked at the cover. He saw little marks on it. "What are those?" he asked. "Those are words," said Grandpa. "Words tell us things." Aaron tapped the words with one finger. "Read them," he said. Grandpa read the name out loud. "That name is the author," said Grandpa. "The author is the person who wrote the words of this book."

"So a person made up Bear!" said Aaron. "Yes," said Grandpa. "A person wrote every word."

Grandpa read one page. Then he turned the page. Then another page. Aaron saw the pages go front to back. Page by page, Bear found his hat.

"Who made up the hat part?" asked Aaron. "The author did," said Grandpa. Aaron hugged the book. "Read it again," he said. "I want to hear the author's words one more time."

Grandpa turned back to the front. "One more time," he said. And he began.

Ibrahim was at the park with his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. He set it on the bench. Then he turned to wave at Briella. When he looked back, the car was gone.

Ibrahim looked on the bench. No car. He looked under the slide. No car. He looked in the grass. Only a yellow leaf and a smooth pebble. "Try the sandbox," said Briella. Ibrahim tried the sandbox. He dug with his hands. Still no car.

Then he remembered last winter. His marble had rolled away at home. He had found it under the couch. Another day, a small ball slid under his bed. Small toys could roll or slide under things. So Ibrahim got down on his knees. He peeked under the park bench. The wood smelled like rain. It was cool and shady under there. And there was his blue car, sitting in the dust. A little red ladybug was resting on top of it.

Ibrahim reached in and pulled the car out. The ladybug flew up and landed on his sleeve. "Hello," said Ibrahim. He held the car up high so Briella could see. "Found it!"

Joshua sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wore his big sun hat. He wanted to paint grass for his picture. But he had no green paint. He looked in his cup. He had only blue and yellow.

Morgan sat next to him. "I need green too," Morgan said. Joshua tapped his brush in the blue. Then he tapped it in the yellow. He stirred them together on his paper. The paint turned green!

"Look!" said Joshua. Morgan leaned in close. The spot was bright green, like the high grass by the lake. Joshua painted a big green hill. Morgan mixed her blue and yellow too. Their brushes went swish, swish.

Ms. Horváth walked by and smiled. The two friends painted side by side. Outside, a bird began to sing. "Green hill for me," said Joshua, "and one for you."

Gabriella went to Abigael's house. Abigael had a big doll named Pip. Gabriella dropped Pip on the floor. "Oh no," said Gabriella. "Pip fell!"

Abigael picked up the doll. "Pip cannot really feel it," she said. "But we can pretend she does." Gabriella looked at Pip's painted skin. There was no bump. There was no tear. Pip was fine.

"But she can get a hug," said Abigael. Gabriella hugged Pip tight. She wrapped Pip in a spotted blanket. "There," said Gabriella. "Now Pip is warm."

Then they played house. Pip was the baby. They fed her a pretend bottle. They put on her swimsuit so she could swim in the pretend pool. "Kick, Pip, kick!" said Gabriella.

Pip floated on the blue rug, all wrapped and warm.

Asher sat in the big chair at the barbershop. It was his first haircut! The barber put a cape on him. It looked like a superhero cape. Snip, snip went the scissors. Then Asher began to squirm. "My neck itches!" he said. He wiggled and wiggled. Tiny bits of cut hair sat on his neck. The barber held a soft brush in her hand. She brushed the little hairs away. The itch went away too! Asher sat very still. "Do it again," he said. "That tickles!" The barber laughed and brushed his neck one more time. Then Asher saw his friend Lennox in the next chair. Lennox was squirming too. "My neck itches!" said Lennox. Asher called out, "Wait! The brush makes it stop!" Lennox stopped wiggling. The barber brushed his neck too. Lennox smiled a happy smile. Both boys jumped down from the chairs. They looked in the mirror. "Two haircuts!" said Asher. "We did not miss one bit of fun." They waved bye-bye to the barber and skipped out the door together.

Mia was ready for bed. Her toy horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. She looked in the toy box. No horse. Mia felt angry. She stomped her foot. "My horse is gone!" she said. Her dad sat down next to her. "Try a slow, deep breath," he said. "Will that help?" Mia asked. "Yes, it helps your body calm down," said Dad. Mia took a big breath in. She let it out slowly. She did it again. Her foot felt still. Her tummy felt calm. Then she saw something white by the window. Snow was falling outside. And there, on the sill, sat her horse. Mia smiled. She hugged her horse tight. "Goodnight, little horse," she whispered.

Brielle stood in the sunny backyard. A red hoop sat on the grass. A soft beanbag sat in her hand.

"Watch me, Faye!" said Brielle. She looked at Faye. She threw the beanbag. It fell in the grass. It missed the hoop.

"Try again," said Faye.

Brielle picked up the beanbag. One, two, three. This time she looked at the hoop. She looked and looked. She threw the beanbag. It went in! The hoop went wobble, wobble, wobble.

"I did it!" said Brielle. "I looked at the hoop!"

Then Nick came with a big blue ball. "Catch!" he said. The wind began to blow. The ball was too big. It bumped her tummy. It fell down.

Brielle held out both hands. One hand, two hands. She looked at the ball. Nick threw it soft and slow. She caught it! The ball made a little sound, like a pat.

"Again! Again!" said Brielle.

Nick threw it high. Brielle looked and caught it with both hands. She jumped up and down. "Big catch!" she said. Faye clapped and clapped.

Emile was at Grandma's house. The soup was hot. Grandma poured it into bowls. Steam went up, up, up.

Then everyone held hands. They closed their eyes. Grandma said, "Thank you for our food. Amen."

Emile peeked with one eye. He wanted to peek with two!

At dinner the next day, Emile held out his little hand. "My turn," he said. Grandma smiled. "We say grace before we eat," she said. "Would you like to say it?"

Emile sat up tall like a big boy. He squeezed Grandma's hand. He squeezed Grandpa's hand too.

"Thank you, soup," said Emile. "You are warm. Amen."

Grandpa laughed a warm, big laugh. Grandma clapped her hands.

Then everyone ate the soup. Emile took a big sip. "Soup tastes extra good after grace," he said. He wore his hat at the table, just to be fancy.

Beatrice loved the big blocks at school. Today she wanted to build a robot. A tall robot. A nice robot with block arms and block feet.

Viraj wanted to build too. Madina wanted to build too. But Beatrice pulled all the blocks to her spot. All of them. "My robot," she said.

Viraj sat with empty hands. Madina sat with empty hands. Their faces looked sad. Beatrice looked at her tall pile. Then she looked at her friends. She counted out some blocks. She pushed them to Viraj. She pushed more to Madina. "One for you, and one for you," she said.

Ms. Wong came over and smiled. "That is fair," she said. "Fair means everyone gets a chance." Now everyone had blocks. Viraj built robot legs. Madina built robot arms. Beatrice built the big robot head.

At circle time, the three friends waved at their robot. It stood tall in the middle of the rug. "Our robot," said Beatrice. "All three of us," said Madina. Viraj clapped his hands.

Everett ran to the game table at daycare. Mr. Vogel held up a big cloth bag. "Put your hand in," he said. "Guess what you find!"

Rosalia went first. She felt inside the bag. "It is a ball!" she said. "It is a red ball!" She pulled it out. The ball was blue. Rosalia laughed. "I could feel the ball," she said. "But I could not feel the color!"

Everett could not wait. He put his hand in the bag. Something was smooth and round. It had little ears. "A mouse!" he said. "A cute yellow mouse!" He peeked inside. The mouse was green!

Devin tried next. He felt a bumpy car. "I think it is blue," he said. He looked. It was blue! "How did you know?" Everett asked. "I saw one before," said Devin.

Mr. Vogel put paint cups on the table. "Now look with your eyes," he said. Everett dipped his brush. He painted a red sun. Then he painted white snow, just like outside the window. "My turn, my turn!" said Rosalia, grabbing a brush.

Raphael stood by the big window at the community centre. Sun came in and made his hands warm. "Where is everyone?" he asked. "Here!" said Josiah. Kali ran in next.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya put out two trays. One had three big red balls. One had three tiny beads. "Which group has more?" she asked.

Raphael pointed at the balls. "The balls! They are so big."

Josiah shook his head. "Count them," he said.

Raphael touched each ball. "One, two, three." Then he touched each bead. "One, two, three."

Kali clapped. "Same! Both are three!"

Raphael laughed. Big or small, three was three. He held up one ball and one bead. "Still one and one."

Then came the small surprise. One bead was stuck inside a plastic cup. Raphael tipped the cup. Out rolled the bead, plus a little paper star. "A star!" said Kali. "You found it."

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya smiled. "That star was lost last week."

Outside, snow began to melt on the window ledge. Josiah found a toy truck with a broken wheel. Raphael counted the wheels. "One, two, three good wheels." Then he pointed at the star, the bead, and a ball. "One, two, three again."

"Can big things and small things both be three?" asked Josiah.

"Yes," said Raphael. "I counted them."

Leah found a big cardboard box at school. She sat inside it. "Beep beep! This is my car," she said. She turned a paper plate. That was her steering wheel.

Kamryn ran over. "No, it's a boat," said Kamryn. "I want to row it." They both pulled on the box. The box did not move. It was too hard to pull.

Tatum came with a bucket. "Let's take turns," said Tatum. "First it is a car. Then it is a boat. Then it is a house." Leah drove the car to the snack shop. Then Kamryn rowed the boat across the rug. Then all three made the box into a house. Leah put a teddy bear inside. "Sleep, baby," she said. She patted its back with a soft, careful hand. When the bell rang, Leah patted the box too. "Good night, house," she whispered.

Cooper ran into the art classroom. He sat down at the big table. Ms. Khoury put out cups of blue paint. Cooper loved blue paint.

"Time for aprons," said Ms. Khoury. Rayyan put on his apron. Makai put on her apron. Cooper did not. He wanted to paint right away. He dipped his brush in the blue cup. He painted a big sun. He painted a noisy truck. Then he looked down. Blue paint was on his shirt. His shirt had a duck on it. Cooper felt like crying.

Ms. Khoury came over with a towel. She helped wipe his hands. Then she held out an apron. "Try this now," she said. Cooper put it on. He painted a green frog and a glass of juice. He painted and painted. When he was done, he looked down at the duck shirt. No paint on it! The paint was all on the apron instead.

The next day, Cooper ran to the art room first. He grabbed his apron before anything else. "My turn," he said, and slid it over his head. Makai smiled. Rayyan gave him a thumbs up. Cooper picked up his brush. "Now my duck can stay clean," he said.

Sarah sat with Mom at the restaurant. Julian and Raymond sat close by. Mr. Carvalho was there too. A big screen glowed on the wall. A big game was on.

The red team ran with the ball. Sarah jumped up. "Go red team!" she cheered. She clapped and clapped. But the whole room went quiet. Then everyone yelled for the blue team.

Sarah looked around. Everyone wore blue shirts. "Oh!" she said. "This is the blue team's place." She started to laugh. Julian laughed too. "You cheered so loud for the wrong team!" he said. "Sorry," Sarah said, still giggling.

Then the blue team scored a goal. The whole room cheered and clapped. Sarah clapped loudest of all. "Now I cheer for blue!" she said. Mr. Carvalho smiled and gave her a high five.

Avery went to the store with her dad. The store had big bright lights. Avery saw a pillow. It was bright yellow. It had a bunny on it. Avery wanted the bunny pillow.

She grabbed at the pillow. Her dad said, "Wait, Avery." He held her hand. Then Avery remembered. She let go of the pillow. She looked up at her dad. "Pillow, please," she said. Her dad smiled. He put the pillow in the cart.

At the cart, Avery saw her friend Crew. Crew wanted a sticker. Crew grabbed for it. Then Crew stopped. "Sticker, please," Crew said. The cashier gave Crew the sticker. "Please," said Avery again, just to hear it. The cashier smiled.

They waited in line. One person went first. Then the next person went. Then it was Avery's turn to pay. Her dad paid for the bright pillow. Avery held the bag with two hands. "Say bye-bye, pillow store," she said. She waved at the door. "Bye-bye, pillow store!"

Henry went to the hospital with his dad. His mom had a new baby there. The baby was Henry's little brother. He was very small. He had tiny hands.

The baby began to cry. He cried and cried. Henry felt sad. "Why is he crying?" Henry asked. Dad said, "A new baby cannot talk yet. He cries to show he needs something." Dad gave the baby some milk. The baby drank and stopped crying.

Later the baby cried again. Henry said, "He needs something." Mom changed his little shirt. The baby stopped crying. Then the baby fell asleep. Henry gave him a soft kiss on his head. The baby made a small sound. Henry smiled. "He likes me," Henry said. Mom smiled too, and held them both close.

Eva wanted a book about moons. She grabbed a moon book from the shelf. It was heavy and big.

Mira sat at the little table. "What did you find?" Mira asked.

Eva opened the book. But the moon looked so funny! The moon hung at the bottom. The stars pointed down. The girl in the picture stood on her head.

"Look, Mira! A silly moon book!" Eva said.

Eva turned the page. The words looked silly too. They stood on their heads. "The words are upside down," Eva said.

Mira laughed. "Turn it around!" she said.

Eva turned the book around. Now the moon sat up high in the sky. The stars twinkled at the top. The girl stood on her feet. The words sat straight.

"I can read the front," Eva said. She pointed at the first page. She turned one page, then the last page.

"Once upon a time, there was a big round moon," said Eva.

"That is my best story," said Mira. "Read it again!"

Benjamin ran to the playground after lunch. He wanted to find his friend Kinsley. She was not on the swings. She was not on the slide.

Then Benjamin saw her by the sandbox. Her mouth turned down. Her eyebrows came together. She looked sad.

"Kinsley, are you sad?" Benjamin asked. "My red truck fell in the water," Kinsley said. "It went down the drain."

Benjamin looked at the drain. It was not scary at all. It was just a small hole. He got a stick. He poked the stick in the sand. The truck was not there.

Mr. Wright walked over. He watched Benjamin look. "Try the big sandbox," Mr. Wright said. "The wind blows toys there."

They ran to the big sandbox. The red truck sat on top of the sand. Kinsley smiled a big smile. Benjamin felt happy too. "Race you to the swings!" he said.

Ali ran into the big kitchen. The toast was waiting on the plate. Ms. Pritchard smiled. "Time to spread the butter, Ali!"

Ali held the little knife with the smooth edge. He pushed the soft butter. It slid across the toast. Swipe, swipe, swipe! The toast turned shiny and yellow. "I did it!" said Ali. Mahdi clapped next to him.

"Now pour the milk," said Ms. Pritchard. Ali lifted the jug. He poured and poured. Milk went up to the very top of the cup. The cup was full to the brim.

Ali walked to the table. One step, two steps. The milk wobbled. Then splash! Milk spilled onto the floor. "Oh no," said Ali.

He got a towel and wiped it up. Then he tried again. This time he poured the milk only part way up the cup. He stopped before the top. Ali walked slowly to the table. The milk stayed inside the cup. Nothing spilled at all!

"The cup did not spill!" Ali shouted. Sloane looked over. "Look at the snow out the window," she said. "It looks so cute on the trees!" Ali blew on his toast to cool it and took a big happy bite.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor skipped around the backyard with her. "What will we do today?" Eleanor asked.

"Today I will show you my bread," said Grandma. "My mother taught me. Her mother taught her." Eleanor's eyes got big. "Bread from long ago?" she asked. "Yes, our family bread," said Grandma.

In the kitchen, Grandma let Eleanor pour the flour. Eleanor poked the dough. It was soft and squishy. Grandma put the pan in the hot oven herself. "You stay back here," she said. Eleanor watched from her chair.

Soon the kitchen smelled warm. Grandma pulled out a round loaf. Eleanor touched the tiny crack in the middle. Then she took a big bite. "It tastes like more, please!" she said. Grandma laughed and cut another slice.

Asher went to the store with his dad. He wanted a book about a soft bunny. Asher looked and looked. No bunny book on the shelf. Then he saw Bilal from his class! "Come with me," said Bilal. "The bunny books hide down low." They bent down together. There it was! A soft bunny on the cover.

Asher grabbed the book. He opened it from the back. "That page says THE END," said Bilal, giggling. "Silly book! It starts at the end!" Asher flipped the book over. Now he was at the front cover. He turned page one. Page two. Page three. The bunny hopped through his whole day. "Front to back!" said Asher. He hugged the book tight. "This one, Dad," he said. "This one, this one!"

Theodore woke up early. Today was a big day. He was going to make a cake for his family! First he went to the farmers' market with his dad. "Eggs," said Theodore. "We need eggs!" He picked out six brown eggs. He bought flour and milk too. At the next stall, Abdul was there with his mom. "Look," said Abdul. "A big lion made of squash!" Theodore laughed. The lion had a mane of tiny pumpkins. Then they walked past the frozen fish stand. Brrr, it was cold there!

At home, Theodore cracked the eggs into a big bowl. Dad helped him pour in the milk. Theodore stirred and stirred. He added the flour bit by bit. The batter got smooth and runny. It looked like thick cream. Theodore frowned. "This is too runny," he said. "It will never be a cake!" He knocked on the bowl with his spoon. Tap, tap. The batter just wobbled.

Mom came to help. "It goes in the oven like this," she said. She poured the runny batter into a pan. Then she slid it into the hot oven. Theodore watched from his stool, far from the heat. He could not see the pan anymore. He waited. He wiggled. He looked at the oven clock.

Then Mom opened the oven door. Out came the pan. The batter was gone! Now there was a real cake. It was golden and puffy. Mom tipped it out onto a plate. She took a knife and cut a slice. A slice! The cake held its shape, just like bread. Theodore clapped his hands. "It was runny," he said. "Now I can slice it!"

The whole family sat down to eat. Dad took a big bite. Theodore took a bigger one. "Best cake ever," said Dad. Theodore grinned and reached for a second slice.

Nolan was at Grandpa's house. Today was a big day. Nolan was getting his very first haircut!

Grandpa held his hand. They walked to the salon down the street. The door went ding!

Nolan saw the big chair. It was tall and shiny. He tried to hop up. He was too small. His feet did not reach the floor!

Then a man came over. "I am Mr. Rajapakse," he said. "I cut hair here." He looked at the big chair. He looked at Nolan.

Mr. Rajapakse went away. He came back with a small seat. "Small children sit on a booster seat," he said. "Then I can reach your hair."

Nolan climbed up. The booster seat made him taller. Now Mr. Rajapakse could reach the top of his head!

Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the clean floor. Nolan watched them fall. He giggled.

"All done!" said Mr. Rajapakse. Nolan looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat.

Grandpa clapped his hands. "What a handsome boy!" he said.

After the haircut, they went back to Grandpa's house. Grandpa gave Nolan a snack. Then Grandpa said, "Time for a nap." Nolan did not want to sleep. He was too excited.

But his eyes felt heavy. The booster seat and the snipping had made him tired. Nolan yawned a big yawn.

He snuggled into the clean, soft bed. "My chair was too big," he whispered. "But my seat was just right."

Grandpa smiled. He patted Nolan's head. The new haircut felt smooth under his hand.

Nolan dreamed about the salon. In his dream, the big chair went up and up. And Nolan sat on his booster seat, taller than the playground, taller than Grandpa's roof!

When he woke up, Grandpa was waiting. "Want to show everyone your new hair?" Grandpa asked.

Nolan jumped out of bed. "Yes! To Leonardo! To Cadence!" he shouted. He grabbed his shoes.

They ran out the door together, hand in hand.

Eliana sat on the big soft rug. Grandpa sat next to her. Christophe and Coralie sat on the floor too. The game was on TV. The room smelled like warm popcorn.

"Who is winning?" asked Christophe.

Eliana tried to remember the score. She could not. She pulled her teddy close and thought hard. Then she saw the big bright board on the TV. It had two numbers on it. Coralie pointed too. "Look, the scoreboard," said Coralie. "It shows how many points each team has."

Eliana looked up. One team had more points. "That team is winning!" she said.

A door closed softly. Mom came in with more popcorn. The crowd on TV got loud. A player scored, and the number on the scoreboard grew.

"It went up!" said Eliana. She clapped her hands.

Grandpa laughed and shared his blanket.

Weston ran to the toy shelf at daycare. He saw a big basket of pictures. Mohammad tipped it over. All the pictures fell out. "Oh no," said Weston. "They are all mixed up."

Ms. López sat down next to them. "Let's make piles," she said. Weston picked up a picture of a cow. Mohammad had a picture of a dog. "These are animals," said Mohammad. They put the cow and the dog in one pile. Soon a cat and a duck joined them too.

Weston found a picture of a ball. It did not look like a cat. It was not food either. He put it with a picture of a teddy bear and a toy train. "Toys," he said. Then he found an apple, some bread, and a sticky honey pot. "Foods," he said. He made a third pile.
