Merrick came over to look. "Where does this go?" he asked. He held up a picture of a triangle. Weston giggled. "Not in the animal pile!" Merrick laughed too. Ms. López smiled at the three neat piles. "Now it is tidy," she said. Weston clapped his sticky hands and sat down for snack time.

Kai sat at the art table. It was summer, and the sun felt warm on his hands. He wanted to paint a traffic light. "Big kids stop for those," he said. Leilani sat down next to him. "I saw one on my walk," she said. "The red light made all the cars stop." Kai picked up the red paint. He made a big red circle. "Red means stop," he said. Then he painted a yellow circle. Skylar drove a toy car across the table. Kai held up his painting. "Stop!" he said. Skylar stopped the car fast.

But the traffic light needed one more circle. It had to be green. "Green means go," said Leilani. Kai looked for the green paint. The green jar was empty. That was bad. He looked and looked. Then he saw blue paint. He saw yellow paint too. What if he put them together? He dipped his brush in blue, then in yellow. He mixed them on the paper. Zip went the brush, round and round. The paint turned green! "Look!" said Kai. Ms. Asante came over. "What a nice green," she said. Kai painted the green circle at the bottom.

He held the painting up high. "Green means go!" he called. Skylar zoomed the toy car past the table. Kai laughed and got a new sheet of paper. "I want to make another one," he said. The brush went zip, zip, zip through the bright green paint.

Ryan was at summer camp. Lunch time was coming soon. Ms. Joseph said, "Wash your hands first. Count to twenty while you scrub."

Ryan put soap on his hands. He scrubbed and counted. Yusra counted next to him. One, two, three, all the way to twenty.

Then Ryan shook his hands. They still felt slippery. The soap was still there. He put his hands under the water. The water washed the soap off. Now his hands felt smooth and clean.

Taim's hands were slippery too. "Put them under the water," Ryan said. Taim did it. The soap went down the drain.

"Now our hands are clean," said Yusra. Ryan smiled and sat down with his sandwich.

Gabriella sat at the art table. She had one small block and a sheet of stickers. She wanted to put a sticker on every face of the block.

Francesco sat next to her. "How many faces does it have?" he asked.

"I don't know," said Gabriella. "I will find out."

She put a red sticker on the top face. Then she turned the block over. She put a blue sticker on the bottom face. She counted, "One, two."

Then she put a green sticker on a side. She turned the block again and again. "Three, four, five, six," she said.

"Six faces!" said Francesco. "A cube has six flat faces."

Gabriella looked at her stickers. Each sticker was square and flat. Each face was a square too, just like the stickers.

Aviraj crawled under the table to find a dropped sticker. "Got it!" he said. His hands were sticky, so Mr. Gill helped him wash them clean.

"Now let's build," said Gabriella. She stacked her block on Francesco's block. Six square faces fit just right.

"My rabbit picture can go on top," said Aviraj. He drew a circle for the rabbit's face and two long ears.

"Square blocks, circle bunny," said Gabriella with a smile. She put the picture right on top.

Willow sat in the family car. Her tummy felt jumpy. Today she would see the dentist for the first time. "What if I don't like it?" she asked. Mom said, "We will try together." Willow held her small bag of toy cars. The car bumped over the road. Willow counted the cars in her bag. One, two, three, four.

At the dentist, a big chair waited. It was not like a chair at home. The dentist said, "Hop in, Willow." Willow climbed in. Then the chair tips back! Willow was lying down now. She giggled and held on. The chair tips back, and now she lay down like at nap time. "It moved!" she said. The dentist smiled.

Willow opened her mouth wide. The dentist looked in with a little light. "Nice work," the dentist said. "You lift your chin a tiny bit." Willow lifted her chin. Soon it was done. Mom gave her a smart new toothbrush. In the car, Willow smiled big. "The chair moved like a ride!" she said.

Sadie ran to the sink at summer camp. It was time for snack. Tate was already there. He had soap on his hands.

Sadie turned the tap. The water looked hot. She pulled her hands back. "Mr. Silva, can you check?" she asked.

Mr. Silva came over. He put one finger under the water. "Still hot," he said. "Let's wait a small bit." They waited. Then he checked again. "Now it's warm, not hot," he said.

Sadie put her hands in. The water felt good. She pumped the soap. Mr. Silva sang a song. "Sing while you scrub," he said. Sadie scrubbed and sang. The song was short. She kept going till the end.

Then she rinsed the soap off. The bubbles went down the drain. Her hands were clean and shiny.

Leni held out the crackers. Sadie took one. "Nice hands," said Leni. Sadie smiled and took a big bite.

Mason was playing on the floor at home. His friend Charlie came to visit. Charlie brought a soft toy lion. The lion had a fuzzy mane. Mason wanted to hold it very much.

Mason reached out and grabbed the lion. Charlie's face went sad. Charlie held on tight. The lion began to shake between them. Mason's dad sat down next to them. "Try asking," Dad said. Mason let go of the lion. "Sorry, Charlie," Mason said. Then he took a big breath. "May I have a turn, please?"

Charlie smiled big. "Yes! That was polite," Charlie said. He put the lion in Mason's arms. The lion was soft and warm. Mason hugged it gently. Then he said, "Thank you, Charlie." Charlie said, "You can keep it a long, long time."

Mason made the lion jump on the rug. Then he handed it back. "Your turn," Mason said. Charlie made the lion roar. Both boys laughed. Dad clapped his hands. "Two polite boys," he said. Mason patted the lion's fuzzy mane one more time. "Roar!" he said.

Sienna ran to the door. Her dog, Biscuit, ran too. "Woof!" said Biscuit. Sienna patted his soft head. She patted his back. Then Mom called, "Lunch time!"

Sienna looked at her hands. They had dog hair on them. She held them up. "Look, Mom!" she said. Mom smiled. "What do we do now?" she asked. Sienna knew this one. "Wash hands!" she shouted.

Sienna ran to the sink. Mom turned on the water. Sienna pumped the soap. Bubbles came out. "Bubbles!" said Sienna. She rubbed her hands. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" The bubbles went far down the drain.

Then something small and surprising happened. Biscuit put his paws on the sink too. He wanted to see the bubbles. "Silly dog!" said Sienna. She dried her hands on the towel. Then she ran to the table.

The soup was hot, and Mom carried it carefully. Sienna sat on her bed-shaped booster seat and waited. After eating, she would wash again. "Clean hands!" said Sienna. She lifted her spoon up high.

Brielle sat in her reading nook. She had a big pile of letters. Ms. Mercado had given her the letter S. "This is S," Brielle said. "It says sss."

Brielle wanted to find more things with S. She looked around the nook. The sun shone in the window. "Sun!" said Brielle. She held up her letter. "Sss. Sun starts with S!" Then she found a sock under the pillow. "Sss. Sock!" She put the sock next to the sunbeam.

Brielle looked and looked. What else could she find? She picked up a toy truck. "Ttt," she said. She was mad for one second. Then she put the truck down. She looked at the sand in her little jar. "Sss. Sand! Sand starts with S too!" Brielle set the jar in the sun. She clapped her hands. "Three things! Sun, sock and sand!" Then she picked up the letter S and gave it a big kiss.

Elizabeth went to the farm with her friend Luc. They saw a big black cow. "Let's play the sense game," said Luc. "I will find things for your five senses."

Luc held up a soft feather. Elizabeth touched it with her fingers. "Touch is a sense!" she said. "I use my hands." Then Luc pointed at the bright yellow sun. "I see with my eyes," said Elizabeth. Next Luc rang the cow bell. Ding, ding! "I hear with my ears," said Elizabeth.

Then they came to the flower garden. Elizabeth had a runny nose. She could not smell the flowers at all. "Oh no," she said. "Which flower smells sweetest?" Luc laughed. "Close your mouth and sniff with your nose." Elizabeth sniffed and sniffed. "This pink one smells like candy!" she said. "We smell with our nose. My nose is my smell helper." The farmer let them give the black cow a bath. Elizabeth touched the warm water with her toes. "Tasting is for later," she said, "at snack time with my tongue." Luc giggled and splashed a little.

Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad took her hand. They walked to the playground.

Violet wanted to play on the slide. But the slide was busy. Laurie was there, and Amyra too. Violet hid behind Dad's itchy scarf. She peeked out with one eye.

A grown-up waved from the bench. It was Mr. López from next door. He said, "Hello, Violet!"

Violet stayed behind Dad. Her tummy felt small and tight.

Then Amyra slid down the slide. She ran to Violet. "Hello!" said Amyra. "Want a turn?"

Violet looked at Amyra's big smile. She stepped out. She said, "Hello, Amyra."

Amyra laughed and clapped. "Yes! Come on!"

Violet went up the steps. She slid down, fast. "Again!" she said. Amyra held her hand in the line.

Soon Violet saw Mr. López again. This time she did not hide. She waved her hand. "Hello, Mr. López!" she said.

Mr. López smiled a big smile. He gave a little wave back.

"Time to go," said Dad. Violet held his hand. "Bye, Amyra! Bye, Laurie!" she called.

They waved all the way to the gate. Violet skipped all the way home.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down a pencil and paper. "Can you write your name?" she asked. Jackson grabbed the pencil and stood up. He waved it in the air. He wanted to run to the door and show Dad.

"Hold the point down," said Mom. "A pencil can poke if it faces up." Jackson looked at the point. He turned it down toward the floor. Then he walked to the door, slow and careful.

Dad smiled. "Show me your name." Jackson sat back down. He held the pencil the right way. He missed some lines at first. He tried again. There it was. A J. Then an a. "That's me!" said Jackson. Dad clapped, and Jackson laughed.

Bennett ran to the slide. Big kids zoomed down fast. Bennett wanted to zoom too. But the top was so high up. He stood at the bottom and looked. The ladder went up. The slide came down. "Up and down," said Juliette. "They are opposites." Juliette was a big child, and she climbed up, up, up. Then she slid down, down, down. Bennett put one foot on the ladder. He held the rail straight and tight. Up he went, one step at a time. At the top, the wind felt cold on his nose. "Ready, brave knight?" called Juliette. Bennett sat down. He zoomed down fast. "Again!" he said. Then a small green frog hopped onto the bottom of the slide and sat there, watching them.

Sophie sat at the dinner table. She looked at her peas. "Mom," she said, "is today library day?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now. And right now, we eat dinner."

Sophie ate one pea. Then another. "Yesterday we went to the park," she said. "Audrey was there. We picked one flower each."

"That was yesterday," said Mom. "It already happened."

"But the library is today?" Sophie asked again.

"Yes. After dinner. You just have to wait a little."

Sophie looked at her plate. She wanted to go now. But the peas were still there. So she ate them, one by one. She took her time.

At last the plate was empty. Mom wiped Sophie's hands. "Now we can go," said Mom.

Sophie reached for her coat. "Today is the best day," she said. "The library, and Mom, and all done peas."

Addison played at Grandma's house. Grandpa had put a big box of toys in the den. Addison pulled out blocks. She made a tall tower. Then she made a long road. Blocks went all over the rug.

Grandma called, "Snack time!" Addison jumped up. She began to run to the kitchen. Grandma stood in the door. "The toys you played with wait for you," she said. Addison looked back. The blocks were everywhere. Her friend Leandre had cars out, too. He put his cars in his bin. Addison picked up one block. She put it in the box. The rug began to show at the bottom of each pile. Soon all the blocks were in. The rug was clear.

Then Addison ran to the kitchen. Grandma gave her a tasty apple slice. Addison sat on her bottom on the little chair. She took one slice, then sent the plate down to Leandre. He took his turn. After snack, Grandma said, "You can play again now." Addison and Leandre ran back to the den together. "My turn with the red car," said Leandre. Addison smiled and picked up the blue one.

Grandpa's big car came up the street. Harrison stood at the door. He hid one foot behind the other.

Grandpa got out of the car. He opened his arms wide. "Hello, Harrison!" he said.

Harrison wanted to hug Grandpa. But his tummy felt funny. He was shy. He could not move.

Mom held his hand. "You can wave hello," she said softly.

Harrison looked at Grandpa. Grandpa smiled. Harrison lifted his hand. He waved hello. His hand went back and forth, fast and slow.

Grandpa waved back. "Hello to you too!" he said.

Harrison's tummy felt better. He took one small step. Then one more step. Then he ran on his big feet, right into Grandpa's arms.

"Hello, Grandpa," Harrison said, with his face against Grandpa's soft sweater. It smelled like mint.

"Hello, my boy," said Grandpa. He carried Harrison inside, just like a big hug that could walk.

Weston was in the backyard with his friend Aryan. Weston had a big box of chalk. "Let's draw a blue bird," said Aryan. Weston looked in the box. He found a dark blue chalk. "This is not blue," said Aryan. "It is too dark. It is black."

Weston held the chalk up to the sky. The sky was light blue. The chalk was dark blue. Hmm. Were they both blue? Weston drew a small dot of dark blue. Then he drew a dot of light blue. "Look," said Weston. "They look like brothers." Aryan squinted at the dots.

Then Weston put all the blue chalks in a row on the grass. Light blue. Middle blue. Dark blue. A line of blues, like steps going down. "See?" said Weston. "Light blue and dark blue are both still called blue." Aryan picked the dark one. "Then we can draw a night bird!" The birds under the tree got a mama in light blue and a baby in dark blue. A noisy crow flew over and landed in the tree, as if it wanted a chalk color too.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Sienna showed Grandma her truck toys. She showed Grandma her itchy new sweater. "Wear it for a picture," said Grandma. Every day they did fun things. One, they baked cookies. Two, they fed the ducks. Three, they read books in the big chair.

Then the week was done. Grandma packed her bag. Sienna's eyes went sad. "You can call me on the phone," said Grandma. "We can see each other on a video call, too. Or you can send me a letter." A letter! Sienna had a big idea.

Sienna drew a picture fast. It showed Grandma, the ducks, and one truck. Mom helped her mail it. In three days, guess what? The phone rang. Grandma was on a video call, holding up the picture! "My favorite mail ever," said Grandma. Sienna waved both hands and said, "Draw one more tomorrow!"

Kayden woke up in his bed. The sun was bright at the window. He heard dishes in the kitchen. He heard his dad say, "Good morning!"

Kayden ran down the hall. Mom and Dad sat at the table. There were eggs and toast. "Is it morning now?" Kayden asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." Kayden climbed into his chair. He took a big bite of toast.

Yesterday, Kayden had cried at breakfast. He had wanted pancakes, and there were none. Mom had said, "Not today. Pancakes are for tomorrow." Now Kayden looked at the plate. There were pancakes! "Today is tomorrow!" he said. Mom laughed. "That's right, sweet boy. Today is the pancake day." Kayden smiled big.

A plane flew over the house. It made a loud hum in the sky. Kayden waved at it. "Where is it going?" he asked. "Far away," said Dad. "It will land later." Kayden ate his pancake. It was warm and sweet.

After breakfast, Kayden felt shy. He wanted to play outside, but the yard seemed big. Mom held his hand. They stepped out together. The grass was soft under his feet. "We can go inside later if you want," Mom said. Kayden picked up his red ball. "Now I want to kick it," he said. And he did.

Maverick planted seeds in the community garden. He patted the soft brown soil. His friend Beckett planted seeds too. Every day they came to look. Dirt, dirt, and more dirt. No green yet.

"It takes time," said Mr. Kaminski. "You water, and you wait." So Maverick watered the little row. He slipped his watering can under the spout. He counted the days. One, two, three, four. Still just dirt. Maverick felt sad. Maybe his seeds were no good.

On day nine, Beckett yelled, "Look! Look!" A tiny green tip was poking up. Maverick got down on his knees. He touched one small leaf.

"That is a sprout," said Mr. Kaminski. "A tiny new plant poking up is called a sprout."

"A sprout!" said Maverick. "I have one too!" He pointed at a second green tip. Then a third.

"I grew this," said Maverick. "From just a seed."

Josephine sat at Emma's table. Emma's mom put a tablet in front of her.

"Press the round button with your finger," said Emma. "Then tap the little paint box."

Josephine pressed the button. The screen lit up. Then she tapped the paint box. A drawing app opened.

"I did it!" said Josephine.

She drew a thin green snake. Then she drew a big red sun. Then she drew Emma with yellow hair.

Emma laughed. "That looks like me!"

"Can I draw a cat too?" asked Josephine.

"Yes," said Emma. "There is lots of time."

Josephine started the cat. She drew one ear. Then two ears. Then the screen went black.

Josephine sat very still. "Is it broken?" she asked.

Emma's mom came over. "No, it ran out of power after being used," she said. "It needs charging. Watch me."

She plugged the charger into the wall. Then she plugged it into the tablet. A little picture of a battery showed up on the black screen.

"See?" said Emma's mom. "It is getting power now."

"It was tired," said Josephine. "Like me at bedtime."

Emma giggled. "It has to rest and eat!"

Emma's mom said, "You can draw more later. Can you put the tablet away now?"

Josephine picked up the tablet. She set it down on the shelf, right next to Emma's crayons.

"Bye bye, tablet," said Josephine. "Rest well."

Emma took her hand. "Come play blocks until it is full again."

Josephine smiled and followed her friend to the toy corner.

Sienna held her little blue bag. She was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. They rode on a big train. "Look, one seat, two seats, three seats," said Sienna, counting them.

Papa looked worried. "I don't know our stop," he said. "This place is new to us." The train went clickety-clack. Fields and cows went past the window. Sienna looked around. She saw a paper on the wall. It had lines and little dots. "What is that?" she asked. "That is a map," said Mama. "It shows the roads and the places."

Sienna stood close to Mama. She put her finger on the map. "Here is our town," she said. "I see the word." Papa looked too. "Yes! And the line goes to the next place," he said. "That is our stop." Sienna clapped her hands. The map showed the way.

A girl sat across from them. Her name was Braelynn. She was going to the same place. "You can sit by me, friend," said Braelynn. They shared fresh apple slices from Mama's bag. One slice was warm from the sun and felt soft, like it might melt in Sienna's mouth.

Then came a small surprise. Braelynn had a tiny map in her pocket. It was a map of the zoo! "We can find the pandas," she said. "The map shows where they are." The train slowed down. "Our stop!" said Papa. Sienna held Braelynn's hand. "Maps show the way," she whispered, and off they went.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. It was yellow and shiny. "I will write my name!" said Lucas.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. His mom smiled. "Try two fingers on top," she said. "Like this." Lucas changed his grip. One finger, two fingers, thumb below. The pencil felt smooth and cool. He started to write. L, U, C. He began at the right side of the paper. He wrote and wrote. Then his pencil bumped the edge. No room! No more letters! Lucas frowned. "My A is stuck!" he said.

"You ran out of room," said Mom. "Watch me." She wrote her own name. She started at the left side. The letters marched across, left to right, all the way to the right. Lucas gasped. "Start here!" he said. He put his pencil at the left edge. L, U, C, A, S. Five letters! They all fit!

"It's beautiful!" said Lucas. He clapped his hands. The letters sat in a row like little friends. Then he grabbed a new sheet. "Now a story about my name!" said Lucas. The pencil went scratch, scratch on the paper. He began at the left again.

Grayson walked on the nature trail with Ms. Hoang. She held a bag of things. "Let's play a puzzle," she said. "Tell me which things are soft and which are rough."

Grayson pulled out a feather. He touched it with his fingers. "Soft," he said. Then he touched a pinecone. It poked his skin. "Rough!" he said. Next came a small purple blanket. He rubbed it on his hand. "Soft," he said. He had solved the puzzle with his skin.

"Now close your eyes," said Ms. Hoang. She put something in his hands. It was bumpy and hard. Grayson laughed. "Rough! My skin can tell!" His skin could feel soft things and rough things, even with his eyes shut.

They walked on. Grayson touched a smooth gray rock. "Rough?" he asked. He felt it again. "No. Smooth. That's a new one!"

Eliana went to the store with her dad. She held his hand. "Stay close," said Dad. "One, two, my hand and you."

At the store, they saw the fruit first. The apples were cold. Eliana touched one. "Brrr," she said. Dad picked warm bread from a shelf. The bag felt soft and hot. "This one is for grown-up hands," said Dad, and he held it up high.

Then Eliana saw something on the floor. It was small and shiny. It was a little lighter. A man had dropped it. Eliana did not pick it up. She kept her hands behind her back. "Dad," she said. "That is not for me."

Dad looked down. He bent and picked it up. "You did good," he said. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." A kind lady at the counter smiled. She called out, "Whose is this?" The man came back. "Mine! Thank you," he said.

Dad cleaned Eliana's hands with a wipe. Then they counted their bags. "One, two, three." Outside, the sun felt warm on Eliana's face. She held Dad's hand all the way home.

Emilia ran to the park with her mom. It was a beautiful summer day. Danica and Devon were already there, digging in the sand.

"Can we play all day?" Emilia asked.

"Not all day," said Mom. "We go home later."

Emilia played with Danica. They dug a big hole. Devon ran down the slide again and again. Then Emilia stopped and looked up.

"When is later?" she asked. "Is it now?"

Mom held up her phone. "See this little clock? A clock shows what time it is."

Emilia looked at the numbers. "The clock has numbers on it!"

"Yes," said Mom. "Now the short hand points here. Later it will point there. Then we go home."

Emilia watched the sand. She filled her bucket. She tipped it over. The sand made a tall tower. One bucket made one tower.

"Look! My bucket made a hill," she said.

"Can I try?" asked Devon.

"Yes! Watch," said Emilia. She filled his bucket too.

Yesterday they came to this park. Today they were here. Tomorrow they would come back.

Emilia ran to Mom again. "What does the clock say now?"

Mom showed her. "Still play time."

"Good," said Emilia. She stood by the tower and clapped her hands.

"I love today," she said.

William sat on the clean bench in the backyard. He wanted to learn his five senses. "What do I use to hear?" he asked. He put his hands over his eyes. Then he sat very still.

A bird sang. His ears heard it. "Ears!" said William. "We hear with our ears." A bee buzzed. His ears heard that too. The wind made the leaves go shush. His ears heard it all.

Emiliano came over with a seed in his hand. "Look," said Emiliano. William looked with his eyes. He sniffed with his nose. Then a dog barked next door. Both boys sat still and listened. "Ears again," said William, and he pointed to his ears.

Hunter was four today. His party was at the community hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a big cake on the table.

Katrina came in with a small box. "Happy birthday," she said. "Are you four now?"

"I was three," said Hunter. "Today I am four."

Nicole ran over. "You got bigger," she said. She touched the top of Hunter's head. "You are taller than me now."

Hunter stood up very straight. He looked at the balloons. He looked at the cake. On your birthday, you turn one year older. Yesterday he was three. Today he was four. Next year he would be five.

Mr. Le helped with the cake. He was careful with the little candles. He lit them one by one. "Now make a wish," he said.

Hunter took a big breath. He blew out all the candles. The smoke went up like a soft feather.

"Happy birthday, Hunter!" everyone sang.

Hunter grinned. "I am four," he said. "Can I have the first piece of cake?"

Sofia went to the library with her dad. Story time was today. Mr. Kang read a book about shapes. He held up a round plate. "This is a circle," he said. He held up a box. "This is a square."

After the story, there was a craft table. Sofia wanted to make a paper sailboat. The boat needed two triangles for sails. But there were no triangles left. There was only one square piece of paper. Vanessa had no triangles either. Madeline had one, but her boat needed it.

Sofia asked her dad, "Can a square become triangles?" Her dad picked up the scissors. "Watch," he said. He cut the square from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell into two pieces. Two triangles! Sofia clapped. One triangle was loose on the table, and she gave it to Vanessa.

Then they sang a little song about boats. "A triangle sail for me and you," sang Sofia, holding up her triangle.

Matteo went to the big hall with his grandma. The hall was next to the old temple. Today there was a shared lunch. Long tables. Folded napkins. A pot of soup steaming at the end.

Matteo helped set out spoons. One, two, three, four. His friend Francesca came. His friend Jawad came too. Ms. Hassan brought warm bread on a big plate.

Before the meal, grandma held Matteo's hand. "Say it with me," she said. "Itadakimasu." Matteo tried. "Ita... daki... masu." He bumped his spoon and it rolled under the table. He picked it up. He tried again, slower. "Itadakimasu."

"In Japan, people say itadakimasu before eating," grandma said. "It gives thanks for the food."

Francesca clapped. Jawad said it too. Ms. Hassan said it. The whole table said it. Then everyone began to eat.

Matteo ate his soup. He ate his bread. "Lucky soup," he said, because there was a carrot shaped like a star.

After lunch, Matteo drew with a crayon. He drew the table and the spoons. On the top he wrote the letters he knew.

At dinner that night, Matteo folded his hands. "Itadakimasu," he said, just right.

"Very good," said grandma, and she filled his bowl.

Iris was hungry. She wanted her snack now. Mom set out three things on the table. There was a red apple. There was soft bread. There was a long orange carrot.

Iris picked up the carrot. She marched it over to her toy box. She put the carrot next to her white robot. "Carrot can play too," she said. The robot did not play. The carrot just sat there.

Then Iris looked at the apple. Mom cut the apple into slices. Mom gave one slice to Iris. Crunch! It tasted sweet. Iris watched the bread. Mom tore the bread and shared it too. Iris chewed and wiped her mouth with a napkin.

Iris ran back to the toy box. She picked up the carrot. She carried it to the table. She put it down by the apple and the bread. "You go here," she said. The carrot had found its friends. Mom smiled and gave the carrot a little wash. Iris bit it. Crunch, crunch!

Weston's class had a guessing game. Ms. Krause held up a big card. "Name an animal," she said. Weston raised his hand fast. "A dog!" he said. Leighton said, "A cow!" Ms. Krause smiled. "Good. Dogs and cows are animals."

Then Ben held up a picture of a fish. "A fish is not an animal," said Weston. "It has no legs." Ben looked sad. The fish card fell to the floor. Ms. Krause picked it up. "A fish is an animal too," she said. Weston made a funny face. A fish? An animal? He was not sure.

The class went to the small tank by the window. Weston leaned in to listen. The water made soft blips. The fish opened its mouth. It wiggled its tail. It swam all by itself. Weston watched and watched. "It moves," he said. "It swims. It is alive." His head went up and down. "A fish is an animal!" he said. Ben clapped. Leighton clapped. Weston's face felt full of happy.

"Now name more animals," said Ms. Krause. Weston said, "Dog, cow, fish!" Then he stopped. He peeked under the table. "Is a table an animal?" he asked. Everyone laughed. "No, a table just sits there," said Leighton. Weston giggled. "Okay. Dog, cow, fish," he said again. "Dog, cow, fish." The fish blew one tiny bubble. Pop.

Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She folded her napkin into a little square. "Can we read the bear story now?" she asked.

Dad put the bowls on the table. "Now we eat dinner," he said. "The story is not now. The story is later."

Eleanor looked at her spoon. She wanted the story at this very moment. But first came the peas. First came the rice. She took one bite. Then another bite.

"Is it later yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Now we are eating."

Eleanor ate some more. She folded her napkin again. "Now?" she asked.

"Now we wash hands," said Dad. They washed hands at the sink. The water was warm. Dad held the towel for her.

Then they sat on the couch. Dad opened the book. "Is it now?" Eleanor asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "It is now."

Eleanor snuggled close. She had been brave and waited all through dinner. The bear story started. She turned the first page with her own hand.

"One more page," she said. "Right now, please."

Alexander dug a little hole in the backyard. His dad helped him pat the seeds into the dirt. "Now we water them," said Dad. Alexander tipped the can. The water made dark spots on the soil.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He saw only dirt. No sprout. "Where is my plant?" he asked. His tongue poked out as he thought. He watered the seeds again. A bird swung on the fence and watched him.

Ila came to play. They watered the seeds together. Still only dirt the next day. And the next day. Then one morning, Alexander looked down and gasped. A tiny green sprout stood in the dirt. "Ila! Come see!" he called. Ila ran over fast. "It's new," she whispered. Alexander watered it again, very carefully.

Lydia stood at the little desk in the reading corner. She was getting her first library card. Her name was on it in blue letters. She held it up high.

"I can borrow a book now!" she said. Her voice was big and loud. A boy nearby was reading a dinosaur book. He put his finger on his lips. Mr. Papadopoulos leaned down close. "Many libraries ask people to use quiet voices so others can read," he said softly. Lydia looked around. Fiadh was reading. Lia was reading too. Lydia made her voice tiny, like a mouse.

"Watch this," she whispered to Fiadh. She tiptoed to the shelf. She found a book about a red fox. She gave her card to Mr. Papadopoulos. He scanned it. Beep! The book was hers to take home.

Fiadh clapped her hands, very softly, like quiet rain. "That was the quietest clap ever," she whispered. Lydia giggled. Then she covered her mouth fast. The boy turned his page and smiled at them. "Next time I will pick a book about the moon," Lydia whispered. She hugged her book and walked on tippy toes all the way to the door.

Myles sat at the big art table. He had a new yellow pencil. He wanted to draw a big furry dog. Ms. Murphy put out white paper for everyone.

Myles pressed down very hard on the paper. He made one dark line. Then he made another. He wanted the fur to look dark and thick.

Snap! The pencil point broke. The little black tip fell onto the table. Myles picked it up. "My pencil broke," he said. Raya leaned over to look. "Mine still works," she said. She was drawing softly.

Myles got a new pencil from the box. This time he pressed gently. The line was light and smooth. The point stayed on the pencil. He drew the furry dog, one soft line at a time. He even drew a swing for the dog to sit on. Ms. Murphy hung his picture on the wall. "Look at that fluffy dog," she said.

Lennon went to the library with her dad. She wanted to draw on the big tablet there. But the screen was dark. She did not know how to make it work.

Ms. Nair came over. "Press the round button," she said. Lennon pressed it. The screen lit up! She saw small pictures everywhere. "Those little pictures are called icons," said Ms. Nair. Lennon looked at each icon. One icon had a paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush icon. The drawing app opened! She drew a fluffy cloud. She drew a noisy black crow too.

Soon it was time to go. Lennon pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on its shelf, just like the other kids did. Jensen smiled and said, "Thank you, Lennon."

Norah stood at the paint table at school. Ms. Chowdhury put out big cups of paint. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. Norah sniffed the air. "This paint smells stinky," she said. "That is okay," said Ms. Chowdhury. "It washes off with soap."

Norah wanted to paint a pumpkin. But pumpkins are orange. There was no orange paint. "Where can I get orange?" she asked. Dhruv sat down next to her. "Try red and yellow," he said. "Mix them in your cup."

Norah dipped her brush in the red paint. Then she dipped it in the yellow paint. She stirred and stirred. The paint turned orange. It looked just like a pumpkin. "I did it!" she said.

She painted a big round pumpkin. She painted a green stem on top. Avreen leaned over to look. "I like your orange pumpkin," said Avreen. Ms. Chowdhury hung it on the wall to dry. Norah pointed at it and said, "I made orange all by myself."

Madeline went to the park with her dad. There was a paint table by the swings. Mr. Pereira was the teacher at the table.

"I want to make a pink flower," said Madeline. "It is for Grandma's card."

Mr. Pereira looked in the paint box. "We have red, blue, yellow and green," he said. "But no pink."

Madeline counted the paints. "One red. One blue. One yellow. One green. No pink. No pink." She felt sad.

Lily came over on the swing. The swing went high, high, high. Then Lily jumped off and ran to the table. "I will help you," said Lily.

Madeline picked up the red paint. She made a red flower on the card. "Too dark," she said. "Grandma wants pink."

Remington brought the white paint. "Try this," he said.

Madeline stirred the white into the red. Round and round went the stick. She had to fold the white in slowly. The red got lighter and lighter.

"Pink!" said Madeline. "White and red make pink!"

She painted a pink flower on the card. Lily painted a green stem. Remington painted a yellow sun.

"One red. One white. One pink flower," said Madeline. She held the card up to the sun.

"It is beautiful," said Mr. Pereira.

"Grandma will love it," said Madeline. She put the card in her bag, nice and flat.

Alexis went to the park with his drum. Bang, bang, bang! The drum was loud and fun. Alexis felt excited.

Camden ran over. Camden put his hands on his ears. "Too loud," said Camden. Camden looked scared of the big sound.

Alexis stopped drumming. He felt sad that Camden was sad. Then he had an idea. "Let's count clouds," he said.

They lay in the cozy grass. One cloud looked like a plate. Two clouds looked like a bunny. Alexis counted to ten.

Ms. Perera sat nearby on the bench. "Nice counting, boys," she said.

Then Wells came by with a whistle. Toot, toot! Wells loved the loud whistle. He jumped and laughed. But Camden covered his ears again.

So Wells put the whistle away. Wells and Alexis kept counting clouds quietly. Camden smiled and pointed up. "That one is a dragon!"

Alexis banged his drum very, very soft. Bang. Camden clapped. They all watched the dragon cloud float away.

Penelope stood in the kitchen with her mom. She wanted to make pancakes for the family. "The recipe tells us what to use," Mom said. "And what to do, one step at a time." Penelope looked at the card. Flour, milk, one egg.

Penelope poured the flour. She poured the milk. Then she saw the egg. "I want to mix now," she said. She skipped the egg. Mom put the pan on the stove. Penelope stood back and watched. Mom poured the batter. The pancake came out flat. Flat like a plate. "Oh no," said Penelope. "It did not puff up."

Mom read the recipe again. "We skipped a step," she said. "The egg step." Penelope put one egg in the bowl. She mixed it all up. Mom poured the new batter. This time the pancake puffed up big. "It's tall!" said Penelope. She hung her dish towel on the hook. The smelly dog came in, hoping for a bite. Dad sat down. "Pancakes for dinner!" he said. Penelope smiled and put a big one on his plate.

Rowan ran onto the basketball court. It was a long walk from the car. His sister had gone to sleep on the way, and Mom carried her to a bench.

Rowan's team was called the Bluebirds. He counted his friends. One, Ally. Two, Taylor. Three, Rowan. Three Bluebirds on the court. Rowan got the ball and hugged it tight. Then he ran with it, all the way to the hoop.

A whistle blew. A man in a striped shirt held up his hand. "Traveling," he said. The ball went to the other team.

Rowan frowned. He ran to the coach. "Who is that man?" he asked. "He is the referee," the coach said. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Rowan watched the referee. The referee watched all the players. Rowan got the ball again. This time he bounced it. Bounce, bounce, bounce. The referee smiled and let him play on.

Ally clapped. Taylor clapped. Rowan shot the ball. It hit the rim, then went in. "Good rules," Rowan said, and he gave the referee a big wave.

Levi stood at the running track. The sun felt warm on his arms. Ms. Nur put a hoop on the grass. She gave Levi a real beanbag. "Throw it in," she said.

Levi threw. The beanbag sailed high. It landed in the hoop. "I did it!" he shouted. Archibald ran up. He wanted a beanbag too. Levi held the whole bag of them. Archibald's face went sad. Was there a way to make it fair? Levi thought hard. Then he held one out. "Your turn now," Levi said. Archibald threw one, then Levi threw one. One kid, then the next kid, over and over.

Next came the big ball. Levi caught it with both hands. It felt bumpy and cool. "My turn!" said Archibald. Levi passed the ball right over.

The train went clack, clack, clack. Hannah sat by the big window. She was going on a trip with Dad. "Look," said Dad. "The sea is outside." Hannah saw blue water and yellow sand. She saw a little pig on a farm by the tracks. The pig looked the same as the pig in her book at home. The train door slid shut with a soft whoosh.

Hannah saw children by the water. One small girl ran to the waves. She stopped. She looked back. A big grown-up came to her. Then the girl held his hand. Together they went near the water. Splash, splash! Hannah watched and watched. Another boy waited too. He waited until his mom walked down with him. Then he jumped in the waves.

At last the train stopped. Hannah and Dad got off. Hannah ran to the sand. She saw the water up ahead. But she stopped. She looked back at Dad. "Come with me, Daddy," she said. Dad smiled. He took her hand. They walked down to the water together. Hannah put her toes in. "Cold!" she said, and laughed.

Kinsley was at the mall. She was not late. She was just in time for her first haircut.

The hairdresser smiled. "Time for a cape," she said. She put a cape around Kinsley's shoulders. It was blue and shiny.

"Why a cape?" asked Kinsley.

"So the cut hair stays off your clothes," said the hairdresser.

Kinsley giggled. "I look like a superhero!"

The hairdresser began to cut. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. One, two, three little hairs. Not on her shirt. Not on her lap. Just on the cape.

"Snip, snip, snip," said Kinsley.

Her friend Keziah waved from the next chair. "You look like a blue pig with a cape!" she teased.

"A superhero pig," said Kinsley. "Oink, oink!"

The hairdresser brushed the hairs away. She lifted off the cape. Kinsley's clothes were clean. No hairs at all.

"Look, Mom," said Kinsley. "My shirt has no hairs!"

She spun in a circle. "Snip, snip, snip!"

Rowan sat at the dinner table. He took a big drink of water. "Yum," he said. "Water is so good."

After dinner, Rowan had to use the toilet. He ran down the hall. He was in a hurry.

Then he ran back to the table. But wait. Had he flushed? He did not think so.

Rowan ran back to the bathroom. He pressed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. It made a loud, swishy sound.

Next, he turned on the tap. He rubbed his hands with soap. Bubbles, bubbles! The water felt warm. His dad had made it warm for him.

Rowan patted his hands dry on the soft towel. Then he pulled off his sock to show his dad a bubble had landed on his toe.

"All clean?" his dad asked.

"All clean," said Rowan. "I flushed, then I washed."

He yawned a big, sleepy yawn. Bath time came next, then warm pajamas. Rowan wondered, did the toilet swirl every time? He would listen for it tomorrow.

Theodore sat down at the art table. Mr. Goh gave everyone paper and paints. "Today we paint a house," said Mr. Goh. Theodore was so excited! He wanted to paint a big red house. But then he stopped. He did not know what shape a door was. He looked at his paper. He looked around the room. Matthew was painting a sun with a circle. Mara dipped her brush in the blue bucket. "I need a door shape," said Theodore. Mr. Goh smiled. "Look around the room," he said. Theodore looked. He saw the door. The big classroom door! He jumped up and ran to it. He put his finger on the door. He counted the corners. One, two, three, four. Four corners! And he counted the sides. One, two, three, four. Four sides! "It has four sides and four square corners," said Theodore. "Just like a rectangle!" He ran back to his table. He painted a rectangle door on his red house. It had four sides and four square corners, just like the real door. Then he painted a tiny circle for the doorknob. "My house is done!" said Theodore. Mr. Goh held it up high. "Look at that fine rectangle door!"

Felix woke up sleepy but excited. Today was a big family day. Grandma was in the kitchen. She had a bowl and a box of raisins. "Come help," said Grandma.

Felix helped stir the dough. Then he patted it flat. Grandma put the tray in the oven. The oven was hot, so Grandma did that part. Felix watched from his chair.

The cake smelled so good. Felix wanted some now. He reached for the tray. "Not yet," said Grandma with a smile. "This is a special cake. We make it only for today." Felix waited. It felt very long.

At last the family sat together. Felix took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "It tastes like the party!" Grandma laughed. "Have another piece," she said. Felix lifted his plate up high.

Jake ate breakfast at home. He used his fork to pick up his eggs. Today he had to get a shot at the doctor's office. His tummy felt tight.

"Will the shot hurt?" Jake asked his mom.

"Just a tiny pinch," she said. "Then it is done."

Jake held his cute teddy bear tight. In the car he counted things. One bag. Two shoes. Three big breaths.

At the office, Jake sat on the big bed. The nurse cleaned his arm. It felt cold. Jake wanted to hide.

"Smell a flower," his mom said. "Breathe in slow. Then blow out slow, like a candle."

Jake tried it. He smelled a big flower. In went his slow breath. Out it went, slow and soft. One flower. One candle. Again.

His shoulders came down. His tummy felt less tight. The nurse said, "All done!"

"Already?" said Jake. "I did not even feel it!"

The nurse gave him a bandage with stars. At home, Jake helped feed the fish. He smelled a flower breath again, just for fun.

"That is my trick," Jake said, and blew out slow like a candle.

Ayla went to the park with her stuffed bunny. Mavis was there too. Mavis had a teapot and little cups. "Let's play tea party," said Mavis.

Ayla sat down on the grass. She looked inside the teapot. It was empty. No water. No tea. "Uh oh," said Ayla. "There is no tea."

Mavis laughed a happy laugh. "It's okay! It's pretend tea. Look." Mavis tipped the teapot over a cup. Nothing came out. But Mavis said, "Here is your tea!" Ayla picked up the cup. She drank pretend tea. It tasted like nothing at all. That was funny!

Ayla hugged her bunny. "Tea for you," she said. She tipped the pot. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" Mavis giggled so much she almost fell over. Ayla put a leaf by the cups. "Pretpretend cookies," she said. "Yum, yum!"

Then Ayla set her cup down too fast. It did not break. It just tipped over. "Pretend spill!" said Mavis. They wiped it with pretend rags.

"This is like grandma's house," said Ayla. "Grandma has a cozy table just like this." Mavis poured one more cup. Ayla held it up high. "More pretend tea, please!"

The lights went out. Leo's whole living room went dark. "Mama!" he called. Mama came fast with a candle. She lit it carefully with a match. The little flame tickled the air and made shadows dance on the wall.

Leo wanted to see more. "Can we have more candles?" he asked. Mama lit two more and set them on the table. Now the room glowed warm and orange. "We make a good team," said Mama. Leo giggled.

Then Leo looked out the window. "Mama, come look!" he said. All the houses on the street were dark too. Every window was black. Not one light anywhere. "The power cut made the whole street go dark," said Mama. Leo pressed his nose to the cold glass. It was so quiet and so dark outside.

Then, far away, one window lit up. Then another. Then their own lamp blinked on. "The power is back!" shouted Leo. He jumped up and down. "Can we blow out the candles now?" Mama smiled and helped him puff. The flames went out, one, two, three, and the lamp shone bright.

Charlie was building a tall tower. Marvin came to play at her house. He ran fast to see the blocks. He bumped the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down.

Charlie looked at the blocks. She looked at Marvin. Marvin's face looked funny, like he might cry. "Why do you look sad?" Charlie asked. "I knocked your tower down," Marvin said. "It was too fast. I did not mean it."

Marvin took a big breath. "Sorry, Charlie," he said. Charlie picked up one block. "Sorry means you know you bumped it?" she asked. "Yes," said Marvin. He picked up a block too. Then they took turns. Marvin put one on. Charlie put one on. The tower grew tall again.

Charlie's mom called them for lunch. "Should we leave the tower up?" asked Charlie. "Yes," said Marvin. "We can build more later." They ran to the table together.

Athena went to the store with her mom today. Yesterday the store had no pink yogurt. Athena wanted some. She looked and looked. There it was! A pink cup with a strawberry on it.

She held it up. "Can we get it now?" she asked.

"Not now," said Mom. "We need bread first. Then we pay. Soon."

"Soon?" said Athena. "What is soon?"

"Soon means in a little while," said Mom.

Athena frowned. A little while felt big. She held the pink cup and walked with Mom. They got the bread. They got apples. Still no checkout.

"Is it soon yet?" asked Athena.

"Not yet," said Mom. "Soon."

Athena waited. She counted the apples in the cart. One, two, three, four. Then she saw Agastya from her class by the bus toys! He waved. She waved back. He showed her a little yellow bus. "Beep beep!" he said. Athena laughed.

"Now it is soon," said Mom. "Look, it is our turn."

The cashier scanned the bread. Then she scanned the apples. Then she scanned the pink cup. Athena held the bag all the way home.

"Tomorrow we can eat the pink yogurt," said Mom.

"No," said Athena. "Later today. It is soon!"

Mom laughed. "Yes. Very soon."

It was game morning at Charles's house. Dad put snacks on the table. Salem and Flavie came over to watch the big game with Charles. Everyone sat on the rug.

"Who is that man?" Flavie asked. She pointed at the TV. A man in a striped shirt ran back and forth. He kept watching the players. He blew his whistle, and everyone stopped.

Charles felt a little scared of the loud whistle. Dad said, "It's okay. Come sit by me." Charles sat close.

"He is the referee," said Salem. "A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules."

Then a player pushed another player. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his finger. The player put his hands up and said sorry.

Charles counted the players. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He counted the referee too. "Six!"

The whistle blew again. The game went on. Dad gave Charles a snack.

"That man helps them play nice," said Flavie.

Charles waved at the TV. "Good watching, referee!" he said.

Asher stood at the school gate. His backpack was on his back. It was very heavy. He tried to walk to the door. His legs wobbled like a little duck.

Gloria stood by the gate too. "Why do you walk like that?" she asked. "My bag is too heavy," said Asher. He took the bag off his back. He set it on the ground. He opened it up.

Out came a toy truck. Out came a farm puzzle. Out came a big red ball. "I packed too many toys," said Asher. Now the bag was light. He put it back on his back. It felt easy now. He could walk tall.

Then the bag went squeak, squeak. Something was still in there! Asher peeked inside. A small white rabbit sat on his snack. "A bunny!" laughed Gloria. Ms. Sadeghi came to the gate. She helped the rabbit into her hands. "We will find his farm home," she said. Asher waved to the bunny. "See you, little friend."

The car was warm. Luca sat in his seat. The baby sat in her little seat. She had a soft blanket. "Baby sister," said Luca. "One, two, three of us now."

Luca wanted to hold her. He reached out his hands. "Not yet," said Dad. "Your hands are dirty from the park." Luca looked at his hands. They had sand on them. He rubbed them on his pants. The sand did not go away.

The car stopped at home. Dad carried the baby inside. Luca followed. Dad ran warm water at the sink. Luca washed his hands. He counted, "One, two, three, bubbles." He dried them on the towel.

Then Dad sat on the big chair. He put the baby in Luca's arms. Her blanket was soft. She made a small sound. She grabbed Luca's finger. Luca laughed. "She likes me," he said. "Big brother."

Arlo ran to the park with his dad. He wanted to see the ducks. Blair was there by the pond.

"I saw the ducks tomorrow," said Blair. Then she stopped. "No, wait. I saw them yesterday. Yesterday already happened."

Ms. Suryanto was sitting nearby. "Yesterday is the day before today," she said with a smile.

Arlo thought about that. Yesterday, it had rained. Yesterday, he stayed inside. Today, the sun was out. Today, he was at the park.

But the ducks were not at the pond now. The water was still and empty. Arlo grabbed a stick and poked at the grass. He waited. Blair waited too. They watched and watched.

"I wanted to give them bread," said Arlo. "I forgot it at home."

Then Ms. Suryanto stood up. She pulled some seeds from her bag. She poured them near the water. The seeds sat on the ground. Nothing came.

"Sometimes we just have to wait," said Ms. Suryanto.

Then they heard soft feet. One duck came out of the tall grass. Then two more. The ducks nibbled the seeds, one by one.

"Tomorrow we can come back," said Blair. "We can bring more seeds."

"Tomorrow," said Arlo. He waved at the ducks. "See you tomorrow!"

Grandma had a little card on her wall. It said "Hair Day." Today was Iris's turn for her very first haircut. Grandma drove her to the salon.

Iris sat in the big chair. It went up and up. The hairdresser, Ms. Santos, held shiny scissors. "Watch what I do first," said Ms. Santos. She picked up a comb. She combed Iris's hair until it lay smooth and neat. Then she made one snip. Iris counted in her head. One comb, one snip. Two combs, one snip. She waited to see more. Three combs, one snip.

"Grandma, why does she comb so much?" Iris asked. She watched closely and found her answer. When the comb stopped, the hair stuck up in a tuft. When the comb ran through, the hair sat neat, and the scissors cut a straight little line. "The comb keeps my hair neat for cutting," said Iris. Ms. Santos smiled. "That's right!"

Iris kicked her feet in the big chair. She got to see the cut hair on the floor. It curled like tiny springs. At the end, Ms. Santos gave her a card with a sticker on it. Iris held it all the way home. "My hair is short and neat," she said, and she spun around in a circle.

Victor sat at the little table in the school library. Ms. Walker gave him a pencil and paper. "Now we write your name," she said.

Victor held the pencil in his fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The first letter came out wobbly and big. It did not look like a V at all. Victor felt sad. "My letter is wrong," he said.

Ms. Walker put a pink thing in his hand. "This is called an eraser," she said. "Try it." Victor rubbed the pink eraser on the wobbly letter. He rubbed and rubbed. The wobbly line went away! The paper was clean again. What a surprise!

Victor held the pencil the new way, with his fingers. He made a V. It was a good V. He made an i, a c, and more letters. His friend Anayat came to look. "You wrote Victor!" said Anayat. Victor smiled and rubbed the eraser on his sleeve like a little drum. Then he wrote his name one more time.

John was at Grandma's house. He wanted to put on his coat all by himself. "I can do it," he said. He pushed his arm in one sleeve. Then he pushed his other arm in. "Look, Grandma! My coat is on!"

Now came the tricky part. The zipper. John pulled it up. It went crooked and stopped. He pulled it down. He tried again, slowly. This time the zipper went up, up, up to his chin. "Zipped!" said John. Grandma clapped her hands.

He ran outside to the big tree. A loud frog sat by the pond. "Ribbit!" said the frog. "Ribbit!" said John. Then he took off his coat to catch a bug. He dropped the coat in the grass and ran after the frog.

Later, John could not find his coat. He looked and looked. It was hiding in the tall grass! Grandma found it. "Next time, hang it on the hook," she said. She pointed to a little hook by the door. John hung his coat on the hook. It stayed up high, off the floor. "Good hook!" said John, and he patted it.

It was Blake's first day of school. She marched down the hallway with her new lunchbox. It was blue, with a huge dog on the front. Her tummy felt like popping corn.

At lunch, Blake saw a boy with the same blue lunchbox. "That is mine!" said the boy. "No, it is mine!" said Blake. Then Arnav opened the lid. "Look," he said. "My name is here. Arnav." Blake opened her lid. Her name was not there. Uh oh. Her lunchbox looked just like his. Which one was hers?

After lunch, Mr. Ramos helped. "Whose sandwich is this?" he asked. "I have cheese," said Arnav. "I have jam," said Blake. Mr. Ramos looked in both boxes. Arnav's name was on the jam box. So the jam box was Blake's! Mr. Ramos wrote Blake's name on her lid with a marker.

At pickup time, Blake's mom gave her a hug. "Will your lunchbox get lost again?" she asked. "No," said Blake. "My name will bring it back to me." Then she held up her lid and smiled at the letters.

Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Snow had fallen in the night. The snow covered the grass and the trees. Gabriel looked out the window. The snow was white, all white.

"I will draw the snow," said Gabriel. Grandma gave him white paper. Gabriel picked a crayon. He found a red crayon. Red was not snow. He found a yellow crayon. Yellow was not snow. He found a white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up on the white paper. Gabriel frowned. "Where did my snow go?"

Grandpa was looking at his map by the door. He waved Gabriel over. "Try this," said Grandpa. He gave Gabriel a blue paper. Gabriel drew with the white crayon. White lines showed up on the blue paper. "I see the snow!" said Gabriel. He drew white snow on the blue sky. He drew a green tree under the snow. He drew a red hat on a little yellow bird.

"Time for lunch," said Grandma. The soup was warm and salty. Gabriel waved at his picture while he ate. Outside, the real snow was still white on the grass. "Snow matches my crayon," said Gabriel, and he took one more bite.

Willow had a little bunny toy. She loved that bunny very much. But one morning, bunny was gone. Willow looked in her toy bag. Bunny was not there. She wanted to run to the big attic all by herself.

Then she remembered something. If you lose something, you tell your grown-up first. So Willow found her mom in the kitchen. "Bunny is lost," she said. "Will you look with me?"

Mom wiped her hands on a towel. "Yes, let us look together." They walked through the house side by side. They peeked under the bed. They found a yucky dust ball, but no bunny. Willow heard a scratch, scratch sound by the couch. Mom lifted the cushion. There was bunny!

Willow hugged bunny close. "We found her together," she said. Mom smiled and kissed the top of Willow's head. "Next time, tell me first too," said Mom. Willow nodded, and bunny's soft ear tickled her chin.

Lena sat at the little table. There was a tablet in front of her. Mr. Singh had put it there. Lena wanted to draw a yellow sun on it. Amari sat next to her, drawing already.

Lena pushed the screen with her whole hand. She pressed and pressed. The screen stayed dark. Amari looked over. "Try one finger," Amari said. Lena lifted one finger. She gave the screen a small tap. The screen lit up! Lena tapped a picture of a paintbrush. The drawing app opened. She picked the yellow color. She drew a big sun with a smile.

Brayden came to the table. He wanted a turn too. Lena drew one more yellow ray. Then she was done. "All done," she said. She tapped the button that closed the app. She helped Mr. Singh carry the tablet back to its basket.

Mr. Singh smiled. "You can have a turn tomorrow," he said. Lena waved to the tablet in the basket. "Bye, sun," she said.

Zoey sat at the little table. She had a big white card. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

Mr. Hoffmann pointed to the letter Z on the wall. "That is the first letter in your name," he said. "It says zzz."

Zoey picked up her crayon. She wrote zoey, with a small z first. She looked at the card. It looked almost right. But something was not right.

Alanna leaned over. "Look at my card," she said. Alanna had written Alanna. The A at the start was big and tall.

"A name starts with a big letter," said Arianna. "A big capital letter."

Zoey looked at Arianna's card too. Arianna had a big A at the start of Arianna.

So Zoey made a big Z. She pressed hard with her red crayon. Z-o-e-y. Now the Z was big and tall, like the girls' letters.

"That's it!" said Mr. Hoffmann. "Zoey starts with a big Z."

Zoey held up her card. "Z says zzz," she said. "And my name has a big Z!"

She pulled on her sweater. The card would go home in her pocket. "Maybe Mom will hang it up," she said.

"It's beautiful," said Alanna.

Zoey smiled and wrote it one more time. Big Z. Big and tall.

It was cold at daycare. Hayden put on his red scarf. Abbas had a blue scarf. "Let's race to the playground," said Abbas. They ran fast. Then they walked slow.

Moshe sat on the step. His scarf was very short. It did not cover his neck. "My neck is cold," said Moshe. Hayden looked at his own scarf. His scarf was long. It went around and around.

Hayden unwound his long scarf. He wound it around Moshe's neck too. Now the scarf was short for two boys, but it covered them both. They sat close together. Mr. Campbell came out with warm cocoa. "Hot cocoa for cold boys," he said. Moshe smiled and sipped. "Warm," said Moshe. Hayden squeezed his hand. "Warm," said Hayden too.

Addison sat in a big booth at the restaurant. A big screen filled the whole wall. The game was on. Her dad pointed at the ice.

"Where is the ball?" Addison asked.

Aylin slid in next to her. Aylin was from her class. Ethan sat across with his smooth cup of milk.

"There is no ball," said Aylin. She pointed at the ice. "That flat disc is called a puck."

Addison looked hard. The players ran on skates. Each one held a long stick. A player hit the puck with his stick. The puck slid fast across the smooth ice.

"I see it!" said Addison.

Another player hit the puck. It went into the net. The crowd on the screen cheered. Everyone in the restaurant clapped too.

Addison sipped her root beer. A player hit the puck again. It slid past the net and missed.

"Next time it will go in," Addison said. She watched the sticks tap the ice. Then she waved at the screen. "Go, puck, go!"

James went to the pharmacy with his dad. There was a little sink by the door. James had messy hands from the park.

"Time to wash," Dad said. James turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. He looked down. There were no bubbles. His hands were still sticky.

James looked at the empty soap bottle on the sink. "Dad, it's empty!" Dad found a new soap bottle. He put it by the sink.

James got one pump of soap. He rubbed his hands again. Now bubbles came! Big bubbles, little bubbles. James rubbed and rubbed. He counted to twenty while he rubbed. Dad helped him count.

Then James rinsed his hands. The bubbles went down the drain. Dad gave him a towel. James wiped his hands all dry.

Outside the window, a little boat went by on the river. "Clean hands," said James. He held Dad's hand all the way home.

Paint day was here. Charlotte looked at the paints. There were only three pots. "Where are the rainbow paints?" she asked. Mr. Ma smiled. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," he said. Charlotte frowned. "How can I paint a rainbow?" she asked. She thought for a minute. Then she had an idea.

She dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. She swirled them together on the paper. The spot turned orange! Charlotte gasped. One colour plus one colour made a new colour. Krish, the boy at the next table, leaned over. "How did you do that?" he asked. "Red and yellow make orange," said Charlotte. She mixed yellow and blue next. Green bloomed on the page.

Outside, a dog barked at the window. The door stood open, and the sun came in. Charlotte painted her rainbow, stripe by stripe. "There," she said. "Now I need purple." She dabbed her brush into blue, and then into red.

Hailey went to the library with her dad. It was cold outside, so winter hats were hanging by the door. Mr. Baptiste smiled at the desk.

"Story and craft time today," said Mr. Baptiste. Hailey ran to the craft table. Hayden and Erika were already there. Today they would make shape pictures!

Hailey wanted to draw a circle for the sun. She drew it. It came out wobbly and ugly. She frowned. "My circle looks funny," she said. Hayden's circle was wobbly too.

Then Hailey saw her cup of water. She had an idea. She held the cup upside down on her paper. She traced all around the bottom of the cup with her crayon. She lifted the cup up. A perfect circle! "Look, look!" she shouted. Erika clapped. Hayden begged to try. He traced around his cup too. His circle was perfect as well!

Hailey made more shapes. She cut a square for a house. She cut a triangle for the roof. She cut a rectangle for the door. Mr. Baptiste hung her picture on the wall. Hailey pointed up at it. "The sun is my best circle," she said.

Jasper sat on his bed. He held his little blue bag. "I want to go to Muhammed's house now," he said.

Dad sat down beside him. "Not now, Jasper. Today is today. Tomorrow we go."

"Where is tomorrow?" asked Jasper.

"Tomorrow is the day after today," said Dad. "First you sleep. Then you wake up. Then it is tomorrow."

Jasper frowned. "Sorry, little bag," he said. "You have to wait too."

He put the bag by the door. He put on his pajamas. He counted his bedtime things: one blanket, one bear, one kiss from Dad.

"Sleep, wake, then a new day," he said softly.

Jasper closed his eyes. He slept all night. He woke up when the sun came in. He looked at the door. The blue bag was still there, waiting.

"Today is the new day!" said Jasper. "It is tomorrow!"

He hugged the bag. He ran to find Dad. "Wake up, wake up! Now is tomorrow! Now we go to Muhammed's house!"

Dad laughed and picked him up. "Yes," said Dad. "Now we can go."

The wind came whooshing into the backyard. It was a noisy wind! Theo held out his hands to feel it. His fingers felt the cold air.

"Ida, come see!" Theo called. Ida ran over. The wind blew dust and bits of dirt. Some flew at Theo's face. He blinked fast, fast, fast. His eyes were okay!

Theo saw a hammer on the grass. He picked it up. It was heavy and hard. He put it down again.

Then he smelled flowers. He sniffed with his nose. Sweet! He tasted a berry his dad gave him. Yummy on his tongue.

"Why do I blink so much?" Theo asked.

"Your eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes," said Ida.

Theo blinked again. "My eyelashes are little helpers!" he said. Blink, blink, blink.

Charles went to the art studio with his dad. He brought his box of crayons. He wanted to draw a big red sun.

Charles sat at the little table. Clemence sat next to him. Elia sat next to her. "I will draw the sun," said Charles. He opened his box.

Uh oh. The crayons were soft. They bent like noodles. Charles tried to hold one. It flopped over in his hand. "My crayons are bendy!" he said.

"I left my box in the car," said his dad. "It was sunny and hot today." Charles touched a red crayon. It was warm and shiny. He pushed it on the paper. The soft crayon made a thick, shiny red mark. It did not look like a line. It looked like a fat red sun!

Charles pushed the crayon again. The red sun grew bigger. Elia said, "It looks like a real sun!" Clemence clapped her hands. Charles mixed the red sun with a soft orange crayon. The colors mixed into one big glow.

Ms. Bighorn came to look. "What a big sunny picture," she said. Charles held up his bendy crayon. He smiled at it. "You are my sun crayon," he said. He gave it one more push across the paper.

Eloise got a little card in the mail. It had her name on it. It was her first library card. "What does it do?" she asked. Her dad said, "It lets us borrow books. We take them back later."

At the library, Eloise looked and looked. She wanted a book about trucks. She saw books about cats. She saw books about soup. But no trucks. She could not find any.

Then she saw a woman at a big desk. The woman smiled. "I am the librarian," she said. "I work here. I help people find books." Eloise asked, "Can you find a truck book?" The librarian walked to a shelf. She pulled out a big red book. "Trucks!" said Eloise.

At home, Eloise read the truck book on the rug. Outside, rain went splash on the window. She waited and listened. Then she turned the page. "Big truck," she read. "Beep, beep," said Eloise, and she turned one more page.

Brielle ran to the pool with her friends Zaina and Maren. Today was her birthday party. Balloons bobbed by the water. Brielle wore a big paper hat. "Why does everyone make a fuss today?" she asked.

Grandma held out a small photo. "Look at this baby," she said. "This is you on the day you were born." Brielle looked and looked. The baby had tiny hands. "That was me?" she asked. Grandma nodded. "Your birthday is the day we celebrate the day you were born."

Brielle jumped up and down. "I was born!" she said. She chased Zaina and Maren around the pool. Then they ate crunchy snacks at the picnic table. Mom lit the candles, and everyone sang. Brielle blew and blew. The candles went out. "Happy birthday, Brielle!" said Ms. Krause, the swimming teacher. Brielle grinned. "It is my born day!"

Juliette wanted the big red blocks. But Conrad was using them now.

"Can I have the blocks?" Juliette asked.

"Later," said Conrad. "I am building a bear house."

Juliette sat down. She hugged her squishy bear. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Conrad. "I am still building."

Juliette watched him stack the blocks. One block fell down. Then another fell down.

"Is it later yet?" she asked again.

"Not yet," said Conrad. He put the blocks back. He added a roof.

Juliette looked out the window. A bird flew by. Then the bird flew away. The sky got a little darker.

"Is it later yet?" she asked.

Conrad stood up. "Yes! Now it is later. The bear house is done."

Juliette jumped up. Later did not come right away. Later came after the building, after the bird, after the waiting. She took the blocks and began her own tower.

"Do you want to help me?" she asked Conrad.

"Yes," said Conrad. "I will help now."

Mr. Mokoena smiled. "A tower for the bears," he said.

Juliette placed the last red block on top. "Our tower is tall," she said.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to make a house with paper shapes. He found a brown square for the wall. He found a long rectangle for the door. But the top of his house looked flat and strange. He needed a roof shape. He did not know which one.

Lexie sat next to him. She had her snack. Ms. Paquette had cut her sandwich into triangles. Lexie held one piece up. "Look, a triangle," she said. Ibrahim looked close. He touched the corners with one finger. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Lexie counted too. "One, two, three. A triangle has three sides and three corners."

Ibrahim asked, "Can a triangle be my roof?" Lexie said, "Yes! A pointy top like a house." He took a triangle from the shape box. It was brown like toast. He glued it on top. Pointy side up. Now his house had a roof.

Ms. Paquette walked by with a spoon of glue to share. "What a fine house," she said. Ibrahim pointed at the roof. "Triangle! One, two, three corners," he yelled with joy. Lexie laughed and clapped. She was still hungry, so Ibrahim gave her one of his crackers. Then he drew a yellow sun. It was a big circle in the sky. "My house is done," he said.

Maya went to her dad's office. Dad had a tablet on his desk. Maya wanted to draw on it.

Dad showed her the round button. Maya pressed it. The screen lit up. "I did it!" she said. Dad helped her find the drawing app. It had a little paintbrush on it. Maya tapped it. The app opened. Now she could draw a sun.

Maya put her cup of milk on the desk. It sat right by the tablet. Dad shook his head. "The tablet stays away from drinks," he said. Maya picked up her cup. She carried it to the little table by the window. Then she ran back, fast as a bunny.

Maya drew a big yellow sun. She drew a red cat too. Then she was done. Dad showed her the top button again. Maya held it. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in the drawer, all by herself.

"I can do it," said Maya. Dad clapped his hands.

Alice was hungry for a snack. Her dad set a bowl of strawberries on the table. The berries were red and shiny. Alice looked at them with her eyes. She heard a little "plip" as one fell off the bowl. "Be careful," her dad said with a smile.

Alice picked up a big strawberry. She touched it with her fingers. It felt bumpy with tiny seeds. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled so sweet. She took a big bite. Mmm, it tasted sweet and juicy too.

Then Alice had a funny idea. She pinched her nose closed. She took another bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. Her eyes went wide. She let go of her nose. She sniffed and bit again. Now it tasted sweet once more.

She tried it again with a small berry. Nose closed, plain taste. Nose open, sweet taste. "Dad, my nose helps me taste!" she said. Her dad laughed and gave her one more strawberry. Alice sniffed it first, very slowly, like a little bunny.

Nora ran to the playground gate. She held her dad's hand. It was a windy day. The wind pushed her hair over her nose.

Then Nora saw the small bikes. Hoorain was riding one. Nora wanted to ride one too. She jumped on a red bike and pushed the pedals.

Mr. Çelik knelt down. "Where is your helmet?" he asked. Nora looked at the helmet rack. One, two, three helmets sat there. She got off the bike and ran back.

She put on the blue helmet. It clicked under her chin. Then she rode round and round, past one tree, past two trees. Hoorain rode beside her.

Near the fence, Henley was waiting for his turn. He held his helmet in both hands. The wind was cold on Nora's cheeks, but her head felt snug and warm.

She rang the little bell. Ding, ding, ding. Hoorain laughed and rang hers too.

Nolan sat at the small table. Ms. Wardak put a card in front of him. The card had a letter K on it. The K was bumpy. Nolan could feel it with his finger.

"Now we write K," said Ms. Wardak. Nolan picked up his crayon. He wrote a K. But it came out wrong. The legs went the wrong way. Nolan made a sad face. "Try again," said Ms. Wardak kindly.

Thomas sat next to him. Thomas traced his letter with his finger first. He went down, then up to the corner, then up again. His K looked good.

Nolan watched. Then he put his finger on the bumpy K. He traced it. Down, up to the corner, up again. The bumps tickled his finger. He traced it again and again.

Then Nolan picked up his crayon. Down, up to the corner, up again. He looked at his paper. The K was right! "I did it!" said Nolan. Ms. Wardak smiled. "Hang it on the wall," she said. She pointed to a spot above the coat hooks.

Nolan carried his paper to the wall. He hung it up next to Avery's letter A. He stood back and looked at it. "K," he said out loud. "Kuh, kuh, K."

Stella stood on her stool in the kitchen. She wanted to make pancakes with Dad. The bowl was big and white. Dad had a wooden spoon ready.

"First we need eggs," said Dad. He put two eggs on the counter. "You crack the shell open to get the egg out." Stella held one egg in her small hand. She tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap, tap. The shell cracked. She pulled it apart. The egg slid out into the bowl. "I did it!" said Stella.

Then she saw something in the bowl. A little bit of shell had fallen in. Stella took a spoon. She fished out the bit of shell. She had to try two times, but then she found it and lifted it out. Dad smiled. The batter got milk, flour, and a stir from the wooden spoon. Stella stirred slow, then fast.

Dad poured the batter onto the hot pan. Stella watched from her stool. The pancakes puffed up like little clouds. Soon the family sat down to eat. Stella took a big bite. "I made these," she said. "With eggs from inside the shells."

Edouard went to the park with his friend Kayce. Kayce had a big red ball. Edouard wanted to bounce it very high. But first, Kayce said, the ball was stuck under a bush.

Edouard got down on his knees. He touched the leaves with his hands. They were sharp and scratchy. He pulled the ball out. Then a man came with a loud leaf blower. It roared and roared. Edouard did not like the loud sound at all. Kayce put her hands over her ears. Edouard put his hands over his ears too. The sound got quieter. "Better," he said.

The leaf blower blew the leaves far away. Edouard could smell the leaves and the green grass. Ms. Chatterjee, the park helper, came with cold water. "Will the loud sound come back?" Edouard asked. "No, it is done now," she said. Edouard drank the water. It tasted cool and good.

Then Edouard and Kayce bounced the red ball. It went up, up, up, round like the moon in the sky at night. Edouard watched it come down. Kayce caught it. "Your turn," she said. Edouard held out his hands.

Zayn sat at the little table. He had cardboard, glue, and a marker. He wanted to make a bus. The bus could drive all over the rug.

He cut out a big rectangle for the bus. He drew four square wheels. He glued them on. "Go, bus, go!" he said. He pushed the bus on the rug. The bus would not roll. It just slid and flopped over. Hmm.

Lyanna sat down next to him. She was rolling her toy car. It went fast and far. Zayn looked at her car. Its wheels were round, like circles. How interesting, he thought. Could round wheels roll?

He asked Ms. Leung for help. She held the scissors and cut four circle wheels for him. Zayn glued them on. He pushed the bus again. This time it rolled! It rolled all the way to Lilly's feet. "Beep beep!" said Lilly. She pushed it back.

Zayn turned the bus over and over. He touched the round wheels. They felt smooth and cool. "Round wheels roll," he said. He made another bus with triangle wheels, just to see. That one flopped too. So he went back to circles. Then he drove his busy bus all around the rug, round and round.

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had paper and glue. He wanted to make a car.

"I need to cut the paper," he said. He saw the big scissors on the counter. He reached for them.

His dad shook his head. "Those are too big," Dad said. He handed Mohamed small scissors. "These are safety scissors. They have round tips. You cut while I watch."

Mohamed held the safety scissors. He squeezed them on the paper. Snip, snip, snip. The paper fell into little bits.

Mohamed pasted the bits on a flat sheet. "This is my car," he said. "It is blue." The doorbell rang. It was Kelsey.

"Wow," said Kelsey. "Can I try too?"

Dad gave Kelsey her own safety scissors. Kelsey snipped while Dad watched. The paper bits fell like snow.

Mohamed glued a round bit on his car. "Look, a wheel," he said. "Now my car can go."

Kelsey laughed and clapped her hands. Mohamed held his car up high. "Beep, beep," he said. "Off we go!"

Emilia went to the farmers' market with her dad. She wanted a little plant for her garden. She picked a small tomato plant in a pot.

At home, she dug a hole in the soil. But then Emilia saw a weed near her plant. She grabbed it and pulled. Out it came, all wiggly. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom. "Look, Dad! Strings!" she said.

Dad laughed. "Those are the roots. A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Emilia looked at her tomato plant. She put it in the hole. She spread the roots down, so they could live in the dark soil. Then she patted the dirt on top.

Celeste came to see. "Where is your plant hiding?" she asked.

"It lives under the sun," said Emilia. "And its feet go down!"

Each day Emilia watered it. One morning, a sleepy sun came up, and there was a tiny yellow flower. Emilia clapped her hands.

"My plant grew up!" she said. "And its roots grew down!"

She ran to tell Celeste, holding her watering can high.

Gianna wanted to draw a cat. She had a tablet in her bag. She pressed the round button on the side. The screen lit up. It glowed bright and green.

She tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. Gianna drew a spotted cat with long whiskers. She gave it a piece of cheese to eat. Then she was done. The screen stayed on and bright.

"Does it stay awake?" she asked. Her dad shook his head. "Not if you press the button."

Gianna pressed the power button. The screen went dark. Pressing the button when you are done makes the screen go dark. She slid the tablet into the basket.
