"Night night, cat," said Gianna.

Carter held the small box. Something inside went squeak. It was his new puppy!

Dad drove to the doctor. Carter felt worried. "The puppy does not like doctors," he said. Dad smiled.

The waiting room was full of animals. A cat sat in a lap. A bunny sat in a cage. "Where are the people patients?" Carter asked.

A kind man came out. "I am Mr. Nair," he said. "I am a vet. A vet is a doctor for animals." The puppy barked, as if to say hello.

Mr. Nair looked at the puppy. He felt her smooth fur. He mixed some food in a bowl. Carter held his puppy's toy so she would feel calm. Mr. Nair gave her a clean bill of health.

At home, Carter put the bowl down. The puppy ate it all up. Then she curled up next to Carter's shoe and slept. "Goodnight, puppy," Carter whispered.

Rose and her family were going on a big trip. They stopped at a roadside diner to eat. Rose sat in a red booth. She put her backpack on the seat. Inside the backpack was her teddy bear, Mr. Bits.

The waiter brought pancakes. Rose ate slowly. She held Mr. Bits in her hand. The pancakes smelled sweet and warm. Then it was time to go to the airport.

At the airport, Rose put her backpack on a moving belt. The backpack went into a machine. It was gone. Rose felt bad. "Where is Mr. Bits?" she cried. A kind worker said, "Watch the other side." Rose watched. Out came her backpack, safe on the belt. Rose opened it fast. There was Mr. Bits!

"The machine checked what was inside," said Rose's mom. Rose gave the worker a big smile. She held Mr. Bits tight all the way to the plane.

John was at Grandma's house. Mom came in with a little blanket. Inside was John's new baby brother. "He is so small," said John. He touched the baby's tiny hand.

Grandma sat in her big chair. Mom put the baby in her arms. Grandma put one hand under the baby's head. John watched. "Why do you hold his head like that?" he asked. "A new baby cannot hold up his own head," said Grandma. "So we hold it for him."

John wanted to help. He rolled a soft ball across the rug. The baby did not look. The baby could not even hold up his head yet. So John pushed his toy truck next to Grandma's chair instead. "I will wait until you are bigger," he said.

Then it was time for Dad to carry the baby. Dad put his big hand under the baby's head too. John saw the hand go under, and the head stayed safe and still. John leaned close and whispered, "I will hold your head someday, little brother. I promise."

Wren stood in the kitchen. Her coat lay on the chair. "I will do it myself," she said.

She put her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. She pulled the zipper up. It went up, then it went down. She tried again. Up, up, up. The zipper stayed. "I did it!" said Wren.

Her mom handed her mittens. "Here are your mittens for school." Wren held them in her hands. She could not carry her lunch too. Then she saw the little pocket on her coat. She tucked one mitten in. She tucked the other mitten in. Both mittens fit inside. The pocket held them snug. "Mittens live in there," said Wren. She picked up her lunch bag. She remembered her mittens were safe. She smiled a pretty smile.

"Ready for school," said her mom.

Wren zipped her coat one more time, just to see it go up.

Noah planted tiny seeds in the school garden. He patted the dirt with his hands. Ms. Reyes gave him a watering can. "Now we water them," she said. Noah tipped the can. Drip, drip, drip.

Every day Noah came back to look. Malaika came too. They saw little green leaves. Then they saw curly stems. The stems climbed up a tall stick.

One day Malaika picked a long green pod. "What is this?" she asked. She squeezed it. Pop! It opened up. Inside was a row of little green peas. Noah picked one pod too. Pop! More peas, all in a neat line. "Peas grow inside pods," said Ms. Reyes. Noah laughed and clapped his hands.

Noah had a small hurt on his finger from a stick. "It stings," he said. Ms. Reyes kissed it better. Then she picked a pink flower from a pot by the garden floor and put it in Noah's pocket. "Snack time," she said. Noah held his pod all the way home.

Ayla sat on the grass at the big field. Her friends Anahat and Leopald sat close by. The red team and the blue team were playing soccer.

The blue team ran and ran. They ran so fast! "The blue team runs a lot," said Ayla. "Maybe they win."

Mr. Chaudhry smiled. "Look at the board," he said. Ayla looked up. The board said red two, blue one.

"Red has more points," said Ayla. "Does red win?"

The whistle blew. The game was over. The red team jumped and cheered. They got a big shiny cup.

"So the team with more points wins," said Ayla. "Not the team that runs more?"

"Look, mud on the ball," said Leopald. The muddy ball rolled to Ayla's feet. She kicked it back, and everyone laughed.

It was Matthew's birthday. His mom brought cupcakes to the classroom. The party would be in the big room after snack time. Matthew wanted all his friends to come. So he made invitations with crayons.

Taim looked at his invitation. He was worried. "What if I get lost?" he said. "Where is the party?" Matthew looked at his paper. Oh no. He had drawn a cake and a balloon. But he had not written where. Taim had the wrong paper to help him. Hasrat had one too. She could not tell where to go either.

Matthew got a new card. He wrote the room number on it. He drew the cubbies too. "Now it says where," said Matthew. He gave the new card to Taim. Taim smiled. "The big room! I know that room."

After snack time, everyone came to the big room. Nobody got lost. Then the door opened. Mr. Demir walked in with a tall tower of cupcakes. The top one had a candle. His mom lit it with a match, far from the children. Matthew made a wish. "Happy birthday, Matthew!" said Taim. Matthew blew out the candle.

Brooks sat at the dinner table. The room went dark. "Oh no," he said. He could not see his plate.

His nose sniffed the air. He could smell the warm pasta. His ears heard it bubble in the pot. His hands felt the table, soft and smooth. "Where is my fork?" he asked. His fingers touched a spoon instead.

Then his mom clicked on a lamp. Light filled the room. Now Brooks could see everything. His eyes found the fork right away. "There it is!" he said.

He took a bite. The sauce tasted sweet and tangy on his tongue. He piled his pasta into a big mountain.

Ms. Harper, their neighbour, knocked on the door. She brought fast bread rolls. "The light helps me see," Brooks told her, and he took another big bite.

Kayden stood on the warm sand. He was learning his five senses with Ms. Pierre.

"Ears hear," said Ms. Pierre. Kayden heard the big waves go splash. "Eyes see." Kayden saw a red bucket. "Hands touch." He touched a smooth, white shell. "Tongue tastes." He drank his water because he was thirsty. He remembered the taste of salty water, yuck.

Then Kayden stopped. He sniffed the air. "I smell cookies," he said. "I smell them with my nose!" But he did not see any cookies. He looked left. He looked right. No cookies anywhere.

"Your nose can smell some things before you can see them," said Hayden. Hayden was his friend from school. "My nose found the cookie truck once!"

Kayden followed his nose. Sniff, sniff, sniff. He walked past a sleeping pet dog. He walked past Elowyn's sandcastle. The smell got stronger and stronger.

Then he saw it. A little cart with cookies baking inside. A grown-up was taking them out with big gloves. Ms. Pierre bought one cookie for each child.

Kayden took a big bite. "My tongue tastes it too," he said. "My nose found them first!"

Elowen giggled and clapped. Hayden gave Kayden a high five.

"Five senses," said Kayden. "Nose, ears, eyes, hands, tongue. I did it!"

He licked the last crumb off his thumb.

Beatrice sat on the school bus. Her purple backpack sat next to her. Her brother sat behind her, humming a soft song. Beatrice had a little book on her lap.

Landon sat down beside her. "What is that?" he asked.

"It is my letter book," said Beatrice. She pointed at a page. "That big letter is A. The wall in our room has a big A too."

Then she saw a small, round letter below it. "But this one is new," she said. "It looks like a little circle with a tail."

Landon leaned close. "That is a small a," he said. "It is the same letter. Big capital letters and small lowercase letters are the same letters."

Beatrice blinked. She put her finger on the big A. Then she put her finger on the small a. "Same letter," she said slowly.

"It makes the same sound too," said Landon. He took a bite of his apple. "Ah," he said, and they both laughed.

The bus hummed under them. It was warm in the sun. Beatrice turned more pages. Big B, small b. Big D, small d. "Same letters," she said, again and again.

Adelie called from her seat, "What are you doing?"

"Letter hunting," said Beatrice. She held up the book so Adelie could see.

The bus stopped at school. Mr. Demetriou stood at the door, smiling. Beatrice hopped down the steps with her book. "Small a," she said to him, pointing at the page, "same as big A."

Mr. Demetriou clapped his hands. Beatrice ran up the walk, holding her book tight against her purple backpack.

Maeve stood at the kitchen table. Her tummy rumbled. She wanted toast, but not plain toast. She wanted toast with shapes on it. Her dad was at the stove, being careful with the hot pan. "Can I help?" Maeve asked. "You can fix the toast at the table," said her dad.

Halima came over to play. Maeve laid out the food. A round cracker was a circle. A cheese slice was a square. A tortilla chip was a triangle. And a graham cracker was a rectangle. "Where is the square?" asked Halima. "Here," said Maeve. She turned the cheese so one corner pointed up. Halima frowned. "Now it is a new shape," said Halima. Maeve turned the cheese back. The corner sat flat again. It was the same square! Maeve turned it once more, corner up. Still a square, just turned. Halima laughed. "A square turned is still a square," she said.

The girls made a shape picture on their plates. Circle, square, triangle, rectangle. Then they ate every shape up. "That square was my best one," said Maeve. She carried her plate to the sink. Her dad gave her a warm hug.

Joshua went to the art gallery with his class. Ms. Johansson showed them a big paint table. There were three plates of paint. One plate was red. One plate was yellow. One plate was blue.

"I want green," said Deborah. "I like green."

Joshua put his brush in the blue paint. Then he put it in the yellow paint. He stirred on his paper. The paint turned green! It looked wet and shiny.

Deborah leaned close. "Green!" she said. She poked the paint with her finger. It was still wet. Her fingerprint stayed there. The green got a smudge.

"Wet paint can smudge if you touch it," said Ms. Johansson. "We have to wait."

Joshua made a red and yellow circle next. It turned orange. It smelled like paint, sharp and fresh. He wanted to poke it. He held his hands behind his back.

"I will wait," said Joshua. He counted slowly. One, two, three.

Arzoyi waited too. She blew soft air on her paper. The paint got dry. Then she poked it. No smudge! Her paper stayed smooth.

Joshua touched his orange circle. It was dry. No fingerprint. Deborah clapped for him.

"Look at my green," Deborah said. "It has my finger in it. That is okay. I like it too."

Luke sat at the kitchen table. His mom put down two bowls of crackers. "Which one has more?" she asked. Luke pointed at the big bowl. "That one!" He counted them. The big bowl had six. The little bowl had two.

His friend Aviraj came over with his toy plane. The yellow plane zoomed over the bowls. A cracker fell off the table. Luke picked it up and put it in the little bowl. He counted again. Two and one made three. Still fewer than six.

Aviraj pointed at the little bowl. "This one has fewer," he said. Luke nodded. Fewer meant the small amount. More meant the big amount. His mom gave each boy an apple. "One apple for you. One apple for Aviraj. Same, same!" Luke laughed and took a big bite.

Peyton stood in the kitchen. She wanted a nice cold drink. Her cup sat on the table. It held apple juice.

Mom gave her a small ice cube. "You can put it in," said Mom. Peyton picked it up with her fingers. Ooh! The ice cube felt so cold. She dropped it in the cup fast. Plop! It went splash. Peyton laughed. She touched the cup. The cup felt cold too. The ice made her juice cold.

Peyton looked at the ice. It was clear and shiny. She heard it go click, click on the glass. She sniffed the juice. It smelled like sweet apples. She took a sip. Mmm, cold and sweet on her tongue.

Hazel came to play. Peyton gave her an ice cube too. Hazel held it in her hand. "So cold!" said Hazel. She dropped it in her cup. Plop! The two girls watched the ice dance in the juice.

Mom sat close by. "All safe and cozy," she said. Peyton took another sip. The cold drink felt just right.

Nolan sat on the school bus. He had letter cards in his lap. He wanted to put them in a row.

He put A down. Then B. Then C. Then N. Then M. Then D. Was that right? He scratched his head.

Lyra sat next to him. "Sing it," she said. "The alphabet song sings the letters in order." Nolan began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." He stopped. Where did M go?

He sang some more. "H, I, J, K, L, M, N." M came before N! He moved the M card. Then he put the N card after it. The row looked better now.

A noisy truck went by outside. The bus began to drive again. Nolan sang the whole song from A to Z. He tapped each card as he sang. All the letters were in order.

Mr. Santos looked back from his seat. "That is a long, long row," he said. Nolan grinned and sang the song one more time. When he got to Z, Lyra clapped. "Now do it fast!" she said. Nolan took a big breath and began.

Lena wanted to see the bubbles. Dad had a pot on the little stove in the backyard. White steam went up, up, up. Lena took a step closer. Then she took another step.

Dad held out his hand. "Stay back, stay safe," he said. Lena stopped. The steam rose high over the pot. Dad put his hand near it, far above. He pulled his hand back fast. "The steam is hot," he said. "Steam can burn." Lena looked at her own small hands. She held them behind her back.

Her friend Aliya came to play. Aliya wanted to see the bubbles too. "Stay back, stay safe," Lena said. The two kids stood by the fence, far from the pot. Soon Dad called, "The corn is ready!" He carried the pot away all by himself. The kids sat on the grass. The corn was warm and good. Aliya smiled. "You are a kind kid," she said. Lena smiled too. The corn would grow tall in the garden next year, and they would watch it from far, far back. "Stay back, stay safe," said Lena, and she clapped her hands.

Olivier was going to the dentist for the first time. His mom took his hand at the door. The waiting room had a picture of a lion on the wall. The lion had big white teeth. "I wonder how many teeth a lion has," Olivier said.

A kind dentist called Mr. Rahman came out. "Hello, Olivier," he said. "Let's look at your teeth." The chair went up and down. That was funny. The light was bright, not cloudy at all. Mr. Rahman counted Olivier's teeth one by one.

Then it was time to brush. Mr. Rahman put minty toothpaste on a little brush. He brushed all around. Soon Olivier's mouth was full of white foam. It tasted like mint. Olivier was about to swallow it.

Then he remembered what Mr. Rahman had told Georgia at school. Georgia had asked about the foam, and Mr. Rahman had said, "You spit it out, not swallow it." Olivier turned his head. He spat the foam into the sink. It went down with a swirl.

"Good job," said Mr. Rahman. "Your teeth are clean and shiny." Olivier looked in the little mirror. His teeth were white like the lion's teeth. "Can I take a sticker?" he asked. "Yes," said Mr. Rahman, and handed him a shiny gold tooth sticker.

Ivy had one toy drum. Her friend Kailey came to play. Kailey saw the drum. "I want to bang it," said Kailey. Ivy grabbed it fast. "My drum!" she said. Kailey's face went sad. She sat on the floor.

Ivy's mom brought two cups of milk. Ivy took a sip. She looked at Kailey. Ivy tapped the drum one time. "Want to try?" she asked. Kailey smiled and banged it. Boom, boom! Then Kailey held it out. "Your turn," she said. Ivy banged it too. Boom!

They took turns all morning. Ivy played for a while. Then Kailey played for a while. "That is smart sharing," said Ivy's mom. Later, they went outside to dig in the sand. "You are fun to play with," said Kailey. Ivy banged the drum one more time. "Boom!" she said.

Maeve stood at the hotel pool. Her toes wiggled on the warm tiles. Her friend Rudy was already in the water.

"I want to swim way over there," Maeve said. She pointed to the far side. "Where the big kids jump in."

Ms. Nkosi held her hand. "Come to the shallow end first," she said. "This end is shallow. That end is deep."

Maeve stepped in. The water came up to her tummy. She giggled. "It's like a big bath!"

She kicked her legs, slow at first. Then faster. "Look at me!" she splashed.

"Hey, you splashed my feather!" Rudy said. He held up a wet pool toy shaped like a feather. It dripped and drooped. "Now it's a sad feather." He laughed.

"Sorry!" Maeve said. She swam a little more. Then she looked across the pool. The big kids stood in water up to their chins.

Maeve squinted. "Ms. Nkosi, the water is taller over there."

"That's the deep end," Ms. Nkosi said.

"Then I'll stay here," Maeve said. "Where the water is small, like me."

She pulled her rubber ring close and floated on her back. The ceiling lights blinked at her. "Rudy," she called, "come float with me. The shallow end is the best end."

Rudy paddled over. "Only if no more splashing my feather."

Maeve grinned. "No promises."

Mila sat on the school rug. Mr. Bui had big news. "A puppet show is coming today," he said. Mila felt so excited. Her legs wanted to bounce. Her mouth wanted to shout. She bounced and bumped into Amber. Amber dropped her red crayon and looked sad. "Sorry," Mila said. She picked up the crayon. Then Mila felt excited again. She jumped up high and shouted, "Puppets!" Maeve covered her ears. Mila saw that her shouting made Maeve scared. Mila sat down. She put her hands in her lap. She squeezed them tight and counted, "One, two, three." The bouncing feeling got small and slow, like ice cream starting to melt. The door opened. The puppets had big yellow shapes on them. Mila clapped her hands softly. "I waited," she whispered to Amber. Amber smiled and made room on the rug.

Miles wanted to hide. His dad was in the bathroom, filling the big tub. "Can I hide here?" Miles asked. "You can hide behind the towel," Dad said.

Miles stood behind the towel. Then he covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the tub. He could not see Dad. He could not see the bucket of toys.

Dad laughed. "I can still see you, Miles." Miles peeked. His eyes saw Dad smiling. His ears heard the water splash. His nose smelled the sweet soap. His hands felt the soft towel.

"I want to try," Miles said. Dad covered his own eyes. "Now I cannot see you," Dad said. Miles tapped Dad's arm. Dad's hands found him and hugged him.

Then Miles put one toe in the tub. "Warm," he said. Dad helped him in. Miles splashed. Water went splash, splash. Dad held the soap near. "Smell this," he said. Miles sniffed. "Sweet!"

Miles closed his eyes again, just for fun. Everything went dark. He opened them. There was Dad, all along.

Lena sat on the big rug at the little temple. Mr. Augustin played his drum. Boom, boom, boom. Lena wanted to clap along, but her hands went too fast. "Try again," said Mr. Augustin. Lena watched the drum. Boom. She clapped. Boom. Her hands matched the drum now. Mr. Augustin smiled.

"Now we will sing," he said. Indie sang a loud, loud song. The song was so loud. Then the teacher showed them a baby, sleeping in a heavy blanket nearby. "A song can be sung loudly or softly," said Mr. Augustin. Lena sang her nursery rhyme very softly, like a little whisper. The baby kept sleeping. Indie sang softly too. They counted each clap, one number at a time, as they sang. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. Lena sang again, soft as a feather.

Lucas ran into his classroom. His friend Emaan was already there. "Good morning, Lucas!" said Emaan. Lucas stopped. "How do you know it is morning?" he asked. "We call it morning when we wake up and eat breakfast," said Emaan. "I woke up today and ate eggs. So it is morning now."

Lucas thought about that. Yesterday he had woken up late. He had no time for breakfast. His tummy had growled all morning. Today he ate a big bowl first. Now his tummy felt happy. That was the difference. Waking up and eating made the morning.

Ms. Buchanan rang the bell. "Snack time comes later," she said. Lucas sat down to wait. He looked out the window. A red leaf began to fall. It landed softly on the grass.

At last Ms. Buchanan called, "Snack time now!" Lucas grinned at Emaan. "Morning is over. Now is snack." Emaan laughed and passed him an apple.

Alexander went to the store with his mom. He saw apples, and he wanted one. He tugged his mom's sleeve. "Give me an apple!" he said. His mom shook her head and went on shopping. Alexander watched a boy at the bread shelf. The boy said, "May I have bread, please?" The baker smiled and gave him a bun. Alexander counted on his fingers. One, try loud. No apple. Two, try "please." He walked back to his mom. "Apple, please?" he asked. His mom smiled big this time. She put an apple in the basket. Then she let Alexander hold it.

At the checkout, Alexander put the apple on the belt. "Thank you," said the cashier, and she gave him a sticker of an ant. "Thank you," Alexander said back. He held the sticker up high. In the car, his mom washed the apple and cut it with a safe knife. The apple was sweet and yummy. Alexander chewed slowly and thought about the bread boy. Then he drew an ant on the foggy window with his finger. "Ant, please," he said to the window, and he laughed. His mom laughed too, and they drove home with the sticker on his hand.

Aria woke up under her warm blanket. The sun came in the window. Her tummy made a little rumble. "Hmm, what was that?" she wondered. She could smell toast from the kitchen.

Aria got dressed all by herself. Socks first, then her red dress. Then she padded to the kitchen. On the shelf she saw the cookie jar. Cookies! she thought. She reached up on tiptoe.

"Not yet," said her dad with a smile. "Your tummy slept all night. It needs the first meal of the day. That meal is called breakfast." He held up two plates. "You can pick. Toast or yogurt?"

Aria looked at the toast. She looked at the yogurt. The cookies had to wait. "Toast, please," she said. She put the bread in the basket herself. Her dad put it near the stove, where it was safe.

The toast popped up warm and hard on the outside. Aria took a big bite. Her tummy felt happy. After breakfast, she would wash up, brush her hair, and play. Maybe the cookies could come later, after lunch. She patted the cookie jar on her way to get her brush. "Wait for me," she whispered.

Sofia walked into the school computer lab with her class. Mr. Nkosi held up a tablet. "First, we press the round button," he said. Sofia pressed the round button. The screen lit up. It was like magic.

She tapped the drawing app. A big white page appeared. Sofia drew a blue lake with green grass around it. She drew a little duck on the lake. Her friend Emberly leaned over. "That duck is so cute," Emberly said. Sofia smiled and drew a tiny duck friend.

Then it was time to go. Sofia put the tablet on a chair and started to walk away. Annie came over to sit down. "Wait," Sofia said. She grabbed the tablet just in time. Mr. Nkosi pointed to the shelf. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place." Sofia slid it into its spot on the shelf. "That was smart," said Annie.

Peyton ran to the sink. Lunchtime was next, and she was hungry. She pumped soap into her hands. Then she rinsed it off fast, super fast, and ran to the line.

Ms. Hamdan looked at her hands. "Peyton, come back, please. The soap needs more time. We scrub for twenty seconds. That is a long, slow count." Peyton sighed. Her tummy was hungry and her arms felt tired.

Vamika stood next to her at the sink. "Count with me," said Vamika. "One, two, three..." They scrubbed and counted together. The bubbles grew big and white. "Ten, eleven, twelve..." Peyton wiggled her fingers like little fish. "Nineteen, twenty!" Then they rinsed.

At the table, Peyton looked at her clean hands. They smelled like flowers. She took a big bite of her sandwich. Outside, the sun was warm on the window. After snack, Peyton marched back to the sink all by herself. "One, two, three..." Sylas heard her and came to count too.

Grace stood on the warm sand. Her toes wiggled in it. "The sand feels fuzzy," said Grace. Ms. Singh smiled. "That is your skin," she said. "Skin tells you how things feel."

Grace and her friend Aydin sat down for a snack. Ms. Singh held up a lemon slice. "Close your eyes," she said. "Guess sweet or sour." Grace put the lemon on her tongue. Her mouth made a funny face. "Sour!" she said. Aydin laughed and clapped.

Next came a little cup of ice. Grace licked it. "Cold," she said. "And sweet! It is juice ice." Her tongue told her so. Aydin tried one too. "Sweet," he said. They both licked again. Then they waited for more juice. They watched the waves. The ice got smaller and smaller in the sun.

After the snack, Grace ran to the water. The sea touched her feet. She could hear the big waves crash. She could smell the salty air. "My ears hear the sea," said Grace. "My nose smells it."

"Can you taste the sea?" asked Aydin. Grace touched a wet finger to her tongue. "Salty," she said. "Sour lemon, sweet ice, salty sea. My tongue knows them all." Then she jumped over a little wave and laughed all the way back up the beach.

Natalie ran into Raina's kitchen. "Toast time!" said Raina's grandma. She put two warm slices on the plate. Natalie picked up the hard butter from the fridge. She pushed it on the toast. The bread tore. A hole! "Oh no," said Natalie. "My toast has a hole." She was afraid to try again. Raina's grandma set out a soft dish of butter. "This one sat out," she said. Natalie dipped her knife. She spread the soft butter. It slid on so easily! No hole at all. The toast turned shiny and gold. Then Raina poured milk into cups. Natalie poured her own. Not one drop spilled! Natalie took a big bite. "Best toast ever," she said. "Can we do it again tomorrow?"

Evan ran onto the court at the community center. He wore his real team shirt. It had a big green number one. His friend Loan was there too. The coach gave Evan the ball.

"Score a basket!" Loan said. "Get the ball through the hoop." Evan looked up. The hoop was high, high up. He pushed the ball with both hands. It hit the rim. It fell down. No basket. Evan tried again. Miss. Again. Miss.

Then Evan had an idea. He stood closer to the hoop. He aimed up, not out. He pushed the ball soft and high. It went up, up, up. Then it dropped right through the net. Swish! Loan clapped. Ms. González, watching from the bench, clapped too. "You did it!" she called. Evan passed the ball to Loan. "Now you," Evan said.

Leon was at home in the kitchen. Mom had baked cookies. The cookies sat on a big blue plate. Leon wanted to count them all by himself.

He touched each cookie with one finger. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the cookies on the small plate. "One, two." Leon looked at both plates. The big plate had more. He could see it. He told Mom, "This plate has more cookies." Mom smiled and gave him a cup of water to drink.

Emmy came over to play. Emmy was grumpy because she had no cookies at her house. So Mom gave each of them one cookie. Leon watched Emmy hide her cookie behind her cup, then eat it slowly. Leon ate his too.

Leon counted again. "Three, four," he said, as two cookies went away. Then Dad came in and took more. Leon counted one left. Then Emmy took the last one. Leon looked down at the plate. He tried to count. There was nothing to touch.

"Mom, how many now?" he asked. Mom looked at the plate. "Zero," she said. "Zero means none. There are zero cookies left." Leon nodded. He held up the empty plate. "Zero cookies," he said. Emmy laughed and clapped her hands.

Weston sat at the big art table. He was making a paper crown. Ms. Gupta helped him cut the shapes. Then Weston put glue on each point. He pressed the pieces together.

"Now can I wear it?" Weston asked.

"Let's see," said Ms. Gupta.

Weston picked up the crown. Oh no! The pieces began to slide. One piece slid right off and dropped to the table. Weston's lip went down.

"Is the glue still wet?" said Ms. Gupta. "Wet glue needs time to dry before the pieces hold together."

Weston touched the glue with one finger. It felt cold and sticky. He looked at the shiny wet spot. How long would it take? Would it dry like a puddle in the sun?

Robyn sat down next to him. She was gluing a red star. "Mine slid too," she said. "Now I wait."

So Weston put the pieces back. He pressed them down. Then he waited. He watched the glue. The shiny wet spots grew smaller and smaller. Slowly they looked dull and dry.

Weston picked up the crown again. He lifted it up high. The pieces stayed on! Not one piece slid off. The crown held together.

"I did it!" said Weston. Ms. Gupta smiled.

Weston put the crown on his head. Robyn clapped her hands. Then she held up her dry red star. "Look, mine held too," she said.

Weston spun around once, but not too fast, so he would not get dizzy. The crown stayed on tight. "Glue is magic," he said. "It just needs to wait."

Adam walked in the forest with his teddy bear. The teddy's name was Robot. "Robot feels sick," Adam said. His friend Brinley was there too. "Let's help Robot get better," she said.

Adam found a big flat rock. He laid Robot on the rock. "Robot needs medicine," said Adam. He picked up a little acorn cap. He tipped it to Robot's mouth. "Drink your medicine," he said softly. Then Brinley passed him a soft green moss square. Adam tucked it around Robot like a blanket. "Now sleep, Robot," he said. He patted the moss blanket.

Robot lay still under the green blanket. Adam waited. Then he smiled big. "Robot feels better!" he said. Brinley clapped her hands. Adam picked up Robot and hugged him tight. "Time to go home," Adam whispered. He carried Robot all the way home.

Nathan stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook, Ms. Oyelaran, smiled at him. "Let's make toast," she said.

Ms. Oyelaran put warm bread on a plate. She gave Nathan a little knife with butter. The knife was dull and safe. Nathan spread the butter. It went squish, squish. The toast turned shiny and gold.

Next came the milk. Nathan held the cup tight. He poured fast. Splash! Milk went all over the table. "Oh no," said Nathan. His friend Bowen came to look. "It's okay," said Bowen. "Try again."

Ms. Oyelaran wiped the table tidy. She gave Nathan more milk. This time Nathan poured slowly. The milk went up, up, up in the cup. Not one drop fell out.

Then Ms. Oyelaran opened a small jar. Inside was a tiny seed for the bread. "A surprise topping," she said. Nathan sprinkled it on his toast. He took a big bite. "Yum!" he said. Bowen gave a little knock on the table. "More milk, please!"

Maverick stood in the school hallway. His shoes were new and red. He held his dad's hand tight. There were so many doors. One, two, three doors, and more.

A boy stood by the wall. He looked at the floor. He did not talk to anyone. Maverick let go of his dad's hand. He walked over to the boy. "My name is Maverick," he said. "What is your name?"

The boy looked up. "I am Raphael," he said. "I have a furry cat at home. And a baby sister." Maverick smiled. "My dad bakes banana bread," said Maverick. "Maybe your cat would like to smell it."

Mr. Clarke opened the classroom door. "Time to come in," he said. Raphael held out his hand. Maverick took it. They walked in together, side by side.

"Sit by me," said Raphael.

Madelyn wanted to play rocket ship at daycare. But Niko was already in the big cardboard box. "I am the pilot," said Niko. Madelyn frowned. She wanted a turn.

Ms. Marino knelt down beside them. "We can fit two astronauts," she said. "One, two. Hop in." Madelyn climbed in next to Niko. The box smelled like stinky crayons, but she did not mind.

"Rocket ships need a countdown," said Niko. "Ms. Marino told me. Counting backward from ten down to one is a countdown." Madelyn listened. Niko began. "Ten, nine, eight." Madelyn joined in. "Seven, six, five, four." They said the rest together. "Three, two, one. Blast off!" They both jumped up out of the box.

A bird outside the window flew up too, right at blast off. It surprised Madelyn and she laughed. "The bird is a rocket too," she said. Niko laughed too. Then Madelyn remembered something. "Now I get a turn to say the countdown," she said. She took a deep breath. "Ten, nine, eight."

Ezra was at Grandma's house. Ayra came to play too. The red scooter sat by the door. It was Ezra's favorite toy. "My turn first," said Ezra. He held the handle tight.

"No, my turn," said Ayra. She pulled the handle. Grandma came out. She held up a little glass timer. "Look, it is full of sand," she said. "When the sand runs out, the turn is over." She turned it over. The sand began to fall. It made a soft hiss, like tiny rain.

Ezra rode up the path. The wheels went clack, clack. He watched the sand. Down, down it went. Then the last bit fell. The sand had run out. His turn was over. Ezra stopped the scooter. He let Ayra have it. Grandma turned the timer again.

Ayra rode and rode. Ezra waited. He counted the falling sand grains. Clump, clump, went the wheels on the path. Then the sand ran out again. "My turn!" said Ezra. Ayra handed him the scooter. They took turns until the sun went down. "Same again tomorrow night?" asked Ayra. "Yes!" said Ezra, and he hugged the little timer.

Levi was at Grandma's house. It was raining outside. He could not play in the yard. He wanted to play, but the rain said no.

Grandma put two cushions on the rug. "Pretend the floor is a river," she said. Levi looked down. The floor did not look like a river. It was just a rug. "Can I walk on the river?" he asked. "No," said Grandma. "You will splash! Pretend to hop on the rocks."

Levi hopped from cushion to cushion. He made a splash noise with his mouth. "Look at me!" he said. Grandma pointed and laughed. Then Levi held his teddy bear. "The baby can't swim," he said. So he pretended to carry the baby across the river, hop by hop.

Levi got to the sofa. "We are safe now," he told the bear. Grandma clapped. The rain went tap, tap on the window. Levi sat close to her, warm and dry, and gave the bear a friendly hug. "More river tomorrow?" he asked. "More river tomorrow," said Grandma.

Asher loved the big slide at school. The slide was tall and red. Jaxson and Malek wanted to slide too.

The children stood on the floor by the ladder. Asher saw a line of feet. Mr. Torres held up his hand. "A line means you stay in your spot until it is your turn," he said.

Asher stood behind Malek. Malek had curly hair. Asher waited in his spot. Jaxson ran up fast. He pushed past Asher. He got to the ladder first.

Mr. Torres knelt down. "Go back to your spot," he said. Jaxson walked back down. He stood behind Asher. "Wait in your spot," said Mr. Torres. Jaxson waited in his spot.

Malek went down the slide. Whee! Then it was Asher's turn. Asher climbed up the ladder. He slid down, down, down. It was fast and fun. Then it was Jaxson's turn. Jaxson slid down too. "My turn again!" said Asher. He ran to the line. He found his spot at the end. "Wait in your spot," he said to himself.

Malek patted his curly hair. "You can be in front of me," said Malek. Asher stood in the new spot. The line moved, one child at a time.

Jaxon ran to the door. The sun was out. It was a sunny day.

"Race you to the swings!" he said.

His dad held up a little bottle. "Wait. Sunscreen first."

Jaxon stood still. Dad put sunscreen on his nose. He put it on his cheeks. He put it on his arms. One arm, two arms, all done.

"Now you can go," said Dad.

Jaxon ran to the playground. His friend Nate was there. Nate had been in the sun all morning. His nose was red. "Ow," said Nate. "My nose is hot."

Jaxon touched his own nose. His nose felt fine. His sunscreen was helping keep his skin safe from sunburn.

"Where did the wind go?" said Nate. The windy day had made the flags stop flapping. Now it was just sunny and still.

"Want to win a race?" said Jaxon.

"Yes!" said Nate.

"One, two, three, go!"

Jaxon was brave at the tall slide. He went down fast. Then he went down again.

"Your turn," he said to Nate. "You can win this one."

Livia stood by the hotel pool. She held her mom's hand. "I want to swim today," she said. Ms. Santos-Reyes, the swim teacher, waved from the water. "Come in, Livia!"

Livia stepped down the steps. The water was warm and cozy. She grabbed the edge of the pool. She held on tight. "Now kick your legs," said Ms. Santos-Reyes. Livia kicked. Her legs went up and down, up and down. Big splashes flew everywhere. A drop of water hit the big window near the pool. Plop!

Spencer was there too. He held the edge and kicked. His splashes were huge. Water hit Ms. Santos-Reyes right on the nose. Everyone laughed. Livia kicked harder. She bounced her legs fast, fast, fast. More splashes! More plops on the window!

Then Ms. Santos-Reyes let go of the wall. She swam all the way across the pool. Livia watched with wide eyes. "Again!" she shouted, kicking and splashing all the way.

Thomas held Dad's hand at the big cultural center. Music played. Bright flags hung from the ceiling. It smelled like warm bread and sweet oranges.

Thomas saw Roland from his class near a food stall. "Roland!" he called. He let go of Dad's hand and ran. There were so many people. Tall legs everywhere. Where was Dad now? Thomas could not see him.

Mr. Torres, the teacher, knelt down. "Where is your grown-up?" he asked. "I don't know," said Thomas. His tummy felt stormy, like dark clouds. "What do I do?" he asked. "We stay put and look," said Mr. Torres.

Then Thomas saw the desk with the bright red paint on it. Dad was standing right there! Thomas ran and grabbed Dad's leg. Dad picked him up and held his hand again. They walked to the food stall together. "Can we get the warm bread?" asked Thomas. Dad smiled and said, "Yes, one for you and one for Roland."

Nicholas was in the playroom. Blocks lay on the soft rug. He wanted to build a tower of ten blocks. He put one block on the rug. "One," he said. Then he put another block on top. "Two," he said.

Daphne sat beside him. She held a red block. "What comes after two?" she asked. Nicholas rubbed his chin. Then he heard Ms. Tanaka singing quietly by the shelf. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Daphne smiled and sang along. "Three, four, shut the door." She put her block on the tower. "Three!" she said. The rhyme helped her remember.

They sang as they built. "Five, six, pick up sticks." "Seven, eight, lay them straight." The tower grew tall and the color changed from red to blue at the top. The last block did not fit. It was too big. So Nicholas found a small green block. It fit just right. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen," they sang together. Ten blocks! It was a good tower. Daphne clapped and said, "Let's count it again. One, two, buckle my shoe!"

Madeline set up her pretend kitchen. She put a big red pot on the toy stove. Her stuffed dog sat in a chair, waiting for soup.

"Soup time!" said Madeline. She stirred the pot. Spoon, spoon, spoon. Then the phone rang. It was her friend Reed.

"Come play!" said Reed. "My mom is here."

"But my kitchen is a mess," said Madeline. Pots and cups were everywhere. The spoon was on the floor. The dog was tipped over.

Mom came to the door. "Time to go," she said. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away."

Madeline picked up the spoon. She stacked the cups. Reed helped too. He stood the dog up straight. "Sit, dog," said Reed. The dog just stared with his button eyes.

Madeline put the red pot on the shelf. The kitchen looked beautiful and neat. She patted the dog's soft ears.

"Bye, dog," said Madeline. "Bye, kitchen."

Then she took Reed's hand. They skipped out the door together.

Theodore ate his sandwich at daycare. "I am thirsty," he said. Angel gave him his cup. After lunch came naps. Theodore lay on his mat and closed his eyes.

At nap time, he thought about his morning. He had brushed his teeth after breakfast. "Why did I do that?" he wondered. He asked Ms. Whitehead when he woke up. "You brush in the morning," she said. "And before bed too."

That night, Theodore got into his pajamas. He pulled his blanket up. Then he sat up tall. "Wait!" he said. He hopped out of bed. He ran to the sink. He brushed and brushed. His teeth felt clean and shiny.

"Did you brush?" his dad asked from the hall.

"Yes! Morning and night," said Theodore. He climbed back into bed and smiled his clean smile.

Daniel sat at the dinner table. He wanted the apple juice. It was far away. He pulled the tablecloth. Uh oh. The black cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table like a little river.

"Mama, help please," said Daniel. Mama ran over with a towel. She wiped up the milk. Then Daddy put a triangle of bread on Daniel's plate. "Thank you," said Daniel. Daddy smiled.

Daniel looked at Mama's wet sleeve. Her sleeve got milky when she helped him. "Sorry, Mama," he said. Mama gave him a soft hug. "Thank you for saying that," she spoke quietly.

Then something surprising happened. Mama gave Daniel a new cup. It had juice in it, not milk! Daniel took a sip. It was cold and sweet. He held his cup with two hands, very carefully this time.

"More bread please," said Daniel. Daddy gave him another triangle.

Jade sat in the music classroom. A big drum sat in front of her. Ms. Carvalho handed her the drum stick.

Jade hit the drum very hard. BOOM! The sound was huge. Saint covered his ears. Amos jumped in his seat. Even the toy shelf seemed to shake.

"Whoa," said Saint. "That was so loud."

Jade looked at her friends. She did not want to scare them. So she tried again. This time she tapped the drum softly. Tap. The sound was small and low, like a little footsteps sound. Saint smiled. Amos clapped his hands.

"Better!" said Amos.

Jade tapped softly again and again. Tap, tap, tap. Then she hit hard one more time, just to hear it. BOOM! Then back to soft. Tap.

Ms. Carvalho knelt down beside her. "Jade, can you play the quiet beat for us? Amos will shake his bells with you."

Jade tapped the soft beat. Amos shook his bells. Saint patted his knees. The music room filled with gentle sounds.

At the end, Jade gave the drum one loud boom, and everyone laughed.

Nathan sat at the little table in the playroom. He wanted to paint grass. Green grass, like outside the window.

He looked for the green paint pot. He found the red pot. He found the blue pot. He found the yellow pot. The green pot was empty. "Oh no," said Nathan. "No green!"

Florian came over. "I need green too," she said. "I am painting a big green boat on the grass. One boat, two boats, three boats!"

Nathan dipped his brush in the blue paint. He made a blue spot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He touched the blue spot. The spot turned green!

"Green!" shouted Nathan. "The blue and the yellow made green!" Florian dipped her brush too. Blue, then yellow. Green! She painted her boat sitting on green grass.

"Your boat has green grass," said Nathan. "My itchy socks match it." He wiggled his toes and laughed. The paint pots sang a happy clink as he put the lids back on. One red, one blue, one yellow, all done.

Clara sat on the sofa. Malachi sat next to her. Ms. Berg sat on the other side. The big game was on TV. The players ran and ran. Clara leaned her neck forward to see.

"Who is winning?" asked Clara.

"The red team," said Malachi. "Two to one."

Then a blue player kicked the ball. It went in the net. The score said two and two now. Clara looked and looked.

"Who won now?" she asked.

"Both teams have the same score," said Ms. Berg. "That is called a tie."

"A tie," said Clara. She said it again, soft. "Nobody wins?"

Nobody won. The game was over. Dad gave out cheese and crackers. Clara helped sort them onto plates. Malachi took a cracker and made a stinky face at the cheese.

"It is not stinky," said Clara. She ate hers all up.

Louis was at daycare. He could not find his red car. It was his favorite toy. He looked in the toy box. No red car there.

Louis looked under the little table. He looked by the blocks. Still no red car. Adriel came to help. "Where did you see it last?" Adriel asked. Louis thought hard. "I had it at snack time," he said. "I was holding it by the snack table."

They ran to the snack table. Louis got down on his knees. He peeked under the chairs. There was something red! It was Mr. Kim's smooth red apple. Louis laughed. "Hello, apple," he said. He gave the apple a little pat.

Then Louis remembered more. At snack time, the car had rolled off the table. It had bumped his cup and rolled away. Where does a car go when it rolls? It goes somewhere low. Louis looked at the low shelf near the floor. There it was! The red car sat next to a small toy bear. "We meet again," Louis told his car. He drove it along the smooth floor, all the way to Adriel.

Isaiah sat in his car seat. Mom was driving. "Is the library today?" he asked. "Yesterday we did not go. We ran out of time."

"Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day that is happening right now. And right now we are in the car. So today is library day."

Isaiah looked out the window. A little dog was digging in the dirt by a fence. "Cute dog!" said Isaiah. "Can we pet it later?"

"Not this trip," said Mom. "We can look again tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today."

The car stopped at a red light. Isaiah waited. He looked and looked at the light. Then the light turned green. The car moved! "The light made us go," said Isaiah.

"Yes," said Mom. "Green means go now."

At the library, Isaiah found a book about a dog. He sat down to read. He turned one page. Then he turned another page. His shoe had come untied. He tried to tie it himself. He pulled the strings slow and careful. Mom waited, patient.

At last the bow held. "I did it!" said Isaiah.

"Good work," said Mom. "Now let's check out that book."

Rehmat was four today. She counted the guests at the door. "One, two, three, four," she said. Richard came, then Amin, then Ms. Mokoena from next door.

The cake sat on the table. Her dad lit the candles. "Make a wish," he said. Rehmat squeezed her eyes shut. She wished for a big butterfly cake next year. But there was a problem. Richard and Amin started to sing, and Rehmat did not like loud singing. She hid behind her hands.

Then she heard it. "Happy birthday, dear Rehmat." Her name was in the song! She peeked out. They sang her name again. She smiled behind her hands.

"Sour lemons!" said Amin, making a funny face. "No, sweet cake!" said Richard. Everyone laughed.

Rehmat took a big breath. She blew out the candles. One, two, three, four, all out. Ms. Mokoena clapped. "Sing it again," said Rehmat, "with my name!"

Elizabeth was in her room with her friend Amal. They were making piles on the rug. One pile was for animals. One pile was for toys. One pile was for food.

Elizabeth held her brown stuffed dog. She put it in the animal pile.

Amal shook his head. "The toy dog is a toy, not an animal," he said. "It is not alive."

Elizabeth picked it up. She looked at it. It did not bark. It did not wag its tail. It did not eat.

She put the toy dog in the toy pile. Then she put her toy banana in the food pile. She thought again. It was not real food. She moved it to the toy pile too.

"Good sorting," said Amal. He clapped his hands.

Elizabeth covered the toy dog with a small blanket. "Sleep now," she said.

Victoria wanted to make a magic spell. She stood by the mirror in her bedroom. "Spell, spell, make me happy," she said. Then she made a big smile. The girl in the mirror smiled too. Victoria clapped. Her spell worked.

Next she tried a sad face. Her mouth went down. The mirror girl looked sad too. "Oh no," said Victoria. "The spell is too strong."

She stomped her foot and made an angry face. The mirror girl looked angry. Victoria jumped back. That was a little bit scary. She hid behind her toy car.

Then she had an idea. She made one more big smile. The mirror girl smiled right back. Victoria laughed out loud.

Her cat walked in. He looked lazy and sleepy. Victoria leaned close to him. She made her biggest happy face at him.

The cat blinked. Then he purred.

Mason went to the animal shelter with his dad. Many dogs and cats sat in little rooms. "They wait here for a family," said Dad. "Then a family takes one home." Mason walked past the dogs. He walked past the cats. Then he saw a small brown rabbit. "This one," said Mason. The rabbit came home in a box.

In the backyard, Mason made a pen with soft grass. He sorted the food into two bowls, one for pellets and one for greens. "Good rabbit," said Mason. The rabbit sniffed his hand. Then it thumped its big back foot. Thump, thump! Mason jumped. "It talks with its foot!" he said. Dark clouds came. A storm was near. Dad helped carry the rabbit inside, safe and dry. The rabbit thumped one more time. "Good night, rabbit," said Mason.

Leo was at Grandpa's house. He wanted his favorite book. It was the one about the big red truck. But Grandpa's shelf was tall and full of books.

Leo pulled one book down. He opened the front cover. That page had small marks. He turned to the first page. "Not this one," he said. He put it back.

Then Grandpa came in. "What do you need, Leo?" Leo said, "The truck book. The big truck book." Grandpa smiled. "A book's title is its name," he said. "Let's find the name."

Grandpa held up books. Leo looked at the marks on the front. "No. No. No," he said. Then he saw red marks. "That one!" he said. Grandpa opened it. There was the big red truck!

Grandpa sat in his soft chair. Leo sat on his lap. Grandpa read from the front to the back. At the end, the truck went beep, beep!

Leo gave the book a kiss. Grandpa laughed. "More truck book tomorrow," he said. "And now you know its name."

Leo held the book tight. "Goodnight, truck book," he whispered.

Joseph woke up and put on his striped socks. He got his bag ready for school. Then his mom looked out the window. "No school today," she said. "It is a snow day." "What is a snow day?" asked Joseph. "It means school is closed because of snow."

Joseph ran to the window. Snow was everywhere. It covered the grass. It covered the steps. It made a big white mountain on the picnic table.

Joseph put on his boots. He stepped outside. The snow went crunch, crunch. He made a snowball and threw it at the fence. The fence wobbled, and snow slipped off the top. The snow fell down with a soft plop.

Joseph laughed. His throw made the snow fall! He threw another snowball. More snow slipped down. His mom smiled from the door. "Hot cocoa when you come in," she said. Joseph waved his red mittens in the air.

Ivy ran to the yellow truck at the playground. But Oskar was already pushing it. "Vroom, vroom!" he said.

Ivy reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She put her hands behind her back instead. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked.

Oskar kept pushing the truck. Then he stopped. "Okay. You can have the last turn," he said. He gave her the truck. "Vroom!" said Ivy. She pushed it fast, then slow. One wheel began to dance as it spun around.

Alya came next. She reached for the truck. Then she stopped too. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked.

"Yes," said Ivy. "You can have this piece of fun next." She pushed the truck one more time. Then she gave it to Alya.

"Vroom, vroom!" said Alya.

"Good waiting," said Ms. Müller. She clapped her hands.

Ivy smiled. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked Alya.

Alya pushed and pushed. Then she held out the truck. "Here you go, Ivy," she said.

Evelyn walked into her classroom. Ms. Owusu had set out five little cups on the table. "We will use our senses today," said Ms. Owusu. Evelyn wanted to know what was in the cups.

First Evelyn used her eyes. She saw orange juice, warm and yellow. She used her ears. She heard Jai tap his cup. She touched Esme's cup. It was cold. "Use your nose now," said Ms. Owusu. Evelyn sniffed. She could smell orange!

Evelyn looked in the little mirror. "You have two nostrils," said Ms. Owusu. "The openings in your nose." Evelyn counted them. One, two. Then Evelyn sipped her juice. It tasted sweet. Esme covered one nostril with her finger. She could not smell the orange well. She uncovered it and sniffed again. The smell came back! They had to clean up before it got late. Evelyn helped put the cups away, and she was still smiling.

Stella went to the farmers' market with her dad. They bought fresh bread and a little jug of milk. "I want to make my own snack," said Stella. "You can learn how," said her dad.

At home, Dad toasted the bread in the hot toaster. Stella waited far away, safe. Then she sat at the table. She took her knife for butter, the dull one. She spread the butter slowly. The bread tore a little. She kept going. Soon the toast was all yellow.

Next, Stella poured the milk. She tipped the cup too fast. Milk ran out onto the table. A little white puddle sat there like a cloud. Stella wanted to cry. But she remembered something. If milk spills, you can wipe it up with a cloth. She got a cloth all by herself. She pushed the cloth over the puddle. The milk went away. The table was dry.

"I did it," said Stella. Her dad smiled. She poured again, very slowly this time. Every drop went into the cup. She took a big bite of squishy, buttery toast. "Yum," she said. "I want to pour yours too."

Adam sat at the dinner table. He had pasta on his plate. His hands were dirty from playing in the sand.

His mom said, "Wash your hands first." Adam went to the sink. He turned on the water. He rubbed the soap. Bubbles grew on his hands!

Adam rubbed more soap. He rubbed more water. More bubbles came. He put the bubbles on his chin. "Look! I have a bubble beard!" he said. He giggled and giggled.

His mom laughed too. "Silly Adam," she said. "Your beard is bigger than Dad's!" Adam made the bubbles fly off his hands. Then he rinsed all the soap away. His hands were clean at last.

He ran back to the table. He ate his pasta with a fork. It was yummy. Then he yawned a big yawn. "Bath time, then bed," said his mom. Adam smiled. He hoped the bath soap would make bubbles too. "Maybe I can make bubble hair next," he said.

Gabriel went to the store with his dad. He wanted red apples. One, two, three apples in the bag. Gabriel was excited.

Then the store man said, "No red apples today. All gone." Gabriel felt sad. His face went down like a rain cloud.

His dad said, "Let's look at the high shelf." One, two, three yellow bananas sat there. Gabriel could not reach. His dad lifted him up high, safe in his arms.

"Can we mix bananas with apples at home?" Gabriel asked. "Yes," said Dad.

They paid and walked home. At home, Dad cut the fruit. Gabriel put one, two, three pieces in a bowl. He took a big bite. His sad feeling was gone. Now he was happy.

"Bananas are yummy," said Gabriel, and he smiled.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Emma ran around the backyard. She picked three yellow flowers for him. "But where will Grandpa sleep?" she asked her dad. Dad smiled. "We need to make him a bed." Emma gasped. A guest who stays needs a sleeping spot!

Emma carried a big soft pillow to the spare room. It smelled like sunshine. She hugged it tight. Then she found her favorite blanket. It was blue with white stars. She laid it on the bed. Dad put clean sheets on too. Emma patted the pillow three times to make it fluffy.

At last the car came up the drive. Grandpa stepped out. Emma pulled his hand. "Come see your bed!" Grandpa touched the soft pillow. He sniffed the yellow flowers by the lamp. He tucked the star blanket up to his chin. "This is the yummiest, coziest spot," he said. "I will sleep like a happy bear." Emma climbed up beside him for one little snuggle. The blanket was warm and soft. Grandpa kissed the top of her head.

Charlie sat in her car seat. She wanted her red ball. It was in the toy box at home. “I beg you, can we go get it?” she asked. “Yes,” said the dad. “Fast!”

The big car went fast on the road. Then it went slow near home. Charlie put her hands in her pockets. Her mittens were hot inside. The cold air felt cold on her nose.

At home, Charlie put toys in the box. Out came a small hand. Her baby brother took each toy out. In went the bear. Out came the bear. In went the ball. Out came the ball. “In and out are opposites,” said Charlie. She laughed and gave the ball to her brother. He hugged it tight.

The dad made warm milk. Charlie drank it in her cozy chair. “Ball,” said the baby. He held it up high.

Arlo stood at the park with a red beanbag. A wooden hoop lay on the grass. He wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Arlo threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew high and far. It landed in the dirt, way past the hoop. Nellie ran to get it for him.

"Try it like this," said Ms. Wu. She held her arm down low. Then her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop. "That is an underhand throw," she said.

Arlo held his arm down low. He swung it forward and up. The beanbag sailed and fell into the hoop. "I did it!" said Arlo.

Then Ms. Wu tossed him a big ball. Arlo hugged it with both hands. It did not fall. Nellie clapped, and Arlo laughed.

Jaxon wanted to sing a song all by himself. Mama knew a song about a little boat. Jaxon tried to clap while he sang. His claps went fast, fast, faster. "My claps are running away!" he laughed. Then the song got all mixed up.

Moma stood up. "Let's march," she said. She marched around the rug. Step, step, step. Jaxon marched too. His feet went even, like hers. "The beat is like footsteps when you march," said Mama. Step, step, step. The beat stayed even and kept going.

Jaxon sat down. He clapped the same way his feet had stepped. Clap, clap, clap. It stayed even! He sang, "Row, row, row your boat." Every word fit. Jaxon drew a little boat on paper and clapped again. "I did it!" he said. "Quiet, boat, you can sing too."

Jaxson put on his skates at the ice rink. His team had a game soon. But first came practice.

"I want to play now," Jaxson said. "Not practice."

Ms. Kelly smiled. "Practice is when we learn skills," she said. "Then we get ready for the game."

Jaxson slid onto the smooth ice. He fell down. He got up. He fell again. Kyrie fell too. Ved wobbled like a penguin.

"Nice penguin," Jaxson said. They both laughed.

They practiced stopping at the red door. They practiced gliding past cones. Every day, Jaxson fell less and less.

Then came game day. The puck slid toward Jaxson. He stopped. He glided. He scored!

Kyrie hugged him. "Practice helped!" Ved shouted.

Jaxson spun in a circle. "More practice tomorrow," he said.

Mateo was going on a big trip. He was going to his grandma's house. He grabbed his little red bag. He put in his crunchy crackers and his toy truck. "The car is ready," said Dad.

Mateo ran to the car. He was so excited. He climbed in fast. He sat on his car seat. Dad looked back at him. "I don't hear the click," said Dad. The car did not start. The car just waited.

Mateo looked down. The buckle was not buckled. He pushed the two parts together. Click! The car could go now. "All buckled," said Mateo. Dad smiled and started the car.

At grandma's house, Mateo ran to the door. Grandma gave him a big kiss. "Did you ride safe?" she asked. "Yes! I clicked my buckle," said Mateo. He bit into a crunchy cracker and held up his truck.

Elias stood on the soccer field. Ms. Paquette held up a hoop. "Throw the beanbag in," she said. Elias threw it. The beanbag went straight up. Then it came down on Lyam's shoe. "Ow," said Lyam, laughing. "It didn't go in!"

Elias tried again. He looked at the hoop. He threw the beanbag low and slow. It dropped right in. "Yes!" said Elias. Lyam clapped. Sierra clapped. Even the coach clapped.

Then Ms. Paquette rolled a big ball to Sierra. Sierra caught it with one hand, like a big kid. It bounced off her fingers. The ball rolled away. "Why did it get away?" Sierra asked. Elias ran after the ball. "Try two hands!" he said. He held out both hands. Ms. Paquette rolled the ball to him. He caught it. It sat in his arms like a big red world. Sierra held out both hands too. "Throw it to me!" she said. Elias threw it, and she hugged it tight.

Charles walked into the big hall. It was warm inside. Winter was cold outside, but not in here. A tall green tree stood by the window. It was a Christmas tree. Lots of families had come to decorate it.

Mr. Brown handed Charles a box of ornaments. Charles picked a shiny red ball. He hung it on one branch. Then he hung a gold star on the same branch. Then a little bell, right there too. The branch bent down low. It looked sad and squished.

"Let's spread them out," said Mika, his friend. She hung her ornament on a far branch. Charles tried too. He put his bell up high. He put his star on the other side. The branches stood up straight again. The tree looked full and pretty.

Bryce hung a silver snowman next to Charles's star. "Now it's Christmas," Bryce said. Soon every branch had something shiny. The lights came on, and the tree glowed.

Charles yawned. He was sleepy. He tasted sweet cocoa from his cup. His dad lifted him up to see the whole tree. Every branch was bright. "We did it," said Charles, and he patted the soft, green tree.

Mohamed was at Grandma's house. She had new paint pots. "Can I paint?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandma.

Mohamed looked at the pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. He said each colour out loud. "Red. Yellow. Blue." Grandma smiled.

"I want green," said Mohamed. "How do I make green?" Grandma put a little yellow in a small cup. Then she put a little blue next to it. "Try," she said. Mohamed mixed the cup with his brush. The paint turned green! He laughed.

Then Mohamed wanted more green. He pushed his brush into the big yellow pot. The blue on his brush went in too. The whole yellow pot turned green. "Oh no," said Mohamed. "Can I pull the blue back out?"

Grandma shook her head. "No, kid. Once two paints are mixed, you cannot pull them apart again." Mohamed looked at the pot. Then he looked at the small cup.

Next time, Mohamed was careful. He kept a little red aside. He kept a little blue aside. He mixed the two little bits together. The paint turned purple, just like he wanted. "I did it!" said Mohamed. Grandma clapped. Mohamed held up his purple brush. "Now I know," he said. "Keep a little bit for next time!"

Rosalie looked out the window. The sky was gray. Rain dripped down the glass. Drip, drip, drip.

"I want to play outside," said Rosalie. She ran to the door. She stepped out with no coat. The rain fell on her hair. The rain fell on her arms. Her sleeves got wet. She ran back inside.

Her mom held up a red raincoat. "Put this on," she said. Rosalie put her arms in. She did up the big buttons. The hood covered her hair.

Rosalie stepped out again. The rain fell and fell. It tapped on her hood. Tap, tap, tap. She held out her arms. The rain ran down the red coat. It slid right off. Her arms stayed dry.

Rosalie found a puddle. She stomped in it. Water splashed everywhere. Her boots were wet. Her socks were dry.

A rabbit hopped under a bush. It was hiding from the rain. Rosalie watched it from her puddle.

"I'm hungry," said Rosalie. She went inside. She took off the red raincoat. It was wet. Her body under it was dry. She hung the coat on its hook. Drip, drip, drip, said the coat. Rosalie smiled and ate her snack.

Sebastian ran to the toy shelf at daycare. He wanted his red car. But the big toy bin was a mess!

"Where is my car?" he said. Samrath came to help. "Let's sort the toys," Samrath said. Sebastian put all the red blocks in one pile. Samrath put all the blue blocks in another pile. Then Lydia came with a big smile. She took the same blocks and made a new pile. "Look," she said. "Big blocks here. Small blocks here." The same blocks, but now they were sorted by size!

Sebastian stared. Wow! One pile was red and blue. One pile was big and small. Then he saw something. Under the small pile was a slow, shiny snail toy. And right next to it was his red car!

"My car!" he shouted. He held it up high. Mr. Mensah hung a sign on the shelf. It said "Sort by color or sort by size." Lydia laughed. "Next I will sort by shape!" she said. Sebastian put the car on the floor and pushed it to her.

Miles stands by the sink. He wants to wash his hands. The sink is too high. His hands cannot reach the water.

Ms. Kelly brings a step stool. She puts it by the sink. "Here is your step stool," she says. She stays close by. Miles climbs up. Now his hands reach the water. "I did it!" he says.

Ms. Kelly squirts soap on his hands. "Rub and count," she says. Miles rubs the soap. Anastasia counts beside him. They count to twenty. The bubbles are real and slippery. Robin makes a train of bubbles down the drain. Whoosh, the water pulls the bubbles away. Miles pulls a paper towel. He dries his hands all by himself.

Then it is snack time. Miles sits down with clean hands. "My hands smell like flowers," he says. Anastasia sniffs her own hands. "Mine too!" she says. "Flower hands for snack," says Robin.

Wyatt stood in the garage with Dad. Rain tapped on the big door. Wyatt wanted to play outside after the rain stopped. But first he had to put on his coat all by himself.

He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. "I did it," Wyatt said. He pulled the zipper up. But it got stuck. His sweater was caught in the zipper. Wyatt pulled hard. It would not move. "Uh oh," he said.

Dad knelt beside him. "Try pulling the zipper back down a little," Dad said. Wyatt pulled it down, slow and gentle. The sweater came free. Wyatt pushed the sweater flat. Then he zipped it up, up, up. It worked! He zipped it all the way to his chin. "Zip it up, up, up," Wyatt sang. Dad smiled and opened the garage door. The rain had stopped. Wyatt ran out into the wet, shiny yard.

Maverick was on a family trip. The car stopped at a roadside diner. It was different from home. "It has shiny red seats," said Maverick. His mom ordered pancakes. Maverick drank his juice. It was fun to eat in a big booth. "Do you think the beach will be fun too?" his mom asked. "Yes," said Maverick. "I want to find shells."

After the beach, the family drove home. Home again! Mom said, "We unpack our bags now." Maverick pulled his little bag to his room. He put his socks in the drawer. He put his shirt away too. Then he took off his shoes. Something went crunch. What was that? He tipped his shoe over. Sand popped out onto the floor. Little grains, soft and warm. "Look, Mom! The beach came home in my shoe!" His mom laughed. Maverick touched the sand with one finger. Then he put his shoes away, all by himself.

Isabella was at George's birthday party. There was a big pile of balloons. There was one small red truck. Everyone wanted it.

George held the truck first. "My turn," he said. Isabella wanted it so much. She reached out her hand. Then she sat on her hands instead.

Next to the truck was a box of feathers. Isabella picked up a white feather. She blew on it. The feather floated up. "Look, George!" she said. George peeked at the feather and laughed.

Then Holden held the truck. Isabella stacked cups while she waited. She made a tall, tall tower. "Beep beep!" said Holden, driving the truck to the tower. He pushed one cup over. It was silly.

"Isabella's turn now," said George. She took the truck. It was bumpy and fast. "Vroom!" she said. Holden took a feather and tickled her arm. "Tickle tickle," he said.

Isabella drove the truck in a big circle. Then she gave it back to George. "Your turn," she said. George smiled and drove it under the chair. "Beep beep!" he said.

Mackenzie sat in the family car. Her tummy felt funny. "Today I see the dentist," she said. "My first time." Dad drove the small car down the road. "The dentist will look at your teeth," said Dad. "That is all." Mackenzie held her toy bunny tight.

At the dentist's office, Mackenzie sat in a big chair. It went up and down. A light was above the chair. The dentist turned it on. The light was so bright! Mackenzie made a squinty face. Her eyes went small. "Here you go," said the dentist. She gave Mackenzie sunglasses to wear. Now her eyes felt better. She could open them wide.

"Open your mouth big," said the dentist. Mackenzie opened wide. The bright light above the chair helped the dentist see inside her mouth. "I can see all your teeth," said the dentist. "They are so clean." The little tool tickled Mackenzie's tooth. She wanted to giggle. "That tickles!" she said.

Soon it was done. Mackenzie got a sticker. She rode back to the car with Dad. "The light was so bright," she said. "But my sunglasses helped." Dad smiled and buckled her in. On the way home, they passed a big yellow bus. Mackenzie waved at it. She held her sticker up to the window. "Next time, I will wear the sunglasses again," she said.

Luna sat on the small red mat at school. Ms. Gallagher held up a picture of a big yellow sun. "We have five senses," said Ms. Gallagher. "Today we will name them."

Luna wanted to name one first. She put up her hand fast. "Eyes see!" she said. Ms. Gallagher smiled. "Yes, Luna. Eyes see."

Then Luna looked out the window. The sun was there. It was so bright. She wanted to see it up close. She leaned toward the window and squinted. Alexy shouted, "Don't look at the sun!"

Luna turned away. Her eyes felt funny and watery. She blinked and blinked. Ms. Gallagher knelt down next to her. "Never look straight at the sun, because it can hurt your eyes," she said.

Luna rubbed her eyes. Then she pointed at her ears. "Ears hear Alexy shout," she said. She touched a bumpy triangle block. "Fingers feel bumps." She sniffed the play dough. "My nose smells it!" Then Mouhamed shared his crackers, and Luna took a shy little bite. "Mouth tastes salty," she said.

Ms. Gallagher clapped. "You named all five senses, Luna." Luna looked up at the sky. She kept her eyes on the clouds instead. The clouds were soft and white and did not hurt at all.

Milo wanted to make soup. It was sunny outside, and the play kitchen sat by the window.

"I am the soup maker," said Milo.

Harry put pinecones in the pot. "One pinecone, two pinecones, three," said Harry. "Now it is pinecone soup."

Milo stirred it with a big spoon. He smelled it. "Mmm," he said. "It smells so good."

Then Milo lifted the spoon to his mouth. He was going to take a big bite.

"Stop," said Mr. Ramírez. He sat down next to Milo. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat," he said.

Milo looked at the spoon. He looked at the pinecones.

"Oh," said Milo. He put the spoon near his lips and made a slurpy sound. "Sluuurp!"

"Pretend eating!" said Harry. He slurped too.

Meredith came over with her teddy bear. "Teddy is hungry," she said.

"I will sell you soup," said Milo. He held out the pot. "One bowl for one teddy."

Meredith held the teddy up. The teddy pretended to eat and eat.

Then a train went by outside the window. Choo, choo!

"The soup train!" said Milo. "More soup for the train!"

Milo filled three more bowls. One for teddy, one for Harry, one for himself.

"Sluuurp," said Milo. He smiled. Pretend soup was the best soup of all.

Alexis woke up early. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He put on his t-shirt and shorts. Mom took him to the playground. Ved and Jaxson were there too.

"We can slide fast!" said Ved. Alexis ran to the slide. The wind began to blow. It was windy now. His hat blew right off his head. Jaxson chased it and caught it. "Here you go," said Jaxson. Alexis put the hat back on.

Then the sky got dark. Raindrops fell. It was rainy. Thunder rumbled, big and loud. "When you hear thunder, go indoors," said the coach. She held the gate open. Alexis took Ved's hand. They ran inside together. Jaxson ran too. They watched the rain from the window. "Good running," said the coach. Alexis smiled at his friends.

Sadie sat at the kitchen table. She had a plate of crackers. "Is this one a square?" she asked. Her dad smiled. "Let's find out," he said. He gave her a piece of string.

Sadie put the string along one side. Dad helped her cut it to fit. Then she moved the little string to the next side. It fit too. "See? Same," said Sadie. She tried the third side. It fit. She tried the fourth side. It fit again.

"A square has four sides," said Dad. "And they are all the same length." Sadie clapped. Then she held up a slice of cheese. She put the string on one side. That side was longer. "Not a square," said Sadie. "It's a rectangle!" She laid the cheese on the cracker and took a big bite. "This is my beautiful square snack," she said. "Now it is a secret. Nobody else gets one."

Kayden sat in a big chair at the mall salon. His friend Nathanael was there too, waiting for his own turn. The hairdresser picked up her scissors and put a blanket around Kayden.

"Wait," said Kayden. "Will my hair stay short forever?"

"Do you want it to grow again?" asked the hairdresser.

"Yes," said Kayden.

"Then you are lucky," she said. "Hair grows back after it is cut."

She snipped and snipped. Little bits of hair fell on the blanket. Kayden watched one piece slide down, slow as snow.

When she was done, Kayden felt his short hair. It was soft and tidy.

"Your turn, Nathanael," said Kayden. "And don't worry. It grows back."

Nathanael climbed up and grinned at the mirror.

John wanted to play shop in the playroom. He had a big red box. He put apples in the box. He put a toy cake in it too.

Colter came in. "I want to be the shopkeeper," said Colter. John sat down by the box. "Then I can be the shopper," said John. Colter stood behind the box. John stood in front of it.

John picked up the toy cake. He looked at it for a long time. Colter waited. Colter did not grab it. John put the cake down. Then he picked up an apple.

"I will take this one," said John. Colter held out his hand. John put a small square block in it. "One coin," said Colter. "Thank you for shopping."

"Now it is my turn," said John. They switched spots. Colter stood in front. John stood behind the box. Colter looked at the apples. He looked at the cake. He thought and thought. John waited for him.

"I want the cake, please," said Colter at last. John smiled and took the square block. "Here is your cake," said John.

Ava ran onto the soccer field. Today was her first game! Her team wore blue shirts. All the blue shirts matched.

The whistle blew. Ava got the ball. She looked up fast. She saw a green shirt. She kicked the ball to the green shirt. But the green shirt was Olivier! Olivier was on the other team. Olivier ran away with the ball.

Ava stopped and thought. She looked around. Blue shirts meant her team. She saw Hukam in a blue shirt near the goal. "Look for blue!" said Mr. Thompson, the coach.

The ball came back to Ava. She looked for blue. She kicked the ball to Hukam. Hukam kicked it in. Goal! The blue team cheered. "Nice pass, Ava!" Hukam said.

After the game, the sky turned rainy. The players had a snack under the big tree. "Same shirt, same team," Ava said to Olivier. Olivier laughed and gave her a high five. Then Ava cut her orange into two pieces and shared it.

Myles went to the farmers' market with his dad. He saw a man with an old red truck. The truck was full of little green plants. Myles picked two small plants. One was a carrot. One was a tomato.

At home, Myles planted them in a pot. He watered them every day. Soon tiny green leaves popped up. But then Myles saw a small leaf he did not like. "That is a weed," he said. He pulled hard on it.

His dad ran over. "Stop! That is your baby carrot!" Myles let go fast. His dad knelt down beside him. "See the feathery little leaves? That is the carrot. A weed is a plant growing where we do not want it. This one we want!" Myles looked closely. The carrot leaves were soft and feathery. The weed leaves were long and pointy.

Myles pulled the pointy one instead. Out it came, roots and all. The baby carrot stayed safe in the dirt. Later, Myles picked one ripe tomato. He shut the gate to the garden. He put the tomato on a blue plate. "Dad, look!" said Myles. "We grew lunch!"

Anna wanted to write her name. She had a new pencil with a shiny yellow coat. But the letters kept going crooked. The A looked like a little wobbly tent.

"Grandma, my letters go all silly," said Anna.

Grandma put a paper on the table. The letters of Anna's name were there. But they were made of dots. Little dots, all along the letter shapes.

"Look," said Grandma. "You can trace over the dotted letters. That is one way to practice."

Anna gripped her pencil in her fingers. Grandma helped her hold it just right, not too tight. Anna put her pencil on the first dot. Then she drew a line to the next dot. Then the next one. The big letter A appeared, straight and tall!

"Ooh," said Anna. "The dots show my pencil where to go!"

She traced the small n. Then another n. Then a. Her hair fell into her eyes and she pushed it back. She did not stop tracing.

The last letter was a. Anna traced it slowly. But wait. After the last dot, there was one more little dot, all by itself. Anna tapped it with her pencil tip. It moved! It was a tiny ladybug, sitting on the paper!

"Grandma!" laughed Anna. "A dot came alive!"

Then she looked at her whole name, all traced and tidy.

"Now I know how to make my letters," she said. She picked up a clean paper and began to draw the big A by herself, no dots at all.

Dylan wanted to be a firefighter. But he was just Dylan. He did not feel like a firefighter yet.

He found a big red hat. He put it on. Now he looked in the mirror. "I am a firefighter!" he said. The hat helped him pretend to be someone else.

His teddy bear was stuck on the sofa. "Don't worry," Dylan said. "I am strong." He lifted teddy down. Then he gave teddy a drink from a toy cup. "Drink this," he said. "You will grow big again."

Dylan's dad made a paper flag for him. Dylan waved it high. "The fire is out!" he called. Dad clapped and cheered.

Asha came to play. She put on a big blue hat. "Now I am a doctor," she said. Dylan lay down on the rug. He pretended his leg hurt. Asha checked it with a toy tool. "All better," she said.

They played all afternoon. Then Dad called, "Snack time!"

Dylan kept his big red hat on. "Firefighters need snacks too," he said.

Rosalie went to Paris's house. Paris's mom had a tablet on the table. It was big and shiny. Rosalie wanted to draw on it. She put her hands behind her back. "Can I use the tablet?" she asked. "Yes," said the mom. "That was smart of you to ask. Children ask a grown-up first."

Paris showed Rosalie the button. Rosalie pressed it. The screen lit up! Her press made the light come on. "Again," said Rosalie. She pressed a little picture on the screen. The drawing app opened. It had blue and red and yellow.
