Rosalie drew a green boat. It went on the blue water. "I will write BOAT," said Paris. He tapped letters under the boat. Then Rosalie yawned. Her eyes felt sleepy. She pressed the button again and the screen went dark. She put the tablet in the drawer. "All done," said Rosalie. Paris clapped his hands.

Madeline went to the cemetery with her dad. They carried a basket and a blanket. Grandma's stone was big and flat. Dad spread the blanket on the grass. He set out bread, cheese and apple slices. A little paper flower was glued to the basket lid. Madeline had made it at school.

"We sing our blessing before we eat," said Dad. "Grandma liked it sung, not said." Madeline wanted to sing it. She took a big breath. She began the tune. But the tune came out wrong. It went up when it should go down. Madeline stopped. Her face went hot.

"Try again," said Dad softly. "I will clap." Madeline held her toy rabbit close. Then she sang the tune again. This time it went up and then down, just right. Dad clapped. A bird hopped near the flat stone, as if it listened too.

"Now we eat," said Dad. He gave Madeline the first apple slice. Madeline smiled. "I sang it good," she said. The bird flew up into the tree.

Everett ran to the water table at daycare. Today there was a big pink tub full of water. He wanted to splash right away.

"Stop, please," said Mr. Leblanc. "I check the water first." He put his hand in the tub. "A grown-up checks the bath water to make sure it is not too hot before you get in." Everett watched and waited. He made the water spin with one finger. Round and round it went.

Then Everett had a problem. His friend Zainab came running. She did not know the secret. She tried to climb in fast. "Wait!" said Everett. He held her hand. "Mr. Leblanc checks first. Watch." Mr. Leblanc put his hand in again. "Just right now," he said. Zainab smiled at Everett. They climbed in side by side. "Splash!" they said, together.

Iris was playing in the living room. The sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the rug.

She saw something on the low table. It was a little bottle. Some round things had spilled out. They were red and yellow. They looked like candy.

Iris wanted one. She loved candy. She reached out her hand. Then she stopped.

"Maybe they are not candy," she said. She thought hard. She asked herself a question. "What if they are medicine?" She knew the answer. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.

Medicine can be scary if you take it alone. Iris did not touch the pretty round things. She put her hands behind her back. Then she walked to the kitchen. She stayed close to the wall the whole way.

"Mom, come see," she said. "There are red and yellow balls on the table. I did not touch them."

Her mom came with her. Mom looked at the table. "Those are pills," Mom said. "They are medicine, not candy. You did the right thing, Iris."

Mom picked up the pills and put the cap on tight. Iris watched from her spot on the rug. The warm sun was still there. Iris sat down in it.

"Can I have real candy now?" she asked.

Mom smiled and held out her hand. "Come with me," said Mom.

Gabriella ran to school. She was not sleepy today. She had eaten a big breakfast. She felt excited. It was painting day in Ms. Horváth's class.

Isabel was carrying the paint jars. She tripped on the mat. The jars fell down. Blue paint went splash. Isabel sat on the floor. Her face looked sad and scared.

Gabriella ran over. "Are you okay?" she asked. Isabel stopped crying. She looked up at Gabriella. "My knee hurts," said Isabel. "But you asked about me. That makes me feel better." Ms. Horváth came with a wet cloth. She cleaned the little cut. Then Isabel smiled a small smile.

Gabriella helped pick up the jars. She got a towel for the paint. Isabel kept painting next to Gabriella. She made a big blue cat. "Blue is my best color," Isabel said.

Mila wanted to build a rocket in the playroom. She found a big red box. She pushed it. It would not move.

Zaid came in. "You try," said Mila. Zaid pulled the box. It stayed put. "This box is heavy," said Zaid.

Then Mila saw a small white pillow. She picked it up. Up it went, easy as that. "This pillow is light," she said. "Heavy and light are opposites!"

"I can be a fast rocket," said Japji. She zoomed around the rug. Mila zoomed slow, like a moon boat. Ms. Fernando laughed from the door. "One, two, three, blast off!" she said.

Mila put the light pillow on top of the heavy box. The rocket had a soft white nose. "Buckle up," said Mila. "We will drive to the stars."

Zaid held the pillow. Mila counted down. "Five, four, three, two, one!" Japji jumped up high.

Samuel sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "One red car," he said. "Two dogs. Three trees." His dad smiled. They sang a counting song together. "One, two, three, four, five," they sang. Then the song went on. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

The car stopped at the park. Samuel jumped out onto the soft grass. He saw Adelina and Amelia by the pretty flowers. "Hello!" he called. "Can we play hide-and-seek?" asked Adelina. "Yes!" said Samuel. "I will hide," said Amelia. "I will seek," said Adelina.

Amelia ran to hide behind a big tree. Adelina covered her eyes. She counted, "One, two, three, four!" Then she shouted, "Ready!" Amelia was still running. "You counted too fast," said Samuel. "Count slowly so we can hide." Adelina covered her eyes again. She counted slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Now everyone was hidden. Adelina turned around and giggled. "I hear you behind the tree!"

Clara sat down at the dinner table. She had ten little peas on her plate. "I will count them!" she said. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Then she ate one pea. Now there were nine.

Clara looked under the table. She saw something blue. It was a sock! Just one sock. "Whose sock is this?" she asked. Her dad laughed. "It is mine. I lost it this morning." Clara held it up. "You need the other one," she said. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks!" Her dad nodded. "Yes! Can you help me find its partner?"

Clara jumped up, feeling excited. She looked by the door. She looked on the stairs. Then she saw a blue sock on Goldie, her toy bear! "Goldie was wearing it!" she shouted. Dad put on both socks. "One sock, two socks. A pair!" said Clara. "Ten toes in there!" Dad counted them out loud, and Clara giggled. "Dinner and a sock hunt!" said Dad. Clara hugged Goldie tight.

Alexis was going on a trip. He rode a bus to the airport. Then he rode an airplane to the national park. Alexis had a seat by the window.

He wanted to stand up. He wanted to reach the window with his fingers. "Sit down, Alexis," said his dad. "Buckle your seat belt." Alexis clicked his belt. Click! The plane began to roll. Then it went up, up, up. The plane tipped back and Alexis slid down in his seat. The belt held him snug. The plane zoomed into the sky.

Alexis looked out the window. The clouds looked soft. The sun made the seats warm and hot. "Wow," said Alexis. Later the plane came down. The belt held him again. His dad smiled. "Look, deer!" said Alexis. He pointed at the park below.

Owen went to the community kitchen with his dad. Today they would make bread for the family. Owen wanted to help pour.

Mr. Marino set out a big bowl. He gave Owen a bag of flour. "You can pour it in," said Mr. Marino. Owen held the bag up high. He tipped it fast.

The flour made a little cloud. It went up and up. Then it came down like snow. Owen had flour on his nose. His dad had flour on his nose too. Camilo, at the next table, got a dusty nose as well. "Puff," said Owen, and he laughed.

The cloud settled slowly onto the table. Owen looked at the flour in the bag. It was a dry powder, soft and light. When he poured it fast, it made the cloud. Now he wanted to try again, but a small cloud this time.

"More flour," said Mr. Marino. This time Owen tipped the bag slowly. The flour slid out like sand. No cloud came. No dusty noses. The flour made a soft little hill in the bowl. Camilo leaned over to look. "No snow today," said Camilo.

Owen stirred the bowl with a big wooden spoon. Mr. Marino put the bread in the oven, because ovens are hot. Owen watched from his chair. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and good. The bread came out golden. "I poured it slow," Owen told his dad. His dad gave him a kind smile and a warm slice.

Emily woke up early. Today she turned five. She ran to the kitchen in her white socks. Mom was there with a big cake. It had pretty pink frosting.

"Let's count the candles," said Emily. She touched each one with her finger. "One, two, three, four." Then she stopped. "That is only four candles. But I am five today!"

Mom smiled. "You are right. A cake has one candle for each year." She went to the drawer. "Can you fetch the candle box for me?" Emily brought it carefully with both hands. Mom put in the fifth candle.

Adriel and Edouard came over. They sang happy birthday. Then Dad lit the candles, one by one. The little flames danced. "Make a wish," said Mom. Emily took a big breath. She blew and blew. All five candles went out at once.

"Five candles for five years," said Adriel. Emily grinned. Then Mom cut the cake, and everyone got a big slice.

Milo walked on the nature trail with Ms. Rao. Farah and Coen walked next to him. Ms. Rao had a game. "Tell me a sense," she said. "Nose!" said Milo. "Good. You smell with your nose." Milo smelled a flower. It smelled sweet.

Then Coen laughed. He pinched his nose shut with his fingers. He sniffed the flower. "I can't smell it!" he said. Milo tried it too. He pinched his nose shut. He sniffed and sniffed. No smell came. He let go. The sweet smell came back. Milo sniffed the flower again. It smelled sweet once more.

Milo touched a rough tree. He listened to a loud bird. He looked at a red leaf. Then Ms. Rao said, "Snack time." She took cookies from her bag. The cookies came from her kitchen. Milo smelled them with his nose. "Yum," he said. He took a big bite. "Can you spell yum?" asked Farah. "Y-U-M," said Ms. Rao, slow and clear. Milo ate his cookie and smiled.

Sara wanted to play house at school. She saw Loic and Aminata in the corner. They rocked baby dolls in their arms. Sara stood near them. She did not know how to join. She looked down at her shoes. The dolls were soft and squishy. Sara wanted to hold one.

Aminata saw Sara. "Do you want to play?" she asked. Sara nodded, but she stayed quiet. She picked up a small towel. She wanted to dry the doll's tiny face. Loic just looked at her. He did not know what she was doing.

Then Sara took a big breath. "Let's pretend I am the doll's mom," she said. Loic smiled right away. He handed her a doll. Aminata gave her a little bottle. "The baby is hungry," Aminata said. Sara fed the doll. Then she patted its back.

Outside, the sky was bright. Mr. Huang peeked in at the door. "What a happy home," he said. Sara hugged her doll close. "Time for sleep, little one," she whispered.

Matteo put on his skates at the ice rink. His team was going to play a game! The ice felt cold and shiny. His breath made little white clouds.

The other team was fast. They skated and skated. The buzzer went beep. The other team won. Matteo did not win. He sat down on the bench. His tummy felt tight and his face felt hot.

Mr. Rivera called, "Line up, everyone!" Matteo looked. His whole team made a long line. The other team made a line too. Zendaya was first. She skated past each player. She said, "Good game." Each player said, "Good game," back to her.

Matteo went next. He skated past a boy from the other team. "Good game," said Matteo. The boy smiled big. "Good game!" he said. They tapped hands. Matteo's tummy felt better. It felt warm, like cocoa.

"Can we drive home now?" Matteo asked his dad. "Can I tell Mom the whole story?" Dad laughed. "Yes! She will be so happy to hear it."

At the next game, Matteo lined up first. He could not wait to say, "Good game."

Cooper got on the school bus. He held his toy dinosaur tight. Gurfateh sat next to him. "Can I hold him?" Gurfateh asked. Cooper pulled the dinosaur close to his chest. "He is my very best toy," Cooper said. Gurfateh's face went sad. Cooper did not like that at all.

Then Cooper had an idea. "Do you have a backpack?" he asked Gurfateh. "Yes," said Gurfateh. Cooper smiled. He put his dinosaur in his own backpack. He zipped it up all the way. The dinosaur was hidden and safe. Nobody had to share him now. "Where did he go?" asked Gurfateh. "Into my secret store," said Cooper. Gurfateh laughed.

Cooper dug in his backpack again. He pulled out a small red car. "Want to try this one?" he asked. "We can take turns." Gurfateh pushed the car down the seat. Then he rolled it back. Vroom, vroom! Addison leaned over from the seat behind. "My turn next?" she asked. Cooper nodded and passed her the car. The bus bumped and giggled all the way to school.

Mason sat in his car seat. His cup had nothing in it. "My cup is empty," he said. His dad was driving to Ms. Addo's house. Dad said, "We can stop and fill it up."

They stopped at a little shop. Marina and her mom were there too. Marina held a big cup. Mason's cup was small. Dad bought a cold bottle of water. The water was cold, but the coffee cup in Dad's hand was hot, so Dad held both carefully.

Dad let Mason help pour. Mason poured fast. Water came up and spilled over the top. "Oops," said Mason. He tried again. This time he poured slow, slow, slow. The water went up and up. It stopped right at the top. "Now it's full!" said Mason. Dad gave him a kiss on his head. "You were brave to try again," Dad said. Ms. Addo was baking cookies when they got there, and Mason carried his full cup in slowly, one step at a time, so not one drop would spill.

Ali wanted to play in the backyard. But his toy box was empty. "Where did my toys go?" he said.

Ali looked behind the big tree. He found a red ball. He looked under the chair. He found a soft doll. He looked by the flower pot. He found a little toy mouse, grey and cool in the shade.

Ali put each one in the box. Ball. Doll. Toy mouse. His friend Sahib came to the fence. "You found them!" said Sahib. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," said Sahib. "You can put them all in one box."

Ali ran inside for his blocks. He stacked them tall, then made the tower spin around with one finger. It wobbled and fell with a soft plop. Ali laughed.

Then Ali put the blocks in the box, too. Now the box was full. "All my toys are home," said Ali. He gave the box a gentle pat.

Elliot went to the park with his dad. Azaan and Sehaj were there. They were throwing beanbags into a big hoop on the grass.

Elliot tried. His beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed in the stinky trash can. "Yuck," said Elliot. He tried again. He missed again. He felt like crying.

"Try again," said Azaan. So Elliot picked up a new beanbag. He threw it. Miss. He threw it again. Miss. Then he threw it one more time. Whoosh! The beanbag went right into the hoop.

"Again," said Elliot. He threw and threw. Now most of his beanbags went in. His arms knew just what to do.

Then Sehaj rolled him a big ball. "Use both hands," she said. Elliot held out his hands. The ball bounced off his tummy. He tried again. He tried a lot. Then he caught it with both hands. He held it tight.

"You caught it!" said Sehaj.

Elliot looked at his hands. "My hands got smart," he said. The sun went down like a big orange ball over the ocean, far away. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "I want to throw some more."

Georgia was at Grandma's house. It was bedtime, and the room was dark. Grandma said, "Pick your socks, sweet pea." Georgia reached into the sock bag. In the dark, the socks all felt the same. She could not tell what color they were. She held one up close. Still no color, just dark. "It's too dark," said Georgia.

She put on two socks. She felt warm and cozy. "Good night, Grandma," she said. The dark was a little scary, but her blanket was soft. Soon Georgia was asleep.

In the morning, the sun came in. The window turned bright and yellow. Georgia looked down at her feet. One sock was red. One sock was green. She laughed. "Grandma, look! Red and green!" Grandma smiled and said, "The light helps us see colors." Georgia stomped her feet. Clomp, clomp, went the red sock and the green sock, all the way to breakfast.

Layla sat in the family car. Her bunny was gone! "Where is Bunny?" she cried. Daddy buckled her in. "Let's look when we stop," he said.

The car went bump, bump over the road. Layla looked under her seat. No bunny. She looked in her cup holder. No bunny. Then she saw her coat on the seat. The coat had a big pocket. Things could end up inside other things! Maybe bunny was inside the pocket. Layla pushed her hand in. Something soft was in there. She pulled and pulled. Out came Bunny! "Bunny was in the pocket!" she shouted. She hugged Bunny tight. Bunny's ear felt warm from the sun.

"Good looking, Layla," said Daddy. Layla giggled. "Bunny was hiding in my coat!" She kissed Bunny's nose.

Daniel stood in Grandpa's garage. On the wall hung a small violin. "Can I try it?" Daniel asked. Grandpa took it down. "A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument," he said. "Let's go see Mr. Adeyemi."

Daniel held the violin upside down. He plucked one string. It made a funny little sound. He plucked again. Still funny. He tried one, two, three strings. Not one made music. Daniel frowned. "It sounds wrong," he said.

Mr. Adeyemi knelt down. "Let's turn it around," he said. He helped Daniel hold it the right way. Daniel put his chin on the soft rest. He pulled the bow across one string. A long, sweet note filled the room. Then he pulled two, three, four times. Each pull made a new sound.

Daniel played soft and slow, like snow in winter. He played fast and bouncy, like popcorn. Vincent and Hadley came to listen. They clapped their hands. Grandpa sat in his chair and smiled. "Play one more," said Hadley. Daniel lifted his bow and began again.

Theodore put on his little apron. He was at the big community kitchen with his dad. Today he would make cookies for his family. Ms. Sinclair smiled at him. "One, two, three scoops of flour," she said. Theodore counted along. "One, two, three!" He poured the flour into the bowl. Then he cracked two eggs. A bit of shell fell in. His dad helped him fish it out. "Good try," Dad said. "Try again." The next egg came out clean.

Theodore mixed the dough. He mixed and mixed. His arm got tired, but he kept going. Then the dough was ready. Dad slid the tray toward the oven. Theodore wanted to open the oven door himself. He reached out his hand. Dad caught his arm gently. "A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven when children help cook," Dad said. "You can watch from here." Theodore stepped back and nodded.

The kitchen window rattled. It was windy outside. A paper napblew off the counter and sailed across the room. Theodore giggled and chased it. He caught it and set it back down. Then the oven beeped. Dad put on big mitts. He opened the door. The cookies were golden. But there was a surprise. One cookie had a hole in the middle, shaped like a little star. "Look, Dad!" Theodore said. "A star cookie!" He counted the tray. "One, two, three, four, five, six cookies for my family." He carried the plate, walking slowly, all the way home.

Caleb stood at the bus stop with his dad. The wind blew. His coat flapped open like wings. "Brrr!" said Caleb. "My tummy is cold."

His dad held the coat. "Look," he said. "A zipper has two sides." Caleb looked down. Yes, two sides, one on the left, one on the right. "Where do they go?" Caleb asked. His dad smiled. "You try. Pull the tab up."

Caleb found the little tab. He pulled it up, up, up. Click, click, click. The two sides joined together! The wind stopped sneaking in. "My coat is closed!" said Caleb. He jumped. His cup of water bounced in his hand and went blub, blub.

Hallie ran up with her mom. Her coat hung open too. The wind puffed it out like a balloon. "Can you help me?" she asked. Caleb showed her the tab. "Pull it up!" Hallie pulled and pulled. Click, click, click. Her coat closed too.

The bus came down the bumpy road. Caleb held his dad's hand. "I did my zipper all by myself," he said. Hallie patted her zipped-up coat. "Me too," she said. "Warm tummies for the bus!"

Aaron went to the store with his dad. Aaron wanted a cookie. Where were the cookies? Aaron saw a sign on a shelf. The sign had words on it. Dad read the words out loud. "It says cookies are here," said Dad. Wow! The words told Dad something.

Aaron wanted to make a sign too. At home he drew one for his friend Laurier. He wrote all his letters in one long line. IMADEACOOKIEFORLAURIER. "Can you read my sign?" Aaron asked. Laurier looked and looked. "No," said Laurier. "It is all squished."

What could Aaron do? He looked at a book. The book had words too. Aaron opened the front cover first. He saw little gaps between the words. A space here. A space there. Aaron copied that. He put spaces in his own line.

I MADE A COOKIE FOR LAURIER.

"Spaces between the words," said Aaron. Laurier read it out loud, slow and happy. "A cookie for me!" Then Laurier took a big chew of the cool cookie Aaron had saved. "Your words work," said Laurier. Aaron smiled and drew one more sign. It said AARON.

Arlo sat in his little chair at the temple hall. There were big bowls of bread and fruit on the table. Arlo was hungry. He grabbed a piece of bread and took a big bite.

Then Arlo looked up. Everyone else sat still. Nobody was eating. Grandma held her hands folded. Coen had his hands folded too. Priscilla whispered, "We say thank you first." Arlo put his bread down on his tidy plate. He folded his hands.

Grandma smiled. She said the blessing out loud. She thanked everyone who grew the food. Then she said, "Now we eat." Arlo picked up his bread again. "Now we eat!" he said. Coen laughed. Priscilla laughed. Arlo took another big bite.

At the next meal, Arlo folded his hands all by himself. He waited, and he waited. Then Grandma said the blessing. "Now we eat," said Arlo, and everyone smiled at him.

Hailey wanted to wash her doll. She ran to the bathroom. The faucet had two taps. One was red. One was blue.

Hailey reached for the red tap. Her mom stopped her fast. "Let me check it," Mom said. Mom turned the red tap a little. Steam came up. "That one is hot," Mom said. Mom turned the blue tap. The water felt cool and nice. Mom filled the sink partway.

Hailey washed her doll in the warm water. Then she saw her rubber duck. It had been lost for weeks! "You were hiding," Hailey said. She gave the duck a wash too.

After the bath, Hailey wanted to go to the park. The park was across the road. Cars went by. Hailey saw the swings. She wanted to run. But she waited. She held out her hand. Mom took it. They crossed the road together, hand in hand.

At the park, Kaleb was there with a toy animal. "Fetch!" he called. His dog ran for the stick. Hailey laughed and swung high beside him.

Amira was home with a snuffly nose. Her tissue box sat on the table. Her apple slices sat on a plate. She was hungry for one.

First Amira blew her nose. The tissue went into the bin. Then she reached for an apple slice. She stopped. Her hands had touched the tissue. She asked herself, "Are my hands clean?"

"Wash first," said her mother. Amira ran to the sink. One pump of soap, two splashes of water, three big rubs. "Soap and water, soap and water," she sang. Her hands came out bubbly and clean.

Then Amira took an apple slice. It tasted sweet. She ate one, two, three. Later she blew her nose again, and put the tissue in the bin. "Wash first," Amira said, all by herself. She carried her stool to the sink, careful and slow. Clean hands, sweet apple. She smiled and took another slice.

The end came at snack time the next day. Amira blew her nose, and Mavis said, "Snack time!" Amira held up her hands and said, "Wash first." Mavis followed her to the sink.

Today was Maria's birthday. She wore a paper hat with stars. The party was at the bowling alley. Zackary and Alaina came too.

Maria rolled her ball. One pin fell, then two pins, then three pins. Zackary clapped. Alaina clapped. Maria wanted to see her balloons float. Dad had blown up three balloons with his own breath.

Maria let go of a red one. She watched the sky. The balloon did not go up. It went down, down, down to the floor. It sat by Zackary's shoe.

Maria picked it up. She let go again. Down it went again. It drifted like a soft leaf. Ms. Smith, from next door, smiled and gave it a little sweep with her hand. The balloon slid across the floor.

Alaina found one gold balloon on a string near the party table. That balloon pulled up on its string. Maria held the red one up high and let go. It fell right onto her hat.

"This one stays with me," Maria said. She hugged the red balloon. Zackary yawned and rubbed his eyes. The little ones at the next lane were asleep in their strollers.

Maria carried her red balloon to the car. She held it tight all the way home.

Isaiah went to the park with his dad. Isaiah wore his striped shirt. He saw a big robot toy in another boy's hands. "Can we stop and look?" Isaiah asked. "Yes," said his dad.

Near the swings there was a little snack shop. A man was cooking corn on a hot grill. Isaiah pointed at it. "That grill is hot," the man said. "I will hold the corn. You stay back here." Isaiah stood far away and watched. The corn went sizzle, sizzle.

Then Isaiah saw a red kite high in the sky. He turned and turned to watch it. When he looked down, his dad was not there. Isaiah could not see him anywhere. He felt like crying, but he stopped and thought. His dad always said a shop worker can help. So Isaiah walked to the snack shop man. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The man smiled. "Let's look together."

They waited by the shop. The man gave Isaiah a cup of cold water. Isaiah sipped it slowly. Then he heard a voice. "Isaiah!" His dad was running over from the pond. "I stopped to feed the ducks," said his dad. "You found a good helper." Isaiah asked, "Did the water help me wait?" The man laughed. "Yes. Cold water is a good waiter too." Isaiah held his dad's hand all the way to the swings.

Naomi sat at the dinner table. Her hair was a big mess. It went up and out and everywhere. She had slept on it funny. She had played hard at school, too.

"Mama, my hair has tangles," said Naomi. She pulled a bit with her fingers. "Ow."

"Finish your carrots first," said Mama. "Then we will fix it."

Naomi ate one carrot. Then she ate one more. She drank her milk. She put her plate in the sink, nice and slow.

Then Mama got the brush. Naomi sat on the little stool. Mama started at the bottom of her hair. She brushed slowly, so it did not pull. Naomi watched in the hall mirror.

One tangle came out. Then another tangle came out. Naomi could see it happen. The brush went through, and the tangle was gone. Her hair began to hang down, soft and smooth. Her eyes went wide.

"Brushing gets the tangles out!" said Naomi.

"Yes, it does," said Mama. "One, two, three, four. All done."

Naomi touched her hair. It felt like silk. She smiled a big smile.

"Now bath," said Mama. "Then pajamas. Then bed."

"Can I bring the brush?" asked Naomi.

Mama laughed and put it in her hand.

Iris was three today. There was a big party at home. Balloons bobbed by the kitchen door. Tyler and Reyna came to play. On the table sat a box with blue paper and a bow.

"What is inside?" asked Iris. She shook the box. She squeezed the box. The paper hid everything. She could not see one bit of it. Reyna shook it too. "I can't see either," said Reyna.

Iris wanted to peek. She pulled at the paper a little. "Not yet," said Mom gently. "We open it after cake." It was hard to wait. So Iris ate her cake first. Then Mom helped her open the box. The paper fell away. Inside was a soft brown teddy bear! Iris hugged him tight. "Hello, bear," she said. "You were hiding all along." The party went late into the happy afternoon, and Iris fell asleep with her bear in her arms.

Riley sat in the big concert hall with her sister. The stage had a drum and a big gray piano. Riley wanted to clap along to the song. She clapped and clapped. Then her hands got tired. "How can I keep going?" she asked. Her sister pointed down. "You can stamp the beat with your feet."

Riley stamped her feet. Boom, boom, boom. The beat kept going. Mr. Anderson saw her from the stage. He smiled and tapped his drum. Boom, boom, boom. Riley stamped too. The drum and her feet went the same way.

Then Riley sang a nursery rhyme she knew. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She stamped while she sang. Melina and Kimberly stamped too, from their seats. Soon everyone was stamping and singing together. Riley tapped her knees, then stamped her feet, then clapped again when her hands felt better. The song grew big and warm. "More!" said Riley. And the drummer played one more song, just for her.

Iris sat at the little table in the library. A big box of crayons sat in front of her. She had all of them. Alaina came and sat down too. Alaina had no crayons. She looked at the paper. Then she looked at the floor.

Iris picked up the red crayon. She put it in front of Alaina. Then she gave her the blue one too. "You can use them," said Iris. "Sharing means you use them too."

Alaina smiled and drew a big red cat. Iris drew a blue dog. They pushed the crayons back and forth across the table.

Ms. Ngo came by with a book. "The truck book is back," she said. "You two can look at it together."

Iris turned the pages. Alaina pointed at the truck with the sharp ladder on top. "My turn," said Alaina. Iris gave her the book and kept coloring.

Axel ran to the park with Lilianna. Ms. Pelletier had two hoops and a big red ball.

"Throw the beanbag in the hoop," said Ms. Pelletier. Axel threw it. It hit the rim and fell out. Lilianna threw hers. It went in with a soft plop. "Good try," she said to Axel. Axel picked up his beanbag. He took a big breath. He threw again. This time it went in. "I did it!" he said.

Then Ms. Pelletier rolled the big red ball to Axel. His hands were in his pockets. The ball bumped his tummy and rolled away. Lilianna giggled, but not in a mean way. "Watch me," she said. She held her arms out. Her hands were open. The ball came, and she caught it with both hands.

Axel pulled his hands out of his pockets. He was afraid the ball would bump him again. But he held his arms out too. He opened his hands wide. The ball rolled to him, soft and bumpy. He caught it! It felt cool and smooth. "My turn again," said Axel. He bounced the ball on the grass and ran after it.

Luca sat on the little red mat at Ms. Goh's music studio. Ms. Goh clapped her hands. "Listen," she said. "Clap when you hear the beat." Luca clapped. Then he clapped some more. Clap, clap, clap, just like the drum.

"Now let's sing a rhyme," said Ms. Goh. Zahra and Cameron sang too. Luca knew the first line well. But the second line went missing. He stopped and frowned. "My words fell out of my head," he said. "Like a sour lemon dropped them." Cameron laughed. "Sing it again, silly!"

So they sang it again. Then again. Then one more time. Luca thought hard. The mountain of the song grew smaller each time. On the fifth try, the second line jumped right out of his mouth. "I did it!" he shouted. Ms. Goh clapped the beat. "One, two, ready, sing!" And Luca sang the whole rhyme all by himself, clapping loud at the end.

Emily went to the park with her dad. Mr. Dang was there with the big chalk. He was drawing a yellow sun on the path.

Emily had big news. She found a red leaf. She wanted to tell Mr. Dang right away. "Mr. Dang! Mr. Dang!" she said. Mr. Dang was still talking to her dad. Emily tugged his sleeve. "Mr. Dang!" Mr. Dang held up one finger. He did not turn around.

Emily's face felt hot. That felt scary, a little bit. Her dad smiled at her. She watched Mr. Dang's mouth. He was still talking. Then his mouth stopped. There was a quiet little pause.

"Now," Emily whispered to herself. "Mr. Dang, please look. I found a red leaf!" Mr. Dang turned around. "A red leaf! May I see it?" "Yes. Thank you for waiting," said Emily. "Thank you for the leaf," said Mr. Dang.

"I am sorry I pulled your sleeve," said Emily. Mr. Dang smiled. "You waited for the quiet part. That was kind." Emily held the leaf up high. "My turn to talk," she said.

Muhammad found a big cardboard box under the table. He tipped it over. It made a cave! He put his bear inside.

Zack came to play. Zack saw the cave and jumped. "A dragon lives in there," Zack said. "A scary dragon!"

"No," said Muhammad. "The dragon is friendly. He sleeps in the cave."

Zack frowned. "Dragons are scary."

Muhammad thought hard. What could they do? Then he had an idea. "Let's say the dragon is friendly," he said. "He can be our pet."

Zack smiled a big smile. "Yes! A pet dragon. His name is Rex."

The boys patted the box. One pat, two pats, three pats for Rex. They fed Rex a pretend apple. Rex waved his pretend tail. He was a friendly dragon after all.

"Rex is hungry again," said Zack.

"I will cook," said Muhammad. He stirred a pretend pot. The dragon was far away, waiting by the cave. He blew pretend smoke, but no fire. Friendly dragons do not do fire.

Then Rex yawned. He was sleepy. They tucked him in with a small towel. "Night night, Rex," said Muhammad. Zack patted him one more time. The friendly dragon snored.

Everly ran to the big sports field. Her family sat on the soft green grass. Ms. Mercer was there too. So were Gwen and Zavier. A big game was about to start.

Everyone around them wore blue shirts. Deep blue, like the night sky. Everly looked down. Her shirt was plain white. She felt a small worry fill her tummy.

"Where is your blue?" asked Gwen. "Wearing team colors shows which team you cheer for," said Zavier.

Ms. Mercer opened her bag. It was full of blue shirts. She held one out to Everly. "Would you like one?"

Everly put it on. It was soft and warm. It smelled like clean laundry. Then she glued herself to her spot next to Gwen. Everyone clapped.

The blue team ran out. The crowd waved and cheered. Everly waved too.

"Go, blue team!" she called in her loudest voice. "Go, blue team!"

Ella went to the library with her dad. It was a sunny day. The big windows let in warm light. Story time was about to start.

Mr. Grewal put out a mat. On the mat were toy cars. Red cars and blue cars. Then Ella saw something yellow. It was long and curved. "A banana!" she said. "A banana does not go with cars."

Raegan pointed too. "The banana is the odd one out," she said. Ella held the banana up. Everyone laughed. Mr. Grewal smiled.

Then Mr. Grewal held up a picture card. It had a cat, a dog, a bird, and a shoe. Ella looked and looked. She picked the shoe. "The shoe is the odd one out," she said. "A cat, a dog and a bird are animals. A shoe is not."

After story time, Ella found the food books. Emeraude was there too. They read about apples and bread. Then Ella hung her coat on her little hook. She checked the pocket. Out fell a small toy duck.

Emeraude giggled. "A duck with apples?" she said. Ella laughed and hugged the duck. "You are the odd one out," she whispered. "But you can come too."

Hayden rode the bus with his mother. The floor was slippery, so he held her hand tight. Today he would get a library card.

At the library, Ms. Malik smiled. "Here is your card, Hayden." Hayden took it. The card had his name on it. He picked a big red book about buses.

A cat in the book went scratch, scratch on a tree. Hayden laughed.

Then he had to give the book back. He felt sad. "All done?" he asked Ms. Malik.

"No, no," she said. "Watch this."

She slid his card again. Beep! Out came a new book, a green one about frogs.

"My card works again!" said Hayden.

He hugged the card all the way home on the bus.

"Next week, more frogs?" asked his mother.

"Next week, more buses!" said Hayden.

Lily walked into the mall with her mom. She was going to get her very first haircut! Her hair was long and full of tangles. She wanted it short, like her friend Valentino.

At the salon, a hairdresser put a big cape on Lily. She snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Lily watched the hair fall down. It looked like soft rain.

Then the hairdresser was done. Lily looked in the big wall mirror. She could see the front of her hair. It was so short and neat! But she could not see the back.

"Mom, I want to see the back!" said Lily. She turned her head. She bent way over. Still no back. She laughed at herself in the mirror.

The hairdresser smiled. She held up a little hand mirror behind Lily's head. Lily looked at the big mirror. There it was! The back of her hair! Two mirrors made it show.

"I see it! I see the back!" said Lily. "It looks like a fox, all orange and smooth!"

On the way out, they saw Aarya from school. "Wow, Lily!" said Aarya. "Your hair is so cute!"

"Come here," said Lily. "You have to see the back. The salon has a magic little mirror, and it is very gentle with your hair."

Josephine climbed onto the school bus. She sat by the window and held her letter cards. Today she would learn the whole alphabet!

She sang the letter song with her friend Ashton. They sang all the way to the letter P. Then Josephine stopped.

"Is P the last letter?" she asked.

"No!" said Ashton. "Keep singing!"

So Josephine kept singing. Q, R, S. The bus rumbled over ice on the road. T, U, V, W. She saw a sharp corner turn. X, Y, Z!

"Z is the last one," Josephine said. She put her Z card at the end of her row. Then she put her A card at the front.

"The alphabet starts with A," she said, "and ends with Z!"

She would remember that all day. She sang the song again, fast, and laughed all the way to school.

Scarlett ran to the toy cars at daycare. Beatrix was already there. Gordon came too.

"Let's race," said Gordon. "The cars go to the red boot. Then they stop."

They all pushed their cars. Scarlett watched her little car zoom. It went far. Beatrix's car went far too.

Then Gordon said, "New rule! Now my car wins every time."

Beatrix put down her car. Scarlett put down her car too. Nobody pushed any cars. The game stopped.

"That is not the game," said Beatrix softly.

Gordon looked at the quiet cars. He thought for a moment. "Okay. Cars go to the red boot. Then they stop."

The race started again. Scarlett laughed. Her car wobbled like a furry caterpillar.

Then something small surprised her. Under the red boot sat a tiny toy mouse. "Look!" said Scarlett.

"A prize!" said Beatrix.

"Now we all follow the rules," said Gordon. "So we all get turns with the mouse."

Scarlett held the mouse first. Then she gave it to Beatrix. "Your turn," she said.

The cars zoomed to the red boot again.

Willow sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a little rumble. "Is it time to eat now?" she asked. "Not yet," said her mom. "It is time to eat later." Willow sighed. Later felt very far away.

She wiggled her toes under the table. She stretched her neck to see the counter. Then she saw the round clock on the kitchen wall. "What is that?" she asked. "That is the clock," said her dad. "The clock shows what time it is." The short hand pointed up high. The long hand went round and round, slow, not fast.

Willow watched the long hand move. It ticked and it ticked. Then her dad called, "Dinner time! Come and eat." Willow looked up at the clock. The hands were in a new spot. She clapped her hands. "The clock told you!" she said. Her dad laughed and set down the warm bowl. The steam came up soft and smelled like butter.

Willow ate her noodles one by one. "Can we do this again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "Tomorrow, and the day after that too." Willow smiled. After dinner, she slid off her chair. She patted the wall right under the clock. "Good night, clock," she whispered. "See you tomorrow."

Nolan sat at the dinner table. He could smell the soup. He used his nose to smell it. He touched his warm bowl with one finger. Then he tasted a spoonful. It was yummy.

Grandpa sat down next to him. Grandpa picked up his spoon. He looked at his book. He could not read the words. "I need my glasses," Grandpa said. He put them on his nose. Now he could see the words clearly. Nolan saw the glasses help Grandpa see.

Nolan heard the cat purr under the table. He remembered the first time Grandpa read to him. Nolan leaned his ear toward Grandpa's voice. "Read to me," Nolan said. Grandpa turned the page and began.

Juliette turned four today. Her party was at the big swimming pool. Abir and Inaya came too. They splashed in the shallow water. Ms. Ong, the pool teacher, gave them all kind smiles.

Then it was cake time. Juliette saw the cake. It had four little candles. She grabbed a box of matches. She wanted to light the candles herself.

Dad took the matches gently. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," he said. "You get the wish." Juliette watched Dad light each candle. The flames went flick, flick, flick. Then she took a big breath. She blew out all four candles at once. Everyone clapped. Inaya handed her a card. Juliette smiled at the tiny candles, still smoking. "Next year, you can light them again, Dad," she said.

Jasper sat at the little table in art class. The light came in the big window. Ms. Ortiz put out paper shapes. There was a square, a triangle, and a rectangle. There was also a big red circle.

"Cut out the circle, Jasper," said Ms. Ortiz. She gave him the old blue scissors. She stayed right beside him. Jasper looked at the circle. He wanted to find a corner to start cutting. The square had corners. The triangle had corners. Jasper ran his finger all around the circle. He could not find a corner anywhere.

"The circle is round," said Louana next to him. "It has no corners." Jasper touched it again. Round and round his finger went. No corner at all. So he made a little pinch in the paper. Then he cut. Round and round he went, all the way. He held up the red circle to the window. "I found no corners!" said Jasper. Louana clapped. Dario held up his square. "I found four corners," said Dario. Jasper smiled and put his circle on his picture, right on top.

Freya got a new card from the library. It had her name on it. "My own card!" she said. Freya showed it to Ria. Ria had a card too.

They went to the library with a grown-up. The shelves were tall, tall, tall. The books were big and heavy. Freya could not reach them. She felt tired. "Too big," she said.

Then Ria pulled her hand. "Come and see!" There was a little corner at the desk. The shelves there were small. The books had bright colors. "Many libraries have a children's area," said the grown-up, "with books just for young kids." Freya picked a book about a puppy. She gave her card at the desk. The librarian stamped the book.

At home, Freya sat on the rug. She tried to tie the puppy's ribbon to her toe. "Silly Freya," said Ria, laughing. Freya laughed too. "Read the puppy again," she said.

Rowan wanted his animal book. It was gone. He looked under his bed. He looked in his toy box. Silly toy box, no books in there.

"Let's make a shelf like the library," said Dad. "The library puts its books on shelves in groups. The animal books sit all together."

Rowan wiped the shelf with a cloth. It was dusty. He put the animal books in one group. He put the truck books in one group. He put the ocean books in one group. The ocean book had a big blue whale on it.

Then Rowan found his animal book. It was hiding with the sock books. "Silly book," said Rowan. He put it with the animals, right by the cow.

"Now I can find them," said Rowan. Dad read him the cow page.

Luka loved the dress-up corner at school. Today the basket was all mixed up. "Where did my red hat go?" he asked. Saint looked too. "Maybe it is under the heavy crown," said Saint.

Luka dug in the basket. He found a shirt. He found a sock. He found another sock. But no hat. Then he looked at the toy shelf. Something soft was sticking out of the truck bin. It was his hat!

"Why is a hat with the toys?" Luka wondered. Rehmat laughed. "That was my joke," she said. "I hid it there." Luka laughed too. He put the hat back in the basket. He put the shirts and socks in too.

"Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," said Ms. Xu, peeking in. "They live together." Luka looked at the toy shelf. Trucks and blocks are toys, he thought. They live over there.

He carried the heavy basket to the shelf. The dress-up corner looked just right now. "Tomorrow can I wear the red hat?" he asked Ms. Xu. She smiled and said, "Yes, at play time."

Bennett ran to the toy shelf at daycare. He wanted the big red magnet. Yesterday the magnet had picked up paper clips, and he wanted to try it again today. But the shelf was empty. Where did the magnet go?

Nivaan was playing at the sand table. "Tomorrow I went to the park with Dad," said Nivaan. Then he stopped. "No, not tomorrow. Yesterday. It already happened." Bennett thought about that. Yesterday was the day before today. The park trip was over. It was done. So the magnet play from yesterday was done too. But today was still new. "Did you see the red magnet?" Bennett asked. "Mr. Foster put it up high," said Nivaan. "We can have it later, after snack."

Later felt far away. Bennett brushed the sand off his hands and sat down for snack. He was afraid the magnet might be lost. But Mr. Foster smiled and took the magnet down from the tall shelf. "Now it is your turn," said Mr. Foster. Bennett held the magnet near a paper clip. The clip jumped up and stuck. He pulled it off and tried again. The clip jumped again! "It comes every time," said Bennett. Viola laughed and lined up three more clips. Bennett tapped the magnet on top.

Wren looked out the kitchen window. Snow was falling! Dad said, "No school today. It is a snow day!" Wren jumped up and down. She drank her cocoa while Dad held the warm cup. Then she ran outside.

She scooped up snow. She patted it into a ball. The ball fell apart in her hands. Wren tried again. It fell apart again. Gianna came over to play. Gianna said, "This snow is dry. Dry snow will not stick." Wren touched the new snow falling now. It felt a little wet. She patted it. It stuck!

The wet snow packed together well. Wren rolled a big ball. Gianna rolled the middle one. The snowman grew tall and cool. Wren got a carrot for the nose. Dad smiled from the window. Wren said, "Come see our snowman!"

Kinsley sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma was baking bread. Kinsley wanted to show Grandma something new. She wanted to say all five senses on her five fingers.

Kinsley held up her hand. She pointed to her thumb. "Seeing," she said. "I see the bread with my eyes." She pointed to her next finger. "Hearing," she said. "I hear the oven with my ears." Grandma smiled and nodded.

Kinsley sniffed the air. "Smelling," she said. "I smell the bread with my nose." She touched the cool table. "Touching," she said. "I touch with my hands." Then she stopped. She looked at her last finger. She had forgotten one. Her lip wobbled a little. "Grandma, I forgot one."

Grandma came close. "That is okay," she said. "Take your time." Kinsley looked at her hand. Then she looked at the bread. Grandma gave her a tiny taste on a spoon. Kinsley licked her lips. "Tasting!" she said. "I taste with my tongue. All five are true!"

Grandma clapped. "You did it," she said. Kinsley held up her hand again. She counted every finger, one by one. On the shelf, a little cow bell rang. "I hear the bell!" said Kinsley. "That is my ears catching the sound." Grandma laughed and hugged her tight.

Isaiah sat at the little red table at the tutoring centre. Mr. Guo put out two bowls of buttons. "Which bowl has more?" he asked.

Isaiah looked and looked. One bowl seemed big. But was it more? He could not tell. He said, "That one?" Mr. Guo shook his head and smiled.

Then Maddie, the girl next to him, counted the buttons in her bowl. She held up one finger for each button. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Her fingers stayed up. Five fingers. Five buttons. Nothing got lost.

Isaiah tried it too. He touched a button and put up a finger. Touch, finger. Touch, finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers stood up like a little fence. Before, he had lost his count two times. Now he did not lose it.

"Seven!" he shouted. Maddie laughed. "My fingers smell stinky," she said, and she waved them near Isaiah's nose. Isaiah giggled and waved his own fingers back.

Mr. Guo said, "So which bowl has more?" Isaiah held up his seven fingers. Then he looked at Maddie's five fingers. He put his hand next to hers. His row was longer.

"This one," said Isaiah. "Mine has more."

Mr. Guo gave him a big gold star sticker. Isaiah pressed it right onto his shirt.

"Look, Maddie!" he said. "My star can count too. One star."

Lillian sat at the big table. She wanted to draw a cat. She got her green crayon. Then she saw it was broken in two.

Lillian made a sad face. She pushed the crayons away. She put her head down on the table. Her tummy felt heavy.

"Are you okay?" asked her dad. He was washing cups at the sink. Lillian did not answer. She just frowned at the floor.

Then Lillian sat up. She looked at her dad. "I feel sad," she said. "My green crayon broke."

Her dad came over. He looked at the two pieces. "I can fix this," he said. He got the tape. He wrapped it around the middle. The crayon was long again.

Lillian picked it up. She pressed it on the paper. It made a green line! She drew a big green cat. Then she drew green grass under the cat.

"I feel happy now," said Lillian.

"Me too," said her dad. He went back to the sink. Soon it would be bath time, and the cat would wait on the table.

Lillian held up her picture. "Look, cat!" she said.

Gianna stood at the little table in the art room. She wanted to paint a big orange sun. But her paint pots only had red, yellow and blue.

"I want orange," she said. "I don't have orange."

Lylah held up a flat tray with little holes in it. "This is a palette," she said. "You can mix paint on it."

Gianna dipped her brush in the red. She put a dot on the flat tray. Then she dipped in the yellow. She put a yellow dot next to it. She stirred them together with her brush. The paint turned orange!

Gianna gasped. "Red and yellow made orange!"

She tried more on the palette first. Blue and yellow made green. She tested each new colour on paper before she painted her sun.

Ms. Buchanan smiled. "What a bright sun, Gianna."

Gianna painted orange rays all around it. Then she painted green grass at the bottom. Her picture had every colour she made.

"Look, Lylah," said Gianna. "The sun is orange like a big round peach."

Logan dug in the dirt with his small trowel. He planted little tomato plants in a row. He planted carrot seeds in another row. Then he planted bean seeds by the fence.

The next day, Logan forgot which row was which. "Where did I put the tomatoes?" he asked. He looked at the green sprouts. They all looked the same to him. A noisy chicken walked past his feet and pecked at the dirt.

Ms. Pritchard was his neighbour. She leaned over the fence. "Pass me that stick," she said with a smile. Logan passed her a stick. She gave it back with a paper card on it. The card had a red tomato painted on it.

Logan pushed the stick into the dirt by the tomato plants. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," said Ms. Pritchard. Logan made more labels. He painted a orange carrot. He painted a green bean.

Soon every row had its own picture card. Then came the small surprise. The bean seeds grew fast. They curled up the fence like tiny green arms. Logan ran to get his watering can. He gave each row a drink, row by row, and patted the label by the beans.

Daniel was at the playground. He saw the big yellow truck. It was the best toy there. Simeon was holding it.

"I want a turn," said Daniel. He reached out fast. His hand hit the truck. Some sand began to spill from the back.

"Ouch," said Simeon. "You almost knocked it down."

Ms. Virtanen came over. She held up a little timer. "Simeon has two more minutes," she said. "Then it will be your turn, Daniel."

Daniel sat on the bench to wait. He ate his snack. The apple slices were crunchy. He watched Simeon push the truck up the ramp. It looked like fun.

The timer rang. Ding! Simeon stopped the truck. He lifted it high. He looked like he might toss it far.

"Wait," said Daniel. "Please hand it to me gently."

Simeon smiled. He walked over slowly. He put the truck in Daniel's hands, soft as giving a present. "Your turn," said Simeon. "I can wait too."

Daniel drove the truck through the sand. Lina sat down next to him. "I would like a turn next," she said.

The timer rang again. Ding! Daniel stopped the truck. He held it out with two hands. Lina took it gently.

Then Simeon brought Daniel a crunchy leaf to look at. "We can play together after," said Simeon.

Daniel watched Lina drive. He waved. "Beep beep," he said.

Lily sat on her bed with her bear. Dad came in with a book. It had a forest on the cover. "Read it, please," said Lily.

Dad opened the front of the book. He read the words on each page. His finger went under them, left to right. Lily saw that when Dad touched the little black marks, he said the story out loud. When he turned pages, he went one by one, front to back.

One page had only a picture. A wet duck sat in a pond. "Read this one," said Lily. Dad looked. "There are no words on this page," he said. "Nothing is written here to read." Lily looked close. The page had no little black marks at all. "So the duck stays quiet," she said.

She gave the page a kiss anyway. Then Dad read the words on the next page, and the story went on. "This is the front," said Lily, patting the cover. "We read this way, to the back." Dad smiled and turned the page.

Nicholas climbed the big school bus steps. He held the rail with both hands. He found a seat by the window. His tummy felt jumpy.

A boy sat down next to him. "I am Caden," said the boy. "Are you scared?" Nicholas nodded a little. "My mom said the teacher looks after us," Caden said. "The teacher is the grown-up who helps the kids in our class." Nicholas looked out the window. The sun made his shadow on the seat. The shadow was long and wiggly.

The bus stopped at school. A tall man stood at the door. "Hello, I am Mr. Sow," he said. "I am your teacher. I will help you today." Nicholas took a big breath. He was brave now. He knew the man's name. "Hello, Mr. Sow," said Nicholas. Mr. Sow smiled and held out his hand.

Grayson was going to the dentist today. It would be his very first time. "I want to win a big smile!" he told his mom. He ran to the bathroom mirror at home.

Grayson opened his mouth wide. He looked at his tiny teeth. Then his tongue came out and said, "Ahhh." But every time he tried to talk, his mouth closed. His teeth went away. He could not see them anymore.

He tried again. He held his mouth open. He did not talk. There were all his teeth! Then his lips met and the teeth hid again. Mom laughed. "You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth," she said. "So don't talk in the chair. Just hold it open like a lion."

At the dentist, a big chair waited. The dentist said, "Let me see your teeth, Grayson." Grayson roared like a lion. He opened his mouth very wide. He kept it open and did not say a word.

The dentist looked at tooth after tooth. "I can see every one," she said. "What strong teeth you have." Grayson's mom gave him a thumbs up. At the end, Grayson got a tiny new toothbrush. He held it up high and roared again, "Roooar!"

Sienna played in the playroom. Blocks were all over the floor. "Time to clean up," said Mr. Holloway. "Put the same colors together."

Sienna looked at the blocks. Could she make a red pile? She picked up a red block. Then another red one. She stacked them in one spot. "Red pile," she said.

Giuliana made a blue pile. Amar made a yellow pile. Soon there were three piles on the floor. All the red blocks sat together. All the blue blocks sat together. All the yellow blocks sat together.

Then Sienna saw something funny. A yellow block was hiding in the red pile! "How did you get there?" she asked it. The block did not answer, of course. She picked it up and put it in the yellow pile. Now it was with all the yellow blocks, right where it belonged.

Mr. Holloway clapped his hands. "Good tidy piles," he said. Sienna smiled. Maybe there was a green block too? She looked under the little glass table. Yes! One green block, all alone. Where should it go? Not with the red ones. Not with the blue ones. It needed its very own pile. She set it down by itself. "Green pile," she said. "One, two, three, four piles!"

Rose and Alaya found a small house in the forest. It was made of sticks and old plastic bags. "Let's play house here," said Alaya. "Yes!" said Rose.

They set out leaves for plates. They set out pinecones for babies. Rose picked up a pinecone. "I am the parent," said Rose. "I feed the baby." "No, I am the parent," said Alaya. "I want to feed the baby too."

Both girls wanted to be the parent. Both girls stood still. The baby pinecone sat on the ground. Nobody fed it. Mr. Nasser, their neighbour, was walking by with his dog. He stopped and smiled. "You can both be the parent," he said. "Just not at the same time. One of you can be the baby, and then you can switch halfway."

"Alaya first," said Rose. "Then me." Alaya held the pinecone. She rocked it and sang. "Baby, baby, time to eat." Rose got down on her knees. She was the baby now. She drank pretend soup from a leaf. "More, please," said Rose. Alaya laughed and filled the leaf again.

Then they switched. Rose was the parent now. She held the pinecone up high. "Time for a hug, baby!" Alaya was the baby. She yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy, sleepy," said Alaya. Rose patted her back, very soft.

They played all afternoon. Parent, then baby. Baby, then parent. "Best house ever," said Rose. Alaya hugged the pinecone tight and said, "See you tomorrow, baby."

Kai was at Grandma's house. It was dark. The lights went out. "Power cut," said Grandma. She lit a big red candle. "Watch from here," she said. Kai sat on the sofa.

The house felt strange. Kai held his teddy tight. "Grandma, it is so quiet," he said. "Why is it so quiet?" Grandma said, "Listen. What do you hear?" Kai listened. He heard no humming. The fridge had stopped humming. "The fridge is asleep," said Kai. Then he heard a new song. It was a cricket outside the window. Then he heard the clock. Tick, tick, tick. He had never heard the clock before.

Grandma gave him paper. Kai drew a picture by the candle. He drew the little cricket singing its song. Grandma smiled. "The lights will come back," she said. Kai kept drawing in the warm red glow. "Tick, tick, tick," went the clock.

Jade sat at the dinner table. Her dad set out ten little cups. "Let's count them," he said. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Jade counted too. She held up her fingers as she said each word.

Then Jade saw the mailbox through the window. It had a big number on it. "What is that?" she asked. Her dad said, "That is a five. It is the same five you just counted." Jade looked at her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Five fingers. And the number five is on the box."

Jade peeked at her plate. She had five peas on it. She counted them one by one. Then she ate one pea. Now she had four. "Four is one less than five," she said to herself. She put the pea back? No, that would not work. She laughed.

Jade looked out at the big tree. "Dad, if I find a five, will you count five peas for me?" she asked. Dad smiled. "One, two, three, four, five," he said, and put five peas on her fork.

Grandma was coming on the train. Madelyn went to the station with Dad. "Grandma will stay a whole week," said Madelyn. "The same bed every night!"

They stood on the platform. Madelyn heard a faraway choo choo. She tiptoed to the edge to peek. Dad held her hand. "Stand back from the edge," he said. "We wait until the train stops."

Madelyn stepped back behind the yellow line. The big train zoomed past. Whoosh! It made her hair fly up like feathers. Madelyn laughed and laughed.

The train slowed down. Then it stopped. Now it was safe to walk. The doors opened with a pop. Grandma stepped out with her little red bag.

"Grandma!" Madelyn hugged her tight. "I stood back and the wind tickled me!"

"Smart girl," said Grandma. "Now let's go buy some bread for tea."

They walked to the car, all the family together.

Maeve went to the store with her dad. She wanted a new crayon. Her old blue crayon was stuck in the toy box. It would not come out.

Maeve looked at the crayons. She saw red, yellow and green. She saw a gray one too. "I will get the gray one," she said. "I want to draw the sky."

Then Maeve looked out the big window. The sun was out. The day was clear and bright. The sky was blue! The whole sky was blue.

Maeve put the gray crayon down. She picked up the blue one. "This one," she said. "The sky is blue today."

At home, Maeve drew a big picture. She drew the yellow sun. She drew green grass. She drew the blue sky, all the way to the top. Her dad hung it up. "Blue sky," said Maeve, and she smiled.

Quinn stood in the band room. A shiny trumpet sat on the stand. She wanted to play it for the spring show.

Ms. Ndlovu gave her a paper with dots and lines on it. "What are these marks?" Quinn asked.

"Those marks are called notes," said Ms. Ndlovu. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play."

Quinn put the paper on the stand. She blew the trumpet. Nothing came out but a squeak. Her friend Taha clapped anyway. "Try again," he said.

She puffed her cheeks and blew once more. A big sound came out! Quinn looked at a dot on the paper. She pressed her fingers and blew. A new sound came out.

"It's late, time to pack up," said Ms. Ndlovu. Quinn grinned and hugged her trumpet.

Arnaud wanted to win the guessing game. Ms. Cho had a big box on the table. Ewan and Jay stood in a line. Ms. Cho held up a long string. "Tie it on your eyes," she said. Arnaud could not see. He heard Jay giggle next to him.

Ms. Cho put something in Arnaud's hands. It was small and heavy. He touched it with his fingertips. His fingertips felt it all over. Smooth. Very smooth. "A stone!" he said. "Yes," said Ms. Cho. She gave him a new thing. His fingertips felt little bumps everywhere. Bumpy, bumpy, bumpy. "A pinecone!" he said. Jay clapped.

Then Arnaud held something light. His fingertips said soft, like a tickle. He smelled it too. It smelled like nothing much. He touched it again, soft and smooth. "A feather," he said. Ms. Cho took off the string. There it was, a white feather. Arnaud touched it one more time with his fingertips. "Soft," he said.

Claaire stood at the front door. She looked out the glass. The sky was gray. Rain dripped down the window.

"Can I go out?" Claire asked.

"Put on your rain boots," her mom said. "And take your coat. It is rainy today."

Claire pulled on her yellow boots. She zipped up her red coat. Then she pushed the door open. The rain went tap, tap on her hood.

At the playground, Claire met Lana. Lana pointed down. "Look! A big puddle!"

The puddle was wide and brown. Claire stepped in it. Splash! Water flew up. Her boots got messy. Lana laughed and jumped too. The rain made the puddle, and the puddle made the splash.

Later the rain stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny now. Claire took off her coat. She hung it on the fence.

"Time for breakfast," her mom called.

Claire ran to the door. "That was fun!" she said. "Thank you for my boots!"

Anna was at the community centre. Ms. Bennett put out two bowls of crackers. One bowl was for Anna. One bowl was for Brett.

"Which bowl has more?" said Brett.

Anna looked and looked. She could not tell. The crackers were all messy and jumbled.

Then Anna had an idea. She touched each cracker in her bowl. "One, two, three, four," she said. She held up four fingers. "Four!"

Brett counted his bowl. "One, two, three," he said. He looked sad. "Three."

"You have more," said Brett. "You win!"

Anna laughed. "Wait!" She moved one cracker to his bowl. Now they both had the same.

Ms. Bennett came by with a plate of orange slices. "More counting?" she said.

"Yes!" said Anna. "One, two, three, four, five. Five for me!"

Brett giggled. "Five for me too!"

Mya woke up and saw white. Snow had fall en all night. "No school today!" said her dad. "Snow day!" Mya cheered. She wanted to find her friend Kameron. So Dad took her hand and they walked to the park.

The park was soft and quiet. Mya's boots went crunch, crunch. She looked down. Her feet made marks in the snow! "Look, Dad! My feet make pictures!" Dad laughed. "Those are footprints," he said. Mya took big steps. Then baby steps. Then one silly hop. Each foot made its own print.

Then Mya saw more prints. They were small, like hers. They went past the slide. They went past the swings. "Follow me, Dad!" said Mya. She stepped in each print, one by one. The prints stopped at the bench. And there sat Kameron, wrapped in a big red coat, holding a book.

"You found me!" said Kameron. Mya grinned. "Your feet told me where to go!" Kameron giggled and held up the book. "Want to read about a sick dragon? He sneezes snow." Mya sat down close. "Achoo!" she said, and they both fell over laughing into the soft white snow.

Lily went to the grocery store with Dad. She held her bunny toy in her hand. The store smelled like fresh bread. Lily put bunny in the cart seat. Then she turned to look at the apples. They were red and shiny.

At the checkout, Lily looked at the cart. Bunny was gone! "Dad, bunny is lost," she said. Her eyes felt hot. Dad gave her a hug. "We can look together," he said. "When we both look, more people are searching." Lily looked down the bread aisle. Dad looked by the apples. Then Lily heard a squeak. Bunny was stuck under the bread bags, next to a stinky cheese. Dad laughed and pulled bunny out.

Lily hugged bunny tight. Bunny smelled like bread now. They walked to the car. "We win," said Lily. Dad smiled. "More eyes found bunny," he said. Lily waved to the store. "Bye, store," she said. Bunny got a soft pat on the head all the way home.

Grandma's car stopped outside. Claire ran to the door. Grandma had a big bag with wheels. "What is that?" Claire asked. "My suitcase," said Grandma. "It holds my clothes for a whole week." Claire helped pull the suitcase into the kitchen. It was heavy. It went bump, bump on the floor.

Claire wondered about the suitcase. "Is it full of toys?" she asked. Grandma laughed. "No, it is full of socks and shirts. Guests who come to stay pack their clothes and things in a suitcase." Claire unzipped it a little bit. She saw a red sweater. She saw warm socks. No toys at all.

Then Claire saw something cool. Grandma put her slippers by the door. Claire put her shoes by the door too. Now the row was bigger. "We filled the whole row!" said Claire. Grandma smiled.

At bedtime, Grandma unpacked more things. A hairbrush. A soft scarf. A shell from the beach, white and smooth. "For you," said Grandma. Claire held the shell to her ear. "I hear the sea," she said. Grandma tucked her in and patted the pillow. The suitcase sat by the wall, waiting for morning.

Grandpa came to stay at Logan's house for a whole week. "Let's play a game," said Grandpa. They sat on the blue mat in the backyard. Grandpa brought out the cards.

Logan wanted to go first. "Me first!" he said. He grabbed the cards. He put down his card. Then he put down another card. Grandpa laughed. "Wait, wait, little man," he said. "We take turns. You go, then I go."

Logan tried again. He put down one card. Then he waited. Grandpa put down one card. "Your turn," said Grandpa. Logan clapped his hands. "My turn now!" he said. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Do you like taking turns?" Logan thought. "Yes. It goes back and forth, like a swing!"

They played the game all week. On the last day, Logan said, "Grandpa first." Grandpa smiled big. He put down his card. Then Logan put down his.

Chloe sat on the city bus with her mom. They were going to the dentist for the first time. Chloe looked out the big window. "How will the dentist see my teeth?" she asked. Her mom smiled. "You will see."

At the dentist's office, Chloe sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. The dentist held up a little tool. It was a tiny mirror on a handle. "Open wide," she said. Chloe opened her mouth. The mirror went inside. It was small and shiny.

"How can you see behind my teeth?" Chloe asked. The dentist turned the mirror. "Look," she said. Chloe saw her own teeth in the tiny mirror. The backs of her teeth were there too! "The mirror shows me the backs of your teeth," the dentist said. Chloe got to hold the mirror after. She looked at her teeth again. "I can see me!" she said.

Camille was at Grandma's house. The new baby was there too. Camille had a red ball. She wanted to play with the baby.

"Baby, catch!" said Camille.

But the baby was sleeping. His eyes were shut. Camille waited. She drank milk from her orange cup. She took a bite of her bread. The baby kept sleeping.

Then the baby woke up. He made a small cry. Camille's mom picked him up. "He was sleepy," Mom said. "New babies sleep for much of the day."

Camille held out the red ball. The baby looked at it. He did not catch it. He just watched it roll. Then he yawned. His eyes closed again.

"Oh," said Camille. She sat down next to him. She patted his blanket, very soft. Grandma gave her a small pillow for her lap.

"I will wait," Camille said. She held the ball in her lap. The baby slept. Camille watched him breathe, up and down, up and down.

Grandma came with two cookies. "One for you," she said. "One for later, when he wakes."

Camille took a bite of her cookie. She smiled at the sleeping baby. "Wake up soon," she whispered. "Then we can play."

Sophia sat at the big table in the art room. Sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Ms. Tang put out the paints. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. Sophia wanted to paint grass. But there was no green paint.

"I need green," said Sophia. Her tummy felt tight. "There is no green!" Ms. Tang sat close by. "You can try," said Ms. Tang. Zakary dipped his brush in yellow. Ariya dipped hers in blue. Sophia looked at the two pots. She put yellow on her paper. Then she put blue on the yellow spot.

She moved her brush round and round. The yellow spot turned green! Real green! Sophia dipped her brush again. She filled the grass with green strokes. "Look!" said Ariya. Sophia painted tall green grass all the way to the flowers. At snack time there was bread and milk. Ms. Tang smiled. Sophia held up her painting. "I made green," she said.

Alexis wanted to read the big red book. It had a bird on the cover. The bird could fly over a dark, dark wood. Victor and Azriel were already on the rug. "A monster is in this book," said Azriel. Alexis sat down fast. He opened the book. He put his finger on the page. He started on the right side. His finger slid and slid. The words did not talk to him. Mr. Wong sat down. "Try the left side," said Mr. Wong. Alexis put his finger on the left. He slid it to the right. Mr. Wong said each word with him. The words talked! They told about a bird family in a tree. Alexis turned page after page. The story grew and grew. "The bird flies home," read Alexis. He smiled at the dark wood picture. "Turn the page!" said Victor. Alexis turned it. "The end," he read, all by himself.

Willow ran into the band room. A big piano stood by the wall. "I want to play a bear!" she said. Natan was there too. He wanted to play a bird.

Willow pressed a key on the left. Boom! A low sound came out. "That sounds like a big bear!" she said. She pressed it again. Boom, boom. She stomped her feet like a bear.

Then she pressed a key on the right. Ping! A high sound came out. "Can a bear be that high?" she asked. "No! The high side is for the bird." Natan pressed the right keys. Tweet, tweet! He flapped his arms.

"Your turn, Ms. Dang!" said Willow. Ms. Dang sat down. She played low, low, low on the left side. The room rumbled like a giant bear. Then she played high, high, high on the right side. It sparkled like a tiny bird at the beach.

Willow clapped. "Left is low! Right is high!" she said. She played bear sounds all the way down the left side. Boom, boom, boom. "Growl, big bear, growl!"

Charlotte was going on a trip. She was going to Aunt Rosa's house. Aunt Rosa lived near the snow. Charlotte got her little red suitcase. She wanted to pack it all by herself.

Charlotte put in her swimsuit. "I will swim at Aunt Rosa's house," she said. She put in her sun hat too. Then she showed her mom.

Mom looked at the suitcase. Mom looked out the window. The snow was far away, but it was waiting. "Let's check the weather where we are going," said Mom. They looked together. Snow! Lots of snow. "We pack warm clothes for the snow," said Mom. "A swimsuit is for the beach."

Out came the swimsuit. Out came the sun hat. In went the warm coat. In went the mittens. In went the little fuzzy hat. Charlotte pulled the zipper shut. Click.

At Aunt Rosa's house, the snow was deep and white. Charlotte stuck out her tongue. A snowflake landed on it. It turned to water, quick as a wink. "Do it again!" said Charlotte. And a little snowflake landed again.

Hayden went to the library with his dad. He hung his coat on the little hook. The library was big and quiet.

Then Hayden heard a loud noise. It went bang, bang, bang. He did not know what it was. His tummy felt tight. He felt scared. He held his dad's hand tight.

"I'm scared," Hayden said. "It's a scary noise." His dad said, "I can help. Let's go look together." They walked slowly. They looked behind a shelf. It was only Mr. Pérez, the librarian, pushing a heavy cart. Bang, bang went the wheels.

Hayden smiled. "Just a cart!" he said. He was not scared now. He was happy. Mr. Pérez gave him a truck book. Hayden sat in the tidy reading corner. He read it with his dad. "Good book," said Hayden.

Jacob ran onto the soccer field. The sun was big and hot. His shirt got warm. His nose got warm too.

"Time for a break," said Mr. Zhou. Jacob sat on the grass. Sienna sat next to him. She held up her blue bottle. "Water time," she said. She took a big drink. Raymond took a big drink too.

Jacob looked in his bag. He did not see his water bottle. It was at home on the table. Jacob felt worried. His mouth felt dry.

Then Mr. Zhou came over. He had a green bottle in his hand. "Here you go," said Mr. Zhou. "Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days." Jacob took the bottle. He drank and drank. The water was cool.

Jacob looked at the sky. The hot sun made him thirsty. The cool water made him feel better. He could see how that worked.

"Thank you, Mr. Zhou," said Jacob. He gave the bottle back. Then the whistle blew. Jacob jumped up and ran to kick the ball. "This is my favorite game," he said.

Sadie was at home. Her friend Rachel came to play. Rachel had her coat on and her head down.

Then Sadie heard a small sound. Rachel was crying. Big tears ran down her cheeks. Sadie felt scared for a minute. She did not know what to do.

Sadie looked at Rachel's wet face. She thought about her bunny. Her bunny made her happy. Maybe it would help Rachel too.

Sadie went to her room. She found the bunny on her bed. She ran back with the soft bunny in her hand. "You can hold him," said Sadie. Rachel took the bunny. She held it tight.

The tears slowed down. Then they stopped. Rachel wiped her face with her sleeve. "He is soft," said Rachel. She gave a little smile. Sadie felt excited and clapped her hands.

"Want some jam toast?" Sadie asked. "Yes," said Rachel. They went to the kitchen. Sadie's dad made the toast. Sadie watched from her stool. The jam was sticky on her fingers. She licked them clean.

Rachel held the bunny on her lap. She ate her toast bite by bite. "Thank you for Bunny," said Rachel. Sadie smiled. She had seen the bunny stop the tears.

After lunch, the girls drew pictures. Rachel drew a bunny with long ears. Sadie drew Rachel's smile.

Beau waited at the train station. Grandma was coming to stay for a week. The big train came in. A door opened. Grandma stepped out with her white bag.

"Grandma!" said Beau. He ran to hug her leg. Then he saw Mom hug Grandma too. Beau looked and looked. "Mom, why do you hug my grandma?" he asked.

Mom laughed. "Grandma is my mom," she said. Beau's eyes got big. "A grandparent is a parent of your mom or your dad," said Mom. "So Grandma is my very own mommy."

At home, Beau drew a picture. He drew Grandma, Mom, and himself. Grandma sat down and helped. She drew a little train. "Choo choo," said Beau, and he hugged her again.

Eleanor woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted milk in her cup too. "I can do it," she said.

Dad put the toast on the table. He cut it into squares. Eleanor took the butter knife. She spread the butter. She spread it slow. Some squares got lots of butter. One square got none. "Silly square," she said.

Next came the milk. Eleanor held her cup in one hand. She held the milk jug in the other hand. The cup wiggled. The milk splashed. A little puddle sat on the table. Dad mopped it up with a cloth. "Watch," he said. He set his cup down on the table first. Then he poured.

Eleanor set her cup down too. The cup sat very still. She poured. The milk went in, not out. "It's staying put!" she said. Dad gave her one more square of toast. It was the last one. "We can talk about it at snack time," said Eleanor, and she took a big bite.

Georgia sat at the big table. Grandma put warm bread on a plate. Lots of family came to eat. Georgia held her spoon up high. She was ready to eat.

Then everyone reached out their hands. Cousin hands, grandma hands, grandpa hands. They made a big circle around the table. Georgia looked and looked. Why were the hands holding? Her spoon was still in her fist. She could not hold hands and a spoon too. So she set the spoon down. Click, it went on the plate. Then she took two hands. One was grandma's. One was cousin Aylin's.

"Can we sing now?" Georgia asked softly. Grandpa smiled. Everyone closed their eyes. They said thank you for the bread. Georgia said it too. Then everyone picked up spoons at the same time. Outside, the street was quiet and sleepy. Georgia ate her bread and watched it melt butter on top. "More hands tomorrow?" she asked.

Jackson sat in the family car. The car went over a bump. The baby was in the car seat. The baby was his new baby sister.

"I want to hold her," said Jackson.

"Not in the car," said Mom. "The car seat keeps her safe. You can hold her at home."

The car went over another bump. The baby kept sleeping. Jackson held his own arms out. He practiced cradling them, like a little bed.

At home, the cat came to look. Jackson sat down on the couch. Dad sat right beside him.

"You can hold her now," said Dad. "Sit still, and I will help."

Dad put the baby in Jackson's arms. Dad kept his hands under her, too. The baby was small and warm. Jackson was very still.

"Hello, baby," said Jackson.

The baby opened her eyes. She looked at Jackson. Jackson smiled so big.

"My arms hold her," said Jackson.

"Yes, they do," said Dad.
