The cat jumped up and sat close. The baby made a tiny sound. Jackson rocked his arms, slow and soft. The baby closed her eyes and went back to sleep.

Zachary sat in the family car. He buckled his seat all by himself. "Today I get my shot," he said. "I am big now!" Mom smiled and started the car. The car went bump, bump over the road. Zachary held his toy dinosaur tight. "You can come too," he told the dinosaur.

At the doctor's office, Zachary took a big step inside. The nurse said, "Time for your shot." Zachary held still. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick! It was done. "That was fast," said Zachary. "It was just a little poke!"

Then Zachary saw something on the wall. It was a little red box. It had a small door. "What is that box for?" he asked. The nurse opened the little door. She dropped the used needle inside. It went clink! "The needle goes in there," she said. "It is a special hard box so nobody gets poked."

Wow! Zachary looked and looked. The needle went in, and the box did not let it come out. Nobody would get poked. Not the nurse. Not Mom. Not Zachary. "The box keeps the needle safe inside," he said. He said the word "safe" two times. "Safe, safe!"

On the ride home, Zachary told the dinosaur all about it. "Needles go in a hard box," he said. "Nobody gets poked!" Then he found a loose thread on his sock and wiggled it. The car went bump, bump again. Zachary waved at the doctor's office out the window. "Bye, bye, red box!"

Eli sat in the school computer lab. His teacher, Mr. Sokolov, held a black tablet. "You can learn to turn it on today," said Mr. Sokolov.

Eli pressed the round button. The screen lit up. His push made the light come on! He tapped the little paint icon. A drawing app opened. He drew a fast blue swing, back and forth. Saige sat next to him and drew a doctor with a red bag. Then the screen went dim. "It needs power," said Mr. Sokolov.

Eli found the charger cord. He carried it over. He wanted to plug it in himself. "I will plug it in," said Mr. Sokolov. "You can bring me the charger." A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall. Mr. Sokolov pushed the plug in. The screen lit up again. Then it was time to go. Eli pressed the button and put the tablet away on the shelf. "All done," he said.

Logan sat at the dinner table. His house smelled like warm pasta. He had a little truck in his pocket. "Tell us about school," said Dad. Logan put the truck on the table.

"I wanted the truck," said Logan. "Sutton had it. I grabbed it." He showed Dad how he grabbed. "Sutton cried. One big grab, one big cry." Sutton's face had gone sad and mad at the same time. Logan gave the truck back. "My turn?" he had asked. Sutton wiped his eyes and nodded.

"Then we took turns," said Logan. "One turn for Sutton. One turn for me. One turn for Sutton. One turn for me." Dad smiled. "That was kind," he said. Logan kissed the cute little truck. "Trucks are for sharing," said Logan. Dad gave him a big hug and another bite of pasta. Logan held out his fork. "Your turn, Dad."

Beatrice stood in the reading corner. She held a new card. It was her very own library card.

"I can pick any book?" asked Beatrice.

"Yes, one book today," said Ms. Aziz.

Beatrice picked a book about a shy little duck. The wind outside made the window rattle as they walked to the desk. Ms. Aziz stamped the book. "Bring it back next week," she said.

All week Beatrice hugged the duck book. She read it at breakfast. She read it in the bath. Then the week was done.

At the library, Ms. Aziz pointed to a small door in the wall. "This is the book return slot," she said.

"A book return slot," said Beatrice. "What does it do?"

"It is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library," said Ms. Aziz.

Beatrice looked at the slot. It was dark in there. She held her book tight. "My duck will be all alone!"

The duck book sat in her hands. Then Beatrice kissed the cover. She held it out. She let go.

The book slid in. Gulp!

Beatrice peeked at the slot. "Bye bye, duck," she said. She waved at the little door. "See you next time!"

Ms. Aziz laughed. "You can pick a new book now."

Beatrice ran to the reading corner. She came back hugging a book about a bus. She gave the slot one more wave.

John sat on the school bus. He held his show-and-tell card. It had a big S on it. "S says sss," said Ms. Nowak from the front seat. John was to find three S things before school.

Rae sat next to him. "I found one," she said. She pointed at the window. The sun was coming up. "Sun starts with S," said Rae. "Sss-un," said John. He laughed. The sss sound was funny, like a small snake in his mouth.

Quinn waved her foot. She had one sock on. The other sock was lost. "Sock starts with S," said Quinn. "Sss-ock," said John. Now he had two. He still needed one more. The bus went bounce, bounce. Then rain began to splash on the roof. "No," said John. "Rain starts with R."

Quinn tipped her shoe. Sand fell out. Sand from the beach yesterday. "Sand," said Quinn. "Sss-and," said John. Three S things! He sat up tall. "Sun, sock, sand," he said. "All S." Rae clapped. John looked out at the wet road. The sun came back out. "Sss," he whispered to it.

Athena was playing in the yard. She saw something soft on the grass. It was small and gray. "A feather!" she said. She held it up to the sun. It felt tickly on her cheek.

Her dad came out. "Where did it come from?" Athena asked. "Birds are animals that have feathers," said Dad. "So a bird lost this one." Athena looked up. She saw a big tree. She saw a little bird on a branch. The bird dropped another feather. It floated down, down, down. It landed in the pond. Ripples filled the water in circles.

"The bird did that!" said Athena. She laughed. She put her gray feather in her pocket. "I will keep it," she said. Dad took her hand. They walked inside together. "Such a beautiful feather," said Dad. Athena smiled.

Zayn put on his new blue shirt. Today was Eid, and the community hall was full of people. His dad said, "When someone comes in, you say 'Eid Mubarak.'" Zayn practiced in the air. "Eid Mubarak," he said, very small.

Then his friend Luka arrived with his mom. Zayn wanted to say hello. But he felt shy. He stood alone by the door. His dad smiled and stood close behind him.

Zayn took a big breath. He fold his hands together, like at practice. "Eid Mubarak, Luka!" he said.

Luka's mom beamed. "Eid Mubarak to you too!" she said. Luka laughed and waved. Then Orson came in. "Eid Mubarak, Orson!" said Zayn. Then Ms. Santos came in. "Eid Mubarak!" said Zayn again. Each time, the words made big smiles appear. One greeting, one smile. Two greetings, two smiles.

Zayn counted them in his head. Then he ran to find Luka near the treat table. "One sweet for you," said Zayn. Luka grinned and said, "Eid Mubarak, Zayn!"

Sara ran to the park. She saw the big gray slide. She wanted to go down it fast.

Lisa was there too. Lisa had a red ball. She rolled it to Sara. Sara caught it and laughed. Then Sara put the ball in her pocket to keep. Lisa looked sad. Her lip went down. Sara saw Lisa's face. She gave the ball back. "Your turn," said Sara. Lisa smiled again.

Then Sara wanted a turn on the swing. All the swings were full. Mr. Charles came to help. He found one free swing at the end. "Here you go," he said. Sara ran to it. Her mom called, "Sara, what do we say?" Sara ran back to Mr. Charles. "Thank you," she said. "You helped me find a swing." Mr. Charles smiled big.

Then Lisa rolled the ball to Sara again. Sara caught it. "Thank you, Lisa!" she said. Lisa clapped her hands. They took turns rolling the ball. Back and forth it went. "My turn," said Sara. "Your turn," said Lisa. The sun went down behind the trees. Sara waved to Lisa. "Come back tomorrow," said Lisa. Sara held her mom's hand all the way home.

Aria was three today. The community hall had deep blue balloons. Mom had let her pick them out. Aria could smell cake and soap from the sink nearby.

Presents sat in a pile. Adam handed Aria a small box. She opened it fast. Inside was a red toy car. She hugged it and ran to the next box. It was from Brianna. It had a soft bunny inside.

Aria stopped. She looked back at Adam. He sat with his hands in his lap. She walked over to him slowly. "Thank you, Adam," she said. Adam smiled big. "You are welcome," he said. Then Aria went to Brianna too. "Thank you," she said. Brianna gave her a hug.

Aria held the bunny in one arm. She pushed the red car with her other hand. It rolled all the way across the floor.

Theodore went to Mr. Chaudhry's music studio. He wanted to play a song for his mom. The big piano stood by the window. Its keys looked slippery and shiny. Theodore counted them. "One, two, three," he said. Some keys were white. Some keys were black.

"Try the black keys," said Mr. Chaudhry. Theodore pressed one. Plink! He pressed another. Plonk! He played only the black keys, one by one. The sounds hopped up and down like a bunny. "It sounds like a song!" said Theodore. His friend Ishan laughed. "Play it fast!" So Theodore played fast. Plink-plonk-plink! Ishan did a little swing with his arms.

Then Theodore pressed two black keys at once. BONK! The sound was big and funny. Ishan fell over, laughing. "That one is like a duck with a hat!" he said. Theodore pressed it again. BONK! The keys were black and white, and every one made a sound. Theodore grinned and played his black-key song all the way to the end. "Again!" said Ishan. "Again!" said Theodore, and his fingers danced.

Ryan ran to the park with his dad. The sun felt hot on his face. Then he stepped into the shade under a tree. "Brrr, now it's cold," he said.

His friend Kiana was there. "Let's play a game," she said. "I say a word. You shout the opposite."

"What is an opposite?" asked Ryan.

"Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be," said Kiana. "Like big and small."

Kiana held her arms out wide. "Big!" Ryan made himself tiny like a mouse. "Small!" They laughed and laughed.

Then Kiana pointed to a dog. "Fast!" she said. Ryan tried to say "slow" but he ran instead. "Too fast, too fast!" he giggled. The dog ran after him and it was not scary at all. It licked his hand.

Then the wind blew. Ryan saw the tall grass bend. The wind made the grass bend, and then the grass rose up again. Ryan touched the grass. It went down, then up, down, then up.

"Kiana, look! The wind bends it and it stands back up!"

"That's like up and down," said Kiana. "Opposites!"

Ryan picked up a big stick. "Big stick!" he said. Kiana found a tiny one. "Small stick!"

Then a leaf let go of the tree. Ryan watched its slow fall all the way down. "Slow fall," he whispered.

Kiana grinned and shouted one more word. "Day!"

Ryan thought hard. He looked at the sky. Then he pointed to the dark shade under the slide. "Night!" he shouted.

Kiana clapped. "You got it!"

On the walk home, Ryan held his dad's hand. He looked up at the sun, then down at his shoes. "Up and down," he said softly. "Opposites."

Julia ran into the cooking classroom. Her hands were dusty from the sandbox. Mr. Kamau was mixing pancake batter.

"I want to stir," said Julia.

Mr. Kamau pointed to the sink. "Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food," he said.

Julia looked at her hands. They were dusty hands. Pancake batter was food. She did not want dusty hands in the food.

Katerina was already at the sink. She made bubbles with the soap. "Wash, wash, wash," she sang. Rhodes came to the sink too. He made bubbles as well.

Julia pumped the soap. She rubbed her hands under the water. The bubbles felt squishy. She rinsed all the bubbles off. Her hands were clean now. "My turn to stir," she said.

Julia stirred the batter. Round and round went the spoon. The batter became smooth. Mr. Kamau poured it into a hot pan. Julia stood back from the hot pan. Mr. Kamau flipped the pancake high. It landed in the pan.

The pancakes went into Julia's coat pocket, wrapped in paper. She would take them home for supper. Mr. Kamau gave her one more pancake. Julia ate it with Katerina and Rhodes.

"Wash, wash, wash," they sang again, all together.

Lea went to the farm with her class. Nael and Arjan came too. Ms. Sánchez had a game. "Name a sense," she said. "Then name the body part."

Lea heard a cow. "Moo!" she said. "I hear with my ears." Nael touched a soft sheep. "I touch with my hands," he said. Arjan smelled the hay. "I smell with my nose," he said.

Then Lea wanted to find the last one. She covered her eyes with her hands. It got dark. She could not see the cow. She took her hands away. The cow was right there! "I see with my eyes," said Lea. Ms. Sánchez clapped. The farmer gave them clean cups of milk. He did not sell the milk today. It was a gift. "We see with our eyes," said Lea. She waved at the cow.

Eli ran to the park with a big cardboard box. The sun was warm and the sky was blue. His friend Jade was already there.

"Let's make it a car," said Jade. She sat in the box and turned a pretend wheel.

"No, a boat," said Eli. He wanted a boat so much. They both pulled the box.

Then Jade had an idea. "We can take turns," she said. "A box can be anything."

First it was Jade's car. "Beep beep!" she yelled. Eli waited and counted to ten. Then it was his turn. "My boat is on the sea," said Eli. He rowed with his hands. Jade clapped for him.

Iyla came by with her doll. "My baby needs a house," she said. Eli looked at the box. "It can be a house too," he said. He held the box steady while Iyla tucked her doll inside.

Ms. Jung sat on a bench and smiled. "What a nice game," she said.

The box was a car, then a boat, then a house. Eli patted the box. "Good box," he said.

Livia sat at the dinner table. She wanted more rice. She reached and reached. The bowl was too far away.

"Please pass the rice," she tried. Her papa passed the bowl. "Thank you, Papa," said Livia.

Then Salman came to dinner. Salman was a new friend from school. He was a little shy. He sat down slowly.

Livia gave Salman a roll. "Thank you," said Salman. Then he said, "Gracias."

Livia blinked. "What is gracias?" she asked.

"It is thank you too," said Salman. "It is Spanish."

"Spanish?" asked Livia.

"Yes. Other languages have their own words for thank you," said Salman. "I can say gracias."

Livia tried. "Grah-see-as," she said slowly.

"You did it!" said Salman.

Salman dropped his spoon on the floor. "Sorry," he said. Livia picked it up for him. "Gracias," he said.

"Gracias," said Livia, and she smiled. Then she took a big bite of rice.

Isaiah held his dad's hand at the street festival. There were lanterns and music and a big stage. Isaiah saw Mr. Chea standing by a tall golden menorah. "Hello, Isaiah," said Mr. Chea. "It is the third night of Hanukkah." Isaiah's dad used a long match to light the candles. Isaiah stood far back and watched. First the middle candle was lit. Then the flame touched two more candles. Three candles glowed bright.

Isaiah counted them out loud. "One, two, three!" Mr. Chea smiled. "One more candle each night," he said. "We light them for eight nights." Isaiah patted his dad's arm. "Will there be four tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Mr. Chea. "Four tomorrow, and eight on the last night."

Casey ran up with her mom. "I love the candles," said Casey. "They are my favorite part." The kids sat on a bench together. Isaiah looked at the shining lights. He held up his fingers and counted to three again.

Then he made a plan. Every night he would ask his mom to help him count on the computer. He would draw a candle picture each night too. Tonight he drew one, two, three little flames.

Casey leaned over his paper. "Draw four flames tomorrow," she said.

"Okay," said Isaiah. "One, two, three, and then four."

Elizabeth wanted to make muffins for her family. Her mom said, "Yes, let's cook in the backyard." They set a little table by the friendly oak tree.

Elizabeth grabbed the sugar bag. She poured it straight into the bowl. Sugar went everywhere. Too much sugar sat in a big hill. "Oops," said Elizabeth. Her back felt sticky.

Mom held up a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Elizabeth scooped sugar with it. She filled it up and tapped it flat. Then she used a measuring spoon for the vanilla. Just the right little bit went in. Not too much. Not too little. The batter looked smooth and good.

Mom put the pan in the hot oven. Elizabeth watched from her chair, far away and safe. Soon the muffins were done. The family sat on the grass to eat. "Yum," said Dad. Elizabeth caught a crumb in her hand and smiled. "I made these," she said.

Livia was going to the beach. The car was packed with bags. "Look, a farm!" said Livia. Cows stood by a fence. The sun did shine on the water tower.

Then Livia had a problem. "I need to pee," she said. "It is so far to the beach." Dad said, "We can stop." The car turned off the big road.

They pulled into a rest stop. Livia jumped out. She used the bathroom there. Then she stretched her arms up high. Tyler would never believe this. "A rest stop is a cool place," said Livia. Dad laughed. "You stretched like a cat."

Back in the car, Livia watched for more rest stops. "Are we there yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "But look, the sea!" The water did shine and shine. Livia clapped her hands.

Rosalie went to the store with her dad. Evaan and Crew were there too. They saw a big box of toy bears near the door. One bear had soft brown fur. Rosalie wanted that bear so much.

Rosalie grabbed the brown bear fast. But Evaan was holding it first. Evaan's face went sad. He started to cry. Rosalie heard him sniffle. Her tummy felt funny and tight. She did not want that.

Then Rosalie remembered. She put the bear back in Evaan's hands. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. "When you are done?" Evaan wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You asked. Okay." He hugged the bear once. Then he gave it to Rosalie.

Rosalie held the soft brown bear. "Your turn now," she said after a bit. She gave it back. Evaan smiled big. Crew clapped his hands. Dad came close and smiled too. "Time to go," he said. Rosalie waved to Evaan and Crew. "Bye, bear," she said. "Bye, friends."

Everett wanted his bear book. Mom had read it last night. He loved the part with the wind.

At the library, Everett found the blue book. It was thin, with a shiny bear on the front. He held it up. "This one!"

Dad sat down on a soft rug. He opened the book. He started at the first page. "The wind began to blow," Dad read. "The bear held his hat."

Everett sat very still. Those were Mom's words! Mom had said the very same thing.

Dad turned the pages one by one. He went from the front to the back. At the end, the bear got a kiss goodnight.

"Mom said that too," Everett whispered.

"She did," said Dad. "The words stay the same."

Everett smiled. "Read it again."

Emmett sat in the family car. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Doctor today," said Mom. Emmett held his round toy ball. He did not want a shot.

At the office, a kind woman in white said, "Time for your shot." Emmett began to shake. Mom held his hand. One, two, three. Quick! The shot was done. Then the woman put a small bandage on his arm. Emmett looked at it. The bandage had stars on it. Little stars, big stars, one, two, three, four stars.

"Look at my stars!" said Emmett. In the car again, they stopped for ice cream. Mom got him a round scoop. Emmett held up his arm. "Stars," he said. The cashier smiled. Emmett licked his ice cream. "One star, two stars, three stars," he counted, all the way home.

Gabriella was at Grandma's house. Grandpa had a big drum in the den. It was dark red and shiny. "Can I try it?" asked Gabriella. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Sit here. Tap it soft."

Gabriella tapped the drum. Boom! The drum made a big sound. She tapped again. Boom, boom! Grandma came in to listen. So did Aria, who lived next door.

Then Grandpa picked up his flute. He played a little song. Gabriella and Aria clapped. Grandpa bent down low, all the way to his knees. "Why did you bend?" asked Gabriella. "When people clap, we bow," said Grandpa. He laughed. "It is our hello to the claps."

Now it was Gabriella's turn again. She played a boom boom song. Aria clapped loud. Grandma clapped loud. Gabriella started to run away. Then she stopped. She turned around. She bent down low, like Grandpa. Aria laughed and clapped more. "Look at me!" said Gabriella. "I am bowing!" Then she bowed again, just for fun.

Theodore stood at the airport. He held a paper sign. It said "Grandma." People walked and walked. Then Theodore saw her. Grandma hugged him tight.

At home, Theodore looked at a photo. It showed Dad as a boy. "Dad was little?" said Theodore. "Tell me!" Grandma smiled. She told about Dad's first bike. Dad fell in the wet grass. Dad spilled his juice on his shoe. Dad had a stuffed pig that Dad loved. Theodore laughed and laughed. "Dad was a boy like me!" he said.

The next day, Theodore wanted more. He brought the old photo to Grandma. He sat close on the soft chair. Grandma told about Dad's spotted dog, too. Theodore clapped his hands. "One more story," he said.

Luca went to the pharmacy with his dad. Luca needed to wash his hands. He had just used the toilet. Dad lifted him up to the little sink. The soap came out like white glue on his hands. Luca rubbed twice and stopped. "Too fast," said Ms. Wu from the door. She was the kind pharmacist. "Sing your song," she said. Luca sang his camp song. "Happy hands, scrub scrub scrub." He sang all the way to the end. The soap bubbles grew big and white. The water rinsed them away. His hands came out clean and shiny. "Beautiful hands," said Ms. Wu with a smile. Luca looked at them under the light. Then he ran to find his dad, singing the song all the way.

Miles climbed the big school bus. He held the rail with his hand. The bus was loud and full. Miles sat by the window. His tummy made a little growl.

"I am hungry," said Miles. "I want my snack now."

A boy named Blaire sat next to him. "The teacher will tell us when," said Blaire. "There is a time for eating at school. It comes after we get there." Mr. Ortiz stood at the front of the bus. He smiled at Miles. "Almost there," said Mr. Ortiz.

The bus went beep, beep, beep. Miles counted one tree, two trees, three trees. His tummy growled again. "One more block," said Blaire. "One more block," said Miles.

At school, Mr. Ortiz held up his hand. "Snack time!" he said. Everyone sat at the little tables. Miles opened his bag. He had crackers and a banana. Miles ate his snack with Blaire. "My tummy waited," said Miles. "What a smart tummy," said Mr. Ortiz. Miles took another big bite.

Jacob wanted to help make breakfast. He pulled a chair to the kitchen counter. His dad was there, cracking big eggs into a bowl. Jacob tapped his small egg on the edge. Tap, tap, knock. It cracked open too.

The pan was hot, so Dad held the spoon. Jacob stirred the eggs in the bowl, slow and slow. "Faster?" asked Dad. Jacob stirred fast, and the eggs spun around. He laughed.

Then Jacob filled a cup with cold water. He carried it very carefully. But his sleeve dipped in, and water ran down his arm. His sleeve went from dry to wet. Dad got a towel. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Dad with a smile. Just then, Blake knocked on the door. "Come see," Jacob called. "I made breakfast, and I made a wet sleeve too!" Blake giggled, and the eggs went onto the plates, steaming and warm.

Henry went to the park today. Yesterday the park was wet with rain. Today the sun was warm on the slide.

Raya was there with her rabbit. The rabbit sat still in the grass. Henry ran up fast. The rabbit did not move. Then it hopped away quick.

"If you freeze, it will come back," said Raya.

Henry froze. He did not move his feet. He did not move his hands. The rabbit came back to the same spot. It sniffed his shoe. Henry giggled inside but stayed still.

"Can we give it a carrot now?" Henry asked.

Mr. Tang was sitting on the bench. "The carrots are not now. They are after snack. Now means at this very moment."

Henry looked at the rabbit. Now it was sniffing Raya's pocket. Raya had a carrot there all along.

"Snack now?" Henry asked.

"Snack now," said Mr. Tang, and he laughed. Tomorrow they would bring more carrots.

Athena wanted to make a tower of blocks. She wanted it to be very tall. "I will count the blocks," she said. "One, two, four."

Her little brother laughed. "That sounds funny," he said.

Athena frowned. Something was wrong. She tried again. "One, two, four, five."

Eleanore came over to play. Eleanore was her big friend from next door. "Say the numbers with me," said Eleanore. "One, two, three, four, five."

Athena said it with her. "One, two, three, four, five." The words sounded neat now, like a little song.

"Again!" said her little brother.

"One, two, three, four, five, six," they sang. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Athena put one block on the tower for each word. One, two, three, four, five. The tower grew tall and tall. She wiggled her nose at it. Then she added more. Six, seven, eight, nine.

"One more," said Eleanore. "Ten!"

Athena set the last block on top. The tower stood tall and straight. Her little brother clapped.

"Now we say it backwards," said Eleanore. "Ten, nine, eight."

Athena took one block off for each word. The tower got shorter and shorter. Seven, six, five, four, three, two, one.

"Zero blocks!" said Athena. "Now we count the cookies."

"One, two," said her little brother, "one for me!"

Louis lost his red dinosaur. He looked under the bed. He looked behind the big chair. "Not here," said Louis. He looked in the garden. His grandpa was picking beans. "I can't find Dino," said Louis. "I had him at the park yesterday." Grandpa held his hand. "Then let's go look," he said.

The park was not far. They walked past the swings. They walked to the little gate. A man was putting something in a big box. "What is that box?" asked Louis. "The lost and found," said the man. "People put things they find in here. Then the owners can come and get them back." Louis stood on his toes. He peeked in.

A red dinosaur sat on a hat. Louis gave Dino a big hug. "You were waiting for me!" he said. The man smiled. Grandpa smiled too. Louis waved all the way home.

Wren sat on the back step with Zackary and Bodhi. Ms. Rosen had a big question for them. "Can you name the five senses?" she asked. Wren wanted to get them all right.

She held up her hands. "We touch with our hands," she said. Zackary pointed to his ears. "We hear with our ears." Bodhi sniffed the air. "We smell with our nose." They all looked at each other. Eyes! "We see with our eyes," said Wren.

But then they stopped. "What is the last one?" asked Zackary. Ms. Rosen put a lemon slice and a strawberry on the table. She cut them with a safe knife, and the kids kept their distance. Then Wren tasted the lemon. Her whole face went tight. "Sour!" she said. Then she bit the strawberry. "Sweet!" She stuck out her tongue. "We taste with our tongue!"

"Five senses," said Bodhi. "You did it," said Zackary. A monkey shook a branch in the tree, and they all laughed.

Milo was at school. He saw a big box of toys. He wanted to play house with his friend Kareem. Kareem took the baby doll. Milo took a little stuffed dog.

Kareem dropped the doll on the floor. It fell with a soft thud. Kareem's face looked sad. "The baby fell," said Kareem. "Maybe the baby is sad too."

Ms. Lindqvist came over. She knelt down by the doll. She picked it up and looked at it. "The doll is fine," she said. "Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Kareem gave the doll a big hug. Then he rocked the doll in his arms. The doll's eyes stayed open and did not cry. "Shh," said Kareem. "Sleep now."

Milo looked at his stuffed dog. He pretended the dog wanted a bite of lunch. He held a toy cup to its mouth. "Eat it all up," said Milo. The dog did not really eat. Milo laughed and patted its head.

Then Ms. Lindqvist sat close by them. Milo rocked his dog too. Kareem fed his doll more pretend food. "My baby is happy now," said Kareem. Milo hugged his dog tight and said, "Night night, dog."

The big farmhouse went dark. Matthew flipped the light switch up. Nothing happened. He flipped it down. Nothing happened. "Oh no," said Matthew.

"It is a power cut," said his dad. "The electric lights are off. The switch will not turn them on." Dad found a flashlight. Dad turned it on. A bright circle splashed on the wall. Matthew laughed.

They sat on the couch. The winter wind went whoosh outside. The flashlight made a bunny shape on the ceiling. Matthew clapped his hands. He flipped the light switch one more time. Still nothing. That was okay. The flashlight worked fine.

Then the lamps came back. The whole room glowed. Matthew flipped the light switch up. The light came on, fast! "It works now!" he said. Dad smiled and gave him a big hug.

Zachary sat at the little table in the art classroom. He wanted to paint a big red apple. Ms. Chan gave him a brush and a juicy red color. Zachary painted round and round. The apple looked so good. Ruth painted a yellow sun next to him.

Then it was time for snack. Zachary put his brush down in the red paint. He ran to the fruit bowl. The next day, he came back to paint more. He picked up his brush. It was hard. It would not bend at all. "Why is my brush so stiff?" he asked. Ms. Chan said, "The paint dried on it. We rinse the brushes so the paint does not dry on them."

She showed him the sink. The water ran cool and soft. Zachary rinsed his new brush all clean. He watched the red swirl away down the drain. After painting his green leaf, he carried the brush straight to the sink. "Brush goes in the water," he said, and he washed it all by himself.

Thomas went to the grocery store with his dad. He held his little toy plane in his hand. But at the bread shelf, Thomas looked down. His plane was gone!

"Where did I go first?" Thomas asked. "The carts," said his dad. "Then the apples. Then the bread." So they went back to each place, in the same order. They walked to the carts. No plane there. They walked to the apples. No plane there. Thomas waited and looked slowly. Then they walked to the bread.

There, under the bread shelf, sat the little plane. Thomas picked it up with gentle fingers. "My plane!" he said. A shop worker smiled. "Thank you," Thomas said to her. Dad said, "We went back the same way you came. That helped us find it." Thomas held his plane all the way home.

Aria sat in the big waiting room. Her mama sat next to her. Aria wanted her turn right now. "Soon," said Mama. "We wait here until the nurse calls us." Aria wiggled her shoes. She was not alone. A boy sat with his dad. A grandma sat with a little girl. Aria looked at the fish tank. The fish swam round and round. Then the door opened wide. A nurse called, "Aria!" Aria jumped up. That was her name! The nurse had called her because it was her turn. Aria walked in fast. The doctor was kind. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then the nurse gave her a farm sticker. Aria spelled out the word on it, "C, O, W!" She held the sticker up high all the way home.

Levi sat at the kitchen table. He had a big red crayon. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

"Can I write my name?" he asked.

"Yes, you can," said his dad.

Levi drew the first letter. It was small. He drew more letters. "L, e, v, i," he said, one by one. "L, e, v, i. That says Levi!"

Then Dad put a paper near Levi's hand. It said Levi too. But the first letter looked different. It was a big L. It stood tall like a duck standing up straight.

"Why is your L so big?" asked Levi.

"A name starts with a capital letter," said Dad. "A big one at the start."

Levi looked at his small L. He looked at Dad's big L. He wanted a big one too. He grabbed a new paper. He did not rip it. He drew slowly. A big tall L came out.

"One big letter, then little, little, little," said Levi. "L, e, v, i. Levi!"

Dad smiled. "That's it. You did it."

Levi held up the paper. "Read it!" he said.

"Levi," said Dad.

Levi jumped up and down. "Again!" he said. "Read it again!"

Hannah put on her red dress. Today was a big family party. Grandma had baked sweet cookies for it. The house smelled warm and good.

Hannah saw her cousin get a small red envelope. She wanted one too. "Where is mine?" she asked. Grandma smiled and held one out. Hannah grabbed it fast. She pulled the paper to open it. "Wait," said her cousin. "You say thank you first. Then you open it."

Hannah stopped. She looked at Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma," she said. Grandma gave a big nod. Then Hannah opened the red envelope. Inside was shiny money. "It has money in it!" said Hannah. Her cousin laughed. "That is the best part."

Later, Uncle Tom held out another red envelope. Hannah remembered what to do. She folded her hands like a polite little girl. "Thank you, Uncle Tom," she said first. He smiled wide. Then she opened it and hugged him. At bedtime, Hannah put the red envelope under her pillow. "Best party ever," she whispered.

Mason sat at the big art table. Ms. Siddiqui gave him white paper. She gave him bright pink paint too. Mason wanted to make a butterfly. But he did not know how.

He painted one wing on half the paper. Then his elbow bumped the paper. The wet half folded over onto the dry half. Paint dripped onto the floor. "Oh no," said Mason.

Ms. Siddiqui helped him open the paper. There was a surprise. Two wings now. Both were pink. Both looked the same. "A butterfly," said Frankie from the next seat. Mason was happy. He painted green on one half of a new paper. He folded it fast. He opened it. Two green wings. He laughed and put his brush down on the table. "Now I remember how," said Mason.

Avery sat on the little red bench at Mr. Doyle's music studio. The sun did shine through the big window. "Today we will clap," said Mr. Doyle. "We will clap along with the steady beat." He played a song on the piano. Clap, clap, clap. Avery clapped too. The beat was steady, steady, steady. Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Avery sang it all by herself. She did not miss a word.

Then Avery clapped. But Mr. Doyle was still playing. He stopped and smiled. "Wait for the end," he said. "At a concert, people clap when the music is over. It is how they show they liked it. It is a polite thing to do." So Avery waited. She made the waiting into a game. She held her hands very still. The last note rang out. Then Avery clapped and clapped. Mr. Doyle bowed. "Bravo, Avery," he said. She clapped some more.

Arya was at Grandma's house. It was dark outside. Then all the lights went out. Beep! The TV went off too.

"Power cut," said Grandma. "Let's find the big flashlight." Grandma found it on the shelf. She clicked it on. A bright circle shone on the floor.

Arya felt scared in the dark. Her tummy felt hungry too. "I want a snack," she said. Grandma got some bread and apple slices. They sat on the rug.

Arya held her hands near the light. The light shone on her hands. A big black shape popped up on the wall! "Look, Grandma!" she cried. She moved her fingers. The shape grew long ears. It was a bunny!

"Make a secret shadow," Arya whispered. She hid one hand. The bunny lost an ear. She put her hand back. The ear came back!

Grandma clapped. Arya made a bird next. It flapped on the wall.

Then the lights came back on. The shadows were gone. Arya laughed and said, "Again tomorrow! Bunny, come back!"

Georgia wanted her red block. It sat by the door. But Daddy stood in the doorway. He was talking on the phone. Georgia tried to squeeze past him. Daddy did not move.

She tapped her chin. What could she do? She took a big breath. "Excuse me," she said in a small voice. Daddy heard her. He smiled and stepped to the side. "Thank you," said Georgia. She picked up her block. It felt smooth and cool in her hands.

She sat on the rug and stacked it up tall. "Excuse me," she whispered to the cat, who lay on the rug. The cat blinked but did not move. Georgia built her tower around him. "Tasty," said Daddy, sniffing the bread in the oven. Georgia sniffed too. It smelled warm and good.

Eliana planted little seeds in the garden. One, two, three, four, five. She planted lettuce and carrots. Peter planted peas next to her. Mr. Novák gave her a small watering can.

Every day Eliana came back. She counted her plants. One, two, three, four, five. They grew green and tall.

Then came a very hot day. Eliana looked at her lettuce. The leaves hung down low. "Oh no," said Eliana. "The lettuce looks sad. That is a problem."

She filled her watering can at the tap. She gave the lettuce a drink. Drip, drip, drip.

"We can water mine too," said Peter. He filled his can.

The next morning, Eliana ran to the garden. She counted. One, two, three, four, five. The lettuce stood up tall again. The leaves were crisp, not squishy.

Then Eliana saw something small. A ladybug sat on her biggest leaf. "Hello," said Eliana. "Do you like the water too?" The ladybug flew up, up, up, and landed on her nose.

Aurora was at Grandma's house. It was getting dark outside. "Can we play ball before bed?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Please roll it gently."

Gianna was there too. She had come after school. Aurora rolled the ball to Gianna. Gianna caught it and ran off down the hall. Then she stopped. She turned around and said, "Thank you, Aurora." Aurora smiled big.

"Can you send the ball back?" Aurora asked. Gianna rolled it. But the ball went under the big chair. "Oh no," said Aurora. "I can't reach it. Grandma, can you help me, please?"

Grandma lifted the chair. Out popped the ball. And out popped something else too. A little red sock, lost for a long time! "My sock!" said Gianna. "I looked everywhere at home." Aurora picked it up and gave it to her. "Thank you," Gianna said again.

"Sorry I rolled too hard," said Gianna. "That's okay," said Aurora. "Try again." Gianna rolled the ball slowly this time. Aurora caught it. Then she ran down the hall, just like Gianna did. She stopped and turned around. "Thank you for the ball, Gianna!" she called.

Nora wanted to draw a nest on the tablet. The screen was dark. She tapped it again and again. Nothing happened. "Why won't you wake up?" she asked.

Mr. Lindqvist sat down next to her. "Try the little button on the side," he said. "Press it once." Nora pressed the button. The screen lit up bright. She smiled. One little press made the dark screen turn on.

Nora opened the drawing app. She drew a big brown nest. She drew two blue eggs inside it. "Who will meet the eggs?" she asked herself. "A mama bird," she said, and drew the bird too.

Then it was time for snack. Nora pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in the basket, soft and safe, just like the eggs in the nest.

It was Luna's first day at school. The playground had a big wooden bus. It had seats and a wheel. Elie sat in the driver's seat. "Climb in," Elie said. Luna climbed in and sat down.

Then Luna saw Elie's little brother outside the fence. She stood up on her seat to wave. Elie stopped the wheel. "On the bus, we stay sitting in our seats," Elie said. Luna sat back down. Elie turned the wheel again. The bus game went on. Vroom, vroom!

Soon Luna felt thirsty. She let her tongue rest on her lip. Ms. Carvalho came with cups of water. Luna drank slowly. Then she ran back to the bus. She sat down first. Then she waved at Elie's brother through the window. Elie smiled and honked the horn.

Zayn dug in the dirt with his hands. His dad made the holes. "One seed, two seeds, three seeds," said Zayn. He dropped them in and patted the soil. Then he gave the seeds a drink of water.

Every day Zayn looked at his garden. He saw dirt. He saw dirt. He saw a tiny brown leaf ride past like a little boat on the wind. Still, he saw only dirt. "Come up, little seeds," he said. The sky grew gray, but no snow fell, only soft rain.

On the ninth day, Zayn ran outside. Something green was poking up out of the soil! "Mom, a sprout!" Zayn called. "A tiny new plant is called a sprout," said his mom, smiling. Zayn clapped his hands. "Hello, sprout," he whispered, and gave it one more drink.

Everly went to the park with her friend Iyla. Ms. Yilmaz was there with a big basket. She had cold juice and crackers for everyone.

Ms. Yilmaz held out a green cracker. "Would you like one?" she asked. Everly looked at it. It had seeds on it. "Yuck!" Everly shouted. Ms. Yilmaz blinked. Iyla put her hands over her ears. Everly felt her face get hot.

Iyla took a green cracker next. "No, thank you," said Iyla. Ms. Yilmaz smiled. "Okay, Iyla. Maybe you would like a plain one?" "Yes, please," said Iyla. She got a plain cracker. Then she got some juice, too.

Everly waited her turn. Ms. Yilmaz held out the green cracker again. "No, thank you," Everly said. "May I have a plain one, please?" "Of course," said Ms. Yilmaz. Everly got a plain cracker and cold juice. The cup was not frozen, but the juice was nice and icy.

Then came the surprise. A small dog ran by with a wheel in its mouth. It dropped the wheel at Everly's feet. "No, thank you, dog," said Everly. Iyla laughed and laughed. Ms. Yilmaz laughed too. The dog wagged its tail and took the wheel back. "Thank you for sharing!" Everly called. Then she sat down on the grass and ate her cracker, one slow bite at a time.

Gabriella went to the library with her dad. The shelves were tall. The room smelled like paper. "Books, books, so many books," she whispered.

Gabriella wanted a big red book. It sat high on the shelf. She stood on her toes. She reached and reached. Her fingers touched the edge. The book did not move. She pushed. Still it did not move. One pull, two pulls, three pulls. Nothing.

Her friend Viola came over. "That looks too hard," Viola said. Gabriella frowned. Then she remembered something. She walked to Mr. Bouchard, the library man. "Can you help me, please?" she asked.

Mr. Bouchard smiled. "Of course!" He lift ed the big red book down. "Thank you!" said Gabriella. She hugged it tight. The cover felt smooth and cool.

Viola wanted a blue book up high too. "Can you help me, please?" Viola asked. Mr. Bouchard brought it down. "Sorry I dropped my marker," Viola said, picking it up. The two girls sat at the little table. They played a looking game inside the book. "I see a cat!" said Gabriella. "I see a smart owl!" said Viella. "I see a moon!" said Gabriella.

"Smart girls," said Mr. Bouchard. Gabriella turned the page.

Maria was at Grandpa's house. Her baby cousin was asleep upstairs. Maria wanted to show her friend Mona the big toy train.

"Look!" Maria shouted. "A train!"

Grandpa put his finger to his lips. "Shh," he said. "The baby is sleeping. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice."

Maria looked at the stairs. She thought a shout might wake the baby. So she tried something new. She made her voice very small.

"Look, Mona," she whispered. "A train!"

Mona whispered too. "I want a turn."

Maria handed her the train. Mona pushed it slowly on the floor. The wheels made a soft little sound. Then Mona gave the train back to Maria.

"My turn," Maria whispered. "Then your turn."

Grandpa brought them two pieces of apple. One piece for Maria. One piece for Mona. Same size. Maria smiled. That felt fair.

The two girls rolled the train back and forth. They whispered a choo-choo song. It was not scary to be quiet. It was like a game.

Soon the baby cried upstairs, loud and happy. The baby was awake now.

"Can we be loud now?" Mona asked.

Grandpa laughed and nodded. Maria clapped her hands and shouted, "Choo choo!"

"Hello, sleepy baby," she said.

The lights went out. Clara sat in the dark. "Mama!" she called. "I want a snack. Can I have cold pizza from the fridge?"

Mama lit a little candle on the table. "We keep the fridge door shut," she said. "Then the food stays cold longer."

Clara pouted. "But I want pizza now."

"Come here," said Mama. She gave Clara bread and cheese from the cupboard. "We can save the pizza for tomorrow."

Outside, it was a rainy night. The rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

Clara held her bread. She looked at the big fridge. Its door stayed shut, like a mouth staying quiet.

Then the lights came back on! The lamp glowed. The fridge began to hum.

"Now can we look?" asked Clara.

Mama smiled. "Yes. The power is back."

Clara helped Mama drop cheese onto bread. They made warm toast. The pizza stayed cold inside the fridge, waiting for tomorrow.

"Good night, pizza," said Clara, and she waved at the fridge door.

Maeve was going on a big trip. First she rode in the car to the airport. Then she would sleep in a tent at a campsite.

The airport was very busy. So many people! So many feet walking fast. Maeve saw a big plane out the window. It was huge. She wanted to run to it.

Maeve let go of her dad's hand. She took one step. Then she stopped. The crowd was big and fast. A lady with a suitcase walked right in front of her.

Maeve looked back. Her dad held out his hand. "Stay close to me," he said. "In busy places like this, children hold hands."

Maeve grabbed his hand. She held it tight. Now the busy feet did not feel so big. They walked together, past all the people.

Later, the plane flew up high. Maeve sat by the window with her mom. At the campsite, they put up the tent. Dad made the campfire, and Maeve watched from far away. Her mom gave her a clean cup for water.

At night, Maeve heard a horse. "Neigh," it called. It was a horse at the farm next door. "Can we see it?" Maeve asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Hold my hand. The field is dark."

Maeve held on. They walked together to the fence. The horse looked at Maeve. Maeve waved.

"Good night, horse," she said.

Hailey went to the store with her mom today. Yesterday it rained, so Hailey wore her warm sweater. She wanted red apples for a snack.

"We will get apples soon," said Mom.

"Is soon now?" asked Hailey.

"Soon means in a little while," said Mom.

First they got bread. Then they got milk. Then Mom said, "Now we get apples." Soon had come!

At the checkout, Hailey saw her friend Mannat. Mannat looked afraid of the big line.

"Don't worry," Hailey said. "Soon means in a little while. Our turn will come soon."

The line moved. It was their turn. Hailey waved to Mannat.

"Tomorrow we can eat apples together," said Mannat.

"Okay!" said Hailey. She held the apple bag all the way home.

Kayden went to the library with his dad. Kayden wanted a book about trucks. He looked at the books on the shelf. The books had little words on the front. Dad said, "This word says trucks." Kayden said, "Where is my name?" Dad helped him look. On the desk was a card with Kayden's name on it. Kayden pointed. "That says me!" Then Kayden found his name on his library card too. He looked and looked. The letters were the same both times. Same letters, same order. Kayden laughed. He sat on the soft rug with Dad. Dad opened the book at the front. "We start here," said Dad. Kayden turned each page. Page by page, he got to the end. "The end," said Kayden. He gave Dad a big hug.

Juliette stood in the big restaurant kitchen with Ms. Morningstar. On the counter sat a loaf of soft white bread. Juliette poked it with her finger. It felt soft like a pillow.

The bread went into the toaster. Juliette waited. One, two, three, she counted. The toaster popped. Out came the bread. It was brown now. It was crunchy now. "It changed!" Juliette said. "The heat made it brown and crunchy," said Ms. Morningstar. Juliette tapped the toast. Tap, tap, tap. It sounded rough and dry.

"Now try the butter," said Ms. Morningstar. She gave Juliette a butter knife, a safe one. It was not sharp. Juliette held the knife like a tool. She spread the butter. One stroke, two strokes, three. The butter melted on the warm toast. It went smooth and shiny.

"Now the milk." Juliette picked up the cup. She poured slowly. The milk went up the side. One inch, two inches. She set the jug down. Not one drop spilled! "I did it!" she yelled. Ms. Morningstar clapped her hands. Juliette took a big bite of toast. Crunch.

Mila sat in her big bed. Her green book was on her lap. She opened the front cover first, the way Papa showed her. Papa read page one, then page two, all the way to the end.

Mila loved the pictures. There was a bear. There was a cat. There was a big bowl of ice, cold and shiny. The bear poured juice over the ice.

"Papa, who drew the bear?" Mila asked.

Papa turned back to the first page. He pointed to a line of little words. "The name is right here," he said. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator."

"Ill-u-stra-tor," said Mila slowly.

"Look, here is the name," said Papa. He read it out. Mila touched the words with one finger. The words said the name. The words told her who drew her bear.

"Can we say thank you?" Mila asked.

"We can," said Papa.

Mila looked at the page. "Thank you, illustrator," she said. "I love my bear."

Papa turned off the lamp. Mila held the green book close. The moon came in the window, soft and white.

"Good night, bear," Mila whispered.

Lillian was drawing in the playroom. She drew a big sun and a small sun. "The big sun is hot," she said. "The small one is not so hot."

Mr. Villanueva brought two cups. "This one is cold," he said. "Mine is hot, so I hold it." Lillian touched her cold cup. It felt nice.

Zach rolled a ball fast. Lillian rolled hers slow. Zach's ball hit the wall hard. Dirt from the plant pot fell on the floor.

Then the room went dark. Lillian thought it was morning. "Time to get up!" she said.

Mr. Villanueva laughed softly. "Look out the window. It is still night. Day and night are opposites. Night is dark. Day has light."

Lillian waited. She drew in the dark. It was hard to see.

Slowly, slowly, the sky turned light. Day was here.

"Morning!" said Lillian. Zach clapped his hands.

Eliana sat on the rug at book club. Mr. Kapoor held up a card with a big K on it. "Can anyone make the K sound?" he asked. Eliana hugged her teddy tight. She did not know that one yet.

Then Mr. Kapoor asked them to write K on their papers. Eliana picked up her crayon. She drew a K, but it came out wrong. The little lines went the wrong way. Jocelyn leaned over. "Mine looks funny too," she said.

Mr. Kapoor gave them bumpy letter cards. "Trace the letter with your finger," he said. Eliana sat up tall. She put her finger on the K. She traced down the straight line. Then up the hill, and up the other hill. The bumps tickled her finger.

She tried her crayon again. This time her K looked just right. "I did it!" she said. Amira clapped. Mr. Kapoor smiled. Eliana traced the K one more time, slow and careful, just to feel the bumps again.

Charlie had a big red drum. She wanted to bang it. Boom, boom, boom!

But the baby was taking a nap. "Shh," said Dad. "Loud will wake the baby."

"Can I drum and stay quiet too?" Charlie asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Try a little tap."

Charlie tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. It was quiet. The baby kept sleeping. The drum was still fun.

Outside, snow began to fall. It came down slow. Charlie watched it from the window. She tapped slow, like the snow. Tap, tap, tap.

Then Anika came to play. Anika put her hands over her ears. "That was loud before," she said.

"Now it is quiet," said Charlie. "Loud and quiet are opposites."

The baby woke up at last. Now everyone could be loud. Boom, boom, boom! The two friends played together.

Ethan stood by the library door at school. He saw a sign with words on it. "What do the words say?" he asked. Benicio looked too. "They say Library," said Benicio. "The words tell us where to go." Ethan smiled. So words could talk!

Inside, Ethan found a box marked Crayons. He opened it. The crayons were right there. He tapped the box. "The words knew," he said. He looked at a label on a jar. It said Paint. And it was paint! Words were on signs, labels and boxes, and they told him things.

Khai sat with a big book. Ethan peeked in. "You started at the front," he said. Khai nodded. "Yes, you read front to back." Ethan picked his own book. He turned page one, then two, then three. "I am brave," he whispered. He would not cry, not even at the wolf. He read on, page by page, all the way to the end.

Michael ran onto the soccer field. "Game time!" he shouted. Connor and Zayn were already there. Mr. Yilmaz blew his whistle.

"First we warm up," said Mr. Yilmaz. "One, two, run and stretch. One, two, run and stretch."

Michael stopped. "What is a warm up?" he asked.

"It is running and stretching before a game," said Zayn.

Michael sighed a big sigh. He wanted to kick the ball right now. But he got in line anyway. One, two, run and stretch. One, two, run and stretch. Michael ran fast like a horse. Connor laughed. "Silly horse!"

Then the game began. Michael kicked the ball. He ran and ran. His legs felt good and strong.

"Where did the fast horse go?" teased Connor.

Michael grinned. "Right here! Neigh!"

After the game, Michael patted his legs. "Thank you, legs." Then he looked up. A real bunny was hopping across the field, right past the ball.

"Bunny!" said Michael. "Do bunnies warm up too?"

"No," said Zayn. "Bunnies are ready all day."

The bunny hopped away. Michael waved. "Bye, bunny. See you at the next game."

Levi was in his bed. He had a cough. Mom gave him warm soup. The soup tasted a little sour, but Levi drank it all up. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

Levi wanted to play. He could not go outside. He looked around his room. Then he saw his toy doctor bag. Out came a little tube with two round ends. "What is this?" Levi asked. Mom said, "That is a stethoscope. A doctor can listen to your chest with it."

Levi put the round end on his teddy bear's chest. He put the other end on his ear. He heard nothing. He moved the round end. He waited. He listened again. Then he heard a sound. Thump, thump. Thump, thump. It was his teddy's heart! No, wait. It was too loud for a teddy. It was his own heart, under the tube. Levi laughed.

Levi put the stethoscope on Mom's chest. Thump, thump. Fast and strong. He put it on his own chest. Thump, thump. Slower and small. He tried one more time, just to be sure. Yes, the stethoscope could hear it. Every time.

Later Levi fed his teddy a pretend snack and tucked it in. The rain kept tapping on the window. Levi yawned. He held the stethoscope in his hand. "Listen to my chest too," he told Mom, already closing his eyes.

It was snack time at school. Amelia had one square napkin. She wanted a flag for her cracker castle, but a flag had to be small. She looked and looked. Then she had an idea.

She folded the square napkin in half, edge to edge. She pressed it flat. "Look!" she said. "My square is gone. Now it is long!" Japji leaned over. "That is not a square anymore," he said. "It is a rectangle." Ocean clapped. "A rectangle flag!"

The weather outside was sunny, and a brown leaf blew in the door. It landed right on the castle. "A knight!" laughed Amelia. Ms. Becker smiled. "Every castle needs a guard," she said. Amelia stuck the rectangle flag on top. "Hooray for rectangle land!" she said.

Iris sat in the big barber chair. The chair was tall. Her papa stood right beside her. The barber had silver scissors. He cut a little curl of hair. Snip. The curl fell on the cape.

Then the barber cut some more. Snip, snip. Iris watched in the mirror. Her hair got shorter and shorter. The curl was the very first one. It lay on the cape like a tiny puzzle piece.

Papa picked up the small curl. He put it in a white envelope. "What is that for?" Iris asked. "Some families keep a little lock of hair," Papa said. "It helps them remember the first haircut."

The barber kept cutting. He took his time. Iris sat very still and waited. At last her haircut was done. Papa helped her down from the big chair. He gave her the envelope to hold.

At home, Papa taped the envelope in her baby book. Iris opened it a tiny bit. There was her little curl. It was soft and brown. "That is me," she said. Papa smiled and patted the page. "All safe," he said.

Claire was in the playroom. There was one big rocking horse. Claire wanted to ride it. But Lyana wanted to ride it too.

They both held the horse. It did not rock at all. Claire looked at Lyana. Lyana looked at Claire. "We can take turns," said Lyana. "You go first, one after another. Then me." Claire nodded.

Claire climbed on. She rocked and rocked. The horse went squeak, squeak. "Silly horse," said Claire, and she laughed. Lyana counted to ten. Then Claire got off. Now it was Lyana's go. Lyana rocked fast, and her hair flew up. Claire waited. She tapped her toes on the grass-green rug. It was hard to wait. But then Lyana got off, and Claire got another go.

Ms. Choi came over with two scarves. She tied a red scarf on the horse. "It looks like a knight's horse now," said Ms. Choi. Claire gasped. A surprise! Lyana rode the silly knight horse first. Then Claire rode it after her. One go, then another go, all the way to snack time. "My turn again?" asked Claire. "Yes," said Lyana. "After me!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Mya wanted to be a good host. She showed him her toys. She showed him the backyard, where an ant crawled on a stone. "Where do you sleep, Grandpa?" she asked. "I sleep in the room at the end of the hall," he said.

The next day, Grandpa took a bath. Mya played with her blocks outside the door. Soon Grandpa called out. "Where are the towels?" he asked. He could not find one. Mya opened the little cupboard in the hall. The towels were stacked inside. She took one soft towel and gave it to Grandpa. "Here you go," she said. "Thank you," said Grandpa.

After that, Mya showed him more things. "This is the bathroom," she said. "This is the cup you use." Grandpa smiled big. Each morning he asked, "What will my host show me today?" Mya laughed and ran to the cupboard. She pulled out a fresh towel and held it up like a flag. "Bath time!"

Felix sat at the little table. Ms. Mensah put out shape cards. There was a big circle, a square, and a triangle.

Felix held up a small red button. "Look, a tiny circle!" he said.

Josiah shook his head. "That is too small," he said. "The big clock is a circle. Your button can't be one too."

Felix felt worried. He carried the button to the wall. He held it next to the big clock. Both had round edges. Both had no corners.

"Josiah, come see," said Felix. "Big circle, tiny circle. Both are circles!"

Josiah looked and looked. "Both circles," he said. "One is big and one is small!"

Ms. Mensah smiled. "Let's pass out the shape cards. Then we can build a robot from squares and rectangles."

They made a tidy robot with a circle head. Felix put his button on the robot's tummy. It was a tiny circle button on a big robot friend.

Isla planted seeds at the school garden. Ms. Yang helped her pat the dirt. "Where is my sprout?" Isla asked. "First we water the seeds," said Ms. Yang. Isla filled her little can. She poured the water on the dirt. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Isla ran to the garden. She looked and looked. There was only dirt. "Oh no," said Isla. "Is this bad?" "No," said Ms. Yang. "A sprout does not come up right away. Keep watering, and we wait." So Isla watered the seeds every day. Her friend Rowan came to help. He clapped when the water went splash, splash.

One morning, Isla saw something green. A tiny sprout was peeking out of the dirt! "It came up!" Isla shouted. Rosemary ran over to see. "What is its name?" Rosemary asked. "It is a little carrot sprout," said Ms. Yang. Isla gave it more water from her can. The sprout stood up tall in the sun. "Hello, little sprout," said Isla.

Beatrice sat at the little table. She wanted to write numbers for a counting song. Ms. Boateng sang, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Beatrice wrote one, two, three. Then she wrote four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Each number had one shape. Ten needed one more shape, but she got stuck.

Mivaan came over. "Ten is written with two digits," he said. "A 1 and then a 0."

Beatrice tried it. She wrote a 1. Then she wrote a 0 right after it. "Ten!" she said.

Aila clapped. "Now we can sing to the end."

They sang the song all together. Beatrice held up her paper so everyone could see. "One, two, three, all the way to ten," she sang.

Raphael ran to Manuel at daycare. "Can I come to your house now?" he asked. "I want to see your beach ball."

Manuel smiled. "Not now," he said. "We go after a sleep. Tomorrow."

Raphael frowned. "What is tomorrow?"

Ms. Toussaint knelt down beside them. "Tomorrow comes after today," she said.

"But I want to go now," said Raphael.

"Now we play here," said Manuel. "Then we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Raphael looked out the window. The sun was up. Today was now.

After school, Raphael ate his snack. Then he slept in his bed. When he woke up, the sun was up again. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked his dad.

"Yes," his dad said, smiling. "Today is the new day."

At Manuel's house, they threw the beach ball high. Raphael held up his drawing with the sharp point of his pencil.

"I waited, and now it is today!" he said.

Charlotte went to the park with Elia. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Charlotte wore her warm red hat.

Then the wind began to blow. The big trees started to sway. "Look," said Elia. "The trees are dancing." Leaves flew off the branches. The leaves blew all around the grass. Charlotte chased a leaf. It rolled away from her hands. She chased it again. "The wind pushes the leaves," said Elia. Charlotte laughed and jumped on a pile of them.

The wind pushed hard on her hat too. Off it flew! The hat tumbled over the grass. Charlotte ran fast. Elia ran too. They chased the hat all the way to the slide. Charlotte picked it up. She zipped her coat up to her chin. The coat kept her warm.

"Good job," said Elia. Charlotte put the hat back on. She held it with both hands. Then a gray cloud came. Small drops fell. "Now it is rainy," said Elia. They ran to the bench. A mom held out two umbrellas. "Snowy days need boots," said the mom. "Rainy days need these." Charlotte took the blue one. The rain made little taps on top. The trees still swayed and swayed. Charlotte watched one more leaf fly by. "Catch it if you can," she said to Elia.

Arlo sat on the big bed. A basket sat next to him. In the basket was his new baby sister. "She is so small," said Arlo. "Smaller than my bear."

The baby made a little cry. Then she made a funny smell. Dad picked her up. "Time for a new diaper," said Dad. Arlo watched Dad open the diaper. "So many diapers," said Arlo. "She has a whole big box!" Dad took off the old diaper and put on a new one. The baby stopped crying. Arlo laughed. "One little smell, one big change!"

The next day Oskar came to play. Oskar peeked at the baby. "Why does she need so many diapers?" asked Oskar. Arlo stood up tall. "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet," said Arlo. Oskar nodded. "Not like us. We use the toilet."

Then the baby made another funny smell. "Again?" said Arlo. "Again," said Dad. Arlo held up a fresh diaper like a flag. "Diaper helper to the rescue!" The baby kicked her tiny legs. Arlo patted her soft head and said, "I eat big food. You eat milk. But we both make funny smells."

Elijah was at Anton's house. Anton had a big red truck. Elijah wanted it so much.

"My turn soon," said Anton. He pushed the truck across the rug. Elijah's hand reached out. He wanted to grab it. Then he stopped. He sat on his hands.

Elijah took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His body felt calm. He watched the truck go zoom, zoom, zoom.

"Your turn now," said Anton. He held out the truck. Elijah took it gently. He pushed it all the way to the toy barn.

"That was fun," said Elijah. "You can have it after me."

Anton smiled. They sat side by side and watched the wheels spin together.

Jaxon loved story time at the library. Ms. Tran had a new song today. "One, two, three," she sang. All the kids sang along. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Jaxon patted his knees to the beat.

Then Gia sat down next to him. Ms. Tran asked, "Gia, how old are you?" Gia held up four fingers. "I am four," she said. Jaxon looked at his own hands. He held up four fingers too. "I am four too!" he said. Gia laughed and showed him her fingers again.

After the song, they read a wild book about ten silly monkeys. The monkeys jumped on a street in the pictures. Jaxon counted them. "One, two, three, four," he said. "Just like my age!" Gia held up her fingers. "Me too," she said. "Four!"

Samuel stood by the pool. His coach held a big red ball. "Catch it, Samuel," she said. Samuel held out his hands. The ball came to him. He shut his eyes. The ball went bounce, bounce, away. "Oh no," said Samuel. He ran to pick it up.

Ananya was next. She kept her eyes open. Her hands caught the ball. "My turn again," said Samuel. The coach threw the ball. Samuel watched it all the way. He did not shut his eyes. He watched it right to his hands. His hands closed around it. He caught the ball!

"I got it, I got it!" said Samuel. A sleepy man by the pool woke up and clapped. Then Samuel threw his beanbag into the hoop. It went in. "Two tricks," said Ananya. Samuel laughed. "Watch the ball," he told her, "all the way to your hands."

Austin stood by the lemon tree in his backyard. His eyes saw four yellow lemons on a branch. His ears heard a bee buzz by. His nose smelled something sharp and fresh. "Lemons," said his dad. "They are ready to pick."

Austin wanted lemonade. He thought lemons would taste like orange juice, sweet and yummy. His dad picked one lemon and cut a thin slice. Austin put the slice in his mouth. His tongue tingled. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!"

His friend Evan came over with a big grin. "You made a sour face," Evan said. Austin laughed and gave Evan a tiny taste. Evan's face scrunched up too. Then the boys touched the lemon skin. It was bumpy and cool.

Dad squeezed the lemons into a jug. He added water and sugar. Austin stirred it with a long spoon. The juice and the sugar sank and swirled together. They drank cold cups in the shade. Austin took a sip and smiled big. "Sweet now!" he said. "And a little bit sour too."

Theodore ran to the block corner. He wanted to build a big tower, taller than him. His friend Keon ran over too.

"I help," said Keon.

They stacked one block, then two. The tower grew tall. Then the wind from the open door began to blow. The tall tower wobbled. It fell down with a loud crash. Theodore felt angry. His face got hot and his eyes got wet.

"Teddy has feelings," said Ms. Joseph. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups. I feel sad when my towers fall too."

"You do?" asked Theodore.

"I do," said Ms. Joseph. "So I take a big breath and build again."

Theodore took a big breath. Keon patted his back. They built the tower again, slow and steady. This time it stood tall.

"Look!" said Keon. "It did not fall!"

Theodore clapped his hands. He felt happy and excited. He spun in a circle.

"Now let's build it even taller," said Theodore.

Blake ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. But first she had to wash her hands.

She climbed onto her tall stool. She put soap on her hands. The soap was white and bubbly. She rubbed and rubbed. Her dad sang the counting song, and Blake counted to twenty.

Then Blake turned off the tap. Her hands were dripping wet. She shook them hard. Water flew everywhere. A drop landed on a small rock that sat by the window. Another drop landed on her dad's sleeve.

"Wet hands make wet messes," said her dad. He pointed to the hook. "The towel is the last step."

Blake held the soft towel. She dried one hand, then the other. All the drips went away.

Blake looked at her clean, dry hands. "Towel last!" she said, and she smiled all the way to her sandwich.

Arya wanted to find her blue doll. It was lost in the backyard. She looked with her eyes. She saw the swing. She saw the flowers. No doll there.

Then she heard a sound with her ears. Beep, beep. It came from the tall grass. Arya stopped and listened. The sound was small. It went beep again.

She sniffed with her nose. She smelled the sweet flowers. She smelled something else too. It smelled like her doll's soft soap. Arya followed the smell to the grass.

The grass was prickly in her shoes. She sat down on the step. She took off her shoes. Her bare toes touched the grass. The soft grass tickled her feet. "My feet can feel it too!" she said. Her toes felt something round. Arya reached down with her hands. There was her blue doll!

Arya hugged the doll. Then she tasted the cold water her dad gave her. "My doll was hiding," she said. Dad laughed and carried her inside, shoes swinging from her hand.

Connor woke up and looked out the window. "Snow!" he said. The grass was gone. White snow was everywhere. No school today! It was a snow day at home.

Connor put on his boots and his coat. He ran out the door to play. But the sidewalk was icy. His feet went slip, slip, slip! Down he went, right on his bottom. "Oof," said Connor.

His dad came out too. Dad did not run. Dad took small, slow steps. His feet went tap, tap, tap. "Watch me," said Dad. Connor stood up. He took small, slow steps too. Tap, tap, tap. His feet did not slip! "I did it!" said Connor.

Connor stomped in the soft snow. The snow was bumpy in some spots. He found a surprise under a bush. Little bird tracks, like tiny stamps! "Who made these?" Connor wondered. He followed them, slow and careful, tap, tap, tap, all the way to the fence.

Sara packed her little brown bag. She was going on a trip. Her family would stay at Grandma's house. Grandma lived near a big lake.

At the lake, Sara saw a snake. It was long and brown. It slid into the grass. "Can we keep it?" Sara asked. Her dad shook his head. "But we can take a photo," he said. He held up his phone. Click!

Sara wanted to know more. She looked at the photo. There was the snake! There was the lake! There was Grandma waving! "Take more," said Sara. Click, click, click. A duck. A yellow flower. Grandma's brown front door.

Then it was time to go home. Sara felt sad in the car. "I miss the snake," she said.

At home, they sat on the sofa. Dad opened the photos. There was the lake again! There was the snake! There was Grandma! Sara pointed at each one.

"Look," she said. "The snake went into the photo."

It was Myles's birthday at home. There were balloons in the kitchen. Grandma made a big cake. Dad lit the candles, and Myles watched from his chair.

The doorbell rang. It was Yousuf and his mom. Yousuf was a new friend from down the street. "Happy birthday!" Yousuf said. Then Yousuf asked, "How old are you today?"

Myles looked at his hands. He held up three fingers. "I am three!" he said. His dad smiled and shook his head. "Try again," Dad said. Myles looked down at his hand. He put up one more finger. Now he had four fingers up. "I am four!" he said.

Yousuf held up four fingers too. "I am four also," he said. They laughed. Then they all sang the birthday song. Mom used her phone to take a photo of the four fingers. Later they ate cake, but they were not late for bed, because four-year-olds still need sleep. Myles waved goodbye and held up four fingers one more time.

Maverick ran to the swings at the playground. He wanted the red swing most of all. But Coen was already on it. Maverick opened his mouth to say "My turn!" Then Leana began to talk. "Coen, look at my new shoes," she said. Coen looked at her shoes. Maverick held his words in his mouth. He waited. He watched.

The playground was noisy. Kids were laughing and calling. But Maverick kept waiting. Leana finished her words. Then Coen said, "Nice shoes, Leana." Then Coen looked at Maverick. "Do you want the red swing now?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Maverick. Coen hopped off. Maverick got on.

Mr. Shapiro stood near the slide. He gave Maverick a big thumbs up. Maverick pumped his legs. The swing went up, up, up. It felt like flying. "This is fun!" he called. Leana and Coen ran to push him gently. When the swing slowed down, Maverick jumped off into the soft sand. "Now you can have a turn," he said to Leana. She smiled and climbed on. Mr. Shapiro clapped his hands. "Good swinging, everyone," he said.

Axel went to the park with his dad. There was a big party there. It was a celebration for the new season. Flags waved on tall poles. A long table held plates of warm bread and salty pretzels.

Axel held his dad's hand. Drums began to play. Then some people began to dance. They clapped and spun around. Axel stood very still and watched. He stomped his foot in the grass, just a little. The drum went boom, and his foot went too. When the music went fast, his feet went fast too.

"Come on," his dad said. Axel held his dad's hand tight. First they took slow steps. Then big steps. Then a spin. Mario and Ciara were dancing too. They waved at Axel. Axel waved back and kept dancing.

Later Axel sat on the bench. He was tired and happy. His dad gave him a pretzel. The band played one more song. Axel listened and clapped along. Then he said, "More dancing, please."

Blake was so excited. Grandma was coming on a plane! Blake and her dad drove to the airport. They stood in a big room with lots of people. "Where is Grandma?" Blake asked. "We wait here," said Dad. "This is the arrivals area. Families wait here to meet people coming off a plane."

Blake watched the doors. The doors opened. A tall man walked out. "Grandma!" said Blake. "No, that is not Grandma," said Dad. The doors opened again. A lady in a red shirt walked out. "Grandma!" said Blake. "No, not yet," said Dad. Then the doors opened one more time. Grandma! Grandma hugged Blake tight. "I found you!" said Blake. "You found me!" said Grandma.

At home, Blake showed Grandma the guest bedroom. Grandma would sleep there for a whole week. Blake patted the wooden bed. "This is your room," said Blake. Grandma put her folded shirt in the little drawer. Blake opened the curtains so the sun could come in. "Good night, Grandma," said Blake. Grandma smiled and waved from the wooden bed.

Hayden stood at the basketball court. The sun was warm. His friend Lana was there too. Mr. Nwosu had a big bag of balls.

"Hayden, try this beanbag," said Mr. Nwosu. Hayden threw the beanbag. It hit the hoop. It fell down on the ground. He ran to get it. He threw it again. This time it went through the hoop. "Yay!" said Lana. Hayden clapped his hands.

Next came a big ball. Hayden held out his arms. Mr. Nwosu tossed the ball. Hayden touched it. The ball bounced out of his hands. It rolled across the court. He tried again. The ball bounced out again.

Then Hayden caught the ball and pulled it right in. He hugged it to his chest. The ball stayed. It did not bounce out. "I got it!" said Hayden. He hugged it tight. "My turn now," said Lana. Mr. Nwosu smiled and picked up another ball.

Rose was sick at home. Her nose was red. Her tummy felt funny, and she was not hungry at all.

Then Mommy put on her coat. "We need medicine," Mommy said. "The doctor said so." Rose held Mommy's hand in the pharmacy. She saw big shelves and bright lights. It smelled like mint.

A kind man stood behind a high counter. Mommy gave him a paper from the doctor. The man looked at it. Then he brought out a little white bag. "Here is the medicine the doctor said you need," he said. Rose watched him hand it over. So that is how it works, she thought. The paper goes in, and the medicine comes out.

At home, Mommy gave Rose a spoon of medicine. It tasted like cherry. Soon Rose yawned. She slept like a little cat by the river in her dream. When she woke up, her tummy growled. "I'm hungry!" said Rose. Mommy brought her warm soup, and Rose ate it all up.

Zachary sat at Grandma's big table. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. Grandma sat next to him.

Zachary made a Z. Then he made an A. But the paper slid away. His pencil line went crooked. He tried again. The paper slid again.

"Try your other hand," said Grandma. Zachary put his other hand on the paper. He held it still. He wrote a Z. The line stayed straight! He wrote A, then C, then H. The paper did not move at all.

Grandpa brought apple slices. They were crunchy. Zachary ate one. His tummy felt happy. Then he went back to his paper. He held it still with one hand. He wrote A, R, and Y.

"You did it," said Grandma. Zachary held up the paper. "Zachary," he read. "I can kick the paper away now, but I won't."

Lena was at the campsite with her family. In the cooler there were fresh carrots from the farmers' market. Lena wanted to cook them for dinner. "I will make soup for everyone," she said.

The carrots were covered with dirt. Lena put one in the pot. The dirt stayed on it. "Yuck," said Lena. Her dad helped her carry the carrots to the water bucket. Lena dipped a carrot in. She rubbed it with her fingers. The dirt came off in little clouds. The water turned brown. The carrot turned clean and orange.

Lena scrubbed each carrot, one by one. Then she scrubbed the potatoes too. Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables before cooking them, and now Lena knew why she did it too. She made a circle of clean carrots on the plate.

Dad cut the carrots into rounds at the table. Lena helped him stir the big pot. The soup bubbled soft and slow. It smelled warm and sweet.

"Soup is ready," said Dad. Lena held her bowl out. She took a big sip. "I cooked this," said Lena. "And I washed it too."

Louis sat in the big salon chair. His feet did not touch the floor. He was a little afraid of the scissors.

A fish tank sat by the window. Little fish swam round and round. Louis turned his head to see them. Snip! The hairdresser stopped. "Please sit very still," she said. "Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly."

Louis turned again. Snip, snip. The cut went crooked. A piece stuck out like a twig.

Louis thought of his dream. He wanted hair like his dad, all neat and shiny. So he made a plan. He would sit like a statue. He looked at the fish in the window glass. He could see them without turning. The light made the water shine.

He sat very still. Snip, snip, snip. The hairdresser cut and cut. It felt like little tickles.

"All done," she said. She held up a mirror. Louis saw a neat, short haircut. "I sat like a statue!" he said. His dad gave him a big smile.

Eliana wanted to zip her own coat. But the zipper was stuck at the bottom. She pulled and pulled. It did not move.

She called her dad. "Count while you pull," he said. "One, two..." Then Eliana forgot what came next. She stood very still.

Then she remembered a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. "Three, four, shut the door." Dad smiled and clapped the beat. The words rhymed, so they came out easy. "Five, six, pick up sticks." On "pick," she grabbed the zipper tab with her fingers. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." The zipper slid up, up, up. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" The coat was zipped all the way to her chin.

Eliana picked up her red hat. "I did it with my song," she said. Dad gave her a real hug. "Sing it at school for Krew," he said. Eliana ran to the door. "One, two, buckle my shoe!" she sang.

Theo sat at the art table. He wanted to make a robot. Ms. Bondarenko gave him a wood block and a sheet of stickers. "What can I do with these?" Theo asked. "Count and see," said Ms. Bondarenko.

Theo put a red sticker on the front of the block. Then he turned it. Another flat side! He put a blue sticker there. He turned the block again and again. Top. Bottom. Left. Right.
