"One, two, three, four, five, six!" said Theo. Six stickers on six flat sides. Each sticker was a square, and each flat side was a square too!

Alexis came over. "How many sides does it have?" she asked. Theo held up the block. "Six! Count my stickers!" Alexis clapped. Theo glued the block onto his robot for a head. He drew two circle eyes and a triangle nose. "My square-headed robot has a tail," said Theo. He taped on a paper rectangle. The robot waved its arm.

Gabriel sat in his car seat. Dad was driving to the park. Gabriel had a little bag of grapes.

"You can have three grapes," said Dad. "Not more."

Gabriel looked at his grapes. Some were small. Some were big. Did big grapes count as more?

"Is a big grape still one?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three means three grapes. Big or small."

Gabriel picked three big grapes. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Then he ate them, one by one.

He heard rain tap the roof. One tap, then more taps. The rain made a song. Dad sang, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

A grape fell from Gabriel's hand. It rolled under the seat. He could not reach it.

"I will pay attention and hold on tight," Gabriel said. He held the next grape with both hands.

The rain stopped. The sky looked beautiful and blue.

"We are here," said Dad. He helped Gabriel out of the car. They held hands and walked to the swings.

"Can I have three grapes later?" asked Gabriel.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three is three, every time."

Gabriel smiled. He swung his arms and counted the swings. "One, two, three!"

Hailey sat at the little red table. Art class was starting. "Today we paint the street," said Ms. Qureshi. Hailey wanted to paint cars. But what colors did cars need? She picked up a blue brush. She painted a long street. Jakob painted a yellow car. Sukhmani painted a green tree. The paint smelled like soap. Wind tickled the paper on the table.

Then Hailey saw something on the wall. It was a picture of a traffic light. It had a red circle and a green circle. Ms. Qureshi held it up. "Red means stop," she said. "Green means go." Hailey painted the red circle on top. She painted the green circle at the bottom.

After class, Hailey held her mom's hand. They stood at the snowy corner. The light turned red. The cars all stopped. The light turned green. The cars all went. "Look!" said Hailey. "Red means stop. Green means go." Her mom smiled. Hailey looked up and down the street. Would the next light be red or green? It was green. The cars went. Hailey waved at a yellow bus.

Sadie stood at the big table in the community kitchen. Ms. Cho had made warm toast, and now it was Sadie's turn.

"Watch me," said Ms. Cho. She held the butter knife. Sadie took her own knife, the safe one with the curly edge. She dug up a pat of butter. One pat, two pats, three pats on the table. She counted them, then took just one.

Sadie spread the butter on her warm toast. She spread it slow. She spread it fast. The toast was warm, and the butter sat on top. Then the butter began to shine. Then it got soft. Then it slid into the toast and was gone!

"Where did it go?" Sadie asked.

"It melted into the warm toast," said Moses. "Look, your bread is all shiny now."

"Can I do the milk too?" Sadie asked. "Yes," said Ms. Cho.

Sadie held the cup with both hands. She poured and poured. Not one drop spilled!

"Toast and milk, toast and milk," sang Bea from the sink, where she liked to swing the towel in the air.

Sadie took a big bite. "My butter is still in there," she said. "I can taste it!"

Max ran onto the baseball diamond. His shoes went crunch, crunch on the dirt. His cap was orange, and his juice box was in his bag. Today was his first game!

"Where do I stand?" Max asked. He looked left. He looked right. The bases looked far away. One base, two bases, three bases, and home plate. Max did not know.

Then the coach called out. "Come here, Max. I will show you." The coach was Mr. Lau. He put his hand on Max's shoulder. He pointed to a spot near second base. "Stand right there," said Mr. Lau. "Watch the ball."

Max stood on the spot. He held his glove up high. He thought about the ball flying through the air.

Rishi hit the ball. It went pop! The ball came right to Max. Thump! It landed in his glove.

"I caught it!" Max shouted. "I caught it!"

Rishi clapped. Maelie clapped. Mr. Lau clapped big claps.

The next ball came too. Max stood on his spot. Thump! Caught it again.

Mr. Lau gave Max a thumbs up. "Same spot, same catch," he said.

Max grinned so big his cheeks hurt. After the game, he drank his juice. It was sweet and cold.

"I can't wait for the next game," said Max. "Same spot, same catch!"

Natalie sat in the waiting room. She hugged her toy lion tight. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt funny.

A nurse came out. "Natalie, come this way," she said. Natalie walked slow. She held her lion close.

First came the scale. Natalie stood on it. She wiggled her toes. The numbers jumped up and down. The nurse shook her head.

"Stand still," the nurse said. Natalie stopped wiggling. The numbers stopped too. Now the scale showed one number. It showed how much Natalie weighed. "Big girl," said the nurse. Natalie smiled.

Then it was time for the shot. Natalie sat on the big bed. She squeezed her lion. "You can do it," said Mom. The nurse counted. "One, two, three." The shot came, quick as a blink. It was done!

Natalie looked at her arm. There was a small bandage on it. It had little stars on it! "A surprise for you," said the nurse. Natalie held up her arm to show Mom. "My stars," she said.

Billie stood at the edge of the hockey rink. The ice was far away. A big mat sat on the floor for gym day. Ms. Desir put out hoops and beanbags.

"Watch me first," said Ms. Desir. She tossed a beanbag up. It went right into the hoop.

Billie tried. Her beanbag hit the stick holding the hoop. It fell out. "Why did it fall?" Billie asked.

"You threw it too hard," said Ms. Desir. "Try a little toss."

Billie tried a small, soft toss. The beanbag went in. Billie clapped.

Then Ekam threw the big ball to Willa. He threw it fast and hard. It bumped her hands and rolled away. Willa looked mad.

"Throw it soft," said Billie. "A gentle toss is easier to catch."

Ekam tossed it gently. Willa caught it with both hands. She did not let go.

"Now to me," said Billie.

Ekam spoke with a big smile. "Here it comes, slow and easy."

Billie held out both hands. The ball came down soft as snow. She caught it.

Ms. Desir sat close by on the mat. "Good work, friends," she said. Billie hugged the big ball and smiled.

Miles sat at the table. Mom put down a big pot. It smelled warm, like rice and peas.

"Tonight we say the blessing first," said Mom. "It is special. We fold our hands."

Miles wanted to eat right now. The rice smelled so good. But Mom said, "Watch Grandpa."

Grandpa bowed his head. He closed his eyes. Miles peeked. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut and Grandpa's head down. Miles closed his eyes too. He bowed his head. "Thank you for our food," he said, in his little voice.

Then Miles opened one eye. Grandpa was still bowing. Miles closed his eye fast. He waited. The room was very quiet. He could hear the pot steam going tss, tss.

"Amen," said Grandpa. Everyone said "Amen." Mom smiled big. "Miles said it with us!"

Miles clapped. The blessing was done, and now it was time to eat. Miles took his spoon. "I did it!" he said. "Can we say it again tomorrow?"

Charles wanted to read his book about a pet cat. It was his favorite book. But the sun was going down and it was getting late.

He sat on his bed. He held the book up. The cat looked funny. Its feet were at the top! The words looked funny too. They were at the top of the page.

Charles laughed. "Silly cat!" he said. He turned the book around.

Now the cat sat right side up. Its feet were at the bottom. The words sat at the bottom too. The cat looked like a cat again.

Dad came in. "Read to me," Dad said. Charles opened the front of the book. He pointed at each word. Dad smiled.

"I can read the cat book," Charles said. He turned the page. The cat began to paint a big red picture.

Charles read to the very end. Then he hugged the book tight. "Good night, cat," he whispered.

Lea sat in a big chair at the health clinic. Her friend Monroe sat in the next chair. They both waited for their turns.

"I am not sick," said Monroe. "So why do we need a shot?"

The doctor heard him. "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said. "Even when you feel fine."

Lea watched the nurse rub her arm with a cool, wet cloth. Then came the tiny pinch. It was over fast. Lea got a loose bandage and a sticker with a star.

Monroe stood up next. He squeezed his eyes tight. But then he saw Lea's sticker. He opened his eyes and smiled. "I want a star too," he said.

The pinch came and went. Monroe got his sticker and held it up high. On the way out, Lea saw her long shadow on the sunny floor. She waved at it, and the doctor waved back.

"See you next time," said the doctor.

Lea held her sticker all the way home.

Naomi walked in the forest with her teddy bear. She wanted to have a tea party, but she had no tea.

She found a flat stump. She set out three empty cups. One for teddy. One for a pinecone. One for a rock. She counted them out loud. "One cup, two cups, three cups."

An owl called softly from a tree. "Whoo, whoo," it said.

Naomi picked up an empty cup. She tipped it over teddy's cup. Nothing came out. Then she smiled.

"Look, teddy. The cup is empty, but the tea is pretend." She poured pretend tea again and again. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" she said.

"Can a rock drink pretend tea?" she asked. "Yes, if it is a pretend thirsty rock," she answered.

Naomi used a leaf to sweep the stump clean. "All tidy," she said. "More pretend tea, anyone?"

Ezra wanted his yellow pajamas. They had a duck on them. But first it was bath time.

His father ran the bath. Ezra splashed in the warm water. He washed his curly hair. He played with his blue boat.

Then bath time was done. Ezra jumped out. He ran down the hall. Drip, drip, drip went the water. It made little wet spots on the floor.

"Ezra, you are all wet," his father said. "Come and get your towel."

Ezra came back. His father wrapped him in the big soft towel. It was warm and fluffy. Ezra patted his arms. He patted his legs. The towel rubbed the water away. Now his skin was dry.

"The towel dries me," said Ezra.

"Yes, it does," said his father. "Now show me your arms. All dry!"

Ezra put on his duck pajamas. He brushed his teeth with help. Then he got into bed.

His father read one book. Ezra hugged his bear. His father turned off the light.

"Night night, duck boy," said his father.

"Night night," said Ezra. He closed his eyes. The wet floor spots were gone too.

Maverick wore his bright red shirt to daycare. It was animal day. Everyone brought a picture of an animal. Maverick brought his dog picture. "A dog is an animal," said Mr. Hamdan. Skye held up a cow picture. "A cow is an animal too," said Mr. Hamdan. "Moo," said Skye, and everyone laughed.

Then it was Maverick's turn again. He had a fish picture too. "Fish has no legs," said Maverick. "Fish is not an animal." Louane shook her head. Mr. Hamdan put the dog, the cow and the fish on the table. He tapped each one slowly. "Animal. Animal. Animal." Maverick looked and looked. He touched the fish picture with one finger. It tickled his mind like a new idea.

"Dogs, cows and fish are all animals," said Maverick. "Even fish with no legs!" He clapped his hands. At snack time, Maverick ate his apple. He looked at his fish picture one more time. "Swim, little animal," he said.

Theo sat on a wooden bench. The bench was hard and smooth. Apollo sat next to him. Leanne sat on the other side. They were at the big stadium. A basketball game was on. Lots of people were watching. Theo clapped his hands.

A player held the orange ball. He threw it up. The ball went through the hoop. The crowd jumped up. "They score when the ball goes in the hoop," said Apollo. Theo watched. Another player threw the ball. It went through the hoop too. The scoreboard changed to a bigger number. "Did you see that?" Theo asked. "The ball went in, and the number grew."

A big mascot ran by. He had a fuzzy tail. The tail bounced as he ran. Theo laughed and waved. Then the game was over. Theo's team did win. "Hooray!" shouted Leanne.

After the game, they went to a small hoop. It was short, just Theo's size. Theo held the ball. Could he do it too? He threw the ball. It hit the rim and fell off. He tried again. The ball went up, up, and through the hoop. It dropped down under the net. Theo jumped high. "It went in!" he said. "Throw it again," said Leanne. Theo picked up the ball.

Layla wanted to make a picture book. But her basket of pictures was all mixed up. She tipped it over. Out fell a cow, a ball, a banana, an owl, a teddy bear, and an apple.

"Too messy," said Layla. She put the cow in one pile. She put the owl with the cow. "Cow, owl," she said. "Animals." Next she made a new pile. "Ball, teddy bear," she said. "Toys." Then one more pile. "Banana, apple," she said. "Foods."

Her dad came to help. He looked at the piles. "You sorted them into groups," he said. "Nice work." Layla chose the owl for her book. She glued it in. Her fingers got sticky from the glue, so her dad wiped them with a wet cloth.

Then Layla turned the page. "Now the animals," she said, "one, two, three, four!"

Eleanor went to the corner store with her dad. Apples sat in a big box. "Can I count them?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Eleanor pointed at the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." But she pointed at one apple two times. "Six!" she said. Dad shook his head. "Count again," he said. "Point to each apple one time."

Eleanor tried again. She tapped one apple and said one number. "One, two, three, four, five." Five apples! She had said one number for each apple. She jumped up and down. "Five apples!"

Next, Eleanor looked at two little piles of pears. She counted the first pile. Four pears. She counted the second pile. Seven pears. "This pile has more!" she said, pointing. Mr. Korhonen, the store man, smiled. He put one pear in the middle of the small pile. "Now count again," he said. Eleanor tapped each pear one time. "Five!" she said. Still not more than seven. She giggled and gave the pear back.

At home, Eleanor counted her toy cars. One car got two taps by mistake. She lifted her finger and started over. "One, two, three, four." She ran to Dad with all four cars. "I counted just right!" she said. "Can we go back tomorrow?"

Arnaud loved the big red blocks at school. Today he got to the block corner first. He stacked one, then two, then three. The tower grew tall.

Hallie and Matheo came over. "Can we play too?" Hallie asked. Arnaud looked at his tower. "These are my blocks," he said. "All of them?" Matheo asked. "All of them," said Arnaud.

Hallie walked away. Matheo walked away. Arnaud built alone. The room felt quiet. He looked at Hallie. She was drawing with her finger in the air. He looked at Matheo. He was spinning in a circle. Nobody was building.

Arnaud pushed the blocks into one big pile. Then he stopped. What if he made three piles? He counted them out. "Hallie! Matheo!" he called. "Look. One pile for me. One pile for you. One pile for you."

Hallie ran back fast. Matheo ran back fast too. Each child built a small tower. "Can I put my block on top of yours?" Arnaud asked. "Yes," said Hallie. "You say please, that's polite." "Please," said Arnaud.

The three towers stood side by side in a row. Matheo clapped his hands. Hallie moved her tower closer so they touched. Arnaud grinned and said, "Blocks for everyone."

Bennett was in his bedroom. He built a big tower of blocks. It had ten red blocks and ten blue blocks. He felt so happy. "My tower is tall!" he said.

Then the phone began to ring. The loud ring scared Bennett. His hand bumped the tower. The tower fell down. Now it was broken. Bennett felt angry. He stomped his foot. "My tower is broken!" he shouted. He wanted to throw a block.

Dad came in fast. "I am here," Dad said. "Let's try slow, deep breaths." Bennett blew out one slow breath. Then two slow breaths. Then three. His body began to calm down. His mad feelings got smaller and smaller.

Bennett saw that slow breaths helped him feel calm. He looked at the broken tower. It was not so bad. "I can build it again," he said. Dad helped him stack the blocks. Up, up, up went the tower. Bennett felt excited. He hugged Dad. "All done!" said Bennett.

Emile ran into the backyard. The sky was sunny, but white snow covered the grass. The wind blew. It was windy and cold. He wore his big puffy coat and his warm red mittens. "I want to keep some snow," he said. He scooped up a snowball. It was round and cold in his hands. His little sister watched from the door. She was busy stacking cups. Emile carried the snowball inside. "Where can it stay?" he asked. He put it in a bowl on the table. Then he went back out to play. The snow squeaked under his boots. Later, he came in and scratched his head. The bowl held only water. The snowball was gone. "It melted," he said. "Inside is warm, so snow melts into water." He ran to show his sister. "Look! Water!"

Mason sat in the cafe with his mom. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. The letters came out wobbly. The M looked like a squiggle. "It's too hard," said Mason.

"You can try again," said his mom. "I will sit right here with you."

A lady at the next table smiled. She was writing on a big pad. Her letters were neat and small. "I write my name every day," she said. "Now it is easy for me."

Mason looked at his paper. He tried again. He held the pencil with his fingers, not his fist. He wrote M, a, s, o, n. It was a little better.

Each day they came back to the cafe. Mason wore his blue shirt and wrote his name on fresh paper. Write, write, write. His letters got straighter. Soon the M stood tall like two little mountains.

One morning Mason wrote his whole name fast. "Look, Mom!" he said. "Look, look!"

His mom gave him a hug. Mason mixed his apple juice with a spoon and smiled at his neat, sweet name.

Isaac stood in the garage. A big drum sat by the wall. He tapped it once. Boom! The sound filled the garage. Isaac jumped. Where did that big sound come from? He looked at his hand. Did his little tap do that?

He tapped again. Boom! He smiled. His drum had a song, but it was long. Isaac tried to play it. Tap, tap, boom. Then he missed a part. He tried again and missed again. His shoulders went down. "This song is too hard," he said. Luciano came in with his dad. "Play it for me," said Luciano. Isaac played the start. Then he stopped. He missed the end.

The next day, Isaac came back to the garage. He played the start. Then he played a little more. The next day, he came again. He played the start and the middle. Each day he played a little more. One morning, Isaac took a big breath. He played the whole song, all the way to the end. Boom, boom, boom, boom! Luciano clapped. "You did not miss one beat," he said. Isaac patted the drum. "We did it," he whispered, "a little bit every day."

Chloe sat in her reading nook with a big red book. On the wall hung a poster with a big letter A. In her book, she saw a small, round letter. "Who are you?" she asked it. "You are not the big A from my wall. You must be a new letter!"

Chloe ran to her friend Roy's house next door. His friendly dog, Biscuit, barked hello. "Roy, look," said Chloe. "This little letter is in my book. Is it a new letter?"

Roy laughed. "No, it is the same A. It is just small."

"The same?" said Chloe. "Big A and little a?"

"Big letters and small letters," said Roy. "Same letter, big and small."

Chloe looked at her page. The little a sat right at the start of "apple". She said, "A, a, apple!" The rain began to tap on the window, but Chloe kept reading through the little storm. "A, a, ant!" she said. "A, a, apron!"

Chloe turned the page. "B!" she said. "Big B, little b. Bat!" Biscuit barked again, as if he liked that one too.

Peyton put on her skates at the ice rink. Her team was the blue frogs. Ms. Khoury handed her a small blue jersey. "Time to play, frogs," said Ms. Khoury.

Peyton chased the puck across the ice. Her legs felt wobbly. Her friend Samantha skated beside her. "You can do it," Samantha said. Peyton swung her stick. She missed the puck. It slid far away.

Peyton stopped and looked down. Then she heard something. Her teammates were clapping. "Try again, Peyton!" they cheered. Cassius banged his stick on the ice. Even Samantha clapped for her. The team was loud and warm and happy.

Peyton skated after the puck again. She chased it to the wall. She swung her stick once more. This time she hit it! The puck slid right to Samantha. Samantha pushed it toward the goal. It went in! Everyone cheered again.

Later, Cassius missed the puck too. It slid under the bench. Peyton skated over to him. She clapped her mittens together. "Try again, Cassius!" she called. Cassius smiled and chased the puck. Peyton clapped louder.

The big farmhouse went dark. Emile stood very still. He wiggled his toe inside his sock. "Mom, the lights went out!"

Mom found her flashlight. "The power is out," she said. "We will be fine." The light made a neat white circle on the wall. Emile held his own small flashlight too. They sat on the couch together. Emile listened to the quiet house. No fan. No fridge hum. Only the wind outside.

Mom lit one candle on the table. She kept the matches up high, far from Emile. The flame made little shadows dance. Emile watched them hop and dip. "They look like they bite the air," he whispered. Mom smiled.

Then the lights came back on. The fan hummed again. Emile clapped his hands. But something looked funny in the kitchen. The clock on the oven was blinking. Blink, blink, blink.

"Mom! The oven clock is blinking!" said Emile.

"That is what happens after a power cut," said Mom. "It needs to be set again." She pushed the little buttons. Emile stood beside her and watched. The numbers stopped blinking. The clock showed the right time again.

Emile looked at the microwave too. Its clock was blinking as well. "That one too, Mom!"

Mom laughed. "Good eye, Emile." She set that clock too. Then she said, "Time for bed, clock helper."

Emile followed her up the stairs, his flashlight still glowing in his hand.

Ryan sat in Mr. Zhang's music studio. A guitar sat on a little chair. Ryan patted the big round back. Bomp, bomp, like a drum. "Is this how it plays?" he asked. Mr. Zhang shook his head. "You play a guitar by plucking or strumming its strings," he said. He pointed to the long strings.

Ryan looked at the strings. They were shiny and thin. He put one finger on a string. He pulled it and let go. Twang! A pretty sound filled the room. Ryan smiled big.

Then Ryan moved his thumb across all the strings. Strum! It sounded like rain, soft and quick. His friend Evren clapped from the corner. "Play more!" Evren said. Ryan strummed again, slow this time. The sound was warm like honey. "Can I try?" Evren asked. Ryan nodded and held the guitar out to his friend.

Leon sat on the rug at school. He had five toy monkeys. Stanley sat next to him. "Let's sing the monkey song," said Stanley. Leon clapped. "One little, two little, three little monkeys," they sang. Leon counted all the way to ten on his fingers, just for fun.

Then they sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head." Leon made one monkey drop. He looked at the rug. "Now there are four," said Stanley. They sang again. One more monkey fell. Now there were three. Leon's eyes got big. "One monkey falls off each time," he said. "The number gets one smaller!" They sang and sang. Then there were two. Then there was one. Then there were none.

Leon held the last monkey softly. "Did he bump his head too hard?" he asked. Ms. Esposito sat down close. "He is fine," she said. "Monkey bumps are pretend bumps." Leon smiled and set all five monkeys in a row. Then it was snack time. The muffins were warm. "Blow on it so it does not burn," said Ms. Esposito. Leon blew and blew. "Now it is cool," he said, and he took a big bite.

Nolan looked out the window. Snow! School was closed. "Snow day!" he cheered.

Dad took Nolan to the park. Kelsey was there too. The paths were all white and slick. Kelsey tried to walk. She slipped and fell on her bottom. "Oof!" she said.

A big truck came. A grown-up got out with a shovel. He pushed the snow off the path. Left, right, left, right. The path turned from white to brown. "Look!" said Nolan. "The snow is gone!"

Nolan stepped on the clean path. His boots did not slip at all. Kelsey stepped on too. "It's easy now!" she said.

Then Nolan saw something under the big tree. It was a pink mitten, half covered in snow. "I can get it!" he said. He walked on the clear path. No slipping. He picked up the mitten and held it up high.

"Nice work!" said the grown-up with the shovel. Nolan grinned. "Shovel snow, then you can walk!" he said.

Mya woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow!" she said. School was closed. It was a snow day at home.

Mya wanted to play in the backyard. But the snow was too deep. Her boots went down, down, down. She could not walk. Her boots got stuck!

Then Mya heard a big noise. She looked out the window by the gate. A big truck was on the road. It had a big shovel in front. "A snowplow," said her dad. The snowplow pushed the snow off the road. The road turned black and clear. Where did all the white go?

The snowplow had made a big pile by the curb. Mya looked at the pile. Then she looked at her yard. She had an idea. "Can we make a path?" she asked.

Her dad got the red shovel. He pushed the snow, just like the snowplow. Mya held his hand and walked behind him. Step by step, they made an open path to the swing.

Mya ran down the path to her swing. "We did it!" she said. Then she sat down and pumped her legs.

Mohamed sat on the big rug in the living room. The game was on TV. Papa sat next to him. Layne came too, with her teddy bear. Mr. Brennan, the neighbour, sat on the sofa.

One, two, three, four men ran on the green grass. They ran after one ball. Mohamed pointed. "The ball goes over the net!" he said. Papa shook his head. "Watch the net," he said.

A man kicked the ball. The ball went into the net. Layne jumped up. "Goal!" she said. Everyone clapped. The crowd on TV clapped too. The ball went in, and everyone cheered.

Mohamed made a big sign with his hands. It said GOAL. Layne shared his crackers. They were yummy. The man kicked again. The ball went in. "Goal!" said Mohamed.

Levi sat at the little table at summer camp. Ms. Munro put out three paint pots. One was red. One was yellow. One was blue. Levi dipped his brush in the red. He made a red circle. Then he dipped the same brush in the yellow. His circle turned orange. He looked at it. He made another one. Red and yellow made orange again.

Levi forgot about his brush. He left it in the red pot. He went to play. The next morning, Levi came back to paint. He picked up his brush. It was hard. It would not bend. The red paint had dried on it. Levi showed it to Ms. Munro. "We wash the brushes with water," she said. "Then they dry soft for tomorrow."

Levi carried his brush to the sink. He turned the water on. The red paint came off. The water ran pink, then clear. He set the brush on a towel to dry. His friend Arthur came to look. "It's soft again," Arthur said. Levi smiled. He dipped the clean brush in the blue. Then he dipped it in the yellow. A big green line went across his paper. "Green!" said Levi.

Jake stood in the bathroom. The water was warm. Jake dipped his toes in. "Splash!" went his foot. Small water drops flew up. Jake made a circle in the fog on the mirror with his finger.

Then Jake sniffed with his nose. Something smelled good. It smelled like soup. "Mmm," said Jake. His tummy made a little growl. He could smell dinner before he saw it. "Is it soup?" he called.

"Yes, it is," said his dad. "Good nose, Jake." Dad helped Jake wash. The soap smelled like flowers. Jake touched the soft cloth. He heard the water go drip, drip, drip. His ears heard that.

After the bath, Jake sat at the table. He took a taste of soup. "Yummy," said Jake. He slurped it up. He had known it was soup with just his nose, before his eyes saw the bowl. Dad smiled and gave him more bread. "Warm tummy," said Jake.

Grandpa had a busy morning planned. He put five things on the big table. Olivier wanted to name them all with his five senses.

"First, use your eyes," said Grandpa. Olivier looked. He saw a red apple, a smooth shell, a soft sock, a little bell and a lemon. "I see them with my eyes," Olivier said. He clapped his hands.

"Now close your eyes," said Grandpa. Olivier listened. Ding, ding! "I hear the bell with my ears!" Next he sniffed the lemon. "I smell it with my nose." He took a tiny bite of apple from Grandpa's hand. "I taste it with my mouth."

Then Olivier touched the shell. It felt bumpy. He touched the sock. It felt soft. "My fingers feel it," he said. Grandpa smiled. "Yes, we feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips." Olivier touched his own neck. His fingertips felt warm skin there too. He laughed and touched the shell again. "Bumpy! My skin knows it!"

Parker sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sun was out. "Sunny day!" he shouted. The car drove to school.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell. Drip, drop, drip. "Rainy now," said Parker. The wind blew too. It blew a paper bag down the street. "Windy!" said Parker. He watched the bag fly away.

At school, Parker and his dad had to walk to the door. The rain came down fast. Dad opened a big umbrella. He held it over Parker's head. The rain went tap, tap, tap on top. Parker stayed dry! The umbrella kept the rain off his head. "My head is dry, Dad!"

Inside, his friend Thalia was hanging up her snowy boots. "It snowed at my house!" she said. Parker clapped. "Sunny, rainy, windy, snowy!" said Parker. Thalia laughed. Then they ran to the toy cars.

Ava held the violin under her chin. She held the bow in her left hand. "What do I do now?" she asked. Mr. Chukwu smiled. "Try it and see," he said.

Ava poked the strings with the bow. The violin went squeak, squeak, squeak! Ciara laughed and put her hands over her ears. "It sounds like a duck!" she said. Jind was awake now, wide awake, and he laughed too. Ava counted the squeaks. "One, two, three squeaks," she said. "My duck is singing."

Mr. Chukwu came over. He turned the bow in her hand. Then he pulled it across the strings, slow and smooth. A big, warm sound filled the room. Ava pulled the bow across the strings herself. One long song came out. "Bye bye, duck," said Ciara. Ava laughed and played some more.

Emily sat on the bright mat at the community centre. Ten little cups stood in a row. "Let's count them," said Ms. Ong. Emily pointed at each cup. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She clapped her hands.

Sadie had cups too. Sadie's row was short. "One, two, three," counted Sadie. Emily looked at both rows. "My row has more," she said. Sadie giggled. "I want more too!" Ms. Ong gave Sadie seven more cups. Now they each had ten.

Then Emily gave one cup to Hana. Hana made a little tower with it. Emily counted her cups again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." She looked up fast. "One went away! Now I have nine!" Sadie counted her own cups. "Ten is more than nine!" Emily laughed and put her doll on the last cup, like a hat. "Do it again," she said.

Henry sat on the playroom floor. Jamal held a big cloth bag. "It is a feely bag," said Jamal. "Put your hand in. Don't peek!"

Henry pushed his hand into the bag. He felt something round and bumpy. "It is a ball!" he said. "It is a red ball!" Jamal laughed. "Open your eyes and look." Henry pulled out the ball. It was blue, not red.

Henry tried again. He felt something soft with corners. "A blanket!" he said. "A green blanket!" He pulled it out. It was yellow. Henry sat back on his knee and laughed too.

Mr. Tanaka came in with a scarf. "Cover your eyes with this," he said. "Then touch the crayons." Henry felt a long thin crayon. "This one!" he said. He lifted the scarf and peeked. The crayon was green. He covered his eyes again and felt another one. This time he could not say the color at all.

"You see colors with your eyes," said Jamal. "Your fingers can't tell!"

Henry found a red crayon and a blue crayon. He held them behind his back. "Close your eyes, Jamal. Now guess!" Outside the window the sky looked stormy and grey. Jamal grinned and covered his face with both hands. "I feel a crayon," he said slowly. "But what color? Tell me, tell me!"

Olivier sat on the small red rug at school. Mr. Rahimi held up a big book. On the cover was a bear in a green forest.

"Who made up the bear story?" Olivier asked.

"Guess," said Haroun, who sat next to him.

Olivier pointed at the bear. "The bear did it!"

Rivaan laughed. "Bears cannot write!"

Mr. Rahimi smiled. He turned the book to the front. He put his finger under a name. "This is the author," he said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book."

Olivier leaned in close. He saw little black marks. "That says a name?" he asked.

"It says a name," said Mr. Rahimi.

Olivier looked at the marks. They were small and shy, hiding at the bottom of the cover. But they were there. Someone with a name made the bear up!

"Read the front page first," said Mr. Rahimi. He opened the cover. "Books go front to back."

He read page one. Then page two. Olivier listened to every word.

After story time, Olivier found a little book on the shelf. He turned it to the front. He found the small marks at the bottom.

"Rivaan!" he called. "Look! This one has a name too!"

Charlotte ran to the block corner at practice. Giovanni was already there. He held the red blocks in his arms. Charlotte wanted them too. She reached out to grab them.

Then Ms. Marino knelt down beside them. "You can both use the blocks," she said softly. Charlotte let go. She looked at the tall pile. "We could build one big tower," she said. Giovanni smiled and nodded.

They sat side by side. Charlotte chose a blue block. Giovanni added a red one. The tower grew tall. "Silly tower!" laughed Giovanni, when it wobbled like a wobbling egg. Charlotte waited while he found one more block. Then she put it on top. The tower stood big and strong. "Look what we made," said Charlotte. "Together," said Giovanni, and he patted the very top block.

Jules sat at the craft table at summer camp. He was painting a big picture. It had a sun and a blue sea. Next to him, Aarya painted a turtle with a green shell. The paint smelled like rain, and the paper felt cool.

Jules put his finger on the sun. The yellow paint was still wet. It smushed and made a big smudge. "Oh no," said Jules. "My sun is blurry now."

Mr. Nguyen came over with a fan. He set it on the table near the paintings. Jules and Aarya watched the air blow on the papers. They waited and waited. Then Aarya touched her turtle. It was dry! The green paint stayed smooth. Jules touched his sun again. It was dry too.

"Let's make more," said Aarya. She went to the shelf to get more paper. Jules picked up a wooden stamp and pressed it in red paint. He stamped little fish on his sea. Then he folded his hands in his lap. He would not touch the fish yet. He would wait for them to dry.

Mr. Nguyen smiled. "Your fish look great, Jules." Jules grinned and kept his hands very still.

Leon ran to the swing at the playground. Ty was already there. Leon wanted the swing so much. He grabbed the chain with both hands.

Ty held on too. "My turn," said Ty. "My turn," said Leon. Nobody could swing. The swing just stood still.

Mr. Gallagher came over. "We take turns here," he said. "Ty, you go first. Leon, you go next."

Ty swung up high. Then Ty got off. "Your turn now, Leon," said Ty.

Leon sat on the swing. "Push, please," he said. Mr. Gallagher pushed. Up went Leon, high like Ty. It was fun.

Hussein came by with a red ball. "My ball got lost," he said. "I found it!" Leon got off the swing. "Your turn, Hussein," he said.

Hussein swung. Leon and Ty rolled the ball on the grass. The ball went round and round.

"Swing, please," said Leon, when the swing was free again. Hussein smiled and hopped off. Leon pumped his legs. The swing went up, up, up.

"Again," laughed Leon. "This is fun."

Leo woke up and saw white outside. "Snow!" he said. No school today. It was a surprise snow day. Dad said, "Let's get you ready."

Leo put on his warm coat. He put on his boots. He put on his hat. But he ran out the door fast, and his mittens stayed on the table. Mr. Thompson was outside shoveling next door. Leo picked up snow with his bare hands. Then his fingers hurt. "Cold!" he said. "My fingers are cold!"

Dad came out with the mittens. "Try these." Leo put them on. His fingers felt warm again. He made a big snowball. He made another one. He stacked them up tall. Mr. Thompson smiled. "Nice snowman, Leo."

Leo waved his mittened hands. "Snow day!" he said.

Theodore sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. He wanted to see the sun. "The sun is hiding," he said. "The clouds are in the way," said the driver. The big gray clouds covered the sky. Theodore waited. He watched the clouds. One cloud moved slowly. Then the sun peeked out. "The sun came out from behind the clouds!" said Theodore. The light was warm on his face.

Then the clouds came back. The sun hid again. "Where did it go?" asked Theodore. He thought about it. The clouds could hide the sun. Then the clouds moved. The sun came back. It was like hide and seek.

The driver said, "It might rain soon. It is windy too." The trees bent and waved. Soon little drops hit the window. Tap, tap, tap. Theodore saw people with umbrellas. One kid wore red rain boots. "I have boots too," said Theodore. He got sleepy watching the rain. The car drove home. His dad took him out and hugged him tight. "Warm and dry," said Dad.

Andrew went to the park with his dad. The wind began to blow. It blew hard. Dust flew up in the air.

Andrew blinked and blinked. "Dad, my eyes blink at the dust!" he said.

"Dust went toward your eyes," said Dad. "Your eyelashes stopped it. Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes."

Andrew touched his little eyelashes. Soft, like tiny feathers. He looked at Miley on the swing. Her eyelashes were soft too. He heard her laugh, loud and happy. He smelled the grass. He touched the cool slide. At snack time, he tasted a sweet apple.

Then Andrew asked, "Do eyelashes work every day?" Dad said, "Yes, every day."

Andrew blinked one more time. "Good," he said. "My eyes are safe."

Sebastian went to the store with his dad. He wore his shoes with laces. His dad had to tie them first. "Big knots for big shoes," said Dad.

Sebastian wanted cold milk. He walked fast down one aisle. Then he walked slow down the next aisle. He saw a big cart and a small basket. He picked the small basket. "Good choice," said Dad.

At the milk case, the door was open. The cold air came out. A man put his hand near it. "Open and closed are opposites," the man said. "Like a door that is open or shut." Sebastian pushed the door shut. It clicked. He pulled it open. He got the milk. He pushed it shut again. "I closed it," said Sebastian.

At the hot food counter, a lady used long gloves. She did not touch the hot pans. The steam went up. Sebastian stayed back with Dad. They bought milk, bread and a lemon. Dad said lemons taste sour. Sebastian made a funny face just thinking about it.

On the way out, Sebastian saw a toy elephant. It was gray and soft. "Big elephant," said Sebastian. He waved to it. "Bye, elephant," he said. The doors slid open. Then the doors slid closed.

Samuel stood by the hotel pool. He wanted to get out of the water. He grabbed the smooth edge. He pulled and pulled. His arms slipped. His tummy splashed back down.

"I can't get out," Samuel said. His dad was standing close by the pool. "Try the ladder," his dad said. He pointed to the metal steps in the corner.

Samuel marched through the shallow water. His friend Colton was already climbing the ladder. Samuel watched Colton put his feet on the metal rungs. Colton held the rails and stepped up, up, up, and out.

Samuel put his foot on the bottom rung. He held both rails. He stepped up, one foot, then the other. Soon he was out of the pool. "That was easy," Samuel said. Colton handed him a warm towel.

Later, Samuel got sleepy on the big chair by the pool. He watched the water shine. His dad sat right beside him. Samuel closed his eyes and fell asleep.

Grandpa had a jar of buttons. Elijah wanted to choose ten buttons for a picture. He sat at the big table. Grandpa helped him pour some out.

Elijah made a long row. The buttons spread out far. Then Grandpa made a second row. His buttons were pushed close together in a bunch. Elijah pointed at his row. "Mine has more. Mine is huge and long."

"Let's count them," Grandpa said. Elijah touched each button. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." His row had nine. Then Grandpa's row. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Grandpa's row had nine too.

"Same," Elijah said. He pushed his row close. He spread it out again. He counted once more. Still nine. Elijah looked out at a cloud in the window. Then he made both rows into one big bunch. "Now let's count all of them," he said.

Lena was at Timothee's birthday party. A big red train sat on the rug. Lena wanted to push it right away.

Timothee was holding the train. Lena reached out her hand. Then she put her hands in her lap instead. She watched Timothee push the train far across the rug.

"Can I have a turn?" Lena asked. "Yes, when I stop at the station," said Timothee. The train chugged back. Timothee gave it to Lena. "This is sharing," he said. "You use it too."

Lena pushed the train. It went under the table and back. Timothee waited with his hands in his lap, just like she had done.

At lunch they ate sandwiches. After lunch, Lena skipped to the rug. She held out the train to Timothee. "Your turn now," she said.

Athena sat on the rug at school. Her teddy bear, Boo, lay in her lap. Boo had a sad face. "Boo is sick," Athena told Andie.

Andie looked at Boo. "Boo needs medicine," she said. Athena held a small cup to Boo's mouth. She tipped it slowly. "One sip," she whispered. "Good teddy." Belle ran over with a spotted blanket. "Blankets help sick bears," she said.

Athena wrapped Boo up. She patted his head. Then she made a little bed from blocks. She laid Boo down on the blanket. "Shh," said Athena. "Boo is sleeping." The girls tiptoed around the bed.

Mr. Nowak peeked at Boo. "How is the bear?" he asked. Athena put her finger to her lips. "Sleeping," she whispered. Mr. Nowak nodded and tiptoed too. Boo stayed very still under the spotted blanket. "He will be all better soon," said Athena. Andie smiled and tucked the blanket in tight.

Norah ran to the snack table at summer camp. Her hands looked clean. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said.

Addilyn shook her head. "Mine aren't dirty either," she said. "But we still wash them. Come on."

Ms. Cho turned on the water. She put soap on Norah's hands. "Wash while we count to twenty," she said. Norah rubbed and counted. The bubbles grew big and low on her fingers. One, two, three. Madina counted too. "Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!" Then they all sang the rest. "Twenty!"

The water took the bubbles away. Norah dried her hands on a soft towel. Then she sat down with her soup and crackers.

"Next time I wash after the toilet too," Norah said. Madina grinned. "Me too. Twenty whole seconds." Norah took a big bite of her cracker and smiled.

Muhammad was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to draw a picture of the sky. He looked in the crayon box. He found a crayon that was dark like the night. "Is this blue?" he asked. His cousin Aira shook her head. "That is not blue," she said. "Blue is like the sky."

Muhammad held the crayon up to the window. The sky was lighter. His crayon was darker. He began to cry a little. His lips went tight. "I want blue," he said.

Grandpa came over with a smile. He put three crayons in a row. One was light like the sky. One was in the middle. One was dark like the night. "Look," said Aira. "This one is light blue. And yours is dark blue." Muhammad smiled big. He lined up all the blues from lightest to darkest. Then he drew the whole sky, and the night sky too.

Violet ran to the bathroom at Grandma's house. She used the toilet. Then she ran out fast to play with her toy sheep.

Grandpa was coming in. He used the toilet too. Then he went to the sink. He put soap on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed. Violet stopped and watched. Bubbles grew on his hands. He counted slowly, "One, two, three," all the way to twenty. Then he rinsed the bubbles away. The water took the bubbles down the drain.

Violet looked at her own hands. She went back to the bathroom. She pushed the door shut. She reached up on her tiptoes. She put soap on her hands. She rubbed them together. Big bubbles came. She counted to twenty with Grandpa. Then she rinsed all the soap off. Her hands were clean and shiny.

Soon it was lunchtime. Violet sat at the little table. Grandma gave her a warm bowl of soup. Violet ate it all up. Her tummy felt full. She hugged her toy sheep tight. Grandpa smiled at her clean hands. "Big girl," he said. Violet held her hands up high to show him.

Romy sat in her car seat. Her friend Eddy sat beside her. They were going on a picnic.

Dad put a bag by their feet. "Let's sort the bag," said Romy.

She pulled out a toy plane. That went in the toy pile. Then she pulled out a carrot. She put it with the plane.

"Is a carrot a toy?" asked Eddy.

Romy looked at the carrot. She bit it softly. No, it was not a toy.

She pulled out bread and apples too. She put them all together. "Apple, bread, carrot, food," she said.

Eddy held the toy pile. The car went over a bump. The apples did not spill. "Lucky," said Romy.

Outside the window, a real plane flew up high.

"Look," said Eddy. "Our plane has wings too."

Ella went to the store with her dad. She wanted a big box of cookies. The box sat on the top shelf. It was too high.

"I can't reach," said Ella. "Can we go up?"

Her dad laughed. "Watch this." He pushed a button. A big stair moved up, all by itself. Ella held his hand and rode it up, up, up.

Leena and her mom were there too. Leena giggled. "We went up the stairs!"

"Now we go down!" said Ella. They stepped on the other stair. It carried them down, down, down.

"Up and down are opposites," said Leena.

"Yes!" said Ella. "Up goes this way. Down goes that way!"

Then Ella smelled something warm. The baker was stirring a big pot of soup. He let Ella watch from far away. "It's hot," he said. "This pot is hot, not cold."

"Can I stir?" asked Ella.

"No, little one. Hot pots are not for little hands. But you can smell it!"

Ella sniffed. "Mmm! Hot soup smells so good."

After the store, they stopped at the playground. Ella climbed up the ladder. Then she slid down the slide, fast. A little boy slid down slow, like a sleepy snail.

"What a big day," said her dad.

"Up, down, up, down!" sang Ella, climbing again.

Jackson ran to the park with his blue bag. He wanted to play house with May. But May was not there yet. Jackson sat on the bench and waited.

Then May came with her teddy bear. "The teddy is sick," said May. Jackson peeked into his bag. He took out a furry sock. "This can be his blanket," he said. May smiled. Jackson patted the teddy's head. "Drink your milk," he said. He held up a leaf like a cup. There was no real milk. There was no real blanket. But they acted as if they were real. The teddy got "better" right away.

Mr. Reddy walked by with his dog. "Is the teddy okay now?" he asked. "Yes," said May. "Jackson is the daddy. I am the doctor." Mr. Reddy gave them two shiny coins as pretend money. Jackson put the coins in his blue bag. "Time to buy pretend bread," he said. "The store is by the slide."

Grandma had big jars of paint. Olivia wanted to paint so much. But Grandma said, "Wait. You have a new shirt today." Olivia looked at her new shirt. It was yellow and clean.

Grandma held up an old shirt. "This old shirt keeps paint off your clothes," she said. Olivia put it on. It was big and soft. Her new shirt stayed clean underneath.

Olivia opened the red jar. She made a red dot. She opened the blue jar. She made a blue dot. Then she mixed them with her brush. "Look!" she said. The paint turned purple, like a plum.

Grandma smiled. Olivia mixed yellow and blue. That paint turned green, like the grass. She mixed red and yellow. That one turned orange, like a carrot.

It was getting late. Soon it would be time to sleep. Grandma said the paint had to dry. "We will look early tomorrow," she said. Olivia washed her hands. She took off the old shirt. Her new shirt was still clean. She hung the old shirt on the hook. "See you tomorrow, purple dot," she said.

Gianna stood at the hotel pool in her short swimming suit. Her friend Simeon was already splashing. "Come in!" he called. Gianna wanted to jump in so much. She looked around. Ms. Nkosi was not there yet. Gianna stopped at the edge. She had learned one big rule. A grown-up must always watch children in the water.

She sat down and waited. Her toes reached the cool water. Simeon made a big splash. "You look like a little mountain sitting there," he said. Gianna laughed. "Why do I have to wait?" she asked herself. Then Ms. Nkosi walked out with a whistle. "I am watching now," said Ms. Nkosi. "Jump when you are ready!"

Now a grown-up was watching. Giana held her nose. She jumped! Plop! The water went everywhere. Simeon clapped. "That was the biggest splash," he said. "Bigger than a mountain!" Gianna blew bubbles in the water. "Now I know," she said. "I swim when Ms. Nkosi watches." She kicked her legs and zoomed like a little fish.

Ellie sat on a little chair at the campsite. Dad handed her warm toast. He gave her a small knife with butter. Ellie painted the butter on the toast. Slow, slow strokes. The butter made the bread shiny. She took a bite. It was good toast.

Next to the toast was a big milk carton. Ellie lifted it with two hands. It was too big. Milk sloshed near the edge. Her cup stayed empty and her face felt sad. Dad saw the big spill waiting to happen. "Let's try this," he said. He poured some milk into a little jug.

The little jug was light. Ellie tipped it over her cup. Milk poured out, smooth and slow. Not one drop spilled. She drank it all and smiled. "More milk, please," said Ellie. She picked up the little jug again.

Brielle wanted the red truck. Callum had the red truck. Brielle reached out her hand. She wanted to grab it. She stopped her hand. She sat on the rug instead. She looked at the truck. She looked at her shoes.

Then Callum drove the truck to her. "Here," he said. "Your turn." Brielle held the truck. It was big and red. She pushed it across the rug. Vroom!

Brielle remembered something. When a friend shares, you say thank you. She turned to Callum. "Thank you," she said. Callum smiled a big smile. He patted the truck.

Ms. Nasser called from the other room. "Snack time!" The children were hungry. Brielle drove the truck back to Callum first. Then she ran to the snack table with him.

Harper wanted to bake cookies with Dad. She asked, "Can we bake now?"

"Not now," said Dad. "We will bake later."

Harper frowned. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"No, not yet," said Dad.

Harper followed Dad to the laundry room. He put a shirt in the washer. Then he put a towel in. "One shirt, one towel," he said.

"Is it later yet?" asked Harper.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Harper waited. She counted the socks. "One sock, two socks, three socks."

The washer went swish, swish. Then it stopped.

"Now is it later?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Yes! Now it is later."

They washed their hands. Harper helped pour the sugar. She was careful and stood back from the hot oven. Dad put the cookies in.

"One cookie, two cookies, three cookies," said Harper.

"Tomorrow we can bake more," said Dad.

"Tomorrow!" said Harper. "I love tomorrow."

Isaiah was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa was making soup. The pot was big and heavy. Grandpa lifted it himself.

Auntie came in with bread. She smiled at Isaiah. "Bon appétit!" she said.

Isaiah tilted his head. "What does that mean?"

Grandpa sat down. "In France, people often say 'bon appétit' before a meal. It means they wish everyone a good meal. Try it!"

Isaiah stood up tall. He took a big breath. "Bon appétit!" he said.

Auntie clapped her hands. Grandpa laughed a happy laugh. Isaiah's words had made them smile!

Isaiah said it again. "Bon appétit! Bon appétit!"

"Now let us share the bread," said Grandpa. He tore off a soft piece for each child at the table. Isaiah munched his bread. Everyone was smiling.

Isaiah looked around the table. His words had done that. He said it one more time, nice and loud.

"Bon appétit!"

Penelope went to the library with her dad. It was quiet inside. She wanted a book about trucks. She could not find one on the shelf.

Penelope walked to the desk. Mr. Leung was there. "Please," she said, "can you help me find a truck book?" Mr. Leung smiled. "Yes, I can help," he said. He bent down. He found a big blue truck book. "Thank you," said Penelope.

"You're welcome," said Mr. Leung. Penelope heard that. It was a new thing to say.

Then Caden came in. He dropped his crayon on the floor. Penelope picked it up. She gave it back. "Thank you," said Caden.

Penelope knew just what to say now. "You're welcome," she said. Caden gave her a little hug. Then they sat together in the quiet room. Penelope opened her truck book. "I hope it has a big digger," she said.

Ezra sat at the dinner table. His carrots made a little pile. His cup sat next to his sheep cup, the one with the dirty face on it from breakfast.

Ezra pushed a carrot with his spoon. He counted it. "One." He pushed another. "Two." He kept going. "Three, four, five." He peeked at his dad. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Ten carrots!"

"That is a lot of carrots," said Dad. "You could share some."

Ezra wanted to eat them all. But he wanted something else too. He wanted to play rocket ship. "Dad, can we play rocket ship after dinner?"

Dad smiled. "Yes. But first, the carrots."

Ezra ate them one by one. He counted down as he ate. "Ten, nine, eight." He chewed. "Seven, six, five." He drank from his sheep cup. "Four, three, two, one." The plate was empty.

He jumped up. "Blast off!"

Dad laughed. "That was a countdown! You counted backward from ten down to one."

"A countdown," said Ezra. He said it again. "A countdown." He ran to the couch and sat like a rocket. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" He popped up so high his socks slid on the floor.

Then the doorbell rang. It was Micah, holding a toy rocket of his own.

Micah sat down next to Ezra. "I want to blast off too," he said.

"Then you need a countdown," said Ezra. "We count backward from ten."

They sat side by side. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" They jumped up together, and Micah's rocket flew over their heads.

Eli ran to the little playhouse in the backyard. Kayla was already there. "We can cook lunch," she said. Eli put a toy pot on the toy stove. It was just pretend. He stirred it with a big spoon. The spoon went clack, clack, clack. Kayla fed her baby doll. The doll had soft arms and a small hug-ready body.

They played a long time. Then the sun went low. "Time to go home," called the dad from the door. Eli looked at the playhouse. The pot was on the floor. The cups were on the grass. The baby doll lay under the chair.

"Wait," said Eli. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." Kayla smiled. They picked up the cups. Eli put the pot back on the shelf. Kayla tucked the baby in. Then Eli ran home, waving his hand all the way.

Rehmat woke up early on Saturday. Her dad was in the garage, and she went out to see him. The garage was cold. Rehmat shivered in her little coat. Her dad was busy with his toolbox, so she tried to zip her coat by herself. She found the zipper tab. She held it and pulled it up. The coat closed! She was warm now.

Then her dad turned on the big heater. Soon the garage felt like summer. Rehmat got too warm. "My coat is hot," she said. She held the tab again and pulled it down. The coat opened! Cool air came in. Danielle, her friend from next door, peeked in the door. "You did it all by yourself," Danielle said. "Pulling the tab down opens it," said Rehmat. She smiled and pulled the tab up, then down, one more time, just to watch it happen.

Mateo was at home. He set out his purple blocks. His friend Hasrat came to play. Hasrat sat down fast. His mouth turned down. His eyebrows went low. Mateo looked at Hasrat's face. "Are you sad?" Mateo asked. Hasrat nodded. "My kite got a hole," he said. Mateo ran to his toy box. He took out his red kite. He put it in Hasrat's hands. Hasrat's mouth turned up. His eyes got big and bright. "A kite!" Hasrat said. "Now I feel happy!" They went to the garden to play. They ran in the soft green grass. Then the wind blew hard. Both kites went up, up, up. Hasrat laughed. But the red kite flew over the little pond. It landed in the water. Mateo looked at Hasrat's face again. Hasrat was laughing still. So Mateo laughed too. The dad waded in and got the kite. It dripped and dripped. "It wanted to swim," said Hasrat.

Nolan sat in a big chair. He was near the fish tank. He waited with his dad.

Nolan was going to see a doctor. He knew doctors. They looked at your ears. They looked at your tummy too.

A door opened. A man smiled. "Hi, I am Mr. Ortiz," he said. "I am the dentist."

Nolan looked up. "What does a dentist do?" he asked.

"A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth," said Mr. Ortiz.

Nolan opened his mouth wide. He wanted the dentist to see his teeth. But Mr. Ortiz did not look at ears. He did not look at tummies. He only looked at teeth. Nolan counted them out loud.

The fish swam near the glass. Nolan watched them. Mr. Ortiz said, "Your teeth look great."

"I teach my teeth to be clean," said Nolan. "I brush them every day."

"That is a good job," said Mr. Ortiz. He gave Nolan a sticker.

On the way out, Nolan held the sticker up high. "Next time, teeth only," he said. "No tummy checks!"

Ibrahim wanted to go on the slide. It was his own slide in the backyard. Dad was cooking pizza on the grill. "Stay where I can see you," said Dad. Ibrahim stayed close.

Ibrahim climbed up the ladder. It was tall for him. He got to the top. He lay down on his tummy. His head was at the top of the slide. He started to slide head first. "Wait," said Dad. Dad came over fast. "Turn around, little one." Dad helped him turn. Now his feet were at the top. "Feet first," said Dad. Ibrahim went down the slide feet first. Whee! It was fast and fun.

Ibrahim ran back to the ladder. He climbed up again. He turned himself around all alone. Feet first, down he went. He did it again and again. Then Dad called, "Pizza time!" The cheese was hot, so Dad cut it and waited. Soon the pizza was warm. Ibrahim sat next to Dad and took a big bite. He looked at the slide and smiled.

Sofia sat in the backyard with her markers. She was making a card for her mom. It had a big red heart on it. Her friend Yana sat next to her.

"I will draw a sun too," said Sofia.

She grabbed a yellow marker. She held her paper on her hand. Then she drew fast. Oh no! The yellow line went right onto her hand!

Yana looked at her hand. Sofia looked at her hand. Now she had a yellow sun on her skin.

"I am afraid it will stay forever," said Sofia. "Mom will see it. It looks like a big yellow mistake!"

Yana jumped up. "Let's show Ms. Kapoor! She is watering her flowers."

They ran to the fence. Sofia held up her hand. "Look! I drew on myself!"

Ms. Kapoor smiled. "Come here, Sofia. Washable markers wash off skin with soap and water."

Sofia ran to the garden tap. Ms. Kapoor helped her. They used the soap. They splashed the water. Sofia rubbed her hand.

The yellow sun began to fade. Then it was gone! Her hand was clean.

Sofia gasped. "It went away!"

She ran back to her card. She made the sun on the paper this time. Then she drew a secret flower on it too, just for Mom.

"Sofia!" called Yana. "Can I draw a rainbow?"

"Yes!" said Sofia. "But keep it on the paper. Or we will wash again!"

Arthur was going to the beach. He sat in his car seat. He held his cup of juice. "Are we there yet?" he asked.

The car stopped. Dad made a funny face. "Oh no," said Dad. "I think we took a wrong turn." The road was small and bumpy. There were no waves anywhere.

Mom opened a big paper map. "The map shows roads and places," she said. Arthur leaned over to look. The map had lines everywhere. There was a little blue sea on it! "Beach! Beach!" said Arthur, pointing.

Mom put her finger on the little blue sea. Then she followed a line with her finger. "This road goes to the beach," she said. Dad turned the car around. Soon the road got big and smooth.

Arthur saw the water. The beach smelled a little smelly, like fish and salt. "The map found the way!" said Arthur. He ran to the sand and dug with his shovel.

Mackenzie stood at the bus stop with her dad. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," she said. She took off her hat.

Then the wind came. It blew her hat away. "Windy!" she cried. Her hat landed on the bench. A lady picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," said Mackenzie.

Then the sky turned grey. Rain fell. Pop, pop, pop on the roof. Dad opened a big umbrella. Mackenzie stood under it. Her shoes stayed dry.

The next day, snow fell at the bus stop. Snowflakes landed on Mackenzie's nose. Poppy was there too. Poppy made a snowball. She patted it with bare hands. "My hands are cold," Poppy said. She looked upset.

Mackenzie had red mittens. She patted a snowball too. Her hands stayed warm. "Look, mittens!" she said. She held out one mitten. "You wear this one."

Poppy put it on her hand. She made another snowball. "My hand is warm now," said Poppy. "Yay!"

A little snake of steam rose from a cup in Dad's hand. He held it up high, away from the girls. "Warm hands and a warm drink," said Dad. "Snowy days are good days."

Lily sat on the library rug. Big letter cards were spread all around her. Ms. Adebayo had asked the class to put them in a line.

Lily picked up the M card. Where did it go? She looked and looked. Sehaj held the A. Giovanni held the B. The line grew longer and longer. But Lily could not see where M belonged.

Then she had an idea. She began to sing, very soft. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She tapped a card for each letter she sang. When she sang L, her finger landed on the L card. M came next in the song! She put her card down, straight and neat, right after L.

"Look, Ms. Adebayo," she said. "The song shows me where M goes!"

Ms. Adebayo smiled. "Try the next one," she said.

Lily picked up the Q card. She sang all the way from A again, and her finger climbed from card to card. P! Q sat right after P.

"Where was Q hiding all this time?" Lily wondered, and she laughed.

Jules sat in a big blue chair. He waited with his dad in the salon waiting room. There was a fish tank up high on a shelf. "One fish, two fish, three fish," said Jules. His hair was long and his dad said it was time for a haircut. But Jules did not want one. "Scissors might hurt me," he whispered. His dad held his hand. "The hair cutter will tell you all about it," he said.

Soon a grown-up called, "Jules!" Jules climbed into the tall chair. It went up high, like a dream ride. The hair cutter picked up the scissors. Snip, snip. Jules shut his eyes tight. Then he opened one eye. "Did it hurt?" he asked. "Not one bit," said the hair cutter. "Cutting hair does not hurt." Jules felt his head. Nothing hurt at all.

"More, more!" said Jules. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little pieces of hair fell down, soft as feathers. "One snip, two snips, three snips," Jules counted. Then the chair went down low. Jules looked in the mirror. He saw a big smile and short hair. "I want to tell Boden about this," he said. His dad laughed. Jules waved to the three fish on his way out.

Benjamin put on his shoes. He liked to wear the blue ones. Then he walked down the street with his dad. They walked slow, because the library was close.

In the library, Benjamin saw books. One, two, three big shelves. On the top shelf was a book about trains. Benjamin wanted that book very much. But the shelf was too high. He could not reach it.

Then he saw his friend Megane. She held a puppet. Constance came over too. Constance reached for the puppet. Megane pulled it away. Then Constance said, "May I have a turn?" Megane smiled. She said, "Yes, you may." She gave Constance the puppet.

Benjamin watched. He had a question. Would that work for him too? He walked to Ms. Grant, the librarian. He said, "May I have the train book, please?" Ms. Grant smiled too. She reached up, up, up. She put the train book in his hands.

"Thank you," said Benjamin. He sat down on a soft rug. He turned page one, then page two, then page three. The train went choo, choo.

"Read it again?" he asked his dad.

"Yes," said his dad. "We can read it two more times."

It was a rainy day at daycare. Elias looked out the big window. Drops went tap, tap, tap on the glass. "Rainy days mean puddles," said Mr. Wong. "Puddle day, puddle day!" Elias sang.

Elias put on his rain boots. They were red and they went squish, squish when he walked. His friend Gurnawab wore sneakers. "Look at the big puddle!" said Gurnawab. He jumped in. Splash! Elias jumped in too. Squelch went the water, cold and brown.

Gurnawab made a sad face. "My socks are all wet," he said. "My feet are dry," said Elias. He wiggled his toes in his red boots. One dry foot, two dry feet. Gurnawab looked down at the puddle, then at the boots, then at the puddle again.

"Mr. Wong!" Gurnawab called. "Can I wear rain boots too?" Mr. Wong laughed and went to the cubbies. He found blue boots with yellow ducks on them. Gurnawab pulled them on fast. Then both boys ran outside. Splash, splash, splash went the puddles.

Elizabeth sat at the dinner table. She wiggled her toes under her chair. One foot had a red sock. The other foot was bare! "Where is my other sock?" she said. Daddy set down a pot of warm soup. It smelled like tomatoes.

Elizabeth peeked under the table. She saw a spoon, one shoe, and a dust ball. No sock. Then she felt something on her bare foot. It was soft and small. "A sock!" she said. She pulled it on. Now she had two red socks. "Look, Daddy. A pair!" Daddy smiled. "That's right. A pair means two, like a pair of socks."

Elizabeth counted her socks out loud. "One, two." She picked up her spoon and counted peas. "One, two, three, four, five." She ate two. Three were left. The cat, her pet, jumped on a chair. Did the cat want peas too? Elizabeth laughed. Then she counted her toes, wiggling each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten toes, all warm in socks. "Is that true, Daddy? Ten toes?" Daddy nodded and slurped his soup. Elizabeth grinned at her two red feet.

Matthew ran into the music room. Mr. Munro was holding his drum. "Today we learn a song!" said Mr. Munro. "And we clap the beat!"

Mr. Munro tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Matthew clapped along. His friend Edmund clapped too. Krew clapped fast. "Too fast," said Mr. Munro with a smile. "Keep it steady, like walking." Tap, tap, tap. Krew slowed down. Now all the boys clapped the same.

Then they sang. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," they sang. Matthew knew that part. Then came the next line. Matthew forgot the word. He stood alone in the middle of the rug. He wanted that word so much!

He thought hard. Star. What sounds like star? "Car!" he said. Edmund laughed. "No, it's jar!" said Krew. "Jar rhymes with star!" said Mr. Munro. "Jar and star end the same." Matthew clapped his hands. He tried again. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are." That was it!

They sang it three more times. Matthew did not stop. He clapped the beat and sang every word. "Again!" he shouted. Mr. Munro tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. "One more time, big and loud!"

Billie sat at the dinner table with her family. Her dad put a bowl of peas on the table. Billie wanted some peas. She reached far, far over. The bowl tipped. Peas went everywhere. Some peas fell on the floor.

"Sorry, Dad," said Billie. "Can you help me?" Dad helped. He picked up the peas. He did not throw them. He put them in a little dish for the birds. Then Billie said, "Peas, please." Dad gave her some. "Thank you," said Billie. "Thank you," said Dad.

Then the doorbell rang. Ding, dong. It was Ms. Taylor from next door. She was holding a smelly cheese pie. Billie hid behind her chair. Then she peeked out. She asked herself, "What makes Ms. Taylor smile?" She tried it. "Hello, Ms. Taylor," said Billie. Ms. Taylor smiled a big smile. "Hello, Billie," said Ms. Taylor. "Hello, Billie," said Billie again. The pie came to the table, and the family ate.

Mila looked out the big window. The sun was gone. The sky was gray. The trees bent and swayed. The leaves flew around the yard.

"It is windy today," said Mom. "Wear your warm hat."

Mila put on her red hat. She zipped up her coat. Then she ran outside to play. The wind whooshed past her ears. A bird held tight to its branch. Its feathers puffed up in the wind.

Then the wind gave a big push. Mila's red hat flew right off her head. It tumbled over the grass. Mila chased it. The hat rolled and rolled. She felt upset. "Come back, hat!" she called.

Mom came out with a smile. "A strong wind can blow a hat right off your head," she said. She caught the hat near the fence. She put it back on Mila's head. This time she tied the strap under Mila's chin.

The wind blew again. But the hat stayed on. Mila laughed. The wind was strong, but the strap was stronger.

"Good hat," said Mila. She patted it with her mitten.

Margot ran to the sandbox. She saw the big red truck. She wanted it so much.

Gustave had the truck first. He filled it with sand. Margot waited. She watched him pour. Then Gustave said, "Your turn now." Margot smiled. She pushed the truck. The wheels went bump, bump, bump. Gustave sat and waited too. He hummed a little song while he waited.

Then Miriam called, "Snack time!" Everyone ran to the bench. The truck stayed in the sand. The buckets stayed out too. The sandbox looked messy.

Margot looked back. She saw Mr. Russo standing by the toy box. He did not say anything. He just looked at the sand too. Margot walked back. She picked up the red truck. She put it in the box. Gustave came back and got the buckets. Miriam carried the little shovels. Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with.

One shovel had yucky wet sand on it. Margot had to bend down low to reach it. She wiped it with her hand and dropped it in the box. Mr. Russo gave her a big thumbs up.

"Now we all get crackers," said Miriam.

"Two for me," said Margot. She held up two fingers and grinned.

Zoey sat on the playroom floor with a big sheet of paper. She wanted to make a sailboat. The boat needed two triangle sails. But her paper was a square. "How can a square become triangles?" she wondered. She knocked on the door frame to call Mr. Somsak. He came in and held the paper up high. "I need two triangles," said Zoey. Mr. Somsak took the safety scissors. "Watch," he said. He cut from one corner to the opposite corner. Snip, all the way across. The square fell open in his hands. Now there were two pieces. Each piece had three sides. "Triangles!" said Zoey. She clapped her hands. "Can I see them touch?" She put the two triangles side by side on the rug. Together they made the square again. She slid one away, and there were two sails, one for each side of her boat. Zoey taped them onto a paper boat. Then she placed a round apple beside it for the captain's snack. "Which shape is the apple?" she asked herself. She looked and looked. Round like a ball. A circle. She picked up the triangle sails. "Where do you want to go, boat?" she asked. The boat did not answer. So Zoey pushed it fast across the rug, all the way to the toy box.

Lennon ran onto the big green field. The grass tickled her shoes. It was soccer day. Mr. Becker blew his whistle, and Lennon chased the ball with her friends Penelope and Kyler.

After practice, Mr. Becker set up a tee. "Now we try batting," he said. Kyler ran to the tee first. He picked up the bat. The sun was warm and the ball was bright white.

Mr. Becker called, "Wait, Kyler! You need your helmet." Kyler stopped. Mr. Becker set a blue helmet on Kyler's head. It covered Kyler's head all around. "Now you can bat," said Mr. Becker. Kyler swung the bat. Tock! The ball went wild and far.

Then it was Lennon's turn. She started to run to the tee. She remembered Kyler. Lennon stopped and pointed to the helmet. Mr. Becker smiled. He set the yellow helmet on her head. It felt smooth and snug. Lennon held the bat tight. She swung. Tock! The ball rolled across the soft, warm grass. "Yay, Lennon!" cried Penelope, clapping her hands.

Leah skipped to the salon with her mom. Today was her very first haircut! She could not wait.

Inside, the big chair was tall. Leah climbed in, but she slid down. She was too short. "I cannot reach your hair," the hairdresser said. Then she brought a booster seat. "Small children sit on this," she said. Leah sat on the booster seat. Now her head was up high. The hairdresser could reach every bit of her hair.

Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Leah watched a little piece fall. The piece floated down like a wing. When it was done, Leah looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat. She smiled all alone in the big mirror. "Look at me!" she said. "I look so big now!" Her mom clapped, and Leah bounced out the door.

Florence had big news today. A rabbit was coming home with her! She held the cage tight in the car. "Hello, rabbit," she said. The rabbit had one floppy ear.

At home, Florence put hay in the cage. She petted the rabbit's soft back. Then she heard the snack bell. Cookies! Florence ran to the snack table.

Her mom held up a hand. "Wash your hands first," she said. Florence looked at her hands. They had rabbit fur on them. "Okay," said Florence. She washed her hands with soap. The water was warm. Her mom had turned it on for her.

Then Florence ate her cookie. "Yum!" she said. After the cookie, she went back to the rabbit. "Pet, then wash," said Florence. The rabbit wiggled its ear. Florence laughed and laughed.

Joseph wanted to draw a chicken. But his crayons were all gone. Mom showed him the tablet on the table.

"Push the round button," said Mom. Joseph pushed it. The screen lit up white. "Now tap the little paint box," said Mom. Joseph tapped it. The drawing app opened.

Joseph put his finger on the screen. He moved his finger across the screen. A line appeared! A long, squiggly line. Joseph gasped. He moved his finger again. Another line, this time green. He moved his finger round and round. The squiggly line looked like a snake. "A snake!" Joseph shouted. He gave the snake a yellow head and two small eyes.

Then Joseph drew his chicken. The chicken had a white body and red legs. "Tap the little X now," said Mom. Joseph tapped it. He put the tablet in the basket, all by himself. "I can do it," said Joseph. "Show me again tomorrow!"

text:
Daniel had a little red guitar. He loved to strum it. Plink, plunk, plink. "That sounds funny," said Daniel. His friend Ismael was visiting. "It sounds like a duck with hiccups," said Ismael. They both laughed.

Daniel showed Ismael the strings. "One, two, three, four, five, six," they counted together. Six strings. Daniel strummed each one. Plink, plunk, plonk. Each string sounded different.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya lived next door. She came over with her umbrella, because it had started to rain. "Can you help?" asked Daniel. She turned the little pegs at the top, one by one. Plink went up. Plonk went smooth. "There," she said. "Now it is tuned. The notes sound right."

Daniel strummed a big chord. It sounded clean and sweet, like ice sliding into a cup. Ismael clapped. Daniel strummed again. "Play it one more time!" said Ismael.

Elliot liked the singing time at daycare. Ms. Munro sang, "One, two, three, four, five." Everyone held up fingers. Elliot held up five fingers too.

Then Elliot saw a door. It had a 5 on it. He stopped. "What does that mean?" he asked. Maisie came to look. "That 5 is the same as five," she said. "Like this." She held up five fingers.

Elliot looked at his fingers. He looked at the door. The 5 was five! He counted his fingers again. "One, two, three, four, five." The same.

After singing, Elliot brushed his hands on his pants. He heard a soft sound at the door. Jonas was knocking five times. "Knock, knock, one, two, three, four, five!" said Jonas.

Elliot laughed. "Five knocks for the door with five!" he said. He knocked five times too.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Ava ran to her at the gate. "Come see my backyard!" said Ava. The sun was bright. Grandma smelled the mint and the basil. "Can we make your special bread?" Ava asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "My mother taught me. Now I will teach you." They washed their hands. Ava poured flour into the big bowl. Grandma added water and yeast. Ava mixed and mixed. Then they set the bowl by the sunny window. "Watch it," said Grandma. Ava peeked in. The dough was bigger! "What made it grow?" asked Ava. "The little yeast made it puff up," said Grandma. Ava clapped her hands. They went out to the backyard and picked two basil leaves. Ava pushed the leaves into the dough. "Now it is our bread," said Ava. "You and me." Grandma smiled big. The oven was hot, so Grandma put the bread in all by herself. Ava waited by the window. Soon the whole house smelled warm and good. "Ding!" went the timer. Grandma set the bright golden loaf on the table. Ava tore off a piece and took a big bite. "Mmm," said Ava. "We made this together. Can we make it again tomorrow?" Grandma laughed. "Every day this week," she said.

Sofia stood at the edge of the lake. The water went splash, splash at her toes. Today she would learn to swim.

A tall chair sat by the water. A person sat up on the very top. "Who is that?" Sofia asked her dad. "That is the lifeguard," said a girl named Rylee. "A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it." Sofia looked up. The lifeguard could see everyone from up there. She could see the whole huge lake!

Sofia held her dad's hand. She let the water come up to her knees. It was cool and soft. She kicked one foot. The water went splash on Rylee. Rylee laughed. A little yellow flower floated by on a small wave. Sofia kicked again. The flower bobbed away.

Then Sofia slipped. She sat down in the water. Before she could cry, the lifeguard blew a whistle and pointed. Sofia's dad was already lifting her up. "I saw you from my chair," the lifeguard called down with a smile. "Up high, I see everyone."
