Sofia looked at the tall chair. "Can you see a fish too?" she asked. The lifeguard laughed. "Look by your feet," she said. A tiny silver fish swam right past Sofia's toes.

The bookmobile stopped on Myles' street. Myles ran up the steps with his dad. Mr. Mansour smiled and handed him a card. "Your very first library card," he said. Myles held it with both hands.

Myles picked a book about tools. There was a hammer on the cover. He read it in the corner. Then he slid it onto a shelf by the door.

"Wait," said Mr. Mansour. "See that little white label on the spine? That label shows where the book belongs." Myles looked at the letters. He pulled the book out and matched the label to the shelf. It slid right into its spot.

"Did the label do that?" Myles asked. His dad nodded. "It did."

Then the bookmobile began to beep. "Time to go," Mr. Mansour spoke softly. "Take your book home. Bring it back soon."

Myles carried the hammer book down the steps. He held his card up high.

Lily sat at the art table. She wanted to paint a pink flower for Grandma's card. But there was no pink paint.

She looked in the paint cups. She found red. She found blue. She found yellow. She found green. "No pink," said Lily.

Oaklynn sat next to her. "Make a red flower," said Oaklynn. "Grandma likes pink," said Lily. Her voice was quiet.

Then Lily saw the white paint. It sat in a big cup. She dipped her brush in the red. She put red on her paper. Then she stirred in white paint. She mixed it round and round.

The paint turned pink! "Look!" said Lily. "Pink!" said Oaklynn.

Lily painted a big pink flower. She painted green leaves too. Then she added a blue sky.

Mr. Sadeghi came over. "What a pretty card," he said. Lily held it up high. After school, she would skip to the car and give the card to her mom. "This is for Grandma," Lily would say.

Juliette sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. She looked out the window. "One tree," she said. "Two trucks. Three birds!"

Dad sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Juliette clapped her hands. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The numbers danced in her mouth like popcorn. Her tummy felt happy.

At the park, Juliette saw Elaine and Evan. "Let's play hide-and-seek!" said Elaine. "You seek, Juliette. Close your eyes and count." Juliette closed her eyes. "Onetwothreefourfivetensix!" she said, very fast.

"No, no, no!" laughed Evan. "You counted too fast! We did not have time to hide." Juliette giggled. Evan was still standing in the open. He was not hidden at all.

"I will count slowly," said Juliette. She closed her eyes again. "One... two... three..." She heard feet go pitter-patter. "Four... five..." She heard a giggle behind a bush. "Six, seven, eight, nine... ten! Ready or not, here I come!"

She found Evan first, behind the big tree. Then she found Elaine, hiding like a little fox, crouched down low. "You counted slow," said Elaine. "So we could hide!" Juliette laughed so hard her face went sour like a lemon, all squeezed up. "Again, again!" she said. "My turn to hide!"

Victoria had a cold. Her nose was red. Mom said, "We need medicine. Let's go to the pharmacy." Victoria put on her coat. She got to choose her own hat.

At the pharmacy, the shelves were tall. Victoria saw cough syrup. She saw tissues. She saw a little box with a sticker of a mouse on it. "What is in the mouse box?" she asked. Mom said, "A thermometer." The cashier put it in the bag.

At home, Mom took out the thermometer. It was small and smooth. "What does it do?" Victoria asked. "A thermometer is a tool a grown-up uses to check how warm your body is," Mom said. Victoria held very still. Mom slid it under her arm. They waited. Victoria watched. Then it beeped. "All warm, no fever," said Mom. "How lucky." Victoria smiled and hugged the mouse box.

Lucas was in the playroom with Zahra. They were playing house. Zahra was the cook. Lucas was the dad with a teddy bear baby.

"I made soup!" Zahra said. She held out a pot full of pompoms and paper.

Lucas was so hungry for pretend. He opened his mouth wide. He put a pompom right on his tongue.

Zahra jumped up. "Stop! Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth!"

Lucas spat the pompom into his hand. "Can we slurp it instead?" he asked.

"Yes! Slurp it like this," Zahra said. She lifted the pot and made a big slurpy sound. "Sluuurp!"

Lucas slurped the air over the pot. "Sluuurp! This is the best soup ever!"

The teddy bear baby needed food too. Lucas held a pompom near the bear's mouth. He made munching sounds. "Num num num," he said. The bear was safe and happy.

Then the teddy bear got messy. Zahra pretended to wash him with a splash. "Splash, splash!" she said. "All clean."

"My sister does this at home," Zahra said. "She feeds her dolls every day."

"Let's do it again tomorrow," Lucas said. He held the pot up high. "More soup, please!"

Layla stood at the running track with her class. Ms. Brown held a big bag of beanbags. "Today we throw beanbags into hoops," said Ms. Brown. She put a shiny red hoop on the ground, far away.

Layla picked up a beanbag. She threw it. The beanbag landed in the grass, not in the hoop. She tried again. It missed again. Her friend Jayla threw one too. It missed. "This is hard," said Layla. They kept trying. They waited for their turns. They waited for the wind to stop.

Then Ulysse took three little steps forward. He stood closer to the hoop. He threw his beanbag, and it went right in. "My turn," said Layla. She walked closer too, step by step. She threw her beanbag. It landed in the hoop with a soft plop.

After that, Ms. Brown brought out a big ball. "Catch with both hands," she said. Layla held out her arms. The ball bounced off her fingers. She tried again. This time her two hands caught it and hugged it tight.

At lunch time, Layla sat with Jayla on the grass. She had a sandwich in her lunch box. "Want to mix our crackers and berries together?" asked Jayla. "Yes," said Layla. They shared their food and watched the clouds go by. "Tomorrow I want to throw from far away," said Layla, "and then walk closer and closer until I get it in."

Dylan ran onto the big field at the community center. His team wore blue shirts. Mr. Munro blew the whistle.

"Today we play soccer," said Mr. Munro. "One net here. One net there. Kick the ball into the net to score a goal."

Dylan looked at the net. It was huge, with white strings like a spiderweb. How could a ball fit through that? He wondered if it would get stuck.

The game began. Dylan kicked the ball. It went sideways. Camilo kicked it too. Still no goal.

Then Dylan kicked the ball again, harder. The ball rolled and rolled. It went right into the net. The strings moved. The ball sat inside.

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Camilo hugged Dylan. Jonas jumped up and down.

"Did you see that?" Dylan asked. "The ball went in. So that is a goal!"

Dylan kicked the ball again. It went into the net one more time. He counted, "One, two goals!"

He could not wait to write about it with Grandma that night. "A goal is when the ball goes in the net," he would tell her.

Mr. Munro gave out juice. Dylan drank it all. Then he ran back to kick the ball once more.

Luke ran to the park with his dad. Today was a big day! A lady had a box of kittens by the pond.

"Can we take one home?" Luke asked.

"Yes," said his dad. "Just one."

Luke picked a small kitten. It was yellow. "I will call him Sunny," said Luke.

At home, Luke put Sunny on the floor. Sunny ran under a chair. Then Luke had a question.

"Dad, where will Sunny go pee?" he asked.

"Come and see," said his dad.

His dad set down a small box. It was full of soft sand. "This is his litter box," said his dad. Sunny slipped out from under the chair. He sniffed the box. He climbed in. He dug a little hole. Then he used the box as his toilet.

"Wow!" said Luke. He clapped his hands.

Luke sat down to watch. Sunny stepped out. He shook sand off his paws. Little sandy marks went onto the floor. Luke giggled.

Then Luke got a small scoop. He helped his dad clean the box. The sand looked smooth again. Sunny came back and jumped onto Luke's lap.

"Good kitty," said Luke. He stroked Sunny's soft yellow fur. Sunny closed his eyes. Luke asked, "Do you like your new home?" Sunny purred very loud.

Eleanor ran to the kitchen with muddy hands. "Soup time!" she called.

Her dad pointed to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat," he said.

Eleanor looked at her hands. They were brown. "My hands are wearing mud shirts!" she said. Her dad laughed.

She went to the sink. He turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Eleanor rubbed her hands together. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

Back at the table, there was soup and bread. Eleanor dipped the bread in. "Salty!" she said, and made a funny face. "Salty soup, clean hands."

Her dad held up his own hands. "Wash first, eat after," he said, and winked. Eleanor giggled and took another big bite.

Stella sat at the dinner table. She had her spoon in her hand. Dinner was soup and bread.

"I want pancakes," said Stella. "Pancakes, pancakes!"

Mom smiled. "Pancakes are for tomorrow," she said. "We had pancakes yesterday, remember? Now it is dinner time."

"Tomorrow is too far away," said Stella. Her lip went down.

"When is tomorrow?" asked Mom.

Stella thought. "Tomorrow is... now?"

Mom shook her head. "No, now is dinner. Later comes bath time. Then sleep. When we wake up and eat breakfast, that is morning. Morning is tomorrow."

Stella looked at her bowl. The soup had a round carrot shape in it. She poked it with her spoon. "So I sleep first," she said. "Then morning comes?"

"Yes," said Mom. "You sleep, and then morning comes with pancakes."

Dad gave Stella a hug. "Eat your soup now," he said. "Then bath, then bed, then pancakes."

Stella took a big bite. The soup was warm and good.

"Wrong spoon," she said, holding up her fork. She giggled and took her spoon.

She ate all her soup. She ate her bread too.

At bath time, Stella splashed. At bed time, Mom tucked her in.

"Wake up fast, morning," whispered Stella. She closed her eyes.

The sun came in the window. Stella ran to the kitchen. Everyone was at the table.

"Good morning, Stella!" said Mom.

"Morning!" said Stella. There were pancakes on her plate, big and round.

Stella clapped her hands and picked up her fork.

Elliot sat at the little table in the school library. Ms. McKenzie gave him a pencil and some paper.

"Today you will write your name," she said. Elliot was so excited!

He squeezed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The letter E came out wiggly. "Oh no," said Elliot. Ms. McKenzie showed him how to hold it with three fingers, like a bird sitting on a stick. Elliot tried. He made the E again. This time it stood up tall!

Then came the L. Elliot drew it. "Look! Straight lines!" he said. He drew more straight lines. Then came the O. Elliot tried to draw it with straight lines. It looked like a box, not an O. "That is not my O," he said.

Ocean leaned over. "The O is round," she said. Elliot wiped the box away with his toe of his paper towel. He drew a big round curve instead. "O!" he shouted. The library was noisy with kids writing.

Elliot looked at his name. Straight lines and round curves, all together. "Ms. McKenzie! My E and L are straight. My O has curves!"

"Yes," she said with a big smile. "Now write it one more time."

Elliot picked up his pencil like a bird on a stick. E, L, L, I, O, T. "I did it!" he said.

Miles sat at the dinner table. He took a bite of his rice. His dad gave him apple slices too.

"Can I wear my robot shirt to bed?" Miles asked.

"Robot shirts are for the day," said Dad. "You need pajamas for sleeping."

Miles looked down at his shirt. It was not soft like his pajamas. His pajamas had little stars on them. They felt cozy and warm.

"Where are my star pajamas?" Miles asked. "Are they lost?"

"Let's look," said Dad.

First they looked in the drawer. One, two, three shirts. No pajamas. Then they looked under the bed. No pajamas there. Then Miles looked in the laundry basket. His star pajamas were at the bottom!

"I found them!" said Miles. He held them up high.

Dad helped him run a warm bath. Miles washed his toes and his tummy. Then Dad helped him dry off. Miles put on his star pajamas, all by himself. One arm, then the other arm. Snap, snap went the buttons.

Miles climbed into bed. His pajamas were soft and warm. He gave his star pajamas a little pat.

"Good night, stars," said Miles. "Good night, Dad."

"Good night, Miles," said Dad. He turned off the light.

Luca was sleepy after his bath. He took off his shirt and dropped it on the floor. His socks fell next to it. The bathroom floor looked messy.

"Where do dirty clothes go?" Luca asked his dad. His dad pointed to the basket. "In there. Then they can be washed."

Luca picked up his shirt. He dropped it in the basket. Then he made a game. He held a sock like a ball. He aimed at the basket. The sock went in. "Score!" said Luca. The other sock went in too. Now the floor was all clean.

Luca put on his pajamas. He brushed his teeth, listening to the little brush sound. A green leaf was stuck to the towel by the window. He pulled it off and put it in the bin.

The basket was full. "Dad, will my socks be clean tomorrow?" Luca asked. "Yes," said Dad. Luca smiled. He hung his towel on the hook and ran to bed.

Georgia went to the store with Dad. "I want apples!" she said. Dad said, "Yes! You can pick some."

The apples sat in big rows. Georgia put all the red apples in one pile. Then she put all the green apples in another pile. "Look, Dad! Red apples here. Green apples there."

A girl named Amalia came by with her mom. "I sort apples too," said Amalia. She put the big apples in one pile. She put the small apples in another pile. Georgia stared. The same apples, in new piles!

"You sorted by color," said Georgia. "Did you sort by size?"

"Yes! Big ones and small ones," said Amalia.

Georgia laughed. "Apples can go in different piles!" She put one red apple with the big pile. Then she sent a small green apple rolling down the fruit ramp. It rolled and rolled. Dad caught it and smiled. "Apples for the road," he said, and he carried the frozen peas too.

Mason ran fast in the classroom. He wore his blue hat. His arms went out like wings and he pretended to fly.

There was a block tower on the carpet. Charles-Edouard had built it. It was very tall. One, two, three, four blocks.

Mason ran too close. He bumped the tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down. Charles-Edouard looked sad.

Ms. Rowe knelt down. "You can say sorry," she said. Mason looked at his shoes. "Sorry," he said to Charles-Edouard. Charles-Edouard looked up.

"Can I help build it again?" Mason asked. "Yes," said Charles-Edouard. So they stacked the blocks together. One, two, three, four blocks. Then one more on top.

"Now it is taller than my hat," said Mason. Charles-Edouard laughed. Mason felt tired from running, so he sat down to look at the tower.

"Can we build two towers next time?" asked Mason. "Yes," said Charles-Edouard. "Two towers, one for you and one for me."

Ivy sat in the new chair at the doctor's office. She saw a big picture of an ear on the wall. She touched the cool paper on the bed. Then she smelled something funny. "What is that smell?" she asked. "It is my soap," said Ms. Nakamura, the nurse. "Can you smell it with your nose?"

Then a machine by the sink went BEEP, BEEP, BEEP. It was so loud! Ivy wanted to yell. She did not like the loud sound. What could she do?

She put her hands over her ears. The beeping got quiet. How did that happen? She took her hands off. Loud again! She put her hands back on. Quiet again.

Then Ms. Nakamura gave her a sweet drink. Ivy tasted apple. "I like apple," said Ivy. She kept her hands on her ears until the beeping stopped.

Ms. Nakamura smiled. "All done," she said. Ivy took her hands off. The room was quiet. She looked at the picture of the ear one more time. "Ears are for hearing," said Ivy.

Milan was at Grandma's house. He had a cough and a runny nose. His summer pajamas were soft and light. Grandma had put his blanket on straight, just the way he liked it.

At lunch, Grandma made warm soup. Milan took one bite. Then two. Then he pushed the bowl away. "All done," he said. Grandma felt his head. "You have a cold," she said. "When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much. That's okay."

Milan was quiet. He drank a little water. Then he lay on the couch and watched the leaves fall outside the window. One leaf fell. Then another. His eyes followed each one down.

At dinner, Grandma made toast with butter. Milan took a small bite. Then he took another. Then he ate the whole piece. Grandma smiled big. "Look at you," she said. Milan held up his empty plate. "My tummy woke up," he said. Grandma laughed and kissed his warm little head.

Madelyn sat in the family car. Her tummy felt jumpy. Today she would get a shot at the doctor.

"I think the needle is big," said Madelyn. "Big like a boat!"

"Say what you see at the doctor," said Mom. "Then we will come back to the car."

At the doctor, Madelyn held her bear tight. The doctor held up a thin, thin needle. "One quick poke," said the doctor. "Ready?"

Poke. Done. Madelyn blinked. "It was tiny! Not big like a boat. Just a quick poke in my arm." She looked at her arm. A small bandage sat there like a little white boat.

"That was so fast!" said Madelyn.

"Very fast," said Mom. "You did it."

Back in the car, Madelyn grinned. "Shots are just a quick poke with a thin needle. That is all!" She waved her bandage out the window. "Can we get a tasty snack now?"

"Yes," said Mom, starting the car. "You earned it."

Madelyn hugged her bear. "Quick poke, thin needle, all done!"

"Home we go," said Mom, and the car rolled down the road.

Georgia waited at the window. Michael was coming to her house. It was not a birthday, just a play day. But Georgia felt so excited. Her tummy jumped like a frog. Her feet began to bounce. Bounce, bounce, bounce. She shouted, "Michael! Michael!"

Her blocks fell over. The tower went crash. Georgia dropped her green cup on the rug. "Oh no," she said. Her legs just wanted to jump and jump.

Her mom sat with her on the big soft rug. "Let's find a calm way to wait," Mom said. Georgia took a slow breath. Then one more. Her feet stopped bouncing. Her tummy went quiet and still. She sat and watched the road. Wait, wait, wait.

Then a car pulled up. Georgia saw Michael! She waved her hand, not her whole body. She smiled so big. Michael ran to the door and hugged her. "I waited so calm," said Georgia. "Now let's play!"

Emile sat at the big table. It was pasta night at school. Ms. Dlamini had a big pot. All the kids wanted pasta. Beatrix was first in the line by the table. Brett was second. Emile ran up and pushed in front of Brett.

"Hey," said Brett. "You jumped the line."

Ms. Dlamini looked at Emile. She did not say much. She just pointed to the back. Emile looked behind him. Two more kids were already there. Was the last spot his spot? He walked back and stood behind them.

Then he watched. Beatrix got her pasta. Then Brett. Then one kid, then the next. Everyone stayed in one spot. Nobody pushed. The line moved like a slow little train.

"It is your turn," said Ms. Dlamini.

Emile froze. His turn? Already? He held out his plate. Warm pasta, just for him. It was the key that made the line work, he thought. You stay in your spot, and your spot brings you pasta.

After dinner, Emile lined up his toy cars on the table. "You wait there," he told the blue car. "Your turn comes after the red one."

Brooks was in the playroom. The sun made a warm spot on the rug. His friend Dexter was there too.

"Let's put things in piles," said Dexter. "Animals here. Toys here. Food here."

Brooks picked up a cow. It went in the animal pile. He picked up a banana. It went in the food pile. He picked up a little red car. It went in the toy pile.

Then Brooks found a soft brown dog. He put it in the animal pile. Dexter shook his head. "That is a toy," he said. "It is not alive."

Brooks looked at the dog. It did not bark. It did not wag. It just sat there, soft and quiet.

The real dog at home barked. This one did not. Brooks picked it up. He put it in the toy pile, next to the red car.

"Now it is not lost," said Brooks.

"Wait," said Dexter. "The food pile is empty."

Brooks smiled. He ran to the toy kitchen. He came back with a apple, a carrot, and a egg. They went in the food pile, one by one.

Mr. Jung looked in the door. "Nice tidy piles," he said.

The soft brown dog sat with the toys. It was quiet. It was not alive. It was right where it belonged.

Sofia had a little red drum. At bedtime, she wanted to play it. She felt so excited. "Can Penny hear my drum?" she asked. Penny was sleeping over at Sofia's house. "Yes, let's go ask her," said Mom.

Sofia tapped the drum. Boom! Boom! Sofia laughed. She felt happy. But Penny put her hands over her ears. "Too loud," Penny said. Penny looked scared. She hid under the blanket.

Sofia stopped tapping. She looked at the drum. Then she looked at Penny. The drum made Sofia feel happy. The same drum made Penny feel scared. Sofia thought and thought. "Can we play a quiet game?" she asked. "Yes," said Penny, peeking out.

Sofia found a soft white feather. She put it on the drum. She patted the drum very, very softly. The feather went up. The feather went down. Penny giggled. "Again," Penny said. Sofia patted again, very gently. The feather floated up and down.

"Do you like the drum now?" Sofia asked. "I like the quiet drum," said Penny. Sofia hoped Penny would play with her all night. They watched the little feather dance in the lamp light. Then Mom turned off the lamp. "Sweet dreams," Mom said. The two friends whispered, "Good night, drum. Good night, feather."

Gianna saw a box on the table at school. Ms. Tanaka put a little mirror in it. "This is our mirror station," said Ms. Tanaka. She gave Gianna a small key. Gianna turned the key and lifted the lid. It was easy to open.

Gianna looked in the mirror. She smiled big. The mirror girl smiled big too. Then Gianna made a sad face. The mirror girl made a sad face too. Then Gianna made a scared face, and an angry face. The mirror showed each one.

Keenan sat down next. "My face looks mad," he said. He frowned at the glass. "Try a happy face," said Gianna. Keenan smiled. His eyes went bright. "There," said Gianna. "Your face is happy now." Sahib clapped, and Keenan laughed at his big smile in the mirror.

Leon was at Mira's house. Mira had a big red truck. Leon wanted the truck too.

Leon grabbed one side. Mira held the other side. Pull, pull, pull. The truck did not move. Mira looked sad. Leon felt worried.

Then Leon had an idea. "Let's ask your mom," he said. They found her in the kitchen. She was pouring milk into cups.

"We both want the truck," said Mira. "Can you help us take turns?" Her mom smiled. "Yes. Mira first, then Leon."

Mira pushed the truck. Vroom! Then she gave it to Leon. Leon pushed it. Vroom! It was fun to wait and then play.

After the truck, they sat at the table. The milk was tasty. Leon took a sip and smiled. "Your turn, Mira," he said, holding out the cup of crackers.

Quinn ran to the swings. She wanted to play with Robin. Robin was on the bench with a stuffed bear. Quinn stood by the bench. She did not know what to say. Robin looked at her boot, then at the ground.

Then Quinn had an idea. She held up a striped leaf. "Let's pretend this is soup," she said. Robin jumped up. "Yes! Let's pretend I am the mama bear." Robin poured pretend soup for the bear. Quinn clapped her hands.

Hadassah ran over too. "Can I play?" she asked. "Let's pretend you are the baby bear," said Robin. Hadassah made a little roar. They fed the bear soup from the striped leaf.

Ms. He walked by with the water bottle. "More soup, please," she said. Quinn poured more pretend soup. Ms. He said, "Yum, thank you." Quinn smiled big. She said the magic words again. "Let's pretend the bear is sleepy now." All three friends tucked the bear under Robin's jacket. "Shh," said Hadassah. "Night night, little bear."

Eliana held her new book up high. It was bedtime, but she wanted one story first. "One little story," she said. Dad smiled and sat down on the bed.

Eliana opened the book. She looked at the page. The pictures looked all mixed up. A bear was at the end. A boat was at the top. "Oh no," said Eliana. "The story is broken."

Dad tapped the back of the book. "Try the other side," he said. Eliana turned the book over. Now she saw the front cover. It had a picture of a little red boat. "Start here," said Dad. Eliana opened the front cover.

Page one had the little red boat. Page two had a big wind. The wind blew the boat, and the sail went up. Eliana turned the page. One, two, three. She turned and turned until she reached the back cover. "The end," said Dad. The story was all in order now. The bear came at the end, right where he belonged.

Eliana hugged the book. "Good night, boat," she said. "Good night, bear." Dad kissed her head. The wind made a soft sound at the window. "It is late," said Dad. "Sleep now." Eliana closed her eyes. Then she felt something small and warm on her toes. It was her cat, curled up like a little ball at the end of the bed. "Good night, cat," whispered Eliana.

Ezra went to Cameron's house. Cameron had a big box. It had a flap on top. "This is my shop," said Cameron.

Ezra wanted to play. He picked up a toy banana. "I will sell it," he said. Cameron shook his head. "One person can be the shopkeeper," said Cameron. "And one can be the shopper."

So Cameron stood behind the box. Ezra was the shopper. Ezra waited. His hands did not grab. He looked at a teddy bear. Then he looked at a tiny cup. At last he pointed. "This one, please."

Cameron gave him the cup. Ezra paid with a pretend coin. Cameron smiled. Ezra took his hair brush too, and brushed the teddy's hair. Then Ezra spun around and got dizzy, and Cameron laughed.

"Your turn to be the shopkeeper," said Ezra.

Penelope stood at the bus stop with her mama. The bus was coming soon. Penelope wanted to put on her red coat all by herself. "Can I do it?" she did ask. "Yes," said mama.

First, Penelope held the coat up high. Then she pushed one arm in. Then she pushed her other arm in, too. But wait. Both arms went into the same sleeve! The coat hung funny on one side. Penelope laughed and laughed. "I look like a one-arm bear!"

She wiggled her arms out. She looked at the coat. The coat had two sleeves. She counted them. "One sleeve, two sleeves." Each arm goes into its own sleeve. So she tried again. One arm in this sleeve. One arm in that sleeve. The coat sat just right on her.

Now the zipper. Penelope pulled it up, up, up. It stuck near the top. She tugged it again. Zzzziiip! It went all the way. "I did it!" she said.

A voice said, "Nice coat!" It was Mr. Visver, the neighbour, holding a little desk he was taking home on the bus. "Would you like to sit on the bus like a lucky girl with a warm zip?" he asked. Penelope smiled and held the zipper pull. "Look, it goes up and it goes down," she said. The big bus rolled in.

Nova sat on the train with Mama. The train went clickety-clack. "Are we at the sea yet?" Nova asked. "Not yet," said Mama. Nova looked out the window. A cow went by. Then a river went by. Then the sea came! It was big and blue and shiny.

The train stopped. Nova and Mama got off. Nova saw the sand. She saw the waves. She wanted to splash right now. She ran to the water. "Wait," said Mama. "At the beach, you go near the water only with a grown-up watching." So Nova waited. She wiggled one toe in the warm sand.

Mama held her hand. Then they walked to the waves together. A wave splashed Nova's toes. It was cold and tickly. "Again!" said Nova. Mama gave her a kiss on her wet cheek. Another wave came. Nova laughed and laughed.

Aurora sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist. It was her first time. She held her little bag on her lap. Inside was her toothbrush, ready to show.

"One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She liked that.

Mommy started the car. Aurora peeked in her bag. She saw a toothbrush. But it was blue. Her toothbrush was green. This one was not hers. It was the baby's toothbrush. "Not mine, not mine," said Aurora.

Mommy looked in the mirror. "The baby uses that one," she said. "Each person uses their own toothbrush." Then the car went on. Aurora held the blue toothbrush. She did not use it. She just looked at it.

At the dentist, Aurora opened wide. The dentist counted her teeth. One, two, three, up to twenty. Then Aurora smiled a big smile. "No bad teeth today," said the dentist. "Good brushing!"

Back in the car, Aurora held her bag tight. At home, she ran to the bathroom. She put the blue toothbrush back by the baby's cup. She took her own green one. "One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She gave it a big hug.

Connor wanted to go to the library. Mom had said, "We will go tomorrow." That was yesterday when she said it.

Now it was dark. Connor was in his small bed. He wore his blue pajamas. He could not sleep.

"Mom," he called, "is today the library day?"

Mom came in. She sat on the bed. "Yesterday I said tomorrow. Now that day is here. Today is the day that is happening right now."

Connor sat up. "So today is library day?"

"Yes. Today we go. But first we sleep."

Connor wiggled his toes. "I sleep now. Library later?"

"That's right. Sleep now. Library later today."

Connor heard the clock tick. He heard his dog scratch at the door. Mom let the dog in. The dog jumped up and curled on the rug.

Connor closed his eyes. He thought about books. He thought about his red boots by the door. They would go on his feet later.

Then Mom kissed his head. "Little surprise," she whispered. She put a small book under his pillow. "From the library yesterday. To read tonight."

Connor hugged the book. "Today is a good day," he said.

Mom turned off the light. "Yes, it is."

Arya was at Grandma's house. On the shelf sat big books. Arya saw one with a blue butterfly on the front. She wanted that book. But Grandma was in the garden, and Arya did not know which book it was.

Grandma came in with a basket of apples. "Can I have the butterfly book?" Arya asked. Grandma smiled. She pointed to the top of the book. "Those words are its name," she said. "This one is called Butterfly Day." Arya traced the letters with her finger. The book had a name, just like she did.

"Now I can ask for it," Arya said. Grandma sat down. She opened the front of the book first. Arya snuggled close. They read page by page, all the way to the back. Then they went to the kitchen to eat apple slices. "Butterfly Day again after snack?" said Grandma. Arya nodded. "Yes, please. Butterfly Day."

Rosalie held her mother's hand. They walked into the big library. Rosalie wanted her very own library card.

A librarian sat at a small desk. She typed on her computer. Then she gave Rosalie a card with her name on it. Rosalie smiled and put it in her pocket.

There was a rug with children on it. A librarian held a book up high. Rosalie did not go sit down. She stood near the shelf and watched.

The librarian opened the book. It was a funny book about a frog. The children laughed. Rosalie laughed too.

Then Rosalie walked over. She sat down next to Yuna. She listened to the whole story.

After storytime, Rosalie found a book about a red bus. She gave her card to the librarian. The librarian scanned the book.

"Take it home," said the librarian. "Bring it back next week."

Rosalie hugged the book all the way home.

Sophie stood at the train station with her mama. They were waiting for Grandma. Grandma would stay for a whole week. Sophie held a red bag. Inside the bag was a picture she had drawn.

The station was big and noisy. Trains went whoosh. People carried bags. Sophie heard a whistle blow. The train would come soon.

Sophie felt shy. Grandma lived far away. Sophie had not seen her in a long time. "What if Grandma wants a big hug?" Sophie asked. Mama held her hand. "You can wave hello instead," said Mama. "A hug, a wave, or a hello. Any one is good."

The train came in. The doors opened with a swish. Grandma stepped out. She had a deep blue coat and a little bag. Grandma saw Sophie. She opened her arms wide.

Sophie was not ready for a hug yet. So she waved her hand. "Hello, Grandma!" she called. Grandma waved back. "Hello, Sophie!" she said. Grandma waved and waved. Then Sophie ran to her. Now she wanted the hug. Grandma held her close. Her coat was soft and warm.

They walked to the car. Grandma would drive home with them. Sophie gave Grandma the red bag. "A picture for you," she said. Grandma smiled a big smile. "Hello, my Sophie," she said again.

Kinsley sat at the little table in the library. Ms. Bélanger gave her a fat pencil. Kinsley wanted to write her name. She squeezed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letter K came out wobbly and big. It did not look right at all.

Her friend Aura sat down next to her. Aura wrote her own name. Her letters stood up straight and small. Kinsley felt her face get hot. She looked at her paper again.

Ms. Bélanger knelt down beside her. "Watch my hand," she said. Ms. Bélanger pinched the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then she let the pencil rest on her middle finger. It looked like a little spider sitting still on its web.

Kinsley tried it. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. She rested it on her middle finger. Then she wrote. The K came out neat. The I came out neat. The N, the S, the L, the E, the Y. All seven letters, all in a line.

"Can I send it to Grandma?" Kinsley asked. "I will mail it after story time," said Ms. Bélanger. Aura clapped. "May I see it?" Aura asked, very polite. Kinsley held the paper up high. At the bottom, in small neat letters, it said Kinsley.

Lillian ran to the dress-up corner. She wanted to be a snow queen. But the box was stuck under the shelf. Rubani came to help. Together they pulled it out.

Lillian found a long scarf. It went down to her shoes. Rubani found a short scarf. It stopped at his chin. "Mine is so long," said Lillian. "Mine is short," said Rubani. "Long and short are opposites," said Anaiah, who was watching.

Then the scarf tripped Lillian. She fell on the bumpy rug. Almost. She lifted her arms and caught herself. The long scarf was too long for running. Rubani held the end of it in his hand. "Now you can run fast," he said. Lillian ran. The scarf flowed behind her like a river.

Outside, the sun was hot. The slide was hot too. Ms. Ndlovu touched it first. "Wait for the shade," she said. They waited by the cool wall. Then they slid down, slow and then fast.

At song time, everyone sang the snow song. Anaiah had no scarf at all. Lillian wrapped her long scarf around both their necks. One scarf, two friends. "A surprise!" said Anaiah, and she laughed. They sang the song together, all wrapped up warm.

Margot woke up and saw white outside. "No school today!" said her mom. "Snow day!" Mom had to work, so Margot went next door to Mr. Fernando's house. His grandson Wren was there too.

"Let's go play in the snow," said Wren. They put on boots and mittens. Mr. Fernando brought out a sled and a warm blanket on the table for later. "I'm hungry already," said Wren, laughing.

Then Wren lay down in the snow. He swept his arms up and down. He swept his legs out and in. Then he jumped up fast to show Margot. His boots pressed big holes in the snow. The shape was smudged.

"Oh no," said Wren. "I stood on it."

"Try again," said Margot. So Wren lay down once more. He swept his arms and legs again. This time he rolled to the side, far from the shape, and stood up there. The snow showed wings and a gown.

"It's a snow angel!" said Wren.

Margot lay down too. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. Then she rolled to the side and stood up. Her angel had wings too.

"You made one!" said Wren. Mr. Fernando clapped from the porch. "Come in soon, you two. I made soup."

Margot threw one soft snowball at Wren. Wren threw one back. Then they ran inside, ready for lunch.

Declan sat in his car seat. He was going home from the park with his dad. His tummy rumbled. He wanted a warm bath and his pillow right after.

"Big bath tonight," said Dad. "You got very muddy."

Declan smiled. At home, Dad turned on the water. Declan wanted to jump in. He stopped. "Wait," he said. "You check first."

Dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot," he said. "Watch this."

Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Steam went up, then it stopped. Dad checked the water again. "Now it is warm," he said.

Declan put in his toes. Warm, not hot. He slid in all the way.

Declan had an idea. "Does the tap make cold water too?" he asked.

Dad showed him. Declan put his hand near the cold tap. Brrr. He pulled back fast.

"So taps can be hot or cold," said Declan. "And you check first."

"Check first," said Dad. "Every time."

Declan splashed and played. His rubber duck floated past his knee. Then he hugged his towel, warm and soft like a big pillow. "Bath time is the best," he said. "After you check first."

Abigail sat in the family car. Her big brown bear was lost. "Where is Bear?" she said. She looked under her seat. She looked by the door. Then she picked up something from the floor. It was a shiny blue toy car. But it was not hers. It belonged to Miles from daycare.

The car stopped at daycare. Abigail held the shiny car in her small hands. The sun made it glow. She wanted to keep it. Miles was standing by the gate. His face looked sad. His skin was hot from crying. "Miles," said Abigail. "I found your car."

Miles ran to her. His eyes got big. "My car!" he said. He hugged it tight. Then he smiled a big smile. Abigail felt warm inside. Miles held her hand. They walked to the door together. "You can play with my car too," said Miles.

It was a rainy morning. Eliana woke up early. Her tummy was full of toast. Mom took her to the library for story time.

Ms. Chen had a game ready. "Today we hunt for shapes," she said. She held up a card with a red rectangle. "Find me a rectangle, just like this." Vivaan found a square block. "A square has the same kind of corners," he said, "but this one is small and boxy." Mia found a circle in a round clock. Nobody had found a rectangle yet.

Eliana looked and looked. Then she saw the big door at the front of the library. She walked over and put her finger on the edge of the door. She slid her finger down one side. Then she went across the bottom. Then up the other side. Then across the top. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Four sides." She tapped the corners with her finger. "One, two, three, four. Four corners, and they are square corners." Ms. Chen smiled. "A rectangle has four sides and four square corners," she said, "just like the shape of a door." Eliana held up the red card next to the door. It matched.

Vivaan clapped. Mia clapped too. Ms. Chen gave Eliana a star sticker shaped like a rectangle. Eliana stuck it on her raincoat. "Now my coat has a rectangle too," she said, and she spun around on her toes.

Isla sat at the dinner table. It was a cold winter night. She wanted her doll at dinner, but her doll was not there.

"Where is my doll?" said Isla.

"Your toys are all over the floor," said Dad. "Eat first. Then we will look."

Isla ate her warm soup. She ate her bread. Soon her bowl was empty.

Then Isla looked at the floor. She saw blocks by the chair. She saw a ball by the door. She saw her doll under the table.

"I found her!" said Isla.

Isla picked up the blocks. "Blocks are toys," she said. She put them in the toy box.

She picked up the doll. "Dolls are toys," she said. Into the box.

She picked up the ball. "Balls are toys," she said. In it went.

The toy box was full. The floor was clear.

"Now it is time to bathe," said Dad. He warmed the water. Isla splashed in the tub. Then Dad wrapped her in a big, dry towel.

"Good night, toys," said Isla.

Eliana sat at the little red table. It was snack time at school. She wanted the crackers very much.

Bentley sat next to her. "Give me juice!" he said loudly. Ms. Ngo shook her head. "Try again," she said. Bentley thought. "Juice, please," he said. Ms. Ngo smiled and gave him the cup. The juice smelled like sweet apples.

Eliana watched. She saw Bentley say a word. Then she saw Ms. Ngo give him the juice. One thing made the other thing happen.

Eliana felt hungry. "Give me crackers," she said. Ms. Ngo waited. Eliana thought of Bentley. "Crackers, please," she said. Ms. Ngo gave her three crackers.

One cracker fell on the floor. Eliana picked it up. "Yucky," she said. She put it in the trash.

Gracelyn dropped her string of beads. They rolled under the chair. "I can help," said Eliana. She got down on her knees. The beads felt smooth and cold. She gave them back, one by one.

"Thank you," said Gracelyn.

"You are welcome," said Eliana. She ate her crackers and smiled.

Emmett ran to the playground. He wanted to meet his friends there. Clark was on the slide. Alaina was near the sand. Emmett felt so excited.

Then Clark tripped near the swing. He fell down in the soft sand. His face looked sad. His eyes had tears. Emmett walked over to him. He bent down low. "Are you okay?" Emmett asked.

Clark looked up. His tears stopped. "You asked me," Clark said. "That makes me feel better." He smiled a little smile. Then a rabbit hopped out of the bushes! One, two, three big hops, right past the boys.

Alaina ran over. "I saw the rabbit too!" she said. Emmett and Clark laughed together. Clark stood up. "One, two, three, let's play!" he said. They ran to the slide, all three.

Joshua wanted warm milk. He looked at the big stove. The pot sat on top. The stove did not look hot. No steam. No fire. Nothing.

"Maybe it is cold now," Joshua said. His hand came close. Then he stopped. He remembered his rule. Ask first, touch never.

"Mom, is the stove still hot?" he asked.

His mom came over. She held her hand above the pot. "Yes, it is hot," she said. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it."

Joshua stepped back. He watched from his spot at the table. The floor felt cool on his toes. The kitchen smelled like sweet cocoa.

Mom poured the warm milk into his blue cup. "You can pretend to pour with your toy pot," she said.

Joshua poured pretend milk for his teddy. "Careful, teddy," he said. "Only grown-ups touch the stove."

Mom gave him a big smile. "That is a neat rule," she said. Joshua took a sip. The milk was warm and yummy. He stayed close to Mom the whole time.

Anna sat on the small red mat. The music room had a drum, a bell, and a big spotted drum with dots. Mr. Morin picked up his guitar.

"Today we will learn a nursery rhyme," said Mr. Morin. "A nursery rhyme is a short rhyming song for little ones."

Anna wanted to sing it all by herself. But the words felt tricky. She clapped too fast. Then she clapped too slow. Fionn clapped fast too. Ian clapped and laughed.

Mr. Morin played the song again. He clapped one, two, one, two. Anna watched his hand. His hand went up, then down, slow like a big rabbit hopping. Anna clapped when his hand came down. The claps fit the song now.

Then she sang the rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The ends of the lines sounded the same. Star, star, are. She sang it again, all alone.

Fionn clapped along to her voice. Ian bent down low and hopped like the rabbit. Anna sang the last line. Then she clapped once, big and loud, right on the beat.

Hudson ran to the sand pit at the park. Siena was there. She was building a big sandcastle. It had three tall towers.

Hudson wanted to see it close up. He ran fast. His foot hit the castle. One tower fell down. Siena's mouth turned down. She looked like she might cry.

"Sorry," said Hudson. "It was a mistake." Siena looked at him. Her mouth turned up again. "Help me fix it," she said. Hudson patted the sand. He made a new tower. It was even taller.

Mr. Nkosi walked by with a ball. "Nice castle," he said. "Can we play later, please?" asked Hudson. "Of course," said Mr. Nkosi.

Then Siena put a leaf on top. "A flag!" she said. Hudson smiled at the tall tower in the sun.

Nora wanted to play the flower fairy game with Wren and Mivaan. The rules were simple. You pick a flower card. You hop two hops. Then you send your fairy to the flower house.

Nora picked a card. She hopped four hops. She zoomed straight to the flower house. "I win!" she said.

Wren put down her card. "That is not the game," she said. Mivaan folded his arms. He sat down on the smooth rug. Nobody hopped. Nobody picked a card.

Nora looked at the empty flower house. Her fairy sat all alone. "Okay," she said. "Two hops. Then I send my fairy."

She picked a new card. She hopped two hops. She sent her fairy to the flower house. Wren clapped. Mivaan jumped up and picked his card. All three fairies sat in the flower house together. "Now we all win," said Wren.

Ella ran to the big sandbox at the playground. She had the only red shovel there. It had a rough handle and a smooth red top.

Ella dug a deep hole with her shovel. Oakland came and sat down next to her. He looked at the hole. He looked at the shovel. He had nothing to dig with.

"Want to dig too?" Ella asked. Oakland nodded his head.

"Here," Ella said. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too."

Oakland took the red shovel. He dug and dug. Ella used her hands to pat the sand. A little cloud moved across the sun. Then Oakland gave the shovel back.

"Your turn," he said. Ella dug a long river. Oakland patted the sand flat.

Then Carlos came over. He had no shovel either. Ella looked at him. Could three friends share one shovel?

Ella held out the shovel. "We take turns," she said. Carlos smiled.

They dug one big hole, all together. Ms. Foster called out, "Time for a snack!" The three friends put the shovel back in the toy box.

"One, two, three, my turn!" said Carlos, jumping up and down.

Jackson sat at the dinner table. He had ten green beans on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

He touched a bean. "One," he said. He touched the next one. "Two." His mom smiled and waited. "Three, four, five." The beans were round and little. "Six, seven, eight, nine." One bean was left. "Ten!" Jackson clapped his hands.

Then Jackson wanted to write the number ten. He had a paper and a crayon. He wrote a big 4 first. No, that was four. He rubbed it out. He drew a huge 7. No, that was seven. He looked at his mom.

"Ten is written with two numbers," she said. "A 1 and then a 0." Jackson drew a small 1. Then he drew a round 0 right after it. He held up the paper. "Ten!" he said.

At school the next day, his friend Zaya was counting sheep on a card. "One, two, three," she said. Jackson sat next to her. He wrote 1 and then 0 on his paper. "That means ten sheep," he said. Zaya counted the last sheep and laughed. "Ten!"

Aiden walked in the forest with his dad. He saw a big red hat on a log. "Who lost this hat?" he asked. "Maybe a firefighter," said his dad. Aiden put it on his head. The hat was too big. It tickled his ears.

Something felt different now. Aiden looked down at his boots. "I have firefighter boots!" he said. He puffed up his chest. "My job is to put out fires," he said. The red hat made him feel like a whole new person.

Aiden found a soft grey rabbit made of leaves and moss. He picked it up gently. "Don't be scared, little one," he said. "I will keep you safe." He rocked the leaf rabbit in his arms. He patted its back like a baby. "Shh, time for sleep," he whispered.

Then Aiden saw smoke far away. It was just dad making tea at the little camp stove. Dad waved him over. "Firefighters need a snack," said dad. He gave Aiden a warm biscuit. Aiden sat on the log with the leaf rabbit on his lap. He tipped his big red hat back. "Firefighter Aiden, reporting for tea!"

Mila ran into the library. It was story day! She was so excited.

But the story room door was shut. A sign hung on it. "Closed today," said Mr. Baptiste. "The ceiling has a leak. The rain came in."

Mila felt sad. Her lip went down. Her friend Karam stomped his foot. He was angry. "I wanted the bear story!" he said.

Then they heard a loud drip. Drip, drip! Emaan covered her ears. "That sound is scary," she said.

Mr. Baptiste smiled. "We can fix our day," he said. He pulled big cushions off a shelf. He laid them in a ring. He draped a red blanket over two chairs.

"A fort!" said Mila. "In the library!"

They all crawled inside. Emaan picked the bear book. Mr. Baptiste read it out loud in his big bear voice. Karam laughed and laughed.

Mila looked around the fort. She had been sad before. Now she felt happy. The day had changed, just like that.

"Mila," called her mom at the door. "Time to go home for dinner."

"I'm coming!" said Mila. She hugged the bear book first. "Same time next week?" asked Mr. Baptiste.

"Yes!" said Mila. "The fort too?"

Leon held his drum in the school auditorium. Jonas held a drum too. Ms. Lavoie said, "Let's play together, boys."

They played. Leon tapped fast. Jonas tapped fast too. Soon their drums went zippy quick. The sounds bumped into each other. The song fell apart. Jonas frowned.

Ms. Lavoie stomped her foot. Tap, tap, tap. It was a steady beat, slow and even. "Now grab your sticks," she said. Leon tapped with her foot. Tap, tap, tap. Jonas tapped too. Tap, tap, tap.

Then they played the song. One drum, two drums, steady and neat. The sounds matched. Macy clapped from her seat. "Play it again!" she said. Ms. Lavoie held up a card with a star on it. "Steady wins a star," she said.

Leon counted as he tapped. One, two, one, two. Jonas smiled big. The two friends played the whole song, steady and slow, all the way to the end.

Henry was at summer camp. There was one big red drum. Henry wanted to bang it. But Paul wanted it too.

Henry grabbed for the drum. Ms. Joseph held up her hand. "Wait," she said. "Paul has it now."

Paul banged the drum. One, two, three, four! Then Paul stopped. "Your turn, Henry," he said.

Henry took the drum. He banged it. One, two, three, four! Was that all? Yes, it was Paul's turn again.

Paul played for a while. Then Henry played for a while. Back and forth it went. One, two, three, four!

Later, Henry found a toy frog near the sandbox. His hands were dirty, but the frog was fun. Paul came over and looked at it.

Henry smiled. "Your turn," he said, and held out the frog.

Ryan woke up early. He found his toy monkeys on the rug. "Five monkeys for my song," he said. He set them on his bed.

Ryan sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" He pushed one monkey off the bed. It fell on the rug. Now he counted. "One, two, three, four. Four monkeys left!"

He sang the next part. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Another monkey fell. He counted again. "One, two, three." Hmm. Was it three now? Yes, three monkeys sat on the bed.

"One fell off and bumped his head!" Ryan laughed. He counted, "One, two." Then one more monkey fell. "One," said Ryan. Then that monkey fell too. "Zero monkeys! All done!"

Mack came over to play. "Where are the monkeys?" he asked. Ryan pointed at the rug. "They all fell off. Want to put them back?" Mack put five monkeys on the bed. "Sing it again," said Mack. "One, two, three, four, five. Ready?" Ryan smiled. "Ready!"

Brooklyn and her mom walk to the bank. It is cold outside. Brooklyn has her red coat on. But the coat is open.

"I want to zip it," says Brooklyn. She pulls the little tab. Up, up, up. But the zipper will not go. She pulls again. Still no zip. Wind blows in at the door.

Mr. Delgado works at the bank. He sees Brooklyn at the wall by the high counter. He kneels down. "Look at the bottom," he says. Brooklyn looks. There is a little box there. One side of the zipper has a pointy end. Brooklyn slides the end into the little box. Click. It fits!

"Now pull the tab," says Mr. Delgado. Brooklyn pulls. Zip! The zipper goes all the way up. Her coat is closed. No more cold wind.

"Thank you," says Brooklyn. Mr. Delgado smiles. Mom takes her hand. "Nice warm coat," says Mom. Brooklyn pats her zipper. "I did it," she says.

Jaxson went to the library with his dad. A big sign said "Story Time Today." Jaxson wanted to sit in the front row. But the front row was full.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya held up her hand. "Let's count the chairs," she said. "One, two, three, four, five." Then Francesca counted too. "One, two, three, four, six." She frowned. "That sounds funny."

Jaxson listened hard. "Six comes after five," he said. Francesca tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She smiled big. "Now it sounds right!"

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya gave Jaxson a job. "Count the mats for me," she said. Jaxson touched each mat. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten mats for ten kids. Everyone sat down. Finley patted the mat next to him.

The story was about ten little ducks. Jaxson counted them on the pretty blue pages. One duck went away, then two, then more. At the end, all ten ducks came back.

Story time finished. Jaxson gave back his mat. "One," he said, putting it on the pile. He waved to Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya. "Ten tomorrow?" he asked. She laughed and said, "Ten tomorrow."

Today Ms. Abdi brought a big picture to circle time. It showed eyes, ears, a nose, a tongue, and hands. "We use our body to learn about the world," said Ms. Abdi. "Our five senses help us." Athena wanted to say them all by herself. But she could only remember two. Eyes see, she thought. Nose smells. What did ears do?

Just then a big black truck rumbled by the window. It was very loud. Athena put her hands over her ears. Ruth did too. The sound got much quieter. Athena moved her hands away. The rumble came back loud again. She put her hands back. Quiet again. "My ears hear the truck," Athena said.

"Now I know three," said Athena. Alexandre smelled an orange with his nose. That made four. Then Athena touched a soft blanket with her hands. That made five. "I did it," she said. She waved to Ms. Abdi with both arms. "Ears, eyes, nose, tongue, and hands. All mine."

Rowan sat on the big rug in the living room. The game was on TV today! Koen and Isabelle came over to watch too. Mr. López brought popcorn.

"Which team is ours?" Rowan asked.

"The blue team," said Mr. López. "Look at their shirts. Our team wears blue. The other team wears red. Each team wears its own colors. That is how you tell the two teams apart."

Rowan looked hard. Blue ran one way. Red ran the other way. Now he saw it! A blue player kicked the ball. "Go blue!" shouted Rowan.

Outside, a big truck went by. It honked its horn. Isabelle was not afraid of it. She just laughed.

The red team got the ball. A red player ran fast. "He is going to score!" said Koen.

"No! Blue, come back!" said Rowan.

The blue keeper jumped. He caught the ball! Everyone cheered. Dad clapped so loud.

"Can you teach me that catch?" Rowan asked Mr. López after the game.

"Sure," said Mr. López. "But we use a soft ball."

"Blue team, get ready!" said Rowan. He threw the ball up high.

Sophie went to the store with her dad. She held his hand on the road. "I want to find a banana," she said. Dad smiled. "Let's look in the fruit aisle."

Sophie saw apples and oranges. She saw a big pile of toy cars on a low shelf. Then she spotted something yellow. It was a banana! But it was hiding among the toy cars.

Sophie picked it up. "The banana does not fit here," she said. Sophia, her friend from school, was there too. "The banana is the odd one out," Sophia said. "It is not a toy car."

Sophie put the banana in the cart. Then she played a game with Sophia. They found a book in the bread bin. "That's the odd one out!" said Sophie. They found a sock in the apple bin. "The sock is the odd one out," they said together.

Dad laughed. "You two are good at this." At home, Dad peeled the banana. Sophie took a big bite. "Found it, fixed it, ate it," she said. Sophia giggled, and Sophie smiled a deep, happy smile.

Mateo wanted to wear his new shoes to school. It was bedtime, but he got them out anyway. "Shoes for tomorrow," he said. His dad smiled and put them by the door.

Mateo had his bath first. The water was warm and bubbly. He washed his toes. Then he put on his soft pajamas. He ate a banana for a small snack. He brushed his teeth. At last it was time for bed.

But Mateo wanted to try the new shoes now. He sat on the rug. He pushed his bare feet into the shoes. They felt bumpy inside. The dog barked once, as if to say something was funny.

Mateo laughed too. He pulled the shoes off. He found his warm socks. He put the socks on his feet first. Then he put the shoes on. Now his feet felt cozy and smooth. "Socks first, then shoes," Mateo said. His dad tucked him in under his sweater blanket. Mateo closed his eyes. He dreamed of cozy feet at school.

Sophia wanted her teddy. It was bedtime. Her room was dark. She looked with her eyes. She could not see teddy. Where could he be?

She heard a sound with her ears. Tap, tap. It was just the tree by the window. She touched her blanket with her hands. It was soft, but it was not teddy. She sniffed with her nose. Teddy smelled like soap, not smelly at all. But in the dark, she could not find him. She tried to crawl across the rug. Still no teddy.

"Why can't I see him?" she asked. Her mom came in. "It is hard to see in the dark," Mom said. "Let's turn on the light." Mom clicked the lamp. The room lit up. There was teddy, under the chair! Sophia hugged him. He was soft and warm. She kissed his nose. "I see you now," she said. Mom smiled and turned the light back off.

Addison sat at the kitchen table. She had a big new pencil. Mom gave her paper with lines on it. "You can write your name," said Mom.

Addison wanted to write the big A first. She held the pencil tight. She pressed very hard on the paper. Snap! The pencil tip broke off. The little black tip rolled on the table. Addison gasped. Her pencil had a flat top now. No point! No A!

"Uh oh," said Addison. Mom brought the pencil sharpener. She turned the pencil round and round. A sharp new tip appeared. Mom put the pencil back in Addison's hand. "Try a soft touch," said Mom. Addison touched the wet sponge on the table to wipe her shirt sleeve clean. Then she took a deep breath.

This time she pressed soft and slow. The pencil did not break. A line! A curvy line! Then a big letter A. Then a little d. Addison made letter after letter. "Look, Mom! It says Addison!" Mom clapped her hands. Addison held up the paper, and the wet pencil tip made one more happy dot on the page.

Myles stood in the kitchen. Ms. Clarke-Williams was baking bread. "Can I help?" Myles asked. "Yes," she said. "We will play a senses game."

"What can your eyes do?" she asked. "See!" said Myles. He looked at the bread. It was a pretty golden color. "My eyes see the color," he said.

"What can your ears do?" "Hear!" The oven ticked. Myles heard it. "My ears hear the oven."

Then the bread came out. Ms. Clarke-Williams held the warm pan. She gave Myles one small piece of bread on ice to cool it. He touched the ice. "My fingers feel cold!" he said.

"Now the big question," said Ms. Clarke-Williams. "Smell the bread. What do you use?" Myles leaned in close. He sniffed with his nose. "My nose smells it! We smell with our nose!" He sniffed again. "Mmm. It smells so good. Can we taste it too?"

Josephine did not eat much breakfast at home. Now her tummy made a little growl. At daycare, Ms. Jung put strawberries on the table.

Josephine looked at them with her eyes. They were red and shiny. She heard Madeleine say, "They smell so good." Josephine sniffed with her nose. The smell was sweet.

But Josephine did not like new foods. She pushed her plate away. "I don't want a bite," she said.

Myra was eating her strawberry. Then Myra held her nose closed with her fingers. She took a bite. "It tastes plain now," Myra said. "Like nothing much."

Josephine watched. One thing made another thing happen. Myra's nose was closed, and the taste went away. Josephine wanted to see for herself. She held her nose closed. She took one small bite. The strawberry tasted flat, like a plain cracker. "Oh," said Josephine. "It is true."

Then she let go of her nose. She took another bite. Now the taste came back, big and sweet. "It tastes good now!" she said. She touched the strawberry with her fingers. It felt bumpy with little seeds.

After snack, the kids went outside. Josephine kicked a red ball on the flat grass. "Strawberries again tomorrow," she said.

Mia stood at the edge of the hotel pool. Her friend Isha was already in the water. The swim teacher smiled and patted the water.

"Time to put your face near the water," the teacher said. Mia shook her head. The water looked big and wet. She did not want her face in it.

The teacher had an idea. "Can you blow bubbles into the water through your mouth?" she asked. Mia tried one little bubble. It went pop. She tried again. This time she made big bubbles. The bubbles floated up and broke near her nose. Isha laughed. Mia laughed too. Her face had been in the water, and it was fine.

A green float shaped like a frog drifted by. Mia chased it with Isha. They kicked and splashed. When they got out, Mia's towel had an itchy tag. Her dad tucked it inside.

"More bubbles tomorrow?" asked the teacher. "Yes," said Mia. "Big ones."

Jack put on his swim shorts. He ran to the hotel pool. His friend Mayson was already there. Jack stepped to the pool stairs.

A pool worker held up a hand. "Hold on," she said. "We take a shower first."

Jack looked at Mayson. "Where is the shower?" he asked. Mayson pointed to a small shower by the wall. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in," said the worker.

Jack stood under the shower. The water was warm. It ran down his arms. He picked up a towel that fell. Then he walked back to the pool.

He went down the stairs, one step at a time. The water felt good. Mayson held out a long noodle. "Hold this," he said. Jack held the noodle with both hands. He kicked his legs.

Ms. Siddiqui, the pool teacher, counted. "One, two, three," she said. Jack kicked and kicked. Then he let go of the noodle for one second. He paddled his hands.

He grabbed the noodle again. He smiled big. "I did it!" he said. Mayson clapped. Jack paddled to the wall. Then he paddled back. He took his time. The water held him up. "Again," said Jack.

Eloise lost her soft bunny. She looked under the table. Bunny was not there. She looked in her toy box. Bunny was not there. "Where are you, bunny?" she said.

Eloise looked behind the sofa. No bunny. She looked by the fire place. Her dad said, "Come away from there, Eloise." She came back to the rug. Then she saw her bed. The blanket was bumpy. She picked up the blanket. There was bunny! Bunny had been hiding under the soft blanket all along.

Eloise hugged bunny tight. But she did not want to lose bunny again. She found a small basket. She put the basket by her bed, right where she could see it. "This is bunny's home," she said. Her dad smiled. Every night, Eloise put bunny in the basket. Every morning, she knew just where to look.

One day, her friend Ollie came to play. He lost his truck. He looked and looked. Eloise said, "I know where bunny is, every time. Bunny has a home." She showed Ollie the basket by the bed. Bunny sat inside, waiting.

Aaron stood in the reading corner. He wanted a library card of his own. Finley had one. Westley had one too. Aaron's card would let him take a book home.

Aaron walked to the big desk. He asked, "Can I get a card all by myself?" The librarian shook her head. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," she said. Aaron's dad was right there, holding his keys. "I can help," said Dad.

Dad held the pen. Aaron wrote the letters of his name. A is for Aaron. The letters looked a little messy. The wind from the fan made the paper lift up. Aaron held the paper flat with one hand. He brushed the crumbs off the desk first. Then he wrote the last letter.

The librarian gave Aaron his card. It was blue and shiny. Aaron picked a book about a big red truck. He asked, "Does the card let me take this?" The librarian said, "Yes, it does." Aaron smiled and put the book in his bag.

Arthur sat in his car seat. Mama was driving. "Where are we going now?" asked Arthur. "To the store now, and to Grandma later," said Mama. "Later is after the store," said Arthur. "Yes," said Mama. "You got it."

At the store, Arthur saw Huda and her dad. Huda held a big pot. "We went to the park tomorrow!" said Huda. Arthur blinked. "Tomorrow?" he asked. Huda thought hard. "No, not tomorrow. It already happened. It was yesterday," she said. "Yesterday is the day before today." Her dad smiled and nodded.

Arthur thought about that all the way to the car. Yesterday was the day before today. Yesterday he played in the sand. Today he saw Huda at the store. Tomorrow was still coming, after he slept.

In the car, Mama gave Arthur a fresh apple slice. "Mama, yesterday we had apples too," said Arthur. "And tomorrow, can we play at the park?" "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow we can go." Arthur smiled big. The trees went by the window. He watched them, one, two, three. "Grandma now?" he asked. "Almost now," said Mama. "Just up this road."

Sofia put on her red dress. Today was a big party at the community hall. "Who will come?" she asked. "All the family," said Mama. "Family comes together on special days."

Sofia held Mama's hand. They walked in. The hall was tall and bright. There were balloons and a long table.

Then Sofia saw her cousin Leo. She had not seen Leo in a long, long time. "Leo!" she shouted. Leo ran to her. They jumped up and down.

A big dog stood by the door. His tail began to brush against Sofia's leg. She laughed. The dog wagged and wagged.

More and more people came. Aunts, uncles, and cousins filled the hall. "So many family!" said Sofia. "Family comes together on special days," she said again.

The lights went low. Ms. Eze began to sing. Sofia clapped her hands.

"Shall we dance too?" asked Leo.

"Yes!" said Sofia. "Let's dance!"

Carter went to the pharmacy with his mom. In the back was a little doctor's room. Today Carter needed a shot.

A nurse pointed to the big table. "Climb up here," she said. Carter looked at the table. It was high and cold. His tummy felt tight. He shook his head fast.

His friend Clayton was there too. Clayton was getting a shot as well. Clayton's dad sat down on a chair. Then Clayton sat on his dad's lap. Clayton held his dad's arm. The nurse gave Clayton the shot. Clayton did not cry one bit.

Carter watched. Then he said, "Mom, can I sit on your lap?" His mom sat down on the chair. Carter climbed up. She held him snug with both arms. Carter took a deep breath.

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done. It was so fast!

"You were so brave," his mom said. The nurse gave Carter a sticker. On the way out, Carter waved to Clayton. "See you at school," he called.

Felix ran into the playroom. "Look at all the toys!" he said. There were blocks and a toy plane and a soft bear. Cassandra was there too. She held a toy rabbit.

"We need boxes," said Ms. Ba. "One box for animals. One box for toys. One box for foods." Felix was so excited. He loved sorting!

Felix found the bear. The bear went in the animal box. He found the plane. The plane went in the toy box. He found a toy banana. It went in the foods box. Then he found something soft and red. It was small and had a hole in it. "A sock!" said Felix. He put the sock in the toy box.

Cassandra laughed. "Socks are not toys," she said. "Shirts and socks and hats are all clothes." Felix picked up the sock. He looked at it. It was not a bear. It was not a plane. It was clothes!

"Where do clothes go?" asked Felix. "Not in a toy box," said Ms. Ba. She found a new box. Felix dropped the sock in. Then he found a hat on the shelf. The hat went in too. Then a shirt went in!

"The clothes box will grow big!" said Felix. He clapped his hands. Cassandra clapped too.

After sorting, they sat down for a snack. Ms. Ba gave them crackers. "These are salty," said Felix. He took a big bite. "Yum!"

Then Felix picked up the toy plane again. "Zoom!" he said. The plane flew over the animal box. It flew over the clothes box. "Best playroom day ever!"

Ivy sat on her bedroom floor. She had paper and a fat red crayon. She wanted to write a note for Grandpa. Grandpa was coming today.

Ivy made letters. She made them big and small. She made them all in one long line. The letters were squished together like peas in a pod. She held up the paper. "Look, a note!" she said. Then she put it on the bed for Grandpa.

Mom came in. She picked up the note. She turned it upside down. She looked and looked. "Hmm," said Mom. "My eyes feel weak today. I cannot find the words." Mom tapped her toe, thinking. Then she smiled. "Ivy, there is a space between one word and the next." She showed Ivy with two fingers. A little gap. Like that.

Ivy tried again. She wrote a word. She left a gap. She wrote the next word. Gap, word, gap, word. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," the note said now. She did not forget the gaps at all. She ran and put the note by the door, face up, so Grandpa would see it first.

The door opened. Grandpa came in. He picked up the paper. He read it right away. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," he said out loud. He laughed a big laugh. Ivy jumped up and down. "You read my words!" she said. Grandpa held out his hand. "Come on," he said. "Let us play."

Maya put on her skates at the ice rink. Her team was playing a game today. The ice was shiny and cold. Francesca skated beside her. Corbin was the goalie.

The game began. Maya skated fast after the puck. Then she fell down. She got up and kept going. Corbin blocked the puck with his pad. Maya reached out and pushed it in with her hand. The crowd made a funny sound. A man in a striped shirt blew his whistle.

Maya was upset. "Why no goal?" she asked. Her coach skated over. "That man is the referee," he said. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules." Maya watched the referee drop the puck. Francesca won it and scored. Maya drew a picture of the referee after the game. She drew his stripey shirt too.

"Next time I will use my stick," Maya said.

Edouard was at Grandma's house. Lunch was hot soup. Grandma set the big pot on the table.

"Bismillah," said Grandma. She said the word before her first bite.

Edouard opened his mouth. He wanted the soup now! But he stopped. He had a little problem. He could not remember the word.

"I forgot it," said Edouard. "It went out of my head!"

"Maybe it hid under the soup," said Grandma. They both looked. They saw only noodles. Edouard giggled.

"Say it with me," said Grandma. "Bismillah."

"Bismillah," said Edouard. It means "in the name of God." Then he took his first bite. Yum!

Then Edouard had an idea. He picked up his toy duck. "Duck, say Bismillah too!" he said.

The duck said nothing. Ducks cannot talk. So Edouard said it for the duck. "Bismillah, duck!"

Grandma laughed. Then she put one noodle on the duck's plate, just to meet the duck.

Edouard looked at the noodle. He looked at his bowl. One little word had made everyone happy. Even the duck had soup now.

"More Bismillah, please," said Edouard, and he held out his bowl.

Kinsley sat on the small red chair. The sun did shine through the big window. Mr. Côté picked up his guitar. "We will sing a rhyme today," he said. Gregoire and Julianne sat beside Kinsley.

Mr. Côté played very fast. Kinsley clapped fast. The words got all tangled. Julianne laughed. Gregoire looked grumpy. "My mouth can't say it that fast," he said.

Mr. Côté smiled. He played very slow. The words came out one by one. Kinsley clapped on the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Her hands made the sound match the song. She sang the whole rhyme from her head, all by herself.

"A song can go slow," said Kinsley. She clapped again, soft and steady. Mr. Côté nodded and played on.

Aaron sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a little rumble. "I want my noodles now," he said.

Mom put the pot on the stove. She stirred the warm water. Aaron watched from his chair. "Now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Now means at this very moment. The noodles need to cook first."

Aaron slid down from his chair. He hopped across the kitchen floor. Hop, hop, hop. His socks made a soft sound. He looked up at Mom. "Is it now?" he asked again.

"Not yet, sweet boy," said Mom. Aaron felt a big feeling in his tummy. Waiting felt so long.

Then Mom turned around. She held a steaming bowl. "Now!" she said. Aaron clapped his hands. He ate his noodles fast, fast, fast. The noodles were warm and squishy.

"Can I have a cookie now?" Aaron asked. Mom laughed a kind laugh. "A cookie later," she said. "Tomorrow you can help me bake more." Aaron smiled. "Today noodles, tomorrow cookies," he said. "That's right," said Mom, and she kissed his head.

Colton ran to the playground with his bear. He saw Avery by the slide. Avery was playing pretend.

"I am a dragon," said Avery. "A scary dragon!"

Colton hugged his bear tight. "A scary dragon?" he asked. He did not like scary dragons. His bear did not either.

"You be a dragon too," said Avery.

"No," said Colton. "I want a nice dragon. My bear wants a nice dragon."

Avery stopped and thought. "Okay," said Avery. "The dragon is nice. The dragon gives bear rides."

Colton smiled big. He held his bear up high. "Ride, bear, ride!"

Avery flapped her arms and stomped. They ran around the slide together. A spider sat on the fence and watched them play. Its web had a little hole in it. The spider worked and worked. Soon the hole was gone.

"Look, a spider web," said Colton.

"The dragon sees it too," said Avery. "The dragon says hello to the spider."

Colton laughed. "Nice dragons say hello to everyone."

They gave the bear one more ride. Then they sat in the shade. Mr. Murphy, the playground helper, waved from his bench nearby.

"Time for a snack," said Colton's dad.

Colton waved goodbye to Avery. "Play dragons tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Avery. "The nice one."

Elias was at Grandpa's house. He wanted a cookie. But the cookie jar sat up high. "First we wash the plate," said Grandpa. Elias sorted the spoons while Grandpa ran the water.

Then a girl next door came to play. Her name was Gwendolyn. "How old are you?" Grandpa asked her. Gwendolyn held up four fingers. "I am four," she said. Elias gasped. He held up four fingers too. "I am four too!" he said. They laughed and jumped.

Grandpa gave each of them one cookie. "Count them," he said. "One, two," said Elias. Gwendolyn counted the spoons next. "One, two, three, four, five." Elias counted the plates. "Six, seven, eight." Grandpa counted the cups. "Nine, ten."

After the cookies, they yawned big yawns. The cat was asleep in the sun. Grandpa tucked them under a soft blanket. "One blanket for two sleepy kids," he said. Elias closed his eyes and whispered, "One more cookie tomorrow?" Grandpa smiled and patted his head.

Naomi wanted to see Judy. "Can Judy come today?" she asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Now it is breakfast time. Judy can come later." Naomi frowned. Later felt very far away.

Naomi ate her eggs. She kicked her feet under the table. She asked again, "Is it later now?" Mom smiled. Mom pointed up at the wall. "That is a clock," Mom said. "The clock shows what time it is." The clock had a round face and two hands. Naomi watched the hands. They moved very slowly. She could hear a little tick, tick, tick.

Naomi watched the clock all morning. She built a tower. The hands moved a little. She painted a sticky honey cat. The hands moved a little more. The big hand went all the way around. Then the doorbell rang!

Judy was at the door. "It is later now!" Naomi shouted. Judy laughed. "My tummy rumbled," said Judy. "And then Mom said it was time."

The two girls played and played. Then Naomi looked up at the clock. The hands had moved again. "Mom!" she called. "Is it tomorrow yet?" "Not yet," said Mom. "Tomorrow comes after you sleep." Naomi nodded. Tonight she would watch the clock some more. Then she ran back to Judy and gave her a big hug.

Felix ran to the book corner at daycare. He had a big red book about trucks. "Ms. Wardak, read this one!" he said.

Ms. Wardak sat down. She opened the front cover first. Then she turned the pages one by one. She read the words out loud. "The truck goes up the hill," she said.

Felix looked at the little black marks on the page. "What are those?" he asked.

"Those are the words I am reading," said Ms. Wardak.

Felix turned a page. This page had only a picture. A big picture of a stinky garbage truck. "Read this page!" said Felix.

"There are no words on this page," said Ms. Wardak. "There is nothing written here to read. So I will just look at the picture too."

Abygael came over. "Let me try," she said. She started at the front. She turned pages the right way. "This page has words," she said. "Read it to me!"

Ms. Wardak read it. Abygael clapped.

Felix picked up a little book about a team of dogs. He started at the front. He turned each page. He pointed at the words. "These tell the story," he said. "This page has none. So we just look."

Ms. Wardak smiled. "You can tell me the story of the picture," she said.

Felix looked at the dogs. "The stinky team found a big bone!" he said.

Mya ran to the playground. Her friend Cruz was there. He was trying to stack big red blocks. His tower fell down. Cruz made an angry face. He kicked the soft grass.

Mya felt scared of his loud voice. She stepped back. Then she saw Cruz's nose turn red. A little tear came out. He sat down by the fence.

"Cruz, are you sad?" Mya asked. Cruz nodded. "I feel sad," he said. "My tower keeps falling."

Mr. Karimi came over. He heard Cruz's words. "I can help," said Mr. Karimi. He held the bottom blocks steady. Cruz stacked the top ones. Mya clapped. The tower stood tall and did not fall.

"My turn!" said Mya. Her fuzzy socks slipped on the grass. Cruz held her hand. "You can do it," he said. Mya stacked one block, then two, then three.

"I feel so happy!" Mya shouted. Cruz laughed. "Me too," he said.

Madison went to the laundromat with her dad. The washing machine spun round and round. It was not empty anymore. It was full of socks and shirts. Madison's new coat was warm, but it had no zipper at all. It had buttons instead.

"How do I make it close?" she asked. Her dad smiled. "Look for the little holes," he said. Madison pushed one button through one hole. Pop! It went through. She pushed the next button through the next hole. Pop! She counted out loud, "One, two, three, four." The coat closed all the way down. The wind outside could not get in.

Just then, the dryer stopped. Madison jumped up to see. Her dad pulled out the warm clothes. A little paper slip fell out of a pocket. "Look," said Madison, "my coat works, and the dryer works too." She did up her buttons again, all by herself, one, two, three, four.

Claire sat high in the big stadium. Her friend Niam sat beside her. They were watching the soccer game.

The players ran fast. They kicked the ball. Then a man blew a whistle. Toot! All the players stopped running.

"Why did they stop?" asked Claire.

"That is the referee," said Niam. "The referee blows a whistle to stop play."
