The referee put his hands out too. He waved one way, then a different way. Then he dropped the ball. The players ran again.

Later, Claire got a gift from her dad. It was a small toy whistle. She blew it. Toot!

"My turn," said Niam. He took the whistle and blew it too.

Claire laughed. "We are referees!" she said.

At the end, the big screen showed a player jumping like he could swim through the air. Everyone cheered. Claire blew her whistle one more time, very softly.

"Play on!" she said.

Beau went to the store with his dad. Beau loved the fruit part best.

"I want grapes," said Beau. "Can I have three?"

"Yes," said Dad. "Three grapes. Just three."

Beau opened the bag. He picked three big grapes. Then he found tiny grapes. He held one tiny grape. It was so small!

"Do little grapes count as one too?" asked Beau.

Dad smiled. "Three is three," he said. "Big or little."

So Beau put in one big grape. Then one little grape. Then one middle grape. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." It was still three grapes. Three always meant three!

At the register, the cashier said, "That will be ten dollars." Beau counted the bills with Dad. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

In the car, Beau ate his grapes. "Same three grapes I picked!" he said. He held up the little one.

"This one is my favorite," said Beau. "It is grape number two!"

Quinn was going to the national park. She packed her purple hat. The car was full of bags.

Quinn climbed into her seat. She looked out the window. She saw a big bird fly by.

Dad sat down. But the car did not go. "Click," said Dad. "Your buckle, Quinn."

Quinn looked down. Her buckle was not done. She had forgotten. She tried again. She pushed the buckle in.

Click! The car started to move.

The air came in the window a little bit. It smelled like pine trees. Quinn held her hat on her head.

At the park, Quinn saw deer. She saw a stream. She and Dad walked on a soft dirt path.

"Look, Dad," said Quinn. She pointed at a stick in the water. The water pushed the stick. The stick floated away.

Back at the car, Quinn climbed into her seat. Click! She did it all by herself. Dad smiled.

"Ready, Quinn?" said Dad.

"Yes," said Quinn. "Click!"

Ella ran to the park. The grass was bumpy under her shoes. She held her bunny toy tight.

Then Ella saw Emilia. Emilia sat by the slide. Tears ran down her face. "Emilia is crying," Ella thought. "She is sad."

Ella watched her friend. Emilia wiped her eyes. Her mouth turned down.

Ella ran over fast. "Bunny wants to hug you," she said. She held out her toy.

Emilia sniffled. She took the bunny. She hugged it soft. Then Emilia smiled a big smile. "Thank you," she said.

A happy feeling grew in Ella's tummy, warm like a bath.

"Bunny loves the slide," said Emilia. "Let's go!"

Ella felt so excited. She jumped up and down.

Together they climbed the steps. Bunny went first, whee, down the slide.

Theo went to the pharmacy with his dad. Theo did not wish to go. He was going to get a shot.

A nurse in a white coat came out. She had a tube around her neck. Theo pointed at the tube. "What is that?" he asked.

The nurse smiled. "This is my stethoscope," she said. "A doctor uses a stethoscope to listen to your heart beating. Would you like to hear yours?" Theo sat very still. The nurse put the little ends in his ears. She placed the round part on his chest. Then Theo heard a sound. Thump, thump. It was his own heart. "That is me!" said Theo. He listened again. Thump, thump.

Then it was time for the shot. Theo held his dad's hand. "Be brave, Theo," said his dad. The nurse counted one, two, three. It was done. Theo had one small bandage on his arm.

"Can I hear my heart again?" Theo asked. The nurse put the stethoscope on his chest once more. Thump, thump, it went, even faster now. "My heart runs fast," said Theo.

Hailey and her family were going on a trip. They stopped at a big diner by the road. Hailey sat in a red booth. Her tummy made a little growl. A nice waitress brought pancakes. Hailey ate them all up.

In her backpack, Hailey had her teddy bear. His name was Boo. After the diner, they drove to the airport. Hailey held her backpack tight. It was her carry-on bag. It would ride with her on the plane.

At the airport, a man in a uniform said, "Put your bag on the belt." Hailey put her backpack down. The belt moved. The backpack went into a big machine. The machine checked what was inside it.

Then Boo was gone! Hailey could not see him. "Boo!" she called. Her dad held her hand. "Watch the other side," he said. Hailey watched and watched. The belt kept moving. Then her backpack came out the other end. It popped out, safe and whole!

Hailey unzipped the bag. Boo was right there, soft and warm. She hugged him close. "You went through the machine," she whispered. A phone began to ring near by. It was time to walk to the plane. Hailey carried Boo all the way.

Beau wanted to help make breakfast. His family was in the kitchen. The table was wooden and warm in the sun.

"Mama, can I help?" he asked. Mama was making eggs. "You can wash the apples," she said. "The pan is hot, so I will stir."

Beau looked at the stove. It made a sizzle sound. Mama's hand stayed far from the heat. Beau stayed back too. He washed the apples in cold water. Brrr, it was chilly.

Then Beau saw something on the wall. It was a small hole with two little slots. It was behind the toaster. He wanted to put his finger in it.

He looked at his finger. He looked at the hole. Then he stopped.

"Mama, there is a hole here," he said. "It has slots. I did not touch it."

Mama came over. "Good job, Beau. Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet." She plugged the toaster into the slots. The bread popped up warm and brown.

Beau chewed his toast slowly. He looked at the wall one more time. Then he picked up another apple. "This one is for you, Mama," he said.

Eva went to the park with her friend Ella. They wanted to find something special. Ella peeked under a bush. She found a piece of paper. It was not special. Then Eva saw something in the deep grass. It was small and soft. It was gray and fluffy.

"What is it?" asked Ella. "A feather," said Ms. Schneider, who was walking by. "Birds are animals that have feathers," she said. Eva looked up. A big bird sat in the tree. The bird flapped its wings. A little feather fell down. It landed right by Eva's shoe.

The bird had lost a feather. Eva had found it. She held the feather up high. "It came from the bird!" she said. Ella clapped her hands. They put the feather in Eva's pocket. Then they waved at the bird. The bird flew away, over the swings and up into the sky.

Grandma came on the big train. Maverick held his dad's hand at the station. The train went choo, choo. Grandma hugged Maverick tight.

Grandma stayed for a whole week. They baked bread. Grandma let the oven. Maverick poured the sugar. They played trains at home. Every night Grandma read him a story.

Then the week was done. Grandma had to go home. Maverick felt sad. His eyes got wet. "I will miss you," he said. "We can keep in touch," said Grandma. "We can call on the phone. We can see each other on a video call. And we can send letters."

At the station, a plane flew up in the sky. The big train came in. Grandma waved from the window. The train went away. Maverick waved and waved.

At home, Maverick made a plan. He drew a picture of Grandma's train. His dad helped him write a letter. They put it in an envelope. Then they called Grandma on the phone. Her voice came right through. "I got a video call!" said Grandma's face on the screen.

"Draw me the plane next time," she said.

"Okay, Grandma," said Maverick. "I will draw a big one."

Snow fell all night! Brielle looked out the window. The sky was gray. The backyard was all white. "No school today!" said Dad. "It is a snow day!" Brielle jumped up and down. This was big news.

Dad said they could drive to the big hill. Mom packed a thermos of soup in a pot. Brielle pulled her red sled. Abbas and Gurfateh were there too. The hill was tall and fast.

Brielle got on her tummy. She wanted to go down head first. Dad held the sled. "Sit up, please," he said. "Face the way you are going. Hold on tight. I will watch you the whole way down." Brielle sat up. She faced forward. She held the string. Dad let go. She went fast, fast, fast! She did not tumble one bit. "Again!" she called. "Again!"

Luna set her books on the grass. Her dad helped her carry a little shelf outside. "Let's make a backyard library," her dad said. Luna clapped her hands.

Nash came over with his wagon. Sahib came too. "I want a book about animals," said Nash. Luna put all the animal books on one shelf. She put all the toy books on another shelf. She put all the food books on the last shelf. "Here are the animal books," said Luna. Nash found a book about a big brown bear.

Luna's dad put a magnet on the shelf door. It held a picture of a puppy. The picture did not fall down. "The magnet holds it," said Luna's dad.

Then Sahir looked and looked. "I can't find a book about food," he said. Luna pointed to the food shelf. The books stood there in a group. Sahib found a book about tasty apples. Nash read about the bear. Luna read about a red wagon that could drive down a hill.

The sun went warm on the grass. The friends sat in a little row. "Next time," said Luna, "the books will be easy to find." Nash turned a page and smiled at the bear.

Max went to the store with his dad. Max wanted the big red box. The box had words on it. "What does it say?" Max asked. "It says fish crackers," said his dad. Max looked and looked. The letters were like little bugs on the box. He could not hear them talk.

Then Max saw a small book. It had a fish on the front. He wanted that book so much. Max opened it and put his finger on the right side of the page. He slid his finger that way. Mr. Nair, the store man, shook his head with a smile. "Start here," he said. He pointed to the left side. Max put his finger on the left. He slid it to the right. "Fish!" Max read, all by himself.

Max held the book tight. His dad gave him a hug. "This book is special," Max said. At home, he slid his finger from left to right, page by page, all the way to the end. "Good night, fish," he said.

Madelyn went to the pharmacy with her dad. The shelves were tall and full. The soap bottles made the lights shine like little stars. Madelyn picked a pink soap. It smelled like juice!

At home, Dad put crackers on the table. Madelyn reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She hopped down and ran to the sink. Dad helped her turn on the water. It was warm. Madelyn pumped the soap. Bubbles grew and grew.

"Count with me," said Dad. They counted all the way to twenty. One, two, three, all the way to twenty! Madelyn rinsed the bubbles off. Then she held up her clean hands. "Look, Dad! All gone!" She sat down and ate her crackers. Dad gave her a big smile. Madelyn felt proud. Her hands smelled like sweet pink soap. She took another cracker and clapped her clean hands.

Lydia walked into the school cafeteria. It was her very first day. She held her lunch box with both hands. The room smelled like warm bread and juice. So many tables! So many chairs!

Mr. Berg stood by the wall. He clapped his hands once. Everyone sat down. Lydia blinked. Why did everyone sit? She stood there, wondering. Mr. Berg clapped again. Lydia looked around and sat down too. "You sat because of the clap?" she whispered.

A boy named Rayan leaned close. "We have rules," he said. "Everyone follows them." He pointed to a big poster. It had thick letters and a bright yellow star. Lydia looked at the poster. She traced the letters with her eyes.

Then it was time for milk. Lydia wanted to run to the front. But she saw everyone else wait in a line. A line was a rule too! She stepped in behind Rayan. The line moved, one step at a time.

At the table, Lydia opened her lunch box. She took out her thick red cup and her apple juice. "One more rule," said Rayan with a smile. "We color at the big table, and we eat at this table." Lydia looked at the crayons far away. Rules were everywhere!

She took a big sip of juice. Then she picked up her apple and held it high. "Apple for everyone?" she asked.

"No," laughed Rayan. "Apples are just for you!"

Juliette sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was full of warm soup. "One more bite," said Dad. Juliette took a big bite. Yum.

"I want to stay up late," said Juliette. "I want to play with my blocks." Dad said, "Okay, a little late." Juliette played and played. She did not sleep much.

The next morning, Dakota came over. They ran out to the yard. Juliette tried to run fast. Her legs felt slow. Her eyes felt heavy. She sat down on the grass near the swing. "I am too tired," she said.

That night, Juliette ate her dinner. She had a bath. She put on her soft pajamas. Then she said, "I will go to sleep now. Sleeping at night gives my body rest for the next day."

She slept and slept. In the morning, Dakota came again. Juliette ran fast in the yard. Her legs felt strong. "My rest worked!" she said. Dakota laughed, and they ran to the swing together.

Hazel went on a trip with her family. They slept in a tent at a campsite. Hazel helped put the sticks in a pile. Her dad made the fire, and Hazel watched from far away.

The next morning, Hazel walked to the lake. She took off her shoes and dug her toes in the sand. Then she put the shoes back on. "Time to go home," said her mom. Hazel hopped into the car with her sand shoes.

When they got home, her mom said, "Now we unpack." Hazel pulled out her shirt. She pulled out her socks. Then she shook out her shoes. Sand fell all over the floor! Hazel laughed and laughed. "The lake came home with me," she said. Her mom got the little brush. Hazel helped sweep the sand into her hand. They put the sand in the plant pot. "The plant will like it," Hazel said. Then she put her shoes by the door, all ready for the next trip.

Edouard loved basketball day in the school gymnasium. His team was the Blue Foxes. His friends Khalid and Abir were on the team too. But Edouard had a problem. The ball never went in. He threw it high. It hit the wall. He threw it low. It rolled away. "The hoop is playing tricks on me," he said.

Mr. Do blew his whistle. "Watch Abir," he said. Abir held the ball up. She bent her knees. She let it fly. Swish! The ball went through the hoop. The scoreboard changed. Two points! A shy boy on the bench whispered, "That's how our team scores." Edouard opened his eyes wide. The ball had to go through the hoop.

Edouard tried again. He bent his knees like Abir. He aimed up. The ball sailed through the net. "I did it!" he shouted. Khalid laughed and gave him a high five. Mr. Do clapped. After the game, they helped clean the floor. Edouard put the ball in the bag. "Same time next week?" said Abir. Edouard grinned. "Yes! I want more hoops!"

Ellie had big news. Her class was a team today, and they planted a little seed.

Dad was talking on the phone. Ellie pulled his sleeve. "Dad! Dad!"

Dad held up one finger. He kept talking. Ellie frowned.

Mom leaned close. "It is polite to wait until someone finishes talking," she whispered.

Ellie sat still. She smelled the warm soup. She heard Dad's voice go on and on.

Then Dad went quiet. Ellie saw the pause. "Dad, may I tell you something, please?"

"Yes, Ellie."

"We planted a seed! Salem watered it. I said thank you to Mr. Wong."

"That is happy news," said Dad. "May I see it soon?"

"Yes! I will show you."

Ellie gave Dad a kiss on his cheek. Dad smiled and finished his soup.

Wesley sat at the big table in the library. Ms. Ngo had set out paper and paint. Wesley wanted to paint a pumpkin. The pumpkin shape was big and round on his page.

But there was no orange paint. Wesley looked in every jar. Red, yellow, blue, green. No orange. He began to beg Ms. Ngo for more paint. "We are out," she said with a smile. "Try mixing what you have."

Wesley dipped his brush in the red paint. He made a red stripe on the pumpkin. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He painted right over the red. He rubbed it with his brush. The paint turned orange! Wesley gasped. He painted the whole pumpkin orange. Nicholas leaned over from his seat. "How did you do that?" he asked. "Red and yellow," said Wesley. He made one more stripe to show him.

Then Wesley painted a small orange cat beside the pumpkin. It was a tight little ball, sleeping in the grass. Nala came to look. "An orange animal!" she said. "I want to paint one too." She took the red jar and the yellow jar, and she began to stir.

Nora went to the library with her dad. She was excited to pick new books. She found a book about bears and hugged it tight.

Then Nora heard a big noise. It went bang, bang, bang. It came from behind the tall shelf. Nora felt scared. Her tummy felt small and tight. She wanted to run and hide under the table.

But Nora remembered something. When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help. She ran to her dad. "I am scared," she said. "There is a big noise." Her dad held her hand. They walked to the shelf together. Mr. Nolan, the library man, was there. A heavy book had a big fall from the top. Bang! That was the smelly old book that made the loud noise.

"Nothing bad," said Mr. Nolan. He picked up the book and smiled. Nora felt happy again. She was not scared anymore. Her dad read her the bear book in the soft chair. Nora leaned on his arm and turned the pages. "Again," she said.

Penelope ran out to the playground. The sun was big and bright. "Sunny today!" said Dax. Penelope looked up. The sun made her eyes go small. She could not see the slide. She held Emmitt's hand tight.

"Why are my eyes squinting?" she asked. Ms. Sokolov smiled. "Try a sun hat," she said. She got a blue hat. Penelope put it on. The hat made shade over her face. Now her eyes opened wide. She could see the whole slide. She could see Dax waving. She could see the swing.

It was windy too. The wind blew Emmitt's scarf. It flapped like a tail. "Your scarf looks funny," said Penelope. Emmitt laughed and held it.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain came down. Rain was not scary. Ms. Sokolov opened umbrellas. "Rainy days need umbrellas," she said. They walked inside. Penelope kept her hat on. "My hat helps in the sun," she said. "I want to wear it again tomorrow." Dax said, "Me too!"

Hayden was wide awake. Today was the big lunch at the community hall. His friend Jorawar was coming too. There was a long table with bread, cheese, and apples from the garden.

A bell did ring. "Ding, ding!" Everyone sat down. Hayden saw the bread. His tummy was growling. He was so hungry. He reached out his hand and grabbed a big piece.

Jorawar shook his head. "Not yet," he said. "We say the blessing first."

"But I'm hungry now," said Hayden.

"In my family, we all wait," said Jorawar. "We wait until the blessing is done. Then we eat."

Hayden looked at the bread. He put it back on his plate. He folded his hands. Jorawar's dad said some soft words. Hayden listened. Ms. Hughes, the neighbor, was listening too. So was Ariel, from down the street.

The blessing was finished. "Now we eat!" said Jorawar.

Hayden picked up his bread. He took a big, big bite. "Mmm," he said. "Waiting made it taste extra good."

"Maybe it did," laughed Jorawar. "Or maybe you were just very, very hungry."

Hayden laughed too. He passed the apples to Ariel. Then he rang the little bell himself, just for fun. "Ding, ding!" he said. "More bread, please!"

Milan stood by the fruit bins in the corner store. His mom let him pick apples. He put apples in the bag, one by one. "One, two, three, four," he said.

Next to him, his friend Jaylen picked oranges. Jaylen put oranges in his bag. "One, two, three," said Jaylen.

Milan looked at both bags. "My bag has more," he said. "I have four. You have three."

Jaylen picked one more orange. He put it in his bag. "One more," said Jaylen.

"Now we count again," said Milan. He pointed with one finger. "One, two, three, four." Jaylen's bag had four apples now, too.

"Same!" said Milan. His mom smiled and gave him a hug. Milan winked his eye at Jaylen. "Want one more, too?" he asked.

Jaylen picked up one more orange.

Rose was at Grandma's house. Then the lights went out. All dark!

Grandma found a candle. She lit it herself. The little flame danced.

"Can I hold the candle?" Rose asked.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "Only a grown-up lights candles. And only a grown-up looks after them. Here is your own light."

It was a flashlight. Rose shook it. She clicked it on. A quick white beam lit the hall!

Grandma walked with the candle. She set it on a safe table. She watched it there.

Rose walked with her flashlight. She pointed it at the wall. She pointed it at her teddy. One beam, two feet, three toes. "I see your toes, teddy!"

Then the lights came back on. Rose clicked the flashlight off. The candle was out too, and Grandma blew a little smoke away.

"Where does the light sleep now?" Rose wondered. She held the flashlight close, like a magnet to the fridge, all the way to bed.

Isabella ran into the music room at the community center. Ms. Pelletier had a big box on the table. "Recorders for everyone!" she said. Isabella picked one up. It felt smooth and cool in her hands.

Juniper sat next to her. "Let's play!" said Juniper. Isabella blew into her recorder. It made a loud squeak. Juniper laughed. Then Juniper's recorder squeaked too. Isabella felt a little sad. She wanted a pretty sound, not a squeak.

Ms. Pelletier came over. "Look at your fingers," she said. Isabella looked. One finger was up a tiny bit. A hole was showing. Isabella pressed her finger down. She covered the hole all the way. She blew again. Out came a clear, pretty note. "I did it!" she shouted.

It was like a puzzle. Cover the holes one way, get one note. Cover them another way, get a new note. Isabella covered a different hole. A new note came out. Lucille clapped. "Play it again!" she said. Isabella took a big breath and played the new note one more time.

Ayla was at Ariyah's house. Ariyah had a shiny red truck. It had a big button on top. Ayla wanted to push the button very much.

Ariyah pushed the button. The truck made a funny sound. Ayla reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She put her hand in her lap instead. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked.

Ariyah looked at Ayla. Ariyah smiled big. "Yes! You can go next." She pushed the button two more times. Then she gave the truck to Ayla.

Ayla pushed the button. Beep, beep! The truck rolled past a paper flower on the rug. Ariyah clapped her hands.

Ariyah's mom came in with apple slices. "You two are sharing so nicely," she said.

"Next it is your turn again," Ayla said. She held the truck out to Ariyah.

"You push it," said Ariyah. "I like the sound."

Ayla pushed the button one more time. Beep!

Romy wanted to wear her red coat all by herself. She pushed one arm into a sleeve. Then she hunted for the other sleeve. The sleeve was hiding behind her back. She twisted and wiggled. The sleeve still hid.

Her friend Lochlan came to play. He saw her arm waving in the air. "Put the coat on the floor," he said. Romy laid the coat flat on the grass-green rug. "Now put both arms in," said Lochlan. Romy knelt down. She pushed one arm in, then the other. "Now flip it over your head," said Lochlan.

Romy stood up and flipped. The coat jumped up over her head and landed on her. Both sleeves were on. She pulled the zipper tab. Up it went, zzzz, all the way to her chin. "I did it," said Romy. Outside, the rain began to tap on the window. "Rain," said Lochlan. "Good thing we have coats." Romy looked at her slimy-wet rain boots by the door and smiled. "Let's go splash."

Ruby wanted to say the blessing all by herself. Grandma was coming for dinner, and Ruby had a big job.

"What is the bread blessing called?" Ruby asked.

"It is called the Hamotzi," said Mom. "Many Jewish families say it over the bread."

"Can I say it tonight?" asked Ruby.

"Yes," said Mom. "Let's practice."

Ruby practiced all day. She said it to her teddy bear. She said it to the cat. She said it fast and she said it slow. Her words felt loose at first, tumbling out all mixed up.

Then Mom called, "Grandma is here!"

Ruby ran to the door. Grandma picked her up and hugged her tight. Ruby's tummy did a happy jump.

Dad put the warm bread on the table. It was Friday night. Snow was falling outside the window. Everyone washed their hands and sat down.

"Who will say the Hamotzi?" Grandma asked.

"Me!" said Ruby. "I practiced all day!"

Ruby took a big breath. She said the words slowly and clearly. When she finished, everyone said "Amen" and smiled at her.

Grandma kissed the top of her head. Then Dad tore the bread and gave Ruby the first piece.

"It tastes even better tonight," said Ruby, taking a big bite.

Ava sat in the kitchen. Her mom cut an apple into small slices. "After snack, we go to the dentist," Mom said. Ava looked at her apple. She did not want to go.

"Open big," said the dentist. Ava opened her mouth. The dentist looked at her front teeth. "Front teeth are for biting food," the dentist said. Then he looked way in the back. "Back teeth are for chewing it." Ava got a shiny sticker. The dentist smiled.

On the bus home, Mom gave Ava an apple slice. Ava bit it with her front teeth. The apple came off in her mouth. Then she chomped it with her back teeth. Chomp, chomp, chomp. "I did it!" Ava said. Mom began to laugh. "My big dentist girl," she said. Ava held up her sticker to the window, and the sun made it shine.

Declan sat at the kitchen table. The bowls were warm with soup. His spoon sat by his hand. He wanted to eat right away.

"First we say our blessing," said Dad. Declan folded his hands. Dad began to speak. Declan waited. The soup smelled good. He watched steam rise. Still Dad kept talking. When would it end?

Then Dad said one word. "Amen." Mom said "Amen" too. Their hands opened. Their spoons came up. So that was the end word. Declan dug his spoon into the soup.

"Amen," said Declan, nice and loud, before his next bite. Mom laughed. "You can say it with us next time," she said.

At dinner the next night, Declan said the word with them. Then he picked up his spoon.

Benjamin woke up early. The sun was shining in the sky. It was a sunny day. He wanted to run into the backyard right away.

"Wait," said his dad. "Sunscreen first. Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn."

His dad rubbed white cream on Benjamin's arms. One arm, two arms, one nose. Then Benjamin ran outside. The sun felt warm on his skin. His skin did not turn red. His friend Braelyn came over. She had sunscreen on too. "Look," she said. "My skin is not red."

Then the wind began to blow. It was windy. The wind made the leaves dance. Benjamin's hat went up, up, up. He did not want to lose his hat. He held it with his hand.

"Where does the wind come from?" Braelyn asked.

Benjamin pointed at the big tree. "It comes from there," he said.

The wind blew a little more. Then it stopped. The leaves sat still on the grass. Benjamin and Braelyn sat down too. The warm sun shone on them, and they ate apple slices together.

Emile sat at the dinner table. His dad put eggs on his plate. Next to the salt was a little glass timer. It was full of sand.

"How was school?" Dad asked.

Emile took a big breath. "Gio had the scooter," he said. "I wanted it too. I grabbed it. Then we both pulled."

"That sounds hard," said Dad.

"Then Mr. Choi came," said Emile. "He had a sand timer, just like that one. He turned it over. The sand went down, down, down. Gio rode the scooter until the sand ran out. Then it was my turn!"

Dad smiled. "Did you wait?"

"I waited," said Emile. "I watched the sand. When it ran out, Gio gave me the scooter. I rode fast. It tickled my tummy to go so fast! Gio clapped for me. Then the sand ran out again, and I gave it back. Gio is my friendly friend now. We said we will ride again in the summer."

Dad picked up the little timer. He turned it over. "Watch," he said.

The sand went down, down, down. Emile watched every bit of it.

"When the sand runs out, you get dessert," said Dad.

Emile laughed. "I can wait! I am good at waiting now!"

The last bit of sand fell. Dad brought a bowl of strawberries. Emile shared one with his dad.

Iris wanted to give her cookie to the new girl. The new girl sat by the fence. Her name was Louisa. Iris walked over slowly. She held out the cookie. "Here you go," said Iris. Louisa took it. Then Louisa said, "Gracias."

Iris stood still. That was a new word. She looked at Louisa. Louisa smiled. "It means thank you," said Louisa. "It is how we say thank you in Spanish." Iris tried the word in her mouth. "Grah-see-as," she said slowly. Louisa nodded. Iris said it again. "Gracias!" This time it came out fast.

Louisa ran to get her ball. She came back and rolled it to Iris. "Please can I have a turn?" asked Iris. She rolled it back. Then Louisa dropped the ball. "Sorry," said Louisa. "It is okay," said Iris. They kept playing until the sky turned orange. Louisa waved. "Adios," she said. Iris waved too. "Adios!"

Declan was hungry at daycare. It was snack time. Ms. Diallo had a tray of sandwiches. Some sandwiches were squares. Some were cut into triangles.

Declan picked a triangle piece. He held it up. "Look, Avreen," he said. "Mine has corners." Avreen held hers up too. "Count them," she said. Declan touched each corner with one finger. "One, two, three," he said. "Three corners!" Avreen counted the sides of her piece. She drew a line in the air with her finger. "One, two, three," she said. "Three sides."

Then Declan wanted a square piece too. But Lisa had the last square. Lisa looked sad because she wanted a triangle. "We can trade," said Declan. Lisa gave him the square. He gave her the triangle.

Declan bit a corner off the square. He counted what was left. "One, two, three," he said, laughing. "Now mine has three corners!" Lisa took a big bite of her triangle. "Yummy," she said. "Not yucky at all."

Beau wanted the red hammer from the toy shelf. It was the best hammer in the whole class. Today it was a magic hammer, and he was a builder with a big job.

But Selena stood right in front of the shelf. She was building a tall, tall tower. Beau tried to squeeze past her. He bumped the tower. Blocks fell everywhere. Selena looked angry.

"Sorry," said Beau. He put the blocks back one by one.

Then he remembered. Ms. Kapoor said the magic words. "Excuse me," said Beau. "Can I get past you?"

Selena stepped aside. "Excuse you!" she said.

Beau reached the shelf. He picked up the red hammer. "Thank you," he said.

Selena smiled. "Build a magic house for my tower?"

Beau tapped the hammer in the air. "One magic house, coming up!"

Henry sat in the school library. He had a glass of water on the table. Next to it was a bowl of crunchy crackers. Mr. Islam put out big letter cards.

Henry picked up a card. "That is A," said Alexandre. "A says ah." Henry tapped it. "Ah," he said. He found B. Then he found more and more.

"Stop," said Henry. "The letters end here. This is P." Alexandre shook his head slowly. He waited. Henry looked and looked.

Then Henry began the alphabet song. He sang it all alone. L, M, N, O, P. He kept singing. The song did not stop. He sang all the way to the end. "Z!" said Henry. "The alphabet ends with Z."

Mr. Islam smiled. "Try it again," he said. Henry started over at A. He took a slow bite of a crunchy cracker. Then he tapped each card, one by one, and sang the letters like fish that swim in a long, long line, all the way to Z.

Oliver sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump down the road. He had a basket of picture cards. Oh no. The basket tipped over. All the cards fell to the bottom of the car. What a mess.

"I can fix it," said Oliver. He picked up a card with a cow. Then a card with a duck. He put them in one pile. "Animals," he said. Then he found a card with a ball. Then a card with a teddy bear. He made a new pile. "Toys," he said. Then he found a card with an apple. Then a card with bread. He made one more pile. "Foods," he said.

Riley sat beside him. Riley held out a card with a carrot. "Where does this go?" Oliver took it. He put it in the food pile. The car was quiet now. Every card had its own pile. "You can send the basket back now," said Riley. Oliver slid it over with his foot. Then he held his animal pile up to the window. "Look, cow," he said. "Moo."

Wyatt ran to the park with his juice. The wind blew hard. It was a windy day. "Where is the ice cream truck?" he asked. The truck came on Saturdays.

Yesterday the truck came. Yesterday Wyatt had a red ice pop. Today Wyatt wanted one again.

Aicha was at the swings. "The truck is coming soon," she said. "Soon?" said Wyatt. "Soon means in a little while." Wyatt sat on the bench. He counted the clouds. One, two, three.

Would soon be long? Wyatt did not know. He watched the gate. He sipped his juice. A little while went by.

Then he heard it. Music! The ice cream truck turned the corner. "It came!" Wyatt shouted. He jumped up. "Soon was not long at all," said Aicha. Wyatt waved to Mr. Aquino, who drove the truck. "One ice pop, please," said Wyatt. "Maybe tomorrow I will get two."

Ellie sat at the dinner table. She held her spoon with both hands. "Can we go to Juliette's house now?" she asked.

Mom shook her head. "Not now, sweet pea. We go tomorrow."

Ellie frowned. "What is tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow is the day after today," said Mom. "First comes today. Then comes tomorrow."

"But I want it now," said Ellie.

"Today we eat dinner," said Mom. "Then you sleep. When you wake up, it is tomorrow. Then we go to Juliette's."

Ellie ate a bite of pasta. She thought about that. Yesterday she had gone to the playground. That was over and done. Today was right now, pasta in her spoon, Mom beside her. Tomorrow was still coming, like a friend walking toward the door.

After dinner, Ellie put on her pajamas. She brushed her teeth. Dad read her a book about a small red hen. Then Ellie closed her eyes and slept.

The sun came up. Ellie opened her eyes. She looked out the window and saw the light. "It's tomorrow!" she shouted.

Mom smiled. "Yes. Now it is today, a new today."

At Juliette's house, they played with blocks. Juliette stacked them tall. Ellie put one on the very top. The tower stood up, and Ellie felt proud.

"Yesterday I wanted to come," said Ellie. "And now I am here!"

Juliette laughed and hugged her. "Let's build another one," she said.

Brooklyn went to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on the slide. "The slide is hot from the sun," said Dad. He touched it first, so Brooklyn could see. Brooklyn slid down the cool side, where the shade was.

Then Brooklyn saw the big red ball. It rolled far, far away. It went past the swings. It went to the tall trees at the far end. Brooklyn ran after it. She ran and ran. Then she stopped. She looked back. She could not see Dad. The trees were in the way.

Brooklyn stood very still. She did not like this. So she picked up the ball and walked back, past the swings, past the sandbox. Dad waved from the bench. "I can see you now!" he said. Brooklyn ran to him and hugged his leg. She stayed close and rolled the ball back and forth with her feet.

At snack time, Dad put juicy apple slices on a plate. A dog near the fence began to bark. Brooklyn looked up. "Stay here where I can see you," said Dad, "and we will watch the dog together." Brooklyn sat and ate her apple, bite by bite. Then she said, "Can we go on the swings?" Dad smiled and held out his hand. "Yes, but stay where I can see you," he said. Brooklyn took his hand and they walked to the swings side by side.

Caleb woke up early. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. "What if I get lost?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Your teacher will help you," she said. "You will see."

Caleb put on his red shoes. Then he zipped up his bag. The zipper went zzzzip, and the bag was closed. One thing made another thing happen. Mom laughed. "That was easy," she said. "Easy, peasy," said Caleb. He said it two times. "Easy, peasy!"

Then they walked to school. Caleb began to hurry. He ran ahead on the path. "Wait," said Mom. At the school door, Caleb saw his class. The children stood one behind the other. They were walking in a line. Misha stood in the line too. "Where do I go?" Caleb asked. "Find your spot in the line," said Mom. "The line? The line?" said Caleb. He stepped in behind Misha. Misha turned and waved. Caleb waved back. The line moved, and Caleb moved with it.

Felix was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make soup for the family. Grandma said he could help. First they got a big pot. It felt rough on the sides. Felix put carrots in the pot, one by one. Then an onion went in too.

Grandpa picked up the knife. He cut the onion, slowly and carefully. Then Grandpa's eyes began to water. Tears ran down his face. Felix stopped. "Grandpa, are you sad?" he asked.

Grandpa shook his head. "The onion makes my eyes sting," he said. "They water like this." Felix looked at the onion. He looked at Grandpa's face. So the onion did that! Felix waited by the door while Grandpa cut the rest. Grandpa blinked and blinked. Then his eyes were fine.

The soup sat on the stove, where Grandma watched it. Felix sat on a stool and waited some more. The kitchen began to smell good. A little mouse ran past the window outside. Felix hopped off his stool to see. The mouse was gone, but the pot was bubbling. "Soup is ready!" Grandma called. Felix smiled and got the spoons.

Romy sat in the big chair at the barbershop. Her hair was long and curly. Today she would get her first haircut. Mr. Luo smiled at her. He held up a big blue cape.

"Where does that go?" Romy asked.

"It goes around your shoulders," said Mr. Luo. He wrapped it around her and snapped it shut. "The cape keeps the cut hair off your clothes."

Mr. Luo picked up his scissors. Snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off the cape and onto the floor. Not one bit went on Romy's shirt.

Romy looked at the cape. She held out her arms. "I'm a superhero!" she said.

Mr. Luo laughed. "A winter superhero," he said. "It is cold outside today."

He unlocked the door lock to let Romy's mom come in. The door swung open. Romy waved her cape arms.

"My hair is short now," said Romy. "And my shirt is still clean!"

Noah ran to the sandbox at summer camp. James was already there. James had the big blue truck. Noah wanted it right now.

Noah reached out his hand. "My turn!" he said. He grabbed at the truck. James held it tight. Ms. Nair came over fast.

"Noah, we take turns," she said. "James is playing now. You can have the truck next."

Noah sat down. Waiting felt so long. He puffed out his cheeks. Then he saw the sand. It was loose and soft. Noah patted it. He piled it up high. "A sandcastle!" he said. "It looks like a castle by the ocean!" James looked over and laughed.

Noah made a door. He made three little towers. The sandcastle grew tall. Then James said, "Here, Noah. Your turn now." He held out the blue truck.

Noah took the truck. Vroom, vroom! He drove it around the sandcastle. "Now I know," Noah said. "When I wait, I can build!"

"Want a turn again?" Noah asked James. James nodded big. Noah handed the truck back. Then he patted more sand. "This time I will build a bridge!"

Jaxon was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big drum. "You can play it," said Grandma.

Jaxon hit the drum hard. BOOM! The drum made a loud sound. The baby woke up and cried. "Oh no," said Jaxon. "Too loud, too loud, too loud."

Grandma sat close by him. "Try again," she said. Jaxon hit the drum soft. Tap. The drum made a little sound. The baby went back to sleep. "Little tap, little sound," said Jaxon. He tapped again and again. Tap, tap, tap. The cozy room stayed quiet.

Jaxon took the drumstick in his hand. He made one long line of taps, all soft. The baby slept on. Grandma smiled. "Play for the baby," she said. Jaxon tapped his soft song.

Jules sat at the old kitchen table. On the table were three things. There was a feather. There was a pinecone. There was a small blanket.

"Let's play a game," said his grandma. "Sort them. Soft things go here. Rough things go there."

Jules picked up the feather. He rubbed it on his cheek. It tickled. It felt soft. He put it in the soft pile. Then he touched the pinecone. "Ow," he said. "It is bumpy." It felt rough. It went in the rough pile. Last, he touched the blanket. It was soft and warm. He hugged it.

"My hands did it!" said Jules. "My skin can feel soft and rough."

Grandma smiled. "Yes. And what do your eyes do?"

"They see the soup!"

Grandma stirred the hot soup on the stove. Steam went up. "Sniff," said Jules. "My nose smells it." He listened too. "Blub, blub," went the pot. "My ears hear it!"

"Time to taste," said Grandma. She gave him a cool spoon of soup.

"Mmm," said Jules. "My mouth tastes tomato!"

He licked his lips and patted the soft blanket. "Five senses," he said. "I used them all."

Hudson sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. Ms. Chanthavong put a cape on him. It was soft and it fit just right. "Time for your first haircut," she said.

Hudson's dad stood close by. Ms. Chanthavong picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some landed on Hudson's neck. Hudson began to wiggle. He scratched his neck with his hand.

"Why are you wiggling?" Ms. Chanthavong asked. "My neck feels itchy," Hudson said. She smiled and picked up a soft brush. She brushed the little hairs away, tick tick tick. The itchy feeling went away too. Hudson sat very still. "Where did the hairs go?" he asked. "Into my brush," she said. She tapped it over a bin. The bin was empty, and now tiny hairs fell inside.

Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. When a hair landed on his neck, Hudson said, "Itchy!" Ms. Chanthavong brushed it off right away. Then the haircut was all done. Hudson looked in the mirror. "I see a big boy," he said. Dad gave him a thumbs up, and Hudson grinned all the way home.

Kinsley woke up at Grandma's house. Today was the big party! It was a festival day for the whole family. Kinsley ran to her little bag of clothes. She pulled out her red coat. She pulled out her bunny pajamas. She pulled out her sparkly gold dress. "Which one?" she said. She could not pick.

Grandma came in with a shiny blue dress. It had tiny stars on it. "Look what I made for you," said Grandma. "People often wear special clothes to a celebration," said Grandma. Kinsley touched the stars. They were soft.

"Special dress for a special day!" said Kinsley. She put it on. It swished when she twirled. Her cousin pointed a paper plane toward her. "You look like a star!" he said. Grandma sent Kinsley to the kitchen to see the tasty bread. The whole family wore their bright, pretty clothes too. Kinsley twirled again and again. "Festival day!" she said.

Mya was at Grandma's house. Grandma made hot toast. Mya wanted to spread the butter all by herself. "You are a big girl now," said Grandma. She gave Mya a dull knife, safe for small hands.

Mya poked the toast with the pointy tip of the knife. The toast got holes in it. Butter chunks fell off. "That is a mess," said Mya. Grandma smiled and waited.

Then Mya turned the knife over. She used the flat side. She pushed the butter across the bread. The butter went soft and did not stick to the knife anymore. It covered the toast all over. "I did it!" said Mya. Then she poured milk into her cup. A little spilled. She poured again, slow and slow. Not one drop fell. Grandma clapped. Mya took a big bite, and the toast popped a crumb onto her nose. Mya giggled and licked it off.

Ibrahim went to the store with his dad. The store smelled like fresh bread. He heard the carts squeak on the floor.

Ibrahim saw a little book on a shelf. It had a red truck on the front. "Can we get it?" he asked. "Please?"

"Yes," said his dad. "You hold it in the cart."

At home, Dad opened the book. "I start at the front," Dad said. He turned page one, then page two. He read, "The red truck goes up the hill."

Then Mom came in. She sat down by Ibrahim. "My turn to read," she said. She opened the front of the book too. She read, "The red truck goes up the hill."

Ibrahim sat up tall. "Mom, you said the same words as Dad!"

"Yes, I did," said Mom.

"Even though you are not Dad?"

"Even though," said Mom, with a smile.

Ibrahim looked at the page. The little black marks sat there, quiet and still. "Dad," he asked, "can the book say something new tomorrow?"

"No," said Dad. "The words will say the same thing. Every time."

The next morning, Ibrahim brought the book to his friend Remington. "You read it," he said. Remington turned to page one. "The red truck goes up the hill," Remington read.

Ibrahim clapped his hands. He pointed at the last page, where the truck was missing its driver. "Now turn to the back," he said. "That part is my favorite."

Ellie sat at the dinner table. She had a big glass of water with her pasta. She drank and drank. Then she felt it. "I need to go!" she said. Her mom took her to the little toilet.

Ellie ran back to the table. Her mom followed. "Ellie, did you flush?" her mom asked. Ellie looked at the hall. The toilet was still full. She had forgotten!

Ellie ran back. She pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled away. Then she turned on the sink. She washed her hands with soap. Bubbles!

"Wash hands after the toilet?" Ellie asked. "Yes, every time," said her mom. Ellie remembered both steps now. Flush, then wash.

Back at the table, Ellie got a big hug. The pasta was still warm. Ellie smiled and took another bite.

Eloise went to the store with her dad. Snow was falling outside the big window. "We need apples," her dad said. "Can you count them?"

Eloise put apples in the bag. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. Oh no. What came after two? She could not remember. This was a problem.

Then Eloise heard a song in her head. It was the song from school. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang softly. "Three, four, shut the door." Nyah had sung it with her in class. The song rhymed, and the rhymes pulled the numbers out, one by one.

"Five, six, pick up sticks," she went on. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." An apple rolled off the pile. Eloise caught it and put it back. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!"

"Ten apples," she said. "I did it!"

A voice sang from behind the apples. "A big fat hen!" It was Mr. Cardinal, her neighbor, holding a basket of eggs. "I love that song," he said. He held up the basket. "And look, I have the hen's eggs right here."

"Ten eggs?" asked Eloise.

Mr. Cardinal laughed and counted them out loud. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

At home, Eloise bit into a red apple. It was a little bit sour. She made a funny face, and her dad laughed. "Want a sweet one next time?" he asked.

"Yes," said Eloise. "I will count to ten again."

Ezra loved snack time at daycare. Today Mr. Desir had a big bowl of green peas. "Would you like some peas, Ezra?" he asked. Ezra put out his cup. "Yes, please," he said. The peas went plop, plop, plop.

Mehreen sat next to him. Mr. Desir held the bowl out to her. Mehreen looked at the peas. "Yuck!" she shouted very loud. Mr. Desir jumped a little. His spoon fell on the floor. Mehreen's face went red. Nobody said anything for a minute.

Then Mehreen tried again, in a small voice. "No, thank you," she said. Mr. Desir smiled. "Thank you for telling me," he said. He picked up the spoon and washed it. Then he found some orange crackers just for her. Mehreen munched her crackers. Ezra munched his peas. The table felt happy and quiet.

After snack, Ezra and Mehreen played dragons. The blocks became a dragon castle. "Help, my dragon is stuck!" said Ezra. Kacey came over. "I can help," said Kacey. They pulled the dragon out together.

At rest time, Ezra lay on his mat. His bottom was cozy under his blanket. His eyes felt heavy. He closed them and began to sleep. Before he drifted off, he heard Mehreen whisper, "No, thank you, dragon. This mat is mine."

John ran to the play corner at daycare. Hayes was there with a big toy kitchen. A purple pot sat on the little stove. A stuffed horse lay in a small bed.

"I want to be the dad," said Hayes.

"I want to be the dad too," said John.

Ms. Mensah knelt down beside them. "When you play house, each person can pick a role," she said. "Someone can be the parent. Someone can be the baby."

John looked at the stuffed horse. The horse could not be the baby. It was just a toy. "Then who will be the baby?" he asked.

"I can be the baby first," said Hayes. "You be the dad. Then we switch."

"Switch?" asked John.

"Yes. Halfway through, we trade jobs."

So John was the dad first. He stirred the purple pot. He fed the horse from a small bottle. Then he gave Hayes a blanket, and Hayes pretended to cry like a baby.

"Now we switch," said Hayes.

John lay down in the little bed. Hayes patted his head. "Sleep, little baby," Hayes said.

John closed his eyes and smiled. Being the baby was fun too. Which job would he pick next time? Maybe he would pick both.

Maverick sat on the back step. His dad had asked him a question. "Can you name your five senses?" Maverick knew only one. "Eyes see," he said. He wanted to know the rest. He sat very still and waited.

His ears began to pick things up. A bird sang. A dog barked next door. The wind whooshed in the tree. Maverick pointed at his ear. "Ears hear!" he said. Then he touched the warm step with his hand. "Skin feels!" He sniffed the air. Dad was cooking, and the smell made his tummy rumble. "Nose smells!" He licked his lips and tasted an apple Dad gave him. "Tongue tastes!"

Then a small surprise came. His friend Damien climbed over the low fence. "What are you doing?" Damien asked. "My five senses," said Maverick. "Want to meet them?" Damien sat down too. He closed his eyes. He heard a bird, then a bee, then his own tummy. "Ears hear," Damien said. Maverick smiled and pointed at the empty apple core. "That one is all done."

It was a sunny day at the park. Maverick played a game with Jayda and Zayn. It was hide-and-seek. Ms. Farah counted to ten by the swings. Maverick ran to the big tree. He stood by the trunk and put his hands over his eyes. Everything went dark. Now he could not see the swings or the slide.

"I hope Jayda can't see me," he said. He heard Jayda's feet on the grass with his ears. He smelled the flowers near the tree with his nose. He touched the rough bark with his fingers. Then Jayda said, "I see you, Maverick!" Maverick took his hands off his eyes. He saw Jayda pointing at him.

"Can you see me when my eyes are closed?" he asked. "Yes," said Jayda. "You cover your eyes. You don't cover mine." Maverick laughed. Next time, he hid behind the tree with his eyes open.

Emile sat on the soft mat at the community centre. Ms. Chen put out two groups of toy cars. "Which group has more?" she asked. Emile wanted to know, but the cars were all mixed up on the floor. He had to count them. Counting felt a little scary with so many cars.

Emile began at the red car. He touched each car as he counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven cars! His friend Oakley sat on the other side. Oakley started at the blue car, the far end. He counted the same cars, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven too!

Emile frowned. "You started at a different car," he said. Oakley nodded. "I started at the blue one." They counted again, slowly. Emile started at the blue car this time. The number stayed seven. Oakley started at the red car. The number stayed seven. Emile clapped his hands.

Then Ms. Chen held up the second group. It was a long line of cars, like a little ocean of colours. Emile counted from the left side. Oakley counted from the right side. Both of them said "ten" at the very same time. "Ten is more than seven," said Emile. He picked up the ten side and hugged the whole row of cars.

Alice ran to the community garden with her dad. "Today we plant seeds!" she said. Mr. Toussaint handed her tiny carrot seeds. Alice made little holes in the dark soil. She dropped the seeds in. Then she covered them up. "Grow, grow, grow," she sang.

Every day Alice came back with her watering can. Jameson came too. They looked and looked. Then one morning, green tops peeked out! "It happened!" Alice shouted. Jameson clapped his hands.

A thick green weed grew next to the carrots. "I will pick that weed," said Alice. She pulled it gently. Up it came. Alice stared. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom. "Look, look, look!" she cried. Jameson leaned close. "Those roots grew down into the soil," Alice said. Mr. Toussaint nodded. All over the town, under every plant, roots were growing down.

Alice patted the soil flat again. She watered her carrots. "Your roots go down," she whispered. "Grow big." The green tops waved in the sun. Alice waved back.

Evan went to the library with his friend Kacey. Mr. Kerr had a big box of new books. "One book each," said Mr. Kerr. Evan picked a book about trucks. Kacey picked a book about a bear.

Kacey read fast. Soon she wanted Evan's truck book too. Evan held it close. Then he looked at her book. The bear had a big, wide yawn. Evan wanted to see it. "You read mine," said Evan. "I read yours." They swapped books. That worked well.

At the desk, Mr. Kerr stamped Evan's book. Evan took it and ran to the door. Kacey stopped him. "Wait," she said. "What do we say?" Evan thought hard. He ran back to the desk. "Thank you, Mr. Kerr," he said. Mr. Kerr smiled a big smile.

"Thank you too," said Mr. Kerr. "For remembering." Evan gave his book a little kiss and hugged it tight.

"Can we cook pretend soup with the bear book?" Kacey asked. Evan laughed all the way to the car.

Jules went to the store with his dad. The store smelled like bread and apples. Jules held the small list. "Milk, jam, apples," he said. "One, two, three."

Jules wanted the jam. The jar was on a low shelf. He reached for it. He got it! But the lid would not open. He pulled and pulled. His hands hurt a little. He made an angry face at the lid.

"Too hard," said Jules. Then he remembered something. He walked to his dad. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. His dad smiled. "Yes, I can help you." He turned the lid. It popped open. Jules hugged the jar.

At the checkout, Jules put the apples on the belt. One, two, three. The cashier gave him a sticker. It was a little red animal with a long tail. "Thank you," said Jules. "You are welcome," said the cashier.

Jules dropped the sticker on the floor. "Sorry," he said. He bent down to pick it up. But a surprise! Under the shelf sat a tiny toy cat. "Look, Dad!" said Jules. His dad wiped the cat clean with his sleeve. "It can ride home with us," he said. Jules held the jam in one hand and the cat in the other. "Milk, jam, apples, cat," he said. "One, two, three, four."

Mia sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Look at the big wheel," said her dad. The wheel spun round and round. Soon the car stopped at Ms. Friedman's house. Mia and her dad got out to say hello. Mia stayed close to her dad's hand. Then she saw something shiny on the grass. It was a small lighter. Mia did not touch it. "Dad, I see a little fire thing," she said. Her dad came right away. He picked up the lighter. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," he said. He put it high in his pocket. Ms. Friedman smiled. "What a smart, careful girl," she said. On the drive home, Mia stacked her toy cups in her lap. She felt very proud. "I kept my hands to myself," she said. Her dad smiled at her in the mirror.

It was Gianna's first day of school. Her new shoes felt bouncy on the playground. The swings made a loud squeak. Children ran and laughed everywhere. Gianna saw Edward and Emil digging in the sand. She wanted to play too. But then her tummy felt funny. She needed the bathroom, and she did not know where it was.

She looked around. She saw Ms. Balogun, her teacher, by the slide. Gianna walked over slowly. Her feet went clip, clip on the ground. "Ms. Balogun, I need help," she said. "I need the bathroom." Ms. Balogun smiled and held out her hand. "Come with me, Gianna," she said.

They walked inside together. The bathroom was right there, cool and quiet. Gianna washed her hands. The soap smelled like flowers. Then she ran back out to the playground. Edward and Emil waved at her. "Come dig with us!" said Emil. Gianna sat down in the warm sand. She patted a tall sand tower. "I asked for help," she said, "and it worked."

It was book club day at school. Mr. Chanthavong held up a big card. It showed the letter S. "This letter makes a hissing sound," he said. "Sss, sss, sss." Emile listened. Then he whispered, "Sss." Jamie found a picture of the sun. "Sun starts with S," Jamie said. "Sss, sun," said Emile. Nayla found a picture of a sock. "Sss, sock," she said. Emile smiled. He looked around the reading nook. He wanted to find his own S word.

Emile hunted slowly. He looked at the shelf. It was empty. He waited. He looked again. Then he saw the sand table in the corner. "Sand!" said Emile. "Sss, sand." He said it three times. Sun, sock and sand. They all started with S. They all made the hissing sound. Emile clapped his hands.

Mr. Chanthavong sat down beside him. "Can you find one more?" he asked. Emile looked and looked. Then he pointed at his own shoe. "Sss, shoe!" he said. Mr. Chanthavong laughed. "Yes," he said. "Sss, shoe. Good hunting, Emile."

Maeva planted little seeds in the garden. She watered them every day. Amin planted seeds too. But her pot stayed empty for a long time. "Where are my peas?" Maeva asked.

One morning, Maeva woke up early. She ran to the garden. The plants were tall! She looked closely. She saw a small green pod. "What is that?" said Louna. "Not a toy," said Maeva. She held it gently.

Maeva squeezed the pod. It popped open. Inside were little round peas, all in a row. "Look, Louna!" she said. "The peas grow in there!" They picked more pods together. Mr. Bondarenko brought a bowl. He washed the peas with cool water. Maeva ate one. It was sweet. "More pods!" she said, and ran to the next plant.

Sarah wanted to help set the table. Dad said, "Can you put out the cups?" Sarah loved cups. She carried them one by one.

She put one cup in front of each chair. One cup for Dad's chair. One cup for Mom's chair. One cup for her own little chair. Then one cup for Emmie's chair, because Emmie was coming for tasty pancakes.

Sarah looked at the table. Every chair had a cup. "Dad, look! One cup on every chair," she said. "There are no cups left in my hands." Dad smiled. "Yes, one cup for each chair."

Then Emmie arrived with her dad. Emmie sat down. Emmie had a cup! Sarah counted the chairs. One, two, three, four. She counted the cups. One, two, three, four. "Same!" said Sarah. "Every chair has one cup. Every cup has one chair."

Emmie held up her cup. Sarah held up hers. "Cheers!" said Emmie. Sarah tapped her cup to Emmie's cup, very softly. "Cheers!" said Sarah.

Lily went to the store with her dad. She wanted to feed the fish at home. So she wanted fish food in a big bag.

Lily could not reach the shelf. The bag was too high. "Can you help me, please?" she asked. A store worker smiled. He got the bag down. "Thank you," said Lily. The worker gave her the bag.

Lily held the bag tight. She walked slow so she would not drop it. At the line, she saw Ms. Hussain, her neighbour. "Hello, Lily," said Ms. Hussain. "Hello," said Lily.

Lily stepped on her toe by accident. "Sorry," said Lily. "That is okay," said Ms. Hussain. Then the cashier gave Lily the bag. "Thank you," said Lily again.

At home, Lily put the food by the fish tank. Her dad poured some in. The fish swam up fast. They ate and ate. "They like it," said Lily. The little fish blew a bubble.

It was snack day in Mr. Bennett's class. Sophia sat next to Lauren and Sahib. "Today we learn our five senses," said Mr. Bennett. "And we will play a game!"

First came the eyes. "Eyes see," said Sophia. She looked at a picture of a butterfly on the wall. "I see the butterfly with my eyes!" Then came ears. The class covered their eyes and listened. "Ears hear the bell," said Sahib.

"Now the tongue game," said Mr. Bennett. He held up two cups. "Guess this one. Sweet or sour?" "Sweet!" shouted Sophia. She took a tiny taste. It was lemon juice. Her whole face went funny. "It's sour!" she said. "My tongue told me!"

Lauren tried the next cup. "I guess sour," she said. She tasted it. It was honey. "No, it's sweet!" Everyone laughed. One more cup came around. Sophia tasted it. "Sweet!" she said. Her cup was empty now, but her smile was full.

"Last two senses," said Mr. Bennett. "Noses smell, and hands feel." Sophia touched a soft, full pillow. "My hands feel the soft pillow!" she said. Mr. Bennett clapped. "Sophia knows all five senses!" Sophia jumped up. "Tongue, eyes, ears, nose, hands! Me, me, me!"

Maria ran to the playground. The sky was gray. Big drops began to fall. "Rain!" said Maria. The rain went pitter, patter, plop.

Mohammed ran to the slide. He had no raincoat. The rain touched his shirt. Soon his shirt was wet. "I am all wet!" he said. He ran back to his mom. She helped him put on his red raincoat. Then Mohammed slid down the slide. His raincoat kept his body dry. "Look, I am dry under here!" he said.

Maria wore her yellow raincoat too. She jumped in a puddle. Splash! Her socks stayed dry. Mohammed jumped too. "Careful," laughed Maria. "My boots are full of water now!" Desmond shook his umbrella. The wind blew it inside out. "Silly wind!" said Desmond.

Then the sun came out. It was sunny again. The three friends took off their raincoats. They hung them on the fence. "Now we can play tag," said Maria. They ran and ran. Nobody missed a turn. "Best rainy day ever," said Mohammed. "Even my socks are dry again!"

Mia sat on the wood bench. The singing lady stood up front. Everyone would sing soon. But Mia did not know the song.

"Try clapping," said Esteban. He clapped his hands. Clap, clap, clap. Mia clapped too. The claps fit the song! She smiled so wide.

Now they had to sing. Mia opened her mouth. The tune came out, and she blinked. She knew this tune! It was the ABC song. A, B, C, D. She sang every letter.

The singing lady laughed. "You found our song," she said. "It has two names. 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' and the ABC song use the same tune."

Mia clapped and sang again. This time she sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Esteban sang the letters. Dustin sang them both together, very fast.

The whole room clapped with them. Clap, clap, clap. Mia stood up on her knees and sang louder.

Paint day was here at last. Henri sat on his low chair at the big table. He wanted to paint a sun, a big yellow sun. He dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He painted a round sun. It looked good.

Then he wanted green grass. He dipped his brush in the blue paint. But his sun spots mixed in. His yellow turned muddy and dark. Henri frowned at his paper. Yoel sat next to him. Yoel pointed at the water cup. "Rinse your brush in the water," Yoel said. Henri put his brush in the water. He swished it around. The water turned cloudy yellow. He wiped the brush on his towel.

Now his brush was clean. Henri dipped it in the blue paint. Then he dipped it in the yellow paint too. Blue and yellow touched on the paper. Green! The grass came out bright and clean. Henri held up his painting. "Look, Ms. Sandhu! Green!" Ms. Sandhu smiled. "That is a lovely green, Henri." Henri painted more grass, swishing his brush in the water each time. "Want to share my green?" he asked Yoel. Yoel nodded and held out his paper.

Lucas went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm on the slide. Lucas felt happy. He wanted to go down the big slide today.

Lucas climbed up the little steps. Then he looked down. The slide was very tall. His tummy felt funny. He felt scared. He sat at the top and did not move.

Martha came up behind him. "You can do it," she said. Lucas shook his head. "Dad was scared of slides too," said Martha. Lucas looked down at his dad. "Is that true?" he called. Dad nodded. "I was scared. I held on tight. Then I slid."

Lucas was surprised. He thought only small kids felt scared. Dad was big and tall. Dad had feelings too. Everybody had feelings, even grown-ups. That was a new thought for Lucas.

Lucas took a big breath. He let go of the rail. Down he went, fast and smooth. The wind pushed his hair. He laughed all the way. At the bottom, Dad clapped. "Again!" said Lucas. He ran back to the steps, and Dad followed with a smile.

Aiden wanted to make bread for his family. Mom said he could help. He poured flour into a big bowl. He added water and mixed it with a spoon.

Then he touched the dough. "It is sticky!" said Aiden. "It is all over my hands. It is ruined!" The sticky dough felt scary on his fingers. "Can we throw it out?"

Mom smiled. "Cooks knead the dough," she said. "They push it and fold it with their hands. Try it!" Aiden pushed the dough with his palm. Then he folded it over. He pushed and folded again and again.

Soon the dough was not sticky at all. It felt soft and smooth like a pillow. "It changed!" said Aiden. "My hands are clean!" Mom put the dough near the warm oven to rise. Later the bread went into the hot oven. Aiden watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and good.

Dad and Aiden's big sister came to the table. Aiden tore off a piece of bread. He put it in his mouth. "Mmm," he said. "I made this!" Dad took a big bite. "Best bread ever," said Dad. Aiden laughed and clapped his hands.

Brooklyn sat in her car seat. She had a little red bag. Her toys were in the bag. She wanted to keep them there.

The car went fast. Bump! A ball came out of the bag. Brooklyn put the ball in. Bump! A duck came out. She put the duck in. "In you go," she said. Then Bump! The ball came out again.

Brooklyn felt worried. Her toys would not stay in. Sulaiman sat next to her. He held his teddy tight.

"Mom, the toys keep coming out!" said Brooklyn.

Her mom looked in the mirror. "Hold the bag upside up," she said. "Then close the top."

Brooklyn turned the bag up. She pushed the toys in. She closed the top tight. The car went fast, then slow. The car went over bumps, big and small. Nothing came out. The toys stayed in.

"In and out are opposites," said Sulaiman.

Brooklyn smiled. Her toys went in. Her toys stayed in. Nothing came out. The sun was hot outside. The air inside was cold.

At home, Mom would bathe the duck in warm water. Brooklyn would sit at her desk and draw a fast car.

The car stopped. Brooklyn hugged her bag. "My toys stayed in," she said. Mom gave her a proud smile.

Colton sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. The sun needed a big round circle. Colton drew and drew. His circle came out bumpy. It wobbled like jelly. He frowned at it.

Zain sat next to him. "My circle is wobbly too," said Zain. Mehreen held up her paper. Her sun had a perfect circle. Colton leaned close. "How did you do that?" he asked.

"I traced around a cup," said Mehreen. She put her cup down on the paper. Then she drew all around the bottom of it. She lifted the cup up. There it was. A big round circle!

Colton grabbed a cup. He pressed it down on his paper. He drew around the bottom. Lift. A circle! He made another one. Another circle! "Wow!" he said. His whole page was full of circles.

Then he made squares with blocks. Ms. Buchanan came over. She held up a triangle sticker. "Can you make a house?" she asked. Colton put a square down. He put a triangle on top. He added a circle sun. "A house!" he shouted. Mehreen clapped. The three friends kept drawing until it was time to sleep for naps. Colton yawned and smiled. "Circles are the best sound in my tummy," he said, giggling. "Snack time soon!" said Ms. Buchanan. Colton hugged his paper tight.

Abigail could not find her bunny. She looked in the toy box. She looked under the table. Bunny was not there.

Abigail asked her friend Lena, "Did you see my bunny?" Lena shook her head. Then Faris ran over. "Bunny is in the bus!" he said. "I saw it on the seat!" Abigail felt sad. The bus had gone away.

Mr. Bakker sat down next to her. "We can ask the bus driver tomorrow," he said. "But how will he know it is your bunny?" Abigail thought hard. Lots of kids had bunnies at daycare.

Then Abigail had an idea. She took a paper tag. She asked Mr. Bakker to help. He wrote the name Abigail on the tag. They tied the tag to bunny's ear the next day. Abigail colored a little heart on it too.

At nap time, the door opened. The bus driver held up bunny. He read the tag. "This says Abigail," he said with a warm smile. "So it belongs to you." Abigail hugged bunny tight. Lena clapped her hands. "Now bunny always comes back," Abigail said. She gave bunny a drink from her cup. Bunny was home.

Weston opened his eye and saw white outside. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on the big tree. "No school today," said Dad. "It is a snow day!"

Weston put on his warm coat. He put on his boots and mittens. Dad walked with him to the sledding hill. Weston's friend Ameer was there. Ameer slid down fast on his red sled. Weston slid down too. Whoosh! They slid and slid until lunch.

After lunch, Weston wanted to go back out. He grabbed his mittens. "Oh no," said Weston. His mittens were all wet. His boots were wet too. His hands felt cold inside them. Weston wanted to cry a little.

Dad helped him hang the wet mittens on the radiator rack. They set the boots by the door, toes up. "They will dry while we wait," said Dad. Weston waited. He drank warm milk. He watched the mittens. Slowly, the mittens were not wet anymore. Weston touched them with his hand. They were dry and warm!

Weston put on his clean, dry mittens. He put on his dry boots. "All better!" he said. Dad smiled and zipped Weston's coat. They opened the door together. The snow sparkled outside. "Race you to the hill," said Dad.

Milan ran to the big tire swing at the playground. His friend Liam was already there. "Let's play rocket ship," said Liam. Milan wanted to be the rocket ship. But he did not know how to start it.

Liam held the tire with both hands. "Watch me," he said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Liam jumped high on "blast off." The tire swing swung back and forth. Milan clapped his hands.

"My turn," said Milan. He got in the tire and held on tight. The tire felt bumpy under his tummy. Liam counted, "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Milan giggled. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Milan jumped up and the swing went whoosh.

Ms. Thompson was sitting on a bench. "That is called a countdown," she said. "You counted backward from ten down to one." Milan smiled a big smile. His fuzzy hair blew in the wind. "Again!" said Milan. Liam laughed. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!"

Quinn was at the park with her class. Ms. Yoon said, "Today we learn our five senses." Quinn wanted to name them all by herself.

First Quinn touched the grass. "Hands!" she said. That was one. Then she heard a dog bark. "Ears!" That was two. Then she saw Wylder on the swing. "Eyes!" Three. Then she tasted her apple at the picnic table. "Tongue!" Four. Quinn stopped. She could not think of the fifth one.

Then a smell came on the wind. It was warm and sweet. "Cookies!" said Quinn. "I smell cookies." But she did not see any cookies. She did not see a bakery either. She just followed her nose. Issa ran with her. Behind a big tree, there was a little cookie cart. A baker was pulling a tray from a small oven, and Ms. Yoon was waiting there with a grin.

"Nose!" said Quinn. "The nose is five! I smelled them before I could see them!" Ms. Yoon gave each child a cookie. Quinn pushed her chair to the table and took a quick, happy bite. "Five senses," she said. "I did it."

Alexis sat on the big couch. His dad sat next to him. Valerie and Sulaiman came over too. The game was on TV. Everyone was shouting and clapping.

Alexis wanted to know who was winning. He asked, "Who has more points?" Dad said, "Watch and see." Alexis could not remember the numbers. They kept changing in his head.

Then Alexis saw it. The big board on the TV had numbers. One number was for the red team. One number was for the blue team. Mr. Kovalenko, the neighbour, pointed at it. "Look at the scoreboard," he said. "It shows how many points each team has." Alexis looked and looked. The red team had the bigger number. The red team was winning!

Alexis clapped his little hands. He got Valerie a spoon so she could eat her yogurt. Sulaiman spilled his juice, and Alexis helped wipe it up. Then the red team scored again. The number on the scoreboard went up. Alexis jumped and shouted, "The number got bigger!"

The game ended. The red team won. Dad said, "You watched the whole game, Alexis." Alexis smiled at the screen. "Same time next week?" he asked.

Jayden ran to the snack table at school. He saw a big plate of cookies. He wanted a cookie so much. "Cookies now, please!" he said.

Ms. Ferreira smiled. "Not yet," she said. "We eat breakfast first. Breakfast is the first meal of the day." Jayden blinked. First? Before cookies? He looked around. Riyan was eating oatmeal. Jordyn was eating a banana.

Jayden could help make breakfast too. He picked up a cup. He helped pour milk. Ms. Ferreira held the warm pot. Jayden watched from his chair, nice and safe. He took a bite of oatmeal. Yum! His tummy felt happy.

After breakfast, the cookies came out. Jayden got one small cookie. It tasted sweet. "First breakfast, then cookie," he said. On the shelf, a stuffed striped monkey sat and watched. Jayden waved at the monkey and took another bite.

Eva went to Zeke's house. Zeke's mom put on a song. It had a bumpy, jumpy beat. Eva wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" with Zeke and clap too.

Eva clapped whenever she liked. Clap! Clap! Clap! Zeke shook his head. "You are clapping too fast," he said. "It sounds all mixed up." Eva got upset. Her claps and the song did not match. It was like a dream where her feet ran the wrong way.

"Listen first," said Zeke. "The song goes boom, boom, boom. Clap at the same time as the boom." They stood still and listened. Boom, boom, boom. Eva waited. Then she clapped on the boom. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps landed right on the song! She felt her hands find the music like a friend holding hands.

Then they sang. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva sang it all by herself. She did not miss one word. Zeke clapped along with her singing. Eva laughed and clapped too, right on the beat, all the way to "what you are."

The light went out. The TV went dark too. Isaac patted the TV screen. "Wake up," he said. His dad came in with a flashlight. The flashlight made a big yellow circle on the floor.

Isaac tried the TV again. It stayed dark. He pushed the button two times. Nothing happened. "No power," said Dad. "We have to wait." Isaac sat down on the rug. He waited. The TV did not pop back on.

Dad shined the light on the shelf. "Look," he said. "Books. Puzzles. And board games." Isaac picked the puzzle. He put in one piece. Then another. Then another. The puzzle worked with no TV. His mom came and held the light close so he could see.

After the puzzle, they played a board game on the floor. Isaac moved his little red piece. Mom rolled the dice for him. The flashlight made everything glow. "This is beautiful," said Mom. Isaac clapped when his piece won. Soon the lights came back on. The TV popped on too. But Isaac still had one turn left. "My turn," he said. Dad laughed and sat back down on the rug.

Jasper went to the library with his dad. He wore his red socks that morning. But at the story rug, Jasper looked down. One foot had a sock. One foot had no sock at all.

"Where did my sock go?" he asked. Mr. Suzuki sat down next to him. "A pair means two," said Mr. Suzuki. "Like a pair of socks. We need to find the other one."

Jasper began to look. He peeked under the rug. He counted the rug squares out loud. "One, two, three." No sock. He walked past the shelves. He counted books. "Four, five, six." Still no sock. His friend Linden was stacking blocks. Jasper helped her count them. "Seven, eight, nine."

Then Jasper heard a soft sound near the door. Something was stuck to the mat. It was small and red. It was his sock! He picked it up and pulled it on.

"Ten toes," said Mr. Suzuki, laughing. "Two feet. One cool pair of socks." Jasper wiggled his toes in his shoes and clapped his hands.

Sofa girl Sofia got to daycare with her dad. "Good morning," said Ms. Ndlovu. Sofia yawned. "It is not morning," she said. "I did not eat breakfast."

Hayley was stirring oatmeal in a little bowl. Ms. Ndlovu helped her stir it round and round. "Breakfast time is morning," said Ms. Ndlovu. "You woke up today, and now you can eat."

Sofia sat down. She took a spoon. She stirred her oatmeal too. Round and round it went. "Now it is morning for me," she said.

Destiny ran over with a toy snake. "The snake was asleep yesterday," she said. "Now he is awake." Sofia fed the snake one pretend bite of oatmeal. The snake liked it. He was not asleep anymore.

"Sofia, can you come paint now?" asked Destiny. "Later," said Sofia. "First I eat." The oatmeal was warm and yummy.

After breakfast, the girls painted the sky. Sofia painted a big yellow sun. "That is the morning sun," she said. "He wakes up and eats too, like me." Destiny laughed. The snake got a sun painted just for him.

Lincoln sat in his car seat. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "We get to Dawson's house later. Later means some time after now, not right away." Lincoln looked out the window. He saw a big truck. He saw a red light. He saw a dog. One truck, one light, one dog. "Is it later yet?" he asked again. "Soon," said Dad. The light turned green. The car went. "Now we move," said Dad. Lincoln clapped his hands.

The sun began to hurt his eyes. Dad pulled down the sun shade. "Better?" Dad asked. "Better," said Lincoln. A loud horn went beep. That was a scary sound. Lincoln held his teddy tight. "It is okay," said Dad. "The horn is far away now." Lincoln peeked out. No truck. Just trees. One tree, two trees, three trees.

"Is it later yet?" asked Lincoln. Dad smiled. "Look. Here is Dawson's house. It is later now!" Dawson ran to the car. "Lincoln! We can play blocks today!" said Dawson. The blocks had waited all day. Lincoln hugged his teddy. "We played later," he said. "Later came!" Dawson laughed and gave him a red block.

Aiden ran to the water table at the playground. It was a hot summer day. His friend Lou was there too. Lou held a big cup. It was empty. Nothing was inside it at all.

Aiden turned the faucet on fast. Water rushed out. Splash! Water went all over his shoes. Lou laughed. "Look," Lou said. "The cup is full to the top now."

Aiden got a small cup. It was empty too. What would happen if he poured slow? He turned the faucet just a little. Drip, drip, drip. He could hear the quiet sound. He waited and watched. The water went up, up, up. He stopped before it spilled. "My cup is full," Aiden said. "Yours was full and splashed. Mine is full and dry."

Lou poured again, slow this time. He filled his cup to the top. Not one drop fell out. Aiden smiled. "Full cups feel heavy," he said, lifting his cup with two hands.
