William sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to make a toy car. His mom gave him a box and some sticky tape. Anaiah came over to play too.

William taped on four square wheels. "My car is done!" he said. He pushed it across the floor. It would not roll. He pushed it again. It would not roll. "Hmm," said William. "Why will it not roll?"

Anaiah pointed at the cookie sheet on the counter. "Look. That can is round. It rolls." William gave the can a tap. It rolled all the way to the wall. Round things roll!

His mom got the scissors. Grown-ups use scissors, so she cut for him. She cut four circles out of the box. William taped the circle wheels on. He pushed his car. It rolled! It rolled fast, far, past Anaiah's feet.

"Circle wheels!" said William. He colored them red with his crayon. Then he rolled the car again and again, all around the kitchen.

Nora had a little violin at home. She picked it up. She held it upside down. "Will it sing like this?" she wondered. She plucked a string. It made a tiny sound, but the violin felt funny in her hands.

Her dad sat beside her on the rug. "Let's ask Ms. Owusu," he said. "She is a music teacher." Ms. Owusu came to their house. She knelt down next to Nora. "Can you show me how you hold it?" she asked. Nora held it upside down again. The chin rest sat near her knees.

Ms. Owusu turned the violin around. She lifted it up to Nora's chin. "A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument," she said. Nora held it the right way now. It felt smooth under her fingers and warm against her cheek.

Nora pulled the bow across one string. The sound came out big and sweet. One string, two strings, three strings, four. Each one sang a different song. Nora was so happy she stomped her feet. Ms. Owusu began to clap. Nora's dad clapped too. "Play it again," said Ms. Owusu. Nora pulled the bow back and forth, and the violin sang.

Jules went to the park with a big cardboard box. He pushed it under a tree. "A house!" said Jules. He sat inside it.

Axelle ran over. "A boat!" she said. "No, a house," said Jules. They both pulled the box. It tipped over. Jules almost fell, but his dad held his hand.

"Let's take turns," said Axelle. Jules went first. His box was a house. He patted his plastic bear. He gave it a pretend hug. Then Axelle had a turn. The same box was a boat now. They rocked side to side. "Row, row!" said Axelle.

The sky looked stormy, so they carried the box home together. "Same box, new game," said Axelle. "Tomorrow it can be a car," said Jules.

Georgia loved her soccer team. But today she did not want to go to practice. "I just want pizza and play," she said.

Her mom drove her anyway. Ms. Haddad blew the whistle. "Time for practice," she said. "This is how we get ready for our game."

At practice, Georgia kicked the ball to Zoe. Zoe kicked it back. Again and again they kicked. Georgia's foot got good at it.

On Saturday, the game began. The ball flew right at Georgia. She caught it with her foot and stopped it. Then she kicked it in the goal!

"Zoe!" Georgia called. "Can you guess why I caught it?"

"Yes!" said Zoe. "Practice!"

Amira stood at the park with a red beanbag. Winnifred held a big yellow hoop. "Throw it in!" Winnifred shouted.

Amira threw the beanbag down hard, like a ball. She thought it would bounce up and hop into the hoop. But the beanbag just went flop. It landed soft and stayed still on the grass.

"Try again," said Mr. Hu, the park coach. "Aim it at the hoop." Amira picked up the beanbag. She tossed it up high. Flop! It dropped right into the hoop. "I did it!" Amira shouted. Zahra clapped her hands.

Then Mr. Hu rolled a big blue ball to Amira. The sky turned sour and gray, like a storm was coming. Amira held out both hands. She squeezed them tight. The ball came closer, closer. She caught it! "Both hands!" she shouted, and tossed it back.

Mila sat on the big couch. She had a cold. Her nose felt stuffy, then runny. She sniffed and sniffed.

"Can I have a tissue?" Mila asked. Her dad brought a soft box. She pulled one tissue out. She wiped her nose, one slow wipe. Her nose felt better.

She sniffed again. Drip, drip. "Why does my nose run?" she asked. Dad said, "A cold can make your nose runny or stuffy." Mila listened to his quiet voice. She put her hand on her chest. She could feel her heart go thump, thump, soft and slow.

Outside, a bus was noisy. Inside, the couch was quiet and warm. Mila got a warm blanket. She pulled it up to her chin.

"I need one more tissue," she said, holding the box.

Rosalie ran into the book club room. "I want to write my name!" she said. Mr. Novák smiled. "Let's try," he said. Rosalie took a crayon. She wrote the letters one by one. r, o, s, a, l, i, e. She counted the letters. Seven! But her name looked funny.

Evana looked at the paper. "My name starts with a big E," she said. She pointed to her paper. There it was. A big capital E at the front. Noah held up his paper too. "Mine starts with a big N," he said.

Rosalie looked at her little r. Then she picked a red crayon. She drew a big R right on top. Now her name read Rosalie. The first letter was big and tall. "Look, look!" she shouted. Mr. Novák clapped. Evana and Noah clapped too. Rosalie held her paper up high. She raced to show her mom at the door.

Jasmine sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. "One truck. Two birds. Three bikes," she counted. The third bike had a tiny bell. It went ring, ring.

The car stopped at the park. Emy was there on her bike. Emy wore a helmet on her head. Jasmine jumped out. She wanted to ride Emy's bike right away. She ran to the pedals. Then Emy's wheel wobbled. Emy fell down. Her helmet went bonk on the ground. Emy stood up. "I am okay," she said. She rubbed her helmet, not her head.

Jasmine looked at the car. "I need my helmet," she said. Her dad opened the trunk. He pulled out her red helmet. Jasmine put it on. She pulled the strap. "One, two, three, ready," she said. Then she rode in a big circle, round and round, like a wave in the ocean. "Look at me!" she called. "Look at my helmet!"

Madison got to school with a big smile. Her friend Aaira waved. "Sleepover night!" Aaira said. Tonight Madison would sleep at Aaira's house.

At school, Mr. Wang read them a story. Madison sat on the rug. She sucked her finger while she listened. Then it was snack time. Madison ate a juicy apple. Crunch, crunch, yum.

At bedtime, Madison put on her pajamas. She picked the ones with stars. She brushed her teeth at the little sink. Then she and Aaira hopped into bed.

But wait. Madison sat up fast. "Aaira, we forgot!" she said. "We brush our teeth before bed too!" They both jumped out of bed. They ran to the little sink. Brush, brush, brush. Their teeth felt clean and smooth.

Aaira's mom peeked in. "Back in bed, sleepy heads," she said. The girls giggled. They snuggled under the blanket. "In the morning we brush again," Aaira whispered. Madison smiled. Then she closed her eyes.

The sun peeked in the window. Madison woke up first. "Morning teeth time!" she called.

Gianna ran to the train station with her mom. Grandpa was coming today. He would stay for a whole week!

But Grandpa had no bed at Gianna's house. Giana felt worried. "Where will Grandpa sleep?" she asked.

Mom smiled. "We can make a bed for him," she said. "A guest needs a sleeping spot."

Gianna picked out a soft pillow. She got her prettiest blanket, the blue one with stars. She put them on the big bed in the guest room. Then she put her teddy bear on the pillow too.

The train pulled in. It went choo, choo! Grandpa stepped off with his bag. He gave Gianna a big hug.

"Come see your bed!" said Gianna. She pulled his hand. Grandpa saw the pillow and the star blanket. He laughed and laughed.

"A soft bed for me," he said. "And a bear to keep me company!"

Daniel sat in a big chair at the restaurant. The big screen showed a game. Edmond and Anita sat next to him. Daniel had a cool red cup with a straw.

The red team ran with the ball. Daniel stood up and clapped. He cheered, "Yay, go red team!" But everyone else was quiet. The blue team had the ball, not the red team. Anita giggled. "We like the blue team," she said. Daniel sat down. He waited and watched.

Then the blue team scored a goal. The whole room got loud. Everyone stood up. They clapped and cheered, "Blue team, blue team!" Daniel clapped too. Now he knew. When his team scored, he could cheer loud. He licked his chocolate stick and waved it in the air. "Go blue team!" Daniel said. Anita gave him a high five.

Emma put on her swim class suit. It had little ducks on it. Her mom took her to the big hotel pool.

Emma hoped she could swim today. Her class was by the steps. Mr. Bui was the teacher. "Hello, Emma," he said. "We will kick and blow bubbles."

Chelsea ran fast to the pool. "Wait," said Mr. Bui. "The floor is wet. Wet floors are slippery. Walk, please." Chelsea stopped her feet. She walked very slow, like a turtle. Emma laughed. "Slow turtle feet," she said.

Emma got in the water. She held the rail. She kicked and kicked. She blew ten bubbles. Then she let go. She kicked all by herself. "Look at me!" she called.

After class, Emma felt fresh and clean. She walked, not ran, to her towel. Chelsea walked too, turtle style. "See you next time," said Mr. Bui. Emma waved and waved.

Riley sat in the family car. Today was a big day. She was going to get her very first haircut!

"Hooray!" said Riley. "I want short hair like Ellis!"

At the salon, the hairdresser said, "Hop up, Riley." Riley sat on the big chair. She felt very tall.

Then the hairdresser picked up a comb. She combed Riley's hair. Then she made one snip with the scissors. Riley watched with wide eyes.

"You combed first!" said Riley. "Then you snipped!"

"That's right," said the hairdresser. "The comb keeps the hair neat while I cut it."

Riley began to count. "One, two, three combs. Snip!" she called. "One, two, three combs. Snip!"

A little girl with an animal shirt sat and watched. "She is counting!" the girl said to her mom.

One piece of hair got stuck to Riley's nose. Riley laughed and blew it off. "Puff!"

Soon the haircut was done. Riley looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat, just like Ellis.

"Can we bake cookies now?" she asked her mom. "Short hair needs a cookie!"

Her mom laughed. "Yes, we can. Let's go!"

Riley ran to the car. "Three combs, one snip!" she sang all the way home.

Kinsley ran into the big room at the cultural center. There were rows and rows of little clay cups. Her mom held a box of them. "Can I help?" Kinsley asked. "Yes," Mom said. "Put them in a long row."

Kinsley set out the little cups one by one. She counted them as she went. Her friend Ryder came to help too. He put wicks in each cup. Then a grown-up poured oil into them.

"What are these called?" Kinsley asked. Mom said, "They are called diyas." Ryder rolled a diya across the table to Kinsley. She laughed and set it back in the row.

Soon Mr. Kelly came with a small flame. He touched it to the first wick. A little light popped up. Then he lit the next one, and the next. Kinsley watched from far back, where it was safe.

The whole row glowed now. One little cup had made one little light. Then all the little lights made a big bright line. "Look, Ryder!" Kinsley said. "They all shine together!" The diyas blinked like tiny stars on the table.

Milo sat at the kitchen table. His striped socks tapped the floor. His mom put on a song. "Let's sing the star song," she said.

Milo began to sing right away. But the song was not starting yet. His voice came out all alone. He stopped and felt shy.

Mom held up her hand. "We can count first," she said. "One, two, three, four." Then she began to sing. Her claps moved with the beat. Clap, clap, clap, clap.

Milo waited this time. Mom counted, "One, two, three, four." Then they both sang together. Milo clapped his hands at the same time. The claps matched the song. His socks tapped under the table too.

They sang the whole star song. They did not stop once. At the end, Milo clapped all by himself. "Again," he said. "Count with me!"

Nicholas wanted the red fire truck. Harvey was playing with it. Nicholas grabbed it fast. Harvey's face went sad. He put his hands over his eyes.

Nicholas looked at the truck in his hands. He did not like making Harvey sad. "Why is Harvey crying?" he wondered. "Because I took it." So Nicholas held the truck out. "Harvey, can I please have a turn?" he asked.

Harvey wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You can have a turn. Then it is my turn again." Nicholas pushed the truck across the floor. It went fast under a cup on the table. Julie came to watch. She bent down to see the truck zoom by.

Nicholas gave the truck back. Harvey smiled. Then Julie asked, "Can I have a turn too?" "Yes!" said Nicholas. "Let's take turns all day." Julie rolled the truck to Nicholas. "My turn is over now," she said. Nicholas laughed and made the siren sound.

Abigail sat on her bed. She looked at her red shoes. "Is the library day coming?" she asked. Mom smiled. "It is today," she said. Abigail jumped up. Today was now! Today was this very day!

"But when is now?" Abigail asked. Mom tapped the window. "Now is the sun in the sky. Now is when we eat breakfast."

Abigail put on her clean socks. They smelled like soap. Yesterday she had mud on her socks. Yesterday was over. It was the day before this one.

"After the library, we read a story," said Mom. Abigail clapped. "Is later after now?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Later comes when now is done."

At the library, Abigail hugged three books. Mr. Weber was there. He read about a big red truck. Abigail heard the truck go vroom in the story.

At home, she sat with Mom. Tomorrow they could read more. But now, Mom opened the first page. "Once upon a time," Mom read.

Oliver ran to daycare with a card in his hand. It was his birthday card. His grandma had given it to him.

At his cubby, he hung up his coat. He bumped his head on the cubby door. "Ouch," he said. Then he saw the name on the cubby. It said Oliver.

He looked at the card. It said Oliver too. Same letters. Same order. He held the card next to the cubby. Both names looked the same.

"Look, Adley," he said. Adley came over. She was friendly. She pointed at her own cubby. "That one says Adley," she said.

Ms. Addo smiled. "Come read a book," she said. Oliver opened the book. He turned page one, then page two, front to back.

He put his card in his cubby. The two names sat side by side. "Same, same," he said.

Anna was going to the dentist today. It was her very first time. Her tummy felt funny. "What will the dentist do?" she asked. Her dad said, "Let's play dentist at home."

Dad sat in a big chair. Anna wanted to look in his mouth. She put her finger near his lips. Then she stopped. "Wait," she said. "Is my finger clean?" Her dad shook his head. "Not yet," he said.

He went to the kitchen. He washed his hands with soap. Then he pulled something from a box. He slid them on. His hands turned blue! Anna giggled. "Your hands are blue!" she said. "These are gloves," her dad said. He opened and closed his blue fingers. Snap, snap. The gloves made a funny sound.

Anna put on small gloves too. They were too big for her. She pulled one, and it went snap. She counted her dad's teeth with one gloved finger. "One, two, three," she said. The glove felt smooth and cool, like air was inside it.

Anna looked at her gloves. "The dentist wears these too?" she asked. Her dad nodded. "The dentist wears gloves when putting fingers or tools in your mouth." Anna thought about that. It was a good plan. Clean gloves for every mouth.

At the real dentist, the chair went up and down. It was like a ride. Then the dentist came in. Anna saw his hands. They were covered in blue gloves! "I know those," she said. "I wore them at home." She opened her mouth wide. The check was quick. It was not too hard.

On the way home, Anna held her dad's hand. "Next time, can I count my own teeth?" she asked. Her dad laughed. "Maybe the dentist will give you blue gloves too," he said. Anna smiled all the way home.

Amira sat at the art table. She wanted to make a house picture. Ms. Ramos put out paper shapes.

Amira found a red square. It was just right for the house wall. She found a triangle for the roof. She found a little square for the window.

Dane sat next to her. His square slipped on the glue. It turned. One corner pointed up.

"Look," said Dane. "You made a new shape."

Amira looked at it. She tipped it back flat. It was the square again. She turned it once more. Corner up, it was still the square. Same four sides, same square.

Amira smiled. She put the tilted square on her paper. It became a window for the attic. The corner pointed up like a little roof.

"I like it turned," she said.

Elena came to look. She saw the house, the roof, and the two windows.

"It's a good house," said Elena.

Amira hung it up to dry on the street of pictures by the wall, where all the art went home at the end of the day.

Layla sat on the library rug. She had bumpy letter cards and a pencil. Her friend Bowie sat next to her. He had a soft blanket over his legs because the library was cold.

"I want to write K," said Layla. "But my K looks funny." She wrote a K. It came out wrong. The arms went the wrong way. Bowie looked at her paper. "Try the bumpy card," he said. Layla put down her pencil. She traced the K with her finger. Up, down, out, in. The bumps tickled her skin. She traced it again and again.

"Now I will write it," she said. She picked up her pencil. She wrote a K. "Look, Bowie! My K is right!" Bowie clapped. "Which letter next?" he asked. Layla smiled. "B," she said. "B is for Bowie." She traced the bumpy B with her finger, slow and careful. "One, two, three," she counted. Then she wrote it on her paper. Ms. Islam walked by with a stack of books. "That is a beautiful B, Layla," she said. Layla held her paper up high.

Mia went to the park with her friend Samson. Mr. Almeida was there too. He had a big net and a little bucket.

"Let's find animals," said Mia. They saw a dog first. The dog ran and jumped. "A dog is an animal," said Mia. Then they saw a cow behind the fence. The cow said, "Moo." "A cow is an animal," said Samson.

Then Mia looked in the pond. She saw a little fish. "Is a fish an animal?" she asked. "No way," said Samson. "It has no legs. Animals have legs." Mia had to guess. "I guess a fish is not an animal," she said. Then Mia splashed her hand in the water. The fish swam away fast. It moved all by itself. It was not a scary fish. It was a small, silly fish.

Mr. Almeida scooped the net in the pond. He held it up. "Look here," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Mia laughed. "A fish with no legs is an animal too!" Samson clapped his hands. "That is a funny story," he said. The fish wiggled its tail. Mr. Almeida tipped the net. Splash! The fish went back home.

Milo sat at the small red table at the tutoring centre. Mr. Horváth put out three big balls and three tiny beads. "Which group has more?" he asked.

Milo pointed at the balls. "The big balls! They look like lots more." The balls were soft and round. The beads felt smooth and small, like little river stones.

"Let's count," said Mr. Horváth. Milo touched each big ball. "One, two, three." Then he touched each tiny bead. "One, two, three." He sat very still. His friend Lila leaned over to see.

"They are the same!" said Milo. "Both are three!" He counted again to be sure. One, two, three. One, two, three.

Lila clapped her hands. "You did it, Milo." Mr. Horváth smiled and slid three more beads across the table.

Milo counted them fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six. Now the beads have more!" He lined up all the beads in a row, and Lila lined up the balls beside them.

Charlotte ran to the park. Today was her birthday! Her friends Spencer and Callahan were waiting by the big slide. "I was three yesterday," said Charlotte proudly. "Today I am four. On your birthday, you turn one year older!"

"Wow!" said Spencer. "Then tomorrow will you be five?"

Charlotte laughed. "No, silly! Only on my birthday!"

A parent lit the candles on the cake. Charlotte watched from far away, because candles are for grown-ups. Then everyone sang. Charlotte took a big breath. She blew and blew. One by one, the candles went out! Her breath made them go out!

"Happy birthday, Charlotte!" said Mr. Bélanger, their neighbour. He gave her a wrapped present. She tore off the paper. It was a shiny red sled!

"I can't wait for snow!" she said. "We will slide down the mountain hill."

"Me too," said Callahan. "Don't miss the cake!"

Charlotte ate her cake. It was chocolate, her favourite. "Best birthday ever," she said. "And next year, I will be five!"

Zayn loved the big red book on the shelf. It had a picture of a dog with long floppy ears. The dog was drinking juice from a blue cup.

"Who drew this dog?" Zayn asked his friend Daksh.

Daksh shook his head. "I don't know. Maybe nobody did. Maybe it just grew there."

Zayn held the book. He looked at the front. He looked at the back. The dog was on the front page. Zayn turned the pages one by one, from the front to the back. At the very end he saw small black marks. The marks made words.

Zayn carried the book to Ms. Costa. "What do these words say?" he asked.

Ms. Costa pointed. "This part says the illustrator. The illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book. This name is the illustrator's name."

"So a real person drew the dog!" said Zayn. "A person with a name!"

Just then Mitchell knocked on the playhouse door. "Come see," he called. Zayn ran over, hugging the red book tight. He could not wait to show Mitchell the name of the person who drew the dog.

Thomas walked into book club. He was not late. Ms. Gauthier smiled at him. Big letters hung on the wall. There was a big A. Thomas knew that one. "A," he said. "A says ahh."

Emmeline held up a book. "Look at this," she said. Thomas looked. He saw a small round letter. "That is not A," said Thomas. "A is big. That one is small." He felt worried. Would he be wrong?

Ms. Gauthier sat down next to him. "Look close," she said. Thomas looked close. The small letter was a. The big letter was A. She put them side by side. "Big A," said Thomas. "Small a," said Thomas. "Ahh," he said again. He made the ahh sound twice. It was the same sound!

Emmeline passed him the glue. Thomas glued both letters on paper. The big one went on top. The small one went under it. "They are a team," said Thomas. Caiden clapped. Then all the kids said "Ahh!" together.

Colton sat in his car seat. It was a hot summer day. Dad was driving to the park. Colton wanted to play hide-and-seek with Kilian and Malik.

"Dad, can we sing the counting song?" said Colton.

"Yes!" said Dad.

They sang together. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

At the park, Kilian ran to a tree. Malik ran behind a bush. Colton covered his eyes. He counted, "One, two, ten!"

"Too fast!" called Kilian. "We need more time to hide!"

"Count slowly," said Malik.

Colton covered his eyes again. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." It was slow and good.

"Now I will find you!" said Colton.

He peeked around the tree. He looked behind the bush. Malik laughed and laughed.

"You found me!" said Malik.

"Let's hide again," said Kilian. "You count, Colton!"

Colton grinned and covered his eyes. "One, two, three..."

Sadie sat in the art room at school. Ms. Wang put out three paints. "Red, yellow, blue," said Sadie. She pointed at each one. Ocean sat next to her. He was painting a sky. His sky was very dark. Too dark for daytime. Ocean frowned at it. Ms. Wang gave him white paint. Ocean stirred the white into his blue. The blue got lighter. Now it looked like a soft daytime sky. Sadie watched with big eyes. She wanted to try too. She painted a red cat. Then she stirred in some white. Her red cat got lighter. It turned pink, like a little pig. Sadie laughed. "My cat is pink!" she said. Ocean laughed too. Then Sadie mixed red and yellow on her paper. It made orange. She counted her paints: one, two, three. "I made new colours," said Sadie. Ms. Wang smiled. "A happy painter," she said. Sadie held up her pink cat and her orange sun.

Xavier waited by the gate. Ms. Grewal called the names. "Yunus! Neo! Xavier!" Xavier ran to his dad.

At home, Dad said, "First we wash hands. Then we eat." Xavier looked at the soap. It felt smooth. He rubbed it. Nothing happened. "Where are the bubbles?" he asked.

Dad turned on the tap. Water ran cool and fast. Xavier held his hands under it. He rubbed the soap again. Bubbles! Lots of soft, white bubbles covered his fingers.

"Look, Dad! Bubbles!" Xavier piled them on his chin. "I have a beard!" Yunus made one too, at school. Xavier giggled and giggled.

He washed the bubbles off. His hands were clean and shiny. Then he ate his lunch. After that came a bath, with more bubbles. Then he would wear his soft pajamas with the little animal on the front.

"Soap and water," said Xavier. "Bubbles every time."

He rubbed his soapy tummy and blew one bubble off his hand.

Henri sat in the big waiting room. His mom sat right beside him. Today was his first haircut. A lady called his name, and Henri held his mom's hand.

Henri climbed up into the tall chair. The barber picked up the scissors. Henri looked worried. "Will my hair be gone forever?" he asked. His mom smiled. "No, sweet boy. Hair grows back after it is cut." Henri watched in the mirror. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell down, soft as snow. Henri touched his ear. It felt funny and light. "My ear is cold!" he said, and he laughed.

Then Henri saw something surprising. On the floor, a little pile of his own curls. He pointed. "That was on my head!" he said. His mom laughed too. The barber gave him a sticker of a dog. "New hair, coming soon," said the barber. Henri grinned at his short hair in the mirror and dreamed about the dog sticker all the way home.

Emilia was wide awake in her car seat. She held her basket of play things. "We are going on a picnic!" she said. Dad drove the car. The sun was bright outside.

Emilia looked at her basket. She had a toy bear. She had a toy truck. She had a toy ball. "Those are my toys," she said. She put them in a row on her lap.

Then she found an apple, some bread, and a carrot. She made a picnic game. She put the apple with the toys. She put the bread with the toys too. Then she put the carrot next to the bear.

Dad looked back at her. "Is the bear going to eat the carrot?" he asked. Emilia laughed. "No, Dad! Bears don't eat carrots at picnics." She thought hard. The apple was for eating. The bread was for eating too. She looked at the carrot.

"The carrot is food," she said. "It goes with the apple and the bread." She picked up the carrot. She put it in a new pile. The apple, the bread and the carrot sat together. Her toys sat in the other pile.

"We can mix them up and sort them again!" said Emilia. Dad smiled. "When you feel sick, you take your medicine. When you are hungry, you eat food like that." Emilia clapped her hands. "Picnic food! Apple, bread and carrot!" Then she handed the carrot to the bear, just to be silly, and giggled all the way to the park.

Olivia wanted the crackers at snack time. The shelf had two boxes. "Which box has crackers?" she asked. Ms. Singh said, "The words tell us." Olivia pointed to the little marks on the box. Ms. Singh read them out loud. "Crackers," said the box. So Olivia took that box. Words tell us things, she thought.

Then Kevin wanted milk. Olivia looked at the bottles. She saw little marks on one. "This says milk," she said. Kevin smiled. The milk was cold and good.

After snack, Ms. Singh read a book. She opened the front cover first. Then page one, then page two. She turned the pages one by one. "Where does the story start?" Olivia asked. "At the front," said Ms. Singh. At nap time, Olivia fed the fish. Then she helped put the shelf back in order, all tidy. "The words can help us," she said.

Lea went to the store with her dad. She held his hand. On the shelf she saw a small striped sock puppet. It looked like a little animal with two soft ears. "Can I hold it?" asked Lea. "Just for a minute," said Dad.

Then Ruby came by with her mom. Ruby pointed at the puppet too. "I want that animal," said Ruby. Both girls reached for it. Lea grabbed it fast. Ruby stomped her feet. Her face turned red. She was angry. She sat down on the floor.

"Ruby, come here," said her mom. She sat with Ruby on a small bench. "Try slow, deep breaths with me," said her mom. Ruby breathed in slow and big. Then she let it out slow and big. She did it again. Her face got calm. She was not angry anymore.

Lea watched all of it. She saw the slow breaths make Ruby feel better. "Do you want to hold it now?" Lea asked. "Yes, please," said Ruby. She hugged the striped puppet. Then she made it talk. "Hello, I am a sock lion," said Ruby in a lion voice. Lea laughed and clapped.

Dad said it was time to go. But then he had a small surprise. He bought two sock puppets, one for each girl. Lea jumped up and down. "A lion and what else?" she asked herself. She peeked in the bag. "A striped zebra!" she said. The lion and the zebra waved goodbye at the store door.

It was Sense Day at school. Emma was so excited. "Today we name our five senses," said Ms. Fortin. Emma wanted to name them all by herself.

First came eyes. Eyes are for seeing. Then ears. Ears are for hearing. Then nose, tongue, and hands. Emma counted them. "One, two, three, four, five. Five senses. Five is my best number!" said Emma. Bo clapped. Mohammed clapped too.

Then Emma wanted to try her eyes on something big. "I will look at the sun up close," she said. Ms. Fortin ran over fast. "Stop! Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes." Emma was sorry. She shut her eyes tight instead.

Then something surprising happened. Emma closed her eyes, and she could not see Bo. She opened her eyes, and Bo was right there. She closed them again. Gone! She opened them. There! "My eyes make seeing happen," said Emma. "Eyes for seeing. Ears for hearing. Nose for smelling. Tongue for tasting. Hands for touching. It all fits!"

Emma ran home singing her five senses. Then she saw the sun going down. She made a peeking hole with her fingers, and did not look straight at it. "Five senses, zero sun in my eyes," said Emma.

Oliver had a new baby sister at home. She was tiny and red and very loud. Now Oliver was at nursery, playing with the doll babies. "Feed the baby, feed the baby," he sang. He gave his doll a bottle.

Adele held her doll too. "My baby sleeps all night," she said. Oliver shook his head. "Not real babies," he said. "Real babies wake up in the dark. My mummy feeds the baby in the night. And in the day too. Again and again and again."

Taim giggled. "Again and again and again!" Ms. Hughes laughed. "That sounds like a hungry baby."

At nap time, Oliver heard a tiny cry. It was not a baby. It was Timmy the teddy, stuck under the shelf! Oliver pulled him out. "Did that hurt?" he asked. He gave teddy a bottle. Then teddy needed a star sticker. Teddies love stickers. "Feed the teddy, feed the teddy!" said Adele.

Then Oliver saw something. He patted teddy's tummy. Teddy stopped crying. "Look," said Oliver. "Full tummy, happy teddy!" Outside the window, one red bus went by. "One bus!" said Taim. "Two buses!" said Adele, pointing. Ms. Hughes said, "Time for a snack." Oliver stood up tall. "I am like the baby," he said. "I eat in the day. But I sleep all night!"

Felix sat at the kitchen table. He had a big piece of paper. He had one yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He pressed the pencil down. He made a line for the letter F. But the line was fat and fuzzy. "That is not a good F," said Felix. He made another line. That one was fuzzy too. His letters looked like little grey clouds.

Felix looked at the pencil tip. It was dull and round like a tiny potato. He carried the pencil to his dad. "Can you sharpen it?" asked Felix. "My letters look sleepy." Dad held the pencil in the sharpener and turned it around and around. "Watch with your eye," said Dad. Wood curled out like a party streamer. Then the tip was long and pointy.

Felix carried the pencil back. It was not heavy at all. He pressed down again. Now the line was thin and dark. The pencil did work so much better! Felix wrote F. Then E. Then L, I, X. His name sat on the paper, neat and sharp.

"Dad! Come look!" shouted Felix. Dad ran over. He read the name out loud. "Felix," he said. "Felix," said Felix, and he gave the pointy pencil a little kiss on the tip. "Ouch," said Felix. Dad laughed and got him an ice cube.

Josephine planted seeds at the farm. She planted carrot seeds in a little row. Mr. Shapiro gave her a small watering can. "Water them every day," he said. Josephine watered them every day. Every single day.

One morning, green leaves popped up. Josephine was so happy. Then she saw more green leaves. They were not in her row. "Weeds!" she said. A weed is a plant growing where you do not want it. She pulled one weed out. Then another. Then she saw a small leaf in her row. "A weed!" she said. She grabbed it.

"Stop," said Mr. Shapiro. "That one is a carrot. It is growing where you want it." Josephine let go of the little leaf. She patted the dirt around it. A worm wiggled by her shoe. "Hello, old friend," she said. She hurried to get her watering can. The carrot drank and grew and grew.

Austin stood at the big kitchen table. His mom had a tray of cookies. The cookies were circles. Austin wanted to help cut paper shapes for the cookie party.

His mom gave him paper and safe scissors. Austin cut a square first. He found the corner and cut. Snip, snip. The square had four corners. Then he cut a triangle. It had corners too.

Next he wanted to cut a circle. He looked for a corner. He looked and looked. "There is no corner," he said. His mom smiled. "A circle is round," she said. "It has no corners." Austin turned the paper round and round. He started anywhere and cut slowly. He cut and cut. At last, a circle!

"Now I know how," said Austin. He held it up to the cookie. They matched.

Harper was at Grandma's house. She wanted to make toast for lunch. Grandma got out the bread and the butter.

Harper took the butter from the fridge. She pushed the knife on it. The butter was too hard. It would not spread. It tore a big hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Harper.

Grandma put the butter on the counter. "We will let it sit," she said. Grandma used a sharp knife to cut apples. Harper drew a pig on paper while they waited. She filled the pig's nose with pink crayon.

Then Harper touched the butter. It was soft now. She spread it slowly. The bread stayed whole. Harper made toast for Grandma too. Grandma took a big bite. "Yum," said Grandma. "This is the best toast."

Harper smiled. "Tomorrow I want to make toast again," she said.

Hazel sat in a big chair at the clinic. A nurse came in with a small tray. On the tray was a tiny needle.

"Can I hold it?" Hazel asked. "I want to see it up close."

The nurse shook her head. "Only I touch the needle. That is my job. But you can hold my sticker sheet."

The sticker sheet had beautiful stars on it. Hazel picked one star. "Will the shot hurt?" she asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said the nurse. "Then it is done."

Hazel held her sticker tight. The nurse used the needle all by herself. Then she put it in a special box.

"All done!" said the nurse.

Hazel looked at her arm. There was a small round bandage on it. "It was just a pinch!" she said. "I did it!"

The nurse clapped. Hazel put her star sticker on her shirt. "Next time," she said, "I will pick two stars."

Everly went to Grandma's house. Grandma had a big pink cake on the table. "Can I have some, please?" Everly asked. "Of course," said Grandma. She cut a big slice.

Everly took her plate outside. Her friend Reese was there. Reese slid down the grassy hill. Then Reese ran up. He looked at the cake. Everly wanted to share. She held out the plate. "Here, you can have some," she said. Reese ate a bite. "Mmm, thank you," said Reese.

Everly did not know what to say back. She ran inside. "Grandma, help," she said. "Reese said thank you. What do I say?" Grandma smiled. "Say you're welcome," Grandma said. Everly ran back down the hill. "You're welcome!" she called. Reese laughed and waved. Everly ate her cake with a big pink grin.

Scarlett was awake early. She wanted to wash her face all by herself. Dad put a small ice cube in her cup of water. Scarlett picked up the ice cube with her fingers. It felt so cold! She dropped it into the cup fast. Plop! Her ears heard the little splash. Then she washed her hands with warm, soapy water. The soap smelled like strawberries. She touched the soft towel to dry off. Dad held out his hand. "Here is your toothpaste," he said. It tasted like mint on her tongue. Scarlett looked in the mirror. Her eyes saw the ice cube floating in the cup. She touched it once more, very quick. Still cold! She laughed and poked it with her toothbrush. "Brrr," she said, and waved at the girl in the mirror.

Grace went to the store with her dad. She wanted to buy ten apples. Ten was her very big number!

In the fruit part, Grace counted out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." The apples went into the bag, one by one. "Six, seven, eight, nine." Just one more to find!

Then Grace saw a big sign. It said 10. She stopped and stared. "Dad, why does ten have a 1 and a 0? One and two and three have just one number each. Ten has two!"

Dad smiled. "Ten is written with two digits," he said. "A 1 and then a 0." Grace put the last apple in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" she shouted. "Ten apples, and ten has a 1 and then a 0!"

At home, Dad cut the apples into crunchy slices. Grace shared them with Lilly. Grace looked up at the white cloud out the window and took a big bite. "Crunch!" went the apple. "Ten is the best number," said Grace, and she ate one more slice.

Aria sat in her seat in the family car. It was a sunny day. The family was going on a big trip. They were going to visit Grandma, who lived far away. First they would drive. Then they would fly in an airplane.

Daddy put Aria's bag in the boot of the car. "All packed," he said. Aria clicked her seat belt. Click. The car went down the road. Aria saw a cow. She saw a big red barn. Then she saw the airport. The airplane was so big.

On the plane, Aria had a seat by the window. She wanted to stand up. She wanted to look out the window. She unbuckled her belt. Then the plane began to move. It went faster and faster. Aria wobbled in her seat. Mommy held her hand. "Buckle up," Mommy said. "We buckle for takeoff." Aria clicked her belt. The plane lifted up into the sky.

Aria looked out the window from her seat. The cars looked tiny. The clouds looked soft. When the plane came down to land, Aria kept her belt on. The plane touched the ground. It slowed and stopped. Then Aria heard a little ding. "We can get up now," said Mommy. Aria stood up tall and held Daddy's hand. "I saw the whole sky," she said.

Beau went to the library with his dad. The library was quiet. Beau found a book about a wiggly worm. He wanted to check it out all by himself.

At the desk, Ms. Flores said, "You may take ten books, Beau." Beau piled his books on the counter. He began to count them. "One, two, three, four, six," he said. Ms. Flores smiled. "You skipped five," she said. "The counting words go in the same order every time. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Beau looked at his pile. He touched each book, nice and careful. "One, two, three, four, five, six," he said. He had six books. He hopped back to the shelf for more. His friend Christine was there. "Help me count," Beau said. They touched the books together. "Seven, eight, nine, ten," said Christine.

Then Beau heard something. A small sound came from his worm book. He opened it. A paper worm popped up from the page. It was green and long and wiggly. "Hello, worm," said Beau.

Ms. Flores stamped each book. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," she said. Beau carried his books with both arms. "Same order every time," he said to Christine. She nodded and waved goodbye.

"Ten books," said Beau to his dad. "And one worm."

Aaron sat at the little red table. It was snack time at school. He had one cracker on his plate. Jocelyn leaned over and said, "That cracker is a square."

Aaron looked at his cracker. "I'm not sure," he said. "It looks almost like a square."

Rachel came over with a piece of string. "We can check," she said. "A square has four sides that are all the same length."

Aaron held the string on one side of the cracker. Rachel marked it with her finger. Then they laid the string on the next side. It matched. They laid it on the third side. It matched too. The fourth side matched as well.

"It is a square!" said Aaron. He smiled big.

Ms. Shevchenko walked by. "What a soft piece of bread you have too, Aaron," she said. Aaron put his bread on top of the cracker. It did not cover it all. The bread was round like a circle.

"Mine is a triangle," said Jocelyn. She held up her cracker with three pointy sides.

Aaron picked up his square cracker and took a happy little bite.

Sophie sat on her big bed. Dad was folding socks nearby. Sophie had her book about a red cat. She held it up to "read" it. "Cat goes up a tree," she said.

But the cat looked funny. The tree was funny too. "The cat is on his head!" Sophie laughed. The words looked funny too. "Silly letters," she said. One letter, two letters, three letters. All of them stood upside down.

Sophie turned the book around. Now the cat sat right side up. The tree stood tall. The letters stood up straight too. Sophie pointed at the letters. "That says cat," she said. Dad smiled and nodded. "That says cat," he said.

Sophie turned the book upside down again. Upside-down cat! She turned it back. Right-side-up cat! She did it one more time. Upside down, then around. Sophie giggled and giggled.

She opened the front cover first. She turned page one, page two, page three. The red cat found his mama at the end. Sophie closed the book softly. "Good night, cat," she whispered. Dad tucked the blanket up to her chin. Sophie hugged the book and closed her eyes.

Ali walked into the library with his dad. The room was big and quiet. High on the wall hung a round clock. "That clock looks like a circle," Ali said.

Ms. McKenzie was setting out a shape bucket. It was full of buttons, blocks and paper shapes. "Would you like to help, Ali?" she asked. Ali put his hand in the bucket. He pulled out a tiny red button. His friend Natalie came to look.

"That is not a circle," Natalie said. "The clock is a circle. It is big. Your button is too small." Ali held the button up. He looked at the clock. Then he looked at his button. Both of them were round all around. No corners anywhere.

Ali put the button next to a square block. The block had four flat sides. His button had none. He put the button next to a triangle. The triangle had three pointy corners. His button had none of those either.

"Ms. McKenzie, come look," Ali said. She held the button up high, next to the big clock. "Both round," she said. "Big circle, tiny circle." Natalie clapped her hands. Then she dug into the bucket and held up another button. "Tiny circle!" she said. Ali smiled and dropped his button back in the bucket.

Dylan ran to the water table at daycare. He wanted to wash his teddy bear first. "Bath time, Bear!" he said. But the water tub was empty.

Ms. Mensah turned on the tap. Steam curled up like little clouds. Dylan jumped up and down. "Hurry, hurry," he said. He put one foot near the tub.

"Stop there," said Ms. Mensah. "A grown-up checks the bath water first." She put her hand in the water. She waited. Dylan waited too. He counted out loud. "One, two, three."

Ms. Mensah added cool water. She put her hand in again. "Now it is just right," she said. Dylan touched the water with his toes. Warm, not hot. In went Bear. "Splash, splash," said Dylan. Atlas and Samy came over with their dolls. Three toys in the bath. Then Samy brought a rubber duck. Four!

After the bath, Dylan dried Bear with a small towel. He had taken off his own wet sock, and it stuck to his foot, tight and wrinkly. "My sock is tight," he said, pulling it off. He talked to Bear while he worked. "All dry now."

Ms. Mensah helped him put on a dry sock. Then it was snack time. Dylan sat with Bear on his lap. He gave Bear a pretend cracker first. "You eat, then I eat," he said. Outside, a bird sang at the window.

Arnaud stood by the daycare window. Outside, the sun was bright. He wore his yellow sun hat. Edison wore his too. "Sunny days need hats," said Edison.

Then the sky turned grey. Wind whooshed through the trees. Leaves rolled across the grass like little turtles walking. Arnaud tapped the glass. "Look at the wind!" he said.

Then came a big sound. Rumble, rumble. Thunder! River gasped. "What was that?"

"That was thunder," said Ms. Bear. She opened the door. "When you hear thunder, go indoors. Everyone inside now."

"But I want to keep playing," said River.

Ms. Bear held his hand. "Rain is coming. Boots and coats, quick quick."

Rain pattered on the roof. Drip, drip, drip. Arnaud watched from the window. The sunny hat sat on the wrong hook, all alone outside. He felt sad for it.

Ms. Bear went out and brought the hat in. She shook off the rain. Arnaud hugged it. "Someday it will snow," he said. "Then we need mittens."

River smiled. "And snow boots too."

The thunder rumbled once more, far away. Arnaud and River built a tower with blocks. They stayed cozy inside, and the rain came down.

Anna loved the blocks at daycare. Today she wanted the big red blocks. She ran to the block table.

"Not so fast," said Mr. Yip. He put his finger to his lips. Shea was sleeping on the little blue mat. "When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice," said Mr. Yip.

Anna stopped. She looked at Shea. Shea's eyes were shut. His blanket went up and down. Anna tried a tiny whisper. "Blocks?" she said. Shea did not wake up.

Ananya tiptoed over. "I want blocks too," she whispered. There were three red blocks. Anna took one. Ananya took one. One block was left on the table.

"My turn?" whispered Ananya. "Yes," whispered Anna. "Then me." They took turns. One for you, one for me.

The room got dark at the windows. Nap time was almost over. Anna stacked her block on top. The tower was tall. It stood very still, like Shea on his mat.

Then Shea opened his eyes. He sat up. "Blocks!" he said in a big loud voice. Anna laughed. Now they could all be loud.

"Can we buy more red blocks?" Shea asked Mr. Yip.

"Maybe," said Mr. Yip. Anna held out the last block to him. "Your turn," she said.

Zoe sat on the train with her bag. She was going on a family trip to the snow. She opened her bag to peek inside. Her swimsuit was right there on top. "For the snow!" said Zoe. Her dad laughed. "Snow is cold, Zoe. You need warm things." Zoe felt the window. It was cold and hard. Outside, snowflakes began to pass by the window. "Ooh," said Zoe. Snow needed mittens, not swimsuits.

Zoe looked in her bag again. She dug down deep. She found one mitten. Where was the other one? "It is hiding from me," she said. Her dad helped her look. He lifted the socks. No mitten. He lifted the hat. No mitten. Then Zoe wiggled her toes and something fell from her boot. It was the mitten! "You were hiding in my shoe!" said Zoe. She put on both mittens and clapped. Then she ate her apple, all warm and cozy, watching the snow fly by.

Elizabeth sat at the big art table. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked in the paint cups. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. There was green paint. But there was no orange paint. Elizabeth felt worried. A pumpkin had to be orange.

Richard sat next to her. He saw her sad face. "What do you need?" he asked. "I need orange," said Elizabeth. "My pumpkin can't be green."

Richard smiled. "Stir red and yellow," he said. He scooped a bit of red. He scooped a bit of yellow. "Now mix them with your brush."

Elizabeth dipped her brush in the red. Then she dipped it in the yellow. She stirred them on her paper. Round and round went the brush. The red and yellow swirled together. The paint turned orange! Elizabeth's eyes went wide.

She painted a big round pumpkin. She painted a fuzzy little stem on top. Mr. Holloway came over and looked. "What a fine orange pumpkin," he said. "Did you find the orange paint?"

Elizabeth shook her head. "I made it," she said. She held up her brush. On the tip was orange paint, still shiny and wet. "I can make more any time I want."

Gabriel went to the pool by the lake. The water looked big and shiny. Ms. Chen was his swim teacher. "Today we float," she said. Gabriel wanted to float like a little boat. But when he leaned back, he wobbled. His tummy felt funny. "I might bump my head," he said.

Ms. Chen put her hands under his back. "I will hold you," she said. One hand, two hands. Gabriel leaned back. He did not sink. He did not bump. He lay on the water like a leaf on the lake. "Kick, kick, splash," said Gabriel. His feet made a little noise. The water felt fresh on his toes.

Then Ms. Chen took one hand away. Gabriel still floated. Then she took both hands away. Gabriel floated all by himself. "Look at me!" he called. Boaz and Dua waved from the pool steps. Gabriel looked up at the sky. The clouds went by, slow and soft. "I am a boat," he said. "A little, little boat."

Clara loved her dog, Spot. Every morning she patted his soft fur. Then one day, Clara patted Spot and ran to the table. "Lunch time!" she said. Her mom shook her head. "Hands first, Clara." Clara looked at her hands. They looked the same as always. But she went to the sink anyway.

Clara turned on the water. It was warm. Her mom gave her the soap. Clara made bubbles. She rubbed and rubbed. "Sing the sun song," said her mom. Clara sang. When the song was done, her hands were rinsed. Then she got her favorite sandwich.

The next day, Clara played outside in the sand. She came in hungry. She looked at her sandy hands. She did not wait for her mom. Clara walked to the sink all by herself.

"Look at you!" said her mom. Clara smiled and made more bubbles. Clean hands, then lunch. Every day, the same way. That afternoon, Clara patted Spot by the door. "Wait right there," she said. She ran to the sink and sang the sun song, loud and happy.

Jack was at the beach with his dad. There was a little pool near the sand. Jack wanted to swim in it.

Ms. O'Brien was the swim teacher. "Let's start here," she said. "This is the shallow end." Jack put his feet down. The water was small on his legs. He could touch the bottom.

Kaius was already swimming. Kaius was at the deep end. The water went up to his chin. Jack wanted to go there too. But when he walked, the water got taller and taller. Jack stopped. His feet could not touch anymore. Ms. O'Brien lifted him up. "Back to the shallow end," she said softly.

Jack saw the rain clouds far away over the sea. Then the clouds came close. Rain began to fall on the water. Little rings grew in the pool. Jack watched each drop make a ring.

After the rain, Jack tried again. He kicked his legs in the shallow end. He paddled his arms. He was swimming. Kaius clapped. "Look at Jack!" he said. Jack drank his juice from his cup and smiled at the water.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a week. Owen wanted to make him a welcome sign in the kitchen. He found paper and glue. He glued on a tiny picture of a train. "Grandpa loves trains," said Owen. "Where does his train stop?" Mom pointed to a photo on the fridge. "He waits on the platform," Mom said. Owen saw Grandpa standing behind a yellow line. "Stand back from the edge until the train stops," Mom said. "Then it is safe to step in." Owen made his own platform with kitchen chairs. He taped a line on the floor. He stood behind it and waited. Then he pulled a toy train slowly in. Only when it stopped did he step in. Later, at the real station, Owen watched Grandpa's train arrive. Grandpa stepped off, smiling. Behind him came a second person, carrying a cake. It was Grandma! "Surprise," she said. "I came too." Owen laughed and hugged them both.

Madelyn sat at the big table at home. Caroline was coming to play. Madelyn wanted to share her toy monkeys.

She made two groups. One group had four monkeys. One group had six monkeys. She counted each group out loud. "One, two, three, four," she said. Then she counted the other pile. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

"I want this pile," said Caroline. She pointed at the pile of four.

"But that one has fewer," said Mom from the kitchen. "Fewer is the other word. This pile has more. That pile has fewer."

Madelyn looked at the two piles. She counted again. The big pile had more. The small pile had fewer. So Caroline got fewer monkeys!

"Wait," said Madelyn. "Take the big pile. Then we both have lots." She pushed the six monkeys to Caroline.

Caroline smiled and hugged a monkey. Its ear was sticky from jam at lunch.

"Let's count them again," said Caroline.

"Together," said Madelyn. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

Maya ran into the kitchen. Something smelled so good! "Muffins!" she said. Mom had made the batter. Mom put the pan in the hot oven. Maya stayed back and watched.

"Smell with your nose," said Mom. Maya sniffed. The sweet smell went up her nose. It went in two little holes! Maya wanted to see them. She climbed onto her step stool. She looked in the shiny toaster. There was her face! She found her nose. She counted the holes. One, two. Two little openings! "What are they called?" she asked. "Nostrils," said Mom. "Your nose has two openings called nostrils." Maya giggled. "Two nostrils! One and two!"

The timer went ding! Ding! Maya heard it with her ears. Mom took the muffins out with big gloves. The muffins sat on the rack. Maya waited and waited. At last Mom said, "One for you." The muffin felt warm on Maya's fingers. She took a tiny bite. Mmm! Sweet banana on her tongue! Maya touched the top with one finger. It was soft like a feather. "A special muffin for a special girl," said Mom. Maya held up her muffin. "And a special nose with two nostrils!" she said, and she took another big bite.

Mason sat in the family car. His tummy felt funny. Today he would meet the dentist for the very first time.

"Mason, are you scared?" his dad asked.

"A little bit," said Mason. "Is it bad there?"

"No," said Dad. "Your friend Aryan goes too. He likes it."

Mason counted the cars out the window. One, two, three blue cars. Four, five red cars. Soon they were at the dentist's door.

A big chair sat in the room. It looked like a giant seed, round and tall. Mason climbed up with the dentist's help. Then he pressed nothing at all, but the chair began to move. It slowly leaned back, back, back. Mason lay down, just like lying in bed!

"It moved!" Mason giggled. "The chair tips back!"

"That's right," said the dentist. "Now hold still and open wide."

Mason opened his mouth. The dentist looked and looked. "Nice clean teeth," she said.

Mason got a sticker. He stacked it on his hand like a little badge.

"Can we come back?" Mason asked his dad.

Dad laughed. "Next time, buddy. First, let's show Aryan your sticker."

Camille ran to the park. Her boots went crunch, crunch in the snow. She touched the snow with her mittens. It was cold and soft. Brrr!

Ms. Kobayashi was there with the class. She pointed up. Gray clouds sat in the sky. Camille heard the wind. It went whoosh past her ears. "What is that smell?" she wondered. It was popcorn from a cart. She sniffed with her nose. Yum!

Camille got a warm cup of popcorn. She tasted it with her tongue. Salty and good! Then her friend Judah ran by. Camille chased him. He laughed and she laughed.

Then Camille saw something odd. Ms. Kobayashi was looking for her mitten. She walked right past it. "It is by the bench," said Camille. Ms. Kobayashi put on her glasses. She looked again. "Why, there it is," she said. She picked up the mitten. Camille's eyes got wide. The glasses helped Ms. Kobayashi see it! Camille wondered, "Do my eyes need glasses too?" She blinked at the gray clouds. She could see them just fine. "My eyes see clear," she said. Then she chased Judah one more time, all the way to the swings.

Olivia sat at the dinner table. She wanted spaghetti tonight. Mom had said spaghetti was for tomorrow. Olivia did not want to wait.

"When is tomorrow?" Olivia asked.

"Eat now, and sleep, and tomorrow comes," said Mom.

Edith was there too. "I went to the park tomorrow!" said Edith. Then Edie stopped. "No, wait. I went yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." The park day was all done. It was behind them now.

Olivia took a quick bite. She dropped her fork, and Mom picked it up with a smile. The light above the table glowed warm.

"So yesterday is done, and today is now?" asked Olivia.

"Yes," said Mom. "And later comes bedtime."

Olivia ate her noodles. Tomorrow felt far away. But tomorrow, the spaghetti would come.

Andrew sat at the little table in the tutoring centre. Mr. Rajapakse put down two plates. One plate had three cookies. The other plate had one cookie. "Which plate has more?" asked Mr. Rajapakse. Andrew pointed at the plate with three cookies. "That one!" he said. "Good counting," said Mr. Rajapakse, and he smiled.

Then Mr. Rajapakse picked up a cookie and ate it. Now there were two. He ate another one. Now there was one. He ate the last one. Andrew looked at the plate. It was all empty. "How many now?" asked Mr. Rajapakse. Andrew looked and looked. There were no cookies left at all. "Zero," said Mr. Rajapakse. "Zero means none." Andrew tapped the empty plate. "Zero cookies," he said. "That plate has more!" And he pointed at the other plate, where three cookies still sat.

Aryan clapped from the next table. Ozgy gave Andrew a kind smile. Mr. Rajapakse said it was time for a summer game. He had brought a small pot, and each child could plant a seed in it. Andrew counted the seeds. "One, two, three," he said. Then he gave one seed to Aryan and one to Ozzy. He looked at his own hand. It was empty. "Zero seeds," said Andrew. Mr. Rajapakse laughed and put a new seed in Andrew's hand. Andrew planted it in the pot and patted the dirt down with his little hands.

Abigail sat at the art table. She was making a house picture. She had a square for the house. She had a triangle for the roof. She had a circle for the sun. But she needed one small rectangle for the door. "I can't find a rectangle," she said. "Not one. Not anywhere." Macie looked in the paper tray. "No rectangles here," said Macie. Nate looked too. "Only squares," said Nate. "Square, square, square."

Then Abigail picked up a square napkin. She folded it in half, edge to edge. She pressed it flat. She opened one eye. Then both eyes. "Look!" she said. "My square is a rectangle now!" Macie clapped. Nate laughed. "Do it again," he said. So Abigail did it again. Fold, press, look. A rectangle every time. Mr. Eze walked over and smiled. "That door fits just right," he said. "And you didn't have to pay one penny for it." Abigail pasted the small rectangle on her house. Then she drew a star above the roof. "A rectangle door and a star," she said. "Best house ever."

Everly sat at the dinner table. Mama set down a bowl of warm soup. It smelled like tomatoes. Everly's friend Gregoire sat next to her. He had a big frown on his face. His eyebrows went down low.

Everly looked at his face. She remembered what Ms. Park said at school. "You can often tell how a friend feels by looking at their face." So Everly asked, "Are you sad, Gregoire?"

Gregorie nodded. "I dropped my toy car," he said. "It broke."

Everly felt excited about an idea. She slid her bread across the table. "You can have some," she said. Gregorie took a bite. Then his frown went away. His mouth made a big smile, the same shape as a happy banana.

Gregorie giggled. "Yum," he said. Everly smiled too. The kitchen felt warm, and the soup smelled good. Mama patted both their heads.

"I like dinner," said Gregorie.

Grandma had a gift for Lena. It was a shiny pencil with a thin yellow body. "You can learn to write your name," Grandma said. Lena was so excited. She held the pencil tight in her fist.

"Not like that," said Grandma. She showed Lena how to pinch the pencil with two fingers. Lena tried. The pencil felt funny, but good. "Now write L-E-N-A," said Grandma. Grandma wrote the letters first. Lena looked hard.

Lena started to write. She began at the right side of the paper. She wrote L. Then E. Then she ran out of room! The paper ended. No space for N and A. Lena frowned. "My name won't fit!"

Grandma smiled. She put her finger on the left side of the paper. "Watch me," she said. Grandma wrote her own name, starting at the left. The letters went across, toward the right. They fit! Lena clapped her hands.

Lena tried again. She started at the left. Pinch, pinch, went her fingers. L. E. N. A. All four letters fit on the line! "I did it!" said Lena. She held up the paper. Her name went across the page, just like Grandma's. "Again!" said Lena, grabbing a new sheet.

Nolan went to the library with his dad. Ms. Augustin smiled at the desk. She had a tablet just for Nolan.

"I will show you how to turn it on," she said. She pushed the little button. The screen lit up. It glowed bright. Nolan clapped his hands.

Nolan tried it himself. He pushed the button. The screen lit up again! He pressed the picture of the crayon. A drawing app opened. It had huge rainbow colors.

Nolan picked blue. He drew a big round circle. "A birthday cake!" he said. He drew red candles on top. Amelie sat next to him. She drew a yellow sun.

Then it was time to go. Nolan picked up the tablet with one hand. It slipped. It slid down, down, down. Nolan caught it fast with his other hand. His heart went boom boom.

He held the tablet with two hands now. It did not slip. It felt steady, like a hug. He carried it slowly to Ms. Augustin. He set it down on her desk, soft and careful.

"All done," said Nolan. "I know just where it goes." Ms. Augustin gave him a high five. "See you next time," she said. Nolan waved at the tablet. "Bye, bye, cake."

Sophie wanted to wear her yellow dress. She pulled it from the drawer. But her arms were cold and sticky. "Bath first," said her dad. "Then you can wear it."

Dad ran the warm water. Sophie saw the steam rise. She patted the water with her hand. It felt nice. She climbed in with Dad's help. The water went splash, splash. She rubbed the soap on her tummy. It smelled like flowers.

Then Sophie jumped out. She wanted that dress now! She ran across the room. Drip, drip, drip went her feet. Water made a wet path on the floor. The dress would get all yucky and wet. Sophie ran back. She grabbed the big blue towel. She rubbed her arms. She rubbed her legs. The towel drank up all the water! Now her skin was dry and warm. Dad helped her put on the yellow dress. It stayed soft and pretty. Sophie climbed onto her bed. She pulled the blanket up. "Good night, towel," she said.

Axel ran to the park with Bastien. Ms. Bennett had a big red bag. "Let's play a guessing game," she said. "Close your eyes. No peeking!"

Axel closed his eyes tight. He held out his hands. Something landed in his palms. He felt it with his fingertips. "It is bumpy all over," said Axel. "It is a pinecone!" He opened his eyes. He was right! Bastien clapped.

Next came a feather. Axel touched it with his fingertips. "It is soft," he said. "A feather!" Then came a stone. It was not bumpy and not soft. His fingertips said it was smooth. "A smooth stone!" Axel laughed.

Then Axel heard a bird singing. He used his ears to hear it. He smelled pretty flowers with his nose. Ms. Bennett gave them a sweet apple slice. Axel tasted it with his tongue. Yum!

Axel's heart beat fast from all the running. He walked slow to the bench. "Again, again!" he said. "My fingertips want one more guess!"

Ruby woke up early. Today was her first day of school. She put on her red shoes. She ate a banana for breakfast. Mom gave her a big hug. "Time to go," said Mom.

At school, Ruby saw a long slide. It was tall and shiny. William was already there. Ruby climbed the stairs fast. She wanted to go down right away. But William stood in front of her at the top. "You have to wait," said William. "At school, children take turns on the slide." Ruby stepped back and waited. William went down. Then it was Ruby's turn. Whee! She slid down fast. The wind made her mouth feel cold. She laughed and ran to the stairs again.

Maksim was at the front now. Ruby got in line at the back. She waited her turn. Soon she slid down again. "Your turn came fast," said Maksim. Ruby blew a kiss to the slide and got back in line.

Evelyn stood at the front door. She looked out the glass. "Where did the sun go?" she asked. The sky was gray now. It was rainy. Rain went drip, drip, drip on the step.

Mom helped Evelyn put on her rain boots. She put on her yellow coat. The wind blew. It was windy too. The wind made a loud sound. It whooshed the tree back and forth.

After the rain, Evelyn went out to play. She found a big puddle on the ground. "Wow," said Evelyn. She stomped her boot in it. Splash! Water went up and up. Her friend Maddox came by. He jumped in the puddle too. Splash, splash!

"I want to see a monkey puddle," said Evelyn. She held her hands like a monkey. She crawled to the puddle on all fours. "Ooh ooh!" she said. Maddox laughed.

Then Evelyn saw something. The puddle was smaller than before. Where did the water go? She looked and looked. The sun had come back out. It was sunny now.

"Bye-bye, puddle," said Evelyn. She waved her hand. Then she jumped in one more time, quick, before it was all gone.

Eva's cat ran fast down the hall. "Come back!" said Eva. The cat liked to sleep in a secret spot.

Dad had put number cards on the doors. Eva walked and read them. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten doors! But which door was the cat behind?

Then Eva saw it. A little tail! It stuck out under a card. The card said 5.

Eva held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." Five fingers!

She looked at the card. It said 5. She looked at her fingers. Five!

"That says five," said Dad.

"It does!" said Eva. "Five is five!"

She pushed open door five. There was the cat, curled up on the big bed. Fast asleep!

Eva counted her pats. "One, two, three, four, five." The cat blinked at her.

"Purr," said the cat.

Grayson sat in the cafe with his mum. He had a big pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. He tried to make a G. The letter looked yucky and wobbly. "Why is my G so messy?" he asked. "Try holding the pencil near the point," his mum said. Grayson moved his fingers down. He made a G again. This time it came out clean and round. Then Grayson stood up to find his friend Lyra. He waved the pencil as he walked. Lyra came close. "Point it down," his mum said softly. Grayson turned the pencil so the point faced the floor. He walked over to Lyra and showed her the paper. "Look," he said. "That says Grayson." Lyra clapped her hands. "Do the robot next," she said, and Grayson laughed and drew one with his good G.

Madeline went to the store with her dad. She wanted a red balloon. Yesterday the store had lots of balloons. Today there was only one left, high on a shelf.

"When can we get the balloon?" Madeline asked. "Now?" "Not now," said Dad. "We have to shop first. Later we can buy it."

Madeline heard a big noise. Beep, beep! A cart bumped a shelf. The last red balloon popped. Madeline felt like crying. "No more balloons today," she said.

Dad pointed at the clock on the wall. "A clock shows what time it is," he said. "See the hands move. We shop now. The truck brings new balloons tomorrow."

So Madeline helped put apples in the cart. She watched the clock the whole time. Then Dad said, "Time to drive home now." Madeline waved at the clock. "Bye, clock. Balloon tomorrow!"

Emily was going on a big trip. First the family rode a train. The train went fast past dark trees. Emily looked out the window. She saw the wheels push the train. Then the whole train moved. One thing made another thing happen!

Next, the family got in a car. The drive was very long. Emily wiggled her legs. "I need the bathroom," she said. Dad kept driving. Would the car stop?

Then Dad pulled into a big place. "Look, a rest stop," Mom said. "Here we can use the bathroom and stretch." Emily ran in with Mom. Then she stretched her arms way up high. "The car stopped, and now I feel better!" she said. "Can we bring a snack too?"

Ivy had on her party dress. It was pink and twirly. "I want to sleep in it," she said. Her mom shook her head. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," said Mom. She held up soft blue pajamas with stars.

Ivy touched her dress. It was scratchy on her arms. She touched the pajamas. They were soft like her teddy. The dress had a shiny wheel of ribbon that spun when she pushed it. She pushed it one more time. Then she reached for the pajamas.

"Can my dress sleep too?" Ivy asked. "It can hang on the door," said Mom. "It will be there in the morning." Mom helped Ivy pull off the dress and put on the pajamas. Ivy looked at herself in the mirror. The stars glowed in the dark.

Mom tucked her into bed. Ivy hugged her teddy. His fur was a little sticky from jam at dinner, but he was still good for hugging. "Do stars sleep?" Ivy asked. "Yes," said Mom. "They sleep when the sun wakes up." Ivy closed her eyes. The door was quiet. The dress hung still. Outside, the streetlight glowed, and Ivy slept.

Nova wore her fuzzy socks to the party. The community hall had balloons on every chair. Her friends Florian and Aiza ran in with big smiles.

"Why is everyone making a fuss?" Nova asked. "Is it a holiday?"

Grandma held up a small photo. "This is you, the day you were born," she said. "A birthday celebrates that day. Today is your birthday!"

Nova looked at the photo. The baby was tiny. The baby was her! She laughed and laughed.

"So the party is for me?" she asked.

"It is all for you," said Mr. Barrett, the neighbour. He carried in a big cake. A grown-up lit three little candles. Nova watched from her spot. She made a wish. Then she blew out the candles. Whoosh, the flames went out!

At lunch, Aiza gave Nova a gift. Florian gave her one too. Nova hugged them both.

"You were that tiny baby," said Florian, pointing at the photo again.

Nova puffed up her cheeks like a baby. Everyone giggled. Then Nova took a big bite of cake and said, "Best born day ever!"

Jules ran to the park with his red bag. Inside was his soft brown dog, Woof. Mr. Diallo had made two big circles in the grass. "One circle is for animals," he said. "One circle is for toys." Jules put Woof in the animal circle. A pigeon pecked the grass nearby. It flapped. It hopped. It blinked its little eye. Woof did not hop. Woof did not blink. Woof just sat. Jules picked Woof up and turned him over. No wiggles. No tail wag. Jules carried Woof to the toy circle. He set him down by a ball and a truck. "Easy," said Jules, and he gave a little wave to the pigeon. Then it was time for lunch. Jules sat on the bench with an apple. The pigeon walked close to him. The pigeon was warm and alive. Jules peeked into his bag. Woof sat on a sandwich, soft and still as a stone. "Silly Woof," said Jules. He held Woof up to watch the clouds.

Jack had a new bedtime book. It had a bear on the cover. The bear wore a red hat.

"Read it, please," said Jack. Mom sat on the bed. She opened the front of the book. "We start here," she said. "The pages go one by one." Jack turned a page. The bear found a deep, dark hole. Jack turned another page. The bear fell in. "Oh no!" said Jack.

"Who made the bear fall in?" Jack asked. He wanted to know. Mom turned back to the cover. She put her finger on a name. "This is the author," she said. "The author wrote the words." Jack looked at the name. The name was small black marks. "The words say that name," said Mom. Jack ran his finger over the marks. "Marks mean words," he said.

"I want to see more marks," said Jack. "Can we fetch my other book?" Mom got it from the shelf. It had a duck on the cover. Jack found small marks there too. He pointed. "Author!" he said. Mom smiled.

Then Jack held his fork from dinner time in his mind. No, he put that away. He snuggled down instead. Mom read the last page. She closed the back of the book.

"Night night, bear," said Jack. "Night night, author."

Felix put his arms in his coat. The zipper would not go up. He pulled and pulled. The little slide stayed at the bottom.

Stevie zipped her own coat. It made a zzzz sound all the way up. Felix felt the cold air on his neck. "How did you do that?" he asked.

"I practiced a lot," said Stevie. "Every day at school."

So Felix practiced. He lined up the two sides. He pushed the slide. It stopped again. Outside the window, a butterfly landed on the wall. Felix watched it open and close its wings. Then he tried again.

Zzzz! The zipper went up. His neck felt warm now. The coat hugged him snug.

Ms. Ahmadi smiled. "Time for the walk to the bank, Felix."

Felix ran to the door. "I can zip it myself!" he said.

Isabelle went to the playground with her friend Robert. The sun felt hot on her face. The slide was cool and smooth under her hands. What a funny mix, she thought. Hot up here, cold down there!

Robert ran to the big sand box. "Help me move this box of toys," he said. Isabelle pulled and pulled. The box did not move. It was very heavy. Then she saw a small yellow feather on the ground. She picked it up with one hand. It was so light! It almost floated away. "Heavy and light are opposites," said Robert, laughing.

Isabelle put the feather in her pocket, next to her red crayon. She took one step, then another. The feather weighed nothing at all. A naughty breeze tugged at it. She held on tight.

"Look, Robert!" she said. "My pocket can carry a feather all day."

Zachary went to the store with his dad. It was a sunny day. Zachary felt excited. He wanted to look at the toy drums.

He found a big drum and tapped it. Boom! He loved the loud sound. He laughed and tapped again.

Then he saw Nelly from his class. She covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. She looked scared of the boom.

Zachary stopped tapping. Could he like the drum and she not like it? That felt like a funny idea. Same drum, two feelings.

"Want to play something quiet?" he asked. Nelly nodded. They found a soft bunny puppet. Nelly hugged it and smiled.

"I like the bunny," she said. "I like the drum," said Zachary. They both laughed.

Dad came back with the milk. "Ready?" he asked. Zachary waved to Nelly.

"Boom for you, bunny for me!" he said.

Natalie stood at the campsite table. She wanted to bake a cake for her family. Her friend Ezra came to help.

Natalie cracked the eggs. Ezra poured the milk. They mixed and mixed. The batter was runny. It went plop into the pan.

"It is so runny," said Natalie. "It will never be a cake. It will just be a pancake puddle." Ezra laughed. "A puddle cake! Squish, squish." Ezra made a silly squishy dance. Natalie waved a spoon like a magic wand. "Batter, be a cake!"

Her dad lit the little oven. Natalie stood back, far from the hot part. She watched the pan go in. The oven was noisy and warm.

"Maybe we should drink the cake," said Ezra. "With two straws." Natalie giggled so hard she snorted.

Then Dad opened the oven. He took out the pan. The batter was not runny now. It was a real cake. A cake they could slice!

Natalie jumped up and down. "Look, Ezra! The puddle got thick!" Dad cut a slice for each friend. Natalie took a big bite. "Best puddle ever," she said.

Michael went to the music room at the community center. His friend Halle was there. So was Mr. Novák. On the table was a big drum. Michael gave the drum a pat. It made a loud boom.

Then Mr. Novák held up a big paper. It had little dots and lines on it. "What are those?" Michael asked. Mr. Novák smiled. He pointed to a dot. "These marks are called notes," he said. "They show which sounds to play."

Michael looked at the paper. He saw a dot up high. He patted the drum. Boom, boom! Then he saw a dot down low. He patted it soft. Boom. Halle clapped her hands. Michael patted the drum again and again. "Look at my notes!" he said. "Boom, boom, boom!"

Lea ran into the big gym. Her team was ready to play. Mr. Wu gave out the shirts. Lea's shirt was green. Celine had a green shirt too. Joud had a green shirt too. "We all match!" said Lea.

The game began. Lea had the ball. She saw a shirt ahead of her. It was red. Was that Celine? No, it was not. The red shirt was on the other team. Lea stopped and looked around. Where was a green shirt? There! Celine waved her arms by the wall. Lea passed the ball to the green shirt. Celine caught it and ran. "Good pass!" said Mr. Wu.

At snack time, Lea had a sweet apple. She had an idea. She looked at all the teams. Every team had one color. Could her shoes hide on the green mat? She laughed. They could! Lea smiled big. "Same colors find each other," she said.

Gianna sat on her bed. She wanted to read her bear book all by herself. She hugged Bear first. Then she opened the book. But the pages felt wrong. The bear in the picture was going to sleep. Then the bear was eating honey. Then the bear was waking up. "That is all mixed up," said Gianna. The story was jumbled, like socks in the wrong drawer.

Gianna looked at her book. She saw shiny squares on the cover. There were little marks on the squares too. "Those marks are words," said Loic at school, and Gianna had heard him. Gianna turned the book over. Now the bear woke up first. Then he ate honey. Then he went to sleep. "One, two, three," said Gianna. "The bear is doing it right!" She turned each page, one by one, until she reached the back.

Gianna read the words out loud. "Good night, bear." Her voice made the story sing. She tucked Bear under her blanket, safe and warm. "I read it front to back," said Gianna. "You are clean like a bath, bear. Good night." She patted the soft cover and closed her eyes.

Eva sat in the waiting room at the vet. She wore her thick winter hat. On her lap was a box with holes. Inside was a little brown dog.

"Can we take him home today?" Eva asked.

"Yes," said the vet. "He is all healthy now."

The vet helped her lock the box. Eva hugged it all the way home.

At home, Mom poured dog food into a bowl. The dog ran to it. He crunched and munched.

Eva wanted to play. She reached for her ball.

"Not now," said Mom. "When a pet is sleeping or eating, it is best to leave him alone."

Eva sat on the floor. She waited. The dog crunched some more. Then the bowl was empty. The dog licked his lips. He looked at Eva.

"Wanna play?" Eva asked.

The dog wagged his tail. Eva rolled the ball. He chased it all around the room.

Nolan had a big story about the dog next door. He ran to the table with his coat still on. He wanted to tell it now.

At dinner, Mama began to talk. "Today I saw a big red truck," she said. "Stop! Dog story!" said Nolan. Mama stopped talking. Papa stopped talking. The story about the truck got lost.
