Nolan tried again. Papa began to talk about the park. Nolan opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He took a bite of bread. He waited. Papa finished talking about the ducks. "Your turn," said Papa. "Dog story time!" said Nolan. "The dog had one white paw and two black ears!"

"Good waiting," said Mama. Nolan ate one more bite. His eyes were sleepy. "Ducks tomorrow," he said. "And dog stories after that."

Eva ran to the gate at school pickup. Her hair was all puffy and wild. She had slept on it funny during nap time. Mikaela pointed and laughed, not mean, just surprised.

"Your hair looks like a cloud," Mikaela said.

"Why does it look like that?" Eva asked.

"Because it has tangles in it," Mikaela said. "My mom combs mine slow so it does not pull."

Ms. Tehrani bent down. She held a little comb from her pocket. "Brushing or combing your hair gets the tangles out," she said. "Want to try?"

Eva nodded. Ms. Tehrani started at the top. She pulled the comb down slow. It tugged a tiny bit. Then the comb went through, and one piece of hair lay flat and smooth.

Eva watched the mirror on the fence. Puff, then flat. Puff, then flat. Each slow comb stroke made a soft place in her hair.

"There," Ms. Tehrani said. "All done."

Eva's dad came through the gate. He was carrying her green sweater and the backpack. "Time for home," he said. "Then a bath with soap, then dinner, then bed."

"And my hair will be smooth for tomorrow," Eva said. She held the comb in her fist all the way to the car.

At home, the phone would ring, and dinner would smell good, and Eva would put on her soft pajamas. But first she stood by the hall mirror. She pulled the comb down, slow, slow, all by herself.

"Look, Dad," she said. "The tangles went away."

Nicholas woke up and saw snow. Lots and lots of snow. There was no school today. It was a snow day at home.

Nicholas ran to the window. He wanted to keep a snowball forever. He put on his boots and his coat. His mom helped with his mittens. Outside, the snow was huge and soft. He scooped up a big white snowball. He carried it inside to the kitchen.

"I will keep you," Nicholas said. He put the snowball in a bowl on the table. Then he went to draw pictures of snowflakes. His snowflakes had points like a feather.

At lunch time, Nicholas came back. He looked in the bowl. The snowball was small now. There was water in the bowl. He dipped his finger in it. It was wet and cold. The snow had turned to water inside the warm kitchen.

Nicholas scooped a new snowball from the door. He set it in the bowl too. He watched and watched. Drip, drip, drip went the snowball. A little puddle grew. Nicholas clapped his hands. "Snow makes water in here," he said. Then he ran to draw that too.

Ayla's bunny was gone. She had brought him to daycare. Now she could not find him anywhere.

Ayla ran to the block room. She looked fast. She ran to the art room. She looked fast again. "I can't find bunny," she said. Avleen was there too. Mr. Chukwu knelt down beside her. "Try the block room first," he said. "Look at every spot in that one room."

Ayla went back to the block room. She looked by the shelf. She looked under the table. Then she dug through the soft pillow pile, one pillow at a time. There was something spotted and soft in the corner. It was bunny!

Ayla hugged him tight. "I found him in the pillow pile," she said. Avleen clapped her hands. Mr. Chukwu smiled. "Bunny can sit with us at snack time," he said. Ayla set bunny on the little town rug, next to the toy houses. Bunny was home safe.

Natalie had a cold. Her nose ran and ran. She sat on the couch with a soft blanket. Her mom brought her a box of tissues. "Blow, honey," Mom said. Natalie blew her nose. Honk! The tissue felt damp and crumpled. She dropped it on the couch.

Soon there were tissues everywhere. One on the cushion. One on the floor. One on her sock. Then Mom set the bin down by the couch. "Each tissue has a job now," Mom said. "It goes in the bin." Natalie picked up a tissue. She held it high. She let it drop. Plip! It fell in the bin.

Natalie giggled. She tried again from far away. Plip! She tried with her eyes shut. Plip! She picked up every tissue, one by one. The couch was clean. The bin was full. Natalie sniffed and smiled. "I did it, Mom. All in the bin!"

Elliot sat in the playroom with his paint. He wanted to paint grass. But the green pot was empty. "Where is green?" he asked. Mya looked too. "It's all gone," she said. Elliot felt tired of looking. Then he saw the blue pot and the yellow pot. He poured some blue paint into a cup. He poured some yellow paint in too. He mixed it with his brush. The paint turned green! "Look, Mya! Blue and yellow make green!" Mya clapped her hands. Elliot painted long green grass at the bottom of his paper. Then he painted a red sun and a blue sky. Ms. Schneider came to look. "What nice grass," she said. Elliot held up his brush and said, "I made green all by myself!"

Naomi ran to the door. "I want to go to the bus stop now," she said. "No coat today."

Outside, the wind blew. The cold air went up her arms. Naomi shivered. She looked at the big trees. The sky looked stormy and gray.

She ran back inside. She found her red coat on the hook. She pushed her arms in. One sleeve, then the other. The zipper was hard. She pulled it up, up, up. Click, zip! She did it all by herself.

Naomi went back outside. The wind blew again. But now she felt warm. "My coat keeps my body warm when it is cold," she said.

At the bus stop, Palmer was there. "Brrr," said Palmer, hugging his arms.

Naomi smiled. "I can help you zip up," she said. "First you put your arms in. Then you pull the zipper up, up, up."

Palmer pulled. Zip! His coat was closed too.

"Nice work," said Naomi. "Now the cold air can't get us."

Maya was at the beach with her dad. Near the sand was a little pool. Maya wanted to swim in it. "I will swim like a fish," she said.

But Maya could not swim yet. Her tummy felt wobbly. She held the edge of the pool with both hands. Ms. Munro, the teacher, said, "Hold on tight. Now kick your legs." Maya kicked one leg. Then two legs. Then she kicked very, very fast. "One kick, two kicks, three kicks!" The water went splash, splash, splash. A big splash hit Ms. Munro right on her nose. Her hair was all wet. "Oh my," she said. "Is the pool angry with me?" Maya laughed and laughed. "No, that was me!"

After the pool, the sky made dark clouds. Rain began to fall. "Quick," said dad. "Let's feed the ducks and then go home." Maya threw little bits of bread. One duck, two ducks, three ducks came to eat. Maya still held her towel like she held the pool edge. She gave one last kick for fun. "Splash!" she shouted on the sand. Maya hugged her dad and said, "I can kick. Tomorrow I will kick all the way across the pool."

Hudson wanted to build a big block tower. He tipped out all the blocks. There were so many! He counted them, one, two, three, four, five, six.

Tiffany came in. Then Wendy came in. They wanted to build too. But Hudson had all the blocks. Tiffany had zero blocks. Wendy had zero blocks. Wendy sat on the rug and looked at the empty basket.

Hudson saw Wendy's face. He counted the blocks again. "You can have some," he said. He put blocks in the basket. "One for you, one for you, one for me." Tiffany clapped. Wendy smiled big.

Then something made a pop sound. A sunny yellow ball had rolled in from the yard. "My ball!" said Wendy. "We can roll it after we build," said Tiffany.

The three of them built towers. One, two, three towers, side by side, all tall.

Blake ran to the park with her little red bear. "One, two, three swings!" she counted. But when she got to the swings, her hands were empty. Bear was gone!

Blake looked and looked. She checked the clean picnic table. No bear. She checked the big tree by the street. No bear. "One spot, two spots, three spots, no bear," she said.

Then Blake came to the tunnel slide. It was dark in there. She peeked in. She could not see anything at all. Her friend Kendrick peeked too. "Too dark," he said.

Mr. Rao walked over. He had a flashlight. "This can help you," he said. He clicked it on and held it for Blake. The light shone into the dark tunnel. There, at the end, was red fur!

"Bear!" Blake shouted. She reached in and pulled him out. She hugged him tight. "The flashlight helped us see in the dark spot," she said. Kendrick clapped his hands.

"One bear, two friends, three big smiles," said Blake. She slid down the slide with bear on her lap. "Wheee!"

Madeline sat at the art table. She had a new idea. She wanted to draw snow. Outside the window, snow was falling. It lay soft on the ground. Fresh snow is white, she could see. So her snow would be white too.

Madeline picked up a white crayon. She drew on white paper. She looked down. She could not see her snow at all. The white crayon hid on the white paper. "Oh no," said Madeline. "My snow is gone." Marko leaned over. Letty leaned over too. "Where is it?" asked Letty.

Madeline looked at the paper stack. She saw red paper, yellow paper and green paper. Then she saw blue paper. She took the blue sheet. She drew her snow again with the white crayon. Now the snow showed up big and bright. "There it is!" said Marko. Madeline drew white snow on the blue sky. Letty drew red mittens on her own snow.

Ms. McKenzie came to look. "What lovely snow," she said. "It will dry fast, and then you can hang it up." Madeline was tired and happy. She put her head down for a tiny nap. When she woke up, her snow was dry. She hung it on the wall, next to the window, right beside the real white snow.

Cooper was in the playroom with his friend Alexander. They were playing house. Cooper was the dad. Alexander was the doctor.

Cooper had a soft bunny. He hugged it. Then he tripped on a block. The bunny fell far across the rug. Cooper picked it up fast.

"Bunny got hurt!" said Cooper. He looked worried. He touched the bunny's soft ears. He held its floppy shape in his hands.

Ms. Lindqvist came over. She knelt down. "The bunny is fine," she said. "It is just a toy. Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Cooper thought about that. Then he smiled. He gave the bunny a big pretend hug. One hug, two hugs, three hugs.

"Here, doctor," said Cooper. He handed the bunny to Alexander. "Please fix it."

Alexander tapped the bunny with a toy spoon. "All better!" he said.

Then Cooper folded a small blanket. He wrapped the bunny up snug. "Sleep now," he whispered. The bunny closed its eyes. Well, Cooper made them close, with his fingers.

Parker went to the community center with his dad. There was a big piano in the music room. Ms. Ivanova smiled and said, "You can play it."

Parker sat on the bench. He wanted to play a big growly bear. He pushed a key on the right. It made a high sound, like a little bird. That was not a bear. Parker looked sad. "That's not growly," he said.

His friend Rania came to sit next to him. She pointed to the left side. "Try way over here," she said. Parker reached far to the left. He pushed a big key. Boom! A low sound came out. "That's my bear!" said Parker. He pushed it again and again. Growl, growl, growl.

Then Parker wanted a little chick too, like from an egg. He reached way to the right. He pushed a small key. Tweet! A high sound came out. Rania laughed. "That's the chick," she said. Parker played the bear, then the chick. Low, then high.

Ms. Ivanova clapped. Parker pulled the bench closer so Rania could reach too. Rania made the low bear sound. Parker made the high chick sound. They played together, bear and chick, all the way to the end of the song.

Elliot stood in the school hallway. He held his dad's hand. The classroom door was open. Bright pictures hung on the wall. Elliot could smell crayons and glue. He heard kids laughing inside.

"My tummy feels funny," Elliot said. "It feels like worms wiggling in there."

Dad knelt down. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," he said. "Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay."

Elliot looked at the door. A boy named Eugene ran past with a paper airplane. It would float, then dip, then float again. Elliot laughed. His wiggly tummy felt smaller.

"Want to go in?" Dad asked.

Elliot nodded. He walked to the door. Eugene held out the paper airplane.

"You fly it next," Eugene said.

Elliot took it. He threw it high. The airplane floated over the desks and landed on a soft rug.

Leah was at school. It was a busy day. Mr. Park said, "Time to change for gym."

Leah took off her painty shirt. Paint was on the sleeve. She dropped it on the floor. Her friend Blair dropped her socks on the floor too. Then Blair picked them up fast.

"Look, Leah," Blair said. She threw a sock at the basket. Swish! It went in. "Laundry basketball," Blair said. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed."

Leah threw her shirt. It missed. It fell on Louis's foot. Louis laughed. "Try again," he said. Leah threw it high. Swish! It went in.

Then Leah threw her sock. It landed on Mr. Park's head. Everyone laughed. Mr. Park wore it like a hat. He walked to the basket. He dropped it in. "One point for me," he said.

After gym, the class had a birthday snack for Louis. Leah looked at her clean shirt in her bag. It was the other shirt, not the painty one. The painty shirt was in the wash now, all ready for tomorrow.

Blair said, "Basketball again tomorrow?" Leah nodded. "But Mr. Park keeps the sock hat," she said.

Paisley sat at the dinner table. Morgan sat on one side of her. Zorawar sat on the other side. Mom set out one big bowl of corn. There was also a small silver salt shaker.

"I want the salt first," said Morgan. "I want it too," said Zorawar. Both hands reached for the little shaker. It started to slip off the table. Paisley caught it with both hands.

"Wait," said Paisley. "You can take turns." Morgan looked at her. "Like this. First Morgan gets a go. Then Zorawar gets a go." She put the shaker in Morgan's hands. Morgan shook a little salt on his corn. "Your go is done," said Paisley. Then she passed the shaker to Zorawar. He shook a little salt too. He gave the shaker back to Paisley. "Now it is my go," she said. She shook a tiny bit on her plate.

After that, the water pitcher came around too. Morgan poured, then Zorawar, then Paisley, one after another. Everyone got a turn. Nobody grabbed. The table felt quiet and calm.

Dad brought out warm bread last. Paisley waited with her hands in her lap. She looked at the fox picture on her placemat. The fox had two bread rolls in its paws. Paisley giggled. "That fox is not taking turns," she said. Morgan laughed too. Zorawar held out the bread basket. "Your go, Paisley," he said.

Hayden wanted a big garden. He dug little holes in the backyard dirt. He put tomato seeds in one row. He put carrot seeds in another row.

The next day, Hayden forgot which row was which. "Oops," he said. "Where are my tomatoes?" His friend Harris came over to help. Harris held out some paper squares. "We can make picture labels," Harris said.

Hayden drew a red tomato. He drew a long orange carrot. He stuck the labels in the soil. Now every row had a picture to show what was planted there. Hayden clapped his hands.

Days went by. Little green sprouts popped up. Hayden ran to the labels. He pointed at the tomato picture. "That row is my favorite!" he said. Harris laughed. "Let's give the sprouts some water," he said. Hayden grabbed his little watering can and ran.

Matthew was playing outside in the mud. He made a big, heavy mud pie. Then the bell rang. It was snack time.

Matthew ran to the table. His teacher, Mr. Morin, held up his hand. "Stop," said Mr. Morin. "Look at your hands." Matthew looked. His hands were brown with mud. "We wash our hands before we eat," said Mr. Morin.

Matthew walked to the bathroom. The light was on. He stood on his step stool at the sink. Mr. Morin turned on the water, because it was warm. Matthew put his hands under the soap pump. He pushed it himself. He rubbed and rubbed. The soap made white bubbles.

His friend Harlow came in. She had mud on her hands too. "Watch," said Matthew. He held his hands under the water. The mud went down, down, down the drain. His hands were clean and pink. "You do it too," he said. Harlow got her own soap. She rubbed and rubbed. Her mud went down the drain too.

Then they ran back to the table. Mr. Morin gave them each a plate of crackers. "Clean hands first," said Matthew, and he picked up his cracker.

Today was the puppet show at school. John felt excited. He wanted to jump and bounce and shout. He jumped so much that he bumped Kabir. Kabir fell down and felt sad. John felt bad too.

"Sit on your hands," said Mr. Almeida with a smile. John sat on his hands. He still felt excited. But now he could not jump. He looked out the window. He saw a big tree. A bird sat on a low branch. The bird sat very still. Was the bird waiting too?

John watched the bird. His body got calm. Soon the puppets came out. John clapped with everyone. "I waited like the bird," he whispered to Kabir. Kabir smiled and clapped too.

It was raining at daycare. Natalie looked out the big window. The rain made little taps on the glass. Then the rain stopped, and the sun came out.

Natalie ran outside with Adonis. There was a puddle on the ground. It was big and shiny like a magic mirror. Natalie jumped in it. Splash! Her socks got wet. Her socks got cold too.

"Wet and dry are opposites," said Adonis. He pointed at his own socks. "Mine are still dry."

Natalie touched her wet sock. Then she touched her dry sleeve. The sock felt squishy. The sleeve felt soft and warm. She counted her squishy toes through the wet sock. One, two, three, four, five.

Ms. Ross came out with a busy smile. "Natalie, let's get you new socks." Inside, Natalie pulled off the wet socks. She wiggled her toes in the dry, warm new ones.

"Can we splash again tomorrow?" she asked.

"Bring extra socks," said Ms. Ross, and she hung the wet ones by the sunny window.

Sienna sat at the big library table. Mr. Farah gave her a pencil. "Hold it like this," he said. He showed her how to pinch it near the tip. Sienna tried. The pencil felt funny in her hand.

She wanted to write her own name. She made a big S. Then a wobbly i. Then a letter that did not look like anything at all. "That one looks ugly," said her friend Ariella, peeking over. Ariella was reading a book about a chicken.

Sienna turned the pencil around. There was a pink part on the end. She rubbed it on the ugly letter. The mark went away! The paper was clean again.

She made a new letter. It came out neat. "It rubs out," Sienna whispered. She wrote e, then n, then n, then a. She sat back and read it out loud. "Sienna."

Mr. Farah smiled. Sienna jumped up and did a little run around the table, then sat back down. She picked up the pencil again. Maybe she could write it one more time.

William got to the pool first. He could see the big blue water. It went splash, splash against the side.

William wanted to jump in. Beverly and Zane were still putting on their shoes. Ms. MacLeod was not there yet. William sat down at the edge. He put his toes in the water. Brrr, it was cool! He waited. He loved the pool, but he waited anyway.

Then Ms. MacLeod came in with a big bag. "I will watch you now," she said. William stood up. He jumped! Splash! The water went everywhere. Beverly laughed. Zane jumped too. Ms. MacLeod smiled and kept watching.

The water made rings around William. He made his arms go round and round. The rings got bigger and bigger. "Look, Ms. MacLeod!" he said. She said, "I see you, William. I am careful, and I am watching." William kicked his legs. Splash, splash, splash.

Willow ran up the hill to Marlee's house. She could not wait to meet Marlee's new toys! At the door, Marlee smiled big. "Come see my room!"

There was a shiny red car on the rug. Willow wanted it right now. She grabbed it. Marlee's mouth went sad. Willow's tummy felt funny.

Then Willow saw a fluffy bear up on a high shelf. "Who is that?" she asked. "That's Mr. Bits," said Marlee. "I put him away before you came. My mom said I can keep him just for me."

Willow thought about her bunny at home. So a special toy could go away first! "Can I try the car gently?" she asked. "Yes! Then it is my turn." Willow rolled the car slow and gentle. Then she passed it to Marlee. "Vroom," said Marlee. "Your turn again!"

Jack wanted his red hat. He could not find it anywhere. He looked under the swing. He looked by the sand box. No hat.

Then he saw something move. It was a leaf. Then more leaves blew across the grass. The trees swayed back and forth. "It is windy today," said his dad. Jack watched the big tree bend. Its branches moved like arms waving.

The wind pushed a red thing along the fence. It was his hat! Jack ran after it. The hat rolled and stopped by the bushes. Jack grabbed it. He put it on his head and held it with one hand. The leaves kept blowing past his shoes. Jack laughed and chased them too. The wind made the leaves dance, and Jack danced after them. Then he sat on the step with his dad. His hat stayed on. What a fun, windy day.

Arya sat on the rug at school. Amari had a shiny red kite. It had a long tail. Arya wanted to hold it very much.

She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She looked at Amari's face. She put her hand in her lap. "May I have a turn?" she asked.

Amari smiled big. "Yes! You said may I!" He put the kite in her hands. Arya felt the string. It was smooth and long. "Thank you," she said.

Jose ran over too. He grabbed for the tail. "No, no," said Ms. Sinclair softly. "Try asking, Jose."

Jose thought for a moment. "May I hold the tail?" he said. "Yes, you may," said Arya. She held the kite safe and snug. Jose held the tail. They walked round and round the rug, humming a little song. "Zoom goes the kite!" said Amari, pushing it through the air.

Elizabeth went to the store with her mom. Her friend Haley was there too. Haley had a big cart. Elizabeth had a small basket. "Big!" said Haley. "Small!" said Elizabeth. They laughed.

"Those are opposites," said Haley. "Two words as different as they can be." Elizabeth nodded. Then she had a want. She wanted cold milk for her lunch. "Let's find the cold milk," she said. They walked past the bread. It sat on a warm shelf. They walked past the soup. A lady held a hot pie with two mitts. Elizabeth watched from far away.

Then they came to the freezer. The freezer hummed. Cold air came out. Elizabeth touched nothing. She just felt the air on her nose. "Cold!" she said. "Hot!" said Haley. They laughed again.

Ms. Greco from next door worked at the store. "Can you find me the slow turtle?" she asked, pointing at a toy shelf. There was a fast rabbit toy too. Elizabeth found the turtle. It was short and green. She found the rabbit. It was tall and white.

At the checkout, the belt moved fast. Then it stopped. Slow. Fast. Slow. "Watch this," said Elizabeth. Haley watched. The belt stopped and started all by itself. "The girl made it stop," said Haley. "My basket made it go," said Elizabeth. Mom smiled and put the milk in the bag. "Cold milk for lunch," she said.

Hailey was at the beach with her dad. The beach had a big pool next to the sand. Hailey wanted to learn to swim. Her friend Harper was there too.

Hailey got in the pool by the steps. Step by step, she went down. The water was cool. She held the side and kicked her legs. Then she wanted to get out. She tried to climb over the edge. It was too high. Her arms hurt. Her feet slipped on the wet wall.

Then Hailey saw a ladder in the corner. She wondered, "Can the ladder help me?" She grabbed it. She put her foot on the first bar. Up she went, one bar at a time. It was easy. She was out of the water in no time. She brushed the water off her arms.

Harper climbed out too. "The steps are good for getting in," Hailey said. "The ladder is good for getting out." Harper smiled. "Race you down the steps again!"

Jacob woke up in the dark. He thought it was morning. He walked fast to the kitchen.

The kitchen was dark too. The big window showed no sun. Only a small moon was up. "It is still night," said his mom. "Day and night are opposites."

Jacob peered out at the dark yard. An ant crawled on the cold windowsill. It moved very slow. Jacob tapped his foot very fast. Then he yawned and moved slow too.

His mom poured milk into a pot. She made it warm on the stove. Jacob stood back, watching from a safe spot. The milk got hot. His mom gave him a cup of cold water first. He drank it down.

"Now try the warm milk," she said. Jacob took small sips. "Tasty," he said.

They sat by the window together. The moon glowed over the big tree. The kitchen clock ticked slow. Jacob's eyes began to close. His mom lifted him up.

"Night now," Jacob said softly. "Morning comes later."

"That's right," said his mom. She carried him back to bed.

Aubrey sat at the kitchen table. Athena sat beside her. Mom put down two bowls of crackers. "Which bowl has more?" Athena asked. Aubrey looked and looked. She could not tell.

Aubrey began to count. "One, two, three, four." Then a cracker rolled. Aubrey looked up. She forgot where she was. "Oh no," she said. "I lost my count." Her face felt hot and her eyes felt watery. Athena patted her arm. "Try again," Athena said softly.

Aubrey had an idea. She held up one finger. "One," she said. She held up another finger. "Two." She kept going, one finger for each cracker. "Three, four, five, six, seven." All her fingers were up. Seven crackers! The crackers did not roll away this time. Her fingers held the number for her.

Then she counted Athena's bowl the same way. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten crackers! Ten was more than seven. "Your bowl has more," Aubrey said. Athena laughed and clapped. Mom came back with a small plate. On it was a cracker shaped just like a wiggly worm. "That one is special," said Mom. "It is for the girl who counted all by herself." Aubrey held up one finger and grinned. "One special worm cracker!"

The lights went out. Isabelle's whole apartment went dark. "Oh no," said Mama. "The power is out." The fridge stopped humming. The TV went dark too.

Mama patted the shelf. "Where is the flashlight?" she said. Isabelle thought hard. Did flashlights like drawers? She clapped her hands. "The kitchen drawer!" she said. Mama opened it. There was the flashlight. Mama clicked the button. The flashlight made a huge circle of light on the wall. Isabelle peeked at it. The power was out, but the light still shone. "The batteries make it glow," said Mama. Isabelle waved the light across the ceiling. The circle danced like a fish swimming in the dark.

Isabelle and Mama sat on the rug. They made shadows, a bunny and a bird. Soon the lights came back on. The fridge hummed again. "All done," said Isabelle, and she clicked the flashlight off.

Billie sat in her car seat. Mom was driving to Ms. Kamau's house. "We will have tea," Mom said. Billie liked tea time.

At the house, Ms. Kamau put water in a kettle. She turned it on. Billie wanted to see the bubbles. She began to walk to the stove. Mom held her hand. "Stay back with me," Mom said.

They stood by the old lamp in the corner. Billie could still see the pot. Soon the water went hiss, hiss. White steam rose up. It looked like a cloud. "The steam is hot," said Ms. Kamau. "It can burn you. So we stay back here." Billie watched from far away. The steam went up and up. It made the window foggy. Billie touched the foggy window with one finger. The glass was cool.

Ms. Kamau poured the tea into cups. Billie got warm milk in a little cup. "I choose milk," she said. Everyone sat down together. Billie sipped her milk. Outside, the car waited in the sun. "More steam," Billie said, pointing at the window. Ms. Kamau laughed. "Yes," she said. "Let's watch it together."

Lennon sat at the dinner table. She ate her peas, one by one. She drank her milk. Mom said, "After dinner, we go outside." Lennon looked down at her feet. Her feet were bare. "I need shoes," she said.

Lennon ran to get her shoes. She pushed them onto her bare feet. She pulled and pulled. The shoes felt bumpy inside. She tried to walk. "Ouch!" she said. She sat down on the floor. What was wrong? She peeked inside a shoe. Her toes rubbed on the bumpy part.

Then Lennon saw her socks on the chair. Maybe the socks came first. She pulled the shoes off. She put the socks on her feet. Then she put the shoes back on. Now the shoes felt soft and warm. She stood up and stomped. "Socks first, then shoes!" she said. Mom held the door open. Lennon ran outside with her coat on.

Aubrey sat on the big couch. She had a cold. Her cup of water sat beside her. She hugged her bear, Mr. Flop.

A sneeze was coming. One, two, three. "Achoo!" Germs flew all over Mr. Flop.

Her grandma came in with a tissue. "Try your elbow next time," Grandma said. She lifted her own arm and showed the elbow trick.

Aubrey held Mr. Flop up high. "Your turn," she said. She waited. She was ready.

The next sneeze came. One, two, three. Aubrey bent her arm fast. "Achoo!" The sneeze went into her elbow. Mr. Flop stayed clean.

"Now you," she told Grandma.

Grandma laughed and shook her arm like a swing. "Achoo!" she said, into her own elbow.

Aubrey clapped. "We did it, one, two, three."

Victor sat in his car seat. He held his little blue car. Then the car went over a bump. The blue car jumped out of his hand. It was gone!

"Mom, I lost my car," said Victor. Mom stopped the car. They looked on the seat. No car. They looked in Victor's bag. No car. Victor felt sad. He loved that little blue car.

Then Victor thought of something. At home, his marble had rolled away. It had slid right under the couch. Small toys could roll and slide under things like couches and beds. "Look down low," said Victor. Mom bent over and peeked under the car seat. "I see something blue," she said. She reached in and pulled it out. It was the little blue car!

"Thank you, Mom," said Victor. He gave the blue car a big hug. Then he held it tight, all the way home under the moon.

David went with his dad to the phone repair shop. A man with kind eyes fixed phones there. "Can I wait?" David asked. His dad said yes.

The man handed David a tablet. "Press this button," he said. David pressed it. The screen lit up like magic. David tapped the drawing app. He wanted to draw a red sun. He saw little circles at the bottom. He tapped the red one. Then his finger made red lines. "Red!" said David. He tapped blue. A blue fish appeared on his screen. He tapped white and drew white clouds.

When the picture was done, David pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the counter. "All done," he said. The repair man smiled and gave him a thumbs up.

Leon stood at the bus stop with his mom. It was cold. Snow fell on his red hat. Snow fell on his yellow boots. Leon stomped his toe in the white snow.

Then Leon had a big idea. He would keep a snowball! He scooped up some snow. He patted it round. He put it in his pocket. "My snowball can ride the bus with me," he said.

At home, Leon looked for his snowball. His pocket was all wet. There was a puddle on the floor. "Where did it go?" he asked. Mom knelt down next to him. "It is warm in here," she said. "The snow melted into water." Leon touched the puddle with one finger. It was wet and cold. Leon laughed. "Snow turns to water!" He got a towel and wiped it up. Then he put on dry pants and had warm milk with Mom.

Elliot sat on the playground bench. The wind moved his hair. He had five little toy monkeys in his pocket. He wanted to sing his song. But he was alone on the bench.

Then Meher ran over. "What do you have?" she asked. "Five little monkeys," said Elliot. He put them on the bench in a row. "Let me see them," said Meher. They counted them together. "One, two, three, four, five."

Elliot began to sing. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." He pushed one monkey over. It fell off the bench. Meher laughed. "Now there are four," she said. "One, two, three, four." They sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." One monkey fell off. Then there were three. Then two. Then one. Then the last monkey fell off too.

Mr. Lin came by with the balls. "Where are your monkeys?" he asked. "They all fell off the bed," said Elliot. He picked them up, one by one. He put them back in his pocket. "Five monkeys," he said. Meher held his hand. They walked to the slide. The wind was soft and warm.

Miles went to the park with his dad. They had a small box with holes. Inside was a guinea pig. "His name is Pepper," said Dad. Miles wanted to carry Pepper all around.

Miles picked up Pepper with one hand. He stood up tall. Pepper wiggled. Miles got a little mad. "Why do you wiggle so much?" he asked.

Dad sat down on the grass. "Come sit with me," he said. "Watch this." Dad used two hands, one under Pepper and one behind. Then Dad passed Pepper to Miles. Miles was sitting down, so Pepper could not fall far. Pepper sat still and made a soft sound. "He likes this," said Miles.

Louie ran over with his ball. "Can I pretend Pepper is a puppy?" asked Louie. "No," said Miles. "He is small. You have to sit." Louie sat down. Pepper sniffed his shoe. Everyone laughed. Miles held Pepper close with two hands. "Gentle hands," said Miles. "Gentle hands."

Chloe sat on the little red mat in the school library. She had letter cards in her hands. Shawn sat next to her with more cards.

"Let's put them in a row," said Shawn.

Chloe put down A, B, C. Then she put down M. Shawn shook his head. "That one is wrong," he said.

Chloe looked at the M card. She wanted it to fit. "Where does M go?" she asked.

Ms. Hughes knelt down beside them. "Try your song," she said softly.

Chloe sang the alphabet song in a small voice. She sang past H. Then L came. Then she sang M. She stopped and looked at the row. She picked up the card and put it after L.

"That is the right spot," said Shawn.

They sang together to see the letters all lined up. Then it was time for lunch, so they left the cards neat on the mat, A to Z.

Liam ran into the library. Story time was his favorite. Yesterday he missed it. Yesterday the library was closed. But today it was open.

"I want a story now!" said Liam.

Ms. Shapiro held up her hand. "The story is not now," she said. "The story is after snack. Now means at this very moment. Right now, we wash hands."

Liam looked at his hands. Now they were dirty. He washed them with soap. Now they were clean. "Now my hands are clean!" he said.

Marigold sat down next to him. "I wanted the story now too," she said.

"Now we eat crackers," said Liam. He gave Marigold the last cracker from the bowl. She smiled at him.

A baby made a loud noise near the shelves. The baby began to cry. Yanis found a soft book and gave it to her. The crying stopped. Now the baby was happy.

The clock made a tick tick noise. Ms. Shapiro clapped her hands. "Snack is over. Story time is now!"

Liam clapped too. "Now! Now!" he said.

He sat on the carpet with Marigold and Yanis. Ms. Shapiro opened a big book.

"Tomorrow we will read another one," she said.

"Tomorrow," said Liam. "But now, the story!"

Addison sat on her bed. She wanted to wear her new socks tomorrow. But tomorrow felt far away. Where did yesterday go? Yesterday she had played in the rain. Now the rain was gone. Time was a funny thing.

Mom came in with a small bag. "Is it my birthday now?" Addison asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "Soon." Addison frowned. "What does soon mean?" "Soon means in a little while," Mom said. Addison thought about that. A little while. How long was a little while?

She put on her pajamas. She brushed her teddy bear's fur. She picked out three books. Then Mom knocked again. She held a birthday crown and one cupcake. "It is morning now," Mom said. "Today is your birthday!" Addison gasped. Soon had come while she was busy. She put on the crown and yelled, "I am ready!"

Victoria ran to the playground. One, two, three, four steps up the little slide. She felt so happy. She smiled a big smile.

Then she saw her friend Leighton. He sat by the swing alone. His mouth turned down. His eyes had tears. "Why the sad face?" Victoria asked. "I miss my sister," Leighton said. "She went to visit Grandma."

A shiny puddle sat near the swing. Victoria looked in. She saw her own face. She made a big smile. The face in the water smiled too. Then she made a sad face. The face looked sad too. "Look," she said. "Faces show feelings."

Leighton looked in the puddle. He tried a smile. One, two, three, four teeth showed. He giggled. Victoria gave him a gentle hug. Then they took turns on the swing, one push, two pushes, three.

"I feel better," Leighton said. "Me too," said Victoria. They smiled all the way to the sandbox.

Ayla went to the store with her mama. She held the shopping list. The list was small. The cart was big.

Ayla saw Ms. Do in the store. "Hello, Ayla," said Ms. Do. Ms. Do was buying soup. The soup can was cold from the shelf. Mama picked a warm loaf of bread. "Hot and cold," said Ms. Do with a smile.

Then Ayla saw it. A toy drum sat on a shelf. It was red and round. "Can we get it?" asked Ayla. Mama said yes. Ayla tapped the drum. BANG! It was so loud. A man by the bread put his hands over his ears. A baby began to cry. Ayla made her hands go fast on the drum. Loud, loud, loud.

Ayla stopped. She made one small, slow tap. Tap. That was quiet. The baby stopped crying. The man took his hands down. "Loud and quiet are opposites," said Ms. Do. Ayla tapped loud. Then she tapped quiet. One drum, two sounds!

A cart rolled by, fast. A old man walked by, slow. A box began to drop from a shelf. A worker caught it. He put it back in a tidy line.

At home, Ayla played her drum. She tapped quiet like a little rain. Then she tapped loud like a big storm. Mama laughed. "Play your quiet rain for me," she said. Ayla tapped, tap, tap, tap, soft as a spring day.

Axel stood on his shoe stool in the bathroom. He wanted to brush his teeth all by himself. First he squeezed the paste. It smelled like mint. His nose knew that smell. He rubbed a little on his finger and touched it. It felt cool and slippery.

Then he heard a knock on the door. "Can I come in?" called Milana, his friend from next door. She was staying for dinner. Axel opened the door. He saw her holding a lemon slice. "Try it," Milana said. "It looks like orange."

Axel licked it with his tongue. Yuck! His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!" Milana laughed and laughed. "You made a naughty face," she said.

Axel drank some water. Then he looked in the mirror. He stuck out his tongue at himself. The mirror boy made a sour face back. "Hello, sour face," said Axel.

Evelyn sat on the rug at home. Her blocks were all around her. She wanted to give her best block a sticker on every side. But she did not know how many sides it had.

First she looked at her snack. Her cookie was a circle. It was round like a ball. She stuck out her tongue and licked a crumb from her lip. Then she put the cookie down and looked at the block.

"One," said Evelyn. She put a red sticker on a flat side. The side was a square. She turned the block over. "Two." She put a blue sticker there. That side was a square too. "Three, four, five." A sticker went on each flat face. Her socks were stinky, so she wiggled her toes and kept going. She turned the block one more time. "Six." The last sticker was yellow.

"Mom, how many sides does a block have?" Evelyn asked. Mom came to look. "Count your stickers," said Mom. Evelyn lifted the block up high. "One, two, three, four, five, six," she said. Six stickers. Six flat faces. Each one was a square, just like her red sticker.

Evelyn held the block to the window. The sunlight made six shiny squares glow. "Six," she said again, and gave the block a hug.

Luca was at the ice rink. His team wore blue hats. Luca held his stick with both hands. He saw his friend Lyra on the red team.

The red team won the game. Luca sat down on the cold bench. He felt grumpy. Why did he feel like that? Then Mr. Mokoena blew his whistle. "Line up, everyone," he said.

The blue team stood in a line. The red team stood in a line too. The lines came close together. Each player tapped gloves with a red player. "Good game," said Luca. "Good game," said Lyra.

Luca skated off the ice. His grumpy feeling had gone away. He looked back at the closed rink door. "Can we do that again?" he asked. Mr. Mokoena laughed. "Next game," he said. "Good game, Luca."

Amira loved her socks. She had red socks, blue socks, yellow socks and green socks. Tonight she wanted to wear her red socks for school. But her room was dark. Mommy had turned off the lamp.

Amira peeked in her sock drawer. She could not tell the colors apart. "Which socks are red?" she asked. She pulled out two socks anyway. They felt the same. She hoped they were red. She put them by her shoes and went to sleep.

In the morning, the sun filled her room. Amira looked at her socks. One sock was red! One sock was green! "Not a true pair," she said with a laugh. So she asked Mommy to turn on the lamp next time. In the light, she could see every color. She picked two red socks. Then she blew a kiss to her socks. "Your name is Red Team," she said. Off she ran to find Syed and show him her big news. "Look! Both red! Both!"

Julia wanted cold milk for snack time. She opened the little fridge at daycare. The door swung wide. She took out the milk. Then she ran to get a cup.

Mr. Kaya called, "Julia, the fridge is open. Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut." Julia looked back. The door was wide open. Cold air spilled out onto her hand. She pushed it shut. Click. Now it was closed.

She poured slowly. The milk was cold on her lips. Elyana sat on a small chair beside her. Sean drank his milk fast. Julia drank hers slow. Outside the window, a curly dog trotted by, big and fluffy. Julia held up her cup. "Cold milk is the best," she said.

Henri woke up in his bedroom. His tummy felt funny. He ran to the toilet all by himself. He used the toilet. Then he ran back to his room to stack his blocks.

"Henri, come back," his mom called. "You forgot something."

Henri ran back. He looked with wide eyes. He pushed the big handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. The toilet was clean again.

"Now wash your hands," his mom said.

Henri stood on his little stool. He turned the water on. He made bubbles with the soap. He rinsed his hands. The water went down the drain. His hands were clean and shiny.

That night, Henri heard his toy car beep under his bed. He crawled and got it. Then he yawned a big yawn.

"I have to go," Henri said. He used the toilet. He pushed the handle. Whoosh! Then he washed his hands all by himself.

"Good job, Henri," his mom said.

Henri smiled. He put on his pajamas. He got into bed with his car. He closed his eyes.

"Night night, car," Henri whispered.

Tomorrow Liam would go to the dentist for the first time. He wanted his teeth to be shiny. So Dad helped him at the sink.

"Brush the top teeth," said Dad. "Now the bottom teeth." Liam brushed round and round. His mouth filled with minty foam. It tasted good. Liam was about to swallow it. Then he stopped.

"No, no," said Dad with a smile. "Spit it out." Liam leaned over the sink. He spat the foam out. It went down the drain. His mouth felt clean.

"Again?" asked Liam. Dad laughed. "Once is enough tonight." Liam looked in the mirror. His name was on his little cup. He opened his mouth wide. His teeth looked white like tiny stars.

"Look, Dad!" said Liam. "Ready for the dentist."

"You sure are," said Dad. He gave Liam a big hug goodnight.

Max went to the art gallery with his dad. There was a paint table for kids. Max saw red paint and yellow paint. There was no orange paint at all.

Max wanted to paint a pumpkin. Pumpkins are orange. Max looked and looked. No orange. He felt like crying a little.

Gunner was at the table too. "I want orange," Max said. "There is none," said Gunner.

Max dipped his brush in the red paint. Then he dipped it in the yellow paint. He touched the paper. The paint turned orange! Max made a big round pumpkin. "Orange!" he said.

Mr. Campbell-Brown, the gallery teacher, came over. "What a fine pumpkin," he said. Max painted a green turtle next to it. On the wall behind him hung a painting of a sour lemon. Max held up his pumpkin for his dad to see.

Leah sat at the big table in math club. Ms. Sharma put down two bowls of buttons. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Leah looked and looked. She could not tell by looking. The bowls were too full. Lea and Esmee counted their own buttons next to her. Leah wanted to know too.

She picked up her buttons one by one. She made a pink line on the table. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. She touched the last button. "Five!"

Then she counted the other bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." She touched the last button again. "Seven!" The line with seven was longer. Seven was more than five. Leah clapped her hands.

Ms. Sharma smiled. She gave each girl a paper cup. "Feed the cup five buttons," she said. Lea counted slowly. "One, two, three, four, five. Five!" Esmae bounced on her seat and tried too.

Leah tried again with a new pile. She counted to her knee, back and forth, one touch for each word. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She stopped and said, "Eight!" She looked at the long, long line. "Eight is more than seven!"

Esmae leaned over. "Do it again, Leah. Count mine." Leah touched each button. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She sat back and grinned. "Ten buttons! Ten is the most."

Samuel sat on a chair by the hospital bed. His mom held a tiny bundle. "This is your baby sister," she said. Samuel looked at the small face. He missed sitting on Mom's lap all by himself. His eyes felt hot and teary.

Then Dad called out, "We need a clean diaper." Samuel jumped down from the chair. He found the diaper bag by the door. It was soft and smelled like soap. He carried a clean diaper to Dad. Dad smiled big. "Big brothers can help fetch things," said Dad. "You did a good job."

Samuel ran back for a small blanket too. It was blue and fuzzy. He laid it gently over his sister's legs. She made a tiny sound. It sounded like a kitten. Samuel laughed. "She likes me," he said. Mom lifted Samuel up for a big, warm hug.

Jake sat in the family car. He held his toy dinosaur tight. "Dentist today," said Dad. Jake's tummy felt jumpy. "The dentist will count my teeth," said Jake. "Roar," said the dinosaur, in a small voice.

At the dentist's office, Jake climbed into a big chair. It went up and up, like a ride. Then a bright light turned on above him. Jake squeezed his eyes shut. It was too bright! "Here, these will help," said the dentist. She gave Jake little sunglasses to wear. Now his eyes felt fine. The dentist leaned close. The bright light helped her see inside Jake's mouth.

"Open wide," said the dentist. Jake opened wide. "One tooth, two teeth, three teeth," she counted. "Ten teeth! So clean, like after a bath." Jake grinned. "The chair is slippery," he said, sliding down. "Roar!" said the dinosaur, riding on his lap.

Lincoln sat at the dinner table. He had peas, carrots, and noodles on his plate. He wanted his fruit cup. But first he had to eat his vegetables. That was the problem.

"One pea, two peas, three peas," said Lincoln. He pushed the peas into a green pile. He pushed the carrots into an orange pile. "Sorted by color!" he said.

His friend Benjamin was eating too. Benjamin pushed his peas to one side. "Look," said Benjamin. "Big peas here. Small peas there. Sorted by size." Lincoln looked at his own plate. The same peas! But a new way to sort them.

Lincoln found a round carrot. He found a long carrot. "Round ones here. Long ones there," he said. "Sorted by shape!" He counted the round ones. "One, two, three, four."

"Nice sorting," said Benjamin. Lincoln ate a pile. Then another pile. His plate was empty at last.

"Can I have my fruit cup now?" asked Lincoln. Dad put it on the table. Lincoln wiggled his foot under his chair. "One strawberry, two strawberries, three," he said. Then he sorted them by size, biggest to smallest, and ate them all up.

Noah was in the playroom with his friend Noam. Noam had a big bag of blocks. He poured them out on the clean rug. "Let's count them," said Noam. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Noah clapped. Ten blocks!

Noah wanted to build a tower with all ten. He put one block down. Then another. "One, two, three," he said slowly. The tower grew tall. He put on one more block. It wobbled. Then it fell down. Crash! The blocks went everywhere.

Noah waited a moment. He took a deep breath. Then he started again. "One, two, three, four, five." Mr. MacLeod came to the door. He smiled. "How old are you, Noah?" Noah held up three fingers, and then he said, "I am three!" Mr. MacLeod laughed. "And how old am I? I am four, no wait, I am much more!"

Noah giggled. "You are big." He looked at his three fingers. Three was his number. He was three, just like three little bites of his apple at snack time. Noam held up his fingers too. "I am four," said Noam. Four fingers, one more than Noah.

Back went the blocks. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Noah put the last block on top. The tower stood still. It did not fall. Noah looked and looked. "The answer is ten blocks," he said. Noam patted the top block, very softly.

Maya stood in the garage with her dad. An old piano sat in the corner. "Can I play it?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Be gentle."

Maya pressed a white key. It made a sound. Ding! She pressed another one. A different sound! Then she saw the black keys. The piano has black keys and white keys. Maya liked the black keys best. They looked like little bear noses.

Maya played only the black keys. Tap, tap, tap. It made a tune! Samir came in to play. "I want a turn," he said. He chased his fingers up the keys, fast. His tune sounded funny. "Silly tune!" said Maya. They laughed.

Then Maya pressed a key very hard. Boing! The sound was big. She pressed one softly. The sound was small. Big press, big sound. Soft press, small sound. Maya tried it again and again. "Listen, Samir!" she said. Samir made a small sound too. Then they made big sounds together. Boing, boing, boing! From the house, Dad called out, "What is going on in there?" Maya grinned and pressed one more key, very soft. Ding.

Paisley was at the park with her mama. She was excited to go on the slide. "Big slide today!" she said.

Then a cold wind blew. Big gray clouds came. Drop, drop, drop. Rain fell on Paisley's nose. The rain made the park close. "No slide," said Paisley. Her face felt sad. Her eyes got wet, like the rain.

Rupert ran by with his dad. "Bye, Paisley," he called. "I feel sad too." Paisley waved at him. She held her mama's hand. They walked home in the rain.

At home, Mama had a question. "Do you want to build a blanket fort?" Paisley wiped her eyes. "Yes," she said. They put a big blanket over two chairs. Paisley crawled inside with her bear. It was warm and cozy. She giggled.

Mama peeked in. "How do you feel now?" Paisley smiled a big smile. "Happy!" she said. Her sad feeling had gone away. Now she felt happy inside the fort. Paisley hugged her bear tight.

"More blankets," said Paisley. Mama laughed and brought one more.

Theodore sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy hurt a little. "May I wash my hands?" he asked. The nurse said yes. Theodore saw the little sink. He turned toward the tap. The nurse stopped him fast. "Wait. I check the water first." She put her hand under the tap. "Warm, not hot," she said. Theodore waited. Then she nodded. "Now you." Theodore put his hands in. Warm! He got soap. "How long do I scrub?" he asked. "Twenty seconds," said the nurse. "That is two happy songs." Theodore sang and scrubbed. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles. He saw a spotted fish on the soap bottle. Then the doctor came in with a sticker shaped like a seed. "Clean hands!" she said. Theodore smiled and clapped his soapy hands.

Jules sat in the family car. He hugged his bag. Then he peeked inside. His teddy was not there!

"Teddy is lost," said Jules. His eyes felt hot. "I want to run and look now."

The car stopped in a busy lot. There were so many cars. So many people. Jules put his hand on the door.

Then he turned to Dad. "I lost teddy. Will you help me look?"

"Yes," said Dad. "We will look together. Hold my hand."

Jules held Dad's hand. They walked past the big hill of shopping carts. They peeked under a bench. No teddy. They peeked by the door. There was teddy, sitting on a step!

Dad picked teddy up. Jules hugged him tight. "You came back," said Jules.

They walked back to the car together. Jules waved to teddy from his seat. He was happy all the way home.

James sat at the dinner table. He had a string of pasta on his fork. He twirled it round and round. "One twirl, two twirls, three twirls," he counted.

"I don't want to sleep tonight," said James. "I want to stay up late." Dad shook his head. "Bath first, then pajamas, then bed," said Dad. "One bath, two pajamas, three kisses," said James. "That is silly," said Dad. "But yes."

James ran the bath water from far away, where it was safe. Dad checked it. James got in and splashed. Then he put on his pajamas. One leg, two legs, one arm, two arms. "I will stay awake all night," said James. But his eyes closed fast.

The next morning, Elodie and Griffin were playing tag. James was too tired to run. He sat on the grass. He was upset. Elodie ran over. "Come play!" she said. "I can't," said James. "I stayed up too late." That night at dinner, James twirled his pasta. "One twirl, two twirls," he said. Then he yawned. "Bath, pajamas, bed," he said. Dad laughed. "That's my boy." The next morning, James ran and ran. "Catch me!" he called to Griffin.

Lea sat at the kitchen table. She wanted to paint a rainbow. But her paint box only had three pots left.

The pots were red, yellow and blue. Her mom said, "Those are the primary colours."

Lea frowned. "How can I make a rainbow?" A rainbow had so many colours. She looked and looked at the pots.

Then she had an idea. She dipped her brush in red. She dipped it in yellow too. She made a big dot on the paper. The dot turned orange!

Lea gasped. "It changed!" One paint plus another paint made a new colour. She tried blue and yellow next. Green spread across the paper, green like a leaf.

She tried red and blue next. Purple! Her rainbow was growing. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. All from three little pots.

Her mom sat down beside her. "What will you mix next?"

Lea held up her brush and grinned. "I want to see what red and green make!"

Maria walked to school with her boots on. There was mud by the gate. She stepped over it and went inside.

It was snack time in Ms. Pritchard's room. On the table sat a basket of bread. Maria was hungry. She reached out and grabbed for the bread. Ms. Pritchard put her hand on the basket. "Wait," she said. "We say please when we ask for something."

Maria let go of the bread. She looked at the basket. She looked at her friend Lily-Rose. Lily-Rose folded her hands and said, "Please may I have some bread?" Ms. Pritchard smiled and gave her a piece.

Maria tried it. "Please may I have some bread?" she said. Ms. Pritchard gave her a warm piece. "Here you are," she said. "It is hot, so blow on it first." Maria blew on the bread. Sultan sat down beside her. "Please may I have some bread?" he said. He got a piece too.

Maria ate her bread slowly. It tasted good. Then she asked for one more thing. "Please may I have some water?" Ms. Pritchard poured a little cup. Maria took a sip and said, "Thank you." Lily-Rose held out her cup too. "Please may I have some water?"

Audrey wanted to find her red ball. The playroom was messy. Blocks were on the floor. Dolls were on the rug. The toy box was empty.

Mckinley came to help. "Let's put them away," she said. Audrey picked up a block. It felt hard and cool. She put it in the box. "Blocks," she said. Mckinley held up a doll. The doll had soft yellow hair. "Dolls," said Mckinley. She put it in the box too.

Walter rolled something across the floor. It bumped Audrey's toe. It was the red ball! "Balls," said Audrey. She put the ball in the box with the blocks and the dolls. "Blocks, dolls and balls," said Mckinley. "They are all toys." Audrey clapped. "We win! The box is full."

Mr. Silva peeked in at the door. "What a clean playroom," he said. He pointed at the rug. A little bug was sitting there. "The bug needs a home too," said Audrey. She put her hand down low. The bug crawled onto a leaf by the window. Audrey waved. "Bye bye, bug. Bye bye, mess."

Tonight Iris's family had a party. There were candles on the table. Iris wanted to light one. "I can do it," she said.

"Not yet," said her dad. "The flame is hot. It can hurt your skin. Grown-ups light the candles." Iris felt sad. Then her dad said, "But you can pick one for me to light. Pick any candle you like." Iris looked at all of them. She chose the little blue one.

Dad struck the match. The wick caught. The flame grew small and bright. Iris had chosen it, and it was lit! "I picked that one!" she did not need to shout. She said it quietly, and she felt proud.

Dad lit one more candle. Then Mom called, "Snack time!" Iris ran to the table, still watching her little blue flame shine.

Emma wanted to go to Bjorn's house. She wanted to go right now. "Can we go now?" she asked. Mom shook her head. "It is bedtime now. You can go tomorrow." Emma made a sad face. "What is tomorrow?" she asked.

Mom opened a little book. The pages showed days. "Today is now," Mom said. She turned one page. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Emma touched the page with her finger. "Tomorrow comes after sleeping?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "First we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Emma got into bed. Her pillow felt soft and warm. She looked up with wide eyes. The night light made a yellow circle on the wall. Bath bubbles from earlier still floated in her mind, popping one by one. "Sleep first," Emma whispered. "Then tomorrow. Then Bjorn." She closed her eyes. She hugged her bear tight. In the morning, the sun was up. "It's tomorrow!" Emma called. Mom laughed. "Go get your shoes," she said.

Theo ran to the park with his red dinosaur. He played on the slide. He dug in the sand. Then it was time to go home. Theo looked in his hands. His dinosaur was gone.

"Where did you have it last?" asked Saif. Theo thought hard. "I held it at snack time," he said. "I ate crackers by the bench." The boys ran to the bench. Theo looked under it. No dinosaur. Then Theo saw a young woman sitting nearby. A big leaf had fallen from the tree. It lay over something red in the grass. Theo lifted the leaf. There was his dinosaur!

"Where did I leave you?" Theo asked. "By the crackers," he said, and hugged the dinosaur tight. Ms. Hussain smiled and walked them home.

Henry had a cough. Mom said, "We must see the doctor. We are not too late."

At the office, Henry was scared. Ms. Sutton, the nurse, smiled at him. "You can trust me," she said. "Let's play a game."

First Ms. Sutton held up a card. "Use your eyes," she said. Henry looked. He saw a red bird on the card. "A bird!" he said.

Next she made a sound. Tick, tick, tick. Henry used his ears. "A clock!" he said. Ms. Sutton laughed. Then she held a cotton ball near his nose. Henry sniffed. It smelled like flowers. Then the doctor looked in his mouth. Henry stuck out his tongue, but he did not taste anything yet.

"You get one small gift," said Ms. Sutton. It was a sticker shaped like a star. Henry touched it with his fingers. It was smooth and shiny. He moved it onto his shirt all by himself.

At home, Henry played with his toy truck. He was in the living room. Then he sniffed the air. He smelled something warm. He ran to the kitchen. Mom was stirring a pot, far from the hot stove. Henry stayed back.

"Mom, is dinner soup?" he asked.

Mom smiled. "Yes! How did you know?"

"I smelled it first," said Henry. "I smelled it before I saw it."

Aaron wanted to have a tea party. He set his teddy bear and bunny on the grass. He put out three little cups. There was just one problem. He had no tea.

"Where can tea come from?" he asked. His mother was hanging clothes on the line. She smiled and looked at the empty teapot. Aaron looked too.

He picked up the teapot. He tipped it over a cup. Nothing came out. He tipped it again, slowly. Nothing came out at all.

Then Aaron had an idea. He tipped the pot once more. This time he said, "Plop, plop, plop!" He watched his hand make the pouring motion. He heard his own plop sounds. And just like that, the cup felt full of pretend tea.

"Teddy, here is your tea," said Aaron. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" He blew on the empty cup. He counted slowly: one, two, three. Then he handed it to Teddy.

Haley jumped over the fence gate. "Can I come to your party?" she asked. "Yes!" said Aaron. "But do we have enough tea?" Haley looked in her cup. It was empty. "Is empty tea still tea?" she wondered.

Aaron tipped the pot for her. "Plop, plop, plop," he said. Haley laughed and drank it all up. The bunny got a cup too. "Plop, plop, plop!"

The sun went down slow and orange. Aaron hugged his teddy bear. "More tea tomorrow?" he asked. His mother said, "Any time you like." Aaron stacked the cups and grinned.

Jack ran onto the soccer field. The sun felt big and hot. His shadow stuck close to his feet. "Where is my water bottle?" Jack asked. He looked in his bag. He looked by the fence. It was not there.

The coach blew the whistle. "Break time!" Jack sat on the grass. His friend Fatoumata sat next to him. She took a long drink from her bottle. Jack felt thirsty. His mouth felt dry like sand.

Mr. Pierre walked over. He held a bottle in his hand. "Here, Jack. Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days." Jack took a big drink. The water was cool. "Can I try again now?" he asked. "Yes, you can," said Mr. Pierre. Jack stood up. He kicked the ball. It went right past the loose defender, Donovan. "Nice kick!" Donovan called. Jack smiled and ran on.

Lucas ran to the picnic table in the yard. His dad had set dinner outside. The table sat right on the green grass. Lucas took off his shoes first. Then he took off his socks.

"Look, Daddy!" Lucas said. "My toes are in the grass!" The grass felt soft and tickly under his bare feet. He wiggled his toes. "My feet can feel it too!" He laughed and stamped a little. The soft grass tickled more.

Daddy had helped bake bread that morning. Lucas could smell it, warm and good, with his nose. On his plate sat a sandwich cut into a triangle. One corner of the triangle looked sharp. Lucas touched it with his finger. "Ooh, pointy!" he said. Then he took a big bite. The bread tasted yummy on his tongue.

Finnley came over with his mom. He sat down and pulled off his shoes too. "Why did you do that?" he asked. Lucas pointed at his own bare feet. "Try it! The grass is soft!" Finnley put his toes in the grass. His eyes went wide. "It tickles!" he said. "It really tickles!" Both boys laughed and wiggled their toes together while they ate.

Parker had a new toy truck. It was big and red. Kaya came over for dinner. She saw the truck right away. "Can I play too?" she asked. Parker hugged the truck tight. He did not want to let go.

Dad set a small timer on the table. "When the timer dings, it is a new turn," said Dad. Parker played with the truck. He made it go straight across the table. Ding! The timer rang. Parker almost tossed the truck to Kaya. He stopped. "Can the worm ride in the truck?" he asked. "Yes," said Kaya. So Parker put a little toy worm inside. Then he handed the truck gently to Kaya. "Your turn now," he said.

Kaya made the truck go straight too. The worm went for a ride. Ding! Kaya handed it back gently. Parker smiled. "My turn is over, your turn is over," he said. "Then it comes back!" After dinner, they each got a cookie. Parker did not beg for two. He shared his cookie too, piece by piece. "Truck," said Kaya, "one more turn before bed?" Dad nodded. Ding! Ding! The timer sang.

It was William's birthday. The party was in his backyard. A green flag hung on the fence. The cake sat on the picnic table. William carried his party invitations in his hand.

His friend Ariel came to the gate. She looked sad. "I was scared I would get lost," she said.

William held up his card. "Look. My mom wrote it all here."

Ariel looked at the card. It had a picture of a cake. It said the party was on Saturday. It said the party was at William's house in the backyard.

Ariel smiled big. "The card told me when to come. It told me where to come too!"

"Want to plant a birthday seed?" William asked. He had a small pot and one little seed. Ariel patted the dirt on top. They poured water slowly. They would wait and wait.

Then Alya ran in through the gate, waving her card. "I read mine! Saturday, backyard!"

"Come on," said William. "Cake time."

Brooklyn sat at the big table. She had fresh paper and bright paints. She wanted to paint a sun for her grandma. It was a present for Grandma's birthday.

Her friend Manuel came to play. He sat down too. He also painted a sun. A big yellow sun with orange rays. Brooklyn painted a big yellow sun with orange rays too.

Then the wind came in the window. It blew both papers off the table. Mom picked them up. "They look the same," said Mom.

"Which one is mine?" asked Brooklyn.

"Can you guess?" asked Mom.

Brooklyn looked and looked. Both suns were yellow. Both suns had orange rays. She could not tell. Manuel could not tell either.

"Write your name on it," said Mom. "Then everyone knows who made it."

Brooklyn took her crayon. She wrote the letters. B for Brooklyn. Manuel wrote M for Manuel.

Now the papers were not the same at all. Brooklyn held hers up high. "This one is mine! It says Brooklyn!" Manuel held his up too. "Mine says Manuel!"

Mom put both suns on the fridge. Brooklyn smiled at her name.

Arnaud loved the letter song. He sang it at the library with Ms. Islam. He sang A, B, C, all the way to P. Then he stopped. "The song is done," he said. Avyan shook his head. "No, it keeps going," he said. Arnaud was upset. He wanted the song to be done.

Ms. Islam opened a big book. It had all the letters in a row. "A comes first," said Oaklynn, pointing. Arnaud looked at the last letter. It was Z. The alphabet ends with Z, he saw. The song was not done at P at all.

So Arnaud tried again. He sang Q, R, S. He sang T, U, V. Avyan clapped. Oaklynn poured water from a small cup for Arnaud, because his voice was tired. Arnaud drank it and laughed.

Then he sang W, X, Y, Z. "Now it is done!" he said. Ms. Islam smiled and held the door open. Arnaud waved to Z on the page. "See you next time," he said.

Elliot went to the park with his dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Elliot wore his cap and his light shirt.

Then the wind came. The wind blew the leaves. It blew Elliot's cap right off. "Hold it tight," said his dad. Elliot held his cap tight with both hands.

Then the sky turned gray. Drip, drop. Rain fell on Elliot's nose. Rain fell on his head. "We need an umbrella," said his dad. He opened a big red umbrella. He held it up high over them both. The rain tapped on top. Tap, tap, tap. But no rain fell on Elliot's head. No rain fell on his dad's head either. The umbrella kept the rain off!

They marched home under the umbrella. It rained and rained. They stayed dry. At the door, Dad shook the umbrella. Out came a small surprise. A little green leaf had been hiding on top. It fell down, down, down. Elliot laughed. "Bye-bye, leaf," he said. "Bye-bye, rain."

Sophia wanted to sing the whole song. Not just some of it. The whole song, all by herself. Mom sat with her on the big soft rug after nap time.

"Let's try the spider song," said Mom. "The itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water spout." Mom made her fingers climb up, up, up. Sophia watched. She made her tiny fingers climb too. But her spider went down, down, down. Mom laughed gently. "The spider climbs up," she said. Sophia tried again. Up, up, up went her fingers. Then the rain came down. Down, down went her hands. Then the sun came out, and the spider climbed up again.

Sophia clapped along too. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps matched the song. When she clapped, the song felt steady. When she stopped, the steady feeling went away. She clapped again and it came back.

Then Mom stopped singing. Sophia kept going. "The itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water spout," she sang. Her fingers climbed up. The rain came down. The sun came out. She did not miss one part. Her feet gave a little kick of joy on the rug.

"I did it, Mom! I did the whole song!"

"You did the whole song," said Mom, and she clapped too.

Amelia woke up and put on her socks. She was ready for school. She heard her dad speak on the phone. Then he called to her. "No school today," he said. "It is a snow day. School is closed because of snow."

Amelia looked out the window. White snow covered everything. The snow had closed her school! She ran to get her boots.

Next door, Kayla was outside too. Kayla patted a big snow ball. "Want to make a snowman?" she asked. Amelia patted snow onto the ball. It got bigger and bigger. Then she pushed it down the hill. It rolled and grew fat. One push made it grow! Amelia laughed. "That was silly," she said. "My little push did that."

They set a rock for the snowman's eye. They added a stick arm. Kayla clapped. "Good job, Amelia," she said. Amelia patted one more ball of snow. It rolled and grew too. She smiled and gave it a nose.

Raphael sat at the little red table. Snack time was grapes today. Mr. Romano walked around with a big bowl. "Each friend gets three grapes," he said.

Emmitt got his grapes first. His grapes were small. Then Lia got hers. Her grapes were big and sweet. Raphael had a question in his head. Did big grapes count more?

He held out his cup. Mr. Romano dropped in one, two, three big grapes. Raphael counted them with his finger. One, two, three. Then he looked at Emmitt's cup. Emmitt counted his out loud. One, two, three.

"You have three and I have three," said Emmitt. "Same!" Raphael smiled. Three was three. Big grapes, small grapes, it did not matter.

After snack, they used blocks to build a tall tower. Raphael put one block on top, and the tower stood up straight. He laughed and clapped his hands.

Ruby ran to the gate at school pickup. Her tummy made a little growl. She saw her grandma waiting with a bright yellow bag.

"Can I have cookies now?" Ruby asked. Grandma shook her head. "Not yet. First we eat breakfast."

Ruby stopped. "What is breakfast?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day."

They walked home. The sun felt warm on Ruby's face. Grandma's shoelace came untied, so they had to wait while she tied the string into a bow.

At home, Grandma said Ruby could help. Ruby looked in the cupboard. She saw cookies on the top shelf. "Those come later," said Grandma. Ruby saw oats in a big jar. She picked the jar up with both hands.

Grandma cooked the oats on the stove. Ruby stood far away and watched. The oats went pop, pop, pop. They smelled sweet like warm honey.

Ruby ate her bowl of oats all up. Her tummy felt happy and full. Then it was time for the rest of the day. Grandma helped her get dressed in a red shirt and blue pants.

"Can I have a cookie now?" Ruby asked. Grandma laughed and put one cookie in her hand. Ruby took a big bite. It was soft and sweet.

"This is the best cookie," said Ruby. Grandma wiped oat milk from Ruby's chin with a warm cloth. "That is because your tummy is full," said Grandma. Ruby held the cookie up to the window, and the light shone through the little hole in the middle.

David wanted to make bubbles. He tried water alone in the sink. He rubbed his wet hands and rubbed them again. No bubbles came. Just wet hands.

Then David got the soap. He held it under the water. He rubbed the soap with his wet hands. Bubbles popped up between his fingers. Lots of bubbles! "Look, Mom!" he called. "The soap and the water make bubbles!"

David rubbed more. He made a bubble beard on his chin. It was long and white and fluffy. He giggled and giggled. His mom laughed too. "Time to rinse," she said. The bubbles washed away down the drain.

Next came his pajamas. David pulled them on all by himself. He brushed his teeth at the sink. Then he climbed into bed. His mom read one book. David yawned a big yawn. "Tomorrow I will make more bubbles," he said. His mom kissed his head and turned out the light.

Jaxson stood in a big circle of people at the festival. Long tables were set with open boxes of warm bread. His friend Hallie waved at him. Her whole family stood beside her.

"Hands, everyone," said Hallie's grandma. "We say our blessing first."

Jaxson folded his hands. The blessing said thank you for the food. Everyone said it together. Then it was time to eat, but Jaxson did not move.

"Where does bread come from?" he asked.

"A farmer grew the wheat," said his dad. "The sun helped it grow tall."

So Jaxson cleared his throat. "Thank you for the food," he said. "And thank you to the farmer, too."

Hallie smiled and clapped. Her grandma blew him a little kiss. Then everyone took warm bread, and Jaxson took the biggest piece he could find.

Arya climbed the big school bus steps. Her backpack sat on her back. It was very heavy. She wobbled as she walked.

She sat next to her friend Zaiden. "My bag is too heavy," Arya said. She pulled it off her back. She looked inside. There were three toy animals, five crayons, and a hard rock from the yard.

Zaiden peeked in. "That is a lot of stuff," he said. Arya took out the toy animals and the rock. She left them on the seat beside her feet. Then she lifted the backpack again. It was light now! She put it back on her back and stood up tall.

Mr. Carvalho, the bus driver, smiled at her. Arya waved with one free hand. "Look at me!" she said. "My backpack rides on my back, and it is easy now."

Beau ran to school. His bike was too slow today. His legs went fast, but the bike went slow. "Hurry, bike," said Beau.

At circle time, Ms. Njoroge held up a big toothbrush. "Who brushed teeth this morning?" she asked. Mannat raised her hand. Jujhar raised his hand. Beau looked down. He had not brushed. "Can I pass the toothbrush?" asked Mannat. She passed it to Jujhar. Jujhar passed it to Beau. Beau held it up high. "One, two, three, brush, brush, brush!" said Ms. Njoroge. Everyone laughed.

"You brush in the morning," said Mannat. "And before bed," said Jujhar. Beau nodded his head.

At bedtime, Beau put on his pajamas. He hopped into bed. Then he popped right back out. "My teeth!" he said. "I brush before bed." He ran to the sink. His dad helped with the toothpaste. Beau brushed, brush, brush.

"Good job," said Dad. Beau smiled a big, clean smile. "Morning and night," said Beau. "One, two, three!" He jumped back into bed and pulled the covers up to his chin.

Sienna ran to the sandbox. Briella was there! Briella had the big red truck. Vroom, vroom, it went up the hill.

Sienna wanted that truck so much. She grabbed it fast. The truck jumped out of Briella's hands.

Briella's face turned sad. Her lip shook. Then she began to cry. Big tears ran down her cheeks.

Sienna looked at the truck. She looked at Briella. Sienna gave the truck back.

"Here, Briella," she said. "Can I have a turn next?"

Briella stopped crying. She hugged the truck. "Okay," she said. "One turn for me."

Then Sienna counted. "One, two, three, my turn!"

Briella pushed the truck down the hill. Then she held it out. "Your turn, Sienna!"

Sienna held the truck. It felt warm from the sun. Vroom, vroom, up the hill it went.

Later, Mr. Paquette called out, "Snack time, everyone!" Sienna and Briella ran to the bench. Sienna had a letter cookie, and Briella had sour lemon drops. Briella made a funny face. Then she let Sienna try one.

"One, two, three, my turn!" said Sienna, and she popped it in her mouth.

Ellie was in her bedroom. She had a cold. Her nose was red and her throat hurt.

Mom brought her warm soup. Ellie took a little sip. Then she took another. She put her teddy bear on the pillow next to her.

Ellie wanted to play with her blocks. She sat up and tried. But her head felt heavy. She felt bad, not good at all.

Then her throat began to hurt more. It hurt a lot. Ellie thought about hiding it. She could just be quiet. But she remembered something.

She called out, "Mom, I feel sick. My throat hurts bad."

Mom came fast. She touched Ellie's head. "You told me," Mom said. "That was the right thing to do." She gave Ellie some medicine and a cool drink.

The next day, Ellie felt a little better. The day after that, she felt better still. Soon she was not sick at all.

Ellie sat on her bed and stacked her blocks. One, two, three, four, five. The tower stood up tall.

"Look, Teddy," Ellie said. "We can play again."

Today was Ruby's birthday. She was four years old now. Grandpa had lit the candles on the cake, and Mom blew them out with Ruby. Ruby watched the smoke curl up. The room was full of people.

Then everyone began to sing. Ruby heard something. Were they saying her name? Yes! "Happy birthday, dear Ruby." Her name was in the song. She hid her smiling face behind her hands and peeked out.

Sam stood next to her. "Why are you hiding?" he asked.

"Everyone said my name," Ruby whispered. She looked at Sam's mom. Would Sam's name fit in the song too? She wanted to find out.

"Can we sing to Sam?" Ruby asked.

"Sure," said Sam's mom.

Everyone sang again. This time they sang "dear Sam." Sam laughed and hid behind his hands too. Ruby peeked at him.

Then Ruby ripped open a present. It was a paint set. One box was empty of paper, so Grandpa found some more.

"Sing one more time," Ruby said. "Sing Eunice!"

And everyone sang again.

Lucas looked out the kitchen window. Snow was falling on the grass. "No school today," said his mom. "It is a snow day." Lucas put on his boots and his red coat. He marched out into the yard.

First, Lucas tried to make a snowman. He patted the snow into a ball. The ball fell apart in his hands. He tried again. It fell apart again. The snow was soft and dry. It would not stick together. Lucas sat down in the snow. His snowman would not work.

Back inside, the kitchen smelled like warm soup. Lucas watched his dad stir a big bowl. Steam made the window foggy and wet. Later, they looked outside. The new snow looked a little shiny and wet. "Try your snowman again," said his dad.

Lucas marched back outside. He patted the wet snow into a ball. It stuck together. It made a big, round ball. Then he made a smaller one on top. The snowman stood up tall. Lucas smiled at the window. "Hello, snowman," he said.

Benjamin sat at his little table in the backyard. He wanted to draw a picture for his dad. He had red, yellow, green, gray and blue crayons.

He drew a red apple. He drew a yellow sun. He drew a green tree. Then he picked up the gray crayon for the sky.

Keziah came to the fence. "What are you drawing?" she asked.

"A sunny day," said Benjamin. He looked up. The sun was bright. The sky was not gray at all. On this clear, sunny day, the sky was blue. Benjamin put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He filled the top of his paper with blue.
