"The sky is really blue," said Keziah.

"Yes," said Benjamin. "Blue like my cup."

His dad came out with his phone. "Can I take a picture?" he asked. Benjamin held up his drawing next to the real sky. Click!

Benjamin could smell the flowers nearby. He smiled and drew one more thing. He drew a small blue butterfly, flying up into all that blue.

Zachary played in the sand box all day. His shoes were full of sand. His socks were sandy too.

"Time for a bath," said his dad. Zachary ran to the bathroom. He wanted to jump right in.

The tub was filling with water. It looked warm and bubbly. Zachary lifted one foot up high.

"Wait," said his dad. "The water might be too hot. A grown-up has to check it first."

His dad put his hand in the water. He moved it slowly. Then he turned the tap a little.

"Now it is just right," his dad said.

Zachary touched the water with his toes. It felt warm and nice. He slid in and sat up straight. He washed off all the sand.

After the bath, Dad helped him put on his pajamas. Zachary ate a warm snack. Then Dad tucked him into bed.

"Next bath, can I watch you check it?" Zachary asked.

"You can sit right beside me," said his dad. "I will show you every time."

Ezra went to the store with his dad. It was a cloudy day. Ezra wanted a book about boats. He loved how boats float on water.

The book shelf was big. Ezra could not find his book. He pulled out one book. It was about cats. He put it back. He pulled out another. It was about bugs.

His dad helped him hold the book. He showed Ezra the front cover. "That word is the book's name," his dad said. "It is called the title." Ezra looked at the big letters. He turned the pages from the front to the back. Cats on every page.

Then Ezra saw more big letters. He pointed at them. "Boats, Boats, Boats!" said the letters. He opened it front to back. Boats on every page. His heart felt happy.

A girl named Chelsea stood close by. She looked sad. She wanted a book about dogs. Ezra showed her the front cover. "The big word tells you the name," he said. Chelsea found a dog book all by herself. Ezra hugged his boat book tight. "We can read it front to back at home," said Dad. Ezra held the door for Chelsea on the way out.

Paisley stood at the front door. She wanted to wear her yellow shoes. Those shoes were for sunny days. She looked out. The sun was not out. Big white clouds sat in the sky.

"Where did the sun go?" she asked her dad. "The clouds are hiding it," he said. Paisley watched and waited. She could not see the sun at all.

The wind began to blow. It blew hard on the door. Paisley helped her dad close the door. Then she heard little taps. Rain was falling. The sky turned gray. "Now we need rain boots," her dad said. Paisley put on her plastic rain boots. They were blue. She put on her rain coat too.

Then the rain stopped. The wind blew the clouds away. The sun came out. It made the steps warm and bright. Paisley ran to get her yellow shoes. "Sun!" she said. She stepped out into the light.

Muhammad sat in his car seat. The wind whooshed past the window. He was going to the shop with his dad. He wanted a juice box. He wanted it so much.

"Dad, give me juice!" said Muhammad. Dad shook his head. "We are in the car," said Dad. "There is no juice here. But you can ask me at the shop." Muhammad tried again at the shop. "Give me juice!" he said. Dad shook his head again. Muhammad tried a big breath. "Juice, please," he said. Dad smiled wide. "Juice, please, coming up," he said. Muhammad held the juice box. It was white and cold. "Thank you," said Muhammad. "You are welcome," said Dad.

In the car, Muhammad bumped his cup. Juice spilled on the seat. "Sorry, Dad," said Muhammad. Dad gave him a small towel. Muhammad wiped the seat. He kept wiping until it was dry.

Then Muhammad saw something. When he said please, Dad smiled. When he said please, Dad helped. One little word made good things happen.

"Juice, please," Muhammad said again, just to try. Dad laughed. "Yes, Muhammad. Here you go." Muhammad looked out at the wind in the trees. "Thank you," he said. "Thank you, thank you."

Lena sat on the soft rug at daycare. Big blocks were all over the floor. Time to clean up, said Ms. Bennett. "Let's make color piles."

Lena picked up a red block. She put it with the red blocks. One red block, two red blocks, three red blocks. Next came the blue blocks. One blue, two blue. Then the yellow blocks. One yellow, two yellow, three yellow.

Walter found a green block. He looked and looked. There was no green pile yet. So he made one.

Then Lena counted her piles. Something was missing. One yellow block was not there. She peeked behind the toy mouse. There it was, hiding. But it was sitting in the red pile.

Lena held it up. "This one is yellow," she said. She put it with the yellow blocks. Now all the yellow ones were together.

Benicio clapped. Lena yawned. Snack time came next, and Lena got to eat a warm roll.

Ms. Bennett smiled at the neat piles. "Red here, blue here," she said.

"Yellow here," said Lena, and she patted the yellow pile.

Cooper was at Grandpa's house. It was winter, and snow sat on the window. Cooper had a big red truck. It could roll down the hall very fast.

Then Merrick came to play. Merrick wanted the truck too. Merrick held out his hands. Cooper pulled the truck close. His tummy felt tight. He almost grabbed Merrick's sleeve.

Grandpa was careful with the teapot. He set it down and came close. "Grandpa," Cooper said, "I feel like grabbing."

Cooper took three slow breaths. One, two, three. His tummy felt softer. "Your turn," he said. He gave Merrick the truck.

Merrick rolled it down the hall. It bumped the wall. Merrick laughed big. Cooper waited and took three more slow breaths.

Then Merrick pushed the truck back. "Your turn, Cooper," he said.

Cooper rolled the truck all the way to the door. Merrick clapped his hands. Grandpa smiled and poured two cups of warm milk.

"Again!" said Merrick.

Hannah had a big bag of blocks. She wanted to build a tower now. "Can Bowie come play now?" she asked. Her dad was folding clothes. "Later," said Dad. "First I make the beds."

Hannah sat on the rug. "Is it later yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Dad. Hannah looked at her blocks. She could not touch them yet. She made a little song instead. "Wait, wait, wait," she sang, softly.

She watched Dad pull the sheet. The messy bed got smooth. One pull, one smooth side. Then he did the next bed. Then the last bed. Hannah sang her song all the way through.

"Now it is later," said Dad. Hannah clapped her hands. She poured out the blocks. Bowie came in and they stacked them tall. The tower wobbled and did not fall. When bedtime came, Hannah sank into her pillow. "Tomorrow we build it again," she said. "Yes," said Bowie. "Tomorrow."

Amelia sat on the warm sand. Her friend Jawad ran up with a big bucket.

"Amelia, look!" he said. "A smooth shell!"

Amelia held it. "My hands feel it," she said. "Hands are for touching."

She put the shell to her ear. "I hear the sea! Ears are for hearing."

Jawad laughed. "Yes! Now try this." He held up a slice of orange.

Amelia looked at it. "My eyes see it. Eyes are for seeing." Then she sniffed. "My nose smells it! Nose is for smelling."

Jawad grinned a silly grin. He pinched his nose shut. Then he sniffed the orange.

"I can't smell it!" he said. His voice sounded funny.

Amelia laughed and laughed. She pinched her nose too. She sniffed and sniffed.

"Nothing!" she said. "No smell at all!"

She let go of her nose. The sweet smell came back.

"Hey!" she said. "Where did the smell go when I pinched?"

Jawad said, "It hid from your fingers!"

Amelia was not mad. She thought it was funny. She took a tiny bite of orange. "My tongue tastes it! Tongue is for tasting."

"That's five!" said Jawad. He counted on his fingers. "See, hear, touch, smell, taste."

Then Amelia ran to the wet slide of sand by the dune. She slid down on her bottom. The sand was cool and scratchy.

"My bottom can feel it too!" she called.

Victoria wanted to count her beads. She had a bowl of beads and a long string. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. What came after two? She frowned. "I forgot," she said.

Her grandma sat close by on the low step. Grandma was threading beads too. "Try your song," said Grandma. Victoria knew a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. "Three, four, shut the door!" The words rhymed, and the rhymes helped her remember. "Five, six, pick up sticks! Seven, eight, lay them straight!" Each rhyme gave her the next number.

Victoria pushed a red bead onto the string. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" she sang. Ten beads on her string. Grandma clapped. "Ten beads!" said Victoria. "I did it!" Grandma gave her a hug.

Josephine sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. "Where are we going?" she asked. "To the shop," said Dad. "We need apples and bread."

At a red light, Josephine saw Mr. Santos. He was walking his dog by the road. Josephine hid behind her blanket. She was a little scared of big dogs. Mr. Santos waved at the car. Josephine peeked out. Then she rolled down her window, with help from Dad. "Hello, Mr. Santos!" she called. Mr. Santos smiled a big smile. "Hello, Josephine!" he said back. "Hello, little dog!" she said. The dog wagged its tail. One hello made one smile. Then the light turned green, and the car drove on.

At the shop, Josephine picked three apples. One, two, three. She gave them to the cashier. "Please, can we have a bag?" she asked. "Of course," said the cashier. The bag broke! Apples rolled on the floor. "Oh no," said Josephine. "Sorry," said the cashier. "Let me get a new bag." A new bag came, and Dad picked up the apples.

Back in the car, the sky grew dark. Street lights came on, one by one. "Dad, can you turn on my light?" Josephine asked. "Yes, I can help," said Dad. The small light glowed. Josephine held her bear up to it. "Look, Bear," she whispered. "Hello, light." And the light shone on Bear's smiling face all the way home.

The wind blew hard at the park. Elias held his coat tight. Sand flew up from the sandbox. Some sand went toward his eyes. He blinked fast, and the sand did not get in. "Why did I blink like that?" he asked. His friend Margaux ran over. "Mr. Fernando calls those eyelashes," she said. "Mine blinked too!" They both blinked at each other.

Elias wanted to know more. He looked at a dog with the coach. The dog had a long tail. The dog wagged it in the wind. The wind blew dust at the dog's face. The dog blinked. The dust stayed out of its eyes too. Elias heard the dog bark. He patted its soft, warm back. He smelled popcorn nearby. Mr. Fernando bought a bag and shared it. Each piece was warm and yummy. Elias tasted the salty kernels.

The wind got bigger. "My eyes feel funny," said Margaux. She rubbed them with dirty hands. "Don't," said Mr. Fernando kindly. "Sand on hands can get in. Come, we will wash them." He took them to the water tap. He washed Margaux's hands with soap. Then he gave them each a big drink of water. Elias looked up at Mr. Fernando and smiled. "Eyelashes and clean hands," said Elias. "My eyes are safe."

Logan wanted to find his purple toy car. He looked under his bed. He looked in his toy box. He pulled out cars, cars, and more cars. One, two, three, four, five cars. Then he found something long and yellow. "A banana!" said Logan. "In my toy box!"

Savreen came over to play. "That is silly," she said. She picked up the banana and held it high. "Cars, cars, cars, banana," she said. "The banana is the odd one out. It does not belong."

Logan laughed. "Bananas are foods, not toys!" He put the banana in the fruit bowl with the apples and the orange. Then he looked and looked again. Apples, apple, orange, and there, peeking out, was something small and purple. "Found you, little car!" said Logan. He drove it fast across the floor. "Beep beep!"

Arya was building a tall sand castle at school. It had one tower, two towers, three towers. "It is a magic castle," said Arya.

Aya ran by fast. Her foot hit the castle. Crash! One tower fell down. Aya stopped. She looked at the fallen tower. "Sorry, Arya," said Aya. "I did not mean to knock it down. I feel bad."

Aya patted Arya's head, gentle like a feather. Then she helped build the tower again. They patted the sand. They patted and patted. One tower, two towers, three tall towers! The castle was whole again.

"Thank you, Aya," said Arya. Aya smiled. "You are welcome. Now the magic castle can shine!"

Mr. Pereira rang the bell. "Time to finish and come inside," he said. Arya and Aya held hands and ran to the door.

Alexander sat with his class at the little church hall. Mr. Sadeghi picked up his drum. "Clap with me," he said. Alexander clapped fast. Then slow. Then all mixed up. His claps did not fit.

Mr. Sadeghi tapped his knee. Tap, tap, tap. "Try the steady beat," he said. Alexander watched. He clapped with the taps. Tap, clap. Tap, clap. His hands fit the song now. He smiled big.

"Now we sing," said Mr. Sadeghi. They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Alexander sang as loud as he could. He was very loud. In the corner, a baby was asleep in a pram. The baby began to wiggle. Mr. Sadeghi put his finger to his lips. "Softly now," he said. Alexander sang very soft. The baby stopped wiggling. The baby went back to sleep. The room felt warm, like a fresh egg from a hot pan at breakfast. Alexander clapped his steady beat, very quiet, and sang the whole song from start to end. "Again," he whispered.

Theodore's teddy bear, Boo, looked sad. His fur was all flat on one side. "Boo is sick," Theodore told his mom. "He needs help." His mom smiled and brought a small blanket. "You can take care of him," she said.

Theodore laid Boo on the couch. He got his toy cup and filled it with air. "Here is soup, Boo," he said. He tipped the cup to Boo's mouth. He patted Boo's head very softly. Then he wrapped the gray blanket around Boo, all the way up to his ears.

Boo still looked a little sad. Theodore hugged him tight. He sang a small song, the one his mom sang at night. Boo's eyes began to close. Theodore tucked the blanket under Boo's chin. "Sleep now, Boo," he whispered.

The next morning, Theodore ran to the couch. Boo sat up straight and fluffy. Theodore held him high. "Boo is all better!"

Xavier put on his red boots. Selena wore her blue boots. Livia wore her yellow hat. It was a snowy day at daycare.

"Let's walk to the park," said Ms. Schneider. She held Xavier's hand. They came to the big road. There was a tall light there. It had three round colors.

The light turned red. "Red!" shouted Xavier. All the cars stopped. He laughed. "The cars have to wait!"

Then the light turned green. "Green means go," said Selena. The cars all went zoom. "Red means stop," said Xavier. He clapped his cold hands.

At the park, Xavier found a stick. He held it up like the tall light. "Red!" he said. Selena and Livia froze like cars. "Green!" he said. They ran and laughed.

Then Xavier held up the stick and said, "Green!" and he ran too, right into a big snowy pile.

Emmett sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to play rocket ship after dinner. But first he had to eat.

His baby sister sat in her high chair. She dropped her spoon again. "Naughty spoon," said Dad, with a smile.

Emmitt ate one pea. Then another. He counted, "Ten, nine, eight." He ate and counted. "Seven, six, five." The peas went down. "Four, three, two, one." His plate was empty!

"Emmett, what was that?" asked his sister Haniya, sitting beside him.

"A countdown," said Emmett. He jumped up from his chair. "Blast off!"

Dad laughed and held out his hand. They zoomed around the table together. "Ten, nine, eight," said the baby, banging her spoon.

Snow fell all morning at daycare. Everett pressed his nose to the window. "Snowy!" he said. Charli clapped her hands.

Mr. Huang opened the door. "Coats on, everyone. It is cold and windy out there." Everett zipped his red coat. He put on his boots. But he could not find his mittens. They were still at home on the table.

Outside, the snow was soft and white. Everett scooped up a big handful. He patted it into a snowball. He threw it at Malcolm. "Got you!" Malcolm laughed. Then Everett looked at his hands. They were red and cold. "Ow, ow, ow," he said, blowing on them.

Malcolm held up his fuzzy blue mittens. "My hands are still warm." Charli wiggled her green gloves. "Warm too!"

Mr. Huang had an extra pair in his pocket. "Here, Everett. Try these." Everett pulled them on. They were too big and floppy. He looked like a bear. Everyone giggled.

Everett patted a new snowball. His hands stayed warm inside the mittens. He made one snowball, then two, then three. "I can count five snowballs!" he said.

Later, everyone came inside for warm soup in a bowl. Everett was thirsty and drank all his water. "Tomorrow," he said, "my mittens are coming to school." Mr. Huang smiled. "Good plan, snowball boy."

Wren went to the library with her dad. There was a playroom there. Wren saw a big box of blocks.

Clarke was there too. He was building a tall tower. "Can I have a turn?" Wren asked. "Yes," said Clarke. He put a block on top. Then Wren put one on top. They took turns, one by one.

Samantha came in. She wanted a block. Clarke gave her one. Wren gave her one too. Now they all shared.

Then the bell rang. Playtime was over. Wren ran to the door. Then she stopped. She looked back at the blocks. They were all over the floor. The floor was a mess because everyone had played.

"Ms. Rossi, do we clean the blocks?" Wren asked. "Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with," said Ms. Rossi. Wren pointed at the blocks. "I played with those!"

Wren ran back. She put the blocks in the box. Clarke helped. Samantha helped too. Soon the floor was clean.

"What a nice surprise," said Ms. Rossi. "Such friendly helpers!" Wren smiled. She held her dad's hand. "Can we come back?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Tomorrow we can come back."

Jake was in the kitchen with his mom. They were going to bake cookies. The dough was cold. Jake loved to roll the dough flat with the rolling pin. The oven was hot, so his mom put the cookies in herself. Jake stood back and watched.

They needed sugar, but the jar was empty. "We will go to the store," said Mom. "Stay close to me there." Jake held her hand all the way to the store.

In the store, Jake saw a big bin of bouncy balls. One ball began to roll across the floor. Jake ran after it. When he picked it up, he looked around. He could not see his mom anywhere. His tummy felt funny and scared.

Then Jake remembered. He walked to the checkout. A store worker in a green vest stood there. "I can't find my grown-up," said Jake. The worker smiled and spoke into her phone. Soon Mom came running. "What a lucky boy you are," she said. "You did just the right thing."

At home, the cookies came out of the oven. They had to cool because they were hot. Jake heard the timer make a loud sound. He waited and waited. Then he took a big bite of a cool cookie. "Best cookie ever," said Jake. Mom laughed and gave him a glass of milk.

Arya stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim suit. It was too twisty. One arm would not go in. "Let me help," said her mom. Together they fixed it. Now the suit was not twisted. It was not broken anymore.

Arya walked out to the pool. The water looked big. She saw a tall chair. A man sat up high in it. "Why is he up there?" Arya asked her friend Sylas. "He is the lifeguard," said Sylas. "He watches the swimmers. He helps anyone who needs it."

Arya kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. Then she slipped. Splash! The lifeguard saw her right away. He blew his whistle. He reached out his long pole. Arya held on tight. He helped her to the side.

"You saw me from up there," Arya said. "I watch everyone," said the lifeguard. After swim time, Arya told her mom, "He helps people. Like at the playground, when I fell and a grown-up helped me." Her mom smiled. Next week, Arya blew more bubbles. She kicked and kicked. Then she floated all by herself. The lifeguard clapped from his tall chair.

Emily stood on the big stage. She held her little drum. The auditorium was quiet. She saw her friend Reign in the front row. She saw her friend Keanu too. Mr. Nowak stood by the curtain. He gave her a nod.

Emily patted the drum. Pat, pat, pat. She counted as she played. One, two, three. One, two, three. The people watched. Emily patted faster. Pat, pat, pat, pat. Then the song was done.

The people clapped and clapped. Emily did not know what to do. She looked at Mr. Nowak. He bent his body down low. Emily bent her body down low too. The people clapped even more. "They like your bow," said Mr. Nowak. Emily smiled. She bowed one more time. "Bow," she said. "Bow like me."

Victor sat in a big chair in Ms. Malik's kitchen. She was a neighbour who cut hair at her table. She had scissors, a comb, and a spray bottle. This was Victor's very first haircut. His hair had gone wild and curly. It covered his ears and poked into his eyes.

"Snip, snip," went the scissors. Ms. Malik cut slowly. She took her time. Victor sat still and waited. Little curls dropped onto the cape like dark rain.

Then the haircut was done. Victor looked at himself. He could see the front. His forehead showed now. His eyes felt free. But he wanted to see the back too. He turned his head left. He could not see it. He turned his head right. Still no.

"I can't see the back!" said Victor.

Ms. Malik smiled. She picked up a little mirror in her hand. She held it up behind Victor's head. The little mirror met the big mirror on the wall. Victor looked. There it was. The back of his head! Short and neat and smooth.

"Hi, back of me," said Victor. He waved at the mirror. "Mom, can we buy a mirror like this for home? I want to look at the back of my turtle too."

Henry put on his blue coat. He was going to the doctor. Mom held his hand in the waiting room.

"Time for your shot," said the nurse. Henry sat very still on the big chair. The nurse cleaned his arm. Then the shot went in, quick and small. It was done! Henry got a sweet red sticker.

In the car, Henry rubbed his arm. "It hurts a little," he said. "The spot where you got your shot can feel sore for a little while," said Mom. "It will feel better soon."

Henry looked out the window. He watched the trees go by. Then he touched his arm again. It felt better already. Henry smiled and put his sticker on his coat.

Emily ran to the big slide at the playground. Hank was already there. "Watch me!" he said. Hank climbed up the ladder. Then he slid down the slide. Up, then down. Emily clapped her hands.

"Can I try?" she asked. Hank nodded. Emily put her foot on the first step. She climbed up and up. At the top, the wind felt cool on her face. She looked way down at Hank. He looked very small from up here. She sat down and slid fast, fast, fast. Whee! Down she went, slow at the end.

"My turn again," said Emily. She went up the ladder one more time. Then down the slide. Then up. Then down. "Why do you keep going up?" asked Hank. Emily laughed. "So I can come back down!" she said.

The bell rang for lunch. "Time to eat," said Mr. Wong from the bench. The sun was hot on the slide now. Emily touched it. Ouch, so hot! Mr. Wong handed her a cold juice box. Emily took a big sip and watched the tall slide. "After lunch, I'll climb all the way up," she said.

Logan stood by the grocery cart. His little bunny was gone. Logan looked in the cart. No bunny. Logan looked under the apples. No bunny.

"Where is bunny?" he asked. Mom said, "Let's look again." Logan looked by the bread. He looked by the milk. Ms. Hu worked at the store. She came to help. "Let's check the shelves," she said. They looked at a short shelf. They looked at a tall shelf. No bunny anywhere.

Then Logan felt something in his coat. His coat pocket was bumpy. He put his hand in. There was bunny! Bunny had been tucked inside his pocket the whole time. Logan hugged bunny tight. "You were in my pocket!" he said. Ms. Hu laughed. "Things can end up inside other things," she said. Logan patted his pocket. "Bunny rides with me now," he said. At the checkout, Logan waved bunny's soft tail at the cashier. "Bye bye, store," said Logan.

Clara woke up in her big girl bed. Her hair was a big mess! She pulled her comb off the shelf. She combed the front. Ouch, that pulled. So she went slow, little bit by little bit. The tangle came out! Clara combed some more. The tangles all came out. Her hair was soft and smooth now.

She ran to show her mom. "Look! My hair is not puffy!" She picked her blue dress. She pulled it on all by herself. Mom held her hand to the bathroom. Clara washed her face with a warm towel.

"Breakfast time!" Mom called. Clara ate fast, fast, fast. Then she said, "Can I comb your hair too?" Mom sat down. Clara held the comb up high and smiled. "Your turn!"

Aria went to the animal shelter with her dad. It was a sunny day. She wanted a puppy of her own. She walked past the cats. She walked past the rabbits. Then she saw a small brown puppy with floppy ears. "This one," said Aria. Her dad said, "Let's ask the shelter lady first." The lady smiled and said yes.

The puppy was soft and warm. Aria named him Biscuit. A lady at the shelter clipped a leash to Biscuit's collar. Then she put the leash in Dad's hand. They walked out into the big world.

On the way to the car, a bird hopped on the grass. Biscuit wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash was clipped to his collar. The leash held him close to Dad. Biscuit could not run away. Aria felt glad. Her puppy stayed safe by her side.

At home, Aria gave Biscuit water. She gave him a soft blanket. She counted his paws. One, two, three, four. Biscuit licked her hand. Then he curled up and went to sleep.

Stella sat on the big blue rug. The game was on TV. Mama held popcorn. Wallace sat beside Stella with his toy ball.

A man in a striped shirt ran on the screen. He blew a whistle. "Who is that?" Stella asked. "That is the referee," said Mama. "He watches the game. He makes sure players follow the rules."

Stella watched the referee closely. A player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle again. He pointed and shook his head. The player looked down. The game stopped.

"He saw it!" said Stella. "The referee saw the hands." Wallace clapped his toy ball. "He watches everything," said Stella.

At snack time, Mama brought bread with jam. Stella took a piece. "I can be the referee," she said. Wallace ran with the jam jar. "No running!" said Stella. She blew a pretend whistle. Wallace stopped and giggled.

"Good call," said Mama. Stella held her bread up high like a trophy.

Victor ran to the playground. He wore his red socks today. He loved his red socks. He took off his shoes to feel the soft sand. Then he ran to the slide. One red sock fell off in the sand. Victor did not see it.

He sat down for his juice. He felt his foot. One foot had a sock. One foot had no sock. Victor looked upset. "Where is my sock?" he said. His friend Luna came over. "We can find it," she said. Mr. Moretti sat on the bench. "One, two," he counted Victor's feet. "A pair means two," said Mr. Moretti. "You need two socks."

So Victor went looking. He took a step. Then another step. Luna came too. They looked by the slide. They looked by the swings. "One, two, three, four, five," counted Luna, touching the flowers. "Six, seven, eight," said Thatcher, who joined the hunt. "Nine, ten," said Victor, counting the stones.

Then Luna pointed. "Look!" There was the red sock, half under the sand. Victor picked it up. He put it on his foot. Two red socks. A pair! "Thank you," said Victor. He gave Luna a big hug. Then they ran to the swings together.

Sadie stood in the kitchen on her tip-toes. "I want to do it myself!" she said. Her dad put toast on her plate. The toast was cool now. Sadie held the little knife. She spread the butter. One swipe, two swipes, three. The butter melted and made the toast shiny. "It worked!" she laughed.

Next came the milk. Sadie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly, slowly. One drip ran down the side. She wiped it with her thumb. The counter looked tidy again. Then Maxine knocked at the door, and Sadie ran to see her new red boots. What a surprise!

The milk sat on the counter. The clock ticked. Sadie looked back. "Wait!" she said. She ran and put the milk in the fridge. Cold milk stays in the fridge. She closed the door and smiled. "All done!"

Aubrey went to Rose's house. Rose had a big rug on the floor.

"Watch this," said Rose. She pointed at the rug. "The floor is a river now. We can't touch it. We have to hop on the cushions." Rose jumped onto a cushion. Then she jumped to the next one.

Aubrey looked at the rug. It was just a rug. But Rose acted like it was water. So Aubrey jumped onto a cushion too. "Look at me!" she said. "I'm swimming with the fish!" She put her hand in the pretend water. Rose laughed.

They put a teddy bear in a box. "The boat is here," said Rose. They pushed the box across the rug. The teddy bear rode on the boat. Then Maxim came in. "Why is the bear in a box?" he asked.

"It's not a box," said Aubrey. "It's a boat. We're pretending." Maxim was scared of the river at first. He held Aubrey's hand. Then he hopped onto a cushion too.

"Big jump!" said Rose. Maxim jumped. He made it! All three kids cheered. The teddy bear floated past a pretend shoe that had fallen in the river. Rose fished it out. "Got it!" she said. They hopped all the way to the couch, and Aubrey shouted, "Land ahoy!"

Nolan ran into the library with his mom. Craft day was here! He saw Teo and Alivia at the big table. They were making paper sailboats. Alivia held hers up. It had a triangle sail. Teo's boat had a triangle sail too.

Nolan wanted a triangle sail. But his paper was a square. He frowned at it. He turned it around. Still a square, not a triangle. "I need two triangles," he told Teo. Ms. Yip came over with the scissors. "Watch," she said. She pointed at one corner. Then she pointed at the far corner across from it. "Cut from this corner to the opposite corner."

Nolan watched her cut. Snip! The square fell apart in her hands. Two triangles! It was a surprise. "Now you try," said Ms. Yip. She handed him a new square and cut for him where he pointed. First one corner. Then the opposite corner. Two triangles again!

Nolan taped one triangle to his boat. It stood up tall. He shook the boat in the air. "Look, Alivia!" Alivia laughed. "Your sail looks like a pizza slice!" Then Nolan sniffed his paper. "It's not smelly like pizza," he said. Everyone giggled. Ms. Yip clapped her hands. "Boats to the rug!" she said. Nolan sailed his boat all the way there.

Jaxson ran to school. He saw Timothee by the door. "Is today the library day?" Timothee asked. Mr. Kaur smiled. "Yes, it is today. Today is the day that is happening right now." Jaxson jumped up and down. The library trip was now, not later!

"Yesterday we played with blocks," said Timothee. Jaxson nodded. That was over. "Tomorrow we paint," said Timothee. That was not here yet. Today was library day!

The big bus came. Iman climbed on. Jaxson held the rail tight. "Don't be scared," said Mr. Kaur. "I sit with you." Jaxson sat by the window.

At the library, Jaxson found a book about a silly dog. The dog begged for a cookie on every page! Jaxson laughed and laughed. He hugged the book all the way home on the bus.

It was nap time at daycare. Grayson wanted to sleep in his dinosaur boots. They were his favorite things. He stamped his feet. One boot, two boots. Stomp, stomp, stomp.

Mr. Lavoie shook his head gently. "Boots are for outside," he said. He held up something soft and blue. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said. Grayson touched them. They felt loose and warm. He sat down on his little mat.

Grayson pulled off one boot. Then the other boot. He put on the pajamas. They had little stars on them. Alivia was already asleep nearby, snug in her own pajamas. Grayson patted his mat. He closed his eyes. The stars on his pajamas glowed softly in the dim room. "Sleepy stars," he whispered. Then he was fast asleep, cozy as can be.

Penelope woke up in her bedroom. The room was still dark. She wanted it to be morning. Morning was the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast. "Not now," she said to her teddy. "Not yet."

She climbed down from her bed. She looked out the window. The world was dark and sleepy. No sun came to shine in the sky. Penelope heard Daddy in the kitchen. She heard a spoon clink in a bowl. She smelled warm porridge. But it was not morning yet, so there was no breakfast for her.

Penelope sat on the rug. She waited. She waited more. Then the window turned pink. Then it turned gold. The sun began to shine. Light came into her bedroom. Penelope ran to the door.

Down the hall, Daddy was at the table. Mommy was there too. There was porridge and there was a banana. Penelope said, "Good morning!"

"Good morning, Penelope," said Daddy. "Did the sun come up?"

"Yes," said Penelope. "The sun came up first. Now it is morning."

She sat in her little chair. She took her first bite of breakfast. The sun shone right onto her bowl. "Now," said Penelope, "I eat."

Elias loved water play day at daycare. Mr. Boateng filled the big tub outside. Juliana and Zephyr splashed with cups. Elias splashed too. Soon his arms were wet. His shirt was wet. Even his hair was wet!

Water dripped down his arms like little drops. "Where is the drippy going?" he asked. Zephyr held up a big soft towel. "The towel drinks it up," she said. Elias rubbed his arm with the towel. The drips went away. His arm was dry! He rubbed his hair too. The towel made his hair soft and dry.

Then Elias saw something on the grass. It was a rainbow in the spray of water. "Juliana, come look!" he called. Juliana ran over, all wet. She had no towel. She shivered and hugged her arms. Elias ran to the cubby room. He found a towel for her. He rubbed her arms until they were dry. "Thank you, Elias," Juliana said.

Mr. Boateng put out dress-up clothes. Elias picked a red cape. He pulled it on over his dry shirt. It felt warm and cozy. Zephyr put on a yellow hat. "Can I buy a hat too?" Elias asked, playing shop. Mr. Boateng smiled and handed him a blue one. Elias wore the cape and the hat. Then it was time for lunch, and everyone sat down together.

Liam was at daycare. Mr. Joshi put out three big baskets. One basket was for toys. One basket was for animals. One basket was for clothes. "Can you help me sort?" asked Mr. Joshi. "Yes!" said Liam.

Liam put a teddy bear in the animal basket. He put a ball in the toy basket. Then he found a little red sock. Where did it go? He dropped it in with the toys. Emiliano laughed. "That is not a toy," he said. Liam picked up the sock. Could a sock be an animal? He looked at it. No, it had no ears. His sister had socks just like this at home.

Liam held up the sock. "Where does this go?" he asked. Mr. Joshi smiled. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," he said. Liam put the sock in the clothes basket. Next to a shirt. Next to a hat. It fit right in. Liam clapped. He did not miss one sock. Jorawar brought a hat. Liam pointed at the basket. "Clothes!" said Jorawar, and dropped it in. "This sorting game is wild," said Liam. The baskets filled up fast.

Jaxson sat at the big table in the library. He was painting a garden. He had blue paint. He had yellow paint. He wanted green paint for the grass.

"Where is the green paint?" Jaxson asked. Ms. Moretti smiled. "We are all out of green today," she said. Jaxson looked at his paper. His garden had no grass yet.

Matias sat next to him. Matias was painting a big orange carrot. "Put your paints in one cup," Matias said. Jaxson dipped his brush in the blue paint. He put it in the cup. Then he dipped in the yellow paint. He put that in too.

Jaxson stirred slowly. He stirred and stirred. The paint began to change. "Look, look!" Jaxson began to yell. The blue and yellow made green paint. Green like real grass.

Jaxson painted his grass. He painted it all along the bottom. Mara leaned over to see. "Nice grass," she said. Jaxson held up his wet painting. "I made green myself," he said. He stirred the cup one more time, just to watch it swirl.

Cooper sat in his car seat. The sky was bright and sunny. He wore his sun hat. "Off we go," said Dad.

Then the trees began to sway. The wind whooshed past the car. "It is windy," said Cooper. Dad parked by the park. Cooper and his friend Lambert jumped out onto the grass. The wind blew hard. It blew Cooper's hat right off his head!

"My hat!" said Cooper. The hat rolled across the grass. Lambert ran with him. The wind pushed it again. It moved fast, then it stopped by a shoe. Cooper grabbed his hat. He held it tight with both hands.

The wind turned gentle. It did not bite his nose anymore. "I will hold my hat next time," said Cooper. Lambert laughed. They put their hats on and held them tight, all the way to the swings.

Sarah sat on the big rug in the living room. The game was on TV. Dad, Etta and Saoirse sat on the couch. Everyone was watching the ice hockey game.

"Where is the ball?" asked Sarah. The players slid on the ice. They did not kick a ball at all.

"There is no ball," said Etta. "They hit a puck. It is flat like a little pan."

Sarah watched close. A player swung his stick. The stick hit the puck. The puck zoomed fast across the ice. "The stick makes it go!" said Sarah. She clapped her hands.

The door opened. A parent came in with snacks. "I remember you like cheese," they said to Saoirse. Saoirse smiled and got the first piece. Sarah got one too. Etta's socks were smelly from playing outside, so she took them off and put them by the door.

Then a plane flew past the window. Sarah heard the loud hum. But she kept her eyes on the TV. A player hit the puck again. It slid right into the net. Everyone jumped up. "We saw that!" said Sarah. "The stick hit the puck, and it went in!"

Ellie went to the farm with her dad. She had a watering can and little seeds. "I will plant lettuce," she said. Her dad helped her make a row in the dirt. Ellie put the seeds in. She patted the soil down. Then she gave the seeds a drink.

Every day Ellie came back. She looked at the dirt. One morning, tiny green leaves were open to the sun. Ellie clapped her hands. "Hello, little plants," she said. Katrina and Beau came to see them too. They counted the leaves together.

Then came a very hot day. Ellie ran to the garden after lunch. The lettuce was drooping. The leaves hung down like sad little ears. "Oh no," said Ellie. She thought for a minute. Then she filled her big watering can at the tap. She tipped it over the plants. The water began to sink into the soil. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Ellie came back. The lettuce stood up tall. The leaves were open and bouncy. "They wanted a drink," Ellie said. Beau smiled and touched a soft green leaf. The big clock by the barn said it was time for a snack. "First, more water," said Ellie, and she picked up her can.

Jade wanted to play hide-and-seek at school. Frederic wanted to play too. Jeffrey said, "I will hide first!" Jade said, "I will count."

Jade shut her eyes. She counted fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then she turned around. Jeffrey was still standing in the middle of the rug. Frederic was only half behind the table.

"Hey!" said Jeffrey. "You counted too fast. We did not hide yet." Frederic laughed. "Count slowly, Jade. Slow like a snail."

Jade guessed a snail was very slow. So she tried again. She shut her eyes tight. "One... two... three..." Jeffrey ran behind the table. "Four... five..." Frederic hid under Ms. Farah-Ali's big coat. "Six... seven... eight..." Jade heard little feet go tip, tap, toe. "Nine... ten! Here I come!"

Jade looked by the blocks. No one there. She looked at the sharp corner of the art shelf, where the coat hung. Two shoes peeked out. "I see Frederic!"

Then the coat said, "Boo!" It was Jeffrey's voice, not Frederic's. Jade jumped and laughed. Frederic popped up from behind the table. "You found the wrong boy!"

"Okay," said Jade. "My turn to hide now."

Sebastian held his small blue bag at the airport. The plane was big. It went "whoosh" up into the sky. Sebastian and his dad and his mom flew far away to the beach.

At the beach, Sebastian found soft sand. He patted the sand into a hill. Then a wave came in. The wave washed his hill away. "Oh no!" said Sebastian. His dad laughed. "Let's take a photo of you first," he said. Dad held the camera. He clicked. The photo showed Sebastian and his hill of sand.

Then it was time to go home. Back home, Sebastian missed the beach. He missed his sand hill. He felt sad.

"Come here," said Mom. She opened the photo on the screen. There was Sebastian, with his hill. There was the wave, coming to get it.

"That is me!" said Sebastian. He laughed. "The wave ate my hill!"

"Let's look again," said Mom.

Sebastian looked at the photo one more time. "Click," he said.

Noah and his dad got to the hotel room. Noah put his small bag on the table. The room had a big window. "Look, Dad!" said Noah. He could see planes far away.

Then they went down to the airport to meet Grandma. It was very busy. Noah saw a big plane out the window. "I want to run and see it!" he said. He started to go. Dad took his hand right away. "In busy places, you hold my hand," said Dad. Noah looked around. So many people! He held on tight. They walked together, hand in hand. Noah saw the big plane through the glass. It was huge. A boy near them held his mom's hand too.

Back in the hotel room, Dad gave Noah a juicy apple. Dad read a book on the bed. Noah stood by the window. He waved at the sky. "Bye, plane," he said. "I held Dad's hand the whole way."

Lucas sat on a big chair at home. Mr. Kelly had a little salon in his house next door. Today Lucas would get his very first haircut.

Lucas held onto his mother's hand. "Will it hurt?" he asked. "No," said his mother. "The scissors just snip the hair. Hair does not feel it." Mr. Kelly showed Lucas the scissors. They went snip, snip. Lucas watched a little curl fall down. It landed on the cape like a tiny bird.

Then Lucas saw something. Mr. Kelly held up one small curl. He handed it to Lucas's mother. She put it into a little envelope. Lucas had a question. "Why do you keep my hair?" he asked. His mother closed the envelope. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut," she said. "It helps us remember this day."

Lucas touched the top of his head. His hair felt soft and short. He looked in the mirror and smiled. "All done!" shouted Mr. Kelly. Lucas ran to show his mother the envelope. She put it in her pocket, safe and warm.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. She pulled a big suitcase behind her. "Can I hold it?" asked Mackenzie. The suitcase was heavy. It went bump, bump on the floor.

Grandma put the suitcase in the guest bedroom. Mackenzie sat on the soft rug. "What is inside?" she asked. "Open it and see," said Grandma. Grandma turned the little zipper. Click, click, click. The top opened up.

Mackenzie peeked in. There were Grandma's shirts, folded flat. There were Grandma's socks. There was her hairbrush and her soft pink sweater. "You packed your clothes," said Mackenzie. "Yes," said Grandma. "Guests who come to stay pack their clothes and things in a suitcase."

Then Mackenzie saw something shiny at the bottom. Grandma lifted it out. It was a small picture frame. Inside was a photo of baby Mackenzie! Grandma had carried it all the way here. Grandma set it on the table by the bed. "Now you are here too," she said.

Lucas stood in the new nursery room. The walls were soft brown. A tiny bed stood by the window. One, two, three little wheels on the baby cart, and a wheel squeaked when his dad pushed it.

Lucas had a problem. The baby was coming home today. Lucas wanted to hold the baby. But the baby was too small. "You can sit next to him," said his mom.

The baby came in. He was small and wrinkly. He looked at Lucas with big eyes. Lucas waved. The baby did not wave back.

"Try this," said Mom. "Put your finger in his hand." Lucas poked his finger into the little fist. The tiny fingers closed tight. The baby held on! Lucas laughed. He pulled a tiny bit. The baby held on more. "He likes me!" said Lucas.

The doorbell rang. Ayah came to see the baby. "Watch this," said Lucas. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he put his finger in the baby's hand. The baby grabbed Ayah's finger too. Ayah giggled so hard her tummy hurt.

"Silly baby," said Ayah. "He thinks we are toys."

"He thinks we are his," said Lucas.

Nolan sat at Grandma's big table. There was a paper with dotted letters on it. The letters spelled N-O-L-A-N.

"What are the little dots for?" Nolan asked.

Grandma smiled. "You can trace over them. That is one way to practice making letters."

Nolan held his pencil. Grandma helped him bend his fingers around it. She showed him how to make his eyes go wide and look close.

Nolan drew a line on the first dot. Then the next dot. The dots made an N! He traced the O, slow and round. He traced the L, tall and straight.

A duck waddled past the window. Nolan laughed, then kept going. He traced the A and the N.

"Look, Grandma! I made my name!"

"That is your name, all by you," said Grandma, and she hung the paper on the fridge with a magnet.

Madison sat on her bed with a big crayon. She wanted to write a note for Daddy. The note would say "Come see my bear." Daddy would read it in the kitchen and smile.

She wrote the letters one by one. M, A, D, I, S, O, N. Then more letters, all in a row. All the letters touched each other. They looked like one long, huge word. "C O M E S E E M Y B E A R." All squished together, like a train with no gaps.

Daddy came in and looked at the paper. He tilted his head. He turned the paper around. "I want to read it," he said, "but the letters are stuck together." Madison frowned at her paper. Then she looked at her bedtime book on the pillow. She opened the front cover first, like always. The words on the page had little gaps between them. Little spaces. One word. A space. Then the next word.

Madison picked up her crayon again. She copied her letters, and this time she made little gaps too. One word. A space. Then the next word. "Here, Daddy, this one," she said. Daddy held the paper. His eyes went along the row. "Come see my bear," he read out loud. Madison clapped. "You read it!" she said. Daddy picked up the bear and hugged them both.

Wren stood at the edge of the pool. She held her teacher's hand. Mr. Yoon smiled at her.

"Time to try bubbles," he said. "Swim teachers have kids practice blowing bubbles into the water through their mouth."

Wren looked at the water. It was blue and shiny. She did not want to put her face near it.

"What if the water tickles me?" she asked.

"Maybe a little," said Mr. Yoon.

Wren leaned over. She took a big breath. Then she blew through her mouth into the water. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles popped up. They tickled her chin. Wren laughed and laughed.

"Look, Willa!" she called. "I made bubbles!"

She blew again. More bubbles came. Willa ran over to see.

Then a bubble popped right on Wren's nose. It felt like a tiny kiss.

"Do it again," said Willa.

So Wren did.

"Hello, bubbles," she said.

Elena went to the library today. She wanted the book about bears. She saw it on the table yesterday. Now her friend Hukam was holding it.

"I went to the park tomorrow," said Hukam. Then he stopped. "No. I went yesterday. The park day is done." Elena laughed. She was not afraid to say when she got words mixed up too.

Mr. Fitzgerald sat down with them. "Yesterday is the day before today," he said. Then he opened the bear book. Elena and Hukam looked at it together. They turned the pages. They saw a big brown bear and two small cubs.

"Can we read it again tomorrow?" asked Elena. "Yes," said Mr. Fitzgerald. "Today we read it now." After the story, Elena picked out a book to buy at the little shop by the door. Hukam picked one too. Elena held her book tight all the way home. "Same table tomorrow," she said.

Natalie stood at the park with Kenan. There was a hoop on the grass. Ms. Ahmadi held a little beanbag.

"Watch this," Kenan said. He looked at Natalie. He threw the beanbag. It fell far from the hoop.

Natalie took the beanbag. She looked at Kenan too. She threw it. It missed.

Ms. Ahmadi waited by the hoop. The sun felt warm on Natalie's neck. The grass smelled fresh and green.

Natalie tried again. This time she looked at the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in.

"You did it!" Kenan said.

Kenan looked at the hoop too. He threw his beanbag. It went in.

Then Ms. Ahmadi rolled a big ball to Natalie. Natalie held out both hands. She looked at the ball. The ball went right into her arms.

"Again," Natalie said. She laughed and hugged the big ball.

Isabella was at Grandma's house. In the corner stood a little piano. Grandma gave Isabella a soft smile. "You can play it," Grandma said.

Isabella pressed one key. Plink. She pressed two keys. Plink, plink. Then she tried a song. It came out wrong. The song ran away from her fingers. Isabella frowned. "It is too hard," she said.

"You can try again tomorrow," said Grandma. So Isabella did. One day, she played three keys. Plink, plink, plink. The next day, she played four keys. Then five. Then the whole line of the song. Outside, soft rain tapped the window. Isabella was careful with her fingers, slow and small.

On the last day, Isabella sat up tall. She played the song all the way to the end. Plink, plink, plinkety, plink. Grandma clapped. "Play it again," she said. Isabella laughed and put her fingers on the keys.

Wesley woke up excited. Today was paint day! He put on his favorite shirt. It had a big yellow star on it. Mom set out red and blue paint. Wesley grabbed his brush.

But wait. Where was his apron? Mom looked in the bag of art things. No apron. Wesley dipped his brush anyway. He painted a curly snake. Blue dots went everywhere. One dot landed on his star. "Oh no!" said Wesley. "My shirt!"

Mom held up an old shirt of Dad's. "Put this on," she said. Wesley pulled it over his clothes. It was big and soft. He painted a red sun, a blue fish, and green grass. Paint splashed on the old shirt. Paint splashed on the old shirt again and again. But his star shirt stayed clean!

Wesley jumped up and down. "The paint can't get me now!" he said. Mom laughed. "Wear it every paint day," she said. Wesley painted one more curly snake. "I love this shirt," he said. "It keeps paint off my clothes." He hung it on his hook, ready for tomorrow.

Parker ran into the backyard. Mr. Joshi had built a little library there. It was a small wooden house for books. It had three little shelves inside.

Parker wanted a book about animals. He looked at the first shelf. Those books were about toys. He looked at the second shelf. Those books were about foods. There were books about apples and bread. No animals. Parker felt sad. He sat down on the grass. The grass felt cool and soft.

Then his friend Alena came by. She opened the little door. "Look, Parker. The books sit in groups," she said. "The animal books are all together on the last shelf." Parker stood up. He pushed the door wide. He looked at the third shelf. Yes! There were animal books, all in a row. He took one about a big elephant. Alena took one about a small red bird.

The two friends sat under the tree. The leaves made a soft shushing sound. Parker turned the pages slowly. "I like the elephant," he said. Alena smiled and pointed at her bird. The man next door waved from his garden, and Parker waved back, holding his animal book up high.

Beatrice had a toy kitchen at home. She wanted to play house with her toy duck. "You be the baby," she told the duck.

She put the duck in a pot. She stirred with a spoon. Clang, clang, clang! Then she gave the duck a pretend bottle. The duck was a rough baby. It fell on the floor. Beatrice picked it up and patted its back. "One pat, two pats, three pats," she said. The duck felt better.

Then her friend Angad came over. He wanted to play too. He made pretend soup with round buttons. Slurp, slurp! They fed the duck together. "We win at playing house," said Angad. They laughed and laughed.

Soon Angad had to go home. But the kitchen was a big mess. The pot was on the floor. The spoon was under the chair. The buttons were everywhere. Her mom said, "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." So Beatrice and Angad cleaned up. One pot, two spoons, three buttons. They counted each toy into the box.

Then Angad went home. Beatrice hugged her duck. Mom tucked them both in for a cozy rest. "Night night, baby duck," said Beatrice.

Music time was starting at school. Mr. Campbell picked up his drum. "Let's clap the beat," he said. "Steady, like this. Boom, boom, boom."

Jake clapped and clapped. He tried to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" too. But his hands got tired. They felt loose and floppy. His claps went all wobbly. The song fell apart.

Then Jake looked down. Mr. Campbell was tapping the drum. Boom, boom, boom. Jake saw his own shadow on the floor. Could his feet do it?

Jake stamped his feet. Stamp, stamp, stamp. The beat came back! "My feet can keep the beat!" he said.

Kaysen stamped too. Brayden tapped his knees. Pat, pat, pat.

They all sang together, loud and happy. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star."

"Nice beat, Jake," said Mr. Campbell. "Shall we pick a new song now?"

Jacob was at Grandma's house. He was hungry. He wanted his lunch right now.

Grandpa was on the phone. He was talking to Uncle Ben. Jacob tugged Grandpa's sleeve. "Grandpa! Grandpa! I want lunch!"

Grandpa held up one finger. He kept talking. Jacob waited. His tummy made a tiny growl, like a small bear.

Then Grandpa stopped talking. There was a quiet moment. Jacob took a breath. "Grandpa, may I have lunch, please?"

Grandpa smiled big. "Yes! You waited for me to finish talking. That was very kind."

Grandpa made cheese sandwiches. He cut them into star shapes, like magic stars.

"Thank you," said Jacob. He bit into a star. It was the best lunch ever.

"More stars tomorrow," said Grandpa. "We can buy more cheese together."

Aubrey found a small grey feather on the playground. She held it up high. "Look, Raelynn!" she said. "A soft little leaf!"

Raelynn shook her head. "That is not a leaf," she said. "It is a feather. Birds are animals that have feathers."

Aubrey looked up at the tree. A little brown bird sat on a branch. It fluffed its feathers. One more small feather floated down. It landed on Matias's shoe.

"The bird is sending us feathers!" said Aubrey. "Like magic mail."

Ms. Lim smiled. "Let's play feather post office," she said. She gave each child one feather and one seed. Aubrey pretended her feather was a boat. She set the seed on top. "Sail away, little boat!" she said. "Sail before the sky gets stormy!"

A soft wind blew. The feather boat lifted up. It spun and floated away, over the fence and gone. Aubrey waved at the bird. The bird chirped twice and flew after it.

Matthew wanted to read the bunny book. But Noelie had it first. Noelie sat on the rug and turned the pages fast. "I can't find the bunny," said Noelie.

Matthew sat down next to her. "Can we look together?" he asked. Noelie gave him a careful hug and said, "Yes, let's look."

Matthew put his finger on the page. He started at the right side. He moved his finger to the right. Mr. Virtanen came over and shook his head. "In English, the words go from left to right," he said. He put Matthew's finger on the left side. Then he slid it all the way to the right. "See? Left to right."

Matthew tried it himself. Left, then right. He did it again and again. Left to right, left to right. "The words are like a path!" he said. He turned the pages front to back, one at a time. Then, on a page near the end, they saw the bunny. It was hopping over a big green hill.

"There he is!" said Noelie. "Your finger found him." Matthew laughed and kicked his feet with joy. Then he started at the left side again. "Left to right," he said, all by himself.

Rehmat ran to the table. Dinner was hot rice and peas. Everyone sat down, but Rehmat was confused. At home they ate right away. Here at Nathaniel's house, they all held hands first.

"Would you like to say grace?" Nathaniel's mom asked.

"What is grace?" Rehmat asked.

"It is a short prayer of thanks," Nathaniel said. "Many Christian families say it before meals. Like this one."

Nathaniel folded his hands. "Thank you for this food," he said. Then everyone said, "Amen."

Now it was Rehmat's turn. She patted her tummy. She thought hard. "Thank you for the rice," she said. "Thank you for the peas. Thank you for my friend Nathaniel!"

Everyone smiled big smiles. "Amen!" they all said together.

Then came the surprise. Nathaniel's dad gave Rehmat the last warm cookie on the plate. Rehmat took his hand and squeezed it tight.

"Cookie first," she whispered. "Grace next time!"

Mila went to the store with her dad. She wanted a little book about a duck. The book had a rock on the cover. The duck sat on the rock. Mila found it on a low shelf.

"Read it, Daddy," said Mila. Dad opened the front of the book. "The words start here," he said. He read each page. One duck. Two ducks. Three ducks on a rock.

Then Mila turned a page. It had no words at all. Just a big picture. "Read this page, Daddy," said Mila. Dad looked at it. He shook his head. "There are no words on this page," he said. "I read the words, not the pictures. You can tell me what the ducks do."

"I can do that," said Mila. She held the book up high. "The ducks go splash!" Dad laughed. "Read it again," said Mila. "All the way to the back." So Dad did, and Mila told every picture page herself.

Quinn found a big guitar at home. It was shiny and brown. She wanted to make music.

Quinn tapped the guitar like a drum. Tap, tap, tap. But the guitar made no big sound. Just little thumps. Quinn frowned.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Try this," he said. He moved his fingers across the strings. His fingers went swish, swish. A bright sound filled the room. It went zing, zing, zing!

"Strings!" said Quinn. She put her little fingers on the strings. She pulled one string and let it go. Pop! The string made a sound. She pulled another one. Pop!

Quinn pulled the strings one by one. Each string sang its own note. Then she moved her whole hand across them, swish. All the strings sang at once.

"More music, Daddy!" said Quinn. Her dad helped her strum again.

Then something funny happened. The cat came running. It popped its head around the corner. The cat's ears went up at the zing, zing sound.

Quinn laughed. "The cat likes my song!" she said. She strummed the strings again. The cat sat down to listen.

Quinn played and played. Her song went pop, zing, swish. The cat stayed and listened, and Quinn smiled a big smile.

Olivia sat on the rug in the music room. Ms. Vogel picked up her drum. "Let's clap the steady beat," she said. Olivia clapped. Clap, clap, clap.

But Olivia got excited. Her claps went fast. Clap-clap-clap-clap! Then faster! Her hands flew like two little birds. Soon the claps were a big jumble. The song fell all apart. Zeke laughed and fell over sideways. Olivia frowned at her hands.

Ms. Vogel stood up. "Try this. March with me." Olivia stood and marched. Step, step, step. Her feet went even, and they kept going. "Like this," said Olivia. "A steady beat stays even and keeps going, like footsteps when you march." She marched in a circle, past Agamveer, past the class pet in its cage, past the drum. Step, step, step.

Then she stopped marching and clapped the same way. Clap, clap, clap. Even and steady. The claps matched the drum. Olivia sang the nursery rhyme, all the way from the top, and she did not miss one word. Zeke clapped with her. Agamveer clapped too. Olivia smiled so big her cheeks went round. She stood up and did a little dance, still clapping, still steady, all the way to the safe soft rug by the door.

Wyatt was at Grandpa's house. In the big room stood a shiny violin. It sat in a case like a little bed.

"I want to play it," said Wyatt. Grandpa held up a long stick. "This is the bow," he said. Wyatt grabbed the bow with both fists. He pushed it on the strings. SQUEAK! The violin made a funny noise. Wyatt laughed. "It sounds like a duck!"

"Watch," said Grandpa. He held the bow his way. Then he pulled the bow across the strings. A sweet song rang out. One pull, one song. Wyatt tried it. He pulled the bow, slow and long. The violin sang.

Grandpa clapped. "Play it again," he said. Wyatt pulled the bow one, two, three times. The violin sang and sang.

The lights went out. Hayden's whole apartment went dark. He could not see his toys. He could not see the door.

"I want my water cup," Hayden said. He began to run to the kitchen. His leg bumped a chair. It hurt a little. Dad found him in the dark.

"Run and you can trip," Dad said. "Walk slowly. Hold my hand." Hayden held Dad's big hand. They walked slowly, one small step at a time. Nobody tripped. Nobody bumped the chair.

They sat by the window. The moon gave a little light. Hayden patted his furry bear. They sang a soft song together. Then, click! The lights came back on. Hayden saw his water cup on the table. He picked up a small rock from his shelf and set it by the cup. "We did it," he said. Dad smiled.

Hazel sat at the dinner table. She ate her noodles one by one. "Can I go to Elodie's house now?" she asked. Mom shook her head. "Not now, sweet pea. Elodie was sick yesterday." Hazel put down her fork. "Today, then?" "Today Elodie is still resting," said Mom. "You can go tomorrow."

Hazel frowned. "Where is tomorrow?" Mom smiled. "First you sleep. Then it is tomorrow." Hazel looked out the window. The sky was getting dark. She helped Mom carry the plates to the sink, one at a time, slow and careful.

Hazel had a bath. She picked out string for her hair, a blue one. Mom braided it in. Then Hazel climbed into bed. She closed her eyes. She woke up in the morning. The sun was on her blanket. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked. Mom nodded. Hazel slipped on her shoes fast. At the door stood Elodie, holding two muffins, one for Hazel.

Luna wants to paint at school. She loves painting with her curly paintbrush.

"Now we play outside," says Ms. Suryanto. "Painting comes later."

"Later? When is later?" asks Luna.

Ms. Suryanto points to the big clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is," she says. "When the short hand points up, it is paint time."

Luna runs outside with Samy and Charley. They wave to the birds. They dig in the sand. But Luna keeps looking at the clock. The short hand moves a tiny bit. "It moved!" says Luna. "Does the hand know it is paint time?" she wonders.

She waits. She builds a tower with Charley. She looks again. The short hand points up now!

"Now!" says Luna. "The hand went up. It is paint time now!"

Ms. Suryanto smiles. "Yes, it is time now."

Luna dips her curly brush in blue paint. Yesterday she painted a sun. Today she paints a big round moon. Tomorrow she will paint stars.

"Look at my moon," says Luna. "The clock told me when."

Emile looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "A snow day!"

Emile put on his boots. He put on his big coat. Then he walked into the snow. His boots made marks. Each step left a shape in the snow. Step, step, step.

Then Emile saw more marks. They were not his marks. They looked like little feet. "Look, Dad!" said Emile. "Little feet walked here!"

The little footprints went across the yard. Emile followed them. Step by step, he walked. The footprints went past the swing. They went under the big tree. They stopped at the fence.

The footprints led to a small door in the fence. It was the neighbour's door. Emile heard a sound. "Neigh!" A huge white horse stood there!

"Hello, horse," said Emile. The horse was gentle. It did not hurt Emile at all. The neighbour came out. "She escaped this morning," she said. "But her feet left footprints in the fresh snow."

Emile looked back at his own footprints. His feet made marks too. "My feet made footprints, Dad!" said Emile. Dad smiled. "You found the horse all by yourself."

Emile patted the horse's soft nose. "Good feet," he said. "Good footprints."

Elliot wanted to play the feely bag game. Lya was coming over, and Mom had a big sock full of toys. "You close your eyes," said Mom. "You feel with your fingers. Then you guess."

Elliot went first. He put his hand in the sock. He felt something round. "A ball!" he said. "A red ball!"

"Open your eyes and look," said Mom.

Elliot looked. The ball was blue! He laughed. His fingers could tell it was a ball. But his fingers could not tell the color.

Then Lya felt something long. "A pencil! A yellow pencil!" She looked. It was orange! "My fingers tricked me," said Lya.

"No, your fingers did not trick you," said Mom. "They told you the shape. Your eyes need to tell you the color."

Elliot tried again. He felt a small car. "A car," he said. "But I need to look for the color." He peeked. "Green!"

Then Mom put in one more thing. Elliot felt it. It was soft and small. He squeezed it. A car? No. A sock? No. He pulled it out. It was a green frog! It hopped in his hands.

"A frog!" said Lya.

Elliot held it up high. "Hello, green frog," he said. "Your eyes are very big."

Mackenzie turned four today. Her party was at the park. Her dad blew up a big red balloon. He tied it and gave it to her.

Alba and Roman ran over. "Let it go!" said Roman. "It will fly up to the sky!" Mackenzie held the string tight. She was a little scared it would fly away too far.

Mackenzie let go of the string. The balloon did not fly up. It went down, down, down. It landed softly in the messy grass. Roman picked it up. "It did not go up at all," he said.

Mr. Abdi, the park helper, walked by. "Want a game?" he asked. He showed them how to hit the balloon up with their hands. The balloon went up, then it came back down every time.

"We need shoes off for the grass," said Dad. Mackenzie sat on the picnic blanket with Alba and Roman. They ate cake. Mackenzie hugged her red balloon. "Stay right here," she said. And it did.

Raphael sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a little growl. "I want my pasta now," he said. Dad put the pot on the stove. "The pasta is not now. It is later," said Dad. Raphael frowned. Now was this very moment. Later was not. He could see the pot. He could hear the water bubble. But he could not eat yet. He waited. He looked at the salt shaker. It was stuck to a bit of sauce. Mom washed it off. Mom gave Raphael a carrot stick. "You can eat this now," she said. Raphael ate it up. Now felt better. He heard the timer ring. Dad poured the pasta into a bowl. Dad sprinked cheese on top. "Is it now?" asked Raphael. "It is now!" said Mom. Raphael took his fork. He twirled a big bite. "Yesterday I had rice," he said. "Today I have pasta!" "And tomorrow," said Mom, "you can have soup." Raphael laughed. He drew a little hill on the foggy window with his finger. He pushed a pea up the hill. The pea rolled back down. He ate the pea. "The story of the hill comes after dinner," said Mom. "Not now. Later." Raphael nodded. He knew that word now. Later came after now. He took one more big bite and said, "Now I am ready for the story."

Violet wanted to build a little house. It was for her toy cat, Mitten. The cat needed a door.

Violet looked at her blocks. Some blocks were circles. Circles rolled away when she stacked them. Some blocks were squares. Squares sat flat and still. Some blocks were triangles. Triangles had pointy tops, like little hats.

Myra came to play too. Myra held up a long flat block. "What is this one?" she asked. It was not a square. It was longer than a square.

Mr. Islam was in the playroom, fixing a shelf. He smiled at the girls. "That is a rectangle," he said. "A rectangle has four sides and four square corners."

Violet wanted to see. She looked at the big playroom door. She touched each corner with one finger. "One, two, three, four," she counted. Four square corners. The door was a rectangle, just like the long block.

Now Violet could build. She used squares for the walls. She used a triangle for the roof. She used the rectangle block for the door. It stood up tall and did not tip.

Myra found a small circle of clear glass on the shelf. It was a little window. Violet set it into the wall. The house had a door, walls, a roof, and a window.

Outside, the sky was turning stormy. Big grey clouds moved past the real window. But Mitten was safe and dry in her new little house.

Violet put her cat inside. She knocked gently on the rectangle door. "Welcome home, Mitten," she said.

Zoey ran to the swings. The sun was bright on this warm day. She felt so excited. Then she saw Antonella trip on the black rubber path. Antonella fell down. She began to cry. She looked sad.

Zoey stopped swinging. She walked over to Antonella. "Are you okay?" she asked. Antonella looked up. Her tears slowed down. "My knee hurts," she said. "I got scared when I fell."

Ms. Almeida came with a small bandage. She put it on Antonella's knee. "That was kind, Zoey," she said. Antonella stood up. She did not cry anymore. "Thank you, Zoey," she said. "Want to swing with me?"

Zoey nodded. They sat side by side. Their legs pumped high. Zoey watched the birds fly over the trees. Antonella laughed. "This is fun," she said. "Best day ever," said Zoey.

Elijah ran into the gym at the community center. He was on a soccer team this season. His friend Yasmin was there too. The coach had the balls out.

"I want to play now," said Elijah. He grabbed a ball and kicked it. His leg felt stiff. The kick went crooked.

Ms. Van Dijk clapped her hands. "Time to warm up," she said. "We run first. Then we stretch."

The team ran one lap. Then they stretched. They touched their toes. They counted together. "One, two, three, four, five."

Elijah kicked the ball again. The kick went far and straight. It flew right to Yasmin. She caught it.

"Sorry, I made you run," Elijah said to his legs. Yasmin laughed. "Your legs like the warm-up."

The game began. Elijah ran fast. "One, two, three, four," he counted as he dashed down the field. He passed to Samir. Samir scored.

"Good team," said Ms. Van Dijk. She held up her hand. Elijah gave her a high five. Then he closed his eyes, took a big breath, and ran back for the next kick.

Kinsley sat at the dinner table. She ate her noodles, one by one. "Big bite," said Dad. Kinsley opened her mouth wide.

After dinner, it was bath time. Kinsley splashed in the bubbles. Then she put on her soft pajamas. Her old clothes sat on the floor. "One sock, two socks," she counted. "One shirt, two pants."

Kinsley looked at the laundry basket. She held a sock. She tossed it. It went in! "Yay, Kinsley," said Dad. He clapped his hands. She threw the shirt. It missed and landed on the floor. Kinsley picked it up. She tried again. In it went! She threw the pants, one and two. All the clothes were in the basket now.

"Dad, the basket is full," said Kinsley. Dad smiled. "Tomorrow the washing machine will clean them all." Kinsley looked at the clock on the wall. "Now bed," she said. Dad tucked her in. "Sleep tight, big girl," he said. Kinsley pretended her teddy was tossing socks too. "In the basket, teddy," she whispered. "One, two, splash."

Elizabeth sat at the dinner table. She wanted the apple pie. It sat on the counter, far away.

"Can I have pie now?" she asked.

"Not now," said her dad. "We eat pie soon."

Elizabeth frowned. "Soon is a long time," she said.

"Soon means in a little while," said her dad.

Elizabeth took one bite of her chicken. She took another bite. She drank some milk. She looked at the pie again. It was still there.

"Now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said her dad. "Eat a little more."

Elizabeth ate her carrots, one by one. She waited some more. Then her dad stood up. He cut the pie. He put a big piece on her plate.

Elizabeth looked at her plate. The waiting was done. The pie was here now.

"Yesterday I had bread," she said. "Today I have pie. Tomorrow I can have pie again?"

"Maybe tomorrow," said her dad, smiling.

Elizabeth took her fork and played a little game. She made her pie into a moon shape. Then she ate it all up.

"Now pie is all gone," she said.

Her dad laughed. "And tomorrow," he said, "we can bake a new one together."

Blake stood at the front door. She looked outside. The sky was gray. Rain dripped down the glass. "Rainy day," said Dad. Blake wanted to jump in the big puddle by the steps. She ran out in her sneakers. Splash! Her socks got wet. "Yuck," said Blake. "Smelly, soggy socks." She had to go back in.

Dad helped her take off the wet socks. "Fetch your rain boots," he said. Blake fetched them. They were yellow with red ducks on them. She pulled them on. One boot, two boots. Then she ran outside again. Splash! This time her feet stayed dry. The rain boots kept her feet dry in the puddle.

The wind blew Blake's hat. "Windy too!" she said. Just then the rain stopped. The sun came out. It made the puddle shine like a little lake. Eliot walked by with his umbrella, all bundled warm. "Snow is coming soon," he said. Blake looked up at the sunny sky and laughed. "Sunny now!" she said, and jumped one more time.

Andrew sat at the big art table. Mr. Girma put paper in front of everyone. "Today we paint shapes," said Mr. Girma.

Andrew picked up his brush. He wanted to paint a house for his dog. He painted a square for the house. He painted a rectangle for the door. He painted a circle for a window. Then he stopped. The roof was hard. He tried a round roof. It looked like a cloud. It slid down the paper like something slippery.

Zakaria sat next to him. Zakaria was eating his snack. His sandwich was cut into triangles. "Look," said Zakaria. He pointed at a piece. "A triangle." Andrew leaned close. He touched the corner of the bread. Then he counted on his fingers. "One, two, three." The triangle had three corners. He ran his finger along the edges. Three sides too.

Andrew found a triangle on the table. It was a yellow paper triangle. He counted the corners again. One, two, three. He picked up his brush. He painted a triangle roof. It sat right on top of his square. It did not slide.

Mr. Girma came to look. "A triangle roof," he said. Reign came to look too. "Nice house," said Reign. Andrew painted a little triangle door for the dog. Then he wrote his name at the top. "Done," said Andrew.

Arnaud was at Grandpa's house. In the garden he found three pinecones and one pink flower petal. "I will make soup," he said.

He put the pinecones in a little blue pot. He stirred with a stick. The soup smelled like nothing at all, but in his head it smelled like berries. He held the pot up to his mouth. Then he stopped. He remembered Mom's words: "Pretend food is for pretending to eat."

So Arnaud tipped the pot near his lips. He made a big slurpy sound. "Slurp! Mmm! Yummy soup!" Not one pinecone went in his mouth. He put the pot down and patted his tummy.

Grandpa peeked around the door. "Was the soup good?"

"Best soup ever," said Arnaud. "But you can't have real bites. Only pretend bites."

Grandpa sat down on the grass. He took a leaf spoon. He slurped too. "Slurp! Oh, so good!"

Then Arnaud kicked a pinecone that rolled off the table. It rolled under a bush. He got down on his knee to look.

A ladybug was sitting on the pinecone. It was very small and very red.

"A guest for soup!" said Arnaud. He put the pinecone back in the pot. "More soup for everyone."

Jaxson stood on the big green soccer field. Ms. Crowchild put a tiny beanbag in his hands. "Now we throw," she said. Jaxson threw it. The beanbag went up and came down. It landed in the red hoop. Jaxson jumped up and down.

Sloane stood next to him. Abraham stood next to her. Jaxson picked up the next beanbag. He picked up another one too. He held them both tight. He wanted to throw them all.

Sloane reached out her hands. She had no beanbag. Her face looked sad. Ms. Crowchild knelt down. "Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn," she said. Jaxson looked at the beanbags in his hands. He looked at Sloane. He gave her one beanbag.

Sloane threw it. It went up and came down into the hoop. Then Abraham took his turn. Then it was Jaxson's turn again. He threw his beanbag far. Then Ms. Crowchild rolled him a big ball. Jaxson caught it with both hands. "Good catch," said Sloane. "My turn now?" Jaxson rolled the ball to her.

Luca ran into the hair salon with his dad. It was his very first haircut! There was a big fish tank by the wall. The fish were busy swimming round and round.

Mr. Nasser put the cape on Luca. He held the scissors. Snip, snip! Luca turned his head to see the fish. Mr. Nasser stopped. "Oops," he said. "Your hair is all bumpy now." Luca looked in the mirror. One side was long and one side was short.

Luca had an idea. He would sit very still, like a statue. He kept his eyes on his knees. Snip, snip, snip! Soon Mr. Nasser said, "All done!" Luca looked up. His hair was neat and smooth all over. He jumped down and ran to the fish tank. "Dad, the fish saw my new hair!"

Paisley wanted her bedtime book. It was on the shelf, under a book about a spider.

"Please read it, Dad," she said. Dad sat on the bed and held the book. He opened it the right way, front cover first.

"This line says, 'The little bear tiptoes to the moon,'" Dad read.

Then Mom came in. "My turn," she said. Mom held the book too. She read the same page. "The little bear tiptoes to the moon."

Paisley sat up. "Say it again, Mom."

"The little bear tiptoes to the moon," Mom said again.

Dad read it once more. Same words. Mom read it once more. Same words. Paisley pointed at the little black marks on the page.

"Do those marks say the bear part?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "The marks stay on the page."

"Even when you read it?" asked Paisley.

"Even then," said Dad.

Paisley turned to the front. She tapped the first page. "Start here," she said. Dad smiled and turned the pages one by one, all the way to the end. The tidy stack of books sat waiting for tomorrow night. Paisley yawned and whispered, "Same words tomorrow?"

"Same words tomorrow," said Dad.

Ivy went to the playground with her dad. The sun felt warm on her face. "Why do I hold your hand?" she asked. "So we stay close," said Dad. They walked close together all the way to the swings.

Tenley was there too. She waved from the sandbox. "Come play!" said Tenley. Ivy ran to the sand. It was soft and cool between her toes. Then Ivy saw something shiny on the bench. It was a little box. Bright little dots sat inside. They looked like candy. Red ones and yellow ones.

Ivy did not touch them. "Is that candy?" Tenley asked. "I don't know," said Ivy. "It might be medicine. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy." She ran to Dad and pulled his hand. Dad came and picked up the box. "Good job, Ivy," he said. "I will keep it safe."

Tenley brought Ivy a leaf as a present. "This is for you," she said. "Sorry I almost touched the box," said Tenley. They dug in the cool sand until the sun went low. "Swing time," said Ivy, and off they ran.
