John was a young boy. He was going to the big pool by the beach. He ran past the sand. He ran past the ice cream cart. "Swim, swim, swim!" he sang.

Clarke and Osman were at the pool too. John saw the water. It went splash, splash, splash. He wanted to jump in right away. He pushed his feet fast, fast, fast. But Ms. Abdi stood by the door. "Stop, John!" she said. "Take a shower first. Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." John looked up. He saw the shower. The water went tinkle, tinkle on his toes.

One shower, two friends, three big splashes. John stood under the water. It was warm. It tickled his nose. Then Ms. Abdi said, "All clean! You can swim now." John jumped in. "Wheee!" said Clarke. "Wheee!" said Osman. That night, a lamp shone by John's bed. He dreamed of the pool. "Shower first," he whispered, "then splash."

Emile was at Seth's house. The toast was warm and golden. Seth's dad had made it, and now it was Emile's turn. Emile took the little knife with butter on it. He spread the butter slowly, slow and smooth. The butter melted into the warm toast. "I did it," said Emile.

Next came the milk. Emile held the cup and poured. He poured and poured. The milk came up to the very top, all the way to the rim. He walked to the table. One step, two steps. Milk sloshed over the side and made a little puddle.

Seth's dad wiped it up with a cloth. "Try again," he said kindly. Emile poured a new cup. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He left some room. He walked slowly past the bright window, past the muddy boots by the door. Not one drop spilled. Emile climbed onto his chair and took a big sip. "Milk stays in," he said.

Madeline sat in her car seat. She had a basket of picture cards. Oh no! The basket tipped over. All the cards fell out. They went everywhere.

"I can fix it," said Madeline. She picked up a card. It was a cow. She picked up another. It was a dog. "Cow and dog," she said. "They are both animals." She put them in one pile. Then she found a card with a ball. The ball was not an animal. The ball was a toy. She made a new pile. Then she found a card with an apple. "Apple is a food," she said. She made a third pile.

Her dad drove on. It started to rain. The rain went splash on the window. "Look, a boat card!" said Madeline. The boat was a toy, so it went in the toy pile. Soon the piles were done. The basket was tidy again. "We are not late," said Dad with a smile. Madeline hugged her sorted cards. "Animals, toys, and foods," she said.

Alexis ran fast across the playroom at daycare. His shoes slip on the shiny floor. He fell right into Sultan's tall block tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sultan's mouth turned down. His eyes got big. "My tower," he said. Alexis felt his tummy go tight. He did not mean to knock it down. Mr. Toussaint knelt down next to them. "Alexis, do you have words for Sultan?" he asked softly.

Alexis took a big breath. "Sorry, Sultan. I did not mean it. Sorry means I know I hurt you." He looked at the fallen blocks. "Can I help build it again?" Sultan nodded. "Okay. Let's build it big."

They stacked the red blocks first. Then the blue ones. Then the yellow ones. Joey came over with a cold juice cup from snack time. "Can I help too?" he asked. "Yes!" said Sultan. "It is going to be a birthday tower for my dog."

The tower grew tall, taller, tallest of all. "It did not fall," said Alexis. "We built it together." Sultan smiled and put one more block on top.

Chloe was painting at the kitchen table. She painted a big blue flower. She wanted more yellow paint for the middle. The jar was too high on the shelf. "Dad, can you help me, please?" she asked. Dad got the jar down. "Thank you," said Chloe.

Then the doorbell rang. It was Ms. Desir from next door. She brought a little pot of yellow flowers. Chloe jumped up and down with joy. She took the pot with both hands. "Thank you!" she said. Ms. Desir smiled a big smile.

"Gracias," said Ms. Desir. Chloe blinked. "What does gracias mean?" Ms. Desir laughed softly. "It means thank you in Spanish." Chloe tried the new word in her mouth. "Grah-see-as," she said slowly. "Gracias!" said Ms. Desir, and she clapped.

Chloe ran to her painting. She painted the words on the blue flower. Dad read them out loud. Chloe hugged the yellow pot. "Gracias, flowers," she whispered.

Anthony woke up with a big idea. Today he would make his own breakfast! Dad put two pieces of toast on a blue block of wood. The toaster was hot, so Dad had used it himself. Anthony got the butter and a soft round knife.

First came the butter. Anthony held the knife and spread. The butter went on in thick, bumpy stripes. "Look, Dad! I did it!" Dad gave him a thumbs up. Anthony grinned so big his eyes went closed.

Now for the milk. Anthony picked up the big jug. He tipped it fast. Splash! Milk jumped out of the cup and ran across the table. "Oh no," said Anthony. Dad wiped it up. "Try again," said Dad. Anthony took a deep breath. This time he poured slowly. The milk slid down, quiet and smooth. It filled the cup all the way. Not one drop came out!

A bit of butter floated on his milk from his sticky fingers. Anthony laughed and got a cloth. Then he lifted the cup and took a big sip. "Best milk ever!" he said.

Josephine ran to the park with her dad. The sun was big and bright. It was a sunny day. Josephine climbed up the slide. She squinted her eyes. The sun was on her face. "Too bright," she said. Her dad said, "Let's get your sun hat." He pulled it from the bag. Josephine put it on. The hat made shade over her face. Now she could open her eyes wide. "Better," she said.

Maisie came to the park too. Maisie wore rain boots. "It was rainy this morning," Maisie said. "My boots went in the puddles." The puddles were gone now. The sun had dried them.

The wind began to blow. It was windy now. The wind made the tree leaves shake. The wind tried to blow off Josephine's hat. She held it with her hand. The naughty wind tickled her hair.

Kaden ran over with a towel. "I went swimming," he said. "My hair is all wet." He rubbed his hair with the towel. Then he sat in the sun to get warm.

Josephine slid down the slide again and again. Her hat kept the sun off her face the whole time. At the top of the slide, she looked at Kaden and Maisie. "My turn again," she said, and down she went.

Ethan went to the garden center with his dad. He wanted to grow vegetables. He picked little seeds and a big bag of soil. "I will plant them all by myself," he said.

At home, Ethan put soil in a pot. He poked holes with his finger. He dropped the seeds in. He covered them up. Then he watered them. Every day he looked at the pot. Nothing was there. "Where are my plants?" he asked. "Maybe it is a big problem," he said. His dad said, "Not yet. Just wait a little more."

Ethan waited and waited. One morning he saw something tiny and green. It poked up out of the soil! Ethan ran to his dad. "Come see!" he shouted. His dad smiled. "That is called a sprout," he said. "A sprout! A sprout!" Ethan sang. He watered it again. "Grow big, little sprout," he said. "You will be a silly big carrot soon."

Ibrahim wanted to make breakfast all by himself. His dad put two pieces of warm toast on a plate. The butter was cold from the fridge. Ibrahim tried to spread it. The butter was hard. It made a hole in the toast. "Oh no," said Ibrahim.

His dad got a friendly smile on his face. "Try this bowl," he said. The butter in the bowl had sat out on the table all morning. Ibrahim dipped his knife again. He spread the soft butter. It went on smooth and easy. No holes at all!

Now for the milk. Ibrahim held the cup with two hands. He poured slowly. One small drip ran down the side. He wiped it with a cloth. That was his answer to the drip.

"I did it myself," said Ibrahim. His dad sat down next to him. Ibrahim took a big bite of toast. "Pretend you are a milk man," he said, "and I will pour you a cup."

Emmett waited at the airport. His grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. "There he is!" said Emmett. Grandpa came off the plane with a small red bag. "Hello, Emmett!" said Grandpa. "Hello!" said Emmett. Grandpa's coat was wet. "The rain made me damp," said Grandpa. "We can hang it up to dry," said Emmett.

At home, Grandpa took out some cards. There were sheep on the cards. "A card game!" said Emmett. "I go first!" Then he said it again. "Me first again!" Grandpa laughed. "No, no. We take turns. You go, then me, then you." Emmett put down one sheep card. Then Grandpa put down one. Then Emmett again.

They played all week. "My turn," said Emmett. "My turn," said Grandpa. "You are good at this," said Grandpa. Emmett smiled and put down his last sheep card. "I win!"

Ryan put on his little apron. It had a funny cat on it. He was at the big community kitchen with his dad. Today they would bake blueberry muffins for the family.

Ryan helped mix the batter. He gave the spoon a big stir. Then he dropped three blueberries in the bowl. His mom slid the pan into the oven. She set the timer. "What is that?" Ryan asked. "The timer," his mom said. "It will ring when it is time to check the muffins."

Ryan and his dad sat on a soft pillow near the door. They played a game with red and yellow cups. Ryan stacked the cups up high. Then he stacked them again. He forgot all about the muffins.

Suddenly, a loud beep filled the kitchen. Beep, beep, beep. Ryan jumped up. "The muffins!" he said. His mom opened the oven door. She pulled out the pan with her big mitts. The muffins were round and golden. Ryan counted them, one, two, three, four. He put them in a basket to take home. His dad said, "You heard it first, Ryan." Ryan smiled and held the basket all the way to the car.

Wesley woke up early. Snow was falling outside. He and his dad rode the bus. They were going to the doctor.

At the doctor's office, Wesley sat on a big chair. His tummy felt tight. "I don't want a shot," he said. His friend Harlow was there too. She held her teddy bear close.

A nurse came in. "Wesley, it is your turn," she said. Wesley held his dad's hand. Then Harlow whispered, "Breathe in slow. Like smelling a flower." Wesley took one slow breath in. Then he let it out. His shoulders came down. His tummy felt less tight. He breathed in slow again.

The nurse cleaned his arm with a soft cotton ball. It felt cool. Then the shot was done. "All finished," said the nurse.

"That was fast," said Wesley. He got a bandage with a star on it. He looked at Harlow and smiled. "Slow breaths helped me," he said.

Jackson sat in the family car. They were going on a big trip. Papa drove and drove.

Then Papa took a wrong turn. "Oh no," said Papa. "This is not our road." Jackson saw a big paper on Mama's lap. It had lines on it. "What is that?" asked Jackson. "A map," said Mama. "It shows roads and places."

Mama turned the map around. Jackson looked at the lines. He saw a little blue line. "That one!" said Jackson. "It goes to our place." Mama looked where his finger pointed. "You found the road," she said. Papa turned the car around. Soon they saw the right road. "We are not alone," said Jackson. "The map helps us too." Papa smiled and honk went the horn.

Victor sat at the big table. His block tower had fallen down. He felt sad. He pouted and hid his face in his arms.

Mom walked into the room. "Victor, are you okay?" she asked. Victor did not answer. He just frowned at the floor.

Then Victor took a big breath. "I feel sad," he said. "My tower fell down." Mom sat next to him. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Let's build it again together."

Victor felt a little better. He and Mom stacked the blocks. Red block, blue block, green block. The tower grew tall. Victor clapped his hands. He felt happy now.

Later, his friend Wren came to play. Wren dropped a crayon and began to cry. Victor handed it back to her. "You can say how you feel," he said. Wren wiped her eyes. "I feel sad," she said. "But now I feel better."

Mom smiled. "What a smart idea," she said. Victor grinned and put the last block on top.

Wesley sat at the dinner table. He had a toy dog next to his plate. He had a toy cow, too. He loved his toy animals.

Dad put fish on Wesley's plate. "Yum," said Wesley. Then he made a face. "Fish is not an animal. Fish has no legs. My dog has legs. My cow has legs."

Ms. Ivanova was there for dinner. She smiled. She held up the toy cow. "This is an animal," she said. Then she pointed to the plate. "And a fish is an animal, too."

Wesley looked at his fish. He looked at his dog. "A fish can be an animal with no legs?" he asked.

"Yes," said Ms. Ivanova. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals."

Wesley took a small bite. He chewed. "The fish is good," he said. He made his toy dog hop on the table. "Woof, woof," he said. "Time for dinner, fish!"

Then Wesley held up his toy cow. "Moo," he said softly. He gave the fish one more big bite.

Eleanor and her dad walked into the hospital. Mom had a new baby here. Eleanor wanted to hold him very much.

The baby was tiny. He had small hands and small feet. Mom said, "You can touch him. But a new baby must be touched very gently."

Eleanor patted the baby's head. She patted too hard. The baby began to cry. Eleanor felt bad. "Too big," she said. "My pats are too big."

Mom took Eleanor's hand. She turned it over. "Try this," Mom said. "Stroke his little hand, soft like a feather."

Eleanor reached out one finger. She stroked the baby's hand. She did it slow and soft. The baby stopped crying. His tiny fingers wrapped around her finger. "He likes it," Eleanor whispered. She stroked again, soft as a whisper.

Later they sat in a cozy chair. A nurse came by with a computer on a cart. She smiled at the sleeping baby. "He knows your touch now," she said.

Eleanor gave the baby one more gentle stroke. "I will always touch you gently," she told him. The baby held her finger tight.

Theodore sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. He saw trees out the window. Then he saw the park. The swings were there. "The park!" said Theodore. "I want to swing." The car stopped. Dad got out first. Theodore saw the swings across the road. A big truck went by. It was loud. Theodore waited on the grass. Dad held out his hand. Theodore put his little hand in Dad's big hand. They looked both ways. Then they crossed the road together. The slide felt cool in the shade. Theodore found a small white bone in the wood chips. "Leave it there," said Dad. "It belongs to the dog who lost it." Theodore patted his own arm. "I have bones too," he said. "Me too," said Dad. Then Theodore ran to the swings. "Push me high!" he said. Dad gave one big push.

Benjamin ran into the kitchen. It was morning, and Dad was making breakfast. Benjamin saw big red strawberries in a bowl. He touched one with his finger. It felt bumpy and cold.

"I want a crunchy apple too," Benjamin said. Dad washed an apple. Then Dad turned on the blender for the smoothie. The blender was very loud. It was too loud for Benjamin's ears. He put his hands over his ears. His hands covered his ears. Now the loud sound was quieter. That was better. Benjamin smelled the strawberries. They smelled sweet.

The blender stopped. Benjamin took his hands off his ears. Dad gave him a slice of apple. Benjamin tasted it. Crunch, crunch. "Can Josh and Luna hear the blender?" Benjamin asked. "No, it stopped," said Dad. Benjamin listened. The kitchen was quiet again. "All done," said Dad.

Scarlett went to the store with her dad. Today was the big shopping day. Yesterday they had no bread. Today they would get some.

Scarlett saw a big bin of fuzzy peaches. She touched one. It felt soft like a feather. "Can I hold one now?" she asked.

"You can hold it now," Dad said. "But we buy it, and you eat it later." Scarlett held the peach all through the store. "Is it later yet?" she asked at the milk. "Not yet," said Dad. "Is it later yet?" she asked at the bread. "Not yet," said Dad.

At home, Dad washed the peach. Scarlett counted, "One peach, two hands, one big bite." Now it was later. Now she could eat it. She dug her little teeth in. "Sweet!" said Scarlett. "Now it is later!"

Lily went to the park with her teddy bear. She saw Syed under the big tree. He had set up a little box on the grass. Toys sat on top in a row.

"Welcome to my shop," said Syed. "I am the shopkeeper."

Lily had an idea. "Then I can be the shopper," she said. "I want to buy the red car."

Syed shook his head. "You have to wait. The shopper looks first." Lily looked at all the toys. She picked up a duck. She put it down. She picked up the red car again.

"I choose this one," said Lily. She gave Syed a leaf for money. Syed laughed. "Thank you, shopper," he said. He put the leaf in his pocket very carefully.

"Now it is my turn," said Lily. "I will be the shopkeeper. You be the shopper." They swapped places. Syed looked and looked. He chose the duck.

Then Kendra ran over to the tree. "Can I play too?" she asked. "Yes," said Lily. "I am the shopkeeper. You can be the shopper." Kendra took her time choosing. Lily waited with her hands behind her back, just like a real shopkeeper.

At the end, the shop had no toys left. Everyone had bought one. "The shop is now closed," said Lily. She turned the box upside down.

"New shop tomorrow?" asked Syed.

"Yes," said Lily. "Open at the swings."

Hazel sat at the little red table. Megan had a bowl of apples. "I will count them," said Hazel. She touched one apple. "One, two." Then she touched it again. "Three!" Megan frowned. "That looks like two apples."

Ms. Gupta came over. She knelt down by the table. "Try again," she said. "Point at each apple one time." Hazel took a big breath. She pointed at the first apple. "One." She pointed at the second apple. "Two." She did not point at the first one again.

"Two apples," said Hazel. Ms. Gupta smiled. Then she put out a plate of crackers. "Which has more?" Hazel pointed at each cracker. One, two, three, four. "The crackers have more!"

Megan clapped her hands. Hazel counted the apples once more, just to be sure. "Two," she said, and took a happy bite of her snack.

Michael rode in the family car. His mom drove. The seats felt warm. Michael held his toy lion. "Where are we going?" he asked. "To see the dentist," said Mom.

At the dentist, a kind lady smiled. "Open your mouth wide," she said. "Then I can see every tooth." Michael opened. Then he closed his mouth to talk. "Is my lion okay too?" he asked. The lady could not see his teeth now.

Mom held the lion up. "Roar like your lion," she said. Michael took a big breath. He opened his mouth wide and roared. "Aaaa-roar!" The lady looked in. She saw every tooth. She counted them all.

"Your teeth are clean and strong," she said. Michael hugged his lion. He got a bright sticker for his shirt. In the car, Mom turned on the radio. Michael looked out at the clouds. He made one more roar, very soft, and his mom laughed.

Madison was at Grandma's house. The toast was warm on her plate. Grandma put out soft butter. "Can I try?" asked Madison. "Yes, you may," said Grandma.

Madison picked up the butter knife. She held it flat, not pointy. She spread the butter, slow and slow. The butter made a shiny path on the toast. "I did it myself!" said Madison. Grandma smiled big.

Next came the milk. Madison held the cup with one hand. She poured with the other hand. Glug, glug, too fast! A little milk ran onto the table. A small white puddle sat there. Would it stay forever? What could help?

Madison saw a cloth by the sink. She took the cloth and wiped the table. The milk went away. All gone! The puddle had vanished, like a bird can fly away. Then Madison drank her milk. Grandma clapped. "Yay for Madison!" she said. Madison wiped one more spot, just to be sure.

Jasmine sat at the big art table. Mr. Li put a paper in front of her. He gave her a soft gray pencil. She wanted to draw a cat with a long neck.

Taim sat next to her. He was drawing a sun. Jasmine pressed down very hard on her paper. The line got dark and thick. She pressed even harder for the cat's long neck.

Snap. The pencil point broke off. It fell on the table. Jasmine looked at the little gray piece. "Guess I pressed too hard," she said.

Mr. Li gave her the pencil sharpener. He turned the pencil and made a new point. Jasmine held the pencil again. This time she pressed soft and slow. The line came out thin and light. The long neck grew tall, little by little.

Taim leaned over. "Nice cat," he said. Jasmine drew one soft ear, then the other. Then she drew a tiny nose.

Caleb put his lunchbox on the shelf. Maxim put his lunchbox on the shelf too. Both boxes were red. Both boxes looked the same.

After play time, Caleb got a box. He opened the lid. Inside was a squishy banana, not his apple. "This is not mine," said Caleb. Maxim opened the other box. "This is not mine," said Maxim.

Ms. Yip came over. "Look inside the lids," she said. Caleb saw letters on his lid. "That says Caleb," said Ms. Yip. Maxim looked too. "That one says Maxim," he said.

They swapped the boxes. Caleb opened his lid again. His apple sat there, round as a rock. He took a big bite.

At pick up time, Caleb held his box tight. "Name on the lid," he said to his dad. "It comes back to me."

Amelia went to the store with her dad. She saw her friend Dorian there. Dorian had on a red scarf. It went down past his knees. Amelia wanted a scarf too. She found a pink one with a cow on it. She held it up. It stopped at her waist. It was short.

"Your scarf is long," Amelia said. "Mine is short."

"Long and short are opposites," Dorian said.

Amelia put her scarf next to his. She could see it. One scarf was long. One scarf was short. She held them up high. Then she let them drop. The long one took more time to fall.

Dad said, "The store has hot cocoa at the back." They walked slowly to the counter. A grown-up poured the cocoa. Amelia waited until it was warm, not hot. She took a little sip. "Yummy," she said.

Dorian gave her a hug. Amelia smiled and wrapped her short cow scarf around her neck twice. Dad laughed. "It fits you just right," he said. Amelia looked in the big mirror by the door and waved at the small girl waving back.

Maverick rode the city bus with his dad. He held his old blue bag. Then he opened it. His little toy bear was gone.

"I can't find Bear," said Maverick. He looked under the seat. He looked by his shoes. No bear. He looked in his dad's coat pocket. No bear. Maverick sat very still. His eyes felt hot.

"Dad, will you help me look?" he asked. Dad smiled. "Yes, let's look together." Dad bent down low. He shone his phone light under the seat. Maverick got down too. He pointed at a tiny paw. "There!" Two people looking found it fast.

Dad pulled Bear out. Maverick hugged Bear tight. The bus stopped. "Our stop," said Dad. Maverick waved to the driver. "Bye, bus!"

One bright morning, Scarlett ran to the playground. She wanted to find her friend Hukam. She saw the big slide first. "One slide," she said. Then she saw two swings. Then three, four, five steps on the climbing wall!

Near the little playhouse, a number sat on the door. It looked like this: 5. Scarlett pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked.

Hukam came around the corner. "That says five," he said. "It is the same five as my fingers." He held up his hand. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five!"

Scarlett held up her hand too. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The number on the door meant her five fingers! It was a real five.

"Let's count more," said Hukam. They jumped on the bridge. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" they sang out loud.

The singing worked. Dario heard them from the sandbox. He ran over fast. Now three friends played on the bridge, jumping and singing all the way to ten again.

John woke up in his bed. The sun was up too. He heard plates in the kitchen. Mom and Dad sat at the table. They were eating breakfast.

"Good morning, John," said Mom.

"It is morning now," said John. "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast."

Today was a big day. John was going to the park with his friend Charlie. "The park is later," said Dad. "First we finish breakfast."

John ate his cereal from his bowl. He ate fast. He wanted to go now.

Then Dad's phone rang. Dad could not go to the park today. John felt his eyes go hot. "But I want to go today," he said.

Ms. Weber was outside watering her flowers. John asked her about the park. "I am going to the park today," she said. "You can come with me."

They walked to the park. A naughty squirrel took Charlie's hat. Charlie laughed. John helped him step over the big puddle to get it back.

They played on the swings. Then it was time to go home.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" asked John.

"Yes," said Ms. Weber. "Tomorrow we will wake up, eat breakfast, and come back."

Florence was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big old dog. His tail would swing when he was happy. He was not lazy at all. He ran to sniff Florence's shoe.

"Grandma, why does he smell my shoe?" asked Florence.

"Animals smell with their nose," said Grandma. "Smelling is a sense. Do you know your senses?" Grandma held up one hand. "Look. You have five fingers. You have five senses too."

Florence looked at her own hand. She put down one finger. "Eyes see." She put down another. "Ears hear." One more. "Nose smells." Then she stopped. She frowned. "I forgot one."

Grandma gave her a slice of apple. Florence took a bite. "Mmm! Tasting! My tongue tastes!" She put down a fourth finger. Then she touched the dog's soft ears. "And my hands touch! Touching!" All five fingers were down. She had said them all.

"You got it," said Grandma. She picked Florence up for a cozy hug. The dog's tail began to swing again.

"Five senses, five fingers," said Florence. Grandma laughed and gave her another slice of apple.

Eva was at home in the kitchen. Her dad was washing strawberries. Eva wanted to taste one.

First she used her eyes. She saw the red strawberries. She saw the little green leaves on top.

She used her nose next. She sniffed a strawberry. It smelled sweet. Then she used her ears. She heard the water splash in the sink. She touched the strawberry with her fingers. It felt bumpy with little seeds.

Her dad let her have one. Eva bit it. "Yum!" she said. It tasted big and sweet in her mouth.

Then Eva held her nose closed. She bit the strawberry again. She chewed and chewed. The taste was very small now. It tasted plain, like nothing much. She let go of her nose. The sweet taste came back! Eva laughed.

She tried it again with a second strawberry. She held her nose. Plain again. She let go. Sweet again.

Her dad peeked over her shoulder. "What are you doing?" he asked.

Eva held up her strawberry. "My nose helps it taste big," she said.

Then her little bike bell rang in the hall. Ding, ding! Eva had not touched it. It was the cat, batting the bell with her paw.

Caleb went to the grocery store with his dad. "We need flour and eggs," said Caleb. He held the list in his hands. "This is my recipe," he said. "A recipe tells me what to use." At the store, an owl picture hung on the wall by the bread. "That owl is watching us," Caleb giggled. They bought eggs, flour and milk. The milk carton was a little smelly, so they got a new one.

At home, Caleb helped mix. Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Caleb stood back and watched. The first pancake came out flat. "Oh no," said Caleb. "It looks like a plate!" Dad laughed. They read the recipe again, step by step. One step was skipped. The recipe said to add baking powder. Dad had left it out! They mixed a new bowl, and Dad added the powder. The next pancake came out big and fluffy. "Look!" said Caleb. "It puffed up like a cloud!" He clapped his hands. Dad flipped it high in the pan. Caleb yelled, "Flip it again, Dad! Make it touch the owl picture on the wall!" Dad said, "One flip at a time, chef."

Grayson sat in his car seat. The window was cool on his hand. "We can feed the ducks today," said Dad. "Yes, please!" said Grayson.

They stopped to pick up Sheldon. Sheldon's mom handed Grayson a snack cup. Grayson grabbed it fast and looked out the window. "Grayson," said Dad softly. Grayson looked back. "Thank you!" he said. Sheldon's mom smiled. "You are welcome," she said.

At the pond, Sheldon passed Grayson the bread bag. Grayson ran off with it to the ducks. Then he stopped. He turned around. "Thank you, Sheldon!" he called. Sheldon laughed. "That was a good joke, Grayson," said Dad. "No, thank you is real," said Grayson. He tore a little bread and dropped it. The ducks came close. "More, please," said Grayson, holding out the bag to Dad. Dad gave him one more piece.

Blake sat at the big table. She had all the red crayons. Toby sat next to her. He had no crayons at all.

Toby looked at the paper. He looked at the crayons. "Can I use one too?" he asked.

Blake held the crayons close. Then she saw Toby's empty hands. She thought hard. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too," her mom had said at breakfast. Blake lifted two red crayons out of the pile. She put them by Toby's hand.

"Thank you," said Toby. He drew a big red bird. The bird had wings held high.

Blake drew a bird too. "Why is your bird so big?" she asked.

"Because I had a fat crayon," said Toby. They both laughed.

Outside, a real bird flew by the window. It flew high, high up. Blake and Toby watched it go. Then they shared the crayons again.

Luke ran to the table. He wanted his snack now. But his hands were muddy from the garden.

Ms. Côté held up her hand. "We wash our hands before we eat," she said.

Luke looked at his hands. One hand, two hands. Both hands were brown with mud. He sighed a big sigh. Then he walked to the bathroom.

Diego and Aila were already there. They stood by the sink. Luke tapped the tap with his mom. The water came out. It felt warm. The soap felt slippery. Luke rubbed and rubbed.

"Bubbles," said Diego. "One, two, three bubbles."

"More bubbles," said Aila. "Four, five, six bubbles."

Luke made bubbles too. He counted them. "Seven, eight, nine." The bubbles were white like a little cloud. The mud went down the drain. Luke watched it swirl away.

Soon his hands were clean. He could see his skin again. He dried them on the soft towel.

Then Luke ran back to the table. Aila and Diego sat down too. Ms. Côté gave them apple slices. Luke took a big bite. It was crunchy and sweet.

Luke looked at his clean hands. Clean hands, yummy snack. He held up his apple slice. "All clean," he said.

Noah sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all. He tapped a pea with his spoon. "One, two, three, four," he said. Then he stopped. "Five... no, six?" He looked at his peas. He was stuck.

His big sister sat next to him. "Try again," she said. "I will help you." Noah tapped slowly. "One, two, three, four." His sister held up one finger. "What comes next?" Noah looked at her finger. "Five!" he said. "Then six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He tapped each pea as he said each word. All ten peas were counted.

"Now the counting words are all used up," his sister said. "They always go in the same order." Noah grinned. He scooped up his peas, one by one. "Ten, nine, eight," he said as he ate. His sister laughed.

After dinner, Noah drew a little mouse on his paper. He gave it ten whiskers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," he said. Then he drew a frozen pond, all blue. "Daddy can drive us to the pond tomorrow," he said. "I will count the skates. One, two, three, four." His daddy smiled. "And what comes next, Noah?"

"Five!"

Asher ran into the kitchen. His teddy was lost! He had left it somewhere after lunch.

The kitchen was dark. The sun had gone down. Asher could not see. He peeked behind a chair. He felt a towel with his hands. He listened with his ears. He heard only the fridge humming.

Asher smelled something sweet. Cookies! His mom was baking. His tummy wanted a cookie, but first he wanted teddy.

"Mom, I can't see!" Asher said.

"Let's turn on the light," Mom said. She flipped the switch. Click! The kitchen got bright.

Now Asher could see with his eyes. He looked at the counter. There was teddy, sitting by the bread box! Asher hugged teddy soft against his neck.

Then Mom gave him a warm cookie. Asher took a little bite. It tasted sweet and good. He licked his crumbs and went to wash his hands at the sink. Teddy watched from the counter.

"One more cookie for teddy?" Asher asked.

Mom laughed. "Teddy can just smell it," she said.

Austin sat at the little table. He had a red crayon and some paper. He wanted to draw a sun. The sun needed a big round circle.

Austin tried to draw a circle. His circle came out wobbly. It looked like a squished egg. "Oh no," said Austin. He tried again. That one was wobbly too.

Mael sat down next to him. Mael had a cup in her hand. She put the cup down on her paper. She traced her crayon all around the bottom of the cup. Then she lifted the cup up. A perfect circle was on the paper. "Round!" said Mael.

Austin's mouth went open wide. He grabbed his own cup. He set it down on his paper. He traced around the bottom, slow and careful. He lifted the cup. There it was. A perfect circle!

"Now my sun can shine," said Austin. He drew little sticks all around the circle. Mr. Ma came over and looked. "What a sunny circle," he said. Austin patted his paper. "My cup made it!"

Ezra ran to the slide at daycare. The sun made the yellow slide shine. A line of kids stood by the ladder. Mehdi was first. Elle was second. Ezra was third.

Ezra wanted to go down fast. He pushed past Elle and grabbed the ladder. Elle frowned. "You jumped the line," she said. Ms. Sato came over. "The line means you stay in your place until it is your turn," she said. Ezra looked at the ladder. Then he let go.

He walked back to his spot behind Elle. He waited. He counted his shoes. He watched Mehdi go down, whee. He watched Elle go down, whee. Now it was his turn. Ezra climbed up, step by step. He slid down so fast his tummy felt dizzy. He laughed and laughed.

"Again?" Ezra asked. "Yes," said Elle. "Get in line." Ezra ran to the back and stood still. He held his spot. "My turn soon," he said. Elle smiled and patted the ground next to her.

Axel woke up with a big smile. "Park day!" he said. He ate his sandwich fast. It was cheese and it was yummy. Then he ran to get dressed. He pulled on his shirt all by himself. He found his shiny red shoes. He pushed them onto his toes. But the shoes felt funny and bumpy inside. He tried to walk. He fell down on the soft rug. He laughed and laughed.

His feet were bumpy because of his toes, not socks! Axel pulled the shoes off. Then he found his blue socks. He wiggled them onto his feet. They were warm and soft. Now he pushed his shoes on again. This time they felt smooth and snug. He stamped his feet. Clomp, clomp!

"Ready!" said Axel. He ran to the door. His mom said, "Shoes on feet, socks first!" Axel giggled. "I did it!" he said. Then he zipped his jacket and ran outside.

Thomas sat at the dinner table. He had ten green peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

He pointed at each pea. "One, two, three," he said. Then he counted some more. "Four, five, six, seven." His friend Ananya sat next to him. She held up her milk cup.

"Eight, nine," said Thomas. He looked at the last pea. "Ten!" He was so proud. But then he wanted to write the number ten on his paper.

He wrote a big 1. He stopped. "Where is the ten part?" he asked. Ananya laughed, not in a mean way. "Ten is two numbers," she said. "A 1 and then a 0."

Thomas was afraid he would forget. So he looked at his plate. He pushed one pea away from the rest. Then he pushed another pea next to it. One pea, then a round pea alone. They looked like his numbers!

"That is my ten!" said Thomas. His dad smiled and gave him a marker. Thomas wrote 1, then 0. "Ten!" he shouted. Ananya clapped and Thomas ate the round pea last.

Ryan sat at the kitchen table. The toast was warm and golden. Mom had made it for him. Now Ryan wanted butter on it, all by himself.

He took the butter knife. He spread slow, soft strokes. The butter made little waves. "It looks like a pond," said Ryan. Mom laughed. "A butter pond," she said.

Next came the milk. Ryan held the cup in one hand. He poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk plopped onto the table. "Oh no," said Ryan.

Mom helped wipe it up. Then Ryan set the cup down on the table first. He poured again. The cup sat still. Not one drop spilled. The milk went right in.

Ryan drank it all up. "The cup likes to sit," he said. Mom smiled. "Just like you at snack time," she said. Ryan giggled and took a polite little sip, pinky up, like Jamieson's fancy dad in the car that one time.

Luka sat on the little red mat. He had a book about a big green truck. The pictures were so nice. Luka wanted to know who drew them.

"Mr. Oliveira, who made the truck?" he asked.

Mr. Oliveira sat down next to him. "Let's look," he said. He opened the front of the book. The front, not the back. "This page has names," he said. "See the words? Words tell us things." He pointed with one finger. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator. Here is the name."

Luka looked at the letters. He touched them with his sticky fingers. "Alma! Come see!" he called.

Alma came and sat close. "Who drew it?" she asked.

"The illustrator drew it," said Luka. He turned to the first page. "We start at the front. You wait, I will read."

He pointed at each word. The words told about the truck. Beep, beep!

Then Alma got her own book. "Look, my book has words too," she said.

Luka smiled and turned his page.

Sophia walked in the forest with her dad. The leaves were wet from the rain. She saw Charley by a big log. Charley was poking a stick in the mud. Sophia wanted to play with him. But she did not know how to start.

She stood by the log. She looked at Charley. Then she had an idea. "Let's pretend we are bears," she said. Charley jumped up. "Rawr! I am a big bear," he said. "Let's pretend this log is our bear house," said Sophia. Charley ran to get some leaves. He put them by the log. "The leaves are our bed," he said.

Sophia found a round stone. "This stone is our coin," she said. "Bears buy berries with coins." Charley laughed. "I will sell you berries," he said. He picked up three small red leaves. "One coin, please," said Charley. Sophia gave him the stone. Then she ate pretend berries. They were yum yum pretend berries.

After that, Sophia held a long stick. "Let's pretend this stick paints," she said. She drew a bear in the mud. Charley drew a bear too. Then he drew a little bear. "That is the baby," he said. Sophia patted the mud drawing. "Good night, baby bear," she said. "Rawr," said Charley, very softly.

Michael went to the store with his dad. Mr. Popal worked at the store. He had big boxes of apples.

Michael wanted a red apple. So did his friend Dania. They both reached for the apples. Mr. Popal held up his hand. "One at a time," he said. Dania went first. She picked a small apple. Then it was Michael's turn. He picked a big red one.

The apples felt rough in his hands. Michael helped sort them. He put red apples in one basket. He put green apples in another basket. A little worm poked out of one apple. "Look, Dad!" said Michael. Dad laughed. That apple went in the bad basket.

Mr. Popal gave Michael a sticker. Michael ran to the door with his dad. Then he stopped. He had not said anything to Mr. Popal. Michael ran back.

"Thank you for my sticker," said Michael.

Mr. Popal smiled. He reached into his pocket. He gave Michael one more sticker, a shiny gold one.

"Wow," said Michael. "Thank you again!"

Ivy sat on the bath mat. Her dad turned the taps. "Hot tap first," he said. "The hot tap is for grown-ups." Ivy watched the steam rise. The cold water made the bath warm. She put in her toy slide and her little frog.

"Time for breakfast after this," Dad said. The soap smelled like apples. Ivy smiled.

The frog wanted to slide. First he lay down head first. Bump! His head hit the water too hard. "Poor frog," said Ivy. She picked him up. She turned him around. Now his feet went first. Whee! He slid down and landed soft. "Feet first," said Ivy. She sent him again. Whee! Soft landing every time.

Dad was not far away. He stayed right by the bath. "One more slide," said Ivy, "then breakfast." She held the frog up high. "Feet first, little frog. Here you go!"

William sat at the dinner table. Daddy put three carrots on his plate. William wanted all the big carrots too. "More carrots," he said. "Ryker has some," said Daddy. "You have your own."

William grabbed the salt shaker. He shook it on his carrots. Then he shook it on Ryker's carrots. "Stop," said Ryker. "Too salty! My carrots taste bad now."

Ryker pushed his plate away. He did not eat. William looked at Ryker's plate. The carrots looked sick with salt, all white and bumpy.

William had an idea. He got a new carrot from the bowl. He put it on Ryker's plate. "Here," said William. "A new carrot."

Ryker smiled. He took a bite. "Good carrot," said Ryker. Then Ryker gave William a piece of bread. "Share," said Ryker.

Daddy clapped his hands. "Good sharing, boys." William ate his carrots, one by one. The salt shaker sat by the wall, far away from the food.

"More carrots tomorrow?" asked William. "Yes," said Daddy. "And Ryker can come too."

Brielle was at Grandma's house. It was night. Then all the lights went out. The whole room went dark. "Oh no," said Brielle. "I can't see anything at all!"

Grandma found a big candle. Grandpa lit it with a match. Then he set it on the table. "We will give the room a little glow," said Grandma. Grandpa got his tool box. "I will go look at the power box," he said. He went out with a flashlight.

Brielle sat very still. At first she could not see anything. She waited a little while. Then she saw one thing, the big sofa. Then two things, the sofa and a chair. Then three things, the sofa, the chair, and her pink teddy bear. "Grandma! My eyes can see now! The dark got softer!" "Yes," said Grandma. "Your eyes get used to it."

Brielle found Grandma's shawl on the chair. She carried it to Grandma. "Here, so you are not cold," she said. The lights came back on. Grandpa came in. "All fixed!" he said. Brielle hugged her teddy bear. "I could see you," she whispered. "One, two, three."

The wind blew hard outside. It howled at the windows. Then all the lights went out. The TV went dark too.

Harrison held his furry teddy bear tight. "The lights are gone," he said. His mom lit some candles. Dad put them on the table. The room glowed warm and soft.

"The wind was so strong it knocked out the power," Mom said. Harrison listened. He heard the wind again. Whoosh, whoosh. Then the lights in the hall blinked on. Then off again. The wind blew, and the power wobbled.

Harrison ran to the window. He waited. The wind stopped. The lights stayed on. "The wind stopped and the power came back," he said.

Dad opened the curtains a little. They all looked outside. The street lights were on now. The woman next door waved from her window. Harrison waved back. Then he gave his teddy bear a big goodnight squeeze. "Night night, bear," he said. "The wind is all done now."

Mason sat at the dinner table. He wore his striped pajamas. His cup sat by his plate. One spoon, two carrots, three peas. Mason counted them all.

Then he heard a noise. Thump, thump, thump. It came from under the table. Mason felt scared. His tummy felt tight. He did not want to look under the table alone.

"I am scared," Mason said. "Will you help me?"

Dad put down his fork. "I can help you," Dad said. He bent down low. He looked under the table. "Come and see," he said.

Mason peeked too. It was only the cat. The cat was batting a swing toy. Thump, thump, went the little ball.

"Oh," said Mason. Now he was happy. Dad picked up the cat. Dad sent the cat to her soft bed in the corner.

Mason ate his carrots. One, two, three bites. The house was quiet again.

"Night, night, cat," said Mason.

Everett sat on his bed. He lifted one foot, then the other foot, into his pajamas. It was bedtime, but he had a big question.

"Is today the library day?" he asked Mom.

Mom smiled. "No, that was yesterday. We went to the library yesterday."

Everett thought and thought. Yesterday he had picked three books. One, two, three books. Yesterday was all done.

"When is the library day again?" he asked.

"That is tomorrow," said Mom. "We will go tomorrow."

"Is tomorrow now?" asked Everett.

"No," said Mom. "Today is the day that is happening right now. Now it is bedtime."

Everett looked at his window. Now the sky was dark. Now the moon was out. Today was still here, but it was almost done.

"Can I read one book now?" he asked.

Mom shook her head. "Not now. Later, tomorrow, you can read at the library."

Everett lay down. He pulled his blanket up. He thought of yesterday, today, and tomorrow. Yesterday was done. Tomorrow would come. Today was right now, and right now was sleepy time.

"Tommow, library," he whispered.

"Yes, tomorrow," said Mom. She kissed his head.

Everett closed his eyes. One, two, three little snores.

Arnaud sat at the big kitchen table. He had a small box of toy cars. "This is a treasure chest," he said. His baby sister crawled over. She grabbed a car. She took it out of the box. Arnaud put it back in. She took it out again.

"She keeps taking them out!" said Arnaud. His dad laughed. "In and out are opposites," said Dad. "You put them in. She takes them out."

Then Arnaud had a big idea. He held the box up high. The box was far from his sister's hands. He dropped a car in. Then he dropped another in. His sister clapped. She wanted the fast cars, but they were up too high. "Too slow, baby," said Arnaud. He spun one car on the cold table. It went fast, then it stopped. His sister grabbed that one. "You win," said Arnaud.

Alexis sat at the dinner table. His bowl was full of warm soup. He blew on it, and a carrot began to float. "Look, it floats!" he said. His tummy felt happy.

Then Alexis heard a sound. His little sister was crying. Big tears ran down her eye and down her cheek. Mom said, "She is sad. She dropped her spoon." Alexis knew about sad. When he felt sad, he cried too. So his sister must feel sad.

Alexis picked up her spoon. He put it back on the table. Then he gave her his soft bunny. She grabbed it and hugged it tight. Her tears stopped. She smiled a big, wet smile. Alexis smiled too. "She is not sad now," he said. Mom clapped her hands. "Good job, Alexis." Alexis ate his soup, and the carrot still floated.

Joseph sat at home in his big chair. "Today we go to the doctor," said Mom. "You will get a little shot." Joseph wondered, what is a shot like?

At the doctor's office, Joseph sat up tall. The nurse cleaned his arm with a cool, wet wipe. Then came a tiny bump of a pinch. It was over fast. "All done," said the nurse.

Then Joseph saw a red box on the wall. It had a closed lid. "What is that?" he asked. "A special hard box," said the nurse. She dropped the used needle inside. It made a small sound, like click. "So nobody gets poked," she said.

Joseph peeked at the box again. So that is where old needles go. On the way out, he waved. "Bye, box," he said. "Bye, needle."

Brielle was at daycare. It was lunch time. The children stood in a line.

Erik stood right in front of her. He was big like a wall. Brielle wanted to get to the fruit bowl. She tried to squeeze past him. He did not move.

Brielle looked around. What could she do? Ms. Wanjiru was pouring the milk. Brielle walked over to her.

"Ms. Wanjiru, Erik is in my way," said Brielle.

"Try saying excuse me," said Ms. Wanjiru. "That is a polite way to get past someone."

Brielle walked back to Erik. She tapped her chin. Would it work? She took a little breath.

"Excuse me, Erik," said Brielle.

Erik turned around. Then he stepped aside. "Oh! Sorry, Brielle," he said. "I did not see you."

Brielle walked past him. She got an apple from the fruit bowl. It was red and shiny.

Lilya was stuck too. A big chair blocked her way. "Help," said Lilya.

"Try it," said Brielle. She pointed at the chair.

"Excuse me, chair!" said Lilya.

Brielle laughed. That was funny. Then Erik moved the chair for Lilya.

"Thank you, Erik," said Lilya.

They sat down together. Brielle bit into her apple. It crunched very loud. All three of them giggled.

At snack time, Brielle saw Ms. Wanjiru by the door. A parent stood in the way, holding a big box. Brielle waited.

"Excuse me," said Brielle.

The parent smiled and stepped aside. "What a polite girl," she said.

Brielle beamed. "You're welcome," she said, and ran off to dig in the sandbox.

Arthur sat at the dinner table. He could smell the soup with his nose. He could hear it bubble with his ears. He could see the steam go up with his eyes. He touched his cup with his fingers. The cup felt warm.

But Arthur did not want the soup. He put his hands over his eyes. Now he could not see the soup at all. "No soup," he said. "I can't see it."

Mom smiled. She took the bread basket and hid it behind her back. "Can you see the bread?" she asked.

Arthur peeked. No bread! He opened his eyes wide. There was the basket, hiding behind Mom. "When my eyes are closed, I can't see things!" he said.

He tried one little spoonful of soup. He tasted it with his tongue. It was warm and good. He took another bite. "Mom, this soup is pretty yummy. Can you help me get more?" he asked.

Mom filled his bowl. Arthur looked at his full bowl with his eyes. He ate it all up.

Romy stood at the school gate. Her bag had a star on it. Her tummy felt jumpy.

"Have a lucky first day," said Mom. She gave Romy a hug. Then the gate opened with a click.

Romy walked in. Kids ran everywhere. They laughed and played. But Romy did not know anyone. She stood still by the wall.

Then she saw a girl. The girl stood alone too. She looked at her shoes.

Romy took a big breath. She walked over.

"My name is Romy," she said. "What is your name?"

The girl looked up. "I am Alexandria," she said. "Want to play?"

"Yes!" said Romy. They held hands and ran to the slide.

The bell rang. Mr. Costa came to the door. "Line up, friends," he said.

Romy and Alexandria lined up together. Romy waved at Mom outside the gate. Mom gave a big wave back.

"See you after school," said Alexandria.

"Lucky day," said Romy. They walked in side by side.

Harper wanted to be a mommy today. But she felt too small. Her mom gave her a big blue coat. "Dress-up clothes help you pretend," Mom said. Harper put it on. Now she was Mommy Harper, big and tall!

Mommy Harper got to work. One spoon for Bunny. One spoon for Bear. "Time to eat," she said. Bunny had weak little arms, so Mommy Harper held him. "One more bite," she said. "Then we bake a cake." She patted air in a pan. Pat, pat, pat. The cake was pretend, but it smelled like rainbows.

Then the baby cried. "Waa, waa," said Mommy Harper for Bunny. She rocked him fast. She sang low. Bunny stopped crying. Mommy Harper smiled. She fixed Bear's hat too. Then she looked up at Mom and said, "Can I be a firefighter next?"

Ivy sat at the school table. Mr. Çilik put a bowl of ice cubes down. "We will use our five senses," he said.

Ivy peeked at the cubes with her eyes. They were shiny and white. She heard them clink in the bowl with her ears. She smelled them with her nose. They smelled like water, like nothing at all.

Then Ivy picked one up. She touched it with her fingers. "Ooh!" said Ivy. The ice cube felt so cold. She dropped it into her cup fast.

Bo tried it too. "Cold, cold, cold!" said Bo. He dropped his cube in too.

"What is in the cup now?" asked Khadija.

Ivy took a little sip with her tongue. "Cold water!" she said. "Ice makes it cold."

Ivy picked up one more cube. She was not alone at the table. All her friends held the ice, then let it go. "So cold, so fast!" they said, and laughed together.

Ayla went to the store with her dad. She held a small basket. Her job was to find three things: an apple, bread, and a carrot.

In the toy aisle, Ayla saw Charly from her class. "Look at this soft bunny," said Charly. He put a toy carrot in his basket. Ayla had a real carrot. Where should it go? She looked at the bunny. The bunny was a toy. The carrot was not a toy. Could she eat a toy? No. "Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," Charly said, pointing to the food sign. Ayla carried her carrot to the food aisle. She put the apple there too. Then the bread.

"What else is a food?" Ayla wondered. She looked at the shelves. Bananas! Milk! She filled her basket. Dad helped her wash the apple at home. Then Ayla ate it under her warm blanket, and she smiled. "Apple," she said, "you are a food."

Wren ran to the reading corner. Today she would get her very first library card! Mr. Szabó smiled and handed it to her. "Now you can borrow a book," he said.

Wren picked a big red book about trucks. She sat down with her friend Isabel. Isabel had a marker. Isabel began to draw on the truck page!

"No, wait!" said Wren. "This book is shared. Lots of kids read it. If we write in it, the pages get messy."

Isabel stopped her marker. "So many people share this one book?"

"Yes," said Wren. "So we take care of it. No tearing. No writing. Let's get paper instead."

Mr. Szabó gave them a plate of paper and some crayons. Isabel drew a big blue truck. Wren drew a good, tall tower.

Then Wren held out her card. Mr. Szabó stamped the book. Wren hugged it tight.

"My first borrowed book!" she said. Isabel clapped. "Good job, Wren!"

Theodore ran down the cereal aisle. "We need eggs!" he said. Mom put the carton in the cart. Theodore held it all the way to the car. "Tonight I cook," he said.

At home, Theodore set out a big bowl. He wanted to make eggs for the whole family. He picked up an egg. It had a thin shell all around it. He tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap. Crack! The shell broke open. The egg slid out into the bowl.

"Yay!" said Theodore. He cracked another one. But this time, a tiny bit of shell fell in too. "Oh no," said Theodore. Then he had an idea. He grabbed a fork. He dipped it in. The shell bit stuck to the fork. He lifted it out. "Got it!"

Mom cooked the eggs in the pan. Theodore watched from his chair. Soon the family sat down to eat. Taha and Raina had come over to share.

Theodore took a bite. "The egg came out of the shell," he said. "And now it is on my fork!"

Wesley was at home with Dad. It was raining. "I miss the park," said Wesley. He felt sad.

Then the lights went out. Wesley felt scared. He held Dad's hand. Dad lit a candle with a match. Wesley stayed back, far away, and watched.

Dad sat down by the candle. His face looked worried. "Are you scared too?" asked Wesley. "Yes, I was," said Dad. "You feel scared? You are big!" "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups," said Dad. Wesley thought about that. He looked at Dad's face. He saw Dad take a big breath, in and out. So Wesley took a big breath too.

The cat came in. Her tail was up. She was not scared at all. Soon she was asleep by the warm candle. Wesley felt calm now. He and Dad made shadows on the wall with their hands. Wesley laughed. He felt happy again.

Then the lights came back on. "Hooray!" said Wesley. He felt so excited. Dad gave him a big hug. "Night night, rain," said Wesley. He waved at the window.

Sofia had a tiny new kitten. His name was Milo. He was soft and gray.

Sofia put his bed on the floor. She put out his water bowl. But Milo ran under her bed. He stayed there. Sofia could only see two bright eyes.

She sat down on the rug. She sat very still. Her mom brought a little snack for Milo. Sofia set it near the bed. She waited. She could hear the clock tick, tick.

Milo sniffed the air. One small paw came out. Then his whole body came out. He ate the snack. His rough tongue licked Sofia's finger. Then he gave a hop and pounced on her sock.

"He likes my house," Sofia whispered. Milo curled up in her lap and purred.

Maeve sat at the big table. The day was cloudy outside the window. She wanted to make a toy car. Dad gave her a small box and some cardboard. "I can cut the wheels," said Dad. "You tell me the shape." Maeve held up a square. "These," she said. Dad cut four square wheels. They taped them on. Maeve pushed the car across the floor. The car bumped and stopped. It would not roll. "Why won't it go?" she asked. She looked at the squares. Then she looked at her ball. The ball was round. It rolled under the chair. "Round wheels," said Maeve. "Like circles!" Dad cut four circles. They taped them on. Maeve pushed the car again. It rolled all the way to the door. A little wind of air came from the window. Maeve brushed the dust off her car. She pushed it again. "Round circles roll!" said Maeve. The car rolled past her feet and bumped the wall.

Charlie wanted to make her own breakfast. Dad made the toast, because the toaster was hot. Then Dad put the warm toast on Charlie's plate.

Charlie held the butter knife. She spread the butter, slow and slow. A little pat of butter sat on top. Then Charlie watched. The butter got shiny. The butter got soft. The butter melted away into the warm toast.

"Where did it go?" said Charlie. "It disappeared!" She touched the toast with one finger. It tasted like butter. The butter was still there. It had just melted.

Next came the milk. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured, slow and slow. One drip ran down the side. Dad gave her a small cloth. Charlie wiped the drip up herself.

"I did it," said Charlie. "I did it all by myself." She took a big bite of toast. "Mmm," she said. "The butter is hiding in there." Dad smiled and poured milk for himself, slow and slow, just like Charlie.

Charlie sat at the table for dinner. Mom put a big bowl in the middle. "We can all share it," she said. Charlie looked at the bowl. He thought about school. At school, Ember had the blocks. Charlie had grabbed them. Ember looked sad. The teacher, Ms. Sultani, had brought them back to the rug.

"Ember took the blocks first," Charlie said. Mom nodded. "What did you do then?" she asked.

"Ms. Sultani helped us. We made one big tower. I put a block on. Then Ember put a block on. We played with one toy together."

"That sounds nice," said Mom.

After dinner, Charlie helped hang his coat on his hook. He got his bear from the shelf. "Ember can play with my bear tomorrow," he said. "We can build one big road together."

Mom smiled. "That sounds like a good dream," she said.

Charlie hugged the bear tight. "Two hands, one bear," he said.

Aria put two slices of soft white bread into the toaster. Her dad pushed the lever down. "Now we wait," he said. "We wait, we wait," sang Aria. Pop! The bread jumped up. But it was not white anymore. It was brown. It was crunchy. "What happened?" asked Aria. Dad said, "Toast." "Toast," said Aria. "The bread got hot and turned brown and crunchy." Now she wanted to spread the butter all by herself. She held the knife. Dad watched close by. The butter was too cold. It would not spread. So she pressed a little, then a lot. The warm toast made the butter go soft. One, two, three strokes. The butter covered the toast. Then she poured milk into her cup. "Slow, slow," she whispered. Not one drop spilled. "Look at my toast," said Aria. "Brown and crunchy, just like that." She took a big bite. Crunch. "Baby steps," said Dad with a smile. "You did it, one, two, three." Aria held up her cup. "Milk next time, no spills, no break, all by me."

Raphael stood by the wooden counter in the corner store. He wanted apples for his class picnic. Ms. Huang put out two baskets. "Can you count them?" she asked.

Raphael counted the red basket. "One, two, three, four, five." He counted the green basket. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." The wind rattled the door. "Which basket has more?" asked Ms. Huang.

"The green one!" Raphael shouted. But the red apples were his favorite. He took one red apple out of the basket. Then he counted again. "One, two, three, four. It went down to four!"

Emmanuelle ran in from the cold. "Can I have a red apple too?" she asked.

"Yes," said Raphael. He took one more out. "Now watch. One, two, three."

Emmanuelle clapped her hands. "You are so good at counting!"

Raphael smiled and put the apples in a bag.

Bennett ran to the bathroom. It was bath time. He wanted to jump right in.

The tub was full of water. Steam went up, up, up. Bennett put one toe near the water. "Ouch," he said. "Hot!"

His dad came in fast. "Wait, little one," said Dad. "A grown-up has to check the water first."

Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Bennett watched the steam go away. Dad put his hand in the water. He moved it slowly. Then he smiled. "Warm now. Not hot."

Bennett touched the water with his hand. It felt nice. He climbed in with Dad's help. His rubber duck floated by his knee. Bennett laughed. "Duck is warm too!"

He heard the water go swish, swish. He saw the soap slip and slide. Dad washed his little toes, one by one.

"Is the water warm or hot?" Dad asked, like a joke.

"Warm!" said Bennett. He hugged the duck. Then he made a big splash with both hands.

Miles stood at the big table. Ms. Hu had set out bowls. Today the class would make bread for the family night. Miles wanted to make the best loaf ever.

Ms. Hu gave him the bag of flour. "Pour it in the bowl," she said. Miles tipped the bag fast. Whoosh! A little cloud puffed up. The flour landed on his nose. It landed on Zayne's curly hair too. Amaya laughed and laughed. She had white spots on her cheeks.

"Look at us," said Miles. "We all look like snowmen." He looked at the flour bag. It was dry powder, soft and light in his hand. He poured some more, but this time he poured slowly. No cloud came up. The flour slid down quiet as a fish learning to swim.

"Now we can see," said Amaya. Ms. Hu helped them mix and knead. She put the loaves in the oven, because ovens are for grown-ups. Soon the bread smelled warm and good. Miles carried his loaf to the table for his family. "I made this," he said, with one white smudge still on his nose.

Nova held her old teddy bear. It was bedtime, but she wanted a story.

"Tell me about the park," she said. Dad sat on the bed.

"You went to the park tomorrow," said Nova.

Dad smiled. "No, that was yesterday," he said. "Yesterday is the day before today."

Nova thought. "So today is now?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Now, in your bed."

"We got ice cream at the store," said Nova. "The dog tried to lick it!"

"You counted ducks," said Dad. "One duck, two ducks, three ducks."

"Four ducks, five ducks!" said Nova. "Can we go to the park again?"

"That will be tomorrow," said Dad. "First we sleep, then we play."

Nova hugged her bear. She closed her eyes.

"Tomorrow," she whispered. "One sleep first."

Dad kissed her head and turned off the light.

Layla stood at the little table in cooking class. Ms. Bautista put warm toast in front of her. The bread was soft, and the butter was cool. Layla felt shy about the big knife. "This one is safe and dull," said Ms. Bautista. "Just spread, spread, spread." Layla spread the butter. One, two, three strokes. The white butter melted and sank into the warm toast.

Next came the milk. The big carton was tall and heavy. Layla lifted it with both hands. It wobbled. Milk dripped down the side and made a puddle. Faris brought a towel. "Oops," said Layla. Ms. Bautista poured some milk into a small jug. "Try this," she said. The small jug was light. Layla tipped it slowly. The milk went up, up, over the edge, and down into her cup. Not one drop spilled.

Layla took a bite of her toast. The butter tasted good on the soft bread. She poured more milk into Faris's cup, nice and slow. "You did it," said Faris. Margaret clapped her hands. Layla scratched an itch on her arm and smiled at her full, milky cup. "More toast, please," she said.

Alice sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint the sky. She found a blue paint pot and made a big blue stripe.

Arian held up a crayon. "This one is not blue," he said. "It looks too dark."

Daphnee shook her head. "It is blue," she said. "It is just dark blue."

Mr. Malik came over with a smile. "Let's line them up," he said. The three children lined up all the blues. Light blue went first. Then plain blue. Then dark blue. Then the navy crayon.

"Look," said Daphnee. "They are all still blue."

Alice picked up her brush. She painted a light blue sky at the top. Then she painted a dark blue sea at the bottom. She added a yellow sun and a red boat with a green flag.

"What a lucky boat," said Arian. "It sails on your dark blue sea."

Alice smiled and dipped her brush again. "My whole blue family," she said.

Harper sat on the blue rug at school. Ms. Augustin held up a picture of an eye. "Can you find your eyes?" she asked. Harper touched her eyes. Koa touched his eyes too. Camilla made a silly face with her eyes.

Then it was time to go outside. "What will we play?" Harper wondered. The weather was warm and sunny. Koa ran to the grass. He put his hands over his eyes. "You can't see me!" he said.

Harper covered her eyes too. It was all dark. She could not see Koa. She could not see the slide. She opened her hands. "I see you!" she said. "I see the slide and the sky!" Koa opened his eyes too. "We see with our eyes," he said.

A little ant began to crawl near Harper's shoe. Harper bent down low. She kept her eyes open wide. "I see the ant," she said. "Its legs go fast." Camilla came to look too. The three friends watched the ant crawl straight across the grass, all the way to the big tree.

Willow held her mom's hand at the pharmacy. Tomorrow she would go to the dentist. It was her very first time.

"I want to be brave," said Willow. "But I have a question." She looked at her turtle toy in her other hand. "How can the dentist see my back teeth? They hide behind my front teeth!"

At the pharmacy, Mom had to buy some things. Willow waited by the shelf. She saw a little mirror there. It was tiny. It had a long, thin handle. Willow picked it up and looked.

She held the little mirror near her mouth. She could see the backs of her teeth in it! "Mom, look!" said Willow. "The mirror sees behind my teeth!"

The next day, Willow sat in the big chair. The dentist smiled. He held up a tiny mirror on a handle. "This helps me see the backs of your teeth," he said. Willow giggled. She already knew!

Afterward, the dentist let Willow hold the little mirror. She looked at her teeth one more time. Then she hugged her turtle tight and said, "That was easy. Can we come back tomorrow?"

Zachary sat in the waiting room. His mom read a story to him. Zachary did not listen much. He was thinking about scissors.

"It will hurt," Zachary said. His mom said, "Wait and see."

Kyson was there too. He was in front of Zachary. Kyson climbed up into the big chair. The barber turned the chair, and Kyson got dizzy. The chair spun around and around.

Then the barber picked up the scissors. Snip, snip. Kyson sat very still. Zachary watched Kyson's face. Kyron was smiling. Zachary looked hard. No tears. No ouch.

"Did it hurt?" Zachary asked.

"Nope," said Kyson. "It feels like nothing at all."

Soon it was Zachary's turn. The chair spun. Zachary held tight. Snip, snip. The hair fell down. It landed on his cape like little soft bits of string.

Zachary looked in the mirror. "My turn is done already?"

The barber swept the floor clean. Zachary picked up a piece of his hair. He put it in his pocket.

"I will show Kyson," he said.

Nora ran into the big gym. The floor was smooth, not rough like the sidewalk. Her team was ready to play. Keon waved at her. Clayton waved too.

Nora did not know where to stand. She asked, "Where do I go?" Ms. Lewandowski said, "Stand by the tall net. I will show you." Ms. Lewandowski was the coach. She took Nora's hand and pointed. Then Nora stood in the right spot.

The game started. Nora hid her face behind her hands. The ball came fast. It went right past her. "Oh no," said Nora. Ms. Lewandowski blew her whistle. She showed Nora how to catch the ball with both arms. They tried it together. Nora tried again and again.

The ball came again. Nora caught it. Keon clapped. Clayton clapped. Nora ran to the coach. "Did you see me?" she asked. Ms. Lewandowski smiled. "I saw you," she said. Nora held the ball up high.

Sarah was at the park with her friend Emrick. They were riding their bikes on the straight path. The sun was warm. The grass smelled fresh and green.

Then Emrick's bike fell over. His water bottle rolled into the mud. Emrick stomped his feet. His face turned red. "I'm so angry!" he shouted. He kicked a stick. Sarah felt scared of his big loud voice.

Ms. Oliveira walked over slowly. She sat down on the bench. "Come sit with me," she said. Emrick sat down. She showed him how to take slow, deep breaths. In went the air, slow and long. Out it came, soft like wind. Emrick copied her. He breathed in. He breathed out. Sarah watched and copied too. The air felt cool in her nose.

After many breaths, Emrick's face was not red anymore. His shoulders came down. "I feel calm now," he said. A dog began to bark far away. Emrick laughed. Sarah felt happy. They picked up the bottle and washed it at the fountain. Then they rode their bikes again, side by side, all the way to the swings.

Georgia went to the park with her dad. Her friend Hanna was there. Georgia wanted to throw the ball to Hanna. But first she wanted to know one thing.

"When do we go home?" Georgia asked.

"Later," said Dad. "Not now."

Georgia threw the ball. Hanna caught it. Then Hanna threw it back. The ball went too high. It did not fall on the ground. It fell into the bushes. Georgia ran to look. She saw a big bug. It was not scary. It was small and black.

"I want to go home now," said Hanna.

Dad held up his phone. There was a clock on it. "A clock shows what time it is," Dad said. "See the big hand? When it points up, we go home."

Georgia watched the clock. The hand moved a little bit. She threw the ball to Hanna again. She watched the clock some more.

Then the big hand pointed up. "It is time!" said Dad.

"Now we go home," said Georgia. She took Hanna's hand. They walked to the gate together. "We can come back tomorrow," said Georgia.

Elijah was at home. His tummy was hungry. His dad was making lunch. Elijah smelled warm soup.

The doorbell rang. It was Emmett. Emmett came to play. "Hello, Emmett," said Elijah. Dad put three cups on the table. He gave each boy a cup of milk. "Thank you," said Elijah. Emmett said thank you too.

Dad held out a bowl. It had green peas. "Would you like some peas?" Dad asked. Elijah made a face. "Yuck!" he shouted. Emmett looked down at his cup. His cheeks turned red. Dad waited. He patted Elijah's back. "Try again," Dad said kindly. Elijah took a breath. "No, thank you," he said. Dad smiled. "Okay. How about bread?" "Yes, please!" said Elijah.

Emmett pushed his chair in. "Can you help me open my bread?" he asked. Elijah helped him. Then Elijah patted Emmett's arm. "You are a kind friend," said Emmett. They ate their bread and drank their milk. "More milk, please," said Elijah. Dad poured. "Thank you, Dad!"

Kayden stood in the school cooking classroom. His class was making cookies today. The cookies were for his family. That made them special cookies.

Mr. Watanabe gave Kayden a bowl. Kayden poured in the sugar. He cracked two eggs with a fork. Then he used the fork to mix. Rohan poured in the flour next. Jane added the chocolate chips. Kayden used a big spoon to fold it all in. He went slow. He folded again and again. Soon the dough looked just right.

Mr. Watanabe rolled the dough into balls. He lined them up on a tray. Then he carried the tray to the big oven. He turned the hot oven all by himself. Kayden watched from far away. The oven was hot, so a grown-up was in charge.

The cookies baked and baked. Kayden wanted to peek inside. He walked toward the oven. Mr. Watanabe held up his hand. "The oven is hot," he said. "Only I open it." So Kayden waited. He looked at the timer. He waited some more. Waiting felt long.

At last the timer beeped. Mr. Watanabe opened the oven door. He pulled out the tray. Golden cookies, warm and round! Kayden clapped his hands. He put six cookies in a little box, one for each person in his family. He held the box all the way home. At dinner, everyone took a bite. "Yum," said Dad. Kayden smiled big.

Claire dug a little hole in the backyard. She dropped in a fat seed. "Grow, little seed," she said. She gave it water from her blue watering can. The can looked like a tiny boat with a spout.

The next morning, Claire ran outside. She saw only dirt. "Hey! Where is my plant?" she said. Her friend Zakaria laughed. "Maybe the seed is still sleeping." "Seeds can't sleep," said Claire. But she gave it more water anyway.

Every day she asked her dad, "Is it up yet?" Every day he said, "Not yet." So she kept watering. The dirt got dark, almost black, and wet.

On the seventh morning, Claire saw something green. A tiny sprout! "Zakaria! Come see!" she shouted. "It was sleeping," said Zakaria. Claire grinned and patted the dirt. "Good morning, sprout," she said. "I brought you more water."

Jordan sat in a big chair at the health clinic. He held his teddy bear tight. The nurse said, "Time for your shot."

Jordan felt scared. He squeezed his teddy. The nurse said, "You can look at the wall. Take a deep breath." Jordan took a deep breath. The nurse gave him the shot. It was quick. It hurt just a little.

Then something good happened. The nurse put a small bandage over the spot. It was an orange bandage with stars on it. Jordan looked at his arm. "Stars!" he said. The nurse smiled and said, "The bandage helps protect the spot."

After the shot, Mom took Jordan on the bus. They rode to the ice cream shop. Yassine was there with his dad. Jordan rolled up his sleeve. "Look at my bandage," he said. "It has orange stars." Yassine leaned in close. "Cool," said Yassine. "My shot next week." Jordan held his arm up high and took a big bite of his ice cream.

Leo went to the farm with his class. Anika and Blaire came too. Ms. Jung said, "We will find our five senses today."

First Leo touched a sheep. Its wool was soft. "We touch with our hands," he said. Then he heard a cow. "Moo!" went the cow. "We hear with our ears," said Blaire. Then Leo saw a red barn. It was a big shape like a box. "We see with our eyes," said Anika.

Then Ms. Jung held up a lemon slice. Leo put it on his tongue. His face went tight. "Sour!" he said. Then she held up a strawberry. Leo tasted that too. It was sweet. "The strawberry is sweet and the lemon is sour," said Leo. "My tongue knows both!" He stuck out his tongue and looked at it.

On the way home, Leo sniffed the air. "I smell hay with my nose," he said. Anika laughed and sniffed too. "I smell it too," she said. Leo counted on his fingers. Eyes, ears, nose, hands, tongue. "Five senses," said Leo. "All mine."

Colton went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big red book about trucks. It sat up on a high shelf. Colton reached and reached. His hand was too small.

Colton felt a big frown in his heart. He almost pushed a stool over to climb. "Stop, that is not safe," his dad said. He shut the tall step stool away.

Mr. Reyes walked by with a cart of books. Colton remembered something. He stood up tall. "Can you help me, please?" he asked.

Mr. Reyes smiled a warm smile. "Yes, I can help you." He reached up with his long arm. He got the red truck book down.

"Thank you," said Colton. He hugged the book to his chest.

"You are welcome," said Mr. Reyes. "I like that book too."

Colton sat at the little table. His dad helped him open the pages. The trucks were big and red and one looked hot like a fire truck.

On the way out, Colton bumped the book drop with his elbow. A book fell. "Sorry," said Colton. He picked it up and put it back.

His dad held his hand. "Good asking today," he said. Colton looked up at the big shelves. "Can we come back tomorrow, please?"

Andrew was at Grandma's house. Grandma had big paper and paint. She put out red paint and yellow paint.

"I want to paint a sun," said Andrew.

He dipped his brush in the yellow. He made a big circle. Then he wanted orange. But where was orange? There was no orange cup.

Andrew put his brush in the red. Then he put it back in the yellow. He stirred. The yellow turned orange!

"Look, Grandma! Yellow and red made orange!" he said.

Then Andrew touched his sun. Oh no. His finger went right in the paint. The wet paint smudged. Now there was a fingerprint on his sun.

"The paint is still wet," said Grandma. "It can smudge if you touch it."

Andrew made a new sun. This time he did not touch it. He stepped back and looked. He waited and waited. He looked at his hands. He looked at the clock.

Then the paint was dry. Andrew tapped it with one finger. Nothing smudged. The sun was still a big round orange sun.

"Time for dinner," said Grandma.

Andrew carried his cool painting to the table. He set it down by his chair.

"Grandma, tomorrow can red and blue make something too?" he asked.

Grandma smiled. "We can find out," she said.

Jacob was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose ran and his voice was small. Grandma said, "You need rest. Rest helps your body get better."

But Jacob wanted to play outside. He saw the big red ball. He wanted to kick it. He ran to the door. Grandma caught his hand. "Not yet, Jacob. Come and rest."

Grandma tucked him on the couch. She gave him his bear. She gave him a warm cup of water. "One blanket, two pillows, one bear," she said. Jacob counted too. "One, two, one."

Jacob rested. He smelled the soup Grandma made. He hugged his bear. He closed his eyes.

Jacob woke up and rested more. "One blanket, two pillows, one bear."

Later, Jacob sat up. His nose did not run. His voice was big again. He jumped off the couch and ran to the door. He kicked the red ball high, high, high.

Grandma clapped. "Rest did its job," she said.

"Again!" shouted Jacob.

Margot stood on her step in the bathroom. She wanted to wash her face all by herself. The soap was a pink square. It smelled like flowers. She sniffed it with her nose.

Her dad was close by. "Your nose has two openings," he said. "They are called nostrils." Margot felt shy about the big word. Then she looked in the mirror. She leaned in close. She saw her nose. She counted the openings. One, two. Two nostrils! She touched one nostril with her finger. It was soft and small.

She turned on the tap. The water made a splashing sound. Her ears heard it. The water felt warm and wet on her hands. She rubbed the soap on her cheeks. It tickled. She stuck out her tongue at the mirror. The soap tasted yucky! "No tasting soap," said Dad, and he gave her a fluffy towel. Margot planted a big kiss on her own reflection in the mirror.

Brielle ran to the picnic table. Her dad was making pancakes at the campsite. "Can I stir?" she asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "But first, cooks wash their hands." He pointed to the water jug and the soap. Brielle looked at her hands. They had dirt on them. She had been digging near the tent.

Brielle poured water on her hands. She rubbed the soap until it made white bubbles. The bubbles felt soft and tickly. She rinsed them off in the bowl. Now her hands were clean and shiny.
