Then Dad gave her the big spoon. She stirred the batter. Round and round it went. It went plop, plop, plop. A drop fell on the table. Brielle laughed.

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot grill. Brielle stood back and watched. She was a little shy about the flames. But Dad held her hand, and she felt safe.

Then came the surprise. Dad flipped a pancake high in the air. It landed right back in the pan! "Do it again!" said Brielle. Dad smiled and said, "After we eat these."

Sofia wanted to play the drum. She got it for her birthday. It was big and red. Her cat liked it too.

Evie came over to play. Evie had two sticks. "Let's play together," said Evie. They hit the drum. Bang, bang, bang! Sofia went fast. Evie went slow. It sounded like a big mess. The cat ran under the sofa like a shy little snake.

Sofia stopped. "We need to be the same," she said. "Let's tap our feet first." Evie nodded. They tapped their feet. Tap, tap, tap. One, two, one, two. Then they played the drum at the same speed. The sound was smooth and friendly. It made a real song!

Sofia's dad clapped from the kitchen. Even the cat came back out. "More drum," said Sofia. "Okay," said Evie. Tap, tap, tap. One, two. Bang!

Mila went to the library on a sunny day. She saw a basket of toy monkeys. Each monkey had a long tail. Mila wanted to sing the monkey song.

She asked Mr. Zhao for help. He sat down on the rug. Sacha and Kacey came to sit too. "Let's sing," said Mila. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

Sacha lined up the monkeys. One, two, three, four, five. Then Mila sang the next part. "One fell off and bumped his head!" Kacey took one monkey away. Now there were four.

They sang again. One more monkey fell off. Mila took it away. Now there were three. Mila counted them. Three monkeys, then two. Then one. Then none.

Mila showed her empty hands. "All done!" she said. "The monkeys went one by one," said Sacha. Mr. Zhao smiled. "Sing it again?" he asked.

Mila put all five monkeys back in a row. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" she sang. One monkey fell off, and Mila laughed.

Kai sat at his little table in the backyard. He had red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. He wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green paint in his box.

"What will I do?" Kai said. He looked at the yellow pot. He looked at the blue pot. Maybe he could try something. He put a big yellow dot on his paper. He patted the brush into the blue pot too.

Kai stirred the paints round and round. The spot turned green! Bright, shiny green. Kai laughed out loud. He painted bumpy grass all along the bottom. Then he painted a little boat on blue water above it. "Green!" said Kai, and he held the paper up to the sun.

Hunter stood in the garage. Dad's old guitar leaned by the wall. Hunter wanted to play it for Vardaan.

Hunter plucked the strings. The notes sounded funny. Boing, wobble, squonk. Vardaan laughed and held his ears. "It sounds like a duck!" he said. Hunter plucked again. Funny again. Hunter thought hard.

Ms. Santoso came from next door. She held her striped bag. "Can you fix it?" Hunter asked. "Strings need tuning," she said. She turned the little pegs. Turn, turn, turn. Then she plucked one string.

The note came out clean and sweet. Vardaan clapped. Hunter plucked the string himself. Sweet again. He plucked the next one. Sweet too. Hunter strummed all the strings. It sounded like a song at last. "Duck is gone!" said Vardaan. Hunter played and played, and Ms. Santoso tapped her foot.

Lena was at Grandma's house. She wanted to draw a letter for Grandma. It would say "I love you." But her crayons were still in the car. "Where are my crayons?" Lena asked. Grandma took her hand. They went out to the car.

Lena opened the crayon box. "Oh no!" she said. The crayons were soft. They were bendy too. One red crayon drooped like a noodle. "Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day," said Grandma. Lena looked up at the big sun. So the hot car made her crayons go soft!

"But I need red," said Lena. Then she had an idea. She pressed the soft red crayon onto the paper. It made a fat, shiny red mark. Lena pressed green. She pressed yellow. "Look, Grandma! Fat colors!" Grandma clapped. Lena drew a big heart with the soft crayons. Then she drew a letter A. Her letter was ready at last. "Can we mail it, Grandma? Can we, can we?" "Yes," said Grandma. "And after, we will grow a flower and eat a yummy snack." Lena hugged the paper to her chest. "I made a letter with melty crayons!"

Hailey stood at the paint table at the art gallery. There was red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. Mr. Otieno smiled. "You can mix two colours," he said. Hailey dipped her brush in the blue. Then she dipped it in the yellow. She stirred and stirred. The paint turned green! "Cool!" said Charles-Edouard. He painted a green snake on his paper. Hailey wanted more blue. She looked in her pot. All her blue was gone. It had all gone into the green. She poked at it with her brush. The blue would not come back out. It was stuck in the green. "Oh no," said Hailey. Next time she put a little blue in a cup first. Then she mixed the rest with yellow. "More green snake!" said Gabriel. Hailey laughed and painted one too.

Natala woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said Dad. "Snow day!" Natalie jumped. She wanted to play at the park.

Dad wrapped her in her red blanket. Then he said, "Let's get your boots on." At the park, the ground was hard ice. Natalie ran out on it. Whoosh! Her feet slid and she sat down fast. "Ouch," she said. It did not hurt much, but it was a surprise.

Her friend Inayah was there too. Inayah took tiny steps. Step, step, step. She walked so slow, like a little penguin. Natalie tried it too. Small steps. Slow steps. Her feet did not slide at all! "You did it," said Inayah. Natalie smiled a big, proud smile. "Ice is slippery, so we walk slow," said Natalie. She and Inayah walked all around the icy park, step by step, holding Dad's hand.

John went to the park with his toy dragon. He held it up high. "Roar!" he said.

Sara ran over. She had a toy bunny. "Let's play house," she said. "The bunny is the baby." John shook his head. "The dragon is scary. He roars loud." Sara hugged her bunny. "The baby will cry." John looked at the bunny. He thought hard.

"Okay," said John. "The dragon is not scary. He is friendly." Sara smiled. "Yes! He helps the baby." John made the dragon kiss the bunny. Sara gave the dragon a cup. "The dragon is thirsty," she said. "His cup is empty." John tipped the cup. "Now it is full," he said. "We made tea."

They played until the sun went down. "Same dragon, same bunny, tomorrow?" asked Sara. "Yes," said John. "Friendly dragon. Big roar for happy."

Clara wanted her new book. It was on the high shelf. "Can I have it?" she asked. Her mom reached up with a stick and tipped it down.

Clara sat on the rug. She opened the book. The cat was on the first page. She turned the pages one by one. The cat kicked a ball. Then the cat found a fish. The end page was at the back.

"Now we will write your name," said Mom. She took a card and a pen. She wrote C-l-a-r-a on the front. Clara looked at the letters. Then Mom wrote Clara's name on her drawing too. Clara put the card next to the drawing. She looked and looked. The letters were the same. They went the same way, in the same order.

"It is still me," said Clara. She held the card up high. Mom put the card on the fridge with a magnet. Clara kicked off her shoes and sat down to read her book again, from the front.

Quinn ran into her classroom at school. It was cake day for their friend Nia! Ms. Mendoza held up a big pink cake.

"Who wants to sing?" said Ms. Mendoza. "Me, me, me!" said Quinn. All the friends sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Quinn clapped at the end.

Then Selene asked Nia a question. "How old are you today?" Nia held up her fingers. She showed four fingers, and she said, "I am four!" Quinn's eyes went wide. A number word for your age!

Quinn jumped up and down. "Ms. Mendoza, ask me! Ask me!" Ms. Mendoza smiled. "Quinn, how old are you?" Quinn held up four fingers, just like Nia. "I am four!" she said. "I am four, I am four!" Selene laughed and clapped.

"Time for tasty cake," said Ms. Mendoza. She cut the cake with a safe knife, far from the little hands. She gave each friend one piece. Quinn counted the pieces on the table. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Ten friends, ten pieces! Just right.

Quinn took a big bite. "Best cake day ever," she said. Then she held up four sticky fingers. "I am four!"

Zachary ran to the door. He wanted to go to the playground. It was a sunny day. The sun made the slide shine.

"Wait," said his dad. "Sunscreen first." He rubbed white cream on Zachary's arms. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Zachary touched his arm. The cream felt soft and smelled like coconut. Then they went out.

At the playground, Zachary saw Anaelle. Anaelle was wearing a big red hat. "It is sunny," she said. "My hat keeps the sun off my face." Zachary patted his own sun-creamed arms. He could play a long time and not get red skin.

One lazy cloud sat high in the sky. Zachary counted things. One sunny sun. One big cloud. Two friends. Three swings. The wind blew a little. It flapped Anaelle's hat like a bird. Zachary held the hat for her. "Thank you," she said.

Then the wind blew harder. Dark clouds came. Drip, drip, drop. Rain fell on the slide. Rain fell on Zachary's head. "Rainy day!" said Anaelle. Her mom opened a big umbrella. Zachary sat under it with Anaelle. They listened to the rain go tap, tap, tap.

Zachary counted again. One umbrella. Two friends. Lots of raindrops. The sun hid behind the cloud. But Zachary was dry and cozy. "See you next time," said Anaelle. Zachary waved his hand. "Bye, rain," he said.

Elizabeth was at school. She saw a big red truck on the rug. Clovis was playing with it. He made it drive over a small hill of blocks.

Elizabeth wanted the truck. She grabbed it fast. Clovis yelled, "Hey! That is mine!" His lip went down and his eyes got big. He sat with his arms crossed.

Elizabeth looked at his sad face. She gave the truck back. Then she said, "Can I have a turn, please?" Clovis smiled. He said, "Yes, after two more drives." He pushed the truck over the hill twice. Then he put it in her hands.

Elizabeth made the truck go fast. Gunner came over and said, "Can I have a turn too?" Elizabeth nodded. "Yes, after my turn," she said. Ms. Lim watched from the doll corner and gave them a good smile. The truck drove all around the rug, one kid at a time.

Xavier had a toy rabbit. He took it everywhere. One night he sat at the kitchen table. He held his rabbit close. "I want to stay up late," he said. His dad said it was time for bed. Xavier said no. He wanted to watch the big clock. His dad let him sit a little longer. Xavier stayed up and up. His eyes felt heavy. At last his dad picked him up and carried him to bed.

The next morning, Xavier came to the kitchen. Gael was at the door. "Come and play," said Gael. Xavier sat down. His spoon was slow. His toast sat untouched. He yawned and yawned. He could not run. He could not jump. He felt upset. "I stayed up too late," he said. Gael was sad too. They had wanted to play all morning.

That night, Xavier ate his supper in the kitchen. He had a bath. He put on his pajamas. He brushed his teeth. Then he looked at his dad. "Bedtime now," he said. His dad smiled. Xavier hugged his rabbit and went to sleep. He slept all night.

The next morning, Xavier jumped out of bed. He ran to the kitchen. His legs felt strong. His eyes felt happy. "Come on, Gael!" he called. They ran and jumped in the yard. "I slept all night," said Xavier. "Now I can play all day!"

Gianna sat on the rug at Giuliana's house. A big red hammer toy sat in front of her. It had balls to pound. Bang, bang, bang, went the balls.

Dev came to the rug too. He reached for the hammer. Gianna held it tight. She turned her back to him. Dev sat down with no toy. His hands were empty. His face looked sad.

Gianna looked at the hammer. Then she looked at Dev. She slid the hammer across the rug. "Your turn," she said. Dev smiled big. Bang, bang, went the balls. Dev laughed out loud.

Gianna waited with her hands in her lap. The balls went up and down. She watched them pop. Then Dev slid the hammer back. "Your turn now," he said. Gianna took it and hit one ball. The bell inside went ring, ring.

They passed the hammer back and forth all afternoon. Nobody grabbed. Nobody felt bad. At the end, Giuliana's mom called them for juice. Gianna and Dev ran to the table together. "That was fun," said Dev. "Again tomorrow?"

Olivier was at Grandma's house. He had a little red car. Now the car was gone. "Oh no," said Olivier. He looked under the table. He looked in his shoe. No car.

Grandpa sat in his big chair. "Where did you go today?" he asked. Olivier thought. "I went to the garden. Then I watched the birds. Then I had a snack." Grandpa smiled. "Then we retrace your steps. We go back to each place, in order."

So Olivier walked to the garden first. He bent his neck down low. He looked by the flowers. No car. Then he walked to the window where he had watched the birds. He looked by the big plant. No car. Then he walked to the kitchen. He looked at his snack chair.

There it was! The red car sat on the chair, waiting. "Grandpa, I found it!" Olivier ran to show him. Grandpa laughed. "My beautiful red car," said Olivier. He held it up to the light. "Home again, little car."

Michael was at home. He had a little toy car in his hand. The car was not broken. It went zoom on the floor.

"Big day," said Mom. "We will get your first library card." Michael wondered, what is a library card? He put on his shoes. He took one step out the door. Mom held his hand. They walked to the library.

At the desk, a lady gave Michael a card. It had his name on it. Michael picked a book about a big red truck. He hugged it tight. "Can I keep it forever?" he asked. The lady shook her head. "This book goes back on the due date," she said. "Borrowed books have to come back by that day. Then other kids can read them too." Michael looked at the truck book. Maybe Maisy would like it too.

At home, Michael read the book three times. He turned every page. When the due date came, Mom helped him pack it in his bag. Back at the library, Michael slid the book across the desk. Then he looked at all the shelves.

"Can we take a new one home?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Pick one out."

Michael ran to the truck shelf. "This one!"

Victor went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm. Victor saw a big bug on a leaf. "Hello, bug," he said.

Near the trees, a man was cooking on a grill. Mr. Toussaint said hello too. Victor could hear the food sizzle. It made a hiss, hiss, hiss sound. The grill did not look hot at all. Victor wondered, was it hot? Was it cold? He wanted to touch it.

Dad saw Victor step close. Dad held his hand. "Only grown-ups touch the grill," Dad said. Then Mr. Toussaint held his hand near the top. He pulled it back fast. "Hot," he said. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot." Victor nodded. He took one big step back.

Later, Victor watched ducks bathe in the pond. He saw ants walk in one straight line. They went around a stick. The stick was big to them. Victor followed the line with his eyes, all the way home.

Eliana sat at the paint table. Ms. Aydın put out red, yellow, and blue. "Red like my boots," said Eliana. "Blue like the sky," said Talia. Eliana wanted to make a big green leaf for the class tree. She mixed blue and yellow right on her paper. It turned into a wet, muddy blob. The paper got a hole. Eliana felt like she might cry.

Then Ms. Aydïn held up a flat little tray. "This is called a palette," she said. "It is a tray for holding paint." Eliana put dots of paint on the wide, flat tray. She dipped her brush and made yellow. She dipped again and made blue. She mixed the two colours on the palette first. Green! Bright, leafy green.

Eliana looked at the green blob of paint. She tapped her brush and one small drop did fall, right onto her paper. Now she had a green leaf, not a hole. Talia clapped. Kinley made orange on her own palette. Ms. Aydïn hung the leaf on the class tree, way up high. "Look what I made," said Eliana.

Arnaud put on his swim shorts. He was going to the pool with Nael. "Swim day!" said Nael. "Swim day!" said Arnaud.

At the pool, Arnaud saw water on the floor. Lots of water. One splash, two splashes, three splashes. Nael started to run. Ms. Wu called out, "Walk, please! The floor is wet. Wet floors are slippery." Nael stopped running. He walked slowly to the pool.

Arnaud wanted to run too. He wanted to jump in fast. But he remembered the wet floor. He walked, one step, two steps, three steps. His feet stayed under him. He did not slip.

"My turn to buy you a juice after," said Nael. "You walked so carefully." Arnaud smiled. The pool water went up to his mouth when he jumped in. The wall by the steps felt rough on his hands.

"Kick," said Ms. Wu. Arnaud kicked. He splashed. He was swimming, one kick, two kicks, three kicks.

Mya was at Chaya's house. It was cold outside. Winter had come, and the snow was yucky and slushy. So the girls played inside.

Chaya had a big red bucket. She put blocks in it. Mya wanted the bucket. She reached out her hand to grab it. Then she stopped. She put her hands in her lap instead.

"Mya, you can have a turn," said Chaya. Chaya gave her the red bucket. Mya held it tight. "Thank you, Chaya," said Mya. Chaya smiled a big smile. She looked very happy.

Then Chaya took the blocks. She began to fold paper hats for the bears. Mya watched. She counted to herself, slowly. Then Chaya said, "Your turn again, Mya." Mya took the bucket and said, "Thank you!" again.

Chaya clapped her hands. "This is fun," she said. "You always say thank you to me." Mya hugged the red bucket and grinned.

Max ran to the toy corner at daycare. He wanted the little red truck. But Lilith had it first.

Max stopped and looked at Lilith. Her mouth was turned down. Her eyebrows made a sad line. "Are you sad?" Max asked. Lilith nodded. "I dropped my cracker," she said. "It fell in the sand."

Max thought hard. He got a napkin from the snack table. He put a new cracker on it. He carried it back slowly. Lilith saw the cracker. Her mouth turned up into a big smile. "Thank you, Max!" she said. Max felt happy inside, warm like the sun.

Then Nadine yelled from the wood bench. "My tower fell down!" Her face was red. Her hands were tight little fists. Max could see she felt angry. He picked up two blocks and handed them to her. "I help you build," he said. Nadine's fists opened. Her face went soft again.

Ms. Sultani clapped her hands for snack time. Max looked at Nadine's face again. Her eyes were wide. She was bouncing on her toes. "You look excited," said Max. Nadine laughed. "Snack time has apples!" Max sat down between his two friends. He took a big bite of his apple.

Everett stood by the little pool near the beach. The sun was warm on his toes. He looked at the blue water. He wanted to float, but he was scared.

Elina and Samuel were in the pool. "The teacher holds you," Elina said. Ms. Mercer smiled. "I will hold your back," she said. "You can float." Everett stepped in. The water was cool. He lay back slowly. Ms. Mercer's hands were under his back. He did not go down. He floated! He saw the big white clouds up above.

Ms. Mercer took one hand away. He still floated. Then she took the other hand away. He floated all by himself. He felt like a little boat. After the pool, he sat on a gray rock. His wet hair turned black in the sun. The sand was hot. "The sand can burn your feet," his dad said, and carried him to the towel. Everett looked back at the pool. "I floated," he told Samuel. "All by myself."

Rehmat waited by the gate at school pickup. She swung her lunch bag back and forth. Makai stood next to her, hopping on one foot.

"I need the toilet," said Makai. He ran inside. Rehmat waited and waited. Where was he?

Makai came back, smiling. But then Albert sniffed the air. "Something smells funny in here," he said. Rehmat peeked into the little bathroom. The toilet had not been flushed. Oh dear.

"Sorry," said Makai. "I forgot." Rehmat wondered what to do first. Makai pressed the silver handle. Whoosh! The water swirled away. Then he turned on the tap. He washed his hands with soap. Water dripped from his fingers.

"Now I need a towel," said Makai. Rehmat pointed to the little towel by the sink. Makai dried his hands, one finger at a time.

Mr. Traoré walked over. "Ready to go home?" he asked. Makai nodded. Rehmat took his hand. Outside, the sun was going down. Soon she would eat dinner, have a bath, and sleep in her cozy bed.

At the gate, Makai turned around. "Next time I will flush first," he said. "Then I will wash my hands." Rehmat smiled and waved goodbye.

Jackson stood at the basketball court. Mr. Van Dijk put a big hoop down low. "Throw the beanbag in," he said.

Jackson threw it. It hit the rim. It fell out. He threw it again. One miss, two misses, three misses. Forrest and Scout watched and waited.

Then the beanbag went in. "It went in!" said Jackson.

Next Mr. Van Dijk rolled a big ball to him. Scout caught a ball with one hand, like a big kid. Jackson tried one hand too. The ball bounced off and rolled away. He ran after it. He was thirsty, so he took a little sip from his water bottle.

Then Jackson put out both hands. "Ready," he said. The ball came. He held it with both hands. It stuck like glue.

"One ball, two hands," said Jackson. Mr. Van Dijk rolled it again. Both hands caught it again.

Joshua sat high up at the ice rink. His dad was next to him. His friend Fionn sat on his other side. Down below, two teams skated fast. One team wore purple socks.

The purple team skated and skated. They zoomed all around the ice. The other team skated less. They stood near their goal a lot.

"The purple team skated the most," said Joshua. "So they win, right?"

Fionn shook his head. "Let's look at the big board," he said.

Joshua looked up. The big board showed the score. The purple team had two points. The other team had four points.

"Four is more than two," said Joshua.

The whistle blew. The game was over. The team with four points got a big shiny cup. The purple team clapped for them.

Fionn waved at the players. Joshua waved too. One player waved back at them.

Joshua gave his dad a kiss on the cheek. "Next time I will look at the board first," he said.

"Good plan," said Fionn. "Skating a lot is still fun, though."

Joshua laughed. "Yes! But the points get the cup."

On the way out, the purple team walked past them. One player had a big box. He opened it. Inside were little purple stickers for every kid.

Joshua put one on his coat. "A surprise!" he said.

Avery sat in her bed. It was bedtime. Her tummy felt full of soup and bread. Avery looked out the window. The sky was dark. "Papa," she said, "can I have cookies tomorrow?" Papa shook his head. "Cookies are not for breakfast," he said. "What is breakfast?" asked Avery. "The first meal of the day," said Papa. "First?" said Avery. "The very first?" "Yes, the first," said Papa. "It comes after sleeping."

Avery lay down and thought. First she would sleep. Then the sun would come up. Then she would eat breakfast. She said it again and again. First I sleep, then breakfast. First I sleep, then breakfast. Her eyes got heavy. She waited for sleep, nice and slow.

In the morning, the sun peeked in. Avery ran to the kitchen. She helped put eggs and toast on her plate. She took one big bite. Then Papa opened the oven door with his big glove. "Surprise," he said. There were warm muffins, and one ugly, bumpy one that was all Avery's. Avery laughed and ate it up. "Breakfast is first," she said. "Muffins are second!"

Hudson went to the barbershop with his dad. It was his very first haircut. He sat in the big chair. The barber smiled and tried to cut. But Hudson was too small. The barber could not reach the top of his head.

The barber went away. Hudson waited. He chewed his cookie slowly. He stacked the blocks in the corner, one by one. The barber came back. He had a small seat in his hands.

"This is a booster seat," said the barber. "Small children sit on it so I can reach their hair."

Hudson climbed onto the booster seat. Now he was high up. The barber snipped and snipped. Soon Hudson had fresh, short hair. He looked in the mirror and grinned.

"I can see me!" said Hudson. His dad clapped his hands.

Myles wanted his story now. He ran to his mother with his book. "Read now, please," he said.

His mother smiled. "The story is not now," she said. "Now is bath time. The story comes later." Myles did not want a bath. He sat on the floor and hugged his book. "But now means at this very moment," said his mother. "Right now, the water is running. Later, we read."

Myles listened. He could hear the water. It was running now. He put one hand in the air. The water was not on his hand yet. That was later. So Myles went to the bath. His mother washed his toes. He gave the towel a little bite to make her laugh. It worked! She laughed a soft, warm laugh.

After the bath, his pajamas felt cool, almost frozen from the drawer. Then they got warm from his body. His mother tucked him in. "Is it later now?" asked Myles. "Yes," she said. "It is later now." She opened the book. Myles snuggled down. "Now means at this very moment," he said, "and this moment is my story."

"That's right," said his mother, and she began to read.

Grace ran to the library with her dad. She wanted the big red book about trucks. It had shiny wheels on every page.

At the desk, a librarian gave Grace a little card. "This is your library card," she said. Grace held it with two hands. It was cool and smooth.

Then Grace saw the red truck book on a shelf. She hugged it tight. "Can it come home with me?" she asked. "Yes," said the librarian. "Your card lets you borrow books and take them home to read." Grace beamed. She tapped the card on the desk, like magic. Beep!

At home, Grace read the truck book on the rug. The page had a crunchy gravel road for the trucks. Her friend Hugo came over. "How did you get a library book?" he asked. Grace held up her card and grinned. "Beep," she said.

Arya wanted to sort her toys. She made two big piles. One pile was for animals. One pile was for toys.

Jamal came over to play. He held her stuffed dog. "Put him with the animals!" he said. Arya put the dog in the animal pile.

Then she looked and looked. Her cat licked her hand. The cat ran! The dog did not run. The dog just sat there.

"The dog is a toy," Arya said. "It is not alive." She moved the dog to the toy pile. Jamal clapped.

Arya found her rubber chicken. It did not run either. Into the toy pile it went!

Later Arya washed her hands. The towel was wet. "Let's speak about the animals," she said. Jamal pointed at the cat. "That one is alive!" The cat purred very loud.

Quinn sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. "When do we eat?" she asked. "Soon," said her dad. "Soon means in a little while." The lamp posts went by, one by one. The car went into a deep, dark tunnel. Quinn waited. She counted the lights. One, two, three. Then the tunnel ended. The sky was bright again.

Soon, soon, soon. Quinn said the word to herself. The car turned a corner. Then she saw it. Grandpa's house! There was Grandpa, waving by the door. "We are here!" said Dad. "It was not a long wait," said Quinn. She climbed out of her seat. Grandpa hugged her soft and warm. "Did you bring cookies?" he asked. "Yes," said Quinn. "We will eat them soon." Grandpa laughed. "Then just a little while," he said, and held the door open wide.

Ruby waited at school pickup. She held her coat. She saw her friend Iris walk by with her dad. "We eat dinner early," Iris said. "Then bath, then pajamas." Ruby waved. Her mom came at last.

At home, Ruby ate her pasta. She had a big drink of milk. Then Mom ran the bath. Ruby saw the steam. Mom felt the water first. "Just right," Mom said. Ruby washed her toes and her arms. She got dressed in soft pajamas with stars.

Mom read one book. Ruby got into bed. Then she sat up. "My teeth!" she said. She hopped out of bed. Mom had put the toothbrush by the pot of water. Ruby brushed up and down. She brushed the front and the back. "I brush at night," she said. "And in the morning too." Mom closed the bathroom door. Ruby snuggled under her blanket. She thought about her clean, sparkly teeth. Then she closed her eyes.

Ivy stood by the shelves in the bookshop. She held a small book with a big S on the front. Ms. Patel smiled. "S says sss," said Ms. Patel. "Like a gentle snake."

Ivy looked around. Sun, sun, where was a sun? She found a picture book with a sun on it. "S is for sun," said Ivy. One.

She went on. She saw a shelf with socks in a basket. "S is for sock," said Ivy. Two.

Livia came over. "What are you doing?" she asked.

"I am hunting for sss," said Ivy. "Sun, sock. I need one more."

Livia pointed at a book about the beach. There was sand on every page. "Look," said Livia.

"S is for sand," said Ivy. Three.

Ivy counted on her fingers. "Sun, sock, sand," she said. "S, s, s."

Ms. Patel clapped her hands. "You found them all," she said.

"Can we leave the bookshop now?" asked Livia.

"Soon," said Ms. Patel. "First, one more page."

Ivy sat down. She opened the beach book. She ran her finger over the letters. S, s, s. Then she turned the page, slow and gentle, one more time.

Nathan went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big red book about trucks. He ran to the shelf, and he wanted to shout with joy.

But then Nathan saw a baby. The baby was sleeping in a stroller. The baby's mom sat close by. Near the baby, a girl named Mahee was looking at a book. Mahee saw Nathan run. She put her finger by her lips and whispered, "The baby is sleeping. We use a quiet voice."

Nathan stopped. He made his voice very small. He tiptoed to the shelf. He took the red truck book down. Then he saw his friend Faris at the low table. Faris had a box of blocks. Faris wanted the truck book too. So Nathan held the book between them. They turned the pages together, one page each.

Later the librarian, Ms. Carvalho, came by. "Please do not throw the blocks," she said kindly to a boy who tossed one. The boy put the blocks back in the box, one by one. Faris and Nathan helped too.

The baby woke up and made a sweet little sound. "You were so quiet," the baby's mom said with a smile. Nathan smiled back. Then he whispered to Faris, "Trucks go vroom, but softly."

Paisley ran to the shelf. It was almost lunch time. She wanted the cracker box for her table.

"Where is it?" she asked. There were three boxes. One, two, three.

Kade picked up a box. "This one?" The box said BAGELS on it.

"No," said Asha. She pointed at the front. "Those words say bagels."

Paisley looked hard. The letters were big. "So this box has bagels," she said.

Mr. Sato smiled. "Yes. The words tell you what is inside."

Paisley picked the next box. She traced the letters with her finger. "This says crackers!" she said. The word had a c at the start, like her cat.

"Good looking," said Mr. Sato. "Now stop at the door first. See the sign?"

Paisley stopped. The sign said WASH HANDS. "Wash hands," she read.

"That sign tells us what to do," said Asha.

Then Mr. Sato held up a story book. "Front cover first," he said. He turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back.

Paisley washed her hands and carried the cracker box. "The naughty crumbs went on the floor," she said, pointing.

Mr. Sato laughed. "We will wipe them up after lunch."

Luke stood by the classroom door. His mom held his hand. He did not want to let go.

A big man smiled at him. "Hello, Luke," the man said. "I am Mr. Mensah. I am the teacher. I look after the children in this class. I help them too."

Luke looked at the floor. He was shy. Mr. Mensah was new to him.

Then Luke saw a girl drop her crayons. Mr. Mensah knelt down. He helped her pick them up. "There you go, Lili," he said. He gave her a white cup of water. She took a drink and smiled.

Luke let go of his mom's hand. He walked to Mr. Mensah. "Hello, Mr. Mensah," he said, very small.

Mr. Mensah grinned. "Hello, Luke! Come and see the blocks."

Luke sat down next to Lili. She gave him a red block. His mom waved from the door. Luke waved back.

"Look," said Luke. He stacked one block, then another. The tower went up, up, up.

"Nice tower," said Mr. Mensah. "Now let's build one more."

Clara wanted to build a house for her toy bee. The bee was small and yellow. Clara set it on the playroom rug. "You need a home," she said.

Asiya came to help. "I will get blocks," Asiya said. She was careful with the tall tower in the corner. She carried the blocks one by one. Clara picked a square block. It had four sides that matched. She put it down flat. Then she picked a circle block. It rolled away under the chair. Sadie got down on her knees. She reached far and pushed it back. "Here," Sadie said.

Clara stacked a triangle on top. It looked like a little roof. Then she turned a square block. One corner pointed up. Sadie frowned. "That is a new shape," Sadie said. "It is not a square now."

Clara tipped her head. She looked and looked. Then she turned the block back. The flat side went down. "See," Clara said. "It is the same square." Sadie clapped. "A square turned is still a square!"

They put the square at the door. The bee sat on top. Clara made the bee sing a little song. "Buzz, buzz, home sweet home." Asiya laughed and patted the roof.

Wyatt wanted to build a big tower at school. But the block box was all mixed up. Red blocks hid under blue blocks. Big blocks sat on little blocks.

Wyatt made piles. "Red here," he said. "Blue there. Yellow there." Now the box was tidy. He started his tower with the red pile.

His friend Holland sat down. "I can sort them too," she said. Holland made one pile of big blocks. She made one pile of little blocks. She passed him a big red one. "Start with these," she said.

The big blocks made the bottom strong. The little blocks sat on top. The tower grew tall, tall, tall.

Then snack time came. Ms. Müller gave Wyatt a fork for his noodles. A shy girl at the next table peeked at his tower. "It's so tall," she whispered.

After snack, Wyatt ran back. He put one more block on top.

"Can it touch the ceiling?" Holland asked.

Wyatt grinned. "Let's find out."

Sophia wanted to make a paper sun. She found yellow paper on the shelf. Ms. Tesfaye put out glue and stickers. "I need to cut the rays," Sophia said.

She saw the big scissors in the cup. They had sharp, pointy tips. Sophia reached for them. Ms. Tesfaye caught her hand. "These are the safety scissors," she said, handing Sophia small ones. "Children cut with these while I watch." The tips were round, like little spoons.

Sophia squeezed and snipped. Snip, snip, snip. The yellow paper fell into long rays. Onyx laughed. "Your sun has a haircut!" Sophia glued the rays in a circle. It looked like a bright, tidy sun. "Now it can catch the sky," she said.

Mia went to the park with her mother. Bridget was there too. "Let's play a guessing game," said Bridget. "You close your eyes and guess!"

Mia closed her eyes. She heard birds singing with her ears. She smelled pretty flowers with her nose. Then Bridget put something in her hands.

Mia touched it with her fingertips. "It feels bumpy," said Mia. "Is it a pinecone?" "Yes!" laughed Bridget. "Your fingertips are so smart!"

They played again. This time Mia felt something soft. "A feather!" she said. She was right. Next she felt something smooth and cool. "A stone," said Mia. She was right again!

"Your turn, Bridget," said Mia. Bridget closed her eyes. Mia held out something soft and bumpy at the same time. "Hmm," said Bridget. "A nice fuzzy sock with a pinecone inside?"

Mia laughed so hard she fell over in the grass. "How did you know?" she asked. Bridget grinned and held up the sock. "My fingertips told me!" Then she tickled Mia with the feather, and Mia grabbed it and tickled her right back.

Victor was at Grandpa's house. It was Lunar New Year. There was red bread on the table. "Look, the lion is coming!" said Grandpa.

The lion dancers came down the street. Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! Victor covered his ears. "Too loud!" he said.

Grandpa held his hand. "Watch the lion," he said. Victor peeked out. The lion jumped. The drum went boom. The lion jumped again. Every boom made the lion move!

Victor let go of Grandpa's hand. He clapped with the drums. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! The lion bounced to his claps. Jett clapped too, from his porch across the street. The lion blinked its big eyes at Victor.

The drums stopped. The lion bowed. Grandpa gave Victor a red envelope. Victor's hands were full, and his heart was happy.

"Again?" asked Victor. Grandpa laughed. "Next year, little one." The lion danced away down the street.

Matthew ran into the backyard. His big red toy box sat under the tree. He wanted to clean it up before his nap. But first, he wanted to find every toy.

He picked up a block. He put it in the box. "Block," he said. Then he saw his teddy under the swing. "Doll," he said, and in it went. Then he found his blue ball in the grass. The grass was cool and soft. The ball was still bouncy. He bounced it once, twice. "Ball," he said. In it went, too.

Danny climbed over the fence. Danny held a green apple. "That's not a toy," said Danny. "Apples are food." Matthew looked at the apple. It was shiny and smelled sweet. Danny bit it. Crunch! Matthew laughed. Danny gave Matthew his toy truck. Matthew pushed it. The truck made a long line in the dirt.

The wind began to blow. The tree branches bend and swish above them. Leaves fell down, one, two, three. The sun felt warm on Matthew's head. He yawned a big yawn.

"Time for your nap," his mom called from the door. Matthew looked in the toy box. Blocks, dolls, balls, all in one place. "Toys sleep too," he whispered. He closed the lid softly, like tucking them in. Then he ran inside, holding Danny's hand. "Goodnight, toys," he said.

Penelope wanted to go to Emery's house. She wanted to go now.

"Now we eat lunch," said Mom. "You can go tomorrow."

"Where is tomorrow?" asked Penelope.

Mom smiled. "Tomorrow is the day after today."

Penelope made a picture for Emery. She drew on white paper with a spotted crayon. "Will you like this tomorrow?" she whispered to the picture.

Then it was night. Penelope put on her pajamas. She brushed her teeth. She got into bed.

"Sleep now," said Mom. "Then tomorrow comes."

Penelope closed her eyes. She slept and slept.

The sun came up. Penelope opened her eyes. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Yesterday you made your picture. Today you can bring it."

Penelope held the paper. Emery opened the door.

"For me?" said Emery. "Come and play!"

Wren was at Grandma's house. Today they would bake cookies.

"Can I pour the sugar?" asked Wren.

"Yes," said Grandma. "Pour it in the cup."

Wren tipped the big bag. Too much sugar came out. It went all over the bowl. Some fell on the floor.

Grandma did not look cross. "Let's try again," she said. "The measuring cups and spoons help us put in the right amount of each thing."

Grandma gave Wren a small cup. Wren spooned sugar into it. She filled it up to the top. Then she poured it into the bowl.

"Just right," said Grandma.

Wren measured the flour too. She used the big cup. White powder made her sneeze. She laughed. Grandma laughed.

"Now the chocolate chips," said Grandma. "One spoon."

Wren filled the spoon. Brown chips piled up on it. She tipped them into the bowl. She ate one chip. It was yummy.

Grandma put the pan into the hot oven. Wren stood back and watched. The kitchen began to smell sweet.

The timer rang. Grandma took out the cookies.

Wren took a big bite. "I made these!" she said.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You measured each thing just right."

Jake came over with his mom. Wren gave him a cookie. "I used a cup," she said. "It was the right amount."

Jake took a bite and smiled.

Samuel wanted to draw a cute animal for his mom. He looked for a plug to see. There was a little outlet near the kitchen table. It had small holes in it.

Samuel pointed. "What is that, Dad?"

"That is an outlet," said Dad. "Fingers and toys never go in there."

Samuel nodded. He kept his hands in his lap.

"I will plug in the lamp," said Dad. Dad pushed the plug in. Click! The light came on.

Samuel's eyes went wide. The plug made the lamp glow.

"Now we can see your paper," said Dad.

Samuel drew a cute bunny with long ears. He stayed close to Dad the whole time.

"My bunny!" said Samuel.

Dad smiled and hung it on the fridge.

Xavier sat on the playground wall. He had a bag of crackers. Edwin ran over.

"Can I have three?" asked Edwin.

"Three crackers," said Xavier. He counted them out. "One, two, three."

Edwin looked at his hand. "The big ones too? Big ones still count as three?"

Xavier thought hard. He picked three big ones. "One, two, three. Big or small, three is three."

Edwin laughed. "Three is three!" He ate them all up.

Rylan climbed down from the slide. "I want three too."

"One, two, three," said Xavier. Rylan got three, just like Edwin.

Then they played hopscotch. "One, two, three," they sang, hopping. "Four, five, six." A spider crawled by the chalk line. "Don't step on it!" said Edwin. They covered the spider with a leaf and let it go.

The sun felt hot. "Count to ten and race me," said Rylan. Xavier counted, "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" and ran laughing across the grass.

Asher stood in the backyard. The new baby was inside. Everyone was looking at the baby. Not at Asher.

Asher picked up his watering can. He poured water on the grass. The water made a puddle. A leaf fell in the puddle. The leaf began to float. Asher blinked. The water made the leaf float.

"Look," he called. But nobody came. Asher felt a small, sad spot in his tummy.

Then Dad came out with the baby. The baby was sleepy. Her eyes closed. Dad wrapped her in a soft towel. "Can you show her the leaf?" Dad asked.

Asher poured more water. The leaf floated again. The baby opened her eyes. She watched it.

Dad sat down next to Asher. "You are my big helper," said Dad. Asher leaned on Dad's arm. He poured the water again. The leaf floated and floated.

Michael sat at the little table in the backyard. He was making a paper crown. He put glue on the strips of paper. His hands got a little dirty with glue.

Michael wanted to wear his crown right away. He picked it up. Oh no! The pieces slid apart. The crown was not sticking yet.

"Maybe we need to wait," said his dad. "Wet glue needs time to dry."

So Michael put the crown down on the table. He and his friend Forrest watched it. They counted clouds in the sky. They touched their own skin, not the glue.

Then Forrest poked the paper. "It feels dry now," he said.

Michael picked up the crown. The pieces held together! It did not slide apart.

Dad put the crown on Michael's head. "All done," said Dad. "You had to wait, and the glue worked."

Michael smiled under his crown. "I will make one for you too, Forrest."

Charles was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to paint a pink flower on a card for Grandma. But there was no pink paint. "Where is the pink?" Charles asked. Grandpa smiled. "Look in the box," he said.

Charles opened the paint box. He saw red, blue, yellow, green, and white. He counted them out loud. "One red, one blue, one yellow, one green, one white." No pink anywhere. He felt worried. His flower could not be pink.

Grandpa put a little red paint in a cup. "Now add some white," he said. Charles stirred with his brush. Round and round he went. The red grew lighter and lighter. "Pink!" Charles shouted. He painted a pink flower, one pink petal at a time. Grandma got her card, and Charles got a glass of milk that was not sour. "Pink again tomorrow?" asked Grandpa. "Pink again," said Charles.

Madelyn was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big box of paint. "Red, yellow, blue," said Madelyn. She said the names one by one.

Madelyn wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. She looked and looked. She felt a little sad. Then she had an idea. She mixed yellow and blue in a dish. She pulled her brush through it. The paint turned green! "It's green!" she shouted. Her dream frog could be green now.

She painted one green frog. She painted two green lily pads. She painted three blue drops of water. It was the best painting ever.

Then Madelyn left her brushes in the paint. She went home for the night. The next day, she came back. She picked up a brush. It was stiff. It would not bend at all. "Oh no," said Madelyn.

Grandma helped at the sink. They washed the brushes with water. The paint came off. The brushes were soft again. Madelyn laid them out to dry. Then she got clean paper. "One frog, two lily pads, three water drops," she said. Grandma clapped her hands. "Paint us a big one," said Grandma. Madelyn dipped a clean brush and started to paint.

Lucy sat in a big chair at the barbershop. It was her very first haircut! Ms. Esposito smiled and put a cape on her.

Snip, snip, went the scissors. Then Lucy began to wiggle. "My neck itches!" she said. "Why does it itch?" She reached up to scratch.

Ms. Esposito gently stopped her hand. "Little cut hairs are on your neck," she said. "Tiny bits of cut hair can feel itchy." She took a soft brush and swept the hairs away. Whoosh! The itchy feeling was gone.

"Oh!" said Lucy. "The hairs made my neck itchy. Now they are gone, so it stopped!" She sat very still, like a statue, and the cold brush tickled her arm.

"Can Juliet get a haircut too?" Lucy asked. "Yes, next week," said Ms. Esposito. "Then I will tell her my secret," said Lucy. "Sit still, and the brush will fix the itch!"

Ms. Esposito finished the last snip. Lucy looked in the mirror. She saw short, bouncy curls. She jumped down from the big chair and waved the brush goodbye.

Alexander sat in his cozy reading nook. He had big letter cards on his lap. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He picked a pencil. He wrote "alexander" on his paper. He looked at it. It did not look quite right. His tummy felt a little scary. Then his dad came and sat close by.

"Your name starts with a big letter," his dad said. "Watch me." Dad drew one big letter A. Alexander looked. The big letter A made his name look strong, like a pet lion waking up. Alexander erased the small letter a. He drew a big letter A. "Alexander!" he read out loud. He hugged his paper. Dad gave him a kiss on his head. Alexander started to draw the big letter A again, just because he liked it.

Henri sat at the big table in the library. Mr. Aquino gave him a paintbrush and red paint. Henri painted a big red cat on his paper.

"Henri, time to go home," said the librarian. Henri put his brush down in the paint cup. He did not rinse it. The brush sat there all night.

The next day, Henri came back with Mika. He picked up his brush. It felt hard. It did not bend at all. "Oh no," said Henri. "My brush is stiff."

Mika held up her brush. Hers was soft and shiny. "I rinse mine in the water cup," she said.

Henri carried his stiff brush to the sink. Mr. Aquino helped him run the warm water. Henri rinsed and rinsed. The red paint came off. The bristles went soft again.

"So if I rinse it, the paint won't dry on it?" asked Henri. Mr. Aquino smiled and nodded.

Henri looked at the clean brush. "Nice brush," he said. "Now sleep in the drawer."

Avery wanted to make a library in her backyard. She set a big box by the door of the shed. The box had her books. But the box was stuck! Avery pulled and pulled. Then it popped open. Out came books about animals, books about toys, and books about food.

Daisy and Rudransh came to play. "Welcome to my library," said Avery. She made three shelves from an old bench. "Animal books go here," she said. "Toy books go here. Food books go here." One, two, three shelves!

Daisy wanted a book about animals. Rudransh wanted a book about food. Avery found each one fast. Then big rain drops fell. The children ran inside. Ms. Zhao, the neighbour, waved from her window. "Next time, can I borrow one?" she called. Avery smiled and held up a book about toys. "This one is for you!"

Myles was playing in the backyard with Flavie. They were digging in the dirt. They wanted to feed the birds later with the seeds they found.

Myles saw something shiny under the leaves. He bent down to look. It was a little lighter. It had a button on the side.

"Look, Flavie," said Myles. "What is it?"

Flavie shook her head. "Don't touch it. Let's show a grown-up. Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use."

They ran to Myles's father. "We found something!" said Myles.

His father came to the leaves. He picked up the lighter with care. "Good job not touching it," he said. "That was smart."

Myles felt tall and proud. His father put the lighter in his pocket, far away from little hands.

Then they fed the birds together. The birds came flying down, wild and fast. They pecked at the seeds on the grass.

"Again tomorrow?" asked Flavie.

"Yes," said Myles. He waved at the birds.

Grandpa turned on the big game. Henri sat on the rug with his furry dog toy. Halle came over too. Yohan came with his dad. Everyone shouted, "Go, go!"

The red team kicked the ball. Score! Henri clapped his hands. Then the blue team kicked the ball. Score again! Henri jumped up and down. The game got loud and fast.

At the end, Henri looked at the numbers on the screen. He saw two big fives. "Who won?" he asked. Grandpa smiled and said, "It is a tie." Henri tilted his head. Halle asked, "What is a tie?" Grandpa said, "When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie." Henri lifted his furry dog up high. "Both teams win!" he shouted. Yohan laughed and clapped. Grandpa handed out cookies for everyone. Henri took a big, happy bite.

Eli loved the big red toy box at daycare. Today it looked funny. The lid was open wide.

Eli peered inside. He saw toy cars. Red cars, blue cars, and one green car. Then he saw something yellow and long. "A banana!" he said. "In the car box!"

Mehar ran over. "A banana cannot live with cars," she said. "It is the odd one out."

"The odd one out," Eli repeated. He picked up the banana. It was soft and squishy. Then he had a big idea. "The banana is a magic dragon egg!" he said. "The cars are guarding it!"

Giulia clapped her hands. "I will get a towel," she said. "The egg needs a blanket." She wrapped the banana in a small blue towel. It looked cozy.

Mr. Sánchez walked by. "Where does the egg sleep now?" he asked.

"Not in the car box," said Eli. "It goes with the food." He carried the egg to the snack table. Mehar and Giulia followed him.

"Thank you for guarding the egg," Eli told the cars. He patted the box.

Mr. Sánchez smiled. "You found where it belongs," he said. Eli stood tall and proud. The dragon egg sat on the table, all wrapped up, waiting for snack time.

Eva sat at the art table. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. But she had no orange paint. She looked in the paint cups. There was red. There was blue. There was yellow. There was green. No orange anywhere.

"I need orange," said Eva. Her friend Kaliyah came to help. "Put red in your dish," said Kaliyah. Eva put red paint in her dish. "Now put yellow in too," said Kaliyah. Eva put yellow paint in. She stirred it round and round with her brush.

The red and yellow made orange! Eva dipped her brush. She painted a big round pumpkin. Adriano looked over from his windy day picture. "That is a nice orange," he said. Mr. Virtanen smiled and put more paper on the table. Eva painted one more pumpkin, and one more after that.

Lucas ran into the backyard. The sun was warm on his face. His friend Colten was there too.

Then the sky turned gray. Big drops began to fall. "Rain!" said Colten. The rain made wet spots on Lucas's shirt. It made wet spots on his arms. Lucas ran inside to his mom.

"My shirt is all wet," said Lucas. His mom held out a red raincoat. "Here is your raincoat," she said. Lucas put it on. He pulled the hood up over his hair.

Lucas went back outside. The rain went pitter-patter on his hood. It slid down the raincoat. His hair stayed dry. His shirt stayed dry. But his boots went splash in a puddle, and his socks got wet! "Silly rain," said Lucas. "You got my socks, but not my shirt!" Colten laughed. Colten had no raincoat, and his shirt was very wet.

"I will bring you a towel," said Lucas. He ran inside. Mom gave him a big soft towel. Lucas brought it out for Colten. "Next time, wear a raincoat," said Lucas. Colten nodded. "Next time, I will!"

The new baby was home. Olivier looked at her little face. She slept in a soft square blanket.

Then the baby woke up. She cried and cried. "Why is she crying?" Olivier asked. "She cannot talk yet," said Dad. "So she cries to show she needs something."

Olivier thought. Maybe the baby was hungry. Dad gave her milk. She kept crying. Maybe she was cold. Olivier found a small sock. Dad put it on her foot. Still she cried.

Then Olivier saw her wet diaper. "Maybe she needs a clean one!" he said. Dad changed it. The crying stopped. The baby made a little coo.

Olivier laughed. "She talked to us!" he said. He patted her hand quick and soft. The baby held his finger.

"Again!" said Olivier. Dad smiled. "She will talk like this a lot," he said.

Olivier sat close on the floor. He waited for the next cry. He was the big brother who could help.

Olivia was in the kitchen with her dad. She wanted to help make toast. Dad put the bread in the toaster. "Watch from here," Dad said. Olivia stood on her spot, a thin rug by the door.

The toaster got hot. Olivia could feel it a little on her face. Dad used a fork to get the toast out. He did not let Olivia touch the fork. "Hot things are for grown-ups," Dad said. Olivia nodded. She gave the butter a little push across the bread. It made a shiny line.

Then Olivia saw something. A little mouse ran under the fridge. "A mouse!" she said. She wanted to see it. She ran to the far corner, way behind the big table. It was dark back there. She could not see Dad. Her tummy felt funny. She stopped. She ran back fast to the thin rug.

"There you are," Dad said. "Stay where I can see you." Dad could see her on the rug. That felt good. Olivia took a bite of her toast. It was warm and sweet. The mouse stayed under the fridge, and Olivia stayed right by her dad.

Noah ran to the playground after dinner. He was not sleepy yet. He wanted to play on the swing. But the swing was taken. A girl was on it. It was Hannah from his class.

Noah waited by the fence. He watched the swing go up. He watched the swing come down. Hannah pumped her legs hard. Then the swing went slower. Then it stopped.

"Can I have a turn, please?" asked Noah. Hannah slid down off the swing. "Sure," she said. "Thank you!" said Noah. Hannah stood still. She did not know what to say next. Her mouth opened, then shut.

Dane was close by, sharing his crackers. He gave one to a small boy. "Thank you," said the small boy. "You're welcome," said Dane. Hannah watched too. Her eyes got big.

Noah pushed the swing with his legs. Up he went. Down he came. Then a ball popped out of the sand and rolled to his feet. "Can you help me?" called the small boy. "Sorry, I can't reach it alone," said Dane, who tried and missed.

Noah jumped off the swing. He picked up the ball. He handed it to the small boy. "Thank you," said the small boy. "You're welcome," said Noah. Then Noah looked at Hannah. She smiled. "Want to push me now?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Noah.

Mya went to the doctor with her dad. The waiting room was big. Mya saw a fish tank. She saw a little bug crawl up the glass. She heard the fish go "blub, blub." She smelled something like soap in the air.

Then the doctor called her name. Mya was so excited. The doctor looked in her ears. Mya heard the doctor say, "Your ears hear well." The doctor put cold gel on Mya's tummy. It felt slimy and cold. Mya touched it with one finger. "It's cold!" she said. Then the doctor gave her a sweet, orange drink. Mya tasted it. "Yummy orange!" she said.

Next, the doctor pointed at a chart on the wall. "Tell me what you see," she said. Mya looked hard. The pictures were all fuzzy. She could not see the little star at all. Mya felt sad. "I can't see it," she said.

The doctor smiled. She put some little glasses on Mya's nose. Mya opened her eyes. Wow! Now the pictures were clear. Now she could see the little star! "Glasses help some people see more clearly," said the doctor. "These can be yours."

Mya wore her new glasses all the way home. She read her book with her dad. She saw every star on every page. Mya clapped her hands. "I see it! I see it!"

Brooks went to the baby store with his mom. A new baby sister was coming soon. Brooks wanted to pick a gift for her. He saw a soft toy and a tiny cup. He chose the cup. It had a funny face on it.

In the next aisle, Brooks saw baby crackers. He held up his box of crackers at home too. "She can share mine," he said. His mom shook her head. "A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food," she said. Brooks put the crackers back on the shelf.

Then Brooks found a bottle. It was small and clean. Milk could go inside it. "This one," he said. His mom smiled and put it in the cart. At home, Brooks set the bottle by the baby's bed. "Milk for you," he whispered, "and crackers for me."

Arya sat at the table. Her hair was short and curly. Daddy put pasta on her plate. After dinner, Sheldon came over to play.

Arya had a little blue car. Sheldon wanted the car too. He grabbed one end. Arya grabbed the other end. "My car!" said Arya. "No, my turn!" said Sheldon. The car could not move at all.

Then Arya thought of something. "Let's ask Daddy," she said. Daddy came over. "We both want the car," said Arya. Daddy said, "I can help you take turns. Arya first, then Sheldon." Arya pushed the car fast. "Beep beep!" she said. Soon she gave the car to Sheldon. He pushed it too. Then Arya got another turn. "This is fun," said Sheldon. Arya smiled big. "Your turn now," she said, and rolled the car across the floor to him.

Jordan sat at the quiet table. Mr. Ho put a tablet in front of him. Jordan pressed the round button. The screen lit up. He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. Jordan drew a big red swing, just like the one outside. He drew green grass under it. Then the screen went black. All his green grass was gone. Jordan looked at Mr. Ho. "Did I break it?" he asked. "No," said Mr. Ho. "It ran out of power. It needs charging." Mr. Ho picked up the charger and plugged it in. Jordan watched the little battery picture fill up. When the screen came back, his swing was still there. Jordan smiled. He drew one more swing, then put the tablet away.

Ali had a big red drum in his bedroom. He loved his drum. He hit it. Boom! Boom! Boom! Ali felt so excited. He was a loud dragon, and the drum was his roar.

His friend Andrew came to play. Ali hit the drum again. Boom! Andrew covered his ears. Andrew did not feel excited. Andrew felt scared of the loud sound. He sat near the bed and hid his face.

Ali stopped drumming. He looked at Andrew. Then he looked at the drum. Same drum. Ali felt happy. Andrew felt scared. Ali put down the drumsticks.

"Let's be quiet dragons," said Ali. They patted the drum very softly. Tap. Tap. Tap. Andrew peeked out. He smiled and patted too. Ali got the toy plates. They shared pretend cake. "Yum," said Andrew.

Felix held the puppy's big paws. "Our first pet!" he said.

At the pet store, Ms. Szabó smiled. "Every pet needs a collar," she said. Felix picked a red one. It went click, click.

Then Ms. Szabó held up a small tag. "This goes on the collar," she said. Felix looked at it. It was shiny and cold. His mom typed their phone number on it.

"Why the number?" Felix asked.

Ms. Szabó said, "So people can reach his family if he gets lost."

Felix put the tag on the collar. Ding! It made a little sound.

At home, the puppy licked Felix's hand. His tongue was warm and soft. Felix gave him a gentle pat on his big head.

The puppy ran to the door. Ding, ding! The tag jingled.

"Mom, he's here!" Felix laughed. "The tag tells us where he is!"

Eleanor went to the park with her friend Maci. Ms. Whitehead brought a hoop and a big red ball. She put the hoop on the grass. "Toss the beanbag in," she said.

Eleanor held the beanbag up high. She flung her arm over her shoulder. The beanbag flew far, far away. It landed near a little butterfly. The butterfly flew off fast. Maci laughed and laughed. "Too far!" she said. Eleanor ran to get the beanbag. She felt a bit cross.

Ms. Whitehead knelt down beside her. "Watch me," she said. "This is an underhand throw." She held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up, up, up. Then it dropped right into the hoop. "Yay!" said Maci.

Eleanor tried it. She held the beanbag low. She swung her arm forward and up. The beanbag sailed into the hoop. Eleanor jumped up and down. "I did it!" she said. Then the beanbag fell out of the hoop and rolled on the grass. Eleanor shut her eyes and giggled. "Silly beanbag," she said.

Then it was ball time. Maci threw the big red ball to Eleanor. Eleanor held out both hands. The ball was too big for one hand. Both hands caught it, hug tight. Maci clapped. Ms. Whitehead clapped too. "Throw it back," said Maci. Eleanor hugged the ball, swung low, and let it fly up to Maci.

Hunter turned three today. His party was at the big park. Grandma came with a cake box. The box lid was open. "Count the candles," said Grandma. Hunter counted. "One, two, three!" he said. He got three candles because he was three. Giovanni came to the table. Giovanni said, "I am five. My cake had five candles. One for each year." Then Killian ran over with the plates. Mr. Islam, the park helper, blew up a red balloon. Hunter held the balloon. It was open sky above him. The balloon stayed up high on its string. Hunter tugged the string. The balloon came down a little. He let go. The balloon went up again. "Mommy, look!" said Hunter. "The string makes it stay close to me." Mom smiled. Dad lit the candles with a match. Hunter stayed back, safe. Everyone sang the birthday song. Then Hunter blew. Out went the candles. Grandma cut the cake. Hunter got a big piece. "Happy birthday, Hunter!" said everyone. Hunter waved his balloon.

Isaiah ran to the park with his doll. Khaled was there by the little playhouse. "Let's play house," said Khaled. Isaiah smiled big.

"I want to be the dad," said Isaiah. "I want to be the dad too," said Khaled. They both stood still. The doll sat in Isaiah's arms and waited.

Then Isaiah had an idea. "You be the dad first," he said. "I will be the baby." Khaled tucked a thin blanket around a teddy bear. "Time for dinner," said Khaled in a big dad voice. Isaiah made a tiny baby sound and bounced on his seat.

"Now we switch," said Isaiah. So Khaled became the baby, and Isaiah became the dad. Isaiah fed the doll a pretend bottle. Khaled giggled and clapped.

Just then Lillian came by with a puppy puppet. "Can I play too?" she asked. "Yes," said Isaiah. "You can be the puppy."

Isaiah patted the puppy's soft head. "Good puppy," he said. "Time for bed, everyone." Khaled yawned a big pretend yawn and closed his eyes.

Claire stood on her balcony with a big flat pot. She filled it with soil and patted it down. "One seed, two seeds, three seeds," she said. She made a wish for each little seed. Then she watered them and waited.

One morning, a tiny green leaf poked up. But a stringy weed grew right beside it. Claire grabbed the weed and pulled. Out it came, with long white strings hanging down. "What are these?" she asked her dad. "Those are roots," he said. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil." Claire looked at her seeds. Were roots growing down under there right now?

She dug very gently at one seed. Thin roots were going down, down, down. Claire smiled. That night she looked at the moon and said, "Grow down, little roots."

Charlie was at the park with her dad. She held a small box with holes. Inside was a tiny gray kitten.

"Hello, little mouse," said Charlie. "You are not a mouse. You are a cat!" The kitten mewed. She was small and soft.

Charlie wanted to name her. "One, two, three names," said Charlie. "Whiskers, Socks, Puff." The kitten licked her nose. "Puff it is," said Dad.

On the path they saw Mathias. He was throwing a ball for his big dog. The dog ran fast. Then the dog stopped. He drank from a bowl by the bench.

"Dogs get thirsty," said Mathias. "Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day." Charlie looked at her box. "Puff will need water too," she said.

At home, Dad put a bowl on the floor. Puff sniffed it. She drank and drank. Then she fell asleep in the bowl. Her paws were in the water.

"Oh no," said Charlie. "Puff is sleepy and drippy."

Later the bowl was empty. Puff licked the empty bottom. Charlie reached for the bowl. It was too high on the shelf, so Dad helped. He filled it with fresh, clean water from the tap. Charlie set it down. "One bowl for Puff," she said.

Puff woke up. She drank. Then she chased her own tail. "Silly Puff," said Charlie. "Water first, then tail."

Lillian ran into the playroom. Adelie was already there. A big cardboard box sat on the floor. It had round paper windows. It was a rocket ship!

"I want to blast off," said Lillian. "Me too!" said Adelie. They climbed in. They pushed buttons that were just tape. They wiggled the steering wheel, which was a paper plate.

"Rockets need a countdown," said Adelie. "A countdown is counting backward from ten down to one. Then we jump up and yell blast off!" Lillian nodded fast.

Adelie started. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Lillian said the next ones with her. "Six, five, four, three." They held hands. "Two, one. Blast off!"

They jumped up so high. They froze like astronauts in the sun light from the window. Then they fell down, giggling. "Again!" said Lillian. They got back in the box. Adelie took a big breath. "Ten, nine, eight," said Julia, popping her head in the door. "Can I count too?"

Eli went to the park with his mom. It was a big festival day. There were flags and drums and lots of people. There were food stalls too.

Eli saw a food stall with sweet bread. He let go of his mom's hand. He walked toward the smell. The crowd was big. People walked in front of him. He could not see his mom. His tummy felt dizzy with worry.

Then Eli remembered. At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up. He stood still and looked around. His mom was not far away. She was waving at him. He ran back and held her hand tight.

"Stay close now," his mom said. "The crowd is too big for little feet." They walked to the sweet bread stall together. His mom bought one piece. Eli took a bite. It was soft and warm. A little crumb fell, and a cloud of birds flew down to peck at it. Eli laughed and licked his sticky fingers. He held his mom's hand all the way home.

Madison was at the park with her dad. She looked in her bag. Her little pink car was gone. "I can't find my car," she said. Her tummy felt worried.

"We will look together," said Dad. They looked by the swing. They looked by the big tree. Then Madison saw something shiny in the grass. It was a beautiful blue car. But it was not her car. It was Cash's car. Cash was crying by the bench.

Madison picked up the car. She ran to Cash. "Here is your car," she said. Cash stopped crying. He smiled big. Then Cash pointed at the sandbox. "Is that yours?" he asked. There was a pink car in the sand. "My car!" said Madison. She caught it up in both hands and hugged it tight. "You found mine too," she said.

Charles was at Grandma's house. It was a big holiday day. Grandpa was making dumplings, just for today.

Charles wanted one now. "Can I taste one?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandpa. "They have to cook first." Grandpa had a hot pan on the stove. Charles stood back and watched. Grandpa let him pour the flour into the bowl. Charles poured it slowly. Little puffs of white came up. Grandpa mixed the flour and water. Then he rolled it flat. Charles helped press the green spinach into the dough. The dough turned green like grass.

"Today we eat dumplings," said Grandpa. "We only make them on this day." Charles nodded. He waited by the table. The dumplings went into the pan. They sizzled and popped. Charles watched and watched. Soon they came out, all warm and steamy. Grandpa put three on Charles's plate. Charles took a big bite. Then he held one up and said, "These are holiday dumplings!"

Jayden was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to feed the pet fish. But Grandpa said, "First we count the fish flakes."

Jayden got the little cup. He tipped one flake in. "One," he said. He tipped another. "Two," he said. Then he stopped. He could not remember what came next. His face felt sad.

Then he heard singing from the porch. It was his cousin Vanessa. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Jayden ran to her. "What comes after two?" he asked.

"Sing it with me," said Vanessa. "Three, four, shut the door." Jayden sang it too. The words rhymed and tickled his ears. "Again!" he said. They sang all the way to "nine, ten, a big fat hen."

Jayden ran back to the fish. "One, two, buckle my shoe," he sang. He tipped a flake. "Three!" He tipped another. "Four!" He counted all the way to ten flakes. The fish swam fast and gobbled them up. Grandpa helped him clean the wet cup. Then Grandpa clapped.

Jayden sang to the fish, "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!"

Lea loved the library. There was a big red truck there. Today Mustafa was holding it. Lea wanted it too. She reached out her hands. Mustafa held the truck tight. Uh oh. Now what?

"Truck, please?" said Lea. Mustafa shook his head. Then Ms. Gallagher came close. She sat down on the little rug. "Whose go is it now?" she asked. "Mustafa's," said Lea. "And after him?" asked Ms. Gallagher. Lea thought hard. "Me!" she said. "We send the truck to each other," said Mustafa. He pushed the truck across the rug. Vroom! It rolled right to Lea. She laughed and caught it.

Lea drove the truck to the pretend kitchen. It carried a toy fork and a spoon. Beep beep! Lunch for the truck. Then she looked at Mustafa. He was waiting. Waiting, waiting, so still. She pushed the truck back to him. Vroom! "My turn again soon?" she asked. "Yes," said Mustafa. "One after another." But wait. The wheel felt funny. One wheel spun and spun. Oh no. Was the wheel broken? Lea turned the truck over. A tiny stone was stuck in it. She popped the stone out with her finger. The wheel spun smooth again. Mustafa clapped. "Good fixing!" he said. Lea smiled and pushed the truck back to him one more time.

Lennon went to the store with her dad. She had a hole in her sock. "Dad, where do socks live?" she asked. "Socks live with the clothes," said Dad. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Lennon looked at the toy aisle. There was a big teddy bear wearing a tiny hat. She giggled. "The bear wears clothes too," she said. Then she saw a rack of socks. She pulled one off. It was long and stretchy. She pulled it onto her leg like a silly snake. "Look, Dad! A sock snake!" Dad laughed. "Pass me the other one," he said. Lennon passed it to him. He made it hop like a bunny.

Nearby, Reese from her class was shopping too. Reese held a wet umbrella and dripped on the floor. "It rained on me!" said Reese. "I need new socks too." Lennon held up a pink pair. "These are clothes," she said. "Try these!"

At home, Dad washed the wet umbrella in the sink. Lennon put her new socks in the basket with the shirts and hats. "All together," she said. Dad nodded. "Good sorting, Lennon." She gave the teddy bear a pat on his hat.

Dylan was in his bedroom. Maxime was coming to play today. Dylan felt so excited. His tummy was bouncy like a frog.

"I want to jump!" said Dylan. He jumped on the rug. He bounced on his bed. He shouted, "Maxime is coming!" He was so loud. His teddy fell over. Teddy looked angry about the big noise.

Dylan stopped. He sat down on the rug. He took a big, slow breath. He gave teddy a hug. "Waiting is hard," he said softly. He patted his bouncing legs, one pat, two pats. The frog in his tummy got small and still.

Then the door went ding-dong. Dylan walked slowly, slow like a snail. He opened the door. "Maxime!" said Dylan. "Come see my bedroom!" Maxime ran in, and they both laughed.

It was Sebastian's birthday. He ran into the classroom. Mr. Yip had set up a big table.

"Look, Sebastian!" said Ayana. "Presents!" There were three boxes on the table. Each box was covered in wrapping paper. Constance pointed at the biggest one.

Sebastian picked it up. He shook it. He squeezed it. He held it up to his ear. "I can't see inside!" he said. "The paper hides it."

"Guess what it is," said Ayana.

"A dinosaur!" said Sebastian.

"A truck!" said Constance.

Sebastian waited a long time. Then his dad came in. "Time to open them!" he said. Sebastian pulled the paper off the big box. Out came a red truck with a honking horn.

"Constance was right!" Sebastian laughed. He pushed the truck in a big circle around the table. "Next year, I will wrap your presents," he told Ayana. "Then you can't peek either!"

Wesley was at the farm with his friend Russell. They planted little seeds in a long row. "What will these be?" asked Russell. "Peas," said Wesley. They patted the dirt down and went home.

Every day they came back. Sun and rain helped the plants grow tall. Soon little green swings hung on the stems. Wesley touched one. "Is this a bean?" he asked. "No, look," said Russell. He popped one open. Inside sat a row of peas, snug like beads.

Wesley picked a pod and popped it too. "Peas grow inside pods!" he said. He picked more pods until his hat was full.

At night they ate the peas with dinner. "Sweet," said Wesley. He swung his empty pod like a tiny sword. "More pods tomorrow!"

Jasmine found a big cardboard box in the backyard. She wanted to play with it right away. Her friend Mya came over to play too.

"A car!" said Jasmine. She sat in the box and turned a pretend wheel. "Beep, beep!"

"A boat!" said Mya. She wanted the box to be a boat. "Row, row!"

They both wanted the box. Mya frowned. Jasmine frowned too. Then Mya had an idea.

"Let's take turns," said Mya. "First a car. Then a boat."

Jasmine smiled. She drove the box car around the grass. "Vroom!" The wheels were loud in her head. Then she climbed out and gave the box to Mya.

Mya rowed the box boat across the grass. "Splash, splash!"

Jasmine got her teddy bear. The bear needed a house. "The box can be a house now," she said. She put the bear inside and patted its head. Mya added a leaf for a blanket so the bear could dry off after the pretend bath.

"Time for bed, little bear," said Jasmine softly.

Then the girls climbed in together. The box was a house for everyone.

Ms. Holloway peeked over the fence and waved. "What a fine house," she called.

Jasmine waved back. "Come to our house!" she said.

Raphael had a cold. He had coughed and coughed. Today his mom took him back to the doctor's office. Ms. Chowdhury looked in his ears. "Your cold is almost gone," she said. "A grown-up can give you the medicine at home. Only a grown-up gives a child medicine."

At home, Raphael felt warm and sleepy. The little purple bottle sat up high on the counter. Raphael looked at it. He wanted to feel strong again. He reached up on his toes. His mom came in fast and soft. "I will pour it," she said. "You can watch."

She poured a small spoon. The medicine tasted like sweet grapes. Raphael drank it all. Then he played a quiet game with his blocks. His mom hugged him. "Medicine time is over," she said. "Now it is rest time." Raphael yawned and held his teddy bear tight.

Everly ran to Ms. Andersen's house. The big game was on TV today. Everyone was coming to watch. Everly wanted to wear her red shirt. But she could not find it anywhere.

She looked under her bed. She found one sock. That was silly. She looked in the toy box. She found a banana, not a shirt. "Not a shirt!" she said.

At Ms. Andersen's house, Phillip wore a blue shirt. Barkat wore a blue shirt too. Ms. Andersen wore blue from head to toe. "We cheer for the blue team," said Phillip. "Our shirts show our team!" Everly looked down at her polka dot shirt. She did not look like anyone.

Then Ms. Andersen held up a soft blue scarf. "Try this," she said. Everly put it on. Now she looked like her friends. "We match!" she laughed. Everyone sat on the big soft couch. The game was loud and bright. Everly clapped when they clapped. She munched popcorn, warm and salty.

When the blue team scored, Phillip jumped up. "Hooray!" he said. Everly jumped too, scarf flying. "I love my scarf," she said. Barkat grinned. "Blue team forever!"

Madison went to the store with her dad. She wanted new socks with elephants on them. They had to be blue socks. Madison had lost one old sock at home. Only one was left.

Dad held up two socks. "A pair means two," he said. "Two socks make one pair." Madison held the two elephant socks. She put them together. "One, two," she said. "A pair!"

Then she counted the socks on the shelf. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten socks. Then she counted again, slowly. Ten socks made five pairs. She picked her blue pair and pulled one sock on. It felt tight, so she wiggled her toes until it sat just right.

At home, she washed her hands and dad filled the sink. Madison dropped the new socks in. Water went splash. She counted them in the water. "One, two. A pair," she said, and hung them up side by side.

Aurora went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about fish. She could not find one by herself. "Let's ask," her dad said. They went to meet Ms. Le at the big desk.

Ms. Le handed Aurora a fish book. Aurora held it up to look. The fish looked funny. The fish was upside down! The words were upside down too. Aurora laughed and laughed. "Silly fish!" she said. Ms. Le smiled. "Turn the book around," she said. Aurora turned it around. Now the fish swam the right way. Now the words sat the right way too.

Victoria and Aylin came over. "What's so funny?" asked Victoria. Aurora flipped the book upside down again. "Look! Upside-down fish!" Aylin giggled. Then Aurora turned it the right way. She opened the front cover first. She pointed at the words. "These say fish," she said. "My dad reads them to me." On the last page was a picture of a big blue whale. It was a surprise! "A whale!" said Aurora. She hugged the book tight. "Can we take it home?" Her dad said, "Yes."

Milan sat on the big red couch. Dad put the game on TV. Players ran with a orange ball. Milan watched one player stop and throw. The ball went up, then down through a hoop. The crowd cheered loud. "The ball went in the hoop!" said Milan.

Krish and Celeste came over with his mom. They all sat on the couch too. Milan wanted to try. "Can I throw a ball in a hoop?" he asked. Dad said yes. They had a little ball and a toy hoop on the door. But first Dad said, "We wash our hands." Milan rubbed the soap on his hands. Bubbles everywhere!
