Then Milan threw the ball. It hit the rim. He threw again. It went up and down through the hoop. "I did it!" said Milan. Krish clapped. Celeste clapped. Krish threw the ball too. It went in! "Good try," said Dad. "One more time," said Milan.

Stella stood at the bus stop with Kade. The sun was warm on her face. She wore her yellow hat and her light shoes.

Then the wind came. It blew and blew. The wind took Stella's hat right off her head. The hat flew into a bush. "My hat!" said Stella. Kade helped her get it. She held it tight.

Dark clouds rolled in. Rain began to fall. Plop, plop, plop. Then Stella heard a big sound. Rumble! Rumble! "Thunder," said Kade. Stella knew what to do. When you hear thunder, you go indoors. She and Kade ran to Ms. Li's little shop by the road.

Ms. Li opened the door. "Come in, come in," she said. She turned the lock so the wind would not push the door. Inside it was dry and cozy. Ms. Li gave them each a sweet biscuit. Through the window they saw rain and one wet cow walking home. "There goes the bus," said Stella. Kade laughed, and they waved at it together.

Felix wanted his gray bunny. Bunny was not in his bed. Bunny was not under the chair. Felix looked in the toy box. No bunny there.

"I had bunny on the bus," said Felix. "I held him on my lap." Dad gave Felix a hug. "We can look for him," said Dad. Dad made a phone call. A man at the bus place said, "We have a lost and found. It is a place where people put things they find, so the owners can get them back."

"Is a gray bunny there?" asked Dad. The man said, "Come and see." So Felix and Dad rode the bus. Rain made a splash on the window. Felix watched the drops run down the glass.

They got to the bus place. There was a big box. It had hats and mittens and one gray bunny. Felix picked bunny up. He held him tight. "Hello, bunny," said Felix. Bunny's ear was still soft. Felix waved to the man. "Thank you," said Felix. On the bus ride home, bunny sat on Felix's lap, all the way.

Natalie sat in a big green chair. The chair was soft. Mom sat next to her. A fish swam in a tank by the wall. Its tail went swish, swish.

"Is it my turn now?" Natalie asked.

"Not yet," said Mom. "This is the waiting room. Families sit here until it is their turn."

Natalie watched the door. A boy went in. Then a grandma went in. Then a nurse came to the door. "Natalie," the nurse called. Natalie jumped up. It was her turn at last!

In the small room, the nurse rolled up Natalie's sleeve. The needle was very small. Natalie held Mom's hand. Plop. It was done. It hurt just a tiny bit, like a prickle from the grass outside.

"Was that all?" Natalie asked.

"That was all," said the nurse.

Then came the surprise. The nurse gave Natalie a bandage with a cat on it. The cat had pink ears.

"I want to buy more of these," Natalie said.

"You cannot buy them," Mom said, laughing. "But you can wear one all day."

Natalie looked at her arm. The little cat smiled up at her. "You are not wrong, cat," she said. "Today was a good day."

The fish in the tank went swish, swish, goodbye.

Theodore put on his skates at the ice rink. His friend Isaiah came too. Everlee came too. Mr. Li helped them zip their coats. They skated round and round until Theodore was tired. Then they sat on a long bench with warm cocoa.

A big game was on the screen above the snack bar. It was soccer, not skating. Theodore watched the players run. He saw the net at the end of the field. "The ball goes over the net," said Theodore. "High, high up!" Isaiah shook his head. "Watch," he said.

A player ran fast. He kicked the ball. The ball went into the net. The whole crowd stood up. "Goal!" they shouted. Everyone at the rink shouted too. Mr. Li clapped his hands. Theodore clapped his hands.

Another player kicked the ball. It went into the net again. "Goal!" shouted Theodore. Now he knew. The ball goes into the net. That is how players score. Theodore hugged his soft pillow from home. He had brought it for the long ride. He was sleepy but still awake. Isaiah waved. Everlee waved. Theodore waved back and said, "Goal!"

Elliot went to the library with his dad. The library smelled like old, smelly books and warm paper. Elliot wanted the big red book about trucks. But Kaysen was holding it. Kaysen hugged it tight.

Elliot wanted to grab it. His dad shook his head. Then Elliot remembered what his teacher said. He tapped Kaysen's arm. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Kaysen smiled. "Yes! May I have it back after?" "Okay," said Elliot. They sat side by side. Kaysen pointed at a dump truck. Elliot turned the page.

Later Elliot found a green book about frogs. He brought it to Mr. Martínez at the desk. "May I take this home?" he asked. "Yes, you may," said Mr. Martínez. "Thank you," said Elliot. "You're welcome," said Mr. Martínez. Elliot held the frog book all the way to the car. "May I read it first?" he asked his dad. His dad laughed. "Yes, you may."

Myles stood by the cubbies at school. His coat was big and red. Ms. Mokoena smiled at him. "You can do it, Myles," she said. Myles pushed his arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It made a little sound. Zzzz! He did it all by himself.

Then Myles wanted to play outside. But where were his mittens? One mitten was on the floor. Lochlan picked it up and gave it to him. "Thank you," said Myles. He put it on his hand. Then he looked at his coat. There was a pocket! Myles tucked both mittens inside. They fit just right.

Outside, Myles took the mittens out. Warm hands! He ran to the slide with Lochlan and Aadvik. When it was time to go in, the mittens went back in the pocket. No more lost mittens. "Good work, Myles," said Ms. Mokoena. Myles gave a big, tired smile. He zipped his coat again. Zzzz!

Florence sat on her bed. She had a new book. She wanted to know who made it up.

She looked at the front cover. Then she opened the book. "One page, two pages, three pages," she counted. The pages had little marks on them. "What are those marks?" she wondered.

Everly came in to play on the swing outside, but first she sat down too. Florence turned the pages from front to back. "That is how a book goes," Everly said. "Front to back."

Everly pointed at the cover. "See the name there? That is the author. The author is the person who wrote the words of the book."

Florence looked again. "So that name made my story?" she asked.

She traced the letters with her finger, one by one. Then she hugged the book tight and read the first page to Everly.

Audrey sat down at the dinner table. She smelled the soup with her nose. It smelled like carrots. She heard the spoons clink with her ears. She touched her cup. The cup felt cold in her hands. Then Dad set a lemon slice by her plate. It was yellow and round. She saw it with her eyes.

"Juice!" said Audrey. She loved orange juice. Orange juice was sweet. Maybe lemon was sweet too. She licked the lemon with her tongue. Yuk! Her whole face scrunched up.

"Sour!" Audrey did not shout it, but she almost did. Dad laughed. "Try it again," he said kindly. "Lemons are sour." She touched the lemon again with her tongue. Sour again! The lemon had a moon shape and a sour taste. Outside the window it was windy. The tree bent and waved. Audrey sipped her milk. Sweet milk! Her tongue knew the difference now. She took another tiny lick. "Still sour!" she said.

Eloise stood in the band room. It was winter, and the radiators ticked softly. Mr. Cho handed her a small recorder. "Put your fingers on the holes," he said. Natalie and Eden each took one too.

Eloise blew into her recorder. It made a squeak. Natalie laughed, then made a squeak too. Mr. Cho bent down. "Look at your thumb," he said. Eloise looked. Her thumb was half off its hole. She moved it until it covered the hole all the way. She blew again. Now a real note came out.

She lifted one finger. She blew. A new note came out. She lifted two fingers. The note changed again. "The holes make the notes!" she said. Eden covered all her holes and blew a low, smooth sound. Eloise kissed her recorder on the top. "You were not sick," she whispered. "You just needed my fingers." Then she played her low note one more time.

Milan was at Grandma's house. He wanted a story about a big red truck. Grandma was stirring hot soup, so she could not read yet. "Find the truck book," she said. "It is on the shelf."

Milan found the book. He opened it. The pages looked all mixed up. The truck was at the end. The words went the wrong way. "This book is broken," he said.

Grandma looked over. "Hold it up," she said. "The front cover shows the truck." Milan turned the book over. Now the truck cover was at the front. He opened the front cover. The first page said, "Here is the big red truck." He turned the pages one by one. The truck drove through the whole story, all the way to the back cover.

Grandma blew on the soup and smiled. "That was a real fix," she said. "Now bring it here. We will read it together while the soup cools." Milan climbed onto the chair beside her and opened the front cover again.

Victoria had a cold. Her nose was red. Her voice was small. She sat in her bed in her pajamas.

"Drink your water," said Dad. He brought a special cup. It was yellow with a straw that bent. Victoria did not want it. Water was not fun today.

Then Lorelai came to visit. Lorelai knocked on the door. She held a picture she had made. It was a cat in the mud. The mud was brown and heavy on the page.

"Sip with me," said Lorelai. She pretended to sip from her hand. Victoria laughed a small laugh. She picked up her cup. She took one sip. Then she took another.

Soon her voice came back. It was not small anymore. "Let's play cats in the mud!" said Victoria. She jumped out of bed. The water had helped her. She felt ready to hurry and play.

Isabella came to Grandma's house with her sister. Her sister had mud on her shoes. Isabella had mud on her hands. "Bath time," said Grandma.

Isabella wanted to jump right in. The tub was big and white. But Grandma held up her hand. "Wait," said Grandma. Grandma put her hand in the water. "A grown-up checks the bath water first," she said. "It must not be too hot."

Isabella waited. She held her red rubber duck. She watched Grandma's hand move in the water. Then Grandma turned the tap a little. Cold water ran in. Grandma put her hand in again. "Now it is just right," she said.

Isabella climbed in with help. The water was warm and soft. Her duck floated beside her. Isabella put her hand in too. "My hand checks too," she said. Grandma smiled. "Splash time," said Grandma.

Maverick sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. It was a gift from his dad. "Now you can write your name," Dad said.

Maverick held the pencil tight. He made an M. But the paper slid away. His M went crooked. He tried again. The paper slid again. Maverick felt grumpy. He puffed out his cheeks.

Dad sat down next to him. "Let's try one thing," Dad said. He showed Maverick how to put his other hand on the paper. Maverick pressed down. The paper stopped sliding. Now the pencil stayed on the line. He made a big straight M. Then an A. Then a V!

"I did it!" Maverick said. "Look, it says Maverick!"

Dad clapped his hands. "It sure does," he said. "Should we leave it on the table for Mom to see?"

Maverick nodded. He put his pencil down right on top of his name.

Miles sat at the long table in the community hall. His shoes were tucked under his chair, all tidy. His friend Aylin sat beside him. Aylin's grandma was there too. She had brought rice and soup for everyone.

Aylin's grandma put her hands together. She smiled and said, "Itadakimasu." Then she began to eat. Miles looked around. Everyone at the table said it too. What was that word? Why did they say it first?

Aylin leaned over. "We say itadakimasu before we eat," she said. "It gives thanks for the food." Miles sat up tall. He put his hands together, just like Aylin's grandma. He took a big breath. "Ita... daki... masu," he said slowly. Aylin's grandma clapped her hands. "Very good, Miles," she said.

Then Miles picked up his spoon and ate his warm rice. It tasted good. He looked at his bowl and wondered. Maybe he could say itadakimasu at home too, before his very own dinner. He would practice the word all the way home, one step at a time, all the way to his own door.

Quinn was at the library. It was a quiet place. Mr. Ngo had letter cards on a big plate. Each card was bumpy. Quinn wanted to write the letter K. She drew it on her paper. "That looks wrong," said Blair. "It's backwards." Quinn felt sad. She might lose her turn to show the card. Mr. Ngo sat by her. "Put your finger here," he said. Quinn traced the bumpy K. Up, down, out, and out again. She traced it two more times. Then she picked up her crayon. She wrote a K on her paper. "You did it!" said Blakely. Quinn held up her paper. The K was just right. "K says kuh," said Quinn. Mr. Ngo smiled. "Let's try the next letter," he said.

Jade was at Grandma's house. Grandma was baking bread. Jade wanted to help. "Can I help, please?" she asked. "Yes, you can pour the flour," said Grandma. Jade poured it slow, slow, slow.

Then someone knocked on the door. Knock, knock. Jade hid behind Grandma's skirt. Mr. Vargas stood outside. He waved at Jade. Grandma said, "Hello, Mr. Vargas." Jade peeked out with one eye. She peeked out with two eyes. Then she said, "Hello, Mr. Vargas." He smiled a big smile. He was not angry at all. He gave Grandma a jar of jam.

"I made this jam," he said. "Would you like to taste it?" "Yes, please," said Jade. Grandma spread the jam on warm bread. Jade took a little bite. "Thank you," said Jade. Mr. Vargas laughed. "Hello again tomorrow?" he asked. Jade nodded and waved.

Gabriel sat at the little table in the library. Ms. Sokolov gave him a fat pencil. "Can you write your name?" she asked. Gabriel held the pencil in his fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The G came out big and wobbly. The A looked like a naughty squiggle. "It won't stay in the lines," Gabriel said.

"Try it again," said Ms. Sokolov. She showed him how to pinch the pencil like a bird holding a twig. Gabriel picked it up. Pinch, pinch. He wrote G-A-B. His tongue peeked out like a little tooth. It was still wobbly, but the G stood up tall.

Every day Gabriel came back to the library. He wrote his name on new paper. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. The letters grew neat and small. "Look!" said Gabriel. He held up the paper. Jovan leaned over. "Your name looks so easy now." Gabriel smiled and wrote it one more time.

Snow fell all night. Mila looked out the window. The whole yard was white. "No school today," Mom said. "It is a snow day."

Mila wanted to see the mail carrier. But the path was deep in snow. Mom got the big shovel. Mila got her little red shovel. They pushed the snow away. Mila made a small pile. Then she made a bigger pile.

Soon the path was flat and clear. "Grown-ups shovel snow off paths," Mom said, "so people can walk without slipping." The mail carrier came up the path. Her boots went tap, tap, tap. "What a nice clear walk," she said. "Thank you, Mila." Mila patted her shovel. "I can do it again tomorrow," she said.

Ayla was at Grandma and Grandpa's house. It was evening. Then all the lights went out. The TV went off too. Everything went dark.

"The power has gone out," said Grandpa. "It is a power cut." Grandma lit a little candle. The flame sat low and small. Grandpa held it carefully. Ayla stayed back, safe and close to Grandma.

Ayla looked out the big window. "Grandma, look!" she said. The house next door was dark. The house across the street was dark too. Every house on the street was dark. "All the houses went out together," said Ayla. "Just like ours."

Grandma smiled. "Yes. Now, let's make shadows on the wall." Ayla stuck up her hand. Her fingers made a butterfly shape. It flapped on the wall, big and soft.

The lights blinked. Then they came back on. "Yay!" said Ayla. "The whole street is bright again!"

Michael went to the library with his class. Mr. Tang sat on a big red rug. He held up a book about a dragon. Jamal sat very still. Wes sat very still too. Michael had a big idea. He wanted to tell it now.

"Mr. Tang! A dragon flew over my house!" he said. Mr. Tang kept reading. Michael talked more. Mr. Tang could not read the words. The story stopped. Jamal looked sad. Wes said, "Michael, my ears can't hear two sounds." Michael whispered, "I am sorry." He put his hand on his knees. He made his mouth a quiet button. He watched Mr. Tang's mouth make the words. The dragon's shadow looked big on the wall. It looked like it might fly!

At last Mr. Tang shut the book. "Now it is your turn, Michael," he said. Michael stood up tall. "A dragon flew over my house," he said. Everyone listened. Everyone waited. Jamal clapped. Wes clapped. "A library sells nothing," said Wes, "but it gives us dragon shadows!" Michael smiled. His turn had come because he waited. He sat down and folded his hands. "Next story, please," he said.

Ibrahim stood in the changing room. He pulled on his swim shorts all by himself. "I did it!" he said. His goggles were in his bag. He put them on his eyes. They went pop, pop over his hair. Niyamat laughed next to him. "Your hair is sticking up like a duck," said Niyamat. "Quack," said Ibrahim.

They walked out to the pool. The sun made the water shiny. Ryleigh was already there with the teacher. "Hello, Ibrahim," said Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya. Ibrahim looked at the pool. One side was full of kids standing up. The water came to their tummies. The other side had big kids. The water came up to their chins.

"Can I swim on that side?" Ibrahim asked. "That is the deep end," said Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya. "We start in the shallow end." Ibrahim stepped in. The water was small on his legs. He could touch the bottom. He kicked and splashed. Then his foot slipped and he started to fall. But the floor was right there. He stood up fast. "Ha! The shallow end caught me," he said. Ryleigh splashed him. Then something touched his toe. It was a rubber duck, floating by all alone. "A duck in the pool!" said Ibrahim. "Quack," said the duck's squeaker. Nobody knew how it got there.

At the end, the big kids went to the deep end. Ibrahim stayed in the shallow end and reached for the duck. The door to the changing room was closed. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya opened it. "Next time, deep end?" asked Ibrahim. "Next time," said Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya. "The duck comes too," said Ibrahim, and held it up high.

Victor had a little green dinosaur. It was soft and squishy. He took it to the school playground. He loved that dinosaur very much.

Victor played on the slide. He played in the sand. Then he looked in his pocket. The dinosaur was gone! "Oh no," said Victor. "I dropped my dinosaur."

Margot and Scarlett came to help. They looked under the slide. They looked by the swing. No dinosaur. Then Victor saw the sand box. He had dug a big hole there. He looked in the hole. There it was! The green dinosaur was sitting in the sand.

Mr. Lombardi walked over. "Where will you keep him next time?" he asked. Victor thought hard. He pointed to his coat pocket. "Right here," said Victor. "The same spot every time." He put the dinosaur in the pocket. He patted it softly. At home, he set a small basket by his bed. The dinosaur went in the basket. Every night, the dinosaur slept there. And every morning, Victor knew just where to look.

Quinn sat down at the dinner table. Her hands were messy from paint. "Wash first," said her dad. Quinn did not want to wait. The soup smelled so good.

She went to the sink. Her dad turned on the water for her. Quinn held out her hands. The water felt cool. Then she rubbed the soap.

Look! The soap made bubbles on her hands. White bubbles, lots of them. Quinn patted them on her chin. Now she had a bubbly soap beard. "I am a bubbly man," she said. She giggled and giggled.

She rinsed the bubbles off. Her dad helped her close the tap. Her hands were clean now. She saw their picture on the wall, a boat on a stormy sea. Back at the table, she picked up her spoon. "All clean," said Quinn, and she ate her warm soup.

Emile was at summer camp. A big red drum sat on the grass. Emile wanted to bang it. But Mamadou got there first. Mamadou banged the drum. Boom, boom, boom.

Emile reached out his hand. He wanted to grab the drum. Ms. Russo put her hand on his arm. "Wait, Emile," she said. Emile let go. He sat down on the grass. He looked up at a white cloud. He wondered, "When will it be my turn?"

Mamadou stopped banging. "Emile, you can play now," he said. Emile took the drum. He banged it. Boom, boom, boom! Mamadou waited and watched. He did not grab.

Then Emile stopped. "Mamadou, your turn," he said. Mamadou banged the drum again. Boom, boom, boom! They went back and forth, one at a time.

At tidy-up time, Emile put the drum in the basket. "Can we share it tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Mamadou. "Boom, boom, boom!"

Hazel sat on the rug at school. Ms. Chowdhury held up a big card. It had a big red A on it. "A," said Ms. Chowdhury. "A is for apple."

Then Hazel looked at her new book. She saw a small a on the page. It looked round and little, not tall and big. Hazel frowned. She put up her hand. "Is that a different letter?" she asked.

Ms. Chowdhury smiled. "No, Hazel. That is the same letter A." She put the big card right next to the small a in the book. Hazel looked at both. Big A, small a. Same letter, two shapes. "Can I try one more?" asked Hazel. "Yes, you can," said Ms. Chowdhury.

Hazel turned the page. She found a big B and a small b. She pointed at them. "Same letter," she said. A little green frog crawled across the window outside. Hazel laughed and waved at it. Then she pointed at her book again and said, "B, b, B, b."

Harper sat on the big rug in the living room. Theo and Oceanne sat next to her. On the TV, a big game was on. Lots of people were running with a ball.

"Which team is mine?" Harper asked. She pointed at the TV. "They all look the same to me!"

Theo laughed. "They do not look the same. That team is red. That team is blue."

Harper looked hard. She saw one group in red shirts. She saw one group in blue shirts. "Oh! Red team and blue team!"

"Each team wears its own colors," said Mr. Kaur from the couch. "So you can tell the two teams apart."

The red team ran fast. A red player kicked the ball. It went into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted. Harper jumped up and down.

Then the weather outside turned rainy. Rain tapped on the window. But inside, the game went on.

"Now I can help," Harper said. She clapped for the red team. "Go red! Go red!"

The blue team got the ball. "Oh no," said Oceanne. "I like blue."

"That is okay," said Theo. "You pick blue. I pick red."

Harper made a kind offer. "You can share my team too, Oceanne."

Oceanne giggled. "No thank you. Blue is mine."

The game went on and on. Harper watched the red shirts run. She watched the blue shirts run. She never mixed them up again.

Mr. Kaur passed out cups of juice. Harper took a big sip. On the TV, the red team kicked the ball again.

"Here it comes!" Harper shouted. "Watch the red one!"

Axel was at the school garden. He had tiny seeds in his hand. He wanted to grow carrots.

"Put them here," said Ms. Rivera. Axel made a little hole. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the dirt down. Then he poured water from a small can.

Every day Axel came. He watered the seeds. The sun shone warm. One day, little green leaves popped up. The water and sun made the seeds grow.

Then Axel saw tiny leaves he did not plant. He pulled one up. Then he grabbed another leaf to pull.

"Stop," said Ms. Rivera. "That one is a carrot. It is not a weed."

"A weed?" asked Axel.

"A weed is a plant growing where we do not want it," she said.

Axel looked closely. The weed had thin, stringy leaves. The carrot had soft, feathery leaves. He let go of the carrot. He pulled the weeds and set them on the road path, where they could not grow back.

Gurbaaz came to help. Thiago came too. They folded paper cups into little pots for new seeds. The wind felt cool on Axel's face.

Soon the carrots grew tall and green. Axel pulled one up. It was orange and long. "My seed did that!" he said.

Ms. Rivera smiled. "Wash it first," she said. They washed it in cool water and shared big, crunchy bites.

Harrison was in his bedroom. His toy dog, Wags, was lost. "Where are you, Wags?" he said. He looked under the bed. He looked in the closet. He looked behind a big green leaf on his poster. One, two, three places. No Wags. Harrison made a sad face in his mirror. Then he heard a bark. Bark, bark! His friend Abdul was at the door. Abdul held Wags. "He was by my shoes," said Abdul. "I am sorry I took him home." Harrison made a big smile in the mirror. His face looked happy now. "See, Abdul! My smile shows I am happy." Abdul smiled too. Harrison gave Wags a little bite of pretend cookie. Then the two boys hugged.

Amelia turned four today. The community hall had balloons and a big cake. Her friends Riggs and Otto ran to the table. On the cake sat four little candles. "Can I light them?" Amelia asked. She reached for the matches.

Dad shook his head. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," he said. He took the matches. Amelia watched him strike one. A small flame jumped up. Then he touched it to each wick. One by one, the candles lit. How did one little flame send light to all four? Amelia leaned in close to see.

"Now you," said Dad. "You make the wish." Amelia thought hard. Riggs and Otto waited with big eyes. Everyone began to sing, loud and happy. Amelia took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four flames went out. Her hair bounced as she clapped. "Dad lit them, and I made them go out!" she said. "Wish time," said Dad. Amelia closed her eyes tight.

Emile sat on the grass at the big sports field. His mom gave him a cookie in a napkin. Luciano and Kashton sat next to him. They all watched the soccer game. The players ran fast up and down the field.

Emile wanted to see a goal. He kicked his feet like he was playing too. Then something odd happened. The referee put a whistle to his mouth. He blew it. Tweet! Every player stopped running. Emile blinked. "Why did they stop?" he asked.

Mr. Morningstar was sitting close by. "The whistle says stop," he said. Emile watched some more. The players ran again. Then the whistle went tweet, and they all stopped again. Emile laughed. The whistle was like a stop sign that players could hear.

Then a player fell down. The referee blew the whistle. All the other players stood still and waited. A coach helped the player up. His knee was not broken, just a little sore. He got up and smiled.

Later the game was done. Emile got to choose what to eat. He chose another cookie. "When we play," he said to Luciano, "I will be the whistle man." He took a big breath and puffed out his cheeks. "Tweet!" said Emile.

Jaxon wore his striped coat on the city bus. He held Dad's hand. The bus would pass the big library soon. "First stop for books," said Dad.

At the library, a man gave Jaxon a small card. It had Jaxon's own name on it. Jaxon saw a book with dinosaurs. "DINOSAURS!" he shouted in a big voice.

A girl at a table looked up. She was reading. So was a man by the window. The librarian put one finger near her lips. Dad bent down. "Quiet voices here," he said softly. "People are reading."

Jaxon made his voice small. "Dinosaur book," he whispered. The girl smiled at him. He gave his card to the librarian. She stamped the book.

On the bus home, Jaxon sat close to Dad. "We read quiet," he whispered, and opened the dinosaur book.

William ran to the sandbox. He wanted the big bucket of trucks. He held the bucket tight. "All mine," he said.

Ari came to the sandbox too. Ari had no trucks. Ari sat on the little chair and looked down. Martin came too. Martin had no trucks. He dug with one clean spoon and nothing else.

Mr. Nasser walked over. "Let's count the trucks," he said. "One, two, three, four, five, six." William counted out loud with him. Six trucks, three friends.

William looked at Ari. Ari looked sad. William put two trucks in front of Ari. Then he put two trucks in front of Martin. He kept two trucks for himself.

"Thank you," said Ari. Martin made a big hill fast. William made a bridge. Ari made a ramp for the trucks. William skipped around the sandbox. He was happy to share.

"Want a turn with my blue truck?" William asked Martin. "Yes please," said Martin. They pushed the truck down the ramp together. Mr. Nasser smiled and sat on the chair to watch.

"More trucks coming!" said Ari. Down the ramp they went, one, two, three, four, five, six.

Ezra stood in the backyard. He had a red beanbag and a hoop. Lenny held a big yellow ball. "Watch me," said Ezra. He threw the beanbag. It missed the hoop and landed on the grass.

"Try again," said Lenny. Ezra threw it again. It missed again. A green frog hopped by the hoop. The frog sat very still. Ezra picked up the beanbag. He threw it one more time. Miss. His eyes felt hot and sharp with tears.

Lenny patted his back. "Keep trying," Lenny said. So Ezra kept trying. He threw the beanbag again and again and again. Then one throw went in. It went right through the hoop. "I did it!" said Ezra. The frog hopped away.

"Now catch," said Lenny. Lenny tossed the big ball. Ezra held out both hands. The ball bounced off. Lenny tossed it again. Ezra missed again. But he kept his hands out. He kept trying, again and again.

Then the ball came down. Both hands caught it. Ezra held the big ball tight. "I caught it!" he said. Lenny clapped and clapped. Ms. Buchanan looked over the fence and smiled. "Nice work, Ezra," she said. Ezra threw the beanbag next. Whoosh. In it went.

Ryan ran to the toy shelf at school. A big basket sat on the floor. It was full of picture cards. Colin tipped it over. All the cards fell out.

"Uh oh," said Ryan. "So many cards." The pile looked like a big mess. Mr. Brown knelt down next to them. "Let's make it easy," he said. "We can sort them. Animals go here. Toys go here. Foods go here."

Ryan picked up a card. It had a cow on it. A cow was an animal. He put it in the animal pile. Colin found a ball. "A ball is a toy," said Colin. He put it in the toy pile. Cali held up a card with bread on it. "Bread is food," she said. She put it in the food pile. Ryan clapped. Each card went to its own group.

Then Ryan found a shiny apple card. He looked and looked. Where did it go? It was food, not a toy. He put it with the bread. "Good sorting, Ryan," said Mr. Brown. Cali gave him a big smile.

Soon all the cards were gone. Three neat piles sat on the mat. Ryan looked at the animal pile. He saw a sheep. "Maybe sheep dream," he whispered. Colin laughed. Ryan put the sheep on top of the pile, right where he could see it.

Eva held her cup at the water table. It was empty. Nothing was inside it at all. She turned it over. Still empty.

"I want it full to the top," said Eva. Aurelia stood next to her. Sullivan stood on her other side. Sullivan had a big cup. Eva had a small cup.

Sullivan poured water fast. It went splash over the edge. "Too fast," said Aurelia. "Try slow."

Eva wondered how slow she should go. She tipped the jug just a little. Drip, drip, drip. That was very slow. "The cup is still empty," she said. She tipped a bit more. Now the water ran quick and smooth.

"Stop, stop!" said Aurelia. Eva stopped. The water sat right at the top. "My cup is full," said Eva. She looked at Sullivan's cup. His was empty now. All his water was on the table in a big puddle. Ms. Ricci came with a towel and wiped it up.

"Want to try again?" asked Ms. Ricci. Sullivan poured slow this time. His big cup filled all the way up. Eva clapped. The two full cups sat side by side on the table.

"Snack time," said Ms. Ricci. Eva carried her cup past the window. Outside, the children ran fast on the playground. Eva chewed her apple and looked at her cup. Full now. Empty before. She took a big drink.

Quinn sat in the family car. They were going to the beach! She held her toy crab. One claw was broken, but she loved it still. "Can I splash in the waves now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "At the beach, you go near the water only with a grown-up watching." The car stopped. The sea looked big and blue. Quinn jumped out. She wanted to run to the water right away. But she stopped and stood still on the sand. She waited. Dad put down the big bag. Then he held her hand. "Now we can splash," he said. Quinn ran to the waves with Dad. The water tickled her toes. She laughed so hard her tooth felt funny. "The water came in!" she said. "And then it went out again!" Dad smiled. "Waves do that." Quinn splashed and splashed. Her crab got a little splash too.

Isaiah sat at the table with a dry cracker. He wanted to know one big thing. Was his cracker a square? He was not sure.

"I will find out," said Isaiah. He ran to fetch a piece of string. He laid the string on one side. He cut it to fit. Then he moved the string to the next side. It fit! He counted out loud. "One side, two sides, three sides, four sides." Every side was just as long as the string. All four sides were the same length.

"It is a square!" said Isaiah. He held up the cracker. His mom clapped. Then Isaiah looked at his plate. He saw a round cookie. "That one is a circle," he said. He took a big happy bite.

Bennett stood at the bus stop with his dad. The sky had been rainy. Now it was sunny again. Bennett wore his rain boots and his yellow coat.

"I want to splash," said Bennett.

"Look down," said Dad.

Bennett looked. The rain had left a big puddle on the ground. He stepped in it. Splash! Water went up and up. His boots kept his feet dry. Bennett laughed and laughed.

The wind blew his coat. It flapped like a flag. Soon the bus came. A girl got off. It was Vayda from his class!

"You met me at the bus stop," said Vayda.

"I did," said Bennett. "Want to splash with me?"

Vayda jumped in the puddle too. Splash, splash! They were both happy. Dad held their hands all the way home.

Snow was falling outside the daycare window. Andrew watched the snow ride down on the wind. He clapped his hands.

"I want to draw the snow," said Andrew. Ms. Pereira gave him white paper. Andrew took his white crayon. He drew and drew. But he could not see the snow. The paper was white too.

Andrew made a sad face. He tried again. Still no snow. His friend Marlee came to look.

"I know a trick," said Marlee. "Try blue paper. Fresh snow is white, so it will show." She gave Andrew a big blue sheet. Andrew drew with his white crayon. The white snow popped out on the blue.

"Snow!" said Andrew. "White snow!" He drew more snow. He drew a big white hill. He drew a little white snowman with a yellow scarf. Marlee drew a red hat on the snowman. Carlos drew green trees under the snow.

Ms. Pereira hung the picture up high. "Look at all that snow," she said. Andrew pointed at the window. The real snow fell and fell. His paper snow fell too, all over the blue.

Andrew smiled. "More snow," he said. "More snow, please."

Thomas ran into the yard. The grass was wet and cold on his toes. Then he saw it. A small grey feather lay by the big tree.

"Look, Mommy, look!" he called. He picked it up. It was soft like his cat's tail. He petted it with one finger.

"Birds are animals that have feathers," said Mommy. "So a bird lost this one."

Thomas looked up. He looked at the tree. He looked at the roof. "Bird!" he shouted. A fat bird sat on the fence. It had grey feathers, all over!

The bird flew down. It hop, hop, hopped. It found a crumb. Then it flew away. Thomas waved.

"Come back!" he called. He held the feather up high. He was proud of it.

Inside, Mommy gave him toast and apple slices. Thomas ate his food. He put the feather on the window sill.

"Maybe the bird will see it," said Thomas. He watched and watched the yard. The toast was warm and good. Then he saw something move outside.

A bird was back on the fence. "It came back!" Thomas shouted. He ran to the window and tapped the glass, very soft. "Hi, bird. Hi!"

Andrew was drawing at the table. His mom was cooking at the stove. She stirred the big pot.

Andrew sniffed with his nose. "I smell something yummy," he said. He closed his eyes. The smell was warm. It was a little sour, like lemon. "Is it soup?" he asked.

"Yes, tomato soup," said Mom. "You smelled it before you saw it. Good nose!"

Andrew laughed. He wanted to taste it. But the pot was hot. Mom said, "Stay back. I will pour it."

Andrew touched his cold cup of milk. His ears heard the soup bubble. His eyes watched Mom pour. The bowl was red like the ocean is blue, all one color.

Raya knocked at the door. "I smell soup!" she said from the hall.

"Come and see," said Andrew. "We can dip bread together."

Mom set out two bowls. "Blow on it first," she said. Andrew blew. Then he took a taste. "Mmm," he said. "My nose was right!"

Billie sat on the big gray bus with her mama. She was going to see a doctor today. Billie held her small toy cat. The bus hummed under her feet. A man looked at a computer up front. Billie chose the seat by the window.

"I do not like doctors," Billie said. "They look at my whole body." Her mama smiled. "This one is different," she said. "You will see."

At the office, a nice man in a white coat said hello. "My name is Mr. Kim, the dentist," he said. He did not look at her arms. He did not look at her tummy. He looked only at her teeth. He counted them one by one. "A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth," he said.

Billie sat very still. She opened her mouth wide. Mr. Kim gave her a little mirror. She saw her teeth in it, small and white. "They look like tiny moons," she said.

On the bus ride home, Billie hugged her toy cat. "The dentist looked at my teeth," she told the man with the computer. "Only my teeth." She smiled her moon-white smile all the way home.

Alexis sat in the family car. His mama drove to the doctor. "I have a question," Alexis said. "Will the shot hurt?" "Just a tiny pinch," said mama.

At the office, a nurse asked Alexis to stand on the scale. Alexis wiggled his toes. The numbers jumped up and down. They would not stop. "The scale shows how much you weigh," the nurse said. "Stand still." Alexis stood very still, like a statue. Then the numbers stopped jumping. One number stayed put. "I did it!" said Alexis.

Then it was time for the shot. Alexis felt shy. He hid his arm behind his back. The nurse smiled. "Look at your teddy," she said. Alexis hugged teddy tight. He felt one small pinch. Then it was over. "All done," said the nurse. Alexis got a shiny bandaid with stars.

Back in the car, Alexis held up his arm. "Look, mama! Stars!"

Eli looked out the window at daycare. The sky was stormy and dark. Big rain drops hit the glass.

"No park today," said Mr. Watanabe. "The rain is too heavy."

Eli felt sad. He wanted to swing and slide. Wallace felt sad too. His lip went down and his eyes got wet.

Then Mr. Watanabe got two big blankets. "Let's build a fort," he said. Eli helped drape the blankets over the wood chairs. Wallace stepped inside. "Come in, Eli!" he called.

Eli crawled in too. It was cozy and warm inside. The fort wobbled, so Mr. Watanabe held the wood steady. "Safe now," he said.

Eli smiled big. His sad feeling was gone. Now he felt happy. "Rain made the park stop," said Eli, "but rain made our fort day!"

"Again tomorrow?" asked Wallace.

"Yes!" said Eli.

Brielle sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump down the road. She could see the pizza shop near the corner. "Pizza," said Brielle. "Yes," said her dad. "We will get pizza soon."

Brielle was thirsty. There was a juice box in the bag by her feet. "Give me juice!" she said. Her dad did not pass it to her. He kept both hands on the wheel. "Try again," he said. Brielle thought for a moment. "Juice, please," she said. Her dad smiled in the mirror. Then he reached back at the red light and gave her the juice box.

Brielle drank her juice. It did not hurt her tummy. It felt good and cold. "Thank you," she said. "You are welcome," said her dad.

At the pizza shop, the man gave Brielle one warm slice. "Please may I have more?" she asked. The man laughed and gave her a second slice. Brielle took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "More, please!"

Lena went to the library on a sunny day. She saw a big red truck book on the table. She wanted it very much.

Leo had the truck book in his hands. Lena grabbed for it. Leo held on tight. Mr. Cheung knelt down beside them. "We say please when we ask for something," he said. Lena let go of the book. She took a breath. "May I have the truck book, please?" she asked.

Leo looked at the book. Then he looked at Lena. "You can have it after me," he said. Lena sat on the rug and waited. She counted the pictures on the wall. One cat, two cats, three cats. Soon Leo held out the book. "Your turn," he said. Lena hugged the sweet red truck book to her chest. "Thank you," she said. "This is the best day at the library."

Sienna went to the library with her dad. Mr. Russo showed her a new tablet.

"Can I draw?" Sienna asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Russo. He pushed the button. The screen lit up. Lots of small pictures sat on the screen.

"Those are icons," said Mr. Russo.

Sienna looked and looked. She wanted the drawing app. She saw a little paintbrush. She tapped it with one finger. The drawing app opened! What a surprise.

She drew a big red cat. Then she drew a sun. She liked the sun best.

"Time to put it away," said Mr. Russo. Sienna pressed the button. The screen went dark. The tablet was off.

"Did I do it?" she asked.

"You did it," said her dad.

Sienna hugged the tablet gently. "Bye-bye, paintbrush," she said.

Henri ran to the sand toys at the park. He wanted the orange shovel first. But Augustin was already digging with it. "Can I have a turn next?" Henri asked. "Yes, after I make my hole," said Augustin.

Henri waited. He watched a turtle crawl near the pond. The turtle went slowly, slowly, step by step. Then Augustin held out the shovel. "Your turn," he said. Henri dug a big hole all by himself.

Then Henri saw Collins walk away. Collins had left trucks all over the grass. Henri ran after him. "The trucks are still out," said Henri. Collins looked back. "Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with," said Collins. He ran back and picked up two trucks. Henri picked up two too. They put them in the basket side by side.

Ms. Li smiled at the clean grass. "Time for a snack, then the turtles can sleep," she said. Henri waved to the turtle. "See you tomorrow, turtle," he said. And he carried the empty basket with both hands.

Anthony stood at the sink in the backyard kitchen door. He had carrots from the farmers' market. The carrots had dirt on them. "Why are they dirty?" he asked. His dad said, "They grew in the ground." Anthony held a carrot under the water. He rubbed it with his fingers. The dirt washed away. The water turned brown in the sink. Then the carrot was clean and orange.

Anthony laid the clean carrots on a towel on the floor of the counter. He scrubbed a potato too. The potato had more dirt. He rubbed and rubbed. The water splashed a little. The potato came out clean.

The sky looked stormy, but the rain held off. Anthony's dad used the stove. Anthony watched from far away. Soon the carrots and potatoes were soft and sweet. "You rinsed the dirt off," said Dad. Anthony smiled and took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "My carrots taste good."

Blake sat at Grandma's big table. Her plate had toast on it. The toast was hot, so Blake waited. She counted while she waited. One, two, three, four, five. Now the toast was warm.

Then Blake wanted her favorite book. Grandma had a shelf full of books. "Which one?" asked Grandma. Blake pointed and pointed. She got a blue book. Not that one. She got a fat book. Not that one.

Grandma held up a little red book. "This one has a name," said Grandma. "It is called The Sleepy Bunny." The words on the front said The Sleepy Bunny. Blake looked at the words. "The Sleepy Bunny," she said slowly.

Grandma nodded. Blake held the book. She opened the front cover first. She turned the pages one by one, all the way to the back. After the story, Blake helped wash up. The plate went into the sink with a splash.

"One, two, three," said Blake, drying the plate. "Can we read The Sleepy Bunny again tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Grandma. "The Sleepy Bunny will be right here, waiting on the shelf."

Axel was awake early. He ran to the kitchen in his sock feet. "I want to help cook," he said. His dad smiled. "You can help make pancakes."

Axel used his eyes to watch the bowl. He used his ears to hear the pan go sizzle. His dad poured the batter, because the pan was hot. Axel stood far away, safe.

Then something smelled good. Axel used his nose. "I can smell it!" he said. "The pancakes smell sweet."

The pancakes were ready at last. Axel used his tongue to taste one. "Yum," he said. He used his hands to touch the blueberries. They felt little and round.

Axel carried his plate to the back door. He sat on the step. The grass was right there, wet and green. Axel took off his socks. He put his bare toes in the grass. He wiggled them.

"The grass is soft," said Axel. "My toes feel it!" His toes felt the soft grass under them, and it tickled. He laughed and kicked his feet.

His dad came out with his own plate. He sat down too. "Nice spot," said Dad. Axel ate his pancake and wiggled his toes some more. "Grass feet!" he said.

David ran to the paint table at summer camp. He wore his new blue shirt. He wanted to paint a dragon with a wide, wide tail.

Mr. Hoffmann held up an apron. "Paint goes on clothes," he said. "An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes." David put on the apron. He was ready.

Isra and Catherine sat down too. Isra picked red paint. Catherine picked yellow paint. David picked blue paint. "This is blue," said David. "My shirt is blue too."

Then David wanted a green dragon. He looked and looked. There was no green paint. He thought and thought. He dripped blue into the yellow cup. He mixed it with his brush. The paint turned green! "Magic!" said Catherine. Isra clapped her hands.

David painted a big green dragon. The dragon had a wide tail and red eyes. Paint splashed on the apron. David looked down at his new blue shirt. It was clean! He felt a happy feeling all over.

Isra dripped red into the yellow cup. Orange paint! Catherine dripped red into the blue. Purple paint! "We are paint wizards," said David. He waved his brush like a wand.

"More green for the dragon," said David. He mixed and mixed.

text:
Isabella ran into the kitchen. Her mom was baking bread. A big paper bag of flour sat on the counter. The kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Isabella sniffed with her nose. "Mmm," she said. "I smell bread!"

Her mom opened the bag. A little puff of flour went up. It floated like soft snow. Isabella got some on her cheeks. She felt it with her fingers. It was soft, not hard like a spoon. "The flour flew at my face," she said. "But my eyes feel fine." She blinked and blinked.

She looked in the shiny toaster. She saw little white bits on her eyelashes. "Look, Mom! My lashes have flour on them." Her mom smiled. "Your eyelashes helped keep the dust out of your eyes," she said. Isabella blinked again. Her lashes were like tiny umbrellas. Eyelashes keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes, she thought. What a job for such little hairs!

Then came a small surprise. Her mom gave her a tiny taste of honey on a spoon. Isabella touched it with her tongue. "Sweet!" she said. She heard the oven door close with a soft thump. Soon the bread would be ready. Isabella blinked one more time. "Thank you, eyelashes," she whispered.

Maya went to the pool with her father. It was early, and the water was calm. Maya wanted to swim, but she could not swim yet.

Mr. Murphy said, "Hold the edge of the pool, Maya. Now kick your legs." Maya held the edge with her hands. She kicked her legs. Her feet made big splashes! Splash, splash, splash. Mr. Murphy got wet and laughed. "Kick more," he said. So Maya held on tight and kicked again. More splashes flew up. Her friend Cormac held the edge too. He kicked beside her. Splash, splash, splash.

"Your legs are getting strong," said Mr. Murphy. Maya practiced every day. Hold the edge. Kick, kick, kick. One day her father counted, "One, two, three!" Maya let go and kicked all by herself. She glided through the water like a little fish. "I did it!" Maya called. "I swam!"

Maverick ran into the backyard. The sun was out. He wore his sunny day hat. Then the sky turned grey. Big drops fell. "Rain!" said Maverick. He ran to the porch and felt safe there. His dad handed him a rain coat.

The rain stopped. But the trees began to move. "Why are the trees dancing?" Maverick asked. His dad smiled. "It is windy." Maverick watched the wind make the trees sway. Leaves blew all around the yard.

Maverick chased the leaves. He chased a red one. He chased a yellow one. The yellow one slipped right out of his hand. Then a leaf landed on his head. He laughed. Abir came over with his coat on. "Where did the leaf go?" Abir asked. Maverick pointed up. It was flying over the fence.

Elena waited at the bus stop with Ms. Jung. The wind blew cold. "I want to put my coat on all by myself," Elena said. Ms. Jung smiled. "Show me," she said.

Elena laid her coat on the bench. It looked like a little pillow. She slid one arm in. Then the other arm. Now came the tricky part, the zipper. She pulled it up. It stuck halfway. Elena felt dizzy from looking down so hard. She planted her feet and pulled again. Zip! The zipper went all the way to the top.

"I did it! All by myself!" Elena shouted. Her friend Ariel ran up to the bus stop. "You did it all by yourself?" Ariel asked. "Yes! All by myself!" said Elena. The bus came down the street.

At school, Ariel dropped her coat on the floor. Later, Ariel could not find it anywhere. "My coat is lost," she cried. Then Elena pointed near the wall. "Look! Hang it on a hook," she said. Ariel hung her coat on a hook. It stayed up high. It did not touch the floor at all. "Tomorrow I will put my coat on all by myself," said Ariel, "and hang it on the hook."

Hazel woke up with very puffy hair. One part stood up like a little tree. She patted it. It bounced right back. "Oh no," she said. "My hair has tangles."

She went to the kitchen. Her dad was there. He poured milk into her cup. It made a splashy sound at the bottom. The kitchen was quiet and warm. Hazel showed him her hair. "Can tangles come out?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "Try your brush. Go slow so it does not pull."

Hazel found her brush. She counted the tangles. One, two, three. She brushed the first one. Slow, slow, slow. Ouch, a tiny bit. Then it was smooth. She brushed the second one. It went smooth too. "Look at that," she said. She brushed the last one. Her hair lay down flat and shiny.

Then someone knocked. It was Bella from next door. Bella's hair was sticking up too. "My hair is a bird nest," said Bella. Hazel held up her brush. "Brushing gets the tangles out," she said. "One, two, three, then you are done." Bella sat on the little stool. Hazel brushed very slowly. One tangle, two tangles, all gone. Bella shook her head and her hair flew like a pony tail. "Silly hair," said Hazel. "It sleeps all wild." Bella laughed. Then they ate their toast.

Milan was in the backyard. His friend Adonis came to play. Milan had a hoop and a beanbag. He threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. He threw it again. It hit the hoop and fell out.

"You were busy looking down," said Adonis. "Look at the hoop." Milan looked at the hoop. He threw the beanbag. It went in! Milan jumped up and down.

Then Adonis rolled a big ball across the grass. Milan had his hands in his pockets. The ball bumped his legs and rolled away.

"Try again," said Adonis. Milan held his arms out. He kept his hands open. Adonis rolled the ball. The ball came right into his hands. Milan caught it!

"Now me," said Adonis. He held his arms out too. Milan rolled the ball to him slowly. Adonis caught it with both hands.

"Nice catch!" said Milan. He picked up his cup of water from the step. He drank it all up. Then he held out his arms again. "One more!"

Matthew put on his red coat. One arm went in. The other arm went in too. Now came the zipper. Matthew pulled it up, up, up. Then it stopped. It would not move at all.

Matthew looked down. His sweater was caught in the zipper. He pulled hard. The zipper did not budge. Would it stay stuck forever? Then Matthew tried something new. He pulled the zipper down, just a little. The sweater came loose. The zipper was free.

Matthew pulled the zipper up again. This time it slid all the way to the top. He was warm and dry inside his coat. "I did it," said Matthew. His mom smiled and took his hand. They walked into the big grocery store together. "Can we look at the train set?" asked Matthew.

Athena sat at the big table in the library. Mr. Fischer gave her paper and pink paint. "Make something pretty," he said.

Athena painted a wing on one half of her paper. Then she folded the paper. She pressed it down with her hands. She waited. She ate her cookie while she waited.

Athena opened the paper. She gasped. There were two wings now! The paint had gone on the other half. "A butterfly!" she said. The wings matched.

Madyson leaned over. "Mine looks wrong," she said. "Only one wing." So Athena folded Madyson's paper too. They waited and waited.

Madyson opened her paper. Two wings! The two girls held up their butterflies. "Let's make one for Lianna," said Athena, and she picked up the brush.

Bennett stood in the kitchen. The toast sat on his plate. Mom had made it, and now it was cool. Bennett wanted butter on it. He wanted to do it all by himself.

He held the knife. He poked the toast with the pointy tip. The butter made a hole. The toast tore into little bits. "Oh no," said Bennett. Mom sat down next to him. "Try the flat side," she said. "Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread." Bennett turned the knife over. He pushed the flat side across the bread. Would it work? The butter swept over the toast in a smooth, yellow sheet. "Look at that!" said Bennett. The toast was not torn at all.

Next came the milk. Bennett picked up the jug with two hands. He poured slowly into his cup. Not one drop spilled. He carried his toast and milk to the table. Mom poured the last of the milk into a bowl for the cat. Bennett took a big bite. "I did it," he said.

Lydia sat in the school library with her friend Blair. They had a big pile of yellow blocks. Mr. Takahashi gave them two baskets. "Count them," he said.

Lydia put four blocks in her basket. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Blair had six blocks in his basket. Lydia pointed at Blair's basket. "You have more," she said. Blair smiled.

Then Mr. Takahashi handed Lydia one more block. She put it in her basket. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." Lydia's eyes got big. She picked up another block from the pile and added it too. "Six," she said. She looked at both baskets. "Now we have the same."

Blair added one more to his basket and counted, "Seven." Lydia laughed and reached for the pile again. "My turn," she said.

Josephine ran onto the soccer field with her team. Her friend Jethro ran beside her. "Kick it to me!" he called.

The ball came to Josephine. She kicked. The ball went past the goal. She hung her head.

Then Miguel yelled, "Good try, Josephine!" The other kids yelled too. "Try again! Try again!" Even Mr. Quinn clapped. Josephine laughed and stood up tall.

Soon the ball came back to her. She looked at the goal. She kicked hard. The ball went in! "Hooray!" said the team.

Then Jethro kicked and missed. The ball rolled into a slimy, muddy puddle. Jethro looked sad.

Josephine knew just what to do. "Good try, Jethro!" she called. The whole team cheered with her. "Try again! Try again!"

Jethro picked up the ball. He wiped the mud off on the grass. Then he kicked it far across the field.

"Nice job!" said Mr. Quinn.

Josephine held Jethro's hand as they ran back. "We cheer for everyone," she said. "Even when we miss."

Madelyn put on her little apron. Today was cooking class at school. Ms. Demetriou held up a spoon. "This is our tool for butter," she said. The bread was already toasted and cool. Madelyn dipped the spoon in butter. She spread it slow and soft. The toast turned shiny and gold. Zaiden made a butter mountain on his toast. "Mine has a snow hill," he said with a laugh.

Next came the milk. Madelyn held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. Cleo clapped. "Nice pouring," she said. "You are polite to the table," said Madelyn, and everyone giggled.

Then the bell went ring. Class was over. Madelyn started to walk away. The milk was still on the table. She ran back and picked it up. "Milk goes back in the fridge," she said. She opened the door and set it inside. The milk sat in the cold. Madelyn waved to it. "See you tomorrow," she said. Then she ate her toast, all gone.

Luke sat in the big waiting room. Today he would see the dentist for the first time. Rain tapped on the window. Luke watched the drops run down the glass.

Romane sat next to him. She had a little bag. "Look," she said. She pulled out two toothbrushes. One was blue. One was green. "The blue one is my brother's," she said. "I took it by mistake."

Luke looked at the blue brush. "Can I try it?" he asked.

"No," said Romane. "Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes."

"Oh," said Luke. "Where is yours?"

Romane looked in her bag again. She dug past a book and some money for the dentist. Then she found it. The green one. "This one is mine," she said. She put the blue one back in the bag. She would give it to her brother at home.

Luke smiled. He had his own toothbrush at home too. It had a rocket on it.

The door opened. Ms. Taylor, the helper, said, "Luke, it is your turn." Luke stood up tall. He held his dad's hand. Romane waved. "Bye, Luke," she called.

Luke walked through the door.

Isaiah had a bath before bed. Mama washed his curly hair. Then Isaiah jumped out of the tub. He ran down the hall. Drip, drip, drip went the water. It made little wet spots on the floor.

"I forgot something," said Isaiah. He ran back to the tub. His blue towel was hanging there. He picked it up. He rubbed his arms. He rubbed his tummy. He rubbed his curly hair too. The water went into the towel. His skin was dry now.

"Why is my tummy dry?" Isaiah asked. "The towel dried me," said Mama. She smiled. "Good thing you came back for it."

Isaiah put on his soft pajamas. They went on easy now, because he was dry. He drank a little milk. Then Mama read him a story. His puppy curled up on the bed. His tail went swish, swish.

"Sleep now," said Mama. Isaiah closed his eyes. The puppy gave one small yawn.

Leo sat on the big red couch at Mr. Wu's house. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Leo's friend Willa sat next to him with her milk.

"Who is winning?" asked Leo.

"I forgot," said Willa. She spun her cup and got a little dizzy. "Maybe the blue team. Or the red team!"

Mr. Wu laughed. "Look up there," he said. He pointed at the TV. "That is the scoreboard."

Leo looked. The scoreboard had two big numbers on it. One number was for each team. The blue team had the bigger number.

"The blue team is winning!" said Leo. He clapped his hands.

The red team kicked the ball into the net. The scoreboard changed. Now the numbers were the same.

"It's a tie!" said Willa.

"Look at that," said Leo. "The scoreboard always knows. I never have to remember!"

Leo dreamed of the day he would play in a big game too. But for now, he sipped his milk and watched the numbers go up and up.

"Willa, check the scoreboard," he said. "Quick, quick!"

The blue team scored again. Leo jumped up and did a happy dance.

Daniel was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to make soup for the whole family. Grandpa said yes. Daniel put a big pot on the table. He put in carrots and potatoes. Then he held up an onion. "This one too," he said.

Grandpa cut the onion with a knife. The knife went chop, chop, chop. Then Grandpa's eyes began to water. Tears ran down his face. "Grandpa, are you sad?" asked Daniel. "Do you miss your car?"

Grandpa laughed and wiped his eyes. "No, no. The onion did it. Grown-ups' eyes sting and water when they cut onions." Daniel giggled. "Silly onion! You made Grandpa cry!"

Daniel stirred the pot from his chair. The soup bubbled and smelled so good. Soon Mom and Grandma came to eat. Everyone slurped it up.

"I helped!" said Daniel. He gave his loose tooth a little wiggle. Grandpa hugged him and said, "Best soup ever, my little chef."

Muhammad stood at the art table with his friend Viktor. He picked a red crayon. His eyes saw the bright red on the paper. He heard the glue bottles click as Viktor put them away.

Then Ms. Vargas turned on the blender in the little kitchen corner. The blender was very loud. Muhammad did not like the big sound. He put his hands over his ears. The loud sound got smaller. It was quieter now, like a soft hum. Muhammad peeked at Viktor. Viktor covered his ears too, and smiled.

"The blender stops soon," said Ms. Vargas. She watched the blender from the counter. Soon it went quiet all by itself. Muhammad took his hands off his ears.

Ms. Vargas gave them each a cup of pear smoothie. Muhammad touched the cold cup with his fingers. He smelled the sweet pear. He took a sip and the taste was yummy. Viktor drank his all up.

"My tummy feels happy, not sleepy," said Viktor. Muhammad laughed. His classmate Mattias ran over, his shirt tail flying out behind him.

"Can I have some too?" Mattias asked.

"Sit here," said Muhammad, and he patted the chair next to him.

Emile was at Grandpa's house. Rain tapped on the window. The sky looked stormy and grey. "Let's write your name," said Grandpa. Emile dug in the big drawer. He found a fat red pencil. He held it in his fist, like a spoon.

He pushed the pencil on a square of white paper. His lines went every which way. The letters did not look like letters. Emile frowned. Grandpa sat close. "Try two fingers on top," he said. Emile pinched the pencil near the tip. He pressed down. A clean straight line appeared! "Again!" he shouted. He made another line, then another.

Emile wrote E, M, I, L, E. "Mine is all straight lines," he said. Grandpa wrote HELLO under it. Emile leaned in close. "Your O goes round and round," he said. "Mine never does that!" He traced the O with his finger. It felt curvy, like a slide. Then he drew a big red O of his own. "Look, Grandpa! Round letters and straight letters!" He held the paper up to the window, and the stormy sky made his red letters glow.

Scarlett was four today. Her party was at the big park. There was a table with cups of juice. Gray clouds sat far away in the sky. Scarlett sat down to open her presents.

First she opened a small box. It was a red ball from Katherine. Then Scarlett saw a big box. She jumped up and ran to it. She pulled off the ribbon fast.

Katherine looked down at her shoes. Scarlett stopped. She held the red ball. She ran back to Katherine.

"Thank you for my ball," said Scarlett.

Katherine smiled big. "You are welcome!"

Then Gurbaaz gave Scarlett a bunny. "Thank you, Gurbaaz," said Scarlett.

"You say thank you, and your friend smiles," said Scarlett. Ms. Pritchard poured more juice, and everyone clapped for the birthday girl.

Eloise planted seeds at the farm. She planted peas, carrots and tomatoes. Her friend Jaxx helped dig. Safiya patted the soil down. Then they watered every row.

But the next day, Eloise forgot something. "Where are the tomatoes?" she asked. The little plants all looked the same. Ms. Brown smiled. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," she said. Eloise got a big idea. She drew a tomato on one card. She drew a pea on another. She drew a long orange carrot too. She stuck each label in the soil by its row. "Peas, carrots, tomatoes," she said. "Peas, carrots, tomatoes."

Every day the seeds grew a little more. The labels stayed in their spots. Jaxx read them out loud. "Peas, carrots, tomatoes. Peas, carrots, tomatoes." Safiya counted the labels. One, two, three.

At last a red tomato peeked out. It grew right by the tomato label. Eloise felt proud. "The label kept the secret," she said. "It told us where you live, little tomato." Jaxx picked it gently with both hands. Safiya laughed and held it up to the sun. "Peas, carrots, tomatoes," Eloise sang, all the way home.

Miles sat in a big chair at the barbershop. He was scared of the scissors. His dad stood right beside him and held his hand. "The scissors will not touch you," Dad said.

Mr. Vargas came over with a soft blue cape. "This cape keeps the cut hair off your clothes," he said. He put it around Miles' shoulders. Miles looked down. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell. They landed on the cape. They did not land on his shirt. "It works!" Miles said.

Mr. Vargas laughed. "You can be a cape hero next time," he said. Miles giggled. He patted the cape like a superhero. When the haircut was done, Mr. Vargas brushed off the hairs. Miles jumped down. His shirt was all clean.

"Can we come back next month?" Miles asked Dad. Dad smiled and took the key from his pocket. "Yes," he said. "We can come back."

David went to the store with his dad. He saw a big cart and a small basket. "I can push the small one," said David. He pushed it fast, then slow, down the aisle.

David wanted to help carry things. He saw a big box of cans. He pulled and pulled. The box did not move. It was too heavy. Then he saw a feather pillow. It was fuzzy and soft. He picked it up with one hand. It was light. "This one is easy," said David. He gave the pillow a hug.

Rayne and Braelyn were at the store too. Rayne patted the big box. "That one is heavy," Rayne said. "Heavy and light are opposites." David put the light pillow in his basket. "My basket is full," he said. Dad smiled and took his hand.

It was bedtime. Jackson brushed his teeth in the bathroom. Then he ran to his room.

Jackson had a plan. He took out his crayons. He wanted to write a note for his dad. Jackson loved the playground, so he wrote, "LETSGOTHEPLAYGROUND." He put the paper under his pillow. His tummy felt happy and jumpy.

Dad came in to tuck him in. Jackson held up the note. "Read it, Dad!" Dad looked and looked. He turned the paper sideways. "Hmm. I cannot read this yet." Jackson's face went sad.

Dad picked up Jackson's bedtime book. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He pointed at the page. "See the words? There is a space between one word and the next." Jackson leaned in close. He saw the little gaps. The words sat apart, like friends on a bench.

Jackson took his crayon. He drew little gaps in his note. Now it said, "LETS GO THE PLAYGROUND." Dad read it out loud. "Let's go the playground! Yes, tomorrow we can go." Jackson laughed and clapped. Dad kissed his head. "Sleep now, my writer."

Jackson hugged the note to his chest. "Goodnight, words," he whispered.

James went to the store with his dad. He held Dad's hand. The store was big and bright.

"I want a toy animal," said James. He saw a shelf of toys. There was a pink pig. There was a little dog. There was a big cow. James picked up the dog. "A dog is an animal," he said.

His friend Khai was there too. Khai pointed at a toy fish. "Look, a fish!"

James shook his head. "A fish is not an animal. It has no legs. The dog has legs. The cow has legs."

Khai held the toy fish. He swam it through the air. "It is an animal," said Khai. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals."

James looked at the fish. Then he looked at the dog. Then he looked at the cow. "Fish too?" he asked. "Fish too," said Khai.

Dad smiled. "You can pick one toy animal," said Dad. James looked and looked. The pink pig was soft. The dog was soft too.

Then James saw a little toy forest. A deer stood in the trees. The deer had legs. "Is a deer an animal?" James asked. "Yes," said Dad. "But the fish is too. Legs or no legs."

James hugged the toy fish. "The fish won't hurt me," he said. "It is soft." He put the fish in the cart. Khai waved goodbye.

At home, James put the fish on his bed. "Swim, fish," he said. "You are my animal." The fish sat still, and James smiled.

Arthur was at summer camp. It was time for a juicy watermelon snack. Mr. He called everyone to the water table.

Arthur pumped the soap. He rubbed his hands and counted with Aidan. One, two, three, all the way to twenty.

Then Arthur ran to the bench. His hands felt slippery. The soap was still on them. He looked at his palms. They shined and slid against each other.

Arthur went back to the tap. He held his hands under the water. The water ran over his fingers. The slippery soap slid away. The water carried it down the drain. Now his hands felt smooth and clean, not slippery at all.

Tatiana was next to him. Her hands were still slippery too. "Rinse under the water," said Arthur. "The water washes the soap off." Tatiana rinsed her hands. She watched the soap bubbles swirl away.

The three friends sat on the springy grass by the picnic table. They talked about the tadpoles in the pond. Arthur bit into his watermelon slice. His clean hands held it tight. The juice ran down his chin, and he laughed.

Aurora went to the store with her mom. The store had a big window by the door. Sun came in through the window. Aurora wanted new stickers for her art box.

She saw the stickers on a high shelf. They were too high. "Mom, can you help me, please?" she asked. Her mom reached up with a smile. "I can help you," she said.

Aurora was so happy. She spun around fast. Then she bumped a shelf. Apples rolled everywhere. Thump, thump, thump. Her friend Zoravar was there with his dad. An apple hit Zoravar's foot. He rubbed his toe.

"I am sorry," said Aurora. Zoravar looked at her face. He saw she felt bad. He smiled a little. "It's okay," he said. "You said sorry." Then they picked up the apples together. One by one, they put them back. The man at the store said, "Thank you for helping."

Aurora got her new stickers. "Thank you, Mom," she said. On the ride home, she held them tight. "Stickers for my art box," she said.

Lucy sat in the backyard with her paint. She was painting a big yellow sun. Her friend Memphis came over on his bike. He rode round and round the tree. Then he stopped to look.

"Can I touch the sun?" Memphis asked.

Lucy nodded. Memphis put one finger on the painting. The yellow sun smudged. It spread into a wobbly smear. "Oh no," said Lucy. "My sun is all blurry now."

Lucy touched the paint too. Her finger came away yellow. The paint was still wet and gooey. She wondered, what would happen if she waited? The sun looked wet now, but paint can change.

So Lucy and Memphis sat on the grass. They watched the painting. They watched and they waited. A ladybug crawled by. The wind licked the paper's corner. The sun began to look dry.

Lucy touched the very edge. Her finger stayed clean. "It's dry now!" she said. She was brave enough to touch the middle. The paint did not smear. It stayed smooth and bright.

Lucy painted a new sun on the other side. This time she said, "We wait. We don't touch." Memphis counted to ten, very slowly. Then he said, "Ten!"

Lucy smiled and held up her painting. "The sun waited for us," she said.

Elijah stood at the train station. He held a big red sign. It said GRANDMA in wobbly letters. It was hard to write letters that big.

The train rolled in. It was long and shiny. The doors went whoosh. People walked out one by one.

Then Elijah saw her. "Grandma!" he shouted. Grandma hugged him tight. Her coat smelled like flowers.

"Grandma, you are staying at my house for a whole week," said Elijah. "Are you my friend Andie's grandma too?"

Grandma laughed. "No, sweet pea. I am your mommy's mom."

Elijah blinked. "My mommy has a mom?"

"She does," said Grandma. "I am her mommy, just like your mommy is your mommy."

Mommy came over with the car keys. "Hi, Mom!" she said, and hugged Grandma too.

Elijah looked at Mommy. Then he looked at Grandma. Mommy's mom. Grandma was Mommy's mommy!

On the walk to the car, Elijah held Grandma's hand. "Grandma," he said, "when we get home, can we have warm milk?"

"We can have warm milk," said Grandma. "Your mommy can heat it. She learned that from me."

At home, Mommy heated the milk. Elijah held his cup with two hands. It was warm and sweet.

"Grandma," he said, "tomorrow can you read me a book? The train book?"

Grandma sat down beside him. "Every day for a whole week," she said.

Elijah snuggled close. The book had a shiny train on the cover. "That train looks just like your train," he said.

"It does," said Grandma. She opened the book to page one.

Athena ran to the scooter. Gurasees was already on it. Athena grabbed the handle. "My turn!" she said. Gurasees held on tight.

Mr. Gagnon came over. He had a little sand timer. "When the sand runs out, the turn is over," he said. He turned it over. The sand began to fall. Gurasees rode in a circle. Athena watched the sand. It went down, down, down. The sand ran out. Gurasees stopped. "Your turn now," he said.

Athena got on the scooter. She rode to the fence and back. She peeked at the timer. The sand was almost gone. Athena stopped all by herself. "Sand is done!" she said. Gurasees laughed and took his turn.

Then Athena and Gurasees built a big sand hill together. They dug with their hands. Athena said, "I am hungry." Mr. Gagnon smiled. "Snack time," he said. "First, brush the sand off." Athena brushed off her hands. Then she sat with Gurasees and ate crackers, side by side in the sun.

Eli went to the library on a stormy day. Rain tapped the big window. Plop, plop, plop.

Eli wanted to play hide-and-seek with Dustin and Zaynab. "I will hide," said Zaynab. "I will hide too," said Dustin. "You count," they said to Eli. Eli did not know how to play. "What do I do?" he asked. "The seeker counts while we hide," said Zaynab. "Count to ten, then come find us."

Eli covered his eyes. He counted very, very fast. "One-two-three-four-five-six-seven-eight-nine-ten!" Zaynab popped out from behind the plant. "Too fast!" she laughed. "We did not hide yet." Dustin's shoes showed under a chair. "Count slow, please," he said.

Eli tried again. "One... two... three..." He counted slowly, like a sleepy turtle. Zaynab hid behind the plant. Dustin squeezed behind a shelf. "Four... five... six..." A fire truck went by outside. Wooo, wooo! Eli kept counting. "Seven... eight... nine... ten. Here I come!"

Eli looked behind the plant. He found Zaynab! Her shoes peeked out. He looked under the chair. Nobody there. Then he heard a giggle by the shelf. "Found you, Dustin!" said Eli.

Dustin laughed. "Your slow counting worked. Now you hide, and I count." Dustin covered his eyes. "One... two... three..." Eli ran to hide behind a book cart.

Ayla sat on the rug at school. Mr. Koné held a big book about a pet dog. The dog was small and cute. Ayla wanted to hear every word.

Mr. Koné opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. His eyes moved along the little black marks. Then his voice made the story come out.

"Read this page too!" said Ayla. She pointed at a page with just a picture of a bone. There were no little black marks on it.

"There are no words on this page," said Mr. Koné. "So there is nothing for me to read."

Ayla looked hard. The marks were gone! She turned back to the dog page. The marks were there. Mr. Koné read them, and the dog barked in the story.

"Keep going," said Ayla. She leaned in close. Mr. Koné turned to the last page. Ayla saw the marks grow big and wide. Then he read the very last word, and the story ended with the dog fast asleep.

Myles stood at the big kitchen table. He was making bread with his mom. He mixed flour and water in the bowl. Then he poked the dough with one finger. It was sticky and soft. "Oh no," said Myles. "It is stuck to my hands. The bread is ruined!"

His mom smiled. "Cooks knead it," she said. "They push it and fold it with their hands."

Myles tried it. He pushed the dough down. Then he folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold. The dough came off his fingers, bit by bit. Soon it felt smooth like a little pillow. "It is not stuck anymore!" said Myles.

They left the dough in the bowl to rest. Later it was big and puffy. His mom put the pan in the hot oven. Myles stood far away and watched.

Soon the kitchen smelled warm and good. Myles set the table while he waited. His dad came in with the dog, whose bone clicked on the floor. At last the bread came out, brown and round.

"I kneaded it myself," said Myles. "Push and fold, push and fold." He tore off a warm piece and took a big bite.

Luca ran into the kitchen. "Can I ride my bike now?" he asked. His dad was at the stove. The pan was hot and it went sizzle. Luca stopped far away and stayed by the door.

"You need your helmet first," Dad said. Luca looked at the window. His helmet was outside on the step. He did not have it. He wanted to ride right away. But then he thought about his helmet. Luca ran back and got it. He put it on his head. Dad gave him a thumbs up. "Nice and safe," said Dad. "Wear a helmet when you ride a bike."

Luca patted his helmet with both hands. Then he looked at the pan. "That is hot," he said. "Yes," said Dad. "Only I touch it." Luca nodded. He stayed close to Dad while the water boiled. Soon Dad turned everything off. The stove was cool now.

Luca found his friend Emil by the gate. "Look at my helmet," said Luca. Emil smiled. "That is a kind helmet," he said. Luca climbed on his bike. He pedaled down the path. His helmet sat snug on his head. "Ready!" he called. Emil ran behind him, waving all the way.

Amelia was building a block tower in the sunny kitchen. Jessica came to play. Jessica made a tower too. The two towers sat in the middle of the rug.

Amelia reached for a big red block. She leaned too far. Her elbow bumped Jessica's tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. Jessica's mouth turned down. Her eyes got wet.

"Sorry, Jessica," said Amelia. She looked at the fallen blocks. Then she picked up one block. She set it down softly. She picked up another. Jessica wiped her eyes. She picked up a block too. Amelia passed her the red one. "Here," said Amelia. "You can go first."

They stacked the blocks, one by one. Up went the tower, taller and taller. Jessica put the last block on top. It wobbled. Amelia held her breath. The tower stood still.

"Again?" said Jessica.

"Again," said Amelia, and she handed over the red block first.

Ethan went to the store with his dad. It was snowy outside. The store had a big shelf of books. Ethan wanted a book about a red lamp.

He found one. He sat down to read it. He opened the back page first. He ran his finger from right to left. The words felt mixed up. "Dad, the story is broken," he said.

His dad sat close beside him. "Turn to the front cover first," he said. Ethan turned the book around. He put his finger at the left side of the page. Then he slid it to the right. The words went in a row, one after another. It sounded like a real story.

A girl named Maksim from his class peeked over. "That is my favorite book," she said. Ethan smiled and read on. His finger moved across the page, left to right, all the way to the end.
