Thomas went to the pet store with his dad. There were fish and birds and a rabbit with soft ears. Then Thomas saw a small brown puppy. The puppy had a white paw and a wagging tail. "Can we take him home?" asked Thomas. Dad said yes.

In the car, Thomas had a chocolate treat in his pocket. He took it out. "Here, puppy," said Thomas. Dad stopped the car and looked at him. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick," said Dad. "Dogs are never given chocolate." Thomas put the treat away fast.

Back at the pet store, a man named Mr. Villanueva worked behind the counter. Dad asked him what a puppy could eat. Mr. Villanueva handed Thomas a small bone-shaped dog treat. "Try this instead," he said. Thomas held it out to the puppy. The puppy took it gently and wagged his tail. His wing of a tail, Thomas thought, flapped with joy.

At home, the puppy drank from his water bowl. He had been thirsty. Then he fell asleep in a soft blanket. Thomas colored a picture of him. He drew the puppy holding a dog treat, not chocolate. "Good boy," Thomas whispered. The puppy's tail wagged in his sleep.

Audrey woke up early. The sun was bright on her street. "Picnic day!" she said. She held her dad's hand and walked to the park. Her friends Martha and Killian were already there. Mr. Goldberg sat on the bench with a big basket.

"Let's play picnic shop," said Martha. Audrey laid everything out on the grass. "One apple," she said. "One bread. One ball. One carrot. One drum." She counted each thing with a tap. Martha picked up the carrot. She put it next to the ball and the drum.

Then Thumper came by. Thumper was Audrey's pretend rabbit, made of one strong sock. Thumper sniffed the ball. Thumper sniffed the drum. Thumper did not eat them. "Is a carrot a toy?" Audrey asked herself. "No. A carrot is a food." She picked up the carrot and put it with the apple and the bread. "Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," she said. Thumper munched the carrot and went hop, hop, hop down the path.

Brooklyn had a cold. Her nose was stuffy and runny. She sat on the couch with a soft blanket. Her tummy made a little rumble. "I want a snack," she said.

Her mom put crackers and apple slices on a plate. Brooklyn took a tissue. She blew her nose. It made a big honking sound. Then she reached for a cracker.

"Wait," her mom said. "Your hands need soap and water first." Brooklyn felt a bit sad about waiting. But she slid down from the couch. She went to the sink. She pumped the soap. She rubbed her hands under the water. Bubbles grew between her fingers. "I will tell my teddy," she said. "He should wash his paws too."

Then Brooklyn sat back down. She picked up a cracker with clean hands. She crunched it. The apple was sweet and juicy. Her mom smiled and tucked the blanket around her. Brooklyn gave one apple slice to her teddy, and pretended he took a big bite.

Olivier ran into the store with his dad. "I want new socks!" he said. "Red ones!" His dad smiled. "Okay, pick them out."

The sock shelf was in a dark corner. The lights were off in that part of the store. Olivier grabbed two socks. He held them up. They both looked the same to him in the dark. "I found two red socks!" he said.

Then Mr. Sánchez, the store worker, turned on the lights. The corner got bright. Olivier looked again. One sock was red. One sock was green! He laughed. "It was too dark. I could not see the colors!"

"Young man, you picked fast!" said Mr. Sánchez. Olivier found the bin and got two red socks. At the door, he waved at Amar, who was coming in with his mom. "Amar! Turn on the lights before you pick!" Olivier called. He skipped to the car with his red socks in a bag, and held them up to the sun.

Gabriel sat on the rug at daycare. He had ten little blocks in a row. He wanted to build one tall tower. He touched each block as he counted. "One, two, four," said Gabriel. "Wait," he said. "Where did three go?"

Louisa sat down next to him. "Three comes after two," she said. "Try again." Gabriel tapped the blocks slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All ten blocks! The tower stood up tall. Gabriel clapped his hands. "Again!" he said.

He counted the blocks again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words went the same way every time. Then Louisa looked sad. "My tower fell down," she said. Gabriel gave her three of his blocks. "One, two, three," he said. She stacked them up high. Mr. Marino turned on the little lamp, and the blocks seemed to shine. At home time, Gabriel waved. "Bye, blocks! One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," he called from the door.

Raphael stood in the kitchen. The back door was open a little bit. Cold wind came in. His coat hung open and flapped.

Brrr! Raphael shivered. The wind puffed his coat like a big balloon. "Silly coat," he said. His mom was stirring soup at the stove. "Zip up, Raphael," she said. "I will do it myself," he said.

He pulled at his coat. He pushed the tab down. Nothing joined. The wind came in again. His tummy felt cold.

Then he looked down. The coat had two sides. There was a little pin on one side. There was a little box on the other side. He pushed the pin into the box. Click!

"Now pull the tab up," said his mom.

Raphael pulled the tab up. Up, up, up. The two sides joined together. Zzzzip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. "I did it!" he shouted. His mom clapped her spoon. "My cozy zipper boy!"

Raphael zipped the tab down. Zzzzip. He zipped it up again. "Zip, zip, zip," he sang. He drew a picture of his coat with a green crayon while the soup cooked. The picture had a big tab on it. "Look," he said. "I can do it. Zzzzip!"

Mateo sat at the little red table. He wanted to draw a big sun on the tablet. He pressed his whole hand on the screen. He pressed and pressed. The screen did nothing. "Oh no," said Mateo.

Tommy sat next to him. "Try one finger," said Tommy. "Tap the screen with your finger to choose things." Mateo lifted his hand. He held out one finger. He gave the screen a gentle tap. The tablet lit up fast. "It works!" said Mateo. He heard Allie clap behind him.

He tapped once more. The drawing app opened. Mateo drew a big yellow sun. He drew fast little rays all around it. Then Mr. Mehta rang the small bell. Time to put the tablet away. Mateo tapped the button, slid the tablet into its box, and smiled. "Tap, tap, done," he said.

Joshua ran into his classroom. He had big news in his pocket. A red leaf from the big tree outside.

Ms. Ionescu was talking to Noelle. Noelle was showing her a drawing. "Ms. Ionescu!" Joshua called. "Look at my leaf!" Ms. Ionescu kept talking to Noelle. She did not turn around. Joshua called again. She still did not hear him.

Joshua stood still. He watched Noelle's mouth. Noelle stopped talking. There was a quiet space. Then Joshua said, "Excuse me, please. Look at my leaf." Ms. Ionescu turned to him right away. "What a big red leaf," she said. "Thank you for waiting, Joshua."

"You're welcome," said Joshua. "May I put it on the table?" "Yes, you may," said Ms. Ionescu. Joshua skipped to the table. Anika came over to look. "It is a good leaf," she said. "Can I hold it?" Joshua gave it to her. "Here you go," he said. Then he asked himself a question. Did waiting really help? It did. Waiting gave him his turn.

Thomas was at Grandpa's house. He wanted his small red car. Grandpa said, "Your car is in a box." The boxes sat on a shelf. Each box had a number on it.

Thomas looked up. He saw a box with a 5. He counted on his fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Five! The 5 is five!" Grandpa smiled and nodded.

Thomas pushed a chair? No. Grandpa lifted the box down. Thomas opened it. He counted the cars. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten cars! His red car was there.

Thomas fixed the car. Its small wheel had come off. He pushed it back on. Then he rolled the car on the floor. It went far. His shirt pulled up as he leaned. "My car goes fast," said Thomas. "Fast, fast, fast."

Sophia sat at the little table in the playroom. She wanted to paint grass. Ms. Clarke-Williams gave her a big smile. "What will you paint today?" she asked.

"Green grass!" said Sophia. "Tall, tall grass!"

She looked for the green paint pot. It was empty. Oh no! No green meant no grass.

Theodora sat next to her. "I have blue," said Theodora. "Blue for the sky."

"And I have yellow," said Zia. "Yellow for the sun."

Sophia had an idea. "Can I mix them?" she asked.

Ms. Clarke-Williams nodded. "You can try."

Sophia put a blob of blue paint on her paper. Then she put a blob of yellow next to it. She stirred them with her brush. Round and round and round.

The paint turned green! Bright, bright green!

"Green!" shouted Sophia. "I made green!"

She painted the tall grass. It went up and up. Theodora painted the blue sky above it. Zia painted the big yellow sun.

"Now we all made one picture," said Zia.

Sophia was tired and happy. She hid her green brush behind her back. "Look, Ms. Clarke-Williams! No brush!"

Then she pulled it out fast. "Surprise! The grass brush!"

Everyone laughed. The grass looked so green and so tall.

Jack stood at the bus stop with his mom. Snow was falling on his red hat. The wind blew the snow sideways. "It is windy today," said Jack.

Marigold came with her dad. She was making a snowball. Jack helped her pat it round. "I want to keep it," said Marigold. "Then it will be mine forever." She put the snowball in her coat pocket.

They skipped to the bus. The bus doors were closed, then they opened with a hiss. Inside, the bus was warm. Marigold pulled out her snowball. It was small now. Then it was just a wet spot on her mitten. "My snowball is gone," she said. Her eyes got wide. Jack held her other hand. "Snow melts in the warm bus," he said. "We can make a new one in the snow." Marigold smiled and looked out the window at the white, white street.

Margot stood in the gym with a red beanbag in her hand. Mr. Nasser had put a hoop on the floor. "Throw it in," he said. Margot threw it. The beanbag hit the edge and rolled away. She tried again. It rolled away again. "What could help?" she wondered. She looked at the hoop. She looked at her hand. She stepped closer. She threw slowly. The beanbag dropped right in. "I did it!" said Margot.

Then Mr. Nasser brought out a big blue ball. He rolled it to Azlan. Azlan closed his eyes tight. The ball bumped his tummy and fell. Azlan made a sad face. Then Mr. Nasser rolled the ball to Margot. "Where are my eyes?" she wondered. She kept them wide open. She watched the ball all the way to her hands. Her hands closed. She caught it!

"Try again," said Margot to Azlan, in a polite voice. Azlan opened his eyes. The ball came. He watched it all the way. His hands closed around it. "I got it!" he shouted. Margot clapped. Azlan threw the ball back to her. She watched it come and caught it again.

Lena was drawing at home. Her toy pig sat next to her. Then she heard a thump. Her friend Caden had fallen in the hall. He sat on the floor. His face looked sad.

Lena felt scared for a second. Her mom was close by. "Go ask him," Mom said with a smile. Lena walked over. She looked at Caden's face. "Are you okay?" she asked.

Caden wiped his eyes. "My knee hurts," he said. Lena stayed by his side. Mom came with a soft bandage. She put it on his knee. Then Caden smiled a big smile. Lena felt happy inside.

"It is hard when you fall," said Lena. "But I came to ask." Caden hugged his pig tight. Then he held out a red crayon to Lena. "Want to draw a pig with me?"

Everly had a sparkly pink dress. She wore it all day at Katelyn's party. She twirled. She jumped. She ate cake until her tummy was full.

Now it was dark. Everly did not want to take off her dress. "I want to sleep in my dress," she said. Her dad helped her change anyway. He put on her soft pajamas. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said.

Everly got into bed. The pajamas felt warm and cozy. Her dress had been scratchy. The pajamas were soft like a blanket. She snuggled down and felt safe. Her dad tucked her in.

"Night night," he said.

Everly closed her eyes. "Night night, dress," she whispered. "You can come out tomorrow."

And soon she fell fast asleep.

Amelia and her dad drive to the doctor's office. She wants to be brave today. The nurse has a red strawberry chew for her. Last time it tasted so strong, and Amelia made a face. That is her problem today. In the waiting room she hears a dog bark outside. She sees a picture of a chicken on the wall. She smells soap near the big desk. She touches the soft chair. Then the nurse says, "Here is your strawberry chew." Amelia holds her nose closed with her fingers. She pops the chew in her mouth. It tastes plain, not strong at all! Her eyes open wide. "It worked!" she says. The nurse laughs and claps. Amelia lets go of her nose. Now the taste comes back, big and sweet. She grins and takes another bite.

Amira sat at the big art table. She had a nest craft to make. She drew leaves with a friendly green marker. Then she drew a little brown bird. Her hand slipped. A green line went right on her skin.

"Oh no," said Amira. She looked at her hand. The green mark would not leave. Saira leaned over. "You can wash it off," said Saira. "These markers wash off skin."

Amira walked to the sink with Mr. Tang. He helped her get soap and water. She rubbed her hands together. Bubbles grew soft and white. The green line got lighter. Then it was gone!

Amira held up her clean hand. She smiled big. She went back to her nest. She glued on two leaves and her little brown bird. Then she picked up the marker again. This time she drew a slow, careful line on the paper only. "See my bird!" she said. "It lives in the nest now."

Gabriella went to the park with her dad. She saw a big sandbox. She wanted to dig in it. But her shovel was gone. "Oh no," she said. "Can you help me?" she asked her dad. "I can ask Mr. Khoury," said Dad. Mr. Khoury watched the park. He had a box of toys.

Mr. Khoury looked in his box. He found a thin red shovel. "Here you go," he said. "Thank you," said Gabriella. She ran to the sand.

A new girl sat in the sandbox. Her name was Winifred. She had a toy owl with big eyes. "Wow," said Gabriella. "Can I pat the owl?" Winifred nodded. Gabriella patted it, soft and slow.

Then Gabriella gave Winifred the red shovel. Winifred smiled big. "Gracias!" she said. Gabriella stopped. What did that mean? "Gracias means thank you," said Winifred. "It is Spanish." Gabriella tried it. "Gracias!" she said. "You said it right!" said Winifred. They dug a big hole together, side by side.

Willow sat at the kitchen table. Mom put out three pots of paint. "Red, yellow, blue," said Willow. She pointed at each one. "I know them all!"

She wanted to paint a big sun. She dipped her brush in yellow. Then she dipped it in blue. She made a stroke on the paper. It was not blue. It was not yellow. It was muddy and dark. "Oh no," said Willow. "My yellow is all dirty!"

Mom said, "Let's rinse the brush in water first." Willow put the brush in the water cup. She swished it around. She wiped it on the cloth. The brush was clean now.

Willow asked, "Will the yellow stay yellow now?" She dipped the clean brush in yellow. She made a stroke. It was bright yellow! "Yes!" said Willow.

Then she painted red next to the yellow. She rinsed the brush again. Where the red touched the yellow, a new colour appeared. "It's orange!" said Willow. She clapped her hands. "Red and yellow make orange!"

She painted and painted. Rinse the brush. Then a new colour. Rinse again. Her sun had a bright orange sky. "Mom, come look!" said Willow. "Clean brush, clean colours!" Mom gave her a kind smile and a high five.

Milo sat at the little table in the backyard. He had a big paper pumpkin to paint. He looked in the paint box. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. But there was no orange paint. "Where is the orange?" he wondered.

His friend Hayes came over. Hayes held up the red jar. "Want to paint it red?" asked Hayes. Milo shook his head. He wanted a real orange pumpkin. Then he had an idea. What if the paints could mix?

Milo put a dot of red on his brush. Then he put a dot of yellow next to it. He picked up the brush and swirled them together. Round and round they went. The red spread into the yellow. The yellow spread into the red. Then something new appeared. Orange! Bright, orange paint!

Milo dipped his brush in the orange. He painted the pumpkin. He painted the stem green. He touched the wet paint with one finger. It felt a little slimy. He laughed and wiped it on the paper. "Look, Hayes! Red and yellow made orange!" said Milo. Hayes grabbed a brush too. "My turn to mix!"

Georgia ran to the bathroom. Her mom had a surprise for her there. On the sink sat a big glass of water. Next to it was a bowl of ice cubes. "Can I touch one?" asked Georgia. "Yes, you can try," said her mom.

Georgia picked up an ice cube. It was slippery in her fingers. "Ooh, it feels cold!" she cried. She dropped it fast into the glass. Plop! The water splashed a little drop onto her nose. She licked her lips. The water did not taste like anything. She heard the ice go clink, clink in the glass. "Do my ears hear that?" she asked. "Yes, they do," said her mom. "My nose smells soap," said Georgia. She sniffed the pink soap by the sink. Then she touched it with one finger. It was smooth and warm.

Georgia picked up another ice cube. She wanted to hold it longer this time. But it was too cold! Her hand pulled back fast. "Brrr!" she said. She dropped the ice cube into the glass. It clinked again. Georgia laughed and clapped her hands.

Maverick had a cold. His nose was red. His cough went honk, honk.

"Time for the doctor," said his mom. Maverick held her hand in the waiting room. The doctor looked in his ears. She wrote on a paper. "This paper says what medicine he needs," she said.

Then they went to the pharmacy. It had a black door and a tall counter. A pharmacist stood behind the glass. Mom gave the paper to the pharmacist. The pharmacist reached up high for one box. Then the pharmacist reached down low to the bottom shelf for a small bag. She put the medicine in the bag. She handed the bag to Mom. Maverick watched the whole thing. "She gives out the medicine," he said. At home, Mom poured the medicine onto a little spoon. Maverick drank it. Slowly, slowly, his cough went quiet. His breathing was soft. He held his stuffed bear close. "Honk, honk, all gone," he whispered. Then he closed his eyes and slept.

John was at daycare. It was nap time. The room was dark and quiet.

John could not find his teddy. He wanted his teddy now. He looked with his eyes. But the dark room made it hard to see. He listened with his ears. He heard Maximus snoring on his mat. He touched the floor with his hands. He touched a shoe. He touched a sock. No teddy.

"Ms. Hosseini," John whispered. "My teddy is lost." Ms. Hosseini came over. She slid her hand along the wall. She found the little lamp. Click. The light went on.

Now John could see! There was his teddy, under Taylor's chair. John picked it up. He hugged it. It smelled like soap, a clean smell.

"I see it with my eyes," said John. "My eyes needed the light." He gave the teddy a little kiss. Teddy fur was soft on his lips.

Ms. Hosseini smiled. "The sun outside is bright and hot," she said. "But in here we just needed a small lamp."

John lay down on his mat. He held his teddy close. His tummy felt warm, like a baby bird under a wing. Ms. Hosseini turned the light off again. The room went dark. But John did not need to look anymore. His teddy was right there in his arms.

"Goodnight, teddy," John whispered. And he closed his eyes.

Connor stood at the bus stop with Grandpa. The sky was gray. Little drops began to fall. "Rainy," said Connor. He felt the drops on his nose. They were cold.

Connor started to cry. "My head is wet," he said. Grandpa smiled. He opened a big red umbrella. It went pop over their heads. The rain tapped on the top. Tap, tap, tap. But no drops fell on Connor. "The umbrella keeps the rain off your head," said Grandpa.

The wind blew. The umbrella wiggled in Grandpa's hand. "Windy," said Connor. He held the pole, too, to be a helper. "Thank you, Connor. That was polite," said Grandpa.

The bus came. Its lights were shiny and yellow. Connor climbed the steps. His head was dry and warm. "Sunny days need no umbrella," he said. Grandpa laughed all the way to the seat.

Madison went to the store with her dad. She held his hand. She wanted apple juice, and she wanted to pick the box all by herself.

At the deli counter, Madison saw a big silver pot. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop inside it. White steam rose up from the pot. It looked like a little cloud. Madison wanted to see the bubbles up close. She let go of her dad's hand and took one step.

The lady behind the counter said, "Stay back, please. Steam is hot and can burn you." Madison stopped. Her dad took her hand again. They stood far away from the pot. From far away, Madison could still see the bubbles. Pop, pop, pop. She watched the steam curl up high.

Then something surprising happened. The steam made a fog on the cold glass case. The fog turned white. Madison drew a big circle in the fog with her finger. Then she drew a smile inside the circle. The lady laughed. "That is a happy face," she said.

Madison helped her dad put the juice box in the cart. It was a new juice, with a strawberry on the front. She pushed the cart a little way, holding on with both hands. At the checkout, the cashier gave her a sticker. It was a shiny red apple. Madison put it on her shirt and smiled all the way home.

"Pop, pop, pop," she said.

Jake had a cough. He could not sleep at night. His mom took him to the pharmacy down the street. The shelves were tall and full. Jake smelled mint and soap. Mr. Reddy worked behind the big counter. "Time to see the doctor," Mom said.

In the small room, Jake held his toy horse tight. The doctor had a shiny thing around her neck. "This is called a stethoscope," she said. Jake sat very still. She put it on his chest. "Breathe in," she said. Jake breathed in. He heard a soft thump, thump inside him. "That is your heart," she said.

At home, Jake put the cold end on his horse. He waited. No thump at all. He put it back on his own chest. Thump, thump. He smiled. His mom tucked him in. "Now you can sleep," she said. Jake whispered to his horse, "I heard my heart."

Ivy sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. Her mama held her hand. Ivy was not sick. She felt fine. So she asked, "Why do I need a shot?"

The doctor smiled. "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said. Then she cleaned Ivy's arm with a soft cotton ball.

The shot came. It felt like a quick pinch. Ivy did not cry. She blinked, and it was done. The doctor put a small round bandage on her arm. "All done," said the doctor. "You were so brave." Ivy looked at the bandage. It had a little duck on it.

Then mama took Ivy to the ice cream shop. Ivy got pink ice cream in a bowl. Her friend Maximus was there with his dad. Maximus saw Ivy's duck bandage. "What happened?" he asked.

"I got a shot," said Ivy. She held up her arm to show him. "It helps protect my body."

Maximus nodded. His ice cream dripped onto his hand. "My hands are dirty now," he said. Ivy gave him a napkin. He wiped his fingers.

The ice cream man brought out a big pot of sprinkles. He scooped some with a spoon. He put sprinkles on both bowls. Red ones and green ones. Maximus shared his cookie with Ivy. Ivy shared her sprinkles with him.

At home, Ivy showed the duck bandage to her cat. The cat sniffed it. Ivy patted the cat very softly. "Shots help protect you too," she whispered. The cat blinked and curled up on her lap.

Grandma made a warm apple pie. Willow could smell it from the yard. "Pie time!" said Grandma.

The kids made a line by the table. Thalia was first. Then Alora. Then Willow. Grandma cut the pie with a big knife. Willow watched from far away. Then Grandma gave out the forks.

Thalia got her slice. Alora got her slice. Willow wanted to be first too. She ran up and pushed to the front. "Hey," said Alora. "You took my spot." Willow looked back. The line had a hole where she had been. Alora was standing there with no pie.

Willow stepped back. She went to her spot at the end. Grandma smiled. She cut one more slice. It had shiny apples on top. Grandma set it down with a fork. "Here you go," she said. "You waited in your place." Willow took a big bite. The pie was warm and sweet. Alora sat down next to her. "Want to share my chair?" asked Alora. "Yes please," said Willow. The sun began to shine through the window.

Victoria got on the city bus with her dad. The bus was going to the dentist. Victoria had never been to a dentist before.

"My tooth feels funny," said Victoria.

"Let's go and see," said Dad. "The dentist will help your teeth."

The bus smelled like warm bread. A man sat with a big paper bag. Victoria held Dad's hand.

At the dentist, Victoria sat in a big chair. It went up and up. Ms. Ito looked in Victoria's mouth.

"Your front teeth are for biting food," said Ms. Ito. "Your back teeth are for chewing it."

Victoria got a small mirror. She saw her teeth. They were little and white. Not bad at all!

On the bus home, Felix was there. Felix had an apple slice. He bit it with his front teeth. Then he chomped it with his back teeth.

Victoria laughed. She opened her mouth wide. "Front teeth bite," she said. "Back teeth chew!"

"Like a sheep," said Felix. "Sheep chomp all day."

Felix's mom gave Victoria an apple slice too. Victoria bit it with her front teeth. Then she chomped with her back teeth. The bus went bump, bump, bump. Dad smiled at her.

"There's a dog outside the window," said Victoria.

The dog was wearing a tiny red hat.

Isaac sat at the art table. There was a big box of crayons. He pulled all of them close to his side. He wanted to draw a red fire truck.

Harlow sat down next to him. She looked in the basket. The basket was empty. No crayons were left. She put her hands in her lap and looked at the paper.

Isaac looked at his big pile. Then he looked at Harlow. He slid three crayons across the table. "You can use these too," he said. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too." Harlow picked up the blue one. She drew a big blue truck.

They worked side by side. Harlow handed Isaac the green crayon when he needed it. Mr. Lau came by and smiled at their pictures.

At dinner that night, Isaac told his mom about the blue truck and the red truck. He gave her a hug. "We used the crayons together," he said.

Everett went to the store with his mom. He held her hand at the door. The store was big and bright. Apples sat in a red pile. Everett saw a balloon on a shelf. It was yellow with a happy face.

"I want the balloon," he thought. He pulled his mom's sleeve. She was looking at bread. Everett made a sad face. He hung his head. His mom did not see. He stomped his foot, and his face felt hot and angry. Still, his mom did not know.

Then Everett said, "I feel sad." His mom looked down right away. "You feel sad? Thank you for telling me." He pointed at the balloon. She smiled and put it in the cart. "I did not know what you wanted," she said. "Now I can help you."

Everett felt excited. He held the balloon all the way home. At home there was milk to drink and cookies for a little party. Solomon came over to play. "A balloon!" said Solomon. Everett let him hold the string too. "It has a happy face," said Everett, "just like me."

Sophia loved hide-and-seek at school. Today she wanted to hide so well that no one could find her.

"Follow me," said her friend Aoife. They ran behind the big furry rug on the wall. Sophia heard Ms. Marino counting. She heard Alfie's shoes on the floor. She put her hands over her eyes. Now it was all dark. "Nobody can see me," she thought.

But Alfie found her right away. "I see your shoes," he said. Sophia peeked with one eye. Alfie was pointing and laughing. She took her hands off her eyes. She looked at Aoife. Aoife had covered her eyes too. Sophia could still see Aoife's red socks and her yellow bow.

"Try hiding your whole body instead," said Ms. Marino kindly. So Sophia crouched down small behind a chair. She smelled paint from the art table. She touched the cool floor with her fingers. She closed her eyes and it got dark again. But she knew the chair was still there. She opened her eyes and saw it again.

Alfie walked past the chair. He did not see her. He did not find her socks. He did not find her bow. Sophia waited very still.

Then a small surprise came. Something soft bumped her arm. It was the class key on its string. Ms. Marino had hung it on the chair. "Found you too," said Ms. Marino with a warm smile. She gave Sophia a sweet cracker to taste. It was yum.

Sophia laughed. "Next time I will hide my feet too."

Matteo sat at the little table. There was a tablet in front of him. It was dark and still.

"Mr. Tehrani, how do I make it go?" he asked.

"Press the round button," said Mr. Tehrani.

Matteo pressed the button. The screen lit up. He made a happy sound. He pressed a green square, and a drawing app opened. He drew a thin blue line. Then he drew a big red circle. It looked a bit like an egg.

Jaylen came to sit beside him. Jaylen set his cup of juice on the table. It sat right next to the tablet. Mr. Tehrani shook his head.

"Not there, Jaylen," he said. "Tablets stay away from water and drinks."

Jaylen picked up his cup. He carried it to the other table. Then he came back and watched Matteo draw.

"Can I draw too?" Jaylen asked.

"Yes," said Matteo. He moved over so Jaylen would fit.

Jaylen drew a yellow sun. Matteo drew a green frog under it. The frog had big eyes.

Soon the timer rang. It was time to clean up. Matteo pressed the button to make the screen dark. He slid the tablet into its soft case. It fit just right. He set it on the shelf, all by himself.

"Well done, Matteo," said Mr. Tehrani.

Matteo smiled and went to wash his hands.

Milan walked in the forest with Adam. Milan held his teddy bear. The leaves went crunch, crunch under their shoes. The wind smelled like pine.

Milan jumped over a big root. His hand slipped. The teddy fell down, right into a mud puddle. "Oh no!" said Milan. His eyes got wide. "He fell! He is sad now."

Adam picked up the teddy. "Look," said Adam. "He cannot really feel sad. Toys cannot really feel. But we can pretend he does." Milan thought about that. Then he smiled a little. "So he is fine? Just muddy?" "Just muddy," said Adam.

Milan gave the teddy a big pretend hug. Then he patted the teddy's arm, very soft. The mud fell off, bit by bit. "Look!" said Milan. "My pat made the mud fall!" He patted again. More mud dropped onto the leaves. "Pat, pat, pat," said Milan. "You are all clean now, teddy."

Then Milan yawned. He felt sleepy. He put the teddy inside his jacket. "Shh," he whispered. "The teddy is sleeping." The two boys walked home. The wind went whoosh in the trees. "Was the mud cold?" Adam asked. "No," said Milan. "It was squishy. Like soup." Adam laughed all the way to the gate.

Matteo ran into the dental clinic. He held his toy train tight. Today was his first dentist day!

A man sat in a big chair. He waved at Matteo. His hands were blue!

"Your hands are blue!" said Matteo. He wanted to cry. Blue hands felt scary.

The man pulled one blue finger. It came off! Then it was just a hand.

"They are gloves," said Mr. Kapoor. "I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

Matteo looked close. A glove sat on the tray. It looked like a big blue mitten.

"Now my turn," said Matteo. He opened his mouth wide, wide, wide.

Mr. Kapoor put on new gloves. Snap, snap! He counted Matteo's teeth. One, two, three!

"All done!" said Mr. Kapoor. "Your teeth are nice and clean."

Matteo hugged his train. "I like blue gloves!" he said. "We come back soon!"

Kinsley rode the bus with her mom. They were going to the big library. Today Kinsley would get her very first library card.

At the library, Kinsley wanted a book about trucks. She looked and looked. She saw books about cats. She saw books about the sea. But no trucks. Where could they be?

Then she saw a woman at a desk. Books were stacked all around her. Kinsley asked, "Do you work here?"

"Yes, I do," the woman said. "I am the librarian. I help people find books."

"Can you help me find truck books?" asked Kinsley.

The librarian walked to a shelf. "Here they are." There were so many trucks!

Kinsley picked a big red one. She shut the book under her arm. She held her new card up high.

On the bus home, she whispered, "I found it all by asking."

Kayden sat in his car seat. It was a rainy day. The window was foggy near his face.

He counted cars going by. "One, two, three." Then more came. "Four, five, six." He kept going. "Seven, eight, nine." One more car went past. "Ten!"

Kayden wanted to write the numbers on the foggy window. He drew with one finger. He wrote a 1. He wrote a 2. He wrote 3, then 4, then 5. Each number was just one mark.

Then he tried to write ten. He made a 1. He stopped. Ten did not look done. He looked hard at the window. He thought and thought.

He drew a 0 next to the 1. Now it said 10. Kayden smiled. "Ten needs two numbers," he said. "A 1 and a 0."

His mom said, "We have to hurry, or the store will close. We need eggs."

At the store, Kayden counted the eggs in the box. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten eggs. The box had 10 written on it, a 1 and a 0, just like his window.

Kayden tapped the box. "I know you," he said. "You are ten."

Isabelle wanted to make cookies. Her mom said yes. First they would cut paper shapes for the cookies.

Mom gave Isabelle safe little scissors. She gave her a square of paper. "Start at a corner," said Mom. Isabelle found a corner. She snipped it off. Then she found another corner. Snip, snip.

Next Mom gave her a circle of paper. Isabelle looked at it. She turned it around with her arm. She looked again. "Where is the corner?" she asked. She ran her finger all along the edge. There was no corner anywhere. The paper was round all the way around. "A circle is round and has no corners," said Mom. Isabelle touched the edge one more time. It was true.

So Isabelle started cutting anywhere at all. Snip, snip, snip. The round paper fell away. Inside was a little triangle. She held it up. "Look, Mom!" she said.

Mom rolled out the dough. She cut a square cookie and a triangle cookie. Then she cut a circle cookie. Isabelle watched Mom put the tray in the oven. The oven was hot, so Isabelle stood back.

Soon the cookies came out. The square one had four sides. The triangle one had three. The circle one was round, with no corners at all. Isabelle picked it up. She took a big bite. "Round all the way," she said, and smiled.

Joshua was at school. He saw his friend Bo by the block shelf. Bo's face was sad. Bo's eyes were wet. Tears ran down his cheeks. Joshua did not know why Bo was crying.

Mr. Fernando sat down next to Bo. "Bo feels sad," Mr. Fernando said. Joshua looked at his own hands. He was holding his toy car. It was his favorite car. Joshua pulled the car out of his pocket. He held it out to Bo. "You can hold it," Joshua said.

Bo took the car. He turned its wheels. He made a soft vroom sound. Soon Bo's tears stopped. Bo smiled a big smile. Joshua felt happy inside. The two boys rolled the car on the rug, back and forth, by the little lamp. "My turn," said Bo. "Okay," said Joshua.

Lydia was at Grandma's house. It was a hot summer day. Grandma said, "Let's make bread." Lydia loved bread.

Lydia helped Grandma mix the flour. Grandma put the bread in the oven. Lydia watched from her chair. Soon the kitchen smelled yummy.

"Now we need butter," said Grandma. She gave Lydia bread and a knife with no sharp edge. Lydia tried to spread the butter. The butter was hard and cold. It tore a hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Lydia.

Grandma smiled. "The butter came from the fridge. Cold butter is hard. Let's put some on the counter." They set the butter on the counter. Lydia waited. She sang a song. She drew a picture of a cow. Then she poked the butter with one finger. It was soft now! Lydia spread it all by herself. The bread looked lovely.

Grandpa came in. "Is that stinky cheese I smell?" he asked. "No, it's my bread with butter!" said Lydia. Grandpa took a big bite. "Yum," he said. Lydia poked the soft butter one more time and laughed.

Grandma was coming on the big train. Thomas waited at the train station with Dad. The train came in, slow and long. Grandma stepped down with her furry red bag. "Grandma!" said Thomas. He hugged her soft coat.

Grandma was staying for a whole week. At home, she tied Thomas's shoe in a big bow. Then Thomas found a photo in her bag. It was a little boy on a blue bike. "Who is that?" asked Thomas. "That is your dad," said Grandma. Thomas looked at Dad. Then he looked again. "Dad was little? Like me?" "Yes," said Grandma. "He fell off that bike two times."

Thomas sat close on the couch. "Tell me more," he said. Grandma told about Dad's dog, who hid a bone under his bed. She told about Dad's first train ride, holding Grandma's hand. Thomas laughed and clapped.

The next day, Thomas went back to the train station with Grandma. They waved at the trains going by. Thomas said, "Grandma, tell me a Dad story now." Grandma smiled and began, "When your dad was little, he loved to splash in puddles." Thomas jumped in a small puddle too. Splash, splash.

Scarlett woke up early. She put on her socks fast. "Sun hat day!" she said. Mom had packed her hat. It was a big yellow hat.

At daycare, Scarlett looked out the window. The sun was not there. Big gray clouds sat in the sky. "The clouds hide the sun," said Ms. Wong. Scarlett pressed her nose to the glass. She wanted the sun to come out. Then it would be sunny. Then she could wear her hat outside.

Helena came to the window too. "I want sun," said Helena. Elias came too. His ear was full of news. "It's windy out!" he said. The tree branches bent and swayed. A leaf flew past the window.

The three friends watched and waited. The clouds moved. Slow, slow, slow. Then a little bit of blue showed. Then a yellow edge peeked out. "The sun!" Scarlett shouted. The clouds slid away and the sun was back. Everything turned bright and warm.

"Outside time!" called Ms. Wong. Scarlett grabbed her yellow hat. Helena got her sunglasses. Elias held his coat, because the wind was still blowing. They ran out into the sunny, windy day. The wind lifted Scarlett's hat. She laughed and held on tight. "Sunny and windy at the same time!" said Helena.

Scarlett wanted her bear book at bedtime. But Mom was busy giving the baby a bath. The soap had made a big mess of bubbles.

"Dad can read it," said Mom. So Dad came in. He sat on the bed. He opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. He read, "Little Bear spilled his milk."

The next night, Mom came instead. She opened the front cover too. She turned the pages one by one. Scarlett leaned close. "Little Bear spilled his milk," Mom read.

Scarlett pointed at the little marks on the page. "Those marks say it!" she said. Mom smiled and turned to the next page.

Scarlett ran her finger under the marks. Dad had said them. Mom had said them. The very same words, both times.

"Again," said Scarlett. "Same page." She turned back to the front and tapped it. "Read."

Lily ran into the playroom. Blocks were everywhere! Red blocks. Blue blocks. Yellow blocks. Green blocks. What a mess.

"Clean-up time!" said Ms. Bouchard. "Let's sort by color," said Cora. "That means all the same color blocks go together in one group."

Lily grabbed a red block. She put it in the red pile. Thunk! She grabbed another red block. Thunk! Soon the red pile was big and tall. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Cora made a green pile.

Lily looked at the red pile. Wait! One block was hiding in the wrong pile. It was blue! Lily picked it up. She walked it over to the blue pile. Thunk! Now every block sat with blocks just like it.

Cora clapped her hands. "All sorted!" she said. Cash held up a green block and grinned. "Look! Green pile wins. It's the tallest!"

Then Lily heard a quiet flutter by the window. A little bird spread one wing, then the other. It pecked at a yellow block on the sill. "The bird likes yellow too!" said Lily, and she waved hello.

Peyton woke up early. She held her bunny's soft ear. Then she saw a hole in her bag. Bunny was not there.

"Bunny fell out," said Peyton. "Maybe at the park."

Peyton and her dad walked to the park. They went past the bumpy path. They went past the log that looked like a snake. Peyton looked under the swing. She looked by the slide. No bunny.

Mr. Ho was sweeping near the bench. "Hello, Peyton," he said. He held up a soft bunny. "I found this on the grass."

Peyton ran to him. "That is my bunny!"

"How do you know?" asked Mr. Ho.

Peyton turned the tag on bunny's ear. Her name was there. "It says Peyton," she said. "My mom wrote it."

Mr. Ho smiled. "The tag helped me know it belongs to you."

Peyton hugged bunny tight. She waved to Mr. Ho. Then she and her dad walked home on the bumpy path, bunny riding safe in her arms.

Nova was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma held up Nova's thick red coat.

"Can you put it on by yourself?" Grandma asked.

Nova pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat was on! But the coat was open. Cold air came in at her tummy.

Nova pulled the little zipper tab up. Zzzzzip! The coat closed. Nova was warm now.

Nova and Grandma went out to the yard. There was a big puddle by the gate. Nova stomped in it. Splash! Her boots got wet and shiny.

Then Nova ran and ran. She ran to the fence and back. Now she was hot. Too hot! Sweat ran down her back.

Nova pulled the zipper tab down. Zzzzip! The coat opened. Cool air came in. Nova felt better.

"You did that all by yourself," said Grandma. "Yes I did," said Nova. "Down makes it open."

They walked to the gate. Nova pulled the tab up again. The coat closed and she was warm. She pulled it down. The coat opened and she was cool. Up and down, up and down.

"Time to come in, little one," said Grandma. Nova held her hand. They stepped over the puddle together.

Natalie was in the kitchen with her dad. She wanted her juice cup from the counter. But her dad stood right in front of it. He was stirring a big pot, and the stove was hot.

Natalie tried to squeeze past him. She wiggled this way. She wiggled that way. It did not work. Her dad was too big, and the space was too small. Natalie stopped and thought. What could she say?

Then she heard a word in her head. "Excuse me," she said out loud. Her dad looked down and smiled. He stepped to the side. Now the way was clear. Natalie walked past him and got her cup. "Thank you, Daddy," she said.

She sat at the table and took a long drink of juice. The bottom of her cup felt cold in her hands. Later, her mom stood in the doorway, and the way was blocked again. Natalie tugged her sleeve. "Excuse me," she said. Her mom smiled and moved aside. "There you go," said Mom. Natalie skipped through the door.

Layla wanted to smell the bread. Her dad was baking it in the oven. "The bread will be ready soon," he said. Layla could not smell it yet. She sat at the table and waited. She heard the oven hum. She saw the bread rise through the glass door. She touched the warm table with her hands. Still no smell.

Then Dad opened the oven door. A big smell came out. Layla smelled it with her nose. "Mmm," she said. Dad gave her a warm slice. She tasted it with her tongue. It was sweet and soft.

Later, Layla looked in the mirror. She saw her nose up close. She counted the little holes in it. One, two. Her dad came over. "Those are your nostrils," he said. "Your nose has two openings called nostrils." Layla looked again. One on this side. One on that side. Then she smelled the bread again, still on the table. "I can smell it two ways," she said. She laughed and took another bite.

Thomas had to wash his hands. Lunch was coming, and he had just used the toilet. He turned on the tap. He rubbed his hands fast under the water. Then he dried them on the green towel. The towel had little trees on it, like a tiny forest.

At the table, Miraya looked at his hands. "Where are your bubbles?" she asked. "What bubbles?" said Thomas. "Look at mine," said Miraya. She held out her hands. They smelled like soap.

Thomas went back to the bathroom. He wet his hands again. He rubbed the soap all over. Bubbles popped up, small and white. "Bubbles!" said Thomas. He counted while he rubbed. "One, two, three, four." Gianna came in and counted too. They counted all the way to twenty together. The bubbles were everywhere, soft as foam.

Thomas rinsed the bubbles away. The dirt went down the drain with them. His hands were clean and shiny. He ran to lunch and held them out to show. "Look at my hands," he said. "Now I smell like soap too."

Brooklyn went to the store with Mom. First they got bread. Then they got apples. Then they got milk. The milk case was cold. "Brrr," said Brooklyn. "My hands feel cold." The bread shelf was near a warm oven. A worker pulled hot rolls out with big gloves. Brooklyn stayed back and watched.

Brooklyn wanted to see the toy aisle. She looked and looked. Then she turned around. Mom was not there. Brooklyn could not see Mom anywhere. Where did Mom go?

Brooklyn remembered something. She walked to the front of the store. A worker in a red vest stood by the checkout. "I can't find my grown-up," said Brooklyn. "Can you help me?" The worker smiled. She used the big speaker. Soon Mom came running. "There you are!" said Mom. She gave Brooklyn a big warm hug. The worker put the bread in the bag. Brooklyn held Mom's hand all the way home.

Snow was falling at school. Big white flakes, small white flakes. Ivy stood at the window with her teacher.

"Time to play outside," said Mr. Liu. "It is a snowy day."

Ivy put on her boots. She put on her puffy coat. She put on her hat. Mr. Liu gave her red mittens for her hands.

Outside, Ivy saw her friend Kabir. Kabir was making a snowball. He patted it and patted it. Then he stopped. He held his hands up.

"My hands are cold," said Kabir. "I forgot my mittens."

Kabir did not have mittens, so his hands were cold. Ivy looked at her own hands. Her mittens were on. Her hands were warm.

"I can help," said Ivy. She had an idea. She helped Kabir roll the snowball with her mittened hands. Then Mr. Liu came with spare mittens, blue ones.

"Try these," said Mr. Liu.

Kabir put them on. He made a new snowball all by himself. He patted it and patted it. His hands stayed warm.

"Look, a big round ball!" said Kabir.

"It looks like a triangle next to the small one," said Ivy, and they laughed.

The wind blew. The snow fell. The friends swept snow off the bench with their mittens and sat down together, warm from boots to hands.

Sadie stood at the big table in the community kitchen. Mr. Karimi had made toast, and the toast was still warm. "Can I put on the butter?" Sadie asked. "Yes, you can," said Mr. Karimi. He gave her a small knife and a soft pat of butter. Sadie spread the butter slowly. The butter melted and made the bread shiny. "It looks like paint," said Sadie. Remy laughed next to her. "Shiny toast is yummy toast," he said.

Then Sadie wanted milk. She held her cup under the milk jug. Mr. Karimi poured with her. The milk went up and up. It stopped just below the top. "Why did we stop?" Sadie asked. "Watch and see," said Mr. Karimi. Sadie picked up the cup. She walked to the table. Not one drop spilled. Remy filled his cup to the very top. He walked, and milk sloshed over his hand.

Remy got a cloth and wiped it up. Then he poured again. This time his milk stopped below the top too. He walked slowly to the table. His hands stayed dry. "Mine did not spill," said Remy. Sadie carried her cup back for more toast. The milk moved a little in the cup. But the cup had room, so the milk stayed in. Sadie took a big bite of her buttery toast. "Milk and toast," she said. "The best snack ever."

It was bedtime, but Addison could not find her book. "Look in your bag," said Mom. Addison held the bag open. Out came a birthday card. On the front she saw letters. "That says Addison," said Mom. Addison ran her finger under the letters. A, then d, then d, again.

"Look at your cubby," said Mom. Mom had a photo from preschool. Addison looked at the photo. Then she looked at the card. The name looked the same. Same letters. Same order. "It is me, both times," said Addison. She held the card next to the photo.

"Here is your book," said Mom. Addison opened the front cover. Her name was there too. It was windy outside, but Addison was cozy and warm. She ate a small apple slice. Then she turned the pages, one by one, from front to back.

"Read to me," said Addison. Mom sat close and began.

Anna went to the park with Henri. She heard a funny sound with her ears. "Quack, quack!" said the ducks, far away on the pond.

"I want to see the ducks," said Anna. She looked with her eyes. The ducks were too far. They looked like little fuzzy dots.

Mr. McKenzie sat on a bench. He took something out of his bag. He put on his glasses. "Ah, now I can see the ducks," he said. "Glasses help me see more clearly."

"Can I try?" asked Anna. Mr. McKenzie held them on for her, just for a moment. The ducks looked big! She saw one duck splash. She touched the cold water with her hand. She smelled the sweet grass. Then Henri shared his snack, and her mouth tasted the yummy apple.

The ducks came close. "They think we have food!" said Henri.

"Full tummy, no bath for ducks," laughed Mr. McKenzie. Anna giggled too.

"Quack!" said a duck, right at her toes.

Jaxon had a small red card. It was his very own library card. He kept it under his pillow.

Lilliana came to play in his bedroom. "Let's play library," said Jaxon. He put his teddy bear on a shelf. The bear would be the librarian.

Lilliana picked a book about trucks. She held out her hand for a card. Jaxon gave her his red card. Beep, he said, like the real machine. Lilliana took the truck book and hugged it.

Then Lilliana put the book back. "All done," she said. "I want the dinosaur one now."

Jaxon looked at his card. He thought it was all used up. He squeezed it. It did not bend. It did not hurt his hand. It still felt fresh and smooth.

He tried again. Beep. Lilliana jumped up and down. "It works again!" she said. "One card, more books!"

Jaxon put the card back under his pillow. Then he ran to show his mom.

Quinn sat on her bed. She had a big book about a rainbow. The rainbow was red, blue, and yellow. It was so pretty.

"Who drew the rainbow?" Quinn asked.

Her dad was folding socks. "Let's look," he said.

Quinn opened the book. She turned to the very first page. She saw little words there. Dad read them out loud. One name was for the writing. One name was for the pictures.

"That one is the illustrator," said Dad. "An illustrator draws the pictures."

Quinn looked at the name. She said it out loud, slow. "The illustrator! The illustrator!" She said it two times, then three times.

Then she wanted the rainbow page again. She turned pages one by one. First this page, then that page. The rainbow came near the end. Dad said, "Books go front to back. The end is at the back."

But wait. Quinn turned one more page. There was a tiny cat hidden in the corner. A surprise cat! The illustrator had drawn it there.

Quinn laughed. She closed the book, back cover down. "Good night, rainbow. Good night, little cat."

She gave the book a soft pat and slid it under her pillow.

Madelyn wanted the crackers at snack time. But the shelf had three big boxes. She did not know which box had crackers. "One box, two boxes, three boxes," she said. She looked at each box. Each box had little marks on the front. "Marks, marks, marks," she said.

Mannat came over. "Those marks are words," he said. "Words tell us things." Madelyn looked closer. Ms. Anderson pointed at one box. "These words say crackers," she said. Madelyn opened that box. Crackers! She laughed. "The words told me!"

At story time, Ms. Anderson held up a book. Madelyn saw words on the cover too. "That says bunny," said Jude. Ms. Anderson opened the book at the front. She turned one page, then two pages, then three. "Front to back," said Madelyn, and she turned a page herself.

On the page was a bunny with a snowy white tail. "Soft as a feather," said Madelyn, and she petted the page with one finger. Jude giggled and petted it too. Then Madelyn pointed at the marks under the bunny. "Read those words," she said. "All of them, front to back."

Charlotte sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. Mama was driving to Ms. Novák's house. Charlotte wanted to bring her teddy bear inside for play time.

At last the car stopped. Charlotte held Mama's hand in the parking lot. She stayed close, right by Mama's knee. Cars were big and fast, so she did not run.

Inside, Ms. Novák had juice and crackers. "Careful, the tea is hot," Ms. Novák said. She put the tea cup up high. Charlotte did not touch it. She drank her cold juice instead.

Then Charlotte saw something on the low table. It was a little box. Round things inside looked like candy. They were red and yellow and small. Charlotte reached out her hand.

Then she pulled it back. "Mama," she called. "Candy on the table."

Mama came over fast. "Those are not candy," Mama said. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine."

Ms. Novák picked up the box. She put it in a high cabinet. "Thank you, Charlotte. That was smart."

Charlotte found her teddy bear in her bag. She hugged it tight. "Teddy helps too," she said.

It was a rainy day. Freya sat at the kitchen table. Her dad put on a song.

"Can you clap with me?" he asked.

Freya clapped. Her claps were too fast. Then her claps were too slow. She tried again. Clap, clap, clap. At last her hands matched the beat.

"Now let's sing the rhyme," said Dad.

"Twinkle, twinkle, little star," sang Freya. Then she stopped. She could not remember the next line.

"What comes next?" she asked.

"Sing it again and see," said Dad.

So they sang it again. And again. Freya felt the claps in her hands, warm and tingly. She heard the rain tap, tap, tap on the window.

The fifth time, something happened. The words just came out. "How I wonder what you are!"

Freya sang the whole rhyme all by herself. She clapped the beat too, right on time.

"Dad! I know it now!" she said. "Can we pay it one more time?"

"Sing it again," said Dad, laughing. So she did.

Logan sat at the little red table. Ms. Ferreira put out letter cards. "Can you put them in order?" she asked. Logan picked up the card with M. He put it after P. Sydney giggled. "That is not right," she said. Logan made a sad face. The letters were all mixed up, like socks in a drawer.

Then Jake had an idea. "Let's sing the song," he said. They all sang the alphabet song together. Logan sang too. A, B, C. He tapped each card as he sang. When the song got to L, then M, then N, Logan saw it. He picked up the M card and put it in its real spot. It was a real fix.

Logan clapped his hands. Then he chased Jake around the play flag in the corner. "You helped me!" Logan said. "Sing it again with me," said Jake. So they sang it again, all the way to Z, right there by the flag.

Colton sat at the little red table. Mr. Bui put out two groups of toy cars. "Can you count them?" said Mr. Bui. Colton loved cars. He picked up the first one. It felt smooth and cool. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Five cars!"

Ayden sat next to him. Ayden took the same cars. But Ayden started from the other end. "One, two, three, four, five," said Ayden. Colton frowned. He felt upset for a second. "You counted wrong," he said. "You started from the other side!"

"But I got five too," said Ayden. Mr. Bui smiled. "Count them again," he said. "Start anywhere you like." Colton started from the middle. "One, two, three, four, five." Still five! He started from the blue car. Five again. Colton clapped his hands. How funny, he thought. The cars did not care where he began.

"Now look at the other group," said Mr. Bui. There were some sticks on the table. Colton pointed at each stick. "One, two, three." Then he looked at the cars. "Five cars. Three sticks. The cars have more!" Jayla came over to see. "Can I try?" she asked. She counted the cars from the top of the pile. "One, two, three, four, five."

"Five," said Colton. "I know that number. It's the same!" Jayla laughed and held up a stick like a magic wand. "Vroom," she said, "five cars coming through!"

Julia sat in her car seat. She held her small red pillow. The car doors were closed. "Are we there yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "We will see Azaan later."

"Now?" asked Julia. "No, not now," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away." Julia looked out the window. A cow stood in a green field. The car went past. "Is it later yet?" asked Julia. "Not yet," said Dad. Julia watched the cow get small and small.

Julia had an idea. She would bring her pillow to Azaan. Then they could build a pillow house. She put the pillow on her lap. She waited. She sang a little song. A red car went by. Then a bus went by.

"Now?" she asked again. Dad laughed softly. "Now it is later," he said. "We are here." The car stopped. Azaan ran to the door of his house. Julia brought her pillow. "Let's build!" said Azaan. They stacked the pillow with two more. The little house stood up tall. Julia clapped her hands. "Later did come!" she said.

Zoey sat on the playroom floor. "Let's make piles," said Ms. Holloway. "One pile for animals. One pile for toys. One pile for food." Zoey picked up a toy apple. It went in the food pile. Then she found a toy cat with soft fur. She threw it, and it did not run away. It just sat where it fell.

Zoey held a toy dog. "Woof," she said. She put it in the animal pile. Then she stopped. The toy dog did not wag its tail. It did not blink. "It is not alive," said Cassius, sitting next to her. Zoey tapped the toy dog. It stayed very still. She picked it up. She put it in the toy pile instead.

"Good sorting, Zoey," said Ms. Holloway. Ayoub clapped his hands. Zoey smiled and patted the toy dog on its soft head.

Lucy made a card at school. It said "Good Morning" on it. She wanted to give it to her friend Neriah. But where was Neriah?

"Not here now," said Ms. Santos. "She will come tomorrow."

Tomorrow. Lucy tapped her foot. When was tomorrow? Yesterday they had painted together. Today Neriah was not at school. So tomorrow must be the next day.

The next morning, Lucy woke up. She peeked out of her room. The family was at the table eating breakfast. Morning was here! It was the part of the day when they woke up and ate. So today had come.

"Good morning!" Lucy said.

At school, Lucy held her card tight. The door opened. Neriah peeked in.

"I came today!" said Neriah.

Lucy ran to her. "A card for you. Good morning, Neriah!"

Aiden ran into the kitchen. His sock slipped off his foot. It landed on the floor.

"Pick it up," said his dad. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed."

Aiden looked at the sock. He looked at the basket. The basket was far away. It looked like a big net.

Aiden had an idea. He held the sock in his hand. He threw it up. The sock went in the basket. "Yay!" said Aiden.

He ran to his room. He found another dirty sock. He threw it too. It missed. The sock fell on the floor. Aiden picked it up. He tried again. This time it went in. "Two socks!" said Aiden.

His friend Amira came to play. She was a pretty girl with a red bow. Amira had dirty socks too. "Want to play?" said Aiden. "Yes!" said Amira.

They threw socks together. One, two, three. Some went in. Some fell out. "Missed it," laughed Amira. She tried again. The sock went in. "Nice throw," said Aiden.

The basket got full. Dad carried it to the washing machine. Soon the socks were clean and warm. Dad put a clean sock on Aiden's foot. It was soft.

Aiden smiled. "Socks in, socks clean," he said. He patted the basket with his little hand.

James was in his bed. He had a cold. His nose was red. His sock was missing.

His dad came in. Dad held a little stick. It was a thermometer.

"What is that?" asked James.

"It checks how warm your body is," said Dad. "Grown-ups use it."

James looked at the little stick. Could it see his warm? He wanted to know.

"Hold very still," said Dad.

James held very still. One, two, three. The stick made a small beep.

Dad looked at it. "Your body is warm," he said. "So you need rest."

James had an idea. Could the stick check other things? He held it near his teddy bear. Nothing happened. The bear was not a body. Then James held it under his own chin. Beep! It was warm too.

"Now rest," said Dad. He turned on the night light. It glowed soft, not like fire.

James counted his toys. One bear, two cars, three books. He watched his eyes start to fall shut, one blink, two blinks, three.

"Night night, thermometer," James whispered.

Felix stood at the front door. He put on his red hat. "It is windy today," said Dad. Felix opened the door a little. The wind blew his hair. The wind blew the leaves.

Felix stepped outside. A big gust came. The wind blew his hat right off his head! The hat flew over the grass. "Come back, hat!" said Felix. He ran after it. The hat rolled and rolled. Otis was playing outside. He ran too. He caught the hat with both hands.

"Here is your hat," said Otis. He gave it back. "Thank you," said Felix. Dad came out with a warm coat. "Hold your hat on windy days," said Dad. Felix held the hat with one hand. The wind blew again. But the hat stayed on. Felix smiled at Otis. "Let's play," said Felix.

Julia was in her bed. Her blanket was soft and warm. She hugged it tight.

Then Julia heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Julia felt scared. Her eyes went wide. She hid under her blanket.

Julia thought for a minute. She could tell a grown-up. "Mama," she called. "I am scared. I hear a tap."

Mama came in fast. She stood by the bed. "Let's look together," said Mama.

Mama opened the curtain. A small branch was outside. The wind made it tap, tap, tap on the glass.

"It is just a branch," said Mama. Julia was not scared now. She felt happy.

Mama closed the curtain. She gave Julia a kiss. "Tap, tap, tap," said Julia, like a little song.

Her eyes closed. The wind went tap, tap, tap, all night long.

Lennon went to the store with her dad. She wanted a new book. She had her own little bag to carry it.

She found a shelf with small books. She picked one about a cat. She sat down on the floor to look at it. She held it upside down. The cat looked funny. The cat's feet were up. The words looked funny too. The letters went the wrong way. Lennon laughed and laughed.

A girl named Gwen sat down next to her. "Your book is upside down," Gwen said. Lennon turned the book around. Now the cat stood on its feet. The words looked neat in a row. Lennon pointed at the words. "That says cat," Gwen said. Lennon turned the book upside down again. The cat's feet went up again. She turned it back. The cat stood right again. Lennon and Gwen giggled.

Dad helped Lennon pay at the cashier. She put the book in her bag. At home, she read it to her stuffed bear. She held it the right way, front to back. "Goodnight, cat," she said. Then she closed the book with a pat.

Maverick sat in his car seat. He was going to Abby's house for pizza. He held five toy monkeys on his lap.

"Watch this," said Maverick. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." He bounced the monkeys on his knee. "One fell off and bumped his head." He let one monkey drop to the seat.

"Now there are four," he sang. He bounced the four monkeys. "One fell off." Another monkey dropped.

"Now there are three." He kept singing. One more monkey fell. Two monkeys sat on his knee.

"One fell off," Maverick sang. One monkey dropped. Just one monkey was left. It jumped all alone. Then it fell off too.

"Now there are no monkeys," said Maverick. He picked them all up. He counted them: one, two, three, four, five.

"How many are left now?" his dad asked from the front seat.

Maverick looked at his lap. "Five! We start again."

He began the song again. Outside the window, the wheels went around. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," he counted to the wheel sounds.

"We are almost there," said his dad. "Abby will like your song."

Maverick smiled. "Abby gets a monkey. A nice monkey."

He lined up the monkeys on his knee. The car stopped. There was Abby's door. Maverick held his monkeys tight.

Samuel was drawing at his desk. He made a big red ball. Then he made a messy blue sky. His crayons rolled under the desk. He had to reach far to get them.

"Time for the park," said Dad. Samuel ran to the door. He could see the swings across the road. The swings looked fun. Samuel wanted to run. He stopped at the curb and waited.

"Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street," Dad said. Samuel held Dad's big hand tight. They looked left. They looked right. They walked across together. Then Samuel let go and ran to the swings. Rosa was there too. "I held my dad's hand all the way," Samuel said. Rosa smiled and pushed the swing for him. "Higher, please!" Samuel said. His shoes touched the sky, almost.

Emile was a small boy in a big white seat. The lights went low. A woman with a violin walked out. Hasan sat next to Emile. Mr. Nolan sat on the other side. The music began, soft and slow.

Emile clapped his hands. Clap, clap! Mr. Nolan held up one finger. He pointed to the stage. The music was still playing. Emile put his hands in his lap. He listened. The song went on and on. Would it ever stop? He tapped his toe, one, two, one, two. He sang a little rhyme in his head, Twinkle, twinkle, little star.

The last note rang out. Then the music stopped. Mr. Nolan clapped, and Hasan clapped, and everyone clapped. Emile clapped too, fast and loud. One, two, three! The violin woman smiled and took a bow.

"When do we clap next?" Emile whispered.

"When the next song ends," said Hasan.

Emile nodded. His hands waited in his lap, ready.

Willow sat at Grandma's big chair. She had a long piece of paper and a box of crayons. She wanted to draw a picture for Grandma. It would be the garden and the sky.

Willow drew red flowers. She drew yellow flowers. She drew green grass, so green and soft. Then she picked up a gray crayon. "The sky is gray," she said. She made one gray line.

Grandma looked out the window. "What a sunny day," she said. Willow looked too. The sun was bright and warm on her face. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue! Willow put the gray crayon back. She took the blue crayon. She filled the whole top of her page with blue.

"Look, Grandma!" said Willow. Grandma held the picture up to the window. The blue on the paper met the blue in the sky. "It matches," said Grandma. Willow smiled and drew one yellow sun.

Arya knelt in the school garden with her friend Madyson. They had planted tiny lettuce plants. Every morning they came to look. "Will they grow big?" Arya wondered.

One hot day the lettuce looked sad. The leaves hung down low. "Why are they drooping?" Arya asked. Ms. Guo handed her the watering can. Arya tipped it over the plants. Water dripped onto the mud. Drip, drip, drip.

The next day Arya ran to the garden. The lettuce stood up tall. The leaves were wide and perky. "It was thirsty!" Arya said. Madyson clapped her hands. Arya picked up the watering can. "Let's give them another drink before we're late for class."

Kayden sat at the big table. Everyone was at Grandma's house today. Auntie carried in a big hot pot. Uncle put down baskets of bread. Kayden wanted to help start the meal.

"You can lead us," said Grandma. "Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it. We are a singing family." Kayden stood up tall. He took a big breath. Then he opened his mouth. Out came the wrong tune. It sounded like a silly song about ducks. Paul and Sage giggled. Kayden's face went hot.

"That's okay," said Grandma. "Try again." Sage wiped the table with a square cloth, slow and calm. "You can do it," said Paul. Kayden counted to help himself. One, two, three. He took another breath. This time the tune came out right. It rolled along, curly and sweet, like Grandma's own voice.

Everyone joined in. Mr. Jean-Louis, the neighbour, sang too from his chair. The song went around the table. Then the bread baskets opened. Kayden sat down and smiled at his plate. "Again tomorrow?" he asked Grandma. She patted his curly head. "Every meal," she said.

Madison was at Grandma's house. It was almost time for dinner. Grandma called, "Come and wash your hands."

Madison ran to the sink. She put soap on her hands. She rinsed it off fast. Then she held up her wet hands. "Done!"

Grandma smiled. "Not yet, sweet pea. Scrub with soap for twenty seconds. That is a long, slow count."

"Twenty?" said Madison. "That is so many!"

Grandma turned on the water. "Let us count together." They counted, "One, two, three." Madison scrubbed and scrubbed. The soap made white bubbles. Bubbles went up her arms. They counted all the way to twenty.

Then Madison rinsed the bubbles off. Her hands were clean and shiny. Grandma gave her a big towel. Madison dried each finger.

At the table, Grandma gave Madison a warm bun. Madison held it with her clean hands. "My hands smell like flowers," she said.

Grandma laughed. "They sure do."

After dinner, Madison had to use the toilet. When she came out, she went straight to the sink. "I have to do the big count," she said.

She counted to twenty all by herself. Her voice went slow so she would not rush. "Nineteen, twenty!"

Grandma peeked around the door. "My big girl," she said. "Now come give me a hug."

Chloe stood at the bus stop with her dad. The sun was warm on her face. Then the wind blew hard. It tossed her hair all around.

"Rain is coming," said Tala. Tala was waiting too. She wore yellow rain boots. Big drops began to fall. Chloe jumped in a puddle. Splash! Water went into her shoes.

"My socks are all wet," said Chloe. She wiggled her toes. Squish, squish. Tala looked down at Chloe's feet. "My boots keep my feet dry," said Tala. She stepped in a big puddle. Splash! Tala smiled. Her feet were still dry inside.

The rain turned to snow. Soft white flakes fell on the bus stop. They landed on the wooden bench. Chloe held out her hand. A flake sat on her glove. At school, Mr. Kaminski helped Chloe. He put her wet socks by the warm radiator. "My mom will bring my boots tomorrow," said Chloe. Tala gave her a high five. "Then we can splash together," said Tala.

Charlotte wanted to play the word game again. Yesterday her friend Ophelie had shouted a word, and Charlotte had shouted back. "Big!" said Ophelie. "Small!" said Charlotte. "Big and small are opposites," Ophelie had said. Two words, different as can be!

Today Charlotte looked around her kitchen for words. "Big!" she shouted at the fridge. Then she whispered, "Small," at a cup. She counted on her fingers. One pair! Two pairs!

Her dad was cooking soup. The pot went gurgle, gurgle. "Careful," said Dad. "The stove is hot. You stay back." Charlotte touched the cold window instead. Brrr! "Hot and cold," she said. "Opposites!" Three pairs!

Outside, a dog ran by, fast fast fast. Then it stopped to sniff. Slow, slow, slow. Charlotte laughed. "Fast and slow! Opposites!" Four pairs! Her dad smiled and tapped the pot with a wooden spoon. Then he said, "Sharp knife next, so watch me cut, not you." Charlotte watched. The knife cut a carrot with a snick.

"Can we pay the game tomorrow?" Charlotte asked. "Play the game," said Dad, laughing. "Yes! Play it with Ophelie." Charlotte ran to the window, fast as the dog. "Ophelie!" she called down the street. "Big news! I know four pairs!"

Grandpa had a big drum in the attic. Jules tapped it with his hand. Boom! "Wow," said Jules. He hit it harder. BOOM! The loud sound filled the whole room. Downstairs, the baby woke up and cried. "Oops," said Jules. Grandpa came up the stairs. "That was a big sound," said Grandpa. "Try a little sound."

Jules tapped the drum softly. Tap. The sound was small and quiet. He tapped again. Tap, tap. The baby stayed asleep. Jules giggled. "I can make little sounds too," he said.

Then Jules played a game. He hit hard for a big boom. He tapped soft for a little tap. Grandpa clapped. "You are a drum man now," said Grandpa. Jules tapped one more soft tap. "Shh," he whispered. "The baby is sleeping."

Miles stood on his stool in the kitchen. It was Mama's birthday today. Miles wanted to bake her a cake. He cracked two eggs into the big bowl. Mama helped with the sharp part. Miles poured in the flour and the sugar. He stirred and stirred with the wooden spoon.

The batter was runny. It went drip, drip, drip. Miles frowned at the bowl. "This can't be a cake," he said. "It's just soup! Birthday soup!" He stuck his finger in and tasted it. Yum. It was sweet, juicy, runny birthday soup. "Mama will get soup for her birthday," he said. He tried not to giggle.

Mama poured the batter into a pan. She put the pan in the hot oven. Miles watched from his spot at the table. He waited and waited. Then the timer rang. Mama opened the oven. Out came a real cake! It was big and round and firm. "It's not soup anymore," said Miles. Mama cut one slice from the top. Miles took a bite and smiled. "Happy birthday, Mama!"

Kayden's class was having a shape hunt. Mr. Mehta gave each child a card. Kayden's card had a circle on it. So did Mohamed's card.

"I will find the big circle," said Mohamed. He ran to the wall clock. "Look! The clock is a circle."

Kayden looked down at his shirt. He saw a tiny button. He held it up. "My button is a circle too," he said.

Mohamed shook his head. "No way. Your button is too small. The clock is a circle."

Mr. Mehta came over. He was calm and kind. He put the button near the clock. "Put them side by side," he said.

Kayden looked at the big clock. He looked at his tiny button. He turned the button around. He traced it with his finger. Round and round it went. Round and round the clock went too.

"Both are circles!" said Kayden. "Big circle, small circle, both circles."

Mohamed traced the button too. "Both circles," he said. He smiled.

Then the boys counted their circles. One clock. Two buttons. Three stickers on the door. Kayden found a cookie in his lunch box at snack time. "The cookie is a circle too," he said. It was a cool find.

Mr. Mehta laughed. "Good hunting, boys," he said. Kayden put his button back on his shirt. He would remember this day.

"One circle," said Mohamed.

"Two circles," said Kayden.

"All circles," they said together.

Ethan was playing cars in the playroom. Angel was there too. They had lots of shiny cars. Ethan wanted his cars to be magic.

"I know," said Ethan. "Let's make a road!" He put down a yellow scarf. It looked like a big sunny road. Angel put down a blue scarf next to it. Now the road was long.

Then Lily-Rose held up a green card. "Green means go!" she said. Ethan pushed his little red car fast, fast, fast. It zoomed down the scarves. Then Lily-Rose held up a red card. "Red means stop," she said. Ethan stopped his car. It stopped right away, like magic!

Angel smiled. She drove a yellow truck to the end of the road. There sat a stuffed bunny. The bunny held a paper flower. "Truck, take the flower to the bunny!" said Ethan. Lily-Rose held up the green card. The truck went. She held up the red card. The truck stopped.

The cars stopped and went all morning. Stop, go, stop, go. Then Ethan's dad came to the door. "Time to go home, Ethan." Ethan picked up his red car. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked. His dad smiled and said, "Yes, we can." Ethan waved the little car at his friends. "Beep beep," said the car.

Bennett woke up early. "Is it today?" he asked. "Is today the library day?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now."

Bennett looked out the window. The sun was up now. That meant it was really today. Yesterday he had waited all day. Yesterday was gone. Today was here!

He put on his shoes. He brought his fuzzy bear. "Bear wants a book too," he said.

At the library, Ms. Sow was there. "We went yesterday!" said Kenna.

"No," said Ms. Sow gently. "Yesterday you came with Lewis. Today is a new day, and today Bennett is here."

Bennett picked a big book about trucks. "Can we read it now?" he asked.

"Yes, now," said Mom. They sat on a soft rug and read it now, not later.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" Bennett asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow comes after today."

Bennett hugged his fuzzy bear. He borrowed three books to bring home for dinner time.

"Tomorrow, truck book!" he said.

Sadie wore her red sweater to the pet store. She held her dad's hand. There were fish and birds and one small brown puppy. "Can we take him home?" she asked. Her dad said yes. Sadie smiled so hard her cheeks hurt.

At home, the puppy spilled his water bowl. Water went all over the floor. Sadie got a small broom and helped sweep. The floor was dry again. The puppy wagged his tail.

The next day, the puppy did not want to play. He just lay in his bed. "Is he sick?" Sadie asked. "We will take him to the doctor," her dad said. Sadie felt worried. "A big people doctor?" she asked. "No," said her dad. "A vet."

At the vet's office, Sadie looked around. A cat sat in a box. A rabbit sat in a lap. A dog waited with a bone. "Where are all the people patients?" she asked. A lady in a blue coat laughed softly. "A vet is a doctor for animals," she said. "I only see animals here."

The vet looked at the puppy. She gave him some medicine. The puppy licked her hand. At home, the puppy ran in a circle. He chased his tail. Then he jumped up beside Sadie.

"You feel better!" said Sadie. The puppy licked her nose.

Riley sat on the big couch. She had a cold. Her nose was red and her head hurt a little. She was awake, but she was very tired.

Her dad brought soup and toast. Riley loved toast. She took one bite. Then two bites. Then she put the toast down. "More?" her dad asked. Riley shook her head. "My tummy says no more."

Dad smiled. "That's okay. When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much." Riley looked at the plate. One, two bites. That was all. So that was why her tummy felt that way!

Then Riley heard a sound. Jingle, jingle. It was the key in the front door! Rae came in with her mom. Rae held a small banana. "For you," Rae said.

Riley took a tiny bite. It tasted good. She took one more tiny bite. Then she snuggled under the blanket. "Thank you, Rae," she said. "Two bites today. Maybe ten tomorrow."

Evan woke up and saw snow. So much snow! School was closed. It was a snow day at home!

He ran to the window. A big truck was coming down the street. It had a big blade in front. "That is a snowplow," said his dad. "A snowplow pushes snow off the road." The blade pushed the snow to the side. The road turned black and clear. Evan pressed his nose to the cold glass. Wow!

"Can we go sledding now?" Evan asked. "Yes!" said Dad. "The road is clear, so we can walk to the hill." Evan put on his boots. They climb up the big hill. Then they zoom down, fast, fast, fast!
