Whitney was there too. "Watch me!" Evan shouted. He lay on his sled and flew down the stormy white hill like a bird.

Florence had a big box of blocks. She wanted to build a rainbow tower. "Which block goes first?" she asked. "The red one," she said. She made a red pile, then a blue pile, then a yellow pile.

John came to play. He sat down and looked at her piles. "My turn," said John. He put all the small blocks in one pile. He put all the big blocks in another pile. Florence gasped. The same blocks, but different piles!

"You sorted by size," said Florence. "I sorted by color." She tried it too. Big blocks here, small blocks there. Then she dropped a small red block on the tower. "Too small," she laughed. "It wobbles!" John found a big red one. The tower stood tall and still, like a castle in a story. "Perfect," said Florence. "Now we need a dragon."

Everett ran to the dinner table. His hands were muddy from the garden. "Time to eat!" said Mom.

But Mom held up her hand. "Stop, Everett. We wash our hands before we eat." Everett looked down. His fingers were brown with mud. Mud on hands, and dinner on a plate. That did not go together.

Everett walked to the sink. Mom turned on the tap. The water felt cool. He put his hands under it. He rubbed and rubbed. The mud went down, down, down. Mom gave him a towel. His hands were clean and pink now.

Back at the table, Everett sat on his square placemat. His plate had pasta and peas. Fiona and Rita were eating too. "Look at my clean hands!" said Everett. He held them up high. "Nice hands," said Rita. Mom filled his cup with milk. Everett took a big bite of pasta. Clean hands, yummy dinner. He smiled at Mom. "Wash first, then eat," said Everett, and he picked up his spoon.

The lights went out. The whole living room went dark. Dad lit some candles on the table. Victoria sat on the rug and waited. It was very quiet.

Dad gave her a flashlight. "This is for you," he said. Victoria held it in her hands. She turned it on. The light shone on her fingers. Then she saw something on the wall. It was a big dark shape. It moved when her hand moved. She wiggled two fingers up. "Look, Dad! A bunny!" she said. The shadow bunny had long ears. Dad laughed and made a shadow dog.

Victoria tried again. She bent her fingers slowly. The bunny ears went down. She slid her hand along the wall. The bunny hopped far away. "It can share the wall with your dog," she said. Dad moved his dog next to it.

The candles glowed on the table. The two good friends sat in the dark, playing with light. Then the lights came back on. The bunny was gone. "Make it again!" said Victoria. Dad clicked the flashlight off and on. The bunny came back.

Olivia ran to the park with her dad. Adelyn and Wayne were there. They were playing a game. It was Duck, Duck, Goose. Olivia said, "I want to play too." Adelyn said, "Okay, but we follow the rules. One, you tap a head. Two, you say goose. Three, you run around." They all sat in a circle. Wayne tapped Olivia's head. "Goose!" Then he ran fast. Olivia ran fast too. Wayne got to her spot first. Olivia had to sit. She was not happy. Then Wayne said, "New rule. Only I get to be it." Adelyn stood up. "That is not fair." Olivia stood up too. Adelyn and Olivia walked away. Wayne sat all alone. Then Wayne said, "Okay, okay. Same rules for all." They came back. They played one round, two rounds, three. A duck waddled by the pond. Olivia laughed. It was almost time to go. "We are not late yet," said her dad. Olivia tapped Adelyn's head. "Goose!"

Ellie looked out the kitchen window. Dad was at the grill in the backyard. The grill was hot. "Stay back, Ellie," said Dad. Ellie stayed on the grass.

Her friend Malakai came over to play. He brought a little slide from his yard. Ellie wanted to slide down it first. She climbed up the ladder. Then she lay down on her tummy. Her head pointed down the slide.

"Wait," said Malakai. "At the playground, go down the slide feet first." Ellie sat up. She turned herself around. Now her feet pointed down the slide. Whoosh! She slid down and landed on the soft grass.

"Again!" said Ellie. Up she went. Feet first, whoosh, down. Each time, her feet touched the grass first.

Then Ellie saw something pink in the tree. "Look, Malakai!" she said. It was a pink ribbon on a branch. Was it part of a nest? A small bird sat on the nest. The bird looked at Ellie. Ellie looked at the bird.

"Do you think it has eggs?" asked Malakai.

"Maybe," said Ellie. "We can look from here. We will not touch."

They sat side by side in the shade. The grill sizzled. The bird sang. Ellie whispered, "Hello, bird."

Aiden had a dream. He wanted to grow carrots on the balcony. His dad helped him put seeds in a big flat pot. Aiden patted the soil down with his hands. "Now we wait," said Dad.

Every morning Aiden checked the pot. The soil was brown and still flat. Nothing was there. He gave the pot a little water. Then he waited some more.

One morning Aiden looked again. A tiny green thing was poking up out of the soil. "Dad, come quick!" said Aiden. Dad came to look. "That is a sprout," said Dad. "A tiny new plant poking up is called a sprout." Aiden smiled big. "A sprout! A sprout!" he said.

Aiden ran to tell his friend Raina. She lived next door. "My carrot has a sprout," said Aiden. Raina came to see it. The sprout was small and green. They sat by the pot and watched it together. "Hello, little sprout," said Raina.

Clara was at Mr. Pelletier's house. She sat on his big soft rug. Then all the lights went out. The lamp went dark. The clock stopped glowing.

"Stay right there," said Mr. Pelletier. He found a flashlight. He turned it on. The room had one bright circle of light.

Clara sat very still. She listened. "It is so quiet," she whispered. The house had been humming before. Now the humming was gone. The fridge had stopped. When the power goes out, the machines stop. The machines stop humming. So the house gets quieter.

"What is that sound?" Clara asked. She heard a tiny tick, tick, tick. Mr. Pelletier shined the light on the wall. It was his old wind-up clock! Clara had never heard it before. The humming had hidden it.

She heard another sound too. Tap, tap, tap at the window. Mr. Pelletier moved the light. A moth was walking on the glass.

"Can I write this down?" Clara asked. "So I remember the quiet sounds?" Mr. Pelletier gave her paper. She drew a triangle clock with three tick marks. He gave her a lemon drop. It was sour and good.

The lights came back on. The fridge began to hum again. The little clock got quiet once more. Clara held her paper and smiled.

"Goodbye, tick, tick, tick," she said.

Paisley ran to the park with her red ball. The gate was open, but the lock hung on the chain. It was loose, and it rattled. Paisley pushed the gate. It swung wide.

Ray was there by the big tree. He had a book on his lap. He was looking at the pictures. Paisley held out her ball. "Kick it to me, please," said Ray. Paisley kicked the ball. It rolled straight to his feet.

Ray jumped up. He ran off with the ball, all the way to the slide. Then he stopped. He turned around. "Thank you, Paisley," he called. He ran back and gave her a turn on the slide first.

Paisley sat on the slide. She saw Ray hold her ball. She saw him say thank you. When her turn came, she slid down slow, then fast. "Thank you, Ray," she said. Ray smiled and kicked the ball back to her. It rolled over the soft, green grass and stopped right at her toes.

Parker sat near the big TV at Mr. Haddad's house. Brinley and Vyom sat beside him. Everyone was watching a big game.

The blue team ran fast. Then the blue team scored! All the big people jumped up. They clapped and cheered. "Yay!" they shouted. Parker saw that. When a team scores, people clap.

Parker wanted to clap too. So he clapped. He cheered very loud. "Yay, blue team!" But Mr. Haddad laughed. "Parker, we like the red team!" Parker looked at the TV. The blue team was winning. His team might lose! Parker made a sad face.

Then the red team ran and scored! Everyone clapped again. This time Parker clapped too. "Yay, red team!" he cheered. Vyom patted his back. Brinley gave him a high five. Parker laughed. He had cheered for the wrong team before. Now he cheered for his team, loud and happy.

Mr. Haddad sat down by Parker. "Want a snack while we watch?" he asked. Parker nodded and clapped one more time.

Liam ran into the backyard. The sun was big and bright. He wanted to dig in his sandbox. But the sun was in his eyes. He made a funny squinty face. "Too sunny!" he said.

His dad came out with a hat. It was a blue sun hat. It had a big brim all around. "Try this," Dad said. Liam put it on. The brim made shade over his face. His eyes went wide. He could see the whole sandbox! "My hat makes shade!" he shouted.

Liam dug a big circle in the sand. It was a beautiful circle, round and neat. The wind blew a little. The leaves on the tree went flip, flip, flip. Liam laughed at them. Then Mona came over to play. She wore a sun hat too. "Sunny day, sun hat!" she said.

They dug together in the shade of their hats. Liam piled sand high, high, high. He put a leaf on top like a flag. "Look, Mona! My sand mountain!" The wind flipped the leaf again and again, and both of them clapped.

Avery ran into the store. She had been playing in the little play yard outside. "Where is the baby?" she asked. "I want to hold my baby sister!"

The baby was in a cart. She was sleeping in a soft blue blanket. Mommy smiled. "First we wash your hands," she said.

"Why?" asked Avery.

"Big sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby," said Mommy.

Avery looked at her hands. They had dirt on them. She had been digging in the play yard. Her hands made marks on her dress when she touched it.

Mommy took Avery to the sink. The water was warm, but Mommy turned it on. Avery watched from her step. She rubbed the soap all over. The bubbles tickled. Mommy helped her rinse. Now her hands were clean.

"Clean hands!" said Avery. She clapped them together. The water drops flew up like little sparkles.

Then Mommy sat down on the bench. She put the baby in Avery's lap. Avery held her arms very still. The baby opened her eyes. She made a small sound.

"Hello, baby," said Avery. "I washed my hands for you."

The baby grabbed Avery's finger with her tiny hand.

Mia stood on the big grass field. Mr. Kelly put a hoop on the ground. He gave her a small red beanbag. Mia threw it. It missed. It landed in the messy grass.

"Try again," said Mr. Kelly. Mia counted, "One, two, three." She swung her arm back. She threw it soft and slow. The beanbag went up. Then it went down. It fell right into the hoop. "I did it!" said Mia. Lilith clapped. Cynthia clapped too.

Then Mr. Kelly rolled a big ball to Mia. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out. It bounced away. "Oh no," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out again.

Then Mia had an idea. She waited with her arms open. The ball came. She caught it. Then she hugged it to her chest. The ball did not bounce out. It stayed right there. "One, two, three, I got it," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again, faster this time. Mia caught it and hugged it tight. The ball stayed.

Lilith ran over. "Can I try?" she asked. Mia opened her arms wide and smiled.

Camille was at the park with her friend Shayan. Mr. Suryanto held a big cloth bag. "Put your hand in," he said. "Guess what you find."

Camille put her hand in the bag. She felt something round and bumpy. "A ball!" she said. "A red ball!"

She pulled it out. The ball was green. Camille laughed. "I was sure it was red!"

"You can feel it is a ball," said Shayan. "But you cannot feel the color. Your eyes have to look."

They played again and again. Shayan felt something soft and small. He peeked. "A yellow duck!" Next Camille felt something flat and wide. She looked fast. It was a blue boat.

Then Camille felt something cold and wiggly. She jumped. "Yikes!" Out came a wide orange fish toy, and everyone laughed by the pond.

"Your turn again," said Shayan, holding out the bag.

Addison sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma set out a beautiful bowl of soup. Addison picked up her spoon right away. She took a big bite.

Then she looked up. Grandma was not eating. Papa was not eating. Auntie was not eating. Everyone sat still with their hands folded. "We say thank you first," said Grandma. Addison put down her spoon. She felt her cheeks get warm.

"Can I say it too?" asked Addison. "Yes," said Grandma. "You can say thank you with us." Everyone held hands. Addison squeezed Papa's big hand. "Thank you for the soup," said Addison. "Thank you for the water in my cup." Grandma smiled. Then everyone picked up a spoon at the same time. Addison took another bite. The soup tasted good after the thank you. Addison colored a picture after lunch. She colored the soup bowl and all the hands holding hands. "This is us," she said. Grandma hung it up by the table.

Cooper sat in his car seat. The wheels went spin, spin, spin on the road. "We go to Calder's house," said Dad. "His mom is making soup."

At Calder's house, the soup smelled good. Cooper stood in the doorway of the kitchen. He stayed close to Dad, just like always. Calder's mom stirred the big pot on the stove.

Cooper looked at the stove. It did not look hot. There was no fire. There was no smoke. Cooper wanted to touch it. He reached out his hand.

"Is the stove still hot?" Cooper asked Dad.

Dad held his hand softly. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot," said Dad. "Only grown-ups touch the stove." Cooper pulled his hand back. He stood by Dad's neck and held on.

Calder's mom used a big glove. She lifted the pot all by herself. Then she poured the soup into two small bowls.

The soup was too hot to eat. Cooper blew on his spoon. One, two, three. Then he took a little sip. It was warm and cozy in his tummy.

"The soup is all gone," said Cooper. He gave Dad a big hug.

Josephine came to the store with her dad. She held his hand. She saw apples in a big pile. She wanted a red apple. She was excited.

Josephine reached for the apple. It fell down. It rolled under the shelf. She felt sad. Her dad said, "Let's try again." He got down on his knees. He reached far. Out came the apple.

Then Josephine saw her dad's face. He looked worried. "Are you scared?" she asked. "A little," said Dad. "I was nervous too, like you at the doctor." Josephine stared. Grown-ups had feelings too! Even dads!

"I cry sometimes," said Dad. "And I get happy, like now." Josephine gave him a big smile.

They walked to the bread aisle. Josephine picked a box with a bird on it. A yellow bird, flying up high.

At the car, Dad blew up a balloon for her. She hugged it all the way home. It went pop in the door, and it was flat. Josephine laughed. "It's flat, Daddy! Flat like a pancake!"

Dad laughed too. "We can blow it up again tomorrow."

Nora stood by the door with her red coat. "I want to do it all by myself," she said. Her mom smiled and waited.

First Nora found the sleeves. One sleeve hid behind her back. She wiggled and pulled. Then her arm popped out. "Got you!" she said. Next came the zipper. She tried to pinch it. The zipper was slippery in her fingers. It slipped down, down, down. Nora tried again. She held the bottom tight with one hand. She pushed the zipper up with the other. Zip, zip, zip. It went all the way to her chin. "I did it! I did it!" said Nora.

Then they stepped outside to wait for the bus. Drip, drip. Little rain fell. Nora felt drops on her hair. Then she remembered. Her coat had a soft part on the back. "That's the hood," said her mom. Nora reached back and pulled it up over her head. The hood covered her. The drops went plip, plip on top of it, and her hair stayed dry. "My hood keeps me dry," said Nora. She pulled it down. Drip, on her nose. She pulled it up again. Dry! Nora laughed under the hood and jumped in a small, wet puddle.

Grandma put a brown pot on the table. "Shall we sing?" she asked. Eliana nodded. She wanted to sing the whole cat song by herself.

Grandma clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Eliana clapped too. Her hands went slow, then fast, then slow again. "Try steady," said Grandma. "Like this." Clap, clap, clap. Eliana watched Grandma's hands. She clapped just like her. The claps matched the song!

Then Eliana sang alone. "The cat sat on his..." She stopped. She had lost the word. She frowned. "What sounds like cat?" she wondered. She tried "hat." "The cat sat on his hat!" Grandma laughed and clapped. "Yes! Cat and hat end the same," she said.

Eliana sang it again. Then she touched her own hat. She ran to the store bag by the door and pulled out a small brown hat. She put it on the cat picture in her book. "Now the song is true," she said. Grandma clapped the steady beat. Eliana clapped too, and sang every word.

Florence ran into the backyard. Her little pool was full of water. She wanted to jump in right away. "Can I get in now?" she asked.

Dad held up his hand. "Wait, let me check the water first," he said. The hose had sat in the sun all day. Dad touched the water with his hand. Then he touched the side of the pool. "It is warm, not hot," he said. "Warm is good. Hot would hurt your toe." Florence touched the water too. It felt like her bath at night. It felt nice.

Mr. Nwosu was next door at his grill. The grill was very hot. He turned the food with a long fork. "Stay back from the fire," Mr. Nwosu said. Florence stayed close to Dad. She sat down at the pool edge. Her loose hat fell off. "Let me fix your hat," Dad said. He tied it under her chin.

Florence put one toe in the water. Then she put in her whole foot. Then she climbed in all the way. "The water is warm!" she called. Mr. Nwosu smiled and waved. Florence splashed her hands. Dad sat right beside her on the grass.

Aiden went to the store with his dad. He wanted a big red apple. He held his dad's hand and skipped to the fruit bins. The apples looked wild and shiny in a tall pile.

At the checkout, a cashier put the apple in a bag. Then she gave Aiden a shiny sticker. Aiden took it and said nothing. His dad tapped him gently. Aiden thought, "Why?" A lady helped June reach a cart, and June said, "Thank you." Then Gabriel dropped his bread, and the cashier picked it up. Gabriel said, "Thank you" too.

Aiden looked down at his sticker. He turned back to the cashier. "Thank you," he said. She smiled a big smile. Aiden smiled too. He held up his sticker all the way to the car. "A party for my apple," he said.

Penelope stood in the school library. She wanted to count the red books. Mr. Han put ten red books on the table. "Can you count them?" he asked.

Penelope touched each book. "One, two, three," she said. She kept going. "Eight, nine, ten." Ten red books! Then Mr. Han put out blue books. Penelope counted them too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Now she wondered. Which pile had more?

She looked and looked. The red pile looked big. The blue pile looked small. She felt a little scared to guess. She might get it wrong.

Adelaide came to help. "Make a line," she said. Penelope put each red book in a line. Then she put one blue book next to each red book. One red, one blue. One red, one blue. She went all the way to the end.

Every red book had a blue friend. Not one book was left out. "They match!" said Penelope. "Ten and ten. The same!"

Mr. Han smiled. "Would you like to try the green books next?"

Penelope grabbed the green pile. "Watch me," she said.

Benjamin ran to the bathroom after the rainy walk. His socks were wet. His shoes were wet. One, two, three drips fell on the floor.

He saw a little hole in the wall. It was low down, near the sink. What was it? It had two small slots. Did an ant live in there? Benjamin bent down low. His fingers came close.

"No touching," said his dad. "Fingers go in your pocket. Dad puts things in the outlet."

Benjamin put his fingers in his pocket. He watched his dad push the plug into the slots. One push. Then the little heater by the door hummed. Warm air came out.

"Hot," said Dad. "Stay back, please."

Benjamin stayed back. He counted the warm puffs. One, two, three. The plug made the heater work. He would pay attention to that.

"Can I tell Shivansh tomorrow?" Benjamin asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Good noticing, Benjamin."

Rowan went to the baby store with his mom. A new baby was coming to his house soon. Rowan wanted to pick a gift all by himself. He saw a soft gray rabbit on a shelf. "That one," he said. "The rabbit is not too heavy."

On the next shelf there was a doll for practice. Ms. Navarro worked at the store. "You can try holding it," she said. Rowan picked up the doll. The doll's head flopped way down. "Oh no," said Rowan. "Its head fell!"

Ms. Navarro showed him how. She put her hand under the doll's head. "See? I hold the head," she said. "A new baby cannot hold up its own head. So grown-ups hold the baby's head when they carry it." Rowan tried it. He put his small hand under the doll's head. This time the head stayed up. "I did it!" he said.

Then Rowan found his mom. She was buying little socks. Rowan held up the rabbit. "For the baby," he said. "And I know how to hold it. I will hold the head, like this." He showed her with the doll. His mom smiled big. At home, Rowan put the rabbit by the empty crib. He patted the soft head, very, very gently.

Zoey sat at the little table. Mr. Dhillon put out three big red balls. Then he put out three tiny yellow beads. "Which group has more?" he asked.

Zoey looked at the balls. They were so big! "The balls," she said. "They are more."

Mr. Dhillon smiled. "Let's count and see."

Zoey touched each ball. "One, two, three." Then she touched each bead. "One, two, three."

She blinked. The same! Three big balls and three tiny beads were both three.

"Wowl," said Zoey. "Big ones and small ones count the same."

Emery leaned over from the next table. "Can I try?" She counted four little frogs. "Four frogs," she said. Zoey counted three blocks. Emery had more.

Zoey did not feel sad. She jumped up and bent down to pick up a bead that rolled away. "Again!" she said. "Let's count again!"

Mr. Dhillon laughed and put out ten buttons.

Madeline sat in the playroom with her doll. She wanted to know how old Rayyan was. She did not know how to ask.

Rayyan held up some fingers. Madeline held up her fingers too. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six fingers! Madeline felt sad. Rayyan was so big, and she was so small.

Mr. Karimi came in with blocks. "How old are you, Madeline?" he asked. Madeline held up her hand. "Four," she said. Then she asked, "Did I say it right?" "Yes," said Mr. Karimi. "You are four."

Ziyad ran in. "I am five!" he said. He held up five fingers. Madeline counted them. Then she counted Rayyan's fingers again. "Six, seven," she said. "I am seven!" Rayyan laughed. He shook his head. He put down one finger. Now he held up five.

Madeline had to wait for her turn with the blocks. She counted the blocks while she waited. "One, two, three, four, five." She made a tower. Mr. Karimi put the last block on top. Madeline hugged her doll and smiled. "I am four," she said to the doll.

Elijah was at home. He did not want his shot. "The needle will be big," he said. "It will be as wide as my thumb!" His mom packed his toy frog. "You can hold Frog," she said. Elijah held Frog all the way to the doctor. He missed his warm breakfast at home. His tummy felt funny.

The nurse came in. She wiped Elijah's arm. The wipe felt cool. "Look at Frog," said Mom. Elijah looked at Frog. Then, quick! One thin needle poked his arm, and it was done. "That was so fast," said Elijah. His eyes went wide. The nurse put a band-aid on his arm. It had stars on it.

At home, Elijah showed his frog the star band-aid. "Frog, a shot is one quick poke," he said. "It is not wide at all." He kissed Frog's head. Then he ran to play.

Dylan ran to the front door. The sun was out. It was a sunny day!

"I want to play outside!" said Dylan.

"First we get sunscreen," said his dad. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn."

Dylan stood very straight. Dad rubbed the sunscreen on his arms. Then on his face. It felt cool and smooth.

"Now I can go out!" said Dylan.

Dylan played with Soleil in the sun. They ran and jumped. The sun shone and shone.

Later, Dylan looked at his arms. No red spots! "My skin is okay," he said.

"It is okay," said Soleil. "You got sunscreen."

Clouds came. The sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. "Rainy now!" said Dylan.

They ran to the front door. Dad had two raincoats waiting.

"Rainy day, raincoat day!" said Dylan.

Dad laughed. "That's right!"

Logan stood in the pool changing room. He pulled off his shoes. His socks went into the bag. His feet felt cold on the wet floor. "Swim time," he said.

He walked out to the pool with his friend Abigail. The water was big and blue. Logan wanted to jump in right away. He ran to the edge. Then he looked around. Ms. Torres was not there yet. No grown-up was watching the pool. Abigail held his hand. "We have to wait," she said. Logan stopped at the side. He sat down on the cool tiles. He put his toes near the water, but not in.

Then the door opened. Ms. Torres walked in with the whistle. "My eyes are on you now," she said. Logan stood up. He jumped in with a big splash. The water went up and up. Then the water came back down on his head. His jump made the splash! He laughed and laughed. Abigail jumped in too. "Splash!" she said.

The bookmobile came to Adam's street. He held his dad's hand. Today Adam would get his very own library card.

Inside, the shelves were tall. The books were way up high. Adam stood on his tiptoes. He could not reach them. The books had tiny words and no pictures. He felt like giving up.

Then he saw his friend Priscilla. "Come here," she said. She pointed to a small corner. There was a little rug and low shelves. "This is the children's area," she said. "The books here are just for young kids." The covers were red and yellow and blue.

Adam knelt down. He did not have to reach at all. He found a book about a big red truck. He carried it with careful hands to Ms. Tanaka, the bookmobile lady. She smiled and made his new card. "One book," she said. "Due back next week."

Adam put the card in his shoe so he would not lose it. Then he waved to Priscilla. "See you next week!" he said.

Brooklyn ran to the living room. The Christmas tree stood tall and green. "We decorate a tree at Christmas," said Grandma.

A big box sat on the floor. It was full of ornaments. Brooklyn picked up a shiny red ball. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a snowman there too. Then a little drum. Soon one branch was full.

"Look, Mama!" said Brooklyn. "My branch is so pretty."

Maci, her cousin, came close. "The tree is empty on top," Maci said. "Only one branch has ornaments."

Brooklyn looked up. Maci was right. She took a golden star from the box. She hung it high on another branch. Then a bell. Then a silver bird. Her hands reached out, one branch at a time.

Grandma plugged in the lights. Brooklyn stood back with Maci. The whole tree danced with tiny lights.

"Now it is a dream tree," said Brooklyn. Maci laughed and held her hand.

Lennon went to the grocery store with her dad. They needed eggs, milk, and blueberries. "We can bake muffins!" said Lennon. Her dad said yes. Lennon picked the biggest blueberries she could find. They were fat and blue. She held the bag like a treasure.

At home, Lennon helped mix. Dad put the pan in the hot oven. Then a bell went off in Dad's pocket. "What is that?" asked Lennon. "It is the kitchen timer," said Dad. "It beeps to tell the cook it is time to check the food." Lennon listened hard. Beep, beep, beep!

Then Brianna came over to play. They built a tall block tower. They turned on the lamp to see better. They laughed and laughed. Dad sat on the couch. He was feeling lazy after shopping. Everyone started to forget the muffins!

Beep, beep, beep! The timer rang out loud. "The muffins!" yelled Lennon. Dad jumped up and ran to the kitchen. He took out the pan. The muffins were big and gold. But one was not gold. It was giant, as big as a plate! "How did it get so big?" asked Lennon. Dad smiled. "It grew in the oven." Lennon took a tiny bite. "Best muffin ever," she said.

Hayden sat at the big kitchen table. Dad was washing dishes at the sink. Hayden had five cards in front of him. Each card had a body part on it. "Let's play the sense game," said Dad. "One card for each sense."

A big truck rumbled by outside. Rumble, rumble, rumble. It was so loud. Hayden covered his ears with his hands. Then the truck sound got quiet. He took his hands away. The rumble came back loud. He put his hands back. Quiet again. Hayden smiled.

"Dad, my hands make it quiet," he said. Dad clapped and laughed. "Good finding, Hayden." Then Dad held up the card with the ear on it. "What do ears do?" Hayden patted his ears. "Ears hear the truck," he said. He put the ear card in the middle of the table.

Then Dad held up the nose card. Hayden sniffed the cold milk on the table. "Noses smell," he said. Next came the eye card. "Eyes see the milk," said Hayden. Then the tongue card. "Tongues taste the milk." Last came the hand card. "Hands touch, and hands make loud sounds quiet too," said Hayden. Dad smiled wide. "All five senses. You did it."

Hayden lined all five cards up in a row. Then a dog barked outside. Hayden covered his ears and whispered, "Woof, woof, quiet woof."

Declan ran to the window. "Rain!" he shouted. Big drops hit the glass. Plip, plip, plip.

"I want to splash in puddles!" said Declan. He ran to the door. He opened it fast. He ran straight out into the yard.

The rain fell on his head. The rain fell on his shirt. It was cold and wet. Declan was wet all over. He ran back inside fast.

His mom held up a red coat. "Your raincoat," she said. "Put it on." Declan pushed his arms in. He zipped it up. He pulled the hood on too.

Then he ran back out. The rain fell on the hood. Plip, plip. The rain fell on the coat. Plip, plip. But Declan stayed dry under it. Not wet at all!

He touched his sleeve. The rain sat on top. It did not go through. "Dry!" he yelled. He jumped in a big puddle. The water went splash.

Maci came by in her yellow boots. "Look at all that rain!" she said. "My coat keeps me dry too!" They stomped and stomped. Two dry kids, two big puddles, one happy rainy day.

Kai ran into the library with his mom. "Tablets today!" he said. Ms. Desir smiled and held up a big box. The box was full of tablets.

Kai picked one. The screen was dark. He pressed the round button. The screen lit up! "Look, Mom! I did that!" said Kai.

Flora sat next to him. "Tap the little paint pot," she said. Kai tapped it. A drawing app opened. There were bright colors everywhere. Kai drew a big red truck. Then he drew rain falling on the truck. "Rain!" he laughed.

Then the timer rang. Time to put the tablets away. Kai did not know what to do. Flora pressed her round button. Her screen went dark. Kai pressed his button too. His screen went dark! The tablet was asleep now.

Kai put his tablet back in the box. Ms. Desir gave him a sticker. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Kai asked his mom.

"First the truck," said Flora. "Tomorrow the rain!"

Paisley stood by the backyard pool. Her tummy did a little flip.

"Can I get out all by myself?" she asked.

"Yes, you can try," said her dad. He stayed right beside her.

Paisley kicked and splashed. She blew bubbles. Then she swam to the edge. She pushed on the side. She pulled and pulled. Her arms got tired. She slipped back with a plop. A puddle of water dripped from her nose.

Rafael was there too. "Use the ladder," he said. He pointed to the silver bars.

Paisley swam to the ladder. She put her feet on the steps. Step, step, step. She climbed right up and out. It was easy!

"Where do the steps go?" Rafael asked her.

"Up and out of the water!" said Paisley.

Then she jumped back in with a big splash. The water flew far and hit Rafael's hair.

"Hey!" laughed Rafael. "My hair is all wet now."

Paisley laughed too. "Come and get me!"

Rafael chased her to the ladder. Step, step, step, and out she went, fast as a bunny.

Rose sat at the kitchen table. Mom was baking bread. "I want to help," said Rose.

"First, you can feel the dough," said Mom. Rose poked it with her fingertips. "It is soft and squishy!" she said. "I feel it with my skin. My fingertips feel it!"

Mom rolled the dough into a ball. Rose rolled a small piece too. "My hands feel the dough," said Rose. "What else can my skin feel?"

Rose touched the wood table. "The wood is hard," she said. She touched a cold spoon. "The spoon is cold." She touched a warm towel. "The towel is warm." Her skin told her each thing.

"Now let's name the five senses," said Mom. "Eyes see. Ears hear. Nose smells. Tongue tastes. And skin feels!" Rose touched her cheeks, her hands, her fingertips. "My skin is everywhere!" she said.

The bread went into the oven. Mom put it in, because ovens are hot. Rose waited at the table. Soon the smell filled the kitchen. "My nose smells bread!" said Rose.

The bell rang. Ding! "My ears hear it," said Rose. Mom set down a warm slice. Rose took a little bite. "My tongue tastes it. Yum!"

Then Rose touched the crust with one fingertip. "The crust feels bumpy," she said. "I found it all by myself."

Mom smiled. "One more sense to use," she said. Rose looked at the bread. "My eyes see it," she said. "All five!"

Axel was going on a big trip. First his family rode a train. The train went clickety-clack. Axel sat by the window with his small blue bag. Inside the bag was his toy bunny.

A girl sat across from him. "I am Lya," she said. She had a backpack with a teddy bear. "We are going to the airport," she said. "My dad says the bags go on a little ride there."

Axel held his bag tight. A machine that takes bags? That sounded scary to him. What if bunny did not come back?

The train stopped. Everyone walked into the big airport. A man in a uniform stood by a machine. Lya's dad put her backpack on a belt. The backpack slid into the machine. "My teddy!" Lya cried.

Axel watched. Out came the backpack on the other side. The teddy bear was right there. Lya laughed and hugged him.

Then it was Axel's turn. He put his blue bag on the belt. He watched it go in. His tummy felt funny. Then he looked at the other end.

Out came his bag. Bunny was safe. "It checks what is inside," Lya's dad said with a smile. Axel hugged bunny to his chest.

"Good ride, bunny," Axel whispered.

Gabriel stood on the big soccer field. Mr. Choi held out a red beanbag. "Toss it into the hoop," he said. Gabriel threw it hard. The beanbag flew over the hoop and landed in the grass.

"Try again," said Mr. Choi. Gabriel rubbed his tummy. He felt a little worried. Mr. Choi smiled at him. "I will stay right here," he said. Gabriel looked at the hoop. He took a soft, slow swing. This time the beanbag went right in. Gabriel clapped his hands. Anne clapped too.

Next, Mr. Choi brought out a big yellow ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. Anne went first. She threw the ball very hard at Gabriel. It was too fast. It bumped his arm and rolled away. Gabriel ran after it across the grass.

Gabriel picked up the ball. He thought about the beanbag. He did not throw hard. "Here comes a gentle toss," he said. Anne held out both hands. The ball came slowly. She caught it! "Again," said Anne. They played until the sun went down. Then Gabriel waved and said, "Bye, Mr. Choi."

Olivia stood at the train station. She held her mom's hand. Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. The train pulled in. It was long and gray. Grandpa stepped off with a big bag. "Olivia!" he said. She hugged him tight.

At home, Grandpa had a bath. Mom ran the water. Olivia waited outside the door. Soon Grandpa called, "Oh dear. Where are the towels?" Olivia heard him. She opened the cupboard in the hall. The towels were stacked inside, all soft and warm. She knocked on the door. "Here is a towel, Grandpa," she said. He took it and laughed. "What a good helper you are."

The next morning, Grandpa brushed his hair. He could not find the brush. "It fell under the bed," Olivia said. She picked it up and gave it to him. Grandpa smiled. He showed her the picture on his brush. It was a little gray cat.

All week, Grandpa asked where things were. Olivia showed him the bathroom. She showed him the cups. She showed him the coats by the door. On the last day, Grandpa packed his bag. "I know where everything is now," he said. "You showed me." Olivia helped zip the bag. Then she waved at the window and said, "Come back soon, Grandpa."

Madelyn sat in the backyard with her box of crayons. She was busy drawing the sky. Adem came over with his crayons too. "I want to draw the sky," he said. "Give me the blue."

"This is my blue," said Madelyn. She held up a light blue crayon.

Adem held up a dark one. "This one is not blue. It looks like night."

Madelyn tipped her head. "Can a color be night and blue too?" She thought hard. "Let's see!"

They lined up all the blue crayons on the grass. "One, two, three, four," they counted. Lightest first, darkest last. They made a little row, like a parade of blues.

The light blue looked like morning sky. The dark blue looked like night sky. Both were still blue!

"Now we can draw day and night," said Adem.

Madelyn drew a yellow sun on light blue. Adem drew white stars on dark blue. They made a card for Ms. Morales with both skies on it.

Madelyn found a green leaf and let it float onto her paper. "The leaf can be a boat," she said.

"Two boats!" said Adem. He floated a red petal next to it.

"Can I take your dark blue home?" Madelyn asked.

"Yes," said Adem. "It is blue, so it belongs with you."

Eloise went to the park with her dad. The sun was warm. The grass smelled green. "Stay where I can see you," said Dad. Eloise ran to the slide. She slid down, fast. It was fun.

Then Eloise saw something red. It was far away, by the big trees. She wanted to see it. She ran and ran. She looked back. She could not see Dad. Her tummy felt small and tight.

Eloise stopped. She stood still and called, "Dad! Dad!" A big voice called back, "Eloise!" She saw Dad's blue shirt. She ran to him, and he hugged her tight. "Stay where I can see you," said Dad again. Eloise held his hand.

They walked together to the red thing. It was a fire truck, parked by the grill. A man in a big hat was cooking. "The grill is hot," said Dad. "You stay back with me." Eloise watched from far away. The man flipped the food with a long fork. Later, they sat on the bench. Dad had cookies from home. "Yummy," said Eloise, chewing. The cookies were all gone.

Victor was going to the national park! He grabbed his striped backpack and ran to the car. "We will see big trees!" he sang.

Victor climbed into his seat. He was so excited. "Go, go, go!" he said. But the car did not go. Dad looked back at him. "Where is your click, Victor?"

Victor looked down. His buckle was not clicked. He pulled the strap across himself. He pushed it in. Click! Now he was buckled into his car seat. Dad started the car. Off they went!

At the park, Victor saw a tall, tall tree. A leaf broke off and began to fall. It twirled down, down, down. It landed right on Victor's shoe. He laughed and held it up high. "Look, Dad! A big tree made a leaf fall!"

Aaron went to the store with his dad. He held his dad's hand tight. The store was big and bright. "Stay close to me," said Dad. Aaron stayed close.

At the store, they got milk, bread and apples. Near the apples was a little rack. A shiny lighter sat on the floor by the rack. It was small and pretty. Aaron looked at it. He did not touch it. "Dad, that is on the floor," said Aaron. Dad picked it up with two fingers. He slid it into his pocket. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," said Dad. "Thank you for telling me."

Then Aaron saw Mr. Hughes from next door. Mr. Hughes waved. Dad let Aaron slide his hand free to wave too. Then Aaron took Dad's hand again. They paid for the apples. "You were a big helper today," said Dad. Aaron smiled and held on all the way to the car.

Eleanor sat in the playroom. She wanted to make a little paper house. She found a square piece of red paper. It had four sides, all the same. She held it up. "This will be my roof," she said.

Duke came to sit beside her. "My house needs a door," he said. Eleanor looked at her square paper. She turned it around. It was still a square. She frowned a little. Her mouth went sour. Then she had an idea. She folded the paper in half. She pressed the edge with her hand.

She opened her eyes wide. The paper was not a square now. It was long on two sides and short on two sides. "A rectangle," said Ms. Nur from the doorway, smiling. Eleanor ran her finger along the long side. "The rectangle is my door," she said. Duke clapped his hands.

They made more shapes together. Duke cut a circle for a window. Eleanor made a triangle roof. When the work was done, they sang a happy little song about their house. Eleanor held up the rectangle door one more time. "Square goes in," she said, "and rectangle comes out."

Isabella stood at the basketball court. Her friend Eli was there too. Mr. Grewal gave Isabella a red beanbag.

"Try to throw it in the hoop," said Mr. Grewal. The hoop was up high on the big pole. It was Isabella's favorite game now.

Isabella threw the beanbag. It missed. It fell on the ground. She threw it again. It missed again. Isabella looked at the hoop. Then she took a few steps closer. She threw the beanbag once more. It went in! "Yay!" said Isabella. Eli clapped his hands.

Next, Mr. Grewal rolled a big ball to Isabella. She held out both hands. The ball bounced off her tummy. She tried again. Both hands out, arms open wide. The ball came. This time she caught it! "I got it!" she said. A big cloud moved over the sun, like a little storm was coming. "One more throw," said Mr. Grewal. Isabella stood close to the hoop. She tossed the beanbag up. It went in again.

"Again," said Isabella, holding out her hands for the big ball.

The lights went out. Rehmat ran to the wall. She flipped the switch up. Nothing happened. She flipped it down. Still nothing! "Mama, the light is broken!" she called.

Mama came in with a candle. The flame was shiny and small. "It is a power cut," said Mama. "The lights are off. Flipping the switch will not turn them on." Rehmat tried the switch one more time. Click, click. The room stayed dark. Only the candle glowed.

So Mama lit more candles. Rehmat counted them. One candle, two candles, three candles! Then she spelled her name with blocks on the floor by candlelight. R-E-H-M-A-T. "Let's make shadows next!" said Rehmat. She held up her hands, and a big bird danced on the wall.

Dylan went to the art gallery with his class. Ms. Gupta showed them a big painting. "What colour is this?" she asked. "Red!" said Dylan. "Yellow!" said Jayke. "Blue!" said Emy.

Then the class sat at a paint table. Dylan wanted to paint a pig in the snow. He mixed red and yellow on his paper. The brush turned orange. "My pig can be orange!" he said. He laughed. A silly orange pig.

He painted a blue sky. He looked at it. It was very dark blue. His snow pig looked frozen and sad in the dark. "My sky is too dark," said Dylan. He frowned at it.

Emy had a pot of white paint. She passed it over. Dylan dipped his brush in the white. He stirred it into his blue. Round and round went the brush. The blue got lighter. Then it got lighter still. Now it looked like a soft morning sky.

"Look, Ms. Gupta!" said Dylan. He held up his painting. The orange pig stood in the white snow under the pale blue sky. Jayke clapped his hands. "Your pig has a sunny day," said Emy.

Dylan stacked the paint pots in a neat little tower. "Next time I will paint a green frog," he said. "I will mix blue and yellow!"

Iris went with her dad to the shelter. Lots of dogs and cats sat in little rooms. "They wait here," said the man at the desk. "They wait for a family to take them home." Iris walked past a big dog. She walked past two cats. Then she saw a small brown rabbit. "Hello," said Iris. "Will you come home with me?" The rabbit twitched its nose. "That one likes you," said the man, laughing.

At home, Iris set the cage in the backyard. She put in water and hay. The rabbit made the hay all messy. "You are a funny rainbow of trouble," said Iris. "No, wait, you are just brown." Her friend Luciano came to see. "Can I pat it?" he asked. Iris showed him how, soft and slow. The rabbit sat very still. Then it hopped one little hop. "She likes that," said Iris. She gave it a green leaf from her dad. The rabbit munched and munched. Iris clapped her hands. "Hello, Mopsy," she whispered. Mopsy's ears went up, up, up.

Lucas ran to the playground. He saw the big kid, Selina, on a bike. "I want to ride," said Lucas. He jumped onto his little bike. Then Selina called, "Wait! Wear a helmet when you ride a bike."

Lucas stopped. He looked at the red helmet by the bench. He got off his bike. He walked back, one, two, three steps. He put on the helmet. It clicked under his chin.

Then Lucas rode in a slow line. Amaira rode beside him. "One wheel, two wheels, purple helmet, red helmet," said Amaira. A plane went by up high in the sky. Lucas waved at it and kept pedaling. "Nice helmet," said Selina. Lucas smiled and rang his little bell, ding, ding, ding.

Jackson sat on the school bus. He sang the alphabet song with his friend Heidi. They sang all the way to P. Then Jackson stopped. "The song is done," he said. "P is the last letter."

Heidi shook her head. "There are more letters," she said. "Keep singing." Jackson felt worried. More letters? He thought his song was all done.

So Jackson took a big breath. He sang on. Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y. Then came one more letter. "Z!" Jackson shouted. The letter Z was shiny and new to him. Ms. Nakamura, who sat at the front of the bus, smiled. "You found the very last letter," she said.

Jackson tried again. He sang from A to Z, all by himself. When he got to Z, the bus stopped at school. Jackson laughed. The song had a start, A, and an end, Z. He sang it one more time, soft and happy. "A is first and Z is last," he said to Heidi. "Let's sing it again!"

Leon stood in the backyard with his friend Peyton. Ms. Eze had a big question for them. "Can you name your five senses?" she asked. Leon wanted to win this game. But he could only think of two.

" Eyes see," said Leon. He looked at a duck on the grass. "Ears hear," said Peyton. They heard the duck quack, quack, quack. "What comes next?" wondered Leon.

Then Leon got down low. He saw a little ant crawl by his shoe. He put his nose close to the flowers. Sniff, sniff. Mmm, the roses smelled sweet! "We smell with our nose," said Leon. "The nose knows!" laughed Peyton. They sniffed every flower to find the sweetest one.

Then Leon touched the warm grass with his hands. "Hands feel!" he said. Ms. Eze smiled. "One more to go," she said. Leon thought and thought. His tummy felt funny, like when he was sick in the car. Then he tasted a sweet berry his dad gave him. "Tongues taste," said Leon. "I did it! Five senses, five body parts!" He jumped up high and yelled, "Five! Five! Five!"

Anna sat on the big couch in the living room. Mama was beside her. Greyson and Bruno sat on the floor. They were all watching the big game on TV.

"Who is that man?" Anna asked. He wore a striped shirt. He kept running and looking at the players.

"That is the referee," said Mama. "The referee watches the game and makes sure the players follow the rules."

One player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his finger. The player looked sad and let go of the ball.

"He saw it!" said Bruno.

"Yes," said Anna. "The referee watches everything."

Anna stayed awake until the end of the game. The referee blew his whistle one more time. The game was over. Mama gave Anna a warm hug. Then Anna looked at the picture of a referee she drew in her book, and smiled.

The lights went out at Lily's house. Lily was at her neighbor's house with her dad. Everything went dark. "Oh no," said Lily. "Where did the lights go?"

Lily wanted a snack. She walked to the big fridge. She pulled on the door. Her dad put his hand on it. "Keep the fridge door shut," he said. "The food stays cold longer that way." Lily let go of the handle. The door stayed shut.

Lily looked around the dark room. Her dad lit a little candle. The candle made a warm glow. Lily could see again. She sat by the candle and ate a tasty apple. Outside the window, the whole street was dark, like one big mountain against the sky. "When will the lights come back?" Lily asked. Then, click! The lights came back on. The fridge hummed again. Lily ran to see. The door was still shut, and the food inside was still cold. "We kept it shut the whole time," she said. "And the cold stayed inside."

Daniel sat at the table. His tummy made a little growl. The soup smelled good.

Papa put the pot down. The pot was hot, so Papa used a big pad. "Time to hold hands," said Papa. "Some families hold hands around the table while they say a blessing."

Daniel had his spoon in his hand. He wanted the soup now. But Mama reached for his hand. Daniel looked at his spoon. He set it down on the table. Then he took Mama's hand and Papa's hand.

"Now we say thank you," said Papa. They all said the blessing together. It was short and soft.

Then Papa let go. Daniel picked his spoon back up. "Why did I put my spoon down?" Daniel asked. "So you could hold hands," said Mama. "Now you can eat."

Daniel took a big sip. The soup was warm and good. Outside, the moon was coming up, big and round. Daniel licked his lips. "More, please," he said. Papa smiled and filled his bowl again.

Sofia wanted to paint a pumpkin. But not a green pumpkin. Not a yellow pumpkin. She wanted a big orange pumpkin, just like the one at the farm.

Sofia looked in her paint box. She had red paint. She had yellow paint. She had blue paint. But there was no orange paint anywhere. "Oh no," said Sofia. "No orange!"

Her dad was cooking soup in the kitchen. The soup was orange like a sunset. Sofia held up her paint brush. "Dad, I need orange!" Dad smiled. "Try mixing two colours," he said. "Stir them like soup."

Sofia dipped her brush in the red paint. Plip. She dipped it in the yellow paint. Plip. She stirred them together on her paper. Round and round, like a tiny spoon in a tiny pot. The red and yellow swirled. They mixed. They turned into... orange!

"Orange! Orange! Orange!" Sofia cheered. She painted her pumpkin round and bright. She painted it orange like the fresh soup on the stove. Then she painted a tiny red cat sitting on her orange pumpkin. The cat said, "Meow," and Sofia giggled and painted a yellow moon.

Samuel sat at the dinner table. He could smell the soup. "I smell it with my nose," he said. His tummy made a hungry sound. But the soup was too hot, and he had to wait.

Mom put a cloth bag by his plate. "A guessing game," she said. "Close your eyes." Samuel closed his eyes tight. The light went dark behind his eyelids.

"Now use your fingers," Mom said. Samuel put his fingers in the bag. He touched the first thing. It felt bumpy all over. "Bumpy!" he said. It was a pinecone. He touched the next thing. It felt soft, and it tickled his fingertips. "Soft!" he said. It was a feather. The last thing felt smooth and cool. "Smooth!" he said. It was a stone.

"You used your fingertips," said Sam, his brother, from across the table. Samuel looked at his fingers. His fingertips could tell soft, rough, smooth and bumpy. He touched the pinecone again. Bumpy, bumpy, bumpy. He laughed.

The soup was cool now. Samuel tasted it with his tongue. "Yum," he said. He heard spoons clinking with his ears. Mom smiled a friendly smile. Samuel touched his smooth stone one more time. "My fingertips know," he said.

Alexis sat in his car seat. Mama was going to drive them over the big hill. "Can I have crackers?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "You can have three crackers. Just three."

Mama handed him the bag. Alexis took one cracker. He took two crackers. He took three crackers. But one cracker was very big. He looked at it. "Do big crackers count as more?" he asked.

"No," said Mama. "Three is three. Big or small, three is three."

Alexis counted his crackers. "One, two, three," he said. Three crackers. Not more, not less. Just three. He smiled and took a big bite of the big one.

Then Mama turned on a song. Alexis sang along. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" His voice filled the car. Mama tapped the wheel and sang too.

The song made the long ride feel short. They went up the hill. They came down the hill. Alexis still had two crackers left. He counted them. "One, two," he said. "Two left!"

"Save one for Nihaal," said Mama. "He is waiting at home." Alexis put one cracker in his pocket. He held the other in his hand. "One for Nihaal," he said. "One for me."

The car stopped. They were home. Nihaal ran to the door. Alexis held out his cracker. "One for you," he said. Nihaal took it and grinned.

Maria was hungry. Lunch was on the table. It was a big, juicy apple.

"First we wash our hands," said her dad. Maria ran to the sink. She stood on her toes. The sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water.

"I can't do it," said Maria. Her tummy felt worried. She wanted the apple so much.

Her dad came close. He brought the step stool. He set it by the sink. "Here you go," he said. He stood right next to her.

Maria climbed up on the stool. Now she could reach the water. She got soap on her hands. She rubbed them together. Her dad helped her count. They counted all the way to twenty.

The bubbles went down the drain. Maria dried her hands on the towel. She climbed down with her dad's help.

Then she sat at the table. She took a big bite of the juicy apple. Crunch!

"Now my hands are clean," said Maria.

Rowan sat at Grandpa's big table. The bowls were smooth and warm. Soon they would eat the soup. But first came the blessing. Rowan did not know how to do it.

Grandpa said, "Fold your hands, little boy." Rowan folded his hands. He closed his eyes tight. Then he heard Grandpa's soft voice say the blessing. Rowan peeked. He saw Grandpa's eyes were closed too. Grandpa's head was bowed down low. Rowan quickly shut his eyes again.

The blessing was done. "You peeked!" said his cousin, and she laughed. Grandpa laughed too. "Some people close their eyes or bow their heads during a blessing," Grandpa said. "I did both," Rowan said. He took a step toward his chair and sat down. The soup was hot, but Grandpa helped him blow on it. Rowan took a big spoonful. "I can do the blessing next time," he said. Grandpa smiled and gave him more bread.

Victoria sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to count them for her dad.

"One, two," said Victoria. Then she stopped. "What comes next?" she asked. Her face felt worried.

Her dad smiled. "Try the song," he said. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door. Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight. Nine, ten, a big fat hen."

Victoria sang the rhyme. The words rhymed, like shoe and two. "Three, four, shut the door!" she sang. Now she remembered!

She looked at her plate. She pushed one pea with her spoon. "One," she said. She pushed another. "Two." She sang all the way to ten. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!"

"Ten peas," said her dad. "You did it."

"I sang it," said Victoria. "The song helped me remember."

Dad laughed. "Sing it again," he said. "Then you can eat your peas, and the lazy old mouse under the sink will get nothing tonight."

Victoria sang it again. "One, two, buckle my shoe." She counted every pea. Then she ate them all up.

"Goodnight, lazy mouse," she whispered. "No peas for you."

Jack ran to the farm with his friend Calum. "We can plant seeds today!" said Jack. Mr. Le gave them three little seeds each. Jack dug a small hole. He put his seeds in the dirt. He patted the dirt down, pat, pat, pat. "Now what?" asked Calum. Mr. Le brought a big watering can. "Seeds need water to start growing," he said. Jack poured the water on the dirt. It went drip, drip, drip.

The next morning, Jack ran to the farm. He looked at the dirt. There was only dirt. "No sprout yet!" said Jack. He poured more water on the spot. Calum poured water on his seeds too. A loud tractor drove by. Jack jumped, then laughed.

Jack watered his seeds every day. One morning, Jack saw something green. It was a tiny sprout! "Calum, come see! It came up!" Calum ran over fast. "Mine too!" he said. "Our seeds grew!"

Madison held her dad's hand. They walked down the long road to school. The school had a tall gate and a big playground.

Madison saw kids running and laughing. Her dad waved goodbye. Then he was gone. Madison felt her tummy make a little sound. She was hungry! She wanted a snack now.

A boy named Eason ran up to her. "Hi! I'm Eason," he said. "Want to play?" Madison and Eason went down the slide. They dug in the sand. They pushed a red ball. But Madison's tummy grumbled again.

Then Ms. Navarro rang a little bell. "Snack time!" she said. All the kids ran to the picnic table. Madison sat down next to Eason. She opened her little bag. Out came a banana and a tiny cup of crackers.

Madison took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "Snack time comes after playing!" Eason laughed and held up his apple. "Now we have lots of energy," he said. "Race you to the slide!" Madison jumped up from the bench. "Ready, set, go!" she shouted.

Isla loves painting at school. Today she wants to paint a big yellow sun. But the paint pots are empty. "We will fill them later," says Ms. Chan. "Later is not now," Isla says. She waits. She squishes the squishy sponge in the water. It drips.

Cassian sits down beside her. "I went to the park tomorrow," he says. He looks down at his shoe. "No. Not tomorrow. Yesterday. It already happened." Isla thinks hard. Yesterday is the day before today. Yesterday, the paint pots were full. Today, they are empty. Tomorrow, they might be full again.

"I know a game," Isla says. "You say a day. I say if it is done." "Yesterday, I had a coin," says Cassian. "That is done," says Isla. "Today, I hug my bear," says Cassian. "That is now," says Isla. They both laugh.

Ms. Chan comes back. She fills the paint pots with bright colors. "Now we can paint," she says. Isla dips her brush. Today the sun is yellow. Tomorrow she will paint a moon. "My turn now," says Cassian, holding out his brush.

Sofa wanted to go to the park. "When do we go?" she asked Mr. Demir. "Later," he said. Sofia made a sad face. Later felt very far away.

Mr. Demir pointed to the wall. "Look at the clock," he said. "The clock shows what time it is." Sofia looked up. The long hand sat on the six. She watched it move. It went tick, tick, tick. She sat down and waited.

Yesterday the park was wet from rain. Today the sun was out. Tomorrow Sofia would come back to daycare again. Right now she stared at the clock. The long hand moved and moved. Then it pointed up high. Mr. Demir clapped his hands. "Now it is park time!" Sofia jumped up. At the park, Edgar and Ivy were already on the swings. "We watched the clock too," said Ivy, laughing.

Iris was at home. Her friend Alana came to play. Alana had a little toy rabbit. It was soft and gray. Its ears felt like velvet.

Iris wanted the rabbit. She took it fast. Alana's face turned sad. "That is mine," Alana said in a small voice.

Iris looked at Alina's sad face. She gave the rabbit back. "Can I hold it, please?" Iris asked.

Alana smiled. "Yes. You can have a turn."

They sat on the rug. The world outside was noisy with a big truck. Inside, it was quiet. Iris held the rabbit. Then she gave it back. "Your turn," she said.

"Now we both played with it," said Alana. Iris hugged the soft gray rabbit one more time and handed it over gently.

Livia stood by the cubbies at school. It was cold outside. Mr. Ahmadi said, "Coats on, everyone!"

Livia picked up her red coat. She pushed one arm in. Then she pushed her other arm in too. But both arms went into the same sleeve! The coat hung funny on her. Haniya laughed. Livia laughed too.

"Where did my other sleeve go?" Livia asked. She looked at the coat. The empty sleeve swung back and forth. "Hmm," she said. "Maybe one arm goes in here." She pulled her arm out. She put it in the other sleeve. Now the coat sat just right on her shoulders.

"Now the zipper," said Mr. Ahmadi. Livia held the little tab. She pulled it up, up, up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to her chin.

"Your coat is on!" said Simeon.

Outside, big drops began to rain. Livia stayed dry and warm. She zipped the zipper up high. Then she jumped in a puddle and laughed.

Matthew had a little blue car. He loved that car. He took it to the playground. Now the car was gone. "Oh no," said Matthew. He ran to the slide. He ran to the swings. He ran to the sand box. He ran so fast, and he did not really look.

Ollie came over. "You ran past me twice," said Ollie. "Let's go slow." So Matthew tried again. He picked one spot first. The slide. He looked under it. He looked behind it. No car. Then he went to the swings. He looked under each swing, one by one. Still no car.

Then he went to the sand box. He got down on his knees. He looked in one little corner at a time. There, half covered with sand, was the blue car! Matthew wanted to shout with joy. "Ollie! I found it!" Ms. Wanjiru smiled. "Time for juice now," she said. Matthew drank his juice and held the car tight. After his nap he would be awake again, and he would take his car to the sand box, one careful step at a time.

Gianna stood by the hotel pool. The water looked big and blue. Vance was already in, kicking his feet. "Come in!" he called.

Gianna wanted to swim. But she could not swim yet. She looked up at the tall white chair. A man sat up there, way up high. "Who is that?" she asked her dad. "That is the lifeguard," Dad said. "His job is to watch the swimmers. He helps anyone who needs it."

Gianna held the steps. She kicked and kicked. Then she let go of the rail. Splash! She slipped under the water. Bubbles flew up all around her. The water went in her eyes.

A whistle blew. The lifeguard slid down fast. He reached out his big hand. He pulled Gianna up. "I saw you from up high," he said. "That is why I sit there." Gianna held on tight. The sun was sunny and warm. Vance patted her back. Mr. Chen, the coach, brought her a towel. "Try again with me," he said. Gianna smiled. She looked up at the tall chair. The lifeguard waved. She kicked and kicked, all the way to the steps.

Jules ran to the toy corner first. He wanted the big red truck. But Orion was there. Orion's mouth went down at the corners. His eyebrows made a big frown. Jules looked at Orion's face. He saw that Orion felt sad.

"Are you sad?" Jules asked. Orion nodded. "The truck is stuck," Orion said. Jules pointed at the truck. One wheel was under the shelf. "We can pull it together," Jules said.

Jules held the back. Orion held the front. They pulled and pulled. Out popped the truck! Now Orion's mouth turned up. He had a big smile. "I am happy now," Orion said. Jules felt happy too. Ms. Ma clapped her hands. "Great teamwork," she said. Jules and Orion pushed the truck around the room. Vroom, vroom!

Daniel sat in a big room. His name was called out loud. He walked in with his mom. There was a big table in the room.

Daniel had to get a shot today. He felt scared. The table was tall and cold. "Can I sit on the big table?" he asked. "You can," said the nurse. But Daniel did not want to.

Then Mom sat down on a chair. She held out her arms. "Come sit on my lap," she said. Daniel climbed up. Mom held him snug. She gave him a soft hug. He felt safe on her lap. A grown-up can hold a child on their lap during a shot. Daniel did not know that before. Now he did.

"Will it hurt?" Daniel asked. "Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick! It was done. "That was fast," said Daniel.

After the doctor's office, they went to an ice cream shop. Daniel got a strawberry cone. The phone did ring at the counter, and Mom got a call. "Can we come again next time?" Daniel asked. Mom laughed. "If you need another shot, yes," she said. Daniel licked his cone. The young boy smiled big. "I want to sit on your lap every time," he said. Mom gave him a kiss on his head.

Anthony was on the Bee team this summer. After every game, the team went to the big pool. The water was cool and splishy. Anthony could smell the sunscreen on his arms.

Today it was Anthony's turn to bat. He ran to home plate. He ran too fast. He forgot his helmet. The coach called him back. "Anthony, you need your helmet," she said. She put it on his head. It was hard and smooth. It clicked under his chin.

Anthony swung the bat. He hit the ball! One big hit, one happy shout, one run around the bases. The ball flew high, but his head was safe.

After the game, they all went to the pool. Anthony saw an old boot by the fence. Then he and Otis got to feed the fish at the little pond. One fish, two fish, three fish. "The fish know us," said Otis. Anthony laughed and jumped in with a splash.

Olivia got a small blue card. It had her name on it. "Your first library card," said Grandpa. "Now you can touch a book, take it home, and keep it a while."

They went to the library. Grandpa helped her pick a book about ducks. "This one," said Olivia. She held it tight all the way home.

At home, Olivia read the duck book many times. She read it to her teddy bear. She read it to Grandpa. Then Grandpa said, "Time to take it back. But we will get a new book too."

At the library there was a little hole in the wall. "That is the book return slot," said Grandpa. "A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library." Olivia held the duck book. She did not want to let it go.

"I will miss it," said Olivia. "You can pick a new one right away," said Grandpa. Olivia held the book up to the slot. She waved to the ducks. "Bye bye, ducks," she said. Then she dropped the book in. It slid down, down, down. It was gone.

Olivia looked at the slot. The book had gone in, and now the slot was empty. She had put it in, and it had gone away. She jumped a little jump. "I did that!" she said.

Then she ran to the shelf. She touched the covers, one by one. "This one," said Olivia. It was a book about a loud, bumpy truck.

Louis ran to the playground. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He wore his small red cap.

Onyx was on the swings. Alita was at the slide. Louis climbed up, up, up. Then he slid down fast. "Again!" he said.

The wind began to blow. It was a windy day now. Leaves flew past Louis. His cap blew right off his head. Alita laughed and caught it. "Your cap went flying!" she said.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Big drops, small drops. Louis held out his hands. "It's rainy now," said Onyx. "My boots are happy."

Then came a big sound. Rumble! Rumble! Louis looked up. Ms. Wijaya clapped her hands. "Thunder!" she called. "Everybody come inside."

"But I want to slide more," said Louis.

"Thunder says go indoors," said Ms. Wijaya. "We can come back later."

Louis ran inside with Onyx and Alita. They sat by the window. Louis found a book about weather. He turned the pages. Rain, sun, wind, snow.

Outside, thunder rumbled again. Louis was cozy inside. "Goodbye, thunder," he said. He turned another page.

Olivier ran down the hall at the hospital. His mother held his hand. "The baby is here," she said. Olivier wanted to play peek-a-boo right away.

The baby was in a soft blanket. His eyes were shut. "Is he looking for me?" Olivier asked. "No," said his mother. "He is sleeping. Babies sleep a lot, all day long." Olivier waited. He listened to the tiny snores. They sounded like a little cat.

Olivier showed his toy truck to the baby. The baby kept sleeping. Olivier held up his sock puppet. Still sleeping! Then the baby opened one eye. Olivier waved. The baby yawned and shut his eye again. "Okay," said Olivier. "Truck can wait." He sat down by the bed and yawned too. "Baby, you sleep more than me."

Ezra went to the library with his dad. He wanted a book about rocket ships. The library had big gray shelves and soft carpets. Ezra marched down the aisle. He saw a book with a red rocket on it. "This one!" he said.

Callan was there too. "Let's play rocket ship," said Callan. They stood by the carpet squares. Callan began to count. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Ezra listened. The numbers went down, one by one. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Both boys jumped up high. A girl named Agathe clapped. "That's a countdown," she said. "You count backward from ten down to one."

Ezra wanted to try. He took a deep breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" He jumped so high his socks almost flew off. Ms. Leblanc, the librarian, smiled. Ezra held his rocket book tight. "Ten, nine, eight," he whispered all the way home.

Declan went to the store with his dad. The store was big and bright. It smelled like fresh bread. Declan held his dad's hand.

Declan wanted the yellow truck on the shelf. It had big black wheels. He pointed at it. "Can I hold it?" he asked.

"Only one toy today," said Dad. "You already have the red ball."

Declan's face got hot. He stomped his foot. He wanted to yell. His hands made tight fists.

"Try this," said Dad. "Take a slow, deep breath with me." Dad breathed in slowly. Declan watched his dad's chest get big. Then Dad let the breath out slowly, like a little river of air.

Declan tried it. He breathed in slow and deep. Then he let it out. He did it again. His hands were not fists anymore. His foot stopped stomping. "My body feels calm now," Declan said.

At the checkout, they saw Mr. Singh. He smiled and waved. "That yellow truck is nice," he said. "But that ball is good too."

At home, Declan rolled the red ball on the floor. It bumped into a chair. "Oops," he said. "That was an ugly bump. But I can fix it." He rolled the ball again, soft and slow.

It was bedtime, but Violet wanted to sleep in her shoes. "Big kids wear shoes," she said. She sat on the bed. She pushed her feet into her shoes. But her toes felt funny. Her feet were cold, too.

"Wait," said her dad. "Where are your socks?" Violet looked. Her socks were on the floor. She laughed and laughed. Off came the shoes. On went the socks, one, two. Then the shoes went on top. "Socks first, shoes last," she sang. She stomped her feet. Tap, tap, tap!

Violet ran to the tub first. She washed with her yellow duck. The duck floated. "Splash," said the duck, in duck talk. Then she put on her pajamas. They had dancing bears on them. The bears did a little dance when she wiggled. At last, off came the shoes and socks. Her toes were free. "Goodnight, toes," said Violet. "See you in the morning!"

Axel was at Grandpa's house. It was snowing outside! Axel wanted to play in the snow. He grabbed his big red coat. His bear wanted to come too.

Axel pushed his arms in the sleeves. Then he grabbed the zipper tab. He pulled and pulled. The zipper did not move. He pulled again. Still no moving. "Oh no," said Axel. Grandpa leaned down. "Look at the bottom," said Grandpa.

Axel looked at the bottom of the coat. He saw a little box there. He saw the end of the other side. Axel pushed the end into the little box. Click! Now he pulled the tab. The zipper went up, up, up! The coat was closed and clean and warm.

"Snow time!" shouted Axel. He hugged his bear tight. Then he ran out the door.

Elena sat at the big table. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her name. She held the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out wobbly. One letter looked like a wiggly worm.

Mom sat down next to her. "Watch me," said Mom. Mom put the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then the pencil rested on her middle finger. "It is called a pinch," said Mom. Mom wrote the word pinch. The letters were neat and small. Elena laughed. "That is not a worm!"

Elena tried it. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and first finger. She let it rest on her middle finger. Now the pencil did not sink into her fist. She wrote the big E first. Then L, then E, then N, then A. There it was. Elena, on the paper, all neat.

"I did it!" said Elena. Mom clapped her hands. Elena gave Mom a gentle hug. Then she wrote her name again.

It was a rainy day. Jasmine and her dad went to the store. They needed paint for a card. Jasmine wanted to paint a pink flower for Grandma. She looked and looked. The store had red paint. It had blue paint. It had yellow paint. It had green paint too. But there was no pink paint anywhere.

"I can't make my flower," Jasmine said. Her tummy felt tight. "Grandma loves pink." Her dad said, "Let's try mixing some paints. We can ask for help." A kind store lady came over. She put red paint in a cup. Then she added white paint.

Jasmine stirred the cup round and round. The red got lighter and lighter. "Pink!" Jasmine said. "The white made the red turn pink!" The store lady smiled. "Yes it did," she said.

Jasmine painted a pink flower on the card. Next to it she painted a green stem and blue rain drops. Then she drew a yellow sun. "Grandma will love it," her dad said. At home, Jasmine put the card by her bed. In the morning it was dry. She hugged it all the way to Grandma's door.

Freya and her dad rode the city bus. They were going to the library. Freya was getting her very first card. She held her dad's hand and waited. The bus stopped, then went, then stopped again. "Soon," said Dad. "We wait, then we get there."

At the desk, a librarian gave Freya a small card. It had her name on it. "Now you can borrow a book," said the librarian. Freya picked a big red book about dogs. Luke from her class was there too. He put his book back on the shelf, but it slid into the wrong spot. It fell on the floor. Luke looked upset. The librarian picked it up. "See this little label on the spine?" she said. "It shows where the book belongs on the shelf." Luke looked at the label. He put his book back in the right spot. It stayed put.

Freya looked at her own book. It had a spine label too. She turned it in her hands. "My book has one too," she said. The librarian smiled and stamped the book.

Then Freya and her dad got on the bus again. Freya set the red book on her lap. She ran her finger down the spine, over the label. She would put it back in the right spot when she was done. She sat very still, all the way home, with her hand on the label.

Mackenzie stood in the kitchen with her mom. On the table were three things: a feather, a pinecone, and a soft blanket.

"Can you sort them?" Mom asked. "Which ones are soft?"

Mackenzie picked up the feather. She touched it with her fingers. "Soft," she said. She put it in one pile. She touched the pinecone. "Ouch. Bumpy and rough." She put it in the other pile. She touched the blanket. It felt like a hug. "Soft!" It went with the feather.

Then Mackenzie touched Mom's cheek. "Soft," she said, and laughed. She touched the counter. "Rough? No. Smooth!" She touched her own shirt. "Soft."

"My hands can tell!" she said. She waved her fingers in the air like they could dance. "Mom, can my hands feel the window too?"

"Try it," said Mom.

Mackenzie pressed her hands on the cold window glass. "Ooh. Cold and smooth!"

Just then the toaster popped, and Mackenzie jumped. "That was a scary pop!"

Mom laughed. "Did your ears hear that?"

"Yes! My ears heard it. My nose smells the toast. My eyes see it. My tongue will taste it. And my hands feel it!"

Mom put the warm toast on the plate. "Only grown-ups touch hot things," she said. "But you can touch your chair. Is it soft or rough?"

Mackenzie touched the chair. "Rough," she said. "And my toast is warm and yummy. Yum, yum!"

Rehmat held her new library card. It was red and small. She wanted a book about tigers. But the tiger book was not on the shelf.

She looked by the chairs. She looked by the door. She heard a voice in the storytime room. "Ms. Sinclair reads books aloud to us," said Auston. Rehmat peeked in.

There sat Frank. There sat three more kids. Ms. Sinclair held the tiger book. "This one is my favorite," she said. "It is about a big dream."

Rehmat felt shy. She waited. One step. Two steps. Three steps. She sat down.

Ms. Sinclair read the funny part. Rehmat bumped knees with Frank. They both laughed.

After the story, Ms. Sinclair said, "Would you like to take it home?" Rehmat held out her red card. The tiger book went into her bag. "Bye, tigers," she whispered. "See you next time."

Myles was at Grandma's house. He wanted her to read his new book. Grandma was making soup, so Myles waited. He held the book. He turned the pages. First page, second page, third page. He turned them back again. The book went front to back.

Myles looked at the cover. He saw a name there. He asked, "Grandma, who made up this story?"

Grandma came over. She pointed at the name. "That is the author," she said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book."

Myles looked again. "The author wrote the words," he said. "One, two, so many words!"

Grandma laughed. "Yes, a messy pile of words, all in a line."

"Now I can show you," said the little boy. He opened the front. "Start here, Grandma."

Grandma sat down and began to read.

Liam was a dragon at home today. He wore his soft green blanket like wings. His mom was making soup. "Try a taste, little dragon," she said. She held out a small spoon.

Liam looked at the soup. It had big white bits in it. "Yuck!" he shouted. He hid under his blanket. His mom's face went sad. Liam did not like that.

He remembered his friend Agatha. Once she got peas and said, "No, thank you." The teacher smiled at her. Liam tried it now. He came out from under the blanket. "No, thank you," he said in his best dragon voice.

His mom smiled big. "Okay, dragon. How about bread instead?" She gave him a warm slice. "Thank you," said Liam. He tied the blanket around his neck like a cape and flew to the table.

Isaac ran to the kitchen in his pajamas. He wanted eggs for breakfast. "Eggs, please!" he said. His dad was at the stove. "First, wash your hands," said Dad.

Isaac stopped. He looked at his hands. They had jam on them from yesterday. Yucky!

"I need the toilet first," said Isaac. He ran down the hall. He used the toilet. Then he ran back to the kitchen.

"Did you flush?" Dad asked. Isaac put his hand on his head. Oh no. He forgot! He ran back. He pushed the handle. Whoooosh! The water swirled away.

"Now I wash my hands," said Isaac. He turned the tap. Bubbles came. He rubbed and rubbed. "Smelly soap!" he said. "Like flowers."

A little bird sat at the window. It looked at Isaac. It tapped the glass. "Tweet tweet!" said the bird. Isaac laughed. "The bird wants clean hands too," he said. He held up his soapy hands. The bird tapped again.

Isaac rinsed his hands. He did not spill any water on the floor. He dried his hands on the little towel.

"Clean hands, ready for eggs," said Dad. Isaac climbed into his chair. He ate his eggs. The bird watched from the window. "Tweet!" it said. "Tweet to you too," said Isaac, with egg on his chin.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. She slept in the guest bedroom next to Ezra's room. Every morning Ezra heard her hum.
