One day Grandma said, "Come. I will show you my bread. My mother made it this way too." Ezra wondered, "Did she make it a long time ago?" Grandma smiled and nodded.

In the kitchen, Ezra helped pour flour. He patted the dough. It felt bumpy like the road to the farm. "Why does it get big?" he asked. "Watch and see," said Grandma. She put the pan in the hot oven, and Ezra stood back.

Soon the bread rose, big and round. It smelled warm. "It grew!" said Ezra. Grandma cut a slice. "Stop, wait one minute," she said, "it is hot." Then Ezra took a bite. "It tastes like a cow is happy," he said, and Grandma laughed.

The sun was warm at summer camp. A little flag flapped by the sand pit. Freya saw the big red truck. Rio was holding it. Freya wanted it so much.

She ran over. Her hand reached out. She grabbed, and Rio held on tight. "Mine turn!" said Rio. "No, my turn!" said Freya. The truck did not move at all. Mr. Watanabe knelt down beside them.

Freya took a big breath. She let go. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked. Rio smiled. "Yes! When I'm done." Rio drove the truck round and round. Then he set it down. "Your turn now," he said. Freya hugged the truck. "Can you have a turn when I'm done?" she asked. Rio nodded and sat beside her. They waited together in the warm sand. The little flag went flap, flap, flap. "Beep beep!" said Freya.

Max got a new truck. He wanted to play with it all night. "One more minute," he said. But he stayed up very, very late. The moon went to sleep before Max did.

In the morning, Mama woke him up. Max put on his shirt. He put on his pants. His socks went on his feet. At school, Catherine was building a big tower. Max sat on the mat. His eyes felt heavy. "Play with me!" said Catherine. Max tried. He yawned a big yawn. The truck sat on the floor. Max was too tired to push it.

Ms. Teo sat down next to him. "You look sleepy," she said. That night, Max took a warm bath. He washed his hands and his back. "Tonight I will sleep," Max said. He put his truck by his bed. He closed his eyes and slept all night.

The next morning, Max woke up with big eyes. At school, he ran to Catherine. "Let's build!" he said. They pushed the truck together, fast, fast, fast. "You have lots of play today!" said Ms. Teo. Max laughed and pushed the truck again.

Adam played in the playroom. He wore his blue socks. Remi tipped over a cup of water. Splat! A big puddle sat on the floor. Adam stepped in it. His socks got wet. "My socks are wet," said Adam. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Jannah. Adam felt the wet sock. It was not dry anymore. Ms. Ortiz came over. "Let's pick some dry socks," she said. She opened the little drawer. Adam sat on the rug to wait. He waited. He waited. Then he picked red socks. Ms. Ortiz helped him pull them on. Dry socks! Warm toes! Adam smiled. Then he looked down. The puddle was gone! "Where did the water go?" he asked. Ms. Ortiz held up a towel. "The towel drank it," she said. Adam laughed and laughed.

Isaac went to Jaxon's house. Jaxon had a big teddy bear and a small bunny. "Let's play tea party," said Jaxon.

Jaxon set out little cups. The cups were empty. Isaac looked in his cup. "There is no tea," he said. He felt sad. He wanted real tea for the bear.

Jaxon picked up the teapot. He tipped it over Isaac's cup. Nothing came out. "Look, pretend tea," said Jaxon. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" Isaac blew on his cup, just in case.

Isaac tipped the teapot too. He poured pretend tea for the bunny. Then for the bear. Then for himself. He took a big pretend sip. "Mmm," he said. "So good!"

Then Goldie came in with a toy plate. "Sandwich time!" she said. She put an invisible sandwich on the plate. Isaac pushed the plate to the bear. The bear fell over, and everyone laughed.

Isaac gave the bear a pretend hug. "More tea?" he asked. The bear sat very still. So Isaac poured him some more.

Isaiah ran to the playground. His brown shoes went clip, clip on the path. He was excited to see the big drum.

Ms. Okonkwo had put the drum by the sandbox. Isaiah hit it once. Boom! He hit it again. Boom, boom! He laughed. "One boom, two booms, three booms," he counted.

Then Lilith came near. She put her hands over her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked scared. Isaiah stopped his hands. He felt sad that his friend felt scared.

But Oakleigh ran over. She was smiling big. "I love the drum!" she said. She hit it too. Boom! Isaiah looked at Lilith. He looked at Oakleigh. Same drum. One friend was happy. One friend was scared.

"Ms. Okonkwo," said Isaiah, "can Lilith and I play something quiet?"

"Yes," said Ms. Okonkwo. "The sandbox is a quiet spot."

Isaiah and Lilith dug in the brown sand. One scoop, two scoops, three scoops. Oakleigh kept the boom, boom, boom far away by the fence. Lilith smiled now. Isaiah was happy too.

"We can all play," said Isaiah. "Loud over there. Quiet over here." Lilith patted the sand. "This is just right."

Jaxon was at home with his mom. He wanted to help tie his own shoes. His mom showed him how the laces made loops. Jaxon pulled one loop with his finger. The bow got bigger. He pulled it again. The bow fell apart. "Try again," said Mom. Jaxon tried once more. This time the loops stayed tied.

Then Mom said, "We need to go to the store." Jaxon held Mom's hand in the parking lot. Inside the store, Jaxon saw big apples. He looked at the apples. He looked up. Where did Mom go? He could not see her anywhere. Mom was missing.

Jaxon saw a man at the checkout. The man had a store shirt on. Jaxon walked to him. "I can't find my grown-up," said Jaxon. The man called out on his phone. Soon Mom came around the corner. She hugged Jaxon tight. "You found a store worker," said Mom. "That was just right." Jaxon smiled and held her hand all the way home.

Wesley sat at the little table in the school library. Mr. Santoso gave him a pencil and some paper. "Can you write your name?" Mr. Santoso asked.

Wesley wanted to write a big W. He held the pencil tight and pressed down hard. Snap! The pencil tip broke off and fell on the table. Wesley froze. How would he write now?

"Here is a new pencil," said Maxim, who was sitting nearby. Wesley took it and watched his own hand. This time he pressed gently, very softly. The pencil made a W. Then an E. Then an S.

"It works!" said Wesley. He made the letters again, light as a cat's tail. The pencil tip stayed on. His whole name was on the paper.

Declan was four years old today. He was having his party at the bowling alley. Veda and Rosie came too. Declan rolled his ball down the lane. It bumped the pins over. Then a new boy came to play with them.

"How old are you?" the new boy asked. Declan held up his fingers. He looked down at his hand. One, two, three fingers were up. That was not right. He was not three. He put one more finger up. Now there were four.

"Four!" said the new boy. "I am four too." He held up four fingers too. They counted them together. One, two, three, four.

"Nice rolling," said Mr. Grewal, the man at the next lane. "Take your time and try again." Declan waited for his turn. He rolled the ball slowly. All the pins fell down.

After bowling, they ate cake. Each child got a piece. Rosie said, "Thank you," and Declan said, "What polite friends I have." Then he held up four fingers at the new boy one more time, just because he liked it.

Ali was three. He had a book about dinosaurs. He loved that book. But he wanted more books.

"I want a library card," Ali said. "A card of my own."

His mom smiled. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," she said. "Come on. I will help you."

They walked to the library together. Ali held his mom's hand. The library was big and friendly.

At the desk, Ali stood tall. His mom helped him sign up. Then Ali got his very own card. It had his name on it!

Ali picked a book about a red fire truck. "This one, please," he said. The lady scanned his card. Beep!

Ali carried the book all the way home. He sat on the rug. His tummy felt happy. He opened the book.

"Read it again," Ali said.

Jules sat in the cafe with his mama. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his own name.

He held the pencil tight. He pushed hard on the paper. The J came out fat and fuzzy. "Why are my lines so big and soft?" Jules asked.

Mama looked at the pencil tip. "It looks dull," she said. "Let me sharpen it." Mama turned the pencil in the sharpener. Jules watched from his seat. Thin curls fell down like little apple peels.

Then Jules tried again. He made a thin, dark line. The pencil moved so fast now. He wrote J, then u, then l. "Jules!" he said. "I did it!"

Mama gave him a brave sticker for his shirt. Jules shook his paper a little, to make it dry. "More paper, please," he said.

Isla was at Brock's house. Brock's dad had made hot toast. The toast was ready to eat now. Isla wanted to spread the butter all by herself. She held the soft butter with the knife edge. Her dad had put the knife out for her. She pushed it slowly across the toast. The butter made a bumpy little cloud on top. She spread it more, and the bumps went flat.

Then Brock got the milk. He tipped the cup fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. Brock looked at the wet table. "Oh no," he said. His dad wiped it up with a cloth. "You can try again," he said kindly.

Isla took her turn next. She tipped the cup just a tiny bit. The milk went in slowly. It did not splash. Not one drop came out. Brock watched with wide eyes. "Your milk stayed in the cup," he said. Isla poured some more, nice and slow. The milk rose up to the top. Then she picked up her toast and took a big, happy bite.

Madelyn put on her skates at the ice rink. Today her team was playing a fun game. Mr. Chen put a big ball on the ice. He put a net at each end too. "What game is this?" Madelyn asked. "It is soccer on ice," said Mr. Chen. "We try to get the ball into the net." Her friend Elliana skated fast. Her friend Baby skated slow and wobbly.

Madelyn pushed the ball with her skate. The ball slid far across the deep white ice. It missed the net. It went into the boards instead. The boards were hard like a big box all around the rink. The ball bounced off and came right back. "Try again," said Elliana.

Madelyn skated after the ball. She pushed it with her foot. The ball slid and slid. Then it went into the net. Everyone shouted, "Goal!" Mr. Chen clapped his hands. Madelyn looked at the net. The ball was inside it. "I did it," she said. "The ball went in the net!" Baby skated over and gave her a hug. Then Elliana took the ball out of the net. "Now it is my turn," she said.

Theo was at the playground. He found one red sock on the grass. "A sock!" said Theo. He held it up. It was soft and flat.

Scarlet ran over. "You need two," she said. "Two makes a pair. Like a pair of socks." Theo looked at his one sock. He wanted its partner.

So Theo went hunting. He counted the places he looked. "One, the slide. Two, the swing. Three, the sandbox. Four, the bench. Five, the little wall." No sock. Arzoie came to help too. "Six, the tunnel. Seven, the steps. Eight, the bushes," they counted together.

Then Mr. Ngo called out. He had a flat piece of paper in his hand. The paper was from the shop, and it was wrapped around something. "Is this yours?" he asked. It was the other red sock!

Theo put on both socks. "One and one," he said. "Two! A pair!" He jumped high. Scarlet clapped and counted, "Nine, ten, jump again!"

Mateo went to the garden center with his dad. He wanted to grow a vegetable garden. He picked little tomato plants, little carrot seeds, and a big bag of soil. "One bag, two bags, three bags," said Mateo. Dad helped him stack the bags in the cart.

At home, Mateo found a problem. Weeds were in his garden spot. He pulled one weed, gently. Out it came, with long stringy roots hanging down. "Wow," said Mateo. "Where did those come from?" His friend Damon came over to help. "The roots grow down into the soil," said Damon. Mateo pulled another weed. Down came more stringy roots. Mateo laughed. The roots went down, down, down.

Then Mateo made a hole for his tomato plant. He set it in and patted the soil. "Grow down, little roots," he said softly. He counted his plants: one, two, three.

Every morning Mateo ran outside. His tummy felt jumpy with waiting. One day his tomato plant had a tiny green ball on it. Mateo did a happy dance. "My garden is growing!"

Xavier ran to the playground with his teddy bear. He set the bear on a low wall. Then Kenai ran by fast. The teddy fell off the wall onto the ground.

Xavier picked up his teddy. "Are you sick?" he asked. "Maybe a big fall made you feel bad." He felt the teddy's head. "You feel hot," said Xavier. What could he do?

Liliane ran over with her doll. "My doll has a bed," she said. "You can tuck your teddy into it." She put her doll down and gave Xavier a small blanket. Xavier wrapped the teddy up. "Now pretend medicine," said Liliane. She held up a little cup. Xavier tipped it to the teddy's mouth. "Drink this," he said softly.

Then Xavier rocked the teddy in his arms. "Time for bed," he whispered. He laid the teddy on a chair under the blanket. "Do you feel better now?" he asked. He waited and waited. Then he lifted the teddy and made it nod. "Yes!" said Xavier. "The blanket and the medicine helped!"

Liliane clapped her hands. "Good job, teddy doctor," she said. Xavier smiled and held up the teddy. "My turn to be sick tomorrow," he said.

Anthony woke up in the dark. He walked to the kitchen. "Is it morning?" he asked. His dad shook his head. "Look out the window," Dad said. The sky was black. "It is still night," Dad said. "Night is the opposite of day."

Anthony thought about that word. Night was dark. Day was light. They were opposites.

"I want warm milk," said Anthony. Dad got the small pot. Dad poured the milk. The stove was hot, so Anthony stood back. Dad stirred it slow, slow, slow.

Dad looked out at the sky. "Cloudy tonight," he said. "No stars to see." A bird began to fly past the window. It was going home to the big forest.

The milk was ready. Anthony held his cup. It was warm, not cold. He took a little sip. "Night milk is cozy," he said. Dad smiled. Soon Anthony gave a big yawn.

Mackenzie went to the store with her mom. She held her mom's hand in the parking lot. "Stay close," said her mom. Mackenzie stayed close.

Inside, Mr. Hosseini was at the deli counter. He had a big pot of soup. Mackenzie wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. She started to walk toward it. Her mom held her hand. "Steam from a pot is hot," her mom said. "It can burn. We stay back." Mackenzie stopped. She took one step away. Then one more step.

From far away, Mackenzie could see the pot. The bubbles went pop, pop, pop. The steam went up, up, up. Mr. Hosseini stirred the soup with a long spoon. He did not touch the pot with his hand. Mackenzie watched him from her safe spot. Stay back, stay back, she thought.

Next they went to the fish counter. Mackenzie saw a slimy fish on the ice. She wanted to pat it. "Let's just look," said her mom. So Mackenzie looked. The fish was cold. The ice was cold too. Cold felt very different from hot.

At home, her mom made tea. The kettle sang. Mackenzie stood back. She watched the steam rise from far away. "I see the steam," she said. "I'm staying back." Her mom smiled and blew on the cup.

Zachary stood in the bathroom. His dad ran the water for his bath. Zachary heard the water splash. It made a funny plop, plop, plop sound.

He touched the water with one toe. It felt warm. He saw white bubbles in the middle of the tub. The bubbles bobbed up and down. "Look, they ride on the water," said Zachary. The soap smelled like flowers.

On the sink, Zachary saw a lemon slice. "Is it sweet like orange juice?" he asked. "Try it and see," said his dad. Zachary licked it with his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. His dad laughed. "Lemons are sour," he said.

Zachary wanted the sour taste to go away. He drank some water. Then he got in the tub. He washed the lemon smell off his hands. The bubbles stuck to his tummy. They felt soft and tickly.

His dad wrapped him in a big towel. It felt fluffy and warm. Zachary yawned a big yawn. He looked at the lemon slice one more time. "You stay there," he told it. "You are too sour for me." His dad smiled and turned off the light. Zachary's teddy sat on the shelf, still asleep, waiting for bed.

Luna sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. But she looked and looked. There was no orange paint. "Oh no," said Luna. "My pumpkin needs orange."

Mahdi sat down next to her. "Red and yellow," he said. He scooped red paint into a cup. He scooped yellow paint, too. Luna took a stick and stirred. She stirred slow, then quick. "Look, look!" said Luna. "It turned orange!"

Luna painted her pumpkin. It was big and round. She painted one green leaf, two green leaves, three green leaves on top. Ella came to watch. "That is a good pumpkin," said Ella. Luna smiled and held it up high. "Red and yellow," she said. "That makes orange!"

Theo went to the store with his dad. Theo wanted a new ball. He could not find one anywhere.

First Theo saw apples and milk. "Those are foods," said Dad. Next Theo saw a big dog on a leash. "That is an animal," said Theo. Then he saw a shelf with dolls. He saw blocks too. Then he saw a red ball behind the blocks!

"Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," said the cashier, smiling. She pointed to the toy shelf. Theo reached for his ball. It was cold like ice. "It sat by the frozen peas," said the cashier with a laugh.

Theo held the ball tight. Dad paid for it. At home, Theo bounced it on the floor. The ball made a happy sound. Bounce, bounce, bounce.

Clara sat at Grandma's big table. She had a fat pencil and clean paper. "I will write my name," she said. Grandma sat next to her.

Clara began at the right side of the page. She made a C. Then an L. Then an A. Then another A. There was no room left. The R fell off the edge of the paper. Clara frowned. "My R ran away," she said.

Grandma smiled. "Let's help that R," she said. "Start here." She pointed to the left side of the page. Clara put her pencil down there. C, L, A, A, R. This time they all fit. The letters went across, all the way to the right.

Clara held up the paper. "It says Clara!" she said. Grandma clapped. "Write it again," she said. Clara started at the left once more.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Adam went to the airport with Dad. Dad said, "We wait here in arrivals. Grandma comes out those doors." Adam watched the doors. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" said Adam. It was not Grandma. A lady with a big hat came out. "Grandma!" said Adam. It was not Grandma either. Then the doors opened one more time. It was Grandma! She hugged Adam tight.

The next day the summer sun was warm. Grandma and Adam went to the park. Salma and Aidan were there. "Let's play airport," said Adam. The slide was the plane. Aidan and Salma slid down fast. Then they ran out through the gate, like people coming off a plane. Adam and Grandma stood by the bench. "This is the arrivals area," said Adam. "We wait here for you!" Salma ran right into Grandma's arms. "Welcome off the plane!" said Grandma. They played and played until snack time.

On the way home they stopped to shop for bread. Grandma wiped Adam's hands with a clean napkin. "Same game tomorrow?" asked Salma. "Yes!" said Adam. "And I will wait at arrivals first."

Benjamin stood in the small guest bedroom. Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. He wanted to give her a big hug. But Benjamin felt shy when the car pulled up.

Grandma got out of the car. Benjamin hid behind his dad's leg. His heart went thump, thump, thump. Grandma held out her arms.

"You can hug me," said Grandma. "Or you can wave. Or you can just say hello."

Benjamin peeked out. He lifted his small hand. He waved. Grandma waved back, big and wide. Then he whispered, "Hello, Grandma." One ear turned a little pink.

"That is a fine hello," said Grandma. "I like waves too."

On day two, Benjamin waved again. On day three, he said hello loud and clear. On day four, he gave her a hug, quick and small. By day five, the hug was big. He did not cry once.

At bedtime, Grandma tucked him in. "Wave or hug?" she asked.

Benjamin hugged her tight.

Eloise was at school. It was naptime. The room was quiet. But Haylie had a drum. She banged it loud. The loud drum woke Martha up. Martha rubbed her eyes. She looked mad.

Mr. Swampy walked over. He sat down next to Haylie. "Loud and quiet are opposites," he said. "Can you play the other way?" Haylie thought hard. Then she tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. The tap was quiet. Martha did not wake up again. She went back to sleep.

Eloise watched the whole thing. She wanted to try too. She picked up a small drum. First she played it loud. The loud sound made Martha stir. Then Eloise played quiet, quiet, quiet. Nobody stirred. A flower on the shelf stood still. "I need the quiet drum for naptime," Eloise whispered. Tap, tap, tap.

Jordan went to the art studio with his dad. He wanted to paint a rainbow. But there were only three paint pots on the table. Red, yellow, and blue. No green. No purple. No orange.

Jordan had a question. "How do I paint a rainbow with only three paints?"

Mr. Holloway smiled. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours."

Jordan poked his brush in the blue. Then he poked it in the yellow. He swirled them on his paper. Green! Like dragon grass! He gasped. One paint plus another paint made a brand new colour.

He tried red and yellow. Orange! Like a yummy carrot. He tried red and blue. Purple! Like a magic wizard hat.

Jordan painted his whole rainbow. He gave his painting a hug. "Look, Dad! Three paints made all of this!"

Olivier woke up in his bedroom. The sun was on his pillow. His tummy made a big growl. He wanted cookies. Cookies were the best.

He found his loose sock on the floor. He pulled on his pants, one leg at a time. Then he ran to the kitchen. "Cookies please!" he said. Mom laughed. "Cookies are not breakfast. Breakfast is the first meal of the day." Olivier made a silly face. "Then I will eat cookies second!" Mom smiled. "First, breakfast. Then we will see."

Olivier looked at the table. There were eggs, toast and a banana. He helped Mom feed the toast into the toaster, one slice at a time. The toast popped up with a jump. "It jumped!" Olivier said. He made his toast into a chicken shape with the banana for a beak. Mom clucked like a hen. Olivier took a big bite. His tummy felt happy.

"Mom, can breakfast come two times a day?" he asked. Mom laughed and handed him a napkin. "Eat your chicken beak," she said.

Maria got in the big car with her family. They were going to a campsite. She hugged her teddy bear tight.

At the campsite, Maria played near the water. She dug in the sand with her hands. She found a smooth white shell. She put the shell in her pocket. Her feet went squishy in her wet shoes.

Then it was time to go home. The car took them back. Maria fell asleep on the way. Her dad carried her inside.

The next morning, Mom said, "Time to unpack our bags." Maria pulled her shoes out of her little bag. She shook them, and sand fell out. "Sand came from the beach!" she said. The sand tickled her toes on the floor.

She put her shell on her shelf. She put her teddy bear on her bed. She put her shoes by the door. Then she helped Mom put the towels away too.

"Thank you, Maria," Mom said. "You put everything away."

Maria smiled and clapped her hands. "All done!" she said.

Caleb stood in the cooking classroom at school. He wanted to make pancakes for his family. Mr. Patel gave him a card. "This is called a recipe," said Mr. Patel. Caleb looked at the card. "What does it tell me?" he asked. Mr. Patel smiled. "It tells you what to use and what to do, one step at a time."

Caleb read the first step. He put flour in the bowl. Then he put in milk. Eleanor helped him stir. Then Caleb saw a step about eggs. "We can skip that," he said. He wanted to be fast. The batter went into the pan. Mr. Patel watched the hot stove and turned the pancakes.

The pancakes came out flat. They looked like little foot prints. Lennyn looked at the card. "We missed the egg step," she said. Caleb felt his face get warm. He read the card again, one step at a time. This time he did not skip anything.

The new pancakes came out big and puffy. Caleb put them in a box to take home. "My family will eat these," he said. Mr. Patel gave him a thumbs up. Caleb held the box with two hands. "Step by step," said Caleb. He carried the warm box out the door.

Daniel had a big red truck. Lev came over to play. Lev wanted the truck too. Lev reached out his hand. Daniel held the truck tight. What could he do?

Daniel looked at his blocks. There were so many blocks on the rug. He had an idea. "You can have the truck first," Daniel said. "I will build a tall tower."

Daniel stacked the blocks. One, two, three, four. The tower grew and grew. It looked so cool, tall like a rocket going to the moon. Soon the tower was done. Then Lev gave the truck back. "Your turn," Lev said.

Daniel pushed the truck across the floor. It was his turn now. Waiting had not felt long at all. "Want to build another tower?" Daniel asked. Lev laughed and nodded yes.

It was snack time at school. Ms. Ong put crackers on two plates. Tara got one plate. Jackson got the other plate. Jackson looked at his plate. It looked small. Tara's plate looked big.

Jackson counted his crackers. He touched each one as he counted. "One, two, three, four." Then he counted Tara's crackers. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Tara had more crackers than him.

"I want more," said Jackson. "I have fewer," said Jackson.

"Fewer," said Ms. Ong. "That is the other word. More and fewer."

Ms. Ong was kind. She waited while Jackson counted again. He got to six on Tara's plate. He got to four on his own. Still fewer. Then Ms. Ong added two crackers. Jackson counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six. Now we both have six!"

Tara broke a cracker and shared her egg salad too. "Now we have the same," said Tara. Jackson smiled and took a big bite.

Jaxon ran to the park with his red truck. He saw Diego there. Diego was putting leaves in a little pile.

"Look, this is my house," said Diego. He pointed at a bench. "The leaves are my soup."

Jaxon sat down. He held out his truck. "Here is more soup," he said. Diego laughed. He stirred the leaves with a stick.

Then Casper came. He was hopping on the stones. "Don't step in the water!" he said. "The ground is a big river!"

Jaxon looked down. The ground was dry. It was not water at all. But Casper hopped like it was real. Jaxon tried it. He jumped from stone to stone. His feet stayed dry. "It's not real water," said Jaxon, "but we act like it is!"

"Mom says that is pretending," said Casper. "Pretending means acting as if something is real when it is not."

Jaxon wanted to try more. He picked up a small stick. "This is my baby," he said. "The baby is alone. It needs a nap." He laid the stick on the bench. He patted it gently. "Shh, sleep now."

Mr. Clarke-Williams walked by with his dog. "Is your baby sleeping?" he asked.

"Yes," said Jaxon. "Please be quiet." Mr. Clarke-Williams smiled. He tiptoed past.

Diego brought over some leaf soup. "Here, feed your baby," he said. Jaxon held the stick up. "Yum, yum," he said softly.

Then the baby stick "woke up." Jaxon made it dance. Casper clapped. Diego clapped too.

They played until the sky turned orange. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Diego.

"Yes!" said Jaxon. He hugged his truck. "And the baby comes too."

The lights went out at Arlo's house. It was dark and Arlo could not see his toys. "Where did the lights go?" he asked. "The power went out," said Mom. "We will sit still and wait."

They went next door to Ms. Hosseini's house. She had a little lamp that ran on batteries. It sent a soft glow over the table. Arlo sat close to Mom. He was sleepy, but he did not want to nap in the dark. Ms. Hosseini gave him a warm blanket. Soon the lights came back on. "Yay!" said Arlo.

Then Arlo saw something odd. The clock on Ms. Hosseini's oven was blinking. "The numbers are blinking!" he said. "What is missing?" he asked. "The time is missing," said Ms. Hosseini. "After a power cut, oven clocks blink and need to be set again." She pushed the little buttons, and the clock showed the right time again.

At home, Arlo ran to the kitchen. The oven clock was blinking there too. "Mom, it needs to be set again!" he said. Mom set the clock, and the numbers stopped blinking. Arlo smiled. Then Mom picked him up and carried him to bed. "Sleep tight, Arlo," she said.

Theo went to the garden center with his dad. He held a little pot of dirt. "I want to grow peas," said Theo. "Then we can bring them home," said his dad.

At home, Theo poked holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the top. "One seed, two seeds, three seeds," said Theo. His dad helped him water them.

Every day Theo looked. The dirt stayed flat. Then one morning, green leaves popped up. The plant grew tall. Then it grew little green pods. "What are those funny things?" asked Theo. His friend Joshua came to see. Joshua picked a pod and squeezed it. Pop! It opened up. "Look!" said Joshua. Inside sat a row of little green balls.

"Peas!" said Theo. "The peas grow inside the pods!" He picked a pod and popped it too. They counted the peas together. "One, two, three, four." Theo ran inside to show his dad. "Our plant made a snack," he said. "Can we pop some more?"

Violet sat at the big table in the art classroom. Mr. Watanabe was near the paint pots, smiling. Violet dipped her brush and made a big yellow sun. The paint smelled like rain. She put her paper on the drying rack to dry.

Sultan sat next to her. He made a yellow sun too, almost the same as hers. Later, two papers fell off the rack. They landed in a pile on the floor. Violet picked one up. She looked and looked. "Which one is mine?" she asked. Her tummy felt tight.

Mr. Watanabe came over. He held both papers. "People often write their name on their artwork so everyone knows who made it," he said. Violet turned her paper over. On the top corner, small letters said VIOLET. Sultan turned his over. His said SULTAN. "There you go," said Mr. Watanabe. Violet smiled. Her tummy felt better.

She got a crayon. On her next painting, a yellow cat, she wrote her name all by herself. Sultan wrote his name too. Then, surprise, Violet wrote SULTAN on the back as well. "Now we both know," she said, and tapped the top of the cat's head with her crayon. "Mine and yours, sun friends forever."

Brielle sat at the kitchen table. She was painting a big park. She had blue paint and yellow paint.

She wanted to paint the grass. But she had no green paint. "Where is green?" she asked. Her paint box was full, but no green cup.

Then a drop of blue fell in the yellow cup. Brielle looked. She stirred it with her brush. The paint turned green! She stared at the green cup. How did that happen?

She dipped her brush in blue. She dipped it in yellow too. Green again! She laughed. "It stays green!" she said.

She painted grass all along the bottom. Then she painted a green frog by a tree. A surprise frog!

"Look, Mommy!" she said. "I made green." She held up her wet painting. The frog sat on the green grass and smiled.

Elena walked down the street with her dad. The farmers' market was busy and loud. There were apples, bread, and big jars of milk.

Mr. Moose had a toast stand. "Would you like to try, Elena?" he asked. He had a grown-up toast the bread in the toaster. Then he gave Elena a cool little knife, safe for spreading.

Elena took the hard butter from the fridge box. She pushed it on her toast. The toast got a hole in it. "Oh no," said Elena. "Why did my toast rip?"

Mr. Moose smiled. "Let's try again." He set some butter on the warm sun table. They waited. Elena watched a bird play in the grass. Then she touched the butter. It was soft now.

Elena spread the soft butter. It went on smooth and easy. No holes! Next came the milk. Elena poured slowly, slowly, into her cup. Only one small drop spilled. She wiped it with a cloth.

Her friend Elie ran over. "Can I try too?" Elie asked. Elena handed her the soft butter. "Use this kind," she said. "Watch me pour, and then you pour."

Elie poured the milk. Not one drop spilled. They clinked their cups together. "Yucky hard butter," Elena laughed. "Soft butter is the best." They ate their toast, every last crumb.

Haraper sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. She had to get a shot today. Her tummy felt funny and a little sad.

The doctor came in. A shiny tube hung around her neck. Harper pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked. "A stethoscope," the doctor said. "I use a stethoscope to listen to your heart beating."

"Can I hear it too?" Harper asked. The doctor put the round end on Harper's chest. She put the tubes in Harper's ears. Thump, thump, thump! Harper heard her own heart. It beat fast, like a drum. She took a big slow breath, and the thumping went slow.

Then it was time for the shot. Harper held her mom's hand. She listened to her heart thump, thump in her head. Quick as a blink, the shot was done. "All done," said the doctor with a smile.

Harper spun around once on her sock feet. "My heart says thank you," she said. The doctor laughed. "Come back and hear it any morning you like."

It was dark at Grandma's house. The lights went out. Louis held Mom's hand. "Silly lights," Louis said.

Grandma got a candle. Grandma lit it with a match. The flame was small and warm. It smelled like vanilla. Louis wanted to carry the candle to his room. He reached out his hand.

"Only a grown-up lights candles and looks after them," said Grandma. She gave Louis a flashlight instead. Louis pushed the button. Click! The light turned on. He aimed it at the wall. A big white circle appeared. He moved his hand. The circle moved too. Louis laughed.

He walked to his room with the flashlight. The beam showed his toys. It showed his bed. Grandma came too. She carried the candle carefully with two hands.

The lights came back on. "Say goodnight to the flashlight," said Mom. Louis clicked it off. "Goodnight, flashlight."

Ayla went to the vet with her dad. There was a big cage near the door. Inside was a small brown rabbit. "Can we take him home?" Ayla asked. "Yes," said her dad. "He will be our first pet."

The vet put the rabbit in a box with holes. Ayla peeked in. The rabbit had a round shape, like a soft ball. At home, Ayla held him. He was warm and fuzzy. Then she saw crackers on the table. She ran to grab one. "Wait," said her dad. "Wash your hands first." Ayla looked at her hands. She had just touched the rabbit. She washed her hands with soap. The bubbles made a pretend beard on her chin. Then she ate her cracker.

The next day, Ayla cleaned the rabbit's cage with her dad. The hay went in the bin. "Hands?" she asked. "Hands," said her dad. She washed them again. The rabbit watched from his box. Ayla waved at him. "We wash hands, then we eat," she said. Then she gave him a carrot, and he made it disappear, crunch by crunch.

Leah was going on a big trip. First she rode a ferry across the water. She held the rail and watched the waves bite the shore. "Where are we going now?" she asked. Dad said, "To the airport, to fly in a plane."

On the plane, Leah found her seat. She buckled her seat belt. It felt tight and snug. She saw a green forest far below the window. She wanted to stand up to see it better. "Stay buckled," said the flight attendant. "We are taking off." Leah stayed in her seat. The plane went up, up, up. She watched the forest get smaller and smaller. When the plane came down for landing, she stayed buckled again. Then the wheels touched the ground. Dad smiled and said, "You can stand up now." Leah jumped up and looked out the window one more time.

It was a sunny day at daycare. Snow had fallen in the night. The snow was white, white, white. Hannah wanted to draw it.

She took a white crayon. She drew on white paper. "Where did my snow go?" she asked. Dylan came to look. "I can't see it," he said. "Me neither," said Hannah.

Then she had an idea. She found blue paper. She paid one sticker to Keanu for it, because it was his favorite sheet. She drew with her white crayon on the blue paper. The snow showed up at last. Big white blobs, small white dots, all of it shining.

"Look, look, look!" said Hannah. Keanu clapped. "That looks like real snow," he said. Ms. Sato hung it by the window. Hannah looked out at the white snow. Then she looked at her drawing. "Same white snow," she said. She patted her green shirt and smiled at Dylan. "Now you try one."

Aubrey sat in the school computer lab. She pushed the round button. The screen lit up. Pop! Aubrey tapped the little sun. The drawing app opened. She drew a red ball. She drew a blue slide, like at the playground. Drew sat next to her. He drew a green tree.

The timer rang. Time to stop. Aubrey set her tablet on the big beanbag chair. She ran to the line. Then Drew ran to the beanbag. He was going to sit down! "Careful!" said Ms. He. She held out her hand. Drew stopped. The tablet was right there, under his bottom. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," said Ms. He. She pointed to the shelf.

Aubrey used two careful hands. She carried the tablet to the shelf. It fit in its spot just right. The next day, Aubrey pushed the button. Pop! She drew a purple flower. Then she carried the tablet back to its special place, all by herself. "I did it!" said Aubrey. Ms. He clapped.

Ryan dug a little hole. He put in a carrot seed. He put in a pea seed. He put in a lettuce seed. "Grow, seeds, grow," he said.

Every day Ryan came to the community garden. His friend Bani watered the seeds. His friend Macy looked for birds. "No birds can make a nest here yet," Macy said. "The plants are too small."

One morning, green leaves popped up. Ryan saw a tiny leaf. He saw another tiny leaf. He saw a third tiny leaf. "A weed!" said Ryan. He pulled his hand back to grab it.

Mr. Novák knelt down. "That is not a weed," he said. "Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them." Ryan let go of the little leaf. "So this is a carrot?" he asked. "Yes," said Mr. Novák. "We want it right there."

Ryan looked at the tall grass near his row. Nobody planted that grass there. "That one is a weed," he said. Mr. Novák smiled. "Pull it out," he said. Ryan pulled the weed. He pulled the next weed. He pulled the last weed. "My carrots are safe," said Ryan. Bani clapped. Macy clapped. Ryan watered his row one more time.

Grayson could see the big playground from the sidewalk. The slides shone in the sun. The swings went up and down. He wanted to run to them right away.

But a street was in the way. Cars went by, fast. Grayson looked at the street. Then he looked at his grandma. He put his hand up and waited.

"Hold my hand," Grandma said. "We cross the street together." Grayson held her hand the whole way across. His feet did not let go of her.

On the other side, his friends were waiting. Kiana waved from the swing. Brooklynn was digging in the sand. "We saw a train go by!" said Kiana. "It was so loud it made the ground shake!"

Grayson ran to the sandbox. Brooklynn had found a wet worm. "It feels slimy," she said. She put it on a leaf. "It needs shade." Grayson found another leaf. Together they made a little roof over the worm.

Then the whistle blew. Time to go. Grayson looked at the street again. He found Grandma's hand and held it tight. "My turn," he said, and he squeezed her fingers all the way home.

Wesley stood in the backyard with a beanbag in his hand. A hoop lay on the grass in front of him. Celine and Finley stood beside him.

"Throw it in," said Celine. Wesley threw the beanbag high. He thought it would bounce. He thought it would bounce right into the hoop. But the beanbag came down with a soft flop. It landed on the grass and stayed still.

Wesley blinked. "Why did it just flop?" he asked. Celine smiled. "A beanbag lands with a soft flop," she said. "It does not bounce like a ball."

Wesley picked up the beanbag. He threw it again. Flop. It landed in the hoop and lay flat. "It stayed in!" said Finley. Wesley clapped.

Then Mr. Eze rolled a big ball to Wesley. Wesley held both hands out wide. He caught the ball with both hands and hugged it close. "Can I do the hoop again?" Wesley asked. "Yes," said Mr. Eze.

Wesley took off his cap and set it on the towel on the bench. Then he threw the beanbag, one more time. Flop. Right in the hoop.

Amira sat at the big kitchen table. She had a small blue block. She wanted to give it a sticker on every side. But how many sides did it have? Mom was baking, and she let Amira use the round stickers.

Amira put one sticker on the front. She turned the block over. She put a sticker on the back. She pointed to the top. "Sticker there too," she said. One, two, three. Then the bottom. Four. Then the two little sides. Five. Six.

She counted the stickers out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six sides! Every side was flat. Every side was a square. "It has six squares," said Amira. Mom smiled and gave her a high five.

Then Amira looked around the kitchen. The cookie Mom cut was a circle. The cheese slice was a triangle. The door of the fridge was a big rectangle. "I see shapes," said Amira. She held up her block. "And this one has six square faces." Mom laughed. "Good work, Amira," she said. Amira gave the block one more sticker, right on top.

Riley looked out the glass door. The sky was gray. "Rain," said Dad. Riley put on her rain boots. The rain made a tap-tap sound on the roof.

The rain stopped. Riley ran to the backyard. Vyom was there too. "Look!" said Vyom. He pointed at the ground. A big puddle sat in the grass. Riley stepped in it. Splash! Her boot went down in the water. She laughed and jumped again. Splash, splash. The puddle got smaller and smaller.

Soon the sun came out. It was sunny now. The wind started to blow. It blew Riley's hair all around. "My puddle is going," said Riley. She filled her glass of water and poured a little on the ground. A tiny puddle came back. "There you are," she said, and she jumped one more splash.

Rowan was at daycare. He wanted more milk with his snack. He held up his cup. "Please," he said to Mr. Nolan. Mr. Nolan smiled. He poured more milk. The cup felt smooth in Rowan's hands.

Nayla sat next to Rowan. She had no crackers left. Rowan gave her one of his. "Thank you," said Nayla. Then she looked down. She did not know what to say after that. Mr. Nolan said, "You're welcome, Rowan." Nayla looked up fast.

At play time, Ayoub bumped Rowan's tower. The blocks fell down. "Sorry," said Ayoub. "It's okay," said Rowan. Then Ayoub helped him. They built the tower again. It was tall and smooth at the top. Ayoub gave Rowan a blue car. "Thank you," said Rowan. Nayla stood close by. "You're welcome," she said. Ayoub laughed. Rowan laughed too. Then they pushed the car across the rug together.

Rehmat was at Grandma's house. She wanted honey on her bread. The jar sat on the big table. Grandma had put it there for her.

Rehmat pulled the lid. It did not move. She pulled again. Still stuck. "Oh no," said Rehmat. Outside the window, a bee buzzed by the flowers. Rehmat watched it go round and round until she felt a bit dizzy. Then she looked at the jar again.

She took a big breath. "Can you help me, please?" she asked Grandma. Grandma smiled. "Of course I can." Grandma's strong hands turned the lid. Pop! It opened. Grandma gave her a spoon of honey. "Thank you," said Rehmat. Later, Grandpa dropped a napkin. "Can I help you, please?" said Rehmat. She picked it up and gave it back. Grandpa clapped. "What a good helper." Rehmat grinned and took a bite of her bread.

Ava's baby brother was sleeping. Ava wanted to play the big drum. She lifted the drumsticks up high. "BOOM!" she shouted, just for fun. The baby woke up. He cried and cried. Mom came in with a tired face. She rocked the baby in her arms. Ava put the drumsticks down. She felt sad in her tummy.

Mom put the baby back in his crib. Then Mom held up one finger by her lips. Ava copied her. "Shh," Mom whispered. Ava tried it too. "Shh," she whispered back. Mom nodded and smiled. Ava saw the baby's eyes close again. He stayed asleep this time. Ava tip-toed out of the room. She carried her drum in a bag, so it would not bump the door.

Ava found her friend Rylie outside. Rylie had a dirty, shiny bike. The sun did make it shine, even with the mud. "My brother is sleeping," Ava whispered. "We can be quiet." Rylie whispered too. They took turns with the drum, pat, pat, pat, soft as a cat's feet. The baby slept and slept. "Quiet is fun," Rylie whispered.

John loved craft time at school. Today the class would make paper sailboats. John wanted a big red sail for his boat.

Leland had a triangle already. Charly had a triangle too. John looked in the paper box. He found a red square. But he needed a triangle.

He held the square up. He turned it around. "I want two triangles," he said softly. His shoulders went down.

Ms. Haile knelt beside him. "I have scissors," she said. "The scissors are sharp, so I will cut." She placed the square on the table. The paper felt smooth and cool.

"Watch," said Ms. Haile. "Cut from this corner to the opposite corner." She cut slowly across the square. Snip, snip, snip.

The paper fell open. Two red triangles lay on the table. John clapped his hands. One, two!

He glued a triangle on his boat. The little sail stood up tall. "My boat is ready," said John.

"Let's sail them," said Leland. The boats slid across the big table. John laughed and pushed his boat again.

Camille walked into the big hall with her mama. There were long tables and paper stars on the wall. Camille's friend Jocelyn waved from a tall chair.

"Come see," said Jocelyn. "It is Hanukkah. We light candles on a menorah."

A grown-up lit the candles with a long match. The flames burned bright and small. Camille counted them with her finger. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Only four candles!"

"That is tonight's number," said Jocelyn. "There are eight nights."

Camille made a face. "I want all the candles now. Eight is better than four."

"You have to wait," said Jocelyn, and she laughed. "Tomorrow night there will be one more."

The next night they came back to the hall. Ms. Pritchard from next door was there too. The grown-up lit the candles again. Camille counted fast. "One, two, three, four, five!" She jumped up and down. "One more than yesterday!"

Each night the candles grew. Six. Then seven. On the last night, all eight candles burned together. Camille held her mama's hand and watched the flames.

"Good night, candles," said Camille. "See you next year."

Sarah had a little slide in her yard. Her dad sat on a chair close by. "Can I go on the slide?" Sarah asked. "Yes, I am right here," said Dad.

Sarah climbed up the little steps. She got to the top. She saw a bird on the fence. It was a spotted bird. "I hear you, bird," she said. The bird sang back.

Sarah wanted to go down fast. She lay down on her tummy. Her head was at the top of the slide. She was going to slide head first. Dad came over fast. "Turn around, Sarah," he said. He helped her turn. Now her feet were at the top. Sarah held on with her hands. Then she let go. Down she went, feet first, all the way to the grass.

"I did it!" said Sarah. She heard the spotted bird sing again. Dad clapped his hands. "Again," said Sarah. She ran back to the steps. She climbed up, turned herself around, and down she went, feet first, one more time.

Norah had a cold. She sat at the table with her toast. Her nose began to drip. Sniff, sniff. She sniffed again and again. "Why does my nose do that?" she wondered.

Her dad handed her a tissue. "Blow," he said. Norah pressed the tissue to her nose and blew. Out came the runny stuff. Her nose felt better. Then it got stuffy. She could not breathe through it at all. She tried one side. Then the other side. "My nose is all stopped up," she said.

So Dad took her to the pharmacy. They walked past the shampoo. Past the bandages. One, two, three shelves of tissues. Norah picked a soft blue box. On the way home they passed a muddy puddle. Norah saw the mud, but she did not step in it. At home she held her new box. "I have tissues now," she said. She blew her nose with a big honk and smiled. "That is better."

Sofia sat on the grass at the park. Her class was painting pictures. Ms. Guo gave each child three pots. Sofia had a red pot, a blue pot and a yellow pot.

She wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green pot at all. "I need green," said Sofia. Her friend Harvin looked too. "No green here," he said.

Sofia looked at her blue pot. Then she looked at her yellow pot. She put her brush in the blue paint. She put it in the yellow paint. She mixed them round and round. The brush turned green! "Look, look!" said Sofia. Harvin clapped his hands.

Sofia painted tall green grass. Avnoor came over with a dirty brush. "Can you show me?" she said. Sofia put blue and yellow on Avnoor's brush. Avnoor mixed them round and round. Her brush turned green too. The three friends painted green grass all morning.

"Mixing is fun," said Sofia. She held up her green, green painting for everyone to see.

Grandpa came to stay at Maya's house for a whole week. Each morning they walked to the park together. Grandpa pushed Maya on the swing, way up high. "I can see a big white cloud," Maya called. Grandpa laughed and pushed her again.

They sat on the warm bench and shared a full bag of bread crumbs. The ducks came running. Maya dropped a crumb, and a duck gobbled it up. Then she dropped another crumb, and another duck ran over. "One crumb, one duck," said Grandpa.

One day Grandpa packed his suitcase. Maya felt sad. "I will miss you," she said. At home, Maya drew a picture of the big white cloud. Her mom helped her put it in an envelope. They walked to the mailbox together. Then Grandpa called on the phone, and Grandma waved on a video call. Maya held up her cloud picture to the screen. "I will draw you more," she said. Grandpa smiled.

Athena was playing in the backyard. The sun was warm on her hair. Her mom was fixing the grill. The grill would get very hot. Athena stayed back and watched.

Then Athena saw something on the picnic table. It was a small yellow bottle. Little red balls sat next to it. They looked like candy. Athena loved candy.

She walked closer. She wanted to touch the red balls. But then she stopped. She remembered something. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy. Were these candy or medicine?

"Mom, come look," Athena called. Her mom came right away. "I see little red balls," Athena said. "I did not touch them."

Her mom looked at the red balls. "Good job," Mom said. "Those are medicine, not candy. A kid must not touch them." Her mom put the bottle and the red balls up high, far away.

Athena went back to her toy truck. Her friend Dean peeked over the fence. "Come play," he said. Athena waved. She stayed close to her mom and played in the shade. The grill was hot, so she kept her distance. She rolled her truck down the little hill, back and forth, back and forth.

Hunter sat on the big rug. The TV was on. It was the big hockey game. Jerome and Lina came over to watch too.

"Where is the ball?" Hunter asked. He looked and looked. The players skated fast. They held long sticks.

One, two, three sticks, Hunter counted. Still no ball.

Then a player hit something small and flat. It slid fast on the ice. Hunter pointed. "There! What is that?"

"That is the puck," said Lina. "The players hit the puck with their sticks."

Hunter watched the puck. A stick hit it. The puck zoomed. It went into the net. A goal!

The room was quiet for a second. Then everyone cheered.

After the game, Dad cut the cake. Hunter ate his slow. "The stick hits the puck," he said. "The puck goes in the net."

Dad smiled. Hunter shut his eyes for a big, happy bite.

Ruby sat at the dinner table. Daddy put a big bowl of rice on the table. Ruby wanted to tell about her day. She had found a ladybug at school!

"Guess what!" said Ruby. "A ladybug!"

"Shh, my turn," said Andreas. He was telling about his new shoes.

Ruby opened her mouth again. But Andreas stopped talking. He looked down at his plate. Ruby wondered why. Hmm, what happened?

Then Melodie said, "Ruby, wait for Andreas to finish." So Ruby closed her mouth. She waited. She waited a little more.

Andreas finished his story. "Now you, Ruby," he said.

"My turn!" said Ruby. Her heart felt happy. She told all about the red ladybug with black spots. Everyone listened. Nobody talked over her. Everyone waited.

Then Ruby waited for Melodie's turn too. "When someone is talking, we listen and wait," sang Ruby. Waiting was hard. But listening was fun.

"Now who wants more rice?" asked Daddy.

"Me, me!" said Ruby, waving her hand.

Athena was at the park. Hannah had a big red kite. The kite went up, up, up. Then it began to float on the wind. Athena wanted to hold it very much.

She ran over fast. She put out her hand to grab the string. Hannah pulled the kite away. "No," said Hannah. Athena felt sad. Her shoes stood still in the grass.

Then she tried a new way. She looked at Hannah. "May I have a turn, please?" she asked. Hannah smiled a big smile. "Yes! You said may I. Of course you can." Hannah put the soft string in Athena's hands. The kite danced above them.

A noisy dog ran by. Athena held the string tight. "Thank you, Hannah," she said. "You can have it back now." They took turns until the sun went low. "Same time tomorrow?" said Hannah. Athena nodded and waved all the way home.

Nathan sat on a log at the campsite. His tummy was hungry. He wanted toast and milk, all by himself.

Dad handed him a cool slice of toast. Nathan took the butter knife. He spread the soft butter. Slow, slow, slow. The toast turned shiny and gold. "I did it!" said Nathan.

Next came the milk. Nathan held the cup with one hand. He tipped the carton. Glug, glug, glug. Some milk went in the cup. But a little milk ran over the edge. It made a small white puddle on the table.

Nathan's lip wobbled. His friend Elie came over. "Don't be sad," she said. "Get a cloth."

Nathan found a soft cloth. He wiped the puddle. Wipe, wipe, wipe. The table was dry again. Just like that!

He tried pouring again. This time he poured slowly. Every drop went into the cup. Nothing spilled.

Elie gave him a hug. Ms. Sow, the neighbour at the next tent, called out, "Nice pouring, Nathan!"

Nathan drank his milk. It was cold and sweet. He took a big bite of buttery toast. Under the log, a root poked up like a little bump. Nathan put his cup safely on the flat table.

"No more spills," said Nathan. "But if they come, I know just what to do." He folded the cloth and put it next to his cup.

William sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny and he was a little scared. His mom held his hand. "The doctor is kind," she said. A nurse came in. "Time to wash your hands," she said with a smile. William looked at the little sink.

William wet his hands and rubbed the soap. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he stopped. Was that long enough? He looked at his wet hands. The soap was still on them. He had stopped too soon. "Try again," the nurse said. "Sing a song while you scrub."

William began to sing his favorite song. He sang and scrubbed the backs of his hands. He sang between his fingers too. The song was not done yet, so he kept scrubbing. When the song ended, the soap bubbles were everywhere. He rinsed them all off. His hands were clean and shiny.

The doctor came in and said, "What clean hands you have!" Then she listened to his heart with a soft tool. It tickled a little. William laughed. On the ride home, he sang the song again in the car. "I scrubbed the whole song," he told his mom. She smiled at him. "Sing it for me at bath time," she said.

Kinsley went to the farmers' market with her brother. The market had big baskets of seeds. Kinsley picked tomato seeds and carrot seeds. "I will plant a garden," she said.

At home, Kinsley planted the seeds in two rows. Then she watered the soil. Every day she looked. But soon she forgot which row had tomatoes.

Then Kinsley had an idea. She drew a red tomato on one card. She drew a long orange carrot on another card. She stuck the cards in the soil, one in each row.

Soon green sprouts came up. Kinsley looked at the tomato card. She knew that row was tomatoes. She looked at the carrot card. She knew that row was carrots.

Kinsley picked a red tomato. "Look, brother!" she said. "My card knew first."

Caleb sat at the little table in the school library. He wanted to write his name. Ms. Do gave him a pencil. "Hold it like this," she said. She showed him her fingers. Caleb tried to hold the pencil the same way.

He made a big C. Then he made a wobbly A. "Oh no," said Caleb. "My A looks funny." He wanted to fix it. Alayah sat next to him. "Use this," she said. She held up the pink end of the pencil. "It is called an eraser."

Caleb rubbed the pink eraser on his wobbly A. He looked at the paper. The wobbly line was gone! "It rubbed it out," said Caleb. He made a new A. This one was straight and tall. He wrote L, E, and B. His whole name was on the paper. Adriana clapped for him. Ms. Do put his name up on the shelf by the window, right next to the books about grass.

Julia went to the park with her dad. Ms. Nikolaidis was there with a big red hoop. "Come and play," said Ms. Nikolaidis. "You can throw a beanbag."

Julia held a small blue beanbag. Liliana stood by the hoop. Julia looked at Liliana and waved. Then she threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass, not in the hoop. Julia was scared she could not do it.

"Try again," said Ms. Nikolaidis. Julia counted, "One, two, three." This time Julia looked at the hoop. She looked and looked. Then she threw the beanbag. It went right in! "You did it," said Liliana.

Then Ms. Nikolaidis rolled a big yellow ball. Julia opened her arms wide. She caught it with both hands. "One, two, three, we did it," they all said together. Julia threw the beanbag again and again, looking at the hoop each time. Each time it went in. "Again," said Julia, laughing.

Eliana turned four today. Her party was at the big swimming pool. Himmat and Willa came too.

First they swam in the shallow end. Eliana kicked her legs fast. Her kicks made big splashes. The water went up and came down on Willa's head. Willa laughed and wiped her eyes.

Then Mommy called them out of the pool. There was a cake on the picnic table. It had a soft, furry teddy bear sitting next to it. One little candle stood on top.

"I will blow it out," said Eliana.

"Not yet," said Mommy. "First, everyone count."

They counted the candle. "One!" said Himmat.

"I was three yesterday," said Eliana. "Today I am four."

"That's how birthdays work," said Ms. Harper, the lifeguard, smiling.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew hard. The flame went out. Smoke curled up like a little gray cloud. Everyone clapped.

Then Eliana saw something. Willa was shivering. Willa's towel was far away on the bench. Eliana ran and got it. She wrapped it around her friend.

"Thank you," said Willa.

Eliana sat close beside her. Then she ate her cake, all of it, down to the last bite.

Oliver was at daycare. It was snack time. He wanted cold milk from the little fridge. He pulled the door. The door was open. Cold air came out. Oliver got his milk cup. Then he ran to the table.

"Leanna, look!" said Oliver. "The fridge is open." Leanna looked. Mr. Santoso came over. He touched the fridge. "Open and closed are opposites," he said. He pushed the door. Click. Now it was closed.

Oliver wanted to try. He opened the door again. Open. Then he pushed it. Closed. "I did it!" said Oliver. Leanna tried too. Open. Closed. Orion tried. Open. Closed. They laughed.

Then Mr. Santoso brought out a big cake. "This cake was in the fridge," he said. "It stayed cold because the door was shut." The cake was cold and sweet. Oliver took a big bite. Leanna took a small bite. "Yum," said Oliver. He gave Leanna a hug.

Mr. Santoso smiled. "Who can shut the fridge next time?" Oliver put up his hand. "Me! I will close it," he said. He ran to the fridge, fast. He pushed the door. Click. Closed.

Raphael ran to the red swing at school. But Riggs was already there. Riggs held the swing with both hands.

"I want the swing," said Raphael.

"I want it too," said Riggs.

Milena came over. She pointed at the second swing. "One swing is free," she said. But Milena wanted a turn too. Three kids. Two swings. That was a problem.

Ms. Malik clapped her hands. "Let's take turns," she said. "Each person gets a go, one after another."

Riggs went first. He pumped his legs. The swing went up high. Raphael counted out loud. "One, two, three!" Then Riggs hopped off.

Now it was Raphael's turn. The wind touched his face. He flew up, up, up. The swing felt like spring under him, bouncing and light. Milena counted. "One, two, three!" Raphael held on tight and slowed down. He hopped off.

Then Milena had her go. She laughed the whole time. Raphael and Riggs held the swing for her, so it was cozy and safe.

After that, Riggs got another turn. Then Raphael. Then Milena. One after another, around and around, until the bell rang.

"Same time tomorrow?" asked Milena.

"Yes!" said Raphael. He ran to line up next to Riggs, holding hands with his friend.

Beau lost his toy car. It was his favorite one. He looked in the sand. He looked by the swing. No car. Then Hoorain pointed at the tunnel slide. "It is dark in there," she said. Beau got down low. He peeked inside. He could not see anything in the dark spot. He reached in his hand. He felt only cool metal. Ms. Goh came over with a real flashlight. "Here, try this," she said. Beau held it and shone the light in. The tunnel was bright now. There was his car, sitting at the bottom! Beau crawled in and got it. He came out smiling. "My family gave me that car," he said. Then he rolled it down the slide, and Hoorain clapped.

Isabelle sat at the little table in the school library. Ms. Wanjiru gave her a pencil and some paper. "Today we write the I in your name," said Ms. Wanjiru. Isabelle held up her pencil. She waved it in the air. The point went near Qasim's nose. Ms. Wanjiru knelt down beside her. "Turn the pencil around," she said softly. "Let the point face down when you walk." Isabelle looked at her pencil. She turned the point down. She held it near her tummy. Then she walked to her chair, slow and careful.

Back at the table, Isabelle tried the letter I. One line down, one line on top, one line on the bottom. Her first try was wiggly. Her second try was too small. Qasim leaned over. "Mine was wiggly too," he said. "Try again." Isabelle took a big breath. She gripped the pencil with her whole hand. She made one line down. Then the top. Then the bottom. There it was. A big, tall I on the paper.

"I did it!" said Isabelle. Ms. Wanjiru clapped. Gracelyn clapped too. "Tomorrow we do the S," said Ms. Wanjiru. Isabelle smiled. She stood up with her paper. She held her pencil with the point facing down. "I love writing," she said.

Avery sat at the dinner table. Ricardo sat beside her. The bread basket sat in the middle. Avery could smell warm bread. One basket, two friends, one basket of bread.

Avery reached out fast. She grabbed for the bread. Ricardo's hand was already there. "My bread," he said. "My bread," Avery said too. Mr. Guo put his hand on the table. He waited. He did not say anything.

Avery looked at Mr. Guo. Then she looked at Ricardo. She let go of the basket. "May I have some bread, please?" she asked. Mr. Guo smiled. Ricardo passed the basket. "You say please too," Avery said. "Please," said Ricardo. They each took one piece.

After dinner, Avery helped sweep the crumbs. She swept them to the bottom of the table legs. Her arms felt tired. She yawned. "Bread, please, and sweep," she said. "That was a good dinner."

Benjamin ran to the park with his bike. Gordon and Esmae were at the big sand pit. They had all the trucks and buckets in one pile. Gordon held every single truck.

"Can I have one?" asked Benjamin. Gordon shook his head. "They are mine right now," he said. Esmae had no truck either. She just sat with her hands in the sand. Benjamin wanted to dig so much.

Then Benjamin had an idea. He held out his bike helmet. "You can take a turn on my bike," he said to Gordon. Gordon smiled big. He put one truck in the sand. "Here," he said. Then he put another truck by Esmae. "Here," he said again.

Now everyone had something different to play with. Gordon rode the bike in a slow circle. Esmae filled her truck with sand. Benjamin dug a deep, deep hole. Mr. Bélanger, the park helper, walked by with his dog. The dog gave Benjamin's hand a little kiss.

Gordon came back and parked the bike. "My turn for the truck now?" he asked. Benjamin gave it right over. Everyone got a turn. The sand pile grew taller and taller, one truck load at a time.

Andrew was going on a big trip. His family drove to a roadside diner. They would eat, and then drive to the snowy mountains.

Andrew looked in his bag. He pulled out his swimsuit. "I will swim in the snow!" he said.

His dad shook his head and smiled. "Snowy places need warm clothes," he said. "We pack clothes that fit the weather where we are going. A swimsuit is for the beach. A warm coat is for the snow."

Andrew put the swimsuit back. He looked again. He found his mittens instead. He put them on. Then he gave his dad a big hug.

At the diner, Ms. Koné, the waiter, brought warm cocoa. She set it far from Andrew's hands. Andrew bent down to smell it. "Snow trip, mittens trip!" he said.

His dad laughed. "Yes. Mittens trip."

Andrew waved his mittens in the air. "Mittens trip! Mittens trip!"

Sophie went to the library with her black bag. In the playroom, Emmeline was building a tall block tower. "The castle of the moon," said Emmeline. Sophie wanted to add one block. She waited and waited. "Your turn," said Emmeline. Sophie placed the block on top. The tower grew taller.

Then Ms. Bouchard rang a little bell. "Story time now," she said. Emmeline ran to the rug. Sophie started to run too. She looked back at the blocks on the floor. The moon castle had fallen down. Blocks were everywhere.

Sophie did not run. She got the blocks and put them in the bin. One by one, into the bin. Then Emmeline came back. She picked up blocks too. Soon the floor was clear. "You helped," said Emmeline. They sat down side by side. Ms. Bouchard opened a big book. "Once upon a moon," she read.

Mya was at home. Her little red ball was lost. It rolled away at breakfast.

"Maybe it went up the stairs," said her dad.

Mya went up the stairs. Step, step, step. Up was high. She looked in the big room. She looked under the small chair. No ball.

Down the stairs she went. Step, step, step. Down was low. It felt fast to go down. Going up had felt slow.

She felt a bit dizzy at the bottom. She sat down. Then she stood up again.

"Mya, up and down are opposites," said her dad. "You went up. Then you came down."

Mya looked at the stairs. Up was high. Down was low. She smiled.

Then she saw something red. It was the ball! It sat by the cold front door. The warm sun made a red spot on the floor.

Mya picked up her ball. She hugged it tight.

"I found you!" she said.

She rolled the ball to her dad. He rolled it back. Mya laughed and jumped up high.

Asher was at Grandpa's house. On the desk sat a small violin. It was new and shiny. "Can I play it?" Asher asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Mr. Das will show you how."

Mr. Das came after lunch. Asher grabbed the violin. He held it upside down. He plucked the strings. The sounds were funny and small. "Why does it sound so silly?" Asher asked. Mr. Das smiled. "Let me show you how to hold it."

Mr. Das turned the violin around. He helped Asher put it on his shoulder. Asher held the bow. He pulled it across the strings. A big, sweet sound filled the room!

"Again!" Asher said. He pulled the bow again. The music rang out to the window. Grandpa clapped his hands. "Play one more," he said. Asher pulled the bow slow, then fast, and laughed out loud.

Miles ran to the block corner. He wanted to build a tall tower with his friend Beckham. But the lights were off in the little play room. It was very dark in there.

"I will get the red blocks," Miles said. He reached into the dark bin. He could not see the colors. He grabbed two blocks anyway. Maybe they were red!

Mr. Becker turned on the light. The room got bright. Miles looked at his blocks. One block was red. One block was green.

"Look at that," said Miles. "In the dark, I could not tell!"

Beckham bounced his ball on the floor. "Let's pick again," he said. Beckham held up a blue block. Then he held up a yellow one.

Miles smiled. Now he could see every color. He put the red block on the green one. The tower began to grow. It grew tall and long across the rug.

Miles put his doll on top. "She can see the whole room," he said. Beckham laughed and clapped his hands.

Dinner was outside tonight! Mom set the table on the grass. Luka ran to his seat. But his shoes felt tight and bumpy. "Ouch," he said. He sat down and could not wiggle his toes. Mom helped him pull off his shoes and socks. "Now your feet are safe and free," she said. Luka put his bare toes on the grass. The grass tickled! "My feet can feel it!" he laughed. "Soft grass under bare toes!" He sniffed the soup. It smelled like carrots. He heard Dad slurp, loud and silly. He saw steam rise up. He touched his warm cup with one finger. Then he tasted the soup. Yum! "My feet liked the grass," said Luka. "Can we eat out here every night?" Mom laughed. "Yes, little bare-feet boy."

Declan loved his big brown bear. He hugged it every night. Today Ocean was coming to play. Declan held his bear tight. "What if Ocean grabs my bear?" he asked his mom.

His mom smiled. "You can put your special bear away before friends come," she said. "Then you don't have to share it." Declan looked at his bear. Then he put it up on the high shelf. It sat there, safe and snug.

Ocean arrived with a big smile. Declan showed him the toy cars. "My turn first," said Declan. He pushed the red car down the ramp. It zoomed fast. Then he waited. He kept his hands in his lap. Ocean pushed the blue car next.

They took turns, back and forth. When Ocean grabbed too soon, Declan said, "Wait for your turn." Ocean stopped and waited. Then it was his turn again. Later they ate apple slices at the table.

That night, Declan took his bear down from the shelf. "Nobody grabbed you," he whispered. He thought about the fun day. He hugged his bear close and closed his eyes.

Ryan sat on the city bus with his dad. He was going to the dentist for the first time. "I wonder what the dentist will do," said Ryan. Out the window, he saw a river. Boats floated on it. Then the bus turned. The river went away! Ryan clapped. The bus had made the river hide.

At the dentist, a nice lady looked at Ryan's teeth. Then she gave him toothpaste to try. It was minty. Ryan brushed his little teeth. Bubbles grew in his mouth. He was about to swallow them!

The dentist shook her head. "Spit it out," she said. Ryan leaned over the sink. He spit the foam out. Plop! It went down. "I did it!" said Ryan. He grinned at his shiny teeth in the mirror.

Sofia was going to the dentist. First she went to the pharmacy with her dad. She wanted a new toothbrush. There were so many on the shelf. She found a little one with a cat on it. "This one," she said. Her dad scratched his head. "It is the same as yours at home," he said. "But the cat is new," said Sofia. Dad smiled and put it in the basket.

After the pharmacy, they went to the dentist. Sofia sat in a big chair. Then the chair slowly tipped back! Sofia was lying down now. She giggled. It felt like a little ride. "Ready?" asked the dentist. He looked in her mouth while she lay still. Sofia held her new toothbrush tight. "All done," said the dentist. "Your teeth are sparkly." Sofia sat up. "The chair went back like this," she told her dad, tipping her hands in the air. "Can we do it again?"

Charlie was at Grandma's house. The lights went out. The TV went dark too.

"Oh no," said Charlie. "The TV is off." Grandma found a flashlight. She clicked it on. The light made a bright circle on the rug. Charlie tried the TV again. Still dark. He waited. Still dark.

"No TV," said Grandma. "But look at this shelf." She set a board game down. She put the flashlight on the table. The light shone straight across the board. Charlie rolled the dice. He moved his sheep piece around the board. No plug needed! Then they did a puzzle. Then Grandma read him a book by the flashlight. The pictures showed a cow and a sheep.

Soon the lights popped back on. Charlie kept playing. "Let's finish," he said. Grandma sat down and moved her piece. "My turn!"

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything went dark. "Oh no," said Axel. "The power is out." His dad felt along the wall. "Where is the flashlight?" he asked. Axel thought hard. "Is it in the kitchen drawer?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I think it is."

Axel held Dad's finger in the dark. They walked slowly together. Dad pulled the drawer open. The flashlight was there. Dad clicked it on. The light still shone! "Wow," said Axel. "The power is out, but the light works." Dad smiled. "Good batteries," he said. The beam made a circle on the wall. Axel waved his hand in it. His shadow danced big and small.

Axel found his toy truck in the dark. "Found it," he said. Dad found the stinky dog biscuits too. The dog ran over, happy. Axel shone the light on the floor. The dog chased the circle. Round and round it went. The lights stayed out all evening. The flashlight stayed bright. "We make our own light," said Dad. Axel giggled and clicked it on and off. On, off, on, off. "Good night, light," he whispered.

William zipped up his red shirt. It was his first day on the baseball team. The field was a big green circle of grass and dirt. His friend Linden ran over. They stood by the bench together.

A man in black pants walked out to the base. William wondered, "Who is that man?" Linden said, "That is the umpire."

William hit the ball. He ran to first base. He was safe! Then Linden hit the ball. William ran to second base. The umpire put his hands out. William was out. William felt mad. He wanted to stomp his feet.

The coach came over. "The umpire makes sure players follow the rules," the coach said. William looked at the umpire. The umpire was not scary at all. He just wanted the game to be fair.

William took a big breath. He watched the umpire call the next play. "Safe!" the umpire said loudly. William clapped for Linden. Maybe next time, the umpire would say "Safe" for him.

Mackenzie ran to the backyard. Her friend Auguste was already there. He had a little play kitchen by the fence. It had pots and cups and a small red spoon.

"Let's play house," said Auguste. "You be the mom." Mackenzie picked up a teddy bear. She gave it a hug. She pretended to stir soup in a pot. The teddy bear got a cup of pretend milk. Auguste made a loud pretend soup bubble sound. They laughed and laughed.

Then the sky got cloudy. Mackenzie's mom called from the door. "Time to come inside, sweet girl." Mackenzie looked at the kitchen. Cups and pots were all over the grass. Auguste began to put them in the basket. Mackenzie helped him. The pots went in first. Then the cups. The teddy bear sat on top with the red spoon in its lap.

"Bye, Auguste," said Mackenzie. "Bye, teddy bear." She patted the bear on its soft head. Then she ran to her mom with a warm, happy heart.

Jackson sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma had made him a paper. On the paper was his name in little dots. "You can trace the dots," said Grandma. "Then the letters will be yours."

Jackson held the pencil. Grandma helped him grip it near the tip. He went over the first dots. Slowly, slowly, the dots turned into a line. The line made a big J.

"I did it!" said Jackson.

"You traced it," said Grandma. "Trace them all."

Jackson traced the a, the c, and the k. His name sat on the paper. It was crooked, but it was there. He smiled at it and chewed his toast while he looked.

Grandma put a purple crayon next to him. Jackson picked it up. "Now I make a turtle," he said, "with a J for its tummy."

He started on the dots again.

Clara ran to the playground. Her red scarf flew behind her. Neo was there too. His scarf was blue and little.

"Look," said Neo. "Your scarf is long. Mine is short."

Clara held her scarf out. It went down past her knees. Neo's scarf stopped at his tummy. They put the scarves side by side. Long. Short. Long. Short. Clara laughed.

"Long and short are opposites," said Neo.

The wind blew hard. Clara's long scarf flapped and flapped. It wrapped around her legs. She sat down on the grass. Neo's short scarf just sat still on his neck.

"I will wait," said Clara. She sat and waited. The wind blew again. She turned her back to the wind. The scarf stopped flapping. Slowly, slowly, she stood up. The scarf hung down, quiet and still.

"Now run with me," said Neo. They ran to the swings. Clara heard the swings squeak. The big swing went high. The small swing went low.

"I'm tired," said Clara. They sat on the bench. The sun felt warm on their faces. Clara ate her lunch. The long scarf lay in her lap, all folded up.

"Fast run, slow swing," said Neo.

"Big swing, small swing," said Clara. Then she took one more big bite.

Mohamed wanted the owl book. It sat on the rug in the reading corner. Rachel was reading it, and now she was done. Mohamed picked it up. He opened it. He looked at a page. The owl was already home in her tree. The owl was already asleep. "This is all mixed up," Mohamed said. He turned to another page. The owl had an egg. Then the owl was a baby. It felt like the story was walking backwards. Rachel came over. "Try the front cover," she said. Mohamed turned the book over. He found the front. He opened it. There was the egg, right at the start. He turned the pages, one by one. The baby owl grew. She learned to zip through the dark sky. At the back cover, the owl was tired and fast asleep. Mohamed smiled. "I started at the front," he said. Mr. Çelik gave him a thumbs up.

Mya stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook had made toast, and it was cool now. "Your turn," said the cook. "Spread the butter."

Mya picked up the little knife. She dipped it in the butter. She spread it on the toast. It went on thick in one spot. She spread some more. Slowly, slowly, the butter covered the whole slice. "Good job," said the cook. "Now the milk."

Mya held the cup in one hand. She held the milk jug in the other hand. She poured. The cup wobbled in her hand. Milk went drip, drip, onto the table. Mya frowned. She set the cup down on the table. The cup sat still. She poured again. This time the milk went right in. Not one drop fell.

The cook smiled. "You found a good way," he said. "Now you can drink your milk with your toast."

Mya ate her buttery toast. She drank all her milk. Then she said, "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

The cook laughed. "Yes. And on Saturday, we can drive to the store together and buy more milk. You are lucky, Mya. You are my new helper."
