Mya beamed. "I will pour for you," she said. "I will set the cup down first."

Natalie went to the library with her dad. She saw Senna at the block table. Senna was building a tall tower.

Natalie ran fast to see it. Her arm bumped the tower. The blocks fell down with a big crash. Senna's mouth turned down and her eyes got wet.

"Sorry, Senna," Natalie said. "Sorry means I know I bumped you." Senna wiped her eyes with her sleeve. Natalie sat down slow and careful. She picked up the red blocks first. Senna picked up the blue ones. They stacked them one by one.

The tower grew tall again. Taller than before! Senna clapped her hands. "It's your turn to put the top on," Senna said. Natalie placed the last block, soft as a pat in the bath.

Ms. Petrov came by with a cart of books. "What a fine tower," she said. "You two built it together."

Natalie smiled big. "We took turns," she said. "Can we build one more?"

Joshua ran into the kitchen in his pajamas. His tummy was making a big rumble. "I want breakfast," he said. His dad was at the stove. The stove was hot, so Joshua stood back. He watched his dad cook the eggs. Joshua got his own cup. He put it on the wooden table. The table was made of wood. It felt smooth under his hands.

After breakfast, Joshua got dressed. He put on his red shirt. He put on his blue pants. His socks were smelly, so he picked clean ones. "Good morning, Joshua," said Mr. Menon from the door. Mr. Menon waved and went to his own house.

That night, Joshua had a bath. The water was warm. His mom washed his hair. Then Joshua tasted warm milk before bed. He brushed his teeth after the milk. His teeth felt clean and shiny. He got into his little bed.

But Joshua could not sleep. He sat up. "Wait," he said. "I need to brush again." He hopped out of bed. He went to the sink. His mom helped him reach. He brushed his teeth before sleep. "All clean," said Joshua. He went back to bed and closed his eyes.

Everly stood in the kitchen. Her new coat was on the chair. It had no zipper. It had little round buttons.

"I can do it," said Everly. She pushed one button. It would not go in. She found the small hole next to it. She pushed the button through the hole. The coat closed!

"Look, Mommy! The button goes through the hole!" She did the next one. Push, wiggle, through. Two sides came together.

Her mom was drying dishes by the sink. "Take your time," said Mommy. Everly did the last button. It was slow. But she did not stop.

A big truck went by the window. Everly ran to see it. It was quick and red and loud. Then she came back. She unhooked every button. She wanted to do it all again.

Push, wiggle, through. The coat closed up warm. Everly hugged herself. "I did it," she said. "All by me."

Penelope woke up early. Today was shot day. She did not want to go. But Mommy said they would get ice cream afterward. So Penelope held Mommy's hand and walked in.

The nurse had a little tray. On the tray was a tiny needle. Penelope pointed at it. "Can I hold that?" she asked. The nurse smiled a soft smile. "Only I hold the needle," she said. "That is my job. But you can hold my sticker sheet." Penelope took the sticker sheet. It had a cow sticker on it. The cow was white with big black spots.

Penelope shut her eyes very tight. She felt one small pinch on her arm. Then it was done. The nurse put a bandage on. "Was that all?" Penelope asked. "That was all," said the nurse. Penelope picked the cow sticker for her shirt.

Then they went to the ice cream shop. Penelope got pink ice cream in a cup. She held her spoon all by herself. "Mommy, can I hold my spoon?" she asked. Mommy laughed. "Yes, that one is yours." Penelope licked the spoon and smiled. The cow sticker sat on her shirt, looking at the ice cream.

Emily held her dad's hand at the street festival. The road was full of people. There were flags and balloons everywhere. Emily saw a big bounce house. It was red and black.

Then she saw her friend Waris. He was with his grandma. Waris waved at her. "Eid Mubarak!" he called. Waris hugged Emily's dad too. "Eid Mubarak," his grandma said to everyone at the door of her house.

Emily wanted to say it too. She tried the words in her mouth. "Eid... Mubarak," she said softly. She walked to Waris and his grandma. "Eid Mubarak!" she said, loud and clear. Waris smiled big. His grandma smiled too. She put a sweet in Emily's hand. It was sticky and warm.

The bounce house was next. Emily and Waris jumped up and down. Her words had made everyone smile. "Eid Mubarak!" she shouted, bouncing high.

Milo woke up in the tent. "Eggs today!" he shouted. Dad laughed. "Yes, you can help."

At the little camp table, Milo held a big brown egg. He tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap, knock. The shell cracked. Milo pulled the shell open. The egg slid out! "It came out!" he said. "Look, Dad, it came out!"

But a little piece of shell fell in too. It sat in the yellow egg like a tiny boat. "Oh no," said Milo. Dad gave him a spoon. Milo dipped the spoon in. He fished out the piece of shell. "Got it!"

"Ready to cook?" said Dad. Dad lit the little camp stove. Milo stood back, far from the hot pan. He watched the egg go round and flat. "It makes a circle!" said Milo. "It makes a sun shape!"

The egg went onto a plate. Milo carried the plate to the tent, low and slow, both hands holding tight. "Breakfast!" he called. Mom sat up and smiled. "For me? Thank you, Milo!"

Milo grinned. "I cracked the shell. The egg came out!"

Madelyn sat at the little blue table. Ms. Huang put a plate in front of her. The plate had cookies on it. Madelyn counted them. "One, two, three, four, five." Ms. Huang smiled.

Then Albert came to sit down. He was hungry. He ate one cookie. Madelyn counted again. "One, two, three, four." Albert ate another one. Madelyn counted. "One, two, three." Albert ate one more. "One, two." Then he ate one. "One." Then Albert ate the last cookie. Madelyn looked at the plate. She counted. There was nothing to point at. "Zero," said Ms. Huang. "Zero means none. The plate is empty."

Madelyn looked at her friend Walker. He had cookies too. He counted them for her. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six was more than zero. "You have more," said Madelyn. Walker nodded. He gave her one cookie. Now they both had some. A small gray mouse ran along the closed cupboard door. Ms. Huang laughed. "We can see the mouse another day." Madelyn bit her cookie and smiled.

Riley went to the park with Dad. There was a little tent there. Kittens sat in a big pen. One small kitten had white paws. It looked at Riley. "This one," said Riley. Dad said, "We can take her home today."

At home, Dad put a box on the floor. It had soft sand inside. Riley pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked. "A litter box," said Dad. "The kitten goes to the toilet in it."

Riley watched the kitten. The kitten sniffed the sand. The kitten moved her paws. Then the kitten used the box. Riley clapped. "Good kitten!" she said.

At night the kitten sang a little song. Riley gave her water. She petted her softly. "Careful," said Dad. "Her claws are sharp." Riley touched the kitten very gently. The kitten purred and purred. "Good kitten," Riley said again.

Madison ran to the park with her dad. She wanted a snack, but the snack bag was empty. "Oh no," said Madison.

Madison used her eyes to look. She saw green grass and swings. She used her ears to listen. She heard birds and a dog bark. Then she used her nose to sniff. Sniff, sniff! Something smelled tasty. She could smell it before she could see it.

"I smell dinner!" said Madison. "But where is it?" She followed the smell with her nose. Her friend Maggie was there too. "I smell it too," said Maggie. They walked past the swings, past the sandbox, past the big tree. One, two, three steps, and there it was.

Mr. Oliveira was cooking at a grill. He was making corn. A grown-up was watching the hot grill, and the girls stayed back. Mr. Oliveira said, "You found it with your noses! Here, take a cool piece." Madison touched the corn. It was warm, not hot. She took a bite. Yum! Her tongue tasted the sweet corn.

"So my nose knew first," said Madison. "Noses are smart!"

Myles sat in his car seat. He was going to the pond with Dad. He wanted to see the ducks now.

"Are we there now?" Myles asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Now means at this very moment. We are still driving now."

Myles looked out the window. A big red truck went by. Then the truck was gone. "The truck is not here now," Myles said.

"That's right," said Dad. "It was here a moment ago. Now it is not."

Myles frowned. "I want the ducks now."

"First we drive," said Dad. "Later we get to the pond. Yesterday it rained. Today the sun is out. The pond will be dry and warm."

The car stopped. "We are here now!" said Dad.

Myles clapped his hands. He ran to the pond with Dad. The ducks were swimming. One duck came up close.

Then the duck flapped its wings. Water flew everywhere! A little drop landed on Myles's nose.

"You said the pond was dry!" said Myles.

Dad laughed. "The ground is dry. The duck is wet."

Myles laughed too. "The duck splashed me now!"

"Tomorrow we can come back," said Dad. "But now, let's watch the ducks."

Myles watched the ducks swim round and round. He held Dad's hand. The sun felt warm and good.

"One more minute," said Myles, "then home later?"

"Yes," said Dad. "One more minute now. Home later."

Myles smiled at the ducks. "Quack, quack," he said.

Zoey stood at the edge of the pool. The water looked big and blue. Mr. López was in the pool already. "Come in, Zoey," he said.

Zoey dipped one toe. The water was warm and cozy. She held the wall with both hands. Shiloh and Rhys were kicking nearby. They laughed and splashed.

"I want to see your bubbles," said Mr. López. "Put your mouth near the water. Blow out through your mouth."

Zoey was shy. She did not want her face close to the water. What would it feel like? She leaned down a tiny bit. She blew one small puff. A little bubble popped up. "Ooh," said Zoey.

She tried again. This time she blew harder. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles danced on the water. Rhys popped them with his hand. Zoey laughed and laughed.

"Again!" she said. She put her mouth down low and blew. The bubbles came out in a line, all the way to Shiloh.

The wind moved the pool flag above them. Zoey watched it wave. "Look at my bubble flag!" she said, and blew a long, wavy row of bubbles across the clean blue water.

Luke ran into Grandpa's cozy house. The room smelled like dumplings. There were red lanterns on the wall. They looked like little red mountains.

Grandma handed Luke a shiny red envelope. It felt stiff and crinkly. "What is it?" Luke asked. "Open it and see," said Grandpa with a smile.

Luke pulled at the corner. He wanted to peek right now. "Stop, stop, stop!" said his cousin, laughing. "First you say thank you." Grandpa nodded. "Many children get red envelopes with money inside at Lunar New Year. But we say thank you first."

Luke put his hands behind his back. He bowed a little bit. "Thank you, Grandma! Thank you, Grandpa!" Then he opened the envelope. A coin sat inside, shiny and gold. "Money!" Luke shouted. He shook the envelope. It went crinkle, crinkle, crinkle.

"Listen," said Grandpa. "It sings for you." Luke held it up to his ear. He giggled. "My envelope is singing!" Then he gave Grandpa a big, warm hug.

Evan was at daycare. He had a big red box. He put a toy bear in the box. He put a little car in the box. He put a shiny ball in the box. The box was his soup pot. "This is bear soup," he said. "It is hot soup!" But then Andreas ran up. Andreas took the bear out. Andreas took the car out. Andreas took the ball out too. The soup pot was empty. Evan wanted his soup back. He put the bear in again. Andreas took it out again. In, out, in, out. "Hey!" said Evan. "You take out. I put in." Ms. González smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. Evan looked at the box. Then he had a neat idea. He turned the box upside down. All the toys stayed under it. "No more out!" said Evan. Andreas tapped the box like a drum. Boom, boom! "Now it is a drum," said Andreas. Evan laughed and tapped too.

Lillian went to the store with her dad. She wanted a book about an owl. She had one at home, but she wanted her own new one. On the shelf she saw lots of books. She did not know which one to pick.

There was a lady at the store. She worked there. "Can you help me?" Lillian asked. "I want an owl book."

"What is the book's name?" the lady asked.

Lillian thought hard. "Do books have names?"

"Yes. The big words on the front are the title. That is the book's name."

Lillian looked at the shelf. She turned a book so the front faced her. "Squishy Owl!" she read on the cover. "That one is mine!"

The lady smiled. "You found it. Look, you open the front first." She showed Lillian page one. Lillian held the book and turned the pages one by one. The owl story began at the front.

At home, Lillian sat with her dad. She held the book up. "This is Squishy Owl," she said. "It has a name, just like me."

Colton ran to the playground with his friends Etienne and Remi. "Let's play a game," said Etienne. "Hide-and-seek!"

"I will hide first," said Remi. "You count, Colton."

Colton covered his eyes. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he peeked. "I see you!" he called. Remi was still running to the slide.

Etienne laughed. "That was too fast. You count while we hide. Please count slowly."

"Okay," said Colton. "I can try again."

Remi ran to hide behind the tire. Etienne hid under the bridge. Colton covered his eyes. He counted slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then he looked up. The playground was quiet. Nobody was in sight. Colton moved past the swing. He moved past the sandbox. He heard a giggle by the tire.

"I found you, Remi!" said Colton. Remi jumped out with a big grin. Together they looked for Etienne. They waited by the bridge. They waited and waited. Then two shoes peeked out.

"Got you!" said Colton.

Etienne crawled out laughing. "You counted so slow. That was fun."

"Me next," said Remi. "One, two, three, four, five."

Zoey wanted warm soup for lunch. The pot sat on the stove. Zoey looked at the pot. She could not see anything hot. The stove did not look hot at all.

"Is it still hot?" she asked her dad.

Her dad held his hand up high, near the pot, not on it. "The stove can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it."

Zoey nodded. She stepped back to the table. She chose to stir the cold juice instead. The juice spoon felt cool in her hand. "Cold," said Zoey. Her dad smiled.

Dad carried the pot over. He poured the soup. Steam went up, up, up. Then Zoey saw something silly. Her spoon stood straight up in the thick soup, like a little tree.

"Wow!" said Zoey. She blew and blew on her spoon. One bite, then another. "Yum," she said. "Summer soup is strong soup!"

Elliot sat at the dinner table. He could not sit still. Kamila was coming to eat with them. Elliot was so excited. He bounced in his chair. He bounced and bounced. His spoon fell on the floor with a clang. The egg on his plate rolled and wobbled. "Elliot," said Dad. "Your bouncing makes the spoon fall. Can you wait another way?" Elliot wondered what to do. He put his hands flat on the table. He took a big slow breath. He counted the peas on his plate. One, two, three. He still felt excited inside, but the spoon stayed quiet.

Then the doorbell rang. Ding dong. Elliot smiled a big smile. He kept his hands on the table. "Kamila is here!" he said. Kamila came in and sat down. "This is my first time at your house," she said. Dad put warm eggs on her plate. Elliot showed her his peas. "I counted them," he said. Kamila laughed and counted hers too. One, two, three. Then they ate together, nice and calm, side by side.

Michael ran to the playground. The slide was warm from the sun. It felt slippery under his hands. Lucca was already there.

"Look," said Lucca. He pointed at a sign by the slide steps. "That sign has a number on it."

Michael looked. The sign had a big 5 on it. "What does it say?" he asked.

"It says five," said Lucca. "The coach told me. Five means five, like this." Lucca held up his fingers. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

Michael held up his own hand. He counted too. "One, two, three, four, five." His fingers matched the sign. The big 5 and his five fingers were the same. He laughed. A sign could count!

Then Marcus came with a water bottle. The slide steps were wet and slippery. Marcus sat down and waited. The sun dried the steps, bit by bit.

"Let's count till it's dry," said Michael.

They counted together. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Marcus touched the steps. "All dry!" he said.

"Watch me," said Michael. He climbed the steps. He slid down fast, whoosh, all the way. "Your turn, Lucca!"

Lydia sat on the big rug in the living room. The soccer game was on TV. Rayne and Philippe sat beside her. Her dad sat on the couch.

The red team ran and ran. Lydia said, "They run so much! They will win!" Philippe clapped. "Go, red team!"

Then the whistle blew. The game was over. Lydia looked at the screen. The red team had two points. The blue team had three points.

"The blue team wins," said her dad. Lydia frowned. "But the red team ran more!" Her dad pointed at the screen. "The team with more points wins."

Lydia looked again. Three was more than two. "Oh! The blue team has more points," she said. Rayne said, "The same thing happened in our game at school!"

Lydia picked up her toy horse. She made it gallop around the rug. "My horse ran the most," she said. "But now I like points better. Points win the game!"

Philippe laughed and clapped. Lydia held the horse up high like a trophy.

Ivy ran to the playground with her dad. She wanted to splash in the little pool. Ms. Munro was filling it with the hose. "Can I jump in now?" Ivy asked. "Not yet," said Ms. Munro. "The water is hot from the sun hose. I have to check it first." She put her hand in the water. "Ooh, still too hot," she said. She turned the tap to add cold water.

Ivy watched the water swirl. How did cold water change hot water? She waited and counted to ten. Then Noa came over with a map he had drawn of the playground. "The pool is here," he said, pointing. "I made the swing here too." Ivy looked at the little drawing. "You didn't miss anything," she said.

Ms. Munro put her hand in the water again. "Now it is warm, not hot," she said. "You can get in." Ivy touched the water with one finger. It felt nice, like her bath at home. Her dad always checked that water too. Ivy stepped in and stomped her feet. Cool splashes flew up onto Noa's map. "Hey!" laughed Noa. "Now my map is wet!" Ivy laughed too and splashed him again.

Xavier went to the store with Dad. He held Dad's hand in the big room full of shelves. He wanted a book about trucks.

Xavier found a small red book. He opened the front cover first. Then he turned the pages one by one. Dad read the words out loud. "The truck goes up the hill," Dad said. Xavier looked at the little black marks on the page. Dad pointed at them as he read.

One page had only a picture of the moon. No black marks at all. "Read this one, Dad," said Xavier. Dad shook his head. "There are no words here," he said. "Nothing is written to read." Xavier touched the smooth page. It felt cool and empty.

So Dad just made up his own sound. "Vroom, vroom," said Xavier. They turned to the back cover and hugged the book tight. "Let's send it home with us," said Dad.

Layla and her dad went to the pharmacy. The shelves were tidy and bright. "We need a new toothbrush," Dad said. "You see the dentist today."

Layla picked a small blue toothbrush. The cashier put it in a bag. Layla held the bag all the way to the dentist.

The dentist's room had a big window. Layla sat in the chair. A bright light shone down above her. Layla squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright!

"Here," the dentist said. She gave Layla tiny sunglasses. Layla put them on. Now she could open her eyes. The light did not hurt.

"Say ahh," said the dentist. Layla opened her mouth wide. The light above the chair helped the dentist see inside. "Nice teeth," the dentist said.

Layla looked at herself in a little mirror. A girl in sunglasses, at the dentist. She laughed. "I look funny," she said.

On the way home, Layla stirred her shoe in a puddle and smiled. "Can I wear the sunglasses again tomorrow?" she asked Dad. Dad laughed and held her hand.

Maeve was going on a big trip. She sat in the car with Mom and Dad. The drive was long. Maeve drank all her juice. Soon her tummy felt funny. "I need the bathroom," she said. "Can I wait?" The road went on and on. "I can't wait," said Maeve. Her voice sounded small.

Dad said, "Don't worry. We can stop." Then Maeve saw a big sign. Dad turned the car in. There was a place to park and a bathroom. "This is a rest stop," Mom said. "On a long drive, we can stop here." Maeve ran to the bathroom with Mom. After that, she stretched her arms up high. She felt much better. "Remember my joke?" said Dad. "Why did the car stop? It needed a rest!" Maeve laughed and laughed.

Soon they drove to the ferry. The ferry was big and blue. A grown-up helped them park inside it. Then Maeve stood with Mom at the rail. The water was smooth and shiny. "We made it," said Maeve. She waved at the seagulls. "Look, they wave back!"

Camille went to the store with her dad. She wanted the brown cereal box. The box had a red truck on it. But there were two boxes with trucks. One said honey oats. One said dog food. Hmm. Which one was her cereal? "The words tell us," said Dad. Camille pointed to the words. Dad read them out loud. "Honey oats. This one!" Camille smiled. Words could tell her things.

Then Camille made a list. She wanted apples too. She wrote her letters all squished together. APPLESALLINAROW. The cashier looked and looked. "I can't read this," she said kindly. Dad showed Camille the cereal box. "See the spaces? There is a space between one word and the next." Camille looked hard. She wrote her word again. This time she left a gap after each word. APPL ES MILK. The gaps made little resting spots. The cashier read the list. "Apples and milk. Aisle two!" Camille held her list all the way to the apples. "The words helped us," she said. She put the list in her pocket, next to the honey oats.

Everett sat in the playroom with a big box of blocks. He wanted to build a tower with ten blocks. He lined them up on the rug. "One, two, four," he counted. Then he stopped. His tower had only six blocks, but it should have ten.

His friend Caroline came over. She sat down next to him. "Listen," she said. She tapped the blocks one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words went in the same order every time. "Three comes before four," she said. Everett tried it himself. He tapped each block. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten blocks, all lined up!

Mr. Tang, from next door, peeked in. "A ten-block tower," he said. "Well done." Then a toy chicken on the shelf went beep, beep. It was a surprise noise! Everett laughed. He stacked his ten blocks up high and put the chicken on top, watching over the tower.

Rose ran into her classroom. Today was Sense Day! Mr. Horváth had a big table full of things.

"Close your eyes," said Mr. Horváth. Rose squeezed her eyes shut. Something rang, loud and bright. Rose jumped. "I hear a bell!" she said. "My ears heard it!"

Lou took the next turn. He hid a crunchy snack behind his back. He bit it. Crunch, crunch. Rose heard the crunch with her ears. "You are eating something!" she said. Lou laughed and laughed.

Then Rose got a turn. She put a soft flower near Zander. She sniffed it. "You smell a flower!" said Zander. "Your nose found it!" Rose clapped. Nose for smelling, ears for hearing! She looked at her hands. Hands for touching the itchy wool on the table. Eyes for seeing. "I want to tell Grandpa all five!" she said.

At home, Grandpa sat on the step. Rose touched his scratchy sweater. She looked at his hat. She sniffed his apple. She licked her cookie. Then she cupped her hands behind her ears.

"Close your eyes, Grandpa," said Rose. "What do you hear?"

"A bird!" said Grandpa.

"We hear with our ears!" said Rose.

Max wanted to paint a house in art class. But his paper looked wrong. The house had no door.

Ms. Nakamura said, "Look around the room. Doors are everywhere." Max looked. There was the big classroom door. He had an idea!

"Can I count it?" he asked. Ms. Nakamura smiled and nodded. Max touched the top corner. "One, two, three, four," he said. The door had four corners.

Katerina came over. She touched the sides. "One, two, three, four," she said. The door had four sides too.

"That is a rectangle," said Ms. Nakamura. Max painted a rectangle door on his house. He painted it red, like a barn door.

Ajooni painted a rectangle window. Max added a circle sun and a triangle roof. His house looked big and strong, almost too heavy to lift.

At snack time, Max found his crackers. He turned one in his hand. It had four sides and four square corners, just like the door. He took a bite. It did not taste like a door at all. It tasted like a square.

"Ms. Nakamura!" he called, holding up his cracker. "Look, my cracker is a rectangle too!"

Scarlett wanted to fill a cup for the tea party. Jacob sat at the small table, waiting. The playroom had a big water jug and a little blue cup.

Scarlett tipped the jug fast. Water rushed out. It went over the top. It made a small pond on the table.

"That cup was full," said Jacob. "Now it is too full."

Scarlett looked at the other cup. It had nothing in it. "That one is empty," she said. She held it up to show him.

She got a towel and wiped the pond away. Slow, gentle wipes. Then she tried again. This time she poured slow. She stopped when the water came to the top.

"Full," said Jacob, and he tapped the cup.

Ms. Cardinal came over. She sent them to get cookies from the shelf. Scarlett carried the full cup slow, slow, slow.

"Not one drop spilled," said Jacob.

Matteo saw the tablet on the table. It was big and shiny. He wanted to draw on it.

He did not touch it yet. He walked to Mr. Tse. "Can I use the tablet, please?" he asked. "Yes, good asking," said Mr. Tse. "Children ask a grown-up before using a tablet."

Mr. Tse showed Matteo the round button. "Push it," he said. Matteo pushed the button. The screen lit up. The button made it work! Matteo clapped his hands.

He opened the drawing app. He drew a red cat and a yellow sun. Then it was time for snacks. Matteo pushed the button again. The screen went dark. He set the tablet down, nice and flat.

"That was good putting away," said Nadia. She hung her coat on her hook. "You did it all by yourself." Matteo smiled big. "I asked first," he said. "Then I pushed the button. Then the screen woke up." Nadia giggled. "You are not a naughty cat like your drawing," she said. "You are a good boy." Matteo laughed and went to get his snack.

Charlie was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Charlie wanted to play in the snow.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. Charlie tried to zip it up. The zipper did not move. She tried again. Still no zip. Charlie felt like crying a little.

"You can get it," said Grandma. "Try it again." Charlie put the zipper in the little slot. She pulled it up slowly. Zip! It worked! Charlie smiled big.

She put on her striped boots too. Then she and Grandma went outside. Charlie zipped her coat all by herself again at the door. The snow was soft and white.

"I did it, Grandma!" said Charlie. Grandma clapped her hands.

Carter stood in the kitchen with his mom. He wanted to help make a fruit smoothie. He could see red strawberries in a shiny bowl. He could smell something sweet, like bananas. "Can I help?" he asked. "You can put the fruit in," his mom said. Carter touched the strawberries. They felt cold and bumpy.

Then his mom plugged in the blender. "Stand back a little," she said. She pushed the button. The blender made a big loud noise. Carter did not like the loud noise. It hurt his ears. He put his hands over his ears. The loud sound got quieter. Carter blinked his eyes. He could still see the blender spinning. He could still hear it, but now it was soft.

Soon the noise stopped. Carter took his hands off his ears. He heard the spoon clink in the cup. He tasted the smoothie from a little cup his mom gave him. It was sweet and cold. "Yum," said Carter. "Can we make it again tomorrow, after my nap?" "Yes," said his mom. Carter smiled and took one more sip.

Everly wanted her little night light on. It had a thin plug with two flat prongs. She carried it to the bathroom, where her mom was drying her hair.

She saw a small hole in the wall. It was low down, by the sink. It had little slots in it. "I can put the plug in there," she thought. She reached out one finger.

"Stop there," said her mom. "Fingers do not go in outlets. Only plugs go in outlets. And only a grown-up puts them in."

Everly pulled her hand back. Her mom plugged in the night light. One push, and it glowed. "See," said her mom. "The plug goes in. Fingers never do."

Everly counted the slots. One, two, three little holes. She touched only the smooth plastic plug.

Then she found her paints. She painted a sign. It said "NO" with a big red hand on it. Her mom taped the sign next to the outlet.

"Now everyone knows," said Everly. She held her mom's hand and carried her glowing night light down the hall.

Samuel was in the kitchen with his dad. The window was open. The wind came in fast. Little bits of dust flew around. Samuel wanted to help sweep. He got his small broom. He swept and swept. Dust flew up into the air. Samuel blinked his eyes. "Dad, my eyes blink a lot!" said Samuel. Dad looked at him. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes," said Dad. Samuel stood very still. More dust came near his face. He blinked. The dust did not go in. His eyelashes stopped it. Samuel smiled. He touched his eyelashes with one finger. They felt soft and tiny.

Then Samuel had an idea. He got his crayons. He wanted to write about his eyes. He drew two big eyes on the paper. He drew lots of little lines on them. "Look, Dad, these are the lashes," said Samuel. Dad said, "That is a great picture." Samuel looked at the snowy yard out the window. He listened to the wind. He smelled the soup cooking on the stove. Dad stirred the hot pot. Samuel stayed back, safe. Soon the soup was ready. Samuel took a little taste. "Mmm, I taste carrots!" he said. The kitchen felt warm on his hands. Samuel blinked one more time. "Good job, little lashes," he said, and he held up his picture for Dad to see.

Olivier went to the store with his dad. It was windy outside. The door went bump as it shut.

Olivier wanted a toy car. He looked at the toy shelf. Cars and cars and cars. Then he saw something yellow. It was a banana!

"That is the odd one out," said Dua. She was there with her mom. "A banana does not belong with the toy cars."

Olivier picked up the banana. He put it in the fruit bin with the apples. Now the banana was with foods, not toys. He clapped his hands.

Mr. Nolan, the store man, smiled. "Thank you, Olivier," he said. "Now pick your car."

Olivier chose a red car. "Vroom," he said, and rolled it down his arm.

Madelyn sat on Grandma's soft rug. The big game was on TV. Grandpa was in his big chair. Jasper and Emily sat beside her. There were popcorn bowls on the floor. The popcorn smelled warm and buttery.

The red team ran fast. The blue team ran faster. Madelyn clapped her hands. "Go, red team, go!" she shouted. Her nose tingled from the salty popcorn. Everyone cheered loud. Then everyone went very quiet. The game was over. The score showed ten and ten.

"Who won?" asked Madelyn. Grandpa smiled. "Nobody won. Both teams have the same score. It is called a tie."

Madelyn thought about that. "A tie?" she said. "Like tying my shoes?" Emily giggled. Jasper stood up. "Then we can all be happy," he said. "Nobody lost either!"

Grandma came in with warm cookies. Madelyn took one and smiled. "I like ties," she said. Grandpa laughed and raised his cup. "Here's to the tie!"

Louis ran to the park with his mom. He wanted to build a big pile of leaves. "I will make it big," he said. Inayah was there too. She had a small purple bag.

Louis found a big rock. He pushed it. The rock did not move. He pushed again. It still did not move. "It is too heavy," said Louis. Inayah pushed too. Still no. It stayed right there.

Then Louis found a feather pillow by the blanket. He picked it up. Up it went, so easy! "This is light," he said. "The rock is heavy, and the pillow is light," said Inayah. "Heavy and light are opposites."

Louis put the pillow on the grass. He put light leaves on top. The pile grew and grew. He jumped in. The leaves flew up. "Soft fall," said Louis. His mom clapped. "Time for a cold drink," she said. Louis smiled and gave Inayah the first cup.

Isaac stood in the garage. It was cold out there. He wanted to put on his coat all by himself.

He pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then he could not find the other sleeve. He turned around and around. The coat swung behind him like a cape. "It hides from me," he said.

His friend Bruce ran in. Bruce was on Isaac's team for the walk to the park. "I know a trick," said Bruce. "Lay the coat on the floor. Put your arms in the sleeves. Then flip it over your head."

Isaac laid the coat down. The floor was dusty and cool. He put his arms in both sleeves. He flipped it over his head. The coat landed on him, warm and snug. "It worked!" said Isaac.

Isaac found the tiny zipper pull. He pushed it up, up, up. Click, it stopped at the top. "Now we can hurry to the park," said Bruce.

Isaac puffed out his chest and zipped his coat again. "Flip and zip," he said. "Flip and zip."

Paisley stood by her bedroom mirror. She had lost her red sock. That made her feel sad. Her mouth turned down at the corners. She saw a sad face in the mirror.

Then Paisley had an idea. She made a big smile. "Happy face," she said. The mirror showed a happy face too. The smile was big and bright. She clapped her hands. Making the happy face made her feel a little happy inside.

Paisley wanted to show someone. She called her friend Rayan to come play. Rayan came and saw the mirror too. He made an angry face, with a frown and scrunched brows. "That is my angry face," he said. Then he laughed and made a happy face. They both smiled at the mirror together.

Paisley looked out the window. She saw the big tree in the yard. The wind made the tree leaves dance. "Look, the tree is dancing," she said. Rayan peeked out too. Paisley ran to the bed. Under it, she found her red sock. She jumped up and down. Her smile was so big it filled the whole mirror. "I will do a happy dance," she said. And she did.

Hannah went to the music room at the community center. Mr. Wright had a drum there. He also had a big paper with dots and lines on it.

"What are the dots?" Hannah asked.

"Those are notes," said Mr. Wright. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Hannah tapped a note. She made a boom on the drum. She tapped a short note and made a quick boom. She tapped a big dot and made a long, loud boom. One dot made one sound. She tapped two dots fast. Boom, boom!

Colter came in. "Play with me," said Hannah. He tapped the notes. She played his sounds. He tapped high, she played high. He tapped low, she played low.

Mr. Wright smiled. "You two can play at the party on Friday."

"I know a song now," said Hannah. She tapped one note and waited. Colter hit the drum. Boom. Hannah laughed and clapped her hands.

Joshua ran into the doctor's office. He saw a big fish tank. "Look, Mom, a blue fish!" he said. A sign on the wall said "Shots Today." Joshua held his mom's hand tight. The nurse called his name.

"Time for your shot," the nurse said. Joshua sat very still. The nurse touched his arm. Then, pop! The shot was done. "That was fast!" said Joshua. The nurse gave him a crunchy cracker. Joshua munched it all up.

In the car, Joshua bumped his arm on his seat. "Ow!" he said. "My arm hurts." Mom looked at him. "The spot where you got your shot can feel sore for a little while," she said. Joshua rubbed the spot gently. Then he squeezed his toy dinosaur. "You can be sore too," he told the dinosaur. "It will feel better soon."

Lydia was drawing at the table. She had glue on her fingers. The glue was sticky and cold to touch. Then she stopped. She smelled something sweet. She sniffed again. "Cookies," she said. "I smell cookies." But she could not see any cookies. Her mom was in the kitchen. Lydia did not know what was baking.

Lydia followed her nose down the hall. Sniff, sniff, step. Sniff, sniff, step. The smell got stronger. She came to the kitchen door. The oven was hot, so her mom stood by it. "Mom, where are the cookies?" Lydia asked. "I can't see them yet," her mom said. "Your nose knows first. A nose can smell cookies before you can see them." Lydia sniffed once more. The kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

"Can I smell with my ears?" Lydia asked. Her mom laughed. "No, you smell with your nose." Lydia pointed at her eyes. "These are for seeing." She touched her ears. "These are for hearing." She touched her tongue. "This is for tasting." She patted her arm. "And my skin is for touch." "Very good," her mom said. Soon the timer rang. The cookies came out, hot and gold. Lydia waited while they cooled.

At last her mom gave her one warm cookie. Lydia took a big bite. "Mmm," she said. "My nose found them first."

Avery sat at the little red table. Mr. Rao put down two bowls of blocks. "Which bowl has more?" he asked. Avery looked and looked. She could not tell. The bowls looked almost the same.

Avery picked up a block from the first bowl. "One, two, three, four," she said, touching each block. Then she smiled big. "Four!" The friendly teacher nodded. She counted the second bowl the same way. "One, two, three." Three blocks. Four was more than three. She pointed at the first bowl. "This one has more!"

Adriel clapped next to her. Ayman counted his blocks too. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Five!" Avery counted a rainbow picture on the wall, one color at a time. Then she stacked her four blocks up high. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Four! Four blocks!"

Michael woke up early. "Is it a party day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is your birthday!"

At the park, Malika and Ricardo ran to him. Balloons bobbed by the swings. "Happy birthday, Michael!" they shouted.

But Michael felt puzzled. "Why is everyone making a fuss today?" he asked. "It is not a big day for you."

Grandma sat down on the bench. She opened her bag. She pulled out a small photo. "Look at this," she said. "This is you, on the day you were born."

Michael looked closely. The photo showed a tiny baby. "That baby is me?" he asked. He touched the little face in the picture.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You were born on this day, three years ago. A birthday celebrates the day a person was born."

"So my birthday is my born day!" said Michael. He jumped up. "Malika! Ricardo! This is the day I was born!"

They clapped and cheered. Dad lit the candles, and everyone sang. Michael blew them out with one big puff. The smoke curled up into the sky like a little grey ribbon.

Henry ran to the art table. Today was shape day! Ms. Cheung put out paper and glue. Henry wanted to make a picture of his house.

Kiera was there too. She held up a paper shape. "This one is a triangle," she said. Henry looked at it. It had three sides. He touched each corner with his finger. One, two, three corners!

Henry wanted a triangle for his roof. He looked in the paper box. No triangles left! He wanted to rip a piece of paper, but that would not make it even. Then he saw a square. He folded it corner to corner. He opened it up. Two triangles! The square had made them.

"Look, Kiera, look!" said Henry. He glued one triangle on top of his square house. The roof was pointy and red. He drew a round circle sun above it. Then he drew his bike next to the house, with two big circle wheels.

Kiera held up her sandwich at snack time. It was cut into triangles. "One, two, three corners," she counted. Henry counted his too. Three sides, three corners, just like his roof! He took a big bite and smiled.

Athena did not want to sleep. "I am not sleepy!" she said. Her dad smiled. "First we wash up," he said. He turned on the warm water. Athena held her hands under it. Then she rubbed the soap. Bubble after bubble grew on her hands! "Look, Dad! Bubbles!" She rubbed more soap. Now her hands were white and bubbly. She made a bubble beard on her chin. "I am a bubbly bear!" she said. Dad laughed. "That is a good joke," he said. He helped her rinse the bubbles off. Her hands were clean and warm. Back in the bedroom, Athena put on her pajamas all by herself. She waved to the moon in the window. Then she climbed into bed. Her dad tucked her in. "Bubble bear needs sleep," he said. Athena giggled and closed her eyes.

Lincoln wanted to help Mom with the laundry. The basket was full and warm. "Let's sort it," said Mom. Lincoln pulled out a shirt. "One shirt!" he said. He pulled out a sock. "Two socks!" Then a hat. "Three hats!"

Mom sang a little song as she folded. Lincoln sent each shirt to the shirt pile. He sent each sock to the sock pile. He sent the hat to the hat pile. "Shirts, socks and hats," he sang back. "They all go in the same big pile!"

Then Lincoln found something silly. A sock was hiding in his toy box! It sat right on top of his teddy bear. "You are not a toy," Lincoln told the sock. He laughed a wild, giggly laugh. "You are clothes! Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes!" He sent the sock back to the sock pile.

Mom clapped. "Good sorting," she said. Lincoln held up the hat. "This is clothes too!" He put it on his head. The hat slid down over his eyes. "I can't see!" he cried, still laughing. Mom lifted the hat up. "There you are," she said. "My silly clothes boy."

Norah was in the backyard. Her new baby brother was coming home today. She wanted to hold him so much. "Babies are so small," she said. "I might drop him."

Her dad sat on the big chair by the sand pit. "Come sit with me," he said. "A big sister can hold the baby while sitting down. I will help you."

Norah sat down on her dad's lap. Dad put a pillow on her legs. Then he laid the baby on the pillow. Norah held her arms just so. The baby was awake. He looked up at her. Norah smiled and smiled.

The baby grabbed her finger. Dad laughed. "He likes you," he said.

After, Norah drove her toy truck in the sand. The baby slept nearby in his little seat. Norah patted his blanket, soft and slow. "I can hold you every day," she whispered. "I sit, and Dad helps."

Henry ran to the park. The sun felt hot on his face. He drank from the fountain. The water was cold. His friend Flynn was there. Flynn had a game. "I say a word," said Flynn. "You shout the opposite." Flynn said, "Big." Henry looked around. He saw a big dog. He saw a small dog. "Small!" Henry shouted. Flynn laughed. "Yes! Those words are opposites. They mean things as different as they can be." They played more. Flynn said, "Fast." Henry watched a fast bird fly by. Then he saw a slow snail on a leaf. "Slow!" he shouted. Mr. Brennan was pushing a girl on the swing. "Good one," he said. The swing went high, then low. "High," said Flynn. "Low!" said Henry. They ran to the sandbox. Henry dug a deep hole. Flynn dug a shallow one. Both holes looked the same size at the end. "Deep," said Flynn. Henry jumped. "Shallow!" A butterfly landed on Henry's shoe. It sat still. Then it flew away, quick as a spring. "That butterfly played too," said Henry. He clapped his hands.

Eleanor went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish, birds, and one small brown puppy. "Can we take him home?" she asked. Her dad said yes. They bought a bowl, food, and a soft bed made of wood chips.

At home, Eleanor wanted to play. She held out a ball. But the puppy was eating his food. Her dad said, "When he eats, we let him be." So Eleanor sat on the floor. She waited and waited. Would the bowl be empty soon?

At last the puppy looked up. The bowl was empty! Eleanor rolled the ball. The puppy ran after it. Then he got sleepy. He curled up on his little bed. Eleanor whispered, "Night night, puppy." She put her hands in her lap and watched him dream.

Felix ran to the fence at school. "Birds!" he shouted. Ten little birds sat in a row.

"Let's count them," said Zaya. Felix counted fast. "One, two, three, um..." A bird hopped. Felix lost count. He scratched his arm and frowned.

"Try again," said Ms. Moose. "Put up one finger for each bird."

Felix held up a finger. "One bird." Another finger. "Two birds." He kept going. Ten fingers, ten birds! The birds flew off the deep end of the fence. His fingers stayed up.

"Ten birds!" said Zaya. "Now look at the slide." Three children sat on the slide.

"Which group has more?" asked Ms. Moose. Felix looked at his ten fingers. He looked at the slide. Three was not ten.

"The birds!" he said. "More birds!"

"Ten fingers, ten birds," said Zaya.

Felix waved his fingers high. "Fingers help me count!"

Arya stood by the big train station door. She held her mama's hand. "Grandpa is coming today," said Arya. "For a whole week."

The train came in. It was long and black. Grandpa stepped off with a small bag. He hugged Arya tight. "I will stay with you," he said. "I sleep here for seven nights."

At home, Arya looked at the guest room. The bed had no pillow. The bed had no blanket. Grandpa could not sleep yet. So Arya got to work. She picked a soft pillow. She carried her favorite blanket, the blue one. She put them on the bed. Then she helped mama clean the little table by the bed.

That night, Grandpa lay down. The pillow was soft. The blanket was warm. The blanket was warm. Grandpa smiled and closed his eyes. In the morning he said, "That was the best sleep, Arya."

Arya patted the pillow. "Soft pillow, warm blanket," she said.

Louis was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa was baking a cake. Louis got to pour the sugar into the bowl. It made a nice white hill.

Then Louis saw a box on the floor. A little cat was inside the box! But the cat would not come out. Louis pulled a string. The cat did not move. Louis tickled the cat's tail with the string. Still nothing.

Then Louis saw marks on the side of the box. "Grandpa, what are these?" he asked. Grandpa said, "Those are words. Let's read them." Grandpa put Louis's finger on the page. "We start here, at the left," he said. They read from the left side to the right side. The words said, "Wet paint."

The cat's fur was wet! Louis got a towel and dried the cat. The cat purred and jumped out at last. "Silly cat," said Louis. "You just wanted to be dry."

Kinsley stood in the kitchen. Her mom was cutting strawberries. Kinsley saw the red berries. She heard the knife go chop, chop. She smelled something sweet.

"Can I have one?" Kinsley asked.

"Yes, here you go," Mom said.

Kinsley touched the strawberry. It felt bumpy with little seeds. She took a bite. It tasted sweet and juicy.

Then Fletcher came in. He was her friend from class. He pinched his nose shut and took a bite. "It tastes like nothing," he said. "So plain!"

Kinsley laughed. She shut her nose too. She took another bite. The strawberry tasted less strong. It was almost like water. She let go of her nose. The sweet taste came back.

"My nose helps me taste!" she said.

The baby sat in his high chair. He was too lazy to fuss. Mom gave him mashed banana. He smiled and clapped.

Kinsley gave Fletcher one more berry. They ate them with their noses open. The kitchen smelled sweet and happy.

"Best strawberries ever," said Fletcher, licking his lips.

Jaxson woke up on a sunny morning. He ran to the playroom. Valerie was already there. She had a little pot and a wooden spoon.

"I made soup," said Valerie. "It is pinecone soup." The pinecones clicked in the pot. They smelled like the short walk through the woods.

Jaxson was hungry. He tipped the spoon into his mouth. A pinecone bumped his lip. It was hard and bumpy. "Yuck," he said. He spit it back out.

"Pretend food is for pretending to eat," said Valerie. She lifted the spoon near her mouth. She made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! Mmm, so good!"

Jaxson laughed. He tried it too. He slurped the air with his spoon. "Slurp! Yummy soup!" The pinecones stayed in the pot.

"Can I have more?" asked Jaxson.

"Yes," said Valerie. "You can have ten bowls."

Then Mr. Johansson peeked in the door. "May I taste the soup?" he asked. He sat down on the small rug. He slurped his bowl of air too.

Jaxson clapped. His soup was warm like the sun, and not one pinecone went in his tummy.

Dylan ran to the library with his dad. The carpet was soft under his feet. It smelled like old books and warm air. Outside the big window, the sky was gray.

Dylan wanted the dinosaur puzzle on the shelf. Max from school was there too. Max reached for the same box. Then Max tripped on the rug. The puzzle box fell. Max sat on the floor. His face looked sad and scared. He rubbed his knee.

Dylan felt worried inside. He walked over. "Are you okay?" he asked. Max looked up. His face began to smile. "My knee hurts a bit," Max said. "But I am okay now." Mr. Nolan brought a small chair. "Sit here and rest," he said. Max sat down. Dylan sat next to him. They opened the box together. Max laughed. "You can have the first piece," he said. Dylan grinned and picked a long green piece.

Hannah went to the library today. Yesterday she had no story. Today she wanted one very much. She found a book with a feather on the cover. "Storytime is soon," said Ms. Campbell-Brown.

Hannah did not know the word soon. She sat down to wait. She waited. It felt long. She waited some more. Eden came and sat by her. Mikaela came too. One friend, two friends.

"Soon means in a little while," said Eden.

Hannah counted the chairs. One, two, three, four. Then the bell rang. Storytime began! Hannah chose the feather book. Ms. Campbell-Brown read it out loud.

"Now it is storytime," said Hannah. The room was noisy with happy voices. Tomorrow she would come back and wait again.

Lydia was at Sebastien's house. She wanted to draw on his tablet. The tablet screen was dark. She tapped it, but nothing happened.

Sebastien's dad was busy making snacks. "Can I plug it in?" Lydia asked, holding the charger. "No, that is a job for me," he said. "A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall." Lydia gave him the charger. She watched him push the plug into the wall. The little light on the tablet turned green.

Then Lydia pressed the round button. The screen lit up. She had made that happen. "I did it!" she said. Sebastien showed her the drawing app. It had a little paintbrush picture on it. Lydia tapped the paintbrush. A white page opened. She drew a big red cat. She drew blue rain. Then she blew on her fingers, like she was blowing out a birthday candle, because tapping so much made them tired.

"Time for a snack," said Sebastien's dad. Lydia knew what to do. She pressed the button, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet on the shelf, right where it belonged.

"Thank you, Lydia," said Sebastien's dad. He gave her a warm kiss on the head. Lydia smiled and picked up her snack. "Cat!" she said, pointing at her red cat picture on the wall where Sebastien's dad had pinned the printed page.

Joshua sat on Grandma's wooden step. He had a small bag of letters. He tipped them out. He wanted to find his favorite letter.

Grandma sat beside him. "Can you find S?" she asked. Joshua looked. The S looked like a wiggly snake. He held it up. "S!" he said.

"Now we hunt," said Grandma. "S makes a hissing sound. Sss. Sun, sock and sand all start with S." Joshua looked around the yard. What else could hiss? He looked down at his feet. His sock had a hole in it. He touched his toes through the hole. "Sss, sock!" he said. Grandma laughed.

Joshua walked to the sand pile. He scooped some in his hands. "Sss, sand!" The warm sand ran between his fingers. Then he pointed up high. The sun was bright. He shut his eyes tight. "Sss, sun!" he said.

Grandma held up the S one more time. Joshua took it and laid it in the sand. He put his sock toes next to it. The letter sat in the sun. "They all go together," said Joshua. Grandma clapped. Joshua picked up another letter. Hmm, what sound would this one make?

Jackson was at Grandma's house. Snow was falling outside the window. Inside, it smelled like warm cookies.

"Cookies soon," said Grandma. Jackson, Miraal, and Brantley made a line by the kitchen door. Jackson wanted to be first. He ran ahead and pushed in front of Miraal. Miraal frowned. Brantley said, "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn."

Jackson looked at his spot at the back. His tummy felt tight. He walked back and stood behind Miraal. He waited. He watched the snow. Soon Miraal got her cookie. Then Brantley got his cookie. Then it was Jackson's turn.

"Here you go," said Grandma, smiling. Jackson took the cookie with both hands. It was sweet and warm. His friends sat with him at the little table. They shared the last cookie, breaking it into three parts, one for each.

After the cookies, Jackson felt sleepy. Grandma tucked a blanket around him on the sofa. "Rest now," she said. Jackson watched the snow some more. Then he closed his eyes.

At daycare, Austin found a big round tub on the floor. Ms. González had put a baby doll in it. "Time to give the baby a bath," she said.

Austin wanted to pour the water fast. Nova came to help too. She held a small towel. Austin turned to the little sink. Hot water was not for him to touch. Ms. González turned the tap herself.

"Can I put the baby in now?" Austin asked. "Not yet," said Ms. González. "First we check the water." She put her own hand in the tub. "Too warm still," she said. "We wait a bit." Austin waited. He could hear the water drip, drip. He liked to listen to it.

Then Ms. González put her hand in again. "Now it feels just right," she said. Austin held the baby doll. He lowered it in slowly. The water splashed a little. Floralie clapped her hands.

After the bath, Austin wrapped the doll in a soft towel. Then he gave it a bottle and laid it down for a nap. He patted its back. "Sleep now, baby," he whispered.

Nova put a toy rabbit beside the doll. "The rabbit wants to sleep too," she said. Austin smiled and turned off the play light. "Shh," he said.

Julia sat in the playroom with her blocks. She wanted to build a tower with ten blocks. She counted out loud. "One, two, three." Colton came to help. "Four, five, six," he said. Millie ran over too. "Seven, eight, nine," she said. The tower was almost done. But it needed one more block. Julia put it on top. "Ten!" they all shouted.

Then Julia wanted to write the number ten. She looked at the big clock on the wall. The clock had numbers on it. She saw nine on the clock. Nine was one number. She wrote nine on her paper. It looked good. Then she tried to write ten. Ten was not on the clock. She wrote a one. Then she stopped. Ten needed more. She thought hard.

Julia looked at the clock again. She was careful with her pencil. She wrote a one first. Then she wrote a zero right after it. "Ten is written with two digits," said Millie. "A one and then a zero." Julia looked at her paper. There it was. Ten!

"Let's drive the toy truck past our tower," said Colton. They pushed the little truck on the floor. It went past the tower. All ten blocks stood tall. Julia clapped her hands. "Ten blocks, one truck, zero crashes," she said.

Benjamin sat at the big table. He wanted to draw a picture of a lake. He drew a yellow sun at the top. He drew fish and a little boat with a triangle sail. He drew a square house with a rectangle door.

Then he tried to draw wheels for his boat on a truck. His circles came out wobbly. They looked like eggs. He tried again. Wobble, wobble.

"I can't make circles," he said. His dad came over. Dad held up a round cup. "Try this," he said.

Benjamin put the cup down on the paper. He held it still. He drew all around the bottom of the cup. He lifted the cup up. There it was. A big round circle!

"It worked!" Benjamin did a loud happy yell. "A circle, a circle!"

He traced the cup again and again. Now his truck had four round wheels. He tapped the paper and smiled. "Off to the lake," he said.

Hunter sat on his bed. His red boot was missing. He looked under the bed. One sock. Two old crayons. No boot.

Hunter felt sad. His face went down. His mom came in. "Hunter, you look sad," she said. Hunter did not talk. He just sat. His mom did not know what to do. She stood by the door.

Then Hunter took a big breath. "I feel sad," he said. "My red boot is lost." His mom smiled. Now she knew how to help. They looked together. They looked under the bear. They looked behind the box. They counted the places. One, two, three. In place three, behind the box, the boot sat. It was dry and dusty.

"Yay!" said Hunter. He felt happy now. He put the boot on his foot. He jumped one time, two times. "Stop jumping on the bed," his mom said, laughing. Hunter stopped. He gave her a big hug. "My boot!" he said.

Nicholas went to the store with his dad. He wanted the red balloon on the shelf. "Can we get it?" he asked. Dad looked, but the balloons were all sold out. Nicholas felt very sad. A tear came, and he began to cry. Dad held his hand. "Maybe next time," Dad said softly.

Then Nicholas saw his friend Leonard by the carts. "Hi, Nicholas!" Leonard said. "Look at my tooth. It is loose!" Leonard wiggled it with his finger. Nicholas touched his own tooth. It did not wiggle yet. The two boys laughed and laughed. Nicholas felt excited. They pushed a little cart together, slow and careful.

At the checkout, the cashier gave Nicholas a sticker. It was a shiny star. "For you," she said with a smile. Nicholas felt happy inside. He had been sad about the balloon. But now he felt glad. The sad feeling had gone away. He waved to Leonard at the door. "See you soon!" he called, holding up his star.

Charlie walked home with her dad. In her arms was a box. Inside the box was her first pet, a small guinea pig named Pip.

The street was quiet. A leaf crawled along the sidewalk in the wind. Charlie wanted to carry Pip around and show him everything. She lifted the box lid. Pip peeked out.

"I want to hold him walking," Charlie said. Her dad shook his head. "Sit down first," he said. "Hold him with two hands. Then he cannot fall far." Charlie sat on the front step. She put both hands under Pip, one under his front and one under his back. Pip sat warm and small in her palms.

Then came the small surprise. Ms. Harper from next door opened her door. Cohen was with her, holding a carrot. "For Pip," Cohen said. Charlie stayed sitting and let Pip nibble the carrot. Pip made a happy little sound.

"He likes me," Charlie said. She carried Pip inside the door, still sitting, still slow, both hands around him like a soft warm egg. "Goodnight, Pip," she whispered.

Zoey was at home with her family. It was a big night. Grandma lit the candles on the table, one, two, three. Zoey watched from her chair.

Then the music began. Papa clapped his hands. Mama tapped her feet. The drum went boom, boom, boom. Everyone started to dance. "Dancing is part of our celebration," said Grandma. She held out her hand.

Zoey felt shy at first. She stayed by the door. The music went boom again. Grandma smiled and waited. One, two, three steps, and Zoey took her hand. They spun around together. Zoey's skirt flew out. Her feet went tap, tap, tap.

"Again!" said Zoey. Grandma laughed. "Good dancing, Zoey." They spun and spun, and the candles glowed warm.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. On Monday, Thomas and Grandpa took a train to the market. Thomas stood on the platform. "Can I lean out to see the train?" he asked. "No," said Grandpa. "People stand back from the edge until the train stops." Thomas stepped back behind the yellow line. He waited with Grandpa. The big train came in. It stopped. Then the doors opened.

At the market, Grandpa bought apples from a farm. Thomas sniffed a big green pickle. "Yucky," he said with a laugh. Grandpa laughed too.

"Grandpa, does your leg still hurt?" Thomas asked. "A little," said Grandpa. "But your hand helps." Thomas held Grandpa's hand all the way. Then the market man gave Thomas a tiny apple. It fit inside his whole hand. "A surprise for you," the man said. Thomas smiled and held it up to Grandpa.

Charlie had a red ball. His dad put a hoop on the fence. "You score when the ball goes through the hoop," said Dad. Charlie threw the ball. It hit the fence. It did not go through. "Oh no," said Charlie.

His friend Quentin came to play. Quentin threw the ball too. It went over the hoop. It did not go through. "The ball keeps missing!" said Quentin. Charlie made a mad face. Then he stuck out his tongue at the ball. "Bad ball," he said, and he laughed.

They practiced and practiced. Charlie threw the ball up, up, up. It went through the hoop. It dropped down. "It went in! We scored!" said Charlie. Quentin clapped his hands. "My turn, my turn!" said Quentin. He ran to get the ball.

Maeva was at school. It was drawing time. She wanted the red color. Joelle had the red color.

Maeva hid behind the big paper shelf. She peeked out at Joelle. She did not say anything. Joelle did not look up. Joelle kept drawing her cat.

Mr. Shin walked over. "Say hello," he said to Maeva, softly. Maeva peeked out again. "Hello, Joelle," she said. Joelle looked up and smiled. "Hello, Maeva!"

"Please can I have the red color?" asked Maeva. "Yes, here you go," said Joelle. "Thank you," said Maeva.

Maeva began to draw. Her hand bumped the cup. Dirty water spilled on the table. "Sorry," said Maeva. "It is okay. I will help," said Joelle. They wiped the table together.

Hello, hello, hello. Maeva said it again at play time, to Maxime too. Everyone smiled back. Then Maeva sat down and drew a big red flower. "Hello, flower," she whispered.

Leon went to the farmers' market with his dad. He saw a big white duck by the crates. "Quack," said the duck. Leon laughed. They brought home a thin bag of flour. Leon wanted to make pancakes for his family. Dad said he could help.

Leon opened the bag. He poured the flour very fast. Whoosh! A little white cloud flew up. It landed on Leon's nose. It landed on Dad's nose too. "We look like snowmen," said Dad. Leon sneezed a tiny sneeze.

They poured the flour again. This time Leon poured it slowly. No cloud. No dusty nose. The bowl was clean and full. Later, Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Leon watched from his chair. The pancakes were round and warm. "Leon made these," said Dad. "With flour," said Leon. "Poured nice and slow."

Harper sat in the playroom. She wanted to make a toy car. She found a small box and some tape. Then she cut four squares of cardboard. She taped the square wheels on. "Go, car, go!" she said. She pushed the car on the rug. The car would not roll. It just bumped and stopped.

Her friend Olive came over. "Try circle wheels," Olive said. "Wheels are round like circles." Ms. Côté helped Harper cut four circles. She used the scissors slowly and was gentle with the cardboard. Harper watched from her seat. Then Harper taped the circle wheels on the car.

She pushed the car again. It rolled across the rug! Harper gave a little jump. Olive clapped her hands. The car rolled right to Drew, who was building with triangle blocks. Drew laughed and rolled it back. Harper got down on her nose-to-floor level to watch the wheels turn. "Round wheels," she said. "Round wheels go."

Sebastian was at daycare. It was nap time. He held his little gray elephant. But then the lights went out. The room got dark.

Sebastian could not see his elephant. He looked and looked with his eyes. He saw only dark. "Where did you go?" he whispered. His tummy felt sad.

He listened with his ears. He heard his friend Bodie breathing. He heard Mikael turning on his mat. But no elephant sound.

Mr. Thompson came in. "The lights went out," he said. He reached up. Click. The lamp went on. Now the room was bright.

Sebastian blinked. Then he saw it. His elephant was under the blanket. He reached out his hand and touched the soft gray ear. He picked it up and hugged it tight.

"Hello, elephant," said Sebastian. He sniffed with his nose. The elephant smelled like soap from his bath at home. Sebastian gave it a little kiss on top of its head. It tasted like nothing at all, just soft.

"Found him," Sebastian told Mr. Thompson. "The light helped." Mr. Thompson smiled and sat down slow. He waited while Sebastian got comfy again. Sebastian patted the elephant. He closed his eyes. "Night night, elephant," he said.

Cooper went to the store with his dad. They needed a party gift for Lionel. Cooper wanted to find a toy.

First they walked past the foods. Cooper saw apples and milk and bread. Then they came to the animal section. There were fish in tanks and birds in cages.

A little bird flapped its wings. A small feather floated down. It landed right by Cooper's shoe. He picked it up. It was soft and blue.

Cooper asked, "Where did this come from?" He looked up. The bird shook again. Another feather fell down. "The bird has feathers," Cooper said. "The bird lost one."

Cooper and his dad picked a red toy car. Dad bought it for the party. Cooper held the blue feather all the way home.

At the party, Lionel opened the car. "Vroom!" said Lionel. Cooper showed him the feather. "A bird gave it to me," he said.

Natalie wanted a book about animals. She wanted to read about a big bug and a thin snake. But the book was not at home.

"Come with me," said Mr. Kamau. "I have a little library at my house."

The library had lots of shelves. Natalie looked and looked. Where were the animal books?

Mr. Kamau pointed. "Animal books stick together on this shelf."

There they were! A shelf of cat books. A shelf of dog books. A shelf of bug books, all in a row.

"So people can find them," said Mr. Kamau.

Then Natalie saw more shelves. Toy books sat in one group. Food books sat in another group. Cake books, apple books, egg books. Yum!

She found a thin book all about snakes. She hugged it tight.

"One animal book for me!" said Natalie.

"Bring it back soon," said Mr. Kamau. He waved at the door.

"I will stick it right back on the shelf," said Natalie.

Zoey went to the library with her dad. There was a big table with crayons. Zoey took all the crayons. She held them in her arms.

She drew a big lion with a yellow crayon. Then she heard a small sound. Matteo sat at the other end of the table. He had no crayons at all. His paper was empty.

"Where are the crayons?" Matteo asked.
"I have them all," said Zoey.
"What will I draw?" he asked.
Zoey looked at her pile. She looked at his empty paper. Sharing means letting someone else use something too, she thought, like Mommy says. She walked over and put some crayons by his paper. "Here, you can use these too," she said.

Matteo drew a lazy lion sleeping in the sun. Zoey drew one too. Ms. Whitehead came by with a book. "Two lions," she said with a smile. "Can I bring you more paper?"
"Yes, please," said Zoey. She pushed the crayon box to the middle of the table so both of them could reach it. "You can use them too," she said again.

Arlo had a cold. He sat on the couch with a box of tissues. He blew his nose. Then he put the tissue down beside him. He blew his nose again. Soon there were tissues all over the couch.

His dad came in. "Time to go to the pharmacy," he said. "We need more tissues and some juice." Arlo hoped the juice would be apple. On the way, Arlo held his dad's hand. At the pharmacy, a nice cashier gave him a little sticker.

Back home, Arlo looked at the messy couch. He picked up one tissue. He dropped it in the bin. It fell right in. He picked up another tissue. He dropped it in the bin too. It was like a game. "In you go," said Arlo. Each tissue went in the bin, one by one.

Soon the couch was clean. "Good job," said his dad. Arlo smiled. He held his sticker up high.

Wren was at school. It was game time on the rug.

"Let's play the duck game," said Dante. "We all hop in a line."

Wren hopped. Ryan hopped. Dante hopped.

Then Dante laughed. "New rule! Now I hop and you sit!"

Wren sat down. Ryan sat down too. No one hopped with Dante.

Dante hopped all alone. "Hmm," he said. "That is not fun."

"Come back to our line," said Wren. "Same rule for everyone."

"Okay," said Dante. "We all hop. Same rule."

The line went again. Wren hopped. Ryan hopped. Dante hopped. Everyone hopped together.

Mr. Goldberg clapped from his chair. "What a good long line!"

After the game, it was snack time. Wren had tiny crackers. Dante had an apple with its red skin.

"I give you a cracker," said Wren.

"And I give you apple," said Dante.

Wren smiled and took a big bite.

Josephine sat on the school bus. She had a brown teddy bear. It was soft and warm.

Jules sat down next to her. "Can I hold the bear?" he asked.

Josephine pulled the bear close. "It is mine," she said.

Ms. Silva stood up at the front of the bus. "We will use the timer," she said. "Josephine goes first. When the timer beeps, your turn is over."

Josephine held the bear. She hugged it. She put her sock feet up on the seat. The bear felt cozy.

Beep! The timer went off.

Josephine almost threw the bear. She lifted her arm way up high. Jules covered his head with his hands.

Then Josephine stopped. She brought the bear down slow. She opened her hands. She placed the bear gently in Jules's lap.

"Soft landing!" said Jules. He hugged the bear. "Your turn, Jules," said Josephine. "My turn is over."

Beep! Jules opened his hands too. He placed the bear gently back.

"Soft landing!" said Josephine. She laughed and hugged her brown bear all the way home.

Peyton ran into the art studio. She wore her favorite shirt. It was blue with a little pig on it.

"Time to paint," said Mr. Hughes. "Put on your aprons."

Abygael put on her apron. It was loose and big. Peyton wanted to paint a pig, so she began right away.

The brush dripped. Red paint fell on her blue shirt. Peyton looked down. Her pig was covered in red.

"Oh no," she said. "Will it come out?"

Mr. Hughes brought her an old shirt. "Wear this," he said.

Peyton put it on. It was long and loose. She dipped her brush again. Drip, drip. The paint fell on the old shirt. Her blue shirt stayed clean underneath.

"Look at that," said Abygael.

Peyton painted her pig. More drips fell. None got on her clothes.

Avery sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her mama held her hand. On the wall was a picture of a yellow duck. Avery liked the duck. But her tummy felt jumpy.

"The nurse will come soon," said Mama. Avery did not want a shot. She wanted to go home. She looked at the duck some more. Her legs swung fast under the chair.

The nurse came in with a small tray. Avery hid her face on Mama's shoulder. "I am scared," she said. "Let's try something," said Mama. "Breathe in slow, like you are smelling a flower." Avery sniffed a big, slow breath in. "Now blow out slow, like you are blowing out a candle." Avery blew out, slow and long.

They did it again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. One more time. Avery's shoulders came down. Her tummy felt less jumpy. "I feel better," she said. The nurse said, "Ready?" Avery held still and kept breathing slow. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done.

Avery got a bright bandage with stars on it. On the road home, she practiced her slow breaths again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. "Look, Mama," she said. "I can do it all by myself."

Avery wanted the red book about the little boat. She took it to Mr. Ngo at daycare. "Please read it," she said. Mr. Ngo opened the cover. He turned page one, then page two, then page three. He read, "The boat went out in the wind. The wind was strong."

Ivaan came to listen too. He sat down on the little rug. Avery held the book on her lap. "The wind gave the boat a bite of cold air," Mr. Ngo read. Ivaan laughed. "The wind bites," he said. "Only in the book," said Avery.

That night, Avery's mom read the same red book. Avery held her breath. Mom read, "The boat went out in the wind. The wind was strong." The very same words. Mom read page one, then page two, then page three. She turned to the last page. "The wind gave the boat a bite of cold air," Mom read.

Avery clapped her hands. "Same words," she said. "Mom reads the same words as Mr. Ngo." The next morning, Avery ran to daycare. She found Ivaan and Cataleya. "One boat, two friends, three readers," she said. She opened the red book. She pointed at the marks on the page. "These say the wind words," she said. Then she turned to the very last page. There, under the last words, sat a picture of a small cat asleep in the boat. "A cat!" said Cataleya. Avery smiled. "He was hiding all along."

Sophia sat in the cafe with her mom. She had a big piece of paper and a little red pencil. "I will write my name," she said. Her name was Sophia. S, O, P, H, I, A. Six letters. Sophia picked up the pencil with her fingers. She made a big S. Then the paper slid away. The O came out wiggly. The P slid right off the page. "My paper keeps running," said Sophia. Her mom sat close by and smiled. "Try again," she said. Sophia made one more try. She put her other hand flat on the paper. She held it still. Then she wrote S, O, P, H, I, A. The letters did not wiggle. The paper did not slide at all. "It stays now!" said Sophia. Her mom said, "I can tell. That is your first whole name." Sophia looked at her letters all in a row. She wiggled her toes in her shoe under the table. Then she wrote her name again, one letter at a time, S, O, P, H, I, A, while her hand held the paper still.

Hudson sat in the computer lab. The tablet in front of him was dark. He tapped the screen with one finger. Nothing happened. He tapped it again and again. Still nothing.

Duke sat next to him. "My screen is dark too," Duke said. Hudson tapped harder. The screen stayed dark. He wanted to draw a big yellow duck. But the tablet would not wake up.

Mr. Smith came over. "Press the little button on the side," he said. "A tablet has a button you press to turn it on." Hudson looked at the side. There it was. A small round button. He pushed it with his thumb.

The screen lit up. It was bright and blue. Hudson laughed. One little push, and the dark screen turned bright! "I did it," he said. Duke pressed his button too. His screen lit up too.

Hudson found the drawing app. It had a paint brush on it. He opened it. He drew a big yellow duck. The duck had an orange beak. He drew squishy mud under the duck. "My duck says quack," he said to Duke.

Then it was time to go. Mr. Smith said, "Time to put the tablets away." Hudson pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet on the shelf, all by himself. Mr. Smith gave him a big smile. "See you tomorrow, Hudson," said Mr. Smith.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. She had a big bag with wheels. "What is inside?" asked Gabriella. "My clothes and my things," said Grandma. "Guests who stay pack a bag."

Gabriella pulled the bag down the hall. It went bump, bump, bump. The guest bedroom was tidy. Her bear sat on the bed. "One bed, one bear, one Grandma," said Gabriella.

Grandma opened the bag. Out came a red sweater. Out came a toothbrush. Out came one, two, three socks. "Silly Grandma," laughed Gabriella. "Socks get lost!" Then Grandma pulled out one more thing. It was a small gift, just for Gabriella. "Shut your eyes," said Grandma. Gabriella shut them tight. "Open!" said Grandma. It was a tiny bear of her own.

Evelyn went to the store with her dad. The sky outside looked stormy. Evelyn wanted the big red apple on the shelf. It was too high up.

A boy named Bryson stood by the juice. "Give me juice!" he said. His mom shook her head. Then Bryson said, "Juice, please." His mom smiled and put the juice in the cart.

Evelyn slid her hand along the cool shelf. Then she looked up at the store man. "Apple, please," she said. The store man smiled big. He reached up and put the apple in her hand.

"Thank you," said Evelyn. "You are welcome," said the store man. Outside, the stormy sky began to clear. Evelyn held the apple all the way home. "Apple, please!" she said again, at her own house, just to hear it once more.

Adam sat at the big table. His friend Thalia sat next to him. Up on the wall was a big, bright screen. A soccer game was on. Adam's dad had brought a gray hat for Adam. It was a little gift for game day.

A player ran with the ball. He kicked it hard. The ball flew low. Adam held his breath. "It has to go over the net," Adam said. Thalia shook her head. "No, watch," she said.

The ball went into the net. The net moved and bulged out. The whole restaurant shouted, "Goal!" Adam clapped his hands. "The ball goes in the net," Adam said. Thalia smiled. On the screen, the player ran and jumped. Adam waved his hat in the air.

Brielle went to Hallie's house. Hallie had set up a little shop. It had a table and a big box. A huge stuffed owl sat by the box. "Welcome to my shop," said Hallie. "You be the shopper. I am the shopkeeper."

Brielle picked up a toy fish. It felt smooth and cool. "How much is this fish?" she asked. "One block," said Hallie. Brielle gave her one block. Hallie put the fish in a small bag.

Then Hallie wanted to buy too. "Now you be the shopkeeper," said Brielle. So they swapped. Brielle stood behind the table. Hallie walked around like a shopper. Brielle had to wait while Hallie looked and looked. She sniffed the play cookies. They smelled like nothing, but she pretended they smelled sweet. At last Hallie chose a toy cup.

Then a surprise. A real doorbell rang. Ding dong! It was Ciara. "Can I shop too?" she asked. Brielle handed her a bag. "Welcome," she said. "Take your time."

Ayla went to the mall with her dad. She was going to get her very first haircut. Ayla held her dad's hand tight. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "The hairdresser is kind."

Ayla sat in a big chair that could swing up and down. The chair went up, up, up. The hairdresser picked up a comb. The comb felt a little rough on Ayla's head. The hairdresser combed Ayla's hair. Then she snipped once with the scissors. Comb, snip. Comb, snip. Ayla counted out loud. "One, two, three!" she said.

The comb made her hair neat. Then the scissors cut it. Ayla watched in the mirror. Her hair looked short and pretty. "All done," said the hairdresser. Ayla jumped down and ran to Dad. "My hair is neat!" she said. Dad gave her a big hug. Then they walked home past the beds in the shop window.

Joshua held his mom's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the very first time. Joshua looked at the clock above the door. The big hand moved a little bit. The bus stopped, and two people got off.

Joshua sat very still. His friend Nixon had told him about the dentist. "You get to sit in a big chair," Nixon had said. "It goes up and down." Joshua was not sure he liked chairs that went up and down.

At the dentist's office, the chair did go up. The dentist said, "Open your mouth wide so I can see every tooth." Joshua opened a little bit. Then he closed his mouth to talk.
