"Is it done yet?" he asked. "Sorry, not yet," said the dentist. "Open wide again, like a lion's roar." Joshua opened his mouth as wide as a lion. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see every tooth now," she said. "All clean."

The chair went down. The dentist put a sticker on Joshua's shirt. It was a lion, roaring, with its mouth open wide. Joshua laughed all the way to the bus stop.

Billie sat at the dinner table. Her friend Saira sat next to her. Saira had a little rainbow car. It was red and yellow and blue. Billie wanted to hold it very much.

Billie reached out. She took the rainbow car fast. Saira's face went sad. Her eyes got big. "That is mine," said Saira. Billie looked at Saira's face. Saira did not smile.

Billie gave the car back. She put it in Saira's hand. Then she asked, "Can I have a turn, please?" Saira smiled. "Yes! You can have it after me." Saira pushed it across the table. Billie held it and made it go vroom. Her itchy sweater sleeve bumped her chin, but she did not mind.

"Time to eat," said Dad. Billie gave the car back to Saira. They both ate their noodles. "Your turn tomorrow," said Saira. "Okay," said Billie. Dad gave them each a warm cookie. "One for you and one for you," he said. Billie took a big bite. "Yum," she said.

Elias pulled off his striped socks in the changing room. He put them in his little bag. Then he ran to the pool door.

"Stop right there," said Ms. Jung with a smile. "Pools ask swimmers to take a shower first." She pointed to the shower on the wall.

Elias stood under the shower. The water made a drip, drip sound. It was warm on his tummy. He got all wet, even his hair.

"Now you can go in," said Ms. Jung.

Elias stepped into the pool. His friend Aidan was already there. "You took a shower too?" asked Aidan.

"Yes! Shower first, then pool," said Elias. He held the edge and kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. Ms. Jung clapped.

"Good kicking, Elias," she said. Elias laughed and kicked some more.

Ella sat at the dinner table. She ate her peas one by one. Mama put more carrots on her plate.

"Can I go to Skyla's house now?" Ella asked.

"Not now," said Mama. "It is almost bedtime. You will go tomorrow."

Eella put down her fork. "What is tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow is the day after today," said Mama.

Ella looked out the window. The sky was getting dark. She saw the moon come up. "So I sleep first," she said. "Then it is tomorrow."

"Yes," said Mama. "First sleep, then a new day."

Ella ate her last carrot. She drank her milk. She picked up her silly bunny cup and set it down again.

After her bath, Ella got into bed. She closed her eyes. She waited for tomorrow.

Then it was morning. Sun was on her blanket. "It's today again!" Ella said. "A new today!"

She put on her shoes all by herself. At the door, she saw Skyla waiting on the steps.

"You came!" said Skyla. "The party can start now."

"Now!" said Ella. And she ran up the walk.

text:
Lily was on the swim team. The team met at the big blue pool. Ms. Cho was the coach. Lily wore her pink swimsuit.

One day Lily saw a spider by the pool door. "I want to look at the spider," she said. "Not practice today."

"First we practice," said Ms. Cho. "Practice gets us ready for games. You can look after."

Lily kicked her legs in the water. She splashed and splashed. Her friend Eva-Rose practiced too. So did Khai. Ms. Cho held Lily's tummy. Lily blew bubbles. Then Lily kicked all by herself.

On Saturday the team had a game. Lily had to swim to the rope. She thought, "I can do this." She kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. She reached the rope all by herself!

"You did it!" said Eva-Rose. Khai clapped and clapped.

After the game, Lily ran to the door. The spider was still there. It sat in its web. Lily waved. "I saw what practice did," she said. "It made me a swimmer!"

Myles ran out to the daycare yard. Rosalyn was there by the big puddle. The puddle was dark and wide. Myles loved to splash.

"Watch me go fast," said Myles. He ran fast and jumped. Splash! Water went up. Water went down. His socks were all wet. His shoes made a squish, squish sound.

Myles frowned. "My socks are wet. I want dry socks." Ms. Goldberg came with a towel. She wiped his feet with her hand in the towel. "Wet and dry are opposites," she said. "Off comes the wet. On goes the dry." She gave him small dry socks from his bag. They felt warm and soft.

"Can I splash again?" asked Myles. Ms. Goldberg laughed. "Yes, but first we take off your shoes. Then wet socks can't find you." Myles pulled off his shoes by the step. Rosalyn pulled hers off too.

"Fast socks off!" said Myles. Rosalyn giggled. They splashed slow. They splashed fast. The water flew up like tiny rain. When they went inside, warm dry socks were waiting, one pair for each hand. "Dry socks are the best," said Myles.

Rose went to the big library with her dad. It was dark and quiet inside. "Can I really take a book home?" she asked. "Yes, today you get your own library card," Dad said. Mr. Yilmaz made the card. It had Rose's name on it. Rose picked a book about a red triangle. She sat down and opened it. She found a crayon in her pocket. She wanted to draw a cat on the page. Then she saw small fingerprints on the paper. Other kids had read this book too. Mr. Yilmaz came over. Rose asked, "Do other people read this book?" "Many people share it, so we take care not to tear it or write in it," he said. Rose listened. She put the crayon away. She drew her cat on her own paper instead. Then she held her new card tight and checked out the triangle book all by herself. "See you soon, book," she whispered.

Colton needed to wash his hands. His dad came with him to the bathroom. Colton climbed up on his little stool.

He saw two taps. One had a red dot. One had a blue dot. He pointed at the red one. "I want that one," he said.

Dad turned the blue tap a tiny bit. Cold water came out. "Hot water lives in that one," said Dad. "Only I touch it." Colton put his hands under the cold stream. The water felt like ice from the fridge.

Then Colton saw something. The water hit the white sink. A small rainbow sat inside the splash. "Dad, look!" he said. He wondered where the rainbow came from. Dad smiled. "It is the same rainbow you see outside sometimes."

Colton rubbed the soap on his hands. Bubbles grew big and round. He clapped once. Bubbles flew everywhere.

Then Colton wanted his toy car from the hall. He jumped down and ran to the door. He peeked out. He could not see Dad's feet anymore. He stopped.

"Dad?" he called.

"Come back where I can see you," said Dad.

Colton ran back in. Dad was right there, holding the towel. Colton dried his hands all by himself.

"My turn for a rainbow," said Dad. He turned the water a little more. Colton watched the splash dance.

Willow was at daycare. It was play time. She wanted to feed the class fish. The fish swam in a small tank. Ms. Robinson gave her a little cup of food. Willow tipped the cup in. The fish went up and ate it.

Ila came to look. "A fish is not an animal," said Ila. "It has no legs. A dog has legs. A dog is an animal." Willow looked at the fish. She looked at the dog picture on the wall. The cow picture was there too. She thought and thought.

Then Willow had a plan. She got the picture cards. She put the dog card down. She put the cow card down. She put the fish card down next to them. "Look," said Willow. "Dog, cow, fish. They all go in the animal row." Ila bent down low. She pointed at each card. "Dog, cow, fish," said Ila. "Animals!"

Ms. Robinson smiled. "Snack time," she said. The snack was crackers and cheese. Myah passed out cups. Willow drank her milk. Some milk went on her shirt. "Yucky," said Willow, and she wiped it off with a napkin.

After snack, Willow went back to the fish. She tapped the glass, very soft. The fish went round and round. "Little animal," said Willow. "Swim, swim." Ila stood beside her. They watched the fish together, quiet and still.

Amira sat at the big table in math club. Ms. Perera put down two trays of apples. "Which tray has more?" she asked.

Avi counted the red apples fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" But Amira looked closely. He had counted one apple two times. "Try again," she said. "Point at each apple once." Avi pointed carefully. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples, not seven.

Amira counted the green tray next. She touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She counted it two times, just to be sure. Eight was more than six. "The green apples have more!" she said in a loud, happy voice.

"Good counting," said Ms. Perera. Shanaya giggled. "Avi, your apple was tricky!"

Avi laughed too. "You silly apple," he told it. Then he tapped it once, like a drum.

Nathan ran to the park with his red bag. Inside was a big basket of picture cards. The cards had fallen out all over the grass.

Arnav came to help. "What a mess," said Arnav.

Nathan picked up a card. It showed a black cat. Then he found a card with a dog. He put them side by side.

"These are animals," said Nathan.

He found more animal cards. A duck. A bee. Bees live in hives, and this bee had yellow stripes. All the animals went in one pile.

Arnav held up a card. "A ball," he said. "Where does it go?"

Nathan thought. "Is it an animal?" he asked himself.

"No. It is a toy," said Arnav. They made a second pile for toys. A truck. A teddy bear. A drum.

Then Charlee ran over with an apple card. "This is food," she said. A third pile grew. Bread. Milk. A banana.

The three friends looked at their piles. Animals here. Toys there. Food over there. All tidy.

"Snack time," said Charlee's dad from the bench.

Nathan grinned and put the cards in the bag, one pile at a time.

James was hungry. It was snack time at school. The children sat in a circle on the soft rug. Mr. Leung put a big bowl of crackers in the middle of the room. He put a cloth over the bowl to cover it. "Wait for everyone," said Mr. Leung.

Gurnaaz went first. She took one cracker. Then she gave one cracker to James. James took it and ate it fast. He wanted more, but it was Rudra's turn. Rudra took one cracker. Then it was James's turn. "My turn!" said James. He took one cracker. Then he gave one to Gurnaaz, just like she did.

Gurnaaz looked at James. She waited. She waited some more. James looked down at his hands. He had not said anything. "Thank you," said Rudra to Mr. Leung. "Thank you," said Gurnaaz to Rudra.

James ran back to Gurnaaz. "Thank you for my cracker!" he said. Gurnaaz smiled a big smile. "You said it!" she said. Then something small fell from her pocket. It was a tiny car, shiny and blue. "Look," said Gurnaaz. "You can hold it after snack." James sat down and held the little car. "Thank you," he said again. "Thank you, thank you."

Aria put on her red shirt. She loved her red shirt. Then she ran to the big field with her dad.

The game was about to start. One team wore blue shirts. The other team wore red shirts, just like Aria. A man with a big horn looked at Aria. "Yay, red team!" he said. He gave her a red flag to wave.

But Aria did not want the red team. She wanted the blue team. Lachlan was there, waving a blue flag. "Blue team is my team," he said. "I wear blue so everyone knows."

Aria looked down at her red shirt. That was why the man cheered at her! So she ran to her dad. "Can I wear my blue sweater?" she asked. Her dad pulled it from the bag. Aria put it on over the red shirt. Now she looked all blue.

The man with the horn looked again. He laughed. "Blue team too?" he said. He gave her a blue flag. A dog near the fence gave one happy bark. The crowd got loud, then quiet, then loud again, like a big ocean of voices.

Aria waved her blue flag high. "Go, blue team!" she called.

Gabriel had a little garden in the backyard. He counted his plants out loud. "One lettuce, two carrots, three beans." His friend Usman came to help. They pulled weeds and put them in a pile to sort.

The sun was very hot that day. Gabriel touched the soil. It felt dry and crumbly like crackers. Then he saw the lettuce. Its leaves hung down low. "It looks tired," said Usman. The carrots and the beans stood up tall.

Gabael had an idea. He filled his watering can at the tap. He tipped it over the lettuce. Drip, drip, drip went the water. The leaves got shiny and wet.

The next morning, Gabriel ran outside in his pajamas. The lettuce stood up straight and green. "Usman!" he called. "Come and look at my answer!" Usman ran over and touched a leaf. It felt cool and soft. Ms. Sokolov, the neighbour, leaned over the fence and smiled. Gabriel filled the watering can again. This time he watered every plant, one, two, three.

Wren woke up with very messy hair. She looked in the mirror. Her hair had big tangles. Mom said, "Let's fix it before school." Wren sat still on the small chair.

Mom brushed slowly. One tangle came out. Then another. Wren said, "Do it again." Mom brushed some more. Soon the tangles were all gone. Wren's hair was smooth and soft. Mom laughed and said, "What soft hair you have." Wren ran to get dressed. She put on her shoes all by herself.

At school pickup, Mom held Wren's hand. They walked to the park. Wren saw Anne there. Anne pointed at Wren's hair. "So shiny!" said Anne. Then Wren saw something in Anne's hair. It was a tiny white feather. It had been hiding all day! Wren picked it out gently. The two friends laughed and swung until the sun went low.

Max ran into the cooking room. Ms. Rahman held up soft white bread. "We will make toast today," she said. Max touched the bread. It was soft and squishy.

The toaster was hot and electric, so only Ms. Rahman touched it. She put the bread in. Max watched with his friend Abdullah. They counted together. "One, two, three," they said. Pop! Out came the bread. Max gasped. It was brown now. It was crunchy now too.

"What happened?" asked Abdullah.

"Heat did it," said Ms. Rahman. "Bread that gets heated turns brown and crunchy. That is toast."

Max tapped the toast with his spoon. Tap, tap. It sounded crisp. Then he spread butter on top. The butter melted fast. One stroke, two strokes, three. The yellow went everywhere on the warm toast.

Next Max poured milk into his cup. He poured too fast. Milk splashed. His tummy felt worried and his face went grumpy. "Slow down," said Ms. Rahman softly. "Try a little bit at a time." Max poured again, slowly. Drip, drip. Not one drop spilled.

Max ate his toast. Crunch, crunch, yum. Abdullah spoke up: "Your milk is all in the cup!" Max smiled and took a big happy sip.

The big game was on TV. Wesley sat on the rug in the living room. Dad was there. Raavi was there too. Alexandria sat on the small chair.

A player ran with the ball. He threw it up high. It went right through the hoop! The crowd went wild.

"He threw the ball through the hoop," said Wesley. "That is how they score!"

"Can I try?" asked Wesley. Dad found a soft ball and a toy hoop. He held it up high on the wall.

Wesley threw the ball. It hit the wall and fell down. He tried again. Too far to the left. Raavi was quiet. Then Wesley stepped closer. He threw the ball up.

Swish! Through the hoop it went. The ball dropped to the floor.

"I did it!" said Wesley. "I scored!"

"Good throw," said Alexandria. She clapped her hands.

"Again," said Wesley. He picked up the ball.

Anthony went to the library with his mom. Ms. Bui smiled at the big desk. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Anthony nodded. The card was orange and shiny. It had his name on it. He held it with both hands.

Anthony found a book about dinosaurs. It smelled like paper and old glue. He hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Ms. Bui shook her head gently. "It has to come back by a certain day," she said. "That day is called the due date." She stamped a little paper. One book, one card, one due date.

Anthony read the book at home, one page, two pages, three pages. Then he met his friend Alaia at the library. She wanted to read the dinosaur book too. Anthony gave it to Ms. Bui at the desk. "Here you go," he said. Alaia took it next. "My turn," she said. Anthony picked a new book about trucks. His mom took his hand, and they walked home together.

James sat in the family car. The seat belt clicked. Dad drove past the shop and the park. They were going to the dentist for the very first time.

"I want to see the dentist," said James. "But how can she see behind my teeth?" Dad smiled and kept driving. James looked out the window. The car went bump, bump over a small hole. "The hole makes the car jump," said James.

At the dentist, James sat in a big chair. It went up and down. The dentist held up a little tool. It was a tiny mirror on a handle. She put it in his mouth. "Say ahhh," she said. James said, "Ahhh." The mirror turned. Now the dentist could see the backs of his teeth. James heard the little click of the mirror each time it moved.

"All done," said the dentist. "You can hold the mirror now." James held it up. He saw his own eye in it. He made a funny face. The mirror made a funny face too. "Can we get lunch now?" he asked Dad. "Yes," said Dad. "And I will take off my smelly shoes at home." James laughed all the way to the car, still holding the mirror.

Music time was here! Hudson ran to the rug. Mr. Oliveira held his drum. "Today we sing a rhyme," he said. "And we clap the beat!"

Mr. Oliveira tapped his drum. It went fast, fast, fast. Hudson clapped fast. His hands got mixed up. Emaan clapped the wrong way too. Augustus sang so fast his words fell in a heap. It sounded bumpy, like a horse trotting on rocks.

"Too fast!" laughed Mr. Oliveira. He tapped again. Slow. Slow. Slow. Hudson clapped slow. One, two, one, two. His hands worked! He sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," all by himself. Emaan and Augustus sang too.

"A song can be fast or slow," said Mr. Oliveira.

"Slow is best," said Hudson. He clapped and sang louder. Mr. Oliveira poured in more taps, and the whole class sang to the moon.

Audrey sat in the school library. Ms. Popescu put two piles of books on the table. "Count them," said Ms. Popescu. Audrey pointed at each book. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Then she counted the small pile. "One, two, three." Ayesha came to sit beside her. "Which pile has more?" Ayesha asked. Audrey looked and looked. She held her mouth tight while she thought. Then she said, "This pile has more. Five is more than three."

Ayesha took one book from the big pile. She hugged it to her chest. "Now count again," she said. Audrey touched each book slowly. "One, two, three, four," she said. The pile had four now. One book was gone, so the number was one smaller. "Four is still more than three," said Audrey. Ayesha put the book back. Audrey counted once more. "Five," she said, and licked the strawberry sticker on her hand. Ms. Popescu smiled. "You counted three times," she said. Audrey nodded. "I like counting slow," she said. She patted the big pile of books, one pat at a time.

Grayson stood at the circle time rug. Music class was starting at the community centre. Ms. Côté held a big drum. She tapped it slowly. Boom. Boom. Boom. Grayson wanted to clap along. But his hands went too fast. They went too slow. He got mixed up and stopped.

Mathilde sat beside him. She tapped her knees with the drum. "Listen first," she said. Grayson listened. Boom. Boom. He clapped one clap for each boom. It worked! The claps and the drum fit together like two shoes.

Then Ms. Côté said, "Now we will sing a nursery rhyme. It is a short rhyming song for little ones." Elyana knew one about a leaf that fell from a branch so low. She sang it once. Grayson tried. He forgot the end. Elyana sang it again. Grayson hummed, then sang the words. The rhyme was short, so it stayed in his head like a small stone in a pocket.

At the end, everyone sang and clapped. Grayson sang the leaf song all by himself. He clapped right on the beat. His dad waved from the door. Grayson clapped louder and sang, "Leaf so low, away you go!"

Gianna stood in the playroom with a big box of things. "Let's make groups," said Mr. Eze. "Put toys here. Put foods there." Gianna picked up a soft brown bear. She put the bear with the toys. Then she found a red apple. The apple went with the foods.

Ilyas held up a long orange carrot. "Where does this go?" he asked. He put the carrot with the toys. Gianna looked at it. She touched the smooth carrot. It did not look like her bear. "Are you a toy?" she asked the carrot. She sniffed it. It smelled fresh, like a snack.

Then she looked at the apple. She looked at the bread next to it. The carrot looked like food, too. Gianna picked up the carrot. She carried it across the rug. She set it down with the apple and the bread. "Foods," she said. Boston clapped his hands. Mr. Eze gave her a clean plate for the carrots. "Snack time," he said.

Billie sat at the little red table. A tablet lay in front of her. Mr. Moose had put it there.

"Press the round button," said Mr. Moose. "The tablet will wake up."

Billie pressed it. The screen lit up. It woke!

She tapped the little paint cup on the screen. A big white page opened. It was the drawing app.

Billie dragged her finger across the screen. A green line followed her finger! She wiggled her finger. The line went curly. It looked like a snake.

"Look!" said Sierra, leaning over. "A curly green snake!"

Billie drew more snakes. One, two, three. Then the timer on the wall went ding.

"Time to put the tablets away," said Mr. Moose.

But the screen was covered in snakes. Billie pressed the round button. The screen went dark and sleepy. Then she slid the tablet back into its box.

"Now the tablet can rest too," said Sierra.

Billie patted the box. "Wake up again tomorrow," she whispered.

Xavier ran in from the backyard. Grandma was making pancakes. "I want to stir!" said Xavier. Grandma pointed to the sink. "Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food," she said. Xavier looked at his hands. They were dirty. He felt sorry for the dirt. He washed with soap. He washed with water. He rubbed and rubbed. One hand, two hands, clean! Grandma smiled. "Now you may stir." Xavier held the big spoon. He stirred the batter. Stir, stir, stir. He counted the pancakes on the plate. One, two, three, four, five. Grandpa came in from town. He ate a pancake and said, "Yum!" Xavier stirred some more. Stir, stir, stir. "I guess we need more pancakes," said Grandma. Xavier clapped his clean hands. "I will stir them all!"

Benjamin woke up early. Today was the big holiday. Mama was cooking in the kitchen. Papa was setting the table.

"Who is coming?" Benjamin asked.

"The whole family," said Mama. "Everyone comes for the holiday."

Benjamin looked out the window. He wanted to see his cousin. He waited. He counted the chairs. "One, two, three, four." Still no car.

He waited some more. He counted again. "One, two, three, four, five."

Then he saw a car. The door opened. Out came Grandma. Out came his cousin.

"Cousin!" Benjamin shouted. He ran to hug her.

They played under the tree. They helped Mama put out napkins. One napkin, two napkins, three napkins, four.

The family sat down together. The table felt warm and full.

"I like holidays," said Benjamin. "Everyone comes to our house."

Grandma smiled. "Yes, they do," she said.

Eva sat at the little table. The shape blocks were in a box. She wanted to build a house for her toy spider. Mr. Sokolov had said it looked stormy outside, so the spider needed a roof.

Jimmy sat next to her. Eva picked up a square block. It had four flat sides. She put it down flat for the floor. Then she picked up another square and stood it up tall. She turned it a little, so one corner pointed up.

"That is a new shape," said Jimmy. "It is not a square now."

Eva looked at it. She turned it back, flat and straight. "Look," she said. "It is the same square." Jimmy turned it again, corner up. Then he turned it back. "Same square," he said. He smiled big.

They made the roof with two triangles. The door was a rectangle. A circle block made a round window. Sama came over and gave them one more triangle for the chimney. Eva put the spider inside, safe and dry.

Then the bell began to ring. Mr. Sokolov clapped his hands. Eva carried the house to the shelf, corner up, just the way she liked it.

Elias ran to the playground with Ira. The sun was hot on the slide. The shady bench was cold. "Let's play the big drum," said Ira. They found the big drum by the sandbox. Ira banged it with her arm. BANG! It was so loud. Little Kenna woke up from her nap. She rubbed her eyes and cried a little.

"Why is Kenna sad?" asked Elias. Ira said, "The drum is loud. Loud and quiet are opposites." Elias thought about that. He tapped the drum very softly. Tap. Tap. It was quiet now. The quiet sound was small, like a tiny cat. Kenna stopped crying. She sat up and watched them.

Elias tapped slow, then fast. The fast taps were louder. The slow taps were softer and smaller. Kenna smiled and clapped her hands. Ms. Farah-Ali came over with water for everyone. Elias was hungry for his snack. He sat on the cold bench and ate his crackers. "More quiet drum tomorrow," he whispered to Ira. Ira nodded and tapped the sand, quiet as can be.

Milo sat at the paint table at school. He had a pot of blue and a pot of yellow. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But he did not know how to get green.

Marina sat next to him. She had red paint on her paper. "I made a red apple," she said. Milo looked at his two pots. He dipped his brush in the blue. Then he dipped it in the yellow. He stirred and stirred. The pot turned green!

Milo painted his green frog. But then he wanted blue water under the frog. He looked in his pot. All the blue was gone. All the yellow was gone too. It was all green now. He could not pull the paints apart again.

Marina gave him a little of her blue. Mr. Wang came over. "Next time, keep a little of each paint aside," he said. Milo nodded. He kept a tiny bit of blue and a tiny bit of yellow in two small cups. He painted the blue water. Then he painted a yellow sun. "Look at my frog," said Milo.

Arya went to the library with her family. She wanted the big red book about trucks. But Nolan had it first. "Can I have it?" asked Arya. "After me," said Nolan. "One turn for you, one turn for me."

Arya watched Nolan turn the pages. One page, two pages, three pages. Then Nolan held out the book. "Your turn," he said. Arya smiled and took it.

Nearby, a family sat by the window. The mama was rocking a baby. The baby was sleeping. Arya got excited and shouted, "Trucks!" The baby woke up and began to cry. The mama rocked and rocked. Arya felt bad. The crying sounded scary.

Ms. Nikolaidis came over. She bent down close. "The baby is sleeping," she whispered. Arya looked at the baby. She looked at Ms. Nikolaidis. Then she made her voice very small. "One truck," she whispered. "Two trucks. Three trucks."

The baby's eyes closed. The crying stopped. The mama rocked some more. Soon the baby was sleeping again. Arya turned one page, then another, all in her quiet voice. Nolan came back and sat close. "Trucks," he whispered. Arya nodded and slid the book so they could both see.

The baby slept and slept. The library was quiet and warm.

Sadie stood in the cart line with her dad. It was a rainy day, and the store was warm. She wanted the bag of ten toy monkeys on the shelf. It had a little song card on it. "Dad, can we get the monkeys?" she asked. "Please?"

"Yes," said Dad. "You can sing the song at home."

At home, Sadie lined up her monkeys on the bed. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. She pushed one monkey off. It fell on the rug. Now there were four monkeys left.

She sang it again. One monkey fell off each time. Four monkeys, then three, then two, then one. "One little monkey jumping on the bed," she sang. That monkey fell off too. Zero monkeys were left.

The next day at school, Elise had a monkey song book. "It goes down to one," said Elise. "One falls off each time."

"I know!" said Sadie. "Let's count it with our fingers." They held up five fingers. Sadie put one finger down at each verse. Five, four, three, two, one.

"Your fingers win!" laughed Elise. Mr. Joseph clapped for them. "Nice counting," he said. Sadie smiled and sang the song one more time.

Parker stood in the backyard. His grandma held a big box. "For the new baby," she said.

Parker wanted to help. He opened the box. Inside were small diapers. So many diapers! "Why so many?" Parker asked.

Wren came over to play. She peeked in the box too. "Babies wear diapers," Wren said. "They cannot use the toilet yet."

Parker blinked. He looked at his toy bear. He tried a diaper on the bear. It fit! The bear could not use the toilet either.

Then the sky turned stormy. Big clouds came. "Hurry," said Grandma. "Bring the box inside."

Parker picked up the box. He did not drop one diaper. The rain began to fall. The diapers stayed dry.

Grandma smiled. "The baby will need these," she said. Parker patted the box gently.

"Now the baby has diapers," said Parker, "because the baby cannot use the toilet yet."

Hannah sits in the waiting room. Raina sits next to her. Hannah holds her bunny tight.

"I don't like shots," says Hannah.

"We can wait together," says Raina.

They look at a book. They count the fish in the tank. One fish, two fish, three fish. Then the nurse calls, "Hannah."

Hannah walks in slowly. She brings her bunny. The nurse cleans Hannah's arm. "Quick and easy," says the nurse. "You can squeeze your bunny."

The nurse gives the shot. It is done. Hannah sees the needle in the nurse's hand.

"What happens to it?" asks Hannah.

The nurse points to a red box on the wall. She drops the needle inside. "The hard box keeps it safe," she says. "Nobody gets poked."

Hannah looks at the red box. The needle went in. The needle stays in there. Now nobody can touch it.

Hannah gets a bandage. She gets a sticker too.

"Was it easy?" Raina asks in the waiting room.

"Quick and easy," says Hannah. She shows her sticker to the fish.

Jules woke up in the dark. "It's morning!" he said. He ran to the window. Nope. The sky was black, not blue. The park across the street was dark too. The big slide looked like a small black hill. His dad came in. "It is still night," Dad said. "Night and day are opposites," said Jules's big sister from the door. "Night is dark. Day is bright."

Jules went back to bed. He counted stars out the window. One star. Two stars. Three stars. Then his eyes shut.

When Jules woke again, the sun was up. The sky was blue. It was summer, and it was hot. "Park time!" said Dad.

At the park, Jules met Aubrie and Reagan. Reagan went down the big slide. Jules went down the small slide. Aubrie ran fast to the swings. Jules walked slow, like a turtle.

"I slid in the dark last night," Jules said. "You did not," said Aubrie. "The park was closed!" "It was night," said Jules. "The park was sleeping."

Reagan laughed. "Slides sleep at night?" "Yes," said Jules. "And in summer, they wake up hot." He touched the slide. "Ouch, hot!" said Reagan. They ran to the shady swings instead.

Amelia ran onto the basketball court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak. Ms. Wilson blew her whistle. "Blue shirts, line up here," she said. Amelia looked down at her shirt. It was blue too. So was Casey's shirt.

The game began. Casey bounced the ball. The ball went bounce, bounce. Amelia waved her arms. "Pass to me!" she called. But Casey threw the ball to a boy in a black shirt. The boy was on the other team. He ran away with the ball. Casey looked sad.

Amelia had an idea. She held Casey's sleeve. "Look, our shirts are both blue," she said. "Look for blue!" Casey smiled. He looked and looked. He saw Amelia's blue shirt. He passed the ball to her. Amelia caught it. The ball felt bumpy under her hands. She threw it up, up, up. It went through the hoop. Ms. Wilson clapped loud. "Nice pass, Casey," she said. Casey laughed and hugged the ball. After the game, they sat in the glue-warm sun on the bench. "We finish our snack before we go," said Amelia. She shared her crackers with Casey, blue shirt next to blue shirt.

Axel went to the farm with his dad. He had three little seeds in his hand. He wanted to grow big carrots. He dug a small hole in the brown dirt. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the soil down. Then he waited.

Every day Axel ran to the farm. He looked at the dirt. He saw nothing. "Where are my carrots?" he said. Kiana came to look too. She pointed at the sky. "Not yet. The sun has to shine first," she said. So Axel waited more. He counted one day, two days, many days.

Then one morning Axel saw something green. It was very small. It poked up out of the soil. Axel pulled his dad's hand. "Come see! Come see!" he shouted. His dad knelt down. "That is a sprout," he said. "A tiny new plant is called a sprout." Axel jumped up and down. "Hello, sprout!" he said. He waved at it like a friend.

Lydia was at home. Her friend Laith came to play. Laith had big tears on his face. He was crying.

"Why are you crying?" Lydia asked.

"I lost my dog toy," Laith said. "He was my best toy. Now I feel so sad."

Lydia felt sad too. She did not want Laith to cry. She ran to her room. She looked under her bed. She looked in her toy box.

Then Lydia found her favorite dog. It was brown and soft. She held it tight. It was hard to give it away. But Laith was still crying.

"Here," Lydia said. "You can hold my dog."

Laith wiped his eyes. He hugged the soft dog. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile.

"Thank you," Laith said. "I feel happy now."

Lydia smiled too. She saw one thing. When Laith felt sad, he cried. When he felt better, the crying stopped.

"Can my dog spell too?" Laith asked. "I can spell my name. L, A, I, T, H."

Lydia laughed. "Dogs cannot spell. But my dog can sit!"

Lydia made the dog sit on the rug. Laith clapped his hands. He was excited.

They played until it got late. Then Laith's dad came to the door.

"Time to go home," his dad said.

"Can I keep the dog?" Laith asked.

"You can borrow him," Lydia said. "Bring him back soon."

Laith waved from the car. Lydia waved back from her window. Her mom gave her a warm hug.

"You were kind today," Mom said.

Lydia held her mom's hand. "Laith can bring my dog tomorrow," she said.

Andrew was at Grandma's house. The toast was warm in the pan. Grandma had made it for him. "You can spread the butter," she said. Andrew was ready to try.

He took the little knife with the round end. It was safe for small hands. He dipped it in the butter. He spread it on the warm toast. The butter sat on top. Then it began to shine. Then it got soft. Then it went away! Andrew looked and looked. "My butter is gone!" he said.

Grandma smiled. "Look at your toast," she said. Andrew looked. The toast was shiny and wet all over. The butter had melted into it. Andrew took a bite. It tasted good. He lifted his cup of milk with two hands. He poured it slow. Not one drop spilled. Grandma clapped. "Yummy toast," said Andrew, and he took another big bite.

Milan sat on his bed with his big dog book. He loved the dog with one brown eye. "Who drew this dog?" he asked.

He took the book to his mom. "Can you help me look?" She opened the front cover. She turned to the first page. There was a name there. "Here it is," she said. "The person who draws the pictures for a book is called the illustrator."

"An illustrator," said Milan. "She drew my dog!" He ran back to his room. He held the book up high.

The next morning, Ariella came to play. Milan showed her the book. He started at the front. He turned the pages one by one. "See? The illustrator made this," he said. He pointed at the little puppy with a bite taken from its bone. Ariella laughed. "Show me again," she said. "From the front."

Beatrice stood at the basketball court with her grandma. There was a big hoop and a basket of beanbags. "I want to throw them all," said Beatrice. She picked up one, two, three beanbags. She held them in her arms.

Emilio came to play too. He put out his hands. "My turn," said Emilio. Beatrice looked at all her beanbags. She did not want to give them up. She threw one. It missed the hoop. She threw another. It bounced off the edge.

Then grandma said, "Let's try turns. One person throws, and then the next person has a turn." Beatrice gave a beanbag to Emilio. "Your turn," she said. Emilio threw it. It went in the hoop. "You did it!" said Beatrice. She clapped her hands.

Now it was her turn again. She threw one beanbag. It went in. "My turn, your turn," she said. They took turns, one and then one. Then Mr. Kang brought a big ball. Beatrice opened both hands wide. Emilio tossed it to her. She caught it and held on tight. "Strong hands," said Mr. Kang. Beatrice laughed and threw the ball back.

Elena sat on the big couch. She had a cold. Her nose was red. Her blanket was soft and warm.

Dad brought her a warm drink. "Sip it slow," he said. Elena sipped. It was yummy. Then her nose tickled. Ah, ah, ah-choo! She sneezed right into her hand.

"Look," said Dad. He bent his arm. He put his nose into his elbow. "When you cough or sneeze, you cover it with your elbow." He made a little cough into his elbow.

Elena tried it. She bent her arm. She put her nose in her elbow. "Ah-choo!" she said, on purpose, just to try. It worked. Her hand stayed clean.

"Now I can play again," Elena said. She held up her clean hand. Dad put his hand on top of hers.

Later her friend Barrett came to the door. He waved from the window. He held up a toy bus. "When you are better, we can ride our bikes," he called.

Dad said pizza was coming for dinner. Elena smiled and pulled her blanket up. Her nose tickled again. She bent her arm fast. "Ah-choo!" she said, right into her elbow.

"Good job," said Dad. Elena kept her arm bent, just in case.

Wren wanted to paint at home. The paint pots were up high on a shelf.

"Not now," said her dad. "We will paint later. First we eat lunch."

Wren ate her sandwich fast. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad.

Wren waited. She heard the clock tick, tick, tick. She looked out the window. A friendly brown dog walked by. Still not later.

"Is it later now?" she asked again.

Dad smiled. "Later means some time after now. Not right away."

Wren helped clear the plates. She washed her hands. The water felt warm and bubbly. Then Dad got a phone call. He talked for a long time.

Wren waited some more. She pretended her toy cat was painting. She drew a sun on scrap paper with a pencil.

At last Dad put down the phone. "Now it is later," he said. "Let's paint."

He set the pots on the table. He poured water into little cups. Wren dipped her brush. The red paint was cool and wet. She painted a big red sun, just like her pencil sun.

"Tomorrow we can paint again," said Dad.

"Tomorrow is after sleeping," said Wren.

"Yes," said Dad. "And right now, we paint."

Wren made a happy yellow dot in the middle of her sun.

Gianna sat at the snack table at daycare. Mr. Johansson put grapes in a little cup. "You can have three grapes," he said.

Kip looked at his cup. "My grapes are big," he said. "Do big grapes count as three too?" He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." He counted again. Still three. Gianna counted hers too. "One, two, three." She had small grapes. But the number was the same. "Three is three," said Gianna. "Big or small, three is three!" Kip laughed and clapped.

After snack, they went outside. A brown bird sat on the fence. Kip threw a soft red ball to Gianna. She caught it and threw it back. "One, two, three, four," they counted the throws together. Then they sang their counting song. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" A ladybug crawled on the fence post. It was small and bumpy and a bit ugly, but its legs were sweet and tiny. "Hello, little friend," said Gianna. She held out one leaf, and the ladybug walked right on.

Parker sat at the big table. Mom put out little cups. "Let's play a game," she said. "Close your eyes and taste."

First came a strawberry. Parker licked it. "Sweet!" he said. His tongue knew.

Next came a lemon slice. Parker's mouth went tight. "Sour!" he laughed. "My tongue told me!"

Mom clapped. "Yes, your tongue can tell sweet foods from sour ones." She held up a cookie. "Sweet or sour?"

Parker closed his eyes. He did not peek. He took a small bite. "Sweet!" he said. He did not miss one.

Then Mom touched his ear. "What is this for?" Parker thought hard. "Hearing!" he said. "I hear the kettle with my ears."

"And your eyes?" Parker looked out the window. "Seeing! I see a rainbow over the houses!" The rainbow had red and blue and yellow in it.

Mom wiggled his nose. "And this one?" Parker sniffed the lemon cup. "Smelling! My nose smells it!"

"What about your hands?" Parker touched his sweater. He felt a loose string on his sleeve. "Touching! My hands feel the string!"

Mom held up one finger. "How many senses is that?" Parker counted on his fingers. One, two, three, four, five. "Five!" he said. He jumped down from his chair and ran to the window. "Rainbow, do you taste sweet or sour?"

Henry went to the store with his dad. Henry sat in a little chair by the carts. He wanted a red apple. Apples were far away on a tall shelf.

Then Hoorain came in with her mom. Hoorain was Henry's friend. She ran over to say hello. Henry's dad smiled. "How old are you, Hoorain?" he asked.

Hoorain held up her fingers. She held up four fingers. Then she said, "I am four." Henry looked. She said four, and she was four. So a number word could tell your age.

Henry held up his fingers too. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Then he said, "I am three!" Hoorain clapped. Henry's dad clapped. Henry felt big.

Now they walked to the apples. They counted them into the bag. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples went in the bag. Henry helped hold the bag. It was heavy but he did not drop it.

At the counter, the cashier gave them a small surprise. She gave Henry a shiny sticker shaped like a star. "For a good helper," she said. After they finish shopping, Henry would sit in his chair at home and eat a tasty apple. "Can I have my apple now?" he asked. His dad laughed and said, "Right after we pay."

The lights went out. It was dark in the backyard. Juliette could not see her toys. She wanted her teddy bear on the chair.

Juliette ran to the chair. Bump! Her leg hit the chair. "Ow," she said. It was too dark to run.

Dad came out with a big flashlight. He turned it on. Juliette could see the chair. She could see her teddy, too. "My leg bumped the chair," Juliette said. "It was not a mean chair. The dark made me bump it."

"In the dark, walk slowly," said Dad. He held out his hand. "Hold my hand so nobody trips." Juliette held Dad's hand. They walked slowly, step by step, back across the grass. Nothing bumped them at all.

They sat on the step together. Juliette found a feather on the ground. It was soft and white. She let it go and watched it float down. Dad shone the flashlight on it. The feather danced in the light. Juliette laughed and let it float again.

Soon the lights came back on. The house glowed. "Now we can see everything," said Juliette. She held Dad's hand all the way to the door and carried her teddy inside.

Aria stood at the campsite table. She wanted to make pancakes for her family.

"Look, a measuring cup," said her dad. "It helps cooks put in the right amount of each thing."

Aria grabbed the sugar bag. She tipped it. Sugar plopped out. Too much! White sugar piled up like a little hill.

"Uh oh," said Aria. "That is a problem."

Her dad laughed. "Pour some back. Now try the cup."

Aria filled the measuring cup. She poured the sugar into the bowl. Just the right amount! Then she used the small measuring spoon for salt. A tiny bit, not too much.

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Aria watched from far away. The pancakes sizzled and popped. They smelled sweet and warm.

"Time to eat!" said Dad.

Aria took a big bite. "Yum! I made these!"

Her mom smiled. "Best pancakes at the campsite."

Aria licked sticky syrup off her fingers.

Mohamed was at Lawson's house. The toast was warm on the plate. There was a big carton of milk on the table.

"I want to spread the butter," said Mohamed. Lawson's dad gave him a small knife. It was not sharp. Mohamed spread the butter. It went on slowly, bit by bit. Soon all the toast was yellow.

Then Mohamed wanted milk. He tried to pour from the big carton. It was too heavy. The milk nearly spilled. "Wait," said Lawson's dad. He poured some milk into a little blue jug. "Try this one." Mohamed held the little jug. It felt light in his small hands. He tipped it, and the milk went right into his cup. Not one drop spilled. He drank some and felt proud.

Outside the window it was windy. The tree was waving its branches. Mohamed looked at the cup. He did it all by himself. He poured more milk, just to know he could. "More toast?" asked Lawson's dad. "Yes, please," said Mohamed, "and I will spread the butter."

Lincoln sat at the big table in the art room. Mr. Virtanen put out three pots of paint. "This is red," said Mr. Virtanen. "This is blue. This is yellow." Lincoln wanted to paint a pig. He wanted the pig to be pink. He looked and looked. There was no pink pot.

First he made a red pig. Roger sat next to him. "Nice pig," said Roger. Lincoln poked the pig with one finger. The wet paint moved. Now the pig had a fingerprint on its back. "Oh," said Lincoln. His paint was wet, and it could smudge. The pig was slow to dry. So Lincoln waited.

Kylian painted a yellow sun. Lincoln waited some more. Then he had an idea. He put yellow on his brush. He put red on the same brush. He mixed them on the plate. The two paints made pink. Pink like a flower. Pink like a pig.

Lincoln painted a new pig, all pink. He kept his hands far away. "I will not touch it," he said. "Not till it dries." Mr. Virtanen hung the pink pig on the wall to dry. Kylian clapped. Roger gave it a slow wave goodbye. Lincoln waved too. "Bye, pig," he said. "Bye."

Asher ran to the playground. The sun was hot. The slide felt fast under his hands. He slid down, down, down.

His friend Yaseen was at the water fountain. "The water is cold," said Yaseen. Asher drank some. Brrr! Cold water on a hot day.

Then Asher wanted his apple juice. It was in the big red cooler by Mr. Sutton. But the cooler lid would not stay up. It fell shut. Bang! Asher tried again. He held the lid open with one hand. He reached in with his other hand. He pulled out his small juice box. It worked!

"Look, Mr. Sutton!" said Asher. "The lid is open now."

"Good job," said Mr. Sutton. "Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut." He closed the lid softly. Tap.

A naughty plastic ball rolled by and bumped Asher's foot. "My ball!" yelled Trinity from the swing. She ran over, slow at first, then fast. Asher picked up the ball and gave it back.

Then he sat in the shade. He opened his juice box. He took a long, slow sip. "Ahh," said Asher.

Arthur sat in his car seat. He had a red bag of things. His mom was driving to school.

"Let's play the sorting game," his mom said. "Animals here. Toys here. Foods here."

Arthur looked out the window. He saw a brown cow. "Animal!" he said. He clapped. Then he saw a big truck full of apples. "Food!" he said. He patted his bag.

Arthur pulled out his small toy dog. It was soft and gray. He put it in the animal pile.

Then he held it still. He waited. He looked at it a long time. The cow had moved its tail. The toy dog did not move at all.

Arthur moved the toy dog to the toy pile. He put it next to his toy car.

"A toy dog is not alive," his mom said.

"I know," said Arthur. "It stays with the toys."

The car stopped at school. Harper opened the door. "Look!" said Harper. She held up a toy cat. "An animal!"

Arthur shook his head. He patted the toy pile. "Toys," he said. Harper put the toy cat in the toy pile.

Arthur saw his mom press a button. The window went down. Wind came in and tickled his face. He pressed his own button. Down went the window next to him too.

"Two windows," said Arthur, laughing in the wind.

Camille sat at the long table in the community hall. The hall smelled like warm bread. Her tummy made a little growl. The food was almost ready.

A boy named Cedar sat next to her. His grandma set down a big pot. Then she smiled and said, "Bon appétit!"

Camille looked at Cedar. "What does that mean?" she asked.

"My grandma is from France," Cedar said. "In France, people say bon appétit before a meal. It wishes everyone a good meal."

Camille wanted to say it too. She tried. "Bon... app... bon app," she said. It came out funny. Cedar laughed, but not mean. "Try again," he said. His grandma nodded.

"One, two, three," said Cedar. "Bon appétit!"

"Bon appétit!" said Camille. This time the words came out right.

Then something happened. The grandma gave Camille the first bread roll. It was warm and soft. Yara, on the other side, clapped her hands. "Say it again!" she said.

Camille sat up tall. "Bon appétit!" she said, loud and clear.

Everyone at the table said it back to her. The hall filled with voices. Camille took a big bite of her warm bread.

Yara whispered, "Teach me tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Camille. "One, two, three. Bon appétit!"

Elizabeth sat at the big table in the library. She was drawing a lake. Mr. Bui had given her a blue crayon and a pencil.

Elizabeth wanted a duck on her lake. She pressed the pencil down very hard. Snap! The pencil point broke off. It rolled onto the table.

"Oh no," said Elizabeth. She held up the little pencil. Mr. Bui came over. He gave her a new pencil.

Elizabeth tried again. This time she pressed gently. The duck got a small eye. Then it got a beak. Then it got two feet.

"Look, Mr. Bui!" said Elizabeth. Mr. Bui smiled and gave her a thumbs up. Aria came to look too.

"Nice duck," said Aria. "Can you draw me one?"

Elizabeth pressed gently again. Soon there were two ducks on the lake.

Snow fell all night. In the morning, Elliot peeked out the kitchen window. The yard was white. "No school today," said his dad. "It is a snow day!"

Elliot wanted to play in the snow. He ran to the door in his sock feet. He opened it and stepped out. The snow was cold on his toes. His fingers turned cold too. He did not have his mittens.

Elliot ran back inside. His dad helped him put on warm pants and a new blue coat. He put on his boots and his hat. He pushed his hands into soft mittens. His toes felt warm now. His fingers felt warm too.

Elliot ran outside again. He made a big snowball with his mittens on. He pressed it and patted it. "Snow day!" he called to his dad. His dad waved from the kitchen window, and Elliot threw his hat up in the air and caught it.

Sofia was in the pool changing room with her dad. She put on her real swimsuit. It had ducks on it. Louie was there too. Louie had on blue goggles.

"Swim time!" said Louie. He started to run. His feet went slip, slip. He wobbled and sat down hard on the floor.

Mr. Tang helped Louie up. "Wet floors are slippery," said Mr. Tang. "So we walk. Not run."

Louie stood up. He took big slow steps. His feet did not slip. Sofia watched. Then Sofia took big slow steps too. Her feet stayed under her, just right.

At the pool, Sofia blew bubbles in the water. She kicked her legs. Her dad clapped. After swim time, they went back to the changing room. Sofia walked all the way. Louie walked too. Sofia held her towel and her sandwich box.

"We walked like turtles," said Louie.

Sofia laughed. "Slow steps, no slips," she said, step by step across the wet floor.

Sebastian held his dad's hand in the school hallway. The floor smelled like wax and oranges. His juice box was in his backpack. He could hear kids laughing behind a red door.

"I want to see Joud," Sebastian said. "Where is Joud?"

"She is by the window," said his dad.

Sebastian looked down the hallway. It was long and shiny. He took one step. Then another step. His shoes made a squeak on the floor. He walked all the way to the window by himself.

Joud was there. So was Selena. Selena was waving at a big yellow bus outside.

"The bus!" said Sebastian. He put his hands on the glass. The bus doors opened. Kids came out one by one.

A boy on the bus stood up. He wanted to wave out the window. The driver turned around. "Sit down, please," the driver said. The boy sat down in his seat right away.

"Why did he sit?" Sebastian asked.

"Kids stay sitting on the bus," said Joud. "That is the rule."

The bus pulled away. Sebastian waved at the window. The glass was cool on his nose.

"There you are," said a kind voice. Ms. Romano smiled at the door. "Ready for our first day?"

Sebastian nodded. He did not forget his juice. He held Joud's hand, and they walked in together.

Jaxon sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The game was on the TV. Everyone was shouting and clapping. Elie and Margot sat next to Jaxon with a big bowl of popcorn.

Jaxon looked at the screen. He saw lots of players running. He saw lots of players. "Who has the ball?" he asked. He could not tell. It was too mixed up.

Grandpa pointed at the screen. "See the shirts?" he said. "This team wears red. This team wears blue." Jaxon looked hard. The red team ran one way. The blue team ran the other way. "Red team, blue team," Jaxon said. "Red team, blue team."

Then a red player kicked the ball. It went in the net. Everyone jumped up. Jaxon jumped too. The popcorn jumped too. One piece flew up and landed right on Margot's head. Margot laughed and laughed. Jaxon laughed too. "Goal for the red team!" he shouted.

Sara went to the grocery store with her dad. She held her little toy bunny in one hand. Then Sara saw the apples. They were red and green, like a rainbow of fruit. She let go of bunny to pick up an apple. When she turned around, bunny was gone.

"Where did bunny go?" Sara asked. Her dad said, "Let's look together." They walked back down the apple aisle. They looked by the bread. They looked by the milk. No bunny anywhere.

Mr. Goh worked at the store. He saw Sara looking sad. "Can I help you look?" he asked. Sara nodded. Then she had an idea. "Bunny is small," she said. "Small toys can roll or slide under things. Maybe bunny rolled under a shelf!" She got down on her knees and peeked.

There was bunny, under the bottom shelf, next to a lost lemon. Sara gave a quick hop of joy. She reached in and pulled bunny out. She hugged him tight.

"Thank you, Mr. Goh!" said Sara. She held bunny with both hands the whole way home. At the door, she waved. "Bye, bunny's helper!" said Sara, and she and dad hopped out into the sunshine.

Jaxon ran to the big red cubby. It was hide-and-seek time at school. He pressed his hands over his eyes. "You can't see me!" he said.

Magnus counted loud. Jaxon heard his feet on the floor. Thump, thump, thump. Jaxon's ears worked just fine. Then he heard Magnus giggle.

"I see your shoes, Jaxon!" said Magnus. "I see your shoes!"

Jaxon peeked between his fingers. Magnus was looking right at him. Jaxon dropped his hands. Oh! His eyes were closed, but Magnus's eyes were not. Magnus could still see him. "Found you!" said Magnus.

Jaxon laughed and laughed. "My turn to hide again," he said. This time he did not cover his eyes. He looked for a better spot.

He sniffed with his nose. Something sweet was near. Cookies! Mr. Jean-Louis was baking in the little kitchen. Jaxon did not go near the hot oven. He just sniffed from far away.

"Can I guess?" said Jaxon. "Sugar cookies!"

"Yes," said Mr. Jean-Louis. "After the game, we will taste one with our tongues."

Hendrix came to hide too. He covered his eyes with both hands. "You can't see me!" he said.

Magnus tapped his shoulder. "I see your shoes, Hendrix. I see your shoes!"

Hendrix peeked out and grinned. Then he touched the soft red rug and hid behind the cubby, eyes wide open.

Emmett ran into the bathroom. Bubbles filled the tub! He could not wait for his bath.

"After your bath, you can put on your new pajamas," said his dad.

Emmett splashed and played. His rubber fox floated by his toes. The water was warm and smelled like soap. He washed his toes and his tummy.

Then it was time to get out. He dried off with a big towel. His new pajamas were on the counter. They had red foxes on them!

"Fox pajamas!" Emmett shouted. He put them on all by himself. They were soft and cozy.

"Do I sit in these?" he asked.

"No," said his dad. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in."

Emmett grinned. He climbed into bed. "Good night, foxes," he whispered. Then he closed his eyes.

Maeve went to the store with her dad. She wanted to buy apples for her class picnic. Ms. Grewal had asked for ten apples. Ten was a big number.

Maeve put apples in the bag. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. What came after two? She could not remember. Her friend Abygael could count so fast. Abygael liked to sing a song at school. "One, two, buckle my shoe," the song went. The song rhymed! Shoe sounded like two. Maeve sang it in her head. "Three, four, shut the door." That was it!

She sang and put in more apples. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." The rhymes helped her remember each number. Her dad smiled and rolled the cart. One cart wheel wobbled. The apples were shiny and red.

"Nine, ten, a big fat hen," Maeve sang. She counted the apples. Ten! Just then Abygael appeared with her mom. "Maeve!" she said. "Do you want a goldfish cracker box? It has a fish that can swim on the front." Maeve laughed. "First, apples," she said. She put the bag on the counter, all ten.

Chloe went to the farmers' market with her dad. She held his hand the whole way. There were big pumpkins and small berries. Then she saw a little paper bag of seeds. The picture showed a carrot.

Chloe wanted to grow carrots. She used her old plastic shovel at home. She put the seeds in the dirt. Then she gave them water from her small can. "Guess what will happen," she said to her dad. He smiled and said, "We will see."

The next morning, Chloe ran outside. She looked down at the dirt. There was no sprout. Just brown dirt. She felt sad. She watered the seeds again. The next day, there was still no sprout. She watered them again and again.

Then one morning, something tiny and green stood up in the dirt. "A sprout!" Chloe shouted. She touched it very softly. A little ladybug sat on the new green leaf. Chloe laughed and gave it more water, drop by drop.

Sienna sat on the big rug at Mr. Bakker's house. Everyone was watching a soccer game on TV. The players ran and ran. Then the referee blew his whistle. All the players stopped running.

Sienna was puzzled. "Why did they stop?" she asked. "The referee blew the whistle," said Marco. "The whistle stops the game." Then the whistle blew again and the players ran once more. Sienna watched. The whistle blew, and the players stopped. The whistle blew again, and they ran. "The whistle tells them to stop," said Sienna.

At snack time, Sienna got a fork for her cake. Her fingers were sticky from juice. "Thank you," she said to Mr. Bakker, who handed her a napkin. Then came a surprise. The game came back on the little TV in the kitchen. The whistle blew. Sienna clapped her sticky hands and laughed. "Stop!" she called to the players. "The whistle says stop!" Marco laughed too, and Mr. Bakker smiled down at them both.

Beatrice ran to the laundromat door. The big dryers hummed and hummed. Her brown coat hung on a hook. She had pulled it off to feel the warm laundry.

"Can I go out like this?" she asked her mom.

"Try it and see," said her mom.

Beatrice opened the door. The cold air touched her arms. "Brrr!" she said. She shivered and shivered. She ran back inside. The coat helps keep my body warm when it is cold outside, she thought.

So she put the coat on by herself. One arm in. Other arm in. Then the zipper. Up, up, up it went. Zip!

"Look, Mom! I did it all by myself!"

"Big news," said her mom. "Now we can walk under the moon."

They pushed the door together. Beatrice felt the cold air again. But this time, she did not shiver one bit.

Joshua was at Grandma's house. On the table sat paints and brushes. Grandpa held up a flat tray. "This is called a palette," he said. "It holds the paint."

Joshua wanted to paint a big dog. But what colour? He dipped his brush in red. He painted on his paper. Then he dipped in blue. The paper turned a muddy smudge.

"Oh no," said Joshua. "What if I try first?" He put a red dot on the palette. He put a blue dot next to it. He mixed them with his brush. Purple! Bright purple!

"Grandpa, look!" cried Joshua. "Red and blue make purple!" He tried yellow and blue. Green! He tried yellow and red. Orange! He painted a purple dog with a green ball. Grandpa laughed and added a brown collar.

"What colour do we get if we mix all of them?" asked Joshua. Grandpa grinned. "Try it on the palette." Joshua mixed everything together. "Brown! Like a bear!" He ran to show Grandma his dog.

Julia sat on the school bus. She held a little red car. The wheels could spin. Kaius sat next to her. He looked at the car. "Can I hold it?" he asked.

Julia wanted it too. She grabbed the car from Kaius. He made a sad face. His eyes got watery. Kaius started to cry.

Julia looked at the car in her hand. She looked at Kaius. She held the car out to him. "Here," she said. "You can go first." Kaius stopped crying. He made the wheels spin. Outside the window, cars went by on the street. Julia watched a dog with curly fur walk past. Then Kaius held the car out to her. "Your turn," he said. Julia took it. They shared the car all the way to school.

Maya wanted to play rocket ship at daycare. She put on a big cardboard tube. It was tall and brown. It smelled like glue and tape.

Kaiya ran over. "I will be the astronaut too," she said. Maya held her hand. They were not scared together.

Mack stood by the tube. He was the mission helper. "Time to count," he said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Maya and Kaiya jumped up high. Their tube went up, up, up. Then they came down with a soft bump on the mat.

"That was a countdown," said Ms. Liu. She clapped her hands. "You counted backward from ten down to one."

Maya tried it herself. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" She jumped even higher this time. Kaiya laughed and jumped too.

After play time, Ms. Liu asked Maya to bring her a red flower from the art table. Maya counted the petals on the way. "One, two, three, four, five." She brought the flower over.

"Can we do the countdown again?" Maya asked.

Ms. Liu smiled. "Ten," she said.

"Nine," said Maya. "Eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!"

Elias put on his coat to go to the store. Dad had to tie Elias's shoe first. "We need a card for Masa," said Dad.

At the store, Elias saw cards with words on them. He could not find Masa's name. He turned a book of cards from the back to the front. The first page said A, B, C. "Start here," said Dad. Elias turned the pages slowly. He waited. He turned some more.

Then Elias saw it. M-A-S-A. "That says Masa!" he said. He put his finger under each letter. M, A, S, A. Then he saw his own card. E-L-I-A-S. Elias looked at his coat label. E-L-I-A-S. Same letters. Same order. "My name looks the same!" he said.

Dad smiled. "A gentle hand on the cards, please." Elias held the card carefully, all the way home.

Victor ran to the park with his friend Kasper. "Let's look at the big sun!" said Kasper. He pointed up at the sky. "I want to see it up close," said Kasper. He began to look up.

Ms. Russo ran over fast. "Stop!" she said. "Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes." Kasper covered his eyes with his hands. "Whoa," he said. "My eyes feel funny already."

Victor had an idea. "Close your eyes," he said. "You can still play." Kasper closed his eyes tight. He could hear the birds sing. "Ears hear!" said Victor. Kasper touched the heavy sandbox truck. "Hands feel!" He sniffed a flower. "Nose smells!"

Then Victor's mom called, "Snack time!" Kasper grinned. "Mouth tastes!" He grabbed a banana slice and ate it up. "Four senses," said Victor. "And our eyes stay safe."

Audrey was at the playground. She saw a big red slide. She wanted to go on it first. But Kip ran up fast. Kip got to the slide first. Audrey felt angry. Her face got hot. Her hands made fists. She stomped her feet on the ground.

Then Mr. Pérez sat down next to her. "Want to be a big lion with me?" he asked. "Lions breathe slow and big." Audrey sat in the cozy shade. She took one slow breath in. She let it out, big and long. She did it again. Her fists opened up. Her tummy felt calm.

Kip came down the slide. "My turn now?" Audrey asked. Kip nodded. Audrey climbed up. She slid down, fast and free. "Again!" she said. "Lion slides are the best!"

Henry was in his bed. It was dark and quiet. Then he heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window.

Henry felt scared. His heart went bump, bump, bump. He pulled his blanket up high. The sound came again. Tap, tap, tap.

Henry thought and thought. What could he do? He could call his mom. "Mom!" he called loud. "I hear a sound. I feel scared."

Mom came fast. She sat on the bed. "Where is the sound?" she asked. Henry pointed at the window. Mom looked close. "Come see," she said.

There was a small branch outside. The wind moved it. The branch tapped the glass. Tap, tap, tap. That was the sound. Henry smiled big. "So that was it!" he said. He was not scared now.

Mom tucked him in. His blanket fit just right under his chin. "If you feel scared again, call me," she said. "A grown-up can help you." Henry nodded. His room felt warm and tidy. He closed his eyes. The branch tapped soft, tap, tap, tap.

"Good night, little branch," said Henry.

Splash day at school! Kayden played in the water table. He splashed with Wynter. He splashed with Zakaria. Splash, splash, splash!

Now Kayden was all wet. Water dripped from his arms. Water dripped from his hair. Drip, drip, drip! Time to go home. Kayden ran to the gate. But something was missing. Where was the towel? Kayden's arms were still dripping wet. He went back to Ms. Rodríguez. "Your towel is in the box," said Ms. Rodríguez. Kayden looked in the box. There it was, big and soft!

Ms. Rodríguez patted the towel on his arms. Pat, pat, pat. The drips went away! The towel dried his body after his bath-time splash. Kayden hugged the towel. Mommy waved at the gate. Kayden did not wait. He ran, dry and warm, all the way home. "Towel!" he shouted. "Towel, towel, towel!"
