text:
Eleanor sat at the paint table at summer camp. She wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green paint. All the pots were empty except yellow and blue. How would her grass look right?

Rudy sat next to her. He was painting a blue lake. "No green," said Eleanor. "My grass needs green." She looked and looked at the pots.

Then she had an idea. What if the paints could be friends? She dipped her brush in the yellow pot. She dabbed yellow on the paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue pot. She swirled the wet blue into the wet yellow spot.

The spot turned green! Real green, like real grass. "Look, look!" said Eleanor. Rudy leaned over. "Green!" he said. "How did you do that?" Eleanor made a big green field. She even gave her painting a green coat of grass at the bottom.

Mr. Wu came to see. "That is lovely grass," he said. Eleanor held up her wet brush. "Yellow and blue made it," she said. "Yellow plus blue." Then she dipped her brush again. "Can blue and yellow make more?" she asked. Mr. Wu smiled and slid two full pots down the table toward her.

Sadie sat at the big table. Her grandma set out warm rice. It smelled so good. Sadie picked up her spoon. Then she put it down.

"Wait," said Sadie. "I forgot my words."

Grandma smiled a gentle smile. "What words?" she asked.

"Bismillah," said Sadie. "Moussa says it at school. He says it before he eats. I guess it means 'in the name of God.'"

"Yes," said Grandma. "Many Muslims say Bismillah before they eat."

Sadie folded her little hands. "Bismillah," she said, soft and slow.

Then she took a big bite of rice. Yum!

The next morning, Sadie sat at the table again. There was toast on her plate. She looked at the toast. She looked at her spoon.

"Do I say it now?" she asked herself. "Yes! Before the first bite."

"Bismillah," said Sadie. Then she munched her toast.

Dad clapped his hands. "You remembered all by yourself!"

Sadie beamed. One small word, then one big bite. Every meal, every day, Sadie said her word first.

At lunch she counted on her fingers. "Bismillah, then bite. Bismillah, then bite."

Grandma laughed and kissed her head. "Bismillah," said Grandma too. Then they both took a bite together.

Theo was in the garden. He dug in the mud with his small shovel. A worm began to crawl away, and Theo laughed. Soon his hands were brown and muddy.

Then his dad called, "Lunch is ready!" Theo ran to the table. Chicken and rice sat on his tall blue plate. Theo reached for a piece of chicken.

"Hold on," said his dad. "Look at your hands." Theo looked. His hands were very muddy. "We wash our hands before we eat," said his dad. Theo walked to the sink. His dad turned on the water, warm but not hot. Theo rubbed the soap on his hands. The mud went down the drain. His hands were clean and pink.

Theo sat back down. He picked up the chicken with his clean fingers. It was warm and good. His dad sat beside him and ate too. Theo looked at his hands, then at his plate, and smiled.

After lunch, Theo yawned a big yawn. His dad said, "Bath time, then a nap." The water in the tub bubbled soft and white. Theo splashed a little and washed his toes. He put on his cozy pajamas.

Theo climbed into his bed. His dad tucked the blanket under his chin. "Wash, eat, bath, sleep," Theo said softly. His dad kissed his head. Theo closed his eyes and held his small shovel tight.

Jacob sat on the big couch. Leo and Opal sat next to him. Dad turned on the game.

"Who is winning?" asked Jacob.

"I don't know," said Leo. "I forgot the score."

Opal shrugged too. Jacob wanted to know. He needed the score.

Then Jacob looked up. He saw the big board with lights. It had two numbers on it.

"Look up there!" said Jacob. "That must show the points!"

Dad laughed. "That's right. That's the scoreboard. It shows how many points each team has."

Jacob watched the numbers. A player kicked the ball. The net wobbled. Then a number on the board went up.

"It changed!" Jacob shouted. "Blue team got more points!"

Leo and Opal looked up too. Now they all knew the score. Jacob wore his pink socks and clapped.

"Blue team, blue team!" they cheered.

Mom brought popcorn from the kitchen. Everyone munched and watched the numbers. Every time a number changed, Jacob jumped up.

"I will always look at the scoreboard," said Jacob.

"Good plan," said Dad. "Now pass the popcorn."

Muhammad fell in the yard. His knee got a big bump. His sister was sad about it, so their mom came to help.

Mom took Muhammad to the bathroom. She turned on the light so his eyes could see. He heard water go drip, drip in the sink. He smelled the pink soap by the tub.

Mom held out an ice cube in a towel. "This will help your knee work right again and feel good," she said. Muhammad touched the ice cube with his finger. It felt cold! He let go fast and the ice cube fell. Plink! It went into the sink. His ears heard the little sound. His tongue tasted mint from his toothpaste when he smiled.

Mom picked up the ice cube. She held it on his knee with the towel. Muhammad felt the cold through the soft cloth. His fingers touched the warm towel too. His eyes watched his knee. The bump looked smaller now.

"There," said Mom. "Does it feel better?" Muhammad nodded. He touched his knee with his hand. The owie was going away. He gave Mom a big hug. She hugged him back. From the kitchen, his sister called out, "Muhammad! Come see!" Muhammad ran to her, one happy step at a time.

Nolan waited at school pickup. His dad was late. Nolan sat on the little bench. He wanted to be all ready to run.

Nolan put on his shoes. The shoes felt funny. They were itchy and bumpy inside. He wiggled his toes. "Ow," he said.

His friend Sulaiman sat down next to him. Sulaiman pulled on his socks first. Then he pushed his feet into his shoes. Sulaiman stood up and stomped. His shoes felt good.

Nolan looked down at his shoes. He pulled them off. Then he put on his socks. The socks were soft and warm. Then he put his shoes back on. He stomped his feet too. "Better!" he said.

"I did it backwards," said Nolan. "Socks go on your feet before your shoes." Sulaiman laughed. "You learn fast," he said.

Their teacher, Mr. Yip, came out with a big bag. "Coats on, everyone," he said. Nolan put on his coat and his hat. His dad waved from the gate.

Nolan ran all the way. His shoes went stomp, stomp, stomp. "Time for dinner," said Dad, "then a bath. Your socks are smelly!" Nolan giggled and ran faster.

Everett woke up in his bed. The sun was bright in his window. He heard a clink and a pour. Was someone in the kitchen? He wanted pancakes today.

He padded down the hall. Mom and Dad sat at the table. There were plates and cups and a big pancake stack. "Good morning," said Everett.

"Good morning," said Mom. "It is morning now. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." She put a warm pancake on his plate. Everett took a big bite. Yum.

Yesterday there were no pancakes. Yesterday they had eggs. "Pancakes today," said Everett. "Eggs yesterday." Dad laughed. "That's right. And tomorrow we can have pancakes again, if you want."

"Tomorrow is after I sleep again?" asked Everett. Dad nodded. "Yes. First today, then sleep, then tomorrow." Everett thought that was a funny order. But he liked it.

After breakfast, Everett wanted to play a game. "Can we play now?" he asked. "We can play later," said Dad. "First the dishes go in the sink." Everett helped carry his cup. He was careful and slow.

Then it was time for the game. Everett and Dad sat on the rug. "I go first," said Everett. He rolled the dice. He moved his little piece two spaces. "Your turn, Dad," he said. Dad smiled and rolled the dice too.

Everett yawned a big yawn. Morning was for pancakes. Later was for games. Sleep would come after that. He leaned on Dad's arm and whispered, "Good morning was good." Dad said, "Good morning still is." Everett rolled the dice one more time.

Emilia was at Grandma's house. Her tummy felt hungry. She wanted a cookie.

Grandma had many boxes in her cupboard. Emilia could not read yet. She pointed at a box with a dog on it. "Is this the cookie box?" she asked.

Grandma shook her head. She ran her finger under the words. "This box says dog food," she said. Emilia looked at another box. Grandma read that one too. "This says oatmeal." The words on the boxes told them what was inside. Then Grandma found the right box. "This says cookies," she said.

Grandma baked more cookies in the oven. Emilia stood far away, because the oven was hot. While they waited, Grandma read her a book. She started at the front. She turned each page. The story went from the front to the back.

At last the cookies were ready. Emilia ate one. "Mmm," she said. "The words found the cookies!"

Alexis sat at the dinner table. His plate had rice and beans. He was hungry, so he took a big bite. "Yum," he said. He felt happy.

Dad was quiet. He looked down at his cup. He did not smile. Alexis saw Dad's hands shake a little. "Dad, are you sad?" Alexis asked. "No," said Dad. "I feel nervous. I talk at a big meeting tomorrow." Alexis was surprised. Grown-ups feel scared too? "Everybody has feelings," said Mom. "Even grown-ups." Alexis thought about that. One, two, three feelings, he counted. Happy, sad, nervous.

Alexis waved his spoon like a little flag. "You can do it, Dad!" Dad smiled a big smile. He stood up straight. He was not scared anymore. Alexis felt excited. After dinner, Dad helped Alexis wash his hands. The water washed away the dry rice. Alexis told Dad, "One, two, three deep breaths. That is what my teacher Ms. Nakamura says." Dad took three big breaths. "I feel better," said Dad. Alexis grinned. "Me too."

Camille looked out the window. No school today! The street was white with snow. She put on her boots and her big red coat. Mom came out to the yard with her.

Camille fell back into the snow. It was soft and cold. She swept her arms up and down. She swept her legs out and in. Then she stood up, right in the middle.

"Oh no," said Camille. Her boots made big dark spots. Her angel was smudged.

"Try again," said Mom. "This time, roll to the side before you stand up."

Camille lay down in a fresh spot. She swept her arms and her legs again. Then she rolled over and stood up at the edge. She looked back at the snow.

There it was. A white angel with wide wings! The arms had made the wings. The legs had made the long angel dress.

"You did it!" said Mom.

"It's a snow angel," said Camille. She laughed and laughed. Then she made another one, and one more, all the way down the yard.

Stella sat on Grandma's big soft chair. She wanted to read the pig book all by herself. She held it up. The little pig looked funny. His feet were up. His ears were down. "The pig is upside down," Stella said. Grandma smiled and did not say why.

Stella turned the book around, slow and careful. Now the pig stood on his feet. His ears were up. Stella laughed. She opened the front cover first. Page by page, she went. The pig found mud. The pig found his mom. Stella pointed at each word. "That says pig," she told her shy toy rabbit, who sat beside her.

"Will you share the story?" Grandma asked. Stella held the book so Grandma could see. "The end," said Stella, and closed the back cover.

Thomas sits on the little toilet. He is done. Now he wants a snack, a red apple on his plate.

Thomas turns on the tap. He pumps the soap. Mr. Bianchi showed the class how to wash. Thomas rubs and rubs. He sings the happy song in his head. The bubbles are white and small.

Thomas turns off the tap. His hands are wet. He shakes them hard. Water drips on his pants. Water drips on the floor. Drip, drip, drip. Thomas makes a sorry face. His pants are dark with water.

He looks around the bathroom. There is a towel on the low hook. It is soft and clean. Thomas presses his hands on the towel. He pats each finger. The towel drinks up the water. Now his hands are dry. Drying hands is the last step, and Thomas did it all by himself.

He runs to his plate. The apple is red and shiny. Thomas holds it with dry, clean hands. He takes a big bite. "Crunch," says the apple.

David wanted to stay up late. "One more show," he said. His dad said no. "Your body needs rest," Dad said. But David wanted to play trucks in the kitchen. He cried a little. Dad sent him to bed with a hug.

David lay in his bed. He did not sleep for a long time. He listened to the clock tick. Finally his eyes closed.

The next morning, Zaid came to play. Zaid had slept all night. Zaid ran to the toy trucks. David sat on the kitchen floor. His eyes felt heavy. His arms felt slow. He could not run. Zaid zoomed a red truck past him. "David, come play!" Zaid said. David yawned and yawned.

That night, David brushed his teeth fast. He put on his pajamas all by himself. "Bedtime," he said. Dad smiled. "That is smart," Dad said.

The next morning, David jumped out of bed. He ran to Zaid at the door. "Trucks!" David said. His legs felt fast. His eyes felt wide. He zoomed the red truck all around the kitchen. "You slept all night!" said Zaid.

Evelyn sat on the blue rug at school. Ms. Nur put out two rows of buttons. One row was spread out long. The other row was bunched up close.

"Look!" said Anhad. "The long row has more!"

Evelyn wanted to know. She pointed at the buttons. "One, two, three," she counted. The long row had five buttons.

Then she counted the bunched row. "One, two, three, four, five." Five buttons! The same!

"Surprise!" said Evelyn. She spread the bunched row out wide with her finger. It looked long now. She pushed it back close. It looked small again. Still five buttons!

Aram clapped his hands. "It is still five!" he sang.

Ms. Nur smiled. "Who has more buttons now?"

"Nobody," said Evelyn. "Both rows have five. Both are the same!"

She pushed the buttons together. Then she spread them out again. Five buttons every time.

Evelyn jumped up. "I can count! I am a strong counter!"

She gave each button a little pat, one by one, all the way to five.

Adam went to the library with his dad. The library had a craft table today. Adam sat next to his friend Charles. Mr. Gauthier, the librarian, gave each child a card to color. Adam wanted to make a sun with his crayons.

Adam looked in his backpack. His crayons were in there, but they felt funny. He pulled one out. It was soft and bendy. It drooped in his hand like a noodle. "Look," said Adam. "My red crayon can bend!" Charles leaned over to see.

Then Adam remembered. His backpack had sat in the car all morning. The sun had shone in the windows. The car was hot inside. "The hot car made my crayons go soft," said Adam. "I wonder if the sun in the sky could do it too." Charles held a crayon up to the window. They watched and waited. But the window glass was cool, and the crayon stayed stiff.

Mr. Gauthier brought over a fresh box of crayons. "Here you go," he said. Adam drew a big yellow sun. He mixed yellow and orange together for the rays. His itchy sweater sleeve rubbed his arm as he drew. "My sun looks hot," said Adam. Charles laughed and held up his bendy red crayon one more time.

Parker ran into daycare with his tiny backpack. He held up a cookie box. "Cookies for breakfast!" he said.

His friend Nirvaan looked up from his bowl. "What is breakfast?" Nirvaan asked. Parker thought hard. He looked around the room. Everyone was eating. Then it would be play time, then lunch, then nap time.

"Breakfast is the first meal of the day," said Parker. The cookie box felt heavy in his hands. But cookies were sweet, and his tummy was hungry for morning.

Mr. Barrett knelt down beside him. "Would you like to pick a morning meal?" he asked. Parker peeked at the table. There were eggs and toast and banana slices. Parker put the cookie box in his bag. He picked toast and banana. He took a big bite.

"Yum," said Parker. "Can cookies come after lunch?" Mr. Barrett smiled. "Yes, they can."

Outside, a tiny bird hoped for crumbs. Parker shared one bit of toast. The bird skipped away, and Parker laughed.

Arnaud was at Grandpa's house. In the garden there was a shiny red swing. Martin was there too. Both boys ran to the swing at the same time.

"I want to go first," said Arnaud. "I want to go first," said Martin. They both held the swing. It did not move at all. Hmm, thought Arnaud. How can two boys use one swing?

Martin's grandma came out with juice. She sat down on the bench. Martin looked at the swing. Then he looked at Arnaud. "We can take turns," said Martin. "Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another."

Arnaud sat on the swing first. He pumped his legs. Up he went, high like a bird. "My turn," said Martin. Arnaud got off. Martin got on. He went high too. One after another, they went up and down.

Grandpa called, "Who wants to glue paper shapes at the table?" Arnaud smiled. "Me first!" he said. Then he looked at Martin. "Then you."

Levi sat in the family car. He held his red bag. His little bunny was not in the bag. "Oh no," said Levi. "Bunny is lost."

The car stopped at the big store. Mom got out. Levi saw many cars and many people. He wanted to run and look for bunny all by himself. He opened his door a little. Then he stopped. He sat back down and called, "Mom! Mom! Bunny is lost!"

Mom came right away. "Thank you for telling me," she said. She took Levi's hand. They walked together, nice and slow. They looked by the store door. They looked by the carts. No bunny yet.

Then they asked the nice cashier. "A red bunny?" she said. "Yes! Someone found it." She held it up. It was bunny! Levi hugged bunny so tight. "You told me first," said Mom. "That was the smart way." Levi smiled big. Outside, the sun was warm. His ice cream cone had begun to melt, so he took one big lick. "Bunny, do you want a lick too?"

Alexis was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big box of blocks. "Let's put them away," Grandma said. "We can sort by color. That means all the same color goes in one group."

Alexis made a red pile. Then he made a blue pile. Then he made a yellow pile. Grandma made a green pile.

A phone began to ring in the kitchen. Grandma went to answer it. Alexis kept sorting. He waited for a tricky block. Was it blue? He looked and looked. He put it in the blue pile.

Then he saw it. One yellow block was hiding in the red pile! He picked it out. He put it in the yellow pile. Now all the same colors were together.

Grandma came back with two cups of milk. "All done!" said Alexis. Grandma smiled. "You sorted them so well. Now let's build a striped tower, red, blue, yellow, green."

Alexis clapped his hands. "A striped tower! Yes!"

Jack was playing at home. His mom said, "Time to go. You get a shot today." Jack did not want a shot. "Shots pinch," he said. "I will come with you," said Mom. "You can hold my hand."

At the doctor's office, Jack sat on the big bed. The nurse was polite. "One, two, three," she said. "All done." The shot was fast. It pinched just a little. Jack held his mom's hand the whole time. Then the nurse did one more thing. She put a small bandage over the spot. Jack looked at it. "Stars!" he said. The bandage had stars on it.

"I picked stars," said Jack. "Can Hendrix see it?" "Tomorrow," said Mom. "First, let's get ice cream." At the ice cream shop, Jack held up his arm. "Look at my stars," he said. The cashier smiled. "One, two, three, four stars," she counted. Jack ate his ice cream and kept his arm up high.

At home, Jack showed the bandage to his dad. "One, two, three, four," he counted again. His dad gave him a glass of water. Jack drank it all. "I was brave," said Jack. "And I got stars." He put his arm on the table so the stars could watch him play.

Nolan sat in his big bed. His throat hurt. His head felt hot. He wanted to hide under the blanket and stay very still.

Then he called out, "Mom, I feel sick."

Mom came fast. She put her hand on his head. "I am glad you told me," she said. She gave him a sip of water. The water was cool in his dry mouth. She brought a cool cloth and it did stick to his warm forehead for a second, then sat soft as a kiss.

Mom pulled the shades down. The room went dim. "Rest now," she said.

Nolan slept a long time. When he woke, his throat did not hurt. His head felt light and fine. Telling Mom had worked.

"Can I have toast?" he asked.

Mom smiled. "Toast is coming," she said.

Alexander walked in the forest with Ayah. They found a big log by the lake. Ayah sat on the log and looked at the water. Alexander wanted to play with her. But he did not know how to start.

He stood next to the log. He patted the bark. Ayah just kept watching the water. Then Alexander had an idea. He clapped his hands and said, "Let's pretend we're bears!" Ayah jumped up right away. "Roar!" she said. "I am a big bear!"

Alexander saw that his words made the game start. He said, "Let's pretend this log is our bear house." Ayah nodded. "You be the baby bear," she said. "I will make you dinner." She picked up leaves and put them in a pile. "Here is your food, baby bear," she said.

Alexander lay down on the soft moss. "I am sleepy," he said. Ayah covered him with more leaves. "Sleep, baby bear," she said. Alexander closed his eyes. Then he peeked at her and growled, "Grr!" Ayah laughed and hugged him. "My baby bear," she said. "Let's pretend it's morning now!"

Amira held her mom's hand on the noisy bus. They were going to the pool by the beach. Amira wanted to float like a leaf on water. But she was scared. "My tummy feels funny," she said.

At the pool, Ms. Demetriou smiled. "I will hold you," she said. "You can lie on your back." Saanvi and Giovanni were there too. "Look at the clouds," said Saanvi. Amira lay back in the cool water. Ms. Demetriou's hands were under her back. The hands held her up. She did not sink!

"I'm floating!" Amira yelled. She felt the sun on her nose. She heard the waves at the beach, swish, swish. Then Ms. Demetriou took one hand away, just a little. Amira still floated. "My turn next!" said Giovanni, splashing his feet. Amira smiled at him. "Ms. Demetriou will hold you too," she said.

Amelia loved her swim team. Every week she played games in the pool. Today was the big game day. Ms. Becker said, "Line up, team!"

The game began. Amelia splashed fast. Saoirse splashed fast too. The other team got the ball in first. Then they got it in again. The whistle blew. Amelia's team did not win.

Amelia felt grumpy. She wanted to stomp. But Ms. Becker clapped her hands. "Line up by the pool wall," she said. Amelia wondered what would happen now.

The two teams stood in one long line. Each player walked past the other players. "Good game," said Amelia. "Good game," said a girl from the other team. Everyone said it, one by one.

Then Lili gave Amelia a high five. "Good game!" said Lili. Amelia smiled big. "Same time next week?" asked Lili. "Yes!" said Amelia. She jumped and made a big splash.

After the game, there was cake by the pool. Amelia sat with Lili. The table felt bumpy under her hands. "That was fun," said Lili. Amelia took a big bite. "Good cake," she said.

Beatrice sat at the big table. Her mama put out three cups of paint. "This one is red," said Mama. "This one is yellow. This one is blue." Beatrice pointed at the red cup. "Red like my coat!" she said. "Yes," said Mama. "A nice red."

Beatrice dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in the yellow cup. She made a yellow blob. But the blob was not yellow. It was orange! Beatrice tipped her head and looked. "Mama, it changed!" she said.

"Now let's mix blue and yellow," said Mama. Beatrice put blue on her brush. Then she added yellow. Green paint spread on the paper. "Green like the grass!" said Beatrice. She clapped her hands.

It was time to stop painting. Beatrice wanted to leave her brushes in the cups. "We wash them with water," said Mama. "Then they dry." They washed the brushes in the sink together. Beatrice put them on a towel to dry. In the morning, she touched the brushes. They were soft and clean. "Ready for orange again," she said.

Juliette sat at the kitchen table. She had a plate of crackers. "Is this one a square?" she asked. She was not sure. Mom gave her a piece of string.

Juliette put the string along one side. She cut it to match. Then she held it against the other sides. "Same, same, same," she said. The string fit each side. Four sides, all the same. "It is a real square!" said Juliette. Mom smiled.

Then Juliette pointed at the kitchen wall. "That door is not a square," she said. "Two sides are long." Mom nodded. "What is it called?" asked Juliette. "A rectangle," said Mom. Juliette looked at her plate. She found a circle cookie and a triangle chip too. "Look, Mom," she said, holding one up high. "This one has three sides!"

Mia ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. Tom was already there. He had on big red boots.

"I am a firefighter!" said Tom. "Boots help me be one."

Mia looked at the toy box. She wanted to be someone too. But what?

Then she saw a little white hat. She put it on her head. She found a toy sheep and hugged it tight.

"I am a sheep farmer!" said Mia. "My hat helps me pretend!"

Danica put on a long scarf. "Now I am the vet," she said. "My sheep is sick. It has a tickle in its ear!"

Mia held the sheep still. Danica patted its ear softly. The sheep felt all better.

Ms. Bennett clapped her hands. "What good helpers!"

Then Ms. Bennett sneezed. "Ah-choo!"

Tom grabbed his boots. "The doctor is coming!"

Mia laughed and patted Ms. Bennett's arm. "You will be okay. My sheep will sit with you."

Ms. Bennett smiled big. "Best sheep ever," she said.

Today was a big day. It was Leo's birthday week! He had a stack of blue cards in his bag. Mom helped him write them at home. Each card said "Leo's party. Saturday. Room 3."

At school, Leo gave out the cards. "Come to my party!" he said. Dhruv took a card. Emile took a card too.

Then Dhruv looked sad. "I don't know where your party is," he said. "I might get lost."

Leo held up his card. "Look! The card says Room 3." Dhruv turned his card over. He read it with his finger. "It says Saturday too!" he said. "Now I won't be lost." He gave Leo's arm a little pat. "Thank you, Leo."

"Nice card," said Emile. "I love the blue."

On Saturday, everyone came to Room 3. Mr. Bui brought a big cake. Dad lit the candles, and everyone sang. Dhruv arrived right on time, holding his card. "I found it!" he shouted. Leo laughed and clapped.

After cake, Leo got a soft toy animal. It was a lion with a fuzzy mane. "Roar!" said Leo. "Want to pat it?"

Dhruv patted the lion. "Soft," he said. "Best party ever."

Grayson woke up early. Today was the big party at the community hall. He could not pick what to wear. He held up his brown sweater. He held up his pajama shirt with stars. "Hmm," he said.

His mom came in. "Everyone wears special clothes to a celebration," she said. Grayson looked in his drawer. He found his red shirt with a golden bird. It had shiny buttons. He put it on all by himself. He looked in the mirror. "Special," he said.

At the hall, Grayson saw his friends. Zendaya wore a purple dress with flowers. Jade wore a green jacket with a dragon. Even Mr. Vargas, the neighbor, wore a long blue scarf. Nobody wore plain old clothes. The hall had bright flags and paper lanterns. A grown-up lit the candles, and everyone watched from far away.

Outside the window, the sky looked snowy and a little storm was coming. But inside, it was warm. Music played. Grayson clapped his hands. Zendaya spun in a circle. Jade stomped his feet. "Your shirt is so shiny!" said Zendaya. Grayson grinned and spun too, his golden bird flying around and around.

Colton wanted his red ball. It was stuck in a big tree. The ball was up high. Colton was down low.

He called his dad. Dad came with a long ladder. "Climb up," said Dad. Colton put his hands on the ladder. He went up one step. He went up two steps. He went up three steps. His heart went boom, boom, boom. Dad held the ladder the whole time.

Up high, the branches smelled like rain. Up high, he could see the small rooftops. Up high, his red ball sat on a branch. Colton grabbed it. "I got it!" he shouted.

Then Colton had to go down. Down one step. Down two steps. Down three steps. His feet touched the soft grass. Dad said, "Up and down are opposites." Colton laughed. He went up fast. He came down slow.

He rolled the ball on the ground. The ball rolled fast. The ball hit a flower pot. The flower pot wobbled. Colton ran and caught it just in time. Dad clapped his hands.

The door opened. It was Ms. Nikolaidis from next door. She held a cold drink. "Is someone ready for a treat?" she asked. Colton counted the ice cubes in her cups. One, two, three. "Me first!" said Colton, and he ran inside to wash his hands.

Aubrey climbed the big school bus. She sat next to her friend Mckenna. Mckenna had a paper name tag. It said "mckenna" with a small first letter.

"Look," said Aubrey. "My tag has a big A. Aubrey starts with a big A!" Mckenna looked down at her tag. She pulled the zipper on her bag and found a fat red crayon.

"Can I fix it?" asked Mckenna.

"You can make it big!" said Aubrey.

Mckenna drew a big capital M over the small one. Now her tag said "Mckenna". The bus bounced. The tags wiggled.

Then Christian sat down across from aisle. His tag said "christian". "Your letter is small too!" said Aubrey. Christian laughed and borrowed the red crayon. He made a big capital C.

The driver looked in the mirror and smiled. Aubrey sang the letter sounds all the way to school. "M says mmm. C says kuh. A says aah!"

"Next stop, school!" called the driver. Aubrey hugged her tag to her chest. "A is for Aubrey," she whispered. "Big A, all mine."

Ayla stood at the campsite table. She had a big job today. She would make dinner for her family. The carrots came in a paper bag. Ayla pulled one out. It had dirt all over it. The dirt left marks on her hands. "Yuck," said Ayla. She looked at the carrot. It was a puzzle. How could dirt come off?

Her dad showed her the little camp sink. He turned the tap on. Cool water ran out. Ayla held the carrot under the water. She rubbed it with her fingers. The dirt washed away. The water turned brown in the sink. Then the water ran clear again. The carrot was bright orange now. "Look, it's clean!" said Ayla. There were three more carrots. And potatoes too, with dirt on them. Ayla washed each one. She took her time. Rub, rinse, rub, rinse. Adem, her friend from the next tent, came to watch. "Can I wash one?" he asked. He scrubbed a potato slow and careful.

After that, the grown-ups cooked the carrots and potatoes over the fire. Ayla stayed back, a safe distance away, and watched the flames bend in the wind. The food began to smell sweet and warm. Dinner was ready. Ayla took the first bite of her clean, soft carrot. "I made this," she said. Adem clapped his hands.

Myles woke up in his bedroom. He looked out the window. The ground was snowy and white. His tummy felt full of breakfast, and he had to use the toilet.

He ran to the bathroom fast. He used the toilet. Then he pulled up his pants and started to run back to his room.

"Myles," his dad called. "Did you flush?"

Myles stopped. He looked at the toilet. The water was still there. He had forgotten. He pressed the big button. Whoosh! The water swirled down and away.

Myles ran to the sink next. He pushed the soap pump. Bubbles came out on his hands. He rubbed them together. The bubbles turned white and foamy. He rinsed them under the water. The bubbles went down the drain. His hands were clean and shiny.

"Now I am all done," Myles said.

He ran back to his bedroom. His dad was there, making his bed. Outside, the snowy yard sparkled in the sun.

"After you wash, you get dressed," his dad said. He held out Myles' blue shirt and warm socks.

Myles pulled on his shirt. He sat on his bed and pushed his feet into the socks. He wiggled his toes. The socks were soft.

Soon it would be lunchtime. Myles would finish a big sandwich with his clean hands.

"Lunch soon," said his dad. "Wash first, then eat."

Myles smiled and jumped once on the rug. His tummy made a little rumble. "Peanut butter, please," he said.

Abigail sat at the little table at daycare. She wanted to cut out a circle for her owl. The owl needed big round eyes.

She picked up her scissors. Romi was cutting a square. Romi found a corner and snipped there first.

Abigail looked at her circle. She turned it around. She looked again. "Where is the corner?" she said. "My circle has no corner! It is just round and round."

Mr. Fortin smiled. "Try anywhere," he said. Abigail touched the edge. She snipped one spot. Then she cut round and round, all the way.

Atreus held up a rectangle. "Mine has corners," he said. Abigail held up her circle. "Mine has none," she said. "It is round."

She glued the circle eyes on her owl. It was not heavy at all. "Nice owl," said Romi. "Let's go talk about it at snack time."

Grayson was at daycare. He wanted to play dragons with Lenna. Grayson picked up a soft green sock dragon. "My dragon is scary," he said. He made a big growl.

Lenna hugged her sock dragon tight. "No," she said. "My dragon is friendly. It helps people." Grayson frowned. "Scary," he said. "Friendly," said Lenna. They both stood very still.

Then Lenna had an idea. "Our dragons are a family," she said. "One can be friendly. One can pretend to be scary, then be nice." Grayson smiled big. "Yes! My dragon blows fire that turns into flowers." They ran around the rug together. The dragons took care of the baby dolls. "Time for dragon naps," said Lenna. Grayson tucked his dragon in with a small blanket. "Night night," he whispered.

Madelyn ran to the sand at the park. The sky was cloudy, but she did not mind. Her friend Sama was there. Sama had built a big sand house with two towers.

Madelyn wanted to see it up close. She ran fast. Her foot hit the tower. Crash! The tower fell down. Sand went all over Sama's shoes.

Sama's lip shook. "My tower," she said. Madelyn felt bad inside. "Sorry," she said. "I ran too fast. That was a mistake."

Sama looked at her. "Okay," she said. "You can help me fix it." Madelyn got the small blue shovel. She patted the sand, pat, pat, pat. Sama stacked it high again. Then Madelyn put a leaf on top. "A flag!" said Sama.

A ball came bouncing near them. Adnan ran after it. "Can you help me?" he called. "My ball went under the bench." Madelyn reached with the shovel. Out came the ball. "Thank you," said Adnan.

Ms. Mendoza blew a whistle. Snack time. Sama shared her crackers. "Please, take one," she said. Madelyn took two, one for each hand. She gave one back to Sama. Then they sat by the tall new sand house and munched together.

Arlo ran to the kitchen in his pajamas. He wanted bread with jam before bed. "One slice," said his dad. Arlo ate it slowly. He drank his milk. He put his plate in the sink.

Then Dad said, "Time for your bath." Arlo splashed in the warm water. Dad washed his hair. Arlo got out and dried off. He put on his clean pajamas. He brushed his teeth at the sink. Dad tucked him into bed.

Arlo closed his eyes. Then he opened them wide. "Wait," he said. He hopped out of bed. He ran to the bathroom again. Dad followed him. "I brushed already," Arlo said, "but now my teeth feel sticky." Dad helped him reach the tap. Arlo brushed every tooth. He rinsed his brush and put it down.

"I brush in the morning and before bed," Arlo said. He climbed back into bed. He pulled the blanket up. "Next, I wish for a good dream," he said. Dad kissed his head and turned off the light. Arlo's eyes closed, one blink at a time.

Charlie was at daycare. Mr. Siddiqui put out a shape puzzle. The square went in the square hole. The triangle went in the triangle hole. Then Charlie held a small red circle. Westyn held a big blue circle.

"That little one is too small," said Westyn. "It can't be a circle like the big clock."

Charlie looked at the clock on the wall. It was round. Her red piece was round too. She held her piece up next to the clock. Both were round all the way around.

"Mine is a tiny circle," said Charlie. "Yours is a big circle."

Westyn smiled. Charlie put her tiny circle in the round hole. It fit. Westyn put his big circle in the other round hole. It fit too.

Justine clapped. "Big circles and tiny circles," she said.

Mr. Siddiqui turned on the light. "Snack time," he said. Charlie ran to the table, ready to eat her round crackers.

Hunter ran to the park with his ball. He saw his friend Jai by the swings. Jai had a red hat on.

"Is today the library day?" Hunter asked. "I want to go with you."

"My mom said the library trip is now," said Jai. "Today is the day that is happening right now."

Hunter looked up. The sun was out. Cars went by the park gate. This was now. Yesterday, it had rained. They could not go out yesterday. Tomorrow would come later, after sleep.

"My shoes are dirty," Hunter said. He had rolled his ball in the mud. His shoes had brown spots.

His mom came to the park door by the gate. "We can wipe them," she said. She used a small cloth. She wiped one shoe, then the other. The spots went away.

"Can I go to the library today?" Hunter asked.

"Yes," said his mom. "Today is happening now. So we can go now."

Hunter held his ball tight. He and Jai walked to the gate. They went through the door together.

"Last night I read about a big red truck," said Jai. "Today I will find a book about a dog."

"I will find a book about balls," said Hunter. He gave his ball one more roll on the grass. Then he ran to catch up with Jai.

Today was Eliana's birthday. Her mom brought cupcakes to school. Ms. Goldberg said, "We will sing for you." Eliana felt worried. She did not like loud singing. She asked her mom, "Will it be very loud?" Her mom said, "Not too loud. Just wait and listen."

Robyn and Clementine helped set out the napkins. Eliana helped too. She carried one cupcake very slowly. Then she had to sneeze. The cupcake began to drop. Clementine caught it with a plate. "Safe!" said Clementine. The cupcake was fine.

Then everyone stood up. They sang, "Happy birthday to you." Eliana waited. Then she heard it. They sang, "Happy birthday, dear Eliana." They were singing her name. She hid her big smile behind her hands. Her cheeks felt warm and happy.

After the song, Ms. Goldberg gave out the cupcakes. Eliana looked at hers. There was a tiny toy duck sitting on top. "A duck!" said Eliana. "For me?" "Yes," said Ms. Goldberg. "It is yours to keep." Eliana put the duck in her pocket. She held up her cupcake and said, "Sing again, please. I want to hear my name one more time."

Isabella sat on her bed with her sleepy teddy bear. She had a little book. She wanted to know who made it up. "Teddy, who made this story?" she asked. She opened the book. She turned the pages one by one, front to back. The pages went from the front to the back. At the end, there was no answer.

Then Mommy came in. "Who made up this story?" Isabella asked. Mommy pointed to the front of the book. "See this name? That is the author," she said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Isabella looked. There was a name on the front.

"Can I taste the words?" Isabella asked. Mommy laughed. "No, you read them." Isabella held the book. She tapped the name with her finger, like a little hammer, tap, tap. "The author made my book," she said. "The author made my book!" She hugged teddy tight and looked at the name one more time.

Jayden ran into the school library that morning. He was so excited. Today he could pick a sticker from the prize box.

Mr. Sultani held up two trays of stickers. "Which tray has more?" he asked. Jayden had to find out. He pointed to the first tray and counted. "One, two, three, four." He pointed to the second tray. "One, two, three." The first tray had more!

"You can pick from that big tray," said Mr. Sultani. Jayden picked four star stickers. He put them on his hand. One, two, three, four.

Then Alice came over. "I lost my sticker," she said. Jayden looked under the table. There it was! Alice smiled. She gave Jayden her sticker to keep.

Jayden put it with his stars. Then he counted again. "One, two, three, four, five!" Now he had five! Adding one more sticker made his number go up. He jumped up and down.

"I have five!" he did not need to yell, but he almost did. Stefano came to see. "Count them for me," said Stefano. Jayden touched each sticker. "One, two, three, four, five."

Mr. Sultani gave Alice a new sticker from the box too. Alice counted hers out loud. "One, two, three. Now I have three!" They all sat at the little table, counting stars again and again.

Louis ran to the toy corner at school. Ten red cars sat in a line on the rug. Bodie was already there.

"I will count them," said Bodie. He touched the cars one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

"Now me," said Louis. He sat at the other end. He started with the car by his knee. He touched each car. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

The boys looked at each other. "Ten," said Bodie. "Ten," said Louis. They both laughed. Bodie had started at the far end. Louis had started at the near end. Both got ten!

Mr. Hoffmann came over. He held two dirty trucks. "Which group has more, trucks or cars?" Louis counted the trucks. "Six." He counted the cars again, from the middle this time. Still ten! "The cars have more!"

"Great counting," said Mr. Hoffmann. Louis felt a happy feeling in his chest. One little car slipped from his hand. He picked it up and put it right back in line.

Benjamin ran into the playroom. Ms. Lavoie had a big box. "Sock hop time!" she said. "Everyone find a pair of socks!" Aliyah and Baby clapped their hands.

Benjamin dug into the box. He found one sock. It was blue with a fish on it. "One sock," he said. He looked in the box again. He pulled out a red hat. He pulled out a smelly shoe. No sock.

He held up his one sock. "Where is your friend?" he asked it. Ms. Lavoie laughed. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks," she said. "You need one more."

So Benjamin hunted. He looked under the toy ocean rug. He looked behind the bear. Then Baby shouted, "I see blue!" The sock was under the chair!

Benjamin fetched it fast. He put the two socks side by side. "A pair!" he cheered. Both fish matched. "Let's hop!" said Aliyah. They counted together, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten hops!" Benjamin hopped on his two socks all the way to ten.

Jake wanted to smell the flower on the science table. He snipped it with his nose. He could not smell it. He tried again. Still nothing.

"Take a big, slow breath in," said Ms. Morales. Jake took a big, slow breath in. Now he could smell the flower. It smelled sweet. His nose worked!

Edith put a small mirror on the table. Jake looked at his nose in the shiny mirror. He saw two little holes. "Those are called nostrils," said Ms. Morales. Jake counted them. "One, two," he said. His nose had two nostrils!

Musa brought apples in a bowl. Jake touched one. It felt smooth and cool. He took a small bite. It tasted sweet and juicy. Musa laughed, and Jake heard his laugh. Jake heard the clock ticking too.

Then the teacher turned on a song. Jake and Edith danced. Musa clapped. Jake closed his eyes. He could hear the music with his ears. He opened his eyes. He could see Edith spinning around.

Jake picked up the flower again. He held it under his nose. He took a big, slow breath in with his two nostrils. The sweet smell went right in. "I smell it," said Jake.

Muhammad sat at the dinner table. He wanted his favorite pudding. But the pudding was not out yet.

"When is pudding time?" he asked.

"It is not now," said Mom. "It is later."

Muhammad looked at the wall. There was a clock on the wall. "Does the clock know?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "The clock shows what time it is."

Muhammad watched the little hand. It moved a tiny bit. He waited. He ate his rice, slow and slow.

The door opened. Lauralie peeked in. "Is it pudding time yet?" she asked.

Muhammad pointed at the clock. "Not yet," he said. "The hand is not there yet."

They watched together. Then the little hand reached the big number. Mom brought the pudding.

"Now!" said Muhammad. He clapped his hands.

Lauralie laughed and took her spoon.

Lea ran to the swings at the playground. Liyana was already there. "Push me!" said Liyana. Lea pushed the empty swing, and Liyana went up high. Lea held her mama's hand when they crossed the big field. "Stay close," said Mama.

Then Lea saw something shiny in the grass. It was a little lighter. It had a small flame button. Lea wanted to pick it up. But she remembered the rule at home. Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.

"Mama! Come look!" said Lea. She pointed with her finger. She did not touch it. Mama came over fast. "Good job, Lea," said Mama. She picked up the lighter and put it in her pocket.

Mr. Lombardi was fixing the water fountain nearby. The water came out cold. Lea put her hands under it. "Cold!" she said. Then he touched the metal top. "That part is hot from the sun," he said. "I will fetch my pot of cool water for it." Lea and Liyana watched from a safe spot. Soon the fountain was cool again. Lea drank some water. "Nice and cold!" she said.

Mackenzie went to Kingston's house. He had a big toy kitchen. He had a soft cow doll and a baby doll too.

"I want to play house," said Mackenzie. "I will be the parent."

"I want to be the parent too," said Kingston. "I can cook the food."

Kingston looked mad. His face got red. Mackenzie did not want him to feel mad.

Then she had an idea. "You be the parent now," she said. "I will be the baby."

Kingston smiled. He fed the cow doll a bottle. He patted the baby doll's back. "Time to sleep, little baby," he said.

"Can we switch?" asked Mackenzie. "Can I be the parent now?"

"Yes!" said Kingston. "I can be the baby."

Mackenzie wrapped the cow in a blanket. She rocked the baby doll. She gave it a soft hug.

"You are a nice parent," said Kingston.

"I thank you," said Mackenzie. "You are a nice baby."

Then they both laughed. Playing house was fun when they took turns.

Carter sat at the dinner table. His plate had peas in a little square section. Daddy put chicken on his plate too. "What did you do today?" Daddy asked.

"I went to the park tomorrow!" said Carter. He took a big bite of chicken. Lexi had been at the park too. They had played hide and seek behind a big tree. One, two, three, Carter counted, and then he found Lexi.

Daddy smiled. "Not tomorrow," he said. "Tomorrow comes after today." Carter frowned. Was tomorrow now? He looked at his plate. The peas were gone now. They were there before. Hmm. He ate them, and then they were all gone.

"You went yesterday," said Daddy. "Yesterday is the day before today. Today is now." Carter looked out the window. Now it was dark. Yesterday it was daytime at the park. Tomorrow would come after sleep. Carter yawned. He counted his forks: one fork, one spoon, one cup. "Tomorrow can I see Boaz?" he asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "After sleep, tomorrow comes." Carter ate one more friendly little piece of chicken. Then he said, "Sleep now. Boaz later."

Charlotte ran into the art studio. She had on her new shirt with the stars. Mr. De Vries waved her over to the paint table. "Today we paint!" he said. Charlotte saw red paint. She saw yellow paint. She saw blue paint. "Can I paint now?" she asked. "First, put on this apron," said Mr. De Vries. "An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Charlotte put it on. Her star shirt stayed clean under it.

Charlotte got a brush. She dipped it in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred them on her paper. "What is this new colour?" she asked. Sadie leaned over. "That's green!" she said. Charlotte gasped. Blue and yellow made green!

A dot of green paint flew up. It landed on her apron, not her shirt. Charlotte laughed and laughed. Then she dipped her brush in red. "Yellow, your turn!" she said.

Liam sat on the playroom floor with his crayons. He wanted to draw the sky for his sun picture. He picked up a gray crayon. He looked out the window. The sun was bright. He counted, "One, two, three sunny beams." Then he looked again. The sky was not gray today. He asked himself, "What color is the sky?" He saw it and answered, "It is blue!"

Liam put the gray crayon down. He picked the blue crayon instead. He drew a big blue sky. He drew a yellow sun in it. Noam came to play. Noam drew a red bird. Brooklyn drew a green tree. The tree went under the blue sky. "Nice sky," said Noam. "Thank you," said Liam. The crayon felt slippery in his hand, so he held it tight.

They taped the picture to the window. Ms. Demetriou, the neighbor, peeked in and smiled. Liam looked at the real sky. Then he looked at his paper sky. They were both blue. He would remember this. "One sky outside, one sky inside," he said. Brooklyn laughed and pointed at the yellow sun. Liam held the picture up to the light.

Rosalie wanted to play the guessing game at daycare. Kolton and Liliana were already at the table. Mr. Mendoza had put three things in a soft bag.

"Close your eyes," said Mr. Mendoza. Rosalie squeezed her eyes shut. She put her hand in the bag. Her fingers found something. It felt bumpy all over. "A pinecone!" she said. Kolton clapped.

Next Rosalie felt something soft. It tickled her fingertips. It was light like a cloud. "A feather!" she said. Liliana laughed and clapped too.

Last, her fingers found a smooth stone. It was not bumpy at all. It was not soft. It felt round and cool. Rosalie was careful and held it gently. "A stone!" she said. "Yes," said Mr. Mendoza. "Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy."

After the game, Rosalie found a feather on the floor. She let Liliana have it. Liliana smiled and put it by the toy bird's nest. "Soft bed for the baby bird," she said.

Beatrice wanted to play hide-and-seek. Leona and Agatha wanted to play too. "You seek first," said Leona. Beatrice put her hands over her eyes. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She counted very, very fast. Then she turned around. Leona and Agatha were still standing in the middle of the room. They had not hidden at all.

"You counted too fast," said Agatha. "Count slowly so we can hide." Beatrice nodded. She put her hands over her eyes again. This time she counted slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Behind her, she heard little feet pitter-patter. She heard a chair scrape. She heard the coat rack jiggle.

When she opened her eyes, the room was quiet. Beatrice looked behind the clean paint pots. She looked out at the white snow on the window sill. Then she saw two shoes under the coat rack. "I see Leona!" she called. Leona laughed and came out. "You learn fast," she said. Beatrice smiled and pointed at the big coat. "And I see Agatha's hair." Agatha peeked out from behind the coat. "Your turn to seek now," said Beatrice.

Mya climbed the school bus. It was her very first day. The seats were deep and soft. The bus gave a big rumble.

Mya sat next to a girl named Elora. "I hope I do everything right," said Mya. "I don't know the rules yet."

"Don't worry," said Elora. "A classroom has rules that everyone in the class follows. You will learn them too."

"Everyone?" said Mya.

"Even Ms. Grewal!" said Elora. She giggled. "She tries so hard to walk in the hall."

The bus stopped at the school. Ms. Grewal met them at the door. She read the rules out loud. Raise your hand. Hang up your coat. Then she hung up her own coat.

"She did a rule!" Mya whispered.

Elora laughed. "Every day," she said. "Want to try one too?"

Mya hung her coat right beside it.

Leah wanted to play with her friend Blakely. Blakely was coming to Leah's house today.

The doorbell rang. Leah ran to the door. Her mom opened it. Blakely stood there with her coat on. But Blakely's mouth was turned down. Her eyebrows were low. Her face looked sad.

"Blakely, your face looks sad," said Leah. "What is wrong?"

"I lost my toy bunny," said Blakely. "I brought him here. Now I cannot find him."

Leah thought hard. "Where did you go first?" she asked.

"We took off our coats," said Blakely.

The two girls ran to the coat hooks. Leah looked down low. Blakely looked up high. There was the coat pile on the floor. Leah picked up Blakely's coat. Something soft fell out.

"My bunny!" said Blakely. Now her mouth turned up. Her eyes were bright. Her face looked happy.

"Your face is happy now," said Leah.

Blakely hugged the bunny tight. "Let's go play," she said. She held Leah's hand. They ran to the toy room together.

Madelyn found a book on her bed. It was a book about a puppy who could chase butterflies.

She opened the book from the back. "That is funny," she said. The puppy was already home. The butterflies were gone. The story was all mixed up!

"What a mixed-up day," said Madelyn. She turned a page. Now the puppy was wet. Then he was dry. Then he was sleepy. "What a mixed-up day," she said again.

Grandpa peeked in the door. "That story sounds funny," he said. He sat down on the bed with her. Madelyn showed him the pages. Grandpa turned the book around in his hands.

Madelyn looked at the front. She saw the puppy at the start. He was a small puppy, waking up. She turned the pages one by one. The puppy chased a blue butterfly. He ran past a nice red flower. He splashed in a puddle. At the end, the puppy went home to sleep.

"So that is his day," said Madelyn. She patted the back cover. "Good night, puppy." Then she hugged the book tight.

Beau ran to the story rug at daycare. Story time! Story time! He sat down next to David and Lev.

Mr. Sutherland held up a big book. Then he put on his glasses. "Why do you put those on?" asked Beau. "Glasses help me see more clearly," said Mr. Sutherland. Beau looked with his eyes. The glasses looked shiny.

Then Beau listened with his ears. Mr. Sutherland read about a soft feather. He passed around a real one! Beau touched it with his fingers. So smooth! He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled like nothing at all.

At snack time, Beau tasted a sweet apple. Yum!

Then Mr. Sutherland carried the book close to Beau's face. "Too fuzzy," said Beau. He held up the glasses. "Can I try?" He put them on. Now the pictures looked big and clear!

"My turn!" said David.
"My turn!" said Lev.
Beau smiled and passed the glasses on.

Ibrahim sat in a big soft chair. His mama sat next to him. The room had lots of chairs and lots of families. A baby was sleeping in a seat. A girl was looking at a book.

"When is my turn?" asked Ibrahim.

"We wait here until the nurse calls your name," said Mama. "This room is for waiting."

Ibrahim did not want to wait. He wanted to go home to his warm kitchen. He did not want a shot. He wanted his cold juice from the fridge. His tummy felt funny.

Then the door popped open. A nurse looked out. "Ibrahim!" she called.

Mama held his hand. They walked in. The nurse rubbed his arm with a soft cold wipe. "Look at the window," she said. Ibrahim saw a bird outside.

Quick! The shot was done. Mama put a small round bandage on his arm. "All done," said Mama.

At home, Ibrahim got his cold juice. He looked at his round bandage. "I waited," he said, "and then it was my turn." He gave Mama a big hug.

Maverick went to the store with his dad. The store smelled like fresh bread. Maverick loved the fresh bread.

"One bread, two apples, three carrots," said Dad. That was the list.

Then Maverick saw the ice cream man setting up. Ice cream! At his store! Maverick felt so excited. He jumped. He jumped again. He bounced on his toes. He wanted to shout, "Ice cream!"

"Whoa," said Dad with a smile. "Your feet are very bouncy."

"My body wants to jump," said Maverick.

"When we feel excited, we might want to jump, bounce or shout," said Dad. "Let's find a calm way to wait."

Maverick held Dad's hand. He counted the floor tiles. "One tile, two tiles, three tiles." His feet got quieter. But his smile stayed big.

While they waited, a little girl dropped her magnet. It rolled under the shelf. Maverick saw it. He got down low and reached. He wiped the dust off with his sleeve and gave it back.

"Thank you," said the girl.

"You found my magnet," said her mom.

Then it was time. Maverick got a small vanilla cone. He held it with two hands. He took one big lick.

"Yummy," said Maverick. "Best wait ever."

Jules was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut!" They walked to the salon down the street. Jules was so excited.

The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Jules saw the shiny blades. He grabbed a piece of his hair. "No!" he said. "I want to keep my hair!" He was scared it would be gone forever. Grandma knelt down next to him. "It's okay," she said. "Hair grows back after it is cut." Jules looked at Grandpa. Grandpa lifted his hat. His head had fuzzy new hair. "See," said Grandpa. "Mine got cut too. Now it is growing back!" Jules touched his own soft curls. He took a big breath. "Okay. Cut it!"

Snip, snip, snip. Little pieces fell down like a warm rain. The hairdresser gave him a mirror. Jules saw a big boy looking back. "Wow!" he said. Then they walked home to Grandma's house. A little snake sat on a rock in the garden, warming itself in the sun. Jules waved at it. "Look, Grandma! I have short hair now!" he shouted. "But it will grow back. Just like Grandpa's!" Grandma laughed and held his hand all the way up the steps.

Audrey stood at the pool with her dad. The water was blue and splashy. Audrey wanted to jump in the deep end, like Austin. Austin was big. He jumped in with a big splash.

Mr. Mori the swim teacher waved. "Come here, Audrey," he said. "This is the shallow end." Audrey looked down. In the shallow end, her feet could touch the bottom. In the deep end, Austin's head went under the water. That end was deep. This end was not.

Audrey held the wall. Mr. Mori helped her kick. "Kick, one, two. Kick, one, two," he counted. Audrey kicked and kicked. The water went stir, stir, stir around her toes. It tickled. She laughed. Austin swam past like a real fish. "Someday I will swim there," Audrey said. Austin laughed too. "Someday," he said.

After the lesson, Dad dried her hair. "Big splash tomorrow?" he asked. Audrey nodded. She looked at the deep end. Then she looked at the shallow end. "Little splashes first," she said. She hopped into her towel with a plop.

A big cardboard box sat in the corner of the classroom. Lydia wanted it to be a car. "Vroom, vroom," she said. But Santiago wanted it to be a boat. "A boat goes splash," he said.

"No, a car," said Lydia. They both pulled on the box. Mr. Fortin came over. "You can take turns," he said. "First a car, then a boat."

Lydia climbed in. She turned a paper plate. It was the wheel. She beeped a toy horn. "My car is going fast," she said. Then it was Santiago's turn. Lydia shut her eyes and helped rock the box. "Splash, splash," they said. "We are on the sea."

Then Lydia had an idea. "Now let's make it a house," she said. They set a doll inside. They gave the doll a blanket. "The box can be anything," said Lydia. "That's true!" said Santiago. Mr. Fortin smiled and wrote the number one on a card. "One magic box," he said.

Lydia tucked the doll in again. "Good night, little house," she whispered.

Sophie was in her bed. It was bedtime. Her toy drum sat on the chair. She remembered lunch today. She had eaten salty popcorn at school. Then the drum came out. Sophie banged the drum. Boom, boom, boom! She felt so excited. She jumped up and down.

Then Sophie saw her friend Shea. Shea put her hands over her ears. Shea looked scared of the big boom. Sophie stopped. She asked, "Do you not like the drum?" Shea said, "It is too loud for me." Sophie felt surprised. She loved the drum. But Shea did not. Two friends felt different about one drum.

Sophie thought hard. She put the drum down. She picked up a soft scarf. She waved the scarf slowly. Shea peeked out and smiled. Now Shea looked happy too. They played the quiet scarf game until Ms. Clarke said it was time to rest.

Now it was bedtime. The drum was far away. Sophie hugged her teddy. Her dad walked in to say goodnight. Sophie asked, "Can Shea like soft things while I like loud things?" Her dad said, "Yes, she can." Sophie smiled. She closed her eyes and dreamed of scarves floating up, up, up.

Athena sat on Grandma's big soft couch. The game was on TV. Grandpa held a fork with cheese on it. He waved it at the screen.

"Watch now," said Grandpa. "The crowd will get loud."

A man kicked the ball into the net. The whole crowd stood up. They cheered and clapped for their team. Athena clapped too, very loud.

Then she saw the other team score. Their fans stood up and cheered too. Athena jumped up and clapped for them, loudest of all.

Gianna started to giggle. "That is the wrong team, Athena!"

Athena looked at the fans. Blue shirts clapped for the blue team. Red shirts clapped for the red team. She laughed and laughed.

"Okay," said Athena. "Next time I clap for blue."

The blue team scored again. Athena stood on the couch cushions. She clapped and cheered, "Go blue, go blue!"

"Feet down, please," said Grandma, smiling. Athena sat back down fast.

Then the room got quiet. Jaxxon sneaked some cheese with Grandpa's fork. "This cheese is smelly," he whispered, "but I like it."

Athena clapped her hands one more time, just because.

Isabelle sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. "Where are we going?" she asked. Mom smiled. "To ride bikes with Caiden." Isabelle looked out the window. She saw a big red truck. It went vroom. She saw a dog on a leash. The dog stayed close to its owner.

At the park, Caiden was there. He had a small bike. Isabelle wanted to ride right away. She ran to the bike and put her hands on it. But where was her helmet? She looked around. Then she saw it. It was still in the car, sitting on the seat! She ran back with Mom. Mom helped her put the helmet on. It snapped under her chin. Caiden had a helmet too. His was blue with stars.

"Look what my helmet can do," said Caiden. He gave his helmet a gentle tap. Tap, tap. It made a funny sound, like a drum! Isabelle tapped hers too. What a surprise! Two helmets, two drums. Then they rode their bikes on the path. Isabelle pedaled and pedaled. Mom stayed close behind. "Look at me!" Isabelle called. And off she went, all the way to the big tree.

Alexis had a cold. His nose was red and his arm felt tired. "Can I run outside?" he asked. "Not yet," his dad said. "Rest first. Then your body gets better."

Dad drove Alexis to the pharmacy. The pharmacist gave them orange medicine. "This will help," she said. "Take it, then rest on the couch." Alexis had a question. "Does rest help too?" "Yes," Dad said. "Resting in bed or on the couch helps your body get better."

At home, Alexis lay on the couch. He counted his pillows. One, two, three. He read his truck book. He spoke quietly to his teddy bear. Then he slept for a long time.

When he woke up, his nose was better. "Wow," said Alexis. "Rest made me well!" He jumped up and hugged his teddy tight.

James and his grandma went to the pharmacy. The doctor's room was at the back. Today James would get a shot. He was very brave and very excited.

First the nurse said, "Step on the scale." James hopped on. He wiggled his toes. The numbers jumped up and down. "Wow!" said James. He wiggled more. The numbers jumped more.

"Hold still," said the nurse. James stood still like a statue. The numbers stopped jumping. The scale showed how much he weighed. "You find your number when you stand still," said James.

Then it was shot time. James looked at his black shoe. He counted one, two, three. The shot was done. "That was fast!" he said. The nurse gave him a smiley sticker. "I did it!" shouted James.

Nathan wanted to cook lunch for his family. Dad said they could make burgers in the backyard. First, Dad turned on the grill. Nathan stood far away and watched.

Nathan got the buns. He put them in a basket. They looked soft and beautiful.

Then Dad cut an onion on the little table. Soon Dad's eyes were wet. Tears ran down his face. Nathan felt worried. He leaned close and whispered, "Are you sad, Dad?"

Dad smiled through his tears. "No," he said. "It is just the onion. When I cut it, it makes my eyes sting and water."

"So you are not sad?" asked Nathan.

"Not one bit," said Dad.

Nathan laughed. He patted Dad's arm. Then he set the buns out, one by one, in a neat little row.

Maria was playing house at daycare. She held her baby doll, Bella. She made pretend pizza for lunch. "Here is your pizza, Bella," she said.

Then Maria dropped Bella on the floor. "Oh no!" said Maria. "Bella got hurt!" Her eyes got big and wet. She picked Bella up and hugged her tight.

Alicia came over. "Is Bella okay?" she asked. Mr. Levy knelt down next to Maria. "The doll cannot really feel," he said. "But you can pretend she does." Maria looked at Bella. Then she patted Bella's head. "There, there," she said softly. "A hug will make you all better."

Alicia brought her toy dog. The dog gave a pretend bark. "Woof!" said Alicia. "My dog wants pizza too." Maria laughed. She gave the dog a pretend slice. Then she laid Bella on a small blanket. "Sleep now, Bella," she said. "Your leg was weak, but now it is strong." Maria covered Bella with a tiny hat. "Shh," said Alicia. The two girls rocked their babies to sleep.

Victor was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa put on a song. It was a song about a little boat.

Victor wanted to sing it all by himself. But he did not know all the words yet. He wanted to clap too, like the big kids did.

First Victor clapped whenever he liked. Clap! Clap! Clap! It sounded all mixed up. "Hmm," said Victor. "The song goes one way. My claps go another way."

Grandpa tapped his foot. "Listen," he said. "Clap at the same time as the beat." Victor listened very hard. The song went chug, chug, chug, steady like a train. Victor waited. Then he clapped when the chug came. Clap! It fit! He clapped again with the next chug. Clap! It fit again.

"Now my claps match," said Victor. He clapped and clapped. Grandpa sang the boat song. Victor tried the words too. "Row, row, row your boat," he sang. The words came out! He had them in his head, like a story he knew.

After the song, Grandpa made popcorn for a snack. "Do not touch the hot pot," said Grandpa. "I will pour. You can hold the bowl." Victor held the bowl very still. The popcorn tumbled in. They each took a bite. "Salty," said Victor, licking his lips. "Yum."

"Again," said Victor. So Grandpa played the boat song once more. Victor clapped right with the beat and sang every word. Grandpa clapped too, at the very same time.

text:
Samuel ran to the playground after snack. He reached into his pocket. His little red car was gone. "Oh no," said Samuel. "Where is my car?"

He looked by the slide. No car. He looked under the swing. No car. He looked in the sand. No car there either. Samuel sat down on the grass. Oaklyn came over to help. "I will help you look," she said.

Then Samuel stopped. He thought hard. "I had my car at snack time," he said. "I was eating my crackers." The snack table was still outside. Samuel ran to it. He looked down. His red car was under the bench, right by the table. "I found it!" said Samuel. He held it up high.

"Your car was hiding," said Oaklyn. "What a silly car." Samuel laughed. He put the car in his pocket. Then he pushed it across the bench. "Beep, beep," said Samuel. "Want to play cars with me?"

Cooper wanted to make bread for his family. Mom said he could help. He poured flour into the big bowl. He added water and mixed it with a spoon. Then he touched the dough with his hands. It was soft and warm and very sticky. The dough stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Cooper. "Is it ruined?"

Mom smiled. "Let me show you what cooks do. We push the dough. Then we fold it over. Push and fold, push and fold." Cooper pushed the dough down. He folded it over. He pushed and folded again and again. The dough felt smooth now. It did not stick to his hands anymore. "It changed!" said Cooper. "My hands made it smooth." Mom laughed. Cooper kicked his feet with joy.

The bread went into the oven. Mom put it in and took it out. The kitchen smelled warm and good. At the last bite, Cooper's dad gave him a big hug. "We will make more," said Cooper. "And tomorrow we can go to the store for more flour."

Eva ran to the park with her water bottle. Today was soccer day! Mr. Greco waved from the grass. Laurier and Bo were already there. The sun was big and hot.

They ran and kicked the ball. Eva touched the ball with her toe. Bo kicked it far. Laurier laughed and chased it. Eva ran and ran. Her face turned red. She did not feel good.

Mr. Greco blew his whistle. "Break time!" he called. Laurier drank from her bottle. Bo drank from his bottle. Eva looked in her bag. Her bottle was not there. It was at home! She had left it on the table.

Just then a naughty dog ran by with a sock. Eva giggled. Then the coach came over. She held out a cup of water. "Here you go," she said. Eva drank it all up. The water was cool. She felt better fast.

Then Mr. Greco blew the whistle again. Eva ran back to the game. She kicked the ball to Bo. "Goal!" Bo shouted. Eva jumped up high. She held her cup up too. "More water at the next break!" she said.

Arlo sat at the little table. Mr. Gagnon put a plate of warm cookies down. "We learn our five senses today," said Mr. Gagnon. "Eyes see. Ears hear. Hands touch. Tongues taste. Noses smell."

Arlo looked at the cookies. He could smell them. Sweet and warm!

Then Laurence pinched his nose shut. He sniffed and sniffed. "I can't smell my cookie!" he said. His voice sounded funny, like a little train toot.

Arlo laughed. He pinched his nose shut too. Sniff. Sniff. Nothing! No smell at all.

He let go of his nose. Sniff. The sweet smell came back!

"You were brave to try," said Mr. Gagnon. Arlo took a tiny bite. "Mmm. My tongue tastes it! And now my nose smells it again."

"Look," said Arlo. "I can rip my napkin for the crumbs." He ripped it into pieces. Laurence laughed and tooted like a train again.

Ivy sat at the big camp table. She was making a paper sun. She wanted to cut out yellow circle shapes.

Abraham sat next to her. He had small scissors with round tips. "Why are your scissors little?" Ivy asked him.

"I don't know," said Abraham. "Ask Ms. Mokoena."

Ivy held up the big sharp scissors. "Can I use these?" she asked.

Ms. Mokoena shook her head. She took the big scissors away. Then she put small scissors in Ivy's hand. "These are safety scissors," she said. "You cut paper with these while I watch."

Ivy squeezed the little scissors. Snip, snip! They cut the paper. The yellow circles fell onto the table. "They catch the paper and cut it!" said Ivy. "Can they pick up a magnet too?"

"Try one thing at a time," laughed Ms. Mokoena.

Ivy glued her circles down. Then she hung her sun in the window. It was beautiful.

"Look, Abraham!" she said. "My sun shines!"

Lucas sat on the red carpet in the music room. Mr. Girma picked up a drum. He tapped it slowly. Tap, tap, tap.

"Clap with me," said Mr. Girma. Lucas tried. His claps came too fast. He stopped and waited. Tap, tap, tap. He tried again. This time his hands went tap, tap, tap too. The drum made the beat, and his claps followed it.

"Now we sing," said Mr. Girma. Zaynab and Axelle sat beside Lucas. They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star". Lucas knew some of the words. He hummed the parts he forgot. Then Axelle sang the ABC song instead. Lucas listened hard. He tilted his head.

"Wait," said Lucas. "The ABC song sounds just like our star song." He sang the star tune, one, two, three. Then he sang the ABC tune. They were the same! Zaynab clapped her hands. "Sing it again," she said. So Lucas sang the star words. Then he sang the letters. Same tune, both times.

Mr. Girma smiled and played his purple shaker. Tap, tap, tap went the beat. Lucas clapped along and sang the star song all the way through, every word. Axelle blew him a kiss. "You did it," she said. Lucas bowed, quick and small, like a big singer on a stage.

Claire was at daycare. It was walk day! "We will walk to the park," said Mr. Owusu. "Hooray!" said Claire. Lacey held one hand. Amin held the other.

At the curb, the cars went zoom, zoom, zoom. "Red means stop," said Claire. The light was red. The cars stopped. Then the light turned green. "Green means go!" said Claire. The cars went. Mr. Owusu laughed. "Now we can go," he said. The children walked across.

At the park, Claire found a red leaf and a green one. "Careful," said Amin. "The slide is hot in the sun." They sat in the shade instead. The cool air felt good. "When we go back, you can call the light again," said Mr. Owusu. Claire jumped up. "Red, stop! Green, go!"

Wyatt ran to Grandpa's garden with his trowel. "Today we plant seeds!" he said. Grandpa helped him dig little holes. Wyatt dropped a seed in each one. Then he patted the soft, brown soil on top. "Now we wait," said Grandpa.

The next day there was big news. A tiny green sprout was up! Wyatt jumped and clapped. But a weed grew right next to it. "That one has to go," said Grandpa. Wyatt pulled the weed, gently, gently. Pop! Out it came. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom. "Wow!" said Wyatt. He looked and looked. The roots had grown down into the soil.

Wyatt touched the soil where his sprout stood. Down there, under the dirt, his plant had roots too. Roots growing down, down, down. He watered the soil and smiled big. "Grow, roots, grow!"

Beatrice sat in the living room on the sunny rug. The cat slept in a warm patch of sun. Beatrice wanted to draw on the tablet. But the tablet was dark and still.

"How do I make it wake up?" she asked. Her mom showed her the little button on the side. Beatrice pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up bright. She had made that happen.

Next came the drawing app. It was a green square with a paintbrush on it. Beatrice tapped it once. Colors bloomed on the screen, red and yellow and blue. She drew a big cat with long whiskers. She drew the sunny window too.

Then it was time for dinner. Beatrice picked up the tablet with one hand. It slipped and wobbled. "Oh no!" she said. She nearly dropped it on the rug. She caught it and held it with two hands. Now it sat steady in her arms. It did not slip at all.

She carried it to the shelf, two hands all the way. She set it down, pressed the button, and the screen went dark. "Night night, tablet," she whispered. The real cat opened one eye. Then it purred and went back to sleep.

Hunter sat at the kitchen table. He had a little pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. But the pencil slipped in his fingers. The letters came out wobbly and mixed up. "This is too hard," he said.

His dad sat down next to him. "Try again," Dad said. He showed Hunter how to hold the pencil. Hunter gripped it the way Dad did. He wrote his name one time. Then he wrote it again. The next day, he wrote it again. Each day, he wrote it more.

One morning, Hunter looked at his paper. The letters were neat and straight. "Did the letters get easier?" he asked. Dad smiled. "You wrote them so many times." Hunter wrote his name one more time. Then he drew a star beside it.

Isabelle could not find her bunny. Bunny was soft and grey with one long ear. She looked under her bed. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. Only blocks and a ball. The floor felt cold on her bare feet.

"Where did you go, Bunny?" she said. She looked in the kitchen. Mom was there. "Did you feed Bunny a carrot?" Isabelle asked. Mom smiled and shook her head. Then Isabelle looked at her coat on the hook. The coat was puffy and fat. She pushed her hand into the coat pocket. Something soft was inside. Bunny was tucked in the pocket, warm and snug.

"You were hiding in the coat!" said Isabelle. She hugged Bunny close. Mom helped her put on her boots. "Let's take Bunny outside," said Mom. Isabelle held Bunny's paw all the way to the door.

Jackson walked to the park with his dad. A small puppy pulled on a rope beside them. The puppy was brown and white. "This is my first pet," Jackson said. "His name is Max."

In the park, Jackson saw Louane and Lennyn. They ran over to see Max. Louane patted Max's soft ears. Lennyn gave Max a little brush with a soft brush. Jackson counted the things Max needed: a bowl, a blanket, a collar, and a leash.

Then a bird landed near the grass. Max wanted to chase the bird! He pulled hard. But the leash was clipped to his collar. Dad held the leash, so Max stayed close. Jackson watched the puppy try and try. Max could not run away. "The leash keeps him close to you," said Louane.

A big truck rumbled past the park gate. Max wanted to chase that too. Dad held the leash tight. Max sat down by Jackson's feet. "Good boy," Jackson said. He gave Max his favorite green ball. Max dropped the ball at Jackson's shoe. "Again," said Jackson, and threw it far across the grass.

Ellie sat at the big table in the community hall. There was warm bread on a plate. Ellie was hungry. Her tummy made a little growl.

Josiah sat next to her. Rosalia sat across from her. Mr. Wilson stood at the head of the table. "We say a blessing first," said Mr. Wilson. "Everyone waits."

Ellie did not know about waiting. She reached for the bread. Her hand stopped in the air. Rosalia shook her head. Ellie put the bread down. Her hands sat in her lap, loose and still.

Mr. Wilson began the blessing. His voice was slow and kind. Ellie listened. Josiah listened. Rosalia listened too. Then Mr. Wilson said, "Amen."

"Now we eat," said Mr. Wilson. Ellie picked up the bread. It was soft and warm. "We waited," said Ellie. "Yes, we did," said Rosalia. Ellie took a big bite and smiled.

Grandpa came to stay with Hazel for a whole week. On Monday they went to the big park near her house. Grandpa brought a small box. Inside was a card game. "You go first," said Grandpa. Hazel put down a card. Then she reached to go again. "Wait," said Grandpa. "Now it is my turn." Grandpa put down his card. Then he pointed to Hazel. "Your turn," he said. They went back and forth like that. One card for Hazel. One card for Grandpa. "We are taking turns," said Grandpa. Hazel laughed and clapped.

Hazel's friend Valerie came over to play. Valerie wanted to go first every time. Hazel felt a little mad. Then she had an idea. "One card for you," said Hazel. "Then one card for me." Valerie tried it. It worked! The game was fun for both of them. After the game, they picked a yellow flower and gave it to Grandpa. "Thank you," said Grandpa. "Shall we mix up the cards and play one more time?"

Axel was painting a big flower at school. He used red and blue paint. Then the bell rang. It was time for a snack. But Axel's hands were covered in paint. "You must wash first," said Ms. Bondarenko. "The paint has to come off." Axel went to the little sink. He held his hands under the water. The paint stayed on his hands. It would not come off. Axel frowned. His friend Moses came to help. "Try the soap," said Moses. Axel rubbed the soap on his hands. Then he added water. Bubbles grew on his hands! Lots of soft white bubbles. "Look!" said Axel. "Soap and water make bubbles!" He rubbed some bubbles on his chin. "I have a bubble beard!" said Axel. Moses laughed and laughed. Mivaan made one too. Then the three friends rinsed their hands. The paint went down the drain.
