"That was brave of you, Moses," said Ms. Bondarenko, "trying the soap too." "Our hands are clean now," said Axel. "Snack time!"

Elias went to the store with his dad. He wanted a green apple. The apples sat high on a shelf. Elias could not reach them.

He waited by the cart. Then he saw Ms. Johansson from his class. She was picking out bread. "Can you help me, please?" Elias asked. "I cannot reach the apples." Ms. Johansson smiled and got one down for him. "Thank you," said Elias.

A new boy stood next to them. He was Michael's cousin. He took the last green apple by mistake. Elias had waited so long. "Sorry," the boy said. He gave the apple to Elias. Then the boy said, "Gracias."

Elias looked up. "What does that mean?" he asked.

"It means thank you," the boy said. "My family speaks Spanish."

"Gracias," said Elias. It was a new word. It felt good in his mouth.

At the grass outside the store, Elias held his apple up high. "Gracias," he said again, and took a big bite.

Elias sat at the dinner table. His plate had warm rice and peas. He had huge news about a wiggly tooth.

"Mom! Mom! My tooth!" he said.

Mom was talking to Dad. "Wait for my pause," she said.

Elias chewed a pea. He waited. He looked at his tooth in his spoon. Would waiting work?

Mom stopped talking. There was a quiet little pause.

"Now?" Elias asked.

"Now," said Mom.

"My tooth wiggles! Look!" He showed her.

Mom looked closely. "Wow! May I touch it, please?"

"Okay," said Elias. "But be gentle, please."

Mom touched it softly. "It wiggles!"

"Thank you, Mom," said Elias. "Sorry I talked over you."

Mom smiled. Dad passed the bread. Elias took a piece. He watched Mom talk, then talk some more, then stop. He waited for the pause. Then he said, "Dad, look too!"

William ran to the snack table at daycare. Today was cracker day! But William had a problem. He wanted a square cracker, and his plate was empty.

Mr. Chea held up a big square napkin. "Look, William," he said. "Watch this." William watched. Mr. Chea folded the square napkin in half, edge to edge. William's eyes got big. The square was gone! Now it was a rectangle.

William wanted to try. Mr. Chea gave him a square napkin. It was hard to line up the edges. William thought and thought. He turned the napkin. He tried again. Yes! The corners matched. He pressed the fold flat. "A rectangle!" he shouted.

Frederic came over. "Can I do it too?" he asked. Lucien clapped. Soon everyone was folding. Then Mr. Chea put a square cracker on William's plate. William smiled and took a big bite. "My square is a circle now," he said, holding up the round chewed piece.

Muhammad went to the temple with his mama. It was Diwali, a big bright party. There were small clay cups on a long table. "What are these?" Muhammad asked. "They are called diyas," mama said. Muhammad saw they were empty and cold. He wanted them to glow like the pretty lights on the wall.

A kind grown-up named Ms. Francis gave him a job. Muhammad set the diyas in a row. One, two, three, four. He was careful. His friend Reece came to help too. Then the grown-up poured oil in each one. She held the match far from Muhammad's hands. She touched the flame to a wick. A tiny light woke up. Then another, and another.

Soon the whole row glowed. Muhammad hid his face in mama's blanket because the room felt too bright. But the little flames were soft and warm. "They stay lit all night," mama whispered. Muhammad watched one small flame dance. "Hello, light," he said.

Connor ran out to the backyard. His brown dog ran with him. Today was soccer day. Emilio and Aura were coming too.

Connor wanted to kick the ball right away. He ran to it fast. Then his foot hit a slick spot of grass. His shoe would slip! He sat down with a bump. "Oof," he said.

Mr. Thompson, the coach, blew his whistle. "Time to warm up first," he said. "We run, then we stretch." Connor and Emilio jogged around the yard. Aura reached down and touched her toes. Connor's legs felt awake now. His heart went thump, thump, thump.

Then the game began. Connor ran to the ball. No slip this time! He kicked it all the way to Aura. She laughed and kicked it back. "Faster than a bunny," Emilio said. Connor giggled and chased the ball again.

Victor was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big garden by the river. Victor wanted to grow peas. He dug little holes with his hands. He dropped the seeds in. Then he covered them up.

Every day Victor came to look. The sun shone. The rain fell. Small green leaves came up. The plants grew tall. Then Victor saw something odd. There were long green things on the plant. They were not leaves.

"What is that?" Victor asked.

"Pick one," said Grandpa.

Victor picked a long green pod. He squeezed it. Pop! It opened. Inside was a little row of peas. They sat in a line, like beads.

Victor laughed. He picked more pods. He popped them open, one by one. Grandpa caught the peas in a bowl.

"These are ours," said Victor. He held one up to the sun. It was round and small and green.

Blake went to the store with her dad. She wanted the yellow box of cereal. Her tummy felt funny because she skipped breakfast.

At the cereal shelf, Blake saw Waris from her class. Waris was telling his mom about the red box. Blake started to talk too. "I want the yellow one!"

Waris stopped talking. He looked down at his shoes. His mom said, "Wait, Waris. Let Blake talk." Blake said her whole wish fast. Then she felt her face get hot.

Blake took a big breath. She put her hand on her mouth. "Sorry, Waris. You talk first." Waris smiled. He told about the red box to the end. Then it was Blake's turn. His mom said, "That was fair. You both got a turn."

They walked to the line together. Waris let Blake go first. Then Waris went next. "Bye, Blake," said Waris. Blake waved her yellow box high.

Zachary woke up early at Grandma's house. The sun was up and he was awake too. Grandma made hot toast. She put it on his plate.

"Now we make breakfast," said Grandma. She gave Zachary a little butter knife. Zachary poked the toast with the tip of the knife. The toast got a hole. Butter went everywhere in little lumps. Grandma waited. "Try again," she said.

Zachary looked at the knife. He turned it over. He put the flat side on the butter. Then he pushed the butter across the bread. The flat side spread it smooth and shiny. "Look!" said Zachary. Then he poured milk into his cup, slow and steady. Only one small drip. He chewed his toast and took a big drink.

"Dinner will be fun tonight," said Grandma. "You can help me pour."

Milan was at Grandma's house. He could not find his blue bunny. He looked under the bed. No bunny. He looked in the toy box. No bunny.

Milan wanted to give up. He sat on the floor. "I will ask for help," he said. He found his big sister. "Will you help me look?" he asked. She said yes. He found his grandpa. "Will you help me look?" he asked. Grandpa said yes too.

Now they were all looking. Milan looked by the couch. His sister looked by the chair. Grandpa used a spoon from the kitchen to dig in the big plant pot. The dirt was cool and soft. There was bunny! Bunny was hiding in the pot!

"More people looking, more places found," said Grandpa with a smile.

Milan hugged his bunny tight. "We found him together," said Milan.

Matthew sat on the rug at school. A big box of blocks sat next to him. He wanted to build a tower.

Arnaud came over. Iyla came over too. Matthew hugged the box close. He gave all the blocks to Arnaud. Iyla got none. Iyla's face went sad. Her hands were empty.

Matthew looked at Iyla. Then he looked at the blocks. He split the blocks into two piles. One pile for Arnaud. One pile for Iyla. Iyla smiled big. She stacked her blocks up high.

"Everyone gets a chance," said Mr. Ito. He pointed to a striped rabbit toy on the shelf. "You can hold the rabbit when it is your turn. You follow the same rule."

Matthew waited for his turn. He waited and waited. Then it was his turn. He held the soft rabbit. He built a little tower next to it. "Look, rabbit," said Matthew. "A tower for you."

Brielle stood on her balcony with Mom. She had three little pots of sand and soil. "One, two, three," she counted. "Carrots, carrots, carrots." She patted the soil and gave each pot a drink of water.

Every morning Brielle looked. Then one day, green leaves popped up. But tall, wild leaves popped up too. "Yucky weeds," said Brielle. "You are grumpy plants." She reached for a small leaf to pull it out.

"Wait," said Mom. "That one is a baby carrot. It grows where we want it. The weeds grow where we do not want them." Brielle looked and looked. She pulled the tall wild one. She patted the baby carrot. "Stay right there," she said. "You are mine." She wiped her dirty hands on her shirt and smiled at her three pots.

Brooks stood by the sink. The bath water was running low and slow. Daddy put a slice of lemon on the edge of the sink. "That is for my drink," Daddy said.

Brooks looked at the lemon with his eyes. It was bright and yellow. He heard the water splash with his ears. The soap smelled like apple next to the tub. "Can I taste it?" Brooks asked. Daddy said, "Just a little lick."

Brooks touched the lemon with one finger. It felt cool and bumpy. Then he stuck out his tongue and licked it. His whole face scrunched up. His cheeks went tight. "Sour!" said Daddy with a smile. "Lemons taste sour."

Brooks drank some water. Then he made the lemon dance on his finger, round and round. "Sour lemon," he said, "you made my face go squish."

Felix wanted his favorite book. It was the one about the little red truck. He could not find it on the shelf.

"I want the truck book," he said. Mom looked too. There were so many books. Big ones and little ones. Some had sticky spots from his jammy hands.

Then Mom held one book up. She put her finger under the words on the front. "These words are the title," she said. "The title is the book's name."

Felix looked hard. The marks were small and black. Mom read them out loud. "Little Red Truck," she said. "That is this book's name."

So words could say a name! Felix took his pencil. He drew the marks on paper. His marks were wobbly. But he tried.

"Now I can find it," he said. He went back to the shelf. He looked at the fronts of the books. He asked Mom, "What is this one called?" She said each title out loud.

"Blue Boat," said one front. "Sleepy Bear," said another.

Then Felix saw it. There, on a big blue book, were the words he knew. "Little Red Truck!" he said. He pulled it out. He held it up high.

Felix sat on the rug. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. Mom sat down next to him.

"Read the title page," said Felix. Mom smiled and pointed. There were the words again, right inside.

"Lucky we stuck with it," said Mom.

Felix patted the book. "Good book," he said. "I found you by your name."

Miles was at the beach with his class. His teacher, Mr. Navarro, took them to the pool by the sea. "Today we learn to kick," said Mr. Navarro.

Miles wanted to swim like a fish. But when he let go of the wall, he wobbled. He held on tight to the edge. Then he tried something. He held the edge and kicked his legs fast. Splash! Splash! Water flew up and hit Mr. Navarro's shirt. "Oh!" said Mr. Navarro, laughing and wiping his face.

"Can I kick here without going under?" Miles asked. "Yes, hold the edge and kick," said Mr. Navarro. So Miles held the wall and kicked. His legs went up and down like a fish tail. The water made big waves. Jannat held the edge too. She kicked and splashed Miles. Miles giggled. Jaxson held on and kicked even harder. He splashed them all.

The sky turned gray and rainy far away over the sea. The water in the pool turned a soft blue color. Miles watched his legs. Kick, kick, kick. "Look, Mr. Navarro, I can kick and stay right here!" said Miles. Mr. Navarro smiled and shook the water from his hair.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. It was dark. Very dark. "Mama!" Ezra did yell. Mama came fast with a hug. "The power is out," she said. "We are okay."

Ezra could not see anything at all. He could not see the sofa. He could not see his toy truck. Was the dark mean? He held Mama's hand. They sat still on the sofa. His bottom sat on a soft cushion, so he knew where he was.

Then something funny happened. Ezra waited a little while. He looked and looked. Slowly, he could see the sofa. Then he could see the table. Then his truck by the door! "Mama, my eyes can see now!" he said. "The dark is not so dark anymore." He smiled at the shapes in the room.

Hayden stood by the school gate. His brother waved and walked away. The playground was big and sunny. Ms. Yoon rang a little bell.

"Time to walk to our room," said Ms. Yoon. Maha stood behind her. Amirah stood behind Maha. They stood one after another. Hayden did not know why. He ran to the front. He ran past everyone. Ms. Yoon stopped walking.

"Hayden, find your spot in the line," said Ms. Yoon. Hayden looked. The line went one after another, all the way to Amirah. There was a space near Maha. Hayden stepped into the space. The line started to walk again.

The class walked through the hall. The hall was long. Hayden saw that when everyone walked in the line, no one got lost. The line moved like one long caterpillar. Hayden grabbed his own strap on his backpack. It was a little heavy. Maha looked back and smiled at him.

The line stopped at a door. It was their room. Amirah went in first. Then Maha. Then Hayden. "I like the line," said Hayden.

Ms. Yoon smiled. "Tomorrow we will walk in the line again."

Elizabeth sat in a big chair. The chair went up and up. The hairdresser put a cloth around her. Then the hairdresser used the scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down like soft snow.

Elizabeth sat very still. She waited. The snipping took a long time. At last the hairdresser said, "All done!"

Elizabeth looked in the big wall mirror. She could see the front of her hair. It was short and neat. But she could not see the back. She turned her head one way. She turned her head the other way. No, the back of her hair was still hiding. Elizabeth was a little mad. "I wish I could see the back!" she said.

The hairdresser smiled. She picked up a small mirror in her hand. She held it up behind Elizabeth's head. Now Elizabeth could see the back of her hair! The little mirror and the big mirror worked together.

"I see it! I see my back hair!" said Elizabeth. She looked and looked. Then she jumped down and gave the small mirror a big smile. "Bye-bye, mirror!"

Luka was in the backyard. He helped Dad stack soft blankets in a basket. "The baby is coming home soon," said Dad. Luka patted the top blanket. It was fluffy like a cat.

That night, Luka heard a small cry. It came from the baby's room. He tiptoed to the door. Mom was holding the baby. "She is hungry," Mom said. "I feed her now. I feed her many times, day and night." Luka peeked. The baby drank and made tiny sounds.

The next morning, Luka played by the hose. He made a little river on the stones. "Babies drink lots of milk," he told his friend Vanya. Then he giggled. "But not from my river!" Vanya laughed too. Then the baby sneezed, a tiny baby sneeze, and Luka gasped. "She is so smart already!"

Nolan was at Grandma's house. He wanted to give his bear a tea party. But there was a problem. The teapot was empty.

"Grandma, can we make real tea?" Nolan asked.

"Grandpa is making some in the kitchen," said Grandma. "We must stay away from the hot stove."

Nolan looked at his empty cups. He felt sad. Then Grandma smiled. She picked up the empty teapot. She tipped it over a cup.

"Pretend tea!" she said.

Nolan gasped. Nothing came out. But it was still tea, in his head. He poured for his bear. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" he said.

The bear drank it all. So did the sleepy bunny. Nolan built a little bed from blocks for the bunny's bottom.

"Pretend tea for you, Grandma," said Nolan.

Grandma sipped from the empty cup. "Mmm. Best pretend tea ever."

Grandpa came in with a real teapot. "Room for me?"

"No, Grandpa. We ran out," said Nolan, and he tipped the empty pot again. "Careful, it's pretend hot!"

Rehmat sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She was not sick. She felt fine. So why a shot?

The doctor said, "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses."

Rehmat listened. She looked at her arm. "A tiny shot can do that?" she asked.

"Yes," said the doctor. "It works inside your body."

Rehmat counted to three. One, two, three. The shot went in, quick like a little pinch. Then it was done.

"Yay," said Rehmat. "My body has help now."

Afterward, her dad took her to the ice cream shop. She picked purple grape ice cream. It was cold and sweet on her tongue.

On the counter there was a magnet shaped like a cone. It stuck right to the metal. Rehmat pointed and laughed. "It sticks, like my shot sticks with me!" she said. "One ice cream, one happy arm, one good day."

Arthur had a cough. His tummy felt funny too. His dad took him to the doctor's office. The room had a big chair and a poster with a duck on it. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Arthur said, "Ahh."

The doctor gave Dad a small bottle. It was sticky and pink. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," the doctor said. Dad put the bottle in his bag.

At home, Arthur felt hot. He wanted the pink medicine now. He saw the bottle on the counter. He reached up his hands. Then he stopped. Only a grown-up gives a child medicine. So Arthur waited on his little stool.

"Dad," he called. "Medicine, please." Dad came with a little cup. He poured the pink medicine. "Can you help me hold the cup?" Dad asked. Arthur held it with both hands. He drank it all down. The pink medicine tasted like sweet pears.

Soon Arthur's tummy felt calm. Soon his cough got small. Dad read him a book about the duck. Arthur yawned and hugged his bear. "Night night, medicine," Arthur whispered.

Eloise knelt in the school garden. Ms. Tanaka gave her three small seeds. Eloise patted them into the soil. Then she watered the dirt with a little blue can.

Blake came to help too. Blake planted tomato seeds in the next row. They patted and watered and patted some more. Then the bell rang. Time to go inside.

The next day, Eloise ran to the garden. Tiny green sprouts poked up everywhere. But Eloise forgot which row was hers. "Where are my seeds?" she said. "I can't tell them apart!" Blake forgot too. Blake frowned at the dirt.

Ms. Tanaka held up a stick with a picture on it. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," she said. Eloise smiled big. She wanted labels for every row! She got paper and crayons. She drew a yellow moon on one label. She drew a red apple on another. Blake colored a green bean on a third. Ms. Tanaka helped push the sticks into the ground, one for each row.

Eloise stood by the little signs. The moon label sat by her sprouts. "There you are!" she said. Then she looked closer. One sprout had pushed a label up out of the soil. The stick was crooked, like the sprout was hugging it. Eloise giggled. She patted the stick back down, right next to her moon.

Aiden wanted to see the bath fill up. Mom turned the tap. White steam rose up. It looked like little clouds.

Aiden stepped close. He put his hand near the steam. It felt hot, very hot. Mom caught his hand. "Stay back, Aiden." Aiden stepped back two big steps. He watched from there.

The steam kept going up. It fogged the mirror. Aiden could not see his striped shirt in the glass anymore. He laughed. "Look, Mom! The mirror is all cloudy!"

Mom added cold water. She put her hand in the tub. "Now it is warm," she said. Aiden waited on his little stool. He held his striped towel. He watched the water go up and up.

At last Mom said, "Bath time." Aiden touched the water with one toe. Warm, not hot. He slid in and gave his rubber duck a big splash.

"I stayed back from the steam," Aiden said. Mom smiled and brought the duck to him.

"Quack, quack," said Aiden for the duck.

Ethan woke up and ran to the kitchen. "Mom, am I going to the doctor?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Not that kind," she said. Ethan put a butterfly sticker on his shirt. He was ready.

At the door, Ethan took a big step outside. "The doctor will look at my whole body," he said. Mom laughed. "No, Ethan. This one only wants your teeth." Ethan opened his mouth wide. He showed his teeth to the butterfly sticker.

At the dentist's chair, Ethan sat very still. The dentist counted his teeth. "Ten up here," she said. "Ten down there." Ethan giggled. His toothbrush at home was dirty and old. He got a new green one to take home.

Back home, Ethan brushed and brushed. "The dentist is a tooth doctor," he told the butterfly sticker. "You have no teeth at all!"

Audrey had a cold. Her nose was red and squishy. She sat at the kitchen table in her pajamas.

"Drink your water," said her dad. "Water helps when you are sick."

But Audrey did not feel thirsty. She pushed the cup away. Her throat hurt and her head felt heavy.

Then her dad brought a new cup. It was green. It had a bendy straw and a picture of a bunny. Audrey zipped her lips around the straw. She took one little sip. Then she took another.

Slowly, sip by sip, the cup went empty. Audrey's throat felt better. Her head felt lighter too.

"More water, please," she said.

Her dad filled the cup. Audrey took a big sip and smiled at the bunny.

Matthew sat at the big piano on the stage. The auditorium was quiet. His class was practicing for a little show.

Mr. Farah knelt beside him. "Matthew, you will play the bear," said Mr. Farah. "Can you make a big, growly bear sound?"

Matthew pressed a key on the right side. The sound went high and tinkly. Liana laughed from her seat. "That sounds like a tiny bird!" she said.

Matthew wanted the bear to sound big and low. He wondered, what if he tried the other side? He pressed a key far on the left. The sound came out low and rumbly. "Grrr!" said Matthew. Billie clapped her hands.

He tried the right side again. High. Then the left side again. Low. Like walking down and up a rainbow of sounds, from bird to bear.

"Play the bear walking now," said Mr. Farah.

Matthew played the low keys. Thump, thump, thump. Liana stomped her feet like big bear paws. The sound was low and deep and growly.

"Now the bear sees a little bird," said Mr. Farah.

Matthew's hands slid to the right. Tink, tink, tink. The notes went high and small. Billie giggled.

"Once more, bear!" called Mr. Farah.

Matthew's fingers came back to the low keys. Grrr, thump, grrr. The whole class stomped along. Matthew grinned and played his growliest note yet.

Blake walked home with her dad. She held a small box with holes. Inside was a gray kitten, her very first pet.

At home, Blake set the box on the floor. She opened the lid slowly. The kitten peeked out with big eyes. Then it ran under the bed. Blake sat down and looked under. Two eyes looked back at her.

Blake wanted to pat the kitten. It did not come out. Her dad said, "A new pet may hide while it gets used to its new home." Blake sat on the rug and waited. She waited a long time. She heard the kitten's little steps on the floor.

One soft paw stepped out. Then the whole kitten came out. It sniffed Blake's shoe. It bumped her hand with its tiny nose. Blake patted its soft fur, gentle as a tooth under a pillow. The kitten purred loud. Blake smiled and stayed very still, and the kitten stepped right into her lap.

Joshua was at Grandpa's house. The wind howled outside. It made the trees bend and shake. Then the lights went out. The whole room went dark. Joshua could not see his toy robot at all.

"I don't like the dark," said Joshua. Grandpa gave him a hug. "The big wind knocked out the power," said Grandpa. "The lights will come back soon." Grandpa found a flashlight. He clicked it on. A bright circle shone on the wall. Joshua held his robot up. The robot made a big shadow. Joshua moved it. The shadow got tall. He moved it again. The shadow went flat. Joshua laughed. He made the shadow skip across the wall.

They sat on the couch together. The wind still howled. But the flashlight stayed bright and warm. Then the lights blinked. The lamps came back on. The room was bright again. Joshua clapped his hands. "The wind stopped being so big," said Grandpa. Joshua hugged his robot tight. "Good night, robot," he said.

Ellie was at her auntie's house. Today the family would fly on a big plane. "Try an egg first," said Auntie. "You need a tasty breakfast." Ellie ate the warm egg. Then they packed the little blue bag.

The airport was full of people. It was loud and busy. Ellie saw the planes out the window. They were huge! She wanted to run and see them. She let go of the bag strap and started to go. A big crowd of legs and feet went past her. She could not see her auntie anymore. Her tummy felt small.

Then Ellie remembered. In busy places like airports, children stay close to their grown-up and hold hands. She turned around. She reached up and found her auntie's hand. She held it tight. "There you are," said her auntie. Ellie held on all the way to the window. Together they watched a plane lift off into the sky.

Ryan wanted the red truck. It sat on the shelf by the window. But Lorelei stood right in front of it. She was building a tall, tall tower.

Ryan tried to squeeze past her. He bumped the tower. The blocks fell down. "Sorry," said Ryan. Lorelei looked sad. Then she said, "It's okay."

Ms. Cohen knelt down. She said, "You can say excuse me." Ryan looked at Lorelei. "Excuse me," he said. Lorelei stepped to the side. Ryan walked right past her. He got the red truck!

Ryan drove the truck through the sand table. "Beep beep, coming through!" he said. Lorelei laughed. She pushed a cute little dump truck behind him. Then Ryan wanted to swing outside. Lorelei was at the door. He puffed out his chest like a dragon. "Excuse me," he roared. Lorelei giggled and moved aside.

Wren sat in her car seat. She had eaten a big breakfast of toast and berries. Now the car was rolling down the road. "Are we almost there?" she asked. "We will meet Zoelie at her house soon," said Dad.

Wren wanted to find Zoelie's house all by herself. She knew Zoelie lived at number five. But she did not know what five looked like on a door. So she watched every door go by. The sun was high in the sky. The road hummed under the wheels.

Wren began to count on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. She held up five fingers. Then she counted more, just to hear the words. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad smiled and counted along, one number for each finger.

A blue door went by. It had a 5 on it. Wren looked at her five fingers. She looked at the 5 on the door. "Five!" she called out. "That sign is five, like my hand!" Dad stopped the car. Zoelie ran out and waved. "You found my house!" said Zoelie. Wren held up her five fingers high in the air.

Harrison loved bath time. Splash, splash went the water. He washed his arms and his tummy. Then the bath was done.

"I want to get out!" said Harrison. He climbed out all by himself. Drip, drip, drip went the water. It fell on the floor. Drip, drip, drip. His feet made wet spots.

He ran to find his blue shirt. "My shirt is all wet!" said Harrison. The water from his body made it wet. Oh no.

"Come here," said his dad, laughing. Dad held up a big soft towel. The towel patted Harrison's arms. The towel patted his legs. Now the drips were gone!

"My body is dry!" said Harrison. He put on his shirt. It was warm and dry now. "Dry shirt, dry me!" he said.

He sat on his bed. Dad tucked him in. "Good night, Harrison," said Dad.

"Good night!" said Harrison. And he closed his eyes.

Adam woke up early. He ran to the mirror. His hair was full of tangles. It stood up in little clumps. "Oh no," he said. He tried to push it down with his hands. The tangles did not move.

Adam found his brush on the shelf. He brushed one small piece at a time. He started at the top. He went slowly, so it did not pull. One tangle came out. Then another one. His hair began to lie flat. Adam smiled. He brushed and brushed, all the way around.

At the dinner table, Adam sat with Miraal and Keenan. Miraal's hair was smooth and shiny. "I brushed mine," Adam said. "The tangles came out." Miraal touched her own smooth hair and nodded. Keenan showed his hair too. It was brushed and neat.

Adam ate his eggs and toast. He took a big drink of milk. Then Ms. Hoang came by. "Nice hair, Adam," she said. Adam grinned and patted his head. After breakfast, he put his brush in his bag. "For later," he said. Miraal laughed, and Keenan gave him a thumbs up.

Lea sat at the dinner table. She took a big bite of pasta. "Yum," she said. Her dad smiled. "Eat it all up," he said. "Then it is bath time."

Lea wanted to jump in the bath fast. She ate fast. She drank her milk fast. "Done!" she said. Her dad carried her to the bathroom. The tub was filling up. Steam rose up like little clouds. The water made a splashing sound in Lea's ear.

Lea put one foot near the tub. "Wait," said her dad. "A grown-up checks the bath water first. I make sure it is not too hot." He put his hand in the water. Lea waited. She wiggled her toes on the cool floor. "Too hot," said her dad. He turned the tap. More cool water ran in. He put his hand in again.

"Now it is just right," he said. Lea touched the water with her toes. It felt warm and nice, like a hug. In she went, splish splash. Then something surprising floated by. It was her yellow duck, hiding under a towel all along. "Sorry, duck, I forgot you!" said Lea. The duck bobbed up and down.

After the bath, Lea put on her soft pajamas. She brushed her teeth. Her dad tucked her into bed. "Night night, Lea," he said. Lea hugged her duck tight and closed her eyes.

Dylan ran to the playground with his red ball. He wanted to play catch, but his arms were too short to throw far. "Can you help me?" he asked Mr. Lim. "Please throw the ball with me."

Mr. Lim smiled. "I would love to," he said. They threw the ball back and forth. Dylan threw it too high. The ball flew past Harley. Harley ran after it.

Harley grabbed the ball and started to run away with it. Dylan watched. Then Harley stopped. She turned around. "Thank you!" she called to Dylan. She threw the ball back to him.

Dylan wondered about that. Harley said thank you when he gave her the ball. What would happen next?

Dylan rolled the ball to Abram. Abram caught it. "Thank you, Dylan!" Abram said. He rolled it right back.

At bedtime, Dylan put his sweet teddy bear on his bed. His mom gave him a kiss. "Thank you, Mom," Dylan said. Then he closed his eyes and smiled.

Ryan went to the pet store with his dad. The store smelled like hay and fish tanks. A small grey kitten mewed at him from a cage. "Can we take her home?" Ryan asked. His dad smiled and said yes.

At home, Ryan set the kitten on the floor. She sniffed the rug and walked in a little circle. Then she sat by her bowl and looked up. Ryan peeked inside. The bowl was empty. "Dad! Her water is all gone!" he called.

Was the kitten thirsty? Dad held the bowl while Ryan turned the tap. Cold, fresh water splashed in. The kitten drank and drank. Her tongue made tiny tapping sounds. Later, Ryan checked the bowl again. It was empty once more. "You need fresh water every day," Ryan whispered. He filled it up. The kitten purred and rubbed his hand.

Zoe ran into the big room at the community centre. Ms. Crowchild was holding a drum. Avianna and Sifat sat on the floor.

"We will sing a song today," said Ms. Crowchild. "First we clap. Then we sing."

The drum went boom, boom, boom. Zoe clapped. But her hands came too fast. Then they came too slow.

Sifat started to sing right away. He sang all alone. He stopped and looked down.

"Too soon," said Ms. Crowchild. "Listen. I will count one, two, three, four. Then we all sing together."

The drum went boom. "One, two, three, four," said Ms. Crowchild.

Everyone sang at the same time. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," they sang.

Zoe asked, "When do I start?"

"After the count," said Avianna. "Watch me."

Boom. One, two, three, four. Zoe sang too. Her voice was strong.

A gray turtle picture sat on the wall. Zoe pointed at it while she sang.

Avianna laughed so hard she did not cry, she giggled. Zoe giggled too. Then she clapped and sang the whole song by herself.

Boom. One, two, three, four. "Twinkle, twinkle," sang Zoe, all the way to the end.

Ezra sat at the dinner table. His chair was wobbly, just a little. He took a bite of his noodles. They were warm and good.

"Can I have a cookie now?" Ezra asked.

His dad shook his head. "Cookies come later, after the chicken."

"But I want it now," said Ezra. "Now means at this very moment."

"That's true," said Dad. "And right this moment, you have chicken."

Ezra looked at his plate. He looked at the cookie jar on the shelf. He ate one more bite of chicken. Then one more. Soon the chicken was all gone.

"Now?" asked Ezra.

"Now," said Dad, with a smile. He put a cookie on Ezra's plate.

Ezra thought about yesterday. Yesterday he had two cookies. Tomorrow he might have cookies again. Today, he had one, right now.

"Tomorrow can I ride the swing at Kendra's house?" he asked.

"That sounds like a good plan for tomorrow," said Dad.

Ezra took a big bite of his cookie. "Today is a good day," he said.

"Tonight we can read a story," said Dad. "But that is later, after your bath."

Ezra looked out the window. The sky was turning pink. Later was coming, little by little, just like bedtime, just like tomorrow.

"Is it later yet?" he asked.

Romy ran to the sand pit at summer camp. A big yellow truck sat by the wall. It was the coolest toy at camp. Mika was already holding it. He filled the truck with sand and dumped it out. Romy wanted a turn so much. Her hand reached out fast. She almost grabbed the truck.

Then she remembered what the coach said at soccer. "Take three slow breaths." Romy stopped her hand. She took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. Her body felt calm. Mika dumped one more load of sand. Then he held the truck out to her. "Your turn, Romy!"

Romy pushed the truck through the cool sand. She made a big pile. Mr. Jean-Louis came by and smiled. "Nice waiting, Romy," he said. Anabia came to watch. "Can I have a turn next?" she asked. "Yes," said Romy. She played fast and hard, but she watched the time too. Then she gave the truck to Anabia. "Three breaths help," Romy told her. Anabia nodded and counted them out loud.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Romy stood in the dark kitchen. "Mama, the lamp went off," she said.

Mama came in. She held a flashlight. It made a big yellow circle on the wall. Romy touched her own hair. "Why is it so dark?" she asked. "Look out the window," said Mama. Romy looked. Davis's house was dark. Bowie's house was dark too. All the houses on the street were dark at once. "Wow," said Romy. "Every house went dark!"

Mama sat down on the rug. "Come sit with me," she said. Romy sat close. The flashlight was warm in Mama's hand. Romy was careful not to touch the hot part. Outside, the wind made a whoosh sound. A cow mooed far away.

Then the lights came back. First the lamp, then the fridge. Romy ran to the window. Davis's house was bright. Bowie's house was bright too. "All the lights came back together!" said Romy. She waved at the window. "Good night, lights."

Jake was at Grandpa's house for the lantern night. Candles sat all along the big table. Jake wanted to light one himself.

"Can I light the candle?" Jake asked.

"Grown-ups light the flames," said Grandpa. "But you can pick the very first one."

Jake looked at all the candles. He chose the tall red one. He pointed to it. "That one!"

Grandpa took the match. He struck it. A little flame came up. He touched it to the red candle's wick. The wick caught. A warm light grew and grew.

"Whoa," said Jake. "My candle is lit!"

"It is," said Grandpa. "Your pick, my flame."

Grandpa lit one candle after another. Soon the whole room glowed. Jake watched the light jump on the walls.

Grandpa's friend from the farm next door came in with a bowl of peeled grapes. "Try one," she said. Jake squeezed a grape. "Ooh, slimy!" he said, and he laughed and ate it anyway.

Jake helped put out little cups for the guests. He was careful with his hands. When the last guest left, one candle still burned. Grandpa blew it out. A thin smoke curl went up, up, up.

Jake waved at the smoke. "Good night, candle," he said.

Abigail ran to the blocks at the playground. The sky was cloudy, but she did not mind. Tegh was already there. He held all the blocks in his arms.

"My turn," said Abigail. She grabbed a block. Tegh grabbed it back. The tower fell down. Plop.

Mr. Leblanc came over. "Let's try again," he said. Abigail sat on the bench. She wanted to play, but she had to wait. She watched Tegh stack one block. Then another. Abigail felt like she might freeze, waiting was so hard.

"Can we build one tower together?" asked Tegh. "Yes!" said Abigail. She put a block on. Tegh put a block on. One tower, side by side hands. It grew tall. Taller than the horse statue by the fence!

"My turn," said Abigail, holding out her hand. Tegh gave her a block. "Your turn," she said, giving one back.

"One tower," said Tegh. "One big tower," said Abigail. They laughed. Mr. Leblanc smiled and waved.

Abigail clapped her hands. "Look at our tower!" she said.

Elliot ran to the bathroom at summer camp. He used the toilet. Then he ran out fast. The water slide was calling him. "Wait for me, Theia!" he shouted.

Theia was at the sink. She was rubbing soap on her hands. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet," she said. She made soap bubbles shaped like a cloud. Elliot giggled and ran back.

Ms. Chowdhury was by the sinks. She helped Elliot pump the soap. "Now we count to twenty," she said. They sang the camp song twice. Elliot scrubbed and scrubbed. The soap smelled like lemons. He sniffed his hands. His nose was happy. "Not yucky anymore!" he said.

Mavrick zoomed out of the bathroom without washing. "Come back, Mavrick!" Elliot called. Mavrick ran back to the sink. He washed his hands too. All three friends sang the song together.

Then they ran to the water slide. Splash! The water was cold. Elliot's hands were clean and wet. Theia held up her soapy-smelling hands. "Twenty seconds, best seconds," she said. Elliot laughed. "Wash first, splash after!" he said. And he brought his clean hands all the way to the top.

Chloe went to the community hall with her family. It was Lunar New Year. There were red paper lanterns on the walls. There was a big table with sticky rice cakes on plates. Her friend Siena was there too.

Boom, boom, boom! Loud drums began. Chloe put her hands over her ears. "Why is it so loud?" she asked. "Wait and watch," said Siena. "The lion is coming." A big lion with a fuzzy head danced into the hall. It hopped. It blinked its eyes. Then the drums went boom again, and the lion jumped at the same time. The drum went slow, and the lion went slow. The drum went fast, and the lion went fast. "The lion dances to the drums!" said Chloe.

The drum went boom, and Chloe clapped with it. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. The lion shook its head at her. Ms. Kapoor laughed and clapped too. "Do it again," Chloe called. Boom, boom, boom!

Emma and her mom went to the library after breakfast. Emma was still a little sleepy. But then she saw the toy corner. Nivaan was there, and Dax too.

"I want to draw," said Emma.

Ms. Santos-Reyes brought over a tablet. "First we turn it on," she said. She showed Emma the small round button. Emma pressed it. The screen lit up like a window in the dark.

Emma tapped the drawing app. It opened. One tap, open. One tap, red. She wanted to make a red sun. But the line came out green.

"Try the colours," said Nivaan. He pointed to the little squares at the bottom.

Emma looked. Red, blue, green, yellow. She tapped the red square. She drew her sun again. This time the line was red. One tap, red.

"There," said Emma. "My sun."

She drew one sun, one red sun, one big red sun. Then she drew grass. Green. Then a flower. Pink.

Soon it was time to go. Ms. Santos-Reyes knelt down beside her. "Now we put it away," she said. Emma pressed the button. The screen went dark.

"Bye, sun," said Emma. She set the tablet on the shelf, just where it belonged.

Wren waited at school pickup in her party dress. It had sparkly stars on it. Layne stood next to her in soft pajamas. Wren looked down at her dress. It was itchy.

"Wren, are you coming to our sleepover?" asked Layne. "Yes," said Wren. "I want to sleep in my pretty dress." Layne shook her head. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," Layne said. Wren thought about that.

Ms. Cardinal smiled and knelt down. "Do you want to wear Layne's spare pajamas?" she asked. "Are they the same as mine at home?" asked Wren. "Almost the same," said Ms. Cardinal. "Soft and warm."

Wren changed into the little blue pajamas. The itchy feeling went away. She yawned a big yawn. At Layne's house, the dad gave Layne her medicine, and Wren took her own little cup too. Then they brushed teeth and climbed into bed.

"Night, Wren," said Layne. Wren snuggled under the blanket. The stars on her dress hung on the door, waiting for morning. "Night," said Wren, and she closed her eyes.

Isabelle went to Liana's house. Liana had a big orange truck. It could shine its light on the floor. Isabelle wanted the truck very much.

"Can I have the truck?" asked Isabelle. "It is my turn now," said Liana. Isabelle reached out her hand to grab it. Then she stopped. She put her hands in her lap instead.

"You can have it next," said Liana. Isabelle waited. She watched the truck light shine on the wall.

Then Liana said, "Here, Isabelle. Your turn." She put the orange truck in Isabelle's hands. Isabelle smiled big. "Thank you, Liana," she said. She remembered to say it before she drove the truck away. Liana clapped her hands.

The two girls sat in the warm air by the window. They took turns all morning. The truck went back and forth, back and forth. "Vroom," said Isabelle. "Vroom," said Liana.

Jasmine went to the grocery store with her dad. She had her little bunny. But now the bunny was gone. "Oh no," said Jasmine. "Where is bunny?"

Mr. Menon worked at the store. He said, "Let's retrace your steps. That means going back to each place you went, in order."

First they went to the apple bin. No bunny there. Then they went to the bread aisle. The bread was in a thick paper bag. No bunny there. Then they went back to the milk case. The floor was cold on Jasmine's toe, where her sock peeked out.

Then Jasmine saw the cart. Bunny had slid down under the carrots. "Bunny!" said Jasmine. She hugged him tight.

"Good retracing," said Mr. Menon. Jasmine smiled and held bunny all the way home.

Hayden sat at the little red table. Snack time was here. Ms. Sato put bread on a big white plate.

Hayden wanted the bread right now. He reached out and grabbed. Cormac was reaching too. Their hands bumped. The plate slid away. No one got any bread.

Hayden sat back and looked at his hands. He thought hard. Then he turned to Ms. Sato. "Bread, please," he said. Ms. Sato smiled and put a piece in his hand. Cormac watched. "Bread, please," Cormac said too. He got a piece as well.

After snack, they went to the rug. Eden was rolling a soft white rabbit toy across the carpet. Hayden wanted a turn. He almost grabbed it. Then he stopped. "Can I have a turn, please?" he asked. Eden rolled the rabbit over to him. Hayden laughed and rolled it back. They took turns all morning, rolling the rabbit back and forth, back and forth.

Sophie was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a special box of letter cards. The cards were bumpy. Sophie ran her skin over the bumps.

"This one is K," said Sophie. "K says kuh."

Sophie tried to write K on paper. She wrote it the wrong way. The legs went the wrong side. She frowned at it.

Grandma smiled. "Try this," she said. "Put your finger on the card. Trace the K."

Sophie traced the bumpy K with her finger. Up. Down. Slant. Her finger went bump, bump, bump.

Then she picked up her crayon. She wrote a K. This time it was right. The legs went the correct way.

"I did it!" said Sophie. "My finger taught my hand!"

She traced the bumpy S next. Then she wrote a wiggly S on her paper. Grandma clapped.

Sophie traced every card, one by one. Then she wrote her whole name.

"Look, Grandma! S-O-P-H-I-E!"

Grandma hung the paper on the fridge.

Muhammad went to the store with his mom. He held her hand at the big door. Inside, the store was bright and cold. "Brr," said Muhammad. His mom zipped his coat. Now he felt cozy.

They walked past the soup aisle. A pot was steaming. It was hot. Muhammad reached out his hand. "Stop," said his mom. "Hot things can hurt you." She picked up a can instead. Muhammad put his hands in his pockets.

Muhammad saw a big bin of carrots. "Can we get one?" he asked. "Yes," said his mom. "You can pick." Muhammad picked the longest carrot. It was cold and bumpy. He put it in the cart himself.

Then Muhammad saw a toy truck. He stopped to look. The wheels could spin. When he looked up, his mom was gone. "Mom?" he called. His tummy felt funny. He looked left. He looked right. He saw a lady at the checkout. She had a vest and a name tag.

Muhammad walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. "You can tell a store worker," said the lady. "That is just right. I will help." She picked up her phone. Soon his mom came running. She hugged him tight. "You were so brave," she said. Muhammad held her hand all the way home. The carrot went splash into the soup.

Ethan sat at the dinner table. He wanted more peas. "Can I have peas?" he asked.

Mom put the bowl in front of him. "You can count them out," she said. Ethan picked up his spoon. He counted slow. "One, two, four."

Joey sat next to him. Joey was eating with them tonight. "You skipped a number," Joey said.

Ethan tried again. "One, two, four." He looked at his spoon. Still no three. "Where did three go?" he asked.

"Try one at a time," Mom said. She passed him one pea. Ethan put it on his plate. "One," he said. Mom passed another pea. "Two," said Ethan. Mom passed one more. Ethan smiled big. "Three! There it is!"

He kept going on his own. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten peas sat on his plate. They made a round shape, like a little green ball.

"Again," said Joey. Ethan pushed the peas back into the bowl. He counted them back in. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out in the same line every time.

Then Ethan opened his mouth wide. But he did not eat. He waited. "Watch this," he said. He dropped one pea into Joey's cup when Mom was not looking. Joey laughed so loud.

"One pea for you," said Ethan. "Nine left for me."

Raphael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make lunch for the family. "Bread with butter," he said. Grandma got the bread and the butter from the fridge.

Raphael tried to spread the butter. The butter was cold and hard. It would not spread. It tore the bread into messy bits. "Oh no," said Raphael. Grandma set the butter on the counter. "We will wait a little," she said. Raphael covered the bread with a cloth. Then he and Grandma washed the tomatoes. The sun shone on the counter.

Soon Raphael touched the butter. It was soft now. He spread it, and it went on smooth and even. He spread slice after slice after slice. Dad came in and took a big bite. "This is the best lunch," said Dad. Raphael smiled and gave him one more piece.

Rosalie sat on the school bus. She held a little yellow car. It was her favorite toy. Her friend Lili sat next to her. Lili had no toy at all.

Rosalie wanted to play. But Lili reached for the car. Rosalie pulled it back fast. "Mine," she said. Lili's face went sad. She looked out the window. The car did not tickle Rosalie's hands anymore. It felt heavy, like a big fall was coming.

Rosalie looked at Lili. Then she looked at the car. She slid the car to the middle of the seat. "You can use it too," she said. "This is sharing." Lili smiled big. She made the car go vroom, vroom. Then Lili slid the car back. "Your turn," said Lili.

Rosalie made the car zoom down her leg. It tickled her knee. The two girls took turns, over and over. Take a turn, then give a turn. The bus ride felt short and happy. Mr. Njoroge looked back from the front seat. "Good sharing, girls," he said. Rosalie held up the car. "We both used it!"

Peyton ran into the hair salon with her mom. It was her very first haircut at a salon. She was so excited. There was a big fish tank by the wall. A little brown fish swam past the glass.

"Can I look at the fish?" Peyton asked.

"First we cut your hair," said the hairdresser.

Peyton climbed up into the big chair. The hairdresser picked up the scissors. Peyton turned her head to see the fish. Snip went the scissors. A piece of hair fell crooked.

"Oops," said the hairdresser. "Your head moved."

"Can I sit very still?" Peyton asked.

"Yes, still like a statue helps me cut neatly," said the hairdresser.

Peyton planted her hands on her knees. She sat very, very still. She did not look at the fish. Snip, snip went the scissors. The cuts came out neat and even.

Then came a surprise. The hairdresser held up a mirror. Peyton saw a tiny bird printed on her new hair clip. The hairdresser gave it to her to keep.

"Look, Mom, a bird!" said Peyton. She jumped down and ran to the fish tank at last.

Logan held the box with two hands. Inside was a small gray kitten with pink ears. He was taking his first pet home. His friend Mavrik walked beside him on the street.

"Does she have a tag?" Mavrik asked.

"What is a tag?" Logan asked.

Mr. Warsame was watering his flowers. He waved them over. "A tag hangs on her collar," he said. He held up a little circle of metal. "It has our phone number on it. If she ever gets lost, someone reads the tag. Then they can call us, and we can bring her home."

Logan helped clip the tag on the collar. It made a tiny ting sound, like a little song.

Then the kitten jumped out of the box. She ran under a bush. Logan got scared. But his neighbor saw her collar shine in the leaves. She read the tag and knocked on Logan's door. "This kitten belongs to you," she said with a smile.

Logan hugged his kitten tight. "I am glad you have a tag," he said.

Eliana stood on the bathroom floor. The bath was full of bubbles. "Bubbles!" she said. Her eyes saw white and pink foam. What would it feel like?

First she touched the water with one finger. Her finger told her, warm! She heard the water go drip, drip. She sniffed the soap. It smelled like flowers. "My nose knows," she said, and laughed.

Eliana wanted to get in, but her socks were wet. They would slip on the floor! She sat on the step and pulled them off. Then her bare toes touched the cool floor. Ooh. She wiggled them. Her feet could feel too, just like her hands! She tapped one foot, then the other. Tap, tap. Then Dad lifted her into the bath. The warm water hugged her toes. "My feet feel it!" she said. Dad smiled and shook the dry towel open wide.

Claire was drawing in her striped socks. It was after lunch, not quite morning anymore. Her tummy made a little rumble.

She sniffed with her nose. Something smelled warm and sweet. She sniffed again. "Pasta!" said Claire. "I smell pasta!"

Her dad laughed from the kitchen. "Come and see," he said. Claire walked in on her toes. The pot was big. The grown-ups stirred it. Claire stood back, safe, and watched.

She listened with her ears. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. She touched the cool wooden spoon with one finger. Smooth!

Soon they sat at the dinner table. Claire tasted the pasta with her tongue. Yummy. She ate one bite, then two, then three.

"You knew before you saw it," said Dad.

"My nose told me first," said Claire. She gave her nose a little pat.

Daniel wanted to find his red ball. He looked under the sleepy teddy bear. He looked behind the big doll. He found a sock, soft and warm. He found a block, bumpy on his hand. But no red ball.

Ms. Harper put a big box on the rug. "Let's tidy up," she said. Tatum ran over with a block. "Block!" she said, and dropped it in. Sutton brought two dolls. "Dolls," he said, and put them in. Daniel heard them naming each toy. Then he understood. Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys. The box was for toys!

Daniel ran to the baby bed corner. His red ball was hiding there. He picked it up. It felt smooth and round. "Ball!" he said. He dropped it in the box. It went plunk.

Then Ms. Harper laughed. "Look at the top," she said. The teddy bear was asleep in the box too. Daniel gently pulled the bear out and hugged him. "Bears are not toys," he whispered. "You can rip my heart if you think so." Ms. Harper smiled. "The bear can sit here and watch us play," she said. Daniel set him on the soft rug, right next to the box.

Alice wanted to feed her teddy bear. But the kitchen felt far away. Mom was busy at the sink. "Can I help teddy?" Alice asked. "Yes, you can pretend," Mom said. "Pretending means acting as if something is not real." Alice looked at the floor. She put down a red cushion. Then she put down a blue one. "The floor is a river!" she said. She hopped from cushion to cushion. Splash, splash went her feet on the rug. Teddy did not get wet at all. Alice reached the play kitchen. She gave teddy a pretend bowl of soup. She remembered teddy liked carrots too. Mom gave Alice a real cracker for herself. "Teddy, is your soup too hot?" Alice asked. "No," she said in a bear voice. "It is just right."

Freya came into the kitchen in the morning. Her tummy made a little rumble. She wanted her yellow socks, but she could not find them.

She looked by the chair. She looked under the table. Then she saw her socks on the floor. They were next to her pajamas from last night. "There they are," she said. But the socks had marks on them. They were dirty from playing outside.

Her dad was putting clothes into a big basket. The clothes went in with a soft plop. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket," he said, "so they can be washed." Freya picked up her socks. She dropped them in. Plop.

Then she found her night shirt under the chair. She threw that in too. Plop. It was like basketball. She laughed and got one more sock from the floor. It sailed in a big arc and landed right in the middle. "Good shot," said her dad.

They took the basket to the washing machine. Her dad put the clothes in and turned it on. The machine made a whooshy sound, like rain. Freya sat close by with her book and her teddy. The socks spun around in the round window, round and round. Soon the clothes would be clean. Then Freya could wear her yellow socks again. "Wash fast, socks," she said.

Asher was at Grandma's house. His hair had grown long and curly. Grandma said, "Today is your first haircut." Asher felt a little scared. Grandma held his hand. "You can be brave," she said. Asher took a big breath and said yes.

At the salon, a lady picked up her scissors. She was the only one who touched them. Snip, snip, snip. Asher watched a little curl fall down. Then the lady cut one small curl and gave it to Grandma. Grandma put the curl into a little envelope. Asher had to ask, "Why do you keep it?" Grandma smiled. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut, to remember it."

That night, back at Grandma's house, Grandma taped the envelope in a book. Asher ran his hand over his short hair. "I was brave," he said. Grandma said, "Yes, you were."

Edouard ran to the park with his teddy under his arm. He saw Kyla sitting under the big tree. She had a doll in a small blanket.

"My doll is sick," said Kyla. "Her nose is too hot."

Edouard sat down next to her. "What can we do?" he asked.

Kyla found a small leaf. "This is pretend medicine," she said. She tapped the doll's nose with it. Then she wrapped the doll in the blanket again.

Edouard looked at his teddy. "My teddy is sick too," he said. He wanted to help. He found another leaf. He tapped his teddy's nose. Then he tucked his teddy into his own jacket, like a blanket.

"Teddy needs a nap," said Kyla.

The children sang a quiet song. The doll slept. The teddy slept too.

"Shh," said Edouard. "They are resting."

Soon both toys woke up. "All better!" said Kyla.

Edouard hugged his teddy tight. "Time for a snack," he whispered to it. He held a pretend cookie near the teddy's nose. "Yum," said Edouard.

Ali was at the park with his friend Paige. Ms. Castillo had a big bowl of grapes. She held it out to Paige first.

"Want a grape?" asked Ms. Castillo.

"Yuck!" Paige shouted. She made a big face.

Ms. Castillo looked sad. She put the bowl down low.

"Try again," she said. "Say no, thank you."

"No, thank you," said Paige. Now she sounded kind.

Ms. Castillo smiled again. "Thank you for that," she said.

Ali watched. He saw the sad face go away. He saw the smile come back.

Then Ms. Castillo held out the bowl to Ali. Ali did not want a grape. He wanted a cracker.

"No, thank you," said Ali.

"Good words," said Ms. Castillo. "Crackers are in my purple bag. Can you help me beg the ants to stay away?"

Ali laughed. He waited while she found the crackers. The crackers were good.

"Thank you," said Ali, with a crumb on his chin.

Ethan sat on the couch at Grandpa's house. The big game was on TV. Lots of people were there. Holly sat next to him. Astrid sat on the floor.

"Look at that man," said Ethan. He pointed at the screen. The man wore a striped shirt. He kept watching the players. He blew his whistle. Then he held up both hands.

"Why is he blowing the whistle?" Ethan asked. "Why is he watching everybody?"

"He is the referee," said Grandpa. "He watches the game. He makes sure the players follow the rules."

One player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle again. He shook his head. The player looked sad. He put his hands behind his back.

"He saw it," said Ethan. "The referee saw the hands."

"Yes, he did," said Holly. "He is always watching."

Later, a player kicked the ball far. It went past the line. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his arm. Ethan jumped up and down.

"I want to be the referee," said Ethan. He put his hands on his hips. He watched the TV with big eyes. The referee blew his whistle one more time. Ethan blew a pretend whistle too. "Tweet!"

Rosalie sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. Her mama held her hand. Rosalie was thinking about her shot. "Will it be big?" she asked. "Is it as big as a pencil?"

The nurse smiled. "No," she said. "It is not big. It is very small."

Briggs was there too. He was waiting for his turn. "I got my shot already," he said. He waved his arm in the air. "Look, I can wave it!"

Rosalie still felt worried. She thought the shot would be like a giant nail. She thought it would take a long, long time. She hid her arm behind her back.

"Let's count together," said the nurse. "One thin needle. One quick poke. All done." Rosalie looked at the tiny needle. It was thin like a little string. It was not big at all.

"Ready?" said the nurse. Rosalie took a big breath. She held her mama's hand tight.

"One thin needle," said Rosalie. "One quick poke. All done."

The nurse touched her arm. There was one quick poke in her arm. Then it was over. That was it. It was so quick!

"It is done?" asked Rosalie. "Already?" The nurse put a small bandage on her arm. It had a star on it.

"That was quick!" said Rosalie. She jumped down from the chair. She ran to Briggs. "One thin needle," she said. "One quick poke. All done." Then she held out her star bandage for him to see.

Violet was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa held up one big hand. "Five senses," he said. "One for each finger."

Violet looked at her own small hand. She counted. "Eyes see," she said. "Ears hear." That was two fingers. "Nose smells," she said. Three. She stuck out her tongue. "Tongue tastes!" Four.

Violet stared at her thumb. She forgot one. She thought and thought. Then Grandpa handed her a soft peach. Violet squeezed it. The fuzz felt warm on her fingers. "Touching!" she said. "My skin touches!" She put her thumb up. Five fingers, five senses.

Grandpa smiled. "You got all five," he said. "Now choose one and use it." Violet chose her nose. She sniffed the peach. It smelled sweet. Then she chose her tongue. Grandpa cut a slice with his knife. Violet took a tiny bite from his plate.

"Mmm," said Violet. "Tasting is my favorite."

"Even more than seeing?" said Grandpa.

Violet looked at the peach. She looked at Grandpa's big smile. "No," she said. "Seeing Grandpa is my favorite."

Asher stood by the grocery store door. His coat was on, but the zipper was stuck at the bottom. He pulled it up, up, up. It went a little way and stopped. He pulled again. This time it slid all the way to his chin. "I did it," he said. His mom clapped.

One red mitten fell off the shelf by the door. Asher picked it up. Where was the other one? He looked under the cart. He looked by the bread. "Mom, where do mittens go?" he asked. She smiled and pointed at his coat. "Look at your side," she said. Asher patted his hip. There was a little door there. He opened it. Inside was the other red mitten!

Asher tucked both mittens into the pocket. He pushed the little door shut. They fit just right. He patted the pocket. It felt squishy and soft, like two small pillows.

The cart rolled past the soap aisle. Asher smelled flowers and lemons. Then a spot of dust slid under his shoe. He swept it away with his toe. At the checkout, Asher pulled both mittens out of the pocket. "Look, Ms. Cashier," he said. "My pocket kept them safe!" He put them back in, one, two, and zipped his coat up all by himself again.

Luke went to the park early with his dad. The sun made everything warm. Luke touched the slide. The slide felt hot. He pulled his hand back fast. "That part is in the sun," his dad said. They waited under a tree. Luke watched the shade creep over the slide. He touched it again. Now it was cool.

Zoya and Daxon came to the park too. They all ran to the sandbox. Luke stayed where his dad could see him. He found a picnic table under a big tree. On the table sat a small bag. Little round things spilled out of it. They were red and yellow and green. They looked like candy.

Luke wanted to pick one up. They were so pretty, like a tiny rainbow. But he stopped his hand. He remembered what his mom had told him. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.

"I will go get a grown-up," Luke said. He did not touch the little round things. He walked back to his dad. His dad held his hand. They went to the table together. His dad looked at the bag. "These are pills," his dad said. "You did the right thing."

A woman came running back. She had been looking for her bag. She thanked Luke. "I did not touch them," Luke said. She smiled at him. Zoya and Daxon clapped. Then they all went back to the sandbox. Luke dug a deep hole. It felt cool and soft under his hands.

Rosalie was playing house in the playroom. She was the mom. Her baby doll was crying, so Rosalie gave her a bottle.

"Time to cook soup," said Rosalie. She stirred a pot in the pretend kitchen. Alexis was the dad. "I will catch the peas!" he said. He tossed pretend peas in the air. They rolled under the shelf. "Silly peas," laughed Rosalie.

Then Mr. Wu rang a bell. "Clean up time," he said. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." Rosalie looked at the messy kitchen. The pot was upside down. The cup was on the floor.

"I can be brave," said Rosalie. She put the pot on the shelf. Alexis found the peas under the shelf. "I catch you, peas!" he said. They put the cups in the basket. They put the doll in her little bed.

Then Rosalie saw something. The room looked big and clean. "Wow," she said. "The toys got put away, and now the room shines!" Mr. Wu smiled. "One more thing," he said. He held up a sock. It was full of pretend peas.

"My soup!" said Rosalie. "The peas went in the sock!" Alexis laughed and laughed. Rosalie poured the peas back in the bag. "Night night, peas," she said. "Night night, room."

Jasmine was at Grandma's cozy house. She could not find her bunny. "Where did bunny go?" she asked. Grandma did not know.

Jasmine looked under the bed. No bunny. She looked in the toy box. No bunny. Then she heard a sound. Rip, rip, rip. Grandpa was opening a big box in the hall.

"Grandpa, what is that box?" Jasmine asked. "This is my lost and found box," Grandpa said. "People put things they find in here. Then the owners can come get them back."

Jasmine peeked inside. She saw a mitten. She saw a hat. Then she saw two soft ears. "Bunny!" she cried. She hugged bunny tight. The mailman had found bunny on the grass and put her in the box.

Then Jasmine saw something else. A little toy tooth, shiny and white. "Whose tooth is this?" she asked. "That is Rabab's toy," said Grandpa. "She left it last week." Jasmine smiled. "Rabab can come get it back," she said. Grandpa helped her call Rabab's mom. Rabab came and took her tooth home. Bunny's ears wiggled all the way to snack time.

Aurora ran to the snack table. Her hands were gray with mud from the garden. She had helped make a little mountain of soil for the seeds. Now she wanted to catch the last apple slice on the plate.

Amanda was already eating. Alessio was already eating too. Aurora reached for a slice. Mr. Rowe shook his head. "We wash our hands before we eat," he said. He pointed to the sink.

Aurora walked to the sink. She turned the tap. The water was warm. The mud ran off her fingers. It swirled down, down, down. Her hands turned pink and clean. She dried them on the little towel.

Then she walked back to the table. She picked up an apple slice. There was one left after all. She took a big, happy bite.

"Good," said Mr. Rowe. He held up his own clean hands. Amanda laughed and held hers up too. Alessio put his apple down and did the same. Aurora giggled and wiggled her clean pink fingers at them all.

Rain fell in the morning. Now the playground was wet. Everett ran to the swings. His friend Gloria was there. A big puddle sat by the slide. Everett looked down at it. He saw his own face in the water. "Neat!" he said. He made a big smile. The face in the puddle smiled too. Then he made a sad face. The face in the puddle looked sad too. "A face can show feelings," said Everett. He laughed, and the puddle face laughed back.

Then a wind came. Leaves began to fall from the tree. One leaf fell on Gloria's head. She pushed her swing, but the swing felt cold and wet. Her mouth turned down. Her eyes looked sad. Everett saw her face. He knew just what to do.

He ran to her. "Look at the puddle, Gloria," he said. Gloria looked down. "Make a happy face," said Everett. Gloria tried. Her mouth went up, up, up. The face in the puddle smiled big. "I see a smile!" said Gloria. "A big smile!" Everett held her hand. They jumped over the puddle together. One jump, two jumps, three. "Again!" said Gloria. They jumped and laughed. The puddle face laughed too.

Colton sat on the soft red rug. He wanted storytime. He looked at Ms. Ionescu.

"Is storytime now?" he asked.

"Soon," said Ms. Ionescu. "Soon means in a little while."

Colton frowned. Soon felt big. Soon felt far away. He watched the clock. The big hand passed the six.

Zola sat down next to him. "I want the story now too," she said.

Gisele passed out papers. "Draw while we wait," she said.

Colton took the paper. He drew a big red truck. Then he drew a dog in the truck. Then he drew the sun.

"Storytime is now!" said Ms. Ionescu.

Colton jumped up. He held his paper. "That was not long," he said.

"No," said Zola. "It was just a little while."

Ms. Ionescu opened the book. "Once there was a small blue boat," she read.

Colton sat close and smiled. Soon was not so big after all.

Ali went to the animal shelter with his dad. The shelter had dogs and cats. One dog had smooth brown ears. The dog wagged her tail. "Hello, dog," said Ali. He wanted to take her home. Dad said yes.

The dog's name was Pip. Pip went into the car with Ali. Pip sat very still. Her ears were soft as a butterfly's wing.

At home, Ali had a chocolate cookie. He wanted to give some to Pip. He held it out to her. Pip sniffed the cookie.

Dad came fast. "No, no," said Dad. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate." Dad took the cookie away. Ali felt sad. He wanted to share with Pip.

Then Dad held out a small bone. "Try this," said Dad. "This is a dog treat." Ali held out the treat. Pip sniffed it. Pip took it in her mouth. She chewed it up. She licked Ali's hand.

Ali patted her smooth head. "Good dog," said Ali. Pip wagged her tail and wagged her tail. The cookie stayed with Dad. The dog treat went to Pip. Ali smiled. "We are friends," he said.

Lucas ran to the playground. He wanted to build a big block tower by the sand pit. Winston was already there. Winston had a tall tower with red blocks.

Lucas ran fast. The ground was slippery from the rain. He slid right into the tower. Crash! All the red blocks fell down.

Winston sat very still. His lip went down at the corners.

Lucas said, "Sorry, Winston." Then he began to pick up the blocks, one by one. He handed them over. Winston took each block and stacked it. Together they built the tower up again, taller than before.

A duck waddled past the sand pit. Winston laughed. "Our tower is as big as that duck is tall," he said.

"Your turn to put on the top block," said Lucas. Winston placed it. The tower stood.

Ava was playing in the playroom with her friend Navy. They built a big tower with pink blocks. Ava made the sky out of a blue blanket on the floor. It was a good game.

Then the bell rang. It was time for a snack. Navy ran out fast. Ava started to run too. But then she stopped. The blocks were all over the floor. The blanket was in a heap. Nobody had cleaned the toys.

Ava picked up one block. Then another. Mr. Zhou, her neighbor, was at the door with her mom. He smiled at Ava. "Can I help?" he asked. "Yes please," said Ava. They put the blocks in the basket together.

Then Navy came back. She looked at the blocks. "Those are mine too," said Navy. She picked up the last pink blocks. She put them away all by herself. Ava folded the blue blanket. The floor was clean now.

"Snack time," said Mom. Ava and Navy sat at the table. They ate apple slices together. "We clean the toys we played with," said Navy. Ava nodded and took a big bite.

Henry sat on the thick rug in the playroom. He looked for a blue crayon. He wanted to draw the sky.

Kairo held up a dark blue crayon. "I have blue," he said.

"No," said Celine. "That one is too dark. Blue is light like the sky."

Henry wondered. Could dark blue still be blue?

"Let's find all the blues," he said.

They pulled crayons from the box. Light blue. Dark blue. Sky blue. Blue like the deep sea. They lined them up on the rug, from lightest to darkest, like little legs in a row.

Henry pointed at the darkest one. "Is it still called blue?" he asked.

"Yes," said Celine. "Dark blue is still called blue."

Henry smiled. He drew the light sky up top. Then he drew the dark sea below. He kissed his paper. "Two blues," he said. "One picture."

Gabriella went to the park with her friend Teagan. Mr. Horváth, the park keeper, had a big cloth bag. "Let's play a game," he said. "Put your hand in. Guess what you feel."

Gabriella pushed her hand into the bag. She felt something round. "A ball!" she said. She pulled it out. It was a red ball. "I was right, but I didn't know the color," she said. "My fingers can't tell colors."

Teagan had a turn. She felt something long and bumpy. "A carrot!" she said. She pulled it out. The carrot was orange. "I can feel it's a carrot," said Teagan. "I had to look to see the color."

Gabriella had another turn. She felt something small and soft. "What is it?" she asked. She peeked. It was a blue berry-shaped toy. Then Teagan found a green leaf and a yellow flower in the grass nearby.

The sky grew dark, so the friends waved to Mr. Horváth. "See you tomorrow," said Gabriella, holding her red ball tight.

Juliette sat at the paint table at daycare. She was making a card for Grandma. She wanted to paint a pink flower on it. But there was no pink paint.

She looked at the pots. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. And there was white paint. "Where is pink?" she wondered.

Marlowe sat next to her. He was painting a blue train. "I want pink," Juliette said. "What can I do?"

She dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a red flower on the paper. It was bright and beautiful. But it was not pink. She looked at the white pot. What would happen if she mixed white with red?

Juliette put some white paint on her brush. She stirred it into the red flower. Round and round she stirred. The red got lighter and lighter. Now it was pink! "Look!" said Juliette. "Red with white makes pink!"

Ms. Cheung came to see. Juliette painted the pink flower again and again. Then she drew a green stem and yellow sun. Marlowe said, "Your pink flower is so pretty."

At home time, Juliette gave the card to her mommy. "For Grandma," she said. "I made pink all by myself."

Matthew sat on the big table at the doctor's office. His legs swung back and forth. He waited for his shot. "This table feels too big," he said. His tummy felt tight. Where could he sit that felt small and safe? Grandpa had an idea. Grandpa sat on a chair and patted his knee. "Come sit on my lap," he said. Matthew climbed down and sat on Grandpa's lap. Grandpa held him with warm arms. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was quick, like a little pinch. Then it was done! Matthew blinked. Did sitting on a lap make it easier? He wondered about that.

Afterward, Grandpa took Matthew to the ice cream shop. Matthew chose strawberry. The man behind the counter poured warm sauce on top. Matthew watched the pink and red swirl together. "Look, Grandpa!" he said. "The sauce goes down and down!" Grandpa laughed. Matthew ate his cold, sweet scoop. He felt a little sleepy and very happy. "Next time, can I sit on your lap again?" he asked. Grandpa smiled and said, "Yes. Every time."

Mila sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. The pumpkin picture had big round shapes. But Mila looked and looked. There was no orange paint. Only red, blue, yellow and green.

Mila frowned. "I want orange," she said. Her friend Mathys sat down next to her. He picked up the red pot. Then he picked up the yellow pot. "Stir these together," he said. Mila dipped her brush in red. She dipped it in yellow too. She stirred them on her paper.

The paint turned orange! Mila clapped her hands. "It's orange now!" she said. She painted her pumpkin all orange. It looked like a big round pumpkin in a field. Her little brother would think it was so cute.

Ms. Kowalski came to look. "What a great pumpkin, Mila," she said. "Let me put it on the wall." Mila smiled wide. Gianna came over with her paper. She pointed at a flower. "Can you make me pink for my petals?" she asked. Mila picked up her brush. She said, "Let's try red and white!"

Mia ran to the park with her friend Aniyah. The wind blew hard. It flapped Mia's coat. It made the tall trees sway. "My eyes feel funny," said Aniyah. She rubbed them with her hands.

Mia wanted to help her friend. She dug in the sand box with a shovel. Then she stopped. She looked up at the sky. She saw the wind carry dust past her face. A tiny bit of dirt came near her eye. Her eyelashes caught it. The dirt did not go in. Mia blinked. "Look, Aniyah," she said. "My eyelashes keep the dust out. That is what they do." Aniyah stood still and blinked too. Her eyelashes caught some dust as well.

Then Aniyah smelled popcorn nearby. They heard the popcorn pop, pop, pop. Ms. Qureshi, the park helper, gave them each a warm, soft cup. Mia touched the fluffy kernels and tasted the salty pop. "My eyes feel better now," said Aniyah. The wind blew again, and both girls blinked and laughed.

Max was at Grandma's house for dinner. Lots of cousins were there. Big bread rolls sat in a basket on the table.

Grandpa called Max over. "You are big enough now," Grandpa said. "You can say the Hamotzi. Many Jewish families say this blessing over the bread before a meal."

Max felt worried. The words were long. "What if I get them wrong?" he asked.

"Just try," said Grandpa. "I will help you."

They practiced together by the window. Max said the words slowly. Grandpa said them with him. The words got easier each time.

Then everyone sat down. The room was quiet. Grandma touched Max's shoulder. "Your turn," she said softly.

Max stood tall. He said the Hamotzi over the bread. His voice was small at first. Then it grew strong.

When he finished, everyone said "Amen." Then they all smiled and passed the bread.

"You did it!" said Grandpa.

Max bit into his warm roll. It tasted extra good. He passed the basket to his little cousin.

"Next time, you can try," Max said.

Sophie went to the library with her dad. It was windy outside, so they hurried in. Sophie picked a big book about a garden.

Dad opened the front cover first. He read from the first page to the last. Sophie saw small black marks under the pictures. Dad said those were words, and his finger moved along them as he read.

Then Sophie saw a page with only a picture of a plant. No small black marks at all. She asked, "Read this page!" Dad smiled. "There are no words here," he said. "Just look at the picture."

Sophie looked at the plant. Then she turned to the next page. More little words! Dad read them all aloud.

Sophie had one more question. "Do words tell you what to say?" Dad nodded and turned the page. "Read the next part," said Sophie.

Ethan ran onto the soccer field. He had his team shirt on. Cruz was there too. "Kick the ball to me!" said Cruz. Ethan kicked it hard. The ball went to the wrong spot. It went to a tree. "Oops," said Ethan.

Mr. Weber blew his whistle. Mr. Weber was the coach. He showed Ethan where to stand. "Stand here, Ethan," said Mr. Weber. Ethan stood on the white line. He kicked the ball again. This time it went to Cruz. "Good kick!" said Cruz.

Anna ran over and bumped the ball with her knee. The ball bounced high. Ethan had an idea. He could kick it when it came down. He waited. The ball came down. He kicked it. The ball went into the net! "Goal!" said Mr. Weber. Ethan jumped up and down. Cruz and Anna clapped. Ethan waved at Mr. Weber.

The lights went out. Athena looked up from her blocks. The whole apartment was dark.

"It is so quiet," said Mama. Athena listened. The fridge had stopped humming. The fan had stopped whooshing. It was quiet, quiet, quiet.

"I can hear new sounds," said Athena. She heard a dog bark outside. She heard Mr. Levy's feet in the hall above. She heard her own tummy rumble. "Listen, Mama! My tummy says hello!"

Mlaughed. She found a flashlight. She clicked it on. The light made a circle on the floor. Athena chased the circle with her feet.

"Shut your eyes and count," said Mama. "When you open them, we will play shadow puppets." Athena shut her eyes tight. She opened them. Mama's hands made a bunny on the wall.

"I want a bunny too," said Athena. She made her hands into wings. "Mine is a bird!"

Then the lights came back. The fridge began to hum again. The fan began to whoosh. The apartment was not quiet anymore.
