"Too loud!" said Athena, laughing. "Turn it off again!" She hugged the flashlight. "That was fun, Mama. Can the lights go out tomorrow?" Mama kissed her head. "Eat your juicy orange first," she said.

Jaxson wanted to write a note for Dad. The note would say, "I love you." Then Dad would see it at bedtime. Jaxson got his crayons and paper.

He wrote all his letters. He wrote them fast. The letters looked like this: iloveyougoodnight. All the letters were squished together. Dad came in to say goodnight. Dad looked at the paper. Dad moved it close to his eyes. "I cannot read this," said Dad. "The words are all squished. They look like one big yucky worm."

Jaxon felt sad. But then he had an idea. "Ms. Bear showed us books," he said. "Words in books have little gaps." He grabbed his crayon again. He drew a space after I. He drew a space after love. Now it said, "I love you." Dad read it out loud. "I love you! Now I can read it!"

Dad gave Jaxson a big hug. "This note is my favorite," said Dad. "Let's put it under my pillow. In the morning, I will catch you at breakfast and read it again." Jaxson smiled. He took his favorite book to bed. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one, all the way to the back. Every word had little spaces. Dad kissed his head. "Goodnight, Jaxson. Read me that book at breakfast."

It was outside time at school. The sun was high in the sky. Harrison ran to the slide. But a line had already formed.

Reese was at the front. Joelle was next. Harrison stood behind Joelle. He bounced on his toes. He wanted to go first.

Harrison slipped around the side. He pushed to the front and put his foot on the ladder. Reese frowned. Joelle said, "Hey, that is my spot."

Mr. Harper knelt down. "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn," he said.

Harrison looked back at the line. He stepped away from the ladder. He walked to his spot behind Joelle. His spot felt lost without him, so he was glad to find it again.

Reese went down the slide. Whee! Then Joelle went down. Whee! Then it was Harrison's turn. He climbed up. He slid down fast.

The wind made his shirt flap, like he could float. Harrison ran to the back of the line again. "My turn will come," he said.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything went dark. Quinn sat very still on the big smooth rug. She could hear the wind outside. "Mama," she called, "I can't see."

Mama came with the flashlight. She clicked it on. A bright circle moved along the wall. "Here," said Mama. "Hold it and keep it pointing down."

Quinn held the flashlight low. Then she lifted her hands up near the light. The light shone on her hands. Big dark shapes appeared on the wall. Quinn wiggled two fingers. The shape had long ears. "A bunny!" she said. She moved her fingers, and the bunny hopped.

Soon Dad lit the lamp in the kitchen. The light came back on. The shadows disappeared. "Where did my bunny go?" asked Quinn. Dad smiled. "Try again tomorrow." Quinn hugged the flashlight. "Bunny, we can have a party then," she said.

Charlie woke up and saw white snow. Lots of snow! No school today. It was a snow day.

"Come to my hill," said Ms. Dela Cruz. She was the neighbor. Her hill was big and white. Charlie pulled his red sled. Dad came too.

Charlie climbed to the top. He lay down on his belly. He wanted to zoom down head first.

"Not like that," said Dad. "Sit up. Face the hill. Hold on here." Dad showed him how. Charlie sat up. He held the rope tight. Ms. Dela Cruz stood at the bottom. She was watching.

"Go, Charlie, go!" she called.

The sled was slow at first. Then it went fast, fast, fast. Snow flew up. It touched Charlie's neck. It was cold and tickly. He laughed all the way down.

Charlie dragged the sled back up. He sat up again. He went down again. The sled went fast every time.

After, they went inside. Ms. Dela Cruz gave the birds some seeds to feed them. Charlie watched the birds peck, peck, peck.

"Snow day again tomorrow?" asked Charlie.

"We will see," said Dad. Charlie hugged his red sled.

It was a cold morning at the park. Snow was falling on the slide. Eli wore his warm coat and his red mittens. Odin wore a big hat. "Snowy day!" said Odin.

Eeli wanted to keep a snowball forever. He made a small, clean snowball. He held it in his mitten. Then he brought it inside the warm little park house. Mr. Malik was there. "I will keep my snowball," said Eli. He put it in a cup on the table.

Eli and Odin played with blocks. Then Eli looked at the cup. The snowball was gone. There was only water in the cup. "It is water now," said Eli. "Snow melts into water inside where it is warm." Mr. Malik smiled and nodded.

Eli ran back outside. He made a new snowball. This one stayed cold and white in the snow. "Look, Odin!" said Eli. "It still works!"

Madison stood by the big window. The sun was warm on her nose. Across the street, she could see the park. The slides were red. The swings moved back and forth.

"Park!" said Madison. "I want to go to the park." Her dad was in the kitchen. A pot sat on the stove. Steam went up, up, up. "That pot is hot," said Dad. "I will carry it. You stay way over there." Madison stayed back. Dad moved the pot to the table. The soup smelled good.

"Can we go to the park now?" asked Madison. "Yes," said Dad. "Get your shoes." Madison pulled her shoes on. One was on the wrong foot. She tried again. Now it felt right. Dad smiled. "Good trying, Madison."

They went out the door. The street was in front of them. A car went by. Then a big red truck. Madison looked at the street. She looked at her dad. She put her hand up high. "Hand!" she said. Dad took her hand. They looked both ways. Then they walked across, step by step.

At the park, Madison ran to the swing. She dug in the deep sand. She found a smooth gray stone. It felt cool in her fingers. She held it up. "Look, Dad!"

Rowan loved to draw. Today he wanted to draw a big forest. He found the green paint. But the jar lid would not open. Rowan pulled. He pulled harder. The lid was stuck. It felt slippery in his hands.

Saira sat next to him. "Try again," she said. Rowan tried again. The lid still would not open. His face felt hot. He wanted to cry. Then he remembered something. He walked to Ms. Cohen. "Can you help me, please?" he asked.

Ms. Cohen smiled. She turned the lid. Pop! It opened. "Thank you," said Rowan. He carried the jar back to the table. He dipped his brush. He drew tall green trees. He drew more trees. Saira drew a little fox under them. "A forest," said Rowan.

Aaron went to the library with his dad. Aaron wanted a book about trucks. He found one on a low shelf. He sat down on the soft rug.

Aaron opened the book. He put his finger at the right side of the page. "Read, book," he said. But no story came out. Aaron waited. He tapped the page. Still no story.

Kinley sat down next to him. "Ms. Gauthier can help," she said. Ms. Gauthier came over. She was careful with the pages. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side. Aaron put his finger at the left side of the page.

Then Ms. Gauthier read the words. "Big trucks carry mud." Aaron moved his finger from the left side to the right. The words said truck things! Aaron turned to the next page. More words waited there. "Again," said Aaron. Ms. Gauthier smiled. "You send that finger left to right," she said, "and I will read the name of each truck." Aaron walked his finger across. "This one is called Digger," she said. Aaron laughed. "Digger!" he said.

Norah wanted to make soup. She put her teddy bear in a chair. "You are hungry," she said.

She found a pot and a spoon. She put in a red sock. "A tomato!" she said. She put in a small pinecone. "A potato!" Then she stirred and stirred. The soup smelled like socks, not like dinner, but that was okay.

Teddy sat next to the pot. Norah held the spoon up to his mouth. "Slurp, slurp," she said. She made a big slurpy sound herself. Then she put the spoon near her own lips.

Her mom came in fast. "Not in your mouth," Mom said. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat."

Norah looked at the sock. She looked at the spoon. She tipped the spoon over the pot instead. "Pretend yum," she said.

Teddy got a big pretend bite. Norah clapped. "More soup for the team!" she said. She stirred the pot again, round and round, and the pretend steam went up, up, up like it could fly.

Ethan had a small piano at home. It sat by the window. He wanted to make a song.

He pressed one white key. It made a soft sound. He pressed a black key. It made a different sound. "Why do some look dark?" Ethan asked. His dad sat next to him. "Those are the black keys," Dad said. "The flat ones are the white keys."

Ethan wanted to play the black keys only. He tapped them, one by one. Bing, bong, boom. The sounds went up and down. It was a little tune! He played the black keys again. Then he played the white keys. They made new sounds too.

"Listen, Dad!" Ethan said. He played his black-key song. Dad clapped his hands. Then they made popcorn in the kitchen. Ethan waited at the table. Dad brought the bowl. The popcorn was a little salty and warm. Ethan played his song one more time before bed. Bing, bong, boom.

Jacob went to the park with his mom. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Jacob wore his little cap.

At the park, Maisie was there. She had a pink kite. "Look at my kite," said Maisie. She held the string tight.

Then the wind came. The trees began to sway. The big branches bent back and forth. Leaves blew around and around. The kite went up, up into the sky.

"I want a leaf," said Jacob. He ran after a leaf. The wind blew the leaf away. He ran again. The leaf danced past the slide.

Mr. Doyle was sitting on a bench. He waved at Jacob. "It is a windy day," said Mr. Doyle. Jacob felt the wind on his face. His cap blew off his head! Maisie caught it for him. "Thank you," said Jacob.

Jacob held his cap with one hand. With his other hand, he chased one more leaf. The wind stopped for a moment. The leaf sat still on the grass. Jacob picked it up. It was big and brown. He gave the leaf to his mom. "A windy day leaf," he said. Mom smiled and put it in her pocket.

Alexander sat in a big booth at the restaurant. His dad sat next to him. His friends Shane and Kaitlyn sat across the table. The big screen on the wall showed an ice hockey game.

"Where is the ball?" asked Shane. He looked and looked. The players skated fast on the ice. But Shane could not see a ball anywhere. Kaitlyn looked too. She could not see one either.

"I will find it," said Alexander. He watched the screen. He waited. He kept watching. Then he saw it. The players hit something small and flat with their long sticks. It slid on the ice. It was not a ball at all. "That flat disc is called a puck," said his dad. Alexander smiled. A puck! The players used their sticks to hit the puck.

Then the puck went up in the air. It started to fall. Everyone in the restaurant shouted. The goalie caught it, and the game went on. "Stay in your seat," Alexander's dad said. Alexander sat politely and kept watching.

Shane pointed at the screen. "I see the puck now!" he said. Kaitlyn clapped. The players hit the puck again and again. It slid fast across the ice. Alexander leaned forward and whispered, "Go, puck, go." Then the puck slid right into the net, and everyone cheered.

Maria wanted to play shop in the backyard. She put her toy apples on a little box. She had a spotted cup for coins. "I will be the shopkeeper," she said. The shopkeeper has the job of selling things.

Colin came to play. "I am the shopper," said Colin. "I will buy an apple." Maria held out her hand. Colin picked a red apple. He gave her a leaf for a coin. "Thank you, kind shopper," said Maria.

Then Maria wanted to be the shopper too. "Your turn, Colin," she said. Colin stood by the box. Maria walked around the yard. She looked at the apples. She looked and looked. Colin waited and waited. At last she chose the green one. "Good choice," said Colin. Maria hugged the apple like a baby doll. "My little apple is sleepy," she said. "Time to catch the bus home!" And off they went, chug chug chug, around the flowerpot.

Jacob stood by the pool with a red beanbag. His coach held up a hoop. "Throw it in," said the coach. Jacob threw it. It hit the rim and fell to the bottom of the hoop stand. "Try again," said Gus. Jacob tried again. Whoosh, in it went! Jacob laughed and did a little dance.

Then the coach brought out a big beach ball. Gus caught it with one hand, like a big kid. "My turn!" said Jacob. He used one hand. The ball bounced off his palm. It rolled past Louise. She laughed and chased it. Jacob tried one hand again. Bump, off it went.

"Maybe try like this," said Louise. She held out both hands. Jacob held out both hands too. The coach tossed the ball. Thump, it landed right in his arms. "I got it!" Jacob shouted. He hugged the big ball. "Again, again!" he said. The coach smiled and tossed the ball once more.

Rosalie woke up and saw snow. "A snow day!" she said. Mom took her to the park.

At the park, Rosalie saw Aaliyah and Scarlette. They made one snowman, two snow angels, three snowballs. Rosalie's mittens got wet. Her boots got wet too.

"I want more snowballs," Rosalie said. But her mittens were soaked. Her hands felt cold.

"Look," said Aaliyah. She hung her mittens on the fence. "My mom says wet mittens and boots are left out to dry." Scarlette put her boots by the mittens. "One boot, two boots," she said.

Rosalie hung her mittens on the fence too. "One mitten, two mittens," she said. She sat with Mom and watched them dry.

Soon the mittens were dry. "Is that true?" Rosalie asked. She touched them. Yes! They were warm and dry now.

"Thank you, mittens," she said. Then she ran to make four snowballs, five snowballs, six.

Levi sat on the big couch at Ms. O'Brien's house. His dad sat next to him. Remington and Lina sat on the floor. Everyone was watching the big game on TV.

The players ran fast. The crowd was loud. Then the game ended. Levi jumped up. "Who won?" he asked.

Ms. O'Brien pointed at the screen. "The score is two to two," she said. "Both teams have the same score. That is called a tie."

"A tie?" said Levi. "So nobody wins?"

"That's right," said his dad. "Nobody wins and nobody loses."

Remington clapped anyway. Lina threw her arms up like a player. Levi filled his hands with popcorn and threw some in the air like confetti.

"Not a lazy ending at all," said Ms. O'Brien. "It was a great game."

Levi munched his popcorn. His other leg bounced up and down. "I like ties," he said. "Can we watch another one?"

Lincoln was awake early. He ran to the balcony in his sock feet. His garden was waiting there. One pot, two pots, three pots. In the pots were little lettuce plants. Lincoln counted their leaves. One, two, three, four.

The sun was hot today. Lincoln looked at his lettuce. The leaves were bent down. They hung low, like sleepy arms. Lincoln spoke to them softly. "Oh no. You look sad."

Mika came over to play. She saw the pots too. "The lettuce is drooping," she said. Lincoln got his small watering can. It was blue and light to hold. He tipped it over the pots. Drip, drip, drip. Water fell on the soil.

The two friends waited. They ate crackers in the shade. Then Lincoln looked again. The leaves were lifting up. They stood tall and green. "Water helped you," Lincoln whispered. Mika clapped her hands. Lincoln gave each pot one more little drink. "One for you. One for you. One for you."

Oliver stood at the big table in cooking class. Mr. Choi put toast in front of him. "Spread the butter," said Mr. Choi. Oliver took his knife and spread slowly. The butter went soft on the warm toast. He did not rip the bread this time.

Then Mr. Choi gave him a jug of milk. Oliver poured the milk into his cup. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. Eliza clapped. "Good job, Oliver," she said. Oliver took a big drink. The milk was cold and sweet.

Then Oliver set the jug down on the table and walked away. Preston tapped his arm. "The milk has to go back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold," said Preston. Oliver nodded. He carried the jug to the fridge. Mr. Choi opened the door for him. Oliver slid the jug inside. Then he ate his toast and sang a little song. "Juicy toast, cold milk, happy kid," he sang.

Evan sat in the big chair at the dentist. He held his teddy bear on his lap. The bear had one arm sewn back on. It had been broken, but it was fixed now. After the checkup, the dentist said, "No holes in your teeth! Here is a sticker." Then she said, "Time for a snack." She put a little cup of crackers on the table.

Evan looked at his hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" he said. The dentist smiled. She walked him to the little sink. "Let's wash anyway," she said. Evan asked, "For how long?" She said, "Twenty seconds. Sing a song while you scrub."

Evan pumped the soap. He rubbed and rubbed. He sang his bear song. Bubbles covered his hands. He rinsed them in cool water and dried them on the soft towel. "Thank you," Evan said to the dentist. He gave a cracker a bite. "Mmm," he said. His bear watched from the chair, and Evan gave him a big, clean smile.

Arya sat in her car seat. Fiadh sat beside her. They were going to the park.

Arya had a snack bag. Inside were round crackers. She held the bag on her lap.

Fiadh looked at the crackers. "May I have one, please?" she asked.

"Yes," said Arya. She opened the bag. She gave Fiadh a cracker.

Fiadh took a small bite. "Thank you," she said.

Arya did not know what to say back. She thought and thought. She looked out the window.

Then the driver spoke. "Thank you for buckling up, girls."

"You're welcome," said Fiadh.

Arya heard it. Her eyes got big. So that was what to say!

Fiadh looked at her and waited. Arya smiled.

"You're welcome," said Arya.

Fiadh smiled too. Then she took another little bite of her cracker.

The car stopped. They were at the park. Arya held up the bag.

"More crackers?" she asked. "Please?"

"Yes, please!" said Fiadh.

Elliot put on his orange hat. He was going to the ice rink with Dad. Ayansh and Zainab came too. They were going to watch a big hockey game.

The players zoomed past on the ice. One team skated and skated. They went so fast! "That team runs a lot," said Elliot. "They run more. So they win, right?" Zainab shook her head. Ayansh pointed up high. "Look at the big sign," he said.

Elliot looked at the sign. It showed the score. The fast team had two points. The other team had four points. The buzzer went buzzzzz. The game was over. The team with four points jumped up and down. They got a big shiny cup. "They won because they had more points," said Zainab.

After the game, the friends got to slide on the ice. Elliot slid on his bottom. Plop! Everyone laughed. Dad gave Elliot a warm drink. It was a gift from Ms. Huang, who worked at the rink. Elliot held the cup with both hands. "Next time I will count the points," said Elliot. "One, two, three, four!"

Wren stood in the band room. She held a little drum. Two sticks sat in her hands. She wanted to play the whole song. But her sticks went tap, tap, boom. The song stopped in the wrong place.

"That song is tricky," said Isaiah. He watched from his chair. Mr. Katz smiled. "Try it again tomorrow," he said. "And the next day too." So Wren did. Each day she played a little. Tap, tap, boom became tap, tap, tap, boom. Outside the window, gentle rain fell while she practiced.

On Friday, Wren lifted her sticks. She played the song all the way to the end. Bradley clapped his hands. Isaiah clapped too. "You did it!" he said. Wren hit one last boom. "More songs!" she said.

Emily went to the store with her dad. She wanted to find a red cup for school. "Stay close to me," said Dad. Emily held his hand.

They walked past the ovens. A worker was baking bread. "That oven is hot," said Dad. Emily put her hand behind her back. She did not touch. She watched from far away. The bread smelled good.

In the toy corner, Emily found a little slide. It was small and black. Banks from her school was there too. "Can I slide?" asked Emily. "Yes," said Banks. Emily climbed up. She started to lie down head first. Then she stopped. She turned herself around. She went down feet first. Whee! "At the playground, go down the slide feet first," said Banks. Emily slid again and again. Feet first, every time.

Then Emily saw the red cups. She picked one out. Dad paid the cashier. Emily spelled her name on the way home. "E-M-I-L-Y," she said slowly. Dad smiled and spelled it back.

At home, Emily drank cold milk from her new cup. "Was the slide fun?" asked Dad. "Yes," said Emily. "Feet first. Every time."

Layla sat at Grandma's big kitchen table. Her eyes were closed. "Guess what I made," said Grandma. Layla could smell it. It smelled sweet, like berries. Her nose helped her guess. "Is it berry cake?" she asked. Grandma laughed. "Yes! Now open your eyes."

Layla opened her eyes. She saw the pink cake on the blue plate. She saw the cup of ice beside it, cold and shiny. "We see with our eyes," said Layla. Grandma smiled and clapped. "That is one sense. Only four more to go."

Layla touched the ice cup. "Brrr, it is cold," she said. "My hands feel it." She listened to the clock. Tick, tick. "My ears hear that." She sniffed the cake again. "My nose smells it." Then Grandma cut a small slice. Layla took a bite. "And my tongue tastes the berries!"

"You found all five senses," said Grandma. Layla jumped up from her chair. "I want to draw them! Can I have paper?" Grandma set out the crayons. Layla drew two eyes, two ears, one nose, two hands, and one happy tongue with berry jam all around it.

Isla was in the music classroom. Today she would play the big drum. The drum had a spotted cover, like a cow. Isla held the little mallet. She gave it a swing. Boom! The drum made a big sound. She tapped again. Boom, boom!

Ms. Costa called everyone to the rug. "Time for our little show," she said. Lincoln sat down to listen. Rosa sat down too. Isla stood by the drum. Her tummy felt jumpy, but she played. Boom, boom, boom!

Then Isla stopped. Everyone clapped for her. Lincoln clapped loud. Rosa clapped loud. What should Isla do now? Ms. Costa bent down low, from her waist. Isla watched. Then Isla bent down low too, just like that. Everyone clapped even more.

"When can I bow again?" Isla asked. Ms. Costa laughed. "At the end, whenever we clap."

Zachary looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "It is a snow day."

Zachary put on his boots. He put on his red mittens. He went outside to play. The snow was soft and cold. It squeaked under his boots. He patted a big snowball. It was round like a ball.

"I want to keep this snowball," Zachary said. His dad helped him carry it inside. They put it in a bowl on the table. Zachary wanted to save it for tomorrow.

Zachary played with his toy butterfly. He painted a picture of the snow. He waited a long time. Then he looked at the bowl. The snowball was small now. The bowl was not empty. There was water in it. "Dad, come look!" said Zachary. "The snow turned into water."

"The snow melted in here," said his dad. "It is warm inside." Zachary touched the water. It was cool on his finger.

Zachary had an idea. He got a fresh snowball from the yard. He put it in a cup. He carried the cup outside to the cold porch. "Stay there, snowball," he said.

The next morning, Zachary checked his cup. The snowball was still there, big and white. Zachary smiled and patted it with his mitten.

Isla sat at the big kitchen table. She was painting a picture. She painted a red bird. She painted a yellow sun. She painted a blue sky.

Now she wanted grass. Grass is green. She looked in the green paint pot. It was empty! "Oh no," said Isla. "My grass will be white. That is not right."

Her friend Aurora peeked at the picture. "Silly white grass!" she laughed. "The sheep will be confused."

Isla dipped her brush in the blue pot. She painted a blue stripe. Then she dipped in the yellow pot. She painted yellow on top. She stirred with her brush.

The paint turned green! Isla peeked at the pot. "Aurora, look! Blue and yellow make green!" She painted long green grass under the tree in her picture. "It is true. The grass looks perfect now," said Isla. Aurora clapped her hands.

David stood in the garage with Rosalia. Ms. Lewandowski turned on a little radio. A song began to play. It had a steady beat. David wanted to clap along and sing, but his hands went too fast. The beat went on without him.

Rosalia clapped her hands slowly. Tap, tap, tap. "Try it like this," she said. David watched her hands. He clapped when she clapped. His claps landed right on the beat! Then he tried to sing. "The itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water spout." But his fingers climbed down, down, down. Rosalia laughed. "The spider climbs up," she said. David turned his fingers around. Up they went, just like the song.

Ms. Lewandowski clapped too. All three of them sang the whole rhyme from memory. Then the radio made a funny beep and turned itself off. "Time to leave for the house," said Ms. Lewandowski. David clapped one more time, just for fun.

Lily was playing on the rug. "Time to clean up," said Dad. Lily wanted to keep playing her car game. But Dad said the cars must go in the red box.

Lily looked at her line of cars. Vroom, vroom, vroom. Then she saw something bright yellow. A banana was sitting with the toy cars! "How did you get here?" she asked the banana.

Isha came over to play. "The banana is the odd one out," said Isha. Lily thought about that. The odd one out is the thing that does not belong. A banana was not a car. A banana was a food. It belonged in the fruit bowl.

So Lily picked up the banana. She drop-planned a big ride. "Cars, carry the banana home!" she said. She pushed the banana on a little truck. Vroom! The wind from the open window seemed to cheer. At the bowl, she dropped the banana in with the apples. All done! The cars went in the red box, one by one.

Lily looked at the bowl. All fruits together. She looked at the red box. All cars together. Nothing odd, nothing out. "Clean up is like a game," said Lily. "Let's play it again!" said Isha. Lily ran to find her toy animals next.

Harper had a cold. Her nose was red and runny. Mom said, "We need tissues from the pharmacy." Harper put on her coat and went with Mom.

At the pharmacy, Mom found the tissues. Harper's nose began to tickle. She blew her nose into a tissue. Then she saw a bowl of candy at the counter. She reached out her hand. Mom said, "Wait. Let's wash your hands with soap and water first." They walked to the little sink. Harper made bubbles on her hands. The soap made her hands clean. Then Mom gave her one candy. "Good girl," said the cashier, smiling.

At home, Harper blew her nose again. She looked at her apple slices. She said, "I need to wash my hands first." Mom laughed and clapped. Harper carried her apple to the clean, happy kitchen table.

Jaxon sat on the playroom floor. He wanted to draw snow. Snow was big and fluffy. He took his white crayon. He drew on white paper. He could not see it! "Oh no," said Jaxon. "My snow is hiding."

Cristian came to watch. "I see white on white," said Cristian. "It looks like nothing at all." Jaxon frowned. He held up his paper. The snow was there, but it did not show. Mr. Kamau came over too. He looked at the paper. He smiled a soft smile.

"Try a new paper," said Mr. Kamau. He put down a blue paper. Blue like the sky. Jaxon picked up his white crayon again. He drew snow on the blue paper. The snow showed up! Bright white dots on blue. "I see it! I see it!" said Jaxon.

Jaxon drew more snow. He added a green tree. He added a red hat. He added a yellow sun. "Snow is white," said Jaxon. "White snow on blue. White snow on green!" Cristian made a picture too. His spotted dog stood in the snow. The spots were white on brown.

"Snow is white," said Jaxon one more time. He hugged his picture. Mr. Kamau hung it on the wall. Jaxon waved at his snow. "Hello, snow," said Jaxon.

Max stood by the little pool at the beach. The water was green and cool. He wanted to jump in right away.

His friend Nirvaan was already in the water. Nirvaan's dad sat on a plastic chair. He watched Nirvaan swim. Max saw that. When a grown-up watched, Nirvaan could jump and splash.

Max's teacher, Mr. Sadeghi, was not there yet. Max waited at the side. He counted the waves. He stirred the water with one toe. The little waves went round and round his foot.

Then Mr. Sadeghi came. He sat down by the pool. "I am watching you now," he said. Max smiled. He sat on the edge. He kicked his legs. He slid in, slow and careful.

The water felt cool on his arms. Max held the side. Mr. Sadeghi kept watching. Max kicked again. He moved a little bit. "I did it!" said Max. Nirvaan clapped from the other side.

Max got out and rested in the sun. Then he went back in. Mr. Sadeghi watched every time. Max kicked, and he moved again.

Owen loved the red cups at school. One day Ms. Koné said, "Can you help set the table?" Owen carried the red cups. He put one cup in front of each chair. One cup, one chair. One cup, one chair. Uh oh. The last chair had no cup! Owen ran back to the shelf. He found one more red cup. He put it down. Now every chair had a cup. "We all get one," said Owen.

After snack, Ms. Koné put out blocks. She made a black tower and a yellow tower. "Which has more?" she asked. Owen did not know. Then he had an idea. He put one black block on each yellow block. One on one, again and again. Every yellow block had a black block on top. Not one was left over. "They are the same!" said Owen. He gave the towers a little shake to check. They still matched.

Ari clapped. "Again, again!" said Ari. Owen counted the yellow blocks out loud, all the way to ten. Then he grinned and pushed the blocks into one big pile. "Now we build one giant tower," he said.

Harper ran to the park with her dad. "I want to play ball!" she said. But her hat flew off in the wind. It landed near the sandbox. Her sock slipped off too and fell in the sand.

Kiaan was digging in the sandbox. He found the sock. He put it with his trucks and shovels. "A new toy!" he said.

Harper ran over. She looked at the pile. She saw trucks. She saw shovels. She saw her sock. She laughed and laughed.

"That is not a toy," she said. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes!" She picked up her sock and shook off the sand. Kiaan picked up her hat. He put both things in her bag.

"Now let's play ball!" said Kiaan. Harper threw it high. Kiaan caught it, and they both cheered.

Gianna was at Grandma's house. Ekam was there too. They sat on the big rug. Gianna held a teddy bear. She wanted to play with Ekam. But Ekam just looked at his truck. Gianna did not know what to say.

Then Grandma's phone did ring. Grandma said hello. Giana had an idea. She stood up tall. "Let's pretend we are a family," she said. Ekam jumped up. "Yes! I will be the dad." He gave his truck a kiss. "This is our baby."

Gianna made the teddy sleep. She patted it softly. "Time for bed, little one." Ekam drove to the store. "I will get food." They played and played all afternoon. Later, Grandma watched them from her chair in the yard. "What a lazy, happy day," she said. Ekam hugged Gianna. "Let's pretend again tomorrow."

Athena sat at the kitchen table. She had one toy block and a sheet of stickers. She wanted to put a sticker on every side of the block.

"One," she said. She put a blue sticker on the top. She turned the block over. "Two." She put a red sticker on the bottom.

She turned the block again and again. Side, side, side, side. "Six stickers!" she said. "The block has six flat faces."

Her mom looked over. "And what shape is each one?" she asked.

Athena held the block up to the light. She looked at one face, then another. Each face had four straight sides, all the same. "They are all squares," she said. "Six squares in one block!"

She set the block by the window. A slow bee buzzed past the glass. Athena did not leave her chair. She just watched it go.

"Six faces," she whispered to the block. "All square."

Muhammad ran to the playground. Aadya was there with a red kite. The kite danced in the wind. Muhammad wanted to hold it so much.

He reached out his hand. Then he stopped. He thought hard. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Aadya smiled big. "Yes! You said may I. Here you go." She put the string in his hands. The kite pulled like a little fish trying to swim away. Muhammad held on tight. He was brave in the strong wind.

The kite made a funny noise, flapping fast. "Thank you, Aadya," said Muhammad. Aadya clapped. "May I have it back now?" she asked. Muhammad gave her the string. "Please hold it with two hands," she said. Muhammad helped her hold it too. The red kite flew and flew, way up in the blue sky.

Gabriel sat at the big table in the library. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name all by himself. He held the pencil tight and made a line. The line went down and then across. "That is a G," said Mr. Silva. Gabriel looked at it. The G had a round curve, like a ball.

Then Gabriel made a straight line down. It had no curve at all. Mr. Silva put out letter cards on the table. Gabriel sorted them. He put G, A, and R in one pile. Those letters had curves. He put L in the other pile. L was made of straight lines only.

"Now write them," said Mr. Silva. Gabriel pressed the pencil on the paper. The curvy letters rolled out in loops. The straight letters stood like sticks. His name popped onto the page, letter by letter. "I did it!" said Gabriel. "G-A-B-R-I-E-L." Mr. Silva smiled and clapped.

Today was Emma's birthday. She was three years old. Dad gave her a red balloon. He blew it up with lots of air. Then Mom gave her a yellow balloon. She blew it up, too.

"One balloon, two balloons," said Emma. Her friends Fallon and Liyana came to play. Liyana had a shiny helium balloon from the party shop. Liyana let go of it. Up, up, up it went to the ceiling.

Emma wanted her red balloon to fly, too. She let go of it. The red balloon did not go up. It drifted down, down to the floor. Emma tried again with the yellow one. Down it went, too.

Emma listened to the balloons go pitter-pat on the floor. She laughed. She held the string and pulled the balloon along like a puppy. "Come on, balloon!" she said.

Then they ate crunchy apple slices and birthday cake. Dad lit the candles and blew them out for her. Emma clapped. "Happy birthday to me!" she said. She gave the red balloon a big hug.

Maeva went to the community center with her dad. There was a music room there. Mr. Nkosi had a big guitar on a stand. Maeva wanted to hear it play. She tapped the guitar like a drum. Tap, tap, tap. The big strings did not sing.

Mr. Nkosi knelt down beside her. "You play a guitar by plucking or strumming its strings," he said. He showed her how. He swept his fingers over the strings. The guitar made a long, sweet sound. Maeva heard it all the way to her toes.

Maeva tried. She touched one string with her finger. Pluck. One little note came out. She tried again. Pluck. Then she swept her hand across. All the strings sang together. Leif clapped from the doorway. Maeva strummed one more time, slow and loud, and the room filled with sound.

In the morning, Athena ran to the kitchen. She could smell something sweet. "Bananas," she said. Her mom was cutting fruit with a knife. Athena stayed back and watched from her chair.

"We will meet the blender soon," said Mom. Athena touched the cold counter. She saw the bright red machine. Then Mom turned it on. It was so loud! Athena covered her ears with her hands. At once, the big sound got small. She asked herself, "Did my hands do that?" She lifted one hand. The noise grew big again. She pressed her hand back. The noise got small. She smiled behind her hands.

The blender stopped. Mom poured a thin, smooth drink into a cup. Athena tasted it. Sweet and cold! "Mmm," she said. "Can we make it again tomorrow?"

"Maybe," said Mom. "But now listen." Athena heard birds outside the window. She uncovered her ears to hear them better, and sipped her drink.

Charles sat at the small red table. He had three big balls in front of him. They were soft and round. Kingston sat next to him with three tiny beads. Ms. Pelletier put out two baskets.

"Who has more?" she asked.

Charles looked at his big balls. They took up all his space. Kingston's beads looked so little.

"I have more," said Charles. "My balls are big."

Kingston looked a bit mad. He held his beads close.

Ms. Pelletier smiled. "Let's count," she said. "Charles, count your balls."

Charles touched each ball. "One, two, three."

"Now Kingston, count your beads."

Kingston touched each bead. "One, two, three."

Charles sat very still. He counted again. Three big balls. Three tiny beads. Both were three. The same number.

"They match," said Charles. "Three and three."

Kingston smiled wide. "Same number," he said.

"Let's stick them in our counting book," said Ms. Pelletier. She held the pages open. Charles pressed his three big ball stickers down. Kingston pressed his three small bead stickers down. Side by side, three and three.

After school, Charles found his mom by the gate. "We counted at school," he said. "Three big balls and three tiny beads are both three."

Milan ran to the big pool with his bear under his arm. He could not wait to swim! Ms. Mercado waved at the water. "Jump in when I say go," she said.

Milan splashed in near Adalyn and Vincenzo. He kicked his legs. He blew bubbles. The water went up and down. "Look!" said Milan. "When I kick, the water jumps!" Adalyn laughed and kicked too. The water jumped even more.

Then Milan wanted to get out. He grabbed the side of the pool. He pulled and pulled. His arms slipped. It was too high to climb over the edge. Vincenzo pointed to the corner. "Try the ladder," he said. "It helps you get in and out of the water."

Milan held the rail. He climbed one step, then two, then three. Step by step, he was out! That was so much easier. "That ladder is neat!" said Milan. He held his bear up high and let his legs swing in the air.

"Can I climb down the ladder too?" Milan asked. Ms. Mercado smiled. "Yes," she said. So Milan went down the ladder, step by step. He jumped back in the water with a big splash. Adalyn shouted, "Again, again!"

Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Ali wanted to make her feel happy. He got out a big bowl. Mom said, "I will pour the milk. You can pass me the spoon." Ali passed the spoon. Mom stirred pancake batter. The stove was hot, so Mom stood near it. Ali stood back and watched.

Then Ali saw a photo on the fridge. It showed Grandma holding Mom's hand. Mom was little in the photo. Ali frowned. "That is the wrong photo," he said. "Grandma is not your mom." Mom laughed softly. "Yes, she is. Grandma is my mom." Ali looked at the photo again. So Grandma was a mom two times!

The doorbell rang. Grandma came in with her bag. Ali ran to hug her legs. "You are Mom's mom!" he said. Grandma smiled a big smile. "That is my best hug today," she said. Then they all ate warm pancakes together.

Isabella went to the laundromat with her dad. Her coat had soft fur inside. She wanted to zip it all by herself. First, one hand. Then the other hand. The zipper went up, up, up. "Look, Dad! I did it!"

Avery was there too. Avery dropped her coat on the floor. One, two, three coats lay in a heap. Later Avery looked for her coat. She could not find it. It had slid far under the bench.

"Where did it go?" Avery asked.

Then Isabella saw a little hook on the wall. She hung her coat on the hook. Her coat stayed up high. It did not touch the floor. Avery hung hers up too.

"Two coats on the hook," said Isabella. "No coats on the floor."

William ran to the dinner table. He held something in his fist. "Look, look!" he said. He opened his hand. It was one small feather.

"I found it in the grass," said William. "Who lost it?" He looked at his plate. There was chicken, rice, and peas. Not the feather owner. There was his toy car by his cup. Not the feather owner. There was his stuffed bear on his chair. Not the feather owner.

Then William thought hard. He knew a big thing. "Birds have feathers!" he said. "A bird lost it!" He jumped up. He was so excited he almost fell off his chair. Dad caught him. "Feet on the floor, brave guy," said Dad.

William looked out the window. A little bird sat on the fence. It hopped. It flew up high.

"Ms. Campbell told us!" said William. "Feathers mean birds. One feather, one bird!"

The bird flew away. William waved. "Bye, bird! Your feather is safe with me!"

Colton was at the park with his new red beanbag. A hoop stood on the grass. Colton wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

He threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew high. It sailed past the hoop and plopped near the lake. "Silly beanbag," said Colton.

Ms. Njoroge came to help. "Watch me," she said. She held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag sailed up and dropped into the hoop. "Wow!" said Colton.

Colton tried it. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up, up, up. It fell right into the hoop. Nour clapped. April clapped. Colton bowed like a fancy duck.

Next, April tossed him a big ball. He caught it with both hands. "Again!" he said. The ball came back. He caught it again. Colton hugged the ball and grinned.

Colton put on his skates at the ice rink. His team was busy getting ready. Mr. Somsak gave him a stick. "Time to play," said Mr. Somsak.

The puck slid to Colton. He tapped it. He tapped it again. Then he tried to shoot. The puck missed the net. It went past the net and hit the boards. "Oh no," said Colton.

Then he heard something. His team was cheering. "Try again, Colton!" shouted Jeremiah. "You can do it!" shouted Zain. Even the other team clapped their sticks. Colton had a warm feeling inside. The puck came back to him. He shot again. This time, the puck went in! The team jumped up and down.

Zain got the puck next. He shot and missed too. Colton clapped his stick. "Try again, Zain!" Zain laughed and tried again. The puck slid in. "We can all try again," said Colton. Then he skated to fetch the puck for his friend.

Emilia walked on the nature trail with Mr. Whitehead. "Let's name our five senses," he said. Emilia wanted to get them all right. She looked up. She saw a bright star shape in a flower. "I see it with my eyes," she said. She touched a fuzzy leaf. "I touch with my hands," she said. Then she heard a bird. "I hear with my ears," she said. "I smell with my nose," she said. One sense was left. Emilia could not think of it. Mr. Whitehead gave her a lemon slice and a strawberry. Emilia tasted the lemon. Her mouth went puckery and sour. Then she tasted the strawberry. It was sweet. "I taste with my tongue," Emilia said. She had all five senses now. Mr. Whitehead smiled. "My tongue likes the strawberry best," Emilia said.

Rose sat in the car with her brother. The sun was bright. "Sunny today," said Dad. Rose put on her sunglasses. They felt silly and she laughed.

Then the sky turned grey. Rain hit the window. Tap, tap, tap. "Rainy now," said Rose. Dad parked near the school. "We will share my umbrella," he said. Rose stepped out. Rain fell on her shoes. Dad opened the umbrella over her head. The rain could not get her hair. It ran down the sides instead. "My head is dry," said Rose. She smiled big.

Her friend Keon ran past. He had no umbrella. His hair was all wet and drippy. "You look like a wet cat," said Rose. Keon laughed and shook like a puppy. Rose held the umbrella high and kept walking to the school door.

Milan wanted to play with Lauralie. She had a new puzzle. It had a red fire truck on it.

"Now?" Milan asked his mom.

"Tomorrow," Mom said. "Today we stay home. Tomorrow is the day after today."

Milan frowned. "That is far away."

"Sleep comes first," Mom said. "Sleep, then a new day."

Milan ate lunch. He took a bite of his cheese sandwich. Then he played trucks on the floor. The sun went down. The sky turned dark blue, his favorite color.

Milan put on his pajamas. He brushed his teeth. Mom read him a book about a bear. Milan closed his eyes.

Then it was morning. The sun was up. Milan looked out the window.

"Is it tomorrow now?" he asked.

"Yes," Mom said. "It is a new day."

Milan cheered. He put on his blue shirt, his special shirt. He brought his own toy truck to share. Mom held his hand. They walked to Lauralie's house.

Lauralie opened the door. "The puzzle is ready!" she said.

They sat on the rug. They found the red pieces first. Then the wheels. Then the little dog with a black nose.

Milan smiled at Lauralie. "I waited and slept," he said. "And now it is today!"

Billie held her book at bedtime. She wanted Mom to read it. But Mom was still in the kitchen.

Dad sat down on the bed. He opened the book. He turned the first page. "One tiny brown dog ran up the hill," he read.

Then Mom came in. "My turn," she said. Dad gave her the book. Mom started at the front. She turned the pages one by one. "One tiny brown dog ran up the hill," she read.

Billie sat up. "That is what Dad said!" She looked at Mom. She looked at Dad. "Say it again."

Mom read the page again. "One tiny brown dog ran up the hill."

"Same words," said Billie. "Dad says it. You say it. The words stay the same!"

Mom turned to the next page. "The dog saw a red ball." Dad read the next page too. "The dog ran to the red ball." Mom read it once more. "The dog ran to the red ball."

"Same again!" said Billie. "The words do not change."

Mom kissed her head. "They will be there in the morning too."

Billie hugged the book. She turned to the front. She pointed at the words. "One tiny brown dog," she said.

"Now close your eyes and dream about that dog," said Mom. She turned off the light.

Billie smiled in the dark. "Goodnight, same words," she whispered.

Arnaud sat at the little red table. He had a big box of crayons. All of them. Red, blue, green, yellow, purple. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

He drew a slide at the park. He made the sky blue and the grass green. Then he heard a sad sound. Sniff, sniff. It was Abir. Abir had no crayons. Abir had a plain white paper with nothing on it.

Arnaud looked at his five crayons. He looked at Abir. "Sharing," said Mr. Quinn, walking by. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too." Arnaud pushed two crayons across the table. "Here, Abir. Red and yellow." Abir smiled a big smile. Abir drew a pretty red flower and a yellow sun.

Arnaud kept his three crayons. He drew a purple slide. Then Abir pushed the red crayon back. "Your turn for red," said Abir. Arnaud colored the slide red, too. It looked so pretty. Two pictures, one box of crayons, two happy friends. "Want to draw a cat next?" asked Abir. "Yes!" said Arnaud. "One cat, two cats, purple cats!"

Rose sat at the dinner table. Her tummy was happy and warm. She ate her peas one by one. Daddy had made the soup, and it steamed cool at the edge of her bowl.

"Tomorrow we go to the park," said Daddy. "You can wear your new red shoes."

Rose wanted to wear them now. She slid down from her chair. She pushed her feet into the shoes. But the shoes felt bumpy and wrong. Her toes were not cozy at all.

Rose laughed. Off came the shoes. She put on her soft blue socks first. Then the shoes went on, nice and easy.

She gave a little hop. The socks were warm like a feather blanket.

"Ready for tomorrow!" said Rose. She patted her shoe, tap tap, on the floor.

Lena ran to the red truck at the playground. Georges ran too. They both grabbed the truck. Lena pulled one end. Georges pulled the other end.

"My truck," said Lena.
"First," said Georges.

The truck wobbled in their hands. Then Lena saw Mr. Oyelaran by the swings. She walked over with Georges. "We both want the truck," Lena said. Mr. Oyelaran smiled. "Let's take turns," he said. "Lena can go first. Then Georges."

Lena pushed the truck down the slide. It rolled fast. Georges laughed and chased it. Then Lena handed him the truck. "Your turn," she said. Georges pushed it into the sandbox.

Lena watched a furry dog walk past with its owner. She thought of the ocean, big and blue like in her book. Then the truck came back to her. "My turn again," she said. Georges nodded. "Truck next," he said.

Elijah went to the music room at the community center. Mr. Korhonen had a little violin. He held it out. "You can try it," he said.

Elijah grabbed the stick part in his fist. He poked the strings with the wrong end. Squeak! Squeak! Rosalie laughed and covered her ears. "That sounds like a duck," she said. Kyro giggled too.

Mr. Korhonen sat down next to Elijah. "Watch me," he said. He pulled the long stick across the strings. The violin sang. "That stick is called a bow," he said. Elijah took the bow the right way. He pulled it across the strings, slow and smooth. A nice sound came out. Rosalie clapped. Kyro clapped. Elijah pulled the bow again and again. He played music all the way to the wall and back. "More duck!" said Kyro. Elijah laughed and made the violin sing.

Arlo went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm and bright. Arlo held his dad's hand by the road. "Stay close," said his dad. Arlo stayed close.

Near the bench, Arlo saw a little metal box on a pole. It had holes in it. His friend Skye came over. "What is it?" she asked. Arlo wanted to put his finger in a hole. He touched it to his nose instead. That was safe. His dad saw them. "That is a plug box," he said. "Never put fingers or things into it." Arlo nodded.

Then something surprising happened. A bird landed on the bench. The bird had one little eye on Arlo. It picked up a nut and flew away. Arlo laughed. He took his dad's hand again. "Bye, bird," he said.

Owen sat on the blanket in the music room. He held his little guitar. He plucked one string. The note sounded funny. It went boing, not ding.

"My guitar sounds wrong," Owen said. "Why does it sound funny?"

Ms. Traoré knelt down beside him. "Strings need tuning," she said. "That makes the notes sound right." She turned the little pegs, one at a time. She plucked the string again. Ding! Now it sounded smooth and sweet.

Owen looked at the pegs. He turned one just a tiny bit. He plucked the string. It went boing again. He turned the peg the other way, slow and careful. Ding!

Barkat clapped his hands. Owen strummed all the strings. "Ding, ding, ding!" he sang.

Anthony ran to the window at school. Rain was coming down. Big round drops hit the glass.

"No park today," said Mr. Rahman. Anthony felt sad. He wanted to slide and run. Rohan felt sad too. He sat down and frowned.

Then Liya had an idea. "Let's build a fort!" she said. Anthony got excited. He ran to the toy shelf. He pulled out a big red blanket. Rohan brought a small blanket too. Mr. Rahman tied a string from two chairs. Anthony helped hang the blanket over the string. The fort was big and cozy.

The three friends crawled inside. It was dark and warm. Rohan laughed. Anthony laughed too. He was not sad anymore. His sad feeling had gone away. Now he felt happy.

"Rain made the park stop," said Anthony. "But the fort is fun!"

Mr. Rahman peeked in the door. "Can I come too?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Anthony, and he lifted the blanket.

Chloe sat at the big table in the library. Ms. Cheung put out paper and glue. Chloe wanted to make a paper sailboat. She needed a square for the boat. She needed two triangles for the sail. The sail had to look like a tiny triangle flag on top.

Chloe found a red square. But she had no triangles. Her friend Brinley had triangles, but they were blue. Chloe wanted red. She frowned at her paper.

Ms. Cheung came over. "I can help with the scissors," she said. The scissors were sharp, so Ms. Cheung held them. She put the point at one corner of the square. "Cut from this corner to the corner across from it," she said. Snip, snip. The square fell open. Now Chloe had two red triangles!

Chloe clapped her hands. One square had made two triangles! She glued them on her boat. Brinley and Maha made sailboats too. Maha cut a green square and got two green triangles.

Then the three friends lined up the boats on the table. "Choo choo!" said Chloe. "Our boats are a train!"

Noah went to the library with his dad. He found a book with a big red truck on the cover. "Read this one!" said Noah.

His dad opened the book. He started at the front. The first page had words. His dad read them out loud. Noah looked with wide eyes. The words made the story! His dad read each page, front to back, all the way to the end.

Noah loved the pictures best. A dog drove the truck. A cat waved a stick. "Who drew the dog?" asked Noah.

Ms. Gallagher passed by. "The illustrator drew the pictures," she said. "The name is right here."

Noah looked at the front of the book. There was the name. "The illustrator made my dog!" said Noah. He hugged the book tight.

Josephine played in the backyard with Yug. They dug in the dirt with a fork. Soon their hands were very muddy.

"Time for a wash," said Josephine's mom. She put a big tub of water on the grass. Josephine wanted to jump right in. But her mom held up a hand. "Wait, let me check," she said. She touched the water. "The hose was in the sun. This water is hot." She added cold water from the shady tap. She touched it again. "Now it is warm. Warm is good."

Josephine looked at the tub. The hot water had made steam. The warm water did not. The two waters felt different, and only one was safe for her. She climbed in and washed her muddy hands. Yug put a toy fish in the tub. The fish floated by her toes.

After the wash, they had a picnic. Josephine ate with her fork. Then she pointed at the tub. "Is the water warm now?" she asked her mom. Her mom touched it and smiled. "Warm all over," she said. Josephine patted the water with one small finger, very softly, and laughed.

Olivier went to the store with his mom. Today was Friday. Yesterday they had no bread. Now the bread shelf was almost empty. "Just one loaf left," said Mom.

Olivier saw cookies on a low shelf. He wanted the bear cookies. "Can we get those now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "We can get cookies later." Olivier put them in his mind and kept them there.

They picked apples. They picked milk. Olivier kept asking, "Is it later yet?" Mom smiled. "Not yet. Later means some time after now, not right away." Olivier thought about that. So later was not now. Later was after.

They paid the cashier. They walked to the car. Then Mom said, "Now it is later. Let's go back for your cookies." Olivier ran back to the shelf. He put the bear cookies in the basket all by himself. "We can eat them tomorrow," said Mom. Olivier hugged the bag. "Tomorrow is after today!" he said.

Brielle wanted her animal book. She looked at her big book pile. It was too tall and too messy.

She pushed the books. She pulled the books. No animal book! "Where is it?" she said.

Dad came to help. "At the library, books sit on shelves in groups," he said. "That is how people find them." Brielle had seen that. The library had a shelf of animal books. It had a shelf of toy books. It had a shelf of food books.

"Same at home!" said Brielle. She began to sort. She made one group of animal books. She made one group of toy books. She made one group of food books. Dad helped her wipe the shelf. It smelled like lemon. Then Brielle put each group on its own shelf.

She found her animal book. It was hiding at the very bottom! And something else was hiding too. A small toy cat had fallen behind the shelf. "Meow!" said Brielle, and she hugged the cat tight.

Alexis sat on the big paper bed. He held his stuffed fish tight. He did not want a shot. The doctor came in with a shiny tube around her neck. Alexis pointed at it. "What is that?" he asked. "This is my stethoscope," the doctor said. "I use it to listen to your heart beating." She put the little ends in Alexis's ears. Then she placed the round end on his chest. Thump, thump. Alexis heard his own heart. "Loud!" he said. He listened again. Thump, thump.

The doctor cleaned his arm. "One quick pinch," she said. Alexis squeezed his fish. It was done. The doctor gave him a fish sticker. Then Mom took him to the ice cream shop. Alexis picked strawberry in a big cone. His arm felt heavy, so Mom helped him hold it. "My heart said thump, thump," he told her. "It said thump, thump fast when the shot came." He took a big lick. "Ice cream makes it slow again," he said. "Thump, thump."

Mia was in the bathroom. The tub was filling up. One splash, two splashes, three. Her dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot," he said. He turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Now the water was warm and nice.

Mia put her toes in. "Warm," she said. She wondered about the kitchen. The soup pot sat on the stove. The stove did not look hot. No fire. No glow. "Dad, is the stove still hot?" she asked. "Yes, it can be hot even when it does not look hot," said Dad. "Only grown-ups touch it." He moved the pot himself. Mia watched from far away.

Back in the tub, Mia made a game. "This boat is pretend soup," she said. "One stir, two stirs, three." Then she slid down too fast. She sat up. The room felt dizzy for a second. Dad held her hand. "Slow and steady," he said. The phone rang. Dad said, "Soup is ready!" He helped Mia out with two hands. "Warm towel for you," he said. Mia wrapped up like a big soft bun.

Evelyn sat on the train with her mama. They were going to the sea for a whole week. Evelyn pressed her face to the window. The trees moved past, fast and then slow. Her seat cushion felt squishy under her, like a pillow.

"Take a picture," said Mama. She held up her phone. Evelyn made a big smile. Click. The screen showed Evelyn and the window and the trees. "Now we will remember the train," said Mama.

At the sea, they took more photos. Evelyn on the warm sand. Evelyn with a big shell. Evelyn eating an ice cream, with a dot on her nose. Click, click, click.

Then the trip was over. They rode the train home. The next morning, Evelyn felt sad. "I miss the beach," she said. Her feet still remembered the squishy sand. Mama sat down next to her. "Let's look at our photos." They looked at the train photo. They looked at the sand photo. Evelyn laughed at the ice cream dot. "There I am!" she said. She pointed at the shell, big and pink. "Can we see the water one too?" Mama moved her finger on the screen, and the blue water appeared. Evelyn leaned close and smiled. "Again," she said. "Let's look again."

Gabriel sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse had a small tray. On it was a tiny needle. Gabriel wanted to see it up close. "Can I hold it?" he asked.

The nurse smiled a soft smile. "Only I hold the needle," she said. "Children never touch it. But you can hold my sticker sheet." Gabriel held the shiny sheet. It had a pig sticker on it, and a windy-day kite sticker too. The nurse cleaned his arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. Then, quick as a cat's scratch, the needle went in and out. "All done," she said. Gabriel put the pig sticker on his shirt.

Afterward, Dad took Gabriel to the ice cream shop. Gabriel got pink strawberry in a cup. The shop window rattled a little. It was windy outside. Then Gabriel saw something. When he pushed his spoon down, the ice cream made a little hill. He pushed again. Up popped the hill again. He laughed. "Again!" said Gabriel, and his spoon went down.

Theodore went to the park with his friend Damian. They wanted to play firefighters. But they only had their own clothes. "I wish I had a fire hat," said Theodore. Then Ines ran over with a big bag. "Look! Dress-up clothes!" she said.

Theodore pulled out a big red hat. He put it on his head. "Now I am a firefighter!" he said. He pushed a toy truck across the grass. "Beep beep! Fire truck coming!" Damian put on a shiny coat. He became a firefighter too. Ines put on a chef hat. "I will cook soup for you," she said.

Theodore found a cute little teddy bear under a tree. "Oh no, the bear is stuck," he said. He climbed the low step and held out his arms. The bear was safe. "You are a good firefighter," said Ines. "Thank you," said Theodore. He drew a fire station in the dirt with a stick, like using a big pencil.

Then it was time to go home. Theodore took off the big red hat. He looked at it and smiled. Tomorrow he would wear it again. "Firefighter Theodore will be back!" he said.

Benjamin went to the park with his red dinosaur. His name was Roar. Benjamin put Roar down on a big square of grass. Then he ran to play with Adley.

Adley had a ball. They kicked it one time, two times, three times. Then Benjamin wanted Roar. He looked at the square of grass. Roar was gone.

Benjamin looked under the bench. He looked by the swings. He looked by the quiet pond. No Roar. He looked again, slowly. Under the slide, he saw something red. It was Arnaud's red truck, not Roar. Arnaud was sad and looking too.

Benjamin picked up the truck. He carried it to Arnaud. "This is yours," he said. "You give it back when you find it." Arnaud smiled big. Then Arnaud pointed at the fountain. "There is a red thing in the water."

Benjamin ran to the fountain. It was Roar, sitting on the edge. A frog sat on top of Roar's head. Benjamin laughed and hugged him. Ms. Hussain clapped from her bench. "One truck, one dinosaur, one happy frog," she said.

Logan sat at the long table in the community hall. His friend Jaxton sat next to him. The bowls were full of warm soup. The spoons were shiny and new.

Logan was hungry. He wanted to eat right now. But everyone sat still with open hands and quiet mouths. Logan looked around. "Why is nobody eating?" he whispered to Jaxton.

Mr. Brennan stood up tall. He folded his hands. "Let us say the blessing," he said. Logan put his spoon down. He waited. The words went on and on. His tummy made a little growl.

Then Mr. Brennan said one word. "Amen." Right away, everyone picked up a spoon. Right away, Jimmy took a big bite. Logan took a big bite too. The soup was warm and yummy.

The next week, Logan was ready. He sat up tall. He held his friend Jaxton's hand. The blessing began. Logan closed his eyes and listened hard. He waited for just one word. "Amen," said Mr. Brennan. Logan smiled and grabbed his spoon before anyone else. "I knew it was time!" he said.

Jordan sat in the family car. He was going to the dentist for the first time. He held a little bag. In the bag was a toothbrush to show the dentist.

"I wonder what the dentist will say," said Jordan.

Dad looked in the mirror. He saw the toothbrush. "That is the baby's toothbrush," said Dad. "It is blue. Yours is green."

Jordan looked down. The baby had grabbed it too. Now the baby had no brush. Jordan could not use the blue one. Each person uses their own toothbrush.

So Jordan swapped them back. He gave the blue brush to the baby. He took his own green one. The baby smiled a big, full smile, like a happy little worm wiggling.

At the dentist, Jordan held up his green toothbrush. The dentist smiled too.

"This is my very own brush," said Jordan. "I use it every day."

Harper sat in her car seat. She held her crayons and a little pad. Her friend Teo sat beside her. They were going to the park.

Teo began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Harper clapped along. "Six, seven, eight, nine," she sang too. Then Teo stopped. "What comes next?" he asked.

"Ten!" said Harper. She wanted to write it down. She wrote a big 1. Then she looked at her paper. "That says one," she said. "But I want ten."

She tried again. She wrote 1 and then 0. She held up the paper. "Ten!" she said. "It has a 1 and a 0. Two numbers!" Teo peeked at it. "Ten is so big it needs two," he said.

The car went over a bump. Harper's crayon did a little fall onto the floor. "Oops," she said. The mom reached back and picked it up. "Here you go," she said. Harper took the crayon. She wrote ten again. 1 and then 0.

Teo counted the cows out the window. "One, two, three," he said. Harper pointed at a red barn. "Ten cows over there!" she said. She held up her paper so Teo could see. "One, zero, ten," she read.

"We are here," said the mom. Harper jumped out with her pad. She showed the paper to Ms. Chen at the park gate. Ms. Chen smiled. "Nice ten," she said. Harper looked at it all the way down the slide line. "One, zero," she said softly. "Ten."

Jade was at her grandma's house. Her cousin Dalia was there too. Grandma had a big red game with dice and little horses.

"We take turns," said Dalia. She rolled first. Then Jade rolled. Then Dalia again. Jade waited and watched. Waiting felt long, but the dice came back to her.

Then Jade rolled a two. She did not like two. "My horse goes six squares," she said. Dalia stopped playing. She put her dice down. "That is not the game," said Dalia. "The game has rules that all the players follow."

Jade looked at the board. She moved her horse two squares. Dalia picked up her dice again. They played and played. Outside, a noisy crow sat on the fence.

Later, Grandma brought warm cookies. She had used the hot oven herself. Jade and Dalia each licked a chocolate chip. Jade bumped her knee on the table, but she laughed. Dalia laughed too.

"Your turn," said Jade, and she held out the dice.

It was play time in the gym at school. Mr. MacLeod put a big hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in," he said. Addison held the red beanbag. She threw it. It went bump, bump, bump on the floor. It missed the hoop. Addilyn clapped for her anyway. "Good try," said Addilyn. Addison frowned a little bit.

Then Mr. MacLeod rolled a big ball to Addison. She held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and rolled away. Yousef ran after it. "Maybe two hands are better," Yousef said. Addison looked at her hands. She wondered about that. Could two hands really be better than one?

Addison picked up the beanbag again. She threw it. It missed again. She threw it again and again and again. The hoop sat under the bright lamp on the gym wall. Her arm began to feel strong. Then the beanbag went in! It landed right in the middle. "It went in!" Addison shouted. Mr. MacLeod rolled the big ball again. Addison held out both hands. Two hands caught it. She caught it again. Again and again and again, the ball stayed in her arms.

"Your turn," Addison said to Yousef. She rolled the ball gently. "Be polite to the ball," she said with a giggle. Yousef held out both hands too.

Layla was at Grandma's house. Grandma made warm toast. Grandpa's cake was on a big plate. "I will teach you something new," Grandma said. She gave Layla a dull, safe knife and some soft butter.

Layla spread the butter. It went on slow and smooth. "Look, Grandma!" she said. Then Grandma held the milk jug. "Now try pouring," she said.

Layla poured fast. Milk splashed out of the cup. It made a little puddle on the table. Grandma wiped it up with a cloth. "Try again," she said softly. Layla poured very slowly this time. The milk went up, up, up in the cup. Not one drop came out. "I did it!" Layla said. She drank her milk and ate her buttery toast. Grandma clapped.

Wesley got to the birthday party and saw a big red drum. He wanted to bang it right away. But Skye was already playing with it. Skye banged the drum. Boom, boom, boom.

Wesley reached out his hand to grab it. Then he stopped. He asked, "Can I have a turn?" Ms. Weber smiled and said, "Taking turns means you play for a while, and then the other person plays for a while." Skye banged the drum two more times. Then Skye held it out. "Your turn now," Skye said.

Wesley took the drum. He banged it. Boom, boom, boom! It was fun to wait and then play. After that, he gave the drum back. They took turns and turns. "Want cake?" asked Skye. They each got a spoon. "Yes!" said Wesley. "Let's walk to the table together."

Samuel sat in his car seat. The wheels went round and round. "Daddy, is it tomorrow now?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. "Yesterday we went to the park. Today we are in the car. Tomorrow we can go again."

Samuel looked out of the window. The shiny sun was coming up. He saw his friend Jorawar's house. "Can we stop now?"

"Later," said Daddy. "First we drive to Mr. Wanjiru's house. Then we stop."

Samuel waited. He hummed a little song. He watched a big truck. Its wheels did spin, fast and slow.

At last, the car stopped. Mr. Wanjiru opened his door. "Good morning, Samuel!" he said.

"Good morning!" said Samuel. He saw a table with bowls on it. "Is it morning because we wake up and eat breakfast?"

"Yes," said Mr. Wanjiru. "Sit here, and we will eat now."

Samuel sat down. He took a big bite of his egg. "Morning is now," he said. "Tomorrow is later."

Mr. Wanjiru laughed and gave him some toast.

Dylan sat in his car seat. His friend Cody sat next to him. Cody had a basket of little pictures. The basket tipped over. All the pictures fell on the seat.

"Now they are all mixed up," said Cody.

Dylan had an idea. "Let's sort them," he said. He picked up a picture of a cow. Then a picture of a dog. He put them together in one straight line.

"Cow and dog," said Cody. "Animals go together."

Next Dylan found a ball and a teddy bear. He put those in a new pile. Cody found an apple and some bread. Those made a pile too.

"Look," said Cody. "Animals, toys, and foods. Three piles!"

"Groups!" said Dylan.

When the car stopped, the piles were done. Dylan and Cody gave the pictures back to Ms. Li, all neat and tidy.

Sarah was at the park with her class. Mr. Hassan had a big paper with a face on it. He asked, "Who can name a sense?"

Sarah wanted a turn very much. Oliver raised his hand first. "Eyes!" he said. "We see with our eyes."

Then it was Sarah's turn. She pointed to her nose. "We smell with our nose," she said. Mr. Hassan smiled.

Next they sat in the sandbox. Sarah picked up a piece of stick. She rubbed it with her fingertips. "It is bumpy," she said. Then she dug her hands deep in the sand. The sand was soft and warm. When she let go of the stick, it sank down under the sand.

Loic held out a smooth round stone. "Feel this," he said. Sarah touched it with her skin. "It is cold and smooth," she said.

"My skin feels it," said Sarah. "My fingertips know!" She touched Loic's fuzzy hat too. It was soft like a kitten.

Mr. Hassan clapped his hands. "Now our picture needs a hand," he said. Sarah ran to the paper and drew her own hand, right on the face.

Jordan wanted to play dragon in the playroom. He put on his red cape. "Is the dragon friendly or scary?" he asked himself. "Scary," he said, and he made a big roar.

Madilyn came in. She wanted to play too. "My dragon is friendly," she said. "My dragon is scary," said Jordan. They both pulled on the toy dragon.

Then Jordan had an idea. "Let's play one dragon together," he said. "A friendly dragon who is a little loud." Madilyn smiled. "Yes," she said. "And it can slide down the big cushion."

The friendly dragon slid down. Roar! Jordan fed it a pretend snack. Then it was late for dragon sleep. "Night night, dragon," said Jordan. Madilyn tucked the dragon in with a soft blanket.

Sadie put on her sun hat. The sun was warm on her face. She ran to the swings at the playground. Myra was there in a yellow hat too.

Then a big white cloud slid across the sky. The sun went away. Sadie looked up. "Where did the sun go?" she asked. "The cloud hides it," said Myra. Sadie waved her hand at the cloud. "Come out, sun!" she called.

The wind began to blow. It lifted Myra's hat right off her head. Sadie ran and caught it. She gave it back to Myra. "Thank you," Myra said.

The cloud moved on, slow and big. The sun peeked out again. Warm light fell on the swings. "It came back!" Sadie said.

Ms. Bondarenko came by with hot cocoa in small cups. She held the cups while the girls drank. The cocoa was warm and cozy.

Then the sky turned grey. Small white flakes came down. "Snow!" Sadie said. Ms. Bondarenko spoke softly. "Time for boots and mittens."

The two girls zipped up their coats. The snow landed on their hats. "Bye, sun," said Sadie. "See you tomorrow."

Alexander stood in the big school gym. Mr. Dang put a hoop on the floor. He put three beanbags in a red basket. "Try to throw one in," said Mr. Dang. Alexander threw the first beanbag. It landed far from the hoop. He threw the second one. It bounced off the edge. Would the third one go in? He threw it. It went in! Alexander clapped his hands. He liked the sound of the beanbag landing inside.

Then Mr. Dang brought out a big yellow ball. He rolled it to Axton. Axton caught it. He rolled it to Harley. Harley caught it. Then it was Alexander's turn. The ball came rolling fast. Alexander's hands were tucked in his pockets. The ball bumped his legs and rolled away.

"Try again," said Mr. Dang. He rolled the ball again. This time Alexander held his arms out. His hands were open and wide. The big ball came right into them. He caught it! "I caught it!" said Alexander. He looked at his open hands. Arms out, hands open. That is what got him ready.

They played a counting game around the circle. One roll for Axton. One roll for Harley. One roll for Alexander. Around and around the ball went. Then the ball rolled past everyone. It rolled under the snowy coats hanging on the wall. It stopped on a sneaker. Whose sneaker was that? Out stepped the coach. "Looking for this?" he said, holding up the big yellow ball.

Natalie put on her skates at the ice rink. Her team was playing a game today. It was a fun game of baseball, right on the ice. Mr. Bianchi set up a soft ball and a plastic bat. Jagger and Tatum lined up to take a turn.

Natalie skated fast to the plate. She gripped the bat. "Not yet," said Mr. Bianchi. He held up a helmet. "The batter wears a helmet to protect her head." Natalie put it on. It felt warm and snug. Then she swung the bat. Tock! The ball rolled across the shiny ice. Jagger chased it, sliding and laughing.

After the game, they sat by the busy kitchen window. The cook handed them warm cocoa. Natalie watched the steam rise. "Next time, helmet first," she said. Then she took a big sip.

Lincoln stood on the big soccer field. The summer sun felt warm. Mr. Lindqvist held up a beanbag and a hoop. "Try to throw it in," he said.

Lincoln threw the beanbag. It went far and missed the hoop. His friend Keon laughed, not mean, just happy. Lincoln tried again. He watched the hoop. He threw the beanbag slow and easy. It dropped right in! The beanbag made the hoop wobble, wobble, stop. "I did it!" Lincoln said.

Then Mr. Lindqvist rolled a big ball to Lincoln. The ball came close. Lincoln squeezed his eyes shut. Bonk! The ball hit his tummy and fell on the grass. "Oh no," said Lincoln.

Sylvie walked over. "Watch it," she said. "Watch it all the way to your hands."

Mr. Lindqvist rolled the ball again. This time Lincoln kept his eyes open. He watched the ball all the way to his hands. He caught it with both hands! It was big and soft like a pillow.

Lincoln rolled the ball back. Then he jumped up and down on the green grass.

Jasper stood in the kitchen. The toast was ready. Mama had made it with the toaster, and now it sat on his plate.

"I want to spread the butter," said Jasper. Mama gave him a small knife with a rounded end. Jasper dipped it in the butter. He spread it across the toast. It went bump, bump, bump. Little lumps sat on top. He spread them flat. The toast was all shiny now.

Next came the milk. Jasper held the cup. He poured and poured. The milk came up to the very top. He walked to the table. Oh no! The milk tipped over the edge. It made a puddle on the floor.

Mama wiped the puddle. "Try again," she said. Jasper poured once more. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He walked slowly to the table. Not one drop fell out. He sat down and took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk.

Then something small and funny happened. The cat trotted in and licked the last bit of spilled milk right off the floor.

"That was Onyx's treat," Jasper said with a laugh. Onyx bumped his leg and purred.

Charlotte sat at the dinner table. Her baby brother sat next to her. He was eating mushy peas.

Then his spoon fell down. Clang! It hit the floor. His lip wobbled. His eyes got big and teary.

"Are you okay?" Charlotte asked. She leaned over to see his face. He looked at her. Then he smiled a big, happy smile. The tears went away, like they could melt in the sun.

Dad picked up the spoon. He gave it back to the baby. The baby banged it on the tray. Bang, bang, bang.

"Are you okay?" Charlotte asked again, just to be sure. The baby laughed out loud.

Mom turned on the kitchen light. It made the table bright and warm. Charlotte felt excited. She clapped her hands.

"He likes it when I ask," Charlotte said.

"Yes, he does," said Mom.

The baby reached for Charlotte's cup. It tipped over. Water went everywhere, splash!

Uh-oh. Charlotte felt angry for a second. But the baby looked scared. His chin began to shake.

"Are you okay?" Charlotte asked, soft and slow.

The baby stopped shaking. He blew a bubble and giggled.

Mom wiped up the water with a towel. "Good asking, Charlotte," she said.

Charlotte sat up tall. She felt happy inside. "Are you okay, baby brother?"

He patted her arm with his wet little hand.

Amira was on a big train with her dad. They were going to Grandma's house. It was far, far away from home.

Amira looked out the window. She saw white clouds. She saw a river with water in it. "Can I have a drink?" she asked. Her dad gave her a water bottle. One sip, two sips, three sips.

Then Dad looked worried. "Oh no," he said. "Which stop is ours? I forgot." A lady in a blue coat came by. Her name was Ms. Desir. She pointed to a big paper on the train wall. "Look here," she said. "This is a map."

Amira stood up and looked. The map showed little dots for places. It showed the road the train went on. Amira put her finger on the map. She found the river on the map. She found the river out the window. "There!" she said. "The river is here, so we are here." Then she moved her finger along. One dot, two dots, three dots. "This dot is Grandma's town."

Dad smiled. "The map shows us the way," he said. The train went on. Soon a voice said, "Next stop, Grandma's town." Amira held her dad's hand. The train slowed down and stopped.

There was Grandma, waving on the platform.

Henry sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small road. Henry looked out the window. The trees got closer and closer.

They were driving to the forest. It was far from home. Henry had his scarf on his lap. It was a short scarf. Celine sat next to him. She had a scarf too.

"My scarf is long," said Celine. She held it up. It went down past her knees. Henry held up his scarf. It stopped at his elbows. "Mine is short," said Henry. "Long and short are opposites," said Celine.

Henry wanted a long scarf too. His dad was driving, so he could not get one now. Henry looked at his short scarf. He had an idea. He put his scarf on his legs. Then he put Celine's scarf tail on top. Now his lap looked long. "Look," said Henry. "Now it is long!"

Celine laughed. "That is my scarf tail," she said. "But it looks long now."

The car stopped. They were at the forest. It was cold outside. Dad had a thermos of hot cocoa. He poured a cup for Henry. Henry held it with both hands. It was warm.
