Then they march march marched on the path. Henry marched fast. Celine marched slow. "Wait for me," said Celine. So Henry stopped and waited.

"Your turn to lead," said Henry. Celine marched ahead. Her long scarf flew out behind her. Henry watched it flap in the wind. "Your scarf can fly far," said Henry. "My short scarf cannot fly." Celine smiled. "Long scarves fly best," she said. Henry patted his short scarf. It was soft and snug. It was just right for him. They marched into the trees together.

Livia ran to the playground with her dad. She saw the big red swing. She wanted to ride it so much. But Carson was on the swing already.

Livia waited by the fence. She watched Carson pump his legs. Then Carson hopped off. "You can go now," he said. Livia got on the swing right away. She swung up so high. Her heart felt happy.

Carson stood by the fence. He looked a little upset. He had been kind, and Livia had run off. She hopped down and went back to him. "Thank you, Carson," she said. Carson smiled a big smile. "Want to stack the blocks with me?" he asked.

They stacked blocks by the slide. Livia put one block on top. Then Carson put one on top. "My turn, your turn," said Livia. The tower grew tall. Then Remington came to play too. Livia handed her a block. "Thank you," said Remington. They all clapped for the tall, tall tower.

Scarlett sat at the big table in the library. Mr. Russo gave her paper stars and glue. "You can make a crown," he said. Scarlett put glue on a star. She stuck it on the paper band.

Alizee sat next to her. Bellamy sat across the table. Scarlett wanted to wear her crown right away. She picked it up. The stars slid off onto the table. The paper band fell open too.

"The glue is still wet," said Alizee. "Wet glue needs time to dry." Mr. Russo nodded. "Let's set the crowns flat," he said. "We can look at books while we wait."

Scarlett laid her crown down straight on the table. Then she found a book about a big gray rock by the sea. She turned the pages slowly. Alizee read a book about birds. Bellamy drew a little wave on his hand.

After the stories, Scarlett touched the glue. It was dry and stiff. She picked up her crown. The stars stayed on. The band held together. Alizee helped tie it on Scarlett's head.

"Ta-da!" said Scarlett. She gave a little wave to Mr. Russo. "My crown is all dry!"

Elijah went to the store with his dad. It was noisy and busy. Elijah wanted apples in his lunch.
His dad said, "Put the apples in the box."
Elijah put one apple in. His baby sister pulled one out. He put another apple in. She pulled another one out.
"In," said Elijah. "Out," said his sister, and she laughed.
In. Out. In. Out. The box never got full.
Elijah had an idea. He gave his sister a soft bread roll to hold. Her hands were busy now. Then he put the apples in, one by one. None came out. The box stayed full.
His dad said, "In and out are opposites. Good thinking, Elijah."
At the front, his dad had to pay for the apples. Elijah held his sister's hand. She held her bread roll.
"Apples in the bag," said Elijah. "Apples in my lunch."

Jaxson looked out the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling on the backyard.

"Snowy day," said Mom. "Put on your boots."

Jaxson pulled on his boots. He zipped his big coat. He ran outside into the snow. His friend Jaiden was already there. Jaiden wore a hat, a scarf and red mittens.

"Let's make a snow wall," said Jaiden.

They patted the snow. They stacked it up. Soon they had a big white wall. It was tall as their knees.

Then Jaxson tried to roll a snowball. The snow felt cold. His hands turned red. They hurt. He dropped the snowball and held his hands.

"My hands are cold," he said.

Jaiden held out his red mittens. "Mittens keep my hands warm," he said. "Try yours."

Jaxson looked down. His mittens were in his coat pocket. He pulled them on. He rolled a new snowball. His hands felt warm. He patted it onto the wall.

From the door, Ms. Suzuki, the neighbour, called, "Cocoa is ready!"

The boys went in slowly. Their legs were sleepy from playing. Mom set two warm cups on the table.

Jaxson took a sip. Something was floating in his cocoa. It was a tiny marshmallow snowman, with little stick arms.

"He looks just like us," said Jaxson, and he waved at it.

Jaxon sat on his bedroom floor. He had a new wallet. Inside was his new card. It had his name on it. "Jaxon," he read out loud. He felt shy about it. He hid it under his pillow.

At the library, Jaxon found a big red book. It had a bear on the front. He hugged it tight. "Can I keep it?" he asked his mom.

"Ask the lady at the desk," she said.

Jaxon felt shy. He walked slowly. He slid his card across the desk. "What is this for?" he asked.

The lady smiled. "It is a library card. It lets you borrow books and take them home."

Jaxon's eyes got big. "Take it home? To my room?"

"Yes," she said. "You can bring it back soon."

Jaxon gave her his card. She zipped it through a machine. Beep! She put the red book in his hands.

"You mean it is mine now?" he asked.

"It is yours for a while," she said.

Jaxon held the book all the way home. He ran to his bedroom. He sat on his bed. He opened the red book. The bear smiled at him. Jaxon smiled too.

"Mom," he called. "My card made this happen. Can we go back tomorrow?"

Sophie was in the playroom with her five toy monkeys. She wanted to sing the monkey song. But one monkey was stuck under the big toy box. She pulled the monkey. It did not come out. She pulled again. Still stuck.

Mishka came to help. "Let's count while we pull," said Mishka. They counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." They pulled and pulled. The monkey popped out. "Hooray!" said Sophie.

Now all five monkeys sat on the little bed. Sophie sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one monkey fell off. Sophie put it in the basket. Now there were four. She sang again. One more monkey fell off. Now there were three. She sang and sang. One fell off each time. Then two. Then one. Then none were left on the bed.

Mr. Khoury brought juice for a snack. "Drink it here, away from the radiator," he said. "It is hot and it can burn." Sophie sat in the safe spot with Mishka. The little monkey under the box winked at her, and she giggled.

Austin ran outside with his class. The sun was not out today. Dark clouds sat in the sky.

"Windy day!" said Mr. Nair. "Hold on to your hats."

Austin put on his red hat. His friend Elie put on her blue hat. The wind blew hard. It pushed the swings. It shook the big tree. Then the wind gave Austin's hat a big tug. Off it went! The hat flew over the grass.

"My hat!" said Austin.

He ran after it. The hat rolled and rolled. Elie ran too. The hat stopped by the sandbox. It landed right in the soft sand. Austin picked it up. Sand fell off like little rain drops.

"Got it!" said Austin. He held his hat with both hands. "Wind, you can't take it again!"

Elie laughed. "The wind blew it right off your head," she said.

Austin looked up at the sky. What else could the wind blow? He watched it spin a leaf. He watched it wave the flag. Then he pulled his hat down tight, very tight.

Mr. Nair held the door open. "Time to come in," he said.

Austin shared a bench with Elie. They looked out the window together. The wind kept blowing outside. But the red hat stayed on, safe and warm, all the way home.

Brielle went to the park with her red ball. She wanted to kick it to Reginald. She kicked it high. The ball went into the cozy little playhouse at the park.

The playhouse was dark inside. Brielle stepped in to find her ball. She looked and looked. "It is hard to tell what color things are in here," she said. Everything looked the same dark gray. She touched something round. Was this her ball? She could not tell.

She carried it out into the sun. In the bright light, she could see. The ball in her hands was green, not red. It was Reginald's green ball! Then Reginald called from the doorway. He held up a red ball. "Is this yours?" he asked. "Yes!" said Brielle. They traded balls and laughed. Then they kicked the balls by the duck pond. The red ball went far. The green ball went far, too. Brielle read her name on the red ball. It was her ball, for sure.

Nova sat on the playroom rug. The toys were in a big jumble on the floor. Ms. González knelt beside her. "Let's sort the toys," she said.

Nova found a box marked with a paw print. "This box is for animals," said Jordan. Nova put in a dog. It went "woof" when she squeezed it. She put in a cow. Then she held up a wooden fish. It was painted blue and smooth like the ocean in her book at home.

"Fish don't go in there," said Jordan. "Fish have no legs. Dogs and cows have legs."

Nova felt worried. The fish was her favorite toy. "But I want it in the animal box," she said. Her tummy felt tight.

Ms. González picked up a book. It had big pictures. She turned the pages slowly. Dog. Cow. Fish. All the pages had one word on top. The word said "Animals."

Nova looked at the fish. Then she looked at the dog and the cow. "A fish is an animal too," she said. She dropped the fish in the box. It landed with a soft tap.

"Let's talk about the food toys next," said Ms. González. Nova found a pretend banana and a pretend carrot. Jordan clapped. Nova squeezed the fish again. "You are an animal," she whispered to it.

Grandpa had big letters on the fridge. Adam knew the big A. "A says ah," he said. Grandpa clapped.

Then Adam found a book on the sofa. He saw a small letter. It looked like a little circle with a tail. "This is not A," said Adam. "A is big."

Grandpa sat down next to him. "That is a small a," he said. "Big A and small a are the same letter."

Adam looked at the fridge. Then he looked at the book. Big A. Small a. Same letter! He tickled the small a with his finger. "Ah," he said.

Grandpa smiled. "You found a match."

Adam ran to Zayd, who was playing with a spoon in the kitchen. "Zayd, look! Small a and big A!" he said. "Both say ah!" Zayd laughed and pointed at his dirty hands. "Show me after I wash," he said. Adam waited, holding the book up high.

Leo went to the farm with his class. Ms. Foster said, "Today we will name our five senses." Leo wanted to try them all before snack time.

First Leo used his eyes. He saw a cow with a short tail. Then he used his nose. He sniffed hay, and it smelled sweet. He touched a soft leaf on a plant. He used his tongue to taste his apple at snack time.

Then a big truck rumbled by. The noise was loud. Leo put his hands over his ears. The sound got quieter, just like that. He took his hands off. The truck was loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again!

"Ms. Foster, my ears can hear," said Leo. "And my hands make it quiet." Asha laughed and covered her ears too. The cows went back to munching their hay.

Georgia sat on the small bench at Ms. Rosen's music studio. Her drum was a big red box. Zane sat next to her with his drum too. "Let's play together!" said Zane.

They tapped their drums. Boom, boom, boom! But Georgia played fast. Zane played faster. Soon it was just BOOMBOOMBOOM! Their drums went tum-tum-tumble into a big noise. Ms. Rosen laughed. "Try this," she said. She clapped her hands slowly. Clap, clap, clap. "We keep a steady beat so we can play together."

Georgia and Zane clapped with her. Then they tapped their drums the same way. Boom, boom, boom. It sounded like one big drum! Georgia stood up tall. "Zane! We match!" Zane grinned. "Like two feet walking!" They played a long, long song, and Ms. Rosen danced.

Grayson put on his red shirt. It was his team shirt for soccer. The coach said, "Time to play!" Grayson ran onto the grass at the park. His friends Jorawar and Salem were there too. A big tree stood near the field. Its shade looked nice and cool.

The game began. Grayson wanted to kick the ball. He ran to it. He kicked it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. Then it went into the net. Everyone shouted, "Goal!" Jorawar jumped up and down. Salem clapped her hands. Grayson looked at the net. The ball was inside it. That was how his team got a point!

Grayson kicked the ball again. This time it missed. It rolled past the net. The coach blew his whistle. Mr. Hoffmann, the neighbour, waved from his chair by the tree. He smiled at Grayson.

Grayson tried once more. He kicked the ball straight. Into the net it went. "Goal!" his team shouted again. Grayson wore a big smile. The coach gave him a thumbs up. "Nice kick," said Salem. Grayson hugged the ball and laughed.

Joshua was in the backyard with Grandma. Grandma was staying for a whole week. Joshua had a red ball. "Grandma, play with me!" he said. Grandma threw the ball, but it went weak and slow. "I am tired," she said. "I need to rest." Joshua found her a chair in the shade.

Joshua still wanted to play. "I wish someone could play ball," he said. Grandma smiled. "I know a story instead," she said. "It is about your dad." Joshua sat down. "Dad is big," he said. "Dad was little once," said Grandma. "He had a small blue bike. He fell off. He cried. Then he got on again."

Joshua laughed. "Dad on a little bike!" he said. "Tell more!" Grandma told about Dad and his sister, who hid Dad's shoe. Joshua asked, "Can you tell stories every day this week?" "Every day," said Grandma. Joshua ran to get her a blanket for her lap. "Story time!" he called. "Story time!"

Elijah ran to the park with his green truck. He loved that truck. He pushed it down the big slide. Vroom! Then he threw a stick for the dog. He laughed and ran. He played and played.

Then it was time to go home. Elijah looked in his pocket. "Where is my truck?" he said. He looked under the swing. No truck. He looked by the sand. No truck. His tummy felt jumpy.

His friend Nala came to help. "Look there," she said. She pointed at the dog. The dog was sleeping. The truck was under the dog's paw! "Silly dog," said Elijah. The dog woke up and wagged his tail. Elijah took his truck. "Thank you, dog," he said. He was happy.

At home, Elijah found a blue basket by his bed. He put the truck in the basket. The next day, he put it there again. Each day, the truck went in the same spot. One morning he wanted his truck fast. He looked in the basket. There it was! "Easy," said Elijah. He wore his red shirt and hugged the basket.

Eva stood by the cubbies at school. Her red coat was on the hook. "Can I zip it all by myself?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said Mr. García. Eva pushed her arms in. The coat felt soft and warm. She pulled the zipper up. It went halfway and stopped. Her sweater was stuck in the zipper. Eva pulled hard. The zipper did not move.

"Ow," said Eva. The sweater pulled her skin. Mr. García knelt down beside her. "Try backing the zipper down a little," he said. Eva pulled the zipper down, just a bit. The sweater came free. Eva puffed out a breath. She smoothed the sweater flat. Then she pulled the zipper up again, slow and steady. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

Rebecca and Fiadh clapped by the door. "Your zipper shines," said Fiadh. Eva smiled. She patted her coat, which had a little animal on the pocket. "My coat is on," said Eva. "And I did it all by myself."

Juliette ran into her classroom. Today was her birthday! There were paper stars on the wall. She had helped draw them with yellow crayon.

Then she saw the cake on the big table. Yazan and Nancy stood beside it. "Look at your candles!" said Nancy. Juliette counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then she stopped. "Only four candles!" she said. "But I am five today."

Mr. Pelletier smiled. He opened a small box. He took out one more pink candle. He pushed it gently into the sweet, squishy cake. "Now count again," he said. Juliette counted. "One, two, three, four, five! Five candles for five years!" Yazan clapped his hands. "You grew a whole candle!" he said.

Dad came in with the teacher to light the candles. Juliette watched from her chair. The little flames danced. Then everyone sang. The cake smelled like sugar and warm butter. Juliette blew out the candles. All five went out at once. Nancy laughed. "You got them all!" Juliette grinned and licked a crumb off her finger. It was a tiny bit salty from her happy tears.

It was bedtime for Arya. She held her blue blanket. She wanted her book about the big red apple. But she could not find it.

Arya looked on her shelf. She found a birthday card. She saw letters on it. The letters made her name. "A-r-y-a," she said. It looked just like the name on her cubby at school. Same letters. Same order. "It is me again!" she said.

Dad helped her look under the bed. There was the apple book. Arya opened the front cover first. Dad read page one, then page two. Arya turned each page to the back. At the end, she saw her name there too. Same letters. Same order again. Arya gave Dad a big hug. "Good night, Arya," Dad said. "Read it again tomorrow?" asked Arya. "Yes," said Dad, and turned out the light.

Olivia was at Grandma's house. Her friend Eunice was there too. Grandma gave them a big basket of toys. "Let's play house," said Eunice. Olivia clapped her hands.

"I want to be the mommy," said Olivia. "I want to be the mommy too," said Eunice. They both held the same toy elephant. Oh no. What could they do?

Then Olivia had an idea. "You be the mommy first," she said. "I will be the baby." Eunice put the elephant to bed. Olivia pretended to cry like a baby. "Waa," she said, and then she laughed.

"Now can we switch?" asked Olivia. Eunice nodded. "Yes! Now you be the mommy." Olivia tucked the elephant in. She gave it a soft blanket. "Night night, little one," she said.

When you play house, you can pick a role. Then halfway through, you can switch! Olivia thought that was very special. She counted the toys. One, two, three, four.

"Who will be the baby next time?" she asked Eunice. Grandma smiled from her chair. "Maybe I can be the baby," she said. Olivia giggled. "Grandma, you are too big for a crib!"

Ali was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had two bowls of red berries on the big table.

"Let's count," said Grandpa.

Ali touched each berry in the first bowl. He counted one, two, three, four. Then he counted the second bowl. One, two, three, four, five, six.

"This bowl has more," said Ali. He pointed at the six berries.

"Yes," said Grandpa. "And this bowl has fewer."

Ali said the new word slowly. "Fewer." He liked how it felt in his mouth.

Then Ali wanted to try again. He went to the toy shelf. He put five blocks in one pile. He put nine blocks in the other pile. He counted each pile, touching every block.

"This pile has more," said Ali. "Nine is more than five."

"And what about this little pile?" asked Grandpa.

"Fewer!" said Ali. "Five is fewer than nine."

Grandpa smiled. "Let's have a snack now."

Ali ate his berries one by one. He put one berry in Grandpa's hand. Grandpa popped it in his mouth.

"Your bowl has more," said Grandpa. "Grandma gave you the special big bowl."

Ali looked in his bowl. Then he looked at Grandpa's empty bowl.

"You have fewer now," said Ali.

Grandpa laughed and hugged him. "My smart boy," he said.

Josephine ran to the swings. Jameson was already there. "Push me!" he called.

Josephine wanted the swing too. But Jameson had it. She stood still. Her face got hot. She wanted to yell.

Then Franklin fell off the slide. He sat on the ground. He did not say anything. He just looked down. Ms. Hughes walked by. She did not stop.

"I feel sad," Franklin said. Ms. Hughes heard him. She came right over. "Let me see your knee," she said. She helped him up.

Josephine looked and looked. Did words make Ms. Hughes come? She walked to the swing. "Jameson, I feel sad," she said. "I want a turn."

Jameson stopped his swing. "Okay. You can have a turn." Josephine sat on the swing. It was a pretty red swing. Ms. Hughes gave her a big push.

"Whee!" said Josephine. "This is fun!"

Peyton walked into the big hall with her mom. There were gold decorations on the walls. The room smelled sweet, like warm honey. Mr. Ferreira stood by a long table. He was rolling soft dough with his hands. Peyton watched him. "This is special bread," he said. "We make it only on this day, for the celebration."

Peyton wanted to taste the bread right away. Mr. Ferreira shook his head kindly. "Not yet, little one. It must bake first." He put the dough on a tray. He slid the tray into the big oven. Peyton stood back, far from the heat. Her friend Joey ran over. "What's in the oven?" he asked. "Special bread," said Peyton. "It is made just for today."

They waited together. Peyton pressed her finger into the squishy dough left on the table. It made a little dent. She giggled. Outside, snow began to fall past the windows. The hall felt warm and cozy.

At last the oven door opened. The bread came out, brown and puffy. Mr. Ferreira cut it into slices. He handed one to Peyton. She took a bite. "It tastes like honey," she said. Joey took a big bite too. "Mmm," he said. Peyton looked at the long table full of food. "Is all of this food just for today?" she asked. Mr. Ferreira smiled and nodded. "Every dish here is made for this one special day," he said.

Peyton held her warm slice in both hands. She sat down next to her mom. Outside, the snow fell softly on the steps. Inside, the hall was full of good smells and happy voices. Joey waved from across the table. Peyton waved back and took one more sweet bite.

Sebastian ran to the truck corner at daycare. He saw a big red truck there. Tenley was holding it. She pushed it across the floor. It made a loud rumble.

Tenley went to get some blocks. Sebastian grabbed the truck fast. He held it tight. Tenley came back. Her mouth turned down. "That's my truck," she said. Her eyes got watery.

Sebastian looked at her face. He put the truck down on the floor. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. Tenley wiped her eye. "Yes. After my turn," she said. She pushed the truck twice more. It rumbled by his feet. Then she gave it to him. "Your turn," she said. The truck felt smooth and warm in his hands.

Phoenix came over too. He waited and watched. "Can I play?" he asked. Sebastian nodded. Soon all three pushed the truck together. It rumbled down the long floor. Mr. Park clapped his hands. "Nice asking, everyone," he said. The red truck zoomed past the pink playhouse.

Mateo sat in the nursery room. The new baby was here. Her name was Coco. Everyone looked at Coco. No one looked at Mateo. He felt small and left out.

Dad said, "Oh no. We need a clean diaper. It is in the basket." Mateo jumped up. Big brothers can help by fetching things. He ran to the basket. He got one clean diaper. He brought it to Dad. Dad smiled big. "Thank you, Mateo!"

Then Mom said, "Can you find the green blanket?" Mateo looked around. He saw a green puzzle box. He saw a green sock. Then he saw the green blanket on the chair. He carried it over, soft and warm.

They wrapped Coco in it. Mom said, "You are such a good helper." Mateo stood tall. The baby made a small sound. It sounded like "Ma." Everyone laughed. Mateo gave Coco a gentle kiss on her head.

Edouard sat at home with his dad. "Today we go to the doctor," said Dad. "You will meet Nurse Amy. She has a small magic bandage for you."

At the doctor's office, Edouard sat on Dad's lap. The nurse wiped his arm. Then came a quick little pinch. Edouard blinked. It was done. The nurse put a blue bandage on his arm. Edouard got a sticker too.

In the car, Edouard touched his arm. "Ow," he said softly. "My arm feels sore." Dad gave it a gentle kiss. "The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while," said Dad. "It will feel better soon." Edouard nodded.

Back at home, Edouard played with his blocks. He stacked them up tall. Then he looked at his arm again. It did not hurt anymore. He smiled at his blue bandage. "All better," he said. "Safe and all better."

The cultural center was full of people. Theo held his dad's hand. The night was coming, and lanterns glowed up high. "Stay close," said his dad. "It is a big crowd."

Theo saw a food stall. It smelled sweet. He let go of his dad's hand. He took one step. Then two steps. The people were tall and thin between him and the stall. He could not see his dad. Theo's tummy felt small.

He stopped walking. He looked back. There was his dad! Theo ran to him and grabbed his hand. He held on tight. "I stayed close," said Theo. His dad smiled. They walked to the food stall together, hand in hand. "One sweet bun, please," said his dad.

Isla sat in the backyard with her paints. She was painting a big yellow sun. Her friend Kali sat next to her, painting a stormy blue cloud. "The sky is dark in my picture," said Kali. Isla dipped her brush in the red pot. Then she left the brush standing in the pot. She ran to play on the grass. The paint dried on the brush while she played.

The next day, Isla picked up her brush. It felt hard. She tried to paint. The brush would not bend. "Oh no," said Isla. "My brush is stiff." Kali held up her own brush. Kali's brush was soft and clean. "I rinse mine in the water pot," said Kali. Isla looked at the water pot. She put her stiff brush in. The paint came off, bit by bit. Isla waited. She swished it slowly, foot tucked under her. At last the brush was soft again.

Isla painted a new red bird. When she finished, she rinsed the brush. She set it on the paper to dry. Then she picked up a leaf and used it to sweep the paint spots off the table. "Look, Kali," she said. "Clean brush, clean table." Kali smiled and held up her painting of the stormy cloud. Isla hung her red bird next to it on the fence.

Jaxon ran to the bike rack at summer camp. The shiny blue scooter was there. But Vincenzo got there first. Vincenzo held the handle tight. Jaxon grabbed at it. "My turn!" he said. Vincenzo pulled it back. The scooter wobbled. It almost fell. Mr. Nolan walked over with something in his hand. It was a sand timer, small and round like a cookie. "Let's watch the sand," said Mr. Nolan. He turned it over. The sand made a soft hiss. It fell like tiny yellow rain. Jaxon watched the sand go down. Vincenzo rode the scooter in a big circle. Round and round, past the water puddle, past the climbing wall. Then the sand ran out. Not one grain was left. The turn was over. "My turn now," said Jaxon. Vincenzo handed him the scooter. Jaxon rode in a circle too. He jumped over the puddle. Splash! When the sand ran out again, Jaxon gave the scooter back. They took turns all morning. The sun felt warm on Jaxon's arms. "Sand all gone," he said. "Your turn, Vincenzo!"

Avery had been sick at home. Her nose ran and her cough was loud. She could not smell her toast. Now she felt better, but her mom said, "Time to see the doctor."

At the doctor's office, Avery sat on a big chair. The doctor held a silver tool. It looked slippery and cold. Avery hid behind her mom. "It will touch me," she whispered.

"This is called a stethoscope," the doctor said. "I can listen to your chest with it." Avery peeked out. "Listen to me? I make sounds?" she asked. The doctor nodded and smiled.

Avery sat very still. The doctor put the stethoscope on Avery's chest. Avery took a big breath in. "I hear your chest," the doctor said. "It sounds clear and strong!"

Avery was surprised. The little tool heard her, just like that. Then the doctor let Avery listen to her own chest. Thump, thump, thump. Avery laughed. "I hear me!"

On the way home, they walked past a tree. Avery's mom held her hand. "Can I go back and listen again?" Avery asked. Her mom smiled and said, "Next time, we will."

Matteo ran into the big school gym. The floor was shiny. It smelled like rubber balls and popcorn. Ms. Harper was there. She smiled and waved.

"Time for practice," said Ms. Harper. "Today we play a game." Matteo loved the game. He wore his purple shirt. Addison wore one too. They pushed the big cart of balls across the floor. There was a soft blue mat like a little hill in the corner. Neve rolled a ball up the hill and laughed.

Then they played. Matteo kicked the ball. It went far, far away. A man in a black shirt blew a whistle. He said the ball was out. Matteo stamped his foot. "No fair!" he said.

"That man is the umpire," said Ms. Harper. "He makes sure we follow the rules." Matteo looked at the umpire. The umpire made a fair face. He was just doing his job.

Matteo took a big breath. He kicked again. This time the ball stayed in. "Safe!" the umpire called. Matteo jumped up and down. Neve clapped for him.

After the game, Ms. Harper handed out crackers. Matteo sat with Addison on the soft mat. His tummy felt warm and happy. "Good kick," said the umpire, walking by. Matteo grinned and took another bite.

Sebastian was sick at Grandma's house. His nose was red. His cough was loud. He wanted to feel good again.

Grandma said, "The doctor says you need medicine. We must go to the pharmacy." Sebastian put on his coat. He zipped it up, slowly, all by himself. Then he held Grandma's hand.

At the pharmacy, a man stood behind a big counter. "That is the pharmacist," Grandma said. Sebastian watched. The pharmacist looked at a paper. The paper had the doctor's name on it. Then the pharmacist put a little bottle in a bag. He gave the bag to Grandma. The bag went zip, zip as it closed.

"Medicine from the doctor," Grandma said. "The pharmacist gave it to us." Back at home, Grandma poured the right amount into a spoon. Sebastian opened his mouth. He took it, one slow sip.

The next morning, Sebastian's cough was small. His nose was not so red. He ran to the window and waved at Mr. Do next door. "I feel good!" he called. "I feel good!"

Maria sat in a big chair. It was a waiting room. Today she would see the dentist for the first time. She squeezed her mama's hand. "Will it hurt?" she asked.

A boy sat down next to her. His name was Justin. He had a loose tooth. He wiggled it with his finger. Maria watched. When he wiggled it, his whole mouth moved. She wiggled her own tooth too. Nothing happened. Her tooth stayed still. Why did his move and not hers?

The dentist called Maria in. He looked at her teeth with a little mirror. "Say hello to your front teeth," he said. "Front teeth are for biting food. Back teeth are for chewing it." Maria bit down on a soft fruit snack. Snip went the front teeth. Then she chomped with her back teeth. Chomp, chomp. The snack got small.

On the bus home, mama gave Maria an apple slice. Maria bit it with her front teeth. Then she chewed it with her back teeth. "It works!" she said. "I can feel it getting smaller." The boy across the aisle smiled at her. "Want to share mine too?" he asked. Maria took one polite little bite. Then she chewed. Chomp, chomp, chomp.

Nova sat on the little bench at the campsite. Her dad gave her warm toast. He put a bowl of butter on the table. The butter was cold and hard from the fridge.

Nova took her knife and spread. The hard butter made holes in her toast. "Oh no," said Nova. "My toast has holes." Her friend Forest looked over. "That is a problem," he said.

Dad had an idea. He set some butter in the sun by the tent. They waited. A loud bird sang in the tree. Nova watched the butter. It got soft and shiny.

Nova spread the soft butter. It went on smooth and easy. No holes! Then she poured milk into her cup. She poured slowly. Not one drop spilled.

"Look, Forest!" said Nova. Forest clapped. Mr. Fernando walked by with his mug. "Nice toast," he said.

Nova took a big bite and smiled. "Soft butter wins," she said.

Mateo was at Grandma's house. A little basket sat on the couch. In the basket was his new baby sister. Mateo wanted her to like him. But she was so small. What could he do?

"Can she play?" Mateo asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "She is tiny." Mateo was afraid he might hurt her. He stood very still. Then Grandma held out his hand. "Put one finger near her hand," she said. Mateo put his finger in the baby's little hand. Her tiny fingers held tight! "She has me!" Mateo said. He pulled a little. She still held on, tight, tight, tight.

The baby let go. Then Mateo put his finger back. She held on again. "She knows it is me," he said. Grandma smiled. Outside, a big wheel spun on a truck. The baby turned her head toward the noise. Mateo giggled and offered his finger one more time. "Hold tight, little sister," he said.

Juliette went to the park with her mama. Jimmy was there too. He had a big cardboard box.

"I want to sit in it," said Jimmy. He sat down inside.

Juliette wanted a turn. She waited. Then Jimmy got out.

Juliette sat in the box. She held the sides. "Beep beep!" she said. "This box is my car!"

Jimmy looked sad. "I want it to be a car too."

"Okay," said Juliette. "You can ride in my car."

Then Jimmy had an idea. "Let's make it a boat," he said. He turned the box and rocked it side to side. "Row, row!"

"The box can be a house too," said Juliette. She tipped it up on one side. It made a little wall. Jimmy laughed and crawled in behind her.

Rosie came over with her toy elephant. "The elephant needs a home," she said. She set the elephant in the box. Juliette patted it gently, like a baby.

Ms. Lewandowski, the neighbour, waved from the bench nearby. "That looks like a nice house," she said.

Rosie almost dropped the elephant. Juliette caught it with both hands. "Got you," she said softly.

The sun went down a little. Mama called, "Time to go home."

Juliette gave the box a pat. "Bye, house. Bye, car. Bye, boat."

Jimmy helped tip the box back down. They all held hands and walked to the gate.

Cooper ran fast to the table. Mr. Chanthavong had set out the tablets. Cooper wanted to draw his grandma's house. He did not know how to turn one on.

Aria showed him. "Press the round button," she said. Cooper pressed it. The screen lit up. Then Aria tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. Cooper drew a green plant by grandma's door. He drew a red door. He drew a big yellow sun.

Then the screen went black. All his drawing was gone. Cooper felt like crying. "It went off," he said.

Mr. Chanthavong came over. He looked at the tablet. "It needs charging," he said. He picked up a charger and plugged it into the wall. He plugged the other end into the tablet. A little battery picture showed up on the screen. Cooper watched from his chair.

"Now it can fill up," said Mr. Chanthavong. Cooper drew a small cat while they waited.

Soon the tablet was full again. Cooper opened his drawing. There was grandma's house. He put the tablet back on the shelf, all by himself. Aria clapped. "Good job, Cooper," she said. Cooper smiled and drew one more cat.

Austin zipped his coat all the way to the bottom. It was cold outside. His family walked into the big cultural center. There was a Christmas party inside.

In the middle of the room stood a tall tree. Austin looked up. The tree had lights and pretty balls. His friend Anika was there too. She had a box of ornaments.

"I want to hang them all," said Austin. He put five ornaments on one branch. The branch bent low. One ornament slid off and fell into Anika's hands.

"Look," said Anika. "Too many on one spot."

Austin wondered what to do. He took three ornaments off. Then he hung one here and one there. He spread them out on the tree. The branches did not bend. Every ornament stayed on.

Mr. Augustin smiled and gave him a black star. It had a silver shine. Austin hung the star near the top. Anika clapped. The tree looked full and bright.

"Where should this one go?" Austin asked Anika, holding up a red bell.

Luke went to the library with his dad. It was hot outside, so the cool room felt nice. Luke wanted the dinosaur book on the high shelf. It was too high for him.

Mr. Jung was reading to the kids. Jenny and Hussein sat on the rug. Luke sat down too. Mr. Jung sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Luke sang along. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The kids clapped.

Then Mr. Jung asked Jenny, "How old are you?" Jenny held up four fingers. "I am four," she said. Luke looked at his own hand. He held up four fingers too. He could say it just like her!

After the song, Luke asked Mr. Jung for help. Mr. Jung got the dinosaur book down from the high shelf. "How old are you, Luke?" he asked. Luke held up his fingers and said, "I am four." Mr. Jung smiled.

Outside, rain began to fall on the street. Luke held his book under his jacket. "One, two, three, four," he counted the big raindrops on the steps. His dad laughed and said, "Let's run to the car!"

Jacob was playing on the big kitchen rug. His mom gave him a basket of play things. "Let us sort them," she said.

Jacob made two piles. One pile was for toys. He put in a truck and a ball and a drum. The other pile was for food. He put in an apple. He put in some bread.

Then he held a carrot. It was orange and long. It looked a bit like a stick. He dropped it on the toy pile.

Mom picked up the apple and the bread. She put them back in the food pile. "Apple, bread, carrot," she said. "All foods." Jacob looked at his carrot. Foods go in the food pile. He picked up the carrot and moved it. Now it sat with the apple and the bread.

"Thank you for the food," said Jacob. He covered the food pile with a blue towel, like a little blanket. "The foods can dream now," he said.

He tapped the drum twice. The food pile did not move. He tapped again. Then Mom took the towel off. The apple was still there. The bread was still there. And the carrot was there too, safe in the food pile. "Good night, carrot," said Jacob.

Hannah went to the store with her dad. She wanted a big red apple.

The fruit stand looked like a rainbow. Green apples sat in one box. Red apples sat in a big box. Bananas made a yellow pile. "The fruit is sorted by color," said the man at the stand.

Hannah picked up two red apples. One was big. One was small. She put the big ones in one pile. She put the small ones in a little pile. Now they were sorted by size!

Then she found round oranges and long bananas. She made a round pile and a long pile. "These are sorted by shape," she said.

A warm light glowed over the fruit. It made the apples shine like a picture.

Dad smiled. "Pick your apple, Hannah."

Hannah held up the biggest red one. "This one!"

Hunter ran to the gate at school pickup. His mom was waiting with a big smile. "I stayed up late last night," Hunter said. "I watched a long movie."

The next morning, Hunter did not want to wake up. He was too tired to eat his breakfast. He was too tired to get dressed. Mom helped him put on his shirt and his shoes. He did not even want to bathe. He yawned and yawned.

At school, Theresa and Juan were playing tag. Hunter tried to run. His legs felt slow. He sat down on the bench. "You look sleepy," said Theresa. "I stayed up too late," said Hunter. "Now my body is tired."

That night, Hunter put on his pajamas all by himself. He brushed his teeth. Mom read him one book. Then he closed his eyes and slept. Sleeping at night gave his body rest for the next day.

In the morning, Hunter ate all his eggs. He got dressed fast. At school, he ran with Juan and Theresa. "You are so fast today!" said Juan. Hunter laughed and blew a big breath at the wind. Then he drew a picture of himself running, with a big smile.

Jackson sat at the big kitchen table. Mom had put out five little bowls. "We smell with our nose," said Mom. Jackson sniffed each bowl. The cinnamon bowl made him smile.

Mom asked, "Can you smell the cookies too?" Jackson leaned near the oven. Mom held the tray, because it was hot. Jackson sniffed from his chair. "Mmm, cookies!" he said. His nose found the sweet smell.

Then they played a game. "What do ears do?" Mom asked. Jackson pointed to his ears. "Ears hear the timer!" Ding, ding! Then he covered his eyes. No cookies to see. He opened them. Now he saw the cookies. "Eyes see!" he said.

One cookie almost did fall off the tray. Jackson caught it with both hands. "Nose smells, ears hear, eyes see," he said. "Mouth tastes. Hands touch." He touched the warm plate. He took a big bite. "My mouth tastes cookies!" said Jackson. Mom clapped her hands.

Declan stood at the bus stop with his mom. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He wore his sneakers with bears on them.

Then the wind blew. The wind made his hat fly up. Declan laughed and held it tight. "Windy today," said his mom.

Madeleine came to the bus stop too. She wore rain boots. They were red and tall. Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip.

Declan saw a big puddle. He wondered, could he jump in it? He jumped. Splash! The water went into his sneakers. His socks got all soggy. His toes felt wet and cold.

Madeleine stepped in the puddle too. Her feet stayed dry. "Rain boots keep your feet dry," she said. Declan looked down at his wet socks. He looked at her red boots. Hmm, he thought.

The next rainy day, Declan wore his rain boots. He stomped in a deep puddle. Splash, splash! His feet were dry. He was a brave puddle jumper.

At home, his mom helped him wash the muddy boots. They set them by the door for the baby to see. "Big boots," said the baby, and pointed.

Outside, the snow began to fall. "Snowy next," said Declan. He put on his mittens.

Henry ran out to the backyard. "Where are my toys?" he said. He wanted to build a big tower before lunch. But the toy box was empty! "Oh no," said Henry. Then he saw something funny. A string was tied to the swing. It went behind the big tree. Henry pulled the string. Out came his blocks, one by one. His dog had moved them! Henry laughed. He put the blocks in the toy box. "Blocks are toys," he said. Then he pulled again. Out came his doll. "Dolls are toys too!" He put the doll in the box. Out came his red ball. "And balls are toys!" said Henry. The box was full at last. Anais came through the gate. "Can we play?" she asked. "Yes!" said Henry. He lifted the red ball up high. "Watch me throw it far!"

Jack woke up in his big bed. The sun was on his sweater hanging on the door. He pulled the sweater on, slow and careful. Then he needed to use the toilet.

Jack used the toilet. He pulled up his pants. He ran to the kitchen. "Jack, come back," said his dad. "You forgot something."

Jack walked back. He looked at the toilet. "What did I forget?" he asked. "The flush," said his dad. Jack pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water went down. "Now wash your hands," said his dad.

Jack turned the tap. The water was warm. His dad had checked it first. Jack rubbed soap on his hands. He rubbed slow. Then he dried them on the towel.

"Now breakfast," said his dad. Jack sat down. He ate his egg. "Flush, then wash," said Jack. His dad smiled. "That's it."

Emile went to the store with his dad. They needed milk and eggs for breakfast. Ava and her mom were there too. Ava waved. "Hi, Emile!" she said.

The store had a big game on a table. There were three big bins. One bin said animals. One bin said toys. One bin said foods. Ms. Chanthavong, the friendly store lady, smiled at the kids. "Put each thing in its bin," she said. "It is a sorting game."

Emile picked up a banana. He put it in the foods bin. Ava picked up an apple. She put it in the foods bin too. Then Emile found a stuffed dog. It was soft and brown. He dropped it in the animals bin. But then he looked at it. He tapped its nose. Nothing. It did not blink. It did not wag. It did not bark. Ava held up a real-looking carrot toy and laughed. "This carrot does not smell!" she said. Emile laughed too.

He picked the dog up again. "You are not alive," he told it. "You are a toy." He put the dog in the toys bin. Ms. Chanthavong gave him a sticker shaped like a star. "You got it," she said.

At home, Emile ate his breakfast. He put his napkin over his plate like a little blanket. "My banana is a food," he said. "And my sticker is a toy." He stuck it on his shirt, right over his heart.

Nolan sat at the kitchen table. Dad put warm bread on the plate. Dad folded his hands and said, "We say a blessing first." Nolan wanted to eat the bread now. But he folded his hands, too. Dad said, "Thank you for our food." Nolan listened. Then Dad took a bite. Nolan could not eat yet. He had not said his part.

Nolan thought hard. The bread came from wheat. The wheat grew in spring. Someone planted it. Someone picked it. "Thank you for the farmer," Nolan said. Dad smiled big. Then Nolan got to eat. The bread was soft and warm. Nolan drank milk. He made a sour face at the lemon water. Soon Nolan would sleep, Dad said. At supper, Nolan folded his hands first. "Thank you for our food," he said. "And thank you for the farmer." Dad clapped softly.

Mia sat in the big concert hall. A lady on stage began to play a song. Mr. Grewal clapped his hands. Clap, clap, clap. Mia tried to clap too, but her claps came too fast. Garrett leaned over. "Listen first," he said. Mia listened. Clap, clap, clap. The beat went slow and steady, like a nice big drum. Mia clapped with the beat. Her claps fit right in.

Then Adelyn stood up. "I know a song!" she said. She sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" as loud as she could. Her voice filled the whole hall. A baby near the front woke up and began to cry. Adelyn stopped. What could she do now?

The baby's dad rocked the baby gently. Adelyn looked at Mia. "Watch this," Adelyn said. She sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" very softly, like a little whisper. Mia clapped her steady claps, very quiet. The baby's eyes closed. The baby fell asleep, off to dream. Adelyn smiled and sang even softer, softer still. "Good night, stars," Adelyn whispered.

Livia sat in the tall chair in the waiting room. Her tummy felt jumpy. Today she would get a shot at the doctor's office.

"I don't want it," she whispered to her dad. A toy bird with a paper wing sat on the table. Livia picked it up and held it tight.

Her dad sat close. "Let's breathe together," he said. "Breathe in slow, like you are smelling a flower."

Livia sniffed in a big, slow breath. Then she let it out. Her dad did it too. They did it three more times. Slow in, slow out.

"Your shoulders look soft now," Dad said.

The nurse came in. Livia sniffed her flower breath one more time. The needle went in, quick as a wing flap.

"All done," said the nurse.

Livia looked at her bandage. "That was fast," she said. She picked a sticker from the basket. It was a big red heart.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked.

Her dad laughed. "Let's go home, brave girl."

Madeline was playing at daycare. She loved the big block bin. "Time to clean up," said Mr. Swampy. He clapped his hands.

Madeline had an idea. "I will make color groups," she said. She put all the red blocks in one pile. She put all the blue blocks in one pile. She put all the yellow blocks in one pile. Kiyan came to help. He drove a green truck over. "The truck can carry blocks," he said. Madeline loaded yellow blocks in the truck. Brmm, brmm! Kiyan drove them to the yellow pile.

Then Madeline saw a green block. It was hiding in the blue pile! "Huda, look!" said Madeline. She picked up the green block. She put it with the other green blocks. "All the green blocks live together," said Huda.

Soon every pile had one color only. The dry play dough sat on the shelf like little moons. Mr. Swampy looked at the piles. "Wow," he said. "Ready for a story?" Madeline sat down fast. "Yes!" she said. "Tell us the one about the red dragon!"

Max ran to the rug at school. The room was noisy today. Blocks fell down with a big crash. Max laughed. Then he saw Ember. She sat in the corner. Tears ran down her face.

"Ember is crying," Max said. "Why is she crying?" He looked closer. Her lips went down, down, down. Max felt sad too. Sad faces and tears went together, like rain and clouds.

Max had a red truck in his bag. He loved that truck. He got it out. "Here, Ember," he said. "You can hold it." Ember wiped her eyes. She took the truck. Then she smiled, just a little.

Ms. Barrett sat down beside them. "Look at that," she said. Ember pushed the truck across the floor. It went vroom, vroom. Max clapped his hands. His father had scratched the truck's paint, and Ember rubbed the scratch with one finger.

"More truck?" Ember asked. "Yes!" said Max. And they zoomed it back and forth, back and forth, all the way to snack time.

Lincoln stood at the big table in the cooking classroom. Ms. Yoon put out a bowl and a spoon. "We will make a cake," she said. Lincoln's family would eat it at home tonight. Jawad and Frankie would help too.

Lincoln cracked the eggs. Oops. A bit of shell fell in. He picked it out with his fingers. Then he poured milk and flour. He mixed and mixed. His sweater felt itchy on his arm. He pushed up his sleeve and kept stirring. The batter was runny. It went drip, drip, drip off the spoon.

"This is not a cake," said Lincoln. "It is soup! My cake will never be a cake." He felt sad. Ms. Yoon poured the runny batter into a pan. She put the pan in the hot oven. "We will meet the cake soon," she said. Lincoln waited. He looked at the oven light. It glowed like a little sun.

Then Ms. Yoon opened the oven door. She wore big mitts. She lifted out a real cake. It was puffy and gold. It was not runny now. She cut one slice so Lincoln could see inside. Lincoln laughed. His runny batter had turned into a cake. He carried the cake to his family. "I made this," he said.

Ivy wanted to find a rectangle for shape day. Ms. Francis said, "Look all around the room." Ivy found a circle clock. Ariana found a square block. Dion stacked triangle blocks into a little tower.

"Where is a rectangle?" Ivy asked. She looked far across the room. She saw the door. She walked over slowly. She put her finger on the door. She counted one side, two sides, three sides, four sides. Then she touched each corner. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Four square corners."

"Ms. Francis, look!" said Ivy. "The door is a rectangle." Dion came to count too. Ariana touched a corner and giggled.

"Cookie time," said Ms. Francis. Ivy looked at her plate. "My cracker has four sides too!"

Milan went to the lake with his dad. It was not too late. The sun was warm. Milan wanted to learn to swim. He held the side of the little pool by the lake. He kicked his feet. Splash, splash.

A lady sat in a tall chair above the water. "Who is that?" Milan asked. "That is the lifeguard," his dad said. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it." She sat up high. She could see everyone in the water.

Milan saw a turtle swim by. He let go to look. His feet went down. He blew bubbles. The lifeguard blew her whistle. She slid down fast and held Milan up. "I have you," she said kindly.

Milan held the side again. He watched the turtle. He paid attention to his kicks. Splash, splash. "I can see you," the lifeguard called from her tall chair. Milan waved up high.

Willow went to the library with her dad. In the storytime room, Ms. Tremblay had something small and flat. It was a library card, just for Willow. Willow held it with both hands. Now she could get a book to take home.

Willow looked for a book about flowers. A boy next to her found a dinosaur book. "DINOSAURS!" he shouted. Willow saw people at the tables. They were reading. They looked up at the shout. Ms. Tremblay put a finger near her lips. "We use quiet voices here," she whispered. "People are reading." The boy made his voice very small. "Dinosaur book," he whispered. Willow made her voice small too. "Flower book," she whispered.

The shelves were tall. Willow walked slowly, row by row. Some books had ugly bug covers. Not those. Then she saw it. A big pink flower on the front. Willow pulled it out gently. She waited in line to use her new card. Ms. Tremblay scanned the book. "All done, Willow," she whispered.

Willow hugged the book to her chest. She waved to the boy. He waved back and whispered, "Bye." Willow tiptoed past the reading tables, all the way to the door.

Colton wanted to find his red ball. It was in the backyard. Dad was washing cups at the sink. Colton opened the door and ran out. "Stay close," said Dad.

Colton looked and looked. The ball rolled far away. It sat by the big tree at the far end of the yard. Colton ran to the tree. Then he turned around. He could not see Dad. He could not see the house window at all. The tall bushes were in the way. Colton stopped. His tummy felt small. He whispered, "Dad?"

Colton picked up his ball. He ran back fast. The bushes went away. There was the window. There was Dad, waving. Colton ran into Dad's warm hug. "I could not see you," said Colton. Dad held his hand. They walked back inside together. Dad made warm milk. Colton sat on his back steps and drank it all. "Next time, stay where I can see you," said Dad. Colton nodded. He hugged his red ball tight.

Aria sat in the family car. The seat belt clicked. The car doors went zip, and they were off. "Where are we going?" Aria asked. "To get your first haircut," said Dad. "For Grandma's big party on Saturday."

Aria was wide awake, but her tummy felt funny. "Will the scissors hurt?" she asked. Dad parked the car. "Let's go and see," he said kindly.

Ms. Berg worked at the salon. She had a big red chair. "Hop up," she said. Aria climbed in slowly. Ms. Berg held up the scissors. Snip, snip, she cut a little piece of her own hair. Then she put the hair on Aria's hand. It felt like soft little threads. It did not hurt at all. It felt like nothing.

"Your turn," said Ms. Berg. Snip, snip. Aria waited. She felt nothing. She looked in the mirror. Little curls fell down, soft as feathers. One curl landed right on her nose! Aria laughed and blew it off. "More snips, please," she said. Ms. Berg smiled and kept cutting.

Lena sat at Grandma's big table. She had paper, red paint, and a fat brush. "I want to make a butterfly," said Lena. Grandma smiled. "Paint one wing first," she said. Lena dipped her brush. She painted one red wing. It was shiny and wet. It had dots too. One dot, two dots, three dots.

Then Lena bumped her elbow. The paper folded in half! "Oh no," said Lena. "My butterfly is gone." Her tummy felt tight. "It's okay," said Grandma. "Open it slowly." Lena opened the paper very slowly.

The wing was still there. And something else was there too. A second wing! It looked just like the first one. One dot, two dots, three dots on each side. The wet paint had printed itself. Lena clapped her hands. "Two wings! They match!"

"I can make more," said Lena. She painted one yellow wing on a new paper. She folded it while the paint was wet. She pressed it with her flat hand. Then she opened it fast. Two yellow wings, matching side by side.

Outside, the rain began to fall. Plop, plop on the window. It was getting late. "Time to wash hands," said Grandma. Lena washed the red and yellow paint off her fingers. The water felt warm and soapy. Grandma hung the butterflies up high to dry. Lena looked up at them. "Goodnight, butterflies," she whispered.

Ayla was at Grandma's house. She wanted some apple juice. "Give me juice!" she said. Grandma did not move. She just stirred her pot.

Ananya was there too. Ananya was Ayla's friend. "Juice, please," said Ananya. Grandma smiled right away. She poured Ananya a big cup.

Ayla looked at her own cup. It was empty. She thought hard. Then she tried again. "Juice, please," she said. Grandma smiled big. "Of course, Ayla." Now her cup was full.

Later, they went to the pond. A thin green frog sat on a rock. "Can you help me open the gate, please?" Ayla asked Grandma. Grandma opened it. The girls waited quietly. The frog jumped in. Splash!

"Thank you, Grandma," said Ayla. Grandma gave them each a warm hug.

Aaron went to the playground with his mom. He wanted to play on the big slide. But a new boy stood by the slide. Aaron did not know him. Aaron felt a bit scared, so he hid behind his mom.

Mr. Wanjiru walked by with the new boy. Mr. Wanjiru waved at Aaron. "Hello there!" he said. Aaron peeked out from behind his mom. Would the wave still work if he hid? He stepped out a little. "Hello," said Aaron in a small voice.

Mr. Wanjiru smiled a big smile. "Hello! This is Jensen," he said. Jensen smiled too. "Do you want to send the toy elephant down the slide?" asked Jensen. He held a toy elephant. "Yes, please!" said Aaron.

Up the steps they went. Aaron slid down first. Then he sent the elephant down to Jensen. "Thank you!" said Jensen. Aaron looked at his mom. His hello had made a new friend. What else could a hello do? He waved at the swing. "Hello, swing!" he said. Jensen laughed and laughed.

Rehmat ran to the bikes at the park. Her friend Lilah was already there. Rehmat jumped onto a red bike. She put her feet on the pedals. Then she stopped. She slid off the bike and ran back to the bench. "My helmet!" she said. She put it on her head. She clicked the strap under her chin. Then she got on the red bike again.

Lilah had no helmet on. "I want to ride now," Lilah said. Ms. Wardak held up a blue helmet. "Wait," said Ms. Wardak. Lilah took the helmet. She put it on too.

The two girls rode round and round the path. The sun was warm in the blue sky. A gentle wind blew on Rehmat's face. Rehmat saw her mama waving from the bench. Rehmat waved back and stayed close. Then she rang the little bell on her bike. Ding, ding! Lilah laughed. "Race you to the tree!"

Mateo sat on a little bench at the campsite. His dad gave him warm toast. The toast was for Mateo to butter all by himself.

He held the butter knife in his hand. He spread the butter. Some spots were thick. Some spots were thin. "I did it!" said Mateo.

Then it was time for milk. Mateo picked up the jug. He poured. The milk went into the cup. But some milk ran over the edge. A little puddle sat on the table.

Mateo felt worried. "Oh no," he said. His dad stayed close. "You can wipe it up," said Dad. He handed Mateo a cloth.

Mateo wiped the puddle with the cloth. The milk went away. The table was dry. He poured again. This time he poured slowly. Not one drop spilled.

Charlie-Rose came over with a cookie. "Can I pour too?" she asked. "I will get a cloth if I need one," she said.

Mateo smiled. He ate his toast and drank his milk. "More milk, please," said Mateo.

Paisley stood by the window. It was dark outside. Inside, it was Hanukkah time.

"Tonight we light the candles," said Dad. He put the menorah on the table. The menorah had holders for candles. Dad took out the candles and the matches.

Paisley wanted to help. "Can I count the candles?" she asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "You count. I will light them. Matches are for grown-ups."

Paisley counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." Dad put four candles in the menorah. He lit them with a match. Then he lit one more candle in the middle. The middle candle helped light the others.

Paisley looked and looked. She had counted four. But now there were five little flames. Something felt wrong to her. She counted again, touching each flame with her eyes. "One, two, three, four, five!"

"That middle candle is the helper," said Mom with a smile.

The next night, Paisley was ready. She got an apple slice to snack on while she watched. Dad put in the candles. Paisley counted. "One, two, three, four, five." She waited. Dad lit them all, and the middle helper too.

"Six!" said Paisley. She clapped her hands.

On the last night, eight candles stood in the menorah. The whole row glowed bright. "We light them for eight nights," said Mom.

Paisley snuggled close in the warm light and took a big bite of her apple.

"Eight candles," she whispered. "All done."

Louis put on his nice new shirt. Today was Eid. Family was coming to his house.

Mom knelt down by the door. "When our guests come, we say Eid Mubarak," she said. Louis practiced. "Eid Mubarak!" he said. He said it again. "Eid Mubarak!"

The doorbell rang. Auntie came in. Louis took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak!" he said. Auntie smiled big. "Eid Mubarak, Louis!" she said, and gave him a hug.

More people came. Uncle came. Louis said, "Eid Mubarak!" Uncle laughed and hugged him too. Grandma came. Louis said it loud. Grandma clapped her hands.

Then his cousin ran in. She hid behind Grandma. She did not know the words yet. Louis held her hand. "You can say it too," he said. "Eid Mubarak!" His cousin whispered, "Eid Mubarak." Grandma kissed them both.

Dad called everyone to the table. There were sweet treats. Louis sat with his cousin. "Eid Mubarak," she said to him. Louis grinned and took a big bite.

Jacob sat on the small blue chair. Ms. Kang handed him a recorder. It was long and white, with little round holes.

Jacob put his fingers on the holes. He blew hard. The recorder made a squeak. It sounded like a duck with hiccups. Vincent laughed. "Your duck is back," he said. Jacob laughed too. He tried again. Squeak, squeak!

"Look at your thumb," said Ms. Kang. Jacob peeked at his thumb. It was half off the back hole. He pressed it down all the way. He blew softly. A sweet, low note came out. Vincent's eyes went wide. Jacob lifted one finger. He blew again. Now the note was high, like a little bird. He lifted another finger. The bird flew even higher.

"Each hole makes a new sound!" said Jacob. He played low, then high, then low. Vincent clapped his hands. Jacob wiggled his fingers like a spider walking. The recorder sang a silly, jumpy tune. "Play it again," said Vincent. "It's my favorite song of the day." Jacob took a big breath and played the duck, the bird, and the spider, all in a row.

Nora's baby brother came home today. He was very small. He had tiny hands and tiny feet.

"Can I pat him?" Nora asked.

"Yes, but gently," said her mom.

Nora patted the baby. Pat, pat. The baby began to cry. Nora stopped. "Was that too hard?" she asked. "Yes, it was," said her mom. "A new baby must be touched very gently."

Nora looked at her hand. What could she do? She put out one finger. She stroked the baby's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The baby stopped crying. The baby looked at Nora.

"Does he like soft touches?" Nora asked.

"He does," said her mom.

The window was cloudy outside. Nora saw the baby close his eyes. Soon he began to sleep. Nora whispered, "Sleep, little baby. Sleep."

Isaac sat on the little red chair. Mr. Ndlovu played a song on the piano. "Clap the beat, Isaac," said Mr. Ndlovu. Isaac clapped his hands. Clap, clap, clap. Soon his hands got tired. They felt hot and achy. Isaac stopped and frowned.

"Try stamping your feet," said Mr. Ndlovu. "Feet can keep the beat too." Isaac stamped. Stamp, stamp, stamp. The song went on and his feet went on. He stamped to the end of the song. Madyson and Mira clapped along with him. Mr. Ndlovu smiled and banged the big drum. Boom, boom, boom. The drum kept the beat too.

"Now let's sing," said Mr. Ndlovu. Isaac sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by himself. He tapped his knees as he sang. Tap, tap, tap. His voice was strong and his knees kept going. "Again," said Isaac. He tapped his knees one more time and began to sing.

Aaron sat in his car seat. The car was going to the farm shop. He wanted to pick a toy from the toy box there.

"Look at that black cow," said Dad. Aaron looked out of the window. He saw a horse too. "Is a horse an animal?" Aaron asked. "Yes," said Dad. "So is a sheep."

At the farm shop, Aaron ran to the toy box. He dug and dug. He found toy cars and toy trucks. Then he saw something yellow. It was a banana, hiding under the toy cars!

Ria was there with her mum. Aaron held up the banana. "Ria, look! A banana in the toy box!"

"That's funny," said Ria. She laughed. "A banana is not a toy. It is food."

"The banana is the odd one out," Aaron said. It did not belong with the toys. Ria put the banana in the food basket, next to the apples.

Aaron picked a little black toy car from the box. He smiled. "The car belongs here. It is a toy." He held it all the way home.

Amelia ran to school with her shoes not straight. One lace was loose. She sat on the floor to fix it. "Breakfast time," called Mr. Do. Amelia had a cookie in her bag. She held it up high. "I want this first!" she said.

Mr. Do shook his head. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day," he said. "So we pick a breakfast food." Amelia looked at the table. Eggs, toast, and milk sat there. "One, two, three foods," she counted. Eve pointed at the toast. "Toast is warm," said Eve. Adley pointed at the milk. "Milk is cold," said Adley. Amelia put the cookie away. She chose eggs and milk.

Amelia ate slowly. Then she saw her cookie bag. The cookie was still there! "You finish breakfast, then cookie later," said Mr. Do. Amelia smiled. The sun came in the window. She counted her breakfast: "One, two, three bites." Then she clapped. "I did it!" said Amelia. Eve and Adley clapped too.

Sara sat on the big couch. She had a cold. Her nose was red and her throat felt scratchy.

Her furry blanket was on her lap. She held her toy fish. She gave the fish a little pat. "Are you sick too?" she asked. "No," she said. "You are a toy."

Her mom came in with a small stick. It was shiny at one end. Sara wondered what it was. "What is that?" she asked.

"This is a thermometer," Mom said. "It checks how warm your body is."

Sara wanted to see how it worked. She sat very still. Mom put it under Sara's arm. It tickled a little. Sara did not wiggle. Then Mom took it out and looked at it.

"Your body is warm," Mom said. "You need rest today."

Sara looked at the thermometer. "Can the fish try?" she asked. Mom smiled and shook her head. Sara hugged the fish and snuggled down.

"More rest, then," said Mom. She tucked the blanket up to Sara's chin.

Aiden ran into the bathroom. He wanted to brush his teeth all by himself. The sun made a brown shadow on the floor. The tap went drip, drip, drip.

Aiden turned the tap. Cold water came out. It felt icy on his fingers. His mom came in and turned the other tap. Steam floated up. "Hot," she said. Aiden touched only the cold side. He brushed his teeth up and down. His mom smiled.

Then Aiden saw something small by the sink. It was black and shiny. It looked like a little toy. He reached out his hand. Then he stopped. He made his hand stay still. "Mom, look," he said. His mom came close. She picked it up. "This is a lighter," she said. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups." She put it high up in a drawer. Aiden heard it click shut.

Aiden washed his brush under the cold tap. He heard a truck go by on the street. Then he ran to the door. "All done!" he called, holding up his toothbrush.

Lea sat in the music room. Ms. Iyer played a song on the piano. "Clap with me," said Ms. Iyer. Lea clapped. Clap, clap, clap. But her claps got faster and faster. Soon they were all mixed up. "My claps run away," said Lea.

Ms. Iyer stood up. "Try marching with me," she said. They marched around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp. The steps went steady. They did not speed up. They kept going, even and slow. Lea looked down at her feet. "The beat is like my marching feet," she said. She clapped along with her steps. Clap, clap, clap. Now the claps were steady too.

Then Lea sang the rhyme all by herself. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She did not stop. She sang every word to the end. "Did I finish the whole song?" she asked. "Yes," said Ms. Iyer. "Every word, even the letter T in twinkle." Lea yawned. Marching made her sleepy. "Is the sun awake still?" she asked. "No, it is going to sleep," said Ms. Iyer. "And we will sing again next time." Lea waved goodbye to the piano. Clap, clap, clap, went her happy hands, all the way to the door.

Hannah held her small blue bag at the airport. The big doors slid open when people walked near them. Hannah stopped and watched. "Mama, the doors moved!" she said. "They open for us," said Mama. Hannah waved her hand at the door. Whoosh. It opened again.

They rode a big plane to the beach. Hannah saw the sand and the water. "Can I splash now?" she begged. "Not yet," said Mama. "At the beach, we go near the water only with a grown-up watching." Hannah asked, "Why not now?" "Because I am still carrying the bags," said Mama.

Hannah waited. She made a quiet little castle in the sand. Her friend Opal waited too. Then Mama put the bags down and took Hannah's hand. "Now we can go," said Mama.

Hannah ran to the water with Mama right beside her. The waves came up and wet her toes. She jumped and laughed. The wave went out, and she followed it a little way. Mama stayed close the whole time. "The water is cold!" said Hannah. "Splash with me, Mama!" And Mama did.

Josephine was at school. The sun was warm on the playground. She was building a big sandcastle with her friend Davis. It had a tall tower and a small door.

Josephine ran to get a bucket. Her shoes were slippery in the sand. She slid, and her foot hit the castle. The tower fell down. It went flat. Davis looked at his tower. His eyes went big and sad.

"I knocked it down," said Josephine. "Sorry." Davis looked at her. "You said sorry," he said. "Okay. Let's fix it." Josephine passed him the bucket. They patted the sand, slow and slow. Then the tower stood up again. Mr. Lewandowski walked by. "What a tall castle," he said. Davis smiled. "We built it two times," he said.

Bennett had a tea party in the playroom. His big teapot was empty. "No tea," he said. Karam and Izabella sat on small chairs. They wanted tea for the farm animals.

Bennett poured water into his cup. He poured fast. Water began to spill. It did not fall into the cup. It fell onto the table. "Oh no," said Bennett. Ms. Moose brought a towel. "Pour slow," she said. Bennett poured slow. The cup filled and filled. Then he stopped. The cup was full, not empty. "The cup is full!" he said. He poured slow into small cups too. Not one drop fell out.

Ms. Moose had warm tea from the kitchen. She held the hot pot herself. "Too hot for you," she said. She blew on it. Now it was not hot. It was warm and sweet. Karam laughed. "Full cups for the farm cows!" said Izabella. Bennett held his cup up high. "Full cups for all!"

Logan held his mama's hand at the pharmacy. There was a little room with a bed. A nurse called his name. "Time for your shot, Logan," she said. Logan felt scared. His tummy felt tight. "It is quick," Mama said. "I will hold your hand."

Logan sat still on the bed. The nurse wiped his arm. It felt cold and smooth. Then came a tiny pinch. Logan blinked. "All done," said the nurse. Logan looked at his arm. A small round bandage sat there, soft and sticky.

Then Logan saw a red box on the wall. It was hard, with a small hole. "What is that?" he asked. The nurse held up the used needle. She dropped it in the hole. It went click. "Used needles go in this box," she said. "So nobody gets poked." Logan waved bye-bye to the needle. On the way out, he patted his bandage and smiled at Mama.

Elizabeth ran to the swings at the playground. She wanted to count everything today. "One, two, three!" she sang, pumping her legs. Then she saw Clay by the sandbox. He looked sad. He was holding a big bucket of pebbles.

"Mr. Ramos said I can have five pebbles," said Clay. "But my pebbles are big. Do big ones count as more?" Elizabeth plopped down next to him. "Let's try!" she said. They laid out five big pebbles in a row. "One, two, three, four, five," said Elizabeth. Then they laid out five small pebbles. "One, two, three, four, five," said Clay. The rows matched! Five meant five, big or small.

"Five always means five," said Elizabeth, clapping. Clay laughed and marched around the sandbox like a happy ant. Then they counted the steps to the slide. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" They slid down together. "Ten steps, one slide!" shouted Clay. Elizabeth held up ten fingers and jumped.

Grace wanted to wash her hands. The tap was too high, so Dad came to help. He turned the hot tap. Steam went up, up, up. Grace leaned in close to see the steam. Dad said, "Stay back a little. Steam is hot." Grace stepped back one step. Dad turned the cold tap too. The water got warm and nice. The steam got small. Grace put her hands under the water. She looked up at Dad. "I stayed back," she said. Dad smiled. "Yes, you did." After that, Grace waited on her little stool. Dad made a card for her with a beautiful gold star on it. Grace held the card in her clean, warm hands. "Steam goes up," she said. "And I stay back."

Evan was hungry for a snack. Mom washed a big red strawberry. Evan sniffed it with his nose. It smelled sweet! He looked at it with his eyes. It was red all over.

Evan took a bite. "Yum!" he said. It tasted sweet and juicy. Then he had a silly idea. He held his nose shut with his fingers. He took another bite. His eyes got big. "It tastes plain!" He let go of his nose. He took one more bite. The sweet taste came back!

He ran to Mom. "Mom, try this! Hold your nose!" Mom held her nose and ate a piece. "So plain!" she said. Evan laughed and laughed. He gave Mom a quick hug. Then he ate the rest of the strawberry, nose open, tasting every sweet bite.

Sadie sat on the pool step. The water was warm on her toes. Her team was playing water basketball today. Lennyn held the big orange ball. Rosalyn splashed by the hoop.

"You shoot now," said Ms. Robinson. Sadie took the ball. It was hard and slippery. She pushed it up. The ball hit the hoop's edge. Plink. It fell into the water with a splash. No point.

Sadie tried again. She pushed harder. The ball flew over the hoop and landed near Rosalyn. No point again. Sadie frowned.

Then she looked at the hoop. It had a hole in the middle. The ball had to go through the hole. Sadie pushed the ball up, soft and straight. The ball dropped right through the hoop. Swish!

"Two points!" called Ms. Robinson. Lennyn clapped. Rosalyn laughed and hugged her.

Sadie's teddy bear sat on a towel by the pool. His fuzzy ears were damp from the spray. Sadie waved at him. Then she got the ball and lined up her next shot. "Through the hoop," she said.

Rosalie sat on the kitchen floor. Her dad was baking bread. The kitchen smelled warm and good. The cat, a furry gray cat, sat by the door.

"Let's sing a song," said Dad. He clapped his hands. Clap, clap, clap. Rosalie clapped too. Her claps were fast and jumpy. Dad's claps were slow and steady. "Try to clap like me," said Dad. Rosalie watched his hands. Clap, clap, clap. This time her claps matched. "I did it!" she said.

Then they sang a rhyme. "Hickory dickory dock," sang Rosalie. Then she stopped. She could not remember the next line. She frowned at her toes. "Sing it again," said Dad. So they sang it again. And again. And again. The furry cat twitched its tail to the claps.

At last Rosalie sang the whole rhyme. She did not stop at all. "Again!" she shouted. Dad laughed. The cat ran to lick a crumb of bread off the floor. Clap, clap, clap went Rosalie's hands.

Victor stood in the reading corner. His hand held a shiny new card. It was his very first library card. He wanted a book about trucks.

He looked on the low shelf. He saw books about bears. He saw books about the moon. No trucks.

His friend Lyana was there too. She wanted a book about dogs. She could not find one either.

"Let's ask the librarian," Lyana said. "A librarian works at the library. A librarian helps people find books."

Ms. Romano smiled at them. Victor asked, "Can you help us find books?"

"Yes, I can," she said. "Follow me."

She walked to a big shelf. She reached up and grabbed two books. One was about trucks. One was about dogs.

"The red color on the spine means trucks," she said.

Victor hugged his book tight. He handed over his new card.

"This is mine," he said. "I will bring the book back next week."

Lincoln loved the red truck at daycare. But today he could not find it. Mr. Fortin brought out a big cloth bag. "Put your arm in," he said. "Tell us what you feel."

Lincoln reached in. He felt something round. Something smooth. "A ball!" he said. "A red ball!" He pulled it out. The ball was blue. "Oh," said Lincoln. "It is blue."

Cora put her arm in next. She felt something soft. "A sock! A green sock!" She looked. The sock was yellow. "I was wrong," she said.

"Your fingers can feel the shape," said Mr. Fortin. "Only your eyes can see the color."

Then Milena found the red truck under the rug. Lincoln laughed. "I see it! I see my red truck!" He turned the truck around and around, and the wheels went round and round.

Everly was at daycare. It was a windy day. The windows made a funny sound. Bang, bang, bang.

Everly felt scared. She held her coat tight. Her friend Ludovic felt scared too. He hid behind the blocks. Emerson put his hands over his ears.

Everly looked around the room. Mr. Ramos was sitting by the art table. Could she tell him? She walked over on her little feet.

"I hear a bang," said Everly. "It scares me."

Mr. Ramos took her hand. "Let's look together," he said. They looked at the window. A tree branch was tapping on the glass. The windy day made it move. Bang, bang.

"Was that the sound?" asked Mr. Ramos.

"Yes," said Everly. "The branch did it!" She felt better now. Ludovic came out from behind the blocks. Emerson took his hands off his ears.

Everly smiled a big smile. "Come and see," she said. "The windy tree says bang!"

Ludodic peeked at the window. "I hope it taps all day," he said.

The three friends watched the branch dance in the wind.

Blake sat at the art table. She wanted to make a house with paper shapes. She had a red square. She had a yellow rectangle. But the roof was missing.

Samir sat next to her. He held up a green shape. "I have a triangle," he said. "A triangle has three sides and three corners." He put it on top of his own paper house. It fit just like a roof.

Blake looked for a triangle in her pile. She found one. She touched each side. One, two, three. Then she touched each corner. One, two, three. "It does have three," she said. She put it on top of her square. The roof sat on the house.

Camilo drew a window next. He made it a square, like Blake's red one. The door was a rectangle, long and thin. Blake tipped her cup to drink her water. "Wait," she said. "Look at my cup. The top is a circle!" Samir peeked at his cup too.

Ms. Katz came by with snacks. She gave Blake a sandwich cut into triangles. Blake counted the corners before she took a bite. One, two, three. "Same as my roof," she said, and took a big bite.

Jaxson sat on the playroom floor. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a big picture.

"I will draw a tree," said Jaxson. He drew a green leaf. Then one more green leaf. The tree was full of them.

Now he wanted to draw the sky. He picked up a gray crayon. He made one gray line. Then he stopped. Blaire was painting at the little table. "Look out the window," she said.

Jaxson looked. The day was clear. The sun was bright. The sky way up high was blue. Not gray at all.

Jaxson put the gray crayon back. He picked up the blue crayon. He drew the sky all blue. Blaire held her painting up next to his paper. Her sky was blue too.

"Blue sky," said Jaxson. "Blue sky," said Blaire. Leia clapped from the rug.

Jaxson drew a yellow sun in his blue sky. Then he got tired. He lay down by his picture. The blue crayon was still in his hand. "Blue sky, sunny day," he said softly, and his eyes closed.

Grandpa had a big chair by the window. He picked up his guitar. "We will have a little concert," he said. Avery sat on the rug. A small bug crawled by her foot. She did not touch it. Her sock felt itchy, so she wiggled her toes.

Grandpa played a slow, quiet song. Avery clapped right away. Clap, clap, clap! Grandpa smiled and shook his head. "Not yet," he whispered. "People clap when the music is over. It shows they liked it." So Avery sat still. She waited and waited. The song got slower, then it stopped. Now Avery clapped! Grandpa bowed his head. Grandma clapped too.
