Then Grandpa played a happy song. Avery clapped on the beat. Clap, clap, clap, clap! She sang her nursery rhyme from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Grandma sang along. Penny and Eloise came to listen at the door. When the last note ended, everyone clapped at once. Avery clapped the loudest. Grandpa took her hand and bowed.

Sara dropped her teddy bear on the kitchen floor. She picked it up fast. She looked at his soft paw. "Are you hurt?" she asked.

Her mom came over. Mom gave the bear a little pat. "The bear cannot really feel," Mom said. "But you can pretend he does." Sara hugged the bear tight. She rocked him in her arms. She made a small bed from a towel. The bear lay down. He looked cozy.

Then Sara heard a shake at the door. It was Khloe, from next door. Khloe held her doll. The doll had mud on her shoe. Khloe looked sad. "She fell in the mud," Khloe said. "It hurt her."

Sara smiled. "Toys cannot really feel," she said. "But we can pretend." Sara got a damp cloth. She wiped the doll's shoe, all clean. Then Khloe tucked the doll into the little towel bed too. Both toys slept side by side. The girls sat alone together, very quiet. "Shhh," whispered Sara. "The babies are sleeping."

Jade rode in the car with Mom and Dad. She held her backpack tight. Her teddy was inside it. "One bear, one bag, one girl," she said.

At the airport, they came to a long machine. Dad put the backpack on a belt. The bag went in. Then it was gone. "Where is Teddy?" Jade cried. Would he hide in there forever?

A man in a uniform smiled. "The machine checks what is inside the bags," he said. Jade watched and waited. She counted, "One, two, three." Then the backpack slid out the other end. Teddy was still inside. "You went in and you came out!" Jade said. "The bag took a ride!"

That night, in the hotel room, Jade sat on the big bed. She put Teddy beside her. She talked to him softly. "In and out," she said. "That is how it goes." Then she gave him a quick hug and closed her eyes.

Naomi woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted milk in her big blue cup. "I can do it myself," she said.

Her mama put two warm slices of toast on a flat plate. She gave Naomi a soft round spreader. Naomi dug the butter. The toast tried to slip away. Naomi held the plate with one hand. She spread slow and soft. The butter went all over. Every bit of the toast turned yellow.

Next came the milk. Naomi held her cup in one hand. She poured with the other. The cup wobbled. Milk made a little puddle on the table. Naomi got a cloth and wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go. The cup sat still. She poured again. The milk went right in. Not one drop spilled.

Naomi took a bite of toast. She took a sip of milk. "I did it all by myself," she said. Her mama smiled. Naomi gave her cup a little pat.

Maeva sat in her seat in the car. Mom was driving to the park. Ayah and Cooper would be there. They would play a counting game at the big gate. Maeva wanted to count all the way to ten. She began. "One, two..." Then she stopped. What came next? She had lost the words.

"Mom, what comes after two?" she asked. Mom kept her eyes on the road. "Sing your shoe song," she said. Maeva smiled. She knew that one. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door. Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." The words came out easy, one by one. The rhyme carried her along like a little boat on deep water.

She sang the last part. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen." Then she said the numbers all alone. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She had them now. Outside, a truck full of wood went by. "Bye, wood truck," said Maeva. She sang the song again, soft and slow, all the way to the park gate.

Luca sat at the art table. The sun was warm and sunny on the paper. He wanted to draw a ball for his dog picture. He tried to draw a circle. It came out bumpy and wobbly. "Oh no," said Luca. "My ball looks like a potato."

Rosemary sat next to him. She held her cup of paint water. Then she turned it over on the paper. She traced all around the bottom. Lift the cup. There it was. A round circle, nice and neat.

Luca gasped. He turned his cup over too. He traced around the bottom. "A circle!" he said. "A perfect ball!"

Then he drew a square house. He drew a triangle roof. He drew a rectangle door. He tried to draw the dog. He missed the tail. The tail went on the floor.

Rosemary laughed. "Silly tail," she said. Luca taped it on anyway. "Now my dog has a floor tail," he said.

Mason stood in the pool changing room. He pulled on his little swim shorts all alone. Then Moshe came in with his towel. "Swim class time!" said Moshe.

At the pool, Mr. Fraser sat by the water. "Today we blow bubbles," he said. Mason looked at the water. It was close to his chin. He did not want to put his face down. What would the water feel like?

"Watch me," said Mr. Fraser. He put his mouth near the water. He blew out. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles popped up. Mason's eyes went wide. Bubbles came from a mouth? He leaned over. He blew out through his mouth. Bloop! Little bubbles. He blew harder. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles!

Moshe blew bubbles too. Rayaan laughed and blew some more. Mason blew and blew. His face was in the water and he did not even mind. Mr. Fraser clapped. "Nice bubbles, Mason!"

After class, they went back to the changing room. Mason's wet hair stuck up like a feather. "Again tomorrow?" he asked. "Bubbles again," said Moshe. Mason zipped his bag and smiled.

Theodore stood in the big room at school. Ms. Novák put a hoop on the floor. She gave him a small beanbag.

"Throw it in the hoop," said Ms. Novák. Theodore threw the beanbag. It hit the edge. It fell out. He tried again. In it went! Theodore was happy.

Then Ellie came with a big ball. "Catch," she said. She threw it very hard. It was too fast. It bumped Theodore's hands and rolled away. He ran after it.

Abdul wanted a turn too. Abdul held out his hands. Theodore thought about the fast ball. He did not throw hard. He made a soft, slow toss. Abdul caught it with both hands. Abdul laughed.

"My turn," said Ellie. She held out her hands. Theodore tossed the ball slow and easy again. Ellie caught it. She hugged the ball.

Ms. Novák made a triangle with her fingers. "Look," she said. "You can all play together." Theodore picked up the beanbag. He aimed at the hoop.

"Watch me," he said.

Mia's class had a special day. They were going to the park. Ms. Van Dijk held up a red card. "Red means stop," she said. Everyone stopped. Even Victoria stopped. Even Kingston stopped. Then Ms. Van Dijk held up a green card. "Green means go," she said. Everyone walked on.

At the door, there was a big red box of toys. Ms. Van Dijk pointed to it. "Put on your yellow coats," she said. Mia found her yellow coat. It had a green frog on it. Victoria had a blue coat. Kingston had a blue coat too.

Then they came to the road. There was a tall traffic light. It had a red light on top. Mia held Ms. Van Dijk's hand. The red light made the cars stop. All the cars stood still. Mia watched and watched. Then the light changed to green. The cars went. They zoomed past, one by one.

"Now we go," said Ms. Van Dijk. Mia stepped off the curb. "Red means stop," she said. "Green means go." Victoria laughed. Kingston spun around once, like a little car. The class walked to the park, and Mia called out the colors all the way.

Benjamin was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to play the drum. Boom, boom, boom! He hit it loud. Then the baby woke up. The baby cried and cried.

Grandpa held the baby. He rocked her slow. Soon the baby went back to sleep. Grandpa put one finger by his lips. "When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice," he said. Benjamin nodded big.

Benjamin wanted the drum again. This time he tapped it soft. Tap, tap, tap. The baby kept sleeping. Devon came over to play. Devon wanted a turn too. Benjamin handed him the drum. "You can go next," Benjamin whispered. Devon tapped it soft too. Tap, tap, tap. The baby slept and slept.

Grandpa smiled. He gave them each a warm cookie. Benjamin ate his slow and quiet. "Shh," he said, with a big grin.

Paint day at school! Dylan ran to the art table. Ms. Van Dijk gave him a special plastic cup of water and a brush.

"I want yellow," said Dylan. He dipped his brush in yellow. He painted a big sun.

Next he wanted blue. He dipped his brush in blue. He painted the sky.

Then he wanted yellow again. He dipped his brush in yellow. But the yellow came out green and muddy!

"Yuck!" Dylan yelled. "My yellow is dirty!"

Willow leaned over. "Wash your brush," she said. She pointed at the cup.

Dylan swished his brush in the water. Bubbles wiggled in the cup. The brush came out clean.

He dipped the brush in yellow again. This time the yellow was bright like a lemon. Dylan painted a shiny yellow moon.

Arjan looked over. "Nice moon!"

"Watch this," said Dylan. He swished his brush in the water. Then he dipped it in blue. He tapped the blue on top of the yellow moon. The sky turned green, green, green.

Willow clapped. "Green!"

Dylan held up his brush. "Water first, then paint," he said. He dipped his clean brush in red.

Rehmat woke up and looked out the window. The snow was wild and white. She put on her shoes for school. Her mom came in and smiled.

"No school today," Mom said. "It is a snow day. School is closed because of snow."

Rehmat tilted her head. "Closed? Like a shop?" she asked.

"Yes, just like that," said Mom.

Rehmat ran to the kitchen in her pajamas. "Can we make dinner early?" she asked. Mom laughed. "We can cook soup," she said. Rehmat pushed her stool far from the stove. She watched Mom chop carrots. The carrots went into the big pot. Then the snow outside made the window fog up.

"Mom, look! The hot pot made the glass cloudy," Rehmat said. One thing had made another thing happen.

After the soup, they went outside and made a big snowman. Rehmat put a carrot on its face. "He can have my carrot too," she said.

Freya went to the little pool by the lake. Mr. Rosen was the swim teacher. "Swim time!" Freya shouted. She ran for the water.

"Wait," said Mr. Rosen. "Shower first, pool second. Shower first, pool second." He turned on the warm shower. Freya stood under it. The water tickled her toes.

Freya wanted to skip it. She looked at the pool. She looked at the shower. Shower first, pool second, she said to herself. Tatum and Eloi were already wet from the shower. Freya counted, "One, two, splash!" The water ran down her arms.

Then Mr. Rosen showed a small surprise. It was a long green snake. It was a toy for the pool! It floated like a wiggly stick. Freya laughed. She was a brave girl in the shower, so now she could swim. She stepped into the pool. The toy snake bobbed beside her.

"Look at me!" said Freya.

Luka went to the park with his dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Luka ran to the sandbox. He followed his friend Sara to the big bucket of toys. But the sun was very bright. Luka squinted his eyes. He could not see the shovel. He rubbed his eyes. "My eyes feel funny," he said.

Then Sara put on her sun hat. "My hat shades my face," she said. Luka looked at her. She was not squinting at all. "Dad, can I have my hat?" Luka asked. Dad pulled the sun hat from the bag. Luka put it on. The brim made shade over his face. Now he could open his eyes wide. He could see the whole sandbox.

Luka filled the bucket with sand. He made a big, tall tower. "What a lucky hat," said Luka. "On a sunny day, my sun hat shades my face." Sara laughed and clapped. Dad sat close by on the bench. The wind blew a little. It tickled Luka's nose. Luka patted his tower and smiled at Sara. "Let's build another one," he said.

Henri sat in the big concert hall. The lights were bright like paint on the walls. Mr. Rivera stood on the stage. He said, "Let's clap along. One, two, three, four." Henri clapped. His clap went too fast. Then too slow. Mr. Rivera waited and smiled. He clapped again. One, two, three, four. This time Henri clapped just right. His clap and the song fit together like two shoes.

"Now we sing," said Mr. Rivera. Henri began, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you..." He stopped. He lost the last word. Tage sat beside him. Tage whispered, "Think of a word that rhymes with star." Henri thought. Car? Far? Jar? Then he said, "Are! How I wonder what you are!" The word rhymed with star, just like cat rhymes with hat.

Zephyr clapped the steady beat. Henri sang the whole rhyme from memory. Everyone clapped, one, two, three, four. Then a small surprise. Mr. Rivera played one shiny note on the piano, and Henri's clap made his chair squeak. Squeak, clap, squeak, clap. Henri laughed. "Again!" he said. "One more time," said Mr. Rivera. And the music began.

David ran to the front door. The sun was bright outside. "Sunny today!" said Dad. David grabbed the handle. "Wait," said Dad. "Sunscreen first." Dad rubbed it on David's face and arms. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," said Dad. David wiggled while Dad counted. "One arm, two arms, done!"

Then David looked out the window. Rain was falling. "Rainy now!" said David. "Get your boots," said Dad. David found one boot. The other boot was missing! He looked by the door. He looked under the mat. There it was, under Samy's coat!

Samy knocked at the front door. "Play outside!" said Samy. David pulled on both boots. He zipped his raincoat up, up, up. The two boys jumped in one puddle, then two puddles, then three. "Splash!" they shouted. David laughed in the rain.

Kai went to the park with his mom. There were red flags and paper flowers everywhere. It was Lunar New Year.

Kai saw his friend Leland. Leland was holding something small and red. "What is that?" Kai asked.

"It is a red envelope," said Leland. "There is money inside."

Kai wanted one too. He watched the big people. A grandma gave Leland an envelope. Leland folded his hands. He said, "Thank you." Then he opened it.

Kai waited. He watched a dancer in a furry lion costume. The lion did a little jump. Kids clapped and waveed their hands.

Then a grandpa came to Kai. He held out a red envelope. Kai folded his hands like Leland. "Thank you," Kai said.

The grandpa smiled. Kai opened the envelope. He peeked inside. There was money in there!

"Mom, look!" said Kai. "I said thank you first."

Mom gave him a big hug. Kai held his envelope up high. The lion dancer waved right at him.

Rosalie went to the baby store with her dad. A new baby sister was coming soon. Rosalie wanted to pick a gift. She saw a little red cup. She held it up high.

"I will give her my crackers too," Rosalie said.

A man who worked at the store smiled. He was stacking little bottles. "New babies only drink milk or formula," he said. "Not regular food yet."

Rosalie put down the little red cup. She thought about her crackers. She could not feed them to the baby. So she picked a soft blanket instead. It had a bunny on it.

At home, Rosalie met her baby sister. The baby was very small. She made a tiny sound. The baby drank milk from her bottle. Rosalie watched from her spot on the rug.

"Here is your gift," Rosalie said. She laid the bunny blanket by the baby. The baby grabbed it with one little hand. Rosalie laughed. "You win the blanket," she whispered. The baby held on tight.

Arlo sat at math club. Mr. Papadopoulos put out two bowls of buttons.

"Which bowl has more?" he asked.

Arlo looked and looked. Kylie counted the buttons in the blue bowl. "One, two, three," she said. Then she kept going and got mixed up. She shrugged.

Arlo pointed at the blue bowl. He counted again. "One, two, three..." Then he forgot where he stopped. He frowned.

He looked at his hand. He put up one finger. "One." He put up another finger. "Two." One finger for each button. "Three, four, five, six."

Six fingers were up. Six buttons!

Now he counted the red bowl the same way. One finger for each button. He got four fingers up. Four buttons.

"Blue has more," said Arlo. "Six is more than four."

"Yes!" said Mr. Papadopoulos. "Well done, Arlo."

Kylie clapped. Francesco clapped too.

Arlo held up his six fingers. He wiggled them like they were singing. "My fingers are special helpers," he said.

Then he counted the crayons on the table, one finger for each crayon.

Emile went to the park with his class. Ziva and Hudson came too. Mr. Mensah had two hoops and one big red ball.

"Time for a throwing party," said Mr. Mensah. Emile threw his beanbag. It missed the hoop. He threw again. It went in. Ziva clapped. Hudson clapped. "One, two, three throws," they said. "Emile can do it!"

Then it was time to catch. Mr. Mensah rolled the big red ball to Emile. Emile touched it with his hands. The ball bounced away. He tried again. The ball bounced away again. "That ball is too big," said Emile.

Ziva rolled the ball. This time Emile caught it. Then he pulled it close and hugged it to his chest. The ball did not bounce away. It stayed right there. "I hug it, I hold it," said Emile.

"Let's call that the big ball hug," said Mr. Mensah. Emile laughed. A rainy cloud went by, but the sun stayed. He hugged the ball all the way to the bench.

The new baby was home. His name was Sam. Sam cried and cried. Mom picked him up and fed him. Then Sam went to sleep.

Scarlett looked at Sam. She wanted Mom to play. But Mom was busy. Scarlett felt a small sad spot in her tummy. She tugged Mom's sleeve. "I miss you, Mom," she said. "Just you and me."

Mom put her hand on Scarlett's head. "Thank you for telling me," Mom said. She put Sam in his cot. Sam stayed asleep.

Then Mom sat on the floor. "Now it is our turn," she said. They made a long line of blocks. Red, blue, red, blue. "Look how neat!" said Scarlett. Mom clapped. From the cot came one tiny snore. Scarlett giggled and added one more block.

Edouard sat at the picnic table at the campsite. Mom put two soft white slices of bread into the toaster. The bread went down with a click.

"Why does it go down?" Edouard asked.

"It is getting warm," said Mom. "Watch it pop up."

Ping! Up came the bread. But it was not white and soft now. It was brown and crunchy. Edouard tapped it with his spoon. Tap, tap.

"The bread got hot," said Mom. "Now it is toast."

"Toast," said Edouard. He smiled.

Mom gave him the toast and a small knife with butter. "You can try," she said. Edouard dug the knife in. The butter made a big hole. He laughed and tried again. This time he spread slow and soft. The butter went all the way to the edges.

Gregoire came over with a cup. "Can you pour the milk?" he asked. Edouard picked up the small jug. He poured too fast. Milk made a puddle on the table. Theresa ran to get a cloth.

"Try again," said Theresa.

Edouard poured again, very slow. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell. He bit his crunchy toast. "I did it!" he said.

Gregoire raised his cup like a flag. "To Edouard!" he said, and they cheered.

Isaiah stood in the bathroom next to the big tub. Dad turned the silver tap. The water came out fast. "That side is hot," said Dad. He put his hand under the other tap. "This side is cold." Isaiah touched only the cold water. It felt like snow from the sky. Dad filled the tub with warm water. Isaiah put in his blue boat. The boat went round and round.

After his bath, Isaiah and Dad went to the store. Isaiah wanted to see the apples. He looked at the red apples. Then he looked up. Dad was not there. Isaiah looked down the aisle. He saw shoes. He saw carts. He did not see Dad.

Isaiah remembered a word Dad had taught him. The word was "worker." A worker wore a green vest. Isaiah saw a woman in a green vest at the checkout. He walked to her and held the edge of her counter. "I can't find my grown-up," he said.

The worker spoke into her phone. Soon Dad came around the corner. He knelt down and hugged Isaiah. "You did it just right," said Dad. Isaiah held Dad's hand. The apples were red and shiny in the cart.

Evan woke up early. Today was his big day. He was going to the dentist for the very first time. "I get to sit in a big chair!" he told his gray cat. He counted his teeth with his finger. "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

He packed his small pillow in a bag. He wanted to hug it in the car. Mom smiled and buckled him in. The seat clicked.

At the dentist, a kind lady waved. Evan looked at her hands. Her hands were blue! "Why are your hands blue?" he asked. The dentist held them up. "These are my gloves. I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

Evan touched one glove. It felt smooth and stretchy. The dentist pulled it and let go. Snap! Evan laughed out loud. He opened his mouth wide, just like a lion.

At home, Evan put his pillow on the couch. He snapped his own pretend gloves on his hands. "Open wide, cat!" he said. The cat yawned big.

Jules wanted to build a big tower at daycare. He found a heavy box. He pulled it. He pushed it. The box did not move. "It is so heavy," said Eloi.

Ms. Tan brought a pillow. "Try this," she said. Jules lifted it up high. It was light. "Heavy and light are opposites," said Kaya with a giggle.

Jules put the light pillow on top of the heavy box. The tower stood tall. It did not fall down.

Jules colored a small piece of paper. He stuck it on the box like a flag. "Our tower!" he said. Kaya clapped. Eloi patted the box. Jules stood very proud, next to his big, tall tower.

It was Wren's birthday. She brought a big box to school. The box was all wrapped up in blue paper. Mr. Tesfaye put it on the table.

Abigail and Jayson ran over. They wanted to see the present. But the paper hid the box. Nobody could see inside.

"Shake it!" said Jayson. Wren shook the box. Something went thump, thump. "Is it a truck?" he asked. "Maybe a drum," said Abigail. Wren squeezed the box. It felt hard on one side. Still, she could not see it. The paper was in the way.

"I can't tell," said Wren. Her tummy felt funny. She wanted to know right now. "Just wait," said Mr. Tesfaye kindly. "Presents open at snack time. It is not long to wait." He sat down next to her. Wren took a big breath.

At last it was time. Wren pinched the paper and pulled. Rip! The paper tore open. There was the box. She lifted the lid. It was a red tea set! "Cups!" said Abigail. "So smart," said Jayson. Wren smiled big.

"Tea party!" said Wren. She poured a pretend cup for Abigail first.

Madeline was at Grandma's house. In the yard there was a big tree. Under the tree there was a swing. Madeline wanted the swing. But Louna was on it. Louna was her cousin's friend, and she was already going high.

Madeline stood and watched. She held the rope. She waited. Grandma said, "You can ask, sweet pea."

Madeline asked, "Can I have a go?" Louna slowed down. "We can take turns," said Louna. "You get a go, then I get a go. One after another."

So Madeline sat on the swing first. Grandma pushed her gently. Madeline went up and down. Then she hopped off. "Your go," she said.

Louna had her go. Then it was Madeline's turn again. One after another, back and forth.

Then something small surprised Madeline. A dark little bug sat on the swing rope. It did not move. The girls waited for it to fly away. It flew to the big tree.

Madeline laughed. "Now it is your go again," she said, and she gave the swing a push.

Samuel sat on the rug at school. Mr. Mercado had a drum. He tapped it slowly. "Clap when I tap," said Mr. Mercado. Samuel clapped too fast. His claps ran ahead of the drum. Gordon clapped just right. Samuel stopped and looked at Gordon's hands.

"Why do your claps fit the drum?" Samuel asked. "I wait and listen," said Gordon. Samuel tried again. He listened first. Then he clapped. His claps landed with the drum, one, one, one. Joanna smiled and clapped with him.

Then Mr. Mercado said, "Now we will sing a rhyme. Nursery rhymes are short rhyming songs for little ones." Samuel knew one from his grandpa. He stood up tall and sang it all the way through. The whole class clapped the beat. Samuel sang it again, louder this time.

The lights went out. Isaac flipped the switch up. Nothing happened. He flipped it down. Still nothing!

"Mom, the switch is broken!" he called.

Mom came with her phone. The phone made a bright little light. "It is a power cut," she said. "The lights are off in the whole building. Flipping the switch will not turn them on."

"Can we see Eunice?" Isaac asked. "She lives down the hall!"

Mom knocked on Eunice's door. Eunice held a flashlight. Her dad had lit a candle, way up high where Isaac could not touch it.

"Watch this," said Eunice. She flipped her switch. Her lamp stayed dark. "See? No power, no light."

Isaac grinned. "Then flashlights are our lights tonight!"

They built a car from glue and paper. They made pretend salty popcorn. The flashlight glowed on the wall.

Then the lights popped back on. The lamp glowed bright. Isaac flipped the switch down, just to see.

"Goodnight, big light," he whispered.

Today was Madison's birthday. She was three years old. Her party was at the swimming pool. Hannah and Adalyn came too. Mr. Navarro, the pool teacher, waved hello.

First they splashed in the small pool. The water felt fresh and cool. Adalyn fell down in the water. Madison held her hand. Adalyn stood up and laughed. Then they all got out. Mom wrapped them in big warm towels.

Then Dad brought out the cake. It was by the pool wall. The cake had three pink candles. Madison wanted to light them. She reached for the matches. Dad shook his head fast. He took the matches up high.

"Only a grown-up lights candles," Dad said. "You can blow them out. And you make the wish."

So Dad lit the candles. One, two, three little flames. Madison thought hard. Then she took a big breath. She puffed and puffed. The candles went out. All gone! Hannah clapped. Adalyn clapped too. Mr. Navarro knocked on the table like a drum. Everyone sang happy birthday.

Mom cut the cake. Madison gave the first slice to Adalyn. "For you," she said. Adalyn smiled big. Then they all ate cake by the pool. The sun went down slow. "Happy birthday, Madison," said Dad. Madison waved her fork in the air.

Sofia sat at Grandma's big table. There was fish for dinner. Grandma had cut it into small pieces. Sofia felt bumpy with worry inside. She did not know the words.

At Grandma's house, everyone held hands first. Grandma said, "We say grace before we eat." Sofia squeezed Grandpa's hand. She did not know what to say.

Grandma smiled. "Just say thank you for something," she said. Sofia looked at her plate. The fish was warm. The rice was soft.

"Thank you for the fish," said Sofia. "Thank you for Grandma." Everyone said amen. Then they all began to eat.

The next morning, Sofia held out her hand before breakfast. Grandpa laughed and took it. "You remembered," he said. Sofia said thank you for the eggs and for Grandpa too. Then she ate her warm egg, and Grandpa gave her a big hug.

Hazel sat on the soft rug in the school library. Mr. Janssen put a big picture book in front of her. "Count the cookies with me," he said. Hazel pointed at the plate in the picture. "One, two, three," she said. Petra sat down next to her. "My turn," said Petra. "Four, five, six, seven." Aarav came with a second book. His plate had cookies too. "One, two, three, four, five," he counted.

"Now look at both plates," said Mr. Janssen. Hazel looked and looked. "Petra's plate has more," she said. Petra smiled and clapped. Then they turned the page. The dog in the story ate a cookie. Then he ate another. The plate got emptier and emptier. Hazel counted each time. "Three, two, one." Then the plate had nothing on it at all.

"Zero," said Mr. Janssen. "Zero means none." Hazel said it back to him. "Zero. The plate is empty." A little bug crawled across the page, and Aarav helped it onto a leaf by the window. "Sleep now, little bug," Petra whispered. On the last page, the dog baked more cookies. "Yummy," said Hazel, and everyone laughed. Hazel counted them all, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Mr. Janssen gave her a big thumbs up. "Zero cookies left for me," said Aarav, holding out his empty hands.

Rehmat was at her grandma's house. Grandma had a big red hat on the table. "Sing with me," said Grandma. Rehmat wanted to clap and sing the whole rhyme. But she did not know it yet.

Grandma sang very fast. Rehmat tried to clap. Her hands slipped and missed. Her words came out all jumbled. "Sorry," said Rehmat. "I can't do it."

"Let's try it slow," said Grandma. Grandma sang the rhyme slow, slow, slow. Rehmat clapped one clap for each word. Clap, clap, clap. It fit! Grandma sang it slow again. Rehmat sang every word from her memory. Then Grandma sang it fast. Rehmat clapped fast and sang fast too. No slipping. No jumbles.

"Again!" said Rehmat. She put the big red hat on her head. She clapped and sang all by herself. Grandma clapped along with her.

Amelia put muffin cups in a pan. Her dad mixed the batter. Amelia helped him pick blueberries and drop them in. Then Dad put the pan in the oven. "We need the timer," he said. He turned the dial, and it went tick, tick, tick.

Amelia ran out to the backyard. Legend was there. They played a game with a big red ball. "Catch!" Legend called. Amelia threw with her whole arm. The ball bounced on the grass. They laughed and forgot about the muffins.

Then they heard it. Beep, beep, beep! "That means it is time to check the food," Amelia said. She ran to the door. Dad was already pulling out the pan. The muffins were big and golden. Amelia smelled the warm blueberries. "We made those," she said, feeling proud. "Timer, will you beep for cupcakes next?"

Joseph turned four today. His party was at the big park. His mom set a cake on the picnic table. The sky was blue, not rainy at all.

Presents sat in a pile on the grass. Joseph ran to them fast. He grabbed a red one first. It was from his friend Agastya. Inside was a little toy truck. Joseph held it up. "A truck!" he said.

Then Joseph saw a green present. He put the truck down. He ran to the green one next. But Agastya stood there, still waiting. Agastya looked at his shoes.

Madeleine ran over to Joseph. "You forgot something," she said. Joseph looked at Agastya. Then he looked at the truck. He ran back to Agastya.

"Thank you for my truck," Joseph said. Agastya smiled big. "You are welcome!" he said.

Joseph opened the green present next. It was a soft baby doll from Madeleine. Joseph hugged it. Then he turned to her. "Thank you, Madeleine," he said.

Ms. Mercado, from next door, gave him a book. Joseph took it with both hands. "Thank you," he said, right away.

Everyone clapped. Joseph ate cake with his truck in his lap. Agastya sat close by his side. "Happy birthday, Joseph," said Agastya.

Kinsley rode in the car with her dad. They were going to the hospital. Her mom was there. A new baby was coming today.

"Is the baby here yet?" Kinsley asked.

"Soon," said Dad. "We have to wait a little."

They walked down the hall. They counted the doors together. One door, two doors, three doors. Then they saw Mom. Mom held a small bundle. A tiny baby was inside.

"This is your baby brother," said Mom.

The baby had a little nose. He had little hands. Then the baby began to cry.

"Why is he crying?" Kinsley asked. "Is he sad?"

Mom shook her head. "He cannot talk yet," she said. "So he cries to show he needs something."

"Maybe he is hungry," said Dad.

Mom held the baby close. She fed him. The crying stopped. The baby made a small sound. Then he went to sleep.

"He cried, and you helped him," said Kinsley. "Now he is happy."

Later, the baby cried again. Kinsley looked at him. "He needs something," she said. "Maybe his blanket fell off."

Mom picked up the blanket. She put it back on. The baby stopped crying. His eyes closed.

"He is strong," said Kinsley. "He can tell us things with his cry."

"Can I hold him?" she asked.

Mom helped Kinsley sit just so. The baby rested in her arms. Kinsley hoped he would stay asleep.

"Hello, baby," she whispered. "I am your big sister."

The baby made one small sigh. Kinsley smiled and held him very still.

Milo had a big story about a bird's nest. He saw it in the tree by his door. The nest had three little eggs in it.

At dinner, Dad began to talk. "Today I fixed the gate," Dad said.

Milo jumped in. "A nest! I saw a nest!"

Dad kept talking. Milo's words fell on the floor. Nobody heard them.

Milo tried again. "The eggs! The eggs!"

Mom was talking now. Milo's tummy felt tight. His story was stuck inside.

Mom put a crunchy cracker on his plate. "When someone is talking, we listen and wait until they finish," she said.

Milo chewed his cracker. Crunch, crunch. He looked at Dad. Dad was done now. He looked at Mom. Mom was still talking. Milo folded his hands and waited.

Mom took a sip of water. She was done.

"Now Milo can talk," said Mom.

Milo sat up tall. "I saw a nest in our tree!" he said. "It has three little eggs!"

"Wow," said Dad. "Show me after dinner."

Dad helped Milo hang his jacket on the hook. Then they went out to the tree together.

"Can we see the eggs?" Milo whispered.

Dad lifted him up, way up high. "Look," said Dad.

The eggs were still there. Three little eggs, warm in the nest.

Maverick went to the park with his dad. Henry and Gurasees were there too. They ran to the slide. The sun made the slide very hot. Maverick touched it with one finger. "Ow! Hot!" he said. His dad said, "Wait for the shady side." They slid down the cool side instead.

Then Maverick saw something on the bench. It was a little box. Inside were round red things. They looked just like candy. Gurasees leaned close. "Yum," said Gurasees.

"No," said Maverick. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." He did not touch the pretty things. He kept his hands behind his back. He ran to his dad and pulled his sleeve. "Dad, come look!" His dad looked at the box. "That is medicine," said his dad. "You did the right thing, Maverick." His dad put the box high up, away from everyone. The boys ran back to the slide. Henry yelled, "Last one down is a string bean!" Maverick laughed and slid down fast, all the way into the soft sand.

Ella was at Grandma's house. Chase came to play too. Grandma had one red scooter. Chase got it first. He zoomed down the path. Ella wanted a turn right now. She reached out her hand to grab it. Then she stopped. She put her hands in her pockets. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" she asked. Chase looked at her. He nodded. Ella sat on the step to wait. She watched Chase zoom and zoom. Soon he rolled the scooter to her. "Your turn," he said. Ella zoomed fast. The scooter was a bit slippery, so she held on tight. When she was done, she gave it back. "Can I have a turn when you're done?" Chase asked. "Yes," said Ella. They took turns all afternoon. Grandma watched from the door and smiled. Then she folded a blanket for the porch seat. "Two tired riders," she said, patting the soft shape. Ella and Chase sat down together, side by side. "Same time tomorrow?" said Chase.

Joseph ran into the kitchen. "Toast time!" he shouted.

Dad put the toast on the plate. Dad put the butter dish beside it. "You can spread it," said Dad.

Joseph took the little knife with the round top. He dug into the butter. He spread it across the toast. The butter made the toast shiny. One more swipe, and all the bread was covered. "Look, Dad! I did it!"

"Now the milk," said Dad. He put out the big carton. Joseph tried to pour it. The carton was heavy. Milk almost sloshed out. "Too big!" said Joseph.

Dad poured some milk into a small jug. "Try this," he said. Joseph picked it up. It was light in his hands. He tipped the jug, and milk went into the cup. Not one drop spilled!

The dog trotted in and sniffed the empty jug. Joseph laughed. "More milk, please!"

Mya stood in the kitchen in her sock feet. One shoe was on. One shoe was hiding under the table.

"Toast time," said her mother. She put two warm slices on Mya's plate. Mya loved warm toast.

Mya picked up her little knife. It was dull and safe, just for her. She dug a small pat of soft butter. She patted it onto the toast. Pat, pat, pat.

Then Mya looked down. The butter was gone! "Where did it go?" she cried. "My butter ran away!"

Her mother peeked at the plate. The butter had turned shiny and wet. It had melted into the warm toast. Now the toast looked glossy, like a snowy hill in the sun.

"It did not run away," said her mother. "Look close. It is still there."

Mya leaned way down. She patted the toast again. The butter was hiding in the warm bread. She put another pat on the second slice. It got shiny too. Mya giggled. "The toast drinks the butter!" she said.

Next came the milk. Mya held the small cup with two hands. She poured slowly, slowly. A tiny drop ran down the side. She wiped it with her finger. No big spill.

Mya took a big bite of toast. It tasted buttery all the way through. "Mmm," she said. She wiggled her toes and looked under the table. "Shoe, are you hiding too?"

Elias stood in the kitchen. The toast sat on his plate. Mama put a small knife beside it.

"I want to spread the butter," said Elias. Mama handed him the knife, flat side down.

First Elias poked the toast with the pointy tip. The bread tore into little bits. Butter clumped in one spot. "Oh no," said Elias. "My toast is a mess."

He looked at the knife. It had a flat side. What could that side do? Elias turned the knife over. He scooped a bit of butter. He pushed the flat side across the bread. The butter slid and spread. It covered the whole toast, corner to corner. "Mama, look! The flat side works!"

Now for the milk. Elias held the cup with two hands. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. The sun began to shine on the table. Elias took a big bite of toast.

"Can the baby have milk too?" he asked. Mama smiled and poured a small cup. Elias carried it, so careful, so slow, all the way to his little sister.

Leo sat at the dinner table. The pasta smelled warm and good. His dad was talking to Aunt Meg about her new job.

Leo had big news. "Dad! Dad!" he said. "Ulysse found a coin today!"

Dad kept talking. Aunt Meg kept talking. Leo felt afraid his news would float away.

He tried again. "Dad! The coin was shiny!"

Dad held up one finger. He did not stop talking.

Leo looked at his pasta. He took a bite. He waited.

Dad stopped talking. There was a quiet little pause.

"Now, Leo?" Leo asked.

"Yes, now," said Dad.

Leo sat up tall. "Ulysse found a shiny coin at school. He let me wave it goodbye when the bus came."

"What lovely news," said Aunt Meg.

"Thank you," said Leo.

Dad smiled. "May I have some bread, please?"

"Please," said Leo too.

Dad passed the bread. Leo took a warm piece. It felt soft in his hand.

He chewed slowly and listened. When Dad stopped again, Leo said, "Can you help me cut this, please?"

"Of course," said Dad.

After dinner, Leo waved to Aunt Meg at the door. "Come again!" he said.

Kinsley went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about pink flowers. Ms. Dlamini showed her a little shelf.

Kinsley found a book. She held it up. The bear on the page stood on his head. The words sat at the bottom of the sky. "Look, Milo!" she said. "The bear is upside down!" Milo came over and laughed.

Ms. Dlamini turned the book around. Now the words sat at the bottom of the page. The bear stood on his feet. Kinsley blinked. She turned the book upside down again. The bear stood on his head again. The words flew up to the top. "Funny bear," she said. She turned it back. The bear sat down. The words sat at the bottom, all in a row.

Kinsley put her finger on the row. "These are the words," she said. "They tell about the bear." Milo leaned in close. Kinsley turned to the first page. "This is the front," she said. She opened it and began. "Bear woke up. Bear saw pink flowers."

Rose ran in the sunny yard at daycare. The sun felt warm on her nose. She wore no coat at all. Sasha wore a round yellow hat. Braelynn laughed as the wind blew it off. "The wind wants my hat!" Sasha said. Rose chased the hat and caught it. Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to tap, tap, tap on the slide. Thunder rumbled, big and low. Rose still wanted to play on the swings. Mr. Reyes clapped his hands. "When you hear thunder, go indoors," he said. Everyone ran inside fast. Rose watched from the window. A bird with one wet wing sat under the roof too. Rain poured down. Rose said, "Good thing we came in." Sasha's hat dripped on the floor, drip, drip, drip.

Muhammad went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm on his face. It was a sunny day. He wore his short sleeves.

Then the wind came. The wind lifted the leaves up high. It was a windy day. Muhammad held his hat with both hands. His friend Ellis was there. Ellis had a paper boat.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was a rainy day. Ellis ran in the rain. Soon his shirt was all wet. Muhammad's raincoat kept his body dry. He put his hood up too.

Ellis went back home with his mom. He came back wearing his raincoat. Now Ellis was dry too.

Then something small and white fell on Muhammad's nose. "Snow!" said Ellis. The rain had turned to snow. The boys watched it fall on the tall tree.

"Snow on my boat," said Ellis. The little paper boat sat white and still. Muhammad laughed softly and held out his hands.

Lea wanted the big red truck. She could not find it anywhere at daycare. The toy shelves had little signs on them. Lea looked at the signs. They had small black words.

Malakai came over. "What does that sign say?" Lea asked. Malakai pointed to a sign. "It says blocks," he said. Lea looked under the shelf. Yes! Blocks were there. Then he pointed to another sign. "That one says trucks." Lea ran to that shelf. The red truck was waiting for her. The words had told her where to look.

Next Lea found a box on the table. It had words on it too. Eden sat beside her. "Let's read a book," Eden said. Eden held the book flat. "You start at the front," Eden said. He turned the pages one by one, front to back. Lea heard the pages flip, flip, flip. They saw a dog, then a cat, then a big red truck in the book.

Outside the window it was cloudy. Lea's shadow looked soft and grey on the floor. "My turn," Lea said. She took the book. She opened the front page. She turned each page slowly. Flip, flip, flip. "Look, the truck again!" she said. Ms. Hughes smiled and sat down to hear the whole story.

Parker wanted to play tea party at school. But the teapot had no tea in it. He looked inside. It was empty. He felt sad.

Briggs said, "Come see." He turned the little cup over. Nothing came out. "The cups are empty too," Briggs said. Parker frowned. "No tea? Then we can't play."

Briggs smiled. He picked up the empty teapot. He tipped it over Parker's cup. "Here is your tea," Briggs said. Parker picked up the cup. It was light, not heavy at all. He took a pretend sip. It tasted like nothing. But it was still fun!

Parker set his stuffed bear in a small chair. He tipped the empty teapot again. "More tea for you," he said. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" The bear wore a red color hat. Parker wrapped him in a soft blanket and patted his back.

Ms. Kobayashi came over. "What a nice tea party," she said. Parker held up his empty cup. "Would you like some tea?" he asked. She took a pretend sip. "Just right," she said. Parker clapped and poured her some more.

Lydia could see the park from her front step. The swings were far away, across the road. It was a hot summer day, and the slide would be cool and shady.

"Are you ready?" her dad asked. "Yes," said Lydia. She took his big hand. They stopped at the curb and looked both ways. They walked across the street together, hand in hand. Lydia held on tight the whole way.

At the park, her friend Mika was already there. Mika was picking red flowers that grow by the fence. "Don't eat those," Lydia said. "They are just for looking." Mika nodded and put the flower behind her ear instead.

They swung high, then low. Lydia saw her dad wave from the bench. She waved back. When it was time to go home, she ran to him and took his hand again.

"We cross the street like this," Lydia told Mika. Mika held her own dad's hand too. They all walked together, one big line of hands.

Henri held his new puppy, Pip, in his lap. They were going to the doctor. Henri felt worried. Doctors were for people, not for puppies. Would the doctor help Pip?

The door opened. Henri looked around with big eyes. A cat sat in a basket. A bunny sat in a box. A big dog wagged his tail. "Where are all the people?" Henri asked. "These are pets," said a girl named Evelynn. She held her guinea pig.

A kind man came out. "I am Mr. Qureshi," he said. "I am a vet. A vet is a doctor for animals." Henri looked up. A doctor for animals! Pip barked one small bark, as if he understood.

Mr. Qureshi looked at Pip's ears. He gave Pip some medicine. It was pink. "Pip needs this to stay strong," said Mr. Qureshi. He passed a little brush to Henri. "You can brush him each day." Henri brushed Pip, slow and gentle. Pip closed his eyes.

At home, Henri put water in Pip's bowl. Pip drank fast. Then he curled up to sleep. Henri sat beside him and brushed his soft fur one more time. "Good night, Doctor Pip," Henri whispered.

Kai wanted to make pancakes. He wanted to make them all by himself. Dad said, "We can cook together. First we read the recipe." The recipe was a paper with words. Dad said, "A recipe tells us what to use and what to do."

Kai helped pour the flour. He put in an egg. He got to stir the bowl. The spoon went round and round. But Kai was excited. He did not wait for Dad to read the next part. He missed a step on the paper.

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Kai stood back and watched. He was careful near the stove. The pancakes came out flat. Flat like little mats. Kai felt sad. "Our pancakes are squished," he said.

Dad hugged him. "Let's read the recipe again," he said. "One step at a time." They read each part. They did not skip anything. This time Dad put the pan on the stove. The pancakes came out big and fluffy. The family ate them in the backyard. Mom said, "These are the best ones yet!" After the meal, Kai had a warm bath. He played with his rubber duck. "Tomorrow," said Kai, "we read the recipe first."

Jasper was at a big festival with his dad. There were flags and drums and food smells everywhere. Jasper wanted the little rice balls at a food stand. His dad bought three on a plate.

Then Jasper saw his friend Zohan. Zohan was with his grandma. Zohan's grandma put a bowl of rice on the table. She put her hands together. "Itadakimasu," said Zohan's grandma. Zohan said it too. Then they picked up their spoons and ate.

Jasper watched. He wanted to say the word too. He opened his mouth, but nothing came out. The word felt big in his mouth. He tried again. "Ita... itadakimasu," said Jasper. Zohan smiled. Zohan's grandma smiled too. She clapped her soft hands. Jasper's dad put the plate down. Jasper put his hands together. "Itadakimasu," said Jasper. Then he ate a rice ball. It was warm and good.

Zohan's grandma poured Zohan a small cup of milk. Zohan said "Itadakimasu" again before he drank. Jasper ran to get his own cup of milk. His hands were a little wet from the rice ball, so he wiped them on his shirt. He held his cup up high. "Itadakimasu!" said Jasper, very proud. Everyone at the table began to eat.

Maeve wanted to make breakfast for her family. She set up her little table in the backyard. Her dad brought out a bowl and three eggs. "You can have this one," he said. A fast mouse ran by the fence and hid in the grass.

Maeve held the egg. It was smooth and cool. She tapped it on the bowl, tap, tap, tap. The shell cracked open. The egg slid out into the bowl. "I did it!" said Maeve.

Then she saw a tiny piece of shell in the bowl. She used her spoon to fish it out. Out it came, small and white. She tapped the next egg, and out came the egg.

Dad cooked the eggs in the pan. Maeve gave everyone plates at the table. "Breakfast is ready," she said.

Lincoln held his mama's hand at the dentist's door. The room smelled like mint. A big chair sat in the middle. It was bigger than his chair at home. Lincoln did not want to sit in it.

His friend Paislee was there too. She had been to the dentist before. "Watch me," she said. Paislee climbed up and lay down. Then the chair moved. It leaned back, slow and smooth. Paislee giggled. "It's like a ride!" she said.

Lincoln's turn came. His tummy felt funny. He sat on the big chair. He squeezed his toy snake tight. The dentist pushed a small button. The chair leaned back, and Lincoln was lying down. Now the dentist could see inside his mouth. "Open wide," the dentist said kindly. Lincoln opened his mouth. The dentist looked at every tooth. "Your teeth are clean and strong," she said.

When the chair came up again, Lincoln felt a tiny bit dizzy. Paislee laughed with him, not at him. He gave his toy snake a kiss on the nose. "See you next time," the dentist said. Lincoln waved. He wanted to ride the chair again.

Wyatt looked out the window. The sky was gray. Rain fell down, down, down. "I want to play outside," said Wyatt. His dad smiled. "First we wait for the rain to stop."

The rain stopped. The sun came out. Wyatt put on his rain boots. He and his dad went to the backyard. Wyatt stopped. There was water on the ground. "A big puddle!" said Wyatt. "Rain makes puddles on the ground," said Dad. Wyatt stepped in the puddle. Splash! Splash! Splash!

The wind blew. Wyatt's hat flew off his head. "It is windy!" said Wyatt. Dad laughed and caught the hat. Wyatt put it back on. The wind blew again. The hat flew again. Wyatt held his hat with both hands. "Stay on, hat!" said Wyatt.

Wyatt's furry dog ran to him. The dog jumped over the puddle. Splash! Water went everywhere. Wyatt laughed and laughed. Dad said, "Time for a warm hug inside." Wyatt held Dad's hand. They walked to the door, past the puddle. "Bye bye, puddle," said Wyatt. "See you after the next rain."

Juliette planted little seeds in the dirt at the farm. She patted the soil with her hands. Her friend Atharv planted seeds too. "When will they grow?" Juliette asked. "Soon," said the farmer. "We will wait and see."

Every day Juliette came back. She looked and looked. The dirt just sat there. Then one morning, she saw something green. It was very tiny. It poked up out of the soil. "What is that little green thing?" she asked. The farmer smiled. "That is a sprout," he said. Juliette got close to see it. It was smaller than her finger. It looked like a small green curl.

Juliette ran to find Atharv. "Come see! Our seeds made sprouts!" she said. They counted one, two, three sprouts. "Will they be big tomorrow?" Atharv asked. "I don't know," said Juliette. "Let's look again and find out." The next day, the sprouts were a bit taller. Juliette clapped her hands. "Hello, little sprouts," she said.

Ryan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny. "The shot might hurt," he told his mom. "Just a little pinch," said the nurse. "Then I have a surprise for you."

The nurse cleaned Ryan's arm with a cool, wet wipe. Ryan counted with his mom. "One, two, three." The pinch came. It was small, like a bug kiss. Then it was done.

Ryan saw the nurse open a small paper wrapper. She put a small bandage over the spot on his arm. The bandage had yellow stars on it. "A star bandage!" said Ryan. He could not stop looking at it. The spot felt better already.

Afterward, Mom took Ryan to the ice cream shop. Ryan got pink strawberry ice cream in a cup. It was cold and sweet on his tongue. A man at the next table waved. "Nice stars," he said. Ryan held up his arm to show him. "One, two, three, four, five stars," he counted.

Conner from school came in with his dad. Conner ran over to see. "I got a shot too," Conner said. He pulled up his sleeve. His bandage had blue dinosaurs on it. Ryan laughed. "Next time, I want dinosaurs," he said, and he took another big bite of ice cream.

Juliette sat at the big table in writing club. Mr. Lombardi gave each child a pencil. Juliette wanted to write her name all by herself. She grabbed the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard on the paper. The J came out wobbly. It looked like a squiggle, not a letter. Juliette frowned at the line she had made.

Mr. Lombardi sat down next to her. "Try this," he said. He pinched the pencil between his thumb and his first finger. Then he let it rest on his middle finger. He drew a J. It was tall and neat. Juliette watched him. Then she pinched her pencil the same way. It rested on her middle finger, just like his.

She drew a J. It was neat! She drew u and l and i and e. Her whole name sat on the paper. Ziyad leaned over. "Juliette!" he read out loud. Juliette smiled. Outside the window, the snowy yard was white and quiet. She wrote her name one more time, slow and proud.

Willow ran to the big slide at the playground. She wanted to be a rocket ship today. She held her arms up high.

Louis ran over too. "I am a rocket!" he said. "Me first!" But Willow wanted to be first. They both stood very still. Then Willow had an idea.

"Let's go at the same time," she said. "We can count first. Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Then we jump!" Louis nodded. They held hands.

Ms. Schneider sat on the bench nearby. "That is called a countdown," she said. "You count backward from ten down to one." Willow smiled big.

Willow had to tie her shoe first. She sat down on the spring toy and pulled the string tight. Louis laughed. "Your bow looks ugly!" he said. Willow looked at it. It did look silly. They both giggled.

Then they stood by the slide. "Ready?" said Willow. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" They jumped up together. Up, up they went, down the slide. Whee! Willow laughed so hard. "Again!" she said. "Count with me, Louis!"

Louis squeezed her hand. "Ten, nine, eight," he began.

Zachary sat in the family car. He was going to meet the new baby. The baby had tiny brown eyes and very small hands. Zachary could not wait.

"Can I hold the baby?" Zachary asked. He tried to reach over the seat. Dad said, "Not yet. First we wash our hands."

At home, Dad carried the baby inside. Zachary ran to the sink. He turned the tap and washed his hands with soap. He rubbed and rubbed. Then he showed Dad his wet, clean hands.

"All clean!" said Dad. He put a soft blanket on Zachary's lap. Then he set the baby down, very gently. The baby looked up with big brown eyes. Zachary held his little brother and smiled.

The baby grabbed Zachary's finger. Zachary laughed. "I washed my hands," he told the baby. "So I get to hold you."

Dad took a picture. The baby held on tight and would not let go.

Axel was in the kitchen with Grandma. He wanted to make a toy car. Grandma found a cardboard box and some tape. Axel taped on four square wheels. He pushed the car on the floor. The car would not roll. It just stopped. Axel got mad. He pushed it again and again. It still would not roll.

"I can help," said Grandma. She held the scissors. Grandma is a grown-up, so she did the cutting. She cut the squares off. Then she cut four circles instead. The circles were round. Axel taped the circles on the car. He pushed the car again. This time it rolled across the kitchen floor. It rolled fast, all the way to the fridge.

"It rolls!" Axel shouted. He clapped his hands. Grandma laughed. Axel made the car roll back to her. Then he made it fly off the ramp he built from a book. The car zoomed down and rolled some more. Axel pushed it one more time and said, "Round wheels win!"

Muhammad was in his bedroom. He had a cold. His nose was red and his throat felt scratchy.

His mama brought him soup on a tray. Muhammad took one small sip. Then he took two bites of bread. He pushed the tray away.

"No more?" asked Mama.

Muhammad shook his head. "My tummy says no thank you."

"That's okay," said Mama. "When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much. Just a few bites is fine."

Muhammad looked at his bowl. The soup was warm. The steam went up, up, up. Where did the steam go? Maybe it popped out the window. It was a rainy day, so the window had little drops on it. Tap, tap, tap went the rain.

Muhammad drank a little juice. The juice was cold and sweet. Then he drank a bit more. His tummy said yes to juice.

He lay back on his pillow. He heard the rain. He heard Mama wash the bowls downstairs. Clink, clink, clink.

Soon his friend Samir came to the door. Samir could not come in, because Muhammad was sick. Samir waved from the doorway.

"Feel better!" said Samir. He held up a drawing of a big red truck.

Muhammad waved back. He felt sleepy. He closed his eyes. The rain went tap, tap, tap on the window, and Muhammad fell asleep.

Julia walked to the shelter with her dad. Many dogs and cats sat in little rooms. They were waiting for a family. "They wait for someone to take them home," said her dad.

Julia looked at a brown dog. She looked at a white cat. Then she saw a small gray cat with one black tooth spot on her ear. The cat reached out a soft paw. "This one," said Julia. The shelter lady put the cat in a box with holes.

At home, Julia set out water and food. The rain made the cat's fur dry spot by the warm towel. Julia brushed her every day. On the street, Selah came to see. "What is her name?" asked Selah. Julia held the cat close. "Her name is Rosie," said Julia. Rosie purred and closed her eyes.

Clara went to the store with her dad. She held his hand by the big glass door. "Stay close," said Dad. Clara stayed close.

Near the toys, Clara saw a small slide. Gemma was there too. Gemma climbed up. She lay down on her tummy, head first, at the top. Clara watched. "Gemma, wait," said Clara. "At the playground, we go down feet first." Gemma turned around. She put her feet in front. Then she slid down. "Wheee!" said Gemma.

Clara had a turn too. Feet first, down she went. One slide, two slides, three slides. Her socks felt warm from the floor.

Later they passed the ovens in the back. "Is that hot?" asked Clara. "Very hot," said Dad. He opened the tall oven door himself. Clara watched from far away. Then Dad bought her a warm bun. "Hot now, cold later," said Clara, and she blew on it, one breath, two breaths, three.

Matthew held his dad's hand at the street festival. There were red lanterns everywhere. There was a big dragon made of paper. There was food and drums and so many people.

"Can we dance too?" Matthew asked.

"Watch first," said his dad.

The drums went boom, boom, boom. The dancers hopped and turned. The dragon spun around. Zavier from Matthew's class was dancing too! He held his mom's hand and hopped. Ms. Tang waved from the stage. "The music makes us dance!" she called.

Then the music stopped. The dancers stopped too. Everything was quiet and still.

The music started again. The dancers danced again!

"The music makes the dancing!" said Matthew. "That is how it works!"

"Yes!" said his dad. "Dancing goes with the music."

Matthew pulled his dad's hand. "Let's dance now!"

They hopped and turned. Matthew saw a spider web shine on a lantern, slippery with rain drops. He laughed and spun again.

Boom, boom, boom went the drums. Matthew went hop, hop, hop.

Camille wanted a story about a bunny. She could not find one at school. "I will look," she said.

She found a book on the rug. It had a bunny on the front. But when she opened it, the first page had no bunny at all. It showed a big truck. "This is not a bunny book," said Luc. Camille turned to the front cover again. Then she started at the very first page, right after the cover. She turned each page one by one. The bunny came on page after page. "Books go front to back," said Harper. "See? The bunny is here!"

Then Camille asked, "Who made up this bunny story?" Mr. Kang, the teacher, sat down with her. He pointed to the cover. "See this name?" he said. "That is the author. The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Camille put her finger on the name. It felt smooth under her hand. "Thank you, author," she whispered.

Camille was tired after all that looking. She sat in the cozy chair with the bunny book. She held it front to back. She read every page to Luc. "The bunny hops," she said. "The bunny takes a nap." Luc smiled and turned the page for her. Camille was happy to be a reader.

Addison sat on her big soft rug. She had a new book about a green snake. The snake looked very slippery in the pictures.

Addison wanted to read it all by herself. She opened the book. But wait. The pictures looked all mixed up. The snake was swimming before it woke up. Addison frowned. "That is not right," she said. She turned the book over in her hands. Now she saw the front cover. The green snake smiled at her from the front. She opened the front cover. Ah, this way the story started just right. First the snake woke up. Then it slid down the slippery rock. Then it went swimming.

Addison turned one page. The snake found a red shoe. Addison turned another page. The snake hid under the bed. She turned the pages one by one, all the way to the back cover. Then the story was done.

"Where do books begin?" Addison wondered. She picked up another book. She looked for the front cover first. She opened it there. "Hello, story," she said.

Arthur was going next door. Ms. Doyle was having a big game day. Arthur wanted to wear his red shirt. But where was it? Not in his drawer. Not on his bed. Not on the hook. Arthur was mad.

At Ms. Doyle's house, everyone wore green shirts. Parker wore green. Christine wore green too. "Why does everyone wear green?" Arthur asked. Parker pointed at the TV. "Green is our team's colors. We wear them to show we cheer for our team." Arthur looked down at his blue shirt. Hmm.

Then Christine ran to the toy box. She found a green cape. She held it out. "You can wear this!" Arthur put it on. One, two, three tucks, and it stayed.

The game started. The team got a goal. Everyone stood up to clap. Ms. Doyle gave out cookies. Arthur clapped with his cookie in his hand. "We all match," said Parker. Arthur grinned under his green cape.

Jaxon plays on a soccer team. The team goes to the park every Saturday. Ms. Aziz is the coach.

One morning, Jaxon does not want to practice. "I just want to play the game," he says. Ms. Aziz smiles. "Practice is when we learn skills and get ready for games," she says. "Come try one little kick."

Jaxon kicks the ball. It goes to the side. He kicks again. It rolls to Dominic. Dominic stops it with his foot. "Good kick," says Dominic.

The team practices passing the ball. Jaxon tries once. He tries twice. Then the ball goes right to Kyle. Kyle catches it with his feet. Kyle laughs and claps.

On Sunday, the game begins. The other team runs fast. The ball comes to Jaxon. He passes it to Dominic, just like in practice. Dominic kicks it into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouts.

After the game, Jaxon runs to his mom. "Can I write about my goal?" he asks. His mom helps him write the word "goal" on paper. Jaxon draws the net and the ball too.

The next Saturday, Jaxon is the first one at the park. He puts his ball down on the grass. "Ms. Aziz," he calls, "I am ready to practice." Ms. Aziz tosses him the ball. Jaxon traps it with his foot.

Ibrahim went to the farmers' market with his dad in the morning. They bought fresh bread, red apples, and a big bag of white flour. Ibrahim wanted to make pancakes for his family.

At home, Dad put the bowl on the table. "You can pour the flour," said Dad. Ibrahim picked up the big bag. He tipped it fast. Whoosh! A little white cloud flew up. The flour landed on Ibrahim's nose. It landed on Dad's nose too.

"Ah-choo!" said Ibrahim. He looked like a snowy snowman. Dad laughed and wiped his nose with a towel. Ibrahim looked at the cloud of flour in the air. "It went up like smoke," he said.

"Try again," said Dad. "Pour it slow this time." Ibrahim took a small cup of flour. He poured it bit by bit. No cloud. No dusty nose. Just quiet white flour in the bowl.

Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Ibrahim watched from his chair. Soon the pancakes were golden. The family sat down to eat. "Yummy," said Ibrahim. "We feed the flour slow, and it feeds us back."

Eleanor had a bath. The water was warm and smooth. Mama washed her hair. Then Mama helped her put on her soft pajamas.

Eleanor picked two books. Mama read them slow. Eleanor looked at every picture. Then Mama kissed her head. "Time to sleep," Mama said.

Eleanor got in bed. She pulled the blanket up. She closed her eyes. Then she sat up fast. "My teeth!" she said. "I forget to brush!"

Eleanor hopped out of bed. She walked to the sink. She got her little toothbrush. Mama put the paste on it. Eleanor brushed up and down. She brushed the front and the back.

"Teeth get brushed two times," said Eleanor. "In the morning and before bed." Mama nodded and smiled.

Eleanor rinsed the brush. She looked in the mirror. Her teeth were clean and shiny. She yawned a big yawn.

Back in bed, Eleanor snuggled down. The house was quiet. The blanket was warm. Mama hummed a little song.

"Good night, Eleanor," Mama said.

"Good night, teeth," said Eleanor.

Theo ran to the playground with his friend Mavrik. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. They wore their sun hats.

Then a big white cloud came. The wind began to blow. Theo heard it whoosh in the trees. The trees began to sway. "Look, Mavrik!" said Theo. "The trees are dancing!" The leaves blew around and around. Leaves flew across the grass. Theo chased one leaf. Mavrik chased another. The leaves blew fast. The boys ran fast.

"Caught it!" said Theo. He held a big red leaf. "I got a smelly one," said Mavrik. He sniffed it. "Pee-yew!" Theo laughed so hard. The wind blew again. The trees swayed again. "More leaves!" Theo whispered. He got ready to run.

Isla sat on a big red rug at Mr. Toussaint's house. The TV was loud. A basketball game was on. Her friends Amina and Myriam sat beside her. A tall man ran with the ball. He wore a shiny blue shirt. The man threw the ball up. It went right through the hoop. The crowd jumped and cheered.

"Look at the furry dog," said Amina. A big furry dog lay by the door. He wagged his tail at the noise. Isla wanted to try throwing a ball through a hoop too. But there was no hoop in the house. Her face felt sad. "I can't play the game," she said.

Mr. Toussaint smiled. "Come with me," he said. He had a toy hoop and a small ball. He hung the hoop on the fence outside. The fence was low and safe. "Throw it through," he said.

Ila threw the ball. It missed. She threw again. It went in! "I scored a point!" she shouted. Myriam clapped. Amina clapped. The dog barked. Mr. Toussaint said, "One more time, Isla." She threw the ball, and it went through the hoop again.

Luke was at school. He was going to sing in a show. His tummy felt funny. His hands felt cold. "I am scared," he told Ms. Paquette.

Ms. Paquette sat down next to him. "I feel scared too," she said. "Grown-ups have feelings, just like you." Luke looked up. "You too?" he asked. "Yes," she said. "Even teachers."

That made Luke feel better. He saw Laurie was scared too. He held her hand. "Grown-ups get scared too," he told her. Laurie smiled.

Then it was time to sing. Luke took a big breath. He sang loud and strong. He felt happy now. The parents clapped and clapped. Luke waved at his dad. His dad was waving back with tears in his eyes. "Dad is crying," Luke said. "Dads have feelings too!"

Ayla stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. Her tummy felt jumpy, like a frog lived in there.

She had to find the bathroom. Fast. She looked left. She saw a door with a fish on it. She looked right. She saw a door with a mop and bucket. No bathroom anywhere.

Her friend Brycen walked by. "Hi, Ayla!" he said. Then he was gone, quick as that.

Ayla wiggled one leg, then the other. The frog in her tummy jumped higher. Doors were everywhere. Big ones, small ones, one with a tiny window. Which one was the bathroom?

Then she saw Ms. Kaya. Ms. Kaya was the teacher. She had kind eyes and red shoes. Ayla took a big breath. She walked over, quick on her little legs.

"Ms. Kaya, I need help," said Ayla. "Where is the bathroom?"

Ms. Kaya smiled. "That was easy! You asked me, and now I can help. Come with me."

They walked down the hall. The bathroom was right there, past the fish door.

"Thank you," said Ayla. She hurried inside.

Later, Brycen looked lost too. He scratched his head at the mop door.

"Ask Ms. Kaya!" Ayla called. "It works!"

Ruby was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut." Ruby felt a small worry in her tummy. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Grandma. "We will stay together the whole time."

The salon had a big blue chair. Ruby climbed up into it. But she was too small. The hairdresser could not reach her hair. "I will get a booster seat," he said. He placed the booster seat on the big chair. It was not heavy at all. Ruby sat on top. Now she was tall enough. The hairdresser could reach every bit of her hair.

He put a soft towel around Ruby's shoulders. "You can help by sitting very still," he said. Ruby sat very still. Snip, snip, little by little. Snip, snip, little by little. Curly bits fell down like little clouds. Grandma smiled and held her hand. Soon the hairdresser turned the chair around. Ruby saw a girl with short curly hair in the mirror. "That's me!" said Ruby.

Carter wanted his bedtime book. It was the book about the little red truck. But the shelf was too tall, and the book was gone.

"I want the truck book," said Carter. "Where is it?"

Dad sat down on the bed. "A book has a name, just like you. The name is on the front."

Carter looked at a book on the floor. He opened it and turned the pages. Page one had a moon. Page two had a hill. Page three had a sheep on the hill. Carter turned the pages front to back, one by one, like walking down a path.

"This one is about a sheep," said Carter.

"That book is called Sheep on the Hill," said Dad.

"Not my truck book," said Carter. He picked up another one. He turned it over. He pointed at the big letters. "What does this say?"

Dad read it out loud. "The Little Red Truck."

"That is its name!" said Carter. He hugged the book tight. He brushed the cover clean with his hand, like tucking it in.

Dad opened the book. "Ready?"

"Read it front to back," said Carter. "All the way to the end."

The truck went up the hill on the last page. Carter smiled and said, "Good night, truck."

Kayden dug in the dirt. He had three little seeds. Mr. Castillo helped him put them in the ground. "Now what?" Kayden asked. "Now we water them," said Mr. Castillo. Kayden poured water from a small can. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Kayden ran to the garden. He saw only dirt. No sprout. "Where is my plant?" he asked. Destiny pointed at the dirt. "Maybe it needs more water," she said. Kayden felt sorry for his seeds. He watered them again. Rhodes watered them too. Every day they came back. Every day they poured the water.

Day after day, there was still no sprout. "Did I lose?" Kayden asked. Mr. Castillo smiled. "No. Seeds take time. Keep going." So Kayden kept watering.

One sunny morning, Kayden saw something green. A tiny sprout stood in the dirt. "It came up!" Kayden shouted. He clapped his hands. Destiny and Rhodes clapped too. Kayden ran to get the water can. "More water for you," he said.

Abigail stood at the basketball court. She held a soft red beanbag. Ms. Moretti put a small hoop on the ground. "Try to get it in," said Ms. Moretti. Abigail threw the beanbag. It fell far from the hoop. She threw again. It missed again.

Her friend Grady ran over to meet her. "I keep missing," said Abigail. "Why does it fall short?" She took three little steps closer to the hoop. Then she threw the beanbag. It went in! "It went in!" she said. She pushed her hair out of her eyes and smiled. She threw again from close by. In it went again.

Next Ms. Moretti rolled a big ball to Abigail. Abigail held out both hands. She opened them wide. The ball came right into her arms. She hugged it tight. "Again!" said Abigail. Ms. Moretti rolled the ball again.

Isabella wanted to win the word game. Musa said one word. Then you had to shout a word as different as it could be. "These are opposites," said Musa. "Big and small!"

Isabella held her green rabbit. It was small. The big teddy bear sat beside it. "Big and small," she said. "Opposites!"

Musa ran fast around the playroom. Isabella walked slow behind him. "Fast and slow!" they both shouted.

Then Musa said, "Cold." Isabella looked at her toy cup. It was not hot. The tea was pretend. She did not know the other word. She squeezed her rabbit and thought.

"Cold is like ice," said Musa. "Think of the sun."

Isabella's eyes got wide. "Hot!" she shouted. "Cold and hot!"

"That's it," said Musa. "One, two, three, you win!"

Isabella hugged her rabbit tight. "Opposites," she said. "Big and small. Fast and slow. Cold and hot. Let's dream up more tomorrow."

"Okay," said Musa. "Big and small, big and small!"

Gianna stood in the school cooking classroom. Ms. Kaya had big bowls on the long table. Today they would bake cookies for Gianna's family.

"Mix the dough," said Ms. Kaya. "I will need a big circle of it." Gianna patted the dough. Elowen patted it too. Khalid patted it too. Pat, pat, pat, a round circle.

"Can we put them in the oven?" Gianna asked. "No," said Ms. Kaya. "The oven is hot. A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven." Ms. Kaya slid the tray in herself. Gianna watched from far away. The oven glowed warm inside.

Soon the kitchen smelled sweet. Gianna wanted to check the cookies. She walked one step. Then she stopped. "Who opens the oven?" she asked herself. "A grown-up does," she answered. She stood still and waited.

The timer rang. Ms. Kaya opened the oven door. The cookies were gold and warm. One, two, three, four, five cookies for the family.

Gianna carried the plate with both hands. Dad smiled big at the door. "Hot oven, warm cookies," said Gianna. "You baked these all by yourselves," said Dad. Gianna took the biggest cookie for him.

Rehmat was at Grandma's house. She was getting over her cold. She sat at the table with her toast. Her nose tickled. She sniffed and sniffed. Then her nose began to drip. A drop landed on her plate. Rehmat looked down. She did not know what to do.

"Your nose is runny today," said Grandma. Grandma picked a tissue from the box. "Try one of these." Rehmat held the soft tissue. She put it up to her nose. She wiped, and the drip went away. "It works!" said Rehmat.

Grandma put the tissue box close to Rehmat's chair. "Now you can reach it all by yourself." Rehmat ate her toast. Her nose tickled again. She picked a tissue all by herself. She wiped her nose, and it felt better.

Later, her friend Alaina came to play. They built a tower in the safe, sunny corner of the kitchen. Alaina sniffed and sniffed. "I have a cold too," she said. Rehmat held out the tissue box. "Runny noses need these," she said. Alaina picked one and wiped her nose. "Thank you," said Alaina. The tower grew taller and taller.

Charles ran to the toy box at summer camp. The red truck was there! It was the best toy of all. Charles grabbed it fast and hugged it tight.

Then Colton came over. "I want the red truck too," said Colton. Charles held the truck with both arms. He did not want to give it up. Colton reached for it. Charles pulled it away. Colton's face went sad. "Sorry," Charles said quietly. Mr. Pham knelt down beside them. "Colton can have a turn next," he said. Charles looked at the truck. He looked at Colton. He did not want to grab, but waiting felt so long.

Then Charles saw the sandbox. "I can build while I wait," he said. He dug his hands into the cool sand. It was soft and squishy between his fingers. He patted and patted. Soon he had a big sand tower with a stick flag on top. He was so busy, the time went fast.

"Your turn now," said Colton. He held out the red truck. Charles pushed it across the sand. It made a bumpy track. Vroom! Then Colton kicked a pinecone near the sandbox and they both laughed. "Let's build a garage," said Colton. Charles clapped his sandy hands. Waiting was easy when there was sand to dig.

Arnaud was at Grandma's house. Today he was three years old. There were balloons on the door. The cake sat on the table, waiting.

Flavie came with her mom. Flavie was a new friend. She looked at Arnaud and asked, "How old are you?"

Arnaud held up his hand. He showed three fingers. "Look," he said. Flavie counted them. "Three?" she said.

Arnaud looked at his hand. That was not right. He put one more finger up. Now there were four. "No, four," he said. Hmm, that was not right either.

Grandma knelt down beside him. "Show me too," she said softly. Arnaud tried again. He held up three fingers, then one more. Four. He tucked one finger back down. Three! "Three," he said, and laughed.

Flavie held up three fingers too. "I am three as well," she said.

Then they opened a big present. It was a fuzzy toy car, soft and blue. Arnaud pushed it across the rug. Flavie pushed it back. The wheels made a little humming sound on the floor.

"Happy birthday, Arnaud," said Grandma. She lit the candles with a match, far from the little hands. Arnaud blew and blew. The candles went out, all three at once.

Max wanted a dinosaur book. The big dinosaur book was at the library. But Max did not have a card. "You can get your very own card," said his dad. So they went.

A lady at the desk made Max a card. It was blue. It had a little circle on it. "My card!" said Max. He held it tight. The lady scanned the card. Beep! Then Max took the dinosaur book home.

In his bedroom, Max read the book. He made a pretend roar. "ROAR!" said Max. "You are a sour little lemon dinosaur," he told the picture. The dinosaur looked grumpy. Max laughed.

Soon the book was done. All the pages, all done. They took the book back to the library. Max felt sad. But the lady said, "Pick a new one." Max gave her the same blue card. Beep! The card worked again! Max picked a truck book. He ran to show his dad.

"I can get a new book every time," said Max. "Beep!"

At bedtime he hugged the blue card. "ROAR," he whispered to it.

Mason ran to the bookmobile. His mom held his hand. The door opened with a little step. A big book shelf stood inside. The books went up, up, up. Mason could not see any pictures on them. They were all brown and thick. He felt small next to the tall shelf.

"I want a book like mine," said Mason. "With pictures." Ms. Henry smiled. She pointed to the back of the bookmobile. There was a little corner with a red rug. The shelves there were short. The books were red, blue and striped. "This is the children's area," said Ms. Henry. "The books here are just for young kids." Mason touched a striped book. He pulled it out. It was little, like his hands.

Then Ms. Henry gave him a card. It had his name on it. "Your very first library card," she said. Mason held it with two hands. The card made the book his to take home. He put the card on the desk. Ms. Henry beeped the book. Beep! "All done," she said.

Mason hugged the book. Was the bear in the story sleepy? He would find out tonight. "Bye, book corner," said Mason. "Bye," said Ms. Henry. Mason waved all the way down the step.

Andrew was at home. He wanted to build a tall block tower. He asked his mom, "Please can you help me find the big blocks?" His mom smiled and helped him carry them.
