Soon his friend Shiloh came to play. Shiloh handed Andrew a red block. "Here you go," said Shiloh. "Thank you," said Andrew. Shiloh laughed. "My grandma says gracias. That is her word for thank you. She speaks Spanish." Andrew blinked. A whole new word for thank you!

Then the tower wobbled. A block slipped and fell. It hit Shiloh's foot. "Sorry," said Andrew. Shiloh rubbed his foot and waited. "It's okay," he said. Andrew was careful now. He placed each block slowly, one by one. He waited after each block. The tower stood tall.

Shiloh pointed at the top block. "Can I add one?" "Yes, please," said Andrew. Shiloh set a blue block on top. "Gracias," said Shiloh. Andrew grinned and said, "Gracias to you, too!" They both laughed and looked up at the tall tower.

Bennett was going to a big park with tall trees. "Let's take the car," said Dad. Bennett ran to the car fast. He hopped in and sat on his seat.

But the car did not go. Dad did not start the car. "Click," said Dad. "Your car seat needs a click." Bennett looked down. He pulled the buckle. Click! The strap went snug across him.

"You forgot your click!" said Dad with a laugh. Bennett laughed too. "I am buckled now!" he said. The car started. It went bump, bump down the road.

At the park, they found pink flowers by a big tree root. Bennett pointed at the root. "The tree has big feet!" he said. Dad laughed and laughed. Bennett held Dad's hand and said, "Trees wear their buckles underground."

Hunter wanted to make his own breakfast. His dad put warm toast on a plate. Hunter held the butter knife with a careful hand. He spread the butter slow, slow, slow. The butter made little lines on the toast. "I did it," said Hunter. Then he chewed a big bite. It tasted good.

Next came the milk. Hunter took the big carton with both hands. He poured slow, slow, slow. A little milk ran down the side of the cup. Hunter wiped it with a towel. He did not spill it wrong. He poured just right. "Good job," said Dad.

Then Hunter ran off to play. The milk sat on the counter. Hunter stopped. He looked at it with one eye on the clock. Dad came back. "The milk goes back in the fridge," said Dad. Hunter picked up the carton. He set it inside the cold fridge. The door shut with a soft thump. "Nice work," said Dad. Hunter smiled and took his cup to the table.

Peyton stood at the pet store with her dad. She peeked into a big glass box. A soft white rabbit sat inside. "Hello, rabbit," said Peyton. The rabbit wiggled its little nose.

"We can take him home," said Dad. "His name can be Snowy." Peyton smiled so big. She petted Snowy's soft hair. It felt like a cloud. Elie was there too. Elie petted Snowy's hair as well. Then the pet store man put Snowy in a small box with holes.

At home, Peyton fed Snowy a green leaf. Snowy munched it fast. Then Peyton wanted her crackers. She started to run to the snack table. Elie called out, "Wash your hands after touching a pet!" Peyton stopped. She went to the sink. Dad helped with the warm water and soap. Her hands got all bubbly. Then she sat down alone with her crackers. "Best snack ever," said Peyton.

Arnaud went to the hotel pool with his dad. Arnaud wanted to jump in fast. He ran on the wet floor. His feet slid out. Plop! He sat down in the water on the floor. It did not hurt, but it was a big surprise. A lifeguard came right away and helped him up.

"Why did I fall?" Arnaud asked. "The floor is wet, so we walk," said the lifeguard. "Wet floors are slippery." Arnaud looked at his feet. "Then I will walk," he said.

He walked, one step, two steps, three steps. He walked to the pool. He walked to the bowl of sweet grapes his dad had. "Thank you, Dad," he said. Then he walked again, one step, two steps, three steps, right to the water.

Dylan stood at the snack table. Big kids were all around it. He wanted the red cup of juice. He could see it. He could not reach it.

Dylan tried to squeeze past a big kid. The big kid did not move. Dylan tried again. Still no room. He frowned and stood still. He did not know what to do. Then he heard a voice behind him.

"Excuse me," said Inaaya. She was trying to get past too. The big kid heard her and stepped aside. Inaaya walked right through. Dylan opened his mouth. He wondered if those words were magic.

Dylan took a little breath. "Excuse me," he said. The big kid looked down at him. The big kid moved to the side. Dylan walked past and picked up the red cup. "Thank you," he said to the big kid. The big kid smiled.

At the paint table, Dylan sat next to Aurelie. She was painting an old shoe box. It was the color of the sky. "Can you help me open the glue?" Dylan asked Mr. Eze. "Of course," said Mr. Eze. He opened the cap for him.

Dylan dripped a dot of glue. He pressed down a yellow leaf. It stuck. The leaf stayed on the box. Dylan looked at it and grinned. "Excuse me," he whispered to the leaf, "you live here now."

Beau was at Grandma's house. A new baby was coming home today. Beau waited by the window.

The car came up the drive. Mom got out with a small bundle. It was the baby! Grandma clapped her hands. "Come see," she said.

Mom sat on the big couch. She held the baby in her arms. Her hand held the baby's head, too. Beau looked and looked. "Why do you hold her head like that?" he asked. Mom smiled. "A new baby cannot hold up her own head yet," she said. "So I hold it for her."

Beau wanted to help. He found his small bear. He held the bear in his arms. He put his hand under the bear's head. The bear's head did not fall. "Look, Grandma!" he said. Grandma said, "That is a nice way to hold a bear."

Then the baby made a little sound. Mom said, "Do you want to sit by us?" Beau climbed up next to Mom. He sat very still. Mom let him touch the baby's soft hand with one finger. Beau whispered, "I will hold your head when I am big."

The baby yawned. Her eyes closed. Beau watched her sleep.

Eli stood in the kitchen. He wanted his bath now. He could hear the water running. It made a noisy sound. "Bath time soon," said his dad.

Eli climbed one step toward the tub. "Stop," said his dad. "I check the water first." Dad put his hand in the tub. He waited. Eli held his toy rock and waited too.

"Too hot," said Dad. "We make it warm." Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Eli watched. Then Dad put his hand in again. "Now it is warm," he said. "Warm, not hot. You can get in."

Eli touched the water with his toes. It felt nice. It was not hot. Dad helped him sit down. The water went splash. Eli made his rock swim. "The rock likes warm water," said Eli. Dad laughed and clapped. Eli splashed again.

Asher ran to the park with his box of chalk. Maika was already there, drawing on the ground. "I drew a big blue triangle," she said. Asher sat down next to her. He picked his navy chalk. He drew a fast rocket ship under her triangle.

"That rocket is not blue," said Maika. "It is too dark."

"It is so blue," said Asher. "Look how blue it is."

They both held up their chalk. One was light like the morning sky. One was dark like the night sky. Maika made a sad face. Asher made a grumpy face. Their chalk pieces sat apart, like strangers.

Then Asher had a big idea. "Let's pour all our chalk out," he said. They tipped the whole box onto the ground. It made a happy, busy tumble of colors. Red rolled one way. Yellow rolled another way.

"Find every blue," said Asher. They hunted through the pile. Light blue, dark blue, and blue in between. They lined them up in a row, lightest to darkest, like a little train.

"See?" said Asher. "They are all blue."

Maika touched the lightest one. "Even this pale one is blue." She touched the darkest one. "And this one too."

Maika drew a whale with the dark blue chalk. Asher poured water waves with the light blue. The waves splashed up to her blue triangle, and the triangle became a sail. Their rocket ship waited on the sand beside them, dark and blue, ready to fly.

"Zoom," said Asher, and off it went, up past the sail, into the sky.

Riley waited at school pickup. She held her coat in her arms. She wanted to put it on all by herself. One sleeve hid inside the coat. It was like a little puzzle. "Where did my sleeve go?" she asked. Her friend Liyana looked too. "It went inside," said Liyana. Riley pulled the sleeve out. Then her arm slid right in. She had caught the sleeve just in time.

"Time to wash hands," said Ms. Buchanan. "Then we can eat our snack." Riley rubbed the soap. She added water. The soap made bubbles on her hands. The bubbles grew and grew. Riley made a bubbly beard on her chin. Liyana giggled. Riley giggled too. She was not afraid of the soap now. It felt soft and light.

The water rinsed the bubbles away. Riley dried her hands on the towel. "Bubbles need soap and water," Riley said. Ms. Buchanan smiled. Riley zipped up her coat. Then she waved to Liyana. "See you tomorrow," said Liyana. Riley held her parent's hand and walked to the car.

Noah sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The game was on TV. Grandpa, Kane and Tina sat there too. They all had popcorn in a big bowl. It smelled warm and buttery.

The players ran fast on the green grass. They kicked the ball again and again. Noah frowned. "Who has the ball?" he asked. "There are so many players. I can't tell them apart." All the little men on TV looked the same to him.

Grandpa laughed a kind laugh. "Look at their shirts," he said. "Each team wears its own colors." Noah looked hard. One team wore red shirts. The other team wore blue shirts. A red player kicked to another red player. A blue player ran after the ball. Now Noah could see two teams, not one big crowd. "Red has the ball!" Noah shouted. "Now blue has it!" Kane clapped. Tina clapped too.

Grandpa's cat jumped onto the couch. It was a lazy animal. It curled up and went to sleep. "The cat likes the game too," Noah said. "Red team, kick the ball!"

Elliot stood in the kitchen. His toast was on the plate. His mom let him spread the butter. He held the knife, and his mom helped his hand. One, two, three, smooth strokes. The butter went all over the toast. "I did it!" said Elliot.

Next came the milk. Elliot held the cup. He poured and poured. The milk came up to the very top. He looked at the cup. It was full, full, full. Elliot picked it up and began to walk. One step, two steps. The milk sloshed. It spilled over the edge onto the floor. A wide puddle grew by his feet.

The mom got a towel and wiped it up. "Try again," she said with a smile. Elliot poured more milk. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He left some room. He walked slowly. One step, two steps, three steps. Not one drop spilled. Elliot sat down and drank his milk. "Look, Mom!" he said. "Nothing fell!"

Nova went to a big festival with her mama. There were paper lanterns and long tables full of food. Nova's tummy made a little growl.

At the tables, people did something new. They did not just eat. First, some of them sang. Nova pulled her mama's hand. "Why are they singing?" she asked. Her friend Emery was there with her dad. Emery smiled. "Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it," Emery said. Nova watched. The singing families held hands. Then they ate.

Mr. Watanabe, the teacher, called everyone to sit down. The rice was hot and steamy. He asked, "Who wants to lead the blessing?" Nova stood up tall. She wanted to sing it too.

She opened her mouth. But the tune came out wobbly and wrong. Some kids giggled. Nova's face felt hot. Her mama squeezed her hand. Nova took a breath. She tried again. This time the tune went up, then down, just right. Everyone sang along with her.

Then it was time to eat. "This rice is tasty!" said Emery. Nova helped fix the cups, setting one by each plate. Mr. Watanabe gave her a nod and a big spoonful of rice.

Nova ate it all up. Then she sang the blessing again, soft, just for herself.

Snow fell all night. The park was white and quiet. Maria put on her warm red coat. She put on her mittens and her hat.

"Let's play in the snowy park," said Lana. Lana wore a yellow scarf. Moses wore big black boots. The wind blew hard. "It is windy too," said Moses. His hat flew off. Maria picked it up for him.

Maria made a snowball. It was round and cold. "I want to keep it forever," she said. "Can I keep it, Mama?" Mama said, "You can try."

Maria put the snowball in her bucket. She carried it inside. Inside it was warm. Maria set the bucket on the table. Then she went back out to play.

Later the sky turned dark. Rain began to tap on the window. Maria ran in to see her snowball. "Where did it go?" she asked. "Look down," said Mama. The bucket held only a little puddle of water. The snowball was gone.

"It melted," Maria said. "The warm room turned it into water." The next day it was sunny. The snow outside began to melt too. Little wet spots grew on the slide.

Maria picked up her bucket. "Snow comes back when it snows again," she said. Lana clapped. "Your snowball found out first," she said. Maria laughed and held her bucket up high.

Arthur sat at the table. The soup was hot. Steam went up, up, up. Arthur picked up his spoon. He was ready to eat.

But Papa did not pick up his spoon. Mama did not pick up her spoon. They sat still. Their hands were in their laps. Arthur looked at his spoon. He looked at them. Why was everyone waiting?

Papa smiled. "We say thank you first," said Papa. "Many families do that before they eat." Arthur put his spoon down. He put his hands in his lap too. Then Papa said the blessing. Mama said it too. Arthur listened to every word.

"Now we eat," said Mama. Arthur picked up his spoon again. He ate his soup. It was warm and good.

The next night, Arthur got to the table early. He sat very still. He put his hands in his lap and waited. "Ready," he said. Papa laughed and held his hand.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Riley clapped her hands. "I will show you everything," she said. Grandpa put his big bag by the door. It was raining outside. Rain tapped on the kitchen window.

Riley showed Grandpa the kitchen. "Here is the cup cupboard. Here is the spoon drawer. Here is the bread box." Grandpa smiled at each one. Then it was bath time. A grown-up ran the warm water. Grandpa had his bath and sang a song.

After his bath, Grandpa looked and looked. "Oh dear," he said. "Where are the towels?" Riley picked up his hand. She walked him down the hall. "Here is the cupboard," she said. "Towels live inside." Grandpa took a big blue one. "What a good host you are," he said. Riley stood tall.

The next morning, Grandpa made breakfast. He did not call for help. He knew right where the spoons were. He knew the bread box too. Riley laughed a sweet laugh. "You remember my kitchen," she said. Grandpa winked. "You showed me so well," he said. Then he cut her toast into a star.

David was at daycare. He wanted the big red ball. Umar had it first. Umar kicked it high. The ball rolled far away. David ran to get it. Then he held it tight. He wanted to keep it. Umar called out, "Can I have my turn?" David looked at Umar's face. David rolled the ball back. "Thank you, David," Umar said. Umar smiled a big smile. David felt warm inside.

Mr. Balogun drew a picture on the board. It was a boy sharing a ball. "That can be you," he said. David sat next to Umar. "Pass it to me, please," said David. Umar passed it. David caught it. "Thank you," said David. Then David threw it back. Back and forth the ball went. David's arms felt weak. He sat down to rest. Umar sat too. "I like your game," said Umar. Then something surprising happened. The ball rolled all by itself. It stopped right between them. "Be careful," laughed David. "It wants a turn too!"

Ivy sat at a low table in the ice rink café. Her skates were off. Her toes were warm again. A big screen hung on the wall. A soccer game was on. Tatiana and Blair sat with her. Mom brought hot cocoa, and the mugs warmed Ivy's hands.

"One team, two teams, one ball," said Ivy. She counted on her fingers. "The ball goes over the net," said Tatiana. "No, into the net," said Blair. A player ran fast. He kicked the ball low. The ball rolled into the net.

"Goal!" everyone shouted. The whole café cheered. Mr. Banerjee, their coach, clapped his hands. Ivy planted her feet on the floor and cheered too. She sipped her cocoa. It was sweet and hot.

"I get it now," said Ivy. "The ball goes in. Then they cheer."
"And the player tried to get it in," said Blair.
Another player ran. Ivy leaned in close. "Kick it low," she whispered. "Kick it into the net."

Penelope ran in from the backyard. "I want to stir the batter!" she said. Mom was mixing pancakes at the counter.

"Not yet," said Mom. "Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food." Mom pointed to the sink.

Penelope looked at her hands. They had dirt on them. She turned on the water. She rubbed the soap. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The bubbles went down the drain.

"Now can I stir?" she asked.

"Yes, you may," said Mom. "Please pass the spoon."

Penelope passed the big spoon. She stirred round and round. The batter was smooth and shiny.

"I washed my hands and now I stir," she said. "One wash, one stir!"

Mom laughed. She poured the batter into the pan. Penelope watched from her stool. Soon the pancakes were golden and warm.

Penelope set three plates in a line on the table. One for Mom, one for Dad, one for her. She ate every bite.

Eleanor wanted to write a note for her baby brother. At daycare she found paper and a fat blue crayon. She wrote her letters: ILIKEYOU. All the letters ran together in one long line.

She ran to Mr. Lawson. "Read it, read it!" she said. Mr. Lawson squinted. He turned his head this way and that. "Hmm," he said. "It looks like one big squishy word."

Colt came to look. Pierce came to look too. "That's a lot of letters stuck together," said Colt. "Like a train with no gaps!"

Mr. Lawson held up a storybook. "Look here," he said. He opened it at the front. "See? There is a space between one word and the next." Eleanor looked. Between each word was a little empty bit. A small gap. Like a door between rooms.

Eleanor went back to her paper. She wrote it again. I LIKE YOU. She tapped each space with her finger. "Space. Space. Space," she said.

Mr. Lawson read it out loud. "I like you!" he said. "What a nice note." Eleanor laughed. "My baby will smell the paper and like it too," she said. Then she drew a big smiley face under the words, just the right size for a baby.

Jade was at daycare. It was sock day. Everyone had taken off their shoes. Mr. Cohen put on a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," the children sang.

Jade looked down. She had one red sock on her foot. Where was the other one? She felt inside her shoe. It was empty. She hopped on one foot. "My sock is gone," she said.

Louane saw her hop. "What is wrong?" she asked. "I have one sock," said Jade. "Just one." Fox looked under the cubby. No sock there. Then Mr. Cohen held something up. "A pair means two," he said. It was her red sock! He had found it near the dog toy box.

Jade put it on. Two red socks. One, two. "A pair!" she said. Fox clapped. Louane clapped. They sang louder. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then the dog toy barked, a wild woof from inside the box. Jade peeked in. A small stuffed dog was hiding there. She laughed and hugged it. "You can keep my sock warm," she told it.

Arya sat at the dinner table. The soup was hot. Her dad stirred it. Arya touched the bowl. It felt warm on her fingers.

"Lights out for a minute," her dad said. The room went dark. Arya could not see her teddy. "Where is Bear?" she asked. She listened hard. She heard nothing but the soup bubbling.

Her dad turned on the lamp. Now Arya could see! There was Bear, under the chair. "My eyes see him!" said Arya. She picked Bear up. His loose arm hung down. A magnet on the fridge held her drawing nearby.

"Smell the soup," said her dad. Arya sniffed with her nose. "Yum," she said. She took a small taste with her tongue. "Warm and good!" She started to hug Bear tight.

"Dinner is ready," her dad said. Arya smiled at Bear. "You sit right here," she told him. "Where my eyes can see you."

Hunter turned four today. There was a party in his backyard. His friends Irha and Samir came to play.

"Hunter, how old are you?" asked Irha.

"I am four," said Hunter. "Yesterday I was three. Today I am four. On your birthday, you turn one year older!"

Samir laughed. "You got bigger in one day?"

"No, just older," said Hunter. "One whole year older!"

They ate watermelon. The seeds were slimy and Hunter giggled. "These seeds feel like tiny fish!"

Dad set a cake on the table. Dad lit the four candles. Dad was careful with the fire. Hunter watched from his spot.

"Make a wish," said Irha.

Hunter took a big breath. He blew. All four candles went out. His blow made the flames go away.

The lamp by the door shone on the cake. Everyone clapped.

"Happy birthday, Hunter!" said Samir.

Hunter grinned. "Now help me eat the cake!"

Kinsley sat at the little red table. Mr. Tran brought snack time around. "Would you like some banana?" he asked Leon. "Yes, please," said Leon. Leon got a banana.

Mr. Tran held the bowl toward Kinsley. Inside were green grapes. Kinsley did not like green grapes. "Yuck!" she shouted. Leon put his hands over his ears. Mr. Tran blinked. Kinsley felt her face get hot.

Mr. Tran sat down next to her. He said, "You can say no, thank you." Kinsley looked at the grapes. She took a breath. "No, thank you," she said. Mr. Tran smiled. "Thank you for those nice words," he said. Then he brought out a quick bowl of crackers. "Cracker, please," said Kinsley. He gave her two.

Then the class sang a quiet song together. Kinsley clapped along. "No, thank you," she whispered to the grapes, just to do it again. Leon laughed. Mr. Tran laughed too.

Audrey sat on the grass in the backyard. Her teddy bear, Boo, lay beside her. His tummy was muddy from a fall in the flower bed. "Oh no," said Audrey. "Boo is sick."

She wondered what to do. Mom was hanging up towels on the windy day. Audrey asked, "Can Boo have pretend medicine?" Mom smiled and found a small cup. "Here is his medicine," she said. Audrey held the cup to Boo's mouth. "Drink it all up," she said. She touched his forehead. It felt soft and warm.

Then Audrey got a towel from the pile. She wrapped Boo up like a blanket. "Now Boo needs a bed," she said. She patted the grass flat and laid him down. "Sleep tight, Boo." She patted his head very gently.

Boo lay still under the towel. The wind made the corners flap. Audrey waited and waited. Then she peeked under the towel. Boo's eyes looked shiny and happy. "All better!" said Audrey. She hugged him tight. "Time for a pretend snack, Boo."

Ryan stood in the kitchen. Mom had a big bowl. Inside were a feather, a pinecone, and a small blanket. "Can you sort them?" Mom asked. "Put the soft ones here. Put the rough ones there."

Ryan picked up the feather. He rubbed it on his cheek. It was soft. He put it in the soft pile. He picked up the pinecone. He touched it with his hand. It was bumpy. "Ooh," said Ryan. "This one is rough." He put it in the rough pile. The blanket felt soft and warm. He put it with the feather.

"My skin can tell!" said Ryan. He patted his own head. "My skin is all over me." Mom smiled. "Yes, your skin feels soft and rough. That is one of your five senses."

"Can I use my ears too?" asked Ryan. "Yes," said Mom. "Listen." She shook the bowl of rice. Ryan had to freeze and stand very still. He heard the rice go swish, swish. "My ears heard that!" said Ryan. He picked up the feather again and tickled Mom's arm, and she laughed.

Edouard wanted to play hide-and-seek. Kimberly said, "I will seek first!" She covered her eyes and began to count. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" It was too fast. Edouard was still standing by the letter blocks. He had not hidden at all.

"That was too quick," said Krishiv. "Count slowly so we can hide." Kimberly laughed. "Okay, okay!"

She covered her eyes again. "One... two... three..." Edouard ran on his little feet. The rug was soft under his toes. He squeezed behind the big teddy bear. The spot was tight and warm. He held his breath.

"Eight... nine... ten!" Kimberly turned around. Krishiv was under the table. Edouard was very quiet. Kimberly looked and looked. Then Edouard's shoe went squeak.

"Found you!" she shouted. "Your shoe told on you!"

Benjamin stood in the kitchen. He wanted a snack. His dad was baking bread. The bread smelled beautiful, and Benjamin's nose knew it. He could hear the mixer humming. His ears liked that sound.

"Dad, can I have some?" asked Benjamin.

"Soon," said Dad. "Close your eyes and wait for the beep."

Benjamin closed his eyes. It was dark. He could not see the bread. He could not see the mixer. He could not see his dad. He heard a voice. "I see you, Benjamin!" It was Nia. She had come in the door. Benjamin opened his eyes wide. There she was, waving.

"Your eyes were closed, but I could still see you," said Nia. She laughed. Benjamin laughed too. He had thought the dark hid him. It did not.

The oven beeped. Dad used a tool, a big wooden spoon, to move the bread. The bread was hot, so Dad did the hot part. Then Dad gave Benjamin a small piece that was cool. Benjamin touched it. It was soft and warm. He took a bite. His tongue said yum. The bread tasted beautiful.

"More please," said Benjamin, and held out his hand.

Austin ran to the block corner. He loved blocks. He took the whole bin. "All mine," he said. He made a big tower. It was very tall.

Then Cedar came over. Cedar had no blocks. Cedar just stood there. Kali came too. She had no blocks. Kali looked at the floor. Austin looked at his tower. Then he looked at his friends. He began to count. "One for Cedar. One for Kali. One for me." He put blocks in three small piles. Cedar smiled big. Kali clapped. "Let's all build," said Austin. Ms. Diallo peeked in. "Being fair means everyone gets a chance," she said. The three friends built one giant tower together.

The tower wobbled. It fell down with a crash. Something flew out from behind it. It was a butterfly! It had been hiding there all along. It landed on Kali's shoe. "Smelly old shoe!" laughed Cedar. The butterfly stayed a minute. Then it flew out the window. Austin waved. "Bye, butterfly!"

James went to the garden center with his dad. He wanted to grow carrots. He picked a small bag of seeds. Mr. Rahman gave him a pot and some soil. James put the seeds in the dirt. He gave them a drink of water.

Every day James looked at his pot. Then one morning, little green leaves popped up. James jumped up and down. His friend Shepherd came to see. A little weed was growing in the pot too. Shepherd said, "Let's pull it out."

James held the weed and pulled. It came out with a pop. Long stringy roots hung down from the bottom. "Look!" said James. "The roots grow down into the soil." The roots were slippery and wiggly like worms. James asked, "Do carrots have roots too?" Shepherd laughed. "Big fat ones," he said. James patted the soil flat again and said, "Grow, carrots, grow."

Raphael was in the kitchen. A bright bowl of soup sat on the table. His spoon waited next to it.

Raphael reached for the spoon. Then he stopped. He looked at his hands. They had dirt on them from the sandbox. Raphael ran to the sink. He turned the tap. The water was warm. He rubbed the soap all over. He counted with his mom. "One, two, three." She helped him count to twenty. Bubbles went down the drain. His hands were clean now.

Raphael sat down at the table. He picked up his spoon. He ate his soup, one spoon at a time. Ms. Petrov was his neighbor, and she came in with bread. "Wash hands first," said Raphael, and he showed her his clean hands. She smiled and washed hers too. Then they both ate the warm bread.

The rain had been stormy all morning. Willow jumped in one big puddle on the way inside. Splash! Her socks got wet. Her feet felt cold and squishy.

"I want dry socks," said Willow. Her mom sat her on a chair in the middle of the kitchen. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mom. "Let's get you dry."

Mom peeled off the wet socks. They went drip, drip on the floor. Mom got a small towel from the shelf. She patted Willow's feet until they were warm and dry. Then she pulled on soft new socks.

Willow wiggled her toes. The wet socks lay in the sink. The dry socks felt warm and cozy on her feet. The kettle began to sing on the stove. Mom turned it off and poured hot cocoa into a big cup. Willow held her small cup with two hands. She took a slow, careful sip.

Outside the stormy sky rumbled. Inside, Willow was warm and dry. She hummed a little song while she drank. Mom sat beside her and clapped to the beat.

Liam stood at the edge of the backyard pool. The water was blue and cool. His tummy felt funny. "I want to float," he said. "But what if I sink?"

Mr. Warsame stepped into the pool. "I will hold you," he said. "My hands go under your back. Now you can let go of me."

Liam lay back in the water. He felt Mr. Warsame's hands under his back, like a soft plastic mat. Liam opened his eyes. The sky was up there. A cloud looked like a big white dog. Was the water holding him too?

"I'm floating!" Liam said. "I'm not sinking!" Aanya clapped from the pool steps. "Next it's my turn," she said.

Then Mr. Warsame took one hand away. Liam did not sink. He did not go under. He just lay there, light as a leaf.

"Can you take your other hand away?" Liam asked. Mr. Warsame smiled and let both hands go. Liam floated all by himself. He saw the cloud drift by, slow and slow.

"Look at me, Aanya!" Liam called. Aanya kicked her legs in the water. "Can a cloud ride on the sky like that?" she asked.

"Maybe it can," Liam said. He lay still and watched it go.

Sara was at school. She had a big pile of paint. She wanted to paint a dragon. It would be a friendly, green dragon.

Coen grabbed her brush. He pulled it away. Sara felt hot and mad. Her face went red. She stomped off to the rug.

Then Ms. Quinn sat with her. "Try a slow, deep breath," said Ms. Quinn. Sara breathed in, big and slow. She let it out like a sleepy dragon. Her body felt calm.

She walked back to the table. Coen gave the brush back. "Sorry," he said. Sara painted her dragon. Krisha added tiny wings.

"Weak wings are small," said Sara. "My dragon has big, strong wings!" The dragon flew right off the paper, in her imagination. It zoomed around the whole room. Sara laughed and clapped.

Gianna sat in the music classroom. A big drum sat in front of her. It was almost too heavy to move. Ms. Kapoor had set it out for drum time.

Gianna hit the drum hard. BOOM! The sound was very loud. April covered her ears. Vanessa jumped in her seat. A baby in the room next door began to cry.

Gianna looked at the drum. She looked at the wall. She lifted her hand again, but this time she tapped softly. Tap. The sound was small and quiet. The baby stopped crying.

"Better," said Ms. Kapoor with a smile. Gianna tapped again, soft as a sweep of wind. April and Vanessa picked up little drums too. They all tapped together, quiet and slow, like rain on the slide outside the window.

Gianna tapped one more time. Tap, tap, tap.

Grace was at daycare. It was snack time. There was juice and bread on the table.

Theo grabbed for the bread. His hand went right past Grace's nose. Mr. Do shook his head. He held the bread plate up high.

"Try again," said Mr. Do.

Theo sat up tall. He looked at Mr. Do. "Bread, please," he said.

Mr. Do smiled. He gave Theo a big piece. Grace's eyes went wide. Theo grabbed, and nothing. Theo said please, and bread! Was that how it worked?

Grace wanted some bread too. She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She put her hand down. She tried it the other way.

"Bread, please," said Grace.

Mr. Do gave her a piece right away. "Here you are, Grace."

Grace took a bite and began to chew. The bread was soft and warm. One piece for Theo. One piece for Grace. One, two, pieces on the table.

Siena came to the table. No bread for her yet. What would she do? Siena thought and thought. Then she said, "Bread, please."

Mr. Do laughed. "Bread for everyone who asks so nicely."

Grace drank her juice. Please, bread. Please, bread. She said the magic word all day long. "Juice, please." "Crayons, please."

At home time, Grace waved to Theo. "See you tomorrow, please."

Jasmine sat in the waiting room with her mom. The chairs were blue. Jasmine counted them. One chair, two chairs, three chairs. "Is it my turn now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "We sit here until the nurse calls us." Jasmine waited. She counted the coats on the hooks. One coat, two coats, three coats, four coats. A boy named Oskar sat down too. He was waiting with his dad. "Waiting is wrong," said Jasmine. "Waiting is slow," said Oskar. Then the door opened. A nurse stood there. She called out, "Jasmine!" Jasmine stood up fast. That was her name! The nurse made the shot quick and small. It felt like a tiny pinch. Then the nurse gave her a sticker. It was a party sticker with a clown on it. Jasmine held it up high. "My turn came!" she said.

Andrew held his dad's hand at the pet store. The cages were bright and full. One small cat pushed its paw through the bars. Andrew felt a warm feeling in his chest. "That one," he said.

His dad smiled. "We can take her home," he said. Mr. Lin, the store man, put the cat in a soft box with holes. Andrew carried the box very carefully. It was light.

At home, the cat walked around the kitchen. She sniffed the table. She sniffed Andrew's shoe. Then she meowed at the door. "Does she need to go out?" Andrew asked. His dad shook his head.

"She is an indoor cat," Dad said. He set a pan on the floor. It had soft sand inside. "This is her litter box." The cat sniffed the pan. Then she stepped in. She scratched the sand. She dug a little hole. Andrew watched with wide eyes. The cat used the litter box as her toilet. Then she jumped out and walked away.

Andrew knelt down and looked. The sand was smooth in one spot and bumpy in another. "So the pan is her toilet," he said. Dad nodded. Every morning, Andrew helped scoop the sand. The cat purred and rubbed his leg. "Good cat," Andrew said. "Good toilet, too."

Grandpa had a big rug on the floor. It showed all the letters from A to Z. Aurora sat on the rug. She wanted to learn every letter.

Her friend Maeve came to play. They put the letter cards in a row. But one card was lost under the sofa. It was the letter M. When Aurora found it, she did not know where it went. "Try the song," said Maeve. "The song sings the letters in order." So Aurora sang. She sang past the rough carpet edge, past the sand tray Grandpa kept for writing letters. She sang, "L, M, N." She put M right after L. It fit!

Grandpa clapped. "Now do the M sound," he said. Aurora pressed her lips together. "Mmm," she said. "Mmm for Maeve!" Maeve laughed and hugged her. Grandpa poured them cold juice from the fridge. Aurora sang the song one more time, all the way to Z. Then she traced an M in the sand with her finger, slow and careful.

Sienna walked in the forest with her friend Madeline. Sienna saw a long stick on the ground. She picked it up and stirred a pile of leaves.

"Now I am cooking soup," she said. "This pot is not real. But I will act like it is. That is my pretend pot."

Madeline found a smooth stone. "This is my baby," she said. "My baby needs a nap." She wrapped the stone in leaves.

Then Sienna saw the ground between two logs. "Look, a river!" she said. "We must hop across."

The girls hopped over the pretend river. They did not get wet at all.

"I like this game," said Madeline. "The river is not real. But hopping on it is fun."

Sienna stirred her soup again. "Happy birthday, baby stone," she sang. "Time for soup."

The leaves did not break. The stone baby slept for a long time.

Sophia put her lunch tray on the long table. It was her first day at school. The tray had a little orange cup of fruit. She sat next to a girl named Esmeralda. Esmeralda dropped her pencil on the floor. Sophia picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," said Esmeralda.

After lunch, Mr. Zhang said, "Play time now." Sophia ran to the slide. It was big and shiny and red. She climbed up and went down fast. Whee! She wanted to go again right away. She started to run to the ladder. But a boy named Keon was already there. He stood in line with two more kids.

"The line goes around," said Keon. "We take turns on the slide." So Sophia walked to the back. She waited. She watched Keon go down. Then the next kid went down. Then it was her turn. Sophia climbed up and slid down again. It was just as fun. At the back of the line, Esmeralda waved at her.

"Want to wait together?" asked Esmeralda. "Yes," said Sophia. They held hands in line. The sun felt warm on the slide. When Sophia got to the top, she looked down at Esmeralda smiling below. "Here I come!" she called.

Luke stayed at Grandpa's house. He ran to the bath and put one foot near the water. "Too hot!" said Grandpa. He held his hand in the water first. Then he turned the tap and added more cool water. Luke watched. The steam went away. Grandpa felt the water again. "Now it is just right," he said.

Luke got in. The water was warm and wet on his toes. He splashed a little. He washed his arms and his tummy. Grandpa gave him a duck to float. On the window, a flower sticker smiled at him. "Look, a yellow flower," said Luke. Grandpa laughed and washed Luke's hair.

After the bath, Luke got dressed in soft pajamas. Then he ate bread and milk with Grandpa. His eyes felt sleepy. Grandpa tucked him into bed. Luke yawned. "The duck can sleep too," he said. He closed his eyes and held the duck tight.

Charlotte dug a little hole at the farm. "In you go, pea seeds," she said. Her friend Alden dug a hole too. "Mine is a baby garden," he said. "Mine too," said Charlotte. They patted the rough dirt down flat.

Every day Charlotte came to look. She followed the long green vine with her eyes. It grew tall. It grew taller than her knee. One day she found a small green pod. "Alden! A funny little green boat!" Alden touched it. It made a soft noise when he squeezed it. "What is it?" he asked.

Charlotte popped it open. "Peas! Peas inside!" A neat row of little round peas sat in the pod. Alden popped his open too. "Peas in mine too!" Charlotte ran to Mr. Tehrani. "My seeds grew into peas hiding in pods!" she said. Mr. Tehrani laughed. "Look at that," he said. Charlotte held her pod up high. "Hello in there, little peas!"

Benjamin went to the park with his friend Emilie. A little cart stood by the trees. A man was selling cold drinks there. "I want lemonade," said Benjamin. His dad bought two cups, one for Benjamin and one for Emilie.

The man put an ice cube on the counter. Benjamin wanted to hold it. He picked it up with his fingers. The ice cube was so cold! Benjamin let go fast. The ice cube dropped into his cup with a splash. "It's cold!" said Benjamin. Emilie laughed. "That was a funny joke," she said. "It wasn't a joke," said Benjamin. "Ice really feels cold."

Then Benjamin looked at his cup. He saw the lemonade, yellow and bubbly. He heard the ice go clink, clink. He sniffed the lemon. It smelled sharp and fresh. He took a sip. The juicy lemon taste made his mouth happy. He touched the cup with both hands. The cup felt cold too.

Emilie touched her cup. "Mine is cold as well," she said. Benjamin held his cup with both hands. That helped his fingers feel warm again. He drank slowly and watched the ducks on the pond. The ice went clink one more time.

Jasmine stood in the backyard with her baby brother. He was new and very small. His blanket was pink and soft.

"I want to play ball," said Jasmine. "Baby, wake up!"

The baby did not wake up. He was sleeping again. Jasmine looked at the clock on the porch. The big hand went all around. The baby still slept.

"Does he sleep all day?" she asked.

Mom came out and sat on the step. "New babies sleep for much of the day," said Mom. "That is how babies grow."

Jasmine waited. She watched a bird fly over the fence. She patted the baby's blanket, very gently.

At last the baby opened his eyes. Jasmine held up the ball. He smiled at her. Then his eyes closed again.

Mom laughed. "He will play soon," she said.

Jasmine sat close to Mom. She kissed the baby's head. "Sleep, baby," she whispered. "I will be right here."

Jules ran to the playground with his dad. His friends Fateh and Kaiya were already there. "Look, a picnic!" said Kaiya. There was a little camp stove on the picnic table. Jules's dad was cooking warm milk for cocoa.

"Stay close to me near the stove," said Dad. Jules stood right beside him. He did not touch the stove. The stove did not look hot at all. It was small and tidy and silver. No fire. No smoke. Nothing.

"Is it still hot?" Jules whispered to Dad. "It does not look hot." Dad held his hand up high, far above the stove. "Yes, it is still hot," said Dad. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it." Dad poured the milk into cups. He turned the stove off himself.

Jules picked up his cup with two hands. The milk was warm and sweet. "Yum," he said. Fateh and Kaiya drank theirs too.

Later, Jules found a fat worm on the ground. It wiggled near a sharp stick. "Don't touch the sharp stick," said Ms. Weiss, the neighbour, walking by with her dog. "I won't," said Jules. He watched the worm crawl into the grass.

"Only grown-ups touch the stove," Jules told the worm. "That is the rule." Then he ran back to Dad, and they swung on the swings together.

Jaxon was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a card for her. He wanted a pink flower on it.

Grandma got out the paints. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. There was white paint too.

But there was no pink paint. Jaxon looked and looked. "I need pink," he said. "My flower has to be pink."

He saw a big square of paper on the table. He saw his brush by the cup. He put red paint on his brush. He painted one red petal.

Then he dipped his brush in the white paint. A little white went onto his red petal. He stirred the red and the white together.

The petal turned pink! Jaxon sat very still and looked at it. "Pink," he whispered. "Red and white make pink."

He stirred more white into more red. He painted more pink petals. He painted a green stem and yellow dots.

Grandma came to see. "A pink flower," she said. "My favorite." Jaxon painted one more petal, slow and careful.

Nathan put on his brown sweater. Mom held his hand. They walked into the big community hall.

"Who will be here?" Nathan asked. "Everyone," said Mom. "Families often gather together to celebrate special holidays."

The hall was full. Nathan counted the people. One grandma, two grandpas, three aunts. Then Nathan saw someone small by the table.

"Jayce!" Nathan called. His cousin Jayce turned around. They had not seen each other for a long time. Jayce ran over. They waved to each other and laughed.

The girls brought flat bread. Uncle brought a big pot. Ms. Hosseini, the neighbour, brought sweet cookies. More families kept coming in the door. The hall got fuller and fuller.

Nathan watched Mom light the candles. She did it slowly, one by one. Nathan clapped when all the candles were bright. Then everyone sat down together.

Jayce sat next to Nathan. They shared a cookie. "More family?" Jayce asked, pointing at the door.

Nathan looked. Another aunt walked in with a big smile. "Yes," said Nathan. "A family party means everyone comes."

Jayce took another cookie and put it in Nathan's hand.

Naomi went to the store with her dad. She wanted to find a small blue lamp. Dad held her hand in the big store. The store had bright lights and long shelves.

Naomi saw a shelf with lamps. One lamp was not plugged in. Dad picked it up. "This one?" he asked. Naomi nodded. It was blue and small.

Near the shelf there was a little hole in the wall. It was an outlet. Naomi pointed at it. "Hole," she said. Dad crouched down. He put the plug into the outlet. The lamp made light. Naomi clapped her hands.

Naomi reached out her little finger toward the outlet. Dad held her hand softly. "No fingers in there," he said. "Only plugs." Naomi watched again. Dad took the plug out. The light went off. He put it back in. The light went on. Naomi laughed.

At home, the lamp sat by her bed. Dad plugged it in, ready for her nap. Naomi touched only the lamp's cool shade. "Night night, lamp," she said.

text:
Theo woke up in the dark. He put on his itchy sweater. "It is morning!" he said. Dad smiled. "Come and see," said Dad. They went out to the car. The sky was still black. The moon was up. "It is still night," said Theo.

Dad drove to the store, slowly. The big store was open all night. It had big lights. Theo got a small cart. It was little, like him. Inside, the freezer was cold. Theo touched the glass with one finger. Brrr. The bakery corner was warm. Dad held the hot bread with a glove. Theo watched from his spot.

A man named Mr. Leblanc worked there. He waved. "Hello, Theo!" he said. "The sun comes soon," he said. "Then it is day. Day and night are opposites." Theo yawned. They bought milk and bread. Dad carried the small bag. Theo held Dad's hand. Outside, the sky turned pink. "Look," said Theo. "The sun!"

Lillian sat in the backyard with her paper. She was painting a big yellow sun. "Look, my sun is so bright!" she said.

Lucien came to play. "I want to hold it," he said. He put his finger on the sun. The yellow smeared into a big smudge. Lillian gasped. "My sun! It is smudged now."

"That was not so scary," Lucien said. "We can fix it." They put the paper in the sun to dry. "We have to wait," said Lillian. "Wet paint smears if you touch it. I know that now."

They waited and waited. Then Lillian touched the paper with one finger. It was dry! She painted a new sun on top of the smudge. It looked even brighter than before.

"I will always wait for paint to dry," said Lillian. Lucien clapped his hands and said, "Me too!"

Victoria sat at the little table in the school library. Ms. Popal gave her a pencil and some paper. "Today you will write your name," said Ms. Popal. Victoria looked at the letters. V for Victoria. That one came first.

Victoria squeezed the pencil very tight. She pressed down hard on the paper. She wanted the letter to be big and dark. Snap! The tip broke off and rolled onto the table. Victoria stared at the broken tip. Pressing too hard made it break.

"Can I try again?" Victoria asked. Ms. Popal sharpened the pencil and smiled. "Here you go," she said. Victoria held the pencil softly this time. She pressed gently. Slowly she made a V. Then an i. Then a c. The letters appeared on the paper, one by one. Nothing broke.

Rosie came over to see. "Look at your name!" said Rosie. Victoria pointed at each letter. "That's me," she said. Outside the window, snow began to fall on the trees. Victoria picked up her paper with both hands. "I will show my mom," she said, and she zipped it safe inside her spotted backpack.

Ibrahim went to the backyard with a mirror. He wanted to find the smell of the cookies his dad was baking. He could smell them with his nose. He held the mirror up to his face. He looked at his nose. He saw two little holes in it. He counted them. "One, two," he said.

Aiza came to play. "What are you doing?" she asked. "Looking at my nose," said Ibrahim. "It has two openings," said Aiza. "They are called nostrils." Ibrahim looked again. Yes, two nostrils. He touched one nostril with his finger. The cookie smell went away on that side. He let go. The smell came back.

Desmond came with a shiny spoon. It clinked when he tapped it. They heard it with their ears. Then they saw a turtle walk by the fence. They touched its shell, very gently, with their fingers. Dad called out, "Cookies are ready!" They ran to eat one. It was sweet on their tongues. Dad laughed and said, "Ibrahim, you have chocolate on your nostrils." Ibrahim giggled and held up the mirror again.

Natalie went to the park with her toy bag. She set out her toys on the grass. There was a ball, a truck and a little duck.

Kyra came to play too. She brought her picnic basket. Inside were apples, cheese and crackers. "This is a tasty lunch," said Kyra. They sat on a big red shirt to eat it.

Then Jayson ran over. His hat fell off. A sock fell out of it too. "Look at this," said Natalie. She laughed. She put the sock with the ball and the truck. Then she looked at it. It did not fit there. She looked at Jayson's hat. She looked at the red shirt under them.

"Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," said Natalie. She put the sock in the shirt. She folded the hat on top. Jayson put it all in his bag to take home. "Come on," he said. "Let's choose a swing."

Adam sat in a waiting room with his mom. There was a big toy truck on the floor. Adam turned its wheels round and round. "Soon it is your turn," said Mom.

A nurse called Adam's name. First Adam stood on the scale. He wiggled his toes. The numbers jumped up and down. "The numbers are dancing!" said Adam. "Stand still and see," said the nurse. Adam stood still like a statue. The numbers stopped jumping. One number stayed. "That is how much you weigh," said the nurse. "A scale at the doctor's office shows how much you weigh." Adam looked down at his feet. What else could stillness show?

Then it was time for the shot. Adam held his mom's hand. He stood very still. The nurse said, "All done." Adam had not even cried. The nurse gave him a sticker shaped like a deep blue hill. "Wow," said Adam, "standing still helped twice."

Jade was a little girl on the skate team. She had a red shirt. All her team wore red shirts. The other team wore blue shirts.

Jade had the puck. She looked up fast. Who was on her team? She saw a red shirt. It was Zac! She pushed the puck to Zac. Zac caught it. He passed it back. How did Jade know? She looked for red.

Then Jade saw a blue shirt zoom past. That was Abigaelle. Abigaelle was not on Jade's team. Jade did not pass to her. Red was her team. Blue was the other team.

After the game, Mr. Cruz gave out juicy orange slices. "Nice passing, Jade," he said. Jade smiled and looked at her red shirt. Then she waved to Zac in his red shirt too.

Addison had a cold. She was at home on the couch with a soft blanket. Her nose was runny and red. She reached for a tissue and blew her nose. Then she put the tissue on the couch. Soon there were tissues everywhere.

Her dad came in with warm soup. "Let's put those in the bin," he said. "After you blow your nose, the used tissue goes in the bin." Addison picked up a tissue. She dropped it in the bin from far away. Swish! In it went.

"Again!" said Addison. She threw each tissue, one by one. Swish, swish, swish. The couch was quiet and clean. Then she drank her soup and felt cozy. Dad smiled. "Good throwing," he said. Addison held up her cup. "More soup, please!"

Grandma was coming on a plane. Charlie went to the airport with his dad. Lots of people waited by big doors. "This is the arrivals area," said Dad. "We wait here for people coming off the plane."

The doors opened. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" said Charlie. But it was not Grandma. The doors opened again. A boy came out. "Grandma!" said Charlie. Dad laughed softly. "Not yet," he said. Charlie held Dad's hand tight. The floor was shiny and cold. A cart beeped by with lots of bags.

Then the doors opened one more time. Grandma walked out with her small red bag. Charlie let go and began to run. Grandma opened her arms wide. She picked him up in a big hug. "I found you!" said Charlie.

The next day, Grandma took Charlie to the park. His legs got weak from running so much, so they sat on a bench. Grandma shared her crackers. The sun was warm. Aliya waved from the swings, and Charlie waved back.

Eloise went to the library with her dad. She wanted the big red book about dogs. It sat on a high shelf. She reached up. She reached higher. Her fingers could not touch it.

She pulled a chair. Her dad said, "No climbing, please." He moved the chair away. Eloise frowned. The book was too far up.

She saw Ms. Leblanc at the desk. Eloise walked over slowly. She waited for a lady to finish talking. Then she said, "Can you help me, please?" Ms. Leblanc smiled. "Yes, I can help you."

Ms. Leblanc got the red dog book down. "Thank you," said Eloise. She hugged the book to her chest.

Eloise sat on a soft rug. Calder and Cecelia were there too. Calder was building a tower of blocks. It looked wild and tall. Eloise turned a page. Her elbow went out. It hit the tower. The blocks fell down with a bump.

"Sorry," said Eloise. "It was my elbow." Calder looked at the blocks. Then he smiled. "Let's build it again," he said. Eloise put the book down. They stacked the blocks one by one. The tower grew tall. Eloise laughed and put the last block on top.

Leon stood in the kitchen. He wanted to help make soup. Dad had the big pot on the stove. The stove was hot, so Leon stayed back. "You can wash the carrots," said Dad. Leon carried a carrot to the sink. The water was cold. Brrr, cold water on his little hands.

Then a red ball rolled under the table. Leon ran to the far end of the kitchen. It was dark back there. He could not see Dad. Dad could not see him. Leon looked around the corner. No Dad. "Dad?" he called. No answer came. Leon picked up his ball and ran back fast. Now Dad could see him. "There you are," said Dad. "Stay where I can see you, okay?" "Okay," said Leon. "I will stay right here."

Dad spoke a soft word. "Look now." He turned the lid. Hot steam rose up and away. Leon did not touch. Then, surprise, inside the pot was a carrot shaped like a star! Dad had cut it just for him. Leon laughed. "My star!" he said. He sat on his little stool, close to Dad, and watched it swim in the soup.

Wyatt ran into the band room. A small violin sat on a soft mat. It was just his size, not too big, not too small.

Wyatt picked it up. He held it upside down. He pulled the short stick across the strings. But no music came out. Only little squeaks.

Mr. Campbell knelt down next to him. "Let me show you how to hold it," he said. He turned the violin the right way up. He helped Wyatt tuck it under his chin. "Now try," said Mr. Campbell.

Wyatt brushed the stick across the strings. A sound rang out! It was a real note, long and sweet. Wyatt's eyes went wide. He played it again. The note came again.

Drew and Isobel clapped from their seats. "Play more!" said Isobel. Wyatt played one note, then two, then three. Mr. Campbell gave him a gentle hug. "Good playing, Wyatt," he said. Wyatt held his violin up high, the right way, and smiled.

Jasmine sat at the dinner table. She was so excited. Dinner was soup with big noodles. Alaya sat next to her. Alaya loved the soup. She smiled and clapped her hands. "Yum, yum!" said Alaya. But Arzoyi sat across the table. He did not smile. He looked scared of the soup. He hid behind his cup. "Too hot," he said in a tiny voice. Jasmine looked at Alaya. Then she looked at Arzoyi. The same soup, but they felt differently. Jasmine had an idea. She took her spoon and made it a magic wand. She waved it over Arzoyi's bowl. "Cool, cool, noodles," she sang. Arzoyi peeked out. He blew on his soup like a dragon. The steam went away. Then he took one small bite. His eyes got big. "Happy!" he said. Alaya kicked her feet under the table. She was happy too. Then Jasmine waved the spoon again. "Magic for me too!" said Alaya. Ms. Côté brought bread. The bread was warm and soft. Jasmine tore a piece. The strong smell filled her nose. She gave a piece to Arzoyi and a piece to Alaya. Everyone ate together. "More magic soup," said Arzoyi. Jasmine waved her spoon one more time.

Paint day! Grace ran to the art table. Ms. Petrov had put out three cups. Red, yellow, blue. "Red, yellow, blue," Grace said. She said it again. "Red, yellow, blue!"

Sawyer sat next to her. He held up his paper. "I'm painting my favorite egg," he said. "It's yellow." Grace looked at her own paper. She wanted to paint a big pumpkin. Pumpkins were orange. She looked in the cups. No orange cup. Her tummy felt tight. "Where is the orange?" she asked.

Ms. Petrov smiled. "Try mixing two paints," she said. Grace tapped her chin. She put her brush in the red cup. Then she put it in the yellow cup. Swirl, swirl, swirl. Her brush turned a new colour. Orange! Bright orange! Grace gasped. "Look, Sawyer, look!" She painted her pumpkin. Round and orange and big.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Sawyer. "And orange now!" Grace laughed. She painted a little egg on her pumpkin too. Then she held her paper up high. "My pumpkin rides home with me today!"

Samuel sat at the dinner table. His toy car was next to his plate. Benoit sat beside him. Benoit had a tall tower of blocks on the table. The tower went up, up, up. Samuel reached for his car. His elbow pushed the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. Benoit's lip wobbled. "My tower," he said.

Samuel felt his tummy go tight. Ms. Sun knelt down close. "You can say sorry," she said softly. Samuel looked at Benoit. "Sorry," said Samuel. Then Samuel picked up a red block. He put it down flat. Benoit put a blue block on top. Samuel found a yellow one. They pushed the blocks together, click, click. The new tower grew tall. It was even taller than the first one.

Benoit smiled big. "Our tower," he said. Samuel smiled too. He rolled his car around the plate. "Beep, beep," said Samuel. Benoit laughed. Ms. Sun clapped her hands. "First the tower, then the beeping," she said. Both boys put one more block on top. The tower stood tall and safe.

Declan looked out the window. The weather was gray and rainy. "No park today," he said. Then the doorbell rang. It was his friend Kyle.

Kyle sat on the floor. Declan got out the blocks. They began to build a tall tower. Crash! The tower fell down. Kyle made a sad face. His mouth turned down. His eyes looked watery. Declan looked at Kyle's face. Was Kyle sad? "Are you sad?" Declan asked. Kyle nodded. "My tower fell."

"I can help," said Declan. They built the tower again. It went up and up. This time it stayed tall. Kyle's mouth turned up into a big smile. His eyes looked happy now. "You look happy!" said Declan. Kyle laughed.

After the rain, they went outside. They dug in the wet dirt with a small shovel. Declan found a pink stone. "For you," he said. Kyle held it tight. "Best day," said Kyle. His face said so too.

Eloise stood in the kitchen with her dad. She wanted to see the cookies baking. She looked with her eyes. She listened with her ears. The oven went hum, hum, hum.

Dad put on Grandpa's glasses. "Glasses help me see more clearly," said Grandpa. He read the recipe. "One plate, two spoons, three eggs. Count with me, Eloise!" Eloise counted to three.

Then Grandpa took the glasses off. He held the book far away. He squinted. "Funny face!" said Eloise. She laughed. He put the glasses back on. Now he read the words fast. "My glasses help me see more clearly," he said. Eloise clapped her hands.

The cookies came out of the oven. Dad held the hot pan. "Smell with your nose," said Eloise. She sniffed. Sweet! She touched one cool cookie with her finger. She took a little bite. Yum. "Grandpa," she said, "you can read me a story now. Put on your glasses!"

Grandpa smiled and slid the glasses on his nose.

Liam went to the library with his dad. There was a little playroom with toy trucks. Liam wanted the big red truck. Ayat had the big red truck. "Can I have a turn?" Liam asked. "Yes, after me," said Ayat. Liam waited. He played with a small blue truck while he waited. Then Ayat gave him the red truck. "Your turn," she said.

Liam pushed the red truck all around the rug. He made a loud truck sound. Mr. Hu smiled. Then it was time to go. Liam jumped up and ran to the door. The trucks were still all over the rug. Mr. Hu called, "Liam, the trucks." Liam looked back. Ayat was putting her truck on the shelf. Fatoumata was putting the blocks in the bin. Liam ran back. He put the red truck on the shelf. He put the blue truck next to it.

Now the rug was all clear. "Good helper," said Mr. Hu. Liam held his dad's hand. The sun was still bright outside. "My hands need washing," said Liam. Dad helped him wash and dry his hands. "I had a turn with the red truck," said Liam. "Tomorrow can I have another turn?" "Yes," said Dad. Liam smiled all the way home.

Weston stood at the beach pool with his mom. The pool was big and blue. Weston wanted to swim like the big kids.

He saw Koda and Sehaj in the water. They were splashing and laughing. Weston held his mom's hand tight.

"Can I swim there?" he asked. He pointed to the far side of the pool. The big kids jumped in there. The water looked very far down.

"That is the deep end," said Ms. Saleh, the swim teacher. "This side is the shallow end. You start here."

Weston sat down in the shallow end. The water came up to his tummy. He could touch the bottom with his feet. He kicked his legs and swept his arms through the water. Whoosh!

Koda came to sit by him. Sehaj held his hand. They were a team in the shallow end. They practiced kicking together. Splash, splash, splash.

After swim time, they ate yummy crackers on the towel. Weston looked at the deep end. The big kids were still jumping in. He looked at his feet touching the bottom.

"Next time, more kicks," said Ms. Saleh. She gave him a high five.

Weston clapped his wet hands. "More kicks!" he said.

Luna wanted to play a game. Mom said, "Let's play the touching game." She put a pinecone, a feather, and a stone on the table. "Close your eyes," said Mom. Luna closed her eyes tight.

"Touch with your fingertips," said Mom. Luna touched the first thing. "Ow! It is bumpy," she said. "It's the pinecone!" She touched the next thing. It was soft like a bird. "The feather!" She touched the last thing. It felt smooth and cool. "The stone!" Luna opened her eyes. "My fingers told me everything!"

Then Mom filled a bowl with apples. "Smell this one," she said. Luna sniffed with her nose. It smelled sweet. Mom cut the apple. Luna heard a little crunch with her ears. She saw the shiny red skin with her eyes. Then she took a bite. It was juicy and yummy on her tongue.

Luna looked at her fingertips. "Little helpers," she said. She petted the feather again, very softly. "Guess what this is," she said to Mom. Mom closed her eyes and smiled.

Aurora woke up early. The sun was bright in the kitchen. Mom was making pancakes. "Can I help?" asked Aurora. "Yes, please bring the plates," said Mom. One plate, two plates, three plates. Aurora counted them all.

Then the doorbell rang. It was Albert. "We are going to the park," said Mom. "Would you like some pancakes first?" Albert sat down. Aurora shared her blueberries with him. Albert smiled big. "Thank you," he said. Aurora froze. She did not know what to say back. She looked at Mom.

Mom gave Albert more blueberries. "Thank you," said Albert. "You're welcome," said Mom. Aurora's eyes went wide. That was the answer! Albert looked at her again. "Thank you, Aurora," he said. Aurora took a big breath. "You're welcome!" she said. Albert laughed. Then a butterfly flew in the window and landed on the syrup jar. "A spring butterfly!" said Albert. Mom opened the door. Off it flew, up into the sky.

Kinsley stood at the airport with her mom. Grandma was coming on a big plane. Kinsley held a wooden sign. It said "Grandma" in red letters.

Kinsley wanted to hug Grandma. But her tummy felt funny and shy. Then Grandma walked out of the gate. Kinsley hid behind her mom's leg.

"You can hug me," said Grandma. "Or you can wave. Or you can just say hello."

Kinsley peeked out. She gave a little wave. Grandma waved back with a big smile. "Hello, Grandma," said Kinsley. Grandma knelt down and waited. Kinsley ran to her and hugged her tight.

Then Grandma opened her bag. A small stuffed dog peeked out. "He wanted to come and play," said Grandma. Kinsley laughed and hugged the dog too.

Dylan ran to school with his dad. His hair was all messy. It stuck up in little bumps.

At school, Mr. Patel said, "It is picture day." Dylan looked in the little mirror. His hair had tangles. "One tangle, two tangles, three tangles," he counted.

Jace sat next to him. "My hair was messy too," said Jace. "I combed it slow." Gage got a small comb from the box. The comb had soft teeth.

Dylan started to comb fast. Ouch. It pulled. He stopped. He combed slow, so it did not pull. One tangle gone. Two tangles gone. Three tangles gone. His hair was smooth now.

At snack time, Dylan did not spill his juice. He kept the cup closed to his chest. He ate his crackers and drank it all up.

Mr. Patel called, "Dylan, your turn for the picture." Dylan stood by the wall. "Smile," said Mr. Patel. Dylan smiled big. He patted his smooth hair with one hand. "All the tangles are gone," he said.

Cooper woke up and saw white. Snow was on the street! "No school today," said his dad. "It's a snow day!" Cooper jumped up and down.

Cooper ran outside. He wanted to make a big snowman. He patted the snow. The ball fell apart. He patted again. It fell apart again. "Oh no!" said Cooper. A young bird hopped nearby and watched him.

Then Cooper picked up a handful of snow. It felt a little wet. He squeezed it. It stuck together! He rolled it and rolled it. The ball grew big. He rolled two more balls. He stacked them up. "Look, Dad! My snowman!"

His friend Stefano came by with his mom. "Can I make one too?" Stefano asked. He grabbed the wet snow and squeezed. His ball stuck together too. Cooper put a hat on his snowman. "Hello, Mr. Snowman!"

Xavier wanted to make his own snack. His dad made the toast and put it on a plate. Xavier picked up the butter knife. He spread the butter, slow and soft. The butter made little lines on the toast. He tried again. This time the butter went all over, corner to corner.

Next came the milk. Xavier held the cup with one hand. He poured fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. A little puddle sat there by his cup. His dad wiped it up with a towel. "You can try again," Dad said.

Xavier got more milk in the cup. This time he poured slowly. The milk went up, up, up. It stayed in the cup. No splash at all. Xavier took a big bite of toast. "I did it," he said. Dad gave him a thumbs up.

Everly was home with a cold. It was a rainy day. She sat on the couch with her blanket. A rock she had painted sat on the table beside her. It had a happy face on it.

Everly felt a tickle in her nose. Then she sneezed. The sneeze went right into her hand. Her hand felt wet and yucky. Mom brought a tissue and wiped her hand.

"Try this," Mom said. She lifted her arm and put her nose near her elbow. "When you cough or sneeze, you cover it with your elbow." Mom made a little fake cough into her elbow. Everly giggled.

Everly wanted to try. She lifted her arm. She made a cough into her elbow. "Again," said Mom. Everly coughed into her elbow again. Then she sneezed into her elbow too. "I did it!" said Everly.

Mom brought warm soup. Everly held her spoon and took a little lick of the broth. It tasted good. Her tummy felt warm. Then the tickle came back. Everly lifted her arm fast. She sneezed right into her elbow.

"Good cover," said Mom. She gave Everly a hug. Everly hugged her back with her dry, clean hands. Outside the rain went drip, drip, drip on the window. Everly coughed into her elbow one more time, just to show her rock.

Olivia was at Grandma's house. The lights went out. Everything was dark. "The power is out," said Grandma. Olivia felt hungry. "Can I have a yogurt?" she asked.

She pulled at the fridge door. Grandma held it gently. "We keep the fridge shut now," she said. "Then the food stays cold longer." Olivia let go of the handle. She would wait.

Grandma lit a little lamp. She used a wipe to clean the table. Then they sat together. They made shadow bunnies on the wall with their hands. Olivia told Grandma about the playground. Soon the lights came back on. Everything was bright again.

"Can I have my yogurt now?" Olivia asked. "Yes," said Grandma. The yogurt was still cold. Olivia smiled and took a big spoonful.

Parker wanted to find the toy car. It was hidden in the playroom. Mr. Carvalho had made a number hunt for him.

"Look for the numeral five," said Mr. Carvalho. "Your car sits by it."

Parker knew how to count. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He held up five fingers. He looked at his hand. Five fingers. Then he looked at the playroom.

Daxon was stacking soft blocks. Izaiah was hugging his furry bear. Parker did not see any fingers on the walls. He saw paper squares instead. Each square had a mark on it.

He found a square with a mark like this: 5. He held up his hand next to it. He counted his fingers again. "One, two, three, four, five." Five fingers. The mark said five too.

"Is that the same five?" Parker asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Carvalho. "That mark means five."

Parker looked under the paper square. There was his toy car! He waved it high, like a flag against the sky in the window. "I found it!" he said.

Daxon and Izaiah clapped. Then Parker helped them count the blocks. "One, two, three," he said, and he counted slowly. Some blocks fell down. They waited. Then they stacked them again.

"Let's count to ten," said Izaiah.

So they all counted together. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Emily wanted to wear her party dress to bed. It was gray and silver and full of sparkles. She twirled in front of the mirror. "I will sleep in my pretty dress," she said.

At dinner, Emily used her fork to eat her noodles. She still had on the party dress. After dinner, Dad ran her bath. The bubbles were big and white. She hoped the sparkles would stay shiny.

But when she sat in the bath, the skirt got wet and heavy. It clung to her legs. It did not twirl at all. Dad helped her take it off. "Now what will I wear?" Emily asked. Dad held up her soft pajamas. "Pajamas," he said, "are clothes we wear to sleep in." Emily touched them. They were warm and fuzzy, like her teddy bear.

She pulled them on all by herself. She buttoned the top, slow and careful, one button at a time. Then she climbed into bed. The pajamas felt cozy. She wiggled her toes under the blanket. "Good night, party dress," she whispered. The dress hung on the door, waiting for the next party. Emily closed her eyes and snuggled down.

Luca loved his red fire truck. He pushed it on the floor. It made a loud siren sound. Vroom, vroom!

One day Adalynn came to play. Luca grabbed the truck fast. He held it tight. Adalynn cried. Luca's mom knelt down beside him.

"Your bear can go up high," Mom said. "Then you can share your other toys." Mom lifted the red truck to the top shelf. Luca looked up. The truck sat there, safe and cool.

Luca put his blocks on the rug. Adalynn put a block on top. "Let's build a big tower," Luca said. Adalynn smiled. The tower grew tall. It wobbled. It fell down with a crash. They laughed.

Then Luca wanted the yellow tool set. Adalynn was holding the hammer. Luca took a deep breath. He put his hands in his lap. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. Adalynn gave him the hammer. "Now it is your turn," she said.

Luca tapped the block. Tap, tap. Adalynn waited too. Then it was her turn again.

When Adalynn went home, Mom took the red truck down. Luca hugged it tight. "We built a tower," he said. "And I waited." Mom clapped her hands.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. He wore his blue shirt. Today he had to get a shot. He did not want to go.

"I am not sick," said Jackson. "I feel fine."

His mom sat down next to him. "The doctor will tell you more," she said. "First, one hug. Then, two shoes on. Then, three big steps to the car."

Jackson tried the hug. That was warm. He put on two shoes. He took three big steps to the car. He held his mom's hand the whole way.

At the doctor's office, a friend was there too. It was Hoorain from his class. She held a small teddy bear.

"Are you scared?" Jackson asked her.

"A little," said Hoorain.

"You can hold my hand," said Jackson.

The doctor came in. "I am not sick," said Jackson. "Why do I need a shot?"

"Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," said the doctor.

The shot was quick. It felt like one little pinch. Then it was done.

"See, all done," said Jackson. "One pinch and it stopped."

Hoorain sat up tall. She got her shot too. She squeezed the teddy bear, and then it was over.

Back at home, Jackson got a blue bandage on his arm. He looked at it. He smiled at Hoorain, who came over to play.

"We are protected," said Jackson.

Hoorain held up her arm. "One bandage for me too," she said.

Hazel sat on her bed. She held her big red library bag. "Is it library day?" she asked. Mom poked her head in the door. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now," Mom said. "The library visit is today."

Hazel jumped up and down. "Now?" she asked. "We go now?"

"Soon," said Mom. "First we put on shoes. Then we go." Hazel looked for her shoes. One was under the bed. One was by the door. A dry leaf had come in on her sock. It was brown and crunchy. She picked it up and put it in her pocket.

Yesterday, Hazel had cried. The library trip had been postponed. "Not today," Mom had said then. "Tomorrow." Hazel had not liked waiting.

But she had waited. And now the waiting was done. Today had come at last.

"Shoes on!" Hazel called. "Shoes on, shoes on!"

Mom laughed. "Ready now?"

"Now!" said Hazel. She grabbed her red bag. It flapped like a wing.

"Today is a good day," said Mom.

"The best day," said Hazel. She held the leaf up high. "The library gets to see my leaf too!"

The door opened, and out they went.

Hannah stood on the soccer field. Ms. Hernández put a big hoop on the grass. "Toss the beanbag in," she said.

Hannah threw her red ball first. The ball hit the ground. It bounced up and hit the hoop. Bonk! It knocked the hoop over. "Silly ball," said Hannah.

Next she picked up the beanbag. It felt soft, like a little pillow. Hannah threw it high. She waited for the bounce. But there was no bounce. The beanbag just went flop. It flopped right down into the hoop.

George clapped. "It stayed in!" he said. "It flops like a sleepy frog," said Hannah. She laughed.

Lilian threw her beanbag too. Flop! It landed inside. "Soft things don't bounce," said Lilian. "They just flop down." Hannah threw again. Flop! In it went.

Then Ms. Hernández rolled a big ball to Hannah. Hannah held out both hands. The ball was too big for one hand. She squeezed with two hands. She caught it! "You did it alone," said Ms. Hernández.

Hannah hugged the ball. "My hands are stuck like glue," she said. Flop, flop, catch! It was a good day.

Harper stood at the little hoop. She held a red beanbag in her hands. Mr. Nakamura set a big ball on the ground. "First, try the beanbag," he said.

Scarlette was next to her. Harper looked at Scarlette. She threw the beanbag. It missed the hoop. It landed on the ground.

Harper picked it up. This time she looked at the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! It dropped through with a soft push of air.

"Quick, catch!" said Scarlette. She rolled the big ball to Harper. Harper held out both hands. The ball came right into them.

Harper laughed. On her shirt, a little sheep bounced too. She threw the beanbag again, her eyes on the hoop. In it went again.

Zoe wanted to ride the small red trike. It was the best one in the yard. There was only one trike and many kids.

Mohamed was first in line. Then came Kaya. Then came Zoe. Zoe watched Mohamed zoom around the cones. He laughed and pedaled fast. Zoe waited in her spot.

Then a boy ran up. He pushed past Kaya. He jumped onto the trike. "Hey!" said Kaya. "That was not your turn." The boy looked at the line. He got off the trike. He walked back to his spot. Mr. Bui said, "A line means you stay in your place until it is your turn."

The boy waited at the end. Mohamed had one more ride. Then Kaya had her turn. She rode slowly and smiled. Then it was Zoe's turn at last.

Zoe pedaled the red trike. The wind tickled her face. It felt just like her dream. "My turn came!" she called. Kaya clapped for her. Mohamed clapped too. After that, Zoe went to the back of the line and waited again.

Zachary sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. Today he was going to Sunny's house. He could not wait.

"Yesterday I went to the park," said his friend Adrien from the next seat. "No wait. I went tomorrow." He chewed his pink gum slowly and thought.

"You went tomorrow?" asked Zachary. "Tomorrow is not here yet." He pointed out the window. The sun was in the sky now. Later the sun would go down. Then tomorrow would come.

Adrien laughed. "No, no. I went yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." He counted on his fingers. "Park day was before this day."

The car stopped at Sunny's house. Zachary jumped out. "Come to my house tomorrow," said Sunny. "We can play in my pink playhouse. Now we can run in the yard."

The two boys ran around the tree once. Then they sat down to wait. Later they would have snacks. "Tomorrow is next," said Zachary, clapping his hands. "But now is for running!"

Felix was at Benson's birthday party. There was a big red truck on the rug. It had a horn that really beeped. Felix wished he could hold it first.

Paxton picked up the truck. He beeped the horn. "My turn first," said Paxton. Felix reached out fast. He almost grabbed the truck. Ms. Carvalho knelt down by his knee. "Let's set the timer," she said. "When the timer runs out, you hand the toy gently to the next person."

The timer ticked and ticked. Paxton drove the truck in a circle. Then the timer rang. Paxton lifted the truck up high. He looked like he might toss it across the rug. Felix held his hands very still. Paxton put the truck into Felix's hands, slowly and gently. "There you go," said Paxton.

Felix beeped the horn two times. He drove past a cute little paper dog on the party table. Then the timer rang again. Felix stood up. He walked over to Benson and put the truck in Benson's hands, gently. Benson smiled and beeped the horn. "It's your turn now," said Felix.

Rain was falling on the window. Audrey put her hand on the glass. The drops made little lines slide down. Was it rainy outside? Yes, it was rainy outside.

Audrey put on her boots. Dad held a big umbrella. It looked like a triangle. "Can it catch the rain?" Audrey asked. "It can," said Dad. They walked to daycare under it. The rain tapped on top. Tap, tap, tap. Audrey stayed dry. Her head was dry. Her coat was dry. "The umbrella keeps rain off my head," she said.

At daycare, Ms. Farah looked out the window. The wind blew. It was windy too. A leaf flew past, fast. Audrey laughed and pointed. Later the rain stopped. The sun came out. Now it was sunny. Audrey and Elianna played outside. The sun felt warm on her face.

Dina was at the craft table. She made a snowman picture with cotton balls. "Snow!" said Dina. "Snowy," said Audrey. She wondered: when it is snowy, do you need mittens? "Yes, you need mittens," said Dina. Audrey looked at the umbrella rack by the door. The umbrellas sat there, still and quiet, waiting for the next rainy day.

Avery sat in her car seat. Her father was driving. They were going home early from the park. Avery wanted to sleep in the car. But she could not sleep. There was a big truck outside. It made a loud sound. "Too loud," Avery said. She covered her ears.
