Next to her sat Lilly. Lilly had a small toy drum. Lilly hit the drum hard. It went boom, boom. That was loud too. Avery's eyes stayed open. The baby in the back was awake now too. He made a loud cry.

"Lilly, can you make it quiet?" Avery asked. Lilly tapped the drum softly. Tap, tap. That was quiet. The truck went far away. That got quiet too. Soon the car was all quiet. The baby closed his eyes. Avery closed her eyes too.

"Did the quiet help him sleep?" Avery whispered. Lilly smiled and tapped one more soft tap. "We win," she whispered back. Avery felt the slow, soft taps on her arm. Then she fell fast asleep.

Charles ran to the big table. Grandma had made soup and bread. Everyone was coming to eat.

Charles picked up his spoon. He was ready to have soup right away. Then Uncle Sam held out his hand. So did Grandma. So did Mama. Everyone was holding hands around the table!

Charles still had the spoon in his fist. He could not hold hands and the spoon too. He looked at his spoon. He looked at Uncle Sam's open hand. So he set the spoon down by his bowl. Now his hand was free!

He took Uncle Sam's hand and Mama's hand. Everyone closed their eyes. "Thank you for this food," Grandma said. Charles said it too. Then everyone said, "Amen!"

A frog sat near the window in the garden. Charles could see it while he ate. He counted the people holding hands before the blessing. One, two, three, four, five, six! Six hands made a circle around the table.

After the blessing, everyone let go. Charles picked his spoon back up. The soup was warm and good. "Can we do hands again tomorrow?" he asked. Grandma laughed and squeezed his fingers. "Every meal," she said. "Every single meal."

Luke sat at the big table. It was Grandma's birthday party. Everyone had a plate of warm noodles. There was a salty soup in a blue bowl.

"First we say the blessing," said Mom.

"What is a blessing?" Luke whispered.

"It is a little thank-you we say together," Mom whispered back. "Close your eyes."

Luke closed his eyes. Then he peeked. He saw Grandpa. Grandpa's eyes were closed too. Grandpa's head was bowed down low, like he was looking at his shoes.

Luke giggled. He bowed his head too. He peeked again. Now Grandpa was peeking at him!

"Peeking boy!" Grandpa whispered.

"Bowing boy!" Luke whispered back.

Everyone said the blessing. Then everyone opened their eyes. Grandma rolled a meatball across the table to Luke.

"Now the noodles!" said Luke, and he picked up his fork.

Jack was in the family car. He looked in his bag. "Where is Bunny?" he asked. Bunny was his soft gray rabbit. It was small and very cute.

Dad drove to the school. Jack hopped out and ran to Mr. Bekele. "I lost my rabbit!" said Jack. Mr. Bekele smiled. He held up a soft gray rabbit. "Is this it?" he asked. Jack grabbed it. "Yes! But how did you know it was mine?" Mr. Bekele pointed at the tag. "Your name is on the tag. Writing your name on a toy's tag helps people know it belongs to you."

Jack squeezed Bunny tight. "One rabbit, one tag, one name," he said. Dad laughed. "Smart boy." In the car, Jack held Bunny all the way home. "Bunny, you are a clever rabbit," said Jack. Bunny said nothing. He was just a toy. But his tag said Jack.

Victor loved nap time at daycare. But after nap time came a problem. His socks were on the floor. His shirt was on the floor too. He could not find his other sock anywhere.

His friend Izhaan had a big idea. "Shoot your socks like a ball," Izhaan said. He pointed at the basket. Victor looked. The basket had a name tag. It said "Laundry Basket."

Victor picked up his squishy sock. He threw it. It went in! He found his other sock under the cot. He threw that one too. It went in as well. Izhaan clapped. "Good shot," he said.

Ms. Whitaker came to help. She smiled at the full basket. "These clothes are dirty," she said. "Now they can be washed." Victor helped her carry the basket. His shirt went in last. Victor waved at the basket. "Bye, bye, socks," he said.

Jackson ran into the big gym. The floor was shiny and squeaky under his shoes. His team wore blue shirts. Ms. Nasser blew her whistle, and the game began.

Jackson tried to kick the ball. It felt heavy on his foot. The other team kicked it far. Then the whistle blew again. The blue team had lost. Jackson frowned. His tummy felt tight.

Ms. Nasser said, "Time to line up." The two teams made a long line. Each player said, "Good game," to the other team. Jackson put out his hand. A boy on the red team shook it. "Good game," the boy said. "Good game," Jackson said back. His frown went away. Then he let Valentina hold his hand, and they went to get cold water cups.

Isla ran out to the playground. The wind blew cold on her nose. Her coat hung open and flapped like wings.

Kyson ran past her. His coat was zipped up tight. "Your coat is open," he said. Isla looked down. She saw two sides of her coat. They were apart.

Ms. Nielsen knelt beside her. "See the little tab?" she said. Isla found the tab at the bottom. She put one side in the other side. Then she pulled the tab up. Zip! The two sides joined together. "I did it!" Isla shouted.

The wind blew again. But now it did not touch her tummy. She was warm inside her coat. She felt like giving her coat a big hug. So she did.

Leonard was by the swings. His coat was open too. The wind made him shiver. "I can help," said Isla. She showed him the tab. He pulled it up. Zip! His coat closed too. Then something small fell out of his pocket. It was a tiny toy car, shiny and red. "A surprise!" said Leonard. He laughed and laughed. "Let's race to the slide," said Isla. They ran, zipped up warm, all the way.

Sebastian wanted his milk at snack time. He ran fast to the little fridge. Ms. Mercado was already there. She held a big jug of cold milk. The door of the fridge was open.

"Look," said Ms. Mercado. "Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut." She pushed the door. It went click. The door was closed. Then she pulled it. The door was open again. Sebastian laughed. He pulled the door shut. Then he pulled it open. Shut, open, shut.

Ariella came over with her cup. She slipped a little, but she did not fall. "My cup has a tight lid," she said. "My milk will not spill." Keira held her cup up high. It was a big cup. Sebastian's cup was small.

Ms. Mercado poured the milk. It was cold from the fridge. The door stayed closed now. "Good helper," said Ms. Mercado. Sebastian smiled and took a slow, big sip.

Aaron sat in the backyard with his markers. He was drawing a big red truck on paper. Flynn sat next to him, drawing a sun.

Aaron reached for the blue marker. It slipped in his hand. The blue tip touched his skin. Now his hand had a blue stripe on it.

Aaron looked at the stripe. His lip began to wobble. "It won't come off," he said. He thought he might cry.

Mr. Goh was watering the flowers nearby. He came over and looked at Aaron's hand. "Let's try soap and water," he said. "These markers are washable. Washable means they wash off."

Aaron went to the outside tap. Mr. Goh put soap on his hand. Aaron rubbed and rubbed under the water. The blue stripe got smaller. Then it was gone. His hand was clean.

Aaron laughed. "It went away!" He ran back to Flynn. "Look, one stripe, two stripes, three stripes!" he said, drawing on his paper. "And if I get one on my hand, I can wash it off."

Flynn smiled and drew a big yellow snowman with a bumpy carrot nose. "The snowman has no snow," Flynn said.

"Then we will draw him some," said Aaron, and he picked up the white marker.

Benjamin had a little dog. The dog was brown and white. His name was Pip. Pip came home in a small box with holes. Benjamin wanted to play right away.

Mom put food in Pip's bowl. Pip began to eat. Benjamin reached for his tail. "Not now," Mom said softly. "Let Pip eat." Benjamin sat on his hands and waited. He watched the bowl. Crunch, crunch, crunch. The bowl became empty. Pip looked up. Then Benjamin petted him, and Pip wagged his tail.

Later that day, Pip curled up on his soft mat. His eyes closed. He was sleeping. Benjamin wanted to read him a story. He wanted Pip to see the stormy sky out the window. But he remembered the empty bowl. He tiptoed past the mat. He found Mom instead. "Pip is sleeping," Benjamin whispered. "I will wait."

Pip woke up and stretched. He bounced to Benjamin. They played with a red ball on the rug. After that, Benjamin helped clean the bowl. He filled it with water, with Mom's help. Pip drank it all. Benjamin hugged him gently. "Good dog," said Benjamin. "Do you want to hear my story now?"

Splash day was here. Anthony put on his swim shorts. He had gotten dressed all by himself. Mr. Janssen filled the little pool with water from the safe hose.

Anthony and Kaysen jumped in. Splash! Water went everywhere. Miley laughed and splashed too. Soon Anthony was dripping wet. Water ran down his arms. He ran to the grass to play tag.

"Wait!" called Mr. Janssen. "You are all wet!" Anthony looked down. Drip, drip, drip. His shorts were soaked. He was cold and shivery. Then Mr. Janssen held up a big soft towel. Anthony came back for it. Mr. Janssen rubbed his arms and legs. The towel dried his body. Now he was warm and dry. Anthony giggled. "The towel ate all the water!" he said.

After splash time, Anthony helped hang the wet towel on the fence. The sun would dry it too. Then he got dressed again in his dry school clothes. All that splashing made him thirsty. Mr. Janssen gave him water. Kaysen sipped his cup too. Anthony hung his own towel on the hook, all by himself, like a big kid with a job to do. "Look at me," he said. "I hung my towel up high!"

Dylan sat in the kitchen. He wanted a sweet drink. Mom poured him orange juice. It tasted sweet and yummy.

Then Mom cut a lemon. Dylan saw the yellow slice. It looked like a little sun. He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled sharp and lemony. "That looks like juice," said Dylan. "Can I try?"

"You can touch it," said Mom. "It is a bit sticky." Dylan touched the lemon slice. His fingers felt wet. Then he stuck out his tongue and licked it. His face scrunched up. "Wah! Not sweet!"

Mom laughed. "A lemon is sour," she said. "Not sweet like your juice."

Dylan shook his head. He took a big sip of orange juice. Sweet again! He heard the fridge hum behind him. He smiled at Mom. "Lemon for you. Juice for me."

Paint day was here at last. Mila wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. Not one drop.

"Where can orange come from?" she asked.

Aidan held up two cups. "Watch this," he said. He poured red paint into a bowl. Then he poured yellow paint in too. Mila stirred it round and round with her brush.

One, two, three, four. Red and yellow grew into orange! "It is a magic pumpkin color," said Mila.

She painted her pumpkin orange. She painted one green leaf. She painted two blue stars. She painted three yellow moons. Her shoe tapped on the floor, loose on her foot, tap, tap, tap.

"Look, Ameera!" said Mila. "My pumpkin can fly to the moon."

The pumpkin winked from the paper. "Take me with you," it said.

Arnaud was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to feed the baby chicks in the yard. Grandpa said, "First we count them. Ten chicks need ten seeds."

Arnaud began to count. "One, two, four," he said. Grandpa shook his head. "Something is wrong," he said. "Try again, slow and easy."

Arnaud counted the fluffy yellow chicks. "One, two, three," he said. The chicks peeped softly and wiggled. "Four, five, six," he said. More chicks came to his shoes. They felt warm and tickly.

"Seven, eight, nine," said Arnaud. One little chick looked up at him. "Ten!" said Arnaud. Grandpa smiled and put ten seeds in his hand. Arnaud dropped the seeds, one at a time. Each seed made a chick run over. Peck, peck, peck.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," said Arnaud. All the chicks were eating. The tenth chick sat down by his foot and fell asleep.

Georgia put on her special boots today. She wore them to the hair salon. Mama held her hand as they walked in.

Georgia sat in the big chair. The hairdresser put a soft cape on her. Then she picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Georgia counted. "One, two, three," she said softly.

Soon Georgia wiggled in the chair. She rubbed her neck. "It itches," she said. Tiny bits of cut hair had landed there.

The hairdresser smiled. "I will brush them off," she said. She took a soft brush. She swept Georgia's neck. One, two, three little sweeps.

The itching stopped. Georgia sat very still now. She looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat.

"You can shop for a bow at the front desk," the hairdresser said. Georgia picked a pink one. She clipped it in right away.

"Pretty girl," said Mama.

Georgia smiled at her boots. "Big girl," she said.

Freya wore her striped dress to the big dinner at the temple hall. Long tables ran across the room. Bowls of warm soup sat on every table.

A boy named Ameer sat down beside her. His grandma smiled at everyone. Then she said, "Bon appétit!"

Freya looked up. What did that mean? It sounded like a song.

"Bon appétit," Ameer said. "It means have a good meal. In France, people say it before they eat."

Freya tried the words in her mouth. "Bon appétit," she said. Ameer's grandma clapped. The whole table said it too. Then everyone picked up their spoons.

At home that night, Freya sat on her bed. Mom brought milk and bread. Freya took a big breath.

"Bon appétit, Mom!"

Mom laughed and picked up her cup.

Liam ran to the big window at daycare. The sun was out! He put his hand on the warm glass. "Sunny day!" he said. Ms. Pérez smiled. "Sunny days need sun hats," she said. She put a little blue hat on Liam's head.

Then Liam saw a big grey cloud. It slid over the sun. The glass went cool. The room went dim. "Where did the sun go?" asked Clementine. "The cloud is hiding it," said Kelly. Liam waited. He watched and watched. The cloud did not move. "I want my sun," said Liam. He felt sorry for the warm glass.

Then the wind came. The tree by the window waved its leaves. The wind pushed the cloud along. Slowly, slowly, the cloud slid away. The sun popped out! The glass was warm again. "The sun came back!" Liam shouted. Ms. Pérez said, "Windy days need coats." She gave everyone a coat and a big hug. Liam ran outside in the sun and the wind. His coat flapped like wings.

Avery ran to the sandbox. She had a big red shovel. She had a small blue bucket too. The sun felt warm on her hat.

Reece was there. He sat in the sand. He had no shovel. He had no bucket. He dug with just his hands. The sand fell through his fingers. "I want to make a hill," he said. His voice was small.

Avery looked at her shovel. She looked at Reece. She held out the red shovel. "You can use it too," she said. Reece smiled big. He filled the bucket with sand. He patted it down. He tipped it over. A hill!

Then Reece gave the shovel back. "Your turn," he said. Avery scooped and scooped. The sand was cool and a little sticky on her palms. Together they made three hills. Then they made one big castle.

Mr. Luo walked by. "What a tall castle," he said. Avery and Reece sat back and looked at it. "We both dug it," said Avery. Reece nodded and patted the last hill flat.

Lena woke up and saw snow at her window. "Snow!" she said. She felt so excited.

Today Jaxtyn was coming to play. Lena was excited about that too. She jumped on her rug. She bounced on her bed. She shouted, "Jaxtyn is coming!"

Then she heard a small crash. Her bouncing made her toy bunny fall down. Bunny looked sad on the floor. Lena felt sad too. She picked up Bunny and hugged him.

"Mama, I can't stop bouncing," Lena said. Mama sat with her. "Let's find a calm way to wait."

Lena tried sitting still. That was hard. Then she took slow, big breaths. In and out. In and out. Her bouncing stopped. Her tummy felt hungry, so Mama got her some toast.

Then came a knock at the door. "Jaxtyn!" Lena said. She walked to the door, nice and calm, holding Bunny tight. "Jaxtyn, I made a calm way to wait. Want to see the snow?"

Isabelle went to the pet store with her dad. She wanted to buy a toy for her cat. First they walked past the foods. There were big bags of cat food. There were little cans of fish. "Look at all this food!" said Isabelle.

Next they saw the animals. There were fish in tanks. There were bunnies in cages. There were birds on a perch. Then Isabelle found a small feather on the floor. It was soft and blue.

"A bird must have lost this!" said Isabelle. "Birds are the animals with feathers!" A man who worked there smiled. "Yes, that feather came from one of our birds."

"Can we look at the birds?" asked Isabelle. Her dad said yes. Isabelle drew a circle in the air with her finger, all around the bird cages. A yellow bird dropped one more feather. It floated down, down, down, right into Isabelle's hand.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Matthew wanted to make something with him, something just theirs. In the kitchen, Grandpa got out a big bowl. "I will show you my special bread," he said. "My mother made it, and her mother made it too. Our family has made it for a long time."

Matthew poured the flour. Grandpa showed him how to mix and press the dough. Matthew pressed it flat, then folded it, then pressed again. It was soft and warm, like a cloud. They put the dough in the bowl and covered it with a towel. Then they had to wait. Matthew wanted to peek. "Not yet," said Grandpa, and they sat down to talk about the park instead.

After a long time, Grandpa lifted the towel. The dough was big now. Matthew's eyes went wide. His pressing had helped make it grow. Dad put the pan into the hot oven, and Matthew watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

The next day they took the bread to the park. Marion was there by the lion statue, and Ariel was on the swings. Matthew gave them each a piece. "My grandpa taught me," he said. "It is our family bread." Ariel took a bite and smiled. "Can I help next time?"

Eva sat at the big table. It was cooking class at school. Mr. Quinn put warm toast on her plate. Eva wanted to spread butter all by herself.

She picked up her knife. The butter was cold and hard. It came straight from the fridge. Eva pushed the hard butter on her toast. The butter made a hole in the toast. "Oh no," said Eva. Timothee looked over. Beckham looked over too.

"Let the butter sit out," said Mr. Quinn. "We will wait a bit." So they waited. They poured milk into cups while they waited. Eva poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. Outside, the rain tapped on the window.

Then Eva touched the butter. It was soft now. She pushed the soft butter on her toast. It spread and spread. No holes! The toast was smooth and sweet-smelling. Eva took a big bite. "Yum," she said.

Eva looked at the cold butter dish. She looked at the soft butter dish. She pushed the soft butter on one more piece of toast. Smooth again. "Soft butter is the best," said Eva. Beckham clapped his hands. Timothee laughed. Mr. Quinn smiled and said, "One more round of toast for everyone."

Addison sat on the playroom floor. She had a big box of blocks. She wanted to build a purple house. First she picked a purple square. It had four sides, all the same. She set it flat on the rug.

Her friend Brooklyn came in. Brooklyn held a triangle. It had three sides. "Look at my roof," Brooklyn said. "It points up." Addison clapped. Then Addison wanted a roof too. She looked and looked in the box. She found a circle, but it was round like a pancake. She found a rectangle, but it was long like a train. No triangle for her.

Then Addison had an idea. She took her purple square. She turned it. Now one corner pointed up at the ceiling. "This is a new shape," she said. Brooklyn leaned close. "Turn it back," said Brooklyn. Addison turned it back, slow and careful. It lay flat again. Four sides, all the same. It was still the same square. Addison turned it again. The corner pointed up again. It still fit together just the same.

Addison turned it back and forth. "Square. Square. Square," she said. It was a square both ways. Then she stacked two more squares and made tall purple walls. She begged Brooklyn, "Please pass the little plane." Brooklyn gave her the toy plane. It had little square windows and one round window, too.

The two friends flew the plane over the purple house. It zoomed in a big circle. It zoomed past a rectangle block that stood like a door. Then the plane landed on the roof. "Safe landing," said Brooklyn. Addison smiled and spun the plane's wheels.

Maeve stood by the pool. The water was blue and still. Tiara and Viora stood by the big hoop. Mr. Tse held a box of beanbags.

"Your turn, Maeve," said Mr. Tse. Maeve took a beanbag. She held it with both hands. She threw it. The beanbag went up. Then it came down. It landed in the hoop. Splash, into the pool it went.

Maeve wanted to throw them all. She grabbed another beanbag. She grabbed one more. Tiara stood and waited. Viola stood and waited too.

Mr. Tse knelt down. "Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn," he said. He put the beanbag in Tiara's hands.

Maeve watched. Tiara threw one beanbag. Then Viola threw one beanbag. Then it was Maeve again. One, two, three, one, two, three. Maeve liked the counting.

Then Mr. Tse brought a big red ball. "Catch with both hands," he said. The ball came to Maeve. She opened her arms wide. She caught it with both hands. The ball was big and furry and soft.

Maeve hugged the ball. "My turn, then your turn," she said to Tiara. She rolled the ball across the wet floor.

Connor went to the park with his friend Emberly. The sun was warm. Connor felt thirsty, so he drank from his little water bottle. Then he saw kids playing a game by the swings. "Can I play too?" he asked. A girl named Dahlia said, "Yes! We are playing tag. You run when I count to three."

Connor played and laughed. But then a boy said, "New rule! Now nobody can tag me!" He tagged everyone, but no one could tag him back. The other kids stopped running. They sat down on the grass. "That is not fair," said Dahlia. "We all follow the same rules in a game." The boy looked sad. "Okay," he said. "Same rules for everyone."

The game started again. Connor picked a daisy while he waited his turn to be the tagger. Then he counted, "One, two, three!" and everyone ran. Emberly laughed and ran fast. Connor tagged her gently. "Your turn!" he said. They played until the sky turned orange. "Time to go home," his dad called from the gate. Connor waved to his friends. "Same game tomorrow?" asked Dahlia. "Yes!" said Connor.

Elena was at Grandpa's house. She wanted to make a card for his birthday. "He is ten today," said Mom. Elena got paper and glue. She glued on ten red buttons. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Then she counted some more. "Four, five, six, seven." The last buttons went on. "Eight, nine, ten." Elena wanted to write the numbers too. Mom wrote 1 to 9 in a row. Elena looked for the number ten. She could not find it. "Where is ten?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Ten is a 1 and then a 0," she said. Elena wrote a big 1. She wrote a 0 right after it. There it was! Grandpa was far away in the garden. Elena ran to him and waved the card high. "Happy birthday, Grandpa!" she said.

Milan had a little box of books. He wanted the animal book. He dug in the box. He found a truck book. He found a ball book. No animal book!

"Where is it?" said Milan. "I want the animals. The dog. The cat. The duck."

His mom came to help. "Let's make a shelf like a library," she said. "A library puts its books on shelves in groups. Then people can find them."

Mom put a little shelf by the grass-green rug. "Animal books go here," she said. "Toy books go here. Food books go here."

Milan clapped. He put the truck book on the toy shelf. He put the apple book on the food shelf. One, two, three books!

"Now the animals," said Milan. He looked on the animal shelf. There was the dog book! There was the cat book! There was the duck book! He found them all by himself.

"I found them!" said Milan. "Groups help!"

The doorbell rang. It was Ms. Harper from next door. She had a plate of cookies she had baked.

"Could I borrow an animal book?" asked Ms. Harper. "My grass is full of birds and I want to read about them."

Milan ran to the shelf. "Bird books live here!" he said. "With the dog and the cat and the duck!"

He handed her the bird book, the top one in the group.

Joseph woke up early. Today he would see the dentist. It was his very first time.

"I want clean teeth," said Joseph.

His mom helped him at the sink. She put minty toothpaste on his brush. Joseph brushed his little teeth. Up and down. Up and down. The brush made white foam. The foam grew and grew.

Joseph closed his mouth. The foam tasted like mint. He wanted to swallow it.

Then he remembered. His mom had told him, "Spit it out, don't swallow it."

Joseph leaned over the sink. He spit the foam out. Ptoo! The foam went down the drain. All gone. His mouth felt clean and dry.

"Good job," said his mom. "You spat it out, just like at the dentist."

Joseph smiled a big smile. He brushed one more tooth and spat again. Ptoo!

Then he took a cookie for later. He walked to the door, hand in hand with his mom.

"I am ready," said Joseph.

Camille sat on the rug at school. Ms. Otieno picked up her drum. She played a slow, steady beat. Boom, boom, boom.

"Let's sing our song," said Ms. Otieno. "Clap too." Camille clapped fast, fast, fast. Her claps did not match the drum. Nolan clapped whenever he liked. His claps did not match either. Londyn put her hands in her lap. She looked sad.

"Listen first," said Ms. Otieno. She played again. Boom, boom, boom. Camille listened with a still face. Then she clapped at the same time as the drum. Her claps and the beat fit together. Londyn tried it too. She smiled her big brown smile.

"Now we sing," said Ms. Otieno. Camille sang the rhyme all by herself. She did not miss a word. Londyn clapped along, and Camille shared her drum beat with a happy clap, clap, clap.

Wesley was on the swim team. He loved the pool. The big trees by the pool looked like a little green forest. Today the sun was very hot.

Wesley forgot his water bottle at home. He swam his laps. Then his legs felt slow. His mouth felt dry. At break time, he sat on the side of the pool. His friend Siena sat down too. She took a big drink from her bottle. "Players drink water during breaks," she said, "especially on hot days." Wesley watched her drink.

Then Ms. Nwosu came over. She held out a blue bottle. "Here, Wesley. You can use this one." Wesley reached for it. He drank and drank. Soon his legs felt fast again. He swam his best lap of the whole day. "Thank you, Ms. Nwosu," he said. "That was polite," said Siena with a smile. Wesley waved his arms in the air.

Owen sat at the big table in writing club. Mr. Islam gave each child a pencil. Owen held his pencil tight. He tried to write the O in his name. His lines came out fat and fuzzy. They were not round like a real O. He looked at Jenny's paper. Her letters were thin and neat. Owen frowned at his own big fuzzy circles.

Owen held up his pencil. The tip was dull and flat. Jenny's pencil had a sharp pointy tip. Owen walked to Mr. Islam. "My pencil tip is dull," he said. "Can you sharpen it?" Mr. Islam smiled. "Yes, a dull pencil needs sharpening," he said. He turned the pencil in the sharpener. Then he gave it back. The tip was sharp and pointy now.

Owen held the pencil the way Mr. Islam had shown him. He sat by the open window next to the bowl of crayons. He drew his O again. This time the line was thin. It made a neat round circle. Then he made a W, an E, and an N. His whole name sat on the paper. "Look, Jenny!" Owen said. "I did it. That is my name."

Brielle sat at the dinner table. Her spoon was empty. Her bowl was empty too. That made her face turn down, down, down. "Where is my soup?" she asked. Dad pointed at the pot. "It is too hot right now," he said. "I will blow on it to cool it down. Then you can eat."

Brielle waited. She was sad. Her tummy made a little growl. Then Dad blew and blew on the soup. He poured some in her bowl. "Try one sip," he said. Brielle sipped. It was warm and good. Her mouth went up into a big smile.

"Look at that!" said Dad. "Your face is happy. Your smile shows it." Brielle made another face next. She pushed her mouth into a sad shape. "That is my sad face," she said. Dad laughed. "Your face is awake and telling me everything," he said. Brielle sipped more soup. Her smile got bigger and bigger. "More, please!" she said. Dad filled her bowl again.

Xavier put on his red hat. The sun was warm on his face. But the trees began to whoosh and sway. "It is windy today," said Mr. Chatterjee.

The wind blew hard. Xavier's hat flew right off his head! It tumbled over the grass. Xavier ran after it. His friend Rhett ran too. "Grab it!" Rhett shouted. The hat rolled near the sandbox. Rhett stopped it with his foot.

Then the sky turned grey. Rain began to fall, big drops on the slide. "Rain!" said Xavier. Everyone ran to the bench under the roof. Xavier looked at his wet hat. "The answer is simple," he said. He put the wet hat on the bench. Then he pulled his hood up over his head.

The rain stopped. The sun came back out. "The sun is my friend," said Xavier, and he held his hat in both hands all the way home.

Addison sat at the kitchen table. The bowls were warm. The spoons were shiny. Mama set down the rice, and Addison grabbed her spoon fast.

"Wait," said Mouhamed, her friend. "We say Bismillah first."

"What is Bismillah?" asked Addison.

"It means in the name of God," said Mouhamed. "Many Muslims say it before they eat."

Addison put her spoon down. She folded her small hands. The steam rose up, thin and white, like a little spring from the bowl. "Bismillah," she said. The word felt good in her mouth.

Mama smiled. "Now we can eat," she said.

Addison took one big bite. The rice was warm and soft. Then she spoke again, quiet and happy. "Bismillah," she said, "before my next bite too."

Mouhamed laughed and clapped his hands. "You said it all by yourself."

Addison held her spoon up high like a flag.

Colton sat at the kitchen table. He had three paint pots. Red, yellow, blue. He wanted to paint a rainbow. But a rainbow had more colours. He only had three!

"Those are the primary colours," said Ms. Levy. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours."

Colton stood on his chair to look at all the pots. He dipped his brush in red. Then he dipped it in yellow. He made a dot on the paper. The dot turned orange!

"Orange!" Colton shouted. "One more colour for my rainbow!"

He painted fast. Red and yellow made orange. He mixed blue and yellow. Green! He mixed red and blue. Purple!

Colton painted every day that week. On Friday, Adina came over. She sat near him at the table.

"I only see three pots," said Adina. "Where is the orange paint?"

Colton just smiled. He dipped his brush in red, then yellow. He made a big orange sun on the paper.

"Now you try," he said. Adina took the brush.

It was evening at the farmhouse. The lights went out all at once. The kitchen went black. "Oh no," said Mom. She lit a little lantern.

Elizabeth held Mom's hand. They walked slowly. One step, two steps, three steps. "I can't see the clock," said Elizabeth. "The clocks are off too," said Mom.

They found Daddy in the hall. He had a flashlight. "Follow me," he said. The light made a bright spot on the floor. Elizabeth followed it all the way to the sofa. They sat together and counted the lantern glows. One lantern, one flashlight, one moon in the window.

Then the lights came back on. Everything was bright again. Elizabeth looked at the oven. The clock on it was blinking. Blink, blink, blink. "The clock is blinking," she said. "It needs to be set again," said Mom. Elizabeth watched Mom push the buttons. Mom read the numbers out loud, and Elizabeth said them with her. The clock stopped blinking.

"There," said Mom. "Now it's bedtime, my friend." Elizabeth smiled at the steady little numbers. "Good night, clock," she said.

Zoe went to the pharmacy with Dad. Today was a big day. Zoe would meet the dentist. "Let's pick a toothbrush," said Dad. Zoe found a pink one. She held it tight.

At the dentist, a big chair waited. Zoe climbed up with help. A light hung above the chair. The dentist turned it on. Zoe squinted. The light was so bright!

The dentist smiled. He gave Zoe small sunglasses. Zoe put them on. "Now the light won't hurt my eyes," she said. The light shone into her mouth. The dentist looked at all her teeth. "Nice clean teeth," he said. The bright light above the chair helped him see inside Zoe's mouth.

Zoe got a sticker. It had a playground on it. "Can we go to the real playground?" Zoe asked. Dad laughed. "Yes, Zoe. Let's go."

Ruby went with her dad to the phone repair shop. There was a little table by the wall. On it sat a big tablet with a bright screen.

The repair man, Mr. Krause, smiled. "Want to draw, Ruby?" He tapped the button. The screen woke up. It went from black to bright! Ruby tapped too. The screen lit up again. Her tap made that happen.

"Now find the paintbrush," said Mr. Krause. Ruby looked at the screen. Many small pictures sat there. She saw a cat. She saw a star. Then she saw a little paintbrush. "The small pictures are icons," said Mr. Krause. Ruby tapped the paintbrush icon. Tap! The drawing app opened. A white page was ready.

Ruby drew a big red circle. Then she drew dots for rain. She drew a house with a yellow door. "That one is lovely," said her dad.

Then it was time to go. Ruby tapped the top of the screen. The tablet went dark. She set it on the table. "All tidy," she said. Mr. Krause gave her a wave. "Come draw again soon."

The lights went out. Henri stood still in the dark. "Mama?" he called. "I am here," said Mama. She found him and held his hand. The house was very quiet. No fridge hum. No fan.

Henri wanted light in his room. Mama lit a candle on the table. The flame was small and orange. Henri reached for it. He wanted to carry it with him. "Only a grown-up lights candles and looks after them," said Mama. She took the candle away. She put it in a safe spot. Then she gave Henri a flashlight instead.

Henri pressed the button. Click! The light came on. He shone it on his teddy bear. The bear looked bright in the dark. Henri laughed. The candle gave one orange glow. The flashlight gave a big white beam. His mama watched the candle. Henri watched his beam.

They sat together on the back step. The sky outside was soft and dark. Henri held the flashlight on his lap. Soon the lights came back on. "All done," said Mama. Henri gave his teddy bear a goodnight squeeze under his blanket.

Sofia sat at her little desk in the nursery room. Her baby sister was coming home today. Sofia wanted to hold her so much.

"When can I hold her?" Sofia asked.

"You can hold her while sitting down," said her mom. "I will help you."

Sofia waited on the couch. Her mom sat right beside her. Then Dad came in with a full basket. The baby was inside!

Sofia patted the soft blanket. The baby made a tiny sound. Sofia's heart went boom boom boom.

"Hold your arms like this," said Mom. Sofia sat very still. Mom placed the baby in her arms.

The baby grabbed Sofia's finger. Her hand was so small!

Then the baby rolled her head and made a funny face. Sofia laughed.

"I am your big sister," Sofia whispered. The baby blinked one eye.

"Hello, little one," said Sofia.

Scarlett ran to the snack table. She had been digging in the sand. Her hands were very muddy. Mr. Singh held up his hand. "Stop, Scarlett," he said. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Scarlett looked at her muddy hands. Muddy hands and yummy crackers? She turned and went to the sink. Mika was already there. "Watch," said Mika. He rubbed soap on his hands. Bubbles grew big and white. The mud went down the drain. Where did the mud go, Scarlett wondered?

Scarlett washed her hands too. She rubbed and rubbed. Now her hands were clean. Mr. Singh gave her a plate. She ate her crackers and her apple slices. The crackers were yummy. Would the crackers taste like soap? No. They just tasted like crackers.

After snack came story time. Mr. Singh read a book about a woman who baked bread. Scarlett sat with Emerson. She looked down at her hands. Clean hands, then snack. "Wash first," she whispered to Emerson. Emerson nodded and smiled. Then Scarlett turned the page corner up, just a little, to see the bread.

Arthur sat at the dinner table. His face was sad. His dad put a plate in front of him.

"No park today," said Arthur. "The rain came."

"I know," said Dad. "That made you sad."

Arthur pushed his peas around. "I wanted the swings. I wanted to see Noelie and Micah there."

Dad sat down too. "Rain made the park close. But we still have dinner."

They ate together. Then Dad had an idea. "Do you want to be a team after dinner?"

"A team?" said Arthur. His eyes got big.

"Yes. We can build a blanket fort in the living room."

Arthur felt something new inside. He was excited! He ate his peas fast. He ate his bread fast too.

"That was a naughty thing," he giggled, "eating so fast!"

Dad laughed. "It was a bit naughty. But it is fine."

They carried soft blankets to the couch. They used chairs and pillows. Arthur tucked a blanket over the top. The fort stood up tall.

"Come in!" said Arthur.

Dad crawled in with him. It was cozy and warm inside.

"I was sad," said Arthur. "But now I am happy."

Dad smiled. "Feelings can change like that."

Just then the phone rang. It was Micah. "We made a fort too!" said Micah.

"Come see ours tomorrow," said Arthur. He gave a big, happy shout, and the blanket roof wiggled above their heads.

Arthur ran to the swings at the playground. The sun felt warm on his face. His mom sat on a long bench nearby. Josiah was already on the swing. "Can I go high?" Arthur asked. "Yes, stay where I can see you," said his mom.

Arthur and Josiah pumped their legs. The wind blew past Arthur's ears. Then they saw Mr. Bianchi by the park grill. He was cooking corn. Little flames jumped up under the grill. Arthur felt hot air on his cheeks, even from far away. "The fire makes it hot," said Josiah. Arthur stood back with his friend.

Then Arthur saw something shiny in the grass. It was small and silver. He bent down to look. It was a lighter. The kind grown-ups use. Arthur did not pick it up. He kept his hands behind his back.

"Mr. Bianchi!" Arthur called. "There is a lighter in the grass." Mr. Bianchi came over. He picked it up and put it in his pocket. "Thank you, Arthur. Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," he said. "Can I have some corn?" asked Arthur. "When it is cooked and cool," said Mr. Bianchi.

Arthur and Josiah sat on the long bench with his mom. The corn smelled sweet and smoky. Soon Mr. Bianchi brought over two warm pieces. Arthur blew on his corn, one, two, three. Then he took a small bite. "Yum," he said. "Still a little hot, but yummy." Josiah laughed and blew on his corn too.

Luka was going to the car. He had his red flag toy in his hand. Then he dropped it. "Oh no!" said Luka. "Where did my flag go?"

He ran around the car. He looked fast. He looked under the car. He looked by the door. He could not find it. "Did I look everywhere?" he asked himself. "No. I looked too fast. I missed places."

So Luka tried a new way. He stood at one door. He looked and looked there. Then he moved to the next door. He looked there too. One place at a time. Not fast. Slow and careful.

At the back door, he got down on his knees. He peeked under the seat. There it was! The red flag was stuck by the seat belt. "I found it!" said Luka. He waved the flag high.

Papa came out. "Are you ready?" he asked. "Yes!" said Luka. He held his flag all the way to school.

The lights went out. The TV went dark too. Harrison poked the big screen. "Wake up, TV," he said.

Dad came in with a flashlight. He clicked it on. "The power is out," Dad said. "No TV tonight." Harrison frowned. "What can we do with no plug?"

Then he looked at the shelf. His book was there. His puzzle was there. His board game was there. Harrison picked up the book. He turned a page. It worked! No plug needed. "Dad, look! Books work in the dark!" Dad laughed. "Fetch your game too," he said.

They sat on the floor. Dad held the flashlight up high. Harrison rolled the dice. He moved his little red piece. Then Dad rolled a six. "Oh no!" said Harrison. Dad was winning!

Mom brought two cookies. Harrison munched his cookie and rolled the dice again. He moved all the way to the end. "I win! I win!" he said.

Just then, the lights came back on. The TV blinked awake. Harrison looked at the TV. Then he looked at the game. "One more game, Dad," he said. "A brave player never quits." Dad grinned and picked up the dice.

Grace went to the pharmacy with her dad. Ms. Ramírez worked there. She had pink bottles of soap on a shelf.

Then Grace saw a little dog. The dog was soft. Grace petted the dog. She petted him again and again.

"Lunch next," said her dad. He held up a sandwich.

Grace looked at her hands. They had dog hair on them. "I need to wash," she said.

"Yes! Soap first, then food," said her dad.

Ms. Ramírez showed Grace the sink. Grace pumped the pink soap. She rubbed her hands. She counted to twenty. One, two, three, all the way to twenty!

"Now my hands are clean," said Grace. She held them up. No more dog hair.

She got her sandwich and took a big bite. "Mmm," said Grace.

Ms. Ramírez smiled. "Come back soon," she said.

"Wash, wash, wash," sang Grace. Then she waved to the dog.

Addison got a little blue card. It was her very own library card. She held it with both hands. "My card," she said. Her dad smiled. "Yes. Now you can borrow a book."

They walked to the library. Addison picked a book about a dirty pig. The pig liked to eat apples. Addison hugged the book all the way home. She sat on the bottom step and looked at every page. Then she looked at it again.

After three sleeps, the book had to go back. Addison did not want to let it go. "It's my book," she said. "It is a borrowed book," said her dad. "See that slot in the wall? That is the book return slot. We drop books there when we bring them back." Addison held the book tight. She waited. She waited a little more. Then she held it up and waved. "Bye bye, pig book," she said. She pushed it into the slot. It slid down, out of sight.

The next day they went back inside. Addison used her card again. She found another pig book. She waved at the return slot as they walked by. "See you soon," she said.

Alice went to the hotel pool with her dad. She saw Fatoumata and Aira playing in the water. "Come in, Alice!" said Fatoumata. Alice held the edge of the pool. She wanted to swim, but her feet felt wobbly.

"Hold on tight," said the coach. Alice held the edge of the pool. Then she kicked her legs in the water. Kick, kick, kick! Big splashes flew up. Aira laughed. "The water jumped!" said Aira. "It jumped because you kicked!"

Alice kicked harder. Kick, kick, kick! A loud splash hit the coach. Water ran down his face. He laughed too. "Good kicking, Alice," he said.

Fatoumata wanted to try. Alice showed her how. Fatoumata held the edge of the pool. She kicked her legs. Kick, kick, kick! A big splash went up, up, up. "My turn!" said Aira. The three friends kicked and splashed. A big white owl flew over the pool. It looked down at them. Alice kicked one more time. "Bye, owl!" she said, waving her wet hand.

Kai sat at the paint table at summer camp. He had red paint. He had yellow paint. He wanted to make a new colour.

"Try mixing them," said Ms. Kaya.

Kai stirred red and yellow together. The paint turned orange! "Wow," said Kai. He poked the wet paint with his finger. Now there was a fingerprint in it. The orange had a smudge. "Oh no," said Kai.

"That paint is still wet," said Amirah. "It smudged your picture."

"Next time I will wait," said Kai. He painted a thick blue cat next. Then he painted a red nose on it. He sat on his hands and counted to ten, slowly.

Amirah leaned close. "Is it dry yet?"

"Not yet," said Kai. "Don't touch my cat nose!"

The cat nose turned purple, and Kai waited and waited, sitting on his hands.

Layla sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to draw snow. Big soft snow, all over the paper. She took her white crayon. She drew and drew on the white paper. But nothing showed up. "My snow is gone," said Layla. She held the paper up to the light. Still no snow. Her finger felt sticky, but it did not hurt. Then her shadow fell across the paper. She could see the shadow. It was dark on the white. So dark things showed up, and white did not.

Amayah came in. "I want to draw a cute red mitten," she said. She picked red paper for the mitten and a yellow crayon for a star. Layla looked at the paper stack. There was green paper, yellow paper, and blue paper. Layla took the blue paper. She drew with her white crayon again. The snow showed up! White dots on blue, like real snow. Fresh snow is white, and on blue it looked white and soft.

Amayah clapped her hands. "It looks like a snowy day!" she said. Layla drew one more white dot. Then she smiled and held the picture up to the window.

Parker was at Grandma's house. The table was set for dinner. Parker saw a big basket of warm bread. His tummy made a little growl.

Parker pulled a piece of bread from the basket. He was just about to take a bite. Then Grandma held up her hand. "Wait, Parker," she said. "First we say the blessing." Grandma said the blessing. She said thank you for the food. Parker looked around. Everyone had empty hands. Nobody was eating yet.

So Parker put his bread down on his plate. He folded his hands too. He waited and waited. Then Grandma said "Amen." Everyone picked up their food at the same time. Parker took a big bite of bread. It was soft and warm.

At the next meal, Parker did not reach early. He put his hands in his lap. He waited for the blessing all by himself. When Grandma said "Amen," Parker smiled and picked up his bread. "Can I say it too sometime?" he asked. Grandma said, "Yes, next time, sweet boy."

William looked out the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling down. "Snowy day!" said William. He put on his red coat. He put on his boots. He ran to the playground with his dad.

Boaz was there. Alivia was there too. They all wore mittens. William did not wear mittens. He had left them at home.

"Let's make snowballs," said Boaz. William picked up snow. He packed it with his hands. He made a big snowball. Then his hands felt cold. Very, very cold. "Ow," said William. He held his hands under his arms.

Alivia came close. "My hands stay warm," she said. She held up her blue mittens. Boaz held up his green gloves. "Mittens keep your hands warm," said Alivia.

William's dad had a pocket. He pulled out a small pair of mittens. "Try these," he said. William put them on. He picked up more snow. He packed a new snowball. His hands stayed warm this time.

The wind blew a little. It was windy and snowy. But William kept playing. He threw the snowball to Boaz. Boaz laughed and threw one back.

At home, William looked out the window again. The snow kept falling. He put his mittens by the door. He patted them softly. "Warm hands tomorrow," he said. Then his dad tucked him in, and William fell asleep.

Maverick sat at the dinner table. His mom set down a big basket of picture cards. "These fell in the soup box," she said. "Can you help?" Maverick dumped them out. Cards went everywhere!

"Look, a cat," said Maverick. He heard the cards go swish on the table. He put the cat card in one pile. Then a dog card. Then a bird card with a blue feather. "Animals," he said. "Animals go together."

Then he found a ball card. It was not an animal. He made a new pile. A teddy bear card. A drum card. "Toys!" he said. Siya would love this game. Then he found an apple card. Not an animal. Not a toy. New pile! A carrot. A banana. "Foods," he said.

His mom looked at his piles. "So neat," she said. Maverick felt proud. "Mom, the cards are a zoo, a toy shop, and a store!" he said. He patted the biggest pile, and the bird with the blue feather sat right on top.

Hailey put on her swimsuit. She was on the swim team now. Today was the big meet at the pool.

"I want to swim fast right now," Hailey said. Ms. Kaya smiled. "First we warm up," she said. "Teams warm up before a game."

Hailey watched the team run around the pool. Then they stretched their arms way up high. Hailey peeked at her friend Andrei. He was stretching too. So Hailey ran with him. She stretched her arms and legs.

"Race time," said Ms. Kaya. The whistle blew. Hailey jumped in. Her arms felt strong. Her legs felt strong too. She swam all the way to the wall.

She looked up. Andrei was clapping. So was Davis. "You were so fast," said Andrei. "I warmed up first," said Hailey. "That helped me."

After the race, Hailey sat on the towel. Her little brother was asleep in the stroller. Ms. Kaya gave her a warm hug. "Next race soon," said Hailey, and she jumped back to the pool.

Rehmat wanted to wear her red shoes to sleep. "Shoes are for morning," said her mother. "But you can pick them out now." Rehmat smiled. She ran to get her red shoes. She pushed them onto her bare feet. But her toes felt shy inside the hard shoes. It did not feel right. Her shoes felt cold and bumpy.

"Watch me," said her mother. She took one white sock. She put it on her foot first. Then she put her shoe on over the sock. Rehmat looked and looked. "Socks before shoes," said her mother. Rehmat took her shoes off. She hid her toes in soft socks. Then she put the red shoes on. Now her feet felt warm and good.

Then Rehmat had her bath. The warm water made her toes clean. She put on her pajamas and brushed her teeth. Her mother tucked her into bed. The red shoes sat by the door. They were waiting for morning. "Goodnight, shoes," said Rehmat. "Goodnight, socks." Her mother gave her a kiss. Rehmat closed her eyes and smiled.

Zayn planted little seeds in the backyard. He planted them in a row by the wall. Dad helped him pat the dirt down soft. "Now we wait," said Dad.

Every day Zayn looked. One green sprout. Two green sprouts. Three green sprouts. Then more sprouts came up everywhere. Some were not in Zayn's row. Zayn grabbed one little sprout to pull it out. "Wait," said Dad. "Look close. That one has feathery leaves. It is a baby carrot." "What are the other ones?" asked Zayn. "Weeds," said Dad. "Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them." So Zayn pulled only the weeds. He gave the carrots more room.

Zayn watered the row. He waited. He waited some more. Then one day, orange tops peeked out of the dirt. Dad pulled one up. It was a carrot! They washed it and tasted it. "Yum," said Zayn. "A little salty?" asked Dad, with a smile. Zayn laughed and held his carrot up to the sun.

Nova stood at the running track. She held a small beanbag. Ms. Bennett put a hoop on the grass. "Try to throw it in," she said. Nova threw the beanbag. It did not go in. It came down on the gray track. Nova tried again. She threw it up high. This time it dropped into the hoop. "I did it!" said Nova. Capri clapped her hands.

Then Malek came with a big ball. He caught it with one hand, like a big kid. Nova tried that too. The ball touched her fingers. It fell on her skin and bounced away. Nova picked it up. She held out both hands. Malek rolled the ball to her. She caught it! "Both hands," said Nova. She laughed and held the ball tight. "Throw it to me now," she said.

Evan ran to the park with his mom. He saw Jordan there. Jordan had a big red bike.

"I want to ride it," said Evan.

"Where is your helmet?" asked Jordan.

"I left it home. Can I ride without it?" asked Evan.

"Wear a helmet when you ride a bike," said Jordan. "That is the rule."

Evan looked at his mom. "Can we go get my helmet?"

"Yes," said Mom. "Let's go."

They walked home fast. Evan put on his blue helmet. It had a stripe on top. Mom helped him snap it under his chin. "I am ready!" said Evan.

Back at the park, Jordan waited. "I am ready too," said Jordan.

Evan pedaled the bike around the path. He went past the swings. He went past the slide. His helmet felt snug on his head.

"You did it," said Jordan. "Fast and safe."

"Fast and safe," said Evan. "Again!"

Mom blew him a kiss. Evan pedaled one more time.

Julia and Mahmoud found a tall tree in the forest. Under it was a little playhouse made of sticks.

"Let's play house," said Julia. "I will cook." She put leaves in a pot. She patted a pinecone like a baby. "Sleep, baby turtle," she said. Mahmoud stirred the pot with a spoon. "Soup is ready!" he said. They laughed and tapped bowls together. "Yum, yum," said Julia.

Then the sun went low. Ms. Mokoena called, "Time to go home!" Julia started to run. Leaves and bowls fell everywhere.

"Wait," said Mahmoud. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away."

Julia came back. They put leaves in a pile. They set the pinecone turtle on top. They put the pot by the tree.

"Goodnight, baby," said Julia. She patted the pinecone one more time.

Athena turned three today! Her party was at the bowling alley. Kian came. Layne came too. Grandma and Grandpa came. One kid, two kids, three kids, four people, and Athena!

Athena pushed the big red ball. It rolled slow. Then the pins fell down. Clang, clang, clang! Athena jumped up and down. "I did it! I made the pins fall!"

Then Kian had a turn. His ball went into the gutter. No pins fell. Layne rolled hers. One pin wobbled. Then it fell. "The ball makes them fall!" said Athena. She rolled again, gentle and slow. Down went two more pins.

Later, the lights went low. Mom carried a cake. The little candles did shine. Athena asked, "Why is everyone singing for me?"

Grandma took out a photo. It showed a tiny baby. "That is you, on the day you were born," said Grandma. Athena looked and looked. "A birthday is for the day I was born!" she said. "That is me, small like the pins before they fall!"

Mom blew out the candles with one gentle puff. Then Athena took a big bite of cake. "Happy birthday to me!"

Ryan was at home in the backyard. He wanted to feel the sun on his face.

"I see the sun," said Ryan. His eyes saw it. It was big and yellow.

Then he heard a sound. His ears heard it. "Beep, beep!" It was the ice cream man. The man waved from his truck.

Ryan smelled something. His nose smelled it. It was cookies! Mom was baking inside. Mom let Ryan watch from a safe spot. The oven was hot, so Mom did all the hot parts.

Then Mom gave Ryan one cookie. His tongue tasted it. "Yum!" he said. "Sweet!"

Ryan took his cookie outside. He sat on the grass. His shoes felt tight, so he pulled them off.

His toes touched the grass. "It tickles!" he said. He wiggled his toes. The soft grass tickled his feet.

"One foot, two feet," said Ryan. "Tickle, tickle, tickle!"

He was not scared of the tickle. It made him laugh. "I wish the grass could tickle me all day," he said.

Mom came out and took off her shoes too. She put her feet in the grass.

"Tickle, tickle," said Mom.

Ryan giggled and wiggled his toes in the soft green grass.

Wesley ran into the big kitchen. It was the community kitchen on his street. Today he would help cook soup for his family.

Mr. Costa smiled. "We need rice," he said. Wesley grabbed the bag. He tipped it over the pot. Too much rice fell in! The pot got very full.

"Oh no," said Wesley. Mr. Costa poured the extra rice back. He did not hurry. He showed Wesley a measuring cup. "This is a measuring cup," he said. "It helps cooks put in the right amount of each thing."

Wesley looked at the cup. He filled it with rice. The rice made a little hill. He poured it into the pot. Not too much. Not too little. Just right. Then Mr. Costa handed him a big spoon. "This is a measuring spoon," said Wesley. "Now I get it." He filled it with salt. One small spoon. Just enough.

Zia and Younes came to help too. Zia brought carrots. Younes brought paint for a poster. The poster said "Soup Night." Wesley drew a lucky cat on it.

The soup sat on the stove. Mr. Costa stirred it. Wesley waited. He waited some more. The smell floated up. It smelled warm and good.

At last the soup was done. Wesley's family came in. They sat at the long table. Wesley carried the bread basket, careful and slow. His mom took one sip. "Mmm," she said. "How much rice did you use, Wesley?"

Wesley held up the measuring cup. "This much," he said.

One sunny morning, Iris and her dad rode the city bus. They were going to the big library. Iris was going to get her very first library card.

At the desk, a librarian typed on her computer. Then she handed Iris a small blue card. "It is yours," she said. Iris smiled and held it tight.

Iris picked a book about a red bus. Then she saw a boy put a book back on the wrong shelf. The librarian walked over. "Look at the spine," she said. "The label on the spine shows where the book belongs on the shelf." The boy looked at the label. He put the book in the right spot. Iris looked at her own book. It had a label on the spine too!

Iris gave her card and her book to the librarian. The librarian stamped the book and shut the cover. On the bus home, the fresh air came in through a little window. Iris hugged her book all the way. "Again tomorrow?" she asked her dad. "Yes," said Dad. "Again tomorrow."

Gianna looked out the daycare window. The sky was gray. Rain tapped on the glass. "It's rainy today," said Mr. Bear. He put on his big boots. Gianna wanted to jump in puddles at playtime. She looked at her shoes. They were sneakers with smooth, pink toes. Her friend Reese had on rain boots. His boots were blue and shiny.

At playtime, the rain was soft. Gianna stepped in a big puddle. Splat! Water went into her sneakers. Her socks got wet and squishy. "My socks are all soggy," she said. Reese stepped in the same puddle. His boots went splash, splash. His socks stayed dry. "Rain boots keep your feet dry," said Reese. He stomped again. His feet were still dry inside.

Gianna watched the wind blow a leaf. She held out her hands to feel it. Then she sat on the smooth bench with Mr. Bear. "Next rainy day, I will wear my rain boots," she said. Mr. Bear smiled and helped her put on dry socks, warm and soft. "Let's glue a picture of your boots in your weather book," he said. Gianna pressed the paper down with both hands. Then she drew rain, drop by drop, all around the boots.

Mia wanted the big green toy snake. It sat in the dark corner of the playroom. Vivaan had it first. He made it hiss and slither.

"Can I have a turn?" asked Mia.

Vivaan held the snake tight. Then he looked at Mia's face. He reached out and put the snake in her hands.

Mia ran off to play. The snake slithered up her arm. It was soft and bumpy.

Melissa tugged Mia's sleeve. "You forgot," said Melissa. "When someone gives you something, you say thank you."

Mia stopped. She walked back to Vivaan. "Thank you, Vivaan," she said. Vivaan smiled a big smile.

Later, Ms. Gagnon helped Mia reach the blocks on the high shelf. "Thank you," said Mia.

Ms. Gagnon smiled too. "You are welcome, Mia."

Romy went to the store with her dad. She wanted a special scarf. It was cold outside, so a scarf would help.

Inside the store it was warm. Romy saw big scarves and small scarves. She touched a big red one. It was soft.

Her friend Joey was there too. Joey held up his scarf. "Look, mine is long," he said. Romy held hers next to his. Hers stopped early. Joey's went down and down.

"Mine is short," said Romy.

"Long and short are opposites," said Joey.

They laid the scarves on the floor. Joey's scarf was long. Romy's scarf was short. They swapped to see. Now Romy had the long one. It dragged behind her when she walked. It was fun to walk slow. Then she walked fast and it flew out like a tail.

Romy picked the short red scarf to take home. The cashier put it in a bag. "Good pick," said Dad.

Outside, the cold wind blew. Romy put on her new scarf. "Nice and warm," she said. Dad took her hand, and they walked home slow, looking in all the shop windows.

Gabriella was at the campsite with her family. She wanted to help cook dinner. "Can I make the soup?" she asked. Her dad smiled. "You can wash the vegetables," he said.

Gabriella found the carrots in the bag. They were covered in dirt! "Yuck," she said. Her toe poked the bag, and more dirt fell out. "Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables," her dad said. "Scrub them in the sink."

Gabriella turned on the cold water. She scrubbed one carrot. The dirt went down, down, down the drain. The carrot turned bright orange. She laughed. "Squeaky clean!" she said. She scrubbed the potatoes too. Scrub, scrub, scrub. Dirty potatoes, then clean potatoes.

Dad put the pot on the camp stove. The soup bubbled and smelled yummy. The friendly dog next door gave one happy bark. "Good soup," said Gabriella, and she wiggled her toes by the fire.

Sophie ran to the playground. She wanted to try the big slide. But the slide looked so tall. Her tummy felt funny.

Kira climbed the ladder first. She went up and up. Then she slid down and down. "Up and down are opposites!" Kira said with a giggle.

Sophie looked at the ladder. She put one foot on a step. Then another foot. She went up. The top felt very high. Ms. Singh stood close by. "I am right here," said Ms. Singh. Sophie sat at the top. She took a big breath. Then she slid down, down, down. She landed in the soft sand.

"Again!" said Sophie. She went up fast. She came down slow. Then she went up slow and came down fast. Navy ran over to join them. After sliding, they drank cold water from their bottles. The sun felt hot on their backs. Then a naughty breeze blew Sophie's hat right off her head. Kira caught it. "It fits you again," Kira said, putting it on Sophie's head. They all laughed.

Eva wanted to stay up all night. "No sleep tonight!" she called to her teddy. Her mom said, "Time for bed, Eva." Eva hid under her thin blanket. She giggled. She wiggled. She stayed awake a long, long time.

The sun came up. Eva sat up slowly. Her eyes felt heavy. Her legs felt slow. Nivaan knocked on the door. "Eva! We play today!" Eva tried to run. Her feet went plod, plod, plod. She yawned and yawned. "I am too tired to play," she said.

The next night, Eva got into bed fast. She pulled the blanket up. She drank her cup of warm milk. She closed her eyes. "Goodnight, teddy," she whispered. She slept and slept. In the morning, her feet went quick, quick, quick. She ran to the door and flung it wide. "Nivaan! I can play all day!"

Samuel went to the library today. Yesterday he had found a book about a big red boot. He wanted it again.

"Where is my boot book?" he asked Mr. Santos-Reyes.

"A girl took it yesterday," said Mr. Santos-Reyes. "She brings it back tomorrow."

Samuel felt sad. He wanted the book now, not later.

Mr. Santos-Reyes pointed up. "Look at the clock," he said. "A clock shows what time it is. Story time starts when the short hand points to the ten."

Samuel watched the clock. The short hand moved slow. Then it pointed to the ten.

"Story time now!" said Irha. She sat down and patted the chair next to her.

Samuel sat with her. "I like stories," he said.

The book about the red boot could wait until tomorrow. Today there was a story, a friend, and a big open space on the rug.

Sofia ran into the health clinic. She was getting her shot today. In the waiting room, she saw a picture of a sheep on the wall. The sheep looked soft and warm.

"I think the needle is big," said Aadhya, sitting beside her. "Big like my crayon!" Sofia gasped. She imagined a huge crayon poking her arm. She squeezed her sheep toy tight.

Then Mr. Zhang the nurse called, "Sofia, it's your turn!" Sofia sat on the big chair. Her mom held her hand. Mr. Zhang wiped her arm with a warm, wet cloth. It tickled a little.

"Look at the sheep picture," said Mr. Zhang. Sofia looked. He gave her one quick poke with a thin needle in her arm.

"All done!" said Mr. Zhang.

"Already?" said Sofia. She stared at her arm. It was just one little poke! Sofia laughed and jumped down. "Aadhya, it was quick! It was thin like a tiny stick!"

Aadhya stood up. "My turn," she said. She held her head high.

Sofia waved from the door. "It's just one quick poke!"

Today was Raphael's birthday party at the park. His mom held a big paper card. "This is the invitation," she said. "It tells everyone when the party is. It tells everyone where the party is."

Raphael ran to the picnic table. One table, two table, three tables. His party was at table three!

Then Everlee came down the path. Her face looked worried. "I thought I might get lost," she said.

Raphael held up his card. "Look! The invitation says Saturday. The invitation says the park." He pointed to the words.

Everlee smiled big. "Saturday, the park! Now I know just where to go."

Albert came next. Then Mr. Virtanen came too. Saturday, the park. Saturday, the park. Everyone said it together.

They played catch by the trees. Raphael threw the ball high. It landed in the soft snow and made a funny spot.

The wagon ride felt bumpy and fast. Raphael laughed and laughed.

"Happy birthday, Raphael!" said Everlee. He blew out his candles with one big puff.

Oliver sat at the long table. The bread smelled warm. His tummy made a little growl. "Shh," said Oliver to his tummy. Everyone held hands. Ms. Greco bowed her head. Oliver watched her. Was the blessing over? He did not know. His tummy growled again, like an angry little bear. Cedar giggled next to him. "Wait," Cedar whispered. "Not yet."

Ms. Greco spoke soft words. Oliver saw a paper letter in her hand. It had the blessing written on it. Her finger moved down the page. Oliver waited and waited.

Then Ms. Greco said, "Amen." Everyone said, "Amen!" Hands let go. Arms reached for bread. "Now?" asked Oliver. "Now," said Cedar, grinning. Oliver took a big piece of warm bread. It was soft like a pillow.

At home, Oliver held hands with his dad. Dad said the blessing. Oliver squeezed his eyes shut. He waited for one word. "Amen," said Dad. Oliver's eyes popped open fast. "Bread time!" he shouted.

Edouard sat at the snack table. There were crackers on his plate. Rocco sat next to him. Rocco pointed at his cracker.

"Is this a square?" Rocco asked. "It is hard to tell."

Edouard looked at the cracker. Ms. Huang came over. She gave them a piece of string.

"Try this," she said.

Edouard held the string along one side of the cracker. He pinched the string where the side ended. Then he put the string on the next side. It was just the same. He tried the third side. The same again. And the fourth side too.

"It fits every side," Edouard said. "A square has four sides. They are all the same."

"So my cracker is a square!" said Rocco.

Alan walked over with his snack. His cheese was a triangle. It had three sides. Edouard's napkin was folded into a rectangle. It had four sides, but two were long and two were short.

Later they played a shape game. Ms. Huang held up a clock. "Circle!" said Edouard. He got it right and did a little jump.

"You win the round," said Ms. Huang. She laughed.

At lunch there was warm soup. Edouard looked at his bowl. Round like a circle, all the way around. He dipped his square cracker in.

Gianna ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" she said. "Rainy, rainy!" Little drops went tap, tap on the glass. Mr. Kowalski laughed. "Rain boots today," he said. Otis put on his boots. Kieran put on her rain coat. Gianna zipped her coat up, up, up.

At play time the rain stopped. The sky turned sunny. The sun was big and bright. Gianna went outside and made a squinty face. "Too bright!" she said. Otis made a squinty face too. Kieran held her paws over her eyes like a lion. "Rawr," she said. "I am a sleepy lion."

Gianna thought and thought. Then she got her sun hat. She put it on her head. The hat made shade over her face. Her eyes went big and round. "No more squinty face!" she said. Otis clapped. "A sun hat! A sun hat!" he sang. Gianna smiled. Then something tickled her nose. A leaf flew by in the windy air. It landed right on Kieran's lion nose. "Rawr!" said the leaf, in a small small voice, and everyone giggled.

William ran into the library. He was ready for story time. Mr. Greco sat on the big red chair. Lilianna sat close by, hugging her toy horse.

"Today we read about animals," said Mr. Greco. He held up a book. First came a dog. "A dog is an animal," said William. Next came a cow. "A cow is an animal too," said Lilianna.

Then a fish swam across the page. William frowned. "A fish is not an animal. It has no legs!" Lilianna laughed. Mr. Greco smiled.

"Look at the cover," he said. He pointed to the title. It said Animals. The fish was right there with the dog and the cow.

"A fish is an animal too," said William. He turned the page fast. A horse ran next. William hugged the book tight.

"A horse can chase the fish," he said.

Asher stood in the kitchen on his stool. "I want to make soup," he said. Dad said, "Yes! You can help." Asher dropped carrots into the big pot. One, two, three. Then he saw Dad pick up a knife and cut an onion.

Dad's eyes began to water. Tears ran down his face. Asher pulled on Dad's zipper sleeve. "Why are you sad?" he asked. "Don't cry!" Dad laughed a little. "It is just the onion," he said. "When I cut it, my eyes sting and water."

Asher looked at the onion. He had not touched it, and his eyes were fine. Dad put the last piece in the pot. Asher stirred the soup with a wooden spoon. Soon the soup was hot and ready. Mom came in and took the lid off. "Mmm," she said. Asher grinned. "Dad's tears are gone now," he said. "And I made the soup!"

Kinsley sat at Grandma's big table. The bowls were full of corn. The corn was yellow and a little salty. Everyone held hands. It was time for the family blessing.

Kinsley did not know the blessing yet. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She looked down at her lap.

Grandma squeezed her hand. "Take your time," said Grandma. "We can wait." They all waited. The room was quiet and warm.

Kinsley thought about the corn. "Grandma, where did the corn grow?" she asked. "On a farm," said Grandma. "A farmer picked it for us."

Kinsley thought about that. The farmer had pulled the corn from the tall plants. Then the corn came all the way here. Kinsley took a big breath.

"Thank you for our food," she said. "Thank you for the corn. And thank you to the farmer." Grandma smiled wide. "That is a good blessing," she said. "It says thank you."

Then Grandma passed the bread. Kinsley took a warm piece and ate it all up. "Can I say it again tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma laughed and squeezed her hand one more time.

Camille stood in the kitchen. A big bread sat on the table. It was warm and it smelled good. Camille wanted to say the blessing all by herself tonight. But the words felt tricky in her mouth.

"Baruch atah," she tried. Then she stopped. "What comes next?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Adonai," said Mom. Camille said it again. "Baruch atah Adonai." The words came out smoother now. She said them three times. Three times, three times, three times.

Ziyad came over to play. He sat at the table too. "What are you singing?" he asked. "It is called the Hamotzi," said Camille. "Many Jewish families say it over bread. Will you say it with me?" Ziyad nodded. They said it together, slow and loud.

Then the family came to the table. Daddy put the bread down. Everyone grew quiet. Camille took a big breath. Her heart went thump, thump. "Baruch atah Adonai," she began. The words came out clear and strong. She did not stop once.

When she finished, Daddy touched her hair. Mom kissed her cheek. Ziyad clapped his hands. "Did the bread taste different?" Camille wondered. She took a bite. It tasted warm and soft. "That much is true," she said. "It tastes like our happy table."

David went to Raiden's house. Raiden had a big toy kitchen. There were tiny pots and tiny cups.

"Let's make soup," said Raiden. He put a rubber carrot in a pot. He stirred it with a spoon.

David saw the pretend soup. It smelled like nothing at all. He lifted the spoon to his mouth.

Raiden shook his head fast. "Don't put it in your mouth!" he said. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat. Watch."

Raiden tipped the spoon near his lips. He made a big slurpy sound. "Sluuurp! Yum, yum!" he said. He did not eat it at all.

David tried. He held the spoon up high. "Sluuurp!" he said. "So yummy!"

Raiden laughed. David laughed too.

Then David touched his own tummy. "All full!" he said.

"Me too," said Raiden. "Time to feed the bear."

They tucked the teddy bear into bed. Raiden patted its head.

"Shh," said David. "The bear is sleeping."

The soup pot sat still on the little stove. Nobody turned it on.

Freya stood in the new nursery room. A small bed sat by the window. Her baby sister was coming home tomorrow! Freya wanted to help get ready.

Dad opened a big box. It was full of diapers. So many diapers! Freya counted them. Ten, twenty, more and more.

"Why so many?" Freya asked.

Dad smiled. "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet," he said.

Just then her friend Gael came in. Freya held up a diaper like a prize. "The baby needs these!" she said. "Lots and lots!"

Then Freya heard a scratch at the door. It was the cat! The cat walked across the floor and jumped into the empty box.

Freya laughed. "Silly cat," she said. "The box is for the baby!"

She patted the soft diaper. "Our baby is coming soon," Freya whispered. "I will be the best big sister ever."

The cat purred inside the box.

Clara waited at the bus stop with her dad. The sun was bright. "Where is the bus?" she asked.

"I want to run in the sun!" said Clara. Her dad held her hand. "First we stop," he said. "Sunscreen first." He rubbed it on her arms and face. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," he said. Clara smelled it. It smelled like summer.

Then the wind blew. Clara's hat flew off! "My hat!" she cried. Her dad caught it. The wind was strong today. Clara watched the leaves dance on the ground.

The bus came. Zara was on it with her mom. "Clara!" said Zara. "It was rainy at my house. I wore my boots!" Clara looked down at her own shoes. The sun was warm on her sunscreened arms. "It is sunny here," said Clara. Zara laughed and sat next to her. The bus rolled away down the bright, sunny street.

Sophie found a book at daycare. It had a bear on the front. She wanted to hear the bear story. She took the book to Ms. Fortin. "Please read this," said Sophie. Ms. Fortin sat down on the little red rug. She opened the front of the book. She began at the first page.

Sophie looked at the page. There were little black marks. "What are those?" she asked. Ms. Fortin pointed with her finger. "These are the words," she said. "I read the words." She moved her finger along the marks. Then she said the words out loud. The bear went beep, the words said. Sophie laughed. So that was how it worked!

Then they came to a page with just a picture. The bear was in a tree. There were no little black marks at all. "Read this page too!" said Sophie. Ms. Fortin shook her head. "There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read." Sophie leaned in close. She looked and looked. It was true. Just a picture, no marks. "We can make up our own words," said Ms. Fortin. Sophie clapped her hands. "The bear says hello to the birds!" said Sophie. After the story, it was time for a nap. Sophie put the book on the shelf. "Read it again after nap?" she asked. Ms. Fortin smiled and turned the book back to the front page.

Luke sat in the waiting room. He touched the big green plant by the chair. Its leaves felt smooth. A nurse came out with a key clipped to her pocket. "Time to wash your hands," she said. Luke had just used the toilet. He wanted to wash all by himself.

Luke ran to the sink. He turned the tap. The nurse shook her head fast. "Wait," she said. "Let me check the water first." She put her own hand under the tap. "Too hot," she said. She turned the tap the other way. She put her hand under again. "Now it is warm. Warm, not hot. You can wash."

Luke put his hands in the water. It felt nice. The nurse gave him soap. "Wash for twenty seconds," she said. She showed him how to count. "Five, six, seven..." Luke rubbed the soap all over. Bubbles grew between his fingers. "Eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" Then he rinsed the bubbles off. His hands were clean and shiny.

The nurse gave him a crunchy cracker. "My hands are clean now," said Luke. He looked back at the tap. "Will you check the water next time too?" "Every time," said the nurse. She turned the tap off with a click.

Alice wakes up in her soft, warm bed. The sun is bright at her window. She hears Dad making breakfast in the kitchen. "Eggs today," he says. Alice wants to help, but first she has a small problem. She needs to use the toilet.

Alice sits on the toilet. Then she pulls up her pants and runs to the kitchen. But wait. The toilet is still full. She forgot something! What did she forget? Alice runs back to look.

"First we flush," says Dad, following her. Alice presses the big silver handle. Whoosh! The water spins round and round. She watches it all go down. That was the first step. But there is one more step after that.

"Now we wash our hands," says Dad. He turns on the tap. Warm water runs over Alice's little hands. The soap is slippery and smells like flowers. One, two, three, four, five bubbles. She counts them all. Then she dries her hands on the blue towel.

Now her hands are clean. Now she can help Dad. Alice sits on her chair and cracks nothing, but she does open the egg box for him. "Nice work, Alice," says Dad. Alice smiles and eats her warm egg.

Muhammad wanted to sing a song all by himself. His problem was big. He only knew half of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star."

His mom put on music. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. The claps went with the beat, nice and steady. Muhammad tried too. Clap, clap, clap. His claps were fast at first. Then they got steady, like feet walking.

"Now the song," said his mom. Muhammad sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Then he stopped. He forgot the rest. He frowned and looked at the floor.

Then he began to hum. It was the ABC song from school. A, B, C, D. He hummed more. His eyes got wide. It sounded just the same as the star song! Same tune, all the way through.

"Mom! The ABC song is my star song!" he said.

His mom laughed. "Then you know the whole tune."

Muhammad clapped and sang, "How I wonder what you are." His hands went clap, clap, clap, right on the beat. From the window, a bird in a nest chirped along.

Muhammad sang the letters too, all the way to Z. "Now I know two songs!" he said. Clap, clap, clap.

Claire ran up to Nelly's door. "Come play!" said Nelly. Inside, a big box sat on the floor. It had a sign on it. The sign said SHOP. Nelly held a toy phone. "I am the shopkeeper," said Nelly. "You can be the shopper." Claire jumped. "Yes! I love shops!"

Nelly stood behind the box. Claire picked up a basket. She walked around and around. Nelly waited and waited. At last Claire put a toy pear in her basket. Then she put in a little cup. Then a toy man with a red hat. "Careful," said Nelly. "That man is my best one." Claire held him gently. "I want this one," she said. Nelly smiled. "That will be two buttons, please."
