Claire dug in her pocket. She found two buttons. She put them in Nelly's hand.

"Now you be the shopper," said Claire. "My turn to wait!"

Maya went to the music room at the community center. The room smelled like soap from the clean tables. Ms. Wright had a little drum, a bell, and a flute.

"Today we play the flute," said Ms. Wright. "One, two, three, blow with me."

Maya blew. The flute made no sound. She tried again. Still no sound. Jai and Ariana made sounds right away.

Then Maya saw the music sheet on the stand. It had dots and lines. Long lines and little dots, one, two, three, many more.

"What are the dots?" Maya asked.

"Those marks are called notes," said Ms. Wright. "They show which sounds to play."

Maya looked at a note. She put her fingers down low on the flute, like the low dot. She blew. A low sound came out! She moved her fingers up high. Now the sound jumped up high too.

Ariana clapped. Jai played her bell, ding, ding.

Maya tapped the paper. "Dots make sounds," she said. Then she blew one more long, high note.

Audrey sat at the dinner table. The bright lamp made a warm circle of light. Her dad set down three bowls. One was for animals. One was for toys. One was for foods.

Audrey picked up a carrot. "Food," she said. She dropped it in the foods bowl. Then came a little cow from her farm set. "Animal," she said. Clunk. Then a soft toy dog. She held it near the animal bowl. Her dad waited. She squeezed its furry arm. It did not wiggle. It did not bark. It just sat in her hand.

"Not alive," said Audrey. She moved it over. "Toy dog." Clunk, into the toy bowl. Her dad smiled and swept the crumbs off the table with his hand.

"Now dinner," he said. Audrey put one strawberry in her own bowl. "Food," she said. She took a big bite.

Ethan stood at the school gate. His tummy felt funny, like little butterflies. His mom held his hand tight.

"My tummy feels fluttery," Ethan said.

Mom knelt down. "That means you feel nervous. It is okay to feel nervous on the first day of school. I felt nervous on my first day too."

"You did?" said Ethan.

"Yes! And then I saw my teacher and it got better."

Just then, a boy named Salem ran up to the gate. He was holding a special red truck. He rolled it on the ground and sent it right to Ethan's feet.

"Want to play trucks?" said Salem.

Ethan picked up the truck. The butterflies in his tummy flew away. Across the street, the school bell rang, warm and loud.

"Let's go together," said Salem.

Ethan smiled and took his new friend's hand. "Let's go!"

Rehmat stood by the pool in her red swimsuit. Today was game day! Ms. González held a big box. Inside were beanbags and a hoop. "First we throw," said Ms. González. "Then we catch. Then we jump in and drink our juice."

Rehmat grabbed a beanbag. She swung her arm high and let go. The beanbag flew way over the hoop. It landed near Marvin's feet. "Too far!" laughed Marvin. "One, two, three misses," counted Paige.

Ms. González picked up the beanbag. She held it low, near her knees. Her arm swung from down low, forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the middle of the hoop. "Try that way," she said.

Rehmat held her beanbag down low. She counted, "One, two, three!" Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed through the air. Plunk! It landed in the hoop.

"You did it!" said Paige. "One, two, three baskets!" said Marvin. Now it was catch time. Paige threw the big beach ball. Rehmat opened both arms wide. She caught it and hugged it tight. The ball smelled like sunscreen and felt bumpy.

Then everyone jumped in the pool. The water was cool and splashy. Rehmat was so tired and happy. After juice, she yawned a big yawn. "You might fall asleep right here," said Ms. González. Rehmat laughed and hugged her wet beanbag. "More hoop tomorrow!"

Aurora ran to the sandbox at the park. She saw a shiny red truck. It was Tommy's truck. Tommy was digging a big hole nearby.

Aurora wanted that truck very much. She grabbed it fast. Tommy turned around. His face went sad and he began to cry.

Aurora looked at Tommy. Then she looked at the truck. She held it out to him. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked.

Tommy wiped his eyes with his hand. He smiled a big smile. "Yes!" he said. "You can have a turn."

Aurura pushed the truck through the sand. It was easy and fun. The truck became a magic dragon in her pretend game. It crawled over sandy hills. It sang a roaring song.

Then Aurora gave the truck back. "Your turn," she said. Tommy made the dragon jump. They laughed and played together until the sun went home.

Madison went to the playground with her dad. She saw a big red box of toys. The toys were all over the ground. "Who can help me put them in?" said Ms. Weber.

Madison picked up a quiet little egg shaker. She put it in the box. A baby reached in and pulled the egg out. Madison put it back in. The baby took it out again. "In and out are opposites," said Zoey with a laugh.

Madison had an idea. She put the egg in, then gave the baby a soft ball. The baby held the ball. The egg stayed in the box. "The toys are in!" said Madison. Ms. Weber smiled. The playground was quiet and sunny, and Madison gave the box a happy pat.

The bookmobile came to Matthew's street. It was a little truck full of books. Matthew held his dad's hand. He wanted his very own library card.

Mr. Castillo smiled at the desk. "What is your name?" he asked. "Matthew," said Matthew. Mr. Castillo made a card with Matthew's name on it. Now Matthew could take a book home.

Then Matthew saw a rug and small chairs. Amanat stood far away by the door. She looked at the rug, but she did not sit. Matthew waved to her. He patted a chair. Amanat did not move.

Mr. Castillo sat down on the rug. He held up a big book. It had a monkey on the cover. "Storytime!" he said. "I read books aloud to the children." Then he opened the book. The monkey made a mean face on page one, and all the kids laughed.

Amanat looked at the funny monkey. She slipped out of her shoes and sat down next to Matthew. Mr. Castillo turned the page.

Hailey sat on a big towel at the beach. Mr. Mori said, "Close your eyes. What can you hear?" Hailey closed her eyes. She heard a seagull. She heard the water go splash, splash. She heard a boy laughing. "My ears hear all of it," she said. Mr. Mori smiled. "That is right. We hear with our ears."

Then Hailey opened her eyes. She wanted to name all five senses. She looked at the blue water. "Eyes see," she said. She touched the warm sand. "Hands touch." She smelled her snack. "My nose smells." She took a bite. "My mouth tastes." One was left. What was it? She put her hands over her ears. The sounds went away. She took her hands off. The sounds came back.

"I did it," said Hailey. "Five senses!" Sama ran up the beach. "Listen," said Hailey. "The waves are calling us."

Ivy went to the store with her dad. She held his hand in the long line. The store had a hot food counter. A big pot sat behind the glass.

Ivy could smell the soup. It smelled warm and good. She wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. She let go of her dad's hand and took one step closer.

A worker lifted the lid. White steam went up, up, up. "Careful," her dad said. He took her hand again. "Stay back from the steam." The steam was hot. Hot steam could burn. Ivy took three steps back.

The worker stirred the pot with a long spoon. Bubbles popped in the soup. Ivy watched from far away. She could still see them. She could still smell them too.

"Can I have soup?" Ivy asked. "Yes," her dad said. He put a cup in the cart. Ivy held the cup with two hands. It was warm on her fingers, not too hot. She sipped it slow.

On the way out, they saw the doctor's office next door. "Hi, Doctor," Ivy said, and waved. Then she took her dad's hand and held it tight. "I will stay close," she said. "Good plan," said her dad. They walked home together in the sun.

Mya stood in the kitchen. Her tummy said it was breakfast time. She wanted toast with butter, all by herself. Her dad put two warm pieces of toast on her plate. Then he handed her the butter knife.

Mya dug the knife into the soft butter. She spread it across the toast, one, two, three strokes. The butter made shiny lines. Some spots were bare. She spread some more. Now the toast was covered, and it smelled yummy.

Next came the milk. Mya held the small cup. She poured the milk slowly, slowly. The milk rose up in the cup. Then her hand wiggled. A little white puddle sat on the table. Mya's lip went down at the corners.

She reached for the curly blue cloth. She wiped the puddle, one wipe, two wipes. The table was dry again. Mya poured one more time. This time her hand was steady. Not one drop spilled. She took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk. "I did it," said Mya, "all by myself."

Nicholas waited at the bus stop with his dad. His coat was all zipped up. The sun came out. It got warm.

"I'm hot," said Nicholas.

His dad's hands were full of shopping bags. "Can you try it yourself?" he asked.

Nicholas looked down at his coat. He found the little zipper tab. He pulled it down. Zip! The coat opened up. Cool air came in.

"I did it!" said Nicholas.

His friend Keon stood at the bus stop too. "Do it again," said Keon.

Nicholas pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed. He pulled it down. Zip! It opened. Up and down, up and down. Keon laughed and laughed.

"Now do mine," said Keon.

Nicholas pulled Keon's tab down. Zip! Keon's coat opened too.

The bus came round the corner. It stopped with a big hiss. The two boys climbed the steps. Nicholas sat by the window, coat open, nice and cool.

"Watch this," he said. He zipped it up fast, then down fast, like magic.

The bus went bump, bump, down the clean street. Keon clapped. "Zipper boy!" he said.

Nicholas grinned. "Zipper boy to the rescue," he said, and pulled the tab down one more time.

Connor stood in the yard with a red beanbag. Stefan was there too. Ms. Ricci had set a big hoop on the grass.

"Watch me," said Stefan. Stefan threw his beanbag. It went in.

Connor threw his beanbag. It landed far away by the bear-shaped bush. Connor sat down on the step.

"You can try again," said Ms. Ricci. She handed him a fresh beanbag from the box.

Connor threw it. It missed again. He picked it up. He threw it again and again and again.

Then the beanbag went up. It came down. It landed right in the hoop.

"I did it!" said Connor.

Stefan clapped. "Good throw!"

Then Ms. Ricci rolled a big blue ball to Connor. He held out both hands. The ball bumped his tummy and fell. He tried again. It fell again.

Connor kept his hands out. He kept trying. The ball came again. Both hands caught it and held it tight.

"Again," said Connor, and he tossed the ball back.

Lily wanted short hair. Her hair was long and it got in her eyes. "Today we cut it," her mom said. "Yes!" said Lily.

At the salon, a lady smiled. "I am the hairdresser," she said. She held up a big cape. "This cape goes around your shoulders," she said. "It keeps the cut hair off your clothes."

Lily sat up tall. The cape snapped around her. It was soft and blue. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell down. The hairs landed on the cape. Lily looked. Her clothes were clean!

"Why is my shirt clean?" Lily asked. "The cape keeps the hairs off," the hairdresser said. "The cape does that?" asked Lily. "The cape does that," said Mom.

Lily giggled. "I am a cape girl!" she said. Snip, snip. More hairs fell on the cape, not on her.

Soon the hairdresser took the cape off. She shook it, and all the hairs fell away. Lily looked in the mirror. Her hair was short and neat. "I love it," said Lily. She patted her clean shirt and smiled at the cape, folded up small on the counter.

Logan was in the kitchen. He wanted a napkin for his snack. The napkin holder was too tall for him. He could not reach it.

"Let me help," said his dad. Dad took out one square napkin. It had four sides, all the same. "Here you go."

The napkin felt bumpy on Logan's fingers. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He patted it flat. Then he looked and looked. The napkin was not a square now. It was long and thin.

"Rectangle," said Logan. He held it up for Dad to see.

Dad laughed. "You made a new shape, Logan."

Logan unfolded it. The square came back. He folded it again. "Rectangle!" he said. He kicked his feet under his chair, he was so happy.

Then he set the rectangle by his plate. "Snack time," said Dad, and put down a plate of round crackers.

Aaron sat on his bed in his bedroom. He had a new book about the moon. He wanted Dad to read it, but Dad was busy.

Aaron opened the book himself. He put his finger at the right side of the page. He slid it to the left. Then he turned to the last page. The moon picture was there, but the story felt mixed up. "Hmm," said Aaron. "Is this the end or the start?"

He ran to find Dad. Dad wiped his hands and came in. "Can we read the moon book?" asked Aaron. "Yes," said Dad.

Dad sat on the bed. He opened the front cover. "Watch my finger," he said. His finger started at the left side. It slid to the right. Then it went down to the next line, left to right again. The pages made a soft swish sound.

"Again!" said Aaron. Dad read page one, then two, then three. Aaron tapped his own finger on the words. "One word, two words, three words," he said. "The words talk to you!"

At the end, Dad closed the book. Aaron hugged it and yawned. It was getting late. "Read it again tomorrow?" asked Aaron. Dad kissed his head. "Front to back, left to right, every time," he said. Aaron smiled and patted the cover.

William loved the playroom floor. It had a big striped rug with squares on it. He wanted to build a house for his toy bear.

He found a round plate. "That is a circle," he said. He put it down for a wall. Then he found a tiny button. Mackenzie shook her head. "That can't be a circle," she said. "It is too small. The plate is a circle."

William held the button up. He looked at the plate. Then he looked at the button. Both went round and round, with no corners at all. "Look," he said. He spun the button on the floor. It rolled just like the plate rolled.

"Big circle, tiny circle," said Mackenzie. She clapped. They used the button for a little window. William found a triangle block for the roof. The bear had a house at last.

Wesley went to the library with his dad. Story time was today. Mr. Torres had a big table set up. On it were paper shapes of every color.

"Today we make shape houses," said Mr. Torres. "First pick a square for the walls." Wesley picked a red square. It had four corners. He put a triangle on top for the roof. The triangle had three corners.

Then Wesley wanted a round window. He found a shiny blue circle. He wanted to cut it out himself. But he did not know where to start. He looked for a corner to begin cutting. He slid his finger all around the edge. There was no corner anywhere.

Jerome leaned over. "A circle is round and has no corners," he said. Wesley slid his finger around again. Round and round. No corner, just curve. So he started anywhere at all. He snipped along the curve. The circle came out whole.

Wesley pasted it on his house. Jerome clapped. Mr. Torres spelled the word C I R C L E with letter cards. Wesley said each letter out loud. Then he read it back. "Circle," he said.

It was a surprise. A shape with no corners could be so good. He put his house in the middle of the table. "Look at my round window," he said.

Luna stood in the kitchen by the window. Her coat lay on the chair. She wanted to put it on all by herself.

She pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. She shook it and tried again. This time it sat just right.

"Mommy, watch me zip!" said Luna.

She pulled the little tab up, up, up. The zipper went halfway and stuck. Luna frowned. She held the coat flat and pulled again. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

Then Luna saw rain outside the window. Little drops fell on the big tree. "Oh no," said Luna. "My hair will get wet."

Mommy smiled. "Look at the back of your coat," she said.

Luna reached back and found soft cloth. She grabbed it and pulled. The hood came up over her head. "A hood!" said Luna. "It hides my hair from the rain!"

She ran to the door. "Let's go out under the tree!"

Brielle lived in a small house with a red door. Andrea came to play today. Brielle was so excited. She clapped her hands.

Brielle and Andrea built a big tower. It had ten blocks. The wind blew outside the window. The curtain went whoosh. Andrea got scared and jumped back. Her foot hit the tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Andrea sat on the floor. Her face looked sad. Brielle felt angry at first. She wanted to yell. But she looked at Andrea's face. Andrea was holding her knee. It had a little red mark.

Brielle walked over to Andrea. She sat down close. "Are you okay?" she asked. Andrea looked up. Her sad face went soft. "My knee hurt," said Andrea. "But now I feel better." She gave Brielle a small smile.

Brielle helped Andrea up. Then they built the tower again. This time it was even taller. Brielle's mom brought them a tasty snack of apple slices. Under the couch, Brielle found a surprise. It was her old blue bunny, lost for weeks! "Bunny!" she said. Andrea laughed. They hugged the bunny and ate the apples.

Milo ran to the shelf at daycare. He saw the cookie jar sitting there. "Cookies!" he said. "I want cookies now." His tummy made a little growl. Alaia was already at the table. She had a bowl of warm porridge. Judy had toast with jam. Milo wanted cookies, not porridge. Ms. Sow came over with the big breakfast tray. "Breakfast comes first," she said. "It is the first meal of the day." Milo put his cookie back in the jar. Then he took a cup of milk. The cup felt cold in his hands. He sat down next to Alaia.

Milo took a bite of porridge. It was warm and sweet. "Yum," he said. He took another bite, and another. His tummy felt nice and full. Alaia laughed. "You ate it all up," she said. Judy helped Milo stack the empty bowls. Clack, clack, clack. The bowls made a tall tower.

After breakfast, the class went outside to play. Milo ran fast. He jumped. He did not feel wobbly at all. Then it was nap time. Milo lay on his little mat. His blanket was soft. Ms. Sow patted his back. After nap would come lunch, and after lunch would come play. But now it was time to sleep. "Cookies are for later," Milo whispered. He closed his eyes, and Alaia whispered back, "After nap, my friend."

Anna sat at the dinner table. She had five toy monkeys. She lined them up by her plate. Mom said, "Monkeys can watch, but they cannot touch your food." Anna smiled. Her face was a little messy from the sauce.

Anna began to sing. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One monkey fell off. She took one monkey away. Now there were four monkeys. How many would be left next? She sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One fell off. She put that one in her coat pocket.

Her dad whispered, "Sing it again." Anna sang, "Three little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One fell off again. She moved it away. Then two monkeys were left. Then one monkey was left. Then the last monkey fell off. Her pocket was full of monkeys. Anna looked at the empty table by her plate. "No more monkeys!" she said. Then she clapped her hands and took a big bite of dinner.

Ruby was staying at Grandma's house. She loved Grandma's big squishy bed. At night, Grandma helped Ruby put on her soft pajamas. Ruby picked the ones with little stars.

In the morning, Ruby ate eggs and toast. Grandma poured the milk. Then Grandma said, "Time to brush your teeth." Ruby brushed her teeth in the bathroom. She made lots of bubbles. Her teeth felt smooth and clean.

They went out to shop for a toy plane. Ruby saw a red plane in the window. "That one, please," she said. Grandma bought it for her. In the bath that evening, Ruby sailed the plane over the bubbles. The plane went zoom, zoom. Then Grandma helped her wash her hair.

Ruby put on her star pajamas again. She hopped into the big squishy bed. Grandma turned off the light. Ruby snuggled under the blanket. Then she sat straight up.

"I forgot to brush my teeth!" she said. Ruby hopped back out of bed. She padded to the bathroom. She brushed her teeth with more bubbles. Then she jumped back into bed.

"I brushed this morning and now before bed," Ruby said. Grandma smiled. "Good job, Ruby." The red plane sat on the shelf. Ruby closed her eyes. "Night night, plane," she whispered.

Mohamed went to the corner store with his dad. Ms. Le smiled from behind the counter. She had a bin of bright red apples.

"Can I count them?" Mohamed asked.

"Yes," said Ms. Le. "You can help me."

Mohamed counted the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," he said. But Ms. Le looked puzzled.

"Let me check," she said. She counted too. "I got five."

Mohamed felt worried. He tried again. This time he touched each apple with one finger. He said one number for each apple. "One, two, three, four, five." He heard his own voice say each number just once.

"I counted one apple two times before," Mohamed said. "Now I touched each one once."

Then he looked at the pear bin. "Five apples and two pears. The apples have more!"

"Yes," said Ms. Le. "The apples have more."

His dad put a small rock from his pocket on the counter, smooth and round. "One more thing to count," he said.

"One!" said Mohamed. "One rock. One is less than five!"

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She was playing with her toys. There was a teddy bear and a little truck. She also had a carrot on her plate.

Aubrey put the carrot next to the truck. "Now you drive, carrot!" she said. Her dad smiled. "Is a carrot a toy?" he asked. Aubrey looked at the carrot. Then she looked at her apple and her bread.

"Where do apples go?" she asked herself. She looked at her plate. The apple was on the plate. The bread was on the plate too. "Oh! Apples, bread and carrots are all foods!" She picked up the carrot. She put it back on her plate.

Then a small surprise jumped out of her toy box. It was Nadia, hiding under the teddy bear! "Boo!" said Nadia. Aubrey laughed and let Nadia sit beside her. "Be careful with the carrot," Nadia said. "The teddy wants a bite!" Aubrey held it up. "Teddy can pretend," she said, "but the carrot is food for me." She took a big, careful crunch.

Michael went to the corner store with his dad. It was a sunny day. Michael wanted to buy apples for his class snack. He needed to count them all by himself.

Michael put apples in a bag. He touched each one and counted. "One, two, three, four, five." He looked at his dad. "Five!" His dad smiled and nodded. Michael had counted five apples, and the last number he said was five.

Then his friend Anhad came in with his mom. Anhad was buying oranges. Anhad put oranges in his bag. He counted, "One, two, three, four." Then he said, "Four!" Anhad had four oranges.

"Now let's see which bag has more," said Michael's dad. Michael looked at both bags. "Five is more than four," said Michael. "My bag has more apples." Anhad peeked into Michael's bag and giggled.

The cashier let Michael wipe the counter with a cloth while his dad paid. The cloth was thick and soft. Then Anhad helped too. They took turns, one wipe at a time. Michael held his bag of five apples and Anhad held his bag of four oranges. They walked out the door together.

"See you at snack time," said Anhad.

Zoey sat at the kitchen table. She had a big pencil and some paper. Mom sat next to her. "Can you write Zoey?" asked Mom. "Yes! I will try," said Zoey. She held the pencil in her fist. Mom helped her pinch it with two fingers. "Like this," said Mom. Zoey patted the pencil with her other hand. Then she began. She started at the right side of the paper. She made a Z. Then an O. Then a Y. Then an E. Then the paper ran out! There was no room for the last Y. "Oh no," said Zoey. Mom smiled. "Try starting over here," she said. She pointed to the left side. Zoey began there. Z, O, Y, E, Y. It fit! All five letters sat in a high row across the page. Zoey drew a little house under her name. "This is my house," she said. "And this is me! I wrote it all by myself."

Edouard built a big tower at school. The blocks were red and blue. He wanted to show his friend Destiny. He took a big breath. Then he saw Destiny. She was sleeping on the little mat. Her eyes were shut. Her blanket went up and down.

Edouard opened his mouth to shout. But Mr. Pham put one finger by his lips. He made a small shh sound. Edouard looked at Destiny again. She was still sleeping. So Edouard made his voice very small. "Come see my tower," he said in a whisper.

Mr. Pham smiled. He whispered too. "You used a quiet voice," he said. Edouard nodded. A quiet voice did not wake Destiny up. Her sleep stayed soft, like night. Edouard sat down next to her mat. He waited for his turn to talk.

Soon Destiny opened her eyes. She sat up slow. Edouard whispered, "My tower is strong. Want to see?" Destiny gave him a kiss on the cheek, quick and light. Then they walked to the blocks on quiet feet.

Macie came over too. She handed Destiny a red block. "You can add one," Edouard said. Destiny put it on top. The tower stood tall. "Our tower," said Destiny.

Max sat in the family car. The new baby sat beside him. The baby was his little brother.

The baby started to cry. Max did not know why. It was a puzzle. "Maybe he wants my bear," Max said. He gave the baby his bear. The baby still cried.

Dad pulled the car over. "He is hungry," Dad said. Dad fed the baby a bottle. The baby drank and drank. Then the baby stopped crying. Then the baby fell asleep. Max looked and looked. The milk made the baby sleepy.

Later, they drove home. It got dark outside. The baby woke up and cried again. Max said, "He is hungry again." Dad said, "Yes. Babies eat at night too. They eat many times, day and night."

Max got his bear ready. He held it near the baby. Dad fed the baby in the car seat. The baby drank the whole bottle. Then the baby went back to sleep.

Max felt big. He had solved the puzzle. "Good night, baby," Max whispered. He wished his bear could talk. The baby slept all the way home.

Aubrey sat in her seat in the family car. Click, click went her buckle. The car hummed under her feet. Today was shot day at the doctor. Aubrey did not like shot day. "I am afraid," she said.

Mom kept driving. "We will go together," said Mom. "I will be with you the whole time." Aubrey looked out the window. One tree, two trees, three trees went by. Then the car stopped. They were at the doctor's office.

In the office, Aubrey climbed on the big, high table. It felt cold and too big. Her legs swung in the air. The nurse came in with a little tray. Aubrey's eyes got wide. She started to cry.

"Come here," said Mom. Mom sat on a chair and pulled Aubrey onto her lap. Mom's arms went around her, warm like a blanket. Aubrey held Mom's hand. She squeezed it tight. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done, that fast. It barely hurt at all.

They walked back to the car. The seat felt cozy now. The sun made a warm spot on her knee. "My turn for a sticker," said Aubrey. She stuck it right on her shirt and smiled.

Lily sat on the big chair at the health clinic. A shot was coming next, and she did not want it. "I want to go home," she said.

The doctor had a tube around her neck. Lily pointed at it. "What is that?"

"This is my stethoscope," the doctor said. "A doctor uses a stethoscope to listen to your heart beating."

The doctor put the little ends in Lily's ears. Then she placed the round part on Lily's chest. Thump, thump. Thump, thump. Lily heard her own heart.

"That is me!" said Lily. She listened to her heart some more.

Then it was time for the shot. Lily looked at a fish swimming in the tank. She held the paper on her arm. Thump, thump went her heart.

"All done," said the doctor. "You were so brave."

Lily smiled. "My heart is still beating," she said.

Hudson ran into the playroom. He wanted to play with Aviraj and Nevaeh. But they sat in a corner. They were feeding a teddy bear. Hudson did not know what to do.

He stood by the blocks. He looked at the teddy. Nevaeh held a yellow cup to the bear's mouth. "Drink, baby bear," she said. Aviraj patted the bear's head. Hudson wanted to feed the bear too. But the game had already started. And he was not in it.

Then Hudson had an idea. "Let's pretend!" he said. "Let's pretend I am the baby's big brother!" Nevaeh looked up. Aviraj looked up. "Okay!" said Aviraj. "You can feed the bear." Hudson got a train from the toy box. "The baby wants a train ride," he said. "Toot, toot!" Nevaeh laughed. "The baby loves the train," she said.

Hudson gave the bear a ride around the rug. One lap. Two laps. "Night night, baby," said Hudson. "Let's pretend it is bedtime!" So they all tucked the bear in with a small yellow blanket. "Shh," said Nevaeh. And the baby bear went to sleep.

Eli sat at the dinner table. His plate had pasta on it. Steam went up, up, up.

"Story now," said Eli.

"Not now," said Dad. "Now we eat. The story is later, after dinner."

Eli looked down. He ate one pasta piece. He ate another. He looked out the window. The sky was bright and orange. A small spider sat on the glass. The spider sat very still.

"Is it later now?" asked Eli.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Now means this very moment. Right now, you are eating."

Eli ate some more pasta. His plate got empty. "Now?" he asked.

"Now the plate is empty," said Dad. "So now it is story time."

Eli found his soft blanket. He found his teddy bear too. He sat on Dad's lap. The spider was still on the window. The sky was not bright anymore. It was dark and calm.

"Yesterday we read the bear book," said Eli.

"Yes," said Dad. "Today we read a new one. Tomorrow you can pick again."

Dad opened the book. Eli snuggled close. "This is now," said Eli.

"Yes," said Dad. "This is now." And he began to read.

Eli wanted to build a tower at school. But the block corner was a big mess. Mr. Addo said, "Let us sort them first."

Bethany went first. She picked up a red block. "Red goes here," she said. Then a blue one. Then a yellow one. Soon there were three piles. "One, two, three colors," she said. "Red, blue, yellow."

Now it was Eli's turn. He looked at the piles. He picked up a small red block. Then a small blue one. Then a small yellow one. "These are all little," he said. He put them together. Then he made a pile of big blocks. "One, two, piles," he said. "Little and big."

Bethany watched. "The same blocks," she said. "But you made new piles."

Eli nodded. Little, little, little. Big, big, big. He stacked the big ones at the bottom. He stacked the little ones on top. The tower stood tall and did not fall.

Mr. Addo handed Eli a crayon. "Draw your tower," he said. Eli drew the big blocks first. Then he drew the little ones on top. He wrote a wobbly E for Eli at the bottom.

"One, two, three, four big blocks," said Bethany, pointing at the drawing.

"And one, two, three little ones," said Eli.

Avery went to the big lunch at the community hall. Mr. Islam was there with her friends Musa and Zander. Long tables held bread, soup, and apple slices. Avery sat down and grabbed a slice right away.

"Wait," said Musa. "We say grace first."

"What is grace?" asked Avery.

"It is a short prayer of thanks," said Zander. "Many Christian families say it before meals."

Avery put the slice down. Mr. Islam smiled at her. "Would you like to say grace today?" he asked.

Avery nodded. She closed her eyes. "Thank you for the food. Thank you for my friends."

When she opened her eyes, everyone was smiling at her. Musa gave her the biggest apple slice. Zander clapped his hands.

"Can I say grace next time too?" Avery asked.

"You sure can," said Mr. Islam.

Avery ate her soup and dreamed of next week's lunch. Maybe there would be soup, bread, and a horse cookie just for her.

Today was Emmett's birthday. The party was at the big swimming pool. Emmett wore his blue swimsuit. His friends Emersyn and Taya came too. Ms. Robinson brought a cake.

Emmett sat by the water. He put one foot in. He kicked his foot. The water went splash! The splash made his face all wet. Emmett laughed. He kicked again. Splash! Wet again.

Then everyone gathered round. His dad carried the cake. The candles were little flames. His dad held the cake for him. Emmett did not touch the flames. He just looked.

"Time to sing," said Ms. Robinson. "Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday, dear Emmett." Emmett heard his own name in the song! He hid his smiling face behind his hands. "They sang my name!" he said.

Taya sang her part next. "Happy birthday, dear Emmett," she sang. Emersyn clapped her hands. One clap, two claps, three claps.

Emmett blew out the candles with one big puff. Then he got to choose the first cake slice. He gave it to Emersyn, because she was next to him. Then everyone jumped in the pool. Splash! Splash! Splash!

Claaire sat in the backyard with her paints. She wanted to paint a pumpkin on her paper. But there was no orange paint in the jar. "Oh no," said Claire. "The orange is all gone."

Her friend Jazlyn came over to play. Jazlyn looked at the jars. "I see red paint," said Jazlyn. "I see yellow paint too." Claire dipped her brush in the red. She made a red circle on her paper. Then she dipped her brush in the yellow. She painted on top of the red circle.

The paint turned orange! "Look, look!" said Claire. Red and yellow made orange. The circle looked just like a little pumpkin. "Let's pretend it is real," said Jazlyn. Claire painted a green stem on top.

Then Claire painted more circles. She gave one to Jazlyn. She gave one to Ms. Bekele, who was watering the flowers next door. Ms. Bekele smiled and held it up to the sun. "My pumpkin looks warm," she said. Claire laughed and dipped her brush again.

Ezra wanted his bedtime story. He found his book on the floor. The cover was flat and smooth. He carried it to Dad.

"Read it, read it," said Ezra.

Dad opened the front of the book. He read the first page. "The little bear went up the hill."

Then Dad had to help Mom. "Dad will be back soon," he said. Ezra waited. He held the book.

Mom came in. She opened the front of the book too. She read the first page. "The little bear went up the hill."

Ezra sat up. "Mom, you said the same words as Dad!"

"Yes, the words say that every time," said Mom. She turned the pages one by one. She read to the end. Then she closed the back cover.

Dad came back. Ezra held up the book. "Read it again! Read it again!"

Dad read it. The words were the same again. Ezra clapped his hands. The book did not break. The words did not change.

"Tomorrow I will read it to you," said Mom.

"From the front?" asked Ezra.

"From the front," said Mom.

Ezra hugged the book tight.

Jordan went to the store with his dad. Jordan held his dad's hand. They came to get apples. Apples are tasty. Jordan saw a big red apple up high. He could not reach it. He tried to reach. His dad said, "Stop. You might fall."

Jordan wanted the apple very much. He almost grabbed the fruit stick. Then he stopped. He looked at the man in the store. The man had a tall ladder. Jordan said, "May I have that red apple, please?" The man smiled. "What good words," he said. "May I is a nice way to ask. Yes, you may." He got the apple down with a long stick.

Then Manuel and his mom came in. Manuel wanted to push the small cart. His mom said no. Jordan heard his dad say, "Thank you so much." Jordan gave the apple to his dad to hold. A lady bumped Jordan with her basket. She said, "Sorry." Jordan said, "It is okay." At home, Jordan did not forget the kind man. He ate his apple. "May I have one more tomorrow?" he asked. His dad laughed. "Yes, you may."

Beatrice came home from Grandma's house. She had a big blue bag. The trip was over now.

"Time to unpack," said her mama. Beatrice put her bag on the floor. She opened it up. Out came her shirt. Out came her soft bunny. Out came her little red shoes.

She tipped her shoe upside down. Sand fell out! Sand from the beach at Grandma's house. Beatrice laughed and laughed. The sand made a small pile on the rug.

"That is beach sand," said her mama. She helped sweep it up. Beatrice put her shirt in the drawer. She put her bunny on the bed. She put her shoes on the shelf. The bag was empty at last.

Beatrice smelled her shirt. It smelled like Grandma's flowers. Her feet felt funny without shoes, like something new.

"Unpack, unpack," sang Beatrice. She hugged her empty bag. "All done!"

Ruby went to the store with Dad. The store was long and bright. Ruby wanted red apples.

A boy stood by the apples. He said, "Give me apples!" The man did not look. The boy tried again. He said, "Apples, please." The man smiled. He gave the boy an apple. Ruby saw that. She blinked her eyes.

Ruby walked to the fruit too. She had a question. She said, "May I have two red apples, please?" The man smiled big. He put two apples in a bag. He said, "Here you go." Ruby said, "Thank you."

At the bread shelf, Ruby bumped a cart. A loaf fell down. Ruby said, "Sorry." The woman picked up the bread. She said, "That is okay, sweetie."

At the checkout, the line was long. Ruby held the apples. She waited and waited. Then Dad paid. They walked out to the car. Ruby held the bag all the way home. She said, "We can shop again tomorrow."

Charles was at school. He wanted to build a tall tower. But the tall blocks were on a high shelf. He could not reach them.

A new boy stood by the door. He had curly hair. He hid behind Mr. Zhao. Mr. Zhao waved at him. The boy did not say anything.

Charles walked over. He looked up at the new boy. "Hello," said Charles. "My name is Charles." The boy peeked out from behind Mr. Zhao. "Hello," he said. "I am River."

"Mr. Zhao, may we please have the tall blocks?" asked Charles. Mr. Zhao smiled. He took the blocks down. "Thank you," said both boys together.

River handed blocks to Charles. Charles stacked them up. The tower grew tall. Then it fell with a soft sound. "Oops," said Charles. "Sorry, River." River laughed. "It is okay. Let's build it again."

At play time, River did not hide anymore. He sat next to Charles. They read a book about towers together. "Hello, River," said a girl with a ponytail. River smiled big. "Hello!" he said back.

Charles picked up the first block. "Let's make it taller," he said.

It was Kai's birthday. He was four years old today. The backyard had balloons and cake. His friends Alia and Bowen came to play. Dad blew up a big red balloon. He tied it with a knot. Kai held the balloon up high.

"Watch it fly!" said Kai. He let go of the string. The balloon did not fly. It went down, down, down. It landed soft on the grass. Kai looked very surprised. "Why did it fall?" he asked. Alia picked it up. "It fell because it is not a floating balloon," she said. "Dad blew it up with air from his mouth."

Then Mom came out with a surprise. She had three shiny helium balloons from the store. Those balloons floated all the way up. They pulled straight up on their strings. Kai held one and felt it tug. "This one wants the sky!" he said.

Kai gave Dad a big hug. "Thank you for my red balloon," he said. Dad smiled. "We can bounce it on the floor," he said. So they did. Bounce, bounce, bounce. Bowen threw it high. It came right back down. "Again!" said Kai. It was the best birthday fun ever.

Wesley was at Grandma's house. He sat at the big table. Emmie sat next to him. They were painting pictures.

"One cat," said Wesley. "Two cats. Three cats." He painted three orange cats. Emmie painted three orange cats too. Grandma put the paintings in the sun to dry. The paint began to shine.

Then Wesley wanted his painting. But there were two papers. Both had three orange cats. "Which one is mine?" he asked. He looked and looked. He could not tell.

Emmie held up her paper. Her name was on it. Letters at the top said Emmie. "Look," she said. "I wrote my name." Wesley picked up a crayon. He wrote W-E-S on his paper. Now everyone knew which painting was his.

"How did you know?" he asked Emmie. "Grandma helped me," she said. Wesley smiled. He carried his cats to Grandma. "This one is mine," he said. "It says Wesley."

Victoria went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a red dragon. The dragon flew over a castle in the picture.

Victoria wanted to know who drew the dragon. "Dad, who made this picture?" she asked. Dad did not know. They took the book to Ms. Yoon.

Ms. Yoon opened the book. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator," she said. She pointed to a name on the first page. "This is the illustrator. Her name is right here."

Victoria looked at the name. Then she looked at the words under the picture. "Do the words say something too?" she asked. Ms. Yoon read them out loud. The words told about the dragon flying home. Victoria turned one page, then the next page. The story went front to back, all the way to the end.

Then Victoria found a thin little book about a cat. "Axelle! Come look!" she called. Her friend Axelle ran over. Victoria held up the book. "The words talk to you," she said. "And the illustrator draws the cat." She put her finger on the cat's whiskers. "This cat looks like my grandma's cat," said Axelle. Victoria opened the book to the very first page. "Then let's read it," she said.

Owen sat at the dinner table. It was a rainy night. The kitchen smelled like soup. Daddy put a warm bowl in front of him.

But Owen did not want soup. He pushed his spoon away. He made a sad face. He put his head down on his arms. Daddy looked at him. Daddy did not know what was wrong.

Then Owen sat up. "I feel sad," he said. "I wanted noodles, not soup." Daddy smiled. "Thank you for telling me," he said. Daddy went to the kitchen. He reached up for a box of noodles.

Soon Owen had a new bowl. He took a big bite. "I feel happy now!" he said. Daddy laughed and clapped his hands. "Yay for Owen!" said Daddy.

Hudson woke up early. Today he had to go to the doctor. He put his purple block in his pocket. It made him feel brave.

At the doctor's office, a nurse came in. She held a small needle. "A shot today," she said. Hudson wanted to see the needle up close. He reached out his hand. "Can I hold it?"

The nurse shook her head kindly. "Only I hold the needle," she said. "That is the rule for everyone, even for big kids." Then she smiled. "But you can hold my sticker sheet."

Hudson took the sticker sheet. It had a dog and a star on it. The nurse touched his arm. "One, two, three," she counted. The shot was done, fast like that.

"You held the sheet, so you stayed very still," said the nurse. Hudson looked at her hands. She was the one who put the needle in the tray. She was the one who put the bandage on. She did all the needle things.

Hudson picked a star sticker. He put it on his purple block at home that night. "The nurse did the needle," he told his block. "I did the sticker part."

Xavier ran into Grandpa's garage. He found a big red truck there. It had a loud horn too!

Angel came over to play. She saw the truck. She reached for it. Xavier grabbed it fast. He pulled it away.

Angel's face went sad. Her eyes filled with tears. "Now you made me cry," she said.

Xavier heard her sniffling. He looked at the truck. He looked at Angel.

He gave the truck back. "Can I have a turn next?" he asked.

Angel smiled. "Yes! You can have it after me." She pushed the truck across the floor. "Beep, beep!" she called.

Then she handed it over. Xavier took his turn. "My turn now! Vroom, vroom!"

They played together all afternoon. Grandpa peeked in and grinned. "That lazy old truck is working hard today," he said.

"Beep beep!" said Angel.

Ryan went to the bank with his mom. It was cold outside. Ryan held his coat in his hands.

"I will put it on myself," Ryan said. He pushed one arm into a sleeve. Then he pushed his other arm in too. Both arms went into the same sleeve! The coat looked like one long tube. Ryan laughed and laughed. He waved his arms like a big flipper.

His mom smiled. "Try again," she said. Ryan shook the coat out. This time he looked at it. One arm went into one sleeve. The other arm went into the other sleeve. Each arm had its own sleeve. The coat sat just right on his shoulders.

Now the zipper. Ryan pulled it up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He pulled again, slow and steady. Click. The zipper closed all the way.

At the bank, the warm air felt good. Ryan patted his chest. "I did it," he said. "All by myself."

His mom said, "Next time, we can work on your hat."

"Maybe," said Ryan. "But the coat was my big dream today." He zipped it down and zipped it back up, just to hear the sound.

Eliana ran to her cubby at daycare. She touched the tag on it. The tag said "Eliana." "That is my name," she said.

Ms. Boateng held out a card. "This came for you today." The card was smooth and red. Eliana opened it. It was from Louie. The card said "Eliana" at the top.

Eliana looked at the cubby. Then she looked at the card. "Same!" she said. "The letters are the same." Ms. Boateng smiled. "Louie can spell your name."

Jane came over. "How do you spell it?" she asked. "E, L, I, A, N, A," said Eliana, pointing at each letter. The letters went in the same order both times.

Eliana turned the pages of the card, one by one, front to back. On the last page, there was a picture of bread. It was a picture of bread with a candle in it.

"Happy birthday, Eliana!" said Louie, running in the door.

Riley ran to the playground. Tommy was by the slide. "Guess how old I am," he said. He held up four fingers.

Riley looked at his fingers. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four."

"I am four," said Tommy. He grinned.

Riley held up her own hand. She had sticky hands from her juice. She opened four fingers. "I am four too," she said.

Then Violet came over. She held up five fingers. "I am five," she said. "I had my birthday."

Riley wondered. Five fingers meant five years. Four fingers meant four years. What did three fingers mean?

A little boy was playing in the sand. Riley walked over to him. "How old are you?" she asked.

The boy held up three fingers. "I am three," he said.

Then came a surprise. He held up one more finger. "But soon I will be four," he said. His mom laughed from the bench. Far away, someone was cooking on a grill, and a little puff of smoke went up into the sky.

Riley counted all the fingers on one hand. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Five fingers. Five years. But what about six?"

Violet opened her other hand. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," she said, wiggling them all.

Riley giggled. She wiggled her ten fingers too. "Ten," she said. "That is a lot of years."

Madelyn sat in the family car. Her new baby brother sat in his seat beside her. He was very small. He had a red blanket. Madelyn wanted to help, but she did not know how.

The baby began to cry. His face was scrunched up. "He needs a clean diaper," said the parent, keeping eyes on the road. "It is in the bag." Madelyn looked at the bag. It sat by her feet. She pointed at it. "I can get it," she said.

Madelyn reached down slowly. She pulled the zipper. It stuck a little. She tried again. The zipper slid open. Inside she saw a soft blue diaper. She took it out. She also found a small gray elephant toy. "Here," she said, holding the diaper up.

The car pulled over, and the parent took the diaper. Madelyn gave the elephant to her brother. He stopped crying. He held it in his little hand. He looked at Madelyn with big eyes.

"Now you are a big helper," said the parent. Madelyn sat back in her seat. The fresh diaper made her brother comfy. The elephant made him smile. Madelyn smiled too. "I will get things for you," she whispered to him. The baby held on tight to the elephant.

Aurora woke up and looked out the window. The snow was deep and white. "No school today!" said her dad. "A snow day!" Aurora took her bowl of oatmeal to the table. She ate fast. Then she pulled her zipper up to her chin.

Outside, the yard was smooth and soft. "Where did the birds go?" Aurora wondered. Then she saw little marks in the snow. "Dad, look! Feet leave footprints in fresh snow!" she said. The prints were small, with three toes each. "Can we follow them?" asked Aurora.

They walked slowly. The footprints went around the tree. They went under the bush. They went up the porch steps next door. At the top stood Ms. Nowak, filling her bird feeder. "So that is where the birds eat!" said Aurora. Ms. Nowak laughed and waved. A little brown bird landed on the seed.

Jackson had a cold. He had to stay in his bedroom all day. His throat felt sore and scratchy. His nose was red.

He wanted to hide it. He wanted to play trains now. So he got out his trains quietly.

Then his throat hurt more. It hurt to swallow. Jackson thought hard. "When you feel sick, you tell a grown-up," he said to himself.

He went to find his dad. "Dad, my throat hurts," he said.

Dad touched his forehead. "You are warm. Let's have a rest." Dad brought him water in a small cup. Dad brought a cool cloth too.

Jackson drank the water. The cool cloth felt good on his head. His trains could wait on the rug. Soon his eyes felt heavy.

"I will have a nap," Jackson said. "The trains can have one too."

He lined three trains by his pillow. Outside, the wind blew wild in the trees. It made a soft whoosh sound.

Jackson closed his eyes. Dad read a story in a low voice. The wind went whoosh, whoosh. Jackson fell fast asleep, with his trains beside him.

Colton sat on the big blue couch. Taqdeer sat next to him. Winnifred sat on the floor. The big game was on TV.

The players ran and ran. Colton ran in place too. "Go, go, go!" he cheered. Then a referee blew a whistle. Tweep! All the players stopped running.

Colton gasped. "Why did they stop?" he asked. Ms. Balogun, from next door, held up her hand. "The whistle means stop," she said. "When the referee blows it, play stops."

Taqdeer put his fingers to his lips. "Woooo," he said, like a whistle. Winnifred froze like a statue. Colton froze too. His skin got goosebumps. It was exciting!

Then the whistle blew again. The players started running once more. Colton jumped up. "They can run again!" he shouted. He clapped his hands loud. Taqdeer clapped too. Winnifred spun in a circle.

Colton blew a pretend whistle at the TV. "Tweep!" he said. The players kept on running. Colton laughed. "My whistle is pretend," he said. "That one is real."

Athena sat in the playroom with her friend Tiffany. Big blocks were in a red box. Small blocks were in a blue box. Athena wanted to build a tower. "You can have three blocks," said Tiffany. Athena picked three big blocks from the red box. Then she looked at the blue box. She frowned. "Do three small blocks count as less?" she asked. "No," said Tiffany. "Three is three. Big or small, three means three." Athena put three small blocks in a row. She counted them. "One, two, three." She put three big blocks in a row. "One, two, three." The rows looked the same in number. Athena laughed and clapped. Ms. Chanthavong smiled from her chair by the door. Athena sang her favorite counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then she built her tower, block by block, all the way up into the air.

Jackson was at daycare. He was building a sand robot. "One arm, two arms, one leg, two legs," he said. The robot had a lazy smile made of a leaf.

Allyson walked by with her bucket. She tripped. Crash! The sand robot fell down. Jackson wanted to cry.

"Sorry," said Allyson. "I feel bad I knocked it over."

"Can you help me fix it?" asked Jackson.

"Please, can I help?" asked Allyson. "Yes, please help," said Jackson.

They patted and patted. "One arm, two arms, one leg, two legs." The robot stood up again. It looked even taller now.

"Thank you," said Jackson.

"You're welcome," said Allyson.

"Was your robot sleeping?" she asked.

"Yes," said Jackson. "He was having a dream. In his dream, he could fly." Allyson laughed, and the two friends gave the sand robot two leaf wings.

Scarlett was at Mr. Ivanova's house. It was evening. Then all the lights went out. The room went dark. "Oh no," said Scarlett. "Where did the lights go?"

Mr. Ivanova lit a little lamp. "The power went out," he said. "We will be safe." Scarlett wanted her juice cup. It sat by the big chair. She ran fast in the dark. Her foot hit the chair leg. Bump! She fell down and her knee began to hurt.

Mr. Ivanova came to her. "In the dark, we walk slowly," he said. "And we hold a grown-up's hand, so nobody trips." Scarlett took his hand. They walked slow, step by step. No bumps at all. She found her cup. It felt a bit slimy, so Mr. Ivanova washed it for her.

"Why is it dark?" Scarlett asked. Mr. Ivanova said, "The lights will come back soon. Let's watch." They sat by the window, hand in hand. Then, click! The street lamp outside came on. The room lit up too. Scarlett smiled and clapped her hands.

Elena had a shiny red block. She wanted to give it to her friend Ellis. "I will put a sticker on it," she said. "One sticker for each side."

Elena sat on the rug at home. She put a star sticker on the top. Then she turned the block over. She put a dot sticker on the bottom. "Two," she said. She touched each flat side with her hand. Side. Side. Side. Side. "Four more."

She got more stickers from the store bag. A circle sticker. A square sticker. A triangle sticker. A rectangle sticker. One for each side. She counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

Mom looked at the block. "Let's check," she said. She held it up. "How many stickers do you see?"

Elena pointed. "One, two, three, four, five, six. Six sides!" Each sticker sat on a flat face. Each face was a square, just like the square sticker. She smiled. Six little squares, all covered up.

The next day, Elena ran to Ellis. "Look!" she said. She turned the block in her hands. "Count with me."

Ellis touched each sticker. "One, two, three, four, five, six," he said. "Six!"

"Six sides," said Elena. "All squares."

Audrey was at Grandma's house. The sky got dark. Then all the lights went out. "Oh," said Grandma. "The power is out."

Grandma felt for the flashlight. "Where is it?" she said. Audrey thought hard. "The kitchen drawer," she said. Grandma felt her way to the drawer. One, two, three pulls. Click, click. It opened.

Inside was a toy frog. Inside was the flashlight. It was orange. Grandma picked it up and turned it on. The light shone bright. The room was not dark anymore.

"Even with no power, the flashlight shines," said Grandma. "Look." Audrey held her toy frog in the beam. She saw every spot on it.

Later, Audrey sat by the light. "Can we buy a new flashlight?" she asked. "The shop down the street sells them," said Grandma. "We can go tomorrow." They waited together in the warm, glowing room. Audrey counted the spots on her frog. One, two, three, four.

The lights came back on. Audrey blinked. Grandma smiled. "Night night, frog," said Audrey.

Max sat on his little chair at the tutoring centre. Mr. Delgado put out two bowls of blocks. "Which bowl has more?" he asked. Max had to guess. He pointed at the small bowl. "That one!"

Mr. Delgado smiled. "Let's count," he said. Max counted the red blocks. One, two, three, four, five. Then he counted the blue blocks. One, two, three, four. The red bowl had more! Max laughed. His guess was silly.

Then Gordon came over. "Can I have a red block?" he asked. Max gave him one. Gordon ran off to play. Max counted his red blocks again. One, two, three, four. Now the bowls were the same! Max took a cold juice cup from the tray and grinned. He held up one finger. "One block gone, one number gone," he said. Mr. Delgado clapped. Gordon peeked around the corner and popped the block back in the bowl.

Muhammad was in the backyard with a big cardboard box. Ms. Tanaka, his neighbour, had drawn five pictures on it. One picture was an eye. One was an ear. One was a nose. One was a mouth. One was a hand.

"Stick your hand here," said Ms. Tanaka. Muhammad put his hand on the hand picture. Then he touched a leaf. "I feel it with my hand," he said. He stuck a leaf next to the hand. He listened to a bird. He stuck a feather next to the ear. He looked at a red flower. He stuck a petal next to the eye.

Then Muhammad smelled something sweet. He did not see anything. He did not hear anything. "Cookies," he said. "My nose knows first. My nose smells cookies before my eyes can see them." Ms. Tanaka smiled. "Go to the kitchen window," she said. Muhammad walked slowly. The sweet smell got stronger and stronger. At the window, his dad was holding a warm cookie tray with oven gloves. Muhammad laughed. "My nose found them first," he said. He stuck the last sticker on the box, right by the nose.

John wanted to show Ms. Teo his picture. He had colored a big blue boot. The boot had wings, like a flying boot!

Ms. Teo was talking to Oaklee. "Teacher! Teacher! Look!" said John. Ms. Teo held up her hand. Oaklee kept talking about her new shoes.

John tried again. "Teacher, please look!" Ms. Teo did not turn around. John felt like a sad little rain cloud.

Ayzal whispered, "Wait for a little stop. She looks then." John watched Ms. Teo's mouth. It went quiet. It was like magic. The talking had stopped!

"Ms. Teo, may I show you something, please?" said John. Ms. Teo smiled big. "Yes, John! I am all done talking now."

John held up the flying boot. "It flies slow, like a sleepy bird," he said. Ms. Teo clapped. "What a wonderful boot!" Oaklee and Ayzal clapped too.

"Thank you," said John. Then he bumped Ayzal's elbow with his paper. "Sorry, Ayzal." Ayzal giggled. "It's okay."

Later, John told his dad all about it. He waited for a little stop in the talking. Then he said, "Dad, my boot can fly!"

Henry wanted a jam sandwich for lunch. But first he had to wash his hands. Mom said, "Soap for twenty seconds. Count with me."

Henry pumped the soap. It was pink and smelled like flowers. He rubbed his hands together. One, two, three. His hands felt slippery. They made little bubbles that slid down his fingers. "I can guess what comes next," he said. "Ten, eleven, twelve."

He counted all the way to twenty. Then he put his hands under the water. The water ran and ran. The bubbles went down the drain, one by one. Henry rubbed his fingers. They were not slippery anymore. The water had washed the soap off.

He held his hands up to the light. They were clean and shiny. "All gone," he said. He gave his hands a big sniff. No more flower smell, just clean hands. He ran to the table, low and fast like a little duck. "Jam time!" he said. Mom laughed and put the sandwich on his plate. Henry took a big bite. His clean hands rested beside his plate, still a little wet.

Mila went to the library with her dad. She wanted the bunny book. But she could not reach it. The shelf was too tall. "Please, can you help me?" she asked her dad. Dad reached up and got the book. "Thank you," said Mila.

A girl sat at the little table. It was Leanne from her class. Leanne had the red crayon. Mila leaned too close. The crayon rolled off the table. "Sorry," said Mila. She picked it up and gave it back. Leanne smiled. "Gracias," said Leanne. Mila blinked. "What does that mean?" she asked. "It means thank you in Spanish," said Leanne. Mila tried it. "Gracias!" she said. It was easy to say.

Mila sat down with her bunny book. She turned the soft pages. "This is my favorite. I love bunnies," she said. Leanne nodded and drew a bunny too.

Rosalie took the big road with her dad. They walked to the wide doors of the temple. Inside, Ms. Chaudhry was waiting with her drum.

"Hello, Rosalie," said Ms. Chaudhry. "Today we will clap and sing. You will meet the beat."

Ryan and Reese sat on the mats too. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum. Rosalie began to sing right away. But Ryan and Reese did not sing yet. Rosalie sang all alone. She stopped and her face felt warm.

"Wait for the count," said Ms. Chaudhry, kindly. "I will say one, two, three, four. Then we all start singing together."

Ms. Chaudhry lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four." Ryan and Reese began to sing. Rosalie began too, right on four. Now they all sang at the same time.

Then they clapped. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum, boom, boom, boom. Rosalie clapped her hands on each boom. She saw that when her hand went down, the drum went boom. Clap, boom. Clap, boom.

They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Rosalie knew all the words. She did not look at anyone. She sang them all by herself.

"Again!" said Rosalie.

Ms. Chaudhry smiled and lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four."

Emmett ran to the bathroom after supper. It was time to wash his hands. His dad turned on the water. The water was warm, but not too warm.

Emmett got one pump of soap. It felt slippery on his fingers. He rubbed his hands under the water. Then something happened. Bubbles! Little bubbles, big bubbles, bubbly bubbles. "Look, Dad!" said Emmett. "Soap and water made bubbles!"

He rubbed more soap. He rubbed more water. More bubbles came up. Emmett spread the bubbles on his chin. "I have a bubble beard!" he said. He giggled and giggled. His dad laughed too. "That is a kind old man beard," said Dad.

Then it was time for a bath and then night-night. Dad helped Emmett wash his toes and his tummy. Emmett stopped making bubbles so he could splash one time. Dad wrapped him in a big towel. Emmett put on his soft pajamas all by himself.

"One story, one hug, one kiss," said Dad. Emmett smiled a bubble smile and went to bed.

Aiden was busy in the playroom. He wanted his red ball. He looked under the little chair. He looked behind the big plant. "Where is my ball?" he asked. His dad said, "Look in the toy box."

The toy box was full of everything. Blocks were on the floor. A doll was on the rug. The ball was under the teddy bear. Aiden put a block in the box. The box had one less thing on the floor. He put in another block. Now the floor had more room.

Aiden held up the doll. "Doll goes in," he said. Dad said, "Yes, it does. Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys." Aiden smiled. He put the doll in. He picked up the ball. "Ball goes in too!" he said.

Then Aiden wanted to make a picture. Dad got the glue and some paper. Aiden spread the glue with a stick. He stuck on a red circle. He pressed it down. The paper was heavy with glue, so it sank down flat on the table. Aiden held his ball up high. "My ball can sit here," he said, and he set it right on top of the full toy box.

Declan ran to the tub. He wanted to get in right away. But the water was still filling up. Steam went up, up, up.

"Can I get in now?" asked Declan.

"Let me check the water first," said Dad. Dad put his hand in the water. "It is too hot right now. We will wait a bit." Declan sat on the step. He waited. He watched the steam float away. Dad turned the tap a little. Cold water came in. Dad put his hand in again. "Still too hot." Declan waited some more. He splashed his toy duck on the floor. Dad checked one more time. "Now it is just right."

Declan touched the water with his toes. It was warm and nice. He got in and made a big splash. His duck got wet too. "Bath time!" said Declan. Dad smiled and handed him the soap.

Olivia sat in the big salon chair. Her hair had grown long and wild. It was her very first haircut at a salon! Ms. Visser, the hairdresser, smiled at her.

"Now we will make it neat," said Ms. Visser. She picked up a comb. First she combed a little piece of hair. Then she snipped it with her scissors. Olivia watched closely. "One comb, one snip," she whispered. She counted. Comb, snip. Comb, snip. Comb, snip.

Then Olivia wiggled her foot. The chair bumped. Her hair went fuzzy again! "Oh no," said Olivia. But Ms. Visser just laughed. She combed the fuzzy piece back to soft and neat. Then she snipped. "The comb keeps the hair neat while you cut it," said Ms. Visser.

Yellow hair fell like soft snow. A piece landed on Olivia's nose. She giggled. Ms. Visser held up a mirror. Olivia saw a short, neat bob. She patted it. "I love it!" she said. She gave Ms. Visser the biggest smile and skipped out the door.

Everly was at Grandma's house for Diwali. There were flowers and sweets and lots of cousins. Grandma gave Everly a basket of little clay lamps.

"These are called diyas," Grandma said. "We light them for Diwali."

"Can I put them out?" Everly asked.

"Yes, one by one," Grandma said.

Everly set a diya on the step. Then she set another one next to it. She made a long row. Her legs got tired, so she sat down. She kept going slowly. One, then one, then one.

Grandma came with a small flame. She touched it to the first diya. A little light blinked on. Then the next one. Then the next. The whole row glowed.

Everly's eyes got big. "The fire made them all shiny!"

Her cousin pointed at the last diya. "That one is still dark."

Grandna waited, then touched it too. It glowed at last.

"Now the row is all lit," Everly said, and clapped her hands.

Grace went to the park with her dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Grace wore her sun hat. She saw a windy corner, too. The wind blew a paper bag along the ground. Grace laughed and chased it.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was a rainy day now. Grace had her raincoat on. Her friend Bella ran out to the slide. Bella had no raincoat. The rain fell on Bella. Her shirt got all wet. Bella ran back to the bench. "I am wet," she said. Her mom helped her put on her raincoat. Then Bella ran out again. The rain fell on the raincoat. But Bella stayed dry underneath. "Look, my tummy is dry," Bella said. Grace patted her own raincoat. Her tummy was dry, too.

Grace and Bella played until the rain stopped. "In winter, snow will fall here," said Bella. "A snowy day," said Grace. "Then we will wear big warm coats." Her dad smiled. "Yes, but now it is time to go home," he said. "Little tired kids need to sleep." Grace held her dad's hand. Her boots made splashy sounds all the way home. "Splash, splash," said Grace.

Sienna sat on the small red mat at Ms. Rahimi's music studio. Ms. Rahimi played a happy song on the piano. "Now we clap," said Ms. Rahimi. "Clap, clap, clap." Sienna clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps made a sound like little drums.

"What comes next?" asked Ms. Rahimi. "A rhyme about a spider," said Sienna. "The itsy bitsy spider!" said Amalia, who sat beside her. They began to sing. Sienna made her fingers climb up, up, up. Then she wiggled them down, down, down. Amalia giggled. "The spider climbs up, not down," said Amalia. Sienna looked at her own fingers. Oh! The spider went up the water spout. She put her fingers back at the bottom.

Sienna tried again. Up, up, up went the spider. The rain came down and washed it out. Out came the sun. Sienna clapped along with the beat, clap, clap, clap, and sang the whole rhyme all by herself. "You did it," said Ms. Rahimi. Sienna yawned a big yawn. Singing made her sleepy. "After my nap, can we sing more?" she asked. Ms. Rahimi played one more song, and the spider climbed up and up again.

Aaron sat on his bed. His teddy bear had one ear bent down. Aaron held a book, but it was not his book. It was Yanis's book. "I want my own book," said Aaron. Yanis had a library card. Aaron did not have one.

His mom said, "Let's go get your card." At the big desk, his mom helped him sign up. "A grown-up helps a child get a first card," said the librarian. She smiled. She made a card with Aaron's name on it. It was blue. It was shiny. It felt a little squishy in his pocket.

Aaron picked a book about a big red truck. He gave the card to the librarian. Beep! The card made the truck book his. "Wow," said Aaron. "My card did that!" The librarian laughed. "It sure did."

Back home, Aaron sat on his bed. He fixed teddy's soft ear. He read the truck book out loud. He read it to teddy. He read it to his socks. "Time for sleep," said his mom. Aaron hugged the book. "I will miss you, truck book," he said. He put teddy's paw on the cover, so teddy could hold it too.

Leah sat on a big train. She was going on a trip with Dad. "We ride the train, then we fly in a plane," said Dad. Leah held her card with a cute bunny on it.

At the airport, Leah saw the plane out the window. It was so big! She got in her seat next to Dad. The seat belt went click. Then Leah wanted to see out the window. She stood up.

The plane began to lift off. Leah wobbled and fell back into her seat. Dad hugged her. "Sit, buckle," said the flight lady. Dad clicked the belt again. Everyone in their seats buckled up. Leah looked out the window from her seat. She could see the clouds!

The plane came down slow and soft. Leah stayed buckled the whole way down. Dad held her hand. "Good sitting, Leah," he said. "Now let's go find Grandma."

Ayla sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist for the very first time. "I want to see everything!" she said. Outside, white snow was starting to drop from the sky.

At the dentist's office, Ayla climbed into a big chair. It went up and up, like a rocket. "Open your mouth wide," said the dentist. "Then I can see every tooth." Ayla opened wide, like a lion's roar. "Ahhh!" she said. Then she closed her mouth to ask, "Do I get a sticker?" The dentist could not see her teeth anymore.

Ayla thought for a minute. She opened her mouth wide again. Now the dentist could see every tooth. "All clean!" the dentist said. Ayla picked a pink sticker, her favorite color. She wore it all the way home, grinning big at the snow.

Sara sat at the paint table. Ms. Park put out three cups. "Red, yellow, blue," said Ms. Park. Sara said each one. "Red. Yellow. Blue." Dani said them too. "Red, yellow, blue!"

Sara wanted to make green paint. She had seen green leaves outside. She took her brush. She dipped it in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred. The paint turned green! Sara clapped. "Green!"

But then Sara looked at her cup. All the yellow was gone. It had gone into the blue. Sara tried to pull the yellow back out. She pulled with her brush. The yellow would not come back. Her eyes got big. "My yellow is stuck," she said.

Ms. Park came over. She gave Sara a hug. "It is okay," she said. "We cannot pull them apart now. But we can get more." Ms. Park gave her a fresh cup of yellow. Sara kept a little yellow to the side. She kept a little blue too. Then she mixed the rest. Green again! Dani laughed. "Green!" said Sara. She painted one green leaf, then two, then three.

Adam was at the park. The sun was out. It was a sunny day.

Adam wore his old red hat. He played in the sand with Amaya. The wind blew. It was a windy day too. Adam watched the wind move the leaves. "Look, the leaves dance!" he said.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Adam felt cold drops on his nose. "Where does the rain come from?" he asked. Then came a big sound. Rumble! Rumble! It was thunder.

Adam wanted to keep playing in the sand. But Ms. Sokolov called out. "Thunder! Time to go indoors," she said. Adam held Amaya's hand. They ran inside with Ms. Sokolov. It was warm and dry indoors.

Adam looked out the window. The rain fell and fell. "When we hear thunder, we go indoors," he said. Ms. Sokolov smiled. "That's right, Adam."

Adam dreamed about snowy days. Snowy days need warm boots and a big coat. "Can we play in the snow someday?" he asked. Ms. Sokolov nodded. "We can," she said. Adam watched the rain slide down the glass.

Abigail was drawing in her room. She drew a small duck on a pond. Then she smelled something warm. She sniffed the air with her nose. It smelled like bread and cheese.

"Mom!" she called. "Are we having grilled cheese?"

"Yes!" said Mom from the kitchen. "Come and see."

Abigail ran to the kitchen. She did not see the sandwiches yet. Mom stood by the stove. The pan was hot, so Mom watched it. Abigail kept her feet far away.

"First I smelled it," said Abigail. "Now I will hear it." She used her ears. The pan went sizzle, sizzle. Mom flipped one sandwich over.

"Almost done," said Mom. "You can wait at the table."

Abigail sat down. She patted the smooth table with her hand. Soon Mom brought two plates. The sandwiches were gold and brown. Abigail could smell them up close now. She took a small bite. Her tongue tasted cheese, warm and salty.

"Yum," said Abigail. "My nose knew before my eyes did."

Mom laughed and slid the plate closer.

Clean-up time came to Connor's room at daycare. Mr. Okonkwo said, "Let's make color piles. Red things go here. Blue things go there. Yellow things go over there."

Connor picked up a red block. He put it on the red pile. Fatima put a blue block on the blue pile. Hargun put a yellow block on the yellow pile. "Same colors together," said Connor.

Then Connor saw a green block. It was hiding in the red pile. "Look," he said. "Green does not go here." He picked it up. He looked and looked. Then Mr. Okonkwo held out a box. "Smart boy, Connor. Make a green pile." Connor put the green block in the box. All the green blocks sat together, and Connor smiled.

Jaxon sat at the art table. He wanted to make a paper sailboat. He needed two triangles for the sail. But his paper was a square.

"Oh no," said Jaxon. "I only have a square."

Izaiah looked over. "Ms. Gill can help," he said.

Ms. Gill was a kind woman. She came to the table. She took the scissors and cut the square. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner.

Jaxon watched. The square fell into two pieces.

"Two triangles!" said Jaxon. "I see it now!"

He taped the triangles on a stick. Then he made the boat. It had a circle window and a square door too.

"That is a cute sailboat," said Emelia.

"Want to make one too?" said Jaxon. "I can help you cut."

Emilia sat on the park bench with her friend Akira. Mr. Hassan had a big basket of snacks. "Let's play a game," he said. "Guess the snack with your senses."

Emilia put her hands over her eyes. "I can't see it," she said. "Eyes see." Akira covered his ears. "I can't hear it," he said. "Ears hear." Emilia sniffed the snack. "My nose smells banana," she said. She touched it next. "My hands feel something squishy."

Then she took a little bite. Her face went funny. "Yuck! Sour!" she said. "That is a lemon. Mom packed it from our kitchen. She said it was a bad idea to bite it." Akira laughed and laughed. "A lemon is not a treat, Emilia!"

"Now it's my turn," said Akira. He closed his eyes. He sniffed. He licked his snack. "Sweet! My tongue says sweet!" His tongue was right. It was a sweet, ripe strawberry.

Emilia tried again with a new snack. Her tongue told her, sweet. It was honey bread. "My tongue is so smart," she said. Mr. Hassan smiled. "One more snack," he said. He held out a slice of orange. Emilia licked it. "Sweeeeet," she sang.

Then Mr. Hassan held out a small green apple. Emilia licked it. She made a big, silly face. "Sour! Sour! Sour!" Everyone laughed. "My tongue can tell," said Emilia. "Sweet snacks and sour snacks. It always knows!"

Akira clapped for her. Emilia took a big bite of the sweet honey bread.

Nova woke up early. Today was the Eid party in the park. She looked at her small blue coat. "Can I wear my coat?" she asked. Her mom shook her head. "No, today we wear special clothes. People often wear special clothes to a celebration." Nova put on her pretty green dress with gold flowers. It swished when she twirled. Her mom helped her tie the little ribbons on her shoes.

At the park there were balloons and sweet smells. Nova smelled warm cardamom and buttery cookies. She saw her friend George. George wore a long white shirt that shone in the sun. "Your shirt is so white!" said Nova. George laughed and spun around. Then Nova saw something surprising. Phillip was there too. Phillip wore a bright red jacket covered in tiny mirrors. When the sun touched it, sparkles danced on the grass. Nova gasped. She clapped her hands.

Then Nova had a question. "Why does everyone look so fancy today?" she asked her mom. Her mom smiled. "Because it is a celebration. Special clothes make the day feel special." Nova looked down at her green dress. She twirled again and the gold flowers caught the light.

They sat on a soft blanket. Ms. Saleh, from next door, waved hello. She wore blue silk that shimmered like water. Everyone ate sweet treats from big plates. Nova licked sugar off her fingers. A breeze blew and all the pretty clothes fluttered together, red and green and white and blue. Nova leaned against her mom and watched the sparkles dance on the grass.

Madison sat at the big art table. She was painting grass for a cow. Ms. Augustin had put out paint pots. There was a red pot. There was a blue pot. There was a yellow pot.

Madison looked for the green pot. It was empty. Only a stuck lid sat on the bottom. "Where is the green?" she asked. "Maybe we can make green," said Kasey. Kasey was painting next to her.

Madison put her brush in the blue pot. She added some yellow paint. She stirred it with her brush. The paint turned green, just like grass. Madison smiled big. She painted tall green grass under her cow. Kasey painted a green frog. "Dad will like this," said Madison. Her brush sank into the fresh green paint.

Jaxon walked in the forest with Ms. Ricci. He saw a box under a big tree. The box had a hat, a scarf, and some shiny boots. "Who wears this?" he asked. "You can wear it," said Ms. Ricci. Jaxon put on the big hat. He stood very tall. "Now I am a firefighter!" he said. "The dress-up clothes make me someone new."

His friends Shepherd and Judith came down the path. "Look, look!" said Jaxon. "I am a firefighter!" Judith put on the scarf. "Now I am a mama," she said. Shepherd put on the boots. "I am a farmer now," he said. They all laughed.

The farmer had a carrot. "My baby bunny is hungry," said the mama. The firefighter helped. "I will bring the carrot fast!" said Jaxon. He ran, but not too fast, and gave the carrot to the soft toy bunny. The bunny was not hungry anymore. "Is the bunny okay now?" asked Jaxon. "Yes, all better," said Judith.

Then the pretend phone rang. Beep, beep! "Come quick!" said Shepherd. "A little cat is stuck!" The firefighter put on his big hat again. He held his toy hose. He sprayed pretend water on a pretend fire. The cat was saved. The mama hugged the cat. The farmer clapped. Jaxon took off the big hat at the end of the day. He was just Jaxon again. But he smiled all the way home. "Can we play again soon?" he asked Ms. Ricci. "Yes," she said. "Tomorrow we play again."

William got his first pet today. It was a small guinea pig. His dad carried the box to the park. They sat on the soft green grass to open it.

"Can I carry him around?" William asked.

William stood up. He held the guinea pig with one hand. The guinea pig wiggled. He nearly fell.

"Not like that," said Ms. Clarke-Williams, his neighbour. "Sit down on the grass. Hold him with two hands."

William sat down. He cupped both hands under the guinea pig. The guinea pig sat in his two hands. He wiggled, but he did not fall. He was close to the ground. William could not drop him far.

"Soft," said William. He petted the fur with one finger.

A girl from school ran by. "Can I hold him?" she asked.

"You have to sit down first," said William. Lucia sat on the grass. William set the guinea pig in her two hands. The guinea pig sniffed her sleeve.

Then it was time to go home. William stood up slow. His dad put the guinea pig back in the box. William carried the box with two hands, like a big stack of blocks.
