At home, William sat on the floor. The guinea pig climbed onto his lap. "Good little pig," said William. "I will always sit down."

Ali went to the farm with Ms. González. He wanted to learn his five senses. He wanted to say them all by lunch time.

First, Ali smelled bread. "I used my nose," he said. Next, he heard a cow. "I used my ears." Then he touched a small, soft lamb. "I used my hands." He tasted a sweet apple from his bag. "I used my tongue." One sense was left. Ali looked up at the sky. He wanted to see the sun up close. He began to look straight at it. "Stop," said Ms. González. "Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes." Ali looked down fast. He blinked and blinked. He felt a little scared. "Your eyes are okay," said Ms. González. "You looked away in time."

Then Ali saw a duck by the river. It jumped in and made a splash. "I used my eyes!" said Ali. "That is five! Nose, ears, hands, tongue, eyes." Ms. González smiled. "You did it," she said. "Now let's go catch a bus home."

Aiden ran onto the soccer field. The sky was cloudy. "Kick, kick, kick!" he said. The ball went this way and that way.

Aiden did not know where to stand. He stood in the middle of everything. Harley bumped into him. Roy bumped into him too. "Too many feet!" said Roy. Aiden sat down on the grass. "I am all mixed up," he said.

Mr. Ba blew his whistle. He was the coach. "Come here, team," he said. Mr. Ba showed Aiden a spot near the corner. "Stand here," he said. "Watch for the ball." Aiden stood on the spot. He watched and watched. Then the ball came rolling. He ran to it. He kicked it far, far away. "Goal!" shouted Harley. "Goal!" shouted Roy. Aiden laughed and did a happy jump.

The big clock on the field said it was time to go. "Same time next week," said Mr. Ba. Aiden filled his water bottle with his dad. "I know where to stand now," said Aiden. "Stand on my spot. Wait for the ball." He kicked a pinecone all the way to the car.

Luke had a toy snake at school. It was green and long. He loved that snake.

At play time, Luke saw Liana. She sat by the wooden blocks. Tears ran down her face. She was crying. Luke felt sad too.

He ran to his cubby. He got his toy snake. He held it out to Liana. "You can hold him," Luke said. Liana wiped her eyes. She took the soft snake. She hugged it close.

Then Liana smiled a big smile. "His name is Sam," she said. Luke sat down next to her. They made a little home for Sam out of blocks. Mr. Lin came over and helped them cover the snake with a small blanket.

"More blocks," said Liana. She handed one to Luke.

Elijah went to the library with his dad. He wanted the pink bunny book. He saw it on a low shelf.

A tall man stood in the way. Elijah tried to squeeze past. He bumped the man's bag. "Sorry," said Elijah. The man smiled and moved his bag. But he still stood there.

Elijah waited. He tapped his feet. Then he remembered. His dad said, "Say excuse me." So Elijah said, "Excuse me, please." The man looked down. He stepped to the side. "Go right ahead," he said.

Elijah walked to the shelf. He took the pink bunny book. "Thank you," he said to the man. The man said, "You are welcome."

Elijah sat with his dad. In the book, the bunny had a little brother. The brother liked to chew a big carrot. Elijah turned the pages slowly. The pink bunny shared the carrot at the end. Elijah hugged the book and said, "Again."

Everly went to the store with her dad. She wanted milk for her cereal. But the store was big. Where was the milk?

Everly looked up. There was a sign. It had letters on it. The sign said "Milk". Her dad pointed. "The words tell us what is here," he said. Everly smiled. Words could tell her things!

She looked at more signs. One said "Bread". One said "Apples". The apples sat on a low shelf. She could see them just fine.

Then Everly saw a box on the bottom shelf. She had to lift it up to see the front. The front had words too. "Cereal," Everly read. Her dad clapped. "You found the signs and the box words!"

Everly held her dad's hand. She skipped past the crayons on the way to the milk. "Milk is this way," she said, pointing at the sign.

Max went to the farmers' market with his dad. He saw a big pile of little plants. He picked one pot. It had small furry leaves.

"Can we plant it?" Max asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We can plant it at home." Mr. Guo sold them the plant. He put a stick in the pot. A little picture of a tomato was on the stick. "The stick shows what it is," said Mr. Guo.

Max and his friend Ricardo planted the tomato in the garden. Ricardo planted a carrot too. Then Max forgot which spot had the tomato. He looked and looked. All the spots looked the same. Max sat down by his shoe. Then he had an idea.

He asked Dad for more sticks. Max drew a red tomato on one. He drew an orange carrot on the other. He pushed the picture sticks into the soil. Now he could see the tomato spot. Now he could see the carrot spot. Every day Max watered them. The tomato grew tall. A round red tomato hung on the plant. Max held it in his two hands. "It grew!" said Max. "It grew from our little stick spot," said Ricardo.

Hayden had a little garden in the backyard. He planted lettuce, carrots and beans. Every morning he skipped out to look at it.

One hot day, the lettuce looked sad. The leaves hung down low. "Oh no," said Hayden. "My lettuce is drooping!" Amal came over to play. He looked at the leaves too. "It droops when it does not get enough water," said Amal.

Hayden ran to get his watering can. The grass was slippery from the sprinkler, but he did not fall. He gave the lettuce a big drink of water. Mr. Huang, the neighbour, waved over the fence. "Nice job," he said. The next morning, the lettuce stood up tall and green. "Look, Amal!" said Hayden. "It is happy now!" Amal clapped his hands.

Arya sat on the big rug. The room was full of people. Dad was there. Amaira was there too. They were all watching the big game.

The players ran fast. They kicked the ball. Then a loud horn blew. "Who is winning?" Arya asked. Dad said, "The red team." Arya clapped her hands.

The players ran again. Someone kicked the ball hard. The crowd on TV cheered. "Who is winning now?" Arya asked. Amaira said, "I forgot." Arya could not remember either. She beg ged Dad to tell her, again and again.

Then Arya looked up at the TV. She saw a big box with numbers. One name was on top. One name was on the bottom. Each name had a number beside it. "What is that?" she asked. Dad said, "That is the scoreboard." Arya looked and looked. She pointed at the numbers, one, two, three. The red team had more points. The blue team had less.

The game went on. Arya did not ask anyone. She looked at the scoreboard herself. Every time a team got a point, one number grew bigger. The little arrow moved up too.

Then something funny happened. Arya's cat jumped onto the rug. He sat right on her picture book. He watched the game too. "He likes the red team," said Amaira. Arya giggled and patted his soft ears. Then she looked at the scoreboard one more time. "Red team wins," she said.

Kayden woke up in the morning with a big problem. His hair was full of tangles. "Oh no," he said. He looked in the little mirror. His hair stood up like a bird's nest. He wanted to look nice for school. His friend Lia was coming today.

Mom gave him his small brush. "Go slow," she said. "Slow does not pull." Kayden started at the top. He pulled a little. Ow. That part was stuck. He went slower there. Brush, brush, brush. One tangle came loose. His hair got smooth in that spot.

"Wow," said Kayden. "The brush gets tangles out!" He brushed the other side. Brush, brush. Smooth! He felt dizzy spinning around to see the back. Then he ran to get dressed. He pulled on his shirt and tied his shoes. He was so fast.

At school, Lia touched his hair. "So soft," she said. Kayden smiled. "I brushed it slow," he said. "Slow makes the tangles go away." Lia giggled and patted his head again.

Maria went to the hospital with her papa. Her mama was there. Mama had a new baby. The baby was a girl. Maria peeked at her tiny hand. "Can I touch her?" Maria asked. Mama smiled. "Put your finger in her hand," Mama said. "Watch what she does."

Maria put her finger in the baby's hand. The baby held tight! The little fingers wrapped around Maria's finger. They did not let go. Maria laughed. "Papa, look! She is holding me!" Papa laughed too. "She is strong," he said.

Maria pulled her finger a tiny bit. The baby held on more. Maria wondered, how small are her hands? The hand was smaller than Maria's whole thumb. "Does she dream?" Maria asked. Mama said, "Little babies sleep a lot." The baby's eyes were shut. Her hand was still tight on the finger.

A nurse came in with a soft blanket. It was a cozy yellow blanket with a rabbit on it. The nurse wrapped the baby up. Now only the baby's face and hands showed. Maria touched the rabbit on the blanket. Then she felt her finger again. Still holding on!

Mama yawned. She was tired. "Say night night," Papa said. Maria waved at the baby. She tapped the small hand once. The fingers opened. The baby let go. Maria smiled. "She held my finger the whole time," Maria whispered to the rabbit blanket.

Olivier ran to the park with his red coat on. His friend Douglas wore a blue coat. Gavin wore a yellow hat. The sun went down and the sky turned orange. A dog barked by the swings. It was time to go home.

"Where is my coat?" said Olivier. He had left it in the play tunnel. The tunnel was very dark inside. Olivier reached in with both hands. He felt something soft. He pulled it out. In the dark, he could not tell what color it was. Mr. Hussain held up his phone light. "Let's look together," he said. The coat in Olivier's hands was green, not red. "That one is mine," said Mr. Hussain with a smile. "Let's try again."

Olivier reached back into the dark tunnel. He felt another coat. He pulled it out into the light. This one was red! "You found it," said Douglas. Olivier put on his red coat. Gavin waved his yellow hat. "See you tomorrow!" said Gavin. Olivier waved all the way home.

Margot looked out the window. The sky was gray. Rain fell on the grass. "Rainy day," said Mom. "We need boots today."

Margot put on her yellow boots. She put on her raincoat. Mom held the umbrella. They went outside to walk to the car.

Then Margot saw something. A big puddle sat on the driveway. She pointed at it. "Where did that come from?" she asked.

"It rained," said Mom. "Rain makes puddles on the ground."

Margot stepped in the puddle. Splash! Water went up on her boots. She laughed. She stomped again. Splash, splash!

Then Margot felt a big gust. The wind pulled at her hood. "Windy too!" said Mom. She held Margot's hand tight.

Margot's legs felt a little weak from stomping. Mom picked her up. "Time for warm cocoa at home," she said.

At home, Mom took off Margot's wet boots. Mom made the cocoa, because cocoa is hot. Margot waited on the couch.

She looked at the window again. The rain was stopping. The sun came out. "Sunny now!" said Margot.

Mom smiled. "Tomorrow we can look for more puddles," she said. Margot hugged her cup with both hands.

Lennon sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She waited with her mom. She heard a soft beep from the hall. She used her ears for that.

Ms. Guo came in. Ms. Guo was the doctor. "Hello, Lennon," she said. "I heard you got dust in your eye at the park."

"Yes. The wind blew it in," said Lennon.

"Close your eyes," said Ms. Guo. "Look in the little mirror."

Lennon looked. She saw her own eyes. She saw tiny hairs on her eyelids. "What are those?" she asked.

"Those are your eyelashes," said Ms. Guo. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes."

Lennon blinked. She blinked fast, then slow. A tiny speck sat on her lashes. She touched it with one finger. Her finger felt the little dot.

Then she opened her lunch box. She smelled her apple. She took a bite. Her tongue tasted the sweet apple juice.

"Your eye looks all clean now," said Ms. Guu.

Lennon blinked one more time. She watched her eyelashes go down and up in the mirror.

"They did a good job," she said.

Carter went to the playground with his mom. First he went down the slide. Then he ran in the green grass. "One slide, two swings, three big steps," he counted. His mom waved from a bench.

After play time, they walked to the little store next to the playground. Mom said, "Stay close." Carter saw apples. He saw a big tower of cans. Then he looked up. Mom was not there. The tall shelf had hidden her.

Carter remembered what his dad had taught him. He walked to the front. The cashier had curly hair. "I can't find my grown-up," Carter said. The cashier called out, and Mom came running around the shelf. "You told a store worker," Mom said. "That was just right."

Then a small surprise came. Azalea from his class popped out from behind the juice boxes. "Carter! We play at my house next door," she said. Carter counted again: "One apple, two friends, three happy people." Mom held his hand all the way to the door.

Muhammad sat at the big clean table in the library. Ms. Perera gave him a pencil and some paper. Muhammad wanted to write his name. He held the pencil in his fist. The letters came out wobbly. "Try three fingers," said Ms. Perera. She showed him how. Thumb, finger, finger. Muhammad tried. The line was smoother now.

Then Muhammad got up to find Austin. He waved the pencil as he walked. The point was up. Ms. Perera tapped the table softly. Muhammad stopped. He turned the pencil around. Point facing down. Austin walked past, close to the pencil. Nothing poked him. Muhammad kept walking, very careful.

Back at the table, Muhammad spun the pencil once between his fingers. He pressed down. M-u-h-a-m-m-a-d. "I did it!" he said. Austin clapped. Ms. Perera smiled. Muhammad held his paper up high.

Layla ran to the big tree at the park. Ayra and Beatrix were already there. They had a doll, a toy carrot, and a small blanket.

"Let's play house," said Ayra. "You can each pick a role," said Beatrix. "One person can be the parent. One person can be the baby."

"I want to be the parent," said Layla. "I want to be the parent too," said Ayra. Both girls frowned. The toy carrot sat in the grass.

Then Layla had an idea. "Let's switch halfway," she said. "You first. Then me."

Ayra smiled. She held the doll and fed it the carrot. Layla curled up like the baby under the blanket. "One, two, three, halfway now!" she called.

They switched. Layla rocked the doll. She gave it a kind pat. Ayra snored like a sleepy baby.

Ms. Ortiz walked by and laughed. "Whose turn is next?" she asked.

Luna ran to the sandbox at the park. The sand was warm. It felt a little itchy between her toes. Lucia was there, playing with toy cars. Red cars, blue cars, one yellow truck.

"Look," said Lucia. "Something is hiding in the cars." Luna dug in the sand. She found a banana! A yellow banana, sitting with the toy cars.

Luna laughed. "That's the odd one out," she said. "It does not belong." The cars could roll. The banana could not roll. The banana was a food, not a toy. Lucia put the banana in her lunch box.

"I have apples too," said Lucia. "And crackers." Luna patted the sand flat. Then she lined up the cars, one by one. She put her red hat at the end.

"Now the hat is the odd one out," said Luna. Lucia giggled. They rolled the cars down the hill, all together, whee, whee, whee.

Anthony sat in the family car. Dad was driving to the salon. "First haircut," said Dad. Anthony held his hat. He did not want his hair to go.

At the salon, Anthony sat in a big chair. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. She was the grown-up with the sharp thing. Snip. One bit of hair fell. Snip, snip. Two more bits fell. "One, two, three," counted Anthony. The tiny bits dropped down, down, down.

Anthony's lip wobbled. "My hair is gone!" he said. Dad smiled. He bent his big head down low. "Touch it," said Dad. Anthony patted Dad's head. It was fuzzy, like a peach. "My hair was cut too," said Dad. "Then it grew back. Hair grows back after it is cut." Anthony patted again. Fuzzy, fuzzy, fuzzy.

Back in the car, Anthony looked in the little mirror. His hair was short and neat. It fit under his hat now. "Bye, hair," said Anthony. "Grow, grow, grow." Dad laughed all the way home.

Addison went to the music studio. Mr. Wilson had a drum. "Now it is your turn," he said. Addison put out her hands.

"Clap, clap, clap," said Mr. Wilson. "One, two, three, one, two, three." Addison clapped along. At first her claps were too fast. Mr. Wilson swung his arm slow like a swing. Addison watched. She clapped slow too. Now her claps matched the song. "One, two, three, one, two, three."

"Now we sing," said Mr. Wilson. Addison sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" very loud. Lou covered his ears and laughed. Then Kobe put the baby doll in the little bed. "The baby is sleeping," he said. "Be careful."

Addison took a big breath. Then she sang very, very soft. Her voice was small like a whisper. The baby doll stayed asleep. Lou sang soft too. Kobe sang soft too. They sang the whole song, quiet as mice.

Mr. Wilson smiled. "Same song," he said. "Soft this time." Addison patted the doll's back. "Shh," she whispered. "Sleep, baby, sleep."

Jaxon stood at the edge of the hockey rink. The ice was far away. The class had the soft floor by the boards today. Ms. Wang held a big box of beanbags.

"Watch me," said Ms. Wang. She tossed a beanbag into a hoop. The beanbag went in. Jaxon clapped. He picked up his own beanbag. He threw it. It hit the rim and fell out. Abeer threw hers. It went in. Jaxon tried again and again. On his fifth try, the beanbag dropped right in.

Next came the big ball. Kehlani rolled it to Jaxon. Jaxon had his hands in his pockets. The ball bumped his tummy and rolled away. He ran after it. Ms. Wang waited. She did not say anything. She just put her own arms out. Her hands were open. Kehlani rolled the ball to her. She caught it.

Jaxon looked at his pockets. Then he took his hands out. He stretched his arms out wide. His hands were open. Kehlani rolled the ball again. It came slow and soft. Jaxon held on with both hands. "I caught it!" he said.

"Again," said Kehlani. Jaxon kept his arms out. He was careful. The ball came and he caught it again. Then he drew a big smile in the air with his finger to show how happy he was. "My hands are ready," he said.

Sienna stood in the kitchen with her dad. She wanted to help make a smoothie. First she looked at the red strawberries with her eyes. She sniffed them with her nose. They smelled sweet.

Then Dad put the fruit in the blender. "Cover your ears!" he said. The blender was very loud. Sienna did not cover her ears fast. The noise was too big! She put her hands over her ears right away. Then the loud sound got quiet. Her ears felt better under her hands.

The blender stopped. Sienna took her hands off her ears. "It is quiet now," she said. Dad poured the smoothie into a cup. Sienna touched the cup with her fingers. It was cold. She took a sip and tasted strawberries. "Yum!" she said. She let Dad have a sip too.

The next morning, the blender roared again. This time Sienna was ready. She covered her ears with her hands before the noise. It stayed quiet and small. Sofia came over to play. "That sound is big," Sofia said. Sienna showed her how. "Put your hands on your ears," she said. Sofia tried it, and she smiled. The two friends drank their smoothie by the open door. "Nice and quiet," said Sofia.

Lily sat at the little table. It was paint time at daycare. She wanted to paint the sky over her house. She picked up the gray paint. Her friend Jethro sat next to her.

Jethro looked out the big window. "Look at the sky," he said. Lily looked too. The sun was bright. There were no clouds at all. The sky was blue, not gray. Lily put the gray brush down. She dipped her brush in blue. She painted a big blue sky with a yellow sun.

A dog barked outside. Jethro felt scared of big dogs. He covered his ears with his hands. Lily gave him her green crayon to hold. Jethro held it and stopped covering his ears. Then he painted green grass under Lily's blue sky.

Ms. Do came to look. "What a sunny day," she said. She hung the painting by the window. The real sky and the paint sky were both blue. Lily smiled and pointed at them. "Two blue skies," she said.

Eloise set her teddy bear on the rug. She was playing house! She gave him a toy cup.

Then her friend Nina came over. Nina held a toy dragon. "The dragon is scary," said Nina. She made a big ROAR noise.

Eloise frowned. She did not like that game. "The dragon is friendly," said Eloise. "It wants to feed the teddy bear."

"Scary dragon," said Nina.

"Friendly dragon," said Eloise.

They both looked at the dragon. The game stopped. That was no fun at all.

"Wait," said Nina. "We can pick together. One dragon. Both of us."

"A friendly dragon who roars at breakfast?" asked Eloise.

"Yes!" said Nina. "One friendly dragon. ROAR!"

The dragon flew to the teddy bear. It fed him pretend toast. It made one big noise, and then it gave a hug.

"One dragon," said Eloise. "Both of us."

"Best dragon ever," said Nina. "ROAR again!"

Rosalie sat high up in the big stadium. Her mom sat beside her. Rupert and Hassan were there too. The game was about to start.

The players ran out onto the field. The crowd began to roar. Rosalie held her red flag. She waved it up and down.

Then a boy in blue kicked the ball into the net. Rosalie jumped up. She clapped her hands and cheered very loud. "Yay! Yay!" she shouted.

But nobody else was clapping. Rupert looked at her. Hassan looked at her. Everyone around them sat still and quiet.

"Rosalie," said Rupert. "That was the other team."

Rosalie looked at the field. The blue players were hugging. The red fans were not happy at all. She started to laugh. "Oops!" she said. "I cheered for the wrong team!"

Hassan laughed too. "Watch," he said. "When our team scores, everyone will clap."

Soon a boy in red kicked the ball in. The whole crowd stood up. They clapped and cheered and stomped. The seats seemed to shake. Rosalie clapped hardest of all.

"Now I get it," she said. She waved her red flag and waited for the next goal.

Michael was in the pool changing room with his dad. He pulled off his sock and put it on the bench. He stacked his sock on top of his shoe. "Look, Dad. One sock, one shoe."

"Nice stacking," said Dad. "Now let's put on your swimsuit."

Michael pulled on his swimsuit. It had blue fish on it. He was going to learn to swim. His friend Coralie was already in the water. She was splashing her arms.

"Can I jump in now?" asked Michael.

"Not yet," said Dad. "A grown-up must always watch children in the water. Mr. Martínez is not here yet."

Michael counted the people in the pool. "One lifeguard, two kids, three towels. But no Mr. Martínez." He wanted to jump so much. He stood at the edge of the pool. He put one toe in. The water was warm.

"Who will watch me?" Michael asked.

"Mr. Martínez will watch you," said Dad. "He is coming now."

The door opened. Mr. Martínez walked in with a tall stack of floats. "Hello, Michael! I see you waiting. That was smart."

Michael jumped into the water. Mr. Martínez was watching. Coralie clapped her hands. Michael kicked his legs and splashed.

"I did it!" said Michael.

"Again?" asked Mr. Martínez.

"Yes, again!" said Michael. He held the float and kicked. Mr. Martínez stayed close, watching. Then Dad wrapped Michael in a big towel. "Warm sock, warm shoe," said Michael, and he smiled.

Paisley was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big red swing on a tree. Paisley wanted to swing right away.

But her friend Oceanne was on the swing. Oceanne pumped her legs. The swing went up high. Paisley waited by the tree. She did not push. She did not yell. She held her seed from lunch in her hand and looked at it.

Then Oceanne jumped off. "Your turn now," said Oceanne. Paisley got on the swing. She kicked her legs. The swing went up and up. Grandma said, "Look at you go!" Paisley laughed.

After a long time, Paisley saw Oceanne standing by the tree. Oceanne's face looked a little sad. So Paisley slowed down. She jumped off. "Your turn now," said Paisley. Oceanne ran fast and got on.

The girls took turns all morning. One would swing, then the other. Then one would swing again. Grandma brought out paper. "Come color with me," she said. Paisley drew the swing. She drew Oceanne's ugly old shoes, which Oceanne loved very much. "I will draw you next," said Paisley. Oceanne smiled and picked a crayon.

Aurora went to the store with her dad. She held his hand tight. She liked to wave at Mr. Nolan, the man who stacked the shelves. Mr. Nolan waved back.

Near the checkout, Aurora saw something on the floor. It was a little bottle. The lid was off. Round red things had spilled out. They looked like candy. Were they candy? She wanted to pick one up. But then she remembered. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy. So she did not touch them.

"Dad, come and see," she said. Her dad looked. "Good girl," he said. "Those are pills, not candy. Let's find Mr. Nolan." Mr. Nolan picked up the bottle. He put the pills back in. "You solved the puzzle," he said. Aurora smiled. She held her dad's hand tight all the way to the car.

Theodore sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint the long grass by the lake. But there was no green paint in his tray. He had red, yellow, and blue. He looked and looked. Still no green.

His friend Khaled sat down next to him. "I need green for the grass," Theodore said. "I only have yellow and blue." Khaled pointed at the jars. "Yellow is a sun colour," he said. "Blue is a sky colour."

Theodore dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He painted a big yellow stripe on his paper. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue paint. He made a blue stripe right on top. He swirled his brush round and round. The colours touched. The wet paint moved together.

The stripe turned green! Theodore jumped up. "Khaled, look! It's green!" He painted long green grass all the way across his paper. He even gave the stick figure in his picture green shoes. Ms. Pérez came over and smiled. "What lovely grass, Theodore." Theodore held up his wet painting so she could see. "It's yellow and blue," he said.

Emmett hurried to the dress-up corner at school. He wanted to wear the firefighter hat. But his shoe felt funny. One sock was gone!

"Where is my sock?" Emmett asked. He looked under the chair. No sock. He looked in the short basket of hats. No sock. He looked in the toy box. Yes! His sock was lying on top of a teddy bear.

Emmett picked up the sock. He laughed. "A sock is not a toy," he said. "It goes with clothes. Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Yousuf came over. He was holding his shirt. "My shirt fell in the toy box too," Yousuf said.

"Then we can fix it," Emmett said. He put his sock in the clothes basket. He counted out loud, "One sock, one shirt, one hat." Yousuf added his shirt. "Now two shirts!" he said.

Ms. Munro smiled. "You made the corner neat," she said. "Thank you, boys."

Emmett put on his sock and shoe. Then he put on the firefighter hat. He looked out the window at the big tree. "Firefighter to the rescue!" he said.

Water day was here at school. Weston put on his swim shorts. He had a small towel in his bag too. Mr. Taylor set out a big tub of water. "Splash all you like," he said.

Weston stepped into the water. Splash! Splash! Water went everywhere. His arms got wet. His legs got wet. His hair dripped and dripped. Maeve got wet too. Rowan got wet too. Everyone was dripping.

Then Weston ran off to sit for a story. Drip, drip, drip went his hair on the mat. "You are making a puddle," said Maeve. Weston felt a bit sad. His shirt was cold and wet. "I want to be dry," he said. He looked in his bag. He found his small towel. He rubbed his arms. The towel took the water off. He rubbed his legs. Dry! He rubbed his hair. Dry! Mr. Taylor smiled. "Your towel dries your body after a bath," he said. Weston nodded. It was true.

Then Weston sat down, all dry and warm. Rowan came over, still dripping. "Can I use your towel too?" asked Rowan. "Yes," said Weston. "Towels are for friends."

Charlie was in her bedroom. She had a sniffly nose and a cough. Outside, the sun was warm. She wanted to run outside and play on the big hill.

Her dad stopped her at the door. "Not today," he said. "Rest helps your body get better." He tucked her into bed with her bear and her favourite book. The blanket was soft. It smelled like soap. Her cup of water sat close by.

Charlie read her book. She rested. She napped. The next morning, her nose did not sniffle. Her cough was gone. "Can I go out now?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "You rested, so you got better." Charlie hugged her bear. Then she ran out the door and up the hill.

Freya sat on the big soft couch at Grandma's house. The big game was on TV. Everyone was watching. Papa clapped. Lucian and Zoe sat on the floor with their snacks.

Freya saw a man on the screen. He wore a black and white striped shirt. He ran up and down the field. He did not kick the ball. He just kept watching. "Who is that man?" Freya asked. "Why does he run so much?"

"That is the referee," said Papa. "The referee watches the game."

A player grabbed another player's shirt. The man in the striped shirt blew his whistle. He put his hand out. The game stopped. Then the players lined up and started again.

"Wow," said Freya. "He stopped the whole game!" The referee watched and watched. When someone did not follow the rules, he blew his whistle. When the players were fair, he let them play on.

Freya looked around the room. Zoe was sharing her crackers with Lucian. "You two are following the rules," Freya said. "Good players!" Lucian laughed. Zoe held up a cracker like a little trophy.

At the end, everyone cheered. Grandma brought out a special cake with a rabbit on it, because Freya loved rabbits. Freya took a big bite. Then she stood up tall, put her hand out like the referee, and said, "Play fair, everyone!"

Lucian giggled and blew on a toy whistle. Zoe raised both arms. Freya smiled and took another bite of cake.

Everett ran to the big red truck at the playground. But Armin got there first. Armin pushed the truck along the sand. "My turn," said Armin. Everett wanted to grab it. His hands felt tight.

Ms. Lau knelt down beside him. "Waiting can feel hard," she said. "Take three slow, deep breaths." Everett breathed in slowly. He breathed out slowly. He did it three times. His hands felt loose. His tongue stopped pressing against his teeth. He watched Armin push the truck up the little hill.

Then the truck rolled back down. "Your turn now," said Armin. Everett took the truck and pushed it far. Silas came over too. He wanted a turn as well. "You can go after me," said Everett. Silas waited and took three slow breaths, just like Everett. The sky looked rainy, so they played fast under the roof.

Armin laughed and clapped his hands. "Good truck, Everett!" he said.

Maverick sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint a nice town with a red fire truck. But his paint cups were only red, yellow and blue.

"Red truck," said Maverick. He painted the red on the paper. Then he wanted an orange sun. He had no orange. He put yellow on top of the red, right on the paper. Now his sun looked like mud.

"Uh oh," said Augustin. "Your sun is all mixed up."

Ms. Asante came over. She held out a flat tray with little holes in it. "Try this. It is called a palette. You can mix your paint on it first."

Maverick dipped his brush. He put red on the palette. He put yellow next to it. He stirred them with his brush. The paint turned orange!

"Orange!" he shouted. He counted his colours out loud. "Red, yellow, blue, orange!"

He painted a big orange sun over his town. Aiden clapped. "Nice sun!" he said.

Maverick looked at his brush. "Now I mix blue and yellow," he said.

Eliana was going on a trip. She was going to Grandma's house. Grandma lived near big snowy mountains. Eliana got her small blue bag.

She put in her yellow swimsuit. She loved her swimsuit. It was for the beach. "I will wear it at Grandma's," she said.

Her dad looked in the bag. "Fetch your mittens too," he said. "It is cold up there. Snow is not beach weather." Eliana peeked out the window. Snow fell at Grandma's house on the picture. The snow was white and deep. Her swimsuit would not fit the snow. The snow needed warm things.

So Eliana put in her mittens. She put in her warm red coat. She put in her fuzzy hat. The swimsuit stayed home this time.

At Grandma's house, snow covered the ground. Eliana wore her coat and mittens. She made a snowball with her mittens on. Her tongue caught a tiny snowflake. "Cold," she said with a giggle.

"Try one more thing," said Grandma. She opened a big box. Inside was a tiny snow swimsuit, just for dolls. Grandma laughed. "Your doll can wear it. Not you!" Eliana hugged her doll tight. "Snow coat for me, swimsuit for you," she said.

Gabriella sat on the mat at the community centre. Mr. Weiss had a drum. He tapped it slowly. "This is the beat," he said. Amina clapped with the drum. Elizabeth clapped too. Gabriella clapped, but her claps went fast, then faster. Her claps did not match.

Mr. Weiss tapped again. "Try marching, Gabriella," he said. Gabriella stood up. She marched around the room. One, two. One, two. Her steps were even. They kept going. Her curly hair bounced with every step. Mr. Weiss tapped the drum to match her feet. Then Gabriella clapped as she marched. One, two. One, two. Now her claps matched the drum.

"Now we sing," said Mr. Weiss. The children sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Gabriella clapped the beat while she sang. Her voice floated out like a boat on the ocean, slow and steady. Amina smiled. Elizabeth smiled. Then Mr. Weiss stopped the drum, and the claps kept going all by themselves. Gabriella laughed. "The beat is still in my feet!" she said. One, two. One, two.

Mya went to the store with her dad. Her friend Gabriel was there too. Gabriel was telling his mom about the red apples. Mya jumped in. "I want apples too!" she said. Gabriel stopped talking. He looked sad. His story was not done.

Mya tried again to talk. The cashier held up her hand. "One at a time," she said. Mya waited. She pressed her lips together. She looked at Gabriel with one eye on him and one eye on the apples. Gabriel went on. "The red apples are sweet," he said. "My grandma makes a short pie with them." Then he was done.

Now it was Mya's turn. "I like apples too," she said. "I want a big red one." The cashier smiled. "What good waiting," she said. "You let Gabriel finish." Mya felt tall, like a big girl.

At the checkout line, Mya wanted to talk to her dad. But he was talking to the cashier. Mya closed her mouth. She waited. She counted the apples in the cart. One, two, three. Then her dad was done talking.

"Mya, did you want to say something?" her dad asked. "Yes!" said Mya. "Gabriel taught me. When someone is talking, we wait. I waited for you!" Her dad gave her the big red apple to hold. "You waited so well," he said. Mya hugged the apple all the way home.

Evelyn was starting school today. She had a big red backpack. It went on her back, and it was very heavy.

"Too heavy," said Evelyn. She sat down on the floor. She could not stand up! The backpack pulled her backward. Claire came over to help. "What is in there?" asked Claire. Evelyn opened it up. Out came a doll. Out came a tiny truck. Out came three blocks and a ball.

"That is a lot of toys," said Claire. Evelyn looked at her backpack. Then she looked at the toys. A backpack was a bag you carry on your back, and her back was small. She put the doll back in. She left the toys in the cubby.

Mr. Chanthavong smiled. "Ready for circle time?" he asked. Evelyn stood up fast. The backpack felt light now. "Ready!" she said. She and Claire ran to the rug, and Evelyn sat down with a happy bump.

Sofia was at Grandma's house. She wanted to read the cat book all by herself. Grandma was folding a warm towel in the kitchen. "Read to me when you are ready," said Grandma.

Sofia sat on the soft rug. She held the cat book. She opened it. The cat looked so funny. His feet were up. His ears were down. Sofia laughed and laughed. "Grandma, the cat is upside down!"

Grandma came over and sat close. "Turn the book around," she said. Sofia turned the book. Now the cat stood on his feet. His ears were on top. But the letters still looked funny to Sofia. "The words are upside down too," she said.

Grandma helped Sofia hold the book right side up. Sofia turned the pages one by one. She started at the front. The words sat in straight little lines. Sofia tapped each word. "Cat," she said. "Cat," she said again. The word looked the same each time.

"Can I ask you something?" said Sofia. "Do the words say cat?" Grandma smiled. "They do. You found the cat word all by yourself." Sofia hugged the book. She turned it upside down one more time. The cat's feet went up again. Sofia giggled. "Silly cat." Then she turned it back and patted the page. "Good cat."

Hailey stood at the edge of the hockey rink. The ice was gone today. Instead, hoops lay on the cold floor. Ms. Joseph held a box of beanbags and a big red ball.

"Watch this," said Ms. Joseph. She tossed a beanbag into a hoop. It landed with a soft plop. Hailey threw her beanbag. It sailed past the hoop. Her friend Rose clapped anyway. "Good try," Rose said. Hailey tried again and again. On her fifth try, the beanbag dropped right in. "I did it!" Hailey shouted.

Then it was time to catch. Ms. Joseph rolled the big ball to Mikhail. He caught it with both hands. She rolled it to Hailey. Hailey squeezed her eyes shut. The ball bumped her tummy and rolled away. "Oh no," Hailey said. Rose ran after the ball. The bright lights made a long shadow on the floor.

"Try again," said Mikhail. Hailey stood ready. This time she kept her eyes open. She watched the ball all the way to her hands. She caught it with both hands! "Again!" Hailey cried. Ms. Joseph rolled it once more. Hailey's eyes stayed on the red ball, and she caught it again. "My turn," said Rose, holding out her hands.

Leah was almost asleep. Then she heard a sound. Tap. Tap. Tap. It came from under her bed. Leah sat up fast. Her heart went boom, boom. She was scared. She pulled the blanket up high. The sound came again. Tap. Tap. Tap. Leah did not like it one bit.

She thought for a minute. She was a young girl, but she knew something good. When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help. So she called out, "Mom! I hear a sound!" Mom came in fast. She sat on the bed. "I'm scared," Leah said. "It goes tap, tap, tap." Mom held her hand. Leah pointed one finger down at the floor. "It's under there," she said.

Mom got down on her knees. She looked under the bed. Then she laughed a little laugh. Out came the cat! He had been batting a toy. Tap. Tap. Tap. That was his little game all along. The cat jumped up on the bed. He curled up by Leah's feet. His tail was soft and warm.

Leah was not scared anymore. She felt happy and sleepy too. Mom kissed her head. "Call me any time," Mom said. "I will always come." Leah closed her eyes. The cat purred by her toes. It sounded like a tiny motor. Tap. Tap. Tap, said the toy on the floor. The cat did not care. He was already asleep.

"Good night, cat," Leah whispered.

Arya sat on her knees at the kitchen table. Grandma put down two warm bowls of rice. "We say a word first," said Grandma. "In Japan, people say itadakimasu before eating. It gives thanks for the food."

Arya wanted to say it just right. She took a big breath. "Ita... takki... moose!" Grandma smiled. "Almost. Try again, little one." Arya said it slowly, one bit at a time. "I-ta-da-ki-ma-su." Her voice was strong now. Grandma clapped her hands.

"Why do we hurry to say it?" Arya asked. Grandma laughed. "The rice is hot, and the word comes first." Arya put her small hands together. "Itadakimasu!" she said. Grandma said it too. Then they picked up their spoons and ate the warm rice together.

Wren wanted to see Jase's new puppy. She asked Mom in the morning. "Can we go now?"

"Not now," said Mom. "Today we stay home. We go tomorrow."

Wren put on her red shoe anyway. She slid her foot in and stood by the door. "Today," she said.

Mom shook her head. "First comes sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Wren ate lunch. She played blocks. She waited and waited. The sun slid down the sky. Then it was dark.

Wren put on her soft pajamas. Mom read her a book. Wren closed her eyes and slept.

In the morning, the sun was up. "Is it tomorrow?" Wren asked.

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is tomorrow now."

Wren clapped. She grabbed her shoe and hopped to the door. "Puppy day!" she said.

Madison sat at the dinner table. Vienna sat next to her. There was one big basket of bread. Madison grabbed the whole basket. "All mine," she said.

Vienna looked down at her empty plate. "I want some too," she said. Madison held the basket tight. Then she looked at Vienna's plate. It was empty. Her own plate was very full.

"Would you like to share?" asked Mom. "Being fair means everyone gets a chance." Madison thought for a moment. She put one roll on Vienna's plate. Vienna smiled. Vienna put butter on it with the little knife, because Mom helped with the sharp part. "Thank you," said Vienna.

"I like sharing," said Madison. She ate her bread. It tasted good. After dinner, Mom said, "Who wants a push on the new swing?" Madison raised her hand. Vienna raised her hand too. "Me first!" said Madison. Then she looked at Vienna. "You can go first," said Madison. Vienna jumped up. "Let's both swing," she said.

Maeva stood in the reading corner. It had soft mats and a little lamp. The lamp made warm light on the books. Today Maeva got her first library card. It was a small card with her name.

Mr. Lombardi gave her a red book. "This book is shared with many other people," he said. "So we take care of it. We do not tear it. We do not write in it." Maeva turned the pages. So many hands had held this book before her! Maybe Sehaj had held it. Maybe Ariane had held it too.

Maeva wanted to draw the duck in the story. She found a crayon. She was about to draw on the page. Then she stopped. The book was shared! She got her own paper instead. She drew the duck there. She showed Mr. Lombardi. "I drew on my paper," she said. "Can the next kid have a turn with the book now?"

Luca ran to the kitchen. Lunch was ready on the table. His hands were dirty from the garden.

He turned on the tap. He rubbed his hands under the water. He looked at his hands. There were no bubbles. Something was missing.

Luca found the soap. He rubbed soap and water on his hands. Bubbles popped up, white and small. He counted while he rubbed. One, two, three, all the way to twenty.

His friend Lewis came in. Lewis held up his own hands. "No bubbles," said Lewis. Luca showed him the soap. Lewis rubbed and rubbed. Bubbles covered his hands too.

They rinsed the bubbles off. The water carried them down the drain. Luca bumped the tap closed with his elbow. The two boys sat down at the table.

Luca picked up his sandwich. His hands felt clean. He took a big bite. "Bubbles next time too," said Lewis.

Hailey went to the park with her little bag. The grass was green and soft. The swings went up and down. Mr. Bouchard was there with Clarke and Mickael.

Hailey wanted a turn on the swing. Clarke was on it. Hailey reached out and grabbed the swing chain. Clarke held on tight. The swing stopped.

Mr. Bouchard sat on the warm bench. "Say please," Clarke said. Hailey took a breath. "Swing, please," she said. Clarke slid down slow. "Your turn now," said Clarke. Hailey sat on the neat blue seat. The wind touched her face. Up she went, and down.

Then Mickael came running. "Swing, please," he said. Hailey pumped her legs two more times. Then she hopped off. "Your turn," she said.

Mickael swung so high. "You win," said Hailey. She clapped her hands. Then she took a cracker from her bag and shared it, because Clarke had asked, "Please?"

Edouard sat at the kitchen table. His sister had made him five cards. Each card had a body part on it. Edouard wanted to say them all right.

"Let's try," said his dad. He held up the first card.

"Eyes!" said Edouard. He covered his eyes with his hands. "Now I can't see you."

He opened his eyes. "I see you, Dad! We see with our eyes." He clapped. "One sense done!"

Dad held up the next card. "Ears," said Edouard. He covered his ears. The room went quiet. He uncovered them. "I hear the clock! We hear with our ears. That's two."

Dad held up a card for a nose. Edouard sniffed. "Soup! We smell with our nose. Three!"

Then came the tongue. "We taste with our tongue. Four!"

The last card showed hands. Edouard touched the table. It felt smooth and cool. "We touch with our hands. Five!"

"You said all five senses," said Dad. Edouard spun his chair around, one big happy spin.

"Can we spin again?" he asked.

Isla went to the garden center with her dad. She picked a small bag of seeds. "Carrot seeds," she said. She held the bag like a little ball all the way home.

In the yard, Isla dug in the dirt. She made the soil clean and soft. Her dad helped her break up the big lumps. Isla patted the seeds down into the dirt. Then she gave them a drink of water.

Every day Isla ran outside to look. She saw only brown dirt. She saw a worm. She saw a leaf blow by. But no carrots came up. "Too slow," said Isla. Her dad laughed. "Wait more days," he said.

At last, Isla saw something tiny and green. It was poking up out of the soil. She ran to the fence. "Hector! Come see my sprout!" she called. Hector ran over fast. "A sprout?" he said. "Yes," said Isla. She pointed at the little green tip. "That is a sprout. My seeds made it." Hector bent down low. "It is so small," he said. "It will grow big," said Isla. She gave the sprout one more drop of water.

Rosalie was in the playroom. She wanted the big red truck. Brady had the big red truck.

"My turn soon?" Rosalie asked.

"First me, then you," said Brady.

Brady drove the truck round and round. Rosalie watched. She waited. Then Brady held it out. "Your turn now."

Rosalie took the truck. It was heavy. It went far across the floor. Brady waited too. Her heart felt warm.

Then Mr. Santos-Reyes clapped his hands. "Clean-up time," he said.

Rosalie put down the truck. She ran to the door. But Brady did not run. Brady picked up the blocks. He put them in the bin. Amelya put the dolls away. They had played with the dolls.

Rosalie came back. The truck was hers to put away. She rolled it to the toy shelf. She lifted it up. It fit just right.

"Good helping," said Mr. Santos-Reyes.

Rosalie looked at the clean floor. She felt proud. Brady smiled and gave her a small toy star. A surprise in his pocket!

"You kept my turn fair," said Brady.

"Your turn tomorrow?" said Rosalie.

"Yes," said Brady.

David sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. David wore his sunglasses.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell on the window. Tap, tap, tap. "Rainy now," said David. His dad turned on the wipers. The rain went away, swish, swish.

"Where is my hat?" David asked. "We might need it." His dad said, "Look at the trees."

The trees swayed back and forth. Leaves blew all around. They blew across the road. They blew past the car. "It is windy!" said David. He counted the leaves as they flew. One, two, three. The wind took them far away.

"Wind makes the trees dance," said David. His dad smiled. The last leaf flew up, up, up. Then it landed on a big hill.

"The hill is white," said David. "Snow!" His dad said, "Yes. We will need warm coats."

David hugged his hat. "I am ready," he said.

Riley stood in the restaurant kitchen. The cook had made hot toast, and it sat on a plate. "Now you can butter it," the cook said. Riley took the knife and scooped soft butter. She spread it slow, corner to corner. "Look, shiny toast!" she said. Mr. Kaminski smiled. "Nice work, Riley."

Next came the milk. Riley held a cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk plopped onto the table. "Sorry, milk," Riley said. Mr. Kaminski handed her a cloth. Riley wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go of it. The cup sat still. Riley poured, and the milk went right in. Not one drop spilled. Riley hopped up and down. "The cup stays still when I put it down!" Jolene clapped from the door. "Can I try too?"

Violet stood in the bathroom in her pink party dress. Tonight was her birthday sleepover. She wanted to wear the dress to bed.

"Can I sleep in this?" she asked her mom.

"You can try," said Mom.

Violet sat on the bathtub edge. The dress was stiff. It poked her arms. The glitter rubbed off on the towel. She tried to lie down on the bath mat. The skirt went crunch, crunch. It sounded loud in the quiet room.

Mom held up soft pajamas. They had a cloudy sky on them. "These are for sleeping," Mom said.

Violet touched them. Soft. Warm. Not scratchy at all.

She pulled the pajamas on over her feet. She gave the party dress a pat. "Night night, dress," she whispered.

In the morning, the sky outside looked cloudy too, just like her pajamas. Violet hugged her red ball. "Today we play," she said. "Tonight we sleep again."

Amelia sat at Grandma's big table. There were letter cards all over it. Grandma held up a card. "This is A," said Grandma. "A says ah, ah, apple."

Amelia picked up a card too. "B," she said. "B says buh, buh, ball!" Grandma clapped her hands. The cards felt smooth and cool in Amelia's fingers.

Then Amelia put the cards in a long line. She sang the letter song. She got to P and stopped. "All done," she said. "The letters end at P." Grandma shook her head and smiled. "Keep singing," she said. Amelia felt a little worried. She sang on. Q, R, S, all the way to the very last card. She picked it up and looked at it. "Z!" she shouted. She hugged the soft, beautiful card to her chest.

"The alphabet starts with A," said Grandma, "and ends with Z." Amelia laughed and sang the whole song again. Then she ran to the shelf and opened the toy box. She pulled out her blocks and lined them up too. "A first," she said. "Z last!" Grandma sat close by, and Amelia sang one more time, all the way to Z.

Emilia was at Grandma's house. After her bath, she dropped her wet towel on the floor. She pulled off her socks too. She left them by the bed.

The next morning, Emilia wanted to wear her blue socks. She looked on the floor. Her socks were gone. "Grandma, where did my socks go?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket," she said. "Then they get washed."

Grandma carried the basket to the washing machine. Emilia watched from the door. The socks went round and round in the water. Then they came out warm and clean.

After lunch, Emilia had an idea. She rolled her socks into little balls. She stood by the basket. Toss! The first sock went in. Toss! The second one went in too. "Grandma, look!" she said. "My socks are in the basket, ready to be washed." Grandma laughed. "What a big throw," she said. Emilia picked up one more sock and tossed it high.

Maya sat on the rug at school. Ms. Novák held up one hand. "We have five senses," she said. "Let's find them all."

Maya held up her hand too. She counted on her fingers. "One, eyes for seeing. Two, ears for hearing. Three, nose for smelling." She stopped. "Four, tongue for tasting." She looked at her thumb. She had one finger left, but she forgot the last sense.

Troy sat next to her. He was stuck too. He wiggled his fingers. Edith reached over and touched his hand. "Touching!" she said.

Maya laughed. "Yes! Five senses. Fingers are for touching." She touched the sticky tape on the floor. She touched the wood block. She touched Troy's sleeve, very soft.

Ms. Novák smiled. "Now let's pay attention to our senses," she said. She rang a little bell. Maya's ears heard it. She covered her eyes. She could still hear it.

Then a surprise came. A smell filled the room. Something was baking. "I smell it with my nose," said Maya. Troy sniffed the air. Edith sniffed too.

Ms. Novák opened the door. There were warm buns on a tray. "Taste them with your tongue," she said.

Maya took a small bite. "Mmm. All five senses," she said, holding up her whole hand.

Jade stood at the airport with her dad. She held a big paper heart. "Grandma's plane comes today," she said.

The doors opened. Grandma walked out with a tiny blue bag. Jade ran to her and hugged her tight. "You stay seven days," said Jade. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Grandma laughed and held up seven fingers.

Grandma stayed and stayed. They went to the playground. They made pancakes; Dad held the hot pan, and Jade watched. Every night Jade counted the days left. "Three days." Then "two days." Then "one day."

Then it was time to go. Grandma's plane went up in the sky. Jade felt like crying. She wanted Grandma to stop and come back.

Her mom sat with her. "We can call Grandma on the phone," Mom said. "We can see her on a video call too." Jade watched Mom tap the phone. Grandma's face came on the screen. "Hello, Jade!" said Grandma.

Jade had one more idea. She drew a picture of the playground. Mom put it in an envelope. It was a letter for Grandma.

"Call you soon, Grandma," said Jade. She waved at the phone until the screen went dark.

Luke was wide awake in the playroom. He wanted to play cars with Kenan. Kenan had a big red car. Luke had a small blue car. Aariz had a yellow bus. There was one problem. All the cars kept bumping into each other.

Then Luke found a green toy on the shelf. It looked like a tall light. It had a red circle and a green circle. "What is it?" asked Kenan. Luke held it up high. "Red means stop," said Ms. Ahmed from the door. "Green means go."

Luke had an idea. He held up the red side. All the cars stopped. Not one wheel moved. Then he held up the green side. The cars went, went, went! The yellow bus zoomed past the red car. Luke listened to the wheels on the floor. Rumble, rumble, rumble.

They played the game all morning. Red, and everyone stopped. Green, and everyone went. Then came the small surprise. When Luke held up red, Aariz's puppy sat down too! "Good puppy," laughed Luke. He patted its soft head. "Green means go, puppy!"

Aubrey stood by the art table at school. She was making a card for her dad. It had a big red heart on it. Tomorrow was Show and Tell. She wanted to bring the card. She felt excited.

Then she dropped the glue. It fell on the floor. The heart got a big wet spot. Aubrey felt sad. Her eyes went hot and her mouth turned down.

Ariah came over. "Are you sad?" Ariah asked.

"Yes," said Aubrey. "My heart is all wet."

Ms. Katz knelt down. "You know, I felt sad this morning too," she said. "My mug broke at home. I liked that mug."

Aubrey looked up. "Grown-ups feel sad?"

"Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups," said Ms. Katz. "Dads too. Mommies too. Teachers too."

Aubrey felt a little better. Nathaniel brought a paper towel. He held it tight and dabbed the wet spot. The heart dried. It looked bumpy, but still red. Outside a dog began to bark. Aubrey laughed.

"I like the bumps," she said. "My dad will feel happy."

Clara went to the store with Mom. She brought her little toy truck. Clara set it down to pick an apple. When she looked back, the truck was gone.

"My truck is lost," Clara said. She felt like crying. She looked by the bread. She looked by the milk. No truck.

Then Clara saw a big shelf. It was dark under there. She could not see anything at all. Mom reached into her bag. "Here is a flashlight," she said. "It helps you see into dark spots." Mom clicked it on and held it low.

Clara peeked under the shelf. The light made the dark spot bright. There was her truck! "I see it!" she said. Clara reached in and picked it up.

"Yay, Clara!" said Mom. Clara hugged the truck tight. "No more dark spots," she said. The flashlight stayed on all the way home.

Eloise went to the library with her dad. She wanted storytime to start now. But the sign said storytime was soon.

"Is soon now?" Eloise asked.

"Not yet," said Ms. Haddad. "Soon means in a little while."

Eloise frowned. A little while felt big. She looked out the window. The flag blew in the wind. A boy knocked on the table. His mom gave him paper to draw on.

Eloise got paper too. She drew a cat. Then she drew a dog. Then she drew three cats.

"Storytime is soon," said Ms. Haddad again.

"Now?" asked Eloise.

"In a little while," said Ms. Haddad.

Eloise drew a sun. She drew a frozen pond with skates on it. June and Abigaelle came in and sat down. They drew too. The paper pile grew tall.

Then Ms. Haddad rang a little bell. "Storytime starts now!" she said.

Eloise jumped up. "Soon came!" she said.

Ms. Haddad laughed. "Yes. Soon always turns into now."

Eloise sat on the rug next to June. Yesterday she had been too late for storytime. Today she was just right. Tomorrow she would come back again.

"Once there was a bear," Ms. Haddad began. Eloise smiled and hugged her paper cat.

"I will bring you tomorrow," she told it.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Clara stood in the dark. She could not see anything at all. "Mama!" she called. "I can't see!"

Mama found her by the couch. Mama lit a candle with a match. Clara watched from far away, because Mama held the hot flame. But the candle was small. The big room stayed dark. Clara's toy cat was lost somewhere. Clara wanted her toy cat very much.

"Stay here," said Mama. "The dark is not bad. Your eyes will get used to it." Clara sat on the step. She blinked and blinked. At first she saw nothing. Then she saw a little. Then she saw more. The dark slowly got easier for her eyes.

Clara looked around the room. She saw the shape of the sofa. She saw the big bowl on the table. She saw a round shape by the chair. It was small and soft. "My cat!" said Clara. She picked it up and hugged it tight.

Clara sank down next to Mama on the sofa. The candle made a warm little light. "I found him all by myself," said Clara. "My eyes got used to the dark." Mama smiled in the candlelight. Outside, one farm light came back on. Then the room lights came back too. Clara waved to her cat. "Hello, cat," she said. "I saw you first."

Sofia stood in the kitchen with her mom. The pot on the stove was hot. Mom held Sofia's hand. "Hot things can hurt," Mom said. Sofia stayed back and watched.

The kettle went hiss, hiss, hiss. Mom poured hot water into a cup. Steam went up, up, up. Sofia felt warm air on her face. "Can I help?" she asked. Mom gave her a cold cup from the fridge. The cup felt cold in her hands.

Then Jaylen knocked on the door. "Come to the park!" he said. Sofia looked out the window. The park was across the road. Cars went by, fast and loud. Sofia waited. She held Mom's hand tight. Mom looked both ways. They crossed together. Jaylen took his dad's hand too.

At the park, Sofia spun around and around. She got dizzy and fell in the grass. Jaylen laughed and fell down too. Then Sofia heard a small sound. A puppy was stuck by the fence. "I will get help," Sofia said. She ran to Mom. Mom lifted the puppy out, safe and sound. The puppy licked Sofia's hand. It was warm and soft.

Mia sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her toy worm, Wiggly, sat on her lap.

"Will the shot hurt?" Mia asked.

"Just a quick pinch," said Ms. Fortin, the nurse. "Take a deep breath."

Mia took a deep breath. She held Wiggly tight. The shot was quick. It was done!

"Can I climb down now?" Mia asked. She climbed down from the big chair.

In the car, Mia rubbed her arm. "My arm feels sore," she said.

"That can happen after a shot," said Dad. "It will feel better soon."

Mia looked at her arm. Was the sore spot making her rub it? She rubbed it again, soft and slow. The spot felt a little warm.

"I wonder if Wiggly's tummy is sore too," Mia said.

Dad laughed. At home, Mia put a sticker on Wiggly's tummy. Then she put one on her own sore spot.

She looked at the sticker. It was a shiny star. She smiled and patted it gently. "All better," she said.

Raphael looked out the window. The sky was gray. Big drops fell. "Rainy!" said Raphael. He ran to get his boots. But where was his umbrella? He could not find it. "The rain will wet my head," he said.

His mom held up one big umbrella. "We can share," she said. They walked to school under it. The rain tap-tapped on top. Raphael touched his hair. It was dry! His shoes were dry too. The rain slid off the umbrella, drip drip drip. "It keeps the rain off my head," said Raphael. "What good work it does!"

At school, Mr. Byrne hung his wet coat on a hook. Jonathan shook his hat. It was all soggy. Raphael pointed at his own dry hair. "Want to share my umbrella tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes!" said Jonathan. The rain went drip drip drip on the window. Raphael smiled. His umbrella was waiting by the door.

Ruby was at the park with Ms. Russo. Markus and Raavi were there too. Ms. Russo had a basket of orange slices.

"I want to learn my five senses," said Ruby. "I am ready!"

"Okay," said Ms. Russo. "Eyes see. What do your eyes see?"

"I see a red ball!" said Ruby.

"Ears hear," said Ms. Russo.

"I hear a dog bark," said Markus.

"Noses smell," said Raavi. He sniffed the orange slices. "Mmm, orange!"

Then Ruby had a silly idea. She pinched her nose shut. Snug and tight. She sniffed the orange slices. She sniffed and sniffed.

"I can't smell them!" said Ruby. Her voice sounded funny. Markus laughed.

"You sound like a duck!" said Markus.

"I can't smell like a duck either," said Ruby. She let go of her nose. Sniff, sniff. "Now I smell orange again!"

Raavi tried it too. He pinched his nose shut. "No smell!" he said, like a duck. Then Ruby tried it again. Pinch, no smell. Let go, orange smell. Pinch, no smell. Let go, orange smell.

"Fingers touch," said Ms. Russo, smiling. "So your fingers can stop your nose!"

Ruby touched the orange slice. It was cool and bumpy.

"Tongues taste," said Ms. Russo. Ruby ate her slice. Yum.

"I did it," said Ruby. "Eyes, ears, nose, fingers, tongue. All five!" She jumped up high.

"Now let's play duck noses again," said Markus. He pinched his nose and waddled in a circle.

Rowan was at the park. He wanted the yellow ball. It sat under a big tree. Ariane had the ball first.

Ariane rolled the ball to Rowan. "Here you go," she said. Rowan caught it. Then he ran away fast. He ran to the slide. He forgot something.

Ariane put her hands on her hips. She looked sad. Rowan stopped. He looked back at her.

He ran back. "Thank you, Ariane," he said. Ariane smiled. Now she looked happy again.

Then Aayan fell down near the sandbox. A block fell too. It fell right on his foot. "Sorry," Rowan said, because he had dropped it there before.

Aayan held up the block. "Can you help me?" he asked. Rowan helped him stack it up tall. Ms. Pierre came over and clapped. "Nice work, boys," she said.

The sun went behind a cloud. The three friends sat on the bench. They shared the yellow ball, one roll at a time.

Elena went to the grocery store with her dad. She held her little toy bunny in her hand. The bunny was small and soft and gray.

Then Elena saw the apples. She let go of bunny to pick one up. "Hello, apple," she said. When she looked down, bunny was gone.

"Bunny is lost," said Elena. Her tummy felt tight. Dad knelt beside her. "We will find bunny," he said. "Let's look together."

They looked by the apples. No bunny. They looked by the bread. No bunny. Then Elena saw a shelf, low to the floor. Small toys can roll or slide under shelves, just like under beds and couches. She got down on her knees. She peeked under the shelf. There was bunny! "Bunny rolled!" said Elena. "The floor is slanted, and bunny slid under."

Dad smiled. "What a neat find," he said. "You thought to look down low." Elena hugged bunny tight. "Never roll away again," she whispered.

Outside, a soft rain began to fall. Elena held bunny in one hand and Dad's hand in the other. "Bunny likes rain," she said. Dad laughed. They walked to the car, warm and dry, together.

Emmett went to the store with his mom. Yesterday it had rained. Today the sun was out. Emmett saw a big red ball on the shelf. He squeezed it. It felt soft and bouncy.

"Can I have the ball now?" asked Emmett.

"Not now, sweetie. Later," said his mom.

Emmett pushed the cart. He helped put apples in a bag. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said his mom.

They found milk and bread. The aisle was all tidy and neat. Emmett touched the cold milk jug. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Now it is later," said his mom, smiling. She put the red ball in the cart.

Emmett bounced the ball at home, on the soft rug. "Tomorrow we can bounce it again," said his mom. Emmett hugged the ball tight.

Gianna was at daycare. She loved the round red ball. It had her name on it. "My ball!" she said.

Then Conrad grabbed the ball. "No!" said Gianna. "My ball!" Her face got hot. Her hands made fists. She stomped her foot. She wanted to yell.

Ms. Ho knelt down beside her. "Try this," said Ms. Ho. "Take a slow, deep breath." Gianna breathed in, slow and big. Then she breathed out. Ms. Ho said, "Again." Gianna took one more slow, deep breath. Her fists got soft. Her tummy felt calm.

"I feel better," said Gianna. Conrad gave the ball back. "Sorry," he said. "Want to play?" Gianna hugged the round ball to her chest. Then she rolled it fast to Conrad.

"My turn!" said Conrad. He laughed and rolled it back.

Rehmat sat on Grandpa's porch steps. She was counting hens in the yard. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. What came next? She could not remember. She frowned at the hens.

Grandma came out with a bowl of beans. "Sing with me," said Grandma. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." Rehmat sang along. The words rhymed, so they were easy to hold. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." Rehmat giggled. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" she sang, and pointed at a fat hen by the fence.

Now she tried again. "One, two, three," she said, "four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The words came out just right. The song helped her remember. Grandpa clapped his hands.

"There are ten beans for you," said Grandma. She held out ten beans from the bowl. Rehmat counted them into her little hand. "One, two, three," she said, all the way to ten. One bean rolled off the step. It landed by a tree root. "I hope it grows," said Rehmat. The bean looked small and weak next to the big root.

Grandpa helped her plant it in soft dirt. He patted the soil down. "Water it a little each day," he said. Rehmat nodded. Then she sang to the bean. "One, two, buckle my shoe." The fat hen came close to listen.

David went to the park with his friend Hubert. David had a big red strawberry in his lunch box. He wanted to win a taste game. "Can we play a game?" he asked. "Yes," said Hubert. "Let's guess what we eat!"

First they used their eyes. "I see something red," said David. "I see little seeds," said Hubert. Then they used their ears. They heard the swing go squeak, squeak, squeak. Then they used their hands. David touched the strawberry. It felt bumpy and cold.

Mr. Wijaya sat on the cozy bench with them. "Close your nose with your fingers," he said. "Now take a bite." David held his nose shut and bit the strawberry. He made a funny face. "It tastes plain!" he said. "So plain!" Then he let go of his nose and took another bite. "Now it tastes sweet! Now it tastes like strawberry!"

"So my nose helps me taste?" asked David. "Try it again and see," said Mr. Wijaya. David held his nose. Plain. He let go. Sweet! He counted out loud, "One, two, three, let go!" Every time it worked.

Hubert tried it too. "Plain! Sweet! Plain! Sweet!" they laughed. David waved his strawberry in the air. "My nose wins the game!" he said.

Layla ran into the backyard. Her friend Rhett was waiting by the little pond. "Let's play the senses game!" he said. Layla clapped her hands. She wanted to win the game.

"My eyes see the pond," said Layla. "My ears hear the noisy birds." Rhett nodded. Then he held up a lemon slice and a strawberry. "Now what?" he asked. Layla popped the lemon in her mouth. Her whole face went squinty. "Sour!" she said. She tried the strawberry next. "Sweet!" She stuck out her tongue. "My tongue tastes it. That is the tongue's job!"

Rhett laughed and clapped. Layla dipped her hands in the pond water. Then she sat on the warm step to dry them in the sun. "The sun makes my hands dry," she said. "That is the sun's job!" Rhett giggled so hard he fell over in the grass.

William wanted to wear his new shoes to bed. Not for sleeping, of course. He just wanted to put them on first, to see them.

He sat on his bed. He pushed his feet into the new shoes. Then he tried to push his socks on over the shoes. The socks would not go. They slid off. William laughed and fell back on his pillow.

His dad peeked in. "Time for a bath, buddy."

After his bath, William was clean, with no dirt on his toes. He put on his pajamas. Then he picked up his socks. "Socks first," he said. He pulled them on. Then his shoes slid right over them. "It works!"

Dad tucked him in. "Shoes stay on the floor tonight."

William put the new shoes by the bed, toes pointing out. He yawned and closed his eyes.

"Good night, shoes," he whispered.

Camille was at home. She was excited. Her friend Anahat was coming to play. The doorbell rang. Ding, dong!

Camille opened the door. She looked at Anahat's face. Anahat had a big frown. Her mouth was turned down. Camille had not seen that before.

"Your face looks sad," Camille said.

Anahat spoke in a small voice. "I lost my pink hair clip."

Camille thought. Then she had an idea. "Come and see my dolls," she said. The dolls had little clips. Camille found a pink one.

"You can use it," said Camille. Anahat put it in her hair. Now Anahat's face changed. Her mouth went up. She was smiling!

"Thank you," said Anahat. "I feel happy now."

The girls played with the toy dog. It had a bone in its mouth. They laughed and laughed.

"You are my best friend," said Anahat.

Camille hugged her tight.

Elizabeth sat in the school library with Mr. Wright. He held up a big card. It had one letter on it. The letter was S.

"S says sss," said Mr. Wright. "Like a snake. Can you find things that say sss?"

Elizabeth looked around the reading nook. She wanted to find one all by herself. She saw a book with a sun on it. "Sun!" she said. "Sss. S is for sun!" Mr. Wright smiled.

Then Joanna came over. Joanna was sad. She could not find an sss thing. "Look at your sock," said Elizabeth. She pointed at Joanna's foot. Joanna wiggled her toes. "Sock! Sss!" said Joanna. She laughed and clapped.

Ellis found one too. There was sand in a little jar on the shelf. "Sand starts with sss," said Ellis. Mr. Wright put the S card on the table. Sun, sock and sand all sat with it.

"Now the pink card," said Mr. Wright. He held up a letter P. Elizabeth jumped up. "My turn!" she said. Off she went to hunt again.

Asher played with his toy truck in his bedroom. The truck had a green cab and little black wheels. It rolled over a soft brown rug. Asher pushed it with one finger. Then he pushed it right into the mud on his shoes. Now his hands were muddy too.

Mom came in with a plate of apple slices. Asher ran to the plate. He grabbed for an apple slice.

"Not yet," said Mom. "First we wash our hands. We wash our hands before we eat."

Asher went to the bathroom sink. Mom turned on the water. Asher rubbed his hands under it. The mud went down the drain. His hands came out clean.

He ran back to the bedroom. He picked up an apple slice. It was crisp and sweet. He took a big bite. No mud got on his apple.

Asher finished his snack. He put on his soft pajamas. He brushed his teeth with Mom. Then he climbed into bed.

He yawned a big yawn. "Night night, green truck," he said. He hugged the truck close. Mom turned off the light. Asher closed his eyes and fell fast asleep.

Jack ran to the playground. The sun was hot on his back. Zeke was at the water table. Zeke wore a big yellow hat. "Come pour with me," said Zeke.

Jack picked up a small cup. The cup was empty. Nothing was inside it. Zeke poured water fast from the big jug. Splash! The water ran over the top. The cup was too full. "Oh no," said Zeke. His shoes got wet.

Mr. Greco came over with a towel. He helped Zeke dry his shoes. "Try pouring slow," said Mr. Greco. Jack poured slow, slow, slow. The water went up and up. He stopped just at the top. Now his cup was full to the top. Not one drop fell out.

"I did it!" said Jack. He poured his water on the little plants near the fence. A cat ran out from the shade. It was fast. The cat drank a drip from the ground, then walked away slow. "That was neat," said Zeke. Jack held up his cup. "It's empty again," he said. "Watch me fill it one more time."

Victor looked out of the car window. The sun was warm on his face. "It is sunny," said Victor. Dad drove on. Then big drops hit the glass. Tap, tap, tap. "Now it is rainy," said Victor. He put on his rain hat. The wind whooshed the hat askew. "It is windy too," said Victor. He held the hat with both hands.

The rain turned soft and white. Flakes fell on the window. "Snow," said Victor. Snow piled up on the grass. On a fence. On a big red hat that someone lost. Victor rolled down his window a little bit. He scooped up some snow. He made a small snowball. "I want to keep it," said Victor. He put it in his mitten. He was lucky. The snowball felt cold and round and good.

When the car stopped, Victor ran inside. Mom helped him take off his wet boots. Victor put the snowball in a cup on the table. He would look at it after his bath. The bath was warm and bubbly. Victor washed his toes and his tummy. Then Mom lifted him out in a big towel.

Victor ran to the table. He looked in the cup. The snowball was gone! There was only water in the cup. A little puddle sat on the table too. "My snowball," said Victor. Mom said, "Let's look." They leaned close. Victor dipped his finger in the water. It was cool. Victor put on his coat and his mittens. He ran back outside into the snowy yard. He scooped up fresh white snow. He patted a new snowball. This one would stay in the cold. "This is your home," said Victor. The snowball sat on the porch, white and small.

Adam wanted to draw a farm picture. He had paper and crayons. But he needed a shape for the barn door. "I need the door shape," he said. "But which one is it?"

Mom was cooking at the stove. Adam stayed back from the hot stove. He looked around the sunny kitchen. He saw a plate. "That is a circle," he said. He saw a window. "That is a square." He saw a slice of toast. "That is a triangle!" But no door shape yet.

Then Adam looked at the big kitchen door. He ran to it. He touched one side. Then another side. "One, two, three, four sides!" He poked each corner. "One, two, three, four corners. And they are square corners!" The dog barked, as if to say yes. "A rectangle has four sides and four square corners," said Adam, "like the shape of a door!"

Adam ran back to the table. He drew four sides and four square corners. He drew a red barn around it. He drew a sunny sky and a cow. "The farm is done!" he shouted. Mom clapped her hands. The dog barked again, loud and happy.

Benjamin ran out to the backyard. His teddy was missing! He looked in the grass. He looked by the big tree. But the sky was dark now. "It is so dark," said Benjamin. He could not see his teddy anywhere.

Then he heard a sound. Crunch, crunch. His feet on the wet grass! He sniffed with his nose. He smelled the flowers by the fence. He touched the cool grass with his hands. Still no teddy. "Where can he be?" Benjamin wondered.

Dad came outside. He reached up and turned on the porch light. The backyard glowed bright. Benjamin blinked his eyes. Then he saw it! Teddy was sitting on the swing. Benjamin ran over and hugged him. Teddy's fur felt soft on his cheek. "I found you!" said Benjamin. Dad smiled. "Light on, teddy found," said Benjamin, and he gave teddy a little kiss.

Emily woke up and looked out the window. Snow! Big white snow everywhere. "No school today!" said her mom. "It is a snow day!" Emily jumped up and down. A snow day was a surprise, like a gift.

After breakfast, Emily wanted to play outside. She put on her boots and her red coat. Then she ran out the door. She ran fast on the sidewalk. But the sidewalk was icy. Her feet slid. She fell down on her bottom. "Oof!" said Emily. The ice was cold and squishy on top.

Her mom came out too. Her mom did not run. Her mom took small, slow steps. Step. Step. Step. She did not fall at all. Emily stood up. She tried small, slow steps too. Step. Step. Step. Her boots did not slide. "Look, Mom! I can walk on the ice!" she said.

"I guess slow feet are the best feet," said her mom. Emily laughed. Then they made tiny slow footsteps all the way to the swing set, side by side.

Austin sat on the big rug in the living room. He wanted to draw a picture on the tablet. He pushed the screen with his whole hand. The screen stayed dark. He pushed harder. Still dark. "Silly tablet," he said.

His mom sat down next to him. "Try your finger," she said. Austin held up one finger. He gave the screen a little tap. The screen lit up. "It glowed!" said Austin. He tapped the drawing app. It opened. A green crayon popped up on the screen.

Austin tapped the green crayon. He drew a wiggly snake. Then he tapped blue and drew the windy sky. The snake wore a hat, which made Austin laugh.

"Can I pass it to you?" he asked his mom. She took the tablet. Austin pressed the button with one gentle tap. The screen went dark again. The tablet went to sleep on the shelf. Austin waved at it. "Night night, snake," he whispered.

Elias went to the library with his dad. Mr. Tanaka was reading a story about a plane. Elias sat down on the wide, soft rug.

Rishi and Celia sat close by. Mr. Tanaka said a puppet dog would come out soon. Elias felt excited. When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout. Elias bounced on the rug. He bounced so much he bumped Celia. Celia looked sad.

"Sorry, Celia," Elias said. He looked at his hands. He made them slow. He took a big breath. Then he sat very still and waited. The puppet dog popped out. Everyone laughed. Elias wanted to shout, but he squeezed his hands instead.

Rishi whispered, "I feel excited too." Elias smiled wide. "Me too," he whispered back. The puppet dog shook its floppy ears.

Jasper was at the pool with his dad. He was learning to swim. He splashed and kicked in the shallow water. Jenna from his class was there too.

"Look at me," said Jenna. She held the wall and kicked fast. Jasper held the wall too. "I can kick like a frog," he said. His dad laughed. "You make big splashes, Jasper."

Then it was time to get out. Jasper tried to climb over the edge. His arms were wet and slippery. His tummy pressed on the cold wall. He slid back down with a plop. "Oh no," he said. Jenna called to him, "Use the ladder!" Jasper looked. There it was, shiny silver steps right in the water. He held the rails and climbed up, step by step. It was easy.

"Where do we get in again?" he asked Jenna. "The steps," she said, pointing. "The steps are like a ladder in the water." Jasper walked down the steps with his dad beside him.
