The water came up to his tumpy tummy. "The ladder is my best friend," said Jasper, and Jenna giggled. "Race you to the big beautiful floaty cow," she said. "Ready, set, splash!"

Jake waited at the airport with his mom. He held a sign with big letters. It said GRANDPA. People came and went. Then Jake saw a big smile. "Grandpa!" he shouted. Grandpa hugged him tight. "I will stay for a whole week," said Grandpa.

At home, Jake had a problem. Grandpa was sleeping over. But where would Grandpa sleep? "We need a bed for a guest," Mom said. "A guest who stays the night needs a sleeping spot." Jake ran to the spare room. He found a soft pillow. He put it at the head of the bed. Then he got his favorite blanket. It had blue stars on it. He spread it out, careful with the corners. "This blanket is soft," he said. Mom helped him color a picture too. It said WELCOME. He set it on the pillow.

Grandpa came in. He saw the bed. He saw the pillow and the blue-star blanket. "A bed all ready for me," said Grandpa. He gave Jake a big hug. Jake grinned. That night, Grandpa slept under the stars, and Jake slept happy down the hall.

Hudson ran to the park with his dad. The sun was bright on the swings. His hair bounced as he ran. Anais was there with a bag of grapes.

"Want a grape?" Anais asked. Hudson shook his head. "Yuck!" he shouted. Anais put the grapes away. She looked sad and sat alone on the bench.

Hudson sat on the swing. He wanted Anais to play. He thought and thought. He walked back slowly. "Anais, can you push me, please?" he asked. She jumped up and pushed him high. Hudson laughed. Then Anais held out one grape again. Hudson shook his head. "No, thank you," he said quietly. Anais smiled a big smile.

"That's okay," she said. "Want a cracker instead?" Hudson took the cracker. "Yes, please!" he said. Then he climbed down and they both ran to the slide together.

Maria sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse had a question for her. "Did you wash your hands today?" she asked.

Maria held out her hands. She had rinsed them fast, quick quick, under the tap. The nurse smiled. "Let's look," she said. She put a tiny bit of pretend germ dust on Maria's hands. It was like soft sparkles. Maria rubbed her hands together. The sparkles stayed on.

"Now let's wash with soap," said the nurse. "We scrub for twenty seconds. We count slow." Maria put on soap. She rubbed and counted. One, two, three. The bubbles grew big and white. The sparkles hid in the bubbles. She kept counting all the way to twenty. Then the water washed the bubbles down, down, down. The sparkles went away too!

Maria looked at her hands. They were clean and shiny. "My quick wash left the sparkles," she said. "The long wash took them off!" The nurse laughed softly. "Yes it did," she said. Maria clapped her clean hands. At snack time, she washed first, and she counted all the way. Then she took a big happy bite of her apple.

Romy was at home. Omar came to play. "I have a big drum," Romy said. She hit the drum. Boom! Boom! Boom!

Romy felt excited. She jumped up and down. But Omar put his hands on his ears. His face looked sad. "Too loud," he said. Romy felt surprised. The drum made her happy. The same drum made Omar sad.

Romy touched the drum softly. Tap. Tap. "Is this okay?" she asked. Omar smiled. "Soft is nice," he said. Now they played together. One, two, three, tap. One, two, three, tap.

The cat woke up. She had been asleep in her nest of blankets. She walked over on little quiet paws. She sat down next to the drum. Omar giggled. "The cat likes the quiet drum," he said.

Romy tapped soft and slow. The cat purred. Omar purred too, like a small gray cat. They all sat close together on the floor. "More soft drum," said Omar. Romy smiled and tapped, tap, tap, tap.

Kinsley went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish. She saw a bunny. Then she saw a small puppy. "This one," said Kinsley.

Mr. Patel worked at the pet store. He gave the puppy a red collar. Then he clipped on a leash. "The leash clips to the collar," he said. "It keeps the puppy close to us."

Kinsley held her dad's hand. Her dad held the leash. The puppy walked beside them. It sniffed a shoe. It sniffed a stick.

Then a bird flew by. The puppy wanted to chase the bird. It pulled and pulled. But the leash held tight. The puppy stayed close to Dad. It could not run away. "Good puppy," said Kinsley. She clapped her hands.

At home, Kinsley gave the puppy water. The puppy drank it all. It made a circle on the rug and fell asleep. "Sleepy puppy," said Kinsley. The puppy's tail wagged, just a little, in a dream.

Camille sat at the dinner table. She had a little white feather in her hand. She had found it at the farm today.

"Look," said Camille. "A feather."

Hazel peeked at it from her chair. Hazel was eating with them tonight.

"Birds are animals that have feathers," said Hazel.

Camille looked at her plate. There was corn. There was bread. There was milk.

"I see food," said Camille. "Corn and bread and milk."

"On the farm I saw animals," said Hazel. "A cow. A pig. A duck."

"The duck has feathers," said Camille. "So a duck lost my feather!"

Dad came with a sharp knife. He cut the bread for them. Camille watched from her seat.

Camille set the feather by her plate. She took a bite of corn.

"The bird will come back for it," she said. "Maybe tomorrow."

Noah sat in a small chair at the pharmacy. The room smelled like mint and soap. His tummy felt jumpy.

"I am here to get my shot," Noah told his mom. "Will it hurt?"

"Just a tiny pinch," Mom said. "Then it is done."

Mr. Nolan, the nurse, came in. He had a sticker sheet on his tray. Noah liked the bear sticker best.

Noah looked at the little needle. His legs felt weak. He wanted to hide behind Mom.

"Try this," Mr. Nolan said. "Breathe in slowly, like you are smelling a flower."

Noah sniffed in a big slow breath. It smelled like mint and soap. Then he let the air out, slow and long.

Mr. Nolan tapped his arm. "One more slow breath, like smelling a flower."

Noah breathed in slow. He breathed out slow. His tummy felt less jumpy. His legs felt strong again.

There was a tiny pinch. "Ow," said Noah. Then it was over. Mr. Nolan put on the bear sticker right away.

"You did it," Mom said. "Do you remember what helped you?"

"The slow, slow breaths," said Noah.

On the way out, Mom bought him a cookie. Noah took a big bite. It was sweet and warm.

"I want to smell the flowers at home," Noah said. "Can we go now?"

"We can go now," said Mom, and she held his hand all the way to the door.

Nova was going on a trip. The car was packed with bags. Nova sat in her special seat. She hugged her teddy bear tight.

The car drove and drove. Nova looked out the window. Then she felt it. "I need the potty," she said. "We are far from home," said Dad. "But we can stop soon."

The car turned off the big road. Dad parked by a square building with a sign. "This is a rest stop," Dad said. "People stop here to use the bathroom and stretch." Nova held Dad's hand and walked in.

Nova used the potty. She washed her hands. Outside, she stretched her arms up high. She chose to hop like a bunny. Dad laughed and hopped too. Then they got back in the car. Nova waved at the rest stop. "Bye bye!" she said.

Juliette wanted to wash her hands all by herself. But the sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water. "Too high, too high!" she said.

Her dad brought a step stool. "Here is your step stool," he said. He stayed close by her side. Juliette climbed up. Now her hands could reach the water. "I can do it!" she said.

She put soap on her hands. She rubbed and rubbed. "Bubbles, bubbles!" she sang. She counted to twenty. It took a long, long time. The bubbles went down the drain. Her hands were clean and shiny.

"Now we can eat," said Dad. He held up a cookie. Juliette looked at her hands. "Clean hands get a party treat!" she said. Dad laughed. "A cookie party for two." Juliette rode her step stool down and ran to the table. She clapped her soapy-clean hands. "Cookie time!"

Sebastian went to the ice rink with his dad. Kara and Akram came too. Ms. Bélanger from next door was there as well. They sat on the green bench by the wall.

The big game began. Sebastian looked and looked. "Where is the ball?" he asked. Kara pointed at the ice. "Look. The players hit a flat disc. It is called a puck," she said. Sebastian watched. One player swung his stick. Tap! The puck slid fast across the ice. Another player hit it back. Tap! Tap!

"I don't see a ball anywhere," said Sebastian. He counted the players. One, two, three, four, five, six. All of them held sticks. The sticks hit the puck. The puck flew into the net. The crowd cheered. Sebastian clapped his mittens.

Akram was small and could not see. Sebastian stood up and made room. "You can sit by me," he said. Akram smiled and slid close to the wall. The puck came again. Tap! Both boys shouted, "Goal!"

Leah put two slices of soft white bread into the toaster. Grandma pressed the switch down. The bread went in pale and soft. Soon it popped out brown and crunchy. "What happened to it?" Leah asked. "The toaster made it hot," Grandma said. "Hot bread turns brown and crunchy. That is toast."

Leah wanted to butter the toast all by herself. But the butter was cold and hard. It would not spread. It tore a hole in her toast. Leah frowned at the hole. Then Grandma sent the butter dish to sit near the warm toaster. Soon the butter was soft and loose on top. Leah tried again. The soft butter slid across the toast. Now the whole slice was golden.

Next came the milk. Leah held the cup with one hand. She poured slowly. A little milk dripped down the side and pooled at the bottom of the cup. She got a cloth and wiped it up. Then she tried again. This time she poured even slower, and not one drop spilled.

Leah carried her toast and milk to the table. She took a big bite. Crunch! "I made this myself," she said. Grandma clapped her hands.

Penelope sat at the dinner table. Her plate had peas, cheese and bread. Under her chair, her boot tapped the floor. One boot was on. One boot was lost somewhere.

"I want a book about animals," said Penelope. "The cat book. With the big tiger."

"We can go to the library tomorrow," said her dad. "The animal books sit together on one shelf. The toy books sit on another shelf."

Penelope looked at her plate. She had an idea. The dinner table could be a library!

She pushed all her peas into one group. "These are the animal peas," she said. She pushed her bread into another group. "These are the toy breads." The cheese got its own spot too. "Food books," she said, and giggled.

Then she dropped some cheese, and it went splat. "The cheese is glue now," she said. "It sticks my groups down."

Her dad laughed and helped wipe the table. "Now the table is clean again," he said.

The next day they went to the library. Penelope held her dad's hand. She found a big shelf full of animal books. Tigers, cats and elephants, all together. She picked the tiger book and hugged it tight.

"Peas go with peas," she said. "Animal books go with animal books."

She found her other boot by the door on the way out. She sat down and put it on, right there on the library steps.

"Tiger time," she said.

Aria had a slide in her backyard. She wanted to go down it all by herself. She climbed up the little ladder. At the top, she lay down on her tummy. She pointed her head down the slide.

Her dad saw her. "Turn around, Aria," he said. Aria turned herself around. Now her feet went first. She held on with both hands. Then she let go. Whee! Down she went, feet first, all the way to the soft grass.

Her friend Macy came over to play. Macy climbed to the top too. Macy started to lie down, head first. "Feet first," said Aria. Macy turned around. Down she slid, feet first. Then something surprising happened. Macy sat at the bottom and laughed and laughed. An ice pop in her hand had begun to melt in the sun. "Quick," said Aria. "Eat it before it melts more!" The two girls sat by the window in the shade, being careful with their sticky hands, and smiled.

Rosalie went to the store with her dad. She wanted to buy a red balloon. She held his hand in the big door.

First she saw Agam. Agam had a big smile. "Why is your face like that?" Rosalie asked. "I am happy," said Agam. "I got a toy car."

Then Rosalie saw a mirror by the hats. She looked in. One, two, three faces she made. First a happy face, and there it was, a big smile in the mirror. Then a sad face, and her mouth went down. Then a mad face, and her eyebrows came together. The mirror copied her every time.

But then she could not find her dad. She looked left. She looked right. Her tummy felt scared. Where did he go?

Rosalie thought about the mirror. If she was scared, would her face show it too? She made her scared face. A lady in a green coat saw her. "Are you lost?" the lady asked. She took Rosalie to the counter.

Dad was right there, holding a red balloon. "Surprise!" he said. Rosalie smiled so big. One smile for Agam, one smile for Dad, and one happy balloon ride home.

Milo loved the red bag at school. Ms. Hamdan held it up at circle time. "Let's play the feely bag game," she said. "Put your hand in. Feel. Then guess."

Emma went first. She put her hand in the bag. "It is round," she said. "It rolls. It is a ball!" Ms. Hamdan smiled. "Now open your eyes wide and look." Emma peeked in the bag. "The ball is yellow!" she said. "I could feel it was a ball. But I had to look to see yellow."

Then Malia had a turn. "Bumpy," she said. "It is a crayon!" She looked in the bag. "A blue crayon," she said. Feel the crayon, look for the blue. Feel, then look. Feel, then look. That was the game.

Now it was Milo's turn. He closed his eyes. He put his hand in the bag. He felt something soft. Something small. "Is it a car?" he asked. He answered himself. "No. A car is hard. This is soft." He pulled it out and looked. It was a green sock! Everyone laughed, soft and kind. "You found it," said Ms. Hamdan. "You win the soft sock prize." She gave him a pretty green sticker.

Milo stuck the sticker on his hand. He gave the sock a little kiss, right on the toe. "My hand did not know green," he said. "My eyes know green!" He waved the sock high in the air.

The wind howled outside the apartment. Jasmine watched the big tree by the window. Its branches bent and bent. Then all the lights went out. The whole room went dark.

"The power is out," said Dad. "The strong wind knocked it out." He lit a little lamp with a click. It was safe and soft. Mom found a blanket. Jasmine followed them to the big chair. She held her soft toy animal, a gray rabbit.

Outside, the wind pushed the tree again. Jasmine listened. "The wind is strong," she said. Dad nodded. "That is why we have no lights tonight." Jasmine looked out at the dark windows all up and down the building. Every window was dark too. All the wind, all the dark.

Mom gave her a sweet apple slice. They sat close together. The lamp made a small warm circle of light. Jasmine put her rabbit on her lap. The wind howled on. But inside, the blanket was warm, and the apple was sweet. Soon the lights blinked. Then the whole room glowed again. Jasmine clapped her hands. "Hello, lights," she said.

Ibrahim got a new bunny today. He named it Fluffy Ears. He carried the cage to the backyard. "You can hop here," he said.

Ibrahim opened the cage door. But Fluffy Ears did not hop out. Fluffy Ears hid behind the water bowl. Ibrahim waited and waited. Still no bunny.

His friend Weston came to see. Weston peeked in the cage. "Maybe the bunny is shy," said Weston. Ibrahim sat down on the bumpy grass. He stayed very still. He sipped his juice slowly. He did not make a sound.

The sun moved across the sky. Then one little nose came out. Then two soft ears. Then hop, hop, hop! Fluffy Ears jumped onto the grass. Fluffy Ears nibbled a clover leaf.

"He likes it here!" said Ibrahim. Weston laughed. "He likes your juice too." Fluffy Ears was sniffing at the cup. Ibrahim giggled and held it up high. "No juice for bunnies," he said. "Just clover for you."

Norah stood at the bus stop with her grandma. The wind blew. Norah felt cold.

"Put on your coat," said grandma. Norah held her yellow coat. She pulled the zipper tab up. It did not move. She pulled again. The zipper stayed open.

Tyler was at the bus stop too. He looked at her coat. "Mine did that too," he said. He pointed at the bottom. "Look at the little box."

Norah looked down. There was a small box at the bottom of one side. The other side had an end. She slid the end into the little box. It clicked in.

"Now pull," said grandma. Norah pulled the tab. The zipper went up, up, up. Her coat was closed. She was warm.

The bus came. Norah climbed the steps all by herself. "I did my zipper!" she told Tyler.

"Me too," said Tyler. They sat down side by side. Norah zipped her coat up and down, just to feel it move.

Sadie sat on the school bus. She held a name tag in her hands. She wanted to write her name all by herself. She wrote s, a, d, i, e. But it looked small and wrong.

Fox sat next to her. "That's not how a name goes," Fox said. Fox held up his own tag. It said Fox with a big F. "Look at my F," said Fox. Sadie looked at the big F. Then she looked at her small s.

Sadie took out her pencil. She erased the small s. She drew a big S. Now her tag said Sadie. Conor leaned over from his seat. "S is for Sadie," he said. "S, s, s," said Sadie, making the sound. Mr. Ito smiled from the front of the bus. Sadie gave her tag a little hug. Through the window, she saw the spring trees go by. "Big S," she whispered. "Big S for me."

Margot wanted to build a house for her tiny cow. She found blocks on the shelf. One block was round like a ball. "That is a circle," said her friend Alita. Margot rolled the circle across the floor. It went fast. It would not stack for walls.

She tried a square block. Four sides, flat and neat. It stacked up well. Then she tried a long block. "That one is a rectangle," said Presley. Margot put two rectangles side by side. The walls grew tall. The tiny cow peeked out from inside.

Now she needed a roof. She held up the circle. It rolled off the wall. She held up the square. It sat flat, like a lid. Then she found a block with three sides and three corners. She counted them. "One, two, three," said Margot. "It's a triangle!" said Alita. The triangle sat on top like a pointy hat.

Ms. Nakamura brought snack time. She had cut the sandwiches into triangles too. Margot counted the corners of her piece. One, two, three. She took a big bite. Then she ran back to the blocks. "Your house has a triangle roof," said Presley. Margot put the tiny cow under it. "Night night, cow," she said.

Caleb was at Grandma's house. On the table sat a big glass jar. It was full of fresh strawberry jam. Caleb wanted some jam on his bread.

He picked up the jar. He pulled the lid. The lid did not move. He pulled again. His hands slipped. He made a sad face.

His grandpa walked in. Caleb said, "Can you help me, please?" His grandpa smiled. He held the jar and turned the lid. Pop! The lid came off.

"Thank you," said Caleb. His grandpa put jam on his bread. It smelled sweet. Then Caleb knocked over his spoon. "Sorry," he said. His grandpa picked it up and gave him a clean one.

Caleb took a big bite. The jam was yummy. He drew a picture later with a red crayon. It was a picture of the jam jar. He drew his grandpa too, with a happy face. "More jam tomorrow," said Grandma. Caleb smiled and licked his spoon.

Maverick stood in the backyard. Taha and Van were there too. Ms. Nowak put a hoop on the grass.

"Throw the beanbag in," said Ms. Nowak. Maverick threw it. It hit the rim and fell out. He tried again. It went in! Taha clapped. Van smiled.

Then Ms. Nowak rolled a big ball to Maverick. He touched it with his hands. The ball bounced out. He tried again. It bounced out again.

"Why does it keep jumping away?" Maverick asked.

"Watch Van," said Ms. Nowak.

Van held out both hands. The ball came to him. Then he hugged it to his chest. The ball stayed.

Maverick tried. He held out both hands. The ball came. He hugged it to his chest. He held on! He did not drop it.

"I did it!" said Maverick. "I got it that time!"

"Now throw it back," said Ms. Nowak. Maverick tossed the ball to Taha. Taha hugged it to his chest too.

"Let's take a picture," said Ms. Nowak. She held up her phone. The three friends stood by the hoop. Maverick held the beanbag up high. In the last picture, they were all smiling.

Ryan wanted his bath right now. He ran to the tub and put one knee on the edge. "Stop," said Dad. "The water is too hot. Wait for me." Ryan sat down on the mat. He watched Dad stir the water with his hand. Steam rolled up in little clouds. Ryan put his fingers near the tap. "No, no," said Dad gently. "That tap can get very hot. I will turn it." Dad turned the cold tap too. The water got warm and quiet. Dad put his elbow in and smiled. "Now it is warm, not hot. You can get in." Ryan climbed in slow and careful. The water felt nice on his toes. His rubber duck rolled over in the waves. Ryan laughed and gave it a little push. "Warm water is the best," he said. Dad knelt beside the tub and stayed close.

Matteo sat on the rug at Grandpa's house. He made a tall tower. One block, two blocks, three blocks, four.

His friend Gia came over. She made a tower too. Douglas made a straight wall. They sat in a circle of blocks.

Matteo reached for a red block. He leaned too far. His hand bumped Gia's tower. It fell down. All four blocks went crash.

Gia looked at her blocks. Her eyes went small and sad.

Matteo said, "Sorry, Gia." He picked up one block, two blocks, three blocks, four. He put them back, one by one. Gia put the last one on top.

Then Gia handed Matteo the red block. "Your turn," she said.

Matteo zipped the red block onto his tower. Grandpa came in with a plate of crackers. "Crackers for the tower builders," he said.

Douglas laughed. "We build, we bump, we fix," he said. Matteo smiled and took a cracker.

Gianna sat at the big table. She had red paint and yellow paint. She wanted to make something new.

First she dipped her brush in red. She made a long red slide on her paper. Then she dipped the same brush in yellow. She painted over the red.

"Look!" said Gianna. The red and yellow made orange. It looked like a pumpkin. She touched the paint with one finger. It was cool and wet.

When she was done, her hands were busy and sticky. Her mom helped her wash the brushes with water. They put the brushes on a towel to dry.

The next day, Gianna saw her brushes. They were soft and clean. She smiled and picked up her favorite one.

"More orange today," she said.

Joseph wanted to stay up late. "One more story," he said. Mom read one more book. Then Joseph asked, "Can I skip sleep tonight?"

"Sleeping at night gives your body rest for the next day," said Mom. But Joseph shook his head. He played with his blocks. He watched the moon in the window. He stayed awake a long, long time.

The next morning, Joseph was so tired. Elisa came to play. She was going to ride the toy bus with him. Joseph tried to run. His legs felt slow. He tried to build a tower. His hands dropped the blocks. "Why am I so slow?" he wondered.

Elisa had gone to bed early. She zoomed the bus fast. She laughed and jumped. Joseph sat on the warm rug. He yawned a big yawn. He took a bite of his banana, but even chewing felt slow.

That night, Joseph got dressed in his soft pajamas all by himself. "Mom," he said, "I want lots of rest tonight." He climbed into bed. He closed his eyes.

The next morning, Joseph jumped out of bed. He ran to the toy bus. "Watch me, Elisa!" he called. And he zoomed fast, fast, fast.

Lena sat at her big table. She had a pile of crayons. She wanted to draw the sky.

She found her blue crayon. But it was dark like the night sky. "I need light blue," she said.

Erica was there to play. She held up a navy crayon. "This one is blue," said Erica.

Lena shook her head. "That one is too dark. Blue is light like the sky."

They put all the blues on the table. There were five blue crayons. Lena lined them up. The palest one went first. The darkest one went last. They made a long row, light to dark.

"Look," said Erica. "They are all still called blue."

Lena smiled. She picked the lightest blue crayon. She drew a big sky shape with soft clouds. Then she drew the sea with the dark blue crayon. The sea was still blue too.

At bath time, Lena splashed the water with her hand. The water looked light blue in her little cup. The big tub looked dark blue in the shadow. "Two blues," said Lena. "One light, one dark."

Jaxon went to the park with his dad. There was a big festival there. Lots of lamps sat in a long row on the grass. "Can I light one?" Jaxon asked. "Grown-ups light the flames," said Dad. "But you can pick one." Jaxon looked and looked. He found a lamp with a root painted on it. "This one!" he said. "That is a nice one," said Dad. Dad used a little stick. He held it to the lamp. A small flame came up. It glowed and glowed. Jaxon waved hello to Addilyn across the grass. She had picked a lamp too. Her dad was lighting it. "Look, a flame!" said Addilyn. Jaxon held his dad's hand and watched the little lights shine all along the park.

David woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! "No school today," said Mom. David jumped up and down. "Snow day!"

He put on his boots and his red hat. Mom took him to the big sledding hill. His friend Kingston was there too. They sled down fast, fast, fast. Whee!

Then David tried to walk to the sled hill steps. His feet slipped. He sat down in the snow with a plop.

Mr. Cruz was shoveling a path. He pushed the snow away with his big shovel. "Try walking here," he said. David walked on the clean path. He did not slip at all!

"Can I help?" David asked. Mr. Cruz gave him a small shovel. David pushed snow off the path. The mail carrier came by and waved. "Thank you!" she said.

Then Mom called, "Time to go cook soup!" David slid down the hill one more time. He heard the sound of Kingston laughing all the way down.

Charles went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big white book about trucks. It sat on the shelf, and Charles could see it from far away. He began to walk faster and faster. Then he ran right to the front of the line of kids. Safa and Dani were standing there, waiting for their turn.

"Charles, you went past us," said Safa. Ms. Korhonen knelt down beside him. "This is the line," she said. Charles looked behind him. So many kids, all standing one after another. He wondered, what is a line for? He went back to his spot, behind Dani. His feet stayed still. It was hard to wait. He counted the flowers on Dani's shirt, one, two, three, four.

A boy at the front got his book. Then it was Safa's turn. Then it was Dani's turn. And then it was Charles's turn. He held out his hands. Ms. Korhonen gave him the big white truck book. "My turn," said Charles, and he hugged it tight.

Miles went to the beach with his dad. There was a little pool by the sea. Mr. Malik, the lifeguard, sat in a big tall chair. Miles was learning to swim in the pool.

"Why do you sit up so high?" Miles asked. "So I can watch all the swimmers," said Mr. Malik. "And I help anyone who needs it."

Miles got in the slow, shallow water. He held the side. He kicked his feet. His friend Mariana was there too. She splashed and laughed.

Then Mariana slipped. She went under for just a second. Miles could not reach her. But Mr. Malik blew his whistle. He climbed down fast. He reached out his long pole. Mariana held on tight. He pulled her to the side.

"That was so quick!" said Miles. "I saw you from up high," said Mr. Malik. "Now you know why I sit there."

Miles felt a small surprise in his tummy. But Mariana was fine. Her mom ran over and gave her a big hug.

"Can you watch me too?" Miles asked. "I watch everyone," said Mr. Malik. "You too."

Miles kicked his feet again. The water felt warm. He looked up at the tall chair. Mr. Malik waved. Miles waved back.

Evelyn ran to Grandpa's house. A big rain was starting outside. Grandpa had a surprise. It was a big cardboard box!

"Let's make it a car," said Ziva. Ziva was visiting too.

"No, a boat," said Evelyn. "Rain, rain! A boat goes in rain!"

They both pulled the box. It nearly tipped over.

"Take turns," said Grandpa. "First a boat. Then a car."

Evelyn sat in the box first. "Row, row!" she said. She used a wooden spoon as an oar. Ziva splashed her hands. "The rain makes waves!" she said. A toy frog hopped in. "The frog rides too," said Evelyn. She tucked the frog in a small blanket. "Sleepy frog," she said.

Then it was Ziva's turn. "Beep beep! A car now!" said Ziva. Evelyn pushed the box slowly across the rug. Grandpa made the car sound. "Vroom, vroom!" he said.

Then Evelyn had a big idea. "It can be a house too!" she said. She tipped the box onto its side. Ziva crawled in. Evelyn crawled in too. The frog came too.

They peeked out of their box house. The rain tapped on the window. "Home, sweet home," said Evelyn. Grandpa laughed and clapped his hands.

Matthew dug a little hole in the backyard. He dropped in a seed. "Grow, little seed!" he said. His dad helped him pat the dirt down. It was not a broken pot, just a round, flat shape of dirt.

Matthew got his small watering can. He poured water on the dirt. "More water, more water!" he sang. His friend Jalen came to see. "Where is the plant?" asked Jalen. "It will come!" said Matthew.

The next morning, Matthew ran outside. He looked and looked. There was only dirt. "I miss my plant," he said. But he watered the dirt again. Every day, Matthew watered it. Then one morning, a tiny green sprout stood up in the dirt. "Jalen! Jalen! Come quick!" yelled Matthew. Jalen ran over and bent down low. "It came up!" said Jalen. Matthew smiled and filled his watering can again.

Caleb got a small blue card today. It was his very own library card. His name was on it in wide letters. He held it up to the light. "My card," he said.

The librarian helped him pick a book. It was about a big red truck. The librarian stamped a paper inside. "It's called the due date," she said. "Bring the book back by that day." Caleb put the card in his pocket. He carried the book home with two hands.

At bedtime, Caleb sat on his bed. His dad read the truck book to him. Caleb laughed at the mud part. He wanted to keep the book forever. He hid it under his pillow. "Mine," he whispered.

The next morning, Caleb showed the book to Aydin on the steps. Aydin's eyes went wide. "I want to read that one too," said Aydin. Caleb looked at the stamped paper. The book had to go back by the due date. Then Aydin could read it. Then Caleb could borrow it again.

Caleb put the book in his bag. At breakfast he ate his cereal with a big spoon. He did not let the book catch any milk. After school, Dad walked him to the library. Caleb put the book on the desk. The librarian smiled and stamped it.

"Can I take it again?" asked Caleb. The librarian nodded. Aydin came in with his mom. Caleb held the truck book out to him. "Your turn," said Caleb.

Clara got to daycare and hung up her coat. She painted a big black cat at the paint table. Her friend Laura painted a dog.

Then Clara needed to use the toilet. She went in all by herself. She pulled up her pants and ran out to play.

Mr. Clarke was passing the little bathroom. "Someone forgot to flush," he said kindly. Clara looked. The water was still in the toilet. It was her turn!

Clara remembered what came next. She pressed the handle. Whoosh! The water swirled away. Then she washed her hands with soap. The bubbles felt warm and bubbly.

Later, Clara ate her snack of crackers and apples. Then it was nap time. She lay on her mat and watched a ladybug crawl across the floor by the wall.

After nap, Clara used the toilet again. This time she remembered both steps. Whoosh went the flush. Then she sang a little song while she washed her hands.

"Nice work, Clara," said Mr. Clarke with a smile.

Alexander sat at the white table in the library. He wanted to make a toy car. Ms. Cho gave him cardboard and tape.

He cut four square wheels. He taped them on. He pushed the car. The car would not go. It just sat there.

Jayla sat down next to him. "My car has circle wheels," she said. She rolled her car across the table. It went fast, all the way to the end.

Alexander looked at his square wheels. Then he looked at Jayla's round ones. Wheels are round like circles, and round wheels roll.

"Can you help me cut circles?" he asked. Ms. Cho used the scissors and cut four round wheels. Alexander taped them on his car.

He gave the car a little pull. It rolled! It rolled past the triangle blocks. It rolled past the rectangle books on the shelf.

Aurelia clapped her hands. "Your car goes so far!" she said.

Alexander rolled the car again and again. Then he sat back in his chair and smiled.

"Round wheels win," he said.

Rose was at Grandma's house. Her friend Inaya came to play. Grandma put a big box of crayons on the table. Rose took the whole box. She hugged it close. "They are all mine," she said. Inaya sat down with no crayons. She looked at her empty hands.

Rose drew a shiny yellow sun. Then she looked at Inaya. Inaya had no paper sun. She had no colors at all. Rose felt a small pull inside her tummy. She opened the box. She gave Inaya three crayons. "You can use them too," Rose said. Inaya smiled so big. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too," said Inaya. She picked the red one first.

They took turns with the blue crayon. Rose drew two birds. Inaya drew one cat. Then Grandma called, "Snack time!" Rose yelled, "Coming!" They ran to the kitchen. On the table sat a surprise. It was a gift for Rose and Inaya. Inside were two new coloring books, one for each. Grandma winked. "You shared so well," she said. Rose gave Inaya the shiny sticker on top.

Aiden ran into the kitchen. "Picnic day!" he shouted. He wanted to help pack the big basket.

He grabbed a big box of apples. He pulled. He pulled again. The box did not move. "Oh no," said Aiden. His dad came over and slid the box onto the table. "That one is heavy," said Dad. Aiden picked up a small bag. It went up, up, up in his hands. "This one is light!" he said. Heavy and light are opposites.

Then Aiden wanted to carry everything to the car. "Can I take the soup?" he asked. "No," said Dad. "It is hot. I will carry the hot soup. You carry the cold juice." Dad carried the slow, careful walk with the pot. Aiden ran fast to the door and then came back. "Again!" he said. He ran fast, then walked slow, then ran fast again.

"Can we count the apples?" Aiden asked. "Yes!" said Dad. "One, two, three!" Aiden put them in one by one. At last the picnic basket was full. Dad smiled. "Sweet cookies on top," he said. Aiden held the little cookie bag up high. It was light, light, light. He marched out the door, and Dad followed with the big, heavy basket.

Sarah wanted to make a card for Daddy. She took out her paper and crayons. First she drew a sun. But her circle came out wobbly. It looked like a squished egg. She tried again. It was still wobbly. Sarah frowned at the paper.

Then she saw her cup on the table. The cup had a round bottom. Sarah held the cup down on the paper. She traced around the bottom with her crayon. She lifted the cup up. There it was. A big round circle! "Look, Mommy!" she called. Mommy came to look. "That is a fine circle," Mommy said. Sarah laughed. It was so smooth and round.

Sarah traced the cup again and again. She made three circles. She colored them yellow like the sun. Then she drew little square windows and a triangle roof for a house. She added a sweet smile on the sun's face. "Daddy will love this," said Mommy. Sarah ran to find the tape. "Daddy!" she shouted, holding up the paper.

Mason sat at the big kitchen table. He was painting a picture of a mouse in the grass. His mouse was gray. His sun was yellow. His sky was blue.

Then Mason stopped. He had no green paint. "Oh no," he said. "My grass needs green." He looked in his paint box. Only blue and yellow were left.

Mason dipped his brush in the blue. Then he dipped it in the yellow. He gave the paints a gentle stir. The paint turned green on the paper! Mason laughed out loud.

"Mom, look!" he said. "Blue and yellow made green!" His mom came over and smiled. "That is a lovely green meadow," she said.

Mason painted tall green grass. He painted the little gray mouse hiding in it. "You are a sneaky mouse," said Mason. He pulled his picture close and added one more tuft of grass on top. "There," he said. "Now you can hide from Kevin!"

Wesley sat at Diya's little table. Diya had a tablet. Wesley wanted to draw on it too.

Diya's mom showed Wesley the button. "Press here," she said. Wesley pressed it. The screen popped on. It was bright and full of colors. Wesley tapped the drawing app. He drew a big red wheel. Then he drew a rough brown dog.

Diya drew a blue sun. "It's a surprise sun," she said. Wesley laughed. A blue sun was silly and fun.

Now Wesley was done. He wanted to put the tablet away. But the screen stayed on. He looked at the button. He pressed it. The screen went dark. It was quiet and still now.

"You did it," Diya said. Wesley carried the tablet to the shelf. He set it down soft and slow. Diya's mom smiled. Then she opened her hand. Inside was a small sticker of a wheel.

"For you," she said. Wesley stuck it on his shirt. "A wheel for the wheel boy," said Diya. Wesley patted his sticker all the way home.

It was Lincoln's first day of school. He put his lunchbox on the shelf. Peter put his lunchbox there too. The two lunchboxes looked the same. They were both red with a bear on them.

After play time, the class sat down for lunch. "Whose is this one?" asked Ms. Carvalho. She held up a red lunchbox. Lincoln looked. Peter looked. They both reached for it.

Then Ms. Carvalho opened the lid. "Look," she said. "Here is a name." It said Lincoln. The other lunchbox said Peter. Lincoln got his own lunchbox back. His sandwich was inside. His apple was inside too. "My name found my lunchbox," said Lincoln. After lunch, Lincoln poured water from the little jug into his cup. He put his cup in the tidy row on the shelf. Then he patted his lunchbox with one foot-tapping hop of joy and sat down beside Peter to draw.

Grandpa came to stay at Nora's home for a whole week. In the kitchen, Nora wanted to play train. Grandpa pushed a kitchen chair across the floor. "Here comes the train!" he said.

Nora made a long line with tape. Grandpa said, "This is the platform. We wait on the platform." Nora stood on the tape. She wanted to lean out far to see the chair train coming. "Stand back from the edge," Grandpa said. "Wait until the train stops." Nora took one big step back. The chair rolled closer, closer, then it stopped. Only then did Nora step up and climb aboard.

After the game, flour had spilled on the floor. Nora got her little brush. She helped Grandpa sweep the flour into a pile. "Not a bad mess," Grandpa said. "Good helpers." Nora drove her train home across the clean floor.

Parker went to the library with his dad. Mr. Janssen had a table with tablets on it. Parker wanted to draw a cat on one.

"Can I try?" Parker asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Janssen. "First we turn it on." Parker pressed the round button. The screen lit up. His tap made it wake!

He tapped the little paint app. It opened. The app was open, just like a book. One tap, one picture page. Another tap, a new color. It was like magic, but it was not magic. His finger did it.

Parker drew a big orange cat. Then Tiago sat down beside him. Tiago set his juice cup on the table. It sat right by the tablet.

"Not there," said Mr. Janssen. "Tablets stay away from water and drinks." Tiago moved his cup to the next table. Parker looked at his own cup. He moved it too. Far away.

He drew the cat a pillow to sleep on. Then it was time to go. Parker pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, flat side down.

"Bye, tablet," said Parker. "Bye, cat."

Juliette was at Grandma's house. She wanted a story, but Grandma's big bookshelf was very heavy to look at. Too many books!

"Who made up the stories?" Juliette asked. She chewed her toast while she thought about it. Grandma did not know. "Let's ask Mr. Khan next door," she said. "He has lots of books too."

Mr. Khan was in his garden. He heard them coming and waved. Juliette held up the book. "Who made up the words?" she asked. Mr. Khan smiled. He turned the book to the front cover. He pointed with one finger. "The author," he said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Juliette looked hard. There was a name on the front. She said it out loud, one part at a time. Then she turned the book over. No name there. She turned it back. The name was on the front again!

Back home, Juliette sat with Grandma. She opened the book at the front, like Mr. Khan showed her. "The author made the words," she said. Grandma made a happy noise. Juliette turned page one, then page two, then page three, all the way to the end. "Again," she said. "From the front."

Jayden wanted to look at the truck book. It had a big red truck on the front. Lohan had it first. Lohan sat on the little chair and opened the book from the back. "The words look funny," Lohan said. "The story is all mixed up." He turned a page. Then another. The pictures jumped around. Lohan frowned.

Jayden sat down next to him. "Flip it over," Jayden said. Lohan turned the book over. Now the red truck was at the front. Lohan opened the front cover. Page one had a small truck. Page two had a long truck. The story went in a line, page by page, all the way to the back cover.

"Lohan read it front to back," said Mr. Goh, smiling as he walked past. "See, the words tell us the story," said Lohan. He pointed at the letters. The letters sat under each truck. Jayden looked at them. The words did not sink down like stones in water. They sat still. They meant something. Jayden turned to the front page. "Let's read it again," he said. "From the very first truck."

David stood at the edge of the hotel pool. The water was blue and cool. His friend Ruben was already in the pool. "Come in, David!" Ruben called. But David held back. He did not want to put his face near the water.

Mr. Bear, the swim teacher, knelt down beside him. "Watch me," said Mr. Bear. He bent over and blew bubbles into the water through his mouth. Pop, pop, pop went the bubbles. David's eyes grew wide. Would his mouth make bubbles too?

David leaned down, slow and careful. He blew out through his mouth. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles rose up and popped. David laughed and laughed. "I made bubbles!" he said. Ruben blew bubbles too. Then David splashed in, right next to his friend. A wet leaf floated past his hand. David blew at it. The bubbles pushed the leaf away. He blew again. Away it went again. "Look what my bubbles can do!"

Arthur held his dad's hand at the community hall. There were red lanterns on the walls. "It is Lunar New Year," his dad said.

Then the drums began. Boom, boom, boom! The sound was very loud. Arthur hid behind his dad's legs. "Too loud," he said.

His friend Anaelle ran over. "Look, Arthur!" she said. A big lion was coming in. It was red and gold. The lion moved to the beat of the drums. Boom! The lion jumped. Boom! The lion shook its head.

Arthur peeked out. He clapped his hands with the drum. Boom, clap! The lion moved with him. Then the lion blinked its big eyes at Arthur. A hand came out of the lion's mouth and waved.

Arthur laughed and waved back. "Hello, lion!" he said.

Rain fell on the window. Plip, plip, plip. Miles pressed his nose to the cold glass. "No park today," said his dad. Miles felt sad. His bottom lip went down, down, down.

He climbed off his bed, not up it, and dragged his blanket to the floor. "One blanket," he said. "Two chairs. Three pillows." He made a fort. It was a cave. He was a little brown mouse, skipping through the rain. He spun one time and felt dizzy, then he giggled.

Casey came over with her mom. Casey crawled in the cave too. "Rain outside," said Miles. "Dry in here!" The flashlight made stars on the blanket roof. One star, two stars, three stars. Miles clapped his hands. His sad feeling had gone away. Now he felt happy inside the cave. "More pillows!" he shouted.

Emile loved the book about the smelly troll. The troll lived under a bridge. He splashed in the water all day. He let a fox ride on his back.

Emile wanted that book again. He looked at the shelf. So many books! He could not find it.

Emile asked Ms. Sandhu, "I want the troll book."

Ms. Sandhu said, "Tell me the title. A book's title is its name."

Emile looked at the book in her hand. Big letters sat on the front. He put his finger on them. "Troll Under the Bridge," he said slowly.

"That's it!" said Ms. Sandhu. She pointed to the shelf. Emile found the big letters all by himself. He held the book close. He opened the front cover first, like always.

"Hello again, smelly troll," he whispered.

Eleanor went to summer camp. Her class met by the big yellow tent. Ms. Kapoor said, "Snack time soon. First we wash our hands."

Eleanor ran to the sink. She pumped the soap. She scrubbed fast. Then she rinsed and ran to the table. Sean was still at the sink. He was singing a little song.

"Why are you singing?" Eleanor asked. "It helps me keep washing long enough," said Sean. He kept scrubbing until the song was done. Then he rinsed.

At the table, Ms. Kapoor looked at Eleanor's hands. "Still bubbles," she said. "Try again, please." Eleanor walked back to the sink. This time she sang too. "One little duck, two little ducks, three little ducks, four." She scrubbed the backs of her hands. She scrubbed between her fingers. The song was long!

When the song ended, Eleanor rinsed. The bubbles went down the drain. Her hands were clean and shiny. She held them up for Ms. Kapoor to see. "All done," said Ms. Kapoor.

Eleanor sat down with Sean and Krish. They ate apple slices. "Your hands smell like soap," said Krish. Eleanor smiled and took another bite. Then she whispered, "One little duck, two little ducks, three little ducks, four."

Livia stood in the kitchen. Her dad was making soup. The pot was big. Her cup was small. "Big pot, small cup," she said.

Saira came to play. "Let's play the kitchen game," said Saira. "I say a word. You say one as different as it can be." "Big!" said Saira. "Small!" said Livia. "Hot!" said Saira. Livia touched the cold window. "Cold!" she said. "Those are opposites," said Saira. "Big and small. Hot and cold."

Then Livia got stuck. "Fast!" said Saira. Livia looked around the kitchen. She could not think of the word. The soup bubbled. A horse picture hung on the wall. The horse in the picture had a short tail. Livia stared at the tail. Slow, slow, like a sleepy snail. "Slow!" she shouted. "Yes!" said Saira. "Fast and slow are opposites too."

Livia clapped her hands. She wanted more words. She saw a sticky spoon. Honey dripped off it. "Sticky!" said Livia. Saira laughed. "Sticky is not sticky's opposite! Opposites are two words as different as can be." Livia thought hard. She touched the smooth, dry table. "Smooth!" she said. Saira nodded.

The soup was ready. Dad poured it into two small cups. "Blow slow," said Dad. Livia blew slow, slow, slow. The steam danced away. Saira blew fast. Livia giggled. She held her cup up high. "Big sip or small sip?" she asked. Saira smiled and said, "Small sip, because it is hot, hot, hot!"

Anna wanted to wash her toy duck. She went to the bathroom with her dad. The water ran into the sink. Dad felt it first. "Hot," he said. "Too hot for you." He turned the tap. Now the water felt warm and nice.

Anna washed the duck. It went splash, splash. Then she saw a little box on the wall. It had small holes in it. It was near the sink, close to her elbow.

Anna pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked.

"That is an electrical outlet," said Dad. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet."

Anna looked at her fingers. She kept them on the duck. Dad plugged in his razor, and it made a noisy hum. Anna heard it buzz.

Dad put a little sign over the outlet. "There," he said. "Now it is covered."

Anna washed the duck some more. Splash, splash. "All clean," she said.

"Good girl," said Dad. "You told me. You did not touch."

Mason sat on the big bed at the doctor's office. He held his teddy bear tight. "The bear helps me be brave," he said.

The nurse was friendly. She talked to Mason in a soft voice. "One little pinch," she said. "Then you are done." Mason looked at his bear. The nurse counted, one, two, three. The shot was over. "All done," said the nurse.

Then Mason saw it. The nurse put the needle in a red box on the wall. The box was hard and it had a little door. "What is that box for?" Mason asked. "Used needles go in there," the nurse said. "That way nobody gets poked." Mason watched the little door close. The needle was inside. Nobody could get poked now. Not even the bear.

Afterward, Mom took Mason to the ice cream shop. His friend Cynthia was there with her dad. "I got a shot today," Mason said. "The needle went in a red box. It went click." Cynthia licked her pink ice cream. "My dad got a shot too," she said. Mason took a big bite of his ice cream. He held his bear up to the cone. "You can share," he whispered. The bear got a tiny dot of cream on his nose.

Elias went to Grandma's house. Today was a big party day. There were so many people there. There were lanterns and red paper on the door.

Elias held Mama's hand at the door. Then he saw a big table of food. There were his favorite dumplings. He let go of Mama's hand. He walked toward the dumplings all by himself.

The room was full of legs and coats. Elias could not see Mama. He could not see Grandma. His tummy felt funny. He stood still and thought. At a big party, he must stay close to his grown-up. Grandma found him by the food table. She took his hand. "Stay with me, little one," she said.

Grandma walked with him past all the people. Grandpa was lighting a candle. Grandma held Elias back from the candle. "Only grown-ups touch fire," she said. Elias watched the candle from far away. It was pretty and safe.

Then they found the dumplings together. Elias ate three dumplings. Mama sat right beside him. Grandma gave him a red envelope with money inside. Elias held Mama's hand again. The party was loud and happy. "This is my favorite day," said Elias. Grandma smiled and squeezed his hand.

Florence was at Grandma's house. On the shelf sat a little tablet. Florence wanted to draw on it.

Grandma showed her the round button. Florence pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up. A picture appeared!

"Now the drawing part," said Grandma. Grandma tapped the blue spot. Florence tapped it too. A big white page opened. Florence picked the red crayon on the screen. She drew a red cat. She drew a sleepy sun going down.

Soon Florence got tired of drawing. She put the tablet on the soft couch. Then Grandma came in to sit down. "Wait!" said Florence. The tablet was right where Grandma would sit!

Florence picked up the tablet. "Where does it go?" she asked. Grandma pointed to the shelf. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," said Grandma. Florence set it on the shelf. It fit just right in its spot.

Grandma sat down on the couch. Florence climbed up beside her. On the fridge hung a plastic magnet shaped like a star. Florence pointed at it. "That star can be my next picture," she said. "A red one."

Emma went to the playground with her family. Maxine and Zola were there too. Emma saw a little red stove on the picnic table. Her dad was cooking on it. The pot went pop and hiss. Steam rose up like white clouds.

"Is it hot?" Emma asked. "Can I touch it?" Her dad shook his head. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot," he said. "Only grown-ups touch it." Emma looked at the little red stove. It looked quiet and cool. But she did not touch it. She stepped back and held her dad's hand.

Soon the pot made warm cocoa. The cocoa was hot too. Emma held her cup with both hands and blew on it. Then she took a tiny sip. It was sweet and warm. Maxine's cup was too full. Emma found a napkin and wiped the little spill. Zola could not find a seat, so Emma moved over to make room.

The three friends sat close together. The big slide had looked scary that morning. Now it looked fun. "Watch me!" said Emma. She climbed up the ladder, one step at a time, and down she came. "My turn!" said Maxine.

Olivier sat on the school bus. He held a letter card in his hands. The card had a big K on it. The K was bumpy. Olivier could feel the bumps with his fingers.

Holden sat next to him. "I can write K," said Holden. He wrote a K on his paper. Olivier tried too. He made his K the wrong way. The legs went the wrong side. He tried again. Wrong way again. His eyes got hot and blinky.

Ms. Rajapakse sat across the bus. "Try this," she said. "Trace the K with your finger. Go slow." Olivier put his finger on the bumpy K. Down the straight line. Then slant in. Then slant out. One, two, three lines. He traced it again. One, two, three.

Then Olivier picked up his pencil. He wrote a K on his paper. The K came out right! "I did it!" said Olivier. Holden patted his back. "Good team," said Holden. Olivier kissed his bumpy card. Ms. Rajapakse smiled. The bus was warm and safe. Olivier traced the K one more time. One, two, three.

Lucas turned five today. His family came to the big park. The sky was cloudy but soft and gray. His friends Ariane and Arnaaz came too. There was a table with a cake. It was a berry cake. It smelled sweet like strawberries.

Lucas looked at the cake. He counted the candles. One, two, three, four. Ariane counted too. "Only four," she said. Lucas frowned. He was five now. He wanted to count to his number.

Then Lucas remembered. Each year gets one candle. Four candles would be for a four-year-old. He was not four anymore. "We need one more candle," he said. Mom looked in the picnic basket. She found one pink candle. She pushed it in with careful fingers. Now there were five. One, two, three, four, five.

Dad lit the candles with a match. Lucas watched from far away. The little flames danced. Everyone sang the birthday song. Lucas took a big breath. He blew slow, then fast. All five flames went out. Arnaaz gave him a hug. Then they ate cake on the cool grass.

Violet went to the corner store with her dad. She had one coin in her pocket. She wanted to choose a bag of apples for snack time.

The apples sat in a big bin. Some apples were spread out in a long line. Some apples were pushed close together in a bunch. Violet looked and looked. "That line looks like more," she said. She pointed at the long line.

Then she counted the line. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Then she counted the bunch. "One, two, three, four, five." She blinked. The line was five. The bunch was five too. The long line just looked bigger. It was not more.

The store man at the counter smiled and put down six red plums. He pushed five plums close together. He spread one plum far away. "How many now?" he asked. Violet counted again. "Six," she said. "Same plums, same six." Her dad's phone buzzed in his pocket, and she laughed.

Violet put five apples in a bag. The bin was almost empty now. "I choose these," she said. "Five apples, spread out or squished close." She held the bag all the way home.

Isla sat in the reading corner. She hugged a big red book. It was a book about a rabbit.

"You like that one," said Ms. Côté. "Would you like to take it home?"

Isla shook her head. "Books stay here," she said. She put the book back on the stack.

Ms. Côté held out a small card. "This is a library card," she said. "It lets you borrow books. You can take them home to read."

Ila took the card in both hands. Her eyes went wide. "Home?" she asked.

"Home," said Ms. Côté.

Isla ran back to the stack. She found the rabbit book again. She held it tight.

Aarna came over. "You can borrow two books," said Aarna. "I borrow two."

Isla picked one more, a blue book. Ms. Côté zipped them into a bag.

At home, Isla opened the red book on her bed. The rabbit hopped across the page.

"Goodnight, rabbit," said Isla. "You sleep at my house tonight."

Jaxon sat at the paint table at the park. He was making a card for Grandma. He wanted to paint a big flower on it. Not just any flower. A pink one. Pink was Grandma's favorite color.

But there was no pink paint. Jaxon looked in the box. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. There was white paint. No pink anywhere.

"I need pink," Jaxon said. His friend Nirvaan sat down next to him. She was painting a huge green frog. "Maybe mix two paints," she said. Jaxon put a petal sticker on his card to see how big the flower should be.

Jaxon put red paint on his brush. He painted one petal. It was red. Too dark. Then he had an idea. He dipped his brush in the white paint. He stirred the white into the red. Round and round he stirred. The red got lighter. It turned pink!

"Pink!" Jaxon shouted. Nirvaan clapped. "It did bite the dark out," she laughed, because the pink looked soft, not loud. Ms. Demetriou, the park teacher, came over to look. "What a pretty pink flower," she said. Jaxon painted all the petals pink. Then he painted a yellow sun and a blue sky.

Jaxon held up the card. "Grandma will love this," he said. He put it in his bag, safe and flat.

"Tomorrow I will paint a purple frog," said Nirvaan.

"I know how to start," said Jaxon. "With red and blue!"

David was at Grandma's house. He had a cold. His nose was red. His voice was small.

"Drink some water," said Grandma. "Water will help you." David shook his head. He did not feel thirsty at all. He wanted to lie on the soft couch.

Grandma went to the kitchen. She came back with a yellow cup. It had a bear on it. It had a twisty straw. "This cup is for a sick kid," she said. David sat up. He took one little sip. Then he took another.

He sipped water all morning. He watched birds out the window. They were wild and fast. They made him laugh.

At lunchtime, David jumped off the couch. His nose was better. His voice was big again. "Grandma, my cup is empty," he said. Grandma smiled and filled it up. David took a long, happy drink.

Maria stood in the warm kitchen. Grandma was making bread. It was special bread for the big day. "We only make it now," Grandma said. "Special food for a special day."

Maria wanted a taste. "One bite, please?" she asked. Grandma shook her head. "Not yet, little one. We wait." Maria pouted. Then Grandma said, "You can help."

Maria helped from her safe spot by the door. She watched Grandma mix the flour. She watched the dough sit and sit. Then Maria saw something. The dough got big! It was small before. Now it was big and puffy. Waiting made it grow.

"Again! Again!" Maria said. So they made one more batch together. Maria patted the soft dough. She saw it puff up again. The same thing happened two times.

Outside, a bird sat on the cloudy morning. Inside, the oven did its work. Grandma pulled out the hot bread. The grown-up handled the hot pan, and Maria stayed back.

Soon the family came. The table was full. The special bread was in the middle. Maria took a big bite. "It is so good!" she said. "Worth the wait," said Grandma, and she hugged Maria tight.

Victor was at Grandpa's house. He wanted Grandpa to read the big bear book. But Grandpa was in the quiet room, resting his eyes.

Victor found a crayon. He wrote a note. He wrote all his letters squished together. ICANNTWAITYTHBEERBOOK.

Victor patted Grandpa's arm. "Read my note," he said.

Grandpa held the note. He turned his head. He turned it again. "Hmm," he said. "This looks like one long worm."

Victon laughed. "It is not a worm! It is words!"

Grandpa smiled. "Try a space between one word and the next."

Victor got his crayon again. He copied his note. This time he made little gaps. I CANNOT WAIT.

Grandpa read it out loud. "I cannot wait! For the bear book!"

"Yes!" said Victor. "Front to back, please!"

Grandpa opened the cover. He turned page one, then page two.

"The bear went over the mountain," Grandpa read.

Victor snuggled close and patted the page.

Athena was at daycare. Her bunny was not in her bag. She looked in her cubby. No bunny there. Athena wanted to run down the hall to look by herself. Then she stopped. She walked to Ms. Gupta instead. "My bunny is lost," she said. "Will you help me look?"

Ms. Gupta smiled. "Yes. Let's search together." They looked in the block box. They looked by the play kitchen. Constance was stirring a pot there. "I saw a bunny," Constance said. She pointed to the book corner. Makai sat on the rug. He was holding Athena's bunny.

"Here," said Makai. He gave the bunny a gentle hug, then handed it over. Athena hugged her bunny tight. The bunny's ears were soft and pretty. "Thank you, Makai," she said. "And thank you, Ms. Gupta." Athena held the bunny's paw. They all sat down to hear a story. The sun made a warm spot on the rug, and Athena smiled.

Miles ran to the park with his small blue dinosaur. He loved that dinosaur. At the park, Winnie was kicking a ball. Lea was on the swing. Miles pushed his dinosaur down the slide. Then he played in the sand.

"Where is my dinosaur?" said Miles. His tummy felt tight. He looked by the swing. He looked by the sand. No dinosaur. Mr. Addo sat close by on the bench. "Think," said Mr. Addo. "Where do you last remember holding it?"

Miles thought hard. "The slide!" he said. "I held it at the slide!" He ran to the slide. The wind had blown sand there. He wiped the sand with his hand. Under the sand was something blue. It was his dinosaur!

Miles hugged his dinosaur tight. Winnie rolled the ball to him. "Yay!" said Lea. Mr. Addo smiled and waved. "Snack time," he said. Miles sat on the bench, dinosaur on his lap, munching happily.

Max ran into the library with his dad. Story time was about to start! Mr. Warsame had a big surprise behind a red curtain. Max could hear something jingle behind it. "Is it a truck?" Max asked. "Wait and see," said Mr. Warsame.

Nina and Garrett sat down too. Mr. Warsame pulled the curtain. It was a rocket ship made of boxes! It was tall and silver and long. "We can blast off," said Garrett. "But first we count backward," said Mr. Warsame. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Max jumped up high. Nina jumped too. The rocket shook and rumbled.

"Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown," said Nina. Max wanted a turn. He took a deep breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Up he popped, so high his shoes nearly hit the stars. After story time, Max found his dad. "I did a countdown!" he said. "Can we eat a snack now? Being an astronaut makes me hungry." His dad laughed and held out his hand.

Arnaud woke up in his cozy bed. His tummy made a little rumble. He wanted cookies, lots of cookies, right now.

He found Ada in the kitchen. Ada was eating eggs from a bowl. "Cookies, cookies," said Arnaud. He pulled at the cookie jar on the shelf.

His mom picked him up for a hug. "Not yet, sweet one," she said softly. "This is breakfast. Breakfast is the first meal of the day." Ada held out her spoon. "Want some eggs?" she asked.

Arnaud sat on his chair, nice and straight. He took one little bite. The eggs were warm and soft. Then he ate another bite, and another. A small feather from his pillow clung to his sleeve, and Ada giggled. "You have a feather!" she said.

At last Arnaud patted his tummy. "I love breakfast," he said. Ada laughed and tapped her spoon to his cup.

Olivier had a cough. Mom took him to see the doctor. The doctor looked in his ears. She counted his coughs. "He needs medicine," she said. "One spoon, two times a day." She gave Mom a small bottle.

At home, Olivier felt warm and tired. He wanted the medicine fast. He saw the little bottle on the counter. It was purple. It smelled like grapes when Mom opened it. But Olivier did not touch it. He knew only a grown-up gives a child medicine. So he sat on the rug and waited.

"Ready," he called. Mom came with a spoon. She poured the purple medicine. Olivier opened his mouth. The spoon went in. It tasted sweet. Then Mom gave him his last blanket and a card from Eleonore. It had a cat on it. Olivier laughed. His cough was still there, but he felt better. "Two times a day," he whispered, and closed his eyes.

The lights went out. Hunter sat on the rug. His toy bee buzzed in his hand. "Mama, it is dark," he said.

Mama came with a squishy blanket. She lit a little lamp. It was not a candle. It was a safe lamp, and she held it up high. "Look out the window," said Mama. Hunter looked. All the houses on the street were dark. Every window was black. "The power went out," said Mama. "The whole street went dark at once. Even the neighbors' houses."

Hunter peeked again. The house next door was dark too. Then a small light came on there, far away. Soon the street lights blinked. Then Hunter's own lights came back on. His bee buzzed bright in the glow. "Hello, light," said Hunter. He hugged his bee and smiled.

Alexander wanted the rabbit book. It had a fuzzy cover. He hugged it to his chest. He carried it to Ms. Kamau.

"Read it, please," he said. Ms. Kamau sat down on the small red chair. She opened the front cover first. Then she turned the pages one by one. She read the words out loud. "The rabbit hopped to the garden," she read. The words sat under the picture, small and black.

Then she turned to a page with only a picture. The rabbit drank milk in the sun. Alexander waited. But Ms. Kamau was quiet.

"Read this one too," said Alexander.

"There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read."

Alexander leaned close. He looked and looked. He touched the page with his finger. There were marks on other pages, but not here. Only the rabbit and the milk.

"Turn it," he said. Ms. Kamau turned to the next page. The words came back. She read them all the way to the back cover.

Alexander clapped. Then he opened his fuzzy book again, at the front, all by himself. He traced the little black words with one finger.

"These say rabbit," he told Lachlan. "You wait. I will learn to say them too."

Clara went to the community hall with her dad. It was a shared meal morning. Lots of people brought food. There were breads and fruits and one big pot of soup.

Ms. Kaur clapped her hands. "Time for the blessing," she said. "Some families say it. Some families sing it." Clara's family sang theirs. Today Clara wished to lead the singing all by herself. She stood up tall.

Clara began to sing. But the tune came out wrong. It went up when it should go down. Stephen giggled. "That is a silly song," he said. Clara's cheeks went red. The song felt hard now.

"Try again," said Lev. "Songs like tries." Clara took a big breath. She sang it once more. This time the tune came out right. The whole hall sang with her. Even Stephen sang. The soup steamed and everyone smiled.

When the singing stopped, Ms. Kaur said, "Now we can eat." Clara sat down next to Lev. She got a big warm bowl. "You led it," Lev said. Clara grinned and dipped her bread.

James woke up at Grandpa's house. The sun was up. Grandpa said, "We brush our teeth in the morning." James got his little toothbrush. He brushed up and down. His teeth felt clean.

Then James ate breakfast. He had toast and milk. Later he played with his toy truck. The truck could shake when it rolled. Grandpa laughed at the funny truck.

At night James had a warm bath. Mama washed his hair, slow and gentle. Then James put on his pajamas. He pulled the zipper up all by himself. He got into bed and pulled the covers up.

Then James sat up. "My teeth!" he said. He hopped out of bed. He ran to the sink. He brushed his teeth again. Grandpa smiled and said, "Good job, James. Now the sugar bugs can't play." James got back into bed. He closed his eyes. "Goodnight, Grandpa," he said.

Hunter was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a wooden box of games. "Can we play one?" Hunter asked. Grandpa nodded. He said Hunter could pick one and play with Iqra and Nayla. They came over after lunch.

Hunter picked a game with a spinner. Grandpa read the letter taped inside the lid. The letter told the rules. Each player took a turn. Each player spun once. Grandpa put birdseed on the table, too. Later they would feed the birds with it.

Hunter spun first. He got a one. Then Iqra spun. She got a four. Now Hunter wanted another spin. "I get two spins," he said. He spun again. Iqra put down her piece. Nayla stood up. "We are not playing," Nayla said. Both girls walked to the window.

Hunter looked at the board. Then he looked at the girls. Why did they stop? He handed the spinner to Iqra. "One spin for you," he said. Iqra smiled and sat back down. Nayla came back too. Everyone took one turn each time. The game went round and round. Grandpa watched from his chair. "That looks fun," he said. Hunter spun once and clapped.

Margot went with her mom to the driving school. It was cold outside. Margot watched the cars go round and round. Each car had a big wheel inside.

"Time to go out," said her mom. "Let's put on your coat." But the coat had no zipper. It had little round buttons. Margot pulled the coat close. It fell open again. "Why won't it stay?" she asked.

"Look at the holes," said her mom. Margot looked. Each button had a little hole. She pushed a button through its hole. Pop, it went through! She pushed the next one. Pop! Soon every button was in its hole. The coat stayed closed. Margot was warm now.

"Look, Mom!" she said. She climbed into the car. Her mom held the wheel. "My buttons went through the little holes," said Margot. "All by myself."

Milo ran into the bright backyard. "Let's play hide and seek," said Zak. Milo put his hands over his eyes. "Now you can't see me," he said. Zak laughed. "I can still see you, Milo. Your eyes are the only thing that can't see."

Milo peeked through his fingers. Zak was right. He could see the swing, the grass and Zak's big grin. He ran and hid behind the big tree. He could feel the bark, rough on his fingers. He could smell the flowers by the fence. He could hear Zak counting. "Ready or not, here I come!" Could Zak hear his feet on the grass?

Zak found him fast. "How did you know I was here?" asked Milo. "I saw your shoes," said Zak. Milo looked down. His shoes stuck out from the tree.

They played again. This time Milo tucked his feet in. Zak walked right past him. "Where is Milo? Maybe he is a dream!" Zak called. Milo held his breath and waited, smiling in the dark behind his safe tree.

Emma was four today. There was a party at her house. Balloons sat on the chairs. Eason and Sofia came to play.

A big box sat on the table. It was covered in blue paper. Emma could not see inside it. She shook the box. She heard something go bump. She squeezed it. The paper still hid the present.

"I want to see it now," said Emma.

"The paper hides it," said Sofia. "You have to open it first."

Emma looked at her mom. Her mom smiled. "You can open it after the cake," she said. Her dad lit the candles. Emma watched from her chair. Then she blew them out. Everyone clapped.

The sky outside turned cloudy. But inside, the room was bright.

At last Mom said, "Now you may open it." Emma tore the paper off. Inside was a shiny red drum. "It was hiding in there!" said Emma. She tapped the drum. Boom, boom, boom!

Josephine stood on the soccer field with her class. Ms. Cho held a basket of beanbags. "Watch me," said Ms. Cho. She tossed a beanbag into a hoop. It landed softly inside.

Josephine tried. Her beanbag hit the rim. It fell out. She tried again. It fell out again. Her nose felt itchy and her eyes felt hot. Ms. Cho came close. "Try again," she said. "You are safe here." Josephine took a big breath. She tossed the beanbag slow and high. It dropped into the hoop, clean in the middle. Josephine jumped up and down.

Then Chelsea brought a big ball. Chelsea threw it to Bennett. The ball went too fast. It hit his hands and bounced away. Bennett did not catch it. He looked sad. Josephine picked up the ball. "Try a gentle toss," she said. Chelsea tossed it soft and slow. Bennett caught it with both hands.

Then Bennett tossed it gently to Josephine. She caught it too. The three friends sat on the clean grass. "Nice hands," said Ms. Cho from the bench. Josephine hugged the big ball and smiled.

Hunter woke up. The sun was bright in his room. He heard spoons and cups in the kitchen. His mom was at the table. His grandpa was there too. "Good morning, Hunter," said Grandpa. "Morning is when we wake up," said Grandpa, "and eat breakfast." Hunter sat down. He ate his egg. He drank his milk. One egg, one milk, one piece of toast.

Today Hunter was going to the park. "Now we eat," said Mom. "Later we ride to the park." Hunter waited. He looked out the window. Then Mom said, "Now!" Hunter ran to the door.

At the park, Hunter saw Fox and Niam. They counted the ducks. One duck, two ducks, three ducks. The ducks went into the water. Splash! The water made little rings. Hunter threw a small stick. The stick made rings too. Fox threw a leaf. The leaf made rings. "The water moves when we drop things," said Niam.

Mr. Kaminski sat on a bench nearby. He was not young, and he had a big hat. "Come back tomorrow," he said. "The ducks will be here tomorrow." Hunter nodded. Yesterday he had played at home. Today he played at the park. Tomorrow he would come again. Hunter waved to the ducks. "See you tomorrow," he said.

Mia wanted to build a house for her toy cat. First she found her blocks. One, two, three, four blocks on the floor. One block was round like a ball. One block had three sides like a little hat. Two blocks had four sides each.

Liam came to play. "Let's build the house," he said. Mia put a flat block down for the floor. It had four sides that were all the same. "This one is a square," said Liam. The square made a good floor for the cat.

Then Liam turned the square a little bit. Now a corner pointed up at the ceiling. "Look," said Liam. "A new shape!"

Mia tilted her head. Was it a new shape? She put her finger on the corner. She turned the block back. The corner pointed down again. It looked just like before. She turned it again. Corner up, corner down. It was still the square! The same block, only turned. "It's not new," said Mia. "It's the same square!"

The square could be a roof, too. Mia turned the square so a corner pointed up. It sat on top of the house like a little hat for the cat. But the block began to slip. The roof slid down. Mia pushed it hard with both hands. Now it stayed. "Roof, stay," she said.

Liam laughed. "The cat can be a cat in the forest," he said. He pushed a green tree block next to the house. Mia pushed one, too. One tree, two trees, three trees. Now it looked like a little forest. The cat went inside. "Meow," said Mia in her cat voice. "Come in, come in. This is your square house."

Jack found his bike in the garage. He wanted to ride it right now. He pushed the bike to the driveway. His dad called out, "Where is your helmet, Jack?"

Jack stopped. He looked at the driveway. Then he looked back at the garage. He ran back and found his helmet on the shelf. He put it on his head. Dad helped him click the strap. "Safe," said Dad. "Now you can ride."

Jack rode up and down. Malak came by with his bike. Malak had no helmet. He started to pedal fast. Dad held up his hand. "Wait, Malak. Get your helmet first." Malak rode home and came back with his helmet on. "Good," said Dad. "Wear a helmet when you ride a bike."

Then the two boys rode side by side. Jack watched his wheels go round and round. Malak laughed. Jack laughed too. "Last one to the gate is it!" shouted Jack.

Isaiah sat at the dinner table. His cup was red. His plate had peas on it. One pea, two peas, three peas.

"Tell us about your day," said Dad.

"I went to the park with Leona," said Isaiah. "Tomorrow was so fun."

Dad smiled. "Do you mean yesterday?"

Isaiah looked at the clock on the wall. The clock said now. Now was dinner time.

"Is yesterday the park day?" asked Isaiah.

"Yes," said Dad. "Yesterday is the day before today. Today is peas day."

Isaiah pushed one pea, two peas, three peas with his fork.

"Can we go to the park today?" he asked.

"Not now," said Dad. "Later we will read a book."

"Tomorrow park?" asked Isaiah.

"Maybe tomorrow," said Dad.

Isaiah ate a pea. He was not shy about peas anymore. He hopped down from his chair and ran to get a book.

Kai was hot at the park. The sun was big and bright. He saw Leif by the picnic table. Leif had a cooler.

"Want an ice cube?" Leif asked. Kai nodded. He took one with his fingers. Ow! The ice cube felt cold on his hand. He dropped it fast into his cup. His fingers turned red.

Ms. Traoré sat at the next table. "My hands are hot too," she said. "I will try that." She held her ice cube and counted. Then she dropped it in her cup too.

Kai listened. The ice went plink in the water. He sniffed his cup. It smelled like nothing at all. He took a small sip. The cold water tasted good.

Then Kai touched the wet table. It was not cold. Only the ice cube was cold. Where did the cold go? He looked in his cup. The ice cube was hiding under a lemon slice. He poked it with his spoon. Still cold! Kai laughed and drank it all up.

Camille went to the grocery store with her dad. She wanted to hold her little bunny. But bunny was gone. "Where is bunny?" Camille asked. She looked in the cart. She saw apples and bread. No bunny.

Camille looked under the lettuce. No bunny. She looked by the milk. No bunny. Then she saw her friend Leena. Leena waved. "I lost bunny," Camille said. Leena helped her look by the eggs. Still no bunny.

Then Camille saw her dad put the same carrots into a bag. The carrots went inside the bag. Camille looked at her coat. Maybe things could hide inside other things. She patted her pocket. There was a soft lump. She pulled it out. It was bunny!

"Bunny was in my pocket!" Camille said. She hugged bunny tight. Dad smiled and gave her the key to the toy coin so she could pretend to shop. At home, Camille helped wash the apples. Bunny sat on the counter, safe and close.

Hazel put on her new red shoes. Today was her first day of school. "Who will play with me?" she asked. Her mom said, "You will find out." Hazel ate her breakfast fast. She did not spill her milk, not even one drop.

At school, Hazel saw the toy corner. She saw the paint pots. Then she saw a boy standing all alone by the blocks. He looked at the floor. Hazel wondered, "What is his name? How can I find out?" She walked over to him. "My name is Hazel," she said. "What is your name?" The boy smiled a big smile. "I am Evander," he said. "Do you want to build with me?"

"Yes!" said Hazel. They stacked the blocks up high. It made a beautiful tall tower. Then it fell down with a crash. They laughed and laughed. "This is fun," said Evander. Hazel held his hand at snack time. She had made a friend, just like that.

Mia was in the kitchen with her mom. A pot sat on the stove. It made a small humming sound. The pot was hot, so Mia stayed back. Her mom poured warm milk into a cup.
