Mia saw something small on the floor. It was by the trash can. It looked like a little box. "What is that?" Mia asked. She did not pick it up. "That is a lighter," her mom said. "Leave it there, please."

Her mom picked it up with one hand. She put it high in a drawer. "Lighters are only for grown-ups," she said. Mia nodded. Small hands must not touch them. That would be wrong.

On the table was a flower in a jar. Mia touched one soft petal. "Can I pour the water?" she asked. "Yes," said her mom. Mia poured a little water into the jar. The flower stood up tall.

Hunter sat at the dinner table. He had a big pile of picture cards. The cards had fallen out of his basket. They were all mixed up. Hunter wanted them in neat piles.

Mom put his coat on the back of his chair. Then she sat down next to him.

Hunter picked up a card. It had a cute little dog on it. "That is an animal," Mom said. Hunter put it in one pile.

He found a cat card next. The cat went with the dog. Both were animals.

Then he found a ball card. It was a toy. He started a new pile for toys. A teddy bear card went in the toy pile too.

Then he found an apple card. "Food," said Hunter. Apples and bananas and cheese all went in the food pile. The food pile made his tummy rumble.

Hunter looked at his three piles. Animals, toys, foods. All neat, all sorted.

Mom smiled. She slid his dinner plate closer. "Here is some real food," she said. Hunter took a big bite of banana and grinned.

Romy ran to school with her curly hair bouncing. Yesterday she could not go to the library. It was closed. Today she wanted a book about the lake near her house.

At school, Madyson was swinging her legs on the bench. "Is today the library day?" Madyson asked.

Mr. Papadopoulos rang the little bell. "Yes, it is today," he said. "Today is now. We walk right now, not later."

Romy jumped up. "Now means we go right away!" she said.

Brock held the door. The children walked to the library.

Romy found a lake book with ducks on it. She hugged it tight. "Tomorrow I can read it again," she said.

"Tomorrow is after today," said Madyson.

Then Romy opened the book. A little paper duck fell out.

"Look!" said Brock. "It can swing on a string!"

Romy smiled and hung it on the window.

Emile sat on his low bed. He held his teddy bear. "Teddy needs a story," Emile said. He had a book about summer. The sun was on the cover. Emile opened the front cover. Then he opened the next page. He put his finger on the page. He began at the right side. He slid his finger that way. The words felt mixed up. He tried again, right to left. Still mixed up. His dad sat down next to him. "Watch me," Dad said. Dad put his finger at the left side. He slid it to the right. "One word, two words, three words," Dad said. Emile tried it too. Left, then right. The words went in a line. Emile counted, "One, two, three." He read about the summer sun. Teddy sat up tall. "Again," said Emile, and turned the page.

Eloise stood at the little sink. She wanted to smell the soap, but her nose felt all stuffy. She could not smell a thing.

Ms. Vogel came over. "Hold this mirror," she said. "Look at your nose. Your nose has two openings. They are called nostrils."

Eloise looked in the mirror. She counted them. "One, two," she said. Two nostrils! She touched them gently with her finger. Then she took a big breath in. The cold air went in both nostrils.

She sniffed the soap. Now she could smell it! It smelled like flowers. "I can smell again," she said.

Mavrick ran over from the window. "I can hear a truck on the street," he said. Eloise used her ears to listen. Rumble, rumble.

At snack time, Eloise tasted a sweet apple. She touched her smooth cup. "My eyes see Mavrick," she said. "My ears hear the truck. My nose smells soap. My tongue tastes apple. My hands touch my cup."

"One, two," said Eloise, pointing at her nostrils. "My nose works again."

Livia wanted to help in the kitchen. Mom was busy at the stove. "The pot is hot," Mom said. "You stay back here." Livia stood far from the hot pot. She could see Mom. Mom could see her.

"I will get the big spoon," Livia said. She ran to the far end of the pantry. It was dark back there. Livia looked out. She could not see Mom. "Mom?" she called. Mom did not answer. Livia did not like the far end. She hurried back fast. Then Mom could see her. And Livia could see Mom.

"I like it here," Livia said. Mom gave her a brush. "Brush the crumbs off the table," said Mom. Livia brushed. The crumbs went slide, slide, into her hand. "Good helper," said Mom. Livia smiled and brushed some more.

Eleanor went to the store with her dad. She wanted soup for lunch. The big cart was slow. The small basket was fast. Eleanor carried the small basket.

In the store, the freezer was cold. The soup shelf was far away. The soup can was big and heavy. Eleanor used two hands.

Then Eleanor saw Aarav from school. He had a salty soup can too. They walked to the freezer aisle. A puddle sat on the floor. Eleanor stepped in it. Her sock got wet.

"My sock is wet," said Eleanor.

"My sock is dry," said Aarav. "Wet and dry are opposites."

Eleanor found the socks shelf. She picked new socks. Her dad paid at the till. Eleanor sat on the bench and pulled them on. One sock on, then the other.

"Ahh," said Eleanor. "Dry toes."

Hazel was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a small box for her. "This is for you," said Grandma. Hazel opened it fast. Inside was a red hat with a white pompom.

Hazel put the hat on. She ran to the mirror. "Not ugly at all!" she said. She spun around and around. Then she ran outside to show Madden, her friend from next door.

Madden looked at the hat. "Grandma gave you that?" he asked. Hazel nodded. "Was it a present?" he asked. Hazel nodded again. Then she stopped. She had not said the magic word to Grandma. Her mother had taught it to her. You say it when someone gives you something. Hazel ran back inside. Grandma was washing cups at the sink. Hazel waited by the door until Grandma looked up. "Thank you for my hat," said Hazel. Grandma smiled big. She gave Hazel a hug. "You are so welcome," said Grandma. Hazel held the pompom and smiled too.

Wren went to the park with her dad. She wore her yellow hat. It was a sunny morning.

"Where is the sun going?" she asked.

"Clouds can hide the sun," said her dad.

Wren looked up. A big cloud moved in. The sun was gone. The sky turned gray. Wind began to blow. Wren's hat tried to fly away. She held it with both hands.

Then rain fell. "Rain!" said Wren. Her dad put up her coat hood. They ran to the cozy play house. Harvey and Alie were inside. They shared dry crackers.

Soon the cloud moved past. The sun came back. It made the wet slide shine. A little seed pod blew in the wind. Wren picked it up.

"Is the rain done?" she asked.

"Yes, the sun is out now," said Alie.

Wren and Harvey skipped around the swings. Wren held her seed pod tight. The sunny park felt warm again.

Charlie sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a pencil in his hand. "Let's write your name," she said. "C for Charlie." Charlie held the pencil in his fist. He pushed it hard on the paper. The C came out wobbly and dark. "Sorry, C," Charlie said. He wanted a nice C, not a wobbly one.

Mom turned the pencil around. "Try the pink end," she said. "It is an eraser." Charlie rubbed the pink end on the wobbly C. He rubbed and rubbed. The wobbly C went away! The paper was clean again. Charlie's eyes got big. The wobbly mark was gone.

"Now one finger, one finger, one thumb," Mom said. She helped Charlie hold the pencil with his fingers, not his fist. Charlie looked at the clock on the wall. "Can I try again before the big hand moves?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "You have time."

Charlie drew a new C. This time he pressed softly. The C sat on the paper, round and neat. "C," said Charlie. "One letter down." He laughed. Mom clapped her hands. Charlie rubbed the paper where the old C had been. It was smooth and empty.

"Next is H," said Mom. Charlie counted on his fingers. "C, H, A, R, L, I, E. Six more!" He picked up the pencil again. "Wait for me, H," he said. "Here I come."

Today was Xavier's birthday. He was four years old. The party was at the bowling alley. His friends Martin and Sloan came too. They rolled big heavy balls down the lane. The pins went crash, crash, crash.

After bowling, it was time for cake. The cake had four candles on top. Xavier wanted to light them himself. He reached for the matches on the table. "Not yet," said Dad. He took the matches. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job. Your job is the wish." Dad lit each candle. One, two, three, four little flames.

Xavier knew just what to do. He took a big breath. He blew and blew. All four flames went out. Then Dad handed him something. It was a small wrapped box. "One more candle," said Dad. "For you, next year." Xavier laughed. "Next year, you light it, Dad."

Ibrahim sat at the kitchen table. He had a plate of crackers. He wanted to build a cracker house.

"The square crackers go on top," he said. But he was not sure. Were they really squares?

He found a piece of string in the toy box. He laid it along one side of a cracker. He held the string with his thumb. Then he laid it on the next side. It matched! He patted his knee. "Same!" he said.

He checked the third side. Same. He checked the fourth side. Same too. "Four sides, all the same," said Ibrahim. "It IS a square!"

Shea came over to play. "That's not a square," said Shea. "It's a rectangle."

Ibrahim held up his string. "Look," he said. He measured the sides. One side was short. One side was long. "You're right! That one is a rectangle."

Then Shea laughed. "Look at the round one!"

Ibrahim picked up the round cracker. He put his string around the edge. It went all the way around, like a hoop. "That's a circle," said Ibrahim. "It can be a window!"

The boys built the cracker house. The squares were the walls. The circles were the windows. The rectangle was the door.

Ibrahim took one triangle chip from his bowl. "A roof!" he said.

Then his dad came in. "Is my snack a toy?" he asked.

Ibrahim giggled. "It's a house! Are you ready to eat it?"

"Yes," said Dad, and he took the biggest bite of all.

text:
Luna was in the kitchen with her father. Music was playing on the little speaker. "I want to clap!" said Luna. Her father smiled. "Let's find the beat," he said.

Luna clapped and clapped. The song went fast, then slow, then fast. Her hands got sore. "My hands are tired," she said. She stopped clapping and the beat went missing.

Then Luna looked down at her feet. She stamped one foot. Boom. Then the other foot. Boom. It fit the song! "You can stamp the beat!" she said. Her father tapped his knees too. Boom, boom, boom. Luna tapped her knees, then stamped her feet, then clapped again when her hands felt better.

Then Luna sang her rhyme from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," she sang. She stamped the beat the whole way through. Her father read the words from a card, but Luna did not need it. She stomped and sang to the very last line. "How I wonder what you are!"

Margot wanted to make paper cookies for her kitchen. She pulled out the paper basket. She found a red square. She found a yellow triangle. She found a blue rectangle. "Cookies need to be circles," said Margot. "Round ones."

She found a green circle. She wanted to cut it into two small cookies. Mom held the scissors. Mom said, "Show me where to start." Margot ran her finger along the edge. It curved this way. It curved that way. "I need a corner," said Margot. She looked again. She looked one more time. "Mom, there is no corner! It is round all over!" Mom smiled a gentle smile. "Then I will start anywhere," she said. Snip, snip. Two little round cookies.

Margot set them on a plate. Square cookie, triangle cookie, rectangle cookie, circle cookie, circle cookie. She counted them all. Five cookies. The kitchen smelled like real bread, and outside the night was dark and quiet. Margot held up a circle cookie and said, "Round all over, no corners at all."

Alexis went to the park with Dad. The sun was warm. Alexis held Dad's hand on the path. Ember was there, playing by the sand. "Watch me run," Ember said. Ember ran fast, fast, fast. Alexis laughed. It was not a joke. Ember really could run that fast.

Then Alexis saw a butterfly. It flew near the little park shop. Alexis followed it. He looked up. He could not see Dad. Alexis felt his tummy go tight. He saw the shop worker at the counter. "If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up," Dad had said. Alexis walked to the counter.

"I can't find my dad," Alexis said. "I will help you," the worker said. She took his hand gently. They stood by the counter together. Then Alexis heard, "Alexis!" It was Dad. He had been by the water fountain all along. Alexis ran to him and held on tight. "Let's go see Ember again," Dad said. Alexis took Dad's hand and did not let go.

Arthur held his dad's hand and climbed onto the city bus. The bus was big and warm. Through the window he saw a red car go by. They rode past the bakery and the park. "Are we getting my library card today?" Arthur asked. "Yes," said his dad. "You get to pick a book too."

The bus stopped near the library. Inside, the library was very quiet. Arthur saw a man reading a big newspaper. He saw a girl doing a puzzle. Then he found a shelf with dinosaur books. "DINOSAURS!" he shouted. He was so happy.

The man looked up from his newspaper. The girl looked up too. A lady put her finger near her lips. Arthur's dad bent down. "Many libraries ask people to use quiet voices," he whispered, "so others can read."

Arthur looked around. Everyone was reading. "Why do they whisper here?" he asked. His dad smiled. "So the readers can keep reading," he whispered back. Arthur nodded. "I can whisper," he said, very softly.

At the desk, Ms. Schneider made Arthur's very first library card. It had his name on it. He picked the dinosaur book to take home. "Don't spill juice on it," said Ms. Schneider with a wink. On the bus ride home, Arthur held the book tight. He whispered to his dad, "Rawr."

Scarlett ran into the library with her mom. Story time was her favorite. She wanted the book about the little red truck.

"Is it time for story time now?" Scarlett asked.

"Not yet," said her mom. "It starts later. First we find books."

Scarlett found the truck book. She found a book about a messy dog, too. Marina was there with her dad. Marina wanted the dog book, so Scarlett let her hold it first.

"Is it time now?" Scarlett asked again.

Her mom pointed at the big clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is," she said. "When the short hand points to the ten, it is time."

Scarlett watched the clock. The hands did not zip around. They moved slowly, slowly. She turned pages while she watched.

Then the short hand reached the ten. A bell rang. Ms. Mori sat down on the story rug.

"It is time now!" said Scarlett.

"Yes," said her mom. "You watched the clock. Now we go."

Scarlett sat next to Marina. Ms. Mori read about a train that went chugga chugga. Scarlett listened with her mouth open.

"When can we come back?" she asked after.

"Yesterday we could not come," said her mom. "Today we came. Tomorrow we can come again."

"Tomorrow," said Scarlett. She held the truck book tight. At the desk, the librarian stamped it. Scarlett carried it home with both hands.

William ran into the big gym at the community center. It was his turn to kick the ball. Rio and Violet stood on his team. Mr. Teo held the ball still.

William kicked. The ball went past the net. He missed. He stood alone by the wall. His face felt hot.

Then Rio clapped. "Good try! Try again!" Violet clapped too. "You can do it!"

William looked up. "You cheer for me? Even when I miss?"

"Yes," said Rio. "That is what teammates do."

So William ran back. He waited. He heard the gym hum and the floor squeak. Then he kicked hard. The ball flew into the net, like a paper plane in the wind. The whole team cheered loud.

Jordan wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint! Jordan looked in the cup. Red. Blue. Yellow. Green. No orange at all.

"Watch this," said his friend Oliver. Oliver dipped his brush in the red paint. Then he dipped it in the yellow paint. He stirred and stirred. The paint turned orange!

Jordan gasped. "It's orange now!" he said. He grabbed his own brush fast. He put red in his cup. He put yellow in too. He stirred with his pencil to mix it all up. Orange! Orange! Orange!

Jordan painted his pumpkin orange. Mr. Gauthier came to see. "What a big orange pumpkin!" he said. Jordan lifted the pumpkin up high. "I made the orange myself!"

Ibrahim sat at Grandma's big table. The room smelled like warm bread. Outside, the sky was turning dark. Grandma put a paper in front of him. It had his name on it, but the letters were made of little dots.

"Those are dotted letters," said Grandma. "You can trace over them with your pencil."

Ibrahim held his pencil in his fist. He tried to trace the first letter. It came out wobbly and too big. Grandma smiled. "Try holding it like this." She showed him her fingers. She pinched the pencil near the tip, like a little bird on a stick.

Ibrahim copied her fingers. He traced the dot of the first letter. Then the second. His pencil made a soft scratchy sound on the paper. The wobbly line got smaller. Then it got straight. The letter looked real.

He traced all the letters. He drank some juice from his cup. Then he wrote his name again on a clean paper, all by himself. He held the paper up high. "I did it, Grandma! It says Ibrahim!"

Grandma clapped her hands and pinned the paper to the fridge with a magnet.

Isla wanted to see the pot bubble. Her dad put the pot on the stove. Then the water began to hum. "Can I guess what is inside?" Isla asked. "Just water," said her dad. White puffs rose up from the pot. They curled like little clouds. Isla stepped closer to peek. Her dad held out his hand. "Stay back," he said. "The steam is hot. It can burn you." Isla stopped. She stood by the door, far from the stove. The steam rose higher and higher. It faded before it touched the roof. "Wow," said Isla. "It goes up so fast!" Her dad smiled. He stirred the pot with a big spoon. Isla watched the bubbles pop and roll. They were round and small. She clapped her hands. Then her dad turned off the stove. He poured pasta into a strainer. Isla helped by holding the bread bag. She pulled out two soft slices. "The steam went away," she said. Her dad nodded. "It will come back next time we cook." Isla wondered where the steam would go. "Can we watch again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "You can be my young helper. You stand right there, and you watch." Isla stood very still. The pot sat quiet and cool now. "All done," she said, and patted the counter gently.

Emile ran to the playground. The sun made the slide hot. His dad touched it first. "Too hot, wait a bit," Dad said. So Emile waited. Then the slide felt warm, and down he went.

Emile poured sand from his cup into a bucket. One cup, two cups, three cups. Nihal poured sand too. "My bucket is full," said Emile. "Mine too," said Nihal.

Then Emile saw something on the picnic table. Little pink dots, like candy. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." He did not touch them. "Dad, come look," he called. Dad came fast. "Those are not candy," said Dad. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." He picked up the pink dots and put them in his pocket.

"Good looking, Emile," said Nihal. Emile smiled and ran back to the slide. "One, two, three," he counted, and down he went again.

Nolan woke up and saw white. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on the cars. No school today!

"Snow day!" said Nolan. He rang his bell by the window. Ding, ding, ding!

Then he saw it. A big yellow truck came down the street. It had a big blade in front. It pushed the snow off the road. The snow went whoosh to the side. Now the road was black and clear.

Nolan ran to tell the neighbor, Mr. Tesfaye. "The road is clear!" said Nolan. "The truck pushed the snow away!"

So Nolan and Mr. Tesfaye could walk to the park. It was not easy walking in the deep snow. They stepped high, like big birds.

At the park, an owl sat on a branch. Snow was piled on its head like a little hat. It blinked. Then it flew off, and its snow hat fell down.

"Look out!" laughed Mr. Tesfaye.

Plop! The snow landed on Nolan's nose.

Carter got a new kitten today. He named her Spring because she liked to jump. The vet, Ms. Charles, checked Spring's ears. "She is healthy," said Ms. Charles. Then Carter and his dad took Spring home.

The next morning, Carter ran to Spring. She was licking her empty bowl. "Dad! Spring has no water!" Carter filled a cup at the sink. He poured it into the bowl. Spring drank and drank. Her tummy went up and down.

Now Carter looks at the bowl every day. If it is empty, he fills it up. If the water looks old, his dad helps him pour it out. They add fresh, clean water. Spring laps it all up. Then she crawls into Carter's lap and falls asleep. "Nice kitty," Carter whispers.

Joshua loves snack time at school. Today Ms. Boateng has red apples. "Yum!" says Joshua. "Can I have one now?"

"First we wash our hands," says Ms. Boateng.

Joshua goes to the little sink. He turns on the water. It feels cool on his fingers. He holds the soap under the water. Nothing happens. No bubbles yet.

Then he rubs the soap with his hands. Rub, rub, rub. Bubbles pop up! One bubble, two bubbles, so many bubbles!

Aliyah stands next to him. "How did you get all those?" she asks.

"I rubbed the soap with water," says Joshua. He makes a bubbly soap beard on his chin. He giggles. Aliyah giggles too. "That is a cute beard," she says.

They rinse their hands clean. Then Joshua takes his big bite of apple. Crunch!

Rose had a cold. Her nose ran and ran. Mom said, "We need more tissues. Let's go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy the lights were bright. Rose sat in the cart. The aisles were tall and full. Rose saw one, two, three boxes of tissues. Mom put a box in the cart. Rose held her stuffed bunny tight. At the desk, the cashier gave Rose a sticker. It was a little yellow duck.

At home, Rose felt sneezy. She took a tissue. She blew her nose. Ah-tchoo! The tissue got full. Then Mom set out crackers for a snack.

Rose reached for a cracker. Then she stopped. She looked at her hands. Mom was baking bread, and her own hands were soapy at the sink. Rose said, "My turn too." She pushed a chair near the sink. Mom helped her up. Rose washed her hands with soap and water. She counted the bubbles. One bubble, two bubbles, three bubbles, splash!

Then her hands were clean and warm. Rose ate her cracker. Outside the window the sky was turning dark. On the fridge hung a map Rose had drawn with crayons. Mom said, "After snack, we can look at your map." Rose smiled and took another cracker. She gave bunny a pat on the head.

Max had a big pot on the balcony. It was full of brown soil. He pushed three little seeds down into it. "Grow, grow, grow!" he said.

Every morning Max ran outside. He gave the soil a little water. One day, a tiny green leaf popped up. Max wanted to yell to the whole town, "My plant is here!"

Then Max saw a weed next to his plant. It had little leaves too. He pulled it gently. Out it came, and something long hung from the bottom. Strings, lots of strings, with soil stuck on them.

"What are these?" Max asked. His dad looked and smiled. "Roots," he said. "They grow down into the soil." Max looked at his pot. His plant had roots too, down there in the dark.

Max waited and waited. Then came a red tomato. He picked it. It was warm and hot from the sun. Max held it up high. "Esmee! Look what grew!"

Isabelle loved the big beach. She loved the sand and the waves. Next to the beach was a small pool. Today Isabelle would learn to swim there.

She put on her short swimsuit. It had a crayon print all over it. Blue crayons, red crayons, yellow crayons. "One, two, three colors," she counted. Then she ran to the pool. She wanted to jump right in.

A coach stopped her at the door. "Not yet," he said. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." Isabelle looked up. A shower? At the pool? She wondered who used it.

She stood under the shower. Water ran down her arms. Drip, drip, drip. Then the coach said, "Now you can go in." Isabelle stepped into the pool. The water felt cool. She kicked her legs. Splash, splash, splash. Her friend Sydney laughed. "You made a big splash!" Sydney said.

Isabelle noticed something. When she got out, she saw Bowie run to the pool. "One, two, three steps to the water," Isabelle counted. But Bowie stopped at the shower first. The water ran on him. Then he got in the pool too.

So that was how it worked. Shower first, then pool. Isabelle smiled. She held the wall and kicked again. "Look at me, Sydney!" she called.

Olivia stood in the pool changing room. The floor was wet. One shoe, two shoes, off they came. "Swim time!" she said.

Collins ran past her fast. "Wait for me!" he called. Then his feet slid. Whoosh! He wobbled and put his hands out. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya caught his arm. "The wet floor is slippery," she said. "We walk by the pool."

Olivia looked down at her toes. The floor was shiny with water. She took one slow step, then another. Walk, walk, walk. Her feet did not slide one bit. "I am walking," she said.

Hoorain held her hand and they walked together. One step, two steps, three steps, splash went a puddle under their feet. They both laughed. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya smiled. "Smart walkers," she said.

At the pool, Mom was waiting with a towel. The water was warm and blue. Olivia's hair got wet when she jumped in. She kicked and splashed. "I did it!" she said. Mom clapped and held out the big soft towel. "Swim time again tomorrow," said Olivia.

Parker came home with a small puppy. The puppy had soft brown fur. Parker named him Buddy.

Then Buddy wiggled out the door. He ran across the yard. Parker called and called. Buddy did not come back. Parker felt like crying.

His dad said, "Let's check his collar." Buddy had a tag on his collar. His dad read the tag out loud. It said their phone number. A neighbour found Buddy down the street. She saw the tag. She called the number. Parker and his dad ran to get Buddy.

Parker hugged Buddy tight. "Your tag helped you come home," Parker said. Now Parker held Buddy's leash every day. He filled the water bowl. He gave Buddy soft pats. Parker was a proud big helper. At night, Buddy slept in his new bed. Parker whispered, "Good night, Buddy." Buddy wagged his little tail.

Romy ran onto the basketball court. It was game day! Her whole team was there. Tamara waved. Margaret waved too.

Then the coach said, "Time for batting practice!" She put a tee on the court. Romy ran fast to take her turn. She grabbed the bat. She was so excited!

"Wait!" said the coach. "You need your helmet." She held it out. "It protects your head." Romy put it on. It was a little big. It slipped over one eye. Romy laughed and pushed it back.

She swung the bat. Ping! The ball flew far. It went past Tamara. It went past Margaret. It went right through the coach's open window of her arms. Everyone cheered.

Romy took off the helmet and hugged it. "My helmet helped me!" she said.

The coach smiled. "Same time next week," she said. "Helmet first."

Emma ran to Maxence's house in the car with her mom. Maxence waved from the door. "Breakfast time!" he said.

Maxence's dad made warm toast. He put the toast on Emma's plate. Emma picked up her knife. "I want to do the butter," she said. Her mom said, "I will help hold the knife."

Emma pushed the butter across the toast. It was hard work. Then she stopped. "Look!" she said. "The butter is going away!" The butter had turned shiny. It slid into the warm toast. It melted like snow in the sun. Emma gasped. Maxence leaned close. "It is gone," he said. "No," said Emma. "Look. It is all shiny now."

Next came the milk. Emma held the cup with two hands. She poured slowly, slowly. A drop ran down the side. She wiped it with her finger. The cup stayed full. "I did it!" she said. Maxence clapped. Emma bit her toast. It tasted warm and buttery. "Yum," she said. "More toast, please!"

Margot built a quiet cave under the play table. She put in one big blanket, two small pillows, and a paper map. "This is a bear cave," she said. She crawled in.

The cave was dark. Margot blinked. "Is it morning?" she asked herself. "No. It is still night." She snuggled like a sleepy bear.

Then the lights went on. The cave turned bright. Margot crawled out fast. Bellamy was clapping. "You were slow, sleepy bear," he said. "I am fast bear," said Eesa, and she zipped around the table.

Ms. Pérez brought warm cups. "Careful, this is hot," she said. Margot touched her cold water cup instead. "Big cup, small cup," said Ms. Pérez. She looked out the window. "Look, Margot. The sun is up. The night is gone. Day and night are opposites."

Margot looked at the dark cave. Then she looked at the bright room. She ran back to the cave and pulled the blanket over her head. "Now it is night again," she whispered. One, two, three, and the lights went out for nap time.

Willow wanted to have a tea party. But the teapot was empty. No tea inside at all.

She looked at her teddy bear. "Do you want tea?" she asked. Teddy sat very still. Willow held the teapot up high. She tipped it over a cup. Nothing came out. The cup stayed empty.

Then Willow had an idea. She poured again. "Here is your tea!" she said. The cup was still empty. But it was pretend tea now. She gave Teddy the cup. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" she said. Teddy drank it all up.

Jeremiah came to the backyard. "Where is the real tea?" he asked. Willow showed him the empty cup. "There is no real tea," she said. "The cups are empty. But pretend tea works too!" Jeremiah smiled. He brought his toy dinosaur to the table.

Willow tucked her doll in tight, like a baby in bed. The doll needed tea too. Willow poured. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" she said again. Jeremiah poured for the dinosaur. "Slurp!" he said.

The whole table was full of empty cups. Everyone drank pretend tea. Willow held up her own cup. "More tea, please!" she said.

Felix loved the water table at school. Today Mr. Byrne filled it for a doll bath. Felix ran over fast. "In you go, dolly!" he said.

"Wait," said Mr. Byrne. He put his hand in the water. "The water is too hot right now." Felix looked at his own hand. His fingers wanted to splash. But he stopped and waited. Mr. Byrne turned the tap. Cool water ran in. The tap made the water change, and the steam went away. Mr. Byrne put his hand in again. "Now it is just right," he said.

Felix lifted his doll wide in both arms. "Bath time!" he said. He washed the doll's arms and toes. Corbin brought a towel. The doll got dry and warm. "Time for snack," said Mr. Byrne. Felix patted the doll's head. "You eat after your bath," he told her, and off they went.

The big piano sat on the stage. Zoe walked up to it early that day. Mr. Kapoor smiled. "You can learn one song," he said. Zoe pressed a key. It made a low, growly sound. "A bear!" she said.

Dimitri ran up. "I want to make a little bird," he said. "Chirp, chirp!" He pressed a key on the left. The sound was low and grumpy. "That is a bear bird," Zoe said. They both laughed.

Zoe tapped keys on the right. Those keys made high, tiny sounds. "Birds live here," she said. Dimitri tapped the right side too. Chirp! Chirp! "Now my turn," Zoe said. She played a low bear on the left. Then she played a high bird on the right. Mr. Kapoor clapped from his chair. "Play them both," said Dimitri. Zoe's fingers ran from the bear to the bird.

It was a rainy day. Julia sat by the window. She had her favorite book on her lap. She opened the front cover first. Then she turned the pages one by one.

"I love the bunny pictures," said Julia. "Who drew them?" Her dad was making lunch nearby. "Let's look," he said. He kept stirring the pot.

Julia turned back to the first page. She saw little black marks there. "Dad, these marks say something," she said. Her dad came to look. He pointed. "That says the artist's name," he said. "The person who paints the pictures for a book is called an illustrator." Julia ran her finger under the name. "I want to paint bunnies too," she said.

After lunch, Julia got her crayons. She made her own book. She drew a cover page first. Then she drew the bunny, the rain, and a big red house. She copied some wiggly marks too. Her dad read her marks out loud. "It says Julia!" Julia kissed the page. "My book is done!" she said. She turned the pages from front to back, slowly, one more time.

Paisley wanted cold milk. She went to the big fridge. She pulled the door. The door was open. Cold air came out on her nose.

She poured her small cup. It was full. Then she forgot the door. It stayed open. The duck toy on the floor looked at the fridge.

Her dad came in. "The fridge is open," he said. "Open and shut are opposites." He helped her push it. Click. Now it was shut.

Paisley ran to the window. She wanted to see the fast birds. She saw a slow duck in the yard. "Hello, duck!" she said. The duck did not spin around. It walked slow, slow, slow.

Paisley went back to the fridge. She pulled the door. Open. She looked. She pushed it. Shut. "Open," she said. "Shut." She did it again. It was like a game.

Then she drank her milk. It was still cold. "Yum," said Paisley. She gave the fridge a little pat.

Lucas could see the park. The swings were across the street. He wanted to swing so much.

"Hold my hand," said his dad. Lucas took his dad's big hand. They looked left. They looked right. Then they walked across the street together. They did it again at the next street. Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street. Lucas held on tight.

At the park, Lucas saw his friend Jimmy. Jimmy was by the slide. Lucas ran to him. "Want to swing?" asked Jimmy. "Yes!" said Lucas. They patted the slide first. It was hot from the sun. "Ouch," said Jimmy. He did not slide down. Ms. Luo, the neighbour, was watering a tree nearby. "The water is cold," she said. Jimmy put his hand under the water. The cold water made the hot slide feel better.

Lucas and Jimmy walked to the swings. Lucas looked back. His dad sat on a bench under the tree. Lucas waved. Dad waved back. "Watch me!" said Lucas. Dad gave a thumbs up. Lucas pumped his legs. He went higher and higher. "That is true swinging!" said Jimmy. Lucas laughed and swung some more. "Again!" he called.

Natalie sat in the waiting room. Today she would see the dentist for the first time. She bounced her feet. She looked at the fish tank. One fish, two fish, three fish, four fish, five fish.

Monica from her class sat down next to her. "I saw the dentist before," said Monica. "She looked at all my teeth." Natalie frowned. "But how can she see the back of my teeth?" she asked. "My teeth are in a line. Nobody can see behind them." Monica shrugged. Natalie thought and thought.

The door opened. "Natalie," said the dentist. Natalie held her mom's hand. She climbed into the big chair. "Open wide," said the dentist. Then Natalie saw it. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. She put it in Natalie's mouth. In the mirror, Natalie saw the backs of her own teeth! "I can see them!" she said.

Afterward, the dentist let Natalie hold the little mirror. Natalie showed it to Monica in the waiting room. "The dentist uses a tiny mirror on a handle," said Natalie. "She sees the backs of your teeth with it." Monica looked in the mirror too. "Quick, my turn next," said Monica. The two girls giggled all the way to the car.

Alexis had a big red drum. He wanted to play it for his friends in the playroom. Lilia was there. Jenna was there. Ms. Njoroge was there too. "One, two, three, boom!" said Alexis. He banged the drum. It was very loud.

Then Ms. Njoroge put a finger to her lips. "Shh," she said. "It is naptime. The babies are sleeping next door." The playroom went still. The tick-tock clock sounded small. The sun made a warm square on the rug. Even the wild sock monkey on the shelf looked sleepy.

Alexis wanted to play his drum. But the babies would wake up. What could he do? He tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. That was quiet. The babies did not wake up. He banged it again. BOOM. That was loud. Ms. Njoroge shook her head fast.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Lilia, smiling. Alexis tapped again, soft as a fork tapping a plate at dinner. Tap, tap, tap. Jenna lay down on the rug. Lilia closed her eyes. Alexis played his quiet song all the way to the end.

"Nice drumming," whispered Ms. Njoroge. Alexis patted the drum two times, very gently. "Good night, drum," he whispered back.

Isaiah stood in the restaurant kitchen. His dad worked there, making fresh toast. "Can I help?" Isaiah asked. "Yes," said Dad. "One, two, three things to do."

First, Isaiah put butter on warm toast. He spread it slow, slow, slow. The butter went shiny and smooth.

Next came the milk. Isaiah picked up the big carton. It was heavy. It tipped and dripped. Milk went on the floor.

"Too big for me?" Isaiah asked.

Dad poured some milk into a small jug. "Try this one."

Isaiah held the little jug. He poured. The milk went into the cup, not one drip on the floor. He poured a second cup, then a third.

"That one is just right," said Isaiah. He put the jug down and took a big bite of his buttery toast.

Athena wanted a story. Grandpa sat on the big chair. He picked up her book about a red bike.

"Hold on," said Grandpa. He reached for his glasses. He put them on his nose. His eyes looked bigger behind them.

Athena looked with her eyes. What did the glasses do? She heard the pages turn with her ears. She sniffed the book with her nose. It smelled like paper, not like the yucky sock on the floor. She touched the shiny glasses with one finger. They felt smooth and cool.

Grandpa read without the glasses first. The words looked fuzzy to him. Then he put them on. Now he could see each word. He read all about the bike.

"Now I see it," Athena said. "The glasses help your eyes see the words!"

"Yes," said Grandpa. "Now hop up and we will share the last page together."

Emily wanted to make an animal parade in the playroom. She put her toy dog on the carpet. She put her toy cow next to the dog. They were both animals.

Then Emily found a toy fish. It was small and orange. She held it and frowned. The dog had legs. The cow had legs. The fish had no legs at all.

"Fish can't go in the parade," Emily said. "It has no legs."

Her friend Nawab sat down beside her. "Put it in," he said. "Please? My fish is scared to be alone."

Emily looked at the fish. She looked at her picture book. The book had a page of animals. She turned the pages with Nawab. There was a dog. There was a cow. And there, on the same page, was a fish!

"Fish are animals too!" Emily said.

She set the fish down between the dog and the cow. Then she got a little bowl of water. She let the fish float there so it would not sink to the bottom of the toy box.

"Look, Nawab," she said. "The whole parade is animals. Even the fish."

Nawab clapped his hands. Ms. Tran peeked in from the door and smiled at the long line of animals on the carpet.

"Wag your tail, dog," said Emily. "Swim fast, fish. The parade can go now!"

Beau went to the bookshop with his dad. A big letter A was on the wall. It was red and tall. "A," said Beau. "That is the first letter!"

Then Beau found a little book about cars. He opened it. The first page said "a" in small letters. Beau frowned. "That is not A," he said. "A is big. This one is little."

Mr. Jung came over. He was the bookshop man. "Show me," he said. Beau pointed at the big red A. Then he pointed at the small a in the book. "Two different letters," said Beau.

Mr. Jung smiled. "Big A, small a," he said. "Same letter." Beau looked and looked. He put his finger on the big A. He put his finger on the small a. Round top, little tail. Round top, little tail. "Same!" said Beau.

Beau found more letters. Big B, small b. Big C, small c. He said each sound out loud. "Buh, buh, book!" His dad sat on a soft chair and waited. Beau was tired, but he kept going.

At last Beau picked a book about a dog that could chase a ball. "D," said Beau. "Duh, duh, dog!" He hugged the book. "Can we read it in the car?" he asked. His dad laughed. "Yes," he said. "Let's go."

Ella held up her monkey book. "Read it, Dad!"

Dad sat on her clean, soft bed. He opened the front cover. He turned page one, then page two. He read about a little monkey who did not want to sleep.

Ella laughed. The monkey jumped on the bed. Boing, boing!

Then Dad said goodnight. Mom came in. Ella held up the same book. "Read it too!"

Mom sat down. She opened the front cover. She turned the pages the same way. She read the very same words. "The little monkey jumped on the bed. Boing, boing!"

Ella sat up. "Mom! Dad said that too!"

"Yes," said Mom. "The words on the page say that."

Ella looked at the little black marks. They sat on the page like tiny ants. "The marks say boing?"

"They say boing every time," said Mom. "Dad reads them. I read them. The words stay the same."

Ella pointed at a page. "Read this part again. I will say it too."

Mom read, "The monkey yawned a big yawn."

Ella said it with her. Then Ella turned the page all by herself, front to back, looking for the sleepy part.

"Last page," said Ella. "Now the monkey sleeps."

She patted the book. "Same words tomorrow?"

"Same words tomorrow," said Mom, and turned off the light.

Axel woke up at Grandpa's house. His hair felt funny on top. He ran to the mirror. His hair was full of tangles, like a little bird's nest. "Guess I have a problem," he said. Grandpa laughed softly. He handed Axel a small comb. "Go slow," said Grandpa.

Axel combed one piece at a time. He went slow so it would not pull. Ouch, a little. Then not at all. The tangle came out. He combed the next piece. That tangle came out too. Soon his hair was smooth and soft. He touched it with his hand. "The tangles are all gone!" he said.

"Are they really gone?" Grandpa asked. "Yes, look!" said Axel. Grandpa nodded and got Axel's shirt. Axel pulled it on over his smooth hair. Then they went to the kitchen for warm porridge. Grandpa stirred the pot. Axel carried the spoons. "Tomorrow, can I comb it myself again?" asked Axel. "You sure can," said Grandpa.

The sun came out after breakfast. "It is sunny," said Josephine. She put on her short red coat and went to the backyard.

The wind began to blow. Whoosh, whoosh. The wind made the leaves spin. "It is windy," said Josephine. Her hat flew off. She ran and caught it.

Then the sky turned gray. Drip, drop, drip. "It is rainy," said Josephine. She hid under the big tree. One raindrop, two raindrops, three raindrops fell on her nose.

After lunch, the rain stopped. White flakes came down instead. One flake, two flakes, three flakes, four. "Snowy!" Josephine shouted. Her friend Chloe came over. "Let's make snowballs," said Chloe.

Josephine made a snowball with her bare hands. "One snowball," she said. Then her hands got cold. Very cold. Chloe opened her bag. "My mittens keep my hands warm," said Chloe. She lent Josephine one mitten. Josephine put it on. Her hand felt warm again.

Josephine picked up the snowball. She tossed it gently to Chloe. Chloe laughed and tossed it back. Josephine counted the mittens in the bag. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Bring them all next time!"

Maya stood by the big window at home. The sun was out. "Sunny day," said Maya. She put on her sun hat.

Then the trees began to sway. The wind whooshed. "Windy!" said Maya. The wind blew and blew. Her hat flew right off her head!

Maya chased her hat. It rolled past the chair. It rolled past the cow toy. "Come back, hat!" she called. Her dad caught it at the door. "Good running, Maya," he said.

Outside, the sky turned gray. Rain went drip, drip, drip. Maya put on her rain boots. Splash, splash! One splash, two splashes, three splashes!

Later the rain turned to snow. Soft white snow fell down. Maya wore her warm mittens. She yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy," she said.

She hugged her hat tight. "No more wind, hat." The wind went whoosh again. Maya held on tight. The hat stayed put!

Muhammad was playing at daycare. He ran to the big red wall with chalk. His friend Ryan ran too. Ryan wanted to draw a sun.

Then Ryan tripped. He fell down on the floor. His chalk hit the ground. Ryan began to cry.

Muhammad felt scared for a second. He looked at Ms. Yilmaz. She nodded at him. Muhammad walked over to Ryan. He bent down low. "Are you okay?" he asked.

Ryan stopped crying a little. "My knee hurts," he said. Muhammad helped him stand up. They went to Ms. Yilmaz together. She looked at Ryan's knee. "It is just a small bump," she said. She gave Ryan a sweet sticker shaped like a star.

Ryan smiled a big smile. Muhammad felt happy. Ryan felt excited to show his sticker to Mylan.

Then Muhammad picked up the fallen chalk. He did not let the paper wrapper rip. He handed the chalk back to Ryan.

"Want to draw the sun now?" asked Muhammad. "Yes!" said Ryan. They drew a big yellow sun together on the red wall. "You are a good friend," said Ryan. Muhammad grinned and drew a cloud next to the sun.

Milo sat in the family car. The car went beep, toot, vroom. Milo was going on a trip. "We ride, we ride, we ride away," he sang.

The car stopped at the airport. It was big and bright. Milo saw the planes out the window. "Big planes!" he did not yell. But he wanted to run. He took one step. The crowd was thick like a herd of elephants. So many legs, so many bags.

Then Milo remembered. In busy places, he held a grown-up's hand. He reached up and took his dad's hand. Dad smiled. They walked together, one, two, three, holding hands. They walked past the bags. They walked past the desks. They walked all the way to the big window.

"We ride, we ride, we ride away," said Milo.

"Not yet," said Dad. "First, we wait for our plane."

A bright red plane rolled in. Milo squeezed Dad's hand and pointed. "That one!"

David put on his red shirt. It was his soccer shirt. Today was his first game at the community center.

"Kick the ball into the net," said Jayson. "That is how you score a goal."

David ran onto the grass. The grass was quiet and soft. Then the game got loud. The coach blew the whistle. A big kid kicked the ball far away. Another kid kicked it back.

David looked at the net. It was white. It looked like a giant spiderweb. "What if I kick it there?" he thought. He tapped the ball with his toe. The ball rolled and rolled. It went into the net!

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Even Ms. Andersen shouted from the bench. David jumped up high. Then Jayson jumped too. Then a little dog ran onto the field with the ball in its mouth!

"Drop it, please," said the coach, laughing. The dog let go of the ball. David patted its soft head.

"Good dog," said David. "But next time, that is my goal."

Luna ran to the big slide at the park. Her dad sat on a bench close by. Luna waved at him. He waved back.

At the slide, Luna saw Joey. Joey lay down on his tummy. He put his head at the top of the slide. "Wait," Luna said. "Ms. Sadeghi says go down feet first." Joey sat up. He turned himself around. Now his feet were at the top. Down he went, feet first, whee!

Luna waited for her turn. She counted the kids ahead of her. One, two, three. Then it was her turn. She turned around, feet first, just like Joey. She held the sides with both hands. Down she went, fast and smooth. Luna ran back to the line. She went again, feet first. She went again, feet first. "That's how we slide," she told her dad. Her dad clapped and held up a real gold star sticker. "Feet first," Luna said, and stuck it on her shirt.

Amira went to the library with her dad. Mr. Ivanova was setting up a big game on the carpet. There were three wide mats. One mat had a toy car on it. One mat had a stuffed bear on it. One mat had an apple on it.

"Put each thing on the right mat," said Mr. Ivanova. "We have toys, animals, and foods."

Amira picked up a carrot. It felt bumpy and cold. She put it with the toy car. Raya shook her head. "That mat is for toys," she said. "Try another one."

Amira looked at the mats. She saw the apple. The apple smelled sweet. Apples, bread and carrots are foods, she thought. She moved the carrot next to the apple.

Mr. Ivanova clapped. "Yes! The carrot is food."

Then Kaia held up a piece of bread. "Where does this go?" she asked.

Amira pointed to the apple and carrot. "Right there. Bread is food too."

Mr. Ivanova gave Amira a crayon to draw her three mats. Amira drew the apple, the carrot and the bread, all together.

"Food friends," said Amira.

Iris wanted to paint a big sun. She got out her red and yellow paint. Her favorite shirt was pink with stars on it. She wore it to paint every time.

Today the paint went drip, drip. Red drops fell on her sleeve. Yellow drops fell on her lap. Her pretty pink shirt was a mess now. Iris felt sad about that.

Her mom came to look. "Let's find you an old shirt," Mom said. Mom gave Iris a big blue shirt. It was too long, but that was okay. Iris put it on over her pink one.

Iris painted again. The red paint dripped. The old blue shirt caught it. The paint went drip, drip, and nothing got on her stars. Iris laughed.

She painted a big round sun with yellow rays. She even painted a slippery fish in a blue sea. Mom hung the sun on the wall. Iris pointed at her old blue shirt. "This one saved my stars," she said. Then she dipped her brush and made one more yellow shape.

Dylan wore his blue sweater on the nature trail. His friend Juniper walked beside him. Mr. Andersen led the way. Dylan wanted to learn his five senses. But he could not remember them all. "What if I forget one?" he asked. "We can help you," said Mr. Andersen.

Dylan saw a red leaf. "I see it with my eyes," he said. He heard a bird. "I hear it with my ears." He smelled a flower. "I smell it with my nose." He tasted his apple at snack time. "I taste it with my tongue." Now he had four. One more to go.

Dylan touched a pine cone. It felt bumpy. He touched moss. It felt soft. Juniper asked, "What part do you use for touching?" Dylan looked at his hand. "My skin," he said. "My fingertips feel it." He wiggled his fingers on the moss. Soft, soft, soft.

"I did it," said Dylan. "Five senses. Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin." Juniper clapped. Mr. Andersen smiled. "That was cute," said Juniper. They walked home in the warm sun. Dylan dreamed about soft moss at nap time.

Olivia stood at the school gate. It was her first day. She held her mama's hand very tight. The gate was tall and the yard was big. Olivia did not want to go in.

"Who will look after me?" she asked. "You have to go to work."

Just then, a kind man came to the gate. He smiled at her. A boy named Cassian ran up to him. "Good morning, Mr. O'Brien!" said Cassian. "You always help us in class!"

"That is my job," said Mr. O'Brien. "A teacher looks after the children." Then he waved at Olivia. "Hello! Are you in my class?"

Olivia counted the children at the gate. One, two, three. Then more came. They all ran to Mr. O'Brien. He knew every name. He helped a girl pick up her dirty bag. He helped a boy who dropped his puzzle pieces on the ground. He even got a tissue to cut the tag off Cassian's scratchy new shirt, using safe scissors from his pocket.

Olivia let go of her mama's hand. She took one step. Then two steps. Then she was at the gate. "I am Olivia," she said, in a small brave voice.

"Hello, Olivia," said Mr. O'Brien. "Let us go find your peg for your coat."

Olivia waved to her mama. Then she walked into the yard with her teacher. He looked after her, just like he said.

"Can we do the puzzle first?" asked Olivia.

"We sure can," said Mr. O'Brien.

Edouard was playing in his house. He had a big red truck. He pushed it fast across the floor.

Then the truck hit a chair and broke. A wheel fell off. Edouard felt angry. He kicked the truck. "Bad truck!" he said.

His dad came into the room. "Why is your face so mad?" Dad asked. Edouard sat on the floor and frowned. He would not talk. Dad did not know what to do. He looked and looked at the truck and the chair.

Then Edouard said, "I feel sad. My truck broke." Dad sat down next to him. "I can fix it," Dad said. Dad put the wheel back on. He made it straight and tight. The truck was fixed!

Edouard was excited. He hugged Dad. "Will it roll again?" he asked. "Yes, let's see," said Dad. Edouard pushed the truck. It rolled past his toes. It made his feet tickle when it bumped them. Edouard laughed. He felt happy now. "Fix it again if it breaks!" he said. Dad smiled and said, "Just tell me when you feel sad."

Hailey was drawing in the backyard. It was a sunny day, but the sky was getting dark. Then the lights in the house went out. "A power cut," said Dad. "The power is off."

Hailey went to the back door. She stood very still. "It's so quiet," she said. Dad nodded. "The fridge stopped humming. The power made it go."

Hailey listened hard. She heard a bird in the tree. She heard her own breath. She heard a little tap, tap, tap. "Dad, what is that?" she asked. They listened together. "Rain," said Dad. "It's starting to rain."

Hailey put out her hand. The drops fit right in her palm. Then the rain stopped. The sun came back. Inside, the fridge began to hum again. "The power is on!" Dad called. Hailey laughed. The hum filled the house like a song. "I missed you, fridge," she said. Dad gave her a big hug.

Declan sat on the mat at the community centre. Mr. Iyer held a drum. "Clap with me," said Mr. Iyer. He tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Declan clapped. His claps went too fast. Daphnee laughed. "You are a fast clap machine!" she said. The big room was warm and smelled like popcorn.

"Now we sing," said Mr. Iyer. They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Declan knew the first line. Then his mouth stopped. The second line was gone, like a dark hole with no words in it. Noah knew it. Noah sang on. "I forgot," said Declan.

So they sang it again. And again. And one more time. On the fifth time, the words just jumped out of Declan's mouth. "Up above the world so high!" he sang. His claps fit the beat now, tap, tap, tap. "You found the words!" said Mr. Iyer. "Sing it again," said Declan. "Again and again and again."

Charlie went to Grandma's house. Grandma had a big dirt patch by the fence. "We can plant peas here," said Grandma. Charlie dropped the little seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil with his hands. Then he watered the seeds with a small can.

Every day Charlie looked at the dirt. One day, a green sprout came up. Then the plant grew tall. Then it grew little green pods. Charlie picked one pod. It was small and bumpy. He squeezed it, and it popped open. Inside was a row of round green peas. "Grandma! Look in here!" he said. Grandma smiled. "Those are our peas," she said.

They sat on the porch steps together. Charlie ate a pea from his hand. Grandma read him a book about gardens. A loose page flapped in the wind. Charlie held another pod up to the sun. "More peas live in there," he said.

Raphael ran up the steps to Grandpa's house. He was going to meet the new baby. His tummy felt like a pig was doing jumps inside it.

The baby lay in a soft blue blanket. "I will pat the baby," said Raphael. He patted the baby's head. Pat, pat, pat. The baby's face scrunched up. Then the baby began to cry. A big, loud cry.

"Too pat, too pat," said Grandma. She showed Raphael her hand. She touched the baby's tiny fingers. She stroked them, slow and soft. "Like this, Raphael. A new baby must be touched very gently."

Raphael held out one finger. He touched the baby's hand. He stroked it, slow and soft. The baby stopped crying. The baby held on to his finger.

"He likes me," whispered Raphael. He skipped around the room, one whole skip, then came right back. The baby still held his finger. Grandpa laughed and took a picture. It was a real picture of the two of them.

Ellie ran to the park. The big slide was waiting. A small slide stood next to it. "I want the big one," said Ellie.

First she had to go up. She took the ladder, one step at a time. "One, two, three," she counted. Her friend Aviraj was already at the top. "Up and down are opposites," he said. Ellie kept climbing. "Four, five, six." Now she was up at the top, way up high.

"Ready?" asked Aviraj. "Ready," said Ellie. She sat down. Then she slid. She went fast, fast, fast, all the way down to the sand. Aviraj went slow at first. Then he went fast too.

They climbed up again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." They slid down again and again.

At home, Mom said it was bath time. The water was warm. Mom washed off all the sand. "Can we paint the slide tomorrow?" asked Ellie. "We can paint pictures of the slide," said Mom. Ellie smiled. "The big one," she said.

Victor stood in the school hallway. It was his very first day. He held his dad's hand tight.

His tummy made a little growl. "I am hungry now," Victor said. "Can we eat?"

"Not yet," said his dad. "First you hang your coat. Then you find your name. Then your teacher helps you."

Victor hung his red coat on hook number one. He found his name card with a V. His teacher, Mr. Rahimi, smiled at him.

"You look hungry," said Mr. Rahimi. "Guess what. A school day has a snack time. We all sit and eat together soon."

Soon the bell went ding. All the kids sat at the little table. Victor opened his bag. A sweet apple! A girl named Norah sat next to him. She had crackers.

Victor took a big bite. "Apple!" he said. Norah blew on her crumb and giggled. Mr. Rahimi whispered in Victor's ear, "See? We wait, then we eat."

Victor ate his apple all up. He was not hungry anymore. He patted his coat on hook number one. Then he ran back to play with Norah.

Felix sat in his car seat. Mama was driving. Felix had toys on his lap. He had a little cow. He had a banana toy. He had a soft dog.

Felix wanted to make piles. He made an animal pile. He made a toy pile. He put the cow in the animal pile. "Cow," he said. He put the banana in the toy pile. The banana did not move. It was a toy banana.

Then Felix held up the soft dog. He put it in the animal pile. He waited. The dog did not wag. The dog did not bark. It just sat there. Felix tapped its nose. Nothing happened.

Felix picked up the soft dog. He looked at it for a long time. Then he moved it to the toy pile. It sat next to the banana. "You are a toy," said Felix.

At school, Dorian ran up. "Can I see the dog?" he asked. "Yes," said Felix. "It is a toy dog." Dorian hugged it. It felt nice and soft.

Ms. Halvorsen called from the gate, "Time to come in!" Felix held his toy dog tight. Dorian chased him to the door. Spring flowers grew by the steps. Felix put the toy dog in his backpack, all by himself.

Jade sat in the waiting room at the doctor's office. She wanted to feel brave, but her tummy felt funny. Her friend Arzoyi sat beside her with a big bag.

"Let's play a guessing game," said Arzoyi. "Close your eyes."

Jade closed her eyes tight. Arzoyi put something in her hands. Jade touched it with her fingertips. It felt bumpy all over. "Is it a pinecone?" she asked. "Yes!" said Arzoyi.

Next came something soft and light. "A feather!" said Jade. Then something smooth and cool. "A stone," she said. It was a real, smooth stone.

Jade opened her eyes. "My fingers could see!" she said. The nurse called her name. Jade held the stone in her hand, like a small blanket to carry. "Can I keep it?" she asked. The nurse smiled and said, "It's yours."

Evan was at Grandma's house. His little blue car was lost. Where could it be?

Evan looked under the bed. No car. He looked in the dark closet. No car. He looked by the big chair. No car. Evan sat down. His eyes felt sad.

Then Evan had an idea. "Grandpa, will you help me look?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Grandma, will you help too?" "Yes," said Grandma. Now three people were looking. Evan looked by the door. Grandpa looked near the window. Grandma looked in the kitchen.

"Here it is!" called Grandma. The blue car was by the fruit bowl. Evan ran fast. He hugged the car. "We found it together," he said. Grandpa smiled. "More people looking, more eyes to find things." Evan held the car up high. "Vroom, vroom!" he said.

Mohamed ran to the rug at school. He sat down next to Mathias. He wanted the bear story now.

"Story now?" he asked.

Ms. Joshi shook her head. "The story is not now. It is after snack. Now means at this very moment."

Mohamed looked at the clock. He looked at the empty snack table. "Snack first," said Ms. Joshi. "Story later."

Mohamed ate his crackers. He drank his water. Then the table was empty again.

"Is it now?" Mohamed asked.

"Yes," said Ms. Joshi. "Now it is story time."

Mohamed smiled. He sat very still. The bear story began right then.

"Tomorrow we read it again," said Ms. Joshi.

"Tomorrow," Mohamed said. That word was new.

Mathias leaned over. "Yesterday we read the duck book."

Mohamed hugged the bear book. "Now bear," he said.

Nolan sat in the big concert hall. Ms. Haile was on the stage. She had a little triangle in her hand. She tapped it. Ting! The sound swept all through the hall. The song began. It was quiet and slow.

Nolan felt like clapping. He clapped in the middle of the song. Clap, clap! A lady next to him smiled and put her finger to her lips. "Shh, not yet," she whispered. Nolan stopped. "When do I clap?" he whispered back. "When the music is over," she said. "Then we clap to show we liked it."

Nolan waited. He tapped his feet instead. One, two, one, two. He found the beat! The music got soft, then flat and low, then it stopped. All the people clapped at once. Nolan clapped too, big loud claps. Then he sang his rhyme out loud. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!" Ms. Haile looked right at him. She tapped her triangle again. Ting!

Aria went to the store with her dad. She wanted a book for school. First she looked at the signs. "That says BOOKS," said Dad. Aria saw the letters. The sign showed her the way.

In the book part, Aria found a little book. She opened it in the middle. "It is all mixed up," she said. Dad turned it around. He went back to the front. "We start here," he said. Aria turned the pages, one, two, three. The pictures came in a row.

Then she saw a birthday card. It had a name on it. "A-R-I-A," said Aria. "That is me!" Her name had the same letters, in the same order, every time she saw it. On the card. In her book. Again and again. "My name does not fall apart," she laughed. "It stays!" At school, Mckenzie found her own name on her cubby. It looked the same, too. Aria pointed and clapped.

Lennon was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big jar of pencils. Lennon picked a fat yellow one. She held it in her fist like a spoon. The first letter came out bumpy. "L looks like a broken line," she said.

Grandma sat down beside her. "Try pinchy fingers," Grandma said. She showed Lennon how to hold it light, like holding a feather. Lennon tried. "One L. Two L's. L-L," she said. The L's looked better now. But E was hard. It wiggled like a worm.

So Lennon wrote her name every day at Grandma's house. Monday she wrote it. Tuesday she wrote it. Wednesday too. "One name, two names, three names," she counted. Soon the letters stood up straight. All seven letters, L-E-N-N-O-N, neat on the page. "Look, Grandma!" she said. Grandma clapped and hung the paper on the fridge.

Jack went to a big festival with his dad. There were flags in the wind and lots of food. Jack saw long tables with rice and bread and fruit.

Nihaal waved at Jack from a table. "Sit with us," Nihaal said. Jack sat down and picked up a piece of bread. But Nihaal was not eating. Nihaal's mom was not eating. Everyone sat with their hands still.

"Wait," Nihaal said softly. "First we say thank you." Nihaal's family said a blessing together. Their words were quiet and good. Then everyone picked up food.

Jack put his bread down. He folded his hands too. He waited while Nihaal's family said the blessing. Then Jack took a big bite of bread. "Yum," he said. Nihaal laughed, and the wind moved the flags above their table.

Jack ran to the park with Natalia. The sky was gray and windy. The wind blew a leaf onto Jack's wing of paper, and the paper almost flew away. "Hold it tight!" said Natalia.

Then the rain began. Tap, tap, tap on the slide. Jack stepped in a big puddle. His sneakers got wet. His socks got soggy. "Yuck," said Jack. "My feet feel ugly and squishy." Natalia laughed. "My feet are dry. I have my rain boots on." She stomped in the puddle. Splash! Her feet stayed dry.

The next day was snowy. Jack put on his own rain boots. He stomped in a puddle of slush. His feet were warm and dry. "Look, Natalia!" he said. "Dry socks!" Natalia gave him a big smile. Then they made snowballs until the sun came out.

Peyton stood in the backyard. The new baby was inside. Everyone was looking at the baby. Not at Peyton.

Peylon kicked her red ball. The ball bounced high. It hit the fence. The fence made a big bang. Mom came out fast. "Peyton, are you okay?"

"I miss you," said Peyton. "Just you and me." Mom sat down on the grass. "Come here," she said. "You can feel left out. That is okay. Big sisters feel that way too."

Peyton sat on Mom's lap. Mom gave her a hug. The hug was warm and long.

Then Dalia came by from across the street. "Can Peyton play?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, but first I will hold the baby while Peyton sits with me."

Peyton held Mom's hand. The baby slept on Mom's shoulder. "This is nice," said Peyton. "All three of us." Mom kissed her head. "That is true," said Mom.

Peyton picked up her ball again. She rolled it to the baby's toes. The baby made a small sound. "She likes me!" said Peyton. The ball bounced once more, right over the fence and into Dalia's waiting hands.

Theo was in the backyard. He dug in the dirt with a spoon. Now his hands were very muddy.

"Time to get clean," said Dad. Dad filled a little tub with water. The sun had been shining on the hose all day. Theo wanted to jump right in.

"Not yet," said Dad. "I have to check the water. It might be hot, not warm." Dad put his hand in. "One, two, three. It is hot. We will wait." Theo waited. He counted rocks by his feet. One rock, two rocks, three rocks.

Then Theo touched the grass. The grass was not hot. The tub went drip, drip, drip. Dad put his hand in again. "One, two, three. Now it is warm and cozy. You can get in."

Theo stepped into the tub. The water felt good. Dad washed his muddy hands. "Squeaky clean," said Theo. He splashed one big splash.

Kinsley loved the big red truck at daycare. Kiaan had it now. "My turn next," Kinsley said. Kiaan gave her the truck. Then it was Kiaan's turn again. They took turns, one by one.

Then Jordan ran in with bread for snack time. "Snack time!" Jordan shouted. Little Ben was asleep on his mat. Ben heard the shout. He began to cry.

Kinsley put her hand near her mouth. She made her voice very small. "Shh," she whispered. "Ben is asleep. We use a quiet voice." Kiaan whispered too. Jordan whispered too.

Soon Ben stopped crying. He closed his eyes again. The room was still and soft.

Ms. Chatterjee gave out the bread. Everyone ate in quiet voices. Kinsley ate her bread slow. She looked at Ben on his mat. He was asleep again.

After snack, the truck was free. "My turn," whispered Kinsley. Kiaan whispered, "Then my turn." They rolled the truck across the rug, quiet as mice.

Arthur went to Reign's house. Reign had a big teddy bear named Bob. Bob was lying on the floor. "Bob is sick," Reign said. "He has a sniffly nose."

Arthur wanted to help Bob. He looked around the room. He saw a toy cup. He filled it with air, not water. "Here, Bob," Arthur said. "Drink your pretend soup." He held the cup to Bob's mouth. Then he patted Bob's back, soft and slow.

"Bob needs medicine too," Reign said. Reign found a little wooden spoon. "Open wide, Bob." Reign gave Bob pretend medicine, one spoon, then two. Bob made a tiny cough. "He is getting better," Arthur said.

Then Bob's tummy rumbled. "Oh no," said Arthur. "He is hungry again." They gave Bob more pretend soup. Arthur's father came to pick him up. The floor was messy with cups and blankets. "Bob can sleep now," Reign said. They tucked Bob under a small blanket. Arthur kissed Bob's head. "Bye, Bob," he said. "Feel better soon." Bob's eyes looked shiny and happy.

Ayla sat at the kitchen table. She had a pencil and some paper. Mom sat next to her with a towel and a cup of tea.

"Can you write your name?" Mom asked.

Ayla wanted to try. She held the pencil with her whole fist. She made a big round A. Then the paper slid away. Her line went crooked. The letter looked wobbly.

"My paper keeps moving," Ayla said.

She tried again. She pressed hard. The paper slid again. She frowned and put her head down.

Mom sat close by her side. "You can try again," Mom said softly. "Your hands can work together."

Ayla sat up. She put her left hand flat on the paper. She held the paper still. Then she drew with the pencil.

The paper did not slide. Her A stood up straight. Her Y had two neat arms. Her L had a good tall line.

"Mom, look!" said Ayla. "I did it!"

She wrote the whole name. A Y L A. All four letters, neat and small.

Mom clapped her hands. "Let's ask Dad to come and see," she said.

Dad came to the table. He looked at the paper. "That's your name!" he said. "You wrote it all by yourself."

Ayla smiled big. She turned the paper toward him. "This is me," she said.

Ayla was at daycare. She saw a tiny red fire truck on the rug. It was Joaquin's fire truck. She grabbed it fast and pushed it across the floor. It made a loud siren sound. Vroom, weeoo, weeoo.

Joaquin's face went sad. His eyes filled with tears. "That is mine," he said. "You took it and you did not ask." Ayla stopped the truck. She looked at Joaquin's sad face. Then she pushed the truck back to him. "Can I play with the fire truck, please?" she asked. Joaquin wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You can have a turn."

They pushed the truck back and forth. Weeoo, weeoo! Then Ms. Ortiz called, "Clean up time, everyone." Ayla put the truck in the bin. Joaquin smiled at her. "Do you want to sit by me at snack?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Ayla. She went with him to the little table.

Livia woke up early. Today she would see a doctor. She put her teddy bear in her bag. "The doctor will look at my ears," she told her mother. Her mother smiled. "We will call him the dentist," she said.

Livia sat in a big chair at the dentist's office. It went up and down. The dentist looked in her mouth. He looked and looked. He did not look at her ears. He did not look at her toes. "Open wide," he said. Livia opened wide. He counted her teeth. "Ten on top," he said. "Ten on the bottom." Livia looked in the little mirror. She saw her own white teeth. The dentist was a doctor, but only for teeth.

Back at home, Livia played dentist with teddy. "Open wide," she said. She counted his teeth, one by one. "All done," she said. "You get a sticker."

Mila packed her little red bag. She was going on a trip to Grandma's house by the sea. "The beach!" said Mila. "Sand and waves!"

At the beach, Mila found a big pink shell. She held it up to her ear. "It says whoosh!" said Mila. Grandma laughed. "Let's take a photo of you and your shell," said Grandma. Mila smiled big. Click! The camera went click.

Mila and Grandma took more photos. Click! Mila in the sand. Click! Mila with a frozen treat, cold on her tongue. Click! Mila and the big blue waves. "Help me hold the camera steady," said Grandma. Mila helped with her two hands.

Then it was time to go home. Mila looked out the window. The beach got small and far away.

At home, Mila felt sad. "I miss my shell," she said. "I miss the waves." Grandma sat down next to her. "Look," said Grandma. She opened the photos. There was Mila in the sand! There was the frozen treat! There was the big pink shell! Mila clapped her hands. "The beach came home with us!" she said. "The whole summer, right here in the photo."

Arthur wanted to read his big bear book. But the pages were stuck together. "Hello, book," said Arthur. He held it up to his mouth and blew on the edge. The pages popped apart one by one.

Arthur opened the book. "Is this the front?" he asked his teddy. The cover had a picture of a bear. He turned it over. The back had no bear. "This way," he said. He opened the front cover and peeked inside. Little marks sat in rows on every page. "Those are words," said Dad from the door. "What do words do?" asked Arthur. "They say things," said Dad.

Arthur put his nose close. The pages smelled like pancakes and rain. He pointed at a word. "Say bear," he said. Dad read it out loud. "Bear!" Arthur clapped.

Then something surprising happened. Dad pointed at Arthur's pajama shirt. Words were there too. "What does my shirt say?" asked Arthur. "It says ROAR," said Dad. Arthur looked down and roared like a bear, right at his teddy.

Liam wanted to build a shape house in the playroom. Marion was there too. She had a big box of shapes. Liam found a tiny red button on the floor. "Look, a circle," he said. Marion shook her head. "No, it is too small. The clock on the wall is a circle. A tiny button can't be one." Liam held the button up. He looked at the big clock. Then he looked at his button. Both were round all the way around. He turned the button in the light. Its shadow made a small round dot on the rug.

Liam put the button on the table. He put a square block next to it. Then a triangle block. Then a rectangle block. "Big circle, tiny circle," he said. Marion leaned in close. She touched the button. She touched the clock with her eyes. "Both circles," she said. "Big one and tiny one!" She clapped her hands.

The teacher, Ms. Yang, came over. She helped Liam feed the shapes into the right slots on the shape box. The square block was hard to push. It thumped into the square hole. The button was too small for the circle slot, so it rolled across the table. "Circles roll," said Liam. He chased it and caught it. Marion laughed. "Round things roll, round things roll!" they said together. Liam put the tiny button in his pocket, safe and snug. "My little circle," he said.

Leah stood by the big book bus. It was the bookmobile. Ms. Fraser came out with a smile. "Hello, Leah," she said. "Today you get your very first library card." Leah held the little card in her warm hands. It had her name on it. "My own card," she said. "My own card."

Inside the bus, Leah looked at all the books. She wanted a book about ducks. She could not find one. There were so many shelves. "Who can help me?" she asked. "Can anybody help me find ducks?" Ms. Fraser said, "I can. I am the librarian. That is my job. I help people find books." She reached up and took a book down. "Here is your duck book," she said.

Leah hugged the book. It felt smooth and smelled like paper. "The librarian helped me," said Leah. "The librarian helped me." She gave her new card to Ms. Fraser. Beep went the machine. "Now the book is yours to take home," said Ms. Fraser. Leah walked down the steps, holding her book tight. "See you next week," she called.

Levi woke up on Saturday morning. He jumped out of bed. He wanted to put his socks on all by himself. But there was only one sock on the floor. Just one.

Levi looked under the bed. No sock. He looked by the door. No sock. He counted the socks he had. "One," said Levi. That was not enough. His dad came in. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks," said Dad. "We need to find the other one." So they hunted together. Levi peeked behind the basket. He counted as he looked. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Still no sock.

Then Levi felt something in his pant leg. He shook it hard. Out fell the sock, up high in the air. It landed on his foot. "Two socks!" said Levi. Dad laughed and gave him a big hug. "Nice work," said Dad. Levi wiggled his toes inside his warm pair.

Luke had a small blue card. It was his first library card. He held it very tight.

At the library, Luke found a book about a big red truck. He gave the card to the man at the desk. The man scanned the card. "This card can be used again and again," the man said. Luke took the truck book home.

Dad read the truck book to Luke. Luke liked the page with the shiny tooth on the truck. He was mad when the story was over. He wanted more books.

The next day, Dad took Luke back to the library. Luke gave the card again. He got a new book about a moon. He told Dad, "My card gets books every time!"

At bedtime, Luke put the card under his pillow. Dad laughed softly. "Sleep now, Luke," Dad said. "The card will wait for morning."

Louis stood in the kitchen. The toast was on his plate. Mom had made it warm for him. Louis wanted to butter it all by himself.

He took his knife. He poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast tore. Little crumbs went everywhere. "Oh no," said Louis. Mom handed him a new piece of toast. "Try the flat side," she said.

Louis looked at the flat side. He pushed it across the bread. The butter came off the knife. It spread out smooth and shiny. "It works!" said Louis. He pushed again and again. Soon the toast was all covered.

Next came the milk. Louis held the cup with two hands. He poured slowly. One little drop spilled on the table. But the cup did not tip over. "I did it!" said Louis.

Mom smiled at him. Louis took a big bite of his toast. "Yummy," he said. "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

Avery ran to the park with her dad. It was a sunny day. The sun was big and bright. Avery climbed up the slide. She began to squint. Her eyes went squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. "My eyes feel funny," she said.

Her dad held up a sun hat. "Try this," he said. Avery put it on. The hat made shade over her face. Now her eyes went open, open, open. She could see the swings! She could see her friend Jamieson! "Nice hat," said Jamieson. "You look like a beach carrot." Avery laughed. "A happy carrot," she said.

The wind came by. It was windy now. It blew the leaves round and round. It tugged at Avery's hat. Avery held it with both hands. Then she gave the hat a big hug. "Stay on," she said. The wind puffed once more and stopped. Avery slid down the slide with a full smile and her hat still on her head.

Ella went to the playground with her dad. Her friend Emerson was there too. Mr. Bighorn, the neighbour, was by the fence. He was cooking on his grill.

"Come and see," said Mr. Bighorn. "I have warm buns for you."

Eella wanted a bun very much. She ran to the grill. She saw the buns sitting on top. The grill did not look hot at all. No flames. Nothing glowing. She reached out her hand.

"Not yet, Ella," said Mr. Bighorn. He picked up a bun with a big long tool. He held it out to her. "This one is cool now."

Ella held the bun in her hands. It was warm and soft. Then Mr. Bighorn put his hand near the grill, not on it. He pulled it back fast. "Still hot," he said. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it. Every time."

Later, Ella played on the slide. She went down, down, down. Then she saw a shiny fork on the ground near the grill. It looked fun to hold. But Ella did not touch it. She said, "Dad, there is a fork." Her dad picked it up and put it in a bag.
