Ella helped fold the bag closed. She was not alone at the playground. Her dad was right there. Mr. Bighorn was right there too.

"Want another bun?" asked Mr. Bighorn. "This time you can hand me the plate."

Ella held the plate far from the grill. Mr. Bighorn put a warm bun on it. She carried it back, slow and careful.

"I did it," said Ella. She took a big bite.

Axel went to Mr. Suryanto's music room. A big piano sat by the window. Axel loved the piano. He wanted to play a tune all by himself.

Axel looked at the keys. He saw black keys and white keys. He touched a white key. Pling! He touched a black key. Plong! "Ooh," said Axel.

Then Axel had a silly idea. He would play only the black keys. He pressed a black key. Plong! He pressed the next black key. Plong! Then another. Plong, plong, plong. "It still makes a tune!" said Axel.

Mr. Suryanto laughed. "You found the black keys, Axel. You are brave to try." Alexy and Malika clapped from their seats. Axel played his black key tune again. Plong, plong, plong. Malika tapped her feet. Alexy bounced in his seat.

"Now me!" said Malika. She reached for the white keys. Pling, pling, pling. Axel giggled and played along with her, black keys going plong and white keys going pling.

Aiden was at Grandma's house. Snow was falling outside. He wanted to play in it fast!

Grandma gave him his red coat. Aiden pushed one arm in. Then he wiggled and wiggled. He could not find the other sleeve. The coat fell down. "Oh no!" said Aiden.

Just then his friend Amal came to the door. Amal had her coat on already. "Watch this," she said. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. The coat was on!

Aiden laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. He flipped it over his head. The coat was on him! He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It went zzzzzip!

"I did it!" said Aiden. "We can go far in the snow!" said Amal. Grandma waved from the window. Aiden ran out the door into the white, white snow.

Henry sat at the dinner table. He had pasta and a big glass of milk. "Pasta first, then a bath," said his mom. Henry ate two more bites. Then he ran for the bath.

His dad ran the warm water. Henry got in and splashed. His dad washed his hair with soap. Then the bath was done.

Henry jumped out of the tub. Drip, drip, drip went his feet. Water made little puddles on the floor. "Henry, you are all wet," said his dad. "A towel dries your body after a bath." Henry ran back and grabbed the towel.

He rubbed his arms. The towel soaked up the water. Now his arms were dry! He rubbed his tummy and his legs. All dry. Was the towel wet now? Yes! It was heavy with water. Henry had made the water move from him to the towel. How did it all fit in there?

Henry put on his soft pajamas. He folded the towel and put it on the rack. "Good job," said his dad. "Can I bring my towel tomorrow too?" asked Henry. His dad laughed and turned off the light.

Daniel sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a cat. But his paper was square. "A cat is not square," said Daniel.

Abram sat next to him. Abram had a square napkin. He folded it in half, edge to edge. "Look," said Abram. "Now it is a rectangle." Daniel leaned close. The square had changed. Two sides of it had gone away.

Daniel picked up his square paper. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He pressed it flat with gentle hands. Now his paper was a rectangle too. "It is long like a cat!" said Daniel. Everleigh clapped. Mr. Lin smiled and gave him more paper.

Daniel painted his cat on the rectangle. He gave it a circle eye and triangle ears. His square paper had made a long cat. "More paper, more cats!" said Daniel. Mr. Lin laughed and said, "Here you go."

Rose sat on the little red mat. Mr. Lim tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Rose clapped along with the taps. Her claps went the same speed as the drum.

"Now let's sing," said Mr. Lim. "The cat sat on the mat. The cat wore a big red..."

Amelya stopped. "I forgot the word!"

"Ask Rose," said Mehreen. "Rose knows it."

Rose thought hard. The cat wore a big red... She tried a word. "Mat?"

Amelya laughed. "A red mat on his head? That is so silly!"

"The word ends like cat," said Amelya. "Cat. Hat!"

"Hat!" said Rose. "The cat wore a big red hat!"

They sang it again. Tap, tap, tap went the drum. Clap, clap, clap went Rose. "And next he found an egg," sang Mehreen.

"A red egg?" said Rose. "You are so mean to that cat!"

Everyone giggled. Mr. Lim tapped faster. Rose clapped faster to keep up. "My hands can go fast too!" she said.

Jasmine went to the park with her dad. They came in the car. The car went fast, and Jasmine laughed. She felt excited to play.

At the sandbox, Jasmine saw her friend Ira. Ira was crying. Big tears ran down his face. He looked sad. Jasmine knew that sad people sometimes cry. She wanted to help.

Jasmine had her bunny in her backpack. She held it tight. "Do you want to hold Bunny?" she asked. Ira wiped his tears. He hugged Bunny soft and close. His crying stopped. Soon he smiled a big smile. Jasmine felt happy inside. Then Ira said, "Let's dig a hole!" They dug and dug in the sand. Ms. Bui, the park helper, came by with two juice cups. "A fast runner told me you two might be thirsty," she said. Jasmine and Ira each took a cup. Bunny sat on the sand and watched them dig.

Elijah wanted to reach his blanket. It sat up high on the big bed. He stretched. He stood on his toes. The blanket was too far.

Mom was in the kitchen. She was stirring a hot pot. "I can help soon," she said. Elijah did not touch the stove. He waited.

Then he had an idea. His scarf was hanging on a low hook. He took the scarf. It was long. It went down and down. He threw one end over the bed post. The scarf hung there, long and soft. He pulled the scarf. The scarf pulled nothing.

Mom came in. "Silly scarf," she said. "A scarf is not a rope." She got the blanket down. The blanket was big. The scarf was small next to it.

"Your scarf is long," said Mom. "The blanket is big. Long and short are opposites."

Mom wrapped the blanket around Elijah. It went around him two times, one, two. The scarf went around his neck one time. Long scarf, short wrap.

"Now it is not late," said Mom. "Story time." Elijah hugged the blanket. "Long story," he said. Mom laughed. "A short one," she said. "Then bed."

Freya sat at the big art table. Ms. Wilson put out the paints. There was red paint, yellow paint, green paint and blue paint. Maci picked red. Nelya picked green. Freya wanted to paint snow. "I will make snow," she said. She looked at her paper. The paper was white. The snow was white too. If she painted white on white, nothing would show. Freya frowned at the empty paper.

Then she saw the stack of blue paper. She took one sheet. She dipped her brush in white paint. She made dots on the blue paper. The white dots showed up. They looked like snow falling. Freya made more dots, slow and soft. "Look at my snow," she said. Maci leaned over. Nelya leaned over too. Ms. Wilson smiled. "What a snowy blue day," she said. Freya added one big white dot at the top. "That is the biggest snowflake of all."

Henry sat in a big chair at the mall salon. The chair was striped, blue and white. He wore a cape like a superhero. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. One, two, three hairs on the cape.

"Hair cut!" said Henry. But he had a problem. He could see his front hair in the wall mirror. He could not see the back of his head. Where did the back hair go? "I want to see the back," he said.

The hairdresser smiled. She held up a little mirror. She put it close to Henry's face. Now Henry saw the wall mirror and the little mirror together. And there it was! The back of his hair, short and neat. "I see it!" said Henry. "The back looks good!" He turned his head one way, then the other. The back hair moved too. Henry giggled all the way past the desk and out the door.

Jaxson climbed the school bus with his letter cards. He held them tight in one hand. His friend Deborah sat by the window. She waved at him.

"Look!" said Jaxson. "I have letters!" He put the cards on his knees. "This one is M. It says mmm." Deborah picked up a card too. "This is B," she said. "B says buh." They laughed at the funny sounds.

Then Jaxson dropped his cards. They fell all over the floor. "Oh no!" he said. One card slid under the seat. The cards were all mixed up now. "Which one comes after M?" asked Deborah. Jaxson scratched his head. He did not know.

Then he had an idea. "The song!" he said. "The alphabet song sings the letters in order from A to Z!" He began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." He picked up A. Then B. Then C. He kept singing and picking up cards. "H, I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P." The cards went into a neat line on his knees.

"I found where M goes!" cried Jaxson. "It goes after L!" Deborah clapped her hands. "Sing it again!" she said. Jaxson sang all the way to school. "Q, R, S, T, U, V!" The bus driver smiled in the big mirror. Jaxson held up his neat row of letters. "Now I know my letters, one by one!"

Maverick had a cold. His legs felt weak. He sat at the kitchen table in his pajamas. Mom made warm soup on the stove. Maverick watched from his chair. A bird sat on the window ledge outside. Its small feathers puffed up in the wind.

Mom set down a bowl of soup. She also set down a toy kit. It was Maverick's doctor kit. Inside was a stethoscope. Maverick put the round end on his teddy bear. He put the ear tips in his ears. He heard nothing. "It is just a toy," said Mom. "But the doctor had a real one."

Maverick wondered about that. "The doctor listened to my chest?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "With her stethoscope. She listened to your chest, and it made a thump-thump sound." Maverick lifted the toy stethoscope. He pressed it on his own chest. He held very still. He breathed slowly, in and out.

"Thump," said Maverick. He grinned. "My chest talks!" He listened to Mom next. He listened to the teddy bear again. The bird flew away from the window. Maverick kept the stethoscope around his neck all day. "I am the doctor now," he said. "Soup first," said Mom, and she slid the bowl closer.

Alexander ran to the door. Outside the sun was big and bright. "Sunny day!" he shouted. He wanted to play in the sand right now.

Ms. Henry stood by the door. She held a bottle of sunscreen. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," she said. Alexander held still. She rubbed it on his arms and his face. It felt cool. "It is a bit stinky," he said, and he laughed.

Then Alexander ran outside. Andrea was already at the sandbox. The wind blew her hat off. "Windy!" she yelled. Alexander chased the hat and caught it. He gave it back to her. His skin stayed happy in the sun. He dug and dug, and made a big sand cake. "More sand!" said Andrea. Alexander scooped up another handful.

Thomas dug a little hole in the backyard. He put a carrot seed in it. He patted the dirt on top. His mom gave him a card with a carrot picture on it.

"Water it a little," she said. Thomas tipped his small watering can. The dirt turned dark and damp.

Every day Thomas looked at his spot. One day, tiny green leaves came up. He smiled and clapped. Then more leaves came up, in the wrong place. They were all over the bed. Thomas grabbed one and pulled.

"Stop," said his mom. "That one is a baby carrot."

"What is a weed?" asked Thomas.

"A weed is a plant growing where you don't want it," said Mom. She pointed to the funny grass blades. "Pull those. Leave the carrot leaves."

Thomas pulled the weeds, one by one. His hands got busy and dirty. The baby carrots stayed safe in their row. Zander came by to see them later.

"Look," said Thomas. "Tall weeds out. Short carrots in."

He watered the little leaves again. The sun went down slow and warm.

Maria sat at the table with her spoon. Mom had made warm soup. Dad put the pot down. Then Mom said, "Time to hold hands."

Maria was still holding her spoon. "I can't hold hands," she said. "My spoon is busy!"

Dad smiled. "You can put the spoon down," he said. "It will wait for you."

So Maria set the spoon by her bowl. She reached out both hands. Mom took one hand. Dad took the other. Around the table they all held hands, all the way around.

"Now we say thank you for our food," said Mom. They all said it together. It was quiet now, not noisy at all.

Then Dad let go and picked up his own spoon. Maria picked up her spoon too. "The spoon waited for me!" she said.

Mom laughed. "Good spoon," she said. "Good hands, too."

Gianna went to the pharmacy with her dad. Tomorrow was her first trip to the dentist. "Why do we need the dentist?" she asked. "The dentist looks at your teeth," said Dad.

Gianna picked out a small green toothbrush. Her friend Asma was there too. Asma reached for a pink toothbrush by mistake. It was her brother's toothbrush from home. "That one is not yours," said the cashier. Asma put it back. She took her own pink toothbrush. Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes.

Then Gianna saw a box with a picture of a big tooth on it. "What is that?" she asked. "Open it," said Dad. Inside was a little mirror, just her size. "Now I can see my teeth!" said Gianna. She smiled at the mirror all the way to the car.

Logan had a big box of blocks. He wanted to make a town. But the blocks were all mixed up. "Where are my red blocks?" he asked. He looked and looked. One block felt lost under the couch. Logan pulled it out.

Logan put all the red blocks in a pile. Then he put all the blue blocks in a pile. "Red here. Blue there," he said. His blocks were sorted by color. He patted the red pile. The blocks made a soft tap, tap sound.

Then Meera came to play. "I want to sort too," she said. Meera made a pile of big blocks. She made a pile of small blocks. Logan looked at her piles. "Mine are colors. Yours are sizes," he said. "Can we do it one more way?" Meera asked. So they made a pile of square blocks and a pile of round blocks. Same blocks, new piles. Logan let the round ones roll a little. They went round and round on the rug.

"What if we mix them all up again?" Logan asked. Meera laughed. "Then we can sort them one more time." They tipped the box over. The blocks went crash on the rug. Logan clapped his hands. "Red, big, round. Blocks can go in any pile!" Meera held up a small red block. "This one goes in every game."

Connor stood at Grandpa's house in his dinosaur shirt. Maxwell was coming to play. Connor wanted to give Maxwell a snack, like a big helper.

Grandpa brought a plate of apple slices. "Please may I have two?" Connor asked. "Of course," said Grandpa. Connor carried the plate slowly, like a knight carrying treasure. "Apples for the dragon!" he said.

Maxwell took a slice. "Thank you, Connor," said Maxwell. Then Maxwell went quiet. He did not know what to say back. Connor smiled big. "You're welcome!" he said. Maxwell clapped. "You're welcome!" he said too.

Then Connor shared his juice cup, splash, and the floor got messy. "Sorry, Grandpa," said Connor. Grandpa wiped it up with a towel. "Thank you for helping," he said to both boys. "You're welcome!" they shouted together. Connor laughed. He shared the last apple slice too. "For the dragon," he said.

Sienna sat at the paint table at daycare. She wanted to paint grass. She looked for the green pot. The green pot was empty. "Oh no," said Sienna. "My grass needs green."

Her friend Alden sat next to her. "Try the blue pot," he said. Sienna dipped her brush in blue. She made a blue stripe on the snowy white paper. Then Maddie held up the yellow pot. "Yellow next," said Maddie.

Sienna dipped her brush in yellow. She brushed yellow right over the blue stripe. She looked with her eye close to the paper. The stripe had turned green! Blue and yellow made green. She painted tall green grass all across the bottom. "Green grass!" said Sienna. Alden clapped. Maddie clapped. Mr. Ba came to see. "Look at my green grass," said Sienna, and she painted one more green blade.

Sofa? No, Sofia loved daycare. Today the class made a dragon den under the big table. "Roar," said Jack. "My dragon has one shiny tooth," said Brooke. Sofia was excited.

Then the den went boom. A loud noise came from the ceiling. Sofia was scared. She crawled out fast.

"I heard a scary noise," she told Ms. Chukwu. "Can you help?"

Ms. Chukwu took her hand. They looked up together. It was only a big fan, spinning round and round. It made the whoosh sound. Ms. Chukwu turned it down low. The noise went soft, like a sleepy wind.

Sofia smiled. She went back to the den. "The dragon lives here," she said, "and he is tidy now."

"Roar," whispered Jack, very quietly.

Aurora sat at the dinner table. She had a problem. Her blocks were on her chair. Her doll was on her plate. Her ball was under the table.

"Dinner is for food," said Mama. "Toys go in the toy box."

Aurora picked up the blocks. She put them in the toy box. Then she picked up her doll. She gave the doll a kiss on its thin little nose. The doll went in the box too.

She crawled down and looked under the table. The ball sat by the chair leg. She rolled it across the floor. It rolled right to the box. She dropped it in.

"Blocks, dolls and balls," said Aurora. "All toys." She zipped the toy box shut.

Mama set down the bowls. Aurora climbed onto her clean chair. She picked up her spoon and smiled at her warm soup.

Victoria went to the store with her dad. She saw shelves full of toy cars. The cars were red and blue and green. Then she saw something yellow among the cars. It was long and curved. It was a banana!

"A banana does not fit here," said Victoria. She picked it up. "Dad, why is it with the toys?"

"Maybe someone dropped it," said Dad. "Which one is the odd one out?"

"The banana!" said Victoria. "The odd one out is the thing that does not belong. The cars all go together. The banana does not."

Dad smiled. They took the banana to the fruit section. Victoria saw apples and oranges there. "The banana belongs with the fruits," she said. She put it in the basket with the apples.

At school the next day, Victoria told her friend Aylin about the banana. "Can I try?" said Aylin. She put her toy bear with the crayons. "Which one is the odd one out now?"

"The bear!" said Victoria. "Bears are animals. Crayons are for drawing."

Aylin laughed and put the bear back with the toys. Victoria clapped her hands.

Kinsley wanted to play hide-and-seek. Essa and Savanna came to her house to play. "I will seek first," said Kinsley. "You two go hide."

Kinsley put her hands on her eyes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," she said very fast. Then she turned around. "Ready or not, here I come!"

But Essa was still running down the hall. Savanna was still carrying a pillow to hide behind. "Kinsley, that was too fast," said Essa. "We did not have time to hide."

"You count while we hide," said Savanna. "So count slowly."

"Okay," said Kinsley. She covered her eyes again. "One. Two. Three." She made each word long and slow. Essa's feet made a little noise in the hall. "Four. Five. Six." Savanna shut a door very softly. "Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten."

Kinsley looked up. The house was quiet. She saw an ugly old coat hanging on the wall. It looked too bumpy to be a coat. "I hear you breathing," said Kinsley. She lifted the coat, and there was Essa!

Then Kinsley heard a giggle from behind the curtain. "Found you, Savanna!" she said.

"Now it is your turn to hide," said Essa. Kinsley ran to find her spot.

The lights went out. It was dark in the backyard. Max sat very still on the step. "I want light," he said.

His dad came out with a big flashlight. He clicked it on. The yard was bright again. Dad held the light low. Max put his hands in front of it. A black shape jumped on the wall. "Look! A bunny!" said Max. He bent one finger. The bunny grew long ears. He flapped his hands. Now it was a bird. Dad smiled. "That is a nice shadow duck," he said. Max quacked like a duck.

The lights came back on. The wall was just a wall. Max waved the flashlight at his hands one more time. "Quack, quack," he said.

Leah had a little blue bunny. She took it to daycare. But at play time, bunny was gone.

"Where did you go today?" asked Mr. Tan. "Think of each place, in order. Then walk back to them. That is called retracing your steps."

Leah thought hard. "I painted first," she said. So she went to the paint table. She looked under the chairs. No bunny.

"Then I read a book," said Leah. She went to the book corner. She looked behind the shelf. No bunny.

Brayden came to help. "We can be a team," he said. Leah smiled. A team was a neat thing to have.

"Next, I played with the blocks," said Leah. She and Brayden walked to the block rug. They looked all around. Then Leah stopped.

"I see something blue," she said. It was under the rug's edge. It was bunny!

Leah hugged bunny close. "I went back to every place, in order," she said. "And I found you."

Brayden clapped his hands. "Let's go show Mr. Tan," he said. And off they went, bunny bouncing in Leah's arms.

Jasmine climbed the big school bus. She held her little present for her teacher. Her friend Ila waved from a seat. Jasmine sat down next to her.

The bus began to move. Ila stood up. She wanted to wave out the window. "Look, my dad is there!" said Ila. The bus bounced a little. Ila wobbled and grabbed the seat. The driver looked back. "Please sit in your seat," she said. "Children stay sitting on the bus." Ila sat down fast.

Jasmine held Ila's hand. "You can wave from here," she said. They both waved through the window. Ila's dad waved back big. The bus bounced again, but they stayed sitting. "First day of school," said Jasmine. "We did it!" The bus door opened, and they hopped off.

Julia ran to the playroom. "Block day!" she cheered. Fletcher was already there. He had a big pile of blocks and a sheet of circle stickers.

"I want to play shapes," Julia said. She picked up a square block. "How many flat sides does it have?" she asked.

"Let's find out," said Fletcher. Julia pressed a sticker on the top. Then she turned the block over. She pressed a sticker on the bottom. "Two!" she said.

She held the block up. She put a sticker on each side. "Three, four, five, six!" she counted. She looked at every sticker. "Six flat faces!" she said. "And each one is a square!"

Fletcher clapped. "Give me one," he said. Julia carried a block to him. He pressed on stickers too. "One, two, three, four, five, six," he said. "My block has six too!"

Julia spun in a happy circle. She was not scared of big numbers now. Six was fun!

Then Mr. Aydın came in with a long box. "Block towers!" he said. Julia grabbed her six-sticker block. She put it at the bottom. Fletcher stacked his on top. The tower stood tall.

"Look at our square tower!" said Julia. Fletcher laughed and put one more block on.

Asher stood in the garage with his dad. The car was cold. Asher wanted to sit in the car now. But his coat was not on. "You can do it," said Dad. "One arm. Two arms." Asher pushed his arm in. He pushed the other arm in. The coat was on! But the zipper was not up.

Asher pulled the little zipper. It went up one tooth. Then it stopped. He pulled again. It stopped again. "Not bad," said Dad. "Zipping takes practice." Asher tried one more time. The zipper slid all the way up. Zzzzzip! The coat was closed. Asher laughed. The wind stayed outside. The zipper kept it out. Was that the zipper's secret?

Asher climbed into his warm seat. He looked down at his coat. It was all zipped. He did that. "I did it!" said Asher. Dad smiled and clicked the seat belt.

Billie ran onto the soccer field. The grass was still wet from the rain. Her shoes went squish, squish.

"Look, Lily!" said Billie. "My feet make prints in the wet grass!" Lily laughed and made prints too.

Then the game began. Billie kicked the ball. She kicked it right past Yusra. The ball went into the net. Hooray!

But then a man in a yellow shirt blew his whistle. He shook his head. Billie stomped her foot. "My goal was good!" she said. "Why did he stop it?"

The coach knelt down beside her. "That man is the referee," he said. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Billie watched the referee. He pointed at Lily. Lily had pulled Billie's shirt. That was not a rule. The referee made the other team get the ball.

"Yusra," said Billie, "I have an idea. Let's play by the rules. Then the referee won't blow his whistle!"

So Billie ran and kicked. No pulling. No pushing. Just kicking. The referee smiled at her.

Billie got the ball one more time. She looked at the net. She kicked hard. The ball went in. This time the whistle stayed quiet.

"Goal!" Billie shouted. She hugged Lily. Then she waved at the referee. He waved back.

Luca sat at the dinner table. He wanted to help before the food came. Mama brought a big basket of clean clothes. "Can you sort them?" she asked.

Luca made one pile for his toys. He put a truck there. He put a ball there. Then he held up a sock. "Stinky sock!" he said, laughing. He tossed it on the toy pile.

Mama shook her head. "Socks are not toys," she said. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Luca looked with one eye at the sock. Then he looked at his shirt. Then his hat on the chair. He picked up the sock. He put it with the shirts and hats.

"Look! All clothes," said Luca.

Mama clapped. "Good sorting!"

Madelyn sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house. The sun made the seat warm. "Hot," said Mom. "Let it cool first." Madelyn touched her own soft blanket instead.

The car stopped at the store. Mom got a big red ball. Madelyn held Mom's hand in the parking lot. "Stay close," said Mom. Madelyn stayed close. She counted the steps to the door. One, two, three.

At Grandma's house, Madelyn looked behind the couch. She saw a little hole in the wall. It had two small slots. She wanted to put her finger in it.

Then she stopped. She remembered Mom's rule. Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.

Madelyn got up and found Grandma. "Come look," she said. Grandma peeked behind the couch. "Good girl," said Grandma. "I will put a cover on it." Grandma plugged in a small plastic cover. It filled the slots all the way.

Madelyn patted the couch. "All covered," she said. Grandma smiled.

Then Grandma gave Madelyn a surprise. It was a small toy bed for her teddy bear. "For my teddy!" said Madelyn. She tucked teddy in tight.

"Night night, teddy," said Madelyn. "My turn soon. Then I get my own bed."

Nova sat in her car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small road. Nova held her toy box on her lap. She put a bear in the box. Her baby brother took the bear out. She put the blocks in. He took the blocks out.

"In," said Nova. "Out," said her brother. "In and out are opposites," said Dad from the front seat. "Like big and small?" asked Nova. "Yes," said Dad.

Nova put her bunny in the box. She held the lid down. Her brother tapped the lid. Tap, tap. He could not get the bunny out. The car stopped near home. "Are we far from our house?" asked Nova. "No, we are close," said Dad.

Dad helped them out of the car. Nova's shoes had dirt on them. Dad knocked the dirt off, tap tap on the step. It was cold outside, so Dad zipped Nova's coat up warm. At home, Dad made hot cocoa in the kitchen. Nova watched from her chair. Her brother reached for the box again. Nova gave him a small cup of toys, and she kept the big box. "In," she said softly, and tucked the bunny in for a nap.

Mason got to daycare just as the rain began. Pitter, patter, down it came. Mr. Vargas stood by the door. "Rainy day," he said. "Raincoats on, friends."

Mason looked out the window. He saw sunny days in a picture. He saw windy days too, with hats flying. He saw snowy days with mittens. But today was a rainy day.

Louis-Philippe ran straight outside without his raincoat. His shirt got wet, wet, wet. He came back dripping. "My shirt is all wet," he said. Mr. Vargas helped him put on his red raincoat. Louis-Philippe went out again. This time his shirt stayed dry.

Mason wanted to see. He put on his own yellow raincoat. He counted as he zipped it up. One zipper, two boots, three puddles waiting. Outside, the rain tapped on his hood. Tap, tap, tap. His body stayed dry.

A small frog sat by the big puddle. It hopped once, then twice. "Hello, frog," said Mason. Taya laughed and the frog jumped into the water with a splash.

At lunch, Mason drank his milk. He made a sour face. "This milk tastes sour today," said Mr. Vargas. "Let's get you fresh milk." He stirred a little cocoa into a new cup, just for Mason.

Then it was time to stir the paint for rainy day pictures. Mason stirred the blue paint round and round. He painted rain, a frog, and one big yellow raincoat.

When Dad came, the rain had stopped. Mason was warm and dry. He waved to the frog. "Bye, frog," he said. "Bye, rain."

Anna went to the farmers' market with her dad. The stalls smelled like apples and warm bread. Anna touched a pumpkin. It felt bumpy.

Mr. Hussain had a big garden behind his stall. "Can I plant too?" Anna asked. "Yes," said Mr. Hussain. "Here are tomato seeds." Anna made a little hole. She dropped the seeds in. Then she planted carrot seeds too.

The next week, Anna came back. Little green leaves had popped up everywhere. But Anna forgot which leaves were tomatoes. She felt worried. Then Mr. Hussain held up a small stick. A picture of a tomato was on it. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," he said. Anna pushed the tomato stick into the ground. She made a carrot stick too. Kareem drew a big orange carrot on his.

Every week the garden grew taller and taller. Anna poured water on the leaves. It dripped down like soft rain. One day Kyra ran over and pointed. "Look, look!" A small red tomato was hiding under the leaves. Anna laughed. She picked it with Mr. Hussain's help.

"Which one is next?" Kyra asked. Anna looked at the little sticks. "The carrots!" she said. She pulled one up, and it came out with a pop.

Harrison ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. Belle was already there. "I am cooking soup," she said. She stirred a pot full of red and yellow leaves. Harrison picked up a tiny cup. He poured pretend tea. The cup felt bumpy in his hands. The leaves smelled like dirt and rain.

Then it was time to go home. Ms. Wanjiru rang the bell. Harrison started to run. But Belle stopped. She put the leaves back in the pot. She set the cups in the middle of the little shelf. "We have to clean up," she said. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." Harrison looked at the messy kitchen. So that was the rule!

Harrison picked up the spoon. He put it in the pot. He set the little plates in a neat row. The kitchen looked new again. Would Ms. Wanjiru see it? She smiled and clapped her hands. "What a tidy kitchen," she said. Harrison hugged his pretend pot. "Bye bye, kitchen," he whispered. "See you tomorrow."

Naomi ran up to Stella's door. She could not wait to play. Stella opened the door with a big grin.

"Let's play house," said Stella. "You be the mom. I will be the baby." Stella picked up a toy bunny. "The bunny is sick," she said. Naomi wrapped the bunny in a small blanket. She patted its head. Then she held a toy cup to its mouth. "Drink your milk," she said. "You will feel better soon." Stella giggled and clapped.

Then Stella pointed at the floor. "The floor is a river!" she said. "It is not really a river. We are pretending. That means we act like it is real." She threw down some cushions. "Hop on the rocks!" Naomi hopped from cushion to cushion. She wobbled on one cushion and fell in the river with a splash sound. Both girls laughed and laughed.

"My shoe fell in the river," Naomi said. "It is all wet and slimy now!" Stella pulled her out by the hand. "The crocodile wants your bone," Stella said, waving a toy dog bone. Naomi grabbed a cushion and pushed the crocodile away. Then she ran to the play kitchen. "Time to feed the baby!" she called. "Come on, hop fast!" Stella hopped after her, holding the bunny tight.

Emma held her dad's hand at the animal shelter. The room smelled like straw and warm fur. A small dog with a striped collar looked up at her. His tail went wag, wag, wag.

"I want this one," Emma said. Her dad filled out the papers. A lady brought a red leash. The dog would ride home with them in the car.

The next day, Lucca came to see the dog. Lucca had a chocolate treat in his pocket. "Dog, want some?" Lucca asked. He held out the chocolate.

Emma remembered the shelter lady. She had said, "Chocolate can make dogs very sick." So dogs are never given chocolate. Emma pulled Lucca's hand back, gently.

"No chocolate for dogs," Emma said. "It can make them very, very sick."

Lucca looked sad. He really wanted to feed the dog something. Emma's dad came with a small bag. He gave Lucca a dog treat instead. "You can give him this," Dad said.

Lucca held out the little bone treat. The dog sniffed it. Then he took it, soft and quick. His tail wagged and wagged. Lucca laughed out loud.

The dog sat down by Emma's feet. He was warm and his fur was soft. Emma patted his head, one, two, three. Lucca patted his back.

The dog looked up at both of them. Then he licked Lucca's hand, right where the treat had been.

Noah wanted to make bread for his family. He stood at the big kitchen table. Dad helped him pour the flour. Noah stirred with a big spoon. Then he put his hands in the bowl. The dough was sticky and clung to his fingers. "Oh no," said Noah. "It is ruined. It is all over my hands."

Dad smiled. "We push it," he said. "Cooks knead bread dough by pushing and folding it with their hands." Dad showed him. He pushed the dough down. He folded it over. He pushed it again. Noah tried. Push, fold, push, fold. The dough felt warm and soft. It stopped sticking to his hands. "It worked!" said Noah. "Push, fold, push, fold!" He pushed and folded until the dough was smooth like a little round bear.

Dad put the dough near the warm oven to rise. Noah watched from his chair. Soon Mom came in. "Something smells good," she said. Noah gave her the bread to touch. "I made it," he said. "I pushed it and folded it." At supper, the family ate the warm bread. Noah took a big bite. "Yum," he said. "Push, fold, push, fold."

Grandma came to stay with Joshua for a whole week. On Saturday they walked to the market together. The stalls smelled like bread and peaches. Grandma let Joshua pick three red apples. A little spider sat on a crate of corn. Joshua watched it crawl away.

At the market, they saw Joshua's friend Joy. Joy waved at Grandma. "Who is she?" Joy asked. "My grandma," said Joshua. "She is my mom's mom."

Joy looked surprised. "Your grandma is your mom's mom?" she asked. Joshua nodded. "Yes. A grandma is the mom of your mom." Joy thought that was cool.

On the way home, Grandma held Joshua's hand. The apples felt heavy in the bag. Joshua gave one apple a pat. "We will share these," said Grandma.

Joshua went to the pharmacy with his dad. Joshua needed the toilet. Dad took him to the little sink.

Joshah pumped soap onto his hands. Dad said, "Wash for twenty seconds. I will count." Dad counted slowly. One, two, three. Joshua rubbed the soap. Bubbles grew big and white. Dad counted all the way to twenty. Then Joshua held his hands under the water. The bubbles ran away down the sink.

Joshua shook his hands. Water flew everywhere. Some drops landed on the mirror. Some dripped onto the floor. "Where did all the water go?" Joshua asked. "It flew off your wet hands," said Dad. Joshua looked around. Then he saw it. A clean towel hung on a hook, soft and blue. That was a surprise.

Joshua patted his hands on the towel. Pat, pat, pat. His hands were dry at last. Dad smiled. "All clean," said Joshua. He held up his dry hands to show the quiet little room. Then they walked out past the shampoo shelf, hand in hand.

Amira painted a sun at school today. Brynn painted a moon right next to it. "Come to my house," said Brynn. "We can paint more." Amira wanted to go now. She asked Ms. Bennett, "Can I go to Brynn's house now?" "Not now," said Ms. Bennett. "Brynn's mom says tomorrow." Amira frowned. "But I want it today." "Sleep first," said Ms. Bennett. "Then tomorrow comes." Amira thought about that. Sleep first. Then tomorrow. She said it again. Sleep first, then tomorrow. At circle time, she told Abigail too. "Sleep first, then tomorrow." Abigail clapped her hands. Then the class went outside. Amira found dirt on her shoe. She was not afraid of it. She just stomped, one, two, three, and the dirt fell off. That night, Amira ate dinner. She put on her pajamas. She brushed her teeth. Sleep first, then tomorrow. In the morning, the sun was up. "It is tomorrow!" Amira shouted. Mom laughed. "Run and get your shoes." Amira ran.

Abigail sat at the big kitchen table. She was drawing a snowy hill. On the hill was a little fox with a fluffy tail. Abigail wanted the fox to look dark and bold.

She pressed her pencil down very hard. She pressed and pressed. Then she heard a tiny snap. The pencil point had broken. Now the pencil was short and stubby.

Abigail got a new pencil. She thought about the fox. This time she pressed soft and gentle. The gray lines came out light. The pencil point stayed whole. "There you are, little fox," she said. She gave the fox one more soft ear.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Lydia loved having him there. On Saturday they walked to the market together. Grandpa smelled the warm bread. Lydia touched a fuzzy peach. "Can we play a game when we get home?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "We can play a card game together."

At the table, Lydia grabbed all the cards. "I go first," she said. Grandpa shook his head. "We take turns," he said. "First me, then you." Lydia waited. Grandpa put down one card. Then Lydia put down one card. Back and forth it went. "My turn now?" she asked. "Yes, your turn," said Grandpa.

Lydia laughed at each turn. The cards made a soft slap on the table. When the game was over, Grandpa gave her a big hug. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. "Again tomorrow," he said. Lydia held his hand all the way home.

Willow went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she could not come. The grass was still wet and shiny.

Willow saw the big yellow swing. She wanted to ride on it. But Ava was on it now. Willow asked, "Can I have a turn?"

"Soon," said Ava. Willow frowned. "What does soon mean?"

Ms. Nowak was sitting on a bench nearby. "Soon means in a little while," she said. Willow sat on the wood chips to wait. She counted the birds. One, two, three.

Ava pumped her legs. The swing went up and down. Then Ava jumped off. "Your turn now!" she said.

Willow ran fast. She climbed on and rode the swing. Her hair flew in the wind. She touched the sky with her toes.

Then Khadijah came by with a little carton of milk. She sat down on the wood chips. "I want a turn too," she said.

"You can have it soon," said Willow. Ava pushed the swing soft and slow. Khadijah watched the swing go up. Willow counted to three again.

Then Willow jumped down. "Now it is your turn," she said.

Khadijah clapped her hands and ran to the swing.

Axel held his dad's hand. It was his first day of school. The playground was big and loud. Children ran and laughed everywhere.

A girl with a red bow waved at him. "Hi, I am Ariya," she said. "Come see our class!" Mr. Ahmed stood by the door. He smiled at Axel. "Welcome," he said. "Come take a seat on the blue mat."

Axel sat down. Mr. Ahmed held up a big paper. It had pictures on it. "These are our class rules," he said. "Everyone in the class follows the rules." Axel looked at the pictures. One showed hands keeping gentle. One showed ears listening.

Later, the class made egg shakers. Axel filled his egg with beans. Then he wanted to shake it very fast and loud. Ariya put her hand out softly. "Remember, gentle hands," she said. "That is a rule. Everyone follows it." Axel made his hands slow. He shook the egg gently. Tap, tap, tap. The music sounded nice.

At play time, Axel found a small furry caterpillar on the wall. "Look!" he said. Ariya came to look too. They did not touch it. They watched it crawl, then it went under a leaf.

Axel ran to his dad at the gate. "Dad, we have rules!" he said. "And I shook an egg!" Ariya waved from the gate. "See you tomorrow, Axel!"

Brielle held her bear tight. She and Mom were on the city bus. Today Brielle would go to the dentist for the first time. "I feel sad," she told Mom. "The dentist might put fingers in my mouth." Mom gave her hand a little squeeze.

At the dentist's office, a chair went up. It went down. Brielle sat in it. The dentist waved hello. His hands were blue! "Your hands are blue!" said Brielle. "These are my gloves," said the dentist. "I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth." He pulled one glove and let it snap. Brielle laughed. The blue hand had a finger shape, just like her mitten at home.

Brielle opened her mouth wide. The dentist peeked in with a little mirror. "All done!" he said. He gave her bear a glove too. It fit just right. "Let's go," said Brielle, and she waved the blue bear paw at Mom.

It was evening at the farmhouse. Olivier was building with blocks. Then all the lights went out. The room went dark.

Olivier ran to the wall. He flipped the light switch up. Nothing happened. He flipped it down. Still dark! "Mama, the light will not work!" he called.

Mama came with a big flashlight. She clicked it on. A bright circle shone on the floor. Olivier clapped his hands. He saw the switch do nothing, but the flashlight made light.

Mama found the key to the shed. She came back with a fuzzy blanket. They sat together on the big couch. The flashlight made a warm glow.

Dad made sandwiches in the kitchen. No cooking, just bread and cheese. Olivier ate his sandwich under the light.

Then the lights came back on. The whole room glowed bright! Olivier looked at the switch. "Mama, now can I try it?" he asked.

"Go ahead," said Mama. Olivier flipped the switch. The light went off. He flipped it again. The light came on. "It works now!" he shouted. He jumped up and down on the soft rug.

Jordan went to the library with his dad. It was a big day. Jordan was getting his first library card.

The card was blue. It had his name on it. Jordan held it with two hands.

"Now you can pick a book," said Ms. Tehrani.

Jordan looked at the shelves. They were tall. The books went up and up. Jordan was too small to reach them.

He took one small step. He stretched. Still too high.

Then he saw a little corner. It had small shelves. It had a red rug. It had books with big, bright pictures.

"This is the children's area," said Ms. Tehrani. "It has books just for young kids."

Jordan counted the books he wanted. One dinosaur book. One book about a bone. One book about a naughty little cat.

He picked the dinosaur book. Ms. Tehrani scanned his new card. Beep!

Jordan hugged the book. "Bye, book corner," he said. "I will come back."

Lucas sat in the big waiting room chair. His tummy felt a little sick. Today he would see the dentist for the very first time. "What will the dentist do?" he asked his mom. "She will look at your teeth," she said. A lady at the desk called his name. Lucas held his mom's hand.

The dentist had a bright light and a little mirror. "Open wide," she said. Lucas opened his mouth. "Your front teeth are for biting food," she said. "Your back teeth are for chewing it." She gave him a cup of water to drink. Then he was done. It did not hurt at all.

On the bus home, Mom gave Lucas an apple slice. Lucas bit it with his front teeth. A piece came off. Then he chomped it with his back teeth. The piece got small and soft. He tried it again. Front teeth bite. Back teeth chew. He smiled.

At school, his friend Van had a cracker. "Watch this," Lucas said. He bit with his front teeth. Then he chewed with his back teeth. Van laughed and tried it too. Ms. Nakamura came over. "Show me too," she said. Lucas took a big bite and chewed it all up. "All done," he said, and showed his clean teeth.

Charlie wants to make a paper sailboat. He needs two triangles for the sail. But he only has a square of paper.

He asks Ms. Bighorn for help. "I need two triangles," he says. "I only have a square." Ms. Bighorn smiles. She takes the scissors. She is careful, because scissors are sharp. "Watch," she says. She cuts from one corner to the opposite corner. The square falls into two pieces. "Two triangles!" says Charlie.

Now Charlie wants to try too. Ms. Bighorn holds his hand and the scissors together, so it is safe. They cut slowly, corner to corner. Snip, snip. Another square makes two more triangles.

Ayra comes to see. "You can teach me!" she says. Charlie shows her the square. He points to the corners. Ayra claps her hands.

Charlie tapes the triangles to his boat. He sets it on the floor. The boat has a big triangle sail. Ayra gasps. "It looks like a real boat!"

Then Charlie sees something funny. He puts two triangles side by side. They fit back into a square. He slides them apart. Two triangles. He pushes them together. One square. Charlie laughs out loud.

"Look, Ayra!" he says. "Two triangles make my square again."

Mohamed went to the art studio with his dad. He carried his box of crayons. He had left the box in the family car. The car sat in the sun all morning. Mohamed opened the box. "Oh no," he said. His crayons were soft. They bent like noodles. One gray crayon went droopy in his hand.

Mr. Yamamoto came to look. "Left in a hot car on a sunny day, crayons can melt," he said. Mohamed poked a red crayon. It made a fingerprint. Mohamed had an idea. He could draw with the soft crayons like paint. He pushed the red one across the paper. It left a fat, shiny stripe. Gordon and John came to watch. They wanted to try too.

Mohamed let them each pick one. Gordon took the blue one. John took the gray one. They made big, smooth lines. Then Mohamed helped stack the papers on the table to dry. The soft crayons made his picture look like magic. "Look, Dad," Mohamed said. "My melted crayons."

text:
Ayla pulled on her red boot. She was going to the farm with her dad. "Can I plant something?" she asked. "Yes," said the farmer. "Here are some little lettuce plants."

Ayla dug a hole with her hands. She set a plant in the dirt. She patted the dirt down. Sayed planted one too. "I wonder how big it will grow," said Ayla.

The sun came out. It got very hot. Ayla looked at her plant. The leaves were hanging down. "Your lettuce looks droopy," said Sayed. Ayla filled her watering can at the tap. She gave her plant a big drink of water. Sayed gave his plant a drink too.

The next day they came back. Ayla's lettuce stood up tall. The leaves were wide and green. "Look what the water did!" said Ayla. Ms. Tehrani, the farmer, smiled and cut one leaf. "Taste it," she said. Ayla took a little bite. It was crunchy. "Water and sun," she said. "That is all my plant needs."

Avery walked home on her street. She held a small box with holes. Inside was her new puppy, Sunny. Sunny was brown and furry. He licked her finger through a hole.

The next day, Sunny was not happy. He would not eat. He sat very still. Avery was worried. "He needs a doctor," she said.

Dad put Sunny in the car. Avery held the box on her lap. "Is Sunny going to my doctor?" she asked.

"No," said Dad. "Sunny is going to a vet. A vet is a doctor for animals."

The waiting room was full of pets. A cat sat in a basket. A big dog wagged his tail. His tail made Avery's box tip over, and Sunny almost fell out. Avery caught him just in time.

A kind vet looked at Sunny. She gave him some medicine on a little spoon. Sunny licked it all up. Then he wagged his tail. He gave Avery's hand a small, warm lick too.

On the walk home, Sunny walked beside Avery. He stopped to sniff a leaf. He tried to kick up some dirt with his back paw. Avery laughed and held his leash tight. "You feel better," she said. Sunny barked once, happy and loud.

Hazel had a cold. Her nose was red and her head felt hot. She stayed home in her warm bed.

The doctor said Hazel needed medicine. Her mom said, "We will meet the pharmacist at the pharmacy." Hazel asked, "Who gives us the medicine?" Her mom said, "The pharmacist gives it out."

At the pharmacy, Hazel sat in the cart. She watched the pharmacist behind the big counter. The pharmacist took a small white paper from the doctor. Then the pharmacist put a bottle in a bag. The pharmacist handed the bag to Mom. "Here is the medicine the doctor said Hazel needs," the pharmacist said.

At home, Mom gave Hazel a spoon of medicine. It tasted like cherry. Soon her nose felt better. Hazel hugged her bear and said, "The pharmacist helped me."

Ruby ran into Grandma's house. It was Christmas night. A big green tree stood by the window. It had no ornaments yet.

"Can I help?" Ruby asked. Grandma smiled. "Yes, you can hang the ornaments." Ruby picked up a shiny red ball. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a star there too. Then a sweet little snowman went on the same branch.

The branch began to bend down. One ornament slipped. It fell on the soft rug. "Oh no," said Ruby. "It did not break. It is okay," said Grandma. Ruby felt better.

"Watch me," said Grandma. She spread the ornaments out. She put one here and one there. She filled the whole tree, top to bottom. The tree looked full and bright.

Now Ruby tried. She hung a bell on a low branch. She hung a bird up high. She spread them all out, just like Grandma. The branches did not bend anymore.

Soon Mason came over with his dad. He saw the tree. "Wow," said Mason. "So many ornaments!" Ruby pointed up high. "I hung that gold star," she said. Grandma plugged in the lights. The whole tree glowed. "Merry Christmas," said Grandma, and she gave Ruby a hug.

Norah put on her sun hat. The sky was sunny and bright. She skipped to the front door. Her bag sat by the step, full of chalk. "I will draw a big sun," she said.

Naya and Wells were outside too. They wore light shirts and sandals. It was warm. Then the wind blew. Norah's hat went flying! Wells laughed and caught it. "Silly hat," he said. The trees waved their leaves. The sky turned gray.

Then came a big sound. Rumble! Rumble! Norah stopped still. Ms. Park called from her door. "When you hear thunder, go indoors," she said. Naya grabbed the chalk bag. Wells grabbed his hat. All three children ran to Norah's house. Norah's mom opened the front door. "Good running," she said. "Rain is coming."

Rain tickled the window. Tap, tap, tap. Inside, they drew suns on paper. "When it is snowy, we can wear boots," said Naya. "And puffy coats," said Wells. Norah yawned. The rain sang a soft song. Soon her chalk was asleep on the table. So was Norah, right there on the couch.

Elliot sat at the dinner table. His plate was almost empty. "All done!" he said. "Big day tomorrow," said Dad. "Ayansh is having a party!"

After dinner, Dad ran the bath. The warm water felt good. Elliot washed his toes. Then Dad helped him dry off.

"Now pajamas," said Dad. Elliot shook his head. "I want to sleep in my party shirt!" he said. He pulled it on. It was scratchy. It did not feel cozy at all. He wiggled. He squirmed. Then he took it off.

Elliot picked his soft pajamas instead. They had stars on them. He held them up. "These are for sleeping in!" he said. Dad smiled. Elliot felt the soft air from the fan on his nose. He climbed into bed, and he grew sleepy fast. "Night night, stars," he whispered. Dad turned off the light.

Ruby sat on the grass in her backyard. She was having a pretend picnic. Her friend Kaius came over with a plastic cup. "I brought water," he said.

Ruby's mom brought out a plate of fruit. There were apple slices, orange slices, and one yellow lemon slice. Ruby looked at the lemon with her eyes. It looked like the oranges. She thought it would taste like orange juice. Sweet!

Ruby touched the lemon slice with her fingers. It felt cold and a little bumpy. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled sharp and fresh. She squeezed it, and juice dripped out. The juice made a wet spot on the plate.

Then Ruby took a little bite with her mouth. Her tongue told her something. It was not sweet at all. It was sour! Ruby scrunched up her whole face. Kaius laughed. "Sour!" said Ruby. "My tongue says sour!"

They waited and watched. A bird sang, and they heard it with their ears. A wiggly worm slid by, and Ruby poked the slimy trail with one finger. Then her mom cut the lemon into the water in the plastic cup. "Try a sip," she said.

Ruby spped the lemon water. Still a tiny bit sour, but better. Ruby squeezed one more lemon slice. Drip, drip, more juice fell in. Now it tasted just right. "More, please," said Ruby, holding out her cup.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Joshua wanted to show him the park. "Bring a ball," said Grandpa. Joshua put the ball in his little bag.

At the park, Lilian and Samuelle were playing. Lilian had a small bike with red wheels. "My dad has a bike too," said Joshua. "A big one." Then he frowned. "But Dad was never small." Lilian laughed. Samuelle laughed too.

"Come here," said Grandpa. He sat on a bench near the swings. "Your dad was a little boy once. I remember it. He got his first bike, and he fell off. Then he got up. Then he fell off again." Joshua laughed loud. "Dad fell in the mud?" "Right in the mud," said Grandpa. "His shoes were brown for a week."

Joshua ran to tell Lilian. "My dad was little! And he fell in mud!" Lilian said her grandma told stories too. "Mine tells about my mom and a big cake."

Samuelle rolled the ball to Grandpa. Grandpa rolled it back, fast. Joshua chased it, laughing. "Tell another dad story on the way home," he said. Grandpa said, "I will tell the one about the frog."

Lennon sat at the big table. Her fries were hot and salty. Lisa sat next to her. Penelope sat across. On the wall was a huge screen. A soccer game was on.

"Look at the blue team run!" said Lennon. "They run so fast. They run the most."

The blue team ran and ran. But the ball went in the other net. The red team jumped up high.

Lennon frowned. She pointed at the screen. "Wait. The red team did not run much."

"That is the score," said Lisa. She pointed to the numbers.

Lennon looked. Red had two goals. Blue had zero. The wind blew a plastic napkin off the table and Lennon caught it, giggling.

Then red scored one more. The whistle blew. The game was over.

"Red wins!" said Penelope. "They have more points at the end!"

Lennon clapped her salty hands. "So running fast is not the game. Points are the game!"

She ate another fry and waved at the screen. "Goodbye, blue team. Practice your kicks!"

Charlie sat in her car seat. The car went over a bump. Her toy lion did a little spin in her lap. Her dad was driving. They were going to the library.

"I want a book about animals," said Charlie. "Where will we find one?"

"The library has shelves," said Dad. "The books sit in groups." He parked the car and turned off the phone on his dash.

Inside, the library was quiet. Charlie saw Aadya from her class. Aadya was holding a book about trucks. They walked together past the shelves. One shelf was full of toy books. Another shelf was full of food books. There were books about apples and bread.

Then Charlie saw it. A whole shelf of animal books. "The animal books live together," said Aadya. Charlie picked a big one with a sleepy lion on the cover. It looked just like her toy.

On the ride home, Charlie hugged the book. The sleepy lion smiled at her from every page.

Juliette went to the farmers' market with her dad. The sun made the apples shine. She bought a loaf of bread and a little jar of butter. "I want to do it myself," she said.

At home, Dad toasted the bread. Juliette took her favorite plate. She dipped the knife and spread the butter. It tore the bread at first. She tried again, slow and soft. This time the butter spread all around. "I did it," she said.

Then she poured milk into her cup. A little milk ran over. She wiped it with a cloth and poured again, slower. Not one drop spilled. When she was done, she picked up the milk. She carried it to the fridge and put it back inside. Dad smiled. Juliette took a big bite of her toast and said, "The milk goes in the fridge, and I do it myself."

Lea sat on the school bus. She held her letter cards on her lap. Her friend Julianna sat next to her. "Let's sing the alphabet," said Julianna.

They sang it together. Lea stopped singing at the letter P. "The song is done," she said. Julianna shook her head. "It goes on," she said. "Keep singing."

Lea sang on. Q, R, S, T. The bus rolled past their street. U, V, W, X. Lea pointed at each card. Then came Y. Then came Z.

"Z is the last one," said Julianna. "A is first, and Z is last." Lea looked at her cards. A was at the front. Z was at the back. "So A starts it," said Lea, "and Z ends it."

The bus stopped at their home street. The door opened high up on its steps. Julianna hopped down first. Lea held her cards tight. "A to Z," she said to herself. Then she sang the whole song, all the way to Z, as she walked to her door.

Elijah woke up in his bedroom. It was cloudy outside his window. Today was the day he would shop with Dad. But the shopping trip was later, not now.

"Is it later yet?" Elijah asked Dad. "Not yet," said Dad. "We will eat breakfast now." Elijah ate his eggs. "Is it later yet?" he asked again. "Not yet," said Dad. "First we put on shoes." Elijah put on his shoes. He looked at the clock. He could not read the clock. He looked out the window again. A rain puddle had appeared by the gate. Yesterday there had been no puddle there.

"Now it is later," said Dad. "Time to shop." Elijah jumped up. He saw the shoes on his feet. First breakfast, then shoes, then the puddle outside. One thing came after another, just like that. "Later came!" said Elijah. Dad laughed and held his hand. They stepped out the door, right past the puddle.

Levi went to the park with his dad. The sun was hot on his face. The shade under the tree was cool. Levi saw the big fountain and the small fountain. Ducks swam slow. A dog ran fast, and its balloon pop, pop, popped in the wind.

Levi wanted water for his thirsty duck game. He held his cup under the tap. The water ran fast. The cup filled up to the top. It spilled over his hand. "Dad, the cup is full!" said Levi. His dad smiled and gave him a new cup. "This one is empty," Levi said. He felt it. It was light.

Levi turned the tap just a little. The water ran slow, like a lazy little river. He watched it climb up the sides. He stopped before the top. "Not too full," said Levi. He carried the cup with two hands. It was heavy and wet and just right. The duck game could begin.

Hayden sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to know if his ears worked. "Let's check," said Ms. Brown, the nurse. She held a little bell near his ear. Ding! Ding! Hayden heard it with his ears. "I can hear it!" he said.

Next, Ms. Brown showed him a picture. Hayden used his eyes to see a red apple. She gave him a sticker to touch with his hands. It felt smooth and sticky. Then he smelled a mint with his nose. "Smell this," said Ms. Brown. Hayden sniffed. It smelled cool and fresh.

At the end, Hayden got a snack. He took a bite and tasted sweet banana in his mouth. On the way home, he took off his shoes in the backyard. The soft grass tickled his toes. "Mom! My feet can feel things too!" he said, wiggling his toes in the green, green grass.

Aurora found a book at daycare. It was a book about a doll who could move her arms. Aurora sat down to read it. But something was wrong. The doll looked funny. The doll looked upside down!

Isaac came over. "Your book is upside down," he said. He laughed. "The doll is standing on her head!" Aurora was a little scared. Would the doll fall? Aurora held the book and looked. The words looked upside down too. The pictures looked upside down too. "Poor doll," said Aurora. "I will help you."

Aurora turned the book around. Now the doll stood on her feet. The words stood straight too. "Ta-da!" said Aurora. Then she opened the front cover. "Front first," said Aurora. She read page one. Then page two. Then page three. "I did it!" she said. "I read the doll book all by myself."

Xavier sat in the big waiting room. He waited for his first haircut. The scissors were sharp, so the hairdresser used them carefully. Xavier watched from his chair.

Snip, snip. A little curl fell down. It landed on the cape. Xavier picked it up. It felt soft in his hand.

"Can we keep it?" he asked. His mom smiled. She took out a small envelope. She tucked the curl inside. "Some families keep a lock of hair from a first haircut," she said. "It helps us remember this day."

Xavier felt the envelope. It was light and small. His mom put it in her bag, like a tiny gift.

At home, Xavier showed the envelope to his dad. "Look!" he said. "It is my hair!"

Ivy had a new library card. She held it in her small hand. The card had her name on it. "Ivy," she read out loud.

At the library, Ivy picked a book about a big storm. The storm in the pictures had strong wind. The wind tickled the trees side to side. "I want this one," said Ivy.

Dad read the storm book at home. He read it two times. Then it was time to take it back. At the library, Dad pointed to a slot in the wall. "That is the book return slot," he said. "It is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library."

Ivy hugged the book tight. She did not want to let go. But then she held it up by the slot. "Bye bye, book," she said. She waved at it. She dropped it in. The book slid down, all gone.

Ivy put her hand on the slot. It was quiet now. Then she turned to the shelves. "Can I get a new one?" she asked. Dad laughed and nodded. Ivy ran to find a book about a strong, tickly kitten.

Amelia went to the park with Grandpa. Grandpa was staying at her house for a whole week. He held her hand on the path. They saw the big trees and the swings. A train went by at the edge of the park. It made a loud, rumbly sound. Amelia and Grandpa waved at it.

Then Grandpa sneezed. His nose was runny. "I need a tissue," he said. He looked in one pocket. He looked in the other pocket. No tissue. Amelia knew where tissues were at home, but they were not at the park. She looked around. Camilla was there with her dad. Camilla was kind. She had a small pack of tissues in her pocket.

"Here you go," said Camilla. Grandpa took one. He wiped his nose. "Thank you," he said. Amelia felt happy. At home that evening, Grandpa had a bath. When he came out, he could not find a towel. He did not cry, but he looked worried. Amelia ran to the cupboard. She pulled out a big soft towel. "The towels live here," she said. Grandpa smiled and put it around his shoulders. Then he gave her a piggyback ride to the kitchen.

Elliot was going on a big trip. He sat in the car with Mom and Dad. "We will stop at a diner for lunch," said Dad.

But then Dad took a wrong turn. The road did not look right. Dad stopped the car. "Oh no," he said. "I do not know this road."

Elliot had a big paper map in his bag. He held it up. "Look, Dad!" he said. "The map shows roads and places."

Dad looked at the map. He found the little line for their road. He found the blue dot for the diner. "The map shows the way," said Dad. "We can find the right road again."

They drove on. Soon they saw the diner. Snow was falling outside. Elliot froze at the window and pointed. "Snow! Can we watch it while we eat?"

Inside, Mom ordered pancakes. The waiter brought a naughty fly with them, buzzing near the syrup. Mom shooed it away, laughing.

"I like our map," said Elliot. He folded it up carefully. Then he took a big bite of pancake.

Charlie sat in a big waiting room chair. His feet did not touch the floor. "Today I see the dentist," he told his mom. He was a little scared, and a little excited too.

The waiting room had a yellow rug. It had a fish tank with small blue fish. A girl sat next to him. "My name is Liyana," she said. "I go first!" She skipped through the door.

Charlie waited. He heard a funny sound. It went hum, hum, hum. Then he heard Liyana giggle. "It leans back!" she called. "It is like a ride!"

The door opened. "Charlie, it is your turn," said the dentist. She had a nice smile. "Try sitting in my big chair," she said. Charlie climbed up. The chair was soft and warm from the sun.

"Here we go," said the dentist. She pushed a button. The chair slowly tipped back, back, back. Now Charlie was lying down! He giggled, just like Liyana. "Now I can see all your teeth," said the dentist. Charlie opened his mouth wide. He held very still. Above him he saw a bright little light. "Nice teeth," said the dentist. "You can pick a sticker."

Charlie picked a yellow sticker shaped like a hat. He ran out to show his mom. "The chair went back like a ride!" he said. Liyana waved at him from the fish tank.

Kayden sat at the little table at daycare. Mr. Nowak put a sandwich in front of him. The sandwich was cut into two triangles. Kayden picked one triangle up.

Kabir sat next to him with his juice. "Look at my sandwich," Kabir said. "It has corners." Kayden looked at his own triangle. He touched the corners with one finger. "One, two, three," he counted. "Three corners." He ran his finger along the edges. "One, two, three sides."

Mr. Nowak held up a round cracker. "This one has no corners," he said. "We call it a circle." Then he held up a napkin. "And this one is a square." Kayden looked at the square napkin. It had four sides, not three.

Kayden took a big bite of his triangle sandwich. "Still three corners," he said, with his mouth full. Kabir laughed. Kayden laughed too. He counted the corners again and again, "Three corners, three corners." Then he drank his juice, all gone.

Aubrey was at nursery when Mum came in. She carried a bundle. It was the new baby. Aubrey wanted to help feed him. She got her cracker from snack time. She held it out to the baby. "Bite this," she said.

Ms. Hamdan knelt down beside her. "Babies don't eat crackers," she said. "A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food."

Aubrey watched Mum hold a bottle. The baby drank and drank. Aubrey saw that. Milk went in, and the baby got sleepy. One thing made another thing happen.

Then Messiah stepped close to see. He looked out the window. "The sky is cloudy," he said.

The baby fell asleep. Mum wrapped him in a soft blanket. "Ice for my drink," she joked, sitting down.

"Can I hold him?" asked Aubrey.

Mum smiled. "Sit on the cushion first."

Aubrey sat very still. The baby snuggled close. He was warm and small.

"Hello, baby," whispered Aubrey.

Aubrey went to the playground with her dad. The sun was warm on the slide. The slide felt hot under her hand, so she slid down fast. "The slide is hot today," said Dad.

Aubrey saw a red ball near the tall fence. The fence was far, far away. She ran to the ball. She picked it up. Then she looked back. She could not see Dad. The big climbing frame was in the way. Aubrey stood still in the quiet air and waited. She waited, and she waited. Then she walked back around the climbing frame. There was Dad, waving.

"Found you," said Aubrey. She held up the red ball. Then dark clouds came, and soft drops of rain began to fall. Dad opened the umbrella. Aubrey stayed right under it, close to Dad, all the way home.

John went to the store with his dad. They had come early, before the big crowd. "We need a gift for Mom," said Dad. John felt excited. A gift! A real gift!

John looked at the shelves. One shiny cup. Two soft socks. Three red flowers. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three!"

Then the flowers fell over. Crash. John felt scared. His dad looked sad. "Oh no," said Dad. "Mom wanted those."

John looked up. "Daddy, are you sad?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Grown-ups get sad too. Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

John thought about that. Then he had an idea. He picked up one flower. It was still okay! "This one is fine," he said.

Dad smiled a big smile. John felt happy.

They bought the one red flower. John held it all the way home.

"A flower for Mom," he said.

Jaxon wanted to build a house for his teddy bear. He looked for shapes to use. He found a round plate. "That is a circle," he said. He found a book with four sides. "That is a rectangle," said his dad, walking by with the laundry.

Jaxon held the book up. He touched each side. One, two, three, four. Then he touched each corner. One, two, three, four. "Four sides and four square corners," he said. The corners felt pointy on his finger.

He looked around the room. Where were more rectangles? He asked himself, "Can a door be a rectangle?" He went to the door to find out. He counted the sides. Four. He counted the corners. Four. "Yes! The door is a rectangle, like my book!" He laughed. Teddy could have a door that looked like a real door.

He asked his mom, "Will you help me make the roof?" She cut a triangle from paper. The triangle had pointy corners too. It sat on top of the rectangle. "A triangle roof," said Jaxon. He put a little square inside for a window. He drew a small pond next to the house, and a circle sun above it.

Teddy sat inside the new house. He was not afraid of the dark now, because Jaxon left the door open. "Good night, Teddy," said Jaxon. Four sides, four square corners, and one happy bear.

Julia sat on the red rug at school. Mr. Nakamura held up a big card. It said FIVE SENSES. "We see, hear, smell, taste and touch," he said. "Can you say them?" Julia tried. "See with my eyes," she said. Timothy said, "Hear with my ears." Dion said, "Smell with my nose."

Julia wanted to say all five. She counted on her fingers. "Eyes, ears, nose," she said. Then she was stuck. "What comes next?" she asked. Mr. Nakamura smiled. "Take your time," he said. Dion whispered, "Mouth for taste." Julia counted again. "Eyes, ears, nose, mouth." One finger was left. "Hands for touch!" she said.

A huge truck rumbled by the window. It was so loud. Julia put her hands over her ears. The sound got quieter. She took her hands off. The rumble was big again. She put her hands back. Quiet again. "My ears hear," she said. "My hands help them."

Mr. Nakamura clapped. Julia held up five fingers. "Eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands," she said. Then she gave her hand a little kiss. "Good counting," she said.

Zachary was going for a car ride. Vroom, vroom! The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small road. "Fast and slow," said his dad. "They are opposites." Zachary laughed. Opposites!

At the store, Dad bought one big box and one small bag. Zachary wanted to help carry the big box. He pulled. He pushed. It was too heavy! The small bag was light. Zachary lifted it up high. So easy!

"Big and heavy," said Dad. "Small and light. Heavy and light are opposites too." Zachary hugged the light bag.

In the car, Zachary held his soft pillow. He put it on his lap. The pillow was light, so it stayed. He tried to put the box on his lap. Too heavy! Dad put the box in the back. Zachary told his pillow a story about a fast car and a slow turtle. Then he yawned. "Home soon," said Dad.

Addison sat at the red table. Viraaj had the whole box of crayons. Addison had none. She looked at the paper in front of her. It was all white. Would her picture stay white?

Ms. Bouchard knelt down beside her. "You can ask for a turn," she said softly. Addison reached out her hand. She wanted to grab the box. But she stopped. "Viraaj, can I have a turn?" she asked.

Viraaj looked at his crayons. Then he looked at Addison's white paper. He pushed the box to the middle of the table. "Sharing," he said. Addison picked a red crayon. She drew big circles. The circles looked like they could dance across the page. Viraaj took a blue one. They both drew at the same time. Soon the red table was covered with colors. Addison slid the box back to Viraaj. "Your turn," she said. Viraaj smiled and drew a sun.

Gabriella was at Grandma's house. Her friend Markus came to play too. On the floor sat one big box of blocks. Gabriella wanted them all. She grabbed the box with both hands. "My blocks!" she said. Markus looked sad. His foot tapped the floor. Grandma sat nearby in her soft chair. "There is one box," she said gently. "You can both play."

Gabriella held the box tight. Markus held his hands behind his back. He did not grab. He just waited. Gabriella peeked at him. He was still waiting. His face looked kind of sad and kind of patient at the same time. The room was quiet. The clock ticked on the wall.

Then Gabriella had an idea. She poured out all the blocks. They made a loud clatter. "We can build one big tower," she said. "Together." Markus smiled big. "Yes!" he said. They sat side by side on the rug. The rug felt warm under Gabriella's legs. Markus put one block down. Gabriella put the next one on top.

The tower grew tall. It was taller than Markus. It was almost as tall as the shelf. A little red block wobbled at the top. Gabriella reached out one finger. She tapped it very softly. The whole tower fell down. The blocks went crash. Then Markus laughed. Gabriella laughed too.

"Again?" asked Markus. "Again," said Gabriella. This time she passed him the first block. Grandma looked over from her chair and smiled. "What a tall tower," she said. Markus pushed a short green block toward Gabriella. "You start," he said. Gabriella put it down, and the tower began to grow again.

Evan was on the swim team. The team met at the big pool. Evan's family came to watch. Evan wore his orange swim cap.

By the pool there was a basketball hoop. It stood in the shallow water. Zachariah had the ball. He threw it. It hit the rim. It went splash into the water.

"Can I try?" asked Evan. "Yes," said Zachariah. Evan threw the ball. It went over the hoop. It went splash. "Miss again," said Evan. "Miss again!" He tried a big throw. Too hard. Too far. Splash.

Mr. Virtainen, the coach, came over. "Try a soft throw," he said. Evan held the ball up high. He aimed at the hoop. He threw it soft and slow. The ball went through the hoop. Then it fell down and went splash.

"A point for Evan," said Zachariah. Adriano clapped. "Again, again!" said Evan. He threw the ball through the hoop two more times. Splash, splash. Zachariah laughed. "The ball goes in the hoop and we get points," said Evan. "In the hoop. Points!"

Jasper stood at the far end of the soccer field. He had a red beanbag in his hand. In front of him was a big hoop on the grass.

"Throw it in, Jasper!" called Alessandro.

Jasper threw the beanbag. It flew up. Then it plopped on the grass. Not in the hoop.

Raven giggled. "The hoop ate a daisy instead!"

Jasper tried again. He threw it high. It bounced off the hoop. Still not in.

Jasper made a sour face. "Bad hoop," he said.

Then Jasper took three big steps. He walked closer to the hoop. He threw the beanbag again. This time it went in!

"Yay!" said Jasper. He jumped up and down.

"Your turn, Raven," said Alessandro.

Raven stood very far away too. She threw and missed. Then she walked closer, just like Jasper. Her beanbag went in too.

"Now the ball," said Mr. Walker. He rolled a big yellow ball to Jasper.

Jasper held out both hands. The ball came right at him. He squeezed it tight. He caught it!

"I got it!" said Jasper.

Alessandro rolled the ball next. Jasper held out both hands again. The ball bumped his tummy. He grabbed it and hugged it like a bear.

Then Jasper ran to the hoop with the beanbag one more time. He stood close. He tossed it up.

"In!" he shouted. "Easy peasy!"

Raven clapped her hands. "Do it again, Jasper!"

Jasper picked up the beanbag. He smiled a big smile. "Watch me," he said.

Ali stood in the backyard with his friend Paris. Today the new baby came home. Ali was going to have a party for the baby. He had a red balloon and a paper hat.

Then the baby began to cry. The cry was loud. It was not a small cry at all. Ali frowned. "Why does the baby cry so much?" he asked. Paris tipped her head. "Maybe the baby is scared of the balloon?" she said.

Ali let the balloon go. It floated up to the tree. But the baby still cried. The baby's cry sounded weak, like a little kitten. Ali wondered what to do. He jumped back inside the house. His dad was there. The dad picked the baby up. The dad gave the baby milk. Then the baby stopped crying and made a small sound. A happy sound!

Ali ran back out to Paris. "The baby was talking!" he said. "The baby can't talk with words yet. So the baby cries when it needs something. The cry means, please help me." Paris clapped her hands. Then the red balloon came down from the tree. It landed right on the baby's blanket. The baby grabbed it with one tiny hand and held on tight. "Look," said Ali. "The baby likes parties after all."

Rose rode the city bus with her dad. The bus was big and a little heavy when it rumbled. Rose held his hand. "Library next," she said. She drank her milk at the stop, quick and cool.

At the library, Rose got her very first card. It was red, like her name. "Now pick a book," the librarian said.

Rose found a book about puppies. She put it back on the wrong shelf. A boy named Salem did that too. The librarian smiled. "Look at the spine," she said. "The label on the spine shows where the book belongs on the shelf." Rose looked. The label matched the shelf! She put the puppy book in its right spot. Salem put his back too.

On the bus home, Rose hugged her card. "My book goes back to its spot," she said. Her dad laughed softly. Rose patted the book, right on its spine.

Olivia ran into the art room. She wore her new shirt with the white stars. Mr. Navarro put big paint pots on the table. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

"Can I paint now?" Olivia asked.

"First put on this apron," said Mr. Navarro. "It keeps paint off your clothes."

Olivia slipped the apron over her head. It was long and black. Then she picked up a spoon and scooped some red paint. She dropped it on her paper. She scooped some yellow too. She mixed them round and round. The paint turned orange! Her new shirt stayed clean.

"Look, Kacey!" said Olivia. "Red and yellow make orange."

"Can I try?" said Kacey.

Mr. Navarro gave her an apron too. Kacey mixed blue and yellow. Her paint turned green.

Olivia clapped her hands. "Mixing colours is fun!"

Evelyn put on her boots at daycare. Yesterday it was rainy. She could hear the rain on the roof then. Today the sun came out.

"Let's go to the playground," said Kaison. Evelyn ran outside. The sun felt warm on her face.

Then she saw it. A big puddle sat on the ground. It was right by the slide. "A puddle!" said Evelyn.

Kaison jumped in. Splash! His boots got all wet. Evelyn wanted to splash too. But she looked down. She had her sneakers on, not her boots.

"I need my boots," she said. Ms. Weber was kind. "They are by the door," said Ms. Weber. Evelyn ran back inside the little house. She found her red boots. She pulled them on all by herself.

She ran back out. She stepped in the puddle. Splash! Water went up and down. Her socks stayed dry.

"Rain makes puddles," said Evelyn. Kaison laughed. "Big ones!" he said. Then the wind blew a little. It moved the water in the puddle. Evelyn watched it wiggle.

It was a sunny day with one rainy-day puddle left. Evelyn splashed it all gone.
