Peyton went to the farm with her class. Maximilian held her hand on the path. Ms. Virtanen had a big box. "We will learn our senses today," she said.

First Peyton touched a feather. "Soft," she said. Her skin felt it. Then she touched a pinecone. "Ow. Rough," she said. Her skin felt that too. Vyom touched a red blanket. "This one is soft," he said. Peyton put the feather and the blanket in the soft pile. She put the pinecone in the rough pile. They counted the piles together. One, two.

Then they heard a cow. "Moo!" Peyton used her ears. She smelled hay and used her nose. She saw a duck far away and used her eyes. Maximilian was sad he could not hear the cow. Peyton took his hand and put it near the gate. "Listen," she said. The cow mooed again, and Maximilian smiled.

Elias ran out to the school yard. It had rained all morning. Now the sun made the puddles shine like little blue mirrors. A big puddle sat by the gate. A small puddle sat by the wall. Elias stomped right into the big one. Splash! Cold water went into his shoe. His sock was wet. Very wet.

"Wet and dry are opposites," said Mr. Grant. "Come with me." Elias walked slow through the hall. Squish, squish, squish. Mr. Grant found a dry pair of socks in the big box. Elias pulled off the wet sock. He blew on his cold toes to warm them up. Then he put on the dry sock. It felt soft and warm. Then came a surprise. The lamp on the shelf blinked on. The lamp had a plug on a timer, and it buzzed a little. "What made the lamp go on?" Elias asked. Mr. Grant smiled. "Something inside," he said. Elias sat under the warm lamp until his other shoe dried.

Max sat on the soft rug. He had a box of blocks. The blocks were red and blue. Each one had a square shape.

Max made two piles. He touched each block. "One, two, three, four," he said. The first pile had four blocks. He counted the second pile. "One, two, three," he said. The second pile had three blocks.

"Which pile has more?" Mom asked. Max looked and looked. He pointed at the pile of four. "This one has more," he said.

Then Mom gave him one more block. It was blue. Max rolled it on the rug. It did not roll far. He put it on the small pile. Now he counted again. "One, two, three, four," he said. His eyes got wide. "Now it has four too!"

Max stacked the blocks into a tall tower. It stood up high. He touched the top block with one finger. "My tower has four," he said. "Same, same, same."

Myles was playing in the yard. He wanted to find a pinecone for his truck. He looked under the big bush. He saw something small and shiny there. It was a little lighter.

Myles knew about lighters. His dad used one for the grill. The grill got hot. His dad had said, "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." Myles did not touch it.

He ran to the door. "Dad! Come see!" he called. His dad came out. Myles pointed at the bush. His dad picked up the lighter. "Good job telling me," he said. He put it high on a shelf inside.

Then Dad let Myles help with lunch. Myles washed tomatoes at the sink. The water felt warm on his hands. The water from the other tap was cold. Myles laughed. "One tap is warm, one is cold!" he said. His dad smiled and tickled his ear.

They ate sandwiches together at the table. Myles looked out the window at the yard. His pinecone was still under the bush. "Can you get it later?" he asked Dad. Dad said, "Yes, right after lunch, buddy."

Iris was at Grandpa's house. She wanted to play in the garden. "Can I go out now?" she asked. "It is cold outside," said Grandpa. "A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold."

Iris ran to the door without her coat. She opened it a little. The cold air touched her arms. "Brr!" said Iris. She shut the door fast. "My arms are cold," she said. "I need my coat."

Grandpa held her orange coat. "Try to put it on yourself," he said. Iris pushed her arm in one sleeve. It went the wrong way. She tried again, slow and careful. This time her arm went in. Then the other arm went in too.

"Now the zipper," said Iris. She held the bottom of it. She pulled it up. It got stuck. She waited. She pulled again, little by little. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

Iris ran outside. The cold air was there, but she was warm. A small bird sat on the fence. "Bird, are you warm too?" Iris asked. The bird hid its head under its wing. Grandpa laughed from the door. "I did it all by myself," said Iris, and she jumped in a pile of leaves.

Gabriella wanted to wear her red socks. It was bedtime, but she knew just where they were. They sat in her drawer, by the wall.

The room was very dark. Gabriella could not see much at all. She felt in the drawer with her hands. She found two socks that felt soft. She pulled them on her feet. Then she went to sleep.

In the morning, the sun came in. The window was bright. Gabriella looked down at her feet. One sock was red. One sock was green. She laughed out loud.

"I picked them in the dark," she said. "The dark room hid the colors."

Her dad came in. "Nice socks," he said, and smiled.

Gabriella took off the green sock. She put it back in the drawer. "I will look in the light," she said. She picked two red socks. Now both feet matched.

At lunch, she sat with Robyn. Robyn had a yummy sandwich. Gabriella had one too. Robyn pointed at Gabriella's socks. "Both red," said Robyn.

"Yes," said Gabriella. "I got them in the morning light." She wiggled her toes, and the two red socks wiggled too.

Clara sat on the big red couch at Mr. Marino's house. Her mom sat next to her. Imran and Emberly sat on the floor. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Clara loved game night.

The players ran up and down the field. One team kicked the ball into the net. Everyone clapped. Then the other team kicked the ball in too. The numbers on the screen showed two and two. Clara leaned in to see them.

"Who won?" Clara asked.

Mr. Marino smiled. "Nobody won," he said. "Both teams have the same score. It is called a tie."

"A tie," Clara said softly. She looked at the numbers again. Two and two. The same. She pointed at the screen. "See, Mom? The same. So it is a tie."

Emberly held up two fingers on each hand. "Same, same," she said. Imran laughed and did it too. Clara laughed with them.

At bedtime, Clara found two socks, one blue and one red. She put one on each hand. "Look, Mom. Two and two. Same score. It's a tie!" Her mom laughed and kissed her head.

"Tie game," Clara whispered to her socks.

Aurora wanted warm milk. Her dad poured it into a big cup. The cup was too hot to touch. Dad held it high and counted. "One, two, three. Blow, Aurora." She blew slow puffs. The milk got cooler. It went from hot to cold enough to sip.

Shehbaaz came over to play. They sat at the small kitchen table. Shehbaaz kicked off one sock under the table. "Let's play the opposite game," he said. "I say a word. You say one as different as it can be." He said, "Big." Aurora shouted, "Small!" He said, "Fast." Aurora ran her finger round the cup quick. Then she said, "Slow," and moved it gentle.

Dad brought cold apple slices. The fridge hummed loud, then quiet. Shehbaaz said, "Hot." Aurora touched her warm cup. "Cold," she said, and hugged the apple slices to her chest. Shehbaaz found his lost sock. He put it back on. "Big sock," he said. Aurora laughed and said, "Small toes!" Then they ate every slice, one, two, three, four, five.

Isabella went to the animal clinic with her dad. Behind the clinic was a room with cages. Cats sat in some. Dogs sat in others. A sign said "Adopt Me."

"Adopt?" said Isabella. "What does adopt mean?"

Mr. Banerjee worked there. "Adopt means a pet waits for a family," he said. "Then the family takes the pet home."

Isabella looked in every cage. So many pets were waiting! A small black cat reached out one paw. Isabella pointed at her. "This one is waiting for me."

The cat purred when Isabella touched her soft fur. Isabella was so happy.

They put the cat in a box with holes. A truck outside honked its horn. The cat's ears went up.

At home, Isabella filled the water bowl. The cat drank right away. Food went in, and the cat munched. Isabella gasped. "Dad! I gave her water. Then she drank it!"

The cat curled up on Isabella's lap. "Now we are your family," Isabella whispered.

Zoey sat at the kitchen table. Mom was baking bread. "What is that smell?" Zoey asked. "It smells sweet and warm." Mom smiled. "You smell it with your nose," she said. Zoey sniffed. The sweet smell went right into her nose.

Zoey had a job from school. She had to name her five senses. She was a little sad. She could only think of one. "I know smelling," she said. "My nose does that." Mom said, "Let's find the rest together."

Mom held up a lemon. "Close your eyes," she said. Zoey closed her eyes. She sniffed the lemon. "I smell it," she said. Then she touched it. "It feels bumpy." She opened her eyes. "My hands feel things." She looked at the yellow lemon. "My eyes see it." Mom cut a slice. "Taste this little bit," she said. Zoey tasted it. "Sour!" she said. "My tongue tastes it." Then the toast popped. Pop! "I heard that with my ears."

"Smell, touch, sight, taste, hearing," said Zoey. "My nose, my hands, my eyes, my tongue, my ears." She counted them on her fingers. Five senses, all found. Mom gave her warm bread with honey. "My tongue likes this one best," said Zoey. She gave Mom a big hug.

Madison found a red book on the rug. She opened it in the middle and looked. The letters made squiggles on every page. "What do they say?" she wondered.

She carried the book to Ms. Qureshi. "Who made this up?" she asked. Ms. Qureshi turned to the front cover. She pointed to a name there. "This is the author," she said. "The author wrote the words." Madison touched the name with her finger. The words had a person!

Then Ms. Qureshi turned to the first page. "We start here," she said. She turned page after page, one at a time, all the way to the end. Madison watched the story grow.

After rest time, Madison picked up the red book again. She opened it at the front, where the author's name sat. Jocelyn came over and sat down close. Madison pointed at the name. "This person wrote the words," she said. She turned the first page.

James looked out the window. The big tree was moving. Its branches swayed back and forth. Leaves flew across the yard. "Look at the tree dance!" said James.

James wanted to catch one leaf. He put on his boots. He zipped up his coat. He ran outside. The wind pushed the leaves around. They rolled and tumbled. James chased a red leaf. He chased a yellow leaf. His leg went fast, fast, fast. The leaves blew away from him every time. "Silly wind!" he laughed.

Then the wind blew a leaf right at him. It landed on his head. "I got one!" he said. It was a neat orange leaf with pointy edges. James hoped the wind would blow one more. It did. It blew one right onto the gate. James picked it up too. "Two leaves!" he said. "The tree gave me a present."

Sadie sat in the family car. Her hair was long and full of knots. "Today is your first haircut," said her dad. "Hooray!" said Sadie.

At the salon there was a big fish tank. Blue fish swam round and round. Sadie turned her head to watch them. Snip, snip went the scissors. But Sadie kept turning. One piece of hair came out too long. One piece came out too short. "Oh dear," said the hairdresser. "Please sit very still. Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly."

Sadie thought of the strong statue by the lake near her house. That statue never moved at all. "I will be a statue," said Sadie. She looked straight ahead. She sat very still, still, still. Snip, snip, snip. The hairdresser smiled. "Look now," she said. Sadie turned at last. In the mirror was a neat, shiny bob. It was even and smooth all over.

In the car, Sadie asked her dad, "Can we show Leonidas and Tenley?" "Yes," said Dad. "First let's drive past the lake." Sadie waved at the strong statue. "You helped me," she told it. The little blue fish swam on in her mind, round and round.

Milan was playing in the playroom. He poured toy animals out of a big red box. A lion, a pig, a duck, a rabbit. Then he saw something soft near the rug. It was a small grey feather. It tickled his nose.

Elowyn came to play. "Look," said Milan. "A real feather!"

"Who lost it?" asked Elowyn.

Milan held the feather up to the duck. "Not you. Your feathers are plastic." He looked around the room. He looked at the window. Then he made a circle with his finger on the cold glass.

"A bird has feathers," said Milan. "So a bird was here!"

Outside, a little grey bird sat on the windowsill. It flapped its wings. Tiny feathers puffed into the air. The bird tapped the glass. Tap, tap.

"Hello, bird," said Milan. He waved the feather back.

Xavier sat at the dinner table. He had five carrots on his plate. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

His dad set down a box of crackers. There was a big 5 on the box. Xavier looked at it. He looked at his carrots. He held up five fingers. "Five," he said. Then he pointed at the box. "Five."

"That 5 means five," said his dad. He poured some milk into Xavier's cup. The milk went splash, splash.

Xavier wanted to share his crackers with the cat. "Can the cat have one?" he asked. "Just one cracker," said his dad. The cat got one small cracker. Xavier counted again. "One, two, three, four, five carrots. And one cat."

His friend Mona was coming after dinner. He wanted to save her a cracker. So he counted his crackers, too. "One, two, three, four, five. Five crackers! Same as my carrots." He put three crackers in a bowl for Mona. The bowl had a little 5 on the bottom.

"What a good dinner," said his dad.

Xavier smiled and took a big bite of carrot. "Six, seven, eight carrots next time," he said. "Maybe nine. Maybe ten."

Maverick stood in his bedroom. His socks were on the floor. His shirt was on the floor too. He wanted to play basketball, but the ball was far away in the garage.

Then he saw the laundry basket. "Socks can be my ball," he said. He picked up one sock. He tossed it. It went in! "One point for Maverick!"

He picked up the other sock. Toss. "Two points!" He threw his shirt too. "Three points!" Now the floor was clean. All the dirty clothes were in the basket.

Kaitlyn came to play. "Watch me," said Maverick. "One sock, two socks, three socks, in the basket!" Kaitlyn laughed and tossed her sweater too. "Four!" she said.

His mom came in. "The dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed," she said. "Thank you, Maverick." She carried the basket away.

Later, Maverick put on his pajamas. They smelled like flowers. "My basketball socks got washed!" he said. He jumped into bed.

"Goodnight, basketball star," said his mom. She pointed at a picture on the wall. It showed a big player with a ball.

"Tomorrow I will score five points," said Maverick. He closed his eyes.

Florence sat at the dinner table. Her basket of little pictures had tipped over. Cards went everywhere. Some fell under her chair. One landed in her dirty bowl.

Florence wanted to find her cat card. It was her best card. But the cards were all mixed up on the table.

"Let's make piles," said her dad. He sat down next to her. Florence picked up a card. It had a dog on it. "Animals go here," her dad said. He made a pile.

Florence found a card with a ball. She put it in a new pile. "Toys," she said. Then she found a card with a banana. She made a third pile. "Foods," she said.

She put the dog with the cow and the bird. She put the ball with the teddy bear. She put the banana with the bread and the egg.

The cat card was not in any pile yet. Florence looked under her chair. It was not there. She looked at her dirty bowl. There it was, stuck to the rim.

She pulled it out. It was a little wet. Her dad wiped it with a napkin. Florence put the cat on the animals pile. The pile was big now.

All the cards had a pile. The table looked tidy again. Florence put the basket back on the shelf.

"Can we do it again after dinner?" she asked.

"Maybe with a treat," said her dad. "A cookie can be first in the foods pile."

Lennon woke up early. She looked out the window. The sun was up. "Is it today?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is today. Today is the day that is happening right now." Lennon clapped her hands. Today was the pond day!

Yesterday, Mom had said, "Not today. Tomorrow we go to the pond." Lennon had waited. She had eaten dinner. She had slept in her little bed. Now the waiting was done. Yesterday was gone. Today was here.

Lennon put on her red boots. She looked for her sun hat. It was under the bed. "Found it!" she said. Mom packed some crackers and water. "We will meet Zia there," said Mom. "Zia is coming today too."

At the pond, Zia was already waiting. "You came!" said Zia. "It is today!" The two girls sat by the water. They watched the ducks swim. A young duck wobbled behind its mom. Lennon dropped a small leaf in the pond. The water moved it. The leaf floated away. "Look," said Lennon. "The water pushes it."

Later, they ate crackers on the grass. "Can we come back tomorrow?" asked Zia. Lennon looked at Mom. "Tomorrow is not right now," said Lennon. Mom laughed softly. "That is right. Tomorrow comes after we sleep." Lennon yawned a big yawn. "Now it is time to go home," said Mom. Lennon held Zia's hand. "See you another today," she said.

Jaxson went to the library with his mom. He saw a big red book on the shelf. He wanted to look at it all by himself.

He pulled the book down. He opened it up. But he opened it at the wrong end. The pages went from left to right the wrong way. "This story is all mixed up," Jaxson said. The dog in the picture came before the boy. That was silly. Then the dog began to bark, but the page was before the part where they met the dog.

His friend Natalie came over. "That book is backwards," she said. Jaxson looked at the covers. He saw the shiny side with the title. He turned the book around in his hands.

Now the book started at the front cover. Jaxson turned the pages one by one. The boy met the dog first. Then the dog barked. Then they ran fast through the mud. It all made sense now. Page by page, the story went on and on.

Mr. Malik, the library man, smiled at Jaxson. "You read that book from front to back," he said. Jaxson held the big red book to his chest. "I can read it again," he said. "From the front!"

Mila sat at the big table. Grandma put down a warm bowl of rice. It smelled sweet and steamy. Everyone held hands.

"Now we say our blessing," said Grandpa.

Mila did not know the words yet. She wanted to say them too. She looked at Grandpa. His eyes were closed. His head was bowed down low.

Mila peeked at Grandma. Grandma's eyes were closed too. Her head was also bowed. Mila peeked at her cousin. Closed eyes. Bowed head. Even the baby rabbit on her cousin's shirt looked asleep.

Grandpa said the blessing. Mila listened to every word. Then everyone said, "Amen," and opened their eyes.

"Now we eat!" said Grandma.

Mila fixed her little napkin on her lap. "Can we say it again?" she asked.

"After the next meal," said Grandpa. He smiled and gave her a soft piece of bread.

Mila held the warm bread in both hands. "Close eyes," she whispered to herself. "Bow head." She closed her eyes tight, just for fun. When she opened them, her plate had a scoop of rice on it.

"Grandma put it there!" said her cousin.

Mila giggled and took a bite.

Brielle carried her little drum to the community center. Today was the big music day. Riley and Aliya were there too. Mr. Lin smiled and said, "Time to play!"

Brielle tapped the drum. Boom, boom! Riley clapped. Aliya clapped. The teacher clapped. Brielle felt so happy. Then she saw the big kids on stage. A girl played a song. The people clapped and clapped. The girl bent down low. She bowed! Brielle watched with wide eyes.

Now it was Brielle's turn on stage. She played her drum. Boom, boom, boom! Everyone clapped. Brielle almost ran off. Then she stopped. She remembered the big girl. Brielle bent down low, just like her. She bowed! The claps got louder. Riley called out, "Do it again!" Brielle took her last bow and hugged her drum.

Luca was on the swim team. The pool smelled like water and sunshine. His friend Austin was on the team too. Coach said, "Time for practice. We learn skills and get ready for games."

Luca wanted to play with the baby duck he saw at the edge of the pool. "Can I skip practice?" he said.

"Not yet," said the coach. "First we practice." Luca kicked his legs at the wall. He blew bubbles in the water. The water felt cool on his cheeks.

Then the game began. Luca had to swim to the other side. He kicked and kicked. His arms went round and round. Was the practice helping him?

He touched the wall first! Austin clapped. "You got so fast!" he said.

The baby duck paddled by. It was practicing too, splashing its little feet.

"Can we practice again tomorrow?" Luca said.

Sara and her dad walked to the pool. The pool was next to the beach. Sara could hear the waves. They went swish, swish on the sand.

Sara wanted to swim in the far end. Waylon was already there. The water was up to his shoulders. Sara stepped in. The water was only up to her knees here. She walked a little more. Still just her knees. Then she looked far across the pool. There, the water was over Elora's head.

"This end is shallow," said Mr. Augustin, the teacher. "That end is deep." Sara looked down. The water near her feet was clear and light. The deep end looked blue and dark.

Sara held the soft foam bar. She kicked and kicked. Little waves went up and down. The water felt cool on her toes. Waylon clapped for her.

"Now let's try the old ladder," said Mr. Augustin. Sara touched the wet metal rail. She climbed one step. She looked at the beach. The sun was warm on her nose.

"When I am big, I will say hello to the deep end," said Sara. Mr. Augustin smiled. "One day," he said. Sara kicked her feet in the water, and the little waves kissed her chin.

Gabriel sat at the piano in Ms. Yilmaz's studio. He tried to play his song. His fingers went bump, bump, wrong. "This song is too hard," said Gabriel. "My fingers kick each other instead of playing!"

Ms. Yilmaz laughed a kind laugh. "Play just a little today," she said. "Then a little tomorrow too." Gabriel played the first part. Then he played it again. It was still tricky.

The next day, Gabriel came back. He was not late, because he ran fast like a little plane zooming to the studio. He played the first part. It came out smooth! "Wow," said Gabriel. He played the next part too. Then he played the whole song, all the way to the end. Ms. Yilmaz clapped her hands. Gabriel clapped too. "Again!" he said, and his fingers began to dance.

Elijah stood on the balcony. The pots were empty. He wanted to plant seeds. His dad helped him fill the pots with soft brown soil. Elijah pushed three little seeds into the dirt. He patted the top. "Grow, seeds," he said.

Every morning Elijah came to look. The soil stayed brown and quiet. He gave the seeds a little water. He waited and waited. His friend Darius came to see. "Where are your plants?" Darius asked. "Still sleeping," said Elijah.

One sunny morning, Elijah peeked at the pot. Something small and green was there. It stood up out of the soil. It was a tiny new plant! Elijah ran inside. "Dad! Dad! A little green thing came up!" Dad smiled. "That is called a sprout," he said. Elijah clapped his hands. "Hello, sprout," he said. "Do you want more water?" The sprout stood in the sun, small and green and new.

Jayden sat in his reading nook at home. He had a pad of paper and a fat crayon. Mom sat close by in the big chair.

Jayden wanted to write his name all by himself. He made a small j. Then he made a, y, d, e, n. He looked at his paper. "Mom, why does Drew's name look different?"

Mom held up Drew's card from the desk. "Look at the first letter," she said. "Drew's name starts with a big D."

Jayden looked at his paper. His j was small and little at the start. The big letters seemed scary to make. They were so tall! "Can a big j get stuck?" he asked.

"Just try it," said Mom. "Start at the top and pull down."

Jayden tried. The big J came out tall and strong. He smiled. He could fix his name himself. He wrote JAYDEN with all big letters. Then he wrote it again with just one big J at the start.

Mom clapped. Jayden held up his paper high. "J is for Jayden!" he said.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Rowan stood in the dark kitchen. "Mama!" he called. "The lights are stuck off!" Mama came in with a big torch. "The power is out," she said. "We will keep the fridge door shut so the food stays cold longer."

Rowan wanted his yogurt. He ran to the fridge and put his hand on the door. Then he remembered. Shut stays the cold in. He pulled his hand back. "I will keep it shut!" he said.

Moma laughed. "Good job, Rowan." They sat by the window with a blanket. It was winter, and stars filled the sky. Rowan counted them out loud. Soon the lights came back on. Rowan clapped his hands. "The power is back!" he shouted. "Now can I open the fridge?" "Yes," said Mama. Rowan opened the door. The milk was still cold. He hugged the cold milk jug and laughed.

Freya was at home in the yard. Lyle came to play. They both saw the red swing. Freya ran fast. Lyle ran fast too. They got to the swing at the same time.

"I want it first," said Freya. "I want it first," said Lyle. Freya held the swing rope tight. Her tummy felt tight too. Mom came outside with a yummy snack of apple slices. "You can share the swing," Mom said. "Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another."

Lyle went first. Freya counted to ten. The swing went up and down, squeak, squeak. Then Lyle jumped off. "Your go now," he said. Freya climbed on. The wind touched her face. She kicked her legs high. Lyle rolled a soft ball to her. She laughed. "My turn again after yours," said Lyle. Freya nodded and swung higher.

Hazel stood at the little paint table at the art gallery. Mr. Navarro had set out red, yellow and blue. "We need a mountain picture," he said. Hazel wanted a big orange mountain. She knew red and yellow could make orange. She had seen it once.

She dipped her brush in the red. She painted a small sun. Then she dipped the same brush in the yellow. But the yellow pot turned a muddy brown. Hazel frowned. Her sun looked dirty now.

Louane was painting next to her. "Watch," Louane said. She dipped her brush in the water cup. She swished it around. Then she took fresh yellow. It stayed bright and clean.

Hazel dipped her brush in the water. She swished it well. Then she picked up red, and then yellow. She mixed them on her paper. Orange! A big, clean orange mountain grew under her sun. Kayla leaned over and said, "That orange is so bright."

Gianna sat in the big chair at Grandma's house. She held her little book of letters. "I want to find them all," she said. "But some letters look tricky." Grandma smiled. "Let's look around the room," she said.

Grandma pointed out the window. "Sun," she said. "S. It says sss." Gianna said, "Sss. Sun!" Then she looked down at her feet. Her sock had a duck on it. "Sss. Sock!" she said. Grandma laughed and clapped.

Gianna ran to the toy box. She scooped up sand in her toy cup. It was sand from the beach jar. "Sss. Sand!" she said. "Sun, sock, sand. They all say sss!" She gave her teddy bear a big hug. "You start with B, bear. You say buh." The bear did not mind. He was not an ugly bear. He was soft and sweet.

Grandma sat down next to Gianna. "You found three S words," she said. "Sun, sock, sand." Gianna kissed the bear's nose. "Tomorrow we find more," she said.

Jack got to school with his yellow truck. "Today is truck day," he said. Mr. Aziz smiled. "Yesterday you forgot the truck," he said. "Now you have it!"

Jack wanted to show Kevin. But Kevin was not there yet. "Where is Kevin?" Jack asked. "He will come later," said Mr. Aziz. Jack waited. He counted his truck's wheels. One, two, three, four.

At circle time, Kevin came in. "I woke up this morning," said Kevin. "I ate breakfast fast. Then Mom drove me here." Jack looked up. Morning was the wake-up time. Morning was the breakfast time. That was why Kevin came after Jack!

"Now we play," said Mr. Aziz. Jack rolled the truck to Kevin. "Tomorrow we play trucks again," said Jack. Kevin laughed. "Tomorrow, yes! One truck, two friends, all morning long."

Bennett wore his blue swim shorts to the pool. The pool sat right by the big beach. His friend Luka was already there. So was Mr. Fraser, the swim teacher.

"Today we float on our backs," said Mr. Fraser. Bennett looked at the water. He did not want to float. The water looked too deep. A little green frog sat by the pool edge. It kicked its legs and swam away. "That frog is neat," said Luka.

Mr. Fraser put his hands under Bennett's back. "My hands will hold you," he said. Bennett lay back. He felt the hands under his back. He did not sink. He lay on top of the water like a leaf.

"My turn!" said Luka. Mr. Fraser held Luka's back too. Luka floated. Then Bennett tried again, with the hands still under him. He looked up at the sky. He heard the waves on the beach. "I can float!" said Bennett. Mr. Fraser smiled and kept his hands right there.

Theo wants to help at snack time. He takes the cup basket to the table.

"Count the cups," says Mr. Rivera. "We need ten."

Theo touches a cup. "One." He touches another. "Two." Then he says, "Four."

Ria frowns. "You jumped. Try again."

Theo counts, "One, two, four." Still four. He looks at the cups. They are squishy and easy to squeeze. He squeezes one and thinks.

Ria lines up the cups in a row. "Now touch each one," she says.

"One," says Theo. "Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten."

"Ten cups!" says Mr. Rivera. "Snack can start."

Theo counts the crackers too. "One, two, three, four, five." He hands a plate to Ria first. She smiles.

"I know the numbers now," says Theo. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Mila sat on the playroom floor. She wanted to build a tall tower. Noa came to help.

"One, two, three," said Mila. She stacked the blocks. Noa added more. "Four, five, six." The tower wobbled a bit. "Seven, eight, nine." The tower was so tall now. Then Mila put on one more block. "Ten!" she shouted. Ten blocks!

Mila wanted to make a sign for the tower. She found paper and a crayon. She wrote a big 6. Noa laughed. "Silly! We need ten."

Mila tried. She drew a 1. Then she stopped. "That says one," said Mila. Noa looked at the paper too. Then Mila drew a 0 right after the 1. She held it up. "Ten!" said Noa. "Ten is one and zero!"

Mr. Whitaker came in. "What a neat tower," he said. His phone did ring, ring, ring in his pocket. He showed the kids a toy medicine kit. "Doctor kit," he said.

Mila taped the sign on the tower. "Ten," she read. Ten is one and zero!

Grandma was coming on a big plane. Sophia held her papa's hand at the airport. "We wait here," Papa said. "This is the arrivals area. People come out of that door." Sophia watched the door. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" said Sophia. "No," said Papa, smiling. "Not yet." A lady with a red bag came out. "Grandma!" said Sophia again. "Not yet," said Papa. Sophia waited. She heard shoes going tap, tap. She smelled coffee. Then the door opened one more time. Grandma! Sophia ran and hugged her deep and tight. Later they sat on the train at the station. Grandma had a small plant for Sophia's desk at home. "I get to stay a whole week," said Grandma. Sophia clapped. The train blew its whistle, and off they went.

Mackenzie woke up in the tent. "Toast time!" she shouted. At the campsite table, her dad set down warm bread. Mackenzie took the butter knife. She spread and spread. The butter got stuck in one lump. She tried again, slow and small. One, two, three little strokes. Now the butter covered the whole slice!

Next came the milk. Mackenzie wanted to pour it all by herself. She tipped the cup high. Milk went glug, glug, glug, right up to the very top. She grabbed the cup with both hands. She took one step. The milk wobbled. Then the milk spilled all over the table. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

She got a towel and wiped it up. Then she tried again. This time she poured and stopped before the cup was full to the top. She left some room. Mackenzie picked up the cup. One step, two steps, three steps. The milk stayed in! "I did it!" she said. Kaysen clapped from his seat. Mackenzie took a big drink and smiled. "More milk, please," she said.

Evelyn sat at the paint table at summer camp. She wanted to paint the sky. She had seen it on the walk that morning. It was big and soft and blue.

She dipped her brush in the blue paint. Her brush was a good tool. She painted a long stripe across the paper. But it was dark blue. Very dark blue. It looked like night. The real sky was much lighter.

"Mr. Khan, why is my sky so dark?" she asked.

"That blue is strong," he said. "Try a little white."

Evelyn looked at the white paint. She put some on her brush. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round the pot went. The blue got lighter. It got lighter and lighter.

"Look, Leila!" said Evelyn. "My blue is soft now!"

"It looks like the morning sky," said Leila.

Evelyn painted her whole sky. It was soft and light, just like the one outside. She held her paper up to the window. The two blues matched.

Samuelle came over to see. "How did you do that?" she asked.

"I put white in it," said Evelyn. "The white made my blue light."

Then she painted a little white cloud on top.

Xavier went to the library with his dad. Today was story day. He wanted the new book about bears.

Rylee was there too. "I saw the bear book," Rylee said. "I got it tomorrow!"

Xavier frowned. "Tomorrow?" he asked. "Tomorrow comes later. Not yet."

Rylee laughed. "Oops. I got it yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today."

Xavier ran to the shelf. The bear book was gone! His arm reached up high. He felt sad. He missed the bear book.

Mr. Grant came over. "The book comes back tomorrow," he said. "Let me show you now." He held up a fuzzy puppet bear. The bear waved its little paw.

"Can I hold it?" Xavier asked. Mr. Grant put it in his hands. The bear was soft like a kitten.

"Tomorrow I will get the book," Xavier said. "And now I have the bear!"

Rylee clapped. "Story time starts now," she said.

Xavier sat down with the bear. "You can listen too," he whispered.

Elias woke up early. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny.

"I feel scared," he said. "Will I get lost?"

"No," said his dad. "Your class stays together. You will not forget your bag. I packed it."

Dad drove Elias to the school. A big flag waved on top of the building. Raymond and Sama were there too. Mr. Whitaker smiled at everyone.

"Now we walk to our room," said Mr. Whitaker. "We walk in a line."

Elias did not wait. He ran ahead fast. But then he could not see where to go. The hall was big. He stopped.

"Where do I go?" he asked.

Raymond pointed. "Find your spot in the line. It is right here."

Elias walked back. He stood behind Sama. The line moved together, slow and calm, not fast and lazy. Everyone got to the room.

Elias sat down at his little table. He was not lost at all. Sama slid a crayon over to him.

"Want to draw a flag?" she asked.

"Yes," said Elias. "A big red one."

Victor ran to the park with his dad. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Victor wore his red cap. The wind blew. It was a windy day too. The wind made his cap shake. "Hold on to your cap," said Dad.

Then big clouds came. Rain fell. "Oh no," said Victor. "My head will get wet." Dad opened his umbrella. He held it over both of them. The rain dripped down the sides. Victor's head stayed dry. "The umbrella keeps the rain off my head," said Victor.

Then something silly happened. The wind blew the umbrella up. It looked like a big bowl. Dad laughed and pulled it back down. A little river of rain ran along the path. Victor and Veer jumped over it. "It stopped raining," said Veer. The sun came back out. Victor shook his wet cap and put it on. "Home for warm milk," said Dad. Victor held Dad's hand all the way.

David sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to draw a duck. The duck had a long neck and a round body. David drew one circle. It came out wobbly. It looked like a potato. He drew another one. That one was wobbly too. David frowned at his paper.

His mom was cutting apple slices at the counter. She watched David try again. His circle wobbled once more. Then David looked at his cup. The cup sat by his plate. The bottom of the cup was round. David turned the cup over. He held it still on the paper. He drew all around the bottom. He lifted the cup up.

There it was. A perfect circle. "Look, Mom! A circle!" said David. "A good one," she said. David traced the cup again. Now the duck had a round body. He added a long neck and a small triangle beak. "Quack," said David, and he smiled at his duck.

Luka sat on the rug at daycare. The blocks were everywhere. Mr. Crowchild clapped his hands.

"Clean-up time," he said. "Let us sort by color."

Oakley made a red pile. Luka made a blue pile. Kane made a yellow pile. Then Oakley made a green pile too.

All the red blocks went in one place. All the blue blocks went together. Yellow sat with yellow. Green sat with green. Luka did not lose even one block. He was slow and careful, and that felt good.

Then Luka looked at the red pile. Something blue was hiding in it. A blue block had snuck in with all the red ones.

"Hello," said Luka. "You do not go here."

He pulled the blue block out. He carried it to the blue pile. It fit just right.

Then the pile wobbled. It turned into a tall blue hill.

"Whoa!" said Kane. "How did it get so tall?"

Luka grinned. "Every blue block is here now."

Mr. Crowchild laughed. "One more block was hiding in the basket."

He held up a yellow block. It had been under the rug all along. Kane took it to the yellow pile and set it on top.

Freya ran inside from the swing in the yard. Her hands were muddy. In the kitchen, Dad was putting bread and apple slices on the table.

"Snack time," said Dad.

Freya ran to her chair. She reached for an apple slice.

"Hold on," said Dad. He looked at her muddy hands. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Freya looked at her hands. They were brown and dirty. She walked to the sink. Dad turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. He helped her rub the soap. The bubbles felt slippery. The mud went down the drain. Her hands came out clean and pink.

Freya walked back to the table. She held up her hands to show Dad. Then she picked up an apple slice and took a big bite. Crunch!

"I will remember," Freya said. She ate her bread and her apples. Then she yawned a big yawn.

"Almost bath and bed time," said Dad. He filled the tub with warm water. Freya splashed and washed her toes. After her bath, she put on her soft pajamas.

Freya climbed into bed. She thought about the sink, and the soap, and the crunchy apple. Her eyes closed slowly.

"Wash hands first," she whispered, "then eat."

Paisley held her mom's hand at the big library door. Today she would get her very own library card. She wanted a book about the beach to take home.

First they went to the desk. The librarian typed on her keyboard. Then she handed Paisley a small blue card. "Now you can borrow books," she said. Paisley smiled so big her cheeks hurt.

Near the window, kids sat in a circle on a flat rug. A librarian sat in a little chair and held up a book. "Storytime!" she called. "At storytime, a librarian reads books aloud to a group of children." Paisley saw her friend Nathanael standing by the shelves. He was hiding behind a plant.

"Nathanael, come sit with me," said Paisley. He shook his head. His tummy felt jumpy about the circle. Paisley waited. She did not pull him. She just sat down and patted the rug.

The librarian opened a funny book. A dog in the book wore a hat and drove a tiny car! The kids laughed and laughed. Nathanael peeked out from the plant. He took one step. Then another step. Then he sat down next to Paisley.

"That dog is driving!" he said. Paisley laughed too. After storytime, she found a beach book and gave the librarian her new card. "My first book," she said. Nathanael whispered, "Can we come back tomorrow?"

Ella ran in from the yard. She had been playing in the sand with Yunus. Now a tiny baby was here, in a soft basket. Her new baby brother.

"Can I hold him?" Ella asked.

"He is sleeping," said Mama. "But you can sit close."

Ella held out her sandy hands. The sand felt gritty on her palm. It left little marks on her clean blue plate at snack time, too.

"Wash your hands first," said Ms. Nair, who had come to visit. "Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby."

"Will the sand tickle him?" Ella asked.

"It might not feel nice," said Ms. Nair.

Ella went to the little sink. Mama turned the warm water. Ella rubbed soap on her hands. She washed between each finger. Then she looked at her hands. They were clean and shiny.

"Now can I hold him?" she asked.

Mama sat down and put a pillow on Ella's lap. Then she laid the baby there, very gently. The baby yawned. He made a small sound.

"He is speaking baby talk," Ella whispered.

The baby opened his eyes. Ella smiled. Her clean hands held him soft and slow.

Ruby sat at the craft table at daycare. She wanted to make a toy car. She cut a rectangle for the body. Then she cut four little squares for wheels.

August watched her. "Can it roll?" he asked.

"Let's find out," said Ruby. She pushed the car. It slid. It bumped. It did not roll. Ruby made a face and stuck out her tongue. "Hmm. Why not?"

She looked across the room. Sabrina was rolling a ball. The ball was round like a circle. It rolled and rolled. Ruby looked at her square wheels. Squares had corners. The ball had no corners.

"Maybe my wheels need to be circles," said Ruby. Mr. Francis helped her cut four circles, nice and safe. Ruby pushed the car again.

This time it rolled! It rolled all the way to Sabrina's feet.

"A circle!" laughed Ruby. "Circles can roll."

Theo went to the store with Dad. Today they needed apples and bread. Yesterday the bread was all gone. Tomorrow they would have toast.

Theo wanted to roll the cart. "Can I push it now?" he asked. "Later," said Dad. "First we get the apples." Theo looked up. There was a big clock on the wall. It had hands and numbers.

"When is later?" Theo asked. Dad pointed at the clock. "The clock shows what time it is," he said. "When the big hand moves to the top, we will go home." Theo watched the hand. It ticked and ticked. Then it reached the top. "Now it is time!" he said. Dad smiled. "Yes. You watched the clock with your own eye." They rolled the cart to the door. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Theo asked. "Tomorrow," said Dad, "we will get jam."

Charlotte stood at the bus stop with her mama. Snow fell on her red hat. Snow fell on her boots. "Cold day," said mama. "Wear your mittens."

Charlotte made a small snowball. She wanted to keep it. "I will carry it home," she said. She held it in her cupped hands, in her mittens.

Rosa came to the bus stop too. "It is snowy today," said Rosa. "Yesterday it was windy. My hat blew away." Alexy said, "Last week it was rainy. I wore my rain boots." On a sunny day, Alexy wore a green cap.

The bus came. At home, Charlotte put her snowball in a bowl on the table. "Now I will keep you," she said.

She played with her blocks. Then she looked at the bowl. The snowball was small. Then it was gone. Only water sat in the bowl.

Charlotte touched the water with one finger. "You melted," she said. "Snow turns to water inside, where it is warm."

She ran to show mama the bowl.

Sara was at Grandpa's house. She saw a big black guitar on the couch. Sara tapped the guitar like a drum. It made a small thump. She tapped again. Still just a thump.

Grandpa sat down next to her. "Watch me," he said. He moved his fingers across the strings. The guitar sang out loud. Sara's eyes went wide. "You pluck the strings," said Grandpa. "Or you strum them, like this." He strummed again. The sound was big and warm.

Sara put her little fingers on the strings. She plucked one string. It went "ping." She tried again. Another ping. Grandpa waited and smiled. Sara pulled her fingers across all the strings. The guitar sang out just like Grandpa's. "Again!" she said. Grandpa nodded. "Play it for your friend Anabia tomorrow." Sara strummed one more time.

Muhammad sat at the big table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a picture of outside. He picked up a gray crayon. He started to make the sky.

Then he stopped. He looked out the window. The sun was bright. The day was sunny and clear. There were no clouds at all. Muhammad looked hard at the sky. The sky was blue today.

He put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He made big blue strokes at the top of the page. "Blue sky," he said to himself. Under the blue, he made a yellow sun. He made green grass at the bottom. He made one red flower in the grass.

His mom came in with a cup of water. "What a nice day," she said. Muhammad held up his paper. "Look! The sky is blue today," he said. His mom looked at the window. Then she looked at his picture. "Yes, it is," she said. "On a sunny day like this, the sky looks blue."

Muhammad smiled. He drew two birds in the blue. He talked to his mom about the birds. "They fly up high," he said. His mom hung the picture on the fridge. The blue sky looked just like the real one outside the window.

Grayson woke up and looked out the window. The snow was loud on the glass. "Mom, come see!" he called.

It was a snow day. No school today. Grayson wanted to build a snowman. He ran to the door in his pajamas. He opened it fast. The cold air came in. His fingers got cold right away. "Brrr," said Grayson. He ran back inside.

Mom helped him get dressed. He put on warm boots. He put on a big warm coat. Mom found his hat. "Where are your mittens?" she asked. Grayson looked and looked. He could not find them. He almost forgot all about his snowman.

There they were, under the chicken puzzle. Grayson pulled them out. "My mittens!" he said. Mom helped him put them on.

Grayson went outside. His boots went crunch, crunch. His fingers were warm in the mittens. He patted snow onto a big ball. He patted more and more. Soon his snowman stood up tall.

Grayson put his hat on the snowman's head. The snowman wore a hat, just like him. "Goodbye, snowman," said Grayson. He waved his mitten hand all the way to the door.

Lucy sat at the dinner table. Dad poured milk into her cup. She ate her pasta, one bite at a time. "Can I play outside after dinner?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You need socks and shoes."

Lucy ran to the hall. She put on her shoes first. Then she tried to push a sock over her shoe. It would not go. "Why won't my sock fit?" she asked. The sock just sat there, too small for the big shoe.

So Lucy started over. Off came the shoes. On went the socks, one foot, then the other foot. Then her shoes slid on top, nice and easy. Socks first, then shoes. Socks first, then shoes. Lucy laughed at her feet.

Outside, the grass was cold, almost frozen with dew. A little fox ran along the fence. Lucy stomped her feet. "Socks first, then shoes," she said. Her toes were warm. The fox stopped and looked at her. Lucy waved.

John went to the dentist with his dad. Snow was falling outside the big window. John liked to watch the snow. He pulled his chair close to the window to see.

Then John had to use the toilet. He went in. He went fast, because the waiting room had toy cars. He rushed out to play. But then he stopped. He turned around. He went back to the sink. He pumped the soap. He rubbed his hands and counted to twenty. "One, two, three," he said. He counted all the way to twenty. Then he rinsed the soap off.

After that, it was his turn to see the dentist. The dentist looked at John's teeth. "Nice clean teeth," she said. "What strong hands you have too." John looked at his hands. They were clean and shiny.

The dentist gave him a sticker. It was a big tooth with a happy face. His dad said, "You can have a yummy snack after this." John smiled. He held up his clean hands. "All washed," he said.

On the way home, the snow kept falling. John pulled his mittens on. Then he waved his mitten hand at the window. "Bye, dentist," he said. "See my clean hands next time."

Aria looked out the window. The sky was white and the snow fell down. "It is a snowy day," said Aria. She put on her boots. She put on her red coat. She ran outside to play.

The snow was soft and bumpy in spots. Aria made a snowball with her bare hands. The snowball was round like a triangle was not. She laughed and threw it at a post.

Then her hands felt cold. Very cold. Her fingers hurt a little. Aria ran back inside. "My hands are cold," she said. Her mom got her mittens. They were blue with white stars.

Aria put the mittens on. She went back out. She made another snowball. Her hands stayed warm this time. The wind blew, but her mittens kept her hands cozy. Aria made one snowball, then two, then three. "Snowball mountain," she said. She stacked them up tall. Then she gave the top one a little nose made of snow. "Hello, snow friend," said Aria.

Joseph was in the backyard with his friend Zavier. They were playing an animal game. "Woof!" said Joseph. He was a dog. "Moo!" said Zavier. He was a cow.

Then Joseph saw the fish in the little pond. He pointed at it. "That is not an animal," said Joseph. "It has no legs!"

Zavier laughed. "A fish is an animal too," said Zavier. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Joseph looked and looked. The fish wiggled its tail. It went splash, splash.

"A fish with no legs," said Joseph. "That is so silly!" He jumped like a frog. Zavier jumped too. The dog next door barked, and the fish went under a black rock.

"Fish can't jump," said Zavier. Joseph clapped his hands. Then he made a fish face. "Blub, blub," he said. Zavier made a fish face too. "Blub, blub!"

Eva went to the store with her dad. The doors slid open fast. Then they slid shut slow. "Fast and slow," said Eva. Her dad smiled.

They needed milk. Eva found a small carton. Her dad held a big one. "We need the big one," he said. Eva put the small one back.

Next they got bread from the warm shelf. Eva touched the shelf. "Feel it. It is warm," said Dad. Then they walked past the cold freezer. Eva felt the cold air on her face. She shivered. "Brrr!"

Outside, the sky was dark. Eva looked up. "Is it morning?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "It is still night. Day and night are opposites. Night is dark. Day has light."

Eva nodded. "So we sleep at night," she said. "And we play in the day." Dad laughed.

They walked to the car. The store lights went off, one by one. The street was quiet now. Eva held Dad's hand tight.

"Night night, store," she whispered.

Zayn stood in the garage with his dad. It was cold outside. Snow was on the ground near the big door.

Zayn had a new coat. He wanted to put it on all by himself. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in. The other arm went in too. Now for the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck halfway. His dad waited quietly. Zayn pulled again. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

"I did it!" said Zayn.

Then he saw his mittens on the floor. He had dropped one. He picked it up. Where could it go? He found a little pocket on his coat. He tucked both mittens inside. The pocket held them tight.

"Ready to meet Beckett at the lake?" his dad asked.

"Yes!" said Zayn. He patted his furry mittens in the pocket. Then he held his dad's hand and walked out into the snow.

Audrey sat on the rug at school. Five toy monkeys sat in a row by her knee. Hiba sat next to her, and Ms. Ortiz sat in her chair with a book.

"One, two, three, four, five," sang Hiba. Then she sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." She made the monkeys hop. "One fell off and bumped his head." Hiba took one monkey away. She hid it behind her back.

Audrey looked at the rug. Now there were four monkeys. She tapped her heart. "Where did one go?" she asked.

Hiba sang, "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." Again one monkey fell off. Hiba took it away. Now there were three.

Audrey picked up the three monkeys. "I can do it," she said. "Three little monkeys jumping on the bed." She made them hop. "One fell off!" She put one monkey in her lap. Two monkeys were left.

"Two little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. She put one more in her lap. One monkey was left. It hopped all alone. Audrey was scared it would fall too. "Mama called the doctor," sang Ms. Ortiz, "and the doctor said, no more monkeys jumping on the bed!"

Audrey held the last monkey close. Then she let all five monkeys down on the rug again.

"One, two, three, four, five," she said. She spelled out the letters on her block: M-O-N-K-E-Y. "Monkey!"

Then she sang the song all by herself. Each time she sang, one monkey fell off. Five went to four. Four went to three. Three went to two. Two went to one. The number got one smaller every time.

Hiba clapped. Ms. Ortiz smiled. Audrey lined up the monkeys again. "Five little monkeys," she sang, and the monkeys began to jump.

Maria was playing in the kitchen. Her toy snake was black and long. She made it slither on the floor.

Then Maria smelled something. She used her nose to sniff the air. Sniff, sniff. It smelled warm. It smelled like soup.

"I want soup for dinner," said Maria. "Is it soup?" she asked.

Her grandma was at the stove. "Come and see," said Grandma.

Maria looked with her eyes. She saw the big pot. She could not see inside yet. The lid was on. But she could still smell it. The smell came first. The soup came later.

Maria stood back, safe and far from the hot stove. Grandma lifted the lid. There it was. Soup! Maria had guessed it with her nose.

"Your nose knew before your eyes," said Grandma.

Maria touched the toy snake with her fingers. It felt smooth. She held it up high.

"Snake smells soup too," she said.

Grandma laughed. "Then snake can taste it at dinner."

Ezra sat at the craft table at summer camp. He wanted to make a paper sun. He drew a big circle with his crayon. Now he needed to cut it out.

Ezra reached for the big scissors. Ms. Weber shook her head. She gave him small scissors instead. "These are your safety scissors," she said. They had round tips, like little spoon ends.

Would they work? Ezra squeezed them. Snip, snip. The paper cut! Little pieces fell down like snow. He looked at each piece. The circle was turning into a sun.

Mabel sat next to him with her fork from snack time. She used it to poke holes in clay. "Look, it makes stars," she said.

Ezra held up his sun. "I cut it all by myself," he said. Ms. Weber gave him a thumbs up.

Nathan stood on the balcony. He had a wooden box full of dirt. His dad helped him push three little seeds into the soil.

"Seeds need water to start growing," said Dad. "Do you want to give them a drink?" Nathan got his small blue cup. He poured water on the dirt. "Drink up, little seeds," he said.

The next morning, Nathan ran to the box. He saw only dirt. No sprout yet. His friend Vihaan came over. "Where is your plant?" Vihaan asked. "Still sleeping," said Nathan. He watered the seeds again. He watered them the next day too. And the day after that.

One morning, Nathan looked at the box. Something green stood up in the dirt. A tiny sprout! "Vihaan, come quick!" Nathan called. "The water worked. It just needed time." Vihaan bent down low. Nathan touched one green leaf with one finger, very softly.

Austin was at Grandma's house. Nicole was there too. Nicole had a big red kite. It flew up high in the yard. The wind was loud in the trees. Austin wanted to hold the kite so much.

He ran over and grabbed the string. The kite dipped and fell. Nicole frowned. "You pulled it down," she said. Austin felt his face go hot. "Sorry," he said. Nicole picked up the string again. The kite went back up.

Then Austin heard Grandma on the porch. She was reading her book. She smiled at him. "Try asking," she said. Austin walked to Nicole. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Nicole handed him the string. "Yes! You said it so nicely." The kite pulled in his hands. It felt strong, like a big dog on a leash. Austin laughed. The wind was loud, but he heard Nicole giggle beside him. "Your turn now," he said. "May I have it back?" asked Nicole. He gave her the string, and they watched the kite dance.

Camille stood by the big tree. She wanted to play in the sunny spot. The sun made the slide warm and bright.

But the clouds moved in. Big white clouds. They hid the sun. The slide went dark. "Hey!" said Camille. "Where did the sun go?"

Elyas ran over. "The clouds are hiding it," he said. Camille looked up. She could see the sun's edge behind a cloud. "Come out, sun!" she called. Malaika laughed. "Sun, come play with us!" All three called together.

Then the wind came. The wind pushed the clouds. The clouds moved away, slow, slow, then fast. The sun came out again! The slide turned bright and warm. Camille put her hand on it. "Warm!" she said. "The sun did that."

A little bird sat on the swing. It fluffed its feathers. Camille felt proud. She had found the sun. Then the clouds came back and hid it again. "Oh no," said Elyas. Camille giggled. "We wait," she said. She held Elyas's hand. They watched the sky together. The sun peeked out. "There!" said Camille.

"Listen, Grandpa, listen!" said Maeva. "My turn, my song."

Zachary set up his kitchen under the big tree. He had a red pot and a wooden spoon. His stuffed sheep sat in a chair, waiting for lunch.

"I will make soup," said Zachary. He dropped in pinecones and three little flowers. He stirred and stirred.

Fletcher came through the gate. "Can I have some?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Zachary. He held out a spoon full of pinecone soup. He opened his mouth wide to taste it first.

His dad ran over fast. "Stop! Do not eat that," he said. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth."

Zachary looked at his spoon. He made a big slurping sound instead. "Slurp! Mmm!" he said.

Fletcher laughed. He slurped his soup too. The sheep got a bowl of flowers and slurped as well.

"More please!" said Fletcher.

Zachary stirred the pot again. He added one green leaf. Then he carried the whole pot to the sheep. "Here you go," he said, and made the biggest slurp of all.

Zachary stood at the front door. He put on his red hat. The trees outside were bending. The leaves flew all around. "It is windy," said his mom. Zachary stepped outside. The wind pushed his hair. Then the wind blew his hat right off his head.

The hat rolled across the grass. Zachary ran after it. "Come back, hat!" he called. His friend Danika was walking by. "I will help you," she said. She ran too. The hat flew high. Then it landed in a bush. Zachary grabbed it. He held it tight.

He ran back to the door. His dad gave him a clip. The clip held the hat to his coat. Zachary jumped in the wind again. The hat stayed on his head. He laughed. Zachary felt tired from running. "That was fun," said Danika. Zachary smiled and waved. "See you tomorrow!"

Henri went to the store with his dad. Henri wanted the red apple with the shiny star sticker. He reached for it, but the cart rolled and bumped the shelf. The apples fell down. They rolled everywhere. One apple bumped a girl on the foot. She looked sad.

Henri's dad said, "Time to pick them up." Henri felt angry. He stomped his foot. "No, no, no!" he said. His face felt hot. His hands made tight fists.

His dad knelt down. "Try this," he said. "Take a slow, deep breath." Dad breathed in slowly. He breathed out slowly. Henri copied him. In went the breath, big like a dragon. Out it went, slow like a sleepy wind. Henri did it again. His fists opened up. His face felt cool. He was not angry anymore.

Henri picked up the apples, one by one. He gave the girl the red one. "For you," he said. She smiled. Then Henri got a green apple with a frog sticker. He held it up high like a treasure. "Ribbit," he said, and everyone laughed.

Leo was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big shelf of books. "Can we read the dog book?" Leo asked. Grandma looked at the shelf. "There are lots of books here," she said. "Which dog book?"

Leo pointed. He could not read the little marks on the covers yet. Grandma pulled out one book. It had a bear on it. "No, not that one," said Leo. She pulled out another one. It had a truck on it. "No," said Leo again. Leo wanted the book about the little dog and the red flower. He remembered the picture on the front.

Then Grandma found it. "Here it is," she said. She tapped the top of the cover. "This line up here is the name of the book. It is the title." Leo looked closely. The marks sat right above the dog's head. So books had names, just like he did. "Say the name," said Grandma. "Spot Finds a Flower." Leo said it with her.

The next day, Grandpa took Leo to the library. Leo saw shelves and shelves of books. He wanted the dog book again. So he walked up to the lady at the desk. "Can I have Spot Finds a Flower?" he asked. She smiled. She typed something. Then she came back with the dog book in her hands. Leo held it tight. Asking for the name had worked!

At home, Leo sat with Grandma on the soft red chair. He opened the book himself. He turned the first page, then the next. The dog found the flower near the end. "You read it front to back," said Grandma. "Just like that." Leo patted the cover. "Spot," he said. "That is your name."

text: Matteo wanted to bake cookies with Dad. "Can we bake now?" he asked. Dad held up a brown leaf he had found on his coat. "Not now. First we clean, and later we bake." Matteo pouted. "When is now?" Dad smiled. "Now means at this very moment. Right now we are cleaning." Matteo looked around. Toys were on the floor. He picked up a red truck. Then he picked up a bear. Now the floor was clear. "Now we clean," he said, and he laughed at his own joke. Dad poured flour into a bowl. Matteo added the chocolate chips, one by one. "Cookies are not now," said Dad. "Cookies are later." Matteo waited by the oven. He could not touch it, because it was hot. Dad took out the cookies. Matteo took a big bite. "This is now!" he said. Dad laughed too. "Yes. Now is cookie time."

Dylan went to the animal shelter with his dad. He wanted a pet of his very own. He looked at a big dog. He looked at a sleepy cat. Then he saw a small gray rabbit. The rabbit had one black eye patch. "This one," said Dylan.

Ms. Foster worked at the shelter. "You can hold him," she said. Dylan sat very still. He waited. The rabbit hopped onto his lap. Dylan petted his soft fur. Then Dylan saw a snack table with crackers. He began to run to it. Ms. Foster said, "Wait. Wash your hands first. You touched the rabbit." Dylan went to the sink. He washed his hands. Then he ate his crackers.

At home, Dylan helped clean the rabbit's cage. He scooped the old hay. He gave the rabbit fresh water. He saw the rabbit munch and grow sleepy and happy. After the cage was clean, Dylan washed his hands again. Then he waved through the bars. "Good night, rabbit," he said.

text:
Hazel went to the park with her dad today. Yesterday it rained, so the swings were wet. "We can dry them soon," her dad said. "What is soon?" Hazel asked. "Soon means in a little while," he said. Hazel did not want to wait. She wanted to swing now.

Hazel sat on the bench. Her hat was itchy, so she took it off. Blake ran up with a small towel. "Want to help dry the swings?" Blake asked. Hazel wiped the seat with the towel. The wet spots went away. Now the swing was dry!

Hazel climbed on and pumped her legs. The swing went up, up, up. Ms. Visser walked by with her dog. The dog barked one happy woof. "We will come back tomorrow," said Hazel. "And soon we will have a snack!" Her dad laughed and held out an apple. Hazel took a big bite. "That was a little while," she said, swinging her feet.

Jacob and his family were on a trip. The car stopped at a big diner by the road. "Real pancakes!" said Jacob. "Yes, real ones," said Dad. Jacob ate one, two, three bites. Then they drove on to the beach.

At the beach, Jacob saw the water. The waves went splash, splash, splash. He wanted to run right in. He asked, "Can I splash now?" Mom said, "Not yet." She said, "At the beach, you go near the water only with a grown-up watching." Jacob waited. He counted the waves. One wave. Two waves. Three waves. The waves kept coming.

Then Dad came down the sand. "Now I am watching," said Dad. He held Jacob's hand. Jacob stepped in the water. Splash! The water was cool on his toes. "The wave got me!" Jacob laughed. He sang a little song about it. "Wave, wave, go away, then come back another day!"

Jacob would remember this. First a grown-up, then the water. Dad got splashed too. "Hey!" said Dad, laughing. "You got my real shoes all wet!" Jacob splashed one more time. Splash!

At snack time, Georgia bit her juicy apple. There was ice in her cup. One cube started to slip off the table. She caught it.

Mr. Kaur sat down beside her. "Shall we sing a nursery rhyme?" he asked. "A nursery rhyme is a short rhyming song." He sang one his grandpa taught him long ago.

Georgia sang it once. Then she sang it again. Where did the words go? They stayed in her head. She clapped while she sang, boon, clap, boon, clap.

Luca wanted to make a big snow sheep. He tried to roll a snowball. It was too big to push. Then he pushed a small snowball instead. The small one rolled and rolled. It got bigger and bigger as it rolled. Luca saw that the snow made it grow.

Soon he had a round, fat body. He added a round head and two stick legs. "That sheep looks silly!" said Jalen from next door. Luca laughed. Then they went inside for warm cocoa that Dad made. Luca held the cup with both hands. "Best snow day ever," he said.

Muhammad went to the playground with his dad. He marched straight to the slide. Then he saw a little door low on the wall. It looked funny, like a tiny face with two round eyes.

"What is that?" Muhammad asked.

His dad crouched down. "That is an outlet," he said. "Never put fingers or things into it. Fingers do not go in there."

Muhammad looked at his own small fingers. He hid them behind his back. Just then, the juice machine went quiet. No juice came out.

Ms. Huang, the playground teacher, came over. She had a plug in her hand. "The plug fell out," she said. Muhammad watched her push the plug into the outlet. Click! The machine hummed again. Juice poured into her cup.

The plug went in. The machine turned on. Muhammad clapped his hands.

"More juice, please," he said. He kept his fingers far, far away.

"Yes, he is yours," said Dad. "His name is Pip."

Luca wanted to carry Pip everywhere. He grabbed at the box. "I will walk him all around the room!"

Dad sat down on the floor. "Come sit with me," he said. "Watch this first."

Dad put his hands in the box. He used two hands, not one. He held Pip close to his chest. Then he set Pip on his lap, right there on the floor.

"Why do we sit down?" asked Luca.

"So Pip cannot fall far," said Dad.

Luca sat down too. He held out his two hands. Dad placed Pip on them. Pip was soft, not rough like Luca's shirt. Pip wiggled his little nose. He made a happy squeak!

Luca petted Pip with one finger. Pip did not run away. He sat still and munched a bit of grass.

"He likes sitting with me," said Luca. "Pip, you are my best friend."

Dad smiled. "Tomorrow we will sit and hold him again."

"Again and again!" said Luca, and Pip went "squeak."
