Olivier ran into Grandma's warm kitchen. Today was a big family party. Grandma was making special moon cookies. She only made them on this one day each year.

"Can I taste one now?" Olivier asked.

Grandma shook her head. "First they need the oven," she said. "You can help with the dough."

Olivier pressed the dough flat. It was sticky on his fingers. He made a round shape, like the moon. Grandma put the tray in the hot oven. Olivier watched from far away, on his stool.

He waited. He counted to ten. He counted again. Then a sweet smell filled the kitchen. Grandma took out the tray with her big mitts. The cookies were golden.

"Why do they smell so good?" Olivier asked.

Grandma smiled. "These are made just for today," she said.

Olivier took a small bite. The cookie was soft and sweet. He looked at his sticky fingers and licked them. "Grandma," he said, "can we make these again next year?"

Grandma hugged him. "Every year," she said. "Now let's bring the plate to the party."

Olivier carried the plate slow and steady. Blair and Keaton each took a cookie too. Olivier held his last one up to the window, next to the moon.

Ava sat at the dinner table. Mom put a big pot in the middle. It was soup night. Ava was excited. She loved soup.

Then Dad began to bang a spoon on the pot. clang, clang, clang! Ava laughed and clapped. But her baby brother hid his face. He was scared of the loud noise. Dad put the spoon down. He made a soft tap instead. tap, tap. The baby peeked out and smiled.

Ava looked at the baby. Then she looked at Dad. "He likes quiet," she said. "I like loud. Same spoon!" Dad washed the spoon and handed it to her. Ava tapped it softly for her brother. Then she tapped it fast for herself. Her heart felt happy. "Good tapping, Ava," said Dad. Ava tapped the spoon two more times, soft, soft, and the baby giggled.

Isabelle planted lettuce in her backyard. She planted it with her dad in the morning. She patted the dirt with her hands. Every day she looked at the little plants.

One day the sun was very hot. Isabelle looked at her lettuce. The leaves were drooping. They hung down like sad little arms. "That looks scary," she said. "My plants are falling!" Her dad was close by. "Give them a drink," he said.

Isabelle filled her watering can. She gave the lettuce water, drip, drip, drip. The next morning she ran outside. The leaves stood up tall. They were not drooping anymore. Isabelle smiled. She wrote a big letter W on a card for her friend Everett, because W looked like water. "Look, Dad," she said. "My lettuce drank it all up."

Leah ran to Shea's house. A big cardboard box sat on the floor.

"I want it to be a car," said Leah.

"I want it to be a boat," said Shea.

They both pulled the box. The box tipped over. Leah fell into it with a bump.

Shea laughed. "Now it's a boat again!"

Leah sat inside. She made a steering wheel with her hands. "Beep beep! Now it's my car!"

"Take turns," said Shea's mom. "First a car, then a boat."

Leah drove first. She turned the wheel. "I hope we don't get stuck!" Vroom, vroom!

Then Leah climbed out. Shea got in. "Row, row!" said Shea. "Watch out for the big fall of water!"

After that, they made the box into a house. Leah put her doll inside. "Shh, the baby is sleeping," she whispered.

Shea tapped on the wall of the box. "Knock knock! Snowy day outside! Can we come in?"

"Yes! Come in, come in!" said Leah.

The box was a car. Then it was a boat. Then it was a house. It was the best box ever.

"Next time, can it be a rocket?" asked Shea.

"Yes!" said Leah. "Vroom!"

Avery ran to the block corner at soccer practice. Mae got there first. She hugged the whole pile of blocks to her chest.

"I want them too," said Avery. She reached out and grabbed the biggest block. Mae held on tight. The block went boing and rolled under the bench.

Ms. Mercado knelt down. "Hmm," she said. "I see two builders and one pile."

Avery looked at the blocks. Then she looked at Mae. "Want to build one tower?" she asked. "We can build it side by side."

Mae smiled big. "Yes! One big tower!"

Avery put a red block down first. Mae stacked a blue one on top. Avery added yellow. The tower grew tall in the bright light from the window. It wobbled. They both held their breath.

"Whoa!" said Mae, and they giggled.

Together they played until the whistle blew. The tower stood tall, taller than both of them.

"Best tower ever," said Mae.

Avery grinned and put one more block on the very top.

Levi wanted to ride his bike in the yard. He ran to the door. His dad called, "Levi, wait." Levi stopped and looked back.

"Where is your helmet?" his dad asked. Levi patted his head. His hair was soft and bare. He ran back to the porch. His helmet sat on the step. It was blue with a white stripe, straight and shiny. He put it on. Dad helped snap the strap. It clicked under his chin.

Then Levi rode his bike on the grass. The wheels went bump, bump. A big truck drove past the house. Levi stayed near Dad the whole time. After the ride, Levi washed his hands. Dad filled the sink. The water was warm, not hot. Levi dropped in his little boat. It did float! Levi laughed and pushed it gently across the water.

"Again," said Levi, and he sailed the boat back.

Lucas sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small road.

"Daddy, I'm hungry," said Lucas.

Daddy drove to a farm stand. There were big pumpkins on the ground. There were small berries in a basket. Daddy bought a big watermelon and a small basket of berries.

"Can I carry the watermelon?" asked Lucas.

He tried. It would not move. Daddy picked it up with one arm. It was heavy. Lucas picked up the berries. They were light. He held them all the way to the car.

"Heavy and light are opposites," said Daddy.

Lucas looked at his basket. The berries were light, so he could carry them far. The watermelon was heavy, so Daddy had to carry it.

In the car, Lucas ate one berry. It was a little sour. He made a funny face. Daddy laughed.

Then Lucas yawned. The car went slow and soft, like a lullaby. His eyes closed. He began to sleep.

A big tree root made the car bump. Lucas woke up.

"Where are we?" he asked.

Daddy pointed. "Look, we are home."

Lucas carried his light basket to the door. He put one berry in Daddy's hand.

"This one is sweet," said Lucas.

Norah went to the park with her mom. There was a big tree by the pond. Today was Christmas, and lots of families stood near the tree.

Boxes of ornaments sat on the grass. Norah picked up a shiny star. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a rabbit ornament there too. Then a red ball. Soon that one branch was full. The ornaments bumped each other. Two fell right off into the grass.

Atreus laughed. "Your branch is too full!" he said. Norah looked at the whole big tree. It had so many branches. She picked up the star again. She hung it on a branch up high. The rabbit went on a branch far to the side. The red ball went on a low branch near her knees.

The tree looked bright all over. Sophia clapped her hands. Norah's sweater was itchy, so she wiggled and giggled. Later, everyone helped pick up the fallen ornaments. Norah washed her hands at the water fountain. "Look," she said, pointing at the tree. "Now every branch gets one."

Beau sat in his reading nook. He had his letter cards in a pile. He wanted to put them all in a row, from A to Z. He laid out A, B, C. Then he laid out N. Then he laid out M.

His friend Alia came to play. She looked at the row. She giggled. "M comes before N," she said. Beau scratched his head. "How do you know?" he asked. "The alphabet song sings the letters in order from A to Z," Alia said. "We can sing it!"

They sang the song together. "L, M, N, O, P!" When they sang M, Beau moved the card. M went in front of N. "There!" said Beau. "The song tells me where M goes!"

Alia picked up a pink leaf she had brought inside. She put it by the last card. "Z is at the very end," she said. Beau sang to Z and clapped. Then they walked around the nook like sleepy letters going to bed. "Good night, M," Beau whispered. "Good night, Z," said Alia.

Everett was at Grandma's house. Grandma had made warm toast. The toast smelled so good. "Can I put the butter on?" Everett asked. Grandma smiled. "Yes, you can try."

Everett held the knife. Grandma put a little butter on the tip. Everett spread it. He followed the butter with his eyes. The white toast turned yellow. Where the butter went, the toast looked shiny. "It changed!" said Everett. He licked a bit off his tongue. "Mmm, salty."

Next came the milk. Everett held the cup with both hands. He poured slowly. But some milk ran over the side. A little puddle sat on the table. Everett's lip wobbled. "Oh no. The milk spilled."

Then he remembered the cloth by the sink. He reached for it. He wiped the puddle. He wiped and wiped. The table was dry again. "All gone!" said Everett. Grandma clapped her hands. Everett picked up the cup and took a big sip. "Now I drink it," he said.

Isaiah built a library in his bedroom. His teddy bear sat on a shelf. His toy truck sat next to it. "These are my books," said Isaiah.

Daddy knocked on the door. "May I come in?" he asked. "Yes!" said Isaiah. "This is my library." Isaiah wanted to give out cards, like the real library. But he did not know how. "Daddy, how do I get a card?" he asked. "A grown-up helps you sign up," said Daddy. So Daddy helped. He held Isaiah's hand. Isaiah made a big scribble on the card. "My first card!" said Isaiah.

Daddy picked the teddy bear. "I would like this book, please." Isaiah stamped Daddy's hand. "Due back tomorrow!" he said. Then Daddy opened the card. Inside was a sweet little sticker of a garden. "Look, snow is falling on the flowers!" said Isaiah. Daddy checked out the truck, too.

Rose walked home with her dad. She held a little box with holes. Inside was her first pet, a tiny gray kitten.

"Her name is Puff," said Rose. "One kitten, one name."

On the street, Conrad ran up to see. "Can I count her toes?" he asked. He counted them. "One, two, three, four, five on this paw."

Then the door of the box opened a crack. Puff jumped out! She ran under a dark bush. Rose got down on her knees. "Puff, come back!" But Puff did not come.

Mr. Toussaint came out with his big orange cat. The cat wore a collar with a shiny tag. "If my cat gets lost, someone reads his tag," he said. "It has my phone number on it. Then they can call me."

Rose looked at her dad. "Puff needs a tag too!" she said.

First they had to find Puff. Rose shook the food bag. Puff peeked out. Then she ran to Rose's lap.

The next day, Rose picked a pink tag for Puff. The shop helper put their phone number on it. Rose read each number out loud. One, two, three. Puff purred.

"Now Puff can always come home," said Rose. She hugged her soft little kitten, tag jingling.

Michael ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. His tummy made a big growl.

"First we wash," said his dad. "Wash with soap for twenty seconds." Michael rubbed the soap fast. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he stopped. Was that twenty? He looked at his wet hands. They still smelled like mud from the park.

Then Michael remembered camp. Faris had sung a song at the sink. The song was about bunnies hopping. When Faris finished singing, twenty seconds were done! So Michael sang it too. "Hop, hop, hop, little bunnies hop." The soap felt slippery and bubbly in his palms.

The song ended. His dad smiled and turned off the tap. Michael held up his hands. They smelled like clean soap now, not mud. He looked at the bubbles going down the drain. "The song helped me wash long enough," said Michael. "Can we sing it again after lunch?"

His dad laughed. "Yes. But first, sandwiches."

Stella sat at the big table at math club. Mr. Santoso put down two bowls of strawberries. "Count them," he said. Stella touched each berry. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Noelie counted the other bowl. "One, two, three, four," said Noelie.

Stella put one red strawberry in her mouth. It was sweet and cold. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four," she said. She froze. The bowl had one less berry now. "This bowl has five," said Mr. Santoso. "That bowl has four. Which has more?" Stella pointed to Noelie's bowl. "That one!"

"Now they are the same," said Noelie with a big smile. Stella laughed and took a short drink of water. Then she counted the berries again, one by one, all by herself.

Xavier sat in his car seat. The sun was warm on his neck. Dad was driving to school.

"I want my song now," said Xavier.

Dad said, "The song is not now. It is later, after I park the car."

Xavier looked out the window. A big truck went by now. Then it was gone. A red light was on now. Then Dad stopped, and the light turned green.

"Now means at this very moment," said Zayan from the other seat. Zayan was riding to school too. "Like this moment. See my hand? Now it is up. Now it is down."

Xavier put his hand up. Now it was up. He put it down. Now it was down. He laughed.

The car stopped. Dad parked. "Is it now?" asked Xavier.

"Yes, it is now," said Dad. He turned on the song.

Xavier clapped his hands. Yesterday the song was too short. Today it felt just right. Tomorrow he would ask again.

"Let's sing!" said Xavier. Zayan sang too, and their voices filled the car.

Cooper ran to the big red swing at school. But Haroun was already on it. Haroun pumped his legs and flew up high.

Cooper wanted a go too. He stood and watched. The wind moved the leaves above him. He picked up a small stick and drew a circle in the dirt.

Haroun stopped the swing. "You can have a turn now," he said. "Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another. Me, then you, then me."

Cooper sat on the swing. He held the ropes tight. He kicked his legs and went up, up, up. Haroun drew a circle in the dirt with the stick.

"Now my turn again," said Haroun.

"Okay," said Cooper. He jumped off.

Haroun swung high. Cooper counted out loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

Then Haroun jumped off too. "Your turn," he said.

Cooper and Haroun took turns all morning. Up and down. One after another.

Ms. Morin rang the bell. Time to line up. Cooper put the stick in his pocket. He and Haroun walked to the door side by side.

"Same swing tomorrow?" asked Cooper.

"Yes," said Haroun. "You first."

Luca had been sick with a cold. Today he got to go back to the doctor's office. Ms. Vargas, the nurse, looked in his ears. "All better," she said with a big smile. Luca hopped down from the big chair.

At home, Luca sat on his pillow. His nose felt funny. He blew his nose into a tissue. Then he saw crackers on the table. He reached out his hand.

Then he stopped. He remembered Ms. Vargas washing her hands. Luca went to the sink. He used soap and water. He rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles felt warm.

Then he ate his crackers. His dad gave him a thumbs up. "Look," said Luca, holding up his clean hands. "Soap and water!"

Emmett walked into the big library with his dad. He held his new card in his hand. It had his name on it. Emmett wanted a book about trucks.

He looked at the shelves in the red room. He saw books about cats. He saw books about the moon. But no trucks. Where could the truck books be?

Then Emmett saw a woman at a tall desk. She wore a blue shirt. "Who is that?" Emmett asked his dad. "That is the librarian," Dad said. "A librarian works at the library. A librarian helps people find books."

Emmett walked to the desk. He stood on his tiptoes. "Can you help me find truck books?" he asked. The librarian smiled. "Yes! Follow me." She led him down the hall. There was a whole shelf of trucks. Red trucks, blue trucks, and one big sharp crane.

Emmett picked a truck book with a yellow cover. He gave his card to the librarian. Beep went the machine. "All done," she said. Emmett hugged the book tight.

At home, Emmett pointed at a truck in the book. "Dad, look at this one!" he said. "It can dump big rocks!"

Charlotte sat at the big table. It was writing club day. Ms. Mendoza put out paper and pencils. "Today we will write our own names," she said. Charlotte wanted to write her name all by herself. She picked up her pencil. She held it low, near the tip, just like Ms. Mendoza showed her. Then she made a big C. But her C came out all wobbly.

Alyson leaned over. "My A is easy," she said. "It has straight lines." Keith held up his paper. "Look, my K has straight lines too." Charlotte looked at her letters. The C had curves. The H had straight lines. The A had straight lines. The R had a little curve. The L had straight lines. The T had straight lines. She sorted the letters into two piles with her eyes. Curvy letters in one spot. Straight letters in another spot.

"Now I get it," Charlotte said. She tried the straight letters first. She drew slow, straight lines. H came out neat. Then A. Then R. Then L. Then T. The curvy C was last. She went slow, very slow. The curve came out round and pretty. Charlotte lifted her paper up high. "I did it!" she said. Ms. Mendoza smiled. "Let's cover the table with more names," she said. Charlotte got a new sheet and began again. "C is for Charlotte," she said, and she drew the curve.

text:
Brooklyn was playing house in the playroom. Her baby doll sat in a little nest of soft blankets. Brooklyn fed the doll from a tiny cup. Then the doll fell. It slid off the chair and dropped to the floor. Brooklyn picked it up fast. "Oh no," she said. "Baby fell down hard."

Brodie came to look. Brooklyn held the doll close. "The baby is sad," she said. The teacher, Mr. Navarro, sat down beside her. He looked at the doll. "The doll is fine," he said. "Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Brooklyn thought about that. Then she gave the doll a big hug. "Baby feels better now," she said. Brodie clapped his hands. That was a surprise! Brooklyn made a soft bed and laid the doll down. "Shh," she said. "Baby is sleepy." She patted the blanket. "Night night, baby. Night night."

Joshua stood in the backyard with Dad. They picked red tomatoes from the garden. Some tomatoes were smelly and squishy. Joshua put them in a big bowl.

"Let's make pizza," said Dad. They carried the tomatoes inside. Joshua helped pour flour on the table. He patted the dough with his hands. Dad mixed the sauce.

The oven got hot. Dad put the pizza in. Joshua wanted to see it cook. He walked toward the oven door.

"Wait," said Dad. "The oven is hot. A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven. You can watch from here."

Joshua waited by the table. Soon the kitchen smelled good. Dad pulled the pizza out with big mitts. The cheese was bubbly.

Mom and Lenny came over for a pizza party. Joshua gave everyone a slice. "I made this!" he said. He took a big bite of his red, cheesy piece.

Jayden sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint a big green hill. But there was no green paint. He felt stuck. "No green," he said. Mr. Kaya smiled. "Try this," he said. "It is called a palette." He held out a flat tray. It had little holes for paint.

Jayden had put yellow on his paper. Then he put blue on top. The paper got soggy. It started to break apart. "Oh no," said Jayden. Mr. Kaya said, "Try mixing on the palette first." Jayden put yellow on the flat tray. He put blue next to it. He mixed them with his brush. Round and round. One, two, three. The paint turned green!

Jayden tapped his brush. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. "I know them all." His friend Miller came to look. Jayden painted his hill. It was green and shiny. "I made green!" said Jayden. Miller clapped. "Can I try too?"

Eva wanted her red socks. She looked under the table. She looked by the sink. Her socks were not there. "Oh no," said Eva. "My socks are lost!"

Then Eva saw something on the floor. It was one red sock. It was dirty. "Take my hand, sock," said Eva with a giggle. She picked it up.

Her mom was holding a big basket. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed," said Mom. Eva looked at the basket. Then she looked at her sock.

Eva stood far back. She threw the sock. It went up, up, up. It fell in the basket. "Hooray!" said Eva. She ran to find the other sock. There it was, by the chair. She threw that one too. It bounced off the edge and plopped inside.

"Now we wash," said Mom. She carried the basket to the machine. Eva sat on her stool and watched the round door spin. "Bye bye, socks," she said, waving.

Lincoln sat in the nursery room. His new baby sister was here. She was small and warm. She made tiny sounds.

Lincoln had a cracker. He held it out to the baby. "Want a bite?" he asked.

His dad shook his head. "Babies only drink milk," Dad said. "No crackers yet."

Lincoln looked at the baby. She was not alone. Dad held her close. She drank from her bottle. Her eyes stayed shut. Her little hand held Dad's finger.

"She is still drinking," Lincoln said. The milk went down, sip by sip. The baby sighed a happy sigh.

Lincoln ran to fetch her soft blanket. It smelled like powder. He laid it by her cheek. The baby made a small sound, almost like a purr.

Then Lincoln sat down beside Dad. He watched the milk go down. He shared his cracker with himself, one small bite at a time.

Hudson sat at the big table in the art room. He wanted to paint green grass. But his pot of green paint was empty. He shook it. He looked inside. Nothing there.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya gave him yellow paint. She gave him blue paint too. Hudson dipped his brush in the yellow. He made a yellow stripe on the paper. He dipped the brush in the blue. He made a blue dot on top.

Then Hudson mixed them together with his brush. Round and round he stirred. The yellow went away. The blue went away too. Green came out! He stared at his brush. "Green!" he said.

Hudson painted tall grass all along the bottom of his page. His friend Caden leaned over. "How did you get green?" Caden asked. Hudson pointed at his two pots. "Yellow and blue," he said. Caden ran to get his own brush.

The class sang their tidy-up song. Hudson kept painting one more blade of grass, slow and careful. Then he put his brush down and smiled at his green, green field.

Stella sat at Grandma's big table. Her bear sat on the chair next to her. Lunch was warm and the kitchen smelled like bread.

Grandma folded her hands. "We say grace first," she said. "It is a little thank you prayer. Would you like to say it, Stella?"

Stella looked at her bear. "Say grace," Stella whispered. Her grandma said the words. Stella held hands with Grandma. "Thank you for our food," Stella said. "Amen."

Then Grandma passed the bread. Stella took a bite. It was soft and good. The sky outside was cloudy, but the kitchen felt warm and bright.

"Now we eat," said Grandma. "We said grace, and now we eat." Stella smiled. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma kissed her head. "Yes, sweet girl. Every meal."

Hayden sat at the kitchen table. He had red, yellow, and blue paint. Mom had set out three cups of water too. Hayden pointed at each cup. "Red," he said. "Yellow. Blue." Mom smiled.

Hayden wanted to paint a stormy sky. He dipped his brush in the blue. He made big blue strokes on his paper. He sat back and looked. The sky was too dark. It did not look like a morning sky at all. It looked like night. Hayden frowned. "What can I do?" he wondered.

Then he saw the white paint. Would that help? He stirred his brush in the white. He tapped it onto the blue sky. He mixed them round and round. The blue grew lighter. Now it looked soft, like the sky after rain. Hayden gasped. "White made my blue lighter!" he said.

He mixed yellow and blue next. Green appeared on his paper. "Mom, look! Blue and yellow make green!" Mom clapped her hands. Hayden held up his work for her to see.

Charles rode the city bus with his dad. He held his red string for his toy bunny. The bunny had a string tail he loved to pull. But now the bunny was gone.

"Oh no," said Charles. "Bunny is lost." He looked under his seat. It was dark there. He could not see anything at all.

His dad reached into his bag. He pulled out a little flashlight. He clicked it on. "Here," said Dad. He held the light and shined it under the seat.

The dark spot was bright now. Charles could see dust and a gum wrapper. He could see his bunny. "Bunny!" said Charles. He reached down and got it. The light had helped him see into the dark spot.

A sleepy old man sat across from them. He smiled at the bunny. Charles hugged bunny tight. "Say hi, bunny," said Charles. The sleepy man laughed and waved at the bunny's little string tail.

The community hall was full of people. Lights hung from the ceiling. Music played in the corner. Isabelle held her dad's hand.

Then she saw the food table. There were little sweets in a row. Isabelle let go of her dad's hand. She began to reach for the table.

The crowd was big. So many legs, so many coats. Isabelle could not see her dad. She turned around fast. She looked at the chairs. She looked at the door.

Then she saw her dad's blue coat. He was waving to her. Isabelle ran back to him. She grabbed his hand and held it tight.

At a big crowded celebration, she would stay close. "Hold my hand," her dad said. Isabelle nodded and did not let go.

They walked to the food table together. Her dad picked up one sweet sweet for her. Isabelle ate it and smiled.

Ms. Chatterjee came by with a big tray. "Isabelle, would you like one more?" she asked. Isabelle looked up at her dad. He nodded yes.

Isabelle took the sweet with her free hand. Her other hand stayed right where it was.

Maria went to the bank with her dad. She wore her new red coat. Her dad was still doing her zipper for her every day. "Can I try?" Maria asked. Her dad smiled. "Yes, you can try."

Maria pinched the little metal slide. She pushed it up, up, up. Click! The zipper closed all the way. "I did it!" she said. Mr. Lawson, the bank man, clapped at his window. "Nice zipper work," he said. Maria liked his kind face.

Then Maria heard a small sound at the window. Tap, tap, tap. Raindrops! They sat and watched. Maria had a question in her head. Where could her head go? Then she felt the soft part at the back of her coat. She found it and pulled it up over her head. "A hood!" she said. "My coat has a hood." Her dad laughed and pulled his hood up too. They walked out into the drizzle, two red hoods bobbing down the street.

Kayden wanted to play hide-and-seek. He hid behind the big chair. Then he put his hands over his eyes. "You can't see me, Dad!" he called.

Dad laughed. "I can still see you, Kayden." Kayden peeked through his fingers. His eyes were open now. Dad's smiling face was right there. "I see you!" Kayden said.

Then his ears heard a bell. The oven bell! His nose smelled warm cookies. His tongue wanted to taste them. Dad used big mitts, so his hands would not burn on the hot pan. Kayden touched one cookie when it was cool. It was bumpy with chocolate chips.

The mail slot clicked. A letter fell on the mat. Kayden ran to it. He held it up high. "Look, Dad! The mailman can see me too!"

Michael was going to the dentist. It would be his first time. "What will the dentist do?" he asked his mom. "The dentist will look at your teeth," she said.

So Michael practiced at home. He stood by the big mirror. He opened his mouth. Then he wanted to talk, and his mouth went shut. The mirror showed no teeth at all. He tried again. He opened his mouth wide. His mouth went shut again when he said "hello" to the mirror.

His mom had an idea. "Point to a picture of a lion," she said. Michael pointed to the lion in his book. The lion had its mouth open wide for a big roar. Michael tried the roar. "Roooar!" His mouth stayed open. He could see every tooth in the mirror. One open mouth made every tooth show up. "Cool," said Michael.

At the dentist, a kind man looked into Michael's mouth. Michael did not talk. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion. Every tooth was easy to see. "Roooar," said Michael, very quietly, with his mouth still open.

Cooper sat in his car seat. Mom was driving. Violet sat in the middle, next to him.

"Please may I have a cracker?" Violet asked Mom.

"Yes, Violet," said Mom. She passed one back.

"Thank you," said Violet.

Cooper did not know what to say back. His mouth stayed quiet. He asked Mom, "What do I say now?"

"You can say 'you're welcome'," said Mom.

"You're welcome!" said Cooper. Violet laughed. Cooper laughed too.

Then Cooper dropped his cracker on the floor. "Sorry, Mom," he said. "Please help me."

Mom found a new cracker in her bag. "Here you go."

"Thank you," said Cooper.

"You're welcome," said Mom.

They counted crackers together. One, two, three. Cooper ate his and watched the trees go by.

Luca was at the farm with his dad. He had three little seeds in his hand. One seed for a carrot. One seed for a pea. One seed for a bean. Luca made a hole in the soil. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the soil down, pat, pat, pat.

"Where did my seeds go?" Luca asked. His dad said, "They are sleeping under the dirt."

Every day Luca came to look. He gave the soil a little water. He said, "Wake up, seeds." The soil stayed brown and quiet. Mr. Ivanova was fixing a fence nearby. "Still sleeping," he said with a smile.

On the fifth day, Luca saw something new. A tiny green tip was poking up out of the soil. "Dad, Dad, come quick!" Luca ran to the gate. His dad knelt down. "A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout," he said. Luca looked at it. "A sprout," he said softly. The sprout was small and green like a little finger.

Levon and Kairo came to see. They counted together. "One sprout, two sprouts, three sprouts." One for the carrot. One for the pea. One for the bean. A naughty bird flew close, and Levon waved it away from the sprouts. Luca drew a picture of them. He drew three green tips in brown soil. "Grow big," Luca told the sprouts.

Emmett sat in the kitchen. His mom set out four orange plates. Jamal was coming for dinner. So was Zoelie. "I want to say the good-meal words," said Emmett. "Like Ms. Lavoie does."

Emmett picked up his pencil. He drew the words on paper. But he did not know the words yet. He drew a big orange plate instead. One plate, two plates, three plates, four. Then the doorbell rang.

Jamal and Zoelie came in. They sat at the table. The food was hot, so Emmett's mom carried it. Emmett waited. He wanted words, but the words would not come. Then Zoelie folded her hands. "Ms. Lavoie says bon appétit," she said. "In France, people often say it before a meal." Jamal said it. Zoelie said it. Emmett took a big breath. "Bon appétit!" he said. Everyone smiled. Emmett picked up his fork. "Bon appétit," he said again, just because he liked it.

Wesley stood in the bathroom. He wanted to play the guessing game. Caleb had left a bag on the sink. Inside were three things. Wesley could not peek.

His dad held up a towel. "Close your eyes," Dad said. Wesley closed his eyes tight. He put out his hand. His fingertips touched the first thing. It was smooth and cool. "The stone!" Wesley said. He was right.

The next thing felt bumpy and prickly. "The pinecone," he said. Right again. The last thing was soft as a dream. It tickled. "The feather," Wesley laughed.

Then Dad let one drip of water fall. Plop. Wesley heard it with his ears. The soap smelled like flowers, and he sniffed it with his nose. He chewed his apple slice at the sink and tasted the sweet.

Dad ran the warm water and Wesley felt it on his fingertips, soft and smooth. "One more guess," said Dad. He hid something behind his back. Wesley closed his eyes and held out his hand. "It is straight and bumpy," he said slowly. "The comb!" said Dad.

Grandma's car pulled up. Caleb jumped with joy. Grandma was staying for a whole week!

Caleb ran to the car. He saw a big bag on wheels. "What is that?" he asked.

"That is my suitcase," said Grandma. "Guests who come to stay pack their clothes and things in a suitcase or bag."

Caleb helped pull the suitcase in. It was big. It bumped on the step. The cat ran away from the wheels.

"Can I open it?" asked Caleb.

"Yes," said Grandma. She clicked it open. Inside were shirts and socks. There were shoes too. And a small box with a bow.

"That is for you," said Grandma.

Caleb opened the box. It was a toy boat! "It floats in the bath," said Grandma.

At bath time, Caleb put the boat in the tub. The water was warm. Dad checked the water first. The boat floated round and round.

"My clothes are wet," said Caleb, laughing.

The next morning, Caleb saw Grandma put her shirt back in the suitcase. "I will wear it again," she said. The suitcase kept her things safe all week.

At night, Caleb said, "Stay in my room, boat."

Grandma smiled. "The boat can sleep by the suitcase," she said.

"Good night, boat. Good night, suitcase," said Caleb.

Noah sat at the big table in the library. His friend Mateo sat next to him. Mr. Johansson put out paper and fat pencils.

"I want to write my name," said Noah. He held the pencil tight. He made a small n. Then o, a, h. He looked at his paper. "noah," it said.

Mateo held up his paper. It said "Mateo" with a big M at the start. Noah looked again. His tummy felt funny. "Mine looks wrong," he said.

Mr. Johansson smiled. "Watch this," he said. He took a new paper. He wrote "Noah" with a big N at the start. "A name gets a big letter at the start," he said.

Noah grabbed his pencil. The pencil almost did slip out of his hand. He held it again. He made a big N. It was rough and wobbly, but it was big. Then o, a, h. "Noah!" he read out loud.

The big clock on the wall went tick tock. Noah wrote his name again. Big N, o, a, h. "Now it matches Mateo's," he said. Mateo clapped. Noah slid the paper across the table to show him.

Grandpa sat down to read Alexander a story. Grandpa picked up his glasses first. He put them on his nose. Then he opened the big book.

"Why do you wear those?" Alexander asked. "Try them," said Grandpa. Alexander put them on. The page looked big and funny. The words were all soft and swirly. He took them off. Now the page looked clear again, but small. Grandpa put them back on. Grandpa could see the small words clearly.

Alexander looked with his eyes at the pictures. There was an owl in the tree. He touched the owl with his finger. The paper felt smooth and cool. "Listen," said Grandpa. He made an owl sound, "Hoo, hoo!" Alexander heard it with his ears. Then Grandpa sniffed the page. "Smells like an old book," he said. Alexander sniffed with his nose too. It smelled dusty and sweet.

Later, Mom gave Alexander a slice of apple. He tasted it with his tongue. Sweet and juicy! "Can I see the owl again?" Alexander asked. Grandpa held up the glasses. "These help my eyes see it clearly," he said. Alexander leaned close to the picture. The owl stared right back at him. "Hoo," whispered Alexander.

Arthur sat in the playroom with a big box of blocks. His friend Alina came to play too. "Let's sort them," said Alina. She put all the red blocks in one pile. She put all the green blocks in another pile. Arthur tipped the box. Some blocks began to spill out. "Oh no," said Arthur. "Don't worry," said Mr. Demir, who was sitting nearby. "We can pick them up together."

Arthur picked up the blocks. Then he looked at the piles. He had an idea. "Can I sort them my way?" he asked. "Yes, you can," said Alina. Arthur put the big blocks in one pile. He put the small blocks in another pile. The same blocks, but in new piles! "Why do they look different?" Arthur asked. "Because this time I sorted by size, not by color," he said.

Then Alina clapped her hands. Under the blocks was a small paper map. It showed where a toy animal was hiding. Arthur and Alina followed the map to the toy box. There was a little green frog toy waiting. Arthur hugged the frog. "Sorting is fun," he said. Mr. Demir smiled. "Frog says ribbit," said Arthur, and he made the frog jump onto the big pile of blocks.

Mila was going on a big trip. Her family was flying to a lake. Then they would sleep in a tent. Mila put her teddy bear in her little pink backpack. "You can ride with me," she told him.

At the airport, the bags had to go somewhere. Dad put Mila's backpack on a moving belt. The backpack slid away into a big machine. The machine had a long dark tunnel. Mila could not see her bear anymore. "My bear is gone," she said. Her lip went wobbly. She stood on her toes. She watched and watched.

A man in a uniform stood by the desk. "Watch the other end," he said kindly. Mila looked down the other side of the machine. The belt kept moving. And then, out came her backpack! It slid right into her hands. The bear was still inside. He had not gone away. He had just gone through.

"He took a ride," said Mila. She gave the bear a squeeze. Dad laughed and put the backpack on Mila's back. They walked to the plane. Later, at the campsite, the lake was blue and still. Mila felt proud. "The machine gave you back," she whispered to the bear. "Good night, little rider."

Sadie was awake early. Snow had fallen in the night. It sat white and soft outside the window. Her mother gave her a big bowl of buttons to play with.

Sadie made two rows of buttons on the rug. She pushed one row close together. She spread the other row out wide. The wide row looked so long. "This one has more," said Sadie. "It goes all the way to the cat." The cat gave one small scratch at the rug, then went to sleep.

Sadie counted the wide row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the bunched row. "One, two, three, four, five." She sat very still. Both rows were five. She counted again. Five and five, again. Then she pushed the wide row close, and the short row spread out long. She counted once more. Five and five. The buttons were the same all along.

Then Sadie tipped the bowl over by mistake. Buttons rolled under the couch. "Now I have to count them all back," she said. She lined them up in one long row and began. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She looked at the row. "Ten buttons went in. Ten buttons come out."

Noah got his first pet today. It was a small brown puppy. He named the puppy Biscuit. Noah wanted Biscuit to sleep in his sock drawer, but Mom said no. Biscuit needed a soft bed of his own.

In the backyard, Biscuit ran in circles. Then he stopped running. He sat down and would not play. He did not want his ball. Noah felt worried.

"He needs a doctor," Noah said. "But doctors are for people!"

Mom shook her head gently. "Not just people," she said. "A vet is a doctor for animals."

They drove to the vet. Noah looked around the room. A cat sat in a basket. A rabbit sat in a lap. A big dog waited by the door. Noah's eyes grew wide. "Wow," he said. "So many pets!"

The vet looked at Biscuit. She looked in his ears. She felt his tummy. "He is okay," she said. "He just needs rest and water."

At home, Noah filled Biscuit's water bowl. He set it in a deep shade by the fence. Biscuit drank a long drink. Then he curled up and slept.

The next morning, Biscuit jumped on Noah's bed. He licked Noah's nose. Noah laughed and hugged him tight.

Lincoln put on his swim shorts. They were tight at first. Then he pulled and pulled. Now they fit just right. "Are we going to the pool?" he asked. "Yes," said his dad. "The pool at the community center."

At the pool, Lincoln saw his friend Calum. Calum started to run to the water. Then Calum's feet slid out. He landed on his bottom. Splash, right on the wet floor. Mr. Rao came over fast. "The floor is wet and slippery," said Mr. Rao. "We walk, not run." Calum stood up slowly. He nodded.

Lincoln looked down at his feet. The floor was shiny and wet. So that was it. Wet floor, then a slide. He tried one little step. Then one more. No sliding. "I walk, I walk," he said. He said it like a song.

Lincoln got in the water at the steps. He held the rail tight. He practiced kicking. One kick, two kicks, three kicks. Calum practiced too. They counted together. "One, two, three. One, two, three."

When it was time to go, Mr. Rao helped them out. The floor was still wet. So Lincoln walked, slow and steady, step by step. "Look at me, Calum," he said. "I did not slide at all." Calum walked beside him. Their feet went pat, pat, pat all the way to the towels.

Grace wanted to sort her toys. She had three boxes. One box was for animals. One box was for toys. One box was for foods. She picked up her toy apples and bananas. They went in the foods box. Then she picked up her fluffy dog. It was brown and soft.

Grace put the dog in the animal box. Then she stopped. She looked at the dog. "This dog does not run," she said. "This dog does not eat. It is not alive." So Grace put the dog in the toy box instead. It sank down softly next to her teddy bear.

Her friend Maxence came to play. He held the toy dog and hugged it. "The dog is a toy, not an animal," Grace said. Maxence smiled. He found a toy cat and put it in the toy box too. Then they sat together and shared a snack of crackers.

Madison sat with her family at the temple. Tonight was the first night of Hanukkah. Her dad held the candles. He put one candle in the menorah. Then he lit it with a match.

Madison counted the flames. "One," she said. Her friend Sidney leaned over to look. "One little light," he said. Sidney made a joke about the candle wearing a tiny hat. Madison laughed. The candle burned tall and straight, not flat at all.

The next night, Madison came back. Her dad lit two candles this time. She counted again. "One, two!" Every night after that, one more candle burned. On the eighth night, all the candles were lit. Madison counted them all. Then she clapped her hands and sang with everyone.

Muhammad went to the library with his dad. He saw a big red book about trucks. He hugged it tight. "I want this one," he said.

Then Muhammad felt worried. The book lived at the library. How could it come home with him? His dad said, "Follow me to the desk." A kind librarian sat there. "Is this for you?" she asked. Muhammad nodded slowly. "You need a library card," she said. She made a small card with Muhammad's name on it.

The librarian scanned the card. Then she scanned the book. "The card lets you borrow books," she said. "You can take it home to read." Muhammad smiled so big. Outside, the weather was cool and sunny. Muhammad held his card in one hand. He held the truck book in the other. "Let's read it tonight!" he said.

Elias went to his mom's office. He saw a shiny tablet on her desk. The screen was dark. Elias tapped the dark screen. He tapped it again and again. It stayed dark.

His mom came over. "Press this little button," she said. "That is the power button." Elias pressed the button. The screen lit up. He smiled big. His mom opened the drawing app for him. Elias drew a red circle. Then he drew a blue cat.

"Time to go home," his mom said. Elias did not yell. He pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet down on the desk, all by himself. Then he held his mom's hand. "Bye, tablet," he said. "See you next time."

Luna sat in the nursery room. A little basket was on the floor. Her new baby sister was inside. The baby made a small sound.

"Can I hold her?" Luna asked. "Not standing up," said Dad. "You have to sit." So Luna sat down on the low couch. Dad sat right beside her. He put the baby in Luna's arms. "I am a big sister," said Luna. The baby yawned.

The next day, Zachary came to play. "I want to hold the baby too," he said. "First you sit," said Luna. She showed him the couch. Dad sat close and helped. Zachary held the baby very still. The baby fell asleep. "She likes us," Luna said. She kissed the baby's tiny hand.

Eva wanted to go to the library. Mom had said, "We will go soon." Eva was not sure when soon would be.

At dinner, Eva asked, "Is the library tomorrow?" Mom shook her head. "No, Eva. It is today." Eva's eyes got big. "Today is now?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day that is happening right now. Yesterday we made soup. Tomorrow is the next day after this one. But the library is today."

Eva put on her itchy sweater. She let Mom fix the tag so it did not scratch. Then they walked to the library. Eva found a book about a red truck. She hugged it tight.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Mom smiled and said, "Yes. Tomorrow, after dinner." Eva held Mom's hand all the way home.

Sophia held her mom's hand at the cultural center. Red paper lanterns hung from the ceiling. Liya waved from across the room.

Liya gave Sophia a red envelope. "It has money inside," Liya said. "Say thank you first. Then open it."

Sophia wanted to peek right away. Her fingers pulled at the corner. Mom put a gentle hand on her arm. "Wait, Sophia. Try again."

Sophia stopped. She looked at Liya. "Thank you," she said. Liya laughed and clapped. Then Sophia opened the envelope. A shiny coin sat inside. Her tooth showed in a big smile.

Later they watched the grown-ups light small candles, from far away. A purple dragon danced by. Sophia waved her envelope at it.

"Look, Mom," she said. "My red envelope!"

Colton went to the store with his mom. He held her hand at the big door. The store had apples, bread, and milk. One aisle, two aisles, three aisles, Colton counted. Then he saw a cute butterfly on a card. He stopped to look. When he looked up, Mom was not there.

Colton felt his heart go fast. He looked left. He looked right. No Mom. Then he saw a worker in a green vest by the checkout. His mom had told him what to do. Colton walked to the worker and said, "I can't find my grown-up."

The worker smiled. "Let's find her," she said. She spoke into her phone. Soon Mom came running. She hugged Colton tight. "You did it right," Mom said. On the way home, Colton saw one bird, then two birds. "I want to learn about birds next," he said. Mom laughed and held his hand all the way to the car.

Louis stood in the school cooking classroom. He wanted to make pancakes for his family. Mr. Wiśniewski handed him a card. "This is a recipe," he said. "It tells you what to use and what to do, one step at a time."

Louis poured the flour. He cracked the eggs. Aubrie stirred with a big fork. Adley measured the milk. Then Louis got excited and skipped a step. He did not add the baking powder. The teacher poured the batter onto the hot pan. Louis watched from his safe spot.

The pancakes came out flat. Flat like little plates. Louis frowned. "Let's read the recipe again," said Mr. Wiśniewski. They read it together, one step at a time. Louis found the step he missed. The next pancakes puffed up big and soft. They smelled sweet and warm.

Louis carried the plate home. His furry dog sniffed the bag. "Not for you," said Louis with a giggle. His mom took a bite. "These do not hurt my tummy at all. They are yummy!"

Isabella sat at the little table. Ms. Kovalenko gave her a pencil and paper. "Today we will write your name," said Ms. Kovalenko. Isabella wanted to write it all by herself.

She gripped the pencil tight. She pressed down hard. Snap! The tip broke off and fell on the paper. "Oh no," said Isabella. "What happened?" Malika leaned over. "You pressed too hard," said Malika. "Try soft hands." Isabella picked up the pencil again.

She drew the letter I, slow and light. The line was smooth. Then two S's, then a B, then more letters. She made a heart next to her name. Ms. Kovalenko caught the paper and held it up. "Isabella," she read. "You wrote your name." Isabella smiled at her letters. "Can I write it again?" she asked. Ms. Kovalenko nodded and gave her one more sheet.

Evan sat at the dinner table. He had ten green beans on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

"One, two," said Evan. Then he stopped. He could not remember what came next.

His big sister sat beside him. She sang a little song. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

"Three, four, shut the door!" Evan sang too. The words fit together like a puzzle. They rhymed, and that helped him remember.

"Is that how you remember the numbers?" Evan asked.

"It helps me," she said. "The rhyme holds them in my head."

So Evan counted his beans. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All ten beans, in a real row.

Dad slid the carrots over. "One more thing to count," he said.

Evan grinned and began again. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Jacob ran to the block corner at school. Maely was already there. She was building a big horse out of blocks.

"The horse is mine now," said Maely. "You can have the blocks later."

"Is it later yet?" Jacob asked.

"Not yet," said Maely.

Jacob sat down. He looked at the clock. He watched Ms. Almeida wipe the tables. The tables were all sticky with glue from art time.

"Is it later yet?" Jacob asked.

"Not yet," said Maely. She put two more blocks on the horse.

Jacob waited some more. He heard the songs from circle time. Then he had his snack. Then the class went outside. Jacob found a yucky leaf on his shoe and shook it off.

When the class came back inside, Jacob looked at the block corner. Maely was not there anymore. She was painting with Fern.

Jacob picked up the blocks. Now it was later. He stacked them up, up, up. He made a tall horse with a long tail.

"Nice horse," said Maely.

"You can play too," said Jacob. "Now it is your later."

James stood on the big soccer field. The grass felt soft under his shoes. A hoop lay on the ground. Ms. Yang gave him a red beanbag.

"Throw it in the hoop," said Ms. Yang. James looked at his friend Aarush. He waved and threw. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed in the dirty grass.

"Oops," said James. Aaira ran over. "Watch me," she said. Aaira looked at the hoop. She threw her beanbag. It went right in.

James picked up his beanbag. He brushed off the dirt. This time he looked at the hoop. He looked and looked. Then he threw. The beanbag dropped into the hoop. "Hooray!" said Aarush.

Then Ms. Yang rolled a big ball to him. James held out both hands. He caught it against his chest. It was soft and warm from the sun.

"Again," said James. Ms. Yang smiled and rolled the ball again.

Maverick ran into the kitchen at Grandma's house. The room smelled like soup. Grandma was stirring the big pot. Grandpa carried the bread to the table.

"Sit down, Maverick," said Grandma. "First we say our word."

Maverick sat. But he did not know the word. He felt his face go hot. What if he said it wrong?

Grandpa clapped his hands. "Bon appétit!" he said.

Maverick's mouth popped open. "What is that?"

Grandma laughed. "It is what people in France say before a meal. It means we wish everyone a good meal."

Maverick took a big breath. "Bon... appétit!" he said. Grandma clapped. Grandpa clapped. Even the soup seemed to bubble louder.

"I said it!" said Maverick. "Bon appétit, soup!"

Grandma poured the soup into his bowl. "And bon appétit to you too," she said, with a wink.

Isaac went to the animal shelter with his dad. There were dogs everywhere. One small puppy wagged her tail at Isaac. "She is the one," said Isaac. A helper clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. "The leash keeps her close," said the helper.

They walked home. The puppy was soft and warm. She smelled every leaf. Then a bird flew by. The puppy wanted to chase it. She pulled and pulled. But the leash was clipped to her collar, and Isaac's dad held the leash tight. So the puppy stayed close. No chase! The bird flew away.

Isaac smiled. He gave the puppy water in a little bowl. She drank with tiny licks. "Good friend," said Isaac. The puppy gave his hand one soft bite, just playing. Isaac giggled and hugged her tight.

Caleb was at daycare. He needed to use the toilet. He ran to the little bathroom.

He pulled down his blue pants. He used the toilet. Then he pulled his pants back up. He ran to the sink and washed his hands. Sultan came in and said, "Caleb, you forgot to flush." Caleb looked at the toilet. The water was still sitting there.

"I will do both steps," Caleb said. He pushed the handle. Whoosh! The water went down. Then he went to the sink again. He washed his hands with soap. Ms. Nair said, "Nice job, Caleb." Later, Caleb saw Claire wash her hands too. He said, "Did you flush first?" Claire nodded. Caleb smiled and clapped.

Lily ran to the park with her soccer team. The sun was big and hot. "Go, go, go!" said Mr. Morales. Lily kicked the ball one time. Then she kicked it two times. Then she kicked it three times. Kasen clapped. Ibrahim clapped too.

Lily ran a lot. Her face turned red. Mr. Morales blew the whistle. "Break time!" he said. The players sat on the grass. Kasen drank from his water bottle. Ibrahim drank from his water bottle. Lily looked in her bag. Oh no. No water bottle. She had left it at home.

"I am so thirsty," said Lily. Mr. Morales ran to his big bag. He brought a cold water bottle over. "Here you go," he said. Lily drank and drank. Then the whistle blew again. Lily ran fast. She kicked the ball far. "Goal!" said Ibrahim. Lily clapped for herself. Then the team did a big cheer: "One, two, three, water!"

Ethan wanted his bedtime book. He could not find it. "Where is my bear book?" he asked.

Dad found it under the bed. "Here it is," said Dad. Dad opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. Dad read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear goes up the stairs."

Then Dad had to answer the phone. "Mommy, you read it," said Ethan.

Mom sat down on the bed. She opened the front cover too. She turned the pages one by one. Mom read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear goes up the stairs."

Ethan sat up. "Same words!" he said. "You said what Daddy said!"

Mom laughed. "Yes, the same words every time."

Ethan listened to the page. He put his finger on the words. "Say it loud," he said.

Mom read it loud. "Bear hears a big bone go CRUNCH!"

"Again, again!" said Ethan.

Mom turned to the back page. "The end," she read.

"Same end too," said Ethan. He hugged the book tight and closed his eyes.

Andrew stood in the garage with his blue coat. He wanted to zip it up all by himself. It was cold outside, and Mom was waiting by the car.

Andrew pushed one arm into a sleeve. Then he pushed his other arm in too. But both arms went into the same sleeve! He looked like a wiggly worm. He laughed and fell over on the soft rug. "Silly arms," he said.

He shook his arms out. Then he put one arm in one sleeve. His other arm went in the other sleeve. The coat felt just right now. He pulled the zipper up fast. It made a little noise, zip zip. "I did it!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. Andrew ran to the car, warm and happy.

Emile was in the band room. He had an old drum. Lilly had a little bell. They wanted to play a song together. Emile hit his drum fast. Lilly rang her bell fast too. They went faster and faster. The song fell apart. It sounded like a big mess. Emile put down his sticks. Lilly sat on the old bench for a little nap break. Then Emile had an idea. He tapped his drum slowly. Tap, tap, tap. The beat was steady. Lilly listened. She rang her bell with his taps. Tap, tap, ding. Tap, tap, ding. Now the song worked. Ms. Chaudhry came in. She smiled and clapped along. "Play it one more time," she said. Emile locked eyes with Lilly and counted, "One, two, three, go."

Snow fell all night. School was closed. Audrey ran to the backyard in her boots. The snow was deep and white. It was windy, but the sun came out too. Audrey wanted to make something pretty in the snow. She did not know what yet.

She lay down in the snow. She swept her arms up and down. She swept her legs out and in. Then she stood up fast. She looked back at the snow. "Oh no," she said. There was a big smudge in the middle. Her boots had made it. She tried again. She lay down in a new spot. She swept her arms and legs slowly. Then she rolled to the side and stood up away from it. She looked back and gasped.

The snow held a pretty shape with wings. The neighbor, Ms. Siddiqui, waved from her window. "You made a snow angel!" she called. Audrey hugged herself in her big coat. "A snow angel," she said. She made one more, then one more. The backyard was full of wings.

Everett wanted a story. He asked his dad, "Can we read now?"

Dad was washing dishes. He said, "Not now. Now means at this very moment. The story is after bath time."

Everett looked at the dishes. The sink was full. Dad washed one cup. Then he washed one plate. The pile got smaller.

Everett waited. He drew a slow snail on paper. He made the snail skip over a little farm. The bath water ran next.

Dad said, "The sink is empty now. Bath time is now, too."

Everett splashed in the tub. He washed his toes. Then Dad wrapped him in a big towel.

"Now the story?" Everett asked.

"Yes. It is now," said Dad.

They sat on the couch together. Everett held the book. "Today we read," he said with a smile. Dad turned the first page.

Ivy sat with Mom and Dad at the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. Her friends Armaan and Ruby sat nearby too. People were kicking a ball on the screen. There was a net at each end.

"The ball goes over the net," said Ivy. She pointed up high.

Then a player kicked the ball. The ball went into the net. Everyone jumped up. Everyone shouted, "Goal!"

Ivy clapped her hands. "The ball goes in the net!" she said. Ruby gave her a high five. Armaan shared his crayon with her. Ivy drew a picture of the net on her paper. She drew the ball going in.

The waiter brought fries. Mom put some on Ivy's plate. "Happy day," said Ivy. On the screen, another ball went into the net again. The crowd went wild, and so did Ivy.

Elliot was in the yard with his dog. The dog was brown and sweet. Elliot petted her soft fur. Then his mom called, "Lunch time!"

Elliot ran inside. He sat down at the table. He looked at his hands. They had dirt on them. They had dog hair on them too.

"I need to wash," said Elliot. He walked to the sink. His mom turned on the water for him. She made it warm. Elliot got the soap. He rubbed his hands together. Bubbles grew big and white. He sang the color song while he washed. Red, blue, green, yellow. The song took twenty seconds. Then he rinsed the bubbles off.

His mom gave him a towel. Elliot dried his hands all by himself. Now his hands were clean. He sat down and picked up his sandwich. He took one big happy bite.

Mom smiled. "May I ask you something?" she said. "Can you teach the dog song to the baby?"

Elliot giggled. "Dogs don't sing," he said. "But I can wash again later."

Milan went to the library with Grandpa. Grandpa said, "Today you get your own card." Milan held the new card in his hand. It had his name on it. Milan smiled a big smile.

Then Milan wanted a book about trucks. He looked on a low shelf near the window. No trucks there. He looked on another shelf. Still no trucks. Milan stood still and did not know where to look next.

A kind lady in a blue shirt walked over. "I am the librarian," she said. "I work here, and I help people find books." Milan said, "Can you help me find trucks?" The librarian took his hand. They walked to a shelf she knew. There was a big red truck book! Milan hugged it. The librarian put it in his bag. Milan held his card up high and said, "Thank you. I will come back soon."

Kinsley went to Grandma's house. The grass was wet. A black bird sat on the fence. Grandma said, "Mr. Mansour lives next door."

Kinsley wanted to pet Grandma's cat. The cat had soft fur like a feather. But the cat hid under the chair. Kinsley could not reach it.

They went outside to the garden. Grandma picked a red tomato. "Taste it," Grandma said. It was sweet. Then Mr. Mansour came to the gate. He waved. Kinsley hid behind Grandma's legs. She peeked out with one eye.

"Hello," said Mr. Mansour.

Kinsley peeked out a little more. "Hello," she said in a small voice.

Mr. Mansour smiled big. He opened his hand. He had a little bell for the cat. "Thank you," said Kinsley. She took the bell and shook it. Ding, ding.

The cat came out from under the chair. The cat heard the bell and ran to Kinsley. She petted the soft fur at last.

"Hello, cat," said Kinsley. The cat rubbed her hand. Ding, ding, went the bell.

Amelia went to the library. She wanted to find a book about animals. But the animal shelf was a big mess.

Amelia saw a box of toy blocks. She dumped them out. She picked up the red blocks. "Red goes with red," she said. She made a red pile. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Mr. Fischer put a little flag on each pile.

Her friend Navya came to help. Navya did not sort by color. She put all the big blocks in one row. Then all the small blocks in another row. "Look," Navya said. "Big, big, big. Small, small, small."

Amelia gasped. Same blocks, new rows! She stepped back to look. Then she clapped.

The girls put the blocks away. Mr. Fischer found the animal books. Amelia hugged a fuzzy bear book.

"Same blocks," said Amelia. "Sort them again!"

Andrew was at school. It was snack time. Each child got one square napkin. Romie sat next to him.

Andrew folded his square napkin in half. He pressed the fold with his hand. Then he looked at it. The napkin was not a square now. It was long and thin. "What is this shape?" Andrew asked. Mr. Pelletier leaned down. "That is a rectangle," he said. Andrew smiled. He ran his finger along the fold. "A square can become a rectangle," he said.

Zac tried it too. He folded his square napkin in half, edge to edge. His napkin became a rectangle too! Andrew laughed and clapped. The room smelled like crackers and juice. The sun made a big yellow circle on the table. Romie pointed to it. "Look, a circle," she said. Andrew took a slow bite of his snack. Then he folded his rectangle again, just to see what would happen.

Amira ran to the family car. They were going on a big trip. She climbed up into her car seat. She wanted to go right now.

"Click," said her buckle. No, it did not. Amira had forgotten to buckle. Her dad sat down. He looked back. He did not start the car. He waited.

Then Amira heard it. No click, no go. She pulled the straps over her shoulders. She pushed the buckle in. "Click!" The car stayed still before that. Now the car could go.

The car rolled out of the driveway. They drove past a farm. A brown horse stood by a low fence. A shop on the corner seemed to sell ice cream. "Can we stop later?" Amira asked. "Maybe on the way home," said her dad.

Amira sat snug in her car seat. The buckle was clicked. She watched the horse get small and small. "Off we go," said Dad.

Asher stood by the school gate. He held his small blue bag. The gate was big and silver. His mom gave him a hug. "Have fun, Asher," she said.

Asher walked in slowly. He saw Ms. Gauthier at the door. She smiled and waved. Isla ran past him to the toy corner. Hassan was building with soft blocks. Asher sat down next to a furry brown bear. He hugged it tight.

Then Asher needed to pee. He looked around the room. Where was the bathroom? He did not see it. His tummy felt tight. He wiggled on the rug.

Asher stood up. He walked to Ms. Gauthier. "I need the bathroom," he said in a small voice. She took his hand right away. "Come with me," she said. They walked down the hall. She pointed to a little door. "Here it is," she said.

Asher went inside. He came out and washed his hands. The water was warm and soapy. He felt better now. He ran back to the furry bear. "I asked the teacher!" he told Isla. Isla giggled. Asher squeezed the bear and smiled at the big school door.

Ryan wants to play shop at daycare. He has a little box and some toy food. But who will buy his food?

Brooklynn walks over. "I am the shopkeeper," Ryan says. "You can be the shopper." Brooklynn picks up a toy banana. She looks at it for a long time. Ryan waits and waits. Will she choose it?

Brooklynn smiles. "I will buy this banana," she says. She hands Ryan a round puzzle piece for money. Ryan puts the piece in his box. The banana goes into her bag. It worked!

Then Zach comes to the shop. "I am the shopkeeper," Ryan says again. "You are the shopper." Zach looks at the slimy toy pear and the shiny toy apple. He holds one in each hand. Ryan does not grab them. He waits, just like before. Zach picks the apple. "I will buy this," Zach says.

Ms. Lewandowski peeks in the door. "Who wants to play house next?" she asks. Brooklynn hides the banana behind her back. "The baby needs lunch," she says. Ryan laughs and fills a tiny cup with pretend milk.

Billie got a little brown dog at the park. Annie and Raegan came to see him. "His name is Tiny," said Billie. Tiny ran in the grass. He drank water from his bowl.

At home, Tiny ate his dinner. Billie wanted to play. "Wait, Tiny," she said. "I miss playing with you." Tiny ate and ate. Billie sat still and watched. Soon the bowl was empty. Then Tiny jumped up and wagged his tail. He chased the ball with Billie. "You played with me!" she said.

The next day at the park, Tiny curled up under a tree. He was sleeping. Raegan said, "Can we pat him?" Billie shook her head. "Tiny is sleeping. We leave him alone." The girls played on the swings instead. Tiny woke up and barked. "Now we can play!" said Billie. Tiny ran to the ball.

Ayla rode on a big train. She sat by the window with Mama. The train went choo, choo. Ayla held her small bag. Inside was a cookie for later, and her red shoes from the beach.

The train stopped. Then it went again. Ayla watched the trees go by. "We go home now," said Mama. Ayla looked out at the wooden fence by the track. It went fast, fast, fast.

At last they got home. Mama said, "Now we unpack our bags." Ayla unpacked her small bag. She put her pants in the drawer. She put her shirt in the drawer. Then she shook out her red shoes. Sand fell out! Sand from the beach was hiding in her shoe. Ayla laughed and laughed. "Sand came home with me!" she said. Mama gave her the cookie. Ayla sat on the rug and ate it all up, while sand covered her toes like tiny stars.

The bookmobile came to Hudson's street. It was a big truck full of books. The sky was cloudy, but Hudson did not mind.

"I want a card," Hudson said. "My own card!"

He ran to the little desk inside. Esmee was there. Usman was there too.

Ms. Fernando smiled. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," she said. "Is your dad with you?"

Hudson looked back. His dad waved from the door. He came in and helped Hudson write his name. One card, just for Hudson!

"Now I can borrow a book," Hudson said.

He counted the books he wanted. One book about trucks. One book about the moon. One book about a swing. One, two, three, four, five.

"You may take two," said Ms. Fernando.

Hudson picked trucks and the moon. He held his card up high.

Then Ms. Fernando stamped his hand. A little moon stamp! Hudson laughed all the way home.

"Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "Tomorrow, and the next day, and the next day!"

Aria stood at the front door. She looked out at the sky. The sun was big and bright. "It is sunny today," said Maude. The wind blew hard. "And windy!" laughed Margaux. Aria's hair flew in the wind. A squint is what her face did in the sun. Her eyes went small and tight.

The girls walked to the playground. Aria kept squinting. "My eyes feel funny," she said. Mr. Lombardi, their neighbor, was there. He held a smooth blue sun hat. "Try this," he said. Aria put it on. The hat made shade over her face. She opened her eyes wide. "Now I can see!"

The girls played tag. Aria ran fast in the sun. The hat stayed on her head. At lunch time, they sat in the grass. Aria ate her sandwich under her shady hat. Then rain drops fell, one by one. "Run!" said Maude. They ran to the door. Aria helped lock it behind them. She hung her hat on the hook. "Sun hat, you did a good job," she said.

Adam was at Grandpa's house. He had a cold. His nose was red. His cough came back and back.

Rio was outside in the yard. Rio was kicking a big red ball. Adam wanted to kick it too. He ran to the door.

His grandma stopped him. She held his hand. "Come lie on the couch," she said. "Resting on the couch helps your body get better."

Adam sat on the soft couch. Grandma brought his favourite book. She covered him with a warm blanket. His tummy felt cozy. Outside, the ball went bounce, bounce. Adam read about a slow little snail.

After a long rest, Adam's cough got small. His nose felt better too. He looked out the window. "Grandma, can I go out now?" he asked.

She felt his head. "Yes, you may."

Adam ran outside. Rio passed him the ball. Adam kicked it far, far across the green grass.

Kayden wanted the sheep book. It was on the shelf at daycare. Sukhmani had the truck book. Kayden took the sheep book down.

He opened the book. He saw a sheep on a page. Then he saw a sheep with a hat. Then he saw night time. Then he saw the sheep as a baby again. "That is mixed up," said Kayden. He turned more pages. The sheep went backwards.

Sukhmani came over. "Is it a mixed-up book?" she asked. Kayden looked at the book. He looked at the front. He looked at the back. Then he flipped the book over. "I will start at this side," he said. He opened the front cover. The baby sheep came first. The sheep got big. Then came night time. Then the sheep slept at the end.

Kayden smiled. "Sukhmani, look. The sheep starts little here." He tapped the words on the page. "And these are the real talking words," said Sukhmani. Kayden turned the pages slowly, one by one, all the way to the back cover. "The end," he read.

Andrew stood at the edge of the rink. Ms. Ahmed had big hoops on the floor. There were red beanbags in a box.

"My turn! My turn!" said Andrew. He grabbed three beanbags. He threw one. It missed the hoop. He threw another. It missed too.

Lucy held out her hand. "My turn now," she said. Ms. Ahmed knelt down. "Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn," she said. Andrew looked at the beanbags in his hands. He gave one to Lucy.

Lucy threw her beanbag. Plink! It went right in the hoop. "It went in!" she shouted. Now it was Andrew's turn again. He threw his beanbag. Plink! It went in too!

Sifat rolled a big ball to Andrew. Andrew held out both hands. He caught it! "I caught it!" he yelled. He was not grumpy anymore. He rolled the ball back fast.

"Again!" said Andrew. "Your turn first," he said, and handed Sifat the ball.

Isaiah sat in the art room. He had three paint pots. Red. Yellow. Blue.

"I know those," said Cassius. "Red, yellow, blue."

Isaiah wanted to paint a pumpkin. But he had no orange paint. He looked and looked. No orange pot anywhere.

Then he dipped his brush in the red. He tapped it in the yellow. The pot went swirly.

"Orange!" said Chiara. "You made orange!"

Isaiah painted a big round pumpkin. Then his tummy growled. "I'm hungry," he said. "My pumpkin looks good enough to eat."

Mr. Ma laughed. "No eating paint. First we wash the brushes."

Isaiah carried his brushes to the sink. The water turned orange. He rinsed each brush. Then he laid them flat to dry.

"My brother leaves his brushes in the paint," said Cassius. "They get all stiff."

"Not mine," said Isaiah. He set his last brush down, soft and clean.

Zachary was at the campsite with his family. He wanted to make breakfast for everyone. "Can I help?" he asked. "Yes," said his dad. "You can butter the bread."

Zachary opened the cooler. The butter was cold from the ice. He tried to spread it. The butter was too hard. It tore the bread. "Oh no," said Zachary. "Why is it so hard?" His dad said, "Cold butter is hard. Let's put it in the sun on the table."

They set the butter on the table. Zachary waited. He watched a duck chase a bug by the pond. He smelled the stinky campfire smoke. Then he touched the butter. It was soft now! "It changed!" said Zachary. "The butter got soft in the sun."

He spread the soft butter on the bread. It went on smooth and easy. "Wow," said Zachary. "Butter out here is soft. Butter in the fridge is hard." His mom cooked the bread on the grill. Zachary stayed back and watched.

Breakfast was ready. Zachary held up his plate. "I made this!" he said.

Gabriel sat on the rug in the nursery room. There was a new baby in his house. The baby was his little sister. Gabriel wanted to hold her very much.

Dad sat down next to him. Dad had the baby in his arms. Gabriel saw Dad's big hand under the baby's head. "Why do you hold her head?" Gabriel asked.

"The baby cannot hold up her own head yet," said Dad. "So I hold it for her." Dad put his hand under the baby's head, then he took it away, very slowly. The baby's head tipped to one side. Dad put his hand back. The head was safe again. Gabriel's eyes got big. He had made it happen with his question, and Dad had shown him the answer.

"Now you try," said Dad. Dad put a small pillow on Gabriel's lap. Then he laid the baby on the pillow. Gabriel put his hand under her head, just like Dad. His hand was careful and slow. The baby made a tiny sound. She did not spill a single tear.

"She likes me," Gabriel whispered. The baby held his finger. It was very small and very warm. "Hello, sister," said Gabriel.

Felix got on the city bus with his dad. They were going to the dentist. It was his first time. "Big boys sit still," said Felix. A lady next to them smiled. "Look," said Felix. A picture of an elephant was on the bus wall. It had one missing tooth. "He went to the dentist too," said Dad. Felix laughed.

At the dentist's office, Felix sat in a big chair. It went up and up. Then the dentist turned on a bright light above the chair. Felix made a squinty face. It was too bright.

The dentist saw Felix squinting. She handed him small sunglasses. "Here, try these," she said. Felix put them on. Now the light did not hurt his eyes. The bright light helped the dentist see inside his mouth. "Open wide," she said. Felix opened wide. He sat very still, like the big boy on the bus.

His teeth were all clean. Felix walked out wearing the sunglasses. "Can we fly home?" he asked. Dad laughed. "We can take the bus," he said. Felix waved to the elephant picture as they passed it.

Arlo wants to play rocket ship at daycare. But Diego is already inside the big cardboard box. "The rocket is full," says Diego. Arlo frowns. How can he get a turn?

Mr. Virtanen sits down with them. "Rockets need a countdown," he says. "You count ten, nine, eight, all the way down to one." Diego giggles. "Ten, nine, eight!" he calls. Arlo listens. The numbers go backward! "Seven, six, five!" Now Arlo says them too. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Arlo pushes his feet and jumps up high.

Then it is Arlo's turn in the box. He sits down. "Say the countdown with me!" he says. Diego nods. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Arlo jumps out. At lunch, Arlo bites his crunchy sandwich and smiles. "Ten, nine, eight," he whispers. Diego laughs. "Blast off!"

Aurora ran to school in her new shoes. Her tummy made a big growl. She saw her teacher Ms. Shevchenko with a tray.

"Can I have a cookie?" Aurora asked.

"Cookies are for after lunch," said Ms. Shevchenko. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day."

Aurora counted the breakfast things. "One, two, three. Banana, yogurt, toast!" She patted her tummy. It was happy.

Then Justin came in. His tummy growled too. He had no breakfast at home.

"Are you hungry?" Aurora asked him.

"Yes," said Justin.

"Then you need breakfast," she said. "One, two, three. Banana, yogurt, toast!" Justin took a banana and a yogurt. He ate them all up.

"Want a party at snack time?" asked Justin.

"Yes!" said Aurora. "We can share my crackers."

Ms. Shevchenko smiled and poured the milk.

Naomi looked out the daycare window. The sky was gray. Rain tapped on the glass. "It's a rainy day," said Mr. Hamdan. Naomi put on her boots. They were red and shiny. Then she put on her raincoat. It was yellow with a hood.

Benedict ran to the door. He had no raincoat. He went outside into the rain. Soon he came back. His shirt was all wet. "You need your raincoat," said Mr. Hamdan. "On a rainy day, a raincoat helps keep your body dry." Benedict found his blue raincoat. He zipped it up.

Then the children went out to play. Naomi felt the rain on her hood. It went tap, tap, tap. Her coat kept her dry underneath. She touched her arm. Not wet at all. Benedict ran in a puddle. His coat kept him dry too.

After lunch they had warm pizza. Outside it was windy. The wind blew the leaves across the yard. Mr. Hamdan said snow might come soon. Naomi hoped so. "Snowy days need mittens," she said. She held up her hands.

Grandma had a big box of crayons. Leo wanted to draw a boat. Poppy wanted to draw the sea.

"That one is not blue," said Poppy. "It is too dark."

"It is blue," said Leo. "I think it is."

They took out all the blue crayons. One was light blue, like the sky. One was blue, like a blueberry. One was dark blue, like the night.

Ms. Fortin, the neighbor, came in with a cookie for each of them. She looked at the crayons.

"Put them in a line," she said. "Lightest to darkest."

Leo lined them up. Light blue, then blue, then dark blue. "They are all blue," said Poppy. "Dark blue and light blue are still blue!"

Leo drew his boat with dark blue. Poppy drew the sea with light blue. The pictures stayed on the fridge.

"Dark boat on light sea," said Leo. "It looks big."

Bennett stood at the little table in the backyard. He was making Dad's birthday cake. He counted the eggs. One, two, two eggs in the bowl. He poured in milk. He poured in flour. He mixed and mixed.

The batter was runny and wet. Bennett looked at it. "Will this be a cake?" he asked. "It is too runny!" Dad smiled. "It gets thick in the oven," he said. Bennett wondered how. Was the oven like a robot? "No," said Dad. "It is just hot." Bennett watched Dad open the oven door. The oven was warm and noisy. Dad slid the pan in, very carefully. Bennett waited. He counted to ten, then counted again.

Then Dad opened the oven again. Out came a real cake! It was big and round. Dad cut one slice. The slice held its shape. Bennett touched the plate. "The runny batter turned into cake," he said. He carried the plate inside, one step at a time. "Happy birthday, Dad!"

Penelope wanted to draw a cat on the tablet. But the screen was dark. It was a sleepy, black screen.

She pressed the round button. Tap! The screen lit up. She tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared, just like paper. She drew a big orange cat with six whiskers.

Gianluca peeked over. "Your cat has a funny tail!" Penelope laughed. "It looks like a snake!"

Soon the tablet got sleepy too. The screen dimmed. Mr. Farah-Ali clapped his hands. "Time to put the tablets away."

Penelope saw the charger on the shelf. She picked it up and marched across the room. "Here, Mr. Farah-Ali!" Mr. Farah-Ali plugged the charger into the wall. Penelope watched him do it. Only a grown-up plugs the charger in.

Then she put the tablet on the cart. All done. Gianluca waved. "Bye, snake cat!" Penelope giggled. "Bye, snake cat!"

Lucas was a little boy. He was going on a big trip. His family was going to the snowy mountains.

Lucas packed his bag. He put in his red swimsuit. "I will swim there!" he said.

Dad looked at the bag. "Not the swimsuit," he said. "It is cold in the snow. We pack warm things for cold places. For the beach, we pack a swimsuit."

Lucas thought hard. He looked in his drawer. He found his mittens. He found his warm coat. He put them in the bag. "Warm things for the snow!" he said.

"Good packing," said Dad. He helped zip the bag.

At the park, the snow was white and soft. Lucas stomped in it. Crunch, crunch! His mittens kept his hands warm. His coat was cozy.

His friend Miley was there too. She wore a scarf. "Want to make a snowball?" she asked.
