"Yes!" said Lucas. He stirred the snow with his boot. Then he made a big snowball with his mittens on. He threw it softly. Plop!

"The warm coat was the right thing," said Lucas. He laughed and made another one.

Aubrey sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. She saw a big red truck. It went beep, beep. Then the light turned green. The car moved. One thing made another thing happen.

Soon they stopped at the park. Aubrey saw her friend Gursanjh. He had a bike. Aubrey wanted to ride it right away. She ran to the bike. Then she stopped. Where was the helmet? Gursanjh pointed to his bag. The helmet was in the middle of the bag. It felt heavy on her hands. Aubrey put it on her head. Gursanjh helped clip it.

"Helmet on," said Gursanjh.

Aubrey sat in the middle of the seat. She held on tight. Gursanjh pushed the pedals. Round and round they went, past the swings and the big tree.

Lennon hid in the bathroom. It was bath time, but she wanted to play first. She stood by the big round tub. She covered her eyes with her hands.

"I can't see you," she said. "So you can't see me!"

Ana came in. Ana giggled. "I see your knee, Lennon."

Lennon peeked through her fingers. Ana was waving. Lennon moved her hands away. Now she could see Ana's shoes and the fluffy towels too.

"My eyes were hiding," said Lennon.

She splashed one finger in the water. Her ears heard the little splash. Her nose smelled the sweet soap. The towel felt soft on her cheek. Ms. Gallagher helped her into the tub.

"Warm water," said Lennon. She blew a bubble and watched it pop.

Then Ana hugged her, wet and giggly.

"I see you," said Ana. "I always see you."

Luka went to the library today. Yesterday he could not go, because it rained. Today the sun was out.

Luka wanted storytime. He saw Ms. Charles by the big rug. "Is it now?" he asked.

"Soon," said Ms. Charles. "Storytime starts soon."

Luka sat down on the rug. He waited. He picked one book from the shelf. He looked at the pictures.

His friend Mickael came in. Mickael sat down too. "Is storytime now?" Mickael asked.

"Soon," said Luka. "Soon means in a little while."

Mickael looked out the window. He watched a bird hop on the step. Luka turned one page. Then another page.

Ms. Charles picked up her story book. "Storytime is now," she said.

Luka put his book down fast. Mickael clapped his hands.

Luka liked the story about a red truck. "Can we come again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Ms. Charles. "Tomorrow is storytime too."

Luka smiled and clapped with the rest of the children.

Brielle sat in her brown pajamas. It was bedtime now. "I want to fish at school tomorrow," she said. Her class was going to the pond. She could not wait.

At school, her friend Leif said, "I went fishing tomorrow!" He stopped and thought. "No, wait. I went fishing yesterday." He held up one finger. "Yesterday came first. Yesterday is the day before today." Brielle counted on her fingers. "One, yesterday. Two, today. Three, tomorrow!" Scarlet clapped. "You got it!"

"Now it is today," said Mr. Ortiz. "Later we fish." Brielle held her little pole. One, two, three fish swam by. Then she felt a tug. She pulled and pulled. A small fish wiggled on her line. "Tomorrow you can tell everyone," said Leif. Brielle smiled and let the fish swim home.

Sofia stood at the back door. She looked up at the sky. The sun was not there.

"Where did the sun go?" she asked.

Her grandma stood beside her. "The clouds are hiding it," Grandma said. "Clouds can hide the sun."

Sofia put on her yellow boots. She went into the backyard. The wind blew. It was a windy day. The leaves scratched the fence. They made a noisy sound.

Ren was there too. Ren wore a red hat because it was cold.

"I want the sun to come out," said Sofia.

"Wait and watch," said Ren.

They sat on the step. They watched the big white clouds. The clouds moved slowly. They moved and moved.

Then the clouds went away. The sun came out! It was sunny now. The grass looked bright.

"It came back!" said Sofia. She took off her red hat. She felt warm.

A duck waddled across the yard. It quacked at the sun too.

"Hello, duck," said Sofia.

Grandma called from the door. "Time for warm milk, Sofia."

Sofia ran to Grandma. The sun stayed out all the way.

Victor sat on the rug at school. Ms. Han put a big basket of socks on the table. "We will sort them," she said. The class sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," they sang. Victor sang too. Then he sang, "six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Victor picked up one sock. It was soft and blue. Quinton picked up one sock too. Leilani had one red sock.

"Look," said Ms. Han. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks."

Victor held up his sock. He looked in the basket. He dug and dug. He waited. He dug some more. Then he found a blue sock. He put the two together. Two socks. A pair!

Quinton found his pair. Leilani found hers.

"Can we spell the word pair?" asked Victor.

"Yes," said Ms. Han. She wrote it on the board.

Victor put his pair on the table and smiled.

Beau was at Grandpa's house. It was his birthday. There were presents on the table. There was a big cake in the fridge. The cake was cold and sweet.

Beau opened a present fast. It was a soft gray elephant. He hugged it tight. Then he saw another present. He reached for it. But Oaklynn was standing there. She had given him the elephant. Beau looked at her. Then he looked at the elephant again.

"Thank you, Oaklynn," said Beau. Oaklynn smiled big. "You are welcome," she said. She looked happy.

Cristian gave Beau a present too. It was a red truck. The wheels really worked. Beau pushed it on the floor. It rolled far. Beau stopped and looked up. "Thank you, Cristian," he said. Cristian clapped his hands.

Then Grandpa lit the candles. Everyone waited. Beau waited too. He took a big breath. "Happy birthday to you!" they all sang. Beau blew and blew. The candles went out. He hugged his elephant and said, "Best birthday ever."

Brooks woke up early. Today he would get a shot. He put on his yellow shirt. "Will it hurt?" he asked. His mom said, "Just a tiny pinch. Then it is done."

At the doctor's office, Brooks stood on the scale. The numbers jumped up and down. He was wiggling his toes. Mr. Otieno, the nurse, smiled. "Stand still," he said. Brooks made his feet like stones. The numbers stopped. There it was. The scale showed how much he weighed. "That's me!" said Brooks.

Then came the shot. Brooks looked at his mom's eye and counted one, two, three. It was done. The nurse poured two stickers into his hand. One had a dinosaur. A surprise dinosaur! "Can we show Zahra?" Brooks asked. "Yes," said Mom. Brooks held the sticker all the way home.

Romy sat on her bed. It was bedtime, but she was not sleepy.

"Grandma comes tomorrow," said Romy. She felt so excited. When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout. So Romy jumped on her bed. She bounced high. She shouted, "Grandma is coming!"

Dad came in. "It is bedtime, Romy," he said. "You need a quiet body for sleep."

"But I am excited," said Romy.

"I know," said Dad. "Let's find a calm way to wait."

Romy stopped bouncing. She put one finger on her lips. "Like this?" she asked. "Quiet?"

"Yes," said Dad. "Let's draw Grandma a picture. Drawing can help calm your excited body."

Romy drew a big red heart. She drew Grandma's happy face. Her jumping got smaller. Her bouncing got slower. Her shout became a whisper. "Grandma is coming," she whispered.

Dad tucked her in. He kissed her head. "Grandma will be here when you wake up," he said.

Romy held her picture. "Good night, picture," she whispered. Her eyes closed, slow and soft.

Elijah ran onto the basketball court. His team wore blue shirts today. Zion wore blue too. Josiah wore blue too.

The game began. Mr. Castillo blew his whistle. Elijah got the ball. He saw a green shirt nearby. He passed the ball to the green shirt. But the green shirt was on the other team! The boy in green ran away with the ball.

Elijah stopped and looked around. He saw Zion waving. Zion wore a blue shirt, just like him. "Here, Elijah! Pass here!" Elijah passed the ball to Zion. Zion caught it and shot. The ball went in the hoop.

The coach clapped. Elijah smiled. He looked down at his own blue shirt. Then he looked at Zion's blue shirt. Same color. Same team.

Later, the ball came to Elijah again. This time he looked for blue. He found Josiah in a blue shirt. He passed. Josiah passed back. Elijah took a short shot. The ball bounced on the rim. Then it dropped in.

After the game, Mr. Castillo gave each player a paper ribbon. Elijah held his up high. Zion held his up high too.

"Blue shirts win," said Josiah, and he laughed.

Elijah laughed too. "Same shirt, same team," he said.

Isabella sat at the paint table. Mr. Ross put out three cups. "Red, yellow, blue," Isabella said. "One, two, three."

She had a plan. She would make magic green. "Where does green hide?" she asked Rishaan. "In the yellow cup and the blue cup," he said.

Isabella dipped her brush. She stirred blue into the yellow cup. Swirl, swirl, swirl. The paint turned green like a dragon's tail.

But now all the yellow was gone. "I need yellow for my sun," she said. She pulled the brush back and forth. The yellow did not come out. Mixed paint stays mixed.

Mr. Ross gave her more yellow. Isabella hurried to a clean cup. She kept a little yellow safe. Then she mixed a little blue in a little yellow. Green again, green like a warm summer leaf.

"Green, yellow, green," she counted. She painted a sun with a root like golden spaghetti.

"Look at my magic tree," said Isabella.

Raphael got to daycare early. Snow was falling outside. "Snowy day," said Ms. Weber. "Put on your boots." Raphael pointed at the window. The snow looked soft and white. He wanted to keep some.

At play time, Raphael scooped up a snowball. He hid it in his pocket. Nylah and Ryan made snow angels. The wind blew hard. "Windy," said Ryan. His hat flew off. Nylah laughed and chased it.

Later, the sun came out. "Sunny now," said Ms. Weber. Raphael checked his pocket. His snowball was gone. There was only a wet spot. "Where did it go?" he asked. Nylah leaned close. "Your snow melted into water," she said. "It is warm in here." Raphael touched the puddle. His fingers got wet. He tried again with a new snowball. He set it on a tray. He waited. He watched it drip, drip, drip. "It melts inside," said Raphael. "Next time I will keep it in the snow." Ryan looked at his wet shoe. "My sock melted too," he said. "No, silly," said Nylah. "That is just snow from your boot."

Mohamed ran to the reading corner. Today he would get his first library card! Mr. Hu stood by the desk with a big smile. "Here it is, Mohamed," said Mr. Hu. Mohamed held the card with both hands. It had his name on it.

He picked a book about a big red truck. His friend Saanjh sat nearby with crayons. She opened her book and put a crayon tip on the page. "Stop," said Mohamed. "That is a library book. Many other kids share it. If we write in it, the pages get spoiled." Saanjh looked at the page. Then she put the crayon down. "I will ask for paper," she said. Mr. Hu gave her a white sheet. She drew a truck of her own.

Mohamed took his book to the desk. Mr. Hu scanned the card and the book. "Bring it back next week," he said. Mohamed hugged the book. He was tired but happy. "Next week, truck," he whispered, and waved goodbye.

At school, Isla played on the carpet. The toy box was full. One car, two cars, three cars, four cars. Vroom, vroom, vroom!

Then Isla picked up something yellow. It was long and bendy. It was not a car. It was a banana! "A banana in the toy box," said Isla. "That is so silly." Noel laughed. "It does not belong with the cars," he said. Malaika held up the banana. "It is the odd one out," she said. The banana did not go with the toys.

Isla had a big feeling. She wanted to help. So she carried the banana to the snack table. One apple, two crackers, three cups. The banana fit there. Ms. Hosseini smiled. "The banana goes with the foods," she said. "Good spot, Isla."

Then Isla looked at the car box again. One car, two cars, three cars, four cars. And one small sock. "Odd one out!" shouted Isla. The sock was not a car either. She ran far across the room. She put the sock in the dress-up basket. "The end," said Isla. "More odd ones to find!"

Elena sat on the playroom floor. She wanted to build a tall tower for her doll.

"The tower keeps falling down," said Josie.

Elena picked up a block. It was a cube, like all the toy blocks. She looked at it closely.

"Josie, bring me the stickers," said Elena.

Josie brought the sheet of stickers. Elena put one sticker on a flat face of the block. Then she counted.

"One, two, three, four, five, six."

The block had six stickers. Every face was a square.

"A cube like this block has six flat faces," said Elena. "Each one is a square."

"So six blocks make six squares," said Josie.

Elena stacked the blocks flat face to flat face. She matched square to square. The tower stood tall and still.

Amyra clapped her hands. Ms. Mensah smiled from the doorway.

Elena set her doll on top. The doll sat tall and safe.

"I did it," said Elena. She felt proud.

Riley sat on the couch with a blanket. Her nose was red and her throat felt scratchy. She had a cold, and she did not like it one bit.

She saw the medicine bottle on the counter. It was small and purple. Riley wanted some right away. She slid off the couch and walked over. Then she stopped and looked at the bottle. "Can I pour it myself?" she asked. Her mom came in and shook her head. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," Mom said. Riley watched Mom pour the purple liquid into a little cup. Mom held it out. "Here you go," she said. Riley drank it all. It tasted like grapes.

Riley went back to the couch. She looked out the window at the big blue sky. After a while, her throat felt better. The warm drink had made the scratchy feeling melt away. Rudra knocked on the door with a get-well card. It had a full bowl of soup drawn on it, in red crayon. Riley smiled and held it up to the light. "Is that for me?" she asked. "All yours," Rudra said.

Georgia was awake from her nap. She wanted a snack. Ms. Ahmed had a box of crackers on the shelf.

Georgia could not find the crackers. There were many boxes. She picked one up. It had little words on it. "Ms. Ahmed, what does this say?" she asked.

"That says pasta," said Ms. Ahmed. Georgia put it down. She passed it to James.

Georgia picked up another box. It said crackers. Ms. Ahmed read it out loud. "Crackers," she said. "That is the one you want."

Georgia smiled. The words had told her! She opened the door of the snack cupboard. She took the cracker box to the little table.

James held up a jar. "What does mine say?" he asked.

Ms. Ahmed looked. "Yours says jam," she said.

Georgia passed him a spoon. She pointed at the label. "Jam," she said. "The words say jam."

Hallie clapped her hands. Georgia munched her crackers and looked at the box again.

Myles went to the corner store with his dad. On the shelf sat little toy cars. Red ones and blue ones in two rows. Myles wanted to buy them all.

"I will count them," said Myles. He touched each red car. "One, two, three, four." He ran to show his dad. "Four red cars!"

Zola was there too. She counted the red cars from the other end. "One, two, three, four," said Zola. Myles laughed. "You counted the wrong end!" But Zola held up four fingers. "I got four too."

Myles counted again. He started from a blue car this time. "One, two, three, four. Four! Same number!" He jumped up and down. "Start anywhere, still four!"

Then he looked at both rows. "Red cars are more. Blue has two." Myles put his pencil in his pocket, where it would not break. He picked out four red cars, and no broken ones.

"Four cars, four happy friends," said Zola.

Myles waved the cars in the air. "More for me!"

Kayden loved soccer day at the park. His shoes had blue stripes. His team was called the Green Dragons. Yuna played too. Cooper played on the other team, the Red Rockets.

The game was messy in the best way. One, two, three kicks! Kayden ran fast. Mud went on his knees. Yuna got mud on her mouth. She licked her lip and laughed. "Yucky," she said.

The Red Rockets won. Kayden sat down on the grass. He did not want to lose. His face felt hot and his eyes felt rainy. Then the coach blew the whistle. "Line up," she said. Kayden saw the big kids from the last game. They stood in a long line. Each one told the other team, "Good game."

Kayden stood up. He got in line with his team. Cooper came down the line too. One, two, three hands to tap. Then Cooper stood in front of Kayden.

"Good game," said Cooper.

"Good game," said Kayden.

The rainy eyes went away. Kayden smiled a big, muddy smile.

"Same time next week?" asked Cooper.

"Yes," said Kayden. "You drive your mom's car, I ride my bike."

Isaiah wanted his red dinosaur. It was his best toy. He looked under his bed. He looked in his toy box. No dinosaur.

Then rain hit the window. A storm was coming. The sky outside looked dark and ugly. Isaiah kept looking. He brushed the dust off a basket in the hall. The basket had a paper sign on it.

Dad came by. "That is our lost and found basket," said Dad. "We put things we find in there. Then we can get them back." Isaiah peeked inside. There was a mitten. There was a spoon. There was one blue sock.

Then Isaiah saw a red tail. It was his dinosaur! "You were in the lost and found!" said Isaiah. He hugged the dinosaur tight. He gave Dad a big hug too. The rain tapped the window. Isaiah sat on the rug.

"Storms can't scare us now," said Isaiah. He made the dinosaur stomp across the rug. "Roar!"

Elizabeth hopped up the library steps. She held her mom's hand. Today she would get her very own library card.

Mr. Holloway smiled at the desk. "Here is your card," he said. Elizabeth looked at it. Her name was on it, just for her.

She found a big red book all about birds. It had a picture of a blue feather on the front. "Can I keep this forever?" she asked.

Mr. Holloway shook his head. "Borrowed books have to be brought back by a certain day," he said. "That day is called the due date."

Elizabeth looked at the book. There was a little paper slip inside. On the slip was the due date. "So someone else can read it too?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Holloway.

At home, Elizabeth read the bird book on the low couch. She counted the feathers on a big white swan. She read it every day.

At last the due day came. Elizabeth carried the book back to the library. She set it on the desk with a small hop.

Then she saw Yasin pick up her red book. He sat down and opened it. He looked at the blue feather and smiled.

Elizabeth whispered to her mom, "Now the book is his for a little while." She went to the shelf to find a new one.

Hunter went to the library with his dad. Story time was about to start! Ms. Villanueva held up a big card. It had a letter K on it. "K makes the kuh sound," she said. "K is for kite."

After story time, Hunter found a bumpy letter card. He tried to write K on paper. He made the legs go the wrong way. He tried again. Wrong way again! His friend Andreas looked over.

"Try tracing it," Andreas said. Hunter put his finger on the bumpy card. He traced the letter K. Up, down, and kick out. He felt the bumps under his finger. Then he picked up his pencil. He wrote K on the paper. The legs went the right way!

"Look, Dad!" Hunter said. Dad gave him a big smile. Hunter traced the bumpy K again. Then he wrote three more Ks. They all looked just right. "Can we take the card home?" Hunter asked. Ms. Villanueva nodded and said, "New letter cards come in every week." Hunter hugged the card all the way to the door.

Maya went to the library with her dad. She saw a new book about a red flag on a boat. She wanted to read it all by herself. She sat down on the soft rug. She held the book up high. "Once upon a time," she said.

But the boat looked funny. The flag was on the bottom. The water was on the top. The fish swam upside down. Maya laughed and laughed. "Silly fish!" she said. "Silly flag!"

Lorelai came to sit beside her. "My book did that too," Lorelai said. She turned her own book around in her hands.

Maya looked at her book. She turned it around too. Now the flag was on top. The water was at the bottom. The fish swam the right way. The words sat in neat little rows.

Maya pointed at the words. "That says boat," she said. Her dad smiled and sat close. He read from the front page. Maya turned the page herself, one at a time, all the way to the end.

Hudson was at daycare. It was a sunny morning. He wanted to build a big tower with Celeste.

Hudson stacked one block. Then two. Then three. The tower grew tall. "Look, Celeste!" he said. "So tall!"

Then the tower fell down. All the blocks went down. Boom.

Celeste looked at Hudson. Her mouth turned down. Her eyebrows came together. Hudson saw her face. "Celeste, are you sad?" he asked.

"Yes," said Celeste. "The tower fell."

Hudson looked at her face some more. Now her mouth made a little smile. "Are you happy now?" he asked.

"Yes! Let's build it again," said Celeste.

So they tried again. One block. Two blocks. Three blocks. Slow and careful. The tower grew tall again.

Ms. Nowak came over. "Nice work, friends," she said.

Celeste laughed. Hudson laughed too. Then they gave the blocks a big hug, all around the tall tower, so it would feel safe.

"Tomorrow we build it taller," said Celeste.

"Okay," said Hudson. He put the last block on top.

Matthew sat at the snack table at daycare. He wanted to eat his strawberry. But he did not want to taste it much. Ms. Ito had said, "Snack time, everyone."

Matthew looked at the strawberry with his eyes. It was red and shiny. He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled sweet. He touched it with his fingers. It felt wet and bumpy.

Then Marvin sat down next to him. Marvin was eating his snack. He pinched his nose shut with his fingers. He took a bite. He let go of his nose. "Wow," said Marvin. "My apple tastes plain when I hold my nose."

Matthew wanted to try it too. He pinched his nose shut. He took a big bite of his strawberry. It tasted like nothing much. Just plain and soft. He let go of his nose. Then he could taste the sweet again.

One, two, three, he thought. Eyes, nose, fingers, tongue. He tried it again to be sure. Pinch, bite, plain. Let go, bite, sweet.

Pearl came over with her snack. "My shoe has a wet sock," she said. She sat down. She watched Matthew pinch his nose. Then she pinched hers too, and took a bite.

Matthew smiled and took another bite.

The nursery room smelled like crayons and glue. Jordan sat at the paint table. He made a picture with big red paint. Then the door opened. His mom came in. She carried a little basket. A tiny baby was inside. "This is your new sister," said Mom. The baby made a small squeak.

Jordan felt sad. Everyone looked at the baby. No one looked at his paint. Ms. Okonkwo came over. "Can you help?" she asked. "Big brothers and sisters can help by fetching things, like a clean diaper." Jordan jumped up. He ran to the baby bag. He found a diaper. It felt soft and dry. He brought it back. Mom smiled big. "Thank you, Jordan."

Then Jordan fetched a small blanket too. He laid it over the baby's toes. The baby grabbed his finger. Her hand was warm. "Why is she sleeping so much?" Jordan asked. Mom laughed. "Babies are a bit lazy. They sleep a lot." Jordan sat very close. He was not sad now. He was a helper. The baby held on and would not let go.

Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Victoria waited in the kitchen. She sat on her little stool by the wooden table. "Grandma will be here soon," said Mom.

The door opened. Grandma came in with her big blue bag. Mom gave Grandma a hug. One hug, Mom said with a smile. Victoria wanted to hug Grandma too, but her tummy felt funny. She was shy. So she lifted her hand and waved. "Hello, Grandma," she said, very small. Grandma waved back. "Hello, Victoria," said Grandma. "I like your wave."

Victoria felt better. She counted on her fingers. "One wave, one hello." Then she ran over and hugged Grandma's soft coat. Mom poured juice for everyone. Victoria helped carry the cups, slow and careful, so nothing would spill. "Pretty cup," said Grandma, holding hers up. Victoria smiled. She had three ways to say hello now: a hug, a wave, and a hello. She waved one more time, just for fun. Grandma waved back.

Kinsley loved the library. It felt like a big purple castle full of books. Today she was excited. Story time was about dragons!

Her friend Hoorain ran to get a seat. Then Hoorain tripped. She fell down near the book swing, the little seat that hung by the window. Hoorain's face turned sad. A tear rolled down her cheek.

Kinsley ran over. She bent down low. "Are you okay?" she asked. Hoorain looked up. Her sad face grew soft. "My knee hurts," she said. "But you asked me. That makes me feel better."

Kinsley held her hand. Mr. Demir, the librarian, brought a small ice pack. He placed it on Hoorain's knee. Soon Hoorain smiled again.

Then the dragon story began. The dragon was big and green. He was scared of mice! Hoorain laughed so loud that a shush came from behind the shelves. Kinsley laughed too. She held Hoorain's hand and whispered, "Dragons can be scared, just like us."

Hoorain whispered back, "And friends can be brave, just like us."

Lily stood in the school garden with her class. Mr. Tse gave her three little seeds. "These will grow into carrots," he said. Lily made a small hole in the dark soil. She dropped the seeds in. Then she patted the soil down, low and flat.

Every day Lily came back to look. Stefan came too. Nothing grew at first. Then one morning, tiny green leaves popped up. Lily clapped her hands. The leaves grew taller and taller.

One day a weed grew next to her carrots. Lily grabbed the weed and pulled it up. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom. "Look!" she said. "The roots grow down into the soil." Stefan bent close to see. The roots were pale and thin, like little strings.

Lily put the weed in the compost bucket. Then she watered her carrots. Mr. Tse said the farm cart would take the vegetables home when they were big. Lily folded her hands and waited. Soon she would pull a carrot and see its roots too.

Ella went to the community kitchen with her dad. Today they would make a pizza for the family. Ella wanted to help with everything.

"Can I do the eggs?" she asked. Ms. Delgado smiled. "Yes, you can crack them," she said. Ella picked up an egg. She did not know the egg was hiding inside a hard shell. She tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap. The shell broke open, and the egg slid out. "The egg comes out when the shell cracks!" said Ella.

Then a small piece of shell fell into the bowl. Ella looked at it. She was scared it would ruin the pizza. "Don't worry," said Ms. Delgado. "You can get it out with a spoon." Ella used her spoon. She fished and fished. At last the little shell piece came out. The bowl was clean again.

Ella stirred the eggs. Her dad put the pizza in the hot oven, far from Ella's hands. Soon the pizza was done. Ella's family sat down together. Everyone took a big bite. "Yum!" said Ella. "I made this!" Her dad gave her a hug.

Elias went to the library with his dad. The library had a soft carpet in the kids' corner. There were big shelves and little cozy nooks. Keon and Rudra were there too. "Let's play hide-and-seek," said Keon. Keon covered his eyes. He counted, "One, two, three." He zoomed on, "Fourfivesixseveneightnineten!" Elias did not have time to hide. Rudra was still standing in the open. "You counted too fast," Rudra said. "We need time to hide." Keon nodded. "Okay. I will count slowly this time."

Keon covered his eyes again. He counted, "One... two... three... four..." Elias ran on his soft socks. He hid behind a shelf of books about birds. His book had a picture of a duck with one white wing. "Five... six... seven..." Rudra hid under a table shaped like a shop. "Eight... nine... ten! Ready or not!" Keon came looking. He peeked at the bird shelf. Elias held very still. Keon walked on by. Elias smiled inside his hiding spot. Slow counting had given him time to hide. Then Keon's face popped around the shelf. "Found you!"

Jade sat at the art table. She wanted to glue a paper door for her house picture. But her door did not look like a door. It had wobbly edges.

"Look at the real door," said Royce.

Jade looked. The door was a rectangle. A rectangle has four sides. It has four square corners too.

Jade counted the sides. One, two, three, four. Then she counted the corners. One, two, three, four.

"That was easy," said Jade.

She came back to the art table. She cut a rectangle with four straight sides. She glued it on her house. The corners were square, just like the real door.

"That is a joke," said Andre with a laugh. "Now I want a door too!"

"Here," said Jade. She gave him more paper.

Gianna sat at the school table. Mr. Cohen put a tray of ice cubes down. Each cube looked clear and shiny. "Who wants to hold one?" he asked.

"I do," said Gianna. She picked up a cube with her fingers. The ice felt cold. It was so cold! She let it drop into her cup right away. The cube made a little splash.

Zuri picked one up too. Her eyes got big. "Cold!" she said. She dropped hers into her cup too. Cedar listened to the cubes go plink, plink. "I hear them," he said.

Mr. Cohen had warm juice in a big pot. He poured a little into each cup. He gave everyone a slice of orange. Gianna smelled the orange. It smelled sweet. She took a sip and tasted it. Yummy. Then she touched her cup. The cup was not cold like the ice. It was warm from the juice.

Gianna put her hand on the tray near the ice. Cold again. She put her hand on her cup. Warm. "Different," she said.

Zuri laughed. "Ice cold, cup warm."

Gianna picked up one more cube. She held it, counted one, two, three, then dropped it in her cup. Plink. She smiled.

Henry went to the beach with his dad. He wanted to learn his five senses. His teacher, Ms. Yoon, had asked the class to try at home.

Henry put his toes in the sand. "I feel with my toes!" he said. He looked at a big blue wave. "I see with my eyes." His dad smiled and stirred the sand with a stick.

Then Henry saw his friend Hafsa by the water. She had her hands over her ears. A loud seagull was squawking right above her. "Too loud!" said Hafsa. Henry ran to her. He held her hand until the bird flew away.

"Now listen," said Henry. They sat still on the sand. Hafsa heard the waves. Henry heard the bird. "We hear with our ears," said Henry. Hafsa laughed and clapped her hands over her ears, then pulled them off again.

"One more sense," said his dad. He held out a salty cracker. Henry sniffed it with his nose first. Then he tasted it with his mouth. "All five!" said Henry. He ran to the wide blue water and jumped over a little wave with Hafsa.

Georgia wanted to build a big block mountain at daycare. The blocks sat in one tall box. They clacked when they fell. Georgia scooped them all up in her arms. "Mine," she said. "All mine."

Ollie came over. Ollie had no blocks at all. Hussein had no blocks at all. Hussein's face went sad and small. Ollie's lip went down too. Georgia looked at her big pile. She looked at her two friends. Hmm, she thought. Could a mountain grow with no friends to see it?

Georgia counted the blocks. "One, two, three for me." She gave some to Ollie. "One, two, three for you." She gave some to Hussein. "One, two, three for you too." Now everyone had blocks. Everyone got a chance to build.

Ollie stacked his blocks up high. Hussein made a hard, bumpy road. Georgia made her mountain. "It's tall!" said Ollie. Mr. Nasser knelt down. "Can my car ride down the mountain?" he asked. Georgia pushed the car. Whee! It went fast down the side. Then Ollie took a turn. Then Hussein took a turn. Round and round the car went, all morning long.

Sadie went to the laundromat with her dad. The dryer went round and round. Her warm coat came out of the dryer. Dad held it up. "Your turn," he said.

Sadie put one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat was warm like a hug. Now came the zipper. She pulled it up, up, up. But then it stopped. It would not go any more. "Hmm," said Sadie. "What is it holding?" She looked down. Her sweater was caught in the zipper. The zipper was stuck.

What could she do? She pulled the zipper back down, just a little. Then, pop! The sweater came free. The zipper was not stuck any more. Sadie smiled big. She pulled the zipper up again. This time her sweater stayed out of the way. Zzzzzip! All the way to the top.

Just then, Aimee came in with her mom. Aimee had a scarf in her teeth and a coat in her hands. "Can you do it all by yourself?" Aimee asked. "Watch me," said Sadie. She shook out her arms to show how free they were. She stomped her boots on the floor. The crunchy leaves on her boots made a happy sound. "I can zip!" said Sadie.

Rowan went to the store with Mom. He saw a big toy truck. It was red and shiny. Rowan wanted it so much.

He pulled Mom's hand. Mom was busy picking bread. Rowan sat down on the floor. He frowned and went quiet. Mom did not know what was wrong.

Then Rowan said, "I feel sad." Mom knelt down by him. "You feel sad?" she said. "Tell me more." "I want the truck," said Rowan. "But we came for bread today."

Mom looked at the truck. "You can brush the dust off it," she said with a smile. "Let's look at it together." They looked at the truck. Rowan held it gently. Then he put it back on the shelf. He felt proud.

On the way out, Samara and Delphine waved from the lake toys. "Look, a little lake pool!" said Samara. "Cool," said Rowan. He held Mom's hand tight. "That was fun," he said. Mom smiled and kissed his head.

Sebastian went to the store with his mom. He held her hand. The store was so big! Sebastian was small.

First they saw the eggs. Sebastian picked up one egg. It was little and smooth. Mom put twelve eggs in the cart. The cart was fast when Mom pushed it. Sebastian walked slow behind it.

Then they came to the fridge. It had milk and yogurt. The fridge door was open. Brrr! Cold air came out. Sebastian touched his own arms. "Mom, look! The door is open!"

"Open and closed are opposites," said Mom. She shut the door. Now it was closed. "Please help me close it next time, so the cold stays inside."

Sebastian wanted to help. He found another fridge door a little bit open. He pushed it shut. Click! He did it all by himself.

After the store, they got hot cocoa from the counter. The grown-up made it, and it was hot, so Mom held it up high. At home, Mom made the cocoa cool with milk. Sebastian took a sip. Splash! A drop fell on the table. His cup was almost empty.

"More cocoa please!" said Sebastian.

Mom laughed and filled it up again.

Michael wanted a warm bath. His dad turned the tap. The water poured into the tub. White steam floated up. It looked like tiny clouds.

"Can I touch the steam?" Michael asked. He stepped close to the tub.

His dad held out a hand. "Stay back, Michael. Steam is hot. It can burn you." Michael stopped his feet. He took one big step back.

From far away, Michael watched the steam. It rose up and up. Then it went away into the air. He blew at it. The steam moved a little. He clapped his hands. The steam did not clap back.

His dad put his own hand near the steam. "Hot," he said. Then he held Michael's hand under the cold tap. "This is cold." The cold water felt like winter on his fingers.

The tub filled up slow. The steam got smaller and smaller. Soon it was all gone. His dad felt the water with his elbow. "Just right now," he said.

Michael put one toe in the water. It was warm like a blanket. He slid in and made a splash. "The steam went away," he said. "Where did it go?"

His dad smiled and pointed up. "It flies up high, past the ceiling." Michael looked up. He waved at the ceiling.

Jordan loves craft time at school. Today Ms. Kovalenko holds up a paper. "We will make an elephant!" she says. Jordan claps his hands. An elephant! A big gray elephant to take home!

Ms. Kovalenko gives everyone scissors. She keeps the sticky glue safe on her desk. "Cut out the shapes," she says. "Squares for the legs. A triangle for the tusk. A rectangle for the trunk. And one big circle for the body."

Jordan cuts the square. Snip, snip, done. He cuts the triangle. Then the rectangle. Now the big circle. Jordan looks for a corner to start cutting. He looks and looks. He turns the paper around. Where is the corner?

"Rosalie!" he calls. "My circle has no corner! Not even one!" Rosalie peeks over. "A circle is round," she says. "It has no corners." Jordan smiles big. So he just snips anywhere, and around and around he goes. The circle comes out perfect!

He glues on the legs, the tusk, the trunk. Lukas runs over to see. "Your elephant is so big!" says Lukas. Jordan holds it up high. "Round body, no corners!" he says. "That is how an elephant is made!"

Mia sat at the big art table. She was making a paper crown. She drew stars on the paper first. Then she put glue on the ends.

"Look, Raavi!" said Mia. "My crown is done."

Mia picked up the crown. She held it up high. But the ends slid apart. The crown fell open in her hands.

"Oh no," said Mia. Her lip wobbled a little.

Ms. Ivanova came over. She smiled a soft smile. "The glue is still wet," she said. "Wet glue needs time to dry before the pieces hold together."

Mia put the crown down on the table. She looked at the shiny glue. It looked wet and funny.

"Let's draw while we wait," said Raavi.

Mia drew a cat. Then she drew a sun. Then she drew a big cake with three berries.

She peeked at her crown. The glue was not shiny now. It looked dry.

Mia picked up the crown very slowly. She held it up. The ends stayed together! The crown did not fall apart.

"It worked!" said Mia. She put the crown on her head.

Raavi clapped his hands. "Pretty crown," he said.

Mia spun around in a circle. The stars on her crown went round and round too.

Samuel stood at the front door. He wanted to play outside. He looked out the big window. The trees were swaying. The leaves were blowing all around the yard.

Samuel put on his old red coat. He put on his hat. Then he opened the door. Whoosh! The wind blew his hat right off. His hat flew onto the floor of the porch. Samuel felt worried. "My hat!" he said.

His dad came to the door. "It is windy today," Dad said. "Hold your hat with your hand." Samuel picked up his hat. He held it tight. Then he ran outside.

The leaves blew across the grass. Samuel chased them. They danced like a dream. He jumped and caught one leaf. "I got it!" he said. Josie came over to play too. She held her hat too. Samuel laughed in the wind, warm in his old red coat, with Dad watching from the door.

Freya was at Grandma's house. The kitchen smelled like warm bread. Grandma held a big bowl of grapes. "You can have three grapes," said Grandma.

Freya looked at the grapes. Some were big. Some were small. Maybe big grapes counted differently. Maybe three big grapes meant more than three.

Freya picked one big grape. Then one more. Then one more. She put them in a row on the table. "One, two, three," she said. She picked three small grapes next. "One, two, three." She counted them both. Each pile had three grapes. The big pile looked bigger. But it was still three. Three meant three, every time.

Grandma smiled. "Wash your hands first." Freya brushed the dust off her chair. She pulled the zipper on her cardigan, but it was stuck. "Let me help," said Grandma. Grandma zipped it up fast.

Freya ate her grapes slowly. They were sweet and cold. Then a small surprise ran across the floor. Grandma's cat, with a grape in its mouth! "Hey, that's mine!" said Freya. Grandma laughed. "That one makes four."

Arthur was at Grandma's house. He had drawn a picture at preschool. He wanted to show it to Grandpa right away.

Grandpa was talking to Grandma about his itchy sweater. "Grandpa! Look!" said Arthur. Grandpa did not turn around. He kept on talking. Arthur tugged his sleeve. "Grandpa! My picture!" Grandpa held up one hand. "Just a moment, Arthur," he said.

Arthur felt his face go hot. He said, "Sorry, Grandpa." Then he sat on the rug. He began to wonder if Grandpa would ever stop. Grandpa talked about the wool. He talked about the sleeves. Then Grandpa stopped talking. There was a quiet little pause. Arthur waited for the pause. Then he said, "Grandpa, may I show you something, please?"

Grandpa smiled. "Yes, please show me." Arthur held up the picture. "Thank you for waiting," said Grandpa. Grandma set a cookie on a small plate and put it down beside Arthur. "Thank you, Grandma," said Arthur. Grandpa looked at the picture for a long, long time. "A red fire truck," he said. "Can you tell me about it?" Arthur nodded. He talked and talked, and this time, Grandpa waited for him.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Isaac ran to the guest bedroom. The bed was empty and plain. "Grandpa needs a bed all ready," said Mom. Isaac found the big soft pillow. He put it at the top of the bed. It slid off. The cover was slippery! He put it back. He pushed it down. This time it stayed. Isaac got his favorite blanket. It was blue with stars. He spread it over the bed. He smoothed it flat with both hands. The bed looked cozy now. The doorbell rang. Grandpa was here! Isaac pulled him to the room. "This is your bed, Grandpa!" Grandpa sat down on the soft pillow. He pulled the star blanket up to his chin. "Best bed ever," said Grandpa. Isaac had learned how to make a guest feel at home. "Night night, Grandpa," said Isaac. Grandpa gave the blanket one more tug.

Beatrice sat at the little table in the school library. She had a big pencil and white paper. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

She tried a B. It looked wobbly. "Why is B so hard?" she asked herself. She looked at it with one eye. Then she saw it. B had two bumps. Bumps were curves!

Mr. Jean-Louis brought her a card with big letters. Beatrice put her hand on it. "B has curves," she said. "E is all straight lines. L is straight too!"

She sorted the letters of her name. B, A, R, and C had curves. E, T, and I were straight. She counted them. "One, two, three, four curvy ones," she said.

She drew the straight letters first, nice and tall. Then she made the curves slow and round. Her pencil went bump, bump, bump.

Leif looked over. "That looks cool," he said.

"That's my name," said Beatrice. She held up the paper and smiled.

Billie waited at the bus stop with her dad. It was cold. She wanted to zip her coat all by herself. She pulled the little zipper. It went up, up, up. Then it stopped. "It went the wrong way," said Billie. She pulled it down. She tried again, slowly. This time the zipper ran all the way to the top. "I did it!" said Billie. Her dad smiled. Sidra came running with Mr. Hughes. Sidra was holding her coat in a bundle. "It fell in the hall," said Sidra. "I could not find it. It got dirt on it too." Billie looked at the coat. The dirt was on the back, where the floor had touched it. At school, Billie saw a little hook by the door. She put her coat on the hook. The coat hung up high, off the floor. When it was time to go home, Billie knew just where to look. There was her coat, clean and waiting. She put it on and zipped it all the way up. "Ready," said Billie.

Hannah went with Mama to the cemetery. The sky was gray. It did not rain. The grass was soft and quiet.

They sat by a stone with flowers on it. Mama spread a small blanket. She opened a basket with bread and grapes. "We eat here today," said Mama. "Grandma loved this spot."

Hannah picked up a grape. She was about to bite it. Then she stopped. "Mama, do I say the word first?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We say Bismillah. It means in the name of God." Hannah put the grape down. She folded her hands. "Bismillah," she said. Then she took a big bite.

Mama smiled and said Bismillah too. They ate the bread and the grapes together. A small bird hopped near the blanket. Hannah held out an empty hand. "No crumbs for the bird," said Mama. "But you can wave."

After the picnic, Hannah drew in the dirt with a stick. She drew a robot with square arms. "My robot has big feet," she said. A wind blew. The leaves moved. "Bye, Grandma," said Hannah. She waved at the stone, and Mama waved too.

Declan went to the park with his dad. He had his bunny toy. Declan ran to the swings. Then he sat in the sand. Then he slid down the slide. But bunny was gone. "Where is bunny?" said Declan. He looked by the swings. No bunny. He looked in the sand. No bunny.

Snow began to fall. Soft white flakes landed on the bench. A bird sat in her nest above the path. Declan looked up, then down. There, under the bench, was a shiny toy car. It was not bunny. Declan picked up the car. He wanted to keep it. It was so shiny.

Then Stephen ran over. He looked sad, almost sick about it. "That is my car," said Stephen. "I lost it here." Declan held the car. It belonged to Stephen. So Declan gave the car back. "Thank you," said Stephen. "I will help you find bunny."

They looked in three places. One, under the slide. Two, in the sand box. Three, behind the little tree. There was bunny, sitting in the snow! "Bunny!" said Declan. Stephen smiled. The two boys walked home together through the soft white snow.

Lillian was at Grandma's house. Soren came to play too. Grandma had one big red truck. It was a real truck that could carry blocks.

Lillian grabbed the truck. Soren grabbed it back. "My turn," said Lillian. "No, my turn," said Soren. Grandma knelt down. "Let's take turns," she said. "Soren first."

Lillian waited. Waiting felt long. She frowned at the floor.

Then she saw the toy animals. "One, two, three little ducks," she said. She made a pond for the ducks. She made a mom duck plant her feet in the toy grass. The ducks made a quack sound. Lillian laughed.

The floor made a creak sound. Grandma said, "Lillian, it is your turn now." Lillian looked up. The ducks were all lined up. The waiting had gone fast!

"One, two, three, four blocks," said Lillian. She loaded the truck. Soren lined up the ducks. "Your turn soon," said Lillian. "I know," said Soren. "I will play with the cows."

The cows mooed. The truck rolled. Grandma smiled. "More turns," said Lillian, "and more cows." Soren handed her a little cow. It rode on top of the blocks.

Milan was in the backyard. He saw the park across the road. It had a big red slide. He wanted to go there.

Milan ran to the gate. He put his hand on the latch. Then he stopped. A car went by, fast. The road was not the backyard. It was wide and busy. Milan stood still and looked at the road.

His dad came out with a hammer. He was fixing the fence. "I want the slide," said Milan. Dad put the hammer down in the toolbox. "Hold my hand when you cross the street," said Dad. Milan took Dad's big hand. Dad held on tight. They looked both ways. Then they walked across, together, hand in hand.

On the other side, Milan let go. He ran to the slide. His friend Della was there. Her hair was wild in the wind. They slid down, down, down. Later they sat in the shade with cold water. Milan let a drop of ice lick his finger. "Again!" said Della, pointing at the slide. Milan grinned and ran back for one more turn.

Grace wanted to play firefighters at the playground. But she did not feel like a firefighter. She felt like just Grace.

Then she saw a box by the fence. It was full of dress-up clothes. There was a big red hat. There was a loose yellow coat. Mr. Mercado smiled. "You can wear one," he said.

Grace put on the big red hat. She put on the loose yellow coat. Now she felt like a firefighter! "I am Firefighter Grace!" she said. Her friend Emerson ran over. "A storm came!" he said. "The leaves are all wet!" Grace held her toy hose. She sprayed the air. Emerson held out his toy bear. "My bear is cold," he said. Grace wrapped the bear in a small blanket. "Now your bear is warm," she said.

Cadence put on a chef hat. "I will cook soup," she said. Mr. Mercado helped her stir a pretend pot. Grace dropped a pretend carrot in the pot. The firefighters needed lunch, after all.

At the end of the day, Grace took off the big red hat. She was just Grace again. She held the hat close and smiled. "Same time tomorrow?" she asked Mr. Mercado. He nodded and said, "The hat will be right here waiting."

Lennon sat on the rug in the music room. Ms. Karimi clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Now you try," said Ms. Karimi. Lennon clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps were fast, then slow, then fast. The song went one steady way, but Lennon did not.

Fraser sat next to her. He was an old friend from her family street. "Listen first," he said. Lennon listened. The beat went clap, clap, clap, all the same. She clapped with it. One beat, two beats, three beats. Her hands went the same speed as the song. It felt good.

Then it was time to sing. "The itsy bitsy spider," they sang. Lennon made her fingers climb. But her fingers went down, down, down. Magnolia laughed kindly. "Where does the spider go?" she asked. Lennon thought. "The spider climbs up!" she said. Up, up, up went her fingers, just like the song. Ms. Karimi smiled and clapped the steady beat. Lennon sang the whole rhyme from her memory. Her itchy nose made her scratch it once, and then she sang some more. "Again!" said Lennon. "Up, up, up!"

Grace was at daycare. It was walk day. Her class was going to the park.

"Look at the big light," said Charlee. It hung over the road. It glowed red.

Grace squeezed Mr. Reddy's hand. "Red!" she said.

"Red means stop," said Mr. Reddy. All the cars stopped. Their wheels were still.

Then the light changed. It glowed green. "Green means go!" said Grace. The cars went. They rolled down the road. One truck honked. Beep, beep!

The walkers held hands. Grace held Mr. Reddy's hand tight. It was a little sticky from her snack. They crossed the road when the light was red for the cars. Then they were at the park.

Grace found a rock. It was smooth and gray. She used it to dig in the dirt. Dig, dig, dig. What would she find?

"Look!" said Chad. He pointed. A small yellow bug sat under the dirt. Grace gasped.

"Hello, little bug," she said. The bug crawled onto her rock. It sat there like a tiny king.

Then the bug opened its wings. They were blue. Bright, shiny blue. It flew up and away.

Grace waved. "Bye bye, blue bug!"

Livia had a big toy drum. Bang, bang, bang! She loved that drum.

Alycia came to play. Alycia saw the drum. "I want to try it," said Alycia. Livia held the drum tight. "It's mine," she said. Alycia's face went sad.

Livia's mom sat down with them. "You can take turns," she said. "Taking turns means one person plays for a while, and then the other person gets to play." Livia thought about that. She looked at Alycia. "You can go first," said Livia.

Alycia banged the drum. Bang, bang, bang! She played for a while. Then she stopped. "Your turn now," said Alycia. Livia took the drum. She banged it loud. Alycia clapped her hands.

They took turns all morning. The drum went bang, bang, bang for both of them. After playing, they helped clean up the toys. Livia put the drum in the toy box next to her stuffed animal bear.

"Thank you for sharing," said Alycia. "That was sweet." Livia smiled big. "Come play again tomorrow," she said. "We can take turns with the drum."

Natalie sat at the little table in the playroom. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. There was green paint. But there was no orange.

"How will I make an orange pumpkin?" she asked.

"Try the red and the yellow," said Adelie. "Stir them together."

Natalie was careful. She put a big red dot on her paper. Then she put a yellow dot next to it. She stirred them with her brush. Round and round the colors went. The brush turned orange! The paint on the paper turned orange too!

Natalie laughed. "Red and yellow make orange!"

She painted her pumpkin all orange. She painted a green stem on top. Then she painted a blue door on the pumpkin. "My pumpkin has a house door," she said.

Adelie giggled. "Silly pumpkin. Pumpkins do not have doors."

"This one does," said Natalie. She painted a tiny yellow cat walking in.

Then Ms. Doyle looked over. "Oh my. A pumpkin house with a cat!"

"A little orange cat," said Natalie. "I made the orange myself."

Adelie painted a red dot and a yellow dot too. She stirred and stirred. "Mine is orange too!" she said. "Now we both have orange."

Natalie held up her pumpkin so Adelie could see. "Knock knock," said Adelie at the little blue door. "Who lives here?"

The lights went out. The TV went dark too. Everly sat very still on the rug.

"No TV," she said. "No lights. No cartoons."

Her dad came in with a flashlight. He clicked it on. A bright circle chased the shadows up the wall.

"The power is out," he said. "The TV needs power. So do the lights."

Everly frowned. "What can we do now?"

Mom brought a game box. It was her board game with red and blue squares. She set it on the table. Everly put her coin on the blue square. Mom put her coin on the red one. Dad held the flashlight straight above the board. The little light made the squares easy to see.

"Look," said Everly. "The game works! It does not need power."

Then Dad handed her a book. Everly turned the pages in the flashlight glow. Mom found a puzzle next. Everly matched the duck pieces and the cow pieces.

Later, the lights came back on. The TV hummed. But Everly was busy.

"My turn first," she said, and placed her coin on the last blue square.

Rose sat at the dinner table. It was a hot summer night. She had three cups in front of her. One cup, two cups, three cups. Rose stacked them into a tall tower. Tap, tap, tap.

Her friend Saif came to sit down. He reached for the bread. His elbow hit the tower. Crash! One cup, two cups, three cups rolled under the table. "My tower!" said Rose. She felt like crying.

Saif looked at her face. "Sorry," he said. Then he got down on his knees. He picked up cup one. He picked up cup two. He picked up cup three. He handed them all back to Rose.

Rose looked at the cups. Then she looked at Saif. Hmm. He said sorry. Then he helped. Maybe the two things went together, like spoon and bowl?

Rose stacked the cups again. Tap, tap, tap. Then she slid the bread basket toward Saif. "You can have some first," she said.

Dad put down the plates. The table was a little messy now. "What a kind table," said Dad.

Saif smiled and took one piece of bread. "Thank you, Rose," he said. Rose counted the cups one more time. One, two, three. All standing tall.

Theo sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a hungry sound. He could hear it gurgle.

His dad set down a bowl of soup. Theo smelled it with his nose. "Mmm, it smells like tomatoes," he said. He touched the bowl with one finger. It felt warm, not hot. He took a little sip. It tasted salty and good.

Then Theo looked around. "Where is my teddy?" he asked. "I want teddy at dinner." Teddy was not on his chair. Theo looked under the table. It was dark under there. He could not see anything, only black.

"I can't see in the dark," said Theo. His dad reached over and switched on the lamp by the table. The light made a big glow. Then Theo saw something wild. His teddy was under the chair, all curled up like a sleeping cat!

"I catch you, teddy!" said Theo. He lifted teddy up and gave him a hug. Teddy felt soft and fuzzy on his cheek.

"Teddy can smell the soup too," said Theo. He held teddy near his bowl. His dad laughed and gave Theo a spoon.

Theo took another sip. "Teddy, do you hear that?" he said. "The spoon goes clink!" The clink was a small surprise. Teddies and spoons can talk, in their own way.

Theo ate his soup to the very bottom. Teddy sat beside his plate, warm in the lamplight.

Adam held his book up high. "Dad, who drew the bear?"

Dad sat on the edge of the bed. "Let's find out," he said. He turned to the very first page. "We start at the front of the book," he said. "Like walking through a door."

Adam looked at the front page. It had words on it. Dad pointed. "These words tell us a name," he said. He read it out loud. "Pictures by Alice Blue."

"Alice drew my bear?" asked Adam.

"Yes," said Dad. "A person who draws the pictures for a book is called an illustrator. Alice is the illustrator."

Adam said the word slowly. "Ill-us-trate-or." He liked it. It felt big in his mouth.

Dad opened the next page. There was the bear again. The bear had a gray cat on his lap. The cat was pushing a little wooden wheel across the floor.

"That says the cat is rolling the wheel," said Dad. He read the words. And there was the cat, rolling the wheel, just like the words said.

Adam leaned close. "The words know what the cat does," he said.

Dad turned one page, then another. They went all the way to the back. The bear slept. The cat slept. The moon came in the window.

Adam held the book against his chest. "Tomorrow, can you read it again?"

"We can read it front to back," said Dad. He turned off the lamp. "Find the illustrator in the morning."

In the dark, Adam whispered, "Good night, Alice."

Mia sat at the table. The soup was thick and warm. She licked her spoon.

"Guess what," said Mia. "Freya had my toy mouse at school. The grey one with the long tail."

"Did you grab it?" asked Dad.

"I did first," said Mia. "Freya held on tight. Then she held on tighter!"

"So what did you do?" asked Dad.

"I stopped. I put my hands in my lap. Then I said, 'Can I have a turn when you're done?'"

"What did Freya say?"

"She said, 'Okay!' She pushed the mouse to me. Then we both played. I got my turn, and Freya got her turn too."

Dad smiled. "That sounds like good sharing."

Mia held up her spoon. Then she put it down. "Dad, can I have a turn with the bread when you're done?"

Alexis looked out the window. The backyard was white. "Snowy!" he said. Snow was falling on the fence. Snow was falling on the swing.

He wanted to make a snowball. He put on his boots. He put on his big coat. His mom found his hat. But his mittens were not on the shelf.

Alexis went outside anyway. He scooped up soft snow. He patted it into a ball. "My hands are cold," he said. His fingers felt like ice cubes. He dropped the snowball and ran inside.

"Where are my mittens?" he asked. His mom looked in the basket. There they were, under a scarf. "Windy days need that scarf," she said with a smile.

Alexis pulled on his red mittens. He ran back out. He made a new snowball. He held it a long time. His hands stayed warm inside the mittens.

Alyssa came over to play. "Nice mittens," she said. "Want to make a big snow animal?" Alexis laughed. Together they patted and rolled. The snow grew into a round, happy animal with a stick for an arm.

The sun came out. It was sunny now. Alexis and Alyssa sat by the snow animal. "I wish every day was snowy," said Alexis. Alyssa patted the snow animal's head. "Maybe it will snow again tomorrow," she said.

It was circle time at daycare. Ms. Reddy held up a big red bag. "Who wants to play the feely-bag game?" she asked.

"Me! Me!" said Hannah. Elyse and Maha jumped up too.

"Put your hand in," said Ms. Reddy. "No peeking. Tell us what you feel."

Hannah pushed her hand into the bag. It was cool and smooth and round. "A ball!" she said. "A red ball!"

Ms. Reddy smiled. "Are you sure it is red?"

Hannah squeezed the ball. She turned it in her fingers. She felt bumps and a smooth spot. "Um. Maybe blue?" she said.

Elyse had a turn next. She felt a small hard circle. "A coin!" she said. "A yellow coin!"

"Look and see," said Ms. Reddy.

They pulled the bag open wide. Hannah looked. Her ball was green! Elyse's coin was not yellow. It was a silver coin.

"My fingers were lost," said Hannah. "They could not find the color!"

"Mine too," said Elyse.

Then it was Maha's turn. She felt something soft and flat. "A hat," she said. "But I will not guess the color. My eyes have to look!"

Everyone leaned in close. Maha pulled out the hat. It was yellow. Bright, sunny yellow.

"Yellow! Yellow!" they cheered.

"Now finish the game," said Ms. Reddy. "Look first, then say the color."

Hannah clapped her hands. "Eyes for colors," she said. "Fingers for balls!"

Maha put the yellow hat on her head. It was too big. It slid down over her nose.

Wyatt stood at the bus stop with his dad. He held his new coat in his hands. "I can do it myself," said Wyatt. He pushed one arm in. He pushed the other arm in. The coat was on! Now came the zipper. Wyatt pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. He pulled again. It went zzzzip all the way to his chin. "I did it!" said Wyatt.

Hendrix stood next to him. Hendrix had a blue coat. Skyler had a red coat. Then the sky went drip, drip. Little drops fell on Wyatt's nose. Drip, drip, on Skyler's hat. Drip, drip, on the wooden bench.

"Look at my coat," said Hendrix. He pulled something up over his head. "This is my hood." Wyatt looked down at his own coat. There it was, soft and foldy at the back. Wyatt pulled it up over his head. Drip, drip, on the hood. Not on Wyatt! Wyatt laughed. His dad laughed too.

The rain went drip on the hood, like little drum taps. Wyatt tipped his head. The hood went with him. The rain could not get in. "Rain, rain, go away," sang Skyler. The bus came rolling down the street, all big and yellow. "My turn first!" said Hendrix. "No, me!" said Wyatt. Up went the hood, and onto the bus they went.

Sarah sat in her car seat. Dad drove fast on the big road. Then the car went slow on the small street. Sarah held a box of toys. "In you go," she said. She put in one bear. She put in two cars. She put in three blocks. In, in, in.

Her baby brother sat beside her. He had one little hand free. Out came the bear. Out came a car. Out, out, out. The box was empty! "Dad, the toys keep going out!" Sarah said. Dad said, "In and out are opposites." Sarah laughed. She put the toys in again. Her brother took them out again. It was like a real game. "In," said Sarah. "Out," said her brother.

The car went fast, then slow, then fast. Dad said hot soup was waiting at home. Sarah made a new game. She put in a block. Her brother pulled it out. Then he put it in himself. He clapped his little hands. "You did it!" Sarah said. She counted the toys. One, two, three, all in the box. "Home!" Dad said. The car stopped. Sarah carried her box, holding it tight.

Leah had her favorite toy cat in her pocket. It was soft and gray. She got on the school bus and sat down. Safiya sat next to her. "That cat," said Safiya. "Can I hold it?" Leah pulled the cat close. "It's mine," she said. Safiya reached for it. Leah grabbed it back. Then Safiya grabbed too. The cat's ear went flat. "Oh no," said Leah.

Mr. Navarro, the bus driver, looked in the mirror. He held up a little glass timer. "A sand timer," he said. He turned it over. The sand began to fall. "When the sand runs out, the turn ends." Leah watched the sand go down, down, down. One, two, three, four, five. The last bit of sand fell. "My turn is over," said Leah. She gave the cat to Safiya.

Safiya held the cat and pretended it was ice skating on her knee. Sliding, sliding. Leah watched the sand. One, two, three, four, five. The sand ran out again. "Your turn is over," said Safiya. She handed the cat back. Leah hugged it. Then she laughed. "The sand says whose turn it is," she said. Safiya laughed too. "Silly sand," she said. "It never gets a turn." Leah turned the timer over one more time. Down fell the sand, one grain at a time.

Mila wanted a banana smoothie. Dad got the bananas. He plugged in the blender. Mila waited on her stool.

Then the blender went on. It was so loud! Mila jumped. "Too loud!" she said. She put her hands over her ears. Her palms pressed tight. The loud sound got smaller. It got quiet in her ears.

"Does that help?" Dad asked. "Yes," said Mila. "My hands make it quieter." She kept her ears covered. She waited. The blender spun and spun. Then Dad turned it off. The kitchen was quiet again. Mila took her hands off her ears.

She could hear Dad laugh. She could see the pink smoothie in the cup. She could smell the sweet banana. She touched the cold cup with her fingers. She took a little sip. It tasted like banana and yogurt.

"Grandma makes these too," said Dad. "She spells the word with me. S, M, O..." "O!" said Mila. Dad smiled. "You are so proud of yourself," he said. Mila drank her smoothie and nodded.

Hayden had to go. He ran to the little bathroom by the slides. His dad came with him. "I wait right here," Dad said.

Hayden washed his hands at the tiny sink. He touched the cold tap. Cold water ran out. Brrr. He did not touch the red tap. Dad turned the red tap a tiny bit. Warm water came. "Dad does the hot one," Dad said. Hayden shook the water off his hands. He shook and shook, like a turtle shaking rain off its shell.

Then Hayden ran back to the slide. Kayce was at the top. Kayce lay down on her tummy. Her head pointed down the slide. Hayden called up, "Feet first!" Kayce sat up. She turned around. Her feet pointed down. She slid to the bottom and laughed. Hayden climbed up next. He sat down. Feet first. Whee! "My turn again," he said, and he ran to the ladder.

Liam sat on the couch with a blanket. His nose was red. His cough came back, one, two, three times.

His mom brought him warm soup. Liam took a little sip. It felt good on his throat. Then his nose tickled. A sneeze was coming. It was going to be a big one.

Liam sneezed right into his hand. His hand felt wet. He frowned. "That was bad," he said.

His mom sat down next to him. She lifted her arm and bent it. "Watch me," she said. "I use my elbow." She tapped her elbow. "Elbow, elbow, elbow."

Liam had a question. "My elbow?" he asked. He bent his own arm and tapped. "This part?"

"Yes," said his mom. "Try it now."

Liam practiced. He made a fake cough, one, two, three. He put his elbow over his nose each time. His mom clapped. "You got it!"

Then the tickle came back for real. Liam moved fast. He bent his arm. He sneezed into his elbow.

"My hand stayed clean," said Liam. He held it up to show her.

Mom clapped again. "Good job, Liam."

Liam snuggled back into the blanket. He kept his arm bent and ready. "Elbow, elbow, elbow," he said softly, and took one more sip of soup.

Evelyn had a cold. Her nose was red. Her throat felt scratchy. Mom said, "Let's go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy, Evelyn waited in line with Mom. On the shelf she saw a box with a red butterfly on it. "I like that one," she said. "That box has medicine for kids," said Mom. "But we must ask the pharmacist first." The pharmacist, Mr. Tse, smiled. "Tell me how you feel," he said. Evelyn said, "My throat hurts. My nose runs." Mom told him about her cough too. Mr. Tse picked a small bottle. "This will help," he said.

At home, Evelyn took the medicine. It tasted like cherry. She waited. She drank water. She waited some more. Then she napped with her teddy.

The next morning, her throat did not hurt. Her nose felt better. Mom gave her a red butterfly sticker from the pharmacy bag. Evelyn put it on her hand. "Mom," she said, "if I feel sick at Jillian's house, I will tell Jillian's mom." "That is a good plan," said Mom. Evelyn smiled and stuck the sticker on her teddy too.

Lucy woke up early. She ran to the front door. Outside, the rain went drip, drip, drip. It was rainy, not sunny like yesterday.

"I want to wear my yellow shirt," said Lucy. "But I will get wet." She looked up. "Can rain make you sick?"

"You might get cold and wet," said Mom. "Come, we will share my umbrella."

Mom opened the big umbrella. Lucy stood close to Mom. The rain fell on top of the umbrella. It did not fall on Lucy's head. "Look! My head is dry," said Lucy.

The wind blew. Lucy held her shirt tight. The umbrella stayed up over both of them.

They walked to school. Aayra was at the gate in her rain boots and rain coat. "It was snowy last week," said Aayra. "Today it is rainy."

"Yes," said Lucy. "But I am dry. The umbrella keeps the rain off my head!"

Aayra laughed and took Lucy's hand.

Maeva looked out the kitchen window. Snow had fallen all night. School was closed. It was a snow day!

She put on her boots and mittens. She played in the snow for a long time. Then her mittens felt cold and squishy. They were all wet.

She ran inside to the warm kitchen. "I want to go back out," she said.

Her mom shook Maeva's mittens. Drips fell on the floor. "These are too wet to wear."

Maeva hung them by the window. She hung her boots there too. The sun came in and warmed them.

"Can they dry fast?" Maeva asked.

"Let's eat breakfast while we wait," said her mom. Maeva ate her toast. She did not spill her milk, not even one drop.

Then she touched her mittens. Warm and dry! Her boots were dry too. Wet mittens and boots could dry, and then she could play again.

Maeva raced to the door. "Snow, here I come, one last time before lunch!"

Camille loved the counting song at school. She sang it every day. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. Camilo and Soraya sang too. Ms. Nakamura clapped along.

After the song, Ms. Nakamura held up a big card. It had a mark on it. The mark looked like half a square. Camille pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked.

"That is a five," said Ms. Nakamura. Camille looked at her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." She counted five fingers. The card meant five too! Camille smiled very big.

The class went down the hall. Camille saw a number on a door. It was a five. "This door has five!" she said. Soraya came to look. "Yes, that is room five," said Soraya. Camille held up five fingers next to the door. They matched. Camilo held up five fingers too. All the fingers matched.

Inside the room was the water table. The class got to play. Camille dropped in a squishy ball. It did not sink. It did not swim on top either. It bobbed. Then Camille used a magnet on a stick. She fished up a squishy ball. One ball. Then she got more. She counted them. "One, two, three, four, five." Five balls, all squishy.

Camille held up the card from Ms. Nakamura's pocket. The five on the card. The five balls in her hands. The five on the door. "All fives!" said Camille. Soraya clapped. Camilo clapped. Camille counted one more time, all the way to five, and laughed.

Michael played on a basketball team. It was winter, but the court was warm inside. His friends Lucca and Izabella played too. Mr. Sokolov was the coach.

The ball came to Michael. He tried to shoot. The ball hit the rim. It missed.

Michael's face went hot. He wanted to cover his eyes with his hands. Then he heard a sound.

Lucca clapped. Izabella stomped her feet. "Go, Michael, try again!" they cheered. The whole team clapped too.

Michael looked up. They were smiling at him. The ball came back. He held it with both hands. He bent his knees. He pushed the ball up.

The ball went up, up, up. It went through the net. Swish!

"Yay, Michael!" the team cheered. "Yay, Michael! Yay, Michael!"

Michael ran to his friends. "Next time you miss," he said, "I will cheer for you."

After the game, Dad gave Michael a big orange slice. It was cold and juicy. Michael shared half with Lucca.

"One for you," said Michael. "One for me."

Bennett went to the store with Dad. Bennett wanted to build a cake. It was a cake made of bananas. First he needed a list.

Bennett found a paper and a pen. He wrote his letters. He wrote them all in a big squish. The letters sat close, like sardines. "Read it, Dad!" said Bennett. Dad looked and looked. "Hmm," said Dad. "I see a lot of letters. But the words are stuck together."

Bennett frowned at his paper. His ugly squish would not tell Dad about bananas. Then Bennett saw the cereal box. The box had words on it. The words had little gaps. "Dad, why are there holes in the words?" Bennett asked. "Those gaps are spaces," said Dad. "In English, there is a space between one word and the next."

Bennett looked again. Yes! One word. Space. Next word. Space. Like frogs on lily pads. Bennett wrote his list one more time. This time he made spaces with his pen. He tapped a gap after each word. "B A N space A N A space," he sang.

Then something funny happened. Bennett read his own list. "Ba, na, na," he said. "Bananas!" Dad laughed. "You read it, Bennett!" At the fruit stand, Bennett held up his paper. He matched the letters to the sign. Same letters. Same spaces. "Here they are!" he said. He put six bananas in the bag.

On the way home, Bennett held his list like a lion holds its dinner, tight and proud. "Next time I will write a list for soup," said Bennett. Dad said, "That sounds like a very full paper." Bennett grinned and tapped one big space in the air. "That one is for you."

Hayden stood in the school hallway. It was his first day. He held his little blue bag. The sun came in the big window. Mr. Swampy smiled and said, "Time to go to the slide."

At the slide, Hayden saw a line. Arwen was first. Ezekiel was second. Hayden was third. Hayden had just gone down. He wanted to go again right away. He ran to the top. But Ezekiel was there. "You go to the back," Ezekiel said, gentle and kind. Hayden walked to the back of the line. "One, Arwen. Two, Ezekiel. Three, me," he said.

The line moved. One went down. Then two went down. Then it was Hayden's turn. He slid down fast and laughed. At school, children take turns on the slide. He got in line again. He waited. He counted. Then down he went, right behind Arwen, all the way to the bottom.

Mila sat on a flat cushion in the music room. Mr. Becker held up a big card. "We will sing a song today," he said. "I will count first, so we all start together."

Mr. Becker lifted his hand. He clapped a steady beat on his knee. Then he said, "One, two, three, four." Mila loved the song so much that she started singing right away. But Victoria and Luca had not started yet. Mila was singing all by herself.

Mila stopped and looked down at her shoes. Mr. Becker clapped the beat again. He read the song card once more. Then he said, "One, two, three, four." This time Mila waited. She held her song inside like a bird in a nest. On "four," everyone opened their mouths at once. Victoria sang. Luca sang. Mila sang too.

They clapped along while they sang. Clap, clap, clap, clap. The claps matched the beat like feet matching steps. They sang it again, and again, and Mila did not start early once. When the song was over, the music room felt quiet and warm. "Again," said Mila. "Count with me." Mr. Becker smiled and raised his hand. "One, two, three, four."

Jasper walked to Bastien's house for breakfast. Bastien's mom set out warm toast, butter and a big cup. "You can do it yourself," she said.

Jasper picked up the knife. The butter was soft. He spread it slow and easy. The toast turned shiny all over. He took a big bite. It was so good.

Then Bastien poured the milk. He tipped the cup fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. Bastien's mom was not mad. She wiped it up with a cloth.

"Now me," said Jasper. He held the milk carton with both hands. He poured slowly. The milk went up, up, up in the cup. Not one drop came out.

"I did it!" said Jasper. Bastien clapped. The boys lifted their cups and drank.

Muhammad sat in his big car seat. He had been playing in the sand all day. Now his shoes were full of it. "Home soon," said his dad from the front seat. Muhammad wanted one thing. He wanted his bath. He wanted it right away.

"I will jump in fast," said Muhammad. His dad looked in the mirror. "Not yet," he said. "A grown-up checks the water first. Bath water must be warm, not hot. Hot water can hurt you." Muhammad made a grumpy face. He did not want to wait.

The car stopped in front of their house. Muhammad held his dad's hand all the way to the door. In the bathroom, the tub filled up with water. Steam curled up like a little cloud. Muhammad reached out his hand to jump in.

"Stop," said his dad. "Watch me first." His dad put his own hand in the water. He turned the tap a little. Then he smiled. "Now it is warm, not hot. You can get in." Muhammad put his toes in slowly. The water felt nice and warm. He slid in all the way.

"I waited," said Muhammad. "And the water is just right." His dad laughed and handed him the yellow duck.

Muhammad ran to the park with his dad. The big red slide stood in the sun. Muhammad touched it. "Ow, hot!" he said. His dad gave him a cold drink from the bag. "Ahh, cold and good," said Muhammad.

Then Muhammad saw a big rock on the grass. He pushed it with both hands. It did not move. It was too heavy! Then a soft white feather fell from the sky and landed on the rock. Muhammad picked it up. It was so light! He held it high. "Look, Dad! The rock is heavy. The feather is light. Heavy and light are opposites!"

Muhammad put the feather in his pocket. Then he zoomed down the slide, fast fast fast. His friend Georges went slow, slow, step by step. "Who wins?" asked Georges. Muhammad laughed and said, "Me!"

Lily sat in the waiting room. It was her first trip to the dentist. Her sister was busy drawing a cat. Lily did not draw. She was too awake with worries. "How can the dentist see behind my teeth?" she asked. "My eyes only go front ways."

A boy named Franklin sat next to her. He threw a beanbag gently into a basket in the corner. "I know that one," he said. "Come and see." A nurse opened the door and called, "Lily!"

The dentist had a little tool. It was a tiny mirror on a handle. He held it up in Lily's mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Lily saw herself on the ceiling screen. "That's the backs of my teeth!" she said. After, the dentist let her hold the little mirror. She looked at her sister with it. Her sister made a funny face back.

Isabella sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to draw an owl. She drew a round head for the owl. But her circle came out bobbly. It wobbled all over the paper. "That looks bad," said Tiffany, peeking over her shoulder. Isabella tried again. She drew slowly. The new circle wobbled too.

Then she saw her cup on the table. The cup had a round bottom. She held the cup flat on the paper. She traced all around the bottom with her pencil. She lifted the cup up. There it was, a perfect circle! She added two big eyes and a beak. Then she traced the cup again and again. She made three round eggs under the owl.

Tiffany clapped her hands. "How did you do that?" she asked. "I traced around my cup," said Isabella. She held out the cup to Tiffany. "You can try it too."

Eleanor had new paint pots in the backyard. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. She wanted to paint a big cat.

"New shirt," said Mama. "Put on your old shirt first. An old shirt keeps paint off your clothes." Eleanor pulled the old shirt over her head. It was big and brown.

She painted a red stripe. Then she painted a yellow stripe. The stripes touched. She pushed her brush back and forth. A new colour grew on the paper. It was orange!

"Look, look," said Eleanor. "Red and yellow made orange. It is a colour secret."

She looked at her new shirt under the old brown shirt. No paint on it. She patted the old shirt. "Good shirt," she said.

Chase came to the fence. "What is that?"

"Orange," said Eleanor. "Want to see how?"

Eli sat on the little red rug in the school library. Ms. Joshi put out two bowls. One bowl held three big orange balls. The other bowl held three tiny beads. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.
