Eli pointed at the balls. "This one. The balls are big." Then he stopped. He wished to get it right. "Maybe I should count." He touched each ball. "One, two, three." He touched each bead. "One, two, three." He counted both again. "One, two, three. One, two, three."

Fatima clapped next to him. "The same!" she said. "The same!" said Eli. He looked at the big balls. He looked at the tiny beads. "How can big and small be the same number?" he asked. He counted one more time. Three and three. "They match," he said. He put one bead on top of one ball, and it sat there like a tiny hat.

Hannah was at Grandma's house. Dinner was hot rice and beans. Everyone sat at the big table. Grandma folded her hands. "We say a blessing first," she said. Hannah did not know the blessing yet.

Grandma said the words. One, they thanked the sun. Two, they thanked the rain. Three, they said thank you for the food. Hannah listened hard. Her tummy made a small growl, and River would laugh at that!

The next night, Hannah jumped into her chair. "My turn," she said. She held her hands high like a sign. "Thank you, sun. Thank you, rain. Thank you, Grandma for the rice. Thank you, the farmer for the beans!" Grandma clapped. "The farmer too," she said. "That is a good one." Hannah grinned and picked up her spoon. "Now can the beans jump in my tummy?" she asked.

Charlie ran to art class. Today they would paint trucks! Mr. Horváth put a big shape on each table. "Find your shapes," he said.

Charlie looked at her shape. It had three sides. It had three corners. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three!" It was a triangle. Andrew had a square. Calder had a rectangle. It was long, like a truck bed!

"I want a truck," said Charlie. "My triangle has pointy corners." She turned it around. Then she saw it. The triangle could be the roof of the truck! Andrew's square was the cab. Calder's rectangle was the body. They pushed the shapes together. A truck!

Calder laughed. "It is a stinky garbage truck!" he said. "Help me paint green smelly spots."

Mr. Horváth came over. "Three sides, three corners, and one great truck," he said. Charlie dipped her brush. She made the first wheel round and round.

Peyton sat at the little table in the backyard. She had big paper and wet paint. She wanted to make a butterfly with two wings.

Peyton painted one wing on one half of the paper. Then a bee buzzed by. Peyton jumped up to see it. Her elbow bumped the paper. The paper folded in half while the paint was wet.

"Oh no," said Peyton. Brody came to look. "Open it," he said. Peyton opened the paper slowly. The paint had printed onto the other half. Now there were two matching wings!

Peyton gasped. "A butterfly! A real butterfly shape!" She painted more dots on one half. She folded the paper again. She opened it. More dots on the other half.

Brody tried it too. He painted one wing and folded his paper. His paint printed too.

"I will hang them up," said Peyton. Ms. Oliveira helped hang the butterflies on the fence. A bee flew past the new paintings. Peyton waved and said, "Come see our butterflies!"

Hudson sat at the little table in the library. He wanted to write his name all by himself. He held his pencil and made an H. But the line was fat and fuzzy. It did not look like an H at all.

Hudson frowned. "My H looks like a blob," he said. Ms. Mansour came over. She looked at the pencil tip. "The tip is dull," she said. "A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help." She took the pencil to the sharpener on the desk. Hudson watched from his seat. He heard a scratchy sound. Then she came back with a pointy tip.

Hudson tried the H again. Now the line was thin and clear. It looked just right! He wrote U and D and S and O and N. "I did it!" said Hudson. Ms. Mansour smiled and put a star by his name.

Ella stood at the school playground gate. Her tummy felt fluttery, like small wings inside. She held her dad's hand very tight.

"My tummy feels funny," Ella said.

Dad knelt down beside her. "I felt that way on my first day too," he said. "Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay." Then he pointed. "Look, Mohammed is here."

Mohammed ran over to Ella. He had a red car in his hand. "Want to push it with me?" he asked. Ella peeked at the car. It had one flat wheel, but it still rolled.

Ella let go of Dad's hand. She knelt on the ground. She pushed the car to Mohammed. It rolled slow, then fast, then it bumped his shoe. Mohammed laughed. Ella laughed too. Her tummy felt warm now, not fluttery.

"Again," said Ella. She pushed the car once more.

Alexander ran to the playground. The wind moved the swings a little. He felt excited. He wanted to go down the big slide first.

Then Alexander saw Adonis by the sandbox. Adonis was sitting alone. His face was wet. Tears ran down his cheeks. Alexander stopped running. He felt sad now, too.

"Adonis, why are you crying?" Alexander asked. "My toy truck fell in the mud," Adonis said. "It is dirty now." Ms. Wright came over with a tissue. "When people feel sad, they sometimes cry," she said. She wiped Adonis's face.

Alexander ran back to his bag. He got his lucky blue car. He held it out to Adonis. "You can play with my car," he said. Adonis stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Now Adonis looked happy.

They sat in the sandbox together. They made a hill and a road. The wind blew soft sand off the top. Adonis did not throw sand. He was careful. After a while, Adonis gave the blue car back. "Thank you, Alexander," he said. Then they both ran to the big slide, side by side.

Emily went with her dad to the phone repair shop. The sky was cloudy outside. Mr. Jung smiled at the door.

"Hello, Emily," said Mr. Jung. "Want to try the little tablet?"

Emily tapped the big round button. The screen lit up. She had turned it on!

She opened the drawing app with one more tap. Mr. Jung handed her a cookie. "Draw while you wait," he said.

Emily wanted to draw a red sun. But her line came out blue. She tapped the blue dot, then the red dot. Now her line was red! Tap the colour, get the colour. Tap the colour, get the colour. She drew a big red sun.

"Can I tap green too?" she asked.

"Tap it and see," said Mr. Jung.

Green line! Emily laughed. Then it was time to go. She pressed the button, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet on the counter, all by herself.

"Bye, red sun," said Emily.

Kayden sat on the big red couch. It was Ms. Joshi's living room. The game was on her TV. Kayden loved watching with everyone.

"Go, go!" Kayden shouted. Then he stopped. He pointed at the screen. "Which team has the ball?" he asked.

Ayla laughed. "The red team," she said. "See their red shirts?"

Kayden looked hard. The other team wore blue shirts. Red shirts ran one way. Blue shirts ran the other way. Now he could tell them apart!

"The red team has it!" Kayden yelled. He jumped up and down.

Ms. Joshi brought a plate of carrot sticks. Kayden took one. It was crunchy and yellow-orange. Niam took one too.

"Red team, red team!" Niam cheered.

Kayden clapped for the red team. The blue team got the ball next. Kayden saw the blue shirts right away.

"Blue team has it now," he said.

The red team scored. Everyone cheered. Kayden raised his carrot stick up high like a little flag.

"We win! We win!" he shouted.

Axel ran to the playground. He saw a big cardboard box by the slide. Anayat was standing next to it. "It's my car," said Anayat. "Beep, beep!" Axel wanted it to be a boat. "No, a boat," said Axel. "It sails on the ocean." Both of them frowned.

Then Anayat had an idea. "You go first," she said. Axel sat in the box. He held his arms out like a wheel. "I am driving to the sand," he said. "Now my turn," said Anayat. She sat in the box. She rocked it side to side. "Splash! The ocean is pretty today," she said.

Then Axel turned the box upside down. It had a door shape cut in one side. "A house!" said Anayat. She knocked on it. Axel opened and closed the little door. Their teacher, Mr. Kovalenko, waved from the bench. "Dinner time," Anayat called, and put a toy cup by the door.

Elizabeth sat at the little table in the backyard. Jannah and Mackenzie sat next to her. Ms. Clarke-Williams put snacks in the middle of the table. There were strawberries and lemons.

"Let's play a game," said Ms. Clarke-Williams. "Guess if each snack is sweet or sour. Your tongue can tell sweet foods from sour ones." Elizabeth was scared of the lemon. She thought it might taste bad. Ms. Clarke-Williams held her hand. "Just a tiny taste," she said.

Elizabeth licked the lemon. Her mouth went sour and she made a funny face. Everyone laughed, even Elizabeth. Then she ate a strawberry. "Sweet!" she said. "My tongue knows!" She mixed a strawberry and a lemon slice on her plate and tasted them one at a time. Jannah tried next. "Sour!" she shouted, with a big grin.

Lennon sat at the big table at the library. Mr. Nkosi put out paper and paint. Lennon wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint in the jar.

She looked and looked. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. Hmm, she thought. What if she mixed them? She put red on her brush. She put yellow on top. She gave the paint a little stir.

The paint turned orange! "Look, look!" said Lennon. Her friend Theodora came to see. "That is so neat," said Theodora. Lennon painted her pumpkin all orange. Theodora gave the painting a kiss with her fingertip. Then they hung it up to dry. "Orange," said Lennon, with a big smile.

Ava was playing in the living room. She was pretending her blocks were a castle. Then she sniffed the air. Something smelled good!

She smelled bread and cheese. "Pizza!" said Ava. Her mouth watered. She ran to the kitchen. Her dad was by the oven. He wore big mitts. He slid the pizza out carefully. Ava stood back, far from the hot oven.

"How did you know?" asked her dad. "My nose knew," said Ava. "I smelled it before I saw it." Her dad laughed and gave her a small taste. She touched the warm plate with one finger. It was her favorite dinner after all. "Can I smell tomorrow too?" asked Ava. Her dad smiled and said, "Yes, nose helper."

Caleb sat in the library storytime room. His mom held his hand. Today he would get his very own library card. He wanted a book about trucks, but he had a worry. What if he could only use the card one time?

Mr. Weber smiled at Caleb. "Time for your card," he said. Caleb typed his name on the machine. Then the machine made his card. It had his name on it. Caleb picked a book about a big red truck.

Rylee sat at the next table. She gave her old book to Mr. Weber. Then she swiped her card. Mr. Weber handed her a new book about a juicy orange. "Same card?" asked Caleb. "Yes," said Rylee. "It keeps working." Caleb smiled big. He could bring this book back. Then he could get a new one. On the way out, Caleb saw Rayah at the playground window. "I will read my truck book," he said. "Then I will come back for more."

Raphael went to the temple with his mama. Today was a big party of lights. Little lamps sat in a long row. One, two, three, four. So many lamps!

Raphael wanted to light one. He reached for a match on the table. "Stop," said his mama. "Matches are for grown-ups." Raphael felt sad. He wanted to help so much.

Then Ms. Brown came by. She held a long taper. She was a grown-up, so she could light the lamps. "You can pick one for me," she said. Raphael looked and looked. He chose the small blue lamp. Ms. Brown lit it. A little flame came up. The wick made the flame! Raphael clapped his hands.

His mama smiled. "You picked a good one," she said. Raphael watched his lamp glow. One, two, three, four lamps, all shining. His blue lamp shined the most. He held his mama's hand and watched the pretty light.

Hazel went to the grocery store with her dad. She reached into the cart pocket. Her bunny was not there. "Bunny is lost," she said.

Hazel looked under the apples. No bunny. She looked by the bread. No bunny. Then she saw her friend Dylan by the milk. "Did you see my bunny?" she asked. Dylan pointed to the tall shelf with the paper towels. There sat bunny, up high. Ms. Choi, the neighbour, was reaching for a box. She smiled and handed bunny down to Hazel. "Thank you," said Hazel.

Hazel thought about how bunny got lost. Bunny had no same spot. So Hazel set bunny in the cart pocket. The same spot every time. At the river park later, she set bunny in the same pocket again. When it was time to go, she looked in the pocket. There was bunny, right where she left it.

At home, Hazel found a small red basket by her bed. She set bunny in it. Each night, bunny went in the basket. Each morning, Hazel looked, and bunny was there. "Found you," she whispered.

Isaac wanted to bake a cake with Dad. Isaac was very excited. He got out the big blue bowl. Dad read the list. They needed eggs, sugar and flour.

Isaac looked at Dad. Dad's hands were a little shaky. "Are you scared of the cake?" Isaac asked. Dad laughed. "A little nervous," Dad said. "I burned one last time. But I still want to try." Isaac felt surprised. He thought only kids got scared. "You have feelings too?" he asked. Dad nodded. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Isaac felt brave then. He sent Dad to get the eggs. He poured the sugar into the bowl. Dad cracked the eggs, because eggs can be tricky. The cake went into the oven, and Dad did that part. Isaac watched the oven light. "Can I put the truck in the oven?" he asked. "No," said Dad, and they both laughed. Then a warm smell filled the kitchen. Isaac hugged Dad's leg. "We did it," he said. "And we were only a tiny bit scared." Dad cut two thick slices. "Happy cake," said Isaac, with his mouth full.

Zoey was at the laundromat with her dad. It was cold outside. Winter wind rattled the big glass door.

Zoey wanted to go outside soon. First she had to put on her coat. She pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. Now the zipper.

Zoey pulled the zipper tab up. It did not move. She pulled again. Still nothing. "It's stuck," said Zoey.

Her friend Haroon was there too. He was waiting for his mom. "Look at the bottom," Haroon said. Zoey looked. She saw a little box at the bottom of one side. The other side had a small end. Zoey slid the end into the little box. Click. It fit!

Zoey pulled the tab up. The zipper closed all the way to her chin. "I did it!" she said.

Her dad smiled. They walked out into the cold. The warm coat felt snuggly. Zoey jumped once on the wooden bench outside, and her boots made it bounce a little.

"Zip me next time too," said Zoey. "No," said her dad. "You can do it yourself."

Oliver ran into the big gym. Mr. Wu put out a little net. "Today we play soccer," said Mr. Wu. Oliver wanted the ball to go in the net. He did not know how.

Axl kicked the ball hard. It rolled and rolled. Then it went right into the net. Everyone shouted, "Goal!" Oliver's eyes got big. He saw it. The ball went in the net, so it was a goal.

"I want a goal too," said Oliver. He tapped Kenzo on the shoulder. "Can I have a turn?" Kenzo nodded and passed the ball. Oliver ran to it. He kicked with his whole foot. The ball rolled and rolled. It went into the net! "Goal!" everyone shouted. Oliver jumped up and down.

Outside the window, the snowy field looked white and quiet. But in the gym, the game was still loud and happy. Kenzo clapped. "Good kick," he said. Oliver smiled and kicked the ball back to his friend.

Nicholas put on his red hat at daycare. The sky was gray and the wind whooshed. "It is windy today," said Kali. Mr. Do opened the door. "Hold your hats," he said.

Nicholas ran to the grass. The wind pulled at his coat. Then his red hat flew right off his head! "My hat!" he cried. The hat bounced on the grass. Nicholas chased it. Mac chased it too. The hat rolled and rolled. At last it stopped by the fence. Nicholas picked it up. It felt soft and warm in his hands.

"I will hold it now," Nicholas said. He pushed the hat down tight. Mr. Do smiled. "Windy days are tricky," he said. Later the sun came out. It felt warm on Nicholas's face. He sat inside the cozy playhouse with Kali and Mac. "My grandma knitted this hat," Nicholas said. "Now I hold it when the wind blows." He gave his hat a big hug.

text:
Henry sat at the art table. Ms. Otieno held up a big sheet of paper. "Today we paint snow," she said. Henry looked at his white paper. He looked at his white paint. Hmm. Would white paint show up on white paper?

He tried one little dab. Nothing. The white paint hid on the white paper. Where did it go?

Henry looked around the art room. He saw red paper. He saw yellow paper. He saw green paper. Then he saw blue paper. Blue, like the sky! Snow fell from the sky.

Henry picked up the blue paper. He dipped his brush. He made one white dot. It showed up! He made two white dots. They showed up too!

"Look, Reginald," Henry said. "Blue paper. White snow."

Reginald came over. "It looks like a snow day," he said. "Can I try?"

Henry made more snow. Dot, dot, dot. The blue paper turned white and snowy.

"Fresh snow is white," said Reginald.

Henry smiled and painted the biggest snow pile of all.

Addison sat at the dinner table. Her dad put a plate in front of her. "Lemon slices," he said. Addison looked with her eyes. The slices were yellow and shiny. She sniffed with her nose. They smelled like juice, sweet like her morning orange juice.

Addison wanted a sweet taste. She picked up a slice with her fingers. It felt cool and bumpy. She took a little bite with her tongue. Ooh! Her whole face scrunched up. The lemon was sour, not sweet!

"Daddy, it bites my tongue!" she said. Her dad laughed softly. "Lemons are sour," he said. He gave her a glass of water. Addison drank it all up. One, two, three sips. Then her tongue felt better. Her dad sat close by her side. Addison patted the table with her hand. Dinner was warm. The kitchen was cozy. "One more tiny taste?" asked her dad. Addison shook her head. "Water, please!"

Arnaud sat at Grandpa's big table. There was a whole box of crayons. Arnaud took them all. He held the box tight.

His cousin Rabab came to the table. Rabab had no crayons. She just watched. Could she make a picture with nothing? Arnaud looked at his big pile. Then he looked at Rabab. He pushed three crayons across the table. "You use these too," he said. Rabab smiled and drew a red mountain. "Look!" she said. "It goes up and up."

Arnaud drew a lazy cat sleeping on the mountain. The cat was orange. Then Rabab wanted the orange crayon too. Arnaud handed it over. Rabab added orange suns on the sky. Now the picture was both of theirs. Grandpa came to look. "Who made this?" he asked. "We both did," said Arnaud.

He tipped the box upside down. All the crayons rolled out. "Now we can both use lots!" said Arnaud. Rabab laughed and picked the blue one first.

Samuel turned four today. His party was in the backyard. Balloons sat under the big tree. Clay and Joyce came with small gifts.

Samuel wanted to hear the song. He asked his mom, "Is it cake time now?" His mom said, "Soon. Dad is lighting the candles." Dad was a careful man. He lit the candles with a match. Samuel stayed back and watched.

The cake came out on a plate. Everyone stood around it. Then they began to sing. "Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday dear Samuel." Samuel heard his own name in the song. He pulled his hands up over his face. He hid a big smile behind them. Joyce laughed. Clay sang louder.

After the song, Dad helped Samuel blow out the candles. Samuel clapped. "They sang my name!" he said. Clay said, "The song says your name. It is your birthday." Samuel gave out cake slices. He ate his piece and looked at the balloons. One balloon went up, up, up over the fence. Samuel waved at it. "Bye, balloon," he said.

Aiden sat on the red rug at school. Ms. Greco put out three big circles. One circle had a toy car in it. One circle had a picture of a cat. One circle had an apple. "Put things in the right spot," said Ms. Greco. Aiden picked up a carrot. "Where do you go?" he asked the carrot. He put the carrot in the toy circle.

Edmund came over. He picked up the carrot. "The carrot is food," he said. Edmund put it in the circle with the apple. Aiden looked. The apple and the carrot sat together.

Then Theodora brought bread. She put the bread in with the apple. Aiden clapped his hands. "Apple, bread, carrot!" he shouted. "They are all foods!" Aiden found a red leaf outside on the table. "Is a leaf food?" he asked. "No," said Theodora. "A leaf goes with nature." Aiden put the leaf down and waved. "Snack time!" said Ms. Greco. "We have apples!"

Mateo stood on the soccer field. Mr. Chaudhry put a hoop on the grass. He gave Mateo a red beanbag.

"Throw it in the hoop," said Mr. Chaudhry. Mateo threw it. The beanbag sailed over the hoop and landed in the dirt. He threw it again, soft and low. This time it dropped right in. "I did it!" said Mateo.

Nadine ran over with a big yellow ball. "Now catch," she said. She tossed it high. Mateo held out one hand, like the big kids do. The ball bounced off his fingers and rolled away. He chased it across the field, past the chalk line, all the way to the garden fence. Francesca picked it up for him. "Try both hands," she said.

Nadine tossed the ball again. Mateo held out two hands. The big ball landed right in them and stayed there. He squeezed it tight and laughed. "Two hands!" he called. Mr. Chaudhry clapped. Nadine clapped too. "Throw it back," she said, bouncing on her toes. Mateo bent his knees and threw the big ball with both arms.

Hayden was at the playground with his friend Reagan. The sun was out and the weather was warm. Hayden felt hungry after all that running.

He saw Mr. Ma sitting on a bench with a big jar. The jar had crackers inside. Hayden wanted some. He tried to open the jar. The lid was stuck. He pulled and pulled. It would not move. He made a sad face.

Then he remembered something. He walked to Mr. Ma. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Mr. Ma smiled. "Of course!" He turned the lid and it popped open. "Thank you!" said Hayden. Mr. Ma gave him a cracker. It was shaped like a little star. Hayden had not expected that. "A star!" he said. Reagan ran over to look. "Can I have one too, please?" she asked. Mr. Ma laughed and held out the jar.

Zayn wore his cozy red hat to school. Ms. Fraser had put up balloons. There was a big cake on the table. Ila and Casper ran over to Zayn. "Why all the balloons?" Zayn asked. "Is it a party day?"

Ms. Fraser smiled. She held up a small photo. "Look, Zayn. This is you." It was a tiny baby in a blue blanket. "This was the day you were born," she said. "Today is that same day, three years later. That is your birthday." Zayn looked and looked. The baby had his same nose!

"We are happy you were born," said Ila. "Happy birthday, Zayn!" said Casper.

Ms. Fraser lit the candles, then blew them out with the class. Zayn got the first slice of cake. He put his hat on the baby photo. "You get cake too," he said.

Jackson sat on the small blue chair. A lamp glowed beside him. In his hands was a recorder from Mr. Zhang's music studio.

"Blow soft and slow," said Mr. Zhang.

Jackson blew. Squeak! The sound was loud and funny. Jackson felt upset. Zach laughed next to him, but then he patted Jackson's arm.

Mr. Zhang bent down. "Look at your thumb," he said. "It slid off the hole."

Jackson looked. His thumb had moved. The hole was half open. He put his thumb back on the hole. He locked it there, flat and tight.

He blew again. A round note came out. Not a squeak. A real note.

Jackson lifted one finger. He blew. A new note came out, higher. He put the finger back down. He blew. The low note returned.

Zach clapped. "Do it again!"

Jackson lifted a different finger. He blew. That hole made a new note too. He tried all the holes, one by one.

Mr. Zhang smiled and turned on the lamp, so Jackson could see his fingers better.

Jackson played a low note, then a high note. Zach tried to copy him.

"Your turn," said Jackson. "Cover the hole all the way."

Elias had a red ball. He wanted to be on Mr. Holloway's team. On Saturday, they went to the basketball court.

"Try a shot," said Mr. Holloway. Elias threw the ball. It hit the hoop and fell out. Lucian threw one. It fell out too. "Missed," said Lucian. "One miss," said Elias.

They tried again and again. One miss. Two misses. Three misses. Marko bounced the ball in a neat little way. He watched the hoop. He threw the ball up. The ball went through the hoop. It fell down through the net.

"Nice shot, Marko!" said Mr. Holloway. "You get it in, we score." Elias watched the hoop. He threw his ball up. It went through! It dropped through the net and down.

"Again," said Elias. He threw it again. The ball went through the hoop.

Layla sat at the kitchen table. She had three paint pots. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. Her mom smiled.

Layla wanted to paint a sky. She dipped her brush in blue. She painted a big blue stripe. She held it up. It was too dark. The sky in her window looked soft and pale. Her sky looked like night. Layla frowned.

"Mom, my sky is too dark," she said. Mom set down a pot of white paint. Layla stared at it. She scooped some white with her brush. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round went the brush. The dark blue turned pale. It turned soft like morning. Layla gasped. It was the sky now!

She dipped again. "One scoop, two scoops, three," she counted. The paint got lighter and lighter. Her fingers were sticky and blue. She painted clouds with her new soft colour. "Red, yellow, blue, and white," she sang. "White makes blue go light!"

She painted a little bird in the pale sky. "Hello, bird," she whispered. The bird looked like it was flying home.

Leo held his mom's hand at the street festival. There were red lanterns everywhere. They swung in the wind. Red paper, red ribbons, red apples on a stand.

"Look!" said Leo. "A big lion!"

The lion had golden fur and big eyes. It bobbed its head up and down. Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! Boom!

Leo covered his ears. "Too loud!" he said. The drums were very big drums. They made his tummy jump.

But the lion did not look scared. The lion moved. It hopped when the drums went boom. It shook its tail to the beat. When the drums went fast, the lion went fast. When the drums went slow, the lion went slow.

"Mom, the drums make the lion dance!" said Leo.

Leo let go of his ears. He clapped along. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! Tina came by with her dad. She clapped too. A lady tossed lettuce to the lion, and the lion caught it in its mouth.

The lion passed right by Leo. It blinked its big eyes at him. Leo clapped louder than ever.

"More drums!" Leo shouted. "Make him dance more!"

Maverick had to wash his hands. His friend Agamveer was coming over for lunch. Maverick ran to the bathroom.

He turned on the tap. Water ran over his hands. He rubbed them together. Then he looked. No bubbles. His hands were just wet.

Maverick looked at the pink soap by the sink. He picked it up. He rubbed the soap on his wet hands. Then he rubbed his hands together again. Bubbles! Little white bubbles grew between his fingers. "Look, bubbles!" he said.

He kept rubbing. He counted with his dad outside the door. "One, two, three." The bubbles got bigger. "Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty." He rinsed the bubbles off. The water took them down the drain.

The doorbell rang. Agamveer was here. Maverick ran to the table with clean hands. "Did you wash?" Agamveer asked. Maverick held up his hands and smiled. "Bubbles," he said.

Quinn sat on the school rug. Ms. Mansour held up a bright yellow ball. "Let's count how many times it can roll," she said. The ball rolled to Lennon. Everyone sang, "One, two, three, four, five." Then it rolled to Raven. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Quinn clapped. She wanted a turn with the ball too, but she did not know how to ask.

Then Raven pointed at Quinn. "How old are you?" he asked. Quinn held up her fingers. She looked at them. She took a big breath. "I am four," she said. Her voice was small, then bigger. Ms. Mansour smiled. "Four! Now you can roll the ball four times." Quinn rolled it once. She rolled it twice. Three. Four. The ball rolled right to the toy pond in the corner. "My turn!" said Lennon, running to get it.

Julia was at home with her big teddy bear. She wanted to play pretend. "Let's play house," she said to the bear. "You be the baby."

Julia wrapped the bear in a small blanket. She patted his head. "Time for sleep, baby," she said. Then the doorbell rang. It was her friend Bani.

"I want to play too," said Bani. "But I have a dragon. The dragon lives in our house." Bani held up a green toy dragon.

Julia made a face. "The dragon is scary," she said. "He might eat the baby!"

"No, no," said Bani. "The dragon is friendly. He eats toast."

Julia thought about this. She had a question on her face. "Friendly dragons do not eat babies?"

"Never," said Bani. "Only toast."

Julia smiled. "Okay. Friendly dragon it is. He can be the baby's pet."

Bani made the dragon hop. "Roar! Toast time!" The dragon gave the baby bear a gentle pat. The baby bear did not cry. He liked the dragon.

Julia clapped. "Pretend is fun when we pick together," she said.

Bani nodded. "Now the dragon needs a hat."

Julia ran to get a tiny sock. "A hat for a friendly dragon," she said. The dragon wore the sock all day.

Grayson woke up at Aunt Rosa's house. Today the family would drive far away. "It is a long drive," said Dad. Grayson sat in his car seat. He held his little blue towel from the bath. It was clean and soft. The car went and went. Grayson watched the trees go by. Then he watched more trees. His legs felt stiff. Then his tummy felt funny. "Dad, I need the bathroom," said Grayson. "Hold on, buddy," said Dad. "We can stop at a rest stop." "What is that?" asked Grayson. The car turned off the big road. There it was. A rest stop had bathrooms and space to walk. Dad helped Grayson out of the car. Grayson used the bathroom. Then he stretched his arms up high. He wiggled his legs. They did not hurt anymore. Dad poured water, and Grayson dried his hands on his clean towel. Grayson ran in a little circle on the grass. "Ready to go?" Dad asked. Grayson climbed back in his seat. "Rest stops are good," said Grayson. The car went back on the big road. Grayson waved at the next tree.

Jake woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow day!" Dad said with a big smile. Jake pulled on his pink boots and ran outside. One boot, two boots, crunch, crunch.

Jake wanted to build a snowman. He patted the snow into a ball. The ball fell apart in his hands. He tried again. It fell apart again. "Why won't it stick?" Jake wondered. Did the snowman need more snow? One handful, two handfuls, three. Still it crumbled.

Then the sun came out. The snow began to melt a little. It got wet and shiny. Jake picked up a handful. He squeezed it. It stuck together! One ball, two balls, three balls, stacked up tall. Jake pushed two bits of coal in for eyes. His shadow stretched long next to the snowman's round shadow.

A neighbour walked by. "What a fine snowman," she said. "The wet snow helps it hold." Jake patted the snowman's tummy. It felt firm and cold. "Grow big and strong," Jake told it, "just like me."

Anthony sat in the music room at school. Mr. Fortin picked up a drum. "Let's clap the beat!" he said. Anthony clapped. Clap, clap, clap. But his claps went fast, faster, fastest, like a bunny hopping. The song got mixed up and stopped.

"Oops," said Catalina, laughing. "Your claps ran away!" Anthony laughed too. "My claps are so fast!" he said. Margot stood up. "Mr. Fortin says the beat is steady. It stays even and keeps going, like footsteps when you march." So Anthony stood up. He marched around the green carpet. March, march, march. His steps went even, not fast, not slow.

Then he tried again. Clap, clap, clap. Even claps, just like his marching feet. The song kept going and did not stop! "It works!" said Anthony. "Steady feet make steady claps!" Mr. Fortin played the drum. All the children sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" together. Anthony sang every word from memory. He marched and clapped at the same time. "March, march, clap, clap!" he sang. Catalina took his hand. They marched in one big circle, all around the music room, past the shelf with the green drum, past the little toy bike that sat in the corner. "Again!" said Anthony. "Again, again!"

Mateo had a cold in winter. He had to stay home from school. At the doctor's office, the doctor looked in his ears. "You need rest," she said. "You can go back to school soon." Mateo said, "I am sorry I was coughing so much."

At home, Mateo painted a picture. He painted a big red truck. Then his nose felt stuffy. He blew his nose into a tissue. His mom said, "Time for a snack." Mateo reached for a cracker. Then he stopped.

He ran to the sink. "I need to wash my hands first," he said. He used soap and water. He rubbed his hands together. Then he ate his crackers. His truck painting dried on the table. Mateo smiled and took a big bite.

Louis wanted his bath. He wanted his yellow fish toy in the bath too.

Dad turned the water on. Louis saw steam go up, up, up. "In now?" asked Louis. He put one foot near the tub.

"Wait," said Dad. Dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot. We must wait." A grown-up checks the water first, so it will not be too hot.

Louis waited. He counted with Dad. "One, two, three." The steam went away. Dad put his hand in again. "Now it is just right."

Louis got in. He held his fish. "Fish says swim, swim, swim," said Louis. Dad smiled and washed his hair.

After the bath, Louis put on his pajamas. They had neat blue stars. Dad tucked him into bed. Louis yawned. "Night night, fish," said Louis. He closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Arlo was going on a big trip. He had his little backpack. His teddy bear was inside it.

At the airport, Arlo put his backpack on a belt. The belt moved. The backpack went into a machine. It was gone!

"Where is teddy?" said Arlo. "The machine ate him!"

"Wait and watch," said his dad.

The belt kept moving. Then the backpack came out the other end. Arlo opened it fast. Teddy was still there! He hugged him tight. So that was the trick. Bags went in, and bags came out. The machine just looked inside them.

Later, in the hotel room, Arlo sat on the big bed. Mariam from his class was on the trip too. She knocked on the door.

"Is your teddy okay?" she asked.

"Yes," said Arlo. "He rode the machine. Now he needs a snack."

Arlo's mom gave them each a warm cookie from the bakery box. Arlo broke his cookie in two. He gave half to Mariam.

"You can hold teddy too," said Arlo.

Mariam smiled and held teddy very gently. The cookie felt warm on Arlo's fingers. He licked a crumb off his thumb.

"Teddy is hungry," said Mariam.

Arlo held teddy up to the cookie. "Eat, teddy," he said. "Then we sleep in the big bed."

Ivy ran to the kitchen. Pizza night was here! Her hands had mud on them from the garden.

"First we wash," said her grandma. She turned on the tap. Ivy reached up to put her hands in the water.

"Wait," said Grandma. "The water might be too hot. It could hurt you. A grown-up must check it first."

Grandma held her own hand under the tap. "Warm, not hot," she said. "Now you can wash."

Ivy put her hands in the water. It felt warm and nice. Grandma gave her the soap. Ivy rubbed the soap all over. She made white bubbles on her hands. Bubbles on top. Bubbles on the bottom. Bubbles between her fingers.

"We count to twenty," said Grandma. They counted together. "One, two, three..." Ivy counted all the way to twenty.

The bubbles went down the drain. The mud went down too. The water carried it all away. Ivy held up her hands. They were clean and shiny.

Then Ivy got to eat her pizza. It was warm and good. After she used the toilet, she ran back to the sink all by herself.

"Check the water, please," she said to Grandma.

Grandma smiled and tested the tap. "Warm, not hot."

Ivy washed with soap and counted to twenty. "Twenty!" she said, and shook her wet hands.

Ivy wanted to draw a cat. She asked her mom for the tablet. Mom turned it on for her. The screen lit up bright.

The screen had many small pictures. Ivy did not know which one to pick. Mom sat beside her. "Those little pictures are called icons," Mom said. "Tap one and an app will open." Ivy looked and looked. She found a little paintbrush. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" said Ivy.

She drew a cat with a purple tail. Then she drew a bad dog with spots. She laughed at the spots. When she was done, Mom helped her close the app. Ivy slid the tablet into its bag. She hung the bag on the hook, right where it belonged. "Good night, tablet," Ivy whispered.

Luna ran out of her house to the soccer field. It was a windy day. Leaves danced all around her feet. Mr. Bondarenko put a hoop on the grass. "Throw the beanbag in," he said.

Luna held the beanbag up high by her ear. She threw it hard. It flew over the hoop and landed far away. "Oh no," said Luna. She tried again. High, hard, over the hoop. Again!

Mr. Bondarenko picked up the beanbag. He held it down low by his knees. Then his arm swung forward and up, like a swing. The beanbag went up and dropped right into the hoop.

Luna looked at his arm. Could her arm swing that way too? She held the beanbag down low. She swung her arm forward and up. The beanbag sailed up, then plopped into the hoop. "I did it!" said Luna.

Then Leif rolled her a big ball. Luna opened both hands wide. The ball came and she hugged it tight to her chest.

"Again!" said Luna.

Brooklyn's block tower fell down. It fell right at bedtime, before her bath.

Brooklyn felt angry. Her face got hot. Her hands made tight fists. She wanted to stomp and shout.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Let's try slow breaths," he said. "Breathe in slow. Now breathe out slow."

Brooklyn breathed in. Her tummy got big like a balloon. She breathed out. The balloon got small.

They did it again. In, slow. Out, slow. The clock on the wall ticked softly. Brooklyn's fists came open. Her face felt cool.

"I'm not angry anymore," she said. She felt calm.

Then she stacked the blocks again. Dad helped. The tower grew tall. It did not fall.

Dad read her one book about a grumpy bear. The bear spun in circles, then went to sleep. Brooklyn yawned.

She snuggled under her warm blanket. It was soft and smelled like soap. Dad kissed her head.

"Night night, Brooklyn," he said.

"Night night, tower," said Brooklyn.

Elliot did not want to go to practice. He wanted to play the game today. "We practice first," said Ms. Georgiou. "Then we play." Elliot frowned. His friend Reyansh took his hand. They ran into the big gym.

At practice, they threw the ball back and forth. Elliot missed at first. The ball rolled past him. "Try again," said Elie. Elliot threw it again and again. Then he caught it! He caught it two more times. Ms. Georgiou clapped. "Nice catch, Elliot!"

Then the game began. The ball flew toward Elliot. He held out his hands. He caught it fast! Elliot jumped up and down. "I caught it!" he shouted. Reyansh gave him a big hug. In the car, Elliot sang a happy song. "Practice next week too?" asked his dad. "Yes!" said Elliot. "Practice makes me ready for games."

Mila went to the temple with her mama. It was Diwali, a big bright day. There were many little clay lamps on the floor. "They are called diyas," Mama said.

Mila wanted to help. "Can I put them in a row?" she asked. "Yes," said Mr. Rao. "That is an easy job. Just set them down, one by one." Mila put a diya down. Then another one. She could hear people singing far away. Soon the diyas made a long line.

The diyas were dark. Then Mama used a long stick with a small flame. She touched it to a wick. One diya glowed. She touched the next one. It glowed too. Mila clapped her hands. "The little fire made them bright!" she said. Wallace came to look, and they saw all the diyas shine. Wallace had his soft pet dog with him. The dog sat down by Mila's feet. The lamps glowed like little stars all in a row.

Bennett sat in the living room. The big tablet was on the rug. He wanted to draw a rock on it. But first he had to turn it on. Where was the button? He looked and looked. There! A little round button on the side. He pressed it. The screen lit up. The whole thing glowed. "It works," he said.

Now he needed the drawing app. He tapped a red square. No, that was not it. He tapped a blue circle. No. Then he tapped the green paint pot. Yes! A white page came up. He drew a big gray rock. Then he drew a cat sitting on the rock. The cat was orange.

Bennett picked up the tablet with one hand to put it away. It tipped and slid. It almost fell on the rug! He caught it with a squeak. Then he tried again, this time holding it with two hands. It stayed nice and steady, like a book. He carried it to the shelf. He set it down and pressed the button. The screen went dark.

"Is that a little pop sound?" he wondered. He put his ear close to the shelf. Then his dad called, "Bennett, come see this!" On the window, a butterfly was sitting very still. Bennett tiptoed over. The butterfly opened its wings. They were blue, like the sky. "Hello," Bennett whispered.

Isla stood in the bathroom. She held her little red shoe. The tap dripped, drip, drip. She heard it with her ears. The soap smelled like flowers. She smelled it with her nose. The light was bright. She saw it with her eyes. The towel was soft. She touched it with her hands.

Then a big noise began. Rrrrrr! It was the blender in the kitchen. It was very loud. Isla did not like it. She covered her ears with her hands. She pressed them tight. The loud sound got quieter. Rrrrrr, small and far away. "Better," said Isla.

The blender stopped. Isla took her hands off her ears. She heard the drip, drip, drip again. She wiggled her toes in the warm water. "All done," said Isla. She put her shoe on the mat.

Clara sat at the art table. She had a red crayon and a big white paper. She drew a sun with a happy smile.

Then Clara looked up. Her friend Kayce sat across the table. Kayce had a big frown. Her mouth turned down. Her eyebrows came together. Clara thought, "Kayce's face looks sad." She walked over and sat close.

"Kayce, your face tells me you feel sad," said Clara. Kayce nodded. "I lost my toy car," she said. "It was my favorite one."

Clara wanted to help. She and Kayce looked under the table. They looked by the book shelf. They looked in the toy box. Then Clara called, "I see it! It is behind the blocks!" Kayce grabbed the little car. Her frown went away. Her mouth made a big smile.

"Your face tells me you feel happy now," said Clara. Kayce laughed. Ms. Gill came over with two cookies, one for each girl. "Quick, snack time," she said. Clara took a quick, happy bite.

Kayce held up her car. "Your face tells me you feel happy too," she said. Clara smiled her biggest smile.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Leah ran to the car. Grandma had a big bag with wheels. "Pull it with me," said Leah. Grandma held her hand. They pulled the bag up the steps. It went bump, bump, bump.

The bag was heavy. Leah stopped. "What is inside?" she asked. "My clothes and my things," said Grandma. "Guests who come to stay pack a bag or a suitcase." Leah jumped up and down. "Open it! Open it!" she said.

They went to the guest bedroom. Grandma put the bag on the bed. Click! It opened. Leah peeked in. She saw a red sweater. She saw soft socks. She saw a hairbrush and a little lamp? No, that was not a lamp. That was Grandma's shiny teacup!

Leah helped put socks in a drawer. One drawer was too high for her. Grandma lifted her up. "In it goes!" said Leah. The sock went in. Then Grandma pulled the zipper shut on the empty bag. It looked so small now! "The bag ate everything," said Leah. Grandma laughed and laughed.

Sara sat at the little table at the community centre. Mr. Toussaint put out two bowls of blocks. "Count them," he said. Sara pointed. "One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four, five, six." She patted the big pile. "This one has more!"

Benson came over with two bags. One bag was pink. "Snack time," he said. Benson picked the pink bag. Sara peeked in. The pink bag had fewer crackers. The other bag had more. "That bag has fewer," said Sara. "This one has more."

Benson looked. He saw it too. He took the bag with more crackers and shook it gently. They counted together. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Sara smiled and counted her blocks again. "One, two, three, four. Fewer blocks."

Blake stood at the little sink. Lunch was coming soon. Ms. Takahashi had shown the class how to wash hands. "Twenty seconds of soap," she had said. Blake wanted to do it all by herself.

She pumped the soap. She rubbed her hands together. She counted with Rylee, who was at the next sink. "One, two, three," they said. They counted all the way to twenty. Blake's hands felt slippery and bubbly.

Blake turned off the water. Her hands still felt slippery. "Look," she said to Rylee. "My hands are still soapy." Rylee held out her own hands. They were slippery too.

Blake turned the water back on. She put her hands under it. The water ran over the soap bubbles. The bubbles slid down into the sink. Blake rubbed and rubbed under the water. Then she felt her hands. They were not slippery anymore. They felt clean and fresh.

"Rylee, try it," said Blake. Rylee put her hands under the water too. The soap slid off her hands as well. The two girls dried their hands on the paper towels.

Ms. Takahashi came over with a tray of cups. She gave each girl a glass of water for lunch. "My hands are all clean," said Blake. She held them up to show. Then she sat down and took a big drink from her glass. Rylee sat down beside her, and they began to eat.

Rowan sat at the snack table at daycare. His eyes saw a big red strawberry on his plate. His ears heard Shelby clapping. "Yay, strawberries!" she said.

Rowan picked up his strawberry. His fingers felt the bumpy little seeds. His nose sniffed it. It smelled sweet. He took a bite. "Mmm," he said. It tasted very sweet.

Then Mr. Chanthavong said, "Try something fun. Pinch your nose closed. Then bite." Rowan pinched his nose. He bit the strawberry. He blinked his eyes. "It tastes plain!" he said. "Not sweet at all!" Shelby tried it too. "So plain!" she said. Rowan let go of his nose. He sniffed again. The sweet smell came back. He took another bite. "Sweet again!" he said. He clapped his hands.

Outside, an owl called from the big tree. "Ooh," said Rowan. His sweater felt itchy on his arm, but he did not care. He had a strawberry in his hand. He pinched his nose, and he bit.

Ethan woke up and looked out the window. Snow! White snow everywhere. "No school today," said his dad. "A snow day!"

Eann put on his boots and his red coat. He stepped into the soft snow. Squish, squish. He looked back. "Dad! My boots made marks!"

"Those are footprints," said his dad. "Feet leave footprints in fresh snow."

Ethan stomped and counted. "One, two, three, four!" Four footprints behind him. He stomped some more. One, two, three, four, five.

Then Ethan saw more footprints. Big ones! Not his. "Who made these?" he asked. Where did they go? He followed them. Step, step, step. They went past the big tree root. They went up to a door. Mr. Becker's door!

Knock, knock. Mr. Becker opened the door. "Hello, Ethan! I saw your footprints in my yard. Come in. I have warm cocoa."

Ethan and his dad sat inside. The cocoa was warm. The room was cozy. Ethan looked out the window. Splash went snow off the roof. "Dad," said Ethan, "can we make more footprints tomorrow?"

Eva sat on the train with her mama. Her shoes were on tight. Her bag was on her lap. "One bag, one bear, one hat," she said. "And one mama!"

They were going to the sea. Eva looked out the window. A cow stood in a field. The train went fast, and the cow went zoom, backwards. Eva laughed. "The train makes the cow go back!"

At the sea, Eva met a boy named Scott. They dug a big hole. An ant ran over the sand. "Hello, ant," said Eva. The ant tickled her toe.

Then the trip was over. The train took them home. Eva missed the sea. She missed the big hole. She wanted to cry a little.

Mama had an idea. "Let's look at our trip photos." Click, click, went the screen. There was the cow. There was the hole. There was Scott. There was the tickly ant!

Eva clapped. "The photos stay!" she said. "The sea can go zoom away, but the photos stay right here."

She looked at the ant picture one more time. "Hello again, ant," she whispered.

James went to the library with his dad. Today he would get his very own library card. It was red, and his name was on it. He held it with both hands.

Then James saw something. A woman sat on a little chair. Children sat on the floor in front of her. She opened a big book and began to read out loud. All the children listened. "What is this?" James asked his dad. His dad whispered, "It is storytime. The librarian reads books aloud to a group of children."

One boy stood by the shelf. He looked upset. He did not sit down. Then the librarian turned a page. A picture of a fork made everyone laugh. The boy heard the laughing. He smiled and sat down too.

James picked a book about trucks. He gave his red card to the librarian. She stamped the book and handed it back. "Can we come back for storytime?" James asked. "Yes," said his dad. James hugged the book all the way home.

Milo was at the hotel pool with his dad. He wanted to learn to swim. He held his little kickboard under his arm.

Milo ran past the showers. He wanted to jump right in. A man in a white shirt stopped him gently. "Wait, little one," said Mr. Romano. "Take a shower first. Then you can swim." Milo looked at the showers. He stepped under the warm water. It felt bumpy on his skin. He reached up and touched the water. It came down like a little lake of rain.

After the shower, Milo got in the big pool. His dad held his hands. Milo kicked his legs. He kicked and kicked. He moved through the water all by himself. "Look, Dad!" said Milo. "I'm swimming like a fish!"

Theo woke up with messy hair. His hair had big tangles in it. He looked in the little mirror. "Oh no," said Theo. "My hair is all twisty."

It was bedtime bath time next. His dad ran the warm bath. Theo washed with soap. He saw his yellow duck float by. The duck had a spotted back. "Hello, spotted duck," said Theo. He washed his hair too. The water made his hair soft.

Then Theo found the brush on the shelf. He brushed his hair slowly, so it did not pull. One tangle came out. Then another tangle came out. He brushed some more. The tangles got out, one by one. His hair was smooth now! Theo smiled at the mirror. He put on his soft pajamas. He climbed under his blue blanket. "Dad!" he called. "Come see my smooth hair!" Dad peeked in the door. "What a nice surprise," said Dad. Theo patted his head one more time. Then he closed his sleepy eyes.

Stella went to the store with her dad. She had one job. She would get apples for a juicy snack.

"Get ten apples," said Dad. Stella looked at her list. The list said 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. But the number ten was missing. Stella frowned. Nine had one number. Ten needed more.

Stella picked apples one by one. "One, two, three," she said. She dropped them in the bag. "Four, five, six." The bag got heavy. "Seven, eight, nine." Then she held up one more apple. "Ten!"

Mr. Santos worked at the store. He smiled at Stella. "Ten is written with two digits," he said. "A 1 and then a 0." Stella looked at her list. She wrote a 1. Then she wrote a 0 next to it. Ten! It was the biggest number on her page.

Stella gave the bag a hug. "Ten juicy apples!" she said. Mr. Santos laughed. "You counted them all." Dad came over with the cart. "Good helper," he said. Stella carried one apple herself. She left the rest in the bag for home. "One for me," she said. "Nine to share!"

It was a cloudy day at Grandma's house. Charlotte put on her red boot to go outside. Grandma was going to shop, so Sahib and Flora came to play. "Let's play hop to the tree," said Flora. "We each get one hop," said Sahib. Charlotte hopped once, then she hopped again and again. "Hey," said Flora. "You get one hop. That is the rule." Charlotte hopped some more anyway. Flora put her hands on her hips. Sahib sat down on the step. "We are not playing now," he said. Charlotte looked at them. Nobody was hopping. What had made them stop?

Charlotte thought and thought. Then she went back to the start line. "One hop," she said. "Me first." She took one big hop. Then she stood still. Flora smiled and took her hop. Sahib took his hop next. Everyone waited for each turn. "My turn again?" asked Charlotte. "Yes," said Flora. So Charlotte hopped one time, all the way to the tree. "You did it!" said Sahib. Flora clapped her hands. Charlotte clapped too. "Again, again!" she said, running back to the line.

Peyton ran to the library shelf. She wanted the wild animal book. She pulled it off with both hands. "Dad, read this one!"

Dad sat down on the soft rug. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. Peyton waited for the lion part.

Dad's eyes went across the page. His mouth said, "The lion naps in the sun." Peyton laughed. The lion did look sleepy.

Then they came to a big page with just stars. "Read it," said Peyton.

Dad shook his head. "There are no words on this page. There is nothing written here to read. Look, just stars."

Peyton looked. He was right. No little black marks. Just stars.

She tried something. She put her hand over the words on the next page. Dad stopped reading. He only looked at her.

Peyton pulled her hand away. Dad's eyes went across the little black marks again. "The hippo splashes in the mud," he read. Splash! The picture showed mud everywhere.

"So the words make you talk," said Peyton.

Dad grinned. "You found it out, clever girl."

Peyton pointed at the marks. "Read the hippo part again!"

Xavier stood in the kitchen at home. He wanted to help make breakfast. He heard eggs crack in the bowl. His ears heard that! He smelled the toast pop up. His nose smelled that!

Then Daddy shook a rug by the door. Dust flew up in the air. One bit of dust went near Xavier's eye. He blinked fast, fast, fast. The dust sat on his eyelashes. It did not go in.

Xavier looked in the little mirror. "Little hairs on my eyes!" he said. Daddy smiled. "Those are your eyelashes," he said. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes."

Xavier blinked again. One, two, three. The dust fell off. His eye felt fine.

At lunch, Xavier carried his plate to the table. He touched the bread, soft and warm. He tasted the sweet jam with his tongue.

Later he told Maika on the phone, "My eyelashes stop dust!" He blinked, and blinked, and blinked.

Jade ran into the backyard. The sun was bright. "Ow," she said. The sun was too sunny. She squeezed her eyes into little lines. She could not see her sandbox at all. Siya was already there. Siya wore a big sun hat. Siya did not squint at all.

"My eyes hurt," said Jade. "Here," said Siya. "Try my hat." Siya put the sun hat on Jade's head. The hat made shade over Jade's face. Jade opened her eyes wide. Now she could see everything! The sand looked soft and squishy. Jade picked up her small hammer. She tapped a sand cake. Tap, tap, tap.

Then the wind blew. Windy days make hats fly! The hat lifted off. Jade held it close with both hands. She sat down in the shade next to Siya. "Good hat," said Jade. "Good shade," said Siya. They shared it under the big tree.

Zoe wanted to find her name. She had a card from Grandma on the table. "Is my name in there?" she asked. Dad opened the card. "Look here," he said. Zoe looked. She saw the word ZOE. The letters were big and pink. "That says Zoe!" she said.

Then Zoe wanted to see it again. She hurried to the shelf. Her puppy book sat there. Dad helped her open it. "We read this way," he said. He turned the pages from front to back. Zoe turned one page. Then another. On the last page, the book said FOR ZOE. There were her letters again. Z, then O, then E.

Zoe touched the card. She touched the book. The letters looked the same. Same letters, same order. "My name looks like my name," she said. She asked, "Does my name look like this on other things too?" Dad smiled. "Let's go look," he said. Zoe held her card in both hands, like a little pink bone her puppy might hide, and off they went to find more.

Aaron went to the park with his little toy mouse. The mouse was small and grey and very cute. Aaron threw a ball with his friend Cedric. Then Aaron looked in his pocket. The mouse was gone.

"I lost my mouse," said Aaron. "Where did it go?" He looked by the bench. No mouse. He looked by the tree. No mouse. He looked under the slide. It was dark under there. He could not see anything. "Too dark," said Aaron.

Ms. Wong came over with a flashlight. "Try this," she said. She clicked it on. Aaron shined the light under the slide. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots!" The light made the dark spot bright. There was his mouse, sitting in the leaves. "Mouse!" said Aaron. He picked it up and hugged it tight. "All safe now," said Ms. Wong. "Let's go tell Cedric." Aaron ran across the grass with the mouse in his hand. "Look, Cedric! My mouse was under the slide!"

Aaron wanted a tea party for his bear. But the teapot was empty. No tea inside at all. "Where can I get tea?" he asked. Mom was busy at the stove, stirring the pot. Aaron stayed back from the hot stove. Then he had a big idea. The cups could be empty too! He lined up four little cups. He set out cups for Jade, for Bjorn, and for the bear too.

Aaron tipped the empty teapot over a cup. Tilt, tilt, tilt. Nothing came out. But he made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug!" Jade clapped. "Pretend tea!" she said. Bjorn picked up his cup. He took a big pretend sip. "More, please!" Aaron poured again. The empty cups felt light and easy to hold.

Then Aaron held out the teapot to the bear. "Careful," he said. "It's pretend hot!" The bear drank it all up. Aaron found a soft sock and wiped the bear's mouth. "All clean," he said. "More pretend tea, everyone?" The cups went up in the air. "Yes, please!" said Jade.

Charles ran to the toy shelf. He was excited to play trucks. But then he heard a sound. It was a small, sad sound. Marley sat by the blocks. Her face was wet with tears. Charles felt scared to ask. He held his truck tight.

He looked at Ms. Torres. She smiled and nodded. Charles walked over slow. He held out his red truck. "Want to share?" he asked. Marley wiped her eyes. She took the truck. Then she smiled a big smile.

Ms. Torres said, "That was kind, Charles." Charles felt happy in his chest. Daxton came with a bone toy for the toy dog. One truck, one bone, one smile. Marley laughed. Charles said, "Sharing is easy." Then he pushed the truck across the rug to her.

Nicholas sat in a big chair at the mall. It was his first haircut ever. His mama stood close by. The hairdresser, Mr. Yang, picked up his scissors. Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. They fell on Nicholas's neck. They felt tickly. They felt itchy, too.

Nicholas wiggled. "My neck itches!" he said. He wiggled some more. Mr. Yang laughed a kind laugh. "Hold still, little one," he said. He took a soft brush. He brushed the tiny hairs away. Swish, swish, went the brush. The itchy feeling went away too! Nicholas stopped wiggling. "The hairs made me itchy," he said. "Now they are gone."

Mr. Yang brushed and brushed. Nicholas sat as still as sand in a sandbox. Then Mr. Yang held up a mirror. Nicholas saw a brand new boy with short, cozy hair. His mama gave him a big hug. "Handsome!" she said. Nicholas grinned at the mirror boy. The mirror boy grinned right back.

Brielle stood in the gym with a red beanbag. Ms. Murphy put a hoop on the floor.

"Throw it in," said Ms. Murphy.

Brielle threw the beanbag. It missed the hoop. She threw it again. It was missing the hoop again. Alpha and Vamika watched.

"My turn is bad," said Brielle.

"Try again," said Vamika.

Brielle picked up the beanbag. She threw it one more time. It went in the hoop!

"I did it!" said Brielle.

Then Ms. Murphy brought a big ball. "Catch with both hands," she said.

Vamika threw the ball to Brielle. It bounced off her arms. "I keep missing it," said Brielle.

She held out both hands. Vamika threw the ball again. Brielle caught it!

"Now throw it back," said Vamika.

Brielle threw the ball. Vamika caught it. They threw and caught, again and again.

After recess, Ms. Murphy clapped. "Look at you two!"

Brielle smiled. "I did it lots of times," she said.

"One more time," said Vamika. She tossed the big ball.

Brielle held out both hands. She caught it, easy as a pig in mud.

Aria sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her tummy felt jumpy. "Will the doctor hurt me?" she asked. "No," said her mom. "The doctor just checks you." Ms. Charles came in with a kind smile. She had a black bag. Aria heard it zip open. It went zzzz.

First Ms. Charles looked in Aria's ears. Aria saw a little light. Then Ms. Charles put a cold circle on Aria's back. The cold made Aria shiver. The circle made a sound too. It went thump, thump. "That is your heart," said Ms. Charles.

Then it was game time. "Close your eyes," said Ms. Charles. "Your fingertips can tell soft, rough, smooth or bumpy." Aria felt a pinecone. "Bumpy!" she said. She felt a feather. "Soft!" She felt a stone. "Smooth!" Then she felt something rough. "What is it?" she asked. "A bandage," said Ms. Charles. Aria got a shiny sticker. It smelled like strawberries. Ms. Charles dropped it in Aria's hand. Aria held it tight all the way home.

Owen sat at the dinner table. His cup was red. He was happy. "Yum, noodles!" he said.

Then he heard a loud noise. BANG! It came from the kitchen. Owen jumped. His tummy felt tight. He was scared. "Too loud," he whispered.

Mom saw his face. "You look scared, Owen." Owen nodded. "Scared of the bang." Mom held his hand. "You can tell me. I will help." They walked to the kitchen together. Mom looked under the sink. A pot had fallen down. Mom picked it up and put it high on the shelf.

"No more bang," said Mom. Owen smiled big. Now he felt excited. "I want to catch the noise next time!" he said. Mom laughed. "You are quick, Owen. But just tell me first. I will always come."

Back at the table, Owen ate his noodles. Then he saw something in his bowl. A little carrot looked just like a worm! Owen giggled. "A worm in my noodles!" Mom smiled. "That is just a carrot, cut long." Owen took a big bite. "I ate the worm!" he said.

Emily was in the bathroom. She wanted to read the tiny words on her soap bottle. She held it up to her eyes. The words looked like little ants. Her eyes could not make them clear.

Grandpa came in to help with bath time. He had a kiss for her nose. "Time to swing your towel on the hook," he said. He held the bottle up too. He squinted. He held it far away and then very close. The words stayed fuzzy for him too.

Then Emily saw his glasses by the sink. She gave them to him. He put them on. "Now I can see," he said with a big smile. He read the whole bottle out loud. It said, "Bubbles for splashy baths!" Emily laughed. Grandpa blew bubbles low over the water. Emily touched one with her finger. Pop! She heard the tiny sound. "Your glasses are magic," she said. Grandpa winked. He read the bottle again, just for fun.

Weston sat at the dinner table. He had a big plate of orange carrots. He munched them all up. "Bath time next!" said his dad. Weston loved bath time.

He ran to the tub. Dad filled it with warm water. Weston jumped in and splashed. He splashed and he splashed. Then it was time to get out.

Weston hopped out of the tub. Drip, drip, drip! Water fell on the floor. He ran down the hall. He was still very wet. His pajamas stuck to his skin. "Oh no!" said Weston. He looked back at the bathroom.

There was the towel on the hook. Weston ran back for it. Dad wrapped it around him. Dad rubbed his arms and his legs and his tummy. The towel soaked up the water. Soon Weston was all dry!

"Now pajamas," said Dad. Weston put on his soft pajamas. They felt warm and cozy. The towel had dried him, so the pajamas went right on. Weston looked at the towel on the hook. "Good towel," he said. "You dried me!" Then he gave the towel a big pat.

Mya had a little bunny. She took it to daycare. Bunny had soft white ears. Mya loved bunny very much.

At circle time, the class sang a song. Mya sang too. Then it was time for a snack. Mya looked in her bag. Bunny was not there! Mya wanted to run and look all by herself. She looked at the big play house in the corner. Maybe bunny was there. But she stopped. She walked to Mr. Brown first. "Bunny is lost," she said. "Will you help me look?"

Mr. Brown smiled. "Yes. Let's look together." They looked under the table. They looked by the doll house. No bunny. Mya peeked inside the play house. There was bunny, sitting on a little chair! "Bunny!" said Mya. She gave bunny a big hug.

"It's true," said Mr. Brown. "Telling a grown-up helps." Mya sat down with bunny on her lap. "Now sing the song again," she said.

Milo was hungry. He wanted warm soup for lunch. Dad put a pot on the stove. "I will cook it," said Dad. "You can sit here."

Milo waited at the table. The soup went bubble, bubble. The stove did not look hot at all. It was just flat and black.

Milo wanted to touch it. He slid down from his chair. He took one step, then two. Then he stopped and thought. The stove can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it.

"Is it hot?" Milo asked.

Dad held his hand way up high, far from the pot. "Still hot," said Dad. "Hot things can look the same as cold things."

Milo nodded. He went back to his chair. "Can I help?"

"Yes," said Dad. "Fetch a paper towel for me."

Milo walked slowly and carefully. He brought the paper towel. Dad gave him a little job. Milo tore the towel into small pieces. One, two, three. He lined them up on the table.

Then Milo felt something warm near his cheek. It was the steam. It came up from the pot and floated away. Milo watched it go. It was soft and light.

"Soup is ready!" said Dad. He poured the soup into a blue bowl. He blew on it. "Cool, cool, cool," he said. Milo blew too.

Milo took a little sip. "Warm now," he said. "The stove was hot. Now the soup is just right." Dad smiled. The steam curled up and vanished.

Jacob sat at the dinner table. He wanted more rice. He reached far across the table. The bowl was too far away.

"May I have more rice, please?" Jacob asked. His dad smiled. Dad put rice on Jacob's plate. "Thank you," said Jacob. "You're welcome," said Dad.

Jacob ate fast. Then he wanted the bread. He reached again. Uh oh. His cup tipped over. Milk went everywhere. The table was wet. His shirt was wet too.

"I am sorry," Jacob said. "That's okay," said Dad. "Let's get a towel. Can you help me?" Jacob ran to the drawer. He brought a towel. Dad wiped the table. Jacob wiped his spot. The table was dry again.

Miss Abigail came over after dinner. She was a neighbour. Jacob shared his cookie with her. "Thank you for the cookie," said Abigail. Jacob did not know what to say back. He thought hard. Then he remembered dinner. Dad had said it to him!

"You're welcome," said Jacob. Abigail smiled a big smile. Jacob smiled too. He liked those two little words.

Emma sat at the little table at school. She glued paper whiskers onto a striped cat. "Show and tell is tomorrow," said Mr. Warsame. Emma touched the cat's soft paper ears. She wanted to show it now.

"Is it tomorrow yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mr. Warsame. "Today is still today. First today, then tomorrow."

Emma waited. She counted the day. "One, we eat snack. Two, we play outside. Three, we put on coats." She did each thing. Nimrat and Eddie helped her count. Soon the teacher said, "Time to go home."

Emma went home. She ate supper. She had a bath. She went to sleep. Then she woke up. The sun was up. Her mom and dad sat at the breakfast table. There were eggs and milk.

"Good morning," said Emma.

"Good morning," said Mom. "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast."

Emma ate her eggs. Then she got dressed and ran to school. She held up the striped cat. Its whiskers stood up straight.

"Meow," said Eddie.

"Meow," said Emma, and she made the cat wave.

Alexis had big news today. He was bringing home a puppy! The little dog was brown and white. His tail went wag, wag, wag. "His name is Spot," said Alexis.

Dad drove them home in the car. Spot sat on Alexis's lap. Then Dad stopped the car. "Wait," said Dad. "Spot needs his collar first."

Dad held up a small piece of metal. It was a special tag for Spot's collar. "What is it?" asked Alexis. Dad read it out loud. It said Spot's name. It said their phone number too.

Alexis touched the tag with his finger. It made a little tink sound. Spot wagged his tail. Dad clipped the tag onto the collar. Now the collar went jingle, jingle when Spot walked.

"If Spot ever gets lost, someone finds him," said Dad. "They see the tag. They call our number." Alexis nodded. The tag would bring Spot home!

At home, Alexis filled Spot's bowl with water. Spot drank it all up. Then Spot ran around the kitchen. Jingle, jingle, jingle went his collar.

Alexis laughed and clapped his hands. "Good boy, Spot!" he said. Spot jumped up and licked his nose.

Lucy ran to the window at daycare. "Rain!" she said. Big drops went tap, tap, tap on the glass. Sargun ran over too. "No park," he said. His face looked sad. His mouth turned down at the corners.

Lucy felt sad too. She wanted to swing high. She wanted to slide down fast. Now the park was all wet. Sebastien sat on the rug. He hugged his knees. "I am sad," he said in a small voice.

Ms. Sok clapped her hands. "Let's try something new," she said. She brought out two big blankets. Lucy helped spread one on the top of the chairs. It was soft and warm, like a cloud. Sebastien crawled inside. "This is nice," he said. His mouth turned up in a smile. Lucy saw the blanket make his sad face go away.

Lucy crawled in too. It was cozy and dim inside. Sargun peeked in the door. "Can I come?" he asked. "Yes!" said Lucy. They all sat close together. Ms. Sok gave them a flashlight to make stars on the blanket.

"Rain," said Lucy, looking out the window. "But we are happy now." Sargun laughed and shone a star on her hand.

Brielle sat in the big waiting room. Ollie sat next to her. Both of them were there for a haircut. Brielle wanted her hair short, like Mama's.

"Brielle," called the hairdresser. Brielle climbed into the tall chair. The hairdresser put a big cape around her shoulders. It was blue and smooth.

"Now the little hairs will drop on the cape," the hairdresser said. "Not on your clothes."

Snip, snip, went the scissors. Little hairs dropped down. They sat on the cape. They did not get on Brielle's shirt. She saw it happen. The cape caught every little hair, like a soft net.

"I'm a superhero," Brielle giggled, holding the cape out at the sides.

Ollie laughed from his chair. "Me next," he said.

Charlie wanted to build with his blocks. He dumped them out. Crash! They were so loud. The baby was sleeping in the next room. The baby woke up and began to cry. Dad picked her up. "She was sleeping," Dad whispered. Charlie listened. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice. Could a whisper be strong enough for blocks? Charlie tried it. He whispered, "Block, go on top." The block sat on top. No crying came from the baby. Charlie ripped a piece of paper for a window. Rip, rip. He did it slowly and softly. Soon Dad brought out a toy hammer, small enough for young hands. Charlie tapped it, tap, tap, tap. The baby stayed asleep. Charlie whispered to the baby, "Sleep tight."

Blake was shy at bedtime. She wanted her book, but it was lost. "Let's look," said Dad. They looked in the kitchen. One box, two boxes, three boxes. Blake pointed at the boxes. "Those are words," she said. Dad read one. "Cereal," he said. The picture matched the words. Words on boxes tell us things.

They looked at the door. A little sign sat there. Dad read it out loud. "Wet floor," he said. "The words tell us to be careful." Then they found a bottle marked "soap." The words told them that too.

At last they found Blake's book under a soft feather pillow. Blake opened the front cover. "This way round," she said. She began at the front, and Dad read each page. One page, two pages, three pages. Blake snuggled down. "Words are everywhere," she said. Dad kissed her head and turned out the light.

Gabriella lost her bunny at school. It had one ear that flopped down. She ran to the slide. No bunny. She ran to the swings. No bunny. She ran so fast her hair bounced.

Then she stopped. "I run too fast," she said. "I miss places." So she tried a new way. She picked the little playhouse first. It had a red door. She looked in room one, slow and careful. One, two, three corners checked. No bunny. Rory held her hand at the door. "Take your time," Rory said.

Next she went to the garden by the fence. She bent down low. The sun felt warm on her back. She looked at the big leafy plants, one by one. Under a wooden pot, she saw something soft. It was bunny! "You were hiding," said Gabriella. She hugged bunny tight.

Ms. Çelik clapped her hands. "Well done, Gabriella." Graham came over to see. "Bunny was under the pot," said Gabriella. She sat on the warm step and let bunny's soft ear tickle her nose.

Madelyn sat at home on the big rug. Her mom said, "Time for your doctor visit today." Madelyn did not want to go. "I am not sick," she said. "Why do I need a shot?"

At the office, Madelyn waited on the paper bed. She counted the pictures on the wall. One, two, three. The doctor came in with a small tray. Madelyn looked at her knee. She pulled her sock up tight. Then she let it slip back down, just a little.

The doctor said, "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses." Madelyn thought about that. She was fine now. The shot would help keep her that way.

"Okay," said Madelyn. "I am ready." She held her mom's hand. The doctor tapped her arm. "Look at the ceiling," said the doctor. Madelyn looked up at the light.

Quick! The shot was done. "That was fast," said Madelyn. The doctor put a round bandage on her arm.

Madelyn got a sticker of a yellow duck. On the ride home, she held her arm up to show her mom. "My body is protected now," she said. Then she yawned a big yawn. The shot had made her sleepy. When they got home, she lay down on the rug. Soon her duck sticker went up and down, up and down, as she fell asleep.

Alexander sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "I see a cow!" he said. Dad was driving to the farm shop. "Let's count animals," said Dad. Alexander began. "One cow. One dog. One, two, three."

At the farm shop there was a big round pool. Alexander looked in. Fish swam round and round. He counted them. "One fish. Two fish. Three fish. Four fish."

His friend Elon was there too. Elon pointed at the pool. "Look at the animals," Elon said.

Alexander shook his head. "Fish are not animals," he said. "A cow has legs. A dog has legs. Fish have no legs."

Just then a dog jumped up near the pool. It barked. The fish swam fast to the bottom. The dog barked again. The fish hid under a round rock. Alexander's eyes went wide. "The fish is scared of the dog," he said. "Like animals are!"

Ms. Francis, the shop lady, walked over. "Yes," she said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals."

Alexander counted on his fingers. "One cow. One dog. Four fish. Six animals!" A big clock on the wall went tick, tick. "Time to go," said Dad.

In the car, Alexander looked out the window. "Call out if you see animals," he said to Dad. Dad laughed. "I will."

Then Alexander saw a horse in a field. "Animal!" he called. "That makes seven."

Madison went to the park with her mom. She carried her red ball. Her friend Mohammad was there. He was swinging high. "Watch me!" he called. Madison felt excited.

Then her ball rolled away. It rolled under a big bush. The bush was full of sticks. Madison reached in. "Ouch," she said. "That hurt." She pulled her hand back. Her ball stayed under the bush. The sandbox next to her was empty. Nobody was playing. Madison sat down. She felt sad. Her lip went down, down, down.

Mr. Park the teacher came over. He waited by the swing. He waited by the slide. He waited some more. Then Mom knelt down. "Can you tell me?" she asked. Madison took a breath. "I feel sad," she said. "My ball is under the bush." Mom got a long stick and popped the ball out. A small cat ran out too! It chased the ball all around. Madison laughed and laughed. "I feel happy now," she said, and threw the ball far.

Kai sat in the reading nook by the window. The sun made a warm spot on his leg. He had a long row of letter cards on the floor. He wanted to put them all in order.

Kai got to A, B, C, D. Then he got stuck. Where did M go? He tried M after D. He looked at it. It did not look right.

Then Kai had an idea. He sang the alphabet song, nice and slow. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." The song went on and on. He sang until he met the M. M came after L. Kai put M in its spot. Then N came next, and O after that.

His dad came to the door. "Did the cards give you trouble?"

"A little," said Kai. "The song helped me." He pointed at M. "It goes right there."

He sang the last part softly. "X, Y, Z. Now I know my ABCs." The cards lay in a long, neat line from A to Z. Kai smiled and patted M.

Michael sat in the waiting room. He squeezed his squishy ball. His friend Judah sat next to him. "I don't like shots," said Judah. "Maybe it will be quick," said Michael.

A nurse called them in. The doctor had a tube around her neck. "What is that?" asked Michael. "It's called a stethoscope," said the doctor. She put the little ends in her ears. She put the other end on Michael's chest. Thump, thump. "That is your heart beating," she said. Michael listened. Thump, thump. "I hear it!" he said.

The doctor gave Michael his shot. It was quick, like a little pinch. Michael blew on his arm, just like Mama said. "You were brave," said Judah. Michael smiled and held up his squishy ball. "Want to squeeze it?"

Grayson went to the park with his dad. The sun was warm. It made the ice in his cup melt. Grayson wanted to play in the sand next.

A big kid stood in the way. He stood right on the path. Grayson tried to squeeze past him. He bumped the big kid's arm. "Sorry," said Grayson.

"You can say excuse me," the big kid said. "It works when someone is in your way."

Grayson stood still. He waited for the big kid to look at him. Then Grayson said, "Excuse me, please." The big kid smiled and stepped aside. "Thank you," said Grayson. Now the path was clear.

Grayson ran to the sand. His friend Miles was there. Miles had the only shovel. Grayson wanted a turn. He waited. He watched Miles dig. He waited some more.

Then Miles stood up to get some water. "Excuse me, may I have a turn with the shovel, please?" asked Grayson. "Sure," said Miles. "Thank you," said Grayson.

Grayson dug a big hole. The sand was warm and soft. He filled the hole again. He dug it once more.

A small girl walked by. She wanted to get past Grayson. He was in her way. Grayson stood up and moved aside.

"You can say excuse me," he told her. She smiled big. "Excuse me, please," she said. Then she ran on to the swings, and Grayson sat back down in the sand.
