Raphael looked out the window. Snow was everywhere! No school today. It was a surprise snow day. The sky was big and cloudy.

Dad said, "Let us go to the sledding hill." Raphael put on his boots. But the path was deep in snow. Dad had a big shovel. Raphael had a little shovel. "You can have this job," said Dad. "We shovel the snow off the path. Then people can walk without slipping."

Raphael pushed his little shovel. Push, push, push. The snow made a pile. Then the path showed up! It was clear and brown. Then the mail carrier came walking by. She did not slip at all. "Thank you!" she said. "Nice path!"

Raphael patted the pile of snow. "I made that pile," he said. Then he ran to the hill with Dad. He sled down fast, fast, fast. At the bottom, his boots landed on the snow. He stood right up. He did not slip one bit.

Beau sat in his car seat. Today was shop day. Yesterday they had no milk. Tomorrow the truck would come, but not now. "When will we get there?" Beau asked. "Is it later yet?"

Mom pointed at the clock in the car. "Look at the clock," she said. "A clock shows what time it is." The little hand pointed at a number. Beau watched it. The big hand moved a tiny bit. The clock said now, so it was now, not later.

Beau watched out the window. He saw a red light. The car stopped. Then the light turned green. The car went again. The light made the car stop. Then the light made the car go. Beau clapped his hands.

"Look, Mom! The light tells the cars what to do!"

Mom laughed. "Yes, it does."

Beau looked at the clock again. The big hand had moved more. "Is it later now?" he asked. "It is," said Mom. "And now we are here." The shop doors slid open all by themselves. Beau gasped. Doors that open themselves! "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. Mom smiled and took his hand. "First let's get the milk," she said.

Ethan got to school and hung up his coat. He saw his friend Emmanuelle by the window. She was smiling a big smile. "Look at my teeth," she said. "They are so shiny." Ethan looked. They were shiny and pretty. Emmanuelle said, "I brushed my teeth this morning." Ethan thought about his own morning. He had eaten his cereal fast. Then he had gotten dressed to wear his blue shirt. He had not brushed his teeth.

At school, Ms. Chea said it was time to eat. They ate crackers and apples. Then Ms. Chea said it was rest time. Ethan lay on his mat and closed his eyes. He waited and waited. Then it was time to wake up. Rafael stretched his arms. "I feel good," he said. Ethan yawned. He had wanted to rest, and now he did feel good.

After school, Ethan went home. He ate his dinner. Then he put on his pajamas. Then his dad read him a story. Then Ethan got into bed. He pulled the blanket up. Then he sat up fast. "Wait," he said. "Emmanuelle brushes in the morning. I brush at night too." He hopped out of bed. He went to the sink and picked up his toothbrush. He brushed his teeth. He brushed and brushed. He looked in the little mirror. His teeth were shiny too. He climbed back into bed and smiled. "Good night, teeth," he whispered.

Elizabeth ran to the playground. The sun was hot on her face. Her friend Rupert was already there.

"Look!" said Rupert. He pointed at a big puddle. Next to it was one small puddle. "One big, one small."

Elizabeth stomped in the big puddle. Splash! One splash. She stomped again. Two splashes. She stomped a third time. Three big splashes!

Then she felt it. Her socks were wet. Wet, wet, wet. She sat on the soft grass and pulled off her shoes. The water dripped from her toes.

Mr. Owusu came over with a bag. "Wet and dry are opposites," he said. He gave her dry socks. He hung the wet socks on the fence, one and then the other.

The wind blew. The sun shone. Elizabeth and Rupert watched the fence. Slowly, slowly, the wet socks began to dry.

"Fast, fast!" said Rupert, running in circles around the fence. Elizabeth laughed. Then she walked slow, slow, slow. She brushed the grass with her toes.

Mr. Owusu touched the socks. "All dry!" he said.

Elizabeth put them back on. "Nice and dry," she said, and wiggled her toes.

Matthew sat in his car seat. His furry teddy sat next to him. Mom was driving to the store.

"Mom, can I have some grapes?" asked Matthew.

"Yes," said Mom. "You can have three grapes."

Matthew looked out the window. He counted what he saw. "One red car," he said. "Two big trucks." Then a dog ran by. "Three dogs!" said Matthew.

At the store, Mom picked grapes. Some were small. Some were big. Matthew held up a big grape.

"Mom, is this one grape or more?" he asked.

"It is one grape," said Mom. "Three grapes means three grapes. Big or small, it is still one."

So Matthew counted his grapes. "One, two, three," he said. He put them in a little bag.

In the car, Matthew ate his grapes. He gave one grape to his teddy's mouth, just to play. Then he ate it himself.

"When we get home, I will fix your teddy's arm," said Mom.

"Thank you," said Matthew. "Then we can have soup?"

"Yes," said Mom. "Warm soup in a bowl."

Matthew smiled. He counted his teddy's paws. "One, two, three, four," he said. The car went beep as they backed up.

"Carry the grapes careful," said Matthew. He held the bag with two hands.

"Three grapes for you, and I will have three too," said Mom.

"One, two, three," said Matthew. "One, two, three. Same!"

"Same," said Mom.

Sienna was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big round drum. Sienna picked up the soft drum stick. She hit the drum very hard. BOOM! The sound was very loud.

The baby was sleeping by the window. The loud drum woke the baby up. The baby began to cry. Grandma held the baby close. "Shh, shh," said Grandma. Sienna felt bad. She wanted the baby to sleep.

Sienna looked at the drum. She hit it soft, soft, soft. Tap, tap, tap. The sound was small and quiet now. The baby's crying stopped. The baby closed her eyes. Grandma put a warm blanket over her and began to cover her little toes.

A gray cat came to sit by the drum. Sienna tapped again, gentle and slow. Tap, tap, tap. The baby stayed asleep. Grandma smiled. "Play us a song," she said.

So Sienna played her quiet song, tap, tap, tap, all the way to the end.

The lights went out. It was dark in Claire's house. Claire wanted her juice cup. She ran to the kitchen. Bump! Her leg hit a chair. "Ow," said Claire. Dad came fast with a flashlight. "Let's walk slowly," he said. Claire held Dad's hand. They walked step by step. No bump this time!

Then there was a knock at the door. It was Mr. Dhillon from next door. He held a big lantern. "Our lights are out too," he said. "Come sit on my porch." Claire held Dad's hand all the way next door. They walked slowly in the dark. Nobody tripped.

On the porch, Mr. Dhillon had a bowl of ice. Claire put a little ice on her sore leg. "Thank you," she said to Mr. Dhillon. The stars came out first, one by one. Then, pop! The lights came back on. "Hooray!" said Claire.

Austin looked out the window at the big blue sky. "Time for your first haircut," said Mom. They walked next door to Mr. Ross. Mr. Ross cut hair in a little room in his house.

Austin climbed up into the big chair. But the chair was too big. Austin was too short. Mr. Ross could not reach his hair. "I will get the booster seat," said Mr. Ross. Austin sat on the booster seat. Now he was taller. Now Mr. Ross could reach his hair.

Snip, snip, went the scissors. Mr. Ross held them, and Austin sat very still. Little hairs fell down. They stuck to the cape. The cape had ugly green bugs on it. Austin laughed at the bugs. "Funny bugs," he said. Mom clapped. "You sat so still," she said.

The haircut was done. Austin looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I did it," said Austin. He gave the booster seat a little pat. Mr. Ross smiled and said, "See you next time."

Olivier ran to the sink. Lunch was waiting on the table. He got his hands wet and gave them one quick rinse.

At lunch, Emelia looked at his hands. "I can still see paint on your thumb," she said. Olivier looked down. The blue paint was still there. His quick rinse had not washed it off.

Ms. Rowe came over. She took Olivier back to the sink. "Let's try again," she said. "Soap first." Olivier pushed the soap pump. He rubbed the soap all over. Ms. Rowe said, "Health experts say to scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds." Then she helped him count. "One, two, three..." Olivier watched the bubbles dance between his fingers. They counted slowly. "...nineteen, twenty." He rinsed. The paint was gone. His hands were clean.

After the toilet, Olivier went to the sink all by himself. He made the soap bubbles. He counted to twenty. He even wiggled like a dancing bone was ticking inside him, not a weak little wiggle, a big one.

At the lunch table, Emelia held out her hand. "Clean," she said. Olivier held out his too. "Twenty seconds," he said, and they sat down to eat.

Theodore went to the store with his dad. He hopped out of the car like a bunny. The store smelled like bread and oranges.

At the sample stand, a lady held out little cups. "Would you like a peach slice?" she asked. A girl named Linnea stood there too. She took a slice and put it in her mouth. Then she made a face. "Yuck!" she shouted. Her cheeks went red. The lady looked sad.

Linnea tried again. "No, thank you," she said in a small voice. The lady smiled. "Would you like a cracker instead?" Linnea took the cracker. She ate it all up.

Theodore picked up a peach slice. The peach had fuzzy skin, soft like a furry little cat. He licked it. It tasted strange to him. He did not want more. He remembered Linnea. "No, thank you," he said. The lady gave him a cracker too. It was crunchy and good.

Then the lady laughed and held up a tiny cup. Inside was a sticker shaped like a star. "For two polite shoppers," she said. Linnea put hers on her shirt. Theodore put his on his hand. It sparkled under the store lights.

"Thank you!" said Theodore.

"See you next time," said the lady, and waved her sample spoon like a wand.

The lights went out. Hayden stood in the dark. "I can't see," he said. Mom found her phone. The little light was warm on the wall. But then the phone went dark too, to save its power.

Hayden held Mom's hand. The dark was very big at first. He could not see the sofa. He could not see his toy truck. He waited with Mom on the soft rug. Slowly, the dark began to feel smaller. A little while went by. Then Hayden could see the big shape of the sofa. Next he saw his truck, right by his feet. "Mom! My eyes can see now!" he said. "In the dark, they got used to it. I can see more and more!"

He crawled to the truck and rolled it on the floor. "Vroom," he whispered. The wheels clicked in the quiet room. Outside, a neighbor started a car, and its lights swept across the ceiling. Then the house lights came back on, all at once. Hayden blinked at the bright lamp. He waved at the sofa. "I saw you," he said. "I saw you in the dark."

Ellie went to the store with her dad. She wanted to find a red apple. But first she saw Raegan by the toy shelf. "Look, Ellie!" said Raegan. "I put all the animals here. And all the toys there." There was a lion, a cow and a duck in one pile. There was a ball and a drum in the other pile.

Ellie picked up the ball. She made it bounce. Boing, boing! Then Hayes came by with blocks. Hayes put the big blocks in one row. Then he put the small blocks in a row. Same blocks, but Hayes did not sort by kind. He sorted by size!

"You sorted by size," said Ellie. "Raegan sorted by kind. I can sort another way!" Ellie put the red blocks together. Then she made a pile of blue blocks. Then yellow ones. "Red here, blue there!" she said. "Same blocks, new piles!"

Then Ellie remembered her apple. She ran to the fruit. Red apples sat in one bin. Green apples sat in another bin. The store sorted by color too! Ellie picked a big red apple. "This one!" she said. Her dad laughed and put it in the cart. Ellie waved to Raegan and Hayes. "Bye! I found my apple in the red pile!"

Asher ran to the window. "Look, look!" he said. The sun was out. It was a sunny day at school.

Mr. Fitzgerald clapped his hands. "Time to play outside!" Asher wanted to run right now. He wanted to run so fast. But Mr. Fitzgerald held up a bottle. "Sunscreen first," he said. Asher stood still. Mr. Fitzgerald rubbed it on Asher's arms and face. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," said Mr. Fitzgerald. Then Asher ran out the door.

Riley was already on the slide. Lucca was digging in the sand. Asher felt the warm sun on his arms. His arms felt fine. The sun did not hurt them at all. Riley jumped down. "My turn, my turn!" Asher yelled. He climbed up and slid down fast.

Then the wind came. It was windy now. The wind blew Lucca's hat right off. Lucca laughed and chased it. The hat rolled and rolled. Asher chased it too. The wind pushed the hat to the fence. Lucca picked it up. "Got it!" he said.

Clouds came next. Big gray clouds. The sky turned dark. "Rain!" said Riley. Drops fell on Asher's nose. Mr. Fitzgerald called, "Everyone inside!" The children ran. At the door, Asher looked back. The rain was falling on the slide. It made a beautiful shiny puddle. "We need boots next time," said Riley. Asher nodded fast. "Boots and rain hats!" he said. Mr. Fitzgerald smiled and shut the door.

Parker sat in the waiting room. The chairs were blue and squeaky. He counted them. One, two, three, four. "How many chairs, Mom?" he asked. "Four," said Mom. Parker counted again. One, two, three, four.

A boy named Olivier sat across from him. Olivier held a toy mountain. "I came for a shot," Olivier said. "I sat on my dad's lap." Parker looked at the big door. He was next. His tummy felt tight.

The nurse called, "Parker." The room had a big table. Parker climbed up. The table was cold and too big. He wanted to get down. "Can I sit with you?" he asked Mom. Mom sat on a chair. She held Parker on her lap. Her arms went around him like a hug.

The nurse cleaned his arm. "Look at the ceiling," Mom said. Parker looked up. He saw a sticker of a star. Then it was done. "That was fast!" said Parker. He got a bandage with a dog on it. He walked out tall and proud. At the desk, he did not spill his juice. "Next time," he told Olivier, "sit on a lap. It helps." Olivier smiled and hugged his mountain toy.

Elijah went to Adeline's house. Adeline had a tablet. It sat on the little table. "Want to draw?" she asked. Elijah nodded. But how did it turn on?

Adeline showed him the button. She pushed it. The screen lit up. Elijah's eyes went wide. "It came on!" he said. One little push made the big picture. He pushed the button again. The screen went dark. He pushed once more. Light again. "I did that," said Elijah.

Adeline tapped the drawing app. It opened with a soft sound. Elijah picked blue. He drew a big ball. He drew a dog next to the ball. The dog had long ears. "What if I tap green?" he asked. He tapped green. The line turned green. He smiled.

Then the screen went black. "Oh no!" said Elijah. "My dog is gone!" Adeline called her dad. He looked at the tablet. "It has no power now," he said. "It needs charging." He plugged the charger into the wall. The tablet made a small beep.

"Can it fix itself?" asked Elijah. "It will, while it charges," said the dad. Elijah sat and waited. A little picture of a battery showed up on the screen. "Look, a tiny battery!" said Adeline. Elijah put his hands in his lap and watched. Then the screen came back. His blue ball and his green-eared dog were still there. "It's back!" said Elijah. He drew one more cat. Then he pushed the button and put the tablet on the table. "All done," he said.

Jade ran to the big playground slide. Amar was already there. Amar zoomed down, fast fast fast. Jade went down too, slow slow slow, on her bottom.

"Let's go to the water fountain," said Amar. The sun was hot. The water was cold. Jade drank and drank. A fuzzy caterpillar sat by the fountain. "Hello, little friend," said Jade. It was small, so small. The slide was big, so big.

Jade's grandpa sat on a bench. He had a little red cooler. "Would you like cold juice?" he asked. He opened the cooler. The lid went up, up, up. Jade peeked inside. Then grandpa turned to pour. The lid stayed open. Cold air puffed out onto Jade's arm.

"Grandpa, the lid!" said Jade. She pushed it down. Clack. It was closed. "Open and closed," said grandpa with a smile. "They are opposites." Jade opened it. She closed it. Open. Closed. Then she took her juice and ran fast to the slide, shouting, "Watch me, watch me!"

Parker held his new library card in his hand. The card was blue and had his name on it. He and his dad rode the city bus to the library. Parker sat by the window. He begged his dad, "Can I hold the book too?"

At the library, Mr. Rivera smiled. "This is Parker's first book," said Dad. Parker picked a book about a big red truck. Mr. Rivera scanned the card. The book was Parker's to take home. All summer, Parker read the truck book. He read it at breakfast. He read it in the park. Mom made a tasty snack, and Parker read some more.

One day Paris was at the library. She had a book to bring back. "Where does it go?" asked Parker. "Watch," said Paris. She held her book up to the wall. There was a little slot there. "This is the book return slot," said Paris. "You drop your book in here when you bring it back." She let go. The book fell in. Parker put his ear to the slot. Thunk!

"But what if the book gets lonely?" asked Parker. "Should I say goodbye?" "Yes," said Paris. Parker held up his truck book. He waved at it. "Bye bye, truck book," he said. He dropped it in. Thunk! The slot ate it up. Parker laughed and laughed. Then he ran to find a new one.

Jade ran to the park with her soccer team. The sun was very hot. Mr. Kovalenko blew his whistle. "Break time!" he called.

Jade looked for her water bottle. It was not in her bag. Her tummy felt tight and worried. "I forgot my water," she said. Her friend Dorothy peeked into her own bag. Dorothy had her bottle, but it was almost empty.

Mr. Kovalenko saw Jade's sad face. He walked over with a big bottle. "Players drink water during breaks," he said. "Especially on hot days like this." He poured some water into a little cup. Jade drank it all. The cold water felt good.

The whistle blew again. Jade ran fast. She kicked the ball to Dorothy. Dorothy kicked it in the goal. The whole team cheered. Jade was not angry anymore about the sun. She had water, and she had fun. Her sister waved from the blanket by the tree. "Big kick!" her sister shouted. Jade laughed and waved back.

Madeline sat at the table. She had a loose tooth? No, she had an apple. Today she went to the dentist. The dentist looked in her mouth.

"Say ahh," said the dentist. Madeline said ahh. The dentist looked at her front teeth. Then he looked at her back teeth.

Madeline went home with her mom. On the bus, she sat by the window. A big red truck went by. Madeline watched it. Then she took out her apple slices.

She bit one slice. Her front teeth cut it. Snip! Now the piece was small. But it was still too big to swallow. What could she do?

She moved the piece to the back of her mouth. She chomped it. Chomp, chomp, chomp! The piece got small and soft. Then she could swallow it.

Madeline tried another slice. Front teeth first. Then back teeth. "Mom, look!" she said. "Front teeth bite. Back teeth chew!"

Mom smiled. "That's right," she said. Madeline ate all her apple slices. She was not alone. Mom was right there beside her.

At home, Madeline showed her stuffed bear. "Watch, Bear," she said. She bit a soft banana piece. Then she chomped it with her back teeth. "Now you try," she told Bear. Bear just smiled his bear smile.

Georgia was going to the dentist. It would be her very first time. First she went to the pharmacy with her dad. They walked down a sunny aisle. The toothbrushes were on a low shelf.

Georgia picked up a toothbrush. It was green. It had a rabbit on it. Then she saw Saanjh from her class. Saanjh held a blue toothbrush. "That one is mine," said Saanjh. "My very own. My dad has his own too." Georgia looked at her green one. This one was her very own. Nobody else would use it.

At home, Georgia put her toothbrush in a small cup. Her dad put his in another cup. In the morning, Georgia brushed her teeth. Then she drew a picture with her crayons. She drew the green toothbrush. She drew the rabbit too.

The surprise came at the dentist. The chair went up and down, like a ride. The dentist gave Georgia a tiny mirror. "Look at your teeth," she said. Georgia looked. Her teeth were small and shiny, like little white rocks. "They can be happy teeth," said the dentist, "because you have your own toothbrush." Georgia smiled all the way home.

Lydia sat at the kitchen table. She wanted to make a house for her toy monkey. The door of the house had to stay open, so the monkey could walk in.

She found blocks. A circle block was round like a plate. A triangle block had three pointy corners. A rectangle block was long like a door.

Then Lydia found a square block. She set it down with a corner pointing up. "Is this a new shape?" she asked. She looked at it. It looked like a diamond.

Lydia turned the block back. The flat side sat down. "It is the same square," she said. "A square turned so a corner points up is still a square."

She turned it again and again. Square, diamond, square, diamond. She laughed.

Then Lydia built the house. She used the square for the window. She used the rectangle for the door. She propped the door open with the triangle.

The monkey got tired and had to freeze for a nap. Lydia laid him down inside.

"Wake up, monkey," she whispered. "Your house is ready."

Kayden went to the store with his dad. He wanted new socks. He saw socks with a star on them. "I want blue," said Kayden. The sock bin sat in a very dark corner. The light there was off. Kayden dug in the bin. He held up two socks. He could not tell what color they were. The dark made it hard. "I can't see," he said. Mr. Farah-Ali worked at the store. He turned on the light. The corner got bright. Now Kayden could see! One sock was red. One sock was green. Not blue at all. Kayden laughed. He dug again. He found two blue socks with a star. He put the red one and the green one back. All the picking made Kayden thirsty. Dad bought him a little juice. "We can leave now," said Dad. Kayden held his blue socks all the way home. "Star socks," he said.

Lydia did not want to open her mouth at the doctor's office. She wanted to hide. So she covered her eyes with her hands. "Now nobody can see me," she said.

Ms. Levy, the nurse, was still there. "I can see your shoes," she said. Lydia peeked with one eye. Ms. Levy smiled. When your eyes are closed, you cannot see the things around you. Lydia tried it again. She shut her eyes tight. She heard the paper on the bed crinkle. She heard her mom say, "It is okay, Lydia."

Lydia listened some more. She smelled something like soap. She touched the paper bed with her fingers. It felt bumpy. Then she opened her eyes. She could see Ms. Levy again.

"Can you say sorry to my tongue?" Lydia asked. "It does not like popsicle sticks." Ms. Levy laughed. She let Lydia taste a sweet drop first. Then Lydia opened her mouth wide. "You pay attention with your ears and nose and fingers too," said Lydia. "I was still listening the whole time."

Ms. Levy gave her a sticker. Lydia put it on her hand. "I can see it," she said. "My eyes are open now."

Avery went to Grandma's big house for lunch. There were cousins everywhere. There was Elliot, and there was Harmony, too. Avery counted the plates. One, two, three, four, five, six!

The food sat on the table. Avery wanted to eat the crunchy bread right away. She pulled her chair close. She reached out her hand. Then everyone held hands and got quiet. Avery was confused. Why was nobody eating?

"Would you like to say grace?" Grandma asked. "It is a short prayer of thanks before meals." Avery nodded. She squeezed Elliot's hand on one side. She squeezed Harmony's hand on the other side. "Thank you for the bread," she said. "Thank you for my cousins. One, two, three, four, five, six!"

Then Grandma laughed, and everyone said amen. The bread was still warm. The outside crunched when Avery bit it. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma smiled and passed her the butter.

Maya went to Mama's office. Mama had a big desk. On the desk was a tablet. Maya wanted to draw a cat on it.

Mama said, "You tap the screen with your finger to choose things." Maya pushed her whole hand on the screen. She pressed and pressed. The screen stayed dark. Nothing happened at all.

"Tap it," said Mama. "Like a little bite, but soft." Maya held up one finger. Tap. The screen lit up! Tap. A square opened. It was the drawing app. Maya drew a cat. The cat had funny ears. "That is one ugly cat," Mama laughed. "Ugly and sweet," said Maya. She drew a big smile on it.

Then Maya was done. She put the tablet down on the desk. She slid it into its case, all by herself. Tap, tap, tap, she said to her finger. "You are a good little tapper."

Gianna could not find her bunny. She looked under her bed. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

"Where can bunny be?" she asked.

"Maybe you left him on the bus," said her dad. "The driver found a toy today. It had a name tag on it. The tag said Gianna. So he knew it was yours."

Gianna opened the door. The bus stopped outside. The driver held out her bunny. On his ear was a little tag. It said Gianna in big letters.

"Your name helped me," said the driver. The door closed with a ring.

Gianna hugged her bunny tight. "I felt sick without you," she whispered.

At supper, her dad told a joke about a bunny who rode the bus. Gianna laughed and laughed. She held the soft tag in her fingers all through dinner. Then she drew a name tag for her teddy bear too.

Zoe sat on the playroom rug. She had all the blocks in one big pile. Lawson sat beside her with nothing.

"Can I have some blocks?" Lawson asked. Zoe hugged the pile close. "They are mine," she said. Lawson's face went sad. He looked at the empty floor.

Dakota was building a black snake across the rug. She had some blocks, and Lawson had some too. Her snake got long and long.

Zoe looked at her pile. She looked at Lawson's empty hands. She pushed half the blocks to him. Lawson smiled big. He built a tower. Zoe built a tower too. Then they made one long snake together, longer than Dakota's.

Ms. McKenzie shut the door softly. "Time to tidy up," she said. Zoe and Lawson put the blocks in the basket, one each, all fair.

The wind howled outside the apartment. The big tree by the window began to swing its branches. Then, click, all the lights went out.

"Strong wind can knock out the power," said Dad. He lit a little lantern. "So we wait." Wren held her toy bunny tight. She could not watch her show. She could not have warm toast. The room felt dark and quiet.

Wren listened to the wind. It howled and howled. Then it grew soft. It grew still. Click, the lights came back on. Wren clapped her hands. The lamp glowed again. "The wind stopped," she said. Dad smiled and got out the bread. Wren watched from her chair as he made warm toast. It was a pretty golden color. She took a big bite and said, "Hello again, lights."

Clara went to the store with her dad. She saw a big fox toy on the shelf. It was orange and soft. "Can I hold it?" she asked. "Say please," said Dad. "Please," said Clara. The cashier smiled and gave her the fox.

Then Clara saw her friend Akram. He hid behind his mom. Clara waved. "Hello, Akram!" she said. Akram peeked out. "Hello, Clara," he said. Then he smiled. Why did he smile now? Clara wondered. She said hello again, and he waved back.

Clara spun around with the fox. She spun too fast. She felt dizzy and sat down on the floor. "Oops, sorry," she said to a lady's foot. "Are you okay?" the lady asked. "Can you help me up, please?" said Clara. The lady helped her up. Clara held her fox tight. "Thank you," she said.

Jasmine sat in her car seat. She held five toy monkeys. "One, two, three, four, five," she counted. The monkeys were going to jump on a bed, just like her song.

Jasmine sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one fell off and bumped his head. She dropped one monkey on the seat. Now she counted again. "One, two, three, four." There were four now! She asked her dad, "Where did the fifth monkey go?" He said, "He fell off, so now you have one less."

Jasmine sang the next verse. One monkey fell off again. She counted the ones in her hands. "One, two, three." The lazy monkeys could not hang on to the bed at all. Each time she sang, one more fell. Then there was only one. Then there were none. Her tummy made a little growl. "Dinner soon," said Dad.

At the next red light, Dad picked up the fallen monkeys. He handed them back one at a time. "One, two, three, four, five," Jasmine counted. All five monkeys sat on her lap again. "Let's sing one more time," she said, and she held on tight.

Paisley sat at the dinner table. She had a big story about her day. Her friend Heath sat next to her. Their teacher, Mr. Morales, sat across from them.

Mr. Morales started to talk. He said the soup was hot. He said to wait and blow on it. Paisley wanted to talk right now. "I saw a dog!" she said, very loud.

Mr. Morales stopped talking. He looked at Paisley. "Someone else is talking," he said kindly. "We listen and wait until they finish." Paisley closed her mouth. She put her hands in her lap. She waited. It was hard to wait. But she did it.

Mr. Morales finished talking. Then he smiled at Paisley. "Now it is your turn," he said. Paisley told her dog story. Heath listened with his ears open. Mr. Morales listened too. Nobody talked over her.

Heath shared his bread with Paisley. She took one piece and gave one back. The soup was ready to eat now, nice and warm. Paisley helped wipe the table with a towel after dinner. "Good waiting," said Mr. Morales. Paisley smiled big.

Violet was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big rug with red blocks on it.

"Let's put the blocks in piles," said Grandma. "All the red ones go together."

Violet made a red pile. She made a blue pile. She made a yellow pile.

Grandma said, "Look, a boy in your picture book sorts his cars that way too."

Then Violet saw it. One yellow block was hiding in the red pile. She picked it up. She put it in the yellow pile. Now all the yellow blocks sat together.

A knock came at the door. Malia stood there with her grandma. "Can I play?" Malia asked.

"Yes!" said Violet.

Malia found a green block under the thick blue blanket. "Where does this go?" she asked.

"We need a green pile," said Violet.

Malia clapped her hands. The two girls pushed the piles apart and made a new spot. Green blocks went in the green spot.

"Time for a snack," said Grandma. She gave them apple slices on a red plate.

Violet looked at the plate. "Red like the red pile," she said. She smiled and took a big bite.

Quinn is at the campsite with her family. She wants to help make pancakes. Her dad says, "Yes! You can measure." Quinn holds the big bag of sugar. She tips it over the bowl. Whoosh! Too much sugar pours out. The bowl is full of white. "Oh no," says Quinn. Her dad smiles. "Try this. It is a measuring cup. It helps us put in the right amount." Quinn scoops the sugar with the cup. She fills it up. She pours it into the bowl. Just right! Then she uses a little measuring spoon for the salt. One small spoonful. Not too much, not too little. The spoon feels cool in her hand. The sugar smells sweet.

The pancakes go on the hot grill. Dad watches them. Quinn stands back where it is safe. The pancakes bubble and flip. They smell warm and buttery. Soon everyone eats by the tent. Quinn snuggles in a cozy blanket. Her mom wiggles an ear at her like a bunny. Quinn giggles. "These are the best pancakes," says Mom. "Quinn measured them just right." Quinn takes one more big bite. Then she yawns a sleepy yawn. "More pancakes tomorrow," she whispers.

Lennon stood in the garage with her dad. A radio sat on the workbench. Cassian was there too, tapping his shoes on the floor.

"Let's sing Twinkle, Twinkle," said Cassian. Lennon knew the first line. She sang it out loud. Then she stopped. "I don't know the next part," she said.

Ms. Fraser lived next door. She came in with a box of tools. "Sing it again," she said kindly. So they sang it again. Lennon forgot the same spot. They played the song and sang it again and again. Then again. Each time, more words came out of her mouth. After many times, the second line popped right out. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are!" Lennon sang it all alone. Cassian clapped.

The radio played a steady beat. Lennon clapped her hands on every beat. Clap, clap, clap. The claps went with the song. The cat lay asleep on a shelf of dirt-covered pots. She clapped so well that the cat woke up and blinked at her. "One more time!" said Cassian. Lennon took a big breath and sang the whole rhyme from the top.

Elias stood at the front door. He looked outside. The sky was dark. The wind blew the big tree. "Windy," said Elias. He put on his red boots. He wanted to go to the playground with Mika.

Then he heard it. Rumble, rumble. Thunder! "Thunder," said his mom. "When you hear thunder, go indoors." Elias looked at the rain. Drip, drip, drip. The rain got big. He did not go out.

He counted the thunder sounds. One rumble. Two rumbles. Three rumbles. Each one was far away. Then it got quiet. The rain stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny now.

"Playground!" said Elias. Mom held his hand. Mika was already at the swing. Elias ran to her and laughed. "Sun again," he said.

Hudson sat at the little table. It was paint time at school. He wanted to paint a sunny day.

He picked the gray paint. He started to paint the sky. Then he looked out the window. The sun was big and bright. The day was clear. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue.

Hudson put down the gray brush. He found the blue paint. He painted the sky blue. It looked just like the window sky.

"Nice sky," said Harvey. Harvey was painting a red apple next to him.

"Thank you," said Hudson. "It is blue, like the real sky."

Otto was painting green grass. His green was all done. He wanted blue next. But the blue was far away on the shelf. Otto could not reach it.

Hudson saw Otto stretch and stretch. Hudson got up. He walked to the shelf. He took the blue paint with both hands. He carried it back slow and careful.

"Here you go," said Hudson.

"Thank you," said Otto. Otto painted blue water under his green grass.

Mr. Wardak came to look. He held up all three paintings. The red apple, the blue water, the green grass.

"Beautiful colors," said Mr. Wardak. He hung them by the sunny window.

Hudson looked at his painting. He looked at the sky. Both were blue, blue, blue.

Stella stood by the fence at school. Miles had a big red kite. The wind pulled it up high. Stella wanted to hold it so much. Her hands reached out. Miles pulled the kite away. "Don't grab," said Ms. Wanjiru. She knelt down by Stella. "Try saying May I," said Ms. Wanjiru. Stella looked at the kite. Then she looked at Miles. "May I have a turn?" she asked. Miles smiled. "Yes! Hold on tight." He put the string in her hand. The kite jumped and pulled. Stella laughed. The wind was strong, almost stormy. Then the string slipped. "Help!" said Stella. Ms. Wanjiru caught the string fast. "Thank you," said Stella. "Sorry I let go," said Miles. "It was my turn to hold it." "That's okay," said Stella. "May I try again?" "You may," said Miles. The kite flew up, up, up. Stella held on tight and watched it dance.

Leo sat in the family car. His toes wiggled in his sandals. "Are we there yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. The car made a soft noise on the road. Leo held his little red bucket. He was going to the beach for the first time.

The car stopped at last. Leo saw sand. He saw blue water. Big waves went splash, splash. Leo ran to the water. He wanted to jump in the waves right away. But Mom held his hand. "Wait," she said. "At the beach, you go near the water only with a grown-up watching."

Leo waited on the warm sand. He filled his bucket with sand. He patted it flat. He waited some more. Then Dad took off his shoes. "Now I am coming with you," Dad said. Dad held Leo's hand. They walked down to the water together.

The waves tickled Leo's feet. He laughed and splashed. Dad stood right beside him, watching. "This is so much fun!" said Leo. The water went whoosh over his toes. Dad smiled and squeezed his hand. "Splash again," said Dad. Leo splashed one more big splash.

Rehmat sat at Grandma's big table. Grandma put a pencil by her hand. "Today you will write your name," said Grandma. Rehmat wanted to write it so much. Ayat could already write her own name.

Rehmat picked up the pencil. She held it in her fist. The letters came out wobbly and fat. "Try holding it like this," said Grandma. Grandma showed her two fingers and a thumb. Rehmat tried it. Her R came out clear! Then her E came out clear too. One letter, then the next.

Rehmat jumped up to run and show Grandma. She waved the pencil as she went. The point faced up, near her eye. "Stop, hold the point down," said Grandma. "A pencil must point down so it cannot poke anyone." Rehmat turned the point down. She walked the rest of the way. Grandma clapped and gave her a huge glass of juice. "Rehmat," Grandma read, smiling. "You wrote it yourself."

Luna was in the garage with her dad. It was cold. She wanted to wear her red coat.

She put one arm in one sleeve. Then she looked for the other sleeve. It hid behind her back. She turned around and around. She could not find it. The sleeve would not go on.

Her friend Ari came in. "Watch me," Ari said. Ari laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. Then he flipped the coat over his head. The coat was on!

Luna laid her coat on the floor too. She put her arms in. She flipped it over her head. The coat fell right on her! "My turn worked," she said.

The zipper was hard. It got stuck. Ari said, "Hold the bottom, like this." Luna held the bottom. She pulled the zipper up. It went up and up. Zzzzip! It was all the way to the top.

Luna brushed her sleeves with her hands. "Warm now," she said. Dad smiled. "Let's go play outside," he said.

"Last one out is a wet sock," said Ari. Luna ran for the door.

Emile was in the big bathroom with his dad. The room had white tiles and a round tub. One tile had a star shape on it. Emile liked that tile best.

Dad turned the tap. Steam went up, up, up. "Hot," said Dad. He turned the other tap. The water got cool. Emile put one finger in. "Cold!" he said. Dad smiled. "I do the hot water," said Dad. Emile watched from his spot by the star tile.

Dad had to get a towel. "Stay where I can see you," said Dad. Emile waited. He counted the taps. One tap. Two taps. He looked for the star tile. One star. He waited some more. It was nice and quiet.

Then Emile saw the little cabinet. It was shut. He reached up to open it. Dad came back fast. "No, no," said Dad. "That cabinet has things that can hurt." Dad held Emile's hand instead. Emile looked out the small window. "Snowy," he said. The trees were all white. Dad laughed. "Yes, snowy outside." The tub was ready now. Emile took off his socks. One sock. Two socks. He stepped in the cool-warm water. "Splash," said Emile.

Grandpa had a big guitar. He sat by the window at his house. "Time for a song," he said. Andrew jumped up and down. He could not wait.

Grandpa began to play. He sang about a little rabbit. One, two, three, four. The song had a steady beat. Andrew tried to clap along. He clapped too fast. Then he clapped too slow. "Listen with your ears," said Grandpa. Andrew listened. He clapped one, two, three, four. Now his claps matched the song!

Then Grandpa played a slow, quiet song. Andrew clapped right away. Grandpa shook his head and smiled. He held up one hand. "Wait," he said. "At a concert, people clap when the music is over, to show they liked it." Andrew put his hands in his lap. He waited and waited. The song got quiet. Then it stopped. Grandpa took a bow. Now Andrew clapped and clapped! He clapped so hard his hands felt warm, almost like they would burn.

"One more song," said Grandpa. He played the rabbit song again. Andrew sang the words all by himself. He remembered every one. One, two, three, four. His claps were not too fast and not too slow. At the end, the music stopped. Andrew counted to one in his head. Then he clapped loud and long.

Grandpa laughed. He pointed at the flat cushion on the chair. "Come sit," he said. "You can pick the next song."

Ella ran to the festival table. There were rice cakes and fruit and warm soup. Her tummy made a big growl. She picked up a rice cake fast.

Then Ella looked around. Nobody was eating. Ms. Suryanto had her hands folded. Kacey had her hands folded too. Ernest was waiting with a big smile.

"Everyone says thank you first," said Kacey. "Then we eat."

Ella put her rice cake down. She folded her hands too. Ms. Suryanto said the blessing out loud. Everyone said thank you for the food.

"Now we eat!" said Ernest.

Ella took a big bite. The rice cake was yummy. She clapped her hands.

"Can we do it again?" Ella asked.

"After the soup," said Ms. Suryanto. "We say it before every meal."

"Every meal!" said Ella. "Even snack time?"

"Even snack time," said Ms. Suryanto.

Ella giggled and grabbed her spoon.

Matthew was at Grandma's house. Today he was three. There was cake and singing. Grandpa gave him a red balloon. Grandpa blew it up with lots of breath. He tied a knot in it.

Matthew held the string tight. He wanted to see it fly. He let go of the string. He looked up at the ceiling. But the balloon did not go up. It came down, down, down. It landed soft on the floor.

Matthew picked it up. He tried again near the big chair. He let go. The balloon went down again. It did not float up to the ceiling. He laughed and ran to catch it.

His friend Brantley came to the party. Matthew showed him the red balloon. "Watch this," said Matthew. He tossed it high. It came drifting down. Brantley caught it in both hands.

They played balloon catch all afternoon. The balloon bobbed and fell, bobbed and fell. At last Matthew held it close. "You are my birthday balloon," he said. "You stay with me."

Hayden woke up in his bed. He hugged his pillow and looked at the window. The sky was black outside. It was still night. Yesterday he had eaten a blue muffin. Today he wanted to bake more muffins. He wanted them now.

He found Dad in the kitchen. "Can we bake muffins now?" asked Hayden. Dad said, "Later, Hayden. First I have to clean up." Hayden frowned. "Later means some time after now, not right away," said Dad. Hayden sat down on the black chair to wait. He counted the spoons in the drawer. One, two, three, four. Then he counted the cups. One, two, three, four.

"Is it later yet?" asked Hayden. "Not yet," said Dad, wiping the table. "Is it later yet?" asked Hayden again. "Not yet," said Dad, washing the bowl. Hayden held his pillow on his lap. He waited some more.

At last Dad said, "Now it is later! We can bake." Hayden jumped up. Dad cracked the eggs, because eggs can be tricky. Hayden poured in the flour. He stirred and stirred. He put the bowl in the sink when they were done. Dad put the pan in the hot oven, and Hayden stood back, far from the heat.

They waited for the muffins to bake. "Is it later yet?" Hayden asked one more time. Dad laughed. "Yes! It is later now." He opened the oven with his big glove. The muffins were golden on top. Hayden ate one warm muffin. "Tomorrow," he said, "we can bake again." Dad kissed his head. "Yes. Tomorrow."

Bennett ran to the playground. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He wore a t-shirt and shorts. His friend Reina was there in a sun hat.

Then the wind blew. It was a windy day now. Leaves flew straight across the grass. Bennett's hat flew off. He ran to reach it. "Got it!" he said.

Big gray clouds came. Drip, drop. It was a rainy day. Rain fell on Bennett's arms. His shirt got wet. His hair got wet. Reina had on a raincoat. She was dry under it. "My raincoat keeps me dry," she said.

Bennett ran home. "My raincoat, please!" he said. His dad helped him zip it up. Then Bennett ran back. The rain fell and fell. Bennett stayed dry inside his coat.

Then the rain stopped. Something white fell from the sky. "Snow!" said Bennett. Reina laughed. "Snowy days need mittens." Bennett held out his hands. A tiny snowflake landed on his mitten and did not melt.

"Let's wait for more snow," said Reina. They sat on the bench. They waited and waited. Then one big snowflake landed right on Bennett's nose. "Hello, snowflake," he said.

Adam stood by the little pool at the lake. The water looked big and shiny. His tummy felt funny. "I want to swim," he said, "but I am scared." Mr. Friedman smiled. "I will hold you," he said. "One hand, two hands. You are safe."

Adam saw Thatcher run toward the pool. "Walk, please," said Mr. Friedman. "The floor is wet and slippery." Thatcher slowed down. Adam looked down. One wet floor. Two wet feet. Slip, slip, like ice. So Adam walked too. Slow steps, slow steps, all the way to the edge.

A green turtle sat on a rock by the lake. It slid into the water and began to swim. "Look," said Adam. "The turtle swims. Now me." Mr. Friedman held his hands. Adam kicked his legs. One kick, two kicks. The water held him up. "Nice swim, Adam," said Thatcher from the side. Adam laughed and splashed his feet.

Mateo got a small violin. It was his first day in the music classroom. He held it up high. He held it upside down. He plucked the strings, but the sound was funny. "That sounds like a sad snake," said Savanna. Hamza laughed kindly. "It goes hiss, hiss, hiss."

Mateo felt worried. "My violin is broken," he said. Ms. Ngo knelt down next to him. "It is not broken," she said. "Let me show you how to hold it." She turned the violin around, slow and gentle. She put it on Mateo's shoulder. She helped his hand hold the long, smooth stick.

"Now pluck," said Ms. Ngo. Mateo plucked one string. Pling! It sang out clear and sweet. He plucked again. Pling, pling! Savanna clapped. Hamza clapped.

"I can do it!" said Mateo. He played one note, then two notes, then three. Ms. Ngo sat close by and smiled. "Play us a song," she said. Mateo lifted his bow, took a big breath, and began to play.

Victor plays on a soccer team. Today the team plays at the big park. Victor runs and kicks the ball. His friend Gordon kicks it too.

The other team scores more goals. Victor's team loses. Victor sits down on the grass. A little dog comes near. The dog gives Victor a lick on his hand. It tickles. Victor laughs a little, but he is still grumpy.

"Where is everyone going?" Victor asks. Ms. Ndlovu points to the line. "They line up after the game," she says. "Each player says good game to the other team." Victor looks. His friend Sophia is already in the line. She says, "Good game," to a boy on the other team. The boy smiles and says it back.

Victor stands up. He brushes the grass off his bottom. He waits in the line. It is slow, but he waits. Then it is his turn. "Good game," says Victor. The other boy says, "Good game," too. He holds out his hand. Victor shakes it. Now Victor feels like running again. "Want to play more?" asks Sophia. "Yes!" says Victor. They run to the ball together.

Jordan went to the store with his dad. He saw a big table full of crayons. Jordan wanted the blue one. It was for his picture of the sky.

He picked up a crayon. It looked almost black. "Is this blue?" he asked. His friend Monroe was there too. Monroe shook his head. "That is not blue," said Monroe.

A shy girl stood near the table. She held a pale crayon. "Light blue," she said softly. Then she put her crayon next to Jordan's. Jordan put his dark one next to hers. They lined up more crayons. Light blue, then blue, then dark blue. "Both are still called blue," said Monroe's mom.

Jordan clapped his hands. He picked the dark blue one. At home, he drew the night sky, dark blue and full of stars.

Samuel went to the farmers' market with his dad. There was a small table with bread and milk. Mr. Tan was at the table. He gave Samuel a slice of warm toast. Samuel wanted to butter it all by himself.

He held the knife gently. Dad watched and helped hold the plate. Samuel spread the butter. It went on slow and bumpy. Then he poured milk into his cup. Some milk spilled out. A little puddle sat on the table. Samuel felt sad. "I spilled it," he said. Then he saw a cloth on the table. He picked it up and wiped the milk. The puddle went away. The table was dry. He had fixed it himself.

Mr. Tan smiled. "You wiped it up," he said. Samuel took a big drink of milk. He took a bite of toast. It was good. He put on his hat and waved goodbye. "Bye, Mr. Tan!"

Gianna sat in the reading corner. She held a big book about an owl. "I love this owl," she said. "Can I keep it?"

Sage shook his head. "The book lives here," he said.

Ms. Nolan came over. "Guess what, Gianna," she said. "Today you get your own library card."

"What does it do?" Gianna asked.

Ms. Nolan smiled. "Watch."

Gianna slid the card across the desk. The librarian scanned the owl book. Then she put it in a bag. "You can take it home to read," she said.

Gianna's eyes got big. "Home? The owl comes home with me?"

"Home with you," said Abigael, clapping.

Gianna hugged the bag. "My card, my book, my home," she said.

She waved to the owl book. "See you soon, library."

Ms. Nolan laughed. "See you soon, Gianna."

Gianna held the bag tight all the way home.

Margot wanted to cook dinner. "I will make soup!" she said. Her dad said, "Yes! We can shop for carrots first." At the market, they found big carrots with green tops. But the carrots were dirty. Dirt was stuck all over them. "Yuck," said Margot. "Can we eat dirt?" "No," said Dad. "Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables like carrots and potatoes before cooking them."

At home, Margot ran to the sink. She held a carrot under the water. She scrubbed it with her fingers. The water turned brown. The dirt washed away! Now the carrot was clean and orange and shiny. Margot laughed. "The water is doing the work!" She scrubbed every carrot, one by one. Then she scrubbed a potato too. It went from dull to bright.

Dad cut the carrots into thin pieces with a knife. Margot watched from far away. Dad put the pot on the stove. The soup bubbled and smelled sweet. Sahib and May came over to eat. "Mmm!" said May. "This soup is so good!" Margot grinned big. "I rinsed the carrots myself. Clean carrots, yummy soup!" Dad gave her a high five.

Alexander wanted to fill his cup at the sink. First he held up the cup. It was empty. Nothing was inside at all. "Watch me make it full," he said to Josie.

He turned the tap on fast. Water rushed in. It climbed up and up. "Stop, stop!" laughed Josie. Alexander turned the tap off quick. One drop ran over the side and down his hand. The drop was cold. He dried his hand on a small black towel.

"Now it is full," said Josie. "Full to the top." Alexander looked inside. The cup was full now, not empty. He drank some slow. Then he poured the rest into the big pot for the pasta. "Fast water makes a mess," he said. "Next time I will pour slow." Josie patted the cup with the string on her bracelet and said, "Told you so."

Noah sat in his reading nook with a pile of letter cards. He wanted to find the letter S. He looked and looked. He saw A. He saw B. He saw M. No S yet.

Then he found it. "S!" he said. "S says sss." His mom smiled. "Can you find things that go sss?" she asked. Noah wanted the answer. He began to hunt.

He looked at the window. "Sun!" he said. "Sun starts with sss." He picked up his sock. "Sock! Sss!" He touched the little bag of sand by his toy truck. "Sand! Sss too!" He clapped his hands. Three sss things!

He tried more toys. "Ball. No, that is B." He put the ball down. That was okay. Trying was fun. He hunted again. "Snake! Sss!" The snake toy hissed in his hand. Noah laughed.

His mom gave him a big hug. "You found so many S things," she said. Noah lined up his cards and his sun, his sock, and his sand. "S, sss, S, sss," he said. Then he whispered it one more time, soft like the sand.

Maeva sat in the reading corner. She hugged her new book about a furry dog. "Mine forever," she said.

Westley looked over. "That book goes back," he said. "Ms. Koné stamped it. It has a due date."

"What is a due date?" asked Maeva.

"The day the book must come back," said Marissa. "So other kids can read it too."

Maeva licked her finger and turned a page. The dog in the story licked a bowl. Maeva giggled.

Then she turned to the back of the book. There was a little pocket. Inside was a white card. Her name was on it! And a stamp with the date.

"I have an idea," said Maeva. "I will read it fast. Every day. Then it can go back happy."

She put the book in her bag. Ms. Koné smiled and gave her a small card with a bear on it. "Your very own library card," said Ms. Koné.

Maeva held it up high. "Now I can take all the books!" she said.

Arlo ran to the sand. The beach was bright and warm. Ms. Nikolaidis called, "Come play a senses game!"

"I know my senses!" said Arlo. "Eyes see. Ears hear. Hands touch." He touched the warm sand. "See? Touch!"

Mika held up a tiny shell. "You forgot one!" she said. "Noses smell!"

Just then, Bryan pinched his nose shut. He sniffed and sniffed. "I can't smell anything!" he said. He let go of his nose. He sniffed the shell. "Now I smell it!"

Arlo wanted to try too. He pinched his nose shut. He sniffed a sandwich. No smell at all! He let go. Sniff, sniff. "I smell the sandwich now!"

"So noses smell," said Arlo. "But only open noses!"

"One sense left," said Ms. Nikolaidis. "Tongues taste!" They all ate a cold, sweet orange slice. Arlo tasted it with his tongue. "Yum!" he said.

Then Arlo heard a loud cry. "Seagull!" he said. "My ears hear it!" The seagull flew down near a nest in the dune.

Arlo laughed and clapped. "Five senses! Eyes, ears, hands, nose and tongue!" He pinched his nose one more time and giggled. "No smell again!" Then he let go and shouted, "Hello, beach smell!"

Sara had a new baby brother. He was small and warm. He made tiny sounds.

Sara sat next to him. She held her cracker up. "Do you want some?" she asked. The baby did not take it. His little mouth turned away.

"Why won't he eat it?" Sara asked. Her mom smiled. "Babies drink milk or formula," Mom said. "Not regular food."

Sara watched Mom feed the baby. The baby drank and drank. His eyes closed. His tummy went up and down. "Milk makes him sleepy," Sara said.

Then the baby grabbed Sara's finger. His hand held on tight. He was stuck to her finger like a little spider on a web! Sara laughed.

"Can I do that again?" Sara asked. "Yes," said Mom. So Sara gave her finger back. The baby held on one more time.

Madison went to the vet with her dad. They were picking up her first pet. A small brown puppy waited in a crate. His tail went wag, wag, wag. His crate had one green leaf stuck on top. Madison brushed it off.

On the way home, Madison had a chocolate bar in her pocket. She peeled the wrapper. The puppy sniffed the air. He wanted some. Madison held out a piece.

Her dad stopped her fast. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick," he said. "Dogs are never given chocolate."

Madison looked at her piece. She put it away. "Then what can he have?" she asked.

"Dogs get dog treats," said her dad. He opened a bag of little bone treats. Madison gave one to the puppy. Crunch, crunch, crunch. The puppy licked her hand.

Madison smiled. The puppy looked up at her. "We will fix your dinner when we get home," she told him. "And I will keep my chocolate all for me."

Aubrey and Danilo found a little house in the forest. It was made of sticks and moss. "Let's play house," said Aubrey. Danilo was the dad. Aubrey was the mom. A pinecone was the baby. They gave the baby a bath in a deep leaf bowl. Splash, splash! The baby laughed and laughed.

Then it was time for lunch. They stirred acorn soup in a tiny pot. The pinecone baby ate two berries. "Yum," said Danilo. The sun went down low behind the trees. "Time to go home," called Mr. Choi from the path.

Aubrey looked at the little house. The pots were everywhere. The leaf bowl was tipped over. Mr. Choi said, "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." So Aubrey and Danilo put the pinecone in its moss bed. They set the pots by the wall. The little house looked tidy and cozy. "Good night, baby," whispered Aubrey. She waved to the little house and skipped down the path.

Mateo stood in the bookshop with his dad. He looked at a big book of letters. The first page had a red A. "A says ah," said Mateo. He turned the page. There was a B. "B says buh," said Mateo. His heart felt happy.

Then Mateo saw his friend Penny. Penny was writing on paper at the little table. She wrote "penny" with a small p. She frowned at it. Mr. Gagnon, the shopkeeper, came over. He smiled. "Try a big P," he said. Penny made the P tall and big. Now her name looked right. Mateo watched with wide eyes. Why did the big P matter so much?

Mateo took the pencil. He wrote "mateo". It looked small at the start. Then he made a big M. "Mateo!" he said out loud. His name had a capital M at the start, just like Penny's big P. Dad clapped. "Can we climb the stairs to the picture books?" Mateo asked. Up they went, past his favorite shelf.

Chloe wants to draw a flag at school. Mr. Menon shows her the tablet. He taps the little button. The screen lights up. Chloe taps it too. The screen goes dark again. "Oh no," she says. "It went night-night!"

Mr. Menon smiles. He taps the button one more time. The screen wakes up. Chloe laughs. She taps the button herself. Dark. She taps again. Light. "It is a sleeping game," she says.

Now Chloe opens the drawing app. She draws a big flag. It is red and yellow. She makes a squishy green ball under it. Salman peeks over. "Nice flag," he says. "I want a flag too." Chloe helps him find the app.

Chloe is done with her flag. She presses the button. The screen goes dark. She puts the tablet on the shelf, all nice and snug. Salman claps. Chloe claps too. "Night-night, tablet," she whispers.

Matthew sat in a small chair at the doctor's office. The doctor held up a tiny bandage. It had yellow stars on it. "This will be quick," the doctor said. Matthew held his dad's hand. The shot went into his arm. It felt like a little knock. Then it was over. "All done," the doctor said. Matthew got his star bandage.

In the car, Matthew lifted his arm. It felt sore. He touched the spot softly. "My arm hurts a little," he said. His dad nodded. "The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while. It will feel better soon." Matthew held his arm still and looked out the window.

Then they went to the ice cream shop. His dad ordered two cones. Matthew took a lick. His cold treat made him smile. He tried lifting his arm again. It felt better already. "Dad, look!" Matthew said, and raised his arm way up high.

Jade wanted to make soup for her family. She set up her pot on a little table in the backyard. She picked tomatoes from the garden. She picked a big onion too.

Her dad came out to help. He cut the onion with a sharp knife. Jade stood back and watched. Then she saw tears on Dad's face.

"Dad, are you sad?" she asked. "Why are you crying?"

Dad laughed. "I am not sad," he said. "The onion makes my eyes water."

Jade looked at the onion. Could a little onion really do that? She watched Dad cut more. More tears came. She handed him a tomato. No tears then.

Jade put the vegetables in her pot. Her friendly toy sheep sat beside her.

"Soup time!" said Jade. "Can you spell soup, Dad?"

"S O U P," said Dad.

Jade stirred and stirred. The soup was ready. Dad took one more look at the onion. "Ouch, my eyes," he said with a smile.

The lights went out. Madison stood still in the dark. "The power is off," said her dad. He found a big flashlight and turned it on. The beam made a bright circle on the floor.

Madison looked around. The house felt strange. "Why is it so quiet?" she asked. Dad said, "Listen. What do you hear?" Madison listened hard. She heard no humming. The fridge was not humming. The fan was not humming. All the machines were sleeping. That made the house quieter.

Then Madison heard a new sound. Drip, drip, drip. It came from the sink. "I never heard that before!" she said. Next door, her neighbour Mr. Bondarenko called from his yard, "Is your power out too?" "Yes!" said Dad. Madison held the flashlight up high, her neck stretched tall, still wide awake. Drip. Drip. Drip.

Wyatt sat in the big waiting room chair. His legs swung back and forth. Today he would see the dentist for the first time. He held his old red ball tight.

Zoha sat down next to him. "I like your ball," she said. Wyatt rolled it to her feet. She rolled it back. Then a nurse called, "Wyatt!"

The dentist smiled at Wyatt. Wyatt looked at her hands. "Your hands are blue!" he said. "These are my gloves," said the dentist. She pulled one finger of the glove. Snap! Wyatt laughed. "Gloves keep things clean when fingers or tools go in your mouth," she said, and put on a fresh one. Wyatt opened his mouth wide, just like a lion. "Say ah," said the dentist. Wyatt said, "Ahhh!" The dentist gave him a sticker. It was a shiny tooth. Zoha clapped when he came back out.

Mia sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two bowls. One bowl had strawberries. One bowl had crackers.

"Which bowl has more?" Mom asked.

Mia looked and looked. She pointed at the strawberries. Then she pointed at the crackers. "I don't know," she said.

"Try counting them," said Mom.

Mia counted the crackers. "One, two, three, four." Then she looked away to grab her cup. When she looked back, she forgot. Was it four? Was it five?

Mom held up her hand. "Watch me," she said. She put up one finger for each cracker. "One, two, three, four." Four fingers stood up tall.

Mia tried it. She touched a cracker and put up a finger. "One." She touched the next one. "Two." Then "Three." Then "Four." Her four fingers stayed up. She could see them.

Then she counted the strawberries the same way. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six fingers stood up.

Mia looked at her hands. One hand had six fingers up. One hand had four fingers up. Six was taller than four.

"The strawberries have more!" she said.

"Yes," said Mom. "Six is more than four."

Mia drank some water from her cup. An ice cube clinked inside. "The ice is cold," she said.

Mom laughed. "You can count them too, if you like."

Mia sipped slowly. Then she put her cup down. "Can we count again?"

"We can count all day," said Mom.

Mia put up one finger. "One strawberry for me, please."

Logan sat in the family car. He held his teddy bear on his lap. They were going to get the new baby. "Is the baby big?" Logan asked. "No," said Dad. "The baby is very small." Logan thought about that. His teddy was small too.

At the house, Mom carried the baby in. The baby had tiny hands and tiny feet. Logan wanted to pat the baby's head. He patted his teddy that way. But his hand came down too hard. The baby began to cry. Logan felt sick in his tummy. He had not meant to make the baby sad.

Mom held the baby close. She took Logan's hand in hers. "Watch me," she said softly. Mom stroked the baby's hand. Her fingers went slow and light, like a feather. The baby stopped crying. The baby's little fingers curled around Mom's thumb.

"Now you," said Mom. Logan touched one finger. He stroked the baby's hand, slow and light. The baby blinked at him. Then the baby made a small sound. "She likes you," Mom whispered. Logan stroked again, gentle as can be. The baby held his finger tight.

In the car on the way home, the baby slept. Logan sat very still beside her. He did not scratch his nose. He did not wiggle. Dad smiled at them in the mirror. "This is the best party ever," Logan whispered to his teddy. The baby sighed in her sleep, and her hand found his shirt.

Isaac sat in his car seat. The ride was long. His tummy felt hungry.

Dad drove the car. Isaac saw a bag of crackers on the seat. He wanted one.

"Give me a cracker!" said Isaac.

Dad did not hand it over. He kept driving.

Isaac thought for a minute. Then he tried again. "Cracker, please?"

Dad smiled in the mirror. "Yes! Here you go." He passed one back.

Isaac ate his cracker. It went crunch.

Next to him sat Fatoumata. She had a wide book on her lap. She was trying to read it. But her shoe was stuck under the strap.

Isaac tugged her shoe. It did not budge.

"Help, please," said Fatoumata.

Dad pulled over. He reached back and set her foot free.

"Thank you," said Fatoumata.

"Sorry it was stuck," said Dad.

Then Isaac held the book open. Fatoumata pointed at a big red truck. Isaac pointed too.

Outside, a real truck went by. It honked loud.

"Read this page," said Isaac.

Levi ran to the park with his dad. The grass smelled fresh and green. Levi was excited to play on the slide.

His friend Braxton was there. Braxton had the only red truck. Levi wanted it too. He grabbed the truck. Braxton shouted and his face turned red. He stomped his feet. He was angry. He began to cry big tears.

The park helper, Ms. Pereira, knelt down beside Braxton. "Let's try slow, deep breaths," she said. She breathed in slowly. She breathed out slowly. Braxton copied her. In. Out. In. Out. His face got calm. He stopped crying. He handed the truck to Levi.

Levi took a turn with the small truck. Then he gave it back. Braxton smiled. "Your turn," Levi said. They rolled the truck in the sand together. The warm sun shone on their heads.

Austin wanted to move his toy box. It was big. He pulled and pulled. The box would not move. "Why won't you move?" he asked. The box just sat there. He sat down too.

Mom came in with a glass of pink juice. "Can you help me?" asked Austin. Mom knelt beside him. "This box is heavy," she said. "Heavy and light are opposites." Austin looked at his little pillow. He picked it up with one hand. The pillow was light!

So Austin had an idea. He took his toys out, one by one. Each toy went into a small pink basket. Now the big box was not so full. Austin pushed the box. It slid across the rug! The basket was easy to carry too. Mom clapped her hands. Austin clapped too. "The box moved!" he said. "I made it light!"

Mila woke up hungry. She wanted a pancake. Mom said, "We are not late. We have time."

Mila pushed her little stool to the counter. She climbed up, up, up. Then she climbed down, down, down. "Up and down," said Mom with a smile. "Up and down are opposites." Mila climbed up again. "Up!" she said. Then she hopped down. "Down!"

They were a team. Mom held the big bowl. Mila held the small spoon. She stirred slowly. Then she stirred fast. The batter went round and round. Mila touched the cold milk jug. Then she pointed at the warm pan. "That one is hot," said Mom. "I will hold it. You watch."

Mom tipped the bowl. A big drop of batter fell. Then a small drop fell. Mila waited. The pancake bubbled. Mom flipped it high, up in the air. Then it came down, down, down. Plop. It landed right in the pan.

The pancake went onto a blue plate. Mila took a big bite. Then a small bite. "More flips," said Mila. Mom laughed and poured another circle of batter.

Luka ran to the park with his friend Clarke. Ms. Kang had a big cloth bag. "Let's play the feely game," she said. "Put your hand in. Don't peek."

Luka put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and bumpy. "A ball!" he said. He pulled it out. It was hidden in his fist.

"Guess the color," said Clarke.

"Red!" said Luka. "I felt it. It's red."

He opened his hand and looked. The ball was blue. "No, it's blue!" said Luka. He laughed.

"My turn," said Clarke. He felt in the bag. "A car. Green?" He looked. The car was yellow.

"Now I know," said Luka. "My eyes tell me the color. My fingers don't."

They played again and again. Luka felt a soft duck. He could not tell its color yet. He waited. Then he peeked. The duck was red, just like he had guessed.

A bee flew by the yellow flowers. The sun felt warm on Luka's head. He threw the blue ball high. Clarke caught it.

"Again!" said Clarke.

Isla sat at the big table in the library. Ms. Kelly gave her a yellow pencil. "Now we write your name," said Ms. Kelly.

Isla held the pencil in her fist. She pushed it on the paper. The I came out wobbly. The S looked like a curly worm. Isla frowned. "My letters are wrong," she said.

Ms. Kelly turned the pencil around. "Try the pink end," she said. Isla rubbed the pink end on the wobbly letter. She looked down. The wobbly mark was gone! The paper was clean again.

Ila held the pencil with her fingers, the way Ms. Kelly showed her. She tried again. The I stood up tall. The S curled nicely. "I made the letters go away, then I made them again," said Isla.

Ellie sat down next to her. "Can I try too?" she asked. Isla gave her the yellow pencil. "Rub the pink end if it goes wrong," said Isla.

Ellie wrote her E. It wobbled. She rubbed it out. Then she wrote it again, nice and straight. The two girls smiled at each other and kept writing.

"Let's go read our names to the family shelf," said Ms. Kelly. Isla carried her paper to the shelf. Her name was on it. Her very own name, written by Isla.

Jasmine stood at the school gate. Her tummy felt funny. Today was her very first day.

Her new backpack was on her back. But it was very heavy. Jasmine fell forward a little bit. "Too heavy," she said.

Her dad knelt down beside her. "Let's look inside," he said. They opened the backpack. Jasmine had packed her teddy bear, a toy mouse, and three big books.

"Your backpack is a bag you carry on your back," said Dad. "It goes on your back, so it must not be too heavy."

Jasmine took out the teddy bear. She took out the toy mouse. Now the backpack was light. She could stand up tall.

"Can I pay for milk at school?" Jasmine asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Ms. Friedman will help you."

Just then, a girl ran up to the gate. "Hi! I'm Valeria!" she said. "Want to hold hands?"

Jasmine smiled. Her tummy felt better now. She held Valeria's hand, and they walked through the gate together.

Olivier stood in the garage with his dad. The radio played a happy song. Olivier wanted to sing "The Cat in the Hat" all by himself. But he kept forgetting the words.

His friend Wells came over. Wells was holding a drum. "You clap, I drum," said Wells. Olivier clapped. Clap, clap, clap. The drum went boom, boom, boom. His dad turned the music up loud.

Olivier sang, "The cat sat on the..." He stopped. He forgot the last word. His mouth made a sad shape. Wells tapped the drum one slow time.

Then Olivier had an idea. "The cat sat on the hat!" The word hat sounded like cat. Both words ended the same. His dad smiled. "Cat and hat," said Olivier. "They sound the same at the end!"

Wells hit the drum again. Olivier clapped along to the steady beat. The claps and the boom went together. He sang the whole rhyme. He did not miss one word. He clapped so big that his hands felt warm. A low shelf buzzed a little with the drum.

Then the garage door began to rise by itself. Olivier jumped. It was only his mom, pushing the button from inside the house. She waved at him. Olivier waved back and sang one more time, loud and strong, all the way to the end.

Everly went to the park with her mama. She brought a big box of toys. She put her small ball in the box. She put her soft duck in, too.

A baby crawled up to the box. The baby took the duck out. Everly put the duck back in. The baby took it out again. Everly laughed. "Mama, why does the baby keep doing that?" she asked. Her mama smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. "You put in. The baby takes out."

Everly touched the baby's little hand. The baby dropped the duck. It rolled away, fast. Everly ran, but slow was better on the grass. She picked up the duck and sat in the cozy shade.

Then Everly made a game. She put a toy in. The baby took it out. In, out, in, out. It was the best game at the park.

"Let's draw a map home," said Everly. She drew a line in the dirt with a stick. "Here is our street," she said. The baby patted the dirt, right on the map.

"Time to go," said Mama. Everly put every toy in the box. The baby clapped. "Bye bye, box," said Everly.

Beatrice was playing in the playroom. She had a red car, a blue car, a yellow car, and a green car. Maira came to play too. "Let's drive on the mat," said Maira. But the cars all bumped into each other. Bump, bump, bump. "Too many crashes," said Beatrice. "The cars are all mixed up."

Then Beatrice found a coin in the toy box. She spun the coin on the table. It went round and round. "I feel dizzy just watching it," said Maira. The coin landed and lay flat. Beatrice looked at the spinning top of the coin. It made her think of something. She held up a paper circle. "We can make a light," she said. She painted one side red and one side green. "Red means stop," said Beatrice. "Green means go." Maira held the light up high.

The light turned red. Beatrice pointed at the red car. "Stop," she called. The red car stopped. The light turned green. "Go," said Beatrice. The red car zoomed past. Arzoyi drove the blue car. The light turned red again. The blue car stopped right away. The yellow car waited too. No bumps, no crashes. "One more time," said Maira. She held the light up high and turned it green. Beatrice laughed and pushed the red car past the finish line. "Red means stop," she sang, "and green means go!"

Lucas ran to the red swing at the park. But Amaira was already on it. Lucas grabbed the swing chain. Amaira held on tight. The swing stopped moving.

"No grab," said Mr. Carvalho. "We say please when we ask for something." Lucas let go of the chain. He put his hands behind his back. He waited for the swing to slow down. Then he looked at Amaira. "Swing, please?" he said.

Amaira smiled a big smile. "Okay! You can have a turn." She hopped off. Lucas climbed on. He pumped his legs. The swing went up, up, up. It felt like flying to the moon. He was a rocket ship zooming past stars. Amaira pointed at the sky. "You fly so high!" she said.

Then Lucas stopped the swing with his feet. He slid off. "Your turn now," he said. "Thank you, please Amaira." She laughed. They took turns until the sun looked like a big orange ball. Mr. Carvalho called, "Snack time!" Lucas and Amaira ran to the bench.

Ruby was four today. "Time for your first haircut," said Mom. "Yay!" said Ruby. She jumped like a bunny on a hill.

Mr. Eze had a small salon in his house. It was near Ruby's door. Ruby sat in the big chair. It went up and up! Mr. Eze held a comb and some scissors. He combed Ruby's hair. Then he snipped. He combed again. Then he snipped again. Ruby began to count. "One comb, one snip," she said. "Two combs, one snip!" Mr. Eze laughed. "You count well," he said.

Little bits of hair fell down. They did not go everywhere. They fell in a neat line, just where the comb had been. Ruby watched each comb make the hair sit still. Then she watched each snip. Snip, snip, snip! Mom held up a mirror. Ruby saw short hair and a big smile. "Look at me!" said Ruby. "My hair floats when I shake it!" Mr. Eze gave her a sticker. It was a shiny gold star.

Snow was falling at school. Hunter watched from the window. Big white flakes came down. Mr. O'Brien said, "Time to get dressed."

Hunter put on his boots. He put on his puffy coat. Philippe wore a red hat. Sidney wore mittens with stars. Outside, the wind blew. The snow felt cold on Hunter's face.

Hunter made a snowball. It was round and white. He wanted to keep it. "I will keep it forever," he said. He hid it in his coat pocket.

The class came back inside. It was warm inside. Hunter hung up his coat. Then he played blocks with Philippe.

Later, Hunter reached into his pocket. He found no snowball. He found a puddle! Water dripped on the floor. "Oh no," said Hunter. "My snowball is water now."

Mr. O'Brien came over with a towel. "Snow melts into water when you bring it inside where it is warm," he said. Hunter helped wipe the floor.

"Next time I will keep my snowball outside," said Hunter.

Zayn sat at the big table. His tummy was full of pasta. The big screen showed a game with a ball.

Zayn's dad said, "Watch. When our team scores, everyone will cheer." A player kicked the ball into the net. The whole restaurant clapped and cheered. Zayn clapped too.

Then the other team scored. Zayn stood up and cheered very loud. "Yay! We did it!"

A girl at the next table laughed. It was Annabel from his class. "That was the other team," she said. "The blue team scores, the blue fans cheer. The red team scores, the red fans cheer."

Zayn looked at the screen. The blue fans were clapping. The red fans were quiet.

Soon the red team scored. Zayn jumped up. He clapped and cheered with everyone. Mr. González, his neighbour, gave him a high five.

Then Zayn's spoon went bump on the floor. A waiter brought a new one.

"Red team!" Zayn shouted. "Go, go, go!"

Claare lived near a sunny beach. Behind the sand was a big pool. Claire wanted to swim there.

Mr. Popal was the teacher. "Hold my hand," he said. They walked into the water. The water came up to Claire's knees. She could see her toes.

At the far side, Aarya was swimming. Aarya was tall. The water went over her shoulders. Claire blinked her eye at the deep water. "I want to go there," she said.

Mr. Popal shook his head. "This end is the shallow end," he said. "You start here."

Claire kicked her legs. The shallow water made little waves. The waves pushed a toy duck to her hands. She laughed. She kicked again and again.

At the end, Claire looked at the deep end. "One day," she said. Then she blew bubbles in the shallow water.

Eliana ran into the kitchen. "Mom, can I do it tonight?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "You can lead the blessing."

Jasmine was there for dinner too. "At my house, we sing it," Jasmine said. "Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it."

"Singing? I want to sing it!" said Eliana.

Mom put the green beans on the table. One bowl, two spoons, three plates. Eliana stood up tall. She took a big breath and began to sing. But the tune came out wobbly and mixed up. She stopped. Her face got hot.

"Try again," said Mom. "I will hum with you."

Eliana took another breath. Mom hummed one note, then two. Eliana followed. The blessing came out sweet and round like a little song. Jasmine clapped.

"Eliana sang the blessing!" said Jasmine.

Eliana bowed. Then she picked up her spoon and smiled at her green beans. "Again tomorrow?" she asked.

"Again tomorrow," said Mom.

Emilia ran into the nursery room. Her mom had a new baby in her arms. "A baby sister!" Emilia shouted. "I want to hold her now!"

"Not yet," said Mom. "Big sisters wash their hands first." Emilia looked at her hands. They had dirt on them from the snowy yard outside. She had been making snowballs with her friend Myles.

Emilia ran to the sink. She washed her hands with soap. She blew on them to dry them fast. Then she walked back slowly and quietly.

"Now can I hold her?" Emilia asked. Mom sat down on the soft chair. She put a pillow on Emilia's lap. Then Mom laid the baby on the pillow. The baby made a tiny sound. Emilia held her very still.
