The baby opened her eyes. She looked right at Emilia. "Hello, baby," Emilia whispered. "I am your big sister."

Michael sat at the kitchen table. Mom set out his paints. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. "I know all the colours!" said Michael. He pointed to each cup.

"I want to paint a pumpkin," said Michael. He looked for orange paint. There was no orange cup. No orange anywhere. His tummy felt tight. A pumpkin had to be orange. A yellow pumpkin would look funny. A red one would look wrong.

Then Michael had an idea. He put his brush in the red paint. Dab. He put it in the yellow paint. Dab. He swirled the brush on his paper. Red and yellow turned into... orange! "Mom! Look! Look!" he shouted. Mom came fast. "That is the best orange ever," she said.

Michael painted a big round pumpkin. It was orange all over. He wanted to write his name at the top. Mom helped him hold the brush. M for Michael. Then his little sister woke up, and Mom said, "Show her your pumpkin!" Michael ran to get it. "Orange!" he said. "I made it myself!"

Matteo went to the lake with his friend Robin. It was a warm day. Ms. Moose was their swim teacher. She taught little fish at the lake every day.

Matteo wanted to jump in the water. The water was cool and shiny. He looked for Ms. Moose. She was not there yet. She was still folding the towels on the grass. Matteo sat down at the edge of the lake. He put his toes in. He waited.

Robin ran up. "Let's jump now," Robin said. Matteo shook his head. "Ms. Moose is not watching," he said. "We have to wait for a grown-up to watch us in the water." Robin sat down too. They splashed their toes together. The splashes were loud.

Then Ms. Moose came. She stood by the water and looked at both boys. "I am watching now," she said. Matteo stood up. He jumped in with a big splash. Robin jumped in too. Ms. Moose clapped her hands.

Audrey was in the backyard. She had red paint and blue paint. She wanted to paint a big flower. Her friend Elora came to play. Elora wore an old shirt over her clothes.

"You have paint on your arm," said Elora. Audrey looked down. Her arm had red paint on it. She looked at her dress. It had blue paint on it too. Audrey felt sad. It was her favorite dress.

Elora pointed at her old shirt. "My shirt keeps the paint off," she said. Audrey ran inside. Her dad gave her a big old shirt. Audrey put it on. She painted and painted. Paint went on the shirt, not on her dress. It worked, it worked!

Then Audrey saw something funny. A drop of red paint fell on the grass. A little red spot sat there. "Look, Elora," said Audrey. "The paint makes the grass red too."

Ellie sat at Grandma's big table. The bowls were full of soup. Ellie picked up her spoon. She was ready to eat.

Then everyone stood up. They all reached out their hands. Grandma reached for Ellie's hand. Uncle Ben reached for her other hand. Ellie was still holding her spoon. She could not hold hands and a spoon too. What should she do?

Ellie looked at the spoon. Then she looked at the hands. She set the spoon down by her bowl. Now her hands were free. Grandma smiled and held one hand. Ellie held Uncle Ben's hand too. Everyone made a big circle around the table. They closed their eyes and said the blessing together. After that, Grandma gave Ellie a kiss on her head. Ellie picked her spoon back up and poured nothing, because soup needs a spoon! She laughed and took a big bite.

Would her friend Orion's family do this too? Ellie wanted to ask him tomorrow.

Ellie woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow!" she shouted. No school today! It was a snow day.

She ran to the door in her pajamas. She wanted to build a snowman. But her mom said, "Wait! You need your warm coat." Ellie put on her coat. She found her boots and pulled them on. She grabbed her hat and pulled it down over her ears.

Then Ellie ran outside. She patted snow into a big ball. But her fingers began to hurt. They were so cold! She looked at her hands. No mittens! Ellie ran back inside. "My mittens!" she said. She slid them on. Her fingers felt warm again.

Outside, she rolled the snow with her mittens on. Her mom helped her carry the big snowball. They set the head on top. Ellie found a little stick for the snowman's arm. "He looks like he is waving!" she said. Then she waved back at him.

Florence sat on the rug in the nursery room. Ms. Taylor put out the crayons. "Draw your family," said Ms. Taylor. Florence drew Mommy, Daddy, and a tiny baby. She did not draw herself.

"Why no you?" asked Natasha.

"The baby cries," said Florence. "Mommy picks her up. Mommy has no lap for me."

Braelyn scooted close. "That happens," she said. "My mom held my brother a lot."

At home, Mommy gave the baby juice in a little cup. Florence looked away.

"Do you miss me?" asked Mommy.

Florence nodded. "I miss your lap."

Mommy sat down. "Baby sleeps now. Come here."

Florence climbed up. The lap was warm. She drew a picture of the lap.

"Look," said Mommy. "I am proud of you. You told me."

Florence smiled and hugged Mommy tight.

Sarah was playing in the backyard. She had a little red ball. She pushed the ball across the grass. The ball rolled under the big bush.

Sarah got down on her knees. She looked under the bush. There was her ball. There was something else too. It was a small silver thing. It had a little button on it.

Her friend Oakley came over. "What did you find?" he asked.

"I don't know," said Sarah. She pointed at it. She did not pick it up.

Sarah's dad came out to the yard. "Dad, come look," said Sarah. Her dad looked under the bush. He reached in and took out the silver thing.

"This is a lighter," said her dad. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use."

Sarah and Oakley nodded. Dad put the lighter high up in his pocket. Then he pushed the ball out from under the bush with a stick.

Sarah clapped her hands. The ball rolled back to her feet. She picked it up and pushed it to Oakley.

"Your turn!" she said.

It was bedtime for Ryan. He put on his clean pajamas. They had little fish on them. Ryan loved his fish pajamas.

Dad said, "Let's look at a picture before sleep." They looked at a photo from Ryan's birthday party. Ryan saw Catalina in the photo. Her mouth was turned down. Her eyebrows were low. Ryan said, "Catalina looks sad." Dad said, "Yes, she was sad that day. Her ice cream fell."

The next day, Ryan saw Catalina at school. Her mouth was turned down again. Ryan asked, "Are you sad?" Catalina said, "My truck is lost." Ryan looked around. He found the truck under the rug. He gave it to her. Catalina's mouth turned up into a big smile. Ryan smiled too. Her face told him she was happy now. Ryan waved and went to play.

Nathan was at Grandma's house. It was raining outside. He could not play in the yard.

Grandma gave him a big basket of toys. Nathan found a bear, a blanket, and a tiny cup. What could he do with these? Then he had an idea. "I will play house," he said. He tucked the bear in. He patted the bear's back. The bear was not really a baby. But Nathan acted as if it was. "Time for your milk," he told the bear. He held the tiny cup to the bear's mouth. One sip for the bear. Two pats on the blanket. Three soft songs, all hummed low.

Then Nathan put pillows on the floor. He said the floor was a river. The pillows were different colors. Hop, hop, hop, from pillow to pillow. The water was not real. But he hopped as if it was real. He said the exact word out loud: "Pretending!"

"Come close, bear," said Nathan. He sat the bear on the last pillow. He set the tiny cup on the table. Then the rain stopped. Nathan looked out the window.

"Grandma, can the bear splash in real puddles?"

Scarlett wanted a cat book. At the library, she found a green book with a cat on the cover. She sat down fast. But when she opened it, the pages looked all mixed up. The cat came before the kitten. The ending came first. "This book is broken," she said.

Her friend Muhammed came over. He looked at her book. Then he looked at his own book. "Mine starts here," he said. He pointed to the front cover. Scarlett turned her book over. Now the front cover was on top. She opened it again. One page, two pages, three pages. The cat came first. Then the kitten. Then a nap in the sun.

"Fixed!" said Scarlett. She counted the pages as she turned them, all the way to the back cover. Ms. Becker smiled and gave them each a sticker. "Thank you," said Scarlett, very polite. The cat on the sticker winked at her. Or maybe it was just the light.

Evelyn was at summer camp. A big red truck sat on the sand. Gunnar was holding it. Evelyn wanted a turn.

She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She asked, "Can I have the truck after you?"

"Yes," said Gunnar. He drove it through the sand. He piled sand in the middle of the truck bed. Waiting felt hard.

Evelyn took three slow, deep breaths. In and out. In and out. In and out. Her body felt calm. She watched Gunnar pour the sand out. Then he carried the truck to her.

"Your turn," he said. Evelyn held the truck with two hands. The back door was open. She filled it with sand, then dumped it out. Gunnar waited and took three slow breaths too.

"Now me!" he said. Evelyn smiled and pushed the truck across the sand to him.

Maria loved story time at daycare. Today she wanted the bear story now. She ran to Mr. Bondarenko. "Story now, please!" she said.

Mr. Bondarenko shook his head. "Not now," he said. "The story is after snack. Now means at this very moment."

Maria pouted. She looked at the clock. It did not move fast. Then Elijah knocked over his cup. Milk spilled on the floor. Mr. Bondarenko got a cloth and wiped it up.

"Now the floor is clean," he said.

Maria thought hard. Now was this moment. The spill was now. The wiping was now. But the bear story was not now. It was later.

"Is snack now?" she asked Isabelle.

"Not yet," said Isabelle. "First we wash hands. One, two, three, four, five!"

They washed the dirt off their hands. Then came crackers and apple slices. Maria ate them all up, quick.

Mr. Bondarenko closed his empty cup. "Snack is done," he said. "And now?"

Maria jumped up. "Now is story time! Now means at this very moment!"

"That's right," said Mr. Bondarenko. He opened the bear book.

Maria sat close. The bear story was finally here. "Now," she whispered, and hugged her knees.

Sebastian sat on the small stage in the school auditorium. He held his shiny drum. Ms. Andersen put a big paper on the stand. The paper had lots of black dots and lines.

"What are those dots?" Sebastian asked.

"Those marks are called notes," Ms. Andersen said. "They show which sounds to play."

Sebastian tapped one dot with his finger. Then he hit his drum. Boom! He tapped a high dot. He hit the drum fast. He tapped a low dot. He hit it slow. One dot, one boom. Every time!

Violet and Gemma sat in the front row. "Play the dots, Sebastian!" they called. Sebastian's sister waved from the door. She could not stay. She had to leave for her class.

Sebastian looked at the notes. He played them all. Boom, boom, boom-boom, boom. The sound filled the big room. Ms. Andersen smiled. Violet clapped. Gemma clapped too.

"Again!" said Sebastian, and his sticks went up in the air.

Alice was at the park with her friend Bethany. Bethany was building a big sandcastle. It had three towers and a deep moat. Alice wanted to help. She ran fast to the sandbox. Her foot hit the side of the castle. The towers fell down. The sand went everywhere. It was messy now.

Bethany looked at the flat sand. Her eyes got big. Alice felt bad inside. She had knocked the castle down. "Sorry, Bethany," Alice said. "I ran too fast. I did not mean to knock it down."

Bethany nodded slowly. Then she patted the sand. "You can help me build it again," she said. Alice got the small blue bucket. She filled it with sand. She tipped it over, tap, tap, tap. Bethany patted the sides smooth. Together they made one tall tower.

A duck walked past the sandbox. Alice laughed and pointed. "Look, a duck!" she said. "Can we share the shovel, please?" Bethany asked. Alice gave her the red shovel. They dug a new moat. The castle stood tall in the sun. "Thank you for helping," said Bethany. Alice smiled and added one last shell on top.

Levi sat in a big chair at the hair salon. The chair was shiny and tall. His feet did not touch the floor. A hairdresser named Mr. Whitaker put a soft cloth around him. "Snip, snip," went the scissors. Levi watched little hairs fall down. They landed on the cloth like tiny bits of string.

Soon the hair on the floor was getting bigger. Levi thought about dinner at home tonight. He wanted to look nice for it. "Is my hair done?" he asked. "Almost," said Mr. Whitaker. He combed Levi's hair with slow, gentle pulls.

Then Levi had a problem. He could see the front of his hair. The big mirror showed his face. But he could not see the back of his head. "I want to see the back!" said Levi. He turned his head this way and that. He could not see it at all.

Mr. Whitaker smiled. He picked up a small mirror. He held it up next to the big mirror. Levi looked. Now he could see the back of his hair. There it was, short and neat. "I can see it!" said Levi. He sat up very straight and grinned. At home, Axl would see his new hair after dinner.

Beau wanted his red teddy bear. Yesterday he had it in bed. Today it was gone. Where did it go?

He looked under the pillow. No bear. He looked under the bed. Dust and one sock, but no bear. Then Beau had to freeze. He heard a small sound. Snore, snore. Was the bear hiding?

He turned on his lamp. The light shone under the blanket. There was a red lump! "Found you," said Beau. Papa smiled. "Bath time soon," said Papa. "What does soon mean?" asked Beau. "Soon means in a little while," said Papa. Beau waited. He hugged the bear. He looked at the lamp. Then, after a little while, water ran in the tub. Soon was not long at all.

Beau carried the bear to the bath. "Tomorrow you sleep with me again," he said. "Tomorrow, tomorrow," said Beau, and Papa laughed.

Henry was at Grandpa's house. He wanted a story, but Grandpa was napping. Henry saw a big book on the chair. It had a snowy bear on the cover.

Henry opened the book from the back. The pages looked funny. The words ran the wrong way. "I guess I hold it upside down," he said. He turned the book around. Now the bear was on the front. Henry opened the front cover. The words sat in neat little rows. Grandpa woke up and smiled. "Read it front to back," said Grandpa.

Henry pointed at the cover. "Who made up the bear story?" he asked. "Look here," said Grandpa. He tapped a name on the cover. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Henry touched the name with his finger. Then he turned the first page. "Start here," he said. Grandpa laughed and sat down.

Beatrice was at Grandpa's house. It was windy outside. The trees went swish, swish. Soon it was time for lunch. Grandpa made hot soup. The soup smelled good.

"First we say the blessing," said Grandpa. Beatrice felt shy. She did not know the words. "I will help you," Grandpa said. He held her hand. He bowed his head. His eyes were closed. Beatrice peeked. She saw Grandpa's quiet face. His eyes stayed shut the whole time.

Then Grandpa said the blessing. Beatrice said the words after him, small and slow. "Amen," said Grandpa. "Amen," said Beatrice. Grandpa opened his eyes. He smiled at her. "Now we eat!" he said. Beatrice ate her soup. It was warm and good. Grandpa gave her bread. Beatrice dipped it in. "Can we say it again tomorrow?" she asked. "Every day," said Grandpa.

Amira walked into the pharmacy with her dad. It was a sunny day. The doctor had a little room at the back.

"I don't want a shot," said Amira. "I am scared."

"I will hold your hand," said Dad.

The nurse came in with a small tray. On the desk was a tiny needle in a wrapper. Amira looked at it. She wanted to touch it.

"Can I hold the needle?" she asked.

The nurse smiled. "Only I hold the needle," she said. "That is my job. You never touch it."

Then the nurse held up a sticker sheet. "But you can hold this," she said.

Amira took the sticker sheet. It had cats and stars on it. She looked at the cats while the nurse pushed up her sleeve. She felt one small pinch, fast like that.

"All done," said the nurse.

"Was that the shot?" said Amira. "That was so small!"

Dad helped her pick a star sticker. She put it on her hand, right next to the tiny bandage. On the way out, they waved to the pharmacist at the big desk. Amira held Dad's hand all the way to the car.

"Next time I will hold the sticker sheet again," she said.

Elliot went to the library with his dad. There was a big box of blocks in the corner. His friend Giuliana was there. She was building a tall tower.

Elliot ran to see it. He ran too fast. He bumped into the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. All of them.

Giuliana's lip wobbled. Elliot felt dizzy and hot in his face. He looked at his dad. His dad nodded.

"Sorry," Elliot said. "I bumped your tower." Then he bent down. He picked up a red block. He put it on the carpet. Giuliana put a blue block on top. They built the tower again, block by block. It got tall. Taller than before.

Mr. Walker, the library man, came over. "You two can each put the last block on," he said. "One for Giuliana, one for Elliot." Giuliana went first. Then it was Elliot's turn. He fetched the last block and set it on top, very carefully.

"There," said Giuliana. "It's the best tower ever."

Emile wanted to sing a song all by himself. His baby cousin was coming to visit. Emile wanted to sing for her, but he did not know a whole song yet.

Emile asked his grandpa for help. "Can you teach me a nursery rhyme?" he asked. "A nursery rhyme is a short rhyming song for little ones," said Grandpa. "My mama sang this one to me." He sang about a cat and a hat, and then a rat and a mat. The words matched at the end. Emile laughed.

Grandpa clapped his big hands to the beat. Clap, clap, clap. Emile clapped too. His heart felt warm when the words came out right. He sang the rhyme again at snack time. He sang it again in the bath. The words were short, so he could hold them all in his head. When the baby came, Emile stood in front of her. He clapped and sang the whole rhyme. The baby kicked her feet and made a happy sound. "Again," said Grandpa. Emile took a big breath and sang.

Ethan sat at the kitchen table. Mom had put a bowl of apples there. "Let's play a game," Mom said. "Tell me your five senses."

Ethan held an apple. "I can touch it with my hands," he said. "I can smell it with my nose." He took a bite. "I taste it with my mouth."

"Good," said Mom. "Two more to go."

Ethan listened. The sink was dripping. "I hear that with my ears!" he said.

Then he grabbed a coin from his pocket. He covered his eyes with his hand. "Can I see the coin now?" he asked.

"No," said Mom.

Ethan opened his fingers. There was the coin. "I see it with my eyes!" he said. He covered his eyes again. "Now I can't see it. Silly hands." He opened them. "Now I see it again!"

"We see with our eyes," Ethan said. He clapped his hands. Mom smiled and gave him a big apple slice.

John sat on the red rug at school. Ms. Walker said, "We will sing a rhyme today." John wanted to clap and sing it all by himself. He did not know it yet.

Tiara and Andrew stood up to sing. Ms. Walker sang fast, fast, fast. The words got all tangled. Andrew said, "My tongue is in a knot!" Tiara giggled and fell down on the rug.

Ms. Walker said, "A song can be sung fast or slow. Let us try slow." She sang very slow. Clap, clap, clap went John's hands. The beat was steady like a big drum. John peeked at his white shoes. They tapped the floor too. John sang the whole rhyme, all alone. He clapped the last clap. "Again!" he said.

Louis wanted to make a paper owl at school. But his owl needed wings. Mr. Ross gave him a square piece of blue paper. Louis looked at it. The square had four sides, all the same.

Louis tried to make wings. He folded the square in half, edge to edge. He pressed the fold flat. Then he opened his eyes wide. The paper was not a square anymore. It was long and thin, like a door.

"Look, Celine," said Louis. "A rectangle!" Celine came over. She held up her own square. She folded it in half, edge to edge. Hers made a rectangle too. Louis clapped his hands. Now he had two thick wings for his owl. He glued them on. The owl looked round and fat, like a circle with eyes.

Louis held the owl up high. "Whoo, whoo!" he said. Mr. Ross smiled. "Your owl can fly," he said. Louis ran around the table. The paper wings flapped up and down. Celine laughed and clapped.

At home time, Louis put the owl in his bag. He held his dad's hand all the way home. The owl peeked out of the bag, safe and snug.

Jules sat at the dinner table. He had big news about his day. He made a bird house with a hammer at school. His friend Bronson helped him hold the nails.

Dad was talking to Mom. Dad told about his day at work. Jules wanted to talk right away. "Dad! Dad!" he said. Dad kept talking. Mom kept listening. Jules's words got mixed up with Dad's words. Nobody heard his news.

Jules took a bite of his peas. He waited. He took another bite. Dad was still talking. Jules looked at his fork. He waited some more.

Then Dad stopped talking. There was a quiet little pause. Mom smiled at Jules. "Would you like some milk, Jules?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Jules.

Then Dad said, "Now it is your turn, Jules." Jules sat up tall. "I used a hammer!" he said. "The bird house looks wild inside!" Dad laughed. Mom clapped her hands.

"You waited so nicely," said Dad. "Thank you," said Jules. Dad passed him the bread. "Thank you," said Jules again.

At bedtime, Dad told a story about a wild cat. Jules listened all the way to the end. Then Jules said, "My turn. I saw a bird at school." Dad said, "I love that news."

Beau sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to make a pink flower for Grandma's card. But there was no pink paint. "Where did the pink go?" he asked. Ellie looked in the cup tray. "Not here," she said.

Beau had red paint. He had white paint too. The white paint was squishy in the jar. He dipped his brush in the red. Then he dipped it in the white. He stirred them together. Round and round went the brush. The red turned lighter and lighter. "Look!" said Beau. "It's pink now!"

Taha ran over to see. "How did you do that?" he asked. "I put white in the red," said Beau. "White makes it lighter." Taha laughed. "You made pink out of red! That is so silly and so good." Ms. Suryanto came to look. "What a pretty pink flower," she said. Beau painted a big pink petal. Then he painted a green stem and a yellow sun. He added a blue bird in the sky. His brush would swing up and down as he worked.

At story time, Beau told everyone about his card. "Grandma loves pink," he said. He put the card in his bag, safe and flat. "Tomorrow I will paint her a pink cat," said Beau. Taha giggled. "A pink cat? Cats are not pink!" Beau smiled. "Mine will be."

Theo ran into the baby store. "A baby is coming!" he told everyone. He pushed a little cart. Nawab and Sifat came too. They were Theo's friends from class.

Theo saw a shiny rattle. He shook it. Ding, ding! A tiny baby across the aisle began to cry. "The baby is sad," said Theo. He let the baby's dad walk by with a bottle. The dad gave the baby the bottle. The baby drank and stopped crying.

"The baby was hungry!" said Theo. "The baby cannot talk yet," said Nawab. "So the baby cries to show it needs something." Theo shook his head up and down. Then the baby cried again. "Maybe it needs a new sock," said Theo. He picked a soft sock with a star. The dad put it on the baby's small foot. The baby gurgled and smiled. "It talked to us!" Theo laughed.

Camille ran to the library shelf. She wanted to write her name, all by herself. Ms. Huang gave her a bumpy card with the letter K. "K says kuh," said Ms. Huang. Camille tried to write K on her paper. She made the legs go the wrong way. She tried again. Wrong way again! Madina and Edith looked over. "Try this," said Edith.

Camille put her finger on the bumpy K. She traced it, slow and slow. Up. Down. Kick out. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it again and again. Then she picked up her pencil. Up. Down. Kick out. "It is right!" said Camille. "Kuh, kuh, Camille!"

She wrote the K two more times. Then she stuck out her tongue at the paper, so careful was her face. "Look, look!" she said. Edith clapped. Madina got a fresh sheet for more letters. "Now C," said Camille. "C says kuh too!" Her pencil touched the paper. Up. Around. "I did it again!"

Matthew ran to the kitchen. His tummy felt funny. He needed the potty, fast!

He used the toilet. Then he washed his hands. The soap was slippery and smelled like lemons. The water was warm and bubbly. But wait. Matthew looked back at the bathroom door.

"Uh oh," he said. "I forgot to flush!" He ran back. He pushed the handle down. Whoosh! The water swirled away. Then he washed his hands again, because that is what you do.

Back in the kitchen, Mom had a bowl of oatmeal. It was warm and sweet. Matthew sat on his new chair. His face felt happy. He took a big bite.

"All clean, all fed," said Mom.

Matthew giggled. "Potty, flush, wash, eat!" he said. He clapped his soapy-clean hands. Then he took another big bite.

Juliette woke up early. Today was playground day. She ran to the sandbox with her friend Abigail. There was a big toy horse in the sand. Only one horse, and two girls.

"Can I have a turn?" asked Juliette.

"You can ride it next," said Abigail. Abigail rode the horse first. Then she hopped off. Juliette got her turn.

Then the bell rang. Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with. Abigail ran to the swings. But the horse was still in the sand. Juliette felt worried. Would she have to clean it all alone?

"Abigail!" she called. "Come see. Our horse needs us." Abigail ran back. The two girls picked it up together. It was so big, it needed both of them. Abigail brushed the sand off the horse's back. Juliette carried the small bucket.

Ms. Tanaka smiled at them. "Look at that team," she said. The playground was clean and quiet now, not noisy like before. Juliette held Abigail's hand. They walked to the snack table together.

Harrison ran out to the big puddle. He jumped in it. Splash! Water went up high. Then his socks felt cold and squishy.

"Mama, my socks are all wet," he said. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mama. "Your wet socks are not dry anymore." Harrison looked down at his feet. "Can wet socks get dry again?" he asked. "Yes, we will help them," said Mama.

Mama helped him lift off his wet socks. She hung them by the warm window. Harrison put on dry socks. They felt soft and warm. He drew a picture of his puddle. Later, he was not afraid to jump again. This time he wore his red boots. Splash! His socks stayed dry. "My boots are fast," he said, and off he ran.

The lights went out. Carter sat in the dark. "Mama, the lamp is off," he said. "I can't see my toy pond."

Mama came quickly. "Don't be scared," she said. "The power went out." She found a big flashlight. She clicked it on. Click, on. Click, off. On made light. Off made dark.

Carter held his toy boat. He went to the window with Mama. He looked out. The street was dark too. Every house was dark. "The neighbors' houses are dark too," he said. "All of them!" Mama nodded. "The power went out on our whole street," she said. "All the houses went dark at once."

Carter felt a little dizzy in the dark. He sat down on the rug. Mama sat with him. They made shadows on the wall with the flashlight. "Can the shadows talk?" Carter asked. He made a duck shadow. "Quack, quack," said Mama.

Then the lights came back on. Click, the lamp was bright. Click, all the houses outside were bright. Carter clapped his hands. "The power is back," he said. He hugged his boat. Then he turned on his little lamp all by himself, and the room glowed warm.

Emma stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim pants. "One sock, two socks," she said. One sock was inside out. Emma laughed. She fixed it all by herself.

Then Emma went to the pool with her dad. The water smelled like splashes. Ms. Takahashi, the swim teacher, waved. "Hello, Emma! Come to the wall."

Emma did not want to let go of the wall. The water looked big. Ms. Takahashi said, "Hold the edge of the pool. Now kick your legs." Emma held the edge tight. She kicked. Splash! Water went everywhere. It got Ms. Takahashi's nose. "Oh no!" said Emma. Ms. Takahashi laughed. "Kick again!" Emma kicked again. Splash! Her friend Haven was next to her. Haven held the edge too. Haven kicked. Splash! Now two teachers had wet noses.

Emma's tummy felt full of giggles. She counted her kicks. "One, two, three!" Each kick made a big splash. Her dad said, "You are a little frog." Emma stuck out her tongue. "Frogs don't taste pizza," she said. After swimming, they went back to the changing room. Emma's shoes were gone! She looked under the bench. There was one shoe. There was the other shoe. And there was a rubber duck. "A surprise duck!" said Emma. She held it up. "Quack," said the duck's squeaky voice. Emma hugged it tight. "Duck, you can hold the edge too," she said.

Leo wanted his red sock. Mom was washing dishes. The sock was in the tall basket by the door. But Dad stood in the doorway. He was folding warm shirts. His big pile was wide.

Leo tried to squeeze past. He bumped the pile. One shirt fell down. "Sorry, Dad," said Leo. Dad smiled and picked up the shirt. He still stood in the way.

Then Mom called from the sink. "Say excuse me, Leo. Dad will move." Leo looked up at Dad. "Excuse me, please," said Leo. Dad stepped to the side, quick as that. The way was clear now.

Leo walked to the basket. He dug past a towel and a small hat. There was his red sock, soft and warm from the dryer. "Thank you, Dad!" said Leo. He sat on the floor and pulled the sock onto his foot. It fit just right. Dad handed him the other one. "One for each foot," said Dad, and winked.

Lena wanted to play the new game at daycare. Samael and Usman were already playing it. One kid said a word. The other kid yelled back a different word.

"Big!" said Samael. "Small!" yelled Usman. "Fast!" said Usman. "Slow!" yelled Samael. Lena sat down to watch. She did not know the words to say.

Samael saw her face. "You can play too," he said. "We say a word. You yell its opposite." "Opposites are two words as different as can be," said Ms. Nkosi, handing out cups. "Like big and small."

Lena tried. "Hot!" said Samael. Lena did not know. She looked at her cup. Ms. Nkosi had poured the warm milk. Lena touched her own cool cup of water. "Cold!" she yelled. Samael clapped.

Then it was her turn. Lena looked around the room. She saw the big slide. She saw her small shoes. "Big!" she said. Usman yelled, "Small!" Lena laughed. She got it right.

They played until the shiny star on the wall glowed. "Time for a snack," said Ms. Nkosi. Lena took a cracker. She gave one to Usman too. Usman smiled at her.

"Fast eater!" said Sanael. Lena took a tiny bite, very slow. Everyone laughed. "Opposite!" Lena yelled.

Peyton walked into the forest with her friend Zainab. A brown rabbit hopped across the path. It hid under a bush, and the girls kept walking.

"Let's play house," said Zainab. She set a flat rock in the middle. "This is our table." Peyton found three pinecones. She dropped them into a puddle of rainwater. "Soup!" she said. She stirred it with a stick.

A rabbit hopped by their table. Zainab clapped. "Our soup smells so good," she said. She picked up the bowl and tipped it toward her mouth.

"Stop!" said Peyton. "The pinecones are pretend food. We pretend to eat them. We do not put them in our mouths." Zainab put the bowl down. She made a big slurping sound instead. "Slurp, slurp," she said. Peyton laughed and slurped too.

Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth.

Then Zainab held up a leaf. "A pancake for the rabbit," she said. She laid it on the moss. The rabbit sniffed it and hopped away. Zainab giggled and ate her pretend pancake with a big "nom nom" sound.

Natalie sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. "I don't need my coat," said Natalie.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain came down. Tap, tap, tap on the roof. "Now I need my rain hat," said Natalie. Her dad found it in the bag.

Then the rain stopped. The trees began to sway. Whoosh went the wind. Leaves blew around and around. One leaf came close to the window. It stuck to the glass for a moment. Then it blew away. "It's windy!" said Natalie. She watched the trees sway again. The big tree swayed. Then more leaves blew across the yard. She laughed and pointed.

"What a windy day," said her dad. Soon the wind stopped too. Little white flakes came down. Snow! Snow fell on the grass. "Snowy," said Natalie. She hugged her warm coat. "Snow needs boots," said her dad. "And mittens!"

The car came to a stop. There was her friend Paxton, waiting with a big pile of leaves. The wind picked up again. The leaves blew all around Paxton. Paxton laughed and chased them. Natalie put on her mittens and came out. Together they watched the trees sway. The leaves blew in a circle around them both. "Catch one!" said Paxton. Natalie held out her stick. One leaf landed right on it. "I got it," said Natalie, proud as could be.

Ethan ran to the cubby room at daycare. It was time to go outside. The sky outside looked stormy and gray, so Ethan wanted his shoes on fast.

He pushed his feet into his shoes. Then he grabbed his socks. He tried to push a sock over his shoe. It would not go on. It was too tight, like glue that had dried.

Skyler sat down next to him. "My socks go on first," she said. She pulled on her socks. Then she pulled on her shoes.

Ethan laughed at himself. He pulled his shoes off. He pulled his socks on. Then his shoes went on easy.

"See, you keep trying and you get it," said Mr. Ma from the door.

Ethan stood up. "Socks first, shoes second!" he said. "Socks first, shoes second!"

Skyler giggled. They ran outside together.

Wesley went to the store with his dad. The store was big and bright. Wesley saw a toy drum on a shelf. He tapped it once. Boom! He felt so excited. He tapped it again. Boom! He laughed.

His friend Sahib was there too. Sahib covered his ears. "Too loud," Sahib said. He looked a little scared. Wesley stopped tapping. He felt sad that Sahib felt scared. But Wesley still loved the drum.

Then Wesley had an idea. He tapped the drum very softly. Tap, tap. It was quiet now. Sahib smiled. He did not cover his ears. Sahib pointed at a fluffy rabbit toy. "I like this," he said. Wesley liked it too. They petted the soft rabbit together. "Same store, we feel different," said Wesley's dad with a smile. Wesley held the drum under one arm. He held Sahib's hand with the other. The sky outside looked cloudy. They walked to the car, and the drum slept quietly in the bag.

Amira woke up and ran to the window. "Snow!" she said. There was no school today. It was a snow day at home.

But Amira saw a problem. The road was all covered. "How will the mail come? How will Grandpa's car come?" she asked. Her dad looked out too. "Hmm," he said. "Let's watch."

Then Amira heard a big noise. A big orange truck came down the street. It had a big flat front. "What is it doing?" Amira asked. Dad said, "That is a snowplow."

The snowplow pushed the snow off the road. It went scrape, scrape, scrape. The snow slid to the side, into a big pile. The road turned black and clear. Amira clapped her hands. "The truck moved the snow! Now the road is open!"

One snowplow, pushing snow. Two big piles, growing tall. Three happy waves from Amira at the window.

Later, Grandpa's car came up the clear road. Grandpa held up a bag. "Hot cocoa mix!" he said. Dad made the cocoa, and Amira watched from her stool. Then Grandpa pointed outside. "Look at that puddle by the pile." The snow was starting to melt in the sun.

"One puddle," said Amira. She put her boots on and stomped in it. "Two stomps!" said Grandpa. Amira laughed. "The snowplow pushed the snow, and I push the puddle!"

Penelope sat at the ice rink with her dad. The big game was starting. The air smelled cold and clean. Her mittens were warm and pink.

Abir sat next to her. He looked and looked at the ice. "Where is the ball?" he asked. "I can't see a ball anywhere."

Penelope looked too. There was no ball. Then a player hit something with his stick. It slid fast across the shiny ice. It was small and flat and black. "A puck," said Ms. Weiss from the seat behind them. "They hit the puck with sticks."

The puck slid again. It went into the net. The crowd jumped up. Penelope clapped her mittens together. "A goal!" she said.

Abir was sorry he had missed the puck at first. "I will watch for it now," he said. The puck slid by again. This time Abir saw it first. "There it is!" he said.

Penelope smiled. "This is the best story ever," she said. Then she watched the sticks hit the puck, all the way to the end.

Sebastian looked out the window. The rain was falling on the street. "Rainy day," he said with a sigh.

Then the rain stopped. The sun came out. "Sunny now!" said Sebastian. He put on his rubber boots. Mom said, "Let's check the backyard."

In the backyard, the wind blew a little. Sebastian's hat almost flew off. "Windy too!" he said. Then he saw it. A big puddle sat on the ground near his sandbox. It was wide and brown and dirty.

Yara came over with her boots on. "Look!" said Sebastian. "Rain makes puddles on the ground!" He stepped in. Splash! Water went up on his legs. Yara stepped in too. Splash! They laughed and jumped together.

Then Yara slipped and sat down in the mud. Her lip began to shake. "I might cry," she said. Sebastian ran to her. He held out his hand. "Hold on," he said. "I'll pull you up." Up she came, splash-free and smiling.

"I'll get a towel," said Mom. She wiped Yara's dirty hands. "Thank you," said Yara. The wind blew again. "Brrr," said Yara. "My jacket is all wet." Sebastian ran inside. He came back with his warm, puffy coat. He gave it to Yara to wear.

Yara zipped it up. They jumped in the puddle one more time. "Splash!" they said together.

Jack wanted to zip his coat by himself. He pulled the zipper up. It stopped halfway. It would not go any farther.

"Let's try again," said his dad. Jack pulled it down. Then he pulled it up. It stopped again. Jack sat on the step and frowned.

"You can practice," said his dad. "Zipping takes practice." So Jack practiced. He tried at breakfast. He tried after he got dressed. He tried before they went to the bank. Sometimes it stuck. Sometimes it went up.

At the bank, Jack put on his coat. He held the zipper. He pulled it slow. Up, up, up it went. It went all the way to the top. Jack smiled big. "I did it!" he said. His dad clapped. Outside, they saw a big sign with a yummy bread on it. "We can eat a snack now," said Dad. Jack zipped his coat all by himself, and off they went.

Wesley sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The game was on TV. Mila sat next to him with popcorn.

A man ran on the TV. His shirt had stripes. He kept blowing a whistle. The players all stopped. "Who is that man?" Wesley asked. "Grandpa says he is the referee," said Mila. "He watches the game."

The referee watched the players. He blew his whistle. A player had broken a rule. The whistle made everyone stop. Then they played again. "Whistle means stop!" said Wesley. He covered his ears and giggled. The whistle was loud.

A paper plane flew past Wesley's head. "My plane is missing a wing," said Mila. Grandpa laughed and taped it on. The plane flew again, just like the game.

The referee blew his whistle one more time. Wesley puffed his cheeks and blew too. "Peeeeep!" he said. Mila fell over laughing.

Brooklyn was three years old today. Her party was at the big pool. Norman and Nadar came too. Ms. Castillo waved from her chair.

There was a pile of presents. One box had blue paper with stars. Brooklyn picked it up. She shook it. She squeezed it. "What is inside?" she asked. Norman leaned close. "I don't know," he said. "The paper hides it." Brooklyn turned the box all around. She could not see inside. She could not peek. The paper was in the way.

Brooklyn sat down by the pool. Her tummy was full of cake. Her feet went splash, splash in the water. "If I can't see it, how will I know?" she asked. Her dad smiled. "We open it," he said. Brooklyn jumped up. She wanted to open it now.

She pulled the paper off. Rip, rip, rip! There it was. A little yellow duck for the bath. "I could not see it before," said Brooklyn. "Now I can!" Nadar clapped. Norman clapped. The duck went squeeze in her hand.

Brooklyn hugged the box. She was tired and happy. Ms. Castillo said, "Time to go home soon." Brooklyn waved the duck in the air. "Quack, quack," she said.

Sadie planted seeds with Mr. Bautista in the community garden. She planted tomatoes, carrots, and beans. "Which row is which?" asked her friend Sasha. Sadie looked at the soil. All the little rows looked the same. She could not remember where the tomatoes were. "Maybe the tomatoes are here," said Sasha. "Or maybe here," said Sadie. They felt puzzled.

Then Mr. Bautista held up a small stick. A paper picture of a tomato was glued on it. He pushed the stick into the dirt next to the tomato row. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," he said. Sadie smiled wide. She and Sasha made more picture labels. One, two, three, four, five labels went into the ground. A carrot label. A bean label. A tight little row of labels.

Sadie watered the seeds each day. The sun felt warm. The soil smelled like rain. One morning, green sprouts popped up. Sadie looked at the label first. Then she looked at the sprout beside it. "That one is a bean!" she said. Sasha clapped her hands. A long brown snake slid past the fence, far away. "Even the snake wants to see our garden," said Sadie.

David was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to leave Grandpa a note. He took a yellow crayon and wrote all his letters in one long line. He wrote DAVIDTHANKYOU all squished together.

Grandpa picked up the paper. He looked at it a long time. "Hmm," he said. "I cannot read this."

David wondered why. Grandpa wrote on another paper. He wrote THANK YOU DAVID. "See the spaces?" he said. "There is a space between one word and the next."

David looked hard. He saw little gaps. Then he wrote again. He wrote THANK YOU GRANDPA. He put a space after each word.

Grandpa read it out loud. "Thank you, Grandpa!" he said. "Why, David, that is for me."

David nodded. Grandpa put the note in his pocket.

Gabriel went to the art studio with his dad. He sat at the big table. Miriam sat next to him. "I will draw a dog," said Gabriel. He picked up a pencil. He pressed down very hard. Snap! The pencil point broke. "Oh no," said Gabriel. "My point broke."

Ms. Mendoza brought a new pencil. "Try again," she said with a smile. Gabriel held the pencil. This time he pressed soft and slow. The line came out long and gray. No snap. One ear, two eyes, one wet nose. "Look, Miriam! It did not break!"

Later Gabriel drew a puddle by the dog's paws. "Dogs like to splash," he said. Miriam drew a young puppy too. At snack time they sat together to eat crackers. Gabriel kept his pencil on the table, safe and whole. "Press soft," he whispered to the puppy.

Sienna held her mom's hand. It was a rainy day. They walked into the hair salon. Sienna was getting her very first haircut.

The hairdresser patted the big chair. "Hop up," she said. Siena tried. The chair was too tall. She could not get on. Her feet dangled below the seat. The hairdresser could not reach her hair.

"Let's get the booster seat," the hairdresser said. She carried it over. It was small and blue. She put it on the big chair. Sienna climbed up. Now she sat high. The hairdresser could reach her hair.

The scissors went snip, snip. Little hairs fell like soft rain on the cape. Sienna watched the chair spin a tiny bit. Her mom smiled.

"All done," said the hairdresser. Sienna touched her short hair. "I like it," she said.

Logan stood in the school hallway. It was his first day of school! He held his red lunchbox tight. Mr. Nowak smiled and said, "Let's put your lunchboxes on the shelf."

Logan put his red lunchbox down. Then Juliet came. She put down a red lunchbox too. It looked just the same! Two red lunchboxes sat side by side.

At lunch time, Logan ran to the shelf. He grabbed a red lunchbox. He opened it. Inside was a banana. But Logan had an apple! Juliet opened the other one. "That's mine!" she said. "My banana!"

Mr. Nowak came over. "Open the lids," he said. Juliet's lid said Juliet. Logan's lid said Logan. Mommy had written his name at home! Logan picked the lunchbox with his name. His apple was inside. "My name helps my lunchbox find me!" said Logan.

Juliet laughed. "I want my name on my lid too." Mr. Nowak got a marker. They sat in a cozy circle on the floor. After lunch, they went to build a big block tower. Logan stacked a block high. "First day is the best day!" he said.

Thomas wanted his striped socks. He wanted them for the zoo trip tomorrow. "Can I bring my socks now?" he asked. "Later," said Dad. "We will pack later." Thomas sat on his bed. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. Thomas found a coin under his pillow. He turned it over. He looked at the clock. "Is it later now?" he asked again. "Now is bedtime," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away." Thomas yawned. He put the coin on his table. First he had a drink of water. Then he had a cuddle. Then Dad said, "Now it is later. Let us pack." Thomas dropped his socks in the bag. He smiled at the coin. "Tomorrow we go," he said, and closed his eyes.

Amelia was at Grandma's house. She found a big jar of buttons. "I want to count them all," she said. "One, two..." Then she stopped. What came after two? She tapped her finger on her chin. The number word would not come out.

Grandma sat down next to her. "Let's sing it," said Grandma. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." Amelia laughed. The words rhymed! Shoe went with two. Door went with four. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." Amelia sang along. The rhymes helped the numbers stick in her head, like glue.

"Nine, ten," sang Grandma. "A big fat hen!" At that moment, something went cluck outside. A real hen was at the window! Amelia jumped up. "Grandma, the song sent us a hen!" Grandma laughed her gentle laugh. "Maybe she wants to count too."

Amelia picked up one button at a time. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." She laid the buttons in a row. When a button rolled off the table, she watched it sink deep into the couch cushions. "Button, come back!" she called. The hen clucked twice, as if she was counting too. "One, two," said Amelia. "Even the hen knows the song."

Luka sat at the dinner table. He ate his carrots first. Then he ate his bread. "May I have some milk?" he asked. His dad gave him a cup.

After dinner, Luka had a bath. The water was warm. His mom washed his hair. Then she helped him put on his pajamas. Luka brushed his teeth. "Why do I brush now?" he asked. His mom said, "We brush our teeth before bed." Then Luka got two kisses and went to his bed.

His dad read him a story. Luka closed his eyes. Then he opened them wide. "Wait!" he said. He jumped out of bed. He ran to the bathroom. He looked at his toothbrush. It was dry! "I forgot," he said. "Mr. Njoroge says we brush in the morning too." He brushed fast, then ran back to bed. His toothbrush stood in the cup, all wet and shiny. "Goodnight, toothbrush," said Luka.

Aurora sat at the little red table. Mr. Murphy put out two bowls of blocks. "Which bowl has more?" he asked. Aurora looked and looked. She did not know.

"Can I count them?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said Mr. Murphy. She pointed at the blocks. "One, two, three, four, five." That bowl had five. The other bowl had four. "This one has more," she said. Zack clapped. "You did it!" he said.

Nawab came over with a funny owl sticker on his hand. He held up one block. "Put it in my bowl," said Aurora. He did. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She laughed. "It went up!" Zack made a pretend rip sound, like a rocket. "Next stop, number ten!" said Nawab. Aurora put one more block in and began to count.

Audrey was at Grandma's house. It was almost bath time. Audrey wanted to make bubbles, but the soap was dry and smooth.

Grandma turned on the water. She helped Audrey wet her hands. Then Grandma put soap on Audrey's palms. "Now rub them," said Grandma. Audrey rubbed and rubbed. The soap was dry no more. Big white bubbles grew on her hands!

Audrey giggled and put her bubbly hands on her chin. "Look, Grandma! A soap beard!" she said. Grandma laughed too. Audrey rubbed some more soap and made a bunny tail of bubbles. The water was noisy in the tub. What fun!

After the bath, Audrey put on her soft pajamas. She tried to zip them up herself. The zipper was hard, but she pulled and pulled. Then it went up, all the way. Audrey got into bed and hugged her bear. "Bubbles tomorrow," she said, and closed her eyes.

Avery ran into the big gym. "Game time!" she shouted. "Hold on," said Ms. Ivanova. "Teams warm up by running or stretching before a game." Avery made a funny face. "But my legs are already fast!" she said.

Francesco was already jogging in a little circle. He looked like a wobbly duck. Avery giggled. Then she jogged too. Her arms pumped. Her feet went tap, tap, tap on the floor. Aleksander stretched tall like a tree, then folded down like a folded blanket.

Then the game began. Avery zoomed for the ball. Her legs felt warm and quick. She kicked it right to Francesco. He kicked it in! "Hooray!" everyone yelled. Then the whistle blew. Avery patted her legs. "Good legs," she said. "You warmed up just in time."

Florence stood at the bus stop with her dad. The sun was out. It was sunny and warm. Florence wore her little hat.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind blew Florence's hat right off. "Oh no!" said Florence. Her dad picked up the hat. He put it back on her head. "Hold it with your hand," he said. Florence held on tight.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. It was rainy now. Drip, drip, drip. Rain fell on the bench. Rain fell on the road. Rain fell on Florence's arm.

Her dad opened his umbrella. He held it over Florence's head. The rain went plip, plip on the umbrella. But Florence stayed dry. Not one drop fell on her head. "Look, Dad! The rain can't get me!" she said.

Soon they saw the bus. It was not far away. It stopped with a big puff of air. The doors opened. Florence and her dad climbed in. They sat down together. Outside, the rain kept falling. Inside, Florence was warm and dry. "Good umbrella," said Florence. Her dad smiled and held her hand.

Natalie sat on a big chair in the kitchen. Her mom put a towel around her. "Mr. Castillo will cut your hair here today," Mom said. The doorbell rang. Mr. Castillo came in with his scissors and a comb.

Natalie hid behind Mom. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Mr. Castillo kindly. He snipped a little curl near her ear. Natalie watched it fall. It landed on the towel. "Look, Mom! The curl came off!" she said. She touched her ear. It felt the same. It did not hurt at all.

Mr. Castillo kept cutting. Snip, snip. Little hairs fell like soft rain. Then Mom picked up the first curl. She put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Natalie. Mom said, "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut." Natalie peered at the envelope. "Can I see it again?" Mom opened it. The little curl was still there, safe inside. Natalie smiled. Her hair was short now, and the curl would stay.

Parker woke up on a big morning. Mom came home with the baby. The baby was Parker's new little brother. Parker wanted to grab him for a hug right away.

"Sit on the low couch," said Mom. Mom sat down too. She put one hand under the baby's head. She kept it there.

"Why do you hold his head?" asked Parker.

"A new baby cannot hold up his own head," said Mom. "So I hold it for him."

Parker put out his hands. Mom placed the baby in his lap. She put Parker's hand under the soft head. "Like this," she said. Parker held very still.

The baby made a tiny sound. Parker smiled big. "I held his head," he said. "I am a helper now."

Miles sat at the little red table. He wanted to write his name. But the pencil slipped in his hand. The M came out wiggly like a snake. "My letters hide from me," said Miles. Mr. Demetriou sat down next to him. "Try again," he said. "Try again," said Miles.

Mr. Demetriou put out a paper. It had letters made of dots. "Look," he said. "Dotted letters." Miles put his pencil on the first dot. He drew over the dots, one by one. The line went up, down, up, down. Then he saw it. The dots made an M. A real M! "I made a letter!" said Miles.

His friend Evie clapped. She had a dotted paper too. Miles traced the I, the L, the E, and the S. His fingers got dirty with pencil dust, but he did not stop. Try again, try again. The last M was shaky. The first M was fine. Then he wrote the whole name with no dots. MILES.

"Look, Evie! Look, Mr. Demetriou!" said Miles. He held the paper up high. "That is me. That is my name."

Grandpa put on a happy song. "Clap with me, Gabriella!" he said. Gabriella clapped quick claps, all over the place. Her claps did not sound like the song at all. That was a puzzle.

"You clapped whenever you liked," said Grandpa. "Now listen first. Clap at the same time as the beat." Gabriella sat still and listened. The beat went dum, dum, dum. She waited. Then she clapped. Dum. Dum. Dum. Her hands matched the song!

"Again," said Grandpa. So they listened, then clapped. Dum. Dum. Dum. The song grew bigger and brighter in the room.

"Now sing with me," said Grandpa. He sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Gabriella tried. She missed some words. They sang it again. Then again. Soon she sang the whole rhyme all by herself, clapping at the same time as the beat.

Grandpa clapped for her. Dum. Dum. Dum. "You did it!"

Brooks walked home with a small box. Inside was his new puppy, Pip. "I will take good care of you," Brooks said. But Pip made a sad little cough. Brooks felt upset. "What is wrong?" he asked his mom.

"We will take Pip to the vet," Mom said. Brooks stopped walking. "The vet? Is that a people doctor?" He had been to a people doctor. He did not want Pip to sit on a big tall bed. "Puppies don't go there!" he said.

Mom smiled. "A vet is a doctor for animals," she said. "You will see."

The vet room was full of pets. A cat sat in a basket. A big dog wagged his tail. Sabrina from next door was there with her rabbit. "The vet helps animals," Sabrina said. "The vet helps animals," Brooks said again.

Pip came out of the box. The vet looked at him. "He just needs some rest," she said. Brooks tickled Pip's tummy. Pip wagged and licked Brooks's nose.

"Fun puppy," said Brooks. "Fun vet."

Luke sat in the big waiting room. His sister sat next to him with a small book. Soon the door opened. "Luke," said a lady with a smile. "It is your turn."

Luke climbed up into the tall chair. The lady put a cloth around him. She picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Luke felt something on his neck. It tickled. It itched. He wiggled and squirmed.

"Hold still," said the lady. "Tiny bits of cut hair can feel itchy on your neck." She took a soft brush. She brushed the bits away. The itchy feeling went away too. Luke sat very still.

Ananya from his class walked past with her dad. "Hi, Luke," she said. "Your hair looks short."

Luke looked in the mirror. "I like it," he said, and he shut his eyes for one more snip.

Eleanor sat at the little red table. Mr. Nakamura put out two bowls of crackers. "Count them," he said. Eleanor touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The other bowl had three. "This bowl has more!" she said. Arthur clapped.

Then Arthur took one cracker from Eleanor's bowl. He popped it in his mouth. "Hey!" said Eleanor. She counted again. "One, two, three, four. Now I have four." She frowned at Arthur. "You made my number smaller!"

Eleanor thought fast. She chose one dry cracker from the bowl. She moved it over to Arthur's bowl. "Now count yours," she said. Arthur counted. "One, two, three, four," he said. "We are the same now!"

"Same is good," said Savanna from the next seat. She held out her arm and dropped a cracker into Eleanor's bowl. "Now you have more again," she said. Eleanor laughed. "One more cracker, one bigger number!" She crunched her cracker, and it tasted salty and good. "Snack time is counting time," said Arthur. Mr. Nakamura grinned and poured the milk.

Zoey sat in a big chair in Mr. Bouchard's salon. It was really his kitchen, but he had a mirror and a cape. "Will the scissors hurt?" Zoey asked. She held her long hair with both hands. "You will see," said Mr. Bouchard. He picked up his scissors. Snip, snip. A little curl dropped to the floor. Zoey held very still. Then she blinked. "It did not hurt at all!" she said. "Not one bit?" asked Mr. Bouchard. "Not one bit. It feels like nothing." She watched another curl fall. Snip. It did not hurt either. "The hair just comes off and I can't feel it?" she asked. "That's right," he said. Zoey touched her short hair. It felt light, like it could fly in the wind. "More, please," she said. Mr. Bouchard laughed. "One little snip more," he said.

Sadie woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said her dad. It was a snow day. Sadie wanted to play in the park. So Dad helped her hang her coat on the hook. Then they put on boots and walked to the park.

At the park, Sadie saw her friend Ari. Ari lay down in the snow. He swept his arms up and down. He swept his legs out and in. Then Ari stood up. His boot made a big smudge. His angel had a mark right in the middle.

"What happened?" Sadie wondered. Did the boots do that? Ari lay down in a new spot. This time he swept his arms and legs again. Then he rolled to the side, far away from his picture. He stood up next to it. The angel was clean. Its wings were soft and whole.

"Now me," said Sadie. She lay down in the snow. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. Then she rolled to the side. She stood up next to her angel. "Look!" she said. "A snow angel!" Ari clapped his mittens. "Mine has a smudge," he laughed. "Let's make ten more," said Sadie. Dad smiled and sat down on the bench to watch them.

Leah sat in her reading nook. She had her letter cards and her book. The wall had a big letter A on it. The book had a small a on the page.

Leah froze. She looked at the wall. Then she looked at the book. "That is not A," she said. "A is big. This one is little."

She held up her card. The card had a big A on it. She put it next to the book. The small a was not the same shape at all. This was hard to figure out.

Her mom came over. Leah pointed at the page. "What is this little one called?" she asked.

"That is a lowercase a," her mom said. "It is the same letter as the big A."

Leah smiled. She turned the page. There was a small b. She pointed to the wall. "B!" she said. Big or small, it was still B.

Leah found a small c. Then a small d. She said each sound out loud. "Buh. Duh." Her toys sat close by, listening too.

She gave her mom a big hug. "Big letters and small letters," Leah said. "Same letter!" Then she turned one more page.

Aubrey walked into the art studio with her mom. There were paint jars on a long table. There was a slide of paper running down the big paper roll. Jett and Emeraude were already there.

Aubrey wanted to make a paper sun. She needed to cut out a big circle. She saw shiny scissors in a cup. They were big and silver. She reached for them.

Ms. Kim came over. "Those are the big scissors," she said. She gave Aubrey a small pair instead. "These are safety scissors. They have round tips. You cut while I watch."

Aubrey held the little scissors. They fit just right in her hand. Ms. Kim stood close by. Aubrey opened the scissors and cut a slow circle. The paper fell onto the table.

Jett cut a yellow star. Emeraude cut a green leaf. Aubrey glued her sun to blue paper. "Look, it has a big open sky," she said. Ms. Kim smiled and hung it on the wall.

Isabella sat at the little table. She wanted to make a sun for the wall. "A sun is a circle," she said. Mr. Esposito drew a big circle on yellow paper. Then he drew a square, a triangle, and a rectangle too. "One, two, three, four shapes," said Isabella.

She picked up her safety scissors. She wanted to start at a corner. She looked at the square. It had corners. Snip, snip, done. She looked at the triangle. It had corners too. She looked at the circle. She ran her finger all around the edge. It felt a little bumpy, like an egg shell. But where was the corner? She looked and looked. "No corner!" said Isabella. "A circle is round and has no corners." It just went around and around.

"So I can start anywhere," she said. Zian nodded. Gurnaaz held the paper steady. Isabella started at the top. Snip, snip, snip, slow and careful. Round and round she went. At last she cut the whole circle. "Circle, square, triangle, rectangle," she said, and she finished the sun. Mr. Esposito taped it up high. Isabella smiled at her big round sun.

Zayn woke up in his little bed. The sun was up. He was hungry. He ran to the kitchen in his pajamas.

"Cookies please," said Zayn. He pointed at the cookie jar. His mom shook her head. "Not yet," she said. "Breakfast comes first. It is the first meal of the day." Zayn pouted. He wanted cookies now.

"Let's make breakfast together," said Mom. Zayn washed his hands at the sink. The water was warm. He dried them on the soft towel. Mom cracked two eggs into a bowl. Zayn stirred with a big spoon. He made slow circles. Then Mom cooked the eggs at the stove. Zayn watched from his chair, far away.

The eggs went onto a plate. Zayn saw a yellow mountain of eggs, just for him. He took a bite. "Yum," he said. He ate it all up. Mom clapped her hands. Zayn felt proud. After breakfast, Mom got out one small cookie. Zayn smiled big. "Cookie after breakfast," he said. Mom nodded and kissed his head.

It was Dylan's birthday at school. Ms. Villanueva put a big cake on the table. It had four little candles on top. Dylan wanted to light them himself. He picked up the matches.

"Can I light the candles?" he asked. "No, Dylan," said Ms. Villanueva. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job. I will light them for you." She took the matches. She lit each candle, one by one. The flames went flick, flick, flick.

Agam and Yusra came to the table. "Make a wish," said Yusra. Dylan closed his eyes. Then he took a big breath. He shook his arms like leaves in a forest, just for fun. Then he blew. All four candles went out. "Good blowing!" said Agam. Everyone clapped. "Did my wish work?" Dylan asked. "You will see," said Ms. Villanueva. She cut the cake and gave everyone a big piece.

Romy wanted the red ball. It sat near the sand box at daycare. Jay had it.

"Can I have the ball, please?" said Romy.

Jay passed it to her. Romy held it tight. Then she saw Jay's face. He looked sad.

Inaya was playing nearby. She gave Romy a cup of juice. "Thank you," said Romy. Inaya smiled big.

Romy looked at the ball. Jay had given it to her. She ran back to him.

"Thank you, Jay!" said Romy.

Jay smiled. "Want to play catch?" he asked.

"Yes, please!" said Romy.

They played catch by the fence. The ball went too high once. It landed on the roof of the little playhouse.

"Help, Mr. Ramos!" called Romy.

Mr. Ramos got a long pole. He pushed the ball down. It rolled to Romy's feet.

"Thank you," said Romy and Jay together.

Mr. Ramos laughed. "You two say that so nicely."

Romy threw the ball to Jay. He caught it. He ran with it, then turned around.

"Thank you, Romy!" Jay called, waving the ball.

Leon wanted to splash in the big bath. He got his towel from the hook. He found his yellow duck too.

The tub began to fill. Leon put one foot near the water. "Stop," said his dad. "The water may be too hot. I check the bath water first. Then you get in."

His dad put his hand in the water. Leon waited. He made the duck hop on the floor. He counted to ten, slow and easy. "Still too hot," said his dad. He turned the tap. More cool water ran in.

Leon waited some more. He sorted his bath toys into two piles. The duck went with the boats. The cups went with the whale. His dad put his hand in again. "Now it is just right," he said.

Leon stepped in slowly. The water was warm and nice. He squeezed the whale and it went squirt. Then he made a big splash. "That is a messy one," said his dad, laughing. "The duck thinks it is fun." Leon laughed too, and made another splash.

Samuel ran into the backyard. He held up one hand. "I can count my senses!" he said.

Lucy was there by the sand box. "Show me!" she said.

Samuel pointed to his eyes. "Seeing! One." He pointed to his ears. "Hearing! Two." He pointed to his nose. "Smelling! Three." He pointed to his mouth. "Tasting! Four."

Then he stopped. His fingers were all used up. "I forgot one," he said. He looked at his hand. He looked and looked.

Lucy picked up a soft ball. She put it in his hand. Samuel squeezed it. The ball was squishy and warm from the sun.

"Touching! Five!" he shouted. "My skin feels the ball!" He waved his hand in the air. "Five senses on five fingers!"

"Let me try," said Lucy. She counted on her own hand. Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching. She got all five too.

Samuel ran to the water table. He dipped his hand in. "I feel the water!" he said. "I see it too! That is two senses!"

They built a tall sand castle together. Samuel patted the sand. "Touching again!" he said.

The neighbor, Mr. Nguyen, waved over the fence. "What are you two doing?" he asked.

"Counting senses!" said Samuel. He held up his hand again. "One, two, three, four, five!"

"May we have one more game?" asked Lucy. She was very polite.

Samuel closed his eyes. "Listen," he said. A bird sang on the fence. "Hearing! That is sense number two!"

Then he sniffed the air. "The flowers! Smelling!" He opened his eyes wide. "I can find senses all day!"

Lucy laughed and clapped her hands. Samuel clapped too. "Five senses, five fingers," he said. "High five!"

Naomi looked out the window. Snow was falling. Lots of snow. School was closed today. "A snow day!" said Naomi. It was a surprise.

Naomi put on her boots. She had to wear her red hat too. Dad said the sled hill was ready. Naomi pulled her sled up the hill. Then she lay down on her tummy. "I will go head first!" she said. Dad shook his head. "Sit up, Naomi. Face the front. Hold on tight. I will watch you." So Naomi sat up. She faced the front. She held on tight.

Dad watched. Naomi zoomed down the hill. She did not fall off. She zoomed again and again. Every time, she sat up. Every time, Dad watched. Then the sled hit a rock. The sled was not broken. It was fine. "One more time," said Naomi. Dad smiled and watched her zoom.

Madeline climbed into her car seat. She touched the smooth seat belt. Mom clicked it in.

"Is tomorrow the library day?" asked Madeline.

"No," said Mom. "It is today. Today is the day that is happening right now."

"So the library is now?" asked Madeline.

"Yes, it is now," said Mom. "Yesterday we went to the park. That day is all done. Tomorrow we can go to Jayke's house. But today, right now, we ride to the library."

The car went past one tree, two trees, three trees. Madeline counted them out loud.

"Later we will read our new books," said Mom.

"Not now?" asked Madeline.

"Not now. First we pick them. Then, later, we read."

The car stopped. Madeline looked out the window. The big library door was right there.

"We are here now!" she said. She unbuckled her bottom strap all by herself. Mom held her hand all the way to the door.

Nova went to the store with Dad. Today was a big day. Tomorrow Nova would eat breakfast with Zoya. Nova wanted strawberries for tomorrow.

"Now we are at the store," said Dad. "Later we will go home."

Nova held Dad's hand. The sun did shine through the big window. Nova felt wind whoosh from the fan above the door. It made her hair fly up.

Nova looked for strawberries. She could not find them. The cart wheel was broken and went bump, bump.

Then Nova saw Ms. Tremblay, her neighbour. "Good morning, Nova!" said Ms. Tremblay. Nova said it back. Morning is when you wake up and eat breakfast, and today Nova had woken up and eaten eggs.

"There are the strawberries," said Nova. She pointed. Dad put them in the cart.

"Tomorrow we will eat them at breakfast," said Dad. "But now, home we go."

Nova smiled and held the strawberry box all the way.

James woke up in his bedroom. The sun was on his blanket. His tummy made a little growl.

"Am I hungry?" he asked. "Yes, I am hungry."

His mom called, "Snack time!" James had been playing with his trucks. His hands were muddy from the plant pot. He ran to the table fast. He grabbed a slice of bread.

"Stop," said Mom. "We wash our hands before we eat. Look at those muddy hands."

James looked down. His fingers were brown. "Yuck," he said. Mom took him to the sink. She turned on the water. James rubbed his hands with soap. The mud went down the drain. Now his hands were clean and shiny. One of his sleeves was loose, so Mom pushed it up for him.

"Now can I eat?" James asked.

"Now you can eat," said Mom.

James sat at the table. He ate his bread and a banana. He was still in his pajamas. After snack, it was time to get dressed. He put on his shirt and his socks. Then he brushed his teeth with Mom's help.

At his class later, his teacher Ms. Virtanen read a book. His friend Edmond shared a toy car.

"Thank you," said James.

That night, James took a bath. The water was warm. He splashed a little. Mom washed his hair. Then she tucked him into bed in his bedroom.

"Am I sleepy?" James asked himself. "Yes, I am sleepy." He hugged his bear and closed his eyes. The moon came up over his window. "Goodnight, moon," said James.

Logan was at Grandpa's house. He found a big book on the soft chair. The book had a frog on the cover. Logan wanted Grandpa to read it.

"Read the frog book," said Logan. Grandpa sat down next to him. He opened the book from the front. He read the first page out loud. Logan saw little marks under the picture. Grandpa pointed at the marks as he read.

Then they came to a page with no words on it. It was just a picture of a pond. "Read this page too," said Logan. Grandpa shook his head. "There is nothing written here to read," he said. "I can tell you about the picture instead." Logan felt a little sad. He wanted words on that page too.

Grandpa turned to the next page. More little marks! Grandpa read them out loud. The frog said, "Croak!" Logan blew on the page like a pretend wind. Grandpa laughed. Logan turned the page himself, from the front to the back, all the way to the end. "The end," said Grandpa. Logan clapped his hands. "Again!"

Samuel sat in the family car. Mom was driving him to the salon. It was his first real haircut. "I want it short," said Samuel. "Like a little worm on top."

At the salon there was a fish tank. Orange fish swam round and round. Samuel turned his head to see them. Snip, snip went the scissors. "Oh no," said the hairdresser. "Now this side is long and this side is short." Samuel had turned again, and the hair came out crooked. Mom did not look mad. "Try sitting like a statue," she said. "Statues do not turn."

Samuel looked at the fish one more time. Then he sat very still. He did not move his head at all. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft rain. The hairdresser smiled. "Sitting very still helps me cut your hair neatly," she said. "Look how even it is now." Samuel saw the long side and the short side, and now they matched.

The hairdresser had a surprise. She cut one piece of hair and taped it to a card. "Your first haircut," she said. "You can draw a picture on it at home." Samuel held the card all the way to the car.

In the car, Samuel looked in the little mirror. His hair was short and neat, like a little worm on top. "I sat like a statue," he told Mom. Mom smiled and started the engine. "Home for a snack," she said. Samuel waved the card out the window at the salon door.

Snow was falling at school. Big white flakes came down. Parker ran to the window. "Snowy day!" he said.

Kyson and Nico ran to the window too. Mr. Dang smiled. "Get your coats," he said. "We can play outside."

Outside, the snow was deep. Parker stomped in it. His boots went crunch, crunch. The wind blew his thin scarf. "It is windy too," said Nico.

Parker wanted to make a snowball. He scooped up snow with his bare hands. He patted it round. Then he held the big snowball. "Ow," he said. "My hands are cold." His hands turned red.

Kyson held up his mittens. "Put these on," he said. Parker pulled on the blue mittens. He scooped more snow. He patted another snowball. His hands felt warm! "Mittens keep my hands warm," Parker said.

Then Mr. Dang pointed. "Look at the gate," he said. A snow plow truck rumbled by. Snow fell off the roof with a whoosh. Right onto Nico's hat! Everyone laughed. Nico shook his hat like a snowy dog. "Again!" shouted Parker, and he threw his snowball high into the air.

Anna went to a street festival with her mama. There was music and warm food. Anna saw a stand with pretty candles. "What is that?" Anna asked. Her mama said, "It is a menorah. During Hanukkah, Jewish families light candles on a menorah for eight nights."

A kind man named Mr. Somsak stood by the menorah. He was a neighbor. Anna counted the candles. "One, two, three," she said. "How many will be lit?" she asked. "One more each night," said Mr. Somsak. He used a long stick to light one new candle. The flame grew tall and bright.

Anna watched from a safe spot. She held her mama's hand. Next to her, Sterling and Theresa clapped for the light. Anna spotted a stand with fried chicken. Mama went to buy some. Anna shared it with Sterling. Then she looked back at the menorah. The little flames danced. Anna waved and said, "Good night, candles."

Aiden was at the art studio. He was making a paper crown. He put shiny stars on it with glue. "I will wear it now," he said.

He picked up the crown. But the crown was not ready. The stars slid off. The paper strips slid apart too. The glue was still wet. Aiden felt sad. His friend Kylie came over. She saw the wet glue on the table. "It is not late yet," Kylie said. "We can wait."

So Aiden put the crown down. He and Kylie made a baby bird from clay while they waited. Then they stood by the window. They looked at the clouds going by.

After a while, Aiden touched the glue with one finger. It was dry. He picked up the crown. The stars stayed on. The paper strips held together. The crown was ready. Aiden put it on his head. "It works!" he said. He marched around the room like a king.

Logan went to the store with his dad today. He saw a big box of cookies. "I want those," said Logan. "We can buy them later, after the bread," said Dad.

Malcolm was there too. "I went to the park tomorrow!" said Malcolm. Logan looked up. "Tomorrow? Not yet," said Logan. Malcolm laughed. "No, no. I went yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." Logan nodded. Yesterday was already gone. Today was now.

Logan held Dad's hand. They took one step, then another, down the bread aisle. Logan was upset about waiting. Then Dad came back with the cookies. "Today is our day for cookies," said Dad.

At the door, Logan saw the moon in the sky. "The moon is out now!" said Logan. Dad smiled. "And tomorrow we can eat cookies in the park."

Benjamin wanted to see the bubbles. He ran to the stove. "Hot pot," said Dad. "Stay back." Dad put his hand near the top. White steam went up, up, up. "The steam is hot," Dad said. "It can burn. Stay back." Benjamin took one step. Then one more step back. He held Dad's loose sleeve with one hand. From far away, he saw the bubbles. Pop, pop, pop. He heard the water rumble. A little ant walked across the floor. Benjamin watched the ant too. He did not touch it. "I see bubbles!" said Benjamin. "Big ones and small ones." Dad turned off the stove. The steam went away. The bubbles went away. "More bubbles tomorrow," said Dad. Benjamin waved at the pot. "Bye bye, bubbles."

Ruby sat at the dinner table. There was a jar of apple sauce in front of her. She wanted some on her plate. The lid was stuck. She pulled and pulled. Her hands slipped. The lid would not move. Ruby made a grumpy sound. Her tummy felt tight.

Then she remembered the right words. "Can you help me, please?" she asked. Ms. Hussain smiled. "Of course," she said. She turned the lid with a big twist. Pop! It came off. "Thank you," said Ruby. Ms. Hussain spooned the apple sauce onto her plate. It looked cloudy and soft.

Ruby saw her cup was far away too. "Can you help me, please?" she asked again. Ms. Hussain moved it close. Ruby took a drink. Then she mixed her apple sauce with her spoon, round and round. "More please?" she asked. Ms. Hussain laughed and gave her some more.

Iris walked into the baby store with her dad. A new baby was coming soon. Iris wanted to pick a gift. She saw a soft white sheep. It had a sticky tag on its ear. "This one," said Iris. Her dad smiled and put it in the cart.

Then Iris saw a tiny blanket and a tiny sock. She wanted the baby to wear them right away. "The baby is still at home," said Dad. "Can I hold the baby when it comes?" asked Iris. "I want to carry it around."

"You can hold the baby while sitting down," said Dad. "I will sit right beside you."

At home, the baby came. Iris sat on the couch. Dad sat next to her. He laid the baby in her arms. Iris held the sheep by the baby's cheek.

"Hello, baby," said Iris. The baby grabbed the sheep's ear.

Cooper put on his special shirt. It had little gold boats on it. Grandma was having a big party at her house. There were so many people. There were lanterns and sweet smells and drums going boom, boom, boom.

Cooper held Grandma's hand. "Why do I hold your hand?" he asked. "Because it is a big, crowded party," said Grandma. "At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up." Cooper counted the people. One, two, three, four, five. There were too many to count.

Then Cooper saw the food table. There were little cakes with jam. He let go of Grandma's hand. He took one step. He took two steps. The crowd got thick. He could not see Grandma's blue shirt. Cooper stopped. He looked back. He pushed through to Grandma and grabbed her hand again.

"Can we look at the cakes together?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandma. They walked over, hand in hand. Grandma took a jam cake and gave Cooper a small piece. It was sweet and soft. His friend Oakland came by with his grandpa. Oakland held his grandpa's hand too. "Big party," said Oakland. Cooper smiled and held on tight.

Nora sat on the small red chair. The room was warm and bright. A song was playing. Ms. Ito clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. "Now you try," said Ms. Ito. Nora put her hands together. But her claps came too fast. Clapclapclap. The beat ran away from her. Nora wanted to clap just right.
