Nora hummed to help herself. She hummed the ABC song. A, B, C, D. Crew was next to her. Crew was singing "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Nora stopped. She listened. The songs sounded the same! "Crew, do they sound the same?" she asked. Crew nodded. "The ABC song and the star song," said Crew. "Same tune!"

Nora started again. She sang "Twinkle, twinkle, little star" and clapped on each word. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps fit the beat now! Sanad clapped with her. Ms. Ito smiled. "Sing it again," said Sanad. So Nora sang the star song from start to end. She did not forget a word. Her hands clapped the whole way. Clap, clap, clap, all the way to "what you are."

Claire sat at the dinner table. Her pasta was warm. It looked like a short snake on her plate. She touched it with her finger. It felt soft and squishy.

Dad put on his glasses. He picked up his fork. Claire reached for her fork too. She wanted glasses like Dad. "Why do you wear those?" she asked. Dad let her try them on. They were too big. The room looked blurry. Claire took them off. Dad put them back on. Then he could see his plate clearly.

"Your glasses help you see," said Claire. Dad smiled and nodded. He cut the short snake pasta. Claire sniffed her food. It smelled like tomatoes. She took a bite. It tasted yummy. Claire heard Dad slurp his pasta. She slurped too. "More, please," said Claire.

Jasper sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint a dog in the green grass. But the green paint pot was empty.

"No green," said Jasper. "My grass needs green."

Haylee sat next to him. She had blue paint and yellow paint. She dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred them together in her pot.

"Look now," said Haylee.

The paint turned green. Jasper jumped up on his tiptoes.

"Blue and yellow make green!" said Jasper.

He took some blue and some yellow. He stirred his own pot. Green! He painted tall grass all along the bottom of his paper. Then he painted a big brown dog with a furry tail sitting in the grass.

Mr. Ivanova came to look. "What a happy dog," he said.

"Woof," said Jasper, and he held his painting up high.

Henry went to the library with his dad. He saw a big rug on the floor. The rug had a circle, a square, and a triangle on it. Henry put his foot on the circle. Then he put his foot on the square. Nico was there too. Nico had a bag of toy blocks. "Let's build a tower," Nico said.

Nico tipped over the bag. The blocks rolled everywhere. One block went under the shelf. Henry pointed at it. Nico could not reach it. Ms. Wijaya came with a long stick. She pushed the block out. "Thank you," said Henry.

Ms. Wijaya had some stickers. "Put one sticker on each face," she said. Henry turned the block over and over. He counted the faces. One, two, three, four, five, six. Every face was a square. He put a sticker on each one. Six stickers, six squares. "Look, Nico," Henry said. "It has six square faces." Nico clapped, and Henry smiled with a happy feeling.

Xavier was a dragon in the playroom. He had a red cape and a big paper tail. The cape stuck to his back with tape. Dragons love gold, so Xavier wanted the gold wagon first.

But Maeva and Diya wanted it too. Ms. Do clapped her hands. "Make a line," she said. "One at a time." Diya stood in front. Maeva stood in the middle. Xavier stood at the back.

The line moved very slow. Diya pulled the wagon. Then Maeva pulled the wagon. Xavier wiggled his tail. He wanted to zoom up front. He took one big step past Maeva. Maeva put her hand out. "You have to wait," she said. "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn." Xavier looked at his feet. He stepped back to his spot. He counted the wall pictures. One, two, three.

Then the wagon came to him. It was his turn at last. Xavier pulled the wagon around the room. He made loud dragon sounds. The wheels went clack, clack, clack. "Roar!" said Xavier. He pulled it past Maeva and Diya. Maeva laughed. Diya laughed too. The dragon waved his paper tail and flew down the hall.

Mackenzie did not want to sleep. "When is tomorrow?" she asked. Mom pointed at the tall clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is," Mom said. "See the little hand? When it gets to the eight, it is bedtime."

"Is it eight now?" asked Mackenzie.

"Not yet. It is seven now," said Mom. "So it is bedtime later."

Mackenzie watched the clock. The hand moved a tiny bit. Her puppy wagged his tail on the bed. "He wants to wait too," she said.

Yesterday Mackenzie had cried at bedtime. Today she did not cry. She watched the clock instead.

"Is it eight now?" she asked again.

"Now it is eight," said Mom.

Mackenzie hugged her puppy close. "Tomorrow we can watch it again," she said. Mom turned off the light.

Mateo sat on the floor at home. His tummy felt happy and hungry. "I want my toy cars," he said. Mom helped him tip out the toy box.

Out came the cars. One car, two cars, three cars, four cars. Then out came something yellow. It was not a car. It was a banana!

Mateo picked up the banana. He looked at it. He looked at the cars. "You are not a car," he said. "You are the odd one out."

Mom smiled. "That's right. The odd one out is the thing that does not belong in a group."

Mateo put the cars in a line. "One car, two cars, three cars, four cars. No banana." The banana sat all alone on the rug.

Then Mateo had an idea. He carried the banana to Mom. "Can I eat the odd one out?"

"Yes, smart boy," said Mom. She peeled it for him. Mateo took a big bite.

"Yum," said Mateo. "The odd one out is a good one."

He patted his tummy and drew a banana with his crayon, one yellow line and then another.

Juliette woke up early. Today she had to get a shot. She sat in the family car with her toy pig on her lap.

"Will the shot hurt?" she asked.

"A little poke," said her dad. "Then it is done."

Juliette felt sad. Her tummy felt tight. She hugged her pig. Where was the doctor? The car went past the bakery. Then past the park. Then they were there.

In the waiting room, Juliette held her dad's hand. She was scared. Her breath went fast and small.

Dad sat down next to her. "Smell the flower," he said. He held up his hand like a flower.

Juliette sniffed his hand. She breathed in slowly. Then she breathed out slowly.

"Like a pig sniffing apples?" she asked.

"Sure," said Dad, laughing.

Juliette breathed in slowly again. Something changed. Her tummy felt less tight. Her breath got big and calm. So slow breathing made her feel calm! She tried one more slow, deep breath.

The nurse came in. "Ready?" she asked.

Juliette held her pig tight. She took a slow breath in. Then came the little poke.

"All done!" said the nurse.

It was over so fast. Juliette got a bright bandage. On the way back to the car, she sniffed the air like a flower, slow and deep.

"Again?" asked Dad.

"Yes," said Juliette. "I like it."

Olivia was at her aunt's house. Big bowls of rice sat on the table. Olivia was hungry. She picked up her spoon fast.

"Wait," said her cousin. "We say Bismillah first."

"What is Bismillah?" asked Olivia.

"It means in the name of God," her cousin said. "Many Muslims say it before they eat."

Olivia put her spoon down. She felt a little worried. She did not know the words yet. Her aunt sat close to her. "You can say it with me," her aunt said.

Everyone held hands. Her aunt said, "Bismillah." Olivia said it too, small and slow. Then her cousin said it. The whole table said it together.

After that, Olivia took a big bite of rice. It was warm and good. Her aunt smiled at her.

Later there was a bath before bed. The water was warm and bubbly. Olivia splashed her rubber duck. She did not try to break the bubbles on purpose. She just patted them soft.

"Can we say Bismillah at breakfast too?" Olivia asked.

"Yes," said her aunt. "We can say it together."

Olivia hugged her duck. She was happy. "Bismillah," she whispered to the water.

Olivier ran to Adonis's house. Adonis had a tablet. "Can I draw?" asked Olivier. "Yes!" said Adonis. Olivier pressed the round button. The screen lit up. He tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared. He drew a big red park with slides and swings. He drew a yummy green apple in the park. "Is my park done?" he asked himself. "Yes, it is!" Then Olivier put the tablet on the couch. He ran to get juice. Adonis's dad came in. He was about to sit down. "Wait!" shouted Adonis. The tablet was right there on the cushion. Adonis's dad picked it up. He put it on its shelf. "The tablet goes back in its special place," he said. Olivier grabbed his juice and watched. Then he pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet to the shelf all by himself. "I did it!" said Olivier. Adonis clapped.

It was bedtime. Mila did not want to sleep. "Mama, is tomorrow real?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow comes after you sleep." Tomorrow was bath day, and bath day meant bubbles.

Mila looked out the window. The sky was dark and stormy. Rain went tap, tap on the glass. "Is the storm here now?" she asked. "It is here now," said Mama. "But soon it will stop." "What is soon?" asked Mila. "Soon means in a little while," said Mama.

Mila waited. She heard the rain. Tap, tap, tap. Then it got quiet. The rain had stopped! Mila peeked at the window. A car went by on the wet street. Mama sat close and read a little book to her. Mila yawned. The storm was over, and soon it would be morning. She closed her eyes.

Isaac ran to the block corner. Calvin was already there. He had all the blocks in one big pile.

"I want blocks too," said Isaac. He reached out his hand to grab one.

Ms. Malik knelt down beside them. "Let's think," she said softly. She put her hand over the pile like a roof.

Isaac looked at the blocks. Then he looked at Calvin. "Can we build one tower together?" he asked.

Calvin smiled. "Yes! One big tower!"

Isaac put one block down. Calvin put the next one on top. They took turns, one block at a time. The tower grew tall, far taller than before.

"Uh oh," said Isaac. A block wobbled and did not spill all the way. Calvin held it still.

"Good catch," said Calvin.

"My turn?" asked Isaac.

"Your turn," said Calvin.

Ms. Malik clapped her hands. "What a tall tower," she said.

Isaac grinned so wide his mouth hurt. "We built it together!"

Addison sat on the big rug in the living room. Dad turned on the TV. The big game was starting! Soraya came over with her red hat on. Aram came too, with popcorn to share.

"Who will win?" asked Addison. "I hope my team wins!" Everyone shouted and clapped. The teams ran and kicked the ball. The score was two to two. Then it was three to three. Addison jumped up and down.

The game ended. "Who won?" asked Addison. She looked very worried. "Is it scary when nobody wins?" Mr. Yang, the neighbour, smiled. "Both teams have the same score," he said. "It is called a tie."

"A tie!" said Addison. She clapped her hands. "Both teams get to be happy!" Soraya spun around in her red hat. Aram held up the popcorn bowl like a prize. Dad put his hands on his head and laughed. "Same score again," he said. "Every single year!"

Elliot was at Juniper's house. The toast was warm. The butter was soft and yellow. Elliot took his little knife. He held the toast with one hand. He brushed the butter on. Slow, slow strokes. The butter melted into little shiny pools. "Look," said Elliot. "I did it all by myself."

Then Juniper's dad put out a big jug of milk. Elliot wanted to pour his own cup. He held the cup up in one hand. He tipped the jug with the other hand. Milk went splash, splash, splash. It made a puddle on the table. "Oh dear," said Elliot. "Why did it spill?"

Juniper's dad wiped the puddle with a cloth. It was soft and quiet in the sunny kitchen. "Try it down here," he said. He set Elliot's cup on the table. Elliot put his hands in his lap. Then he picked up the jug with both hands. He tipped it, slow and careful. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell out. The cup sat still on the table, and the milk sat still too. "It worked!" said Elliot. Out the window, a little bird looked in. "Hello, bird," said Elliot. "Want some toast?"

Lucy went to Skyla's house. Skyla had a big teddy bear and a tiny cup. Lucy wanted to play too. But she did not know how to start. She stood by the door and watched.

"What are you doing?" Lucy asked.

"I am feeding my teddy," said Skyla. "He is my baby." Skyla patted the bear. Lucy still stood still. Her tummy felt tight.

Then Lucy had an idea. She took a deep breath. "Let's pretend," she said. "Let's pretend I am the doctor. Your baby needs a check-up!"

Skyla's face went bright. "Yes! Knock on my door, Doctor Lucy." Lucy knocked on the wall. Knock, knock. Skyla held the teddy up. "Come in, doctor."

Lucy listened to the bear's heart. "Your baby is fine," she said. "He needs a hug." Skyla hugged the bear. Then Skyla found a special little hat for Lucy to wear.

Lucy smiled. Those two words made the game begin. She said them again. "Let's pretend we are puppies!" Skyla barked and laughed. The two friends played until the sky turned dark.

Mya stood at the bus stop. She held her yellow hat in her hands. The sun was out, and it made the road hot. "Jalen is coming on the bus," said Mya's mom. "I want to show him my hat."

Then the wind came. The wind blew Mya's hair. The wind blew a paper down the street. Mya held her hat tight so it would not fly away.

Then a big cloud moved in the sky. The clouds hid the sun. The road was not hot anymore. "Where did the sun go?" asked Mya. "Look up," said her mom. "The clouds hide the sun sometimes." Mya watched and waited. Rain began to fall. Mya's mom put up her umbrella.

The bus came. Jalen jumped down. He wore his rain boots. "My mom glued my boot strap," he said. "It broke on the swing yesterday." The rain made little taps on the umbrella. Mya gave Jalen her hat. "It will keep the rain off your head," she said. Then the cloud moved away. The sun came back out. Mya pointed up at the bright sky and smiled.

Grace wanted her bedtime book. It was on the shelf in her bedroom. The cover was shiny and blue. She could not find it under the blanket.

"Where is my book?" she asked. Mama pointed to the pillow. There it was, under the fluffy pillow.

Grace sat on the bed. She opened the cover. Then she turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back. The last page had a little seed on it, small and brown.

Mama sat down. She held the book. She read the first page. "The sun can shine on the seed," Mama read. Grace looked at the words. They sat on the page like little black dots.

The next night, Daddy came to read. He opened the same cover. He read the first page. "The sun can shine on the seed," Daddy read.

Grace sat up. "Daddy, you said what Mama said!"

Daddy smiled. "Yes, I did."

Grace put her finger on the dots. "Say it again," she said.

Daddy turned the page. The sun came up over the seed.

Ivy sat with Frederick and Nihaal at the restaurant. The big screen showed a soccer game. The players ran and ran. "The blue team runs so much," said Ivy. "They must be winning."

"Let's check the score," said Frederick. He pointed at the numbers. The blue team had two points. The red team had three points. "The red team wins," said Nihaal. "They have more points."

Ivy looked again. The blue team ran more. But the red team had more points. "So more points means you win," she said.

Later the red team kicked the ball in. The score went up. Everyone cheered. "We are lucky," said Ivy. "We saw the winner!"

On the way home, Ivy saw a sheep in a field. Its wool was soft and white, like a cloud that could color itself pink in the sunset. She waved at it.

"Did the red team run less and still win?" she asked. Her dad nodded. "Yes. More points won the game."

Ivy smiled and held his hand all the way to the car.

Emily sat at the little red desk. It was snack time at daycare. Ms. Popal held a big bowl of green peas.

"Peas for you, Emily?" asked Ms. Popal.

"Yuck!" Emily shouted loud. Beauden covered his ears. Emersyn made a face.

Ms. Popal did not give her any peas. She just looked at Emily.

"Try again," Ms. Popal said. "Say, 'No, thank you.'"

Emily thought about that. Could words be tried two ways? She looked at the peas. They were round and green. She did not want them.

"No, thank you," said Emily, soft and small.

Ms. Popal smiled. "You are welcome. Would you like some crackers instead?"

"Please," said Emily.

Ms. Popal put crackers on her desk. Later, Emersyn spilled water and it went splash on the floor. Emersyn said, "Sorry, Ms. Popal."

Emily munched her crackers. Maybe words were like shoes, she wondered. Some fit nice, and some stomped too loud.

Beauden passed her a napkin. "Here you go."

"Thank you," said Emily.

Then she ate the last cracker, crunch.

Emmett ran to the park with his red car. He carried it in his little hand. First he went to the swings. He pumped his legs up high. Then he went down the slide. Then he played in the sand.

"Where is my car?" Emmett cried. His hand was empty! He looked in the sand. No car. He looked under the slide. No car.

His friend Peyton ran over. "Retracing your steps," said Peyton. "You go back to each place you went. In order!"

Emmett jumped up. "The swings were first!" He ran to the swings. He looked under the seat. No car. "The slide was next." He looked at the bottom of the slide. There it was! The red car sat in the thin grass.

Emmett held his car up high. "I found it!" he shouted. He ran to the water fountain for a drink. Then he put the car deep in his pocket. "You stay in there," he said.

Victoria stood at the little sink. Lunch was coming soon. First she had to wash her hands. She made bubbles, rinsed fast, and turned off the tap. Was that long enough? She looked at her hands and wondered.

Van was washing beside her. "Mr. Doyle taught us a song at camp," Van said. "You sing while you scrub. It goes to twenty seconds." Van started to sing. It was the camp fire song. Victoria sang along. She scrubbed and scrubbed. The bubbles grew big. Her sleeve was loose, so she pushed it up high. The song kept going. She kept washing. Then the song was done, and twenty seconds were done too. Victoria rinsed the bubbles away.

At the lunch table, Victoria looked at her clean hands. "I sang the whole song," she said. Her mom gave her clean hand a little kiss. Victoria smiled and picked up her sandwich.

Jack was at the little table in the art room. He had red paint and a big brush. He painted a fire truck. He painted one wheel, two wheels, three wheels, four wheels.

"Time to go home," said Ms. Dlamini. Jack put his brush in the red paint cup. He forgot all about it. He got his coat and went home.

The next day, Jack came back to the art room. He picked up his brush. He tried to paint. The brush would not bend. It was hard like a stick. "Oh no," said Jack. "My brush is stiff."

Ms. Dlamini held the brush near the water cup. She turned on the tap. The water was warm and safe. She let the water run over the brush. Little bits of red paint came off. They swirled in the sink. Slowly the brush got soft again.

"Now I will rinse," said Jack. He painted a green tree with Beatrix. He painted one leaf, two leaves, three leaves. Then he passed his brush to Finley. Finley rinsed it too. All the brushes went back in the pot, clean and soft. "Goodbye, brushes," said Jack. "See you tomorrow."

Arya woke up with wild hair. She ran to the bathroom mirror. "Oh no," she said. Her hair stood up like a fluffy cloud. She patted it down. It popped right back up.

Arya found her brush. She touched a tangle. "Ow," she said. The tangle was mean to her brush. So she went slow. One little stroke. Then one more. She counted out loud. "One tangle, two tangles, three tangles." She brushed and brushed. Slow strokes, one by one.

The tangles came out. Her hair turned smooth and shiny. Arya made a silly face in the mirror. Then she made another one. "Smooth hair, funny face," she said, and laughed.

Now it was time to get dressed. Arya pulled on her shirt. She tugged up her pants. The zipper was stuck. She wiggled it. Then it zipped up fast. Zzzzip! After that, she went to the table. Her dad had eggs ready. Arya picked up her fork. "Big day," she said. "No tangles, zipped up, and eggs." She took a big bite and smiled.

Liam ran into his classroom. Today was Mystery Bag Day! Mr. Zhang held a big red bag. "Close your eyes," he said. "Use your fingers to guess."

Liam heard the bag rattle. He smelled something sweet inside, like a snack. Onyx went first. She touched something and laughed. "It is soft!" she said. "A feather!"

Daniella touched next. "Bumpy," she said. "A pinecone!" Her fingertips were right.

Now it was Liam's turn. He shut his eyes tight. His fingers found something round. It felt smooth, not rough. Not soft, not bumpy. Just smooth and cool. "A stone," he said. He opened his eyes. Yes! A smooth gray stone sat in his hand.

After the game, Liam touched his friendly teacher's sweater. Soft. He touched the table. Smooth. He touched the rug. Bumpy! "My fingertips can do this all day," he said.

At snack time, Mr. Zhang gave out juice. Liam tasted it. Sweet! "My tongue knows too," he said. Onyx giggled. Daniella clapped.

"Can we do the bag again?" Liam asked. Mr. Zhang smiled and shook the bag. Rattle, rattle, rattle!

Maria ran into the backyard. The sun was out, but the air felt funny. The trees waved their arms. The leaves went swish, swish, swish.

"Look, my new hat!" said Maria. She put it on her head. It was red with a big white dot. McKinley came over to play. "It's windy today," said McKinley. Then a big gust of wind whooshed across the grass. The wind lifted the hat right off Maria's head!

"Come back, hat!" shouted Maria. The hat rolled over the old swing. It tumbled by the sandbox. Maria and McKinley chased it. The wind pushed it again. It slid under the table. Maria got down on her knees and grabbed it.

She held it tight with both hands. "Whew!" said Maria. She pulled her hood up over her head instead. The wind blew and blew, but the hood stayed on. McKinley laughed. Maria laughed too.

"I need a snack after all that running," said Maria. Inside, Mom gave them each a cup of cold milk. Maria took a sip. It tasted so good. She looked out the window. The wind was still bending the trees. Her red hat sat safe on the table, right next to her cup.

James got a drum in music class. Mr. Cheung showed him how to tap it. Tap, tap, tap went James. Ahmad played bells. Remy played a little horn.

"Time for a show," said Mr. Cheung. James wore his spotted shirt for the big day. He tapped his drum for the class. Tap, tap, boom! The children clapped and clapped. Remy jumped up and down. But James just stood there. Then he saw Remy bow. The clapping got even bigger. Ahmad bowed too. So James bowed too. More claps! More claps!

"Again," said James. He tapped his drum one more time. Then he bowed fast and low. The class clapped, and James smiled.

Elena went to the store with her dad. She saw a spotted cup on a shelf. It had little dots all over it. Elena wanted that cup. "Can we buy it now?" she asked.

Her dad looked in the cart. "We got apples today," he said. "The cup can come tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today." Elena made a sad face. "But I want it now," she said. "First we sleep," said her dad. "Then it is tomorrow."

At home, the sun went down. Elena had her bath. Her dad helped her wipe her wet arms with a soft towel. She put on her pajamas. Then she got into bed.

Elena closed her eyes. She slept all night. In the morning, the sun came up. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "It is today now, and yesterday we saw the cup." They went back to the store. Elena held the spotted cup in her hands. "It came true," she said. Her dad smiled and put it in the cart.

Lucy went to the library with her dad. She wanted the bear book. But where was it? Lucy saw one shelf, two shelves, three shelves. No bear book.

Ms. Friedman worked at the library. She waved at Lucy. Lucy hid behind her dad. She peeked out with one eye.

"Hello," said Lucy, very small. Ms. Friedman smiled a big smile. "Hello, Lucy! Can I help you?"

"Please," said Lucy. "I want the bear book." Ms. Friedman took Lucy's hand. They looked at one shelf, two shelves, three shelves. There it was! The bear book!

"Thank you," said Lucy. Ms. Friedman smiled again. Lucy hugged the book like a hug from a friend.

"Say hello to the bear," said her dad. Lucy held up the book. "Hello, bear!" Her dad laughed. Lucy felt proud. She carried the key to the door all by herself.

Naomi sat at Grandpa's big table. She had a pencil and a paper. Today she would write her name!

Grandpa showed her how to hold the pencil. "Pinch it near the tip," he said. Naomi pinched it just like that.

She began her first letter. But the paper slid away. Her N came out wiggly. Naomi frowned.

"Why does my paper keep moving?" she asked.

"Try holding it still with your other hand," said Grandpa.

Naomi put her left hand flat on the paper. She pressed down. Then she wrote her N again. This time the N stood up straight!

"It stopped!" said Naomi. "My hand made it stay!"

She wrote the next letter. A for Naomi. Then O. Then M. Then I. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five. Five letters in Naomi!"

Grandpa clapped. "Let's play a game," he said. "Can you write it again, bigger?"

Outside the sky looked stormy. Big gray clouds rolled by. But inside, Naomi did not look up. She pressed her hand on the paper. She pinched her pencil. She wrote N, A, O, M, I.

"Look, Grandpa!" she said. "I did it two times!"

Julia was at Stevie's house. The bread went into the toaster. Julia watched it pop up. The bread was not soft and white now. It was brown and crunchy!

"What happened?" Julia asked.

"The toaster made it hot," said the dad. "Now it is toast. Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy."

"Toast! Toast!" said Julia. She clapped her hands.

"Now I will spread the butter," said Julia. She held the knife. The knife was not sharp. She spread and spread. The butter made a huge mountain on the toast. "Look at my mountain!" she said.

"You did it," said Stevie.

Then Julia poured the milk. She poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled! "I did it! I did it!" said Julia.

She took a big bite. Crunch, crunch. "Yummy," said Julia. "Can I have more toast?"

Mila got to daycare and saw her friend Tiago. He sat alone by the sand table. His mouth turned down at the corners. Mila did not know why.

Ms. Zhu called the children to the mirror. "Look at your face," she said. Mila smiled big. The mirror showed a big smile. Then she made a sad face. The mirror showed that too. "My face shows my feelings," said Mila. Ms. Zhu nodded. "A big smile means you are happy."

Mila ran back to Tiago. He still had a sad face. "Are you sad?" she asked. Tiago nodded. "My truck is lost," he said. "It is not in the sand."

Mila got a little shovel. "Let's dig," she said. They dug in the sand together. Mila dug and dug. Then she saw something red. It was the truck!

Tiago's mouth turned up. Now he had a big smile. "You made me happy," he said. Mila smiled too. Later they drew trucks on the computer together. Two big smiles in the screen.

Elliot sat on his bed. The sun came in his window. It was bedtime now. "I want my blue sock now," said Elliot. He looked under the bed. No sock.

"Yesterday you wore the blue sock," said Dad. "Maybe it is in the wash." Elliot was sad. His sock was missing. "Can we find it now?" he asked. "Not now," said Dad. "Now is this very moment. Now it is sleepy time. We will look in the morning, after breakfast. That is later."

Elliot thought about later. Later came after sleep. "Will morning come tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Tomorrow comes after today. Sleep comes first."

Elliot put his teddy next to him. He closed his eyes. He slept all night. In the morning the sun came in again. It was a new day. Dad said, "Now we can look." They looked in the basket. There was the blue sock, all clean.

"Now I can wear it!" said Elliot. He put it on his foot. "Now means right this minute," he said, and he ran to breakfast.

Harrison ran to the playground with his mom. The sun made the slide hot. He touched the slide with one finger. "Ouch," he said. The slide was too hot. His mom poured water on it. The water made the slide cool. Harrison slid down and laughed.

Then he saw Kimberly by the bench. She was looking at something on the ground. It was a little bottle. Bright dots fell out of it. They were red and yellow. "They look like candy," said Kimberly. She reached out her hand.

"Stop," said Harrison. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy." Kimberly pulled her hand back. They did not touch the dots. They ran to the coach. The coach picked up the bottle with a tissue. "Thank you," she said. "You two did the right thing."

Harrison jumped down from the bench. He landed on his knee, then stood up fast. He was okay. Kimberly clapped for him. On the way home, Harrison held his mom's hand. He saw one small bug crawl up a green leaf. He wondered, where do red and yellow bugs go at night?

Arlo woke up in the dark. "It's morning!" he said. He ran to the window. No sun. Just stars and one big moon. Dad laughed softly. "It's still night," Dad said. "Day and night are opposites. Day is bright. Night is dark."

But Arlo was awake now. "Can we go to the store?" he asked. Dad said yes, because they needed milk. Off they went into the cold night air. Brrr! Arlo zipped his coat up fast.

The store was bright like day inside. Arlo found the milk. The big carton was too heavy. He picked the small one instead. Next they passed the bakery. A grown-up pulled hot bread from the oven with big mitts. Arlo stayed back and watched. The bread smelled so good. Dad bought Arlo one small roll.

At the checkout, they saw Ms. Yoon. She was buying slow-cooked soup and fast cookies. "Hello, Arlo!" she said. "The moon is still up!" Arlo waved. He munched his warm roll on the way out.

The night sky was still dark. The street lights were on. Arlo looked up. The moon followed the car all the way home. "Good night, moon," Arlo said. "See you at day."

Lucy went to the laundromat with her dad. It was cold outside. The big windows rattled in the wind. Lucy wore her red coat, but the zipper was open.

"I want to feel the air," Lucy said. She pushed the zipper all the way down. Then a cold wind came through the door. It touched her tummy. Lucy shivered and hugged her arms.

"Dad, I am cold," she said. Dad held the zipper for her. "Now you try," he said. Lucy put the two parts together at the bottom. Click. She pulled the tag up, up, up. The zipper ran all the way to her chin. The cold air stayed outside the coat. Lucy was warm inside it.

"That was not a naughty zipper," said Mr. Russo, who was folding towels. "You just had to learn it." Lucy laughed. She paid no mind to the wind now.

On the walk home, they waited at the corner by the road. Lucy zipped her coat up and down, up and down. "I can do it all by myself," she said. Dad held her hand and smiled.

Abigail found a big red book at daycare. She wanted to read it to her stuffed bear. She sat down and opened the cover. But the pages felt all mixed up to her.

She started at the back page. She put her finger on the right side of the page. She slid it to the left. "Bear, why is the story backwards?" she asked. Bear said nothing at all. Salma giggled from the carpet. "Your words are walking the wrong way!"

Ms. Bui came over. "Turn to the front of the book," she said. Abigail turned to the first page. Ms. Bui tapped the left side. "Start here," she said. Abigail slid her finger from left to right. "The cat sat on the pot!" she read. Salma laughed. "The cat is silly!"

"The cat has a young kitten," Abigail read next. "What will the kitten eat?" asked Elea, sitting down close. Abigail ran her finger from left to right again. "Fish!" she said. "The kitten will eat fish!"

Abigail turned one page, then another page, all the way to the back. Then she hugged the book. "Good story, book," she said. She held it up high like a trophy. "I read it all by myself!"

Hudson held his dad's hand at the street festival. There were bright flags and happy songs. There were tables with sweet treats. Hudson saw his friend Lewis with his family.

"Eid Mubarak," said Lewis to a man at a table. The man smiled big. He gave Lewis a cookie. Then Lewis said it again to an aunt. She smiled too and gave him a sticker.

Hudson wanted a sticker. He wanted a smile like that. He watched Lewis some more. A little bee flew by a flower pot. Hudson stayed close to his dad. Then a kind lady walked up to their group.

Lewis looked at Hudson. "Try it," Lewis said. Hudson took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak," he said to the lady. She clapped her hands and smiled. "Eid Mubarak to you too," she said. She gave Hudson a shiny sticker with a moon on it.

Hudson put the sticker on his shirt. He ran to the next table. "Eid Mubarak," he said to the grandma there. She laughed a soft laugh and waved. Hudson waved back. "Last one, then we eat," said Dad. Hudson grinned and looked for the treat table.

Ella ran to the toy shelf at the community centre. Ten little cars sat in a row. She wanted to count them all by herself.

Ella started at one end. "One, two, three," she said. Giovanni sat down at the other end. He started at his end. "One, two, three," he said too.

Ella got to ten. She jumped up. "Ten cars!" she shouted. Giovanni stopped and looked at her. "But I got ten too!" he said. "I started at the bottom end!"

Ella frowned. "That cannot be the same." They decided to try again. Ella started at her end. Giovanni started at his end. They did not talk. They only counted.

"Ten," said Ella. "Ten," said Giovanni. They both laughed.

Ms. Kaur came over with two plates of crackers. "Who has more?" she asked. Ella looked. "Same!" she said. "Both have ten!" She hugged the cars. "You can start anywhere and still get ten!" said Giovanni.

Ella munched her crackers and smiled at the little row of cars. "Ten," she whispered, "from both ends."

Hailey was at school. Mr. Nasser had a big red kite. The kite had a long yellow tail. It looked like a fire bird in the sun.

Hailey wanted to hold the fire bird. She reached out her hand. But Sawyer was holding the string. Sawyer pulled the kite close to his chest.

"May I have a turn?" Hailey asked. Sawyer smiled big. "Yes! May I is a magic way to ask." He put the string in her hands. The kite pulled like a puppy on a leash.

The kite went up, up, up. It tickled a cloud. Hailey felt the wind push her fingers. "Thank you, Sawyer!" she called. Then the kite dipped down. It bumped Romain's elbow. "Sorry!" said Hailey. "It's okay," said Romain.

Then Hailey got tangled in the string. She could not get free. "I need help, Mr. Nasser!" she said. The kind man knelt down. He untangled her, slow and easy. The red fire bird danced in the sky, waiting. "Now you fly," said Hailey, and she gave the string a tiny tug.

Theodore sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint a rainbow. He looked in the paint box. There were only three pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

Layne sat near him. "Only three pots," said Layne. Mr. Pelletier came over. He held up the pots one by one. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," he said. Then he went to help Aariv find a brush.

Theodore dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a red stripe on his paper. Then he put his brush in the yellow pot. He made a yellow stripe next to the red. The colours touched. Where they met, a new colour grew. It was orange! "Look!" said Theodore. Layne leaned over to see. Then Theodore tried blue and yellow. Green! He tried red and blue. Purple! He painted a rainbow with his new colours. Then he gave Layne the red brush. "You can try," he said. Layne smiled and dipped it in the yellow.

Juliette stayed at Grandma's house. She wore her pink party dress all day. She twirled in the kitchen. She ate an apple at the table. She carried her shoes to the door. At night, Grandma said, "Time for bed."

"I want to sleep in my party dress," Juliette said. Grandma held her hand. They went to the cozy room. Grandma laid out soft pajamas with stars on them. "These are pajamas," Grandma said. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in."

Juliette touched the party dress. It was stiff and tight. She touched the pajamas. They were soft like her blanket. She pulled on the pajamas. They felt warm and snug. She climbed into bed. Then she saw something in her pocket. It was a tiny star sticker from the party! Juliette stuck it on her pajama sleeve. "My pajamas have a star now," she said. Grandma smiled and turned off the light.

Harrison ran to the swings at the playground. The big swing was taken. Annabelle was on it. Harrison wanted that swing a lot.

He asked, "Can I have a turn, please?" Annabelle jumped off. "You can go now," she said. Harrison smiled. Then he had an idea. "You can have my snack," he said. He held out his crackers.

Annabelle took one. "Thank you," she said. She stood very quiet. She did not know what to say back. Ms. Dlamini was sitting on the bench. Harrison waved to her. "Please help," he said.

Ms. Dlamini came over. She whispered to Harrison. Harrison nodded. He had heard his dad say it at home. "You're welcome," he said to Annabelle. Annabelle smiled big. "You're welcome," she said back to him.

Then Kaysen ran up with a glue stick in his hand. "My paper bird lost a wing," he said. "Can you help, please?" Harrison and Annabelle helped glue the wing. "Thank you," said Kaysen. Harrison said, "You're welcome." Annabelle said it too. The three friends sat on the quiet grass and shared the crackers, one by one.

Olivia sat in her bed. It was a rainy night. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap. Her book was on the blanket. It had a bunny on the front. The bunny had big soft ears.

"Who drew this bunny?" Olivia asked. She hugged the book. "I want to know." Her sister came in to say good night. "Open the front cover," her sister said. "The name is inside." Olivia opened the front cover. She turned the pages one by one, front to back, just like at story time. There it was. Words on the page. "Drew Byrd," she read slowly. "Who is Drew Byrd?" "The person who painted the pictures," her sister said. "That is called the illustrator."

Olivia clapped her hands. "Drew Byrd made my bunny!" she said. She looked at the words again. The marks on the page had told her a name. The rain went tap, tap, tap. Olivia yawned and chewed the corner of her blanket. She held the book up high. "Good night, Bunny," she whispered. "Good night, Drew Byrd."

Dylan was going on a big trip. His family would visit a national park. First they had to ride on a plane.

At the airport, Dylan put his backpack on a moving belt. Inside was his toy bunny. The backpack slid away from him. It went right into a big machine!

"Bunny!" Dylan shouted. "My bunny is gone!"

Dad held his hand. "Wait and watch," Dad said.

Dylan stood on his toes. His toe tapped the floor. He waited and waited. What would the machine do?

Then Dylan saw it. His backpack came out the other side of the machine! He grabbed it fast and hugged his bunny tight.

The sky was cloudy when the plane landed. The national park had tall trees. Dylan found a smooth gray stone. He set it in the sun, and the stone felt warm. He put it in the shade, and it felt cool.

"Look, Dad," Dylan said. "Sun makes it warm."

Jacob was at home. He put his toy bear in a bag. "Bear needs a checkup," he said. Mom said, "Jacob has a checkup too."

At the doctor's office, the nurse said, "Time for your shot." Jacob held his bear tight. The nurse counted. "One, two, three." The shot was quick. It was done.

Then the nurse did something new. She put a small bandage over the spot. Jacob looked at his arm. The bandage had stars on it. "Stars!" said Jacob. He had a question. "Does Bear get one?" The nurse smiled. She put a tiny bandage on Bear's soft arm too.

Afterward, Mom took Jacob to the ice cream shop. Brayden was there with his dad. "Look," said Jacob. He held up his arm. "Stars!" Brayden leaned in close. "Cool," said Brayden. Jacob held up Bear. "Bear has one too." Brayden counted the stars. "One, two, three, four."

Jacob licked his ice cream. The bandage stayed on his arm. It stayed on Bear's arm too. "My turn next time," said Brayden. Jacob waved his arm. The little stars caught the light.

Matteo went to the library with his dad. He saw a round rug. It was a circle. He hopped on it. "I am a frog on a lily pad," he said.

In the craft room, Kailey was there. "I want to make a sailboat," she said. She had paper sails. "But I need two triangles." She held up one square. "This is all I have." Her lip went down, like a sad little slide.

Ms. Lindqvist came over. She was polite and kind. "Bring your square to me," she said. She picked up the big scissors. Matteo watched from far away, because scissors are for grown-ups. Snip! She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell into two pieces. Two triangles! Kailey clapped. "Now I have two!"

Matteo wanted to try it too. He found a square paper. He gave it to Ms. Lindqvist. "Cut corner to corner, please," he said. Snip! Two triangles fell on the table. One landed on Matteo's arm. He giggled. He held up his triangles like a little roof. Then he spilled the crayon cup, and three red crayons rolled in a line across the floor. Kailey laughed. "Your crayons made a train!"

Chloe hurried to the park with Lylah. They were going to make snow pictures. Chloe held her special white crayon. "I will draw big white snow," she said.

They sat on the green grass by the red slide. Chloe drew on white paper. Her snow did not show. The white crayon looked like nothing at all. "Where did my snow go?" she asked. Lylah held up her yellow paper. "Try mine," she said. Chloe drew on it. Now the white snow showed up bright and pretty, like real snow, because freshly fallen snow is white. "It works!" said Chloe.

They made snow all over the blue and yellow and green paper. Keenan ran over to see. "Snow in the summer!" he laughed. Chloe held up her picture. "Look at my white snow clouds," she said.

Victor looked out the window. Snow was falling on the street. Big flakes, high and slow. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day." Victor's heart jumped.

Victor put on his boots. He put on his puffy coat. He went outside to the sidewalk. His friend Rubani was there too. They made snowballs. They threw them soft and low. One snowball landed in Victor's mitten. He held it tight.

"I want to keep this one," Victor said. "I will put it in my room." He carried the snowball inside. He set it in a little cup on his table. Then he went back out to play more.

Later, Victor came in for lunch. He looked at his cup. The snowball was gone. There was only water in the cup. A wet puddle sat on the table too. "Where did my snow go?" he asked. He tipped the cup. Water dripped out, drop by drop.

Victor carried the cup to Mom. "My snow turned into water," he said. "It was warm in here." Mom helped him wipe the table. Then Victor ran to the door. "Can I lick a snowflake before it melts?" he asked. He stuck out his tongue and waited, tip pointed high, until one soft flake landed.

Addison sat at the dinner table. She pushed her peas around her plate. Her tummy felt sad inside.

"Why the sad face?" asked her dad.

"The park got rained out," said Addison. "I wanted to swing high."

Dad sat down next to her. "Rain made the park wet," he said. "But feelings change. A sad one can turn happy later."

Addison looked at her peas. She did not believe it. She ate one pea. Then she ate three more.

"Can we build a blanket fort after dinner?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Yes. You pick the blankets. I will hold the chairs."

Addison felt something new in her tummy. It felt like bouncing. It felt happy.

"I will pay you a big hug," she said.

Dad laughed. "Deal."

She ate all her peas. Then she ran for the blankets.

Emilia sat at the kitchen table. She felt scared. A nurse was coming to her house today. The nurse would give Emilia a shot.

The nurse came in with a little bag. "Hello, Emilia," she said. "This will be quick." Mama held Emilia's hand. Emilia looked at her teddy bear. She gave the bear a soft pat. Then the nurse cleaned Emilia's arm. The needle went in, just like that. "All done," said the nurse.

Emilia saw the nurse put the needle into a small hard box. It had a red lid and a little hole. "What is that box for?" Emilia asked. "It is called the sharps box," the nurse said. "The used needle goes in there." She dropped the needle in. It did not come back out. Nobody would get poked by it now.

The nurse gave Emilia a bandage with stars on it. "A little gift for being so brave," she said. Emilia smiled and held out her arm to show Mama. "Look at my stars," she said.

Luca sat at the dinner table. His spoon sat next to his plate. His cup sat next to his spoon. But Luca was not eating.

"Mr. Traoré is coming tonight," said Luca. "He tells the best jokes."

His tummy felt jumpy. His feet felt jumpy too. Luca bounced in his chair. He bounced so hard his fork fell down. Clang!

"Careful," said Dad. "You might break the fork if it falls again."

Luca picked up the fork. But he still felt excited. When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout. Luca bounced again. His chair went bump, bump, bump under him.

"Try something else," said Dad. "Try taking a big, slow breath."

Luca took a big breath. Then he took one more. His feet stopped bouncing. His tummy felt calm.

"Now squeeze your hands together," said Dad. Luca squeezed his hands under the table. It felt like holding a tiny ball. He squeezed and let go. Squeezed and let go.

Then the doorbell rang. Ding dong!

Luca wanted to shout. Instead, he squeezed his hands one more time. Then he walked to the door, one step at a time.

"Hello, Luca," said Mr. Traoré. "Why so calm?"

"I learned how to wait," said Luca.

"Good," said Mr. Traoré. "Here is a joke. What is thin and white and smiles at you?"

Luca shook his head. "I don't know!"

"A happy piece of paper," said Mr. Traoré.

Luca laughed so big that he bounced again, right on the soft rug.

"That's okay," said Luca. "The rug is bouncy."

Mia sat on the rug at book club. Ms. Levy held up big letter cards. Mia had to put the cards in a line.

She picked up a card. It was M. Where should it go? She put M way at the end, after Z. "Is this right?" she asked.

Krish shook his head. "M goes in the middle," he said. Mia frowned. The middle was so big. Which spot was the middle?

Then she had an idea. "The alphabet song helps," said Riyaan. "It sings the letters in order from A to Z." Mia began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G..." She sang slowly and pointed at each card. She stopped at L. The next letter in the song was M!

Mia slid the M card into its spot, right after L. "It fits!" she said. Ms. Levy clapped. The dark rug was full of cards now, lined up like a little wood fence.

Mia sang the song again, all the way to Z, and tapped every letter. "Now can we fix my line if I get one wrong?" she asked. Ms. Levy smiled and handed her one more card. It was Q. Mia tipped her head and began to sing, "A, B, C..."

Mason woke up early. Today he would see the dentist for the first time. He did not know what a dentist did.

"Will it hurt?" he asked his dad.

"The dentist just looks at your teeth," said Dad. "You lie down in a big chair."

At the dentist's office, the chair looked like a bed on a stand. Mason climbed up carefully. Then he pressed his hands on his knees and sat very still.

"Ready?" the dentist asked. She pushed a little handle.

The chair slowly tipped back. Mason was lying down! He giggled. It felt like a ride at the park.

"Now I can see your teeth," the dentist said. She counted them. "One, two, three."

At home, Mason told his stuffed bear all about it. "The chair leans back," he said. "Then you lie down, like you sleep."

He showed his bear on the sofa, tipping his toy cup back and forth, slow and careful. His spotted bear fell over, soft and easy. Mason laughed and did it again.

Brielle was home with her dad. Boaz came to play. Boaz had a little red car. He parked it by the blocks.

The dog next door began to bark. Brielle looked out the window. The sun was warm on her face. She could smell cookies baking in the kitchen.

Brielle picked up the red car. She zoomed it fast. Boaz made a sad face. His lip went down. His eyes got big.

"Why are you sad?" Brielle asked.

"It's my car," Boaz said. "I did not say yes."

Brielle stopped the car. She held it out to Boaz. "May I have a turn, please?" she asked.

Boaz smiled. "Yes! Then it is my turn." He rolled the car to her.

They took turns all morning. Vroom, vroom! The car went down the little slide. The dog barked again. Mommy was sick today, so Dad gave them each a cookie. One for Brielle. One for Boaz.

"Yum," said Brielle. Boaz nodded and took a big bite.

Elias went to the store with his dad. He held a small pumpkin in his hands. He wanted to paint it orange. He walked to the paint shelf.

"One, two, three," he counted the little paint pots. Red, blue, yellow, green. He looked again. "One, two, three, four." No orange pot. The orange paint was missing. Elias began to wonder what to do.

Then he saw his friend Rayden. Rayden was looking at a soft pillow in the next aisle. "Hi, Elias," said Rayden. "Why do you look sad?"

"I want to paint my pumpkin orange," said Elias. "But there is no orange paint."

Rayden smiled. "You can make it. Mix red paint and yellow paint."

Easis looked at the red pot. Then he looked at the yellow pot. His dad bought both pots for him.

At the little table in the craft corner, Elias waited his turn. He was patient. He stirred slowly. Round and round went the stick. One, two, three, four stirs.

The paint in the cup turned red, then yellow, then... orange! Real orange! Elias dipped his brush.

"Look, Rayden!" he said. "My pumpkin will be orange now."

He painted one stripe. Then two. Then three. The pumpkin glowed like a little sun.

"My turn to wonder next," said Rayden. "Maybe I will paint my pillow."

Livia sat at the big table at the library. Mr. Tehrani put out paint and paper. "We will make butterflies," he said.

Livia dipped her brush in red paint. She painted one half of her paper. She painted big spots and long lines. Camden painted next to her. He made a blue wing on one half too.

Livia looked at her paper. One wing was missing on the other side. She turned the paper over. Still missing. Mr. Tehrani smiled. "Try folding it," he said.

Livia folded the paper while the paint was wet. She pressed it with her two hands. She counted to ten, slow and slow. Then she opened the paper up.

The red spots had jumped to the other side! Now both halves had the same spots. Two wings, just alike. "A butterfly!" Livia said.

Camden folded his paper too. His blue wing printed on the other side. Arzoyi clapped her hands. Later they walked past the picture books, slow and quiet. A green frog sat on a page in Livia's book. She held it up to show Camden. "Look," she whispered. "A frog has two sides too."

Natalie stood on the basketball court. She held her ball with two hands. The sun made a bright line on the floor.

"Where do I stand?" Natalie asked. She looked left. She looked right. She saw Mark near the hoop. She saw Samar by the wall. Natalie did not know where to go.

The coach blew his whistle. The coach waved his hand. "Stand on the blue mark, Natalie," said the coach. "Now bounce the ball. One, two, three." Natalie bounced the ball. The ball went up. The ball came down. "Again," said the coach. One, two, three. Natalie bounced and bounced.

Then the coach showed her how to aim. "Push the ball up," he said. Natalie pushed the ball up. The ball hit the hoop. It went in! Mark clapped. Samar clapped. The coach clapped too.

A small dog ran across the court. It chased the rolling ball. Everyone laughed. "I wish the dog could play too," said Natalie. The coach picked up the ball. He gave Natalie a big smile. "First basket of the season," he said. Natalie hugged her ball.

Rosalie stood at the running track. Mr. De Vries held up a hoop. "Throw your beanbag in!" he said. Rosalie tossed it. The beanbag went in. "Hooray!" she shouted.

Next came the big green ball. Moshe threw it to her very hard. It was too fast. It hit her hands and bounced away. Rosalie lost her tooth-shaped sticker from her shoe, and the wind made the flags whisper. She picked the sticker up and frowned.

"Try again," said Mr. De Vries. "A gentle toss is easier to catch than a hard, fast throw," Moshe said, and he smiled. He tossed the ball gently. Rosalie held out both hands. The ball came soft and slow. She caught it! Evelyn clapped. "My turn!" said Evelyn. Rosalie whispered, "Toss it gentle." Evelyn did. Rosalie caught it again.

Isaiah wanted to play house with his teddy bear. Robert came over to play, too. Robert grabbed the teddy bear. "I am the parent," said Robert. "No, I am the parent!" said Isaiah. Both boys pulled the teddy. The teddy began to shake in their hands.

Then Isaiah had an idea. "You be the parent now," he said. "Then we switch halfway." Robert smiled big. "I will be the baby after!" So Robert rocked the teddy. He gave it a bottle. Isaiah crawled on the carpet and cried like a baby. "Waa!" he said. "My baby is a funny baby!" said Robert.

Then it was time to switch. Robert crawled and cried. Isaiah rocked the teddy and sang. Then the doorbell rang. It was Mr. Kovalenko from next door. He held a small spotted box. Inside was a toy worm on a string! "A prize for my two little neighbors," he said. Isaiah hugged the teddy tight. "Play house again tomorrow?" asked Robert. "Yes!" said Isaiah.

Lucy's hair had grown long. It got in her eyes at breakfast. "Can we make it short?" Lucy asked. "Yes," said Mom. "We will go next door. Ms. Yoon cuts hair in her house."

Ms. Yoon smiled. She put a big cape around Lucy's shoulders. "Why do I get a cape?" Lucy asked. Ms. Yoon said, "It keeps the cut hair off your clothes." Lucy giggled. The cape felt smooth and light. "I am a superhero!" she said. She waited very still, like a superhero on a hard chair.

Snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off. None got on Lucy's shirt. Lucy looked down. "The cape did its job!" she said. Ms. Yoon laughed. Then Lucy saw something round on the shelf. "Is that a pot?" she asked. "No," said Ms. Yoon. "It holds my brushes." Lucy patted her short hair. "All done," said Ms. Yoon. "Superheroes fly home now," said Lucy.

Arlo woke up early. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. "I don't know anyone there," he told his mom. "I will hang your jacket on this hook," said Mom. "And I will walk you to the door." Arlo ate his favorite breakfast, eggs and toast. Mom put a joke card in his pocket, just in case he felt sad.

At school, Arlo saw a boy standing alone by the blocks. The boy looked at the floor. Arlo remembered what his mom said in the car. He walked over. "Hi. My name is Arlo. What is your name?" he asked. The boy smiled a little. "I am David," said the boy. "Do you want to build?" asked Arlo. "Yes," said David. They stacked the blocks high, then higher, until the tower fell down. Both boys laughed.

At home time, Mom came to get Arlo. "Who is that?" she asked, pointing at the door. "That is David," said Arlo. "He is my new friend. I asked him his name, and he told me." Mom held his hand all the way home. That night, Arlo put the joke card under his pillow. He could not wait for school tomorrow. "Good night, David," he whispered to the ceiling, "wherever you are."

Aria sat at Grandma's big table. The warm bread smelled so good. Grandma put the bread right in front of Aria. Aria's tummy felt empty. She reached out her little hand.

Grandma held up one finger. "Wait," she said softly. "We say the blessing first." Aria pulled her hand back. She put it in her lap. Then Grandpa began to speak. His voice was slow and kind. Aria listened to every word.

The bread sat there, warm and soft. Aria looked at it. She did not touch it. She waited and waited. At last Grandpa said "Amen." Everyone at the table said "Amen" too.

Then Grandma smiled. "Now we eat," she said. Aria took the bread. It was still warm in her hands. "I waited, Grandma," said Aria. Grandma laughed and patted her head. "You did," said Grandma. "You are on our blessing team now." Aria took a big, happy bite.

Max was at Grandma's house. He could not find his red car. It was his favorite toy. He looked under the big chair. He looked by the door. No red car.

Max scratched his head. Where could it be? He asked himself, "Did I leave it outside?" He peeked out the window. He saw only grass and flowers. His car was not there.

Max felt like giving up. Then he heard Dad in the kitchen. Grandma was there too, making soup. Max ran to them. "My red car is lost," he said. "Will you help me look?"

"Of course," said Dad. Dad looked in the hall. Grandma wiped her hands and looked near the couch. Max looked in the toy box. Now three people were looking, not just one!

"I see something red!" said Grandma. She reached behind the couch cushion. Out came the red car. It had been hiding all along.

"You found it!" said Max. He hugged Grandma fast, then hugged Dad. "When we all look, we find it," he said. He pushed the car across the floor. "Vroom!" said Max. "Who wants to race?"

Daniel went to the playground with his teddy bear. Marguerite and Idris were there. They were playing house under the big tree.

"Come in," said Marguerite. "This is our house." Daniel sat down with his teddy. "The teddy is our baby," said Idris. Daniel rocked the teddy in his arms. The teddy got a hug.

Then Idris stood up. "A dragon is coming," he said. He made big stomping feet. Daniel held his teddy tight. He felt scared. "The dragon is mean," said Idris.

"No," said Daniel. "I want a nice dragon." Idris stomped again. Marguerite put up her hand. "Let's agree," she said. "The dragon can be nice." Idris thought. Then he smiled. "Okay. The dragon is friendly."

Idris pretended to be a kind dragon. He flew around the tree. He gave the teddy a soft pat. "The dragon wants to shop with us," said Marguerite. She picked up leaves for money. Daniel took his teddy's hand. They all walked to the pretend shop.

"We need apples for the baby," said Daniel. The dragon reached high for pretend apples. Everyone laughed. Daniel hugged his teddy close. "Our dragon is the best," he said.

Ava woke up and looked out the kitchen window. Snow was everywhere. No school today. It was a snow day at home. Ava ate her toast at the big table. The snow fell in tiny flakes. It looked soft and light.

Ava put on her red coat and boots. She scooped up some snow. She patted it into a ball. She tried to make a snowman. The ball fell apart in her hands. She tried again. It fell apart again. The snow was dry and fluffy. It would not stick.

Later, the sun came out. Ava watched from the window while her dad washed the dishes. The snow on the ground got a little wet and shiny. Ava ran back outside. She scooped up a handful. She patted it into a ball. This time the snow packed together. It stayed in a round shape. She rolled it and rolled it. The ball grew big. She stacked a smaller ball on top. The snowman stood tall. Ava found two pieces of paper in her pocket and made a little hat. "Hello, snowman," she said. Then Ava waved to him from the kitchen window before her nap. The snowman stood outside while she fell asleep.

Luca stood at the little sink. He turned the cold tap. The water felt cool on his hands. Next to it, the other tap had a red dot. Dad said, "That one is hot. I will turn it for you." Luca touched only the cold water and washed his hands.

Then Luca looked out the small window. He could see the park across the road. He wanted to swing. A bird flapped one wing and flew by. The sky was getting dark. Luca said, "Park, please!" Dad said, "First we dry hands. Then we walk there together."

At the door, Luca saw the road with cars. He put his hand up and waited. Dad took his hand. "Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street," said Luca, and Dad smiled. They crossed together, step by step.

At the park, the swing was free. Luca pumped his legs, up and down. "Surprise!" said a voice. His friend Mylan was hiding behind the pole. Luca laughed and jumped off the swing into the soft sand.

Victor went to the farm with his class. His teacher, Ms. Rajapakse, held a big basket. "We will play a senses game," she said. Victor wanted to win the game.

First Victor touched a soft sheep. "I use my hands to feel," he said. Then he heard a loud moo. "I use my ears to hear," he said. Then he saw a brown owl on a barn beam. "I use my eyes to see," he said. Then he smelled fresh bread. "I use my nose to smell," he said.

But then Ms. Rajapakse held up a red strawberry. "What do we taste with?" she asked. Victor pointed to his tummy. His friend Flynn laughed, but not in a mean way. Bo pointed to his own tongue. "Try it and see," Bo said.

Victor took a small bite. The strawberry was sweet! Then he licked a lemon slice. His face went squishy. It was sour! Victor stuck out his tongue. "I taste with my tongue," he said. The lemon made his tongue feel sour, and the strawberry made it feel sweet.

Ms. Rajapakse smiled. "You found all five senses, Victor." Victor put his hands over his ears, his eyes and his nose. He poked out his tongue one more time. "My tongue fits in my mouth," he said, "and it tastes real strawberries."

Isabella stood at the edge of the hockey rink. The ice was bright and white. Ms. Siddiqui had put hoops on the floor. She had put out beanbags and big balls too.

"Watch me," said Ms. Siddiqui. She tossed a beanbag. It went into the hoop. Isabella tossed hers. It missed. She tried again. This time it went in. Julie clapped her hands.

Then Ms. Siddiqui rolled a big ball to Isabella. Isabella tried to catch it. The ball hit her hands. It bounced right out. She tried again. Out it went again. A small mouse ran along the boards, then hid.

"Try holding it close," said Ms. Siddiqui. The ball came again. Isabella caught it. She hugged it to her chest. The ball stayed. It did not bounce out. Julie threw her ball to Kaira. Kaira hugged hers too. It stayed as well.

"Again," said Isabella. Ms. Siddiqui rolled the ball. Isabella caught it and hugged it tight. Then she kissed the top of the ball, just like a goodnight kiss for a teddy bear.

Jacob stood in the kitchen with Mom. Flour was all over his hands. He wanted to make bread for dinner.

The dough felt soft and warm. But it stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Jacob. "It is all sticky." Mom smiled. "Cooks push it and fold it," she said. "Watch me." She pushed the dough down. Then she folded it over. She did it again and again.

Jacob tried. He pushed with his palms. He folded the dough over. He did it slowly. The dough came off his fingers. It turned smooth like a little ball. "I did it!" said Jacob. He pushed and folded some more. Mom turned on the oven. Jacob stood back and watched. Soon the bread smelled warm and sweet. Dad came in and said, "The whole house smells good!" Jacob held up his hands and said, "I made this, Dad. I pushed it and folded it."

Everly was at Grandma's house. Grandma had old paint pots on the table. Everly wanted to paint a flower. She dipped her brush in yellow. Then she dipped it in blue. She made a big green dot on her paper. "Oh no," said Everly. "My yellow flower is green!"

Grandma held up a flat tray. "This is called a palette," she said. "It is for holding paint." Everly put a dot of yellow on the palette. She put a dot of blue next to it. She mixed them with her brush tip. Green! She tried red and yellow. Orange! Everly laughed. "The palette helps me try first."

She made a yellow flower with a green stem. She painted a red pot under it. Then she made one more dot, orange, for a little sun. Grandma hung the painting on the fridge. Everly pointed at the green stem. "Yellow and blue did that!" said Everly. Grandma clapped her hands.

Everett went to the library with his dad. There was story time with Mr. Balogun. Everett felt excited. He sat on a soft red mat.

Mr. Balogun read a book about a horse. "The horse can float on the water," he read. The horse sat on a little boat. Everett laughed. Danielle laughed too.

Then Danielle stood up fast. She tripped over the mat. Her book fell down. Her face looked sad. A tear rolled down her cheek.

Everett felt scared for her. He walked over slowly. He was brave. "Are you okay?" he asked.

Danielle wiped her eye. "My knee hurts," she said. "But you asked me. That makes me feel better."

Mr. Balogun helped Danielle up. He looked at her knee. "All better," he said with a smile.

Danielle smiled back. Everett sat down next to her. Mr. Balogun read one more book. It was about a brave bear.

Danielle shared her book with Everett. "Friends ask friends if they are okay," she said.

Everett nodded. He held the book gently.

Charles stood by the big piano in the band room. Ms. Fraser had said he could try it. Kayson and Israel were waiting for their turn too.

Charles looked at all the keys. He saw white keys. He saw black keys too. He pressed one white key. It made a low sound. He pressed a black key. It made a different sound. Charles wanted to make a tune, but the keys felt too many.

Then he had an idea. He played only the black keys. He pressed one, then another. He pressed them slow. The sounds went up like steps. Israel clapped. "That sounds nice," Israel said. Charles smiled and played them again. This time he went down the steps, slow and soft.

Kayson wrote a little song on paper with Ms. Fraser. Kayson pointed at each note. Charles played it on the black keys. It sounded like a butterfly hopping flower to flower. The band room door was closed, so no other sound came in. Charles played the last note soft. Kayson clapped again.

Billie wanted to play hide-and-seek at daycare. "I will hide first," said Anais. "I will hide too," said Leslie. "You seek, Billie."

Billie put her hands over her eyes. She counted. "One, two, three!" She peeked right away. Anais was still walking. Leslie was bending down behind the blocks. They had no good spots yet.

"That is too fast," said Anais. "Please count slowly, Billie. We need time to hide." Billie nodded. She tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She said each number slow and clear.

Billie turned around. She did not see Anais. She did not see Leslie. She saw a butterfly by the window. Her socks felt itchy, so she sat down to fix them. Then she saw a shoe peek out from the big red curtain.

"One, two, three," she whispered, walking closer. "Found you, Leslie!" Leslie laughed. Outside, Anais called, "You found one, now find me!"

Aurora ran into daycare. She could not find her cubby. The coats were all mixed up. Her bunny was lost somewhere too.

"Ms. Halvorsen, where is my cubby?" she asked. Ms. Halvorsen held up a card. It had letters on it. "Look for your name," she said. "Your name looks like this."

Aurora sat on the floor. She went slow past each cubby. She looked and looked. There. The same letters. The same order. A, u, r, o, r, a. She put the card and the cubby side by side. They matched. "This one is mine!" she said.

Then Mehar held out a card. "Is this one yours?" she asked. Aurora looked. The same letters, in the same order again. "Yes! It says Aurora," she said. It was her birthday card. Inside was a picture of a bunny. "My bunny!" said Aurora.

Ms. Halvorsen smiled. "Time for a story now," she said. Aurora opened the book from the front. She snuggled her bunny close. "My name found me," she said. "Happy birthday, Aurora," said Mehar.

Raphael went to the vet with his dad. His new cat, Milo, sat in a little box. Raphael peered in. "Hello, Milo," he said.

Ms. Buchanan was the vet. "Let's meet Milo," she said. She opened the box. Out came a small orange cat. Milo blinked two big eyes.

"Faye has a rabbit," said Raphael. "Azriel has a big dog." Milo meowed once. "Now I have a cat," said Raphael. "One, two, three pets for us."

Ms. Buchanan looked in Milo's ears. She counted his toes. "Ten toes," she said. Raphael laughed. "Ten toes, just like me!"

Raphael had found Milo at the shelter. He had walked past the dogs. He had walked past the cats. Every pet sat and waited. His dad said, "They wait for a family." Then Raphael saw the small orange cat. Milo reached one paw out. That paw picked Raphael, just like that.

Now it was time to go home. Raphael held the box with both hands. In the car, Milo gave one loud meow.

"Are you hungry?" asked Raphael.

Milo purred all the way home.

Isla stood in the garage. It was cold in there. Her coat hung on a hook by the door.

"I can do it myself," Isla said. She pushed one arm in. She pushed the other arm in. The zipper was hard. She pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. She pulled again. Zip! The coat was on.

She put on her red mittens. Then she went to find her toy magnet on the shelf. When she came back, one mitten was gone.

"Where did it go?" Isla asked.

Her dad looked at the floor. "Maybe it fell near the boxes."

There it was, under the stool. Isla picked it up. She did not want to lose it again. Then she saw the pocket on her coat. She tucked one mitten in. She tucked the other mitten in. The pocket held them both. They did not fall out, even when she jumped.

"My mittens live here now," she said. She put the magnet in too, but her dad said, "Let's keep that one on the fridge."

Isla zipped her coat all the way up. The cold garage could not get in.

"Ready!" she said. "Let's go find Akira."

Aurora stood at the water table at school. The water was warm and blue. She filled a glass cup and poured it out. Splash! Jean poured water too. Zavier filled a big red bucket.

Then Zavier tipped the bucket over. Water ran all over Aurora's dress. Her socks got wet. Her arms got wet. Water dripped from her hands, drip, drip, drip.

"I am all wet," said Aurora. Ms. Campbell-Brown held out a soft towel. It was fuzzy and yellow. Aurora took it. She rubbed her arms. She rubbed her hands. She bent down and dried her legs. The towel took all the water away. Her skin felt dry and warm.

Zavier was wet too. He dripped on the floor. Aurora found another towel on the shelf. "Here," she said. "A towel dries you." Zavier rubbed his hair. Water stopped dripping. His hair was soft and fluffy now.

Then Ms. Campbell-Brown said, "Snack time." Aurora put on her dry socks. She sat with Jean and Zavier at the little table. She drank water from her glass. Outside the window, a bird sat on a branch, quiet and still.

After snack, Ms. Campbell-Brown read a story. Aurora snuggled with the fuzzy towel on her lap and listened.

Lea sat in the family car. Today was her first haircut at a salon. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Mom. "You will see." Lea held her ponytail. "Do not worry," said Mom. "I will tie it back after."

At the salon, a hairdresser put a cape on Lea. Then she picked up a comb. She combed Lea's hair two times. Snip, went the scissors. She combed again. Snip. Lea counted out loud. "One comb, two combs, then a snip!" said Lea. The hairdresser smiled. "That is how I keep your hair neat," she said. Lea watched the comb in the mirror. The comb went first. Then the scissors followed. The hair fell down, down, down, soft as snow.

Back in the car, Lea touched her short hair. "Mom, the comb went first every time," she said. "It was the boss of the scissors!" Mom laughed all the way home.

Wesley ran to the art room. Big pots of paint sat on the table. Red, blue, and yellow. Mr. Berg said, "Your job today is to mix two colours."

Wesley picked blue. He picked yellow. He stirred them with his brush. The paint turned green! It looked like dragon grass. "A magic green!" said Wesley.

Leen came to look. She touched the wet paint. Her finger left a mark on the picture. "Oh no," said Leen. "My finger made a smudge." The green had a fingerprint in it, like a tiny cave.

"My dragon grass has a hole," said Wesley. He made a sour face. Then he had an idea. He painted a new dragon on top of the smudge. The smudge became the dragon's dark, secret cave.

Then Wesley painted one more green hill. "Don't touch it," he said. "We have to wait." He put his hands behind his back. Leen put her hands behind her back too.

They watched the paint dry. Slowly the shine went away. Wesley tapped it very softly. The paint stayed smooth.

"Now it can come home with me," said Wesley. He held the picture up high. "Look at my dragon in his cave," he said.

Ali sat at the picnic table. His toast was warm in front of him. Ms. Szabó put a small pat of butter on his plate. "You can do it yourself," she said. Ali picked up his knife. Grown-ups held the hot pan, but the knife was just for butter.

Ali spread the butter, one, two, three strokes. Some toast peeked out bare. He spread again, four, five. Now the butter sat in a little lump. Ali looked at it. The lump turned shiny. Then it slid into the warm toast. It melted away, all gone! Ali thought the butter had disappeared. He chewed a bite. It tasted like butter.

Next came the milk. Ali poured slowly. One drip ran down the side. "Sorry, my hands wobbled," he said. Maria brought a cloth and wiped the drip. "Good pouring," she said. Ali drank his milk and ate his toast, all buttery and warm.

Jordan woke up early. Today he would go to the dentist for the first time. His tummy felt funny. First, Mommy stopped at the pharmacy. They needed a new toothbrush. Jordan picked a blue one with soft bristles. "That one is good," Mommy said. The cashier put it in a small square box. Jordan held the box all the way to the car.

At the dentist's office, Jordan sat in a big chair. It went up and down. Then a bright light came on above his head. Jordan squinted. The light was too bright for his eyes. The dentist smiled. "The bright light above your chair helps me see inside your mouth," she said. She gave Jordan little sunglasses to wear. Jordan put them on. The bright light did not hurt anymore.

Jordan opened his mouth wide. "Ahhh," he said. The dentist looked at all his teeth. She counted them one by one. Then she said, "All done!" Jordan got a sticker shaped like a star. He showed it to Mommy. On the way out, Jordan waved at the big chair. "Bye, chair," he said. "Bye, bright light."

Eliana ran to her toy box. "Where is Bunny?" she said. Bunny was gone! Eliana looked under her bed. No Bunny. She looked in her closet. No Bunny. She looked behind the big chair. No Bunny. "I want Bunny!" said Eliana.

Mama helped her look. They found a wooden block. They found one sock. They found a book about the ocean. But no Bunny. Then Mama had an idea. "Bunny went to school with you," said Mama. "Maybe Bunny is still there."

The next morning, Eliana could not wait. She ran into her classroom. "Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya!" she called. "Bunny is lost!" Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya smiled. "Come and see," she said. "We have a lost and found box. People put things they find in it. Then the owners can get them back." Eliana peeked inside the box. There was a hat. There was a mitt. And there, on top, was Bunny!

"Bunny!" Eliana shouted. She hugged Bunny tight. Macie and Rylie clapped. "I found Bunny in the lost and found," said Eliana. She held Bunny up high, all the way home.

Joseph went to the pharmacy with his dad. He had to use the toilet. Then he rushed out fast. He wanted to look at the candy.

Mr. Guo the pharmacist called out, "Wait, Joseph. We always wash our hands after using the toilet." Joseph stopped. He turned back to the sink.

He pumped the soap into his hands. Mr. Guo said, "Now rub for twenty seconds. I will count." Joseph rubbed and bubbled. "Ten, eleven, twelve," said Mr. Guo. The bubbles grew big and white. "Nineteen, twenty!" Joseph rinsed the soap away. The germs went down the drain too.

Then came a surprise. Mr. Guo held out a little spoon. On it was a taste of honey. "A smart boy who washes so well gets a treat," he said. Joseph had wished for candy, and this was even better. He licked the spoon. It was sweet and warm on his tongue. Joseph smiled at his shiny, clean hands. "Twenty seconds is not too long," he said. Mr. Guo laughed and put a sticker of a happy soap bottle on Joseph's shirt.

Jules had a cold. He was home in his big bed. His nose was red. His teddy sat next to him.

His dad came in with a small stick. It was smooth and shiny. "What is that?" Jules asked. "It is a thermometer," Dad said. "It checks how warm your body is." Jules wanted to hold it. "Not yet," said Dad. "First we check you. Hold very still."

Jules held very still. He counted one, two, three. The thermometer was slow. Then it made a little beep. Dad looked at it. "Your body is still a bit warm," Dad said. "More rest for you."

Jules looked at the thermometer. "Can I see it now?" he asked. "Can it check Teddy too?" Dad smiled. "Okay. Hold it under Teddy's arm." Jules put the small stick under Teddy's arm. He counted one, two, three. It did not beep. "Teddy is not warm," Jules said. "Teddy can swim and play without me."

Later Jules ate warm soup. He drank his water, sip by sip. His sister drew him a picture. Then he felt sleepy again.

Dad came back at night. "Time to check you again," he said. The thermometer was slow again. Beep. Jules waited. Dad smiled big. "You are cooler now, my boy." Jules hugged Teddy tight. "Check me one more time," he said. "Okay," said Dad. "One, two, three."

Victoria went to the store with her dad. She wanted a book about ducks. On a shelf she saw a little red book. The cover had words on it. Dad read the words out loud. "Duck, Duck, Sleep," he said. The words told them what the book was. Victoria hugged the book. It was hers.

At home, after dinner, Victoria sat on the rug. She peek at the pages. But the duck looked funny. The duck was upside down. So were the words. Victoria laughed and laughed. "Silly duck," she said. Dad smiled. Victoria turned the book around. Now the duck stood right side up. The words stood up too.

She turned the book upside down again. The duck flopped. She turned it back. The duck stood. "Again," said Victoria. Dad said, "You read it front to back." Victoria opened page one.

Caleb sat on the city bus with his mom. He patted his pocket. His little red dinosaur was not there. "Oh no," said Caleb. "Dino is lost."

Caleb looked under the seat. He saw gum and a crumpled paper. No dinosaur. He looked by his knee. He saw only his shoe. His sweater felt itchy, but he kept looking anyway. A big girl named Jenna stood up near the front. "Is this yours?" she asked. She held up the red dinosaur. It had been under her bag.

"Dino!" said Caleb. He hugged the dinosaur tight. "Thank you, Jenna." The bus rattled and hummed. Caleb held Dino on his lap the whole way home.

At home, Caleb found a small blue basket. He put the basket by his bed. He set Dino inside it. "Same place every time," he said to Dino. The next morning, Caleb woke up. He reached into the basket. There was Dino, waiting. Caleb smiled and gave Dino a kiss on his pointy head.

Nolan went to the farm with his dad. They had seeds to plant. Nolan wanted to grow his own carrots.

"Can we plant them now?" he asked.

"Yes," said his dad. "First we dig."
