Nolan dropped the little seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil on top. Then he watered the ground with a small can.

Every day Nolan came back to look. He saw brown dirt. He saw more brown dirt. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. "Just wait," said his dad. "Seeds take time."

One morning Nolan ran to the garden. There in the soil was a small green tip. It was tiny and new. Nolan had never seen one before.

He ran to the big tree by the barn. His friend Oscar was there. "Come see!" said Nolan. They ran to the garden together.

Oscar bent down low. "That little green thing is called a sprout," said Oscar. "My mom grows beans. Sprouts come up first."

Nolan smiled big. "My sprout!" he said. He gave it one drop of water, very gently.

The farmer walked by with a snowy white duck under his arm. "Well done," he said. "Watch it grow tall."

Nolan and Oscar sat in the shade and watched the sprout stand up in the sun.

Julia sat in the big concert hall. The lights were fresh and bright. Ms. Ma stood on the stage. She said, "Clap with me!"

Clap, clap, clap. Julia clapped her hands. The beat went one, two, one, two. Leonard clapped too fast. Linda clapped too slow. Julia laughed and chased the beat with her hands until she caught it.

Then Ms. Ma sang a song. It was "The Itsy Bitsy Spider." Julia knew the spider climbs up, up, up. She made her fingers climb up. But Leonard made his spider climb down!

Julia whispered, "The spider climbs up!"

"Oops," said Leonard. He turned his fingers around. Up went the spider, up, up, up. Linda made a block with her hands for the rain. Down came the rain and washed the spider out. Out came the sun and dried up all the rain.

Julia sang every word all by herself. Ms. Ma smiled big. "Again!" said Julia. The spider climbed up, up, up.

Henri was grumpy at daycare. His sandwich was cut in a strange way. It was not a square anymore. It had pointy bits.

Felix sat next to him. "That is a triangle," said Felix. Henri touched the sandwich. He counted the corners. One, two, three. He counted the sides too. One, two, three. The same number!

Henri took a small bite. Now his sandwich had a new shape. He counted again. One, two, three, four. "A square has four," said Zayd.

Ms. Huang brought a plate of crackers. Some were circles. Henri found a circle and put it on the table. He spelled his name with string at the craft table. Then he made shapes with the string too. He made a triangle with three loops. One, two, three.

"Look, Felix," said Henri. "My string has three sides." He smiled and munched his cracker.

Olivia went to Ivan's house. Ivan had a big red drum. He banged on it. Boom, boom, boom!

Olivia wanted to bang the drum too. She grabbed for it. Ivan held it tight. "My turn," he said.

Ivan's mom came in with sandwiches. "Let me tell you something," she said. "You can take turns. Taking turns means one person plays for a while, and then the other person gets to play."

"Okay," said Olivia. She sat on the floor. She waited.

Ivan played for a while. Boom, boom, boom. Then he stopped. "Now you," he said. He let Olivia hold the drum.

Olivia played for a while. Boom, boom, boom. Then she stopped too. "Now you," she said.

They took turns and took turns. Ivan's mom smiled. "Time for cold milk," she said.

Olivia drank her milk. "Taking turns is fun," she said. Ivan banged the drum one more time. Boom, boom, boom!

Ryan ran to the red swing at daycare. It was his favourite. But Aadya was already sitting on it. She pumped her legs and went up high. Ryan stood and watched. He wanted a go so much.

Aadya jumped off the swing. "You can have a go now," she said. "Then I get a go after you. Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another." Ryan sat on the swing. He held the chains tight. He kicked his legs and went up, up, up. His arms felt strong. Then Mr. Warsame called, "Time to lift the gate and come wash hands." Ryan jumped down.

"Your go," Ryan said to Aadya. She smiled and got on. Ryan counted while she swung. One, two, three. Then they ran inside together, side by side.

Layla sat in her car seat. Rain tapped on the big window. "It rains fast," she said. Her dad said, "Now it rains slow." Layla held a small cup of cold juice. Dad had a big cup of hot tea. He held it with both hands.

Layla had a toy box on her lap. She put her toy cat in the box. Then she took it out. In. Out. In. Out. Ella was sitting beside her. Ella laughed. "In and out are opposites," said Ella.

The car went fast. Then it went slow. Then it stopped. They were at Grandma's house. Grandma held out a juicy red apple. Layla took a big bite. The rain dripped slow off the roof. "Grandma," said Layla, "my apple goes in my tummy." Grandma smiled and hugged her tight.

Athena went to the store with her dad. She wanted apples for snack time. "Can we find the apples?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "They are in aisle five."

Athena looked up. She saw a big number on a sign. It said 5. She held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "This hand says five too!" The 5 on the sign and her five fingers were the same.

She walked to aisle five with Dad. There were the apples, red and shiny. She picked some apples one by one. Dad put them in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten," Athena counted softly.

Near the apples, Athena saw a box with a fire picture on it. It was candles. "I can see it," she whispered. Dad moved the box gently into the cart himself.

At home, Dad cut the apples. Athena took a big bite. "Aisle five has the best apples," she said.

It was snack time at school. Mr. Koné put a big tray of cups on the table. "Maeve, can you help?" he asked. "Put one cup by each chair." Maeve picked a cup. It was cool and smooth in her hand.

She put one cup by the blue chair. She put one cup by the red chair. Mavis sat at the blue chair. Aryan sat at the red chair. Maeve kept going. One cup here. One cup there. Soon every chair had one cup. There were no cups left on the tray. There were no empty chairs.

"Look!" said Maeve. "Every chair has a cup!" Mavis picked up her cup and took a sip of water. Aryan picked up his cup too. "Same number," said Maeve. "Cups and chairs are the same!"

Mr. Koné smiled. Then he held up two plates. One plate had three apple slices. One plate had five. "Which one has more?" he asked. Maeve pointed at the plate with five slices. "That one!" she said. "It has more!"

Then Mr. Koné brought out a small cake with four strawberries on top. "One for you, one for Mavis, one for Aryan, one for me." Four strawberries, four friends. Maeve clapped her hands. Outside the window, a wild wind shook the leaves. "The wind wants cake too," said Maeve. Mr. Koné laughed and cut a slice for her.

Madeline ran to the playground. She wanted to build a big sand wall. Mohammed was there too. He had the only red shovel.

Mohammed sat in the sandbox. He made a sad face. He looked at the ground. He did not say anything.

Madeline waited. Then she said, "Are you okay?"

Mohammed said, "I feel sad. My tower fell down."

Ms. Moose heard him. She came over. "Let's build it again together," she said. She patted the sand. Mohammed patted too. Soon the tower stood up, tall and messy.

Madeline was excited. "Now can I use the shovel?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mohammed. He handed it to her.

Madeline dug and dug. The sand felt warm. The wall grew bigger and bigger. Mohammed danced around it.

"Happy now?" Madeline asked.

"Yes," said Mohammed. "Very happy."

Madelyn stood at the edge of the pool. The pool was right by the beach. She held her dad's hand tight. "I want to swim like Caspian," she said. Caspian was splashing in the water. Madelyn was scared. The water looked so big.

She saw a man sitting on a tall chair. "Why is he up so high?" she asked her dad. Her dad smiled. "That is the lifeguard," he said. "His job is to watch the swimmers. He helps anyone who needs it." Madelyn looked up. From up high, the lifeguard could see everyone. He could see Caspian. He could see Russell, too.

Madelyn stepped into the water. It felt cold on her toes. She poked out her tongue at the cold. Then she held the side and kicked. Her arms floated up like little wings. The lifeguard waved at her from his chair. "Look at me!" Madelyn called. She kicked and kicked. "I am swimming!" she said.

Scarlett ran to the big slide at the playground. Yunus was there first. "My turn!" said Yunus. He went down the slide fast.

Scarlett wanted a turn too. She stood at the ladder. "Give me the slide!" she called. Yunus just looked away. Scarlett waited. Her turn did not come.

Mr. Njoroge sat on the bench nearby. He was putting glue on a paper bird. "Give me the glue, please," he said to the teacher. The teacher smiled and handed it over. Scarlett watched. She saw the smile. She saw the glue go from one hand to another.

Scarlett climbed the ladder steps again. She took a big breath. "Yunus, can I have a turn, please?" she asked. Yunus looked at her. "Okay!" he said. He slid down and stepped aside. Scarlett slid down fast. Whee!

"Thank you, Yunus!" she called. "Your turn again now." Yunus laughed and ran to the ladder. "You said please!" he said. Scarlett remembered the glue, and the smile, and the slide. "Please," she said again, just to hear it. Then down she went, one more time.

Charlie wanted to bake cookies with Mom. The dough was soft and brown, like mud. "Can I use the cutters?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Wash your hands first."

Charlie looked at the cutters. There was a circle, round like a penny. There was a square, with four sides. There was a triangle, with three pointy sides. But where was a rectangle?

"Can I make a rectangle cookie?" Charlie asked. "Let's look around," said Mom. Charlie walked to the kitchen door. She put her finger on one corner. Then she counted. "One, two, three, four. Four corners!" Each corner looked square and neat. She ran her finger up one side. "One, two, three, four. Four sides too!"

So a rectangle had four sides and four square corners, just like the door. Charlie rolled her dough flat. She cut one long side, then another. She made four sides and four square corners. Her first cookie looked a bit ugly and crooked. Mom said, "Try again." Charlie took a breath and cut a new one. This time it was long and straight, like a little door.

Mom put the tray in the hot oven, and Charlie stood back. Soon the smell filled the kitchen. "Your rectangle cookie smells the best," said Mom. Charlie held up her cutter and grinned. "Doors are yummy!"

Emile walked on the nature trail with Samson. Mr. Lin said, "We have five senses. Can we find them all?"

Emile wanted to find one first. He peeked behind a big tree. A fox ran by! "I used my eyes," said Emile. "My eyes see!"

Samson heard a bird. "My ears hear," said Samson.

Mr. Lin held up a flower. Emile sniffed it. "My nose smells it," he said.

Then Emile closed his eyes. He could not see the flower. But he held out his hand. He touched the flower with his fingertips. "Soft!" he said. "My skin feels it. My fingertips feel soft."

"Now one more sense," said Mr. Lin. He had berries in his bag. He gave each boy one. Emile ate his berry. "My tongue tastes it. Sweet!"

"Five senses," said Emile. "Eyes, ears, nose, skin, tongue." He put his fingertips on the tree bark. "This feels bumpy."

Maverick walked into the school cafeteria. It was his very first day. His tummy made a little growl. He was hungry now.

He looked around the busy room. Kids sat at long tables. His friend Bodhi waved at him. Maverick sat down next to Bodhi. "I want lunch now," Maverick said. Bodhi pointed at the big clock on the wall. Ms. Hernández smiled at the boys. "First we go to our room," she said. "Then we come back here for snack time."

Maverick waited with the class. He built a tower of blocks. He drew a happy sun. Then Ms. Hernández clapped her hands. "Snack time!" she said. The class walked to the cafeteria. Maverick sat at the same table. He opened his little bag. He took a big bite of his banana. Bodhi grinned at him. "I waited," Maverick said, "and now it is time."

Sienna had a cold. She sat at the table with her toast. Her nose began to drip. Sniff, sniff, went Sienna. The drip came back again. Mama said, "Your nose is runny today. A cold can do that." Sienna asked, "Can we fix it?" Mama said, "We can get something at the pharmacy." At the pharmacy, Sienna saw big shelves. She saw bandages and soap and toothbrushes. Mr. Yamamoto worked there. He found the soft tissues and gave the box to Mama. Sienna held a tissue to her nose. She blew, gently. The drip went into the tissue. Her nose felt better. On the way home, Sienna waved to a nice cat by the door. "My nose is dry now," she said. "Tissues are my friends."

Caleb woke up and put on his socks. It was a school day. He wanted to see his friend Maxime. Then his dad looked out the window. "No school today," said Dad. "It is a snow day. School is closed because of all this snow." Caleb pressed his nose to the cold glass. The whole street was white. The snow was deep. The car was a big white lump.

Dad said they could go next door to Mr. Le's house. Caleb wore his warm coat and his red boots. At Mr. Le's door, the snow came up past Caleb's boots. It was hard to walk. His feet sank down, down, down. Mr. Le shoveled a little path. Then walking was easy.

Inside, Mr. Le's house was warm. There was a big green plant by the window. "Look," said Mr. Le. He pointed outside. The sun was on the snow. Drip, drip, drip. Water ran down the white hill by the steps. "The sun makes the snow melt," said Mr. Le. Caleb watched the water run and run.

They made cocoa in the kitchen. Mr. Le stirred the pot, and Caleb watched from his chair. Then they looked out the window together. A small animal hopped across the snow. It left tiny footprints. Drip, drip, went the snow by the steps. Caleb took a big sip of cocoa. "More melting," he said, and pointed at the puddle.

Connor sat in the family car. He was going to the dentist for the first time. A plane flew over the car. "Look, a plane!" said Connor. His dad smiled.

At the dentist's office, Connor sat in a big chair. The dentist had a little mirror. "Can you open your mouth wide?" she asked. "Why?" said Connor. "You open your mouth wide so I can see every tooth," she said. Connor opened his mouth a little bit. Then he closed it. "I want to talk," he said. The dentist waited.

"Try this," said his dad. "Open wide like a lion's roar." Connor took a big breath. "Roar!" He opened his mouth very wide. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see every tooth," she said. "Your teeth are strong, too. They can chew apples and bread." Connor felt happy. On the ride home, he asked, "Can we come back?" "Yes," said Dad. "Next time, roar even bigger."

Addison sat at the dinner table. Baby Ben was asleep in his little seat. Addison had big news. She had shared her lunch with Mario at school. Mario had shared his apple back. It was kind.

Addison opened her mouth wide. "I SHARED MY..."

Daddy put one finger to his lips. Then Daddy whispered, "Baby Ben is sleeping. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice."

Addison looked at Ben. His eyes were shut. His tiny hand was curled up like a ball.

Addison tried again, very small. "I shared," she whispered.

Daddy smiled and whispered back, "Thank you, Addison." Ben kept sleeping, soft and warm.

After dinner, Daddy would sweep the crumbs. Addison could help hold the dustpan. But first, she whispered to Ben one more time. "One, two, three, shh."

Ben made a little sleep sound. Addison giggled, very, very quietly.

"Shh," she said.

Norah was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut." Norah held her long hair. "No! It will be gone forever!" she said.

Grandma took her to the salon. The stylist had squishy soap. She put a cape on Norah. Snip, snip, one. Snip, snip, two. Snip, snip, three. Little hairs fell like soft rain. Norah watched them fall. Then the stylist spun the chair. Round and round went Norah.

In the mirror, Norah saw short hair. "It's little now," she said. Grandma smiled. "It will grow back, Norah. Hair grows back after it is cut." Norah touched her head. It felt soft like a baby duck.

At home, Norah took her nap. When she woke up, she looked in the mirror. "Hello, short hair!" she said. She patted it twice. Grandma laughed. "Will you help me brush it?" asked Norah. Grandma got the soft brush. "One, two, three," said Norah. The brush went round and round, just like the salon chair.

Adam sat on the living room couch. He had a blanket on his lap. He was getting over a cold. His nose was red and his voice was small.

His mom brought him a bowl of soup. Adam took one bite. Then he took another. Then he pushed the spoon away. "I don't want more," he said. "I only ate a little bit."

"That's okay," Mom said. "When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much." She put the bowl on the table. Adam felt glad inside. His heart felt warm. He snuggled down into the blanket.

Later his friend Kyrie came to the door. Kyrie waved through the window. Adam waved back, slow and neat. Kyrie held up a drawing of a big orange cat. Adam smiled a small smile. Then he yawned a big yawn.

Mom brought toast for Adam. He took two bites. He shook his head. "Still just a little," he said. Mom nodded. "That's okay while you are sick," she said. She kissed his head.

Adam drank some water. He watched the rain on the window. The drops went slip, slip, slip. He closed his eyes. The blanket went up and down, up and down. "Sleep tight," Mom said from the doorway. "Wake up, little guy," she whispered later. Adam opened one eye. "Soup?" he asked. He ate the whole bowl.

Xavier sat at the big art table. He was drawing a blue animal. It was a big blue cat. Kohen sat next to him. Kohen was drawing a sun.

Xavier reached for a marker. His hand slipped. The marker touched his skin. Now he had a blue line on his hand. "Oh no," said Xavier. "It is on me. It will not leave."

Ms. Zhang came over. She looked at the blue line. "Let's go to the sink," she said. Xavier followed her. The room smelled like paper and glue. Ms. Zhang turned on the water. She put soap on his hand. They rubbed the soap around. The water ran over his skin.

The blue line began to fade. Then it was gone. Xavier held up his hand. His skin was clean. He laughed and waved his wet hand. "Look, Kohen! All gone!"

Hudson ran to Grandma's door. "Big dinner tonight," said Dad. "You can say the Hamotzi."

"Hamotzi," Hudson whispered. He practiced all day. In the car he whispered it three times. One, two, three. At Grandma's house he whispered it to the paint on the wall. "Hamotzi."

The kitchen smelled like warm bread. Uncle pulled the challah from the oven with big mitts. It was hot, so Hudson stood back. He watched Uncle set the bread on a blue plate.

Everyone found a seat. Hudson counted the chairs. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six people, six chairs. But the bread sat alone. Nobody picked it up.

Then Auntie touched the bread. Everyone got quiet. She waited. Hudson's tummy felt jumpy. He took a big breath.

"Hamotzi," Hudson said, loud and clear. The words came out just right. Everyone smiled. Uncle tore the bread and handed pieces around. Hudson's piece was warm and soft. He chewed slowly.

Then Dad turned to Hudson and gave him a thumbs up. "Nice job, buddy," said Uncle. Hudson bit his bread again and grinned.

Luka looked out the window. The sky was gray. Rain fell on the grass. "It is rainy today," said his dad. Luka put on his sneakers. He ran to the backyard.

Raindrops went plop, plop, plop. A big puddle sat by the swing. Luka looked at it. What would happen if he stepped in it? He stepped in with one foot. Splash! Water went into his shoe. His sock got wet and squishy.

"Brr," said Luka. His toes felt cold. His dad came out with rain boots. "Try these," he said. Luka sat on the step. He pulled off the wet sneaker. He pushed his foot into the rain boot. The boot went up, up, up past his ankle.

Luka stepped in the puddle again. Splash! He looked at his toes. They were dry! He jumped in the puddle. Splash, splash! Still dry. "My feet are dry in the boots!" said Luka.

Sutton came over in her rain boots too. They stomped and splashed together. The wind blew the branches. "It is windy too," said Sutton. Later the sun came out. Everything was shiny and wet. Luka found his favorite stick by the fence. He drew a horse in the mud, one big splash at a time.

Scarlett ran into the backyard. "Come on, Reed!" she called. Reed ran too. They wanted to find treasure. Big treasure!

First, Scarlett used her eyes. Her eyes saw something shiny under the tree. "Look!" she said. She used her ears too. Her ears heard a bee buzzing. "Buzz, buzz," she said.

Reed dug with his hands. His hands touched the dirt. It was cool and bumpy. "Here it is!" he said. It was a shiny spoon. Scarlett sniffed with her nose. She smelled the flowers nearby. "Mmm, sweet," she said.

Then Scarlett sat down in the grass. She took off her shoes. "Ooh!" she said. The grass tickled her feet. "My feet can feel too! The grass is soft under my toes." Reed took off his shoes. He wiggled his toes. "It tickles me too!"

The shiny spoon was their treasure. They put it in a safe spot. "We found it together," said Scarlett. Reed laughed and stomped his happy feet in the soft, soft grass.

Sophie wants the crackers. At daycare, the snack shelf has two boxes that look the same. She picks one and shakes it. Blocks fall out. "That box says blocks," says Luc. Sophie looks at the front of the box. Squiggly lines sit there, like tiny magic worms. She holds the box up to Ms. Pritchard. "What do the worms say?" Ms. Pritchard laughs. "Those are words. They say blocks." So the worms tell her what is inside!

Sophie finds the other box. The words on it say crackers. She carries it to the little table. Luc runs over with a book about a stinky dinosaur. He opens it from the back. "Where is the dinosaur?" he asks. Sophie turns the book around. She opens the front cover. There is the dinosaur, right on the first page! "Books start here," says Sophie. Luc claps his big family of dinosaur toys together. On the door, a big paper sign hangs down. "That says snack time," says Ms. Pritchard. Sophie points at it. "The words tell us!" she says. Then she eats her cracker, all crunchy.

Ava held her cup. The cup was empty. Nothing was inside it. "I want water," she said. Her dad got a big jug of cold water. He put it on the low table.

Ava poured the water. She poured fast. Splash! Water went over the top. Ava got upset. Her socks were wet. "Oops," she said.

Her dad helped her dry the floor with a towel. Then he gave her a new cup. "Try slow," he said. Ava poured slow. Drip, drip, drip. The water went up and up. "Stop now," said Ava. The cup was full to the top. Nothing spilled. Ava smiled big.

Then Ava gave water to her pet cat in a small bowl. She poured slow again. The bowl filled up. The cat drank fast. Ava drank slow. "Empty," she said, tipping her cup over to show daddy. "All gone!" Then she ran to get the towel, just in case.

Camille went to the store with her dad. There was mud on her boots from the puddle. Dad helped her brush the mud off at the door. Inside, Camille saw a big basket of apples. She wanted to buy apples for her class. Ms. Kerr had asked for ten apples.

Camille picked apples one by one. "One, two, three, five," she said. Dad looked in the bag. "Count with me," he said. "One, two, three, four." Camille nodded. "Four! Then five!" She kept going. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The bag was full. Ten apples, just like Ms. Kerr wanted.

At the fruit stand, a small boy was counting too. "One, two, four," he said. His big sister held his hand. "Try again," she said softly. "One, two, three." The boy smiled. "Three! Then four!" Camille smiled too. The numbers went the same way every time. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

Camille saw a lemon next to the apples. She sniffed it and made a funny face. "That one smells sour," she said. Dad laughed and put the apples in the cart. "Ten apples for Ms. Kerr," said Camille. She held the bag all the way to the car.

Julia was in the backyard when the lights went out. The house went dark behind her. She ran to the door and flipped the light switch. Nothing happened. She flipped it again. Nothing happened. The lights stayed off.

"The power is out," said her dad. "The lights will not come on when you flip the switch." Julia flipped it one more time, slow this time. Still dark. She put on her sweater. The evening was getting cool.

Dad lit a little lantern, because he was the grown-up. Julia held his hand. They sat on the back step and looked up. The sky was very dark now. Then Julia saw a tiny light blink. Then another one. "Look, Dad! The sky is growing lights!" Dad laughed. "Those are stars, Julia. They need no switch at all." Julia waved up at them. "Good night, stars," she said.

Lucas had a new pet. It was a small rabbit named Fluff. Fluff lived in a cage in the kitchen.

Lucas wanted to hold Fluff all day. "Be gentle," said his dad. Lucas stroked Fluff's soft fur. Then he ran to the cookie plate on the table.

"Stop," said his dad. "Wash your hands first." Lucas looked at his hands. They had soft fur on them. He ran to the sink. He washed with soap and water. The fur went down the drain. Now his hands were clean.

Lucas ate a sweet cookie. It tasted good. Then he brushed Fluff with a little brush. Fur came off on the brush. Fluff wiggled his nose. Outside the window, a bee buzzed by a flower.

The next day, Lucas cleaned Fluff's cage with his dad. There was hay everywhere. "Wash your hands," Lucas said first. He ran to the sink all by himself. The water ran over his hands. Then he picked up an apple slice. He held it out to Fluff. Fluff took a tiny bite. "More?" asked Lucas.

Julia woke up early. Today was the big game. She ran to her room. She pulled out a red shirt. Then she pulled out a blue shirt.

"Which one?" she asked her dad.

"Fans wear the team's colors," said Dad. "Our team wears red."

So Julia put on her red shirt. Sulaiman came over. He wore red too. Ria came over. She wore red too. Ms. Bear from next door knocked at the door. She had on a big red hat. "I cheer for the same team," she said with a smile.

Everyone sat on the couch. Dad made popcorn. Julia helped pour it into one big bowl. The game started. The crowd on TV made a loud noise. When the team got close to the goal, everyone jumped up.

Then came the surprise. The dog ran in fast. He grabbed the popcorn bowl and ran around the room. Popcorn flew everywhere. Everyone laughed. Julia picked up a piece and put it in the bowl.

The team kicked the ball one more time. It went in! Everyone cheered at once. Julia cheered the loudest of all.

Rehmat ran to the block corner. The blocks were all gone. Liv had them. Liv was building a big red tower.

"Can I have the blocks?" asked Rehmat.

"You can have them later," said Ms. Chen. "Right now it is Liv's turn."

Rehmat sat down. She watched the tower grow. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Ms. Chen.

Rehmat picked up her hat and put it on her doll. Then she drew a cat. "Is it later yet?" she asked again.

"Not yet. Later means some time after now," said Ms. Chen.

Rehmat drew a sweet cake next to the cat. Then she helped Delphine pick up a crayon that could drop off the table.

The red tower fell down with a big crash. Liv laughed. "I'm done now," said Liv. "You can have the blocks."

"It is later now," said Rehmat. She stacked the blocks high, all the way to her chin.

"Rehmat, your turn is done," said Liv. "Then it will be my later!"

Stella ran to the line in the gym. It was ball day in gym class. Ms. Visser put a bat in Stella's hands.

"Wait," said Ms. Visser. "You need a helmet first."

"A helmet?" said Stella.

"In baseball, the batter wears a helmet," said Ms. Visser. "It protects your head." She set the blue helmet on Stella's head. It felt snug, like a hat for winter.

Stella swung the bat. Ping! The ball flew far. Her friend Saint clapped. "Nice hit!" he said. Then Saint ran to bat fast, with no helmet.

"Saint, come back!" called Ms. Visser. Saint ran back. She put a red helmet on his head. He smiled and gave the bat a big rip swing. Ping! The ball rolled past Saige.

Stella was happy. She patted her helmet with her hand. "My head is safe," she said. "My turn again!"

Jayden was at home. His friend Wayne came to play. Wayne built a big farm with blocks. It had a red barn and a little cow. "So cute," said Jayden.

Jayden wanted to add a pig. He reached out fast. His hand knocked the barn. The whole farm fell down. Wayne's lip wobbled. "My farm," he said.

Jayden felt bad inside. "Sorry, Wayne," he said. "It was a mistake. I will help you build it again." Wayne looked at him. Then Wayne smiled a little.

They built the barn together. "Can you pass the cow, please?" asked Jayden. Wayne passed it. "Thank you," said Jayden. The new farm stood tall. It looked even better than before. "Knock on wood," said Wayne, and he tapped the barn gently. The blocks stayed up.

Nathan sat on the grass at team practice. The sun was warm. The ball sat in front of him. It was red and white.

Darcy came over. She wanted the ball too. Darcy grabbed one side. Nathan grabbed the other side. The ball squished like a slimy fish in the middle.

"I had it first," said Nathan.
"No, me," said Darcy.
They pulled. The ball went this way. Then it went that way. Nobody got to play.

Ms. Wright saw them. She walked over. "Do you both want the ball?" she asked. Nathan nodded. Darcy nodded too.

"Then let's take turns," said Ms. Wright. "Nathan can kick first. Then Darcy. I will count for you."

Nathan let go of the ball. He waited. Ms. Wright said, "One, two, three." Nathan kicked the ball far. It rolled and rolled. Darcy clapped.

Then it was Darcy's turn. Ms. Wright said, "One, two, three." Darcy kicked the ball. It rolled the other way.

One ball. Two friends. Turn, turn, turn. Nathan had a little secret in his head. Waiting was not so bad. Waiting meant he got to kick again soon.

Ms. Wright said, "One more turn each, then water break." Nathan got in line. Darcy stood beside him. Nathan smiled at his friend. "You kick far," he said. Darcy smiled back and kicked the ball into the goal.

The bookmobile came to Evelyn's street. It was a big truck full of books. Evelyn held her mom's hand. Inside, a man smiled at her. "I am Mr. Santos," he said. "I am the librarian. I work at the library and help people find books." He gave Evelyn a card with her name on it. It was her very first library card.

Evelyn wanted a book about trucks. She looked on a low shelf. She saw books about bears. She saw books about bunnies. One bunny on a cover looked very cute. But no trucks. Evelyn looked on the next shelf. Still no trucks. She let out a small sigh. Her tummy gave a little bite of hunger, too. Then she remembered. Mr. Santos helps people find books.

She walked to him. "Can you help me find trucks?" she asked. "Yes," said Mr. Santos. He pulled out a bin under the shelf. There were truck books! Evelyn picked a big red one. Mr. Santos scanned her new card. The book was hers to take home.

Evelyn zipped the book into her mom's bag. She waved at the bookmobile as it drove away. "Bye, Mr. Santos," she called. "See you next week!"

Jack sat at the dinner table. He had a big want. He wanted a book about animals. He had gone to the library with Dad. But Jack could not find the animal book. Too many books! He felt worried.

Then Mr. Vogel came to help. Mr. Vogel worked at the library. "Come and see," said Mr. Vogel. He pointed to a shelf. All the animal books sat there, side by side. The books were in groups. Jack could see books about toys on one shelf. Books about foods sat on another shelf. Jack got to choose one animal book. He chose a silly book about a big red dog.

At dinner, Jack told Mom all about it. "The animal books have a home on one shelf," said Jack. "And I found them!" Mom smiled and gave him a hug.

Today was Sara's birthday party at the pool. Orhan and Yusra jumped in with a big splash. Sara jumped too. "Why is everyone making a fuss today?" Yusra asked. Grandma held up a photo. It showed a tiny baby. "That is Sara," Grandma said. "This photo is from the day Sara was born." Sara looked at the baby. Then she looked at her party hat. "So my birthday is the day I was born!" she said. Grandma smiled and nodded.

Then Sara saw something small on the table. An ant was walking on the plate! She watched it crawl toward the cake. "Look, the ant smells the cake," said Orhan. Mr. Santos came over. He shooed the ant away and put the plate on a chair.

Later the sun made the ground feel hot. Mr. Santos lit the candles for Sara. He held them carefully. Sara blew them out with one big puff. Everyone cheered. "Thank you, everyone!" said Sara. Yusra gave her a high five. Then they all jumped back into the pool. Splash!

Aaron was at Jorawar's house. The toast was ready. Aaron wanted to butter it himself.

He held the little knife. He poked the toast with the tip. The butter made a hole in the bread. Pieces fell off onto the plate. "Oh no," said Aaron. "My toast is a mess."

Jorawar's mom smiled. "Watch me first," she said. "Take your time." She turned the knife over. She spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread. The butter went on smooth and yellow. The bread stayed whole.

"Now you," she said. Aaron turned his knife over. He pushed the flat side across the toast. Slowly, slowly. The butter covered every bit. "I did it!" said Aaron. Then he poured milk into his cup. A little slopped out the first time. He poured again, slowly. Not one drop spilled. He took a big bite of toast and a big drink of milk. "Jorawar," he said, "your mom makes the best toast."

Lincoln was at home with his grandma. It was Lunar New Year. There were red lanterns on the wall. There was a big round bowl of oranges on the table.

Grandma held out something small. It was a red envelope. "This is for you," she said. Lincoln wanted to open it fast. He pulled at the corner.

"Wait," said Grandma. She smiled. "First you say thank you." Lincoln stopped his hands. He took a big breath. "Thank you, Grandma," he said. Grandma gave him a little nod. Then Lincoln opened the envelope. Inside was money! "Money!" said Lincoln. Grandma laughed. "Many children get red envelopes at Lunar New Year," she said. Lincoln held the envelope up to the lantern light. "More red," he said. Grandma passed him an orange. Lincoln sat down next to her and peeled it, slowly, all the way around.

Jacob wanted to write his name. His mom took him to the library on the bus. The bus went over a bumpy road. The seats seemed to shake. Jacob held his paper tight.

At the library, Mr. Ramos gave Jacob a fat pencil. "Hold it near the tip," said Mr. Ramos. Jacob squeezed the pencil. He made a letter J. Then he tried an O. The O looked like a wobbly egg. He tried again. It looked like a squished potato. Jacob felt grumpy. He pushed the paper away.

Mr. Ramos put out two trays. One tray had sticks, straight like little roads. The other tray had bendy straws and curls. "Sort the letters of your name," said Mr. Ramos. Jacob picked the J. It had a little curve. He put it with the straws. He picked the A. All straight sticks. He made an A with two sticks and one across. It worked! The straight sticks made straight letters. The curls made curvy letters.

Jacob tried his name again. This time his O came out round and smooth. Alessia looked over from the next table. "That says Jacob," she said. Jacob smiled and wrote it one more time. Then he wrote it again.

Addison sat at the craft table at daycare. She wanted to draw a sun for her picture. She tried to draw a circle. Her circle came out wobbly. It looked like a potato. She tried again. This one looked like an egg. Addison put her crayon down.

Then she saw her cup of water. The cup had a round bottom. She held the cup still on her paper. She traced her crayon all the way around it. She lifted the cup. "A circle!" said Addison. It was big and round and just right. Hugo leaned over to look. "How did you make that?" he asked. Addison smiled and pushed the cup toward him.

Hugo traced the cup too. Soon Leonard made one, and then Ms. Sinclair made a long row of circles. Addison drew yellow rays on hers. Now she had her sun. After craft time, they all went out to the playground. Addison looked up at the warm sun in the sky. "My sun looks just like you," she said.

Raphael went to the store with his dad. He wore his red sweater. He was excited to pick a snack.

Raphael saw the apples. He reached for a big red one. But it rolled off the pile. It fell down and bumped his foot. Raphael got angry. His face got hot. He stomped his foot.

His dad knelt down beside him. "Let's try slow, deep breaths," Dad said. "Breathe in with me." Raphael took a slow breath. Then another one. His body began to calm down. His foot did not hurt much anymore. Then Theresa from school came around the corner. She held a pretty yellow apple. "Want to pour the apples into the bag together?" she asked. Raphael smiled and held the bag open wide.

Brooklyn stood in the kitchen with her mom. Dad had a big pot on the stove. It was hot. Brooklyn stayed back and held her mom's hand. Dad stirred the soup from far away. "Hot pot," said Brooklyn. "Yes," said Mom. "We stay back from hot things."

Brooklyn helped with the carrots. Mom held the knife. Brooklyn put the carrots in the bowl. Mom cut off the little root at the bottom. "See, this is the root," said Mom. Brooklyn put the short root piece in the trash. Then she got her toy slide. Zohan came to play.

Zohan put the slide on the kitchen floor. He climbed up. He lay down on his tummy. His head went first. "Wait," said Brooklyn. She helped him turn around. She held his hand. Zohan slid down. His feet went first. Whee! "Again," said Zohan. He went up. He turned around by himself. Feet first, down he came. "My turn," said Brooklyn, and up the short steps she went.

William ran into the health clinic. He was excited and a little scared. He wanted his turn to be over fast.

The waiting room was full of chairs. Families sat and sat and sat. "When is my turn?" William asked. "Soon," said his dad. "A waiting room is where families sit until it is their turn." William sat down next to his friend Orhan. Orhan was there for a shot too. They stacked the blocks in the toy box. One, two, three, four. Then the tower fell down. They laughed.

A nurse opened the door. "William!" she called. It was his turn! William marched in. The doctor was gentle. The shot felt like one tiny pinch. "All done," said the doctor. William got a bright bandage. He ran back to show Orhan the tower was still standing. "My turn is over!" he said. "Now you go!"

Sophie stood in the big room at school. Mr. Ong put a red hoop on the floor. He gave Sophie a soft beanbag.

"Throw it in the hoop," said Mr. Ong.

Sophie threw the beanbag. It landed far away. It did not go in. She threw it again. It landed by her feet, still not in. Olivia threw hers and missed too.

Sophie took three steps. Now she stood closer to the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! "Yay!" said Sophie.

"Try again," said Mr. Ong, smiling.

Sophie stood close and threw. In it went, soft as a pillow. Then Emil moved closer too, and his beanbag went in.

Next Mr. Ong rolled a big ball to Sophie. She held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy but she caught it. She hugged the ball. It felt smooth and warm from the sun in the window.

"You can win a turn to go first," said Mr. Ong. Sophie laughed and hugged the ball again. "My grandma has a big ball like this," she said. "She plays with me in her yard."

Mr. Ong rolled the ball again. Sophie caught it with both hands and threw the beanbag, close to the hoop. In it went, swish.

Victoria ran to the playground. Her friend Constance was already there. "Let's play the freeze game," said Constance. They ran and jumped. When the coach called "Freeze," they stopped like statues.

Soon Victoria's tummy growled. Her dad was at the picnic table. He had a little camp stove. He was making warm cocoa. Victoria wanted to hold the little pot.

She looked at the stove. The flame was off now. The stove did not look hot at all. Victoria's hand reached out. Then she stopped. She remembered her dad's rule. "Only you touch the stove," she said.

"That's right," said Dad. He put his hand near the pot. "It is still hot, even with no flame. See the steam?" Victoria saw the steam rise up. Dad poured the cocoa into her cup. "Careful, it is warm."

Victoria held the cup with two hands. "Sorry I almost touched the pot," she said. Dad smiled. Constance came over, so Victoria shared her crackers. The steam curled up into the cold air.

Today was Jaxson's birthday pool party. His friend Dane jumped in first with a big splash. Arya sat by the small steps and put her toes in the water.

"How old are you now?" asked Dane.

"I am three," said Jaxson. He held up three fingers.

"No, no," said his dad with a smile. "You had your birthday cake. Now you are one year older. Count your candles again."

Jaxson looked at the table. There were four candles on the cake. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four."

"I am four!" he shouted. He held up four fingers this time.

"You turned one year older," said Arya. She clapped her hands.

Jaxson jumped up and down. Then he sat on the pool steps and kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. His kicking made the waves grow bigger.

"Look!" said Jaxson. "My legs make the big water!"

Then Mr. Morningstar, the pool helper, brought out floating toys. He put one in the water. Jaxson kicked again. The toy sailed across the pool.

"That is my wave pushing it," said Jaxson.

Dane laughed and kicked too. Arya kicked too. All three friends made waves together. The toys zoomed around the pool.

Everyone got out and had cake. It tasted sweet like strawberries. Jaxson blew out his candles in one big puff.

"Happy birthday, Jaxson!" said Dane.

"Happy birthday, four-year-old me!" said Jaxson. He took one more big bite of cake.

Thomas was at the playground. He ran to the big slide. "One, two, three," he counted, and up he went.

Then Thomas heard a deep, loud rumble. It came from under the slide. Thomas felt scared. His tummy felt tight.

He remembered what his dad said. "When you are scared, tell a grown-up you trust."

Mr. Andersen was close by. Thomas ran to him. "There is a scary sound," Thomas said.

Mr. Andersen held his hand. They looked together. It was only a big truck, far past the fence.

"Not scary now," said Thomas. He felt happy.

"Want to try the swing?" asked Mr. Andersen.

"Yes!" said Thomas. He was excited. "One, two, three!" he called, pumping his legs. Up he flew, high as a bird.

Theo was at the laundromat with his dad. The big machines hummed and turned. Warm, soapy smells filled the air.

Theo's coat was in the basket. He wanted to put it on all alone. He pushed one arm in. He pushed the other arm in. "I did the arms!" he said. Now came the zipper. Theo pulled it up, up, up. But it stopped. It would not move.

Theo looked down. His red sweater was caught in the zipper. He pulled hard. The zipper still did not move. He remembered the egg in his pocket. He had held it gently so it would not crack. So he pulled the zipper gently back down, just a little bit. The sweater came free!

Theo tried again. Zip, up, up, up to his chin. "Dad, look! My zipper works!" Dad smiled and clapped. Theo zipped it down, then up again, all by himself. Then he sat on the bench beside the warm dryers. "Zip, zip," he said, and grinned.

Jules loved the big red blocks. He wanted them all. At play time, he took every block with both arms. "They are mine now," he said.

Nico had no blocks. Lenna had no blocks. They stood and watched. Nico's lip went down. Lenna turned away.

Jules built one tall tower. Then he looked around. He was alone with the tower. He felt a little scared to say sorry. He asked himself, "What can I do?" He answered, "I can share."

He gave blocks to Nico. He gave blocks to Lenna. "This is fair," said Jules. "Fair means everyone gets a chance."

Now everyone built. Everyone had a tower. Jules found a friend on each side of him.

"More blocks?" asked Nico.

"Yes," said Jules. "Blocks for everyone. Blocks for everyone."

Ella went to the music studio. Mr. Mercer had a big drum. He hit it slowly. "Clap with me, Ella," he said. Ella clapped. But her claps got faster and faster. Soon she was clapping way ahead of the drum.

Ella got upset. "Why can't I stay with the drum?" she asked. Mr. Mercer smiled. "Try marching," he said. Ella stood up. She marched around the room. Her feet went step, step, step. Her feet stayed even and kept going, just like the drum. Mr. Mercer hit the drum beside her marching feet.

"Now clap like your feet," he said. Ella marched and clapped. Her claps went step, step, step too. They matched the drum! Ella laughed. "It stayed with me!" she said.

"Now let's sing," said Mr. Mercer. Ella sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by herself. She sang every word from memory. At the top of her voice, she sang the last line. Mr. Mercer clapped for her. Ella took a bow, and the drum went boom.

Jaxson ran into the big room at the community hall. There were tables everywhere. His friends Ryan and Colt were already there. Tonight all the families would eat together.

"Jaxson, come sit with us," said Ryan. Jaxson sat down fast. The bowls were full of warm soup. A grown-up carried the pot. Jaxson stayed back, safe and out of the way.

"Before we eat, we say our blessing," said Ms. Hernández. "Who wants to help?" Jaxson raised his hand way up high. "I want to try!" he said.

Jaxson stood by his chair. He thought hard. The blessing often says thank you for the food. But who made the soup? "Thank you for the soup," he began. "And thank you for the farmers who grew the carrots!" Colt clapped. Ryan clapped too. Ms. Hernández smiled big. "That was a fine blessing, Jaxson." Jaxson sat down and picked up his spoon.

Juliette woke up in her bed. The sun was in her eye. She heard a spoon drop in the kitchen. "Is it morning now?" she called. Dad peeked in. "Yes. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." Juliette jumped up. "Then I want breakfast now!"

She ran to the kitchen in her pyjamas. Her friend Boston was at the table with his dad. "Good morning, Boston," said Juliette. Boston smiled. "Good morning. We came early today. Yesterday we came late, and the pancakes were all gone." Juliette sat down fast. Dad gave her a warm bowl of porridge. She ate every bit.

"Can Boston come back tomorrow?" Juliette asked. Dad nodded. "Yes. Tomorrow is the day after today." Juliette clapped her hands. "Then tomorrow we eat breakfast again!" Boston laughed and held up his spoon. "To morning," he said. Juliette tapped her spoon on her bowl, and they both grinned.

Arya was playing blocks at daycare. Megan was next to her. The blocks fell down. Crash! Arya heard the loud sound with her ears. "Let's build it again," said Megan.

Then Arya smelled something. She used her nose. Sniff, sniff. "I smell pizza!" said Arya. "I don't see any pizza," said Mario. Arya looked all around with her eyes. No pizza anywhere. But the smell kept coming. "Sniff, sniff," said Arya again. Megan sniffed too. "I smell it too!"

Mr. Sun opened the kitchen door. Out came the warm pizza smell. "You can smell dinner before you see it," said Mr. Sun. There it was! The cook had baked a pizza for snack. Arya touched the table with her hands. It felt smooth. She took a small bite with her tongue. Yum! Her fingers were a bit messy. Mr. Sun helped her wash them. "Pizza time," he said, and Arya smiled.

James stood in the new nursery room. A small bed sat by the window. A tiny blanket lay on the bed. His baby sister would sleep here soon.

Mikayla came to visit with her mom. She looked at the stack of diapers on the shelf. "Why so many diapers?" she asked. James touched one. It was soft like a bunny. "Babies wear diapers," he said. "They cannot use the toilet yet." Mikayla nodded slowly.

Then the baby came home. She drank her milk. Later she cried. "She needs a new diaper," said Dad. James got one from the shelf. He handed it over, nice and slow. Dad changed the baby. She stopped crying. She smiled at James. James patted her little hand. "I can help," he said. "I am your big brother."

The lights went out. The living room was dark. Dad lit some candles on the table. The flames made little yellow circles on the wall.

Sarah wanted some milk. She went to the fridge. She pulled on the door. "Not yet," said Dad. "The power is out. We keep the fridge shut tight. The food stays cold longer that way." Sarah let go of the handle.

Sarah went back to the candles. She held her hands near the warm glow. Then she tried the fridge again, just to peek. Dad shook his head. "Shut," he said, "so dinner stays cold." Sarah patted the door. "Stay shut," she said.

They sat together and waited. The candle flames wiggled. Sarah watched the shadows dance. Then the lights came back on. The room was bright. Dad opened the fridge and poured cold milk into a cup. Sarah drank it all up. "Cold!" she said, and she smiled.

Rosalie went to Cadence's house. Cadence's mom was there. Cadence had a tablet.

"Can I draw?" asked Rosalie.

"First, we turn it on," said Cadence. "One little button."

Rosalie pressed the button. The screen lit up. Rosalie clapped.

Cadence tapped the drawing app. "Look, one tap," she said. "Now we draw."

Rosalie drew a red cat. Then she drew her sister. Then she drew a big old tree.

Rosalie picked up the tablet with one hand. It slipped. It tipped and wobbled.

"Use two hands," said Cadence.

Rosalie held it with two hands. It did not tip. It did not fall.

"Two hands," said Rosalie. "One, two."

"Now we put it away," said Cadence. They tapped the button and the screen went dark. Cadence's mom helped them hang the tablet bag on its hook.

"Bye, tablet," said Rosalie. "See you next time."

Madison skipped into the backyard. Kasey was there with a big leaf pile. The leaves smelled like dirt and rain. Madison touched one leaf. It felt crunchy and dry.

Then Dad turned on the leaf blower near the fence. It was very loud. "Too loud!" said Kasey. He put his hands over his ears. The loud sound got quieter for him. Madison tried it too. She pressed her hands over her own ears. The noise came in soft, like a whisper. "That's neat," she said.

They counted while Dad worked. One, two, three, four hands on ears. Then Dad turned the machine off. The backyard was quiet again. A bird sang. They heard it with their ears wide open. Kasey gave Madison a red leaf. It smelled spicy. "A present," he said. She put it in her bowl of treasures. "For you too," said Madison, and she found him a yellow one.

James wanted the red truck. Elora had it in her hands. She was pushing it across the playroom floor. The wheels made a soft rumble sound.

James grabbed at the truck. Elora held on tight. "Mine," she said. The truck stopped rolling. Mr. Ma knelt down next to them. "You can ask," he said kindly. James looked at the truck. Then he looked at Elora. "May I have the truck, please?" he asked.

Elora smiled. "Okay. You can have a turn." She put the truck in his hands. The wheels rumbled again, faster now. "Your turn next," James said. Elora touched the paint on the blocks shelf while she waited. "This paint feels smooth," she said. James rolled the truck to her feet. "Here. Safe and slow, just for you."

Audrey ran into the art studio. She was so excited! Today she would paint a big sun.

"Look, look!" said Audrey. She dipped her brush in yellow paint. She painted a big round sun. Then she painted white clouds all around it.

Jaxxon came over to see. "Wow!" he said. He poked the sun with his finger. The yellow paint smeared. Now the sun had a big smudge on it.

Audrey gasped. "My sun!" she said. It looked squished and messy now.

Ms. Nikolaidis came to help. "Let's make it dry," she said. "We will wait and wait."

Audrey waited. She washed her hands at the sink. Her sister counted to ten with her. They waited some more.

Then Audrey touched the sun very gently. It was dry! Her finger stayed clean. Nothing smeared at all.

"Watch this!" said Audrey. She painted a new white cloud beside the sun. "Nobody touch it!" she said. Jaxxon and Maggie nodded.

They all sat on their hands and waited.

"Can we touch it now?" asked Maggie.

Audrey checked. Dry! All dry! Everyone clapped.

"My sun is dry," said Audrey. "Now it can go home with me."

Hayden ran to the snack table. His hands were muddy from the sandbox. He sat down next to Dominic and reached for an apple slice.

Ms. Saleh knelt beside him. "First we wash our hands," she said. "We wash our hands before we eat." She pointed to the little sink by the door.

Hayden walked to the sink. He turned the water on. It was warm, not too hot for little hands. He pumped the soap. Bubbles grew on his palms. He rubbed and rubbed. Then he rinsed the bubbles off. The water turned the mud away and ran down the drain.

His hands were clean now. He looked at them. Dominic peeked over. "Your hands are all pink and shiny," Dominic said. Lorelei came to wash her hands too. Hayden showed her where the soap was. She pumped some soap and made bubbles too.

Then they all sat at the table. Hayden ate his apple slice. It tasted sweet. He looked at his clean hands again. Clean hands, then snack. He smiled and took one more slice. "Wash first," he said to Lorelei. Lorelei nodded and passed him the bowl.

Audrey had a cold. She had a runny nose all day. She sat on the couch with a box of tissues. Her mom gave her warm soup in a small cup.

Audrey blew her nose. She put the used tissue on the couch. Then she blew her nose again. She put that one on the couch too. Soon there were tissues everywhere. "Look at this mess," said her mom. "It looks ugly. Used tissues go in the bin."

Audrey looked at the bin across the room. Could she reach it? She stood up and walked over. She dropped a tissue in. It went right in! One tissue in the bin.

She ran back to the couch. She picked up another one. She walked to the bin. Two tissues in the bin. "This is like a game," she said. Three tissues in the bin. Four tissues in the bin.

Soon the couch was clean. The floor was clean too. All the tissues fit inside the bin. Audrey clapped her hands. Her mom gave her a hug. Then the phone rang. It was her friend Oceanne. "Can you come play tomorrow?" asked Oceanne. "Yes," said Audrey. "I will bring my own tissues. And I know just where they go."

Axel ran to the toy corner. He saw the big red truck. He wanted it so much. But Beckett was holding it. The truck went vroom, vroom on the soft blue rug.

Axel reached out his hand. He wanted to grab it. Then he stopped. He sat on his heels and waited. His hands stayed in his lap. Snow fell past the window, slow and white. The rug felt warm under his knees.

Beckett looked up. "You want a turn?" he asked. Axel nodded. "Yes, please." Beckett pushed the truck over. The wheels rolled across the rug. "Here you go," said Beckett.

Axel held the red truck. It felt smooth and cool in his hands. He remembered something. "Thank you," he said. Beckett smiled a big smile. His cheeks went pink and happy. Then Axel made the truck go vroom, vroom, all the way to the block tower. Later they sat together for juice, and Beckett shared his crackers too.

Alexander sat at the dinner table. Ms. Hosseini put a warm bowl in front of him. Alexander was happy. He picked up his spoon.

Then Alexander heard a sound. It was a small sound, like rain. He looked across the table. Joseph was sitting there. Tears ran down Joseph's face. Joseph was crying.

"Why are you crying?" Alexander asked. "I am sad," Joseph said. "I lost my leaf." Joseph had a big green leaf. He found it in the yard. Now the leaf was gone.

Alexander thought and thought. He waited. Then he had an idea. He took his paper and his crayons. He began to draw. He was very careful. He drew a big green leaf, just like Joseph's leaf. He drew it slow, so it looked nice.

"Here," said Alexander. He held out the paper leaf. Joseph looked at it. He stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Joseph was not sad anymore.

"Thank you," Joseph said. "I love my new leaf." Ms. Hosseini smiled too. Alexander felt warm inside, like his happy tummy at dinner. Then Alexander and Joseph ate their warm food together. "Best friends," said Joseph, and he held up the paper leaf.

Rowan lost his small red dinosaur at Grandma's house. He ran to the kitchen. He ran to the bedroom. He ran to the den. No dinosaur anywhere.

Grandma was in the kitchen. "Can I help feed the birds?" Rowan asked. "First let's find your dinosaur," said Grandma. She held out her hand. "Let's look in one room at a time."

They started in the kitchen. Rowan looked under the table. He looked behind the big chair. He looked in the warm bread basket. No dinosaur there. They went to the bedroom next. He looked under the bed. He looked in the shoe basket. Then he saw it! His dinosaur was stuck to a magnet on the fridge door in the den.

"One room at a time," Rowan whispered. "That is how you find things." He hugged the dinosaur tight. "Now can we feed the birds?" Grandma laughed and filled the little cup with seeds.

Isaiah ran outside at school. The wind blew hard. Sand flew up in the air. "Close your eyes!" said Ms. Quinn. Isaiah squeezed his eyes shut. Sand tickled his nose. He smelled the dusty air. Then the wind stopped. Isaiah opened his eyes. "My eyes feel okay!" he said. He touched his eyelashes. They were little and soft.

Clay rubbed sand out of his eye. "Ow," said Clay. "My eye hurts." Isaiah looked at Clay. "My eye does not hurt," said Isaiah. He blinked and blinked. His eyelashes moved. A tiny bit of dirt sat on them. Isaiah brushed it off with his finger.

"Blink fast, Clay!" said Isaiah. Clay blinked fast. A bit of dirt fell off his eyelashes too. "It came off!" said Clay. Ms. Quinn gave them cold milk to drink. Isaiah tasted it. It was sweet and cold. He blinked one more time. "Good little lashes," he said. "Good little helpers."

Olivier ran to the playground with his dad. The sun made the slide very hot. "Ouch, it is hot," said Sadie, pulling her hand back. Olivier touched the shady side of the slide. That side was cool. He slid down the cool side with Sadie.

Then Olivier saw a little pink box on the ground. It had small holes in it. Wires came out of it. A workman was fixing the big fence. "A plug," said Olivier. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet," Olivier said out loud. He remembered his dad saying that word at home. "Outlet," he said again, careful and proud.

Olivier reached for his dad's hand. He did not touch the pink box. He walked away from it.

"Come look," called the workman. He held up a long block of wood. The block fit on the fence hole. One push and the hole was gone.

Olivier and Sadie clapped. The fence was fixed. Then Olivier got a turn on the swing, with his dad close by, pushing him high, high, high.

Nicholas went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big red book about dragons. Nicholas felt excited. His tummy jumped like popcorn.

He saw his friend Alara on the rug. She was not smiling. Her mouth went down at the corners. Her eyebrows made a little frown. Nicholas looked at her face. He remembered that faces show feelings. "Alara, are you sad?" he asked. Alara nodded. "The dragon book is gone," she said. "Someone took it."

Nicholas looked on the shelf. He looked under the chair. There it was! The dragon book hid behind a box of toy bread. "Roar!" said Nicholas, like a dragon. Alara laughed. Her frown flipped into a big smile.

They sat together. Alara held one side. Nicholas held the other. The book felt full of dragons. "Best dragon day," said Alara.

Declan sat in a big red seat. The basketball game was starting below him. Ziyad sat near him. They both held a bag of popcorn.

A player ran with the ball. He threw it up high. The ball went right through the hoop. The crowd went wild.

"They scored!" shouted Ziyad.

"They threw it in the hoop," said Declan. "I want to do that too."

After the game, they found a little hoop by the door. It was just their size. Declan held his ball. He threw it up. It hit the rim and fell off. He laughed.

"Too high, silly ball," he said.

Ziyad tried too. His ball went through the hoop and dropped down. "I did it!" said Ziyad.

Ms. Torres, who was walking by, clapped her hands. Declan stirred his feet in a happy dance, then threw again. This time the ball went through the hoop.

"Through the hoop!" Declan shouted. "Just like the big game."

Sienna ran to art class. Today they would make toy cars! Ms. Iyer put out cardboard, tape, and little wooden sticks.

"First we draw wheels," said Ms. Iyer. Sienna drew a square wheel. It had four flat sides. Finnley drew a rectangle. Lucian drew a triangle. Then Ms. Iyer held up a round shape. "This one is a circle," she said. "See how round it is."

Sienna taped her square wheels on. She pushed her car across the dry table. The car went thump, thump, thump. It would not roll. "My car is stuck!" said Sienna.

She looked at the circle wheels. Round like a ball. Round like the sun over the pond by her house. She cut new wheels, nice and round. She taped them on tight. She pushed the car. It rolled! It rolled so far it rolled past Lucian's feet. "It rolls, it rolls!" Sienna shouted.

"Circle wheels for me too," said Lucian. He cut circles fast. Finnley cut circles too. Soon all three cars zoomed across the table. "Ready, set, go!" said Sienna. The wheels went round and round.

Declan ran to the picture basket at the library. Lillian and Oaklyn ran too. Ms. Santos tipped the basket over. All the pictures fell out. "Oh no," said Declan. "What a big mess!"

Declan picked up a picture. It was an elephant. "Elephant," he said. He put it down. Oaklyn held a picture of a dog. "Animals go together," said Oaklyn. She put the dog next to the elephant. Lillian found a ball. "That is a toy," she said. Then she found a teddy bear. Toy pile! One, two toys. Declan found an apple. Then a banana. "Foods!" he said. One, two foods.

They sorted and sorted. Animals here. Toys there. Foods over there, in a straight line. Ms. Santos clapped her hands. "Look at our three piles," she said. Declan picked up his elephant picture. "You are an animal," he told it. "You go here." And the elephant sat right on top of the pile.

Arya loved the library. It was busy today. Kids sat on the soft rug. Ms. Vogel held up a big book. "Let's count the ducklings," she said. Arya sang along. "One, two, three, four, five." Alivia patted the rug. "Six, seven, eight." Ira clapped. "Nine, ten!"

After the song, Ms. Vogel gave out paper. "Draw ten stars," she said. Arya drew one star. Then two. Then three, four, five. Her friend Alivia drew fast. "I have six, seven, eight, nine," said Alivia.

Arya wanted to write the number ten too. She wrote a 1. Then she stopped. One was not enough. All the small numbers had one shape. She looked at the wall chart. There it was! Ten had two shapes, a 1 and then a 0. She wrote a 1 and then a 0 beside it. "Ten!" she said. Ira peeked over. "How did you do that?" Arya pointed at the chart. "Look right there," she said.

Ms. Vogel came by with a stick of chalk. "Would you write ten on our board?" she asked. Arya stood up tall. She wrote the 1 first. Then she wrote the 0. Then she drew ten little ducks under it, all in a row. Alivia counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ira clapped and clapped. Arya hugged the chalk stick to her chest. "Thank you," she said to Ms. Vogel. On the way out, Arya waved at the number chart. "Bye, ten," she whispered.

Natalie stood at the front door. She looked out at the big bright sky. "Is it rainy today, Mommy?" she asked. "No, it is sunny," said Mommy. Natalie felt the warm sun on her nose. It was very bright. Her eyes went small and squinty. She held her hands over her eyes.

Mommy brought out a basket. "Let's play a game," she said. "We can sort the clothes." Natalie put the rain boots in one pile. She put the snow mittens in another pile. She found a hat with a big brim. "What is this for?" she asked. "Try it and see," said Mommy.

Natalie put on the sun hat. She stepped outside to the front step. The brim made shade over her face. She opened her eyes wide. No more squinting! The sun was still up in the sky, but her face stayed in the shade. "My eyes feel happy now," said Natalie. She jumped once, twice, three times on the sunny step.

Miles sat in his brown car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. His dad sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Miles sang too. He tapped his boot on the floor. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then they stopped at a red light. A girl in the next car waved. She held up four small fingers. Miles waved back. Then he held up four fingers too. The light turned green. The girl smiled big. The cars went on.

"Dad, why did she show four fingers?" Miles asked. "Maybe that is how old she is," Dad said. "You can say it with words too." Miles tried it. He held up his fingers and said, "I am four." His voice made the window buzz a little. That was funny.

"Can I say I am six?" he asked. "Six is not your number," said Dad. Miles looked at his fingers. "I am four," he said again. "Four, five, six." He counted all the way to ten before the car stopped.

Ivy sat with Grandma's big cat book. She wanted to hear the cat story again. Grandma was in the kitchen making tea. So Ivy turned the pages herself.

She turned the pages front to back, one by one. Some pages had words. Some pages had only pictures. She pointed at the words, but the words did not say anything to her.

"Grandma, can you read this page?" asked Ivy.

Grandma came over. She sat down. She read the words out loud. "The little cat jumped into a deep, dark box."

Ivy smiled. Then she found a page with no words at all. Only a big orange cat sat there. "Read this page too!" said Ivy.

Grandma looked at it. "There are no words here," she said. "There is nothing written to read. But we can make up our own words if you like."

Ivy nodded. "The cat took a nap," she said slowly. Grandma laughed. Then Grandma read the next page, and Ivy turned it.

Colton played in the playroom. He wanted to build a bird house. He looked for pieces to use. "One, two, three, four," he counted. He found a wooden block. He found a small box. He found a yellow feather on the rug. He held the feather up. "Where did this come from?" he asked. Nelly came to look. "A bird," she said. "Birds are animals that have feathers." Colton smiled. "A bird lost it," he said. "It must have flown by the window."

Maeve brought her toy animals. "One cat, one dog, one bird," she said. The toy bird had soft feathers too. Colton put the yellow feather on the toy bird. Now it looked more real. Ms. Campbell helped him tape the box together. Colton set it on the shelf. He put the wooden block beside it. "One box, one bird, one feather," he said. Nelly clapped. "The bird house looks good," said Ms. Campbell. Colton patted the box gently. "Come back, little bird," he said.

Quinn looked out the window. Snow was falling. "No school today!" said her dad. "Snow day!" Quinn shouted. She put on her boots. They were easy to pull on. Dad drove her to the big sledding hill.

Quinn pulled her sled up the hill. Where did everyone go? The hill was quiet now. Then she saw marks on the snow. Little marks in a line. "Dad, look! What made those?" she asked. Her feet made the same marks when she walked. Her boots pressed the fresh snow. Every step left a print. "Feet leave footprints in fresh snow," said Dad. Quinn giggled. She jumped. More prints!

The prints went down the path. Quinn followed them. Step, step, step. They led to a red door. It was Mr. Wright's door. He opened it. "Would you like a warm egg?" he asked. "Yes, please!" said Quinn. Dad said the egg was hot, so Dad held the plate. Quinn blew on it. It was easy to wait.

After the egg, they all went back outside. Quinn made new footprints. She made them big. She made them small. Anabia came with her sled. "Who made these prints?" Anabia asked. Quinn pointed at her own boots. "Me! Follow them and see!"

Evan sat at the little red table. A tablet sat in front of him. He wanted to draw a sun on it. But he did not know how to start.

Mr. Nguyen came over. He held Evan's hand. Together they pressed the round button. The screen lit up. Evan's eyes went wide. "It works!" he said.

Next, Mr. Nguyen showed him the drawing app. Evan tapped the green square. The app opened. Now Evan needed red for his sun. He looked and looked. He saw blue. He saw yellow. He saw green. Then he saw it. Red! He tapped the red colour. His finger turned red on the screen. He drew a big red sun with happy rays. "So pretty!" said Celeste, who sat beside him. Grayon leaned over too. "Can I catch you drawing a cat next?" he asked. Evan laughed. "I will try!"

Then it was time for snack. Evan pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. He slid the tablet into its basket, just like Mr. Nguyen showed him. "All done," Evan said. Then he ran off to find his crackers.

Maeva looked at her hands. They looked clean. It was time for snack at school.

"My hands aren't dirty!" said Maeva.

Ms. Zhu smiled. "Let's wash them anyway," she said. "Hands that look clean still need washing before eating."

Maeva stood at the little sink. She turned the water on. She put soap on her hands. The soap made white bubbles. Rub, rub, rub. Were the bubbles hiding things too small to see? Maybe!

"Now we count," said Ms. Zhu. "We wash for twenty seconds. Sing the sheep song."

Maeva sang with Abby and Alejandro. "Baa, baa, black sheep, one for my master..." The song was different from a plain count. It made the time go fast. Bubbles, bubbles, down the drain.

Then it was time to eat. Crackers and apple slices. Yum.

After snack, Maeva used the toilet. Then she hurried back to the sink. Water on. Soap on. Rub, rub, rub.

"Where are you going, Maeva?" asked Abby.

"To wash my hands again!" said Maeva. "Baa, baa, black sheep!"

Kai sat at the little table in the school library. He had a crayon and some paper. He wanted to write his own name all by himself.

Kai wrote the letter K. He looked at it. "Oh no," he said. The K was backwards! The arms went the wrong way. He tried again. Backwards again. His K looked naughty, like it was falling over.

Juliana sat down next to him. "Ms. Katz has bumpy letters," she said. "Come and see." Ms. Katz gave Kai a card. The letter K on it was raised up and bumpy. "Put your finger on it," said Ms. Katz. Kai traced the big line down. Then he traced the top arm. Then the bottom arm. Up, in, out. The bumps felt rough under his finger. He traced it again and again.

Then Kai picked up his crayon. He drew the big line down. He drew the top arm. He drew the bottom arm. He looked. The K was right! "Juliana, look!" he called. "It's a real K!" He wrote the whole name. K, A, I. He gave the paper a big kiss, smack, right in the middle. "I'm going to write it ten more times," said Kai, and he grabbed a fresh sheet of paper.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Brielle loved it. Every day they walked to the park. Grandpa sat on a bench near the swings. He pushed her high, high, up.

One day Brielle found a small stick shaped like a bike. She held it up. "Dad has a bike," she said. Then she stopped. She could not see Dad small. Dad was big and tall. "Was Dad ever little?" she asked. She did wonder about that.

Grandpa laughed a soft laugh. "Yes. Dad was a little boy once. I can tell you about it." He told about Dad's first bike. It was red. Dad fell off in the grass. Then Dad got back on. Soon Dad rode all the way to get pizza.

The next day, Brielle saw Celina at the park. "My grandpa tells stories about my dad," said Brielle. "Your grandma can tell stories about your mom too." Celina ran to ask her grandma. Grandma smiled and began a story. Celina sat down to listen.

Zachary went to Ms. Bekele's music studio. He was learning to play the drum. His friend Shelby played the tambourine. The drums were noisy and fun.

Ms. Bekele put a new song on the stand. "Try this one," she said. Zachary hit the drum. Tap, tap, boom. He got stuck in the middle. He tried again. He got stuck in the same spot. Zachary frowned. "This song is too hard," he said.

Ms. Bekele smiled. "Take the drum home," she said. "Play it a little each day." So Zachary took the drum home. On Monday he played a little. On Tuesday he played a little. On Wednesday he played a little more.

Each day Zachary got a bit further in the song. His dad clapped when he played. On Saturday, Zachary played the song all the way to the end. "I did it!" he said. "Fetch your shoes," said his dad. "Time to show Ms. Bekele."

Back at the studio, Zachary played the whole song. Tap, tap, boom, boom! Shelby shook her tambourine along with him. Ms. Bekele danced a little dance. "Play it again," said Shelby. Zachary lifted his drumsticks up high.

Olivier went to a big family party. It was a celebration with songs and food. His grandma held his hand at the door.

There was music playing. People were dancing in a circle. Olivier wanted to dance too. But he felt shy. He stood very still.

"Come and dance," said Winnifred. She was his cousin. She took his other hand. The music went fast, and their feet went fast too. When the music went slow, their feet went slow too. Olivier laughed and laughed.

"Music and dancing go together," said Mr. Pham, his kind neighbour. He clapped to the beat. Olivier clapped too.

Then Olivier saw something funny. A little worm tried to crawl across the floor near the door. When the music stopped, the worm stopped too. When the music started again, Grandma scooped it up in a cup and carried it outside to the garden. "Safe now, little worm," she said.

Olivier kept dancing with Winnifred. His grandma watched with a big smile. "Beautiful dancing," she said.

The music played on and on. Olivier spun around and around. "Again!" he said.

The lights went out. Samuel sat on the floor. It was dark. "Mama, I can't see," he said. Mama came with a candle. She lit it herself. The flame stood up straight. Mama put it on the table.

Samuel wanted to take the candle to his room. He reached out his hand. "No, Samuel," said Mama. "A candle is for grown-ups to light and look after." She gave him a flashlight instead. Samuel pushed the button. The flashlight made light! He shone it on his teddy. He shone it on the wall.

Samuel walked to his room with his flashlight. He read his book by the light. Then he found his crayons. He began to write on paper. The lines went up and down. Soon his eyes felt sleepy. The lights came back on. "All bright again!" said Samuel. He clapped his hands.

It was cold outside at school. Arnaud put on his blue scarf. Maci put on her red scarf.

"Let's race to the door," said Maci. "Fast is best!" They ran fast across the snow. Then they walked slow, slow, slow, because the snow was deep.

At the door, Ms. Brennan said, "Big door for me, small door for you." Arnaud went through the small door. He did not forget to stomp the snow off his boots.

Inside, it was warm. Arnaud took off his scarf. His scarf was long. It went down to his knees. Maci held hers up. Her scarf was short. It went up to her chin.

"Look," said Arnaud. "Mine is long. Yours is short."

"Long and short are opposites," said Maci.

Arnaud smiled. He put his long scarf on the shelf. Maci put her short scarf next to it. The long one hung down, down, down. The short one did not hang at all. Would a short scarf stay warm on his knees? Maybe he would ask his dad for a long one too.

Later, the class made toys from wood. Ms. Brennan used a hammer. Arnaud watched from far away, because hammers were for grown-ups. His new wool hat felt itchy, so he pulled it off and held it.

"Can we wear our scarves again?" Arnaud asked.

"At play time," said Ms. Brennan.

Arnaud held up his long scarf and swung it like a rope. It swung far. Maci swung her short scarf. It swung just a little bit.

"Long swings far," said Arnaud. "Short swings near."

Avery ran to the playground. A big black box sat by the slide. She stopped and stared. "What can this be?" she wondered.

Himmat came running too. "It's a car!" he said. He sat in the box and turned a pretend wheel. "Vroom, vroom!" Avery wanted a turn, but not as a car. She wanted a house. "It's my house," she said. "You can come in." Himmat shook his head. "Cars go fast. Houses stay still."

Then Avery had an idea. "First it is your car. Then it is my house. We can take turns." Himmat drove the car to the sandbox. Then he climbed out. Avery climbed in. She set a toy bunny on her lap. "Time for bed, little bunny," she said softly. She patted its head.

After that, Himmat came back. "Now it's a boat!" he said. Avery laughed. "A boat on the blue sand sea!" They both climbed in and rowed with their hands. Ms. Kang walked by and smiled. "Where is your boat going today?" she asked. Avery looked at the box and grinned. "Anywhere we want!"

Avery walked into the library with her dad. Ms. Goh smiled at the door. "Time for your library card," she said. Avery held out her hand. The card was blue and had her name on it. She picked a book about a little red fox. Ms. Goh scanned the card. The book was Avery's to take home.

Avery read the fox book every night. Soon she knew all the words. She turned the last page and felt a little bad. "It's over," she said. Her dad said, "Let's go back to the library."

Avery gave the fox book to Ms. Goh. Then she looked at her card. Was it all used up now? She felt worried. "I gave the book back," she told Ms. Goh. Ms. Goh held up the card. "This card can be used again and again," she said. "It keeps working. Pick a new book."

Avery ran to the shelf. She found a book about a big yellow truck. Ms. Goh scanned the same blue card. The door beeped and the book was hers. Avery hugged it tight. "Same card, new book," she said. Her dad laughed, and they walked home together.

Owen loved story time at daycare. Ms. Schneider held up a big book. "Who made up this story?" Owen asked. "A real person did. I want to know!"

Ms. Schneider smiled. "Look here," she said. She pointed to the cover. There was a name on it. "That is the author," she said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book."

Owen leaned in close. He traced the letters with his finger. "You wrote this book," he told the name. He looked at the back cover too. "Is your name back there?"

"No, Owen," said Ms. Schneider. "We start at the front. Then we go page by page." She turned the first page. Then the second. Then the third.

The story was about a slimy green frog. The frog sat on a big wall. One, two, three flies went by. The frog jumped. One, two, three, gulp!

Owen laughed. Then Jemma held up her little book. "Who made up mine?" she asked.

Owen ran to her. He pointed at the cover. "Look! A name!" He read it out loud. "That one. That one made it up!"

"Good job," said Jemma. Then she opened her book at the front. "Read it with me?"

"Front to back," said Owen. He sat down next to her. "One, two, three, go!"
