Blake was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. The bowls were on the table. The spoons were by the bowls. Blake was hungry. She wanted her soup now.

But Grandma held her hands. Everyone else held hands too. Grandma closed her eyes. Blake did not know why. Her tummy made a little growl. She waited. She peeked at her cousin. His eyes were shut tight.

Grandma spoke soft words. Blake listened hard. The words went on and on. Then Blake heard one word. It was "Amen." Everyone opened their eyes. Everyone let go of hands. The blessing was over.

"Now we eat," said Grandma. She smiled at Blake. "You waited so nicely." Blake picked up her spoon. The soup was warm and good. Her cousin gave her a napkin. She had forgotten hers. "Thank you," said Blake.

At dinner, Blake was ready. She held Grandma's hand. She closed her eyes tight. She listened for the word. She waited and waited. Then it came. "Amen," said Grandma. Blake opened her eyes fast. "Now we eat!" she said. Grandma laughed. "Yes, now we eat." Blake dug her spoon into the mashed potatoes. Her black cat hopped onto the chair. He wanted some too. "Not for cats," said Grandma, and she set him back on the floor.

The window in art class was cloudy. Theodore could not see the sun. He sat on the rug with his shape blocks. One, two, three, four, he counted. A circle, a square, a triangle, a rectangle.

"I want to build a house," said Theodore. Warren sat close beside him. Warren took the square block. Then Warren turned it. A corner pointed up.

"Look!" said Warren. "A new shape!"

Theodore felt worried. His house needed a square. Now the square looked like something else. He took the block. He turned it back. The corner sat flat on the floor.

"It is the square," said Theodore. Warren turned it again. The corner pointed up. Warren turned it back. Flat again.

"A square turned so a corner points up is still a square," said Warren.

Ms. Singh smiled. "Build your house," she said.

Theodore stacked the blocks. One, two, three, four. Circle on top, square at the bottom, triangle for the roof. Warren added the rectangle door.

"Nice house," said Ms. Singh.

Theodore gave the block one more turn. The corner pointed up. Then he turned it back and set it down flat.

Mason ran to Skyler's house. It was lunchtime. Skyler's grandma made round pancakes. Mason sat down fast. He was very hungry.

Then everyone held hands. They bowed their heads. Mason did not know what to do. He sat still.

"Would you like to say grace?" Grandma asked Skyler.

"Yes," said Skyler. "Grace is our thanks before we eat." Skyler said thank you for the food and for friends. Then everyone said "Amen" and picked up forks.

Mason felt left out. He wanted a turn too. "Can I say grace next time?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You can say it now."

Mason held hands tight. "Thank you for pancakes," he said. "Thank you for Skyler!"

Everyone said "Amen." Grandma smiled and gave him the biggest pancake. Mason took a big bite. It tasted so good. He was already ready for the next meal.

Miles stood by the cages at the pet store. "I want that one," he said. He pointed at a small gray kitten. "Good pick," said Mr. Bekele. "Let's get what she needs."

Miles picked out a soft bed. He picked out a little bowl. Then he stopped. "Where will she go potty?" he asked. "We have no grass inside."

Mr. Bekele held up a box full of sand. "This is a litter box," he said. "An indoor cat uses it as her toilet."

At home, the kitten sniffed the box. She climbed in. She dug a little hole. Then she covered it up.

"Wow," said Miles. The next morning, he checked the box. It was used again. "It works!" he said.

His friend Sasha came over. She brought a toy robot cat. "My robot doesn't need a box," she said. The real kitten walked by. She beg ged for a treat with big eyes. Miles laughed and gave her one.

Then the kitten ran to her litter box again. Miles followed her. "Come see," he said to Sasha. "This is where she goes."

The lights went out at the farmhouse. It was dark everywhere. Matthew held his mom's hand. "The power went out," Mom said. She found a flashlight and turned it on. A bright circle danced on the wall. Matthew followed it with his eyes.

Mom lit a candle on the table. Matthew watched the little flame from his chair. "What else can we do in the dark?" he wondered. They made shadow bunnies with their hands. Then they looked out the window. The barn looked big and dark. The yard was muddy from the rain. Far away, the snowy hills still shone a little.

Then the lights came back on. Everything was bright again. Matthew looked at the oven. Its clock was blinking. Blink, blink, blink. "It needs to be set again," Mom said. She pushed the buttons. Matthew watched the numbers appear, one by one. "There," said Mom. "All done." Matthew waved at the oven clock. "Good night, blinky," he said.

Declan sat at the dinner table. He wore his little blue shirt with a rocket on it. His cup of milk was far away. He wanted it very much.

Dad stood in the way. Dad was serving the peas. Declan tried to squeeze past Dad's legs. He pushed a little. Dad did not move. Declan could not reach his milk.

Then Mom said, "Try excuse me." Declan looked up at Dad. "Excuse me," he said. Dad stepped to the side. "Coming through," said Dad with a smile. Declan walked past and got his cup.

Declan drank his milk. It was cold and good. "Thank you," he said to Dad. Dad patted his head. Charlee came over to play after dinner. She had a little game with a red ball. Charlee bumped the peas with her elbow. "Sorry," she said. "That's okay," said Declan. Then they played the ball game under the warm kitchen light.

Nathan's baby sister came home. She was small and sweet. Nathan wanted to help.

At night, Nathan heard a cry. He rubbed his eyes. He went to the door. Mama was holding the baby. "Is she sad?" Nathan asked. "She is hungry," said Mama. "Grown-ups feed a new baby many times, both day and night." The baby drank her milk. Then she went back to sleep.

The next night, Nathan heard the cry again. "Mama, it is time to feed her!" he said. Mama smiled. Nathan pointed to the milk on the table. The baby drank and drank. Then Nathan patted her soft blanket. "Good night, little one," he said. The baby made a tiny sound, like a small animal. In the morning, Nathan drew a picture. It showed Mama feeding the baby, with stars in the sky.

Kinsley ran to the pool in her pink suit. She wanted to jump in right away. Her friend Azaan was already in the water, splashing like a happy snake. "Wait," said Ms. Farah-Ali. "You have to take a shower first. Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in."

"A shower?" said Kinsley. "I am not dirty!" "Even so," said Ms. Farah-Ali. "It is a pool rule." Kinsley did not want to wait. She did not want to stand alone under the water. But she did want to swim.

So Kinsley stood under the little shower. The water went drip, drip, drip down her arms. "Drip, drip, drip!" she laughed. Then she ran to the pool. She jumped in with a big splash. "I showered, so I can swim!" she called. Azaan splashed her back. Ms. Farah-Ali helped Kinsley hang her towel on the hook. "Next time I will shower fast," said Kinsley. "Drip, drip, drip!"

Edouard sat in his big car seat. Mika sat next to him in her small one. "Are we there yet?" asked Edouard. "Not yet," said the dad. "Drive fast, drive fast!" said Mika. The dad drove fast on the big road. Then he drove slow on the small street. Edouard saw a big truck. He saw a small blue car too. The sun was hot on his arm. The air from the window was cold. "Hot and cold," said Mika, and they both laughed.

They stopped at the park. Edouard jumped out. He saw a puddle. He stepped in it. Splash! His socks got wet. He made a grumpy face. "My socks are wet," he said. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mika. "You need dry socks." The dad opened a bag. He pulled out dry socks. Edouard sat on the bench and pulled them on. First one foot, then the other. He had to think which foot went where.

The dry socks felt warm and soft. Edouard stood up. He stamped his feet. "Dry feet!" he said. "Nice work," said the dad. Edouard looked back at the puddle. He walked around it this time. Splash-free. "Race you to the swings," said Mika. Edouard ran, slow at first, then fast.

Caleb went to the beach with his dad. His friend Alessio was there too. Mr. Wilson was in the water. He was a swim teacher. "Come and practice," said Mr. Wilson.

Caleb was shy. He did not want his face near the water. "Look at me," said Mr. Wilson. He put his mouth in the water. Then big bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! Alessio laughed and laughed. Caleb looked at the sky. Then he looked at the bubbles.

Caleb put his mouth in the water next. He blew and blew. One bubble, two bubbles, ten bubbles! The bubbles tickled his nose. "Again!" said Caleb. He blew more bubbles. Then a little fish swam by his feet. Caleb gasped and sat up. "Hello, fish," he said. "Watch me blow bubbles again!"

Lennon sat on the bench at the temple. Her friend Zeke sat next to her. Up front, people were singing a song about a river. Lennon clapped. Her claps went fast. The song went slow.

"That's too fast," said Zeke. "Listen first." Lennon watched Ms. Ong. Ms. Ong clapped slow, steady claps. Clap, clap, clap. Lennon tried again. Slow claps. Now her claps matched the song. Zeke smiled and clapped with her.

After the song, Ms. Ong taught them a rhyme. "Row, row, row your boat," she sang. Lennon sang too. She sang as loud as she could. Zeke covered his ears. "Your singing is louder than my stinky socks," he laughed.

Then a baby fell asleep on a grown-up's lap. Ms. Ong put her finger to her lips. Lennon sang the same rhyme again. This time she sang it very soft, like a whisper. The baby kept sleeping. Same song, small voice.

Lennon whispered to Zeke, "A song can be loud. A song can be soft." Then she clapped one more slow, steady clap, and Zeke clapped it back.

Axel sat in his reading nook. He had a book and his stuffed chicken. On the wall, there was a big letter A. "A is for apple," said Axel. He felt happy.

Then he looked at his book. He saw a small letter a. He pointed at it. "That is not A," he said. "A is big. This one is little." He began to cry a little. "Where is my A?"

His dad came to the nook. Axel held up the book. "Is this a new letter?" he asked. His dad smiled. "No," he said. "A can be big or small." Axel looked at the wall. Then he looked at the book. He put one finger on the big A. He put one finger on the small a. "Both are A!" said Axel. "A says ah, ah, ah."

Axel turned the page. He found a small b. Then he found a small c. "Big B, small b," he said. "Big C, small c." He hugged his chicken. "You have a pretty name letter too," he said. "C is for chicken!" Axel read on and on, all the way to his cozy pillow.

Isabelle stood by the big sink. She wanted to wash her hands all by herself. "Can I do it?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said her dad. He turned the tap. The water ran. Isabelle touched it with one finger. "Cold!" she said. Her dad turned the other tap. Steam went up. "That side is hot," he said. "I keep my hands away from hot water." Isabelle kept her hands away too.

Then she saw something on the shelf. It was small. It was black. It had a long shape. "What is that?" she asked. "That is a lighter," said her dad. "It is only for grown-ups to use." Isabelle looked at it. She did not touch it. She pointed with her finger instead.

"I will not touch it," said Isabelle. "I will not touch it," she said again. Her dad smiled. He put the lighter up high, far, far away. Isabelle waved to it. Then she washed her hands in the cold water. "Look, Daddy! Bubbles!" she said. Her dad helped her dry her hands on the long towel. "All clean," he said.

Everett was three years old today. His party was at the big hall in town. Balloons hung by the door. A thick red curtain stood on the stage.

Everett marched in with his box of invitations. He had drawn a cake on each one. His friends came through the door one by one.

Harriet stopped outside. She looked worried. "I got lost on the way," she said. "I did not know where to go."

Everett ran to her. He held up his invitation. "Look," he said. "It says the party is at the big hall." Harriet looked at the paper. She saw the hall on it. She saw a time too. "It says three o'clock," she said. "That is now!"

"So you came to the right place," said Everett. Harriet smiled big. She put the invitation in her pocket.

Mr. Qureshi set out cups of juice. Anita picked a blue balloon. Everyone sat at the long table. The cake came out with three candles. A grown-up lit them carefully. Everett blew hard. The candles went out. All his friends clapped and cheered.

Harriet waved her invitation in the air. "Best paper ever," she said. "Now let's eat cake!"

Willow wanted to paint a green frog. But her paint pots had no green. She had red, yellow and blue.

She looked for green. She looked in the big box. She looked under her doll. No green paint anywhere.

Willow touched her yellow brush. Then she touched the blue paint. She made a big swirl on the paper. The yellow spot turned green! She dipped again and again. Now she had a green frog, and a green cat, and a green furry monster too.

At bedtime, Willow left her brushes in the paint pots. She went to sleep with her doll beside her.

The next morning, the brushes were stiff. They felt hard like sticks. "Oh no," said Willow. "My brushes!"

Mummy came to help. "We wash them with water," she said. Mummy held the brushes under the tap. Willow watched from her stool. The paint ran off into the sink. Then they laid the brushes flat on a towel to dry.

Soon the brushes were soft again. Willow picked one up. "Paint time?" she asked. Mummy smiled and got out the paper.

Beau sat at the dinner table. His cup was empty. He wanted more milk.

Mom held a big pot. It made a loud clang when she set it down. Beau clapped his hands. "Loud! Fun!" he said.

His dad put his hands over his ears. "Too loud for me," Dad said.

Beau looked at Dad. He looked at the pot. "Dad does not like it?" he asked.

"No, I like quiet," said Dad.

Beau wanted Dad to feel happy too. So Beau tapped his spoon softly. Tap, tap, tap. That made a small sound. Dad smiled. Beau smiled too.

"What if I tap a cow picture?" Beau asked. He tapped his placemat. It showed a huge cow. Dad laughed. "Quiet taps are my favorite," Dad said.

Mom brought the milk. Beau took a drink. "Thank you," he said. Then he tapped his cup, very soft, one more time. Dad tapped his cup back.

Andrew sat on his bed with a big piece of dry paper. He wanted to write a note for his dad. The note would say, "I love you." Andrew wrote the letters one by one. "I, L, O, V, E, Y, O, U." He wrote them all squished together in one long line. "ILOVEYOU."

Dad came in to tuck Andrew in. He read the paper. He scratched his head. "Hmm," said Dad. "This says Iloveyou? I cannot read this."

Andrew felt worried. He wanted Dad to read his note. Then he looked at his bookshelf. His book about a red flag sat there. Andrew opened the book. He turned the pages from the front to the back. The words marched across each page. One word. A little space. Then the next word. "Look, Dad! The words have spaces!"

Andrew picked up his pencil again. He wrote one word, then a space, then the next word. One space. Two spaces. Three spaces. "I love you."

Dad read it out loud. "I love you too, Andrew!" Dad gave him a big hug. Andrew yelled, "Hooray!" He put the note under his pillow. Dad turned off the light. "Read it to me again," Andrew whispered, "one more time."

Sarah and her dad drive to the pharmacy. Sarah thinks they are going to see her doctor. "I do not like shots," she says. Dad smiles. "Today we see someone new," he says. The cashier hands Dad a little paper bag.

At the new place, a big chair waits. It goes up and down. A kind woman looks in Sarah's mouth. She counts Sarah's teeth. One, two, three. She looks and looks. She does not look at Sarah's arm. She does not give a shot. "You only looked at my teeth," says Sarah. The woman nods. "A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth," she says.

Sarah gets a new toothbrush. It is her favorite color, red. "Open wide," she tells her teddy at home. Teddy stays very awake.

Jordan was playing in the yard with his red ball. The gate was closed. Then a new boy came to the gate with his mom. The boy was Jaxtyn. He had just moved in next door.

"Can you play?" asked Jaxtyn.

"Yes!" said Jordan. He opened the gate for him.

Jaxtyn kicked the ball. It flew over the flowers and hit a watering can. Crash!

"Sorry," said Jaxtyn.

"That's okay," said Jordan. "You can say sorry to the flowers too."

Jaxtyn laughed. "Sorry, flowers," he said.

Jordan's mom came out with two cups of juice. "Please carry them carefully," she said. The boys carried the cups slowly, one step at a time. Not one drop spilled.

"Gracias," said Jaxtyn.

Jordan looked up. "What does that mean?"

"Gracias means thank you in Spanish," said Jaxtyn.

Jordan tried it. "Gracias," he said. "Did I say it right?"

"You said it right!" said Jaxtyn.

They practiced all afternoon. "Gracias. Gracias. Gracias," they said, and they giggled every time.

When Jaxtyn's mom called him home, he waved at the gate. "See you tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Jordan. "Gracias for playing with me!"

Samuel ran to the baseball diamond. Ms. Bui had red hoops and beanbags. She had one big blue ball too.

"Watch this!" said Samuel. He spun in a circle first. He got dizzy and fell down. Briar laughed. Samuel laughed too.

Then Samuel picked up a beanbag. He looked at Zakaria. "Ready?" he asked. He threw the beanbag. It landed in the grass. It missed the hoop.

"Oops," said Samuel. He got another beanbag. This time he looked at the hoop. He looked and looked. Then he threw. The beanbag went in!

"Wow!" said Zakaria. "Do it again!" Samuel looked at the hoop again. He threw. In it went, again!

Next was the big blue ball. Ms. Bui tossed it high. Samuel held out both hands. He looked at the ball, not at Briar. Thump! He caught it.

"Now pass it to me," said Briar. Samuel passed the big ball. Briar looked up at the sky. The ball bounced off her head. Everyone giggled.

"My turn again!" said Samuel. He held up both hands. "Throw it to the top of my head, Ms. Bui!"

Everly got a violin for her birthday. It was a small gift in a big box. She wanted to play a song for Veer today.

She held the violin under her arm. Then she poked the strings with the stick. The violin made a squeak. Everly laughed. "That was a silly sound," she said. She tried again. Squeak, squeak.

Mr. Sutherland was their neighbor. He came over with his own violin. "This stick is called a bow," he said. He pulled the bow across the strings. A long, sweet note filled the room. Everly watched close. She put the bow on the strings. She pulled it slow, just like him. A real note came out. She did it again and again. Each slow pull made a song.

Veer clapped his hands. "Play more," he said. Everly smiled and pulled the bow one more time.

Josephine sat on the grass at the park. She had paper and crayons. She wanted to draw the tall trees. She wanted to draw the swings. She picked up a gray crayon for the sky. Then she looked up. The sun was out. The day was clear and bright. "Wow," said Josephine. "The sky is blue!" She put the gray crayon down. She picked up the blue crayon instead.

Her friend Amal sat down next to her. "What are you drawing?" Amal asked. "The park," said Josephine. "I looked up first. Then I picked blue." Amal looked up too. "The sky is blue today," Amal said. Josephine drew a big blue sky. She drew a yellow sun in it. A white cloud began to float by, slow and soft.

Josephine waited for the cloud to move. She watched it float and float. Then she drew it. She drew green grass and a red ball. "Nice sky," said Amal. "The weather is good today." Josephine held up her picture. "Blue sky, yellow sun," she said. "Blue sky, yellow sun." The tall trees waved in the wind, and she drew them too.

Olivier ran to Grandpa's big chair. His teddy bear, Blue, sat on the arm. Olivier grabbed him fast. Oh no! Blue fell down. He landed on the floor with a soft plop.

Olivier picked Blue up. He looked at Blue's tummy. "Did that hurt?" he asked. Grandpa leaned down near the chair. "Blue is a toy," Grandpa said. "Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Olivier smiled so big. He hugged Blue tight. "A pretend hug!" he said. He patted Blue's head. He gave Blue a little scratch behind his ear, just like a puppy. Blue felt soft and warm.

Then Olivier set up a house by the sofa. Blue lay on a small blanket. Olivier fed him a pretend bottle. "Drink, Blue," he said. "Then we play more." Grandpa clapped his hands. "What fun!" he said.

Olivier held Blue up high. "Now you fly, Blue!" he shouted. And around the room they went.

Victoria sat at the dinner table. She had big news. She had seen a pink pig at the farm today! The pig had a curly tail and a wet nose.

Mom was talking to Dad. "So Grandpa said he will take the bus on Sunday," said Mom. Victoria bounced in her seat. "Pig! Pig!" she said. Mom kept talking. Victoria said it again, louder. Still, Mom kept talking.

Victoria felt like crying. Her news was stuck inside her, like a balloon. She looked at the pig salt shaker on the table. It looked right back at her. "Wait," the pig salt shaker seemed to whisper. Victoria took a little bread and ate it slowly. She watched Mom's mouth. Mom talked. Then Mom stopped. There was a quiet space, quiet as a feather.

Victoria took a brave, big breath. "Mom, I saw a pig today!" she said. Mom turned to her right away. "A real pig? Tell me!" Victoria told her all about the curly tail. "And it said oink, oink!"

"Thank you for waiting, Victoria," said Mom. "May I have some milk, please?" said Victoria. Mom poured it. Later, Victoria bumped her cup and some milk spilled. "Sorry," she said. Dad wiped it up and smiled.

Victoria held the pig salt shaker close. "Good pig," she whispered. "Oink," she answered, very quietly.

Mateo sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy hurt a little. "Time for your checkup," said Ms. Pérez. First Mateo had to use the toilet. Then Ms. Pérez showed him the little sink. "Now we wash," she said. "We count to twenty." She squirted soap on his hands. One, two, three! The soap got bubbly and white. The bubbles slipped down his fingers. Ten, eleven, twelve! Mateo rubbed and rubbed. Twenty! The water washed all the soap away. His hands looked shiny and clean. Before that, dirt had been on them. Now the dirt was missing! "Lunch time," said his dad. He held out crackers. Mateo looked at his clean hands. "Wash first!" he said. He ran back to the sink. "One, two, three..."

Aaron sat on the big couch. He had a cold. His nose was red and his throat hurt a bit.

Mom brought him warm soup. Aaron took a sip. Then his throat hurt more. It felt scratchy, like a little worm crawling. Aaron wanted to hide it. He did not want more medicine.

But Aaron thought of what Ms. Bianchi said at school. "When you feel sick, you tell a grown-up." Rylan had told the teacher about his tummy, and she had helped fast.

So Aaron said, "Mom, my throat hurts." Mom felt his head. "You are warm," she said. She gave him a cool drink and a soft blanket. Soon his throat felt better.

Myla came by later. They counted ten cars from the window. "You are strong," Myla said. Aaron smiled and took another sip.

Romy was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a small dirt patch by the fence. "Can I plant seeds?" Romy asked. Grandma smiled and gave her three little seeds. They were small and hard.

Romy dug a hole with her hands. She dropped the seeds in. She patted the dirt down, pat, pat. Then Grandma filled a small watering can. Romy poured the water over the dirt. The dirt turned dark and wet. "Will a sprout come up now?" Romy asked. "Seeds need water to grow," said Grandma. "But a sprout does not come up right away."

The next morning, Romy ran outside. She looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. Where was it? She poured more water. She waited. She felt a funny feeling in her tummy, a hoping feeling.

Every day she poured a little water. One morning, something green stood in the dirt! It was a tiny sprout, bent like a small hook. "You came up!" Romy shouted. Then the sprout lifted its head, and on top was a red ladybug. "Hello," said Romy. "Are you visiting my sprout too?"

Rowan ran into the big bathroom at the pool. He wanted to wash his hands all by himself. Dad said, "I will be right here at the door."

Rowan saw two taps. One tap had a red dot. One tap had a blue dot. He turned the red tap. Hot water came out. The steam felt warm on his face. Dad came over fast. He turned the red tap off. "The red one is hot," Dad said. "I will do the hot tap for you." Dad turned the blue tap. Cold water ran over Rowan's hands. It felt cool and nice.

Then Rowan saw a little spider near the drain. "Hello, spider," he said. The spider ran in a circle. Rowan wanted to touch it. But there was a bottle by the sink with a big red label. Rowan reached for it. Dad put it up high. "That one is not for little hands," Dad said. Rowan looked at the spider instead.

Rowan walked down to the far end of the bathroom. It was long like a hall. He looked back. He could not see Dad. He could not see his shoes by the door. Rowan walked back. Dad was still at the door, waving. "There you are," Dad said.

Rowan dried his hands on the soft towel. He had found out something. When he went far, he could not see Dad. When he came near, he could. "Can I wash again tomorrow?" Rowan asked. "Yes," said Dad. Rowan held Dad's hand, and they walked out together.

Benjamin went to the library with his dad. Ms. Weber had three tablets on a table. "Can I use one?" Benjamin asked. "Yes," said Ms. Weber. "I will show you how."

Benjamin pressed the round button. The screen lit up. He had made that happen. He tapped the blue square with the crayon on it. A drawing app opened. He made a big deep blue lake and a yellow sun. "One sun, two ducks, three fish," he counted as he drew.

Then the screen went black. "Oh no," said Benjamin. He pressed the button again. Nothing happened. He tried once more. Still nothing. "The tablet ran out of power," said Ms. Weber. "It needs charging." She plugged the charger into the wall. Benjamin watched. The little battery picture came back on the screen.

"Now we wait," said Ms. Weber. They read a book while the tablet sat still. After the book, the screen was awake again. "Summer!" said Benjamin, and he drew a green tree. When he was done, Ms. Weber helped him press the button, slide the tablet into its box, and put it back on the shelf. "Goodbye, tablet," said Benjamin. "I will press your button next time."

School was over. Aaron waited by the gate. His tummy felt funny.

"I need the toilet," Aaron said to Mr. Charles.

"I will wait right here," said Mr. Charles.

Aaron ran inside. He used the toilet. Then he pulled up his pants. He ran to the gate.

Mr. Charles sniffed. "Aaron, did you flush?" he asked.

Aaron thought. No. He had not flushed.

Aaron ran back. He pushed the handle. The water swirled down. Then he stopped. Something else was missing.

"Wash my hands," Aaron said out loud.

He turned on the water. He put on soap. He rubbed his hands. The bubbles were soft. He rinsed the soap off. The water ran down the drain. His hands were clean.

Aaron walked to the gate. His friend Kailey was there too. Her dad was zipping up her coat.

"There you are," said Mr. Charles. "Your mom is by the tree."

Aaron found his mom. She held his soft blue blanket. "Nap time soon," she said.

"First a snack," said Aaron. "Then a bath. Then my pajamas."

Mom laughed. "Yes, all of those."

Aaron held her hand all the way to the car.

Nicholas was in the playroom with his friend Quinn. On the floor there were three big circles made of string. Mr. Kamau had made them after breakfast. "Let's sort," he said. "Put animals here. Put toys here. Put foods here."

Nichels picked up a toy bear. Was it an animal? No, it was a toy. It went in the toy circle. He counted as he sorted. "One bear, two balls, three blocks." Quinn found a cat puzzle piece. "Cat!" said Quinn. It went with the animals.

Then Nicholas found a carrot. He put it in the toy circle. Mr. Kamau shook his head. "Where does the carrot go?" he asked. Nicholas looked and looked. There was an apple in one circle. There was bread in the same circle. Apples and bread were there, and they were foods.

Maybe the carrot was a food too? Nicholas picked it up. He moved it next to the apple and the bread. He counted again. "One apple, two breads, three carrots." All foods!

Then Mr. Kamau held up something furry with long ears. "What is this?" he asked. It was a rabbit, a real soft rabbit! The rabbit hopped over and sniffed the carrot. "He likes foods too," said Nicholas. The rabbit took a tiny nibble.

Hazel put on her new coat. It was red and smooth. She wanted to zip it all by herself. "I can do it," she said. Mom smiled. "Let's go to the grocery store. You can practice."

At the store, Hazel got warm. She pulled her arms out of the coat. It fell down on the floor. Then the cart rolled right over it. "Oops," said Hazel. She picked it up and put it in the cart, all bunched up.

At the checkout, they saw Mr. Berg, their neighbor. He had carrots and a big potato. "We will cook soup tonight," he said. Hazel helped Mom put the apples on the belt. One apple was green, one was red, one was yellow. "A little rainbow of apples!" said Hazel.

Then it was time to go. Hazel's coat was bunched and twisted. She could not find the zipper. She pulled and pulled. "Where is it?" she said. The coat was inside out and tangled.

Hazel shook the coat flat. She found the zipper pull. She pushed the two sides together. Click. Then she zipped it up, up, up, all the way to her chin. "I did it!" she said. At the door there was a little hook. Hazel took off her coat and hung it on the hook. The coat stayed up, off the floor. Mom laughed. "Look at that. Now let's go home and cook." Hazel grabbed the cart handle and marched out the door.

Isaiah ran up the steps to Grandma's house. Today was his birthday! The door smelled like cake and warm sugar.

Pierre and Farhan were already inside. They had big grins on their faces.

"Guess what!" said Isaiah. "I am four now!"

Grandma set the cake on the table. Grandpa lit the candles with a match. Isaiah watched from his chair. The candles made little dancing lights.

Then everyone began to sing. "Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday, dear Isaiah. Happy birthday to you."

Isaiah heard it. They sang his name! His very own name, right in the song. He hid his big smile behind his hands. But it peeked out anyway.

"They said me!" he said. "My name is in the song!"

Pierre laughed. "Sing it again," he said. So they did. Once more, everyone sang "dear Isaiah" and Isaiah clapped his hands.

Grandpa blew out the candles for him, so the smoke went up in a thin gray line. Grandma cut the cake. Isaiah got the first big piece. The frosting was sweet and cold on his tongue.

Soon Isaiah was sleepy and happy. He did not want to leave. "One more song," he said. "Sing my name again."

So they sang it one more time, soft and slow. Isaiah smiled all the way to the door.

It was Brooklyn's birthday at the bowling alley. She wore a party hat with stars. Her friends Annalise and Ben came too. Ms. Gupta, her neighbor, came as well.

Dad gave Brooklyn a red balloon. He had blown it up himself. "Let go and watch!" said Ben.

Brooklyn held it up high. She let go. She waited for it to fly. It did not fly. It went down, down, down. It landed soft on the floor.

Brooklyn picked it up. She tossed it up again. Down it came again. "Again!" she said. Up, then down. Up, then down.

Annalise laughed. Ben tossed it too. His balloon came down too. Ms. Gupta smiled and said, "You are very polite, sharing the balloon."

Then the lights went low. The pins looked bright and shiny. Dad helped Brooklyn roll her ball. One, two, three pins fell down. The balloon came down too, right beside her feet.

"Happy birthday, Brooklyn," said Dad. She held her balloon tight and gave him a big hug. The moon was coming up outside the big window. "Again," Brooklyn said. "Again tomorrow."

Josephine loved one book at daycare. It had a big brown bear on the cover. The bear was about to sleep in a pile of leaves.

Today the book was not on the shelf. Josephine looked and looked. "Where did it go?" she asked.

Mira pointed to the book corner. "Iqra has a book," she said.

Josephine ran over. Iqra held a book, but the cover showed a frog. A long tongue stuck out of the frog's mouth. It was not the bear book.

Josephine went to Mr. Grewal. She felt sad. "My book is lost," she said.

"What is the book called?" asked Mr. Grewal.

Josephine thought hard. She pointed at the shelf. "The one with the brown bear."

"Let's look," said Mr. Grewal. He turned a book so she could see the front. Big letters sat at the top. "These words are its name," he said.

Josephine squinted at the letters. "Where is the bear book's name?" she asked.

Iqra came over with her frog book. She held it up. "This one says Frog," she said.

Then Josephine saw it. Behind Iqra, on the shelf, was her bear! She grabbed it. The name was on the front, just like the frog book.

"Now I can find it myself," said Josephine.

She sat down and opened the cover. She turned page one, then page two, all the way to the end. The brown bear curled up and went to sleep.

"Goodnight, bear," said Josephine.

Livia walked to the store with her dad. The street was wet from the rain. Livia jumped over a small puddle. Splash!

Inside the store, Livia saw Mr. Reddy. He worked at the fruit stand. "Can I help?" Livia asked. "Yes," said Mr. Reddy. "We sort by color here." He pointed to big bins. "All the same color goes together."

Livia made a red pile. She put in apples and strawberries. She made a yellow pile. She put in bananas. She made a green pile. She put in pears and grapes.

Then Livia saw a blue bin. Blueberries went in there. She looked and looked. One blueberry was hiding in the red pile! It did not match the apples. Livia picked it up. She put it with the other blueberries. "It belongs here," she said.

Mr. Reddy smiled. "Good sorting, Livia." At home, Livia got to chew a sweet red apple. "Yum," she said. "Red is my favorite."

Ibrahim sat on the playroom floor. He had a bowl of crackers next to him. Aaron sat close by, building with blocks.

Ibrahim held up a cracker. "Is this a square?" he asked.

Aaron looked at it. "I don't know," he said.

Ibrahim found a piece of string. He laid it along one side of the cracker. Then he held the string up. "Now let's see," he said. He laid the string on the next side. It was just the same. He laid it on the third side. The same again. One more side to go. He laid the string down. The same!

"Four sides," said Ibrahim. "All the same length. It's a square!"

Aaron clapped his hands. "A square cracker!" he said.

Ibrahim took a bite. Crunch. The cracker was gone. He reached into the bowl for another one. This one was long, not square. "Hmm," said Ibrahim. He got the string again. He laid it on each side. One side was long. The short sides were not the same.

"This one is not a square," said Ibrahim.

"Maybe it's a rectangle," said Aaron.

Ibrahim put the long cracker down. He picked up a block. It was black and square. He laid the string on all four sides. All the same length. "Square!" he said.

Aaron held up a block too. They laughed and lined up their squares on the floor, one, two, three, four.

Ibrahim finished his last cracker. "Square," he said, and smiled.

Emile ate his sandwich at lunch. It was a good sandwich with cheese. After lunch, his dad helped him fold his socks. Emile put them in his drawer.

Then it was bath time. Dad ran the warm bath with his hand on the tap. Emile splashed and washed his toes. He put on his soft pajamas. He brushed his teeth in the bathroom with his little blue brush.

Dad read a book to Emile. Then Emile got into bed. Dad turned off the light. But Emile sat up. "Wait!" he said. "I ate my snack after my bath. My teeth are not clean now."

Emile hopped out of bed. He ran to the bathroom. He brushed his teeth up and down. He spat into the sink. Dad brought the towel and helped him wipe his mouth.

"That was good thinking," said Dad. Emile smiled in the dark mirror. Then Dad tucked him back into bed. "Morning, we brush again," said Emile sleepily. Dad kissed his head.

Naomi sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. "Today you get a shot," said the doctor. Naomi's eyes got wide. She thought a shot would be huge. Maybe as big as a hornet! Maybe it would take all day!

"I don't want a big poke," said Naomi. "It will be quick," said the doctor. "It is one quick poke in your arm." Naomi peeked at the tray. The needle was thin, like a little straw. "That is so small!" she said. "That is silly small!" She asked, "Can I watch?" "You can watch," said the doctor.

Naomi held her mama's hand. She looked at the thin needle. The doctor tapped her arm. Then came one quick poke. "Ow," said Naomi. But then it was done! A bandage was already on her arm.

"That was fast!" said Naomi. "It was one quick poke!" The doctor laughed. Naomi jumped down from the chair. "Mama, can we get milk?" she asked. "A snack after your shot," said Mama. Naomi ran to the door, waving her bandage. "I was so brave!"

It was animal day at school. Alexis brought his toy dog. It was brown and soft. "Dogs are animals," said Mr. Guo. "Show us your animal, Alexis." Alexis held up his dog. Aron held up a toy elephant. "An elephant is an animal too," said Aron. "It is big and gray."

Elliot had a problem. He held up his toy fish. "I can't play," he said. "My fish has no legs. It is not an animal." Alexis looked at the fish. It had no legs at all. His dog had legs. The elephant had legs. Elliot's fish just had a tail and fins. Elliot's lip turned down. He wanted to be in the animal game.

Mr. Guo turned the fish around in his hand. "A fish is an animal," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Alexis clapped. "Your fish can play!" he said. Elliot smiled a big smile. Then they counted their animals. One dog, one elephant, one fish, one cow. Four animals in a row. Later they had snack time. Alexis gave Elliot his crackers and kept the cheese. "Thank you," said Elliot. "Your cheese smells stinky anyway." Alexis laughed and took a big bite.

Clara sat on the big red couch. Her teddy bear sat on her lap. Mr. Toussaint's TV showed a big game. Everyone was shouting and clapping. "Kick the ball!" said Loan. Loan sat next to Clara. Gurfateh sat on the floor.

Clara looked at the TV. She saw lots of running. But she could not tell the two teams apart. "Who has the ball?" she whispered to Loan. "I don't know," said Loan. "All the players look the same to me."

Mr. Toussaint laughed. He sat down beside them. "Look at the shirts," he said. "One team wears blue. One team wears red. Each team wears its own colors." Clara looked hard. The blue team had the ball! "The red team has the ball!" she said. "No, blue!" said Gurfateh. They all laughed.

Clara held up her teddy bear. The bear's ribbon was red. "You are on the red team," she told the bear. She patted the bear's rough paw. On the TV, a blue player kicked the ball. The crowd went wild. Clara jumped up on the couch. "Blue scored! Blue scored!" she shouted.

Romy sat in the backyard with her paints. She wore her old blue shirt for painting. Her friend Niko came to play. They were a team today.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Romy, pointing at the pots. "One, two, three."

Romy wanted to make a sun. She dipped her brush in yellow. Then she dipped it in red. The red came out muddy and dark. "Why is my yellow all dirty?" she asked. Niko looked at the water cup. It was full of red.

"Maybe the brush needs a wash," said Niko.

Romy rinsed her brush in the clean water. She counted, "One, two, three," while she swished it. The water was empty of red now. She dipped into yellow again. Bright yellow! Then she added red. It made a new colour. "Orange!" said Romy.

She painted a big orange sun. "Yellow and red made orange," she said. Niko rinsed his brush too, and painted green grass.

It was Lea's first day of school. She rode the bus with her father waiting at the stop. Lea felt a little sad. She wanted to wave to him out the window. She stood up in her seat. She bounced on her toes. The driver looked back. "Sit down please," the driver said. "On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats." Lea sat down fast. She waved from her seat. Her father waved back big. Lea smiled. Staying sitting still let her wave and wave.

At school, Lea walked down the hallway. She held her little backpack tight. A boy named Shawn stood by the door. He was looking for his classroom. "I lost my room," Shawn said. Lea saw the teacher, Mr. Lindqvist. She took Shawn's hand. They walked to Mr. Lindqvist together.

"Can you help us?" Lea asked. Mr. Lindqvist smiled. He showed them the room. There were tiny chairs and red cups. Lea let go of Shawn's hand. He smiled too. Liya was already at the paint table. "Come paint with us," Liya said. Lea sat down next to her. She picked up a brush and made a long blue line.

Ethan had on his new shirt. It was snowy white. He wanted to paint in the backyard.

His dad said, "Wait. An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Ethan put on the apron. It was big and blue.

Ethan sat at the little table. He named his paints. "Red. Yellow. Blue." He said it again. "Red. Yellow. Blue."

Oakley came over with a seed in his hand. "I found this seed by the fence," he said. He sat down to paint too.

Ethan wanted to paint grass. But he had no green paint. This was his problem. He looked and looked.

Then he put his brush in the yellow paint. He put the same brush in the blue paint. He stirred them on his paper.

The paint turned green! Ethan made green grass. "I made a new colour," he said.

A drop of paint fell on his apron. It did not get on his white shirt. Ethan smiled. The apron kept him clean.

He and Oakley painted a big green hill. Ethan counted his colours. "Red, yellow, blue, and green. Four!"

Oakley held up his paper. "Look at my green leaf," he said.

Wesley went to the library with his dad. The library felt like a big quiet cave. Wesley wanted the dinosaur book on the low shelf. It was too far back. He could not reach it.

Wesley heard a girl say, "Please help me." Ms. Mercado came and got her book. The girl said, "Thank you." Then she ran off with her book, like a fast little fox.

Wesley tried again. Still too far. So he said, "Please help me." Ms. Mercado reached in and got the dinosaur book. She put it in his hands. "Thank you," said Wesley. "You said the magic words," said Ms. Mercado with a smile.

Wesley sat at the low table. Jamie was there, gluing stars on paper. Jamie passed Wesley the glue. Wesley almost ran off with it, like the fox girl. But he stopped. He turned back and said, "Thank you."

Then Wesley made a gluey dinosaur footprint. Jamie put stars on it. It looked like magic dinosaur dust. "ROAR," said Wesley, very quietly. "You're welcome," whispered Jamie.

Grandpa came to stay at Theo's house for a whole week. Theo and Grandpa played in the backyard all morning. They dug in the dirt and found a little worm. Then Grandpa said, "Time for my bath."

Grandpa went inside. Theo heard the water running. Then Grandpa called, "Oh dear. I can't find a towel!"

Theo ran to the bathroom. "Come with me, Grandpa," he said. He opened the tall cupboard door. "The towels are here. This one is blue."

"Why, thank you," said Grandpa. He rubbed his hair with the blue towel. "You are a good little host."

Theo smiled big. "I will show you more things," he said. "The cups are in the low cupboard. The spoons are in the drawer."

After that, Grandpa knew where everything was. At lunch, Dad helped Grandpa cook soup, and Theo showed Grandpa where the bowls sat. Grandpa took a bowl from the shelf all by himself.

"That's the one," said Theo.

Grandpa gave him a warm hug. "My best helper," he said. "Now let's go back outside and find that worm."

Iris sat in her cozy reading nook. The cushion was soft and warm. On the floor were her letter cards, all mixed up.

Iris wanted to put the cards in a line. She picked up the M card. "Where do you go?" she asked. She put M after P. That looked silly. She put M after B. That looked silly too.

Then Iris began to sing. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." She tapped each card as she sang. "H, I, J, K, L, M!" The M card went right after L. Iris clapped her hands. The song knew where M belonged!

Mom came in with warm cocoa in a mug. "I see you are working hard," said Mom. "You can wear your snow socks if your toes are cold." Iris pulled on her fuzzy white socks. They felt soft like snow.

Iris sang the song again. She tapped every card. The letters followed the song, all the way to Z. Iris smiled and took a little sip of cocoa. Then she held up the Z card. "You are last!" she said.

Emily stood by the classroom door. Her purple coat lay on the floor. Ms. Pham smiled. "Try again, Emily," she said. Emily picked up the coat. She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat hung on her, warm and soft. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. It stuck near her chin. She tugged it gently. Click, it closed.

"Your turn, Emily," said Callum. They walked out to the bus stop. Little drops began to fall. Drizzle tickled Emily's nose. A bee bounced away under the slide. Callum got wet hair. Emily got wet hair too.

Then she felt something behind her head. She grabbed it and pulled. The hood came up over her head. The drizzle tapped the top. Tap, tap. "A hood!" Emily said. "The rain stays off me now." Callum looked at his own coat and smiled.

Sophia went to the store with her dad today. She wanted the ocean book with the blue fish. Yesterday she had seen it on the shelf. Today it was still there.

"When can we get it?" Sophia asked. "Now? Or later?"

Her dad pointed up at the wall. "See the clock? The clock shows what time it is," he said. "Now the big hand is at the top. Later it will point down. Then we pay."

Sophia watched the clock. She watched the fish book too. Slowly, the big hand moved. It crept past each number.

"It moved!" she said. "It is later now!"

Her dad smiled. "Yes. Now we can pay."

They took the book to the cashier. Tomorrow Sophia would read it at home. She held it tight all the way to the car.

Julia went to the pool with her dad. The pool was big and blue. Julia held his hand at the door. She saw water splash over the side.

"Look at that," Julia said. The water made the floor wet. She put one foot on the wet floor. Her foot slid a little bit. Whoa. She held the rail and stood still.

Kylo ran past her. He was going fast. Ms. Bekele called out, "Walk, please. Wet floors are slippery." Kylo stopped his running. He walked the rest of the way. Julia walked too, one step, two steps, three steps.

The pool had three steps down into the water. Julia sat on the first step. Then the second step. Then the short third step. The water came up to her tummy. She kicked her legs. Splash, splash.

Kylo brought her a red floaty ring. "This is for you," he said. Julia smiled and put her arms through it. She kicked again and glided past the second step, all by herself.

"I did it!" Julia called to her dad. He waved from the bench. Julia walked out of the pool, step by step, nice and slow.

Ali went to the ice rink with his dad. A big game was on the TV there. It was soccer, not hockey. Laurent from school was there too. Nate was there with his mom. Ms. Rahimi came to watch as well.

The players ran and kicked the ball. Ali watched the net at the end of the field. He thought the ball had to go over the net. "Watch," said Laurent. "The ball goes into the net." A player kicked the ball hard. The ball bumped a player's leg and went in. The net moved. Everyone jumped up. "Goal!" they all shouted. Ali jumped too. He clapped his hands.

Now Ali knew. The ball goes into the net to score a goal. He pointed at the TV. "The ball went in the net," Ali said. "That's how they get a goal." Ms. Rahimi smiled and gave him a hot cocoa. His dad held the cup so it would not spill. "Can we watch more?" Ali asked. "Yes," said Dad. "The game is just starting."

Aiden went to the store with his dad. Near the carts there was a little play spot. It had a red car and a purple truck. Ayla was there too. She had the purple truck. Aiden waited. He looked at the mud on his boots. Then Ayla gave him the truck. "My turn now," she said. Aiden smiled.

Aiden drove the purple truck on the floor. It went fast. Then it was Ayla's turn again. She took the truck. Aiden took the red car. They took turns and it worked. The bell on the door went ding. A man walked in. His shoes were wet from the mud outside.

Then dad said it was time to go. Aiden ran to the door. The trucks were still on the floor. Ayla picked up the red car. She put it on the shelf. Aiden stopped. He walked back. He picked up the purple truck. He put it next to the car. The play spot was all tidy. Dad held the door open. "All done," said Aiden.

Alexander sat on the big rug at home. Snow fell softly outside the window. A nurse came to the door with a black bag. "It is shot day," Mom said kindly.

First the nurse set a small scale on the floor. "Stand here, please," she said. Alexander stood on it. He wiggled his toes. The number jumped up and down. He bounced his knees. The number jumped again.

"Stand still," said the nurse. Alexander held his arms like a cloud, soft and quiet. He stood very still. The number stopped jumping. It sat in one place. The nurse smiled. "The scale shows how much you weigh," she said. Then she wrote the number down.

"Time for the shot now," Mom said. "Hold my hand. It will be quick, and you are safe with me." Alexander squeezed Mom's hand. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." It felt like a tiny pinch, like a small bug tap.

Then it was done. The nurse gave him a round bandage with a star on it. Mom kissed his head. Alexander looked at the snow, soft and white like a big cloud, and waved at the window.

Charlotte ran onto the basketball court. Her team was ready to play. Ms. Grant blew the whistle. "Try to get the ball through the hoop," said Ms. Grant.

Charlotte got the ball. She threw it up. The ball hit the rim. It fell down. It did not go through the hoop. "No score," said Franco.

Charlotte tried again. She threw it too low. The ball did not go through the hoop. "I keep missing," said Charlotte. She asked, "What will help me score?" Franco said, "Throw it high."

Charlotte threw the ball high. The ball went up. Then it came down through the hoop. "A score!" said Leslie. The team clapped.

Charlotte got the ball again. She threw it high again. Through the hoop it went. "Two scores!" said Franco.

"Nice work," said Ms. Grant. "That was so cool." Charlotte smiled. She had a dream to score one more. She ran fast, she threw it high, and the ball went through the hoop once more.

Maverick woke up late. He had stayed up past his bed time. Now his eyes felt heavy.

He walked to the kitchen. His dad was there. Sabrina was coming over to play today. Maverick wanted to run and jump with her.

His dad made eggs. Maverick helped from his step stool. He cracked nothing. Dad did the cracking. A bit of slimy egg white slid onto Maverick's plate. He touched it with one finger. "Oooh," he said. "It feels slimy."

Then Sabrina knocked on the door. "Let's play!" she said. Maverick tried to run. His legs went slow. He tried to jump. His jump was tiny. He sat down at the table.

"You need to eat," said his dad. Maverick took a bite of egg. He took a bite of toast. He drank his milk. Then he tried to jump again. His jump was a little bigger.

Sabrina waited. "Come on," she said. She held his hand.

"Last night I did not go to bed on time," Maverick said. "My body forgot to get its rest."

"Tonight I will go to sleep early," he said. "Then tomorrow my legs can run fast."

His dad smiled. Maverick drank the rest of his milk. Then he and Sabrina walked to the toy box, hand in hand.

Livia loved her blue hat. It was a real team hat. Her coach gave it to her on the first day.

Today Livia did not want to practice. "Can we just play the game?" she asked. Mr. Santoso smiled. "Practice comes first," he said. "Then the game."

At practice, Livia threw the ball. She threw it again and again. Then she tried to catch it. The ball came fast. She held her mitt up high. Thump! The ball went right in. Livia gasped. "I caught it!"

The game started. Aoife hit the ball far. It flew toward Livia. She held her mitt up high, just like at practice. Thump! It went right in again!

Livia looked at her mitt. The ball was a bright white color, like the sun. "Mr. Santoso!" she called. "My hands know the ball now!"

Parker wanted to make a robot at school. He needed a rectangle body. He only had square paper. "Oh no," said Parker. "My robot needs a rectangle!"

Catherine had a square napkin. "Watch this," she said. She folded it in half, edge to edge. Then she held it up. It was not a square now. It was long and flat. "A rectangle!" said Parker. He was not scared anymore. He folded his square paper, edge to edge. He got a rectangle too.

Mr. Holloway came to look. "Your robot has a fine rectangle body," he said. Parker added a circle head and triangle arms. "I will sell it for one cookie," said Parker. Haroun laughed. "I will pay two!" said Haroun. Parker held up his robot and made it stomp across the table.

Emily went to the store with her dad. She wanted to find a gift for her friend Philip. The store had big signs. One sign said Animals. One sign said Toys. One sign said Foods.

Emily found a stuffed dog. It was soft and brown. She put it in the animal pile. Then she froze. The real fish in the animal aisle swam and wiggled. The dog did not move at all. "It is not alive," Emily said. She picked it up and put it in the toy pile. It fit there, next to the balls and blocks.

Dad helped her pick apples and bread for home. "Foods," said Emily, and put them in the cart. At the till, the cashier smiled. She put the toy dog in a small bag with a bow. "A gift," said Emily. At home, Philip hugged the soft brown dog. "Woof," said Philip, and Emily laughed.

Jade sat at Grandma's big table. There was a pencil and paper just for her. "I want to write my name," said Jade. "Can I?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. But first, let me show you how to hold the pencil." Jade grabbed it in her whole fist. She pushed hard on the paper. The line came out big and wobbly.

Grandma put the pencil down. "Now watch me. Pinch it here, between your thumb and your first finger. Then let it rest on your middle finger." Jade looked. Thumb here. First finger here. Middle finger under. She pinched. She rested. "Like this?" she asked. "Like that," said Grandma. Jade tried a line. The line was small and smooth. "It moves!" said Jade. "My fingers make it move!"

"Now we write your name. It has four letters," said Grandma. "J. A. D. E." Jade made a J. Then an A. Then a D. Then an E. "J, A, D, E," she said out loud. "That's me!" The letters sat on the paper in a row. Grandma clapped. Jade held up the paper. "Can we hang it up?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Right on the fridge."

Margot was at Grandma's house. She sat at the big table. She wanted to paint a turtle. She picked gray paint. She painted a big gray turtle. The turtle looked like it could swim in the sea.

Her friend Oceane came to play. Oceane painted a turtle too. It was big and gray, just like Margot's. They set the paintings side by side. "Which one is mine?" asked Margot. The two paintings looked the same. She could not tell.

Grandma brought a marker. "People often write their name on their artwork," she said. "Then everyone knows who made it." Margot wrote M-A-R-G-O-T on her paper. Oceane wrote her name too. Now Margot saw her name and smiled. She pointed and said, "This one is mine!"

Weston sat at the dinner table. He had a wooden cup next to his plate. His friend Samael sat beside him.

Weston reached for the bread. His elbow bumped Samael's cup. The cup fell down. Water went everywhere.

"Oh no," said Weston. Samael's face looked sad.

"Say sorry," said Mr. Sultani.

"Sorry," said Weston. Then he got a towel. He wiped up the water. Samael picked up the cup.

Then something surprising happened. Samael gave Weston the bread. "You can go first," said Samael.

Weston took one piece. Then he held the plate out to Samael. "Your turn now," said Weston.

Samael smiled. Weston touched his wooden cup. It stayed right where it was.

"Sorry," said Weston again, softly. Samael gave him a piece of bread from his own plate.

Raphael got to school early. The sun was warm on the rug. He sat by the window and waved to his dad outside.

Raphael wanted the red crayon. Harry had it. Raphael took a big breath. "Can I have the red crayon, please?" he asked. Harry smiled and gave it to him. "Thank you," said Raphael. Harry opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He looked down at his shoes. He did not know what to say back.

Ms. Leblanc came over. She knelt by the two boys. "Harry, you can say, 'You're welcome'," she said. Harry looked up. "You're welcome!" he said. Raphael laughed. "You're welcome," said Raphael too, like a big rolling drum. Later, Harry shared his crackers with Scott. Scott said, "Thank you." Harry puffed up his chest and said, "You're welcome." Raphael grinned and took another bite of his cracker.

Nathan was at Grandpa's house. He found a huge red book on the big chair. He wanted to know what was inside.

"Can you read it to me?" Nathan asked.

Grandpa sat down. "Yes. We start at the front." He opened the cover. Then he read the pages, one by one, all the way to the back.

The last page said, "Good night, little bear." Grandpa closed the book.

Then Grandma came in. "Read it again, please," said Nathan.

Grandma sat down. She opened the front cover. She turned the pages, one by one. She read to the back cover too.

Nathan froze. His eyes went big. Grandma had said the very same words. "Grandma, you said what Grandpa said!"

Grandma smiled and nodded.

Nathan had an idea. He asked, "Will you say it again tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Grandma. "The words will be the same."

So the next day, Grandpa opened the front cover again. He read to the back. The words were the same. "Good night, little bear."

Nathan said the last line with him.

Isaac stood in the school gym. Ms. Russo put a hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in," she said. Isaac threw it. The beanbag missed and went to hide behind a mat. He ran and got it. He tried again. This time the beanbag dropped right into the hoop. Isaac jumped up and down.

Then Ms. Russo brought out a big red ball. Camille caught it with both hands. Katrina caught it with both hands too. Isaac wanted to be like the big kids. He held out one hand. The ball hit his hand and rolled away. His face felt hot. "I can't do it," he said.

Ms. Russo knelt down. "Big balls are wiggly," she said. "Try again." Isaac looked at Camille. She held out both hands. So Isaac held out both hands too. Katrina tossed the ball. Isaac caught it! It did not roll away.

The three friends played catch. Outside the window, the ground was snowy and white. Inside, the gym was warm. Near the door, a small desk held all the beanbags. Isaac got another turn with the hoop. He threw the beanbag. In it went again. "I did it!" said Isaac. "My turn!" said Camille.

Charlotte sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her mom held her hand. Charlotte did not feel sick at all. "Why do I need a shot?" she asked.

The doctor smiled. "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said. Charlotte looked at the tiny bandage in the doctor's hand. It had pretty stars on it.

The doctor said, "Squeeze your mom's hand and blow out air, like a birthday candle." Charlotte squeezed. She blew. She felt one small poke, quick as that. Then it was done. The doctor put the star bandage on her arm. "See, it worked," said the doctor. "You were very brave."

In the waiting room, Charlotte saw her friend Lohan. He was waiting for his shot, and his eyes looked worried. Charlotte held up her arm. "Look at my stars," she said. "The poke was small. It helps you stay well." Lohan took a deep breath and blew out air like a candle.

"Ready," he said.

Madison was at Grandma's house. She wanted to wear her cozy socks. She opened the sock basket. She held up one red sock. It was soft and warm. But where was the other one?

"One sock," said Grandma. "You need a pair. A pair means two, like a pair of socks." Madison looked in the basket again. She dug past a scarf. She dug past a hat. No red sock.

Madison counted the basket things out loud. "One scarf. Two hats. Three mittens." She kept going. "Four, five, six clips." She found more things. "Seven, eight, nine pins. Ten tissues!" Still no red sock.

Then Madison saw something under the big chair. It was red. She reached for it. Out came the red sock! A tiny button was inside it. The button was shaped like a strawberry. "That is a happy surprise," said Grandma. "That button was lost last winter."

Madison put on her pair of red socks. Two warm feet. "Dinner soon," said Grandma. Madison danced around the young kitten by the door. She counted her happy steps. "One, two, three, four, five."

Florence sat on the big low couch in the living room. She wanted to draw a flower on the tablet. But the screen was dark and still. She pressed her finger on it. Nothing happened.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Tap the little button on top," he said. Florence tapped it. The screen lit up. There were small pictures everywhere. "The small pictures on a tablet screen are called icons," her dad said. Florence looked and looked. One icon had a paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said.

She drew a big yellow flower with a green stem. Then she drew a small red flower too. When she was done, she put the tablet on the table. "All done," Florence said, and she tapped the screen dark again.

Mohamed sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He was waiting for his shot. His tummy felt funny. "I don't want a needle," he said. His mom held his hand. The doctor came in. A tube hung around her neck. Mohamed pointed at it. "What is that?"

"This is my stethoscope," said the doctor. "I use it to listen to your heart beating." She put the cold round end on Mohamed's chest. Mohamed heard a sound in his ears. Thump, thump. "That is me!" he said. His mom laughed. He listened again. Thump, thump.

"Are you ready for your shot now?" asked the doctor. Mohamed squeezed his mom's hand. The needle was quick, like a small pinch. Then it was done. The doctor gave him a noisy bandage to press on his arm, and a sticker shaped like a heart. "My heart is strong," said Mohamed. Thump, thump.

Peyton ran to the backyard. Her bike was by the fence. She jumped on the seat.

"Wait," said Dad. "Where is your helmet?"

Peyton looked at the garage. The door was closed. "In there," she said.

She ran to Dad. Dad opened the door. Peyton took her helmet. She put it on her head.

Dad helped snap it. "Wear a helmet when you ride a bike," said Dad.

Kayce came over with her bike. She had a helmet too. "Let's go!" said Kayce.

Peyton pushed her pedals. The bike went fast. The wind touched her face.

"I see you," Dad called. He stood by the door.

Peyton rode in a big circle. Kayce rode behind her. The circle got smaller and smaller.

"Careful," said Dad. "Stay where I can see you."

Peyton stopped her bike. She looked at Dad. She waved her hand.

"I am here," she said. "I see you too!"

Kayce laughed. Peyton laughed. They rode again, slow and happy, past the big green tree.

Margot was at Otis's house. Otis's dad made hot toast. Margot got to help with the rest.

First she tried the butter. She pressed too hard. The toast tore a little. Otis's dad gave her a new piece. "Go slow," he said. Margot took her time. Small strokes, one way, then the other. The butter melted into the toast. "I did it," said Margot.

Then came the milk. Margot held the cup with two hands. She poured a tiny bit, then a tiny bit more. Not one drop spilled. Otis clapped. Their cat walked by, her curly tail up in the air.

They ate their toast. It was yummy. Then Otis ran off to find a toy. Margot saw the milk still sitting on the counter. She remembered something. Milk goes back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold.

Margot picked up the milk with both hands. She set it inside the fridge. She shut the door and heard it click close. Otis's dad smiled at her. "Good job, Margot," he said.

Margot ran off to play with Otis too.

Nova went to the library with her dad. Today was story day. Mr. Russo sat in the big blue chair. He held a book about a baby bear.

Vera sat down next to Nova. "I went to the park tomorrow!" said Vera. Then she stopped. She made a little frown. "No, wait," she said. "I went yesterday. Yesterday already happened. Tomorrow is not here yet."

Nova thought about that. Yesterday was the day before today. So Vera's park trip was yesterday. Story time was today, right now. "And tomorrow we come back," said Nova. "Mr. Russo said so."

"I was afraid story time was over," said Vera. "It is not," said Nova. "It is starting now."

Mr. Russo opened the book. The baby bear yawned. Nova and Vera leaned in close to see the pictures.

Evan sat at the little table in the school library. Mr. Augustin gave him a pencil. "You can write your name," said Mr. Augustin.

Evan wanted to write the big E first. He held the pencil tight. He pressed down hard. Snap! The tip broke off. Evan felt scared. His letter looked all wrong now.

Koen was sitting next to him. "Mine broke too," said Koen. He held up his pencil. "Try soft," said Koen. Evan got a new pencil from Mr. Augustin. This time he pressed gently. The pencil made a nice dark line. It did not break.

Evan wrote E, then V, then A, then N. Mr. Augustin smiled. "That is your name," he said. Evan looked at his letters on the paper. "Evan!" he said. Koen clapped for him. Evan stood up and did a little jump, his shirt bouncing as he leaped. "I did it!"

Anthony stood in the kitchen with Dad. Grandma was coming today. She flew on a big plane over the ocean. "I miss Grandma," said Anthony. "Soon she will be here," said Dad.

At the airport, Dad took Anthony to the arrivals area. Families waited there to meet people coming off the plane. Anthony watched the big doors. A lady came out. "Grandma!" said Anthony. But it was not Grandma. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" said Anthony. Dad laughed. "Not yet. Watch the doors." Then the doors opened one more time. It was Grandma! She picked Anthony up in a big hug.

Back home, the kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma made pancakes, and Dad flipped them on the hot pan. Anthony set out three plates. "Is breakfast ready?" he asked. Grandma smiled. "Almost, little one."

Margot was at Grandma's house. She was painting a big picture. It had a sun and a house and a tree. It had one dog, two flowers, three clouds.

But the grass was missing. Margot looked in the paint box. She found red. She found blue. She found yellow. No green. "I need green," said Margot. "The grass needs green."

Grandma sat next to her. "Try your pots," said Grandma. Margot had two little pots. One pot had blue paint. One pot had yellow paint. Margot put her brush in the blue. She made a dot on the paper. She put her brush in the yellow. She made a dot on the blue dot.

The dots turned green. Blue and yellow made green. Margot clapped her hands. "Green! I made green!" She painted one stripe of grass, two stripes, three stripes, all the way to the tree.

There was paint on her fingers. Grandma helped her wash it off. The water turned a little green too. Margot laughed. "Even the sink is green now." She held up her clean hands. Then she painted a green leaf on the tree.

Jack loved his little red car. He took it to the playground. But now the car was gone. "Oh no," said Jack. "Where did you go?"

He looked by the slide. No car. He looked by the swings. No car. Then he saw the big tunnel. It was dark inside. Jack could not see a thing. "Maybe my car is in there," he said. Abigail and Jind came to help. "It is too dark," said Jind.

Ms. Suzuki walked over. She had a flashlight. She turned it on. The light was bright. "Now look," she said. Jack peeked in. There was the red car, sitting in the tunnel! "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots," said Jack. He reached in and took his car. Then the bell rang, and all the children came inside. "Snack time," said Ms. Suzuki. Jack smiled. He was hungry, and his car was safe in his pocket.

Max looked out the door. The sun was bright. "Sunny day!" he said. He wanted to run to the bus stop right away.

His dad held up a little bottle. "Sunscreen first," said Dad. Dad rubbed it on Max's arms and face. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn," said Dad. Max patted his cheeks. They felt smooth.

At the bus stop, the wind blew. Max's hat flew low across the ground. Winston ran and caught it. Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Max and Winston hid under the big roof. They built a little pile of dry leaves to sit on.

Then the rain stopped. The sun came back. Max's hat stayed on his head. "Sunny again!" said Winston. Max smiled and held his dad's hand tight.

Mya's class was going outside to play. It was cold. Mya had to put on her coat. She wanted to do it all by herself.

She pushed both arms into one sleeve. "Silly!" said Indie. Indie laughed, and Mya laughed too. The coat hung funny and would not zip. Both arms in one sleeve did not work. What else could she try?

Mya pulled her arms out. She looked at the coat. It had two sleeves. What if each arm got its own sleeve? She put her left arm in the left sleeve. Then she put her right arm in the right sleeve. The coat sat just right on her back.

Now for the zipper. Mya held the bottom and pulled up. It stuck. She pulled again, slowly. Ziiiip! It went all the way to the top. Mya puffed out her chest.

"Look, Ms. Nair!" said Mya. "I did it myself."

"Good work, Mya," said Ms. Nair. "Now let's follow the line outside to the store on the corner. The cold wind is not too scary today, I promise."

Mya walked out into the cold. The wind touched her cheeks. But inside her coat, she was warm and snug. "Zip," she said, patting her chest.

Luca and Riaan found a little log house in the forest. "Let's play house," said Luca. Luca used leaves for plates. Riaan used a pinecone for a baby. "Time for dinner," said Luca. He stirred a pot of tiny stones. Riaan gave the pinecone a soft kiss on top. "Night night, baby," Riaan said.

Then the sun began to drop. "Time to go home," said Mr. Ndlovu, their kind neighbour. Luca jumped up and ran. "Wait," said Riaan. "Our house is a mess." Luca looked back. Leaves were everywhere. Stones were spilled out of the pot.

Luca went back. He put the leaves in one pile. Riaan put the stones back in the pot. They set the pinecone baby on the log to sleep. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away," said Luca. Mr. Ndlovu smiled. "What a lucky forest house," he said. Luca took Riaan's hand, and they walked home through the soft, falling snow.

Alexis ran into the bookshop with his dad. He was excited. Today he wanted a book about cats.

Mr. Nasser worked at the bookshop. "Hello, Alexis!" he said. "The cat books are on this shelf."

Alexis looked at all the books. He saw big letters on the spines. "What is that letter?" he asked. "That is the letter A," said Mr. Nasser. "A says ah, like apple."

Alexis touched the next book. "And this one?" "That is B," said Mr. Nasser. "B says buh, like ball."

Haisley was there too. She was thirsty, so she got a drink of water. Then she sang the alphabet song with Alexis. They sang and sang. Alexis stopped. "The alphabet ends at P," he said. "Where does it go after P?"

"Keep singing!" said Haisley. So Alexis kept going. Q, R, S, all the way to the end. "It stops at Z!" he shouted. "Z is the last letter!"

Mr. Nasser laughed. "And Z is on that shelf, right at the end."

Alexis raced to the last shelf. He found a cat book there. The first page had a big cat with a fluffy tail. "Can we get this one, Dad?" Alexis asked. "It was hiding behind the Z!"

Margot sat with her class at the little temple. Mr. Khoury picked up a drum. "We will sing a song," he said. "Clap along with me." He tapped the drum, one, two, three, four. Margot clapped, one, two, three, four. Her friend Leah clapped too. Annalise clapped beside them. Margot sang the rhyming song about the star and the boat. She sang it all by herself, every word!

Then her hands got tired. They went flop in her lap. "My hands are tired," she said. She looked around the big room. She saw the tall lamp near the window. A thick red curtain stood beside it. Mr. Khoury came over with the drum. "You can keep the beat another way," he said. "Watch me." He tapped the drum with his hand, one, two, three, four. Then he tapped his knees, one, two, three, four. Then he stamped his feet, one, two, three, four!

"Can feet clap?" Margot asked. "No, but feet can stamp the beat," said Mr. Khoury. Margot stood up tall. She stamped, one, two, three, four. Leah stamped. Annalise stamped. All the children stamped the beat. The drum went boom and their feet went stomp. Margot sang the rhyme again, loud and happy. Mr. Khoury smiled and hit the drum one more time. Boom!

Luke came home with a small dog. The dog was brown and soft. Dad put a bowl of food on the floor. The dog began to eat.

Luke wanted to pat the dog. He reached out his hand. "Not now," said Dad. "The dog is eating. We leave him alone when he eats or sleeps."

Luke sat down on the mat. He waited and waited. The dog crunched his crunchy food. At last the bowl was empty. The dog looked up at Luke. He wagged his tail.

"Now we can play," said Dad. Luke patted the dog very gently. The dog licked Luke's hand. Later the dog lay down for a nap by the window. Luke tiptoed past him. He did not wake the dog up. Luke got a crunchy apple to eat instead. The dog slept and slept. "Good boy," Luke whispered.

Kinsley ran to the art table. "Look, Etta! We get to cut shapes today!" Ms. Hughes held up thin paper squares, triangles, and rectangles. Kinsley picked up a red circle. She looked for a corner to start cutting. She turned the paper. She turned it again. There was no corner anywhere! "A circle is round," said Etta. "It has no corners." Kinsley ran her finger all around the edge. Round and round her finger went. It never stopped at a corner!

Keanu held up his square. "Mine has corners. One, two, three, four!" Kinsley giggled. She snipped her round circle. It went snip, snip, snip very slowly. Her scissors slid around and around. Then she held up her circle to the light. "I did it! A round shape, all mine!" Ms. Hughes taped it to the window. The circle spun a little in the breeze. "It looks like a wheel!" said Keanu. Kinsley laughed and spun around too, just like her circle.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Clara gave her the white blanket from her bed. Grandma hugged her tight.

On Saturday they went to the market. "We need flour," said Grandma. Clara counted the bags as they went in the basket. One, two, three! A big wooden owl watched from a stall, and Clara laughed at it.

At home, Grandma rolled up her sleeves. "My mother made this bread with me," she said. "Now I will make it with you." Clara poured the flour. Grandma mixed it with water. Clara patted the soft dough with her hands. Then they put it in a bowl and waited.

The dough grew big and puffy! Clara peeked again and again. "It got so fat!" she said.

The oven was hot, so Grandma slid the pan in herself. Clara watched from her chair. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

The bread came out golden. Clara took one bite and jumped up and down. "It tastes like your bread, Grandma!"

"It is my bread," said Grandma. "Now it is yours too."

Clara held out a slice. "You have to try it!"

Isla sat in the family car with her new backpack. They were going on a big trip. "We ride in an airplane today!" said Dad. Isla clapped her hands. At the airport, they walked up big steps into the plane. Isla found her seat by the window.

"I want to stand up and look out," she said. The seat belt light went on. "It is time for takeoff," said Dad. "Everyone buckles their seat belts for takeoff." Click went Isla's belt. The plane began to rumble and lift. It went up and up! Isla looked out the window from her seat. The cars below looked tiny, like little worms.

"Where do we buckle again?" she asked. "For takeoff and landing," said Dad. Isla smiled and kept looking out. "Goodbye, tiny cars!" she called.

Alice went to the beach with her mom. The beach had a big pool right by the sand! Today Alice would learn to swim. Her friends Forrest and Meher were coming too.

"Look at the water!" said Forrest. Meher jumped up and down. Alice could see little fish in the pool. The sky was a little cloudy, but the water was warm. Ms. Fortin, the swim teacher, waved them over.

"Now we float on our backs," said Ms. Fortin. Alice was nervous. What if she sank? Ms. Fortin put her hands under Alice's back. The hands held her up! Alice did not sink. She lay on the water like a sleepy fish. The warm water tickled her ears.

"I'm floating!" said Alice. Forrest floated too. Meher floated too. Alice looked up at the cloudy sky. She felt like she was flying.

Colton went to the library with his dad. He wanted to find a book about a big lake. Mr. Kelly smiled and pointed to some shelves. Colton looked and looked. He could not find it. Mr. Kelly said, "This shelf is animals. That shelf is foods." Colton found a book about a bear. Then he found a book about bread. "Where are the toys?" he asked. "Next to the foods," said Mr. Kelly. Colton saw a book about blocks on that shelf. But then his friend Gursanjh came with a big pile of picture cards. "Can we sort these?" she asked. Colton put all the red cards together. Then Gursanjh put the same cards in piles, big ones and small ones. "The same cards can go in different piles!" said Colton. At last he found his lake book. A snowman in it began to melt in the sun. Colton hugged the book tight. "Home we go," he said.

Layla went to the library with her dad. Mr. Iyer had a shape table there. Layla wanted the red block, but Farhan had it first. "You can have it next," said Mr. Iyer. Layla waited. She looked at the table while she waited. One, two, three, she counted the shapes. There was a circle, a square, a triangle and a rectangle. Then Farhan gave her the red block. "It's a cube," said Mr. Iyer. He gave her a sheet of stickers. Layla put one sticker on each flat face. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six faces! Each sticker sat on a square. "Look, Dad! Six square faces!" she did not yell. She said it softly, like in a library. Mr. Iyer smiled. "Would you like some juice?" Dad asked. "Yes! My hands are not slippery now," said Layla. On the way to the kitchen door, she held the cube tight. One, two, three, four, five, six stickers. All squares. All hers.

Isla was going to the dentist. It was her first time. Her tummy felt funny.
