"First we stop at the pharmacy," said Mom. They walked along the busy road. Isla held Mom's hand.

At the pharmacy, Isla picked a new toothbrush. It was green, her best color. Annabella from school was there too. Annabella had a toothbrush in her hand. It was green as well.

"Look, same!" said Annabella. The two green toothbrushes got mixed up on the counter. Isla picked one up. Then she stopped. This one had a mark on it. It was Annabella's.

"Each person uses their own toothbrush," said the cashier. "People do not share toothbrushes."

Isla looked at the mark. She put that one down. She took the clean green one. It was hers.

"Thank you," said Isla. She knocked gently on Annabella's shoulder. "Here is yours."

At the dentist, Isla stayed awake and still. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All done," said Ms. Chan, the dentist. "What a big girl."

Mom smiled. "You did it," said Mom. Isla hugged her new green toothbrush tight.

Luca woke up and saw snow. Lots and lots of snow. "No school today!" said his dad. Luca wanted to visit Ms. Rowe, the kind neighbour next door. She had a tall shelf full of toy bears.

Luca ran out the door. The sidewalk was icy. His feet slid fast. Down he went, right on his bottom.

"I slipped," said Luca. He stood up. He thought about the ice. He took one small step. Then another small step. Slowly, slowly, he walked.

At Ms. Rowe's door, his friend Ismail was there too. Ismail began to run on the ice. "Walk slow, like me," said Luca. "The ice is slippery."

Ismail took small steps too. Step, step, step. They got to the door together.

"Two snowy visitors!" said Ms. Rowe. She gave each boy a soft bear from the tall shelf. Luca hugged his bear tight. "We walked so slow," he said, "like little penguins."

Ivy wanted to play the feely-bag game. Mom put a cloth bag on the table. "Close your eyes," said Mom. Ivy put her hand in the dark bag. She felt something round. "A ball!" she said. She squeezed it. It was smooth and small. "It is a red ball," said Ivy. Mom said, "Now open your eyes and look." Ivy pulled out the ball. It was not red. It was blue! Ivy laughed. "My fingers did not know," she said. "I had to look with my eyes."

Mom put a toy fish in the bag next. Ivy felt it. "A fish!" she said. "But what color? I cannot tell yet." She pulled it out and looked. The fish was yellow. Then Mom hid a green frog. Ivy felt its bumpy back. She pulled it out fast. "Green!" she said. The green frog jumped in her hands.

Ivy put the blue ball back in the bag. She ran to find Isra at the door. "Come play with me," said Ivy. "Close your eyes. Now guess!"

Felix went to the cemetery with his mom. They came to see Grandpa's stone. The stone was big and black and shiny.

Today was a special day. The family would eat at the little table by the stone. Felix's mom put out bread and apples and juice. Felix wanted to lead the blessing before the food. But their family did not say the blessing. Their family sang it.

"Your grandpa sang it too," said his mom.

Felix stood up tall. He took a big breath. He began to sing. But the tune came out wrong. It went up when it should go down. He stopped and looked at his shoes.

"That's okay," said his mom. "Try again, slow."

Felix waited a moment. Then he sang it again, nice and slow. This time the tune came out right. The whole family sang with him. The apples and bread waited on the table until the song was done.

Then they all ate. Felix bit his apple and smiled at the black stone.

"We sang it, Grandpa," he said.

Avery wanted the big red truck. Skyler had the big red truck. Avery reached out her hand. Then she stopped. Ms. Müller knelt down beside her. "You can wait for a turn," said Ms. Müller.

Avery sat on the small blue carpet. Waiting felt long. Her tummy felt sad and slow. Then she saw the paper basket. It was full of yellow paper. Avery picked up a piece. She folded it. She folded it again. It became a little hat. She put it on her knee. Waiting felt short now.

Skyler rolled the truck to her. "Your turn," he said. "Thank you," said Avery. She pushed the truck across the floor. Beep, beep. Then she looked at Skyler. He was looking at the truck. Avery picked up the yellow paper hat. "You can play with this," she said. Skyler put the hat on his truck. It was a truck hat now. Avery rolled the truck, and Skyler drove the paper.

Ezra went to the store with his dad. He held his dad's hand. At the deli counter, a lady was making tea. A kettle sat on a little stove. Ezra wanted to see the water bubble. He let go of his dad's hand.

"Ezra, stay close," his dad said. Ezra took his dad's hand again.

Steam rose from the kettle. The steam looked soft, like a little cloud. Ezra reached up his fingers.

"Careful," the lady said. "Steam is hot. Steam can burn. Stay back."

Ezra stepped back. He watched from far away. The water began to pop and bubble. He could see the bubbles from where he stood. His dad smiled. "Good waiting," he said.

Then something small fell off the counter. It was a toy turtle, heavy for its size. It slid right to Ezra's feet. He picked it up and gave it to the lady.

"Thank you," she said. "That turtle popped right off the shelf."

The lady poured her tea. Ezra watched the steam go up and up, far from his face. He waved to the bubbles. "Bye bye, hot water," he said.

Rosalie was at Maisie's house. Maisie had a shiny red truck. Rosalie wanted it very much.

Rosalie reached out her hand. She wanted to grab the truck. Then she stopped. She put her hands in her lap instead.

"Can I have a turn when you're done?" Rosalie asked.

Maisie smiled at her. "Yes! You can have the next turn," said Maisie. Maisie drove the truck around the rug. It went past the blocks and past a little square box. Rosalie sat and waited. She watched the truck. It was fun to watch.

Soon Maisie gave her the truck. "Your turn now," said Maisie. Rosalie held the red truck. It felt smooth and sweet in her hands. She drove it fast, then slow.

"Can I have a turn when you're done?" Maisie asked.

Rosalie drove a little more. Then she gave the truck back. "Your turn," she said.

Maisie clapped her hands. "Let's take turns all day," said Maisie.

Rosalie drove the truck past the square box one more time. "Beep beep," she called.

Eloise loved to ride to the library with her dad. They went every week, even at night sometimes, when the lamps glowed warm and yellow.

Today the library had a shape hunt. Mr. Ma held up a card. It had a circle on it. "Find a circle," he said. Eloise ran to the wall. The big clock was round like the card. "The clock is a circle," she said. Her friend Jade held up a tiny red button she found on the carpet. "This can't be a circle," said Jade. "It is too small. The clock is big and this is small."

Eloise put the button under the clock. She looked at both. Both were round all the way. No corners on either one. "It is still a circle," said Eloise. "Big circle, tiny circle. Both are circles." Jade smiled and clapped. Mr. Ma put a cute round sticker on each of their hands.

Then they found more shapes. The window was a big square. Akira found a small square block. The roof in a picture was a triangle. A door was a tall rectangle. Eloise held her sticker up to the door. "My sticker is round, like the clock," she said. Jade laughed, and Mr. Ma laughed too. "Time for stories," he said, and Eloise sat down next to her dad.

Nora had a little guitar in music class. She strummed it. The notes sounded funny. "Hmm," said Nora. "Why does it sound like that?"

Adem strummed his drum. His drum sounded just fine. Nora strummed again. The funny sound came back. She was not happy.

Mr. Andersen came over. He listened to the strings. "This needs tuning," he said. "Strings need tuning so the notes sound right." He turned the little pegs. Slowly. Carefully.

Nora watched. One turn made the sound go up. Another turn made the sound come back. "Can I try?" she asked.

"You can turn one peg, just a little," said Mr. Andersen. Nora turned it. The note changed! She had made that happen.

She strummed the guitar. Now it sounded sweet. Nora strummed and strummed until her hands were tired. Outside, rain began from a big gray storm. Nobody minded. "Play it again," said Adem.

Bennett sat on Grandpa's warm lap. The big soccer game was on TV. Alina sat close by with a bowl of popcorn. Gabriel sat on the rug. Everyone was watching.

The players ran and ran. Then a loud whistle went "tweet!" All the players stopped running. Bennett sat up. "Why did they stop?" he asked. "The referee blew his whistle," said Grandpa. "The whistle stops the game."

Bennett watched and waited. The players ran again. Then "tweet!" They all stopped again. "The whistle stops them!" said Bennett. He clapped his hands. "Tweet means stop. Tweet means stop."

Alina laughed and hugged the bowl. Gabriel blew a pretend whistle, "tweet!" The room felt warm and cozy. Grandpa said, "Time for juice now, friends." Bennett smiled and took Grandpa's hand.

Mohamed sat on the city bus with his mom. He was going to the dentist for the first time. "I wonder what the dentist will do," he said.

At the dentist, a kind man looked in Mohamed's mouth. "Say ahh," said the dentist. Mohamed said, "Ahh." The dentist looked and looked. "Your teeth are strong. I will fix the one little tooth." Mohamed sat very still. Soon it was done. The dentist gave him a big smile.

On the bus home, Ria sat beside Mohamed. She had an apple slice. First she bit it with her front teeth. Then she chomped it with her back teeth. Mohamed tried his own slice. Bite with the front. Chomp with the back. He counted: "One bite, one chomp." Ria laughed. "My tongue feels the apple get small," Mohamed said. The bus went beep, beep, down the street.

Hailey went to the store with Mom. "Stay close to me," said Mom. Hailey held the cart.

They walked past the bakery. The oven was big and hot. "Hot," said Mom. "We stay back." Hailey saw the bread rise up. The heat made the bread get big.

Then Hailey saw a fluffy toy. She stopped to look. When she looked up, Mom was gone. Hailey felt scared.

A lady in a green vest worked at the checkout. Hailey walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," Hailey said. The lady smiled. She picked up her phone and called out, "Hailey is here!"

Mom came running fast. She hugged Hailey tight. "You told the store worker," said Mom. "That was so smart."

Outside, soft snow began to fall. "Can we go to the park tomorrow?" Hailey asked. "Yes," said Mom. They walked home, warm and cozy in their coats.

Scarlett wanted to play tea party. But the teapot was empty. There was no real tea at all.

"Where is the tea?" she asked. Then she answered herself. "It is pretend tea!"

She set out four little cups. One for Bear. One for Bunny. One for Sara. One for herself. The cups were empty too. That was okay.

"More pretend tea?" asked Sara. "Yes, please," said Scarlett. She tipped the empty teapot. Tap, tap, tap. Nothing came out. But she said, "There! Full up!"

Then Scarlett remembered something. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" she said. She blew on Bear's empty cup. She blew on Bunny's empty cup. Bunny was wearing her itchy sweater, so Scarlett patted it soft and gentle, in case the sweater bothered her.

After tea, they built a house of blocks for the two cups. Rain tapped the window. "What weather!" said Sara. "Our tea party stays inside," said Scarlett.

Bear got sleepy. Scarlett tucked him under a little cloth. "Night night, Bear," she said. She tipped the teapot one more time. "One last drop of pretend tea."

Madeline sat on her bed. She held her bear tight. It was almost bedtime, but she was dirty from playing outside.

"I hope we can still read a story," she said.

"First we wash," said her dad. He took her to the sink. He turned on the water. It was warm, not hot.

Madeline put soap on her hands. She rubbed them together. Then she looked. Bubbles! Little white bubbles sat on her fingers.

She rubbed some soap on her chin. Now she had a bubble beard, just like a bear!

"Bubbles!" she laughed.

"Soap and water make bubbles," her dad said. He helped her splash them all away.

Then Madeline put on her cozy pajamas. Her dad dried her hair with a towel. They read a story in bed.

Madeline yawned. "Night night, Bear," she whispered. Her dad tucked the blanket up to her chin and turned off the light.

Cooper sat at a long table. It was a big lunch at the temple. Grandma put rice in his small bowl. The woman next to them smiled.

"Say itadakimasu," said Grandma. "It is what people say in Japan. They say it before they eat. It gives thanks for the food."

Cooper tried. "Ita...daki..." His mouth got mixed up. Would the words come out right? He took a big breath.

"Itadakimasu!" he said.

Grandma clapped. The woman clapped too. Then everyone at the table said it together, loud and happy.

Cooper picked up his spoon. The rice was warm and soft. He kissed Grandma on the cheek. Then he took a big bite.

"Itadakimasu," he said again, with rice in his mouth. Grandma laughed and laughed.

Ezra sat at the craft table. He wanted to make a paper sailboat. Silas wanted one too. "A sail needs two triangles," said Silas. Ezra had only a square of paper. He frowned. "Where can we get triangles?" he asked.

Mr. Halvorsen came over. He looked at the square. "Watch," he said. He took the scissors, because scissors were for grown-ups. He cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open. Now there were two triangles! "One, two," said Ezra. He clapped his hands.

Ezra made his boat. The wind from the window pushed the sail. Hayley's boat had no sail yet. She looked sad. Ezra gave her one triangle. "Now we match," said Hayley. The two boats sailed across the messy table, side by side.

John had to wash his hands. Lunch was coming, and he had just used the toilet.

He turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. He looked at them. There were no bubbles. His hands still looked plain.

Ms. Leblanc stood by the door. She did not say anything. She just waited.

John looked at the soap. He picked it up. He rubbed it on his hands. Then he rubbed his hands together under the water.

Bubbles! Little white bubbles covered his fingers.

"Bubbles!" said John.

He kept rubbing. He counted with Ms. Leblanc. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. The bubbles grew and grew.

Jazlyn came in to wash her hands too. John showed her the soap. She rubbed her hands, and she got bubbles too.

They rinsed the bubbles off. They dried their hands on the towel.

John felt tired but happy. He ran to the table. He read his animal placemat while he waited for lunch. Then he picked up his sandwich with clean, bubbly-washed hands.

Riley wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Lunch was ready, and her hands had sticky jam on them. She reached for the tap. "Wait," said Dad. He put his own hand under the water. "A grown-up checks first. It must be warm, not hot." Riley felt a little scared of the hot tap. She waited with her hands in her lap.

Dad turned the tap a small bit. He held his hand under the water again. "Warm now," he said. Riley held out her hands. The water felt like a soft kiss on her fingers. Dad gave her the soap. Riley rubbed and rubbed. "One, two, three," she counted. She counted all the way to twenty. Bubbles slid down the sink.

Riley held up her hands. They were clean and shiny. Dad gave her a big smile. Riley clapped her soapy-clean hands together. "I did it!" she said. Dad kissed the top of her head. Then they sat down to eat lunch.

Nolan sat in his car seat. Mom buckled him in. They drove to the doctor.

At the doctor's office, Nolan sat on the big table. It felt too big. His legs hung down. The nurse came in with a small tray. Nolan hid his face.

The nurse wiped his arm with a little towel. It felt cool. Nolan did not want the shot.

Then Mom sat down on a chair. She opened her arms wide. Nolan climbed onto Mom's lap. She held him close.

"Hug time," Mom said.

Nolan held Mom's shirt. The nurse gave the shot in his arm. It was quick. It was small.

"All done," the nurse said. She put a bandage on his arm.

"You can sit on my lap for a shot," Mom said. "It helps you feel safe."

Nolan nodded. Sitting on Mom's lap made the big table feel small.

They walked out to the car. Mom had a juice box for Nolan. He took a long drink.

"That was smart, sitting with Mom," said the nurse at the desk.

Nolan got back in his car seat. He looked at his bandage. "Fast car now," he said.

Mom laughed. The car drove home.

Jordan sat in his car seat. Colson sat next to him. They were going to the park.

Jordan's mom handed back a bag of snacks. "Would you like a cheese stick, Jordan?"

"Yuck!" Jordan shouted. He pushed the bag away.

Colson spoke in a small, quiet voice. "No, thank you," he said to the cheese sticks. Then Colson held up a thin cracker. "May I have this, please?"

"Of course," said Jordan's mom. She smiled at Colson.

Jordan thought about that. He took a breath. "No, thank you," he said to the cheese stick. "May I have a cracker, please?"

"Yes, you may," said his mom. She passed him the crackers.

Jordan took a small bite. "They taste good," he said. He ate another one.

Then he saw a gray mouse by the fence at the park. It ran under a thin bush. Jordan waved at it through the window.

"Thank you for the crackers, Mom," said Jordan.

"You are welcome, sweetheart," she said. She parked the car, and the boys ran out to play.

Addison was at school. It was play time outside. Zayan put his hands over his eyes. "You can't see me!" he said. Addison looked at him. She could still see his blue shirt. She could still see his shoes.

"Zayan, I see you," said Addison. Zayan opened his eyes. He looked down at his hands. "I closed my eyes," he said. "But my eyes still see you," said Addison. Zayan laughed. He put his hands down.

Ms. Sandhu came over with a small bowl. "Let's mix the sand and water," she said. Addison touched the sand with her fingers. It felt cold and wet. She heard the water splash. She smelled the flowers by the fence. Then Ms. Sandhu gave them a cracker at snack time. Addison tasted it. It was salty and good.

Then Zayan hid again. He stood by the big tree. He covered his eyes with his hands. Addison saw his red hat behind the leaves. She walked over and tapped his shoulder. "Found you, Zayan!" she said.

Rehmat sat at the dinner table. The rice pot was warm and full. Mr. Mwangi said, "Make a line for more rice." Rehmat jumped up fast. She ran to the pot. She pushed past Ernest. "Hey," said Ernest. "You were behind me."
Rehmat looked back. Maeve stood in her old spot. Maeve was sad. Rehmat thought, was that my spot? The line was long. "This is the line," said Mr. Mwangi. "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn." Rehmat walked back. She stood behind Maeve. She waited.
First Ernest got rice. Then Maeve got rice. Then it was Rehmat's turn. Mr. Mwangi put rice in her bowl. "Yum," said Rehmat. She carried it to her seat. Her blanket was on her chair. She sat on it and ate. Rehmat was happy. She had waited, and her turn came. "Can I be in the line again?" she asked. Everyone laughed.

Aaron went to the library with his class. Ms. Jean-Louis said, "It is coloring time." Aaron grabbed all the crayons. He held them in a big pile.

Oaklynn sat next to him. She had no crayons. Her paper stayed empty. Aaron looked at his pile. Then he looked at her paper. Could one thing help another thing?

"Here," Aaron said. He gave her some crayons. "This means you can use them too," he said. Oaklynn smiled and drew a big yellow dog. "Woof, woof!" she said. "My dog can bark."

Outside the window, a bee was stuck on the net curtain. It buzzed and buzzed. Aaron watched. The bee crawled and crawled. Then it popped out and flew away.

"Did you see that?" Aaron asked. "The bee got out!" Ms. Jean-Louis smiled at their pictures. "Nice sharing, Aaron," she said.

Aaron gave Oaklynn one more crayon. She gave him her shiny blue one back.

Aubrey ran into the library with her mom. "Paint day!" she shouted. Ms. Joseph had big tables all set up. There were red cups and blue cups and yellow cups of paint.

Syeda and Pia were already there. They had paint on their hands and big smiles. Aubrey wanted to paint a cat. She sat down fast and dipped her brush.

Then Ms. Joseph said, "Aubrey, where is your apron?" Aubrey looked down. No apron. She had on her cat shirt, her best one. Blue paint dripped. Drip! A blue spot went right on her cat. "Oh no," said Aubrey.

Ms. Joseph held up an old shirt. "You can wear this," she said. Aubrey put her arms in. The shirt was long and soft. She painted a big yellow cat. More paint dripped. Drip, drip! The paint went on the old shirt. Her cat shirt stayed clean. Aubrey jumped up. "Look! No paint on me!" Pia clapped her hands. Then Aubrey went back to paint a sun.

Today Isaac was three years old. Mom put a big cake on the table. Isaac counted the candles. "One, two, three," he said.

Gia came to the party. Gia was five. "Look, Isaac," she said. "I am five, so I get five candles." She held up her hand. Gia pointed at her cake. Mom put one candle for each year on it. One, two, three, four, five candles stood high on the cake.

Dad lit the candles with a match. "Stay back, Isaac," Dad said. Isaac watched from his chair. The little flames moved. "Make a wish, Gia," said Tilly. Gia blew out all five candles. Everybody clapped. Isaac gave Gia a smile and a hug. Then Mom cut the cake. Isaac got a big piece with sprinkles.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Norah helped get the guest bedroom ready. She put a bumpy quilt on the bed. She stacked three pillows up high. She drew a map of the house so Grandpa would not get lost.

Then the car pulled up. Grandpa got out with his big bag. Mom opened her arms wide for a hug. Norah hid behind Mom's legs. She was not ready for a hug yet.

Grandpa did not rush her. He stood still and smiled. "You can hug me," he said. "Or you can wave. Or you can just say hello."

Norah peeked out. She waved one small hand. Grandpa waved back, big and slow. Then she said, "Hello, Grandpa." He said, "Hello, Norah."

Grandpa carried his bag inside. Norah showed him the guest bedroom. She pointed at the quilt. "It is bumpy," she said. Grandpa touched it. "I like bumpy," he said.

At bedtime, Norah stood by the door. She felt ready now. She ran in and gave Grandpa a hug. He hugged her back, warm and soft.

"Hug tomorrow too?" she asked.

"Hug tomorrow too," said Grandpa.

Daniel went on a nature trail. It was early in the morning. Ms. Novák walked with him. Joseph and Lillian came too.

"Let's use our senses," said Ms. Novák. "Noses can smell. Hands can touch." Daniel sniffed a pine tree. It smelled sharp and good. He touched the bark. It felt bumpy. "I smell with my nose," he said. "I touch with my hands."

Then a big truck rumbled by. It was very loud. Daniel put his hands over his ears. The truck sound got quieter. He took his hands off. The sound got big again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again! "My ears hear," said Daniel. "And my hands help my ears."

Lillian saw a red bird. "I see it with my eyes," she said. Joseph found berries. He did not eat them. A grown-up said no. Then Ms. Novák had a snack for everyone. Daniel ate his cracker. "I taste with my mouth," he said. He was happy.

On the way back, the truck came again. Daniel covered his ears right away. "Quiet," he said. Ms. Novák smiled. "Do you hear the birds now?" she asked. Daniel listened. He heard a little bird song. He waved at a woman walking by. "Ears, eyes, nose, hands, mouth," said Daniel. Then he skipped down the trail.

Eloise went to the store with her dad. She wanted to buy a gift for Axelle. "A blue crayon," Eloise said. "Blue is her favorite color."

Eloise found the crayon box. She held up a navy crayon. Ishan was there too. "That one is not blue," said Ishan. "It is too dark."

"It is so blue," said Eloise.

Ishan pulled out a pale crayon. "This one is blue," he said.

Ms. Li worked at the store. She came to help. "Line them up," she said. "Put the blues in a row."

Eloise lined up all the blue crayons. She put the lightest one first. Then the next one. Then the next. At the end was the navy crayon. It was the darkest one of all.

"Look," said Eloise. "It is light blue at this end. And dark blue at that end. They are all blue."

Ishan looked at the row. "All blue," he said. "Light blue, dark blue, blue, blue."

Eloise picked the navy crayon for Axelle. Then she found a squishy blue ball. She put it in the basket too. "Now Axelle has two blue gifts," she said.

At home, Eloise gave Axelle the crayon. Axelle drew a big dark blue sky. Then she drew light blue clouds. "Thank you," said Axelle. "Blue is the best."

Eloise smiled and picked up the squishy ball. "This one is for you too," she said.

Owen woke up early. Today was the lantern festival at the park. He wanted to look right for it. He pulled open his drawer. His red shirt was soft and had a golden dragon on it. His gray shirt was for rainy days. Which one was a festival shirt?

He could not decide. "Try one," said his dad. Owen put on the gray shirt. Then he thought and thought. He did not want to forget the dragon. He pulled the gray shirt off. He zipped up his red jacket over the dragon shirt. "Good," said Dad. "You look ready."

At the park, Owen looked around. What would he see? Philemon wore a blue coat with shiny stars. Lorenzo wore a yellow robe with a big sash. Mr. Leung wore a long white tunic. Even Owen's mom wore her sparkly scarf. Everyone had on something special. Owen looked down at his dragon shirt. His dragon fit right in with the stars and the yellow robe. He smiled a big smile.

The sky grew dark. A grown-up lit the first lantern with a long match. Owen watched from far back, holding Dad's hand. The flame went into the paper. Then the lantern glowed. One little light made a big glow! More lanterns floated up, one by one.

Owen pointed at his dragon. "Look, Dad. My dragon can see the lanterns too."

Connor sat at Grandpa's big table. Grandpa gave him a fat pencil and paper. "You can write your name," Grandpa said. Connor held the pencil in his fist. Grandpa showed him how to hold it with his fingers. "Like this," said Grandpa. Connor tried. He picked up the pencil the new way. It felt funny, but he held on.

Connor started at the right side of the paper. He made a big C. Then an O. Then the N hit the edge. There was no room left! "Oh no," said Connor. "Where do I start?" Grandpa smiled. "We start on the left," he said. Connor looked at the left side. Lots of room there!

Connor began at the left. C, O, N, N, O, R. The letters went across the page, one by one. There was room for all of them! Connor was thirsty after all that work. Grandpa brought him cold water. Then Connor turned the paper over. He wrote his name again, all by himself. "I did it!" he said. Grandpa clapped.

Hailey stood by the little mirror at daycare. She made a big smile. "Look at me," she said. Meera came to look too. Meera made a sad face. Her mouth went down at the corners. "Your face looks sad," said Hailey. "I am sad," said Meera. "My dog ran away." Then Meera's face changed. Her mouth went up. "He came back!" she said. Now she looked happy.

Younes was playing in the corner. He was mad about a broken tower. His eyebrows came down. His face looked angry. "Can I help you build it again?" Hailey asked. "Yes," said Younes. They built a big tower together. Soon his face was smooth and smiling again.

Later they pretended the tower was a castle. Its shadow lay long on the floor. Ms. Baptiste turned on the light. "Do faces tell us things?" Hailey asked her. "Yes, they do," said Ms. Baptiste. Hailey ran to the mirror. She smiled her biggest smile. "My face says I am happy," she said.

Everly sat in a big chair at the salon. She was getting her very first haircut. "I need a trim," she said. The chair was too tall for her little legs. So the hairdresser lifted her up with a happy smile.

Snip, snip went the scissors. A small curl fell down. It landed on Everly's hand. She looked at it. "Where did that come from?" she asked. Her mom said, "From your head. It came off when the scissors cut." Everly gasped. "My hair made a little curl!" She held it up to the light.

Then Mom took out a small envelope. She put the curl inside. Everly tilted her head. "Why?" she asked. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut," Mom said. "To remember it." Everly smiled a big smile. "Like a treasure!" She gave the envelope a gentle pat.

Blake wanted to play hide-and-seek. She called to Finley and Adina in the playroom. "I will seek first," said Blake. "You two go hide."

Blake turned to the wall. She counted very fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

She spun around. Finley was still standing by the toy box. Adina was only half behind the curtain. "Blake, you counted too fast," said Finley. "We did not have time to hide."

Blake thought about that. In hide-and-seek, the seeker counts while the others hide. So she would try again, and count slowly.

"Ready?" said Blake. "Go and hide. I will count nice and slow this time."

"One... two... three..." She heard a soft step. "Four... five..." She heard the curtain move. "Six... seven... eight..." The playroom was quiet now. "Nine... ten! Here I come."

Blake looked behind the teddy bear. She looked under the table. Then she saw two shoes by the fresh white curtain. She pulled it back. "Found you, Adina!"

Adina gave her a big hug. "You counted slow," said Adina. "That was a good game. Now you can choose who seeks next."

"I choose Finley," said Blake. And Finley began to count, "One... two... three..."

Isla and her dad stopped at a roadside diner. It was warm inside. The waiter brought soup, and it was brown. Isla took big slurps.

Tomorrow they would see the snowy mountains. "Is it cold there?" Isla asked. Her dad said, "Yes, very cold!"

Isla jumped up. "I will pack my swimsuit!" she said.

Dad shook his head. He held up her mittens. "Snowy places need warm coats," he said. "You pack clothes that fit the weather where you are going."

A girl at the next table smiled at Isla. Her mom held up a tiny swimsuit. "We are going to the beach," the girl said. "Sand and sun!"

Isla looked at the mittens. Then she looked at the little swimsuit. Snowy mountains get coats. Sunny beaches get swimsuits!

"Okay," said Isla. "Mittens it is!" She put them on right there, and waved goodbye to the girl in the diner.

Liam went to the animal shelter with his dad. The dogs barked and wagged their tails. One small puppy licked Liam's hand. His fur was soft and warm. "Can we take him home?" Liam asked. Dad said yes.

A helper clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. "What does that do?" Liam asked. The helper smiled and handed the leash to Dad.

Outside, a bird landed on the grass. The puppy wanted to chase it! He pulled and pulled. But the leash was short, so he stayed close to Dad. Liam laughed. The puppy could not run away. He sat down and wagged his tail instead.

At home, Liam gave the puppy water. At night, the puppy slept in a soft bed. "Good night, puppy," Liam whispered. The puppy licked his nose one more time.

Zachary went to the library with his mom. He wanted storytime. He asked the man at the desk, "Is storytime now?" Mr. Gallagher smiled. "Not now," he said. "Storytime is soon." Zachary sat on the blue rug to wait. His friend Elisha came and sat too. "Soon means in a little while," said Elisha. Zachary looked at the big clock on the wall. He waited. He looked at a picture book about a man who had to sweep the barn. He turned one page. Then he turned another page.

"I think it is still later," said Zachary. He waited some more. He heard feet walk by. He heard a baby laugh. Then Mr. Gallagher clapped his hands. "Storytime starts now," he said. Zachary jumped up. The little while was over. He sat close with Elisha. The story was about a big blue whale. Zachary clapped at the end. "Tomorrow we come back," said his mom. "Okay," said Zachary. "Soon."

Florence went to a big festival with Grandpa. There were tents and drums and food smells everywhere. Florence saw her friends Scarlette and Willa at a long table. Everyone would eat together soon.

"First we say a blessing," said Grandpa. "Some people close their eyes or bow their heads." Florence wanted to do it just right. She peeked at Grandpa. His eyes were closed. His head was bowed. Now she knew what to do.

Florence counted the people at the table. One, two, three, four, five bowls of rice. She helped pick spoons from a basket and put them out. A big pot sat on a stove, but the cook watched it, so Florence stayed back. Willa passed her a dish of peas. "These feel a bit slimy," Willa said, giggling. Florence giggled too.

Then it was time. Florence closed her eyes. She bowed her head, just like Grandpa. The table got very quiet. After the blessing, Grandpa squeezed her hand. "You did it," he said. Florence opened her eyes and smiled at Scarlette. "My turn to help serve," said Florence. She picked up her spoon.

Owen climbed the big school bus. He found a seat by the window. His tummy felt jumpy and happy.

"Is school fun?" Owen asked the driver.

"Oh yes," the driver said. "You will see."

Owen looked out the window. He saw a truck sweep the street. He saw a snowy white cloud in the sky.

At school, everyone got off the bus. Owen ran ahead fast. He ran down the hall all alone. Where was his class? He did not see Klara. He did not see Emelia.

Then Owen looked back. His whole class was walking in a line. Ms. Santos-Reyes was at the front. Owen ran back to the line.

"Is this my spot?" he asked.

"Yes, right here," said Ms. Santos-Reyes.

Klara smiled at him. Emelia waved. Owen put his hands at his sides. He walked in the line, step by step.

"This way," said Ms. Santos-Reyes. "Off we go to our room!"

Levi stood by the bright blue pool. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But his legs felt wobbly in the water.

Mr. Kowalski smiled at him. "Hold the edge of the pool," he said. "You can practice kicking your legs." Levi held the cool wall with both hands. He kicked one leg. Then he kicked the other. Little waves moved near his toes.

Levi kicked faster. Splash! Water flew up and got Mr. Kowalski's face all wet. Levi giggled. He kicked again. Splash! Water went everywhere. Alison and Avery laughed from the steps.

"Good kicking, Levi," said Mr. Kowalski, wiping his face. Levi held the wall tight. Kick, kick, kick. His legs were strong now. The water felt warm and swirly around him. Levi looked at his feet making waves. "Look at me!" he said. "I can kick and kick!" Mr. Kowalski clapped his hands.

Arnaud was at daycare. It was snack time. There was a big bowl of crackers on the table.

Blake grabbed the bowl. "Give me crackers!" he said. Ms. Francis held the bowl up high. She did not pass it. She waited. She looked at Blake and waited some more.

Arnaud watched. He was hungry too. He wanted crackers very much. He thought about what Blake had said. Then he had an idea. He looked up at Ms. Francis.

"Crackers, please," said Arnaud.

Ms. Francis smiled. She passed the bowl to Arnaud right away. Arnaud took two crackers. "Thank you," he said.

Blake tried again. He sat up tall. He waited his turn. "Crackers, please," he said. This time Ms. Francis passed him the bowl. "Thank you," said Blake. Then he hopped off his chair with a cracker in each hand.

Arnaud ate his crackers slowly. They were crunchy and good. Then he tapped Ms. Francis on the arm. "More crackers, please," he said.

She laughed and filled his cupped hands.

Addison held her dad's hand as they walked through the big mall. Today she would get her very first haircut. The salon smelled like soap and apples. Soft music played. A hairdresser named Ms. Walker smiled and said, "Sit right here, Addison."

Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Addison watched little bits of hair fall. They landed on her cape like snow. "One snip, two snips, three snips," she counted.

Soon Ms. Walker said, "All done!" Addison looked in the big mirror. She saw the front of her hair. It was short and neat. "But I can't see the back," said Addison. She turned her head. Still no back.

Ms. Walker picked up a small mirror. She held it up behind Addison. Addison looked at the big mirror, and there it was. She could see the back of her hair.

"Look, Dad, look!" said Addison. She pointed with one finger. "The little mirror shows the back." Dad gave her a proud smile.

In the car, Addison touched her soft hair all the way home. "Drive slow, Dad," she said. "I want to feel my haircut some more."

Evelyn sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. It would have a flower on it. Evelyn had red, blue, yellow and green paint.

She looked at the paints. "Where is pink paint?" she asked. Grandma's flowers outside were pink. But there was no pink pot on the table.

Grandma sat down next to her. "Let's look in the paint box," she said.

Evelyn stirred her brush in the red paint. Then Grandma gave her the white paint. Evelyn dipped her brush in the white too. She stirred them together on her paper.

The red paint turned lighter and lighter. It became pink! "Pink!" said Evelyn. "Red and white make pink!"

"Grandma's favorite," said Grandma with a smile.

Evelyn painted a big pink flower. She painted a green stem and curly leaves. Outside, white snow was falling on Grandma's real flowers.

"Grandma, this is for you," said Evelyn. Grandma hugged her tight.

Zoe went to the library with her dad. Yesterday the library was closed. Today it was open. Zoe was happy.

Zoe loved story time. She wanted a story now. She pulled Ms. Littlechild's hand. "Story now, please," said Zoe.

Ms. Littlechild smiled. "Not now, Zoe," she said. "Story time is after snack." Zoe did not know what now meant. She asked her friend Lorenzo. "What is now?" Lorenzo pointed at the clock. The little hand moved. "Watch," he said. "The hand moves, and now passes."

First they had snack. Zoe passed the crackers to Scout. Scout passed the juice to Zoe. Zoe kept watching the clock. The hand moved a little bit. Then Ms. Littlechild clapped her hands. "Snack is done," she said. "Story time is now!"

Zoe sat down fast. Ms. Littlechild read a pretty book about stars and night. Zoe clapped at the end. "Tomorrow we come back," Zoe told her dad. "Tomorrow we read again." Her dad laughed and took her hand.

Sofia ran to the park with Cedric. The sky was dark and full of clouds.

"I want to splash in puddles," said Sofia.

"Me too," said Cedric. "One, two, three, splash!"

Then the rain came. Drip, drip, drip. Sofia had her yellow raincoat on. Cedric did not.

The rain fell on Sofia's raincoat. It ran right off. Her body stayed dry. The rain fell on Cedric's shirt. His shirt got wet. Drip, drip, drip.

"My shirt is all wet," said Cedric. "I feel cold."

Catherine ran over. She had her boots and her raincoat too. "Rainy days need raincoats," she said.

The wind blew. Whoosh. The rain went sideways. Sofia's hood kept her hair dry. She was warm and dry in her big yellow coat.

"I will run home fast," said Cedric. He ran all the way home.

Sofia and Catherine jumped in the puddles. One splash, two splashes, three splashes!

Soon Cedric came back. He wore a green raincoat and red boots.

"Now I can splash too," he said.

"Be brave, the big puddle is deep," said Sofia.

Cedric jumped. Sploosh! Water flew everywhere.

"Sunny days, rainy days, the world has so many days," sang Catherine.

Then the rain stopped. The sun came out. Sofia took off her raincoat. She hung it on the fence.

"Rain, rain, go away," said Cedric. "Too late, rain. We are dry!"

Catherine laughed. "One, two, three, splash!"

Eva went to the library with her dad. She found a book about fish. The fish swam through blue water on every page. Eva loved the pictures. She wanted to know who made them.

"Who drew this fish?" she asked.

The librarian, Mr. Mercer, smiled. He bent down next to her. "An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book," he said. "Let's find the illustrator's name."

Eva held the book. She opened the front cover. "This way first?" she asked.

"Yes, books start at the front," said Mr. Mercer.

They looked at the first page. There were words there. "Those words tell us the names," said Mr. Mercer. He pointed. "Here is the illustrator."

Eva looked at the letters. "That name made my fish!" she said. She turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back.

At the checkout desk, Eva hugged the book. On the drive home, the window felt cold like a frozen pond. Eva held the book on her lap. At home she set her plastic fish toy next to the pages.

"This is Swimmy," she told the toy. "A real person drew him. I saw the name."

She turned to page one and began again.

Stella ran into daycare with her bunny. "Bunny comes too!" she said. Mika and Yasmine were already at the play table. Stella put bunny down on a chair. Then she slid blocks with Mika. She painted a fish with Yasmine. It was a big, busy morning.

Time to go home. Stella looked for bunny. Bunny was not on the chair. Stella wanted to run and look all by herself. She ran toward the hall. But she stopped. She ran back to Ms. Kobayashi instead. "My bunny is lost!" said Stella. "Let's look together," said Ms. Kobayashi.

They looked by the blocks. They looked by the paint. Then Ms. Kobayashi opened the closed toy box. Bunny was inside, under a hat! "Bunny!" said Stella. She hugged bunny tight. Mika clapped. Yasmine clapped too. "Bunny found!" said Stella.

David sat in the kitchen. He was hungry. The soup smelled so good. His friend Cormac was coming to eat too.

Cormac ran in. "Bon appétit!" he said.

David looked at him. "What is that?"

"It is what my dad says," said Cormac. "In France, people say bon appétit before a meal. It means have a good meal!"

David wanted to try it too. He took a big breath. "Bon appétit!" he said. His voice was a little too loud. The spoon did a big swing in the pot.

Cormac laughed. "You said it!"

David's mom set the bowls down. The butter was soft. It would melt on the warm bread. David held up his spoon like a flag.

"Bon appétit, everyone!" he said.

"Bon appétit, David!" said Cormac.

They ate all the soup. Every drop.

"Same time tomorrow?" asked Cormac.

"Yes!" said David. "Bon appétit at my house every day!"

Lennon wanted her teddy. His name was Bear. She could not find him.

She looked under the table. It was dark under there. Her eyes could not see in the dark. She put her hand in and touched something soft. Was it Bear? She pulled it out. It was a mop rag. "Yucky," she said.

Then she heard a sound. Pop, pop, pop. Her nose smelled something warm and buttery. Dad was making popcorn in the kitchen!

"Come here, Lennon," said Dad. "The popcorn is ready." He turned on the big kitchen light. Click. The room got bright.

Lennon took one little popcorn piece. She put it in her mouth. Mmm, it tasted salty and good.

Then she looked at the table. Under the bright light, she saw something brown and fuzzy. "Bear!" she said. He was under a napkin all along.

"How did you find him?" Dad asked.

"I turned the light on," said Lennon. "Now my eyes can see!"

She hugged Bear tight. Bear smelled like popcorn now. She gave him a lick. "Salty," she said. Dad laughed and gave her a big popcorn card with a bear on it.

At bedtime, the hall was dark. Lennon held Dad's hand. "Light, please," she said. Dad clicked the lamp on. There was her bed, clear as day. She climbed in with Bear.

"My eyes work best with light," said Lennon. Dad kissed her head. "Goodnight, little finder," he said. Lennon smiled and closed her eyes.

Grandma came on a big shiny plane. Ivy waited at the airport with her mom. The doors opened and there was Grandma, waving her hand way up high. Ivy ran to her and hugged her legs. Grandma stayed a whole week. They made pancakes for breakfast. They fed the ducks. They read the same book four times.

Then the week was done. Grandma had to fly home. Ivy felt sad at the airport. "I will forget you," she said. Grandma smiled. "We can still talk. I can call you on the phone. Or we can see each other on a video call." "A video call?" said Ivy. "Yes, I can see your face on the screen," said Grandma. "And you can send me letters too."

So Ivy made a plan. She drew a duck and a pancake and a book. Her mom helped her put the drawing in an envelope. It was a letter for Grandma. On Sunday, the phone rang. It was Grandma on a video call. "I got your letter!" she said. She held it up to the screen. There was the duck, there was the pancake. Ivy laughed and waved. "Draw me another one," said Grandma. Ivy ran to get her crayons.

Luca ran into the playroom. "A sorting game!" he shouted. Mr. Grant had put out three big boxes. One box was for animals, one for toys, one for foods.

Luca peeked in the toy box. "One car, two cars, three cars," he counted. Then he saw something yellow. It was a banana! The banana did not belong there. "You are the odd one out," Luca told the banana. He picked it up and put it in the foods box. Then he clapped.

Ocean came over with a loud laugh. "Look at the animals!" A feather was hiding under the toy lion. "One lion, two bears, three ducks," said Ocean. "The feather is the odd one out!" She put the feather in her pocket.

Amy closed the door of the toy box. "All done!" she said. Mr. Grant held up the banana. "Snack time!" Luca jumped up and down. "Banana for the odd one out finder!" he said.

Zachary wanted to play the ball game. Emma-Rose was already playing. Natalie was playing too. "Can I play?" Zachary asked. "Yes," said Emma-Rose. "We take turns. You throw, then I throw." Zachary nodded. He waited for his turn. Then he threw the ball far. Natalie ran to get it.

Then Zachary had the ball again. He did not give it back. He held it and ran. "My ball now!" he said. Emma-Rose stopped playing. Natalie stopped too. They sat on the grass. Zachary ran and ran, but he was all alone.

Zachary walked back. He gave the ball to Emma-Rose. "Your turn," he said. Emma-Rose smiled. Natalie stood up. They all played again. Zachary waited, then he threw. Natalie caught the fresh orange ball. She clapped. "Good throw!" she said.

Later, Mom called them inside. "Time for a snack," she said. Zachary helped feed the goldfish with Mom. Then he ate his snack. "We followed the rules," he said. Emma-Rose laughed. "Same rules tomorrow," said Natalie. Zachary ran to the window and waved. "Bye, ball!" he said.

Wren planted little seeds in the backyard. She planted carrots and yellow tomatoes. Every morning she said, "Grow, little seeds, grow." But nothing came up.

Then one day, green leaves popped out of the soil. Wren jumped up and down. "You made a plant!" she said.

A big weed grew next to her tomatoes. Wren grabbed it and pulled. The weed came out slowly. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom of it. They were stuck deep in the dirt.

"What are those?" Wren asked.

"Roots," said her dad. "The roots grow down into the soil."

Wren leaned close. She saw white strings going down, down, down. "So my carrots are down there?" she asked.

"Your carrots are roots too," her dad said.

Near the fence, her dad used a hammer to make a small fence post. It would keep the bunnies out. Wren watched from the grass and clapped.

That night, Wren peeked out the window. Her garden slept in the dark. Under the soil, the roots grew down, down, down.

"Grow, little roots, grow," she whispered.

Addison sat at the little red table. Ms. Jung put out two trays. One tray had three big balls. The other tray had three tiny beads. The balls were smooth and cool. The beads felt slippery in Addison's hand.

"Look," said Addison. "The balls win. Big balls are more."

Jazlyn sat down next to her. "Let's count," said Jazlyn. Addison touched each ball. "One, two, three." Then she touched each bead. "One, two, three." She sat very still. The beads looked so small. But they counted the same.

"Three and three," said Addison. "The same!"

Ms. Jung smiled. "Snack time now," she said. Addison picked up her doll. The doll could not come to the table. Addison set the doll on the shelf, safe and snug.

At snack time, Laurence had crackers. Addison had crackers too. Laurence's crackers were big. Addison's were small. She counted hers. "One, two, three." She counted his. "One, two, three."

"Same!" said Laurence.

Addison laughed. "Big ones and small ones. Both are three." She took a bite of her small cracker. Outside the window, the sun sat on the green grass, and the plants by the window began to grow tall.

Henry loved baths at Grandma's house. The tub was big and white. It even had bubbles. But tonight, Henry was very dirty. He had played in the garden all day. "Bath time," said Grandma. Henry ran to the tub fast. He wanted to jump right in.

Grandma held up her hand. "Wait, Henry," she said. "Let me check the water first." Henry sat on the little stool. He watched Grandma put her hand in the water. She moved it slowly, side to side. Henry picked at the hem of his shirt while he waited.

Grandma said, "The water is a bit too hot." She turned the tap. Cold water came in. She put her hand in again. "Now it is just right," she said with a smile.

Henry put one toe in. The water felt warm and nice. He slid in all the way. He splashed and played with his little boat. His bubbles floated on top. He got water in his eye and blinked, then laughed.

"You were brave to wait," said Grandma. "Now you are clean and warm." Henry looked at Grandma's hand. The water was good because she had checked it first. "Bath is done," said Grandma. "Let's pick your pajamas." Henry pointed to the blue ones with stars.

Cooper sat at the little table in the backyard. He had a big white paper. He had his pencil box. He was drawing a snowman with a funny hat.

"I will draw the snow," said Cooper. He wanted lots of snow. He pressed his pencil down very hard. He made dark, dark lines. Then the pencil point snapped right off.

"Oh no," said Cooper. "My pencil!" He held up the short pencil. The point was gone. Averie looked over from her chair.

"You pressed too hard," said Averie with a little laugh. Cooper made a funny face at her. "You try," he said.

Averie took her own pencil. She pressed down soft and slow. Her lines were light and pretty. Nothing broke.

Cooper got a new pencil from his box. This time he pressed gently. He drew soft snow all over the paper. He drew a hat on the snowman. He drew a winter sun, small and round.

"Now we cover the whole page," said Cooper. He and Averie drew side by side. The snow went up and up to the top.

"Look," said Cooper. "It snowed on my snowman." Averie giggled. "And my pencil still has its point!" she said, holding it up high.

Samuel got to pet a big soft dog outside. The dog licked his hand. Then Samuel and his mom went in to see the dentist.

A friendly nurse said, "You can pick a flower sticker after." Samuel was so excited. He did not want to lose his sticker. Then he saw a little sink in the corner. He wanted to wash his hands first. The nurse smiled and helped him.

"Make lots of bubbles," she said. Samuel put soap on his hands. He rubbed them together. The nurse said, "Count with me. One, two, three." They counted all the way to twenty. Samuel splashed the bubbles away. His hands were clean and shiny.

After that, the dentist looked at Samuel's teeth. Samuel got to kick his feet on the big chair. He opened his mouth wide. "All done," said the dentist. Samuel picked a purple flower sticker. He stuck it on his shirt. "I counted to twenty," he told his mom. She gave him a big thumbs up.

The lights went out. The backyard was dark too. Colton wanted his juice cup. It sat in the kitchen. He ran to the door in the dark. Bump! His leg hit a chair. It hurt a little.

Dad came with a flashlight. "Ow," Colton said. Dad held out his hand. "In the dark, we walk slowly," Dad said. Colton held Dad's hand. They walked slowly, step by step. They did not bump into anything. Colton got his juice cup.

They sat on the tall fence step. A frog sang in the grass. "Peep, peep," Colton sang back. Dad laughed. The lights came on. The house glowed bright. "Night night, frog," Colton said. He waved at the dark grass.

Rose wanted a drink of water. She padded into the kitchen in her socks. The kettle was on the stove. It hissed and puffed like a little dragon. "That is hot," her dad said. "Only a grown-up touches it." Rose stood back and watched the steam curl up. How did the water get so hot so fast?

On the table she saw something shiny. A little bottle had tipped over. Round red dots had rolled out onto the wood. They looked just like candy. Rose leaned in close. They were so pretty. Her hand came up slowly.

Then she stopped. She remembered the rule from school. Mr. Abdi had said, "Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy." Rose put her hands behind her back.

"Dad!" she called. "Come and see!"

Her dad turned off the stove and came over. "Good girl. You did not touch them." He picked up the dots, one by one, and put the cap on tight. He let Rose carry her own cool cup of water to the table. She sipped it slowly. The red dots had looked sweet. But they were not candy at all.

Outside, a bird landed on the windowsill. It tapped the glass twice, then flew away. Rose waved at the empty sky.

William lived in a big apartment. Up high, he had a small balcony. He wanted to grow food there. "Can I plant peas?" he asked. His dad said yes.

They filled a long pot with dirt. William pushed the pea seeds down into the soil. Then he gave them water. Every morning, he watered the pot. Every morning, he looked. One day, a little green shoot came up. William began to shout, "It grew! It grew!"

His friend Preston came to see. A tall green plant stood in the pot. William picked a long green pod. "What is this?" he asked. "Is it a pea?" Preston shook his head. "I don't know."

William pressed the pod with his thumb. Pop! It opened. Inside was a row of little round peas. "The peas grow inside the pod!" he said. The pod felt a little sticky inside. William gave three peas to Preston. Then he ran inside. "Dad! The peas were hiding in the pod!"

Isaiah stood in the playroom. The toy box was empty. Toys were all over the floor.

"Time to clean up," said Ms. Bakker. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys. Every toy goes in the box."

Isaiah picked up a red block. He dropped it in. Clunk. He picked up a blue block. Clunk. Samara held up a doll with yellow hair.

"Is this a toy?" she asked.

"Yes," said Isaiah. "Dolls are toys." Samara put the doll in the box.

Amin rolled a bright green ball across the floor. It bumped Isaiah's foot. Isaiah laughed and picked it up. The ball went in too. Bounce, plop.

Then Isaiah found something under the chair. It was a red apple from snack time. "Is an apple a toy?" he asked.

Amin shook his head. "No. Apples are foods. Foods go on the plate."

Isaiah put the apple on the snack table. Then he looked around the room. A wooden dog, a small cat, a drum, a tiny car. He pointed at each one.

"Animals, drum, car," he said. "All toys!" He put them in one by one.

Soon the box was full. The floor was clean. Ms. Bakker smiled.

"Nice work," she said. "Now who wants to share the drum?"

"Me!" said Isaiah. He sat down next to Samara. He tapped the drum softly. Tum, tum, tum.

Anthony went to the library with his mom. He saw a big red book about trucks. He wanted it so much.

Romy was standing by the shelf. Anthony did not know her yet. Romy waved at him. Anthony hid behind his mom's arm. Then he peeked out. "Hello," he said in a small voice. Romy smiled big. "Hello! Do you like trucks?" she said.

Now they were friends. They read the truck book together. But the book was stuck. The pages were sticky and would not turn. "Let's ask for help," said Romy. They walked to Ms. Suryanto. "Please, can you help us?" said Anthony. Ms. Suryanto wiped the sticky pages with a soft cloth. The pages turned easily.

"Thank you," said Anthony and Romy together. Anthony bumped the book shelf. "Sorry," he said, and pushed it back. Ms. Suryanto laughed gently. On the way out, Anthony saw the man at the desk. He did not hide this time. "Hello!" he said, loud and happy. The man waved back and said, "Hello, little friend."

Kinsley went to Grandma's house for Diwali. The front door was open wide. Sweet smells came from the kitchen. Grandma was making treats.

Grandma gave Kinsley a box of little clay lamps. "These are called diyas," Grandma said. Kinsley looked at them. They were small and round, like tiny bowls. "Can I put them out?" she asked. "Yes, you may," said Grandma. Kinsley set the diyas in a row by the window. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. They looked dark and empty.

Then Grandpa came with a long match. He was the grown-up, so he did the lighting. He tipped the flame into each little lamp. Each lamp had oil inside. The first one lit up. Then the next one. Then all of them. Now the whole row was glowing.

Kinsley clapped her hands. "The window looks like the sky!" she said. The little flames made the room warm and gold. Grandma smiled at the shining row. "That is our sign that the party can start," she said.

Cousins came to the door. One cousin wore a silly hat that lit up too. Everyone ate the sweet treats. Kinsley looked at the diyas. Each flame was small. But together they made the whole house glow. "More lamps, more light," she whispered to herself. Then she took one more sweet treat and shared it with her cousin.

Charles went to the playground with his friend Jace. They found the mud kitchen by the sandbox. It had pots, cups, and spoons.

"I will make soup," said Jace. He put leaves and water in a red pot. He stirred it with a big spoon. "Mud soup!" he said.

Charles wanted some too. He made his own soup with tiny stones and water. The stones were sticky from mud. Charles lifted the spoon to his mouth. He wanted to taste it.

Mr. Ong ran over fast. "Stop, Charles!" he said. He took the spoon away. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth."

Charles looked at his soup. Then he made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! Yum!" he said. He did not put the spoon in his mouth at all.

Jace laughed and slurped too. "More soup?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Charles. They stirred and slurped and pretended all morning long.

Peyton lost her red bunny at Grandma's house. She looked under the big chair. No bunny. She looked behind the door. No bunny. She looked in the thin blue blanket. No bunny.

Grandma said, "Where did you hold bunny last?" Peyton closed her eyes. She thought hard. "I had bunny at snack time," she said. "I ate crackers. Bunny sat with me." Grandma smiled. "The last place you remember having bunny is a good place to start looking," she said. "Let's go there."

They went to the snack table. Peyton looked and looked. Bunny was not on the chair. Then Grandma moved the bread basket. Bunny was there! "You were hiding under the bread," said Peyton. She hugged bunny tight. "One cracker for me," she said. "And one for you, bunny."

Emilia was at daycare. It was playtime outside. Kabir had a big red kite. The kite went up and up. Emilia wanted a turn. She reached out her hand. She almost grabbed the string. But that was not good.

"I have a problem," Emilia said to herself. "How can I get a turn?" Then she thought of something. She walked to Kabir and stood still. She took a breath.

"May I have a turn?" she asked. Kabir smiled at her. "Yes! May I" is a nice way to ask," he said. He put the string in her hands. The kite pulled. Emilia held on tight. The kite went higher.

"Thank you, Kabir," she said. "You can say thank you to me too," said Kabir. Emilia laughed. When she was done, she said, "Sorry, one more little turn?" Kabir nodded. Ms. Joseph clapped from the fence.

The wind blew soft and warm. Emilia felt cozy in her sweater. "May I have a turn?" said Kabir. Emilia gave him the string right away. "Here you go," she said. The red kite danced in the sky.

Penelope went to the park with her mama. There was a party there with little lamps. The lamps sat in a long row. Each lamp had a small flame.

Penelope wanted to light one. She reached out her hand. Her mama said, "Stop. The flame is hot." Penelope pulled her hand back. She watched her mama light a lamp. Only grown-ups touched the flames.

Then her mama said, "You can pick one for me to light." Penelope looked down the row. She picked a blue lamp. Her mama held the match and lit it. The little flame went pop, then it glowed.

Aline came by with her papa. He lit a lamp too. All the lamps were open to the sky. Penelope waved at her blue flame. "Hello, little light," she said.

Natalie was at the playground with her dad. She saw Zahra on the swings. Zahra waved her hand. Natalie wanted to wave back close up.

The playground was across the road. Natalie saw a car go by. She stopped at the curb. She held her dad's hand. "Hand," she said. Her dad smiled. They walked across the street together. He held on the same way he always did.

Then Natalie ran to the swing. Zahra gave her a big push. The swing went up, up, up. The girls laughed. Nearby, Knox was climbing the little stairs. His mom stood right beside him. Natalie pumped her legs. "Look at me!" she called to her dad. He sat on the bench and clapped.

Jade looked out the big window. The sun was warm on her face. She could see her shadow on the floor. It was long and dark.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain tapped on the glass. Tap, tap, tap. Jade got her rain boots and her yellow coat. "Can I go out after the rain?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said Mom.

The rain stopped. Jade went outside with Mom. The wind began to blow. The big tree swayed back and forth. Leaves blew across the yard. Jade chased them. She patted one leaf and it stayed still. Then the wind blew again. The leaf jumped up and flew away! Jade laughed. "Where does the leaf go?" she asked. "The wind takes it," said Mom. The trees swayed and more leaves blew around.

Soon the wind stopped too. The leaves sat still on the grass. Jade and Mom went inside. Mom made warm milk. Jade sat in her cozy chair. She looked out at the quiet tree. "Night night, tree," Jade said, and she waved.

Benjamin woke up and saw snow. School was closed today. It was a snow day.

Mom took him to the neighbor's house. Ms. McKenzie was outside. She was busy with a big shovel. She pushed the snow off the path.

"Can I help?" asked Benjamin.

Ms. McKenzie gave him a small shovel. He pushed snow. Pile by pile, the path turned clear.

"Why are we doing this?" Benjamin asked.

"So the mail carrier can walk without slipping," said Ms. McKenzie.

Benjamin looked at the path. It was bare and safe now.

Soon the mail carrier came. She walked on the clear path. She did not slip at all.

"Thank you," she said with a big smile. She handed Ms. McKenzie three letters.

Later, they went inside. Ms. McKenzie put cookies on a plate. Benjamin ate one and smiled. His arms felt tired, but the path was clear.

It was Mason's first day of school. The classroom had red blocks and a big rug. Mason sat next to Eleanora. Then his tummy felt funny. He needed to find the bathroom. But he did not know where it was. He looked around. His face felt hot.

Eleanora saw him. "You can ask Ms. Rosen," she said. "Will she help me?" asked Mason. "Yes. Teachers help kids." Mason took a big breath. He walked to the desk. "Ms. Rosen, I need the bathroom," he said. She smiled. "Come with me, Mason." They walked down the hall. She pointed to a blue door.

Mason washed his hands after. He went back to the rug. Eleanora waved at him. "That was not so bad," said Mason. Ms. Rosen sat in her chair nearby. Mason picked up a red block and started to build.

Eleanor had a small bunny. The bunny was her best toy. She loved it so much.

"Jasmin is coming to play," said Mom. Eleanor hugged her bunny tight. She did not want to share bunny. Not bunny!

Then Eleanor had an idea. She held bunny up high. "Up you go!" She put bunny on the big shelf. Bunny sat up there, safe and cozy.

The doorbell rang. It was Jasmin! "Blocks!" said Jasmin. Eleanor gave her the blocks. "You go first," said Eleanor. She sat on her hands and waited. It was hard to wait. But she waited.

"Your turn now," said Jasmin. Eleanor stacked one block. Then another. The tower grew tall. "We did it!" said Eleanor. Jasmin laughed and clapped.

At bedtime, Eleanor looked up at the shelf. "Hi, bunny," she whispered. Bunny was still there. Eleanor smiled. She hoped Jasmin would come again tomorrow.

Charlie wanted to find his blue train. It was hiding somewhere in the bathroom. He looked with his eyes. He saw the big white sink. He saw the green towel. No train there.

Then he heard a funny sound. Drip, drip, drip. His ears heard it. He listened by the sink. The soap smelled like flowers. His nose knew that smell. But no train yet.

Charlie closed his eyes. "I will use my hands," he said. He put his fingers in the basket. He felt a pinecone. His fingertips said, "Bumpy!" He felt a feather. His fingertips said, "Soft!" He felt a stone. His fingertips said, "Smooth!" He felt one more thing. His fingertips said, "Rough." It was a bumpy sponge? No. It had wheels!

Charlie opened his eyes. It was his blue train, hiding in the basket! He hugged it. The train tasted nothing at all, so he did not lick it again. He tickled his own nose with the feather. "Found you, train," said Charlie.

Layla was playing with her toy snake. It felt smooth in her hands. Then she heard a knock at the door. Grandma was there! Grandma had a small box.

"Open it," said Grandma. Layla opened the box. Inside was a red hat. Layla put it on. It fit just right. She ran to the mirror. She turned around and around.

Then Grandma put on her coat. She was going home. Layla waved at the window. Grandma walked down the path.

Layla looked at her hat. Grandma gave it to her. Mommy came close. "Go on," said Mommy with a smile.

Layla ran to the door. She pulled it open. "Grandma!" she called. Grandma turned around. "Thank you for my hat!" said Layla.

Grandma gave her a big hug. The red hat was warm, and so was Grandma's smile. Layla knocked on the door frame twice, just for fun, and Grandma laughed all the way to her car.

Caleb sat at the kitchen table. The sun made a sunny spot by his cup. He had a big pencil and some paper.

"Write your name," said his dad. Caleb held the pencil in his fist. He made a C. It came out wobbly and crooked.

"How do I fix it?" Caleb asked.

"Try the pink end," said his dad. "That is called an eraser."

Caleb rubbed the pink end on the C. He looked closely. The wobbly line was gone! The paper was clean again.

He waited a moment. He took a breath. He held the pencil with his fingers, just like his dad showed him. He made a new C. This one was round and neat.

"That looks good," said his dad. He gave Caleb a kiss on the head.

Caleb made an A. Then a B. Then another A. He pointed at his writing.

"That says Caleb!" he said. He rubbed the paper gently with his finger. The letters stayed. He smiled at his name in the sunny spot.

Audrey was at daycare. She had a big bucket of wet sand. She patted it and patted it. Soon she had a tall sandcastle with a brown paper flag.

Leah came running with a truck. She did not see the castle. The truck bumped it. The tall tower fell down. Leah stopped. Her face went sad. "Sorry, Audrey," she said. "It was a mistake. I feel bad I broke your castle."

Audrey looked at the flat sand. Then she looked at Leah. "It is okay," said Audrey. "You can help me build it again." Leah smiled. She scooped up more sand. Audrey patted the tower. Leah made two small walls.

Ms. Lin brought a glass of water for the seeds. "Please may we have one more tower?" asked Audrey. "Thank you," said Leah. They put the flag back on top. Then they sang a happy building song together. "Best castle ever," said Leah.

Arthur got a drum for his birthday. It was big and red. He wanted to play it with his friend Lennon.

Lennon came over with his little horn. "Let's play a song!" said Lennon. Arthur hit the drum fast. Lennon tooted fast too. Soon they were going faster and faster. The song fell all apart.

"Wait," said Arthur. He put his hand on his chest. He could feel his heart. Boom, boom, boom. It was steady and strong. "Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together," said his dad from the kitchen. Arthur tapped his drum softly. Boom, boom, boom. Lennon tooted along with the beat. It worked! The song sounded good. They played it again and again.

"Zip up your coat," said Dad. "We will play more tomorrow." Arthur zipped his zipper and grinned. "Best drum ever!"

Levi wanted to make muffins for his family. He loved muffins. His mom said he could help.

First, one cup of flour. Then two eggs. Then three big spoons of honey. Levi counted each thing out loud. "One, two, three!" he said. His mom put the pan in the hot oven. She set a little timer.

Then the family played a game in the kitchen. They laughed a lot. Levi spun around and got a little dizzy. They forgot all about the muffins.

Beep! Beep! Beep!

"What is that?" Levi asked. His mom smiled. "The timer," she said. "It tells the cook it is time to check the food."

Levi ran to see. His mom took out the muffins. They were big and golden. "The timer helped us," said Levi. He tapped it gently. "Good little timer."

The family ate warm muffins together. "One for Mom, one for Dad, one for me," said Levi. Then he asked, "Will it beep for us again tomorrow?"

James had a cold. His nose was red. His cough was small but loud.

He looked out the window. His friend Alistair was riding a bike. "I want to ride too," James said.

His mom felt his head. "Not today," she said. "Resting on the couch helps your body get better."

James frowned. But then his mom brought his furry bear. She gave him a kiss on his forehead. "You can choose a book," she said.

James chose his book about trucks. He snuggled under a blanket. He looked at the big wheels. He looked at the little wheels.

The next morning, his cough was gone. His nose was better too. "Mom! I feel good!"

He ran to the window. Alistair was outside again. James put on his shoes fast.

"Can I ride now?" he asked.

"Yes," said his mom. "Your rest did its job."

James waved. "Watch me go fast!"

Sara walked in the forest with her mom. The trees were tall and green. The path was quiet and soft with pine needles.

Then Sara heard a voice. "Welcome to my shop!" It was Melanie. Melanie sat on a big flat rock. She had set out pinecones, red leaves, and small stones. "I am the shopkeeper," said Melanie. "You can be the shopper."

Sara wanted a pinecone very much. She grabbed for it. "Wait," said Melanie. "The shopper chooses, and then she pays. You have to wait for me." Sara stopped her hand. She looked at all the things. She pointed at the biggest pinecone. "This one, please."

"That one costs one leaf," said Melanie. Sara picked up a yellow leaf. She put it in Melanie's hand. Melanie wiped the rock with her sleeve and handed over the pinecone.

"Now you can be the shopkeeper," said Melanie. They swapped spots. Sara lined up the stones by color, red ones and gray ones. A quiet lady with a dog came by. "May I buy a stone?" she asked. "Yes," said Sara. "One leaf, please." The lady paid with a leaf, and Sara smiled. Mom waved from the bench, close by. Sara held her new pinecone all the way home.

Audrey stood by the pool with her dad. She wanted to get in the water. The water looked big and blue. Her friend Brian was already swimming. He splashed his arms. "Come in, Audrey!" he called.

Audrey tried to climb over the edge. She pulled and pulled. It was too high. Her arms could not hold on. Mr. Iyer, the teacher, saw her. He pointed to the silver ladder in the water. "Try the ladder," he said. Audrey put her feet on the ladder. She held the rail. Step, step, step. The ladder helped her get into the water. Splash! She was in.

A black butterfly flew over the pool. Audrey watched it move from flower to flower. Then she wanted to get out. She did not try the edge. She went to the ladder. Step, step, step. The ladder helped her get out, too. "That was easy," said Audrey. Brian climbed out behind her on the ladder.

Grace woke up from nap time at daycare. Her hair was all squished on one side. It looked like a bird's nest.

"Your hair has tangles," said Raina. Raina pointed at Grace's head.

Mr. Moose brought a little brush. It was blue with soft teeth. "Brush it slowly," he said. "Slow, so it does not pull."

Grace took the brush. She touched her hair. It felt bumpy and knotty under her fingers. The tangles were big.

She brushed one little bit. Ouch. That pulled. She brushed even slower. The brush slid through. The bump was gone. That part felt smooth now.

"Look, a tangle came out," said Roman. He watched from his cot. His own hair was still messy.

Grace kept brushing, slow and careful. Tangle by tangle. Smooth by smooth. Soon all the bumps were gone. Her hair hung down soft and shiny.

"Pretty," said Raina.

Grace gave the brush to Roman. "Slow," she said. "You have to go slow."

Roman brushed his hair, slow and slow. The tangles came out too.

Then they hung their blankets on the hooks. Snack time was next.

"Apples," said Mr. Moose. "Fast, before they run away." He was joking. Apples cannot run. Everyone laughed.

Wren sat in her cozy reading nook at home. She held her big letter book on her lap. "Today I will find S things," she said. Ms. Nowak, her neighbour, was visiting. She smiled and said, "The letter S makes a hissing sound, like sss."

Wren listened. "Sss," she whispered. She looked around the nook. The sun shone in the window. "Sun!" she said. "Sun starts with sss!" She clapped her hands.

Then she saw her fuzzy sock on the floor. She picked it up. "Sss sock!" she said. "Sss sun!" She hunted some more. There was a little cup of sand on the shelf. She touched it with one finger. "Sss sand!" she shouted. "Sun, sock and sand. All S!"

Ms. Nowak gave her a kiss on the head. "You found three," she said. Wren hugged her book. "Tomorrow I will find M things!" she said. Then she ran to show her sock to her mom.

Snow fell in the backyard last night. Bennett ran out quick. He looked at the snow. The snow was white, all white. "I will draw it!" said Bennett. He got his paper and his crayons. He took out the white crayon. He drew on the white paper. He could not see it. "Oh no," said Bennett. "Where did my snow go?" Inara came to play. "Draw snow with me," said Bennett. Inara held up blue paper. "Try this," she said. Bennett drew with his white crayon. The white showed up on the blue. "I see it! One white hill, two white hills, three white hills!" said Bennett. "Snow is white, white, white!" said Inara. Mr. Ito looked over the fence. "More snow is coming," he said. "Rain first, then snow." Bennett held his blue paper up high. "Ready for more white snow!" he said. He drew one more soft white dot.

Emilia ran into the kitchen. "I want a snack!" she said. Mom was cracking an egg into a bowl. "Snack comes after the egg," said Mom. Emilia wanted it now!

"I will find you a shape while we wait," said Mom. "Find me a circle!" Emilia looked fast. She saw the clock. Round like a ball! "Circle!" she cheered. Mom held up a cracker. "Circle too," said Emilia.

"Now find a square." Emilia saw a napkin on the table. She put her finger on it. One, two, three, four sides. Four corners too. "Square!" "Now a rectangle," said Mom. Emilia ran to the door. She touched it. "One, two, three, four sides. One, two, three, four corners!" The corners were square corners. "Rectangle!" said Mom.

Then Mom set down warm toast, and Emilia took a big, happy bite.

Wesley was at the airport with his dad. The airport was very big and very loud. Wesley saw a huge plane out the window. It was white with red wings. "I want to see the plane!" said Wesley. He started to run.

His dad caught his hand. "Wait, Wesley," said Dad. "It is busy here. In busy places like airports, children stay close to their grown-up and hold hands."

Wesley stopped. He looked around. So many people! One man. Two ladies. Three kids with backpacks. The crowd went this way and that way, like a river on a street.

Wesley held Dad's hand tight. They walked past the shops. They walked past the chairs where people sit. Then they came to a big open window.

Wesley counted the planes. "One, two, three, four!" he said. And then he saw a small plane, tiny and yellow. "A little plane!" said Wesley. "Just my size."

Dad laughed. "You held my hand the whole way," he said. "Good job."

Wesley squeezed Dad's hand. "Hand in hand," said Wesley. "All the way to the big red plane."

Elijah was at the playground with his mom. The sun was out. "It is sunny," said Elijah. He wore his sun hat. Vaughn was there too. Vaughn wore a big cap. "Your hat is neat," said Vaughn.

Then the wind came. The wind blew Elijah's hat off. Elijah ran to get it. He put it back on. The wind blew it off again. He held it with his hand this time.

Then the sky got dark. "Rain is coming," said Mom. She opened a big red umbrella. Elijah stood under it with her. The rain fell all around them. But Elijah's head stayed dry. "The rain can't get me," said Elijah. He smiled up at the umbrella.

They walked home in the rain. Elijah held the umbrella handle too. "I want to wear my boots," said Elijah. "Next time," said Mom. "We can jump in puddles then." Elijah looked back at the wet playground. "Bye, playground," he said. "See you when it's sunny again."

Zayn packed his little red bag. His family was going to a campsite by a lake. "I will take my truck," said Zayn.

At the campsite, Zayn saw a round moon come up. He saw a duck turn its head and dive. He built a small tower of stones. His dad took a photo of Zayn by the tower. Then Mom took photos of the lake, the tent, and the duck.

At home, Zayn missed the lake. He wanted to see the duck again. "We can look at our photos," said Mom. They sat on the couch together. Zayn saw the moon, the stones, and the tent. Then he saw the duck. "There it is!" said Zayn. The photos held the trip, right there on the screen.

Cooper wanted to go to Matilda's house. He wanted to go right now.

Mr. Cheung knelt down beside him. "Not now, Cooper," he said. "Matilda's house is for tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today."

Cooper frowned. "Today?" he asked.

"First today, then tomorrow," said Mr. Cheung. "First you eat lunch. Then you sleep. Then the sun comes up again. Then it is tomorrow."

Cooper did not want to wait. But he stacked the blocks with Matilda. He made a tall, tall tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. They both laughed.

At nap time, Cooper lay on his mat. He pulled his soft shirt over his bear. Soon he was fast asleep.

When Cooper woke up, the sky was orange and pink. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Mr. Cheung. "We sleep all night first."

Cooper slept at home in his own bed. He slept and he slept. Then the sun peeked in his window.

"Tomorrow!" Cooper shouted. He put on his blue shirt all by himself.

Matilda's door opened. "Cooper is here!" she said. "It is tomorrow now!"

They played with the blocks all morning.

Jules sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to draw on the tablet. Grandma put the tablet in front of him. "Push the round button," she said. Jules pushed it. The screen lit up. It was like magic.
