"Tap the little paint tool," said Grandma. Jules tapped it. The drawing app opened. He filled a big circle with blue. "I made a sky!" he said. Then Grandma brought his juice. Jules set the cup right beside the tablet. "Does the juice go there?" he asked himself. He looked at the cup. He looked at the tablet. He shook his head. "No. Water and drinks stay away from the tablet." He carried the cup to the little table across the room.

He drew a sun. He drew a green tree. Then he was done. He pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet back in Grandma's drawer. "All put away," he said. Grandma clapped her hands. "What a nice helper," she said. Jules smiled and took a big sip of his juice.

Charlotte stood in the backyard. Her friend Darren was coming over. It was his birthday today. Charlotte wanted to make him a cake. Her dad brought out a big bowl. Inside the bowl was cake batter. Charlotte looked at it. It was runny. It went drip, drip, drip off the spoon. "It is too runny," said Charlotte. "It will never be a cake." She stirred it. It stayed runny. The spoon got all sticky. Darren came through the gate. He looked in the bowl too. "Where is the cake?" he asked. "We have to wait," said Dad. Dad carried the bowl inside. Charlotte waited by the door. The oven was noisy and hot, so Dad did that part. Charlotte and Darren played with the noisy dog. He showed her his loose tooth. Then Dad called, "Come and see!" The cake was out of the oven. It was not runny now. It was big and round. Dad cut it with a knife. He gave each of them a slice. Darren took a bite. "Best backyard cake ever," he said.

Hannah was in a big hotel room. It had two beds and a shiny pot by the window. "Why is there a pot in our room?" she asked. Her dad laughed. "That pot is for tea," he said. "It is not stinky socks, like your shoe bag." Hannah giggled. She put her stinky socks in her bag.

Hannah thought about the long drive. In the car, she had needed to pee. She had wiggled and wiggled. Then Dad drove into a rest stop. "What is a rest stop?" Hannah had asked. "It is a place to stop," Dad said. "We can use the bathroom and stretch." Hannah got out and stretched tall like a giraffe. Then she peed and felt much better.

Now Hannah yawned. She climbed into the soft hotel bed. "Rest stops are good," she said. Dad turned off the light.

Paisley stood by the pool. The water made little splashing sounds. Mr. Andersen had set up a game on the grass. There was a big hoop on the ground. There was a red beanbag. There was a big soft ball, too.

Paisley wanted the beanbag to land in the hoop. She threw it over her shoulder, high. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed in the grass near a small spider. The spider sat very still.

"Watch me," said Mr. Andersen. "This is called an underhand throw." He held the beanbag down low. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop.

Paisley tried it. She held her arm low down. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed straight into the hoop. "I did it!" she said. Then Bennett rolled her the big soft ball. Paisley covered it with both hands. She hugged it to her chest.

"Again," said Paisley. She picked up the beanbag, low down, forward and up.

Nathan wanted to help bake bread. He could not reach the oven. His mom said, "You can watch from here." Nathan used his eyes to watch. He saw his mom pour pink strawberries into the bowl. He used his ears to hear the mixer hum. Then something new came to him. He used his nose to smell the bread. It smelled so good!

Nathan ran to the mirror. He looked at his nose. He saw one hole, then another. He counted them. One, two. "Mom!" he called. "I see two holes in my nose!" Mom smiled. "Those are called nostrils," she said. Nathan touched his nose with his finger. He could still smell the bread through both nostrils.

At last the bread was ready. Mom paid attention and let it cool. Nathan took a small bite. He used his tongue to taste it. Sweet and warm. "Yum!" said Nathan. Outside the window, the sky turned pink too.

Theodore ran to Grandma's big bathroom. Grandpa filled the tub. The water was warm. Theodore splashed and played. He washed his tummy. He washed his toes. Then bath time was done.

Grandpa said, "Here is your towel." But Theodore jumped out fast. He ran down the hall. Drip, drip, drip went his feet. The cat looked up at him. Water made a little trail on the floor. His pajamas were tight to put on over wet skin. They stuck and would not go up.

Theodore went back to the bathroom. He took the soft towel. Grandpa helped him rub his arms. He rubbed his legs. The towel dried his body after the bath. Now his skin felt dry and warm. His pajamas slid right on. Theodore gave Grandpa a big hug. "All dry," he said.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a week! Alexander clapped his hands. "Where will Grandpa sleep?" he asked. Mom pointed to the big guest room. "We need to make a bed for him," she said.

A bed for a guest! Alexander ran to get his favorite blanket. It was blue with round stars. He put it on Grandpa's bed. Then he found a soft pillow. He patted it flat. Mom put a warm quilt on top too.

That night, the rain sounded like a little storm outside. Grandpa arrived with his big bag. He saw the bed and smiled big. "My own bed, all ready!" said Grandpa. He hugged Alexander tight. Grandpa slept under the star blanket. Alexander peeked in the morning. "The blanket kept him warm all night," whispered Mom.

Natalie woke up in the tent. "Pancakes!" she shouted. Today she would cook breakfast for the whole family.

Dad lit the little camp stove. Natalie stirred the bowl. She dumped in flour and milk and one egg. She poured a pancake. It came out flat. Flat, flat, flat. It looked like a big sad circle.

"I want puffy pancakes," said Natalie. Her friend Damon came by with his dad. Damon held up a card. "This is a recipe," he said. "It says what to use and what to do, one step at a time." Natalie looked at the card. Each step had a number. One said to add baking powder. Natalie had skipped that step!

She started again. She read each step. She used what the card said. She did what the card said, one step at a time. Dad poured the batter on the hot stove. The pancake grew big and puffy. Puffy, puffy, puffy!

Mom took a big bite. "Best pancake at this campsite," she said. Damon gave a thumbs up. Natalie flipped the last pancake all by herself with Dad's hand over hers. "More steps, more pancakes!" she shouted.

Emilia planted seeds with her dad. She put carrot seeds in one row. She put tomato seeds in another row. Then she watered them all.

A few days later, tiny green leaves popped up. Emilia forgot which row was tomatoes. She felt worried. "Dad, I don't know where the tomatoes are!"

Her dad smiled. "We can fix that," he said. Emilia drew a red tomato on a card. She drew an orange carrot on another card. They stuck the cards in the soil. "The label shows what is planted in each spot," her dad said. Now every row had a picture label.

Her friend Elliana came to see the garden. A fuzzy caterpillar sat on a leaf. Emilia gave a little wave to Elliana at the gate. "Look!" said Elliana. "Your tomato row has little tomatoes!" It was a happy surprise.

Violet went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a bird. She looked at the first shelf. The books there were all about trucks. She looked at another shelf. Those books were about foods, apples and bread and eggs. No bird book yet.

Violet walked slowly down the aisle. She saw a shelf full of books about toys. A ball was on one cover. A teddy bear was on another. Still no bird. She stood still and waited. She did not give up.

Ms. Barrett came to help. "The books sit in groups," she said. "All the animal books live on that shelf." Violet looked where Ms. Barrett pointed. There was a long shelf with a picture of a cat on the end. Violet ran to it.

She pulled out book after book. Then she saw it. A big blue bird on the cover. "I found it!" said Violet. "You are lucky," said Jamie, who was looking for a dog book. Violet held her bird book tight. Then she sat down with Jamie to read.

Luna had a cold. Her nose ran and her head felt warm. She sat at the kitchen table in her striped pajamas. Her stuffed animal, a little zebra, sat beside her.

Luna wanted to feel better. She saw the medicine bottle on the counter. It was small and purple. She reached for it.

Her mom came in fast. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," Mom said. She picked up the bottle. "You can hold your zebra while I pour it."

Mom poured the purple medicine into a little cup. One spoon, two spoons, three. "All done," said Mom.

Luna drank it down. It tasted like grapes. She hugged her zebra and counted his legs. One, two, three, four.

Mom made warm soup. Mom poured it into a red bowl. Luna took one sip, then another.

Soon Luna felt less sniffly. She yawned big. Mom carried her to the couch, zebra and all. "Sleep tight," Mom whispered.

Elias was at his grandma's house. He wanted to draw a big sun. He looked for his crayons. They had been in the car all morning. The car sat in the hot sun.

Elias opened the crayon box. He pulled out the yellow crayon. It felt soft. It bent like a noodle in his hand. "Oh no," he said. Grandma looked too. "They got hot in the car," she said. "They sat in the sun."

Elias tried to draw. The soft crayon made a fat, smooth line. It looked like melted butter. He tried the orange one. It made a fat line too. Grandma helped him press gently. The sun came out round and bright. He drew warm rays with the bendy red one. Then he counted his crayons. He had six left.

The young artist held up his paper. "Look, Grandma! The sun is big and soft." Grandma smiled and pinned it to the fridge. Elias put his leg up on a little stool and gazed at his work. "Next time, we take the crayons out of the car," Grandma said. Elias nodded. Then he picked up the bendy blue one and drew a cool blue lake under his sun.

Hunter stood in the pool changing room. It was a rainy day, so his swim bag smelled like wet boots. He pulled on his little swim shorts all by himself.

His friend Archibald was there too. Archibald pointed at the pool door. "The water is waiting," he said. Hunter peeked out. The big pool was blue and still. No teacher sat on the tall chair yet. No grown-up stood by the side.

"Can we jump in now?" Hunter asked. Archibald shook his head. "No. Not yet." Hunter wanted to jump so much. He blew out a big breath, slow, like blowing out birthday candles. Then he sat down at the edge. His toes stayed out of the water.

A girl named Rayden sat down too. They waited together. Soon Mr. Schneider walked in with a whistle. He climbed up the tall chair. He looked right at Hunter and gave a nod.

"Now?" Hunter asked. "Now," said Mr. Schneider. Hunter jumped. Splash! The water was warm. Archibald jumped right after him, and a tiny toy duck popped up between them, bobbing by his shoulder.

Maeve stood at the edge of the backyard pool. The water looked cool and beautiful. "I want to swim," she said. The coach held her hand. "Kick your legs," said the coach. Maeve kicked. The kicking made her move forward through the water. She kicked again. She moved some more. "I did it!" she said.

Maeve saw a tall chair by the pool. A lifeguard sat up high in it. "Why do you sit up there?" Maeve asked. "My job is to watch the swimmers," said the lifeguard. "I help anyone who needs it." From up high, she could see everyone.

Maeve let go and kicked all by herself. Splash, splash, splash. She moved all the way to the pool wall. The water touched her lips. It taste like summer, she thought. The lifeguard waved from her tall chair. "Look at me!" called Maeve to the whole world. "I am swimming!"

Matthew sat on his bedroom floor. He wanted his big red blocks. They were up high on the shelf. "Can I have my blocks now?" he asked. His dad said, "You can play with them later. I am busy now." Matthew frowned. Later? When was later? He watched his dad fold the shirts. He heard the clock tick. He looked at his toy map on the wall. Was it later yet? "Is it later now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. Matthew waited. He poked his slimy toy frog. It went boing. The clock ticked some more. At last Dad stood up. "Now it is later," Dad said. He took the blocks down. Matthew clapped his hands. "Later comes after now!" he said. He stacked the blocks up, up, up.

Sara went to the pet store with her dad. She saw a tall cage full of kittens. One kitten was white like a cloud. "Can we take her home?" Sara asked. "Yes," said Dad. "She is your first pet."

At home, the kitten ran under Sara's bed. Sara could not see her. "Did I lose my kitten?" she asked. Dad shook his head. "She is still here," he said. Sara got a soft pillow and sat on the floor. She waited by the bed.

Sara sat very still. She did not make noise. Then two little eyes peeked out. The kitten stepped into the light. Sara held out her hand. The kitten sniffed her fingers. Then the kitten climbed onto Sara's lap and purred. Sara smiled and petted her softly. "Hello, little cloud," she whispered.

Nathan ran into the big open room at the community centre. Mr. Luo had two bowls of crackers on the table. A sign on the wall said, "Snack Time!"

"Count them," said Mr. Luo. Nathan pointed at the red bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he pointed at the blue bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven."

Santiago ran over. "I want the blue bowl!" he said. "It has more crackers." He jumped up and down. Nathan looked at the red bowl. It did not have more. So it had fewer.

"Fewer," said Nathan slowly. "My bowl has fewer."

"Yes!" said Mr. Luo. "Fewer is the other side of more."

Santiago counted his crackers again. "Seven for me. And you have fewer, Nathan!" He laughed a big laugh.

Nathan laughed too. He held up one cracker. "One is fewer than seven!"

"Good counting," said Mr. Luo. He opened a new box and put three more crackers in the red bowl. "Now count again, Nathan."

Ezra was hungry. He wanted his sandwich now. "One minute," said his dad. He cut the sandwich with a safe knife. Ezra watched from his chair.

Dad put the plate down. The sandwich was not squares today. It had pointy pieces. "What shape is this?" Ezra asked. "A triangle," said Dad. Ezra touched one piece with his finger. He counted the corners. "One, two, three." He slid his finger along each line. "One, two, three." Three sides and three corners.

Ezra took a big bite. One corner was gone. He counted again. "One, two, three, four. Four corners now!" He laughed. Dad laughed too. "You made a new shape, Ezra." Ezra held up the piece. "Triangle had three," he said. Then he chased the last crumb around the plate with his finger and popped it in his mouth.

Sadie sat on the camp bench. Her dad gave her warm toast and a little box of butter. She spread the butter with her own knife-safe spoon. The butter made shiny lines. "It goes soft on warm toast," she said.

Next came the milk. Sadie poured and poured. The cup filled up to the very top. She picked it up to walk to the table. Oh no. Milk spilled over the edge and wet her toes.

Her dad poured again. This time Sadie stopped before the cup was full to the top. She looked at the little space left in the cup. She walked slowly. Not one drop fell. The stormy clouds far away rumbled, but her milk stayed in.

Duke ran over from his tent. "Can I pour too?" he asked. Sadie showed him her cup. "Stop before the top," she said. Duke poured and stopped. He carried his cup past the picnic box, safe and dry. They sat together and drank all their milk.

The car ride home was long. Charles sat in his seat. His buckle clicked. Click, click, one buckle done. "Bath time soon," said his dad. The phone began to ring. Ring, ring, ring. Dad stopped the car and answered. Charles looked out the window. Rain made mud by the road. "That mud looks squishy," Charles said. "Yes, squishy mud. We stay in the car," said Dad. Soon they were home. Charles ran to the tub. He wanted to jump right in. But he stopped and waited. Dad put his hand in the water first. "Too hot," said Dad. He added cold water. Then he checked again. "Now it is warm. Warm, not hot. You can get in." Charles touched the water with one toe. It felt just right. He smiled and climbed in slowly. "Bubbles next," said Dad. "Big bubbles, one, two, three."

Elena played in her playroom. She had a big job. Mom brought in a basket of washing. "Can you help sort it?" Mom asked. Elena nodded.

She put a shirt in the clothes pile. She put a hat there too. Then she found a sock. It was soft and stripey. She made it hop like a bunny. She dropped it in the toy basket with the blocks. Then she laughed and laughed. A sock was not a toy! She picked it up and put it with the shirt and the hat. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," said Mom. Elena patted the pile.

Martin came to play. He brought his toy bee. The bee went buzz, buzz. Elena showed him the lemon from the play kitchen. Martin made a sour face. "Yucky, sour lemon!" he said.

Then Martin found one more sock under the chair. He put it in the toy basket. "No, no!" said Elena. She moved it to the clothes pile. Martin clapped. The pile was done at last. Mom held up a sock puppet and made it talk. "Hello, Elena! Hello, Martin!"

Cooper went to Gurfateh's house. Gurfateh had a big box of clothes. "Let's play," said Gurfateh.

Gurfateh put on a red hat. "I am a firefighter now," he said. He sprayed pretend water on the grass. Cooper watched. A hat made Gurfateh a firefighter!

Cooper wanted to be someone too. He looked in the box. He found a white coat. He put it on. He found a little bag. "I am a doctor," he said. "Can I fix your teddy?" asked Gurfateh. The teddy had a sticky spot on its arm.

"Yes," said Cooper. He tapped the teddy's arm. "All better," he said. Gurfateh hugged the teddy. Then Cooper found a tall hat. He put it on. "I am a baker," he said. "I will bake pretend bread." Gurfateh clapped his hands. The two boys played and played. At home time, Cooper waved. "I can be anyone with dress-up clothes," he said.

Matteo sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. He needed a shot today. The nurse opened her tray. Inside was a small needle. It looked shiny and new.

"Can I hold the needle?" Matteo asked. He wanted to see it up close.

The nurse smiled. "Only I can hold the needle," she said. "That is my job. But you can hold my sticker sheet. It has a car on it!"

Matteo took the sticker sheet. It was wide and full of pictures. He turned it over and found a red car on the back. "I see a car!" he said.

The nurse cleaned his arm. Then she gave the shot. It was quick, like a little pinch. Matteo held his sticker sheet the whole time and looked at the car.

"All done," said the nurse. She put the needle back in the tray. Only her hands touched it.

Afterward, Mama took Matteo to the ice cream shop. He wore his car sticker on his shirt. Alfred was there with his dad. "Nice sticker!" said Alfred.

"Want to see it?" said Matteo. He held out his shirt, wide and proud.

They sat by the window and ate pink ice cream together.

Jake stood at the bus stop with his dad. The big yellow bus was coming. Jake wanted to zip up his coat all by himself.

He grabbed the little tab. He pulled and pulled. The zipper would not go up. Jake felt upset. "I can't do it," he said.

"Look at the bottom," said Shayan, his friend from school. Shayan pointed. "Put the pointy end in the little box." Jake looked down. He saw the small box at the bottom of the zipper. He slid the end of one side into it. Click. It fit!

Jake pulled the tab. The zipper went up, up, up. Fast! Now his coat was warm and closed.

The bus stopped with a big hiss. Mr. Sow, the driver, smiled. "Nice coat, Jake. Did you do that zipper yourself?"

Jake nodded big. "I did it all by myself!"

"Wow," said Mr. Sow. "Then you get the very first seat."

Jake climbed the steps and sat by the window, and his dad waved from the stop.

Owen stood on the soccer field. Ms. Chukwu held up a big red hoop. "Throw the beanbag in, Owen," she said. Owen threw it. The beanbag hit the edge and dropped. Neil got his beanbag in. Annabella got hers in too. Owen frowned. "I missed," he said. Ms. Chukwu said, "I missed lots of times when I was small. Try again and again." Annabella handed Owen the beanbag. "You can share my turn," she said.

Owen threw the beanbag. It missed. He threw it again. It missed again. His hands felt sticky from his juice box at snack time, and the beanbag felt slimy on one side. He wiped his hands on his shorts. Then he locked his eyes on the hoop. He threw it one more time. The beanbag went in! "I did it!" Owen shouted. Neil clapped.

Next came the big yellow ball. Ms. Chukwu rolled it to Owen. He held out both hands. The ball bounced off. She rolled it again. It bounced off again. Then Owen pulled both hands together and caught it. "Big ball, both hands," he said. Ms. Chukwu smiled. "Again?" she asked. Owen hugged the ball to his chest. "Again," he said.

Brielle was ready for a big trip. She was going to Aunt Rosa's house. The car was packed with bags.

Dad drove and drove. Then the car stopped. "Oh no," said Dad. "We took a wrong turn."

Brielle looked out the window. She saw no houses. She saw only trees.

Then Mom held up a big paper. It had lines and little pictures on it. "This is a map," said Mom. "It shows roads and places."

Brielle peeked at the map. She pointed at a line. "Is this our road?" she asked.

Mom smiled. "Yes! That road goes to Aunt Rosa's house."

Dad turned the car around. He drove on the right road. Soon there were houses again.

"There is Aunt Rosa's house!" said Brielle.

Aunt Rosa waved from the door. "My little map helper!" she said.

Brielle held the map up high, like a flag.

Wyatt saw Harlow and Nelly in the corner. They were rocking baby dolls. Nelly patted her doll's back. Harlow made a little bottle from a block. Wyatt wanted to play too. But he did not know how to start. He stood and watched. He peeked around the shelf. His nose felt stuffy, and he rubbed it.

Then Wyatt took a deep breath. He walked over and said, "Let's pretend I am the daddy." Harlow looked up and smiled. "Okay! Your baby is crying," she said. Nelly handed him a doll wrapped in a dark blue blanket. Wyatt rocked the doll side to side. "Shh, shh," he said softly.

Mr. Farah-Ali peeked in from the snack room. "What a happy family," he said. Wyatt gave the doll a tiny bottle. The doll went to sleep. "Now let's pretend we cook soup," said Nelly. Wyatt stirred a big red pot with a spoon. "Dinner time!" he called.

Luka went to the park with his red ball. He wanted to play catch. But the ball was too high on the shelf at home, so he had asked his dad. "Please get my ball," Luka had said. His dad smiled and got it down.

At the park, Luka saw a tall slide. He saw a girl near the sand. Her name was Abeer. Luka threw his ball to her. It did not go far. It began to bounce away, right toward a boy with a book. The ball bumped the boy's arm. His book fell in the sand.

"Sorry," said Luka. He picked up the book. He brushed off the sand. The boy smiled. "Thank you," said the boy. Then he said, "Gracias." Luka looked at him. "What is that?" Luka asked. "It means thank you too," said the boy. "It is a Spanish word." Luka tried it. "Gracias," he said slowly. The boy nodded.

Then they all played catch together. When Abeer threw the ball back, Luka called out, "Gracias!" The boy laughed and clapped. Luka waited his turn on the tall slide. When it was his turn, he climbed up and zoomed down. "That was fun," said Luka. "Gracias, slide!"

Leo wanted his bedtime book. It was the one about the little red truck. But he could not find it on the shelf.

Then he saw a card on his bed. It was from Neil. It said "To Leo" on the front. Leo pointed at the word. "That says Leo," he said. "How do you know?" asked his dad. "It is the same word as on my cubby at school," Leo said. "L, E, O. Just like that."

Leo looked at the card. Then he thought about his cubby. The word looked the same in both places. Same letters. Same order. Every time he saw it, it was still Leo.

"Maybe my name is in my truck book too," Leo said. His dad smiled. They opened the book. They started at the front, where the first page was. Leo turned the pages one by one. There, inside the cover, was the word again. Leo.

"That is my name," Leo said. "It was in the card, and on my cubby, and in the book." He traced the letters with his finger. L, E, O.

His dad washed the day's dirt off Leo's little hands and tucked him in. Leo held the book close. "Read it front to back," he said. "Like always."

Snow fell all morning. Ruby watched it from the window. Snowflakes came down, down, down. She put on her warm coat. She put on her red hat. She put on her boots, one, two. Then she went out to play.

The snow was soft and cold. Ruby made a big snowball with her mittens. She loved it. She wanted to keep it forever. "I will take you inside," she said. She set the snowball in a bowl on the table. She took off her wet boots and hung up her coat.

After lunch, Ruby came back to look. Her eyes went wide. The snowball was gone! There was only water in the bowl. "Oh no," she said. "The snow melted." Mom came over and smiled. "Snow melts into water where it is warm," said Mom.

Ruby had an idea. She scooped new snow into a bowl. She set it on the cold step outside. She counted the flakes on her mittens. One, two, three. Then she went inside to watch through the window. The snowball stayed round and white. Ruby made a happy face and waved to it through the glass. "Stay there, snowball," she said. "I will come back for you."

Maverick sat at the dinner table. He had orange carrots on his plate. He wanted to count them all.

"One, two, three," he said. He pushed a carrot with his fork. "Four, five, six." More carrots! "Seven, eight, nine." One carrot left. "Ten!" he shouted. Ten carrots!

Dad put down a fish on his plate. It was a fish stick. Maverick loved fish sticks. "I have ten carrots," he said. "I want to write ten!"

Dad gave him a crayon and paper. Maverick wrote a big 1. Then he stopped. He looked at the paper. He looked at Dad.

"More?" he asked. Dad nodded. Maverick made a round 0 right after the 1. "One, then zero," he said. He tapped the 1. He tapped the 0. Two numbers!

His friend Callen came to the door. "Look, Callen!" said Maverick. He held up the paper. "Ten! It has a 1 and a 0!"

Callen clapped. "Do it again!" he said. Maverick wrote it again. One, then zero. Ten!

"Time to eat," said Dad. Maverick ate a fish stick. He ate one orange carrot. Then he counted what was left. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." He grinned and popped the last one in his mouth. "Zero left!"

Charlotte sat in the music classroom with her class. Each child had a small recorder. Ms. Tanaka showed them how to hold it. Charlotte put the recorder to her lips. She blew. Squeak! The sound was loud and funny. Roman giggled next to her.

Charlotte tried again. Squeak! She looked at her fingers. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. A little hole peeked out. She pressed her finger down flat. She blew. A clear note came out. Not a squeak!

She lifted that finger a tiny bit. She blew. A different note came out. Covering different holes made different notes. She showed Roman. "Press your finger flat," she whispered. Roman pressed flat and blew. His note was clear too. Emma clapped for them both.

At the end of class, Ms. Tanaka gave everyone a crunchy apple slice. Charlotte took a big bite. "Can we play again tomorrow?" she asked.

Alexis went to the pet store with his dad. He saw fish, birds, and one small gray kitten. The kitten was sleeping on a flat rock. "I want that one," said Alexis. Dad said yes. They bought the kitten, food, and two bowls.

At home, Alexis put a soft blanket in a box. The kitten drank from one bowl. Then it ate. Then it slept. The next morning, Alexis looked at the water bowl. It was empty! He showed Dad. "Dogs and cats need fresh, clean water every day," said Dad. Dad held the bowl under the tap. Alexis watched the cool water fill it up.

The kitten ran to the bowl. It drank and drank. Then it gave Alexis a small kick with its back foot and climbed onto his lap. "You like fresh water," said Alexis. The kitten licked his hand.

The lights went out. Isaiah's whole apartment went dark. "Mama," he said. "The lamp is off." "The power is out," said Mama. She felt for the flashlight. It was not on the shelf. It was not under the bed. Isaiah felt shy in the big dark. He held Mama's hand tight. Then he remembered. "The kitchen drawer!" he said. Mama opened the drawer. Her fingers found the flashlight. She pressed the button. Click. A bright beam shot out. The flashlight still shone! It did not need the power at all. Isaiah laughed. "It works, Mama!" Mama swept the light across the room. Isaiah planted his feet and reached for the beam on the wall. He made a dog shadow with his fingers. Then the light found something small on the couch. It was the cat, curled up in Mama's sweater. "There you are," said Mama. Isaiah sat close. The cat purred. The little beam glowed on the wall. Isaiah pointed at the circle of light. "Mama, can we make a big sun?" he asked. Mama moved the flashlight near the wall. The circle grew and grew. "Wow," said Isaiah. "The sun is in our house."

Georgia wanted to make a paper cat. She found red paper on the big table. She needed to cut the paper into shapes.

Georgia saw the big scissors in the drawer. "I want those," she said. Her dad shook his head. "Not those," he said. "These are your scissors." He gave her the little ones with round tips. They were just her size. Her dad sat down next to her to watch.

Georgia squeezed the little scissors. Snip, snip! The paper came apart. One ear, two ears, one round tummy. She cut a long tail too. Then she glued the cat onto a pillow so it would not hide under the table. "A red cat!" said Georgia. Her dad smiled and clapped. "Meow," said Georgia.

Grayson sat in the nursery room. There was a new cot by the wall. It had a shiny new rail. His baby sister was coming home today. Grayson sat very still. He felt like a shadow in the corner. Nobody needed him.

Then Daddy came in with the baby. She was small and wriggly. She made a little cry. Daddy said, "I need a clean diaper, please. Big brothers can help by fetching things."

Grayson ran to the drawer. One, two, three, he counted the diapers. He picked one up. He brought it to Daddy. Daddy smiled. The baby got a dry diaper. She stopped crying.

"Can you fetch a blanket too?" asked Daddy. Grayson fetched a soft blue blanket. He laid it over her toes. One, two, tuck, tuck. She blinked at him.

"You are my big helper," said Daddy.

"Again?" asked Grayson. "One more thing to fetch?"

Ruby was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a friendly cat named Softpaws. Ruby sat at the big table.

"Can I write my name?" Ruby asked.

"Yes, you can," said Grandma. She gave Ruby a fat pencil and paper.

Ruby held the pencil. She tried to make an R. It came out wobbly. She tried again. The line went the wrong way. Ruby pushed the paper away.

Grandma sat next to her. "Try again, little one," she said. "Your hand is small, but it can learn."

Ruby picked up the pencil. She walked across the room to get a chair. She waved the pencil in the air. The point went up, up, up.

"Point it down," said Grandma. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone."

Ruby turned the pencil around. Now the point faced down by her side. She followed Grandma back to the table. Softpaws walked by, and the pencil did not poke him.

Ruby climbed onto the chair. She held the pencil near the point. She made a big R. Then a U. Then a B. Then a Y. Then one more Y.

"RUBY!" she shouted.

Grandma clapped her hands. "You wrote it! You wrote your whole name."

Ruby looked at her letters. They were a little crooked, but they were hers. She picked up the paper and ran to the kitchen. The cat followed her all the way.

"I will show Mama," Ruby said. She held the paper up high. The pencil stayed on the table, point down.

Abigail ran into writing club. Mr. Das smiled at her. "Today we write our names!" he said. Abigail sat down next to Amirah. She picked up her pencil. She squeezed it with her whole fist. The letter A came out wobbly and big. It looked like a fat old bug. Abigail frowned.

Mr. Das gave her a new paper. Her name was on it in dotted letters. "Trace the dots," he said. Abigail held her pencil with three fingers, like Amirah did. She traced the dotted A. Then the dotted b. The letters came out neat and small!

"Look, Amirah! My dots turned into letters!" Amirah jumped up to see. Then Amirah held up her paper. A tiny ladybug sat right on the dot of her i. "A real bug likes my name!" she said. Abigail laughed and clapped. "Draw more dots for the ladybug, Mr. Das!"

Sophia was at the lake with her mama. Near the lake there was a little pool. Sophia wanted to swim in the pool. She had her soft towel under her arm.

Sophia ran from the changing room to the pool. A coach stopped her gently. "Wait, we take a shower first," the coach said. "Many pools ask swimmers to do that." Sophia stood under the warm shower. The water ran down her arms. Her mama held her towel.

Then Sophia got into the pool. She held the edge and kicked. Her friend Leen was there too. Leen splashed and laughed. Sophia kicked and kicked. She moved a little bit all by herself. "Look at me!" she called to mama. Her mama waved from a green pot of flowers by the fence.

Maeva and her family drove to the national park. There was a lake there with little waves. Maeva wanted to splash right away.

"Wait," said her dad. "A child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching. Come hold my hand." Maeva held his hand. They walked down to the water together.

Maeva looked at the waves. She touched one with her toe. The water went splash on her loose shoelace. Her wet shoe made a footprint on the rock. Each wave made a new splash. Each splash made her giggle. "The wave came to me!" she said. Dad laughed and held her hand tight. "Again!" said Maeva, and the next wave came.

Maya was at school for the first time. She carried a big red backpack on her back. It was very heavy. Maya walked slow, slow, slow.

In the cafeteria, Maya sat down. She opened her backpack. Out came a teddy bear. Out came three toy cars. Out came a big book about dinosaurs. The backpack got lighter and lighter. Maya stood up. Now she could walk fast.

"Your bag is on your back," said Natalia, pointing. "It's a backpack!" Maya smiled. She put the teddy bear on the table. The toy cars sat by her milk. "You can carry it again at home," said Mr. Pérez. Maya picked up one toy car. It went zoom, zoom, across the long table. Natalia laughed and clapped her hands. "Again!" she said.

Hannah was at Grandma's house. The kitchen smelled like warm bread. Grandma stood in the doorway with a big tray. Behind her stood Grandpa, holding a picture he wanted to hang. They were both stuck in the small doorway together.

Hannah wanted to get past them. She wanted to help carry the napkins. She tried to squeeze by, very small and very quiet. It did not work. Grandma and Grandpa filled the whole doorway, side to side. Hannah could not get through.

Then Hannah remembered something. She took a breath and said, "Excuse me." Grandma and Grandpa both turned around with soft smiles. Grandma stepped to the left. Grandpa stepped to the right. The doorway was open now, just for Hannah.

"Thank you," said Hannah, and she walked through. She picked up the napkins and set them on the table, one by one. Grandpa hung his picture on the wall. Hannah looked at the doorway again. "Excuse me, please," she said to nobody at all, and she walked through one more time, laughing all the way to the kitchen.

Lucas peeked under the toy box. He found a feather there. It was small and gray.

"A bird must have lost it," said Marvin. "Birds are animals that have feathers."

Lucas looked at his toy shelf. He saw a toy duck. He saw a toy bear. "Did my toys lose it?" he asked.

Marvin touched the toy duck. "No feathers here," he said. "It is soft, but not feathers."

Lucas touched the toy bear too. No feathers. Then he looked out the playroom window. A wet bird sat on the fence. It shook its wings. Little feathers puffed out.

"Look!" said Lucas. "The bird has feathers!"

The bird dropped one more feather. It floated down like a little boat.

"Hello, bird," Lucas called. "That one is yours."

The bird flew away. The feather stayed on the grass.

Nicholas sat with his mother at the temple. Ms. Lau, the singing teacher, stood at the front. She wore a bright orange scarf. She had a kind smile and one tooth that showed when she sang.

"Let's clap," said Ms. Lau. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Nicholas watched. He tried to clap too. His claps went too fast. His claps went too slow. Then he looked at Ms. Lau's hands. He clapped when she clapped. Now his claps were just right!

"Now we sing," said Ms. Lau. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Nicholas sang the first line. Then he stopped. What came next? He could not remember. Myah and Nova sang it, but Nicholas only hummed.

So they sang it again. And again. And one more time. Ms. Lau said, "Singing it again and again helps you learn its words by heart." Nicholas sang the rhyme five more times. Then something wonderful happened. The second line popped out all by itself. "Up above the world so high!" Could a song grow inside him like that? He clapped to the beat and sang the whole rhyme. His mother clapped too. "Sing it one more time," she said.

Beau sat at the art table. There were crayons everywhere. "So many colors," said Ms. Silva. "Let's sort them by color." Blaire made a red pile. Artemis made a blue pile. Beau made a yellow pile. "Sorting by color means putting all the same colors together," said Ms. Silva. Red with red. Blue with blue. Yellow with yellow.

Then Beau shook the crayon box. One green crayon fell out. "A green one!" said Beau. He looked at the red pile. It did not match. He looked at the blue pile. It did not match. He looked at the yellow pile. No match there either.

"I'll make a green pile," said Beau. He put the green crayon down. One, two, three, four. Four piles now. Blaire clapped. Artemis said, "Cool piles, Beau!" Beau smiled and put the lid on the box. "All done!"

Colton sat on the bath mat. "Dad, where are Grandpa's glasses?" he asked. "I don't know," said Dad. "Grandpa cannot read your bath book without them."

Colton wanted to help. He looked with his eyes. He saw the tall shelf, the sink, and the towels. He listened with his ears. He heard water drip, drip, drip. He touched the soft towels with his hands. No glasses.

Then he smelled the soap with his nose. "That smells like flowers," he said. He tasted a tiny bit of toothpaste on his toothbrush. "Minty," he said. Still no glasses!

A little spider crawled along the wall and under the sink. Colton got down on his knees to peek. There, next to the pipe, sat the glasses. "Found them!" he shouted.

Grandpa came in with the bath book. He put on his glasses. "Now I can see the words," he said. Colton clapped. "Did my glasses help?" asked Grandpa. "Yes," said Colton. "You see more clearly now!"

Grandpa read the story while Colton splashed. The water went splash, splash on the tile. Grandpa laughed and turned the page.

Charlotte was at school. She had a shiny red block. She stacked it up high. The tower was as tall as her cat's tail.

Then Leandro ran by. He bumped the table. The tower fell down. Crash!

Charlotte felt mad and sad. Her face went hot. She sat very still and pouted. Mr. Levy looked at her. He did not know what was wrong.

Reyansh sat next to her. He held a smooth gray stone. "Why is your face like that?" he asked.

"My tower fell down," said Charlotte.

"You can say how you feel," said Reyansh. "I felt sad one time. I said it out loud."

Charlotte thought about that. She walked to Mr. Levy. "I feel sad," she said. "My tower fell down."

Mr. Levy knelt down. He wiped her eyes with a soft tissue. "Let's build it again," he said. "Together."

They stacked the blocks. Red, blue, red, blue. The new tower was even taller. It was a castle for a tiny pretend dragon.

"I feel happy now," said Charlotte.

"Me too," said Leandro. "Can I add one block?"

"Yes," said Charlotte. "Put it on the very top."

William went to Isaiah's house. Isaiah's mom put on a song. Isaiah clapped his hands to the beat. Clap, clap, clap.

"Can I do that too?" asked William.

"Yes! Clap like this," said Isaiah.

William clapped. His hands went too fast. Then too slow. Then, clap! He found the beat. Clap, clap, clap. It felt good.

Next they sang a rhyme about a little spotted boat. William forgot some words. Isaiah sang them. William tried again. This time the words stayed in his head.

Then Isaiah's mom played a slow, quiet song. William clapped his loud claps. Isaiah covered his ears and laughed.

"Wait!" said Isaiah. "Where do people clap at a concert?"

"When the music is over," said his mom. "Clapping says we liked it."

So William sat on his hands. He waited. The song went on and on. At last it ended. Then William clapped and clapped.

"More song!" he shouted. "Then more clapping!"

Maeva went to the store with her dad. She wanted a sweet red apple. The apples sat up on a high shelf. Maeva could not reach them.

She saw a store worker nearby. Maeva pulled his sleeve. "Please, can you help me?" she asked. The worker smiled. He came over with a small step. He picked one sweet apple and gave it to her. Maeva held it in both hands. "Thank you," she said. The worker smiled even more.

Then Maeva saw her friend Maira. Maira was looking for the milk. She could not find it. Maeva asked the worker, "Please, where is the milk?" He pointed to the cold door. Maira ran off toward the milk. Then she stopped. She turned back and said, "Thank you, Maeva."

They walked to the checkout together. The moon was big outside the window. Maeva put her apple on the belt. "Thank you," she said to the cashier. The cashier gave her a sticker too.

Claire went to the farmers' market with her dad. She saw a big gray bucket full of little seed packets. She picked one with a carrot on it. "Can we plant these?" she asked. Her dad said yes.

At home, Claire dug a small hole. She dropped the seeds in the dirt. Then she gave them water from her little can. The next morning, Claire ran outside. She looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. Claire felt sad.

Her neighbor Ms. Schneider came by. "Keep giving them water," she said. "A sprout does not come up right away." So Claire watered the seeds every day. She told her friend Kilian, "My seeds have a name. They are carrots." One morning, Claire saw a tiny green tip in the dirt. "It came up!" she said. She clapped her hands and ran to get her watering can.

Cooper ran to the paint table at school. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But the paints were all put away in the dark supply closet.

"Can I get the green paint?" he asked Ms. Tan. She opened the closet door a tiny bit. It was very dark inside. Cooper reached in. He felt two paint pots. He could not see which was which. In the dark, the pots all looked the same.

He pulled one out and held it in the light. It was yellow. "Not green," he said. Where did the green one go? He reached back in. Again the dark closet showed him no colors at all. His friend Taha came to help. Taha held the door wide. Light came in. Now Cooper could see. There sat the green pot, right next to the red one.

"What a surprise," said Cooper. "The dark hid the colors." He carried his green paint to the table.

Ms. Tan brought water so the brushes could bathe between colors. Cooper painted his frog. He wrote his name at the top. Then he tapped the yellow pot with his brush. Yellow dots went on the frog like new little stars.

"Look," said Taha. "A green frog with yellow spots." Cooper smiled and added one more dot.

Beatrice sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. She was three years old today. "A shot?" she asked. "Yes, a little one," said Ms. Chea, the doctor. Beatrice held her bear tight.

The nurse rubbed Beatrice's arm. Then came the shot. It was fast, like a tiny pinch. "All done!" said the nurse. Beatrice got a shiny bandage and a red sticker. She was so proud.

In the car, Beatrice moved her arm up and down. "Ow," she said. "My arm hurts." Dad looked back. "The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while," he said. "It will feel better soon." Beatrice put her hand on the spot softly. She waited. Then she moved her arm again. No ow! She waved it high in the air. "All better!" she shouted. "That was not so bad after all."

Elias went to the store with his dad. They went to shop for paint. Elias held a little paper pumpkin. He wanted to paint it orange. "I need orange paint," he said. He looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. He saw blue paint and green paint too. But no orange paint anywhere. His bottom lip went down, down, down.

Then his friend Luka came by with his mom. Luka had paint cups in his hands. "No orange?" asked Luka. "No orange," said Elias. "Want to see a trick?" said Luka. "Watch me."

Luka got two small pots, one red and one yellow. He dipped his brush in the red paint. He swirled it in a cup. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He swirled it in the same cup. Round and round went the brush. "Stir, stir, stir," said Luka. Elias leaned in close. The red and yellow mixed. The cup turned orange! Orange like a pumpkin. Orange like a carrot.

"It's orange!" said Elias. "You made it!" "You try," said Luka. Elias dipped his brush in the red. He dipped it in the yellow. He stirred and stirred. His cup turned orange too. He laughed a big laugh. "My turn worked!" he said.

Elias painted his paper pumpkin orange. He painted one big green leaf on top. Then he saw a toy elephant on a shelf. It was stuck behind a big box. Elias pulled and pulled. Pop! Out came the elephant. It was blue. "A blue elephant!" said Elias. Luka giggled. "Elephants aren't blue," he said. Elias hugged the elephant anyway. "My elephant is blue," he said. "My pumpkin is orange. Stir, stir, stir!"

Ella went to the park with her dad. The sun was warm on her face. She ran to the swings. "Wait for me!" said her dad. Ella stopped and held his hand.

Then Ella saw a little food truck. It had a stove inside. A lady was making popcorn on it. Ella wanted popcorn so much. "Can I ask her?" said Ella. Her dad said yes, and they walked over together.

Eella and her dad stood back from the truck. Ella could not tell if the stove was hot. It did not look hot. It did not glow. Ella reached out one finger, just a little bit. Her dad caught her hand. "Only the lady touches the stove," he said. Ella put her hand behind her back.

"Is the stove still hot?" Ella asked the lady. The lady smiled. "Oh yes, it is still hot," she said. She held her own hand above it, far away. "See? I do not touch it either." Then she tipped the pan. Popcorn jumped out like little clouds. "Surprise!" said the lady. She gave Ella a paper cup full.

There was one yucky burnt piece at the bottom. Ella picked it out and set it on a napkin. Zakariya came running over from the sandbox. Ella shared her popcorn with him, all but the yucky piece. They sat on the bench in the sun, munching together, while the lady wiped down her stove.

Eliana was at Grandma's house. Grandma held her hand. "Time for your first haircut," said Grandma. They walked to the salon next door. Ms. Malik worked there.

Eliana sat in the big chair. There was a fish tank on the wall. Little fish swam round and round. Eliana turned her head to see them. Snip, snip went the scissors. "Oh dear," said Ms. Malik. "The hair is cut crooked on that side." One piece was too short. It looked a little broken at the edge.

Ms. Malik pointed at a statue in the corner. "Can you sit like the statue?" she asked. "The fish will wait for you." Eliana took a big breath. She sat very still. Her eyes looked straight ahead. She did not turn to the fish. Snip, snip, snip. This time the cut was neat and even all over.

"Look now," said Ms. Malik. Eliana turned at last. She waved at the orange fish. "I want to shout, I did it!" she said. Grandma laughed and clapped. Eliana spun in a circle, and her new neat hair bounced.

It was time for dinner, but Audrey still wore her party dress. "I want to sleep in my dress," she said. Mom carried her plate to the table. "Eat first," said Mom. Audrey ate her peas. She ate her bread. Then it was bath time. Mom ran the warm water. Audrey washed her duck and washed her toes.

After the bath, Audrey looked for her dress. It was wet from a splash. She could not wear it now. Mom held up something soft. "Pajamas," said Mom. "These are our sleep clothes." Audrey touched them. They were cozy and warm. She put them on all by herself. The pants had little ducks on them.

Audrey climbed into bed and hugged her duck toy. "Pajamas are for sleeping," she said, and closed her eyes. Then she felt something under her pillow. It was her party hat, small and shiny. Mom smiled from the door. "A surprise for tomorrow," Mom said. Audrey fell fast asleep.

Jules sat at Auntie's big table. There were warm pancakes and honey. His favorite cup was full of milk. His tummy made a little rumble. He wanted to eat right away.

His cousin put her hands together. She said, "Bismillah." Then she took a bite. Jules looked at his fork. He had not said it yet. He put the fork down. He said, "Bismillah." Auntie smiled at him. "It means 'in the name of God,'" his cousin said softly. Then everyone ate together. Jules dipped his pancake in the honey.

After lunch, they went out to Auntie's garden. Jules helped fill the watering can. Water spilled onto the green leaves. "Bismillah," Jules said again, just for fun. His cousin laughed and took his hand.

Asher went to the library with his dad. The rug in the story room was gray. Ms. Becker sat on a little chair. "We will sing a counting song," she said. Asher sat down fast. He wanted to sing too.

Ms. Becker held up her fingers. "One, two, three," she sang. The children sang with her. "Four, five, six." Asher listened. He tapped his knees. Then he sang too. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Everyone clapped. They sang it again, slow. Asher sang every word.

After the song, a girl held up three fingers. Ms. Becker asked, "How old are you?" The girl said, "I am four." She held up four fingers. Asher looked at his own hand. He held up three fingers. "I am three," he said. Fatima smiled at him. "Want to go look at the ice book?" she asked. Asher nodded, and off they went.

Eloise sat at the little red table. Mr. Georgiou put down two plates. One plate had cookies on it. The other plate was empty.

"Count with me," said Mr. Georgiou. Eloise pointed at each cookie. "One, two, three, four, five." Five cookies. She looked at the other plate. She counted anyway. "One, two..." But there was nothing to point to. The empty plate had no cookies at all.

Desmond sat down next to her. He was hungry. He ate a cookie. Eloise counted again. "One, two, three, four." He ate another one. "One, two, three." Then another. "One, two." Then one more. "One." Desmond picked up the last cookie. He ate it all up.

"Now count," said Desmond. Eloise looked at the plate. It was empty. Not one cookie was left. "It has none," she said. "Zero," said Mr. Georgiou. "Zero means none." Eloise said the new word slowly. "Zero." The empty plate had zero cookies on it.

Then Mr. Georgiou held up both plates. "Which plate has more?" Eloise pointed at the plate with the new cookies, the ones he had just set down. "That one," she said. "It has more. The empty one has zero." Clover clapped her hands. On the shelf, a toy sheep stood by a little bell. Eloise reached up and made the bell ring, ding, ding, ding. Mr. Georgiou laughed and gave her a fresh cookie, still cool, not frozen at all. "One," said Eloise, and she took a big happy bite.

Riley sat with her class at the temple. There was bread on the table. Big, warm, real bread. Her tummy made a loud pop and growl. "Shh, tummy," she whispered.

Ms. Do stood up. "Now we say the blessing," she said. Riley reached for the bread. Her hand went out, out, out. Then Tomas put his hand on the bread too. He pulled it back and folded his hands. Riley looked at him. She looked at Ms. Do. Nobody was eating yet. Riley pulled her hand back too. She folded her hands and waited.

Everyone said the blessing together. It was short. Then it was done. "Now we eat," said Ms. Do. Riley took the bread and took a big bite. "Waiting made the bread taste extra good," she said. Faris laughed. "That is silly." Riley laughed too and passed him the basket.

Jaxon went to the park with his mom. It was Lunar New Year. There were red flags and a big crowd. Jaxon held his mom's hand tight.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! Boom! The drums were very loud. Jaxon covered his ears. "Too loud," he said. His mom knelt down beside him. "It is okay," she said. "Listen. The drums make a beat."

A big lion came out. It was gold and red. Jaxon watched the lion. The lion jumped each time the drum went boom. The lion hopped to the left. Then it hopped to the right. It moved to the beat of the loud drums, again and again.

Jaxon saw his friend Willow there. She was clapping. Jaxon clapped too. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! The lion danced faster. Jaxon laughed. The loud drums did not scare him now.

After the dance, a grown-up gave out warm buns. Mom said they were tasty. Jaxon ate one on the bench. He drew a lion with his crayon later at home. "Boom, boom," he said, and made his lion hop across the page.

Adam looked in the toy box. His shiny red car was not there. "Where did it go?" he said.

Riyan helped him look. They looked under the table. They looked by the blocks. Lawrence looked in the doll corner. No car.

Ms. Sato came over. "Let's look slowly," she said. "Things can end up inside other things. A toy can get tucked in a bag." Adam thought about that. He looked at his own coat on the hook. He put his hand in the pocket. Something was in there!

Adam pulled out his shiny red car. "It was inside my pocket!" he said. He hugged the car. Then he passed it to Riyan. "You can have a turn," he said. Riyan smiled and rolled it down the hall.

Emmett was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to count the apples in the big bowl. He counted, "One, two," and then he stopped. He could not think of what came next.

His cousin Mac was there too. Mac wanted to know the number after two. "I forgot it," Mac said.

Then Grandpa began to sing. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." Emmett listened. The song went on. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight."

Emmett sang along. When he got to "nine, ten," he laughed. The words rhymed, and that helped him remember. "Three comes after two!" he said. Mac clapped his hands.

Emmett pointed at the bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." There were five red apples. Grandpa gave each boy a good apple to eat.

Emmett sang the song all the way to the kitchen door.

Lea sat in the waiting room. She waited for her first haircut. Her mama held her hand.

"Next, please," called the hairdresser. Lea climbed up into the big chair. Her feet stuck out. Her head was too low. The hairdresser could not reach her hair.

"I need a booster seat," the hairdresser said. She fetched a small blue box. It was a cool seat. Lea sat on top of it. Now she was higher up. Now the hairdresser could reach her hair.

"Why do I sit on this?" Lea asked.

"So small children can sit up high," the hairdresser said.

Snip, snip, snip. The scissors made little sounds. Lea watched in the mirror. Bits of hair fell down. Soon her hair was short and neat.

"Can I see?" Lea asked.

"Look in the mirror," said the hairdresser.

Lea looked. She saw a girl with a shiny new haircut. It was her! Lea clapped her hands. Then she hopped down and ran to show her mama.

Baby Milo came home today. Luna wore her red sweater to meet him. She wanted Milo to like her. But Milo only slept and slept.

Luna tried to show him her bear. Milo did not wake up. Luna tried to sing a soft song. Milo still slept. Luna's shoulders sank down low. "Maybe he does not like me," she said.

Mom sat on the couch with Milo. "You can say hello now," said Mom. Luna leaned in close. She put her finger near Milo's small hand. His little fingers wrapped around it. Milo held on tight! He held and held. He would not let go.

"He is holding me!" said Luna. She laughed and laughed. Mom smiled too. "That is his way of saying hello," said Mom.

Luna sat very still so he would not let go. Then Linden came to visit. "Do you want to hold Milo?" asked Luna. Linden shook his head. "Babies are slimy," said Linden. "Not this baby," said Luna. "Here, try one finger." Linden put his finger in Milo's hand. Milo held on tight. Linden's mouth fell open wide. "He likes me too!" said Linden. Milo kept holding both fingers, one in each little hand.

Harper ran to the dress-up corner. She wanted the red scarf. But Bethany had it first. Bethany put it on. It went down past her shoes. "That scarf is long," said Bethany. Harper found a blue scarf. She put it on. It stopped at her waist. "Mine is short," said Harper. "Long and short are opposites," said Bethany.

Then Leopold came over. He had a green scarf. It was long, too. The three friends counted their scarves. One long red. One long green. One short blue. They lined up the ends on the rug. The two long ones went far. The short one stopped soon.

Ms. Paquette helped them fold the scarves. The long ones took two folds. The short one took one fold. Then the children made a paper boat. Harper slid it across the cold window glass. The boat sailed past the rainy day. "Sail, boat, sail," she said.

Sadie sat in her car seat. The car went fast, then slow. "Look, a big truck," said Dad. "And a little bug car," said Sadie. They were going to the store to get a treat. Sadie wanted ice cream, cold and sweet. Dad said the soup at home was hot, so a grown-up would stir it later, not Sadie. "Okay," said Sadie. At the store, they found a small cup of vanilla ice cream. It felt cold in the bag. Sadie held it on her lap, very carefully. Then Dad said, "We will stop at the park first." At the park, Sadie climbed the ladder. She went up, up, up to the top. Then she slid down, down, down the slide. "Up and down are opposites," said a girl named Avery, standing by the slide. Sadie climbed up again. She slid down again. Her ice cream waited in the cool bag. "Last one," said Dad. Sadie touched her cold cup. "My treat is still cold," she said. She took one big lick. "Yum," said Avery, watching with wide eyes.

The wind began to howl outside the farmhouse. It rattled the windows. Myles put his hand on his ear. "That wind is so noisy," he said.

Then the lights went out. The whole room went dark. Myles could not see his toy truck. He could not see the cat. "Mom! The lights are gone!"

Mom came in with a flashlight. She pointed the light at the window. "The big wind knocked out the power," she said. Myles looked out. The big tree bent and bent. The wind pushed it hard.

"So the wind stopped the lights?" asked Myles.

"The wind was too strong," said Mom. "It broke the power line."

Myles felt proud. He knew a big thing now. Then the cat jumped into his lap and licked his nose.

"Oh no," said Myles. "The wind blew dog breath on you too!"

Mom laughed in the dark.

Joseph looked out the window at daycare. Snow was falling on the grass. White flakes fell on the fence too. One, two, three flakes, down, down, down.

"Snowy day!" said Ms. Kaminski. "Boots and coats for everyone." Joseph put on his red boots. He zipped his big coat. Dawson had blue mittens. Meher had green mittens. Joseph looked at his hands. He had no mittens today.

Outside, the snow was soft. Joseph scooped up some snow. He patted it into a ball. "A snowball!" he said. He threw it to Dawson. Then his hands felt cold. Very, very cold. He peeked at his red fingers. "Ow," he said. "Cold hands."

Dawson came close. "Mittens keep my hands warm," he said. Joseph ran to Ms. Kaminski. She pulled fuzzy yellow mittens from her pocket. Joseph slid them on. Warm hands! He scooped more snow. Pat, pat, pat. "Another snowball," he said. "One, two, three!" The wind blew, the snow fell, and Joseph's hands stayed warm.

Wesley ran to the water table. His little blue fish could swim there. He loved to watch it swim round and round.

Then he heard a small sound. It came from the carpet. Noemie sat there all alone. Her face was wet. Tears ran down her cheeks. Wesley had tears like that once. He had them when he felt sad.

Ms. Castillo knelt down beside Noemie. "Big feelings today," she said softly. She gave Noemie a tissue.

Wesley looked at his fish. He looked at Noemie. Sad faces needed help. He ran back and got his fish. "You can hold him," said Wesley. "He can swim later." Noemie took the fish in her hands. She gave it a little squeeze. Then a small smile came. Her tears stopped.

Outside the window the sky was stormy and gray. Inside, Brock clapped his hands. "The fish gets a turn with everyone!" he said. What a surprise, thought Wesley. One little fish made so many smiles.

"Fish time," said Noemie. She held him up high. Wesley laughed and sat down next to her.

Charlotte held her new library card. It was blue and shiny. She and her dad rode the city bus to the library. The bus went bump, bump, bump.

"I can bring home a book now," said Charlotte. "A real book!"

At the library, she picked a book about a big red truck. She gave her card to the librarian. The librarian stamped the book. Charlotte hugged it tight.

A week later, it was time to bring the book back. Charlotte saw a little door in the wall. Books went inside it, one by one.

"What is that?" she asked.

"That is the return slot," said the librarian. "You drop your book in when you bring it back."

Charlotte did not want to let go of her book. She held it close. Then she had an idea.

She held the book up high. "Bye bye, truck book!" she said. She waved it. The book went into the slot with a soft thunk.

Charlotte peeked at the slot. The book was gone. The slot had eaten it all up!

"More books live in there," said her dad.

"Not in there," said the librarian, laughing. "It just takes them back."

Charlotte got to pick a new book. This one was about a blue bus. She hugged it on the ride home. "Next time, you go in the slot," she told it. "But I will wave first."

Isla wanted to play outside. But the grass looked big and green and secret. "What is down there?" she wondered. She pulled off her shoes. She pulled off her socks. One bare foot, two bare feet.

First she touched the grass with her hand. Her hand felt the little blades tickle her palm. Then she stepped out. One foot, two feet. The soft grass tickled her toes too! "My feet can feel it!" she said. She wiggled her toes in the cool green blades. "Feet can feel. Feet can feel."

Then she heard a bird. Her ears heard it chirp, chirp. She saw a red flower with her eyes. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled sweet. A bee sat on the flower. Isla did not touch the bee. She watched it fly away.

There was one wet spot in the grass. Isla stepped in it. "Ooh! Slimy!" she said. The mud squished between her toes. She laughed and laughed. Then Mom called, "Time to come in!"

Isla sat on the bottom step. Mom helped her wipe her feet with a warm towel. Mom wiped one foot, then the other. "The grass was soft," said Isla. "But the mud was squishy. My feet know everything!" She wiggled her clean toes at the door.

Jack woke up early at Grandpa's house. Grandpa was baking bread in the kitchen. Grandpa handled the hot oven. Jack watched from his chair.

Then Audrey came to visit. She had a little red truck in her hands. Jack liked the truck very much. He reached out and took it. Audrey's face turned sad. She started to cry.

Jack looked at Audrey. Then he looked at the truck. He put the truck back in her hands. "Audrey, can I have a turn?" he asked. Audrey wiped her eyes. "Yes," she said. "You can have a turn."

Jack pushed the red truck across the floor. Vroom, vroom. Then he gave the truck back to Audrey. She pushed it too. They took turns all morning. After that, they went to catch leaves falling in the yard. Later, Grandpa called them in for bread. Jack was tired from playing. He lay down on the bed for a little rest. The red truck sat on the shelf, waiting for tomorrow.

Arlo woke up in his bed. The room was bright. He could smell toast. He heard spoons clink in the kitchen. Was it morning now? Yesterday it was dark at night. Now the sun made stripes on his blanket.

Arlo wanted to be the first one at the table. He ran down the hall in his sock feet. His tummy made a little growl. Mom was there. Dad was there. "Good morning, Arlo!" said Mom.

"Is it morning because we woke up?" asked Arlo. "Yes," said Mom. "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." She set down a bowl. The milk was cold and sweet. The toast was warm and crunchy.

"After breakfast, can we play a game?" asked Arlo. "Yes, later," said Mom. "Today we play after we eat." Arlo ate his toast. He looked at the window. The sun was climbing up, up, up. Later, he thought. Later comes after now.

Then Mom put one more piece of toast on his plate. A surprise! It was cut like a star. Arlo laughed and took a big bite.

Lena ran to the school library. Story day! Ms. Luo had set out two big piles of books on the table.

"Look at all the books," said Lena. She began to count the red pile. "One, two, three, five..." Oh no. She lost her count.

"What do I do now?" Lena asked.

"Try again," said Leah. "Start at the first book."

Lena looked at her hands. She held up one finger for each book. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" Six fingers stood up. She did not lose her count this time.

Next she counted the blue pile with her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!" Eight fingers stood up tall.

"Which pile has more?" asked Ms. Luo.

Lena held out her hands. The blue pile had more books. It had eight. The red pile had six.

"The blue one has more," said Lena. She jumped up and down.

Then Ms. Luo picked up a book about the dry desert and the big blue sky. "You can pick a story now," she said.

Lena sat down with Leah and Kaleb. "The sky is so big in this book," said Kaleb.

Lena turned the page and smiled. "Let's count the stars," she said. She put up one finger for each star.

Harper sat at her little table in the backyard. She had red paint. She had yellow paint. She wanted to paint a big pumpkin.

"One pumpkin, two pumpkin, three," said Harper. But her pumpkin was not orange. "I need orange paint," she said.

Her friend Madyson came over. Madyson gave her a cup of juice. "Mmm, orange juice," said Madyson. "Orange like a pumpkin."

Harper looked at her paints. She put red paint on her brush. She put yellow paint on the brush too. She stirred them in the tray. The paint turned orange!

"Look, look!" said Harper. "Red and yellow make orange!"

Madyson clapped her hands. "Paint the pumpkin now," she said.

Harper painted the pumpkin orange. It was loud outside. The wind blew. The pumpkin looked bright and pretty.

"Give me your brush," said Madyson. "I want to try too."

Madyson dipped her brush in red and yellow. She painted a small orange flower.

Harper held up her pumpkin. "Orange!" she said. "My best pumpkin ever."

Hayden was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big game box. On the box was a picture of an eye, an ear, a nose, a mouth and a hand. "This is my senses game," said Grandpa. "Can you play?"

Hayden opened the box. Out fell a feather, a pinecone and a small clock. "First, use your hands," said Grandpa. "Close your eyes and touch." Hayden touched the feather. It was soft. He touched the pinecone. It was rough. "The feather is soft!" said Hayden. "The pinecone is rough!"

"Now use your nose," said Grandpa. He held up a jar. Hayden sniffed it. "Cookies!" he said. "My nose knows cookies." Grandpa laughed. He rang the little clock bell. "My ears hear that!" said Hayden.

Then Grandpa hid the cookie jar behind his back. "Something is missing," said Hayden. "Where are the cookies?" Grandpa held one up. "Use your eyes," he said. "Look, then use your mouth." Hayden took a small bite. He smiled big. "Yum! My tongue tastes sweet!" Grandpa clapped his hands. "Five senses, all found," said Grandpa. "Want to play again?" "Yes!" said Hayden, picking up the soft feather.

Norah got a little blue card at home. It had her name on it. "This is your library card," said Mama. "We will drive to the library and borrow a book."

They drove past green grass and tall trees. At the library, Norah saw big shelves. The books were high, high up. "Too tall for me," she said, with a pout.

Then Halima ran over. "Norah, come see! This is the children's area!"

Norah peeked in. The shelves were small. The books were low. They were red and yellow and sparkly. "Books just for young kids," said Halima, grinning.

Norah picked a book about a silly puppy. Mama scanned her card. Beep! The book was hers to take home.

"You are so smart," said Mama.

Norah hugged the book all the way to the car.

Grandma put two bowls on the table. One bowl had red apples. One bowl had green apples. "Which bowl has more?" Grandma asked. Hannah looked and looked. She wanted to know. She thought the green bowl had more.

"I will count," Hannah said. She pointed at the green apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Then she pointed at one apple again. "Seven!" Grandma smiled. Hannah counted the red apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven."

"Hannah, look at your finger," said Grandma. "You pointed at that green apple two times." Hannah looked. She had! She counted the green apples again. This time she touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Only six! The red bowl had seven.

"The red bowl has more," said Hannah. Grandma gave her the red bowl. Grandpa's furry cat jumped up next to her. Hannah picked the biggest apple and gave it to Grandma. "For you," she said. Grandma took a big, happy bite.

Cooper stood in the school hallway. It was his first day. He held his green lunchbox with two hands.

His friend Krish ran up. Krish held a green lunchbox too. "We have the same lunchbox," said Krish.

At lunch, the lunchboxes sat on the shelf. They looked the same. Cooper grabbed one. He opened the lid. Inside was a sandwich he did not like. "This is the wrong lunch," said Cooper.

Mr. Lavoie came to help. "Open the lid all the way," he said. Cooper looked at the lid. There was writing on it. It said Krish. The other lid said Cooper.

"Can writing find my lunchbox?" asked Cooper. "It can," said Mr. Lavoie. "Your name on the lid helps it find its way back to you."

After lunch, Cooper went to the art table. He found a small paper there. It was not his paper. But it had his name on it. It found its way back to him.

Cooper smiled. He drew a big truck on his paper. Then he wrote his name at the top, all by himself.

"Look, Krish," said Cooper. "Now my truck knows where to go too."

Jade sat on the school bus. Her dress felt itchy. She wiggled in her seat. It was her first day of school. Her new friend Otis sat next to her. He had a turtle on his backpack. "I like your turtle," said Jade. "Thank you," said Otis. "I like your bow." The bus went bump, bump, bump. Then it stopped at school.

At the playground, Jade saw a big slide. She ran to it fast. She wanted to go down right away. But kids were standing in a line. Otis stood at the back. "We take turns on the slide," said Ms. Brown. Jade got in line behind Otis. She waited. One kid slid down. Then the next kid slid down. Then the next. The line moved up, and up, and up.

Now it was Jade's turn. She climbed the little steps. She sat at the top. She slid down, down, down. "Wheee!" said Jade. She ran to the back of the line again. "Good waiting," said Otis. "Your turn soon!" The line moved up, one kid at a time, and Jade smiled all the way back to the top.

Ryan ran into the backyard. He saw the big blue sky up high. His friend Gurman was there too. Gurman had a bowl of water.

"My dog is thirsty," Gurman said. The dog drank. Ryan patted the dog.

"Is a dog an animal?" Ryan asked.

"Yes," said Gurman. "Animals have four legs. Dogs run fast!"

Then they looked at the little pond. A fish swam by. Ryan tapped the water.

"That is not an animal," said Ryan. "It has no legs!"

Mr. Becker was by the fence. He smiled. "Watch the fish," he said. "Fish swim. Dogs run. Cows eat grass. All three are animals."

Ryan looked and looked. "Wow," he said. "A fish is an animal too!"

Later they ate apples on the grass. "Is an apple an animal?" asked Gurman.

"No," laughed Ryan. "It is food!"

The dog barked. His dirty paws made little prints on the porch.

"More animals," said Ryan, pointing.

Julia woke up in her dark room. She jumped out of bed. "Morning!" she shouted. "Park time!" She ran to the window and looked out. The sky was dark. The stars were out. Her mom came in and smiled. "It is still night, Julia. Day and night are opposites. Night comes first, then day." Julia frowned. "I want day," she said. "You must wait," said Mom. So Julia went back to bed.

Soon the sky turned light. "Day!" cried Julia. "Park time for real!" Mom laughed. At the park, Julia saw the big slide and the small slide. She counted them. "One big slide, one small slide!" Julia ran fast down the big one. Then she walked slow up the steps. "Fast and slow," she said. Her friends Mehreen and Aria were there. Mehreen had a cold drink. Aria had a warm bun from home. "Cold drink, warm bun," said Julia. They sat in the shade because the sun was hot.

Mr. Menon was mixing sand and water in the sandpit. Julia and Mehreen helped him mix. They made a tall triangle tower. "One triangle, two triangles, three triangles!" said Julia. Aria patted the sand flat. Then Julia tipped over her bucket and the tower fell. The bucket was empty now. "Sand all gone!" said Julia. The sun went down. The sky grew dark again. Julia yawned. "Night is back," she said. Mom took her hand. "See you tomorrow, park," said Julia, waving all the way home.

Aurora sat at the dinner table. Windy day at the park had made her eye blink and blink. A tiny bit of dust was stuck near her eye. It felt scratchy. She wanted it gone before dinner.

Mom put a warm cup of milk by her plate. Aurora heard it go clink. She saw steam rise up. She smelled something sweet. "Can I have a cookie?" she asked. Mom handed her one. Aurora touched it with her finger. It was bumpy. She took a bite. It tasted good.

Then Aurora felt something soft on her cheek. She looked in the little mirror. A bit of dust sat on her eyelash, not in her eye. "Look, Mom! My eyelash caught it!" Mom smiled. "Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes," said Mom. Aurora blinked again. The dust fell away. Her eye felt fine now. She drank her milk and the last bit of cookie crumbs fell, plip, onto her plate.

Natalie put on her last clean sweater. Today a hairdresser was coming to her house. Natalie did not want a haircut. "The scissors will pinch me," she said. Mom shook her head. "You can watch first," said Mom.

The hairdresser spread a big cape on a chair. She held up her scissors. She cut a little piece of her own hair. Snip. The piece fell down. It did not fly away. It just sat on the floor. The hairdresser smiled. "Hair is like that. Cutting it does not hurt at all."

Natalie sat very still in the chair. Snip, snip. She waited. She felt nothing. "That is it?" she asked. "That is it," said the hairdresser. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little pieces of hair dropped onto the cape, one by one. Natalie watched them fall. "More," she said. "You can cut more."

Naomi stood in the school hallway. Her mom held her hand. Naomi's tummy felt jumpy. "It is your first day," said Mom. "Mr. Bear will be right there."

A girl stood by the door. She wore a big red hat. She was all alone. Naomi wanted a friend. But she did not know what to do.

Mr. Bear smiled at Naomi. "Go say hello," he said. Naomi walked to the girl. "My name is Naomi," she said. "What is your name?" The girl smiled big. "My name is Alora," she said. "Do you like my hat?" Naomi nodded. "It is a nice hat," she said.

Then Madina ran over. "Can I play too?" she asked. "Yes!" said Alora. The three girls walked into class together. They sat in a row. Naomi was thirsty, so Mr. Bear gave her a cup of water. At play time, Naomi and Alora shared the blocks. "You are my friend," said Alora. Naomi smiled all the way to the carpet for story time.

Mohamed was home with a cold. His nose was red. His throat felt scratchy. He sat at the kitchen table in his pajamas.

His grandma set down a big yellow cup. "This is your special cup," she said. Mohamed did not feel thirsty. He shook his head. "Just try one little sip," Grandma said. Mohamed took a sip. The water was cool. He took another sip. Then he took a big drink.

His friend Brooks called on the phone. Brooks told him about the wind at the park. "The wind blew my hat off," Brooks said. Mohamed laughed. His laugh felt better now. His throat did not scratch as much.

Grandma touched his head. "You drank all your water," she said. "Good job." She filled the yellow cup again. Mohamed drank some more. Then he slid the cup across the table to Grandma. "You sip too," he said.

Max was at the water table with Axel. Max wanted to fill his cup to the top. He held the cup under the tap. The water came out fast. It splashed over the edge. "Oh no," said Max. "My cup is too full."

Ms. Byrne came over. "Try again," she said kindly. "Tip the cup out first." Max tipped the water out. Now the cup had nothing in it. "Empty," said Axel. Max put the cup under the tap again. This time he made the water go slow. He watched it climb. He stopped just at the top. "Full!" said Max. He did a little jump.

Ryleigh blew across the water table. "That was loud," she laughed. Max gave her his cup. "You can pour next," he said. The water went slow and steady. Ryleigh's cup filled up, drop by drop.

Iris went to Kyro's house. Kyro had a song on the phone. It had a steady beat. Iris wanted to clap along.

She clapped. Her claps were too fast. Kyro laughed. "Not so quick!" he said. Iris listened some more. She clapped one, two, one, two. Now her hands matched the beat.

They began to sing too. "Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the..." Oh no. Iris forgot the word. She frowned. Kyro's mom held up a hat. "Try cat and hat," she said. "They rhyme. They end with the same sound."

Iris thought. What sounds like diddle? "Fiddle!" she sang. Kyro clapped and cheered. The moon seemed to shine right through the window. Iris sat up straight and sang it again, all the way to the cow jumping over the moon.

Theodore went to the garden center with his dad. He picked out little carrot plants in pots. He also got a big bag of soil. "We can plant these at home," said his dad.

At home, Theodore dug a hole in the dirt. His dad helped him tip a plant out of its pot. The plant would not come out. Theodore pulled a little harder. Pop! Out it came, and something hung from the bottom. Long white strings dangled down. "Look, Dad!" said Theodore. "The plant has strings!" His dad said, "Those are roots.
