A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Theodore set the plant in the hole. He made sure the roots pointed down. He patted the soil on top with his hands. Then he sat back on his heels and looked at his garden.

The dirt was slippery from the watering can. Theodore washed his hands at the sink. Then he painted a picture of his garden. He drew the green leaves on top. He drew the white roots down under the brown dirt. "Goodnight, roots," said Theodore.

Mohamed went to his dad's office. Dad had a big desk and a soft chair. A tablet sat on the desk. It was flat and shiny. Mohamed hoped he could draw on it.

Mohamed reached out his hand. Then he stopped. "Dad, can I use the tablet?" he asked. Dad smiled. "Yes, you may. Let me turn it on." Dad pressed the button. The screen lit up. Mohamed saw that one little push made the light come on.

Dad tapped the drawing app. A white page appeared. Mohamed drew a green fish. He drew a slimy worm for the fish to see. He drew blue water all around.

Then Mohamed was done. He pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the desk, just where it was.

"Can I draw a fish again tomorrow?" Mohamed asked. "Yes," said Dad. Mohamed sat on the soft chair and smiled at his green fish, still safe inside the tablet.

Evelyn went to Jasmine's house. Jasmine had a big doll and a small bowl. "Let's play house," said Jasmine. "I will be the parent," said Evelyn. "No, I want to be the parent," said Jasmine. Both girls wanted the same role.

Then Jasmine had an idea. "You can be the parent first," she said. "Then we can switch halfway." Evelyn fed the doll from the soft little bowl. She rocked the doll and sang. The doll got sleepy. "Now we switch," said Evelyn. Jasmine took the doll and became the parent. Evelyn got to be the baby.

As the baby, Evelyn got tucked in with a soft blanket. She pretended to taste the pretend soup. It was fun to be little. "Can we switch again?" she asked. Jasmine smiled and handed her the doll. "Your turn, Mommy," she said.

Oliver sat at the little blue table at the tutoring centre. It was dark night outside the window. Ms. Singh put down two bowls of blocks. One bowl had red blocks. One bowl had green blocks.

"Which bowl has more?" asked Ms. Singh.

Oliver pointed at the red bowl. It looked bigger. Louane counted the red blocks. "One, two, three, four," she said. Then she said, "Four!"

Now Oliver counted the green blocks. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He looked at his fingers. Five. He had said five last. He held up his hand. "Five!" he said. "Green has more."

Ms. Singh smiled. "Try the cups next."

The cups were different sizes. Some were big and some were small. Oliver counted the big cups. "One, two, three." He counted the small cups. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six. He had said six last.

"Six cups!" said Oliver.

Louane laughed. "You said six last, so there are six."

After the lesson, Oliver chased Louane to the door. He counted his steps all the way. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Zoe put on her red hat. Then she ran to the playground with Annika. "It is sunny today," said Annika. "Yes, and the sun feels warm," said Zoe. They went down the slide, one, two, three times. Zoe chewed her apple on the bench. "Why do the leaves dance?" Zoe asked. "I don't know. Let's watch," said Annika.

The wind came. The wind pulled at Zoe's hat. "Hold on, hat!" said Zoe. But the wind blew her hat right off her head. The hat flew over the grass. Zoe ran and ran. Annika ran too. "One, two, three, four steps!" they counted. Ms. Mercer caught the hat by the fence. "Here you are," she said. "The wind took my hat," said Zoe. "It was too windy for hats," said Ms. Mercer, kindly.

Zoe held her hat in both hands. The wind blew again. The leaves flew up. Zoe pressed her hat on tight. "Stay on, hat," she said. Annika laughed. The sun came back out. They ran to the swings together.

Georgia sat on the cozy couch. Her whole family was there. Her friend Ephraim sat next to her. The big game was on TV.

A man ran on the green grass. He wore a striped shirt. "Who is that?" Georgia asked. "He runs around and looks and looks."

"That is the referee," her dad said. "The referee watches the game. He makes sure the players follow the rules."

A player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle. Toot! He held up a card. Everyone in the room went, "Ohhh!"

"He saw it," said Georgia. "The referee saw the hands."

"Yes," said Ephraim. "He was watching the whole time."

Georgia clapped her hands. She liked the man in the striped shirt. He watched and watched. When someone broke a rule, toot went the whistle.

Later, a player kicked the ball into the net. No whistle this time. "That was okay," said Georgia. "That was fair." Georgia climbed up onto Dad's lap. "The referee is doing a good job," she said. Dad kissed her hair.

Maverick stood in the school gym. The floor was shiny and cold. Ms. Kim had red hoops on the ground. She had a big basket of beanbags.

First, Maverick threw a beanbag. It flew past the hoop. It landed on the floor. "Try again," said Ms. Kim. Maverick tried again. Plink! The beanbag sat in the hoop. "I did it!" said Maverick.

Then Sofie rolled a big ball to him. Maverick's hands were in his pockets. The ball bumped his tummy and fell down. "Oh no," said Maverick. His arms felt tired, but he pulled his hands out. He held his arms out in front of him. His hands were open, like two big cups. Sofie rolled the ball again. Thump! It landed right in his hands. "You caught it!" said Sofie. Cameron clapped.

Ms. Kim rolled the ball next. Maverick held his arms out. His hands stayed open. He caught it again and again. "One more time," he said. He threw the beanbag too. Plink, into the hoop it went.

Billie wanted to draw a circle. She drew one on her paper. It came out wobbly. It had bumps and a flat side. Billie frowned at it.

"I want a good circle," she said. Her mom was washing cups at the sink. One cup was small and round. Billie looked at the cup. Then she looked at her crayon.

She put the cup down on the paper. She held it still with one hand. With her other hand, she traced all around the bottom of the cup. The crayon went round and round the cup. When she lifted the cup up, there it was. A round, smooth circle.

"Mom, look!" said Billie. "It went around the cup!" Her mom smiled. Billie traced the cup again and again. She got a big circle and a small circle.

Then Billie looked around the kitchen. She saw a book. It had four flat sides. She traced around the book. That shape had long sides and short sides. "That one is a rectangle," said Mom. Next Billie found a napkin with four sides the same. She traced that too. It was a square.

Billie drew a triangle at the top of her square. "It's a house!" she said. She put circles beside it for the sun. Her cup sat on the table, ready to roll. Billie gave it one little push. The cup rolled to the paper and stopped. "You made my picture," Billie told the cup.

Liam was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make a paper crown. Grandma found the glue, the paper, and some shiny stars.

Liam put glue on the stars. He stuck them on the crown. Then he picked the crown up right away. "I love my crown!" he said.

But the stars slid off. One star fell on the floor. "Oh no," said Liam. "Why did my stars fall down?"

"Maybe the glue is still wet," said Grandma. "Wet glue needs time to dry before the pieces hold together."

So Liam put the stars back on. He set the crown on the table. He did not touch it. He watched the gentle rain fall in Grandma's yard through the window. He waited and waited.

Then Grandma touched the glue with one finger. "Dry now," she said.

Liam picked up his crown. He tipped it upside down. The stars stayed on! "Look, Grandma! They are stuck!" He put the crown on his head and danced around the kitchen. "I am King Liam of the yard!"

Jade sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse held a small tray. Jade saw the tiny needle. Her tummy felt tight.

Grandpa sat next to her. He held her hand. "Smell the flower," he said. "Breathe in slow. Then blow out slow." Jade smelled the flower. She breathed in slow like smelling a flower. Then she blew out slow. Her shoulders came down. Her tummy felt calm. The nurse said, "All done!" Jade blinked. She had not even felt the pinprick much at all. "I breathed like a flower," Jade said.

Afterward, they went to the ice cream shop. Grandpa poured hot fudge on top. The man scooped a high pink tower for Jade. A butterfly sticker sat on her arm where the bandage was. Naomi waved from the next table. "Did the shot hurt?" she asked. Jade held up her sticker and smiled. "I smelled a flower," she said.

Emmett sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on a small street. Emmett put his toy cars in his bag. His baby sister took them out. He put them in. She pulled them out. "Stop," said Emmett. She smiled and took one out again. Emmett thought hard. He asked his dad, "Is in the other way of out?" Dad said, "Yes. In and out are opposites." Dad stopped the car at the bakery. It was hot inside. Dad came back with warm bread and a cold drink. The bread smelled good. Emmett held the cold cup. He felt safe in his seat. He put his toy cars in the bag one more time. He zipped it shut. His sister patted the bag. The toys stayed in. The car went home, slow and steady. "All in," said Emmett.

Owen woke up and saw white. Snow was everywhere. His school was closed. His mom had to work, so he went next door to Ms. Chaudhry's house.

"Look at all that snow," said Ms. Chaudhry. "Your bike is buried in it."

Owen looked out the window. His red bike sat under a big white hill. He wanted to ride it, but the snow was too deep.

Then Owen heard a loud noise. A big truck came down the street. It had a big blade in front. The truck pushed the snow off the road. The road turned black and clear.

"That is a snowplow," said Ms. Chaudhry.

The snowplow went up and down the street. It pushed and pushed. Soon the road was all clear.

But the sidewalk was still snowy. Owen could not ride his bike there. Ms. Chaudhry laughed. "The plow only clears the road, not your bike."

Owen giggled. He got a shovel instead. He pushed the snow off the sidewalk, just like the big truck.

"The little snowplow!" said Ms. Chaudhry.

At the end of the day, Owen sat inside with warm cocoa. He had stirred it with a spoon. He looked at the beautiful white street. "Tomorrow, bike," he said.

Victoria was at home. She wanted her very own library card. "Can I get one today?" she asked. "Yes," said her mom. "We will go after I clean up."

At the library, a kind librarian made Victoria's card. It had her name on it. Victoria held it with two hands.

Then she saw something. A librarian sat on a small chair. She had a stack of books. A boy named Malakai stood far away. He looked shy. Victoria watched. The librarian opened a book with a funny dog on it. She began to read aloud. Malakai tiptoed closer. Then he sat down. Victoria clapped her hands. "The book made him sit down!" she said. "The book made him sit down!"

Victoria picked a book about a frozen pond. She borrowed it with her new card. "Can I take it home?" she asked. "Yes, that is what the card is for," said the librarian.

At home, Victoria read to her toy bunny. It was their new game. "Tonight I will bathe you, bunny," she said softly. "Then one more page." She turned the page, and the bunny heard all about the frozen pond.

Victoria was going on a big trip. First the family drove in the car to the train station. Victoria had her pink backpack on her lap. She was so excited that she climbed right in and sat down fast.

The car did not move. Dad looked back at her. "Where is your click?" he asked. Victoria looked at her car seat. The belt was not buckled. She pulled the strap over herself and pushed it in. Click! Then the car started to move.

At the station, a man in a blue hat helped with the bags. Victoria held Dad's hand. They walked to the train. The train was big and long. It made a soft sound, like a big sigh. Victoria found a seat by the window with her mom.

The train began to roll. Outside, the trees slipped by, one, then another, then more. Victoria pressed her nose to the glass. "Look how fast the trees go," she said. Mom smiled and pointed at a little river shining in the sun. Victoria waved at the river until it was gone.

Leo was at the park with his dad. His friend Armaan was there too. Armaan had a big basket. "Look at my picture game," Armaan said. He tipped the basket over. All the pictures fell out on the grass.

Armaan looked sad. "Now it is a big mess," he said. Leo looked at the pile. He saw a cat picture on top. He put it to one side. Then he saw a dog picture. He put it next to the cat. "Animals go together," he said. Armaan smiled. He found a cow picture. He put it in the animal pile too.

Leo found a picture of a ball. Then he found a picture of a kite. "Toys," said Armaan. He made a new pile. Leo found a picture of an apple and a banana. He made one more pile. "Foods," he said. Soon all the pictures were in piles. The basket had room again.

Ms. Farah-Ali walked by with her class. She saw the neat piles on the grass. "What nice groups," she said. Kaison ran up fast to look. "Can we play too?" he asked. Armaan put all the piles back in the basket. He hung the basket handle on his arm. "We can mix them up and sort again," said Leo. Armaan laughed. "Best game ever."

Aria made a library in her bedroom. Her books stood on a shelf. Her teddy bears sat on the bed.

Ms. Bighorn came to visit. She had a card in her hand. "This is your first library card," she said. "It is real."

Aria took the card. It was warm from Ms. Bighorn's pocket.

"Now pick one book to borrow," said Ms. Bighorn. Aria picked a book about a puzzle.

Aria put a book back on the shelf. She put it in the wrong spot. Ms. Bighorn pointed to the label on the spine. "See this little label? It shows where the book belongs."

Aria looked. The label matched the shelf. She put the book right there. It fit!

Then Ms. Bighorn helped Aria sweep the rug. Books went home, dust went away.

At bedtime, Aria held her card tight. "The book is mine for now," she said. Her mom smiled and kissed her head.

Declan had a new book. It was about a big red boot. He could not read the words yet.

He held the book upside down. He turned the pages from back to front. "That is backwards," said his mom. She sat down next to him. "We read this way." She turned the book around. She turned the pages from the front.

"Who made up the boot story?" Declan asked.

Mom pointed to the cover. "This name tells us. It says Sam Park. He wrote the words." The words on the cover were little black marks. The marks meant a name.

Declan looked at the marks. He put his finger on them. "Sam Park made the boot!" he said.

Mom laughed. "Yes. Now are you ready for the story?"

They read the whole book, front to back. At the end, the boot found its sock. It was a tiny golden sock, just Declan's size. "Look!" said Declan. "A surprise sock!"

Mila was at school. It was snack time. Then she heard a loud noise. It came from the hall. Boom! Boom!

Mila felt scared. Her tummy felt small and tight. She held her cup with both hands. Peter heard it too. He hid under the table. "What is that noise?" Mila asked.

Mr. Horváth saw her face. He knelt down beside her. "You can tell me," he said. "I can help." Mila pointed at the door. "A loud noise," she said. Mr. Horváth took her hand. They looked in the hall together.

It was only a big box. The janitor was pushing it. The box went boom on the floor. Mila laughed. She was not scared now. "Just a box!" she said. She ran back to Peter. She pulled him out from under the table. "Come see," she said. "It was a box. It was not a bad monster." Peter smiled. They ate their snacks together.

Leon sat at the kitchen table. He held a cracker in his hand. "Is this a square?" he asked. He was not sure.

Mom gave him a piece of string. Leon put the string along one side. He held the end with his finger. Then he put it on the next side. It matched. He put it on the third side. It matched too. The fourth side matched as well.

"Four sides," said Leon. "All the same!" Mom smiled and said, "Yes, we call that a square." Leon laughed. Then he took a big bite. He looked at the bite mark. "Now it has no shape," he said. Outside, the bright moon was coming up for the night. Leon waved at it through the kitchen window.

Daniel went to the beach with his friend Teddy. Mr. Levy, the lifeguard, had a big game. "Name your five senses," he said. "You get a shell for each one."

Daniel held up his hands. "I see with my eyes," he said. He looked at the waves. Mr. Levy gave him a pink shell.

"I hear with my ears," said Teddy. The waves went crash, crash. Teddy got a white shell.

"I touch with my hands," said Daniel. He patted the warm sand. Another shell! Now he had two.

Daniel was stuck. Two more senses to go. He needed those shells. Teddy had two as well. "I want to win," said Daniel. But he could not think of the last two.

Then Teddy dug a hole in the sand. He pulled out something. "Look at this ugly old boot," he said. He held it up like a tool and pretended to dig with it. Everyone laughed.

Daniel sniffed near the boot. "Pee yew," he said. "I smell it with my nose!" Mr. Levy clapped. "Yes! We smell with our nose," he said. He handed Daniel a green shell.

One sense left. Daniel thought hard. Then Teddy's mom called, "Snack time!" Daniel took a bite of a salty cracker. His mouth was happy. "Taste!" he shouted. "I taste with my tongue!"

Mr. Levy gave him a blue shell. Four shells! Daniel and Teddy were tied. They put all the shells in a bucket. They used the ugly boot as a paint pot. Daniel dipped a shell in paint and made a mark on the sand. Teddy laughed and made one too.

Paisley was at summer camp. She saw a new toy truck in the sand. It was big and red. Caspian was playing with it first.

Paisley wanted the truck now. Her hand reached out. She wanted to grab it.

Then she remembered. She counted, "One slow breath. Two slow breaths. Three slow breaths." She breathed in and out. Her body felt calm. Waiting felt hard, but breathing helped.

"Your turn now," said Caspian. He gave her the truck. It was her turn to push it in the sand.

The camp bell began to ring. Snack time! Paisley stuck out her tongue. "I can smell the watermelon," she said.

"One, two, three breaths, then my turn," said Caspian. Paisley smiled and rolled the truck back to him.

Theo and Benicio played in the forest. They found a big stick. "A dragon!" said Theo. Theo held the stick up. "The dragon is scary," said Theo. "It will roar at us."

"No," said Benicio. "The dragon is friendly." Benicio patted the stick. "It wants to play house with us."

"But it is scary," said Theo. "It makes me mad, the big roars."

Benicio frowned. Theo frowned too. They both wanted the dragon. But not the same dragon.

Then Theo had an idea. "Can the dragon be friendly, but roar one little roar?" he asked. Benicio smiled. "Yes! A tiny roar," said Benicio. "Just for us."

Theo made a small roar. "Roo!" Then Benicio made one too. "Roo!"

Now the dragon had a house. Theo used leaves for a bed. Benicio used a pinecone for a pillow. "The dragon needs a blanket," said Theo. Benicio found soft moss. They tucked the dragon in.

"Shh, the dragon is sleeping," said Benicio. Theo tiptoed. He followed Benicio around the tree. Then Theo drew in the dirt with a pencil he had in his pocket. He drew the dragon. It had a big smile.

"The friendly dragon," said Theo. "Our friendly dragon," said Benicio.

The dragon went, "Snore."

Henry planted a little garden at the farm. He put one pea seed in the dirt. Then two more. Then three more. Mr. Cheung helped him pat the soil down low and flat.

"Peas need rain and sun," said Mr. Cheung. "Now we wait." Henry watered the seeds every day. He waited and waited. One day, a tiny green leaf popped up. Then more leaves came. Then little white flowers. Then the plant grew tall, tall, tall. Henry counted the vines. One vine, two vines, three vines, four vines.

Kennedy came to see. "Where are the peas?" she asked. Henry looked. He saw no peas anywhere. He saw long green pods hanging on the plant. "Maybe the peas are lost," said Henry. He picked one pod. He squeezed it. It popped open. Inside was a row of little green peas, sitting like beads. "There they are!" said Henry. "Peas grow inside pods on the plant!"

Kennedy picked a pod too. It popped open. More peas inside. They put the peas in a basket, one pod at a time. "We grew these," said Henry. He held the basket up to the sun.

Natalie went to Papa's office with him. There was a big couch and a small shelf. On the shelf sat a tablet.

Papa showed Natalie the round button. Natalie pushed it. The screen lit up. She made a happy face and stuck out her tongue, the way she did when she was working hard. Papa showed her the little paint picture on the screen. Natalie tapped it. A drawing app opened. She drew a red circle and a yellow sun.

Then Papa had to talk on the phone. Natalie kept drawing. She drew a tall tree. She drew a cat. At last she was done, and she wanted to look at Papa's books. She put the tablet on the couch and climbed down to the floor.

Papa's friend came over to sit on the couch. He did not see the tablet. "Wait," said Natalie. She picked up the tablet fast. She looked at the shelf. Papa nodded to her. Natalie put the tablet on its shelf, in its special spot.

"Good job," said Papa's friend. Natalie smiled. The tablet was safe. When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place, and Natalie knew just where that was.

Ezra loved his little green dinosaur. He brought it to daycare every day. But now it was gone.

"Where did it go?" Ezra asked. "I don't know," said his friend Andrea. "Let's look in the block corner." They looked there. They looked under the table. They looked in the toy box. No dinosaur. Ezra felt like crying.

Then Kaiden came over. "More helpers can look in more spots," said Kaiden. So Ezra asked Ms. Aquino too. Ms. Aquino looked by the bookshelf. Kaiden peeked behind the cubbies. Andrea checked the sand table. Ezra heard the sand crunch under her hands.

"Look!" said Andrea. "It's here!" The dinosaur was tucked in the sand, warm from the sun. Ezra hugged it tight. "Thank you, everyone," he said. "Now let's go play with the dinosaur together."

Hazel was ready for book club. She sat on the red rug. Ms. Côté held up a big card. "This is K," said Ms. Côté. "K says kuh, kuh."

Hazel tried to write K on her paper. Her K came out all wrong. The legs went the wrong way. "Silly K," Hazel said. "You keep flipping!"

"Try this," said Wynter. Wynter handed her a bumpy card. The K on it was rough like a leaf. "You can trace it," Wynter said.

Helix traced the bumpy K with her finger. Up the tall stick. In the little leg. Out the big leg. Again and again. "Kuh, kuh," she said.

Then she wrote K on her paper. It came out just right! Hazel filled the whole page with Ks. "Look, Philippe! Kuh, kuh, kuh!"

Arya was at Grandma's house. Grandma made warm toast. The kettle was hot, so Grandma kept it far away. Arya wanted to help with breakfast.

"Can I put on the butter?" asked Arya. Grandma gave her a small knife with a dull edge. Arya held the toast near her plate. She spread the butter slowly. The butter melted and got shiny. "I did it!" said Arya with a big smile.

Then Grandma put out a small cup. Arya picked up the milk jug. She poured fast. Splash! Milk went all over the table. "Oh no," said Arya. Grandma wiped it up with a cloth.

"Try again," said Grandma. Arya filled the cup once more. This time she poured slowly. The milk went up, up, up. It stayed right in the cup. No splash at all. Arya took a bite of her toast. Then she drank her milk. "Grandma, look! Not one drop came out!"

Avery ran to the front door. She looked out the little window. "Sunny!" she shouted. The sun made the steps glow.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell, tap tap tap. Avery put on her sneakers. She wanted to jump in the big puddle. Splash! Her feet went in. Her socks got all soggy. "Wet feet," said Avery. She wiggled her toes. Squish, squish.

"Try your rain boots," said her dad. Avery pulled them on. They felt tight at first. Then she stamped her feet. The rain boots went up high. Splash! Splash! Her toes stayed dry. "Rain boots keep my feet dry!" she yelled. She jumped again and again. Her friend Patrick came by in his rain boots too. "It's rainy and we are dry!" he said.

The wind blew hard and whooshed her hood off. That night, Avery put her rain boots by the door, all in a row. "For the next puddle," she said. She patted them, one by one.

Edouard ran to the table at school. He sat down next to Ryan. "Is today the library day?" he asked. Ryan shrugged. "Yesterday we painted," Ryan said. "The library is not yesterday. It is a different day."

Mouhamed came in with a big book bag. "The library is today!" he said. "Ms. Ho told me now, this morning." Edouard jumped up. Today was the day that was happening right now. Not yesterday. Not tomorrow. Right now!

The class walked to the library. Edouard wanted a book about big trucks. He looked on the shelf. It was hard to find. He looked again. He looked one more time. Then he saw it, way up high. "I found it," he said. Ms. Ho smiled. "You can keep it until Friday," she said. "That is later." Edouard hugged the book. "Today I found it," he said. "Later I will read it again and again."

Mila was at Grandma's house. She wanted to draw a cat on the tablet. She pressed the big round button. One, two, three. The screen stayed black. "Oh no," said Mila. "Did I break it?"

Grandma looked. "The tablet is asleep," she said. "It needs power." Mila found the charger under the couch. It was a long white cord. She carried it to Grandma. Grandma plugged the charger into the wall. "Now we wait," said Grandma.

Mila counted the cat on the wall while she waited. One cat, two cats, three cats. Then the screen lit up. Mila pressed the button. The tablet woke up! She tapped the little paint pot. One tap, two taps. The drawing app opened.

Mila drew a cat with orange hair. She gave it whiskers. She gave it a hat. Then she was done. She pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf.

Grandma smiled. "You put it away all by yourself."

"I did," said Mila. "Goodnight, tablet."

Ava sat on Grandpa's big soft chair. The soccer game was on the TV. Her friends Arnaaz and Zariah sat on the rug. Grandma brought sticky buns on a plate.

The blue team ran and ran. They ran so fast. "The blue team runs the most," said Ava. "They will win."

The game ended. The blue team still ran more. But Ava looked at the screen. The numbers said red two, blue one.

"Red has more points," said Zariah. "Red wins the game."

Ava clapped her hands. She had a small problem in her head, and now it was solved. Running a lot did not win. More points won.

Then Grandma called, "Snack time. Come and feed your tummies." The kids ate sticky buns. Arnaaz said, "Next time I will watch the numbers." Ava smiled and took one more bun.

Jaxson sat at the big table in writing club. Ms. Morningstar put a pencil in his hand. "Grip it like this," she said. "Two fingers on top." Jaxson tried. His letters came out wobbly. The J looked like a squiggle.

"Maybe you can't write it," said Brandon. Jaxson felt worried. Ms. Morningstar smiled. "Just write it again," she said. Jaxson wrote his name one more time. Then again. Then again. He made a tall mountain of papers, all with his name.

Soon the letters stood up straight. The J had a strong hook. The X had two neat lines. "Look!" said Abdullah. "Your name is easy now!" Jaxson grabbed a fresh sheet. He wrote JAXSON big and clear. "That one is for you," he told Ms. Morningstar. She clapped her hands.

Lily was at the park with her friend Luc. Luc had a big red ball. Lily wanted to play with it too.

Luc threw the ball far. It rolled into the mud. Lily got mad. She stomped her feet and made a big frown. "Luc threw my ball away!" she said.

Ms. Bear came over. She sat down next to Lily. "Try this," she said. "Breathe in slow. Now breathe out slow." Lily took a slow, deep breath. Then she took another one. Her tummy felt calmer. Her feet stopped stomping.

Lily looked at the ball. Luc picked it up from the mud. He washed it at the water fountain. Then he held it out to Lily. "Want to show me how to roll it?" he asked. Lily smiled big. She rolled the ball, and Luc chased it laughing across the grass.

Victoria stood in the school hallway. It was her first day of school. She held her mama's hand very tight. The hallway smelled like crayons and apples. Shoes went tap, tap, tap on the floor.

Victoria saw a door with a red apple on it. Children went in one by one. Victoria did not move. She felt a little sad. She did not know anyone in that room.

Then a grown-up came out. She had a smile and a name tag. "Hello. I am Ms. Morin," she said. "I am the teacher. I look after the children and help them in our class."

A boy named Stevie walked in. A girl named Lya walked in. Then Victoria let go of her mama's hand. She planted her feet and took one step. Then two steps. Then three.

Ms. Morin held the door. "Would you like to sit on the little chair by the window?" she asked.

Victoria sat down on the chair. It was just her size. "Hello, Ms. Morin," she said.

"Hello, Victoria," said Ms. Morin, and she hung Victoria's backpack on a low hook.

Eva was three today. Her party was at the big community hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a ball to play with, too.

Philemon put a box on the table. It was wrapped in blue paper. Eva looked at it. What could be inside? She could not see. The paper hid it all. She shook the box. Something went bump, bump. She squeezed it. It felt a little soft. "I can't see inside," she said. "The paper hides it."

"Maybe it's a scary spider!" said Philemon. Eva laughed. "No, it is not a spider." Gracelyn marched over to look too. "Just open it," she said. But Eva had to wait. First they ate cake. Ms. Navarro, the neighbour, helped cut it with a safe knife. Then it was time.

Eva tore the paper off. Rip, rip, rip! Inside was a soft brown bear. She hugged it tight. "So that is what was hiding in there," she said. Philemon clapped his hands. "Now we can see it!" said Gracelyn. Eva held the bear up high. "Hello, bear," she whispered.

Hayden looked out the window. Snow was all over the backyard. School was shut today. It was a snow day.

Hayden put on his boots. He ran outside. He made a big snowball. It was round and white. "I will keep you," Hayden said. He put the snowball in a bucket. He carried it inside. He set it by his toy box.

Hayden played with his toy cars. Then it was lunch time. After lunch, he went back to his snowball. The bucket felt light. The snowball was small now. There was water in the bottom. Hayden was mad at first. "Where did my snowball go?" he said.

Then he had an idea. He got a fresh cup of snow from outside. He set it on the warm kitchen table. He watched and watched. The snow got small. The snow turned to water. The warm room made the snow melt.

Hayden smiled. He filled a new cup with snow. He put it in the freezer. "Stay cold," he said softly. He shut the freezer door.

Riley woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said Mom. Riley put on her boots and her red coat. She went next door to Mr. Nguyen's yard, where the snow was deep and smooth.

Riley wanted to make a snow angel. She had never made one before. She lay down in the snow. She swept her arms up and down. She swept her legs out and in. Then she tried to stand up in the middle. Her boot made a big smudge. "Oh no," said Riley. "My angel has a muddy foot."

Mr. Nguyen came out with a broom. "Try again," he said with a smile. "This time, move away slowly." Riley lay down in a fresh spot. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. Then she rolled to the side and stood up very carefully. She looked back and gasped. There it was, a beautiful snow angel with wings, and no smudge at all.

A boy ran by with his sled. "Nice angel!" he called. Riley waved. Then she lay down again in the new snow. Sweep, sweep, roll away. She made one more angel, then one more, until the whole yard was full of wings.

Arlo was in the backyard with his striped ball. It was evening. Then all the lights went out.

"Mom! The lights are gone!" said Arlo.

Mom came outside with a big lamp. "The power went out," she said.

Arlo looked up at the house. One dark window. Two dark windows. Three dark windows.

"Did our house stop working?" he asked.

"Let's look at the street," said Mom.

Arlo looked out past the fence. The neighbor's house was dark too. And the next house. And the next one.

"Wow! Their lights are out too!" said Arlo. "So one power cut can make all the houses on the street go dark at once?"

"Yes," said Mom. "All together."

Arlo counted the dark houses. One, two, three, four. He smiled.

Then the lights came back on. The window lit up. The neighbor's window lit up too.

"The power came back for everyone!" said Arlo.

Mom held out her hand. "Let's go in and find the flashlight anyway."

Arlo picked up his striped ball. He ran to the door, and the whole street glowed behind him.

Ivy sat at the little table in the art room. Mr. Wong gave her a fat pencil and a piece of paper. "Now we write our names," he said. Ivy gripped the pencil in her fist. She tried to make an I. But the paper slid away. Her line went crooked. The paper slid again and her pencil almost fell.

August sat next to her. He was not lazy about helping. He leaned over and said, "Watch me." August put his left hand flat on his paper. He held it still. Then he wrote his A with his other hand. His letter was straight.

Ivy looked at her own two hands. She pressed one hand down on the paper. The paper stopped sliding. She drew the I, then the V, then the Y. "I did it!" she said. Mr. Wong smiled. "Ivy wrote Ivy," he said, and taped it to the wall.

Leo sat on the living room rug. The tablet lay dark in front of him. He tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. He tapped it again and again. Still nothing.

Dad sat down next to him. "This little button turns it on," Dad said. He showed Leo the button on the side. Leo pressed it. The screen lit up. Leo laughed. One press, and the dark screen woke up!

Leo tapped the drawing app. He drew a big spotted cat. Then he drew a cat with a bump on its head, like a funny hat. "More cats," Leo said. He drew one more cat.

Soon it was time for dinner. "All done," said Dad. Leo pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in its basket, soft and safe. "Night night, tablet," Leo whispered.

Beatrice loved her basketball team. She wore a red shirt with a big number five. Her coach said, "Run, Beatrice, run!" Beatrice ran fast.

Today the other team won the game. Beatrice felt grumpy. Her face felt hot and her eyes felt watery. She sat down on the bench. "We lost," she said. Her dad sat next to her. He patted her back.

Then Coach blew the whistle. "Line up, everyone," he said. Beatrice saw both teams make one long line. She held hands with Oskar and Violet from her team. Each player walked past each player on the other team.

"Good game," said a boy in a blue shirt. "Good game," said Beatrice. "Good game," said Violet. They said it over and over. "Good game, good game, good game." Beatrice saw the big kids do it too. Even the tall boy said it.

After the line, Beatrice did not feel so grumpy. A boy on the other team told her a joke. "Why did the ball go to bed? Because it was tired!" Beatrice laughed and laughed. "That was a kind thing to say," said her dad. "You said good game to everyone."

At home, Beatrice would bathe and eat warm soup. She held her dad's hand all the way to the car. "Same time next week?" her dad asked. Beatrice nodded and bounced her ball one more time.

Elliot sat at the big table. It was dinner time. His friend Agatha was there too. Her family came for dinner on this warm day. Dad poured milk into two little cups. Elliot had a new toy car in his pocket.

Elliot held the car up. "Want to see it go?" he asked. Agatha nodded. Elliot zoomed the car down his arm. It stopped at his elbow. "My turn now?" asked Agatha. Elliot pulled the car close to his tummy. He did not want to give it up.

"Can we share it?" Mom asked. Elliot thought. At school, Mr. Marino had a big red timer. When the timer rang, Elliot gave the truck to Jerome. He had almost tossed it. Then he held it out slowly, with two hands. Jerome smiled and said, "Thank you." Elliot remembered that now.

So Elliot held out the car. He placed it in Agatha's hands, gently, with two hands. Agatha zoomed it down her arm. It went vroom, vroom. The car smelled like soap and felt smooth and cool. "Why do you give it slow?" Agatha asked. "So it does not break," said Elliot. Then he counted to ten, nice and slow, while he waited. Agatha zoomed the car one more time. Then she held it out to him with two hands.

"Your turn," she said.

Everett sat very still on the backyard grass. He wanted to win the sense game. Ms. Bianchi had said, "Name five senses. Tell me the body part for each." Everett knew four already. He could see with his eyes. He could smell with his nose. He could taste with his mouth. He could touch with his hands. But the last one made him bend his head and think.

Then he heard something. Tweet, tweet, went a bird in the red feeder. "My ears!" said Everett. "We hear with our ears!" He jumped up. He ran to find Collins.

"Close your eyes," said Everett. Collins closed his eyes. "What do you hear?" Collins listened. "A dog," he said. "Woof, woof!" went the dog next door. "And a bee buzzed by my ear!" Everett laughed. "Ears hear it all," he said. "Even with eyes shut."

Everett put his hand on his chest. His heart went thump, thump, fast from running. He touched the soft grass. He sniffed a flower. "Nose, mouth, hands, eyes, ears," he said. "Five senses! I did it!" He did a happy jump. Then he sat down again, very still. His ears heard the bird. Tweet, tweet.

Jake sat at the big dinner table. Lucille and Gurnaaz sat there too. One truck sat on the table. It was Jake's shiny red truck. Lucille reached for it. Jake grabbed it fast, right out of her hands. Lucille's face went sad. Then she began to cry.

"Lucille, don't cry," said Jake. He looked at her wet eyes. He looked at his hands on the truck. He gave the truck back to her. "Your turn first," he said. "Then my turn." Lucille stopped crying. She smiled and pushed the truck. "Beep, beep!" she said.

In the kitchen, a pot hung on a hook. Daddy took the pot down. He stirred thin noodles inside. Jake counted his turns. "One turn for Lucille. Two turns for Gurnaaz. Three turns for me." He waited and waited. Then the truck came back to him. "Vroom!" said Jake. "Now it is my turn. Want to share it again tomorrow, Lucille?"

"Maybe with a big truck," said Lucille.

Owen wore his striped shirt to daycare. He ate breakfast fast, because he wanted the big truck. Kareem wanted the truck too. Mr. Almeida said, "You can take turns." Owen went first. He pushed the truck across the rug. Vroom!

Then Remy lay down on the little cot. Remy closed his eyes. His breathing went slow and soft. Owen shouted, "Kareem, your turn!" Remy's eyes blinked open. His lip began to shake, and he rubbed his nose.

Owen looked at Remy. He made his voice very small. "Kareem," he whispered, "your turn." Kareem whispered back, "Okay." Remy closed his eyes again. His breathing went slow once more.

Owen pushed the truck quietly now. The wheels made a soft, smooth sound on the rug. He handed the truck to Kareem. "Shh," said Owen, with a smile.

Liam ran onto the baseball diamond. He wanted to play right away. "Let's start!" he said. His friend Desmond shook his head. "We warm up first," Desmond said. Ms. Eze blew her whistle. "Run to the fence and back," she said. "Then we stretch."

Liam puffed. He ran with Nihal. They stretched their arms. They stretched their legs. Liam felt his body get warm. His legs felt fast. His arms felt loose.

Then the game began. Liam swung the bat. He hit the ball far! He ran to first base. "Great hit," said Desmond. At home, Liam drew the diamond with his pencil. He wrote his name. "Sorry, no more jumping on the bed," his dad said, and shut the door. Liam smiled and slid into his blankets.

Miles sat at the dinner table. His peas rolled all over his plate. What a messy plate it was.

Dad put down the pot. Dad was not smiling. Dad let out a big sigh. Miles felt sad. He wanted Dad to be happy.

"Why is your face like that?" asked Miles.

"I felt nervous at work today," said Dad. "Grown-ups feel nervous too. Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Miles looked up. He did not know that. He thought only kids had feelings.

Miles picked up his spoon. He tapped it on his cup, ding, ding. Dad laughed a little. Miles tapped again, ding, ding, ding. Dad laughed a lot now.

Miles felt excited. He moved his spoon near the peas. One pea jumped to the spoon, like a little magnet. A surprise pea!

"You caught it!" said Dad.

Miles held out the spoon. "Dinner for you," he said.

Theodore went to the pharmacy with his dad. The pharmacy did not sell forks or toys. It sold real toothbrushes. Theodore picked a small blue one. "For the dentist," said his dad. Theodore was going to the dentist for the first time. He held the toothbrush tight. His tummy felt jumpy.

At the dentist's office there was a big chair. Theodore climbed up with help. Then the chair began to tip back. Slowly, slowly, it leaned. Theodore was lying down! He giggled. "It is like a ride," he said. The dentist looked in his mouth while Theodore lay back. "Open wide," the dentist said. Theodore opened wide.

The dentist counted his teeth. One, two, three, all the way up. "Nice clean teeth," said the dentist. Theodore sat up when the chair came back. He smiled with his whole face. He waved his new blue toothbrush. "Bye, big chair," he said.

Daniel went to the laundromat with his dad. The washers rumbled like a big truck. Daniel watched the clothes roll around in the round window.

Then it was time to go. Daniel put on his coat. He found one sleeve. His other arm could not find the other sleeve. "This is bad," he said.

A girl named Stephanie was there too. She had on a puffy red coat. "Watch me," she said. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. Her coat was on!

"Can I do that?" Daniel asked. "Try it," said Stephanie. Daniel laid his coat down. He pushed his arms in. He flipped it up and over. His coat was on! He pulled the zipper up, all by himself.

Outside, a truck rolled by. Daniel waved at it in his warm coat. "I did it myself," he said.

Nora sat on the rug at home. She had a big job. She wanted to make two piles. One pile for animals. One pile for toys.

She put her cat in the animal pile. The cat was soft and warm. It blinked its wide eyes and went to sleep. Nora put her rubber duck in the toy pile. The duck was yellow and had a funny shape.

Then Nora held her toy dog. It was brown and fluffy. She put it in the animal pile. She looked at it. She looked at the cat. The cat moved and purred. The toy dog did not move at all. Nora picked the toy dog up. She hugged it. It stayed still and quiet. It was not alive. Nora put it in the toy pile, next to the duck.

After her work, Nora was thirsty. She drank some milk from her cup. Then Sabrina came to play. "Look," said Nora. She pointed at the toy pile. "The dog goes here."

Madison woke up and saw white snow outside. "No school today," said her dad. "We can go to the park." Madison put on her boots and mittens. Off they went to the park, and Madison made a big snow hill. Her mittens got very wet and dirty.

At home, Madison wanted to go back out. She pulled on her mittens. They were cold and drippy. "Wet mittens and boots are left out to dry after playing in the snow," said her dad. He hung her mittens by the door. He set her boots next to them.

Madison waited by the door. She watched her mittens drip, drip, drip. Soon the mittens stopped dripping. She touched them. They felt dry! "The park is still there," said her dad with a smile. Madison pulled on her dry mittens. "Next stop, snow hill!" she said.

Claaire was going to the dentist for the first time. She held her mom's hand in the waiting room. There was a fish tank with spotted fish swimming like a little ocean. Claire wanted to see the dentist's chair, but she felt shy.

A kind lady in a blue coat said, "Hello, Claire. Come and sit in my big chair." Claire climbed up slowly. Then a bright light clicked on above her head. Claire squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright!

The dentist saw Claire squint. She handed Claire a small pair of sunglasses. "Try these," she said. Claire put them on and opened her eyes. The light did not hurt now. Claire saw the dentist smile. "The light helps me see inside your mouth," the dentist said. Claire opened her mouth wide, like a sleepy lion. "Good job," said the dentist. Claire took one more peek at the spotted fish on her way out.

Jayden ran to the paint table at school. "I want to paint a big dog today!" he said. But the paint cups were empty. All the paint was gone.

Jayden felt like crying. Mr. Vu knelt down beside him. "Don't worry," said Mr. Vu. "The paint will come later, after snack time. You can paint then."

"Later is too long," said Jayden.

Just then, his friend Colten sat down. "I went to the park tomorrow," said Colten. Then Colten stopped. He peeked at the big calendar on the wall. "No, wait. Not tomorrow. Yesterday. We went yesterday, before today."

Jayden looked at the calendar too. He saw yesterday's picture. It was the day with the red dot. Yesterday was the day before today. Then he had an idea.

"Mr. Vu! Yesterday we had paint!" said Jayden. "We painted the fish yesterday. The paint came from the big box."

"Yes, it did," said Mr. Vu with a smile. "Good remembering. Let's go peek in the cabinet now."

The cabinet was not broken. It opened with a little click. Inside sat the big box of paint. Mr. Vu poured blue paint into the cups. It went drip, drip, drip.

"Now I can paint my dog now!" said Jayden. He painted a big blue dog with spots.

Colten gave him a hug. "Nice dog," said Colten. "Tomorrow we can paint a cat."

"Yes!" said Jayden. "Tomorrow, after today."

Paisley's grandma was coming by train. She would sleep in the guest bedroom for a whole week. Paisley helped Mom make the bed. The blanket was thick and soft. Paisley put a small paper flag on the pillow. "Grandma can have my flag," she said.

Then Dad took Paisley to the train station. They stood on the platform to wait. Paisley heard a loud sound. "The train is coming!" she said. She wanted to lean out to see it. Dad held her hand. "Stand back from the edge," he said. "Wait until the train stops."

Paisley looked down. There was a yellow line on the floor. Everyone stood behind it. The big train went whoosh, whoosh. Then it stopped. Only then did the people walk to the doors.

Grandma stepped off the train. She hugged Paisley tight. At home, Paisley showed her the guest bedroom. Grandma saw the thick blanket and the little flag. "All aboard for bed," said Grandma, with a smile.

Anthony wanted a story about a big red truck. He looked on his shelf in his bedroom. He found a little blue book. He sat on the rug and opened it.

He opened the book from the back. He turned the pages. The pictures looked all mixed up. The truck was at the end. The truck was smashed first, and whole later. "That is not right," said Anthony.

His friend Koda came in. Koda sat down beside him. "Can I see?" asked Koda. He used his polite hand to point, not grab. Anthony held out the book. Koda turned the book over. He opened the front cover. "Start here," said Koda.

Anthony turned the pages one by one. First the truck was shiny and new. Then it bumped a rock. Then a wheel began to wobble. Then the wheel would break off. Then the driver fixed it with a smile. "Now it tells it right," said Anthony. He read to the back cover, all the way to the end.

"Again," said Koda. Anthony flipped the book back to the front. He opened the front cover. He patted the rug next to him. "You turn the pages too," he said. Koda turned page one.

Kai sat in his soft reading nook. He had paper and a fat crayon. He wanted to write his own name.

Kai wrote k, a, i. He looked at it. Something was wrong. The first letter looked little.

His name card lay on the pillow. It said Kai. The K there was big and tall. Why was that K so big?

Kai tapped the small k. Then he tapped the big K. Big K, small k. Same letter, same sound.

He grabbed his crayon. He made the k big and tall. Now his paper said Kai, just like the card.

The cat jumped up. She licked the hair on her paw. "Look, cat," said Kai. "That says me!"

Kai pointed at each letter. "K. A. I. Kai!"

Then he wrote it again, big K first.

Ellie wanted to paint at daycare. She asked Ms. Pritchard, "Is it time now?"

"Not now," said Ms. Pritchard. "Paint time comes later."

Ellie frowned. Later felt very far away. She looked around the room. On the wall was a big shiny clock. It had a face and two hands.

"That is a clock," said her friend Frederique. "A clock shows what time it is."

Ellie watched the clock. She waited. The little hand moved. Then Ms. Pritchard clapped her hands.

"Paint time now!" she said.

Ellie laughed. "Now came!" she said.

Frederique brought Ellie a red paint pot. Ellie dipped her brush and made a big sun.

"Tomorrow we can paint again," said Frederique.

"Tomorrow," said Ellie. She pointed at the clock. "The clock will know."

Sophie was at Grandma's house. Dinner was almost ready. Grandma set the big pot on the table. "First we say our blessing," said Grandma.

Sophie sat very still. She did not know the blessing. It was long and new to her. Grandma folded her hands. Sophie folded her hands too. Grandma began to speak. Sophie listened hard.

Then the doorbell rang. Aarna and Elliana came in to meet everyone for dinner. Sophie still held her hands folded. "Is the blessing still going?" she whispered. She wanted her food, but she did not want to be rude. So she waited.

Grandma said more words. Then Grandma said, "Amen." Everyone said, "Amen!" Then everyone picked up their forks. Sophie saw it. When Grandma said Amen, the blessing was done. The forks all went down to the plates.

Sophie picked up her fork too. She ate a big bite of rice. Aarna made a silly face. Elliana giggled. Sophie smiled. Next time, she would listen for the word. At last Grandma brought out warm bread. Everyone said, "Amen!" and Sophie said it loudest of all.

Eliana sat on a red bench. She was at the big sports field with her dad. There was a game to watch today.

"I don't see a ball," said Eliana. "Where is the ball?"

Her friend Maddie sat down next to her. "There is no ball," said Maddie. "Look at the ice."

The players skated on the ice. They each held a long stick. Eliana watched closely. What would they play with?

Then she saw it. Something small slid past her. It was flat, like a little black rock. It was not round like a ball.

"That is a puck," said Maddie. "The players use their sticks to hit the puck."

A player swung his stick. Tap! The puck slid fast across the ice. Another player hit it back. Tap! The puck went the other way. Eliana followed it with her eyes. The puck was hard to follow. It moved so fast!

Maddie pointed. "Now it is coming to us!"

The puck slid toward the red bench. A player reached out with his stick. He tapped it away. The puck turned and slid back down the ice.

"Can we follow it again?" asked Eliana.

"Yes," said Maddie. "Watch the puck go!"

Eliana clapped her hands. "Tap, tap, tap," she said. "Go, little puck, go!"

Billie sat on the big square rug at the community centre. Ms. Njoroge had a drum. She tapped it slowly. Tap, tap, tap. "Can you clap with me?" she asked.

Billie tried to clap. Her claps were too fast. They ran ahead of the drum. Kaia clapped just right. Billie felt worried. She hid her hands under her legs.

Ms. Njoroge sat next to Billie. "Watch my hand," she said. "Wait for each tap." Billie watched the drum. Tap. Billie clapped. Tap. Billie clapped. Her claps matched the drum now!

"Now let's sing," said Ms. Njoroge. "A short rhyming song for little ones is called a nursery rhyme." She sang about a star. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star. How I wonder what you are."

Billie sang it too. She got some words wrong. Remington helped her. They sang it again. And again. Soon Billie knew every word by herself.

She sang about the star shining up high. She clapped the steady beat. Kaia clapped with her. Billie smiled big. "I did it!" she said. Ms. Njoroge clapped for her, too.

Ethan held Mommy's hand at the grocery store. His bunny was gone. Bunny was not in his pocket. Ethan wanted to cry, but he stopped.

Ms. Mendoza worked at the store. She smiled at Ethan. "Where did you go first?" she asked. "The flower stand," said Ethan. "I saw the yellow flower." They walked to the flowers. The buckets were full of water. No bunny there. "Next we looked at apples," said Ethan. They went to the apples. No bunny. "Then the bread," said Ethan. They went to the bread. No bunny.

"Last we stood at the milk," said Ethan. They walked to the milk. There, on the shelf, sat bunny. Bunny was leaning on a milk carton. Ethan hugged bunny tight. Ms. Mendoza laughed. "You went back to every place, in order," she said. "Smart boy." Ethan held bunny all the way home.

James held his little red backpack. Inside was his toy boat, Bob. Dad said, "It is time to go on the ferry."

At the terminal, Dad put the backpack on a moving belt. The backpack went into a big machine. James could not see Bob anymore. "Bob is gone!" said James. His tummy felt tight.

Then Dad pointed. "Look at the other side." The backpack slid out, all safe and dry. James opened it fast. There was Bob! The machine had checked what was inside, and Bob was still there. James hugged Bob tight. "Good machine," said James. He waved at it.

On the ferry, James held Bob up to the window. "Bob, look! Water everywhere!" The boat went whoosh, and spray tickled James's nose. Bob got one little splash, but he stayed mostly dry. Dad laughed. "Silly Bob. He already had his ride."

Emily sat at the big table. She had a jar of jam. The lid was on too tight. She pulled and pulled. The lid would not come off. Emily pushed the jar away. "Oh no," she said.

Her mom was washing a cup at the sink. Emily slid down from her chair. She walked over and tugged on her mom's apron. "Can you help me, please?" she said. Her mom smiled. "Of course," she said. She wiped her hands on the towel.

They went back to the table. Her mom held the jar. She turned the lid. Pop! It came off. "Thank you," said Emily. Her mom gave her a spoon. Emily dipped it in. The jam was red and sweet. She took a little bite. Then she held the jar out to her mom. "You want some too?" her mom asked. Emily nodded. "Open wide," said her mom, and she did.

Wesley ran to the park with his red bag. He wanted to play the sorting game with Ayoub and Emerson. Ms. Hughes had set out three big circles on the grass. One circle held toy cars. One circle held stuffed animals. One circle was empty.

"Put the food here," said Ms. Hughes. Wesley pulled out a shiny apple. He set it down in the empty circle. Then he pulled out a soft piece of bread. He set that down too. At last he found a carrot. It was long and orange. He put it with the toy cars by mistake.

Ayoub looked at the carrot. "That is not a toy," he said. Wesley picked up the carrot. He turned it over in his hands. Then he put it next to the apple and the bread. "Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Emerson, clapping. Ms. Hughes gave a kiss to the top of Wesley's head.

After the game, the sky turned gray. The children looked up. Big raindrops began to fall. They ran under the roof by the swings. The rain made little ponds on the ground. Then the sun peeked out. Emerson pointed at the sky. "Look, a rainbow!" A big rainbow arched over the park. Wesley waved at it with his carrot still in his hand.

Henri was at summer camp. It was time for a snack. Mr. Clarke said, "First we wash our hands."

Henri ran to the sink. He stood on his toes. The tap was too far away. "I can't reach," said Henri. His ears felt hot and he wanted to cry.

Mr. Clarke brought a step stool. He put it by the sink and stayed close. Henri climbed up. Now his hands reached the water. He put soap on his hands. Sia stood next to him. They rubbed the soap together. "We count to twenty," said Sia. Henri counted, "One, two, three." He sang the rest of the numbers with her.

The water washed the bubbles away. The bubbles went down the drain. Henri looked at his hands. They were clean and shiny. He climbed down and ate his snack. It was a sweet, red strawberry. "Good washing," said Mr. Clarke. Henri smiled and licked his fingers. "All clean," said Sia.

Caleb woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! No school today. It was a snow day.

Dad took Caleb to the sledding hill. The snow was deep and white. It looked like a big, quiet ocean. Caleb saw Lilianna there with her green sled.

Caleb climbed to the top. He lay down on his sled. He wanted to go down head first, like a penguin.

"Wait," said Dad. "Not like that. Sit up on the sled. Face the front. Hold on with both hands."

Caleb sat up. He faced the front. He held on tight.

"I will watch from right here," said Dad.

Whoosh! Caleb went down the hill. He sat up the whole way. He did not tip over. He landed in the soft snow and laughed.

Lilianna lay down on her sled next. Then she sat up too. She faced the front and held on. Dad watched her too. Whoosh! Down she went.

"My turn again!" said Caleb. He pulled his sled up the hill, one small step at a time.

Lucy's birthday party was in the backyard. Lenna and Ilyas came with a big cake. The cake had four pink candles.

Lucy found the matches on the table. She picked them up. She wanted to light the candles herself.

"Stop there, Lucy," said Dad. "Matches are for grown-ups. Lighting candles is a grown-up job."

Lucy put the matches down. "Sorry, Dad," she said.

"But you get the best part," said Dad. "You make the wish."

Dad lit the candles. The little flames glowed in the evening air. Everyone began to clap. Even the neighbor's cow mooed from the other yard.

Lucy took a big breath. She closed her eyes. She made a wish. Then she blew and blew.

All four flames went out at once. The smoke curled up like little grey ribbons. Lucy had not expected that.

"Look!" said Ilyas. "The wish took them all!"

Lenna laughed and clapped again. Dad cut the cake with a big knife, carefully, all by himself. He gave Lucy the first slice.

Lucy took a bite. The cake was sweet and soft. "Best wish ever," she whispered.

Then Lucy watched Dad blow out the last candle on his own slice of cheese. "Hey," she said. "Dad, you did the grown-up job again!"

Rowan was in the playroom with his friend Aveer. They had a big box of toy cars. Aveer grabbed a red car. Rowan grabbed a blue car. They zoomed the cars all over the rug.

Then Malaika held up a green circle of paper. "Go!" she called. Rowan zoomed his blue car fast. Aveer's red car went fast too. Then Malaika held up a red circle. "Stop!" she called. But Aveer's car kept going. It bumped Rowan's car. A little toy frog fell off the rug.

"Oops," said Aveer. He picked up the frog. He put his curly hair behind his ear and looked at the circles. "Red means stop," said Malaika. "Green means go. That is how the big light by the road works. My mom told me."

They tried again. Malaika held up the red circle. Aveer stopped his car. Rowan stopped too. Then came the green circle. Both cars went zooming past the frog. "Green! Go go go!" yelled Rowan.

Ms. Pelletier peeked in at the door. "What a good game," she said. "May I hold a circle too?" She held up red, then green, then red again. Every car stopped just right.

At the end, Malaika held the red circle up high. Rowan parked his blue car in a line next to the red one. The little frog sat on top, like a green passenger waiting to go.

Hunter pulled the zipper on his jacket. Click, click, click! He was going to see Grandpa's special stone. "We will have bread there too," said Mom. "You can say the blessing."

Hunter had practiced all week. "It is called the Hamotzi," he told his friend Duke at school. Duke clapped for him. Now the big day was here!

They walked past the quiet stones. The grass smelled green and fresh. Hunter put one small rock on Grandpa's stone, just like Mom showed him.

Then they sat on a bench. Mom opened the basket. "Oops," said Hunter. He almost spilled the juice, but Mom caught it. "Close one, you naughty cup," Hunter said, and Mom laughed.

Mom held up the bread. "Ready, Hunter?" Hunter took a big breath. He said the Hamotzi, all by himself. His words felt warm in the air.

Mom tore the bread and gave him a piece. "Grandpa would like that," she said. Hunter took a big, happy bite.

Emilia sits in the waiting room. She is at the doctor's office. Today she will get a shot.

"I will miss playing," she whispers to her mom. "My arm might hurt."

Mom holds her hand. "It is very fast," says Mom. "Then we can get ice cream."

The nurse calls Emilia's name. Emilia hugs her bear tight. The nurse counts, "One, two, three." The shot is done.

"Look," says the nurse. "After a shot, I put a small bandage over the spot."

Emilia picks a bandage with shiny stars on it. The nurse sticks it on her arm.

Later, at the ice cream shop, Emilia lifts her sleeve. "See my stars!" she says. Mom smiles and gives her a lick of the cone.

"The stars stay on my arm," says Emilia. "Now ice cream is my fun part."

Kinsley loves her teddy bear. She brings him to school every day. At nap time, Mr. Ndlovu turns off the big lights. The room gets dark. Kinsley holds her teddy tight.

Then teddy falls. Plop. He falls off her mat. Kinsley hears the soft thump with her ears. She looks with her eyes. But the room is dark. She cannot see teddy anywhere. "Where did he go?" she whispers.

Kinsley is afraid to move. The dark hides everything. She smells popcorn from the hall. That is snack time smell. But she still cannot find teddy. She reaches out with her arm and touches the floor with her hand. She feels only carpet.

"Mr. Ndlovu," she calls. "Teddy fell. I cannot see him." Mr. Ndlovu comes over. He clicks on the little lamp. The light makes the corner bright. There is teddy! His soft paw pokes out by the shelf. Kinsley picks him up and hugs him. Then she tastes her sweet popcorn at snack time, with teddy on her lap.

"Dark hides things," says Kinsley. "Light shows them." Mr. Ndlovu smiles and pats the lamp.

Blake woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. Her dad put two pieces of toast on a plate. "Can I butter it?" Blake asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will get the butter for you."

Blake took the hard butter from the fridge. She pushed it on the toast. The butter tore a big hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Blake. Dad smiled. "Let's try again. This butter sat out on the counter. It is soft now."

Blake spread the soft butter. It went on smooth and easy. No holes! Then she poured milk into her cup. She poured slowly. Only one little drop spilled. Dad clapped. Then Cara knocked at the door, holding a jar of jam. "We made fresh jam at my house," Cara said. Blake held up the knife. "Look, I can spread it myself."

Lydia wanted to wear her yellow shirt. It was on the kitchen floor. It had a big jam spot on it. "Yucky jam," said Lydia. "What an ugly spot!"

Her dad picked up the shirt. He put it in the basket by the door. "Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket," he said, "so they can be washed." Lydia looked at the basket. It was tall and round, like a hoop.

She found one sock under the chair. She tossed it. The sock went in. "Basket!" Lydia cheered. She found another sock. Toss. In it went. "Basket again!" She laughed and jumped.

Then her sock hit the edge and fell out. Lydia picked it up. She got closer this time. Toss. In. "You need a hug, sock," she said, and she hugged the basket too.

Soon the water in the washing machine went round and round. The clothes began to float and flip. Lydia watched from her stool. "Wash my yellow shirt," she said. "Then I can wear it after my bath and my nap." The shirt tumbled up, then down. Round and round, round and round. Lydia waved at it through the little window. "Bye bye, ugly spot," she said.

Ryan was at Grandpa's house. It was cold outside. Ryan wanted to wear his new coat.

The coat had no zipper. It had buttons. Ryan did not know what to do.

Grandpa held the coat open. He pointed to a small hole in the cloth. "That is a buttonhole," he said.

Ryan pushed the first button. It would not go. The hole was too far away. Ryan pulled the coat sides close together. Now the button sat by the hole. He pushed it through. It went in!

The coat began to close. One side came to the other side, and the button held them together.

Ryan pushed the next button through its hole. Then the next one. He did them all by himself. The coat was on. It was warm and snug.

"Look, Grandpa!" Ryan said. He spun around fast. His coat spun too, wide like a bell.

Grandpa laughed. "Time to stir the soup," he said. Grandpa stirred the big pot. Ryan watched from his chair. Something smelled good.

Then Ryan heard a little pop. One button had come loose from its hole. Ryan found it and pushed it back through. All by himself again.

Kinsley waited at the airport. Grandma was coming today! She held a big paper sign. It said "GRANDMA" in red letters.

The doors opened. There was Grandma, waving fast. She pulled a big blue suitcase behind her. "That bag is huge!" said Kinsley. "It has all my clothes and things for a whole week," said Grandma. Kinsley helped pull the suitcase to the car. It went bump, bump, bump. It was heavy! "You packed so much," said Kinsley. Grandma laughed.

At home, Grandma opened the suitcase. Out came socks and sweaters. Then came something soft. It was a small pillow, just for Kinsley! It had a cat on it. "Grandma bought this for me?" asked Kinsley. "Just for you," said Grandma. Kinsley hugged the pillow tight. "A whole week is not too long," she said. Grandma smiled and pulled out one more surprise: a bad, wiggly toy snake, and everyone screamed and laughed at once.

Carter sat in his car seat. His bucket of toy frogs was on his lap. One frog felt slimy from the puddle. He wiped it on his shirt.

Tara sat next to him. She looked sad. "I want a frog," she said. "Please may I hold one?" Carter picked his best green frog. He put it in her hand. "Thank you, Carter," said Tara. Carter opened his mouth. Then he closed it. What should he say back?

His mom stopped the car. She gave the coach some tickets. "Thank you," said the coach. "You're welcome," said Mom. Carter watched. His eyes went wide. He heard the coach say thank you. Then Mom said you're welcome. So that was it!

At the next stop, Tara gave the frog back. "Thank you for letting me hold him," she said. Carter smiled big. "You're welcome!" he said. Tara clapped. The slimy frog sat in the bucket. Carter kept his hands on it all the way home.

Norah stood in line with her class. Today was taste day at school. Mr. Holloway held a big box of strawberries.

"First we look," said Mr. Holloway. Norah used her eyes to see the red berries. She used her ears to hear her friend Antonella giggle.

Norah picked up a strawberry. She touched it with her fingers. It felt bumpy with little seeds. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled sweet.

She took a bite. "Yum! It tastes so good," she said.

Then Melanie pinched her nose shut and bit her berry. "It tastes plain," said Melanie. "No sweet taste at all!"

"Why does it taste plain?" Norah asked.

"You held your nose closed," said Melanie. "Try it."

Norah pinched her nose. She bit her strawberry. It tasted like nothing much! She let go of her nose. The sweet taste came back.

Mr. Holloway smiled. "Now let's tie on these nice bibs and try the blueberries," he said.

Norah clapped her hands. "Can I hold my nose for that one too?"

Gabriella sat at the big kitchen table. Her cup was small. Dad's cup was big. She took a slow sip of cold milk.

Kevin came over to play. He ran to the door. He was fast. Gabriella walked behind him. She was slow. "Let's play a word game," said Kevin. "I say a word. You say one as different as it can be." He said, "Big!" Gabriella shouted, "Small!" Kevin laughed. He said, "Hot!" Gabriella thought of Dad's tea. She touched only the cold table, not the cup. She shouted, "Cold!" Kevin clapped. "Those are opposites," he said.

Then Kevin said, "Striped!" Gabriella looked at her socks. They had stripes. What word was as different as it could be? She looked and looked. She had a question on her face. Dad came over with a plate of warm toast. Gabriella pointed at the plain napkin. "Not striped!" she said. Kevin nodded. "Yes! That is how opposites work."

They ate the toast. The dog ran by, fast. Then it fell asleep, slow and still. Gabriella whispered, "Opposites." Then she took one more bite.

Ava went to the park with her dad. Mr. Sow was there with a big cloth bag. Elias and Amaira came to play too.

"Let's play the feely bag game," said Mr. Sow. "Put your hand in. Feel the toy. Then guess what it is."

Ava reached into the bag. Her fingers found something round. It was smooth and bumpy on one side. "A ball!" she said. Mr. Sow smiled. "Yes, it is a ball. Now guess the color."

"Red," said Ava. "My ball at home is red."

Amaira put her hand in next. She felt a small car. She could feel its wheels. But she could not feel its color. "I can't tell," said Amaira. "Why not?"

Mr. Sow said, "You see colors with your eyes. Fingers can't tell a color."

Ava pulled the ball out of the bag. She looked at it with her eyes. It was not red. It was yellow! Ava laughed. "My fingers fooled me!" Elias pulled out the car. It was blue. "Blue!" he said. Amaira held up a green frog. Everyone clapped.

They sat on the bottom step by the swings. They counted the toys: one, two, three, four. "Can we play again?" asked Ava. "Yes," said Mr. Sow. "Close your eyes and feel." Ava put her hand back in the bag.

Sebastian sat in the big waiting room chair. His feet did not touch the floor. "Today I see the dentist," he said. His mom smiled. "You are a lucky boy," she said. "The dentist is a tooth doctor."

Sebastian looked around. One fish, two fish, three fish swam in a tank. He watched the fish spin in a circle. One fish, two fish, three fish. Then a door opened. "Sebastian," said the dentist. "Come with me."

The dentist gave Sebastian a small cup. "Brush here," she said. "Then spit into the cup." Sebastian brushed. His mouth felt minty. He almost swallowed the foam. Then he remembered. He spat into the cup instead. "Good job," said the dentist. "You spit the toothpaste out. You don't swallow it."

Back in the waiting room, Sebastian found Livia. She held her own little cup. "I swallowed mine," she said. "It tasted like mint." Sebastian shook his head. "Spit it in the cup," he said. "Watch me." One, two, three, spit. Livia laughed and spat too. The minty foam went in the cup, not in their tummies. "All done," said Sebastian, and he spun his empty cup around like a drum.

Naomi had a striped bag. Into the bag went her socks. Into the bag went her bear. Into the bag went her shoes. "Time for our trip," said Mommy. Naomi held Mommy's hand the whole way.

The campsite had big trees. Naomi saw a tent. She saw a campfire, but Daddy held the stick. Naomi stayed far from the fire. She sat with her friend Aditya in the sand. They mixed sand and water in a cup. They patted it flat. "A sand cake," said Aditya. Naomi laughed and laughed.

At last they went home. "We unpack our bags and put things away," said Mommy. Out came the socks. Out came the bear. Out came her shoes. Naomi shook a shoe. Sand fell out, sprinkle, sprinkle. "The beach came home too," said Naomi. Mommy laughed and gave her a hug.

Avery ran to the playground with her mama. Today Bree would meet her there. Bree had been away for a whole week. Avery missed her friend so much.

"I feel so excited!" Avery said. She wanted to jump. She jumped up and down. She bounced near the swing. She shouted, "Bree! Bree!" But Bree was not there yet. Jumping did not make Bree come. Avery got tired of bouncing.

Ms. Swampy was sitting on the bench. "Try waiting like a turtle," she said. Avery sat still on the bench. She put her hands in her lap. She counted the birds on the fence. One, two, three. Waiting felt calmer now.

Then a bus stopped by the gate. Bree jumped off and waved. "Avery!" she called. Avery stood up fast. Her legs wanted to jump again. But she held Bree's hand instead. "I was so excited, I almost bounced away!" Avery said. Bree laughed. They ran to the swings together, all the way to the top of the day.

Isla sat with her class at the temple. Mr. Tanaka picked up his drum. He said, "We will sing a song today."

Isla wanted to clap along. But her hands went too quick. They clapped before the drum. They clapped after the drum. They forgot to wait. Maxwell giggled. His hands got mixed up too. Haven bumped her own chin.

"Let's try it very fast," said Mr. Tanaka. The song zoomed like a bird flying to its nest. The words ran into each other. Isla's claps went splat, splat, splat, all wrong. Her cheeks felt hot. She hid her hands under her legs.

Mr. Tanaka smiled at her. "Now we will try it slow," he said. The drum went boom. Boom. Boom. Isla clapped on each boom. Her hands landed right on time. She sang the whole rhyme. She did not forget a single word. Haven clapped with her. Maxwell clapped too.

Then came a small surprise. A little bird hopped to the window sill. It cocked its head. It seemed to listen. "The bird likes the slow song," whispered Haven. Isla clapped soft, soft, soft, so the bird would stay. The bird puffed up its feathers and sang one note back.

Camille was at Grandma's house. She wanted to paint a rainbow. Grandma gave her three little paint pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

Camille looked at the pots. She held a brush in her hand. "Only three colors," she said. Grandma smiled. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," she said. Camille said the words slowly. "Primary colours."

She dipped her brush in the red pot. Then she dipped it in the yellow pot. She stirred on the paper. The paint turned orange! Camille gasped. Then she tried blue and yellow. Green! Then red and blue. Purple!

She painted stripes, one by one. Orange, green, purple, and the three pots too. "Look!" said Camille. Grandma put the painting by the cold window to dry. "My rainbow," said Camille.

Violet stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop. Her friend Nimrat held the hoop up high. Violet threw the beanbag. It hit the grass. She threw it again. It went in! "Yay!" said Nimrat. "The beanbag went through!"

Then Mr. Kim rolled a big ball to Violet. She put out her hands. The ball hit her hands and bounced away. It rolled past a spider on its web. Mr. Kim rolled the ball again. The ball bounced out of her hands once more. "Hmm," said Violet. "The ball is too big for my hands."

Then she had an idea. She held her arms out wide. The ball came. She caught it and hugged it to her chest. The ball stayed! No bounce at all. "Look, Mr. Kim!" she said. "I hug it, and I hold on to it!" She got a little dizzy spinning around with the ball. Mr. Kim laughed and rolled the ball again.

Anna stood in the garage. It was cold in there. Her gray coat hung on a hook by the door.

Anna put her arms in the sleeves. The coat was on. Now came the zip. She pinched the little tab. She pulled it up. The zip stayed at the bottom. It did not move.

"Try again," said her dad. He was putting seed in a jar to feed the birds.

Anna tried again. The zip went up a tiny bit. Then it stopped. Anna made a sad face.

"Practice," said her dad. "Zips like practice."

Anna tried one more time. Slow, slow, slow. Up went the zip. All the way to the top! The coat was closed. Anna was warm now.

Dad clapped. Anna gave the zip a little kiss. "Good zip," she said.

She pushed the garage door button with Dad. The big door went up. Anna ran outside, zipped up tight.

Anna was at the hockey rink. The ice was gray and far away. Ms. Cohen had a big bag of beanbags.

"Throw the beanbag in the hoop," said Ms. Cohen.

Anna held the red beanbag. She threw it. It went past the hoop. She threw it again. It went in! Anna clapped her hands.

Then Ms. Cohen brought out a big yellow ball. "Now catch it with both hands."

The ball came to Anna. Anna squeezed her eyes shut. The ball bumped her tummy and fell down.

"You shut your eyes," said Joel. "Watch the ball all the way to your hands."

Ms. Cohen rolled the ball again. Anna kept her eyes open. She watched it all the way. She watched it all the way to her hands. Anna caught it with both hands!

"Now me," said Joel.

Joel watched his ball all the way too. He caught it. Anna and Joel sat on the stick-shaped bench. They washed their hands at the little sink. Then Anna threw the beanbag one more time. It went in the hoop.

Sophie sat on the school bus. She held her little farm truck. It had a horse in the back. Arnaud sat next to her. He looked at the truck for a long time.

"That is a nice farm truck," said Arnaud.

Sophie held it tight. Then she had an idea. "You can have a turn," she said. "But only one turn."

Arnaud smiled big. He made the truck go down his knee. He made the horse blow out of the back, like the wind did it. Sophie laughed and laughed. It was silly.

"Thank you, Sophie," said Arnaud. He gave the truck back.

Sophie made the horse blow too. Then she said, "Your turn again." The bus went around a deep bump in the road. The horse jumped high.

"My turn!" said Sophie.

Maverick stood by the door. The door was not shut yet. Soon a car would stop outside. Mama was coming home with the new baby.

The car came. Mama got out. She held a small bundle. "This is your baby sister," said Mama. Maverick looked at her little hand. It was so small.

Maverick wanted to pat her. He patted her tummy. He patted too hard. The baby began to cry. "Oh," said Maverick. His apple fell to the floor. He did not even pick it up.

"Touch her very gently," said Mama. She took Maverick's finger. She moved it slow and soft. Maverick stroked the baby's hand. The baby stopped crying. Her eyes looked up at him.

"Gently, gently," said Maverick. He stroked again. The baby held his finger. Her hand was warm, not cold and slimy like the frog Jagger found once. Maverick smiled. "She likes me," he said.

"Yes," said Mama. "She likes you."

Arnaud went to the park with his dad. Scott was there with a big red kite. The kite went up, up, up into the sky. Arnaud wanted to hold it very much.

He ran over and grabbed the string. The kite dipped and wobbled. "Hey!" said Scott. "You did not ask me." Arnaud let go. He felt bad. "Sorry," he said. Scott looked at him. Ms. Ferreira was sitting on a bench near the wheel toy. She called, "You can say, May I have a turn?" Arnaud took a breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked.
