Scott smiled and held out the string. "Yes! You said May I. Now you can hold it." Arnaud held the string tight. The kite went even higher. Then the wind gave a big pull. The kite spun down and landed on the soft grass. Arnaud laughed. "That was not scary at all," he said. "It was fun!" Scott said, "Come on, let's fly it again."

James went to the park with his dad. He carried a carrot for a snack. His friend Sidra was there by the swings.

James found something in the grass. It was small and shiny. It was a lighter. He did not pick it up. He marched to his dad. "I found something in the grass," said James. "It is a little fire thing." His dad looked at it. "That is a lighter," said Dad. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." Dad picked it up and put it in his pocket.

James ran back to Sidra. They dug in the sand. Sidra made a pile of wet sand. It felt cold on James's hands. Then they sat in the sun. The bench felt hot. "Careful," said Sidra. "Hot bench." They sat in the shade instead.

At snack time, James ate his carrot. It tasted a little salty from his hands. "Good find today," said Dad. James smiled and waved to Sidra. "Bye, Sidra! See you tomorrow!"

Everett ran up to Asees's door. Asees opened it fast. "Come see my doll!" she said.

The doll lay in a small bed. It was cozy under a tiny blanket. Asees dropped it that morning. Now she looked sad. "She fell," Asees said. "She fell, and I feel bad."

Everett looked at the doll. It did not cry. It did not move. Then he had a big idea. "It's a toy," he said. "Toys cannot really feel."

Asees gasped. "Really?"

"Really," said Everett. "But we can pretend!" He picked up the doll. He gave it a soft hug. "There, there," he said.

Asees hugged the doll too. "All better!" she said. The doll still did not move. But Asees smiled big now.

They played house in the yard. Everett was the dad. Asees was the mom. The doll was the baby. They fed it pretend soup. They sang it a song. "Pretend hug!" they said again and again.

Then Everett tripped on the grass. Down he went, bump. Asees ran to him. "Are you okay?" she asked.

Everett laughed. "I am not a toy. I really feel!" Asees laughed too. She gave him a real hug.

"Real hugs are the best," said Everett. "Baby gets pretend ones." The doll sat in the sun, snug and fine.

Arlo ran into Grandpa's kitchen. The bread was hot and fresh. Grandpa was cutting it, and Arlo watched from his chair. On the wall hung big letters. Arlo pointed. "That is A!" he said. Grandpa smiled and nodded.

Then Grandpa opened a big book. He put it on Arlo's lap. "Find the A," said Grandpa. Arlo looked hard. He saw a funny round letter. It did not look like the A on the wall. "This is not A," said Arlo. "This is a new letter!" He felt worried. The wall had one A. The book had another one. Which one was real?

Arlo put his finger on the small letter. Then he looked up at the wall. "Grandpa, this is a small a!" he said. "Big A, small a. Same letter!" Grandpa laughed. "Yes! Letters can be big or small." Arlo clapped his hands. He turned the page fast. He found a big B and a small b. He found a big C and a small c.

A bee buzzed by the window. Arlo pointed at it. "B is for bee!" he said. "Big B, small b!" He zipped back and forth from the book to the wall. Then he leaned close to the page and whispered, "Tomorrow I will find all the small letters. Every single one."

Addison ran to the baseball diamond. The sun was big and hot. Her friend Laurence was already there. Ms. Leblanc held a bag of bats.

"Where is your water bottle?" Laurence asked.

Addison looked in her bag. It was not there. "I forgot it at home," she said.

Addison ran to first base. She ran back. She felt hot and slow. Her tummy felt icky too. She sat down on the bench.

Ms. Leblanc walked over with a bottle. "Here, drink this," she said. Addison took a big drink. The water was cool.

"Can water really help me?" Addison asked.

"Try it and see," said Ms. Leblanc.

Addison drank some more. She stood up. Her legs felt fast again. She ran to the base. She tagged it. She smiled.

"Water made me feel better!" she said.

Now the team took a break. Everyone sat in the shade of a big tree. The tree's root poked out of the ground like a little bench. Kasey sat on it. Addison sat too.

"This is my special spot now," said Addison.

"Mine too," said Kasey.

Ms. Leblanc blew her whistle. It was time to play ball again. Addison ran back out to the field. She looked up at the sun. Then she looked at her water bottle in her hand.

She held it tight all the way to the pitcher's mound.

Lincoln was hungry after playing outside. His hands were wet from the rain, so he washed them at the sink. Then he sat at the table.

Mom brought two plates. Each plate had scrambled eggs on it. Nick was visiting, and he had a plate too.

Lincoln looked at his eggs. He did not like eggs. "Yuck!" he shouted. Mom's face went still. Nick put down his spoon.

"No, thank you," Nick said to Mom. "I don't want eggs today."

Mom smiled at Nick. "Okay," she said. "I have some banana." She cut banana slices for Nick.

Lincoln watched. He thought about the banana. He wanted banana too.

He took a big breath. "No, thank you," he said. "I don't want eggs."

Mom smiled at him too. "Thank you for telling me," she said. She cut banana slices for Lincoln.

Lincoln ate every slice. The cat came and sat by his chair. Lincoln dropped one small piece. The cat licked it off the floor.

Mom brought more banana. "Please can I have some?" Lincoln asked.

"Of course," said Mom, and she put three slices on his plate.

Levi stood at the front door. He looked out at the big sunny sky. "Today is sunny!" he shouted. He grabbed his boots. He grabbed his coat. "No, no," said his dad. "Sunny days need a sun hat." Levi put on his sun hat. It had a brown rabbit on it. "My rabbit hat!" he said.

Outside, the sun was bright. Levi ran to meet Zohan at the swing. Zohan had no hat. Zohan made a squinty face. His eyes went small and tight. "The sun is in my eyes," Zohan said. Levi tipped his sun hat down. The hat made shade over his face. His eyes opened wide. "My hat shades my face!" said Levi. He could see the swings. He could see the trees. He could see everything!

Zohan ran home and got his own hat. "Look, my hat shades my face too!" said Zohan. Then the wind came. It blew and blew. Levi held his hat with both hands. His hair began to brush across his forehead. The two boys laughed and ran to the swings. "Sunny day, sun hat, swing time!" they cheered.

Zoe sat at the kitchen table. She hugged her toy elephant. Today the nurse was coming to her house. Zoe was getting a shot.

"I don't want a poke," Zoe said to her elephant. Her mom patted her head.

The doorbell rang. The nurse came in with a small bag. She had a pretty sticker for Zoe. It had a star on it.

The nurse got her needle ready. Zoe held her elephant tight. The nurse said, "One, two, three." The shot was over very fast. Zoe blinked. "That was little," she said.

Then Zoe saw a red box in the nurse's bag. It was hard, not soft. "What is that for?" Zoe asked.

The nurse opened the red box. She dropped the used needle inside. It went clang. "Used needles go in here," she said. "So nobody gets poked."

Zoe leaned close and looked. The box was shut tight. The needle could not get out. Not her, not her mom, not anyone.

"Can the elephant get a sticker too?" Zoe asked. The nurse smiled and put a star on the elephant's ear. Zoe patted its soft head.

"Now the elephant is safe too," she said.

Eleanor went to the pool with her dad. She rode her bike there first, and her dad pushed it along. At the pool, her friend Noa was already in the water. Noa could float on her back.

"I want to float too," Eleanor said. But she sat on the step and did not move. The water felt big. She was not angry, just scared.

Then Ms. Chaudhry came over. "I will hold you while you float," she said. Eleanor lay back. She felt Ms. Chaudhry's hands under her back. The hands held her up. Eleanor opened her eyes and watched the ceiling. The water did not pull her down.

"Now one hand," said Ms. Chaudhry. Then she took that hand away too. Eleanor was floating all by herself. Noa splashed and cheered. Eleanor kicked her feet a little and laughed.

Logan sat on the big red mat. Music class was starting at the community centre. Ms. Mehta had her drum. Lorelei and Ishaan sat close by.

Ms. Mehta tapped the drum. Bump, bump, bump. Logan clapped whenever he wanted. His claps went everywhere. They bumped into Ishaan's ear by mistake. "Ow," said Ishaan, and he laughed. Logan stopped. He felt his face go warm.

"Lorelei, how do you clap so well?" Logan asked. Lorelei clapped with the drum. Bump went the drum, clap went her hands. "I clap at the same time as the beat," she said. Logan put his hands in his lap. He listened. Bump went the drum. Clap went Logan. Bump, clap. Bump, clap. "You did it!" said Lorelei. Ishaan clapped with him too, and their hands made one big sound.

Then Ms. Mehta sang a song about a star in the dark sky. Logan sang too. He knew the words all by himself. Lorelei clapped for him. Logan took a little bow and fell over sideways on the mat.

Jasmine sat at the kitchen table. She wanted a little blanket for her toy bear. Mom gave her a square napkin. "This is a square," Mom said. "It has four sides, all the same."

Jasmine looked at the square. It was too big for the bear. She frowned. What could she do?

Then Tamara came in. Tamara was her friend from next door. "Fold it," Tamara said. Jasmine folded the napkin in half, edge to edge. She pressed it flat with her small hands.

She opened her eyes wide. The square was gone. Now it was long and thin. "Mom, look!" said Jasmine. "It's a rectangle now." Mom smiled and nodded.

Jasmine tucked the rectangle around the bear. It fit just right. "Night night, little bear," she whispered. Outside the cloudy sky grew dim. Tamara tapped her toe under the table, happy and slow. Then Jasmine picked up another square napkin and folded it in half again.

Chloe put on her swim cap. Today was her first swim team day. The pool was big and blue.

Ms. Nielsen stood at the edge. "I am your coach," she said. "A coach teaches the team. I help you learn the game."

Chloe did not know where to stand. She stood by the wrong wall. Ms. Nielsen showed her the spot with a red cone. "Stand here," she said. Chloe stood there. It was the right spot!

"Now we kick," said Ms. Nielsen. "Hold the rail. Kick, kick, kick." Chloe held the rail. She kicked one, two, three times. She made big white splashes. Her kicks made the water fly up!

"I did that!" said Chloe. Malcom kicked next to her. He made splashes too. Celina kicked and laughed.

They kicked one, two, three, over and over. Then it was time to get out. Chloe was a polite swimmer. She said, "Thank you, Ms. Nielsen."

She put on her warm sweater. It was soft and cozy. Her hair was still wet.

"One, two, three," said Chloe. She gave three big waves to the pool.

Matthew ran to the art classroom. "Painting day!" he shouted. Mr. Kim smiled and put out the paint. Matthew dipped his brush in the blue. He drew a big circle. Then he made bumpy dots for snow on top.

Soon it was time for a snack. Matthew dropped his brush in the red paint cup. He ran to find Eva. "Come see my snow!" he said. They looked at his picture. They ate crackers. They laughed a lot.

The next day, Matthew grabbed his brush. He tried to paint. Oh no! The brush was hard. The paint had dried on it. It would not bend at all.

Mr. Kim held the brush under the tap. He washed all the paint away. The bristles turned soft again. Matthew looked and looked.

Then Matthew painted a sun. When he was done, he ran to the sink. He washed his brush all by himself. "Clean brush!" he said. "Ready for tomorrow!"

Penelope sat on her bedroom floor. Her teddy bear had a hole in his arm. Fluff was coming out. That made Penelope sad.

She got her toy toolbox. It was hard to find the right tool. The wrench was too big. The hammer was too heavy. Then she found a big safe plastic needle and some yarn. She asked her dad to help thread it. He sat with her on the rug.

Penelope tried to fix the hole. The yarn slipped out. She tried again. It slipped again. She took a deep breath and waited a bit. Then she tried one more time, slowly. The yarn went through.

Just then her friend Zakary came in. His mouth was turned down and his eyebrows were bumpy. Penelope looked at his face. She saw he felt sad. "What is wrong?" she asked.

"My truck is at home," said Zakary. "I wanted to show you."

Penelope smiled at him. "Teddy has a hole, but I fixed it," she said. She held Teddy up. Zakary's mouth turned up into a big smile. Penelope saw his happy face and laughed. "Do you want to help Teddy find his hat?" she asked. Zakary clapped his hands.

Eva ran to the red truck at the playground. It had a sweet little horn that went beep. But Aayan grabbed the truck too. Eva pulled. Aayan pulled. The truck did not move at all.

"Maybe Mr. Lim can help us," Aayan said. They held the truck together and walked to the bench. "Two of us want the same truck," Eva said. Mr. Lim smiled. "Then you can take turns. Eva first, then Aayan." He set a big round stone as the shape of the spot where each turn would start.

Eeva drove the truck down the hill. Beep, beep! The wheels slipped a little in the sand. Then she gave the truck to Aayan. He drove it to the slide and back. "My turn again?" Eva asked. "Yes," said Aayan, and he handed it over. "This time I will let you go two whole turns," she said, and pressed the horn.

Levi loved the block corner at daycare. Today he had a big plan. He wanted to build a tower that touched the window. He tipped out the whole basket of blocks.

Tatiana came over. She sat down next to him. "I put the red ones together," she said. She pushed all the red blocks into one pile. Then she made a pile of blue blocks. Then a pile of yellow blocks. Her piles looked like little rainbows.

Levi picked up a red block. He looked at it. Then he looked at Tatiana's piles. He put it in the small pile instead. He picked up a blue block and put it there too. Tatiana frowned. "No, that goes with blue," she said.

Levi shook his head. He pointed at his piles. "Small ones here. Big ones here," he said. Tatiana tilted her head. Then her eyes went wide. "Oh! Same blocks, new way!" She clapped her hands.

Ms. Weiss came to see. She gave them a kind smile. "Show me," she said. Levi and Tatiana sorted the blocks together. First by color. Then by size. Then Levi found a round block and made a shape pile all its own. The piles sat on the carpet like little worlds. Tatiana spun a block on the floor. It wobbled and fell. "Tower time," said Levi, and he stacked the first big block.

Lucas dug in the dirt with his small spoon. He was planting seeds in the backyard. His friend Sulaiman came to help. They planted tomato seeds and carrot seeds. Then they planted pea seeds too.

The next day, Lucas forgot which spot had tomatoes. He looked at the dirt. All the little rows looked the same. "That is wrong," Lucas said. "I can't tell where the tomatoes are." Ms. Tse, his neighbour, brought him some paper cards. Lucas drew a red tomato on one card. He drew an orange carrot on another. He drew green peas on a third. He pushed each card into the soil by its row.

The sun began to shine. A big truck rumbled past the fence. Lucas watered the dirt. Soon a tiny green sprout came up by the pea card. "Look, Sulaiman!" Lucas said. "The card tells us what will grow here!" Sulaiman pointed to the tomato card. "Peas there, tomatoes there," he said. Lucas clapped his muddy hands. Every day they checked the cards and the sprouts. The rows grew taller and taller. Lucas touched the soft pea vines. "Hello, little peas," he whispered.

School was over. Bennett sat on the step by the door. The sky was cloudy and big. "Is that an owl up there?" he asked Ms. Nowak. "No, that is a cloud shaped like an owl," she said. Bennett laughed.

Now Bennett wanted to run to the gate. He grabbed his shoes. He pushed them onto his bare feet. They felt bumpy and funny inside. Zavier sat down next to him. Zavier pulled on his socks first. Then his shoes went on smooth and fast.

Bennett pulled his shoes off. He laughed at his mixed-up feet. He put his socks on first. Then his shoes slid right on. "Ready!" he shouted. He took one big step, then another, all the way to the gate. Zavier raced him to the tree. "You are fast!" said Zavier.

Gabriella held her new library card. It was cool and smooth in her hand. She sat on the city bus next to Mommy. The bus seat had wood trim. Gabriella rubbed it with her fingers.

At the library, Ms. Traoré smiled. "Pick any book you like!" Gabriella found a big red book. It had a bear on the front. She wanted to draw a hat on the bear!

Then she saw a name card inside. Many names were on it. "So many kids read this book!" said Ms. Traoré. "It will be shared again and again."

Gabriella looked at her crayon. She looked at the book. She put the crayon away.

"I will draw on my own paper," she said. Ms. Traoré gave her a white sheet.

On the bus ride home, Gabriella drew a big hat. Mommy taped the picture to the window. "A hat for the bus bear!" said Gabriella.

Lena sat in the family car. "Are we going to the doctor?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "A dentist. Your tooth needs a check."

Lena thought about the doctor. Doctors look at your whole body. They listen to your tummy. They look in your ears. Maybe the dentist would do all that too.

At the office, Lena sat in a big chair. A friendly dentist came over. "Say cheese," she said. Lena opened her mouth wide. The dentist looked at her teeth. Then she looked at more teeth. Then she looked at the last tooth, way in the back.

"Wait," said Lena. "You only look at teeth?" The dentist nodded. "That is my job. I take care of teeth." Lena smiled. "So you are a tooth doctor!" The dentist laughed and gave her a small mirror.

Lena looked in the mirror. She saw her own smile. "My teeth look shiny," she said. "Can we come back next time?" "Yes," said Mom. Lena held the mirror all the way home in the car.

It was morning at school. Natalie wanted to play rocket ship with Sullivan. Sullivan said, "We need a blast off!"

"But how do we start it?" Natalie asked.

"Ms. Cardinal knows," said Sullivan. They found her by the paint pots. Natalie's fingers were sticky from the morning glue.

Ms. Cardinal sat with them. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, blast off!" she said. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown."

Natalie and Sullivan ran to the climbing mat. "Ten, nine, eight," said Natalie. "Seven, six, five," said Sullivan. "Four, three, two, one, blast off!"

They jumped up high. Then they did it again. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, blast off!"

At snack time they ate crackers. Sukhmani asked, "Can I be in the rocket too?"

"Yes," said Natalie. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, blast off!"

Zachary ran to the big park with Daniel. The sun felt hot on his face. They walked past a small fountain. Its water looked cold.

Then Zachary saw a puddle. It was big and brown. He jumped in. Splash! His socks got all wet. His shoes made a squish sound.

"Your socks are wet," said Daniel. "Wet and dry are opposites." Zachary touched his socks. They were not dry at all. Could a wet sock get dry? He wanted to find out.

A dad helped them take off the wet shoes. Zachary sat on a bench. He dug in his bag with his hands. He found one piece of dry bread and one pair of dry socks. The socks were tight, but he pulled them on.

The sun kept shining on the wet socks he held up. Zachary watched and waited. Would the sun work?

He felt the wet sock. A corner was dry now. "Look!" he said. "The sun is drinking the water!"

Daniel leaned close and touched the dry piece too.

Hudson ran to the door. Outside the sun was bright. "Wait," said his dad. "The sun is very sunny today. Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Dad rubbed white cream on Hudson's nose and arms. It felt cool and smelled like the beach.

At the playground, Hudson found Greyson. They played on the round tire swing. The wind blew Greyson's hat right off his head. It rolled across the grass. Hudson chased it and caught it. "That was windy!" said Greyson. They laughed and hung the hat on the fence so it would not blow away again.

Later a big cloud came. A few raindrops fell, fat and cold on Hudson's hands. Mr. Gallagher, the neighbor, called, "Rainy now! Boots on tomorrow." The boys ran home fast. At the door, Hudson looked at his arms. No sunburn at all. "The sunscreen worked," he said, and he waved goodbye to the sun going behind the cloud.

Lena wanted to play toy shop. She tipped out her big toy box. Cars went bump on the floor. Blocks fell out too. Then she saw something yellow.

It was a banana. It sat right in the middle of her toy cars.

Lena picked up the banana. "You are not a toy," she said. The banana felt smooth and cool. It did not have wheels.

Gavin came over to play. He looked at the cars. He looked at the banana.

"You found the odd one out," said Gavin. "The banana does not belong with the cars."

Lena made her eyes wide. "Odd one out!" she said. She liked those words.

She put the banana on the table. Her mom cut it into circles. Lena ate three pieces. Bananas were not toys. Bananas were food.

Then Lena found a pine cone in the toy box. It had dirt on its pointy top.

"Look!" said Gavin. "Another one!"

Lena held it up high. "Odd one out!" she shouted. "You are from outside, not from my toy box."

She put the pine cone on the window sill. It could live there, next to a tiny paper star.

Madelyn went to the cemetery with her dad. They brought a picnic and flowers. They were going to visit Grandpa's stone. Madelyn patted the stone, soft and slow. "Hello, Grandpa," she said. Her dad put the flowers down in the grass.

Then they sat on the blanket to eat. Dad folded his hands. "Now we say our blessing," he said. Madelyn folded her hands too. Dad said, "Thank you for this food." Then he started to eat. Madelyn stopped. She wanted to say more. She thought about her bread. Somebody baked the bread. Somebody grew the wheat. The farmer grew the wheat in the sun!

"I want to say a thank-you," said Madelyn. Dad put his sandwich down. "Go ahead," he said. Madelyn folded her hands again. "Thank you for the food. Thank you to the farmer, too." Dad smiled big. "That was a good blessing," he said. A bird walked by the blanket. It pecked at a crumb. "Stinky bird feet," said Madelyn, and she giggled. Dad laughed too.

They ate their bread and cheese. The wind blew soft on the grass. Madelyn looked at the flowers by the stone. "I see a lion," she said. She pointed at a yellow dandelion, round like a lion's mane. Dad said, "It does look fuzzy like a lion." Madelyn patted the ground next to the flower. "Grandpa, we said thank you," she whispered. Then she took one more big bite of bread.

Luka sat at the daycare table. Mr. Rahman put ice cubes in a big bowl. "Who wants to help?" he asked. Luka raised his hand. He wanted to help very much.

Luka looked at the ice with his eyes. It was shiny and white. He heard the ice go clink, clink in the bowl with his ears. Mr. Rahman gave each child one ice cube and one cup.

Tiana picked up her ice cube. Then she dropped it fast into her cup. "Brrr!" she said. "So cold!" Elaahi smelled his cup of juice first. Then he took a tiny taste with his tongue. "Yum," he said.

Now it was Luka's turn. He touched the ice cube with his fingers. It felt cold! It was not smooth like his pet cat at home. He dropped it into his cup fast. "Cold, cold, cold!" he said, and everyone laughed.

The ice cube sat in the juice. Luka watched it get small. "Mr. Rahman, it's going away!" Mr. Rahman smiled. "It melts in the warm juice. Drink up, everyone." Luka took a sip. The juice was cold and sweet. "Best drink ever," he said. Tiana touched her cold cup and grinned.

Everly ran to the playground with her bear. It was a sunny day. Her spotted bear had one brown ear. Hana was there with her bunny. "Let's play house," said Hana. "Okay," said Everly. "You be the mama. I will make tea."

Everly found three empty cups in the toy box. They had no tea in them at all. She held her bear's paws and poured. "Here is your tea," she said. "Careful, it's pretend hot! Blow on it first." Bear blew with his little nose.

Then Raymond came over. "I want tea too," he said. Everly poured an empty cup for him. Raymond tipped it up to drink. Nothing came out. "It's pretend tea," Everly said. "The cups are empty, but we can still drink it." Raymond smiled and took a big pretend sip. "Yum," he said. "More, please." The bell on the playhouse door went ring, ring. "Tea time," said Hana, and all the cups went round again.

Kayden played on his bedroom floor. He made a big tower with soft blocks. The tower fell down with a soft plop. Kayden laughed and patted his head.

Then he heard Mom call. "Snack time, Kayden!" Kayden ran to the door. Mom saw his hands. They were dusty from the blocks and the toy bin. "Wash your hands first," Mom said. She walked with him to the sink. The water felt cool. The soap made white bubbles. Kayden rubbed his hands together. He saw the dust go down the drain. His hands were clean now.

Back in his bedroom, Mom put a small table by the window. She set out apple slices and a cup of milk. Kayden picked up an apple slice. It was sweet and crunchy. He looked at his clean hands. "Wash hands, then eat," he said. Mom smiled and gave him a friendly thumbs up. Kayden drank his milk. Then he yawned a big yawn. Mom said, "Bath next, then pajamas, then bed." Kayden got his pajamas from his little drawer all by himself. "I can do it," he said.

David ran to the park. The sun was warm on his face. His hat went flying off. "Wow, it is windy!" he said. He picked up his hat and put it back on.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. David got wet fast. His friend Katelyn ran by in her red raincoat. She stayed dry. "How are you not wet?" David asked. "My raincoat keeps me dry," she said.

David ran home. He put on his blue raincoat. He ran back to the park. The rain tap-tapped on his coat. His face smiled. His tummy was dry. His arms were dry too. "Rain, rain, you can't get me!" he called. Katelyn laughed and splashed in a puddle. David stomped in it too. Splish, splash, splosh.

Emma went to the library with her dad. The library had a big tree painted on the wall. There was a playroom too. Emma wanted to play there, but the toy box was empty. "Where did the toys go?" she asked.

Blocks and dolls and balls were all over the floor. Justin had dumped them out. Gideon was hiding under the table. "Too many toys!" said Justin. "They go everywhere."

Ms. Rajapakse came in. She knelt down by the box. "Let's put them back," she said. Emma picked up a block. "Block," she said, and dropped it in. "That's a toy," said Ms. Rajapakse. Emma picked up a doll. "Doll," she said, and put it in. Justin threw a ball. The ball bounced off the wall and rolled back. Emma caught it. "Ball," she said. "Ball is a toy too." She put it in the box.

Gideon came out from under the table. He picked up a book. "Book?" he asked. "The book goes on the shelf," said Ms. Rajapakse. So Gideon put the book on the shelf, not in the toy box. Soon the floor was clear. The box was full. Emma yawned. She was tired now. She sat on her dad's lap by the big tree. "One more story," she said. Her dad opened a book and began to read.

Grace was at daycare. She held her teddy, Brown Bear. Brown Bear fell in a puddle outside. Now Brown Bear was all wet. Grace felt mad about the puddle.

"Brown Bear is sick," she told Ms. Wijaya. "He is cold and wet."

Ms. Wijaya helped Grace dry Brown Bear with a soft towel. Then Grace had an idea. She got a small cup. She held it to Brown Bear's mouth. "Drink your medicine," she said. "It will make you warm."

Brooks came over to play. "My dolly gets sick too," he said. He tucked his dolly under a little blanket. Grace watched him. Then she found a blanket too.

Grace tucked Brown Bear into bed. She patted his head. "Sleep now," she said softly. Brown Bear lay very still under the blanket. Grace gave him one more sip of pretend medicine.

Soon it was nap time for the children too. Ms. Wijaya put Grace's mat next to Brown Bear's little bed. Grace yawned and closed her eyes.

"Night night, Brown Bear," she whispered. "You will feel better soon."

The lights went out. Jasmine sat on the couch with her juice. "The power went off," said Dad. He lit a small lamp. It did not shine very far. Jasmine listened. The house was very quiet. "Why is it so quiet?" she asked. "The fridge stopped humming," said Dad. Jasmine put her ear near the fridge door. There was no hum at all. She had never heard that hum before. Now she heard new sounds. Tick, tick, went the clock. Pat, pat, went the tree on the window.

"I am hungry," said Jasmine. Dad made sandwiches. No stove, no cooking. They ate on the couch. Then Jasmine heard a hum. "Listen!" she said. The fridge was humming again. The lights came back on. The lamp shone bright. "The power is back," said Dad. Jasmine clapped. She was glad she had listened so well.

Billie woke up early. She felt excited. Today was a big party at her house.

Many people came. There were aunties and uncles and cousins. There was food on the table. There were lamps in the windows. The lamps gave a warm light.

Billie saw cookies across the room. She let go of her mama's hand. She began to walk to the cookies. The room was full of legs and bags. A big cousin bumped past her. Billie felt small. She could not see her mama.

Billie stopped and stood still. She looked around. Then she saw her mama's red scarf. Her mama was looking for her too. Billie called out, "Mama!" Her mama turned around fast. She came and took Billie's hand.

"Hold my hand in the big crowd," said Mama. Billie held on tight. They walked together to the cookie plate. Mama gave her one, and gave one to Daniel too, who was visiting with his dad. Daniel held his dad's hand as well.

Later the room grew quiet. Billie felt sleepy, but she was still a little awake. She sat on Mama's lap. The lamps still gave their soft light. Her mama wrapped the scarf around them both. Billie ate the last bit of her cookie. "More party tomorrow?" she asked. Mama laughed and kissed her head.

Jayden got to school early. Ms. Wu put paper shapes on the table. "Let's make a sun," she said. She held up a paper circle. "The circle can be the sun."

Jayden wanted to cut the circle out. But he did not know where to start. His friend Oakley cut a square. Oakley started at a corner. Clip, clip, done. Kora cut a triangle. She started at a corner too.

Jayden turned his circle over. He looked and looked. "Where is a corner?" he said. He ran his finger all around the edge. Round and round it went. His finger never stopped at a corner. "There is no corner!" he said. A circle is round and has no corners.

So Jayden just made one little snip anywhere. Then he cut round and round, all the way. Ms. Wu watched. "You found it out," she said. Jayden glued the circle on blue paper. He drank from his water cup while the glue dried. Kora gave him yellow paper strips for sun rays. Jayden opened the glue stick and stuck them on one by one.

The sun was big and round. "It looks happy," said Oakley. Jayden smiled and hung it up high on the wall.

Chloe sat on the big red swing cushion in the school library. Ms. Szabó held up a card with a letter on it. "What sound does this make?" she asked. The letter was A. "Ah," said Chloe. "Yes! A is first," said Ms. Szabó.

Julianne sat next to Chloe. She bounced on her seat. "I know the whole song," she said. "A, B, C, all the way to P." Chloe frowned. Her sweater felt itchy, and she tugged at the collar. "Is P the end?" she asked Ms. Szabó.

Ms. Szabó smiled. "Sing it and see," she said. So they sang. They sang all the way past P. Q, R, S, T. Chloe's voice got louder. U, V, W, X. Then came Y. And then one more.

"Z!" said Chloe. "The alphabet ends with Z!" Ms. Szabó gave her the Z card. Chloe held it up high. "Last one," she said. "I found it."

Blake had a busy day. She played a game with Vaughn. She ate her supper. She had a bath with yellow bubbles. Then it was bedtime.

Blake put on her pajamas. She brushed her teeth. Then she needed to use the toilet. She sat and waited. She took her time. When she was done, she ran to her bed.

"Wait," said her dad. "Did you flush?" Blake looked back at the toilet. The water was still there. She had forgotten. Blake walked back. She pushed the handle down. The water went round and round. Then she turned on the sink. She rubbed soap on her hands. She rinsed them and turned the water off. Her dad held out the towel. Blake dried her hands, one by one. Then she jumped into bed. "Now I am ready," she said.

Amelia ran to the kitchen. It was Hanukkah tonight! Papa held the menorah. It had spots for eight candles, plus one helper candle.

"Can I count?" asked Amelia. "Yes," said Papa. "Count with me." Amelia counted the candles. One, two, three. Last night there were only two. Now there were three! Papa lit the candles with a match. Amelia stayed back, safe and warm. The little flames glowed.

Mama called them to the table. Amelia sat in her cool chair with stars on it. There were latkes on a big plate. Amelia tugged her zipper down and her coat came off. Mama helped her stack the latkes high on her plate. One, two, three latkes!

Then Amelia stopped. She looked at the menorah. Three candles were lit, just like her three latkes! She jumped up and down. "Papa! The candles match my latkes!" Papa laughed. "Count them again tomorrow night," he said. Amelia could not wait. Tomorrow there would be four.

Jade stood by the little tent at the campsite. The morning air felt cold on her nose. Dad had set out a bowl and a pan on the table.

"Can I help make eggs?" Jade asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "You can crack them. Cooks crack an egg's shell open to get the egg out."

Jade picked up an egg. She tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap. The shell broke. She pulled it apart with her thumbs. The egg slipped out into the bowl.

"I did it!" said Jade.

She cracked another egg. This time, a tiny bit of shell fell into the bowl. Jade looked at it. She took her spoon and fished it out. The little shell sat on the spoon. The egg stayed in the bowl.

"Got it," said Jade.

Dad cooked the eggs on the little camp stove. Jade stood back and watched. The eggs turned white and soft.

They ate at the wooden table near the tent. Jade took a bite.

"Taste this, Dad," she said. "We made it."

Dad took a big bite. "Mmm," he said.

A bird sang in the tree above them. Jade held up her spoon and smiled.

Ruby woke up early. Her sister was still asleep. Ruby wanted juice. She went to the kitchen.

"Give me juice!" said Ruby.

Dad looked at Ruby. He did not get the juice. He waited.

Ruby tried again. "Juice, please," she said.

Dad smiled big. He got the cup. He poured the juice. "Here you go," he said.

Ruby held her cup. The juice was orange like the sun. She took a sip. "Thank you," said Ruby.

Then Ruby heard a little sound. Crash! Her cup tipped over. Juice ran across the table like a river.

"Sorry," said Ruby. "Help, please!"

Dad wiped the river away. He gave Ruby a new cup. "You said please," said Dad. "That was nice."

Ruby drank her juice slowly. Then she whispered to her cup, "More juice, please?"

Dad laughed. He poured a little more. The end cup was full again.

Lennon stood on the soccer field. The sun felt warm on her arms. Ms. Haddad set out a big hoop. "Watch me," said Ms. Haddad. She tossed a beanbag up. It dropped right into the hoop. Lennon tried. Her beanbag fell short. She tried again. It went in. "I did it!" she said. Maren clapped.

Next they played catch with a big ball. Sam threw it hard. The ball flew past Lennon's hands. "Too fast," said Lennon. She had to crawl after it into the string net by the goal. Then Sam smiled. He tossed the ball gently. Lennon caught it with both hands. The soft toss was easy to hold.

"Again," said Lennon. Sam tossed it gently again. Lennon caught it. She felt brave. "Your turn now," she said to Maren. Lennon tossed the ball soft and slow. Maren caught it too. "Nice and easy," said Maren. Ms. Haddad blew her whistle. "Good catching, everyone," she said. Lennon held the big ball tight and smiled.

Mya wants to build a tall tower at school. She stacks her blocks up high. The tower wobbles and falls down. Mya stomps her foot. "My tower fell!"

Arzoi comes over with a bucket of stickers. "Put a sticker on each side," she says. Mya takes a block. She puts a sticker on the top. Then she puts one on the bottom. She counts the sides. One, two, three, four. Six stickers fit. Six sides!

Mya looks close at the block. Every side is a square. Each sticker sits on a square. "Six squares," says Mya. Mr. Kim smiles. "Nice counting, Mya."

Mya stacks the blocks again. The square sides sit flat on the floor. The tower stands tall. It does not fall. Amirah jumps up and claps. "So tall!"

Mya puts her last sticker on the very top block. It is a little star.

Arlo sat at the little table at daycare. He wanted to draw a shiny blue car on a road. He found a crayon. It looked almost like the night sky. Was it blue?

Abygaelle peeked at his paper. "That crayon is not blue," she said. "It is too dark!"

Damon held up a pale crayon. "This one is blue," he said. "Look how light it is."

Arlo put the dark crayon next to the light one. Then he found more blue crayons in the box. One was light like the sky. One was in the middle. One was very dark.

"Let's line them up," said Arlo. The three friends put the blues in a row. Light, middle, dark. It looked like the sky going into night.

Mr. Tang came over. "Look at that," he said. "Light blue, dark blue. All of them are still called blue."

Arlo smiled. He drew his shiny car on the road. The road was dark blue. The sky above it was light blue. Both parts were blue, just the way he liked them.

"Which blue is your car?" Abygaelle asked.

Arlo held up the darkest crayon of all. "This one," he said. "The night car."

Josephine held her dad's hand at the dentist. The chair was big. The room smelled like mint. Josephine felt a little scared.

The dentist smiled. "Open wide, please," she said. Josephine opened her mouth. The chair went up. It went down. It was like a ride.

"How can you see behind my teeth?" Josephine asked. "My eyes can't see back there."

The dentist held up a little tool. It was a tiny mirror on a handle. She put it in Josephine's mouth. "Look at this," she said. She turned the mirror. Now Josephine could see the backs of her teeth on it, small like a tiny moon in the sky.

The mirror was cold and shiny. Josephine saw a spot on a back tooth. She had not brushed that spot. She did not want to forget it again.

"All done," said the dentist. She let Josephine hold the mirror. Josephine looked at her own smile in it. It was the same smile as always.

"I like the little mirror," Josephine said. Her dad picked her up for a hug. "Let's go home," he said. Josephine waved to the dentist. "Bye, mirror!"

Hayden sat at Grandpa's big table. He had a pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. Hayden held the pencil in his fist. He pressed hard. The letters came out wobbly and big. "Why is my H so messy?" he asked.

Grandpa sat down next to him. "Try this," Grandpa said. "Pinch the pencil with your thumb and your first finger." Hayden pinched the pencil. "Now let it rest on your middle finger," said Grandpa. The pencil sat on Hayden's middle finger, quiet and still.

Hayden made a slow line down. Then another line. Then one across. "H!" he said. He made more letters. H, A, Y, D. "Look, Grandpa! I made my name!" Grandpa clapped. Hayden smiled and wrote it again.

Anthony pushed the classroom door with one finger. It was too heavy, so Ms. Huang helped him push it with her hand.

Inside, kids sat on a big red rug. Anthony wanted to sit with them. But he ran fast, and his feet went stomp, stomp, stomp. A girl named Stephanie held up her hand. "We walk inside," she said. "That is a class rule."

A rule? Anthony stopped his feet. Ms. Huang read the rules from a paper. Everyone in the class follows them, she said. Walk inside. Use gentle hands. Take turns.

At play time, Ryan grabbed the truck. Anthony wanted to grab it back. Then he remembered. Take turns. "My turn, please?" he asked. Ryan gave him the truck. "Your turn next," Anthony said.

Stephanie sat by him and smiled. "You look silly when you stomp," she said. Anthony laughed. He liked his class. He liked the rules, too.

Aubrey sat with Mom at the restaurant. The big screen showed a game. Hussain and Rhys sat nearby too. Everyone watched. One team got a goal. Then the other team got one too.

Aubrey counted on her fingers. "One and one," she said. "Who won, Mom?"

"Nobody won," said Mom. "The score is the same. It is a tie."

"A tie," said Aubrey. She said it again. "A tie, a tie, both teams tie!"

Hussain clapped. Rhys jumped up. Aubrey jumped too, but not too high. It was getting late, and her bed was waiting at home.

The screen showed the tie score. Aubrey waved at it. "Good game," she said. "Good game, both teams."

Mom held her hand as they walked out.

Jade made a cat at school. She glued on paper ears. She glued on a yarn tail. The glue dried in the sun by the window. She could not wait to tell Dad.

At dinner, Dad was talking to Mom. He was telling about his day. Jade started to talk. "Dad! Dad! I made a cat!" Dad kept talking to Mom. Jade's words got lost in his words. Nobody heard her story.

Jade took a bite of her rice. She put her hands in her lap. She looked at the light above the table. She waited. Dad finished his last word. Then he looked at Jade. "Now it is your turn," he said.

"I made a cat with glue!" said Jade. "It has a yarn tail!" Mom clapped. Dad smiled big. Everyone heard every word. Mom gave Jade some warm bread. It was not too hot. Jade took a bite. "Tomorrow I will tell about the dog I glued," she said.

Hannah sat on the school bus. She held a small lion in her hands. The lion had a soft mane. Hannah loved her lion very much.

Niyamat sat down next to her. He looked at the lion. "Nice lion," he said. Hannah held it tight. She turned away.

Niyamat had no toy. He looked out the window. His hands were empty. Mr. Choi walked down the bus. "Sharing means letting someone else play with it too," he said softly. Then he kept walking.

Hannah chewed her lip. She looked at Niyamat. She looked at her lion. Slowly, she put the lion in his hands. "You can hold him," she said.

Niyapat smiled. He made the lion jump on the seat. "Roaar!" he said. Hannah laughed. "My turn now?" she asked. Niyamat gave the lion back. Hannah made it jump too. "Your turn!" she said.

The bus rumbled on. Two friends, one lion, back and forth, back and forth. "Rooaar!" they said together.

Declan sat at the art table. He had a red paint pot. He had a white paint pot. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. On the card he wanted a pink flower. But where was pink? "Is pink hiding?" Declan asked. Trevor looked in the paint box. "No pink in here," said Trevor. Declan was a little mad. He tapped his pencil on the table. Mad, mad, mad.

Then Declan had an idea. He dipped his brush in the red. He put red on his paper. He dipped his brush in the white. He put white on top of the red. He stirred, stirred, stirred. "Look!" said Declan. The red spot turned pink. Red and white made pink. It really did. Trevor leaned over to watch. "Whoa," said Trevor. "Do it again!"

Declan did it again. Red, then white, then stir. More pink! He painted a big pink flower. Norman painted a green stem. Mr. Suryanto helped them write "Grandma" on the front. "One pink flower for you," said Declan. He held the card up high. "Pink, pink, pink!"

It was a rainy day. Nathan could not skip outside. So he skipped to the bathroom instead.

His dad was washing a plate at the sink. "Can I wash too?" asked Nathan. "First wash your hands," said Dad.

Nathan turned on the tap. The water felt warm on his fingers. The soap smelled like strawberries. He heard the tap go drip, drip, drip. He saw his face in the big mirror. He stuck out his tongue at himself.

"Look at your nose," said Dad with a smile. "Your nose has two openings. They are called nostrils."

Nathan leaned close to the mirror. He counted one, two. Two nostrils! He put one finger under his nose. He breathed out. He felt the air on his finger, one spot on each side.

Nathan giggled. "My nose breathes twice," he said.

Dad laughed too. "All done," he said. "Now taste this." He gave Nathan a sweet apple slice. Nathan chewed happily.

"Rainy days are good days," said Nathan. He skipped out of the bathroom, drip, drip, drip.

Hudson was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to pick the red apples in the yard. But the apples were high on the tree. Hudson could not reach them.

A woman walked by the fence. She had a friendly face. Grandpa waved at her. Hudson hid behind Grandpa's legs. He peeked out with one eye. Grandpa smiled and said, "Hello!" The woman smiled too. Hudson came out a little. He took a big breath. "Hello," he said in a small voice. The woman waved at him. "Hello, Hudson! Those apples look yummy."

"Will you help us pick them?" Hudson asked. "Yes, please," said Grandpa. The woman reached up. She picked three red apples. One fell on the soft grass. Hudson picked it up. "Thank you," he said. The apples smelled sweet, like pie. Grandpa washed them in cool water. He gave one to Hudson and one to the woman. Hudson took a big bite. It was crisp and juicy. "I like apples," said Hudson. Grandpa laughed. "I like hellos too," he said. Hudson waved at the gate. "Bye! Come again!"

Owen did not want to sleep. He wanted to play trucks all night. "One more truck," he said. "No," said Dad. "Time for bed."

First Owen had his bath. The soap felt slimy and bubbly in his hands. Dad gave him a warm towel. Then Owen put on his soft pajamas. Dad read him one book. Owen closed his eyes. Then he popped them open. "I want to stay awake," he said. He wiggled. He squirmed. He stayed awake a long, long time.

The next morning, Tyson came to play. "Let's run," said Tyson. Owen tried to run. His legs felt slow. His tummy felt funny. He yawned and yawned. "I'm too tired," he said. Tyson ran fast. Owen sat on the grass.

That night, Owen brushed his teeth. He put on his pajamas all by himself. He got into bed right away. "Good night," he said to Dad. Dad kissed his head.

The next morning, Tyson came again. Owen ran fast. He jumped high. "I slept all night," Owen said. "Now my body can play!"

Mya went to the laundromat with her dad. The big machines hummed and spun. Mya watched the clothes swing around in the round window. "They are dancing," she said. Her dad laughed.

Then it was time to go. The snow outside looked beautiful and white. Mya ran to the door without her coat. She opened it a tiny bit. The cold air rushed in. "Brr!" said Mya. Her arms got goosebumps. She shut the door fast.

"My coat!" she said. She found it on the chair. She pushed her arms in. One arm hid, then popped out. "Got you," she said. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. It stuck once. She tugged it again. Zip! It was all the way to her chin.

Mya stepped outside. The cold air touched her cheeks. But her body stayed warm inside the puffy coat. "Dad, look! I did it all by myself," she said. She swung her arms like a robot. "Beep beep, warm robot coming through!"

Mya ran to the window at school. The sky was gray. "It is rainy today," said Ms. Guo. Mya put on her rain boots. She put on her yellow raincoat.

At play time, the rain stopped. Now it was windy. The wind sent leaves across the yard. Mya and Rupert went out to play. Hunter came too.

Then Mya saw it. A big puddle sat on the ground. It was right by the slide. "Look!" said Mya. She jumped in. Splash! Water went up and up.

Rupert jumped in too. "The rain made this puddle," said Rupert. Mya stomped her boots. The puddle got wavy. Hunter laughed and stomped too. Their boots were wet, but their socks stayed dry.

Later the sun came out. Now it was sunny. "The sun will send the puddle away," said Ms. Guo. After snack, Mya ran back to look. The puddle was small. Mya waved to it. "Bye bye, puddle," she said. Then she ran to the slide for one more turn.

Wyatt sat at the dinner table. Jake sat next to him. Mom put bread on a tall plate in the middle.

"I want all the bread," said Wyatt. He grabbed every piece. He put them in a big pile by his plate.

Jake looked at the empty plate. Jake had no bread. His face went sad.

Wyatt looked at his pile. Then he looked at Jake. He pushed two pieces across the table. "Here, Jake," he said.

Jake smiled big. "Thank you!" said Jake. He took a bite. Wyatt took a bite too.

Mom brought more bread for the middle. There was enough for everyone.

"Jake's turn, my turn," said Wyatt. They took turns, one piece at a time. Both plates stayed full.

"More please," said Jake, holding up his cup.

Elliot rode the city bus with his dad. They were going to the library. Elliot held his new card in his hand. It was blue and small.

At the library, Elliot found a book about a wild cat in the snow. He loved it. He carried it to the desk. "Can I keep it?" he asked. The librarian smiled. "Your card lets you borrow books," she said. "You can take it home to read." Elliot gave her his card. She scanned it. Then she scanned the book. "Bring it back when you finish," she said.

Elliot hugged the book. He and his dad got back on the city bus. Elliot sat by the window. He opened the book on his lap. "We can read it at home," he said. His dad nodded. Outside, a little cat sat on a wall. Elliot pointed at it. "Look, Dad, a cat!"

Scarlett sat in her car seat. The sky had been sunny all morning. Now it looked cloudy and gray. "Rain is coming," said Dad. Big drops hit the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"I want to play at the park," said Scarlett. Then the wind blew hard. It made the trees bend and wave. "Windy!" said Scarlett. Rumble, rumble. Thunder! It was loud like a big drum. Scarlett covered her ears. Dad said, "When you hear thunder, you go indoors. We will play at home instead."

At home, Dad used a hammer. He fixed the loose board on the porch. Then it began to snow outside. Soft white flakes fell down. Scarlett and Dad watched from the warm window. "Snow," said Scarlett. She held her teddy bear tight. Dad gave her warm milk in her cup. "Safe and cozy," said Dad. Scarlett smiled and watched the snow.

Hazel ran to the park with Melissa. The sun was out. The swings were free. Hazel felt so excited.

Then big raindrops fell. Drip, drip, splash. "Oh no," said Melissa. "The swings are all wet." Hazel wanted to cry. Her tummy felt heavy and sad. She and Melissa ran to the bench by the garden. The pretty flowers had rain on them too.

"Will the rain stop?" Melissa asked. Hazel listened. The rain went drip, drip, then drip, then nothing. The clouds moved away. The sun came back. Hazel reached out her hand. It was dry. "Look!" she said. "The rain went away." Now her tummy felt light again. The sad feeling was gone. She felt happy.

They ran to the swings. "My turn first!" said Melissa. "No, me!" said Hazel. They both laughed and pumped their legs high, high up into the blue sky.

Sebastian went to the store with his dad. He held his dad's hand. Near the door there was a big shiny mirror. Sebastian stopped and looked.

He made a big smile. His face looked happy. He made a droopy mouth. His face looked sad. He scrunched his brows. His face looked angry. "Dad, look!" said Sebastian. "My face changes!" Dad smiled too. "Faces can show feelings," said Dad.

Then Sebastian saw his friend Emmett by the fruit. Emmett's mouth was turning down at the corners. His eyes were wet. Sebastian felt sad too. He knew just what to do. He made his biggest happy face at Emmett. Emmett wiped his eyes. He pointed at Sebastian and laughed. "Funny face!" said Emmett. "One sad face, one happy face," said Sebastian.

Sebastian gave Emmett an apple to hold. Emmett held it carefully. Then Sebastian saw a big balloon floating high. He jumped up and down. "I am so excited!" he said. His hair bounced as he jumped.

At checkout, Sebastian waved to the cashier. He felt shy, so he hid his face behind Dad. Then he peeked out with a small smile. The cashier smiled back. "Bye-bye," said Sebastian. He waved all the way to the door.

Zoey was going to school for the very first time. She held her mama's hand on the big yellow bus. Zoey found a seat next to a boy named Leandro.

The bus began to move. Zoey saw her mama waving outside the window. Zoey wanted to wave back. She stood up on her seat. The driver looked in the mirror. "Sit down, please," the driver said. "On the bus, we stay sitting in our seats." Zoey sat down fast. Then she waved from her seat. Mama waved back big. It worked!

At school, the children went to the playground. Zoey saw Mr. Li, her teacher. Leandro ran to the slide. "Come on, Zoey!" he called. Zoey looked at the tall slide. It looked different from the slide at the park. She did not know if she could climb it.

Zoey tried one step. Then another step. Leandro waited at the top. "You can do it!" he said. Zoey climbed all the way up. Then she slid down, fast. "Again!" said Zoey. Mr. Li smiled. On the bus home, Zoey sat in her seat the whole way. She waved at the clouds out the window. "I did it," she whispered.

Layla sat on her bed. She had a new library card in her hand. It was blue and little, just her size. She hugged it tight.

Her book was about the ocean. It had big waves and blue fish on the cover. Layla wanted to keep it forever. "The fish book is mine," she said. She put it under her pillow.

Her dad came in. "We need to take the book back tomorrow," he said. Layla held the pillow down. "No. I keep it."

"Miss Leen wants the fish book too," Dad said. "The library gave you a day. That day is called the due date. When that day comes, the book goes back, so Leen can read it."

Layla peeked at the cover. The blue fish looked at her. She thought about Leen reading it. Then she slid the book out. It had a small rip on one page, and a dirty mark on the back. She wiped the mark with her sleeve.

"I will take it back," Layla said. She put the book in her bag. Then she put her library card on top. "And then I get a new book."

Dad smiled. "Tomorrow we go together."

Layla lay down. She patted the bag by her door. "Bye bye, little fish," she whispered.

Jade ran into the store with her mom. "Socks first!" said Mom. The socks were soft and red. Jade touched them. "So fuzzy," she said.

A boy named Zakariya was there too. He held one sock. "I only have one," he said. Jade looked at his hand. "Where is the other one?" she asked. Zakariya shrugged. "Do you need two?" he asked. "Yes," said Jade. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks." Zakariya smiled big. "Then let's find its partner!"

They hunted on the short shelf. One, two, three, they looked. Under a lamp nearby, Jade saw something red. It was the sock! "Four hands, two socks," laughed Zakariya. They marched to the register. "We found a pair!" Jade shouted. The cashier rang the bell, ding, ding. Zakariya held up his two socks. "One for each foot!"

Luna had a small patch of dirt in the backyard. She wanted to grow carrots. Her dad helped her drop the tiny seeds into the soil. "One, two, three," they counted together. Then Luna patted the dirt down, nice and flat.

Every morning Luna went to look. "Hello, seeds," she said. She gave them a little water. Day after day, she saw only brown dirt. "Not yet," said her dad. "Keep waiting." Luna waited. She counted the days. One, two, three, four.

Then one morning, Luna saw something green. It was very small. It poked up out of the soil. "Dad! Dad! Come see!" she called. Her dad knelt down. "Look at that," he said. "A tiny new plant is called a sprout." Luna smiled big. "Sprout!" she said. "Hello, sprout."

The next day there were two sprouts. The day after that, there were five. Luna counted them one by one. Her black cat came to sit beside her in the sun. "You can watch too," Luna said. She patted the dirt again, soft and gentle. "Grow, sprouts, grow."

Zachary sat at the dinner table. Mom set a big bowl of spaghetti in front of him. Next to the table was a basket of clean washing. It was laundry night.

Zachary took a big bite. A noodle fell off his fork. Splat! The noodle stuck to his bright shirt. "Oh no," said Zachary. "My shirt has a noodle on it."

Mom laughed. "That shirt goes in the wash," she said. She pulled it off and dropped it on the pile. Zachary looked at the pile. He saw a shirt, a sock, and a hat. "What are they?" he asked. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," said Mom.

Zachary wanted to help. He picked up a sock. He put it with his toy cars. Then he looked and looked. "That is silly," he said. He laughed and laughed. He moved the sock to the pile with the shirt and the hat. He patted it down. "Clothes stay with clothes," he said. Mom gave him a high five. Then he ate one more noodle, very slowly, with his eyes on his fork.

Paisley held her dad's hand at the store. They walked past the red apples. They walked past the plates and cups. Then Paisley heard a sound. Plop, plop, plop.

"The soup pot is here," said her dad. Paisley saw a big pot behind the counter. It had bubbles in it. White steam went up, up, up. Paisley wanted to see the bubbles. She took one step forward.

"Stay back, please," said the worker. "The steam is hot. It can burn." Paisley stopped. She held her dad's hand again. The worker stirred the pot with a long spoon. The steam rose high above her hands. It did not touch anyone.

Paisley watched from far away. The bubbles went plop, plop. The steam went up, up. Then the worker ladled soup into a cup. She set it on the counter to cool. "All done," she said. She gave Paisley a smile and one round cracker.

Paisley played with the cracker on her fingers while they waited. The soup cup sat still. The steam got smaller and smaller. Then it was gone. Her dad touched the cup. "Warm now," he said. At the table, Paisley had soup in her own little cup. It was warm, not hot. She dipped her cracker in. "Plop," she said, and laughed.

It was a rainy morning. Maverick went to the library with his dad. The floor smelled like paper and rain boots. Maverick wanted the big book about baths. It was on a high shelf.

He saw Lennon building a tower of books. Maverick reached up high. He pulled too hard. The book fell down. It hit the tower. Crash! All the books fell on the soft rug.

Lennon's lip wobbled. "My tower," Lennon said. Maverick felt bad inside. "Sorry," he said. Lennon looked at him. Then Lennon smiled a little. "It's okay. Help me?"

Maverick picked up one book. Then two. Then three. They built the tower together. "Let's count them," said Lennon. "One, two, three, four, five!" Then Mr. Ito came with a step stool. He reached up high. He got the bath book down for Maverick.

"Thank you," said Maverick. Mr. Ito smiled. Maverick sat next to Lennon. He opened the book. There was a rubber duck on the first page. Lennon leaned over to look. "A duck in the bath!" said Lennon.

Sebastian went to the art gallery with his dad. Big pictures hung on the walls. "Look at that one," said Sebastian. "It is all red!"

His friend Joy was there too. Joy pointed up. "That one is blue," she said. Mr. Rivera, the guide, smiled. "Red, blue, and yellow are special colours," he said.

Then Sebastian saw a painting with green grass. He wondered how the artist made green. There was a little table with paint pots. Red, blue, and yellow. Sebastian put his brush in the yellow pot. Then he put it in the blue pot. He mixed them on the paper. "Green!" he shouted. "Yellow and blue make green!"

Joy leaned close to a wet painting. She touched it with her finger. "Oh no," said Joy. Her fingerprint sat on the paint. It smudged. "Wet paint can smudge if you touch it," said Mr. Rivera.

Sebastian looked at his own green paint. It was shiny and wet. He did not touch it. He waited and waited. Soon the paint was dry. Then he poked it with one finger. Nothing moved. The green stayed just the same.

Sebastian grinned. "Can we paint one more before we go home?" he asked. Mr. Rivera nodded. Sebastian dipped his brush again. "This time I will mix red and yellow," he said. "I wonder what we will get."

Andrew wanted his best book. It was the one about the big red truck. He looked under his bed. He looked in his toy box. The book was not there.

"Mom, my truck book is lost," he said. Mom sat down on the rug. She picked up a big basket of books. "Tell me its name," she said. Andrew thought hard. "Truck book," he said. Mom held up a book. "The name is on the front," she said. She pointed to the words. Andrew could not read them yet, but he saw the little black marks. Mom ran her finger under them. "These words say the title. The title is the book's name."

Andrew opened a book from the basket. He started at the back. Mom turned it around. "We read this way," she said. "Front first." Andrew turned the pages, one by one. Page by page, he looked. Then he saw it. A red truck on a shiny cover! "Mom, look! This one says truck!" He held it up high.

Dad came in with wet hands from washing dishes. "Story time?" he said. Andrew sat close. He held the book the right way. He turned each page, front to back. "Read it again," he said.

Josephine woke up early. She put on her socks. She was ready for school. She looked out the window. The street was all white. Snow was on the cars. Snow was on the trees. "No school today," said her dad. "It is a snow day. School is closed because of snow." Josephine looked and looked. The snow was deep and soft.

But then Josephine felt sad. She wanted to see her friends. She wanted to paint at the little table with Siena. Just then, the phone made a sound. It was Siena's mom. "Can Josephine play outside?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Josephine put on her snow pants. She put on her big red boots.

Siena lived next door. Josephine walked to her house. The sidewalk was bumpy under the snow. Siena was waiting at her door. The two girls made a big snowball. They rolled it down the street. It got bigger and bigger. The snow stuck to it as it rolled. "Look!" said Josephine. "It grew!" Siena laughed and clapped her mittens.

Then they saw Mr. Russo. He was shoving snow off his steps. He waved at the girls. He made a small snowball too. He rolled it next to theirs. Now there was one big ball and one small ball. "A snowman!" said Siena. They patted the snow with their hands. The snowman had a hat made of a bucket.

At lunchtime, Dad called Josephine home. She had warm soup in her favorite bowl. She looked out the window at the snowman. He stood by Mr. Russo's steps. "School is closed tomorrow too," said Dad. Josephine smiled big. "Another snow day," she said. "More snow for us!" She waved at the snowman from her chair.

Mila sat at the kitchen table. She wanted to make a paper sailboat. She needed two triangle sails, one big and one small. But all she had was one square of paper. "How do I get triangles from a square?" she asked. Mom smiled and said, "Watch me." Mom took the scissors. She was careful, because scissors are sharp. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. Snip! Two pieces fell on the table. Two triangles! "It worked!" said Mila. "A square makes two triangles! It worked, it worked!"

Mila was brave about the next part. She taped a stick to a cork. She pushed a coin into the cork so the boat would stand up. Then she put the boat in the sink. Would it float? The little boat did not fall over. It sat up straight. A spider crawled along the edge of the sink. Mila laughed. "Hello, sailor!" she said. "Do you want a ride?" She gave the boat one small push. "Sail away, triangle sails!"

Isabelle went to Malakai's house in the morning. Malakai's mom put on a song. It had a steady beat. Clap, clap, clap went Malakai. Isabelle tried, but her claps were too fast.

"Can you help me?" Isabelle asked.

"Watch my hands," Malakai said. He clapped one, two, three, slow and steady. Isabelle watched. Then she clapped, one, two, three. Her claps fit the beat now. The song felt like a swing going back and forth.

"Now let's sing," said Malakai. He sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Isabelle wanted to sing too, but she did not know the words yet.

Then she had an idea. "I know the ABC song," she said. She sang it, and Malakai sang too. "Hey," said Malakai, "it sounds just like our star song!"

They sang the ABC song again. This time the star words came out too. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," Isabelle sang, all by herself. Her voice was soft and sweet like morning milk.

Malakai clapped one, two, three. Isabelle clapped with him. Then she sang the new song again.

"How did you learn it so fast?" Malakai asked.

"I used my ABC song," Isabelle said. She smiled and sang louder.

Avery sat at the kitchen table. She had a job to do. She was sorting buttons into shape groups. Round ones here. Square ones there.

Jawad came over to play. He looked at her buttons. "That one is too small," he said. He held up a tiny round button. "It can't be a circle like the big clock."

Avery looked up at the wall clock. It was a big circle. Then she looked at the tiny button. She put the button on the table. She rolled it. It rolled round and round, just like a wheel.

"Look!" said Avery. "It rolls. The clock is a big circle. The button is a tiny circle. Big circle, tiny circle. Both circles!" She clapped her hands.

"Both circles," said Jawad. He laughed. "That is so funny. Big and tiny. Same shape!"

Mom brought over cold juice from the fridge. "Who wants to paint?" she asked. Avery and Jawad both yelled, "Me!"

They got out the blue paint. Avery dipped her tiny round button in it. She pressed it on the paper. It made a small blue circle. Then she dipped the big cup and pressed it down. It made a big blue circle.

"Big circle, tiny circle," said Avery. "Both circles!"

Jawad found a square cracker. He pressed it in the paint. It made a square print. Then he found a triangle chip. Avery found a rectangle spoon. Paint prints everywhere. Round ones, square ones, pointy ones.

Mom helped them tie a string through a button. Avery hung it on the fridge. Her paint was still cold on her fingers.

"Can we hang my square cracker too?" asked Jawad.

Avery giggled. "You can't tie a string to a cracker, silly!"

Arlo went to Ayman's house. Ayman had a big teddy bear. The bear looked sad. "He is sick," said Ayman. "He needs a doctor."

Arlo wanted to help the bear. Ayman said, "You be the doctor." Arlo put on a hat. It was just a paper hat. But when he wore it, he was Doctor Arlo. He gave the bear a kiss on the nose. Ayman covered the bear with a small blanket.

Then Ayman shouted, "Oh no! The floor is a river!" Arlo looked down. The floor did not look like water. But Ayman hopped onto a cushion. Then he hopped to the next cushion. "Don't fall in!" said Ayman.

Arlo stepped onto a cushion too. He wobbled his arms. "Splash!" said Arlo. He was swimming in pretend water. Ayman laughed. The river carried them all the way to the kitchen.

There, a grown-up gave them real crackers. The bear got a pretend cracker. Arlo held it to the bear's paws. The bear ate it all up. Ayman picked up a toy hammer. "The river broke the boat," he said. "I will fix it." He tapped the toy boat with his hammer. Tap, tap, tap.

"Boat is fixed!" said Ayman. Arlo clapped. The bear was not grumpy anymore. Doctor Arlo put away his hat. Then he rowed the pretend boat home.

David was at Grandpa's house. It was cold outside. Snow was on the ground.

"Let's go out," said Grandpa. "First put on your coat." David found his red coat. He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. Grandpa showed him the zipper. David pulled it up. It went zzzz. "I did it!" said David.

Grandpa gave David his mittens. "Hold them tight," he said. David held them in one hand. Then he picked up his toy truck. A mitten fell in the snow. It went missing in the white snow. David looked and looked. "There it is," said Grandpa. He pointed. David picked it up.

Then David saw the pocket on his coat. He put one mitten in the pocket. He put the other mitten in too. He made a little noise with his mouth, like a happy hum. The pocket held both mittens. His hands were free for the truck.

They went outside. David rolled his truck on the snow. The mittens stayed safe in the pocket. Later his hands got cold. He pulled the mittens out. "Warm!" he said.

Grandpa laughed. "Good pocket," he said. David patted his coat. "My pocket," he said.

Thomas went to the library with his dad. Mr. Li was at the craft table. "We are painting today," said Mr. Li. Thomas sat down next to Coen and Kaira.

Thomas wanted to paint a butterfly. He picked red paint. He painted one wing on one half of his paper. Then he bumped his water cup. The wet paper folded over on itself. "Oh no," said Thomas.

He opened the paper with gentle hands. The red paint had printed onto the other half. Now there were two wings, and they matched! "Look, Coen," said Thomas. "My paper folded while the paint was wet. The paint made another wing." Coen smiled and clapped.

Kaira painted green dots on one half of her paper. She folded it while the paint was wet. She opened it fast. Two matching green wings! "Butterfly," she said.

Mr. Li hung the butterflies on the wall near a book about bugs. Thomas looked up at his red butterfly and smiled. "Mine lives on the wall now," he said.

Kai sat in his car seat. He held a small drum. His baby sister sat beside him. She closed her eye. She went to sleep.

Kai wanted to play. He hit the drum. BANG! It was loud. The baby woke up. She cried. The car felt noisy. "Shh," said Dad from the front seat. "One bang is too loud."

Kai looked at his drum. He tried a soft tap. Tap. Tap. Tap. It was quiet. The baby stopped crying. She closed her eye again. She went back to sleep.

Kai counted his taps. "One tap. Two taps. Three taps." All quiet taps. The car went fast on the big road. The car went slow on the small road. The taps stayed quiet the whole way.

At the red light, Dad looked back. "That drum sounds nice and soft," he said. Kai smiled. He gave the drum one little pat. The baby kept sleeping. "Fast car, slow car, quiet drum," said Kai.

Maria woke up in the playroom. It was dark. "Is it morning?" she asked.

Her friend Selene sat up too. Selene looked out the little window. The sky was black. "No. It is still night," said Selene. "Day and night are opposites. When it is dark like this, it is night."

Maria yawned. She wanted the big sun to come. She looked at the window. It stayed dark.

The girls waited in the soft blankets. Maria held her small orange ball. She made it roll slow, slow across the floor. Selene made the big teddy bear dance. They waited some more.

Then the sky turned grey. Then it turned orange. Light came in the window. It touched Maria's arm. The light felt warm on her skin.

"Daytime!" said Maria. She jumped up. The room was bright now.

Outside, a bird sang fast. Then it sang slow. Selene laughed.

Maria's dad came in with warm milk. "Careful, it is hot," he said. "Blow on it first." Maria blew and blew. She took a small sip. "Now it is just right," she said.

The two girls played until the window grew bright and then, much later, dim again. "Night will come back," said Selene.

"I will wait for the day," said Maria. She hugged her orange ball.

David was at Grandpa's house. It was a sunny day. David wanted Grandpa to read him a book. Grandpa was busy in the garden.

David made a note. He drew big letters. He wrote all the letters in one long line. All squished together.

"Can you read this?" David asked.

Grandpa looked and looked. "Not yet," he said. "The letters are all squished."

Grandpa showed him. "In English, there is a space between one word and the next," he said. He put a little space after each word.

David tried again. He wrote his words with spaces. Tap. Tap. His finger made gaps.

"Now can you read it?" David asked.

Grandpa read it out loud. "Bring the book." He jumped up. "I will!"

They sat together. David held the book. He opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one, all the way to the end.

Then Grandpa closed the book. A leaf fell out. A red leaf, flat and small.

"Grandpa put that there last fall," said Grandpa.

David held the leaf up. "A surprise hiding in the pages!"

"Let's put in a new one," said Grandpa. He picked a green leaf from the floor. David laid it inside, near the middle, and patted the cover shut.

Arya ran onto the basketball court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak, squeak. The coach blew a whistle. "Time to practice," said Ms. Nair. Arya's friends Azlan and Ayzal ran too. "One team, two teams, three claps," they said. Then they clapped one, two, three.

Arya got the ball. She looked at the hoop. She threw the ball up, up, up. It hit the rim. It fell down. It did not go in. Arya felt grumpy. Her face went hot and her eyes felt watery. She wanted to sit on the cold bench.

Then she heard something. Ayzal was clapping. Azlan was clapping too. "Try again, Arya!" they called. "You can do it!" Their voices were warm like a hug. Arya picked the ball back up. She bent her knees. She threw it again. This time the ball went swish, right through the net.

"I did it!" said Arya. Then Azlan got the ball. He threw it. It missed the hoop. It rolled far, far away. Azlan's shoulders went down. Arya ran to him. "Try again, Azlan!" she said. She clapped her hands. "One, two, three!" Ayzal clapped too.

Azlan got the ball. He threw it high. The ball went in, and something small fell from the net. It was a soft feather, drifting down like snow. A little bird flew over the court. Ms. Nair laughed. "Even the bird is cheering," she said. Arya held the feather tight. "Good shot, Azlan," she said.

Harrison stood at the train station with his mom. Grandpa was coming today. He was going to stay for a whole week. Harrison looked down the long track. Where was the train?

The train came in with a big whoosh. Grandpa stepped off and gave Harrison a hug. He was carrying a small red bag. "I have a gift for you," Grandpa said. Inside the bag was a card game. "We can play this together," said Grandpa. "We take turns."

They went home and sat on the floor. Harrison wanted to go first. He grabbed all the cards. "Me first! Me first!" he said. Grandpa shook his head. "My turn, then your turn," he said. He put down one card. Then he waited. "Now it is your turn."

Harrison put down a card too. Then it was Grandpa's turn again. Back and forth the cards went. "This is how taking turns works," said Grandpa. Harrison smiled. The game filled the whole afternoon with fun.

The next morning, Harrison ran to Grandpa's room. "Cards again?" he asked. Grandpa laughed. "You can go first this time," he said. Harrison clapped his hands. "Your turn, then my turn," he said. Grandpa dealt the cards, and they began to play.

Adam sat at the dinner table. He had a big want. "I need a book about animals," he said. "For show and tell tomorrow." His plate had brown rice and warm chicken. His tummy was full, but his book bag was empty. "We can go to the library after dinner," said his mom.

At the library, the big door made a whoosh when it shut. Adam looked and looked. So many books! He saw books about trucks. He saw books about princesses. Where were the animal books? Ms. Zhao came to help. "Follow me," she said. "The library puts its books on shelves in groups, so people can find them." She pointed to one shelf. Animal books, all together!

Adam found a book with a big brown bear on the cover. He hugged it tight. "This one!" he said. He carried it to the desk. Ms. Zhao smiled and stamped it. Adam held his book all the way home.

Quinn ran to the living room. The big game was on soon. Her friend Oaklynn was already on the couch. Mom put out cups of juice to drink.

Quinn looked at everyone. Mom wore a blue shirt. Dad wore a blue hat. Oaklynn wore a blue dress too. Only Quinn wore yellow.

"Everyone is blue but me," Quinn said. Her tummy felt funny. She wanted to cheer for the same team. But she did not know what to do.

Then she looked at the TV. The players on the screen wore blue shirts. The fans in the crowd waved blue flags. The people in blue were clapping for that team.

Quinn jumped up. She ran to her room. She pulled open her drawer. There it was, a blue shirt with a star. She put it on all by herself.

She came back and sat next to Oaklynn. "Now we match," Oaklynn said. Quinn smiled big.

When the blue team got a goal, everyone stood up. "Yay, blue team!" Quinn shouted. She waved her arms with Mom and Dad.

"Good call on the shirt," Dad said, and he lifted her up for a high five.

Asher sat in the big waiting room chair. His feet did not touch the floor. A busy woman at the desk said, "The dentist will see you soon."

Asher held his little bag. Inside was his green toothbrush. A boy named Colten sat down next to him. Colten held a bag too. "I have a toothbrush," said Colten. "It is blue."

Colten dropped his bag. His blue toothbrush rolled out. Asher picked it up. He put it in his mouth to try it.

"No, no," said his mom. "That is Colten's toothbrush. Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes." Asher gave the blue one back to Colten. Colten smiled. He took out his green one from his own bag. "This one is mine," said Asher.

Then the door opened. "Asher, you win the first turn today," said the woman. Asher held his green toothbrush tight and walked in. The chair went up. The dentist looked at his teeth and said, "Nice and clean."

Ellie went to the library with her dad. She wanted storytime to start now. She looked at the story rug. It was empty. She looked at the big clock on the wall.

"Is storytime now?" she asked her dad.

"Not yet," he said. "It starts soon."

"What does soon mean?" asked Ellie.

"Soon means in a little while," said Dad.

Ellie sat down on a small chair. She did not want to wait. But then Holden came in. He sat by the rug too. Ammar came next. The rug was getting busy.

"Storytime soon?" asked Holden.

" Soon means in a little while," said Ellie. "So we wait a little."

Ellie picked a book about a swing. She read it with Holden. They turned the pages slowly. Then Ammar let them see his book too.

The door opened. Ms. Moose came out with a puppet. "Storytime now!" she said.

"It was a little while," said Ellie. She ran to the rug and clapped.

Sophia turned four today. Her party was in the backyard. A wide blue table held the cake. Balloons bobbed by the pond.

"Time for presents," said her dad. Sophia ran to the pile. The first box was from Karter. She pulled off the paper. Inside was a little red truck.

Then she saw a big pink bag. She dropped the truck and ran to it. It was from Jeremy. It had a bunny with soft ears.

"What do we say when someone gives us a present?" asked Ms. Farah, the neighbour, who had come over with a plate of cookies.

Sophia thought. "Thank you?"

"Yes," said Ms. Farah, and smiled.

Sophia ran back to Karter. "Thank you for the truck," she said. Karter grinned wide. Then she hugged Jeremy too. "Thank you for the bunny."
