Later, the grown-ups lit the candles. Sophia made a wish and blew them out. Everyone clapped.

"Happy birthday, Sophia," said Karter.

"You learned the birthday rule fast," said Jeremy.

Sophia held the bunny in one arm and the truck in the other. "Let's play," she said.

Miles went to the library with his class. Ms. Dang sat on a big soft hill of cushions. "Today we hunt for the letter S," she said. "S says sss, like a snake."

Miles asked, "Can I find one?" He answered himself, "Yes, I can!"

He looked and looked. He found a book about the sun. "Sun!" said Miles. "Sss, sun." He put it in his pile. He found a picture of a sock. "Sss, sock." In it went. He found sand in a beach book. "Sss, sand."

Sandra peeked at his pile. "That's a strong pile of S's," she said. Miles laughed. "Sun, sock, sand. Three!"

Avery held up a book about a cat. "Cat?" he asked. Miles shook his head. "Cat says cah. Not sss."

Then Ms. Dang held up one more book. "Can you guess?" she said. Miles got up close. On the cover was a big snake. Miles grinned and made his hand slither. "Sss!"

Ruby sat in a bright waiting room. She waited with her mom. A vaccine was coming today.

"When is my turn?" Ruby asked.

"Not yet," Mom said. "This room is where families sit. We sit until it is our turn."

Ruby looked around. A boy sat with his dad. A grandma sat with a little girl. Everyone sat and waited.

Then a nurse opened the door. "Marcus," she called. The boy stood up. He held his dad's hand. They walked through the door.

So that is how it works, Ruby thought. You wait, and then someone calls your name.

Ruby watched the door. Who would be next? Then the nurse came back.

"Ruby," the nurse called.

Ruby stood up tall. She held Mom's hand. Her turn had come at last.

The nurse said, "Pick a bandage."

Ruby looked at the box. She picked the one with a puzzle on it. It had bright colors.

"You can grow tall like this," the nurse said, sticking a tall giraffe sticker on top.

Ruby smiled. "I waited," she said, "and then it was my turn."

Olivia walked home on her street. She held the little red leash. At the end was Pip, her new puppy. Pip had floppy ears and a wiggly tail.

Her friend Amin ran up with a smile. He held a small chocolate treat. "Can Pip have some chocolate?" he asked.

Olivia looked at the treat. "I don't know," she said. "Let's ask a grown-up."

The neighbour was watering her flowers. She shook her head fast. "No, no. Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate."

Amin made a sad face. "But I want to give Pip something."

The neighbour reached into her pocket. She held out a bone-shaped dog treat. "Give him this instead," she said.

Amin held out the dog treat. Pip sniffed it. Then he gobbled it up in one bite. His tail wagged like crazy.

"He liked it more than my chocolate!" Amin laughed.

Pip pulled the leash. He began to dig a little hole by the fence. Dirt flew out behind him. "Silly puppy," said Olivia. "Are you digging for a pig?" Pip just wagged his tail.

The sidewalk had rain on it. It was slippery. Olivia held Amin's hand so they would not fall.

Pip trotted home with them, one happy puppy.

Lucas wanted to eat his lunch. But first, his mom said, "Time to wash your hands." Lucas ran to the sink. He turned on the water. He pumped the soap. The soap made white bubbles on his hands.

"Let's count to twenty," said his mom. "One, two, three." Lucas rubbed his hands together. Bubbles jumped down into the sink. They counted all the way to twenty. Then Lucas turned off the water.

His hands were still wet. He shook them in the air. Drip, drip, drip! Water fell on his shirt. Water fell on the floor. His brown toy turtle sat by the sink, and a drop landed on its little head. Lucas looked around. Then he saw it. A clean towel hung on the hook.

"The towel is the last step," said Lucas. He dried one hand. He dried the other hand. His hands were soft and dry. "All clean," he said. His mom smiled. Lucas sat down at the table and picked up his sandwich. "Yum," he said.

Sophie woke up early. The sun was out. Mom said, "Let's go to the playground." Sophie put on her red shoes. She packed a bowl of crackers for snack time.

At the playground, Sophie saw the swing. She wanted the swing so much. But Aayan was on it. He went up and down, up and down. Sophie ran fast. She grabbed the swing chain. The swing stopped. Aayan looked sad. Sophie let go of the chain. She sat on the gray bench to wait.

Then Sophie remembered. She walked back to Aayan. She said, "Swing, please." Aayan smiled. He jumped off. "Your turn," he said. Sophie climbed on. Mr. Pelletier gave a little push. Up she went, high as the gray clouds. "My turn, please," she called to Aayan. He laughed and held out his hands for a cracker from her bowl. "Cracker, please," he said. Sophie gave him one, and Bjorn got one too.

Everett wanted the dragon book. He pulled it from the shelf. He held it in his tight little hands. He pushed it at his mom. "Read the dragon!"

His mom opened the book. Everett pointed at the words. He began at the far right side. He ran his finger that way. "Dragon!" he said. But his finger slid off the page. The words got all jumbled.

"Start here," his mom said. She put his finger on the left. "In English, we read this way, left to right." His finger slid along. The words made a line, like a path. First word. Then the next. Then the next.

Everett read the line all by himself. "Big dragon!" The dragon flew over a castle. Its shadow covered the whole town.

"Again," said Everett. He started on the left. "Big dragon! Big dragon!"

His mom laughed. "You read the page, Everett."

"I thank you, words," said Everett. He patted the book. The words sat on the page, quiet and still. But now he knew. They were sleeping dragons. Wake them left to right.

Arlo ran to the park with his grandpa. He wanted to find the blue slide. First he looked with his eyes. He saw Malakai and Eesa by the swings. He heard them laugh with his ears. He smelled popcorn with his nose. He could almost taste it with his tongue.

Then Arlo found a duck sitting on a big wheel. It was an old wagon wheel by the pond. Arlo touched it with his hands. The metal felt cold and bumpy. "Look, Grandpa!" he called.

Grandpa squinted and shook his head. "I can't see it yet," he said. He took his glasses out of his pocket. He put them on his face. "Ah, now I see the duck on the wheel!" He waved at Malakai and Eesa too.

Arlo's eyes went wide. Glasses helped Grandpa see! Arlo pointed at a far bird. "Can you see that one now?" he asked.

Grandpa smiled. "Yes! I see its little red feet."

Arlo grabbed his hand. "Come see the popcorn too!"

Sarah wanted her dog book at bedtime. She could not find it in her pile. The dog on the cover was brown and small. Then she saw it under her bed. She pulled it out and ran to Dad.

"Read this one, please," she said. Dad sat on the bed. Sarah jumped up beside him. A dog barked outside, one loud bark. Dad opened the front cover. He read the first page out loud. His finger went along the little black marks. The marks told him what to say. Sarah looked hard. So that was reading!

One page had no marks at all. It was just a picture of a dog at the sea. "Read this page now," said Sarah. Dad shook his head. "There are no words on this page," he said. "Nothing is written here to read." Sarah touched the smooth page. It felt quiet, like a beach with no wind.

Then Dad showed her a card on her shelf. It was the card Bodhi gave her. It had words too. Dad read those words out loud. "Happy birthday, Sarah," he said. Sarah smiled and licked a salty crumb from her finger. "Read the dog book again," she said. "From the front." Dad turned back to page one.

Cooper sat in the nursery room. There was a new baby at his house. The baby was his little sister. Cooper made a puzzle on the rug. Mr. Eze sat down next to him. "Where is your smile today?" asked Mr. Eze. "The baby took it," said Cooper. "The baby cries. Mom holds the baby. Mom can't hold me."

Amirah came over with a drum. "Bang it soft," she said. Cooper banged it soft. The drum made a little sound. Cooper banged it hard. The drum made a big sound. He banged it soft again. The sound got small again. "One bang makes one sound," said Amirah. Cooper nodded. He tried it again and again.

Mr. Eze said, "It is okay to feel left out when a new baby comes. Big brothers can feel that way." Cooper looked up. "Even me?" he asked. "Even you," said Mr. Eze. "You can tell Mom. She will listen."

Mom came to the nursery room. Cooper ran to her. "Mom, I miss you," he said. Mom sat down on the little chair. She pulled Cooper onto her lap. "I miss you too," she said. "We can sing together." They sang a song. Cooper felt warm. The baby was different, and that was okay. Cooper leaned his head on Mom. "Again," he whispered.

Leo was playing in his bedroom. His toy fish was swimming through the air. It swam round and round, all alone.

Then his friend Mathis came to play. Mathis ran in fast. His foot hit the toy truck. Crash! Mathis fell down on the rug. His face went scrunchy. His eyes got wet.

Leo stopped his fish mid-swim. He looked at Mathis. Why was his face sad like that? Leo walked over close. "Are you okay?" he asked.

Mathis looked up. The wet eyes went small. The scrunchy face went soft. "Yes," said Mathis. "My knee hurts a little. But I am okay now." He held out his hand. Leo pulled him up.

"Thank you for asking," said Mathis. "Now let's make the fish swim to me too." Leo grinned and held the fish out to his friend.

Muhammad stood on the balcony. It was a warm summer day. He had three little pots full of dirt. He wanted to grow vegetables.

"What can we plant?" asked Khadijah. She lived next door.

Muhammad held up small seeds. "Carrot seeds," he said. "I want carrots so much."

He made little holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the dirt down. Then he gave the seeds water from a small cup.

The next morning, Muhammad ran outside. He looked at the pots. There was only dirt. No carrots. Not even one.

"Maybe they need more water," said Khadijah.

So Muhammad watered the seeds again. "Grow, grow, grow," he said.

The next day there was still only dirt. Muhammad touched the soil. It felt soft and wet. "Where are you, little seeds?" he asked.

He kept watering every day. Five days went by. Six days went by.

Then one morning, Muhammad saw something green. A tiny sprout! It was not far from the edge of the pot. It stood up like a little green finger.

"It came up!" Muhammad shouted. "Khadijah, come see!"

Khadijah ran over. She bent down low. "It's so little," she said. "Will it be a carrot?"

"I think so," said Muhammad. He gave the sprout one more drink of water.

Jaxson sat at the paint table. It was art time at school. Mr. Almeida put out the cups. One cup had red paint. One cup had yellow paint. One cup had blue paint. One cup had green paint. Four colors, count them, one, two, three, four.

Jaxson wanted to paint a pumpkin. He looked at his paper. He looked at the cups. There was no orange paint. His tummy felt tight and a little scared. "I can't make a pumpkin," he said.

Nevaeh sat next to him. "Look at me," she said. She dipped her brush in the red cup. Then she dipped it in the yellow cup. She stirred the paint on her paper. Round and round it went. The paint turned orange, just like that. "Wow," said Jaxson. "Red and yellow make orange!"

Jaxson dipped his brush in red. He dipped his brush in yellow. He stirred on his paper. Round and round. Orange! The paint smelled like soap. It felt cool and slippery on his fingers. "My pumpkin is orange," said Jaxson. "Thank you, Nevaeh."

Mr. Almeida came to look. "What a big orange pumpkin," he said. Jaxson painted a green leaf on top. Then he painted a blue sky with one, two, three white clouds. Mr. Almeida hung the picture on the wall. "There you go," he said. "Nice and safe up high." Jaxson smiled at his pumpkin. "Red and yellow," he whispered. "Red and yellow."

Jayden made a library in his bedroom. His bed was the desk. His toy box was the shelf.

"Can I have a card?" Jayden asked his dad.

Dad made a little card. It was clean and blue. It said JAYDEN.

"Now I can borrow a book," said Jayden.

Ahmed came to the bedroom library. Lylah came too. They sat on the floor to read. One, two, three readers on the floor. One, two, three quiet readers.

Jayden found the dinosaur book. "DINOSAUR BOOK!" he shouted.

Ahmed looked up. Lylah looked up. Dad looked up.

"Shh," said Dad. "People are reading here. The library asks us to use quiet voices."

Jayden looked at Ahmed. Ahmed was reading. Jayden looked at Lylah. Lylah was reading. Would a big shout make reading hard?

Jayden tried again. He made his voice very small.

"Dinosaur book," he whispered.

Ahmed kept reading. Lylah kept reading. Nobody looked up.

Jayden held out his blue card. Dad stamped the book.

"One card, one book," said Dad.

"One card, one book," whispered Jayden.

He sat on the floor next to Ahmed. He opened the dinosaur book. He turned the pages slowly. He kept his voice tiny like a mouse.

Lylah leaned over. "That one has four legs," she whispered.

Jayden counted. "One, two, three, four," he whispered back.

Dad smiled and picked up his own book.

Jayden turned one more page.

Josephine went to the laundromat with her dad. It was warm inside. Big machines hummed and spun. Josephine wore her red coat with a sheep on the pocket. She started to feel hot.

"Dad, I'm too warm," she said. Dad was busy with the laundry. He could not help right away. Josephine looked down at her coat. She saw the zipper tab. She pulled the tab down, slowly, slowly. The coat opened! The cool air came in. "One, two, three pulls," she counted. "My coat is open!"

Then she pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed. "I can do it," she said. Dad smiled. He helped a neighbour load the warm towels, and Josephine watched from her step. "Dad, watch me," she said. She zipped down, then up. Zip, zip. Then dad lifted her onto the soft, warm towels. "Coat off," he said. Josephine planted her feet on the floor and hugged him.
